When the gourd struck, his heel touched down; when the chant's syllables stretched, his hands rose to symbolize the wind over the mountain. It worked. The dance hung on the sound instead of on a tune, and his steps landed where they were supposed to land. He tried it again with the recording his aunt had played, the same chant, the same drum, and the timing stayed consistent, beat after beat.

The lanai tiles were cold through the thin mat, though the afternoon air was warm, the sort of insulation from heat he was glad of after an hour of practice. He texted Paisley, who had offered to play ukulele for him. "Can't be a song," he wrote. "It's hula kahiko, the old style. It goes with chanting and the gourd drum, not a melody." He had told her yesterday he'd need music, and he'd been wrong, and it felt strange and good to say so. His phone buzzed. "Then I'll learn the drum part," Paisley replied. Emile grinned, set the phone down, and began the chant again from the first line.

Mr. Reyes had read Kayla's story aloud on Friday, and by the third paragraph Rex had put his head down on his desk like a man surrendering. Nikola had yawned twice, which for Nikola was a lot, since she usually stayed awake even during the fire drills. Kayla sat at the kitchen table on Sunday with the draft in front of her, a red pen in her hand, and the beginnings of a grudge.

The story itself was fine. It was about a dog that stole a whole birthday cake and blamed the cat, and Kayla did not think the plot was the problem. She read the first paragraph out loud to the empty kitchen, quietly, so her mother wouldn't ask questions. Each sentence trundled along, and then the next one trundled the same distance, and then the one after that. She tapped her pen against the table at the end of every sentence and noticed something: the taps came evenly, like a metronome.

She tried an experiment, because experiments felt more logical than sulking. She read the paragraph again and counted the words in each sentence on her fingers. Sixteen. Fourteen. Fifteen. Seventeen. Sixteen. She wrote the numbers in the margin. They were all about the same length, every single one, and hearing them read aloud was like walking down a hallway with evenly spaced doors, none of them leading anywhere surprising. That was the trap. When every sentence was about the same length, the writing sounded monotonous. She had built a perfectly even hallway and then made people walk down it.

Her dilemma was that she liked her sentences. They were long and polite and full of words like "very" and "really" and "beautiful," which she'd been told since third grade were good words. She underlined the weak ones anyway. "Very big" could just be "enormous." "Really pretty" could be "gleaming." "Suddenly and quickly" could be a single word, or possibly nothing, since the dog was already moving at speed. The cuts felt rude, like telling guests to leave a party, but each one made the remaining words work harder.

Then she calibrate-tested the rhythm, in her own way: she read the new version aloud and tapped her pen again. Sixteen. Two. Nine. Fourteen. Three. When she hit the two-word sentence, she actually laughed, alone, at her kitchen table, which she decided not to examine too closely. The short ones landed like doorways opening sideways. The long ones had room to carry details. Mixed together, the paragraph had a rhythm you could walk to, or at least stroll.

On Monday she handed in the revision, and Mr. Reyes read the first page aloud. At the two-word sentence, Rex lifted his head off the desk. Nikola mouthed "enormous" back at her with an approving eyebrow. At the part where the dog framed the cat, somebody in the back row said "no way," which was more commentary than her first draft had received all period.

Mr. Reyes set the pages down. "Same story?" he asked.

"Same story," Kayla said. "Different hallway."

The neighborhood cleanup ended at the community center, where a folding table held boxes of slightly bruised apples, crooked carrots and one bizarre potato shaped like a duck. Emily had signed up for the food bank shift thinking she would sort cans, but the produce had come from somewhere, and nobody could tell her where. "Mr. Hussain's orchard, mostly," said Maxime, stacking apples. "And the garden plots behind Rowan's building. But the boxes keep arriving all afternoon." Emily noticed a pattern: each box had a torn scrap of paper taped to it, and each scrap was in the same handwriting, small and slanted. She decided to test whether one person was behind all of it, and dug through the boxes to excavate every last note.

The notes did not say much. "Take these," said one. "They are fine," said another. But the seventh note, stuck to the duck potato, was longer, and Emily read it out loud. "Dear volunteers. You would not know me. In the old story from the Book of Leviticus, farmers are told to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers. My granddaughter calls this gleaning. I leave my edges. Please use them. Signed, E. Bramble." Rowan squinted at it. "So somebody is leaving the edges of their garden on purpose?" "That's the rule," Emily said. "The unharvested edges are for people who need food. And strangers."

Mr. Hussain came in carrying yet another box, and Emily held up the notes like evidence. "Verdict?" he said, setting it down. "We think one woman, E. Bramble, is behind everything, including the duck potato." He laughed. "Mrs. Bramble is eighty-four. She's been leaving her garden edges for years, and she told me once she got the idea from that old story. Nobody ever caught her because she drops the boxes and hurries off."

The twist, when it came, arrived with the last box of the day. Taped inside was a fresh note. "I saw the girl sorting my carrots. Next Saturday I will leave the front edge too. Tell her the potato is a duck." Emily put it in her pocket, and the potato, carefully, on the shelf where everyone could see it.

Samantha taped a strip of masking tape across the living room rug and wrote LEFT on it in marker. The radiator behind the couch continued to radiate heat into the room, even though her mother had turned the thermostat down an hour ago, and Samantha wiped her forehead with her sleeve.

"Again," she said to Muhammad and Viviane, who stood beside her on the rug, facing the couch as if it were an audience. "Ms. Nasser said we exit stage left after the second song, and we only get one run-through backstage before the concert."

Viviane looked down at her feet. "So left is, like, the piano side? Where the curtains are?"

"Left from where?" Samantha said. "That's the whole problem. If I'm facing the couch and Muhammad's facing the window, my left and his left point opposite ways."

Muhammad spun to face the window, then the couch, then the window again, holding out his arms. His left hand pointed at the bookshelf one time and the television the next, depending on where he stood. He stopped. "It flips every time you turn around," he said. "So whose left is it?"

Samantha thought about the diagram Ms. Nasser had sketched on the whiteboard, and about how the arrows on it had seemed backwards to her at first. She turned to face the couch, which was the audience, and raised her own left hand. "Stage left means our left, when we're facing the audience," she said. "The performers' left. Not the audience's."

They practiced it eleven times, walking off past the bookshelf with their backs to the couch.

The night of the concert, the gymnasium lights went hot and bright, and the principal's introduction made the whole thing feel imminent, as if it were already happening before anyone sang a note. They got through the first song. Halfway through the second, Ms. Nasser raised two fingers, the signal, and Muhammad grinned and started walking toward the piano side, the audience's left.

Samantha caught his sleeve and pulled him the other way. He turned, saw the rest of the choir filing off past the far curtain, and mouthed one word at her: "Concept."

"Terminator?" Philippe whispered. "Like a robot that shoots lasers?" They were standing in front of a huge painting of a single orange sphere at the city art gallery, and the word had just appeared on Ms. Szabó's worksheet.

"It's not a robot," Marissa said, reading ahead. "On a sphere, the terminator is the line where the lit side turns into the shadow side. It's the edge where direct light stops reaching."

Mia squinted at the painting. The sphere had a bright spot, like a tiny sun trapped inside the orange, and a curved line ran down its middle. Past that line, everything went dark, and an even darker oval stretched across the table beneath it. Her own drawing, tucked under her arm, looked flat as a pancake. That was the whole reason she'd signed up for this sketching session: her sphere drawings kept looking like circles, and Monday's art assignment was mandatory if she wanted to pass the term.

"The sphere is showing off," Philippe said. "Yours is just lying there."

"Thanks." Mia pulled out her sketchbook anyway. If she could isolate that line, the exact place where light quit, maybe the rest would follow. First the bright spot, the highlight. Then the terminator curving around. Then the dark side, and finally the smudged oval on the table, the cast shadow.

She drew the circle. She imagined a flashlight aimed from the upper left, the way the gallery lights hit the actual wall. Where would the light stop reaching? Right about... there. She pressed harder with her pencil on one side of her curved line, then harder still, then dragged her finger across the table for the shadow.

Marissa leaned over. "Whoa. It actually looks round."

"Round-ish," Mia said, but she was grinning. She held the page up next to the painting. "Okay, Mr. Sphere. You win this round."

Philippe raised his pencil like a sword. "The terminator will be back."

Emmett stood on Grandma's back porch with his speech cards, shuffling them like a card trick he hadn't learned yet. Tomorrow night he had five minutes in front of the city council to argue that the bylaw banning skateboards from Founders Plaza should be changed, and so far his opening line was "Hi, I'm Emmett," followed by a very long silence.

"Hold this," Grandma said, pressing a purple lump into his free hand. She was making a flamingo out of polymer clay for the garden club contest on Saturday, and its neck kept drooping. "If I win, I get the blue ribbon and bragging rights over Mr. Smith's rooster. Now give. Let's hear the speech."

He read it out loud, flat as a workbook page, and Grandma winced. The problem, Emmett realized, went back to April, when he'd mailed a letter about the plaza and gotten nothing but a form reply saying the matter was noted. Noted. He'd wondered for weeks whether anyone at City Hall actually read letters, or whether they fell into some deep drawer that could generate silence forever. Maybe the problem wasn't his argument. Maybe it was the channel it traveled through.

"Grandma," he said slowly, "if I sent a letter and nothing happened, what if there's a way to get in the room? Like, in person?"

She tapped her rolling pin against the table. "There is. Many municipalities let residents ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting. It's called appearing as a delegation. Your grandfather did it once about the garbage schedule."

Emmett felt the pieces click. A letter was a message in a bottle. A delegation was a handshake. He called the clerk's office from the kitchen phone, wrote down what to do, and got a spot on tomorrow's agenda. Then he rebuilt his speech. Instead of paragraphs, he tried three claims: the plaza's smooth stone was built for rolling, the ban pushed skaters onto the sidewalk where collisions were more likely, and a trial hour on Sunday mornings could test it. He tested the speech on Grandma's garden gnome, on Grandma, and finally on Lilith and Kaya, who biked over after dinner and sat on the lush grass by her tomato beds, firing questions at him like a real council might.

"Why should we risk it?" Kaya demanded, playing a difficult councillor.

"Because right now the bylaw generates the exact problem it was supposed to prevent," Emmett said. "Skaters don't disappear. They move somewhere worse."

On Saturday morning, Grandma set her finished flamingo on the porch rail, its neck held straight by a hidden wire. Emmett drove with her to City Hall, cards in his pocket, and when his name was called he walked to the microphone. "Hi, I'm Emmett," he said, and this time the words kept coming.

The moving truck had left forty boxes on the floor of the new house, and not one of them said what was inside. Asher stared at the stack in the living room, all sealed with brown tape, all exactly the same opaque brown. His mom opened three in a row: pots, books, then a tangle of extension cords. "Where are the sheets?" she asked, because his bed had to be made tonight and nobody knew which box held them.

In his old town, his friend Terry had moved the summer before, and Asher remembered the first night at Terry's new place. Terry had dug through box after box in his pajamas, hunting for his bedsheets while his dad held open flaps and said, "Not that one." They finally found the sheets at the bottom of a box marked kitchen towels. Terry had said, "We should have written where each box goes and what's in it." Asher had nodded, but he hadn't really digested the idea until now, standing in front of forty brown mysteries.

So he tested it. While his mom searched, he grabbed a marker and a pad of sticky notes and went to the boxes she had already opened. POTS, he wrote, KITCHEN. He carried the pot box straight to the kitchen himself and set it on the counter, no sorting needed. It took him ten seconds. Then he did it with the books: BOOKS, MY ROOM, and up the stairs it went. His mom stopped rummaging and watched him. "Do the rest," she said. "Any box we open, it gets a note."

They opened boxes together after that, calling out contents, and Asher labeled each one with its room. The sheets turned up in box twenty-six, but by then it hardly mattered, because every opened box had already gone where it belonged and the living room floor was clearing fast. He made his bed and slept without the cold feeling he had braced himself for.

The next morning was his first day at the new school, and Mr. Campbell stood at the door of the classroom shaking hands. "You must be Asher," he said. Two kids near the window looked over, and one of them, a girl with a braid, raised a hand and waved. Asher walked toward the empty desk beside her and said, "Hi, I just moved here. I'm still figuring out where everything goes."

Benjamin sat at the computer with two news tabs open and a notebook page torn nearly in half from erasing. Both stories were about the same poll, the one about the dilapidated gym roof at school and whether the town should pay to fix it. One story said support had gone from 40 percent to 50 percent. The other said support had jumped 25 percent. He read them twice more, then leaned back until the chair creaked.

"Charlie," he typed into the chat window, "how can the same poll be ten and twenty-five at the same time? Somebody's lying."

"Maybe the second reporter can't do math," Charlie wrote back. "Or the first one is asleep. Pick one."

Benjamin wasn't satisfied with either. He opened the school's sports page next, because that always calmed him down, and found Mr. Moretti's article about the basketball team's season. The team's shooting had improved, the article said, by 25 percent since December. He checked the stats table himself: December, 40 percent from the field. February, 50 percent. There it was again. He sat very still, the way he did when a pattern was hiding somewhere just out of reach.

He grabbed a pencil. Ten out of a hundred, that was the rise he could see. But ten sat on top of forty, not a hundred. He wrote 10 over 40, then 25 over 100, and stared at them until they matched. The two numbers weren't fighting. Ten was the raw climb; twenty-five was the climb measured against where you started. "Percentage points," he said out loud to the empty room, trying the phrase on. "That's the ten."

He went back to the chat. "They're both right," he told Charlie. "Ten points and twenty-five percent. Same change, two names."

"That's annoying," Charlie wrote.

"Extremely," Benjamin agreed.

The next morning he found Mr. Moretti by the gym office, holding a clipboard and a mug with a chip on the rim. Benjamin showed him both articles on his phone. "Your story says ten, the other one says twenty-five," he said. "Which do we put in the school paper?"

Mr. Moretti studied the screen. "Which one tells the truth faster?"

"Ten, if you already know the numbers. Twenty-five, if you want the jump to feel big."

"Then print both," Mr. Moretti said, and penciled something on his clipboard. "Side by side. Let the reader do the arithmetic."

That afternoon Benjamin sat at the computer again, cursor blinking in an empty document. He typed the headline, deleted it, retyped it, and hit print. Charlie was going to hate it, which meant it was probably good.

Jaxson stood on the wide marble steps of city hall with a clipboard under his arm and a knot in his stomach. Behind him, Celia counted the signature pages for the third time. "Forty-one," she said. "The same as the last two times."

"Forty-one out of how many houses?" Aria asked, hopping down one step at a time.

"Ninety-something," Celia said. "Half the street didn't answer, and Mr. Pell slammed his door so fast I still feel the wind."

Jaxson looked up at the tall doors. Last month, Milo from his class had been hit by a car at the corner of Fern and Second, right where they all crossed to get to school. He was okay now, mostly, but nobody walked there without looking four times. Jaxson had asked his dad why there was no crosswalk, and his dad had said, "City things don't change because one person asks. They change because a lot of people ask at the same time, in writing." That idea had stuck in Jaxson's head like a song he couldn't shake. One voice was too quiet. So he had tested it. He had written down exactly what they wanted, a painted crosswalk with a crossing guard at Fern and Second, and gone door to door asking people to sign their names under it.

Inside, they followed the signs to the clerk's office. A woman behind the counter peered at them through translucent reading glasses that made her eyes look larger and softer than they probably were. "Can I help you?"

"We want to give this to a councillor," Jaxson said, and slid the pages across. "It's a petition. It's a written request, signed by a lot of people, asking the city to take a specific action."

The clerk smiled at that, like he'd said a magic word correctly. "Then you take it to the councillor's office, room 204, and you can ask to speak at the next council meeting." She stamped the front page. "You'll need to fill in a form, and you might want more signatures. Forty-one is a start, though."

On the way to room 204, Aria whispered, "So we're not done?"

"We're not done," Jaxson said. "But look." The stamp on the page said RECEIVED, in blue ink, right under forty-one names.

Celia grinned. "Mr. Pell is going to sign next time. I'm bringing cookies."

Kate stood behind the folding table at Ms. Hughes's market stall, gripping a wooden spoon like a sword. Ms. Hughes sold cheese sauce over roasted potatoes every Saturday, and today she had promised to teach Kate how to make it, because Kate wanted to surprise her dad on his birthday. He still talked about the lumpy gravy from last Thanksgiving, and Kate had sworn that would never happen again.

"Flour and butter first," Ms. Hughes said. "That paste is called a roux. Then milk, then cheese. Smooth as a river." She was called away to the register, so Kate stirred while her classmate Leonardo, who had wandered over with quarters for honey sticks, watched the pan. "Can I try?" he asked, and before Kate could answer, he had the spoon. He loved watching things turn golden, so he stirred and stirred, hypnotized, until the roux went the color of caramel, then the color of an old penny. When Kate got the pan back, she whisked in the warm milk, added the cheese, and stirred. The sauce refused to thicken. It ran off the spoon like watery juice.

"Did we add enough flour?" Leonardo asked, peeking into the pan as if the answer were submerge at the bottom. Kate thought hard. She remembered her dad's gravy last fall, pale and gluey, thick as wallpaper paste. Same amount of flour as today, she was almost sure, but hers had been white when it went in. The sauce here had gone thin only after Leonardo cooked the roux dark. She tested the idea the only way she could: she started a fresh batch, kept it pale blond, and poured in the milk. Within a minute, the sauce clung to the spoon in a glossy ribbon. She looked at the penny-colored pan beside it and laughed. "The darker a roux gets, the less it thickens. You cooked our thickener away."

"You mean the pretty part was the problem?" Leonardo said, wounded. "That's betrayal." Ms. Hughes came back, dipped a spoon in the new sauce, and nodded. "Nice save, you two." The suspense of the birthday dinner suddenly felt lighter, and Kate ladled the sauce over a test potato. Leonardo took the first bite, closed his eyes, and held up his honey stick like a torch. "Your dad," he announced, "is going to cry."

Luca stood at the shallow end of the backyard pool and counted the plastic flags Mr. Mokoena had strung along the fence. Twenty-five metres, his dad had measured, exactly the length of a real race pool. Last week Luca had promised his friends he would swim the whole way front crawl, with side breathing, before Saturday. So far he had made it twelve metres before coughing, standing up, and retrieving his goggles from the bottom of the drain.

"You're turning your whole face up," said Haris, who was sitting on the wall with his feet in the water. "My cousin does it sideways, like she's resting her ear on the water."

Luca tried resting his ear on the water. He swallowed less, but he still ran out of air halfway. He floated on his back and stared at the flags, wondering. Why did swimmers even bother with this stroke? When they had watched the freestyle race on television, every single lane had used the same arm-winding style, none of them doing breaststroke or backstroke. "Freestyle means you can pick any stroke you want," Haris said, dangling his toes. "So why does everyone pick the same one?"

Luca chewed on that. Maybe the answer was the same reason a lemonade stand made more income when it sold cold drinks on the hottest day: people choose whatever works best. If every swimmer in the race, from every country, all chose front crawl, then front crawl had to be the fastest of the competitive strokes. That felt credible to him, like something you could trust because so many people kept proving it. But if it was the fastest, the problem wasn't the stroke. The problem had to be his breathing.

He had been assuming he needed a breath every two strokes because his body felt desperate. Maybe the desperate feeling came first from splashing, not from real tiredness. He tested it: one slow lap, arms easy, kicking calm, face down until his cheek barely broke the surface, then a small sideways sip of air. No splash in his mouth. He tried again with three strokes between breaths, then five. The water hissed past his ears and the flags slid overhead one after another.

The wall of the deep end bumped his fingertips. He stood up, gasping and grinning, and pushed his goggles up onto his forehead. "Twenty-five metres," he said. "Count the flags if you don't believe me."

"I believe you," Haris said, and jumped in to try it himself.

The group chat lit up at 7:43 on Tuesday night, right after Colton finished the dishes. Wade had posted a photo of the half-built skate park behind the middle school, with the caption: "they're wasting two million dollars on this dump, my uncle says it'll be dead in a month."

Van replied first, three crying-laughing faces, then "rip our tax dollars." Colton started to type "yeah total waste" and stopped, because at dinner his dad had done a thing with a letter to the local paper. The letter said almost the same words, and his dad had tapped it with one finger and said, "Two million dollars, I can check that. Whether it's a waste, that's just the writer talking." His mom had put the letter under the fruit bowl, which in their house meant the discussion was over.

Colton deleted his reply. He typed instead: "the two million part is checkable. the waste part is just a feeling." Then he sat there wondering if that sounded like something a dad would say.

"checkable how," Wade wrote back.

Colton went looking. The town's website had a page about the project, and after some digging he found the actual number in the meeting minutes. The park did cost two million dollars. That part of Wade's sentence was true, which felt strange, because Wade's uncle had still said it like it proved something. It proved the number and nothing else. Colton pasted the link into the chat and added, "so half your sentence has a citation and half of it doesn't."

Van sent a single question mark, so Colton explained the way he could, without using his dad's exact words, since those were under the fruit bowl now. "like, that sentence is two different kinds of sentence glued together. the cost can be checked. 'a waste' can't. they're distinct things even though they're in one line."

There was a long pause, long enough that Colton could hear the dishwasher running in the kitchen. Then Wade wrote, "ok but is it a dump though." Colton looked at the photo again. The concrete was poured, the ramps weren't installed yet, and there was a mountain of gravel with a porta-potty next to it like a flag planted on the moon. Honestly, at this exact moment, it did look like a dump.

"can't check that from a photo," Colton typed. "go look at it."

The next day after school, Wade and Van were already at the fence when Colton rode up. Wade had his phone out, taking a picture of the same gravel pile from a new angle. "For the chat," he said. "This one's just an opinion, but it's mine."

The vinegar bottle was almost empty, and Tyler's little sister's volcano was due at her classroom in forty minutes. The volcano itself was robust, built from clay over a soda bottle, with painted ridges and even a tiny plastic rodent frozen mid-scuttle on the slope. The rodent was supposed to look dramatic when the "lava" came. Instead the whole thing sat there doing nothing, because Tyler had used the last of the baking soda on a test run at seven in the morning and had nothing left to prove.

He called Elisa first. She showed up at the kitchen door holding a box of baking soda like it was a rescue supply. "Hunter's coming too," she said. "He wants to see if it explodes."

"It doesn't explode," Tyler said. "It fizzes."

That was the problem, actually. His sister had asked him, last night, watching the test run bubble over the clay, where the bubbles came from. Tyler had opened his mouth and realized he didn't exactly know. He'd said "the volcano does it," which even he could hear was a bad answer. Ms. Carvalho, her teacher, had told the class they had to be able to explain their projects, or no points.

Hunter arrived and read the recipe card taped to the counter. "It says baking soda inside, vinegar on top. So the bubbles come from them mixing."

Tyler set out two cups while the clock on the stove ticked toward departure time. In the first cup he put a spoonful of baking soda and a splash of vinegar. Bubbles rushed up the sides. In the second cup he put a spoonful of sugar, just sugar, and poured the same vinegar over it. Nothing. The sugar sat there. He tried salt next. Still nothing, just wet salt.

"So it's not the vinegar making bubbles by itself," Elisa said, leaning over the counter.

"And it's not fizzing because something melts," Hunter said. He'd grabbed an ice cube from the freezer and was holding it over the warm dish rack, watching it drip. "When ice melts it just goes liquid. No bubbles."

Tyler looked at the cup still fizzing, then at the paper his sister was supposed to read aloud. He picked up the pencil and wrote at the top: Gas bubbles that appear when two substances mix, like the fizz when baking soda meets vinegar, are one sign that a chemical change has happened. Under it he wrote, in smaller letters, melting is only a physical change, and beside that he drew the ice cube with an arrow.

His sister came downstairs in her boots, dragging the volcano by its base, the plastic rodent riding the slope like it was braced for the end of the world. Tyler handed her the paper and the baking soda.

"Where do the bubbles come from?" she asked him again, right there in the kitchen, one more time, as if testing whether he'd earned his twenty minutes of tutoring.

"The fizz when baking soda meets vinegar," Tyler said, "means a chemical change happened. Read your paper."

She read it. In the doorway, Hunter was already making a second cup fizz for no reason except that he could.

Raphael stood on Dexter's front porch with his phone in his hand and a plan he had been building for three days. He was going to find the noodle shop on Fenwick Street by himself, and he was going to ask for directions in Mandarin, because last summer he had refused to try even one word.

That memory still sat in his chest like something corrosive, eating at him whenever he thought about it. His grandmother had walked him to the market that summer, pointing left and right, teaching him two small words over and over. He had shrugged and mumbled and pretended not to care, and she had gone quiet for the rest of the walk. Now she was back for a visit, and he wanted to show her something.

"Zuǒ means left," Dexter said, holding the door open. "My grandma says it all the time. And yòu means right. They don't sound the same either. Zuǒ goes down at the end, like you're dropping something. Yòu goes up, like a question." Dexter's little brother Cedar ran past with a water gun, shouting both words in the wrong tones, and Dexter rolled his eyes.

"But they're each said with their own tone," Raphael said slowly, trying it out. "So if I get the tone wrong, I might say the wrong thing entirely." He frowned. That was the hidden part. The words weren't just sounds; they were sounds riding on pitches, and the pitch was doing half the work. He said zuǒ out loud, letting his voice sink, then yòu, letting it lift. Cedar shouted "ZOO-oh!" from the yard, dropping his voice so hard it sounded like a dying robot, and Dexter laughed so hard he had to lean on the doorframe.

Raphael decided to test it before he left. He asked Cedar to point when he said each word, using only the tones to know which was which. He said zuǒ, low and falling, and Cedar pointed left. He said yòu, rising, and Cedar swung his finger right. He said zuǒ again and got left again. It was working. The tone really was carrying the meaning, like a second set of words hidden inside the first.

At the corner of Fenwick Street, an old man was sweeping outside a bakery. Raphael's heart hammered, but he stepped forward. "Qǐng wèn, zuǒ háishi yòu?" he asked, dropping his voice on the first word and lifting it on the second, exactly as he had practiced. The man raised his eyebrows, then pointed right, and said something that ended in a clear, rising "yòu."

Two blocks later, Raphael found the noodle shop, steam fogging the window, the smell of broth drifting out onto the sidewalk. He bought two containers, one for his grandmother and one for himself. On the walk home he kept repeating both words under his breath, low and high, low and high, so he would still have them when she opened the door. "Zuǒ and yòu," he said to nobody. "Left and right."

Hazel had twenty dollars of birthday money in her pocket and one goal: new basketball shoes. The old ones had a hole by the left toe, and tryouts were in two weeks. At the mall entrance, a huge screen showed a pro player spinning a ball on one finger while wearing silver HighGlide shoes. "The choice of champions," the caption said. Behind her, a girl around her age was telling her mom that literally everyone at school already had HighGlides.

Tiana caught up with her near the fountain, out of breath. "Tell Paul to hurry. He's still looking at the sneaker wall like it's a museum."

"It kind of is," Hazel said. They joined Paul in front of a display where a poster shouted "Don't be the last one left in boring shoes!" Hazel frowned at it. "That poster is doing something to us."

"Doing what?" Paul asked.

She pointed at the poster, then at the screen near the entrance, then at a cardboard cutout of the famous player. "The screen says a star wears them, so we trust them. The poster says everyone has them, so we feel left out. And 'boring' is a loaded word. It's not describing the shoes, it's describing us if we don't buy them." She had learned the pattern from a library project about wartime posters. While digging through old posters, she had found something better: a group that had worked on exactly this problem. "The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda," she told Tiana and Paul, reciting it the way she had for her presentation. "Ordinary people. That's the whole point. You don't have to be a genius to spot the trick."

"So what do we do, a science experiment in the shoe store?" Tiana said.

"Actually, yes." Hazel counted the tricks on her fingers. "Celebrity, bandwagon, loaded words. My test: if an ad gives me zero facts about the shoe itself, it's probably hiding something." She turned over a HighGlide box. The writing was vague and ambiguous, all "revolutionary feel" and "next-level energy," with nothing about cushioning or durability. Then she picked up a plain box from the bottom shelf. It listed the materials, the support, and a lower price.

Mr. Li, who ran the shop, came over with a stool for Tiana's tired little brother, who had been wobbling on one foot by the stroller. "Kids your size grow out of shoes fast," he said. "The flash sells, but the plain ones hold up." He tapped the plain box. "And this week they're two dollars off."

Hazel tried them on and jumped twice. Good grip, no pinching. Paul held up the silver HighGlides one last time, then set them back. "Twenty dollars more for a famous fingerprint," he said. "I despise being advertised at."

"Same," said Tiana. "Well. Mostly."

At the register, Hazel paid for the plain shoes and still had change left. On the way out they passed the giant screen again, the champion still spinning his ball. Hazel waved at it like an old acquaintance. "Nice try," she said.

Ellie had been on the couch for three days, watching the steam rise off her mug of tea. The vapor drifted toward the ceiling, and she tracked it with her eyes because there was nothing else to do. The flu had knocked her down one abrupt afternoon, right before the school talent show, and she was missing the rehearsals she was supposed to run with Lisa and Chaya. Her part of the act was the juggling routine, and if she missed too many practices, the whole thing could fall apart.

She found her mother in the kitchen. "Can you call the doctor and ask for antibiotics? Strong ones. If I take them today, I could be back at school by Thursday."

Her mother looked up from chopping an apple. "That's not how it works, but call and ask if you want." She dialed and handed over the phone, and Ellie asked the nurse her question. The answer came back plain and simple: antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses, and the flu is a virus, so they would not help her get better even a single day faster.

Ellie hung up slowly. Bacteria and viruses were two different things, and her medicine cabinet was useless against one of them. She sat back on the couch and thought about what a body actually needed to fight a virus, and decided it was the same thing her grandmother was always saying: rest, fluids, and no rushing. To conserve her energy, she canceled everything except sleeping, sipping tea, and one short phone call each evening.

Lisa called that night with a report. "We moved your juggling to the second half so you get more time to heal. Chaya taped the rehearsal on her tablet so you can study it from the couch."

"Send it," Ellie said, and propped the tablet against her pillow, watching the pattern of the pins rise and fall under Lisa's bedroom lamp.

Alexandre kept one eye on the basketball game and one on the trivia sheet folded in his pocket. Between quarters, his school ran a contest, and the winner got courtside seats for the final. Skyler had beaten him in every trivia round this year, and Alexandre wanted this one. The problem was the last question, the one worth double points: "What is the maximum NFL passer rating?" Abbey leaned over from the next seat, munching popcorn, because Abbey only came to basketball games to argue about football.

"A hundred," Alexandre said. "Perfect has to be a hundred, right?"

Abbey shook her head slowly, the way she did when she was about to enjoy being right. "My uncle says it's the weirdest number in sports. He won't disclose it, either. He says I have to earn it." She pulled out her phone, showed a screenshot of a stats page, then covered half of it with her thumb, keeping her expression neutral so Alexandre couldn't tell whether the answer was hiding under her thumb or not. The gym smelled like rubber floors and popcorn butter, and the scoreboard buzzed as the second quarter ended.

Ms. Johansson, who taught math and kept score at every home game, paused in the aisle with her clipboard. Alexandre asked her the question before he could stop himself. She smiled but shook her head, pointing at the contest rules like a doctor refusing to hand over a prescription without an exam. "You can look it up after the buzzer," she said. "Not before."

The third quarter started, sneakers squealing, and Alexandre couldn't focus on it. Skyler had scribbled "100" on his sheet with a smug little shrug. A perfect score being something other than a hundred felt wrong, and that wrongness itched at him. If Skyler guessed 100, Alexandre needed the strange number. He thought about how the scoreboard compressed four quarters into one final score, how a single number could hold a whole game inside it. Maybe a passer rating squashed several stats together, and maybe squashed numbers didn't land where you expected. He wrote 158.3, half guessing, half reasoning, and slid the sheet to the judge.

When the winner was announced at the final buzzer, the judge read his answer aloud. "Correct, one hundred fifty-eight point three." Abbey uncovered her thumb, revealing the same number on her screenshot. "My uncle says it's a perfect game," she said. "Go enjoy your seats."

Gavin had been waiting for Saturday evening all day, because his cousin's house was hosting the Havdalah ceremony and, for the first time, he was old enough to be trusted with a job. When the sky finally went dark, his aunt poured a small cup of grape juice and set out a little silver holder full of fragrant spices. Then she handed Gavin the braided candle. It had several wicks twisted together, and when she lit it, the flames bent toward each other in a way that made him lean closer. His little sister reached for it, and he pulled it back, careful. "It's the Havdalah candle," his cousin Lindsay said from across the table. "Everybody gets to smell the spices."

Gavin wanted to do more than just hold the candle, though. He wanted to know why the spices were there at all. You could see the flame and taste the juice, but a smell was invisible, and he wondered if it had something to do with the day of rest ending. He devised a test. During the singing, when nobody was watching him closely, he covered the spice holder with his hand and took a slow breath through his nose. Then he uncovered it and breathed in again. The sharp, sweet smell rushed into his nose so strongly that his eyes watered, and he understood without anyone telling him: the smell was the whole point, something you were supposed to notice with a part of yourself you couldn't see.

Later, while his cousin Lilianne passed around pieces of honey cake, she asked him what he thought of his first real job. "I think the protagonist of tonight was me," Gavin said, and then went red, because that had come out louder than he meant. Lilianne laughed, but not in a mean way. "You held it like it was authentic," she said. "Like a real one from a real family."

The house emptied slowly, coats and goodbyes and one last slice of cake for the road. When only the paper plates were left, Gavin's sister tugged his sleeve. "Next time," she whispered, "can I hold the candle?" Gavin looked at the twisted wax, still warm in his hand, and set it carefully back in its box with her name written on a sticky note.

Marcus rang Lyam's doorbell with the controller already in his pocket. Today was supposed to be the tournament. They had planned it all week at lunch, eight players, Krish bringing the snacks, the bracket drawn on graph paper in Marcus's backpack right now. Lyam opened the door only halfway, which was strange, because Lyam never did anything halfway.

"Not today," Lyam said. "Just go home."

"Go home? You drew the bracket." Marcus held up the paper, but Lyam was already looking back into the house, toward the kitchen, where his mother's voice was low and quick.

"I don't feel like it. Forget it." The door shut. Not slammed, exactly, but close enough that Marcus felt the air move past his face.

He stood on the porch for a while. Ants had colonized the crack between the bottom step and the walkway, streaming in and out, and he watched them only because he didn't want to watch the door. Lyam was spontaneous, the kind of kid who once started a water fight in January. He didn't cancel things. Unless, Marcus thought, he'd just been pretending all along, the kind of person who dumps you the second something better shows up. That felt true, standing there. It felt true all the way across the street, where Mr. Chaudhry was watering his roses, and Marcus was so busy deciding what kind of person Lyam was that he barely heard Mr. Chaudhry say, "Terrible thing this morning. Did you hear about the dog?"

Marcus stopped. "What dog?"

"Lyam's. The brown one, Biscuit. Car, right out front, before school. His dad drove them to the vet an hour ago." Mr. Chaudhury shook his head and went back to his roses.

So that was it. Not Lyam's personality, not some secret plan, just a terrible morning that Marcus had walked into the middle of. On the bus home, he put one earbud in and let the podcast queue run. A host was talking about a psychologist named Lee Ross, who in 1977 had called it the fundamental attribution error, the way people blame someone's actions on their personality while missing the situation they're in. Marcus rewound it twice. He had done it today, in under a minute, on a porch.

He texted Krish to cancel the snacks, then walked back to Lyam's house and rang the bell again. Through the door he heard slow footsteps, then the latch.

"I'm not playing," Lyam said.

"I know. I just came to say Biscuit was a good dog." Marcus held out the bracket. "And this can wait as long as you want."

Max slid his drawing across the picnic table so Yohan could see it. "It's a sphere," Max said, "with the light coming from up there, like Ms. Ong set it up." He had shaded the curve carefully, leaving a bright highlight on the upper left and a soft shadow along the lower right, exactly the way the demo ball looked on the wooden stool.

Yohan tilted his head at the page. "It's good, but it's kind of floating. Like a planet." He held the drawing next to the real setup, where a baseball sat on the stool under the camp's one bright lamp. "The ball looks stuck to the stool. Yours looks like it's hovering an inch above the table."

Max frowned and compared them side by side. The shapes matched. The shading matched. He squatted down until his eyes were level with the stool, staring at the place where the ball met the wood. Right at the point of contact, there was a ring of almost pure black, so dark it looked like a drawn line. Farther out, the shadow on the stool faded to gray. He hadn't noticed it from above, but down here it was obvious. He grabbed his softest pencil, the 6B, and pressed a small dark crescent exactly where sphere touched surface, then let it fade outward.

"Whoa," Yohan said when Max held the drawing up again. "It dropped! It's sitting on the table now." Max laughed out loud. A counselor walking past asked what all the noise was about, and Max said, "The darkest part of a cast shadow is right where the sphere touches the surface." He said it like he was announcing a score.

By the next afternoon, half the art shed wanted to know the trick. Bronson had been struggling all week with an orange that looked airborne, and he petitioned Ms. Ong to move the whole still-life table closer to the window so everyone could study their own contact points. Ms. Ong agreed, on one condition. "Each of you draws two spheres," she said, "one with the light from the left, one from the right, so you can see what changes."

Max set up fast, pencil already sharpened. He drew the first sphere with its dark crescent tucked against the surface, then started the second one, mirroring the light. "This one will be perfectly symmetrical to the first," he told Bronson, "except flipped. Highlight moves, shadow moves, but the darkest spot stays where the ball touches." Bronson leaned over, watching Max press the pencil down into that same magic spot. "That," Bronson said, "is the best floating orange fixer I've ever seen."

Juliette had made forty-one free throws in a row at practice on Tuesday, and now her left elbow throbbed with every dribble. She stood at the foul line in the gym, rubbing the joint while Katelyn rebounded for her.

"You're holding your elbow again," Katelyn said, tossing her the ball. "Yann says you do it every time you miss."

"I'm not missing." But she was, and she knew it. The pain had started three weeks ago, right after Coach had run those drills where the whole team shot a hundred layups a day. She'd loved those drills at first, loved watching her percentage climb, feeling the improvement almost like a visible thing. Now she wondered if she'd been reckless, piling shot after shot onto an arm that was still growing.

She thought about her little brother's baseball league. Last spring their mom had dragged the whole family to his game, and the pitcher, a tall kid named Danny, got pulled in the fourth inning even though he was winning. "Pitch limit," the other parents had grumbled, and Danny's dad had shrugged and said, "Growth plates. They're areas of growing cartilage near the ends of kids' bones, and they're weaker than the bone around them." Someone added that it was why young athletes had limits on repetitive stress. Juliette had barely listened, half asleep in the bleachers. She listened now.

She had a theory, anyway. She stopped shooting, walked to the bleachers, and sat down. "I'm testing something," she told Katelyn. "Three days of no shots, just running and passing. If it's the repetition doing it, my elbow should quiet down."

"You're going to look like a quitter," Katelyn said.

"Watch me not care."

Ms. Weiss, the gym teacher, noticed her sitting out on Thursday and raised an eyebrow, but Juliette only passed and drove and defended, and by Friday the throb had faded to almost nothing. She stood at the foul line again, alone after practice, and bounced the ball twice.

"Okay," she whispered to her elbow. "Forty-one was plenty."

She rose up and shot.

Sloane's garage smelled like solder and burnt cheese crackers, and the robotics club had been arguing for twenty minutes. "Digby died at the fair because the battery drained," Frank insisted. "It can't consume power that fast unless the motors stalled." Sloane shook her head. "The code looped. I watched the log. The wheels didn't even twitch." Nolan had been standing near the table, where Digby sat with his sensors intact but his emergency light still blinking red, and he kept thinking about the toxic smell he'd noticed right before the shutdown, sharp and chemical, like a leaking battery.

Mr. Torres, whose house backed onto Sloane's yard, had left a note taped to the garage door that morning. Sloane read it out loud: "Heard your robot quit at the fair. Before you fight about it, look at the book on my porch. Borrowed it from the library years ago and never returned it. Old story. Might help. T." On the porch sat a fat paperback of tales from ancient India, and inside, a parable about blind men and an elephant. Each man touched one part. One felt the trunk and called the elephant a snake. Another felt the leg and said it was a pillar. Another felt the ear and swore it was a fan. Nolan read it twice, then carried the book back inside.

"Guys. We're the blind men," he said, and laid the book open on the workbench. "Frank touched the battery. Sloane touched the code. I smelled the leak. Nobody touched the whole elephant." So they tested it. Sloane ran the log again while Frank measured the cells and Nolan checked the air sensor. The power was fine. The code was fine. The air sensor had detected fumes and triggered the emergency shutdown.

"That means Digby didn't fail," Sloane said slowly. "He did exactly what we built him to do."

Frank grinned and pulled the fair results sheet from his backpack, folded into quarters. He smoothed it flat on the table and pointed to a line halfway down the page, and there, in the judge's neat printing, was Digby's name under Safety Award, First Place.

"He got a ribbon," Frank said. "Our robot has a ribbon and we spent a week mad at him."

Nolan laughed and clipped the fresh battery in place. "Sorry, Digby. Now let's go be blind about something new."

Mackenzie had turned the corner of her reading nook into a detective's office. The window seat held her novel, a stack of pink sticky notes, and a mug of cocoa going cold. On page after page she pressed a pink note wherever the old lighthouse lantern appeared, because her teacher had called it a motif, and Mackenzie had formulated a plan: mark every page, then line them up and see what the lantern was really doing in the story.

At first the lantern seemed like decoration. It lit the harbor, it hung in the keeper's window, it flickered during storms. Marcel had said so at school on Friday. "It's just a lamp," he'd insisted. "A lamp that shows up a lot."

"A motif is an image or object or idea that keeps recurring through a book," Mackenzie had told him, tapping her copy. "And if I track where it comes back, I can see what it comes to mean." Marcel had shrugged, but Karter leaned over and asked if she would show him her notes on Monday.

Now it was Sunday afternoon, and the sticky notes were spread across the nook like a pink tide. Mackenzie counted eighteen of them. She arranged them in order, chapter by chapter, and read her own labels aloud in a whisper. Chapter three: lantern keeps the ships safe. Chapter nine: lantern in the granddaughter's window when she is afraid. Chapter fourteen: lantern dark because the keeper has died. Chapter nineteen: the granddaughter lights it herself.

She sat back against the cushion. The lantern was not about lamps at all. Early in the book it meant being watched over; by the end it meant doing the watching over. Same object, new meaning, and she could see the change only because she had followed it page by page. It was like her nightly ritual of checking the lock on the back door before bed, the same small act that meant something different once she was the last one awake.

Monday at recess she spread the notes along the cafeteria table. Karter walked his finger down the row and stopped at chapter nineteen. "Wait," he said. "So the granddaughter becomes the keeper?"

"That's the twist," Mackenzie said. "The lantern doesn't change. Who holds it does."

Marcel picked up the sticky note from chapter fourteen, the dark one, and turned it over in his hands. "Huh," he said. "So it was never just a lamp." He reached into his backpack and pulled out his own novel and a pad of yellow sticky notes. "Show me where to start."

Eleanor set her fork down perpendicular to her plate, which was how she arranged things when she was thinking, and stared at the two columns of numbers she had copied onto a napkin. "Dad, can I ask you something that is not about dinner?" Her dad said sure, as long as she ate her green beans while she asked. She had until eight o'clock tonight to message Ms. Pritchard with her doubles partner for Saturday's table tennis tournament, and the whole choice hinged on one number that she was starting to distrust.

"Rowan and Pearl both average twelve points a game," she said. "Exactly the same. But watch." She read down the napkin. Rowan's games went eleven, twelve, thirteen, twelve, twelve, eleven. Pearl's went nineteen, three, twenty, four, eighteen, four. "If I just tell Ms. Pritchard the average, they look like the same player. They're not the same player at all." The numbers had colonized her brain since last period, spreading until she couldn't think about anything else, and now she had proof on a napkin that the average was hiding something.

Her dad leaned over and read the columns, chewing his beans. "So which one do you want?" That was the real question, and Eleanor realized she hadn't answered it yet, only proven that it needed answering. Rowan had already texted her three times saying please pick me, I've been practicing my serve every day, so Eleanor knew how much Rowan wanted this. And Rowan was steady, which felt safe. But Eleanor kept picturing Saturday as a knockout bracket, where you lose once and you're done. In that kind of tournament, terrible games end you, but spectacular games win you trophies.

She tried a test out loud, tapping the napkin with one finger. "If Pearl plays like her good games, we win the whole thing. If she plays like her bad games, we're out in the first round. Rowan never does either. Rowan just plays." Her dad said, "Sounds like you already know what you're trading." She did. She picked up her phone and typed the message to Ms. Pritchard, then put the phone face down between her fork and her knife, still perpendicular, still thinking.

Before she could exhale, Rowan's reply buzzed through the table: "any news?" Eleanor looked at the napkin one last time, then typed back, "Can I tell you tomorrow? I picked Pearl, and I want to explain why face to face." She pressed send, folded the napkin into her pocket, and ate her green beans.

Peyton flopped into the seat behind Gibson and slid her phone across the aisle. "Settle this. Best hitter, 1995 and 1996. Justice or Jeter?"

Gibson picked up the phone like it was a loaded question, which it was. For a week they had been arguing about it on the bus, on the field, in the lunch line, until the whole argument saturated every corner of their friendship. He scrolled through the stats page. "Justice. Look. Nineteen ninety-five, Justice's average is higher than Jeter's. Nineteen ninety-six, higher again. Two years, two wins. Done."

"That's what I thought too," Peyton said. "But watch." She tapped the screen twice and turned it toward him. "Combine both years. Jeter's on top."

Gibson stared at it. The bus lurched around the corner by the laundromat, and his backpack slid off the seat, and he didn't even notice. "That's impossible. If Justice wins both years, he has to win overall. It's adding. Adding can't flip."

"Numbers don't lie, but maybe they hide," Peyton said. She pulled a spiral notebook out of her bag and started copying the figures down in her careful, intricate handwriting, every digit checked twice, because if she got one wrong Gibson would never let it go.

"You're doing math homework to win an argument," Gibson said.

"I'm doing math homework to find out if I lost an argument." She frowned at the page. Somewhere under those two years, she was sure, there was a rule at work, something she couldn't see straight off. She tested the simplest idea she had: she made up her own two tiny seasons for two made-up players, small enough to add in her head. Ten at-bats one year, a hundred the next, for one player. The other player, the opposite. She worked through it, lips moving, while the bus squeaked to a stop and half the back rows emptied out.

When she looked up, her mouth was open. "It happens with fake numbers too. It's real. It's a thing."

"Show me." Gibson moved across the aisle into her row, closer to the window, and she angled the notebook between them. He read it twice. "Okay," he said slowly. "Okay. I change my mind. You win the bet, and I don't even get why."

"You don't have to get why. Nobody has to get why today." She closed the notebook. "But next time Coach says some kid's got the best average on the team, I'm asking how many games it's from. One number's not the whole story, and now I can prove it."

"Fine. Then prove it at lunch, and buy me a cookie for the bus ride home since you're so rich from my quarters."

Peyton laughed and held out her hand. "Deal. But you're carrying my backpack up the hill."

Grandpa's rock garden ran along the back fence, and Victoria had decided it was going to make her famous. She crouched beside it with a hammer and a shoebox, splitting open the smooth dark stones one by one, because somewhere out there was a fossil with her name on it.

"You've cracked eleven rocks," said her grandfather from the porch, "and buried the pieces like evidence."

"Twelve," Victoria said. "And one of them has to have a fossil. Probably a trilobite. Maybe a whole fish." She held up the newest halves. Nothing but flat grey inside, like the inside of a potato chip.

Her grandfather came down and picked through her reject pile, turning pieces over in his spotted hands. "You know, when I retired from the quarry, they let me keep the truckload of rocks I'd hauled for thirty years. Never found a fossil in a single one." He set down a shard with tiny sparkling crystals, like sugar. "Igneous. That one cooled from melted rock."

Victoria frowned at the pile. She had been choosing the prettiest rocks, the striped ones, the glittery ones, the dense heavy ones that felt like they were keeping secrets. Then she wandered to the garden path, where the flat, crumbly, boring slabs lay in a row, the ones so plain she hadn't bothered with them at all. She pried one up, turned it over, and pried at the edge with her hammer until a layer flaked away.

There it was: a swirl of ridges, pressed into the pale stone like a fingerprint. She carried it to the porch at a run, and her grandfather leaned close to the little shell-shaped mark.

"Sedimentary," Victoria said. "Layer by layer. The sparkle rocks never had a chance, did they?" She set the fossil on the rail, next to his igneous shard, like two ambassadors from very different countries.

He laughed. "In my day, that was a controversial opinion. Old Pete swore he'd find a fossil in lava if he split enough of it. Split them for twenty years."

"Twenty years," Victoria said. She was already heading back to the garden path, hammer over her shoulder, the boring rocks waiting in a long, promising line. "Amateur."

Autumn had circled her favourite paragraph in the novel three times, so many times that the pencil had almost worn through the page. It was the part where the main character, facing exile, gives up her locket to feed a stranger, and Autumn thought it might prove her whole argument. "The theme," she planned to say, "is that a clear conscience is worth more than anything you own." She had even rehearsed an eloquent opener in the mirror, which would have gone better if her little brother hadn't kept making faces behind her.

At the book club meeting in the library corner, with its smell of old paper and the radiator ticking like a slow clock, Ameera went first and quoted one tidy sentence inside quotation marks. Perfect. Then Maelle, same thing. Autumn opened her notebook and read her paragraph out loud, and it went on, and on, past four lines of prose, and Mr. Oyelaran raised his hand gently.

"That's a wonderful passage," he said, "but how are you planning to write it down?"

"I assume I just put quotation marks around it," Autumn said. "Like everybody else."

Ameera slid her style guide across the table, the pages warm from sitting near the radiator. Autumn found the page herself. She read it twice, then flipped back to the mirror morning, when she had been so sure. The rule was simple: a prose quotation longer than four lines becomes an indented block, half an inch from the margin, with no quotation marks at all.

"So I just... move it over," Autumn said, "and take the quotation marks off?"

"Half an inch," said Maelle, holding her thumb up to measure. "That's like this much. Approximately. Scientifically."

Autumn borrowed Ameera's ruler, drew a faint pencil line half an inch in, and copied her paragraph into the new space. It looked different there, alone and important, like a small statue on its own shelf. Then she looked up. "The theme still stands," she said. "Read it now. Tell me I'm wrong."

Zoey had promised Knox that her new game, Space Squid Invasion, would be ready by Saturday, and Saturday was tomorrow. The plan was simple: a squid sprite would invade the screen, the player would zap it, and the score would go up by one every time. On her laptop, the score part already worked. If the squid touched the lightning bolt, then change score by one. Perfect. The problem was the squid itself.

It moved ten steps, then stopped dead in the middle of the screen like it had fallen asleep at the wheel.

"That is the most lethargic invader in the history of invasions," Knox said from the speakerphone on the kitchen table. "My squid could defeat your squid by simply waiting."

"Something in my code is doing this," Zoey said. She narrowed her eyes at the screen. She couldn't see the problem. It was in there somewhere, hidden in the stacks of blue and yellow blocks, and she was going to find it by testing. First she clicked the green flag and counted the squid's steps out loud. Exactly ten. She clicked it again. Ten again. So there was a rule in there, and rules could be found.

She pulled the motion blocks apart, one piece at a time, and there it was, tucked around her "move ten steps" block like a sandwich: a block that said repeat 10. "Ha," she said. "Repeat ten. That's why it moves ten steps and then freezes. It runs the blocks inside it exactly ten times, then it's done."

"Then put it in a forever block," said Knox. "That keeps going until you stop the program. Forever, Zoey. Like my dad talking about his lawn."

She slid the repeat block inside a forever block, snapped it shut, and clicked the green flag. The squid marched across the screen, turned, and marched back, relentless as homework.

"Now do the score," Knox said. "And a census. I want to know how many squids are invading."

"One," Zoey said, dragging out a new sprite. "For now."

Clara had signed up for the model parliament club at the community centre because Anaeve promised it would be fun, but by the second meeting she had begun to despise it. Her bill, a plan for a protected tundra garden on the centre's roof, kept stalling. The other students voted it through the mock House of Commons, through committee, through the Senate, and then it just sat there. "Now what?" Clara asked, tapping the paper against the table.

"Nothing," said Dana, who wanted desperately to win the club's prize for best bill and kept checking the score sheet. "That's the end. It passed."

Clara didn't believe that. Real laws got announced, signed, enacted. Something had to happen after the last vote, and if the process stalled here, her bill was stuck in a kind of no-man's-land, passed but not real. She narrowed it down. "There has to be one more step. A distinct, final step. Otherwise every bill would just pile up." She tried testing it: she marched her paper to the front and declared it law herself, which made Anaeve laugh so hard she knocked over a stack of nameplates. "You can't just declare it," Anaeve said, gathering the nameplates for Mr. Ferreira, who was carrying too many chairs across the room all by himself. Clara ran to take the other end of his stack.

It was Mr. Ferreira who mentioned the courthouse trip, and it was at the courthouse that Clara found her answer. A guide was telling a tour group about royal assent, how a bill only becomes law when it gets the monarch's approval. "And here," the guide said, "the Governor General gives it. If the Governor General can't, a deputy can. Sometimes even a Supreme Court justice steps in."

Clara pulled Anaeve's sleeve. "That's it. That's the missing step." Back at the centre the next week, she presented the bill to Dana, who was wearing a bathrobe borrowed from lost and found. "Royal assent, on behalf of the monarch," Dana intoned, stamping the paper with a rubber stamp he had won at the prize table. Clara held the bill over her head and said, "The tundra garden is law."

Samuel laced his cleats so fast he nearly snapped a lace. Today was the first real practice of the season, and Mr. Suryanto had promised something new: tug-of-war to build strength for the soccer team. Emerson had been talking about it all week, mostly because Emerson wanted to be picked as team captain, and captains, he said, always got to stand at the front of the rope.

The grass smelled freshly cut, and the afternoon sun warmed the back of Samuel's neck as Mr. Suryanto dragged a thick rope onto the field. "We'll start with the whole team against me and my spring scale," the coach announced, looping the rope through a handle on a stake he'd hammered into the ground. Eight boys heaved. The scale needle jumped, then sagged. Mr. Suryanto squinted at it, then at them. "Some of you are easing off," he said. Then, almost to himself: "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller."

Samuel couldn't stop thinking about that on the walk home to the basement flat his family rented. He shared the building with a tenant upstairs, a quiet pianist, and her music drifted down through the ceiling while Samuel turned the coach's words over. You couldn't see anyone easing off. It was invisible. So how would anyone know it was real? He decided to infer it the only way he could think of: measure.

At the next practice, Samuel asked Mr. Suryanto to borrow the spring scale. "Let's each pull alone first," he said, holding up a notebook. Zack, the smallest kid on the team, went first and yanked the needle to a number that made Emerson snort. Then they pulled in pairs, then fours, then all eight. Samuel wrote every number down, tongue between his teeth. When he worked out the averages, his pencil nearly tore the page. Alone, each boy pulled harder. Together, every single average had shrunk. Even Zack's. Even his own. "It's true," he whispered. "Everybody does it, not just lazy people. Nobody even notices."

"But we still have to pull together on Saturday," Emerson groaned, and then his face changed, the way it did when he was about to grab at captain things. "Unless we trick ourselves. What if we count? One, two, pull. One, two, pull. Like a drumbeat."

Saturday came with cold wind flapping the corner flags and mud sucking at their shoes. The other team was bigger and louder, and their supporters, including the pianist tenant from upstairs, waved scarves on the sideline. The whistle blew. "One, two, pull!" Emerson bellowed, assertive as a drill sergeant, and eight boys heaved as one. The rope jerked. The red ribbon slid toward them, and Zack, mud-streaked and grinning, drove his heels in and screamed, "PULL!"

Carter had wanted to win the history club debate ever since he lost it the year before, and tonight, at Matthieu's kitchen table, he finally had a topic he thought nobody could beat. He spread out two photocopied pages, one from a British soldier's account of the morning at Lexington in April 1775, one from a colonial witness. "Both sides swore the other side fired first," Carter said. "Historians still don't know who fired that first shot."

Jayda leaned over the paper, close enough that her ponytail brushed the cookie plate. She slid the plate toward Matthieu's little sister, who had been hovering by the counter, and said, "So the winner is whoever argues best, not whoever's right?"

"Exactly," Carter said. He had a theory, and he wanted to test it before Monday. His idea was that if you told the same story from two different positions, you could replicate the disagreement, and the class would feel how hard it was to know the truth. So he pushed his chair to one end of the kitchen, facing the window, and told Jayda to stand by the fridge.

"Matthieu, you snap your fingers," Carter said. "We'll both write down where it came from."

Matthieu's fingers cracked like a tiny firework. Carter, staring at the window with the late sun glaring off it, wrote that the sound came from his left, near the doorway. Jayda wrote that it came from her right, beside the stove. When they compared papers, Matthieu's little sister giggled and held up the truth: she had snapped too, from the doorway, in perfect parallel with Matthieu at the stove, ruining the test.

"That's the twist," Carter said slowly, and his stomach did a small flip. "Nobody lied. Nobody even knows whose snap we heard." He grabbed a fresh cookie for the little sister, because she had, without meaning to, made his point better than he had. On Monday, he would not argue for a winner at all.

Jayda grinned and tapped the two photocopied pages. "So what do we call your debate now?"

"A mystery," Carter said, and folded both accounts back into his backpack, side by side.

The planetarium's new rock display had opened that morning, and Mr. Yamamoto had posted a sign: Sort the mystery samples correctly, win a star chart. Mia stood at the table with three boxes labeled igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic, and five unlabeled rocks in front of her. She had already sorted the one with visible layers and the one made of squished seashells. Three rocks left.

Arianna hurried over, breathing hard. "Sorry I'm late. My mom had to work a double shift because of the recession, so I had to wait for the neighbour." She picked up a dark pebble. "This one's boring."

"It's not boring, it's a clue," Mia said. Beside the dark pebble sat a chunk of granite from the donation bin, glittering with big crystals, clearly labeled with its name. Mia held both rocks under the lamp. The granite sparkled in fat, obvious speckles. The dark pebble looked plain and smooth. "Granite is igneous. It cools slowly underground, so the crystals get big." She turned the pebble. "This one must have cooled fast at the surface, like basalt, because its crystals are tiny. It's igneous too."

"So the sparkly one and the plain one are the same kind?" Arianna said. "That's weird."

"It's the speed," Mia said. "Slow cooling gives you big crystals. Fast cooling gives you tiny ones." She dropped the pebble into the igneous box.

One rock left: a flat gray slab that looked almost like flaky pastry. Mia wet her fingertip and rubbed the edge, and grains came loose. That was the test she had thought of on the bus, and the result surprised her. She had expected it to be sedimentary because grains rubbed off, but Alayna, walking by with her star chart already won, pointed at the tiny wavy bands folded through the stone like icing. "That happened after it formed," Alayna said. "Heat and pressure changed it. My grandpa's a geologist."

"Metamorphic," Mia said, and slid it into the third box. She checked her answers with Mr. Yamamoto, and when he handed her the star chart, she gave Arianna the first look through the little planisphere window.

Peyton arrived at Andi's house on Saturday carrying her soccer ball and two granola bars, because Andi had texted her nine times about the Monday tryouts. Andi wanted to practice, but every time she touched the ball she stopped mid-dribble and stared at the fence.

Peyton set up cones in the backyard and watched. When a drill was actually happening, Andi was sharp; she trapped a hard pass, turned, scored. Then, standing still between drills, Andi's hands shook and she said her stomach hurt. Peyton thought about that pattern. Sick and shaky while waiting. Fine while doing. She chewed her granola bar and considered what was different between the two moments.

"You're not scared right now," Peyton said. "I mean, you are, but not of anything in this yard. Fear is a reaction to a threat that's happening now. Anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future. Your tryout is Monday. There's no coach here, no whistle, nothing to be afraid of yet."

Andi took a hard shot that dented the fence. "So my stomach is doing tryouts without me."

"Basically."

They made a truce: Andi would practice for forty more minutes, and Peyton would stop talking about Monday at all. It mostly worked. Andi kept asking about the roster, whether Ms. Bear, the neighbour who coached rec league, would be watching, whether she'd freeze in front of everyone, and Peyton kept redirecting her to the next drill.

At dinner, Andi's mother put a whole lasagna on the table, and Andi, who had barely eaten all week, consumed three pieces. "That's weird," she said. "I've been too nervous to eat since Thursday, and now I'm starving."

The twist came when Andi's phone buzzed. Tryouts were moved to Wednesday, not Monday, which meant four more days of waiting. Andi groaned. Then she got her cleats from the garage and walked back out to the fence, alone, in the dark.

"Where are you going?" Peyton called.

"To be scared of something that's actually happening," Andi said, and kicked the ball against the boards until her mother made her come in.

The travel agency window was full of posters, but Florence cared about only one thing: the giant world map behind the counter, covered in thin grid lines. Ms. Kovalenko, the agent, had promised that if Florence could name the coordinates of any city she picked, she would print her a real boarding-pass-style souvenir with the city on it.

"Rome," said Petra, poking at the map.

Florence traced the lines with her finger. Rome sat near the number 12, but there were two numbers near every place, one going around the map sideways and one running top to bottom, and she could not tell which was which. She turned to the departures board Ms. Kovalenko kept by the door, a leftover from her old airport job. A flight to Tokyo read 35N 139E. A flight to Mexico City read 19N 99W.

"I get the N and S," Florence said. "North and south, top and bottom of the map. But E and W go both ways. How do you know which one you're reading?"

Asiya squinted at Tokyo. "Tokyo's east of us. Mexico City's west. So the letters must mean east and west, not just one line."

"So there's a zero somewhere," Florence said slowly, "and places count away from it on both sides." She ran her finger along the map until she found the line marked 0. From there the numbers climbed to 180 going right, marked E, and to 180 going left, marked W. Longitude, the little label on those lines said. She checked Mexico City: its up-and-down line, the one running from pole to pole, was the 99 west of zero. Its sideways line, the latitude, was the 19.

"Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian," Ms. Kovalenko said, handing Florence a magnifier to calibrate her reading of the tiny numbers. "Zero to 180, east or west."

Florence checked Rome the same way and got 42 north, 12 east. Ms. Kovalenko printed the souvenir, and Petra held it up.

"Next stop, a monarchy," Asiya said, pointing at London.

"Spontaneous trip," said Florence. "Tickets, please."

Amelia sat at the corner table of the public library with her draft spread out in front of her. The essay was supposed to persuade the town council to build a fence around the pond so the turtles could hibernate through winter without dogs digging at their banks. She had an introduction, three body paragraphs, and a conclusion, which her teacher, Mr. Krause, had said was the right shape for a persuasive essay. The trouble was the last paragraph, which currently read, "In conclusion, turtles matter, so please build the fence, thank you."

Braxton dropped into the chair across from her and picked up the page. He read fast, the way he did when he was looking for something to argue about. "Half of Richardson Pond's turtles get disturbed every winter," he read aloud. "Says who?"

"What?"

"Says who. Where did you get that number?"

Amelia stared at the sentence. She had gotten it from somewhere, she was sure, but she could not remember where. Maybe a poster. Maybe her cousin. "It's true," she said.

"It sounds true," Braxton said. "It also sounds made up. If I were the town council, I'd want to know."

Margo arrived with three books about ponds and slid one across the table. "There's a turtle count in here from the Parks Department. Same number, half of them, and it says the Parks Department counted them over two winters." Amelia copied the number onto her page and, underneath it, wrote where it came from, the name of the department right there in the sentence. It cost her nothing, took no extra expense of effort, and somehow the paragraph looked more competent, like something a grown-up with a briefcase might have written.

At the council meeting two weeks later, a man in a gray jacket squinted at her essay. "Half the turtles, hmm. Says who?" Amelia pointed to the line. "The Parks Department. You can go check it." The man went quiet. Then he said, "Well. I can, can't I," and voted yes, which was the twist, because Braxton, who had come along to see her fail, clapped loudest of anyone in the room.

Afterward Braxton asked her to look at his own essay, which was about longer recess. He read the first body paragraph out loud, stopped, and crossed out a number with his pencil. "That one's from nobody," he said. "Got anything from the Parks Department?"

Chase ran his monologue for the fourth time in the empty lobby of the community theatre, and for the fourth time he galloped through it like a kid reciting a spelling list. Tomorrow was the audition. Ms. Adeyemi had promised the lead in the winter play to whoever could actually make the speech breathe, and right now Chase's version was flat as the linoleum.

"Again?" Sharon called from the ticket booth, where she was supposed to be stacking programs. "You've done that speech so many times I could narrate your life in my sleep."

"Then help me," Chase said. "It's dead. I say the words right, but it sounds like nothing."

Naomie popped out from behind the curtain, eating a granola bar. "It's the rhythm. You're rushing every line like a bus is leaving."

"There's no bus," Chase said. "There's a rule, maybe. Listen." He spoke one line slowly, then fast, then slow again, tapping his knuckle on the ticket counter under each word. Something clicked. When he tapped his own lines, some beats landed soft and some landed hard, and the hard ones kept arriving in the same places.

Naomie leaned in. "Say it again and tap."
