But he noticed something else, something he hadn't heard while singing. On the recording, the sound never fully stopped. It went thin for a moment, then filled back out. He frowned and tapped the screen. "Play the long note again." He listened twice, three times, with his eyes shut.

"Frank," he said slowly, "you breathe before I do. We're not breathing at the same time." They tried it on purpose, and it worked even better. When John breathed, Frank's note carried, and when Frank breathed, John's was there. Ainsley arrived just then with the sheet music, and John pulled her into the room. "We figured it out. We take breaths at different moments, so the note keeps sounding even though every singer breathes. Mr. Khan never even told us that."

"Then sing it for me," Ainsley said, and stood by the window to listen.

The note stretched out long and steady under their voices, and outside, a bird answered it.

Samanthal knelt beside the campfire ring, holding a lumpy ball of dough that refused to puff. "Come on," she whispered to it. "Do your job." Her family's tent flapped in the morning draft, and somewhere behind the trailers a generator droned like a sleepy dragon, but none of that mattered. What mattered was that she had promised everyone fresh bread tonight, and her dough lay in the bowl looking as lethargic as her brother before breakfast, flat and lazy and completely unrisen.

She pulled a folded letter from her jacket pocket, the one her friend Layne had mailed her the day before camp started. "Dear Samantha," it read, "my grandma taught me bread this summer. Her three rules: give the yeast sugar to eat, keep the water warm like bathwater, not hot like tea, and never rush it. Hunter says bread is alive, which is creepy and also true. Bake something amazing. Your friend, Layne." Samantha read it twice. Bathwater, not tea. She closed her eyes and remembered standing in Mr. Addo's kitchen last spring, helping him knead his famous Saturday loaves. He had let her stick a finger in the water before it went into the bowl, and it had felt like nothing at all, just pleasantly warm. But this morning, she had poured the water straight off the camp stove because she was in a hurry, and it had steamed.

"So it's the yeast," she said out loud. "The hot water did something to it." She thought about what Layne's letter had said about sugar, and about Hunter's creepy idea that bread was alive, and she pieced it together. "Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles," she told the dough sternly, as if scolding it. If the yeast was ruined, there would be no bubbles, and no bubbles meant no puffy loaf. She had a theory, and she could test it. She filled the water pot again, warmed it gently, touched it with her finger the way Mr. Addo had shown her, and started a fresh batch with a new packet of yeast and a spoonful of sugar from the supply box.

An hour later, Hunter's little brother, who was camping two sites over, wandered by and peered into her bowl. "It grew," he said, sounding personally offended. "Like a balloon." Samantha grinned and punched the dough down, watching it sigh flat again, then shaped it into a round loaf and set it in the dutch oven by the coals. Her mother had said camp bread was impossible and they should just eat sandwiches. When Samantha lifted the lid later and the smell of warm, crusty bread rolled out into the trees, her mother took a bite, closed her eyes, and said, "I was wrong. I am officially changing my mind about everything."

"Even about my tree house plans?" Samantha asked. Her mother handed her another slice and said, "Draft me a proposal tonight."

The line outside the mall's game store stretched past the fountain and curved toward the pretzel stand. Sofia held her sixty dollars in a zipped pocket and counted the people ahead of her, thirty-two at least. Giselle and Ireland had saved spots near the front, and when Sofia reached them, Ireland was bouncing on her toes.

"They're selling the new star fox plush for twelve dollars today only," Ireland said. "The toy store two floors up has the same one for thirty."

"Then why would anyone buy it up there?" Sofia asked.

"Because down here they sell out," Giselle said. "Last month it was the dragon plush. Gone in four minutes. My brother says the store keeps the price too low, so everybody wants one, and there aren't enough to go around. He says that's called a shortage."

At ten o'clock the doors opened, and the line contracted into a tight crowd at the register. Sofia watched the shelf of silver foxes through the glass. A clerk carried out one box, then another, and then he shook his head and held up his empty hands. Sofia was still nine people from the front. Around her, fans groaned and checked their phones. A boy near the counter said he'd been waiting since seven.

Sofia turned her logic over as the crowd broke apart. Twelve dollars, three hundred people, maybe sixty plushes. Thirty dollars, and upstairs she'd seen rows of them sitting untouched on a shelf. The price was the difference. When the plush was cheap, more people wanted it than there were plushes to sell. When it cost more, plenty sat waiting. She pictured the two shelves like symmetrical mirrors, one empty and one crowded, and wondered whether the same rule worked for other things.

"Let's test it," she said. "The pretzel stand sells plain pretzels for a dollar and there's a whole rack. The cinnamon ones are four dollars and there's always a line."

They walked over. The rack of plain pretzels stood full and steaming, and only one customer stood there. At the cinnamon window, six people waited while a fresh tray came out and vanished in under two minutes. Ireland watched the last cinnamon pretzel leave with its buyer and nodded slowly. "Same thing," she said. "Cheap and scarce, or pricey and plentiful."

They rode the escalator to the toy store, where Ms. Cho was straightening a display. Sofia walked to the shelf and counted eleven silver foxes, glossy and identical, each with a thirty-dollar tag. She had enough. She picked one up, and the fur was softer than she'd imagined.

"Changed my mind," Ireland said behind her, grabbing one too. "Waiting in line at dawn is not worth it. I'd rather pay more and actually get the fox."

Sofia carried hers to the register and set her sixty dollars on the counter. "One fox, please," she said.

Megan had taped a growth chart to the back of her bedroom door, and every Friday night she stood against it with a pencil while her dog watched from the rug. Nothing. The same pencil mark for three weeks. She was eleven and a half, and she had a theory: something invisible was happening to her, something working underneath like seeds waiting to germinate, and if she could just find the pattern, she would know when to expect things.

That Friday, her classmate Baby came over with a sleeping bag and a letter she refused to open. "It's from my sister," Baby said, dropping it on the bed. "She's away at camp. I'm saving it for later because if it's bad news I want to still have a good evening first." Megan respected that logic, and they ate popcorn and painted their toes instead.

Later, in the dark, Baby finally opened it by flashlight. "She says her bunkmate got her first period and cried, and the counselor says it's normal at twelve. That's the middle, she wrote. Half of girls get it before twelve and half after." Megan sat up. Her own older cousin had gotten hers at ten, which had scared Megan into thinking she was late. "So it's not a race," Megan said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "There's a whole range around twelve, and everyone lands somewhere in it." She felt something settle, like a rule she had finally proven. "My cousin was just at one end."

"So it's like an ecosystem," Baby said, waving the flashlight. "Everybody's on their own schedule, but it all still works." Megan laughed and wrote the rule on an index card and taped it beside the growth chart: not late, not early, somewhere in a wide normal range.

In the morning Baby's nerves had turned into excitement, which was contagious, and the two of them ran the experiment one more time. Megan stood against the door, and Baby drew a careful new line. "Up a quarter inch," Baby announced, tapping the chart. "See? Something's been happening all along."

Emma had promised Ms. Xu a bar graph of her town's ethnic and cultural origins by Monday, and the numbers would not behave. She spread her survey papers across the kitchen table while the relatives talked over the spaghetti. The percentages from the town's census website added up to one hundred and thirty-two percent, which was impossible, and Emma despised impossible numbers more than anything else on a homework sheet.

"Something's wrong with the data," she told her cousin, who was stacking garlic bread like a wall. Emma narrowed her eyes at the page. Either the census people couldn't do arithmetic, or something was hiding in the numbers, some rule she hadn't figured out yet. She decided to test it the only way she could, with the people in this very room.

She grabbed a notepad and worked the long table like a game show host. "Grandma, where's your family from?" "Italy," Grandma said, "and your grandfather's side is Scottish." Uncle Ray raised his fork. "Filipino and Irish. Ask me about the monsoon season sometime, I was born during one." Auntie Priya laughed. "Indian and Ukrainian, and before you ask, yes, my mother makes competent samosas and competent perogies." Emma wrote it all down, then counted. Eleven people at the table. Fifteen origins in her tally. She flipped the page over and did the math again, because fifteen origins from eleven people meant her little survey would show over one hundred percent too, if she graphed it the way she had graphed the town.

She texted her classmate Dorian, who loved census facts the way other kids loved hockey stats. His reply came fast: "Its not a mistake. Since 1981 Canada's census lets people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population." Emma read it twice, then looked at Grandma, then at her tally sheet, and felt the hidden rule click into place like the last piece of a puzzle. The town's numbers weren't broken. They were extra full, the way this table was extra full.

She redrew the graph that evening, adding a note in her best printing: Origins add up to more than one hundred percent because people belong to more than one. Then she added a small legend, using her own family, just for Ms. Xu: Italian, Scottish, Filipino, Irish, Indian, Ukrainian, all in one kitchen.

Madelynn texted a picture of her own graph, which also went over one hundred, with the message "MINE IS BROKEN TOO."

"Mine was," Emma typed back. "Bring your markers tomorrow."

Aurora spread the scraps of papyrus-colored paper across the archive table and glared at them. The city archive smelled like dust and old glue, and Mr. Iyer had said she could stay until closing if she kept quiet, which was hard, because her class calendar project was falling apart. Four seasons, spring, summer, fall, winter. That was how calendars worked. But every book she pulled from the Egypt boxes insisted the ancient year had three seasons, and no book said why. "Maybe the books are biased," she whispered to Erin, who was drawing crocodiles on the margin of their poster. "Maybe whoever wrote them just liked the number three."

"Or maybe you just can't count," said Barrett, sliding into the chair beside her with a box labeled NILE RECORDS. He dumped it out, and out tumbled photographs of the river, month by month, taken over decades for the city's flood maps. Aurora flipped through them slowly. In some, the river lapped high over its banks, drowning the fields. In others, the same fields stood green and striped with crops. In the last ones, workers bent low, cutting grain. She laid three photos side by side. Flood. Growing. Harvest. Then she counted the months on the flood maps and matched them against the photographs, and her pencil hovered over the paper.

She wrote three columns instead of four. At the top of the first she put the word she had found on a museum card: "Akhet." The second she labeled "Peret." The third, "Shemu."

"That's the flood, the growing season, and the harvest," Aurora said, tapping each column. "That's why three. The river did the counting." She wanted to incorporate the whole thing into the calendar before anyone could argue, so she grabbed the glue before Erin could draw another crocodile on it. Barrett leaned over her shoulder, read the labels, and frowned. "Then where's winter?" Aurora opened her mouth, then closed it. She picked up her pencil and wrote, small, in the corner of the poster: "No snow. Not one flake. Barrett checked."

Brielle sat at the kitchen table with her cast propped on a pillow, staring at the drawing she had made of her own arm bone. Three days ago the doctor had told her mother that the break missed the growth plate, and everyone had smiled, but nobody had said why that was good news. Brielle wanted to know. She had drawn a long bone and put little squiggles near both ends, because she remembered the doctor pointing to the ends when she said it.

Faisal came in through the back door carrying a jar of beans. "My bean project," he said, setting it down beside the fruit bowl. "I want mine to germinate first out of the whole class. I'm putting them on your windowsill because your kitchen gets the best sun." He wet a paper towel and folded the beans inside the jar, then turned it so the light hit it.

"That peach is going to ruin your beans," Brielle said. The peach in the bowl had a gray patch spreading across its skin. "That's fungus. My mom says one bad piece can spread to everything touching it." Faisal made a face and carried the peach to the compost bucket under the sink.

Then he leaned over her drawing. "Why does your arm bone have scribbles at the ends?"

"I think I figured it out," Brielle said. She tapped the squiggles. "Those are growth plates. That's what the doctor called them, at the ends of long bones. They're made of cartilage, and that's where the bone lengthens while you're a kid. If a break goes right through one, it can affect how the bone grows after that." She traced her cast with her finger. "Mine didn't, which is why everyone smiled."

"So how do you know it's still growing in there?" Faisal asked.

"I measured my other arm with the tape measure this morning," Brielle said. "I wrote the number in my notebook. I'm going to measure again next week and the week after, and if the number gets bigger, then the growth plates are working. Same as your beans."

Faisal grinned and slid the jar next to her notebook. "Then we'll watch both experiments at once."

Brielle picked up her pencil and wrote "ARM: 46 CENTIMETERS" across the top of a fresh page, then drew an arrow pointing at the bean jar.

Scarlett held the borrowed guitar up to her ear and plucked the fat E string, and the note wobbled like a door that needed oil. Mr. Dlamini had left the music room door open with a sign taped to it that said TUNING PRACTICE, COME IN, along with a small silver pitch pipe. He had played one low note on the pipe before heading down the hall. "Match that," he had said. "By Friday."

The problem was that Scarlett had no idea which way to turn the peg. She remembered last summer at Theodore's grandparents' house, when he had cranked a peg with total confidence and the note sank lower and lower, like a whale diving. Theodore had insisted the guitar was broken. His grandfather had laughed until he had to sit down. Scarlett turned the peg the opposite way from what Theodore had done, just a tiny bit, and plucked again. The note crept upward.

"Is that right?" Marko leaned in the doorway, holding a sandwich he clearly wanted to eat more than anything, since lunch was in ten minutes and he had skipped breakfast. He had come to complain to Mr. Dlamini about the chess club schedule, but the room had a pull on him. "It sounds less like a dying animal now. Progress."

Scarlett plucked the string, then blew the pitch pipe and plucked again, back and forth until the two notes sat together like matching socks. The old strings felt brittle under her fingers, dry as autumn leaves, and she worried that one wrong twist might snap one. She loosened the next string a little too far, heard it dive, and brought it back up again, more slowly this time. If turning one way raised a note and the other way lowered it, she could fix any mistake. She only had to listen.

By the time the bell rang, four strings rang true and the fifth was close. Marko had eaten the sandwich, crumbs down his shirt, and was strumming the air like a rock star. "Teach me that tomorrow," he said, "and I'll trade you my seat by the window on the bus." Scarlett looked at the guitar, at the little silver pipe, and shook the last string's note upward until it locked into place. "Deal," she said, and blew the pipe one more time to check.

James had been sitting on the garage floor for twenty minutes, staring at the shoebox of painted ping-pong balls Ms. Kim had given him after the science fair meeting. The red ones were protons, the gray ones neutrons, and the tiny blue beads were electrons, meant to hang on bent wire. Aleksander sat across from him, already threading a bead onto a coat hanger. "You start with a big one, right?" Aleksander said. "Like oxygen, sixteen of everything, so it looks impressive."

"I did that last year," James said. He thought about how that model had looked, big and crowded and praised by everybody, and how he had not really understood a single part of it. Building it had felt like camouflage, something impressive to hide behind, and the judges' compliments had been wasted on him. He had decided, in a vain sort of hope that this year would be different, to build the smallest atom instead and actually know it. The problem was the smallest one, hydrogen, was giving him trouble before he even started. He kept reaching for a gray ball out of habit.

"Every atom needs a neutron, doesn't it?" he said, holding up the gray ball. "Something in the middle holding it together." He set it down, picked it up again, then turned to his dad's science almanac on the workbench, the one with the crumpled cover and the page corners that had started to erode from being turned so often. He found the table of elements and ran his finger along the first row. "Hydrogen," he read slowly. "The most common kind has just one proton and one electron." He checked twice, because it seemed impossible. "No neutron at all."

Aleksander leaned over to see for himself. "So the simplest atom in the universe is one red ball and one blue bead," he said. "That's it?"

"That's it," James said. He dropped every gray ball back into the shoebox, hung a single blue bead on one loop of wire, and set it orbiting the lone red ping-pong ball on the workbench.

Amelia stood on Aurora's porch holding a wrapped box of mangoes, her gift clutched so tight the ribbon crinkled. Aurora's grandmother had moved in last month from Chiang Mai, and Aurora had invited her over to meet him... no, her. Amelia had practiced the greeting on the walk: press your palms together, bow slightly, say "sawasdee khrap" if you were a boy and "sawasdee kha" if you were a girl. She was a girl, so "kha" it was.

The door opened and a small woman in a blue blouse smiled up at her. Amelia pressed her palms together, bowed, and said "sawasdee kha." The grandmother's face lit up like a struck match, and she returned the gesture and said something warm and quick that Amelia couldn't follow. Aurora pulled her inside by the sleeve. "That was so good," she whispered. "She'll like you forever now."

The living room had a low table already set with bowls, and a canopy of paper lanterns hung from the ceiling, strung by Aurora's dad for the occasion. Amelia handed the gift across with both hands, the way she'd read you should, and the grandmother took it with both hands too and set it aside unopened. Amelia felt a jolt of worry. She had expected thank-yous, maybe some unwrapping. Why set it down like that? She watched, waiting. Aurora's dad disappeared into the kitchen, came back, called everyone to the table, and only then did the grandmother quietly pick the box up again and place it somewhere careful, near a small shelf with a framed photograph. Amelia began to form a guess: gifts here were not opened in front of the giver. She decided to test it by watching what happened with Aurora's present later. Sure enough, when Aurora's dad handed over a small bag of sweets, the grandmother thanked him, smiled, and set it by the box. Nobody opened anything.

At dinner Amelia kept noticing small rules. The grandmother served the eldest person first, and everyone waited until Aurora's dad lifted his spoon before eating. Aurora leaned close. "Watch this," she murmured, and pointed at her little cousin, a boy of about five who was stacking rice into a tower. Amelia reached over to ruffle his hair affectionately, the way her own uncle always did to her, and Aurora caught her wrist. "Don't. In Thailand the head is sacred. Touching someone's head, even just to pat a kid, is rude there."

Amelia pulled her hand back slowly. The rule was invisible, but the evidence had been everywhere once she looked: the grandmother's quick sidestep earlier when a visitor had reached toward the boy, the way she touched her own head and then her chest as if apologizing for something. Amelia had dismissed that little dance as a stretch. It hadn't been.

"Even for someone as sophisticated as you," the grandmother said in careful English, catching Amelia's wide eyes, "new rules take time." Then she spooned a second helping of rice onto Amelia's plate and gestured for her to eat.

The flight to Denver was delayed, which meant Samantha's class trip had turned into two hours of airport chairs, and Gillian had already eaten both her granola bars. Ms. Russo had handed out atlases to keep everyone busy, and Samantha's job was to find the class destination using latitude and longitude. She traced her finger along the lines until it landed on the dot with the airport code.

"There," she said. "Thirty-nine point seven north, one hundred four point nine west. That's us, flying almost to the middle."

Gillian leaned over. "Why are the lines all squished together at the top? Did somebody smash the map?"

Samantha squinted. The longitude lines, straight and evenly spaced at the equator, bunched tighter and tighter toward the top of the globe, like ribs on an accordion. She tested one with her thumb, measuring the gap between two lines at the equator, then sliding her thumb upward. The gap shrank under her finger.

"Look at this," she said. "A degree here is fat. A degree up there is skinny."

"So a degree isn't always the same size?" Gillian frowned at the page. "That's like a ruler that changes its mind."

"It's like lines of longitude meet at the poles," Samantha said slowly, watching the lines converge at the very top. "A degree of longitude spans about a hundred and eleven kilometers at the equator, but it shrinks to zero at the poles."

"Zero," Gillian repeated. "So at the pole, you could walk across every time zone in one step?" She stood up and demonstrated, stomping in a tiny circle. "I'm in Denver. Now I'm in London. Now I'm somewhere with penguins."

"You'd flourish there," Samantha said. "You've already eaten everything in this time zone."

A shop clerk passing by with a cart glanced at them and smiled. Ms. Russo looked up from her coffee. "Finding Denver?"

"Found it," Samantha said, tapping the dot. "And lost about a hundred and eleven kilometers on the way."

Gillian pointed at the snack stand. "Then let's go find those pretzels before they shrink to zero too."

Parker squeezed past a row of knees holding two hot chocolates, one for himself and one for his little sister, who had been shivering in her thin jacket since the second inning. He had budgeted his allowance for weeks to afford seats like these, close enough to see the stitches on the ball, and now the whole family was here plus Nick and Elias from his class. Below them the crowd roared as the home team's shortstop turned a double play, and Parker nearly wore both drinks.

"How does he do that?" Elias said, leaning forward. "That was so fast."

"He's just competent," Nick said, shrugging. "Like, actually competent. Some guys are fast and some guys just know where to be."

Parker was half listening. Something was nagging at him, and he scanned the field, jersey by jersey. Three. Seven. Twenty-one. Five. Eleven. He checked the visiting team's dugout too. Nobody, on either side, wore 42. "Hey," he said. "Look at the numbers. Nobody out there has forty-two. Not one player."

Elias squinted at the field. "Maybe it's bad luck?"

"It's not bad luck," Parker said slowly. "It's on purpose. It has to be." He turned the idea over. If one team skipped a number, fine, superstition. But both teams, every player? That sounded like a rule. He tested it in his head: Mariano Rivera, the Yankees closer, his dad talked about him all the time. Rivera wore 42. So it wasn't banned forever. He dug the program out from under his seat and flipped through the team pages, running his finger down the rosters. Number 42 was simply missing, like a tooth knocked out of a smile.

Nick pulled out his phone while Elias shielded the screen from the glare. "Okay, okay, it says here... in 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team. First time any professional athlete was honored that way. Every team. The whole league."

"Retired it," Parker repeated, and the word felt heavy and good in his mouth, like something an emperor would command. Nobody could ever wear it again except the few already wearing it when the rule came. "So Rivera was grandfathered in. That's why I remembered it." He nudged his sister, who was still shivering, and draped his own jacket over her shoulders even though the night air bit. "Robinson," he said. "That's why it's everybody, not just one team."

The crowd rose around them as the closer struck out the side, and Parker stood up too, jacket-less and grinning, cup held high.

Julia pressed her pencil so hard against the grid paper that the tip snapped. Across the room, the clock above Mr. Georgiou's whiteboard showed only four minutes left in math club, and she had plotted exactly one point for y = 2x + 1.

"When x is one, y is three," she muttered, marking the point. "But we're supposed to show the whole equation, and I've got one dot."

Libby leaned over from the next desk. "I did three points and it took me forever. There's no way you finish."

Julia could perceive the shape forming on Libby's page, though: three dots in a row, all lined up like fence posts. One more point, and a ruler could connect them. But was two enough? She had never tested that. Quickly, she chose x is zero, worked out that y must be one, and plotted the second point beside the first.

She laid her ruler across both dots and drew the line, then stopped. It looked right, but she needed to check. She picked x is three, calculated y is seven, and placed a small circle on the line. It landed exactly on her ruler's edge. She tried x is negative one, and that point sat on the line too, like it had been waiting there.

"Every single one," Julia whispered.

"Every single one what?" Izaak asked, sliding his chair over.

"Every point I test lands on the line, even though I only drew it through two points. So plotting two correct points is enough. You don't need more."

"Two?" Izaak squinted at her paper. "That feels like cheating."

"It's not cheating, it's faster. Try it." She handed him her ruler, its edge still warm from her hand. Mr. Georgiou had begun collecting papers, and the room smelled of pencil shavings and the oranges he kept on his desk. Julia slid her sheet to the front, a genuine solution with a line running clean across the grid.

Next week, she decided, she would show Izaak an adaptation of her shortcut: two points, one ruler, and half the time to spare. "Bring your own ruler," she told him. "Mine's got tooth marks."

The snow came down overnight with no warning at all, and by morning the radio said school was closed. Charlie texted Mack, and they met at ten o'clock in Riverside Park, where the playground looked like a frosted cake.

"Snowman," Mack said, and scooped up two armfuls of powder. Charlie tried to pack hers into a ball, but the snow fell apart between her mittens like sugar. She tried again, pressing harder, and it crumbled even faster.

"It's too fluffy," Mack said, kicking at it. "Look, it won't even stick to itself."

Charlie sat back on her heels and thought. Yesterday the freezing rain had turned to snow, and this morning the thermometer on her kitchen window read just under freezing, near thirty-two degrees. But the snow felt dry and squeaky, more like the cold snaps in January than like today. She remembered last year, when they had made perfect snowballs in the afternoon after the sun had been on the field for hours. Back then the snow had felt almost damp, and it had packed so hard that Mack's brother complained it was "basically ice."

"Maybe it needs to warm up a little," Charlie said. "Last year's good snow felt wetter than this."

"Wetter snow sounds worse," Mack said.

"Maybe not. Maybe wet snow near freezing sticks together, and dry snow like this crumbles." She stood up. "Let's wait for the sun to do its work, then test it."

They sledded down the hill by the baseball diamond while they waited. Near the fence, an old man grumbled to his dog about the sidewalk, saying the landlord never shoveled it, and that a negligent landlord was going to get somebody hurt. Charlie dragged her sled around the icy patch carefully. By one o'clock the sun was bright on the open field, and she noticed her boot prints looked shiny and damp.

She grabbed a handful and squeezed. The snow held. She tossed a test ball against the fence, and it thumped instead of bursting.

"Wet snow near freezing packs," Charlie said, grinning. "Dry cold snow just crumbles. Come on!"

They rolled the bottom ball together, then the middle, then the head, and Charlie ran to find two pebbles for eyes before the light changed.

Rebecca had read the bylaw three times on the bus, and it still said the same tedious thing: no bikes allowed on the riverside path. She and Bentley rode that path every Saturday, and now they would have to push their bikes through gravel beside it. "We're going to the town hall meeting tonight," she told him at lunch. "We'll speak to the council and get it changed." Bentley's own wish was smaller and sharper; he wanted to be the one who talked, because he had never spoken into a real microphone before and it felt like an audition for something bigger.

The hall smelled like coffee and floor wax. Rows of folding chairs, a long table up front, and five councillors who looked tired already. When the meeting opened, a woman from the gardening club stood up, clutching a stack of notes, and asked to speak about the flower beds by the library. The clerk at the side table shook her head. "I'm sorry. Delegations have to register with the city clerk's office before the meeting."

The woman sat down, deflated, and Rebecca felt her stomach drop. She nudged Bentley. "Before the meeting. Nobody told us that." She watched the clerk flip through a binder and noticed the page had names on it, printed neatly, with times beside each one. So the order of speakers was set before anyone even walked in. That meant their plan had a hidden step they had skipped.

Rebecca raised her hand. When the mayor nodded at her, she kept her voice steady. "We're not registered, but can we sign up for the next meeting tonight, so we don't miss it again?" The clerk smiled a little and slid a form across the table. "You can fill that in now," she said, "and you'll be first on the list for next month." Bentley leaned over the form, gripping the pen. "I'll do the talking part," he whispered. "You did the figuring-out part."

Rebecca inhaled the coffee smell one more time, wrote their names in block letters, and slid the form back across the table.

"See you next month," the clerk said.

Nolan set the recipe card on the counter and read it again, because last time he had skipped that step and the muffins had rebelled, flat and gray as river stones. This time he turned the dial to preheat the oven first, measured the flour, and cracked the eggs. Noemy leaned against the fridge with her phone ready, because she wanted a photo of a perfect muffin for the baking club page, and her last three attempts had looked like accidents. "You get one shot at mine," Nolan warned her. "Then you owe me a muffin," she said.

The recipe said to fill the cups and bake right away, but halfway through spooning batter, the doorbell rang. Jimmy stood there holding a frail paper bag that had torn at the bottom, spilling three marbles onto the step. While Nolan helped him gather them, he kept glancing back at the kitchen, where the bowl of batter sat waiting on the counter.

He remembered the Saturday his grandmother let him stir while she talked. "It's double-acting," she had said, tapping the tin of baking powder. "It releases gas twice, once when it gets wet in the batter and again when it is heated in the oven." He had nodded without really listening, too busy licking the spoon. Now he stared at the resting batter and thought about that. If the first gas had already fizzled out while he chased marbles, the muffins would be flat, and Noemy's photo would be another disaster. But if the second release was still waiting for the oven's heat, maybe the batter could afford to sit for a few minutes, exactly like the recipe seemed to hint when it said not to worry about the last few cups.

"That's the buzzer," Noemy called from the kitchen. Nolan slid the tray in, set the timer, and wiped his hands on the towel. "If they come out flat," he said, "I'm blaming your club photo." Twenty minutes later he pulled the tray out, and the muffins stood tall and golden, tops cracked like little mountains. Noemy snapped three pictures before he even set the tray down. "Tallest one is mine," Jimmy said, reaching past him.

Theodor's little brother was home from school with an ear infection, so the two of them were stuck inside on a rainy Saturday, sharing Theodor's phone on the living room floor. They had already scrolled past what felt like a thousand photos, so many pictures of migratory birds that the screen seemed saturated with feathers, because Theodor's science project on bird migration was due Monday.

"Let's search ourselves," Theodor said, grinning. "Everybody does it." He typed his own name first and found nothing but a runner from another country. Then Liam took the phone and typed Liam plus his last name. The second result made his stomach drop. It was a comment he had written two whole years ago, on a public video about their town's skate park, back when he thought only his friends would ever see it. It said the park was boring and so was the coach who ran it, and it still had his full name attached, sitting there for anyone in the world to read.

"How is it still there?" Liam whispered. "That was forever ago." Theodor shrugged and scrolled, but Liam kept thinking, turning the problem over the way he did with math puzzles. His mom had said once that search engines copy public pages using automated programs called crawlers. If a crawler had copied his comment, then it lived somewhere he couldn't see, like a photocopy stuck in a drawer he couldn't open. He tested the idea: he searched the exact words from his comment, without his name. The comment came up again, third result. So it wasn't connected to his name only. It was public, copied, indexed, findable.

He clicked through until he reached the video page and found a delete button next to his own words. His thumb hovered. The coach from the skate park had helped him land his first ollie last summer, before Liam even knew they had met before. He pressed delete, and the comment vanished from the page. Then he typed his own name into the search bar one more time, just to see, and exhaled slowly at what came up on the screen.

Emily slid her French worksheet across the library table and read it a third time. Ms. Nowak's assignment was printed at the top: describe your family and pets in full sentences, in French. Around her, the library hummed with whispers and page turns, and Koen was already halfway down his page, writing fast, which worried her because Koen never checked anything.

"Ma mère a un chat," Emily said under her breath, testing it. My mother has a cat. That one felt solid. She kept going. "Mon frère a deux poissons." Her brother had two fish, a reckless pair who once leapt from their tank and survived because her mother happened to walk past. Writing about them was easy. Then she reached the last line, the one Ms. Nowak had circled twice: tell your own age and your family's ages.

She wrote "Je suis douze ans" and stopped. Something about it snagged in her mind like a sleeve on a nail. She flipped through her notebook to the vocab list. Avoir, to have. Être, to be. Two different verbs, and she had just used the wrong one, she was almost sure, though she couldn't see why she was sure. It was like guessing a fish was sick because it stopped swimming, without ever seeing the sickness itself.

Koen leaned over. "Stuck on the age part too?"

"I think there's a pattern," Emily said. "I just can't see it yet." She grabbed a scrap paper and started collecting evidence like a detective. Their textbook's sample dialogue said "J'ai treize ans" for one character. A photo caption said "Elle a neuf ans." A workbook answer key, which Ms. Nowak had left on the cart, said "Tu as quel âge?" Every single one used avoir. To have. Emily felt the pattern click into place, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. "They say it with have, not with am. J'ai douze ans. It means 'I am twelve,' but word for word it says 'I have twelve years.'"

Koen stared at his own page. "I wrote 'Je suis onze ans.'" He erased it so hard the paper thinned, and the torn corner drifted to the floor. Emily pulled out her pen and wrote her sentence again, cleanly this time, then added her mother's age and her brother's age, all with avoir, all with years.

"One more sentence," Koen said. "The pets."

Emily grinned and wrote, "Mes poissons sont les seuls organismes dans notre maison qui ne crient jamais," then translated for him: my fish are the only organisms in our house who never shout. Koen laughed, but quietly, because Ms. Nowak was already walking their way, holding the stack of corrected tests. She set Emily's last quiz face down on the table and moved on without a word. Emily turned it over slowly, and there, in red ink beside her sentence about age, was a note: "See me. Almost right."

She looked at her new sentence, then at the quiz, then back at her new sentence. "Koen," she whispered, "watch the door. I'm going to try the avoir rule one more time before she comes back."

Arianna had been stuck home for four days with the flu, and today was the deadline: her science fair project, the one she'd been building out of painted cardboard, was due at school by three o'clock, and the doctor's appointment her mother had booked for eleven was the only thing standing between her and the door. At the clinic, Ms. Ferreira, the pharmacist behind the small counter near the waiting room, was sorting bottles while a boy about Arianna's age clutched a wad of bright green tissues and announced that he definitely needed the strong medicine because his snot was green.

"Green means infection, right?" the boy said, his voice brittle with worry.

Arianna sat up. She'd been staring at her own crumpled tissues all week, thinking the same thing. Ms. Ferreira shook her head. "The color comes from your immune cells and an enzyme they release," she said. "It doesn't tell you if it's bacteria or a virus."

The boy frowned. Arianna's mind started turning. If color didn't tell you the cause, then everyone who panicked at green tissues was panicking for nothing, and that included her, because she'd been saving her grossest tissue in a zip bag, planning to show the doctor as proof she needed something strong. She had been incorporating that tissue into her whole plan, like evidence in a trial. She looked at the boy's pale face and the way he kept checking the clock above the counter, probably late for something too.

"Want to test it?" she whispered to him. She held up her bag. "Mine's been green since Tuesday, and I only have a virus, the doctor said so on Monday. Two green samples, two different causes, so the color can't be the thing that tells them apart." The boy's shoulders dropped with relief. He smiled, wadded his tissues into his pocket, and walked out with his dad instead of demanding medicine.

When the nurse finally called her name, Arianna left the zip bag on her chair. On the way out, she caught the boy's eye through the window and waved her project box. "Good luck!" she called through the glass.

Evan had never been so nervous about noodles. His mom's coworker, Mr. Iyer, had invited their whole family to a gathering at his sister's house, and somehow Evan had ended up at the ramen table beside Mr. Iyer's Japanese son-in-law, with a bowl of steaming broth in front of him and absolutely no plan.

The problem was the noise. The moment everyone started eating, the room filled with slurps, big wet ropey ones, coming from every side of the table. Evan froze with his chopsticks halfway to his mouth. At home, slurping meant somebody got the Look, the one that could diminish your dessert to zero in a single glance. His bias said loud eaters were rude eaters, and his brain was screaming that rule at him right now.

"Ramen's better hot," the son-in-law said, then slurped again, cheerfully, like it was music. "You have to hurry."

Evan watched him, then watched Mr. Iyer's sister doing exactly the same thing, then a grandmother down the table doing it loudest of all. Nobody flinched. Nobody gave anyone the Look. So maybe, he reasoned, the rule wasn't about noise at all, it was about where you were sitting. He decided to run a test. He lifted a tangle of noodles, took a breath, and slurped as hard as he could.

It worked. The noodles actually tasted better, cooler and faster, and a fleck of broth flew up and landed on his own forehead, which made a little kid across the table laugh so hard she had to put her spoon down.

"Excellent slurp," the son-in-law said, thumping him on the shoulder. "Better than mine."

"Impossible," said Evan, already going back in for round two. He was, after all, a very frugal eater when ramen was involved, and he didn't intend to waste a single noodle or a single second being polite about it.

Christopher sat on Brennan's kitchen floor while Brennan's dad set the small box on the counter, and he could hardly keep his hands still. Tomorrow was his own phone day, but tonight he got to practice on Brennan's, because Brennan had promised to teach him the rules before he broke any of them by accident.

"Rule one," Brennan said, holding the phone up like a trophy. "Never text during dinner. Rule two, actually read what you typed before you send it."

"I already know those," Christopher said. "I want to know how they work. Like, how long have people even carried phones around? Did cave people have them?"

Brennan laughed so hard he slid into the cabinet. Then he stopped, because he actually knew. "We had this poster in Ms. Chowdhury's class last year. It had a picture of a man on a New York street, April 3, 1973, holding this giant brick thing. It was the first call ever made from a handheld cellular phone. His name was Martin Cooper, and he was an engineer at Motorola."

"From a street?" Christopher stared at the phone in Brennan's hand. "So nobody had a pocket phone before that?"

"Fifty-something years ago, that was the very first one. Everybody else was stuck at home."

Christopher decided to test this. He typed a message to Theodor, who was home with a cold: "Did you know the first handheld cell call was made by a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973?" Then, after a moment, he added, "Feel better. Can you send me a photo of that poster in Ms. Chowdhury's room?"

The reply buzzed back fast for someone with a sore throat. "Already photographed it for you. It depicts him mid-stride, phone to his ear, people staring."

Christopher remembered, suddenly, the mural on the median outside the school, painted with geese flying in a migratory V, and how Theodor had said phones were like that, everyone heading the same way. He showed Brennan the photo of Cooper walking down the street.

"Tomorrow," Christopher said, "I'm putting that picture as my wallpaper."

"Best first phone ever," said Brennan, and handed him the box to hold until morning.

Lily knelt beside the tent at their campsite in the national park, stuffing her toothbrush into her bag, when she noticed something odd. Their bear locker, the big steel box a few steps away, stood open, and her father was carrying armfuls of stuff toward it. Not just food. He put in the sunscreen, the trash bag, even her little sister's cherry lip balm.

"Why the lip balm?" Lily asked. "That's not food."

Dad set it on the locker shelf. "Here they count anything with a scent as food. Toothpaste, sunscreen, trash, all of it goes in the bear locker too."

Lily thought about that all through dinner. A bear couldn't know what toothpaste was. It just followed smells. That meant her minty toothpaste, left in the tent, would be like a signpost pointing straight at her sleeping bag. She remembered her friend Jazmin saying her family's trip had been ruined by a raccoon, just a raccoon, and this park had actual bears. Bears she would never see coming in the dark.

So she tested her idea. She carried every scented thing she could find to the locker: soap, hand sanitizer, the wrapper from her granola bar, even her strawberry shampoo. Her classmate Davin, camping two sites over with his uncle, wandered past and watched her line the items up. "That's a lot of stuff for somebody who hasn't eaten dinner yet," he said.

"It's not food," Lily said. "It's everything a nose could find." Davin looked at the row of bottles, then at his own tent, and jogged back to check his family's supplies. He returned holding a tube of toothpaste and gave her a thumbs up.

That night Lily lay in her sleeping bag feeling optimistic. The tent smelled like nothing but canvas and dust. In the morning, the ranger stopped by to say a bear had visited the campground, and Lily noticed only one tent had a torn screen, the one far down the row. She watched a gray jay land on the locker's steel top, peck twice at nothing, and fly off into the pines.

Ella slid her phone under the table for the third time, and her mother gave her the look that meant put it away. "It's important," Ella said. "Everyone's sharing this flood picture from the storm downtown. The whole riverfront is underwater. Zakariya's mom works there, and he can't reach her." Her father set down his fork. "Then put the phone on the table where we can all see it," he said, "and eat while you look."

The photo was dramatic and distinct: brown water swallowing the steps of the library, a stop sign showing only its tip. Her little brother leaned over her arm, wanting to feel part of it, so she angled the screen toward him. Last summer, Ella remembered, a kid at camp had shown them a shark photo that was supposedly from that morning's news; by afternoon the whole cabin had learned the shark had been swimming through the same street in pictures from years before. Someone had typed the address of a search page into the old camp laptop and dragged the photo in. "A reverse image search," the kid had called it. Ella had thought it was a neat trick then. Now she opened the same kind of page, dropped the flood picture in, and waited, chewing bread her brother had quietly pushed onto her plate because she'd forgotten to take any.

The results stacked up. The library flood photo had appeared online years before, back when her brother was small, under a headline about an older storm. It wasn't from today at all. "It's an old picture being passed off as new," she said. "Zakariya's worrying over nothing that happened this week." Her father rubbed his knee, the one where the cartilage had worn thin, and stood up. "Then call him. Tell his family before they panic over an old photo."

Zakariya answered on the first ring. "My mom's fine," he said, before Ella could even speak. "She texted two minutes ago. She's dry. But thank you, thank you for checking." Ella set the phone face up on the table and finally took a real bite of dinner. Her brother mimicked her, cutting his chicken with exaggerated care, and slid the last piece of bread onto her plate.

Isabella slid her draft across the library table just as Mr. Tran called out, "Ten minutes until we read our essays aloud, everyone!"

The topic was whether the school should keep its bike racks, and Isabella had written with all her heart. There was the story of her cousin who biked to school in the rain, a paragraph about pollution, a paragraph about how bikes give kids freedom, a paragraph about her neighbor who sold her old bike at a yard sale, and a page of other things she couldn't bear to cut. She counted her paragraphs and her stomach dropped. Seven. Somehow she had seven.

Across the table, Maram was calmly stapling her paper. "How many do you have?" Isabella asked, hoping for company in her misery.

"Five," Maram said. "My sister told me the trick. A five-paragraph essay has an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion." She held up her fingers one at a time. "One, three, one. If you're over or under, something needs to move."

Isabella looked at her pages. She couldn't see why five worked and seven didn't; there was no rule posted anywhere, no diagram in her notebook. But maybe it was like a recipe. If a cake called for three eggs, you didn't add five just because you liked eggs. She had to test it. She labeled her first paragraph "introduction," her last "conclusion," and circled the middle five. Then she tried squeezing her neighbor's bike story into the freedom paragraph, the way Lindsey had once delegated half her poster drawings to Maram when the deadline got close.

"Ms. Popularity over here has five paragraphs," Lindsey announced, pointing at Maram, whose reputation in writing club was so solid that even her stapled essays looked confident.

"That's because I follow the recipe," Maram said. "Unlike Isabella, who is writing a spontaneous novel."

"One, three, one," Isabella muttered, cutting and taping. The rain story went. The yard sale went. At last she counted again: five.

When Mr. Tran called her name, Isabella stood up, took a breath, and read her first line aloud: "Every kid at this school deserves a safe place to park a bike."

The bus let them off in front of the science center, where a banner read Living Farms Week. Sadie's class had studied electricity all month, so Mr. Popescu surprised them by leading the line straight past the lightning dome and toward a hot, glassy hall that smelled of straw. In a low pen, two pink pigs lay belly-down in a wide puddle of mud, blinking at the crowd.

"They're filthy," said Nadine, wrinkling her nose. "Why would anybody show off dirty pigs?"

Sadie leaned on the rail. The hall was warm from the sun through the glass roof, and the pigs' mud was dark and wet. On the wall, a screen showed a big view of pigskin, and a small sign sat below it. She read it twice. Then she noticed something: the pigs had flopped into the mud only after a patch of sunlight crossed their pen. Earlier, when they'd been in the shade, they had stood dry by the fence. It wasn't about being dirty. It was about the heat.

"Watch their pen," she told Nadine. "When the shade comes back, see if they get out."

They waited, sharing the last of Alexandra's crackers at their leisure while visitors drifted past. When the sun moved off the pen, the larger pig hauled itself up, crossed to the dry straw, and shook. The smaller one followed.

"They're using the mud like a pool," Sadie said. "The sign says pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water on hot days to cool off."

"Huh," said Nadine. "So the mud isn't the point."

"Right. Cooling off is the point."

Mr. Popescu clapped his hands for the group. "When we get back, each of you will summarize one thing you observed today," he said. "Make your claim explicit. Tell me exactly what you saw and what you concluded."

Sadie wrote one sentence in her notebook, then read it over. In the pen, the sunlight crept back across the mud, and the smaller pig lifted its head, watching the bright patch move.

The dinner table was tranquil, just the clink of forks and his dad scrolling his phone through box scores, when Elliot decided to bring it up. "Dad, do you think Bruno Reese is a bad hitter?"

"Average says he is," his dad said without looking up. "Two-fifty. That's the number."

Elliot's stomach tightened. He had spent all of recess arguing with Leonie and Sacha about this, and he had lost, badly. He flashed back to the blacktop, Sacha waving a printed stat sheet in his face, Leonie saying, "Face it, Elliot, two-fifty is two-fifty. The guy makes outs." Elliot had gone home quiet, but something about the number had nagged at him all afternoon, the way a pebble in a shoe seems small until you walk on it.

"Can I see your phone?" he asked now. His dad handed it over, and Elliot found Reese's page. Batting average, at-bats, hits, all lined up in cold columns. Then a separate column, far down the list, and Elliot's breath caught. Walks: one hundred and four. He counted them twice with his finger on the screen.

"Look at this," he said, sliding the phone across the mashed potatoes.

"A hundred and four walks," his dad read. "So?"

"So walks don't count as at-bats," Elliot said. "A batting average is just hits divided by at-bats, and a walk isn't an at-bat. Every single one of those hundred and four times he got on base, the average gives him nothing. Zero credit. It's like the number insulates you from half the story." He grabbed the sugar bowl and a handful of dried beans from the counter, laying them along the table edge. "These beans are his hits. These sugar packets are his walks. Now take away the packets." He swept them into his palm. "What's left is all the average can see."

His dad was quiet for a long moment, scrolling slowly. He put down his fork. He rubbed his jaw and looked at the little line of beans like it might change on him.

"Huh," he said. "From that perspective, he's on base more than half the time."

"Leonie's going to eat her words at recess tomorrow," Elliot said, scooping the beans into his pocket.

"Bring the stat sheet," his dad said. "I want to see her face."

Brielle sat in the exam chair and read the letters on the far wall. The big E was easy, but the second line smeared sideways, as if someone had dragged a thumb through wet ink. Ms. Diallo flipped lenses into the frame in front of Brielle's eyes, one click at a time.

"Try this," Ms. Diallo said. "Better or worse?"

"Better. The F has a tail again." Brielle squinted at the card Ms. Diallo held up close, at arm's length. Those letters smeared too. That was the part she couldn't figure out. She had hypothesized that she was nearsighted like her dad, because nearsighted meant far things blurred. But if that were true, the near card should have been sharp, and it wasn't. So that idea was wrong.

She turned her head and found a poster beside the sink, a cross-section of an eye with the cornea drawn in. The cornea on the poster wasn't round like a ball. It was egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, and a caption under it said this blurred vision at any distance. Any distance. That matched exactly what she'd noticed: smeared letters near and smeared letters far.

"That's it," Brielle said. "Mine's egg-shaped, curving more one way than the other. Is that called astigmatism?"

"That's what it's called," Ms. Diallo said, clicking in another lens. "Read the line for me."

Brielle read down to the tiny bottom row, every letter crisp and separate, and grinned at the mirror on the wall because now she could see her own grin. She felt optimistic about Monday, when she would pick up the real glasses. On the way out she stopped at the water cooler in the waiting room, pressed the valve for cold water, and drank while staring across the room at the eye chart hanging there. Even the smallest line held still.

"Those letters aren't going anywhere," she said.

Logan slid the book back and pulled out another one. He had promised Ms. Dela Cruz his presentation would answer two things: why the ancient Egyptians built the pyramids, and how the Nile shaped their farming. So far every book showed pictures of the pyramids but explained them about as well as a postcard of a sandwich explains lunch.

"Dead end?" Lux asked, dropping into the chair across from him with a granola bar and zero sympathy.

"Every book says 'amazing engineering,'" Logan said. "Thanks. Very helpful. But why there? Why that spot, why that shape, why bother?" He tapped the page. "And the farming part is worse. It just says the Nile flooded every year. Floods destroy things. My uncle's basement proves that."

Lux chewed for a second. "Okay, weird connection time. My grandpa gardens, and he made me monitor his tomato pots all summer, like a tiny scientist. The pot with the darkest soil went completely bananas. Twice as many tomatoes. The pale dirt pot was a sad little graveyard." She pointed her granola bar at him. "Dirt that's dark is dirt that's loaded. You're welcome."

Logan stared at her. "Dark soil. The flood." He yanked the atlas over and found the Nile, running like a green thread through all that yellow desert. "So the flood isn't the disaster part. The disaster part is when it goes down. And when it goes down, it leaves a layer of dark, fertile mud on the fields." He flipped to the vocabulary page and his finger stopped on a word. "They called their land Kemet," he read out loud. "The black land."

"Sounds like a superhero," said Lux.

"Sounds like the answer." Logan grabbed a blank sheet and started sketching: fat harvests feeding whole cities of workers, farms strung along the river, pharaohs stacking a stone mountain on the black land's edge as a giant billboard of power. Brianna leaned over from the next table, snagged his pencil, and drew a tiny rat on the grain pile. "That's a parasite," she said. "Free of charge."

"That's a rat, and I love it." Logan laughed and kept writing, feeling optimistic for the first time all week. He raised his hand. "Ms. Dela Cruz? Can we have the projector Thursday? I've got a flood, some very good mud, and a rat."

Jaxon set the Monopoly board on the dinner table between the lasagna and the salad bowl, because tonight Deanna and Kendra were staying for family dinner and game night. His dad cleared the plates, and his little brother pulled up a chair, already reaching for the car token.

Everything went fine until Deanna rolled a five and landed on Free Parking. "Yes," she said, rubbing her hands together. "Payday." She reached for the middle of the board, where Jaxon's family kept nothing at all.

"There's no money there," Jaxon said.

"Because you haven't been putting taxes in. I'll take what's owed from the bank, then."

"That's not how it works. Free Parking does nothing. It's just a free space."

Deanna folded her arms. "At my house, whoever lands on it gets the whole pot. Everybody plays that way."

Kendra looked between them. "At my house too. My cousin won once with like five hundred dollars from Free Parking." Jaxon's little brother chimed in that at his friend's house, you got fifty dollars. Nobody, it seemed, could agree.

Jaxon was about to argue louder when he remembered something Ms. Bear, his neighbor, had said about chess disputes: name the problem before you fight about the answer. So he raised his hand like a referee. "Wait. Let's name the actual problem. I think the problem isn't that Deanna's greedy."

"Thanks a lot," said Deanna, but she half smiled.

"The problem is we learned the game at different houses. My family plays one way, your families play another, and nobody ever said it out loud." He fetch the rulebook from the box and flipped to the page about Free Parking while everyone ate the last of the garlic bread. He ran his finger down the text. "See? Officially, Free Parking is just a rest space. The money thing is a house rule. A really common one, but a house rule."

Deanna leaned over and read it herself. "Huh. My dad taught me that. I thought it was a real rule." She seemed almost relieved, as though being wrong was better than being cheated.

"So here's my idea," Jaxon said. "We can't be immune to house rules just by reading the book, because they're fun and lots of families like them. So let's agree on one before we keep playing. We take a vote, majority wins, and nobody argues after that. That way there's no contradiction later when someone lands on it."

They voted. Three to two, they put the luxury tax and income tax payments into the middle, and whoever landed on Free Parking collected the pile. Deanna offered to let his little brother hold the pot so he would feel included even though he kept rolling threes.

"Good call," Kendra said quietly to Jaxon, and she convey her meaning with a fist bump under the table.

On Deanna's next turn, she rolled a five again and landed on Free Parking once more. His little brother slid the pile of bills across the board with both hands. "Payday," he announced.

Aubrey crouched on the patio with her chalk, drawing the biggest arrow she could manage, from the sun down to a patch of grass. "Science homework," she told Lucie, who had climbed over the fence the way she always did. "I have to draw a whole food chain, from the sun all the way to a top predator, and then explain what happens if one link disappears." The backyard was a good place for it, she figured. The sun was right there, warming the stones. Near the fence, the little solar lamps were still blinking off, their voltage drained from the night, which reminded her that everything out here started with sunlight. Even the maple leaves she'd raked into a pile last week were beginning to decompose into dark crumbs, going back into the dirt.

She drew the chain across the concrete: sun, then grass, then a caterpillar munching the grass, then a bird, then a hawk at the very top. Lucie frowned at it. "Okay, but Ms. Reddy said you have to use the right words." Aubrey flipped through her notebook until she found the page she'd copied off the board. "Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers," she read. "That's the caterpillar. Producers are the plants." She tapped the bird. "And the animals that eat them are secondary consumers." Lucie picked up the blue chalk and wrote PRIMARY in wobbly letters over the caterpillar, then SECONDARY over the bird.

"Fine," Lucie said, "but the last part of the assignment is the part you're avoiding." Aubrey knew she was right. She hadn't written a single thing about what happened when a link disappeared, because she wasn't sure. She had a guess, though, and guesses could be tested. "Watch," she said. She wet her sleeve in the wading pool and scrubbed the grass off the patio. No grass. She looked at the caterpillar. No grass meant nothing for the caterpillar to eat, so it would starve or crawl away. No caterpillar, and the bird went hungry too. No birds, and the hawk would have to hunt somewhere else entirely. It went all the way up, like knocking over the first domino in a line.

"Wait," Lucie said slowly, pointing at the bird. "Then the hawk doesn't just lose the bird. It loses everything underneath it, all the way down." Aubrey grabbed her notebook and wrote it out, fast, before she could forget the shape of the idea. Then she redrew the grass, green and tall, right back where it belonged.

At the kitchen door, her mom called that dinner was ready. "Coming," Aubrey shouted, and drew one last arrow, from the hawk straight back down toward the sun.

Lauren had one problem bigger than her notorious locker, which had swallowed three assignments already. Last night her two cousins had argued in the group chat until midnight. One swore the Moon was getting bigger this week, the other said it was shrinking, and both had demanded that Lauren, the science person of the family, settle it. She had typed "idk" and felt it like a stone in her shoe.

At lunch she negotiated with Lyndon for half his pudding, promising him the last word in any argument for a whole day. Magnus just came along because he liked lamps. They carried Mr. Ba's desk lamp, a volleyball, and a marble into the empty art room, and Lauren made one quick adaptation to the plan: she taped the marble to the top of the volleyball, so the marble was the Moon and the volleyball was Earth, and the lamp could stand in for the Sun by the window.

"You're on Earth," she told Magnus, bending him down so his eye hovered above the marble. "Tell me what you see."

"A dark ball," Magnus reported. Then she walked the marble around the volleyball, slowly, the way the real Moon crawls around the real Earth. "Wait. There's a sliver now. Like a fingernail clipping."

"Keep going." Lauren moved it a quarter turn, then half.

"It's filling up," Magnus said. "It's like a cookie getting un-bitten."

Lyndon, who had been sulking into his pudding, leaned in. "So it's growing. That means my cousin's right and yours is wrong, and mine owes me five dollars."

"Only if it's still going this way," Lauren said. She kept walking the marble around, and past the far side of the volleyball, Magnus called out that the cookie was being eaten again, sliver by sliver.

"Oh," Lyndon said, straightening up. "I want to change my answer. It depends on which part of the lap it's on."

Lauren grinned. "A Moon whose lit part is growing night by night is waxing," she said, "and when it's shrinking, it's waning." She pulled out her phone. "Now hold still, Magnus. I need a photo of you being the Earth."

"Best job I've had all week," said the Earth, and did not blink.

At the cultural festival, Penelope pressed her nose against the tent flap and inhaled the smell of fried dumplings and sweet bean buns. Inside, a long table held paper lanterns, ink brushes, and a poster that said Learn a Sentence. A grandparent of one of her classmates, a woman with silver hair and a smile like a comma, was helping kids say things in Mandarin. Penelope wanted one thing: to record a full sentence about her family and her orange cat, Pumpkin, for the festival's video booth, which would play on the big screen at sunset. The line for the booth closed in twenty minutes.

She started strong. "Wǒ yǒu yì māo," she said into the microphone, meaning I have one cat. But when she checked the tablet's sample recording, the fluent speaker had said something different, with a strange extra syllable in the middle. Penelope played both clips again and again. Same meaning, different sound. She scribbled the two versions in her notebook. There had to be a pattern, some small piece her sentence was missing, and she intended to find it before the booth closed.

She grabbed her friend Bree, who was dragging Pierre-Olivier toward the dumpling stand, and marched them to the corner where the silver-haired grandmother was folding paper lanterns. "Could you listen to me say something?" Penelope asked. She tried her sentence slowly, and the grandmother gently added the missing little word, "zhī," right after the number. Penelope's ears went hot. The word sat between one and cat, exactly where the fluent recording had a syllable. She tested it, moving it like a puzzle piece. In front of the number it sounded wrong; after the noun it vanished into confusion. Only that one slot worked.

She raced back to the booth, weaving between a drum circle and a table of mango slices, and recorded fast: her mother, her father, her little brother, and Pumpkin. "Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo," she said, and the volunteer's eyebrows lifted approvingly. At sunset she stood between Bree and Pierre-Olivier, sticky mango juice on her fingers, and watched her sentence transform into glowing characters on the giant screen. Mr. Diallo, her neighbor from two houses down, tapped her shoulder and pointed at the word in the middle of her cat sentence. "What's that little one?" he asked. Penelope grinned and said, "That's zhī. It goes between the number and the cat."

Colton held the thermometer like it was a magic wand and poked it into the chicken breast sizzling on the grill in his backyard. His parents were stuck at his little sister's dance recital across town, and he had promised them dinner would be ready by six. His friend Amar sat on the porch steps, guardedly optimistic.

"You're measuring chicken like a scientist," Amar said. "My uncle just cuts it open and looks."

"That's guessing," Colton said. He had looked it up an hour ago: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer. "Guessing is how you get chewy chicken, or worse. Watch."

He slid the thermometer into the thickest part of the biggest piece and waited. 151. Not done. He turned the heat down a little, because his mom had once told him rushed chicken burns outside and stays raw inside, and rushed anything usually turns out worse.

Amar wanted to try. He had been begging since they started, mostly because he liked gadgets with digital screens. "Can I check the next one? Please. I'll evaluate each piece super carefully."

"Fine, but push it into the middle of the thickest part, not the edge." Colton handed it over. "The edge cooks first, so it lies to you."

"That's a weird sentence," Amar said, but he did it right. 148, 149, then finally the screen blinked up: 166.

"Sixty-six?" Amar squinted. "In this context, is that good or terrible?"

"Fahrenheit, so it's good. Sixty-six Celsius would be a whole different chicken." Colton flipped the last piece onto the platter, and they stood over the steam, grinning like they had won something.

Headlights swept the fence. His mom called through the car window, "Is it edible?"

"Perfectly cooked," Colton announced, holding up the thermometer like a trophy. "One hundred sixty-six degrees, measured scientifically."

"Well, bring the science inside," she said. "I'm starving."

Evelyn pressed the third wire into place and held her breath. At the maker table in the science museum, her bulb had glowed twice already, and twice it had gone dead the moment Lamar nudged the project. Now the bulb sat dark again, and the demonstration started in ten minutes.

"Try it," said Ali, tapping the switch. Nothing happened. Evelyn frowned at the board. The battery was fine, the wires were fine, and she could not see the problem, whatever it was. That was the worst part. Electricity was invisible, and a broken connection looked exactly like a good one. She had learned that trick about light in the optics room downstairs, how a prism could refract a white beam into a rainbow, bending something you could not otherwise see. She needed a way to bend electricity into view.

Then Mr. Weber walked past with a jar of glowing moss, some kind of fungus from the forest exhibit, and Evelyn stared at the tiny lights inside it. Lots of separate little lights. Not one. "Wait," she said slowly. "What if it's one long path right now? One bulb, one path, and if anything breaks anywhere, everything goes dark." She pulled the wires apart and started over, giving the bulb its own pair of wires straight to the battery.

Her fingers were hesitant at first, because if she was wrong, they would have nothing at all. She clipped, tucked, and flipped the switch. The bulb lit. Then, on purpose, she unscrewed the bulb halfway, until it should have gone dead. It stayed glowing. She tightened it again and turned to the others.

"It's a parallel circuit," she said. "Each bulb has its own path to the battery, so if one bulb breaks, the others stay lit."

Lamar grabbed the second bulb and clicked it into place. "So even if I break one, the rest keep going." He turned to the exhibit table. "Mr. Weber, come watch this."

The dressing room smelled like dust and somebody's banana, which Zoya insisted was the most nutritious thing you could eat before a concert. Arianna held her violin under her chin without bowing it, because her hands were shaking too much to trust. In twenty minutes she would walk onto a stage for the first time in her life, and all she could think about was the strange thing she had noticed at the dress rehearsal: the whole orchestra had gone silent and waited for a single note from one small oboe.

"Why do we all wait for that one instrument?" Arianna asked. "Nobody waits for me."

Zoya, who played clarinet, shrugged. "Maybe the oboe's just bossy."

Arianna didn't buy that. She closed her eyes and replayed the rehearsal in her head. The oboe player had held out a steady tone, and every section had tuned to it, one after another. She remembered asking Ms. Fernando later, in the hallway, and Ms. Fernando had only said, "That's the concert A," and walked off with a cart of music stands, as if that settled everything. It hadn't settled anything. But Arianna had a theory, and she tested it right there in the dressing room. She played her open A string, then listened hard while Alec, who sat second chair oboe, played his. Her note wobbled against his, sharp, so she turned her fine tuner a tiny amount and played again. Closer. Another small turn. There. His sound was steady and it cut straight through the room, easy to hear even over five kids warming up at once.

"So that's it," she said, spine straightening even though her knees hadn't gotten the message. "The oboe's pitch is steady, and it's easy for everyone to hear. That's why the whole orchestra tunes to its A."

"Then cite your source," Zoya said, grinning. "Alec, play it again."

Alec lifted his oboe, and the note rang out through the dressing room door just as Ms. Fernando's voice came down the corridor: "Places, everyone!"

Arianna picked up her bow and said, "Let's go."

The synagogue smelled of old wood and someone's lavender perfume, and Ruby sat in the third row holding her folded speech so tightly the paper creased. Her grandmother had died nine days ago, and now everyone expected Ruby to stand up at the front and talk. "It's called a eulogy," her father had explained at the kitchen table. "From Greek roots. It means to speak well of someone." Ruby had thought that was a strange job for words, since she couldn't even say the word "Grandma" out loud yet without her throat going tight.

She had tried writing the speech five times. One version was three pages long and included the family tree, which even she found boring. One version was two sentences. The problem was picking just one memory, because how could one memory hold a whole grandmother? In the row behind her, Drew and Jett from school sat squeezed between their parents, both of them scrubbed and wearing collars they clearly hated. Drew leaned forward and whispered, "You okay? You look like you're solving a math problem." Ruby whispered back, "I'm trying to test a theory." She had decided that if she told the smallest memory she had, the one nobody else would even know was important, it might work better than the big impressive ones.

The rabbi nodded at her, and Ruby stood. Her shoes were quiet on the carpet, like the carpet had been designed exactly for nervous people. "My grandmother had a rule," she said, once she reached the podium. "If you were about to abandon a board game because you were losing, you had to finish it first. She said quitting was the only thing that actually made you lose." A small laugh moved through the rows of chairs. "One time we played checkers on her porch and a seagull, a huge predatory seagull with eyes like a tiny burglar, landed on the table and stole the red king piece. Grandma said that was the only anomaly in forty years of her checker career, and she made me write it down in a notebook she kept called Things That Happened."

Ruby looked out at all the faces, and her father was crying but smiling at the same time, which she hadn't known a face could do. "So that's my eulogy," she said. "I'm speaking well of her, like the word means. She was the person who made you finish the game, and she made even a seagull stealing a checker piece into a story worth keeping."

She walked back to her seat, and Drew slid over to make room. Jett passed her a tissue box even though she wasn't crying, which was somehow funny. "Good theory," Drew whispered. Ruby tucked the crumpled speech into her pocket. "Turns out you only need one checker piece," she whispered back.

The library meeting room smelled like old carpet and lemon polish, and the folding chairs had been arranged in two crooked rows for the spelling bee. Rose sat between Valentina and Dash, holding her word list so tightly the paper crinkled. The prize was a real trophy, small but golden, and Rose had wanted it since third grade, when she had gone out on the word "rhythm" and cried in the biography section.

Ms. Jean-Louis, the children's librarian, stood at the front desk with the official list of words. "Rules, one more time," she said. "You may ask for the definition, the language of origin, and a sentence. You may start a word over. But listen carefully, spellers. Starting over is allowed. Changing any letters you have already said counts as a misspelling." Rose nodded, though her mind was mostly on the trophy.

The early rounds were kind. Dash got "harbor" and spelled it slowly, like he was walking on ice. Valentina got "sapphire" and grinned after the bell didn't ring. Rose had "categorize," which she spelled without trouble, thinking how convenient it was that the hardest part was remembering the z. Two more rounds thinned the field until only Rose, Valentina, and a boy from another school remained.

Then came "vessel." Rose knew the word, and she knew what it meant; the sentence Ms. Jean-Louis read was about a ship, a vessel crossing the harbor. Rose began. "V. E." She paused. In her head she suddenly saw the other spelling, the one with only one s, and it looked right. The room was so quiet she could hear the clock above the returns desk. She could start over. She knew that. But starting over would not let her change anything, because the two e's were already out of her mouth, hanging in the air, and a different letter in that same spot would count as a misspelling. Whatever she said next had to build on what she had said, or repeat it exactly.

She said the rest carefully. "S. S. E. L." The pause before the final letter felt long enough for the clock to tick twice. Ms. Jean-Louis rang the small bell, the bright one that meant correct, and Valentina squeezed Rose's wrist from the seat behind her.
