The boy from the other school went out on "camouflage," and Valentina went out on "bougainvillea," which Rose privately thought was an arbitrary choice for a library bee, like asking someone to spell a word from Mars. That left Rose alone at the front for the championship word.

"Mnemonic," said Ms. Jean-Louis. "It means something that helps you remember."

Rose almost laughed. She thought of her mother's trick, the sentence about eating a small treat after dinner, and she didn't even need it. "M. N. E. M. O. N. I. C. Mnemonic."

The bell rang, and Dash stood up on his folding chair and waved both arms. Ms. Jean-Louis handed Rose the little trophy, warm from sitting under the reading lamp. Valentina shouted, "Take a picture, take a picture," and Dash was already aiming the library's ancient camera.

The long tables at the community hall were covered with food by four o'clock, but nobody was eating. Naomi stood with her plate and looked down the row of samosas, dates, and a big honey cake with white icing, and every adult she could see was holding a cup of tea and talking, hands nowhere near the serving spoons. Her little cousin tugged her sleeve and said he was hungry, and the cake was scheduled to be cut at six, which gave Naomi two hours to figure out what was going on before a room full of children started complaining.

Her first idea was that the food was for later, like a display at a bakery. She tested it by reaching for a samosa, and a woman near her shook her head and pointed at the clock above the stage. Naomi put the samosa back. Her second idea was worse: that nobody liked the food. She found her classmate Rachael by the punch bowl and asked why the feast was just sitting there.

"Because sunset hasn't come yet," Rachael said. "Today is Eid al-Fitr, the celebration at the end of Ramadan." She said the last day of the month still counted, and that during Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn until sunset. "No food, no water, from sunrise to sundown, for a whole month," she said. "Tomorrow we can eat whenever we want. That's what Eid is for."

Naomi thought about that. She had woken at six that morning and eaten two bowls of cereal, and by noon she had been asking for crackers. A whole month of waiting until sunset, every single day, was hard to picture. From her cousin's perspective, missing one snack was a disaster. From Rachael's, tonight was the finish line of something that had lasted thirty days. He could manage another hour. Naomi found him a chair by the window instead of the food table, and told him to watch the sky with her, since the rule depended on the sun and not on the kitchen clock.

The question of which dessert should be served first became controversial when the honey cake and the baklava came out side by side, and a group of kids began arguing so loudly that a man in a gray jacket came over to settle it. Rachael's little brother insisted cake first because it could be cut faster. Rachael said that was unfair to everyone who had been waiting a month and that dates should go first, since that was how her family always broke the fast. Naomi, who had come in wanting cake more than anything, changed her mind and raised her hand for dates.

At 6:41 the sun slipped behind the roof of the building across the street, the waiting ceased, and the room filled with the sound of plates. Rachael pressed a date into Naomi's palm and grinned. "One month done. Try it."

Joshua stood on the courthouse steps with his class, holding the worksheet Mr. Teo had given them, and stared at question three: "Why does the sign say Act while our textbook calls it a bill?" Around him, students from three schools were filing inside for the Youth Legislature Day, where kids would pretend to pass a law about bike lanes.

"It's a typo," said Thiago, peering over his shoulder. "Just write typo."

Joshua didn't think it was a typo. Inside the chamber, he sat between Thiago and Issac, watching a real legislator explain the day's simulation. She kept saying the word bill. "Our bill goes to committee," she said. "Then the whole chamber votes on the bill." But the plaque on the wall honored the Safe Routes Act, and the paper on everyone's desk was titled Bicycle Safety Bill. Same topic, two names. Joshua turned his pencil over and over, feeling like the answer was hiding underneath something.

"Maybe they change the name on purpose," Issac whispered, "like a nickname."

"That's it," Joshua whispered back. He raised his hand, and when the legislator called on him, he asked, "So is it called a bill while it's still going through all the stages, and then it's called something else after?"

"Exactly," she said. "It's a bill until it passes all its stages; once it becomes law, it's an Act." She smiled like he'd unlocked a door.

Joshua wrote it down so fast his pencil tore the paper a little. During the simulation, their bill survived committee, survived debate, survived a vote that Issac nearly lost for them by voting no out of confusion. "Wait, we want yes," Issac said, changing his vote, and the room laughed. When the speaker declared the bill passed, the student clerk crossed out Bill on the sheet and wrote Act above it, and Joshua felt the whole process decompose in his mind into clear, stackable stages, each one visible at last.

Afterward, Thiago read Joshua's answer to question three. "Okay," he admitted, "not a typo. There's some irony in that, too. I was the one who told you to guess." Mr. Teo, gathering worksheets at the door, paused at their pages. "These two are the only ones who got it," he said, and tapped the plaque. Joshua looked up at the brass letters spelling Act, then down at his smudged sheet spelling bill.

Alexis leaned over the bean plants on the back counter and counted leaves for the third time in five minutes, hoping more would appear. The science fair started in twenty minutes, and their display board had a hole in the middle of it where the conclusion was supposed to go.

"Mine says the beans near the window are the prettier plants," Annalise read off her notepad. "That fills the space, right?"

"Mr. Anderson said we need a conclusion that someone can actually check," Alexis said. She scrutinized the two pots, tilting her head to compare the seedlings. The window beans stood tall and crowded with leaves. The ones by the door were pale and slouching like they had given up on life.

April hurried over with a ruler in one hand and a half-eaten granola bar in the other. "I measured the tall ones twice. Sixteen centimeters on Monday, twenty-one today. The door ones only grew one centimeter."

"So," Annalise said slowly, "is pretty the thing he wants?"

Alexis turned a fresh notecard over and wrote two lines. "Look. Saying the fern in the corner is the prettiest plant in this room, that's an opinion. I can't test pretty. Nobody can measure it and find out if it's true or false. But saying the beans by the window grew faster, that's a claim we can check. We have the numbers right here."

Annalise squinted at the notecard. "So if someone said, no, the door beans grew faster, we could prove them wrong?"

"With the ruler," April said through a mouthful of granola bar. "The ruler never lies. Unlike my brother, who says my granola bars taste like cardboard. That's his opinion, and I have decided it cannot be tested."

Alexis laughed and copied the two lines onto the board in her best handwriting: the window beans grew from sixteen to twenty-one centimeters in four days, while the door beans grew one centimeter. Evidence, measured twice. Underneath, in smaller letters, she added that in her opinion the window beans were also the superior plants, but that part was just for fun.

Mr. Anderson began calling tables to the front, and the tranquil hum of the classroom sharpened into a scrape of chairs and chatter. Annalise grabbed the glue, April guarded the ruler like a dragon guarding gold, and Alexis pressed the conclusion onto the board with both hands just as their table was called.

"You three look pleased," Mr. Anderson said, stopping at their display.

"We had a whole reasoning breakthrough," April announced. "Also, you should try the granola bars. That part is an opinion, but it is a strong one."

He raised an eyebrow, picked up their data sheet, and started counting the leaves himself.

John stood in the corner of Mr. Popescu's studio, clutching his sheet music like a shield. The winter concert was in three weeks, and the choir had split into two groups for the first time. Jemma's group sang the high part. John's group sang the low one. Every time they tried singing together, John's ears got tangled and he drifted up to Jemma's notes like a duck following the wrong mother.

"You did it again," Jemma said after the third crash and burn. "You're copying me. It's like you're a mirror."

"I can't help it. Your part is louder in my head than mine."

Mr. Popescu played the two starting notes on the piano, one after the other, over and over. John closed his eyes and scrutinized the sound, hunting for the difference the way he hunted for his missing sock under the bed. The notes weren't the same, exactly. But they felt like twins, one tall and one short, like an emperor standing beside a kneeling servant who was somehow the same person.

"Wait," John said. "Play those two again." He hummed the low note, then the high one. "They're the same note. Just one is... upstairs."

"An octave," Mr. Popescu said. "A note one octave higher vibrates exactly twice as fast."

"Twice as fast? So my note is lazy and Jemma's is hyper?"

"Basically," Jemma said, delighted.

That was the key. If Jemma's note was his note running at double speed, then it was family, not a stranger, and his ears stopped panicking. He tested it, humming his low note while she sang hers above him. They locked together like train wheels on a track.

At the concert, the two groups blended so smoothly that a kid in the front row whispered that harmonies were "controversial," because they sounded too good to be legal. John just grinned and held his part, steady as a stone at the bottom of a river.

Emmett balanced two paper airplanes on the kitchen counter and frowned at them. One had wings bent up at the tips, the other had flat wings, and the flat one was made from the slick paper from a cereal box while the bent one was plain notebook paper. He had thrown each three times down the hallway, and the bent one had glided every single time, but he couldn't say why.

"Maybe it's the fancy paper," Flora said, watching from the stool while she ate crackers. "Maybe the bendy wings do nothing."

"But which one is it?" Emmett flipped the flat-wing plane over. "What if I made one plane with the bendy wings AND the slick paper? Then if it flew, would that disclose which part was doing the work?"

Flora chewed slowly. "It flew before with bendy wings and it flew before with slick paper. If the new one flies, it could still be either one winning."

Emmett set the plane down. She was right, and it annoyed him pleasantly, the way a puzzle annoys you when it starts to open up. "So what if I keep everything the same except one thing? Same paper, same creases, and I only change the wing bend. Then whatever happens has to be because of the bend."

Ms. Zhao, his neighbour, had drifted in through the back door to borrow sugar and was now watching with her mug of tea. "When I ran the science fair," she said mildly, "we had a monopoly on arguments about exactly this. One boy changed his recipe and his oven at the same time and couldn't tell which one made his cake rise."

"So change only one thing," Emmett said.

"On purpose," Ms. Zhao said. "The one thing an experimenter changes on purpose to see what happens. Mine made that rule mandatory before anyone could touch the materials table."

Emmett folded two fresh planes from identical notebook paper, identical creases, identical everything except the wing tips, one bent up, one flat. He threw the bent one down the hallway and it curved in a slow, beautiful arc and landed on the couch. He threw the flat one and it nosedived into the shoe rack.

"Bendy wings win," Flora announced, crumbs on her chin.

"For notebook paper," Emmett said, already reaching for the slick cereal box. "I wonder if slick paper wins with flat wings." He creased a new fold and held it up to the light.

Anais had never slept anywhere but her cousin Thierry's house before, and even there she had always gone home by nine. Now she was staying the whole night, and Linkin, who lived on the same street, had been allowed to join. Thierry's mom had made popcorn and then left them with sleeping bags in the den, where the only light came from the fish tank.

"Tell the one about the lighthouse keeper," Linkin said, and Thierry did, lowering his voice until the last part, which was about a hand on a stair rail in the dark. Anais noticed her own heart banging and her breath going quick and shallow, which puzzled her, because she knew Thierry made the story up on the spot. He had done the same thing last summer at the lake, and she had laughed then. She was still trying to deduce why her body believed him when her brain did not when the stairs creaked for real.

Thierry shot straight up like a spring and yelped. The cat, huge and gray, strolled into the den, sat on Linkin's sleeping bag, and began washing one paw. Thierry laughed, but his hand was still pressed flat against his chest. "It's the story," Anais said, sitting forward. "Your body doesn't care that you made it up. It heard a scary thing in the dark and got ready to run, so a creak on the stairs set you off like a fire alarm." She thought of herself at the lake, insisting she wasn't scared while her heart hammered, and how she had decided then that being frightened meant being weak. Maybe she had been unfair to herself. Her mind had known better all along; her body just hadn't been consulted.

"Prove it," Thierry said. "Tell one yourself, and we'll see if I'm the only one." Anais made her voice slow and quiet, the way the storyteller at her mother's office party had done, an assertive, steady voice that made everyone lean in even though the story was only about a lost dog. By the time she reached the part about the doorknob turning, Linkin's popcorn was scattered across the floor and Thierry was holding the cat like a shield.

"Okay," Thierry whispered. "Point taken." The doorknob turned for real, and all three of them screamed before the cat wriggled free and bolted for the door.

Simon sat at Grandpa's kitchen table with the old laptop, building a game where an emperor penguin dodged a predatory shark that patrolled the ice. The shark moved in a loop, and an if-then block added a point to the score every time the penguin reached a fish. The score was the problem. Every time the penguin touched a fish, the counter jumped by fifty instead of one.

He told himself the code could not be lying. The computer did exactly what the blocks said, so something he could not see had to be making the block run again and again. His first idea was that the fish was too big, so the penguin touched it for many frames in a row. He shrank the fish sprite, but the score still jumped. Then he opened the loop that moved the fish back to its start position and found the score block sitting inside it, running once for every repeat. He dragged it out onto the main stack, and the score ticked up by exactly one.

He wanted sound next, a little chirp for every point. While hunting through the sound library he found a folder of record-scratches, and next to it a note on the website. He read it twice, then spun around in his chair. "Grandpa, did you know Scratch is named after DJ scratching? Like moving a record back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds."

Grandpa set down his coffee. "That I did not know. But I've got a turntable downstairs, if you want to hear the real thing."

In the basement, Grandpa pulled a record from its sleeve. One wire had gone frayed, so they wrapped it with electrical tape first to insulate it, then Grandpa lowered the needle. He nudged the record backward, let it slip forward, caught it again. Simon recorded five seconds of it on the laptop.

"Watch this," he said, and dropped the sound into the game. Every time the score went up, the penguin chirped and the record scratched. Grandpa leaned in close to the speaker. "Play it again."

Rosalie found Jeanne in aisle three, holding a bright orange bottle up to the light like it might contain jewels. "VeloCharge," Jeanne read. "Six ninety-nine. I drank one before the time trial and I dropped four seconds, so obviously it works." A fine settlement of orange grit sat at the bottom of the bottle, which Rosalie felt said something about the contents, though she didn't say what.

Rosalie turned the label around. The ingredients list ran to vitamins, caffeine, and something called "proprietary focus blend," which sounded like a way of not telling you anything. She read the back twice. "It doesn't say it makes you faster. It says 'supports energy.'" She could exclude almost everything on the list as a possible cause of speed, since she'd eaten three of the vitamins that morning in cereal form and remained slow. "I drank one too," she said. "I felt like a cheetah. Nothing changed, but I felt like one." That was the part that bothered her.

Mr. Ho, at the counter, had been listening the way he listened to everything, which was completely and without appearing to. He set down a box of bandages. "We sell sugar pills here, you know. Homeopathic ones. Some people swear by them." He straightened his name tag. "There's a name for it. The placebo effect." He rang up the customer in front of them, a man buying cough drops and a lottery ticket, and added nothing further, because Mr. Ho believed in letting a sentence stand there until someone picked it up.

Rosalie picked it up. That night she looked up the words on her mother's ancient computer, and by morning she had a plan, an empty VeloCharge bottle, and a pitcher of water. The water she dyed pale orange with two drops from the food coloring set, since Jeanne would otherwise notice, and Jeanne noticing would ruin everything. She could not exclude the possibility that Jeanne would also notice the cap was slightly loose, but she decided to risk it.

At the track, Jeanne drank the whole bottle, grimaced at the grit settlement Rosalie had faked with half a teaspoon of Tang, and ran the practice 400 in her second-best time ever. "See!" she gasped at the finish line, waving the empty bottle over her head. "Six ninety-nine well spent." Rosalie considered mentioning that the entire cost had been tap water. Jeanne was, apparently, immune to that sort of information. "Same time tomorrow?" Rosalie asked, and tucked the bottle into her bag for refilling.

Isaac spread the giant map of the Roman Empire across his bedroom floor, weighting the corners with a shoe, a hockey puck, and a suspicious orange from lunch. Tomorrow he had to stand up in Ms. Grewal's class and explain, using the map, why the empire split and fell, and so far his big discovery was that ancient borders were wriggly.

His phone buzzed. A text from Seth: "Don't panic but I heard Ms. Grewal says if you just point at the map and say 'it was big' she will fake her own death on the spot. Do NOT be that guy."

"Help me then," Isaac texted back, and sent a photo of the map.

Seth's reply came fast. "WAIT. Look at the top. The border wiggles along two blue lines all the way across. Why would a border do that? Borders are usually straight like my haircut."

Isaac flopped down and traced the frontier with his finger, half expecting the orange to obstruct his view. It did. He shoved it aside. The northern border ran along one blue squiggle, then another, stretching across the whole map. He checked the map key. Rivers. The Rhine and the Danube. Of course. Rivers were like walls nature had already built.

"So picture this," Isaac said out loud to his poster of a shark, rehearsing. "The Rhine and Danube rivers formed the northern border in Europe, with forts and soldiers posted along their banks." The shark looked skeptical, so Isaac tried again, pointing at invisible classmates. "Rome couldn't just expand forever past the rivers, because the whole edge needed soldiers, and soldiers cost money, and money was the corrosive stuff eating the empire from inside. Too much border, not enough empire." He grinned. "Too much empire, not enough everything."

The phone buzzed one more time: "Found my thing. I'm doing the part where it split in two. You can have rivers. Rivers are the boring half."

"Boring?" Isaac picked up the orange and held it like a microphone. "Rivers are the whole signal, Seth. Get over here and bring snacks."

The cultural festival had filled the gym with folding tables, and Florence had claimed one near the fan-shaped windows to finish her German poster. Her draft read "Ich habe einen hund und eine katze," and the laptop's spell-checker had underlined two words in wobbling red. She stared at it. Why would "hund" and "katze" be wrong when they were definitely spelled right? She checked the dictionary app, and there they sat: Hund, Katze, both with capitals.

"Your computer is broken," said Quintin, leaning over her shoulder.

"It's not broken. Look, it flagged every single noun." Florence tapped the screen. "Hund, Katze, Bruder, Mutter, all of them." She scrolled down her sentence about her family, watching the red squiggles line up under each noun and skip the other words entirely. It was a pattern, like footprints. Could it be a rule? She typed "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," and the squiggles vanished, one by one.

"So every noun starts with a capital?" asked Johnathan, who had drifted over from the origami table with a transparent plastic bag of paper cranes. "Even in the middle of a sentence?"

"That's what it looks like." Florence tried it on "Ich habe einen Bruder," and no red appeared. "The spell-checker was trying to tell me, and I despised it for nothing. All those times I clicked ignore."

Mr. Zhou, who was running the dumpling stall two tables down and spoke six languages, paused beside them. "In German, every noun begins with a capital letter," he said, and moved on with his tray.

Florence rewrote the whole poster, feeling the irony of it: the tool she'd been fighting had been her best teacher all along. She held up the finished sentence for Quintin and Johnathan to see. "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," she read aloud, and every noun stood tall.

Elena stood in Dominique's kitchen with markers spread across the table like a rainbow that had exploded. The poster board in front of them was for Dominique's sign-language club, and so far it said WELCOME TO THE DEAF CLUB in big blue letters, except Elena had written "deaf" with a lowercase d, and Dominique kept frowning at it.

"You spelled it wrong," Dominique said, tapping the word.

"I definitely didn't," Elena said. "D-E-A-F. I can spell, thank you very much."

"Not the letters. The capital." Dominique flipped her laptop around and slid it across the table. "Look. My club leader told us. In 1972, James Woodward proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself."

Elena leaned over the screen, close enough to smell the lemon cleaner on the table. The words stared back at her, and she felt that little flip in her stomach that happened when something she'd always seen one way suddenly had a second shape. So the same word could mean two different things depending on nothing but a capital letter? A whole culture hiding inside one small piece of punctuation? She wondered how many other words were secretly doing that, walking around in disguise.

"That's like a secret code," she said slowly. "The word looks the same, but if you know the rule, you know exactly what somebody means." She picked up the blue marker and began to fix the D, and her palm started to perspire against the plastic, so she switched hands.

Dominique's little brother, Junior, thundered into the kitchen, grabbed a red marker, and drew what he claimed was a mountain. "It's a plateau," he announced. "Flat on top. Very famous."

"That is approximately a potato," Elena said, and Dominique laughed so hard she knocked over a cup of pencils.

They worked until the poster glowed with the big corrected word and a border of hands signing the alphabet. Junior added his potato-plateau in one corner, and somehow it looked right. Dominique held the poster up against the refrigerator, squinting.

"So when people see the capital D," Elena said, "they'll know it's about people and culture, not just ears."

"Exactly," Dominique said. She signed something quick and fluid, her hands moving like they were telling a joke.

"What was that?"

"Poster looks awesome," Dominique translated. Then she signed it again, slower, and pointed at Elena's hands. "Your turn."

Elena's fingers fumbled through the shapes, wrong twice, closer the third time, and Junior clapped like she had scored a goal.

Cameron pressed one key after another on the classroom piano, listening for the note that had been driving him crazy all week. His audition for the youth orchestra was in six days, and if he earned a scholarship, his lessons would be free. But every time he played his piece, one spot sounded wrong, sour in a way he could hear but not see.

Isa slid onto the bench beside him. "Still the same measure?"

"Still the same," Cameron said. He played the measure again, and the bad note buzzed in his ears like a trapped fly. "I'm hitting the right key, I think. So why does it sound wrong?" He stared at the keyboard, all those white and black rows, and an idea came to him. Maybe he was hitting a black key when he meant to hit a white one, or the other way around. He could not see his fingers clearly when he played fast. So he would test it. He played the measure slowly, watching, and found his thumb landing on a black key instead of the white one next to it.

"There," he said. "That's it."

Isa grinned. "You know, my grandpa has a piano like this. I counted the keys once because I didn't believe him. Fifty-two white and thirty-six black. Eighty-eight in all."

Cameron looked down the whole length of the keyboard. "Eighty-eight chances to hit the wrong one," he said, and they both laughed. "But only one I need to fix."

Benedict called from across the room, where he was putting away his trumpet. "Ms. Kovalenko says five more minutes!"

Cameron played the measure ten more times, slowly, then at full speed. The sour buzz was gone, and the line came out clean and warm, like sunlight through the practice room window. It was not the whole piece, and his audition was still a long shot, but it was an approximate version of the thing he wanted, and it was closer than yesterday. He could work with closer.

Isa nudged him. "Again?"

Cameron set his fingers on the keys and began the piece from the top.

Last Tuesday night, Noah could not find the Moon anywhere. He stood on the back step with his dad, scanning the sky from the fence to the oak tree, and it simply was not there. "It vanished," Noah said. "Moons don't vanish," his dad said, but he could not say where it had gone either. That became Noah's problem, and it was still bugging him at school the next morning.

He grabbed Loic near the lockers. "If the Moon is always up there somewhere, why couldn't we see it at all?" Loic shrugged, so Noah wrote the question on a sticky note and stuck it to his binder. He wanted an answer he could actually point to, not just a sentence from a book.

In science, Ms. Okonkwo had set out a task: illustrate the Moon's phases for the class using the lamp on her desk and a white foam ball. Noah's group got Ilya too, and the three of them pushed their desks together. Noah held the ball at arm's length and walked a slow circle around Loic, who sat in the chair playing Earth. Halfway around, Noah stopped.

"Wait. Look at this." The lamp lit the side of the ball facing away from Loic. From Loic's chair, the ball showed only its dark, unlit face, a grey circle against the grey wall. "It's invisible from your seat," Noah said. "The lamp's over there, so the bright side is pointing away from you." Ilya leaned in and squinted. "So if the real Moon is between us and the Sun, its lit side faces away from us, and it looks dark from Earth. We wouldn't see anything." Loic turned in the chair. "Then where's my Moon? Gone."

Nooh checked the sticky note on his binder. "At new moon," he read slowly, working it out, "the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun. That's the night we had. It didn't vanish, it was just turned dark side to us." The missing Moon stopped feeling like an anomaly, some freak event in the sky, and started feeling like a rule he could test. He walked the ball around Loic twice more, watching the lit slice grow and shrink.

Ms. Okonkwo came by as they labelled their diagram, and she did not correct a single arrow. "One kid in my last class said the Moon was endangered because it kept disappearing," she said, smiling. "You three won't be making that mistake." That night, Noah stood on the back step again with his dad and pointed at the thin curve of light low in the sky. "It's coming back around," he said. "Give it a few more nights and you'll see the whole bright face."

The math club room smelled like the leftover brownies Helen had brought for the snack table, and Helen was guarding them like treasure. "Entry fee," she said, sliding the plate toward the middle of the table. "One solved problem per brownie. I need to defend my reputation around here."

Alexandra looked at her worksheet. "One half plus one third." She wrote an answer fast: two fifths. It looked right. One plus one, two plus three.

Keziah leaned over. "Try it with the fraction tiles. Actually move them."

Alexandra dug through the box of red and blue plastic pieces. She set out a half tile, then a third tile, and squinted at them. They were different sizes. Obviously different. She pushed them side by side and the two-fifths tiles she'd counted out sat there, matching nothing. Her answer had treated the pieces as if they were the same, and they weren't.

She sat back. It was like the flour at her grandmother's house last summer. The measuring cup had a line for a half and a line for a third, and when she'd poured them both into the bowl, her grandmother had asked how much she had so far. Alexandra had said two fifths of a cup, and her grandmother had laughed, not meanly, and said count the marks. The lines on the cup between a half and a third didn't match up either. The pieces were different sizes, so you couldn't just count them together.

Back at the table, Alexandra hunted through the tile box for pieces that would make both stacks match. Sixths worked. The half tile equaled three sixths. The third tile equaled two sixths. She snapped them together, counted, and wrote: five sixths.

"That's what I got," Keziah said. "The bottom number has to match before you can add."

Mr. Reddy walked past and dropped a new problem on their table, face down. "Only one rule on that one," he said. "Show me the pieces."

Alexandra flipped it over. One half minus one third. She was already reaching for the sixths.

"That one's mine too," Helen said, pulling her chair over. "Two brownies says you're faster than me."

"You're on." Alexandra laid out the tiles.

The living room was so crowded that Tyler had to sit on the floor between the couch and the coffee table, balancing his plate of nachos on his knees. The big game was tied with ten minutes left, and every save made the whole room groan or cheer at once. But Tyler kept noticing something else. When the camera showed the trophy waiting at rinkside, it looked battered and strange, dented all over, like somebody had dropped it down a staircase. His uncle kept saying it looked older than the team itself, and Cory, sprawled on the rug beside him, announced that the league probably just bought a cheap one and beat it up on purpose so it would seem legendary.

Tyler didn't believe that. "Trophies don't fake age," he said. "There has to be a real reason it looks like that." Cory grinned and folded his arms like a lawyer in a movie. "Fine, defendant," he said, "the court of this living room finds you guilty of making things up unless you can prove it." Tyler looked around the room. On the shelf behind the TV, between his mom's old novels, stood the family encyclopedia, the letter S volume. He remembered seeing hockey in it once. He stood up, wobbled past Naya's knees, and pulled it down while the crowd yelled at a near miss behind him.

The pages of tiny print were tedious to search, and he skipped whole sections about Saskatchewan and satellites before he found hockey. His finger ran down the column. There it was. "Listen," he said, and the room actually quieted a little, because the period had gone to intermission. "The trophy was donated by Lord Stanley, who was Canada's governor general, in 1892, and it was first awarded in 1893. That makes it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports." Naya sat up straight. "Older than football's?" "Older than all of them," Tyler said, and he checked twice to make sure the numbers matched before he closed the book.

"So it's beat up because it's actually ancient," Naya said. "Not because somebody sanded it in a garage." Cory sighed and handed Tyler the last nacho, which in their court clearly meant he lost the case. On the screen the third period was starting, and Tyler scooted back to his spot just as the puck dropped. "Come on," he said, pointing at the battered old cup gleaming in the lights. "You've been waiting longer than any of us."

Olivier stood at the long jump pit behind the gym, holding the clipboard that Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya had left with him while she went to supervise the shot put. His job was to write down every jump in the boys' qualifying category, and the list was getting messy. Timothe had jumped 4.20 meters, then 4.22, then fouled twice. Sacha had one legal jump of 4.25 and kept checking the clipboard over Olivier's shoulder like it might change.

"If I'm second, I make the final," Sacha said. "Fourth, I don't."

"Right now you're first," Olivier said, tapping the page.

Then Timothe walked to the board, ran, and landed at 4.26. One centimeter past Sacha. Sacha's shoulders dropped, and Olivier saw him do the math in his head: second place, final spot still safe, but barely.

Olivier looked at the list again. Timothe 4.26. Sacha 4.25. Two boys, one centimeter, and a ranking that said first and second as if the gap were some fixed thing. He remembered watching the hundred-meter final on TV with his dad last summer, when the silver medalist lost by less than a blink. His dad had said, "Imagine if they'd both been a hundredth slower. Same race, same runners, but the picture would look identical and nobody would know." Olivier had thought about that for days. A ranking shows order but not distance. Timothe could be ahead by one centimeter or by half a meter, and the results sheet would say exactly the same thing.

He tried an idea. "Sacha, you've got one jump left. Instead of just going safe, mark your takeoff a shoe-width back from the board."

"That wastes distance."

"You've fouled zero times, but you keep scraping the board," Olivier said. "One centimeter behind is the same as one centimeter fouled. Both mean second place. But one centimeter in front of the board, and the jump counts."

Sacha stared at the pit, then at his shoes, translucent tape still clinging to the left one from last week's blister. He walked back a shoe-width, ran, hit the board clean, and flew. Olivier leaned over the tape measure and felt his own heart thump. 4.31.

When Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya returned, she read the sheet. "New leader. By six centimeters." Sacha grinned and held up his hand, and Olivier slapped it.

Mya had walked past the corner store a hundred times, but always with an adult holding the door. Today her mother had handed her a ten-dollar bill and a list with one word on it: milk. The laundromat sat halfway there, and Mya timed herself by it, counting the dryers in the window like checkpoints on a race course.

She was almost at the store when she spotted Freya coming out with a slushie, and they walked back in together. The milk cooler had two options. A big two-litre carton sat on the top shelf, and beside it, smaller one-litre cartons were stacked in a pyramid. Mya had enough money for either one, she realized, but not for both without checking her change.

"That one," Freya said, pointing at the pyramid. "Two small ones. More is more."

Mya was hesitant. She remembered last summer, when she had bought the big bag of popcorn at the pool and it had turned out to cost more than two small bags, which had seemed unfair in a way she couldn't explain at the time. Something about sizes and prices didn't always work the way you expected. She leaned closer to the shelf tag under the big carton and found a second, smaller number printed there.

"It says the price per litre," she read slowly. "Like a secret number for comparing." The big carton's per-litre price was lower than the small carton's. So the big carton was cheaper per litre, even though it cost more overall. She did the arithmetic on her palm with a pencil stub, wincing when the numbers wobbled, then checked again. Two small cartons would cost more than one big one, and she'd get the same amount of milk.

"Fine," Freya said, watching the cashier ring it up. "But you've carried it the whole way home. That thing has, like, no stamina."

"I have stamina," Mya said. "The milk just doesn't."

The cashier counted the change into her hand, and Mya counted it again on the counter, coin by coin, matching it to the receipt. Exact. On the walk back, the carton got heavier with every block, and she stopped at the laundromat to shift it to her other arm. Through the window she could see Mr. Johansson folding towels, and he gave her a thumbs-up when she lifted the carton like a trophy.

Her mother was waiting on the steps. "Right change?"

"Right change," Mya said, "and right milk. The big one was cheaper per litre." She set it down on the step and shook out her aching fingers. "Next time, I'm bringing a wagon."

Alexis stood in front of Ms. Bennett's muffin stall at the farmers' market, holding a basket of blueberries like it was a bomb about to go off. "I'm going to bake these into muffins," she announced. "All by myself. From start to finish."

"Even the oven part?" said Sonny, who was next to her, eating a cinnamon bun the size of his face.

"Even the oven part," said Alexis. Her grandmother had always said she'd be ready when she could do it alone, and Alexis had a plan to prove it this very afternoon.

Anne-Sophie jogged up with a printed recipe in her hand. "Found it online. It's from an American website, so watch out."

They walked home, and Alexis laid everything out on the counter like a general arranging a battle. Flour, sugar, eggs, oil, and a bowl big enough to bathe a small cat in. The recipe said to preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Alexis turned the dial and stopped cold. Her oven only showed numbers up to 250, and there was no 350 anywhere.

"Oh no," she said. "This oven is broken. Or American. Or both."

Sonny leaned over her shoulder. "Maybe you're supposed to turn it past the end and it loops around, like a video game?"

Alexis was tempted. Last summer, when the three of them had tried to make a cake at Anne-Sophie's cottage, they had cranked the oven as hot as it would go because hotter meant faster, obviously. The result had been a black disc that Sonny tried to classify as either a Frisbee or a fossil, and that Anne-Sophie's dog wouldn't even sniff. Alexis did not want a repeat of the Charcoal Cake Incident.

"Wait," said Anne-Sophie, squinting at the bottom of the printout. "There's a little line here. It says 350 degrees Fahrenheit is about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius. Our ovens just speak Celsius. It's like the recipe is talking in a different language."

Alexis looked at the dial again. Between 150 and 200, clear as anything, sat 175. She set the dial there and heard the oven click and begin to hum. "So the recipe wasn't wrong and the oven isn't broken," she said. "They just count differently."

While the oven heated, they mixed the batter. Alexis cracked an egg one-handed, missed, and had to fish out a piece of shell, which Sonny called "the monarchy of Shell Island," ruling over the bowl until she dethroned it with a spoon. She folded in the blueberries, filled the muffin cups, and slid the tray in at a confident diagonal, which Sonny claimed was for luck.

Twenty minutes later, the kitchen smelled like a bakery. Alexis pulled out twelve golden muffins, and the three of them stood around the cooling rack, guarding it like it held treasure.

"See?" said Alexis, splitting one open, steam curling up into the light. "One hundred seventy-five. I told you I could do it."

Harrison stood at the kitchen counter with his speech outline spread in front of him and a timer on his mom's phone. Mr. Hoang had assigned a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and Harrison had decided to talk about his grandfather's hardware store. He pressed start, launched into his hook, and stalled. Two minutes later he had barely finished point one.

"That's impossible," he told Peyton on the phone that night. "Two minutes is too short to say anything important. I need at least ten."

Peyton laughed. "Ten minutes? Nobody would listen past three."

"Then three, minimum." Harrison flopped onto his bed and stared at the ceiling. Something about the two-minute rule bothered him, like a puzzle missing its piece. If two minutes were really too short, why would Mr. Hoang pick it? He grabbed his laptop and typed "famous short speeches" into the search bar.

The answer made him sit straight up. Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver. Harrison read it twice, then counted the words on his own outline: 486. He had been trying to squeeze a ten-minute speech into two minutes. The problem wasn't the time. The problem was everything he refused to cut.

He attacked the outline with a pencil. He would exclude the part about the store's income during the rainy summer, which hurt, because it was his favorite fact. He would cut the list of every tool his grandfather sold. What stayed was the story of the day the whole neighborhood showed up when the store almost closed. That was the hook, that was the heart, and that could land in two minutes.

The next morning he rehearsed for Deborah on the front porch. "Go," she said, and clicked the timer. When he finished his closing line, she held up the phone: one minute fifty-one seconds. Her grin was infectious. "Nine seconds to spare," she said. "Say the Gettysburg thing again, the part about 272 words."

"About 272 words," Harrison said, "and roughly two minutes, November 19, 1863. Same time I just had."

Deborah clicked the timer again. "Once more before the bus comes."

Parker stood in the Build-an-Atom workshop at the science museum with a tray of supplies in front of him: blue beads, grey beads, and a fistful of thin copper wire. His best friend Lena slid into the seat beside him and immediately stole three grey beads.

"Those are my neutrons," Parker said.

"They're neutral, they don't care where they live." Lena lined them up on her tray like a tiny jury waiting to judge somebody.

Ms. Ferreira, the workshop leader, walked the rows with her hands behind her back like a museum security guard who could not actually enforce anything. "Today you each build a lithium atom," she announced. "Protons, neutrons, electrons, all in the right places. Go."

Parker got to work. He pushed three blue protons and four grey neutrons into a tight cluster and then, because it looked lonesome, packed more beads around it until his atom was a solid marble of color. He wired on three electrons at the very edge, barely visible.

Lena leaned over. "Yours looks like a meatball. Atoms aren't meatballs."

"You don't know that. Nobody's ever seen one." Parker held it up anyway, and it did look suspiciously like something from a spaghetti dinner.

Last summer, he remembered suddenly, his grandfather had taken him to this same museum. They had stood in the darkened physics hall where a brass contraption sat behind glass, and his grandfather had read the plaque out loud in his big storytelling voice: the gold foil experiment, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford. They had fired alpha particles at a sheet of gold so thin it was barely there. Most of the particles passed straight through, which showed that an atom is mostly empty space. Parker, age ten, had said, "Mostly nothing? Then why does my desk hold my elbows up?" and his grandfather had laughed until a guard glared at them.

"Wait," Parker said now, snapping out of the memory. He pulled the extra beads off his model one by one, dropping them back in the tray with little ticks of sound. Under his fingers the atom went from meatball to a small, lonely cluster with a wire loop swinging far out around it, the electrons rattling like beads on a bracelet three sizes too big.

"Now it looks like nothing," Lena said, but she squinted at her own solid lump, and he could see her deciding he was right. She started unloading hers too, flicking beads at him until he put up his hands like a shield.

Ms. Ferreira stopped at their table and picked up Parker's atom, turning it slowly in the light from the skylight. "Well," she said. "Who told you it was mostly empty space in there?"

"Gold foil," Parker said. "Geiger, Marsden, and the boss, Rutherford."

She raised an eyebrow at Lena's half-dismantled meatball. "And you? Are you biased toward solid atoms, or are you just copying?"

Lena held up her empty tray, beads all dumped, wire loop dangling. "Copying," she admitted. "But from a good source."

Parker spun his atom so the electrons whirred around the quiet middle, and for a second, in the bright museum light, it almost looked like the nothing was something.

Elena spread her poster board on the picnic table in the backyard and weighted the corners with rocks from the garden. Mr. Lewandowski had assigned the class a food chain for Monday: sun to plant to animal to top predator, with arrows and labels. Her motivation was simple. She wanted the neatest poster in the class, the one he taped to the wall, and she knew exactly how to get it. Sun, then duckweed, then a snail, then a duck, then a hawk. Clean and straight, like beads on a string.

Maverick dropped his bike on the grass and looked over her shoulder. "Ducks eat duckweed?" he asked.

"All the time," Elena said. She cherished this part of projects, the part where her facts lined up and nobody could argue. "And snails eat the duckweed too. So my chain is sun, duckweed, snail, duck, hawk."

"Wait," Maverick said. "If the duck eats duckweed, and the duck also eats the snail, then your duck is in two places on your poster."

Eena looked at her paper. He was right. She had drawn the duck once, above the snail, but she had also written duckweed next to duck in her notes from the pond book. The duck ate both. She frowned and erased her careful arrow, and the paper smudged. The neat line was gone.

Malachi arrived with a granola bar in his hand and crumbs on his shirt. "That's nutritious, at least," Maverick said, pointing at it. Malachi shrugged and sat down on the table bench. "Whatcha doing?"

"Breaking my project," Elena said. But she was already drawing again. She sketched the duck in the middle of the poster, then drew one arrow from the duckweed to the duck and another from the snail to the duck. Then she thought about the hawk. It probably didn't eat only ducks; it probably took fish too. And the snail, she remembered, wasn't picky either. Every animal on her poster seemed to eat more than one thing.

"It's not one chain," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "It's a bunch of chains stuck together." She drew crossing lines everywhere, sun to plants to snails to ducks to hawk, sun to plants to ducks, fish to hawk. It looked messy and it looked true. She took a new poster board from the garage and started over.

"What are you going to call it?" Malachi asked.

Elena wrote the word across the top in big block letters. "A food web." Then she handed Maverick the green marker. "Draw the duckweed. You're good at plants."

At dinner, Camille pushed her rice around her plate and finally said it out loud. "The comic convention is Saturday, and I'm fourteen dollars short for a ticket. I have until Friday night, because tickets close then."

Her father looked up from his noodles. "You still have that box of contemporary graphic novels you said you'd outgrown?"

"Thirty-one of them," Camille said. "I was going to sell them at the garage sale on Saturday, but that's too late. The sale is Saturday morning and tickets close Friday night."

Clemence, who was eating with them because her parents were working late, set down her fork. "Then contract with the neighbourhood," she said. "You know, make a deal. Knock on doors tonight and sell them one by one. Ms. Hussain on the corner is always saying she wants to read what kids are reading."

Camille's motive was simple, and she admitted it: she wanted that ticket so badly her stomach hurt. But she had a problem she couldn't see the answer to. What price? Too high, and nobody would buy. Too low, and even if all thirty-one sold, she might not raise fourteen dollars.

She tried five dollars a book. At Clemence's building, two people bought, then a boy complained, and three people walked away shaking their heads. Too many wanted it at a lower price, she noticed, and too few at a higher one. So she dropped to three dollars, and at the corner store, a woman with a baby bought four. By Friday evening, the box felt light, the paper smell of old pages on her hands, and she counted twenty-two dollars. One book was left.

"The last one didn't sell until I hit two dollars," Camille told her mother at the dinner table, sliding the crumpled bills into a zippered pouch. "Clemence said the price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price. I found it by accident."

"Well," her mother said, "accidents count."

Camille grinned and zipped the pouch shut. "Tomorrow, I'm buying my ticket."

The poster on the wall said CALM in big blue letters, which Ariana found funny, because she was the opposite of calm. She sat across from the guidance counsellor's desk, her fingers knotted in her hoodie strings, waiting.

"So," said Mr. Ionescu, "the recital is Friday, and you want to skip it."

"I don't want to skip it," Ariana said. "I want the shaking to stop. My hands shake, my stomach hurts, and last rehearsal I forgot the whole second page of the piece. That's anxiety, right? That's the word my mom uses."

Mr. Ionescu pulled his chair forward. "Tell me what the shaking feels like. Not why it's there. What it does."

Ariana thought that was a strange question, but she tried. "It's like buzzing. Like my whole body woke up." She paused. "Actually, when I forgot the second page, I was in the practice room, comfy, no buzzing at all. And at the last recital, when the buzzing was huge, I played the fast part better than I ever had at home. Weird."

The door opened and Justin stuck his head in. "Mr. Ionescu, the coach says Matis needs to talk to you before his race, he's all jangly." He looked at Ariana. "Oh. Sorry."

"Jangly," Ariana repeated. That was exactly her word for it. Matis got jangly before races, and Matis won races.

"Wait here a second," Mr. Ionescu said, and left. Ariana got up and wandered the office. She found a magnet board with word tiles: stress, coping, boundaries, focus. She slid the tiles around without thinking, and then stopped. Stress. She'd heard that word a hundred times, always bad. But Matis before a race was stressed, and Matis ran his best times. She narrowed her eyes. Maybe the buzzing wasn't a malfunction. Maybe stress was the body answering a challenge, and a short burst of it could actually help a person focus, like before a test or a race. So why had it helped Matis and wrecked her?

She looked at her hands. The difference, she realized, was that Matis never tried to make the jangly feeling evaporate. He jogged in place and let it burn. Ariana fought hers, clenched against it, spent all her energy on the war. She turned the magnet tiles around and spelled out a treaty: she would stop fighting the buzz and let it work.

Mr. Ionescu came back and found her grinning at the board. "Figured something out?"

"I'm going to play Friday," she said. "Shaky hands and all. The shaking is like a spotlight, not a fire alarm."

"Then let's talk coping," he said, sitting down. "What do you do with your hands during a performance?"

Ariana held them out, still faintly buzzing. "Same thing Matis does with his legs before a race," she said. "Nothing. I let them run."

The bus smelled like wet boots and peanut butter, and Romy had been talking about the commercial since the second stop. "It said the candidate made our taxes the highest in the whole country. The whole country. Can you believe that?"

Gabrielle believed approximately none of it, though she said only, "Huh." She had learned from her older brother that the louder a claim got repeated, the more it deserved a slow look. Out the window, a wedge of migratory geese crossed the gray sky, all heading somewhere on schedule, none of them arguing about it.

"The highest in the country," Romy repeated. "My dad yelled at the TV."

"Was it, though?" Gabrielle asked. "Did anybody check?"

Romy shrugged. "It was on TV."

Olivier leaned over the seat, holding his grandmother's pharmacy bag, which he was delivering on the way home and which contained, he announced, a prescription for cough syrup and a box of mints he was absolutely not going to open. "You can't check highest in the country," he said. "That's just somebody's opinion."

"No, it's not," Gabrielle said. "An opinion is like, that candidate has terrible hair. You can't look that up. Taxes you can look up. Somebody keeps the numbers." She thought of the geese again, how they followed rules nobody could see but everybody could test by watching.

Romy crossed her arms. "Fine. Check it, then."

Gabrielle's mother worked evenings and her phone lived in her mother's purse, so Gabrielle borrowed Ms. Liu's phone at the next stop, where Ms. Liu boarded with her umbrella and her crossword. Ms. Liu handed it over with the air of a woman who had already decided sixth graders were beyond surprising. Gabrielle typed the words from the ad, and there it was, a website called PolitiFact, founded in 2007, that rated claims on a scale it called the Truth-O-Meter. She read down the scale out loud. "It goes from True all the way to Pants on Fire."

Olivier laughed so hard he nearly sat on the cough syrup. "Pants on Fire. That's the worst one?"

"That's the worst one," Gabrielle confirmed. She scrolled. The tax claim from the commercial was right there, already checked, and it sat somewhere in the middle, which meant the ad had stretched a small truth into a big one. "So it's not an opinion and it's not a fact," she said. "It's a claim. Claims are the ones you get to test."

Romy peered at the screen, deflating slightly. "So it's not the highest in the country."

"It's not the highest in the country," Gabrielle said. "But try telling your dad that."

Ms. Liu took her phone back, glanced at the page, and said, without looking up from her crossword, "Four letters, 'untruth,' ends in E."

Romy groaned. Olivier wrote LIE on the fogged window with his finger, backwards, so the geese could read it too.

The group chat pinged at 7:40 on a Tuesday night, while Aaron was supposed to be reviewing for his social studies test on the constitution. Adriel had posted a photo of a birthday card, with the message, "My grandfather signed this and it's WRONG and I can't tell if I should fix it before I put it on the shelf." The signature at the bottom read "Kovács Bence." Adriel had captioned it, "He wrote his last name first. He's eighty-three. Is this random or what?"

Aaron zoomed in on the photo. He knew Adriel's grandfather's real name was Bence Kovács, because everyone called him Mr. Kovács, and Adriel called him Bence Papa. So the old man hadn't made a mistake with the letters; he'd made a mistake with the order, or maybe not a mistake at all. Aaron typed, "Was he born in Hungary?" Madilyn answered faster, a thumbs-up and then, "Budapest. Why?" Aaron sat with that for a minute. In class, their teacher had put names on the board in a column, Korean ones like Kim Min-jun and Hungarian ones together, and something about the order had seemed too neat to be a coincidence. He tested it out loud before typing, the way he did with math: if the family name came first in Hungarian, and the same order was used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names, then "Kovács Bence" was exactly right.

He typed it into the chat in two short lines: "In Hungarian the family name goes before the given name. Same order as Chinese, Japanese and Korean names." Madilyn replied, "Wait, so he signed it correctly on purpose?" and Adriel sent, "Hold on, asking him." There was a long silence, long enough that Aaron went back to his notes about the constitution and watched his concentration slowly decompose into checking the chat every twenty seconds.

Then Adriel posted a voice message, thirty seconds long. In it you could hear an old man laughing, warm and unhurried, and saying, "Of course, kisfiam. That is how we write it at home." Adriel typed underneath, "He says thank you for noticing. Also he wants to know if you three are coming for paprikas on Sunday." Madilyn answered immediately, "Yes." Aaron saved the photo of the card, shelf-worthy now, and typed the same.

Jade sat on her bedroom floor with three shoeboxes open around her, lacing up the sneakers she had bought in September. Her toes hit the end like a fist against a wall. She unlaced them, pulled them off, and stared at her bare feet, which looked, she thought, like they belonged to somebody else entirely.

"What are you doing?" Yasmina asked from the doorway, holding two mugs of juice she had transported all the way from the kitchen without spilling, an achievement she clearly expected praise for.

"Science," Jade said. "Watch." She lined up her September sneakers, her old sandals from spring, and the sneakers she'd talked her dad into buying two weeks ago, "for backup." The sandals were smallest, the September pair in the middle, and the newest ones fit perfectly. "Three shoe sizes in one year. Three. And look at this." She stood up and pulled at the hem of her jeans. They still reached her ankles fine. Her favorite hoodie still hit her wrists exactly where it always had. "How can my feet be three sizes bigger and the rest of me exactly the same?"

"Maybe you're going to be a yeti," Yasmina said, handing her a mug. "Just feet and then, one terrible day, the rest."

"That's the thing. My brother went through this." Jade flopped onto the bed. "His shoes stopped fitting twice in one school year, and his jeans were fine the whole time. My mom kept saying he was imagining it, and then in the spring he grew four inches in about two months, like the rest of him was just late." She frowned at the ceiling. "So the feet go first. They're like the delivery notice before the package."

Yasmina considered this while drinking her juice. "So your arms and legs and everything are going to catch up?"

"That's my theory. But I want to test it." Jade grabbed the notebook from her nightstand and flipped past the arid, half-finished pages about her vegetable garden, which had died in August and still produced a small stab of resentment every time she saw it. She ruled a fresh chart: date, shoe fit, sleeve length, inseam. "Measurements every Sunday. If my feet are done and nothing else happens for months, I'm wrong. If my sleeves start riding up my wrists next, I'm right."

"Sunday," Yasmina agreed solemnly, as if signing a treaty.

Mr. Desir, their neighbour, knocked then, holding a parcel that had been left at his door by mistake. He glanced at the shoeboxes scattered across the rug and raised an eyebrow. "Cleaning out already? It's not even Christmas."

"Growing," Jade said.

He laughed and set the parcel on her desk. "My mother used to say you can always tell when a kid's about to shoot up. Buy the shoes, wait for the rest."

Jade sat frozen for a second, then looked at Yasmina, who was already grinning. She wrote Sunday's date at the top of the chart and underlined it twice. "First measurement," she said, reaching for the tape measure. "Hold still, wrist."

The lights went out at Grandma's house just after supper, and the whole kitchen dropped into blue shadow. Ava heard her grandmother's slippers scuffing toward the pantry, where the candles lived on the second shelf beside the birthday napkins.

"Wait," Ava said. "Don't light those."

Grandma's hand was already on the shelf. "We've used candles since I was your age, sweetheart."

Ava stood still, thinking. Last year Mr. Oyelaran had drilled a fire-safety unit into her sixth-grade class until everyone could recite it, and something about it had stuck. She could picture the handout, even the little citation at the bottom naming the safety agency that had published it. "He said safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut," she said slowly, "because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house." She had drawn a flame on her copy of that page, she remembered now, and he had circled it in red.

"Then where are the flashlights?" Grandma asked.

"Kitchen drawer. The one by the sink." Ava had noticed two of them there that morning when she was hunting for the potato peeler. She felt her way along the counter, bumped her hip on a chair, and pulled the drawer open. Her fingers closed around cold metal. She clicked the first one, and nothing happened, so she twisted its base and it blazed bright across the table. The second one worked too, and Grandma laughed and sat down.

"You're a resilient girl, finding those in the dark," Grandma said.

Ava handed her one of the lights. "Jad's house lost power for two whole days last winter. His family kept a flashlight in every room so they could sustain the outage without stumbling around." She swept her beam across the pantry shelf, where the candles waited, then closed the door on them.

Grandma set her flashlight upright on the table like a little lantern. "Well then," she said, "go get the cards."

Victor had circled February 3 on the calendar in red marker, because that was when Lunar New Year happened, and he had told his whole group that the class project on the celebration would be due right after the community hall dinner. Now he stood in that very hall, holding a plate of dumplings, staring at a banner that read Happy New Year, and feeling the date slide out from under him like a rug.

"You look like your dumpling died," said Noa, who had come with her family from the Korean table across the hall.

"It's January 28," Victor said. "I told Caroline the dinner was in February. The project plan is wrong."

Noa popped a dumpling in her mouth and chewed with vigorous enthusiasm. "My grandma says the date never sits still. It lands on a new moon, somewhere between January 21 and February 20."

"A new moon," Victor repeated. "So the sky decides my grade."

"Take it up with the sky," Noa said, and wandered off toward the rice cakes.

Victor found a quiet corner beside the folding tables and worked it out on a napkin. If the holiday could fall on any new moon inside that window, then it could not coincide with any fixed school date, ever. His plan assumed the celebration would cooperate. It would not. He laughed at himself, which startled an aunt carrying a tray of mandarin oranges, and she gave him one anyway.

He found Caroline by the door, still in her coat. "Good news and bad news," he said. "Bad news, our timeline is garbage. Good news, that's actually the most interesting part. China, Korea, Vietnam, and a bunch of other places all celebrate it, and the date drifts every single year. We can make that the whole project."

Caroline peeled off one glove. "So we turn in a project about a moving target?"

"A moving target we can predict," Victor said, "if we watch the moon."

Behind them, Mr. Chaudhry, who ran the hall, was testing the microphone for the lion dance. "Testing, one, two," his voice boomed. "No revolution on the dance floor, please, only the drummers."

"Sir," Victor called, "did you say revolution?"

"Full turn of the lion," Mr. Chaudhry said, and winked. "Every year it comes around different. Like the holiday, no?"

Victor held up his napkin, covered in numbers, and grinned. "Exactly like the holiday."

Oliver pressed his nose against the window of Carter's Travel Agency, where a frail old globe spun slowly on a brass stand behind the glass. Ms. Pritchard had put a sign in the window that said "Map Day: Come Learn Your Coordinates." He had walked past the shop twice already that morning, telling himself he would go in tomorrow instead. Last week he had told Zarah that London was at 90 degrees north, and she had laughed so hard she had to sit down on the gym floor. He still wasn't sure he wanted to be corrected again, but he pushed the door open anyway.

Inside, the shop smelled of old paper. Zarah was already there, standing at the counter with a peach nectar in a paper cup, arguing with Ms. Pritchard about a poster of London. "I need the exact location of the city," Zarah said. "For our project. Oliver promised he could find it, and I'm not letting him wreck my grade." Her grandmother had been born in London, and Zarah wanted to find the street on a map before she asked for a trip there next summer.

Oliver found London on the globe's bumpy surface and looked for the numbers printed along the edges. The horizontal lines counted up toward the pole, and the vertical ones counted from a thick line marked zero. He turned the globe slowly. "So London is at about 51 degrees north," he said, "and zero degrees longitude, because it sits right on that thick line." He tested it against Paris and then Madrid, checking whether the numbers grew bigger or smaller as he moved east and west, and they did, both ways, like a rule the whole world had agreed to.

"That's the prime meridian," Zarah said, pointing at the thick line. "I stood on it. On my trip last spring. There's a real line on the ground at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, and tourists stand on it with one foot on each side." She sipped her nectar. "I asked the guide why the world's zero was there, of all places, and he said it wasn't London's idea at all. An international conference decided it, in Washington, D.C., in 1884. They just picked the observatory."

Oliver stared at the globe. A city in England had been chosen as zero for the whole planet by a meeting in America, an ocean away. He wondered whether the people at that conference had argued about it, and whether some of them had wanted their own cities instead. There was no way to know from where he stood, holding a peach nectar Ms. Pritchard handed him without a word.

"Write it down before you forget," Ms. Pritchard said, sliding a pencil across the counter. Oliver copied the numbers onto the back of the project sheet: 51 degrees north, 0 degrees longitude, Greenwich, 1884. Then he gave the globe one more spin and watched London come around again, right on the line.

The audition for the school storytelling guild was on Friday, and Emilia had been picked to try out, mostly because Brennan had stood up in class and said, "I nominate Emilia, because she tells the best endings." That had been two weeks ago. Since then her stomach hurt almost every morning, she could not fall asleep, and even her favourite cereal tasted like cardboard. Her mom noticed the dark circles under her eyes and made an appointment.

The doctor was brisk and kind. She listened, checked Emilia over, and said, "Nothing is broken. But your body has been running on cortisol. It's a hormone your adrenal glands make, and it rises during stress. When stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high, and that leaves you feeling run down." Emilia squinted at her. "So worry is a chemical?" The doctor shrugged. "It's one piece of it. The good news is that you can help your body lower it." On the drive home, Emilia turned the words over and over, like a stone in her pocket.

That evening she sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with a notebook and a plan. If worry raised this cortisol stuff, and if it hung around when stress went on and on, then maybe her stomach aches were not random. Maybe they were a pattern she could actually see. She drew a grid: seven columns for days, one row for "worry spike," one row for "stomach or sleep." Then she thought back to Saturday, when Archie had come over to practise stories in the garage.

She remembered it clearly. Archie had done his whole tale about the frozen lake twice, perfectly, and then said, "You go." Her hands had gone cold, her mind had gone blank, and she had mumbled something about homework and hidden in the bathroom for ten minutes. That night she had barely slept. She wrote it down: worry spike, Saturday afternoon; terrible sleep, Saturday night. Sunday she had relaxed, watching a movie with her dad, and she had slept fine. One data point each way. It fit.

"Archie," she said on Monday at lunch, "do you ever get scared before you perform?" He looked surprised. "Everyone does. Brennan says nobody's immune to nerves. He counts backwards from twenty and it works for him." Emilia nodded slowly. So the feeling was normal, even for Archie, even for Brennan. What mattered was what you did next. She tried the counting that afternoon in the garage, out loud, and Archie timed her with his watch. Her shoulders came down from around her ears.

By Thursday she had a new rule written in her notebook: spike the worry on purpose once a day, in small doses, then calm down on purpose, so her body could practise settling. She also told her mom she needed one boundary: no more surprise run-throughs at the dinner table, please, because being quizzed while eating made the spikes worse. Her mom agreed. On Friday morning her stomach was quiet. She stood in front of the guild, counted backwards in her head, and began, "Once there was a lake that froze in one night."

The car was packed before sunrise, and Jordan bounced in his seat the whole drive to the coast. His dad had promised a full day at the beach, and Jordan had big plans: a sandcastle with a moat, a swim race with Abraham and Paxton, who were coming with their own families, and maybe, if the waves cooperated, his first attempt at bodyboarding. His mom slathered sunscreen on his shoulders in the parking lot while he squirmed and stared at the shimmering water.

The morning was everything he wanted. The dunes were lush with tall green grass, and the sand was already warm by nine. Jordan, Abraham, and Paxton dug a moat deep enough to flood at high tide, then charged into the waves for the swim race. Jordan won by half an arm. "Best vacation day ever," he announced, wringing out his shirt.

By late afternoon, though, his shoulders had turned an angry pink, and by dinner they stung so much he had to sit very still. That night he lay on the hotel bed, thinking hard. He'd had sunscreen on. He'd watched his mom put it on. So why the burn? He counted backward through the day. Sunscreen at nine. Swimming, sweating, more swimming, and nobody had touched the bottle again until it was too late. His dad, reading a memoir about a sailor crossing the Pacific, looked up and said, "Sunscreen wears off. That's just how it goes." Jordan frowned. He didn't think it just wore off on a schedule. Something about the water and the sweat seemed important, and he wanted to test it.

The next morning he declared a plan. "New rule," he told Abraham and Paxton as they spread towels near the lifeguard stand. "Sunscreen now, and then we do it again every two hours, and right after we swim. Not later. Right after." Paxton groaned, but Jordan set a timer on his watch and stood guard over the bottle like it was treasure.

They swam at eleven, and the moment Jordan's feet hit dry sand he was squirting white cream into his palms and chasing his friends down the beach. "Every two hours, and immediately after swimming or sweating," he repeated, dabbing Paxton's nose while Abraham laughed. At one o'clock the timer beeped and they lined up again without complaint, because by then even Paxton admitted it might be working. When the sun finally sank behind the dunes, Jordan checked his shoulders in the bathroom mirror. Not pink. Not even a little. He grinned at his reflection and pumped both fists in the air. "Same rule tomorrow," he called through the door. "And I call first bodyboard run."

Nathaniel sat at the kitchen computer in his cargo shorts, clicking refresh for the third time, as if the group chat might change on its own. It didn't. The screenshot was still there, pinned by Eli: a private message Nathaniel had sent him two nights ago, the one that said Onyx's science presentation was "a slow-motion disaster." Below it, Onyx had typed a single question mark.

He heard his mom's voice from the hallway. "Ten more minutes, then you have to comply with the screen rule, mister." Normally he would have bargained. Now he just nodded, because his stomach was doing something like a laundry spin cycle.

He thought about how the message had traveled. He had sent it to one person, in a private chat, at ten at night. It had shown up in a group chat with eleven people in it by lunch the next day. He hadn't posted it there. Eli had. The message itself hadn't leaked out like water through a crack; it had been carried, whole and intact, by someone who had it. Nathaniel rubbed his chin. So a private message wasn't guarded by anything except the person on the other end. If that person shared it, it was public, and there was no taking it back.

He had a theory, and he wanted to test it before he lost his nerve. He opened the private chat with Eli and typed: "Did you screenshot it and put it in the group, or did somebody else?" Then he sat on his hands, literally, because otherwise they would keep typing.

The reply came fast. "i screenshotted it to show my cousin bc i thought it was funny. then he musta sent it to the group. im sorry man."

Nathaniel read it twice. Eli hadn't meant to blow anything up, but that hardly mattered now, because the message had still escaped, twice over. He took a breath and typed one more thing, a message he actually meant, not the fast joke from two nights ago. Then he walked to Onyx's house, three blocks away, because some things deserved to be said out loud with actual air between people.

Onyx opened the door with his arms crossed. "If you're here to say it was fake, forget it."

"I'm here because typing was easier than this, and that was the problem," Nathaniel said. "My apology is more authentic in person. Even if it's less convenient."

Onyx stared at him for a second, then snorted. "Less convenient. Yeah, I'll say." He stepped back from the door. "You want the last slice of pizza? It's only slightly a disaster."

The arguments started at the very first practice. Finnegan wanted to take every free kick, Stanley kept shouting at the defenders, and Jake got knocked over twice because nobody passed to anyone. On the walk home, his mom handed him a folded note from the coach's mailbox, the one she'd agreed to deliver. "Your team is new," the coach had written. "Give it time. Skills grow in strange ways. P.S. There is a box of old books at the field shed if you're bored on rainy days."

Jake remembered the shed from last summer, when he and Stanley had hidden in it during a thunderstorm and counted thunder claps until the rain stopped. So after the next disaster of a practice, a game against the Grey Wolves that they lost four to nothing, he went looking. Behind the cones and the rolled-up nets sat a paperback with a cracked spine, and inside it he found a chapter about how groups develop. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed, way back in 1965, that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. Jake read the line three times. Storming. That was exactly his team.

He tested the idea instead of just believing it. At the next practice he counted arguments, quietly, in his head: Finnegan versus Stanley about positions, then Stanley versus the keeper about a dropped ball. Seven arguments in forty minutes. But he also noticed something the others missed, a pattern you couldn't see in any single moment. Each quarrel ended a little faster than the one before, and afterward the players sorted themselves out without being told. It was cumulative, small fixes stacking up, the way snow builds a drift one flake at a time. When a ball rolled into the hedge, Finnegan was the one who ran to extract it from the branches, even though he never did chores like that before.

Still, the biggest controversy was who would be captain. Finnegan wanted it so badly that he'd started wearing an old armband he found at home, and Stanley wanted it too, which was half the shouting. Jake didn't say a word about Tuckman to either of them. He just kept counting practices, watching the storming shrink.

By the fifth week the counting showed almost nothing. One small disagreement about whose throw-in it was, settled in ten seconds. When the Grey Wolves came for the rematch, the passing went sideways and backward, smooth as water finding its way downhill, and Jake scored the second goal in a three-one win.

After the whistle, Finnegan pulled the armband off and held it out. "You take it," he said. "You noticed everything before we did."

Jake slid it on over his sleeve.

Zoe had agreed to try her grandmother's day of rest for one Saturday, which meant no phone from sundown Friday until Saturday night. Her stomach growled all afternoon because she was fasting too, and by dinner she was staring out the window at a sky turning from orange to gray.

"When does this end?" she asked.

"When we see three stars," her grandmother said. "Then we say Havdalah. It's a Hebrew word. It means separation."

"Separation of what?"

Her grandmother only smiled and handed her a translucent blue scarf. "Put this over your eyes and look up. It softens the glare, so stars stand out better. My mother taught me that trick."

Zoe stepped onto the porch with her cousin, and the two of them began the old race in the family, the race to count the first three stars. Zoe held the scarf to her eyes and scanned. One star, then two, both low over the barn. Then clouds rolled in and covered everything. She waited. Her cousin went inside. The sky stayed solid gray, and she thought about the principle behind the whole day: the rest did not end because you were tired of it, it ended because of something outside yourself, something you could not hurry. She tested the idea by trying to spot stars through a thin patch, but nothing came through.
