He wrote about the line that wrapped past the gym doors every day, the kids who gave up and bought chips, and how a second bar would cost less than the vending machine repairs.

"Read me the last line," Kaaden said, leaning in.

Jeremy held the paper up to the window light. "If you care what students eat, give them a real choice." He grinned and slapped the page flat on the table. "Mr. MacLeod is going to read this at lunch tomorrow."

Evan sat in the waiting room with his arms clamped to his sides, because the gray patches on his blue shirt had come back by second period even though he had used Charley's deodorant that morning. He was here for his yearly checkup, but what he really wanted was an answer to a question he could not ask out loud. If the deodorant was working, why was his shirt still damp?

He remembered the day before, in gym class, when Nael had sniffed the air and said, "Okay, which one of us is that?" Nobody had answered. Evan had gone home and taken the longest shower of his life, and in the morning he had borrowed the deodorant from Charley's locker, hoping it would act like an umbrella for his armpits. It had not. He ran his thumb along the parallel stripes of damp on his shirt, one under each arm, exactly matching. Whatever was happening was happening on both sides at once, like a rule he could not see.

The nurse called him in, measured him, and said he'd grown two inches since last year. "That's puberty starting," she said. "Sweat glands wake up. Bodies change." She handed him a little booklet to look at while they waited. Evan flipped through it, past a page about vaccines and one about sleep, and stopped at a line that made him sit up straight. Deodorants do not stop sweat. They fight odor by slowing the growth of skin bacteria and covering smells with fragrance.

So that was it. He had the whole idea backwards. Sweat and smell were two separate problems, and the deodorant only worked on one of them, the bacteria one, the invisible one. When the doctor came in and asked if he had any questions, Evan said, "So deodorant can't keep my shirt dry? Nothing in it stops sweat?" The doctor shook his head, and Evan nodded slowly, deciding he would stop blaming the deodorant, and maybe stop borrowing Charley's too.

On the bus home he sat next to Nael, who was reading a comic. Evan peeled his shirt away from his side, felt the dampness, and let it be. "Guess what doesn't stop sweat," he said. Nael lowered the comic an inch. "What?" "Deodorant. It only fights the smell." Nael frowned. "Then what are you gonna do about the wet part?" Evan looked out the window and said, "Wear a darker shirt tomorrow."

Vincent stomped into the kitchen and dropped his sleeping bag on the floor like it had personally thwarted his entire weekend. "Maia didn't come to the sleepover," he told his mom. "She didn't even text. She's just selfish, that's all." He had planned the whole night, giant fort, three movies, a marshmallow tower contest, and Maia had said yes on Monday. Now the marshmallows sat in the pantry like evidence at a trial where the defendant hadn't bothered to show up.

On Sunday he decided to run a test. His hypothesis: Maia was a bad friend, one hundred percent character, zero percent excuse. To prove it, he would collect testimony. He texted their classmate Abbigail, who lived two houses from Maia. The reply came fast. "Didn't you hear? An ambulance came to Maia's house Friday night. Her grandma's really sick. Mr. Ramos told my dad they took her to the hospital downtown." Vincent stared at the screen so long his tablet went dark. His hypothesis crumbled like a marshmallow tower in rain.

He grabbed his mom's psychology book, the fat one she used for her night class, and flipped until he found it. "The fundamental attribution error," he read aloud to the dog, who seemed interested. "Named by a psychologist, Lee Ross, in 1977." The book said it was the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in. Vincent closed the book slowly. "Well," he told the dog, "that's me. Exhibit A: a total goofball."

He biked to the hospital with a get-well card and a bag of marshmallows, and found Maia in the lobby with her dad. Her grandma was sitting up and complaining loudly about hospital pudding, which everyone agreed was a good sign. Maia hugged him. "I thought you'd be mad." "I was," Vincent admitted. "Then I discovered I have a famous error named after people like me. Seventy-seven. That's the year, not my grade in science." Maia laughed so hard she snorted, and her grandma demanded to know who Lee Ross was. "Marshmallow tower rematch next Friday," Vincent said, holding up the bag, "and this time nobody gets sick."

The gym smelled like floor wax and sweat, and forty kids were fighting for twelve spots on the travel team. Megan had practiced her crossover all winter for this. Two rows over, Muhammed ran the same drills, faster than almost everyone, which implied the coach was already watching him, and Megan needed to be just as impossible to ignore.

Halfway through the scrimmage, Muhammed went up for a rebound and came down wrong, cracking his temple against another kid's shoulder. He sat up slowly, blinking. The coach blew the whistle and jogged over, but Muhammed waved him off, called out that he was fine, and got to his feet. Everyone drifted back to position, and the whistle was about to blow again when Megan saw Muhamced's eyes. They tracked the ball a half second late, like a video buffering.

"Wait," she said, louder than she meant to. The whole gym turned. Her mouth went dry, because stopping a scrimmage could mean the coach remembered her as the girl who caused trouble instead of the girl with the quick hands. "He hit his head. That's a concussion, maybe. There's a rule about that." Mr. Warsame, the coach from the middle school who ran tryouts, folded his arms and asked what rule. Megan had done a history project on it last month, so she knew. "Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, the first state law in the country that says a young athlete with a suspected concussion has to be removed from play until a health professional clears them."

Mr. Warsame nodded once and pointed to the bench, and Muhammed argued the whole way there, saying he was fine, saying he'd lose his chance. Megan tried a hypothetical to test whether he really was fine: "If I toss you the ball, you'd catch it without moving your eyes?" He said sure, so she tossed it, gentle and easy, and the ball bounced off his forearm because he hadn't tracked it at all. He stared at his hands like they belonged to someone else. Somebody called his mother, and Muhammed walked out with a towel pressed to his head, promising the nurse would clear him by Thursday.

The scrimmage restarted without Megan for two minutes, and she spent them sure she had ruined everything. When the whistles finally ended, Mr. Warsame read the callback list, and her name was third from the top. He caught her eye across the gym and tapped the side of his own head, once, the exact spot where Muhammed's had bounced off the bone, not a fracture but close enough to matter. "First cut is Thursday," he said. "Tell your friend to bring his doctor's note."

Carson's grandfather had promised macaroni and cheese for dinner, but his wrist was sore from shoveling the walk, so the sauce was Carson's job. His cousins were arriving at six, and his grandfather had already boiled the noodles and shredded a mountain of cheddar. "The sauce is the whole game," his grandfather said from his chair by the window. "Lumpy sauce and it's a bowl of disappointment." He handed Carson a wooden spoon like it was the last piece in a game of monopoly, the one you refuse to trade no matter what.

Carson melted the butter in the pot, stirred in the flour, and watched it turn into a paste that smelled like warm toast. Then came the milk, and then came the lumps, small pale islands that no amount of stirring would dissolve. He tried to excavate one from the bottom of the pot with the spoon, but it only broke into smaller islands. His grandfather just said, "Try again," which felt tedious and unfair, because stirring flour and butter for five whole minutes was boring enough the first time.

While the second batch of butter and flour bubbled, Carson called Addison, whose dad cooked all the time. "Addison's dad makes this," she said over the phone. "He calls it béchamel. A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel, one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking." She said her dad heated the milk first, in a measuring cup in the microwave, and poured it in a thin stream while stirring the whole time. Carson stared at the smooth paste in his pot and thought about what was different. The lumps had to come from somewhere, and the only thing he had changed before was the milk, cold from the fridge and dumped in all at once. Maybe the hot flour grabbed the cold milk and clutched it into little balls. If the milk was warm already, and if he added it slowly, the flour would have time to let go.

He warmed the milk, set the pot over low heat, and poured a thin ribbon, stirring in slow circles, then faster, until the paste loosened into something glossy. The sauce thickened gradually, like paint, without a single lump. He drew the spoon through it and the trail stayed open for a moment before closing. Then he shut off the heat and folded in the cheddar a handful at a time until the whole pot turned smooth and golden.

At five fifty his grandfather limped in to check, dipped a corner of bread into the sauce, and held it up without a word. Carson tasted it too, sharp and creamy, better than the boxed kind. The doorbell rang, and somewhere down the hall his cousins were already arguing about who got the biggest bowl.

Jeremy's mother had decided that ten was old enough to retire the family rule about never crossing Maple Street alone. So on Saturday morning he stood in the grocery store with a five-dollar bill in his fist and one job: buy a carton of milk and bring back the change.

He found the milk, waited behind a woman with a mountain of coupons, and watched the cashier scan his carton. She handed him a receipt and two coins. Jeremy walked three steps toward the door, then stopped, because his mother had said one thing before he left: always read the receipt before you go. He had thought it was a silly instruction, like being told to look both ways on a sidewalk. He read it anyway.

The receipt listed every item and the amount paid. MILK 2.49. Then, below that, MILK 2.49 again. Two milks, but he was holding one. He counted the change in his palm, and it was short, almost exactly the price of a milk. He turned around and got back in line, feeling like a detective who had just solved a case nobody else knew existed.

"Excuse me," he said, laying the receipt on the counter. "It scanned my milk twice." The cashier frowned at the paper, tapped her screen, and said, "You're right, buddy. Good catch." She gave him another coin and printed a corrected receipt.

Walking home, Jeremy imagined telling Drayden and Gaelle about it. They had a running joke that Jeremy was the least sophisticated shopper in their class, the boy who once paid for a candy bar with a bag of pennies. But Drayden had once been plagued all afternoon by a missing two dollars at the arcade, and he never found out where it went. Jeremy now knew something Drayden didn't. He held the milk against his chest with one arm and read the receipt one more time on the corner of Maple Street, just to see his evidence, then folded it into his pocket and carried it all the way home.

Tristan slumped at the kitchen table with his tablet, watching the group chat scroll. It was called Lunch Crew and it had forty-three people in it, which was already strange, since his grade only had two lunch tables. Last night he had posted a photo of himself in his older brother's dinosaur costume, and he had deleted it after ten minutes because it was dumb and his face looked weird. Now it was fine. Gone. He kept checking his page anyway.

Then Chaya posted a screenshot of the dinosaur photo with the caption "TREX LIVES." The chat erupted. Forty-three people could see his costume, his kitchen counter, and, in the corner, the whiteboard on the fridge with their address written on it for the pizza delivery guy. Tristan's stomach dropped. He typed, "I deleted that." Chaya answered fast: "Deleting just takes it off your page. I saved a copy the second I saw it. So did Ezra, probably."

Ezra sent a message: "Guilty." Then, after a pause: "Also, whoever added all those extra people should know they can see everything, including your address, Tristan."

Tristan thought about that. He couldn't see who had taken copies, or how far the photo had traveled, but the whiteboard was a clue. He tried something. He asked Chaya to crop the address out and post the fixed version, so the newer copy would spread instead of the old one. She did it within a minute, because Chaya wanted to be the person who fixed things, the meticulous keeper of the chat who documented every inside joke in a folder she called The Archive. "Already cropping," she said. "I keep records. Deleting is for amateurs."

By evening the cropped version was the one everyone was replying to. Ezra sent a private message: "Old copies are still out there somewhere. Can't un-save what people saved." Tristan read it twice. He texted back, "I know. But at least the address one is crowded out." Then he got up, walked to the fridge, and erased the whiteboard with his sleeve.

Bennett had never baked anything without his mom standing nearby, so when Jenny invited him over to make blueberry muffins, he decided he would do every step himself, start to finish. Jenny's kitchen smelled like cinnamon from the morning, and sunlight came through the window and hit the sugar jar, scattering little rainbows like a prism on the counter.

"First thing," Jenny said, tapping the recipe card, "preheat the oven to three seventy-five." Bennett turned the dial and watched the orange coils at the back of the oven begin to glow. "It'll emit heat for a few minutes before it's ready," Jenny said, sliding the muffin tin toward him. Bennett lined the tin with paper cups, then cracked the eggs into a big bowl, poured in the milk and oil, and dumped the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt right on top of everything.

"Wait, wait," Jenny said, picking up the card. "It says the muffin method mixes the dry ingredients in one bowl and the wet ingredients in another, then combines them only at the end." Bennett looked at his bowl, where egg was slowly soaking into a mound of flour, and groaned. "I just dumped everything in at once."

Jenny peered at the lumpy mess. "Can we save it?" Bennett thought about it. The wet stuff had only touched the top of the flour pile. He scooped the dry ingredients carefully off the top, spoon by spoon, into a second bowl, and when he reached soupy egg at the bottom, he figured he had most of it. Not perfect, but close. He whisked the wet bowl smooth, stirred the dry bowl, then folded them together until the batter just came together, flecked with blueberries. Jenny's little brother had a nut allergy, so she checked the ingredient labels twice before letting the batter near the oven, and Bennett read every one out loud for her.

While the muffins baked, a message popped up on Jenny's tablet from Bo: "Can smell something all the way from my house. Bring one to practice tomorrow or I'm quitting the team." Twenty minutes later, steam curled up from the muffin rack, and Bennett broke one in half to cool it faster. "The muffin method," he said, handing Jenny the bigger half. "You saw it here first."

The library computer hummed like a refrigerator with secrets, and Scarlett had exactly forty minutes before her mom picked her up. She typed "free math practice games" into the search box and pressed enter. The first result, shiny and blue, promised FREE for the first result on the page. She clicked it. The site loaded, asked for her grade, asked for her favorite animal, then asked for a credit card.

She stared at the screen. Credit card. She was eleven. Her wallet contained one dollar and a library card, and she cherished that library card more than most things she owned, but it would not unlock a math website.

"Stuck?" asked Domenic, sliding into the chair beside her with his own stack of books. He was supposed to be researching volcanoes but had instead spent ten minutes looking at pictures of the world's largest rubber duck.

"The top result isn't free," Scarlett said. "It says free everywhere, in like laser letters, and then it wants a credit card."

Domenic leaned over. "Click the second one."

She hesitated. It felt wrong, like reading the second question on a test first. Last summer, during the great lemonade disaster, she had trusted the first recipe she found, followed it exactly, and produced a liquid that Camryn had politely described as "angry." Camryn had spent that whole afternoon drinking it anyway, out of loyalty, and then texting Scarlett's mom a review that said never again. That was the day Scarlett had started to wonder whether the top of a list actually meant the best of a list.

She scrolled down and looked more carefully at the page. The first result had a tiny gray label next to it, small enough to miss, that said "Ad." The results below it did not have that label. So the first link had paid money to sit up there, above the unpaid results, which meant it was at the top because of money, not because it was good. The first link was not necessarily the most useful one. She tested the idea by searching something else, "free typing test," and sure enough, there was a labeled ad at the top of that page too, above the regular results.

"Ad," she said, pointing. "It bought its spot."

"So the internet is like a school fundraiser," Domenic said. "Whoever pays gets the front table."

"Basically." She clicked the second result, a plain, boring, impartial-looking site with no shiny buttons. It loaded instantly, asked for nothing but her name, and gave her twenty fraction problems. She got eighteen right.

"Rubber duck," Domenic said sadly, pulling his volcano books closer.

Scarlett grinned and typed "free volcano facts, no ads" into the search box for him. The second result looked perfect.

"Try that one," she said. "And check the label."

Evelyn had clicked the little green "Ad" tag on the same search result four times before Fatimah leaned over her shoulder in the computer lab. "Why do you keep doing that?" Fatimah whispered. Evelyn explained her experiment: type "pangolin extinction" into the search bar, count the real results, then count the ads at the top. She wanted to prove she could tell them apart, because Mr. Malik had said it was a crucial skill and she planned to confess in front of the whole class that she couldn't. That was the plan, anyway. The problem was that every time she clicked an ad, it took her to a strange page about "wildlife sponsorships," and she clicked back and clicked it again, testing whether the ad would follow her like a shadow.

"Stop," said Violet from the next station, not even looking up. "That ad's going to keep coming back no matter how many times you poke it."

Evelyn froze with her finger over the mouse. On the whiteboard at the front of the lab, Mr. Malik had written "TODAY: SEARCH LIKE A DETECTIVE," and beside the projector sat his laptop, which was open to a video he had queued for the class. Evelyn could read the title from her seat: an interview with the owner of a small online plant shop. When Mr. Malik finally pressed play, the shop owner held up a potted fern and said, "Advertisers bid in an auction for search keywords, and usually they pay only when someone clicks their ad. It's called pay-per-click."

The room went quiet except for the fan humming in the corner. Evelyn's stomach dropped. Every click. She looked down at her own screen, at the sponsorship ad she had poked four times, and did the math fast: someone, somewhere, had just paid for four clicks from a girl who wanted a pangolin. She wasn't testing the ad. She was spending a stranger's money.

She raised her hand. "Mr. Malik, I have to confess something before we start."

He paused the video and raised an eyebrow.

Evelyn dragged her chair aside so the whole class could see her screen. "I found out how ads work. The expensive way."

Leah clutched her museum worksheet at the edge of the war memorial park, where her class was waiting for the bus to the Egypt exhibit, and her stomach was doing flips. Tomorrow she had to present on why the ancient Egyptians built the pyramids, and right now all she had was one sparse paragraph about pharaohs and tombs. Bennett leaned against the memorial wall, grinning.

"Easy," he said. "Slaves built them. Whip cracks, chains, all of it. I saw the movie twice."

"That's the movie," said Manha, elbowing him. "Leah, ask the museum lady. Ms. Liu from the Egypt centre is meeting us there. She's my neighbour and she said we could look at anything."

Inside the exhibit, Leah drafted her plan on the back of her worksheet: first the pharaoh-as-god part, then farming on the Nile, then, if she could find proof, the builders. She stopped in front of a glass case and read the label twice. Archaeologists had found a workers' town beside the Giza pyramids, and workers' tombs beside it too. She turned so fast she nearly knocked over Manha.

"Bennett! Come see! There was a whole town right next to the pyramids, for the workers. And tombs for them. Right beside the pyramids, where honoured people got buried. You don't build a fancy tomb for a slave."

Bennett squinted at the display. "So they were... paid guys?"

"Organized, fed and honoured labourers, it says. Teams, probably, like a big project." Leah was practically bouncing. "And look, here's the Nile part. The flood made the fields rich, and the farmers had flood season off, so the work matched the farming year. The river shaped everything. That's my whole presentation, right there in two cases!"

Ms. Liu waved from across the hall, and Manha grabbed Leah's sleeve.

"Go tell her your theory," Manha said. "Test it on an adult before tomorrow."

Leah marched over, worksheet first, pen ready.

The sign at the gas station read TWO BOTTLES PER CUSTOMER, and the cooler was almost empty. Ellie had walked three blocks in the heat for the last lemon iced tea on this side of town, and now Colton was reaching for the same shelf.

"Prices," Harlyn said from the door, holding up her phone. "Look, they doubled. It was two dollars yesterday."

"It's the store's fault," Colton said. "They just want more money."

"It's the buyers' fault," Harlyn argued back. "Everyone's buying it, so they can charge whatever."

Ellie stood between them, warm bottle in each hand, thinking. Everybody wanted iced tea today because of the heat wave, and there were only a few bottles left. She had read something in her brother's old economics book last week, something about scissors. "Neither one alone," she said slowly. "In his 1890 book, Principles of Economics, Alfred Marshall said it takes both blades of a pair of scissors. Supply and demand, both together, set the price."

Colton squinted at her. "Scissors?"

"Think about it. If the store had a hundred bottles, nobody would pay four dollars. If nobody wanted tea, they'd have to drop the price to sell any. It's both."

Ms. Petrov, their neighbour, was at the register with a frozen water bottle she would cherish on the long drive home. "You two can settle it," she said, nodding at the shelf. "There's exactly one bottle left behind the ice cream."

Ellie had an idea, and she wanted to test it right there. She checked the cooler again: one lonely bottle. Then she looked out the window at the road, where a line of cars waited for gas in the shimmering heat, every driver wanting something cold. Lots of buyers, few bottles, high price. It fit.

"I'll split mine," Ellie said, and grabbed two cups from the soda machine counter.

Outside, they divided the tea three ways under the awning, the air conditioning leaking through the propped door like the store couldn't quite hold its cool, the thermostat inside fighting a losing battle. Colton raised his cup.

"To the scissors," he said.

"Both blades," said Harlyn, and they clinked.

Sofia stood at the kitchen counter with her note cards fanned out like a poker hand and groaned so loudly that her dad looked up from the dishes. "The speech is tomorrow," she said, "and my ending is worse than flat soda." Her problem was simple: the assignment from Ms. Ramos required a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and Sofia's three points about why the school needed a second recycling bin were fine. The closing, though, was one limp sentence that evaporated the moment she said it.

Ray came over after dinner, transporting a backpack full of snacks and his own note cards, because Ms. Ramos had assigned the speech to the whole class. He flopped onto the living room rug and made Sofia deliver her closing five times. "It just sort of dies," he said each time, waving a tortilla chip. "The ending needs teeth. Predatory, almost." Sofia laughed, but she knew what he meant; a good ending should grab you and not let go.

Then Ray sat up straight. "Wait. Remember the clip Ms. Ramos played, the speech from 1963? Martin Luther King Jr. said 'I have a dream' over and over, and it stuck in your head for days." Sofia grabbed her laptop and found the clip again. She listened to the crowd surge every single time the phrase came back, like waves hitting the same rock. She counted on her fingers. He started whole sentences with the same words, again and again.

"There's a name for that," Ray said. "I wrote it down because it sounded cool. Anaphora." He held up his card, and there it was in his messy handwriting.

Sofia tested it right there on the rug. Instead of her flat closing, she tried, "I want a school where nothing is wasted. I want a school where a bin is waiting where we need it. I want a school that proves we can do better." Ray's chip froze halfway to his mouth. "Okay, that actually gave me chills," he said.

They drilled until Sofia's little brother begged them to stop, and she made him listen too, timing her two minutes on the microwave clock. The next afternoon Ms. Ramos nodded along as Sofia hit her hook, ticked off her three points, and landed the closing. When Sofia said the last "I want a school" line, Ray, sitting in the second row, raised both fists silently, and Elissa mouthed, "chills."

The bell rang, and Ms. Ramos said, "Sofia, stay one second. That ending. Tell me where you found it."

Alexandra crouched between the rows of potato plants at Ms. Sánchez's farm, a worksheet in one hand and a magnifying lens in the other. For her science class she had to draw a plant cell and an animal cell side by side, then label the parts only plants have, and she wanted a real plant to look at while she worked. The problem was that cells were too small to see, even with the lens, which felt like being handed a mystery with no clues.

"Those leaves don't imply much, do they?" said Philippe, kneeling beside her. He had come along because his mother ran the farm stand, and because Alexandra had promised him the last of her licorice.

"They imply plenty," Alexandra said. "Plants stand up straight without bones. Animals can't do that. Something inside the plant must be doing the job." She poked a leaf, watched it spring back, and wrote stiff wall? in the margin. Then she pulled a spade from the shed, chose a plant, and dug carefully around its roots until a cluster of potatoes came up trailing dirt. "And these," she said, holding one, "are the plant's lunchbox."

At the stand, Ms. Sánchez weighed the potatoes and laughed. "Full of starch, those. A potato is how the plant stores extra food." Alexandra wrote starch on her worksheet, then stopped. If plants stored extra food as starch, animals must store their extra food some other way, because she was pretty sure there was no starch sitting in her arm. She turned to Philippe.

"Where do you think my body keeps spare energy? I ate three pieces of licorice and I'm not using it all right now."

Philippe shrugged, so Alexandra made a plan to test it. She skipped lunch, waited until she was hungry and wobbly, then ran laps around the barn until her legs burned. When she stopped, doubled over, she still had energy to keep going if she had to. Something had been saved up and released, and it had not come from any potato. When she got home she looked it up in her science book and found the word glycogen, with a note saying animals store extra food as glycogen, not starch. She copied both words onto her worksheet in her neatest printing.

On Monday Ms. Sánchez visited the class to judge the cell drawings for a small scholarship prize, three books and a ribbon. Alexandra's poster showed a plant cell with its wall and green chloroplasts labeled, an animal cell beside it, and across the bottom, in molten-orange letters she had traced twice: starch in plants, glycogen in animals. Ms. Sánchez studied it a long time, then pinned the blue ribbon to the corner.

"That's the one," she said, and Alexandra grinned so hard her cheeks ached.

Jade spread the old atlas across Grandpa's kitchen table, weighting the curling pages with a teacup and a jar of nails. On Monday she had to stand up in front of her class and explain, using a map, why the Roman Empire split and fell, and right now she could not even find the borders. She had assumed the whole empire would be one tidy shape, like a puzzle piece. It was not. It sprawled.

"It's huge," said Rowan, who lived next door and had come over because Saturdays at Grandpa's were a ritual: cocoa, biscuits, and whatever project Jade was panicking about. Rowan ran a finger from the top of the page downward. "How far does it go?"

Grandpa shuffled over with his reading glasses and a battered encyclopedia. "There's a card in here somewhere," he said, flipping pages. Jade grabbed the book and found the entry herself, reading aloud. "The empire reached its largest size around 117 CE, under Emperor Trajan." She looked at the date under the map, then traced the border with her fingertip. It began in Britain, in the northwest corner of the empire, and went on and on, down past the sea and across to a land called Mesopotamia in the east. Her finger ached before she reached the end of it.

"That's it," she said slowly. "That's my whole explanation. Look how long this line is. Every bit of it needed soldiers, walls, watchtowers." She took the pencil and drew the border onto tracing paper, then held it stretched between her hands, thin and trembling, one end at Britain and one at Mesopotamia. "If you have to guard all of this at once, something has to give. It split because nobody could hold the whole thing."

Rowan leaned in and pressed one finger on Britain and one on Mesopotamia at the same time, arms stretched wide, like a bird trying to cover the atlas.

"That," Jade said, "is exactly my opening line."

The argument started before the bus even reached the corner. Eloi wanted the card game to begin with the red deck going first, and Everleigh insisted the blue deck had earned it because she had brought the cards in the first place. Their voices climbed over the rattle of the windows, and Rosalie, wedged in the seat behind them, could smell the pencil shavings Everleigh always kept in her jacket pocket.

"Blue goes first or we don't play," Everleigh said, arms folded.

"That's not fair," said Eloi. "You just dismiss every rule I make up."

"You're not making rules, you're making wins."

Rosalie remembered last summer, when she and her cousin had fought the same way over who batted first in the dusty lot behind her grandmother's farm. They had argued until the mosquitoes came out and ruined everything, and neither of them had gotten a real game at all. She had walked back through the agriculture fields that evening thinking she would rather lose a fair game than win a sulky one, though she had never managed to say it out loud.

She leaned over the seat now. "Can I try something?"

They both turned, suspicious.

"Name the problem first," she said. "The problem is nobody can tell who should go first, because both decks want it and there's no reason to pick one." She dug in her pocket and found a quarter, warm from her hand. "So we need a rule that isn't on anybody's side. A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance." She showed them the two faces, one glittering, one ridged. "That's why big sports do it. In football, and in cricket too, they flip a coin to decide how the game starts. If it's fair enough for them, it should work for us."

"Cricket does that?" said Eloi.

"Cricket does everything," Everleigh said, but she sounded interested.

"Heads blue, tails red," Rosalie said, holding the coin above her knee. "First toss decides, and we toss again every new game so nobody gets stuck."

The coin spun, caught the morning light through the window, and landed. Tails.

Eloi grinned and began shuffling. "Every game?" he asked.

"Every game," Rosalie said, and dropped the quarter back into her pocket, where it settled with a small, definite click.

Paige pushed a piece of broccoli around her plate and pretended to chew. Tomorrow was the semifinal, and she was the backup goalie, which meant she might stand in the net for the whole game or for none of it, and her stomach could not decide which one was worse.

"You're quiet," her mother said, spooning rice into her bowl. "Bad day?"

"Not bad exactly." Paige set down her fork. "Emaan says I'll probably have to face at least one penalty shot. She's the regular keeper, and she told me her secret. Before a penalty shot, she breathes out slowly, longer than she breathes in. She says it settles her body down so the stress doesn't take over." She glanced up. "Is that a real thing or just a goalie thing?"

"It's a real thing," her mother said. "Slow breathing with a long exhale is a coping skill. People use it on purpose, right before a stressful moment, because it calms the body's stress response. I do it before big meetings." She smiled a little. "I used it today before I told my boss I needed better boundaries around weekend emails. That word means lines you set so people know what you'll accept. My hands were shaking and my anxiety was doing cartwheels, but I breathed out slow, and it helped."

Paige looked at her plate. In science class, Ms. He had taught them that you couldn't just believe a claim, you had to replicate it, which meant trying the same thing yourself and seeing if you got the same result. Devyn had replicated the herbivore experiment with two mealworms and a pile of leaves, and it had worked. Maybe a goalie's trick could work the same way. She sat up straight, breathed in through her nose, and let the air out slowly, counting to eight while her mother kept talking about Saturday plans.

The tight feeling in her stomach didn't vanish, but it loosened, like a knot someone had worked a finger into. She tried it again, this time while imagining the ball on the penalty spot, the whole gym silent. In, then out, long and slow. Her shoulders dropped an inch.

"Feeling better?" her mother asked.

"I think I replicated Emaan's experiment," Paige said. She picked up the brittle cracker from the side of her plate, snapped off a corner, and ate it. "And it worked. Tomorrow, before that penalty shot, everybody's going to wonder why the goalie looks like she's just smelling the flowers."

Levi stood on Grandpa's porch steps, holding five index cards that trembled in the breeze coming off the garden. His speech on the space race was due Monday morning, and it was supposed to be two minutes long with an opening hook, three points, and a closing. He had seven points, and every time he practiced, he ran four minutes and forgot where he was.

"Grandpa," he called through the screen door, "how do I cut this down? My topic is about how satellites revolve around Earth, and the space race, and rockets, and dogs in space, and treaties, and all of it matters."

Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade and sat in the wicker chair. "You sound like my old commander. Everything mattered, so nothing did."

Levi frowned. He read the cards aloud again, and again he wandered. One card was about a treaty banning weapons in orbit, another about a stubborn Soviet engineer, and he couldn't drop either one.

"Did I ever tell you about Caesar?" Grandpa said. "Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words. Veni, vidi, vici."

"What's that mean?"

"I came, I saw, I conquered."

Levi stared at his cards. Three words. Three points. He laid the cards out on the porch boards and counted with his finger. "So if Caesar could win a battle with three, I can do a speech with three." He pulled out the rocket card, the satellite card, and the treaty card, and slid the rest under the lemonade glass. It felt like cheating, but when he timed himself on Grandpa's watch, he finished in one minute and fifty seconds, and he actually remembered point two after point one.

"See if it holds up in front of a real audience," Grandpa said, raising an eyebrow at the roses.

Levi turned to the flower bed and gave the whole speech to an obstinate bumblebee that refused to fly away, hook, three points, closing line and all.

"Ninety-eight seconds," Grandpa announced, tapping the watch. "You came, you saw, you conquered."

The timer still had eight minutes left, but Ryder could already smell the edges turning dark. He pulled the muffin tin out, set it on the counter, and stared at six black-rimmed blueberry muffins, the third ruined batch since Saturday. His grandmother's recipe said twenty minutes at 375, and he had followed every line of it, including preheating the oven like the first step told him to.

"They can't all be for nothing," said Amari, who had come over to help carry the finished muffins to the team bake sale. The coach expected twelve edible muffins on the table at ten o'clock, and it was already eight. Ryder spooned batter into a new set of cups, but this time he didn't close the oven door right away. His dad kept a little dial thermometer on a hook in the garage, the kind with a metal probe, and Ryder fetched it and hung it from the rack inside.

"Genius or desperate?" Amari asked, watching him peer through the glass.

"Both," Ryder said.

The dial on the oven said 375. The thermometer inside read 415. Ryder leaned back on his heels. So the dial had been lying to him, and every batch had baked at a temperature the recipe never asked for. He turned the dial down to 340, and the thermometer crept back to 375 and stayed there. He hadn't been careless with the recipe; his oven simply ran hotter than the number on its dial, and now he knew it.

His mom came down in her robe, saw the thermometer glowing behind the glass, and smiled without saying a word, which Ryder took as a small victory. At nine-forty he pulled out twelve tall, golden muffins, and Amari fanned them with a cookie sheet to cool faster. Ryder set two aside on a plate for his mom, because she had a long shift ahead of her and never stopped for breakfast.

"You had a motive, didn't you," Amari said, nodding at the plate.

"Some things thrive on bribery," Ryder said, and closed the muffin tin with a clang.

On her second night at camp, Rose sat in the dining hall pushing rice around her plate while her cabin mates argued about the campfire ceremony. Salome wanted their cabin to earn the marshmallow roast on Friday, which meant passing the fire safety check on Thursday. "It's easy," Lucian said. "You dump water on it and walk away. Done." Rose wasn't so sure. She had watched the counselor at last night's fire pour water on it, then stir the ashes with a stick, then pour more water, and then crouch down and hold the back of her hand close to the coals. There had to be a reason for all of that, and Rose wanted to know what it was before Thursday.

At breakfast she found Mr. MacLeod, the counselor who ran the fire pit, and asked him straight out. "It's Smokey Bear's campfire rule," he said. "Drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat. If a fire is too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave." He emphasized the word "feel" by holding up his own hand. "You can't trust your eyes. Ashes can look dead and still be alive underneath." Rose turned that over all day. A fire could hide. It could look out and not be out.

On Thursday evening, her cabin built its fire, roasted one practice marshmallow each, and then Lucian grabbed the water bucket and dumped the whole thing on at once. Steam billowed up. "See?" he said. "Out." Rose shook her head. "You have to stir first, or the water just runs off the top." Lucian rolled his eyes, but Salome handed him a stick, and he stirred the black mess until chunks of glowing red rolled up from the bottom. Rose poured the second bucket over them, and they all watched the last ember hiss gray.

Then it was time to feel. Rose knelt and held the back of her hand above the wet ashes, the way the counselor had done. Warm. Not safe. "More water," she said, and Lucian, who had changed his mind about the whole procedure, was already sprinting to the spigot. When he came back and they stirred and poured again, Rose held her hand over the pit a second time. Cold as the gravel around it. "Okay," Lucian said, dropping the stick. "Now it's out." Mr. MacLeod walked over, checked it himself, and said, "Congratulations, girls. Friday, you roast." On the walk back through the dark, Salome said Rose was like an emperor of campfires now, and the title felt almost permanent, at least until breakfast.

Charlie knocked on Griffin's door three times before anyone answered. Griffin's mom opened it a crack and said he was in his room, but she lowered her voice when she said it, the way people talk about someone sleeping.

Griffin was not sleeping. He sat on his floor with his back against the bed, a half-built robot on his knees. "Hey," he said, and then nothing else. His hands moved the screwdriver in tiny circles without actually turning any screws.

Charlie sat down across from him. She had been building a theory all the way over, because Griffin had skipped lunch twice this week and had not laughed at Heinrich's joke on Friday, which never happened. "Is it the competition?" she asked. Griffin's robotics team had won the regional championship in the fall, a big prestigious tournament, and everyone expected them to go to state. "Everyone keeps asking if we'll win again," Griffin said. "Heinrich keeps grabbing my controller to show me stuff. I keep telling him no and he does it anyway." He set the screwdriver down. "I can't sleep. My stomach hurts before school."

Charlie remembered the poster outside Mr. Ngo's health classroom, the one she had read while waiting for the water fountain in September. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She had stood there thinking it was strange that "social" was on the list, right next to emotional, like friends were part of the same system as feelings. At the time it had seemed like a poster fact. Now it seemed like a clue. If social counted, then Heinrich grabbing the controller was not just annoying. It was part of what was making Griffin sick, the same way lost sleep was.

"I made an assumption," Charlie said. "I thought you were just stressed about winning. But it's more than that." She picked up the robot and turned it over. "Heinrich keeps violating your boundaries. You said no and he does it anyway. That's not a small thing."

Griffin looked at the robot in her hands. "I didn't know you could call it that. I thought it meant I was being dramatic."

"You're not being dramatic. Stress is a real thing, anxiety is a real thing, and there are ways of coping with them, and one way is telling the person causing it to knock it off." Charlie handed the robot back. "Want me to text Heinrich?"

Griffin pulled out his phone himself and typed while Charlie watched. He held the screen up so she could read it: "You keep taking my controller after I say no. Stop. I mean it."

"Send it," Charlie said. He did.

The group chat lit up at 7:04, right after dinner. Ella typed first: "My mom said I can have the party. Now I just have to invite the whole class." Leon replied with three party hats and a question mark. Gurshan wrote, "Just put everyone's email in one big email, easy." Ella stared at her screen. Easy was exactly what worried her. Last year a boy in her class had sent a message to twenty people, and every single address showed up at the top, so everyone could see them all, and one kid got messages from strangers for weeks afterward. She typed, "I don't want to share everybody's addresses with everybody."

Gurshan, who was something of a chronic complainer, said that was overly complicated and that nobody cared anyway. Leon disagreed. "I care. My cousin had her address forwarded around once and it was a mess." Ms. Jean-Louis was in the chat too, because she ran the fifth-grade fundraiser and used the group to post updates about the revenue from the bake sale, which had reached eighty dollars. Ella messaged her directly: "Is there a way to email a lot of people without them seeing each other's addresses? I promise I looked before asking."

Ms. Jean-Louis sent back four words. "Look up BCC."

Ella did not ask her what it meant. She opened her email program and found a small link that said Add BCC, sitting quietly under the To line. She clicked it, and a new empty box appeared. She typed her own address into To, all twenty-four classmates into BCC, added the party details, and then, before sending it to everyone, she tested her idea. She sent the exact same message to just Leon and Gurshan, with her own address in To and theirs in BCC. If it worked the way she hoped, she would see proof.

Leon answered in seconds. "I got it. Weird thing though. It only shows your address. Like you emailed me alone." Gurshan wrote, "Same for me. Where's Leon's address?" Leon replied, "Nowhere. She used BCC. It means blind carbon copy. People in that field get the message, but the other people getting it can't see their addresses at all." Ella read the line twice, grinning so wide her cheeks hurt. Her test had worked. Hidden addresses, hidden from everyone but the sender, exactly as she had guessed.

Then she sent the real invitation, To herself, BCC the whole class. Replies poured in all evening, each one arriving as if Ella had written to that person alone. Gurshan sent a single message: "Okay, fine, you were right. Teach me how to do that." Ella typed back, "Saturday, at the party. Bring snacks."

Victor had been trying to figure out the new kid all afternoon, and the new kid was not helping. Cyrus had come to Ayesha's house with a battered suitcase full of photos: a flat in Cairo, a school in Manila, a street market in Kuala Lumpur, an apartment in Toronto. Four cities, four countries, and he could name them all.

"Okay, so where are you from?" Victor asked, pointing at the Toronto picture, because that was the most recent one.

Cyrus shuffled the photos instead of answering. Ayesha's little brother kept leaning over the table and obstructing Victor's view of the pile, so Victor pulled the photos closer and dealt them out like cards, one city in front of Cyrus at a time.

"Pick one," Victor said. "That's the test. Whichever one you pick first, that's where you're from."

"That's a bad test," Ayesha said. "I'm from here, and I'd still hesitate. My parents are from Lagos." She held up a hand when Victor opened his mouth. "But I'm not from Lagos. See the problem?"

Cyrus laughed for the first time all afternoon. "It's a paradox," he said. "Every answer I give is true and wrong at the same time. My parents are from one place, I grew up in other places, and now we're here. If someone asks where I'm from, the honest answer takes ten minutes."

Victor had a theory forming, something half remembered from a book his mother left on the kitchen counter. He pulled out his phone and searched: children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture. The words came up fast, and he read the name twice to be sure.

"There's a name for you," Victor said. "Third culture kid. Some American sociologist, Ruth Hill Useem, came up with it back in the 1950s."

"Say it again," Cyrus said.

"Third culture kid."

Cyris repeated it quietly, then wrote it on the back of the Cairo photo. "Next time someone asks, I'll say that first, then take my ten minutes."

"Perfect," Ayesha said. "Now we just have to teach the whole school the phrase."

Victor grinned and gathered up the cards. "Deal them out again. This time I get to guess which country is next."

"Toronto," Cyrus said. "It was inevitable."

Stella had decided that her pencil was a wand and her paper was a small planet. The planet was perfectly round, because Ms. Tse had set a wooden ball on the picnic table and told the art shed kids to make it look like it was sitting in real light. "Find the highlight," Ms. Tse had said, "the brightest spot where the lamp hits it. Then let the shadow curl around the far side, and let the sphere drop a cast shadow onto the table, like a dark puddle." Stella loved the idea of a puddle made of darkness. She was halfway to making a planet so real that astronauts would want to land on it when her pencil slipped.

Donovan, who was drawing a sphere that looked more like a potato, leaned over. "You just scribbled right across your bright part. The planet has a storm now."

"It's not a storm, it's a disaster." Stella stared at the smudged patch where the highlight should have been, the one place that needed to stay white and glowing. If she shaded harder everywhere else, the spot would still be gray, like a dirty moon. She could not retrieve the whiteness by drawing. Whiteness was the one thing a pencil could not make.

Then she remembered the gray lump in her pencil case, the soft, squishy eraser Ms. Tse had handed out that looked like a piece of dough. It was called a kneaded eraser, and it did not rub like a normal eraser. Stella pressed it flat between her fingers, shaped the edge into a small point, and touched it gently to the gray patch. When she lifted it, some of the graphite had sunk into the eraser, and the paper underneath was paler. She dabbed again. And again. Each press lifted a little more, and slowly the highlight bloomed back out of the darkness like a window opening on the far side of space.

"It's eating the shading," she whispered. "It's like a creature that eats shadow." She rolled the gray-stained eraser in her palm, thinking of the artisan who must have invented it, some old craftsperson in a workshop who wanted to pull light back out of a drawing the way you pull a rope out of a well. She began testing the limits. A flat press lifted a wide, soft band, good for a gentle glow. A pinched point retrieved a single tiny star of white. She could even curve the shadow's edge by pressing along a line parallel to the sphere's round side.

Kayden wandered over from the pottery wheel with clay on her elbows. "How did you get that to glow?"

Stella held up the eraser, now marbleized with gray streaks like a tiny planet of its own. "Shadow-eating space dough," she said, and pressed it once more against the cast shadow's edge, watching the dark puddle shrink back toward the wooden ball.

Naomi had been counting Taha's "I can'ts" all week, and by Wednesday morning at canoe camp the count was up to eleven. He wouldn't get in the boat on Monday, wouldn't eat at the long table on Tuesday, and today he was sitting on the dock with his knees pulled up while everyone else raced to the water. She flopped down beside him, sandals slapping the boards.

"I made a chart," she announced, unfolding a page from her notebook. "Eleven times since Sunday. And here's the thing, it's not random. It spikes before group stuff and drops when it's just us. That's a pattern." She loved patterns. Patterns meant you could categorize things, file them like the insect cases at the nature hut, and once you filed something you could do something about it.

"So what's the category?" Taha asked, staring at the lake like it might stare back.

"That's what I'm figuring out. Ms. Rao keeps a poster in the first aid cabin. I bet there's a formula for this, like, signs plus a grown-up you trust equals help."

She ran up the hill to the cabin, and Ms. Rao listened, then pulled a binder off the shelf and flipped to a page. "Look at this," she said. "A big U.S. survey of teenagers, thirteen to eighteen, found about a third of them had an anxiety disorder at some point. Most common mental disorder among them."

"A third?" Naomi said. She did the math fast. If there were thirty-six campers, that could be twelve kids. Taha wasn't some strange category nobody had seen before. He was practically ordinary math. She grinned all the way back down the hill.

"Guess what," she said, dropping onto the dock. "You're not rare. A third of teens in this whole huge survey had anxiety. And Ms. Rao says talking to her counts as a plan, not as tattling."

Taha looked at her, then at the water. Then came the twist: he pulled a crumpled page from his pocket, his own chart, her name at the top. "I've been counting your worry signs too," he said. "Nine. You grind your teeth before every swim test."

Naomi laughed so hard she nearly rolled off the dock. "Then let's be competent together. We tell Ms. Rao at lunch, both charts."

"Deal," Taha said, and stuck out his hand to shake.

The driving school smelled like burnt coffee and old carpet, and Aubrey sat in the corner doing homework while her dad practiced parallel parking in the lot outside. Mr. Sow, the owner, drank milk in his coffee all day, and because the corner store was only two blocks away, he had started sending Aubrey for a carton each morning. "My first solo mission," she told him, and she liked counting the change into his palm, nickel by nickel, until the numbers matched.

The third carton turned sour after only a day, and the fourth one too. Aubrey refused to resign herself to sour coffee. The store's milk couldn't be bad, because Jessie, who worked the register, said the delivery truck came every morning and the cold case hummed all night. That left one suspect: the little fridge under Mr. Sow's desk. There was a contradiction in it somehow, she thought, a machine made for cold that was letting milk spoil. She borrowed Jessie's cooking thermometer from the store, the kind with the long metal spike, and slid it into a glass of water on the fridge shelf.

"Forty-nine," she read aloud, frowning. She turned the dial one number colder and came back an hour later, hands still cold from walking the two blocks in the wind. Forty-two. She turned it again. Brynlee, waiting for her own ride home from the driving school, watched over her shoulder. "Forty," Aubrey announced the next hour, holding up the thermometer like a prize.

Mr. Sow squinted at the little line on the dial. "My last teacher put a sticker here," he said. "Keeps it at 40 degrees Fahrenheit, 4 Celsius, or colder. I thought that was just decoration."

"So does the milk," said Aubrey, and she set the fresh carton on the shelf, right beside the sticker.

Victor counted the crumpled bills in the shoebox for the third time that afternoon, as if the total might change out of pure stubbornness. Forty-two dollars. The bike at Miller's Sports cost one hundred and sixty, and every Saturday he and Rafael sold lemonade from the folding table on Ms. Chatterjee's corner, earning about ten dollars a week. At that rate, summer would end before the shoebox did. "You should just put it on your mom's card," Rafael said, stirring the pitcher with a wooden spoon. "She said you could, right?"

Victor's mother had said it exactly one week ago, standing in the kitchen with a card in her hand. She would charge the bike now, and Victor would pay her back a little each week from the stand. It had sounded wonderful then, so wonderful that he'd almost run to the store that same night. But something Rafael's cousin had said kept circling back to him: borrowed money isn't free, because a card charges interest. Victor didn't know what that meant in real dollars, and it bothered him the way an itch behind the elbow bothers you, invisible but definitely there.

He worked it out on the back of a napkin while Rafael poured. "If I borrow a hundred dollars at twenty percent interest a year, and I pay it back after one whole year, that's about twenty dollars extra. A hundred borrowed costs me around a hundred and twenty." Rafael squinted at the napkin. "So the bike doesn't cost one sixty. It costs one eighty." Victor nodded slowly. "And my mom said it could be more than twenty, something about interest building on interest. She called it compounding." A cold drop of condensation slid off the pitcher and soaked through the napkin's corner, blurring nothing important, because the numbers were already burned into his head.

Emrik biked past just then, ringing his bell twice, and the sound of it settled the argument before Victor even admitted he was having one. He watched Emrik coast down the hill, wind in his shirt, and remembered how he'd felt a week ago, certain that waiting was for patient people and he was not one of them. Now the waiting felt different. Twenty dollars was two whole Saturdays of lemonade, sticky hands and all, handed over for nothing. A spontaneous plan rose in him, fully formed: he would keep selling, save the full amount, and own the bike outright.

Ms. Chatterjee came out with a plate of biscuits for the boys and stayed to watch a parliament of starlings land noisily in her maple tree, dozens of them chattering and rearranging themselves like a committee that couldn't agree. "You're not charging the bike anymore," she observed, dipping a biscuit in her tea. "I changed my mind," Victor said. "Borrowing costs more than it looks. I'm saving first."

She smiled and didn't say whether she thought that was wise or merely slow, and Victor found he didn't need her to. He taped the napkin inside the shoebox lid, right above the money, and poured Rafael a cup of lemonade with ice.

"First customer of the rest of the summer," Rafael said, clinking his paper cup against Victor's.

The GeoClub challenge ended at three o'clock, and Aubrey had exactly one lunch period left to find Lima, Buenos Aires and Sydney on the giant world map outside Mr. Nair's room. Whoever pinned all three cities first won the atlas. Tommy had already pinned Lima. Grady had pinned Lima and Buenos Aires and was squinting at his slip of paper for the third.

Aubrey unrolled her coordinates. "Buenos Aires. 34.6 south, 58.4 west," she read, and typed the numbers into the old laptop Mr. Nair kept on the cart beside the map. The online map loaded slowly, the way it always did, and then it showed a pin in the middle of a green landmass with tiny roads winding through it. It looked nothing like Argentina. Grady leaned over her shoulder.

"Your pin precedes your city by a whole ocean," he said. "That's not even the right continent."

Tommy laughed, then stopped when he saw Aubrey's face. "Hey, you'll still get it," he said, and slid his own slip across the cart so she could compare. His coordinates for Lima ended with "12.0 south, 77.0 west," and when he typed his, the map showed a coastal city with the Pacific right where it should be. His numbers were positive on the screen, with tiny minus signs in front. Aubrey's did not have them.

She looked at her slip again. She had written 34.6 and 58.4, both positive, because that was how she thought of numbers on a map. But Tommy typed his as negative. So the map must treat south and west as negative numbers, at least in the decimal coordinates it used. That was her idea, and it was testable. She deleted her pin and typed minus 34.6 and minus 58.4. The screen zoomed to a wide river, blocks of buildings, a coastline. Buenos Aires.

"That's it," Aubrey said. "South of the equator and west of the prime meridian. You have to type the minus sign or the map lands on the other side of the world."

"Then Sydney's going to be easy," said Tommy. "It's east, so it stays positive, and it's south, so it doesn't."

They ran through the possibilities together, because Grady was still stuck and the clock above the door showed twelve minutes left. Sydney, minus 33.8 and positive 151.2, appeared on the first try. Grady found Buenos Aires with Aubrey's rule and pinned it with two minutes to spare. On the wall above the map hung a poster from science class about rainforest food chains, and Aubrey pointed at the word decomposer printed beside a drawing of mushrooms. "That poster comes in second place," she said. "Today the minus sign is the most powerful little thing in this hallway."

At three o'clock, Mr. Nair counted three pins in each city and handed Aubrey the atlas, warm from sitting on the sunny shelf. Grady held the door, and Tommy said, "Same time next month?" Aubrey tucked the atlas under her arm and said, "Bring your minus signs."

Grandpa's reading lamp was the brightest thing in the den, so Autumn unplugged it, carried it to the middle of the rug, and clamped the shade so it pointed sideways. Cassia held the orange Nerf ball while Autumn read the assignment sheet aloud. "Mandatory project: demonstrate the phases of the Moon. Anyone who forgets has to enroll in the make-up session Saturday morning."

"Which is basically prison," Cassia said. "Turn on the lamp."

Autumn clicked it on. "You be the Moon. Walk around me." Cassia orbited slowly, holding the ball at arm's length, while Autumn, playing Earth, watched the light slide across the orange surface. Halfway around, the ball showed a fat curve of light like a sideways smile. "That's a crescent," Autumn said. "See? Only a sliver lit."

"No," Cassia said, and Autumn frowned, because Cassia was supposed to be the agreeable one. "The whole half facing the lamp is lit. It's just turned away from you. Come here and look from my side."

Autumn crossed the rug and stood where the lamp stood. The whole lit half of the ball glared back at her, bright and round. She walked back to Earth's spot. Sliver. Back to the lamp. Whole lit half, every time. "Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun," she said slowly, "even when it looks like a crescent from Earth. The phases just show how much of that lit half is facing us." She grabbed her notebook and wrote it down before the idea could escape.

A knock came at the screen door, and Mr. Sow from next door leaned in, squinting at the lamp. "Everything all right in here? Looks like a landing pad."

"We're doing science," Cassia said. "The lamp is the Sun. I'm the Moon. Autumn's Earth."

"Then Earth's wearing one sock and a hoodie inside out," said Mr. Sow.

Autumn looked down, laughed, and kept orbiting the lamp with her pencil tucked behind her ear. "Half of you is always lit," she told Cassia grandly. "Even the parts that look dark."

"I'd rather be the adversary," Cassia said. "The Moon never gets to talk."

Autumn circled her one more time, watching the sliver grow into a half, then a whole glowing face, and held out her hand for the ball. "My turn to orbit."

The bus hadn't left the parking lot yet, and Logan was already holding his phone above the seat like a trophy. "Told you," he said. "Rankings don't lie. Montero is tenth in the league. Tenth. That means nine whole quarterbacks are better."

Ella squinted at the screen. Behind the big ranking number there was a whole wall of smaller ones: completions, attempts, yards, touchdowns, interceptions. "Tenth in what, exactly?" she asked.

"In quarterback rating," Logan said, as if that settled it. "It's one number. One. That's the beauty of it."

Jana leaned over from the seat across the aisle. "One number for a whole season of games? That seems like a lot of squishing."

Eella couldn't stop thinking about it as the bus lurched out of the lot. A season was hundreds of throws. Some were beautiful spirals into tight windows, some were dump-offs where the running back did all the work, some were dropped by receivers who couldn't catch a cold. All of that, mashed together and squeezed out as one number. She was optimistic that she could find the squishing machine somewhere online, but she didn't have service on the bus, so she'd have to wait, which was its own kind of torture.

By the time they reached her street, she had a plan. "Logan," she said, standing in the aisle, "if one number can rank a whole season, how would you rank one game? Like, what's the best a quarterback could possibly do?"

Logan shrugged. "A hundred. Perfect score is always a hundred. Everybody knows that."

"That's what I thought too," Ella said, and she anticipated his face going through three stages: confident, confused, annoyed. "My cousin had a game on yesterday, and the announcer said a perfect passer rating is 158.3."

Jana burst out laughing. "A perfect score of 158.3? Who picked that?"

"The announcer said the passer rating combines a bunch of passing stats into one number," Ella went on, "and it goes from zero up to a maximum of 158.3. So it's not out of a hundred. Montero's rating isn't like a grade on a math test."

Logan looked at his phone again, then at her, then at his phone. "So when they show the one big number..."

"A lot of little numbers, wearing a trench coat," Jana said.

At her front door that afternoon, Ella looked it up before she even took off her backpack. The little numbers were all still there, underneath, like the bus wheels under all those kids. She texted Logan a screenshot and one line: "Your tenth-best quarterback, in six parts."

Her phone buzzed almost immediately. "Fine. But he's still tenth."

Naomi crouched in the corner of Ms. Littlechild's farm, holding her notebook so tightly that the edges dug into her palm. The assignment was due tomorrow: draw a food chain that started with the sun and ended with a top predator, then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. Everyone else had finished theirs in class. Mitchell had drawn grass, a rabbit, and a hawk in about ten minutes and then gone outside to help unload hay. Naomi had written the sun, then clover, then a rabbit, then an owl, because Ms. Littlechild had pointed out the owl box on the barn and said a nocturnal hunter lived there, hunting in the dark while the farm slept.

But when Naomi tested her chain the way the assignment asked, something went wrong. She imagined the clover vanishing, and the rabbits going hungry, and the owl losing its prey; that part made sense. Then she flipped the problem around. If the rabbits ceased to exist, what would happen to the clover? Nothing in her drawing fed the clover except the sun, and she had a sinking feeling that sunlight alone was not the whole answer. She had watched her mother's houseplant wilt in poor soil even by a bright window. Something had to reach the clover from the soil, something invisible, and she could not draw what she could not name.

She walked the fence line with Mitchell, peering under bushes. "I need to see where old plants go," she said, and he shrugged and led her past the compost bins to a shady patch behind the barn. There, on a rotting log half sunk in the leaves, grew a cluster of pale mushrooms. Naomi knelt down. The log was soft and crumbly where the mushrooms touched it, as though something were quietly taking it apart. She poked the wood with a stick and it flaked away into dark, rich crumbs that looked exactly like the good soil in the garden beds.

"Mushrooms are fungi," Mitchell said, reading over her shoulder as she flipped through the battered field guide in the barn. "It says right here they break down dead plants and animals and return the nutrients to the soil." Naomi stared at the page while her pulse hammered. There it was, the missing link, the hidden one that ran backward, from the dead to the living, feeding the clover from below. On the walk back she tried one more test in her head: no fungi, no breaking down, no nutrients going back, and the soil would slowly run out of what the clover needed.

That evening she redrew the chain with a looping arrow beneath it, from the owl and rabbit and clover down to the mushrooms, and back up to the soil and the clover again. The suspense of the blank page was gone. When Ms. Littlechild looked it over the next morning, she tapped the loop with one finger and smiled. "Everyone forgets that one," she said. "What do you call them?" Naomi set her pencil down on the drawing, point resting on the mushrooms. "Decomposers," she said.

Naomi dragged the folding table into the driveway and propped up the cardboard sign her dad had helped her letter: STRAWBERRIES, $5 A PINT. She had spent her birthday money on four crates of berries from the farm stand by the highway, because Mr. Krause had provoked a question she couldn't shake. "Ask me why strawberries cost more in winter," he had said at the bus stop, and she had been chewing on it ever since.

Jayden arrived first, then Kaliyah with a coin purse and a plan. "Five dollars is too much," Kaliyah said, pointing at the sign. "My mom gets them cheaper at the store." Naomi argued back, but the first half hour proved Kaliyah right. Three customers walked past without stopping, and one man laughed out loud, which Naomi felt was rude and also possibly fair.

She flipped the cardboard over and wrote $2. That worked almost too well. Two women bought six pints between them, a jogger bought two, and by three o'clock only five pints remained with a whole hour of selling left. Naomi sat on the curb and made her inference out loud. "Two dollars made people want way more than we had. Five dollars made them want way less. Somewhere in between there's a price where what people want to buy is exactly what we want to sell." Kaliyah squinted at her. "Like, sell out right at closing time?" "Exactly at closing time," Naomi said, and wrote $3 on a fresh sign.

At $3, it wasn't instant. A boy on a scooter bought one pint, then circled back for another. Kaliyah added a sample dish, because she noticed a shy little girl staring at the berries without asking, and gave her the biggest strawberry on top. Naomi thought that was better business than any sign. By 3:55, one pint sat alone in the shade. "Lower it?" Jayden suggested. Naomi changed her mind about holding firm and crossed out the 3 to make it 2. "One pint, two dollars," she called, "last of the day." A woman in a garden hat turned around and came back with her wallet just as the clock hit four.

That night Naomi wrote a message on the fridge whiteboard, in her best printing: "TO TEAM BERRY: We found the price where buyers want to buy exactly as much as sellers want to sell. Mr. Krause says that is the equilibrium price. It was $3. Next weekend: lemonade?" Kaliyah had already texted back before Naomi even put the marker down. "Lemonade. But I'm in charge of samples."

Ethan set the pizza dough bowl on the picnic table and glared at it, because the last two batches had come out of the grill oven dry and cakey, more like biscuits than bread. Markus leaned over the fence from next door, and Ethan felt a stab of envy at the perfect-looking bun Markus was eating. "Your dough still sad?" Markus asked. "It's a paradox," Ethan said. "Follow the recipe exactly, get exactly the wrong thing." Ryder arrived on his bike just then, skidding to a stop on the grass. "You can't follow a recipe exactly," he said. "Nobody can."

That was the problem, Ethan realized. He had been measuring the flour by dipping the cup straight into the bag, the way you'd scoop sand at the beach. His grandma had shown him once, spooning flour gently into the cup and leveling it off with a knife, but he'd thought it was just her being fussy about tidiness. Now he wondered if there was a real difference. So he tried an experiment right there at the picnic table. He scooped a cup of flour straight from the bag, dumped it onto the scale, and wrote the number down. Then he spooned flour into the same cup, leveled it, and weighed that too. The scooped cup was heavier, a lot heavier. Same cup, same flour, two different amounts.

"So the recipe thinks a cup is one thing, and your cup is another," Markus said slowly, watching the numbers. Ethan nodded. "Scooping packs the flour down. Weighing it is more accurate than any cup." He was quiet for a second, then said in his most assertive voice, "New rule. Nobody scoops in this backyard." Ryder raised his hand. "What if it's ice cream?" "Ice cream is exempt."

Ethan weighed out the flour for a fresh batch, kneaded it until it felt like an earlobe, which his grandma said was the goal, and slid the dough into a bowl to rise in the sun. When he punched it down an hour later and it sprang back soft and smooth, he whooped so loudly that Markus dropped his bun over the fence. "Dinner's at six!" Ethan called. "Bring your appetite, not your scooping hand."

The basket handle was a smooth orange polymer, and Aaron carried it through the sliding doors behind his mother, straight into a crowd that was thicker than usual for a Tuesday. His little sister had been up all night with a fever, and his mother had written a list: children's fever medicine, popsicles, tissues. On the way to the pharmacy aisle they passed a tower of strawberry boxes stacked so high it looked like it might tip over, each one marked with a big red tag. Two dollars, down from five.

"Whoa," said Aaron. "Why so cheap?"

"There's too many of them," said Theo, who had tagged along with his own mother and was now trailing Aaron like a second shadow. "My uncle grows them and he won't stop talking about it. Everybody's flooded with berries."

At the medicine aisle, the shelf was nearly bare. Three boxes of children's fever reducer stood alone at the back, and the price sticker read twelve dollars. Aaron remembered it costing six, because he had bought some for his mother in the spring when she had the flu.

"That doubled," he said.

A woman in front of them reached for a box anyway, checked the price, and put it in her basket without a pause. Then an older man did the same with the last adult cold medicine. Behind him, Ms. Shin from next door stood squinting at the shelf with a vague look on her face, like she wasn't sure the box she held was the right one.

"Ms. Shin," Aaron said, "that's the one for kids. The blue box. My sister takes it."

"Thank you, Aaron," she said, relieved, and took the blue box next to his. "My grandson's staying with me and he's burning up too."

Aaron watched the shelf empty out, box by box, at twelve dollars each. He turned it over in his head. Strawberries were cheap because there were mountains of them, and people still walked past. Medicine was double the price and everybody grabbed one anyway.

"So the strawberry price drops and people still only buy so many," he said slowly, "but the medicine price goes up and up and people keep buying it exactly the same."

Theo recounted what his father, who read economics books at breakfast, had told him last winter when the same thing happened. "My dad calls that inelastic," Theo said. "Demand for stuff people need, like medicine, changes little when the price changes."

"Then the store could charge anything," Aaron said, half a question.

His mother put the last box in the basket before he could wonder any further. "Come on," she said, "and grab some of those strawberries on the way out. At that price, we can afford two."

Charles spread his bean seeds across the kitchen table like a general arranging tiny soldiers. His science fair project, he had decided, would prove that seeds sprouted faster in the warm cupboard above the stove than in the cold refrigerator. He wrote his hypothesis on an index card in his best handwriting, which was still fairly terrible, and taped it to a jar of damp paper towels. "Day one," he announced to the toaster. "Warm jar, fridge jar. May the best jar win."

By Thursday, the fridge jar had three fat white sprouts and the cupboard jar had exactly zero. Charles stared at them, then at his index card, then at the sprouts again, as if they might apologize and shrink back into their seeds. They did not. He checked the cupboard for clues. Warm, dark, damp. Nothing obviously wrong. He checked again at breakfast, at lunch, and once at nine at night in his pajamas, holding a flashlight like a detective. Still zero.

At school, Kallie took one look at his face and guessed everything. "Your beans turned out wrong, didn't they." Her own project sat proudly beside her lunchbox: a slice of bread in a plastic container, growing a fuzzy gray-green colony she had named Gerald. "Look at Gerald. He's shaped exactly like an intestine. He's going to make the whole gymnasium gag, and the judges are going to love it." That was Kallie's plan, plainly stated: first place, through maximum disgust.

Charles slid his data sheet across the table. "I can't present this. My hypothesis said warm, and warm lost. Three to zero." He was on the edge of throwing the whole project in the recycling bin, sprouts and all, when a rumor began to circulate through the cafeteria that Ms. Aquino had already picked out her favorite project, and that rumor was, everyone agreed, definitely about a potato battery and definitely unfair. Charles marched to Room 12 to complain about the potato, and found Ms. Aquino watering a fern instead.

"Nobody picked anything," she said. "There is no potato. But tell me about your beans." He showed her the data sheet, braced for her to say too bad, so sad. Instead she read it twice, nodded, and said, "This is good. A result that shows your hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result, and it is worth reporting. Present it exactly as it happened." Charles walked back to the cafeteria feeling like the fridge jar had won twice.

On fair day, he stood beside his poster, which said in enormous letters: I PREDICTED WRONG, AND HERE IS WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED. A judge read it, asked him three questions, and wrote things down. Later, when the ribbons were handed out, the class vote for favorite project was unanimous. Charles looked over at Kallie, who was holding a red second-place ribbon and glaring at Gerald the intestine like it had personally betrayed her. "Second," she muttered. "To beans. Cold beans." Charles patted his jar and said, "Gerald's still shaped like an intestine, though. That's gotta count for something."

Mia held the mixing bowl over the counter like a trophy, because tonight she was making banana muffins for the whole family, all by herself. Her dad would draft her little brother into setting the table, her mom had promised to stay out of the kitchen entirely, and Mia had the recipe spread out where she could see every step. She mashed the bananas until they smelled sweet and faintly nutty, cracked the eggs, and then opened the cabinet for the baking powder.

The tin rattled. Two teaspoons of powder, and she needed two full ones. Not nearly enough.

She texted Ajay first, because Ajay baked cookies every weekend and acted like a science tutor about it. "Out of baking powder," she typed. "Can I just use baking soda? Same thing, right?"
