His answer came fast. "Not the same. Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid."

Mia stared at the message. A dry acid? She looked at the orange box of soda in her hand, then back at the recipe. Buttermilk, the recipe said, and buttermilk was nowhere in the fridge. Then she saw the last line of the ingredient list: plain yogurt. Sour stuff. She scooped a little onto her finger and tasted it, tangy and sharp, and a plan snapped together in her head so fast she laughed out loud.

Jayden wandered in to steal a banana and found Mia scribbling on the back of the recipe. "What are you doing?"

"Being skeptical of my own idea, then fixing it," she said. "I'm using baking soda instead of powder, but I'm doubling the yogurt so there's enough acid in the batter to react with it." She stirred the wet ingredients hard, watching the yogurt swirl in like a cloudy river, then folded the batter gently because the recipe underlined that word twice.

The muffins rose into golden domes, cracked a little on top, and filled the kitchen with a smell so warm that Jayden abandoned his banana on the spot. Her dad walked in, took one bite, and closed his eyes.

"Two more," he said, already reaching. "For science."

Carter stood in the kitchen holding six index cards and a kitchen timer, and he said, for the fourth time, "Today I will talk about bees." His dad looked up from chopping an onion and nodded politely. His little sister kept drawing her dinosaur. Carter stopped. He had a two-minute speech due in Ms. Hoang's class on Friday, and it was supposed to have an opening hook, three points and a closing, and so far every practice run had made his family act like furniture.

He tried again in the living room that evening. "Today I will talk about sharks." His dad flipped a page of his magazine without reading it, Carter was almost sure. That was the strange part. His dad liked sharks. So why did everyone's attention drift away the second Carter began? He sat on the arm of the couch and wondered about it. It was like the audience's focus could fluctuate, rising and falling depending on something Carter couldn't see, some rule hiding underneath the words themselves.

On Saturday his friend Charles-Edouard came over, and they watched old speeches on a tablet. One kid started with "Today I will talk about recycling," and Carter felt his own eyes go fuzzy. The next video opened with "Did you know a single beehive can hold fifty thousand bees?" and Carter sat up without meaning to. He rewound it. He watched three more videos, keeping a tally on a napkin, and a pattern appeared. The speeches that grabbed him began with a question, a surprising fact, or a very short story. The boring ones began with an announcement.

"See, it's the first line," Carter said. "It's called a hook. A question, or a weird fact, or a tiny story."

Charles-Edouard frowned. "So it isn't about the topic at all?"

"It's about the opening." Carter grabbed a fresh card. He wrote three hooks for his bee speech: a question, a fact, and a thirty-second story about the time a bee followed him around the backyard for a whole afternoon like a tiny buzzing protagonist. Then he decided to test it, because a pattern on a napkin wasn't proof. Sunday dinner, his whole family at the table, was his laboratory.

He cleared his throat. "Which is smarter, a bee or a pigeon?" The conversation stopped. His sister put down her fork. "A bee," his dad said, "surely." "Wrong," said Carter, and launched into his first point. His sister interrupted twice to argue, which was rude but also, Carter thought, exactly the point. Nobody picked up a phone. Nobody drifted. He finished with his closing line, checked the timer, and grinned. Monday at recess he found Finlay by the fence.

"Hey, Finlay. Want to hear the smartest insect in the world?"

Nevaeh spread the petition across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with jars of pickled beets so the pages would not curl. Forty-seven people had signed it, asking the city to change the bylaw that banned skateboards on the library plaza, and today the city would say what happened next.

"That's a lot of names," said Phoenix, who had arrived with his helmet still on.

"Forty-seven," Nevaeh said. "Now what? Does the whole council just vote on it?" She had assumed that a petition went straight to a vote, the way a coin goes straight into a vending machine, but when she called the city clerk's office that morning, the woman on the phone had said the petition had been sent to the community services committee first.

"Committee," Phoenix repeated. "Like a smaller group that studies it?"

Jethro, who was reading over Nevaeh's shoulder, tapped the clerk's phone number. "So they look at it and recommend whether the full council should approve it. That's what the lady said. You wrote it down."

Nevaeh studied her notes. So the petition was like a river that hit a gate before it reached the sea. If the committee said no, the whole council might never even see it. Which meant forty-seven signatures might not be enough on their own. "We have to speak there too," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "At the committee. Not just the council meeting."

Her grandmother set down a plate of oatmeal cookies. "Your grandfather got the noise bylaw softened that way, back when this street was part of the old Campbell dynasty, before the wards changed."

"You mean a real dynasty?" Phoenix asked.

"A family that ran everything, close enough," her grandmother said. "Get yourselves over there. Wear something durable, those chairs at city hall are older than me."

The three of them packed the petition into Nevaeh's backpack, along with the cookies, and pedaled hard toward the yellow-brick building on Main Street, Phoenix ringing his bell the whole way.

The community sports field had been turned into a viewing party for the championship game, with a giant screen propped against the backstop and half the neighbourhood spread across blankets on the grass. Ellie sat between her dad and Tobias, who had his trivia notebook balanced on one knee. Tobias wanted more than anything to win the library's sports trivia contest next weekend, and he was collecting facts like bottle caps.

"Why does the game use Roman numerals?" April asked, pointing at the huge painted banner near the concession stand. The banner depicted a golden trophy, a helmet, and the letters "LVIII" in tall red print.

"Because it's fancy," Tobias said. "That's the whole reason."

Ellie wasn't so sure. Fancy didn't explain anything. She thought about the numbers on the banner, and then about something her grandfather had once mentioned while flipping channels. She decided to test it. "If the Roman numerals were part of the name from the beginning, then the first one would have been called Super Bowl I right away, with the numeral in the name. But Grandpa said the first one had a different official name." She pulled out her phone and typed carefully, shielding the screen from the sun with her hand.

The answer came up, and she read it twice to be certain. "It was called the AFL-NFL World Championship Game. The Roman numerals were added later, after people started calling it Super Bowl I."

"So the numerals are like a nickname that stuck," April said slowly, watching the banner again.

"Better than a nickname," Tobias said, scribbling fast. "It's a contest question waiting to happen." He underlined it twice. "Nobody at the library is going to know that."

"You think everyone else is gullible," Ellie said, "just because they don't read your notebook."

"I think they're lucky I do," Tobias said.

On the field beside the screen, the tenant who rented the little equipment shed, a quiet man who refereed youth soccer on Saturdays, leaned over the fence and tipped his cap toward them. "First one I ever watched, we called it the championship game too," he said. "Never thought a number would end up bigger than the game."

The screen flared bright, the crowd on the blankets stirred, and the kickoff sailed up into the darkening sky.

Brooklyn spread her poster board across the library table and set her stack of surveys beside it. On the surveys, students had reported whether they ate breakfast and what their last math scores were. She had found that the breakfast eaters mostly had better scores, and she had typed "BREAKFAST MAKES YOU SMARTER" in giant letters.

Yasmine slid into the chair across from her and squinted at the title. "So if I eat a waffle tomorrow, my quiz goes up?"

"Basically," Brooklyn said.

Safa leaned over, chewing a granola bar. "My brother eats breakfast every day. He also failed a spelling test on Tuesday because he stayed up until two playing games."

Brooklyn looked at her data table. Half the breakfast eaters were the kids on the swim team, the ones who got up early anyway. She remembered her own surveys from last fall, when she had tried to prove that owning a dog made people more responsible, and Mr. Nowak had written one word in the margin: "Correlation?" She had ignored it, mostly because she did not know what it meant.

She flipped through the surveys again, this time sorting by bedtime. The breakfast eaters also mostly went to bed earlier. Kids who stayed up late skipped breakfast and did worse on tests, both because they were lethargic all morning and scrambling for the bus.

"Oh no," Brooklyn said. "The breakfast might not be causing anything. Something else, like bedtime, could be causing both."

"What do you call it when two things happen together like that?" Yasmine asked.

"Correlation," Brooklyn said, deleting her giant letters. "And it doesn't prove one thing causes the other."

She rebuilt the poster as a question instead of an answer, cutting a strip of cardboard to convert the blank board into a flip chart. Yasmine drew a waffle with a graduation cap on it for the cover, and Safa titled it "The Mysterious Third Factor" in her best artisan lettering, which looked suspiciously like fancy cereal-box writing.

By closing time, the poster asked "Does Breakfast Cause Good Grades, or Does Bedtime Cause Both?" and beneath it, in small letters, "Further testing required. Snacks welcome."

Yasmine held up the last granola bar. "For science," she said, and split it three ways.

Charlotte had walked past Yousif's house every school day since second grade, but on Tuesday she crossed to the other side of the street, because Yousif had gone to the arcade on Saturday with Braxton and never even texted her. She had found out from a photo, three blurry figures leaning over a pinball machine, and the resentment had been sitting in her chest ever since, heavy as a backpack full of wet towels.

On Thursday she decided she could not cross the street forever. She wanted her best friend back, but she also did not want to shout, because shouting with Yousif usually ended in a week of silence. There had to be a better way to say it. That was the problem she chewed on all through Ms. Kaminski's class, half filling her notebook with attempts.

"You ditched me," she wrote, and crossed it out, because that sounded like an accusation, and Yousif would get defensive and stop listening. She tried again. "When I saw the photo, I felt left out." She stared at that one. It said the same thing but pointed at her own feelings instead of at him. It felt softer, like a door left unlocked instead of slammed.

The next morning she caught Yousif on his porch, tying one sneaker. "Hey," she said, and her voice came out smaller than she planned. "When I saw that arcade photo, I felt left out. Like everybody forgot me."

Yousif looked up. "Braxton asked me Saturday morning and I said yes before I even thought. I figured you were at your grandma's." He paused. "I should have texted anyway. I'm sorry."

"It's called an I-message," Charlotte said. "Braxton told me about it. He said a psychologist named Thomas Gordon came up with it in the 1960s. You say 'I felt' instead of 'you did,' so nobody feels attacked."

"You got that from Braxton?"

"He got it from his sister. Whatever. It worked." A cat slunk along the fence, low and predatory, eyes fixed on something in the grass, and then pounced on a leaf and sat there looking disappointed. They both laughed, and the laugh felt like the first warm day after winter.

"So, arcade this weekend?" Yousif asked. "All three of us, and I'll send the text myself."

"Deal," said Charlotte. "And I'll actually answer it."

Evelyn had never noticed how many weird little objects lived in Grandma's hallway drawer until the rainy afternoon when the power went out. There were thimbles, a magnifying glass, and a box of Scrabble tiles that smelled like pencil shavings. She carried it to the kitchen table, where her friend Chelsea was visiting and Caden, the boy from next door, had already claimed the window seat.

They were twenty minutes into the game when Chelsea laid down Q and I and announced, "Qi. Twenty-one points, because the Q is on a double letter."

"That is not a word," Caden said. "You can't just put two letters down and call it a thing."

"It is too a word. It's like, energy."

"Then prove it." Caden crossed his arms, and Evelyn could see the whole afternoon curling up and dying right there, like a leaf in Grandma's woodstove. Nobody had a phone that worked without the router. Grandma offered three dictionaries from the shelf, which was the problem: one was so old it called a refrigerator an "icebox," and another was a pocket version that seemed to skip everything after "plume." Chelsea said the old one counted because old dictionaries knew more words. Caden said the pocket one counted because it was newer. Evelyn drummed her fingers on the table and wondered how something as small as a two-letter word could cause such a giant argument.

"Wait," she said. "Maybe the problem isn't the word. Maybe the problem is that we never picked which dictionary is the boss." She proposed a quick negotiation: before any word got challenged, they would delegate the deciding to one single book, chosen now, while everyone was still calm. They picked the big red one from the den. Caden flipped to the Q section, muttering the alphabet under his breath like a spell.

"Qi," he read, his voice going sour. "A vital life force in Chinese thought." He squinted at Chelsea. "Fine. Twenty-one points. But if I put down 'zyn' next turn, the red book decides, and you can't argue."

"Deal," Evelyn said, and slid the dictionary to the middle of the table where everyone could reach it.

At Gate 14, Jeremy watched the departure board flip from DELAYED to BOARDING, and his stomach did a small flip of its own. His family was flying to Portugal, six hours ahead of home time, and his dad had already promised they would walk along the river their first evening there. Jeremy had a plan for those first evenings, or at least the beginning of one. His friend Riaan had sent him off that morning with a warning: "My cousin flew to Europe last summer and said they were zombies for a week. Nobody could sleep at night." Jeremy wanted to test whether that was really true, or just one family being dramatic.

He started a page in his notebook before the plane even pushed back. At the top he wrote: midnight at home versus midnight in Lisbon. Then he made two columns, one for what the clock on the wall said and one for how awake he felt. His little sister slept through dinner and the movie, which fit Riaan's story. Jeremy stayed awake too, but that proved nothing, because he was excited.

The real test came on the second night. In the apartment his parents had rented, the street below was dark and the refrigerator hummed in the corner, and the clock said 12:40. Jeremy was wide awake, and so were his dad and his sister, whispering over a card game in the kitchen. Only his mom had gone to bed, and he could hear her turning over. On the third night it was the same: 1:15, cards shuffling, everyone's eyes bright as noon. Jeremy wrote it down.

By the fourth night, something had shifted. His sister fell asleep at eleven, local time, without a fight. On the fifth night his dad yawned at ten and gave up on the crossword. Jeremy looked at his columns and counted the nights. Six hours of time difference. One night closer to normal for every hour. He sat on the bathroom floor so the light wouldn't wake anyone and did the math again. One day for each hour, exactly, the way water drains out of a tub at a steady rate.

The next morning he found a postcard stand near the bakery and bought one for Riaan. He wrote the rule in two sentences, then added, "I tested it myself. It took our whole family six nights." Ms. Bélanger, his former teacher who lived on Riaan's street, had once told their class that a good scientist could enroll anyone in an experiment just by making it interesting. Jeremy decided his evidence was unanimous: four out of four family members, all adjusting at the same steady pace.

On the seventh night, the whole apartment was asleep before ten except Jeremy, who lay listening to the quiet street. He got up, padded to the window, and looked down at the river his dad had promised, black and gleaming under the lamps. Tomorrow they would walk along it in daylight, and he would be awake enough to actually see it. He pressed his forehead to the cool glass and whispered, "Worth every sleepy night."

The storm was supposed to hit by evening, and Mya's mother had sent her to the gas station on the corner with a list: batteries, granola bars, and two bottles of water. The parking lot was full. Inside, people were carrying baskets piled with canned soup and flashlight batteries, and a man by the coolers was taking the last four cases of water off the shelf.

Mya got in line behind Tyler, who was holding a single bottle of water and a bag of chips. "Three dollars for this," Tyler said, turning the bottle so she could see the sticker slapped over the old price. "It was a dollar twenty-five this morning. I was here this morning. My mom sent me back for a second one."

"That's twice as much," Mya said. "That's more than twice as much." She looked at the shelf behind them, where one lone bottle of sparkling water sat alone between empty rows. Then she thought of the gas station out by the highway, the big one with thirty pumps, where nobody from their street ever shopped because it was too far to walk. "Come on," she said, and pulled Tyler toward the door.

At the big station, the water aisle was full. Cases stacked to the ceiling, coolers humming, and a hand-written sign that said WATER $1.25. Mya picked up two bottles. "Same water," she said. "Same brand, same size. It's a dollar twenty-five here because there's a wall of it, and three dollars at the corner because there were four cases left." Tyler paid for his second bottle and tore the corner store's sticker off the first one, holding them side by side like evidence.

"It's like Mr. Sato's homework," Tyler said as they walked back. "We had to read a page from this guy, Adam Smith. In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, he says nothing is more useful than water, yet water will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." He squinted. "I didn't get it until right now, standing in that empty aisle."

"You need water to live," Mya said. "You don't need a diamond for anything. But water's everywhere, so it's cheap." At the corner station, the man from the coolers was now taping a new sign to the register: WATER SOLD OUT. The cashier was restishing nothing behind the counter, just counting the drawer, and Mya guessed the store's revenue today would be its best of the whole month.

Back home, her mother looked at the receipt. "You incorporated a whole economics lesson into one errand," she said, handing Mya a granola bar from the bag. Mya shrugged. "Tyler says next storm, we buy diamonds instead." From the driveway, Tyler yelled, "No, next storm, we buy the water early and incorporate a markup."

The old quarry above town had become Mr. Goldberg's outdoor classroom, and today he had dumped three buckets of rocks on a folding table. "Sort them," he said. "Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic. You have until noon." Matteo picked up a dark rock with thin wavy stripes, like frosting swirled through a cake. "That one got cooked," he said, dropping it onto the igneous pile. "Igneous means melted, so anything hot goes there." Lilou frowned but didn't argue, because arguing with Matteo before lunch was never worth it.

Eva worked slowly, holding each rock up so the sun refracted through a quartz vein and threw a small rainbow on her notebook. She pulled a striped rock from the igneous pile and turned it over. "If this melted, the stripes would be gone. Melted stuff mixes." Matteo snatched it back. "Then it wasn't hot enough to melt all the way." Eva raised an eyebrow. "So it was hot, and squeezed, and it didn't melt. It changed. What's a rock called when it changes?"

Mr. Goldberg, who was sitting on a stable stack of slate nearby pretending to read, lowered his book. "Metamorphic," he said, and turned a page. That was all. Matteo stared at the striped rock in his hand. He licked his thumb and rubbed the surface, testing the idea that a changed rock would look somehow newer, softer. It didn't. It looked like the limestone down the hill, but pressed, folded, cooked without ever becoming liquid. He thought of bread dough squeezed through fingers, reshaped but never poured.

He rebuilt the piles. The swirly striped ones moved to a new middle pile, and he found more: a rock with glittery layers that had once been plain mudstone, a hard gray one folded like a wrinkled shirt. "Okay," he said to Eva. "I was wrong. Heated doesn't mean melted. Metamorphic means changed by heat and squeezing, deep down, and it never has to melt at all." Eva added her rainbow-making quartz to his pile. "The rock collectors' guild accepts your apology," she said, and held up the next specimen to the light.

Juliette laid out her supplies on the kitchen table: a jar of water, three paint tubes, a canvas board, and the best brushes from Mr. Otieno's art room. He had let her borrow them for the weekend because she was painting a portrait of her grandmother's old residence, the blue house with the crooked porch where Grandma had lived for forty years.

Greta arrived first, then Joel, and they both leaned over the sketch Juliette had taped to the table. "You drew the porch railing better than I could," Greta said. Joel was already squeezing paint onto a palette, blobs of cobalt and white and a dot of gold for the porch light.

The painting went well for an hour. Juliette mixed the blues thin and runny, adding water from the jar whenever the paint got too thick, and the sky spread across the canvas in smooth strokes. Then Joel stood up to get snacks and left his brush lying on the table, its bristles loaded with paint, while he searched the cupboard for crackers. He took his time. When he came back and picked up the brush, he frowned. The bristles had gone stiff, and they held their shape like little frozen fingers.

"That's ruined," he said, pulling at them. Water did nothing. He dunked the brush in the jar and scrubbed it against the bottom, but the bristles stayed hard.

Juliette looked at her own brush, still wet and soft, then at Joel's. Hers had been sitting in the water jar between strokes, and Joel's had been sitting in open air. She thought about the sky she had just painted, how it was already dry to the touch, and how the paint in the tube stayed soft because the tube was sealed tight. "It's the drying," she said slowly. "While the paint is wet, water thins it out, that's why the jar works. But once it dries, it turns water-resistant. That's why your brush won't clean now, and why my sky doesn't smear when I touch it."

"So we have to wash the brushes before the paint dries on them," Greta said, and she fetched a second jar of clean water for rinsing between every color change.

They worked out a system to conserve their remaining good brushes. Juliette set a paper towel by each jar so a wet brush never touched the table, and Joel kept time out loud, calling "rinse" whenever somebody paused too long. At the end, they washed every brush with soap and laid them flat to dry.

When Mr. Otieno came by on Monday to see the finished painting, he stood in front of the blue house for a long moment. "That porch light," he said. "It's eloquent. You can almost hear the crickets." Juliette grinned and handed him the brush case, every one soft and clean, and Joel held up the one ruined brush like a trophy of what they had learned.

Piper knelt on her apartment balcony with a bag of potting soil, six containers, and a paper envelope of lettuce seeds she had bought with her allowance. Down in the courtyard, the community garden beds sat empty of lettuce, though Caylee had planted a whole row there three weeks ago. Not one sprout had come up. "Maybe the seeds were bad," Caylee had said, but Piper wanted to evaluate that idea herself before she believed it.

She filled her containers and pressed the tiny seeds deep into the soil, a full finger's length down, the way the tomato and bean packets had shown. Tomatoes and beans were already up in her warm corner by the door, where she watered them every morning. She kept the lettuce containers beside them, warm and damp, and waited.

Ten days passed. Nothing. Piper tapped the soil, checked that it was moist, and felt the warmth of the balcony bricks. Water, warmth, air; the soil was loose, so the seeds had oxygen too. "It's like a jury that can't agree," she told Margaux, who had come up to see the tomatoes. "Everything looks right, but the verdict is no sprouts." Margaux leaned over the pots and frowned.

Then Piper read her lettuce packet again, the part she had skipped. Sow shallowly, it said, barely cover the seeds, because lettuce sprouts best with light. She sat back on her heels. The courtyard seeds had been buried deep too. That was it. Seeds like tomatoes and beans needed water, oxygen and warmth, and light didn't matter to them, but lettuce was different.

She sowed a new tray, pressing the seeds into the surface and dusting them with the thinnest sprinkle of soil. "That hardly counts as planting," Margaux said. "It counts as not being reckless with depth," Piper said, and set the tray where the morning sun touched it.

Four days later, a haze of green freckled the soil, tiny and even, like pepper shaken across a plate. Piper ran to the railing and called down to the courtyard, where Caylee was kneeling by the empty row with a fresh packet in her hand. "Don't bury them this time," Piper called. "Just tickle them into the top of the soil and leave them in the light."

Everly lined up nine bean plants along the back counter of the science classroom, each one in a paper cup labeled with a letter. Cups A, B, and C would get the fancy fertilizer from the garden store. Cups D, E, and F would get half strength. And cup G would get plain water and nothing else. "It's my control group," she told Dan, who was building a volcano two tables away. "It gets no change at all, so I can compare everything against it."

"Seems boring," Dan said. He wanted the blue ribbon so badly he had painted his volcano three times, and he kept glancing at Everly's cups like they were competition. "Nobody wins with beans."

Two weeks later, Everly measured the plants and her stomach dropped. The fertilizer plants were fine, but the control plant, cup G, was the tallest of all. That made no sense. Plain water shouldn't do that, and if her control was wrong, her whole poster was wrong. She checked the leaves, made a careful diagnosis, early rot, maybe overwatering, but the plant looked healthy. Something hidden was going on.

Then she noticed the dirt in cup G was dark and rich, darker than the dirt in her other cups. On Friday she hid behind Mr. Gallagher's supply cabinet at lunch and waited, hardly breathing, her knees cramping on the cold tile floor. The door creaked. Anas slipped in with a small green bottle and tipped it into cup G.

"Anas!"

He froze. "My grandmother says fertilizer helps everything. I wanted your control to win. I didn't know which cup was which." He pointed at the cup. "Anonymous plant hero, that was the plan."

Everly laughed, then stopped. "You contaminated my baseline. I have to start over with a new control." She dumped cup G into the bin and planted a fresh seed, and Dan, watching from the doorway, set down his paintbrush.

"Guess controls aren't boring after all," he said. "Want help labeling the new cups?"

Madison spread her homework across the library table by the window, where the afternoon light made the pencil marks easy to see. Her ambition for the week was simple: finish every fraction problem before Friday, so she could join the weekend baking day her neighbour was hosting. The only trouble was the page in front of her, which asked her to add one half and one third.

Across the table, Augustin was chewing his pencil. He wrote something, crossed it out, and wrote it again. Skylar sat between them, stacking her books into a tidy tower, because Skylar liked the library shelves to look orderly even when her own notebook was a mess.

"I got two fifths," Augustin said at last, turning his paper around. "One plus one is two, and two plus three is five. So two fifths."

Skylar leaned over and looked at his answer. "Try this," she said. "You started with one half. Is your answer bigger than a half?"

Augustin drew a line on his scrap paper and marked it into five equal pieces. He shaded two of them, then stared at it. His answer, two fifths, was smaller than the half he had started with. "That can't be right," he said slowly. "When I add something, I should end up with more, not less."

Madison pulled her paper closer and tried the same trick with her own problem. She drew a half, then a third, then tried to see how they might fit together. The pieces were different sizes, like puzzle pieces from two different boxes. She thought she could diagnose the exact trouble: the bottom numbers did not match, so the pieces could not be counted straight across. She flipped to the back of her textbook, past the section on equivalent fractions, hunting for the page Ms. Otieno had mentioned on Monday.

"Sixths," she said suddenly. "Both of them can turn into sixths."

She wrote it out. One half became three sixths. One third became two sixths. Now the pieces matched, and she counted them like ordinary things: three pieces plus two pieces made five pieces. Five sixths. She checked it against her drawing, and the shaded bar stretched past the halfway mark, exactly as an answer should.

Ms. Otieno passed by their table on her way to the returns cart and paused long enough to see Madison's paper. "Testing it with a picture first," she said. "That's a good habit." She moved on without saying anything more, which suited Madison fine.

Madison slid her notebook toward Augustin so he could see how the sixths lined up, top and bottom. His pencil hovered over his own page, and his usually rebellious habit of arguing back seemed to have gone quiet. He copied the method once, twice, then covered his work with his hand and tried a new problem alone.

"Eight fifteenths," he announced a minute later. "Want to check me?"

Mila stood at the front of the drama camp's black-box studio, notes shaking in her hand, and began her two-minute speech about why her school should keep its bee garden. "Um, honeybees visit, um, two million flowers just to make one pound of honey," she said. From the front row, Zayden clicked a tally counter with every "um," and by the end of the first run-through it read thirty-one.

Thirty-one felt terrible, but Mila noticed something while she watched the playback on Ms. Friedman's tablet. When she paused silently before her second point, Zayden leaned forward. When she said "um," he glanced at the ceiling. She wondered if the filler words were the problem rather than the nerves underneath, and she had a way to test it. "Count again," she told Zayden, "but this time clap when I pause instead of counting ums."

The second run had fewer than half the ums, because every time she felt one coming, she shut her mouth and let the quiet sit there. The pauses felt enormous to her, like falling, but Zayden clapped twelve times and only sixteen tally marks appeared. Jared, who was writing the closing line of his own speech, looked up and said, "You sound way more confident when you stop like that. It gives me a second to actually take in the point." That matched what Mila had seen on the playback, and she wrote "PAUSE" in red letters at the top of each of her three points.

The camp showcase came on Friday, with parents folding themselves into the small chairs. Mila's opening hook about the two million flowers landed, and when she reached her second point she paused, one second of silence in a room that had been noisy all morning. Nobody fidgeted. Her closing line, "The bees did the work; the least we can do is keep the garden," got a real laugh and then applause.

Afterward Zayden held up the tally counter, which read four. "Four, and two of those were borderline," he said. Mila grinned and tossed her notes into her bag, because even the protagonist of a bee speech deserves a break, and trivial mistakes were just data now. "Same time tomorrow?" Jared asked, waving his still-unfinished closing line at her. "Bring the counter," Mila said.

The argument at the tetherball pole had been going for two minutes, and Grayson could hear it from the canoe rack. Aubrie stood with her hands on her hips while Thea pointed at a scuffed line in the dirt. "The ball was out. You saw it," Aubrie said. "I did not cheat," Thea shot back, and Grayson noticed that every time somebody said the word cheat, the argument got more volatile, like a fire fed with dry leaves. His ankle tendon, sore from yesterday's hike, twinged as he jogged over, and he tried to regulate his breathing the way the swim instructor had taught them, slow in, slow out, because it was hard to think when you were puffed up.

"Okay, wait," Grayson said. "Can I try something? Don't say who's wrong. Just say what we disagree about." Thea crossed her arms but nodded. Aubrie frowned. "We disagree about whether the ball was out," Grayson said, pointing at the line. He was surprised at how different the sentence felt from you're wrong. It was like the problem had climbed off of Aubrie and landed on the ground between them, where everybody could look at it.

That night he wrote a letter to his older brother, who was at a different camp across the lake.

Dear Marcus, I found a weird trick today. When Aubrie and Thea fought about the call, I made them name the problem as one question both of them owned, and then they stopped yelling at each other and started arguing about the line itself. They still fought, but about dirt, which was funnier. Thea got down on her knees with a magnifying lens from nature crafts. Tomorrow we vote on a rule that both teams agree to before the game starts. Wish me luck. Your brother, Grayson.

The next morning, Thea taped a sign to the pole: FAIR RULE, DECIDED BY EVERYONE. Aubrie read it twice, then pulled out a marker and added, AND THE LINE GETS REPAINTED EVERY MONDAY. She had changed her mind about the whole thing, Grayson realized, somewhere between the magnifying lens and the marker. At lunch, three kids from Cabin Four came over to ask how the rule worked, and Grayson pushed his tray aside, ready to explain.

"First," he said, "tell me what you disagree about."

The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Ivy sat twisting the hem of her jacket so hard it was starting to look like a raisin. She was there for her flu shot, which last week had seemed like no big deal. Then Charly had told her about a cousin whose arm swelled up "like a balloon animal" after one, and how he couldn't lift it for a whole month, and now every time Ivy closed her eyes she saw that balloon arm floating over her like a parade float. She hadn't even told her dad why she'd gone quiet in the car. He'd just said, "Big day, huh," and handed her a peppermint.

The waiting room itself was barren, almost empty, just a fern losing a slow war with the fluorescent lights and two other patients: a man asleep with a crossword on his chest, and Ms. Paquette from two streets over, knitting something green. Ivy picked up a pamphlet from the rack just to have something to do with her hands. It was about why people fear rare things, and one paragraph stopped her cold. In 1973, it said, psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described what they called the availability heuristic, meaning that people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.

Ivy read it twice. She thought of Charly's cousin and his parade-float arm. The story came to mind instantly, bright and vivid, which the pamphlet seemed to imply meant her brain would act like swollen arms happened all the time. She decided to run a test, right there, because sitting still was worse. "Ms. Paquette," she said, "do you know anybody who had a really bad reaction to a flu shot?"

Ms. Paquette looked up over her needles. "Can't say I do, dear. I've had one every year since I was your age. Worst that happened was I felt tired and watched game shows all afternoon." Ivy asked the sleeping man too, who woke up, blinked, and said, "I got one Tuesday. It stung for four seconds. I timed it. I was proud of that." Then he went back to sleep. Two people, zero balloon arms. Charly's one story was loud, but it was one story.

"Availability heuristic," Ivy said to herself, quietly, tasting the words. Ms. Paquette smiled like she recognized them.

"Nurse said one thing to remember, though," Ms. Paquette added. "It works both ways. Easy to remember doesn't mean often true."

When the nurse called her name, Ivy stood up so fast the pamphlet slid to the floor, and she felt in her pocket to make sure the peppermint was still there. Her arm already stung in imagination, four seconds' worth, but she walked through the door anyway.

Jaxson's whole week had started to revolve around the science project on Ms. Sánchez's back table: a battery, a bulb, a switch, and three wires that were supposed to make light. Yesterday it had worked. The bulb had glowed like a tiny sun every time he flipped the switch, and Tristen had clapped so loudly that a kid two rooms over probably heard it. Today, on demo day, he flipped the switch and nothing happened. The bulb sat there, dark and smug, like it was keeping a secret.

"Maybe the bulb died of boredom," Tristen said, leaning over Jaxson's shoulder. The table smelled like pencil shavings and the orange peel somebody had left there since Monday.

"It worked yesterday," Jaxson said. "That's the part that's making me crazy." He wiggled each wire where it clamped to the battery. He unscrewed the bulb and screwed it back. He clicked the switch up, down, up, down, and even held it halfway, which Finley said was like standing in the median between on and off. Still dark. Finley offered a replacement bulb from her kit, and the whole class watched, because whether Jaxson's project could be fixed had somehow become the most controversial question of the morning, bigger even than whether cafeteria pizza counted as breakfast.

Then Jaxson stopped moving his hands and thought. Something invisible had to be the problem, because everything he could see looked fine. A circuit was a loop, and the loop only lit the bulb if something was flowing through it. What if the thing flowing had stopped, not because of a broken wire, but because the battery itself had run out? Yesterday he had left the switch on by accident, all afternoon and all night. The battery could have been slowly using itself up the whole time. "Tristen," he said slowly, "hand me the battery out of Finley's kit."

He swapped it in, pressed the wires tight, and flipped the switch. The bulb blazed. The class actually cheered, and Ms. Sánchez raised both eyebrows like she'd won something.

"So what happened?" she asked.

"The battery turns its stored chemical energy into electrical energy," Jaxson said, holding the old battery up like evidence in a trial, "and when those chemicals get used up, it goes flat. Mine went flat, because I left my switch on overnight and drained it." He turned the dead battery over in his fingers and grinned. "This little guy worked himself to the bone."

"Rest in peace," Tristen said, saluting the battery.

Jaxson dropped it in the paper cup marked "dead batteries" and flipped his switch off, very, very deliberately.

Addison slid her story across the desk to Kendra, who read fast and then frowned. "You only fixed the spelling. Mr. Virtanen said we have to revise."

"That is revising," Addison said. "New commas and everything."

Kendra, who wanted the reading corner spot by the window and knew Mr. Virtanen gave it to whoever improved the most, shook her head. "No. He told Liana the word revise comes from the Latin revisere, meaning 'to look at again.' Revising means seeing your draft with fresh eyes."

Addison looked at her page again. All she saw was the same page. She tried standing up, walking once around the desks, and coming back. That was no better. Then she had an idea: if her eyes were the problem, maybe her ears were the answer. She read the first paragraph out loud in a low voice.

"Leila walked slowly and quietly through the very dark and spooky old hallway." It sounded flat, like a hallway itself. She crossed out slowly and quietly and wrote crept. She crossed out very dark and spooky old and kept only the shadowed hallway. Then she noticed something else. Every sentence was long. Every single one had two commas in it. She cut one sentence down to four words: "The floor creaked. She froze."

Her pencil wanted to rebel against deleting words she had worked hard on, but she reminded herself she was being frugal, keeping only what the paragraph truly needed. Reading aloud took stamina, because she kept stopping to slash adjectives, but by the end she had crossed out eleven of them.

She read it to Kendra again. "The floor creaked. She froze." Kendra grinned and pointed at the last line.

"Read that part one more time," Kendra said.

Cameron stood at the sink in the boys' bathroom and studied his forehead in the mirror. Three red spots had appeared overnight, right above his left eyebrow, and they seemed to have plans to multiply. He was supposed to give his candidate speech for class representative in twenty minutes, in front of everyone, and the last thing he needed was a face that looked like a science experiment.

He turned on the tap and scrubbed his forehead with soap, hard, the way he thought you were supposed to. The spots got redder. He scrubbed again. Worse still. That was strange, he thought. If dirt was causing them, washing should help. But it hadn't, which meant the cause was something he couldn't see, something under the skin, and scrubbing was just making things angrier. The idea germinated slowly in his head: maybe the problem wasn't on the surface at all.

The door banged open and Jean came in, dragging Manuel by the sleeve. "I told you he'd be hiding in here," Jean said. "Mr. Aziz has been looking everywhere. You're up after Ravi."

"I can't," Cameron said. "Look at my face."

Manuel leaned against the sink and looked, really looked, not laughing. "My sister had that exact same thing last year," he said. "She was so upset my mom took her to the dermatologist."

"What's a dermatologist?" Cameron asked.

"Skin doctor. She came home and told me something weird. She said about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne. That's basically everybody."

"Eighty-five percent," Cameron repeated. He did the math against his class of twenty-six. That was around twenty-two kids. Twenty-two faces with the same red spots hiding under the same careful haircuts, including probably the two boys standing right here. "So Ravi has it too?"

Jean snorted. "Ravi has it so bad he grows sideburns to cover it. Come on, it's not a disease, it's just being twelve."

Cameron looked at the mirror one more time. His hair was still pushed forward like a curtain, the way he'd fixed it that morning, which explained why his forehead had been an oily, sweaty mess all week. He'd stopped showering at night too, ever since basketball practice moved to mornings, and he'd skipped the deodorant his mom bought because the label said it was for men and he wasn't one yet. But maybe that was backwards. Maybe this was exactly the age when all of it started to matter, the shower, the deodorant, the whole routine, invisible things you did for invisible causes.

He splashed cold water on his forehead, gently this time, and pushed his hair up off his face. He dug the deodorant stick out of his backpack, where it had been germinating at the bottom for two weeks, and used it.

"When I get up there," he said, "I'm telling them my first act as class rep is putting a box of face wash in the gym bathroom."

Jean held the door. "That's actually not the worst campaign promise I've ever heard."

Cameron walked out with his whole face showing.

The locker room smelled like chlorine and rubber flip-flops, and Willow sat on the bench with her tryout card trembling in her damp hands. Ms. Sandhu had pinned the team list to the corkboard by the pool door: anyone who wanted the last spot on the swim team had to beat the cutoff time in tomorrow's trial heat. Willow's card said her best time from summer club was 41 seconds for 50 freestyle, but the cutoff was 38, and the trial heat was in ten minutes.

"That's a contradiction," said Kaysen, peering over her shoulder while stuffing his sneakers into his locker. "You beat kids all summer. How can you be three whole seconds too slow now?" He wasn't on the team himself, but he came to every tryout to yell for her from the bleachers.

Willow chewed the strap of her goggles. Something felt wrong, and it wasn't just nerves. Her summer club practiced in a huge pool, the one downtown with the diving well, while the school pool was so short she counted only a few strokes before hitting the wall. She tried to conserve her energy on the walk to the pool deck, breathing slowly, because Coach only allowed each swimmer one warm-up lap before time trials began.

Ziad was stretching by the lane ropes, and he saw her staring down the length of the pool. "What are you looking at?"

"I swam my summer times in a 50-meter pool," Willow said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Olympic races are held in 50-meter pools. That's called long course." She pointed at the wall she'd have to turn at, way too soon. "School pools like this one are usually 25 yards or 25 meters. That's called short course. So my 41 seconds from the big pool can't be compared with what I'll swim here. It's a different race, even if it sounds the same."

"Then your card time is biased," Ziad said. "It makes you look slower than you are."

Or faster, Willow thought grimly, and there was only one way to find out. The whistle blew. She pulled her cap down, stepped onto the block, and gripped the edge with her toes. Ms. Sandhu raised her clipboard.

"Swimmers, take your marks."

Willow crouched low, staring at the far wall, and when the beep cracked through the humid air she dove.

The community centre had the rink on one side of the hallway and the pool on the other, so Addison could hear skates scraping while she stood shivering at the shallow end in her swimsuit. Through the big window, her friend Raylan was orbiting the ice in slow loops, waiting for Sullivan to finish his goalie drills so they could play one-on-one until Addison's lesson ended. Raylan wanted to score on Sullivan more than anything, and he'd told her that morning, "He's never let me get one past him. Not once."

Mr. Aziz, the lifeguard, blew his whistle. "Twenty-five metres, front crawl, whenever you're ready, Addison." Addison pushed off and kicked like a frog in a blender. Her legs pumped and churned, her knees bending hard on every beat, and she grabbed the wall having travelled maybe five metres, breathing like a dragon. A boy in the next lane, all knobby knees and easy arms, slid past her barely making a splash. That was the part that bothered her. He wasn't trying even half as hard, and he was crossing the pool like a torpedo while she puttered like a bathtub toy.

She floated on her back and thought. Her kick came from her knees, bent and frantic, but his legs stayed almost straight, like two long oars, and the movement seemed to start higher up, at his hips. Maybe her knees were the problem. Maybe all that bending was dragging on the water like a parachute. She had to test it. She pushed off again, kept her legs fairly straight, and let the kick come from her hips instead. It felt lazy at first, like she was barely doing anything, but the tiles of the pool floor slid past faster than before. She turned her head to the side, took a breath, turned back, and kept going. The far wall arrived under her hand.

"That's the one!" Mr. Aziz called, and the boy in the next lane gave her a thumbs up between strokes.

Raylan appeared at the window, hair dripping sweat, holding his stick like a trophy. "I scored on Sullivan! Five-hole! Did you see my lap?" He pointed at the ice, where Sullivan stood in the goalie net, shaking his mitt at the ceiling.

"I was busy," Addison said, grinning, "but watch this." She set off again, hips driving her kick, straight legs slicing, one side breath, two, three, and her hand slapped the wall. She looked up at the window and Raylan shouted, muffled through the glass, "Now who's the five-hole?"

The group chat had been quiet all afternoon, which was strange, because Elora usually posted at least eleven messages before lunch. Emile refreshed the chat on his tablet and stared at the last message, which was from Nellie: "Meet at the park at 4?" Nobody had answered. He wondered whether the others were busy, or whether the message had just slipped up the screen and gotten lost, the way a message could when nobody replied and it sank under newer things.

At 3:52, Elora's name lit up the chat. The message read, in huge letters, "WHERE ARE YOU." Emile sat back. The letters looked enormous on his screen, like Elora had smashed the keyboard with both fists. A second later, Nellie replied, "why are you yelling?" Emile read that twice. Yelling? Elora hadn't made a single sound.

He typed back, "we're coming, meet at the swings." Then, quietly, without the others seeing, he opened a private message to Elora and wrote, "why all caps?" A private chat was different, he had noticed. It was like whispering behind a cupped hand at lunch, while the group chat was more like standing up in the middle of the cafeteria and shouting something everyone could read.

Elora's reply came fast. "nobody answered nellie so i thought caps would get noticed." Emile tilted his head. So the capitals weren't anger at all. She had used them like a bright flag, something to make people look. It was a strange rule, he thought, that big letters made people hear shouting even when nobody was shouting. Where had that rule even come from? Could you find it written down anywhere, or did everyone just agree on it somehow?

At the park, Elora was kicking wood chips near the swings, her phone still in her hand. "Did it work?" she asked. "Did everyone see it?"

"Everybody saw it," Nellie said, arriving on her bike with one pedal still spinning. "Emile's little brother learned about engines this week and even he saw it. He keeps saying 'piston' at dinner."

"That's a machine part," Emile said. "And capitals are like that too. They push the message harder." Elora frowned, then grinned, and pulled out her phone. She typed something and held the screen up so they could both read it. It said, "sorry i yelled. sort of."

"It's fine," Nellie said. "Just do it again if the chat goes quiet for a whole hour."

"Deal," Elora said, and typed one more message into the group chat, small letters, all lowercase: "ok but next time you two answer faster." She pressed send, pocketed the phone, and ran for the swings.

The bus was leaving the historic site at two thirty, sharp, and Ms. Ngo had already promised that anyone left behind would become "part of the exhibit." Dylan took this as a personal challenge, not because he wanted to stay, but because the old farmhouse had one thing he could not stop staring at: a writing desk in the corner with a dark, shiny patch worn right into the wood.

He drifted toward it while the guide talked about candle molds. His fingers were halfway to the patch when Jagger grabbed his sleeve like a lifeguard. "Whoa. You can't touch that. Ms. Ngo said. The oils and salts from your skin build up over time and stain the wood, or damage the surface. That's why they put ropes around everything."

Dylan pulled his hand back and stared at the dark patch again. Something clicked. "Wait. If skin oils build up over time and stain the surface, then that patch is like a fingerprint collection. Hundreds of hands. Maybe the family counted their money there, or wrote letters, or did homework, even." Victor wandered over, chewing the strap of his backpack. "That's not a credible theory. It's a desk. Desks get used. Case closed, detective."

"It's not just used," Dylan said. "The stain has a shape. Look, it's not everywhere, it's in one band along the front edge. That's an anomaly, Victor. It means people stood on one side, over and over, for years." Victor squinted at the desk, then at the window beside it. "Okay, or the sun hits it there." Dylan considered that, then shook his head. "Sun fades wood. This is darker. And shinier."

The guide was already moving the group toward the kitchen, and the clock on the mantel said 2:15, which meant fifteen minutes before the bus became a memory and they became history. Dylan raised his hand like he was launching it off his wrist. "Can you cite any record of who used the desk? Like letters or inventories?"

The guide blinked, then smiled. "As a matter of fact, yes. The middle daughter ran the farm's accounts from that desk for forty years. Standing at the front edge, where the light from this window fell on her ledger."

"Ha!" Dylan spun around to Victor and Jagger, pointing at the dark band of forty years of ledger-keeping. "Standing. Front edge. I told you."

"You got lucky," Victor said, but he was grinning.

"Excuse me," the guide added, "I'd ask you not to high-five next to the desk."

Dylan and Jagger froze, palms hovering in the air, and backed away to the sound of the whole class laughing at them.

Lily slid her draft across the library table until it bumped Archie's elbow. "Read this and tell me what's wrong with it."

Archie read. "Nothing's wrong with it. It's good."

"See, that's the problem. You can't see anything in it." She tapped the page. "My whole field trip essay is 'nice' and 'interesting' and 'good.' My grandmother read it last night and asked me what exactly was nice about the trip. I said, you know, nice. She said the word gives my opinion without showing anything, and a concrete detail lets the reader picture it and judge."

"That sounds like something a grandmother would enforce at dinner," Archie said.

"She did. She wouldn't pass the potatoes until I answered."

Lily picked up her pencil and read her opening sentence aloud, quietly, because Mr. Bekele was reshelving books two rows over and his rule about voices was the one rule he actually enforced. "The science museum was very interesting." She crossed out "very interesting." Now she had "The science museum was." She stared at it.

Himmat dropped into the third chair with his backpack, which was, as always, perpendicular to the table instead of under it, so everyone had to step around him. "What are we doing?"

"Concrete details," Lily said. "Apparently 'good' and 'interesting' are words you write when you haven't decided what actually happened."

Himmat looked wounded. "I use those words."

"You do. Your volcano essay said the demonstration generator was 'cool.' Was it loud? Did it spark? Did it smell like burnt toast? Cool tells me nothing except that you liked it."

"It did smell like burnt toast," Himmat admitted. "The whole lab did."

Lily wrote that down. Then she kept going, testing each sentence the way her grandmother had tested her: if the word only gave her opinion, out it came. The giant turbine became a wheel taller than Mr. Bekele. The good exhibit became the one where you cranked a handle and a light bulb glowed faintly, then died, then glowed again. The nice bus ride home became thirty-seven minutes of Archie humming one song without stopping.

"I heard that," Archie said, not looking up.

"You were meant to." She read her new opening under her breath: sentences short, then long, then short again, like her grandmother's own storytelling, which never used the same rhythm twice in a row. She turned the page around and slid it back across the table. "Now tell me what's wrong with it."

Archie read. "Nothing's wrong with it. It's good."

Lily raised her pencil. "Try that again with a detail."

Emilia counted the boxes in the empty living room of apartment 4C. Thirteen boxes, one cat carrier, and zero friends. Back in her old town, she and Maggie had run a two-person detective guild that met every Saturday, and here there was nothing to detect, unless you counted the strange smell drifting from apartment 3A.

On the fourth morning, Emilia cried into a photo of her old street, the one with the crooked oak and Maggie waving from her porch. She hated that it kept happening. It made no sense, either, because the new apartment was fine, and the new school was fine, so something had to be causing it. She decided to investigate, the way the guild would. She took a notebook and wrote down every time the heavy feeling hit, then looked for a pattern. The notes said: Monday, seeing the photo. Tuesday, hearing her old ringtone. Wednesday, passing a girl in the hallway who laughed like Maggie.

"Hypothesis," she wrote. "It only shows up when something reminds me of home. So maybe if I add new things, the reminders will dwindle." It was a guess about something she could not see, some hidden rule working inside her, but a guess could be tested.

The test was simple. Each day she added one new thing: she learned the names of three neighbors, including Ms. Fitzgerald, who lived downstairs and fed pigeons from her window; she found the bodega that sold the same brand of hot chocolate as the shop on her old street; and she wrote down the smell from 3A, which turned out to be curry, and which Ms. Fitzgerald said came every Friday at six.

By the second Friday, Emilia still teared up at the photo, but only a little, and only for a minute. In the courtyard after school, a girl named Iyla asked what she was writing, then stole the notebook and read her hypothesis out loud in a dramatic announcer voice. "The detective guild needs a local chapter," Iyla declared, "and I already have a case. Somebody keeps leaving mitten yarn on the stairs, and the pattern is volatile, one day green, one day gray, no warning."

Emilia laughed, a real one, the first since the move. That night she video-called Maggie and told her about the yarn mystery, and about the crying, too, because a guild partner deserved the whole file. "My mom calls that homesickness," Maggie said. "It just means missing home and your people. It's basically the official moving side effect."

Emilia wrote it in the notebook: homesickness, being away from home and familiar people, common after a move, usually eases as you settle in. Then, underneath it, she wrote Saturday's plan, underlined twice. "Yarn stakeout, stairs, six o'clock. Bring snacks. Case 002."

Quinn stood at the phone counter with her mother, watching the cashier run the final settlement for her very first phone. "Bus leaves in twenty minutes," her mother said, tapping the counter. Quinn slid the box open right there, because she wanted the flashlight app installed before the mall lights went dim in the parking garage.

She found the app and pressed install. Then a box popped up on the screen, and she winced. The flashlight app wanted permission to use her contacts. All of them. It also wanted her microphone and her camera. A flashlight needs light, she thought, not Avleen's phone number. Behind her, Stefan waved from the accessory shop across the aisle. "Quinn! Try the glow puzzle app, it's amazing!"

Stefan hurried over, his own phone in hand. "Watch, you tilt it and the pieces light up." He held out his screen, and Quinn noticed something odd. The top of his phone showed a tiny green dot, glowing steadily, even though he was only showing her a puzzle. She borrowed the demo phone on the counter and checked. On the puzzle app's page it listed the same strange permissions: camera, microphone, contacts.

"It's not logical," she said. "A puzzle doesn't need to hear me." She pressed install anyway on the demo, denied every permission it asked for, and the game still ran fine. Then she dug into the phone's settings and found the permissions listed there, with little switches beside them. "You can take permission away later in settings," she told Stefan, and she reached over and flicked off his puzzle app's microphone. The green dot vanished.

Stefan stared at the dark dot, then at her. "Wait. Mine's been on how long?"

Quinn grabbed the box, receipt and bag, and caught her mother's sleeve. Ten minutes to the bus. Stefan raced alongside them, already scrolling. "Quinn, it also had my camera on. Can you look at my settings too?"

"Meet me at school," she called over her shoulder, phone warm in her pocket. "First bell, seven forty-five."

Cole crouched at the tide line with three plastic buckets labeled igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic, wondering which bucket deserved the speckled gray rock in his hand. Winnie dropped a black stone into the igneous bucket without hesitating.

"That one's easy," she said. "It came out of a volcano, so it's magma rock."

"Lava rock," said Shreya, from her perch on a driftwood log. "Not magma."

"It's the same thing, Shreya."

"It's not. Molten rock underground is called magma, but once it erupts onto the surface it's called lava." Shreya said it fast, like she'd been saving it.

Cole turned the speckled rock over. Yesterday Ms. Liu had set a chunk of glassy basalt on his desk and asked where it had cooled. He'd guessed wrong then, deep underground, and she'd only smiled and said to look for bubbles. Now he held the rock up to the light and saw tiny frothy holes, like a chocolate bar someone had whipped with a fork. Bubbles meant gas, and gas meant air, which meant the rock had melted out in the open. Not magma. Lava. Igneous, bucket one.

"Winnie," he said, "look at the holes. If it cooled down there, underground, no bubbles. This one erupted." He set it in the igneous bucket with a click.

Winnie frowned, picked up her black stone, squinted at it, then held it out. "Okay, fine, what about this one?"

Out past the breakers a fishing boat roared by, its propeller churning white water, and gulls wheeled up screaming as if a storm were imminent. Cole wished he could coordinate a drone to fly over the cliff at the beach's far end, where dark bands of rock slanted down toward the water, some layers tilted and wavy like someone had folded a sandwich. Metamorphic, probably. But for now he had Winnie's stone.

"Bubbles," he said, pointing at its surface, "and look, little sparkles. That's the same stuff as mine."

Winnie dropped it back in the igneous bucket and grabbed another rock. "Test me on the next one."

The argument started over the potato salad, which was typical for Aunt Renata's backyard parties. Jacqueline, Ellie's cousin, had brought a beaded bracelet she made at her grandmother's reserve up north, and Sarina, who lived next door and had crashed the party because her own family reunion got rained out, took one look at it and said, "You don't count as Anishinaabe, though. Your mom's not status, right? My uncle says you have to prove it with a card."

"The card," Jacqueline said, "is not the boss of me."

Ellie chewed her forkful of potato salad and watched. She liked watching these two, because their opinions tended to fluctuate depending on who had spoken last, which meant the argument could pivot from bracelet to card to blood quantum to Sarina's uncle, sometimes all in one breath. But underneath all that swerving, she noticed a fixed question neither of them had said out loud: who actually gets to decide which group a person belongs to? The card people? The uncles? The person herself?

She had a theory. If belonging were only about cards, then nobody whose paperwork had burned in a fire, or gotten lost, or never been issued, could ever belong to anyone, and that seemed too dumb to be a real rule. Real rules usually got written down somewhere bigger than an uncle's opinion. So she pulled out her phone behind the dessert table and typed in "who decides if you are Indigenous international."

The answer came up fast. She read it twice, then walked back to the picnic table and held the phone out between them like a plate of something.

"United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples," she read. "Adopted on 13 September 2007. It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership."

"That's it?" Sarina said. "Peoples, plural. Meaning the nations."

"Meaning not your uncle," Jacqueline said.

Sarina frowned at the screen, clearly checking whether she'd been gullible, then shrugged. "Fine. Then I'm telling him at Thanksgiving. Also, your bracelet is better than the ones he makes, but don't tell him I said that."

"Too late," said Jacqueline, threading the bracelet onto Sarina's wrist. "It's yours now, that's the rule."

Alice crouched beside the camp stove, turning the chicken pieces with a fork while her dad gathered firewood down the trail. He had put her in charge of supper, which meant she was supposed to supervise the whole meal, and so far nothing had burned. That felt like a victory.

Jude and Darien wandered over from the next campsite, drawn by the smell. "You're making that look good," Jude said, hopping onto the picnic table bench. Darien peered into the pot and asked what else they were having.

"Chicken, rice, and a big salad," Alice said. "The lettuce is in the cooler." She lifted the chicken out of the pan and set it on a plate, then reached for the cutting board to chop the lettuce. Her hand stopped halfway. The board was dotted with spots of raw chicken juice, and a small pool had collected in one corner.

She stood there thinking. She couldn't see anything wrong with the board. It looked almost clean, just damp. But she remembered a poster in the school kitchen from last year's cooking unit, red letters and a picture of a knife. The words had come back to her at exactly the wrong moments, usually during math, and now they arrived at the right one. She had copied it into her notebook once, and she could still picture her own handwriting.

"Wait," she said out loud. Jude and Darien both looked up. "If I chop the lettuce on the board the raw chicken touched, the bacteria from the chicken could spread to the salad. It's called cross-contamination." She pulled a clean board from the dish tub, washed it at the pump, and dried it on a towel. The old board went into the wash bin, and she scrubbed her hands afterward, too, just to be thorough.

"That's why my mom uses different colors," Jude said. "Red board for meat, green for vegetables." Darien nodded slowly, like a rule he'd heard a hundred times had finally become real.

When her dad came back with an armload of wood, Alice told him what she'd almost done. He admitted, a bit guiltily, that their old two-board system back home had gone obsolete when one cracked and they never replaced it. "So we've been using one board for everything since March," he said. "I keep meaning to fix that."

Alice served the salad last, from its own board, under its own clean knife. Jude took a second helping and pointed his fork at the pot. "Tomorrow you supervise, and we'll be your assistants."

Bennett stood in Charlie's kitchen with his shoes off, back against the doorframe where Charlie's family had marked heights every birthday since kindergarten. The pencil hovered an inch above his last mark from June.

"Stop sucking in your chin," Charlie said. "You're not a turtle."

Bennett held still while Charlie drew the line. When he stepped away, they both stared at it. Three quarters of an inch since summer. Three quarters, in five months.

"That's it?" Bennett said. "Aylan grew like two inches over the summer alone. His mom keeps buying him pants and he keeps ruining them."

Charlie leaned against the counter, chewing a granola bar. "My cousin says it stops eventually. Like, your bones just quit."

"That can't be right. Bones don't just quit." Bennett slid down to sit on the kitchen floor, because thinking went better sitting down. If bones quit growing, there had to be a reason, and if there was a reason, there might be a way to check on it. He pulled out his phone. "Ask it."

"Ask what?"

"How bones know when to stop."

Charlie typed it in, his diligent thumbs working fast, and they read the answer off the small screen together. Bones grew longer at the growth plates, near the ends, and once those plates closed after puberty, a person stopped getting taller.

"Growth plates," Bennett said slowly. "So they're like, doors. And puberty slams them shut."

"Locked," Charlie said, and mimed turning a key.

Bennett scrolled further and found an X-ray image, some kid's wrist, with the plates showing as dark gaps. "Look. You can actually see them. They're right there at the ends." He turned the phone so Charlie could see, and Charlie's reputation for being unimpressed by everything took a hit, because he leaned in close and went, "Whoa."

"So the question," Bennett said, "is whether mine are still open."

"You can't X-ray yourself, man."

"No, but I can do math." He grabbed a napkin and a pen from the junk drawer. His marks on the doorframe went back years, and he was the kind of kid who kept a growth chart in his own bathroom at home too. If he was still growing, even three quarters of an inch, the doors were still open. He started copying down the dates.

"Is this why you've been eating all my granola bars?" Charlie asked.

Bennett paused, mid-calculation. "Partly."

"You could have just said."

"I'm building bones here, Charlie. It's a project." He put the pen between his teeth, took another bar, and got back to the numbers.

Levi stood in his grandmother's kitchen on a snowy February morning, staring at the grocery list she had written for his birthday cake. Strawberries, it said, underlined twice, because Levi's favorite cake was strawberry, and his grandmother never did things halfway. Then she coughed in the next room, and Levi remembered why he was the one going to the store: her allergy to cold air made her eyes swell and her throat itch, so on bitter days she stayed inside.

At the little grocery near her house, the strawberries sat in a plastic box, shiny and red, priced at almost seven dollars. Seven dollars! In summer, Levi knew, the farm stand by the river sold whole baskets for two. He picked up the box, put it down, and picked it up again. His friend Molly from school had once portrayed a grocery shopper in their class play, haggling over tomatoes, and now Levi wished she were here to help him argue with somebody.

Instead he studied the label. It said the berries came from a country far to the south, where it was warm right now. Levi turned the box over in his hands, thinking. The strawberries in summer grew in fields nearby, so they just rode a short way in a truck. These winter berries had to be trucked or flown in from warmer places, and that long trip must cost money, which had to be part of why they cost so much. He remembered Mr. Farah-Ali, his neighbor, saying once that when something is scarce and people still want it, the price climbs, and when there is plenty, it sinks.

Levi counted his grandmother's ten dollar bill, took the box to the register, and paid. Back at her house, he set the berries on the counter and sliced them himself so she would not have to touch the cold juice. As he slid the first strawberry onto her plate, he said, "Now you get summer in February."

She smiled and popped it into her mouth.

Camille sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her laptop open to a government website, a granola bar in one hand and a notebook in the other. Her homework was to explain how a bill became a law, and she had picked a real bill about banning single-use plastics to follow. The problem was that the website kept using words like "second reading" and "Senate," and she could not tell how far the bill had actually gotten or how much road was left.

On a video call, Vada leaned toward her own screen. "Just say it goes through the government and becomes a law," Vada said. "That's basically it, right?"

"That's not basically it," Camille said. "Look, I counted the stages on the tracking page. It has to pass three readings in the House of Commons, and then three readings again in the Senate. Six votes total before it can even get royal assent." She circled the numbers in her notebook, one through six, like rungs on a ladder. "This bill just finished its second reading in the House. So I can figure out exactly how many stages are left. Four. That's the part nobody tells you."

Vada looked skeptical, so Camille scrolled back through the bill's history to test her idea. Every line matched: first reading, second reading, then a pause while a committee studied it, then third reading still to come. When Vada insisted that the Senate part probably did not count, Camille pointed at the site's status bar, which showed the House stages checked off and the Senate ones sitting empty. "You can't refute the checklist," she said. "It's right there."

The insight hit her while she was drawing a diagram: the whole thing was like a relay race with two runners, the House handing off to the Senate, and royal assent as the finish line. If either runner dropped the baton, the bill died and they had to start over. She wrote that at the top of her page, then checked the calendar. The site said the third reading was scheduled for next month, which meant she could actually watch the next stage happen in real time, like tracking a package.

"Is watching a bill even a real thing to do for fun?" Vada asked.

"Way more feasible than my last idea, which was memorizing every MP's name," Camille said. She set her alarm for the morning of the third reading, penciled the date onto the diagram, and drew a small crown next to the finish line. "When it gets royal assent, I'm coloring the whole page gold."

Simon had watched the legislature on TV for forty minutes waiting for the big speech about the new bill, and nothing happened. A clerk read the bill's title, the Speaker said a few words, and then everyone moved on. Simon slumped on the couch. "They forgot the debate," he told his dad, who just said the class field trip to the town hall meeting on Saturday might help him figure it out.

At the town hall, Ms. Sow had set up a long table with folders, one for every student. "You each get to move a bill through our model legislature," she said. "Simon, you're first." Simon stood up, gripped his folder, and launched into a speech about his bill to make the skating rink free on Saturdays, listing all the reasons it was fair and how much family income it would save. He talked for two full minutes before Ms. Sow raised her hand.

"That's not what happens at this stage," said Vera from the second row. "Watch." She stood, held up her own bill about fixing the cracked basketball court, and said only, "I move that this bill be introduced and printed." Then she sat down. Simon blinked. "That's it?" he asked. "That's it," Vera said. "It's called first reading. No debate yet. The bill gets introduced and printed so everyone can read it before they argue about it later."

Simon thought back to the TV. No wonder there was no speech. It was the first reading, and the debate came after, once the printed bill was in everyone's hands. He tried again, word for word: "I move that Bill Twelve be introduced and printed." Ms. Sow stamped his folder, and Sophia whispered, "See? Shortest speech ever, and it still counts." Simon grinned and slid the folder down the table to be copied for every member.

Florence dumped a shoebox of supplies onto the kitchen table: translucent blue beads, gray clay, a tangle of craft wire, and a printout of the periodic table she'd been allowed to take home from Mr. Chea's class. Each student had to participate by building a model of an atom, and hers was due Friday. There was only one problem, and it was a big one. She had no idea how many of anything to use.

Her friend Samantha had wanted the coolest element in the room, which was why Samantha had chosen gold and was already painting ping-pong balls shiny. "What did you get?" Samantha asked, appearing at the door with her backpack still on. Florence slid the periodic table across the table and pointed at the box marked C. "Carbon. But look, there's this little 6 on it, and I don't know what it's counting. Six what? Beads? Electrons? Grams of clay?"

Samantha squinted at the paper. "My gold has a 79. If it's counting something, that's a lot of something." They tried a theory: maybe the number counted electrons, since electrons were the small ones that spun around the outside. Florence strung six blue beads onto a wire ring and held it up. Then she frowned. "But if it's electrons, how do I know how many protons go in the middle? There has to be a rule, or nobody could build any of these." She turned the printout over and found a note in Mr. Chea's handwriting at the bottom. It read: "Dear builders. That number is the atomic number. It is the number of protons in the nucleus of each of its atoms. Every carbon atom, for example, has exactly 6 protons. Build carefully, and don't eat the clay. Mr. Chea."

Florence read it twice, then laughed so hard she had to sit down. "It's protons! Six protons, right in the middle!" She pinched off six balls of gray clay and squashed them together with some extra blobs for neutrons, then rehung her six electrons on the wire ring. Samantha held up her gold model, which now had seventy-nine clay balls crammed into a nucleus the size of an orange. "This," Samantha said, "is the heaviest fruit ever."

Florence balanced her carbon atom on a fork so the electrons could spin, and gave it one slow twist to watch it go.

The sign in the window said the trade-in deal ended at six o'clock sharp, and it was already ten past five. Grace stood at the counter while Mr. Vu slid a slim black phone across the glass, the same model her cousin had, though her cousin's had a case made of that synthetic leather that peeled after a month. She picked this one up anyway, holding it like something that might go off.

"First phone," said Mr. Vu, watching her face. "Big deal."

"Big responsibility," Grace said, mostly because of last summer. She could still remember sitting on Dalia's back steps, spelling out her password out loud, letter by letter, so Dalia could log in on the library laptop.
