"Luca, over here," called Ms. Morin, his art teacher, who organized the event. She pointed to a three-tiered table covered with purple paper. "This is our class's ofrenda." Luca set the box down and looked around at the other altars. Every single one had photographs on it, and candles, and little clay skeletons laughing and dancing. His class's ofrenda had the paper and the flowers but no photos at all.

"Why do they all have pictures?" he asked Mathilde, who was folding paper flowers nearby. She shrugged. Morgane came rushing over from the craft table, holding a small framed photo of an old man with white hair and a wooden cane.

"It's my bisabuelo," Morgane said. "My great-grandfather. He came from Oaxaca. My mom said to bring it tonight because the celebration honors family members who have died, and the altars are how we invite them back to visit."

Luca looked at the empty top tier of their table. "So everybody in our class could bring a photo tomorrow? The celebration goes on through November first and second, right? That's what the schedule says." Morgane nodded. "Then tonight we put your photo up, and tomorrow we ask everyone else."

He was a little embarrassed to ask the whole class, in case someone thought it was strange, but Ms. Morin overheard him and said, "That's the best idea I've heard all evening." So the next afternoon, Luca stood at the front of his classroom with Morgane, and they explained that anyone who wanted could bring a picture of a grandparent or a great-grandparent, or even a pet. He held up a photo of his own grandfather, who had died two years before, standing in front of a bakery with flour on his hands.

By the last day, the ofrenda looked nothing like the bare table it had been. There were eleven photos, four candles, a plate of pan de muerto that Mathilde's aunt had baked, and a toy fire truck that Luca had brought because his grandfather had driven a delivery van and loved anything with wheels. Visitors to the center stopped and looked, and one woman pressed her hands together in front of the photos.

"You know," Ms. Morin said quietly, standing beside him, "I was worried nobody would come to our altar. You gave it a reason to be here."

Luca lit one more candle and set it beside his grandfather's picture, watching the flame lean sideways in the draft from the open door.

Ms. Joshi set a white ball on the table under one lamp and said, "Today we make it look round on flat paper." Livia squinted at the ball, at the bright spot near the top, at the dark curve underneath. She wanted her drawing to look solid enough to pick up, and she pressed hard with her pencil to get there fast.

She shaded the whole lower half as dark as her pencil would go, then looked again. Something was off. Next to her, Delphine was doing the opposite, rubbing her eraser along the bottom edge of her sphere until the paper shone almost white. "I read that the shadow side isn't all dark," Delphine said happily. Livia leaned over and frowned. Delphine's ball had a bright spot on top and a pale rim along the bottom, as if two lamps were aimed at it from opposite directions.

"There's only one lamp," Livia said. "So the bottom can't be that light. But it isn't all black either." She held her pencil at arm's length and compared it against the ball. The bottom edge of the shadow side was a little lighter than the middle of the shadow, but clearly darker than anything on the lit side. She decided to test it. She shaded the center of the shadow darkest of all, then lightened her pressure toward the bottom edge, keeping that rim well darker than the top. When she propped the drawing beside the ball, it finally looked like one lamp was doing all the work.

"Mine looks like it has two light sources," Delphine said, her eraser hovering.

"Make the bottom edge lighter than the middle of the shadow, but still darker than the lit side," Livia said. "Ms. Joshi called that reflected light this morning. Light bounces back from the table onto the shadow side." Delphine redid her rim with a careful, gentle stroke, and her sphere turned from a flat cookie into something you could hold. Across the table Elias was hiding a smile behind his hand because his own ball had come out shaped like an egg, and Livia slid her spare pencil, a softer one, toward him without a word.

"Careful with that eraser," she told Delphine. "Keep rubbing and the paper will erode right through." Ms. Joshi walked past their table and tapped Delphine's drawing once. "That's a good sphere," she said. "Remember, it's not a metaphor for anything today. It's just light on a ball." Livia laughed, then turned back to add the soft cast shadow stretching from under her sphere across the table, a smear of gray, transparent where it thinned at the edge, dark where it met the ball. "Hold it still," she said, sliding the drawing next to the real one. "Which one is which?"

The sun was already hot on the barn roof when Chloe climbed the ladder with her sketchpad. She had promised Ms. Lombardi she would document a full food chain from the farm for the science fair, starting with grass and ending with the hawk that circled the north field every afternoon. She drew grass, then a grasshopper, then a mouse, then the hawk, and she felt pretty good about it until her friend Dash came huffing up the ladder with a tablet under his arm.

"You have to watch this," he said. "It's about creatures at the bottom of the ocean. Tube worms as tall as your arm, and crabs, and these fish nobody had ever seen, all living where sunlight can't reach. Zero light. Totally dark." He pressed play and let the tablet rest on the shingles between them. A narrator's voice said that in 1977, scientists in a submersible called Alvin found deep-sea vent communities whose food chains start with bacteria that use chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.

Chloe stared at the screen. "That can't be right," she said. "Every food chain starts with the sun. That's the whole rule. Ms. Lombardi even said so." Dash shrugged and scrolled back so she could watch again. The screen showed pale crabs swarming around a smoking black chimney on the seafloor, and Chloe thought about her drawing, with its neat arrow from the sun to the grass. If the rule was wrong, then her poster was wrong, and the science fair was in three days.

That night she wrote to her cousin Robin, who loved ocean stuff.

Dear Robin, she wrote. Does every food chain really start with the sun? Dash showed me a documentary about the Alvin submarine in 1977, with vent animals living in complete darkness. The bacteria there use chemicals from the vents instead of sunlight. Is that a legitimate food chain or some weird exception? If it's real, I have to change my whole poster. Please answer fast. Chloe.

Robin's reply came the next morning: Legitimate! The ocean floor is full of them. Check whether sunlight is really the necessary variable, or just the one you can see.

Chloe taped a second strip of paper to her poster. On the left, the sun shone down on the farm chain. On the right, in dark blue marker, she drew a vent chimney and its bacteria, crabs above them, and a question mark at the top where a predator would be. She also added a folded flap over the mouse in the farm chain, and when Ms. Lombardi asked what it was, Chloe lifted it to reveal blank paper.

"If the mice disappear, the hawk loses its food," she said. "I'm testing whether the chain still works with one link gone."

Ms. Lombardi leaned closer to the blue side of the poster. "And this one starts with what, exactly?"

"Chemicals," Chloe said. "Not sunlight. The sun isn't the only beginning."

Dash grinned from the back of the room and gave the poster two thumbs up.

The playground had gone soft with late afternoon light, and Maeva sat on the low wall by the fence, her left arm resting in her lap like a question she could not answer. The cast had been white when the nurse wrapped it, but yesterday Maeva had chosen bright green for the new layer, and now Kale was drawing a row of tiny frogs along it. "Green was a bold choice," he said. "Heath said neon casts are controversial. He thinks they're too loud."

"They're not controversial," Maeva said. "They're just green." Her real worry was not the color. Something inside the cast itched, deep down where her fingers could not reach, and she had a theory about it. She had noticed the itch was worst right after PE, when she sweated, and almost gone in the morning. She reasoned it must be moisture trapped against her skin, though she could not see under the plaster to check. So she had a plan: today she would keep the arm completely dry and see if the itch stayed away.

Heath dropped onto the wall beside them, shaking a water bottle. "How did people even fix broken arms before casts?" he asked. "Did they just walk around with flopping arms forever?"

Maeva frowned. She had read a poster in the clinic waiting room while the doctor worked on her arm, mostly because there was nothing else to look at. "No. This Dutch army surgeon, Antonius Mathijsen, invented the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones, and he published how to do it in 1852. Before that nobody used this exact method." Heath looked at the cast with new respect, as if it had suddenly become older than the school.

At PE, Maeva sat out and kept her arm still and dry, holding it away from the sprinkler Ms. Anderson was using to water the flowerbeds by the gate. By the end of the hour the itch had faded to almost nothing, which meant her theory about trapped moisture was probably right, though she would test it again tomorrow to be sure. On the walk home she stopped at the corner store, bought a small towel with her pocket money, and tucked it carefully inside her backpack. "For drying off," she told Kale, "and for hygiene, so the skin under there stays clean."

The note from Mr. Doyle was taped to the gym door on Monday morning. "Class store opens Friday at lunch. Bring your product and your price. Signed, Mr. Doyle." Zack read it twice, then ran to find Kira and Sameer, who were already arguing by the water fountain.

"Strawberry cups," Sameer said. "My mom gets flats of them in summer for almost nothing. That's the whole reason I picked them." Kira frowned and pulled out her notebook. "But we're buying them in winter, Sameer. Winter strawberries cost way more. I looked it up last night." She showed him the numbers, and Zack felt his stomach tighten. If they charged what the berries cost them, nobody would buy.

Zack lay awake that night turning the problem over. Summer meant piles of strawberries everywhere, so prices sank. Winter meant almost none, so prices climbed. That part made sense. What he couldn't see was what would happen if they charged less than the berries were worth on Friday. He decided to test it, because a low price felt friendly, and friendly had to be good for business.

Friday came fast. They set up their table outside the cafeteria, and Sameer wrote "50 cents a cup" on a poster in thick red marker. The bell rang, and the line formed before Zack had even opened the cash box. Kids pressed forward, coins rattling. By the time Zack counted to three hundred seconds, the cups were gone, and behind the counter the table looked desolate, nothing left but empty trays and a smear of pink juice. The line stretched past the library, and the kids at the back were not smiling.

"You said fifty cents," a boy near the front complained. "I stood here the whole lunch for nothing." Kira stepped around the table and held up her hands. "We're really sorry. We'll bring more Monday, and we'll have enough, we promise." A few kids grumbled off toward the cafeteria, and one girl muttered that she'd been waiting since the bell. Zack watched them go and understood, all at once, what he had done. "We held our price below what the cups were really worth," he said quietly. "So buyers wanted more than we would offer. That's why we ran out." Sameer slumped against the table. "My dilemma is I want it cheap and I want there to be enough. Can't have both?"

Mr. Doyle walked over, counted the short, frustrated line, and raised an eyebrow at Zack. "Something you want to clarify for the class on Monday?" Zack picked up the empty tray and smiled. "Yeah. Strawberry economics. Two dollars a cup, and everybody gets one."

Maya set the mixing bowl on the picnic table and stared at the lump of dough inside it. Twenty minutes ago it had been a smooth little hill. Now it was still a smooth little hill, exactly the same size, while Jaida's dough in the next bowl had puffed up like a pillow.

"Why is yours rebellious?" Jaida asked, poking Maya's dough with one finger. It didn't spring back. "Mine's practically climbing out of the bowl."

Maya ran through her logic out loud. Same bag of flour, same packet of yeast, same spoonful of sugar. The only thing they had done differently was the water. Jaida had filled her jug from the big thermos of cool drinking water. Maya, in a hurry, had dipped hers from the pot that had been sitting on the camp stove. She pressed her palm against the side of her bowl. It was warm. Really warm, the kind of warm that would sting if you held your hand in it.

"Water too hot," she said slowly. "I think it did something to the yeast. Dead yeast can't eat the sugar, so it can't let out the gas that gets trapped in the dough as bubbles. No bubbles, no rising." She peeled open a corner of Jaida's dough and leaned close. Sure enough, tiny holes pocked the inside like a sponge. Her own dough, when she tore a piece open, was dense and smooth with no holes at all.

"So can you fix it?" Jaida asked. She wanted fresh bread before dinner, and the last of their trail snacks had dwindled to a sad handful of pretzels.

"There's one more yeast packet," Maya said. "I'll use the cold jug this time and warm it just a little with my finger in it."

They mixed a new batch together, and while they waited, Maya checked every five minutes until the surface of the dough trembled and swelled. Mr. Ivanova wandered past their site and lifted the cloth covering the bowls. "Smells like a bakery already," he said.

Maya grinned and slid the loaves toward the fire. "Watch the bubbles," she whispered.

The gymnasium smelled like potting soil and tape, and Kaylee balanced her poster board against the bleachers while she hunted for a free table. She found one near the equipment cage, right beside Jean, whose two bean plants sat in matching pots under a sign that read Does Music Help Plants Grow?

"Mine's about water temperature," Kaylee said, unpacking her watering bottles. "Cold versus room temperature, everything else the same." She held up a small brass valve she'd borrowed from her dad's garage. "This controls the drip so both pots get exactly the same amount. I have to keep it durable enough to survive three kids bumping the table."

Jean wasn't listening. She was staring at her plants, and one was tall and leaning while the other was short and straight. "They were identical," she said. "Same music, same soil, same water. I even measured. But the tall one only got tall this week, and I don't know why."

Kaylee crouched down to look. The tall plant was stretched sideways, reaching, its leaves turned one direction. She turned the pot slowly, then turned back. "Which one sat closer to the window?"

Jean looked up at the tall windows above the bleachers, then at her table. "The leaning one. It's been in that spot since Tuesday. I moved the whole setup to make room for Tyler's volcano."

"So it's not the music," Kaylee said. "In a fair test, every other condition has to stay the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one thing you changed." She said it slowly, checking it against her own experiment as the words came out. "Your one thing was supposed to be music. But sunlight snuck in there too, so now you can't tell what caused what."

Jean groaned and put her head in her arms. "The fair opens in forty minutes."

"Then swap them," Kaylee said. "Put both pots the same distance from the window, equal light on both sides, and start your counts over. Or, wait." Kaylee pointed at the other side of Jean's sign, which had room left. "You could keep the old data and elaborate on it. Write down what went wrong. Judges like it when you show how you caught a mistake."

Jean sat up. "Really? Not just crossed out and redone?"

"Mine almost fell apart twice," Kaylee said. "The valve dripped unevenly for two days before I caught it. I logged that too." She handed Jean a fresh index card and her own marker. "Here. Start with the window."

Tyler wandered over from his volcano, wiping baking soda off his hands, and read Jean's card while Jean wrote. "So the plant wasn't reaching toward the music," he said. "It was reaching toward the light."

"Exactly one variable," Jean said, and underlined the last line of her card.

By the time Mr. Cohen came around with his clipboard, Jean's table held two evenly lit pots, a drip valve borrowed from Kaylee's kit, and a sign that read, in fresh marker: A fair test keeps every other condition the same. The tall plant still leaned toward the window, stubborn and green, like it was pointing at the answer.

Emilia stood at the back of the town hall with her cue cards shaking in her hand. Her class had been assigned to explain how a bill becomes a law, and Mr. Lewandowski had arranged for three students to present at the actual town meeting, in front of actual adults. Sullivan had drawn a poster of a bill travelling through committee rooms and debate chambers, and Miguel had built a cardboard Parliament, but Emilia had the speaking part, and she had discovered last night that she did not understand her own part at all.

"The bill goes to the House of Commons, and then to the House of Lords," she whispered to Miguel, "and then it becomes law." She frowned at her cards. "But what if the Lords just say no? Forever? Then nothing ever becomes law."

"Then say they can't," Miguel said, indifferent to the whole problem, as he taped a paper flag to a cardboard tower.

Last summer, she remembered, she had sat on her grandmother's porch during a visit to England, complaining that her town council had voted down a skate park. Her grandmother had laughed. "You think that's stubborn? In Britain, the upper house isn't even elected. But they can't hold everything up. The Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 let the House of Commons pass most bills without the House of Lords' consent after about a year's delay." Emilia had been half listening then, more interested in her lemonade, but now the words came back whole.

She grabbed Miguel's arm. "That's the missing piece. The Lords can delay, but they can't block forever. About a year, and then the Commons can go ahead."

"You sure?" Miguel asked.

She wasn't sure, so she tested it. While the adults argued about the town budget, Emilia and Sullivan set up the cardboard Parliament on a folding table and simulated the whole thing, right there behind the coffee urn. Sullivan played the Lords and rejected everything with a lordly sniff. Miguel read a bill aloud. Emilia moved a paper clock around the tower, one printed month at a time, and at the twelfth month she pushed Sullivan's hand aside and marched the bill to the other end of the table. "Passed without your consent," she announced, quietly enough that only they could hear. Sullivan had insisted the Lords could veto anything they liked, and now he crossed his arms and admitted, "Fine. A year's delay, then it goes through. That's actually fair."

When Mr. Lewandowski called her name, Emilia walked to the microphone without the cards. She explained the committees, the votes, both houses. Then she held up the cardboard clock and said, "And if one house keeps saying no, it still isn't stuck. In the United Kingdom, the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 let the House of Commons pass most bills without the House of Lords' consent after about a year's delay." An old man in the front row, the one who had looked bored all evening, sat up straight and started to clap.

From the back, Miguel lifted the paper flag over the cardboard tower.

The cast on Theodore's left arm itched in three places he couldn't reach, and the doctor's office smelled like the inside of a band-aid. She clipped his X-ray to the light board and pointed with her pen.

"Two bones in there," she said. "The radius is the one on your thumb side. The ulna is on your little-finger side."

"Which one did I break?" Theodore asked, leaning closer.

"The ulna. See the crack, right near the little-finger side? You caught yourself with your hand open when you fell off the bike."

Theodore studied the picture. Two pale stripes, side by side like train tracks, and one of them had a thin dark line through it, like a hair laid across the track. He wiggled his little finger inside the cast, then his thumb. One of them was connected to that cracked stripe. It was strange to think about: the bones were under the cast, under the skin, and he couldn't see them, but he could still reason out which was which.

At school the next day, Ms. Zhang rearranged his desk to accommodate the cast, and Eileen carried his tray at lunch without being asked. At recess he sat on the bench by the soccer field, keeping score. Adley flopped down beside him, sweating.

"It was inevitable you'd end up scorekeeper," Adley said. "You fall off one bike and suddenly you're the bench guy."

Theodore ignored that. He was watching Aiden from the other team, who had missed his last three passes. All three went to the left, and all three were too high. "His passes keep going the same wrong way," Theodore said. "That's not bad luck. That's a pattern."

"So? He's just terrible."

"Or something's making it happen." Theodore stood, cupped his hands around his mouth, and called down the field. "Hey! Check your shoe!"

Aiden stopped, looked down, and pulled a folded page of newspaper out of the heel of his left cleat. He stared at it, laughed, and held it up like evidence.

Adley shook his head slowly. "Okay. Bench guy is now detective guy." He patted the empty spot on the bench. "Sit. Tell me everything you see."

Theodore sat, pulled the scorecard onto his knee with his good hand, and said, "Watch the sweeper. She marks on instinct, but she always cheats to the right. Somebody's going to notice that."

The house smelled like Grandma Ruth's lemon dish soap, even though she had been gone for nine days. Hailey stood in the kitchen holding the wooden spoon her grandmother had used for every batch of oatmeal cookies. In the living room, relatives were saying goodbye to the house itself before the sale sign went up tomorrow. Hailey had a problem she could not say out loud. She wanted to take the spoon home and use it, and she wanted to keep wearing Grandma's flowered apron, which she had already tied on that morning. But a magazine in the waiting room at the funeral home had said people needed to "move on" after a death, and she was not sure whether keeping things meant she was doing it wrong.

She decided to run a test. She put the apron and the spoon in a box marked DONATE, went outside, and sat on the porch steps to see how that felt. It felt like the day she had dropped her library book in the pond. She retrieved the apron within two minutes. The test had failed, which meant, if the magazine was right, that she was failing too.

Mr. Kobayashi, the neighbour from across the hedge, was watering his tomatoes. "Big day tomorrow," he said. Hailey told him about her test, and about the magazine. He wiped his hands on his shorts. "You could look up a book called Continuing Bonds," he said. "Ruth had it. 1996." Then he went back to his tomatoes, because he was a man who said things once and stopped.

Hailey found the book on the shelf behind Grandma's chair, between the cookbooks. It argued that keeping a connection to someone who had died, through memories, objects, or traditions, could be a healthy part of grieving. She read the sentence three times. The word "healthy" sat there on the page, plain as a kitchen timer. Nobody in the book said anything about moving on. She checked the index for "moving on" and it was not even listed, which made her laugh once, quietly, in the empty chair room.

On the last night in the house, Hailey invited Ally and Chance over, and the three of them made oatmeal cookies using the wooden spoon, following the recipe card in Grandma's handwriting. Ally creamed the butter while Chance read the steps out loud. Hailey stirred, and she thought about how Grandma had driven her to the clinic every autumn for her flu vaccine, and had always bought her a juice box after, and how none of that was trivial. She put one warm cookie on the windowsill, which Grandma used to do for the mail carrier. "That one's hers," Hailey said, and took the apron off the hook to wear tomorrow.

The puppy had been his for exactly four hours, and Nicholas had already named him Biscuit, mostly because of the pale patch on his back that had a kind of lopsided symmetry to it, like a cookie someone had bitten on one side. Biscuit was small enough to fit in a shoebox, curious about everything, and especially interested in Nicholas's backpack, which was lying open on the kitchen floor. "No, that's homework," Nicholas said, gently pulling the bag away. Biscuit sneezed, wobbled over to the water bowl, and then, while Nicholas wasn't looking, went back for a second try. Nicholas only noticed when he heard the crinkle of a foil wrapper.

He counted the gum pieces left in the pack. There had been eight, the sugar-free kind his mom bought, and now there were five. His stomach dropped. He had seen a poster at the animal shelter that morning, the one beside the cage where Biscuit had been sleeping in a curled-up ball like a nocturnal creature pretending the fluorescent lights weren't real. The poster had listed foods that were dangerous for dogs, and one line had jumped out at him: xylitol. He remembered turning the word over in his head, wondering what it even was. Now he dug the empty wrappers out from under the couch and found the word printed right there on the foil. His mom's sugar-free gum.

"Mom!" he shouted. "Biscuit ate three pieces of gum. The kind with xylitol in it." He was already scooping up the puppy, whose dark eyes refract... whose eyes caught the kitchen light and threw it back at him in two tiny bright points, as if Biscuit had no idea anything was wrong. "That's bad for dogs," his mom said, grabbing her keys. "I read that it makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar. It's not like it is for us. Call the vet, tell them we're coming."

At the clinic, Ms. Sadeghi, who turned out to be the veterinarian and also, impossibly, the mother of Nikola from his science class, took Biscuit behind the counter immediately. Nicholas stood at the window watching the sun refract through the fish tank in the waiting room, a small rainbow trembling on the wall, and tried not to imagine the worst. Through the door he heard her say, "We'll get his blood sugar up and watch him for a while. You caught it fast, and that matters." An hour later Biscuit came out wagging his whole back end, shameless, and Nikola appeared beside Nicholas with two juice boxes. "So my mom says your dog ate gum," Nikola said. Nicholas looked down at Biscuit, who was already sniffing Nikola's pocket. "Check your pockets," Nicholas said. "Check them right now."

The sign at the science museum said MAKE IT LIGHT UP, and Jayden grabbed the little model house before Khaleesi could. "I call dibs on the wiring," he said. "I've done this at school."

Khaleesi raised an eyebrow. "You shorted out a buzzer with a paperclip."

"That was a design choice."

Mr. Littlechild, the volunteer in the blue vest, set out the parts: a battery, a switch, a bulb, and a pile of wire. "The house has to light up when you flip the switch," he said. "That's the whole challenge."

Jayden snapped the wires into place, taped the battery in, and flipped the switch. Nothing. He flipped it again, faster, as if the bulb were just slow. Still nothing.

"Maybe the bulb's dead," Khaleesi said.

Jayden unscrewed the bulb and touched it straight to the battery. It glowed instantly. So the bulb was fine, which meant the problem was hiding somewhere he couldn't see. He stared at the loop of wire. The current had to travel all the way around, through the battery, the switch, and the bulb, or nothing happened. One gap anywhere stopped everything. Somewhere in that loop was a hole.

He'd been naive to trust the tape job, he decided. He walked the loop with one finger, wire by wire, and found it: a clip at the switch had slipped loose. He pushed it back until it clicked.

"Flip it," he said, and closed his eyes.

The bulb blazed. Khaleesi whooped so loudly that a toddler across the room pointed at their house in wonder.

"Okay," Khaleesi admitted, "you may keep your dibs. But when the bulb burns out, I'm rewiring it."

"You'd have to resign from Team Dibs first."

Jayden flipped the switch off, watched the light vanish, and flipped it on again just to feel the whole loop obey him at once. "See?" he said. "One gap, one finger, one click."

Blake sat at the kitchen table with a blank sheet of paper, a pencil, and two very different ideas about strawberries. Mr. Das had assigned each student one question: why do strawberries cost less in summer than in winter? Blake was supposed to explain it with a diagram.

He drew two lines that crossed like an X and labeled one "supply" and the other "demand." It looked right, but he could not say why. He stared at the crossing point and wondered who had first thought of drawing it that way. It seemed like a strange thing to invent, two lines fighting over a dot.

His phone buzzed. Valerie had sent a photo of her own diagram, which was, annoyingly, neater. "Yours looks like a broken kite," she texted. He called her.

"I have to confess something," he said. "I traced mine off a cereal box."

"That's not even a real thing."

"It could be." He put her on speaker and typed into the search bar: who made the supply and demand diagram famous. He read out loud as the page loaded. "Alfred Marshall. A British economist. He popularized it, the two crossing curves, in his 1890 book." He scrolled. "It's called Principles of Economics."

"Nineteen hundred years ago?" Valerie said.

"Eighteen ninety. That's still ancient. That's before television."

Blake looked back at his kite-shaped X and suddenly understood his own drawing. More strawberries in summer meant his supply line slid sideways, and the crossing point dropped to a lower price. Fewer in winter, and it climbed back up. He redrew the lines twice, once for each season, and wrote "cheap here" and "expensive here" in tiny letters.

"What if the whole thing is about empathy?" Valerie said. "Like, the farmer feels bad charging five dollars in January?"

"No, the farmer feels fine. The farmer has almost no strawberries."

Blake carried the paper to the fridge and pinned it under the strawberry-shaped magnet, which was, he now noticed, holding up a grocery list that included strawberries.

Kaitlyn stood alone at the center of the empty auditorium stage, script rolled tight in her fist. Mr. Hu had cast her as the girl who talks to the empty kitchen at midnight, and for three days she had been stuck. "Who am I even talking to?" she called down to the third row, where Leandro and Meadow sat with their feet on the seat backs.

"To nobody," Leandro said. "That's the whole point. It's a soliloquy, a speech a character gives alone on stage so the audience can hear her private thoughts."

Kaitlyn unrolled the script and looked at it differently now. She had presumed the speech needed an imagined listener, a friend standing invisible in the wings, but that was why it felt fake. The character wasn't performing for anyone. She was thinking out loud. She tried the first line again, slower, letting the words arrive like real thoughts instead of launched arrows. When she hit the line about the broken locket, she stopped, looked at her own hand, and let the pause stretch until Meadow leaned forward.

"That pause," Meadow said. "Do that one again."

They ran it six times. Kaitlyn experimented with a hypothetical question she raised for herself: what if she did the whole speech sitting on the stage edge, as if the character had given up standing? The fourth try was clumsy and the fifth was worse, but on the sixth something clicked, and Leandro whistled.

By Friday, word had spread that Kaitlyn's monologue was worth watching, and her reputation pulled a few stray sixth graders into the seats at lunch. Mr. Hu watched from the back, arms crossed, saying nothing until the end. Then he climbed the steps, nodded once, and said, "Opening night, you do it exactly like that."

Kaitlyn grinned and rolled her script even tighter, like a microphone.

At Hadassah's kitchen table, Lily typed her old blog's name into Hadassah's phone, chewing her thumbnail. Two years ago, in third grade, she had written a blog about her hamster, Biscuit, and she had deleted it last spring when she got embarrassed. Now Parker kept saying he'd found something, and she wanted to see for herself. "It's gone," she said. "I deleted it. I watched it disappear."

"Try this," Parker said, leaning over her shoulder. He typed the name of a website she'd never heard of, then pasted her blog's address into a search box. "My cousin showed me. It's called the Wayback Machine."

The page loaded, and Lily's stomach dropped. There was her blog, exactly as it had looked in third grade, pink background, wobbly hamster drawings and all. Below the address, a whole row of dates. "Since 1996," Hadassah read from a little note on the screen, "the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages." She scrolled, and snapshot after snapshot of Lily's old posts slid past. "So deleting it only deleted it for you."

Lily clicked the oldest post. There was Biscuit's cage, and behind it, propped against the wall, a piece of paper she'd photographed without thinking: the school permission slip with her full address printed at the top. She had been so proud of Biscuit's new wheel that she hadn't looked at anything else in the picture. "Anybody could read this," she said quietly. "Anybody at all."

"That's why I don't post where I am," Hadassah said, dunking a biscuit in her milk. "My mum says the internet never really hibernates. It just pretends to."

Parker grinned. "You've been feeding it like a consumer feeds a vending machine, and it keeps everything." Lily stuck her tongue out at him, but she was already drafting a message to the archive's help address on Hadassah's phone:

Dear Internet Archive, I am ten years old and my old blog has my home address on a slip of paper in a photo. I deleted the blog before I knew copies were saved. Could you please take that page down? I would appreciate it very much. Sincerely, Lily.

She read it out loud, and Hadassah said it sounded very grown up, except the part where she'd written that Biscuit had gone to live on a farm, which was technically true but also the defiant lie she'd told in third grade instead of saying he'd escaped for two days.

They sent the message. Then Lily opened the camera app and turned it around, so the screen showed only the ceiling and Hadassah's laughing face. "New rule," she said. "From now on, we photograph the wheel, not the wall."

Vincent stood in the middle of the empty living room, his voice bouncing off bare walls. The moving truck had come that morning, and tomorrow it would carry everything to the new town, six hours away. He had argued against the move for weeks, doing everything he could to oppose his parents' plan, and he had lost. Now his sneakers squeaked on the wooden floor, and the only sound in the whole house was his own footsteps.

His phone buzzed. It was Mika, calling from the porch next door, where she sat on the railing swinging her legs. "I figured out something," she said. "My cousin moved to Denver three years ago and she never calls anybody, and now she doesn't have a single friend from here. But my grandma moved away from her best friend when she was our age, and they still talk every single week. They visit each other and send messages and everything." Vincent turned in a slow circle, thinking. Friends who stayed close were friends who kept in touch, and friends who faded were the ones who let the contact stop. It was a real pattern, not just a guess. If the inference was right, then the whole thing depended on what he and Mika did next, not on the distance. "So we can't just say goodbye and hope," he said. "We have to actually plan it."

"Exactly," said Mika. "That's what I want. Sunday afternoons, video call, every week. Same time, no excuses. If one of us misses it, the other one calls twice as much until we catch up." They hammered out the details right there, Vincent shouting through the window and Mika laughing from her railing. She made him promise to show her his new room first, even if the walls were scuzzy. "If it's dilapidated, I definitely have to see it," she said.

The next morning, Vincent climbed into the car while the movers locked the truck. He looked back at the house shrinking in the mirror, then down at his phone, where he typed a message to Mika: "Sunday, three o'clock. First call. I'll show you everything." Then he pressed send.

Alexis stood on her grandmother's porch with a box of old paperbacks under one arm. Her grandmother had agreed to drive her into town so she could donate the books to the library, but first the car had to be found, because her grandmother had lent it to a neighbour and could not remember which street the neighbour lived on. "Ask Frau Keller," her grandmother said. "Two streets over. But you will have to ask in German, because she answers to nobody in English."

Alexis had been practising German all summer, and she knew the words she needed. She walked down the hill, found an old woman watering roses, and said, "Wo wohnst du?" The woman looked at her, watered another rose, and said nothing at all. Alexis tried again, louder. The woman turned her back. On the walk back up the hill Alexis made a list in her head: the woman was not deaf, because she had flinched at a car horn. She was not unfriendly, because she had waved at a boy on a bicycle. The only variable left was the words themselves, and the one word Alexis had chosen was du.

She had an idea, and it was a small one. Back at the house she found her German notebook and looked up the polite form. Then she walked down the hill a second time and said, "Wo wohnen Sie, Frau Keller?" The woman set down the hose and smiled and pointed left, then right, then said something with drei and Häusern in it. Three houses from the corner, painted green. Alexis found the car parked outside it, and taped to the windscreen was a note with the library's address and a map.

At the library she called her friend Lacey, who was taking Spanish at summer camp. "Ask your counsellor for directions and see what happens," Alexis said. "Try the familiar form first." Lacey reported back an hour later: an older woman at the camp had ignored a casual tú until a boy switched to usted, and then the directions came out all at once, with hand gestures. "My French pen pal says it's vous over there," Lacey added. "Whether the hand gestures help or just confuse you is subjective, but the pronoun part isn't." Alexis laughed and said her dilemma was solved either way, since she now had a ride, a map, and a rule worth testing on her grandmother, who spoke only German to neighbours.

That evening Alexis said, "Oma, hast du mein Buch gesehen?" Her grandmother kept peeling potatoes. Alexis waited, then tried, "Haben Sie mein Buch gesehen?" Her grandmother looked up at once and held out the missing book from under a newspaper. Alexis took it and studied her grandmother's face. "You understood me the first time," she said. Her grandmother went back to her potatoes and said, "Sie hat gut gefragt."

Brayden flopped onto the couch with his phone and opened the group chat, where Van had posted a photo of the whole soccer team outside the pizza place, jerseys on, grinning. "Wait," Brayden typed. "You put our team name AND the pizza place tag on this?" Terrance replied with three laughing emojis, then, "so? it's funny." Brayden frowned at the little map pin under the photo. "It says where we were. Like exactly where."

"You worry more than my grandma," Van sent, and the chat filled up with crying-laughing faces. Brayden set the phone down, then picked it up again, because something was itching at him. Last month Terrance had searched his own name for a school project and found a comment he'd written in third grade on a public fan page, sitting right there in the results like it had been waiting for him. Terrance had howled about it for a week. Brayden had asked his cousin why the old comment showed up, and his cousin had shrugged and said, "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages. Public stuff gets found." Brayden hadn't really believed it until he'd tried it himself.

Now he typed into the chat: "experiment. everybody search your own name right now." He did the same, holding his breath, and there it was, the team photo from last season that Van had posted publicly, with a caption naming the school. Third result. Underneath it, their tournament schedule, including the field they practiced at every Tuesday.

The chat went quiet except for typing dots, then dots, then dots. Terrance broke first: "WHY AM I ON THE INTERNET." Van sent, "okay. okay okay okay. deleting." His typing technique was frantic, whole messages appearing in bursts, half of them misspelled. "Can you delete it everywhere though," Brayden wondered out loud to the empty room. Copies felt kind of inevitable once something was out there, but at least they could stop feeding it.

Van changed the chat settings so only members could see posts, then sent a new picture: his cat wearing a tiny soccer sock as a hat. "location: my couch," he wrote. "you're welcome."

Brooklyn sat at the kitchen table with her half-built robot prototype, a little car made from a sponge soaked so porous with glue it would never roll again. She was supposed to be finishing it for the science club, but she kept checking her phone. Lily-Anne had not texted back in four days.

It had started when Brooklyn joined robotics and Lily-Anne joined track. Their schedules stopped matching, and then their conversations did too. Last week Lily-Anne had said, "You'd rather hang out with Abbas and his circuit boards," and walked away before Brooklyn could answer. Abbas was fine, but he was not Lily-Anne.

Brooklyn scraped glue off the table and thought about it like a science problem. When she and Lily-Anne had liked all the same things, the friendship had practically run itself. Now they liked different things, and it was stalling. She remembered a page Ms. Krause had printed for the class, and dug it out of her backpack. A 2015 study had followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade, and the friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end. "So that's the pattern," Brooklyn said out loud. If sameness was what kept friendships going, she could not magically become a runner. But she could find one new thing they both actually cared about.

She texted Lily-Anne: "Can you come over? I need a runner." Twenty minutes later Lily-Anne stood in the doorway, arms crossed, still in her track warmups.

"I need someone fast to test this," Brooklyn said, holding up the little car. "If it works, we enter it together in the science fair. You'd have to participate, though. Practice runs, timing, all of it."

Lily-Anne uncrossed her arms. "I get to be the one who says go?"

"You're the only one fast enough to catch it."

Lily-Anne took the car gently, like it was a baby bird, and set it on the hallway floor. "Okay," she said. "On three. One, two, go."

The stands at the rink were so loud that Alexis could feel the noise in his teeth. He was squeezed between his dad and Casey, with Markus one row down, watching the championship game. When the home team scored the tying goal, Markus stood up and yelled like his voice alone could push the puck into the net, and Alexis found himself yelling too.

Afterward, waiting in line for hot chocolate while the teams skated warm-ups for overtime, Casey said, "If we cheer loud enough, they'll win. That's how home ice works." Alexis stirred his cocoa. He remembered something Ms. Chaudhry had shown their class back in the fall, a newspaper story from her scrapbook of odd sports facts. In the 2020 NFL season, she'd told them, when almost no fans were allowed in the stadiums because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1. Basically, no home advantage at all. Alexis had rolled his eyes at the time and copied it down only because it might be on a quiz. Now he turned it over in his head. If cheering really made teams win, then a whole season of empty stadiums should have turned out lopsided, road teams losing left and right. It hadn't. It had come out almost perfectly even.

"I don't think the noise does it," Alexis said slowly. "There was that football season with no fans, and home teams went 127-128-1." Casey squinted at him. "So when I scream at the TV, it does nothing?" Alexis shrugged. "Maybe it does something. Just not that." Ms. Chaudhry, in line behind them buying coffee for the zamboni driver she knew, laughed. "Careful," she said. "Half the commerce in this building depends on people believing yelling helps. Pucks, foam fingers, that sign shop that will modify any jersey with your name by the third period."

Overtime started. The crowd rose, and a banner reading HOME OF THE CONTEMPORARY CHAMPIONS unrolled over the rail. Markus was already on his feet again, banging the boards with both fists. Alexis stood up beside him. He still didn't know if it mattered, and he wasn't sure he wanted to know. When the puck dropped, he cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted anyway.

The bench outside the skate park had been removed in May, and Alex wanted it back. His grandfather's house was the quietest place he knew, with the smell of old books and toast, so that was where he spread out his petition papers on the kitchen table. Grandpa sliced apples beside him but said nothing except, "Councillor Rao has her office hours on Thursdays." Alex had gathered forty signatures at school, including Quinton's enormous scrawl and Axelle's tidy loops, and he had written a speech. What he did not have was any idea what happened after he handed the papers over.

On Thursday, Councillor Rao read every signature. "This is good work," she said. "I can bring your bench to a council meeting as a motion. But I can't just stand up and talk. A proposal needs one member to move it and another to second it before council debates and votes on it." She tapped the petition. "Without a seconder, it dies right there." Alex asked if she had a seconder, and she smiled in a way that did not answer him, which worried him for three straight days.

Grandpa drove him to the council meeting on Tuesday night. The chamber smelled like floor polish and coffee, and the chairs were the hard parallel rows of a courtroom, all facing the long curved desk where seven councillors sat. Alex clutched his notes. When his item came up, Councillor Rao stood, said she was moving a motion to restore the bench at Harlow Park, and mentioned the forty names on the petition as testimony from the neighbourhood. Then she sat down, and the room went still.

Alex gripped the edge of his seat. Nobody moved. The chair at the end was empty, its microphone dark, and it dawned on him that one of the seven councillors was missing tonight. If that was the person who would have seconded it, then the whole thing, signatures, speech, apples and worry, was finished. A door at the side creaked. A woman in a raincoat hurried in, whispered something to the clerk, and slid into the empty chair.

"I'll second that," the woman said, still catching her breath. She nodded at Councillor Rao, then turned slightly, as if she knew exactly where Alex was sitting. Later, outside, Grandpa found him still holding his unused notes. "You didn't even get to speak," Grandpa said.

"I didn't need to," Alex said, and he watched the rain begin to dot the pavement, each drop making its own small dark circle.

The app kept asking for her birthday, which Ivy thought was strange, because a game about matching colored tiles had no reason to care when she was born. She sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with the family tablet, tapping the little calendar again. The kitchen light down the hall made a sparse stripe across the carpet, and she could hear her mom humming while she scrubbed a pot that had been saturate d with burnt rice at dinner. The form wanted a year. Any year. Ivy tried typing the year she was born, and the screen flashed red: "You must be 13 or older to create an account."

Thirteen. She counted on her fingers even though she didn't need to. Two years and four months away. That seemed like a long time to wait for a tile game. But why thirteen? Her dad's chess app had never asked his birthday. Neither had the weather site. It was almost like the matching game was something else, something bigger, hiding behind the tiles.

At school the next morning she slid her notebook across the table to Evelina, who was drawing a cat with a suspicious expression. "Why would a game care how old you are?" Ivy asked. "Does yours ask?" Evelina shook her head. "My sister's app does, but she's fourteen, so she just clicks through." Jax leaned over from the next seat. "It's a law thing. My cousin told me. The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998. Websites need parental consent before they collect personal information from kids under 13. That's why so many sites make you be 13."

"A law," Ivy said slowly, turning her pencil over. So it wasn't the game being picky. The app wanted her name, her birthday, maybe her town. Collecting personal information. The tile game was keeping a file on her, and the law said an adult had to say yes first. She wondered how many kids just typed a different year and walked right past the rule, and whether the app could even tell.

That evening she found her mom drying dishes. "Can I sign up for something if you give permission? There's a law, from 1998, and I'm under thirteen, so you have to consent first." Her mom set the dish down and looked at her for a long moment. "Show me the app," she said. "We'll read what they collect together." Ivy carried the tablet over, screen glowing, and tapped the calendar one more time.

Connor spread his notebook across the kitchen table and stared at the two numbers he had written there. His rubber-band launcher had thrown a marshmallow 240 centimeters on the first try and only 90 on the second. Tomorrow he was supposed to tell Khalid the average range, and right now the average was meaningless, because the two trials couldn't even agree on a neighborhood.

"You look like your project bit you," said Khalid, dropping into the other chair and reaching for a marshmallow. Khalid wanted to eat the ammunition, which was a problem, because every marshmallow he ate was one fewer launch. "Just write down the big number," he said. "Two hundred forty sounds amazing on a poster."

Connor thought about last year's fair, when he had claimed his paper airplane flew eight meters off one single throw that had caught a lucky gust. Mr. Lawson had asked him to repeat it, and it had gone two meters, and Connor had stood there with his face burning. He wasn't going to be that narrator of his own disaster twice. "No," he said. "One throw can be a fluke either way. I'm going to run it ten times and average all ten."

"Ten? That's so many."

"You'll comply with the rules of science," Connor said, loading the launcher. "Or at least with mine."

They took turns launching while Connor's mom timed nothing and understood nothing but kept the cocoa coming. Trial three went 110. Trial four went 230, and Khalid insisted the wind from the open window had helped, so Connor closed it and marked the number anyway. By trial ten they had a messy column of numbers from 85 to 250, and when Connor added them up and divided, the average came out 148.

"One forty-eight," Khalid said, chewing a marshmallow he had stolen from trial seven. "That's not amazing."

"It's true," Connor said, and wrote it in big assertive letters at the top of the page. Then he set the launcher down in front of Khalid. "Your turn to record. We're doing all ten again."

Ryan pressed the green flag for the fourth time, and for the fourth time nothing happened. His cat sprite sat frozen in the corner of the stage while the score variable blinked at zero. Around him, the computer lab hummed with other games springing to life, basketballs bouncing and dragons flapping, and Kyleigh two seats over already had a fish dodging sharks.

"It worked yesterday," Ryan muttered. He scrolled through his code. He had the loop set up right, a forever block that moved the cat toward the mouse pointer, and an if-then block that added one to the score whenever the cat touched a coin. Yesterday the cat had chased that coin all over the stage. Today, silence.

Kylan leaned over from the next row. "Did you try the red stop sign?"

"Everything's already stopped. That's the problem." Ryan clicked the stop sign anyway, just to be sure, and the other games in the room kept playing because the stop sign only stopped scripts, not the whole program. Then he sat back and stared at his stack of blocks, starting from the top. Green flag, he thought. Kyleigh's fish moved the second she clicked her flag. Her scripts must all begin with the same block. He scrolled up to his own stack and felt his stomach drop. His forever loop began with a plain blue block, nothing above it. There was no hat block, no rounded yellow block on top saying "when green flag clicked." Yesterday he must have dragged his code out from under it by accident, and clicking the green flag started nothing because no script began with that block. All his fixing had been in vain.

He dragged the hat block back onto the top of his stack and clicked the green flag. The cat sprang to life, streaked toward the coin, and the score jumped from zero to one. He converted the whole game idea right then, deciding he would add a second coin and a timer so the score would actually mean something by Friday.

"That was it?" Kylan said.

"That was it." Ryan saved his file twice, which he now considered his testimony to never trusting a single save again, and watched the cat snatch the coin for the fifth time. "Kyleigh, do you have an extra coin sprite I can borrow?"

Riley stared at the flyer Mr. Munro had taped to the classroom door. "Market Project," it read. "Explain why something costs what it costs." Everyone else had already picked easy things like video games or sneakers, but Riley wanted the thing that had bugged him since Saturday: at the market with his mom, strawberries had cost half what they cost in March. He'd seen the March price himself, four dollars a basket, and now the same basket was two.

"You should do it," said Kaiya at lunch. "You're the one who kept saying 'but why' in the produce aisle until your mom walked away."

"It's like there's a hidden rule," Riley said. "Prices don't just happen. Something invisible is moving them."

After school, he and Wilson stood at the corner where a farm truck parked every June. The farmer was stacking basket after basket of red berries, more than anyone could eat in a week. Riley counted the baskets out of curiosity and got to sixty before Wilson elbowed him.

"Ask him," Wilson whispered.

"Do these all ripen around now?" Riley asked.

"Early summer, all at once," the farmer said. "The whole valley's berries come in together."

Riley wrote that in his notebook. The word that came to him was supply. In March there were barely any strawberries, and in June the supply flooded in. Maybe price went the opposite way? He drew a see-saw in his notebook: supply up, price down. It was only a guess, though. He wanted proof.

So he made a chart. March: four dollars, few berries. April: three fifty. June: two dollars, baskets everywhere. He taped the chart to a poster and stood in front of the class, holding up a drawing of the farmer's loaded truck.

"Supply is how much of something there is to buy," Riley said. "And where strawberries ripen outdoors in early summer, the local berries all arrive at once, so the supply jumps up, and that usually pushes the price down."

"Usually?" said Mr. Munro, one eyebrow up.

"Prices are turbulent," Riley said. "They wobble. One market could still charge more, for a day or so. But the pattern held every month I checked." He paused. "Here's what I still wonder. When summer ends and the berries cease coming, do prices climb back up slowly, or jump? I want to keep a chart through the winter."

Kaiya raised her hand. "Can I help?"

Riley grinned and slid the empty October page across the desk toward her.

Jack got up before sunrise and ate two pieces of toast, because Ramadan had started and he was fasting for the first time, at least until lunchtime. Then Dad said they were driving to the cemetery to visit Grandpa's grave, and Jack put on his camouflage jacket and carried the folded prayer mat even though the mat had a synthetic surface that scratched his arm.

At the cemetery the artificial grass near the headstones was damp. Jack read the dua Dad had written on a card, and then he began to shiver. By the time they walked back to the car, his teeth were knocking together, and his forehead felt hot when Dad pressed a hand against it. Dad gave him a bottle of water, and Jack drank half of it before he remembered the fast. His stomach dropped.

"I broke it," Jack said. "I ruined my first fast."

Dad felt his forehead again. "You have a fever. Islam excuses people who are sick or travelling from the Ramadan fast, and they make up the missed days later."

Jack sat with that. "So I owe one day? Like homework I have to turn in late?"

"Exactly like that," Dad said.

"But you can't prove I'm sick," Jack said, testing the idea. "You can't see a fever."

Dad held up the thermometer from the first aid kit, and it read thirty-eight point two. "There. Evidence." Then he pointed through the fence at the row of graves. "You know who else never fasted a whole Ramadan in his life? Grandpa. He was diabetic, and he was sick, and every year he made up the days after, in small ones, whenever he could."

Jack looked at the headstone with the wet grass around it. Grandpa, who had taught him chess and never missed a Friday prayer, had spent all those years making up days, quietly, one at a time. Jack drank the rest of the water.

"Tomorrow, when I'm better," he said, "I'm starting over."

Louis was sliding the last wet quilt into the dryer when the metal lip of the machine caught his knuckle and opened a line of skin that welled red. He hissed and held his hand over the folding table while Elora, who had come along to keep him company, dug through her backpack.

"You have to let it dry out," she said, tearing a paper towel from the dispenser on the wall. "My grandpa says air is the best thing for a cut."

"That makes a scab, though," Louis said. He was thinking of his elbow from last summer, a scrape he had picked at for weeks, and how it had left a pale mark. There was something he could not see directly here, some rule about how skin fixed itself, and he wanted to find it. He turned the paper towel over and studied the smear of blood, which was thin, not gushing. "It's not deep. It's not going to need a doctor. But I want to test something."

In the laundromat's cramped office, next to a jar of pens and the coin box that was the whole commerce of the place, he found a small tube labeled petroleum jelly and a box of adhesive bandages. Elora raised her eyebrows. "You're putting grease on it? That's so weird. You're being gullible, believing some old jar."

"Watch," Louis said, and he dabbed a thin layer of the jelly across the cut before pressing on the bandage, smoothing the edges flat. "Grandpa's way keeps it dry. Mine keeps it wet. If I'm wrong, my hand falls off." He said it flat enough that she laughed.

They sat on the counter while the dryer tumbled, and the neighbor who ran the place came by to sweep. Louis showed her his bandaged knuckle and asked, quietly, whether air or jelly was better. She nodded at it. "The jelly keeps the surface moist. That helps it heal, and it can mean less of a scar." Elora made a face, but she pulled out her phone to check, then looked up, defeated.

By the time the quilt came out warm, Louis had peeled back one corner of the bandage to look. The cut was closed at the edges, shiny and clean under its thin coat.

"Fine," Elora said, handing him the next load of quarters. "But if it takes longer to heal and prolongs your hand problem, I get to say I told you so."

"Deal," Louis said, and pressed the corner back down.

Gabriel's duffel bag sat on the lakeside dock like it was already boarding a bus without him. Tomorrow he left for two weeks of sleepaway camp, and tonight Martha and Charlotte had dragged him out here for a send-off, which so far meant lying on the rough boards and avoiding the splinters.

Then Charlotte announced her plan. "At camp, when the counselors take your phones the first night, you're going to be helpless. You can't even find north."

"I can find north," Gabriel said.

Martha propped herself up on one elbow. "Prove it. No phone, right now."

Gabriel patted his pockets anyway, out of habit, and felt a jolt of embarrassment when Martha raised an eyebrow at him. He set the phone face down on the dock like a prisoner surrendering a weapon. Above the far shore, the sky had gone properly dark, and there was the Big Dipper, hanging over the water like a giant soup ladle someone had left out.

He remembered something from a library book, half remembered, which was worse than not remembering. The two stars at the outer edge of the Dipper's bowl, the ones called the pointer stars, pointed toward Polaris, the North Star. He found the bowl, traced a line up from those two edge stars with his finger, and landed on a lone, stubbornly bright star. "That's Polaris," he said. "So that's north."

"That's it? One star?" Charlotte squinted. "How do you know it's the right one?"

Gabriel inhaled the cold lake air and considered lying. Instead he picked up a wood chip, set it on the boards, and turned it so its edge lined up with Polaris. "If I'm wrong, we walk toward Canada by accident and become extinct, like the dinosaurs."

Martha stood, marched ten paces in the direction the wood chip pointed, and stopped at the end of the dock. From there you could see the town's water tower, and everyone knew the water tower stood on the north side of the lake.

She turned around slowly. "Huh."

"Told you," Gabriel said, and lay back down on the warm boards to look at the Dipper some more.

Grandma's kitchen smelled like lemon and burned toast, which meant she had been reading again and forgot the toaster. Clara spread her notes across the table and groaned.

"I have to explain how a bill becomes a law on Monday, and I don't get the part after the veto." Clara pushed the paper toward her grandmother. "The president says no, and that's it, right? Dead bill."

Grandma slid the toast onto a plate and sat down. "Hmm. What does your book say?"

"That Congress can do something if enough of them vote again. But it's a weird number and I always mix it up." Clara squinted at the page. "Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate. Both of them. Not just one."

"Then that's the rule. Want to test it?"

Clara was skeptical. "Test it? It's a rule on paper. You can't poke it."

"Sure you can." Grandma pulled a jar of buttons from the windowsill, the way she did before a game. "We'll be Congress."

Earlier that fall, Clara remembered, she had watched a veteran on the news say that one stubborn senator could obstruct a whole bill by talking forever. She had thought laws were like doors that either opened or stayed shut. Now she wasn't so sure. If enough people pushed, maybe a shut door could open again.

They made the House out of twelve buttons and the Senate out of ten. Grandma was the president. Clara's bill, to make Saturday mornings start an hour later, passed both houses easily the first time, and Grandma vetoed it with a smug little tap of her spoon.

"Okay," Clara said, counting. "Two-thirds of twelve is eight, and two-thirds of ten is almost seven, so I need seven there. I need eight House buttons and seven Senate buttons to vote yes again."

Grandma frowned at the piles like a president should. "That's a lot of buttons."

Clara flipped them one at a time, saying yes for each one. The Senate pile reached seven. The House pile stopped at seven. Eight was needed, and there were only seven, because one button, the blue one, had rolled under the sugar bowl.

"One short," Clara said. "So the veto holds? The bill just dies?"

"In our Congress, yes. Both houses, two-thirds, or the president wins." Grandma fished out the blue button and set it back with the others. "You were wrong this morning, you know. You said a veto was the end."

Clara had changed her own mind right there at the table, and she said so. A veto wasn't the end unless Congress was too small or too split. She copied the rule onto an index card and underlined both twice.

Monday morning, Mr. Fischer called on her first. Clara stood up, took out the buttons, and lined them along the chalk tray.

"Volunteers," she said. "I need twelve of you to be the House."

Zack pushed his desk lamp closer to the orange he had stolen from the fruit bowl, until the light nearly touched the skin. He was supposed to be drawing a sphere for Monday's art assignment, but his last three attempts looked like flat gray circles wearing smudges. He wanted this one to look like it could roll off the page, and he had all afternoon to figure out how.

The orange gave him an idea. He grabbed it and carried it to his dark bathroom, where the only light came from the hallway through a crack in the door. He set the orange on the counter and crouched down until his eyes were level with it. Half of the orange glowed bright orange, and the other half sat in a brown dusk. Between the two halves ran a border, a soft but definite line where the glow simply stopped.

He remembered art class on Friday, when Abigael had laughed out loud at Mr. Korhonen's vocabulary list. "The terminator," Mr. Korhonen had read, tapping the whiteboard. "Who can tell me what that means on a sphere?" Corey had immediately spread his arms like a robot and marched in place, and the whole class cracked up. But then Mr. Korhonen had pointed at the globe in the corner, and Abigael traced her finger around its edge and gone quiet. Zack had squinted at the globe then, but now, in the bathroom, he actually saw it. The terminator was the line on a sphere where the lit side turned into the shadow side, the edge where direct light stopped reaching.

Back at his desk, he sharpened his pencil to a needle point. The bathroom orange had shown him something he had missed before: the terminator was not a sharp fence, it was a soft frontier, and the sphere got darker gradually as it curved away from the lamp. He tested it, laying down short strokes that started light right past the bright spot, the highlight, and stacked them heavier and heavier toward that border. Where the shadow side began, he stopped almost completely, leaving just a whisper of gray because the desk bounced light back up. Then, underneath and to the right, he drew the cast shadow, the dark pool the sphere threw onto the table, darkest near the orange where it touched.

He could smell the orange's sharp peel still on his fingers as he leaned the drawing against his lamp. It looked round. It looked real. He grabbed his phone and texted Abigael a photo, then another text: "No robots were harmed in the making of this terminator." Three dots appeared, then her reply: "Send me your orange trick tomorrow. Mine still looks like a gray cookie." Zack grinned and texted back, "Bring fruit. I have monopoly on the bathroom lab until dinner."

Every Saturday, Austin took the bus out to his grandpa's house on the lake, and every Saturday his friend Jad came along. Grandpa liked to say he was a descendant of a lake captain who had rowed mail across these same waters a hundred years ago, and part of the tradition was that whoever visited had to swim off the old wooden dock. Jad always wore his red trunks with the elastic waistband, and every Saturday, somewhere around eleven o'clock, Jad would go quiet, hold his stomach, and announce, "I feel sick. I'm going inside."

Austin started writing it down in the back of his notebook, the way Grandpa tracked the weather. Saturday, stomachache. Saturday, stomachache and headache. He noticed other things too. When they played cards on the porch while they waited for swim time, Jad's heart seemed to pound so hard Austin could almost see it at his collar, and his breathing went quick and shallow, like he'd run the hill. One night they camped in Grandpa's screen tent, and Jad tossed for hours. "I never sleep good on Fridays," he admitted. "Or Saturdays."

Austin had a theory, but he needed proof. The next Saturday it thundered, and nobody swam. Jad ate two grilled cheese sandwiches, won three hands of gin rummy, and laughed until he had to sit down. No stomachache, no headache, nothing. The Saturday after that, the sun blazed, the lake lay flat and shiny, and by eleven o'clock Jad was pale with his hand pressed to his middle. It wasn't the day that made him sick, Austin realized. It was the dock.

"Want to submerge just your feet today?" Austin offered. "Sit on the ladder and that's it." Jad stared at the dark green water below the boards where the minnows swirled. "It's not the water exactly," he said slowly. "It's the jump. Everybody watches. My brother says anxiety means you're scared, but I'm not scared scared. My body just does this stuff anyway."

Austin rowed him ashore and knocked on the screen door of the blue cottage next door, because Ms. Paquette, who was a retired school nurse, knew about this kind of thing. She listened to the notebook being read aloud, all those Saturdays lined up in ink, and nodded. "Bodies send up flares," she said. "Somebody should tell Jad's mom exactly what you told me. That's not tattling, that's the map."

On the bus home, Jad looked out the window for a long moment. "Saturday, I'm going to try the ladder," he said. "And tonight I'm going to tell my mom about the not-sleeping part too." He bumped Austin's shoulder with his fist and grinned. "Bring the notebook. She likes evidence."

Noemie stood at the back of the parish hall in her socks, watching two kids from the older group kneel on the floor with long bamboo poles. The hall smelled like candle wax and old coffee, and through the open door she could hear someone vacuuming the church carpets. In two weeks, dancers from every family in the congregation would perform at the harvest gathering, and Noemie had signed up for tinikling before she understood what it involved.

The poles clattered twice against the floor, then snapped together on the third beat, and the older dancers slid their feet out just in time. "Tap, tap, clap," went the rhythm, over and over, while bare feet stepped in and out. Julia tried first. She lasted four beats before the poles pinched her ankle, and she hopped away laughing, though her eyes looked worried. Adelaide lasted six. When Noemie's turn came, she got pinched on the very first clap.

She sat on the floor to rub her ankle and watched the older kids again. The pattern never changed: the poles hit the ground twice, then closed on the third beat, then the whole thing repeated. The pole players didn't watch the dancers at all; they watched each other, keeping the beat steady like a metronome. Noemie realized she had been watching the poles themselves, which moved too fast to follow. The poles weren't the thing to track. The beat was.

She stood up and went to the middle. "Say the count out loud with me," she told Julia and Adelaide, who had come to hold the poles for her practice. "Tap, tap, clap. Tap, tap, clap." With the words in her mouth, her feet knew exactly when to land between the poles and when to pull out. On the clap beats, her ankles were already clear. She danced eight rounds without a single pinch, and Ms. Campbell-Brown, who was arranging chairs near the folding tables, called out, "Now that's how you negotiate a pair of bamboo poles!"

Fatigue crept in after twenty minutes, and Noemie's counting got slower than the poles, so the second pole player, an eccentric boy who wore a bow tie even to practice, sped up to match her. They grinned at each other.

On the night of the gathering, the hall filled with families and the smell of rice and fried bananas. Noemie took her place, and when the poles began, she heard herself say it, quiet and steady.

"Tap, tap, clap. Tap, tap, clap."

Tristan held the food thermometer like it was a magic wand, which was a metaphor his dad would probably ruin by saying thermometers are actually tools. Dinner was Tristan's job tonight, his first time cooking the whole meal at the campsite, and he had decided on chicken, foil potatoes, and corn. The chicken was the problem. The fire crackled, indifferent to his plans, flaring up whenever the wind shifted and dying down when it didn't.

"You're staring at that chicken like it's going to talk," said Bowen, who was camping two sites over and had wandered over the moment he smelled food. Ayah trailed behind him, carrying a bag of marshmallows like they were already invited.

"It's not talking," Tristan said. "That's the whole point." He flipped his dad's laminated camp cookbook open to the page he'd read four times. It said poultry was safely cooked when its thickest part reached 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which was about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer. Not guessed from the color. Not poked with a fork. Measured. "My grandpa always said if the juices run clear, it's done. But clear juice is a clue, not a rule."

"So you trust the thermometer more than your grandpa?" Ayah asked, peeking into the skillet.

"I trust it more than my eyes." Tristan slid the probe into the fattest piece, right near the bone where the cookbook said the thickest part would be. The numbers climbed: 140, 150, 158. His stomach growled like a fourth camper. Bowen leaned in so far his marshmallow bag nearly caught fire.

At 163, the reading stopped climbing. Tristan waited, watching the fire spit. He thought about how his grandpa would classify this as wasting time, but Tristan wanted proof, not hope. Ten seconds later the display ticked up: 165.

"Done!" Tristan shouted it so loud a kid at the next campsite looked over. He pulled the chicken off the grate and cut into the biggest piece. Steam curled out, and the meat was white all the way through, cooked and juicy at the same time.

His dad wandered back from the lake with Tristan's little sister, sniffing the air. "Smells official," his dad said. "How'd you know it was ready?"

Tristan held up the thermometer like a trophy. "One hundred sixty-five degrees," he announced. "In the thickest part. That's the rule."

Bowen was already reaching for a piece. "Save me the drumstick, chef."

Georgia set four basil pots in a row on the kitchen counter, each one wearing a paper label in her careful handwriting. Marco leaned over them, sniffing. "They smell amazing already."

"That's the problem," Georgia said. "I've been giving them the fancy fertilizer every week, and they look great. But Mr. Rao asked me how I know the fertilizer is doing it." She poked a leaf. "Maybe they'd look this good anyway. Maybe it's the sunny window."

Marco pulled a stool over and sat down. "So do half of them without it."

"Then I wouldn't know if it's the fertilizer or just that they're different plants." She turned a pot so its label faced them. Her instinct said the answer was in keeping everything matched, though she couldn't have said why yet. She got out her notebook and started a list: same window, same water, same soil, same size pots.

She stopped, pen hovering. "Wait. If everything is the same except one thing, the fertilizer, then that's the only thing that could make a difference." She drew a line down the page. "Two pots get fertilizer, two don't. Everything else I do exactly the same to all four."

"Like a race where everybody runs the same track," Marco said, "and one kid gets secret shoes."

Georgia laughed. "Sort of. I need a control group. Pots treated exactly like the others except for the one thing I'm testing."

Cordelia arrived with her mom's old measuring cup, because she wanted the basil for a pizza project on Saturday and had been nagging Georgia about the harvest for weeks. "You're not going to slow them down with some experiment, are you? I need authentic fresh basil, not sad little leaves."

"If the fertilizer works, you'll get more," Georgia said. She held the cup under the tap and measured the water twice, once for each side of her line, so every pot got exactly the same amount. Marco wrote the numbers down while she poured.

Cordelia watched the two plain pots, the unfertilized ones, sitting beside their glossy neighbors. "Fine," she said, changing her mind with a shrug. "Do it right. I'd rather wait for real proof than eat mediocre pizza."

"Saturday," Georgia promised, and turned all four pots a quarter turn toward the light.

Evelyn had one job for the science fair demo: explain how sound travels, and why it moves faster through water than air. She had a drum, a bag of rice, a bucket of water, and a suspicion that Mr. Fitzgerald had assigned this topic specifically because he owned earplugs.

"Hit it soft," she told Ivan, who was holding the drumstick like it might bite.

He tapped the drumhead. The rice on top shivered, barely. Ivan hit it harder, and the rice jumped a full inch, raining down onto the gym floor with a sound like tiny applause. Evelyn leaned in until her nose was almost touching the drum.

"The rice is doing what the air does," she said. "Particles bumping back and forth. Watch the middle of the jump." She drew the arc in the air with her finger. "How far they travel, that's the amplitude. Bigger vibrations, louder sound."

"That's the word," Charlie said from behind the water bucket, where he was supposed to be taking notes and was instead cherishing a rice grain he'd found in his sleeve. "Amplitude. Write it down before you forget it and call it the jumpy distance."

Mr. Fitzgerald wandered over. "You realize you'll be cleaning that rice up."

"It's testimony," Evelyn said, pointing at the floor. "Every grain is evidence of how hard Ivan hit." Then she picked up the tuning fork she'd borrowed from the supply cabinet, struck it against her shoe, and dipped it toward the bucket.

The water erupted. Waves slapped the rim and slopped over Charlie's shoes, and his yelp carried all the way to the far bleachers, where kids doing jump rope turned to look. Evelyn grinned. The smile was infectious; even Charlie, dripping, started to laugh.
