"Some of that," she said, "traveled through your shoe water faster than your scream traveled through air. Write that down."

Megan sat on the porch of her grandfather's house with her laptop open, refreshing the login page for the fourth time. "It still says my password is wrong," she typed to Foster. "And I didn't change it."

"Did you get that weird email from the pet forum last night?" Foster wrote back. "Somebody leaked their whole list."

Megan stared at the screen. Her pet forum password, the one she'd made when she was nine, was dragon16. Her game account, the one she and Damian needed for tonight's tournament at seven, used the same password because it was easy to remember. She typed dragon16 into her email login just to test the idea, and her stomach dropped when it loaded her inbox. If she could get in with a reused password, so could somebody else. That had to be what happened to the game account. Somebody took the leaked forum passwords and, she reasoned, must have tried them automatically on other sites until one worked. She changed her email password right there, fingers shaking a little.

Mr. Wardak, the neighbour who came over every Tuesday to fix her grandfather's fence, climbed down his ladder and leaned over her shoulder. "You look like you lost a war," he said.

"Somebody took my game account. I used the same password on a forum that got hacked."

Mr. Wardak nodded slowly. "That's called credential stuffing," he said, and went back to his nails.

Megan messaged Damian, who negotiated with the tournament organizer for a ten-minute extension while she emailed the game's support team with proof the account was hers. Then she opened a notebook and started over. Instead of a word she loved, she strung together random letters and numbers, different for every site, and wrote each one down. "You're my password notebook now," she told it, which was easier than admitting she'd never had a system before.

At 6:52, support restored the account. Damian sent a single word: "GO." Megan logged in with her new password, and the tournament screen bloomed open in front of her.

Sophie tapped the screen so hard the tablet nearly slid off the lab bench. "Look at this. GlowWater says their drink makes you run faster in one week."

Tyrell leaned over her shoulder. "That website looks amazing. Blue water, a doctor in a white coat, stars everywhere."

"Five stars," Maiya said from the next bench. "And a countdown clock. That means it's real, right?"

Mr. Ong was walking between the rows of benches, straightening beakers, but Sophie noticed he slowed down near their table, listening. She scrolled down the site. The doctor had a name, Dr. Harmon, and a quote in big letters. There were photographs of sweaty, happy runners holding blue bottles. Everything about the page wanted her to believe it, and she almost did.

"Here's the thing," she said slowly. "The site can't stop talking about itself. Every page is another page from the same people." She opened a new tab and typed GlowWater into the search bar. The results made her sit back. A newspaper article appeared first: "GlowWater sold by the same company that makes it." Then a runner's blog: "The 'independent study' was run by the company's owner." Then a small item about Dr. Harmon, who turned out to be an actor in a toothpaste ad.

"That's sneaky," Tyrell said. "The whole website is one big ad wearing a costume."

"It's like when the algorithm on my video app keeps feeding me more of the same thing," Maiya said. "Everything agrees because it all comes from one place." Sophie nodded and copied the idea onto her worksheet: don't only read the site, read around it. Later she found a name for it in one of the newspaper articles, and she underlined it twice. "It's called lateral reading," she announced. "Instead of judging a website by its own pages, you open new tabs and see what other sources say about it."

Mr. Ong stopped at their bench. "Whose idea was the new tabs?"

"Mine, but Maiya gave me the extra battery pack when my tablet died halfway," Sophie confessed, "so really it was a team effort."

Maiya grinned and slid the battery pack back into her pencil case. "And Tyrell found the actor. He has a fertile imagination for detective work."

"I found the toothpaste ad in four seconds," Tyrell said. "Someday I will open my own detective agency. GlowWater will be my first case."

Mr. Ong smiled and moved on, and Sophie looked down at her worksheet, where she had drawn a small blue bottle with a red X through it. She turned the tablet around so Maiya could add a mustache to Dr. Harmon.

The craft fair signup sheet went up on Monday, and Lily was the first to enroll. She wanted a table of her own, mostly because of the wind turbine model she had built in science, a little spinning thing with blades made from plastic spoons. But her friend Alix had different plans. Alix wanted money, real money, for a new skateboard, and she had a shoebox full of woven bracelets to sell.

The fair was loud and crowded. Alix put her price at five dollars a bracelet, which seemed high to Lily, and by lunchtime the shoebox was empty. "Sold out," Alix announced, holding up the empty box like a trophy. Lily looked down the row of tables. Nobody else was selling bracelets at all. There were candles, cookies, painted rocks, but no bracelets. Five dollars, zero sellers besides Alix, and every bracelet gone. Something clicked in Lily's mind, though she couldn't quite say what yet.

Two weeks later the school held a second fair, and Lily decided to be systematic about it. She walked every row with a notebook and wrote down each bracelet seller and each price. This time there were eight bracelet tables. Eight! Yassin had one, two girls from her class had one, even Mr. Tehrani's nephew had one. And the price? Four tables were asking one dollar, three were asking two, and Alix, still trying for her skateboard money, was asking three. Almost nobody bought at three. With bracelets everywhere, buyers could pick the cheapest one, and sellers kept dropping their prices just to make a sale.

Lily found Alix behind her table, chin in her hands. "Nobody wants mine," Alix said. Lily flipped her notebook open. "Watch this," she said. "I'm going to test something." She made a sign for Alix's table that said BRACELETS, $5, and taped it up. Then she waited. Within an hour, two more kids had signed up for the last empty tables, both carrying boxes of string and beads, both having heard that bracelets were going for five dollars.

"Take the sign down," Alix groaned, but Lily was grinning, scribbling in her notebook. "Don't you see? When the price goes up, more sellers show up." At the next table, Yassin was already knotting his next bracelet.

Kate set the mixing bowl on the picnic table in the backyard, where the light was good enough to magnify every lump in her dough. She had promised her family fresh bread by dinner, and she had never made bread before. Last summer, before her grandmother moved away, they had baked a loaf together on the porch, and Kate remembered stirring flour and water and watching her grandmother knead the dough for ten whole minutes while Kate fidgeted. "The kneading matters," her grandmother had said. "You'll see why someday."

Kate had skipped most of the kneading that summer, wandering off to chase dragonflies, and the loaf had come out dense and sad. She still wondered whether that had been her fault. Her premise now was simple: if flour and water made something on their own, and kneading changed it, then a short knead and a long knead should give her two different doughs. So she pulled off a small piece of dough, set it aside, and gave the rest a full ten minutes of pushing and folding on the table, her arms burning by the end.

The neighbor, Mr. Cho, leaned over the fence. "Looks like you're punishing that poor dough."

"I'm strengthening it," Kate said. "Flour has proteins in it, and when they mix with water, something called gluten forms. Kneading makes the gluten stronger and stretchier." She held up both pieces. The short-kneaded bit tore when she stretched it, like wet paper. The ten-minute piece stretched thin without breaking, until she could almost see light through it, a little window in the dough.

She covered the bowl with a towel and left it in the sun. Her grandmother had never gotten to taste the loaf they started together; that choice, to wander off instead of staying, sat with Kate while the dough rose and puffed under the towel. Maybe the old dense loaf had been her fault, maybe not. When she peeled the towel back an hour later, the dough had swelled round and proud, and she carried the bowl inside to the oven, calling over her shoulder, "Mr. Cho, come back at dinner. You get the first slice."

Sawyer had been watching the same glitter card on the marketplace app for three days, and every morning the price climbed higher. First it was twelve dollars, then fifteen, then twenty-two. There were only two listed, and forty-one people had them in their wish lists. He refreshed the page outside the gas station while his dad filled the tank, and the little red "price increased" tag glowed like a warning light.

"Why did it go up again since last week?" a kid at the next pump asked his own father, pointing at the numbers on the sign. His father shrugged, but Sawyer's dad leaned over. "Crude oil is usually the biggest single part of what a gallon of gas costs," he said. "So when crude oil gets more expensive, pump prices go up too." Sawyer stared at the card on his screen, then at the sign. Scarce thing, lots of people wanting it, price rising. He wondered if the same hidden rule ran both places, though nobody could see it working.

He decided to test it. In his room that evening, luminous desk lamp pulled close, he opened his trade folder. He owned six copies of a card that used to be rare, one he'd once traded his best technique guide to get. For months he had opposed selling them, remembering how hard they were to find. Now there were dozens listed online, and the price had slid from nine dollars to two. He posted three copies at two dollars and watched. Within an hour, two other sellers dropped their prices too. Plentiful thing, price falling. His stomach did a small flip.

The next day he showed the screenshots to Meriem at lunch. "So scarcity pushes prices up, and plenty pushes them down," she said, chewing her sandwich. "Even for gas." Sawyer nodded, though a question still bothered him. He'd sold one card cheap to prove his idea, and now that same card felt harder to let go of than he'd expected. "Think it'll ever get scarce again?" Meriem asked. Sawyer refreshed the app under the table. "Fourteen listed," he said. "Ask me next week."

Claire pressed the elevator button for the fourth floor three times before she noticed it wasn't there. The buttons jumped from three to five, like a stair with a missing step. "Wade," she said, "your building's elevator is broken. There's no four."

Wade lived on the eighth floor, above the restaurant his parents owned, and tonight Claire and Andie were coming for a birthday dinner his whole family was throwing. Andie shuffled in beside them carrying a gift bag that rustled like a paper bird, and Claire clutched her own gift, a puzzle she'd wrapped so badly it looked like it had been in a fight.

"It's not broken," Wade said, grinning. "In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death,' so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor."

Claire stared at the buttons. The landlord, she thought, had decided a missing button was better than a floor with bad luck all over it. She counted the buttons again, just to be sure she wasn't missing one. Five, six, seven. Nope. It was like the floor was hiding.

At the restaurant, the smells of ginger and garlic revolved around her the moment the doors opened. Wade's grandmother met them at the table and pressed a small red envelope into each of their hands. Claire had brought money for a gift card, but Wade shook his head quickly behind his grandmother's back and mouthed, "Not money tonight." She slid the envelope, unopened, into her pocket and decided she'd ask later, because clearly there were rules here she didn't know yet.

Dinner was a lesson in itself. Wade's little brother reached across the whole table for the sweet and sour pork, and his aunt tapped his chopsticks with hers like a fencing match. Claire, watching, kept her elbows in and waited until dishes were passed her way. When the tea got low, she refilled the grandmother's cup before her own, because she'd noticed everyone doing that, and the grandmother patted her hand so warmly Claire glowed.

Later, over cake, Andie told the story of the elevator, waving her fork. "So technically we're on the fifth floor, but really we're on the fourth. It's a whole fake floor." Wade's brother immediately announced he lived on a secret floor and planned to revolve around it, spinning in his chair until he got dizzy and had to stop.

"You didn't open your envelope," Wade whispered to Claire as they cleared plates.

"I didn't want to get it wrong," she whispered back.

"Grandma says you keep it. That's the custom. Open it later, not in front of her."

At home, Claire peeled it open and found a crisp two-dollar bill and a note in wobbly handwriting: Come again. She stuck it above her desk, next to the puzzle receipt, and made a plan to learn five words of Chinese before the next birthday, starting with whatever "four" was, since that one was clearly powerful.

She texted Wade: Next time I press the secret button.

He replied with a single eggplant emoji, which she decided was toxic, and she laughed all the way down the hall.

Penelope found the note taped inside her desk on Monday morning, folded into a lopsided triangle the way Emilio always folded them. "Meet me in the computer lab at lunch," it read. "I need you to supervise something. Bring your brain. It's urgent." Emilio's urgent usually meant a lost pencil, but he had been talking about the baseball stats club all week, so she went.

The lab smelled like warm keyboards. Emilio was already there, hunched over a screen, clicking through old player pages. "I'm making a case to Mr. Bondarenko," he said. "The club picks a greatest player of the nineties at the end of the term, and I'm going to win the argument with David Justice. Look. In 1995 he beat Derek Jeter, and in 1996 he beat him again. Justice has the higher batting average both years. Two seasons, two wins. Done." He leaned back with his arms crossed, sure of himself.

Penelope pulled up the second chair. She believed in checking things, the way she believed in checking her answers in math before handing anything in. "So put both years together," she said. "Then the case is closed forever." She started copying numbers into her notebook, which was tedious work, row after row of digits, and behind them she could hear Mr. Bondarenko's class next door reciting vocabulary for their science quiz, someone saying "herbivore" twice because they stuttered on the h.

The room got quiet while she added the columns. Emilio stopped tapping his foot. Outside, a coach blew a whistle three times, and neither of them looked up.

"Wait," Penelope said.

"What do you mean, wait?"

"Look at this." She turned the notebook toward him. She had combined the two seasons, and the numbers had flipped. Jeter's combined average for 1995 and 1996 was higher than Justice's. She checked it twice, then a third time, because it could not be right, except that it was. One player could win each season and still lose when the seasons were put together.

Emilio stared at the screen for a long moment. Then he grabbed a fresh sheet of paper and began folding it into one of his lopsided triangles. "Mr. Bondarenko needs to see this," he said. "Forget the argument. Forget winning. This is better." He wrote on the outside of the triangle in big letters: OPEN THIS FIRST. Then he was out the door and halfway down the hallway, shouting, "Mr. Bondarenko! Mr. Bondarenko, wait till you see what the numbers did!"

Edouard had come to the spring cultural festival with one plan: eat his grandmother's samosas, watch the dancers, and find the booth with the honey cake. But near the fountain, a volunteer in a green sash was handing out wristbands from a shoebox, and the wristbands were the price of admission to the tasting contest. "Close your eyes and pick," she said. Edouard reached in and pulled out a translucent blue band, thin enough to see his skin through.

"Blue," said Zackery, holding up his own. "Me too." Lily-Rose drew red, and her shoulders dropped. "Half my cake samples just walked away," she said, and drifted toward the red tent.

The contest worked like this: the tasting tables were split by colour, and the crowd voted by dropping pebbles in jars. Edouard soon noticed something strange. The blue tent was cheering for a plate of dumplings that, honestly, tasted like cardboard. He had tried one. The red tent was cheering just as loudly for a tray of burnt rice. He tested his idea quietly, the way he tested things: he walked to the red jar and dropped a pebble in for the blue dumplings, then stood back to listen.

"Traitor," someone behind him muttered, though not angrily. A man in a blue band pointed at the red tent and said, "We'll crush them." Edouard frowned. Nobody had chosen their colour. The bands had come out of a shoebox. He found Lily-Rose by the lemonade stand and asked, "Why does everyone care so much about a random wristband?"

She licked sugar off her thumb. "My mom studied this in university. A psychologist named Henri Tajfel did experiments where people favoured their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random." She shrugged. "The bands, yeah. Exactly like that."

Edouard looked back at the two tents. The blue group had started a clapping ritual, three claps and a shout, and the red group had answered with a stomping beat. Neither group had existed an hour ago, and now they had hand signals and battle songs. He tried one more test: he turned his band inside out, so the white lining showed, and walked between the tents. The cheering did not stop for him. Nobody cheered for plain white.

Ms. Berg, his neighbour, was selling bread at a small table between the tents, outside both colours. He bought a roll and told her what he had noticed. She nodded and flipped a pebble into the red jar, then the blue jar, one for each. "My grandmother came from a place that had too much of this," she said. "I vote for both." Edouard ate his roll slowly, watching the jars fill. Then he turned his band back to blue, walked to the red tent, and held out his hand to Lily-Rose. "Save me a piece of that burnt rice," he said. "I want to taste what you're cheering about."

Grace stood in the dressing room with her sneakers half tied, listening to the choir through the wall. Kayleigh had pinned a note to Grace's costume bag an hour ago, and Grace read it a third time before they were called. "You know more songs than you think," it said. "Also I saved you a spot next to me. Don't presume I'll keep it if you're late. Jose says hi from the percussion section." Below that, Jose had scrawled, "Duck when I hit the big drum, I always overshoot."

Backstage, the problem showed itself immediately. Ms. Asante lined the choir up and counted heads twice, because one head kept vanishing. It was the new kid, a small boy whose name Grace hadn't learned yet. Every time Ms. Asante turned around, he shuffled backward until he was behind the whole back row, nearly hidden in the curtains. Ms. Asante called it an anomaly, said she'd never seen someone drift that far in one rehearsal, and jogged off to hunt for a missing music stand. Grace had ninety seconds to fix it or the formation would be a mess on stage.

She thought about what she'd seen. The boy wasn't running away. He was walking backward, one small step at a time, the way you do when you're nervous and want the audience to be smaller. And the stage was deepest at the back, wide and dark near the curtain. That was the pattern. Grace grabbed his sleeve and walked him down toward the edge of the stage where the lights were parked. "Wait," she said. "I figured it out. Upstage is the back of the stage, farthest from the audience, and downstage is the front, nearest the audience. You keep going upstage without noticing. Stay down here with me and you can see the exit door the whole time." He looked at the door, then at her, and planted his feet.

The lights came up and the choir filed on. Grace kept one eye on her new charge and one eye on Kayleigh, who had left the promised spot open even though a tall alto tried to take it. During the second song Grace realized she'd been so busy guarding the formation that she'd forgotten to be terrified, which felt like a trick Kayleigh might have planned all along.

The small boy stayed downstage, exactly where she'd put him, and on the last note he even stepped forward for his share of the bow, quick and agile, like he'd been doing it for years. From the percussion section came one enormous drum hit, and Grace ducked. So did the whole back row, all except Jose, who waved his sticks at her over the cymbal.

The group chat had been quiet for two hours until Sarina posted a photo of a handwritten card, the script looping and dense. "My grandma wrote this for our family story project but I literally can't read any of it," she typed. "I feel like an idiot. My mom says stop saying that."

Mya stared at the photo. She had heard Sarina chat with her grandmother at the winter concert, fast and easy, both of them laughing at jokes Mya couldn't follow. So Sarina spoke the language. She just couldn't read it. Mya typed back, "Wait. Can you say the words if someone reads it to you?"

"Duh," Sarina wrote. "It's a heritage language. We speak it at home. School and everything else is English."

Mya pulled up the project sheet Mr. Mwangi had handed out and read his note again: sources could include interviews, recordings, and citations for anything written down. A citation needed a text. Sarina had a text she couldn't read and a language she could speak fine. Mya thought of a hypothetical version of the problem, like if Lisa had an old letter in Portuguese, and realized the solution was the same in every case. You didn't need the reader to be the reader.

"Call your grandma," Mya typed. "Put her on speaker. Record it. That's your source."

"Wait that's allowed??"

"It's an interview. Interviews are allowed. Read the sheet."

Then Lisa invaded the chat with seventeen messages about her own idea, a story about her great-uncle and a stolen bicycle, and for a minute the plan got buried under arguments about whether a bicycle counted as family history. Mr. Mwangi, apparently added to the chat by someone, posted only: "Recordings count as sources. Cite them as interviews."

At seven that evening a voice note appeared in the chat. Sarina's grandmother read the card aloud, her voice slow and warm, and every so often Sarina's voice came in behind her, translating a phrase for the recording. When it ended there was one last message from Sarina: a photo of the card propped against her laptop, and underneath it, "She says my pronunciation of one word was better than my mom's."

Gabriella crouched at the top of the quarter pipe with her notebook balanced on her knee, because tonight was the night she finally tested her science-fair plan. Her problem was that judges loved demos you could see, and sound was invisible. Her trick was to make sound's logic visible using Eden's long synthetic slinky, the rainbow one that stretched halfway across a room.

"Watch this," she called. Eden and Kali rolled their boards over and sat on the coping. Gabriella stretched the slinky along the flat bottom of the ramp and flicked one end. A wave rolled down the coils, and the slinky snapped back into place. "Okay, so that's the sound. Now here's the crazy part. Watch one single coil. Pick one and stare at it."

Kali squinted. "The one with the ink mark?"

"That one." Gabriella flicked the end again. The wave zipped along the coils, but the marked coil only jiggled forward and backward, then stopped, right where it had been.

"It didn't go anywhere!" Eden said, popping up off the coping. "The wave went, but the coil stayed."

"Exactly. Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle. Each particle only moves back and forth, and the particles do not travel along with the sound. The wave moves. The particles don't." Gabriella could hardly sit still. This was the part she'd gotten wrong for a whole week, until she'd taped a piece of thread to one coil and watched the thread refuse to travel.

"So why is sound faster in water?" Kali asked. "That's the judges' question, right?"

Gabriella had her answer ready, and it involved dominoes. She pulled a box from her backpack and set a line of them across the flat bottom, spaced wide. She tapped the first one. It toppled the second, then the third, and the chain crawled along the ramp, but every fallen domino ended up flat in its own spot. Then she reset them, this time packed tight, nearly touching. She tapped the first domino again and the wave crashed down the line twice as fast, each piece still just falling in place.

"Water particles are packed close, like the tight line," she said. "Air is the spaced-out one."

Kali grabbed a domino. "Do the sound part again. I want to see that marked coil stay put."

Just then Mr. Navarro, who ran the snack shack, wandered over with his broom. "You three playing dominoes on my ramp?"

"It's a science fair," Gabriella said. "Want to see sound?"

He leaned the broom against the fence. "Show me."

She stretched the slinky wide, flicked the end, and pointed at the ink-marked coil. It wobbled back and forth, and the wave raced away from it down the ramp.

Mr. Navarro bent down until his nose nearly touched the coils. "Would you look at that," he said. "Do it again."

Hannah knelt on the wooden boardwalk and squinted through the little field microscope Mr. Grant had brought for the nature trail club. Two slides sat on the platform, and she had to decide which one held leaf cells and which one held cheek cells, because Mr. Grant had mixed up his labels and refused to fix them for her. "A scientist doesn't need the label," he said, "if the evidence is right there."

Through the lens, the first slide showed cells with straight edges, like bricks laid in neat rows, every one a tidy little box. The second slide showed blobby, roundish cells, some of them squished sideways, with no corners anywhere. Hannah thought about her own cheeks. They were soft and could puff out or flatten, nothing about them was stiff. Leaves, though, held their shape even when she forgot to water the classroom plant. That felt like a clue.

"Got it," she said. "The boxy ones are the leaf, and the round blobs are the cheek." Lennox, crouched beside her, shook his head. "No way. The blobs are leaf cells. Leaves are floppy." He had been trying all afternoon to spot a painted turtle, and he wanted a quick answer so he could get back to scanning the pond. "Look again," Hannah said. "The boxy cells have walls around them, like fences. That's why they're stuck in box shapes. The blobby ones just have a stretchy outside, so they can be round or weird. Walls restrict the shape." Lennox leaned in, frowned, and then his shoulders dropped. "Fine. You're right. But if a turtle shows up, I'm gone."

Hannah flipped the cards over and checked the faded pencil marks on the backs. Leaf, boxy. Cheek, blobby. Both right. "It's kind of fundamental," she said. "If you know that one thing, you can name a slide with no label at all." Mr. Grant grinned and clipped a fresh slide onto the platform, an unlabeled one from his shirt pocket.

Hannah bent to the eyepiece. "Onion skin," she announced. "And it's not even my turn to guess." Down at the pond, Lennox suddenly pointed and whispered, "There. Turtle."

The hospital hallway smelled like disinfector and coffee, and Jake kept his eyes on the gray carpet tiles all the way to the family room. His grandmother had died two nights ago, and this was the last morning before the room was cleared out. He had not slept since Tuesday. Not one real night. He would lie there listening to the furnace, then it would be morning and his body felt like wet sand. He had eaten half a piece of toast yesterday and nothing else, and now his stomach hurt in a way that made him wonder if he was catching something. What if grief had let a real sickness in behind it, like a door left open? He turned the question over while the elevator hummed.

Abdulrahman was already sitting in the family room with his own mother, because his grandfather was on the fourth floor. Jake had not expected anyone he knew. He sat down across from him, and after a while he decided to confide in him, quietly, the way you can with someone in a hospital. "I haven't slept in four days," he said. "And I can barely eat. Do you think I'm getting sick?"

Abdulrahman tore his granola bar in half and pushed a piece across the table. "When my grandpa died last year, same thing happened to me. Tired all the time, no sleep, food tasted like cardboard. It's the grief itself. It hits your body too, not just your feelings." He shrugged. "It wears off. Slowly."

They cleared out Grandma's drawer together after lunch. She had been frugal her whole life, so Jake was not surprised to find a rubber-banded stack of greeting cards she had saved, or the pen with her name on it. What surprised him was a card at the bottom addressed to him, in her shaky handwriting, unfinished. "Dear Jake," it said, "if you can't sleep, count the reasons instead of sheep. I got to ninety-one with you in" and there it stopped, right at what would have been the climax of the list. Jake counted the reasons out loud on the drive home. He reached fourteen before he fell asleep against the window, his dad's hand resting on his shoulder the whole way.

The note appeared in Jeremy's locker on Tuesday, folded into a triangle like a paper football. He opened it in the hallway, away from the crowd. "Everyone can smell you after soccer. Please fix it. A friend." His ears went hot. He read it twice, then crumpled it into his pocket before anyone could see.

At lunch he sat with Maxine and Marina and said nothing about the note. He was thinking too hard to talk. After Saturday's game in the heat, Maxine had announced that sweat itself stinks, and Marina had laughed and said no, sweat doesn't stink, but she wouldn't say what did. Jeremy had even done an experiment of his own. He'd wiped sweat off his forearm with a clean towel right after running, sniffed it, and found almost no smell at all. His shirt later, though, was a different story. Something invisible was going on. Sweat was the innocent part, he was almost sure of it, and something else did the damage later.

"You look like a detective," Maxine said, waving a fry at him.

"I'm figuring something out," he said. "Meet me at the pharmacy after school. Both of you."

Ms. Patel, the pharmacist, raised an eyebrow at three eleven-year-olds marching to the deodorant aisle like they were founding a dynasty of hygiene, as Maxine put it. Jeremy studied the shelves. One label had a weird cartoon skunk wearing sunglasses, so eccentric that Marina giggled and took a picture of it.

"Okay," Jeremy said, holding up two sticks of deodorant like evidence. "Saturday you said sweat stinks. But I tested it. Fresh sweat off my arm had almost no smell."

"So?" Maxine crossed her arms.

"So the smell shows up later. It's not the sweat itself." He picked up a bottle labeled antibacterial body wash and turned it slowly in his hand, watching them both. "Bacteria on the skin break down the sweat. That's where the smell comes from. That's why washing every day matters, and why this stuff works."

Marina grinned. "That's what I was trying to tell you, Maxine."

"You could have just said it," Maxine muttered.

At the counter, Jeremy counted out his allowance for the deodorant and the body wash. Ms. Patel rang it up, then leaned over the counter. "Daily shower, every single day, not just when you remember. Got it?"

"Got it," Jeremy said. He slid the crumpled note across the counter so she could see it, then folded it back into his pocket, a mystery solved, a clue kept.

Maxine held the door open. "Same time Saturday?"

"Same time," Jeremy said, and dropped the deodorant into his backpack with the note.

Noah yanked his gym shirt out of his backpack at Grandpa's house and held it at arm's length. Last year his shirts never smelled like this. He sniffed the collar, then the hem, then, carefully, each armpit. The stink lived in the armpits only, which was weird, because his arms barely sweated at all.

"Grandpa, do you have two clothespins?" he called from the laundry room. He clipped the pins over his nose for one sniff, then moved them so each pin isolated one nostril, sniffing the collar with one side of his nose and the armpit with the other. Science, sort of. The armpit side lost. Badly. He was still experimenting when his phone buzzed with a message from Bodhi, who was home recovering from a concussion he got at hockey practice and had been reading his older sister's health textbook out of boredom. Noah read it out loud to the room:

"Dear Noah, you will not believe this. During puberty, sweat glands in the armpits and groin, called apocrine glands, become active and start producing sweat. APOCRINE. It's a real word, I checked twice. So your shirt smells because those glands turned on, like a switch. Also my head is fine, I can come to Grandpa's on Saturday if the doctor says yes. Bring the good snacks."

Noah read it twice, grinning. A hidden switch in his own body, flipped this year and never last year. That meant the fix had to happen where the glands were, every single day, not just when he felt sweaty.

"Apocrine," he said out loud, just to hear it. "Grandpa, can I do laundry here? I'm starting a whole new system."

Grandpa laughed from the kitchen. "Soap's under the sink, and there's a fresh stick of deodorant in the bathroom cabinet, never opened. Help yourself."

Noah stuffed the shirt in the washer, poured the soap, and marched upstairs to claim the deodorant before anyone else could. Then he texted back: "Saturday YES. Bring your sister's book."

The argument started over a plastic spoon, which Hazel thought was bizarre until she heard what came with it. Cale and Michel both wanted to be the conductor for the party game where everyone got a noisemaker and one person stood at the front waving a wooden spoon like a baton. Michel had grabbed the spoon first, and Cale was now holding the other end of it, and neither of them was letting go.

"You always get to be in charge," Cale said. "Give it."

"You don't even want to conduct," Michel said. "You just want to stand where everyone can see you."

Ms. Kobayashi, whose backyard it was, caught Hazel's eye and then went back to slicing the cake, which Hazel understood to mean: your problem. Great. She took a breath and stepped between them.

"Wait," she said. "Cale, why do you want the spoon?"

"Because it's my turn to be in charge." That was what Cale demanded, his position, but it wasn't a reason. So Hazel tried again, asking why being in charge mattered, and the answer came out sideways: Cale's little brother always bossed him around at home, and at this party he wanted one hour where somebody wasn't telling him what to do. Michel's answer came out faster. He had practiced conducting with his headphones on all week, and if he didn't do it now, in front of people, he would lose his nerve.

Hazel stood there holding her cupcake and thinking. She remembered a line from a poster in the library: positions are what you demand, interests are why you want it. Two people could demand the same thing for completely different reasons. The spoon was the position. The reasons underneath were the interests. She looked at both of them and realized the reasons didn't actually collide, if she could get them to revise the plan a little.

"Michel conducts first," she said. "Cale gets to make up the rules for the song, anything he wants, and Michel has to conduct whatever Cale invents. Silly rules, weird rules, all of it. Then you switch for round two."

"Any rules?" Cale said, and a grin started at the corners of his mouth.

"Even a rule that everyone has to hop on one foot," Michel said. He handed over a slip of paper from his pocket, where he had already scribbled a conducting pattern. "As long as they follow this."

Cale took the paper, studied it, and announced that the first rule was that Michel had to conduct while balancing on one leg. Michel laughed so hard he almost dropped the spoon, then hopped up onto the low garden wall and raised it high. "Ready," he called out. "One and two and hop!"

Matteo flopped onto the living room couch with the family laptop and a granola bar, because tonight he was going to beat the login screen once and for all. His school had sent home a note saying every student needed a new password for the class portal, and Ms. Goh had written "make it strong" in red pen at the bottom, as if that explained anything. He typed "matteo123" and stared at the little bar that turned red, then orange, like the laptop was personally disappointed in him.

He called Erica, who showed up ten minutes later with Vicky trailing behind her, drawn by the promise of leftover granola bars. "You need a passphrase, not a password," Erica said, plopping onto the cushion beside him. "Like, four random words. My dad uses one about agriculture, because he says nobody guesses farming words." Vicky snickered. "Nobody guesses farming words because nobody wants to." Matteo typed "purple-tapir-cactus-soup" and watched the bar flourish into a deep, satisfied green. He felt like he'd won something. Then he did what he always did: he opened a notebook and wrote the new password down next to his old ones, and Vicky leaned over and read them aloud in a game-show voice, which was exactly the moment he understood the problem.

"Every site has the same one," he said slowly. "Look. Gaming site, cartoon site, this portal. All matteo123." He remembered, in a flash, the afternoon last spring when his points had vanished from the basketball game and the coach's son had shrugged and said someone "must have guessed it." Matteo had blamed his little cousin. His little cousin had been innocent, which Matteo now admitted, at least silently, and the real culprit had probably been the password itself, reused everywhere like a single key for the whole neighborhood. He went down the list, site by site, and gave each one its own four random words, working so fast Erica had to grab the granola box to safety.

Then the twist arrived. On the cartoon site, after he changed the password, a message popped up: someone had just tried to log in from another country. His stomach dropped. "It's the thief," Vicky whispered, delighted and horrified at once. But before either of them could panic, the screen asked for a code, one sent to his mom's phone. "Two-factor authentication," Erica said. "It wants a second proof." The code request sat there, blocking the stranger like a bouncer at a door, and Matteo realized the stolen password alone was useless now. He'd gotten something wrong and it had still turned out fine, which felt almost like cheating.

His mom's phone buzzed from the kitchen. She called out, "Matteo, why is there a code on my phone?" He grinned at the two of them and called back, "It's a long story! It involves a purple tapir!"

Zack slid his essay draft into the library computer and clicked the readability checker, mostly because Pascal had dared him to. The score came back low, with a note that the piece was "difficult to read." That stung. He'd written about the skate park on Delancey Street with what he thought were vivid, powerful, extremely amazing descriptions.

"Mine better be easy to read," Pascal said, leaning over. "My sister's going to read it aloud at our family thing Saturday, and if she stumbles over a word, everyone will ridicule me for a month." Pascal drummed his fingers on the desk. "I need a seven out of ten. Easy. Simple."

Zack remembered a time back in fourth grade when Mr. Martínez had handed him a dictionary and said something odd. He couldn't recall the whole conversation, just the librarian holding up a page of gray text and saying, "The Flesch Reading Ease test, created by Rudolf Flesch, scores how easy writing is to read using its average sentence length and average syllables per word." At the time Zack had shrugged and gone back to comic books. Now he wondered. Average sentence length. Average syllables per word. Two things you could actually count.

He found Mr. Martínez shelving returns near the study rooms. "Can I test something?" Zack asked. Back at the computer, he counted his sentences and his long words, then tried an experiment: he cut the adjectives. Not the good ones, just the frail ones, the "very"s and "really"s that leaned on stronger words. Then he split one monster sentence into three short ones and joined two choppy ones together. He ran the checker again. The score jumped.

"So it's not magic," Zack said, staring at the number. "It's arithmetic."

"It counts syllables, dude," Pascal said, already typing his own draft. "It doesn't know your sister."

Zack read his first paragraph aloud in a whisper and grinned at how different it sounded. Then he deleted the word "extremely" and ran the test one more time.

Layla stared at her reflection in the mirror above her dresser and poked at the red spots along her chin. Last year her face had been clear. Something had changed, and she wanted to know what. She flopped onto her bed, opened her notebook, and wrote a note for her friend Oceane, who had texted her last week about the exact same problem.

"Dear Oceane," she wrote. "Meet me Saturday. I found something at the pharmacy. Bring your allowance." She folded the note, slid it into an envelope, and set it on the windowsill where she'd see it in the morning. Then she pulled up the pharmacy website on her tablet and started a list of the face washes she remembered seeing, with their prices and the words on their labels. One label kept repeating something strange: "controls sebum." She copied the word down and underlined it twice.

On Saturday, Layla and Oceane stood in the pharmacy aisle with three bottles in their hands. "Sebum," Oceane read off the back of one. "It's the oil your skin makes. The label says hormones in puberty make the oil glands produce more of it, and that can clog pores and lead to acne." Layla turned the bottle around, thinking. So that was the hidden cause. It wasn't the pizza, and it wasn't because she'd been lazy about washing. Her body was simply producing more oil now, and the extra oil was blocking things up. "So we don't need the vigorous scrubbing wash," she said, reading a bottle that promised to blast pores clean. "Scrubbing hard might even fracture the skin, the pharmacist flyer says. We just need something that cuts the oil gently." They each bought the mild wash and split the cost.

Back in Layla's bedroom, they taped a simple chart inside her closet door: one column for washing morning and night, one for new spots. "Two weeks," Oceane said, drawing empty boxes. "Then we check." The first week, two new pimples appeared anyway, and Layla almost quit, but she kept washing, twice a day, gentle and steady. By the end of the second week the chart showed almost nothing new, and the old spots were fading. Layla drew a small star in the corner of the chart to preserve the moment, then held the marker out to Oceane. "Your turn to start a chart," she said. "I'll buy the next bottle."

The departures board flicked to ON TIME just as Norah's dad handed out the boarding passes, and she grabbed hers like a golden ticket. Gate B14, Yellowstone, five days of geysers and bison. The only problem was the crossword puzzle her seatmate Carl had assigned her, because Carl was flying to the same park with his own family and had declared a vacation-long trivia war. One clue had stumped her on the walk through security: "First U.S. national park, two words." Her answer sheet said "vague" next to it, which was her code for no idea.

Waiting at the gate, Norah stared at the clue. She couldn't see the answer anywhere, but she could test an idea about it. Maybe the park itself dropped hints, like a pattern hiding in plain sight. She pulled the park brochure from her backpack and skimmed every paragraph, hunting for anything old, anything official, anything with a date. She flipped it over twice, convinced the answer had to be printed somewhere, because parks loved bragging about themselves.

Then Remington, from their class, plopped into the seat beside her with a giant pretzel. "Sitting behind you on the plane," she announced. "My mom says sorry in advance for my little brother." She leaned over. "What are you scribbling?"

"Crossword war with Carl," Norah said. "I'm missing the Yellowstone clue."

Remington's eyes went huge. "My grandpa quizzes us on that every single trip. He says a ranger stumped our whole family at a campfire talk with the same question." She lowered her voice like it was a secret code. "Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law."

Norah wrote it down at top speed. "Remington, you just won me the war."

"Boarding Group Two," the gate agent called, and Norah shot up so fast she nearly dropped the brochure. A strap on her backpack snagged the armrest, trying to hinder her, but she yanked it free.

Carl was already in the jetway. She waved the crossword at him and shouted down the line, "Ulysses S. Grant! March first, 1872! Ask me anything!"

He groaned, and half the line laughed.

Zoey stood in the gym changeroom holding her shirt sleeve away from her armpit, sniffing cautiously, and wished she hadn't. After gym she smelled like the hallway near the cafeteria on a hot day. Jenson noticed too, because at lunch he slid his desk a few inches away, and Karim whispered, "It's not just you. Half the class smells after dodgeball." That made Zoey feel slightly better, but only slightly. She wanted to fix it, not just survive it.

In Ms. Nowak's health class there was a basket on the shelf labeled "take one if you need one," filled with two kinds of sticks. One said deodorant. The other said antiperspirant, and in smaller letters, aluminum compounds. Zoey took one of each and turned them over. Karim leaned across the table. "Aren't they the same thing?" Ms. Nowak, who enforced the no-talking rule during reading time, was busy at her desk, so Zoey read the back panels herself, mouthing the words. The deodorant stick listed nothing about aluminum. The antiperspirant one said it reduced sweating by temporarily plugging the sweat ducts. Plugging the ducts. She looked at Karim. "They're not the same," she whispered. "This one actually plugs your sweat ducts with aluminum stuff. That's why the labels are distinct." She turned the deodorant stick over again. "And this one just covers the smell." Karim frowned. "So antiperspirant means it plugs the ducts?" Zoey nodded, and copied both labels into her notebook.

Their science project, a poster about the estuary where the river met the sea and fresh water mixed with salt, sat half-finished on the table between them, but Zoey kept thinking about her experiment. For three days she used deodorant on one arm and antiperspirant on the other, and ran laps at recess. Day one: both arms sweaty. Day two: the antiperspirant side barely damp. Day three, after dodgeball, she checked again and grinned so wide Karim asked what was wrong.

That night her mom found a note crumpled in Zoey's gym bag, written on a torn corner of the estuary poster. "Mom. Antiperspirant. The kind with aluminum. It actually works, I tested it. Can we get some? Love, Zoey." Under it she had drawn a smiley face with one wet armpit and one dry one.

The next morning, a brand-new stick sat on the counter with a sticky note in her mom's writing: "For the dry side." Zoey laughed, dropped it in her backpack, and headed for the bus.

The sign at the gas station read "Water: $4.00" in red marker, and Lucy stared at it with her last five dollars crumpled in her fist. The storm was coming that night, and the shelves that usually held dozens of bottles held exactly seven. Two days ago the same bottles had cost a dollar, and she knew it, because she'd bought one after soccer practice.

"Four dollars for water," Adrian said beside her, holding his own money. He had been planning to buy hot chocolate from the machine, but he'd given that up the moment he saw the emptying shelf. "That's robbery." Two men at the register each took one bottle, looked at the price, and put them back, saying they'd fill jugs at home instead. A woman took two, paid, and hurried out. Lucy counted the shelf again. Six bottles. Five. Nobody was grabbing armfuls the way they'd grabbed cheap batteries last summer when the price had dropped to twenty-five cents and the whole rack emptied in an hour.

"Wait," Lucy said. "When the price was low, everybody bought tons. Now it's high, and people are putting it back." She checked the memory against what she was seeing, and it fit. "Adrian, I think when the price rises, people buy less, and when it falls, they buy more. Like, always, as long as nothing else changes."

"That sounds like a rule," Adrian said. "Rules need a name."

"The jury's still out on the name," Lucy said, and he laughed so hard a man at the coffee station turned around. The cashier leaned toward them. "There's a name," she said. "Law of demand." She tapped the sign. "Consistent as sunrise."

Lucy bought one bottle instead of three, and Adrian, instead of sulking, spent his money on her second-choice, a jug of juice that had stayed cheap because nobody wanted it. At the door she paused. "You intervened in the hot chocolate crisis and saved the day," she said, holding up the juice.

Adrian bowed. "The jury of one finds me heroic."

Bentley found the note taped to his locker after last period, folded twice and written in Felicity's round, careful handwriting. "Practice, 4 o'clock. Dylan says he's right and I say I'm right and we both want YOU to decide. Bring your brain." He read it twice on the walk to the field, because being asked to decide felt like being handed something heavy with no instructions.

The argument was about the relay order. Felicity believed the fastest runner should anchor the final leg, since that position got the most attention at the finish. Dylan believed the fastest runner should lead off, to build an early gap before the other teams could respond. When Bentley jogged over, they were already orbiting the coach's clipboard like two moons around the same planet, each talking louder than the other.

"Tell her," Dylan said.

"Tell him," Felicity said.

Bentley opened his mouth to say which idea he actually thought was better, then stopped. Last spring he had picked a side in an argument between two boys on his old team, and the boy he ruled against had barely spoken to him for a month. The team's times had gotten worse during that little recession of trust, and only when the two of them finally worked it out on their own did the passes start connecting again. He didn't want a repeat of that.

"Here's the thing," Bentley said slowly. "I'm not going to announce a winner."

"Then why are you even here?" Felicity demanded.

"Because there's a difference between a judge and a mediator," Bentley said. "A mediator is a neutral third person. I help you two reach your own agreement. I don't decide who's right."

Dylan squinted at him. "So what do you actually do?"

Bentley shrugged. "I ask questions, I guess. Felicity, what happens if we lead off fast and the other teams catch up anyway?"

"Then it doesn't matter who anchored," she admitted.

"Dylan, what happens if we save our fastest for last but we're already behind by half the race?"

"Then even speed might not fix it," Dylan conceded, kicking at the grass.

They walked the course once together, arguing but quieter now, testing each idea against the track's real curves. By the water bottles they had invented a third option: Felicity would run second, where she could protect an early lead, and Dylan would anchor, which he'd secretly wanted all along.

Ms. Girma blew her whistle from across the field. "Line up!"

Felicity grinned and held out her fist, and Bentley bumped it, feeling lighter than he had all afternoon.

"So," Dylan said, jogging backward toward the start line, "same time next argument?"

The lobby filled at 7:03, and Emilia's friends' names popped up in the chat one by one. She despised the way her own username looked now, EmiliaTheBrave, because of what she had posted under it last spring on the game's public clan page: a whole paragraph in ALL CAPS about how Karina was toxic and always stealing loot. She had deleted it an hour later, but Karina had seen it, and Karina had said nothing since.

"You're on," Issa typed in the private party channel, where only the four of them could read it. Emilia joined the match and played badly, missing two easy shots, because she kept thinking about the old post. After the round ended, people hung around the lobby doing the usual things, spamming dance emotes, typing "gg" in all lowercase, arguing in the public chat about who had lagged.

"Wait," Karina typed, in public chat, so everyone in the lobby could see it. "Emilia. Did you write that thing about me and then delete it?" Emilia's hands stopped on the keyboard. Public chat meant forty strangers watching. She switched to a private message, the quiet channel, and typed, "yes. I'm sorry. Can we talk here?" Karina replied, "ask your question in public. I don't hide."

Emilia took a breath and typed in the lobby, in front of everyone: "I wrote something mean about Karina and deleted it. I'm sorry, Karina." A few people typed "oof." One typed "memoir incoming lol," which made no sense to her, and Karina typed, "ok. thanks."

Later that night, Mr. Chowdhury, her neighbour, was out watering his tomatoes when she mentioned it. "The thing is, it's deleted, but it still feels like it's floating around somewhere," she said.

"Try the Wayback Machine," he said. "The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages. Something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found there."

She ran upstairs, opened the clan page's address, and pasted it into the Wayback Machine. A list of saved dates appeared. She clicked the one from last spring, and the page loaded, and there it was: her paragraph, in ALL CAPS, exactly as she had written it.

She screenshotted it, then opened a private message to Karina and pasted the link. "You should see this. It's the proof of what I did. Then I'm writing to the Archive to ask them to take it down." Karina's reply came in thirty seconds: "you'd really do that?" Emilia was already typing the request.

Sofia dropped into the game lobby after school, her avatar's luminous wings glowing against the dark loading screen. Three of her friends were already there, tiny figures hopping in circles around the fountain, which for some reason gurgled like actual plumbing instead of magical water. Christine's chat bubble popped up first, all capitals: "TEAM SNOW WOLF ASSEMBLE."

"Ready," Sofia typed. She liked that the lobby had conventions everyone knew: capitals meant excitement, tildes meant silliness, and the word "gg" after a match meant you were a good sport even if you lost. It was like a secret code, except everybody in the world knew it except grandmothers.

Then a message arrived that made her stomach flip. Cayden had posted a screenshot in the lobby chat, and the screenshot was of a private message Christine had sent to Sofia two days ago: "cayden hogs the treasure chests, he took 3 of mine yesterday." Sofia stared at it. She had read that message alone, in her private chat, and now it sat there in the public lobby where Cayden and everyone could see it. So that was the rule, she realized. A private message was only as private as the people who received it, because anyone who got one could screenshot it and share it anywhere.

She tested her idea before saying anything. She messaged Christine privately: "did you know cayden had it?" Christine's reply came fast: "I sent it to ONE person. You." Sofia typed back, "that's what I thought. it traveled anyway." In the lobby, Cayden was typing, and typing, and typing, the little dots hibernating and waking over and over like a sleepy bear.

Finally his bubble appeared: "I did hog the chests. They were shiny. I'm sorry, Christine." Christine's avatar did a slow backflip. "Apology accepted. Sofia, you're on screenshot patrol forever." Sofia's wings flared bright, and she typed, "Deal. Now can we play before my wolf hibernates for real?"

The lawnmower had refused to start for three days, and Maelie refused to believe it was dead. She knelt on the oil-stained concrete of the garage workshop, one ear pressed to the engine casing while Aariz pulled the starter cord again. The machine coughed, sputtered, and died. "See?" Aariz said, wiping his hands on his jeans. "Dead." But Maelie had heard something underneath the cough, a faint sucking sound that came before it, like the mower was trying to drink and getting nothing. That sound was invisible to Aariz, but she had a guess about it.

"Your hypothesis," Jenson said, reading off the science fair checklist taped to the wall beside the pegboard. "You need one for the board." Mr. Toussaint, their neighbour, had let them use his garage and his old dictionary for the project, and the dictionary lay open on the workbench next to a jar of bolts. Maelie flipped to the H section while Jenson hunted for the word on the poster of weekly vocabulary words, the one that also had "estuary" on it because Mr. Toussaint liked to fish where the river met the sea. "Hypothesis," she read, and then read it again, slower. "It comes from ancient Greek, and it literally means 'putting or placing under.'"

"You're placing your guess under a test," Jenson said, peering over her shoulder. "Like a foundation."

Maelie didn't answer right away. She thought about last summer, when she'd let her cousin convince her the mower was out of gas without checking, and they'd pushed the heavy thing all the way to the gas station for nothing. She had envied her cousin's confidence that day, but she didn't envy being wrong. This time she would place her guess under the test and let the test decide. "My hypothesis," she said, standing up, "is that the fuel line is clogged, so no gas is getting through, and that sucking sound is the engine pulling against a blockage." Aariz wrinkled his nose. "How do you test something you can't see inside?"

"You look at what the hidden thing would cause," Maelie said. She unclamped the fuel line at the carburetor end and held it over a coffee can while Aariz pulled the cord. Nothing dripped out. Then she blew through the line, and a gritty little plug of old gum and dirt popped onto the bench. She reattached the hose, and on the next pull the mower roared to life so suddenly that Jenson jumped and knocked over the jar of bolts.

Later, painting the letters for her board, she printed the Greek meaning under her hypothesis, and underneath that she taped the actual gritty plug of dirt in a plastic bag, labeled in her careful handwriting. Mr. Toussaint leaned in the doorway, watching. "You know," he said, "your grandfather fixed things the same way, and his father before him. Almost hereditary." Maelie looked at the little gray lump behind the plastic, the hidden thing she had never seen directly but had caught anyway, and picked up the brush. "Aariz," she called, "hand me the yellow paint. The title needs to be brighter."

Brody crouched between his two garden beds behind the garage, pressing his thumb into the dirt. In the bed with the straw he had scattered from the farmers' market, the soil was dark and damp right under the surface. In the bare bed beside it, the ground had cracked into a map of little canyons, and three tomato seedlings lay flopped over like they had given up on life. He had watered both beds the same, morning and night, turning the valve on the rain barrel exactly one half turn each time. So why did one bed look like a jungle and the other like a desert?

At school he showed Bowen a photo of the two beds on his phone. "Aliens," Bowen said immediately. "Or your dad is sneaking out and watering one of them." Brody said that theory was plausible, actually, since his dad did weird things at 6 a.m., but he doubted it. Oceanne leaned over Bowen's shoulder and frowned. "The straw one. What's different about the straw one?" That was the question Brody kept circling. The straw covered the ground. The bare bed exposed the soil straight to the hot sun, day after day. He turned that over all through math class, doodling a sun and a cloud of straw in his notebook margin until Ms. Chowdhury cleared her throat at him.

On Saturday he rode his bike to the farmers' market and found the woman who had sold him the seedlings. He bought two more tomatoes and, after standing in front of the straw bales for a long minute, a whole armful of straw. "Good choice," she said, weighing it. "Straw's called mulch once you lay it on the soil." He nodded like he'd known that, which he had not.

Back home, he tucked straw around every seedling in the cracked bed, thick as a blanket, and pulled four weeds that had sprouted in the bare soil but hadn't dared to poke through the straw bed. Then he crouched and pressed his thumb into the dirt again, right at a seedling's roots. Cool. Damp. He grinned at the tomato plant. "Don't tell the others," he said, "but you were always my favorites."

Jack sat under the oak canopy at Riverside Park, digging the toe of his sneaker into the dirt like he could excavate the whole flowerbed if he tried hard enough. He was waiting for Jayden, who was late, which was new. Jayden was never late. But then, Jayden had spent every afternoon this week at the skate bowls with Aila instead of meeting Jack at the climbing wall, so maybe lateness was just the newest symptom of a bigger problem.

When Jayden finally arrived, he didn't sit down. "You texted me four times," he said. "My mom said you knocked on the door."

"Because you disappeared." Jack stood up. "We had a wall day. Tuesday, Thursday. That was ours."

Jayden shrugged, which stung worse than an argument would have.

Ms. Oyelaran, who was running the park's volunteer crew a few meters away, called out to a kid on her team who kept talking over his partner. "Try active listening," she said. "Rogers and Farson came up with it in 1957. Repeat back what you heard, in your own words." Then she went back to counting shovels, and the kid tried it, and his partner stopped looking like she wanted to leave.

Jack watched the two volunteers, and a small rebellious part of him wanted to say it was corny. But he was the one sulking under a tree, so maybe corny was worth a shot. "So you felt like... I was mad, even though I never said it out loud?" he tried.

Jayden blinked. "You were mad. I could tell."

"That's not what I mean. I mean, say what you heard me say."

Jayden blew out a long breath. "So you felt I picked Aila over you. Like she replaced me."

Something loosened in Jack's shoulders. "Yeah. That." He hadn't known that was the shape of it until Jayden said it out loud.

"Nobody replaced you," Jayden said. "Aila's trying to build a skate video for the park's summer contest, and she needed a cameraman who wouldn't laugh at her falls. She doesn't even know you're jealous, man. She asked if you'd hold the second camera."

Jayden finally sat down on the bench beside him. "Wall day tomorrow? And filming Saturday?"

"Both," Jack said. He pulled out his phone and typed a message to Aila: I'm in for Saturday. Bring the good camera.

Lillian stood at the stove with her phone propped against the flour canister, staring at the word "roux" for the tenth time. Kelsey was coming over at six for their movie night, and Lillian had promised real mac and cheese, not the boxed kind, because Kelsey's older sister always teased them about eating like little kids. The recipe said to melt butter, stir in flour, then add milk. It made it sound easy.

She melted the butter, sprinkled in the flour, and stirred until the paste smelled toasty. Then, wanting to prioritize speed because the movie started soon, she poured all two cups of milk in at once. The mixture seized into pale little balls that refused to mix no matter how fast she whisked. She whisked until her wrist ached, and the balls just rolled around the pan like wet dough. She turned the burner off and stared at the ruined pot, and that was when Kelsey walked in, holding her own whisk like a peace offering.

"I already ruined it," Lillian said. "There's lumps everywhere."

Kelsey leaned over the pot, frowning. "My grandma makes this. She goes slow. Like, annoyingly slow." She tilted her head. "Maybe slow is the point?"

Lillian scraped the lumpy mess into a bowl and started over. This time she thought about what had happened before. When she'd dumped the milk in all at once, the flour had nowhere to go, so it had bunched up into balls. Maybe it needed room to spread out. She tested the idea: she melted the butter, stirred in the flour, and then added the milk just a splash at a time, whisking hard after every splash. Splash, whisk, smooth. Splash, whisk, smooth. Each little bit vanished into the sauce before she added the next.

"It's working," Kelsey said, hovering at her elbow. "Keep going, don't stop."

When all the milk was in, the sauce was glossy with no lumps anywhere. Lillian dropped in handfuls of cheddar, and it melted into something that actually looked like the picture. She pointed at the towel too close to the burner and said, "Move that, it's flammable." Kelsey moved it, then grinned and pulled out her phone to take a photo for her sister.

Lillian stirred one last time and held up the spoon, cheese stretching in a long ribbon off the end. "First candidate for movie night menu, approved," she said.

Kelsey was already reaching for the box of pasta. "So can we double it?"

Hazel sat cross-legged on the porch steps with her mother's phone, scrolling through articles about making friends in a new town, because in eleven days a moving truck was going to carry everything she owned to a place called Fairview. The screen smelled faintly of the lemon cleaner her mother had used on it, and the porch boards were warm under her knees even though the evening air was cooling. Then she found it: a 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas, which found that it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.

Fifty hours. She read the number twice, then did the math on the back of a seed packet. At lunch, thirty minutes a day, it would take a hundred school days. More than half a year. "That's so slow," she said out loud, and the cat, agile as ever, leapt onto the railing beside her without a sound.

She thought about last September, when Irene had been new at her school. They had eaten lunch together exactly once, and Hazel had gone home thinking they were friends, and then Irene had sat with three other girls for two weeks straight. Hazel had decided Irene was rude. Now she narrowed her eyes at the seed packet. Maybe Irene hadn't been rude at all. Maybe one lunch was simply one lunch, and nobody had told them the rules.

There was a whole controversy in the comments under the article, people arguing about whether the hours had to be face to face, but Hazel was more interested in testing it. She grabbed a notebook and wrote "FIFTY HOURS" at the top of a page. The moving boxes stacked by the door were labeled KITCHEN and BOOKS, and next week she would have to label one FRIENDS, except that friends couldn't be taped into a box.

Brandon rode his bike up the driveway before dinner, skidding to a stop in the gravel. "You seriously leaving us?"

"For real," Hazel said. "But listen." She held up the phone. "Fifty hours. That's what it takes. So when I get there, I'm keeping count. Every lunch, every walk home, every anything."

Brandon squinted at the screen. "So if I visit you for a weekend, that's like, thirty hours?"

"Depends how long you stay." She grinned and wrote his name at the top of the list anyway.

The bees were still moving between her mother's tomato blossoms, working the last light, each one pollinating as it went. Hazel added a line to the notebook: Day one, find someone who likes gardens. Then she went inside to look up whether Fairview had a community garden, notebook under her arm like something already precious.

The remote-control car kit sat on the shelf between the paper towels and the birthday candles, priced at forty dollars, and it had sat there for three Saturdays in a row while Connor counted his money at home and got fourteen dollars. His mother pushed the cart toward the dairy aisle, and he drifted toward the checkout, where a little stand of credit card pamphlets leaned against the gum display like it was tired.

He picked one up because it was shiny and because the gum was too expensive. The front promised INSTANT APPROVAL in giant letters. On the back, in letters so small they were almost anonymous, he found the letters A, P, R.

"APR stands for annual percentage rate," Aliyah read over his shoulder. She had appeared out of nowhere, the way she did, holding a box of cereal her mom had sent her to compare with another box. "The yearly interest rate a lender charges on money you borrow. My dad reads these when he's bored."

Connor turned the pamphlet over. Nineteen percent, it said. He did the math in his head, slowly, the way his teacher liked. Forty dollars borrowed. Nineteen percent of that, added on, over a year. Almost eight extra dollars for the same car.

"So if I borrowed forty, I'd really pay, like, forty-eight," he said.

"Plus it keeps going if you're slow paying," Aliyah said, and put the pamphlet back. "My dad says that part loudly."

Connor looked at the car kit, then at the pamphlet stand, then at the car kit again, as if the two of them were arguing. His mother was now two aisles away, coordinating her coupons with what was actually on the shelves, which was her Saturday hobby.

"I get two dollars a week for taking out the recycling," he said. He counted on his fingers, which took a while because fourteen weeks needed more than ten fingers and he had to start over on the second hand. "That's the same amount of time, but I pay forty, not forty-eight."

Mr. Çelik, who bagged groceries on Saturdays and lived in the apartment upstairs from Aliyah, dropped a box of oatmeal into a bag and said, "Thirteen weeks, if your landlord of an allowance gives you a raise."

"He's not my landlord, he's my mom," Connor said.

"She is absolutely your landlord," said Aliyah.

Connor put the pamphlet back on its stand, squared it up with the others, and walked back to the car kit. He picked it up, checked the price again, and set it back down with the care of someone handling evidence.

"Thirteen weeks," he told the box. "Wait right there."

Adam had been saving his allowance for three weeks, and today he was finally going to buy a jar of Mr. Aquino's wildflower honey. He and Veer cut through the crowd at the farmers' market, past stalls of zucchini and bread, until they reached the honey table at the far corner.

A hand-lettered sign leaned against the jars: "BIG SALE, $3 A JAR." The regular price was eight dollars, and Adam knew why the table was surrounded. A woman in front of him bought six jars. A man behind her bought four. By the time Adam reached the front, the table was empty except for a smear of honey on the wood and the sign, which Mr. Aquino was now flipping face down.

"Sold out," Mr. Aquino said, sounding apologetic but not surprised. "I brought sixty jars, and they were gone in forty minutes."

Adam stared at the blank space where the jars had been. Sixty jars sounded like a lot, but at three dollars, everybody wanted them. He remembered the concert tickets Veer's older sister had tried to buy, the cheap ones that vanished while hundreds of fans got nothing. Two situations, same shape: a low price, tons of buyers, not enough to go around. He wasn't sure what to call that shape, exactly.

Veer tugged his sleeve. "Come on, Adelle's holding us a spot at the jam stall. She's been waiting since the market opened, and if the plum jam runs out she's going to be an embarrassment to us all." Veer grinned, but his voice had an edge of worry. Adelle wanted that jam for her grandmother's birthday, and there was only one small batch of it each week.

At the jam stall, the plum jam cost eleven dollars a jar, which sounded outrageous until Adam counted the jars stacked behind Adelle. There must have been eighty of them, and only a few people were buying. High price, plenty of jars, still there. He turned the two pictures over in his mind like cards. Then it clicked.

"I think there's a word for the honey thing," Adam said as they walked home, jar-less but with Adelle clutching her plum jam. "My cousin says it. When a price is kept low, more people want the thing than there are things for sale. That gap is called a shortage."

"Sounds about right," Veer said. "So next week?"

"Next week I coordinate with Adelle. She gets to the market when it opens. I get in line with her, and this time I bring eight dollars, just in case Mr. Aquino skips the sale." Adam looked back toward the empty honey table, already planning. "Either way, I'm getting my jar."

Adam sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field, his right arm wrapped in a bright green cast, and watched Jayda take a shot at the far goal. The groundskeeper's generator hummed behind the fence, powering the scoreboard for Saturday's game, and every time Jayda scored, her victory yell was so loud that Adam caught himself grinning behind the crowd of his teammates.

"How long until it comes off?" Jayda asked, jogging over and flopping down beside him. Her breath fogged in the cold air.

"Six weeks," Adam said. "Four more to go." He tugged his sleeve down over the edge of the cast to insulate his fingers from the wind, which Jayda had told him was silly, since casts were already thick. He thought it helped anyway.

"My grandpa broke his wrist last month," Jayda said. "His cast is enormous. The doctor said he'll wear it for months." She frowned at the field. "That doesn't seem fair. He wasn't even doing anything cool. He slipped on ice."

Adam turned that over. Same kind of break, he figured, or close enough, but his was off in six weeks and his grandpa's would take months. What was different? Not the cast, not the doctor. Then it clicked. "It's because of you," he said. "Because you're a kid. Young bones heal faster than adult bones, so kids get the cast off sooner. My dad said almost the same thing when I got mine."

Jayda sat up. "So grandpa's stuck in his because he's old."

"He's not old," Adam said. "He's adult old. Different." Jayda's laugh was infectious, and even the coach looked over and smiled.

"Test it," Jayda said. "Ask Ms. Ndlovu. She broke her elbow in college."

Ms. Ndlovu was marking cones near the halfway line. Adam walked over and asked, holding up his arm. "Yours came off faster than an adult's would have," she said. "That's how it works. Adults heal slower and wear casts longer."

Adam walked back to the bench, arms spread wide like a scoreboard flashing good news. "Told you."

"Grandpa is going to hate this," Jayda said, and grinned.

Claire had one goal by Friday: convince her whole class to boycott the cafeteria. It had started when she found a patch of grey fungus on her hamburger bun, and she had taken a photo of it before anyone could throw the evidence away. Now she had three arguments lined up, a systematic plan for her five paragraphs, and a spot on Ms. Li's list to read her draft aloud.

She read the first four paragraphs to Arie and Benson at lunch, and even Benson, who normally argued with her about everything, nodded along. Then she reached the last paragraph and slowed down, because it was her favourite part. "In conclusion, if we boycott the cafeteria, the school will have to cancel the spring dance too, since the same company runs both." She looked up. "That's my best idea, right?"

Arie frowned at the paper. "Wait. Why didn't you say that earlier? That's a whole new thing."

"It's my conclusion," Claire said. "Conclusions are where the good stuff goes."

They were still arguing when Ms. Li called the class to order, and Claire read her essay aloud, feeling confident all the way to the final line. Ms. Li made one small red circle, around the last sentence only, and said nothing. Claire stared at that circle for the rest of class, because everything before it had passed without a single mark.

At recess she laid the pages out on the bench and read the conclusion over and over, hunting for the hidden problem. Then she noticed something. Her second paragraph was about safety, her third about wasted money, her fourth about healthier options, and her last paragraph did none of those jobs. Instead it said the same things again in fresh words, until the dance line arrived out of nowhere. She tried moving the dance argument up to become a fourth point, and suddenly the ending wrote itself, restating her position and gathering up her three reasons in new language.

"Your dance idea," she told Arie, running down the hall to find Ms. Li, "it gets its own paragraph now."

Piper had been in Japan for two weeks, staying with her aunt and a house full of cousins she barely knew, and everyone kept being kind to her in a way that made her throat hurt. It was their first summer without Gran, who had died in the spring, and Piper carried a flat envelope in her backpack that she could not bring herself to open. She presumed Gran had written it before the end, because the address on the front was in Gran's looping hand, and the word "Piper" was underlined twice.

At the gathering, cousins carried paper lanterns down to the river, and Piper followed without asking, because following was easier than talking. Her cousin Carl, who spoke English in bursts, kept glancing at her, and finally he said, "It's Obon. The lanterns are for the spirits."

"Spirits of who?" Piper asked.

"Ancestors. They come home for a visit," Carl said, and shrugged, as if this were the most obvious thing in the world. "Mid-August, Obon. Some places do it in July, but here it's August."

Piper turned that over all evening. If Gran's spirit was coming home for a visit, then home was across the ocean, and one paper lantern floating down a Japanese river could not possibly point that far. But then she thought about Gran, who used to say that letters were better than phone calls because a letter travels on its own, without wires, finding its person no matter what. Maybe a lantern worked the same way. She decided to test it. She wrote one line on her lantern with a marker: "Follow me home. Room at the top of the stairs."
