Grandna checked the window, where the light was just beginning to turn gold. "About an hour," she said. "The kitchen opens then."

Aiden stared at the group chat, thumb hovering. Dante had sent a photo of a poster from the community centre wall with the message "someone drew a vase with a face on it, weird." Yani replied three seconds later: "That's not a vase, it's two faces looking at each other." Aiden zoomed in. He could see the vase, plain as a glass on his kitchen table, but the more he looked, the more the white in the middle seemed to shift, like the moment rain precipitation on a window refract was impossible, so he typed instead: "It's a vase. Yani, zoom in."

"It's two faces," Yani sent, with a screenshot of the same poster cropped tighter. "Aiden, the outline is two noses." Dante sent a row of question marks, then "you're both looking at the same poster and seeing totally different stuff?" That was the part that bothered Aiden. Same picture, same wall, same afternoon light. One of them had to be wrong, and he wanted it settled before dinner.

Ms. Bianchi, who ran the centre's art room, had her number on the notice board, and Aiden had messaged her once about a lost jacket. He sent her the photo now and asked whose version was right. Her reply came while he was watching rain streak the kitchen window, droplets refracting the porch light into little wobbly stars. "Neither and both," she wrote. "That's a Rubin vase, from Edgar Rubin, a Danish psychologist, in 1915. You can see it as a vase or as two faces, but not both at the same moment."

Aiden read it twice, then looked at the photo again. The vase held steady for a second, then his eyes caught the faces and the vase vanished completely. He typed, "Yani's right," then deleted it, because that wasn't quite true either. Dante was already messaging: "so who won?" Aiden pasted what Ms. Bianchi had written and added, "nobody, that's the whole point." Then he set the phone face down, picked it up again, and sent one more line: "meet me at the centre tomorrow, we'll stare at it until it flips."

The recipe had come from an American website, and Carter read it three times before he touched anything. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees, it said, then mix the dry and wet ingredients separately. His mother's oven, the old one with the sticky door, only showed Celsius. He had promised his friend Charlotte he would bring blueberry muffins to her bake sale table on Saturday, and Charlotte had already texted him twice that morning.

"I'm counting on you," her message said. "I want our table to beat Carina's. She's bringing those lemon bars everybody likes, so my whole plan depends on your muffins. You can do this. You're more meticulous than anyone I know." Carter put the phone down and stared at the dial. He had let the recipe intimidate him all week, but he wasn't going to let a number beat him now.

He turned the dial to 350 and watched the little light blink on. Then he paused. If the recipe was American, he thought, then the 350 was probably Fahrenheit, and Fahrenheit degrees were smaller than Celsius ones. That meant 350 of them should be fewer than 350 of the ones on his oven. But how many fewer? He took out his phone and searched, and there it was: an oven setting of 350 degrees Fahrenheit was about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius. He clicked the oven off, turned the dial back down to 175, and clicked it on again, feeling like he had just cracked a code nobody in the kitchen could see.

While the oven heated, he measured the flour carefully, cracked two eggs, and folded in the blueberries without crushing them. His mother wandered past and asked if he needed help. "I've got it," he said, spooning batter into the paper cups. "Almost." He slid the tray in, set the timer for twenty minutes, and stood in front of the glass door watching the muffins rise like a small ecosystem of their own, each cup leaning into its neighbor.

They came out golden, domed, and slightly blue at the edges. Charlotte texted him a photo of the empty table with one line: "Saturday, 9 a.m., bring all of them." Carter wrapped the muffins in a tea towel, wrote "350 F = about 175 to 180 C" on a sticky note, and pressed it to the fridge for next time.

Arianna spread the map across the kitchen table and weighed the corners with salt shakers. Anabelle leaned over it, holding a list of cities her mom had printed for their family trip: Quito, Cairo, Mexico City, Nairobi.

"I get to pick one extra stop," Anabelle said, "but Mom says I have to prove it's near the equator. She says I need to stop guessing." She tapped the paper with her pen. "My tutor said the answer is on the map, but he wouldn't tell me how to find it."

"Then we'll figure it out ourselves." Arianna traced her finger across a line near the middle of the map. A tiny label read 0 degrees. "This must be it. It says zero right there, and the equator crosses Africa and South America."

"So what do the other lines mean?"

Arianna followed a curved line upward from the equator toward the top of the map, where the numbers climbed to 90. Then she traced downward and found another 90 at the bottom. "Latitude," she said, reading the small word in the legend. "It says latitude measures how far north or south a place is from the equator. Zero at the equator, and ninety degrees at each pole."

"So a smaller number means closer to the equator?" Anabelle grabbed the pen. "Quito is almost on the zero line. Cairo's way up at thirty." She circled Quito so hard the pen tore a little hole in the paper. "Quito! Mom can't argue with degrees."

"See if you can find Mexico City and Nairobi too," Arianna said. "You'll need more than one piece of evidence."

Anabelle frowned at the map, which seemed determined to be obstinate, folding itself at the crease whenever she let go. Arianna dropped two more salt shakers on it, and the paper finally lay flat.

Anabelle measured Nairobi with her thumb, circled it, and jumped up. "Mom! I have proof!" Her footsteps propelled her down the hallway, the list flapping behind her like a flag.

Elena had left her water bottle on the kitchen counter, and by the time she noticed, her mother's car was already pulling into the rec centre lot. The pool here had almost closed last spring until the landlord agreed to fix the leaking pipes, and now the whole neighbourhood thrived on summer swim sessions. Today, though, the lot was packed with kids from school, all trying out for the swim team, and the sky had that volatile grey look that kept flipping between sun and cloud.

"Third heat is the long one," said Connie, knotting her cap. "Four hundred metres. Mr. Perera makes everyone swim it last."

"That's my heat," Elena said. She felt fine during warm-up, fine during the sprint heats too. But halfway through the four hundred, her arms turned heavy, as though someone had poured wet sand into them. Her kick, which had been crisp in the first heat, went sloppy and slow. Heaven touched the wall a full length ahead of her, and Elena dragged herself out at the ladder, dizzy and strange.

She stood dripping by the bleachers, trying to work it out. She had not been slow in the sprints, so it was not her fitness. The difference was the long heat at the end of a hot afternoon, and she had drunk nothing since breakfast. She remembered a poster in the change room about hydration, something she had skimmed and forgotten. On the way past it she stopped and read properly: losing about 2 percent of your body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events. She looked at her own hands, still pruned, and thought, that was me. Two percent. She weighed herself on the lobby scale before and after her soak at the fountain, and the numbers told the same story.

Mr. Perera posted the list at the end of the day. Elena's name was near the bottom, in the last qualifying spot, with a note beside it: last heat times looked off, re-swim Monday. She found Connie by the door. "Monday I'm bringing two bottles," Elena said. "One for before, one for between heats." Connie grinned and bumped her shoulder, and outside the clouds finally split into real rain.

Ryan crouched at the tide line with three buckets labelled IGNEOUS, SEDIMENTARY and METAMORPHOUS, which Ria immediately crossed out and rewrote as METAMORPHIC. "Mr. Pelletier will do a rock census," she announced, tapping her clipboard. "Every rock on this beach gets counted and sorted by how it formed. Igneous from cooled lava, sedimentary from squished layers, metamorphic from heat and pressure." Gregoire held up a gray lump. "And if we get it wrong?" "Then the census is wrong forever," Ria said gravely, as if a government agency depended on them.

Ryan picked up a pale, holey stone that looked like a gray sponge. He dropped it into the sedimentary bucket, because holes made him think of sand. Then he frowned. He knew sedimentary rocks formed from layers, but this stone had no layers at all. He took it out, turned it over, and made a decision scientists everywhere would respect: he threw it into a tide pool to see what happened.

It bobbed. The rock floated, spinning slowly like a tiny gray raft. "Rocks don't float," Gregoire said, staring. "That one does," Ryan said. He fished it out and held it up. "Igneous bucket. It's full of gas bubbles trapped when lava cooled. That's why it's so light." Ria consulted her clipboard. "It's called pumice." Gregoire sniffed. "Saying a rock floats feels subjective." "It either floats or it doesn't," Ryan said, and dropped it back in. It floated again, smugly.

That evening Ryan's grandfather found a message taped to the fridge: "Dear Grandpa, beach census complete. 41 rocks sorted, 3 arguments, 1 floating rock named Admiral Bob. Pumice is igneous, full of gas bubbles from cooling lava, and light enough to float. Come see him do laps in the sink." His grandfather found Admiral Bob in the kitchen bucket and lowered him into a bowl of water. "Well," he said, giving the rock a gentle push, "sail on, little captain."

The group chat lit up at 7:42, right after dinner. Kim had posted first: "Did anyone SEE what happened in the hallway today? The two kids who collided outside the gym?" Jeremy had seen it, sort of, from the water fountain. He remembered books flying and someone yelling, but when he tried to pin down details, they kept sliding around. Anya replied, "Yeah I was right there. It was bad." That was the trouble. "Bad" could mean anything.

Jeremy wanted the truth because Mr. Sadeghi had announced that anyone who saw the collision should write a statement for the office, and he resented having to rely on other people's memories instead of his own. So he tried something. He messaged Kim privately: "How fast was the first kid going when he smashed into the other one?" She answered, "Fast. Like running really hard, maybe a sprint." Then he messaged Anya the identical question, word for word except one: "How fast was the first kid going when he hit the other one?" Anya wrote back, "Not that fast honestly, kind of a jog, he tried to stop."

He sat staring at the two replies. Same hallway, same moment, two descriptions that were nowhere near equivalent. He scrolled up through the chat and noticed the pattern held: people who used dramatic words described the collision as violent, and people who used plain words made it sound small. It reminded him of a page Mr. Sadeghi had shown the class once, about a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, where people asked how fast cars "smashed" into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that "hit." He had thought it was boring then. Now he tested it on himself, asking his own memory both ways, and got two different collisions.

"Wait," he typed to Kim. "Try asking your brother the hit version and see what he says." Three minutes later she sent back a screenshot. Her brother had estimated a slower speed, same as Anya. Jeremy read it twice, then opened his statement for the office and deleted his first sentence, which began "The kid came out of nowhere, flying." He wrote instead, "I was at the water fountain and heard a crash. I saw books on the floor." Then he added one last line to the chat: "Everyone send me your answers exactly as you gave them, and include the question I asked you." Kim replied with a single eye emoji.

John slid a folded paper under his plate before his dad could see it. Across the table, his little sister was telling a long story about a bee, and John used the noise to study the numbers he had copied during recess: every time he touched the ball in Saturday's game, and what happened after.

"John, you're moving your lips," his dad said. "What's under the plate?"

He handed it over, because there was no way out. "It's my touches. Elie counted them for me. Eleven touches, and six times the ball went to somebody on our team after me."

His dad looked at the paper for a while, and then he laughed, which was not what John expected. "You know what this reminds me of? Moneyball."

"Money ball?"

"It's a book," his dad said. "Came out in 2003. Michael Lewis wrote it. It was about how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." He tapped the paper. "A low-budget team, using numbers to compete with rich teams. Everybody else was ranking players the old way, and Oakland was looking at different numbers."

John chewed on that along with his rice. So one number, like a ranking, could squash eleven touches into a single word, good or bad. But what if the single number was the wrong one? He tried to imagine what his coach saw when he looked at him. Probably the two goals John gave away. Nobody had counted the passes that kept the ball moving.

"Can I speculate about something?" he asked, and his dad raised an eyebrow the way he did when John used a word from his vocabulary list. "The coach ranks us by goals. But Parker got six goals and lost the ball like twenty times. Nobody wrote that down."

"Maybe the coach doesn't have a Parker column," his dad said.

"Maybe that's the whole problem," John said. "There's no column for it."

At school the next day, John showed Elie the paper and proposed a truce: no arguing about who was better, just one week of counting everything, both of them, even the boring stuff. Elie agreed, then ruined the truce immediately by arguing that blocked shots should count double, and they spent all of lunch negotiating. By Friday the chart had grown so long it looked like a corroding pipe in science class, spotted and eaten away at the edges, but the numbers held.

On Saturday, John taped the chart inside his binder and carried it to the bench where the coach sat. He waited for halftime, took a breath, and held it out.

"Coach," he said. "I found something Parker does that nobody's counting."

Sadie counted under her breath as she ran toward the first hurdle: one, two, three, jump. The little plastic bar wobbled but stayed up, and she landed, sprinted, counted again, and clipped the second hurdle hard enough to knock it flat into the grass.

"Same foot?" Victoria called from the bleachers, where she was supposed to be resting her twisted ankle but was instead keeping tally on a napkin.

"Wrong foot every single time," Sadie said, walking back to the start. The coach had set the hurdles close together in the far corner of the park, and the morning sun refracted off the dew so the whole row glinted like a string of aquariums. "I count three steps, but I always take off from my left, and my right is my lead leg. I jump crooked."

Tess jogged over, breathing hard from her own turn. "You hit four, then three, then three," she said, squinting at the napkin Victoria waved at her. "You're not consistent."

Sadie stood at the start line and did the math out loud, because thinking while running had not worked so far. "Three steps between hurdles," she said slowly. "Left, right, left. Then I take off from my left again. If I take off from my left at the first one, three steps means I take off from my left at every one after that, too. An odd number of steps keeps the same leg leading." She looked up. "So it's not random. I'm not arriving on the wrong foot by accident. If my first takeoff is wrong, they'll all be wrong."

"Then fix the first one," Victoria said. "Lead with your left at hurdle one, even if it feels weird."

It did feel weird, like writing with the wrong hand, and Sadie's first attempt was a graceless hop that made Tess laugh until she had to sit down on the grass. But the bar stayed up. She walked back, shaking out her arms, and tried again. Left lead, three steps, left lead again, three steps, left lead. The fourth hurdle, the one she had flattened twice, passed beneath her so cleanly she barely felt it leave the ground.

Afterward, sprawled in the shade near the duck pond, Tess pointed at a green film on the water. "That whole slick is one organism, my science teacher says. Algae, all connected." Sadie watched a dragonfly land on it, its wings intricate as lace, and thought that the hurdles were connected too, each one deciding the next.

Victoria limped over with a water bottle and held it out without being asked. "You stopped counting out loud on the last run," she said.

Sadie took a long drink and grinned. "Left, right, left. I don't have to count anymore. I just hear it."

Jonathan stacked the last crate of honey jars and checked his phone. Four weeks of Saturdays at Mr. Martínez's farm stand meant fifty-two dollars in his pocket, and the skateboard he wanted cost one hundred forty.

"You keep counting that money like it's going to hatch," Jaya said, laughing. She worked the cash box on Sundays and was saving for concert tickets, which was all she talked about.

"It's too slow," Jonathan said. "The shop might sell out of the board. My dad said I could put it on his credit card and pay him back later." He paused. "But he said there'd be interest. Like a fee for borrowing."

"Then it costs more than the sticker says," Jaya said. She frowned, then brightened. "Wait. My mom uses her card every single week, groceries and everything, and she never pays interest. I've seen the statements. Zero."

"That's bizarre," Jonathan said. "Borrowing money for free?"

Jaya shrugged. "She said it's called a grace period. She pays the whole bill by the due date, every time." Jonathan inhaled the smell of warm apples and thought so hard he almost dropped the crate. Interest on the card was like an infection, small at first but spreading if you let it grow. If Dad paid only part of the bill, the interest would start. But if the full statement balance got paid by the due date, there was no interest on the new purchases at all.

"I'm going to test it," he announced. "Small. Dad puts the board on the card, I hand him twenty-six dollars every Saturday, and we pay the whole thing off by the due date. If a fee shows up, I was wrong."

Mr. Martínez, who had been listening while weighing tomatoes, gave him the next Saturday off to visit the shop. Jonathan raced home to ask.

"Dad," he called through the screen door, waving his envelope of cash. "I've got a plan."

Arthur had fasted from breakfast until sundown, the way his family did on certain holy days, and now he stood at the front of the community hall with his stomach growling and a plan in his head. His little sister had been promised she could hold the Havdalah candle tonight for the first time, and Arthur had promised Tyson and Cataleya they could come watch. The problem was that they kept asking questions he could not answer by pointing at anything yet, because the tables at the front were still bare.

"So what actually happens at this thing?" Tyson asked, sitting on a folding chair with his sneakers swinging.

"You'll see it in order," Arthur said. "That's how I figured it out myself. First there's a cup of grape juice, then spices you smell, then the candle. I used to think the candle was just decoration, but that turned out to be an illusion. Watch the wicks."

When his sister lifted the candle, Cataleya leaned forward. "It's braided," she said. "And there's, like, more than one wick in it."

"Several wicks," Arthur's sister said, holding it out flat on her palms the way she had practiced in the kitchen all week. "Ms. Pelletier told me to keep it level so the wax doesn't drip on the cloth."

Ms. Pelletier, who ran the hall, dimmed the overhead lights. The cup of grape juice went up first, then the spice box passed from hand to hand. Tyson took a sniff and held it a second longer than everyone else. "Cloves," he whispered to Cataleya, and she whispered back, "I think there's cinnamon too." Arthur noticed that Tyson lingered on the smell while Cataleya shrugged after one breath, which made him think that liking a smell had to be subjective, the same way his sister loved cloves and he only tolerated them.

After the blessings, the flame was dipped into the cup and went out with a small hiss. A thread of smoke rose, twisting, and Arthur waved his hand to pull the scent toward him, the way his father always did. "The smoke dissolves before you can really follow it," he said. "That part you can't hold onto."

"Can I try?" Tyson asked, and stood up.

Arianna spread her worksheet on the flat base of the war memorial, where the carved names caught the afternoon light. Lennox sat on the step beside her, chewing his pen.

"The pyramids were palaces," Lennox said. "Giant houses for the kings. Obviously."

Arianna looked at the model photograph on the sheet, the one from the museum. A palace had windows, halls, kitchens, a place for a hundred people to eat. The pyramid in the picture had one narrow passage leading to a small room with a stone box in it. She turned the paper so Lennox could see. "Would you build your palace with no windows and one room? Where's the throne?" Lennox leaned closer and frowned. She tapped the little room. "That's a burial chamber. The whole thing is a tomb, built to protect the pharaoh's body and his belongings for his life after death." Lennox said his uncle had once told him an anecdote about a king buried with his dogs, which proved nothing, but he wrote "tomb" in the blank anyway.

The second question was harder: why did their farms depend on the Nile? Arianna thought about what she could not see from the picture, the reason underneath. She picked up a stick and drew in the gravel beside the memorial: a river, a line of floodwater spreading over the fields. Every year the river rose, covered the land, and when the water pulled back it left dark mud. She scattered a few pebbles like seeds on the mud. "Seeds germinate in that wet soil," she said. "No river, no mud, no crops." Simeon, who had been copying names off the memorial wall for a project, wandered over. "So the flood was good news? That's backwards." Arianna drew a dry gully next to the flooded field. "Flood, then food. No flood, then that."

Simeon studied the two drawings, then the carved names above them, people the town had built stone to remember. "The Egyptians built stone for their dead too," he said slowly. Arianna nodded and started writing her answer in the last blank.

A barn owl, nocturnal and hunting early in the dusk, swept over the memorial and out toward the river.

The gym was loud with squeaking shoes, and Mr. Banerjee blew his whistle for the third time. Naomi grabbed the rebound and passed to Dereck, who scored, and for a second everything was good. Then Mckayla leaned over during the water break and whispered, "Naomi, no offense, but something smells like a locker room that lost a fight."

Naomi sniffed her sleeve and her stomach dropped. She had put on deodorant that morning, the same kind her mom bought, and she had showered last night. So why did she still smell? She could not stop thinking about it all through math, drawing little arrows in her notebook. If she was clean and wearing deodorant, the smell had to come from somewhere she had not checked. What was left? She looked down at her hoodie, the gray one she wore basically every day because it was not flammable like her cozy fake-fur one, which her dad said was basically a fire hazard near the stove.

After school she found Mckayla at the lockers. "Can I test something on you?" Naomi asked. "It's a science experiment, kind of."

"You're weird, but okay," Mckayla said.

"Hold this." Naomi handed over the hoodie and stood a few feet back in just her T-shirt. Mckayla sniffed the hoodie, gagged dramatically, then sniffed the air near Naomi's shoulders and raised her eyebrows. "Okay, that's the factor right there. You smell fine. Your hoodie smells like a sock that's been through a war."

"So it's the clothes," Naomi said slowly, working it out aloud. "The sweat gets in them, and it just stays there, and it doesn't matter if I'm clean underneath." She thought of the poster Mr. Banerjee had pointed at during health class last week, the one meant to illustrate good hygiene habits, with a little drawing of a shirt in a laundry basket. She had stared right at it and missed the whole point.

That night she pulled the gray hoodie out of the hamper and stuffed it in the washing machine, along with every shirt, sock, and pair of shorts she had worn that week. The next morning she came downstairs in a clean hoodie, fresh socks, and deodorant, and her mom said, "Look at you. What's the occasion?"

"Hygiene," Naomi said.

At morning practice, Mr. Banerjee split them into teams, and Mckayla jogged over to Naomi's side. "I'm guarding you," she said, grinning. "You smell like laundry now. Toughest defense I'll face all day."

Jaxson set his fork down and stared at his grandmother. She had just finished telling the whole table, for the second time, about the ginger tea from Ms. Boateng that cured her monster headache on Tuesday. "Worst one in months," she said, tapping the teapot like it was a treasure. "By Wednesday morning, gone." Jaxson wanted to believe her. But something nagged at him, the same feeling he got when a magic trick seemed too perfect. His dad always said bad headaches come and go. What if Tuesday's headache was going to leave anyway?

He decided to test it. That night he made a chart in his notebook and asked his grandmother to rate her headache every evening from one to ten. She laughed and agreed. Tuesday, the tea day, was a nine. He kept the chart going, even when it got tedious, filling in little boxes while she watched her shows. Kingston came over for dinner on Friday and studied the numbers. "So the tea only got tried on the really bad one," Kingston said slowly. "She never drinks it on a two." Jaxson grinned. That was exactly the hole in the story.

He found the name for it on Saturday, in a library book about how people fool themselves. He ran to Ms. Boateng's porch to speculate about it out loud. "The book called it regression to the mean," he said. "Unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones. So if you try a remedy when symptoms are at their worst, you might improve even if it does nothing." Ms. Boateng nodded. "My mother swore by honey water for the very same reason, I'd guess."

At Sunday dinner, Jaxson laid the notebook beside the mashed potatoes. "Grandma, the tea might work, or the nines might just turn into threes on their own. To know, you'd have to drink it on the mild days too, or skip it on the bad ones and see." His grandmother looked at the chart for a long moment, then at the teapot. "Well then," she said, pouring herself a cup, "we'd better start skipping some Tuesdays."

Juliette spread the Skyrider VR headset box across the cafeteria table like evidence in a trial. Two hundred forty dollars, said the sticker, though the sticker was polite about it and called that a sale price.

"You could just save up," said Thalia, poking the box. "You have ninety in your jar."

"By the time I save the rest, everyone at school will have moved on to something else. Dorian already has one." Juliette turned the box over. "My mom said I could put it on her credit card and pay her back from my allowance. Ten dollars a month. That's the smart way."

Thalia frowned. "Fifteen months of allowance for a headset you could buy in fifteen weeks of saving anyway. Where's the smart part?"

Juliette had no answer, so she ate her fries. That afternoon Mr. Suryanto's math class had bank day, where they ran the school's little savings counter in the gym, and Juliette had been named savings ambassador, mostly because she owned a blazer. A fourth grader came up with crumpled bills to deposit and asked, while Juliette wrote his balance in the ledger, why his father had paid the bank more money last month than he'd borrowed from it.

"Interest," said Dorian from the coin-counting station, not looking up. "Interest is the price of borrowing money. It gets charged as a percentage of what you borrowed."

"Like renting money," the fourth grader said, and Dorian shrugged, which was as close to enthusiasm as he got.

Juliette sat very still behind the counter. A percentage. Of what you borrowed. She took out her notebook and wrote the headset price, then ten dollars a month, and made herself do the multiplication all the way to the end, twice, because she wanted to verify it was wrong and it refused to be. Her mom's card charged interest every month the balance sat there, and Juliette's allowance payments were small, so the balance would sit there a long time. She would end up paying back more than two hundred forty dollars. For the same headset. The one already on sale.

At recess she found Dorian by the fence. "You wanted the Skyrider for months," she said. "How'd you get yours?"

"Birthday. Why?" He squinted at her. "Also, Thalia wants you to save with us for the class trip, but she was too polite to say it at lunch."

Juliette walked to the library, took out a fresh sheet, and wrote SAVE FIRST at the top, then crossed it out and wrote SAVE FIRST, THALIA'S TRIP TOO, which was longer but more honest. She taped it inside her locker, right where the headset ad had been.

Every morning something dug in the seedbed behind the garage, and every morning Kaitlyn counted fewer marigold seeds than she had planted the day before. She had seen no tracks, no fur, no slime, nothing but little craters in the soil. Her mother suggested birds. Ellen suggested squirrels. Kira suggested Kaitlyn count better, which was not helpful.

"You can't see what's doing it," Kaitlyn said, kneeling at the bed with a trowel. "So you make a guess and then you test it. Ms. Rossi calls it a hypothesis." She had written hers on an index card and tucked it under a flowerpot: birds are stealing the seeds. "If I'm right, a cage over the seeds stops it. If the seeds still vanish, I'm wrong, and it's something that crawls."

She set up two dishes in the garden, both on the ground, both in the same patch of sun, since the bees that pollinated the squash nearby seemed to like it warm and she figured seed thieves might too. Ten seeds in each dish, counted twice, because of Kira. She pressed the dishes into the soil at the same depth, so the temperature would be the same around both, and she would check them at the same time each morning. The only difference would be the cage: one dish covered with chicken wire, one open to the sky.

"It's just ten seeds," Ellen said, watching Kaitlyn clip the wire. "Seems trivial."

"It's not trivial if it's the whole test. If I put out different amounts, or check one dish at seven and one at noon, I'd never know whether it was the cage that mattered or something else. Everything except the thing I'm testing has to stay the same. Same amount, same temperature, same timing." She set the cage down over the first dish with a firm little click.

The first morning, both dishes were untouched, which annoyed her more than theft would have. The second morning, the open dish held six seeds and a small crater; the caged dish held ten, flat and undisturbed. The third morning, the open dish was empty, and when Kaitlyn leaned close she found a single grey feather stuck to the rim of the cage.

She pulled the index card out from under the flowerpot and added one word in careful capitals. Behind her, a mourning dove landed on the fence, looked at the chicken wire, and looked at her.

"All right," Kaitlyn said. "The wire stays."

The museum's Egypt wing smelled like dust and old stone, and Colton stood in front of a glass case holding two round loaves so dark and cracked they looked like rocks. Ms. Weiss had given each student a topic to present on the spot, and his was the Nile. He had practiced on the bus, but Bernard had just leaned over and whispered, "You said they grew corn. Corn came from the Americas, genius."

Colton felt his ears go hot. He revised his plan fast, the way he did when a math answer came out wrong and he had to find where the mistake started. Corn was out. But what was in? He stared at the loaves and the little plaque beside them, then at a long table behind the case where Lea was already turning a crank on a model of a canal. Water sloshed through a gate with a brass valve, and when she opened it, the water spread across a flat tray of green paper shaped like a river valley.

"Look," Lea said. "Flood comes, valve opens, water goes everywhere the farmers want it."

Colton joined her at the model. The flood soaked the tray, and when the water drained away, the green paper looked darker, like a field ready for planting. That was the pattern he needed. The river flooded, the water fed the fields, the fields grew the grain, and the grain fed everyone. It was not some sophisticated machine doing the work. It was the river itself, arriving every year without being asked.

When his turn came, Colton pointed at the loaves in the case. "They didn't grow corn," he said. "The main grain crops were emmer wheat and barley. That's what those loaves are made of. Barley went into their beer too, and bread and beer were everyday food for most people." He nodded at the flood model. "The Nile made it possible. And a whole kingdom of people, fed on grain, could build the pyramids."

Ms. Weiss wrote something on her clipboard. Bernard gave him a slow thumbs-up from the back.

"Nice save," Bernard said. "Emmer wheat. Who knew?"

Aurora stood in line at the mall pretzel stand, holding her birthday money, trying to decide between the headphones she had wanted for a month and the sneakers everyone at school seemed to be wearing. Reese had gotten the sneakers first, and after that it was like a rule had spread through sixth grade: two more kids had them by Friday, and Edwin had put them on his birthday list without even trying them on. Aurora could still picture herself last month, begging her mom for a fidget toy because "everyone has one," and how that toy now sat at the bottom of her backpack collecting crumbs. She did not want to do that again with forty dollars.

While she waited, she scrolled her phone. A video popped up of a famous singer raving about the exact sneakers, calling them "revolutionary, legendary, the greatest thing ever made for your feet." Aurora's thumb hovered. The words felt warm and heavy, like the adjectives had been chosen to lift the shoes up and crush every other brand at the same time. Then she noticed the caption. At the very end, in small letters, was "#ad."

She tapped the profile of a second reviewer, a guy who tested shoes for fun. His video was calmer. "Here's the thing," he said to the camera, holding up a box. "In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something." No "#ad" anywhere on his page, and no free sneakers either, as far as she could tell. He actually showed where the stitching rubbed his ankle after a week.

Aurora had a simple test: if a review glowed too brightly, she would hunt for the disclosure before trusting it. She scrolled the singer's page again. There it was on three more posts, tiny as plumbing hidden inside a wall, doing its quiet work where nobody looked. The glowing words suddenly seemed less like facts and more like a paycheck.

The pretzel line moved. Aurora stepped up, ordered a cinnamon twist, and texted Edwin, who was leaning against a pillar near the fountain, waiting. He wandered over, phone out, perpendicular to the pillar like he was too cool to actually lean on it. "Did you see the singer's video?" he asked. "Those sneakers are legendary."

"Legendary and paid for," Aurora said, holding up her screen. "See the hashtag? She got them free."

Edwin squinted at the tiny letters. "Huh," he said, and slowly lowered his phone. "So what are the headphones like?"

Aurora bit into her pretzel and pointed down the corridor with the last of it. "Come on. Let's go listen before the store closes."

The shovel leaned against the fence post like it had been there all summer, and maybe it had. Andrew picked it up and ran his thumb over the blade, which was the colour of dried blood and flaked when he scratched it. In the shed, the spade hung on its nail, clean and grey and sharp. Same iron, same grandpa, two different endings.

"Grandpa," Andrew called, "why is this one all crumbly?"

His grandpa came out wiping his hands on a rag. "Left that out since June, I expect. Rain and all." He tapped the shed wall, where a small wind turbine spun above the roof, charging the light inside. "The one in here stays dry. That matters, apparently."

Andrew set the rusty shovel beside the spade and crouched down to compare them. He was supposed to be learning this at school, physical changes and chemical changes, and Ms. Szabó had said something about it just last week. Melting was physical; the stuff was still the same stuff, just softer. Burning was chemical. He tried to evaluate which this was. If he scraped the rust off, would the shiny iron come back underneath, the way ice came back when water froze? He scratched. What came off was orange dust, and what was left was thinner than it should have been. The iron hadn't just changed shape. It had turned into something else, and it wasn't turning back.

"I think it's chemical," Andrew said slowly. "Like burning, but slow. The iron with the water and the air, it makes a new thing. It's called iron oxide." He'd found the words in his notebook at the bottom of his backpack, half-copied from the board.

"Is that a fact," said his grandpa, which was not really a question.

Andrew carried the shovel to the fence and laid it flat where he could keep an eye on it. Last summer he remembered leaving his bike out in the rain for two weeks because bringing it in felt like too much trouble, and the chain had squeaked all autumn no matter how much oil he used. He still wasn't sure that had been laziness or just a kid forgetting. He'd been planning to bring it in. Planning, he thought, wasn't the same as doing.

He got the wire brush from the shed and started on the blade, orange dust drifting onto his sneakers. The turbine above the roof spun and stopped and spun again. "Can I keep the good spade in here too?" he asked. "Somewhere dry, where it stays dry?"

His grandpa looked at him for a second, then hung it on a lower nail, within reach.

Adam had taped a sign above his project that read "BUBBLES MEAN A CHEMICAL CHANGE," and for the first twenty minutes of the science fair, nobody argued with him. Kyson stopped by, looked at his chart of vinegar and baking soda, and nodded. "The bubbles are the proof," Kyson said. "New stuff got made."

Then Aliya leaned over the table next to Adam's, where her project sat. She had a hot plate, a beaker of water, and a thermometer. "So what's happening in mine?" she asked. The water had gone turbulent, rolling and churning, and bubbles climbed its sides in a steady stream.

"Chemical change," Adam said. "Bubbles. Same as mine."

"Watch the side of the beaker," Aliya said. "See the bubbles form down there, where the heat is." She tapped the glass. "If something new was being made, where would it go after the bubbles pop?"

Adam crouched so his eyes were level with the rim. A bubble reached the surface, opened, and a puff of white drifted up and vanished. He watched another one do the same thing. In his vinegar demonstration, the bubbles had come from the liquid and the powder making something different together. Here there was only water and heat. He straightened up.

"It's steam," he said. "The bubbles are water vapour, the same stuff as a gas. Nothing new gets made." He pulled the marker off the table and crossed out his sign, then wrote underneath, "BOILING IS A PHYSICAL CHANGE." He said it again, quieter, checking it against the beaker. "Still water. Just gas now."

Ms. Abdi came by on her judging rounds and read both lines, the crossed-out one and the new one. "Which one do you emphasize, then, if someone asks you today?" she asked.

"The second one," Adam said. "The first one's how I got here."

Aliya ladled out a spoonful of the boiled water and held it up so the judges could see it was clear, still water, and Adam pointed at the line on his sign.

The planetarium classroom smelled like dust and old carpet, and Hailey stared at the three unlabeled rocks on her tray while Ms. Becker wrote igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic on the board. On Monday each student had to sort five mystery rocks and defend every choice, and Hailey still could not tell them apart. Camila next to her kept turning a gray lump over and over like it might whisper its origin.

"That one's got bubbles in it," Jeremi said from across the table. "Bubbles means volcanic, right? Igneous." He said it with total confidence, and Hailey almost copied him, because Jeremi's dad worked in plumbing and Jeremi claimed to know how everything hidden worked, pipes, wires, rocks. But when she held the lump near the lamp, the bubbles looked stretched and flat, not round, as if the rock had melted and folded rather than bubbled. "I think it changed after it formed," she said slowly. "Like something squashed and heated it until it transformed into something new." Jeremi shrugged. "Metamorphic, then. Whatever."

The third rock was pale and layered, and nobody could decide. Hailey was about to guess sedimentary when she remembered her lunch bag. The vinegar bottle for her sandwich crinkle-crinkled in her hand as she carried the rock to the sink, and she let one drop fall onto its surface. For a second nothing happened. Ms. Becker paused at the board. Camila leaned in, breath held.

Then the wet spot hissed and fizzed, tiny bubbles crowding up like a shaken soda. "Whoa," Jeremi said. "It's alive?"

"It's limestone," Hailey said. "Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, and vinegar makes it fizz because it releases carbon dioxide gas." She had read it in the quarry chapter two weeks ago and almost forgotten. "If it fizzes, it's limestone, so it's sedimentary. It settled in layers, that's why the stripes." She wrote sedimentary beside the rock and underlined it twice.

Ms. Becker looked over her shoulder at the fizzing drop and said nothing, but one corner of her mouth lifted. On the tray, the last unknown rock sat quiet and dark, waiting.

Kaitlyn sat on the low wall by the basketball courts, her right arm propped on her knee inside its hard blue cast. The cast ran from below her elbow to her knuckles, and it had been there for three weeks, ever since she had gone over the handlebars of her bike and thrown her hands out in front of her. Dr. Ortiz had said the break was in her radius, the big bone on the thumb side, near the wrist, and that breaks like hers were the most common kind kids got, usually from landing on an outstretched hand.

Across the playground, Alden was rolling toward the ramp on his new skateboard, and Kaelyn was jogging beside him with the stopwatch from the gym bin. "The talent show tryouts are right after lunch," Kaelyn called over. "You've got one recess left to land it."

Kaitlyn chewed the inside of her cheek. Alden had fallen twice already this morning, and both times he had stuck his arms out straight, palms forward, exactly the way she had done off her bike. She could not see what would happen if he fell again. Nobody could. But she had started noticing a pattern in the way kids fell on this playground, and she wanted to test it before the bell rang.

She raised her good arm and waved them over. "Alden, do me a favor. Fall down on the grass. On purpose, so you're ready for it."

He rolled his eyes, but the bell deadline was close, so he hopped off the board and let himself tip sideways onto the soft grass beside the courts. He tucked his arm and rolled onto his shoulder. Then she asked him to fall the other way, arms out like most people do when they are surprised. This time his hand slapped down first, and all his weight drove straight through the wrist. He sat up and shook out his fingers. "That one felt way worse," he admitted.

"That's what I did," Kaitlyn said. She tapped the cast with her left hand. "Radius, right near the wrist. The doctor said that's the most common break in kids, and it usually happens exactly like what you just did." She kept her voice level, not panicked, because Alden looked a little pale now. "So the problem isn't falling. It's what your hands do when you don't have time to think."

Ms. Sharma, on yard duty near the fence, wandered over with her coffee. "Everything cooperating out here?" she asked, and Kaitlyn said yes, just an experiment. The motivation was simple: Alden's tryout was in twenty minutes, and a trip to the emergency room would end it before it started. Kaitlyn laid out her plan. Alden would practice the tucked roll until his body did it without thinking, so that if the board shot out from under him, a bad wrist would not be the probable outcome.

They used the last ten minutes of recess on the grass, again and again, until Alden could drop and roll smoothly with his arms pulled in. When the bell rang, he stood up with grass in his hair and climbed onto the board.

At the tryout, the board wobbled on the ramp's lip, and Alden pitched forward. He tucked, rolled, and came up standing in the wood chips with his hands empty and whole.

"See you at the show," Kaelyn said, and Alden grinned and held up both open palms to Kaitlyn, all ten fingers wiggling.

Arthur sat cross-legged on the living room rug with his tablet balanced on a stack of board games, scowling at two headlines side by side. Ms. Mwangi's class project was due Monday, and the assignment was to compare how two news stories covered the same event: a downtown crowd that had blocked traffic for three hours on Saturday. One headline said "Protesters March for Clean Water." The other said "Rioters Snarl City Streets." He and Elie had agreed to split the work, but Elie's part sat untouched in his messages, and Arthur could not figure out what the two stories even had in common.

Aleah arrived after dinner, still holding her basketball shoes by the laces, because Elie had texted her that Arthur was stuck. She flopped onto the couch and pulled the tablet onto her knees. "Same day, same street, same number of people?" she said. "Then it's the same crowd." She tapped the first headline. "So why do I want to be on their side when I read this one, and kind of scared when I read that one?"

Arthur read both articles out loud, and something strange happened. Reading the word "protesters," he pictured his neighbor holding a sign about the river. Reading "rioters," he pictured shattered glass, even though the second article never mentioned any glass breaking at all. He sat back. "It's the words," he said slowly. "The words are doing something."

He grabbed a napkin from the coffee table and wrote two columns. Above the first he put "Protesters" and above the second "Rioters," then he copied every word that described the crowd from each article. The first story used "passionate," "united," and "neighbors." The second used "mob," "aggressive," and "lawless." None of the words were lies exactly, but each one carried a feeling that pushed him somewhere. He tried swapping them, putting "passionate" into the second article, and the crowd suddenly sounded brave instead of dangerous. Same facts, opposite feeling. He could almost deduce the rule from it, like solving for a missing number, but he wanted to be sure before he claimed it. It was probable that the words carried strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" could push readers toward opposite opinions, but probable was not certain.

"Test it," Aleah said. "Do it like Ms. Mwangi's simile thing from poetry, where the same idea feels different depending on the picture." So they wrote one plain sentence on the napkin: "A crowd gathered on Fifth Street." Then they read it to Arthur's dad in the kitchen twice, first with "the brave protesters" added and then with "the dangerous rioters." After the first version, his dad said he hoped the city listened to them. After the second, he asked whether anyone got hurt. Same sentence, same man, opposite reaction.

Aleah laughed so hard she dropped a shoe. Arthur copied both versions of the sentence into his project notes and wrote one line underneath: "Check the word before you trust the feeling." Then he texted Elie: bring snacks Monday, and bring your part, because we actually found something. From the kitchen his dad called, "Who's brave and dangerous out there?" and Arthur held up the napkin. "Everyone," he said. "Depends what you call them."

Florence pushed the desk lamp into the middle of her grandfather's den and set a striped beach ball on top of a stool. "Grandpa, can you be the Earth?" she asked. "I have to show the Moon phases for Mr. Somsak's class, and I need somebody standing in the middle." Her grandfather settled onto a kitchen chair beside the stool, holding his teacup like a prop. He had been telling her all morning about how he'd paid off the mortgage on this very house before her mother was even born, and now he was glad for a new subject. "One small step for Grandpa," he said, planting his slippers firmly on the rug.

Florence dimmed the curtains and clicked the lamp on. The room went dark except for that one bright point. She walked the beach ball in a slow circle around her grandfather, watching the stripey sphere catch the light. Half of it was always lit, she noticed, but from where Grandpa sat, the lit part changed shape. When the ball swung to his right side, he raised a finger. "I see a crescent," he announced, "and it's bright on the right."

"That's a waxing crescent," Florence said. She marked the spot on the rug with a sticky note so she could find it again, then kept circling, calling out each shape as Grandpa reported it. That was when her grandfather's tablet buzzed. It was the weekly call to her cousin in Australia, and he propped it on the shelf so everyone could see. On screen, her cousin waved from a balcony, and behind her, hanging in a deep blue evening sky, was the actual Moon.

Florence leaned close to the screen. "Is that a crescent?" she asked. Her cousin turned to look. "Yes, just getting bigger," she said. "It's waxing." Florence frowned at the little luminous sliver on the screen, then back at her beach ball. On the tablet the lit side was on the left. Around Grandpa's chair, it had been on the right. She grabbed the tablet, held it up beside her model, and looked from one to the other until her neck ached.

"Wait," she said slowly. "We're in the Northern Hemisphere. My cousin's in the Southern Hemisphere. A waxing crescent is lit on the right side as seen from the Northern Hemisphere, but on the left side as seen from the Southern Hemisphere." Her cousin, hearing all this from ten thousand kilometres away, held her tablet up to the real Moon again so Florence could double-check. Left side. Definitely left. Florence spun the beach ball and stood on her toes to peer up from underneath it, tilting her head like someone standing upside down on the far side of the world.

"Grandpa, lean sideways," she said, pulling his elbow. "Pretend you're in Australia." He tipped sideways in his chair, nearly spilling his tea, and squinted at the beach ball. "Well, I'll be," he said. "It's backwards from here." Florence wrote it all down in her notebook for Mr. Somsak, then held the tablet up next to her model one more time and grinned at her cousin. "Tomorrow, show Calder," her cousin said. "Make him lean."

Paisley crouched at the edge of the community garden pond with her clipboard, drawing arrows in pencil. The garden tour started at noon and Mr. Cruz wanted every poster finished by eleven, so she had two hours to make her food chain look perfect: sun, then pond plants, then snails, then a duck. Simple. She had copied it off the board in science class, and Mr. Cruz had said a chain had to run from the sun all the way to a top predator. "Done," she said, and held it up for Laura, who was labeling the tomato beds nearby.

Laura leaned over, then squinted at the water. "Wait. Watch the duck." The duck was paddling along the shallow edge, and Paisley watched it tip forward, tail in the air. It nibbled at the green strands hanging from the rocks, and then it snapped at something small and brown. Henri, who was weeding the lettuce, came over and pointed. "That's a snail. It just ate one of your snails. And before that it ate the plants." Paisley stared at her neat chain of arrows. If the duck ate the plants too, then her drawing was wrong. One of her arrows was missing, and if one arrow could be missing, maybe more were.

"So what do I do, put a second arrow from the plants to the duck?" she asked. "Then it's not a chain anymore. It's got a loop in it." She tried sketching it, and the arrows crossed each other and made the whole poster look sinister, like a spider had crawled across her page. Henri tapped the water where a small fish darted past. "That fish probably eats snails too. And maybe the plants." Paisley added the fish and drew its arrows, then wondered whether the duck ate the fish, and whether something ate the duck. Her page filled with lines going every direction. "It's not a chain," she said slowly. "It's a web. Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so it's all linked."

At ten fifty she drew the final version in marker, arrows crossing like string between her fingers. Then she tested the idea Mr. Cruz had asked about, what happens if one link disappears. She imagined the snails gone. The duck would still live, because it had the plants and the fish. But the fish would go hungry, and if the fish starved, whatever ate the fish would starve too. She wrote that in her corner box and walked her poster to the shed, conserving her last blank page in case Mr. Cruz wanted a redo. He read it twice and grinned. "A web," he said. "Better than a chain." Paisley pointed at the duck, still tipping upside down in the shallows, still eating everything it could reach.

The lights went out at the farmhouse just as Jack sat down to dinner, and the wind outside made the whole blackout feel like it had been planned rather than random. His dad found a flashlight while Jack tried the cordless phone to call Ema, who was coming over at seven to work on their science project. The phone was dead. Not a beep, not a flicker on its little screen.

"It has to charge," his dad said from the hallway. Jack was about to resign himself to an evening without talking to anyone when he remembered the old phone bolted to the kitchen wall, the one with the curly cord his grandmother used before she moved out. Everyone joked it was there because Grandma refused to give it up, like some stubborn stereotype of a farmer who hated new gadgets. Jack lifted the heavy receiver, and there it was: a dial tone, steady and clear, even though every light in the house was dark.

"That's weird," he said aloud. The cordless one sat in its cradle, useless without electricity, but this old thing worked fine. He thought about it while punching in Ema's number. If the cordless needed the house's power, then the wall phone must be getting its power from somewhere else. He didn't know how, exactly, but the dial tone was proof enough.

Ema answered on the second ring. "Jack? Where are you calling from? Your cell keeps going to voicemail."

"The farmhouse. Power's out, and the cordless phone is dead, but the old wall phone in the kitchen still has a dial tone. The phone company must power the line itself." He heard her groan. "What's wrong?"

"My mom was going to leave right now to drop off the poster board. If she doesn't leave before the creek road floods, I can't bring anything tonight, and we present tomorrow." Ema's project, her poster, her whole grade, riding on one phone call.

"Then call her. We've got a working phone and thirty seconds. Go!"

He heard Ema take a breath, and then the quick tapping of her dialing his grandmother's old phone number from memory.

Elena sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her laptop open, replaying the video Aliya had sent her from Tuesday's choir practice. Pierre-Olivier had been sailing along on the high note when his voice split in half, one sound for a moment and then a completely different one. Everybody had laughed, even Pierre-Olivier, but not meanly, and then Ms. Warsame had held up her hand and said something Elena had only half heard because Aliya was whispering to her at the time.

She played the clip again with her ear pressed close. There. Ms. Warsame's voice, faint under the giggling: "The larynx grows during puberty, and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, so the voice may crack while that happens." Elena paused the video and touched her own throat, feeling the small hard ridge there when she hummed. She thought about Pierre-Olivier at the spring concert, before any of this, his voice as light and steady as a flute. Now it was like a door swinging between two rooms.

She needed to know if growing longer and thicker would really do that to a sound. She dug through her desk drawer and found two rubber bands, a skinny one and a thick one, and stretched each one over the top of an empty tissue box. The box was porous cardboard, full of tiny holes, and it buzzed like a little speaker when she plucked the bands. The skinny band gave a high note. The thick band, stretched the same distance, gave a low one. Then she tried stretching the thick band slowly while plucking it, and the note slid downward and caught somewhere in the middle with a wobbly, broken sound. She played the clip one more time and plucked at the same moment, and the two cracked sounds matched almost exactly.

Aliya arrived in the doorway with her backpack still on one shoulder. "Are you seriously doing science on Pierre-Olivier's voice?"

"I'm doing science on my voice too," Elena said. "Mine is going to change eventually, just differently." She felt a small pang of resentment that the boys got a whole dramatic transformation and she got braces first, but she plucked the thick band again anyway, and the buzz came out low and croaky, like a frog learning to sing.

Aliya dropped her backpack and sat down. "Do the slidey one again," she said.

Jordan had been to weddings before, but never one where the bride's family came from Malaysia, so he watched everything closely at the reception, because the gift he'd brought was wrapped wrong and he didn't know how wrong until he saw it. His mom had told him to hand the package to the bride's aunt at the welcome table. He'd grabbed it with his left hand, easy and natural, and the aunt had smiled but not taken it. She had waited, palm open, until Jordan noticed that every single guest ahead of him had used their right hand to give envelopes and boxes.

He switched hands. She received the gift with her right hand and pressed her own right palm briefly to her chest, and Jordan stepped aside feeling like he'd almost dropped something important.

At the long tables later, the air from the kitchen made the tent warm and humid, and Jordan sat between his friend Chance and a cousin of the bride named Mr. Byrne, who had married into the family years ago and clearly knew everyone. Rice dishes came around family style. Chance, who was busy telling a story about the school talent show, picked up the big serving spoon with his left hand and started to pass the platter. Jordan noticed something before Chance did: every other person at the table, all the way down both sides, was eating and passing with their right hand only, even the left-handed kid who had switched his fork over. It wasn't accident. It was a rule, the kind nobody announced but everybody followed.

Jordan couldn't see the rule itself, only the pattern, so he tested it the way he'd simulate a guess in science class, one trial at a time. He took the platter with his right hand and passed it on with his right. He accepted the tea with his right. Nobody corrected him. Nobody even glanced. Then Chance reached across with his left hand for the bread basket, and Mr. Byrne caught his sleeve gently and said, "Right hand, mate, right hand for eating and for giving things. It's respect."

Chance switched, and Jordan passed him the butter, right hand to right hand, like he'd known all along.

Jordan had one D battery, one small bulb, a strip of aluminum foil, and five minutes before Mr. Hassan's mandatory science club ended for the day. He and Campbell were hunched over the picnic table at the edge of the playground, where pale lichen crept up the wooden legs and flaked off on their sneakers.

"Watch," Jordan said. He folded the foil into a tight wire shape, pressed one end to the top of the battery, and touched the other end straight to the bottom. The bulb sat untouched on the table, still dark. Nothing lit. Worse, the foil was getting warm in his fingers, then genuinely hot, and the battery itself was heating up like a stone left in the sun.

"Drop it!" Mr. Hassan's hand came down quick, knocking the foil away onto the grass. Jordan's fingertips stung and his heart pounded, but the teacher's voice was steady, not angry. "That's a short circuit," Mr. Hassan said. "A wire joining a battery's two ends with nothing in between." He crouched to their level, elbows on the table. "It lets a large current flow, enough to make the wire and battery dangerously hot. That's why I grabbed it."

Jordan stared at the foil lying in the grass, thin and harmless-looking. So the problem wasn't the battery, and it wasn't the foil. The problem was the empty gap where the bulb should have been, because the electricity had taken the easy road and bypassed the one thing he actually wanted to light.

"Can we try once more?" he asked. Mr. Hassan checked his watch, then nodded. Campbell scooted closer to hold the battery steady while Jordan laid one foil wire to the bulb's side and another to its bottom tip, and then to the battery, leaving the bulb stubbornly in between. The filament glowed orange. Campbell whooped so loudly that Madeleine looked over from the swings across the playground.

"Jordan made fire," Campbell announced, holding the battery up like a trophy. "On purpose this time."

The three boxes on Mr. Popescu's desk said IGNEOUS, SEDIMENTARY, and METAMORPHIC, and the six rocks laid out in front of Lucas refused to announce which was which. Frederic had already dropped four rocks into boxes and was leaning back with his arms crossed. "I just guess," he said. "If it's shiny, igneous. If it's boring, the middle one." Lucas stared at a gray lump with faint stripes across its face and felt his whole premise wobble. Guessing had gotten Frederic a perfect score on the vocabulary quiz, but guessing felt wrong for rocks, because rocks had histories you could not see, and there had to be a way to read them.

Then he remembered the field trip to the quarry last autumn, the one where the class had stood at the bottom of a desolate white pit while the wind plastered their jackets against them. Ludovik had pointed at the cliff and asked why the rock was striped, like a layer cake tipped on its side. Nobody had answered that day, but the guide had said one sentence before the bus came: "Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment such as sand, mud or shells are pressed together and cemented over time." Lucas had forgotten it until now, staring at the striped lump.

He picked it up and turned it toward the window light. The stripes ran in even bands, and when he tilted the rock he saw something small and pale caught in one band, curved like a fragment of shell. If the layers were sand and mud pressed and cemented, then a shell caught between them made sense, the way a pressed flower gets stuck between pages. He needed to check the idea against more than one rock, so he carried the lump to Ludovik's table, where Ludovik was scowling at his own gray lump.

"Look at the bands," Lucas said. "Mine has a shell piece in one. Does yours have anything like that, grains or bits?" Ludovik held his rock under the light, turned it twice, and stopped. "There are little dark specks in the lines. Like sand." They compared the two rocks side by side, and both had stripes, both had specks or shell fragments caught in the bands. Lucas dropped his into the SEDIMENTARY box, and after a pause, Ludovik did the same.

Frederic came over and frowned at their boxes. "But the shiny black one," he said. "I put it in igneous because it's pretty." Lucas turned the black rock over. No bands, no grains, just a smooth glassy face. He said nothing, only set it beside the striped lumps so Frederic could see the difference himself. Frederic bit his lip, picked up the black rock, and moved it back to the igneous box. Then he grabbed the last boring gray one and held it up to the window. "Bands," he announced. "Sedimentary. And I only guessed twice."

Mr. Popescu walked past their tables with his clipboard, paused, and made three small marks. Lucas exhaled and slid the striped lump to the center of the box, shell side up.

Bennett stood in front of the festival's heritage booth with a clipboard under his arm and a problem in his pocket. His class project was a graph of the cultural origins of people in his town, based on the numbers Mr. Bianchi had printed from the Canadian census. The graph looked wrong. His bars added up to one hundred and forty percent, which was impossible, and the project was due Monday.

The gym smelled of fried plantains and cardamom. Down one wall, tables held flags, embroidered cloth, and trays of dumplings that Maxim was sampling with great determination. Bennett needed answers, so he set up his clipboard beside Mr. Bianchi's table and began asking people the question on his sheet: "What origins would you say you have?"

A woman with a woven scarf stopped and said, "I'm Scottish and Cree." A teenage boy said, "Jamaican, Irish, and Chinese." Krish arrived with a plate of samosas and leaned over Bennett's shoulder. "You're counting people twice," Krish said. "No, I'm counting answers, not people," Bennett said, but even as he said it, the thought landed. He drew a quick chart on the back of his sheet: every person at the festival as one circle, every origin as a sticker on that circle. One woman had three stickers. His total counted stickers, not circles. Since 1981, the census had let everyone report more than one origin, so the totals could add up to more than the whole population of Canada itself.

He had wanted to evade redoing the graph all afternoon, hoping the numbers would fix themselves. They would not. So he sat on the floor behind the booth and recollected his count as people, not origins, keeping each person once. His percentages came down to a neat one hundred, and the bar for "multiple origins" was the tallest one on the page.

At the evening's climax, when the lights dimmed and the drummers started, Mr. Bianchi came over to look. Bennett held up the graph, feeling assertive for the first time all day. "It was never a mistake in the numbers," he said. "It was me, counting answers instead of people." Mr. Bianchi tapped the tall bar with one finger. "Put a label on that one," he said, "so everyone at Monday's presentation knows it's the whole town in there."

Ryder lay on his towel at Marlin Beach and watched the waves convert the morning's smooth sand into a rumpled mess of ridges and holes. Tomorrow his family would fly home, and that was the problem. On the flight out, during the landing, his ears had felt like someone was pushing two thumbs against them from the inside. His little sister, Dree, had screamed the whole way down, and a man across the aisle had put his headphones on like a laser beam of annoyance aimed straight at their row.

He thought about last summer, the trip to his grandmother's house. Same thing. Landing, pressure, pain. But on the flight out to the beach this time, something odd had happened. The seatbelt sign had come on, the plane had started down, and his ears had popped and felt fine. What was different? He turned it over like a shell in his hand. On the way out, he had been drinking a juice box when the descent began. On the way to Grandma's, nothing. On the flight to the beach when his ears had hurt, also nothing.

"Could drinking actually do something?" he asked Anaeve, who was building a wall of wet sand with Ariella against the incoming tide.

"Drinking what?" Ariella said, dumping a bucket.

"Anything. On planes." Ryder told them about the juice box and the two bad flights. He did not mention Dree screaming, because Anaeve would do an impression of it for the rest of the day. She had a talent for impressions.

Anaeve squinted at him. "My mom chews gum on every flight. Every single one. She says swallowing opens your Eustachian tubes. She says that exact word, Eustachian, like she's proud of it." Ariella laughed so hard she sat down in her own sand wall, and the tide came in and converted the whole fortress into a puddle.

Ryder spent the rest of the afternoon running a test. Every ten minutes he yawned, big and fake, and swallowed, and paid attention to what happened in his ears. Each time there was a tiny click, like a bubble popping somewhere behind his jaw. Whatever those tubes were, they seemed to answer when he swallowed. It was like finding a secret button in a wall. He could not see it, but he could feel it working.

The next day, the descent home began with an abrupt drop that made the whole cabin go quiet. Ryder's ears started to press, and beside him Dree began to cry, kicking her sneakers against the seat. He yawned, wide, and swallowed, and the pressure in his own ears let go with a soft pop. Then he dug into the seat pocket and found the juice box their mom had packed.

"Hey, Dree. Look. Big girl juice." He held the straw to her mouth. She hiccupped, glared at him, and drank. Three swallows later her crying stopped like someone had shut off a faucet, and she pointed at her own ear with one sticky finger.

"Popped," she said.

"Yeah," Ryder said. "Mine too."

Chase had never fasted before, not even for part of a day, so when his mom dropped him at his cousin Daniel's house on the morning of Yom Kippur, he felt like an explorer walking into unfamiliar territory. His stomach had already started a gradual grumble, and it was not even noon.

"You don't eat or drink until tonight," Daniel explained, setting a pitcher of water on the counter where it sat like a taunt. "That's the fast."

Chase watched his cousin carefully. Adults had told Chase that fasting was about saying sorry and thinking hard, but how could not eating portray anything? It was like a neuron in your brain, invisible but sending some kind of message anyway. He wondered what the message actually was.

Then he noticed something odd. Daniel, who had diabetes, kept glancing at the kitchen clock. At one o'clock, their uncle handed Daniel a glass of juice. Chase blinked. "Aren't you fasting?"

"Fast day," Daniel said, "but the rabbi told me I have to drink when my sugar could drop. When health is in danger, Jewish law waives the fast. In that case, you're actually required to eat or drink." He said it like it was the most normal thing in the world.

Chase thought that sounded backwards. He tested it out loud anyway. "So skipping it would be the wrong thing? For you, not eating would break the rule?"

"Exactly," Daniel said. "If I passed out, that's not holy, that's just a mess."

Their uncle laughed and ruffled Daniel's hair. Chase grinned and looked at the water pitcher again. He understood the fast now, but he still had one question burning. "Can I try it for just this afternoon, then?"

"Ask your mom," said the uncle, and Chase was already dialing.

Ms. Hoang set a white plaster ball on each table and clicked on a single lamp, and Penelope leaned in so fast she nearly knocked over her pencil. "Today we generate light and shadow with graphite," Ms. Hoang said, "so watch the ball, not your paper." Penelope watched. The lamp sat off to the left, and the sphere blazed with a bright spot, then faded along a curved edge into grey, then deeper grey, then a pool of darkness lying on the table.

She shaded fast, eager to finish first, but when she held up her drawing something was wrong. Her sphere looked like a flat grey disc, like a coin glued to the page. Francesca, one table over, was frowning at hers too, and Roland had given up entirely and was drawing a diagonal stripe across his corner of the paper out of pure frustration.

"That's the exact same grey all the way across," Francesca said, tapping the dark half of Penelope's drawing.

Penelope looked back at the plaster ball. The dark half wasn't the same at all. The very darkest band wasn't at the far edge; it sat just past the curved border between light and dark, on the side away from the lamp. After that darkest stripe, the sphere actually got a little lighter again, like some faint bounce from the table. She tried saying the border out loud. "Terminator," Roland said, pointing at his own ball with sudden interest. "Ms. Hoang wrote it on the board. That line there." And the darkest band, Penelope decided, needed its own word, so she wrote "core shadow" beside it in her sketchbook, right where it belonged.

She started over, pressing hard only in that one band just past the terminator, easing up everywhere else, and dropping a soft cast shadow onto the table. Francesca leaned across the aisle to see, then erased her whole dark side without a word.

"Whoa," Roland said, staring at Penelope's page. "It actually looks round."

"Now do mine," Francesca begged, sliding her drawing down the table.

Landon slid his essay across the library table and watched Farah's face fall as she read the first line. "Our school should start a recycling club," she read out loud. "That's it? That's your whole opening?" Behind them, the librarian shushed a group of sixth graders, and somewhere near the biography shelves, Roxanne was supposed to be drafting her own paper but kept drifting over to look at Landon's.

"The assignment says five paragraphs," Landon said. "Introduction, three reasons, conclusion. I did the introduction. It states my thesis." He pointed at his notes, where he had written thesis and underlined it twice. "Ms. Berg said the thesis goes at the start."

Farah pulled the paper closer. She wanted her essay on cafeteria food read at the school board meeting next month, and she was determined to figure out why some papers made people sit up and others made them yawn. "Your thesis is fine. But you buried it. Watch." She flipped her own essay around. Her first sentence was a question: "Did you know the meatloaf has been in the freezer since October?" Then came a surprising fact about the lunch budget, and only after that did she write her thesis.

Roxanne leaned over both their shoulders. "It's called a hook," she said. "My cousin taught me. An introduction opens with a hook, like a question, a surprising fact, or a short story, and then it catches the reader's interest before you state the thesis." She snatched Landon's pencil before he could argue and wrote hook at the top of his page in enormous letters.

Landon wasn't sure he believed it, so he decided to test it. He copied his thesis onto three scraps of paper and wrote a different opening above each one: the plain version, a question, and two sentences about the dormant recycling bins sitting unopened in the supply closet since September. Then he asked a boy shelving books nearby to pick the paper he would keep reading. The boy chose the one about the bins. Landon tried it on a girl at the computers, then on the librarian. Both times, the story version won.

"It's like the bins were under siege by nobody using them," Roxanne said, squinting at his sentence. "That's not what siege means. Never mind."

Farah was already rewriting her own opening. "Ms. Berg said we get five minutes at the board meeting," she said. "If my first line is strong enough, they'll listen to the whole five minutes."

Landon read his new opening once more, then raised his hand toward the far corner of the library. "Excuse me," he called to a boy by the window, "if I gave you one sentence, would you keep reading?"

Luca counted the candles on his grandmother's menorah three times before Cyril arrived, and every time he got nine. That was the problem. Hanukkah lasted eight nights, his grandmother had said so at dinner, and eight nights should mean eight candles. He was still staring at the silver branches when the doorbell rang and Cyril came in, shaking snow off his jacket.

"Whoa," Cyril said. "Why does that thing have nine candles if the holiday is eight nights? That's weird."

"I don't know yet," Luca said, "but I'm going to figure it out before we light it."

He crouched down next to the menorah on the windowsill. One candle stood slightly apart from the others, raised a little higher on its own branch. The eight matched in a neat row, but the odd one sat off to the side like it had a different job. Maybe that was the clue. He took out his phone and snapped a picture, then zoomed in until he could see the branches clearly.

"Look," he said, showing Cyril. "Eight of them are in a line. The ninth one is separate and taller. It's not part of the pattern. It's like the frontier candle, standing outside the group."

Cyril frowned at the screen. "So what does it do?"

Luca's grandmother called from the kitchen that it was time. She handed Luca the matches, and Luca watched her nod toward the tall candle. "You start with the shamash," she said. "The helper."

Luca struck the match and touched it to the shamash, then used that flame to light the first candle in the row. The tall one had to burn first so it could kindle all the others, night after night. That was the whole answer, and he had found the edge of it himself, just from looking.

"So it's nine because one candle is the helper," Cyril said. "Eight for the nights, plus one to light them. Got it."

"Exactly," Luca said, and watched the flame of the shamash consume the wick's edge as the window glowed against the dark.

Ellie spread the map across the library table so fast that it knocked over Orion's stack of books, and he had to scramble to retrieve three of them from under the chair. "Sorry," she said, not sounding very sorry. "I need to figure out Hilltop Road before Saturday, because my dad says if it's too steep, we walk the bikes up it, and walking is for quitters."
