"Orion, look." She traced her finger along a winding line. "The map has these brown contour lines. Where they're squished together, the hill is steep. Where they're far apart, it's gentle." She had read that in the atlas's front pages an hour ago, and it had felt like being handed a secret code.

Gurshan slid into the seat across from them and peered at the squished lines. "Squished how much, though? Squished isn't a number."

"It could be a number," Ellie said. "Everything's a number if you're brave enough." She checked the map's legend. Each contour line meant twenty meters of height, and the scale said one centimeter on the map equaled one hundred meters of real ground. She grabbed her ruler from her backpack and measured where Hilltop Road crossed the hillside. Between the bottom and the top, the road climbed past five contour lines. Five lines meant one hundred meters of rise. She measured the distance along the road: five centimeters, which meant five hundred meters of real ground.

Gurshan drummed his fingers. "So what's that in percent?"

"One hundred divided by five hundred," Ellie said, scribbling on the map's margin. "That's a twenty percent grade." She said the last part with a flourish, like announcing a magician's reveal.

Ms. Holloway, the librarian, paused by their table on her way past with an armload of returns. "Twenty percent," she repeated, and gave a low whistle. "That's a proper leg burner. Some riders can push up that, some can't. Depends on the rider." She raised an eyebrow at Ellie and walked on toward the front desk.

"Depends on the rider," Ellie repeated slowly. She looked at the map again, at the parallel brown lines crowding Hilltop Road like passengers on a rush-hour train. Then she flipped the atlas to the back page, found a beginner cycling book she'd noticed earlier, and pulled it toward her. "New plan," she said, turning to a chapter called Hills. "Saturday, I'm going to be the kind of rider who can."

"Or we take Maple Street," Gurshan offered. "The lines there are practically on vacation."

Ellie narrowed her eyes at him over the top of the book. "Orion, hold him down."

Thomas had assumed a polling station would be boring, but Ms. Lombardi's class was there on a Tuesday because the gym was unavailable, and the assignment sheet in his hand said he had to explain how a bill becomes a law. Not a federal bill. A provincial one. He was supposed to interview one voter and one poll worker, and he had brought his two-column chart to fill in.

"Do you want to do the voter and I'll do the poll worker?" asked Ludovick. Ludovick's actual goal was the little round sticker that said I VOTED, which the clerk was sticking on every adult who came out from behind the cardboard screens. Ludovick had asked twice already if there were any spare ones.

"You can have my sticker if I get one," Thomas said, which was a compromise, because he wanted the chart filled in more than anything on his body. Yusuf tagged along to watch.

The poll worker, a woman with a lanyard and a pen behind her ear, was handing out a sheet that compared elections to the work of the legislature. Thomas read it standing beside the table where people signed in. The federal side showed a bill going through two houses before the Governor General signed it. The provincial side showed one house, then the lieutenant governor giving royal assent. He counted the steps twice. Fewer steps. A whole house missing.

"Excuse me," he said to the woman. "Did they print this wrong? Where's the other house?"

"That's the difference," she said, and pointed at the word unicameral. "All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures."

"So a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent," Thomas said slowly, testing it out loud. He wrote it in the box on his chart, then crossed out his first draft, which had copied the federal column like a lazy photocopy.

"The election here is volatile this year, so we're busy," the woman added, because a man was now waiting behind Thomas to ask about where his polling division had moved. Yusuf pulled Thomas out of the line.

"Out of context that chart made no sense," Yusuf said, "but you just fixed your whole assignment by counting."

Ludovick was already at the far end of the table. The clerk had set aside a single sticker on the edge, and Ludovick held it up like a trophy.

"One left," he called across the gym. "Split it with me?"

Thomas grabbed his chart, folded it into his pocket, and held out his sleeve. "You take the sticky half."

Ariana held the guitar like it might bite her. Ms. Lindqvist had gone to fetch her tuning fork, which meant Ariana, Jenson, and Kierra were alone in the music room with Jenson's guitar and a pile of new strings.

"I restrung the whole thing," Jenson said proudly. "Took it all apart first. Very thorough."

"Too thorough," Kierra said, pointing at the pegs. "You didn't write down which string goes where, did you."

Jenson's face went through several stages. "They're strings. They're all basically strings."

"They're different sizes, genius. Fat ones and skinny ones." Kierra plucked one and it buzzed like a grumpy wasp.

Ariana assessed the problem, turning it over in her head. The fattest string had to sit where the fattest one belonged, lowest and closest to her chin. But which note was it supposed to be? She remembered her cousin complaining about this at Thanksgiving, muttering the notes under his breath like a spell: E, A, D, G, B, E. From the low fat string up to the skinny one. Two E's, which struck her as negligent planning on the part of whoever invented guitars, but it was the rule.

"So," she said slowly, "fat to skinny, it's E, A, D, G, B, E." She strung the fat E, then A, then D, and had just finished B when Ms. Lindqvist came back and struck her tuning fork against the desk.

"This," Ms. Lindqvist said, "is your E."

Ariana matched the fat string to it, tightening the peg in tiny careful turns until the wobble between the two sounds shrank to nothing. Then came the clever part, the part she'd read about: play the A string's fifth fret, and it should sound like the E string open. She tested it, adjusted, tested again, and worked her way up the neck string by string while Jenson and Kierra leaned in.

The final E shimmered, matched and sweet.

"Consumer of one perfectly tuned guitar," Jenson announced, holding it up, "reporting for duty."

"Thank you, negligent repair person," Ariana said, and strummed a big glorious chord.

Kierra put her hands over her ears. "Okay, do that again but quieter."

Victoria stared at the two pots of basil on the kitchen windowsill, one under a bright lamp and one in ordinary daylight, and both of them stubbornly the same size. Her science fair project was due in nine days, and her poster still said, in her best marker letters, "My hypothesis: extra light makes basil grow faster." The plants had other plans. Three weeks of measurements showed a plateau, the little green stems climbing and then just stopping, like they had decided four centimeters was far enough.

"If they don't grow, I'll be humiliated in front of the whole gym," she said to Blaire, who had come over with her own project, an intricate maze made of cardboard that was supposed to test whether her hamster could learn its turns. Blaire's problem was the opposite of Victoria's: her hamster, Peanut, kept solving the maze perfectly, every single time.

"Maybe Peanut's just smart," Blaire said, watching the hamster zoom through the corridors for the eleventh time. "But I can't prove it. He finishes the maze either way, whether he remembers it or smells the cheese. I want to show he learns, not that he's hungry."

Victoria flipped through the book their neighbor Mr. Henry had lent her, a thick one about the philosophy of science. She had only borrowed it because it had a picture of a laboratory on the cover, but one page stopped her cold. She read it twice, then read it out loud. "The philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong."

"So your hypothesis has to be able to lose," Blaire said slowly.

Victoria looked at her poster again. "Extra light makes basil grow faster." If the lamp basil stayed the same height as the window basil, her idea would be wrong, and the plants would show it. That was actually good. It meant her project was a real test, not just a decoration. But then she looked at Blaire's maze. "Peanut finishing the maze can't lose. You need something that could come out differently if he's only using his nose."

Blaire sat up straight. "If he learns, he should still solve it when I move the cheese to the end he's never been rewarded at. If he's just sniffing, he'll go to the old corner." She grabbed a piece of cardboard and started drawing.

Victoria got a fresh sheet of paper and wrote at the top, "What result would prove me wrong?" Then she measured both basils again, carefully, and wrote the numbers down where everyone at the fair would see them. If the lamp plant lost, she would report it, and that would hurt, but it would still be science.

Blaire set Peanut into the redesigned maze, cheese hidden in the new corner, and they both leaned in close. "Go on," Blaire whispered. "Prove me wrong."

The departures board kept flipping, and Florence's flight to her grandmother's city was still three hours away. She sat on the floor by the big wall map near Gate 14, tracing her finger along the faint lines until Ariella plopped down beside her with a bag of pretzels.

"Find Grandma yet?"

"Almost." Florence tapped the grid of curved lines. "Latitude is the sideways ones, longitude goes up and down. If I get the numbers right, I can point to any city on Earth." She formulated a plan: pick a city, read the numbers, then find it again with her eyes shut. Her first try landed her in the ocean. Her second try landed her in the ocean too, which the map seemed to find funny.

Mr. Hamdan, who taught geography and was on the same flight, wandered over with his coffee. "Did you know sailors could always find their latitude easily, just by looking at the sky?" he said. "Longitude was the hard one. In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of up to twenty thousand pounds for a practical way to find a ship's longitude at sea."

Ariella stopped chewing. "Twenty thousand pounds? For a number?"

"A whole fortune back then," said Mr. Hamdan, and he went to check on his boarding pass, leaving the fact sitting there like unclaimed luggage.

Florence stared at the map. Latitude, the easy one, ran neatly sideways. Longitude, the prize-winning one, went up and down, and she suddenly got why the two were not the same problem at all, or at least she felt the edge of it, the way you feel a puzzle piece fit before you can say why. She checked her grandmother's coordinates one more time, carefully, because guessing had already dumped her in the ocean twice and checking was less tedious than drowning.

"Ten degrees north, eighty-four degrees west," she read aloud, and put her finger on the little dot. Ariella leaned in and held the pretzel bag out like a prize.

Sawyer pushed through the festival crowd with a roll of poster paper under one arm, hunting for the booth with the blue tablecloth. Riley's sign-language club had exactly one hour before the storytelling stage opened, and the poster still said, in giant letters, WELCOME TO THE deaf CLUB.

"There you are," Riley said, signing and talking at the same time. "Did you bring the markers?"

"Better," Sawyer said. "A question. Should 'deaf' be capital or lowercase? The banner outside the library says 'Deaf' with a big D, but our poster has a little one, and the booth next door has both."

They stood in the middle of the fairground, surrounded by booths where people described themselves in every way imaginable. At one table, a woman in a woven shawl was explaining that her embroidery patterns came from her grandmother's village. At another, a family had pinned up photographs of the old mill, and a sign explained that the town had nearly emptied out during the recession in the 1980s, when the jobs disappeared, and that new families had brought it back to life. Two teenagers at a mic were teaching a dance from their neighborhood, laughing when the crowd got the steps wrong and starting over without complaint.

Sawyer pulled out his phone and typed carefully. On the club's own website he found a page Riley had never shown him, and Riley read it aloud. "In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself."

"So it's not a spelling mistake," Sawyer said slowly. "It's two different words. Capital D is about the community. Lowercase is about the condition." He looked at their poster, then at the banner near the library, then at the club's flyers, where Riley had used the big D everywhere. "We weren't consistent. That's why it looked wrong."

He tested his idea against every sign he could find. The storytelling stage had a card that said "ASL interpreter provided by the Deaf community," capital D. A health booth had a flyer about hearing tests that used the lowercase word. Each one fit the rule, which meant the rule was real, and it also meant their poster was telling people the wrong thing.

Riley grabbed the markers. "Fix it before Ms. Adebayo brings her class by."

Sawyer printed the big D in gold, three inches tall, and Riley held the paper steady while the ink dried. Then they propped the poster against the front of the booth, stepped back, and watched a man in a hearing aid stop, read it, and flash them a thumbs-up. Riley signed "thank you," and Sawyer copied the sign, his hands clumsy but getting there.

Cole spread his supplies across the kitchen table: a lump of clay for the nucleus, toothpicks, and three wire rings he had bent from a coat hanger. The assignment said his model of lithium had to show protons and neutrons jammed together in the middle, and electrons in the right places around the outside. He pressed the clay onto a cardboard square and squinted at it. The nucleus looked like a blob of gray gum, which was fine, but the wire rings would not cooperate. Every time he wedged one into the clay, it tipped sideways.

"You're doing it in vain if you don't fix the balance first," said Daniella, who had come over with her own half-finished model in a shoebox. She held up a wooden skewer. "Mr. Halvorsen said ours have to stand up on the desk by tomorrow."

Cole ignored her and kept poking the wire into the clay. The ring flopped again. Then it hit him: the ring wasn't the problem, the angle was. He pulled the wire out, bent a tiny foot onto the bottom of each ring, and pressed all three feet into the clay so they stood one inside the other like the lanes of a tiny circular track. The electrons, three seed beads, could ride those tracks without falling.

"Wait," Daniella said slowly, turning her phone toward him. "Why rings at all? Why not just scatter the electrons anywhere? It says here that in 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model in which electrons travel only in certain fixed orbits, or energy levels, around the nucleus." She looked up. "So the rings are actually right. Bohr was the first to draw atoms that way."

"So my wire rings aren't just decoration," Cole said. "They're the whole point." He slid one bead onto the innermost ring and two onto the next, then stood the model on the counter to test whether it would hold until morning. His mother's laser thermometer, borrowed to check that the glue on the base had cooled enough to accommodate the weight of the rings, beeped once from the drawer.

Daniella leaned in close. "Tip it," she whispered. "Just a little."

Cole nudged the cardboard edge with one finger, and the beads shivered along their orbits but stayed on their tracks.

Lucy stood in front of the glass case, notebook open, and read the question she was supposed to answer for Mr. Owusu's museum worksheet: "Why did ancient Egyptians build the pyramids, and how did the Nile shape their farming?" The trouble was that she had missed two days of school with a broken wrist, and everybody else in her group already knew the answers. Emily and Avery had wandered off toward the mummy exhibit, and Lucy had exactly forty minutes before the bus left.

She started with the pyramids. A sign near a model of Giza said the pyramids were tombs for kings, built tall so the king's spirit could climb toward the sky. That part she copied down, but it felt like copying, not knowing. She looked at the tiny model workers hauling stone blocks up ramps and thought about how many people it must have taken, how much food they must have needed, and how that food had to come from farms along a river that flooded and dried on a schedule nobody controlled.

That was when she found the second case, the one about the Nile. A long wooden pole stuck out over a little model field, with a bucket hanging from one end and a heavy clay weight on the other. A boy about her age was tugging at the pole's rope, but it was bolted down, so his mother had to intervene before he wrenched the whole display loose. A small card next to it read: "Egyptian farmers used a shaduf to lift river water up to their fields." Lucy tried the lever herself, gently, and felt how the weight on the far end made the bucket rise with almost no effort. Her wrist, still in its cast and strangely vulnerable whenever she forgot and used it, did not have to strain at all.

She thought of hauling watering cans in her grandmother's garden, each one heavy enough to make her arms shake. If she had a pole like this, she could dip the bucket in the rain barrel and lift it without lugging anything. That was the real trick, she realized: the Nile flooded every year and left wet, rich soil, but the water sat below the level of the fields, and a shaduf could lift it up. Farmers who could water their crops beyond the flood could grow more food, and more food meant thousands of workers could be fed while they stacked a king's tomb toward the sky.

"Found you," Avery said, skidding around the corner. "Did you figure out your question?"

"Better than that," Lucy said, and pulled the lever again, watching the bucket swing up over the little green field.

Mila spread her library books across the table like evidence at a trial. Ms. Johansson's note, clipped to her essay, said the quotation was fine but the page number had to go in parentheses so a reader could check it. Mila had written the quote with nothing after it, which meant the note might as well have said, nice try.

Tia dropped into the chair across from her and slid over a book about a boy who sails a flooded river to find his grandfather. "This one's theme is easy. It's about not giving up."

"That's a topic, not a theme," Mila said, though she wasn't entirely sure what the difference was. She flipped to the page where the boy's grandfather tells him, "A river takes everything, and still it moves." She copied the sentence down. Then she stopped, pencil hovering. Where exactly did the page number go, and did it need a comma?

Vihaan arrived with pretzel smell on his sleeves and leaned over her paper. "You're being very diligent about one sentence."

"I have to be. Ms. Johansson said the quotes need page numbers the reader can check." Mila tried it three ways on scrap paper: (Carter, 44), (Carter 44,), and finally (Carter 44). The last one looked the least like a mistake, so she wrote it after the quote and sat back. Author's last name, page number, nothing between them. If it was wrong, at least it was wrong neatly.

The three of them spent another hour hunting themes, arguing quietly until a librarian informed them that whispering still counted as talking and the cease-and-desist would be enforced. On the way out, past the poster about screen hygiene that advised wiping your phone daily, Mila reread her paragraph one last time.

At school the next morning, Ms. Johansson paused at Mila's desk and tapped the parentheses with one finger. "Perfect. MLA style."

"So no comma?" Mila asked.

"Author's last name and the page number," Ms. Johansson said. "No comma between them."

Mila slid the essay to the middle of the desk, title side up, and moved on to sharpening her pencil.

The kitten was supposed to go home with Alexis by five o'clock, when the shelter's foster program closed for the weekend, and it was already half past four. She stood at the counter of the veterinary clinic with the adoption folder in her hands while the receptionist photocopied her mother's signature on the form that said the family could afford a pet. Her mother had joked in the car that they were not taking out a second mortgage just to feed a cat, and Alexis had laughed, but she was starting to wonder what a cat actually cost.

The problem was the food. On the shelf behind the counter, the clinic sold dog food and cat food in bags that looked almost identical, and the dog food was three dollars cheaper for a bigger bag. Paisley had told her last week that her cousin fed his cat dog food all the time and the cat seemed fine. Alexis picked up both bags and turned them over, hunting for a difference. She could not see one. The ingredients listed chicken, rice, fat, vitamins, a long list of words she could not pronounce. If the difference was hidden, then something in the cat had to be hidden too, something dogs could make for themselves and cats could not. She had read a poster in the waiting room while her mother filled out forms, and one line of it had stuck in her head.

"Excuse me," she said to Mr. Tran, the vet tech who was restocking the shelf. "Does this word, taurine, matter? It's on the cat food but not the dog food." Mr. Tran nodded and said, "Cats can't make enough taurine on their own, so it has to be in their food." Then he pointed at the next line of the poster, which said a lack of it could cause heart disease and blindness in cats. Alexis read it twice. So a cat could eat dog food for months and look fine while something invisible went wrong inside, and by the time anyone noticed, the damage would already be done. Paisley's cousin's cat was nine years old, and Alexis suddenly wanted to text her.

She almost did, standing there with her thumb over the phone, until Mr. Tran cleared his throat and tapped the clock above the counter. Four forty-five. Alexis grabbed the smaller, more expensive bag of cat food, the one with the lush picture of a chicken on the front, and carried it to the register. She had walked in thinking she would save money with the dog food. Now she set the cat food down and counted out the allowance she had been saving since September.

At the door, the carrier meowed, and Mr. Tran called after her, "Check the label again when you buy your next bag, just to be sure." Alexis lifted the carrier so the kitten could see out the window toward the parking lot. "Every time," she said, and pushed the door open with her hip.

Logan dragged the folding table into the driveway before breakfast, because today was his first day volunteering with the neighborhood collection, and Mr. Banerjee had promised him an official job. His mom had signed him up after he begged for a whole week. The morning smelled like cut grass, and the metal table legs clanked as he snapped them open beside the cardboard boxes labeled CANNED SOUP and PASTA.

By ten o'clock, trucks had already rumbled past twice, and Logan noticed something strange. Both trucks wore the exact same blue logo, a bowl with a swoosh under it, but one was from a city two hours south and the other from a town he'd never even heard of. "How can they have the same sign if they're from different places?" he asked Lewis, who was stacking cans with the speed of a kid who had eaten three bowls of cereal and no patience.

"Maybe they're copying each other," Lewis guessed. "Like rivals." Logan shook his head. Rivals wouldn't share a logo. He had a different idea, and he wanted to test it. When the third truck pulled up, its engine rumbling and hot air rippling off the hood, he asked the driver to hand him one of the paper flyers from the dashboard. The flyer had the swoosh bowl on it and a map dotted with tiny marks. Maely leaned over his shoulder, her synthetic jacket squeaking as she crowded in.

"It's called Feeding America," she read off the top. Logan traced the map with his finger, counting dots until he lost track. "So it's not rivals," he said, his voice rising. "It's one giant team. All these food banks everywhere, more than two hundred of them, all across the country, all on the same side." Hunger was the real adversary, and they were fighting it coast to coast. He grabbed a marker and wrote a new sign for the table, then held it up so the whole street could see: EVERY CAN WE COLLECT JOINS A NETWORK OF MORE THAN 200 FOOD BANKS. Mr. Banerjee laughed and rang the cowbell.

Abigail sat on her grandmother's porch with the old accordion strapped to her chest, sweating like the thing was alive. Her objective was simple: play "O Susanna" all the way through without a single squawk before Sunday, when her grandmother promised they would play together. Saturday was her last chance, so she practiced for two whole hours, missing the same note in measure six about four hundred times. The accordion wheezed like an asthmatic elephant. "We're both exhausted," she told it.

Sunday arrived and measure six still squawked. Grandma winced politely and offered cookies instead of a duet. On Monday Abigail stomped next door to Kaden's house, where he was failing to teach his cat to fetch. "I practiced forever," she said. "Two hours. One sitting. And I'm still terrible." Kaden threw a bottle cap across the yard. "I studied spelling that way once, the night before the test. Crammed the whole list in one giant chunk. Then I got 'rhythm' wrong for the fourth week in a row." The cat ignored the cap. The fourth week in a row. Abigail wondered why that was.

She tried an experiment. Instead of one giant Saturday chunk, she played for only fifteen minutes a day, Monday through Friday. Could smaller pieces really add up to more than one big pile of the same time? It felt too easy. On Tuesday she missed measure six. On Wednesday she missed it twice. On Thursday, her fingers found the button without her even hunting for it, like they had been secretly practicing while she slept. She laughed out loud on the porch and scared a cardinal off the railing.

By Friday, "O Susanna" rolled out smooth and elastic, bending and swinging the way her grandmother's version did. On Sunday, Grandma put down her knitting, and they played the duet twice, then three times, and Grandma's slipper kept time like a metronome. "You've been at it every day, haven't you," Grandma said, eyes crinkling. Abigail grinned and squeezed the bellows shut. "Same total practice, Grandma. Just chopped up small. Want to petition the church to let us do this in front of actual people?"

Natalie's note cards were so sparse they were basically blank, and her speech was due tomorrow. Mr. Mwangi had written the recipe on the board: a hook to grab attention, three points, a closing that circled back. She had the three points. What she didn't have was a heart brave enough to say them out loud.

At lunch she watched Eugene draft his speech on a napkin, cross it out, and draft it again on his sleeve. "Mine's about why cafeteria tacos beat cafeteria pizza," he said. "The whole grade will vote. I'm aiming for a landslide."

"My category is 'something scary,'" Natalie said. Her hands had been shaking since Tuesday, which was ridiculous, because she'd known these kids since kindergarten.

Arman slid her his juice box. "My hands shake every time before I talk in front of people. Every single time."

"That has a name, you know," Eugene said, mouth full. "Glossophobia. Fear of public speaking. And it's one of the most commonly reported fears. Mr. Mwangi told me when I asked why my knees wobble."

Natalie stared at him. One of the most commonly reported fears. Not just her, then. Probably half the room. She did the math on her fingers: if everyone was scared, nobody would be watching for her mistakes, because they'd all be busy being scared of their own. She could test that.

"Tomorrow," she said, "when I go up, I'm going to look for shaking hands in the audience. If I spot three, my theory is right."

Thursday came. She walked to the front, hook ready: "Raise your hand if your hand is shaking." Dead silence. Then Eugene raised his, wobbling like a flag in wind. Arman lifted his, and so did a girl in the second row, then half the class, giggling. Natalie gave her three points about fear, closed with the same raised hand, and the room actually clapped before she finished the sentence.

Walking back, she passed Arman. "Three," she whispered. "Plus five."

"I counted eight," he whispered back, and wiggled his fingers at her.

Rosalie knelt at the edge of the pond with her notebook, because the science test was Monday morning and it was already Saturday. "Draw one plant cell and one animal cell," the study sheet said, "and label the parts only plants have." She could not draw what she could not see, so she had dragged Byron and Grace out here to help her interpret the green fuzz of elodea leaves she'd pulled from the water.

"Cells are too small," Byron said, squinting at the leaf. "This is pointless."

"Ms. Chen said pond plants have the biggest cells we can nearly see. And she said something else, something about a timeline at the museum. I can't remember what." Rosalie flattened the leaf against her notebook page and traced its outline. Grace crouched beside her and poked at a snail creeping along a stone, its little foot gripping like a tendon grips a bone, firm and pale.

"My brother went to that museum last year," Grace said. "He's notorious for mixing up facts, but he kept repeating one thing. This botanist, Matthias Schleiden. German guy. In 1838 he proposed that all plant tissues are made of cells."

"1838," Rosalie repeated, writing it down. Then she stopped writing. "Wait. My sheet says animal cells were declared after that. So plants got figured out first. A whole year before animals."

Byron leaned over her shoulder. "Then the parts only plants have must have been the easy part to spot. The wall. The green stuff."

"The cell wall and chloroplasts," Rosalie said, and she started drawing, a thick box around the plant cell and a thinner skin around the animal cell, labeling the wall and the chloroplasts on the plant side only.

"I said it was pointless," Byron said.

"You did." She added spiky green chloroplasts, then a fat nucleus in both cells. "And you were wrong."

Grace held the snail up so it faced the notebook. "Even he has no chloroplasts."

"Poor snail," Byron said. "No cell wall, either."

Rosalie closed her notebook and stood, brushing pond mud from her knees. "Grace, ask your brother one more thing before Monday."

Charlie had one goal at Jannat's house: win the negotiation over the last chocolate chip cookie before Jannat's little cousin Ben could claim it. Ben was four, loud, and fast for someone so small. Charlie was laying out her case, two cookies for him last Tuesday versus zero for her, when Jannat pulled her into the kitchen.

"Watch this," Jannat whispered, holding up a marble. "Elliott showed me this yesterday. It's from a real psychology thing, from 1985. You hide the marble, the kid knows where it is, then the kid leaves and you move it."

"That's just hiding a marble," Charlie said.

"Just watch."

Ben picked blue. Jannat put the marble in the red bucket, asked Ben where it was, and Ben pointed correctly. Then she sent him to wash his hands, and while he was gone she moved the marble to the green basket.

"Now," she said when Ben came back, "where will you look for your marble?"

Ben, dripping slightly, pointed at the red bucket with total confidence. "There!" He lifted it, found nothing, and looked personally betrayed by the bucket. Charlie laughed so hard she had to inhale a whole breath before she could speak.

"Wait, he saw you move it. Didn't he?"

"He was in the other room. That's the point. Kids his age mostly say you'll look where you left it, because they think everybody knows what they know. Elliott says from about age four they usually get it right. Ben's not quite there yet."

Charlie frowned. Was that true of all four-year-olds, or just Ben? She needed more data. She borrowed the marble, found Jannat's other cousin, age five, in the hallway, and ran the whole thing again, hiding the marble in a shoe, moving it to a plant pot. The five-year-old looked in the shoe first, but then, unprompted, marched to the plant pot and found it.

"So it's not age exactly," Charlie said slowly, counting on her fingers. "It's more like a switch that flips around then."

That night she wrote a note and slid it under Elliott's door, since he was apparently the prestigious expert of the street.

Dear Elliott. Today we did your marble test on Ben (4) and Amira (5). Ben said red bucket. Amira said shoe but then fixed it. Questions: Do dogs fail this too? Do grown-ups ever fail it? Also, is there a version with cookies? Urgent. Charlie.

The next morning she found a reply taped to her front door. It said only: "Bring cookies. And the marble."

Max had been late to his lesson for three weeks in a row, and today he was determined not to be. He ran up the stone steps of Mr. Whitaker's studio, past the speckled patches of lichen on the porch railing, and skidded through the door with two minutes to spare. Mr. Whitaker looked up from the piano and smiled.

"Clarinet ready?" he asked.

"Ready," said Max, and he assembled it so fast that the reed nearly flew across the room. Karim and Andie were already there, sprawled on the rug with their sheet music. Today was the big day: Mr. Whitaker had promised that whoever could play the first eight bars of the spring concert piece without a mistake would get a solo. Max wanted that solo more than anything.

But when he set his music on the stand, the notes swam in front of him. He kept losing his place, and every time he did, he paused too long and Andie had to nudge him back in. After the third stumble, Mr. Whitaker called a break, and Max sat staring at the page. His eyes drifted to the curly symbol at the start of every staff, the one he'd never really looked at before. Something about it seemed familiar. He traced the curl with his finger, around and around, and noticed where it looped. It circled one line, wrapped right around it, as if it were pointing.

He counted up from the bottom line. First line, E. Second line, G. The curl circled the second line.

"Wait," Max said. "The treble clef. It's circling the G line."

Mr. Whitaker grinned. "That's why it's also called the G clef."

A memory flashed back to him: second grade, Mrs. Somebody drawing a giant curling line on the whiteboard and telling the class to follow it like a road. Max had thought it was just decoration back then. All this time, the map had been sitting at the start of every line of music he'd ever played. He grabbed a pencil and, on his sheet, traced the swirl down to its loop. G. From G he could climb to B, then D, then F, the line notes stacked like rungs of a ladder. Suddenly the notes weren't swimming anymore; they had addresses.

"Can we go again?" Max asked, already lifting the clarinet.

"Go ahead," said Mr. Whitaker, and he played a tranquil piano chord to set the key.

Max took a breath and played the first eight bars. His fingers found G without a single pause. Andie whooped. Karim drummed the rug.

"How'd you do that?" Karim demanded.

"Follow the curl," Max said, and pointed at the page.

Hailey set the wooden ball on the camp art table and frowned at her sketch. In her drawing, the sphere looked flat, like a plain circle with a scribble underneath, and it was supposed to be the orb in a portrait of an emperor for the camp art show. Mr. Nakamura had said the best entries would show real light, with a bright highlight, a shadow on the dark side, and a cast shadow on the ground. Hers had none of that.

"Try the lamp," said Kai, dragging the desk lamp across the table. "You can move it around." Hailey's first move was impulsive; she swung the lamp down close to the tabletop, nearly knocking over the ball before catching it. The moment the light steadied, a shadow stretched across the table so long it nearly reached Kai's elbow. "Whoa," Hailey said. "Look at that." She grabbed the lamp pole and raised it higher overhead, and the shadow shrank to a stubby puddle at the ball's base. She lowered it again and the shadow stretched out long; she raised it and the shadow pulled in short. "So that's the rule," she said slowly. "The lower the light is, the longer the cast shadow. Like when the sun gets low in the evening and your shadow goes way out in front of you."

She tested it twice more to be sure, sliding the lamp up and down like a lever while Kai held the ball steady. Then she chose a low lamp position on purpose, because an emperor's orb, she decided, should sit in dramatic evening light. She drew the highlight as a small pale spot where the lamp struck the ball, darkened the far side, and dragged a long cast shadow across the paper. Kai leaned over her shoulder. "That actually looks round," he said. Mr. Nakamura passed by, tapped the table, and reminded them to comply with the studio rule about cleaning brushes before lunch. Hailey dipped her brush in the water jar, but she kept her eyes on the drawing, where the long shadow lay across the page exactly the way she wanted it.

Madison lay on the living room couch with a blanket, a box of tissues, and a headache that felt like a drum line practicing behind her eyes. The flu had kept her home for two days, and tomorrow was the science test, which meant Manuel and Blair were coming over at four with their notes and the review sheet she'd missed. That gave her three hours to feel human again.

She got up, shuffled to the medicine cabinet, and found two bottles: one labeled ibuprofen, one labeled aspirin. The aspirin was the bigger bottle, so she reached for that first. Then she saw the fine print on the side. It said children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it was linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain. She read it twice. Her little brother couldn't even have cough syrup without a parent weighing him first, but she was eleven, practically twelve. Maybe the warning was for little kids.

She decided to test it. She carried both bottles back to the couch and called Mr. Desir, the retired pharmacist who lived downstairs and was famously eccentric, the kind of man who planted a lawn umbrella indoors and sang opera to his cat. He answered on the second ring.

"Mr. Desir, does the aspirin rule count for me, or just for little kids?" she asked. "I'm almost twelve."

"It counts for every child and teenager," he said. "Flu or chickenpox, no aspirin, because of Reye's syndrome. Rare, but it hits the liver and the brain. Take the ibuprofen, take the dose on the label, and drink water."

"Even if I feel like a grown-up?"

"Your head can rebel all it likes. Your liver still knows your age." He chuckled. "And tell your mother I said so."

Madison swallowed the ibuprofen with a glass of water and texted Blair: bring the review sheet, I'm contagious but determined. Then she set the aspirin bottle on the coffee table, turned it so the warning faced up, and propped her notes on her knees. When the doorbell rang at four, her headache had shrunk to a whisper, and she was already on question twelve.

The rain hammered the craft cabin roof so hard that Lily could barely hear Braiden shout across the Monopoly board. Mina had just landed on Marvin Gardens, and she was refusing to buy it.

"If you don't buy it, nobody gets it," Braiden said, crossing his arms. "Then we're just stuck going in circles forever."

"That's not fair to me," Mina said. "I want a chance at it too." Lily watched them argue back and forth, and she began to suspect that the real problem was not the property at all. It was that they each assumed the game ended the moment someone declined to buy, so neither of them could see any way forward except winning the argument. Maybe there was a rule hiding somewhere that covered exactly this.

"Wait," she said, holding up a hand. "Let's check the rule sheet before we fight about it." She dug the thin folded paper out of the box lid, where it had been flattened under the money tray, and smoothed it on the table between the dice. The cabin smelled like wet wood and glue, and someone's flashlight buzzed on the shelf behind them. Lily ran her finger down the small print until she found it.

"It says if you land on an unowned property and you choose not to buy it, the bank auctions it," she read. "To the players. It's right here." Braiden leaned in and read the line himself, then sat back with a rebellious look on his face, like he wanted to argue with the paper itself.

"So Mina could still get it," he said slowly. "At the auction."

"That's the inference I'd make," Lily said. "You don't buy it, the bank sells it to whoever bids, and the money goes back to the bank." Mina flipped through her cash, counting, and a smile spread across her face. She had more money than Braiden did.

They tried it. Ms. Petrov, the craft instructor, wandered over and watched from her stool as Mina opened the bidding at one hundred dollars, Braiden pushed to one hundred twenty, and Mina won Marvin Gardens for one hundred fifty. Braiden groaned, but he slid the title deed across the table without complaint, because the rule was printed in black and white and it had applied to both of them equally.

After that, they played the whole afternoon by the sheet. Every time a disagreement popped up, whether it was about rent or jail or who got to be the banker next, Lily would say, "Name the problem first," and they would hunt through the rules before anyone raised a voice. The rain kept drumming, the game kept moving, and when the whistle blew for dinner, Mina was still counting her stacks of orange and yellow bills, guarding Marvin Gardens with one flat hand.

Clara signed in at the library's front desk, where a folding table had been set up beside the return cart. The community room had been turned into a food bank for the afternoon, and boxes of donated groceries crowded the space between the biography shelves and the window. Her job was sorting: cans with cans, boxes with boxes, and a whole crate of apples that looked strange. Some were small, some had brown spots, and one was shaped like a lopsided snowman. Freya grabbed a dented can of beans and held it up. "This one's fine, right? The dent's just on the side."

"That's the rule," Clara said, pointing at the poster Mr. Flores had taped to the wall. Deep dents, no. Small ones, yes. She picked up the lopsided apple and turned it over. It was the third odd-looking apple she'd found, and almost every piece of fruit in the crate had some flaw. She started to wonder if that was why the store had given it away. Maybe stores threw out anything that didn't look perfect, and that could add up to a lot of food.

"I read something about this at school," Kenan said from the next box. "The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted." He stacked a jar of sauce as he said it, like it was no big deal, but Clara stopped with an apple in each hand. Thirty to forty percent. She tried to picture ten apples on the table. Three or four of them never getting eaten.

She decided to test her idea. She sorted the crate into two piles, perfect-looking fruit and flawed fruit, and counted. The flawed pile was bigger by a lot. "So if stores only sell the pretty ones," she said, "this crate is the proof. It's all the weird ones." Mr. Flores passed by with an empty box and glanced at her two neat rows.

"That's exactly what a food rescue group told us," he said. "They pick up produce the stores can't sell."

Clara had come in thinking volunteering would be boring, just hauling boxes after her long commute across town on two buses. Now she asked Mr. Flores whether the library needed a permanent Saturday sorter, someone reliable, week after week. He said he'd have to ask the coordinator, but he wrote her name on the sign-up sheet in pen, not pencil.

Freya grinned and tossed her a slightly dented can of beans. "You could charge for this someday. Be an entrepreneur."

"Or just do it for free," Clara said, and shelved the can with the others.

Leah had monitored every rehearsal for three weeks, watching where her flute section stood, when the lights changed, how Mr. Lombardi raised his baton. But tonight, in the dressing room with her collar buttoned wrong and her music folder gripped in both hands, she realized she had never once seen the ending.

"Elaina," she said, "what happens after the last song? After the clapping starts?"

Elaina was spraying her hair into a bun that kept collapsing. "What do you mean, after? We did the whole concert twice."

"No, we didn't. We stopped at the last note both times. Mr. Lombardi never told us what to do when people applaud." The more Leah thought about it, the more the hole opened under her, like erosion wearing away what she'd assumed was solid ground.

Elaina's bun slid sideways again. "Then we just stand there, I guess. My mom's in the third row with her phone. I want to wave at her when it's over, so standing there works for me."

"Standing there is wrong," Leah said. She had watched her older cousin's choir concert in the spring, and now the memory assembled itself: when the singing ended and the audience clapped, the whole choir came back out to the stage after a short wait, and bowed. She tested the idea out loud. "It's called a curtain call. The performers return to the stage at the end of the show to be recognized. We bow."

"So we bow. Big deal."

"If nobody tells the sixth graders, forty people are going to freeze out there." Leah left the dressing room, found Mr. Lombardi in the hallway holding his baton like a fork, and said, "We never rehearsed the bow."

He blinked at her. "We didn't, did we. All right, spread the word. After the finale, stay in place, then bow together on my count."

The concert ran long. When the final chord faded and the applause began, Leah stood still, counting. Mr. Lombardi turned toward the stage, raised both arms, and the whole group bowed as one. Somewhere in the third row, a phone flashed. Elaina waved.

Ellie sat at her grandfather's kitchen table with the old laptop open to Scratch, a cat sprite waiting on a blank stage. Her grandfather's house was the only place she could work undisturbed, because the upstairs tenant had complained once about noise and her grandfather had laughed about it for a week. Ahmed was coming over after lunch, and she wanted the game finished before he arrived. The plan seemed simple: a little rocket dodging asteroids, with the score going up every second the player survived.

She built it with a loop that repeated forever, a move block, an if-then block that checked whether the rocket was touching an asteroid, and a change score by one block. It ran. The rocket flew, the asteroids tumbled past in parallel lanes, and the score climbed steadily. But something bothered her. When the rocket hit an asteroid, the game just kept going, the score climbing as if nothing had happened. That was wrong, and she could not see why, because the program was invisible. The blocks looked right. Somewhere in that stack was a rule she could not look at directly, only guess at.

She remembered the afternoon, three months ago, when she had quit her first Scratch project entirely. Her butterfly sprite had spun in endless circles no matter what she did, and she had closed the laptop and told herself coding was not for her. Her grandfather had said nothing at the time, just set the laptop back on the table the next morning, and she still did not know whether that had been wise or stubborn of him. Maybe quitting had been the wrong choice. Maybe it had only been too early to tell.

She tested an idea. She dragged the change score by one block out of the loop and put it inside the if-then block instead, so the score would only rise when the rocket touched an asteroid. She ran the game. The score stayed frozen at zero, then jumped by one the instant the rocket collided. She laughed out loud at herself. The if-then block was like a gate with one door, and she had been rewarding the wrong thing.

When Ahmed arrived, she showed him the problem. "I need the score to go up when nothing happens, and a lose message when the rocket crashes," she said. Ahmed leaned over her shoulder and pointed at the blue blocks in the menu. "Use if then else," he said. She clicked it into place and studied the shape of it, one slot for true and one slot for false, two doors instead of one. Into the first slot she put the change score by one block. Into the second she put a say block with the words GAME OVER, YOU LOSE. She pressed the green flag.

The rocket flew, the score counted, and when an asteroid finally caught it, the rocket stopped and the words GAME OVER, YOU LOSE floated over the stage while the score froze in place. Ahmed pounded the table. "Again," he said, reaching for the mouse.

Autumn sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office with her science notebook open, because her appointment was at four o'clock and the ant project was due tomorrow morning. Her poster was supposed to show how a single queen could colonize a bare patch of sidewalk, building a colony out of nothing, but half her facts were still missing and the clock above the reception desk kept jumping forward.

Across the room, Cassie sat with her knees pulled up, picking at her sleeve. That was strange. Cassie was usually the defiant one, the girl who argued with referees and once led a walkout of the entire cafeteria line. Today she looked small.

"Are you here for a checkup too?" Autumn asked.

"Stomachaches," Cassie said. "Mom made me come. They only get worse near tests." She paused, then lowered her voice. "The doctor said a word for it. Anxiety. And she asked how I cope, and I didn't even know what she meant."

"Coping," Autumn said slowly. "It means the ways you handle stress, I think. My mom says it all the time."

"What do you actually do, after a bad day?"

Autumn thought about it honestly. "I run laps around the yard until my head goes quiet, and I go to bed early even when I don't want to, and I tell my mom what happened. She's the one person who never makes it weird." She tapped her pencil. "So that's three things. Exercise, sleep, and talking to someone you trust."

"Talking is my problem," Cassie admitted. "I just hold it in until my stomach holds it for me."

Autumn looked at the clock, then at her half-empty poster. On the back of it, the blank cardboard side, she wrote in big letters: WHAT I DO AFTER A BAD DAY. "Test it tonight," she said, tearing the page out and handing it over. "Run, sleep, and text me. Consider it commerce. You give me ant facts, I give you this."

Cassie laughed for the first time all afternoon. "Deal. Ants for coping."

When the nurse called Cassie's name, she stood up straighter than before, holding the poster board like a shield.

The doctor's door swung shut, and Autumn flipped her notebook to a fresh page. Under the queen ant, she added a new label: builds from nothing.

The line at the gas station started at the pumps and curled past the ice freezer to the door. Natalie counted eleven cars. Her mother had sent her inside for bottled water because the storm was coming Thursday, and the radio kept saying to stock up. On the shelf, the last case of water had a hand-written sign taped across it: 12 dollars. Last week, Natalie remembered, the same case had cost four.

Arman was already inside, holding two energy drinks and staring at the sign. "That's illegal," he said. "The cashier is just ripping people off. Sellers decide the price, so this is his fault." Justin shook his head from beside the chip rack. "No way. If nobody paid twelve bucks, he'd have to drop it. Buyers decide the price. If we all refuse, the sign comes down." They argued in front of the register while the man behind the counter kept scanning granola bars and saying nothing.

Natalie stood between them with her crumpled ten dollars. She looked at the shelf, where only one case remained, and then at the line of people behind her, everyone glancing at their phones, everyone saying the word storm. She thought about the gas price sign outside, which had gone up forty cents since Sunday. It wasn't only the cashier wanting more money. It was also all these people wanting the same few cases at the same time. Maybe that was the hidden part. She tested it out loud: "What if it's both? What if the seller's price and all of us wanting it together set the number, kind of like how you need both blades of a pair of scissors to cut anything?"

Ms. Silva, who taught down the hall from Natalie's homeroom, was third in line with a flashlight battery in her hand. "Alfred Marshall said that exact thing," she said, setting her battery on the counter. "In his 1890 book, Principles of Economics, he compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price." She paid and walked out, and the line shuffled forward.

Arman still looked stubborn, but Justin nudged him. "You were half right," Justin said. "She was half right too. I changed my mind." Arman turned the case of water over in his hands and set it back. "Okay, both. But twelve dollars for water before a storm still feels like it violates some rule of being a decent human." Natalie paid for the case because her mother had asked, though her conscience pinched a little at leaving none for the woman behind her.

Outside, the air smelled like rain that hadn't arrived yet, and the pump numbers ticked upward for the car at the first island. "Check the price Thursday," Natalie said, loading the case into the wagon. "After the storm, when the shelves are full again. If we're right, it'll be four bucks."

Quinn dragged the whiteboard out of the garage and set it against the fence, because tomorrow she had to draw a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, and explain what would happen if one link vanished. She had the sun part. Grass, then a rabbit, then a hawk. But Soraya had said the top of the chain in their woods was an owl, and Giuliano insisted it was a hawk, and Mr. Swampy, who knew everything about the creek behind his yard, had only smiled and said, "Solve it yourselves."

Giuliano and Soraya came over after dinner. Giuliano drew a hawk with huge talons. "Hawk," he said. "Nothing hunts a hawk."

Soraya crossed her arms. "An owl is bigger. An owl eats a hawk."

They stared at the board. Quinn chewed the cap of her marker. "We're thinking about it wrong. It's not about who's bigger. It's about who hunts who, when they're grown up." She wrote HAWK and then drew a circle around it with an arrow pointing outward to nothing. "A top predator is at the end of its food chain, and as an adult it has no natural predators of its own."

Giuliano frowned. "So the owl doesn't count?"

"Only if an adult owl gets hunted by something," Quinn said. "Does it?"

Nobody could name anything. Soraya grinned and wrote TOP beside both hawk and owl. "They're both at the end," she said. "Two chains."

"That sounds like a paradox," Giuliano said. "Two tops, one woods."

"Or just two chains," Quinn said. The three of them were unanimous on that, so she drew a second chain: sun, seeds, mouse, owl.

Then Quinn tested the idea. "Take out the rabbit," she said, and erased it. The arrow from grass stopped in empty space. "The hawk loses its food. Fewer hawks." She erased the mouse. "Fewer owls. And more rabbits eating everyone's gardens, so there's the part where one link disappearing changes everything after it."

Giuliano drew a hawk and an owl side by side at the top of the board and gave the hawk a speech bubble that said WHO'S HUNTING YOU? The owl's bubble said NOBODY.

The science room smelled like chalk and old glue, and Elliot's comparison chart was due at the end of the period. He had drawn two big circles, one for a plant cell and one for an animal cell, and he had filled the animal one first because animals seemed more interesting. Then Mr. Ross had dropped the real challenge on them: whoever named the parts that only plant cells have would get to supervise the class microscope station for the whole next week.

Alan wanted that job too. He had already written "cell wall" and "chloroplasts" on his chart in careful block letters, and he kept glancing over at Elliot's paper like a fox checking on a henhouse. "You forgot the vacuole," Alan whispered. "Big one. Plants have a huge vacuole. Animals don't."

Elliot wrote those three parts on the plant side of his chart, then stopped. Something felt wrong, and he couldn't figure out what. He looked at the animal side, where he had listed the nucleus, the membrane, and the mitochondria. Mitochondria. He had learned that word last week from a video about a venomous snake, of all things, where the narrator said mitochondria release energy from food, keeping the snake's muscles moving. So mitochondria belonged with animals, obviously. He had even drawn a little crown on them, like they were special.

He was reaching for the marker to write "mitochondria, animal cells only" in the center of a Venn diagram when Ryan leaned across the aisle. Ryan didn't care about the microscope station; Ryan wanted to get out early for parliament club, the mock debate group that met on Thursdays, which meant Ryan needed Mr. Ross to sign his pass in the next ten minutes. "Wait," Ryan said, tapping Elliot's chart. "You're putting mitochondria only on the animal side?"

"Plants make their own food," Elliot said. "They don't need to release energy from it. They just..." He trailed off, because saying it out loud made it sound strange.

"Plants make their own food," Ryan said, "but they still have mitochondria. Both plant and animal cells have them. Plants need mitochondria even though they make their own food." He shrugged and went back to waving his pass at Mr. Ross.

Elliot sat very still, marker hovering. Slowly, he crossed out the crown, then drew mitochondria right in the overlapping middle of the diagram, where the two circles met. Both sides. He double-checked the plant-only list on the edge of his page: cell wall, chloroplasts, big vacuole. Three parts, all plant.

When the bell rang, Mr. Ross walked the rows, pausing at each chart. At Elliot's desk he tapped the middle of the Venn diagram twice, and a small smile crossed his face. "Microscope station," he said. "Monday." Across the aisle, Alan let out a groan and dropped his marker, which rolled off the desk and under the radiator, into the dark.

On the third morning of camp, Camille noticed that Leighton had stopped eating the pancakes, and by the fifth morning he wasn't touching anything at all. He used to be the loudest one at the canoe dock, the kid who cannonballed while the counselors were still counting heads, and now he sat at the end of the picnic table picking at the edge of his paper cup until it tore. Camille had watched her grandmother's health deteriorate the same way the summer before, slowly and then all at once, and something about the quietness reminded her of that. She slid onto the bench across from him. "You want to skip the water slide with us?" Leighton shook his head, and when Dominick called his name from the trail, he flinched like the sound had struck him.

That night, when the lamps were off and the bunks creaked, Leighton came and sat on the end of Camille's bed. His voice was so low she had to lean close. He said he'd been thinking about hurting himself, that everything felt like drowning, and then he grabbed her wrist. "You can't tell anyone. Promise. If people find out, it'll get worse." The word "promise" sat in her mouth, and she didn't say it.

She lay awake remembering a health class from the spring, a single principle the teacher had written on the board and Camille had copied down without really hearing it: if a friend talks about hurting themselves, you tell a trusted adult right away, even if the friend asked you to keep it a secret. At the time it had sounded like a rule for other people. Now she turned it over in the dark, testing it against the promise Leighton wanted. A secret could hold a friendship together, or it could hold a person under the water, and she couldn't see which one this was. So she went with the rule she couldn't see the end of.

At breakfast she walked past the affluent families unloading paddleboards at the far dock and knocked on the door of Cabin One, where Mr. Mwangi kept the first aid kit and the schedules and, apparently, the phone number for the camp nurse and Leighton's parents. She told him everything, including the part about the promise. Mr. Mwangi nodded once and picked up the phone. Outside the window, Leighton was standing alone by the flagpole, and Camille pushed the door open and walked over to sit with him in the gravel. "I had to tell," she said. He stared at the flag, and the rope clinked against the pole.

Hannah had exactly one job before the plane boarded, and it was making sure her snack survived the trip. In her backpack sat a sealed bag of cheese puffs, a bag of gummy worms, and, wedged in a side pocket, a party-size bag of chips she had promised to deliver, uncrushed, to her cousin on the other side of the country. The gate agent had already called Group Three. Group Four was Hannah's group, which gave her maybe ten minutes.

"Text me when it lands," Elisa said, still on Hannah's phone from the curb. "I want the whole report. Every crumb."

"It's chips, not a celebrity," Hannah said, but she was grinning. "You'll get a full anecdote. Probably a boring one."

Elisa hung up, and Hannah slid the phone into airplane mode. That was when she noticed the trouble. A woman two rows over in the waiting area was holding a half-empty water bottle with the cap off, squinting at it like it had insulted her. Hannah's dad had once told her a story about a bottle that swelled on a flight until it looked ready to pop, and Hannah had filed it away as one of his exaggerations, like the time he claimed he had outrun a goose. Now the bottle story tickled at her. If the bottle changed, would the chip bag change too? Her cousin's chips were puffy already, sealed tight, and in Hannah's experience, puffy sealed things were vulnerable to just about everything.

"Are you in Group Four?" asked the boy beside her, who had introduced himself ten minutes earlier as Keenan, also ten, also bored.

"Yes, and I'm trying to diagnose my snack situation," Hannah said. "If the plane makes sealed bags puff up, my chips could burst before we land."

"Planes don't do that," Keenan said. "It's just a plane."

Hannah wasn't so sure. She pulled the chip bag out and studied it, squeezing it gently. Firm. Springy. Like it was already at maximum puff. She needed more information and she needed it fast, because Group Four was shuffling toward the scanner.

Then she spotted Mr. Tran, her neighbour from four doors down, standing at the same gate with a paperback and a knowing smile. He flew constantly for work.

"Mr. Tran, quick question," Hannah said. "On the plane, does the cabin feel like sea level or like a mountain?"

"Good question," he said. "The cabin is pressurized, but the rules let the air pressure be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet, about 2,400 meters, above sea level."

"A mountain," Hannah breathed. Mountains meant thin outside air. Thin outside air meant, if her dad's bottle story was true, puffed-up bags. She didn't know exactly why, and she didn't have time to care. She had a delivery to protect.

"Gate agent said the plane's snack bin is full," Keenan offered helpfully. "So you can't buy a replacement."

Hannah thought fast, then knelt over the bag. If it was going to puff, it needed room to puff. She loosened everything around it in the backpack, moved her socks out of the way, and built a little padded cave using her hoodie and the pair of sneakers she had been forced to bring. Then she wrapped the bag in the hoodie like a burrito.

"Now boarding Group Four," the agent announced.

"If it pops, I'll hear it like a firework," Keenan said as they walked down the jet bridge.

Three hours later, Hannah unwrapped the hoodie. The chip bag had swollen up round and tight as a balloon, exactly the shape of a small, successful experiment. But it hadn't burst, and not one corner was crushed.

Elisa's phone buzzed before Hannah even left the gate. She typed back: "The bag puffed up like a parade balloon and lived. Full anecdote coming."

Her cousin waved from arrivals. Hannah held the puffy bag overhead with both hands, like a trophy.

At the youth hostel in Heidelberg, Natalie sat with her notebook open to a page titled "Meine Familie," which so far held two wobbly sentences. She wanted to introduce her family properly at the language exchange tomorrow: her mother, her father, her two brothers, and Digby, the family's fat orange cat who was too obstinate to come when called. She could write Ich habe einen Bruder, but when she tried to say she had two brothers, the words tangled and her eraser wore a grey hole in the paper.

Elisha dropped into the chair across from her, waving a postcard he wanted to send to his grandfather. "Stuck again?" he asked, peering at the hole in the page.

"I keep writing one brother, then another brother, and it goes on forever," Natalie said. Across the room, a boy from the exchange group was telling the host about his family, and she heard him say a word she did not know: Geschwister. He held up four fingers, then pointed at the photos spread on the table, three boys and a girl. Natalie watched, and a pattern began to form in her mind. He was not listing them one by one, the way she had been doing. He used that single word and then simply the number.

She turned to Elisha. "Watch this. I'm going to try it." She marched over to the table, took a breath, and said, "Ich habe zwei Geschwister," holding up two fingers. The boy grinned and gave her a thumbs up, and the hostel host nodded so warmly that Natalie's ears went pink. So that was the trick. One word for brothers and sisters together, the way English said siblings, and the number did the rest.

When the host asked about pets, Natalie patted her notebook. "Ich habe eine Katze," she said, and drew a quick orange blob in the margin. Elisha leaned over and added whiskers. "Now write mine," he said, sliding the postcard toward her. "Grandpa will like a sentence in German." Natalie picked up her pen. "Then he'll have to comply and write back," she said, and Elisha laughed so loudly the boy at the far table looked up and raised his cup of tea to her.

Taylor spread the giant world map across the kitchen table and weighed its curling corners with a mug, a banana, and her mom's slippery shoe, which was the only thing tall enough to accommodate the stubborn northeast edge. Her social studies test was in two days, and she still could not remember which number was latitude and which was longitude. Hunter, sprawled on the counter eating cereal, watched her suffer.

"Give me a city," she said. "Any city."

"Lima," said Hunter, because he liked saying it.

Taylor traced her finger down from the top of the map, then across, then stopped, hesitant. "Is it 12 degrees south and 77 degrees west? Or 77 south and 12 west? They don't even put the words on half of these." She glared at the map as if it had hidden the answer under Peru on purpose.

Then she noticed the line running straight through Greenwich, marked 0 degrees, and the numbers counting up from it both ways, one side labeled east and the other west, all the way to 180. "Wait," she said slowly. "Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from 0 degrees up to 180 degrees east or west." Hunter repeated "prime meridian" in a deep announcer voice, and she threw a folded napkin at him. "So the west number is longitude, and the up-and-down one has to be the other thing. Latitude. It has to be, because there's nothing left."

She tested it on Tokyo, then Cairo, then Auckland, checking each time that the east-west number stayed under 180. It worked every single time. "It's like a secret code where the numbers never lie," she said, and Hunter said, "It's like bingo for the whole planet."

At dinner she quizzed her dad until he surrendered his dessert. "Sydney," she demanded, finger hovering. "Thirty-three south, 151 east. Longitude. Don't even try to fight me."

Colton sat on the wide stone steps of the war memorial, holding his half-finished Egypt project against his knees. The names of soldiers were carved into the wall behind him, and the old cannon at the top gleamed faintly in the afternoon light. He was supposed to present tomorrow, and he still could not answer the question Reina had written in a note that morning: "Why did the Egyptians have three seasons instead of four? It makes no sense. P.S. I saved you a seat at lunch."

He heard footsteps on the gravel path. It was Luciana, carrying a water bottle and a stack of index cards. "Mr. Tehrani said I'd find you here," she said, sitting down beside him. "He said the quiet helps people think." She offered him half of her granola bar before he even asked, which he took gratefully, because he had forgotten his own snack entirely.

"I'm stuck," Colton admitted. "Our calendar has four seasons because of the sun. So why three?"

Luciana spread her cards on the step, and together they began to distribute them into piles, sorting facts about Egypt. Flood. Planting. Harvest. Flood again. Colton stared at the pattern, and his reasoning clicked into place. "It's not about the sky," he said slowly. "It's about the river. Their year followed the Nile."

"Right," Luciana said, checking her notes. "Akhet was the flood, Peret was the growing season, and Shemu was the harvest."

"That's fundamental to everything," Colton said. "The floods left mud on the fields, so that's when they farmed. And with fields underwater, thousands of workers were free to build." He pulled out a pencil and drew three boxes instead of four on his poster paper. The pattern finally made sense.

That evening he wrote a reply to Reina and slipped it into her locker before the bell.

"Dear Reina. I figured it out. Egyptians had three seasons because the Nile flooded once a year. Akhet, flood. Peret, growing. Shemu, harvest. Meet me at the memorial after school and I'll show you the poster. I saved you a seat in return. From, Colton."

He stuck the note through the vent and heard it land softly on her books.

Samantha pressed her pencil so hard against the poster that the tip snapped. Her food chain, drawn in careful marker, read sun, then an arrow, then grass, then an arrow pointing left at the rabbit, then an arrow pointing left at the hawk. Amina leaned over from the next lab table and squinted at it.

"Samantha, why is the grass eating the rabbit?" Amina asked, and Cillian, who was arranging paper arrows across his own desk, burst out laughing before he caught himself and said sorry.

Samantha stared at her poster. She had drawn every arrow backward, from the eater to the eaten, and now the whole chain looked upside down and ridiculous. She remembered third grade, when her reading poster had won a ribbon at the fair, and how sure she had been that this one would be just as good. That memory made her cheeks burn hotter, not cooler.

"Okay," she said slowly, turning the pencil around to erase. "Think it through. The sun gives energy to the grass. The rabbit eats the grass and gets that energy. So the arrow should show where the energy goes, from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it." She flipped her arrows one by one: sun to grass, grass to rabbit, rabbit to hawk. Mr. Oyelaran, checking posters at the front of the science lab, gave her a small nod as he passed, which meant she was on the right track.

But Samantha wanted to be sure, not just probably right. She took Cillian's loose paper arrows and laid out a test chain on the lab bench. She pointed each arrow from the eaten thing toward the eater, then asked Amina to read it aloud without looking up. "Sun to grass, grass to rabbit, rabbit to hawk," Amina read, "and the hawk is the top predator." It worked every time, in both directions they tried. Samantha grinned and taped the corrected arrows onto her poster.

Then Mr. Oyelaran asked the harder question from the board: what happens if one link disappears? Samantha pulled the rabbit card out of her chain and slid the pieces together. "Then the hawk loses its food," she said, "because the energy that flowed through the rabbit stops right there." She decided it would be feasible to add a second chain to the poster showing that, and she asked Amina and Cillian to help her coordinate the drawing so both chains fit on one page. They worked through the last minutes of class, heads bent together, passing the tape roll back and forth, until the poster showed a sun blazing at the top and every arrow pointing the right way.

"Look at it now," Amina said. "Now the rabbit is lunch, not the other way around."

The debate started the moment Mr. Zhou read the note aloud. Someone had slipped it under the classroom door during lunch, and now the whole class knew: a member of the robotics team, whose name the note left out, had told the coach that a missing robot part was lost, when really a friend had taken it home overnight and broken it. The note writer wanted the team to vote on whether the cover-up was right.

Eve raised her hand first. "We can't even vote. We don't know who did it." That was true, but it wasn't her real reason. Her real reason was that she thought she knew, and she didn't want her guess to get anyone punished.

Jax leaned across the aisle. "Who cares who wrote it? The facts are all right there. Part taken, part broken, friend covered. Those aren't in dispute."

"Exactly," said Aviana, spinning her pencil. "Same facts. So how come half of us think the cover-up was wrong and half think it was fine?"

Mr. Zhou wrote two words on the board: fairness and loyalty. He said nothing else, just tapped the board and sat on the edge of his desk.

Eve stared at the words. She remembered the science fair last year, when she had covered for a partner who forgot the sensor logs, telling the judge the data had been misplaced. She'd thought she was being loyal. Her partner had later said she'd wished Eve told the truth, because fairness mattered more to her than being protected. Same event, agreed on every single fact, and they'd never settled it. Eve had never even realized that was the problem until this moment.

"That's it," she said slowly. "We all agree on what happened. We just don't value the same things."

"So the vote's pointless," Jax said.

"No," Eve said. "The vote isn't about the facts at all." She picked up the note, folded it into a small square, and set it in the middle of Aviana's desk. "It's about us."

Aviana flipped the square over and wrote one word on the back: "Tie."

The automatic doors of the bank sighed open, and Theodore followed his mother past the roped queues to the coin machine in the corner. He was on a mission today, and he had the whole plan folded in his pocket: walk to the corner store alone, buy a carton of milk, and bring back the change. First, though, he needed coins for the machine, because his jar of loose change had to become real money before he could practice spending any.

"Dump them all in," his mother said, and he did, listening to the machine rattle and clatter like rain on a tin roof. The screen flashed a running total, and Theodore watched the number climb, thinking the machine must be doing its own private census of his coins, every last penny counted and recorded. He had never thought about counting much before. It was just something you did. But the machine made it seem almost like a trick.

At the corner store he found the milk, $4.35 according to the shelf tag, and carried it to the counter with his heart going like a drum. He handed over a five-dollar note. The cashier gave him a ten-cent coin, then a fifty-cent coin, then a one-dollar coin. Theodore stood there, unsure. Was that right? He tried adding it up in his head and got tangled. Then an idea arrived, quiet as a moth: what if he started at the price and added each coin as it came back? Four dollars thirty-five plus ten cents made four forty-five. Plus fifty made four ninety-five. Plus one dollar made five. It landed exactly on what he had paid.

"Everything okay?" the cashier asked. "Perfect," Theodore said. A kid behind him, Neve from his class, leaned over the counter with her own bag of chips. "How did you check that so fast?" she asked. "You count up from the price," Theodore said, "until you reach what you paid." Neve frowned, tried it with her own change, and grinned. Outside, Theodore walked home with the milk swinging in its bag, adding the whole world up in his head.

Brooke stood in front of the smoothie stand in the mall's food court with her notebook clutched like a shield. On Monday, Ms. Nasser had assigned everyone the same task: explain one economics idea out loud, in your own words, to a real audience. Brooke had drawn "supply and demand," and she had one weekend left to figure out how to say something credible about it instead of just reading a definition off her phone like Josie planned to do.

That was when she saw the strawberry cart. It was a small stand near the escalator, stacked with plastic boxes of bright red strawberries, and the line in front of it stretched past the pretzel shop. A hand-written sign said two dollars a box. Brooke got in line behind Abygaelle, who was already holding three boxes.

"I'm using these for my explanation," Brooke announced. "Strawberries cost two dollars in summer when everybody's picking them, and like five in winter. That's supply. More of something means cheaper."

"That's only half," said a voice behind her. It was the cart's owner, changing the sign. He crossed out the two and wrote four, because, he told them, he was almost sold out and wanted to stretch the last crates through closing time. "Watch the line."

Brooke watched. Within five minutes, the line had shrunk to two people. One man looked at the sign, whistled, and walked toward the pretzel shop instead. Abygaelle put one of her boxes back.

"Whoa," Brooke said, scribbling. "The price went up and people just... stopped buying."

"That's the other half," the owner said. "Price goes up, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes. No rain, no holiday, no new rival cart. Just the price."

"Nothing else changes," Brooke repeated. "So the weather can't be a variable. It's only the price doing the work."

Abygaelle squinted at her notebook. "Okay, but how do you fit this into a Monday presentation? You can't haul the whole cart into class."
