Later, the woman wandered back with a box of crackers. "You're new," she said. "How long have food banks even existed in this country?"

Zoe had only a vague idea, so she guessed, "A hundred years?"

The woman snorted so hard that Cooper looked up from the pasta. "Canada's first food bank opened in 1981, in Edmonton, Alberta. I read it on the poster by the door. Twice."

Zoe checked the poster. It was true, printed right there under a drawing of a shopping cart. She wrote it on her clipboard in case anyone else asked.

Asha held up a can of soup. "Soft or chewy?"

Marcus had one page of notes and zero ideas, which was, he figured, a ratio that had never once earned an A. Mr. Takahashi's assignment sat in the middle of the library table like a dare: find the theme of your novel and prove it with one quotation. Marcus had chosen The Outsiders because everyone said it was good, and now everyone was apparently wrong about it being easy.

"Theme is the big idea underneath," Tyler said, chewing his pencil. "Like the moral." He was writing about a book where a dog gets lost, so his theme was "dogs get lost," and he seemed at peace with that.

"It's not a moral," said Grayden, who had finished already and was now supervising the other two with the patience of a lifeguard at an empty pool. "It has to cover the whole book. One quotation. From the actual pages."

Marcus flipped through his copy. The book was published in 1967, said the page at the front, by S. E. Hinton, which he'd assumed was a man and was wrong about. There were fights and a church fire and a lot of hair product. Any of those could be the theme, probably. Hair product, definitely.

Then he stopped at the letter. Johnny, dying, had written a message to Ponyboy, and near the end of it were two words: "stay gold." Marcus read them, then read the sentence before them, then read the whole letter again, slower, because something was clicking the way a combination lock clicks when you're not even trying. Johnny wasn't talking about treasure. He was telling Ponyboy to hold on to his goodness and innocence, the way gold is the thing that stays bright while everything else tarnishes. Two words in one letter, and suddenly the fights and the fire and even the hair product all pointed the same direction. The whole novel was about keeping what's good in you when the world tries to grind it off.

"Found it," Marcus said. He was agile about getting his notebook open, which was more energy than he'd shown all week.

"Found what?" Tyler asked.

"The theme. Two words." Marcus wrote them down and underlined them, once, twice, then a third time for luck. "Stay gold."

Grayden leaned over. "That works. That actually works."

Mr. Takahashi passed by their table, paused, and read the notebook upside down, which teachers can apparently do. "Nice," he said. "Page number?"

"178," Marcus said, already flipping to it.

The word card said "colour," and Florence felt her stomach drop. She was standing at the front of Mr. Chowdhury's classroom, the last three spellers left in the school bee, and the judges had just handed her a word she had argued about only two weeks ago.

"Can I have the language of origin?" she asked.

"English," said Mr. Chowdhury, who was reading from the official list.

Florence's mind went back to the lunch table, where Liam had been waving his phone around. His cousin in Toronto had sent him a photo of her school spelling list, and half the words looked wrong to him. "Colour," he had said. "Honour. They spell it with a u up there. Who's right?"

They had looked it up together in the library instead of going outside. Florence had found the answer in a dusty reference book while Liam leaned over her shoulder so close she had to compress herself into the corner of the chair to keep reading. Before 1828, English spellings were a tangle, and then Noah Webster's American Dictionary of the English Language pushed simpler spellings, like "color" instead of "colour," and those became standard in the United States. Neither spelling was really wrong. They just belonged to different places, like two doors out of the same room.

Katia, sitting in the second row now, mouthed something at her. Florence couldn't read it. The clock on the wall hung slightly off true, tilted a few degrees from perpendicular, and she fixed her eyes on it to steady herself.

Here was the trap. At lunch, Liam had said the school bee would follow American convention, but Florence had never actually checked the rules sheet. She thought about it now, fast. This was a school bee in Ohio. The pronouncer had given every other word in American spelling when he read the vocabulary sentences. If the card said "colour," then the judges wanted the British spelling, and they had written it that way on purpose to see if spellers knew it was a variant, not a mistake. If she spelled it the American way, she might be marked wrong.

"C-o-l-o-u-r," she said. "Colour."

Mr. Chowdhury checked his sheet and nodded. "That is correct."

Liam, eliminated three rounds earlier on "manoeuvre," smacked the desk softly. "You remembered the lunch argument."

After the bee, which Florence won on the word "perpendicular" of all things, she found Liam by the door. He was holding his phone, probably about to text his cousin the news.

"So who won the spelling war?" he asked. "Webster or the Canadians?"

Florence thought about the book in the library, about her own choice to look things up instead of guessing. "Nobody," she said. "They just went through different doors." She tucked her trophy under her arm and pushed open the classroom door.

Vincent sat at the kitchen table with a pencil, graph paper, and his math worksheet, which had one problem circled twice in red: Graph y = 2x + 5. He had solved two-step equations all week, getting x alone one step at a time, but the graphing part made his stomach knot up. He wanted to get it before Friday's quiz, because Ms. Gupta had promised the class they could graph a real phone plan when they finished, and Marika had already said she was on problem ten.

His mom set down a plate of crackers and peeked at the paper. "That looks like a rocket trajectory," she said.

"It's supposed to be a line," Vincent said. "But I don't know where it starts." He had made a table of values, plugging in 1, 2, and 3 for x, and the points climbed upward like stairs. Somewhere below the stairs, the line had to begin, but his table stopped before he found it. He decided to test the smallest number he could think of: zero.

He substituted 0 for x, and the equation became y = 2 times 0 plus 5, which was just 5. He plotted the point (0, 5), and there it was, sitting exactly on the y-axis, the tall vertical line down the middle of the grid. He checked his staircase points again, and every one lined up in a straight slant through that single dot. "The plus five is where it starts," he said out loud. He remembered Ms. Gupta calling that spot the y-intercept, the point where the line crosses the y-axis. He drew the line in one careful stroke and it looked authentic, like the ones in the textbook, not like a wobbly guess.

When the phone plan day came, Ms. Gupta gave them a plan with a fifteen-dollar starting fee plus three dollars per gigabyte. Marika frowned at her empty grid, but Vincent plotted the first point straight up the y-axis, at fifteen, then climbed by threes. "The fee is the starting point," he told her, and she copied his method, her line rising past his. At the top of the grid their two lines formed a small plateau before the paper ran out of room, and Marika laughed and taped a second sheet to the edge of the first.

Ryan sat on the end of his bed with a printed page in his hands, one he had grabbed off Ms. Bighorn's classroom shelf before the bell rang. His left knuckle still stung where he had punched his desk that afternoon, after Rudy had grabbed his sketchbook and held it open above his head for the whole bus line to see. Ryan hadn't planned to hit anything. His hand had simply gone before the rest of him could vote.

The page was from a science magazine. He read the same sentence three times: the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties. He put the page down on his quilt and looked at his hand, then at the wall above his desk, where a dent from a thrown controller still marked the paint from last spring.

He flashed back to that afternoon, seconds before the desk punch. Rudy waving the sketchbook, the crowd laughing, Isra saying "just give it back," and then a kind of white gap where the punch should have been in his memory. It was like trying to remember a hallway with the lights off. He had walked through it, but he couldn't see it.

That was the part that interested him. If the planning part of his brain was still under construction, then maybe the gap wasn't him being a bad person. Maybe it was like trying to drive a car that was still getting its brakes installed. He decided to test it. He took out a notebook and wrote a rule at the top: any time Rudy grabs something, count to five before moving. It was a way of lending the unfinished part of his brain a substitute. He couldn't eliminate the impulse, but he could build a wall around the part where his hand decided things on its own.

At school the next morning, Rudy snatched the notebook itself right off Ryan's desk. Ryan felt the same hot spark go off behind his eyes, and he counted. One, two, three. Isra leaned over from the next seat and said, "That's the prefrontal cortex thing you were reading about, right? The part that plans stuff?" Ryan nodded, still counting. Five. Then he stood up, walked to Ms. Bighorn's desk, and said, "Rudy has my notebook and I'd like it back." Rudy blinked, handed it over without a joke, and the class went back to its worksheet.

At lunch Ryan told them the whole story, including the dent in his wall, as an anecdote about the controller. "It sounded smart at the time," he admitted. "Thinking I'd never get frustrated." "That was a little naive," Isra said, and Rudy laughed so hard milk came out his nose. Ryan laughed too, and slid the notebook, safely, into the bottom of his backpack.

Every April, Mia dragged the same three pots onto the same corner of the balcony and planted tomatoes, because her grandfather had done it that way and because tomatoes were the only vegetable her little brother would eat without staging a protest. This April, the seedlings came up spindly and yellow, then wilted at the stems one by one. By May she had lost two pots, and she sat on the balcony rail with her chin in her hands, glaring at the third.

"Maybe they're sad," said Viktor, who had come over to steal her wi-fi and stayed to watch the disaster. "Plants can be sad. My aunt talks to hers."

"Plants can't be sad," Mia said, though she had whispered "please" to the survivor that morning. She turned the wilted stem in her fingers and noticed something: the soil in that corner smelled flat, almost sour, and last year's stems had rotted the same way, in the same spot. She tried to distinguish this year's sickness from last year's by size or colour, and she couldn't. It was identical. Same corner, same disease, two years running.

The clue came from Ms. Schneider upstairs, who grew peppers along her railing like a string of lanterns. "My father moved his tomatoes to a new bed every single year," she said over the rail, handing down a dish of lemon cake. "He never put the same family in the same place twice. He called it rotating crops." Mia chewed on that along with the cake. If the same plant family kept going back to the same spot year after year, something in the soil built up and sickened them. She couldn't see it, but the pattern was there in her dead stems.

So she ran a test. She moved the surviving tomato to the opposite end of the balcony, dumped the old corner soil, and planted beans there instead, since beans were not in the tomato family. She drew a chart with arrows and labelled it THE ROTATION SCHEDULE, and underneath she wrote "fundamental rule: never same family, same spot." Viktor pointed out that one plant in one corner was not exactly a giant experiment. "That's true," Mia said. "But if my tomato lives over there and dies over here, that's a hundred percentage of the evidence I need." Viktor said that wasn't how percentages worked, and she threw a peat pellet at him.

By June the tomato had thickened into a green rope with tiny yellow flowers, while the beans in the old corner poked up cheerful and untouched. Mia knocked on Ms. Schneider's door with a bag of bean sprouts and a slice of her brother's abandoned birthday cake, because Ms. Schneider had once mentioned she loved cake and lived alone. "Next year the beans move and the tomatoes come back," Mia announced. Ms. Schneider saluted with her fork. "Your grandfather would be proud," she said. "Though he'd probably want a bigger cake."

Lauren had forty dollars of birthday money in her pocket, and the running shoes she wanted cost fifty-five. She stood in the middle of the mall food court, listening to the sizzle of the pretzel stand and smelling cinnamon and floor wax, drafting a plan in her head. If she could convince her mom to cover the last fifteen dollars, the shoes would be hers by dinner.

That was when she saw the giant screen above the shoe store. A famous sprinter, the one from the Olympics, held up the exact shoes Lauren wanted and said they made her feel unstoppable. Below the screen, a line of kids waited outside the store door, and a voice boomed that these were the shoes everyone was talking about. Everyone. Lauren felt her feet move toward the line before her brain caught up.

"What are you doing?" Aurora asked, appearing beside her with a smoothie. "You said you were saving for the green ones from the other store."

"I know, but look. That's the sprinter. And everyone's buying these."

Evie tilted her head at the screen. "Last month that same sprinter sold the headphones that broke in a week. Remember?" Lauren did remember. She also remembered the poster from the school election in October, when a candidate had put up a picture of himself eating cafeteria lasagna like a regular kid, and everyone voted for him before anyone asked what his plan actually was. He had turned out to have no plan at all. Mr. Nolan had muttered something about it in the hallway afterward, a phrase Lauren hadn't understood at the time: plain-folks.

She looked back at the store. A second poster showed the shoe company's owner in old jeans, grilling burgers in a backyard, with words like honest and real printed underneath. Honest. Real. Loaded words, the kind her English teacher had circled on their persuasive-writing worksheet, words that made you feel instead of think. And behind the counter, she noticed, a clerk was telling every customer the same thing: "You're the tenth person today to buy these."

"Test something for me," Lauren said. She walked to the counter and asked, "Are these actually better than the green ones at the other store, or just more popular?"

The clerk blinked. "Honestly? Same factory. The green ones cost less."

Aurora laughed so hard she nearly dropped her smoothie. "They got you with the famous lady, the big line outside, and the guy in the jeans. All of it."

The committee in Lauren's head was not unanimous. Part of her still wanted the popular shoes, the ones with the line and the screen and the sprinter's smile, because part of her remembered exactly how it felt to want what everyone wanted. But another part remembered the candidate with the lasagna, and how trusting him as one of us had gotten the whole grade nothing.

At the other store she found the green ones, forty-two dollars, and held them up to the light. The rubber smelled like a new eraser, and when she bent the sole it flexed the same way the expensive pair had.

"They even match your jacket," Evie said.

Lauren counted out the money, then paused and turned to Aurora. "Eight dollars left. Pretzel?"

They walked back toward the cinnamon smell, and Aurora said, "So the jeans guy in the poster, that one's called plain-folks. Mr. Nolan said it. Making a big shot look ordinary so you trust him."

"Like the lasagna guy," Lauren said, and took a bite.

Annabelle got to the community centre at nine fifty, ten minutes before the culture festival opened, and the banner over Loick's table still had a problem. It read "Filipino Diaspora Club" in tall red letters, and already two people had stopped, squinted at the last word.

"What does that even mean?" asked a man carrying a toddler.

"Um," said Loick.

"We're supposed to open at ten," Annabelle said. "Ms. Zhu said every table needs a poster that explains the group, and ours has to be up by then." The deadline was real: Ms. Zhu was walking the rows right now with her clipboard, and last year she'd made Eddie's chess club take down a poster with a spelling error.

Eddie arrived with the tape. "I looked up diaspora last night," he said, "but I fell asleep before the page loaded."

"I think I know it," Annabelle said slowly. She'd heard her grandmother use it at a wedding once, and she'd asked about it afterward, which was unusual for her, because she usually let big words pass by. "It's from a Greek word. It means scattering. Like seeds." She traced the shape of it in the air. "So a diaspora is a people living spread out, far away from where their ancestors came from."

Loick blinked. "So the banner's saying Filipinos here, and in Canada, and in Dubai, all scattered from the islands?"

"Right. But nobody at this table can say that out loud, which is the problem. The man with the toddler just left without signing up." Annabelle grabbed a marker and the back of an old pizza box. "Test it. We write it plain, and we see if people stop."

Eddie held the cardboard steady while she printed: "Scattered across the world, far from our ancestors' homeland. That's what diaspora means. Ask us anything." She taped it below the banner at 9:58.

Ms. Zhu came by at 10:07 with her clipboard. She read both signs, then the sign-up sheet, which already had four names on it, including the man with the toddler. "Good," she said, and moved on.

By eleven, the sheet had nineteen names, and Loick's mother had brought out a pot of soup. Annabelle found a note in the club's mailbox at the front desk, addressed in pencil to the table with the pizza-box sign: "My family is from Ghana and I never knew there was a word for all of us everywhere. Can I come to the next meeting? Signed, a girl from the Trinidad table."

Annabelle read it twice, then walked it back to Loick without saying anything, and watched his face as he read it.

"Tell her yes," he said, and went to ladle more soup.

Backstage at the concert hall, Luca's violin was broken and nobody knew it. Not cracked, not smashed, just quietly wrong, because his A string had slipped flat sometime between the school bus and the warm-up room. He discovered it when he played the open string and it landed with a sad, sagging thud instead of a clean note.

"Use the piano in the wings," said Maxine, who was tuning her own violin against it. Luca tried, but the piano was so far away and the hallway so noisy that he couldn't hear if he matched it or not. Lyna covered her ears. "Somebody's kettle is boiling," she announced. "It's Luca."

Then Luca remembered the small metal fork in his grandfather's old case, the one his grandfather had pressed into his hand last weekend. "This is a tuning fork," his grandfather had said, and told him the story that went with it: it was invented in 1711 by John Shore, a trumpeter at the English royal court. Luca had thought it looked like a bent dinner fork with only two tines, something a hungry artisan might have made by accident. He dug it out of his backpack now and struck it against his knee.

Nothing. He struck it harder. Still nothing, and his knee began to sting. His heart picked up speed. Ms. Chukwu poked her head in and said five minutes to places, and the lineup of kids began to circulate through the warm-up room like fish in a too-small tank. Luca held the fork to his ear and held his breath. There it was, so faint he'd missed it, a thin silver hum at one steady pitch, exactly the pitch his grandfather had made him memorize with his eyes shut.

He set the fork's stem against the body of the violin, and the hum bloomed loud enough to hear over everything. One peg, a slow turn, tiny adjustments, his ear testing each one against that ringing A. The string slid up, wavered, and then locked into place with a sound that felt like two puzzle pieces clicking.

"Fixed," Luca said.

"That's legitimate magic," said Lyna.

Ms. Chukwu called them to the stage. Luca put the fork in his shirt pocket, picked up his violin, and walked out into the lights.

Hazel sat cross-legged on Bruce's living room floor with his laptop between them, because Bruce's ambition to run the fastest gaming club at school had somehow become her problem too. He was signing up for a new tournament site, and the password box had turned an ominous red. "It wants a symbol," Bruce groaned, typing G@m3r and then glaring when the bar stayed short.

"That's the weird part," Hazel said. "I read that the rules forcing uppercase and numbers and symbols actually don't help much. Length adds more strength than those rules do." She plucked a marshmallow from the bowl Bruce's mom had left them and popped it in her mouth. "There's this guidance, from NIST, that tells systems not to require mixes of uppercase letters, numbers and symbols at all."

Bruce looked skeptical, so Hazel tested it right there. She typed a long silly sentence, all lowercase, no symbols, no numbers, just lots and lots of letters. The strength bar climbed higher than his G@m3r had ever pushed it. "See? Twenty plain letters beat your seven fancy ones." Bruce abandoned his symbol and typed the name of his favorite sandwich spread, spelled out long, and the bar filled green. Hazel felt a flicker of envy that he'd thought of a passphrase that fast, since she was usually the clever one.

The site swallowed his new password and they went back to planning the tournament bracket. Half an hour later Bruce's phone buzzed with a message from Stephen, and Bruce read it out loud: "Dude, change your password on the club forum NOW. Someone logged in as me and posted garbage. I only ever used one password everywhere and I think that's how they got in." Bruce went pale. He clicked open his tournament account, then his forum account, then his game account, typing with flying fingers. Every single one had the same password on it, the old one, the symbol one.

"That's the other half," Hazel said quietly. "A password can be strong and still get stolen from one site. If you reuse it, it opens every other door too." She watched him hunch over the keyboard and slid the marshmallow bowl closer, because he looked like a person who needed marshmallows. He grabbed a handful without looking up.

They spent the next hour making new passphrases, each one long and plain and different, and Hazel made Bruce say each out loud once so he'd remember it as a phrase instead of a code. When they finished, a new message appeared from Stephen: "False alarm, guys. It was Ms. González. She's running a digital safety lesson for the club and wanted to see who reused passwords. Only three of us passed. Nice work, Hazel." Bruce stared at the screen, then at his row of fresh passphrases, and started to laugh. "We passed a test we didn't even know we were taking." Hazel held up a marshmallow in a silent toast.

Harrison stood in his grandmother's kitchen holding a plate of honey cake he was not allowed to eat. The cake was for after, for the meal that breaks the fast, and everyone kept saying the word "after" as if it were a place far away. Tonight was the start of Yom Kippur, and this year, at eleven, Harrison had decided he would try fasting the way the grown-ups did. His mother had said he could do it for part of the day if it got hard, but he wanted the whole thing. He just did not know how long the whole thing was.

"How long does it actually last?" he asked his cousin Bianca, who was leaning against the counter, also not eating cake, but only because she was saving room.

"Ask your mom," Bianca said. "She's the one with the calendar."

His mother was stirring a pot of soup. "From sunset tonight until after nightfall tomorrow," she said. "About twenty-five hours."

"Twenty-five?" Harrison frowned. "A day is twenty-four. Where does the extra hour come from?" His mother only smiled and went back to the soup, which was deeply irritating. He found a napkin and a pencil and worked it out at the table. If it began at sunset, and sunset happened a little earlier every day in autumn, then tomorrow's nightfall would arrive slightly sooner than today's sunset had left. But the fast did not stop at sunset. It stopped after nightfall, and the sky took its time going dark. That was the missing piece. Sunset to sunset was about a day, and nightfall lagged behind sunset by roughly an hour, which stacked the extra hour on the end. He turned the napkin around to show Bianca. "It's not a longer day. It's a day plus the time it takes the sky to finish."

"Very credible," said Melodie, Bianca's little sister, who had wandered over. "Except you wrote 'nitefall' with no h."

Later, while the family rested, Harrison's grandmother handed him a folded note, because she had lost her voice to a virus that week and the doctor had not authorized her to talk above a whisper at the table. The note said: "When I was your age I broke my fast on a pickle. Nobody saw. You don't have to be perfect on your first try, boychik." He laughed so hard he had to stuff his knuckle in his mouth, since the house was quiet for prayer.

The next evening he stood in the driveway with Bianca and Melodie, all three of them watching the western sky like scientists waiting for a result. The sun went down. Harrison's stomach growled, and he held up one finger. Not yet. The blue faded to gray, then to a soft black, and finally the first stars came out. Somewhere inside, his grandmother was already slicing the honey cake.

"There," Bianca said. "Nightfall. Twenty-five hours, kid."

Harrison ran for the door.

Vincent had never slept anywhere but his own room, so he packed his bag like he was preparing for something aggressive: two flashlights, three snacks, and a folded note his mom had slipped in at the last minute. "Open this if you get homesick," she had said, which almost made him feel homesick right there in the driveway. At Maddex's house the evening went fine until lights-out, when Maddex and Rachael, who was already there in her sleeping bag by the window, kept whispering and giggling and flopping around. Nobody was going to sleep. Vincent remembered something his older cousin had mentioned once, that seeing someone else yawn often makes people yawn too. He could not see whether it was true, but he could test it.

He let out a long, deliberate yawn, the kind that made his jaw click. Within a minute, Rachael yawned mid-sentence, and then Maddex yawned so wide he knocked his water bottle off the mattress. "Quit it," Maddex mumbled, yawning again as he said it. Vincent waited a bit, then yawned once more, quieter this time. Rachael's eyes were already half shut. He tried a third time and nobody copied it, because both of them had drifted off, faces slack, the closet door throwing a thin stripe of shadow across the floor. It had worked, though he could not exactly prove how; he had only the before and the after.

He still felt a small hollow spot in his chest, so he unfolded the note under his blanket with the smaller flashlight. His mom's handwriting slanted uphill: "The commerce of the corner store was slow today, so I bought you the orange soda you like. It is in the fridge for tomorrow. I did not disclose this to Maddex's mom because it is our secret. Sleep well. Love, Mom." Vincent smiled into his pillow.

He decided he would save the soda for after breakfast, and he would yawn at Maddex over the table just to watch it happen again. Outside, a car passed, and its headlights swept slowly across the ceiling and away.

Backstage smelled like paint, because the school had spent all fall trying to renovate the old auditorium and had run out of time halfway through. Benjamin stood between Yann and Ashlynn in the choir line, gripping his folder so hard the paper crinkled. Through the curtain he could hear the piano, and a thin stripe of stage light cut across the floor like the equator, dividing the bright half from the dark half where he stood waiting.

His problem was simple and enormous: he had never performed before, and he could not hold a count. In rehearsal he always lost his place somewhere after verse two, and Ms. Das had marked his part with three red stars, which meant "danger." Ashlynn had leaned over during warm-up and whispered, "Just watch her hand. The downbeat is the first beat of each bar, the downward stroke." Benjamin had nodded, but he hadn't really understood what she meant.

The curtain swept open. Rows of parents sat in the renovated seats, faces pale and watery in the stage lights. The piano started, the choir came in, and everything went fine until the middle section, when a cough in the front row knocked the count right out of Benjamin's head. Bar? Verse? He had no idea. Panic climbed his throat.

Then he remembered Ashlynn's whisper. He stopped guessing and watched Ms. Das. Her hand rose, then dropped, and on each drop the choir sang a new syllable, the first beat of the bar, exactly as Ashlynn had said. Down, up, down, up, like a steady pendulum. He counted the strokes, waited for the drop that landed on his red-starred word, and opened his mouth.

His voice slid in with everyone else's, right on time. Nobody in the audience would ever know. Yann, singing beside him on the parallel riser step, gave a tiny nod without looking over, and Ms. Das's hand went on falling and rising, falling and rising, all the way to the final chord.

The food bank had taken over the library's basement meeting room on Saturday mornings, and Austin's first job was sorting donations at the table by the mystery shelf. Ayaan, who had volunteered since September, worked beside him, stacking cans and checking boxes. The room smelled of old paper and cardboard, and somewhere above them a heater ticked like a slow clock.

Austin had signed up because he wanted the hours for school credit, but mostly because he liked the idea of figuring things out. Now he watched Ayaan lift a box of cereal, squint at it, and drop the whole thing into the bin marked TRASH.

"Whoa," Austin said. "What's wrong with it?"

"It's expired. One day past the date. We have to throw out anything past its date."

Austin picked a box out of the trash and turned it over. "Best if used by," he read slowly. Something about the wording bothered him, the way a word choice bothers you in a sentence you've heard a hundred times. "It doesn't say expires on. It says best if used by."

Ayaan rolled his eyes. "Don't try your lawyer logic on me. Rules are rules."

"It's not logic yet," Austin said. "It's a hunch." He looked around the room. Across the basement, Ms. Warsame, the librarian who ran the program, was handing bags of rice to a woman with two kids. The kids were touching the spines of picture books someone had set out on the waiting table. Austin noticed something else too: the trash bin already held three more boxes of cereal, all tossed that morning. If the rule Ayaan followed was right, the food bank was throwing away a lot of perfectly good food. If it was wrong, someone in this neighborhood was going without cereal for no reason.

He waited until the line thinned, then carried two of the rescued boxes to Ms. Warsame. "Can I ask about these?" Before she could answer, he spotted a printed sheet taped to the sign-in table, a guideline page for volunteers. He read it, and his stomach did a small flip. There it was, in plain print: the USDA says a "best if used by" date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.

"It's a quality date," Austin said, holding up the sheet. "Not a safety date. The cereal's just, like, one day less fresh."

Ayaan crossed his arms. "So you're saying I trashed four boxes for nothing?"

"I'm not going to accuse you," Austin said. "You were following what you thought was the rule. But the rule's different."

Ms. Warsame read the page herself, then looked at the trash bin, then at the three full shopping carts still waiting to be sorted. She pulled a marker from her pocket and wrote a note on the sorting table, big enough that nobody could miss it. "New rule for the whole morning," she said, and pointed at the cart of donations. "Start with the dairy cooler, boys. That part really is about safety."

Austin grabbed a crate of milk cartons, and Ayaan, still muttering about the cereal, snatched up the thermometer.

Florence sat on her bedroom floor with the rented trumpet across her lap, staring at it like it had insulted her family. Three valves. That was it. Three little buttons, and yet the band book promised she could play dozens of notes. Her cat, Walrus, watched from the laundry basket with what looked like pity.

"Three buttons," she told him. "My video game controller has like twelve and it only makes one character jump."

She pressed the middle valve down and blew. A note came out, lower than before. She let go and blew again. Higher. She tried the first valve, then the third, then two at once, and slowly a suspicion formed: the more valves she pushed, the lower the note sank. It was almost like the buttons weren't changing anything inside, just sending her air the long way around.

She grabbed her flashlight and peered into the bell of the trumpet. The tubing coiled back on itself like a brass snail. She pressed the second valve and followed the loops with her finger, and there it was. Pushing the valve opened a detour, an extra loop of tubing, so her air had to travel farther before it escaped. Longer trip, lower note.

"Elly owes me a cookie," she announced to Walrus.

The next afternoon, Elly and Atticus came over, and Florence made them close their eyes and listen while she played the same pitch with different valve combinations. Atticus guessed wrong twice and then gasped when she showed him the tubing trick, tracing the air's path with her finger.

"So more tubing means lower?" Elly said.

"Exactly. Longer path, lower note."

Atticus picked up the trumpet and pressed all three valves, puffing out his cheeks like a bullfrog. The note that came out was so low and wobbly that Walrus fled the room in horror. Florence laughed so hard she had to coordinate herself back onto the chair.

"It's ironic," Atticus said. "I finally find an instrument with only three buttons, and it's still impossible."

"Almost impossible," Florence said. She lifted the trumpet, took a breath, and let a clean, clear G ring out through the open window.

Alice's note cards said two minutes. She had read her speech about the school garden six times at her desk, and every time it took her about a minute and a half. She told Jolene it was fine.

Jolene sat on the stage steps in the empty auditorium and held up her phone. "Ms. Van Dijk wants the hook, three points, and the closing, and she cuts you off at two minutes. Time it for real. Out loud."

"Reading it counts," Alice said.

"Just do it."

Alice stood at the front of the stage and started. Her hook was a question about where cafeteria carrots came from. Then the three points, one about compost, one about the raised beds, one about the harvest lunch. Her voice sounded strange in the big room, and she slowed down more than she meant to, letting each sentence land.

"Stop," Jolene said. "Two minutes. You just started your third point."

Alice looked at her cards. Half the speech was still in her hand. "I read the whole thing in ninety seconds. Sitting. Silent."

"That's the problem, I think. Reading silently is faster than speaking. You can't hear the length until you say it." Jolene waved the phone. "Again."

They ran it twice more. Both times the speech ran long, by almost the same amount, so Alice worked out a rule: whatever the silent reading clocked, she should add to it. She crossed out two sentences about the compost temperatures, and she trimmed the story about the raccoon that got into the beds, though it hurt to cut her favorite part.

At class the next day, Ms. Van Dijk called her name. Alice gave the hook, the three points, and the closing, and Jolene raised one finger, then a second, and stopped.

"One amendment to my plan," Alice said afterward in the hall. "Every speech I ever write, I practice out loud with a timer. It's the only feasible way to know the real length."

Jolene pocketed her phone. "Then you owe me the raccoon story at lunch."

Ryder had waited all morning for the snow to stop, and by ten o'clock it finally did, so he pulled on his boots and ran to the park two blocks away, where Crosby was already packing a snow fort beside the climbing structure. Every step Ryder took made a strange squeaking crunch, like a rubber duck being stepped on, and when he reached Crosby he turned around and walked a small circle just to hear it again.

"It does that when it's freezing out," Crosby said, stomping his own boot. "Really cold snow squeaks because the hard ice crystals rub and break instead of melting a little under your weight." Ryder frowned. Yesterday the snow had gone almost silent, and it had been warmer, but he wasn't sure he believed that one warm day proved anything. He wanted to verify it himself, with a fair test.

So they tried walking in different spots. The snow near the playground equipment, where kids had trampled it into a hard crust, squeaked sharply. Out by the fence, where the snow lay fluffy and soft, their boots went in with more of a hollow crunch and less of a squeak. Ryder crouched and pressed his mitten flat against the packed patch, then the fluffy patch, feeling the difference in how each one gave way. "So packed snow means it was handled more, and the cold makes the crystals squeaky when they break," he said slowly, working it out. "Then anything nobody touched should squeak too."

They stamped a clean rectangle of untouched snow by the pond, and it squeaked loud enough that a woman walking her dog looked over and laughed. At the shelter by the ball diamond, Ms. Zhu was scraping ice off the water fountain with her mitten, and she asked what they were doing. "Science," Crosby said. "Snow squeaks when it's very cold." She told them an anecdote about her brother measuring the squeak one winter with a thermometer and swearing the coldest days were the squeakiest, which made Ryder grin, because his own test had just agreed with hers.

By the time they headed home, the sun had come out but the air was still bitter, and their footsteps squeaked the whole way. Ryder decided no fair test could make him immune to the fun of it, and he walked twice around the park gate just to hear the sound one more time before Crosby shouted, "Race you to the sidewalk!"

Grandpa's kitchen smelled like burnt toast and maple syrup, which was normal for a Saturday, but Jaxson barely noticed. He had his mom's old laptop open on the table, squinting at a website about a bill that might, someday, make school lunches free across Canada. He wanted to write a whole report about it for Monday, and he wanted to be the kid who actually knew what he was talking about.

"Six," he muttered, drawing on a napkin. "Three readings in the House of Commons, then three more in the Senate. That's six stops." He tapped the screen. "It's passed two so far. So Khadijah owes me a dollar."

His grandpa slid a plate of toast toward him. "Why does she owe you a dollar?"

"She bet the bill was basically a law already. But it's only got royal assent after all six. She counted the readings like they were one big thing." Jaxson grinned. "She added wrong, which is beautiful, because she's the math kid."

Grandpa's landlord knocked on the back door right then, complaining about the gutter again, and Jaxson had to carry his napkin diagram to the living room to protect it. There he summarized the whole thing out loud to Josephine on a video call. "So a bill has to pass three readings in the House of Commons, and then three readings in the Senate. Only then does it get royal assent. Boom. Coherent. Monday, solved."

"That's the least coherent boom I've ever heard," Josephine said. "But okay. What if it fails a reading?"

Jaxson paused. He hadn't tested that. He scrolled, found the answer, and let out a groan. "Then it dies. Khadijah is going to be insufferable."

"So make the report a timeline," Josephine said. "Draw six little doors and a crown at the end."

Jaxson grabbed a marker and started drawing the first door, toast crumbs and all.

Emile sat cross-legged on Angel's bedroom floor, holding Angel's phone while Angel dug through the closet for the good controller. On the screen, the group chat with Maddison blinked awake with a new message, all capital letters: WHERE ARE YOU GUYS. Emile read it twice. It looked angry, like a principal calling someone to the office.

Before he could answer, Maddison replied: why are you yelling?? Angel leaned over his shoulder, still holding a controller in each hand. "I wasn't yelling," Angel said, frowning at his own message. "I just wanted it to stand out so you'd actually see it." Maddison typed back a row of tiny laughing faces, which somehow made it worse. "So caps is like shouting on here," Emile said slowly, "even when nobody's mad." He had an idea, and since the phone was already in his hand, he tested it. He typed a reply in ordinary lowercase letters, all friendly: we're at angel's, working on the tower. come over if you want.

Maddison's answer came fast: ok that's better. you sounded so mad before lol. Angel flopped onto the bed, staring at the ceiling like it was personally unfair. "How was I supposed to know? Nobody handed me a rulebook."

"There kind of is one," Emile said. He opened a private message to Maddison, just her, not the whole group, and typed: angel didn't mean to sound mad. he says sorry. in the group it looked like a big deal but it was nothing. In the private chat it felt different, quieter, the way whispering in a hallway is different from announcing something to the whole cafeteria. Maddison replied with a thumbs up and then, a moment later: tell him to advocate for himself next time instead of making me guess.

They rebuilt the tower in the game until it stood perpendicular to the wall of Angel's desk, perfectly straight, and Emile thought about consequences, how one row of capital letters had almost cost them a whole afternoon. When Maddison knocked on the door twenty minutes later, she held up her phone. On the screen was a single message in enormous capitals: I'M HERE. "That one," she said, "is actual yelling."

Sadie marched into the pharmacy like she was on a mission, because she was. In her backpack sat the evidence: a gym shirt with two gray circles under the arms, held up that morning by Bryden during math while the whole back row laughed. Her ambition was simple and enormous. She would never be embarrassed in gym class again.

"Deodorant aisle," she announced to Makena, who had tagged along for the walk home but now looked fully invested. "There has to be a whole wall of it."

There was. Blue cans, purple sticks, ones that claimed to be for men and ones covered in flowers. Sadie picked up the first stick and read the label, because her mother always said the answer was on the label if you stood there long enough. The word DEODORANT ran across the front. She flipped it over and scanned the back, frowning.

"It says it covers smell," she said. "It doesn't say anything about sweat." She grabbed the next one, a green stick with a glacier on it. This one said ANTIPERSPIRANT. The back panel said it reduced sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts. "So they're different things," she said slowly, holding both up like a game show host. "This one stops the wet. That one stops the smell."

"Then get the glacier one," Makena said. "Obviously."

"But wait." Sadie's brain was doing that thing where pieces clicked together. She thought about the kids in gym, about how some of them smelled fine but still had sweaty shirts, and others had dry shirts that smelled like old sandwiches. Two different problems. Two different products. It was a hidden rule, like figuring out which vending machine ate quarters. She tested her idea on a third label, a purple can: deodorant, nothing about sweat. A fourth: antiperspirant, nothing about covering smell. The pattern held.

"We need the one that does both," she declared, and found a stick that said ANTIPERSPIRANT DEODORANT on the front. She felt heat radiate from her face, but this time it was excitement, not embarrassment. She paid the cashier with crumpled bills and walked out holding the bag like a trophy.

At school the next morning, Sadie found Bryden at his locker and held up the bag. "Good news," she said. "I did research."

He went pale. "What research?"

She pulled out the shirt, which she had washed, dried, ironed, and, in a moment of pure eccentric genius, folded around the same green stick with a note taped on it: For you. Two problems, two fixes. Ask me how I know.

Bryden looked at the note, then at her, then whispered, "Does it work on nerves too? I have band solo Friday."

"Get in line," Sadie said. "I have gym at two."

Eleanor had been looking forward to the food stalls at the cultural festival all week, so when her mother steered her toward the temple open house instead, she dragged her sneakers on the pavement. Inside, the hall smelled of incense and something like flower water. A woman with a clipboard handed Eleanor's mother a paper, and Eleanor saw the words "uposatha day" printed at the top.

"Uposatha," her mother said quietly, nodding at the paper. "That's why the kitchen is closed until tomorrow."

Eleanor scanned the schedule anyway, because she didn't believe her stomach, which was already growling, should have to wait. It was barely one o'clock. Then she noticed the pattern herself: everyone with a sticker on their shirt had eaten before noon, and the long table of rice and curries had been cleared at midday, not one plate left. She counted the rules on the paper her mother held. Eight precepts, and one of them, marked with a small star, was not eating after midday.

Taya from her class waved from near the altar, holding a paper cup of tea. "Come sit with us," Taya said. "My grandma does the eight precepts every uposatha. I ate a big lunch at eleven thirty, so I'm fine." Eleanor sat down between Taya and an old man who was folding paper lotuses, his fingers quick and sure. He showed Eleanor how to fold one, and she petitioned him with her eyes until he laughed and gave her a square of gold paper.

She had been biased against the whole afternoon, deciding it would be boring without snacks, but the folding took all her attention. Her lotus came out lopsided. The old man set it on the altar beside a bronze vessel filled with water, next to his own, and pressed his palms together. Eleanor copied him, not sure she was doing it right. Her stomach growled again, loudly, and Taya snorted.

"It's okay," Taya whispered. "My stomach did that at two o'clock last time. Grandma says the hunger passes, like a wave."

Eleanor watched the worshippers, some kneeling, some chatting softly, and thought about how she'd figured out the no-eating rule from the empty tables before anyone told her. It felt like solving a puzzle where the answer had been hiding in plain sight. When her mother touched her shoulder near sunset, Eleanor stood slowly and looked back at the altar, at her crooked lotus floating in the lamplight.

"Can we come back next month?" she asked. "I want to fold a better one. And I'll eat a bigger lunch at eleven thirty."

Taya held up her hand for a high five.

Aiden was halfway through a frozen pizza when every light on the street died at once. The oven ticked into silence, the fridge stopped humming, and the house went so dark he could see the outline of his own hand only when he waved it in front of his face. He fumbled for the flashlight in the kitchen drawer, found a dead one, then a second one that worked, and carried it out to the porch, where his neighbours Camelia and Margo were already sitting on their steps.

"It's the whole street," Camelia said, pointing her phone screen down the road. Every porch light was out, and the streetlamps stood dark and symmetrical, spaced like the teeth of a very tired comb.

"Come over here," called Mr. Toussaint from next door, holding up a lantern. "Power cuts are better with company and lemonade." The lemonade was warm, but nobody complained. Aiden told him about the pizza, and how his mom had gone out to buy a replacement before it could germinate into a full science experiment, and everyone laughed.

"Biggest one I ever saw was August 14, 2003," Mr. Toussaint said, settling into his chair. "A blackout that day cut power to about 55 million people, in parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada. I walked home from work, whole city pouring out of the buildings. Took me four hours. A man sold warm water bottles on a corner like it was treasure."

Aiden turned the flashlight over in his hands, thinking. Fifty-five million people. That was a blackout that spread across a whole region, like ink in water. He looked down the street again. Four blocks away, he could see a glow, faint but definitely there. He stood up. "If this were huge, everything would be dark, right? But it's not. My diagnosis: something took out just our loop." He traced the street with the flashlight beam. "So it's probably a branch on a line, or a transformer, somewhere close."

Margo grabbed her shoes. They walked two blocks, following the boundary between dark and lit houses like a seam, until they found it: a maple limb lying across the sagging power line at the end of Almond Street, its leaves still trembling.

"There," Aiden said. "Fifty-five million people had to walk home in that one. We just have to walk to the end of the block." Camelia was already dialing the power company, and Margo held up her phone and snapped a picture of the branch, saying, "For the pizza's memorial."

Rose pressed her finger on the museum map until the plexiglass squeaked. The Roman Empire spread across the wall in two colours, red in the west and purple in the east, split by a diagonal line that cut through the middle like someone had taken scissors to the world.

"It fell in 476," said Genesis, who had read exactly one plaque and now considered herself an expert. "It says so right there."

"Then why is there purple still on the map after that?" Rose traced the eastern border with her eyes, down through Greece, up around the Black Sea, all the way to a city marked Constantinople. Something about the shape bothered her, the way the purple part went on and on while the red part just stopped.

Jaycee leaned in. "Maybe the map is wrong."

"Maps in museums aren't wrong," Rose said. "They're just not finished being read."

She remembered Ms. Yamamoto's classroom three weeks earlier, the day of the timeline disaster. Ms. Yamamoto had unrolled a long paper strip across the floor and asked them to place cards with dates on it. Rose had squinted at the card that said 1453 and assumed it was a misprint, because everyone knew Rome fell way back around 476, and there was a gap the size of an ocean between them. She had even written "typo?" on it in pencil. Ms. Yamamoto had looked at the pencil mark, then at Rose, and said only, "Cards can go more than one place on a timeline." Rose had gone home and erased the pencil.

She found the exhibit booklet and flipped past the coins and the mosaics until she reached a page headed with a date: 1453. Ottoman Turks, it said. Constantinople. Captured. She read it twice, then three times, her finger moving along each line.

"Genesis. Come here."

"What."

"Read this."

Genesis read. Her face did the thing faces do when a fact arrives that a person had not ordered. "So Rome fell twice?"

"No." Rose pointed back at the big map, at the purple half, at the line of the border that had held for centuries after the red half was gone. "The eastern half lasted longer. Almost a thousand years longer. It got called the Byzantine Empire, and it came to its end right here, in 1453, when the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople." She tapped the city. "It fell there. The west fell earlier. Two different falls, one empire that split."

Jaycee looked at the map, then at Rose, then at the map again. "So when you said maps aren't finished being read."

"I interpret, therefore I win the argument," Rose said.

Genesis took out her phone to photograph the plaque that said 476, then, with visible despair, photographed the booklet page too. Rose slid her museum pencil along the diagonal border, purple edge to the Black Sea, and said, "Same pencil, by the way. Never borrow my pencil."

Abigail typed her name into the login screen and watched the computer lab's old machines groan to life. Mr. Wijaya had written the assignment on the board: write a Python loop that asks the user for a number and prints the whole times table for it. Easy, Abigail thought. She had already written half the program in her notebook during lunch, right after the part where she'd helped Simone install a game on Simone's laptop, which had taken three tries and one very vague error message.

She typed the program carefully. "Which number?" the screen asked. She typed 7. Then she waited. And waited. The cursor blinked. Then a single line appeared: 7 times 12 is 84. Nothing else. Twelve rows should have printed, one for each number from 1 to 12, and instead she had the last row and only the last row, sitting there alone like the final survivor of something terrible.

"That's all I got too," Adriel whispered from the next computer. His screen showed 9 times 12 is 108 and nothing before it. Simone leaned over from across the aisle. "Mine does the same thing. Only the last row. I think the computers are broken." Abigail almost agreed. The lab machines were ancient, half of them still had a drawing of a butterfly larva stuck on as somebody's old screensaver joke, and "the computers are broken" was a perfectly good excuse. She raised her hand anyway.

Mr. Wijaya came over, looked at her screen, and smiled in a way that told her nothing. "Count your lines," he said, and walked away. Count her lines. Abigail stared at the program. The print statement that showed the answer sat at the left edge of the screen, lined up exactly with the word for. The line above it, the one that moved the number forward, started four spaces in. She counted again. Four spaces. Then zero. She remembered Mr. Wijaya saying it once, back in September, and she'd thought it was a small thing: "Python uses indentation to show which lines belong inside a loop." She had assumed the spaces were just decoration, like paragraph margins in an essay.

Her hand hovered over the spacebar. If the spaces were the rule, then the print line, the one with no spaces, wasn't inside the loop at all. It would run only once, after the loop had finished, after the counting had already gone all the way to 12. Which would mean the computer hadn't lost the first eleven rows. It had never printed them. She pressed the spacebar four times, ran the program, and typed 7. Row after row spilled down the screen, 7 times 1 is 7, 7 times 2 is 14, all the way to 84. "Spaces," she said to Adriel. "It was the spaces the whole time."

The toaster popped and the kitchen smelled like a small campfire. Isabelle pried out the toast, black and stiff, and set it on a plate next to two slices that had stayed golden. On the counter waited her science homework: "Give one example of a physical change and one of a chemical change from your own kitchen." The problem was that she wasn't sure which one burnt toast was, and Kimberly had texted her an hour ago insisting it was still bread, just brown, the way ice was still water. "No way," Isabelle had typed back. Then she had stared at the phone, because honestly, she wasn't sure.

She tried the golden toast first. She bent it, crumbled a corner, and even dropped it in a glass of water, where it went soggy and swelled like a tiny white tsunami rising over the rim. Annoying, but interesting. Soft bread, soggy bread, crumbled bread: still bread, she decided. Nothing new had shown up. That felt like the melting kind of change, the kind her textbook called physical, temporary, like ice going back to water.

The burnt slice was different. She scraped the black part with a knife and got a flaky powder that smelled like nothing she could name, certainly not bread. She licked a crumb of the golden toast, then a speck of the black powder, and made a face. Bitter, smoky, wrong. She thought about her grandmother's old bike in the garage, its fender orange with rust that had definitely not been there when the bike was new. The metal hadn't just gotten wet and dried; something else had formed on it, something that hadn't existed before.

That was the piece she'd been missing. "In a chemical change, atoms rearrange to make one or more new substances with different properties," she said out loud to the empty kitchen, testing the sentence like a recipe. Atoms. Rearrange. New substances. She looked at the powder on her knife. Could burnt toast be a new substance with different properties? It tasted different, smelled different, flaked instead of bending. Bread couldn't do that. She felt the idea click into place, the same click as when she'd finally understood why her mother donated blood: something leaves one thing and becomes part of another.

She texted Kimberly: "Come over. Bring your nose." When Kimberly arrived, Isabelle lined up three plates: golden toast, soggy toast, and the black powder. "Bend the first one," she said. Kimberly bent it. "Now try to bend the burnt one." Kimberly pressed down; it snapped and crumbled into flakes that skittered across the plate. Kimberly sniffed it and pulled back. "Okay," she said slowly. "That is not bread." Isabelle grinned and slid the science notebook across the table, already open to a blank page. "So help me figure out if scrambled eggs count too."

Layla pushed the folded note across the lab table toward Zachariah and waited while he read it. "I'm sorry if you got upset at lunch," he read out loud. "Wait. If I got upset?" He set the note down between the beakers. "That makes it sound like it's my fault for being upset. Like I overreacted."

"It was for Nadia," Layla said. "We haven't talked since Tuesday." Nadia had told Layla that her science fair project was copied from a website, and Layla had said something sharp about Nadia's art poster being traced. Both of them had been wrong, but only one of them had written a note.

Zachariah turned the paper over, studying it like it was data. "You know what my sister calls that? A non-apology. It says sorry about the other person's feelings, not about what you actually did." He tapped the word "if." "That little word is doing all the work. Take it out and see what's left."

Layla covered the note with her hand. She had spent all of Thursday drafting it, and now she could see the flaw plainly, the way you suddenly see the pattern in a math problem. "If I only apologize for her feelings, I'm not apologizing for what I said." The insight felt significant, but it also stung. She had been so careful with the wording, and the wording was exactly the problem.

At lunch she found Nadia alone at the far table. "Can I petition for a redo?" Layla asked, sliding into the seat across from her. "I wrote you a note, but Zachariah read it and it was a non-apology. I'm not sorry you got upset. I'm sorry I said your poster was traced. That was mean, and I said it because I was embarrassed about my project."

Nadia looked at her for a long moment, then pulled the traced-and-painted poster from her bag and unrolled it on the table. "Sit closer," she said. "I'll show you the part I'm actually proud of."

The art shed at Camp Wren had exactly one good lamp, and Mia claimed it before anyone else could. She set her paper on the table, clipped it down, and stared at the task Mr. Han had written on the board: draw a sphere with a light source, showing highlight, shadow, and cast shadow. Pencils only, he had said, because pencil can smudge from light to dark. But when Mia opened her pencil case, she found three rebellious pens that had shoved their way past the pencils she thought she'd packed, and not one soft gray stick among them. The pencil sharpener on the shelf was empty too. All she had were lines.

She tested the idea the only way she could. In the corner of the page she drew a small patch of short parallel lines, all leaning the same way, evenly spaced. From a distance it looked like a pale gray wash. That was something. She drew another patch, this time laying a second set of lines across the first, crossing them at an angle, and the patch went darker, dark enough that it read as shadow. She sat back, pleased and a little surprised. Pure black ink, and somehow she had gray.

Elliot dropped onto the bench across from her, holding a half-finished sketch of the lake. He wanted his drawing in the display case by the dining hall before the parents' visit on Friday, and he kept counting the days out loud. "Two more mornings," he said. "What are you doing with all those stripes?"

"It's called hatching," Mia said, turning her page so he could see the corner patch. "And when you cross the lines, it's cross-hatching. Watch." She laid a third set over the second patch and it darkened again, like dusk coming on in stages.

She formulated a plan as she worked: hatching for the sphere's lit side, where the lines could stay thin and far apart, cross-hatching near the bottom curve where the light gave up, and the cast shadow under the sphere darker than anything, since it was the light being blocked completely. For the highlight she would leave a small circle of bare paper, untouched ink-white. Tamara leaned over from the next table and squinted at the drawing. "It looks round," she said, "and it's nothing but lines. That's weird."

Mr. Han walked the rows slowly, hands behind his back. He stopped at Mia's page and tilted his head, and the lamplight fell across the sphere so that the real shadow of her pen lay across her drawn one. "Nice mechanism," he said quietly, tapping the corner where her test patches were. Mia picked the pen back up and began the cast shadow, line over line over line.

Sarah stood on a kitchen chair in the living room because it felt more like a podium, and held her note cards at an angle nearly perpendicular to the floor, which made them impossible to read. "Two minutes," her mother said from the couch, thumb on the timer. "Opening hook, three points, closing. Go." Sarah opened with a question about school lunches, listed her three points about longer recess, and then mumbled toward the end, "So, yeah. Thanks for listening." The timer read one minute forty. "Your closing just kind of fell off a cliff," her mother said gently. "Want to try Devon's trick? He practiced in front of his dog."

That was the problem. Sarah had a strong hook and three solid points, but the ending slid away from her like the last bit of a smoothie through a straw. She flopped onto the rug and stared at the ceiling, where a water stain looked like a lopsided map. Then she remembered Ms. Côté's class, the day they had listened to a recording of a speech from 1963. Martin Luther King Jr. had said "I have a dream" over and over, and even kids who doodled through everything had sat still for it. When Devon asked afterward why it worked, Ms. Côté had said only, "Repeating the same words at the start of several sentences is called anaphora," and refused to say more, which drove everyone crazy. Sarah sat up so fast her pulse seemed to accelerate.

Maybe the repetition itself was the principle, the thing doing the work, like a drumbeat you could feel in the floor. She grabbed a fresh card and wrote four sentences, each one starting the same way: "Recess gives us time to think. Recess gives us time to move. Recess gives us a reason to love Tuesday afternoons. Recess gives us back our brains." She read them aloud to the ceiling and grinned, because the fourth one made her laugh every time.

She climbed back onto the chair and tapped her cards straight. "Timer," she said. Her mother smiled and held up her thumb. "Two minutes. Go."

Clara sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table and pressed two fingers against the small red bump on her chin. Her thumb and forefinger opposed each other, ready to squeeze, because Amira's birthday party was Saturday and she was not going to a party with a pimple. She was ten minutes early for her checkup, alone in the room, and nobody would ever know.

Her phone buzzed. A text from Amira: "DON'T pop it. My sister says squeezing pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin and it can leave scars. She has a scar. It's real. Just wash it and leave it alone." Clara stared at the message, then at the mirror on the cabinet door. A scar, forever, versus a red bump for three days. She lowered her fingers. It felt like the worst trade in history, but she made it.

The door opened and Ms. Çelik, the nurse, came in with a clipboard. She looked at Clara's chin, then at Clara's face. "Ah, the first one," she said kindly. "Your mom mentioned puberty runs early in your family heritage. Grandmothers, mothers, daughters." Clara slumped. "So it's going to keep happening? And I smell like a gym sock even when I haven't done anything?" Ms. Çelik laughed. "Sweat glands wake up around now. Daily shower, deodorant every morning, and wash your face. That's the whole battle plan." She pointed at the barren white wall where a poster showed a kid the same age as Clara, arrows pointing to armpits and a smiling face. "Hormones," the poster said, like that explained everything.

On Saturday, Clara stood in front of Amira's mirror wearing the new deodorant she had bought with her own money. The bump was smaller. Not gone, but smaller, and no scar, and no gym-sock smell. Callum was already in the kitchen yelling about cake. Clara straightened her party hat and walked out to join him.

Antoine stared at his phone in Ms. Tan's classroom after school, waiting for his mom, and typed into the group chat: "Tournament is Saturday. We need a fourth player. Asiya, Vihaan, vote." The basketball tournament allowed only one sub besides the starters, and three names had already come up: Vihaan himself, a kid named Ravi from another class, and Antoine's cousin. The chat filled fast. Vihaan sent, "Ravi and your cousin both average 10 points a game. Same number. So it doesn't matter, pick either." Antoine started to agree, then paused. He had watched both of them play at the park on Saturdays, and they did not feel the same at all.

"Hold on," he typed. "Send me the points from every game, not just the average." Vihaan sent a photo of the rec center's stat sheet, which somebody's older brother had photographed off the corkboard next to the polymer-science-fair posters. Antoine read down the columns twice. His cousin had scored 10, 10, 9, 11, 10. Ravi had scored 24, 0, 20, 1, 5. Antoine counted each column three times, because the totals looked wrong. They weren't. Both added up to 50 points over five games.

"Whoa," he typed. "Same average. But look at Ravi's games. He either goes off or disappears." Asiya replied with a row of laughing faces, then, "So who's better?" Antoine's thumbs hovered. It would be naive to just take the average and call it settled, he thought, because the average hid the thing that actually mattered: one player showed up every game, and one swung between great and terrible. "My cousin," he typed. "He gives us 10 points every single game. Ravi might give us 24. Or he might give us zero, and we lose by two." Vihaan asked him to elaborate, so Antoine sent the five numbers for each player, one after another, like a bar graph made of texts.

There was a long pause, then Asiya sent, "Okay. Steady beats streaky when you only get one shot. Voting cousin." Vihaan sent a single word: "Fine." Then he added, "You're still running the point though, because if I average four turnovers a game, nobody's checking the spread on that." Antoine laughed out loud in the empty classroom, and Ms. Tan looked up from her desk and asked what was so funny. He held up his phone so she could see the stream of numbers. "Saturday's roster," he said. "Official."

The after-school culture club was making a display for the hallway bulletin board, and Kaitlyn wanted her section to be the best one. Every member had drawn a small map with arrows showing where their families had come from. Imane had drawn Morocco and Canada with a bold line between them, and Charly had taped a photo of a grandmother's kitchen in Manila. Kaitlyn's own arrows were easy, from Ireland and from Mexico to here, but the new boy, whose name tag still said hello, I'm Adnan, had drawn nothing at all.

"Where are you from?" she asked him, because that was the whole point of the map.

Adnan turned his pencil over and over in his fingers. "I've lived in Turkey, then Malaysia, then Egypt, and now here," he said. "My parents are from Pakistan. But I was born in Turkey, so I don't really." He stopped and started again. "Every time someone asks, I feel like my answer is too long, and it must sound made up."

Kaitlyn frowned. Everyone else at the table had answered in one word, and his answer needed four countries plus one more. She wondered whether there was a word for a person whose answer was a whole list. While the others worked, she went to the library cart that Mr. Ngo had wheeled in beside the art supplies, the one stacked with books about families and migration. She flipped through one about children who move around the world, and there it was in the second chapter. An American sociologist named Ruth Hill Useem had coined the term "third culture kid" back in the 1950s, for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture. Kaitlyn read the sentence three times to be sure she had it right.

She carried the book back to the table and set it down in front of Adnan. "Third culture kid," she said. "That's an actual term. A sociologist made it up."

Adnan looked at the page, then at her. "That's a legitimate thing? People study it?"

"Look at the author and the date," Kaitlyn said, pointing. "It's real."

Charly leaned over. "So Adnan's map needs five arrows."

"No," said Adnan, and for the first time that afternoon he smiled. "It needs a circle. All the places, and me in the middle." He began to draw, and Imane offered him her good colored pencils, which she never lent to anyone, a small ritual she performed only when something mattered.

Kaitlyn went back to her own arrows and found that they didn't diminish next to his circle. They were just different, side by side on the same board. When Mr. Ngo came by to check the display, he studied Adnan's circle for a long moment, then gave a slow nod and wrote something in his notebook.

At the end of the meeting, Adnan tore a corner off his scrap paper and copied the title of the book. "For my little sister," he said. "She hates that question too."

"Tell her there's a name for it," Kaitlyn said, and slid the colored pencils back across the table to Imane.

Beatrice stood at her grandmother's counter with three onions and her grandmother's biggest knife, and she was determined to make the soup by herself. Grandma was resting upstairs, and the recipe card in her looping handwriting said French onion soup, the one Grandpa always asked for. Beatrice had promised it for his birthday dinner, and tonight was the night.

The first onion was easy. She peeled it, cut it in half, and then sliced through it, and within seconds her eyes were burning and streaming. She blinked, wiped her face on her sleeve, and kept chopping, but by the second onion she could barely see the cutting board. "How can a vegetable do this to a person?" she muttered, sniffing.

Brodie had asked the exact same question last autumn, she remembered, when the two of them had helped his mother chop onions for chili. He had stood at the sink crying his eyes out and insisting something in his own life must be upsetting him, some hidden sadness, because surely a vegetable couldn't make you weep. His mother had just laughed and handed him a paper towel. Beatrice had laughed too, at the time, though now she wondered whether she should have. She had told him it was only an illusion, that his tears meant nothing. That had been wrong, in a way she couldn't quite name yet.

She set down the knife and thought about it. Something had to travel from the onion to her eyes, because her eyes weren't touching anything. That meant the onion was releasing something into the air when she cut it, and the only moment it started was the moment the knife went through. So the whole thing was her own doing, in a sense. She tested it: she set one whole, uncut onion on the counter and stared at it for a full minute. Nothing. Her eyes stayed dry. Then she made one slice in it, and within ten seconds the stinging started again. Whatever it was, the cutting released it.

So she adjusted her plan. She moved the cutting board to the sink, turned the cold tap on low, and chopped with the water running between her and the onions, keeping her face turned away as she worked. It wasn't perfect, but the tears slowed enough for her to finish all three onions and get them sizzling in the buttered pot, filling the kitchen with the smell that meant the soup was really underway.

When Grandpa came in from the garden, he found her at the stove with red-rimmed eyes and a triumphant grin. "Been crying over me, Bea?" he asked.

"Onions," she said, and slid the wooden spoon toward him for a taste. "But I figured out how to fight back."

Florence typed her name into the sign-up page for the third time, and for the third time a red message appeared at the top of the screen. You must be 13 or older to create an account. She was eleven, and the number would not change no matter how many times she refreshed the page. The whole class was on the app already, sharing drawings and jokes, and she wanted in before Monday.

She pulled up a video call, and Anaelle's face appeared in a small square on the screen. "It asked me my birthday and then it just stopped," Florence said. "Like it's checking."

Anaelle held up her phone so Florence could see her older brother, who was flipping through a search page. "It's a law," he said, reading. "The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998. It says websites need parental consent before they collect personal information from anyone under thirteen."

"So that's why they all ask your birthday," Anaelle said. "They have to know how old you are before they can take your name and stuff."

Florence sat back. So the app wasn't being mean on purpose. It was being careful, because collecting her name, her birthday, her drawings, would count as collecting personal information from someone under thirteen. "Wait," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "If my mom consents, would that work?"

She scrolled to the bottom of the sign-up page and found a small grey link she had skipped before: Options for users under 13. Behind it was a permission form, with a space for a parent's email. She called her mom over to the desk. Her mom read the whole form, every line, while Florence waited with her hands folded.

"Some of this really could invade your privacy, you know," her mom said, pointing at a part about location data. "But there's a setting here to turn that off." She clicked it herself, then typed her email and pressed send.

"Can I tell Ms. Goh about the form?" Florence asked. "Azaan couldn't sign up either. He thought he'd been banned."

"Tell him it was the law, not him," her mom said.

Florence messaged Azaan right away: it's not a ban, there's a permission form, I'll send you the link. He replied with a thumbs-up, then a drawing of a judge holding a gavel, with FLORENCE written underneath in block letters. She laughed and set it as her first post.

Naomi spread the old map across her grandmother's dining room table, weighting the curling corners with salt shakers. Grandpa had left a note in his desk before he passed: "The good pen is at 40 degrees, 44 minutes north, 73 degrees, 59 minutes west. You'll know how to find it." The pen was the silver one he'd used to sign every birthday card, and Naomi wanted it more than anything in the house.

Her friend Anaelle leaned over the map, frowning. "Minutes? Like, at 12:44? Do we have to go somewhere at a certain time?" That was exactly what Naomi had assumed at first, but it nagged at her. Her grandfather had written those numbers as a location, not a time. She traced her finger along the faint lines running across the map and noticed tiny marks between the numbered ones. There were sixty of them, she counted, tucked between 40 degrees and 41 degrees. Sixty again between the next pair. The same pattern showed on the lines running the other way.

"So it's not time at all," Naomi said slowly. "The degrees are cut into sixty parts, and they call those parts minutes." She checked the second coordinate the same way, counting along the vertical lines. Sure enough, each degree of longitude broke into sixty minutes too, and when she squinted, each minute had its own tiny subdivisions. "Look. Each minute divides into sixty seconds. It's like a clock, but it's measuring the Earth, not the day."

They had a new problem, though. The seconds weren't written on the note, and the dining room clock's ticking had begun to make Naomi nervous, as if the map itself might cease to exist before they finished. "We only have degrees and minutes," Anaelle said. "That gives us a whole rectangle of city, not one spot." Naomi refused to panic. She marked the rectangle, then pulled out her phone and typed the coordinates in, adding zeroes for seconds. A dot appeared on a bridge in the park, right where her grandfather used to stop and watch the rowboats.

The park was ten minutes away by bike, real minutes, and the two of them rode fast. Under the third bench on the bridge, taped where only someone looking would find it, lay a small velvet box. Inside was the silver pen and a folded card in her grandfather's looping, eloquent handwriting: "Now write back." Naomi laughed out loud, and Anaelle grabbed her arm. "Write back where?"

Juliette sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field, her right arm propped in a blue sling, watching Kingston and Justice run drills without her. Two weeks ago she had fallen off the monkey bars, and now her broken arm lived inside a hard white cast that itched in the afternoons. In her left hand she held the X-ray printout the doctor had given her, because she had asked to keep it, and because she could not stop staring at it.

"Are you looking at your arm again?" Justice asked, jogging over at the water break, sweat sticking her hair to her forehead.
