"Look." Juliette held up the film. "My bones are white. Really white, like chalk. But my skin and my muscles, you can barely see them. Why would a picture show one part of me and not the rest? It's all me."

Kingston leaned in, breathing hard. "Maybe the machine only likes bones."

Juliette gave him a look of gentle skepticism, one eyebrow up. "Machines don't like things, Kingston. But something is different about bones. Something that doesn't coincide with the rest of the body." She tapped the film with her good hand. "What do bones have that muscles don't?"

Justice frowned. "They're hard?"

"Hard how, though?" Juliette had been chewing on this all week. She remembered the milk ads at school, the ones about strong bones. "Milk. My mom is always on me about milk. Milk has calcium, and calcium makes bones hard." She paused, turning the idea over like a stone in her pocket. "Maybe the calcium is why they show up white. Maybe the calcium soaks up the X-rays, more than the soft stuff around it, so bones come out bright and skin almost vanishes."

"So drink more milk, get whiter bones?" Kingston said.

"No, you'd get stronger bones. The white part is just how the picture turns out." Juliette looked around the field, then down at her cast. "I want to test it."

"Test it how?" Justice asked. "You can't X-ray yourself."

Juliette stood up, tucked the film under her sling, and marched across the grass toward Mr. Francis, who was coaching the younger kids' team on the far end. He was a vigorous walker even standing still, always clapping, always moving. She waited for the whistle, then asked him whether the school nurse kept anything from when students got hurt.

"The nurse has an old light board for looking at X-rays," he said. "Why?"

Juliette explained, pointing at her film, at the glowing bones and the ghost of her arm around them. Mr. Francis nodded along but offered no explanation, only said, "Sounds like you've got a theory. Nurse's office closes at four."

So that was where they went, all three of them, the film clipped to the light board, the white bones blazing against the dim gray of everything else. Juliette held up her hand next to it, her real hand, ordinary and invisible to X-rays in all the ways that mattered, and grinned.

"Calcium," she said. "My bones are full of it, and they drink up the picture."

Paisley sat in the computer lab during lunch, refreshing the school club page for the third time. The Robotics Club roster was gone, replaced by a plain notice: "Page under repair." She needed the list because she had promised Mr. Demir she would delegate jobs to each member before Friday's build session, and now she couldn't remember who had signed up for the sensor team.

Iris leaned over from the next computer. "It was up yesterday. I read the whole thing, even the part where Yuna wrote her name in all capitals. YUNA. Like she was announcing an emperor."

Paisley laughed, then stopped. Yesterday. Something nagged at her, and it wasn't the roster. Yesterday she had also seen a different page, the one from last month, the one where the club's old president had posted a photo of Paisley mid-sneeze with the caption "Club mascot." She had been so relieved when someone told her the post was deleted. She had even gone back to check, twice, and it was gone. Deleted meant gone, she had decided. Like erasing a whiteboard.

"Can I borrow your screen?" Paisley asked. Iris slid over. Paisley typed the way Mr. Demir had shown the class one afternoon, on a site he called the Wayback Machine. She remembered him saying only one sentence about it, that it had saved more than one trillion web pages. A trillion. She had thought that sounded like a made-up number, like something a kid would invent to win an argument.

She typed the club page's address and clicked the snapshot dated last month. The page rebuilt itself, sneeze photo and all. Paisley stared at her own crumpled face, mouth open, one hand mid-air.

"Whoa," Iris said. "I thought it was deleted."

"It was." Paisley pointed at the address bar. "It's saved here anyway. Deleted from the page, not from everywhere."

"So the roster might be too," Iris said. "From before the repair."

Paisley typed again, found a snapshot from Tuesday, and there it was: seventeen names, sensor team circled in green marker by whoever had scanned the sign-up sheet. She copied the names onto her palm with a pen.

Yuna appeared in the doorway, lunch bag swinging. "You found it? Wait. Is that the sneeze picture?"

Paisley closed the old snapshot slowly, the way you close a door you don't want to hear. "It was only ever supposed to be temporary," she said.

Yuna came over and stood behind them, looking at the blank screen.

The assignment sheet said "Theme: a statement about life, supported by a quotation," which was easy to print and impossible to fill in. Juliette sat at the corner table in the school library with her copy of the novel open, a pencil, and a legal pad that still showed the ghost of her last attempt, erased so hard it had a hole in it. Her first try had been "Auggie learns to be brave." Mr. Bekele had looked at it during yesterday's class, made a small sound like a kettle deciding not to boil, and written "closer" in green pen. Closer. Not even close. Closer.

"You've been staring at that page for ten minutes," said Alexandra, sliding into the chair across from her. Elliot arrived next, carrying two cookies and no visible intention of sharing either.

"Auggie learns to be brave," Juliette said. "That's what the book is about."

"That's what the book is about for Auggie," Alexandra said.

Juliette was about to argue when she flashed back to September, when she'd spent a whole weekend building a model bridge for science that had collapsed under one textbook. Her father had said the problem wasn't the popsicle sticks, it was that she'd calibrated the load for one book instead of a shelf of them. She hadn't known what calibrated meant then, so she'd looked it up, which was the only part of the weekend she enjoyed.

She looked down at "Auggie learns to be brave." It held up for one character. A shelf would hold more.

"What if I take his name out?" she said slowly. "People learn to be brave even when it's hard to be seen. Something like that."

Elliot stopped chewing. "That's about, like, everyone. That's about me. I'm learning to raise my hand in math."

"Then it's a theme," Alexandra said. "A theme is usually written about people in general rather than one character, so it could apply to your actual life outside the book." She said it the way she said everything, as though it had been obvious since kindergarten.

"That's why he wrote 'closer,'" Juliette said. "My sentence only worked for Auggie. A theme has to work for a shelf of people." Now she needed a quotation. She flipped pages, hunting for the scene where Auggie stands in front of the class on the first day, and found the line where he thinks that if they're going to stare, he'll give them something worth staring at. She copied it out, then tested it against her sentence. It fit. It even fit Elliot, who had once given a book report entirely facing the window.

The motive for her earlier failure was suddenly clear: she'd been writing a book report in disguise. Themes weren't about what happened to somebody. They were about what happens to everybody, a gradual kind of truth, the kind you don't notice arriving.

Mr. Bekele passed the table on his way to shelve a cart of returns. He glanced at her pad, and the kettle sound did not come.

"About time," he said. "Now find your quotation."

"Found it," Juliette said, and turned the pad so he could see.

The minivan smelled like sunscreen and warm vinyl, and Mathis was squished in the back between Lilianna and Nixon, all three of them buckled in for the twenty-minute drive to Mira's pool party. Lilianna kept her towel wrapped around her waist even though the heater was on.

"You okay back there?" the driver asked from the front. "Party starts at two, so we're on schedule."

"I'm fine," Lilianna said, but she pulled the towel tighter.

Mathis had noticed her hovering by the locker room mirror after gym all week, turning sideways, tugging her shirt down over her hips. He had a guess about why, and he decided to test it. "Lilianna. Is it lines? Like, thin lines on your skin?"

Her face went red. "How did you know?"

"Because I have them too." He pushed up his sleeve and showed the inside of his elbow, where a few pale thin lines ran beside the crease. "I grew two inches since June. The nurse at camp called them stretch marks. She said fast growing does that."

Lilianna leaned over and looked, still not touching the towel. "Really? On your arm?"

"On my knees too. Look." He pulled up his pant leg. "Nixon, check yours."

Nixon examined his own knees and shrugged. "Nothing. I haven't grown since third grade."

"That's why," Mathis said. He had worked out the pattern in his head: fast growth, then lines. Slow growth, no lines. "The nurse said they're common and they fade over time. My cousin had a bunch on his shoulders and now you can barely see them."

On the radio, the news was droning about a frog species threatened with extinction, and the driver turned it down. "Everything all right back there?"

"Fine," all three of them said at once.

Lilianna pulled the towel open a crack and looked down at her hips. "They're kind of transparent-looking. Like, thin. I thought something was wrong with me."

"They diminish," Nixon said, proud of the word. "That's what things do when they fade. My science teacher says it about sound."

"They fade," Mathis agreed. "Pool's in ten minutes. You going in the water or sitting on a chair all afternoon?"

Lilianna looked at the towel, then out the window at the first rooftops of Mira's neighborhood. She folded the towel into her bag and zipped it shut. "Race you to the deep end."

The mall speakers hummed as Aiden pressed his nose to the sneaker store window. Behind the glass, a poster the size of a door showed Darius Cole, the best point guard in the league, holding up the Velocity X. "Everyone's wearing them," said Liliana beside him. "Half our grade already has a pair." Aiden had saved nine weeks of allowance, and the cumulative total in his pocket felt heavy. But something bothered him, and it bothered him like a splinter he couldn't reach.

He scrutinized the poster, corner to corner. In tiny gray letters at the bottom it said, "Darius Cole is compensated for this endorsement." He read it twice. "Compensated," he said slowly. "That means paid." Liliana leaned in and squinted like a laser beam had shot from her eyes to the fine print. "Wait. So Darius Cole gets money to hold these up? Does he even pick them himself?" That was exactly the question gnawing at Aiden. The poster made it look like Darius loved the shoes, but Darius was famous for basketball, not for knowing shoes. Being paid didn't prove he'd chosen them at all.

Inside, the shelves shouted words like "revolutionary," "unstoppable," and "legend." Aiden turned one box over. Same basic cushioning as the forty-dollar pair on the bottom shelf. He tried both on and walked the aisle, jumped twice, and ran a short lap past the cashier. His feet couldn't tell the difference. When Liliana texted her brother, his reply buzzed back a moment later: "Dear Aiden, I fell for a famous guy's ad once, spent eighty dollars on headphones he probably never touched. Save your money, or don't, but now you know how it works. Signed, Marco." Aiden laughed out loud in the middle of the store.

At the register, Ms. Dhillon, his neighbor, was buying socks. She raised an eyebrow at the forty-dollar box under his arm. "Smart choice," she said. Aiden grinned. "Famous people can sell anything," he told her. "Even stuff they know nothing about." He laced up the new shoes right there on the bench and stood up. "Watch this," he said, and sprinted a lap around the fountain.

Alexis dragged the picnic table into the shade of the fence and set out her sketchbook, two pencils, and a pink eraser worn round at one end. Liv dropped onto the bench across from her and peered at the page, where Alexis had drawn a horizon line with two dots on it.

"Two dots," Liv said. "That's it? That's your room?"

"They're vanishing points." Alexis set a fresh hard pencil against the paper. "Every edge of the room has to point at one of them. Watch, I'll draft the walls first, all light, like scaffolding." She drew a vertical line for the corner of the far wall, then angled lines out from its top and bottom toward each dot. Soon the page held a whole network of faint lines, fanning out in every direction, with a box of a room caught in the middle of it. Was this how real artists saw the world, she wondered, invisible lines streaming out of everything toward the edges of the page?

"Can I try?" Liv grabbed a soft pencil, the dark one, and pressed hard as she drew a line from the corner toward the left dot. The line gouged shiny gray into the paper. Alexis drew the window, darkened the real edges of the room, then reached for her eraser and swept it across the network of guide lines.

Half of them came away. Liv's line did not.

Alexis erased again, harder. The line only turned smudgy, a ghost stamped into the paper. She rubbed until the eraser squeaked, and the line sat there, bold as a fence post, cutting straight through her window.

"Liv. Look." Alexis held the sketchbook up to the light, and the groove Liv had pressed shone back at them. "You carved it in. It won't come out."

Liv winced. "My brother says our stubbornness is hereditary. Maybe my pencil has it too."

From the other side of the fence, Ms. Smith leaned over, watering can still in hand. "What's the disaster over there?"

"Nothing," Alexis called back, though she was already testing an idea. She took the hard pencil and drew one more guide line, barely touching the paper, quick as a whisper. She darkened a shelf edge over it, then erased. The guide line vanished clean, leaving only the shelf. So that was the trick. Light hands for the guides, heavy hands for the real edges, and the room stayed a room.

"New page," she said, and turned it herself. "This time you get the hard pencil. One line, feather light. If you can see yourself pressing, you're pressing."

Liv took the hard pencil and hovered over the paper like it might bite. "Feather light," she repeated, and drew a line so faint they had to tilt the page to find it.

"Perfect," Alexis said, and pinned the corner of the sketchbook down before the breeze could argue.

Grandpa had been staying with Luke's family for three days, and so far the week was going great. At the breakfast table they had talked about everything, baseball, the old house on Cedar Street, Grandpa's stories about being a paperboy. Grandpa caught every word, even when Luke mumbled. So on Saturday, Luke decided to take him to the Riverside Market, where Forrest and Emerson were helping Mr. Taylor run his vegetable stall.

The market roared. Vendors called out prices, a man played accordion, and somewhere a machine ground coffee beans. Luke steered Grandpa toward Mr. Taylor's stall, where Forrest was stacking tomatoes in an intricate pattern, each row balanced on the one below it.

"Grandpa, this is Forrest," Luke said. "And that's Emerson, the one waving."

Grandpa smiled and nodded, but when Forrest said, "Nice to meet you, sir, do you like tomatoes?" Grandpa answered, "Yes, it's a fine morning." Luke frowned. That wasn't an answer to the question. At home Grandpa never missed anything. He tested it, leaning close to Grandpa's ear and saying the same thing Forrest had said, slowly, and Grandpa answered right away, "Tomatoes? Sure, the red ones."

So Grandpa's ears worked. Something about the market was the problem. Luke watched and began to notice a pattern. When the accordion stopped between songs, Grandpa chatted easily with Mr. Taylor about the weather. When the music started up again, Grandpa nodded politely at things that weren't questions. The noise was doing something that quiet wasn't. That was it, Luke thought. For someone like Grandpa, following speech got harder when there was background noise, even for the same words that worked fine at the kitchen table.

"Emerson," Luke said, "the noise here is like the antagonist of every conversation." Emerson laughed and wrote that down in the little notebook she used to document stuff for the school paper, and then she had an idea. She flipped to a blank page and wrote GRANDPA? in big letters, then TOMATOES? and HOW MUCH?

Grandpa read the page and grinned. "A dollar fifty for the tomatoes," he said, pointing at Mr. Taylor's chalkboard sign, "and yes, I'd like some." Mr. Taylor bagged them while Forrest gave Luke a thumbs-up.

They found a bench behind the market where it was quiet, and Grandpa told the paperboy story all over again, this time to Forrest and Emerson, who had never heard it. When the accordion started up again in the distance, Grandpa just leaned closer to the kids and kept talking.

"Now that," he said, holding up a tomato, "is worth a dollar fifty."

Camille had built the circuit on Tuesday, and the bulb had glowed as soon as she closed the switch. Yesterday it worked. Today, in the back of the science room, she closed the switch and nothing happened. She flicked it three more times, faster each time.

"Maybe the switch is broken," said Dhruv, leaning over her table. "My dad says switches wear out."

Camille shook her head. "It worked yesterday. A switch doesn't wear out overnight." She unscrewed the bulb and held it up to the window. The filament inside looked whole, a thin silver thread, not snapped or blackened. She screwed it back in and closed the switch again. Still dark.

Ms. Francis walked past and set a small tray of fresh batteries on the counter, but she said nothing, which Camille took to mean: figure it out yourself. Camille remembered her grandfather telling her about the old radio on the farm, how the peasant who lived next door once walked ten kilometres to town just to buy new batteries, because the radio had gone silent in the middle of a storm. "No batteries, no radio," he had said. At the time Camille had thought batteries were like water pipes, something that carried power from somewhere far away. Now she wondered if that was wrong.

She took one wire off the switch and touched it straight to the bulb holder, bypassing the switch entirely. If the switch was the problem, the bulb should light. It stayed dark. So the switch was not it. That left the bulb, the wires, or the battery. The bulb looked fine. The wires were copper all the way along, and yesterday they had carried current just fine. She crossed the room, took a fresh battery from the tray, and clipped it into place. She closed the switch. The bulb lit, steady and yellow.

"It was the battery," she said. "The old one ran out."

Allegra frowned from the next table. "Ran out? Batteries don't have anything in them to run out of. They're just, like, blocks."

"They have chemicals in them," Camille said. "That's where the power sits, stored up. The battery turns that into electrical energy, and when the chemicals get used up, it's flat. Ours was flat." She turned the dead battery over in her hand. It weighed the same as the new one, which was strange, since it was empty.

Dhruv wrote FLAT BATTERY on a scrap of paper and taped it to the dead one. "For the evidence board," he said. "Ms. Francis says the circuit has to be fundamental to our project. We can't have it dying the night before the fair."

"Then we get a spare," Camille said, and took two more batteries from the tray.

Gabriel slid the recipe card across the steel counter and read it top to bottom twice. "Step one: preheat the oven to three seventy-five." He spun the dial, listened for the click and the low rumble of heat, and felt like he had launched a rocket. This was his first Saturday at the community kitchen, and Mr. Mori had promised that anyone who finished a full recipe alone would earn an apron with the kitchen's logo stitched on the pocket.

"Blueberry or plain?" asked Paige, who was already halfway through her own card at the next station.

"Blueberry. Obviously." Emanuel grabbed a mixing bowl for him before Gabriel could even ask. The kitchen smelled like cinnamon from the morning class, and sunlight warmed the flour bins along the wall.

Gabriel measured, cracked two eggs, and stirred until his arm ached. He spooned the batter into twelve cups, and that was when the trouble started. The recipe said bake for twenty minutes, but the tops were still pale and wet-looking at the halfway check. He crouched at the little oven window, watching through the opaque glass, and a worry crept in. If they never browned, they would look raw, and Mr. Mori might decide he hadn't really finished the recipe.

Then he noticed something. Paige's tray, already cooling on the rack, had turned a deep golden brown on top, but when she broke one open to taste, the inside was still pale and soft. Same batter color, same oven. So the browning wasn't the batter changing all the way through. Something was happening only where the heat touched the surface. He thought about toast, and how bread goes golden on the outside while the middle stays white, and he had an idea.

He knocked on Mr. Mori's office door. "Is there a name for when the outside browns but the inside stays pale? Like it's the sugars doing it?"

Mr. Mori grinned. "Sugars and proteins react in the heat. It's called the Maillard reaction."

"Maillard," Gabriel repeated, racing back to his oven. At twenty minutes he opened the door, and there they were: twelve domed tops, transformed from wet grey to glowing gold, steam curling up and the smell of blueberries filling the whole kitchen. He bit into one carefully, and the pale inside gave way soft and warm. Paige leaned over and stole the smallest one, and Emanuel was already reading the next recipe card, tapping the oatmeal muffins.

"Same time next week?" Emanuel said. Gabriel tied his new apron strings in a double knot and slid the card into his pocket.

Carson stared at the card Ms. Baptiste had handed out and felt a wave of despair. On Friday, each student in Spanish class had to stand up and describe their family and pets in full sentences, and today was Wednesday. His sentences kept coming out wrong on the practice sheet, and he could not figure out why.

"Tengo un gato negro," said Trinity, reading off her paper in the library after school. She had a photo of her cat, Midnight, tucked under the book she was studying.

"That sounds backwards," Carson said. "You wrote the colors after the animal. Shouldn't it be negro gato?" He looked at his own sheet, where he had written "un perro marrón" and then scratched it out and written "un marrón perro" instead.

Trinity frowned at her paper. "I copied mine from the board. Ms. Baptiste wrote it that way."

Carson sat back and thought about it. Maybe there was a pattern he was missing. He flipped through the class workbook and found three more examples: "una casa grande," "un libro rojo," "una profesora alta." In every single one, the describing word came after the noun. He grabbed a pencil. "I think I've got it. Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe. So a black cat is un gato negro, not un negro gato."

"Then your dog is the brown one coming second too," Trinity said. "Un perro marrón was right the first time."

Carson erased his scratch-out and rewrote it. "We should verify it before Friday, though. Let's ask Ayesha. She spent a summer with her grandmother, and they only spoke Spanish at home."

They found Ayesha at the art table, painting a luminous yellow sun. Carson read his sentence aloud, and she nodded before he even finished. "That's how my abuela says it," she said. "Gato negro, casa grande. Always after."

Carson grinned and wrote four more sentences, each one with the describing word in the right place. When the bell rang, he slid the practice sheet into his folder and tapped the cover twice for luck.

"Ready for Friday?" Trinity asked, gathering her books.

"Almost," Carson said. "I just have to remember my dog's name in Spanish class. At home he only answers to Stinky."

Nora slid into the seat behind Tim and leaned over the backrest, because the argument from lunch was still burning in her. "Jeter," Tim said, not even turning around. "Justice," Nora said. "I looked them up last night. Justice hit for a higher average than Jeter in 1995."

Allyson, sitting across the aisle, pulled out her phone. The bus rattled over the speed bump by the gym, and she steadied the screen with her sleeve so they could both see the numbers. "Here's 1996," she said. "Justice again. Higher average than Jeter both years."

"Ha," said Nora. But Tim jabbed a finger at a lower line on the screen, one she hadn't noticed. "Combined, though. Jeter's ahead." Nora grabbed the phone and scrolled back and forth, checking the two season lines against the combined one, certain one of them had read it wrong. She hadn't. Justice won in 1995, Justice won in 1996, and somehow Jeter won when the seasons were put together. It felt like a magic trick with no magician.

She sat back and tried to infer what was going on, since the reason wasn't visible anywhere on the screen. Maybe it was like when the morning announcements said the eighth grade averaged twenty points a game, and that single number flattened every blowout and every shutout into one tidy figure. The rankings on sports shows did the same thing, squeezing a whole season into one slot. "It's like the average isn't the whole story," she said slowly. "One number can hide stuff. There must be some other variable that changes when you add the years."

Tim turned around fully now, kneeling on his seat despite the driver's rule about knees on cushions. "So who's actually better?"

"I don't know," Nora admitted, and it felt strange and good to say it. Allyson held the phone flat between the three of them, screen catching the window light, so transparent with smudged fingerprints that she wiped it on her jacket first. "Let's check their whole careers," she said.

"Do it before my stop," Tim said. The bus swung around the corner toward Maple Street, and Nora pulled her lunch money out of her pocket to trade for Allyson's seat, the one with the working window latch, so they could see the screen the whole way.

Leo set the two jars on the garden wall where he could watch them from the kitchen window. One held broth he had boiled on the stove; the other held broth from the same pot, but sealed while it was still steaming. For the science fair he needed an answer, and he had a hypothesis, which Sadie had told him meant a guess you could actually test. His guess was this: it was not the broth that went bad on its own, but something floating into it from the air. Three days later, the open jar had turned cloudy and smelled like old shoes. The sealed one stayed clear. He almost cheered, until Stevie leaned over the wall and squinted at the clean jar.

"That doesn't prove anything," Stevie said. "Maybe sealing it just kept it fresh, like cling wrap on a sandwich. Maybe air itself spoils food, not stuff in the air." Leo felt a drop of dread, cold and sudden, because Stevie might be right. A hypothesis was supposed to survive being attacked, and his had a hole in it.

He went to Mr. Korhonen next door, who kept beakers and glass tubes in his garden shed and let Leo borrow what he called "competent equipment, not toy store junk." Leo heated a glass tube with the little burner and bent it, twice, into a long S-shaped neck, then fitted it to a flask of broth and boiled the whole thing. The flask was open at the end. Air could get in freely, so if plain air were the culprit, this broth should spoil too. He set the flask on the wall beside a second one with a straight open neck and checked it every morning, hating how slowly the days moved.

On the fifth day the straight-necked broth had gone cloudy. The S-necked broth sat clear as rainwater. Leo flipped through the book Mr. Korhonen had handed him, and there it was: Louis Pasteur had done exactly this, boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck.

"Microbes," Leo read aloud, then said it again, grinning. "Stevie! Stevie, get over here and look at my flask."

Savannah knelt on her apartment balcony with three buckets in front of her, a bag of soil, and a packet of corn seeds. Downstairs, in the community garden behind the building, Ms. Campbell-Brown's plot was planted in strange little hills, three different plants crowded together, and Savannah wanted to know why. Her own beans had flopped over last summer, snapping where the stems bent, and she refused to let that happen again. This year she had a theory: the garden plot held the answer, if she could read it.

Junior leaned over the railing from the next balcony, because what he wanted was to be the first to eat whatever grew. "That's not a garden, that's a mess," he said, pointing at the buckets. "Corn there, beans there, squash over there."

"Ms. Campbell-Brown didn't plant hers that way," Savannah said. She counted on her fingers. "Corn in a mound, beans right beside it, squash all around the bottom. Every hill, same pattern. That's not a mess, that's a plan." She dragged her fingertips through the cool soil and smelled that dark, rain-like smell of it. "Beans climb. What if they climb the corn?"

Junior made a face, so she kept her voice neutral and said, "We'll see. You can refute me at dinner." She pushed the corn seeds into the middle bucket, dropped bean seeds beside them, and tucked two squash seeds in the outside ring, where their wide, prickly-edged leaves would sprawl. The last squash seed had a hairline fracture running down its pale coat, and she planted it anyway, curious whether it would still sprout.

For two weeks she measured everything. The corn rose first, straight and stiff. Then the beans appeared, and by the time they had two leaves each, they were leaning, curling, reaching until the tips of them found the corn stalks and gripped. "Look," Savannah whispered one evening, holding her ruler against the stalk while the vine wound another slow loop around it. The squash came last, flat leaves spreading until they shaded the whole surface of the bucket.

Junior arrived that morning with a fork in his back pocket. He crouched, inspected the shaded soil, and poked at it. "No weeds," he said, sounding almost disappointed. "There were weeds all over my mom's tomatoes."

"That's the leaves," Savannah said. She lifted one gently to show him the dark, damp ground underneath. "Ms. Campbell-Brown called it the Three Sisters. Corn holds the beans up, squash keeps the weeds down." She picked the first tiny bean pod, warm from the sun, and dropped it into Junior's hand.

Gabriel spread seven paper airplanes across the kitchen table like a fleet of very confused birds. His science fair project was due Friday, and something was wrong with it, had been wrong since Tuesday. He had changed the wing shape on each plane, which was the point, but he had also switched from heavy paper to thin paper halfway through, because he ran out of the heavy kind. Now his distance chart looked like it had been drawn by a sneezing seismograph. Kevin leaned over the papers, chewing a granola bar. "So just say the thin-paper ones went farther," he said. "Problem solved. Snack?"

Gabriel shook his head. He remembered Mr. Moose, the neighbour who had judged the fair last year, tapping Gabriel's volcano poster with one finger and saying, "Nice lava. What exactly did you change?" Gabriel hadn't had an answer then, and the irony of building a second project with the same hole was not lost on him. He picked up two planes. "Listen. The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose. The dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect." Kevin blinked. "You memorized that?" "I wrote it on my hand," Gabriel admitted, showing a smudged palm. "The independent variable is supposed to be wing shape only. I changed the paper too, so the whole thing is a mess." Kevin looked at the chart, then at the planes, then at the last apple in the bowl, clearly prioritizing. "So fly them again, all on the same paper, legitimate test, and I get the apple."

They refolded the fleet from one stack of identical paper and threw each plane three times down the hallway, marking distances in pencil on the baseboard. Gabriel devised a simple rotating order, throwing one plane of each shape per round so his arm getting tired wouldn't sneak in as a third variable. The surprise came at the end. The plane with the plain rectangular wings, the boring one, the one Gabriel had folded first as a "control before he knew the word," sailed past every dart and glider and smacked the bathroom door. Kevin saluted it. Gabriel stared at his chart, where a clear pattern now climbed across the columns. He picked up the boring plane gently, like something that had earned respect. "Friday," he told it, "you're going first."

Hunter stood at the free-throw line in the empty gym, holding his note cards like they might bite him. Mr. Chanthavong had said every seventh grader would give a two-minute speech on Friday, and Hunter's cards numbered seven points, which felt proportional to how nervous he was. The problem was that his practice runs kept hitting three minutes, then four, and the whole thing collapsed into a pile of facts about volcanoes.

Frank sat on the bleachers tossing a volleyball at the wall. "You're going to put the whole gym to sleep."

"I just need to talk faster," Hunter said.

Thiago jogged over from the equipment room with a badminton racket balanced on his chin, because that was Thiago. "Talking faster is not the answer. Remember when I did my book report on Julius Caesar? He reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words. Veni, vidi, vici."

"What's that mean?" Frank asked.

"I came, I saw, I conquered," Thiago said, and the racket slid off his chin and clattered on the floor.

Hunter looked at his seven cards. Three words, three points. Maybe that was the hidden rule, the reason speeches felt solid instead of mushy. He decided to test it right there. He dealt his cards like a magician, keeping only the three best ones, and pushed the rest under the bleachers.

"Ladies and gentlemen," he began, imagining the gym packed and the basketball hoop glowing like a golden gate, "did you know a volcano in Italy once provoked a war? No? Then listen." He gave his three points, slow and clear, and when he said his last line the sound of his voice bounced off the far wall and came back to him like applause.

Hunter clicked the stopwatch. One minute, fifty-two seconds.

"Again," he said, shuffling his cards like a card sharp in a movie. "This time you two heckle me."

Ella stood at the far end of the baseball diamond, where Ms. Grewal had set a row of low hurdles along the outfield grass. The outfield fence smelled like hot dust, and someone's radio played behind the concession stand. Lara and Maddison were already jogging back from the far end, their feet slapping the hard dirt between second base and the wall.

"Three steps between each one," Maddison called. "One, two, three, hop."

Eella tried it. She cleared the first hurdle, counted one-two-three, and then had to stretch and lurch for the second, catching it with her trailing knee. The hurdle tipped and clattered onto the grass. She tried again and did the same thing. On the third try she took four steps and still barely reached it.

She watched Lara go instead. Lara popped over the first hurdle and arrived at the second with room to spare. Ella stood behind her and counted, then walked the gap between hurdles with her own feet. Lara covered more ground in each step than she did. That was the hidden problem, Ella realized. It was not the jumping. It was the distance in between, which her legs could not cross in only three steps.

She thought about how the hurdles were spaced here, wider than what felt right for her stride, like race spacing. She went to Ms. Grewal by the backstop. "Can we move them lower and closer together?" Ella asked. "Just for practice. Then move them apart as I get faster."

"That's exactly how it works," Ms. Grewal said. "Gradual is the whole point. Prioritize the rhythm first, speed later."

Ella and Maddison slid the hurdles together until the gaps felt possible. Ella ran, and this time her feet found one-two-three, hop, one-two-three, hop, all the way down the row without touching a single bar. Afterward she sat on the bench by the fence, drinking a lemonade she had bought, since she was the team's most devoted consumer of concession stand drinks. Lara came over and bumped her shoulder.

"Same time tomorrow?" Lara said.

"Bring your legs," said Ella. "Mine are still figuring it out."

The regional spelling bee had been moved to the public library at the last minute, which meant Amelia was competing between the biography shelves and a poster of a wetland ecosystem, complete with a cartoon heron. She had studied word lists for months, but she still felt a little reckless skipping her Saturday cartoons for this.

"Your word is 'seismometer,'" said the judge, a librarian with reading glasses parked low on her nose.

Amelia's mind went blank. She knew "meter" had to mean measure, but the middle was a swamp. Juliet, sitting in the front row with their whole class, gave her a thumbs up so enthusiastic it nearly knocked Prince's glasses off.

Then Amelia remembered something her older cousin had grumbled about after watching the Scripps National Spelling Bee on TV. "Wait," she said. "Can I ask for the definition?"

"You may," the librarian said. "An instrument that measures earthquakes."

"And the part of speech?"

"Noun."

"Could I have the language of origin?"

"Greek."

Something clicked. Earthquakes, Greek, "seis-" like the word on the earthquake poster in her science classroom, the one Prince had once tried to oppose by arguing that volcanoes were more interesting. S-E-I-S-M-O-M-E-T-E-R. She could see the whole thing now, letter by letter.

"Seismometer. S-E-I-S-M-O-M-E-T-E-R. Seismometer."

"Correct."

Juliet clapped so loudly that the librarian gave her the look usually reserved for people who dog-ear books. During the break, Prince slid over with a granola bar. "I thought you were going to ask for a sentence too," he said. "You know, like a word in a sentence?"

"I almost did," Amelia said, tearing the wrapper. "But once I heard Greek, I didn't need it. I'm saving that one for the final round." She pointed her granola bar at the heron poster. "Watch out. Next word might be about that ecosystem."

The librarian's voice came over the speaker: "Finalists, take your places, please."

David's violin note kept sagging, and he could not figure out why. Every time he lifted his bow in Ms. Nkosi's music classroom, the A string sounded fine for a few seconds and then drooped, like it was tired of being played. Brogan, two seats over, had already started calling it "the sad whale," and the others had laughed along, though Kash at least had the decency to keep his face neutral.

David tried playing harder, then softer, then standing closer to the window, as if the sound needed better air. Nothing helped. At home he sat with the violin on his lap and plucked the string with one finger, watching it shiver. He pressed the string down against the fingerboard with his other hand and plucked again. Lower. He slid his finger up toward the bridge. Higher. The string was getting shorter, he thought, so there was less of it to move. Maybe less moving meant slower moving, and slower meant lower. Faster would mean higher. It was a guess about something invisible, and the only way to check it was to make the string move faster or slower on purpose.

The next morning he got to class early and borrowed the small tuning fork from Ms. Nkosi's shelf. He struck it, held it near the string, and listened. Then he turned the fine tuner a tiny bit and struck it again. Tighter, the note crept up. He loosened it, and the note slid back down, sinking like a paper boat taking on water. So a string that was tighter vibrated faster, and faster vibration made the pitch higher. Looser meant slower, and lower. He wrote it in his notebook in careful letters: faster vibration, higher note. Slower vibration, lower note.

That gave him a new dilemma. His own string drooped while he played, which meant it was going slower and slower, which meant it was slipping loose. The problem wasn't him. It was the peg. After school he asked Ms. Nkosi if he could look at it, and together they pushed the peg firmly into its hole while he tuned. The string held. He drew the bow across it and the A came out round and steady, no sad whale anywhere.

Brogan walked past and said, "Let's hear the whale."

David set the bow down and lifted the violin. "Extinct," he said, and played the note twice, clean as a bell.

Leo sat cross-legged on the flat rock at the edge of Miller Pond, his notebook open to a page with a wobbly arrow chain: sun, then algae, then water bugs, then minnows, then three big bass he'd drawn with jagged teeth because it looked fiercer that way. His assignment was to explain what happened if one link vanished, and he had no idea. Aryan crouched beside him, poking a stick at the green scum near the shore. "That pond behind the school doesn't have any of this stuff," Aryan said. "The water's clear and there's hardly anything swimming in it." Leo stopped drawing. The two ponds were only a mile apart. Same sun, same bugs, same kind of minnows. The one difference he knew for sure was that nobody had ever caught a bass in the school pond.

"That's my test," Leo said. "Fewer predators, different pond." The next Saturday he and Charlie dragged two nets through both ponds, counting everything they caught, and Charlie wrote the numbers down with vigorous scribbles because his pencil kept breaking. In Miller Pond they netted minnows by the dozen and scopped up thick green strands of algae. In the school pond they found minnows, minnows, and more minnows, swarming everywhere, but the water was oddly bare and the rocks were picked clean. Only three bass lived in Miller Pond, Charlie pointed out, out of hundreds of fish, yet those three seemed to matter more than all the minnows put together.

Leo took his two drawings to Ms. Watanabe, who kept a shelf of science books beside her garden tools. He showed her the chain and the counts, and she handed him a worn paperback and let him read at her kitchen table while the cat accompanied her from chair to sink and back. One line stopped him cold. In 1969, Robert Paine had watched a shoreline change completely after he removed a single predator, and he called that kind of animal a keystone species. Leo read the words twice. Keystone. Like the stone in an arch.

On Monday he balanced wooden blocks on the porch railing and built an arch with Aryan and Charlie watching. He set the last block at the top center, then reached in and pulled it out. The whole arch thudded down around his wrist. "Keystone species," Leo said, holding up the block. "Three skinny bass. Take them away and the entire pond belongs to the minnows." Charlie was already stacking the blocks again. "Build it taller this time," he said, "and pull out one of the side ones too, so we can see it not fall."

At six in the morning the farmers' market pavilion smelled like hay and cinnamon, and Taylor was already perspiring over a folding table that Mr. Iyer had lent her for the day. She and Kayleigh had signed up to sell muffins at the school's market stall, and the deal was that everything had to be on the table by nine, when the first customers wandered in with their canvas bags. The motivation was simple: the booth fee had already been paid, and Taylor's mother had said, twice, that she was not going to eat a single rescue muffin.

Taylor's batch came out of Mr. Iyer's big oven looking the way the recipe photo looked, round and golden. Kayleigh's batch, from the exact same recipe, came out squat and pale and heavy as hockey pucks. "We used the same recipe," Kayleigh said, poking one with a fork. "We even measured everything. Same recipe." Taylor turned a muffin over and thought about the one part nobody could see, the part hidden inside the batter before it ever reached the oven.

She watched Kayleigh make the next test batch, and there it was: Kayleigh dunked her measuring cup straight into the flour bag and dug, packing the cup full, then swept it level with a knife. Taylor, for her own batch, had spooned flour gently into the cup and then levelled it off, so hers held less. Taylor weighed both cups on Mr. Iyer's cheese scale, and Kayleigh's was heavier by a margin that made her groan. "So mine has extra flour the whole time," Kayleigh said. "That's why they're dry little bricks."

They remade Kayleigh's batch the spoon-and-level way, slid the pans in, and watched the clock crawl toward nine. At four minutes to, Mr. Iyer strolled past the stall, sniffed, and raised an eyebrow at the two matching rows of muffins. "Dare I ask which ones are whose?" Taylor wrapped the first sample in a napkin and held it out to him. "Guess," she said.

Nicolas set his fork down and stared at his plate. His dad had asked how school was, and Nicolas had said "fine," which was true in the way that a flat tire means the car still rolls.

"You're pushing peas around like they hinder your dinner," his dad said, trying for a joke. It didn't land.

That morning, Nicolas had posted a photo of himself in his gym shorts with a mustard stain shaped like a duck. He'd meant to send it just to Roger, but he'd posted it publicly by accident. Ten minutes later he'd deleted it, and he'd felt the relief wash over him, like closing a door on something embarrassing. Then, at lunch, Cecilia had slid her phone across the table and shown him the group chat. The duck stain was there. Roger had screenshotted it before Nicolas deleted the post.

"The whole basketball team has it," Roger had admitted, looking sorry. "I only sent it to one person. I didn't think it would spread like a plague."

Nicolas had spent the afternoon working it out. He couldn't see where the photo was now, the way you can't see where a cold goes when it travels through a classroom. But he could test one thing. He asked Roger to send it to exactly one friend, then waited. By last period, three kids Nicolas had never met were quacking at him in the hallway. So deleting the post had only taken it off his own page. Every copy that anyone had already saved, they still had.

"Is it the photo?" his dad asked now. "The one with the duck?"

Nicolas looked up, startled. His dad tapped his own phone. "Ms. Santos sent me a message. She's the coach's neighbor, apparently, and she saw it on her son's phone this afternoon. She wanted to warn you before it reached more parents."

So it had jumped even that fence. Nicolas explained what he'd figured out, that deleting wasn't the equivalent of taking a picture off the wall, because people could have copies they'd made before it vanished. His dad listened without interrupting, which was its own kind of help.

"Okay," his dad said. "So what's your plan?"

Nicolas picked his fork back up. He'd already texted Roger and Cecilia and asked them, one at a time, to delete their copies and ask whoever they'd sent it to do the same. It was like pulling weeds from the roots instead of snapping off the tops. By tomorrow the copies would be fewer. And he'd already decided his next embarrassing photo would go to Roger and Roger only.

"Copies first, then captions," he said. "Roger's writing an apology message tonight. He says the duck deserves a better debut."

His dad laughed, and Nicolas took the first real bite of his dinner.

The garage sale at Mr. Hoang's house had three folding tables, and Hannah had exactly four dollars and one nickel. She wanted the old poetry book with the green cover, the one with a stanza about rivers circled in pencil, but Dalia wanted it too, and so did a boy who kept picking it up and putting it down. On the next table sat a whole cardboard box of water bottles, fifty cents each, and nobody was buying them at all. "Why is the box of water so cheap and the little glass stone so expensive?" Hannah asked Mr. Hoang, pointing at a tiny gem marked fifteen dollars. "Because five people have asked me about the stone since eight o'clock," he said, "and nobody has asked about the water."

Hannah thought about that while she waited for Dalia to make up her mind. She was starting to perspire in the heat, and she noticed that people kept walking past the water to look at the stone, the book, and a radio that had only one left of its kind. Then two girls came by and asked Mr. Hoang whether the water was safe, because someone had told them the old bottles could be toxic. He said no, it was fine, but they still didn't buy any, because there was a whole box of it and a store on the corner.

"You know what my mom told me last night?" Dalia said, fanning herself with her hand. "There was a guy named Adam Smith, and in 1776 he published a book, 'The Wealth of Nations', and he said nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." Hannah stared at her. That was exactly the box of water and the tiny stone. "So it isn't about how useful something is," she said slowly. "It's about how many people want it and how few there are."

She had an idea, and she tested it right there. "Mr. Hoang," she said, "there's only one green poetry book, and three of us want it. Would you take my four dollars and nickel if I promise to write my favorite stanza on a card for Dalia so she gets part of it too?" The boy with the wandering hands had wandered off toward the radio, which left two buyers instead of three. Mr. Hoang looked at the box of untouched water, then at the crowd around his rare things, and grinned. "Sold," he said, and wrapped the book in yesterday's newspaper.

Emilia pulled her synthetic rain jacket out of her backpack at Gate C14 and shoved it back down again, because it was snowing in her hometown and twenty-five degrees where she was going. Beside her, Oceane was reading the travel brochure for the fourth time. Oceane's family and Emilia's were flying together to the coast for a whole week.

"There's a beach right behind the hotel," Oceane said. "It says swimming is allowed but there's a lifeguard sign at the entrance."

"What kind of sign?" Emilia asked. She liked to classify warnings into the ones you could ignore and the ones you couldn't, like the difference between "slippery floor" and "do not climb."

Oceane turned the page. "It says rip currents. My mom told me about those, the water pulls you out away from the beach, and people panic and try to swim straight back in and get too tired."

Emilia thought about that. A current pulling out had to be like a river, and rivers weren't wide everywhere. If the pull was narrow, then swimming sideways, along the beach instead of against the pull, might carry you out of it. She had never seen a rip current, but she could picture the shape.

"Watch," she said, and dug a shoelace out of her backpack pocket. At the window she laid it on the sill, laid her finger on the middle of it, and dragged her finger straight back toward the window frame. Then she slid her finger sideways instead, off the shoelace entirely, and touched the bare sill. "That's the beach, that way. If the current is only as wide as the shoelace, you get out of it sideways."

"So you swim parallel to the beach," Oceane said slowly, "not straight against it."

"That's my guess anyway."

"You sound like Mr. Grant in science class."

A man two seats over looked up from his newspaper. "Lifeguard, fourteen years," he said. "That's exactly what we teach. Swim along the beach till you're out of the narrow thing, then come in. Most kids don't figure that out on their own."

Emilia felt her face go warm. She folded the shoelace and put it back in her pocket, and when the boarding call came she stood up, smoothing her peasant blouse, and said, "Race you to the scanner."

On Tuesday morning Ms. Goh set a small box on Jeremy's desk, and by lunch he had learned that his new phone could do eleven things his brain wanted to do all at once. His mother had written a note that morning and tucked it into his backpack, and he read it again during silent reading while the phone sat in his pocket like a warm coin. "This phone will accompany you to school and back," the note said, "but not into your bed at night. Signed, a person who once fell asleep at her own desk for eleven years straight." Jeremy folded the note into his pocket next to the warm coin, which buzzed twice before the bell.

For four nights he scrolled in bed anyway, flashlight games and video after video, because everyone in his class did it and the screen looked best in the dark. For four mornings he dragged himself into Ms. Goh's classroom like a boy wading through syrup. Natasha noticed on Friday. "You look like Kaysen's fish when the filter broke," she whispered, and Kaysen said, "That fish looked bad, though, so fair."

Jeremy decided to test it like a science experiment, since Ms. Goh was always saying a good critique of your own idea beats a perfect guess. Friday night he left the phone charging in the kitchen and lay in bed with nothing but the ceiling. He was asleep before he finished counting the third crack. Saturday night he scrolled in bed until eleven and stared at the ceiling until nearly midnight, wide awake, eyes burning. Sunday he left the phone in the kitchen again and dropped off fast. Same room, same pillow, same ceiling. The only thing that changed was the screen.

On Monday he found Natasha by the cubbies. "I think the light from the screen does something," he said. "Blue-ish light. When I scroll in bed, my body won't let me get sleepy, and when I don't, it does. I looked it up this weekend on the kitchen computer, not in bed."

"Melatonin," Natasha said. "That's what the website called it. The hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening. Kaysen read the same page because his brother plays games under the covers till one in the morning and is basically a zombie at breakfast."

Jeremy considered this. "So the screen delays the melatonin, or slows it, and then you just lie there." He held up the phone. "Which means this thing is a sleep thief that fits in a sock. It's ironic, honestly. The stuff I scroll to fall asleep is the stuff keeping me up."

Natasha peered at the phone in his hand. "Is that a flashlight app?"

"It's a blue-light experiment," Jeremy said, and he turned the screen face-down on the desk.

The note was waiting in Penelope's trumpet case when she opened it after lunch. In Kristian's scrawly handwriting it said, "Practice was wrong today. You sounded like you were whispering the whole song. What happened? Meet me in the gym before rehearsal." She folded the note into her pocket and thought about the morning, when she had sung so quietly that even she could barely hear herself.

At the gym, Ms. Watanabe was hanging the costumes on a rolling rack. "Tomorrow's concert, so today we do the dress rehearsal," she said. "A full run-through, as if it were the real show, and you perform in costume." Penelope had never worn her costume before. It was a silver tunic with a stiff, high collar, and when she pulled it on, it squeezed her ribs like a fist. She tried to take the deep breath she needed for the long note in the second verse, and nothing came. That was the answer to Kristian's note. She hadn't been whispering on purpose. Her old practice shirt had been fine, so her quiet singing in class had seemed like nerves, but now, in costume, she felt the real cause.

She remembered the fall talent show, when Emmitt had frozen halfway through his magic act and stood there red-faced until Ms. Watanabe finally clapped. Afterward he told her the stage lights had been so hot he couldn't think. She didn't want tomorrow to go that way.

Penelope tried an experiment. She unfastened the top hook of the collar, pulled the tunic down a centimeter at the shoulders, and breathed in. Air rushed in all the way down to the bottom of her lungs. "Ms. Watanabe," she called, "could I sing the run-through like this, with one hook open?" Ms. Watanabe walked over, tugged the fabric, and nodded. "Better loose than silent."

Kristian started the piano intro. Penelope filled her lungs, and the long note in the second verse came out strong and clear, bouncing off the gym ceiling.

Joshua had written the same sentence four times, and Mr. Gagnon still wanted more. "Cut 'really big' and 'very dark' and 'kind of scary,'" he had written at the top of Joshua's draft in red pen. "Then look at your sentence lengths." The story was due on Friday, and Joshua wanted it to be the one Mr. Gagnon read out loud to the class, because last time he had picked Katherine's paper, and hers was about a horse.

At lunch, Joshua spread his draft on the table next to his milk. Lucas leaned over from the next seat. "You wrote 'very very quiet' twice," Lucas said. "That's not even an adjective anymore, that's a cry for help." Joshua crossed out "very very quiet," and just "quiet" stayed, which was strange because quiet seemed louder now, like the word had room to breathe.

Then he counted the sentences in his cave scene. Four of them ran long, one after another, all with commas, dragging their feet down the page. The fifth was "He heard a drip." It sat there alone, and when Joshua read the page again, that little sentence jumped off the line at him. He tried an experiment. He moved "He heard a drip" to the middle of the paragraph, and it disappeared, like a minnow in a school of minnows. He moved it back to the end. There it was again.

"Listen to this," Joshua said, and read the cave scene aloud to Lucas. Lucas stopped chewing his sandwich at "He heard a drip," then admitted that was creepy, which for Lucas was a big concession.

On Friday, Mr. Gagnon read Joshua's paper to the class. He read slowly through the long sentences, and then he stopped. "He heard a drip."

The room went silent. Katherine, who thought nothing could beat her horse story, raised her hand and said, "Okay, that part got me."

"Now I just have to convert my dragon story," Lucas whispered across the aisle. "My dragon is imminent, and currently he is very very huge."

Grandma's piano sat in the front room under a lace cloth, and Avery had been told she could practice on it all summer. The only problem was that her lesson book had gone missing somewhere between her house and here, and Mr. Perera, the neighbour who tuned pianos, was coming over in an hour to fix a sticky key.

"Can't you just play without the book?" asked Yusra, who had come along to keep her company.

Avery ran her fingers over the keys. "I only know three songs, and they're all in the book." She frowned at the keyboard, thinking. On FaceTime last week, Ty had bragged that his cousin knew every piano in the world had the same number of keys. Ty liked to exaggerate, so Avery had half believed him and half not. Here was a way to find out. "Help me count these," she said. "You do the white ones, I'll do the black ones."

They started from the left end. Yusra tapped each white key with one finger, whispering numbers, while Avery hopped her finger from black key to black key, up over the hills and down into the valleys. The room was quiet except for their counting and the sparse ticking of the old clock on the shelf. When they finished, Yusra said, "Fifty-two." Avery checked her own total twice, because it seemed small. "Thirty-six." She added them together on the scratch paper. "Eighty-eight."

"That's what Ty said," Yusra reported, holding up her phone. She had texted him mid-count, and he had replied almost instantly, as if he'd been waiting. "He says a standard modern piano has 88 keys, 52 white and 36 black. He copied it from his cousin."

"So he was right," Avery said, and something about that made her feel the piano differently, like it wasn't one long mystery but a pattern she could learn. If every piano in the world had the same 88 keys, then a song she learned here would work on any piano anywhere.

The doorbell rang, and Mr. Perera came in carrying his tool bag. "Sticky key, is it?" he asked, and Avery suddenly perceived the problem she could actually solve today. She pointed at the E she'd been avoiding all morning. "This one. I can show you exactly which it is, because I counted."

Asher drummed the fingers of his right hand on his desk, which was the only hand he could drum with, since the left one had been in a fiberglass cast for six weeks. Ms. Okonkwo had written CAST OFF TODAY on the board beside the date, because half the class had made him promise to describe it. The appointment was at two thirty, and his mother would leave without him if he was not at the office by two fifteen, since she had a meeting she refused to miss.

"Are you scared?" Wilson asked from the next row. "My cousin said they cut it off with a saw. A real saw, the loud kind."

"That sounds toxic," Nikki said, shaking her head. "Like, actual dangerous."

Asher looked down at his cast. He had signed it in green marker and drawn a shark on it, and underneath the fiberglass his arm was fine. He thought about the saw his dentist used, the one that spun and screamed and was only safe because it stopped the instant it touched anything soft. A cast saw would touch skin the whole way down. Unless it was not that kind of saw at all. He could not see inside the machine, but he could test the idea when he got there.

"I have an idea about it," he said. "I'll illustrate. Ask me tomorrow." Ms. Okonkwo raised an eyebrow at the murmur around him and pointed at the clock. He packed his binder one-handed and hurried out.

At the clinic the nurse wheeled over a tray with the saw on it, and a small kid two chairs away began to cry the moment it buzzed. "It won't cut you," the nurse told him. "The blade vibrates back and forth instead of spinning. It cuts the hard cast, but not skin underneath."

Asher held out his arm. "Can you show me on my hand first?" he asked. She pressed the humming blade flat against his palm and dragged it along his skin. It was warm and ticklish, like a phone buzzing, and it left no mark at all. He grinned at the small kid, who had gone quiet. Then the nurse slid the blade into the cast, and a long crack ran down the fiberglass over the shark drawing.

"Want to keep the pieces?" she asked, already reaching for the shears.

The restaurant kitchen smelled like onions and dish soap, which Levi decided was not the correct smell for muffins but was going to have to do. Ms. Eze had left a recipe card on the steel counter, a bag of flour, eggs, a carton of buttermilk, and a note that said only "Oven. 400. You first." Raven leaned against the walk-in fridge eating a pickle she had found somewhere, and Izabella was already reading the card like it was a test she intended to pass.

Levi cracked both eggs into the big bowl, poured in the buttermilk, dumped the flour on top, and started stirring with the confidence of a person who had never once thought about batter. The spoon turned on him almost immediately. Something pasty clung to it in ridges. Something wet sloshed underneath, indifferent to his efforts, refusing to become anything at all. He stirred harder. It got worse.

"Step two says whisk the dry ingredients in one bowl," Izabella read, in the voice of someone delivering bad news gently. "Step three says the wet ones in a different bowl. It says combine at the end." She looked into his bowl, then at him, then back at the card, as if one of the three might explain the other two. Raven peered in over his shoulder. "It's making little flour islands," she said. "That one has a moat."

Levi stared at the lumps and tried to isolate the problem, the way Ms. Eze was always telling him to do instead of panicking. Two bowls, mixed separately, joined only at the end. That was the whole idea, apparently, and he had skipped it. He couldn't see inside a lump to know what had gone wrong in there, but he could test it. He scraped the miserable batter into the trash, measured flour, baking powder, sugar and salt into the big bowl, cracked eggs and poured buttermilk and oil into a smaller one, and kept them apart like two kids who could not sit together yet. Then, at the very end, he poured wet into dry and folded. The batter came together smooth and thick, with no moats anywhere.

The muffins rose into golden domes while Raven stood at the oven window guarding them as if they might escape. When Ms. Eze came back and bit into one, she chewed slowly, and Levi held his breath, trying to read her face for a motive he could not see. She took a second muffin without a word. Raven nudged him. "That," she whispered, "is the review."

Louis had been waiting for the museum trip for weeks, mostly because of one exhibit: a real fire pole, brass and shiny, rising up through a hole in the ceiling beside a rebuilt fire station from long ago. On the bus, Christina argued with Leen about which was faster, sliding down a pole or running down stairs, and it got loud enough that Ms. Nowak had to intervene and move Leen to a different seat. Louis didn't say anything. He just kept wondering. Why would anyone put a pole through a floor in the first place? Stairs worked fine everywhere else, didn't they?

The class swept through the rooms in a clump. In the nature hall, Leen stopped at a slice of rotting log and read aloud that decomposers like fungi and beetles break down dead wood into fertile soil, which made Louis think about how much of the world happens where you can't see it, underground, inside things. He filed that thought away. On the way out, a guide was standing at the fire station exhibit, tapping the brass pole with one finger.

"Guess why stations once had poles instead of stairs," she said. "Anyone?"

"Because poles look cool?" said Leen.

"Because stairs were too expensive?" said Christina.

Louis stepped closer. He noticed the pole went straight down from the sleeping floor above, no turns, no steps, nothing in the way. If speed was the whole point, then straight down had to beat a zigzag. But how would anybody ever prove a thing like that? Someone must have raced a pole against the stairs. He said, "I think somebody slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs, and after that, everybody wanted one."

The guide grinned. "Close. Want to check the plaque?"

Louis leaned in and read it, and his stomach did a small flip. "Chicago's Engine Company 21," he read slowly. "1878. A firefighter slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs, and that's credited as the first fire pole."

"Told you poles were faster," said Christina.

"You said cool, not fast," said Leen.

"Both," said Christina, and she put one hand on the brass, right in the middle, where it was worn the shiniest.

Riley had read the last page of "Wolf Hollow" twenty minutes ago, but his essay was still blank, and the essay was due tomorrow morning.

"That quote you keep muttering," said Giuliano from the kitchen table, where he was building a bridge out of popsicle sticks for his own project. "You've said it four times. It's long."

"It's the only one that shows the theme," Riley said. "Betty hiding in the woods proves the book is about how people decide who to trust." He found the page again and read aloud: "'She was there, then she wasn't, like something the hill had swallowed, and we stood in the spot where she'd been, not speaking, not moving, until the cold made us turn back.'"

Giuliano laid down a popsicle stick. "That's huge. Ms. Ito said one or two lines, maximum. She gets aggressive about it. Remember when Milo turned in a whole page of quotation?"

"Nothing bad happened to Milo," Riley said.

"He got a negotiation. She said he could revise it or take the zero, and he revised it for two days." Giuliano pushed his bridge aside. "Just cut the middle."

Riley stared at the sentence. The beginning showed the swallowing and the end showed them not moving, both proof that the town couldn't distinguish a real threat from a rumor. The middle, "like something the hill had swallowed," was the pretty part but not the proof. He copied the quotation onto his draft and drew a line through it. The problem was that if he just glued the pieces together, it would look like the book said something it didn't. He flipped through his notes until he found the handout on quotations, and there it was, one line he'd skimmed past in September.

He typed three periods, each one with a space between it and the next, where the cut words had been. "It's called an ellipsis," he said, reading the handout's label aloud.

"Sounds like a dinosaur," Giuliano said, without looking up from his glue.

Riley read the shortened quotation back to himself. "'She was there, then she wasn't . . . and we stood in the spot where she'd been, not speaking, not moving, until the cold made us turn back.'" The theme still stood, and now the quotation fit inside his paragraph with room to spare. He typed his sentence about trust underneath it, saved the file twice, and leaned over to press PRINT.

Kate set her guitar on her lap in Mr. Yip's studio and looked at her fingertips. Eight days of playing had left red dents in the skin, and pressing the strings felt like pressing wire into a sunburn. "I think I'm done," she said. "Maybe piano. Piano keys don't fight back."

Mr. Yip only nodded and wrote something in his book. "Same time next week," he said.

In the waiting room, Kate found Jersey, who had been taking lessons for two years and was tuning his guitar on the bench by the window. She held out her hand, palm up, fingers spread. "Does this happen to everyone, or am I just broken?"

Jersey took her hand and pressed his thumb against the tip of her first finger. She winced. Then he held out his own fingertips, and Kate leaned close. The skin there was thicker, slightly shiny, ridged in little circles. "Mine looked exactly like yours at the start," he said. "Pressing the strings hurts like that at first. If you keep playing, the skin toughens into calluses, and after a while it stops hurting. I barely feel it now."

Kate turned that over in her mind. The soreness had a hidden cause, and the cure was hidden too, something that happened slowly inside the skin where she couldn't watch it. She wanted to verify it before she wasted another week. "So it's not about being tough today," she said. "It's about showing up until the skin changes on its own."

"That's it," Jersey said. "Ask Daniyal. He quit for a month last spring and had to start all over with the sore fingers."

On the drive home, Kate told her mother the whole thing, and then sat in the kitchen drawing a calendar in her notebook. The boxes looked symmetrical, four tidy rows, and in the corner she wrote a crown over the word monarchy because her social studies homework was due Friday and she didn't want to forget it. But most of her mind was on the guitar. She played for fifteen minutes that night, wincing, and marked an X in the first box.

At the next lesson, she played the three chords Mr. Yip had assigned, slowly and evenly, and he raised one eyebrow, which for him was a standing ovation. In the waiting room afterward, she pressed her fingertips against her thumb, checking, and found a small hard spot just beginning on her first finger. She ran to the bench by the window and held her hand out to Jersey. "Feel that," she said. "That's week two of a callus."

Willow had come to the skate park to ride, but the maker van was parked by the fence again, its folding table covered in batteries, bulbs, and coiled wire, and Ms. Campbell-Brown was waving her over. Today's challenge: build a circuit with a battery, a switch, and a bulb, then explain why the bulb lights. "Once you've got one bulb going," Ms. Campbell-Brown said, "try two."

Willow clipped wires to the battery, added a switch made from a brass fastener, and screwed in the bulb. Nothing. She wiggled the switch, and the bulb flared bright, then dimmed when she let go. So the switch opened and closed something, she thought. Something she couldn't see. What was actually travelling through that wire? She built a second loop with two bulbs in a line, and both glowed, fainter but steady. Evie skidded up on her board, flipped it, and leaned over the table. "Why's yours dimmer than mine was?"

Then Willow's first bulb went dark with a pop, and the second one died at the same instant. "Hey, they both quit," she said. "But only one popped." She stared at the dead pair, chin in her hand. Maybe the electricity had to go around in a loop, through every piece, and back. She unclipped the burnt bulb and bridged the gap with a plain wire. The second bulb lit at once, bright and robust, brighter than before. Javier, who had been watching from the ramp, rolled closer. "So one dead bulb can knock out the whole line?"

"It looks like it," Willow said. "In this kind of circuit, if one bulb breaks, the loop is broken and every bulb in it goes out." She turned to Evie. "So in a string of holiday lights, one bad bulb could black out the whole string. That's a good candidate for why those old strings always went dark." Ms. Campbell-Brown raised an eyebrow but said nothing, only slid a fresh bulb across the table.

Willow screwed it into the empty socket and snapped the switch closed. The string blazed, two warm points of light against the grey afternoon. "Okay," she said, pulling out her notebook. "Now what happens with three?"

Easton stood at the bottom of the stairs holding his sleeping bag like a shield. It was his first sleepover at Mikaela's house, and the basement rec room already looked nothing like a basement. Strings of fairy lights hung from the ceiling, a bowl of popcorn sat on the ping-pong table, and Elena was sprawled on an air mattress with a bag of gummy worms.

"Claim the couch," Mikaela said, tossing him a pillow. "It's the best spot, and you're the guest."

Easton dropped his bag by the couch. Elena narrowed her eyes at him across the room. "Warning. Mikaela talks in her sleep. Last time she gave a whole speech about a hamster election."

"I do not," Mikaela said. "You're making it up to scare the new kid."

Easton said nothing, but he filed it away. He had read something once about sleep talking, and one detail stuck with him: the talker usually remembers nothing by morning. That meant nobody could settle the argument tonight. The proof would have to wait until morning, and somebody would have to be awake enough to catch it. He decided that somebody would be him.

They played ping-pong until their arms ached, Elena proving surprisingly agile, lunging for shots nobody thought she could reach. Then they watched a movie, and one by one they dropped off. Easton fought to stay awake. Around midnight, sure enough, Mikaela's voice floated out of her sleeping bag, muffled and slow: "Ballot box... under the couch... Mr. Nibbles demands a recount." Easton grabbed his phone and recorded ten seconds of it, grinning in the dark. Then, because the floor was cold and Mikaela had kicked her blanket halfway off, he tucked it back over her shoulders before lying down.

At breakfast, Elena pounced. "Hamster election. Recount. We all heard it."

"Impossible," Mikaela said, cheeks going pink. "I would remember saying something that weird. I remember everything I say." She looked at Easton for backup.

Easton pushed his plate of toast aside. "That's the thing. I read that sleep talking is really common in kids, and it's harmless, but the person almost never remembers it the next morning. You wouldn't remember. That doesn't mean it didn't happen." He held out his phone. "But if you don't trust Elena, you can deduce the truth yourself. Listen."

Mikaela pressed play. Her own sleepy voice filled the kitchen, mumbling about Mr. Nibbles and the recount. Her mouth fell open. Then she started to laugh, a real laugh that bent her over the counter, and when she straightened up she pointed at Easton. "Fine. I believe you. But tonight you're sleeping in the rec room, and I'm recording you."

"Deal," Easton said, and stole the last gummy worm from Elena's bag.

Lydia had noticed something strange about Saturdays. Every week, right before sundown, her mother packed the little box with the juice cup, the spice tin, and the braided candle with several wicks, and instead of staying home, the whole family drove to the cemetery. "Havdalah is for leaving Grandma's Shabbat the way she liked it," Mom always said, and that was all she would say. Lydia's intuition told her there was more to it, some reason hiding underneath, and she decided to test an idea.

That afternoon she carried the box herself up the hill between the rows of stones. Her little brother, who was five, marched behind her with his chin out, because tonight he was allowed to hold the braided candle for the first time. "I won't drop it," he kept saying. "I never drop anything." Lydia privately remembered the dropped bowl of oranges from Tuesday, but she said, "I know. You'll be careful."

They stopped at Grandma's stone. Mom poured grape juice into the cup and set it on the flat top of the granite, and Lydia noticed that Mom always poured before Grandma's name, never after, as if Grandma were being handed the cup first, like a guest. While the shadows stretched long, Lydia asked, "Do the spices signify something? Is that why you pass them around three times?" Mom smiled. "Smell them and wonder," she said. So Lydia smelled the cloves, and her brother sniffed so hard he sneezed, and the sky went from orange to gray to dark blue, and it was time.

Mom lit the candle, all its wicks flickering at once, and placed it in her brother's careful hands. Lydia watched the flames dance over the grave, and she thought she understood: Grandma could not smell the spices or taste the juice, but Mom needed her to be there anyway, every single week, resilient as the stone itself. "Say the blessing," Mom whispered. Lydia's brother lifted the candle higher and said, "For Grandma," and the little flames waved in the wind.

On the drive home from the gym, Hailey sat in the back of Ms. Eze's car between Davin and Darius, her hair still damp, and lifted her wrist to her nose. The sweat there smelled like almost nothing. Then she sniffed the shoulder of her shirt. Not almost nothing. Definitely something.

"You smell like the boys' locker room," Davin said, fanning the window open with his hand.

"You smell the same," Hailey said. "Why do my wrists smell like water but my shirt doesn't? It's all sweat." She turned it over in her head. If sweat itself had the smell, every sweaty part of her should smell the same. Unless the smell wasn't coming from the sweat at all. She remembered Davin complaining last week that he'd never needed deodorant until this year, and what his older cousin had told him. "Your cousin said fresh sweat has almost no smell, right?"

"Yeah. He said body odor comes when bacteria on your skin break down sweat from the glands in your armpits, and those glands don't even turn on until puberty." Davin shrugged. "He was pretty gross about it."
