He dumped his rocks beside theirs and started hunting for something striped, because now he wanted to find the third kind, not just the candy.

By the fire that evening, Mr. Haile walked the line of sorted stones with his hands behind his back. He stopped at the granite and the basalt sitting side by side, and asked nothing at all, only nodded. Then he handed the peach candy to all three of them at once. David bit into his, and the sweet nectar of it ran down his chin while Ariyah held the basalt up to the last orange light, close enough to see the tiny crystals glint.

The rain hammering the classroom windows was supposed to be the most interesting thing about Tuesday, until Maryam slammed her tray down at the table next to Ryder and refused to look at him. Alice set her sandwich aside. Yesterday the three of them had been planning the science fair project together, a volcano with molten lava made from baking soda and vinegar, and today Maryam and Ryder were acting like strangers.

"He said my poster was ugly," Maryam hissed, stabbing her fork into the pasta.

"I never said that," Ryder shot back, his ears going red. "I said the layout was confusing."

Alice's first idea was to pick whoever seemed most upset, but she stopped herself. Ms. Sánchez had put a poster on the wall last week about solving conflicts, and one line kept floating back to Alice: paraphrasing, it said, meant restating what someone said in your own words. She hadn't really understood it then. Now, watching her two friends talk past each other, she decided to try it as an experiment, the way she'd test anything else.

"So, Maryam," Alice said slowly, "you heard him say the poster itself was ugly, like the whole thing, not just the layout." Maryam nodded, arms still crossed, but her shoulders came down an inch. "And Ryder, you meant only that the parts were hard to follow, not that it looked bad." Ryder nodded too. Alice kept going, restating each of their words back to them, and something strange happened. Maryam frowned and said, "Wait. That's not exactly what I meant. I was mostly embarrassed because I stayed up until eleven making it." Ryder blinked. "I didn't know that. I thought you slapped it together at lunch."

That was the crack in the whole fight. Nobody had actually said the poster was ugly; the hurt had grown out of a sentence that was never spoken, the way the garden's dead leaves would decompose into something that looked completely different from what they'd been. Alice felt her own ears go warm. It wasn't a full fix, but Maryam had turned slightly toward Ryder instead of toward the window, where the precipitation still streaked the glass in long silver lines.

"Could I try the layout again," Maryam said, "if you help with the labels?"

"Yeah," Ryder said. "And you can pick the lava color." He grinned. "As long as it's still molten orange."

Alice picked up her sandwich again, and outside the rain finally began to soften.

Lucy counted her styrofoam balls for the third time. Twelve orange, twelve gray, and a bag of tiny blue beads rolling around the bottom of the box like they wanted to escape. In forty minutes the judges would walk the gymnasium floor, and her model of an atom still looked like a lumpy planet with random beads taped wherever they fit.

"What did you do, throw them on there?" asked Lyric, who was setting up the volcano two tables over. Lyric's baking soda smelled like actual science. Lucy's table smelled like glue.

"The protons and neutrons go in the middle," Lucy said, stabbing a gray ball with a toothpick. "It's the electrons I can't figure out. Ms. Sow said they aren't just stuck in one spot."

Everley wandered over, still holding her half-finished poster about magnets. "I read about that at the library yesterday. In 1897, J. J. Thomson discovered the electron. Before him, nobody knew atoms had small pieces like that at all."

"Wait," Lucy said. "So out of the three particles, the electron was found first?"

"First and only, for a while," Everley said.

Lucy stared at her lumpy planet. If the electron was discovered before the protons and neutrons were, then it wasn't just decoration around the edge. It mattered. She pictured the bead paths looping outward from the center, like rings, each electron in its own lane instead of wherever the tape happened to land. She grabbed the beads and started threading them onto loops of wire.

The glue was still tacky when Ms. Sow stopped at her table, but the electron rings spun on their wires, one bead per lane, the whole thing turning slowly under the gym lights.

"A hidden cause, an unseen pattern, and a working model," Ms. Sow said. "That's a revolution in thinking, Lucy."

Lucy gave the smallest ring a push and watched the blue bead ride its orbit around and around.

Charlie sat cross-legged on her bed with a box of tissues and her stuffed kangaroo, Pip, wedged under one arm like a joey riding in a pouch. She had been staring at the same page of her book for ten minutes, which was how she knew the flu was winning. Her head thumped, her throat felt like sandpaper, and her mom had diagnosed her that morning with one look and a thermometer: 102.3, back to bed, no arguments.

She reached for her phone and called Sam. "When did you start feeling sick?" she asked, trying to sound assertive instead of whiny, because whiny made people hang up.

"Tuesday night," Sam said. "The headache came first, then the fever. Jude got it too. Remember, we were all at the sleepover Saturday."

Charlie flopped back against her pillows. Saturday. They had built a blanket fort in Jude's basement and stayed up until two, sharing popcorn from the same bowl, three girls with their heads together over one flashlight. Nobody had coughed. Nobody had seemed the least bit sick. That was the part that kept snagging in her mind like a splinter in a sock.

"How could we all catch it from each other if nobody was sick yet?" she asked.

Sam was quiet for a second. "My mom said people with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms. So somebody at the sleepover already had it Saturday. We just couldn't tell."

"One day before," Charlie repeated. Jude had seemed fine, but so had she, and so had Sam. It could have been any of them, passing it around in the blanket fort, invisible as a draft. She thought about how she'd pressed close between them for the scary story, giggling, and how she'd do it again even knowing what she knew now. Maybe. She wasn't sure yet.

"Mom's bringing soup," Sam said. "Call you tomorrow?"

"Deal." Charlie set down the phone, pulled the blanket up to her chin, and hugged Pip tighter against her aching ribs.

The kitten's name was Biscuit, and she rode home from the shelter in a cardboard box with air holes, meowing like a tiny angry trumpet. Jordan's whole family was vegetarian, so his mom had already bought a bag of plant-based cat food, and Biscuit sniffed it, looked at Jordan as if he had personally insulted her, and walked away.

That had been three days ago, and Biscuit had barely eaten since. Her coat, glossy on day one, was starting to look dull. "She's going to deteriorate if this keeps up," Rosalynn said, crouching on the sidewalk in front of Jordan's house while Biscuit stalked a leaf. "My grandpa uses that word about his fence. It means falling apart bit by bit."

Jordan thought about the shelter volunteer who had squatted next to him, before the box, before any of this, and said, "Feed her what cats need, not what you eat." At the time he'd nodded without really listening. Now he stared at Biscuit, who had gone aggressive on a stick, batting it across the driveway like it owed her money, and an idea ticked in his head. Maybe the problem wasn't the food dish. Maybe it was what was in it. Cats, unlike his family, might actually need the stuff that comes from animal flesh. He remembered the volunteer's exact phrase and said it out loud, almost like a test: "Obligate carnivores. That's what she called cats."

"Sounds like a superhero team," Raelynn said from the porch, where she was holding an ice pack to her head after falling off the curb. "I might have a concussion, by the way."

"You fell eight inches."

"Concussions are serious."

Jordan marched inside and came back out with a can of actual meat cat food he'd found buried in the pantry. He set it down. Biscuit froze, whiskers forward, then charged across the driveway and shoved her whole face into the bowl.

"Told you," Jordan said, and scratched her ears while she ate like the leaf, the stick, and the vegetarian kibble had all been warm-ups for this moment.

On the third night of their trip to Taipei, Jeremy sat on the hotel bed with his notebook, trying to build five sentences in Mandarin about his family before bed. Ms. Ito had assigned it before the trip, and tomorrow the class would video-call from the hotel lobby at nine in the morning, Taipei time. He had his mother's phrasebook app, but no signal on his phone, and his older sister Sophie was asleep in the other bed.

The words for mother and father were easy enough. Then he reached his little brother Sam, who was actually not so little: Sam was his twin, born ten minutes after him. The app listed two different words, gēge and dìdi, and Jeremy realized the book expected him to know which one meant what. He texted his friend Lea, who was on the trip with her own family two floors up. "Do you know if dìdi means older or younger brother?" Her reply came back fast: "No idea. My book just says gēge means older brother."

Jeremy sat with that for a moment. If gēge meant older brother, then dìdi had to be the other one, the younger. He tested the idea against the sentences he had already copied: Lea's phrasebook said "Wǒ yǒu yí gè gēge" for "I have an older brother." The pattern held. So for Sam, ten minutes younger, the word was dìdi. The realization felt like an insight landing softly: the language cared about something English never bothered to mark. Sophie stirred and muttered that his desk light was too bright, which did nothing except provoke him to angle the lamp away from her.

At the lobby call the next morning, Khadijah from Ms. Ito's class went first and described her two big brothers with gēge twice, smooth as anything. When Jeremy's turn came, he said, "Wǒ yǒu yí gè dìdi," and held up a photo of Sam on his ninth birthday. Ms. Ito smiled at the screen and asked, "Ten minutes younger?" Jeremy nodded. "Then dìdi is exactly right." Behind him, the hotel clerk, who had been listening, gave him a thumbs up and called out, "Hěn hǎo!" with infectious delight.

At soccer practice on Thursday, Lianna and Bennett stopped speaking to each other, which was a problem because they were the two center midfielders and had to pass to each other. Rebecca found out why when she sat between them on the bench, catching water bottles. Lianna claimed Bennett had told the coach she was too slow for the starting lineup. Bennett swore he had only said the opposite, that Lianna deserved to start. Neither of them would budge.

Rebecca had finished peer mediation training at school only two weeks before. "You know I trained as a peer mediator," she said carefully. "Want me to try the steps on you two?" Mr. Kerr was watching the scrimmage from the far sideline, and she knew the rules said a trained student helps classmates settle conflicts with an adult supervisor available, so she checked with him first. He nodded and said he would stay where she could see him.

She sat Lianna and Bennett on the end of the bench, facing each other, and made herself a neutral spot in the middle, arms uncrossed, taking neither one's hand or side. "One at a time," she said. "Lianna, tell him what you heard, not what you think it meant."

Lianna took a breath. "Maya said you told the coach I was too slow."

Bennett's face went red. "I said you were the fastest player on the team. Maya must have heard the first half and missed the rest." He looked at the ground. "I was trying to get you more minutes, not fewer."

Rebecca noticed something she couldn't see directly, a hidden cause underneath the whole fight. Both of them had been scared of the same thing, losing their spot, and that fear had shaped what each of them believed. She tested the idea out loud. "So the fear of being benched is what this whole fight symbolizes, not anything either of you actually did?"

Lianna blinked. "I guess that's true. I was terrified about Saturday."

"Me too," Bennett admitted.

Rebecca asked what they needed from each other, which was the step she always forgot in practice role plays. Lianna asked him to come to her directly next time instead of talking to the coach behind her back. Bennett asked her not to believe Maya's version without checking. They agreed on both.

When Mr. Kerr called them back onto the field, Lianna stood up first and offered Bennett her fist. He bumped it. Then he passed her the ball, and she ran onto the grass with it, both of them chasing the play side by side.

Thomas stood at the kitchen counter with ten dollars in his pocket and a note from his mother that said, simply, "Milk. Whole." It was his first solo mission to the corner store, three blocks away, and he had studied the route so many times that he could draw it with his eyes closed. He told his friend Raymond about it at breakfast, since Raymond had done the same run since he was ten.

"The hard part isn't the walking," Raymond said. "It's the change. The cashier talks fast and there's a line behind you, and you panic and shove everything in your pocket."

Thomas had a plan for that. He would count his money before he went in, then count the change at the counter, right there, in front of everyone, even if it took forever. He set out at four o'clock, when the sunlight refracted off the puddle at the end of his street in a way that made the whole puddle look like it was on fire. He walked past it carefully, as if it might be.

The store smelled like cardboard and oranges. He found the dairy case and picked up the first carton of whole milk. Then something stopped him. He looked at the date on top, then lifted the carton behind it. The date on that one was later. He checked a third carton, way at the back, and its date was later still. He stood there holding three cartons of milk like a man playing a very slow game of cards.

"That's first in, first out," said a woman reaching past him for cream. "Older stuff goes in front." She said it the way you'd mention the weather, then left with her cream.

Thomas slid his hand to the back and took the carton with the latest date. At the register he counted his change out loud, one coin at a time, while the man behind him sighed with what could only be described as despair. The cashier waited without complaint, which Thomas decided counted as a small act of kindness. He counted again on the way home, on the bench by the fire hydrant, and it was right: four dollars and sixty-one cents.

Back in the kitchen, his mother opened the bag, looked at the carton, and turned it over. "You got the one with the latest date," she said. "How?"

"The front ones were older," Thomas said. "The good ones hide at the back." He put the change on the counter, coin by coin, in a neat silver line, and slid the last quarter into place with one finger.

Emile was eating toast at the kitchen table with his tablet propped against the nectar bottle, because that was the only spot the hummingbird feeder juice hadn't dripped on, when his class chat lit up. He typed a joke about the math homework: "Ms. Ndlovu said we can skip the whole assignment if we bring her a coffee." It was obviously ridiculous. He hit send and went back to his toast.

Two minutes later Paula messaged him privately. "Are you serious? Is that allowed? I don't have a coffee. Should I bring money instead?" Then Nixon posted in the group: "PAULA IS WALKING TO THE CAFE RIGHT NOW." Emile groaned. At school, if he'd said it out loud, Paula would have heard his voice going silly on the word "coffee" and laughed. In here his words just sat there, flat, with nothing wrapped around them. He typed "IT WAS A JOGG" and deleted it, because spelling errors would only irritate her more when she was already halfway to the cafe.

He set down his toast and wondered. Somebody must have noticed this problem before, right? People writing to each other without faces, jokes landing like bricks. He searched "how to show a message is a joke." That led him to a page about a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman, who had proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. Emile stared at the little sideways face. Nearly forty years before Emile was typing, a grown man had solved Emile's exact problem with three marks on a keyboard. He copied it and pasted it after his joke in the group chat: "Bring her a coffee :-)"

Paula wrote back within seconds. "Oh. OH. Why didn't you put the face on it the first time?" Nixon sent a row of laughing faces, which felt like showing off, like his whole personality was somehow more sophisticated than Emile's three humble marks. Emile tried it on his little brother at dinner, saying "the dog ate my homework" with a straight face, and got no reaction until he drew :-) on a napkin and slid it across the table.

The next morning Ms. Ndlovu collected the assignments and looked at Emile over her glasses. "I hear there was a coffee involved." "It was a joke," Emile said. "I had to prove it." She held out her hand, palm up, waiting, so he drew the smiley in the air with his finger and she nodded once and moved on down the row.

Paige leaned over the glass counter at Mr. Tran's corner store, staring at a chocolate bar broken into pieces. Mr. Tran had cracked it into fourths on one side and sixths on the other, because a shipment had arrived crushed and he was selling the pieces by weight.

"Two dollars for the whole thing," he said, "but you three have to split it and split the price too, before the 4:15 bus comes. I close at four."

Paige, Marilyn, and Ryden had exactly sixteen minutes. Ryden wanted the fourths side because the pieces were bigger. Marilyn wanted the sixths side because there were more of them. Paige, who had gotten a D on last week's fraction quiz, just wanted everyone to pay a fair share.

"Okay," said Marilyn, pulling out a notebook on the counter. "One fourth plus one sixth. I'll use 24 as the denominator, because both numbers divide into it. That's six twenty-fourths plus four twenty-fourths, so ten twenty-fourths each if we each take some of both."

Ryden frowned at her numbers. "That works," he admitted, "but those are huge fractions. There has to be something smaller."

Paige had been making a quiet assumption all week, the one that had wrecked her quiz: that unlike denominators just couldn't be added, period. Now she stared at the broken bar itself. Sixths and fourths lay side by side, and she formulated a new idea out loud. "What if we chop every piece so they're all the same size? Like, cut each sixth in half and each fourth into three." She traced it with her finger on the chocolate. Fourths became twelfths. Sixths became twelfths.

"Twelve," Ryden said slowly. "Both 4 and 6 divide into it evenly."

"And it's smaller than 24," Marilyn said, surprise in her voice. She erased her work. "So the least common denominator is the smallest number both denominators divide into evenly. For quarters and sixths it's 12. I've been doing it the hard way all year." She laughed. "Ironic, right? More pieces, more math, same answer."

They counted: each of them would get three twelfths of the bar, which was a fourth, and pay fifty cents. Mr. Tran weighed the pieces, nodded, and rang it up as the bus rumbled toward the stop outside.

"Wrap it," Paige said, sliding her coins across the counter. "I have a quiz on Thursday, and this bar is coming with me."

Theo pressed the measuring cup into the bag of flour and packed it full, then leveled it off with the back of a knife, the way he always did. Ms. Warsame's community kitchen smelled like butter and cinnamon, and tonight he was making cookies for his family's Friday dinner, the batch he'd been promising for two weeks. His little sister had asked for soft, bendy cookies, the kind you could fold without breaking, and he intended to deliver.

He had made this recipe once before, at home, and the cookies had come out dry and cakey, more like muffin tops than cookies. He'd followed every step meticulously, so it made no sense. He'd blamed the oven, then the butter, and finally given up.

Hashim leaned over the counter beside him, stirring his own bowl of granola. "Mine always work," Hashim said, a little too cheerfully. He wanted to win the kitchen's mini baking table this month, and the chocolate chip category was still open. "Maybe you just have bad cookie karma."

"Karma isn't real," Theo said. "Something else is going on." He looked at his cup of flour, then at the recipe card. It said two and a quarter cups. He had measured exactly that at home too. So what was different?

He watched Vera, who was rolling dough at the next station. She had a small kitchen scale, and she was pouring flour into a bowl on it, bit by bit, until the number read what she wanted. "Why bother weighing?" he asked her.

Vera shrugged. "My grandma showed me. Scooping flour straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup can hold much more flour than a recipe expects. Weighing flour is more accurate." She tapped the scale. "I aim for the same grams every time now."

Theo stood still, holding his packed cup. If his cup held too much flour, then his dough had too much flour in it, even though he'd measured right. That could be why it came out dry and cakey. It was like steering a boat with a bent rudder: he'd been aiming correctly the whole time, but something underneath pushed him off course.

He asked Vera if he could borrow the scale, and she slid it over. He tapped his packed cup of flour out into a bowl on the scale and read the number. Then he spooned flour gently into another cup, leveled it, and weighed that. The numbers were different. He weighed out what the recipe card listed in grams, one bowl at a time, and mixed his dough. It looked softer and glossier than his batch at home, and it sagged a little when he dropped spoonfuls onto the pan.

While the cookies baked, Hashim sneaked over and weighed a scoop of his own flour. He wrote the number on his wrist with a pen, frowning. "I've been packing mine too," he admitted. "Every single batch." The timer rang, and Theo pulled the pan out. The cookies were golden at the edges and soft in the middle, and he bent one gently in half. It folded without breaking. Vera looked over and said, "That one's going on the table board."

Emilie spread her draft across the library table and read her first paragraph out loud in a whisper. Her essay argued that the school should start a lacrosse team, and her strongest reason, the one she had put in the middle paragraph, was that everyone at school wanted it. She had asked around at lunch, and forty-two students had said yes. That felt like proof.

Drake sat down across from her, sliding a graphic novel aside. "Is that the lacrosse essay? Can I read it when you're done? My mom says I have to bring home something I wrote this week, and I want to see how a real one looks." He leaned over her paper.

"Sure," Emilie said. She pointed at her middle paragraph. "But something about this reason feels thin. Forty-two people want a team. So what?"

Drake read it and shrugged. "That's a lot of people."

Emilie tapped her pencil. Last week, she remembered, the whole cafeteria had lined up for the mystery meat special just because the line was long, and half of them had hated it. Everyone doing something had not made it good. She flipped to the glossary of her writing handbook and ran her finger down the F column. There it was: a named mistake where something is treated as right or good simply because many people believe it or do it.

"Oh," she said. "That's the bandwagon fallacy. My whole reason is a bandwagon fallacy."

"You can't build your essay on that?"

"Not and get a decent grade, I think." She crossed out the sentence and started testing a better reason: the school had no spring sport for kids who couldn't afford club fees, and a team would fix that. She wrote fast, hopeful now.

Ms. Kapoor passed their table and paused at the pile of crossed-out drafts. "Revising?"

"Testing," Emilie said, and slid the finished essay toward Drake.

The lights went out all over Grandma's street at exactly 7:14, because Chloe was watching the clock on the microwave when it died. She heard her grandmother sigh from the kitchen, then the scrape of a chair, then footsteps in the dark. "Well," Grandma said, "there go my plans to vacuum."

Chloe found the candles in the drawer by the stove, the drawer that held a flashlight with dead batteries, three rubber bands, and a letter she had never noticed before. It was addressed to Grandma in loopy handwriting, and while Grandma lit the candle, Chloe squinted at it by the flame. "Grandma, can I read this? It's from Haven's mom, from years ago." The wax seal had already been broken long ago, and the paper smelled like the inside of an old book.

Go ahead, Grandma said, so Chloe read it out loud, doing what she privately called her narrator voice, the one she used when Haven and Arwa made her read the announcements at school. The letter was mostly about a camping trip, but the last part said: I read that a 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light. Isn't that something? Eighty percent of us. We stood in a field and there it was, like a spilled bag of sugar across the sky. Haven slept through the whole thing.

"That's us," Chloe said. "The eighty percent. I've never seen it." She thought of last spring, when she'd told Arwa the night sky was boring, just the same five dots every night, and Arwa had looked at her like she'd said books were boring. Chloe had laughed it off then. Now, holding the letter, she wasn't sure she wanted to be the kind of person who laughed things off.

"Whole street's dark," Grandma said. "Might as well test it." They stepped onto the porch in their socks, and Chloe looked up and stopped breathing for a second. There were not five stars. There were hundreds, and across the middle of the sky ran a pale, grainy river of them, exactly like spilled sugar. Somewhere down the block a dog barked twice and quit. Chloe's socks were getting damp from the porch boards, and she didn't care.

Tomorrow she would tell Haven, whose own mother had written that letter and never mentioned it once in six years of carpool. Arwa might ridicule her for taking so long to look up, and Chloe decided she could live with that. "I'm going to draw it before the lights come back," she said, defiant against the whole idea of ordinary skies, and she went inside to find paper.

The bus let them off in front of the museum just as the doors opened, and Jackson was third in line, right behind Leyla and Ryland. Ms. Demir counted heads twice, then passed out the clipboards. The assignment was to sketch three objects, but Jackson kept getting distracted by small silver boxes tucked into the corners of the display cases, each one with a dial and a thin needle.

"It's a humidity gauge," the guide said when Leyla pointed at one and asked what it was. Then she moved on toward the marble statues, her voice transmitting down the gallery in a flat echo.

Jackson stayed behind. The gauge in the case with an old wooden violin read fifty-one, and the needle was steady. At lunch, in the courtyard, he turned his clipboard over and wrote what he knew. Museums controlled the temperature and humidity. That part was obvious, or the gauges wouldn't be there. But why?

He looked at the questions through the lens of the violin itself. Wood, paper, canvas. He pressed his thumbnail into his sandwich bread and watched the dent stay. Soft things soaked up damp air; dry things gave it back. His own bedroom door stuck shut every August and swung free in January, because the wood swelled and shrank with the weather. If the whole violin swelled and shrank, over and over, the seams would pull, and eventually something would crack or warp. That was the whole reason for the gauges.

Back inside, testing the idea, he stood by the tall window near the instrument cases. He pressed his palm to the glass; it was warm, and outside the sun beat down. A delivery door at the end of the hall stood propped open, and he could feel the outdoor air sliding across the floor, humid and heavy, straight toward the violin case. The gauge's needle had crept up to fifty-four.

Jackson found Ms. Demir by the coatroom. "The delivery door's open near the instruments," he said. "I think it's changing the humidity."

She looked at him for a second, then walked down the hall and pulled the door shut herself. Jackson went back to the case. The needle stood still, and behind the glass the violin lay indifferent to all of it, strings quiet, wood safe in its steady air.

Leyla leaned over his shoulder. "You didn't sketch anything yet."

"I sketched a gauge," Jackson said, and turned his clipboard around to show her.

Joseph stood on the porch of the Tanaka family's house holding a box of almond cookies, and he could not stop staring at the floor. It was his cousin's engagement party, and the whole extended family had been invited, which meant Joseph knew almost nobody except his aunt and uncle. The entryway was lower than the rest of the house, a shallow trench of wooden flooring with a whole row of shoes lined up along one edge, toes pointing toward the door. Two pairs of slippers sat waiting on the higher step like they were expecting somebody.

He was still deciding what to do when a girl his age came up behind him with her mother. Without hesitating, she stepped out of her sneakers, set them neatly beside the others, and slid her feet into slippers. Joseph copied her, feeling clumsy, and kept one hand on the doorframe for balance. His dress shoes looked wrong there, tipped over on their side, so he knelt and straightened them to match the row.

"You must be Joseph," the girl said. "I'm Lorelai. Our moms are cousins." She glanced at his cookies. "Those are for the table? My grandpa calls the entryway the genkan. Everybody's shoes live there."

Joseph wanted to ask a dozen things, starting with how anybody remembered all these rules, but he held back and watched instead. At the doorway to the kitchen he noticed a second, smaller pile of footwear, bathroom slippers lined up by themselves, and a boy he recognized from school, King, stepping out of one pair and into another like changing lanes. Was every room in this house its own small country with its own border crossing? He began to classify the shoes by room: hard slippers for the hallway, rubber ones for the bathroom, socks everywhere else.

Dinner was long and wonderful and full of traps. At home Joseph's family passed plates with reaching forks and elbows everywhere; here each dish arrived with a small ceremony, offered with two hands, received with two hands. When he gave his grandmother's gift, the almond cookies, Lorelai's grandfather accepted it with both palms and a slight bow, then set it, unopened, on a shelf near the door. Joseph felt a flicker of worry. Had he chosen badly? But King had brought a wrapped package too, and it also sat unopened, and Lorelai's mother's gift from yesterday was still sitting there in its paper. A pattern, Joseph thought. Not rejection. Patience.

The only real crisis came when Joseph wandered toward the back hallway in his socks, chasing the smell of grilled fish, and Lorelai's grandmother gasped and waved him back. He looked down and saw it: his socked feet had crossed onto the tatami room's raised edge, where another pair of slippers waited, and a fresh set of shoes sat by the back door as if someone had just gone into the garden. It seemed almost paradox to him that a house so full of rules never once scolded him; people just pointed, smiled, and moved him along like a chess piece.

At the end of the night, he found his own shoes exactly where he had left them, toes pointing out, ready for the road. He stepped down into the genkan, pushed his feet in, and heard Lorelai laugh behind him.

"First time?" she asked.

"Is it that obvious?"

"You bowed to your own shoes," she said.

Emma stood at the baseline of the gym with nineteen other kids, all of them waiting for the tryouts to start. Ms. Martínez held a clipboard and a speaker that would do the judging today. "First we run the beep test," she announced. "Back and forth between the cones, twenty meters apart. You have to reach the line before each beep." Emma glanced down the court. The cones at each end looked small and far away, like punctuation marks on a very long sentence.

"Twenty meters is the full width of the court plus a bit more," whispered Bianca, who was beside her, stretching her hamstrings. "I've done this at my old school." Emma nodded, but her mind had already gone somewhere else. A math problem. If the beeps came at a steady pace, she could sprint the first few and rest later. But what if the beeps didn't stay steady? She raised her hand. "Ms. Martínez, does the time between beeps change?" Ms. Martínez smiled like someone who enjoyed that question. "Listen for yourself."

The first level began, and the beeps came slow and lazy, almost polite. Emma trotted, touched the line, trotted back. On the second level the beeps were quicker. On the third, quicker again. So that was the pattern: each new level meant less time to cover the same twenty meters. It was like an algorithm, she thought, one that kept tightening its rules every round. Her original plan, sprint early and coast later, suddenly looked like a bad idea. If she burned everything now, the later levels would eat her alive.

She changed her mind mid-stride. Instead of dashing to the line with seconds to spare, she timed her steps to arrive just before each beep, saving every scrap of energy. Beside her, Raven was sprinting hard and arriving five seconds early every time, then standing still, then sprinting again. "You're going to tire out," Emma panted as they passed. "You have to be fast later, not just now." Raven gave her an acute, skeptical look, the kind that said prove it.

Level six arrived and the beeps snapped at their heels like a small angry dog. Raven, whose legs had turned heavy, missed two beeps in a row and was told to step out. Emma kept her rhythm, arriving with barely a breath to spare, over and over, until the gym blurred and her lungs burned. At level eight, three runners were left. At level eight's final lap, Emma missed by one step and Ms. Martínez blew the whistle.

She bent over, hands on her knees, gulping air. Bianca had also made it through level eight, and the two of them stood together as Ms. Martínez read the list of names for the second round of tryouts. Emma heard her own name and something in her chest jumped higher than she ever had. "Tomorrow," Ms. Martínez said, checking her watch, "we scrimmage at four sharp. Anyone late sits the first half." Emma grinned at Bianca. "Want to petition her for a practice court tonight?" Bianca was already bouncing a ball. "Race you to the outdoor hoops."

Natalie sorted the tray of small balls at her lab station while Scarlette pushed the foam base across the counter. Ms. Visser had assigned each pair of students an element, and theirs was carbon. The instructions said to place the protons, neutrons and electrons in the right positions, with protons and neutrons clustered in the middle and electrons in rings around them.

"Tucker says the middle doesn't matter as long as it looks good," Scarlette said, gluing the nucleus together.

"That's the conventional way people draw it in cartoons, but Ms. Visser wants the counts right," Natalie said. She counted six red balls into the nucleus. "Six protons."

They added six grey neutrons, then Scarlette handed her the bag of blue electrons. Natalie stuck four onto the wire rings before the bag ran out.

At the next station, Tucker leaned over. "Ours is oxygen. Eight of everything." He studied their model and frowned. "You've only got four electrons. Did you lose some?"

Natalie checked the floor under the counter. Nothing. "Maybe Ms. Visser just gave us fewer."

"Then it should balance," Tucker said. "Four is even, six is even."

Natalie looked at the model again. The red protons were marked with plus signs and the blue electrons with minus signs, the way the diagram on the board showed them. She pulled the diagram closer and counted the symbols in the carbon box.

"Protons are positive and electrons are negative," she said slowly. "A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so the charges cancel out."

"So ours doesn't cancel," Scarlette said. "Ours is off by two."

"I was wrong about it balancing," Tucker said. He got up and walked to the supply cabinet.

Ms. Visser came over while Scarlette was threading the fifth blue ball onto the outer ring. "Missing pieces?" she asked.

"The tray was short," Natalie said. "We counted."

Ms. Visser opened the cabinet and shook a fresh bag of electrons into Natalie's palm. Natalie threaded the last one on, counted six and six, and set the finished carbon model beside the diagram, charges matched.

Eve pressed her ear against the long metal trough of water just as Alejandro tapped a tuning fork against the counter. The hum arrived almost instantly, sharp and quick, like someone plucking a wire inside her head. When she lifted her head and he tapped the fork again in the open air, the sound seemed to dawdle on its way to her, softer and slower, though she knew it had only crossed the same distance.

"Did you hear that?" she asked. "It got to me faster through the water."

Sawer frowned. "Sound can't be faster in water. Water's heavier. Heavy things slow you down, like running through a pool."

"That's your legs," Eve said. "Sound isn't legs."

Ms. Bianchi, who was stacking trays at the back of the lab, raised an eyebrow but said nothing. She had a rule for the afternoons when the three of them stayed late: she would hand out equipment and answer questions with only "yes," "no," or "test it." Eve suspected this was her way of making them isolate the real question from all the guessing.

Eve's question was simple now. If sound reached her ear faster or slower depending on what it traveled through, what happened once it got there? She could not see inside her own ear. "There has to be something in there that catches it," she said. "Like a drum catching a stick."

Alejandro dragged the rolling cart closer. On it sat the model Ms. Bianchi had borrowed from the museum, an ear built giant-sized, its outer curve taller than Eve. Alejandro swung open a panel on its side so they could see within. There was a thin stretched sheet, and behind it three little bones in a row.

"That flat part," Sawyer said, tracing it with a finger, "has to be the eardrum. Sound hits it and it shakes."

Eve touched the first small bone. "Then these pass the shaking along, deeper inside." She tapped the sheet gently with a pencil eraser and all three bones wobbled, one after another, quick as a chain of dominoes. "It's like the vibration hops across them." She pointed at each in turn. "That one looks like a hammer. That one's flat like an anvil, and that last one is shaped like a stirrup."

"So the hammer, the anvil, and the stirrup," Alejandro said slowly, as if filing the names somewhere safe.

The door opened and a parent arrived to pick up Sawyer, but Sawyer lingered, holding a paper cup of water to one ear while Alejandro hummed at the other end of the table. In the corner the radiator ticked in the dry, arid air of the overheated lab, and Eve thought the tick sounded fainter than it should.

"Here's what I think," she said. "Sound is just shaking. And the molecules in water are packed closer together than in air, so the shaking gets passed along faster, the way these three bones pass it along. The drum can't do the work alone. It needs things touching it."

Ms. Bianchi, gathering her keys, paused on her way out. "Ambassador of the science fair," she said, dropping a sign-up sheet on the bench beside the model ear, "should probably demonstrate that with the fork and the trough."

Eve picked up the tuning fork and struck it once, hard, against the counter.

The library's computer room smelled like pencil shavings and old carpet, and Maeva had exactly one hour before it closed. Tomorrow her class would debate whether an ad disguised as a search result was fair, and Mr. Chukwu had put her on the "not fair" side. The problem was that she didn't yet know what she was talking about.

"Try searching hummingbirds," suggested Joseph, leaning over from the next computer. "You like hummingbirds." Maeva typed hummingbird food recipe, and a list of links appeared. The first one had a tiny pale box in the corner with the word Ad inside it. She had never noticed that box before, not once, and now she couldn't stop seeing it.

"There are two kinds of results," Kian said from across the table, squinting at her screen. "The ones the search engine finds on its own, and the ones somebody paid to put there." He was supposed to argue the "fair" side tomorrow, and he grinned at her like he already knew he'd win. Maeva scrolled down and clicked the first non-ad result, a site about nectar mixes for hummingbird feeders, because the ad at the top had the same recipe but with a whole online store attached. Something about that felt sneaky, though she couldn't have said why yet.

Then she tried a test. She searched cheap flammable cabinet paint, and then safe cabinet paint, and compared where the paid links showed up. They always sat at the top, dressed up to look like the real results, like a costume. If the Ad labels were small enough, a person in a hurry would click the paid one without ever knowing. Her stomach did a small flip. That was the hidden pattern, and she had found it herself, at a library computer, with forty minutes left on the clock.

She typed federal trade commission search engines into the search box, adding each word carefully the way she'd been practicing, narrowing instead of widening. The result she wanted sat third on the page, no Ad box on it at all. And there it was: in 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users. She read it twice. "It's actually a rule," she said out loud. "Natural results. That's what they call the real ones."

Kian came around the table and read over her shoulder, and his grin faded into something more thoughtful. "Huh," he said. "Maybe I should switch sides." Before the room closed, Maeva grabbed a scrap paper from the front desk and wrote him a note: "Trade you. You take not fair, I'll argue fair, since the rule makes them label the ads. Meet at the playground at nine if you agree." She slid it across the table, and Kian read it, laughed once, and turned the paper over to write back. "Deal," his reply said, "but you're buying the popsicles."

Adam slid his library copy of "The Bridge to Terabithia" across the table and hoped nobody would call on him first. Mr. Toussaint had written one question on the board before book club started: What is this book really about, and can you prove it? Adam knew what the book was about on the surface, a creek, a rope, two kids, but the underneath part, the theme, kept hiding from him like a fish under a rock.

Kaylin went first. "I think it's about how friendship changes you," she said, "and Jess changes because Leslie teaches him imagination." She read her quotation from a sticky note: "She had made him leave his old self behind." Josue frowned at his own copy and turned pages, hunting.

Adam remembered, suddenly, a rainy afternoon last fall when he had tried to fix his grandfather's old radio. He had pulled the back off, thinking he could just dismantle it and see what was wrong, and instead he had found a jumble of parts that meant nothing until his grandfather pointed at one small wire. You don't understand a thing by taking it apart, his grandfather had said. You understand it by noticing what everything has in common. Maybe a theme worked like that. Adam flipped through the book, not looking for one perfect sentence but for a pattern, and he kept finding the same thing: Jess running, drawing, building, pretending. Leslie gave him permission to imagine. He raised his hand. "I think the theme is that imagination makes even an ordinary life fertile, like it can grow things that weren't there before. Like Jess's art." He quoted from memory: "It was up to him to pay back to the world in beauty and caring what Leslie had loaned him in vision and courage."

Mr. Toussaint tilted his head. "Close. Check the page."

Adam found the page, and his stomach dropped. Two words were wrong. The real line said "for beauty and caring," not "to the world in beauty and caring," and it said "in the beauty" somewhere he hadn't remembered at all. "I got some of it wrong," he admitted.

"Then it's not evidence yet," Mr. Toussaint said, sliding a pencil toward him. "It has to be copied word for word, same spelling and punctuation, inside quotation marks."

Adam copied it carefully, letter by letter, checking twice, and even Josue leaned over to verify the quotation marks. At the end of the meeting, Kaylin passed him a folded note: "Yours was the best motive for our next book. Co-present with me Tuesday?" He read it twice, wrote "Deal" underneath, and handed it back on her way out the door.

The storm knocked the power out at Lya's house just after six, and the three of them, Hazel, Lya, and Charles-Antoine, were left in the half-dark living room with a board game half set up and nothing else to do. Lya's father went out to the shed and came back saying the generator would run the fridge and one lamp, so they dragged the game to the kitchen table under the lamp's cone of light.

Then they found the problem. The game needed exactly two territories dealt out for the starting hand, and there was one packet of cards that had already been opened. Lya and Charles-Antoine each grabbed for it at the same time. Charles-Antoine said he was the guest. Lya said it was her house. The mood around the table turned volatile fast, and Hazel could see the whole evening going with it if she didn't salvage the game now.

She thought about her two cousins at a birthday party last spring, screaming over the last piece of cake until her grandmother stepped in. Grandma hadn't just cut the cake. She had made one cousin cut it and let the other cousin pick first, and the screaming stopped, because the cutter suddenly wanted both pieces to be exactly the same. Hazel hadn't understood it at the time, but now, watching Lya and Charles-Antoine glare at each other, she worked out the pattern: the person dividing has a reason to make the parts equal, because the other person picks first.

"Okay," Hazel said. "Charles-Antoine, you split the cards into two groups. Lya picks which group she wants first." Charles-Antoine frowned, then shuffled the packet and laid out two piles, counting each card twice. Lya studied both piles, took one, and pushed the rest across the table.

Charles-Antoine flipped through his pile. "These are actually even," he said, sounding almost disappointed.

"Set them down, it's your move," Lya said, and she shook the dice in her fist.

The trumpet in Jeremy's case felt heavier every Thursday, and he knew why. He'd practice for two whole hours on Wednesday night, his lips aching, and then walk into the community center band room and flub the same three notes in front of Sami and Atticus.

"Again?" Sami said, not meanly, just surprised.

"I practiced forever," Jeremy said. "My cheeks practically fell off."

Ms. López tapped the music stand. "From the top, everybody."

That night Jeremy flopped on his bed and stared at the ceiling. Something didn't add up. Last summer he'd tried to teach himself to juggle by throwing balls for one marathon Saturday, and he'd ended up chasing oranges all over the kitchen. Then he'd juggled for just five minutes every day after breakfast, and by August he could do it without thinking. Was the trumpet like that? He couldn't see inside his own brain to check, but maybe he could run a test.

So he spread his practice out. Ten minutes Monday, ten Tuesday, ten Wednesday, small bites instead of one giant meal. He wrote the times on a sticky note so he'd know if his intuition about the plan was right.

Thursday came. He lifted the horn, and the notes came out clean, one after another, like water from a tap.

"There it is!" Atticus shouted from the second row.

Sami leaned over. "What did you do different?"

"Short practices, every day," Jeremy said. "Same total time, just spread out. One big night of practice doesn't stick the same way."

"Wait," Sami said. "I cram every Wednesday too."

Ms. López smiled and raised her baton. "Then this is going to be an interesting month."

Jeremy raised the trumpet to his lips and thought, with a small thrill, that even his fancy new routine was really just one simple trick. "Count us in," he said.

Lauren stood at the picnic table in the backyard, cracking eggs into a bowl while her father lit the grill. Tonight was her turn to cook, and she had appointed herself head chef of the pancakes, a decision she was starting to regret. Her little brother, Evan, sat on the porch steps with a clipboard, because he had decided the pancakes needed judging, and fairness was his one criterion: five points if they tasted good, zero if they tasted like soap.

The first batch came out flat and strangely bitter. Evan took one bite, made a face like a deflating balloon, and wrote a large zero. "This," he announced, "is the worst contemporary cuisine I have ever reviewed."

"Thanks, Evan."

Lauren looked at the little box she had used instead of baking powder, because the baking powder tin was empty and she'd figured the two were basically the same thing. Clearly they were not. She flipped the pancake over and studied it, thinking. The muffins she made last month had baking soda in them, but that recipe also had buttermilk, which was sour. This pancake recipe had no buttermilk, no lemon juice, nothing sour at all. She turned the empty tin over and read the ingredient list on the paper label she had peeled off earlier. Then she called Adelyn, who baked constantly.

"Baking powder is different," Adelyn said. "Baking powder already has baking soda and a dry acid in it, so it works even when the recipe has nothing sour."

Lauren hung up and stared at the bowl. So the acid had to come from somewhere. She couldn't see it or taste it, but the pancake recipe got its rise from that hidden partnership inside the powder. Since she only had plain baking soda, she would have to supply the acid herself. She stirred in a spoonful of lemon juice, watched the batter fizz and puff up like something alive, and ladled it onto the griddle.

The second pancakes rose into golden rounds. Evan circled the table twice, tasted, and held up his clipboard with a shaky five written on it, plus a star he drew on afterward.

"I'm still the judge," he said, reaching for a third pancake.

The pharmacy smelled like mint and cough drops, and Alyssa stood in the deodorant aisle feeling like a spy on her first mission. Her mom had given her ten dollars and one instruction: pick something, because "your armpits have opinions now." She grabbed a purple stick labeled "fresh rain" and pretended she was sophisticated enough to know what fresh rain was supposed to smell like. Rain smelled like wet sidewalk, in her expert opinion.

Then she heard a familiar groan from the next aisle. Linden was staring at a mirror display, pressing one finger against the three red spots on his chin like he was trying to push them back in.

"It's over," he said. "My face is ruined. I'm the villain of the seventh grade now."

"You're not the antagonist of anything," Alyssa said. "You're the antagonist of one mirror." She came around the shelf and looked at the acne section, which was enormous, wall after wall of creams and washes and tiny stickers you put on spots overnight. That gave her an idea. If acne were rare, why would there be enough products to fill a whole wall?

She turned the nearest box over and found a fact printed on the back, and she read it out loud. "It says here that about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne."

Linden lowered his finger. "Eighty-five? Out of a hundred?"

"Out of a hundred. So in any classroom, look around and most people either have it or will."

"That's basically everyone," Linden said. "Genevieve's going to get it too. And Marcus. Even the principal, if he's under 24." He grinned, then checked himself. "Wait, how old is the principal?"

"No idea, but I'm not asking." Alyssa held up her purple deodorant. "Also, we apparently smell now, so I'm buying this."

"Get me one too," Linden said. "The manliest fresh rain they have."

The community centre camp split into two teams on Monday morning by drawing names from a plastic tub. Ariana drew a red card, so she was on the Red team, and her best friend Daria drew blue and stood across the gym with the others. By Wednesday, the Red team chanted whenever they beat Blue at floor hockey, and Josie, who was on Blue, refused to sit with Ariana at lunch. "It's just a game," Ariana said, and Josie said, "You're on Red, you wouldn't get it."

Ariana thought about that all through swim time. The teams had not been chosen for skill or friendship or anything at all. The cards came out of a tub at random. So why did everyone act like the tub meant something? On Thursday she devised a test. She cut thirty paper squares, wrote A on fifteen and B on fifteen, folded them, and dropped them in an empty tennis ball can. Then she walked the waiting room outside the gym and asked kids to draw one and pin it to their shirts.

Within an hour, the A kids had claimed the good couch by the vending machine and were telling B kids it was full, even when it wasn't. Nobody had said the teams were for anything. Ariana watched a boy named only in her head as Tall Kid grab his square, see the B, and sigh like he'd lost something. Two girls who came in together drew different letters and ended up on opposite sides of the room by choice.

She looked it up later in the community centre's small library, where a shelf held Mr. Lau's old psychology books. One chapter described experiments by a psychologist named Henri Tajfel. People favoured their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random. Ariana read it twice, then copied it onto the back of a red card.

On Friday she left the tennis ball can on the lunch table with a sign that said "Pick a letter." Josie read the sign, drew a card, and looked at the B. Ariana held up her own card, which she had not drawn from anything, and flipped it over to show the copied sentence. Josie read it, then slid her tray around the corner of the table and said, "Sit down, Red."

The group chat lit up at 7:42, right after dinner. Paisley had sent a photo of a birthday card covered in looping handwriting no one could read. "My grandma sent this," the message said. "She writes in Romanian. I can talk to her on the phone for an hour but I have zero idea what this says. None."

Maeva stared at the photo, then at her own reflection in the dark window. That was exactly her. She could chatter with her grandmother in Creole about school, recipes, and the neighbor's suspicious cat, but the luminous gold card on her dresser, from her own birthday last month, was still a mystery. Her grandmother had watched her open it, and Maeva had smiled and hugged her and never admitted the truth. Now Paisley's message glowed on the screen, and the truth felt heavier than it had on her birthday.

"Wait, you speak it but you can't read it?" Drake typed. "How is that even possible?"

Maeva's thumbs hovered. She thought she knew the answer, but she wanted to test it first, because a guess in a group chat stays there forever. She typed: "Question for everybody. Does anyone's family speak a different language at home than the one we use at school?" The replies came fast. Drake's mom spoke Tagalog. A kid in Ms. Otieno's class, according to Paisley, spoke Marshallese with her grandfather. Then Ms. Otieno herself appeared in the chat, since it was her classroom channel. "Heritage language," she wrote, four words, and Maeva read the phrase twice.

There it was. The pattern. A language spoken at home, in the family, that was different from the main language outside, and you could speak it every single day without ever learning its letters. Nobody had taught Paisley to read Romanian, and nobody had taught Maeva to read Creole, because school and books and street signs had all sustained only English. It wasn't lazy or strange. It was a rule, and the rule had a name, and half their class apparently lived inside it.

Then came the message that made her stop breathing for a second. Paisley: "My grandma is calling me tonight. She's going to ask what the card said." The chat went quiet. Maeva could hear her own grandmother humming in the kitchen, could smell the plantains frying, could feel the birthday card's stiff paper in her memory. She had been planning to keep pretending forever. She changed her mind in the space of one deep breath.

She typed slowly. "Tell her the truth. I'm going to tell mine tonight that I can't read her card, and I'm going to ask her to teach me. Want to learn together?" The typing bubble appeared, disappeared, appeared again. Finally Paisley answered with a single line, and Maeva read it out loud to the kitchen.

"Saturday. Bring the cards."

"Sorry, but in chess that matters," Mr. Hernández said, tapping the knight Kayla had just set back down on its square. "Touch a piece on purpose, you move it, if it has a legal move. That's called the touch-move rule."

Kayla stared at the knight. She had picked it up only to look at the horse's carved mane, and now it had to march into danger, where Deanna's bishop waited like a trap. "But we never said that rule," she protested. "We're just playing in your kitchen."

"Formal chess uses it," Deanna said, chewing the end of her braid.

Kayla moved the knight anyway. Deanna's bishop took it two turns later, and the loss felt significant, like a whole door slamming shut on her attack. She slumped until her chair creaked.

Across the table, Adeline, who had been watching from the counter with a mug of cocoa, came and sat down. "You look how I felt last week when Deanna flipped the board," she said. Kayla laughed, a small one, because she could picture it exactly. That bit of empathy loosened something in her shoulders. Instead of giving up, she decided to test an idea: if the problem wasn't the rule but not knowing the rules, she could fix that.

"Okay," Kayla said. "New game. But first let's name the problem. The problem is that some of us know tournament rules and some of us don't."

"So let's agree on one rule," Deanna said. "Say 'adjusting' before you straighten a piece. Then touch-move doesn't bite you."

"And to practice," Adeline said, "we could simulate a tournament round, complete with a clock and everything."

Mr. Hernández slid the timers out of a drawer and set the pieces back on their squares, all thirty-two of them, the pawns clicking down the rank one by one.

Kayla reached toward her queen, stopped, and said, "Adjusting."

Michael needed one more fact for his poster about why the town should build a rooftop garden at the library, and the library's big room was quiet enough to hear the heaters ticking under the windows. He had three surveys on his clipboard, all from his friend Gael, who had asked people whether they would eat vegetables grown on a library roof. Gael had asked his brother, his cousin, and the kid next door, and all three had said no. "Nobody wants it," Gael had said at lunch, tearing his sandwich in half. "Three out of three. Give up."

Michael spread the three surveys next to a fat binder Mr. Sokolov had left on the table, a report from a city that had tried the same thing. In that city, a survey of two hundred people had been taken, and most of them had said yes, they would eat the vegetables. Michael read the page twice. Three people said no, two hundred said mostly yes, and the numbers would not sit together in his head.

Alana dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of books about agriculture, which she had promised to find for the poster's section on how gardens work. "You look like you bit a lemon," she said.

"Three people said nobody eats rooftop vegetables," Michael said. "But two hundred people mostly said yes. Which survey do I put on the poster?"

Alana tapped the binder. "The big one. Results from a large sample are more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in bigger groups." She said it the way she said math formulas, fast and certain, then went back to her books.

Michael thought about that while he sharpened his pencil. Gael's brother hated all vegetables. His cousin hated them too. Maybe the kid next door did as well. Three people who all happened to hate vegetables was possible the way flipping three heads in a row was possible. Two hundred people could not all happen to be vegetable-haters by accident; the odd ones canceled each other out. He wrote "large sample, more reliable" on a sticky note and pressed it onto the poster sketch, right under a drawing of tomato plants in proportional boxes, one square foot each.

Mr. Sokolov came by with a cart of returns and paused at the table. "Rooftop garden?"

"Gael says nobody wants it," Michael said. "But he only asked three people."

Mr. Sokolov smiled and slid the agriculture books closer to Alana. "So recruit more," he said, and rolled the cart on toward the front desk.

Michael turned to a fresh page and started writing names: his whole class, the chess club, the line at the farmers market. Then he drew a bar for the class survey, wide and empty, waiting to be filled in.

Evelyn spread the topographic map across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with mugs so it would lie flat. Grandpa's hike was on Saturday, and his knee was bad on steep ground, so she had promised to find him a route up Miller Hill that would take the gentlest way. The trouble was that the map showed no photographs, no colors of grass, nothing that portrayed the hill as her eyes would see it. There were only thin brown lines, wiggly as spilled noodles, looping around one another.

Keaton leaned over her shoulder, chewing the last of his toast. "It looks like a fingerprint," he said. "How can a fingerprint tell you which side of a hill is steep?"

"That's what I have to figure out before Saturday," Evelyn said. She read the small printing beside one of the lines. Every line had a number beside it, and the numbers climbed as the lines shrank toward the middle of the hill, 200, 220, 240. She put her finger on a line marked 220 and traced it, slow and careful, the way it curved out to the east, bulged south, and swung back around to close itself into a ring. It was like drawing the equator around a globe.

"So this whole line," she said slowly, "every single point on it, is the same height above sea level. Two hundred and twenty, all the way around." She looked at Keaton. "That means the line is like the edge of a bathtub ring. If you stood anywhere along it, your feet would be at exactly that height."

She grabbed a pencil and tested her idea. On the west side of the hill, the 220 line and the 240 line lay almost on top of each other, squeezed so tight she could barely slide her pencil between them. On the east side, the same two lines drifted far apart, with wide white paper between them. If each line was a level you climbed to, then the west side climbed from 220 to 240 in almost no distance at all, while the east side took a long, lazy stroll to gain the same height. The east slope was the equivalent of a ramp; the west was more like a wall. "The steep part is where the lines crowd together," she said. "The gentle part is where they spread out."

She called Grandpa in from the porch and traced the route with her finger, up the wide-spaced eastern lines, then along a single 260 line like a shelf halfway to the top. He tapped the trail she had drawn and grinned at her.

"Saturday," he said, "you're carrying the map."

The crowd on the TV roared as the players jogged onto the field, and Luca squeezed between his dad and his friend Andie on the couch, balancing a bowl of popcorn on his knees. Rain hammered the window so hard it sounded like applause, and under the oak's wet canopy in the yard, their neighbour Mr. Cohen's umbrella had blown inside out again. It was the kind of turbulent weather that made Luca glad to be inside with the final about to start.

"Beautiful game," Mr. Cohen said from the armchair. "You know who won the very first World Cup? Brazil, of course. Pelé everything."

Luca frowned. He was almost sure that was wrong, but he couldn't say why, which bothered him like a splinter he couldn't reach. "Are you sure? Brazil feels like a World Cup country, but that's not the same as being first, is it?"

"Argentina," said Luca's dad, without looking away from the screen. "Definitely Argentina."

"That doesn't work either," Luca said slowly. "If Argentina had won the first one, somebody would have mentioned it by now." Both of them couldn't be right, and maybe neither was. He slid off the couch and went to the hallway where the family kept the big encyclopaedia with the torn spine, because Dad refused to look things up on his phone during a match.

Andie followed him. "What are you going to do, read the whole S section?"

"S for soccer isn't how books work," Luca said, flipping to W. His finger ran down the page until he found it, and he read the sentence twice to be sure. Then he carried the heavy book back to the living room, held it open, and cleared his throat like a referee with a whistle.

"The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final." He looked up. "So you were both wrong, and Dad, you were wrong in the funniest way possible. Argentina lost to Uruguay. Four to two."

Mr. Cohen laughed so hard he nearly knocked over his tea, and Dad covered his face with a throw pillow. "Four to two," Dad's muffled voice said. "Demolished."

"Beaten, not demolished," Luca said, grinning. On the screen, the whistle blew and the match began.

Ryan stood on his grandfather's porch holding a plate of samosas that were supposed to circulate through the crowd, but he kept eating them himself, so the plate was not circulating very well. Below the porch, the Vaisakhi procession rolled down the street like a slow orange tsunami, drums booming, flags whipping, and his grandfather singing along off-key on purpose just to make Ryan laugh.

Ryan's friend Zachary had come along for the food, which Zachary described as "a chronic condition I have." He pointed at a little girl walking beside a man carrying a tall flag. "Why is today such a big deal, anyway? Is it like a birthday for the flag?"

"It's a harvest thing," Ryan said. "Farming stuff. That's why there's so much food." But as he said it, he noticed something that didn't fit. The little girl's uncle was telling her a story, and every few words the crowd around them would cheer, and Ryan caught one piece of it. "Vaisakhi is the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," the girl repeated loudly, the way kids do when they've just learned something and want the whole street to know.

So Ryan had guessed wrong, and now he wanted to test the right answer. He watched what the little girl did next. She straightened her shoulders and marched like the flag bearers did, copying them step for step. When an older woman in the crowd looked tired, the girl darted over and held out her arm for the woman to lean on, just like the men with the flags were helping a wobbling toddler over a curb.

"That's the pattern," Ryan told Zachary, finally handing him the plate. "The story isn't just a story. They heard it, and now they're all taking care of each other like it's the rule."

"Then hand me a samosa," Zachary said. "You've been violating the rule for ten minutes."

Ryan passed the plate and went down to walk beside the little girl, matching her steps.

Ruby wanted the blue kayak in the window of Dunmore's Sporting Goods more than she had ever wanted anything. It cost two hundred dollars, and she had eleven dollars and a birthday coming up in five months, which felt like forever away.

She was staying at Grandpa's house for the week, and she spread the problem out on his kitchen table like a detective. "I could just put it on a credit card," she said. "Mom has one. You buy the thing now and pay later."

Grandpa slid his coffee mug aside and set down a folded brochure from the bank downtown. "Before you decide, maybe evaluate both ways of doing it. We can walk over there at lunch."

At the bank, Ruby's friend Genesis was already there with her own mother, standing by a rack of leaflets. "My mom's refinancing something mysterious," Genesis said. "Want to see the free lollipops?" Ruby held up the brochure instead. One page showed what a savings account paid you, a tiny percent added to your money over time. Another page showed what the card charged you if you didn't pay it all back, and the number was far, far bigger. She read both pages three times because the difference seemed too strange to be real.

"They pay you this little," she said slowly, "but they charge you this much? That's like a seesaw where one kid weighs as much as a truck."

Genesis leaned over her shoulder. "That's an aggressive difference," she said, whistling.

"Credit card interest rates are usually much higher than the interest a savings account pays you," the cashier said cheerfully on her way past with a box of deposit slips. "Been that way my whole career." She kept walking, and Ruby stared at the two numbers again.

"So if I put the kayak on the card and take five months to pay it off," Ruby said, "the kayak gets more expensive every month I don't finish paying. But if I save up first, the bank pays me, even a little, the whole time." She turned to Genesis. "The card way, I'm paying extra for waiting. The saving way, waiting pays me."

Genesis grinned. "Want to hear an anecdote? My cousin bought a game console on a card, took a year to pay it, and it ended up costing like one and a half consoles. He cried into his pizza."

Back at Grandpa's, Ruby taped the two numbers side by side above the desk in the guest room. She had changed her mind about the card completely. Every Saturday she would walk dogs for Ms. Morales down the street, four dollars a walk, and she had done the math on a napkin: fourteen weeks, maybe thirteen if Grandpa chipped in for her birthday. The kayak would wait in the window, and she could wait too, because waiting was now on her side.

She dropped her eleven dollars into an old peanut butter jar labeled KAYAK and set it on the windowsill where it caught the afternoon light.

"Day one," she said, and shook the jar until the coins rattled like applause.

Anas answered the door in socks, holding two pairs of sneakers, and he did not look happy about it. "Third pair this year," he said. "My mom says I'm imagining it."

Inside, Edith was sitting at the kitchen table with a notebook, and she rolled her eyes at her brother. "He says his feet grow one week and stop the next. I think he just stuffs things in his shoes." Keira, who had come over to work on their science project, set down her bag and looked at the sneakers more carefully. One pair was nearly new. The other had a hole worn at the heel of the left shoe only, which was strange, because the new pair was too small for him now even though he had bought it in October. Meanwhile, she noticed, his jeans still pooled a little over his shoes, the same jeans from September. Her phone emitted a soft chime from her bag, her mother checking in, but she ignored it. Something did not add up, and she wanted to figure it out before she lost the thread.

"Stand against the wall," she told Anas. "No, in your socks." She marked his height with a pencil, then asked to see his wrists. His sleeves still reached his knuckles. She wrote the numbers down while Edith made a face that said this was a waste of a Saturday. "Here's my idea," Keira said slowly. "Maybe your feet aren't growing weird. Maybe they're just growing first, before everything else catches up. Hands and feet first, then arms and legs, then the rest." It would explain everything: shoes that stopped fitting twice in one school year, jeans that still fit fine, even the way he'd knocked over the lamp last week, because his feet had already arrived somewhere the rest of him hadn't.

Edith flipped her notebook to a fresh page and started listing the boys in their class, the ones who had shot up over the summer and the ones who hadn't yet. "If it's a pattern, we could check," she said, and Keira saw that Edith had changed her mind entirely, because now this was data instead of a brother complaining. Anas looked almost buoyant, standing there in his socks with his too-short sneakers dangling from one hand. "So I'm not broken," he said.

"You're not broken," Keira said. "You're just arriving in pieces." She picked up her phone to text her mother, and Anas went to find the second-biggest pair of shoes in the closet, the ones his cousin in the family network had passed down, the ones that might last until June.

The film club's supply cupboard door hung open, and the club's only good speaker lay on the floor in two pieces. Victoria knelt beside it while Cara hovered at her shoulder.

"I heard it fall from the hallway," Cara said. "It just went over by itself."

Ms. Dang had prescribed strict rules for the club's equipment: carry the speaker with two hands, never set it near the shelf edge, log every use in the binder. Victoria flipped the binder open. Marina had signed it out last, at 3:40.

"That's bizarre," said Marina, coming in with her backpack still on. "I put it back exactly where it always goes. Ask Theo." She pointed at the fourth member, who was pulling off his headphones.

"Wind from the window," Theo said. "I told you it was gusty in here."

Four people, Victoria thought, and four different stories. Cara heard it fall. Marina insisted she'd placed it safely. Theo blamed the window. And the binder, which couldn't lie, said only that Marina had it last. She remembered the old sandwich she'd found in the cupboard in September, furry with blue-green fungus, and how everyone had blamed a different person for that too. She'd accused Marina then, out loud, and Marina hadn't sat with her at lunch for a week. She still wasn't sure that had been fair.

On the shelf above the broken speaker sat the club's movie stack, and Victoria pulled out a case with a samurai on the cover. The back read: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.

"Cara," she said slowly, "we're in a Rashomon situation."

"A what?"

"A movie. Four witnesses, four different stories." She turned the case over in her hands. "I think we should each write down exactly what we saw, separately, before we decide anything. Then compare."

Ms. Dang appeared in the doorway, coffee in hand, and looked at the speaker. "Well?"

"Rashomon," Victoria said, and held up the case.

Mr. Horváth slid the fraction tiles across the table and said the bake sale committee needed a total for the recipe, then walked away, which was his way of saying figure it out.

"The recipe calls for a half cup of oats and a third cup of sunflower seeds," Avneet read off the card. "I already did it. Half plus third. Two fifths."

Nolan looked at the tiles. He picked up a half piece and a third piece and set them side by side on the mat. They did not match. The half was fat and squat; the third was slimmer. He stacked them and the edges stuck out everywhere, like two counterfeit puzzle pieces from different puzzles, pretending to fit.

"That can't be right," he said. "Look. You can't count them together. The denominator tells you the size of the pieces, and these are different sizes. A half is one big piece. A third is a smaller piece. Putting a one and a two over a five is just, like, lying."

"It's a shortcut," Avneet said, with the confidence of someone who had not anticipated being questioned.

Paige was already hunting through the tile box. "Okay, so we need pieces that are all the same size. Then we can actually count them." She laid down sixths, one after another, like a row of dominoes. Three sixths for the half. Two sixths for the third.

Nolan counted them and wrote it down. Five sixths.

"So I get more oats and seeds than my answer said," Avneet said, squinting at the two fifths tile. "I've been shorting the bake sale this whole concept of a time."

"That sentence made no sense," Paige said.

"Neither did my math." Avneet held up the five sixths tiles to the light. "Five little pieces. That's the whole cup, then?"

"That's the whole cup," Nolan said, and swept the tiles into his hand.

Piper spread the three science fair packets across the library table and glared at them as if they might confess. The library smelled like old paper and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on the shelves, and somewhere behind the front desk a printer chunked out page after page. Olive arrived first, dropping her backpack with a thud, then Cedric, who was still chewing the last of his pretzels and held out the bag as a peace offering.

"It has to be the taste test," Piper said. "People say the fancy brand of hot chocolate tastes better, but I want to know if that's actually true or just what everybody repeats." She flipped to the page she'd marked, where she'd underlined a sentence twice. "The problem is, if I hand someone the fancy cup and say try this, they'll already believe it's better before it touches their mouth."

Olive leaned over the packet, her braid slipping off her shoulder. "So don't tell them which is which. Easy."

"It's not easy, because I know which is which. I might act different. I might hand over the fancy cup like it's a prize." Piper had caught herself doing it yesterday, smiling wider over one sample when she tested her little brother in the kitchen. He'd picked the one she'd smiled about. Twice.

Cedric crushed the pretzel bag flat, thinking so hard his freckles seemed to scrunch. "Then don't let the person serving know either. Get somebody else to pour the cups, swap the labels, write the code on a card and hide it. Even you won't know who got what."

Piper sat back. "That's it. That's the real thing, I read about it last night. It's called a double-blind trial. Nobody knows, not the tasters, not the people running it."
