She had followed the recipe exactly that time too, measuring the flour level with a knife like Grandma taught her, and the tops still came out scorched while the middles stayed gooey. She had blamed herself then and quit halfway through learning to bake, which she sometimes regretted and sometimes didn't.

"Third time," said Neveah, who had come over to help. "Even Amy's batch burned, and Amy never burns anything."

Alice wiped her hands on her aprapron and thought. The recipe was right. The measurements were right. So something they couldn't see had to be wrong. "It's like guessing what an animal eats without seeing it eat," she said slowly. "You have to look for clues. A rabbit has flat teeth for plants, so you know it's a herbivore. The oven has to be leaving us a clue too."

"What kind of clue does an oven leave?"

Alice opened the cabinet above the fridge, where Grandma kept odd gadgets, and found a shelf so bare it looked almost desolate except for one item: a round metal thermometer with a hook. She hung it inside the oven, set the dial to the recipe's temperature, and waited while the batter sat on the counter in its paper cups.

When the little needle stopped moving, Alice fetched Grandpa's magnifying glass to read the tiny numbers. The dial said one thing. The thermometer said the oven was really twenty-five degrees hotter. "That's it," she said. "Many home ovens run hotter or cooler than the temperature on the dial. This one runs hot. That's why everything burns even when we follow the recipe exactly."

She turned the dial down, waited, and slid in the new tray. Twenty minutes later the muffins came out golden, and Neveah split one open so steam curled into the air.

"Still not sorry you quit last summer?" Neveah asked.

Alice took a bite and pushed the rest of the tray toward her. "Try one and ask me again."

Cole pushed through the door of the phone repair shop with his cracked tablet held like a pizza box. Mr. Sadeghi looked up from a half-open phone on the counter and raised an eyebrow.

"It fell off the bus seat," Cole said. "Can you fix it before Saturday? I need it for my science project." Mr. Sadeghi turned the tablet over, tapped the corner where the glass had begun to flake, and said he could, but Cole would have to find the replacement part himself because his supplier was out. "You have the shop's tablet to search on," he added, sliding it across the counter.

Cole typed screen protector into the search bar and got a wall of results. The top four all had tiny gray letters that said Ad. He was about to tap the first one when Mr. Sadeghi winced. "Careful. Advertisers bid in an auction for search keywords. They usually pay only when someone clicks their ad. It's called pay-per-click." Cole froze with his finger in the air. "Wait, so every click costs somebody money? Even mine?" "Even yours," said Mr. Sadeghi, going back to his screwdriver.

Cole stared at the screen like it was a trap with teeth. The ads looked exactly like the real results, same blue links, same bold words. He couldn't see any difference directly, so he decided to test something. He scrolled past the ads to the plain results below and started typing more specific keywords, tablet glass replacement 8 inch, then tablet digitizer Cole's model number. The ad wall shrank. When he decomposed his search into exact parts, screen size, part name, model, the ads that survived looked obviously desperate, shouting FREE SHIPPING in capital letters. The real results stayed calm and specific.

"Look at this," Cole said, pulling Mr. Sadeghi's sleeve. "The ad says 'best deals on everything.' Everything isn't a thing. The real result says exactly my part number." Mr. Sadeghi leaned in, and for the first time he looked interested instead of indifferent. He tapped the fifth result, a parts site with a big percentage off the glass Cole needed, and a phone number printed right at the top.

Cole called on the shop phone, standing on one foot, then the other. A man with a raspy voice confirmed the part was in stock and would ship that afternoon. Cole hung up and did a small punch in the air. "Two days before Saturday. I beat the deadline."

Mr. Sadeghi wrote the order number on the back of Cole's hand with a blue pen. "You found it faster than I would have," he said. Cole grinned and picked up his cracked tablet. "Same time next week? I'm going to teach Antonia and Brennan the click trap, and then we're all searching for parts for the science project." He held the door open with his shoulder. "Nobody clicks an ad without knowing it."

Quinn had spent three days not talking to Willyam, and now Mr. Bekele's classroom felt smaller than ever. The desks had been rearranged into pairs for the history project, and there was Willyam, sliding into the seat beside her, arms crossed. "You signed up with Andy for the science fair without asking me," he said. "You don't even care."

Quinn stared at the vocabulary list on her desk. The argument had started Friday, but she kept replaying it, weighing whether she had actually done something wrong or whether Willyam was just being touchy. She wanted to fix it. She just didn't know how.

Her eyes drifted to the poster Mr. Bekele had tacked above the pencil sharpener. ACTIVE LISTENING, it said. Carl Rogers and Richard Farson, 1957. Below that, in smaller print: try to understand the speaker's point of view by repeating their meaning back in your own words. Quinn had walked past that poster a hundred times without reading it. Now she turned it over in her mind. Maybe the whole fight didn't hinge on the science fair at all. Maybe it was about something underneath, and if she could name it back to him, she'd find out whether her guess was close or only an approximate one.

"So," she said slowly, "you felt like I picked Andy over you. Like he mattered more."

Willyam's shoulders dropped half an inch. He picked at the corner of his notebook. "Yeah. That's it exactly." He hesitated. "I didn't know how to say it before. I restrict myself to being mad because it's easier."

"Andy just asked first," Quinn said. "You were out sick. But next project, I'm asking you before anyone." She held out her fist.

Willyam looked at it for a second, then bumped it. "Deal. Now can we please get an A on this, because Mr. Bekele already gave me the evil eye twice?"

Quinn laughed, flipped her notebook open, and clicked her pen.

Savannah tapped her note cards against the table and watched Kristen finish a practice round in the crowded cafeteria of the tournament host school. Her own speech was in forty minutes, and it was a mess. She had a hook about her aunt's tropical garden, three points about why schools should require the flu vaccine, and a closing that was basically "so, yeah." The problem was her best point, the one about how sick classmates miss weeks of school, was buried in the middle where she kept forgetting it herself.

"Want to time you?" Martha asked, sliding into the seat beside her with a stopwatch shaped like a strawberry. Savannah nodded and stood up, launching into the hook. When she finished, Martha frowned at her notes. "I remembered your garden part and your ending," she said, "but I already lost your middle point, and I was listening on purpose. The judges won't even be trying."

Savannah sat down and stared at her cards. Maybe the order was the problem, not the words. If people's attention soaked up whatever came first and whatever came last, the way a sponge saturates only at its edges when you dip it halfway, then the middle was a dead zone no matter how good the point was. She rearranged the cards, moving the missed-schools argument to the front and the weakest point to the middle. Then she made her closing echo her opening line about her aunt's garden. "Again," she said, and Martha clicked the stopwatch.

In the round, Savannah spoke to the judge, not to her cards, and when she sat down she could tell from the judge's pen that both her garden hook and her strongest point had landed. Afterward, outside the room, Martha bounced on her toes. "I read about this once," she said. "First and last items in a list stick best. It's called the serial position effect." Mr. Kim, who had been listening from the doorway, gave Savannah a thumbs-up and held up the ballot with the top score circled twice. Savannah grabbed Martha's hand and spun her around once in the empty hallway. "Next time," she said, "we bury Martha's worst point in the middle."

Brielle arrived at class with her right arm in a bright green cast and a question already forming in her head. Her grandfather had broken his wrist last spring, and she remembered sitting on his porch while he scratched a pencil inside his cast and complained. His had stayed on for weeks after hers came off, and they had broken the same bone, the radius, in nearly the same spot. Why, she wondered, did his break take so much longer?

"Nice cast," said Duke, sliding into the seat beside her. "My grandpa broke his arm last winter. He was in that thing forever. Yours will probably be forever too."

"It won't," Eva said. "Brielle's a kid. Kids heal faster."

"How do you know?" Duke challenged her. "Maybe grown-ups just break bones worse because they're heavier."

Brielle had been thinking about exactly that. She wrote GROWN-UPS? on her notebook with her left hand, which came out wobbly. There was a hidden rule somewhere, and she wanted to find it. She decided on a simple test. She would ask everyone she knew who had ever worn a cast and write down who they were, how they broke the bone, and how long the cast stayed on.

At lunch she collected her data. Her cousin, eleven years old, had a broken forearm in a cast for about four weeks. The crossing guard, who was older than her mother, wore one for her ankle for more than two months. Ms. Marino stopped by their table and added her own entry: she had broken her wrist as an adult and spent a long stretch in a cast, longer than any kid on Brielle's list. By afternoon Brielle had eleven names in her notebook.

"Look," she said, turning the notebook toward Duke. Every kid on the list, even with the same kind of break as an adult, had the cast come off sooner. "Young bones heal faster than adult bones. So kids spend less time in a cast than adults with the same break." She remembered her grandfather then, leaning back in his chair, holding out his wrist to compare with hers, laughing that she would be swimming again while he was still stuck. It had seemed random that afternoon. Now it seemed like a rule.

"Okay," Duke said slowly. "I guess that's pretty objective. The numbers all point the same way." He frowned at the notebook, then brightened. "So my grandpa's long cast wasn't because he was clumsy. It was just because he's old."

"It doesn't signify that he's clumsy at all," Eva said. "It just means his bones take longer."

Ms. Marino leaned over the notebook and tapped one line with her finger. "You know," she said, "collecting evidence like this is real science. It takes patience and honesty, which is worth more than income to a researcher."

Brielle smiled and added a twelfth line, a prediction: MY CAST, four weeks, maybe five. Then she held up the green plaster for Duke to sign.

The commercial had aired three times during the game, and each time it made Elliot madder. A deep voice declared that the town's old bridge was "rated the most dangerous in the state," and tomorrow at school, Lexie would definitely bring it up, because Lexie's dad wanted the bridge torn down and Lexie argued everything her dad argued. Elliot wanted to beat her to it with facts instead of just his own opinion, which was that the bridge was the best fishing spot in town and should be preserved exactly as it was. So after dinner he sat at the computer, opened a search page, and typed the exact words from the ad.

The first results were just other people repeating the same sentence, which felt like cheating somehow. Then Lexie's name popped up in the chat window. "You watching the game? Did you SEE that bridge ad? It said most dangerous in the STATE." Elliot's fingers hovered over the keyboard. If he said "yeah, it's probably true," he'd lose tomorrow. He typed back, "I'm checking it," and kept digging. One link led to another, and finally he landed on a site called PolitiFact, which his social studies teacher Mr. Becker had mentioned once, a fact-checking website founded in 2007. Its whole purpose, as far as Elliot could tell, was taking claims apart to see if they held up, which seemed like a useful phenomenon in a world where commercials could say whatever they wanted.

He scrolled. At the top of the page was a little gauge graphic. His mom leaned over his shoulder, drying a plate. "What's that meter called?"

"The Truth-O-Meter," Elliot read. "It rates claims on a scale, from True all the way down to Pants on Fire." He snorted. Then he found it, the exact claim from the ad, word for word, and his stomach tightened as he clicked. The page loaded slowly, one agonizing inch at a time, and Elliot gripped the edge of the desk. The gauge appeared. The needle sat on the far left.

"True," he whispered. The bridge really was rated the most dangerous in the state. His mom let out a low whistle and went back to the kitchen. Elliot stared at the screen, his fishing-spot argument suddenly obsolete, and tried to think how he would tell Lexie. He typed, "Checked the ad. It's true. The bridge thing."

"HA. Told you," came the reply, almost instantly.

Elliot drummed his fingers, then typed back, "But tearing it down is still just your dad's opinion. Want to see how they fact-checked it? Bring it tomorrow."

Jack was supposed to be buttering toast, but he kept glancing at the phone on the counter. Leah had texted him four times before eight in the morning, all about the science test they had on Friday, and it was only Tuesday. Her last message read, "What if I throw up in class? I keep thinking about it." Jack typed "you'll be fine" and deleted it, because last week she hadn't been fine. She'd chewed her sleeve during the math quiz until it was soaked, and she hadn't eaten her lunch at all.

He pulled the pamphlet his mother had brought home from the clinic out of the junk drawer, the one with the cartoon heart on the front. His mother was still upstairs, so he read it aloud to himself while the toast went cold. "Anxiety is a normal feeling of worry or fear," he read, "but it may be an anxiety disorder when it is intense, lasts a long time, and gets in the way of daily life." He set the pamphlet next to the phone and counted on his fingers, one for each part. Intense: throwing-up fear over a test three days away. Lasts a long time: she'd been like this since September. Gets in the way: the sleeve, the skipped lunch. Three out of three. It was like checking a recipe, he thought. You couldn't see what was wrong inside a person, but you could test it against the steps.

When his mother came down tying her robe, Jack slid the pamphlet toward her. "Can Leah's mom see this? I think it might be more than regular nerves." He didn't want to be reckless and just tell Leah to relax, because that had made things worse last time. "Will you elaborate on that a little?" his mother asked, so he explained the three checks, and she nodded slowly and said she'd call Leah's mother before school.

At the bus stop, Jack sat next to Leah, who was flipping through her flashcards with trembling hands. He didn't mention tests or pamphlets. Instead he unwrapped the extra toast he'd made and set half on her knee, still warm. "My grandma's recipe," he said. "It's kind of our heritage, she makes it every time somebody in the family has a hard week." Leah looked at the toast, then at him, and took a bite.

Lucy pressed the switch on her science fair project for the tenth time, and the little bulb glowed steady and bright. Across the gym, Fernando slumped over his own table, where a maze of wires sat dark around a potato battery. "It worked last night," he said. "Now nothing." Lucy could see he wanted a ribbon as much as she did, maybe more, because his grandfather had driven two hours to come watch the judging. She left her diagram and walked over.

"Show me your circuit," she said. Fernando pointed at the tangle. Together they lifted wires one component at a time, the battery, the switch, the bulb, and set them out in a straight line. Lucy followed the path with her finger, the way Ms. Krause had taught her class back in September. Then she stopped. "Your switch isn't connected on one side. The loop is broken." Fernando snapped the loose wire into the clip, and the bulb lit. His whole face changed.

Then Amirah hurried over, holding a library book open to a page of circuit diagrams. "Look at this," she said. "The arrows point from the positive end of the battery to the negative one. But my brother says that's backwards. The electrons, the tiny things actually moving in the wires, go the other way, from negative to positive. The book can't be wrong, can it?"

Lucy frowned and traced the arrows in the diagram, then traced her own circuit the same direction and the opposite direction. The bulb did not care. It glowed either way, because the loop was the thing that mattered, not which way you drew it. "Maybe both are true," she said slowly. "The diagram arrows show what the book calls current, positive to negative, but the electrons really move negative to positive. Two different arrows for two different ideas." Amirah copied that into her notebook, and Fernando leaned over to clarify one part. "Wait, so when I followed your finger earlier, I was following the made-up direction?" Lucy grinned. "You were following the useful one."

Ms. Krause stopped at Lucy's table during judging and asked why her bulb lit. Lucy flipped the switch off, then on, and said, "It only lights when the loop is complete, and if you ask which way things flow, that depends which arrows you mean." Ms. Krause raised her eyebrows and made a small mark on her clipboard. Behind her, Fernando waved, his potato bulb still glowing.

Julia cracked two eggs into the bowl and counted the dry ingredients Ms. Gagnon had set out on the long steel counter. At the community kitchen on Saturday mornings, each kid got one recipe card, and today hers said blueberry muffins, makes twelve. Her friend Joshua was already stirring his batter at the next station, faster than the card said, sending flour onto his sleeves.

Julia read the card top to bottom before she started. The first line said to preheat the oven to 375 degrees. She turned the dial, and the orange light beside it came on. Then she measured the flour, the sugar, the baking powder, and folded in the blueberries, keeping the batter lumpy the way the card demanded. Isabella leaned over from the cranberry station and said her oven light had gone out a minute ago, so hers must be ready.

Julia looked at her own oven, still glowing orange. She wanted to finish first, because the three best muffins of the morning got their photo on the kitchen's bulletin board by the door. So she spooned her batter into the tray, slid it into the oven, and shut the door while the light was still on. The rack felt barely warm through her oven mitt. She set the timer for twenty-two minutes and went to wash the bowls.

When the timer beeped, her muffins were pale and flat, with tops that had spread sideways instead of doming, like small planets gone wrong at the equator. Joshua's muffins, which had gone in after hers, stood up round and golden. Julia lifted one of hers out and turned it over, assessing the soggy bottom and the pale crumb. Same recipe, same kitchen, same twenty-two minutes. The only difference she could find was the light.

She looked up at the ovens along the wall. Every oven had a small light that switched off when the machine reached its set temperature, and every tray that had gone in after the light went dark had come out right. Hers had gone in while the oven was still heating up, so the batter had sat in rising heat instead of starting at the full 375 degrees. The card said to preheat, and now she understood what that meant: wait until the oven has reached the set temperature before the batter goes in, so baking starts at the right heat. She had skipped the waiting part.

Julia scraped her tray clean and started over, measuring the flour again and cracking two more eggs. This time she watched the orange light, and she did not open the oven door until it went out. She slid the tray onto the rack, and the heat rolled out over her mitts like something molten. Then she set the timer, and Isabella said, "Now you just have to hope they beat Joshua's."

The timer beeped. Julia opened the door and lifted out twelve muffins with round, golden tops, and Ms. Gagnon came over with the camera and said, "These are going on the board."

On Saturday morning Matteo counted his money twice, because eleven dollars had a way of feeling like more or less depending on the day. He was saving for a jar of Mr. Romano's honey, the dark kind that his grandmother used to preserve tomatoes in the old country way. At the farmers' market he found Mr. Romano's stall, but there was a line six people deep, and a hand-lettered sign that made his stomach drop: HONEY, $14.

"Fourteen?" Matteo said. "Last month it was nine."

Mr. Romano shrugged. "Bad year for the bees. I have twelve jars and, look around, more than twelve people." Sure enough, by the time Matteo reached the front, three jars were left, and a woman bought two of them at once. Matteo walked away empty-handed and found his friend Louise at the tomato stand, where a pyramid of tomatoes sat so tall it cast shade.

"Look at this," Louise said. "The tomato guy is yelling three dollars a basket, and nobody's even stopping. He's got more tomatoes than the whole market could eat." As they watched, the man crossed out his sign and wrote TWO DOLLARS. A small crowd formed. By the time the baskets were nearly gone, he crossed it out again and wrote THREE, and the last few sold anyway.

Matteo pulled out the notebook he carried for exactly this kind of thing. "So when there's lots, the price falls until people buy it all. When there's little, the price climbs until only a few people still want it."

"Mr. Romano said a word for that yesterday," Louise said. "The price where buyers want exactly as much as sellers have, he called it the market-clearing price."

Matteo wrote it down. Back at the honey stall, the last jar sat unsold at fourteen dollars, and Mr. Romano was frowning at it. Matteo waited, then held up his eleven dollars. "I have this much. And the market closes in twenty minutes, and I'm the only one standing here."

Mr. Romano rubbed his chin, thinking of revenue lost on an unsold jar. "Eleven," he said at last, "and you do me a favor." From under the table he pulled a mason jar of cloudy, cream-colored stuff. "This is mandatory for every kid who buys from me. It's whipped honey. Tell your friends where it came from."

That night Matteo wrote a note and slid it under Louise's door: "Dear Louise. Got the honey for eleven. Also, the tomato man ended with zero tomatoes and the honey man ended with zero honey, and I think that means something. Meet me at the market next Saturday. Bring your allowance. Bring the notebook. Bring snacks, because the snack stand had a line out to the parking lot, and you know what that means. Your friend, Matteo."

Louise read the note twice, then went to find her piggy bank.

Zoe stood at the back of Mr. Yilmaz's studio, holding her folder like a shield. In September she had chosen to stand with the altos because her best friend Amar stood there, and because the soprano line had looked scary, full of high notes that floated off the page like birds. That choice had felt temporary at the time, easy to undo later. It was not turning out that way.

"Alto line only," Mr. Yilmaz said, tapping the piano. "Sopranos, hum your part quietly, but do not abandon it."

Zoe sang her notes. The sopranos hummed theirs. Somewhere in the third bar the two lines tangled, and hers drifted upward until it wasn't hers anymore. Mr. Yilmaz stopped playing. "Again," he said, and the studio clock ticked through four more tries, each one collapsing at the same bar.

Between tries, Zoe did a quick analysis in her head. The problem appeared exactly when the soprano part moved in the same direction as hers, toward the same neighbor note. It was like her line kept following the other line out the door. So she tested an idea: she pressed one finger against her left ear, half blocking the bright soprano sound, and wrote tiny arrows in her music pointing down where the other part pointed up. It was a trick she had never seen anyone teach. It might work, or it might do nothing at all.

On the fifth try, the bar arrived. The sopranos rose. Zoe's finger sealed her ear, her arrows held her eyes, and her notes landed where they belonged. Her voice did not follow anyone.

Afterward, Amar leaned over. "You realize what you just did? You held the harmony. Also, I have news. My voice changed. Mr. Yilmaz moved me down to tenor."

"Tenor?" Zoe said. "You told me choir was two parts, us and them."

Amar laughed and pointed at the folders stacked on the piano bench. "Look inside. Four parts, soprano, alto, tenor, bass, highest to lowest. I'm the third one now."

Zoe opened a folder and stared at the four stacked lines, her old picture of the choir gone. "Then where do I actually belong?" she asked, and ran her finger slowly from soprano down to bass.

Ellie slid three quarters of a metre of ribbon across the library table and frowned at the craft flyer beside it. The winter fair's ornament booth wanted each volunteer to contribute a bow, and the instructions said each bow needed one third of a metre. Anaya leaned over from the next chair, where she was reading a news article about a corporation that had been caught selling counterfeit parts, which Ellie only half heard.

"I only brought this much," Ellie said, pinching the ribbon's end. "If I cut off a third, I don't know what's left over. Three quarters minus one third. The numbers don't match."

"So make them match," Anaya said without looking up. "That counterfeit thing is wild. This company copied every screw exactly, but the boxes were wrong."

Ellie stopped listening. Make them match. She grabbed a pencil and drew two rectangles on scrap paper, shading one into quarters and one into thirds. The shaded pieces were different sizes, so of course she couldn't just take one away from the other. Then she tried slicing both rectangles into twelve thin strips, because twelve came up in both lines. Three quarters covered nine strips. One third covered four. Nine twelfths, four twelfths. Same size pieces now. She wrote the subtraction and got five twelfths, then sat very still, because if she was wrong, she'd cut the ribbon and discover it too late.

Anaya finally looked over. "Why are you staring at it like it might explode?"

"Testing first." Ellie converted her paper strips into careful marks along the ribbon itself, counting twelfths lightly in pencil. Nine marks for what she had. She laid her finger on the fourth mark, where a third ended. Then she counted the marks beyond her finger. One, two, three, four, five.

She picked up the scissors and cut at the fourth mark, slow enough to feel her breath. The bow piece came away, and she stretched the remaining ribbon along the table. Five marks, exactly as the paper had promised. Five twelfths of a metre, enough to edge a small card for the fair.

"Anaya," she said, holding it up, "your counterfeit screws. Did the fakes still fit?"

"Perfectly," Anaya said. "That's what spooked everybody."

"Math doesn't spook me anymore," Ellie said, and tied her first bow.

The stone jars in Grandpa's cellar had no labels, only numbers, and Grandpa had offered Liam a deal: sort every rock into three boxes by how it formed, igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic, and the fossil knife on the shelf would be his by summer's end. In the garden that morning, Grandpa was yanking out a tangle of vines that had swallowed the fence whole. "This stuff is invasive," he muttered. "Came from nowhere and took over everything." Liam knelt on the cellar steps with his first handful, listening to the roots tearing.

The dark rocks with bubbles trapped inside had to be igneous; they had cooled from something molten. The layered ones split like old cake, so those were sedimentary, built up layer by layer, sometimes out of the shells of some tiny organism whose shape still ghosted through the stone. But the third jar held the trouble. Its rocks were pale, streaked like frozen cream, and none of them looked formed by anything. They looked like they had always been that way, which Liam knew was impossible. He set one aside, a chunk big as a fist, and worried at it all afternoon.

He tried to summarize his problem out loud over dinner. "I can sort the ones with bubbles and the ones with layers. It's the pale ones I can't place. Jersey would laugh at me. He went to the museum last week and came back knowing everything." Grandpa only raised an eyebrow and said the third box would stay empty until Liam stopped guessing and started testing. That night Liam lay awake, then padded downstairs and called Jersey from the hall phone, whispering so the floorboards wouldn't creak.

"You saw the statue there, right? The big white one?" Jersey said. "The guide told us it's marble, and it's metamorphic, and it started as limestone, all seabed limestone, changed by heat and pressure deep down." Liam's hand tightened on the receiver. Changed. Not formed, changed. In the morning he carried the pale chunk up to the kitchen, ran hot water over it, and pressed down with all his weight against the counter edge, watching the streaks in the stone catch the light. Then he wrote one word on the box lid and carried it down to the cellar, grinning all the way.

The wedding hall smelled like lilies and fried scallions, and Felix had one job: hold the red envelope with money for the bride and groom until the receiving line, then hand it over with both hands the way his mother had demonstrated twice in the car. Yann, whose cousin was getting married, had promised to stick next to him all evening. Ajay had come too, mostly for the dumplings.

At dinner, Felix balanced two chopsticks, a napkin, and a glass of lemonade on a crowded table. Ajay was telling a long story about a soccer ball and a garage roof, so Felix needed a free hand to eat his dumpling before it slid off the plate. He stabbed his chopsticks upright into his mound of rice and reached for the soy sauce.

The table went quiet so fast that Ajay stopped mid-sentence. Yann's grandmother, who had been laughing louder than anyone all night, set down her teacup without a sound. Yann leaned toward Felix and whispered, "You can't leave them standing up in the rice."

"Why not?" Felix whispered back, his hand frozen over the soy sauce. "It's just easier."

"Just don't. Please." Yann's face had gone pale under the paper lanterns.

Felix pulled the chopsticks out and laid them flat across his bowl, and slowly the talking started up again, though Yann's grandmother kept glancing his way. Felix's stomach stayed knotted. He had done something wrong, something big, and nobody would tell him what. He watched Yann's uncle place his own chopsticks neatly on the little rest beside his plate, and then Yann's aunt do the same, and he began to see a pattern. Nobody at the long table, not one of the forty guests, ever left chopsticks pointing straight up out of food.

He decided to petition Yann directly, out in the hallway by the coat rack, away from the ears of the relatives. "You have to tell me what I did," he said. "I'm not being obstinate, I just can't fix it if I don't know."

Yann checked that the hallway was empty. "Standing chopsticks in rice look like incense offered to the dead," he said quietly. "That's why we never do it. At funerals, that's what it means."

Felix thought about the quiet that had dropped over the table, and about Yann's grandmother and her teacup, and it all fit together like a puzzle snapping shut. He went back in, walked to the grandmother, and bowed the way he'd seen the other guests do in the receiving line, both hands pressed together. She studied him for a long moment, then patted the chair beside her.

"Eat," she said, pushing the dumpling platter toward him. "The tall boy talks too much, and the dumplings go extinct fast."

Ajay opened his mouth to argue, and Yann kicked him under the table, and Felix picked up his chopsticks and held them the way Yann's uncle did.

Mr. Hu plucked one string on his guitar and let the room go quiet. "That is your reference note," he said. "In an orchestra, the oboe usually plays the reference A that all the other instruments tune to." He pointed at Jordan. "Your job is to match your E string to my A. Listen, then turn the peg a little and listen again."

Jordan held his guitar and plucked the string. The sound wobbled, like two notes arguing with each other. He tightened the peg, but the wobble only got faster. He tried the other way, loosening it, and the wobble slowed, then spread out until only one clean note was left. So the faster the wobble, the further off he was. He tested the idea by loosening too far on purpose, and the arguing came back. He tightened until it vanished again.

Kiara leaned over from the next chair. "How did you do that so fast? I've been turning mine forever." She held up her guitar. Her string was flat, and when she plucked it alongside his, he could hear the slow roll of mismatched notes.

"That's it, you're close," Jordan said. "Just tighten it a tiny bit." Behind them, Sheldon had stopped pretending to tune at all. He was watching the window, where afternoon light refracted through his water bottle and laid a crooked rainbow across the music stands. "I already know how to do this," Sheldon said, but his pegs hadn't moved once.

After class, Sheldon caught Jordan at the door. "Can you keep a secret?" His voice was abrupt, low. "I can't hear the wobble. At all. I went to the doctor last week. Something with my ears." He looked at the floor. "I didn't want Mr. Hu to take me out of the group before the concert."

Jordan thought for a second. "Don't tune by ear, then. Use the electronic tuner on my phone, every time, before anyone notices. Nobody checks how you got there." He pulled out the tuner, and its needle swung left, right, then stopped dead in the middle, right on the A. "There," he said. "Pluck it again."

Sophie spread three crumpled sticky notes across the library table and glared at them as if they had insulted her. Her book club met in forty minutes, and Peyton had promised to bring the popcorn, which meant Sophie was responsible for everything else, including the analysis she had sworn she could do. "The mockingjay," she whispered to the open copy of The Hunger Games in front of her. The problem was that the pin showed up as a tiny moment at the start, when Madge Undersee gives Katniss the mockingjay pin before Katniss goes into the arena, and then somehow it turned into the biggest thing in the whole series. How did a small gift grow that much weight?

Violette slid into the chair across from her, smelling of rain and mint gum. "You look like you're being transported to prison." She tapped the book. "That's the one with the birds, right?"

"The mockingjay pin. Madge gives it to Katniss in chapter one, and by the end it means a whole rebellion." Sophie flipped pages, hunting. "I want to prove it changes, not just say it does. I thought I could mark every time the pin or the bird shows up and see what it means in each place." She smoothed a fresh sticky note flat. "Like checkpoints."

Ms. Byrne wheeled her book cart past and paused. "Presentation at four?" she asked, glancing at the clock above the paperbacks. Sophie nodded, throat tight. Twenty-eight minutes. Violette grabbed a pencil and started scanning the middle chapters aloud while Sophie wrote: pin, token of home; mockingjay, something the Capitol never meant to exist; mockingjay, a girl defying them anyway. When they laid the notes in order down the table, the pattern showed up like footprints in snow. The pin began as protection, a piece of District 12, and each time it returned it had gathered another layer until it stood for everyone who refused to be controlled.

Peyton burst through the doors at 3:52 with a grocery bag of popcorn and zero apologies. The four other club members gathered around, and Sophie stood, hands slightly shaky, and walked them down the line of notes like a trail. When she finished, nobody spoke for a second, and then a boy in the back said, "So Madge basically handed her a revolution in chapter one and didn't know it."

"Exactly," Sophie said, and Violette raised the popcorn bag like a trophy.

Savannah taped the last flag to the community centre wall and stepped back to check her display for the heritage night. She had made labels for every family on the sign-up sheet, and one label bothered her: "Germany," printed in neat block letters for the Brandt family. Mr. Brandt had signed the sheet himself, and she had copied it exactly, but last week he had said something odd while helping set up tables. "You know we call it Deutschland at home," he had said, laughing, and then walked off before she could ask what he meant.

She found Khaled and Emiliano stacking paper cups by the juice station. "When your family talks about Egypt, what do they call it?" she asked Khaled.

"Misr," he said. "Never Egypt. My grandma says Egypt is what other people call it."

Emiliano frowned. "So there are two names for every country? The one the group uses and the one outsiders use?"

"There's a word for it," Khaled said. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use is an exonym. My sister taught me that in geography. Like Deutschland and Germany."

Savannah wanted to be sure before she changed her whole display, so she tested it like a tiny algorithm: ask the person, write the answer, compare. She went table to table with her clipboard. The woman from Thailand said "Prathet Thai." The grandfather from Greece said "Ellada." Mr. Brandt confirmed Deutschland again and grinned. It was risky to redo the labels an hour before the doors opened, maybe even reckless, but if she left them wrong the whole wall would tell a story about outsiders instead of the families themselves.

She printed new labels and taped them beneath the old ones, so both names showed. When the families arrived, they stopped at the wall. Khaled's grandmother touched the word Misr and said something to him in Arabic that made him laugh. The Greek grandfather stood in front of "Ellada" for a long moment. "This is how it should be," he said, and wrote his name on the sign-in sheet beside it.

By the end of the night the room was loud with people comparing labels, teaching each other pronunciations, arguing gently about spelling. The event had never drawn a crowd like this before; Ms. Anderson, who ran the centre, said the bulletin board club would thrive if they kept this up. Savannah peeled off the old English-only labels and dropped them in the recycling bin. "Next time we start with the endonyms," she said, and clipped the blank labels back onto her clipboard.

The morning after the movers left, Victor sat on the floor of the empty new house and wrote his old address on thirty envelopes, one for every kid in his class back in Maplewood. Lyric had promised to write back weekly, though Victor suspected she would persevere for about two weeks before switching to texting.

"Give the mail a chance," his dad said, dragging a box toward the kitchen. "I filed the permanent change of address with the Postal Service at the counter yesterday."

"What does that even do?" Victor asked.

"First-Class Mail gets forwarded to the new address for twelve months," his dad said, and then he dropped the box on his foot and said a word Victor was not allowed to repeat.

So Victor had one year, exactly. He tested the idea the first week by mailing himself a postcard at the old address, and eight days later it arrived at the new house with a yellow sticker on it, routed like a homing pigeon. He grinned and showed Lyric's first letter to his new neighbor Yosef over the fence. Yosef, who wanted nothing more than a teammate for the basketball net bolted to his garage, studied the envelope like it was a scout report.

"Twelve months," Yosef said. "So if somebody mailed you a scholarship application in month eleven, it would still find you. That's actually wild."

"It's ironic, actually," Victor said. "I spent two months dreading this move, and the mail is the only thing that followed me."

They played one-on-one until the streetlights buzzed on, and Yosef won four games to three by using a sneaky left-hand layup he claimed he'd been hiding since March. Victor went inside sweaty and cheerful and found two more letters on the hall table. He held them up like trophies.

"Dad," he called toward the kitchen, "eleven months and three weeks left. I'm keeping count."

The bus stopped in front of the fire station with an abrupt hiss of brakes, and Connor was the first one down the steps. He had been wondering all week what a real station would look like inside, and it was better than he'd pictured: tall doors, poles, and a big old engine polished until it glowed.

Mr. Chea counted heads while a firefighter led them past the lockers. Near the old engine, a painting of a spotted dog hung in a gold frame. Caleigh squinted at it. "Why would they put a dog picture next to a truck?" she asked. "It's not even a fire dog. It's just... spotty."

Connor studied the painting instead of guessing right away. The engine in the picture looked older than the one beside it, with wooden wheels and a long pole where the ladder went. Were the horses pulling it? He counted them: four horses, and the spotted dog running out in front. He turned the question over. The dog wasn't riding, and it wasn't chasing the engine. It was ahead of the horses, on the road. Why would a dog run ahead?

"There's a logbook on that shelf," he said, pointing to a ledger beside the frame. "From back then." He asked the firefighter if he could look, and she said sure. Connor assessed the faded pages, flipping past alarms and repairs until he found a note from an old captain: "The dog cleared the street ahead better than any whistle. The horses trust him." Yasmin leaned over his shoulder. "Trust him? Horses don't even like dogs usually."

"That's it, though," Connor said slowly, testing the idea as he said it. "These dogs got along with horses. That's the whole reason firehouses kept them. The horses pulled the engines, and the dog ran ahead, clearing the way." He tapped the painting. "That's why he's out in front. He's doing a job." Yasmin looked from the painting to the dog, then back, like she was checking his answer against the evidence, and grinned.

Mr. Chea gave them ten minutes to sketch anything in the station. Connor drew the old engine with its four horses and the small spotted shape leading them down a crowded street. It made him curious about what else a station needed around it, the whole little ecosystem of people, animals and machines that made a fire crew work. "I wonder what the dog's name was," he said. The firefighter passed by and tapped the brass plate under the painting. "Check the bottom of the frame," she said. Connor crouched down and read the small engraved letters: "Buster, 1898."

Joshua slid his math homework under the placemat before his father carried the spaghetti to the table. On the small kitchen TV, a replay of the hundred-meter final was frozen at the finish, and the silver medalist's face filled the screen. "Second place," his father said, spooning noodles. "He must have been way behind." He had spent the whole afternoon insulating the attic pipes and his arms were still gray with dust.

Joshua leaned closer. The two runners had crossed almost together, so close the announcer had said the gap was less than a blink. "He was only a hundredth of a second back," Joshua said. "A hundredth. That's nothing." His father shrugged and said second was still second. Something about that bugged Joshua all through dinner. Being second could mean losing by a hundredth of a second, but it could also mean losing by a whole minute. The ranking told you who was ahead, and nothing about how far ahead. He decided that wasn't good enough, and it seemed logical to test it.

He grabbed the kitchen stopwatch and a notebook. "Everybody clear your plate, starting now." His mother laughed but picked up her fork. Joshua timed each of them and wrote the numbers down: Mom 41 seconds, Dad 39, himself 53. The next night he did it again, and again the night after, so nobody could say one slow dinner ruined the results. By Friday he had a whole column of times, like a tiny census of plate clearing, and he added them up and divided to get each person's average.

At Friday dinner he pushed the notebook into the middle of the table. "Rankings," he announced. "Dad, you're first. Mom, you're second. But look." He turned the notebook so the columns faced his parents. "Dad's average is 38 seconds and Mom's is 39. One second apart, basically tied. Second place here is like that runner's hundredth of a second." Then he flipped to the row from Tuesday, when his mother had stopped to answer the phone and taken 71 seconds. "But that night, second place was a whole minute behind first. Same ranking both times. Totally different race."

His father set down his fork and read the columns twice. "So when the news says we're second in the league," he said slowly, "we might be a whisker behind or miles behind." "Exactly," Joshua said. "You have to ask for the numbers." His mother raised her water glass. "To the champion," she said, "by one single second." Joshua grinned and clicked the stopwatch one more time, just to hear it beep.

Penelope stood on the painted wooden stage of the community theatre, index cards shaking in her hand, and watched her grandmother's face go blank in the third row. "Two minutes on why the theatre needs a costume sale," Mr. Kerr had said, "opening hook, three points, closing, by Friday night." Penelope had rehearsed the opening hook a dozen times in front of her mirror, and it worked, because her grandmother leaned forward when she described a velvet cape from 1987 that smelled like somebody's attic. But halfway through, her grandmother whispered to Mom, "Which point is she on now? Is this the second thing or the third?"

After practice, Terrance was waiting in the aisle with his own cards. He had been meticulous about his speech, numbered cards in a rubber band, and he shook his head. "Your problem is you need a stronger hook," he said. Penelope disagreed, but she couldn't say why, so she sat on the stage edge and thought. When she read her speech to herself, she never got lost. She could flip back a card, reread a line, find her place again. Her grandmother couldn't. A listener had no pages to flip back through, so once she lost the thread, it was gone. That had to be the real hinge the whole speech turned on, not the hook.

She tested it that evening. "Grandma, I'll say it again, exactly the same, but this time I'll say 'first', 'second' and 'finally' before the points." She gave the speech on the back porch, word for word the same except for those three words, and her grandmother nodded along the whole way. "First, the storage room is overflowing," Penelope said, and her grandmother's eyebrows rose like she'd been handed a map. Terrance, sprawled on the porch swing doing his own rehearsal, looked up. "Oh," he said slowly. "It's not my hook either. My brother got lost too." He changed his mind on the spot and pulled out a pencil. "What's that called, the first, second, finally thing?"

"Signposting," Penelope said, "like street signs for your ears."

Friday night, the theatre seats filled. Mr. Kerr stood at the back with a stopwatch. Andrea went first, then Terrance, who planted his signposts firmly and didn't lose a single listener. When Penelope stepped into the lights, she found her grandmother in the third row and took a breath. "First," she said, and watched the whole audience lean in. "The storage room is overflowing."

Brody had sung the high part in the junior choir at the temple for three years, and he liked standing beside James, who hit every top note like it was nothing. Then, on the first Thursday of October, his voice cracked in the middle of a psalm, right on a note he had sung a hundred times. The sound that came out was somewhere between a squeak and a groan. James did not laugh. Karter, two rows back, did not laugh either, though his shoulders shook once before he got them still.

Mr. Patel, the choir director, called a break and walked over. "Brody, sing that line again. Just for me." Brody tried, and this time the note came out, but it felt like carrying a suitcase up stairs that used to be flat. Mr. Patel nodded slowly. "During puberty the larynx grows, so a boy's singing voice usually drops by about an octave. That often moves him to a different part." He said it the way he said everything, calm and quick, like a weather report. "Try the lower line with Karter for a few weeks."

Brody wanted to confess that he hated the idea, because the lower part wove against the high part, and if he drifted, everyone would hear it. Instead he shrugged and moved back two rows. The melody he knew so well now belonged to other people, and his new line seemed to wander off on purpose, like a dog that ignored whistles.

He decided to test an idea. At home he hummed the high part into one ear, using a recording on his tablet, and sang the lower part out loud over it. At first the high part grabbed him and dragged his voice upward every few bars, like a tide. Nobody was immune to that pull, he discovered; even Karter admitted that when the choir split into two parts, his own notes sometimes slid toward James's. So they practiced the trick together at recess, Karter singing the tune while Brody held the lower line, both of them getting it wrong and laughing and trying again.

By the third Thursday, something shifted. Brody's low line settled under the melody like a floor under a room, and when James's part rose, his own stayed put. Mr. Patel raised both hands for the split section, and the two lines crossed and crossed and neither one wobbled. Afterward, at the snack table, Karter passed over the cookies with peanuts without being asked, because everyone knew about his allergy, and handed Brody the plain ones.

"You sound good down there," James said. "Like a whole different instrument."

"Give it a year," Brody said, pointing at him with his cookie. "Your turn is coming."

James opened his mouth to argue, and a small crack came out instead. Karter's laugh rang all the way to the sanctuary doors.

Edouard stood in his grandfather's music room, holding the alto sheet music like it might bite him. The choir concert was in two weeks, and Ms. Novák had said his part needed to be steady, not just guessed at. Every time he sang the harmony line alone it sounded fine, but the moment the melody came in, his voice slid upward to follow it, like a magnet was pulling him.

His grandfather's old piano sat against the wall. Edouard had never really played it, but he knew where middle C was, because his grandfather had shown him that much. He pressed the C key, then hummed his note from the sheet music. Wrong. He checked again, and found his note two keys down, on the A below. He pressed both keys together and listened. The sound was smooth, almost like one fat note instead of two separate ones. He pressed other pairs to compare. C and the key right beside it sounded scratchy, sour. C with the key two down sounded settled, like they belonged together. So that was the trick. His alto note sat under the tune, two letter names below, which his cousin Prisha called a third apart when she texted him that evening.

"Wait, so your whole line is just a third under the melody?" Prisha wrote.

"Not all of it, but a lot," Edouard typed back, and then he tested it, playing the tune with one hand and hunting for his harmony notes with the other. Some places the rule coincided with what was written, and some places it didn't, but even where it differed, he noticed the harmony line still liked to hover just under the tune. It wasn't a strict equation he could plug notes into, like in math class. It was more like a versatile shadow that shifted but stayed close.

The next morning his grandfather sat in the doorway drinking coffee while Edouard practiced. When Edouard slipped and drifted up to the melody, he stopped, found the piano key, and pulled his voice back down under. He did it again and again, until holding his part felt less like fighting and more like standing still while someone walked past him.

At Thursday rehearsal, Ms. Novák split the choir in half. The sopranos lifted the melody into the air, and Edouard planted his note beneath it, steady, a smooth third below. For the first time, the two lines braided together without him tumbling out.

"Edouard," Ms. Novák called across the room, "whatever you did this week, keep doing it."

He grinned and held the next note even longer.

The cut on Cole's palm had stopped stinging, but the memory of it hadn't. He sat on the bench at the bus stop with his hand wrapped in a paper towel, waiting for the 4:10 with Lola, who was staring at the reddish line across his skin like it might move.

"It was a rusty trowel," Cole said. "At my grandma's, in the garden shed. I reached past a spiderweb and grabbed the wrong end."

"You grabbed a rusty trowel." Lola unwrapped her backpack and dug out the little first-aid pouch her mom made her carry, which Cole used to tease her about. Now it looked like treasure. "Grandma didn't take you to a doctor?"

"She put a bandage on it. That was yesterday. Then this morning she called my mom and said maybe a doctor should look at it after all, because it was deep, and because rust means dirt." He frowned at his palm. "She said something about dirt. I didn't get it."

Lola peeled the backing off a bandage and handed it to him, then sat on her hands, which was her way of saying your turn. Cole positioned it crooked, lifted it, and smoothed it down again, gentler, so it lay flat across the cut without sticking to the red part. Lola nodded once, like a judge.

The neighbor from the blue house, Ms. Mansour, came down her walk with a grocery bag and paused at the stop. "Bandaging practice?" she said. "Good skill. I was a nurse for thirty years."

Cole held up his hand. "If it's from a rusty thing, is that bad? Like the rust itself?"

"It's not the rust, it's what's in it," Ms. Mansour said. "Tetanus. Tetanus bacteria live in soil and dust. That's why a deep or dirty wound can mean a doctor visit. Sometimes you get a tetanus shot, just in case." She checked the crosswalk, then looked back at him. "Deep or dirty, remember. A paper cut, no. A hole from a nail in a garden bed, yes."

Cole turned that over. So the rust was only a warning sign, the way smoke meant fire somewhere you couldn't see. The trowel had lain in soil, and soil held these bacteria, and the bacteria could be sitting in the cut right now, invisible, which was exactly why the wound needed more than a bandage. Grandma had figured that out overnight, he realized. Yesterday she'd dismissed the idea of a doctor, and this morning she hadn't. He wondered how often she changed her mind like that, quietly, before telling anyone.

"My mom made me a deal," he said. "I go to the clinic after she picks me up, and she takes me for dumplings after. It wasn't even voluntary. She just said, you're going."

"That's not a deal, that's a treaty," Lola said. "You get dumplings either way."

The bus rounded the corner, brakes hissing. Cole stood, pressed the bandage flat one more time, and picked up his backpack with the good hand. "Tell me tomorrow if you get the shot," Lola called after him, and he raised his wrapped palm out the window as the doors closed.

Sebastian had come to Aniya's house to work on their language arts project, a poster comparing a book with its movie adaptation, but so far the poster was blank and Aniya was holding a dress. "It came this morning," she said, lifting a white dress with a translucent overlay from a tissue-lined box. "From my aunt in Vancouver. I'm wearing it to the family thing on Saturday. My cousin's getting married, I think. Or something."

Asia, who was sprawled on the rug sketching a movie poster, squinted at the dress. "It's very white." From the kitchen doorway, Aniya's grandmother looked at the dress too, said nothing, and went back to washing rice. Sebastian noticed that, because he noticed things like grandmothers going quiet.

He kept noticing. On the fridge hung a calendar with Saturday circled, and beside the circle someone had drawn a small incense stick. On the mantel sat a photograph of a man Sebastian had never seen before, framed in black, next to an old wedding photo of Aniya's grandparents in which the bride wore red, brilliantly red, embroidered with gold. Aniya had once told him her family was Chinese on her grandmother's side, and that the man in the black frame was her great-uncle, who had died in the spring. Sebastian had an idea forming, and ideas, in his experience, were like splinters: better extracted early.

"Can I see the card that came with the box?" he asked. Aniya dug the envelope out of the trash and handed it over. He pulled out the card and read it. It was not an invitation to a wedding. It was an invitation to a memorial gathering for the great-uncle, with a time, an address, and a line about honoring his memory. Aniya read it over his shoulder and sat down on the coffee table, slowly, the way you do when a floor turns out to be softer than expected.

"So the dress," she said. Her grandmother came in drying her hands, and when Aniya held it up, the old woman nodded once. "White is what we wear for mourning," she said, and patted the fabric like it was a cat. Asia raised her hand from the rug as if they were in class. "Weird, because my cousin got married last month and her bride wore white. Big puffy white dress. Whole church full of it."

"Same color, opposite jobs," Sebastian said.

Aniya looked at the dress, then at the red bride on the mantel, then at the dress again. "Fine," she said. "But I'm wearing it to the memorial, not to any weddings. For weddings I'm borrowing your red hoodie, Asia, and that's final."

"You don't have to decide tonight," Asia said, and went back to her sketch, where the movie monster was wearing, of all things, a veil.

Sadie sat on the hard chair beside her dad at the bank, swinging her feet and staring at the flyer in her hands. It showed a purple mountain bike for one hundred and eighty dollars, and she wanted it so badly her teeth ached. Her dad was at the counter asking about his credit card, and Sadie leaned forward when she heard the cashier say the words "minimum payment."

"Dad," she whispered when he came back, "why not just pay the little bit? The small number looks friendlier."

Her dad rubbed his forehead. "That's the trap I'm in. I've been paying the minimum for ages and the balance barely shrinks. Much of each payment goes to interest, so paying it off could take years. Years, Sadie. For a grill I barely use."

Sadie blinked. She thought about that all the way to the car. The money he sent each month was like water poured into a bucket with a hole in it, except the hole was invisible, which made it worse. Was there a ratio hiding in there somewhere, a secret comparison between the part that actually paid off the bike, or the grill, and the part that just vanished? She wanted to see it for herself.

At home she spread notebook paper across the kitchen table. Her friend Sara came over, and Isa joined her through a video call, his face pixelated on the tablet. "I'm testing an idea," Sadie announced. "If Dad had saved up first, he'd have paid one hundred and eighty dollars, once, and then owned the thing. With the card, he pays and pays, and the debt just sits there like it's too frail to die but too stubborn to leave." Sara laughed so hard she knocked over the glue.

They made two columns. Saving column: bike money set aside each week, total cost fixed. Borrowing column: minimum payments stretching on and on, years of them, and at the end Dad would have paid way more than the grill ever cost. Isa held up a hand-drawn chart to his camera, a wobbly bar graph titled "The Hole in the Bucket." Sadie decided she could monitor her own plan instead: five dollars a week from walking the neighbor's dog, plus birthday money, and the bike would be hers by spring.

The next Saturday she marched back to the bank with her dad, holding her envelope of dog-walking cash. She asked the cashier to open a savings account, and when the woman asked if she had any questions, Sadie slid her notebook across the counter, hole-in-the-bucket chart and all.

"That's my plan," she said. "Is the ratio right?"

The cashier studied it, then grinned. "Kid, you just drew the best chart I've seen all year. Let's get you that account."

Levi sat in the game lobby waiting for the countdown, but his mind was on the email he had to send after the match. He wanted to invite his whole class to an online tournament on Saturday, and Mr. Sok had helped him get a list of everyone's addresses. The trouble was that his first attempt, a practice one, had put all the addresses where everyone could see them. Maiya had noticed right away. "You just showed the whole class my address," she said in the lobby chat, and the chat was public, so everyone in the waiting room saw that too. Stefan added a row of laughing faces.

Levi typed "my bad" in the lobby and then turned to the options on the side of the screen, which were private, meant for adjusting his controls, not for talking. He liked that about the lobby. Some things were broadcast, like the countdown clock and the team names, and some things only he could see, like his ping and his settings. The email program had to have something like that too, and he meant to find it before the match started.

Below the To line there was a Cc line and then a third line labeled Bcc. He had skipped it before because it looked like a typo. He clicked it open, dropped Maiya's address into the To field as a test, put his own and Stefan's into Bcc, and wrote one sentence: "Test, reply if you can see anyone's address but mine." Then the match loaded and he set the email aside, because the lobby was filling and he needed to be competent at the game too, not just at invitations.

After the match, which his team lost narrowly, he opened his inbox. Maiya had replied, "Only yours." Stefan had replied with a single question mark. So that was the rule: people added in the Bcc field received the message, but other recipients could not see their addresses. Blind carbon copy, Maiya had written in the lobby afterward, when someone accused Levi of hoarding the secret. He sent the real invitation with every address in Bcc, all forty-three of them hidden from each other.

On Saturday the tournament bracket filled up fast. When one classmate tried to accuse another of inviting a ringer from another school, Levi offered a settlement: the ringer could play, but only on the youngest team. Mr. Sok, watching from the couch with his own controller, gave a slow nod. "Round two," the lobby announced, and Levi hit ready.

Zoe sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her poster board, a marker with a dying tip, and a problem. Tomorrow she had to explain to her class why the ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming, and all she had so far was a title and one sparse paragraph copied from a website. The rest of the page was blank. She pressed her palm against it, as if pressure might push ideas out of the paper.

Carlos arrived after dinner with his notebook and a bag of pretzels. "I found something at the museum last month," he said, flipping pages. "There was this stairway going down into water, with carved lines on the steps, like ruler marks. I stood there forever trying to figure it out." He tapped his drawing. "Then it clicked. They were measuring how high the river rose. It's called a nilometer."

Zoe grabbed a glass from her desk and set it in the bathtub her little brother had left half full. "Okay, pretend this is the Nile," she said, crouching beside the tub. She drew a small mark on the glass at the waterline, then dumped in a cup of water. The line climbed. "Every year the flood came up, and the marks on the stairs or pillars beside the river told them exactly how high it got." She poured another cup and watched the level rise past the second mark. "So a good flood meant a big harvest, and a low one meant trouble. They could predict it before a single seed went in the ground."

"That's the perspective you were missing," Carlos said through a mouthful of pretzels. "The pyramids, the farms, all of it, it runs on the river." Zoe wrote across the top of her poster, then underlined it twice. "Tomorrow I'm going to summarize the whole thing in one sentence," she said, "but first I need to draw stairs going down into water." She picked up the dying marker and shook it, and it came back to life.

Jordan counted the finished posters leaning against the gym wall and came up one short. The Heritage Showcase was Friday, and his club was supposed to have twelve displays, one for every member. His own poster, about northern communities, sat half-finished on the long table because he couldn't get the caption right. He had written "An Inuit hunter builds a snow house" and then crossed out "An," then written it again, then crossed it out so many times the paper had gone grey and soft.

Avril leaned over his shoulder. "You're going to wear a hole through it."

"It sounds wrong," Jordan said. "The whole sentence. But I don't know what part is wrong."

Kallie spun a chair around and sat on it backward. "Then ask Mr. Toussaint. He's got that whole shelf of books by the door."

Jordan didn't want to ask. He wanted to figure it out himself, the way he figured out the club's poster schedule when everyone's names got mixed up. He went to the shelf anyway and pulled down a book about the Arctic. He found a picture of a single man in a parka, and the label under it. The word there wasn't the one he'd written. He flipped to another page, then another, and a pattern showed up, like the median on the graph in math class, one steady thing in the middle of everything else. One page showed a group, and the other word showed a person.

He grabbed a sticky note and wrote himself a message, then read it to Avril:

"Dear Jordan. Stop crossing out words with your whole arm. The problem is one letter. You're welcome. Sincerely, also Jordan."

Avril laughed so hard Mr. Toussaint came over. Jordan held up the book, pointing at the picture of the one man. "It says Inuk," he said. "One person is an Inuk. Inuit means 'the people.'" He looked at the group photo on the next page, then at his own poster. "I had it backwards."

Mr. Toussaint nodded but didn't take over, which Jordan appreciated. The change would be gradual, though, because the poster still needed its map, and its timeline, and half a border of paper snowflakes by Thursday.

"You'll make the deadline," Avril said, trying to reassure him. "You have the hard part done. The one-letter part."

Jordan copied the new caption in careful letters: "An Inuk hunter builds a snow house." Then he taped his sticky note to the corner of the poster, where everyone at the showcase could see it.

The argument had already sustained itself for ten minutes of practice, which was ten minutes nobody had spent actually playing. Michelle said her goal counted because the ball had touched the cone before rolling wide. Emy said a cone was not a goalpost, no matter what it touched, and that anyone who thought otherwise was inventing rules on the spot.

Alexandra stood between them on the chalk line the coach had drawn across the gym floor like an equator, one team's half on each side. She was wondering something else entirely. Michelle wasn't cheating, exactly. She was playing by a rule she truly believed existed, and so was Emy, and the two rules were not equivalent. The problem wasn't either of them. The problem was that nobody had ever written the rule down.

"Wait," Alexandra said. "Before we fight more. What's the actual rule about cones?"

"Cones are the goal," said Michelle.

"Cones are just cones," said Emy.

"See? That's the problem," Alexandra said. "Not the shot. Nobody ever agreed what a cone is. My grandpa plays cards with a rulebook so old it has a name for this."

That night she found the note her grandpa had tucked into her duffel bag after his last visit, folded into a small square. She smoothed it out on her desk and read it again: "When I come at the end of the month, we play whist, and we play it properly, according to Hoyle." Underneath he had drawn a tiny mustachioed face with a question mark. Alexandra had laughed the first time she read it, and she laughed again now, because she still had no idea who Hoyle was. She looked it up, and the answer was better than she'd guessed. "According to Hoyle" means following the rules exactly; it comes from Edmond Hoyle, whose 1742 book set down the rules of the card game whist. A man so serious about rules that people were still quoting him nearly three hundred years later, usually while pointing a finger.

At practice the next day, Alexandra raised her hand like she was in class, which made Michelle snort milk out of her nose from her water bottle, which made even Emy laugh. "New plan," Alexandra said. "We name the problem out loud, then we make one rule everyone agrees on before we play. That's the Hoyle way."

"Who's Hoyle?" Emy asked.

"Some old card player. He wrote the rules down so nobody had to fight about them."

"So cones are... what, exactly?" Michelle asked.

"Officially out," Alexandra said. "Unless both captains agree before the game that they count. That's the fair version."

Michelle stuck out her hand. Emy shook it, then immediately yelled, "Okay, but if she scores off a cone again, I'm writing to this Hoyle guy myself."

"Good luck," Alexandra said. "You'll need a really old envelope."

Emy positioned the ball at the chalk line, Michelle crouched into her stance, and the game finally began.

Kaitlyn stacked the last box of soup cans at the front of the shelf, right where the labels could be seen, and stepped back to admire her work. The whole row looked neat, all the new stock lined up like soldiers.

"You did that fast," said Layan, who was sorting pasta two shelves over. Kayson was behind them, taping a ripped cereal box, and Mr. Quinn, the volunteer coordinator, came around the corner with his clipboard and stopped so abruptly that his shoes squeaked on the concrete floor.

He pulled a can from the front of Kaitlyn's shelf and turned it over in his hand. "Where did these come from?"

"The delivery this morning," Kaitlyn said. "I put the new ones in front because the labels are nicer."

Mr. Quinn held up an older can from the back, its paper label worn soft at the edges, almost eroded away by years of being picked up and put down. "These older ones have to go out first. First in, first out."

Kaitlyn frowned. "But the new ones look better."

"That's what Kayson said last week," Layan offered, and Kayson groaned from behind the cereal boxes.

Kaitlyn looked at the two cans side by side and thought about it. The old can had a date stamped on the bottom, closer than the date on the new one. If the new cans went out the door today, the old ones would sit there, growing older on the shelf, until nobody could use them at all. She tested her idea by checking three more pairs from different shelves. Every time, the front can in Mr. Quinn's system had the closest date, and the new stock waited behind it.

"So the shelf is kind of a line," she said. "The cans at the front are next to leave."

"Exactly like a queue," Mr. Quinn said, and moved on to the next aisle.

Kaitlyn pulled the new cans forward in her arms and restacked everything, older ones in front, newer ones behind. It took twice as long as the first time, and Layan came over to help without being asked, sliding cans down to her one at a time.

A woman with a small boy on her hip came through the line near closing. Kaitlyn handed her one of the old-front cans, and the woman read the label and smiled. "Split pea. My mom's favorite."

Kaitlyn watched the can go into the woman's bag, first in line, first out the door.

Felix crouched at the edge of Miller's Pond with his sketchbook open and a pencil that had been sharpened down to a stub. His problem was due tomorrow: a science project showing a food chain, drawn from the sun all the way to a top predator, with an explanation of what would happen if one link disappeared. He had never drawn anything for science before, and the blank page felt like it was daring him.

Kaila dropped onto the grass beside him, holding a bag of sunflower seeds. "You've been staring at that paper for ten minutes," she said. "The sun's not going to hop onto it by itself."

"I know it starts with the sun," Felix said. "Then the pond plants, because they grow using sunlight. Then something eats the plants." He pointed at a cluster of green stems poking out of the shallow water. "Snails, maybe. And then something eats the snails. A bird? Mr. Wiśniewski said we have herons here."

Bentley jogged up with his sneakers squelching. "I counted four herons on the far bank yesterday," he reported. "Also about a million tadpoles, and I saw a water beetle grab a tadpole. It was intense."

Felix started sketching fast: sun, plants, snails. Then he stopped, pencil hovering. "Wait. The heron is my top predator. It eats the water beetles, right? Or the snails? I can't just guess. I have to get the order right, or the whole explanation falls apart."

"Think about who eats what," Kaila said, cracking a seed between her teeth. "The snails only eat the plants. The beetles eat the snails and the tadpoles."

Felix sat back. "My dad said animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers," he said slowly, watching a snail slide along a stem. "So the snails are the primary consumers. And the animals that eat them are secondary consumers. The beetles. Then the heron eats the beetles, so it's next up the chain."

"That tracks," said Bentley. "So draw it: sun, plants, snails, beetle, heron. Five links."

Felix drew each link as a circle connected by arrows, and labeled them. Then Kaila leaned over his shoulder and frowned. "Okay, but you still have to explain what happens if one link disappears. Pick one."

"Testing time," Felix announced. He held his thumb over the beetle circle. "If the beetles vanish, the herons lose a big food source. But the snails would go nuts with nothing eating them, so they'd eat way more plants, and the plants would shrink, and then the snails would run out of food too." He slid his thumb over the snail circle instead. "And if the snails disappear, the beetles get hungry and the plants overgrow the whole pond." He looked up. "Take out any link and both sides of it get messed up."

Kaila raised her seed bag as if toasting him. "The pond has spoken, and I think we have a consensus."

"Rain's imminent," Bentley said, pointing at a gray bank of cloud rolling in over the far trees. "Draw faster."

Felix added one last detail, a heron standing in the shallows with its neck curved like a question mark, and printed his name at the bottom of the page just as the first fat drops hit the water.

Kayla spread the rocks across the picnic table in her backyard, sorting them into three rows: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic. Her ambition was to beat Sulaiman in Monday's geology quiz, and she had promised Katia a slice of lemon cake if Katia gave up her Saturday to help.

Katia held up a shiny black rock that caught the sun like a mirror. "This one's easy. Somebody melted a glass bottle and it got all over the beach."

"It's a rock," Kayla said, frowning. But when she looked closer, it did look exactly like glass, with a curved edge sharp enough to slice paper. She turned it over in her fingers. It was cold and smooth, with no sparkles inside, while the granite beside it glittered with tiny crystals. That difference had to mean something.

She ran her thumb across the granite's speckles. Crystals everywhere. Then she rubbed the black rock again. Nothing. She remembered Ms. Huang saying rocks told stories about how they formed, if you knew how to read them. Igneous meant cooled lava. So the crystals in granite had somehow had time to grow, and the black rock had not. She had a simple idea. "I think this is lava that cooled so fast the crystals didn't have time to form," she said slowly. "Cooling fast would make it smooth like glass. Volcanic glass."

Katia leaned over the fence and called to Ms. Huang, who was watering her tomatoes next door. Ms. Huang set down the hose and came over, wiping her hands on her shorts. "Let me see that." She held it up to the light, turned it, then handed it back. "That's obsidian. Volcanic glass. Lava that cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form."

Kayla pumped her fist. Then she felt her cheeks go warm, because Katia was still holding the glass-bottle theory like a defiant shield. "I was sure," Katia admitted.

"That's okay. I got the sedimentary and metamorphic ones backwards all last week," Kayla confessed. "Put the obsidian in the igneous row, and I'll cut the cake."

Katia placed it next to the pumice, then stuck her finger against the sharp edge and yelped. Kayla fetched a bandage from the kitchen drawer and pressed it gently around her friend's finger. "Volcanic glass cuts," she said. "Now you'll never forget what it is."

Katia grinned and picked up the lemon cake slice with her good hand. Kayla wrote OBSIDIAN in careful letters on her chart, then set the shiny black rock on top of the granite, where it gleamed like a small black mirror in the afternoon sun.

Wyatt slumped in the desk chair and clicked on the group chat for his science project. Mattea and Karissa had been messaging all afternoon while he was at his grandma's, and the messages had accelerated since the last time he checked, filling two whole screens. They had chosen the topic without him. Volcanoes. His idea about consumer packaging waste was gone, voted out in a poll he never saw.

He wanted them to notice him. He wanted to matter in this chat. So he typed fast and hit enter.

"WHERE ARE YOU"

Three dots appeared under Mattea's name. Then they vanished. Then they came back.

"why are you yelling?" Karissa wrote.

Wyatt stared at the screen. Yelling? His house was quiet except for the fan humming in the corner and the sticky sound of his chair when he shifted. He had typed the same letters he always typed, just bigger.

"I wasn't yelling," he wrote back, and then, because that felt flat, he added, "why did it look like yelling?"

Mattea answered first. "all caps reads as shouting. everybody knows that."

Karissa sent a shrugging emoji. "you sounded mad at us."
