He wasn't mad, exactly. He felt like the last kid picked for a team, standing at the edge of the field. He had been pessimistic about the project all week, and now the chat seemed to prove him right. He decided to test it, though, because Mattea's claim sounded like a rule, and rules could be checked.

He typed, "OKAY, I WILL BRING THE MARKERS TOMORROW."

"still yelling," Karissa replied instantly.

Then he typed it again, small letters, easy: "okay, i will bring the markers tomorrow."

"see? better," Mattea wrote. "also we can still talk about packaging. mr. farah-ali said we could compare volcano damage to plastic waste if we split the poster in half."

Wyatt leaned forward so fast the chair creaked. He wrote, "I can do the packaging side. I already have a pile of wrappers in my closet for evidence." He looked at the capital I and decided one letter was fine.

"deal," Mattea sent. "bring the wrappers."

Wyatt got up, pulled the shoebox of crinkled chip bags and yogurt cups from under his bed, and set it beside the keyboard for morning.

Lincoln had been at Grandpa's house since noon, along with Alexandre and Quinn, because the championship was starting at two and Grandpa had the biggest television on the block. The plan had almost been thwarted when the screen went dark an hour before kickoff, and Grandpa had spent ten minutes hunting for the receipt to check whether the TV was still under warranty. It was not. But then Mr. Wijaya, the neighbor, appeared at the door holding a remote that looked equivalent to the lost one, pressed three buttons, and the picture came back, and everyone cheered as if the game had already been won.

By the fourth quarter, the home team was ahead by three, and Alexandre was pacing behind the couch. "They're only winning because they're at home," he said. "Put this game in the other team's stadium and it flips. Watch."

"That's not a real thing," Quinn said, mouth full of popcorn. "That's just something people say when their team loses."

Lincoln thought about it. He did not say anything at first, because a claim like that could be checked, and checking was better than arguing. He pulled out his phone and started looking up season records, keeping one eye on the screen where the home team was driving down the field. He wrote numbers on the back of Grandpa's TV guide: wins at home, wins on the road, sport by sport.

"Okay," he said during a timeout. "Look. In basketball, football, hockey, baseball, most major sports, the home teams win more than half their games. It's a real pattern, not a feeling. It even has a name. Home advantage."

Alexandre threw both fists in the air, as though he had just scored himself. "Thank you. Home advantage."

Quinn leaned over the list of numbers. His shoulders dropped a little. "That's a lot of seasons," he admitted. "Fine, it's real. I was wrong." Then he squinted at the paper. "But more than half isn't everything. Away teams still win a lot."

Lincoln had been thinking the same thing. If home advantage was real, then the pattern should show up somewhere you could test it. He turned to Grandpa. "Do you still have that binder with all the old standings?"

Grandpa did, in the basement, going back thirty years. Lincoln and Quinn ran down while Alexandre guarded the couch, and they pulled five random seasons, added up home wins and road wins, and the home wins were ahead every single time, by more than half.

Upstairs, the home team kicked the winning field goal, and Alexandre screamed so loudly that Mr. Wijaya knocked on the wall from next door. Quinn looked at the binder still open on the coffee table, then at the celebrating screen.

"Next week they play away," he said. "I still think they win."

"Then you're saying home advantage isn't everything," Lincoln said, and handed him the popcorn.

Andrew stood on the coffee table in the living room, facing the couch, the way Ms. Dang had told the choir to face the audience. On Friday, three days from now, he would sing in his first concert, and the note she had handed out said the whole choir must "exit stage left." The trouble was, he had no idea which side that was, and neither did Simon or Cullen, who were sprawled on the couch pretending to be a crowd.

"It's obvious," Simon said, pointing at the window. "Left is left. We go that way."

Cullen frowned. "But Ms. Dang said stage left from her spot in the wings, and she's on the other side."

Andrew jumped down and tried an experiment. He made his little brother's toy plane, the one with the spinning propeller, stand on the coffee table facing the couch, just like a performer facing an audience. Then he walked around behind it, pretending to be Ms. Dang looking out from the wings. From behind the plane, its left wing pointed toward the window, which was Simon's left too, but wait. He crouched to the plane's side, where its left wing would be if the plane were a person, and it pointed at the bookshelf. The two directions were opposite. "Stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience," he said slowly, testing each word. "So we go toward the bookshelf side. Our own left."

Simon looked doubtful until they practiced. Cullen called out "Exit stage left!" and Simon spun toward the window, then caught himself, laughed, and crossed to the bookshelf side instead. They drilled it four more times, until nobody hesitated. Even the spontaneous round of applause they gave themselves, led by Cullen pounding the couch cushions, couldn't distract them.

The night of the concert, Andrew's stomach flipped as the curtains opened, and his first note came out thin. But when the final song ended, Ms. Dang raised her hand toward the bookshelf side of the stage, and every choir member turned left together, clean and sure. From the dark rows of seats, a single loud whistle cut through the applause, and Andrew knew it by its pitch.

"That's my dad," he whispered to Simon as they walked off.

Christopher stood at the top of the half-pipe with his board under his feet, and his whole body said no. Below him, Zaiden and Brinley waited on the flat concrete, and the drop looked about ten times steeper than it had from the ground.

"You're overthinking it," Zaiden called up. "Just commit."

Christopher crouched, rolled his weight forward, and bailed almost instantly, sliding down on his knees while the board rattled away behind him. When he chased it down, the wheels were still buzzing against the pavement. He picked it up and felt the hum in the deck with his fingertips.

"Sound is just that," Brinley said, tapping the board. "Vibrations travelling through stuff. Air, concrete, water, whatever."

Zaiden sat on the bench nearby and pressed a steel ruler against the edge, flicking the overhanging part so it went brrrrr. Then he slid it shorter and flicked again, and the note climbed higher. "Frequency," he said. "The number of vibrations per second. It's measured in hertz." He flicked a tiny stub of ruler sticking out and got a thin, high buzz. "Faster vibrations, higher pitch."

"Say that again," Christopher said, still holding his humming board.

"Vibrations per second. Hertz," Zaiden said. "Fewer per second, low note. More, high note."

Brinley had pulled out her phone. "Ms. Abdi told us sound goes way faster through water than air. That's why whales hear each other across whole bays."

"That sounds controversial," Zaiden said.

"It's not, it's real. She showed us a video where a whale call travels like a rumour through a whole harbour. And this other one about a microbe that swims toward sound, which, honestly, felt made up."

Christopher set his board down, spun the wheel with his thumb, and felt the vibration tick against his finger, faster than the big slow wobble of the deck when he bounced on it. Fast ticks, high squeak. Slow wobble, low drone. He grinned.

He carried the board back up to the top of the ramp, set the tail on the coping, and breathed in. He thought of the short ruler, the quick buzz, the way a small fast thing could carry a whole clear note.

"Watch this," he called down, and rolled in.

Ivy pulled the kitchen chair up to the family computer and typed the address Kelly-Ann had written on a scrap of paper. The site was called BugBook, and Kelly-Ann and Aida both had accounts already. They had spent all of recess trading beetle stickers on it, and Ivy wanted in before the good ones were gone. She clicked "Create Account," picked a username, and then the form asked for her birthday.

She typed it honestly: March 14. The screen went red. "You must be 13 or older to create a BugBook account." Ivy sat back. Kelly-Ann was eleven, just like her, and Aida was still ten until June. So how did they have accounts? She tried a test. She made a new username, typed every answer exactly the same, except the year, which she changed so the site would think she was fourteen. This time the screen said, "Ask a parent for permission before continuing." The site had a parent-permission option, but only when it believed you were over thirteen.

In the hall above her, Dad was unrolling pink insulation into the attic floor, and the thumping came right through the ceiling. She carried the laptop up the ladder and showed him the permission screen. "Can you do this?" she asked. Dad read it, then scrolled down to a link that said "Why do you need my birthday?" Ivy leaned in and read it out loud: "The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13. That is why many sites require users to be 13."

"So that's it," Ivy said. "The site isn't trying to keep kids out for fun. It's a law about collecting information." Dad negotiated with her for a while: she could have the account if he signed the consent form and she used only her first name, never her school, never her address. Ivy agreed to everything, then sat at the top of the ladder typing while Dad stapled insulation around the vent. She filled out the consent form the way a diligent student fills out a test, checking each box twice before clicking submit.

The account opened with a cheerful chirp. Aida's beetle sticker collection appeared on Ivy's screen, all forty of them, including the rare gold one. Ivy clicked "send trade request" and typed a message. "Hi! It's Ivy. Can I have the green one?" She waited, listening to the stapler thump above her, until the reply popped up. "Took you long enough," Aida wrote. "Deal."

Natalie sat at the corner table in the library, where writing club met every Thursday after school. Her draft lay in front of her, four paragraphs about saving Miller Park from being turned into a parking lot. Ms. Owusu had said a persuasive essay needed five paragraphs, an introduction and a conclusion, and Natalie had counted hers three times. Four. Something was missing, but she could not see what, so she stared at the empty space after her last sentence.

Imran leaned over from the next chair. "You're stuck on the ending, aren't you. Charles-Edouard finished his in ten minutes." Across the table, Charles-Edouard was writing fast, which was annoying but also a clue. If he had finished quickly, maybe there was a pattern she could copy. She read his conclusion upside down. It ended with a direct order: "Sign the petition at the library desk." Natalie sat back. Every strong essay she could remember did something like that. Hers just stopped, like a door left half open.

She wrote one more sentence at the bottom of her page. Then she wrote a note and slid it across to Imran, because Ms. Owonu liked the room quiet during drafting time. "Mine ends by telling readers to sign the petition to preserve the park. Does that count as a real conclusion, or just a demand?" Imran read it, grinned, and wrote back: "It counts. Ms. Owusu calls that a call to action. It tells the reader exactly what to do next."

When the timer rang, Ms. Owusu walked the room and paused at Natalie's page. "Five paragraphs," she said. "Your argument stayed objective until the end, and then you gave your reader a job. Well done." She handed back the draft with a small check mark. Natalie read her last line again, then copied it onto a clean sheet, nice and neat, so the librarian could pin it by the petition forms. "Sign your name today," it said. "Miller Park needs fifty more people."

The office smelled like coffee and printer ink, and Avery had a whole hour to kill while her mom finished a meeting down the hall. She was supposed to be finding a science project topic, but every search she typed gave her a swamp of junk.

At the desk beside hers, Mattias leaned over from the visitor chair, chewing a straw he'd taken from the break room. "Just search 'best water filter,'" he said. "Whatever's on top is the winner, obviously."

Avery typed it. The very first result was a slick site called PureFlow, all glossy photos and a big orange button that said BUY NOW. "See?" Mattias said. "They must have paid Google a ton to sit up there. Number one spot, right? Nobody gets that for free."

Something about it bugged her, though. She scrolled back to the top and looked more carefully. Above PureFlow, in tiny grey letters, sat a small box she'd never once noticed before: the word "Sponsored." Below it, other links wore the same little label, like name tags at a party.

"Those are ads," she said slowly. "The ones without the tag are different." She clicked a help page and read fast, then read it again, because it seemed too weird. "Listen to this. The unpaid ones are called organic results. And Google says advertisers can't pay to move their pages higher in them." She deviseda quick test: search three other things, filter out anything marked Sponsored, and see whether the top organic results were the big famous sites or the loud shopping ones.

They ran it together. Each time, the ads crowded the top like shouting vendors, and just under them, the organic results led to library pages, university sites, and one surprisingly good contemporary science blog. PureFlow didn't appear in any of them.

Mattias dropped his straw in the trash. "So the top ad paid to be there, but the top real one earned it."

"Exactly." Avery copied three keywords into her notebook, folding the page so she wouldn't lose them. "Now, real search: 'science project, water quality, student.'" She hit Enter and leaned in as the results loaded.

Gabriel's kitchen smelled like burnt popcorn, and he was still arguing about it. "The popcorn burned because the microwave is haunted," he said, sliding the bowl across the counter to Carter. "That's just my opinion, so you can't say I'm wrong."

Carter poked at a black kernel. "Wait, that's not an opinion, though. That's a claim you can check." He pulled out his phone and typed while Gabriel groaned. "Watch. We test it. If the microwave is haunted, it would burn popcorn every time. If it's just old and weak, it burns it because the heat is uneven. Mr. Watanabe said something like that last week, about how some statements can be looked up."

"That's boring," said Elyana, coming in from the living room with a bag of unopened kernels. "But I want to see if it happens again, so keep going."

They ran three batches, one at a time, standing side by side and watching the bag spin. The first batch burned on the left side only. Carter turned the bag a quarter turn before the second batch, and the burn followed the same spot in the microwave, not the same side of the bag. "It's the microwave," he said. "The hot spot stays put. No ghost required."

"That's so weird," Elyana said, leaning closer to the glass door like she might catch the hot spot in the act. "You can't see it, but you can tell exactly where it is."

Gabriel still wasn't finished. "Fine, but the haunted thing was my opinion, and opinions can't be wrong. Like, I think the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin. That's my opinion."

Carter laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the bowl. "That's not an opinion, that's just a false claim. 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion. You can look it up. An opinion is like saying burned popcorn smells good, which, gross, but nobody can check it." He showed Gabriel the map on his phone, and Gabriel squinted at Paris like it had personally tricked him.

"Okay," Gabriel admitted. "So if I said my little brother is the loudest kid on the equator, that would be an opinion, but if I said he's taller than me, that's checkable."

"Exactly," said Carter. "Objective. Measurable. You get out a ruler and you know." He was already wondering what else they could test, because suddenly the whole house looked like a list of questions. "Hey, does your dad have any balloons? I want to see if the haunted hot spot can pop one."

Romy spread her graph paper across the folding table in Grandma's basement, where the whole family had gathered for the reunion. Her homework was due Monday: a bar graph of the ethnic and cultural origins of a town in Canada, using real census numbers. She had copied the numbers carefully at school, but something was wrong. Scottish, 32 percent. English, 28 percent. French, 22 percent. Indian, Punjabi, Chinese, Ukrainian, six percent here, four percent there. She added them three times, and every time the total climbed past 130 percent.

"Your graph's broken," said Abbas, her cousin's friend, who had come along because he lived next door. He leaned over her shoulder and pointed at the column of numbers. "Percents can't do that. A hundred is all there is."

Romy didn't argue. She went upstairs to retrieve her notebook, where she had written the source of the numbers, and checked each bar against her notes. Everything was consistent: the same figures, the same town, the same year. The problem wasn't her copying.

"Maybe the census people made a mistake," Zac offered. He was Abbas's little brother, and he was eating a samosa while he talked. "Grown-ups mess stuff up all the time."

Romy considered that premise and rejected it. A national count that millions of people filled out would not be off by thirty percent. Someone would have noticed. She looked around the crowded basement, at her aunts and uncles arguing about cricket, at the table of food where jollof rice sat next to pierogi, and something clicked. "Zac," she said, "what are you?"

"Canadian and Jamaican," he said, like it was obvious.

"And you?" she asked Abbas.

"Pakistani and, well, Canadian. And my mom says Scottish too, from her grandmother."

Romy wrote both names on a napkin and drew a line under each. "So if a form asked your origins, you'd write down more than one thing." She counted on her fingers. "You'd get counted in two or three columns, but you're still one person. One person, three tallies." That was the hidden rule, and it explained everything: the town's totals could stack past one hundred without anyone lying and without anyone being counted twice as a person.

Her grandmother, passing through with a tray of cups, glanced at the napkin. "Since 1981 the census has let people report more than one origin," she said, setting down a cup of tea beside Romy's elbow. "That's why the totals add up to more than the whole population." Then she went back to the kitchen.

At the bottom of her graph, Romy printed a note: origins add to over 100 percent because people can report more than one. She taped the graph to the basement door and stood back. Abbas squinted at it, then at the napkin, then at his samosa. "So in a town like that," he said slowly, "almost everybody's a walking double bar."

Georgia slid her Spanish folder between the napkin dispenser and the ketchup bottle so Jared couldn't see her notes. "Mr. Greco said our family descriptions have to be full sentences, and he won't restrict us to just vocabulary lists, so I actually have to say stuff out loud."

Jared dunked a fry. "So say stuff. I'm your witness."

"Tengo una perra," Georgia began, pointing to the dog photo on her phone. "Wait." She frowned at her own sentence. Yesterday she had written "Tengo un perro," and today she had switched the word, and she wasn't sure why she'd done it. She said both versions under her breath, listening. Perro. Perra. One had an a at the end, like her own name did, and when she'd written about her mother she had used words ending in a too, and her father's words had ended in o. She flipped back a page in her notebook and checked: her, hers, a-endings; him, his, o-endings. A pattern.

Their waiter, Mr. Greco, came by with water and caught the word "perro" as she practiced. "Your dog, he's a boy?" he asked, nodding at the photo.

"She's a girl," Georgia said. "That's why I'm confused. I wrote perro first."

"El perro is a male dog," said Mr. Greco. "La perra is a female dog."

Georgia looked at the photo of Biscuit, tail up, tongue out, unmistakably a girl, and felt the two words click into place like puzzle pieces. She wrote la perra in her notebook and underlined it twice. "So it's tengo una perra. Uno problemo solved."

Jared raised his hand like he was in class. "As anonymous testimony, I heard her get it wrong first, but she fixed it before the deadline."

"Snitch," Georgia said, but she slid the basket of fries closer to his side of the table anyway.

Mr. Greco laughed and topped off her water. "Say the whole sentence for me. Family, pets, everything."

Georgia took a breath, sat up straight, and began, "Mi familia tiene cuatro personas y una perra que se llama Biscuit."

Charles sat at the kitchen table with his mother's old laptop, which had survived three years of being dragged to school in his backpack and was, his dad said, more durable than anything else in the house. On the screen, his Scratch cat chased a mouse back and forth, but the score box in the corner kept showing numbers that made no sense: 7, then 12, then 30. He wanted this to be the first game he actually finished, the one he could show Britany on Monday instead of another half-built project abandoned like last month's maze.

He remembered the maze now, sitting frozen in his account, and wondered whether he had given up too early that time. Not this one. He opened the mouse sprite's script and read it block by block. When the cat touched the mouse, a block said change score by 1, and below it a forever loop spun the whole thing around again. That part looked right. So the mouse was earning points, and the cat was chasing it, but the number had never once started clean. He thought about what he could not see: somewhere, something was deciding what the score was worth before the game even began. He had a candidate for the culprit, and there was one way to test it.

He dragged in a green flag block, snapped a set score to 0 block under it, and clicked the flag. Zero. He touched the cat to the mouse once. One. He sat back so fast he nearly knocked over his water.

A message popped up from Donovan: "Your game is broken. I played it at recess on Britany's account and got 84 points before I even moved." Charles laughed, typed back "Fixed it. Made a variable called score, set it to 0 when the green flag is clicked, then change score by 1 for each point. Come over and lose properly," and hit send. Down the hall, his dad called that dinner was in ten minutes. Charles clicked the flag one more time, just to watch the zero appear.

Wyatt stood at the front desk of the animal shelter, holding the adoption papers for a wiry terrier mix named Biscuit, when a woman rushed in with a muddy beagle draped in a beach towel. The dog was shivering and wore no collar at all. How did anyone know where a dog like that belonged?

Mr. Sato came out from the back room carrying a small handheld device that looked a bit like a chunky remote control. He waved it slowly over the beagle's shoulder blades, and it beeped. "There's a microchip in there," he said. Wyatt leaned closer. A microchip? He had pictured something like a dog tag, but this was inside the dog, invisible from the outside.

"How small is it?" Wyatt asked.

Mr. Sato held up his thumb and finger, barely apart. "About the size of a grain of rice. It doesn't hold an address or anything, just an ID number. The scanner reads the number, and we look it up in a registry to find the owner's contact details." He copied a string of digits off the scanner's screen and typed it into the shelter computer. Sure enough, a name and a phone number came up, and he called while the beagle gulped down water.

Wyatt turned the idea over while Biscuit sniffed his sneakers. A dog could lose every collar and tag in the world and still carry proof of who owned it, tucked under the skin where nobody could see. Was there a chip in Biscuit? The adoption paperwork was vague about it, just a line that said "chipped: yes" with no detail, so Wyatt decided to test it. "Could you scan him?" he asked.

Mr. Sato ran the wand over Biscuit's shoulders the same slow way, and Wyatt watched, holding his breath. The scanner stayed silent for a second, then chirped and flashed a number that was nothing like the beagle's. That was proof, real proof, printed right there. Wyatt copied it onto his adoption folder in careful pencil, thinking that tomorrow he would call the registry and check that the contact details were his family's and not some stranger's.

His friends Kianna and Cedar were waiting outside with the leash they had brought as a congratulations present, blue with little bones on it. "Guess what Biscuit has inside him," Wyatt said, and Biscuit trotted out the door, tail spinning like a propeller.

Grandpa's living room smelled like popcorn and old leather chairs, and every seat was taken. Anthony squeezed onto the rug between Anya and Thea while the screen showed the stadium filling up, thousands of fans waving towels. "Listen to that crowd," Grandpa said from his recliner. "That noise wins games. The home team feeds on it." The blitzing linebackers could hardly hear the quarterback, the announcer said, because it was so loud.

Anthony wasn't so sure. He remembered something he'd found a few weeks ago for a project and pulled it up on his tablet. In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1. Almost exactly even. No home advantage at all. "Grandpa," he said, holding up the screen, "look at this. In 2020, when almost nobody was in the stands, home teams went 127-128-1." Grandpa squinted at it. "That's barely under five hundred," Anya said, doing the math out loud. Thea leaned over. "So the cheering doesn't actually do it?" "It doesn't look like it," Anthony said.

Grandpa rubbed his chin. "Well, now. That's strange, because I retired in 2020 and watched every game that year on this very chair. Empty stadiums, cardboard people in the seats. Contemporary football, I called it, not like the games of my day." He paused. "And you know what? I never noticed any of that myself. The home teams played just fine." Anthony grinned. "So it's not the crowd. Maybe it's travel, or knowing the field, or something nobody can see." "Or maybe," Grandpa said, "football is just football."

Thea poked Anthony's arm. "Test it, then. Watch the whole game and count the false starts when it's loud." Anthony grabbed a notepad from the side table and wrote FALSE STARTS at the top. On screen, the quarterback barked the count, the crowd roared, and the visiting tackle jumped early. "That's one," Anthony said, and Grandpa laughed so hard his chair creaked. "Two can play at this," Grandpa said, reaching for his own pad from the drawer. "Loser does the dishes." On the wall above the TV hung Grandpa's old team photo, part of the family's sports heritage going back three generations, and Anthony thought his own page in that story was just getting started. The kickoff sailed into the lights, and both of them bent over their notepads, pencils ready.

Nolan had saved his question for the bus, because questions on the bus didn't count against the two he was allowed per field trip. "Why do pigs sit in mud?" he asked Austen, who was sharing his seat and most of his pretzels. Austen shrugged. "Because they're pigs. They like being gross." Emerald leaned over the aisle, holding her farm worksheet like evidence. "It says here to observe animal behavior, so maybe we should actually observe instead of guessing." Nolan stared out the window, where the heat shimmered above the road, and decided that "they like being gross" was the kind of answer that felt true but wasn't.

At the farm, the class reached the pig pen right after lunch, when the sun was at its worst. The pigs lay hip-deep in a brown wallow, completely still except for their ears. One pig near the fence wasn't in the mud at all; it stood in the shade, breathing fast. "That one's the anomaly," Nolan said, pointing. "All the others are in the muck, and that one isn't. If they just liked being dirty, why would one pig stay out?" Emerald scrutinized the pig in the shade, then the wallow, then the water trough beside it. "Maybe it's like the trough," she said slowly. "The mud is doing something the water does."

Nolan tested it. He hung back when the class moved on and watched the dry pig, and sure enough, when it finally waddled over, it went straight into the wallow and sank down with a grunt that sounded almost like relief. The farmer came by with a hose and grinned at the three of them lingering at the rail. "Smart, aren't they," she said. "Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days." Austen's mouth fell open. "They're not dirty," he said. "They're air conditioning themselves."

On the ride home, Emerald filled in her worksheet under "animal behavior," and Nolan added a line about the wallow, even though it wasn't required. He wasn't sure he'd get extra credit, but he wrote it anyway, in pen, so it felt permanent. "Next field trip," Austen said, tossing him the last pretzel, "you're asking more than two questions." Nolan caught it and ate it.

On Saturday morning Ethan's dad handed him a phone in a cracked cereal bowl, which was the family's idea of a ceremony. "Group chat's already set up," Dad said. "Your mom, your sister, me. Try not to text us anything before seven a.m."

Ethan spent the afternoon learning the phone. He figured out how to install a chess app, how to silence notifications, and how to send a photo to Jaida, who replied with a thumbs-up and the words "FINALLY." At 4:52 a text arrived from a number he didn't know. "GAME ACCOUNT ALERT: Your account will be deleted in 24 hours unless you verify your password now. Reply with password to keep your account." His stomach dropped, because he did have a game account, and he had just made a password for it that same day.

He typed his password, then stopped. He opened the family group chat. "If a company texts you and asks for your password, is that real?" His mom replied first with a single question mark. His sister wrote, "omg no." Then his dad called him from the garage, and Ethan walked over holding the phone out like evidence. They looked at the message together. Ethan noticed the sender address was a jumble of letters, not the game company's actual name, which appeared in his app. He remembered a poster in Mr. Santos's classroom, in the corner by the pencil sharpener, that he had never bothered to read. On Monday he went early and read it. Then he texted Jaida and Katherine at lunch: "It's called phishing. Somebody pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away your password or private information."

Katherine wrote back, "Wait, like fishing? With bait?" Ethan said basically. She asked if he'd fallen for it. He admitted he had typed the password but deleted it before sending. "The delete button is my best friend now," he said, and Jaida laughed so hard the lunch monitor looked over.

That evening Ethan reported to the group chat like an impartial referee delivering a verdict: "One fake message received. Zero passwords given away. Account not deleted. The company never asks for your password anyway." His sister replied with a GIF of a fish grabbing a hook and spitting it out. His dad wrote, "Good work. Now go look up whether the school's lunch menu is in some database you can check, because I want to know if it's pizza Friday." Ethan was already searching.

The church basement smelled of coffee and old hymnals, and the folding chairs had been pushed against the wall to make room for music stands. Isabella unzipped the case and lifted out the guitar Mr. Brown kept in the storage closet for kids who didn't own one. In three days the youth group was leading the Sunday songs, and she was the only one who could play more than three chords.

She had learned the tuning trick from Ellis at school: press a string at the fifth fret, and it should sound the same as the next thinner string played open. You started from the low E, worked your way up, and listened until the two notes melted into one. Penelope sat beside her with her eyes closed, because Penelope said she could hear the wobble between out-of-tune notes better than she could see anything.

Isabella pressed the low E at the fifth fret and plucked the A string. Wobble. She turned the tuning key a hair at a time, and Penelope raised a hand when the wobble turned into a smooth hum. They did the same for the D string, then the G, then the B, each time matching the fifth fret to the open string above it. Then Isabella strummed a G chord, the one they would need first on Sunday, and it sounded like a dropped pan.

"That's worse than when you started," Penelope said.

They tuned again, even more slowly, and the chord was still wrong. Isabella checked every string against the fifth fret below it, and everything matched. She was starting to think the guitar itself was broken, some barren dead spot in the wood that no amount of tuning could fix, when Mr. Brown came down with the coffee urn.

"Can you hear this?" she asked him, and played the chord.

Mr. Brown listened with his head tipped, then said, "Try your G string again. Check where you pressed it."

Isabella looked. She had matched the G at the fifth fret to the open B, the same as every other pair. She slid her finger down one fret, to the fourth, and plucked. The note landed square on the open B, no wobble at all. The G string was the one exception. She retuned it, strummed the chord, and the whole thing rang out clean and full, big enough to fill the room.

Penelope opened her eyes. "Do it again."

Isabella did it again, and this time she sang along.

Bently held out his arm like a knight surrendering a sword. "Fix me, Doctor Scarlett. I fell off the porch rail practicing my cool lean."

"My grandma charges a cookie tariff for lessons," Scarlett said, tearing open a bandage from the first aid tin. "One cookie per wound. House rules." Grandma, watching from her rocking chair, nodded solemnly, as if this were a law she had signed herself.

Scarlett pressed the pad over the scrape, wrapped the bandage snug but not tight, and checked that Bently could still wiggle his fingers. "Not too tight, or your hand turns purple and falls off," she said. "Probably." Bently wiggled his fingers extra fast, just in case. Grandma glanced at the clock and said, "Ten minutes, you two, or we miss the ferry to the fair. And Scarlett, since you're the expert now, look at this." She held out her hand. Two days ago she had sliced it on a can lid, and Scarlett had bandaged it herself, feeling very professional. Now the skin around the cut was red, and the redness had spread past the edges of the bandage like a stain growing on a shirt.

Scarlett touched the skin near it, careful and light. Warm. Hot, even. The whole area looked puffy and swollen, and when Grandma flexed her fingers she winced. "It hurts worse than yesterday," Grandma admitted. "And there's a bit of pus."

Scarlett stood very still, thinking. A cut was supposed to get better, not worse. Spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus, pain that got worse instead of better. All five. That was the whole checklist from the first aid book she'd read under the covers with a flashlight, and this cut had checked every single box. "Grandma," she said, "this needs a doctor. Not a bandage. A doctor."

Grandma sighed and resigned herself to missing the ferry, the fair, and the candy apples. "Well," she said, reaching for her keys, "suppose you'd better drive." Scarlett was already dialing the clinic, and Bently was wrapping the leftover bandage around the cat, who looked deeply offended.

Violet stared at her tray of ice cubes, which were melting into a puddle faster than she had planned, and tried to draft her display board for the third time. Her poster read "The Great Change Test," and underneath she had taped two photos: her ice cubes, and a rusty old horseshoe from her grandfather's barn. The problem was the line she was supposed to write beneath them. She had guessed "both are changes," but that felt thin, and the judges would walk the rows in twenty minutes.

Mika leaned over from the next table, stretching a blob of bright green slime between her hands. "Mine is the elastic slime dynasty," she announced. "Three generations of slime recipes, perfected by me. Judges love a dynasty. Also I really want to beat Laurent, because he said my project was 'just toy stuff,' and I intend to make him eat those words with a spoon." She snapped the slime back into a ball. "So what's your actual question, Violet? What are you testing?"

"That's the thing," Violet said. "I melted ice and it turned to water. I watched it. And the horseshoe got all orange and flaky. They both changed, but they didn't feel like the same kind of change, and I can't say why without just saying 'they're different.'" She crouched down and peered at the puddle. "The water is still here. Nothing went anywhere." She dipped a finger in it, then looked at the horseshoe photo again. "But the rust... the iron didn't just move somewhere else. Something new is sitting on that shoe." She stood up so fast she knocked over a cup. "Wait. That's the test. If I freeze my puddle, I should get ice back. Same stuff, different shape. But I can't un-rust anything."

Mr. Suzuki, the judge with the clipboard, stopped at her table right then, which was terrible timing and also maybe perfect timing. "So, young scientist, what did you find out?"

Violet took a breath. "Melting ice is a physical change," she said. "The stuff changes its shape or its state, but it stays the same substance. Ice melting into water is still water. Rusting is the other kind, because it makes something new." She grabbed the cup she'd knocked over, now full of meltwater, and held it up. "I can freeze this and get ice cubes back. Nobody can turn a rusty horseshoe back into a shiny one just by cooling it."

Mr. Suzuki wrote something on his clipboard. Across the aisle, Laurent was quietly watching, arms crossed. Mika stretched her slime into a long green rope and let it hang between the two tables like a bridge.

"Ten out of ten for the freeze test," Mika whispered. "Laurent, your vinegar volcano is about to be extinct."

Olivier had both friends in his garage, which was bad, because Cade and Dwayne were not speaking to each other. They stood on opposite sides of his dad's workbench like two cats guarding the same sunny spot. Cade had his arms crossed. Dwayne was kicking a paint can, gently, as if the paint can had done nothing wrong and he knew it.

"You always ditch me," Cade said. "Saturday, the skate park. You said you'd come, then you went with your cousin instead."

"That's not ditching, that's my cousin," Dwayne said, and the paint can rang like a dull bell. "And anyway, you never text me back, so why should I?"

Olivier raised both hands the way he had seen a referee do it in a soccer video. His problem was simple: he wanted his alliance of garage-cronies back, and he wanted it before Saturday, when all three of them had planned to build a ramp. If he took Cade's side, he'd lose Dwayne. If he took Dwayne's side, Cade would storm out and the ramp would be an impoverished, lonely pile of wood. He needed a third option.

Then he noticed something. Every sentence either of them said started with "you." You always. You never. You did. Each "you" made the other one's face contract into a deeper scowl, like a slug touching salt. Olivier had learned about this in Mr. Pierre's class, one sleepy Tuesday, and he had thought it was boring then. It was not boring now.

"New rule," he announced. "Nobody says a sentence starting with 'you.' You have to start with 'I' and say your own feeling. It's called an I-statement. Watch." He turned to Cade. "Say it again, but that way."

Cade rolled his eyes so hard it must have hurt. But he tried. "I feel left out when plans change."

Dwayne stopped kicking the paint can. His shoulders came down from around his ears. "Well," he said, "I feel bad that I didn't tell you about my cousin. I just forgot."

"Forgot," Cade repeated. "Okay. That's annoying, but it's not ditching."

"Bring your cousin Saturday," Olivier said quickly, before anyone could invent a new argument. "He can hold the wood."

Dwayne picked up the paint can and offered it to Cade like a trophy. "Peace offering. It's mostly dried up, but it's blue."

Cade took it. "Blue is literally the ramp color I wanted."

The campfire crackled in the ring of stones, and Xavier poked at it with a stick until a spiral of sparks rose into the dark. Across the fire, Jorge sat hunched with his arms crossed over his shoulders, which were blotchy red and shiny with aloe gel from the first-aid cabin.

"I put on sunscreen this morning," Jorge said, wincing as he leaned back. "Before we even went down to the lake. So how did this happen?"

Xavier thought about that while he turned his stick in the flames. Jorge had slathered on sunscreen at eight o'clock, that much was true. Then the whole cabin had spent the afternoon at the lake, swimming and racing each other along the shore and hauling the canoe. Xavier remembered the counselor calling out the time when they hiked back for dinner: nearly five. He counted on his fingers, and an insight slid into place. "Jorge, you put it on at eight and then stayed out until five. That's a really long time." He flipped the stick over. "And you were in the water all afternoon, too."

Anabel, who was roasting a marshmallow on the other side of the fire, looked up. "My mom says sunscreen wears off," she offered. "You have to put it on again every two hours when you're outside."

"And right after swimming," said Mr. Pham, the camp director, walking past with an armload of firewood. He only paused for a second before going on, but that was enough. Swimming, Xavier thought. That washes it right off. Nobody had reminded Jorge to reapply anything, all day, and so the morning coat had rubbed away hours before dinner.

"Tomorrow," Xavier said, "we set a rule. New sunscreen every two hours, even if we feel fine, and the second anybody climbs out of the lake." He glanced at Jorge's glowing shoulders. "And if somebody's shoulder looks like a stop sign, we restrict the afternoon swimming to the shady part of the shore until it heals."

"Deal," Jorge said, though he smiled like it cost him something. Anabel pressed her cold marshmallow gently against Jorge's arm, and he sighed with relief so dramatic that even Mr. Pham laughed from the woodpile.

"You know," Anabel said, waving her marshmallow like a tiny white flag, "that was almost eloquent, Xavier. Stop signs and shady shores. You should give the campfire speech every night."

"I'll take the job." Xavier fed his stick to the fire and watched the flames catch. "First speech starts now: everybody up, sunscreen meeting at the picnic table, eight sharp."

The box had been in Alexis's backpack all morning, and by the time the bus lurched out of the school parking lot, he could not wait any longer. He tore the tape off, lifted out the phone his parents had given him for his birthday, and held it where Abigail and Emerson could see over the seat. "First one I've ever had," he said. Abigail leaned over the aisle. "Put a flashlight app on it. Mine has one and it's great for the bus when it's dark in winter."

Alexis found the app and tapped Install. A box popped onto the screen, and he stared at it. "It wants permission to see my contacts. All of them." Emerson frowned. "Why would a flashlight need that? It's a light." Alexis thought about Mr. Mansour, who taught science and always said the question comes first, and the answer has to precede the question about whether you trust it or not. Something felt wrong. A flashlight should turn on a bulb. That was all.

"I'm not tapping yes," he said. He pressed Cancel, then went digging through the screens until he found a place called settings, full of lists with little switches beside every app. There it was: each app had to ask permission before it could use the phone's camera, the microphone, or the contacts, and there was a switch to take that permission away later. He tested it with Abigail's help, since she had her own phone. He gave the calculator app permission to use the microphone, then flipped the switch off. The little light beside it went grey. "So you can undo it," Abigail said. "Any time."

Alexis tried the flashlight one more time, just to be sure he wasn't imagining it, and the same box came back asking for contacts. He deleted the app instead. "There's a different one," Emerson said, pointing. "This one only asks for the camera." That still seemed strange, but a camera at least had something to do with light. It wasn't perfectly logical, but it felt feasible, like a small safe step.

The bus rattled past the field where the track team ran laps, and Alexis remembered his coach saying his grades had to come before any scholarship talk, so the phone went into his pocket with the screen off. He would figure out the rest a little at a time. Abigail tapped his shoulder. "Text me when you get home," she said. "Your number's on the card in the box." Alexis pulled the card out and read the digits twice. "One practice text," he said, "before I do anything else."

Alexandre noticed it first during dodgeball, when Eason waved him over and then leaned back a full step. "You smell like the gym lost a fight," Eason said, not meanly, but not quietly either. That was Tuesday. On Wednesday, Noelle slid her chair a few inches toward the window side of the desk they shared in Mr. Martínez's class, and Alexandre spent the rest of math staring at the poster about rainforest extinction instead of at his worksheet.

After school, his mom drove him to the pharmacy. "Get what you need," she said. "I'll wait in the car."

The deodorant shelf had two sticks from the same brand, nearly identical, in green and blue. Alexandre picked them both up and read the labels. One said deodorant. The other said antiperspirant. He read the backs twice. The green one's ingredient list included an aluminum compound; the blue one's did not.

A pharmacist restocking shampoo nearby glanced over. He looked about sixteen and bored. "Antiperspirant," Alexandre read aloud. "What's that word mean?"

"Antiperspirants reduce sweating by using aluminum compounds that temporarily plug the sweat ducts," the pharmacist said, then carried his box toward aisle four. Alexandre stood there holding both sticks. So the aluminum one plugged the ducts, the little tunnels the sweat came out of. The other one just covered the smell. He bought the green one with his allowance money.

The next morning he used it, then did a test. In science they were studying venomous animals, and Mr. Martínez had them run laps around the field to measure heart rates before and after. Alexandre ran hard, came inside, and checked the armpits of his shirt. Damp, but not soaked the way his shirt had been after dodgeball on Tuesday. He asked Noelle, without explaining why, whether she could smell anything from where she sat.

"Sharpie and rain," she said, sniffing. "That's the stick, right? It's fine. Way better than Tuesday."

At lunch, Eason asked where Alexandre had gotten the green stick, because Eason's older brother used some blue one that "doesn't do anything." Alexandre told him about the two labels, and Eason wanted proof. So they ran the fence line twice, came back, and compared shirts. Alexandre's was damp at the edges only. Eason's looked like he had swum across the creek with his clothes on.

"That's completely unfair," Eason said, peeling his shirt away from his chest.

"Trade me your chips and I'll tell you which one to buy," Alexandre said.

Eason looked at his chips, then at his shirt, and pushed the bag across the table.

Grandpa's study smelled like old paper and pencil shavings, and the map spread across the desk was so big it hung over the edges onto a chair. "Find my hometown," Grandpa said, tapping a spot in the far north. "If you can tell me exactly where it is, we'll video call your cousin and you can read it to her yourself."

Matthew leaned over the map until his nose nearly touched the paper. Thin lines curved across it in every direction, some running sideways, some running up and down, and little numbers sat along the edges like tiny measurements. "This one," he said, pointing at a line labeled 49. "It's on the forty-ninth line."

"Latitude," Grandpa said. "The sideways ones are latitude. The up-and-down ones are longitude." He set a magnifying glass beside Matthew's elbow, then shuffled off to make tea, because his knees signaled rain was coming and he wanted to be seated when it arrived.

Matthew traced the line with one finger and found the little black dot of the hometown sitting just above it, close to where a longitude line crossed. So it was near 49 degrees latitude, and near some other number for longitude. He presumed that meant the numbers worked like street addresses, one telling you how far across, one telling you how far up. He checked another city, Toronto, and found it sitting near 43 degrees. Six degrees apart. Then he remembered something from Ms. Addo's class, written on the board while Tyler was trying to throw paper clips into Kenzi's hood: one degree of latitude covers about 111 kilometers, or about 69 miles, of north-south distance. He counted on his fingers. Six degrees. Six times 69 miles.

"Grandpa!" Matthew called. "Your hometown is about 414 miles north of Toronto. Six degrees times sixty-nine miles." He said it twice more while Grandpa settled into his chair with his tea, and then Matthew got out his notebook and wrote the location the way a real navigator might: close to 49 degrees north latitude, west longitude seventy-something, roughly 414 miles north of Toronto, or about 666 kilometers, since six times 111 was 666.

Grandpa squinted at the notebook, then at Matthew, and pulled out his phone. "Let's call your cousin and see if the boy is right." The call connected, and Grandpa held up the notebook without a word. On the screen, the cousin leaned close, then laughed. "He's got it," she announced, and behind her somebody shouted, "Unanimous!" Matthew grinned and drew a small star next to his numbers.

"Tomorrow," Grandpa said, tapping the map's vast blue ocean, "we find the shipwreck."

Alexis stood in the community centre kitchen with a stack of foam cups, listening to her grandmother describe the new bylaw. Anyone who wanted to sell baking at the Saturday farmers' market inside the centre now had to pay for a special licence, and her grandmother said forty dollars a season was too much for her lemon loaves.

"That's bizarre," Alexis said. "You've been selling here for six years." She turned a cup over in her hands, thinking. There had to be a way to change a rule that seemed wrong, and it wouldn't be by ignoring it, because then the market supervisor would just send her grandmother home.

At the front desk, she asked the receptionist who made bylaws. The answer was city council. Then Alexis found the council website on the lobby computer and read the rules for meetings. Her reflex was to look for an email address, but what she found instead was better: a page saying residents could ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting. Five minutes, the page said, and the request had to go in ahead of time. "It's called appearing as a delegation," Alexis read aloud, and copied the phrase onto her wrist with a pen.

That night at her grandmother's house, she practised. Forest came over with Savannah, and the three of them rearranged the kitchen chairs into a pretend council chamber. Mr. Lewandowski, the neighbour whose garden shared the fence, agreed to supervise the rehearsal and play the councillors. Alexis's first try was a disaster. She talked too fast, forgot her numbers, and stood twisting the corner of her note card until it went soggy.

"You have five minutes, so use them," Savannah said. "Slow down at the important part."

The second try was better. Alexis explained who she was, how long her grandmother had sold at the market, and that the licence fee would push out small sellers like her. She ended with a plain request: lower the fee for people who sell only a few weekends a season. Forest held up his phone timer and gave her a thumbs-up at four minutes and twelve seconds.

The real meeting came two weeks later. Alexis stood at the little wooden podium while the councillors watched from their raised desks, and she spoke about lemon loaves and forty dollars and Saturday mornings at the community centre. When she finished, one councillor leaned toward his microphone.

"That was a fine delegation," he said. "Let's look at that fee."

Grandpa Whit had been sleeping in the guest bedroom for six days, and Hayden had one night left to solve the problem. The problem was this: Grandpa told the best stories in the world, about flooding creeks and runaway mules and a one-eyed schoolteacher, and when he drove home tomorrow, the stories would go with him.

Hayden had tried writing them down, but Grandpa talked faster than any pencil. He'd tried memorizing, which lasted about as long as ice cream in July. On Thursday afternoon he sat on the guest bed, chin in his hands, staring at the empty bookshelf like it might hand him an idea. The room felt almost desolate without Grandpa's suitcase exploding socks everywhere, though Grandpa himself was downstairs burning toast.

Then he remembered. Neve had recorded her grandmother last month for a school project, and she'd mentioned a website. He called her from the hallway. "That thing your grandma did," he said. "The recording thing."

"StoryCorps," Neve said. "You record an interview with a family member. They keep it, and with permission it gets saved at the Library of Congress. Like, the actual Library of Congress, in Washington."

"With my grandpa's voice? In a giant library?"

"On a shelf with a spine, probably," Neve said, "right next to a million other people's grandpas."

Hayden tried to evade the awkward part, but Neve sniffed it out anyway. "You have to ask permission, doofus. Grandparents love being asked."

That evening, Hayden borrowed his mom's phone, knocked on the guest bedroom door, and found Grandpa attempting to fold a shirt into something that resembled a dumpling. "Grandpa. One last story before you leave. But this time I record it."

Grandpa raised an eyebrow. "For whom? The FBI?"

"For the Library of Congress," Hayden said, and explained, all in a rush, how the recording could be saved there if Grandpa said yes. Grandpa went quiet, which was rare enough that a tumbleweed could have rolled through the room. Then he sat down on the bed like a man accepting a medal.

"You mean my mule story outlasts me?" he said. "Son, start recording before I remember how to be humble."

Hayden hit the red button. "Question one. The mule. Go."

"The mule," Grandpa began, "was named Biscuit, and he had the manners of a pirate."

The phone hummed on the nightstand, saving every word.

Jace crouched by the fire pit at Camp Widow Creek, turning a gray chunk of rock over in his hands while his friend Greyson poked at a beetle with a stick. Their teacher, Ms. Ferreira, had promised a prize to whoever sorted the most rocks correctly into the three boxes she had labeled igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. Jace wanted that prize badly, mostly because it was a giant chocolate bar, and partly because Greyson kept saying his own pile would crush Jace's pile "by a huge percentage."

"That one's sedimentary," Greyson said, pointing at the rock in Jace's hand. "It's all layered, like a sandwich."

"It's not layered, it's bubbly," Jace said, holding it up. The whole surface was pitted with little holes, like a sponge that had given up. He dropped it into the igneous box anyway, because igneous meant rock from cooled lava, and lava seemed like the sort of thing that would bubble.

They hauled their finds down to the mess hall, where Nia was already waiting with a bucket of lake water she had dragged up the hill for reasons she refused to explain. "I wanted to wash my rocks," she said, as if that were normal, which for Nia it was. The hillside around camp was so barren of anything interesting that washing rocks counted as entertainment.

Jace set his bubbly gray rock on the table to sort his other finds, and Greyson, reaching past him for the bean dip, knocked it off the edge. It landed in Nia's bucket with a splash. "Sorry," Greyson said, and then they all froze, because the rock was not sinking. It sat on the water like a beach ball.

"It floats," Nia whispered. "Rocks don't float."

"This one does," Jace said. His brain started churning. A rock full of gas bubbles, trapped as lava cooled, that would be light, and light things could float. He remembered Ms. Ferreira saying the word at the start of the week: pumice. He grabbed the rock out of the bucket, dripping, and held it up. "It's pumice. It's igneous, from lava, and the bubbles got trapped in it. That's why it floats."

Ms. Ferreira came over, looked in the bucket, looked at the rock, and raised an eyebrow. "Five points for the igneous box," she said, "and five more for the floating demonstration."

Greyson groaned and slid his sandwich-layered rock toward the sedimentary box. "Fine. You win this round." He paused. "Compromise? We split the chocolate bar."

"Sixty-forty," Jace said, wringing out his sleeve. "My percentage."

Nia fished a pebble from the bucket and dropped it back in. It sank, plunk, and she grinned. "One out of two rocks floating is still better than I expected."

Emily had ten minutes before the sleepover movie started, and her old password had just been rejected for the third time.

"That's the one you use everywhere," Elora said, spinning her desk chair around. "You told me. Your email, the game, everything."

"I know." Emily stared at the laptop on Elora's desk. A message had popped up on her favorite writing site: someone in another city had tried to log into her account. It hadn't worked, but the site wanted her to change her password anyway. "It's 'emily2013.' How did they even guess it?"

Elora shrugged. "People guess stuff like that. Want to install the password manager my sister uses? It remembers everything for you."

"Then it has to be one password that guards all the others, and I'd better not mess that one up." Emily pulled a sticky note toward her and started writing. "Okay. How about 'emily2013!'"

"You added one symbol. Come on."

Emily thought about the time she'd used the same password for her bike lock and her locker at school, back in fourth grade. Lena had guessed it in about a minute, and for a week everyone opened Emily's locker as a joke. Emily had laughed along, but she still remembered how her stomach had dropped. Maybe reusing passwords was the same mistake, just invisible.

She tried something new. She looked around the room for random words, ones that had nothing to do with her. "Elora, give me four words. Anything."

"Turtle. Cactus. Lemon. Piano."

Emily typed turtlecactuslemonpiano into the site's tester. "It says it would take forever to guess." She said it slowly, testing the idea. "Four random words. It's long enough that it's hard to guess, but it's easy for me to remember." She tried to picture a turtle balancing on a cactus, holding a lemon, playing a piano, and grinned. There was no way anyone could guess that.

"But you can't use it on your email too," Elora said. "Remember your locker."

"I know, I know." Emily started a second list, her pen moving fast. "Lena. Quick, I need four more words before the movie."

From down the hall, Lena's voice called, "Does 'purple donkey saxophone blizzard' work?"

Olivia slid her worksheet across the table so Lainey could see it. The problem said y = 2x + 3, and Mr. Henry wanted them to solve for y when x equaled four, then plot enough points to draw the whole line. Lainey, who wanted to beat Anastasia in the club's graphing race, had already drawn three lines and was halfway through a fourth.

"Try x equals one," Lainey said. "Then two. The points should correspond, one x to one y, like they match up."

Olivia calculated. When x was one, y came out to five. When x was two, y was seven. She plotted both points, then connected them with her ruler and sat back. Her line went up, climbing from the lower left toward the upper right.

"That's a positive slope," Lainey said, pointing. "A line with a positive slope rises as you read from left to right."

Olivia nodded, then flipped to the next problem: y = -2x + 3. She did the steps again. Two times x, then subtract, then add three. When x was one, y was one. When x was two, y was negative one. She plotted the points and drew the line, and this one went the other way, sliding downhill from the upper left down to the lower right.

"Mine falls," Olivia said. "Same numbers, but the minus sign flips it."

Anastasia leaned over from the next table. "I made a database of all the equations Mr. Henry ever gave us, so nobody has to guess which ones climb. But I put my name on every page, so much for staying anonymous."

"Nobody cares about your pages," Lainey said. "Race you on the last one."

Mr. Henry posted the final equation on the board: y = 3x minus 1. Olivia solved it, plotted two points, and checked which way her pencil would travel. She smiled and drew her line rising to the right.

The tryout list went up on Friday, and Elijah's name was not on it. He found out at school, but he did the real thinking at home, at the kitchen table, with a mug of cocoa going cold beside him.

Isabel had texted him the names of the fourteen kids who made the basketball team. Elijah read the message three times, then grabbed a pencil and retrieved the tryout sign-up sheet from his backpack. Next to each name he wrote the player's birthday, which he mostly knew because the coach had made everyone say it out loud on the first day. When he finished, he counted. Nine of the fourteen were born in January, February, or March. Only two had birthdays after September, and one of those was Milo, who was already the tallest kid in grade six.

He called Isabel. "Can I read you something?" He read his list of names and dates. "The kids born early in the year got picked more. All of them are months older than the December kids like me."

"That's a thing," Isabel said. "My cousin calls it the relative age effect. It happens in lots of sports."

Elijah had spent the weekend deciding he just wasn't good enough. Now he wasn't sure. He wrote a short email to Mr. MacLeod, who coached the team: "I noticed most of the players picked were born early in the year, and studies have found that happens a lot in youth sports. I'd like to try again. Could I come to one practice and show you?" He reread it, deleted the last sentence because it sounded turbulent and demanding, and sent it anyway.

Monday evening, Mr. MacLeod called the house. "Come Wednesday," he said. "Bring your shoes." Elijah packed his bag that night, set it by the door, and shot free throws at the driveway hoop until the porch light came on.

At Wednesday's practice he scored twice, once on a pass from Milo, who grinned at him across the turbulent cluster of bodies under the net.

"After this," Elijah panted, "I'm going to be like a January kid."

"You already play like one," Milo said.

The skate park at dusk smelled like warm rubber and sunscreen, and Autumn spread her science project across the picnic table by the half-pipe. Her battery, switch, and three small bulbs sat in a careful row, waiting to become the light display she had promised Mr. Lim, the caretaker who had said she could set it up for Friday night practice. He had even gone to the office to authorize it, coming back with a signed note that said one line: Autumn's lights, one table, one night.

"It worked at home," Autumn said, clipping the last wire. Mia skated over, wheels rattling the concrete, and Matilda trailed behind with the screwdriver in her back pocket like a tail. Autumn flipped the switch. All three bulbs glowed.

Then Mia leaned in to look closer, knocked the middle bulb with her elbow, and it flickered and died. The other two went dark too. The table went black except for the last molten orange streak of sunset behind the ramp.

"Great," Matilda said. "One dead bulb, zero lights."

Autumn stared at the wires. Last month she had done this same thing on a school project, wiring every bulb in one chain, and when one failed she had panicked, torn it apart, and taken a lower mark rather than trying to fix it. She still wasn't sure whether she had been lazy that day or just scared. She thought about it while Mia fanned herself with the signed note.

"Each bulb has its own path to the battery," Autumn said slowly, following the wires with her finger. "That's how I should build it. Then if one breaks, the others stay lit, because they aren't sharing its path."

"Are you sure?" Mia asked.

"Mostly. Let's find out." She unclipped the wires and rewired them, giving each bulb its own connection, the way the rivers near her grandmother's house split and ran side by side. Matilda handed her the screwdriver without being asked. It took three tries and one bent clip, and Autumn tried not to think about her bias toward quitting when something had already failed once, the way she assumed a broken thing stayed broken.

She flipped the switch. Two bulbs lit. She reached over, unscrewed one of them, and the other kept glowing, steady and small against the coming dark.

"Try it," Autumn said, holding out the dead bulb to Mia. "Break something."

Mia grinned and gave the middle bulb a deliberate tap with her knuckle. The light beside it never even blinked.

Alexis set his pencil down and stared at the lumpy circle on his sketchpad. Across the picnic table, Amelie was already darkening the shadow under her sphere, and Ms. Hughes had said the art show opened in exactly one hour. "Yours looks flat," Amelie said, not unkindly. "Mine looked flat too, until Elin helped me."

Elin leaned over from the next bench. "You put your light where?" she asked. Alexis pointed at the upper left of his drawing. "Okay, so the darkest part goes on the opposite side, and then you shade lighter and lighter toward the light. There's a bright spot, the highlight, right where the lamp hits it."

Alexis adjusted his grip on the pencil and tried again. He curved his strokes around the sphere instead of scribbling straight across, and slowly the circle began to bulge off the page. Then Elin held up her own drawing, and Alexis noticed something strange about it. The bottom edge of her sphere, on the shadow side, was almost white. It looked like two separate lamps were shining on it from opposite directions.

"That's not right," Alexis said slowly. "The lamp's only on one side. Why would the bottom of the shadow side be that bright?" He looked over at the still life on the table, a real ball under a real lamp, and squinted at its dark side. The very bottom edge wasn't pure black. It was lighter than the middle of the shadow, but nowhere near as light as the lit side. He tested the idea on his own paper, keeping that lower edge a middle gray, darker than anything on the lit half but lighter than the deepest shadow.

"Reflected light," Elin said, peering at the real ball. "Light bouncing back from the table onto the shadow side. I made mine too bright."

"You both have ten minutes," Ms. Hughes called from the craft cabin, where she was taping drawings to the wall.

Alexis shaded fast, keeping every part of the shadow side distinct from the lit side, dark against light. Amelie nudged his elbow. "Hang it up before you smudge it." He carried the pad across the grass and Ms. Hughes pinned it beside Elin's, sphere and shadow side by side under the tent.

Mia folded the newspaper page one more time and put it in her jacket pocket before Kate's mom drove them to the cemetery. The page had come out of the stack her father saved from two weeks ago, back when Grandma June first died. Mia had read it so many times she could almost say it from memory, but she still didn't understand one part.

At the cemetery, Kate and Marylou waited by the gate with flowers, and behind them Mr. Haile, the neighbor who used to fix Grandma June's fence, stood with his hat in his hands. The grass in the middle of the hill had been mowed, but the rows near the back were still long, so everyone walked carefully between the stones.

"There's something I have to check," Mia said, and she pulled out the page. "The obituary. It says she 'spent four years at sea with the merchant fleet.'" She looked at Mr. Haile. "Grandma never told me that. Not once. I thought maybe it was a mistake."

Mr. Haile smiled. "An obituary? That's the notice they publish when someone dies, with a short account of their life. Family, work, interests. She wouldn't have left her sailing out of it by accident."

Mia hadn't known that word before she found the page. Now she understood what it meant: whoever wrote it was supposed to tell the whole life, not just the parts people knew. She thought of all those afternoons dismantling old radios with Grandma on the porch, every part laid out on a towel and named. Grandma had named everything. Why not that?

Mia tried an experiment. "Mr. Haile, do you remember her ever talking about water?"

"Every time it rained," he said. "She'd say the deck rolled like the median of a busy road, cars going both ways. Never made sense to me till now."

It was ironic, Mia thought, that she had spent four years eating dinner across from a sailor and never once asked the right question. She knelt, set the folded page under the flowers, and smoothed it flat with both hands.

"Four years at sea," she said out loud. "Next time I visit, I'm bringing a map so you can show me where."

Sara's mother thrust a five-dollar bill into her hand at the front door. "We need milk before Grandma gets here at six, and I have to watch the soup. You're eleven now. You can do this." The clock on the microwave said 5:32. Sara looked at the bill, then at the door, then at the bill again. She had walked to the corner store before, but always with her mother, always with someone else holding the money.

She counted the steps down the front walk, because counting made her feel like she knew what she was doing. Twenty-one steps to the sidewalk. At the store, the cold air hit her face when she pushed through the door, and she found the milk cooler right where she remembered it. The sticker on the carton said 2.65. She carried it to the counter and handed over the five, and while the cashier rang it up, Sara did the arithmetic in her head, slowly, like walking downstairs in the dark. Five dollars take away two sixty-five. Two dollars and thirty-five cents. That was the change she should get.

The cashier handed her two coins and a bill. "Thanks, hon." Sara stepped aside so the man behind her could pay for his lottery tickets, and only then did she look at what was in her palm. Two dollars and five cents. A quarter was missing. Her stomach did a small flip. Was she sure? She checked the milk sticker again through the plastic bag: 2.65, plain as anything. And five take away two sixty-five was still 2.35, no matter how many times she said it to herself.

The line had grown, and the clock behind the counter said 5:41. Grandma arrived at six. Sara thought about just going home, but a missing quarter meant either she was wrong or the cashier was wrong, and she wanted to know which. Her friend Gerald had once told her that being assertive just meant saying what you needed without apologizing for it, and Sara had liked that word so much she'd written it on her arm with a pen. She took a breath and stepped back to the counter.

"Excuse me," she said, louder than she meant to. "The milk was two sixty-five, and I paid with five dollars, so the change should be two thirty-five. You gave me two oh five." The cashier looked at the register, then at her, then counted the coins in her palm with one finger. "Well, would you look at that. You're right, hon." He dropped a quarter into her hand.

Sara walked home grinning at the sky. It struck her as a kind of irony that the smallest coin had made her feel the tallest, and she wondered what other invisible arithmetic was hiding in ordinary afternoons, waiting for someone to count it out. She pushed through the front door and set the milk on the counter. "Two thirty-five," she told her mother, "and I counted every cent."

Alice had always thought the Moon glowed the way a lightbulb does, like it was burning something, and that was exactly what she planned to tell Aubree when she came over. Grandpa's lamp stood in the middle of the darkened den, its shade removed, blazing like a small sun. Alice held an orange ball at arm's length, ready to orbit it.

"Wait," Aubree said, dropping her backpack by the door. "What's all this?"

"Grandpa says if we mess up his den, we restore it with time and leisure after. Sit down and watch." Alice walked the ball slowly around the lamp, keeping her head still, like Earth. Halfway around, the ball's lit side faced away from her. She turned her head carefully, the way Grandpa had shown her, and gasped. "Aubree, look. I can only see the skinny lit edge. That's a crescent."

Aubree leaned in, agile on her knees, circling to see from Alice's viewpoint. "So it's the same ball the whole time?"

"It has to be. It's just..." Alice stopped, frowning. She moved the ball back to the start, where its whole lit face blazed toward her, then walked it half the orbit again and watched the light shrink to a sliver. "The lamp didn't change. The ball didn't change. The only thing that changed was where I was standing." Her voice went quick with excitement. "The Moon makes no light of its own. It shines only because it reflects sunlight. So the shape we see is just how much of the lit part is facing us."

From the doorway, Ms. Sokolov, who had come to return Grandpa's garden shears, clapped once. "Then show me a new moon," she said.

Alice carried the ball to the far side of the lamp, directly opposite herself, and the bright face turned completely away. The ball concealed its light behind its own dark side, a round shadow against nothing. "It's still there," she whispered. "We just can't see it."

Eve slid her draft across the library table until it touched Paula's elbow. "Read the last part first," she whispered. Around them the afternoon crowd murmured, and Mr. Kaur was restacking the returns cart by the window. The three friends had until closing time to finish their essays for the display case by the front desk, where the best one would hang for a whole month with the writer's name in gold letters.

Eve was arguing that the school cafeteria should keep prices low even when inflation pushed them up. She had three solid paragraphs, but her favorite idea, a plan where students could trade cafeteria credits for fresh fruit from the community garden, had arrived late, scrawled into the final paragraph like a guest showing up after the party ended. Paula read it twice, chewing her pencil. "The fruit idea is your best one," she said, "but it shows up at the end like a surprise. It kind of knocks the rest over."

Enoch leaned over from his seat, his own essay about later library hours spread in front of him. "Mr. Kaur has a whole shelf on essays," he said. "The orange binder. I looked at it yesterday." He fetchedit, and Eve flipped through until she found the page on endings. The rule sat there in plain print: a conclusion restates the thesis in fresh words and sums up the main points, but it should not introduce a brand-new argument. She read it twice, then frowned at her own paper.

"So the ending is supposed to echo the beginning, not announce something new," she said slowly. "That means my garden idea isn't a conclusion. It's a whole main point that got born in the wrong place." She felt almost annoyed with the rule, because the idea had seemed so perfect right there, glowing at the bottom of the page. But then she began to see how it worked. She tested it on Enoch. "Listen to my intro. Cafeteria prices should stay low. Listen to my ending. Cafeteria prices should stay low, and here's why the garden makes that possible." Enoch nodded. "The second one sounds bigger," he said, "but it's actually two papers glued together."

Eve got to work. She lifted the garden idea out of the last paragraph and gave it a home of its own as her third main point, then adjusted her introduction so the reader would expect it. For her conclusion she found fresh words: instead of repeating "prices should stay low," she wrote that every student deserved a lunch that did not cost more each year. It summed up prices, the budget, and the garden without dragging in anything new. Paula read it and gave a thumbs-up so wide her elastic sleeve slipped down over her hand.

At the desk, Mr. Kaur accepted the pages with both hands, the way he took everything, as if each returned book were a small treasure. Eve watched him clip her essay to the top of the stack. "May I borrow that orange binder over the weekend?" she asked. "I'm going to need it again." He smiled and slid it across the counter, and the gold letters on the display case caught the evening light.

Cooper stood in the pharmacy aisle with his mother's ten-dollar bill and a list that said "deodorant, the kind with the green cap." Parker had told the whole locker room that Cooper smelled like a wet dog, and Cooper had decided the problem was his armpits. He picked out the green-cap stick, paid the cashier, and marched home to test it.

The next morning he swiped the deodorant on, pulled on the same hoodie he had worn all week, and went to school. Parker sniffed near him in science and said, "Still wet dog, Cooper." Cooper's ears went hot. He had used the product. Something did not add up.

At lunch he laid out the evidence on the table like a detective. Monday he had worn the hoodie and smelled. Tuesday the same hoodie, plus deodorant, and still smelled. The armpit theory was biased, he realized, because he had only ever blamed his armpits and never checked anything else. Aleena leaned over his shoulder and read his notes. "You wore that hoodie both days," she said. "Sweat and bacteria stay in worn clothes and socks. Changing into clean ones every day helps prevent body odor. Even my brother knows that." She pointed at his sleeve. "That thing is a hull of old sweat."

Cooper ran an experiment that evening. He showered, put on a completely fresh shirt and fresh socks, and left the hoodie on his desk. In the morning he sniffed the hoodie first.
