"Today's cuisine at the snack bar is hot dogs and regret," Tucker announced, "but tomorrow it's victory nachos, so pass that test." She kicked off, counting silently. Three strokes, breathe left. Three more, breathe right. Left, right, left, right, all the way down the lane, and the wall of the far end met her hands exactly where it should.

She looked back up the lane she had swum. Straight as a ruler. Behind her, Allan was trying it too, and even from a distance she could hear his whoop. Mr. Kaya, watching from the diving block, gave her a single thumbs up and pointed at the clock, as if to say the water was hers. On Friday, she thought, and she dove straight back in.

Alice had been dreading lunch all morning, because Ziad and Yaseen were still angry at each other over the group project, and Ms. Rajapakse had asked her to sit with them and help sort it out. Last year she had tried the same thing with two other kids and it had gone badly; she had taken her friend's side immediately, and the other girl had never really spoken to her again. She kept thinking about that as she carried her tray toward the corner table.

"I'm not sitting near him," Ziad said, arms folded, looking defiant.

"You didn't do your part, that's all I said," Yaseen shot back.

Alice raised her hands. "Before we talk about the project, I want rules for the conversation itself." She had read a page in the library about mediators the night before, and one line had stuck with her: mediators usually start by setting ground rules, such as one person speaks at a time and no name-calling, which both sides agree to before talking.

"Rules?" Ziad said. "Like ground rules?"

"Right. One at a time, and no name-calling. You both have to agree before we start." She slid a napkin across the table. "Write your names on it if you agree."

Ziad wrote his name first, then Yaseen, which surprised her. When Yaseen began to explain that he'd done the slides alone and the research alone, Ziad opened his mouth, caught Alice's eye, and closed it again. He waited. When it was his turn, he said the reason he hadn't done his part was that his grandmother had been in the hospital and he hadn't wanted anyone to know. Yaseen's shoulders dropped.

"Okay," Alice said, and she drew two stick figures on the napkin to depict them shaking hands. They didn't actually shake hands. But by the time the bell rang, they had reached a consensus to redo the slides together, and Ziad asked her, "Same table tomorrow?"

Gemma shoved her phone across the carpet and refused to look at it. "It's gone," she said. "I deleted it last night, the second I woke up."

Alice picked it up anyway. On the screen was Gemma's old club blog, the public one their whole grade had found in September, still showing the post where Gemma had called the science fair judges "clueless zombies." At least, Alice was almost sure it did. She tapped the address into her own borrowed phone and the page loaded fresh, without it.

"See?" Gemma said. "Deleted means deleted."

But Alice had a funny intuition about that, the same feeling she got when a magic trick obviously had a trick to it. Public things on the internet felt different from private texts. A text vanished into your phone. A blog post had been sitting out in the open where anyone, anything, could walk by and look at it. What if something out there had been looking, and remembering?

"I hypothesize there's an old copy somewhere," she said, typing. "A place that saves pages. My brother mentioned it once, when the school site went down."

She searched: archive of old web pages. A result came up right away, the Wayback Machine, with a search box and a claim on the screen that made her blink. Saved web pages: more than one trillion.

"No way," Gemma said, leaning over despite herself.

Alice pasted in the blog's address and hit the button. A little calendar appeared, full of dates. She picked one from before last night, before the deletion. The page rebuilt itself on the screen, slow and slightly wrong-looking, like a counterfeit version of the original, but there it was. The zombie line, word for word, in Gemma's own font.

Gemma groaned and dropped her forehead onto the carpet.

"Okay," Alice said, already wondering how many of her own deleted posts lived in there. "So what do we do about it?"

Aiden had been chosen to welcome the new student, and he still hadn't decided how. Ms. Fernando had said on Friday, "You can delegate jobs if you like, but the welcome itself is yours," which meant everyone would be watching him. He'd planned a handshake, the kind his grandfather taught him: firm, two pumps, then let go. That was good manners in his house.

The new student, Louis-Felix, arrived on Tuesday morning with a small wrapped parcel in his hands. Aiden noticed the tag said his own name, so Louis-Felix must have known he'd be the welcomer. "In France we bring something," Louis-Felix said, holding it out. "It would be strange not to." Aiden took it with both hands because somehow that felt right, and slid it into his desk, unsure whether opening it now would be rude or not opening it would be rude. Renee leaned over and whispered, "At my grandma's you open it right away so she knows you like it." He decided to wait, and watch.

Then the room went quiet because Ms. Fernando had stood up. "Louis-Felix lived in New Zealand for two years before this school," she said, "and he has something to show us." Louis-Felix turned to Aiden. "I want to do it properly," he said. "In New Zealand, when someone new arrives, there's a greeting called a hongi." He stepped close and pressed his nose and forehead gently against Aiden's. Aiden held still, surprised by how warm it was. "It means we share the breath of life," Louis-Felix said softly, and stepped back.

At lunch Aiden sat across from Louis-Felix and worked something out between bites. His mother said elbows off the table; Renee's family ate with bread torn by hand; Louis-Felix kept his fork upside down in his left fist, European style, and seemed comfortable. So the rules weren't one big rule, Aiden thought. They were more like a ratio, a few parts each family and each country mixed in its own way. No wonder the gullible kids in class believed there was only one correct way to do everything.

He tried his theory out. "Watch," he told Renee, and turned to Louis-Felix. "Do it again, the greeting. I want to get it right this time." Louis-Felix smiled, leaned in, and their noses and foreheads touched. Behind them, Renee whispered, "Okay, now I want one too."

Sarah's phone buzzed at exactly four o'clock, which meant she had two hours before the online deal on VoltBerry vanished at midnight and only one hour before her mom picked her up from Soraya's house. Soraya had the website open on her laptop, and it looked amazing. A sleek blue page, a photo of a smiling runner, and big letters promising that VoltBerry Focus Drink improved concentration in nine out of ten kids.

"I have forty dollars from my birthday," Soraya said, drumming her fingers on the desk. "That's almost enough for the six-bottle pack. It would help with the spelling bee on Friday for sure."

Sarah leaned closer. The site was full of testimonials from people named things like "Verified Mom of 3" and even a quote from somebody calling himself Dr. Halversen, Expert in Nutrition. It all sounded convincing right up until Sarah scrolled to the bottom and found a tiny line: VoltBerry Wellness Group. A thought tickled at her. The website was saying wonderful things about itself, which was a bit like asking a magician whether his trick was real. She couldn't see who was behind the page just by reading the page.

"Can I borrow your laptop for a second?" she asked. She opened a new tab and typed VoltBerry Wellness Group into a search engine. The first result was a news article from last spring: VoltBerry Wellness Group was the company that made the drink. The same company. A second article mentioned that Dr. Halversen, Expert in Nutrition, was actually the company's founder. A third, from a science teacher's blog, called the concentration claims "corrosive nonsense that erodes kids' trust in real nutrition." Soraya's mouth dropped open.

"So the website reviewing the drink and the company selling the drink are one and the same," Soraya said slowly. "That's a straight-up contradiction. They pretend it's an outside opinion."

"My cousin calls that lateral reading," Sarah said. "Instead of judging a site by its own pages, you open new tabs and see what other sources say about it." It made sense to Sarah the way a rule made sense: once you knew it, you couldn't un-know it. She opened one more tab and found an actual university study on berry drinks. Nothing about concentration, nothing about nine out of ten kids. That eliminated the last shred of her doubt.

Soraya closed the laptop with a firm click. "Forty dollars stays in my drawer," she said. "And on Friday, I'm just going to study the old-fashioned way."

Sarah grinned and checked the time. "Race you to practice the word 'preliminary' before my mom gets here."

Sarah's family reunion started at four, and dinner was at six sharp, because Auntie insisted the noodles be eaten hot. Sarah had one job before dinner: look after her little cousins on the back porch. She could hear the grown-ups inside, laughing over plates, someone recounting the story of the year Grandma's pie collapsed. Out on the porch, the youngest cousin, a round-faced boy of four, kept climbing onto the railing.

Lilyanna from next door had been invited too, since her family knew Sarah's aunt from years back. Lilyanna arrived with a small wrapped box, which confused Sarah, because Sarah's family hadn't brought gifts. "We always bring something," Lilyanna said. "It's just what we do." Sarah filed that away.

The boy on the railing wobbled. Sarah darted over and caught his arm, and in relief she reached out to ruffle his hair, the way her dad did to her. Lilyanna's hand shot out, not quite grabbing Sarah's wrist, but close. "Wait, don't touch his head."

Sarah froze. "Why not?" She looked at the boy, who was giggling, entirely fine.

"In Thailand, the head is sacred," Lilyanna said. "Touching someone's head, even to pat a kid, can be rude. His mom's from Bangkok. She's really nice about stuff, but I wouldn't."

Sarah's cheeks went warm. She tried to think back through the afternoon. Had she patted anyone's head already? She remembered steadying the boy once before, near the drinks table, and she could not recall whether her hand had landed on his shoulder or higher. That was the hidden part, the thing she couldn't see directly. She needed a way to find out.

"Watch the railing for a second," she told Lilyanna, and she carried the boy inside on her hip, keeping her hands firmly on his back. His mother was slicing mango near the sink. "Excuse me," Sarah said. "Earlier, by the drinks, I might have touched his head. I just found out that in Thailand the head is sacred, and I'm sorry if I did."

His mother smiled and rinsed her knife. "You are very kind to ask. Maybe you touched his shoulder, maybe not. Either way, he likes you." She offered Sarah a slice of mango on a saucer, and Sarah took it with both hands, the way Lilyanna had taken the noodles earlier, and that felt right too.

Back on the porch, the sun sat low over the fence, and the smell of noodles drifted out through the screen door. Six o'clock was twenty minutes off. Lilyanna raised an eyebrow at the mango. "Plausible plan," Sarah said, "apologizing before you know you did anything wrong." She sat down on the steps, and the little boy climbed into the space beside her, careful this time to keep both feet on the boards.

Anais spread her science fair board across the kitchen table and frowned at the empty middle panel. Her experiment had gone fine. She had filled three bowls with water, left one plain, added salt to the second, and sugar to the third, then frozen them overnight to see which one turned to ice first. The plain water had frozen solid, the sugar water was mushy, and the salt water was still stubbornly liquid, like an obstinate classmate refusing to line up. But the top of the board needed a word she kept seeing in the instruction sheet: hypothesis. She had skipped over it all week, the way she skipped over the word "stanza" in poetry until Mr. Karimi made her class memorize what one was. Now she was stuck.

She called London, who was no help at all. "Just write what you guessed," London said through the phone. "I despise those vocabulary words. Write 'I guessed the salt water would freeze last' and glue it down."

"That's not the same as a hypothesis, though," Anais said. "The sheet wants the exact word." She hung up, dragged the dictionary off the shelf, and looked it up herself. The entry said the word came from ancient Greek. It literally meant "putting or placing under."

She sat back. "Placing under," she said out loud to the empty kitchen. She thought of her mother placing a rug under a wobbly table leg, something slid underneath to hold the whole thing up. That was what a guess did. You put it under your experiment first, before you knew anything, and the experiment either held it up or knocked it flat. Her guess had been that salt water would freeze last, and the freezer had agreed with her. The guess had been placed under, and the evidence stood on top of it.

She wrote HYPOTHESIS in big blue letters across the panel, and under it: Salt water will freeze last. Then she carried the board to the living room to show her mother, holding it the way you hold something that finally makes sense.

"Look," she said. "The word goes underneath everything."

The recipe card came from Ms. Kapoor next door, and Victoria had promised macaroni and cheese for dinner at six o'clock, when her mother got home from her shift. At five fifteen she had a pot of milk, a knob of butter, and a whisk, and by five thirty she had a smooth paste of butter and flour bubbling in the pan. That part, the roux, had gone fine. She poured in the warm milk a splash at a time, whisking like Ms. Kapoor had shown her through the fence, and for one shining moment the sauce looked like liquid silk.

Then it looked like milk. Thin, pale, watery milk. Victoria whisked harder, but the sauce stayed stubbornly runny, and the minutes on the clock seemed to dwindle faster than the liquid in the pot. At five forty she reached for the flour tin. Eve, who had come over to watch and steal cheese cubes, leaned on the counter. "If you add more flour you'll get lumps again," she said. "Remember the first batch? Little dough balls everywhere."

Victoria set the tin down and stared at the pot. The first batch had been lumpy when she dumped cold flour straight into hot milk. This batch was different, because the flour had already gone in, cooked in the butter, every grain coated. She thought about the rice in Ms. Kapoor's pudding, how each grain swelled up fat and soft as it drank the liquid. Maybe the flour grains in her sauce were doing the same thing, soaking up milk and swelling, and maybe that took heat and time. Nothing had told her that yet, because the pot wasn't hot enough.

"So the sauce thickens as it comes up to a simmer," Victoria said slowly, "not the second the flour goes in." She turned the burner up a notch, kept whisking, and waited. Slowly, the milk began to steam, small bubbles formed at the edges, and the sauce thickened under her whisk into something glossy and substantial. She pulled it off the heat, stirred in a big handful of cheddar until it melted in smooth ropes, and tasted it. Her one criterion for tonight was simple: no lumps. There were none.

At six o'clock exactly, her mother walked in the door, sniffed, and smiled. Eve was already setting out three bowls. "Macaroni and cheese," Victoria announced, carrying the pot to the table with both hands. "From scratch. And I only ruined it once."

Chloe had signed up to volunteer at the community food bank because Mr. Kamau said it counted for two hours of service credit, and because she imagined handing bags of groceries to people who needed them. On Saturday morning she stood in the middle of a huge warehouse, shelves reaching to the ceiling, pallets of canned beans stacked in rows like buildings. She waited by the door with her friend Sylas. Nobody came in.

"Maybe people sleep late on Saturdays," Sylas said.

They waited forty more minutes. A forklift beeped past. Chloe counted the doorways: one for deliveries at the back, one for volunteers, and none marked for visitors at all. That was the clue. A place with no checkout counter and no visitor entrance wasn't built for people to shop in. She walked to the loading dock and read the labels on the outgoing crates. Every box was stamped with the name of a church, a school, or a community center, and one word kept appearing: pantry.

"So this is a warehouse," she said slowly. "A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food. The pantries are the local places where people actually pick it up. Like the one on Miller Street." She pointed at a crate. "We're the behind-the-scenes part."

A woman with a clipboard, who managed the floor, overheard her. "Smart kid. Want to help load the Miller Street run? That driver's trying to conquer a whole route before noon."

Chloe carried boxes until her arms ached. The woman talked while they worked, about how she'd started here years ago after her house went into mortgage trouble and a pantry had fed her family for a winter. She said she wasn't biased toward any one pantry, but Miller Street was her favorite because they never let anyone leave with an empty cart.

Then the van door rolled up, and Chloe froze. Climbing into the passenger seat was Sylas's older brother, and stacked beside him, waiting to carry the boxes in, was Macey, holding a shopping bag from Miller Street.

"Don't tell anyone," Macey said, and held up the bag. "Saturday's our day."

Jace had promised his grandmother he would make dinner tonight, chicken and a big salad, and he'd been planning it since Tuesday. The kitchen at her house smelled like cinnamon and old newspapers, and the wooden cutting board by the sink had a scratch down the middle that he ran his thumb over while he thought. First he cubed the raw chicken, then he washed his hands, then he reached for the lettuce. His hand stopped halfway.

Wait, he thought. The board still had chicken juices in that scratch, maybe, or somewhere he couldn't see. If he chopped lettuce on it, whatever was on the lettuce would be eaten raw, straight onto everyone's plates. Nobody cooked salad. So whatever the raw chicken left behind would ride along, invisible, right into his grandmother and his little cousin. Was that a thing with a name? He'd heard a word once in a video at school. "Cross-contamination," he said out loud, testing it. The spread of bacteria from one food to another. That had to be it.

He was a little skeptical of himself, though. Was he being too careful? His friend Shania would say he was overthinking it, but Shania had once eaten a sandwich off the floor of the gym. The rule, if it was a rule, seemed simple: use separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad. He could test it without any fancy equipment. If using the same board was such a bad idea, then the clean board in the cupboard was the obvious candidate for the lettuce. Switching boards would violate nothing except his habit of doing dishes only once. He pulled out the fresh board and set it down with a clack.

His grandmother came in, drying her hands on her apron. "Two boards tonight?"

"One for the chicken, one for the salad," Jace said. "Cross-contamination. You can't see it happen, so you have to stop it before it does."

She looked at the scratched board, then at him, and pulled a third board out of the cupboard for the tomatoes.

David spread his science fair notebook across the library table and frowned at the page. His experiment was supposed to prove that the plant food he had bought actually made bean plants grow taller, but his three sprouts in the kitchen window had all shot up about the same amount, fed or not. He was missing something, and the librarian had pointed him to a shelf of experiment books near the window.

Moses slid into the chair across from him, balancing a stack of books about volcanoes. "Still stuck on the bean thing?" he asked. David turned the notebook around so Moses could see the chart. Each plant had gotten the plant food mixed into its water, just at different strengths, and every row showed nearly identical heights. "If the food works," Moses said slowly, "shouldn't one of them look different?"

David stared at the chart, and an uneasy feeling sharpened into an acute suspicion: maybe all three plants were getting something that made them grow, which would make them look the same even if the food worked. He flipped to an experiment in one of the library books about testing fertilizer on bean plants, and there it was. The diagram showed tested plants, and beside them one extra pot that got no fertilizer at all. He read the label twice. "That one just gets plain water," he said. "Nothing added. It's called a control group."

Chelsey, who had been listening from the next table while she searched the catalog, leaned over. "So how does that help you?" David picked up his pencil and drew a fourth pot on his chart, labeled plain water only. Now, whatever happened to that plant would show him how tall beans grew anyway, and he could compare the others against it. "Without it," he said, "my whole project just proves that bean plants grow, which nobody needs to prove."

Mr. Tang, shelving books two aisles over, had drifted closer and nodded at the diagram. The three of them reached a quick consensus that David would start four fresh beans tomorrow and document their heights every single morning in the notebook. Moses helped him copy the watering schedule onto a clean page, and Chelsey found him a book about roots.

That evening, David set four new pots on the kitchen windowsill, spacing them evenly in the light. He filled the watering can and touched the pencil to the first line of his new chart, ready to document day one. "Grow," he told the little pots, and turned on the tap.

Elliot sat on the spinning chair in the eyeglass shop at the mall, holding his prescription slip like it was a report card. He had wanted glasses for a while, mostly because Sierra said he looked like a scientist in the try-on frames, but now the paper said -2.00 and his stomach dropped. Two days ago in science class he had gotten a minus on a quiz, and minus meant wrong.

"What's the face?" Sierra asked. She was leaning on the counter, eyeing the pretzel stand across the aisle, its butter smell drifting all the way over. "You got glasses. That's the best day of your life."

"It says negative two," Elliot said. "My eyes got a minus. Like they failed."

The optician, a woman with silver rings on every finger, laughed before she could stop herself. "No, no. That's not a score. It's the strength of the lens, measured in diopters." She tapped the slip. "Minus means nearsighted. Plus means farsighted. Yours is minus two, so things far away are blurry for you."

Elliot looked at the slip again. He turned it over, as if the back might hold more clues. Then he tested it, because testing things was what he did. He held the paper at arm's length, where it was sharp, then set it on the counter and stepped back three paces. The numbers went soft, like frost on the tundra photos in geography class, everything white and edgeless. So that was the pattern: near was clear, far was not. The minus wasn't a grade. The minus was just the direction his eyes leaned.

"So if Sierra needed glasses," he asked, "would hers say plus?"

"Only if she's farsighted," the optician said.

"Farsighted people can read the menu at the pretzel stand from here," Sierra said. "Nearsighted people like you need to walk over. It's basically a rule that I have to go get us both a cinnamon twist, since walking is prohibited for you now until your glasses are ready."

"That's not what nearsighted means," Elliot said, but he was grinning, and Sierra was already halfway across the aisle, coins counted out in her palm.

He tried on frames while he waited. The mirror showed a boy who did look a bit like a scientist, in a way that was entirely subjective and possibly influenced by the fact that Sierra had planted the idea weeks ago. The optician said his lenses would take twenty minutes. He watched the machine behind the counter grind the glass, a wheel of light spinning behind a little window, and he thought about the diopters again, the minus, the number that measured not failure but a direction.

"Order up," Sierra called, waving a pretzel at him from across the aisle. She took a bite of what was clearly the larger of the two.

Keira set two jars on the windowsill in Mr. Jung's science room: one with plain water, one with water and a spoonful of salt stirred into it until the salt disappeared. The problem was the quiz on Friday. She had mixed up melting and rusting twice already, and Mr. Jung had written "physical or chemical?" beside a drawing of a burning candle, which she had answered wrong both times. She needed a way to tell them apart that she could actually see, or at least mostly see.

"Salt water," Alivia said, leaning over the jars. "That one looks like nothing happened at all."

"That's the point," Keira said. "If dissolving the salt is a physical change, the salt is still in there, just hiding. If it's a chemical change, something new got made, and the salt is gone forever."

"So how do you find hiding salt?" asked Alexe, who had come over to watch.

Keira thought about the pond behind the school, a tranquil little ecosystem where the water shrank every hot week of summer and left rings of minerals on the rocks. Water could leave. Things left behind stayed behind. "We wait for the water to leave on its own," she said. "Sun's on this window all afternoon."

She taped a label to each jar with the date and put a pencil mark at the water line. For three days the marks crept lower. Alivia checked the plain jar and found nothing at the bottom. On Thursday the salt jar was nearly dry, and Keira scraped the bottom with a spoon. White crystals came up, gritty and square-edged, exactly like the salt from the shaker.

"It came back," Alexe said.

"Dissolving salt in water is a physical change," Keira said, holding out the spoon. "The water left, and the same salt stayed behind."

On Friday, beside the drawing of the candle, she wrote chemical, and thought of smoke that never comes back, and salt that always does. Mr. Jung circled it, and Keira folded the quiz into her pocket with the little crystal still in it, sharp against her fingertip.

The waiting room at the eyeglasses store smelled like plastic and lemon cleaner, and Livia sat between her mom and a rack of frames, still not used to the idea that the world had been blurry for two years without her noticing. Ms. Do, who owned the shop and did the fittings, had shown her the letters on the chart, and now Livia knew why reading had drifted to arm's length, why the whiteboard at school dissolved into smudges unless she sat in front. Near things were blurry. Far things were fine. She kept turning that over, because it felt backwards from what she'd assumed.

Coen had come along because his mom was picking up his new frames too. His glasses, the old pair, made his eyes look small, like pebbles under glass. Livia had never thought about that before, but she thought about it now while Ms. Do fitted a trial frame on her face and swung the mirror around.

"Whoa," Livia said. Her eyes looked enormous. She leaned closer and they got bigger still, like they belonged to some other girl. "Coen, look. Yours make your eyes small and mine make mine huge. Why?"

Coen shrugged and peered at her over his pebble eyes. "Different problem, probably. I can't see far. You can't see near."

Ms. Do permitted them one guess each before she'd say anything, which was her way with kids who liked to figure things out. Livia held up two fingers, one behind the other, and squinted at the wall of frames across the room. With the trial lenses on, she could read the tiny price tags. Without them, she couldn't read her own hand. So the glasses were bending light somehow, pulling it back into focus. She remembered the poster in the exam room, the little cross-section of an eye, the arrow of light landing short or long. Hers landed behind the mark. The lens had to bend it forward, and a lens that bent light inward, thick in the middle, would magnify. That had to be it.

"Convex," Livia said, mostly to herself. "Mine are convex. Thick in the middle. That's why my eyes look big."

"That's the one," Ms. Do said, and handed her a case.

They walked out into an arid, blowing afternoon, and Livia stopped on the sidewalk because she could see individual leaves on the tree across the street, and every crack in the pavement, all at once. She remembered deciding, back in the fall, not to tell her mom about the blurry pages, because she'd been afraid of looking broken. Maybe that had been a mistake. Maybe she'd just needed one more week. She didn't decide, and the climax of the whole thing, she decided, was this exact moment on the sidewalk anyway.

Coen pointed at the bus stop sign down the block and read it out loud, proving his new pair worked too.

"Race you to the sign," Livia said, and ran.

Daniel slid into his seat in science class and immediately noticed something strange. Marwa, who usually sat half a foot away, had scooted her chair until it almost touched the desk behind her. Mayson leaned toward the window, pretending the parking lot was fascinating.

"You okay?" Daniel asked Mayson.

"Fine," Mayson said, eyes still on the cars. "Great view today."

Daniel had skipped his shower that morning, and again after basketball practice the night before. He'd been in a rush both times, and he figured skipping once or twice couldn't matter that much. Now, though, a suspicion crept over him like a shadow. He sniffed the collar of his shirt. His whole body went hot.

At lunch, he cornered Mayson by the vending machines. "Be honest. Is it me?"

Mayson looked at the floor, then at the ceiling, then finally at Daniel. "It's you. You smell like a gym sock that got left in a locker over summer break."

"Practice was only last night!"

"Exactly," Mayson said, and somehow that one word made Daniel feel like he'd failed a test he didn't know he was taking.

That night, Daniel turned detective in his own bathroom. He thought about it like a science experiment, the kind Mr. Farah made them write up. Something invisible had to be causing the smell, because he couldn't see anything. Sweat, he decided. But wait, he thought, fresh sweat had never bothered anybody. It was old sweat, sweat that sat around overnight, that turned disgusting. Something was happening to it after it left his skin.

He tested his idea the next morning. He showered with soap, scrubbed everywhere twice, and even used the deodorant his mom had bought and left on the shelf like it was some kind of obligation he was supposed to figure out on his own. He put it on, feeling strangely assertive about it, like a knight putting on armor.

At school, Marwa sat at her normal distance. Mayson leaned back in his chair instead of toward the window. Nobody said anything, which was the whole point.

"So it was sweat all along," Daniel said at lunch. "Sweat sitting around gets gross. Wash it off, no smell."

"Congratulations," Mayson said. "You solved the mystery of yourself."

After practice that afternoon, Daniel was first in line for the showers, towel over his shoulder like a victory flag. He was so fast that Marwa, waiting for the gym exit, called out, "Did you run here?"

"Basically," Daniel shouted back, and pushed open the locker room door.

Brayden slid his phone across the dinner table so his dad could see the ad glowing on the screen. "It says these shoes change lives," he said. "Change lives. It's like the fourth ad this week that says that."

His dad forked up some rice and squinted at it. "Maybe they do."

"Change them how?" Brayden asked. "By how much? If I bought them and my life didn't change, could anybody prove the ad was wrong?" He thought about Mr. Pereira, his science teacher, who had made the whole class write predictions last spring that could be checked. Brayden had written his prediction wrong on purpose, just to be funny, and still felt a little hot about it when he remembered. Mr. Pereira hadn't laughed. He had just said, "Wrong is fine. Uncheckable is not."

His little sister banged her spoon, contagious in her giggling, and their mom shushed her with a smile. "What are you worked up about, Brayden?"

"The ad makes a claim, sort of, but it's not a claim you could ever test. If a shoe ad said they last two years, I could wait two years and see. If it said they're the lightest shoe under twenty dollars, someone could weigh them and check the price. But 'changes lives'?" He waved a hand. "It gives you nothing to test. Ever. Even if you wore them for fifty years, the company could just say your life changed in some way you didn't notice."

"So don't buy them," his dad said.

"I'm not buying them. I'm going to boycott them and tell Colton and Imogen why. Colton already ordered a pair." Brayden pulled the phone back and started typing a message to Colton: How would you ever know if they were lying? His sister leaned over and tapped the screen with her sticky finger, adding a row of letter j's to the end.

"Send it like that," she said.

Eve had signed up for the voluntary hurdle clinic at the community pool, mostly because it met on the grass strip beside the deck and she was already there every afternoon anyway. Now she stood in the sprinkler smell of wet chlorine and cut grass, staring at a row of low hurdles that her classmate Ilyes had dragged out of the equipment shed. Ms. Pierre, who coached on Tuesdays, had told them to run the row with a three-step rhythm, but Eve had clipped the third hurdle twice in a row, and the second time she had landed hard enough on her palms that the whole deck went quiet.

"That's it," she said, sitting in the grass. "I'm quitting in front of an audience. This is maximum humiliation."

"You're fine," Ilyes said, though he was frowning at the hurdles, not at her. "Honestly, I don't think it's you."

Eve looked up. "What do you mean?"

"I mean I counted them when I set them up, and something's off." He walked the row, tapping each hurdle. "Seven. Ms. Pierre said a real race row should be ten, because both sprint hurdle races, the men's 110 metres and the women's 100 metres, have ten hurdles. We're three short." He wanted a full race row to practice on before Saturday, she knew, so he could film the whole thing for his track channel.

Eve stood, brushed grass off her knees, and thought about it. If the row was short, maybe Ilyes had squeezed the hurdles closer together to fit them in the same stretch of grass. That would explain her third-hurdle clip better than any clumsiness of hers. You couldn't see wrong spacing just by looking, but you could measure it with your feet. She walked heel-to-toe from the start to the first hurdle, counted, then walked between the first and second, and then the second and third. The third gap was short by almost a full foot.

"Move this one back," she said, hauling the third hurdle down the grass. "It's not me. It's the spacing."

They re-set the whole row, ten hurdles long, stretching it toward the pool fence. Caylee, dripping from the deep end, came over to hold hurdles steady while Eve lined them up. Then Eve backed up to the start, breathed, and ran. One, two, three, lead leg up and over. One, two, three, over again. The third hurdle passed under her knee like it was nothing, and the fourth, and the rest, all the way to the fence, where she stopped with her hands on her head, laughing.

"Get the camera," Ilyes shouted, already running for his backpack. "Ten hurdles, one take."

Theo had planned to build the same volcano every kid built, the brown lump that oozed foam down its sides while everyone pretended to be amazed. But Monica had already claimed volcanoes at lunch, loudly, and Ms. Njoroge had a rule about duplicate projects. So Theo sat at the kitchen table with a baking soda box, a jug of vinegar, and a plan he hoped would be better: measure whether more vinegar meant a bigger eruption, and turn the whole thing into a chart.

He set out five clear cups on the table, each with exactly the same small spoonful of baking soda. The label on the box said sodium bicarbonate, which Theo copied onto his data sheet because it looked scientific. The vinegar bottle said acetic acid. He copied that too. Then he lined up the cups like a little army and got his measuring cup from the mudroom, since his mother had made him promise not to use her good glass ones again.

The first test went badly. He poured a whole cup of vinegar in at once, the foam shot up over the rim, and it pooled across the table and dripped onto his sock. His mother walked by with laundry and did not stop, which was how he knew she had decided it was not her problem. Theo mopped up with a dish towel, then sat still and thought. The liquid was opaque once the fizz clouded it, so he could not see whether the baking soda had fully reacted underneath. He could not watch the hidden cause. He would have to judge it by the effect instead, which meant careful pouring and careful counting.

Eleanor knocked on the door halfway through cup three, drawn by the smell like a scavenger sniffing out snacks. She found none, so she sat down to watch instead. "What's actually happening in there?" she asked, chin on her hands.

"Baking soda, which is sodium bicarbonate, reacts with vinegar, which is acetic acid, and it produces carbon dioxide gas," Theo said, reading off his sheet. "The gas is what pushes the foam up."

"That's it? Gas?"

"Gas," Theo said, "and measurement."

Cup two got twice the vinegar of cup one, cup three got three times, and so on down the line, with Theo counting seconds of fizzing and Eleanor calling out when the foam crossed a rubber band he had stretched around each cup as a flood line. The numbers climbed in a pattern so tidy that Theo checked them twice. More acid, more gas, taller foam. He was still graphing it at the table, tongue out, when Monica texted to ask whether he was going to copy her volcano after all.

Theo typed back one word, held the phone up so Eleanor could see, and pressed send. "Jealous."

Daniel pressed his pencil so hard against the paper that the tip snapped, which did not help his mood. Mr. Delgado had promised that anyone who finished a full room in two-point perspective, with two vanishing points off the edges of the page, could hang the drawing in the hallway display case. Daniel wanted that spot. His friend Kody had already drawn a sophisticated-looking living room with a fireplace and tall windows, and every time Kody leaned over to peek at Daniel's page, it irritated Daniel like a fly at a picnic.

"Your walls look great," Kody said, which was fine. "But your rug is weird."

Daniel looked at the round rug in the middle of his floor. He had drawn it as a circle, same as always, and now that he stared at it, the thing looked like a flat sticker pasted on the page instead of a rug lying flat on the floor. The walls receded toward their vanishing points. The rug just sat there, refusing to cooperate.

Akram wandered over from the supply shelf, eating a pretzel rod like a professor with a cigar. "Hmm," he said. "That rug is embarrassing the whole drawing."

"Thanks," said Daniel. But he kept looking at the rug, turning the idea over. The floor slanted away from him in the picture. A round thing sitting on a slanted floor would not show all of itself at once. He remembered the big clock on the far wall, which he had flattened into a narrow oval, and something clicked. He picked up a fresh pretzel rod from Akram without asking and held it flat, level with his eye, then tilted it slowly back. From the side it was a line. Tilted, it flattened into an oval. A circle seen at an angle got squashed.

"So the rug is a circle I'm seeing at an angle," Daniel said. He erased the round rug and drew a flattened oval instead, wider than it was tall, sitting snug between the lines of the floorboards. The rug sank into the room like it belonged there.

"An ellipse," Akram announced, pointing. "That's the word. A flattened oval." Kody groaned and grabbed his own eraser, hunting through his drawing for round things, and Mr. Delgado paused at their table on his rounds, looked down at the oval rug, and quietly moved Daniel's paper to the top of the display case pile.

On the first Saturday of April, William found his grandmother on the back porch with a plastic bag full of small brooms, cloths, and paper money folded into intricate gold shapes. He knew exactly what the bag was for, because Grandpa had explained it last spring, before he got sick.

In the flashback that played in William's mind, he was nine, sitting on this same porch while Grandpa folded the same kind of gold paper. "Next April," Grandpa had said, "I'll take you to my father's grave. It's called Qingming, the tomb-sweeping festival. It usually falls on April 4 or 5. Families visit their ancestors' graves, clean them, and leave offerings." Grandpa had laughed and added, "Your uncle Seamus once swept the wrong headstone and left a whole plate of oranges on a stranger's grave." William had laughed too, and promised he would come.

Now Grandpa was the one being visited. William had worked out a problem on his own: which day should they go? His birthday was April 3, but a festival was not a birthday. He checked the calendar and found that Qingming fell on April 5 this year, so he circled it in red and showed his grandmother. "You figured that out yourself," she said, and she allocated the sweeping to him, the polishing of the stone to herself, and the carrying of offerings to Uncle Seamus and his son Lukas, who was William's age.

On the morning of April 5, they drove to the cemetery. Grandpa's stone had a thin layer of winter grime. William swept it in careful strokes, the way Grandpa had once swept his own father's stone, top to bottom, left to right. Lukas wiped the carved letters until they shone. They set out oranges, the gold paper shapes, and Grandpa's favorite sesame candies.

Then Uncle Seamus told the wrong-headstone story, and Lukas laughed so hard he had to sit down on the grass. William put one last orange on the stone, exactly in the center, and said, "We'll come back next April, Grandpa. I'll bring the broom."

The group chat pinged at 7:04 with the same message it got every Friday: "Court at the park, 3pm, first to five wins respect." Hayden had come to think of the message as a ritual, almost sacred to his friend Ann, who sent it with the seriousness of a royal proclamation. The problem was that "respect" always went to whoever scored the flashiest basket, and Hayden, who was not flashy, kept ending up picked last even though his team usually won when he played.

That Sunday his uncle had dragged him to a sports bar to watch baseball, and between innings the uncle leaned over his nachos and said, "You know the 2003 book Moneyball, by Michael Lewis? It described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used a statistic like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." Hayden had nodded, but the words stuck to him like gum to a shoe. Undervalued. That word was about him, possibly, although it also might just mean "bad at basketball," so he decided to test it.

The test was simple in idea and tedious in practice. He made a chart on graph paper and, for two weeks, tracked every pickup game in the chat: who was on which team, who touched the ball before a score, who got back on defense. Logging it felt like counting ants in a sidewalk crack. But a pattern grew in the numbers, quiet and stubborn, like mold in a lunchbox. Whenever Hayden played, his teams won more, even though he scored the least.

On Friday he posted the chart to the chat, with a caption: "New captain selection system, based on real data, not on Ivana doing one behind-the-back dribble last June." Ivana replied with seventeen angry-face emojis and then, three minutes later, "wait, run it again with me included properly."

Saturday, the picker chose Hayden first, and Ivana's team lost 5-2, which everyone agreed proved nothing at all, since Ann had spent the whole game guarding the wrong basket. "Statistics," Hayden announced solemnly, "never lie, but they do nap sometimes." Ann threw the ball at his head.

The bus doors hissed open at the nature reserve, and Audrey was first down the steps, notebook already in hand. Mr. Karimi had promised a visit to the fire station tucked behind the reserve's visitor centre, where firefighters would show how smoke behaved in a burning building. Audrey had been wondering about that all week. Why did the drills at school always say to crawl? Nobody ever said.

Inside the station, a firefighter set up a small demonstration room with a smoke machine, harmless haze curling from a vent near the ceiling. "Who wants to try crossing the room?" the firefighter asked. Marlee volunteered first and walked straight through, coughing and waving her hands even though the smoke wasn't real. Romy went next, same result, both of them laughing and rubbing their eyes.

Audrey stood at the doorway and watched instead. The haze hung high, drifting along the ceiling like a grey blanket, while the air near the floor stayed clear. She felt her curiosity sharpen into an idea. Maybe it wasn't just where the smoke happened to be; maybe it always gathered up there. She crouched low, then dropped to her hands and knees and crawled under the layer of grey. From down there she could see Marlee's sneakers and the whole clean strip of floor, cool and clear all the way to the far wall.

"Look at this!" she called, and Marlee and Romy dropped down beside her. "The smoke and heat go up," Audrey said, pointing at the ceiling. "The cleaner, cooler air is near the floor. That's why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke." Marlee crawled the length of the room twice, grinning, and Romy timed herself with the stopwatch from her backpack, like it was some kind of ritual.

Back outside on the reserve trail, the demonstration dissolved into ordinary sunshine and birdsong, but Audrey kept thinking about it. When they passed the marsh, she noticed mist floating above the water and wondered whether it moved the same way, buoyant and upward, before it vanished. She crouched at the boardwalk railing, watching the mist rise, and wrote one line in her notebook: the answer is almost always lower than you think. Then she scrambled up and jogged to catch the others.

The note in his hand said: 2 litres of milk, exact change, walk fast. Harrison had read it four times before he even reached the corner store, because this was his first solo mission and he wanted zero mistakes. His mother's coins rattled in his pocket like tiny applause.

Inside, the dairy case was colder than a snowbank, and the shelves hummed. He grabbed a big two-litre carton, then noticed a yellow sticker beside the price, tiny print reading price per litre. Two one-litre cartons sat nearby. He did quick math with his lips moving, then checked the small print again. Two one-litres together cost less per litre than the single big carton. "Whoa," he said out loud. "The big one isn't always cheaper." He set the big carton down and picked up the two small ones, feeling like he'd cracked a secret code nobody else had noticed.

His classmate Cameron was already at the freezer, hunting the tropical popsicles, which were sold out, as usual. Cameron wanted orange-pineapple so badly he'd walked here in the rain yesterday, and today he was hunting again. "It's like a parasite," Cameron groaned, patting the empty shelf. "This store feeds on my hope." Harrison held up his two small cartons as evidence and said the bigger one wasn't always cheaper per litre, and Cameron said that refutes everything his big brother had ever told him about bulk buying, and he changed his mind about the giant juice jug he'd been carrying around, putting it back with a dramatic sigh.

At the till, Harrison counted his coins one by one, sliding them across the counter, then counted his change back into his palm, twice, the coins cool and jingling. The cashier waited without rushing him, which he appreciated. Outside, the streetlights were just flickering on. He ran the whole way home with the milk sacks swinging, and burst through the door shouting, "Change counted! Two litres! And guess what isn't always cheaper?"

Mackenzie crouched at the starting line of the school track, laces double-knotted, eyes on the orange cones ahead. Tryouts for the spring team were one afternoon only, and she had been waiting all winter. Before the sprints began, she watched Stanley, who was a proud carnivore and always chewing beef jerky at lunch, jog the warm-up lap like it was nothing. Then he tripped over the inside rail, tumbled onto the rubber, and sat up slowly, blinking.

"I'm fine," Stanley said, waving off the coach. "I can't skip the hurdles. This is my only shot."

Mackenzie had noticed something, though. He was squinting at the scoreboard as if the numbers were swimming. She began to hypothesize: if he had hit his head hard enough to scramble his vision for even a minute, then something was wrong that she couldn't see, and there might be a rule about exactly that. She remembered a poster in her dentist's office, of all places.

"Stanley, wait," she said, jogging over. "There's a law. Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009. It was the first state law in the country that says a young athlete with a suspected concussion has to come out of play until a health professional clears them."

Stanley stared at her. "That's a real law?"

"First of its kind in the whole U.S.," said Alizee, who was stretching on the next lane and had overheard. "My cousin sat out two weeks because of it."

The coach, an eccentric man who wore a whistle on a beaded chain and a different pair of mismatched socks every day, nodded. "She's right. You're done for today, Stanley. Doc clears you, you get another tryout."

Stanley's shoulders dropped, and Mackenzie thought he might argue. Instead he rubbed the back of his head and said quietly, "Okay. I'd rather sit out one day than the whole season." He walked to the bench and pulled out his jerky.

Mackenzie toed the line again, heart drumming. The starter raised the flag, and she ran.

Nevaeh sat cross-legged on the garage floor beside the workbench, holding the circuit she had built yesterday: a battery, a switch, and a small bulb joined with copper wire. She flipped the switch. Nothing happened. The bulb stayed dark, and that was a problem, because her objective was to demonstrate the circuit to Ms. Rosen's science class tomorrow morning.

She checked the wires first. Each one was still clipped tight, and the switch clicked when she moved it, so the metal parts were touching. She unhooked the bulb and touched its bottom to the battery terminal directly, the way she had tested it before. Still dark.

Joelle came through the side door with her bike helmet still on. "Did you break it?"

"I don't think so." Nevaeh turned the battery over in her hand. It was the same battery from yesterday, when the bulb had glowed bright enough to read by. "Everything looks right. Same wires, same bulb, same switch."

"Then the missing piece is something we can't see," Joelle said. She pointed at the battery. "Maybe it's that."

Nevaeh thought about it. A battery turns stored chemical energy into electrical energy. She said the words out loud, and then the rest came: if those chemicals got used up, there would be nothing left to turn into electricity, even if every wire was perfect. That would explain why it worked yesterday and stayed dark today. It also gave her a test. She found a fresh battery in the drawer, swapped it in, and closed the switch.

The bulb lit, a small luminous circle on the concrete floor.

"Told you," Joelle said. "It went flat."

"The chemicals ran out," Nevaeh said. "A battery only sustains the circuit until they're gone. Then you need a new one." She put the flat battery in her pocket so she could show the class both sides of it, the dark one and the glowing one, and flipped the switch off and on twice just to watch it light again.

Autumn raised her hand so fast her chair squeaked. "Ms. Nwosu, my cousin swears her lucky pencil is why she passed her math test. Could we test that?" She had been wondering about it all weekend, ever since her uncle held up his copper bracelet at dinner and declared it had cured his back pain. Nobody had argued with him. Autumn hadn't either, but a question had been tickling her ever since: how would anyone know?

"Design an experiment," said Ms. Nwosu. "Show me your plan first."

At the lab table, Rosalyn flipped through her notebook. "We could have people take a quiz with the lucky pencil and a regular pencil and compare scores."

"But it's not really her pencil," Autumn said. "It's just a pencil we call lucky. That's the part I want to figure out. When my uncle says the bracelet fixed his back, he's telling a story about himself. Marlee told me there's a word for that."

"An anecdote," Marlee said, popping the cap off a marker. "A story about one person's experience. It can't show that one thing caused another, because other explanations haven't been ruled out."

"Like what?" Rosalyn asked.

"Like his back might have gotten better anyway," Autumn said slowly, drawing two boxes in her margin. "Or he started sleeping differently. Or he just believed it would work." The thought felt like a small revolution in her head, everything turning to face a new direction. One story was not the same as evidence, and the difference between them was suddenly distinct and obvious, like two separate doors she had been treating as one.

They ran the test the next day. Ten classmates took the same ten vocabulary questions twice, once with the "lucky" pencil and once with an ordinary one, with the order flipped for half of them. The scores were almost identical, and the two kids who did better with the lucky pencil had done the easy questions that round.

"Order," Rosalyn groaned, highlighting the pattern in yellow. "The second set was easier for them. That's the other explanation."

"So one person's story can't prove it," Autumn said, "because of stuff exactly like this, hiding in the background." She taped their chart to the whiteboard and stood back. "I'm going to tell my uncle we need thirty uncles and two bracelets."

Mason had never slept over anywhere but his own house, so when his cousin Winter invited him and Chaya for the night, he packed his bag like the weekend might last a month. Winter's house had a basement with a couch, a bowl of popcorn the size of a mixing vessel, and a tablet propped against a stack of board games. They watched video after video until Winter's mom called down that it was eleven o'clock and lights out meant lights out.

The lights went out, and then nothing happened. Mason lay on the air mattress listening to Chaya flip her pillow for the fourth time. "I'm so tired," she whispered, "but my brain won't shut off." Winter groaned from the couch. Mason stared at the ceiling and thought about the order of the evening. The videos had preceded the dark by hours, but his eyes still felt bright, like the screen was still glowing behind them. He sat up.

"Wait," he said. "My grandpa does this thing where he stops looking at his phone an hour before bed. He says the light, especially the blue light, tells your brain to hold back the sleep hormone."

"The sleep what?" Chaya asked.

"Melatonin," Mason said. "That's what he calls it. Bright screens late at night delay sleep because the light signals your brain to hold back melatonin."

"So we basically bathed our eyeballs in blue light for three hours," Winter said, "and now we can't sleep. Great. Science is ruining my life."

Mason found his flashlight in his bag and kept it pointed at the floor, dim and low. "We can't undo it. But maybe we can test it. No screens, no bright lights, just boring dark, and we see who falls asleep first." Chaya suggested they whisper stories instead of watching anything, and the yawning started almost immediately. When Chaya yawned, Mason yawned, and Winter accused them both of making it contagious on purpose.

Before he finally drifted off, Mason wrote a note on the back of a popcorn-stained receipt and left it on the tablet so morning-Winter would find it. "Dear future us: screens make the brain hold back melatonin, which is why we were awake until forever. Turn the tablet off by ten tomorrow. Signed, the scientist on the air mattress." In the morning, Winter held the note up and read it out loud at breakfast, and for once he didn't make fun of anything. "Same time next month," he said, sliding the tablet into a drawer, "but the videos end at nine."

The cafe smelled like cinnamon and burnt toast, and George had rewritten his first sentence four times. His essay was supposed to convince the school to start a recycling club, and Ms. Weber had written one word beside his opening paragraph: "Flat." He stared at the page so hard it was almost like he could scrutinize the letters themselves, hunting for whatever was missing.

Tomas slid into the booth across from him with a hot chocolate and peeked at the paper. "My opening was flat too," he said. "Araya fixed it."

"She did?" George remembered Araya's essay about the library staying open on Saturdays, the one she had read aloud in class. He had actually leaned forward in his seat when she started, and he hadn't even cared about libraries. Something about her first sentence had grabbed him and not let go.

Araya came back from the counter carrying a muffin, and before she even sat down George pushed the essay toward her. "How did you start yours?" he asked.

"With a hook," she said. "Like a question, or a surprising fact, or a tiny story. Something that catches the reader before you tell them your main idea." She pulled the essay closer and read his first line: "Our school should have a recycling club for several important reasons." Then she grabbed a napkin and a pen. "Let's test three."

Tomas counted them off on his fingers. "One, his boring one. Two, a question." Araya wrote, "Did you know our school throws away hundreds of bottles every week?" George frowned. He wasn't sure the number was exact. "Make it approximate," he said, and she added the word "about" so the sentence stayed honest. "Three, a story," Tomas said, so George tried, "Last Tuesday I watched a kid toss a whole water bottle into the trash can right beside the recycling bin."

Then they did the experiment. Araya read each opening out loud in a flat, robot voice, and George closed his eyes and paid attention to his own attention. The first one made his mind drift to the window. The question made him wonder, just a little. The little story made a picture pop into his head, sharp and clear, like one neuron lighting up a whole string of others. "That one," he said, pointing at the napkin. "Definitely that one."

He copied the sentence onto his paper, then crossed it out and wrote it again, changing Tuesday to Friday because that was the day it had really happened. Ms. Weber had said to begin with the truth, even the small truths. He thought about his flat first try and felt a little embarrassed, but also strange and pleased, the way you do when a locked door finally swings open. Tomas stole a corner of his muffin, and Araya said, "Read the whole thing now, robot voice," so George squared his shoulders and began, "Last Friday I watched a kid toss a whole water bottle into the trash can right beside the recycling bin."

Camille set the puppy's crate by the couch, where she could see it from the kitchen. The puppy, a small brown mutt her mom had finally agreed to, watched her every move. She had a list of first-day rules taped to the fridge, and at the top she had written, "Feeding," because feeding seemed like the most important thing a person could get right.

That afternoon Kaleigh came over with a bag of trail mix to celebrate. They sat on the porch floor and let the puppy tumble between them. Camille loves this, she thought, and reached into the bag for a handful of raisins to share. Kaleigh grabbed her wrist. "Wait, you can't. Raisins can hurt dogs. It's their kidneys. Grapes too, so grapes and raisins should never be given as treats." Camille stared at the small wrinkled fruits in her palm. She had been about to hand them over like they were ordinary dog food.

Camille wanted proof, though, because Kaleigh got things wrong sometimes. She texted Kole, whose family had two dogs, and he answered right away: "Never. Not even one. My vet has a poster about it." Then Camille checked the animal hospital's website, part of the big network of vet pages her mom had bookmarked the day they picked the puppy up. Every page said the same thing. She closed her fist around the raisins and carried them back inside to the counter, far from the puppy's reach.

"I was this close," Camille said, holding up two fingers nearly touching. "I thought fruit meant healthy. For everybody."

"For humans," Kaleigh said. "Dogs get their own rules."

Camille wrote a new line at the top of the fridge list and underlined it twice. The puppy bumped her shin with its nose, and she knelt down and offered it a piece of plain kibble instead.

Elijah stood at the pond exhibit in the science museum, staring at a glass tank full of green water. Rex was already scribbling on the worksheet: frog, snake, hawk, done.

"Your chain starts with a frog," Elijah said. "Where does the frog get its energy?"

"From whatever it eats," Rex said. "Bugs."

"Right. And bugs eat... what, exactly?"

Rex tapped his pencil against the glass. "Stuff. Leaves, maybe?"

Kaia leaned in between them, pointing at a sign near the tank. "Algae. Look, it says algae are producers. That means they make their own food."

Elijah frowned at the tank, at the cloud of green drifting under the surface. "Make it out of what? There's no kitchen in there."

"Sunlight," Kaia said. "The sign says most food chains start with the sun, because plants and algae, the producers, use sunlight to make their own food by photosynthesis."

Elijah wrote SUN in big letters at the top of his page, then algae, then bug, frog, snake, hawk. It looked strange, having the sun in a food chain, like putting a lamp on a menu. But the more he thought about it, the more it made sense. The hawk traced back to the snake, the snake to the frog, the frog to the bugs, the bugs to the algae, and the algae to sunlight hitting the water. Nothing started from nowhere.

Mr. Traoré appeared behind them with his hands in his pockets. "Nice work. Now here's the controversial question of the day. Suppose all the frogs vanish. What happens to your chain?"

Rex shrugged. "Fewer frogs. The end."

"No, wait," Elijah said. He covered the word FROG with his thumb and studied what was left. "The snakes lose their food, so they get hungry and move somewhere else. And the bugs go crazy, because nothing is eating them anymore. They'd eat all the algae."

"So the water changes," Kaia said slowly.

Elijah grabbed a fresh worksheet and started again, this time drawing arrows backward from the hawk down to the sun. He wanted to test the idea, to see if one missing link really could pull the whole chain apart from both directions at once. When he finished, he held the page up beside Rex's.

"Same chain," Elijah said. "But now we can see the whole thing, starting with the sun."

Rex looked at both pages, then grinned and erased his first attempt. "Okay. Sun first. No monopoly on good ideas, though, that was all you."

Mr. Traoré tapped Elijah's drawing with one finger. "That one goes on the wall by the tank."

Elijah followed him to the exhibit board, worksheet held out flat so the sun at the top wouldn't bend.

The note was folded into a tiny square and stuck under Piper's toothbrush in the camp bathroom. Camp Pinesong had a rule that the whole week seemed to revolve around: the buddy system, the whistle system, the check-in board where every camper moved a clothespin from "cabin" to "beach." But nobody had a system for notes in the bathroom. Piper unfolded it by the sinks and read: "I can't do the swim test tomorrow. Don't tell anyone. Dev."

At breakfast, Piper watched Dev across the picnic table. Dev hadn't touched his pancakes, though yesterday he'd eaten three. He kept his hood up even though it was already hot, and when Tommy joked about the giant rodent someone had spotted behind the mess hall, Dev didn't even smile. His knee bounced under the table, quick and constant, like a small engine. Piper thought about last summer, when her cousin had stopped eating and stopped sleeping and everyone had said "she's just shy" until it got so bad she couldn't go to school at all. Piper had been ten then and had told nobody. She still turned that over sometimes, wondering if speaking up would have made her cousin better sooner, or just made her mad.

The note said don't tell anyone. But Piper had a theory that "anyone" wasn't the same as "an adult whose whole job is campers." At craft hour she tested it, casually, sliding onto the bench beside Mr. Popal, the water-safety counselor who ran the lake. "Hypothetically," she said, "if someone wasn't eating and couldn't sleep and was scared of the swim test, would telling you count as telling anyone?" Mr. Popal set down his whistle. "Hypothetically," he said, "that's called noticing warning signs, and I'd want to know."

That evening Dev sat with her on the dock, feet dangling over the black water. "Mr. Popal talked to me," he said. "I was mad for about an hour." Then he shrugged. "Last year I saw a counselor for anxiety. It's treatable, that's the first thing she told me. We did cognitive behavioral therapy." He picked at a splinter. "It teaches you to notice anxious thoughts and change them. She said it's one of the most effective treatments there is." He grinned sideways. "So the twist is, I already know the swim test can't actually drown me. I just forgot for a week."

The next morning Dev moved his clothespin to "beach" without being asked, and Piper stood beside him at the lake's edge while Mr. Popal buckled his life vest. "Ready?" Mr. Popal called. Dev took a breath, and Piper cupped her hands around her mouth. "Noticing!" she shouted, and Dev laughed, and dove in.

Stella stood at the edge of the community hall with a plastic cup of juice in her hand and a problem in her head. She had told Kohen and Karlee she was fasting until sundown like her family did during Ramadan, and she had lasted through lunch, through the smell of the bake sale table, through Karlee eating a cookie right in front of her. That part was hard but simple. The confusing part came when her grandmother texted: pray at four, like we do.

Four o'clock found her in the hallway by the coat racks, holding her phone. Kohen was there, retying his sneaker. "What are you doing?" he asked.

"Trying to figure out which way to pray," Stella said. "My grandma says we face toward Mecca. But which way is that from here?" She turned in a slow circle. The hallway looked the same in every direction, water fountain, bulletin board, doors.

Kohen got up. "My uncle prays five times a day. He has an app." He pulled out his phone and tapped at it, then held the screen flat like a tiny tray. A green arrow appeared. "It's called salah," he said. "The prayer. It points to the Kaaba, in Mecca." He turned slowly until the arrow lined up with the far wall. "That way. Northeast, sort of."

Stella frowned at her own phone. She had been about to guess. Guessing the direction seemed like the kind of thing you could get wrong for years and never notice, because nothing would tell you. There was no mark left behind if you faced the wrong wall. She opened the compass app and watched the needle settle, then compared it to Kohen's arrow. They matched.

"It's the same for everybody, isn't it," she said. "Five times a day, from anywhere, everyone facing the same place."

"From what I've seen, yeah," Kohen said.

She set her juice on the windowsill. The hall thermostat on the wall read twenty-two degrees, and outside it was hot enough that Karlee had winced stepping off the bus. Stella found a clear patch of floor near the coat racks, laid her jacket down, and stood facing the direction the two arrows agreed on.

Karlee appeared in the doorway. "You're not drinking your juice?"

"Not until the sun goes down," Stella said. "Four o'clock is prayer time first." She stood still, facing northeast, and began.

Lucy had signed up for the pottery shed at Camp Winnowood mostly because Cohen said the kiln smelled like burnt cookies, but the moment she sat down at the drawing table, she wanted in. Ms. Sok had set a plaster ball on a cloth with a single lamp beside it, and every kid in the room was leaning forward.

"Today we shade a sphere," Ms. Sok said. "Highlight, shadow, cast shadow. And one more thing to find, if you can."

"A robot part?" Cohen whispered.

"Terminator," Remi whispered back, and Lucy laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water cup. Ms. Sok only smiled and said the word was real, and that they would have to figure out what it meant on their own.

Lucy squinted at the ball. The lamp made one bright spot, the highlight, and the side away from the lamp went dark. Her pencil guessed at where the light stopped reaching. She drew a curved line and shaded everything past it. Remi leaned over. "Too far back," she said. "See? The gray part starts here." Lucy looked again, and she could see it, a curving edge on the ball where the lit side turned into the shadow side, where the direct light stopped reaching. She pressed her thumb along the ball's surface to feel the spot go cold and warm, as if her skin could confirm what her eyes already knew. "The terminator," she said quietly, trying the word out, and this time nobody laughed, because they were all hunting for it on their own drawings.

Lucy decided to test her idea. She slid the lamp slowly around the table and watched the terminator crawl across the plaster like something alive, the whole shadow side turning with it, while the dark oval on the cloth, the cast shadow, swung away like a door. She tried it three times to be sure. When Ms. Sok passed by, Lucy spun the sketchbook toward her, finger on the line. "It moves with the light," Lucy said. "Wherever the light goes, that's where the lit side stops."

Ms. Sok gave a nod, the kind Lucy recognized from when someone got it exactly right. "Keep going," she said. "Next week, contemporary portraits, and you'll need this." Lucy bent back over the sphere, compressed the whole night down to one curved pencil line, and beside her Cohen drew a tiny robot, just to be safe.

Mila found Odalys on the bench by the estuary, where the river widened and slowed before it met the sea. The air was humid and heavy, and Odalys was reading Mila's text out loud to Charles in a voice like a judge announcing a verdict. "'Sorry if you got upset about Saturday.'" Odalys looked up. "That's not sorry for anything. That's sorry I got upset, like it's my fault for having feelings."

"It's a non-apology," Charles said, kicking at the gravel. "My sister calls them that. You're apologizing for my feelings instead of for what you did." He shrugged, as if to say he was only the messenger.

Mila opened her mouth to argue and then closed it. She had missed Saturday because her grandmother's visit got moved, and instead of saying so, she had typed that sentence fast, wanting the whole thing to be over. She tested the idea in her head, turning it like a coin: if she crossed out the word "if," what would be left? "Sorry you got upset about Saturday." Still Odalys's feelings. She would have to name what she herself had done. She thought back to three weeks ago, when Odalys had forgotten Mila's birthday picnic in this same park and shown up an hour late with a burnt cake, and Mila had said it was fine. She had nurtured that small hurt quietly, feeding it every time Odalys talked too long about other friends, until it had grown into not answering texts. Maybe the text hadn't started the fight at all. Maybe it only uncovered it.

"I did a bad thing," Mila said. "Not Saturday, exactly. When you were late to my picnic, I said it was fine and it wasn't, and I've been keeping score ever since. I'm sorry I did that." Odalys blinked, then held up her phone. "Then I'm sorry I read your text out loud to Charles like a court exhibit." Charles groaned. "Can I be sorry I had to hear both of you?" Odalys laughed first, then Mila, and then Odalys pulled two melted chocolate bars out of her bag and held one out across the humid air. Mila took it.

Sunlight through the stained glass window refracted into little pools of red and blue on the carpet, and Autumn stared at one of them instead of at her sheet music, because the music was not the problem. The problem was Izaiah. They were both altos, and the choir performed in three days, and every time they landed on the same long note, something in the sound went wrong in a way she could not point to.

"Hold the F," said Ms. Khan, tapping the piano. "Just the two altos. Everyone else, rest."

They sang. The note started clean, then it began to shudder, swelling and shrinking, like a moth beating against a jar. Autumn stopped. Izaiah stopped. The pools of colored light sat there being innocent.

"That pulsing," Autumn said. "It slows down when we get closer. Listen." She sang her F and slid hers slightly flat, and the wobble sped up. She slid back toward his pitch and the wobble stretched out, slower, slower, and then vanished entirely, and their two voices fused into one note so wide and warm that she felt it in her teeth.

"That's called beats," said Izaiah. "My cousin told me once."

"Then we don't listen for the right note," Autumn said, already flipping to the anthem. "We listen for the wobble to stop."

Ms. Khan had them run it again, and this time Autumn tracked the pulsing like following a string through a maze, easing her pitch until the sound smoothed out. On the last held note, the whole choir joined, and nothing wobbled anywhere.

Afterward Ms. Khan said it was the best the altos had ever sounded, which was, Autumn privately noted, not a high bar. She gathered her music, still hearing the shudder in her memory like something swallowed.

"Sunday," said Izaiah at the door. "Don't go larva on me. All curled up and lethargic in the back row."

"Sunday," said Autumn, "I will be the wobble-hunter."

He laughed so hard he dropped his folder, and she walked out through the red and blue pools toward the parking lot.

Jack had exactly forty dollars and one hour before his mom picked him up at the food court entrance at five o'clock. The shoes he wanted, the silver-and-blue ones everybody at school talked about, cost sixty-five. He stood in front of the sports store window, watching a video loop play on the screen inside. A famous point guard sprinted across a court, then looked straight into the camera and said, "I never lace up anything else." Under him, flashing letters shouted MILLIONS AGREE. THE GREATEST GRIP EVER ENGINEERED.

"They're unbelievable," said Brycen, who had appeared beside him with a smoothie. "Legendary. Revolutionary."

"Those are just the ad's words," Jack said. "Loaded words. They don't tell you anything." But he said it without much conviction, because the weird thing was that the shoes did feel unbelievable to him now. He had heard they were the best five separate times today: once from Yousef, once from a kid in math class, twice from the video loop, once from a radio spot in the parking garage. Nobody had shown him a single test, a single number, and yet somewhere in his head the claim had hardened into fact.

He tried an experiment on himself. "Say 'the mall fountain grants wishes' five times," he told Brycen.

"Fine. The mall fountain grants wishes. The mall fountain grants wishes. The mall fountain..." Brycen counted on his fingers through all five, then frowned. "Okay, that actually felt true for a second. That's creepy."

They found Yousef near the fountain, wearing a T-shirt with a cartoon kangaroo on skates, some mascot from a defunct juice stand, and Jack told him about the experiment. Yousef nodded. "My sister read about that. In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true."

"So the repetition is doing the persuading," Jack said slowly, "not the proof." He looked back at the window, at the point guard he'd never meet, at the word MILLIONS, at kids from the affluent side of town walking out with boxes. He checked his budget again. Forty dollars, no matter how many times he counted it.

"Foot Locker clearance rack is two stores down," Yousef said. "Forty-two bucks, and they grip fine."

Jack looked at the clock above the register. Four fifty-one. He jogged toward clearance, Brycen and Yousef right behind him, and pulled a plain gray pair off the bottom shelf. "Hold these till I get back," he called to the cashier, and sprinted for the food court door to intercept his mom and ask for two dollars.

Isaac had been postponing his science worksheet all through lunch because the cafeteria looked different today. Ms. Sutherland had set up long tables diagonal to the windows for International Food Day, and families had brought dishes from home. Safiya, who had signed up three weeks early, was guarding her samosas like treasure, hoping people would try them before the pizza line emptied the room of customers. Isaac's real worry, though, was Marion.

Marion had invited him to her family's table, where her mother had set out a huge pot of ramen. Isaac took a bowl, thanked her, and then nearly dropped his chopsticks. Marion slurped. Not a small slurp either, but a long, loud, glorious one, noodles vanishing into the steam. Her mother slurped too. So did Marion's little brother, who was mostly missing his mouth.

Isaac glanced at Safiya, who raised an eyebrow as if to say, do something. Isaac quietly ate without making a sound, the way he'd been taught at his grandmother's table, and waited for an adult to say something polite and terrible. Nobody did. That was the strange part. When Marion's mother offered seconds, she smiled widest at the brother, whose slurp had been the loudest of all.

So Isaac tested it. He slurped his next mouthful of noodles, feeling his ears go hot. Marion's mother laughed warmly and refilled his bowl before he could say no thank you. "You slurp like my uncle in Osaka," Marion said. "In Japan, slurping noodles like ramen and soba is acceptable at the table. It isn't rude there at all." Isaac, mouth still full, could only nod.

Safiya arrived at the table with the last samosa on a napkin, having calculated that a fair percentage of the crowd had gone for ramen instead. "Trade?" she said, holding it out to Marion.
