"You got the popular dish." Marion split the samosa in half, and Isaac slurped another mouthful so loudly that the little brother stopped, stared, and offered a solemn high five across the table.

Blake stood in Grandpa's kitchen with a heavy pot and a bag of sugar, because tonight he was making caramel sauce for dessert, all by himself. His friend Dillon had come along, mostly to watch and eat. "Is this the same browning as the crust on Grandpa's roast?" Dillon asked, peering into the pot as Blake turned the burner on. Blake thought about it while he sprinkled in the sugar. The roast had browned too, but that had meat juices in it, and meat has protein. This pot had nothing but sugar. "It can't be the same," he said slowly. "There's nothing in here but sugar. It's just sugar alone being heated." Dillon shrugged and leaned on the counter.

Grandpa, who was fiddling with the thermostat because the old house ran cold, called over, "Careful, that melted sugar is volatile stuff. One minute pale, next minute burnt." Blake kept his eyes glued to the pot, whisk in hand. He decided to test his idea. If sugar alone browned, then the browning must happen without anything else in the pot, and he could watch it happen stage by stage. First the sugar melted and went clear. Then, slowly, it turned gold, then amber, then a deep copper. Nothing had been added the whole time. So this browning needed only heat and sugar.

"It's called caramelization," Blake announced, "browning that happens when sugar alone is heated." Dillon frowned. "Then what was the roast doing?" Blake remembered a word from a science video he'd half watched. "That's the Maillard reaction. It also needs amino acids, the stuff in meat. So they're two different reactions." He grabbed a notebook and wrote it down so he'd remember for the science fair. "Two brownings, two causes," he said, and did a small victory spin with the whisk.

Then the smoke alarm shrieked. Blake yanked the pot off the burner a second too late; the copper had gone dark and bitter. He stared at the ruined batch, shoulders dropping. Dillon tried to console him. "It's okay, man, it smelled amazing for a whole minute." Blake dumped the pot in the sink, set out a fresh bag of sugar, and pointed the whisk at the stove. "Round two. You watch the clock this time."

The camp bus wouldn't reach Lake Wendell for another forty minutes, and Quentin had already asked the driver to stop three times. "I need to call my mom," he said, gripping the seat in front of him. "I forgot my allergy pills, and my prescription is at home, and I'm going back." The driver said they didn't turn around for forgotten pills, especially pills Quentin didn't actually take anymore.

Savannah, sitting across the aisle, had her own problem. She was the only one of her friends going to overnight camp, and she'd decided, somewhere around the highway on-ramp, that she was the only person on the bus who felt like her stomach had been swapped with a bag of rocks. She was also, in an impulsive way, a person who counted things. She had once tallied every red car in the school parking lot for a week. So she pulled a notebook out of her backpack and wrote a plan: before the bus arrived, she would ask every camper one question and find out for sure.

She started with Zaynab, two rows up. "On a scale of one to ten, how much do you miss home right now? Don't think about it, just say a number." Zaynab said six. The boy by the window said four. A girl with braided hair said seven and a half. Quentin said eleven, then asked if he could put his name in bold letters on the page. Savannah worked her way down the aisles, keeping her voice low so the driver wouldn't think she was causing trouble, and by the time the bus took the exit ramp she had twenty-eight numbers. Twenty-six of them were higher than one. Most were fours, fives and sixes.

Mr. Munro, the counselor riding up front, came back to collect the sick bags someone had scattered, and the notebook slid off Savannah's knee into the aisle. He picked it up, glanced at the column of numbers, and handed it back without a word, but tucked between the seats he'd dropped his staff binder, and a printed page stuck out of it. Savannah read the heading upside down, then right side up when she pulled it loose. Research on kids at overnight camps had found that most campers felt at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stayed mild. So her numbers weren't weird. They were normal, and normal meant survivable.

She tapped Quentin on the shoulder and turned the notebook toward him. "Twenty-six out of twenty-eight," she said. "You're not special. You're barely above average." Quentin stared at the column, then at the page from the binder, and let out a breath. "Fine," he said. "But if my mom asks, tell her I said ten." Through the windshield, a wooden sign shaped like a canoe came into view, and the whole bus leaned toward the glass to read it.

Julia had been sweeping the front of Mr. García's bike shop every Saturday for a month, and every Saturday the green mountain bike in the window seemed to wink at her. It cost two hundred dollars. She had earned thirty-one dollars so far, plus nine from the lemonade stand she and Kellan had run in July.

"You should just ask your mom to put it on her credit card," Kellan said, leaning on the broom Julia was supposed to be using. "Then you'd have it today. I despise waiting, personally. Waiting is for suckers."

Julia stopped sweeping. "My mom says a credit card is borrowing money. You have to pay it back plus extra."

"That's the boring part. Skip the boring part."

That night, Julia got out a notebook and tested the idea, because Kellan's plan sounded great and her mom's face had not. If her mom borrowed one hundred dollars for her, and the card charged twenty percent interest for a year, then paying it back after one year would cost about twenty dollars extra. She wrote it out. One hundred dollars became one hundred twenty. Two hundred dollars became two hundred forty. And the receipt in her mom's drawer said "compounds," which her mom translated as: if you take longer, it costs more than that.

On Saturday, Julia marched into the shop. "Mr. García, if I borrow one hundred dollars from a credit card and pay it back after a year, it costs about twenty dollars in interest. More if it compounds."

Mr. García looked up from a wheel. "Sounds right. Why are you telling me my own business?"

"Because Kellan says I should do that for the green bike, and I worked it out, and borrowing two hundred dollars means paying back two hundred forty. That's like sweeping your floor for nothing for two whole months."

"Kellan has a monopoly on bad ideas," Mr. García said. "Nobody else can get a word in."

"He does. He's very proud of it."

Julia did the math another way. At her Saturday wages, she would have the bike by spring without owing anyone anything. Spring felt far away, but two hundred forty dollars felt worse. She taped a paper bicycle to her wall and colored in one wheel spoke every Saturday.

In March, Kellan was still paying his mom back for a video game he'd charged in December, plus extra, and he had gone quiet on the subject of suckers. Julia counted her jar one last time: two hundred and six dollars. She rode the green bike to the shop to show Mr. García, ringing the little bell twice, her rebellious ponytail escaping its elastic as she flew down the hill.

He came out and saluted. "Paid for with zero interest," he said.

"Zero," Julia said, and rang the bell again.

"Excusez-moi, où est la pharmacie?" Violet asked the woman at the corner, gripping her clipboard. The woman smiled and answered in a rush of French, and Violet caught only two words: "tout droit." She turned to her group. "She said something about à droite. So we go right."

Alisha frowned at the photocopied map. "The pharmacy is on Rue Saint-Jean. That's straight past the bakery, isn't it?" Behind them, Leonie rubbed her arm where the travel clinic nurse had given her the vaccine that morning before the bus, and Violet's own arm gave a small ache of sympathy. They had fifteen minutes to buy the bandages Ms. Gagnon needed for their first-aid kit project, then meet the class at the fountain.

Violet looked at the map, then at the corner. The pharmacy symbol sat at the top of the page, straight up from where they stood. A street did branch off to the right, but nothing on the map was marked there. If the woman had meant right, the pharmacy should be on that side street. It wasn't. She exhaled slowly through her nose, the way she did before a difficult piano piece, and thought about the sounds. The woman had said "tout droit." Not just "à droite." Two different things, probably, because the woman had used both at some point, or had she? Violet closed her eyes and replayed the answer in her head. "Continuez tout droit." That was it. Continue. You continue when you keep going the way you already are.

"Wait," Violet said. "I think tout droit means straight ahead, and à droite means to the right. They sound almost the same, but she said tout droit, and she told us to continue. So we go straight." Alisha tilted her head. "You're sure?" "Testing it. If we walk two blocks straight and there's no pharmacy, we turn around." They walked past the bakery, where warm sugar and butter drifted out the open door, and past a bookshop with a cat sleeping in the window. At the second corner, the green cross of the pharmacy glowed above the door.

Inside, Violet asked the cashier for bandages in careful French, counted out the coins, and carried the small paper bag outside like a trophy. Leonie checked her watch. "Nine minutes to spare." They ran for the fountain, and when Ms. Gagnon raised an eyebrow at their flushed faces, Violet held up the bag and said, "On y est allées tout droit."

Laurence squinted at her sketch pad and then at the ping-pong ball sitting on the art cabin's wooden table. Mr. Sokolov had set up the still life for everyone: one ball, one flashlight clipped to a shelf, one hour before the camp art show opened at four. Her sphere had a nice highlight on the top left and a soft shadow curving away from the light, but something was wrong, and she couldn't name it.

"It looks like it's hovering," said Vera, leaning over from the next stool. Vera's own page had a lopsided blob that she insisted was "abstract," though what she really wanted was for the judges to hang her drawing next to the canoe rack where everyone walked past. "Mine's hovering too, but on purpose. Yours looks like a magic trick gone wrong."

Emaan, on Laurence's other side, was already halfway done. He had smudged his gray pencil until his ball looked so real that Laurence reached out, half expecting her finger to touch it. "How did you do the bottom?" she asked him. Emaan shrugged and held up his pencil. "I just pressed really hard in one tiny spot. Right under the ball. Don't ask me why it works." He was busy trying to finish before the bell so he could get the good table at the campfire snack, and he'd promised to save Laurence a marshmallow if she made the deadline too.

Laurence bent down until her eye was level with the table. The flashlight didn't emit much light into the thin space where the ball touched the wood, she realized, so that little sliver of contact was where the shadow went almost black. Everywhere else, light crept in from the sides and made the shadow grayer. She picked up her softest pencil and pressed hard, darkening just the crescent where ball met table, leaving the rest of the cast shadow lighter. Then she drew a faint line around the sphere's equator, the halfway curve she'd learned about yesterday, to make the shading turn evenly.

Vera scooted her stool closer and whispered, "Can you show me the pressing thing? Mine's floating worse than a hot air balloon." Laurence demonstrated on the corner of Vera's page, and Vera copied it, tongue sticking out, then let out a whoop when her blob finally sat down on its imaginary table. "It's grounded! It has a home now!" A few kids laughed, and even Mr. Sokolov cracked a smile from the doorway.

At three fifty-eight, Laurence added one last approximate touch of gray beneath the black crescent, so the shadow would fade smoothly outward. The bell rang, and Emaan grabbed both their pages and jogged them to the display table, saving spots side by side. Laurence followed, wiping graphite off her fingers, and stood back to look. Her sphere rested on the table, heavy and real, no longer floating anywhere but exactly where she'd put it. "Marshmallow tax," Emaan said, and held out his hand.

Laurence sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a worksheet, a pencil, and a slice of pizza that was going cold while she glared at the first problem: one quarter plus one third. Her grandmother had already asked twice whether she wanted more cheese on it. Laurence had said no twice.

"You look like the worksheet insulted you," said Simona, who had come over because her own house had no pizza and also no grandmother who made mango smoothies.

"It did insult me. The denominators don't match. You can't add fourths and thirds, that's like adding cats and scissors."

Her grandmother slid a whole pizza onto the table and, without a word, cut a quarter out of it. Then she took that quarter piece, cut it into three skinny slices, and fanned them out. "Three twelfths," she said, and went back to her crossword.

Laurence stopped chewing. She counted the skinny slices, then the twelve slices they would make across a whole pizza. She pulled her plate closer and cut her own slice the same way, muttering as she worked, and began to document her results in the margin of the worksheet like a scientist who suspected something remarkable. One quarter, cut into three pieces, made three twelfths. She tried it with half the pizza, cut into three, and got three sixths, which was still a half, sitting there pretending to be new.

"It works if you multiply the top and the bottom by the same number," she told Simona, with an assertive tap of the pencil. "So one quarter is three twelfths, and one third is four twelfths, and now they're both twelfths and I can actually add them."

Simona looked at the pizza, which now had a grid of cuts across it like a prism throwing lines everywhere. "So the answer is seven twelfths?"

"Seven twelfths." Laurence wrote it down and boxed it, then ate the evidence.

Her grandmother penciled in one more word of the crossword and slid the smoothie across the table.

Antoine had exactly forty minutes before the library closed and before the deadline for Mr. Ionescu's class project expired at midnight, which would not have been a problem if his printer at home had not chosen tonight to release a puff of vapor and die. So here he was at the public library, hunched over a computer between two friends, typing "cats or dogs best pets" into the search bar and getting pages about nothing useful at all.

"Try it again," said Reuben, leaning over his shoulder. "Maybe the internet is just being moody."

"The internet is always moody," said Masen. "It's like a cat. Which is sort of our topic, so that's poetic."

Antoine typed the search a second time and got the same pile of junk. Mixed in with the results were boxes shouting WIN A FREE PHONE and TOP 10 PET DEALS, which he was starting to recognize as ads rather than real results. He remembered the day Mr. Ionescu had shown the class a page covered in blinking boxes and asked them to raise a hand when they spotted the fake one. "You're learning to see the invisible," Mr. Ionescu had said, which at the time had sounded like something a wizard would say. Now Antoine squinted at the screen, skipped anything with a tiny "Sponsored" tag, and felt slightly like a detective.

"Wait," he said slowly. "The word OR is lowercase. What if that matters?" He highlighted the o, deleted it, and retyped it in capital letters. The page refreshed, and suddenly the results showed sites about cats and sites about dogs, pages containing either word, exactly what he'd wanted. "It works! OR has to be in capital letters, all caps, or it doesn't count."

Masen gasped like Antoine had discovered fire. "You just collaborated with the computer and won."

"I didn't collaborate with anything, I just yelled at it in capital letters," Antoine said, but he was grinning. He narrowed his keywords further, adding "behavior" and "care," and the junk results thinned out like fog on a cool morning. Reuben pointed at one box that claimed a puppy could be delivered in an hour. "Definitely an ad," Antoine said, scrolling past it. "Real results don't promise you a puppy like a pizza."

At 8:58, two minutes before closing, Antoine hit print. The librarian appeared at the desk holding his warm pages, and outside the air had turned humid and heavy, the kind of night that made his shirt stick to his back all the way to the bus stop. He slid the report into his backpack, zipped it, and turned to his friends.

"Tomorrow I'm teaching my dad this trick," he said. "He thinks the search engine is out to get him."

Reuben clapped him on the shoulder. "Tell him to fight back in capital letters."

Arthur had heard the story about the first big game so many times that he could almost see it, and that was the problem. Grandpa Joe told it every year at Mr. Mehta's watch party, which was the best party on the block because Mr. Mehta had the biggest television and made samosas by the trayful. Arthur sat on the floor between his friends Tayla and Everly, a plate balanced on his knees, waiting for the moment.

It came in the second quarter. "I remember the very first one," Grandpa Joe announced from the good armchair. "January 15, 1967. Packers against the Chiefs, and the Packers won it thirty-five to ten." He said it the way he always did, like he was setting down a stone.

Everly leaned toward Arthur and whispered, "He says that every year. Do you think he really remembers it? He would have been a kid." Arthur had wondered the same thing. Grandpa Joe's memories sometimes got mixed up, like the time he swore he'd shaken hands with a president at a county fair. Tayla shrugged. "You could just ask him stuff."

Arthur decided to test the story instead. His idea was simple: if Grandpa Joe truly watched that game, he would know details that a person couldn't fake, and if he only knew the numbers, the story might come from somewhere else. So during a commercial, Arthur asked, "Grandpa, where did you watch it? Who was there?"

Grandpa Joe's face changed, going soft and far away. "My father's living room. The furniture was sparse back then, just a couch and two chairs, and the whole building crammed in because half the street didn't have a set yet." He described his mother keeping score on a grocery bag, and how the paper tore and a neighbor taped it back together at halftime. "I kept that bag for years," he added. "Wish I hadn't lost it. That's a choice I regret."

Arthur listened with both ears. The numbers matched every year, but this was different. This had people in it, a torn grocery bag, a neighbor with tape. You couldn't replicate a memory like that by repeating it; you could only have it. From Arthur's perspective on the floor, looking up, Grandpa Joe suddenly seemed less like a teller of tales and more like a man holding pieces of a day almost nobody else remembered.

Tayla nudged him. "So? Real or not?"

"Real," Arthur said, and Grandpa Joe, who had heard the whole exchange, raised his cup toward him across the crowded room.

Bennett slid into his usual seat on the school bus, third row from the back, and pulled out his phone before the doors had even hissed shut. Somewhere behind him, Lucca was laughing with a knot of eighth graders, and the sound of it made Bennett's stomach tighten. Yesterday, in what he thought was a private chat with a kid from math class, Bennett had typed some things about Lucca. He had called him bossy. He had said Lucca acted like he owned the group project. It had felt good to type, the way yelling into a pillow feels good. Now he was not so sure it had stayed between the two of them, because at lunch Lucca had sat at the far end of the table and said nothing to him at all.

He tested his idea the only way he could think of. He opened the chat and reread his own message. Then he checked the other group chat, the big one with half the grade in it, where memes and soccer scores saturated the feed every afternoon. Nothing about him. Nothing yet. But that did not prove anything, and he knew it, because Ms. Wong had once said something in class that stuck in his head: a private message is only as private as the people who read it. Anyone who received it could screenshot it and pass it along, and then it lived wherever they put it.

The bus jolted over the tracks near Aila's stop, and Aila grabbed the seat back as she climbed the steps. She dropped into the seat across the aisle from Bennett and studied him with her eyebrows up.

"You look like you saw a ghost," she said.

"Worse." He turned the phone face down on his knee. "I said something mean about Lucca in a chat I thought was just me and one other kid. And now Lucca's not talking to me, and I don't know if he saw it or if he's just mad about the project."

Aila frowned. "So you don't actually know the cause. That's the whole problem. You're guessing."

"Exactly. There's no way to check the guess." He rubbed his thumb along the edge of the phone case. "Unless I just ask him."

"That's not guessing anymore. That's a test."

The bus pulled up to the school. Bennett stood, then stopped in the aisle where Lucca was gathering his backpack. The eighth graders had gone quiet, and the driver's mirror showed everyone's faces at once, small and staring.

"Lucca. Did you see something I wrote?" Bennett asked.

Lucca held up his phone, and there it was, a screenshot, his own words in somebody else's chat. "Marcus sent it to the big group this morning."

Bennett looked at the image of his message sitting there where it was never meant to be. "I'm sorry," he said. "I should have said it to your face, or not at all."

Lucca studied him for a long second, then shrugged one shoulder. "Then say it to my face now."

"You're bossy about the project. Sometimes. That's all it was."

"Okay," Lucca said. "Now I actually heard it. Get off the bus, bossy is going to be late for homeroom."

The snow had come down all night, and by morning school was cancelled. Aiden pulled on his boots and walked to the park, where the hills were already loud with kids on sleds. On the way, he passed the little house beside the park gate, where Ms. Friedman was shoveling her driveway. She was moving slowly, and she kept stopping, one mittened hand pressed against her side.

Aiden watched from the sidewalk for a minute. His father had said something once about snow and older people, something he couldn't quite remember. Standing there, he made an inference: the stopping wasn't laziness or cold. Heavy snow was hard on the heart, so the stopping must be a way of protecting it. If that was true, then the huge shovelfuls she was heaving were the problem, and small loads would fix it.

"You should let me take a turn," he said, "and take little scoops instead of big ones. And maybe rest between rows."

Ms. Friedman leaned on her shovel. "Small scoops?"

"Half a shovel at a time," Aiden said. "Doctors say take breaks and lift small loads, not big ones. That's what my dad told my grandpa." He wasn't sure his memory was authentic, but she looked at him as if it might be, so he picked up the spare shovel by her porch step.

They worked row by row down the driveway. He shoveled one row while she stood by the gate catching her breath, and then she did the next while he rested and watched the sleds go flying down the park hill. The work went slower than one person digging fast, but by the time they reached the sidewalk she was breathing easy and laughing at something he'd said about the snowman in the park, which wore an actual necktie.

Braeden and Lyanna came trudging past with a sled between them. "Come to the hill," Braiden called. "Best snow all winter."

Aiden looked at the clear driveway, then at the hill.

"Race you," he said, and grabbed his shovel.

Joshua set the two bean pots side by side on the folding table in the gymnasium, smoothing his display board with the heel of his hand so the title stood straight: "Do Beans Grow Better With Music?" The gym smelled like floor wax and masking tape, and the bleachers rattled as other kids dragged in their tables. His left pot, the music pot, had grown tall and pale. His right pot, the silent one, was squat and dark green. On paper it looked like a discovery, the kind of thing people called a scientific frontier, a whole new question nobody had answered yet.

"Wow," said Ameera, leaning over his table. "The music one totally won."

Joshua grinned, but then he stopped. Something about the tall, pale plant bothered him. Pale meant reaching for something, the way plants reached for light. He closed his eyes and tried to picture his bedroom, where he had kept the pots for three weeks. He could almost smell the dusty windowsill, could almost hear the radio humming on the shelf beside it.

Then the flashback hit him whole. His dad carrying the pots upstairs, setting one pot on the sunny windowsill because it fit there, and the other on the dresser across the room because it didn't. The impulsive decision had taken ten seconds. "No, no, no," Joshua said out loud. He had not only played music for one pot. He had also given it the window.

"It's ruined," he said, and his voice cracked a little. "Both things changed. I can't interpret the results at all. Music, light, I don't know which one made the difference."

Ameera frowned at the pots. "So what do you do now?"

Ms. Mwangi passed by with a roll of tape, and Joshua caught her sleeve. "Ms. Mwangi, if I start over, how do I make it right?"

"You keep every other condition the same," she said, already walking on. "Then any difference in results can be traced to the one variable you changed."

Joshua grabbed a marker and wrote across the top of his board: ROUND TWO. Ameera laughed and pulled up a chair.

"New pots," Joshua said, already counting seeds out of the packet into his palm. "Same soil, same water, same shelf. This time the radio is the only thing that's different."

The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and coffee, and the line of voters snaked between the basketball hoops. Chloe stood near the check-in table with her poster rolled under one arm, waiting for her mother to finish her ballot. Tomorrow she had to give a report in Mr. Santos-Reyes's class, and tonight the school was letting students set up civics displays at the polling station. She had picked the topic herself, how a bill becomes a law, and now she wasn't sure she actually understood it.

Jesse jogged over from the juice table, waving a folded newspaper. "Look at this. There are two versions of that park bill. One says the Senate passed it, one says the House passed it. Which one becomes the law?"

Chloe took the paper. Both articles were real, both votes had happened, and the two versions weren't even worded the same. She felt a hot flicker of panic, the same one she'd felt when she'd skipped the reading last week and guessed wrong on the quiz. She had guessed then. She didn't want to guess again.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Watch this." She unrolled her poster on the folding table and drew a quick sketch: two boxes labeled House and Senate, arrows, and a small figure at the end. "I think it's like this. The House passes its version. The Senate passes its version. But if they're not identical, it can't just move on." She traced the arrows with her marker. "It has to pass both, in the same form, before it goes to the president."

Chace, who had drifted over with a cookie, squinted at the drawing. "So in the news, neither one is the law yet?"

"That's my idea," Chloe said. "Let's test it." She walked to the check-in table, where Mr. Santos-Reyes was meticulously handing each voter the correct ballot for their residence, checking addresses line by line. "Mr. Santos-Reyes, quick question, not about voting. If a bill passes the House one way and the Senate another way, is it a law?"

He smiled and held up his hand like a stop sign. "I'm not telling you. That's your report, Chloe. But ask yourself: would you sign two papers that didn't say the same thing?"

She stood there a second. Then it landed, and she almost laughed. Of course. You wouldn't sign two different papers. The bill had to be identical in both places first, and only then did it reach the president's desk. It was a rule you couldn't see, but you could feel its shape, the way you could feel that the line of voters was moving even with your back turned.

Back at the table, she redrew her poster with the two boxes joined by a loop labeled "must match," then the arrow to the president. "Jesse, get your notebook and recount the steps out loud while I write them," she said, capping her marker. Chace read the headline one more time, then flipped the newspaper over. "So that park bill still has a long way to go," he said, and Chloe nodded, already printing the last word in careful block letters.

Connor found the watch in the cupholder, where Grandpa always left it during long drives. The leather band was warm from the sun, and the second hand still ticked, even though the funeral had been three days ago and Grandpa had been gone two weeks before that. Connor slipped it on his wrist. It was too big, so he made a fist to keep it from sliding off.

"Do you think that's weird?" he asked. His mom kept her eyes on the road, so Connor turned to Drayden in the back seat instead. They were driving to Grandpa's house to help sort his things, and Drayden had come along because Connor hadn't wanted to make the trip alone. "Wearing it. Drayden, I'm asking you. Does it mean I'm not moving on?"

Drayden pulled out his phone. "My counselor had this book on her shelf. It's called Continuing Bonds. Came out in 1996." He scrolled, then held the screen up. "It says keeping a connection to somebody who died, through memories or objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving. It's actually a whole idea people study."

Connor looked at the window. The fields outside were barren this time of year, brown and flat, and for a second he felt like that too, like nothing would grow in him again. Then he thought about how Grandpa used to orbit the kitchen every morning, coffee cup in one hand, checking the window for birds. Connor had always thought that was silly. Now he wasn't sure. Maybe he would start checking the window himself.

"Traditions," he said slowly. "Like the drive to get donuts on Saturdays. Grandpa never skipped it. Not once."

"So don't skip it either," Drayden said. "That's not being stuck. That's the watch still ticking."

The jury in Connor's head had been out all week, and it wasn't back yet, but his fist loosened anyway. He rotated the watch until its face caught the light, then looked out at the birds following the car down the fence line. "Saturday," he said. "You're coming with me."

Camille spread her poster board across the library table and frowned at the empty space in the middle. Her report was due Thursday, and she still could not answer the question Mr. Villanueva had written on the board: Why did the ancient Egyptians build the pyramids, and how did the Nile shape their farming? She had a stack of books, a plastic tub of sand Angad had carried in from the art room, and a half-inch of water in a squeeze bottle. Anais dropped into the chair across from her and peered at the sand.

"What's the tub for?" Anais asked.

"Testing," Camille said. She had read that the Nile flooded every year, and she wanted to see what that would do to farmland. She tilted the tub so the sand piled at one end, then pressed a shallow channel down the middle with her finger. "This part is the river. These flat bits are fields." She squeezed water slowly into the channel until it crept over the edges and darkened the sand on both sides. When the water soaked in, she lifted the tub to eye level to magnify the view of the thin layer of wet silt left behind, and the pattern made sense at once. The flood was not a disaster. It was delivery. Wet mud, spread across the fields, year after year.

"Okay, that's farming," said Angad, sliding a book toward her. "Now look at this." It was a cutaway picture of a pyramid, sliced open like a cake. Deep inside, near the middle, was a small room with a stone chest in it. Angad tapped the room. "I thought pyramids were palaces. Like, the pharaoh lived in the top and looked out."

Camille studied the picture. "If it were a palace, where are the windows? The kitchens? There's just this little room buried in all that stone." She turned pages until she found the caption, and read it twice to be sure. "It's a burial chamber. The whole pyramid is a tomb, built to protect the pharaoh's body and his belongings for his life after death." That explained everything else, she realized. The treasure, the narrow passages, the sealed entrances. Nobody seals a palace like a vault.

"Mr. Villanueva?" Camille called softly, and the librarian came over. "Can I check out this model kit? It has a Nile with a little valve you open to flood the fields." He found the box and set it beside her sand tub.

"For the presentation?" he asked.

"Both," Camille said. She copied the cutaway picture onto her poster, drew arrows from the river to the fields, and wrote her answer at the top in careful letters: floods fed the fields, and the pyramids kept the pharaoh safe for the life after this one. Anais read it over her shoulder and nodded.

"One more thing," Angad said, pointing at a drawing of birds in the corner of a page. "The Egyptians watched these migratory birds arrive every year right before the flood. The birds were like a warning sign."

Camille added one bird to her river, wings spread, flying north. Then she squeezed the bottle again and watched the water rise.

Charles had a science worksheet due Monday, a chart comparing a plant cell and an animal cell, and no desk he wanted to sit at on a Saturday. So he brought the worksheet to the community garden, where he was supposed to be helping his neighbor Ms. Khoury repair her dilapidated tomato cages.

"You're drawing instead of weeding," Ms. Khoury observed.

"I'm multitasking." He held up the paper. "Plant cell. I copied it off the board. Animal cell, too."

Alycia and Martin wandered over from the lettuce beds to look. Alycia frowned at the two drawings. "Yours are the same. Basically."

"They're not the same," Charles said. "Mine has the wall, the chloroplasts, and the big water bubble thing."

"Vacuole," Martin said, in the tone of someone who had spelled it wrong on a quiz and never forgiven himself.

Alycia tapped the animal cell drawing with one finger. "Then why does the animal one have this extra bit? Two little rods, right here. My drawing has them too. Did we inherit them from the same board notes, or did you just not copy fast enough?"

Charles stared at the tiny rods. He had copied fast, thank you. He'd checked. Which meant the rods were in the animal cell and not in the plant cell, and that was a real difference, not a rushed one. "That's an inference," he said slowly. "The rods are only in animals. I'm inferring."

"You're showing off," said Martin.

"I'm inferring." Charles flipped the worksheet over and wrote it down. Alycia peered at the board notes on her own sheet and found the label. "Centrioles," she read. "Animal cells have them. And most plant cells don't."

"So plants just divide without them," Charles said. "Show-offs."

Ms. Khoury handed him a bent tomato stake. "Inferring is fine," she said. "Hammering is better."

Charles hammered, worksheet pinned under a rock beside him, centrioles circled twice for good measure.

The bus smelled like wet sneakers and oranges, and Lincoln had his phone balanced on his knee, glaring at the class group chat. Someone had typed twenty-seven walrus emojis at five in the morning. Then someone else had answered with a foghorn sound. Then the chat had somehow become a debate about whether Mr. Grant's mustache counted as agriculture, because Hope had started it and she could make anything sound scientific.

"We need rules," Lincoln said.

Mikaella, two seats over, leaned across the aisle. "You can't just invent rules. People will assume you're being bossy, and then they'll send more walruses out of spite."

"That's exactly why I have to find out if official rules already exist. Like, real ones. Written down somewhere."

He searched, scrolling while the bus lurched around the corner by the farm stand. He typed "official online manners" and then, after another lurch, "old rules for chatting." What came up surprised him: a document called RFC 1855. "Listen to this," he said. "One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995."

"Netiquette," Mikaella repeated. "That's actually a word?"

"That's what it was called." He skimmed further. The old guide said things like don't shout in capitals, and think about how messages sound without a face attached. Lincoln had a theory forming: the walrus problem wasn't really about walruses. It was that in the group chat, everybody talked like they were alone in their bedrooms, which they were, instead of like they were on the bus together, where you could see people wince.

He tested it. He typed a message out loud first, in his normal voice, then changed the capitals to lowercase before sending.

NEW RULE, the message began, then his thumbs deleted it and started over. "New rule," it read instead. "Before you send something at 5 a.m., say it out loud like we're all sitting behind you. Also, the chat goes quiet after nine at night. Vote yes or send one walrus."

One walrus appeared within seconds, from Hope.

"That's a no," Lincoln said.

"That's a yes with an attitude," said Mikaella. "Significant difference."

Caleb stood on an old milk crate in Mr. López's garage, holding his choir folder like it was a shield. Karson and Darwin leaned against the workbench, and the three of them were supposed to sing "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" as a round for Friday's assembly. The problem was that every time they tried it, somebody wandered into somebody else's line.

"Again," said Mr. López, tapping his music stand with a screwdriver. "Group one starts. Group two waits."

Caleb began. "Row, row, row your boat, gently down the stream." Darwin was supposed to come in next, but by the third word Darwin had drifted over to Caleb's words entirely, and the round collapsed into two boys singing the same thing at each other.

"Maybe it just can't work," Karson said. "It sounds wrong on purpose, doesn't it?"

Caleb wasn't sure. He had thought the same thing at first, which now seemed naive, because the upper-school choir had sounded amazing at the winter concert. So the round had to work somehow. He looked at the sheet music and noticed something he had missed before. His part and Darwin's part had the exact same notes, the exact same words. Nothing was different except where each pencil mark said "begin."

"Wait," Caleb said. "In a round, everybody sings the same melody, just starting at different times. Darwin, you're not supposed to sing my words. You're supposed to sing your words."

"That's it? That's all it is?" Darwin asked.

"One way to find out," Caleb said. He inhaled, counted four beats in his head, and started. Darwin came in late, and this time he stayed on his own line instead of chasing Caleb's. Karson jumped in third, and for a second the garage filled with three voices tumbling over each other. It was the sound from the winter concert.

Mr. López lowered his screwdriver and smiled. "From the top."

The kitchen smelled of burnt toast, and Theo had exactly one hour before bed, because tomorrow Mr. Do was giving the retest. Two-step equations. Plotting the line on the grid. Last week Theo had bombed it, and Mr. Do had said, "Persevere, Theo. That's the whole skill." His pencil moved without thinking now; that was the problem. Subtracting before dividing had become a reflex, and the reflex was wrong.

His phone buzzed against the table. It was Armin, from math club. Theo, why does Izaiah keep calling the graph paper Cartesian? is it fancy paper?

Theo frowned at his grid, where three points sat crooked and a fourth had gone wild off the line. He texted back that he had no idea, then remembered Mr. Do writing a name on the board last Tuesday in his looping hand, and Izaiah raising his hand and reading it out loud. Descartes. That's why it's called the Cartesian plane. Then Izaiah had added that Descartes was a French mathematician and philosopher, and that in 1637 he wrote about linking algebra and geometry. Theo had been half asleep that day and figured it was trivia for a prestigious quiz team, nothing to do with him.

But now he stared at his equation, y = 2x + 1. He plugged in 0, then 1, then 2, and marked each point. The toast smell still hung in the air, sharp and bitter. He connected the points with his ruler, and they lay in a perfectly straight diagonal. Algebra, the numbers, turning into geometry, the line, right on the paper. So that was what Descartes had linked. His wrong points, he noticed, were the ones where his reflex had botched the arithmetic. The equation was innocent.

He texted Armin one line: it's not the paper, it's the whole grid, ask Izaiah. Then he erased the wild point, solved the equation again slowly, one step at a time, and set the pencil down where the line crossed the y-axis, dead center of the square.

"Zero, one," he said out loud, and drew the point twice as dark.

The eye chart in Mr. Balogun's classroom had been hanging by the window for as long as anyone could remember, and Willow had never once wondered about it until the letter from the eye clinic arrived in her backpack. Her screening results, the note said, were due back to the school office by Friday, and her appointment was Thursday afternoon. That left exactly one day of wiggle room, which her mother said was not wiggle room at all.

"You can't read the board from your seat?" Liv asked on Wednesday, squinting at her from two desks over.

"I can read it fine," Willow said, which was mostly true if she leaned forward and guessed. Mr. Balogun had moved the science vocabulary list to the board that morning, and Willow had written "habitat" as "rabbitat" because that was what the smudge looked like. She cherished that notebook, and she did not want to fill it with invented words.

During silent reading, she found herself staring at the eye chart again instead of her book. The rows of letters shrank toward the bottom, big E at the top, tiny blur at the base. Someone had designed that, she realized. Somebody, at some point, had sat down and decided how big each letter should be. But who? And when? She raised her hand.

"Mr. Balogun, do you know where eye charts come from?"

He looked pleased, the way he did when a question went sideways from the lesson. "There's a name on the bottom of that one, if you can get close enough," he said. "Which, apparently, you soon will."

Willow walked up and crouched at the bottom corner of the chart. Under a film of dust and tape residue, in faded print, was a single word: Snellen. Beside it, a year. 1862.

"Herman Snellen," she read aloud. "He made this in 1862."

"Same design we still use," Mr. Balogun said, and went back to his grading, offering nothing further, which was his way of making students dig.

Willow stood there doing the math on her fingers. Her great-grandmother was ninety-one, born in a world with cars and radios and telephones. This chart was older than all of that, older than anyone's great-grandparents in the whole school, probably. She tested the idea on Izaiah at lunch, and he worked it out with a french fry as a timeline marker. "So every kid who ever squinted at one of these," he said slowly, "was squinting at Herman Snellen's idea. That's wild."

"Also," Liv said, "you have forty minutes before your mom picks you up for the eye doctor, and you're using them to talk about a dead Dutch guy."

At the clinic, Willow slid into the big chair and found herself facing another chart with shrinking rows, a newer one but the same creature. The optometrist asked her to cover her left eye, and the letters unrolled in front of her one line at a time, sharp and unmistakable, like the world had been holding out on her.

"Ready for the bottom?" the optometrist asked.

Willow leaned forward, optimistic for the first time all week. "Line by line," she said. "That's how Snellen would have wanted it."

Samuel spread the two library books side by side on the table by the window, one open to chapter one and one to the last chapter. His copy of The Great Gatsby had only one bookmark in it, and he kept flipping back and forth so much that Abraham reached over and tapped the second book.

"You're going to wreck the spine doing that," Abraham said. "Just use mine."

"It's the same page," Samuel said. "That's the problem. The green light is the green light. Same words both times. Mr. Khoury says a symbol can shift what it means across the chapters of a novel, and I don't see how."

Carl slid into the third chair with a stack of granola bars. "I already finished it," he said. "It means the same thing. It's a light. It's green. Gatsby stares at it because he likes staring at it."

"It's not that simple." Samuel leaned over the page. In chapter one, Gatsby stood at the edge of his lawn reaching toward the water, toward a single green light, and Daisy was the person he wanted, the whole reason he had bought that enormous house across the bay from hers. Samuel read the last chapter again, slower. Here the light was just one of the "enchanted objects" the narrator names, something already far away, a dream that could not be reached no matter how rich Gatsby became. Same light. Different weight.

"Okay," Carl said, chewing. "So chapter one, it's his hope of winning Daisy."

"And by the end," Samuel said, "it's the dream he can't reach. Rich as he gets."

Carl frowned and pulled the book toward himself. He wanted to be the one who figured things out first, and being second bothered him, so he reread the last page with his finger under the line. "It's like a mirror," he said finally. "There's a symmetry. Same light, but one side is hoping and one side is knowing you'll never get there."

"That's it," Samuel said. "That's what Mr. Khoury wanted us to track." He copied both passages into his notebook and drew an arrow between them. He would have to conserve the exact wording when he wrote his paragraph, because the whole argument depended on what the narrator actually says.

Abraham looked at the notebook page. "So I don't have to reread the whole thing?"

"You should reread it," Carl said, sliding the book back across the table.

Samuel laughed and handed over the second bookmark. "Page one hundred eighty. Start there."

At ten o'clock sharp, the community kitchen on Maple Street had to start cooking, because lunch went out at noon and forty people were counting on it. Anthony tied his apron and stared at the pot of macaroni and cheese he was responsible for, all by himself, for the first time. Ms. Becker had shown him once how to make a roux, that paste of butter and flour, and how to whisk milk into it until it turned smooth. His first batch had gone beautifully. His second batch, the one for today, sat cooling on the counter in a separate pot, and it looked wrong.

"Yours is shiny," said Elissa, leaning over from the salad station. "Kind of greasy shiny." Anthony scooped a little with a spoon and watched oil pool in the dent it left. Johnathan wandered over, sniffed it, and made a face like he'd bitten a lemon. Anthony thought hard. He had made the roux exactly the same way both times, same butter, same flour, same milk. What had been different? Then he remembered: the first time, the pot had been off the burner when he stirred in the cheese. This morning, rushing, he had left it on the flame. It was as if the cheese had a rule he couldn't see, and he'd broken it without knowing the rule existed.

"Stir it in off the heat," he said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "The heat makes the cheese clump up and squeeze out its fat. That's why it's greasy." Elissa raised an eyebrow, so Anthony grabbed the last of the cheese from the walk-in fridge, remelted a fresh roux with milk, pulled the pot off the burner, and stirred the cheese in slow handfuls. The sauce came together like velvet. No shine, no oil, no lumps.

They plated forty containers by noon, plus the special bag for the neighbor whose prescription medicine had to be kept separate from the dairy, just in case. Ms. Becker tasted a spoonful of Anthony's sauce, paused, and looked at him with an almost predatory gleam, the look of a cook who has spotted talent she intends to recruit. "Saturdays," she said. "We do a soup that needs exactly this touch. Do you thrive under pressure, or wilt?" Anthony grinned and held out his spoon for her to see the shine that wasn't there. "Test me," he said.

The trail climbed through pines until it opened onto a rocky lookout where Ms. Villanueva unrolled a laminated map and clipped it to a cardboard board. "Your task," she said, "is to find checkpoint four. I'll give you the location, but I'm giving it the way real geographers do, in numbers." Isla's group had come in second at the last orienteering meet because Isla had guessed at the checkpoints instead of working them out, and she had promised herself this time would be different.

Emil leaned over the map first, because Emil wanted to be the one who found every checkpoint before anyone else. "Give us the numbers, then," he said, bouncing on his toes. Finley pulled out a granola bar and offered half to Isla, who took it even though her stomach was too nervous to want it; it was kind of him, and she ate it anyway.

"Checkpoint four is at roughly forty-four degrees north, seventy-one degrees west," said Ms. Villanueva. Then she sat on a flat rock and pretended to be very interested in a beetle, which meant she was not going to say another word.

"Which one is which?" Emil asked. "North of what? West of what?" He spun the map so the trail pointed downhill, which concealed the little blue lake in the corner, and Finley had to grab the edge before the wind took the whole thing into the ravine.

Isla traced the numbers along the side of the map with her finger. The forty-four ran up and down, in rows that crossed the trail like the rungs of a ladder. The seventy-one ran side to side. Then she remembered the flight screen at the airport last summer, when she and her dad had stared at a string of numbers next to their plane and she had asked him which number meant what. Longitude, he had told her, measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from zero degrees up to one hundred eighty degrees, east or west. Latitude was the other one, the ladder rungs, north and south. She checked it against the map: seventy-one west put them on the left side, the west side, and the checkpoint had to sit where the ladder rung crossed the sideways line, right where the map showed a bend in the creek.

"It's at the creek bend," Isla said, and she could feel her face going warm, not from the climb. "East and west means longitude. Our number is west of the zero line." Emil was already stuffing the map under his arm, and Finley folded the wrapper into his pocket so nothing was left behind.

They ran the trail with the sense of the finish imminent, and Emil let Isla take the last twenty meters even though he was faster, because she was the one who had worked it out. At the creek bend, a red-and-white marker hung from a birch, and this was the climax of the whole afternoon: checkpoint four, orange clipboard, their team name at the top of the sheet. Emil pumped his fist and yelled so loudly that a crow burst out of the pines. "Next one," he said, "you read the numbers, and I'll run."

Henry had exactly eleven minutes to prove his rock was limestone before the museum's rock-sorting challenge ended, and Mr. Gill was already walking toward the last table.

"Quarry rocks," Mr. Gill had announced at the start, dumping a bin of gray, battered stones onto the table. "Sort them into igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic by how they were formed. Formed, not how they look." Henry's three samples all looked like plain gray lumps, which felt like a bad joke. Maryam had breezed through hers in four minutes, holding each rock up to the light like a jeweler. Dennis kept trying to classify everything as metamorphic because, he said, "It sounds the coolest," and when Henry pointed out that coolness was not an objective way to sort anything, Dennis ridiculed him for the rest of the activity. "Oh, look at Henry with his science words," Dennis chanted, grinning. Henry grinned back, but his rocks still sat in one unsorted pile.

He turned the smallest stone over in his hands. Igneous meant cooled from melted rock. Sedimentary meant squeezed together in layers, bits and pieces settling over ages. Metamorphic meant changed by heat and pressure deep underground. None of that was written on the rock. It happened ages ago, out of sight, and he couldn't exactly climb into a volcano or an ancient seabed to check. But then he remembered the museum card he'd read near the cave exhibit, the one Maryam had skipped to look at the glow-worm display. Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, so a drop of vinegar makes it fizz as carbon dioxide gas is released. A fizz you could see. A clue from the past, showing up right now.

"Maryam," Henry whispered, "do you still have the vinegar from lunch? You put it on your chips." Maryam dug the tiny bottle out of her backpack like it was treasure. Henry set his rock on a paper napkin, dripped three drops onto its surface, and held his breath. Nothing. He tried the second rock. Nothing again, just wet gray stone. His heart sank, but he kept his hands steady for the last one. Drop. Drop. A hiss of tiny bubbles fizzed up on the surface like the rock itself was breathing.

"Sedimentary!" Henry shouted, loud enough that a toddler across the room pointed. "This one's limestone, and limestone forms in layers, so it's sedimentary. That means these other two aren't limestone, and this one here has tiny sparkles, like crystals grew in it, so it's metamorphic, and that leaves the fine-grained one for igneous." Mr. Gill leaned over the table, checked his clipboard, and tapped the limestone with his pen. "Correct on all three," he said. "The fizzing gives it away every time. Nicely done." Dennis groaned and slid his own pile of rocks toward Henry. "Fine, oh science-words one," he said. "Sort mine too."

Marcus sat on the lakeside dock with his duffel bag between his knees and tried to look like a boy who had been to camp before. He had not. The bus would come at noon, and until then his only plan was to sit still and let the morning happen to him.

Denis plopped down beside him, already eating a granola bar he had clearly brought for exactly this dramatic moment. "My dad says the camp store charges two dollars for a candy bar that costs a dollar anywhere else," Denis said. "He called it a tariff on chocolate." Marcus nodded slowly, filing that away as important information. Then Parker arrived, out of breath, holding a folded paper. It was a note from Ms. Lin, the neighbor who had gone to this same camp thirty years ago, and it read: The fire rule matters more than you think. Ask them to show you.

"Why would I ask anyone to show me a fire rule?" Marcus said, but Parker just shrugged. Marcus stared at the water and remembered the last time he had seen Ms. Lin, in her garden in October, turning a shovel of dirt that steamed faintly where she had burned leaves the day before. She had said the pile wasn't done, and he had not understood what she meant until later, when the fire truck came. Something about fire, he decided, kept being there after it stopped looking like it was there. That was a hidden thing, and hidden things bothered him more than buses did.

At camp, on the second night, the counselor let their cabin build a fire by the lake. Marcus watched everything: where the wood went, how the flame caught, how Denis blew on the coals with the confidence of a boy who had read one pamphlet. When it was time for bed, the counselor doused the fire, stirred it with a stick, and doused it again. It looked finished. Gray ash, no light, no smoke. The counselor turned away, and Marcus raised his hand like they were still in science class.

"Can I check it?" he asked. The counselor handed him the stick and told him the rule, but really it was Ms. Lin's note coming true: drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat, because if a campfire is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave. Marcus held the back of his hand above the ash, careful, like testing bathwater. It was warm. Not fire warm, but warm. So he poured the last bucket on, stirred the black soup of it, poured again, and waited. Denis tried to replicate his hand hover beside him and yelped anyway, even though the heat was gone, and the yelp was contagious; three boys jumped. Parker just grinned. Marcus touched the ash with one finger and found it cool as the lake.

"Okay," he said. "Now it's out."

Carter had written the same paragraph three times, and each version ended up in the trash. His essay was supposed to argue that the town should replace the cracked, porous concrete at the skate park before somebody got hurt, and he had a statistic for it. The number sat on his notepad: 62 percent of local skaters said they had crashed because of bad surfaces. He had found it somewhere online two nights ago, and now he could not remember where.

Zavier sat on the floor with the draft in his hands, reading it out loud in a newsy voice. "Sixty-two percent of local skaters," he announced, then lowered the page. "Says who?"

"What do you mean? It says right there."

"I mean, where did the number come from? Who counted the skaters? If I don't know that, I just have to trust you." Zavier tapped the sentence. "And I don't, because you ate my fries at lunch last week."

Carter searched his browser history, his downloads, even the pocket of his hoodie where he sometimes stuffed notes. Nothing. The page had vanished, or he had never saved it. He sat very still while the laptop loaded search after search, feeling the essay start to wobble like a loose truck on a skateboard. A number with no home behind it was just noise.

Then he tried a different approach. Instead of hunting for the vanished page, he looked for a group that would actually count skaters, and he found one: a regional parks association that had published a survey, with the exact figure, on its own site. He typed the organization's name into the sentence, and when Crystal came by later to give her critique, she read the line and nodded. "Okay, that's better. I could go look it up myself if I wanted to check."

At the kitchen table, Carter began the final draft. Ms. Fraser wanted them to advocate for something real, with an introduction that grabbed you and a conclusion that landed. He wrote the first sentence, then stopped and read the statistic line once more, the source sitting there beside the number like a hand pointing at a door.

Peyton set the model catapult on the counter at the back of Ms. Bouchard's science classroom and pulled the release lever. The ping-pong ball sailed over the sink, bounced off the window, and rolled under Carlos's chair. Carlos held up his stopwatch. "Four meters, sixty centimeters. That's your launch distance."

"That can't be right," Peyton said. Yesterday in her driveway the ball had barely cleared two meters, and her data table was due at the science fair on Friday. She thought about the moment in class last week when Ms. Bouchard had dropped a crumpled paper ball three times to show how each drop landed slightly differently; the paper was the same, but the landings were not. Peyton had a feeling the same thing was happening here, though she couldn't see any reason for it.

"Hand me the ball," she said, in her most assertive voice. "We're running it ten times." She tugged the folder of graph paper out of her backpack, where she kept everything for the project because the economy of using one folder instead of four meant she never lost her notes. On the top page she wrote a note to herself in block letters: "Dear Friday Peyton, do not trust one launch. Do ten. Then average. Love, Tuesday Peyton." She read it back, decided it counted as a message, and got to work.

Launch one went wild again, all the way to the radiator. Launch two barely reached the edge of the counter. Carlos called out each number while Asia recorded them, and Peyton reloaded the lever every time without changing anything. "These numbers are all over the place," Asia said. "Does that imply your catapult is broken?"

"No," Peyton said. "It implies any single one of them could be wrong. But if I average ten, the wild ones stop mattering so much." She added the column of numbers, divided by ten, and wrote the answer at the bottom: three meters, twelve centimeters. She looked at it, then at her catapult, which had seemed so unreliable a minute ago.

"Steady number," she said. "Now we have something we can actually put on the board."

Emile slid his equation across the table so Solomon could see it. y = 2x minus 4. He had solved it for x = 3, x = 0, and x = negative 2, and now three points sat on his coordinate grid like tiny buoys. Math club had a contest going: whoever plotted the most correct points before the timer went off won a pass to skip one homework problem. Merrick was already on his fifth point, and the timer showed four minutes.

"Check this one," Emile said, tapping the point for x = negative 2, which gave y = negative 8. "It goes left and down. But look, Merrick's point at negative 1 and 5 goes left and up. And Solomon's at 6 and negative 3 goes right and down." He paused, pencil hovering. Was there some order to where things landed? The two axes cut the grid apart like streets slicing a neighbourhood, and every point seemed to belong to one particular block.

Solomon leaned over the empty grid printed in the back of Mr. Wang's practice packet. "Mr. Wang calls those sections quadrants," he said. "He had us label them last year." Emile studied the packet's small diagram. Quadrant one sat in the top right, where x and y were both positive. Then it went counterclockwise: quadrant two at top left, quadrant three at bottom left, quadrant four at bottom right, numbered one to four all the way around.

So his point at negative 2 and negative 8, both negative, lived in quadrant three. Merrick's was in quadrant two. Emile tested a hypothetical point in his head, something like x = 5 and y = negative 10, and traced it: right for the positive x, down for the negative y. That had to be quadrant four. It was like a rule hiding underneath the grid the whole time, and now that he could see it, he couldn't stop seeing it.

The timer beeped. Mr. Wang walked the rows checking points, and when he reached Emile he counted seven correct, then paused at one near the bottom left. "Which quadrant is this in?" Emile looked at the point, negative 3 and negative 6, sitting in the bottom left section. "Three," he said. Mr. Wang nodded and moved on.

Merrick kicked Emile's chair on his way to hand in his sheet. "Ten points. The homework pass is mine." Emile let his eyes drift back to his own grid, where the seven points had begun to line up into a straight path, one that climbed steadily toward quadrant one. He traced the line with his pencil, wondering where it had been before it crossed into quadrant two, up past where his paper ended.

The community art studio smelled like pencil shavings and wet paint, and Elijah loved it more than almost anywhere else. He had signed up to participate in the Saturday drawing workshop because the flyer promised "cities, castles, and impossible rooms," and today was the last day before the youth show, where one drawing from each student would hang on the studio's front wall for a whole month.

"Twenty minutes," Mr. Hughes called out, walking between the easels. "The frames for the show get hung at noon, sharp."

Elijah stared at his paper in despair. He had drawn a fantastic castle corridor with tall pillars and banners, the kind a dragon might guard, but every pillar leaned the wrong way, as if the whole hallway were melting. He had used one vanishing point at the center, the way he always did, and it worked fine when he drew a road running straight at you. It was ruining everything here.

Hafsa leaned over from the next easel, her own paper showing a cozy living room with a fireplace. "Your castle looks kind of venomous," she said. "Like it's going to bite somebody."

"It's not supposed to be venomous. It's supposed to be grand." Elijah pushed the drawing back and wandered to the window, where Katelyn was sketching the corner of the actual studio room, the corner where the brick wall met the plaster wall. Her lines ran off in two different directions, left and right, toward two little dots on the far edges of her paper.

"Why two dots?" he asked.

Katelyn shrugged. "Because I'm looking at the corner. Each wall goes back its own way, so each one runs toward its own dot."

Elijah felt something click, the way a jar lid does when it finally loosens. He was facing the corner of his castle corridor, not staring straight down it. The left wall needed one vanishing point and the right wall needed a different one. He hurried back to his easel, but his paper was smudged and crowded, and there was no time to erase everything.

"Fresh sheet," Mr. Hughes said gently, setting one down. "Ten minutes. The frames are an expense the studio only covers once a year, so we hang them on schedule."

Elijah placed two dots, one near each edge of the paper, and drew the corner pillar first, tall and proud. Then he let every pillar on the left wall lean toward the left dot and every pillar on the right wall lean toward the right dot. The corridor opened up in front of him like a mouth about to sing.

"Time," Mr. Hughes announced. "Bring your drawings to the front."

Elijah carried his castle forward, still warm from his hand. Hafsa looked at it and grinned.

"Still a little venomous," she said, "but in a good way."

Ethan had exactly one hour before his grandmother's bees needed checking, and somehow Elise and Cory had turned her kitchen table into a battlefield. "He deleted the whole database," Elise said, jabbing a finger at Cory. "Three weeks of bee counts. Gone."

"I did not delete it," Cory shot back. "I was sorting it." They talked over each other, louder and louder, while Ethan's grandmother slid a plate of biscuits toward him and disappeared into the garden with a grin, like she knew something he didn't.

Ethan's plan had been simple: figure out who was right, shake the loser's hand, done. But they kept interrupting each other, and every interruption started a new argument about the interruption itself. He watched them go around twice more, and a thought landed like a dropped biscuit. The interruptions were the problem, not the accident. What if nobody got to talk over anybody? He held up both hands. "New rule. One at a time, no cutting in. Elise first, all the way to the end. Then Cory, all the way to the end. That's it."

"That's how mediation works?" Cory asked.

"That's how this one works," Ethan said, feeling oddly official.

Elise told her side without a single interruption, and halfway through, Cory's mouth opened and then closed again, because Ethan pointed at the chair like a traffic cop. When Cory finally got his turn, the story came out whole: he had clicked "sort" while the file was saving, and the records hadn't vanished, they had scattered into the wrong folders. He hadn't deleted anything. He had hidden it. Ten minutes of searching got every number back, and Elise actually laughed.

Out in the garden, the bees were droning over the squash blossoms, busy pollinating the last flowers of summer, and Ethan lifted a frame of comb toward the light. The new hive looked small and fragile, he thought, kind of vulnerable without its big sister colony beside it. He'd have to tell his grandmother they should double-wrap it before October.

"Same time next week?" Cory called from the porch. "Elise says she'll bring her notebook, and we promise to fight quietly."

"Bring cookies too," Ethan said. "Mediators need fuel."

Lillian leaned against the picnic table outside the camp infirmary, reading the letter her mother had tucked into her duffel bag. "Your body is changing this year," her mom wrote, "and that means sweat glands that work harder, oilier hair, and a daily shower even when you're tired. Use the deodorant I packed. It's the purple stick, next to your toothbrush." Lillian sniffed her left armpit, then her right, and decided her mother had a point. She had skipped the shower after the morning hike, and her cabin, Cedar Cabin, smelled like wet socks.

After lunch, Mr. Kaya called the campers to the amphitheater for presentations. Each camper had to recount a nature observation from the week, and Lillian had written hers about the beaver dam by the north creek. She went third, and halfway through her description of the dam's climax, the moment the water finally rose over the top, a boy from Juniper Cabin stood up to present and his voice cracked so hard on his second sentence that a girl in the back row giggled.

He pushed on, but his voice dropped low, jumped high, and broke again on the word "osprey." He sat down red-faced, and Lillian heard two boys behind her whisper that he was faking it for laughs. She thought about her mom's letter. Bodies changing. She had noticed her own arms smelling different this summer, and Nathalie had shot up two inches and needed new sneakers in July. Maybe the boy's voice was changing too, and it wasn't something he could control.

At free swim, Lillian found Isabella, who had a worn and durable paperback about growing up that her older sister had given her. "Can I borrow it?" Lillian asked. "Trade you my second popsicle." Isabella handed it over, and Lillian sat on the dock with her feet in the water, the pages warm from the sun, smelling faintly of sunscreen. In the chapter on voices she found the answer: during puberty the larynx, or voice box, grows larger and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys.

The next morning the boy from Juniper Cabin was called up again to finish his presentation. He stood stiff, braced for laughter. Before he started, Lillian raised her hand. "His larynx is growing," she said. "It's his voice box. The vocal cords get longer and thicker, and that makes the voice deeper." Mr. Kaya nodded and told the giggling girl in the back row to listen closely, because in a few years everyone's body would surprise them somehow.

The boy's voice still cracked on "osprey," but nobody laughed, and he grinned at Lillian on his way back to his seat. That night she lined up first for the shower, purple deodorant stick in hand.

The bus to the regional bee took forty minutes, and Mr. Silva had brought a box of index cards to fill every one of them. "Practice round," he said, standing at the front while the driver pulled out of the school lot. "Autumn and Wren, you're our two regional spellers. Spell against each other. Loser buys the winner a pretzel at the venue."

Autumn slid into a seat near the middle, and Elisha sat down beside her. Autumn had spent three weeks hoping Wren would catch the flu, or trip over a dictionary, or spell one word wrong. Second place meant you watched someone else hold the trophy. She had decided it would be unbearable.

Wren took the seat across the aisle. "Ready?" he asked.

"Not really," Autumn said, which was true.

Mr. Silva held up the first card. "Sustain. Autumn."

"S-U-S-T-A-I-N. Sustain."

"Correct. Wren, brittle."

"B-R-I-T-T-L-E. Brittle."

"Correct."

They went through twelve words that way, then twenty. Every card, both of them, no mistakes. Elisha kept score on the back of her notebook and after a while stopped writing anything at all, because there was nothing to write. The bus hummed, the cards kept coming, and nobody got a word wrong.

Elisha leaned over the notebook. "You know what happened at the real Nationals? The 2019 Scripps bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. Eight winners. They just ran out of words before anyone missed."

"Eight?" Autumn said.

"Eight. Sharing the title."

Autumn looked at the stack of cards in Mr. Silva's hand. She had been thinking about the bee all wrong, like it was a wall with room for only one person on top. But if eight spellers could each get every word right, then the wall had more room than she had imagined. If she and Wren both spelled perfectly, neither of them had to lose. She turned to the aisle.

"Wren," she said, "what if we both just keep going until the cards run out?"

"Then we both get pretzels," Wren said, "and we each buy our own."

"That works too."

Mr. Silva shuffled the deck once more. "Privilege," he said. "Autumn."

"P-R-I-V-I-L-E-G-E. Privilege."

"Correct. Wren, crescendo."

Marcus had been squinting at the whiteboard from the back row for two weeks, and he had a theory about it. His eyes worked fine up close. He could read the tiny text on his dad's phone, count crumbs on the counter, see every detail on a trading card held six inches from his nose. It was only far things that went blurry, like the board, or the street sign at the end of the block. That seemed like a clue, and he wanted to test it before his eye appointment on Saturday.

"So you're saying near stuff is easy and far stuff is fuzzy," said Ali, who had come over to build the pond diorama for their science project. She was painting a lily pad while he talked. "That's the opposite of my grandpa. He holds the menu at arm's length."

"My theory," Marcus said, "is that my eyeballs are the wrong shape. Like, too long, front to back. So the light from far away lands in the wrong place, in front of the back of my eye instead of right on it." He drew a quick sketch in his notebook: a circle with an arrow stopping short of the back wall. "The picture forms too early. That's why it's fuzzy."

"Is that plausible?" Ali asked, squinting at the drawing. "Can an eyeball be too long?"

"That's what I'm going to find out. Want to help me test it?" He taped a page of small print to the fence at the bottom of the yard, then stood at the porch steps and tried to read it. He could make out the headline but not the rest. When he walked halfway down, the words sharpened. He wrote the results on a clipboard, feeling like a real scientist studying the ecosystem of his own backyard, which was a funny thought because normally the ecosystem project was the exciting one.

On Saturday, the optometrist flipped lenses in front of Marcus's face and asked which was better, one or two. Marcus confided his theory right there in the chair, the eyeball being too long, the light stopping in front of where it should land. The optometrist smiled. "Nearsighted," he said. "That's the word for it. You figured out most of it yourself."

When the glasses arrived a week later, Marcus put them on in the kitchen and ran straight to the back door. The fence at the bottom of the yard had letters on it, actual readable letters. He could see the small print from the porch. He could see everything.

"Ali!" he shouted into the phone. "I can read the fence!"

Daniel had exactly twelve minutes to make his bulb light up, and so far the bulb was winning.

"It's not fair," said Jase, peering over the cluttered lab table. "Harlee's bulb glowed on the first try. Hers is obviously immune to failure."

"Nothing is immune to failure," Daniel said, wiggling the wire again. "My proof is this bulb." The battery sat there like a smug gray brick. The switch was flipped, the wires were clipped, and the bulb stayed dark. Mr. Tse had said the demo teams would be picked at two o'clock sharp, and the clock above the whiteboard read 1:48. If Daniel's circuit didn't work, he'd be the only kid in class presenting a table full of dead parts.

He stared at the loop. Battery, wire, switch, bulb, wire, back to battery. It looked exactly like the diagram on the board. "Maybe the battery's dead," he said, and swapped it for a fresh one from the supply drawer. Nothing. "Maybe the bulb's loose." He screwed it tighter. Still nothing.

Then Harlee wandered over, holding her glowing circuit like a trophy. "Try her bulb in yours," Jase suggested. Daniel unplugged his bulb and clipped Harlee's into his loop instead. It lit instantly. "So it's the bulb," Daniel said, feeling both relieved and annoyed. He grabbed a new bulb from the drawer, clipped it in, and the loop glowed warm and yellow. He flipped the switch off and on twice, just to enjoy the power.

"Okay, but why does it work at all?" Harlee asked, tapping his battery. "The electricity's invisible. How do you know it goes around?"

"Because it's a loop," Daniel said. "It has to travel all the way around, through everything, and back. If the loop gets broken anywhere, nothing flows at all." He pulled the dead bulb out of his pocket and held it up. "Watch." He clipped the old dead bulb back into the circuit alongside the good one, so the current had to pass through both. Both bulbs went dark. Even the good one. "See? One dead bulb kills the whole string, because the loop is broken."

"That's kind of dramatic," said Jase.

"That's science," said Daniel, removing the dead bulb. The good one lit again instantly, and he grinned like he'd invented fire.

Mr. Tse checked the clock and clapped his hands. "Two o'clock. Demo teams, to your stations."

Daniel flipped his switch one last time. "Go on, little loop," he whispered. "Make the trip."

Lucy pushed through the door of the science room with her backpack still on one shoulder, and she knew immediately that something was wrong. Delia and Kohen were standing on opposite sides of the workbench, arms crossed, and the invention they were supposed to finish by Friday sat between them like a dropped cake.

"It's a grabber arm," Delia insisted. "I saw Mr. Bélanger's sketch. It has claws and a hinge, and it picks things up."

"It's obviously a launcher," Kohen said. "I was here Tuesday when he tested the base. It flings stuff. I watched a wooden ball hit the ceiling tile."

Lucy tilted her head. Both of them sounded certain, and both of them sounded right, which was strange. How could one machine be two things? She leaned over the workbench and studied the half-built contraption, noticing that the claw end and the spring-loaded base didn't actually touch each other yet. Nobody in the club had seen the whole thing at once, she realized. Delia had come Thursday, Kohen Tuesday, and Lucy herself had only read the supply list. They were each describing a different part.

"It's like that story my grandma tells," Delia said, her arms slowly uncrossing. "The blind men and the elephant. It's a parable from ancient India.
