Izabella pulled her chair over so Lambert didn't sit alone. Marcus had planned a whole sophisticated argument to present on Monday, with diagrams, but listening to Lambert he thought a shorter one might do. He used the back of his notebook instead, where he kept his sketches, and drew the flight path of the airplane in careful pencil. Then he wrote his plan with an economy of words, just four lines. "We're all witnesses," he told them. "The trick is, we're all honest, too." Izabella grinned and stole his pencil to add a fifth line. "Then let's go tell Mr. Qureshi," she said.

Gabriel stood at the kitchen counter on a sticky June morning, staring at three enormous jugs of strawberry lemonade that had not sold the day before. His stand had been perfect, or so he'd thought. He'd built the sign himself, made the letters perfectly perpendicular to the sign's edges so they'd look professional, and set the price at four dollars a cup because the strawberries had been expensive at the farmer's market. Harper had helped him squeeze lemons for two hours. Now the jugs sat in the fridge, and every cup he hadn't sold was money he'd spent and would never get back.

"Maybe we should just charge less," Harper said, arriving with more lemons in a plastic bag. "Dennis bought one cup yesterday and said nobody at the pool would pay four dollars when the gas station sells lemonade for a dollar."

Gabriel frowned. He remembered his mother buying strawberries in February, when the little plastic box had cost almost seven dollars, and the same box in June costing three. He'd asked her why once, and she'd shrugged and said something about how many strawberries exist in each season. He hadn't understood it then. Now he scrutinized the jugs, the price sign, the empty street outside, and something clicked.

"In winter, everybody wants strawberries and there aren't many, so the price goes up," he said slowly. "In summer, there are tons, so it goes down. And if you charge more than people will actually pay..." He pointed at the fridge. "You end up with that. Jugs and jugs nobody wants."

"Surplus," Harper said, grinning. "That's the word Mr. Desir used when he was grumbling about the book fair last year."

They rewrote the sign together, this time with the new price, one dollar fifty, crooked but readable. By four o'clock the jugs were empty, and Gabriel counted the money twice, feeling the weight of the coins in his palm. He still wasn't sure whether the February strawberries and his lemonade were really the same thing, or whether he'd just gotten lucky with the weather. Harper was already talking about next weekend and watermelons.

"One dollar a cup," Gabriel said, and flipped the sign face down against the table.

Jade stood outside room 412 for a long time before she pushed the door open. Her grandmother had died two hours before dawn, and the machines were gone now, which somehow made the room feel louder instead of quieter. A nurse had mentioned that the backup generator would kick in if the storm outside cut the power, and Jade caught herself wondering about that, how a machine nobody ever saw could be waiting the whole time, ready. Maybe grief worked the same way, humming underneath everything, invisible until it wasn't.

Her father was on the phone with the rabbi, writing fast. Jade leaned over his notepad and saw the word shiva circled twice. Seven, he said when he hung up. It came from the Hebrew word for seven, and it meant seven days of mourning after the burial, seven days when visitors would come to the house to comfort them. "Starting tonight," he added, "right after we bury her. The burial has to happen before the storm gets worse."

That was the deadline, and it left Jade with a problem she couldn't stop chewing on. Ameera and Rylen had texted six times already, asking what to say, and Jade didn't know. What words covered a hole that size? She tried drafting something in her head, crossed it all out, and finally decided to run a test. She would tell them the truth: come anyway, say nothing if nothing came.

They arrived that evening with torn, rain-spotted notes they never unfolded. Rylen stood stiffly by the snack table. Ameera sat on the floor next to Jade and just stayed there, and Jade discovered something her scribbled speeches never could have demonstrated: the silence with a friend inside it was different from plain silence.

The twist came at the door. Grandma's oldest friend arrived, took one look at the crowded living room, and said, "Everyone here is being so careful with me, so impartial, like I might break." She laughed a wet laugh. "You children, you got it right without trying."

Jade looked at Ameera, still on the floor, still not saying anything, and patted the space beside her.

Raphael was sitting at the family computer with his poem assignment open on the screen when the message from Arielle popped up. She had sent a photo of her new rabbit, a gray ball of fluff sitting in a cardboard box, and underneath it she wrote that her poem was going to be about him for Mr. Henry's class. Raphael zoomed in on the rabbit, then, out of curiosity, right-clicked the image and chose "Get Info." He had learned that trick last week when he wanted to see how big a file was. A panel slid open with dates and camera settings, and at the bottom, a small map appeared with a pin on it. The pin sat on Maple Court, three streets over from school, exactly where Arielle lived. Next to the map were numbers, a latitude and longitude, pointing straight at her house. He sat back. He had never told Arielle where she lived, and she had never told him either, yet here was her street, written into the picture itself.

He remembered the word from a video he had watched about phones: hidden data written into a photo file. He thought the video had called it EXIF metadata, but he wanted to be sure it worked the way he thought. He took a photo of his own desk with his tablet, sent it to himself, and opened it on the computer. He right-clicked, chose "Get Info," and scrolled to the bottom. There was the map again, and this time the pin pointed at his own house, at the end of his own street, four houses from the corner. So that was it. When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into the hidden data in the file, and anyone who opens the details can see them.

Raphael looked at his poem, which was one stanza long and needed two more, but he typed a message to Arielle first. "Check the details of the rabbit photo," he wrote. "Right-click, then Get Info. Scroll down." While he waited, he turned off location services on his tablet, thinking it would also help conserve the battery. His answer arrived in pieces: "WHAT," then "that's my house," then "how." He wrote back that the hidden data in a photo file is called EXIF metadata, and that hers had her street written right into it. A minute later she sent a thumbs-up and said she had just turned her location off, and that she was only ever sending him rabbit pictures from now on anyway.

He went back to the poem, wrote a second stanza about the rabbit's ears, and decided the third one would be about the cardboard box, because a box was a better home than it looked. Before he closed his messages, Arielle sent one more line: "Shiloh posts ten pictures a day. Should we tell him?" Raphael looked at the photo of the gray rabbit still open on his screen, the map pin gone now that Arielle had fixed it, and started typing.

Sydney sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with her mother's old laptop, chewing the end of her pencil. Tomorrow morning her class was holding a debate, and Ms. Tesfaye had assigned her the opening statement. The question on the board had been: is it fair for an advertisement to disguise itself as a regular search result? Sydney had exactly one evening to build a case.

She typed "are ads fair" into the search bar and got back a mush of opinions, a quiz site, and something about fair trade chocolate. Annabella had told her after school that the trick was specific keywords, so Sydney tried again: "search engine paid results rules." That was better. She tried "paid results versus natural results" and got a page that looked promising.

Then she noticed something odd. The first link on the page had a tiny grey box beside it that said "Ad." The ones below it did not. Sydney had never really looked at that box before. She scrolled down, found another one, and counted three little boxes on the whole page. They were the same size as the other links, the same shade of blue. Only the small grey label made them different. She copied one of the ad links and one of the plain links into a document so she could show the class tomorrow.

Naila rang the doorbell at seven, holding a bag of pretzels and her own tablet. "I found something," Naila said, dropping onto the couch. "In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results have to be clearly distinguishable from natural results." She turned the tablet around. "Or they risk deceiving users. That's a quote."

Sydney felt the tight spot behind her ribs loosen. That was the rule, the whole reason the little grey boxes existed. "So the ads aren't supposed to hide," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "If you can't tell them apart, that counts as deceiving people." She looked back at her screen, at the three ads sitting quietly at the top of the results. Then she tried a small experiment. She typed the name of a popular game and searched it. The first four links all carried the grey "Ad" box, and beneath them came an ordinary fan site with none. The pattern held.

"Can I confide something?" Naila said, lowering her voice even though only the two of them were in the room. "I was hesitant to sign up for the debate team. I thought I'd freeze up in front of everyone." She pushed the pretzel bag toward Sydney. "But this is actually kind of fun."

Sydney took a handful and kept typing. She added a line about the Federal Trade Commission, then a line about her own grey-box count. By eight thirty she had a full page, and on it she had written her closing image: every result wearing its own honest little label, like name plates on the doors of a residence where you could always tell who actually lived there.

She read the last sentence out loud, then hit print and listened to the pages slide out into the tray.

The pot had just started to rumble when Gavin set his notebook on the counter and wrote "bubbles = chemical change" in capital letters. He was so sure of it that he'd told Annie at school, and Annie had laughed at him for a whole lunch period. Now he had a plan. If bubbles meant a chemical change, then boiling water was producing something new, and he was going to catch it.

Mr. Qureshi from next door had lent him the thermometer from his garage. "You'll want to calibrate it first," he'd said, handing it over, "in a glass of ice water. Then you'll know it reads true." Gavin had done exactly that, tapping the dial until the needle settled where ice water should put it. The nectar jar on the windowsill, left over from his mother's tea, held his pencils, and beside it sat a cold metal spoon, a nail gone brown and flaky, and a burnt match. Evidence, he called them. His exhibit.

He remembered the match from last summer, when he'd held it too long over the camp stove and the wood had gone black and would never be wood again. That was chemical. He remembered the nail on the porch railing, rusting year after year, turning into something that crumbled when you poked it. Chemical too. Both of those his teacher had called influential examples, the ones everyone copied into their notes. So bubbles, he figured, belonged on the same list.

He held the cold spoon above the pot just as the water began to boil. Bubbles climbed and burst and the water thrashed, and Gavin held his breath and counted. One, two, three. When he pulled the spoon out, the underside was dripping wet, nothing else. No rust, no ash, no new anything. Just water. The bubbles hadn't made a new substance at all. He stared at the spoon, then at the pot, then at the sloppy capital letters in his notebook.

"That's it," he said out loud. He crossed out the old line and wrote slowly, saying the words as the pen moved. "The bubbles are water vapour. Same stuff as the water, just a gas." He looked up at the steam curling toward the ceiling. "Boiling is physical. Annie is going to lose her mind." He grabbed his phone and started typing.

Tyler ran up the walkway carrying the plate of spring rolls his mom had wrapped in foil, because tonight was the sixth-grade potluck at Mr. Saleh's house and he had been counting the hours since lunch. The garden was lush after all the rain that week, green spilling over the edges of the flowerbeds, and he could smell something garlicky and wonderful from the porch.

At the door, Adalynn's grandmother met him with both hands pressed together and a small bow. Tyler copied her without being sure he'd done it right. Then Adalynn's whole family appeared, and instead of a wave they each nodded to him, one after another, like a line of dominoes. Inside, Mr. Saleh was greeting Jackson's family with a handshake and his hand over his heart. Same doorway, different greetings. Tyler filed that away like a trading card.

He also noticed the shoe pile by the door and the tray of oranges wrapped in red paper that Jackson's dad handed to Adalynn's grandmother. Nobody opened the gift. She just held it against her chest and thanked him twice. Interesting, Tyler thought. At his house, presents got ripped open on the spot, sometimes before the giver even sat down.

The table was incredible: noodles, dumplings, rice cookers steaming like dragons, and a big bowl of soup. Tyler piled his plate and wedged himself between Jackson and Adalynn. When Jackson leaned over to grab the soy sauce, Tyler stuck his chopsticks straight down into his mound of rice so he'd have a free hand, and grabbed the last pork bun at the exact moment Jackson reached for it.

"Hey!" Jackson said. "Are you going to accuse me of stealing, or can I accuse you? Because that bun is mine."

"Finders keepers." Tyler grinned and lifted the bun high, chopsticks standing straight up in his rice like little towers.

Adalynn went quiet. She reached over and laid his chopsticks flat across the rim of his bowl, quick and gentle, the way you'd straighten a crooked picture frame.

"We don't leave them standing up in the rice," she said. "It looks like incense offered to the dead."

Tyler looked at the two pale sticks standing in the white rice and felt his ears go hot. "Oh. Sorry. I didn't know."

"It's okay. My cousin did it at a restaurant once and my aunt nearly dove across the table." Adalynn split the pork bun in half and pushed one half onto his plate. "Trade you. Half a bun for that spring roll your mom made, because I've been staring at them all night."

"Deal." Tyler handed it over, then noticed Mr. Saleh at the head of the table raising his glass.

"Before anyone eats another bite," Mr. Saleh announced, "I should tell you I signed us all up for the spring fair agriculture exhibit, and our class is growing the lettuce."

Jackson groaned. Adalynn cheered. Tyler raised his glass of lemonade so fast it sloshed.

"To lettuce," he said.

Paige sat at the kitchen table with a poster board, a glue stick, and a box of strawberry stickers she had bought for exactly one purpose: to make Ms. Aziz's assignment the best one in the class. The assignment was to explain something about prices, and Paige had picked strawberries. The trouble was, she did not entirely understand her own topic yet.

She flipped through her notebook to the page from last January, when her mother had sent her to the corner store for berries and the cashier had asked for almost seven dollars. Paige remembered standing there, clutching the little plastic box, deciding whether strawberries were worth that much in the middle of winter. She had bought them anyway, because her mother had an audition that night and always wanted strawberries before she sang. That flashback gave Paige an idea, and she grabbed her jacket.

Kian lived two floors down. He was in her class, and his family bought fruit from the Saturday market every single week. "Kian," Paige said when he opened the door, "how much were strawberries at the market last Saturday?" He squinted. "Like four dollars. Same as always in June." Paige wrote it down. "And how many stands were selling them?" Kian held up three fingers, then paused. "Wait. It was six. Three new stands opened just this week." He had complained about it, actually, because the crowd near the berry tables had blocked his shortcut to the honey stall.

Paige stared at her notebook until the numbers seemed to move on their own. High price in winter, almost no stands. Lower price in June, and six stands. She had been thinking that expensive berries meant sellers would stay away, but Kian's three new stands told a different story, and she changed her mind right there at his door. When the price rises, sellers offer more, because selling becomes more profitable. She said it out loud to test it. "That's the law of supply," Kian said, nodding, because Ms. Aziz had written those words on the board on Monday and Paige had copied them without understanding them until now.

Back upstairs, Paige built her poster. On one side she drew a snow-covered market with one lonely stand and a seven-dollar sign. On the other side she drew six sunny stands with baskets stacked high. Ms. Aziz would interpret the pictures as winter and summer, Paige decided, as long as she labelled them clearly, and she carefully printed the prices beside each drawing. Her little brother wandered over and pointed at the winter side. "Why only one stand?" he asked. Paige pulled him onto her lap. "Because that's when berries are scarce," she said. "Come on, you can help me stick these on. The strawberries, not your dinosaur stickers. Those guys are extinct, remember?"

He laughed and reached for the glue stick anyway, and together they pressed a whole row of red stickers across the top of the poster, one for every dollar a summer shopper would save.

Stella had saved eleven dollars for weeks, all for the snow globe at the big garage sale on Maple Street. Last year an identical one had sold for three dollars, and she had regretted not buying it ever since. She arrived at eight sharp, before the tables were even fully set up, and there it was, on the end of the driveway beside a crate of records.

The price tag read eight dollars. Stella frowned. She turned the tag over, hoping for a mistake, but the handwriting was clear.

"That's weird," said Gurnoor, who had come with her. "It was three last year."

"Maybe nobody wanted it then," Stella said slowly. She looked around. The driveway was already crowded, and people kept stopping at that end of the table, picking up snow globes, setting them down, drifting back. A woman held one up to the light and watched the glitter swirl and refract inside the glass, then put it back with a disappointed sigh.

There were four snow globes this year. Last year, Stella remembered, there had been at least fifteen, heaped in a basket nobody touched. She felt hesitant, but she asked the man running the sale anyway.

"Why are these eight dollars? They were three last summer."

"Fewer of them this time," he said. "People were fighting over them, so we put the price up."

Stella's heart sank, and then she noticed something. The four globes sat untouched for a long while. One woman walked away shaking her head. Two kids picked theirs up, saw the tag, and put them back without a word.

"Gurnoor," she whispered, "watch. Nobody's buying at eight."

At noon the man crossed out the tag and wrote five. A girl grabbed one instantly. He crossed it out again and wrote three, and the last three sold in about a minute, including the one Stella snatched. She held it tight on the walk home, shaking it so the flakes swirled.

"Ms. Horváth told my brother there's a name for that," Gurnoor said. "The law of demand."

"Then it works," Stella said, and she shook the globe again.

Addison spread her poster board across the kitchen table and frowned at it. Sun, grass, rabbit, fox. Four boxes, and she had to connect them with arrows before science class tomorrow. Mr. Reddy had said whoever explained the chain best would present it to the class, and Addison wanted that job the way some kids wanted the last slice of pizza.

She drew the sun first, a big yellow circle in the corner. Then she wrote GRASS, RABBIT, and FOX in neat boxes going up the page. She grabbed a marker and started drawing arrows from the fox down toward the rabbit, from the rabbit down toward the grass, because that was the way the animals were looking. Her hand hovered. Something felt off, but she could not say what, so she finished the arrows and went to bed.

The next morning Keagan came by so they could walk to school together. He leaned over the poster where it sat on the porch step. "Wait," he said. "Your fox is eating the rabbit, right? Because from here it looks like the grass is eating the rabbit."

Addison snatched the poster up. "It does not." But she looked again, and Keagan was right. With the arrows pointing the way she had drawn them, the energy looked like it flowed downhill, from the fox back to the sun. She flipped through her notebook, hunting for her notes from Mr. Reddy's lecture, until she found the line she had copied off the board: the arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy flows.

"So the arrow goes from the grass to the rabbit," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud, "because the grass gets eaten." She erased every arrow and redrew them, sun to grass, grass to rabbit, rabbit to fox, going up the chain. Keagan held the eraser and handed her the marker like a surgeon's assistant. "Now it says energy flows up," he said. "Like a ladder."

At school, Mr. Reddy walked the rows checking posters. He stopped at Hillary's desk first, and Addison heard him say Hillary's arrows needed flipping too. Then he reached Addison's table and nodded. "This one works. Can you explain it?"

She stood up in front of the class with the poster and told them what she had figured out, and even cited Mr. Reddy's own lecture as her source, which made him laugh. Then he asked the hard question. "What if the rabbits all disappeared?" Addison traced the chain with her finger, sun to grass to the empty spot to fox. The grass would grow wild, she said, and the fox would go hungry or leave.

After class Mr. Reddy tapped her poster. "You'll be our ambassador at the science fair," he said. "Contemporary ecologists draw their food webs exactly like this." Addison grinned, rolled up the poster, and slid it into her backpack like a sword going into its sheath.

Gabriel stood between Wyatt and Ava in the Hendersons' backyard, where the smell of grill smoke drifted over a table of cupcakes and someone's dog was stealing a napkin off the ground. Ava's arms were crossed so tightly she looked like a knot. Wyatt wouldn't even look at her, which Gabriel had learned, after six years of friendship with both of them, was worse than yelling. He wanted to fix it before the piñata, because once the piñata broke there would be candy everywhere and nobody would listen to anybody.

"He promised to save me the corner piece of cake," Ava said, "the one with the most frosting, and then he ate it at lunch."

"It was in the fridge with my name on it," Wyatt said. "I thought it was mine."

Gabriel's first instinct was to pick a side, but he had watched Mr. Ndlovu, the neighbor everyone said was the most influential coach in the whole rec league, settle a shouting match between two players last month without blaming anyone. Mr. Ndlovu hadn't just said "shake hands and be friends." He had made each player say exactly what he would do next time. Gabriel had a theory: maybe fights ended only when both people promised something specific, so each one knew precisely what he had promised. He decided to test it.

"You two want to just be friends again?" Gabriel asked.

"Fine," Wyatt muttered, and Ava gave a shrug that did its best to conceal how much she still cared about that frosting. They drifted apart anyway, and within ten minutes Ava was telling a fourth grader the whole story of the stolen cake, with sound effects.

Gabriel hurried back. "That didn't work," he admitted. "New plan. Ava, what will you actually do next time there's cake?"

"Write 'AVA' on the box. In marker. Big letters."

"Wyatt?"

"I'll ask before I eat anything that looks too good to be mine."

They stared at each other. "Deal," Ava said, and stuck out her hand.

Just then Mr. Henderson called out, "Piñata time!" and the dog raced past with the entire napkin holder in its jaws. Wyatt laughed so hard he snorted punch out of his nose, and Ava handed him a stack of napkins like an ambassador delivering a peace treaty. Gabriel picked up the bat and said, "I get first swing, since I'm the one who fixed you two."

Jace sat in the hallway outside the auditorium with his monologue pages flat on his knees. The tournament program said Dramatic Interpretation, Round Two, 1:15 p.m., and the clock on the wall said 12:50. He had run the speech twenty times that morning, and every time it came out the same way, smooth and empty, like a robot reading a grocery list.

"You sounded like a text-to-speech app," said Emy, dropping onto the bench beside him. She popped a mint into her mouth and offered him one. "I'm not being mean. I'm being your friend."

"I know," Jace said. The mint tasted like cold pennies. He stared at the page. The monologue was about a boy whose best friend had moved away without saying goodbye, and Jace could not figure out why his voice refused to care. He could articulate every word perfectly. Nobody had ever told him to slow down or speak up. The words were just dead on the page, like a photo of an extinct animal, accurate and completely without breath.

Mathieu came back from the auditorium shaking his head. "The judge in there gave the girl before me a look like he was watching paint dry, and then a kid went up and did a monologue about a broken radio, and the judge leaned forward the whole time. I nearly clapped." He flopped against the wall. "What did the radio kid have that you don't?"

Jace watched a custodian sweep the far end of the hall, back and forth, back and forth. He thought about the radio kid, about the leaning-forward judge. The good performance had not been louder or slower. Something invisible was underneath it. He flipped his page over and looked at the blank side. Maybe the words were only the top layer, and the bottom layer, the foundation, was missing. But missing how?

Ms. Berg, the coach from his school who had driven them here, was reviewing notes down the corridor. Emy jogged over and asked her something, and when she came back she was grinning. "She told me the trick her college acting teacher used. You ask what the character wants in the scene. It's called the objective. Then you play every single line trying to get it."

Jace looked at his page again. What did the boy in the monologue want? He read it once more, hunting. Not just to be sad. The boy kept mentioning the empty porch, the unfilled seat, the letter he never sent. He wanted his friend to answer him. He wanted to be answered so badly he was talking to nobody, in public, hoping the wind would carry it. That was it. That was the want.

At 1:12 the doors opened and a volunteer called his name. Jace walked to the mark on the stage, set his pages down, and did not start right away. He let a silence sit there, heavy as a held breath. Then, instead of reciting the first line, he asked it, out toward the empty back row, as if someone might be back there after all. The judge, a tired man with reading glasses, looked up from his ballot and stopped writing. Jace pressed on, line after line, asking harder each time, his hands opening and closing like he was trying to catch something that kept slipping. When he finished, the last word hung in the air a second longer than he expected, and somewhere in the third row, Mathieu whispered, "There he is."

The letter from the city lay open on Grandma's kitchen table, and Emma read it twice before she dared say anything out loud. The community garden behind the library would be paved over for a parking lot unless someone convinced a councillor to change the bylaw before the vote on Friday. Grandma grew her tomatoes there, and so did half the seniors on her street. "Grandma," Emma said slowly, "who's our councillor?" Grandma peered at the letter. "It doesn't say. It just says contact your local representative." That was the problem, and it itched at Emma all afternoon.

She remembered the spring, when the beehives at school had died off and no one knew why. Finlay had insisted it was vandals, but Emma had tracked the blooming bushes along the fence and realized the bees had simply lost their source of nectar when the groundskeeper cut everything down. Things fail for hidden reasons, she had learned, and you have to look for the cause underneath. Maybe politics worked the same way. If every councillor governed a different slice of the city, then emailing the wrong one would be like writing to a beekeeper about a bush two towns over.

She found the city website on Grandma's old laptop and clicked through maps, but the lines wiggled everywhere and the names meant nothing to her. Sophia texted back "just email the mayor" when Emma asked, which felt too easy. Emma sat very still, staring at the address bar, and then it struck her: she could type Grandma's street address into the ward finder. The cursor blinked. She pressed enter, and the screen hung there, white and blank, for what felt like a full minute.

Then the map bloomed with colour. A shape wrapped around Grandma's neighbourhood, labeled Ward 4. Emma turned to Grandma, hardly believing it. "This is a ward," she said. "In lots of cities, each councillor is elected to represent one area, and that area is called a ward." Grandma leaned in, squinting. "So there's one councillor just for us?" Emma nodded and copied the name and the email address onto a pad of paper.

They drafted the message together at the kitchen table. Emma wrote that the garden was fundamental to the street, that seniors depended on it, and that the bylaw should be changed to protect it. She kept it short and polite, the way Mr. Shapiro had taught them for persuasive writing back in September. Then she read it aloud, one last time, her finger under each line. Grandma reached over her shoulder and clicked Send.

Theo had counted the plates twice, and the math refused to work. Nine adults, nine plates, but only seven scoops of rice, and Grandmother's plate held nothing but fruit and a bowl of sabudana, which was not rice no matter how much it pretended to be. Everyone had gathered at his aunt's house for lunch, and the smell of cumin and warm dal drifted out of the kitchen so strongly that his stomach growled like a small dog.

"Grandmother, you forgot the rice," he said, sliding the pot toward her.

"I forgot nothing," she said, and popped a slice of banana into her mouth as if that settled it.

It did not settle it. Theo had noticed this before, at dinners weeks apart, and he began to wonder whether something invisible was going on, some hidden rule deciding which days Grandmother skipped rice and which days she didn't. He had a theory, but theories needed testing. On the drive home he borrowed his mother's phone, found a lunar calendar, and started hunting. The last time Grandmother had refused rice was eleven days after the new moon. The time before that, eleven days after the full moon. He scrolled further, and there it was again: the eleventh day of each half of the lunar month, like clockwork, except lunar clockwork, which was clearly fancier.

The next Saturday his friend Pearl came over, and Theo spread his notebook on the kitchen table like a detective in a movie. "Every eleven days, twice a month," he announced. "Half a lunar month on each side. That's the pattern."

"What are you two plotting?" his mother asked, setting down two glasses of juice.

"It's called Ekadashi," Pearl said, peering at his notes. "My grandma does it too. She says it's dedicated to Vishnu."

"Vishnu," Theo repeated, and something clicked into place. "So that's why she fasts! No grains, no beans, nothing like that. She's not being negligent about rice, she's following a rule on purpose. This whole time I thought she was just picky." He felt slightly foolish and extremely pleased at the same time, a combination he recommended to everyone.

The following Ekadashi, Theo decided to try it himself, just until sunset. "A half day of rest from rice," he declared at lunch, pushing his plate away with tremendous dignity. It lasted forty minutes. Then the aroma of his father's fresh chapatis drifted down the hallway, and Theo reasoned that a boy who was growing had special needs, and that tomorrow's version of himself could handle the consequences.

He converted his fast into a promise instead: next time, he would make it all the way to moonrise. His stomach gurgled its disagreement, and Pearl, who had come over to watch, laughed so hard she knocked over the juice.

The gym smelled like glue and popcorn, and the folding tables stretched in rows all the way to the bleachers. Brayden set his shoebox on the table and lifted the lid. Inside, on a tangle of floral wire, hung his model of a lithium atom: a cluster of beads for the nucleus, and three lonely beads orbiting on wire rings. Sara leaned over from the next table, where her volcano waited with its lump of red foam.

"Those middle ones are supposed to be different colours," she said. "Yours are all yellow."

Brayden looked down. He had glued three yellow beads into the nucleus and hung three yellow beads on the rings, because yellow was the colour he had the most of. Now that she said it, the whole thing looked flat, like a drawing with only one pencil.

"The label sheet says each particle gets its own colour," he said. He found the paper in his pocket. Protons, it read, were the ones in the nucleus with positive charge. Electrons were the ones on the rings with negative charge. The third kind, neutrons, sat in the nucleus too, and the line after that made him stop. "Neutrons have no charge at all."

Sara read over his shoulder. "No charge? Then how do you colour nothing?"

The whole model seemed to hinge on that one bead. Three protons, Brayden counted, and three electrons, and four neutrons. If he couldn't tell the neutrons apart from the protons, the judges would look at his nucleus and see seven identical beads and no thinking behind them. The差别 between the nucleus particles couldn't be seen directly, only implied by colour, and right now his colours implied nothing.

He tried an idea. "Positive could be red," he said slowly, pulling a red bead from his pouch. "Then electrons are blue on the rings. Opposite colours for opposite charges." He wired the red beads in and hung three blue ones. That left the neutrons.

"What colour is nothing?" Sara asked again.

Brayden looked around the gym. Then it landed on him. He took a black marker and painted four beads solid black. "Black," he said. "No charge, no colour."

Mr. Ba stopped at the table on his judge rounds and studied the model for a long moment. "Walk me through the nucleus," he said.

"Three red protons, positive," Brayden said, pointing. "Three blue electrons out here, negative. And four black neutrons."

"Which have no charge at all," Mr. Ba finished, and made a note on his clipboard. "Now that's a radical improvement from where you started, I'd guess."

He moved on to the volcano, and Sara whispered, "You're welcome." Brayden tilted the shoebox so the light caught the little black beads, then picked up the label sheet and wrote one word beside each colour.

Elijah held the envelope with exactly four dollars and fifty cents, one side of it rubbed soft from being folded and unfolded all morning. Mr. Virtanen had given the class a real-world assignment: walk to the corner store alone, buy one carton of milk, count the change, and bring back a receipt. "You'll modify your plan if something goes wrong," Mr. Virtanen said, "that's the whole point." Coraline, who had gone last week, winked at Elijah as they left. "Check the milk before you pay," she said, and nothing more, which was not helpful at all.

At the store, Elijah found the dairy case and reached for the front carton, then stopped. He had heard Coraline's warning in his head all afternoon, and now he noticed something. Every carton had a date stamped near the top, and the dates in the front row were different from the ones behind. He pulled one from the front and one from the back and compared them. The back one had the later date. He checked another pair. Later again. So that was what she meant: the store put older milk at the front, and the carton with the latest date was often at the back. Somebody had told Coraline that once, and now Elijah had seen it for himself. He slid his hand past the front row and took the freshest carton, feeling clever, like the store's system was a camouflage he had seen straight through.

At the register, the cashier said the milk was four dollars and nineteen cents. Elijah counted out the coins, then counted the change she handed back, coin by coin on the counter, the way he had practiced with Mr. Virtanen. Thirty-one cents. He said thank you, pocketed the receipt, and walked out with the milk hugged against his jacket.

Back at school, he showed the receipt to Mr. Virtanen, who nodded slowly. "And the milk?" Elijah turned the carton so the date faced him and pointed to it. "Got the newest one in the case." Coraline appeared beside them and smiled. "See? I told you to check." "You could have just said reach for the back," Elijah said, and she laughed. "You found it yourself. That's better." Mr. Virtanen gave an eloquent little wave of his hand toward the door. "Same assignment next month," he said. "Different aisle."

Gavin had claimed the corner of the garage his dad was still paying the mortgage on, and turned it into a lab. On Saturday morning he laid out his supplies with meticulous care: a foam ball for the proton, a tiny bead for the electron, and three pipe cleaners for the electron paths. Cadence sat cross-legged on an overturned bucket, reading the assignment aloud from Ms. Nielsen's handout.

"Build any atom," Cadence read. "Protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons outside it." Gavin had planned lithium, which meant hunting down six extra balls, but he'd lent his whole bag of foam to his cousin and the craft store's rules prohibited anyone under twelve from buying the glue he needed without a parent along. He slumped against the workbench. His whole project was stuck.

Then he remembered the chart in his science book. He flipped it open on the dusty floor and ran his finger down the first column. "Cadence, look," he said slowly. "Hydrogen. The most common kind has one proton and one electron. And no neutron at all. Nothing in the middle except the proton." He tested the idea out loud: if that was true, his single foam ball was already a complete nucleus. "I had it backwards. I thought every atom needed neutrons to hold it together. The chart says hydrogen just doesn't have any."

He pushed the bead onto a pipe-cleaner loop and hung it around the foam ball. Cadence held it up to the garage window, and the bead caught the light as it spun. That afternoon Gavin wrote a note to his cousin: "I need my foam balls back, but not for lithium anymore. I only ever needed one. Bring the bag Tuesday and I'll show you why the smallest atom in the universe is hiding in my garage." Cadence stuck the note in an envelope and drew an arrow on it, pointing at the little sun of pipe cleaner and foam. "Address it to the smartest kid on the block," she said, "because that's you now."

Dominic sat on his bedroom floor with his back against the bed, holding his phone in both hands like it might bite him. On the screen, Jaycob's face filled the little square window, one eyebrow up. "So are you coming to Darius's thing on Saturday or not? I've asked three times. I'm doing a census of the whole grade and you're the only no."

Dominic looked at the poster of the eccentric old astronomer on his wall, the one with wild white hair and a telescope aimed at nothing. He liked the poster because the man looked like he did not care what anyone thought. That was the opposite of Dominic lately. "I don't know," he said. "My stomach hurts when I think about it. It's been hurting for like two weeks. Everything feels loud, even when it's quiet in here."

Jaycob leaned closer to the camera. "Two weeks? Dude. My cousin had that. She stopped sleeping, stopped eating basically, and it got in the way of school and everything. My mom said feeling anxious sometimes is normal, everybody gets that. But when it's really intense and it lasts a long time and it stops you doing normal stuff, a doctor can diagnose an anxiety disorder." He shrugged. "That's the actual word, anxiety disorder. And it's treatable. My cousin told a doctor, and she's way better now. She still has stress, but she has ways of coping with it."

Dominic turned the phone over in his hands. He had been telling himself the stomach aches were from the cafeteria pizza, or from staying up too late. But the pizza theory did not fit the pattern: the ache showed up on school nights and on Saturday mornings before parties, and never during the horror movie marathon last weekend. Maybe he had been looking for the wrong hidden cause. He thought about the last party, in this same room, where he had spent an hour deciding what to say to Darius and then said nothing. He could not change that night, but he was still holding it, letting it consume whole evenings.

"Can you even do anything about it, though?" he asked. "I can't just tell my brain to stop."

"You tell the doctor, not your brain," Jaycob said. "That's the whole move. And you set boundaries, like, you don't have to go Saturday. A no is allowed. My cousin says that all the time."

Dominic stood up, walked to his window, and pushed it open. Cold air smelling of cut grass rushed in. Down the street a leaf blower growled and somewhere a dog barked twice. He could hear his mom in the kitchen below, stacking dishes.

"Okay," he said into the phone. "I'll ask my mom to make a doctor thing. And put me down as maybe for Saturday." He paused at the door. "Hey Mom? Can we talk about something?"

Bennett had chosen the lighthouse on purpose. His social studies class had read about refugee families crossing dark seas, and he wanted his model to show how a lighthouse says "land is here" to someone who has nowhere safe to go. He'd spent two evenings wiring it: a battery, a switch, a bulb in the tower. On Friday he pressed the switch, and the little light glowed steady and bright. Perfect.

Then Kaylin walked past his table at the science fair and stopped. "It's good," she said, "but one bulb? A contemporary lighthouse has a big lamp, not a tiny one. Add a second bulb. Two has to be brighter than one." Bennett looked at his tower. Two lights, one above the other, would look stronger. He had a spare identical bulb in his parts box, so he unscrewed the lamp cover and wired the second bulb into the same path, one after the other.

He flipped the switch. Both bulbs lit, but each one glowed more dimly than his single bulb had glowed on the same battery. Bennett stared. He checked the wires, wiggled the connections, even swapped in a fresh battery from his pocket. Still dim, both of them, together. He whispered, "That's backwards."

Kael leaned over from the next table. "What's backwards?" Bennett explained: one bulb on this battery, bright; two identical bulbs wired in a row, dimmer, each of them. Kael suggested they eliminate the switch in case it was the problem, so they took it out and joined the wires directly. Nothing changed. Both bulbs still glowed with less light than either one alone would have shown. "Then it's not the switch," Kael said slowly. "It's the two bulbs themselves."

In his lunch bag Bennett found the note his grandfather had tucked there that morning, because Grandpa couldn't come to the fair. "Dear Bennett," it read, "your grandmother says to tell you: the lamp does not have to be big to be brave. It only has to stay lit. Love, Grandpa." Bennett read it twice, then went back to his table.

He unscrewed the second bulb, reconnected the first one straight to the battery, and replaced the switch. When the judge, Mr. Rahman, stopped at his table, Bennett pressed it. The single bulb glowed bright and steady inside the tower. "One bulb, one battery, one switch," Bennett said. "The electricity goes around in one loop, and when I open the switch, the loop is broken and the light goes out." Mr. Rahman nodded and wrote something on his clipboard. Behind the bright little window, Bennett taped his grandfather's note where only he could see it.

The regional spelling bee had gone online this year, so Alexia sat at her kitchen table with the laptop propped on a stack of cookbooks while her dad hovered behind her with the vacuum switched off. Down in the corner of the screen, in a grid of tiny faces, Yousuf gave her a thumbs up. He had made it to the finals too, and all week they had drilled each other over video calls after homework. His one wish was to beat his older sister's record from three years ago, when she had placed fourth, and he reminded Alexia of it at least twice a day.

Round four began, and the announcer called her name. "Alexia, your word is chef." She asked for the definition, then for the language of origin. "French," the announcer said. Alexia spelled it c-h-e-f, and it was correct, but her stomach still felt tight, because the next word could be anything.

Between rounds, waiting was anything but leisure for her; she kept her hands busy straightening the pencils on the table. Then she noticed something. When the announcer had said French for chef, the sh sound at the start had been spelled with the letters c and h. She remembered Yousuf's practice list, and the word chorus, where the same letters c and h made a k sound. She had missed chorus in a practice round on Tuesday, spelling it with a plain k. Maybe the difference wasn't luck. Maybe the language of origin was the hidden key, and she could test it if the chance came.

"Alexia, your word is chimera." She asked for the definition first, buying a second to think. Then she asked, "Language of origin?" "Greek," the announcer said. Greek, like chorus. If the pattern held, that k sound at the start would be spelled with c and h. She imagined Yousuf on the other side of the screen, mouthing breathe, which is what he always mouthed at her. She started the word slowly, letter by letter, c-h-i-m-e-r-a, and held her breath until the bell that meant wrong stayed silent.

"Correct," the announcer said, and the moderator's voice added that the next round was imminent. In the corner of the grid, Yousuf's face lit up; he had advanced too, which meant his sister's record was still within reach for him. The pronouncer turned to his list. "Yousuf, your word is charisma." Yousuf leaned toward his camera, and Alexia heard him ask, calm and steady, "Language of origin, please?"

Theo stood at the end of the lakeside dock with his duffel bag at his feet, because in exactly one hour the camp van would carry him away for a whole month. Before he left, he wanted one thing: to paddle a canoe, just once, so he wouldn't be the only beginner at camp.

Zaid held the canoe steady against the dock while Luciana sat in the middle seat, paddle across her knees. Theo grabbed the gunwale and swung his leg over the side. The instant his sneaker touched the canoe's edge, the whole boat tipped like a seesaw, and cold lake water slopped over the rim. He jerked back onto the dock, heart hammering.

"That wasn't random," Theo said slowly, watching the canoe rock. "It tipped exactly where I stepped." He thought about Luciana, sitting low and centered, who had barely wobbled at all. Was there a rule hiding in that? He tested it, putting his foot not on the edge but into the middle of the hull, right where Luciana's pack lay flat. The canoe swayed a little, then settled, steady as a table.

"So that's why people step into the middle of a canoe and not onto its side," he said. "The weight has to be low and centered. That's what keeps it stable."

"Your intuition is better than mine was," Zaid admitted. "I fell in last summer. Twice."

Mr. Bondarenko, whose dock it was, ambled down and helped Theo acquire a paddle from the boathouse rack, checking the life jacket straps himself before letting them push off. For twenty minutes the three of them glided past the reeds, Theo crouched low in the center, learning to steer.

When the van finally honked from the road, Theo ran up the hill, waving. "First thing I'm telling everyone at camp," he called back over his shoulder, "is I already know where to step!"

Elizabeth had exactly forty minutes before her flight to Denver, and one enormous problem: she had promised her grandmother she would send the location of every city she visited, written in latitude and longitude, because Grandma wanted to pin them all on a wall map. The only trouble was that Elizabeth had never read latitude and longitude in her life.

She spread the atlas she'd bought at the airport bookstore across two plastic chairs near gate B12, and her friend Desiree leaned over it, cracking gum. "Numbers everywhere," Desiree said. "Which ones are the city?"

"That's what we're finding out." Elizabeth traced her finger across the curved lines. The ones running sideways, wrapping around the world like belts, had to be latitude, because she remembered Ms. Sokolov saying the equator was latitude zero. So the lines stretching from top to bottom, like segments of an orange, were longitude. Denver sat near the number 105 on one of those tall lines. "Thirty-nine north, one hundred five west," she read aloud. "That's Denver."

Then Ayah arrived with a paper cup of hot chocolate and a globe from the gift shop, a frail little thing she was afraid to fracture if she dropped it, which was why she carried it like a baby bird. "Look at the top," Ayah said, spinning it slowly. Elizabeth bent close. Near the equator, the longitude lines stood far apart, but near the top of the globe they squeezed together, crowding in like roads merging until they all touched at a single point.

"They meet," Elizabeth whispered. "At the pole, they actually touch." She grabbed the ruler from her backpack and measured on the map's scale bar. "At the equator, one degree of longitude is about a hundred eleven kilometers. But up at the pole it has to shrink to zero, because the lines have run out of room. Zero!" She checked the atlas key, and there it was in print, exactly what she'd worked out. She felt like a detective who had solved the case before the police.

Desiree wrote the Denver coordinates on a napkin and then, since they had twenty minutes left, they hunted down Tokyo, Nairobi, and Reykjavik, whose longitude lines were packed so tightly toward the top that Elizabeth had to squint. "Grandma's going to need a bigger map," she said, copying the last one down.

The speaker crackled with her boarding call. Elizabeth snapped the atlas shut, hugged both friends, and jogged toward the gate, napkin held high like a flag.

"Send us Reykjavik!" Ayah called after her.

"Already on it!" Elizabeth shouted over her shoulder.

Isla sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field with her X-ray printout balanced on her good knee. Her left arm, wrapped in a bright green cast, rested in her lap, and every few minutes the coach blew the whistle and she had to remind herself she wasn't supposed to run out there. Evelyne plopped down beside her, dusty from drills, and leaned over the film.

"Why do your bones look like glowing white sticks?" Evelyne asked. "Your arm and everything else is just a gray smudge."

Isla held the film up against the sky. The two bones of her forearm stood out sharp and pale, and the break near her wrist made a crooked line she couldn't stop staring at. "The doctor said something about it," she said slowly. "Something in the bones. I think it's the calcium. The calcium absorbs more of the X-rays than the softer stuff around it, so the bones show up white and everything else barely shows at all." She turned the film over, as if the answer might be printed on the back.

"Calcium, like in milk," Evelyne said.

"Like in milk." Isla looked down at her cast, and an idea clicked into place. When they'd taken the X-ray, the thick part of the cast had shown up faintly on the image too, a hazy white shadow behind the bone. Old plaster casts had calcium in them. That was why the technician had angled the machine around it. Her idea wasn't just a guess; the same stuff, the same white glow. "I'm going to ask Martha," she said. "She broke her wrist last year. If her old X-ray shows the cast shadow too, then I'm right."

They found Martha by the goal net, breathing hard while Ms. Sato called out instructions to regulate the pace of the scrimmage. Ms. Sato saw Isla's awkward one-armed attempt to carry her water bottle and jogged over to open it for her, then stayed to fan Martha with a clipboard until she caught her breath. Martha dug out her phone, scrolled through photos, and held up her own X-ray. There it was: the bone, brilliant white, and behind it the ghostly outline of her old cast.

"So the calcium drinks up the X-rays," Martha said, "and whatever drinks up the most shows up brightest."

"The tendon doesn't, though," Isla said, pointing at the thin gray thread of tissue near Martha's wrist. "That's why you can barely see it." She flexed the fingers of her casted hand, the last voluntary movement the doctor had allowed her, and grinned. "Three more weeks, and I'm back on that field."

Ms. Sato handed her the whistle. "You can officiate until then," she said. "First call of the scrimmage, right there."

Brielle taped her last poster word, "HYPOTHESIS," just as Ms. Mendoza opened the gym doors and the science fair began. Her project claimed that a paper airplane with wide wings would glide farther than one with narrow wings. "That's my testable guess," she told Heather, who was guarding the two planes at the table. "If the wide one wins, my guess holds up. If not, it's overturned."

But when Brielle demonstrated, the wide-winged plane nosedived and the narrow one sailed. Heather laughed so hard she knocked over the cup of pennies they were using as table currency for counting trial runs. Something felt wrong to Brielle, and she thought back to last Saturday, when she had folded the wide plane at her kitchen table and thrown it in the still hallway. It had glided beautifully then, past the laundry basket and onto the couch. So what had changed? She looked around the gym and noticed the propped-open door, and the draft of wind rattling the endangered spider plant on the windowsill, one gust away from losing its last three leaves.

"You can't compare them like this," she said. "In a fair test, everything except the thing you're testing has to be kept the same. Same amount of paper, same throws, and same wind, which means none. The wide one just flew into a breeze." Emy-Jade wandered over from the moldy-bread exhibit and offered to stand guard by the door until Ms. Mendoza could authorize closing it, since only adults were allowed to touch the doors during the fair.

Brielle re-threw both planes in the still air, ten careful trials each. The wide wings won eight times out of ten. Her hypothesis had survived after all, once the sneaky wind was taken out of the picture. She crossed out the word "overturned" on her poster and wrote "supported," then held up the wide plane like a tiny silver trophy.

"Ladies and gentlemen," she announced to Heather and Emy-Jade, "never trust a gym with a draft."

Benjamin stood at the start of the row of low hurdles, and his heart was doing the three-step rhythm before his feet were. "Film it again," he begged Shaan, who was crouched by lane four with his phone. Shaan wanted to make the practice highlight reel for the class channel, and he had already built a whole database of clips, tagging each one with Benjamin's times, so nothing about this could stay a secret for long.

"Go on then," Shaan said. Benjamin ran. One, two, three, hurdle. One, two, three, hurdle. His lead knee cracked the third barrier, and the fifth, and he crossed the finish in a tangle of white plastic. Ms. Chatterjee blew her whistle and jogged over, but she only said, "Watch your own video, not my mouth," because that was the rule she had made mandatory for learning new events: figure it out before being told.

They crowded around the phone behind the equipment shed. Brynlee, who had come to time him because she wanted the official numbers for her stopwatch notebook, leaned in too. Benjamin scrubbed the clip backwards and forwards, watching his own legs. There it was. He took off close to each hurdle, and his lead knee shot straight up like a drawbridge, stiff and slow, and that was exactly when he clipped the bar. But on the one hurdle he cleared cleanly, he had pushed off farther back and landed just past it, close on the far side. "Look," he said, jabbing the screen. "I take off way farther away than I land after. When I crowd it, my knee has to go up all steep and it slows me down." Brynlee read out the splits to prove it: the clean hurdle was his fastest split of all.

He walked back to the line, counted his steps out loud, and planted a cone in the grass where the good takeoff had been. "Brynlee, accompany me to lane four," he said grandly, holding out his hand like an announcer. "Somebody has to catch the record."

Shaan hit record. "Three, two, one," he called, and Benjamin flew.

Elena pressed one more gold bead onto her foam sphere and stepped back to look at it. Her model of a gold atom was completely covered, every centimeter packed with beads for protons and neutrons, with electrons glued around the outside like sprinkles. It had taken three evenings, and tomorrow was the science fair, where the winning project would go on to a prestigious regional contest.

"You did the whole thing already?" Prisha set her own half-built skeleton of pipe cleaners on the table beside Elena's. "Mine still looks like a collapsed tent."

"It was supposed to be a collaboration," Darcy said, arriving with the glue gun and a wounded expression. "You said Saturday."

"I know. I got carried away." Elena turned the sphere so Darcy could see the gap where one bead had popped off. "You can do the electron rings. I saved them."

Mr. Johansson paused at their table on his rounds of the gym, coffee cup in hand. He tilted his head at the solid ball of beads. "Interesting. Have you read about the gold foil experiment?"

Elena shook her head, and he moved on to the next table without another word, which felt like a challenge.

At the library after school, she found it. Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working under Ernest Rutherford, had fired tiny particles at gold foil, and most of the alpha particles passed straight through. Elena read the page twice. Passed through gold. Atoms were mostly empty space. She stared at her packed, crowded sphere, heavy as a bowling ball in her lap, and felt like the whole thing was a small rebellion against how the universe actually worked.

The next morning she pried off the beads with a butter knife, and Prisha knelt on the other side and caught them in a cup. Darcy threaded the three of them that remained onto clear fishing line, so the nucleus hung in the middle of a wire frame with nothing but air around it. The electrons went on the outer rings, small and alone in all that space.

At the fair, a judge leaned close to the frame. "So where's the rest of it?"

"That is the rest of it," Elena said. "In the gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, because an atom is mostly empty space."

The judge smiled and moved on, and Prisha squeezed Elena's elbow. Down the row, Mr. Johansson gave them a small nod from behind his coffee cup.

Alicia had one job at the mall's spring market: help Agnes and Liliana sell strawberries at their little table by the fountain, and figure out one thing for her social studies sheet. The question was why strawberries cost less in summer than in winter. She had a hunch it had something to do with how many boxes people would buy, but a hunch wasn't an answer, and the sheet was due Monday.

The morning was slow and tedious, mostly straightening boxes and watching shoppers revolve past on the escalator without stopping. The sign said two dollars a box, and by lunch they had sold only six of forty. Agnes slumped onto the stool. "We're going to carry all these home."

"Then the price is wrong," Alicia said. She was guessing, but it was a guess she could test. "Summer strawberries are cheap, so cheap that people buy tons of them. Let's try one dollar." Liliana found the marker in the craft bag, crossed out the two, and they waited.

It worked almost too well. By two o'clock half the boxes were gone, and by four there were only eight left with an hour of market time to go. Alicia counted the boxes, then the customers drifting by, then the clock above the jewelry store. Some shoppers picked up a box, saw the price, and put it back. Others carried off two at a time. Buyers wanting to buy and sellers wanting to sell, she thought, were like two sides of a seesaw. When the two sides matched, everything balanced.

"Raise it to one fifty," she said. At one fifty, the last eight boxes went slowly, one at a time, to a woman with a stroller, to Ms. Hoang from the music store downstairs, who bought two and said the girl at the next table should save the last box for her. Agnes held it behind the register, and at exactly five o'clock, closing time, the woman came back, and the table was empty. Nothing left over, nothing carried home.

Liliana wrote on the sheet: the price where the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell. "There's a name for it," Agnes said, flipping through the handout. "Equilibrium price."

"So winter strawberries are expensive because at a high price, the small number of boxes matches the smaller number of buyers," Alicia said, stacking the empty crates. "And summer strawberries are cheap because there are so many of both." Ms. Hoang tucked her box into her tote and smiled at the three of them.

"Now we just need something to sell next month," Liliana said. "Something that runs out exactly at closing time."

Hunter dragged the chair across the kitchen and climbed up to the top shelf, where his mom kept the craft box. Moving the old calendars exposed a spool of red ribbon, exactly what he needed for the model bridge due tomorrow. He measured off three quarters of a metre and cut it, then held the roll up to the window. Not much left. He set the piece on the table beside his sketch.

The problem was the sketch itself. It showed a span, two towers, and a strip of ribbon running along the top, but Eliot had called ten minutes ago with news that had made Hunter's stomach drop. "The suspension cable has to be a third of a metre," Eliot had said, "and the anchor cables come off the same piece. Mr. Nair measured them in class today with the metre stick." Their piece was three quarters of a metre. A third went to the span. Would the rest cover the anchors, or was the whole project sunk?

Hunter did not want to cut anything until he knew. He pulled his math notebook toward him and wrote 3/4 minus 1/3. The numbers just sat there, refusing to line up. Fourths were not thirds; he could picture the cut marks on the ribbon, and they did not match up anywhere. He tried counting on his fingers and got nowhere. Outside, a storm was rolling in, and the kitchen light flickered once, which made him feel like the clock was against him too.

Then he thought of the measuring cup. His mom used it for rice, and it had marks all around the inside: halves, thirds, fourths, and a fine set of little lines between them. He found it in the drawer and turned it slowly under the tap light. If he poured to a fourth, the water touched one of the small lines. If he poured to a third, it touched another. He counted the small lines carefully, twice. Twelfths. Every mark on the cup was a twelfth, and both of his fractions landed on them.

Back at the table, he wrote it out. Three quarters was equivalent to nine twelfths. One third was equivalent to four twelfths. Nine twelfths minus four twelfths came to five twelfths of a metre left over after the span. Five twelfths was almost half a metre, and his sketch needed only about a quarter metre of anchor cables. His pencil hovered over the paper while he checked the counting one last time, because if he was wrong, there was no second piece of ribbon in the house.

He cut a third of a metre for the span, then laid the leftover along the ruler. Five twelfths. He measured out the anchor cables, and there was still ribbon to spare. His phone buzzed. "Did you figure it out, or are we building a plank bridge?" Eliot asked. Hunter wrapped the extra ribbon around his finger and grinned at the window, where the first fat raindrops were hitting the glass. "Suspension bridge," he said. "Come over and bring the popsicle sticks."

Stella spread the canvas boards across the picnic table in Gunnar's backyard and counted the brushes in the jar. Three of them stood stiff as sticks, their bristles frozen into sharp little points. She had left them in the studio overnight, and now the mural for Ms. Wiśniewski's community garden sign was due at five o'clock, and it was already noon.

"Soak them in hot water," Gunnar said, filling a bucket from the garden hose. "That always works."

Stella dipped one brush in and swirled it. Nothing happened. The bristles stayed frozen, and when she pressed them against her palm they left a hard line, like a stick of chalk. She thought about what she'd noticed while painting yesterday: the paint had rinsed off her hands easily while it was wet, but the smudge she'd missed on her sleeve had hardened and survived the washing machine. She turned that over in her head. If the paint thinned with water only while it was wet, then once it dried it must resist water completely. That would explain why soaking was doing nothing at all.

"Hot water isn't going to fix these," she said. "The paint already dried on them. Water can't get it off once it's dry."

"That's not a credible plan," Gunnar said. "We need three working brushes for the lettering."

"Then we test it my way first." Stella held a stiff brush under the tap and squeezed dish soap into the bristles, working it in with her fingers, then rinsed. A thin ribbon of softened paint came out, but the core stayed hard. She tried a second time, scrubbing harder, and more came free, but the bristles splayed crooked.

"Two minutes," Reese called from the porch, where she'd been waiting to help with the vines. "My mom said she can drive the sign over to the garden at five, but she has to commute to her evening shift right after, so there's no second trip."

Stella looked at the two clean brushes left in the jar, then at the painted letters already finished, then at the long border of leaves still undone. The landlord who owned the garden plot had promised the sign would hang by the gate this weekend, and half the neighborhood would see it.

"Gunnar, I changed my mind," she said. "Forget the stiff ones. We each take a clean brush and do the leaves together. And after this, we wash the brushes right away, before anything dries. Every time."

They painted fast, trading the water cup between them, dipping and rinsing and rinsing again. By four thirty the border was done, green leaves curling around the letters. Stella carried the brushes straight to the hose and washed them under the cold stream until the water ran clear, then laid them flat on the table to dry in the sun.

Reese held up the finished sign. "Ms. Wiśniewski is going to hang this by the gate tonight."

"Then let's get it in the car before anything else dries on us," Stella said, and she picked up the brushes to keep.

Blake stood at the shallow end of the community pool that shared a building with the hockey rink, listening to the thud of pucks hitting the boards through the wall. Twenty-five metres. That was the whole test, and he had failed it twice, always in the same way.

"Same spot every time," said Mathieu, hanging on the lane rope. "Between the flags and the wall. You turn your head, cough like a seal, and stand up."

"I'm trying to get a big enough breath," Blake said. He wasn't lying. He turned his face to the side, tried to let the old air out and pull new air in during that one quick moment, and every time the water won. It poured into his mouth, and that was that.

Calla swam past them, slow and easy, her face rolling to the side like it was nothing. Blake watched her go. She wasn't taking a huge breath. He could see that much. Her mouth barely opened at all. So why did she have air to spare?

Mr. Dlamini, the lifeguard on duty, blew his whistle at two kids trying to obstruct the lap lane with a pool noodle, and Blake kept watching Calla's face underwater. A stream of bubbles came out of her nose and mouth the whole time her face was down. Then when she turned, she only had to breathe in. One thing, not two things.

"That's it," Blake said. He pushed off before he could talk himself out of it. Face in, he pushed the air out through his mouth and nose, a steady fizz of bubbles, and when his arm pulled back he rolled his head, took one quick sip of air, and put his face down again. Bubbles out. Sip in. The flags went by overhead. Then the wall was under his hand.

He stood up, breathing hard but not coughing.

"You got the tutor after all," Mathieu said, grinning. "Calla's been showing you stuff all week."

"I figured it out myself," Blake said, but not in a defiant way. He looked down the lane. "Mostly."

Calla laughed and pushed off toward the deep end. "Race you to twenty-five," she called over her shoulder.

Blake shoved off the wall after her.

Maeva stood in her grandmother's kitchen with the folded paper in her hand, reading the same line for the tenth time. In two days she would stand in front of everyone at her cousin's quinceañera and deliver the reading at the Mass, and so far she could only get through three sentences without stumbling.

"Taha says he memorized a whole speech once by recording it and playing it while he slept," said Olivia, who was sitting on the counter eating an orange. "You could try that tonight."

"Two nights," Maeva said. "That's not enough sleep to learn two paragraphs." She stared at the paper. Something was wrong with her method, and she tried to figure out what. She had been rereading the words from the top every time, so the beginning was smooth and the ending was shaky. The problem, she realized, wasn't the words themselves. It was that she only ever practiced the easy part first. When she stood up in church, she would have to start at the beginning with no warm-up, so she needed a way to practice starting cold.

"It would be logical to begin in a different place every time," she said slowly. "Random spots. Middle of paragraph two. Last line. Then the beginning would just be one more starting point, not the only one."

"Or," said Olivia, "you could panic, which is what I would do."

Grandma shuffled in with the mop and told them to lift their feet. "Two more days until the big one," she said. "Your mother made a whole controversy out of the cake flavors, can you believe it. Vanilla or tres leches, and now half the family isn't speaking to the other half."

Maeva closed her eyes and recited from the middle of the second paragraph, the part she always fumbled. The words came out clean. She opened her eyes and grinned. "It's working."

They spent the next hour testing each other. Olivia would call out a line, and Maeva would take off from there, sometimes fast, sometimes slow, once while hopping on one foot because Olivia claimed distraction training would accelerate her progress. Grandma declared it the strangest rehearsal she had ever mopped around.

On Saturday morning, in her grandmother's front room, Maeva smoothed her dress one last time. The church organ started. She took a breath and began, and the first sentence came out steady and sure, right on cue, as if she had started there a hundred times before. Somewhere in the third pew, Olivia gave her a thumbs up.

Jonathan had one goal for the season: beat Connor at everything. Connor was the fastest kid on the team, and he knew it, which made beating him even more satisfying in theory. In practice, Jonathan kept coming in second, which was getting old.

Then something strange happened at Tuesday practice. Mr. Sow set up sprint drills, and Jonathan beat Connor. Twice. Connor bent over, hands on his knees, and stared at the grass like it had insulted him. "I've been training every single day since March," he said. "Morning jog, afternoon sprints, evening juggling. I'm the most diligent soccer player in this county." He said it like a badge, but he looked like a melted snowman.

On Thursday, Jonathan beat him again, and this time Atlas noticed too. "You're getting slower," Atlas told Connor, with the kindness of a friend and the delivery of a game show host. "Like, measurably." After practice, Jonathan rode his bike home puzzling over it. Training every day should make you faster, shouldn't it? Unless the getting stronger part happened somewhere he couldn't see, some hidden step between the workout and the speed. His own week suddenly looked interesting: Monday sprints, Wednesday practice, and in between, honestly, a lot of video games and a heroic amount of cheese crackers. He had been resting. A lot. And he had been getting faster.

Friday, he tried an actual test, in the scientific tradition of making stuff up. "Connor," he said, dropping a soccer ball on the bleachers next to him, "take two days off. No jogging, no sprints. Total sloth mode." Connor looked personally wounded. "My legs will forget how to be legs." "Two days," Jonathan emphasized, holding up two fingers. "Then we race Saturday." Connor grumbled, but he agreed, mostly because losing to Jonathan had made him agree to anything.

Saturday morning, the field was still damp and the nets sagged like tired hammocks. Atlas stood at the sideline with a stopwatch he had borrowed from Mr. Sow, who watched from the parking lot with his coffee and one raised eyebrow. They raced sideline to sideline, three times. Connor won the first by a full stride. He won the second by two. On the third, he crossed the line, spun around, and pointed at Jonathan. "You knew! Rest days are part of getting better, you sneaky little scientist!" Jonathan raised both arms like he'd won the World Cup. "Race you to the water bottles," said Connor.

Chase sat on the living room rug with his notebook open, because on Monday he and Yuna had to perform a two-minute improv scene in drama class, and so far every practice had collapsed. Yuna knelt across from him, drumming her fingers on the coffee table.

"Okay," she said. "I'm the captain of a boat."

"There's no boat," Chase said. "We're in a supermarket."

Yuna slumped. "Right. Again."

Chase frowned at his notebook. He thought about Tuesday, when Brent had gone up in front of the class and pretended to toss a ball to a kid, saying, "Fetch, boy!" The kid had answered, "No, that's not my dog," and the whole room went quiet, like someone had pulled a plug. Brent had stood there holding an invisible leash until Mr. Warsame called time. At the time Chase had laughed, but now he wondered whether the same thing was happening to him and Yuna. It was like there was a hidden rule, something you couldn't see, deciding which scenes lived and which ones died. Both times, somebody had refused what the other person offered, and the scene just stopped.

"Let's simulate it," Chase said. "You say the boat thing again, and instead of fighting it, I'll say yes and add something."

Yuna straightened up. "I'm the captain of a boat."

"Yes, and the hull is porous," Chase said, patting the rug, "so we're bailing water with these buckets."

Yuna's eyes lit up. "Yes, and there's a tsunami coming, so we'd better bail faster."

"Yes, and I see an island to the north."

They went back and forth, trading offers, and the scene rolled along like a wheel downhill. A pirate appeared, then a talking seagull, then the seagull turned out to be the coast guard. Chase realized he'd been wrong earlier. He'd thought a good scene meant winning, keeping his own idea on top, but it worked the opposite way. The scene got better when he let go of his plan and built on hers.

"Wait," Yuna said, grabbing his arm. "I get it. When you said 'there's no boat,' that was blocking." She said the word carefully, the way Mr. Warsame had said it once in passing. "Blocking. That's what it's called."

"Then no more blocking," Chase said. He flipped his notebook to a fresh page and wrote the words YES, AND across the top in big letters, underlined twice, then tore it out and taped it to the coffee table where they couldn't miss it.

Yuna picked up her invisible bucket and grinned. "Bail faster, sailor. That wave's getting closer."

Camille slouched at the lunch table, poking at her noodles while Hayden flipped through a stack of crumpled papers. "Ms. Pham wants us to find five checkable facts in these product reviews by tomorrow," Hayden groaned. "But every sentence says stuff like best or boring, and I can't tell what counts."

Camille pulled one review toward her. It was for a metal water bottle, and the reviewer had written in fat, cheerful handwriting. She read it aloud under her breath. "This is the best bottle I've ever owned. It holds twenty-four ounces. The lid leaks. You should buy the purple one. The design is beautiful." Something about the words snagged in her mind, the way a thread catches on a splinter. She grabbed Hayden's green highlighter and dragged it across "best," then "boring" in the next review, then "should," then "beautiful," then "worst." When she circled what was left, only a few thin sentences remained, holding an amount of liquid, a leaking lid, a color. She looked up slowly. "Judgment words like best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signals that a sentence is an opinion, not a fact."

Hayden leaned over, chewing the cap of a pen. "So the leak we could test? Actually test?" That was the idea that had lain dormant in Camille's head since morning, and now it woke up. She reached into her backpack and pulled out her own purple water bottle, the same brand as the review. She filled it at the water fountain in the hallway, listening to the cold stream plink against the metal, then screwed the lid on tight, flipped it upside down over a paper towel, and counted. At ten seconds the towel stayed dry. At thirty, one dark dot bloomed near the rim.
