"That's our checkable claim," Camille said, her stomach doing a small flip of excitement. "The review said it leaks. It does. That's not opinion, that's something anybody could test." Kash wandered over from the vending machines with a bag of pretzels and read the highlighted pages upside down. "You turned opinions into a treasure map," he said. "The judgments govern nothing. The leftover sentences are where the facts hide."

That evening Camille wrote a note and slipped it into Hayden's locker before the buses were called.

Hayden, I checked. Best, worst, boring, beautiful, should, all highlighted, all signals of opinion. Everything left over in all three reviews was testable: twenty-four ounces (I measured mine with the kitchen measuring cup), leaky lid (confirmed, upside-down test, thirty seconds), purple color (confirmed, looked at it). Five facts found, no guessing. Bring your highlighter tomorrow. Camille.

In class the next morning, Ms. Pham walked between the desks, tapping the pages. When she reached Camille and Hayden, she picked up their sheet, studied the green stripes and the neat circles, and raised her eyebrows. "You found the pattern yourself?" Camille nodded, and Hayden pointed at the highlighted "best" in the first line. "That word tried to trick us," Hayden said. Ms. Pham smiled and set the page back down. "Then read us your favorite checkable claim," she said. Camille took a breath and stood up.

Eva set the microscope on the picnic table and weighted the instructions with a pinecone so the wind couldn't take them. Mr. Asante had lent her the scope for the weekend along with three slides, a razor blade in a folded paper sleeve, and a single demand: draw one onion cell and label the cell wall, the cell membrane, and the nucleus. "Extra credit," he had said, "but only if all three labels are there."

Violet arrived on her bike with an onion from her mother's kitchen, and Cade came over the fence the way he always did, dropping into the grass without using the gate. Eva peeled a thin layer from the inner curve of the onion, the layer so fine it looked like fog, and laid it on the slide. Under the lowest lens the cells appeared like a brick wall, each one a neat rectangle with a darker dot near the middle. "Nucleus," she said, and wrote it. The outer edge of each brick was plain too, a firm line all the way around. She wrote "cell wall."

Then she sat back and frowned. The assignment called for three labels, and she had two. There was no second line anywhere inside the rectangles, nothing between the wall and the inside of the cell. "Maybe onions just don't have one," Cade said, chewing a blade of grass. "Mr. Asante wouldn't ask for it if it didn't exist," Violet said. "He's not like that."

Eva turned the fine focus very slowly, watching the edge of one cell. She remembered how the squash had looked when she'd forgotten to water it, how its skin had pulled away from the flesh in a loose ridge. What if the membrane was there but hidden, pressed flat against the inside of the cell wall so tightly that it couldn't show as a separate line? She couldn't see that directly. But she could test it. If something made the cell lose water, would the membrane pull away from the wall and become visible?

"What could make it shrink?" she asked. Violet suggested salt, and Cade told an anecdote about his grandmother sprinkling salt on cucumber slices and watching puddles form within minutes, which made his point better than any argument. Eva fetched a glass of water from the kitchen, stirred in a spoonful of salt, and let the slide sit in a shallow dish of it. They waited, swatting mosquitoes, while the sprinkler next door made its vigorous sweep across the neighbor's lawn.

When she looked again, she leaned so close her braid fell against the stage. Inside several cells the membrane had drawn back from the wall, curling inward like a deflating balloon, and now it stood out as its own clear line. She drew one cell twice, before and after, and labeled the membrane on the second drawing with an arrow and a note: pressed tight against the wall normally, you only see it when the cell shrinks. "So it was there the whole time," Cade said, peering into the eyepiece. Eva took the slide off the stage and held it up to the light, looking at the thin wet sheet that had kept its secret until the salt asked the question.

At dinner Leah pushed her noodles around her plate and said, "Deklan told everyone today that most students at our school walk to school. Ms. Krause asked him how he knew, and he just said everybody does, obviously. But does everybody? I see bikes jammed into the rack every morning."

Her dad set down his fork. "So is he wrong?"

"That's the thing. I don't know if he's wrong. That's what's bugging me." She pulled the folded paper out of her pocket and smoothed it beside her glass. "Ellia said it's just his opinion and opinions can't be wrong. But it doesn't feel like an opinion. An opinion is like when I say the cafeteria pizza is better than the pasta. Nobody can check that. Deklan said a fact about how many kids walk, and that seems like something you could actually count."

"So count it," her dad said, spooning more sauce onto her noodles whether she wanted it or not.

Leah looked at the paper, where she had scrawled a tally grid on the bus ride home. Rows for walk, bike, car, bus. Empty columns. "That's what I was thinking. Ms. Krause postponed our quiz until Friday so we'd have time, actually. She said if we're going to argue about it, we should find out. I asked her how, and she said a survey would work, and that was all she'd tell us. Ellia and I figured out the rest after class." She tapped the grid. "We stand at the front doors tomorrow morning and mark one line per kid. Ellia takes the eighth graders, I take everyone else. Deklan, if he shows up, can count bikes, since he was so sure of himself."

"Seems fair," her dad said. "You know nobody's ever counted this before, right? You three could be the first."

Leah stopped, fork halfway to her mouth. She hadn't thought of that. "Huh. So right now, this minute, nobody in the world knows if Deklan's right?" The idea gave her a strange, fizzy feeling, like discovering an unopened room in a house she thought she knew. "I kept thinking a fact had to already be written down somewhere, in a book or on a website. But a thing can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet." She said it slowly, testing it. "It's just sitting there waiting."

"It's like the dinosaurs," her dad said. "Their extinction wasn't a mystery forever. Somebody found the bones and checked."

"I guess." She was already folding the paper into quarters, then into eighths, so it would fit in her jacket pocket without ripping. At lunch she would get Ellia's answer about Deklan, and if he was in, all three of them would have to agree on the plan. She hoped it would be unanimous, because arguing took longer than counting, and she wanted to be at the doors by seven forty.

She ate a real bite of noodles at last. Tomorrow morning, one tally mark at a time, she was going to find out what was true.

Audrey set down the platter of noodles and listened to her grandfather start the lake story for what had to be the hundredth time. He claimed Aunt Rosa had shown up two hours late to the family reunion picnic and ruined the group photo. Her mother, ladling sauce, said no, Rosa had been exactly on time, and it was Grandpa who had wandered off to the dock and made everyone wait. They argued the way they always did, with the fond stubbornness of people who had been disagreeing for decades. Nicole, sitting beside Audrey with her napkin folded in her lap, raised her eyebrows.

"That's not even possible," Nicole whispered. "Someone has to be wrong."

Audrey had invited Nicole and Kyson over for dinner partly to escape homework and partly because her mother made better noodles than anyone, but now she had a new reason to be glad they'd come. For months she had been chewing on a question she couldn't digest: how could two people remember the same afternoon so differently and both be certain? Grandpa said Rosa ruined the photo. Mom said Grandpa did. Each of them thought the other was being unreasonable, and neither would budge.

She remembered a day in October when she had done the same thing. Nicole had borrowed her calculator and returned it with a cracked screen, and Audrey had spent a whole weekend certain that Nicole was careless and didn't care. Then Nicole showed her the dent in her backpack where a locker door had slammed shut on it. Audrey had felt her certainty tilt sideways, and the feeling had never fully settled back into place. Maybe everybody walked around like that, she thought, believing they saw things exactly as they were and assuming anyone who disagreed was just misinformed. She wanted to test it while everyone was still at the table.

"Grandpa," she said, "tell the story again, but pretend you're Aunt Rosa." He grumbled, but he tried it, describing himself waiting at the picnic tables while a man strolled off toward the water. Then Mom told it as Grandpa, watching the clock while Rosa's car finally pulled in. By the time the noodles were cold, each of them had paused at least once, and Mom laughed at her own version, which she had never done before.

"Mr. Foster calls that naive realism," Kyson said, reaching for the bread. "Thinking you see things as they really are, so anyone who disagrees must be uniformed or biased." He shrugged. "He says everybody does it."

Nicole turned her fork over. "So who's right about the lake?"

Nobody answered. Grandpa spooned more sauce onto his plate, and Mom went to the drawer for the old photo album, the one with the durable cracked spine, and set it down in the middle of the table.

Muhammad raced across the frosty park with a paper flyer flapping in his hand, weaving between the lanterns already being strung between the oak trees. The Lunar New Year festival started in two weeks, and his class project on family celebrations was due the day after the big dinner. There was just one problem: he had told Mr. Dlamini the project would be presented on February second, and now the flyer said the festival was January twenty-ninth.

"Corbin! Kingston!" he shouted, skidding to a stop at the picnic table where his friends were stacking paper lanterns for the volunteer booth. "The dinner is on the twenty-ninth. My whole project plan is wrong."

Corbin shrugged. "So move your plan. Big deal."

"You don't get it. Last year the dinner was in February. I remember because it was after my cousin's birthday." Muhammad flipped the flyer over, then pulled out his phone and opened the calendar app, thumbing back through months. January. He tapped the moon symbol again and again. "Every year it's different. It jumps around."

Kingston leaned over his shoulder. "My mom says it's the moon calendar. She's Korean, and her friends from Vietnam and China all celebrate the same day."

"Then it's a new moon thing," Muhammad said slowly. He scrolled back to last January and found it: a new moon, and the festival right on it. He scrolled to this January. Another new moon, late in the month. "It lands on a new moon between January twenty-one and February twenty. That's the rule. That's why it moves."

"Diagnosis: you planned your project around the wrong date," Kingston said, grinning. "Prescription: ask Mr. Dlamini to move it."

Muhammad had tried that already, sort of. On Monday he had stammered out a request and Mr. Dlamini had waved him off, saying the schedule was the schedule, notorious for never changing. This time Muhammad would bring proof. He spent the rest of the afternoon photographing the flyer, the calendar app, and the huge banner the volunteers had just finished hanging over the park gates, red and gold letters announcing the festival date.

On Monday he laid the pictures on Mr. Dlamini's desk before the teacher could dismiss him. "My family's dinner is on the twenty-ninth. New moon between January twenty-one and February twenty. I can't present after it happens, it won't make sense."

Mr. Dlamini studied the photos for a long moment, then looked up. "Move it up a week, then. And Muhammad?"

"Yes?"

"Bring mooncakes to the presentation."

Charles had exactly forty minutes of coding club left, and his program still thought that 1 was prime. He had typed it himself: ask for a number, divide it by everything smaller, and if nothing divides evenly, print "prime." It worked on 7. It worked on 13. Then Jeremie, leaning over from the next laptop, had typed 1 and the program had announced, with total confidence, "prime."

"That's wrong," Jeremie said.

"It can't be wrong. It did the math."

"It did your math," said Devyn from across the table, without looking up from her screen.

Charles stared at the loop. The problem was that 1 had nothing smaller than it except, depending on how you counted, 1 itself, so nothing ever divided it, so the program declared victory. He could fix it with one line, an if statement that threw out 1 before the loop even started. But that felt like cheating. He wanted to know why 1 shouldn't count, not just that it shouldn't.

Ms. Marino wandered past, hands behind her back, the way she did when she was checking on people but pretending to consume a poster on the wall instead. She paused at his screen.

"Why is 1 not prime?" she asked. "That's your bug, by the way."

"I know it's my bug. I don't know why it's a bug. One is just one. It's not divisible by anything else, so it sounds prime to me."

"Mathematicians exclude it," she said, "so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." Then she walked away, because she was the sort of teacher who dropped a sentence like a match and left the fire to you.

Charles sat with that. A product of primes. He grabbed the scrap paper next to his keyboard, the one covered in a vague sketch of a robot he'd drawn during announcements, and flipped it over. Twelve, he wrote. Twelve was 2 times 2 times 3. Was there another way? He tried 3 times 4, but 4 wasn't prime. He tried 2 times 6, but 6 wasn't prime either. Every road led back to the same three numbers.

Then he tried it with 1 allowed. Suddenly 12 was 2 times 2 times 3, or 1 times 2 times 2 times 3, or 1 times 1 times 2 times 2 times 3, forever. One way became infinite ways. That was the whole motive behind the rule, he realized: not that 1 had done anything wrong, just that letting it in wrecked the one-way promise for everybody else.

He typed the if statement, ran the program, and typed 1.

"Not prime," the screen said.

"Of course," Charles told it, and saved the file.

The gym was closed for floor repairs, so Ms. Barrett had hauled a portable hoop out to the asphalt beside the baseball diamond and told the team to practice there until further notice. Hudson was supposed to be learning to run the offense, calling plays as if he were a point guard, even though the season hadn't started yet. "You wanted this," she reminded him, tossing him the ball. "So call something."

Hudson called for a pick and roll. Sharon jogged over and planted herself beside him, arms crossed, while Clarissa, playing defense for the drill, bumped into the screen and stumbled backward. That was the moment. Hudson drove past her, looked for someone to pass to, and found nothing. Sharon was still standing where she'd set the screen, watching him, her hands on her hips. Clarissa recovered and knocked the ball away before Hudson could decide what to do with it.

"Try again," Ms. Barrett said from the bleachers by the backstop, and she said it in a way that told Hudson she'd seen exactly what had gone wrong. He wasn't sure he had. The screen had worked. Clarissa had gotten caught on it. So why had nobody been open? He thought about it while Sharon's dad arrived to pick her up early, which meant Clarissa had to play Sharon's spot and Sharon jogged off waving goodbye.

Second time through, Hudson set the screen himself this time, so he could feel the play from the other side. He planted his feet, took Clarissa's bump, and then, out of instinct more than anything, pivoted and slipped toward the basket. Clarissa's dad's car horn honked somewhere beyond the outfield fence, and in that second Hudson raised his hand and Clarissa, now with the ball, fired a bounce pass that he caught in stride and laid up off the backboard. It rattled in. He stood under the rim with the strange, bright feeling of a thing clicking into place. After setting the screen, the screener doesn't stay put. The screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler. Sharon had stood still because nobody had ever told her that part, and Hudson had never known to look for it because he'd only ever watched the ball.

"Once more," Ms. Barrett called, "then I'll let you commute home before dark." She was already texting Sharon's dad, asking if Sharon could come fifteen minutes early tomorrow. "She's a component you need," she said to Hudson, nodding toward the empty spot where Sharon had been standing. "That play doesn't work without her."

The next afternoon, Sharon arrived early, water bottle in hand, and found Hudson waiting at the portable hoop. "Yesterday I didn't know what I was supposed to do after I blocked Clarissa off," she admitted. "You roll," Hudson said. "Watch me once, then I'll watch you." He set the screen, felt Clarissa crowd into him, pivoted, and cut hard toward the hoop with his hand up, calling for the ball.

The season was only two weeks old, and Gavin's new team already had a reputation. At every practice on the dusty diamond behind the middle school, the catcher argued with the pitcher, Hazel argued with the right fielder about who should catch pop-ups, and the coach's clipboard had a dent in it from being thrown once. Gavin wanted one thing that spring: a team that actually played like a team. But every time they took the field, it fell apart in a new way.

That night he found his older sister's psychology book lying open on the couch, next to a half-eaten bag of pretzels. He only meant to move it, but a page heading caught his eye: stages that groups go through. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups pass through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. Gavin read it twice. Forming was when everybody was new and polite. Storming was the arguing part. His whole team was living inside a page of his sister's homework, and nobody knew it.

He couldn't wait to test the idea, so he texted Hazel, who was the only one who would actually listen. "I think the arguing is a stage, not a disaster," he wrote. "Teams are supposed to fight at first. It's called storming." He went on to explain that after the storming came norming, when a group settles into shared habits, and after that, performing, when things finally click. Hazel replied with a wall of question marks, then added, "If this is wrong, we're going to look so weird."

The next morning Gavin noticed something small. At batting practice, Hazel handed the bat to Anne without being asked, and Anne tapped the plate for her the way Hazel liked, two quick taps. Their little rituals had started to coincide, moving in step without anyone planning it. Was this norming? He watched for it all week like a bird-watcher with a checklist. When the pitcher and catcher stopped shouting and started using the same shorthand sign for a curveball, a warm feeling spread through him that had nothing to do with the sun.

The test came Saturday. In the third inning, a pop-up sailed into the gap between Hazel and the right fielder, the exact spot that had caused three screaming matches already. Gavin held his breath. Hazel called it, the right fielder peeled away, and Hazel made the catch, and then, even stranger, the right fielder jogged over and bumped her glove like they'd planned it. Two weeks ago that ball would have started a war.

Gavin ran in from shortstop, grinning. "Stage four," he said to Hazel. "Performing."

She flipped the ball to him. "Your book better be right all season," she said, "because if we storm again, I'm blaming Tuckman."

Behind them, the coach wrote something on his clipboard, carefully, without throwing it.

The living room smelled like pizza, and the ceiling fan spun overhead like a small turbine, pushing warm air around because Dad refused to turn on the air conditioner during a "big game." Declan had the best seat, the corner of the couch, with Ty on the floor and Quinten wedged into the armchair with a plate balanced on his knee.

In the third inning, Quinten pointed his crust at the screen. "Every team has like forty numbers. Why has nobody ever got 42? That's the one I'd pick."

Ty shrugged. "Maybe it's bad luck."

Declan didn't think it was luck. Luck didn't remove a number from every team at once. He pulled out his phone and opened the roster page for the away team, then the home team, and scrolled. Nobody wore 42 on either side. He checked the bench players too, all the way down. Still nothing. That was a rule, not a coincidence, and rules had to be written down somewhere.

"Bet you a slice it's a rule," he said to Ty.

"You're on," Ty said.

Declan searched the number. He read for a minute, then put the phone face down on the cushion. "In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team. First time any professional athlete got honored that way."

"Retired how?" Quinten asked.

"The number. Nobody on any team wears it. Ever since then."

Quinten squinted at the screen. "Wait, there's a 42 on the mound."

They all leaned in. Declan paused the picture and checked the pitcher against the roster. "That's a 2 and a 4. Number 24. My sister's TV is so small the numbers squish together."

Ty groaned and slid his plate over. Declan took the biggest slice, which was a legitimate prize, since he had won it fairly.

"You knew that already," Ty said.

"I didn't. That's why I checked the rosters before I said anything."

Quinten was quiet for a while, chewing. During the seventh-inning stretch he said, "So if Robinson wore 42, and nobody can wear it now, then every time you see a 42 somewhere, like on a shirt, that's basically a sign pointing at one guy."

"It's like his number went into hibernation," Ty said. "Asleep, but still there."

Declan shook his head. "Not asleep. Retired. A bear wakes up."

Ms. Ndlovu, who had come over to watch with the neighbors and was sitting by the door, raised her cup without looking away from the screen. "Play ball," she said.

Alexander had been fast his whole life, which was exactly the problem. In the schoolyard, fast meant winning, because races there lasted ten seconds and ended at the fence. The park track was different. Two laps around it made eight hundred metres, and Mr. Novák had entered him in the district meet anyway, even after watching him run exactly once.

"You went out like your shoes were on fire," Bella said from the bleachers, where she was supposed to be timing him with her phone. "Then you looked like the fire won."

It was true. In his first time trial, Alexander had sprinted the opening lap so hard that by the far turn of the second one he was jogging, and Mael, who wasn't even racing, had caught up to him while eating a granola bar. Alexander had laughed then, because it was funny, but the loss had sat with him all week. Maybe being fast in short bursts wasn't the same as being fast where it counted.

On Saturday morning the three of them met at the track, and Mr. Novák marked the start line with a cone. "Two laps," he said, and walked off toward the storage shed before Alexander could ask anything else, which was his way.

Alexander stood on the line and tried to make the invisible visible. He couldn't see his own energy, couldn't measure how much a lap would cost him, but he could see the track, and the track was honest. Eight hundred metres meant the first lap and then the second lap, nothing more, and if he spent everything in the first one, the second lap would collect the debt. A plan began to germinate somewhere behind his ribs: run the first lap like a boy who had somewhere to be, not like a boy being chased. He thought of his father complaining about prices at the grocery store, how everything cost more now, and joked to Bella, "If I sprint the first lap, the second lap charges me inflation."

"Write that on a T-shirt," said Bella. "I'll buy two."

Mael ran beside him as a pacer, calling the splits. The first lap felt almost insultingly easy. "Sixty-eight seconds," Mael shouted as they crossed the line the first time, and every nerve in Alexander's legs screamed at him to go, because going was what he did. He remembered the granola bar instead. He held, he held, and then at the back stretch of lap two he let the leash out slowly, and something unexpected happened: he got faster while everyone else's plan fell apart. A runner from the other end of the park, who had blazed past them early, was suddenly shrinking ahead of him, legs gone wobbly. The boy even started pumping his arms and driving for the finish. But the finish wasn't there. That was still one lap away, and the boy didn't seem to know it.

Alexander passed him at the final bend and Bella was screaming numbers that didn't matter anymore. He crossed the line, bent double, and Mael clapped him on the back so hard he coughed.

"Two fourteen," Bella announced, holding up her phone like a trophy.

Mr. Novák came back from the shed with a clipboard, looked at the time, and said nothing, which meant everything. Later, walking home, Alexander found himself thinking about the runner who had kicked a lap too early, and about his own schoolyard self, the fastest kid at the fence. He wasn't sure which of them he'd been that first day at the park. Maybe both.

"Same time next Saturday?" Mael asked.

"Bring two granola bars," Alexander said. "One for each lap."

Beatrice set the microscope case on the flat rock beside the creek and knelt to open it, because Mr. Gauthier had said the seventh-grade trail lab counted the same as a classroom lab, and her grade in science needed the help. Her job was to peel a paper-thin layer from an onion, mount it on a slide, and label three parts: the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. The wall she could see already, brick-shaped boxes in neat rows. The nucleus showed up as a dark dot once she added the stain. The membrane was the problem. It lay so flat against the wall that it might as well have been invisible, and her diagram, worth half the marks, had an empty arrow pointing at nothing.

Aveer crouched beside her with the field kit, holding a dropper bottle of plain creek water and, in his other hand, a second bottle he had filled from his own lunch, the salty water left over from his pretzels. "You could just evaluate what you've got," he said, squinting through the eyepiece. "Draw the wall, draw the nucleus, and take the partial marks."

"I need the whole diagram," Beatrice said. She thought about it while a jay screeched somewhere up the slope. She had a hypothetical idea, the kind Mr. Gauthier liked: if the membrane was pressed flat against the wall like a wet shirt on a window, maybe it would show if something pulled it loose. She didn't know what could pull it, but she knew she could test the idea fast. "Give me your pretzel water."

"You want my spit-water on your slide?"

"It's just salt water. Hand it over." He did, and she laid one careful drop at the edge of the coverslip and watched it seep under. For a moment nothing changed, and she held her breath, afraid she had flooded the whole slide and ruined everything. Then, slowly, row by row, each cell seemed to shrink from the inside. Something thin and clear peeled away from every brick-shaped wall and crumpled toward the center, like a balloon letting go of the inside of a box. The arrow on her diagram finally had something to point at.

Agam came over from the tree station to see why she was grinning. "What happened to them?"

"Salt water pulls the water out of the cells, so the membrane shrinks away from the wall," Beatrice said, already sketching. "Aveer says it's called plasmolysis."

"It's on the poster in the classroom," Aveer admitted. "I read it this morning."

Beatrice laughed and wrote the word across the top of her page, then bent back to the eyepiece to catch the last row before the light shifted. "Draw fast," she said, holding out a pencil to Agam.

The computer lab smelled like warm plastic and the lemon cleaner Ms. Sadeghi sprayed on the keyboards every Friday, no matter what. Jonathan had claimed the machine by the window because its screen didn't flicker, and he was supposed to be finishing his social studies slide about inflation, which so far consisted of one title and a picture of a sad coin. Behind him, Kye was typing fast, the way he did when he was pretending to work.

"Did you see it?" Kye whispered, sliding his chair over. He turned his monitor so only Jonathan could see. On the screen was a screenshot, clearly a screenshot because of the clock and battery icon at the top, showing a message that read: "Maelly thinks she's the boss of the group project. Someone should tell her the universe doesn't revolve around her." Below it, in the group chat for the whole class, Maelly had written: "real classy, whoever this is." The screenshot's header showed it came from a private chat, just two names.

Jonathan looked from the screenshot to Kye, then to Maelly, three rows up, arms crossed, staring at her screen like it had insulted her family. "Who sent it to the group?" he asked.

Kye shrugged, but the shrug was too fast. Jonathan thought about it. A private chat had two people in it, the sender and the receiver. The sender wouldn't share it. So the receiver had, and the receiver knew exactly who wrote it. The message was only as secret as the person who read it. "You told someone," Jonathan said quietly. "You sent it to one person to complain, and that person pasted it into the group."

"It was private," Kye hissed. "Between us. I said don't show anyone."

"You said that to the wrong guy, apparently." Jonathan turned back to his slide. The coin looked even sadder now. "If it got screenshotted, it isn't private anymore. It's as private as the person you sent it to, and that person has a big mouth."

Ms. Sadeghi walked the rows, pausing at Maelly's computer, then at Kye's. Her expression stayed neutral, which somehow made it worse. "Whoever needs to apologize," she said to the room, not to anyone in particular, "I'd coordinate that soon, before I have to." On Maelly's screen, the group project document sat open and barren except for her name at the top, all alone.

Kye stood up. His chair squeaked the length of the lab. He stopped beside Maelly's desk and said, so quietly Jonathan almost missed it, "That was about somebody else. Same name. Different Maelly."

Maelly looked at him for a long moment and typed one word into the document: "Prove it."

Rose sat on her bed with her phone balanced on her knees, watching the group chat light up. Forty-three messages had appeared since dinner, and all of them were about Volt Blast.

"It actually works," Fanny had written. "I drank one before practice and shaved ten whole seconds off my mile. TEN."

Jericho had replied with three lightning bolts. Mr. Quinn, who somehow ended up in every chat he wasn't supposed to be in, had typed, "Is that the one with the green label? My nephew sells it."

Rose typed slowly, then deleted, then typed again. She wanted to believe Fanny. But ten seconds was a lot, and Fanny had also once claimed a magnetic bracelet cured her hiccups. Rose had spent her leisure time that whole weekend reading about things like that, which maybe said something about her, but she didn't mind.

"Question," she posted. "Did you time yourself before the Volt Blast too?"

Fanny answered with a shrugging emoji, which was not an answer. Rose flopped back on her pillow and stared at the ceiling. She remembered the hiccup bracelet. She remembered how Fanny's hiccups had stopped exactly when she decided, really decided, the bracelet worked. Rose had borrowed the bracelet later and hiccuped for half an hour like a defective frog.

She sat up and made a plan. It was simple: she'd fill one bottle with Volt Blast and one bottle, an identical one, with water plus a drop of lemon so it looked the same. Then Jericho would drink one, run the mile, and later drink the other and run again. He wouldn't know which was which. Rose would be the only one holding the secret, and she'd hold it like a hot potato.

At the track the next morning, Jericho stretched dramatically. "I can feel it already," he announced, after drinking bottle one. "Tingling. Powerful. Like a horse."

"Run," said Rose.

He ran the mile in 7:52 and collapsed in the grass, indifferent to the ants marching over his shoe. On Sunday they came back, and he drank bottle two, the lemon water, and ran it in 7:49.

"Wait," Jericho wheezed. "Which one was the real one yesterday?"

"The real one was Sunday," Rose said. "Yesterday was lemon water."

Jericho lay in the grass, processing. "So Monday I felt like a horse because I believed I was a horse."

"There's a name for it," Rose said. "It's called the placebo effect. When people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, like a sugar pill, just because they expect it to help."

Fanny arrived then, holding a Volt Blast. She looked at Jericho sprawled on the track, looked at Rose's two empty bottles, and took a very long, slow sip. "I'm still buying it," she said. "It tastes like green apples."

Jericho raised one finger from the grass without lifting his head. "Get me one."

The permission slip had prescribed long pants and closed shoes for the field trip, so Joshua had swapped his sandals for sneakers before the bus pulled away from school. He sat across the aisle from Haya, who was reading the fire safety pamphlet for the third time, and behind Khaleesi, who kept turning around to ask whether they would see a real dog. When they arrived at the fire station, the smell hit him first, diesel and burnt toast from the kitchen, and then the trucks, enormous and polished, with hoses coiled on their sides like a giant intestine.

A firefighter led them past the trucks to a wide gray mat on the garage floor. Beside it hung a poster with big orange letters. Joshua leaned close to read it while the others crowded toward the trucks. The poster said that if your clothes catch fire, the rule is stop, drop and roll, because running feeds the flames more oxygen. He read it twice, then a third time, mouthing the words. Running feeds the flames. That was strange. His legs had always seemed like the answer to every problem, and here was a poster telling him the opposite.

"Who wants to be a volunteer?" the firefighter asked, standing on the mat. Khaleesi's hand shot up so fast it nearly hit Haya in the chin. The firefighter pointed at her, and she bounced forward, then froze halfway, her face going pink. "In front of everybody?" she said, half to herself. Joshua could see her heels already edging backward.

"You can do it," Joshua called out. "I'll go after you, so you won't be the only one rolling around on the floor looking silly." Ms. Nasser, who had been counting heads by the door, gave him a small nod, and Khaleesi's shoulders came down from around her ears.

"Stop, drop and roll," Khaleesi said to herself like a spell, and she did it, stopping dead, dropping to the mat, and rolling until the firefighter called out that the imaginary flames were out. The class cheered. Joshua went next and rolled so hard he bumped into her knee, and they both cracked up.

On the way to the smoke room, where the firefighter warned them that smoke was toxic and to stay low, Haya tugged Joshua's sleeve. "Earlier," she said, "when the alarm went off in the kitchen, that cook ran out flapping his apron. Why did he run, if running makes it worse?"

Joshua thought about the poster, and about how nobody had told the cook. "Because he panicked before he could think," he said. "The rule works only if you know it before you need it." He looked at Khaleesi, still brushing mat fuzz off her elbow, and decided he was going to teach the rule to his little brother tonight, before dinner, on the living room carpet.

Chase stood at the kitchen counter on Thursday night, staring at the permission slip for the geography bee. His name was on the list for Monday's assembly, in front of the whole school. His mom had signed the form, which meant there was no backing out. His hands were cold and his stomach hurt, even though he had not eaten since lunch. He assumed the stomach ache was from the cafeteria pizza, until he noticed his shoulders were up near his ears and he had been grinding his teeth since dinner.

He texted Winter, who had done the spelling bee last year and had not fainted, which made her the expert as far as he was concerned. She called him back right away.

"Did you eat something weird?" she asked.

"Pizza. But my hands are cold too, and I keep grinding my teeth."

"That's not pizza. That's stress. Your body does stuff before your brain catches on." She paused. "Remember Arizona at the science fair? She was tracing a square on the desk with her finger before her turn, over and over. It's called box breathing. Four counts in, four counts holding, four counts out, four counts holding, then you just repeat the pattern. The square she drew had one side for each count of four."

"So I breathe in for four seconds, then hold for four, then out for four, then hold again?"

"That's the whole thing. You can draw the square on your leg if your hands shake, like hers did."

He hung up and tried it at the counter, drawing a square on the countertop with one finger. In for four counts along the top edge. Hold for four down the side. Out for four along the bottom. Hold for four going back up. After five squares his shoulders had come down off his ears. His hands were still cool but not ice. He kept going until the microwave clock changed by two minutes.

The stomach ache faded, which proved Winter's point. His body had been running an alarm with no fire. The irony was that the thing he feared, standing up Monday, was being ruined in advance by the fear itself, in his own kitchen, three days early.

There was still the night problem. Every time a bee came up, he lay awake replaying the time in fourth grade when he blanked on the word "isthmus" and a kid in the second row had laughed for a solid minute. He decided to test an idea: what if sleep needed a pattern too, the same way breathing did? He made a routine and wrote it on the fridge whiteboard. Phone on the counter at nine, not in his room. Same three stretches. Lights out at nine thirty, every night, bee or no bee, starting tonight.

Friday he slept through the night for the first time all week. Saturday he did the routine again and added the square breathing while lying in bed, finger tracing the shape on the blanket. Sunday night he caught his shoulders climbing toward his ears while he thought about the auditorium, so he ran ten slow squares until his jaw unclenched.

Monday morning, before the bus, he practiced one last time at the counter. His mom watched him draw the invisible square on the countertop and pour his cereal with a steady hand.

"Feeling ready?" she asked.

"Approximately," he said, and traced the first edge. "In, two, three, four."

Grandpa's laptop had a sticky E key, so every time Scarlett typed "SUM," it came out "SUME" and the formula sulked at her in a little green triangle. She pried the key up with a butter knife, blew a crumb out from under it, and tried again. This time the cell at the bottom of her Allowance column flipped to a number: 46.75. She had actually done it. She had made a formula that added a whole column by itself.

"Whoa," said Jeremi, leaning over her shoulder at the kitchen table. "It did math without you."

"It did math without me," Scarlett agreed, and did a small drumroll on the table. Grandpa's plan was simple. He kept a jar of coins, and he'd promised to accelerate the rewards if Scarlett tracked his mysterious candy spending for one week and showed him a chart by Sunday dinner. Sunday dinner was in ninety minutes.

Aryana arrived with the coin jar hugged against her chest like a baby. "I counted it last night while you two were fighting with the E key. Grandpa spends the most on licorice. I want him to see that in giant letters."

"Bars," Scarlett said. "Not letters, bars." She selected her candy data, clicked Insert, chose the first chart that looked right, and hit Enter.

The chart appeared sideways. The licorice bar lay flat along the bottom like it had fallen asleep. Aryana gasped as if the computer had committed a crime. "It's broken. Fix it before Grandpa sees. He'll blame me, I'm holding the jar."

Scarlett frowned at the screen. Every chart she'd ever imagined had bars standing up. She scrolled through the chart options and found two names sitting side by side: column chart and bar chart. She picked the column chart instead, and the bars straightened up into tall towers, licorice towering over everything. "It wasn't broken," she said slowly. "I picked the sideways one. A bar chart has horizontal bars. A column chart has vertical ones."

"So a bar chart isn't even a column chart," Jeremi said, poking the screen. "That's like a hot dog not being a sandwich."

"It's exactly like that," Scarlett said. She added a title, and because the anonymous culprit behind the missing chocolate coins deserved blame, she labeled the licorice bar "GRANDPA'S DOWNFALL."

At dinner, Grandpa held the laptop at arm's length, squinted, then laughed so hard he nearly dropped his fork. "Licorice, my downfall indeed." He slid three chocolate coins across the table to Aryana, who caught them midair.

"Your hierarchy of candy is officially exposed," Scarlett told him, tapping the tall licorice tower one last time.

Audrey's family was supposed to leave the campsite by nine, but the fire pit was still warm. Her dad had dumped a bucket of water on it an hour ago, and the ashes had stopped smoking, but when Audrey waved her hand over them, she could still feel heat, like a radiator in spring. "It's fine," her dad said, loading the cooler into the trunk. "Water beats fire. That's the whole fight."

Audrey wasn't so sure. She crouched beside the stone ring and studied the ashes. The top layer was grey and dead-looking, but a piece of charred log near the edge had a dull orange line along its underside, like a secret. She deduced that the water had only drowned the surface, and that the hot part was hiding underneath, where the water hadn't reached. If that was true, then pouring more water on top would do the same thing twice: cool the lid, leave the stove.

She found Emmie and Gerald at the picnic table, scraping maple syrup off their fingers with napkins. "I need your bucket," Audrey said. Gerald groaned. "The fire's out. I saw steam. Steam means out." "Steam means the water's out," Audrey said. "The fire might still be under there." Emmie, whose goal in life was a scholarship to a science camp where she could set things on fire legally, stood up so fast she knocked over the syrup bottle.

Audrey filled the bucket at the pump and dumped it on the ashes. Then she took a stick and stirred, digging down through the grey layer into black chunks underneath. A puff of steam hissed up, smelling like wet charcoal and old hot dogs. "Told you," she said. She poured on a second bucket, drowning everything until the water pooled in the low spots of the pit, dark and gritty. She kept her voice neutral when she said "touch test" to herself, because part of her wanted to brag.

The back of her hand hovered over the ashes. Warm. She stirred again, knocked the chunks apart, and dumped a third bucket. This time, when she touched the ashes with her fingertips, they were cool and clammy, like wet sidewalk. No orange lines anywhere. Gerald poked a black chunk with his shoe. "Okay," he said. "That was actually kind of great."

Her dad leaned against the car, arms crossed, watching. "Where'd you learn that?" "Nobody told me," Audrey said. "The middle was still hot, so the middle needed the water." She rinsed her hands at the pump, dried them on her shorts, and picked up the last bag of marshmallows. "You owe me the window seat," she said.

The first time Lea ran the eight hundred metres in gym class, she sprinted off the line like the ground behind her was on fire. She led the whole first lap, her ponytail streaming, and Landen shouted, "You're winning!" Then somewhere on the second lap her legs turned to noodles, and five people passed her before the finish. She ended up sixth and spent the walk back to the changeroom trying not to cry.

Mr. Nakamura handed out strips of paper the next day. "Time trials on Friday," he said. "Eight hundred metres again." Lea stared at hers. Sixth place she could live with. Sixth place while feeling like a melting snowman, she could not.

At lunch she watched Landen eat his sandwich, and an idea began to bother her. "Landen, on Monday, when I blew up, where was I at the start of the second lap?" Landen thought with his mouth full. "First. Easily first. Then Yanis passed you by the water fountain, and after that it was like a parade going by you." A parade. Lea drew two circles in her notebook. She had gone out fast, faster than a pace she could hold, and she had slowed sharply on the second lap. Every runner who had passed her had looked comfortable on lap one, like they were saving something. She wrote underneath: fast first lap, slow second lap. Test: even laps.

Wednesday after school she tried it on the track alone, with Yanis holding the stopwatch. "Don't fly out like a startled pigeon," Yanis advised. "Noted," said Lea. She counted her steps, held back when her legs begged to zoom, and crossed the first lap slower than she ever had on purpose. It felt almost embarrassing. Then, on the second lap, she found she still had something left, and she sped up instead of slowing down. Her two laps were nearly the same time. Yanis showed her the watch and raised both eyebrows. "Huh."

Friday, Mr. Nakamura blew his whistle. Lea stuck to her plan even when a girl from Mr. Nakamura's other class tore away at the start, arms pumping, clearly the fastest thing on the track. Lea ran her own race. Sure enough, on the back curve of the second lap, the fast girl began to fade, her steps shortening, and one by one the parade went by her: Lea included, right on the final straight.

Lea finished second, breathing hard, her shirt starting to perspire in the cool air, and Landen wrapped her in a hug that smelled like peanut butter. "You passed that girl like she was a mailbox!" Yanis jogged over, grinning, and said, "You looked durable out there. Like a good pair of boots." Lea laughed. She had felt many things during that race, but boot-like was new. "That girl who faded," she said, pointing to the leader-turned-mailbox, who was now bent over, hands on her knees. Yanis nodded. "Happens every year. Somebody always burns it all on lap one." Lea thought about walking over to tell the girl what she had figured out, because she knew exactly how that felt. Empathy, her mom called it. She grabbed her water bottle, trotted across the infield, and said, "Hey. Want to see something I wrote in my notebook?"

The argument started before homeroom, when Alexi held a phone screen up to Mila's face and demanded, "Tell me this dress is white and gold."

Mila looked. The photo showed a lacy dress on a hanger, shot in bad lighting. "It's blue and black," she said. "Obviously."

Alexi made a sound like a kettle. Leonardo leaned over from the next desk and studied the same screen. "White and gold," he said. "Sorry, Alexi, I'm on your side, but that thing is white and gold."

"You're agreeing with me by disagreeing with her," Alexi said. "That counts as winning."

By lunch, the whole cafeteria had picked sides. Mr. Lombardi, who monitored lunch duty, walked past the table, glanced at the phone, and said, "Blue and black," then kept walking with his tray of meatloaf as though nothing unusual had occurred. Mila's table erupted. Someone at the far table claimed white and gold, and a seventh grader stood on a chair to conduct a poll by shouting.

Mila kept thinking about a Saturday three weeks earlier, when her cousin had gotten a mild concussion at the skate park and spent the evening in a dim room. At one point her aunt held up a translucent curtain and asked what color the light through it looked like, testing her cousin's eyes, and her cousin had said one thing and her aunt had sworn the light was another. The doctors had shrugged. Brains, they said, report things differently sometimes. Mila had filed it away as a weird family story. Now she wasn't so sure it was just a family thing.

She had a theory, and she wanted to test it. If two people saw the same photo differently, then the same two people should still agree on something ordinary, like a marker. She borrowed a blue marker from Mr. Lombardi's desk on the way to fifth period, marched it back to Alexi, and held it beside the phone. "What color is this?"

"Blue," Alexi said. "Duh."

"And the dress?"

"White and gold. Next to a blue marker. Which is insane, and yet."

Leonardo tried it too and got the same split, marker blue, dress gold. Mila revised her first idea, which had been that Alexi was simply wrong on purpose to be annoying. That theory was dead. Something stranger was going on, and it clearly wasn't about eyesight in any ordinary way.

After school she looked it up in the computer lab. The photo had gone viral in February 2015, and the whole internet had split exactly the same way, some people seeing blue and black, others white and gold. She scrolled further and found the ending of the mystery: the real dress was blue and black.

She ran the search result out to the courtyard, where Alexi and Leonardo were waiting by the bike racks. "Okay," she said, holding up the screen. "The actual dress is blue and black. It's a real dress, in a store."

Alexi stared at the screen. "Then my eyes are lying to me."

"Mine too," said Leonardo, "which is somehow worse."

Mila grinned and put the phone away. "Tomorrow I'm bringing a printout. Let's find out what Mr. Lombardi's meatloaf really is."

The bus rattled past the hardware store where workers were going to renovate the old front, and Daniel barely glanced at it. He had the sign-up sheet for Saturday's three-on-three basketball tournament folded in his pocket, and he was down to the last roster spot. Samy slid into the seat beside him, backpack first.

"Tell me you picked someone," Samy said.

"Not yet. It's between Nolan and Marcus from Ms. Santos's class. I wrote down every game they played at lunch this week." Daniel unfolded a page of pencil marks. "Nolan scored eight, nine, eight, nine, ten. Marcus scored zero, zero, eighteen, eighteen, eight. Both of them add up to forty-four points, so their average is the same."

Samy leaned over to read the page. "Then flip a coin."

"It's not the same," Daniel said. "Watch." He covered Marcus's scores with his thumb, then uncovered them one at a time. "Nolan gives you eight or nine every single game. Marcus gives you nothing half the time. If he has a bad game Saturday, we're playing two against three." He tried it again with the numbers, moving them around, and the pattern stayed put. Same average, but the games underneath it looked nothing alike.

"So you're saying a coin flip is wrong," Samy said.

"I'm saying the average can't tell them apart. Something else has to." Daniel tapped the pencil against the seat back. The bus stopped, and a group of sixth graders pushed past, arguing about a video game ranking. Daniel listened to one of them insist he was ranked higher even though his percentage of wins was lower, because he had played twice as many matches. Numbers squashing a whole season into one line, Daniel thought, just like his lunch scores.

At the next stop Marcus got on. He dropped into the seat across the aisle, saw the sheet, and raised his eyebrows. "You picking me or Nolan?"

"Neither of you yet," Daniel said. "You both average the same points. But Nolan's steady, and you're either brilliant or invisible, and I can't tell which one shows up on a given day."

Marcus grinned. "Take Nolan then. Even I don't know which one shows up."

Daniel circled Nolan's name. "Tell you what, though. If we're losing at halftime, you're my first substitution."

"Deal," said Marcus, and held out his fist over the aisle.

Grace's phone buzzed against her math homework, and she almost knocked over her water glass grabbing it. The new class group chat, the one Ms. Reyes had approved on Friday, already had sixty-two messages, and Grace had left it alone for twenty minutes. Twenty minutes. She scrolled up through a wall of capital letters. SOMEONE TOOK MY SPOT IN THE LAB LINE, Myriam had written, and then Imran had answered in capitals too, and then three other kids she barely knew had piled on, each message louder than the last, as if shouting were contagious, like a virus spreading through the chat one ALL CAPS message at a time.

Ms. Reyes had put Grace in charge of the chat's rules, which had seemed like an honor at the time and now felt like being handed a leaking bucket. Grace sat cross-legged on her bed, chewing the end of her pencil. She knew the rules for talking to people face to face. You didn't shout at Myriam in the hallway, and you didn't announce embarrassing things in front of the whole class. But online, everyone seemed to forget. And the worst part was that Grace couldn't tell what was a joke and what was real anger. Myriam's message could be either. That was the hidden problem, and Grace couldn't see it directly, only its shadow: sixty-two messages, escalating.

She typed a test. "Hey, Myriam, were you actually mad or just joking?" The reply came fast. "joking obviously." Then, a second later: "everyone thought i was mad though." Grace sat very still. That was it. Myriam's tone had come across wrong because caps and no punctuation and no face, all the things that normally told you how someone felt, were missing. In private, between the two of them in direct messages, Myriam wrote calmly, lowercase, patient. In the public chat, she performed for an audience. Same girl, two different voices.

Grace needed rules, but she wanted them to be official, not just made up by her. "Did anyone ever actually write down manners for the internet?" she muttered, and pulled her laptop over. She searched, expecting nothing, expecting that online manners were as extinct as the dinosaurs. Instead a page came up that made her sit up straight. One of the first written guides to online manners, called "Netiquette Guidelines," had been published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855. She read it twice. 1995. Before she was born, before smartphones, and people had already noticed the exact problem in her chat: it was hard to read tone, and shouting in capitals made things worse.

At school the next morning, Ms. Reyes gave the class five minutes of chat business before the lab. Grace stood up, her ears radiating heat, and held her phone like a tiny podium.

"Turns out this isn't a new problem," she said. "There's a real guide. It's called the 'Netiquette Guidelines,' and it was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855." A couple of kids snickered at the number. "Before any of us existed," Grace said, "and it says don't type in all caps, because people can't tell if you're joking or yelling." She paused. "So I made us a rule. Public chat, normal letters only. Jokes get an emoji or a 'jk' so nobody panics."

Imran raised his hand slowly. "So yesterday, when Myriam wrote in caps, and I wrote back in caps, we were both yelling at nothing?" Myriam spun around in her seat.

"We were fighting a war that didn't exist," she said, and started laughing, and Imran laughed too, and Grace watched sixty-two messages of pretend anger collapse into three seconds of real giggling. Then she pulled up the chat and pinned the new rules to the top.

The carrier wobbled in Evan's hands all the way from the car to his bedroom, and inside it the kitten, Nutmeg, yowled like a tiny storm. "Welcome home," Evan whispered, setting the carrier on his bed. His dad had signed the papers at the shelter an hour ago, and the woman at the desk had said the words Evan couldn't stop thinking about: "She's microchipped."

Kenzi and Drew showed up before he'd even latched the carrier door. "You said it has a chip," Drew said, leaning over Nutmeg, who flattened her ears and backed into the corner. "So where's the map?"

Evan pulled out his phone, grinning. That was the plan. He'd imagined it on the drive home: a little orange dot, Nutmeg's dot, moving across a map of the neighborhood whenever she squeezed through a fence or vanished under the porch. He typed "microchip tracker" into the search bar and waited, thumb bouncing against his knee.

Nothing came up that looked like a map. The results were pages about scanners and ID numbers, and the more he scrolled, the more his grin went brittle around the edges. Kenzi took the phone, read for a minute, and handed it back. "It says a microchip has no GPS and can't track where an animal is," she said slowly. "It only gives its ID number when a scanner is held close."

"Close like how close?" Drew asked.

"Like at the vet's office," Kenzi said.

Evan stared at the phone, then at the kitten. "So if Nutmeg runs away, the chip won't tell me where she is. It just tells whoever finds her who she is." He thought about the dots on the map he'd imagined, all those invisible little signals he'd assumed were flying around, and felt almost embarrassed. He had wanted so badly to see that map that he'd read the word "chip" and made up the rest. That was a bias, he decided, toward good news.

"So we test it," Drew said, because Drew always wanted to test things.

Nutmeg chose that moment to bolt. She shot out of the carrier, ricocheted off a pillow, and vanished somewhere behind Evan's desk. Evan lunged, dropped the phone, and crouched with his cheek on the carpet, peering into the dark gap where two amber eyes blinked back at him.

He held the phone out flat on the floor, screen glowing. "Nope," he reported. "No dot. I have no idea where she is except that I can see her."

Kenzi laughed and grabbed the half-full carrier. "Then we catch her the old way. Drew, get the string."

Nutmeg's tail twitched once at the edge of the shadow.

The gate of Hillcrest Cemetery was old enough that it squeaked in two different notes, and George noticed that the low note came when he pushed it slowly and the high note when he pushed it fast. Everything had a mechanism, his dad always said, even squeaky gates. George had come with his class on a foggy Saturday morning because Mr. Jung, who took care of the grounds, had invited the school to see the historic Jewish section before it got restored.

"You two are coming with me," Mr. Jung said to Lane and Annabel, because the teacher wanted the Jewish kids to help read the worn headstones. "You're cousins, right? You can translate faster than I can."

"Faster than each other, anyway," Annabel said in her assertive way, the way she talked in class when she was sure she was right and wanted everyone to know it. "Lane's from the other side of town. Different synagogue."

They walked between rows of stones with Hebrew letters softened by a hundred winters. George trailed behind them, thinking about something he had wondered for weeks. His grandmother had died in the spring, and he had overheard adults at the funeral saying things about where she was now, and the strange part was that they didn't all say the same thing. He had a hypothesis, which was a word he'd learned in science class: maybe the differences weren't random. Maybe they followed a pattern, and he could find it by asking the same question twice.

"So," he said, keeping his voice casual, "what happens after you die? Like, in your religion." He asked Lane first.

Lane wiped lichen off a stone with his sleeve. "The dead will be resurrected. That's what we believe. Someday, at the end, they rise up again."

Annabel frowned at him like he'd said something backwards. "That's not what we say at our synagogue. We focus on this life. What matters is what you do now, how you live."

They stared at each other. "We're both Jewish," Lane said. "How can we believe two different things?"

George's pulse did a small jump, the way it did when an experiment worked. Here was his evidence. Lane's family was Orthodox, Annabel's was Reform, and the two answers split exactly along that line, the way iron filings line up with a magnet. He could deduce the rule from only two data points, which was thin, but it was a start. He wanted more.

"Mr. Jung," he called, "do you know the families buried here? Which were which?"

Mr. Jung ran his thumb along a carved name. "Some of these stones have hands carved on them, some have stars, some have nothing at all. Different congregations, different centuries. Even among the Jewish families here, the old records show they didn't all describe the world to come the same way." He handed George a clipboard. "Write down the symbols, row by row. Let's see what we find."

So George counted. Hands, forty-one. Plain stones, sixty-three. Stars, nine. He graphed it in his notebook, and the numbers clustered in sections, as if whole groups had sorted themselves by belief before they ever got buried. He was still puzzling over what the mechanism could be, whether people chose neighbors who shared their hopes, when Lane pointed at a small stone near the fence.

"That one has both," Lane said. "Hands and a star. Same grave."

"Two families?" Annabel guessed.

"Or one family that split," George said slowly, "like you two."

Annabel opened her mouth, closed it, and then started to laugh. "Okay, that's actually possible. Lane, our great-great-something might be right there."

Lane got down on his knees in the wet grass to read the half-vanished name. "Gershon," he said. "Gershon, son of Leah."

"Then we're related to a mystery," Annabel said, kneeling beside him.

Brooklyn slapped three sticky notes onto the lunch table like she was dealing cards. "Topic is banning homework. I say we win this thing."

Wilson leaned over his tray. "Your first note just says homework is bad."

"That's my claim," Brooklyn said. "The point being argued. Write it down, Wilson, that's your whole job."

Greta pulled the note toward her. "And the other two?"

"Reasons homework is bad." Brooklyn grinned. "Reason one, it ruins weekends. Reason two, it turns kids into zombies."

Mr. Rao, who ran the debate club and apparently had radar for sticky notes, appeared behind them with his coffee. "Zombies," he repeated. "Interesting. In the Toulmin model, a claim is the point being argued, and the grounds, sometimes called the data, are the evidence that supports it. So." He pointed at each note in turn. "Claim. Opinion. Opinion." Then he walked off toward the vending machine, humming.

Brooklyn stared at the notes. Last year she had done this exact thing, she remembered, standing up in Ms. Park's class to declare that school lunches were a crime, and Tomas Reyes had simply asked, "Says who?" She'd had nothing. She had sat down next to the humid radiator and felt her face burn hotter than it.

"Not again," she muttered. "Wilson, we need data. Real data."

Wilson raised his hand like they were still in class. "My cousin had a double ear infection last month and still had to do a math packet. Is that data?"

"It's a story," Greta said. "One cousin is not a pattern."

But Brooklyn was already flipping her notebook open. Here was her idea, and it was so simple she felt silly for not testing it sooner: she would put every sentence they planned to say through one question, "where's the evidence," and anything that died there got cut. "Homework ruins weekends," she read aloud. "Evidence?"

Wilson shrugged. "We could count how many kids did homework last Saturday."

Greta grabbed a fresh sheet of paper. "We survey the whole grade at lunch. Two questions. Then we have numbers."

They spent the next lunch stationed outside the cafeteria, sweating in the humid hallway air, collecting answers from anyone who would stop. Twenty-eight kids, and nineteen of them had done at least an hour of schoolwork on Saturday. Two claimed they were zombies already, which Greta crossed out.

"So the claim is homework takes weekend time," Brooklyn said slowly, writing, "and the grounds are nineteen out of twenty-eight students. And then we need the part that connects them. Why do those numbers prove the claim?"

Wilson squinted at her page. "Because an hour on Saturday is an hour not spent riding bikes?"

"Elaborate," Brooklyn said, tapping her pen.

"Because... time is finite? Like, you can't get it back?" Wilson threw his hands up. "I don't know, it sounds smarter when I say it out loud."

"It sounds like a link," Brooklyn said. "Claim, grounds, link. Every point gets all three or it goes in the trash." She held up the zombie note, considered it with great ceremony, and dropped it into the garbage can by the door.

At Thursday's practice debate, the other team stood up and announced that homework built character, that homework taught discipline, that homework was a sacred tradition. Brooklyn stood, pointed at their first speaker, and asked, "Where's your evidence?"

Nobody said anything for a full five seconds. Mr. Rao smiled into his coffee.

Brooklyn leaned toward the microphone. "Nineteen out of twenty-eight students, folks. Check the sticky notes."

Aaron spread the two newspapers across the coffee table in his living room, one on top of the other like an archaeologist about to excavate a buried city. Dexter flopped onto the couch beside him with his laptop. "Same rally, same day, same park," Aaron said, tapping the first headline. "Read this one out loud."

"'Thousands of protesters filled the square demanding cleaner water,'" Dexter read. Then he slid the laptop over. "And this site says, 'Rioters clashed with police downtown.'" He frowned at both. "Okay, that's weird. It feels like two different things happened."

Aaron remembered their teacher saying the class project had to compare how the same story got told in different places, and he had shrugged at the time. Now the shrug felt brittle, like it might crack, because the difference was sitting right in front of him. He read both headlines again, slower. Thousands of peaceful people versus a violent mob. Same crowd. The only thing that had changed was the word.

"Try this," Aaron said. He copied both headlines into a blank document and swapped the words. "'Rioters filled the square demanding cleaner water.' Ugh. I picture broken windows, and they were just holding signs." Dexter typed fast, then leaned back. "'Protesters clashed with police.' That almost sounds reasonable, like a disagreement." He looked at Aaron. "So the word does it. The word pushes you." Aaron nodded. "My dad says they're loaded words. They carry a feeling, like a backpack full of rocks. 'Protesters' makes you feel a little empathy for them. 'Rioters' makes you want them stopped."

Then Dexter spun the laptop toward the TV, where a commercial was playing. A famous basketball player grinned at the camera and said he only drank a certain sports drink, and everyone was drinking it, millions of fans, everybody. "See, that's the other stuff," Dexter said, counting on his fingers. "Celebrity guy says buy it, and then they tell you the whole world already did. My little sister fell for that last week with some sneaker thing." Aaron laughed. "They're stacking the tricks. Famous person plus 'everyone has it' plus, I bet, some loaded word in there." He grabbed a pen and circled "revolutionary" in the ad's caption on the screen. "That's a loaded word too."

They worked until the room went dim, marking every technique they could find in a pile of ads and headlines. Aaron's list had three columns now: bandwagon, testimonial, loaded words. Outside, a leaf blower roared, and their neighbor Mr. Mendoza waved from his porch. Dexter snapped the laptop shut. "So for our project, we show people the same crowd with two different words and see if they fall for it?" Aaron was already pulling out his phone to record. "We'll ask five people. Watch this."

He hit record and held up the first headline. "Read this and tell me what kind of people they are."

Arthur had been to Emelia's house a dozen times, but he had never been past the kitchen until Saturday, when her mother asked if he wanted to help with the surprise. Emelia's grandmother was turning eighty, and the plan was a board of family photographs to hang above the cake table. Emelia spread the pictures across the living room carpet like a giant game of memory, and Arthur's job was to sort them into two piles, nice ones and extra nice ones.

He worked through them one by one. There was Emelia at age six gap-toothed on a tropical beach, there was her parents' wedding, there was a cousin graduation. Then he found a wide photo of a whole family standing in rows, everyone dressed in plain white shirts and white headbands. It looked formal and calm, like the kind of picture taken at a wedding. He set it in the extra nice pile, right beside a photo of Emelia's aunt in a lacy white gown cutting a cake.

When Emelia came back with lemonade, she stood over the piles with her hands on her hips. "Good," she said, tapping the wedding picture. Then her finger stopped on the family in white. "Why did you put this one there?"

"It's a wedding," Arthur said. "Everybody's in white, like your aunt."

Emelia picked it up and studied it the way Ms. De Vries studied a suspicious book report. "This is my great-grandmother's funeral," she said finally. "Everybody's wearing white. In traditional Chinese culture, white is worn for mourning at funerals."

Arthur looked at the two photos side by side, one family in white for a funeral, one bride in white for a wedding, and felt his whole sorting system wobble. "So white can mean two opposite things?"

"Apparently." Emelia set the funeral photo gently in a third pile she made on the arm of the couch. "I didn't know that either until I asked my mom last year. I used to think Western brides were copying us, but it's just different."

Arthur wanted to make sure he had it right before they glued anything down. At the party a week later, he watched for himself. Emelia's grandmother, dressed in deep red, laughed at the photo board, and when she reached the funeral picture she touched the edge of the frame and said something quiet in Cantonese to Emelia's mother. Later, at the cake table, the grandmother pointed at Arthur and asked Emelia a question. Emelia translated: she wants to know why you keep staring at everybody's clothes.

"She's checking something," Emelia said, grinning.

Arthur admitted it. He had counted, and in every photo from the wedding side the bride wore white, and in every photo from the funeral side the whole family wore white, and now he was watching the guests to see if anyone would show up to the party in white by accident. The grandmother listened, then shook her head at him with warm, amused eyes.

"Wear red," she said in English, and patted the sleeve of her own crimson blouse.

Clara had thirty-two dollars in her pocket and one goal: buy a ticket to the Silver Comets concert at the mall kiosk before anyone else did. The tickets were twenty dollars, which was the whole point. Her friend Raiden had texted her that morning: "Tickets go on sale at NOON. The line starts at the pretzel stand. Bring snacks. This is not leisure, this is war."

By eleven-thirty, the line curved past the pretzel stand, around the fountain, and halfway to the shoe store. Clara counted heads as she walked. She got to one hundred and forty and gave up, because the line kept going. Behind the kiosk counter, Mr. Yamamoto was stacking a small box on top of the register. Clara stood on her toes. The box was shallow. She did the math in her head and felt something go brittle in her chest, like a pretzel snapped in half. One hundred forty people, probably more, and maybe fifty tickets. Maybe fewer. She couldn't see the exact number, but she could see the shape of the problem, and the shape was bad.

At noon the line surged. Twenty minutes later Mr. Yamamoto flipped the sign to SOLD OUT, and a groan rolled down the corridor like a wave. A girl near the front held her ticket over her head and cheered, which did not help. Clara was still a hundred people back. She stomped toward the food court, where Raiden sat with an empty plate and a grim expression. "I had two thoughts on the walk over," he said. "Thought one: pretzels without cheese are a crime. Thought two: they priced those tickets too low. At twenty dollars, everybody in this mall wanted one, and there weren't enough for everybody."

Clara slid into the seat across from him. "My sister would call that a shortage," she said. "When a price is kept below the, uh, the right price, more people want the thing than there are things for sale." She'd overheard the phrase once and now it clicked into place like a puzzle piece. "So here's my test. If that's true, the tickets that exist should be worth more than twenty dollars now. Watch what happens."

They watched. Near the escalator, the girl who had cheered was surrounded by three boys, cash in hand. "Sixty," one said. "Eighty," said another. The girl grinned and held up a finger, making them wait. Clara leaned toward Raiden and whispered, "Tickets left the store in twenty minutes. Hundreds of fans got nothing. And the price just went up on its own, like it knew." Raiden pulled out his phone and started typing. "I'm messaging my cousin. She has a birthday next week and zero patience." He turned the screen so Clara could read it: "Dear Cousin, I have survived the Ticket War of the Mall. I fought bravely. I lost. Send money. Love, Raiden." The girl by the escalator pocketed her eighty dollars, and the boys chased the next ticket down the corridor.

Joshua's mom had left for the weekend with one instruction taped to the washer: "Dark clothes together, cold water, don't shrink my sweater." That meant the laundry was his, all of it, and Wesley had come over mostly to watch and partly because he wanted his lucky shirt washed before Monday's tryouts. "It's my tryout shirt," Wesley said, holding it out like evidence. "Kevin's mom does his, but my mom says I'm old enough now."

They sorted piles on the kitchen floor, argued about whether gray counted as dark, and ran two loads. When everything came out damp and wrinkled, Joshua remembered the iron in the hall closet. His dad used it for work shirts, and it had a dial with names like cotton and wool and a little chart of symbols on the handle. Joshua turned it to cotton, the hottest-sounding setting, because cotton seemed like it should mean business.

The trouble was Wesley's shirt. It was some shiny game-day material, and when Joshua pressed the iron onto the sleeve, a patch of it went dull and flat, like frost on a window. "What did you do?" Wesley grabbed the shirt and stared at the shiny spot. "This is my tryout shirt." Joshua's first motive for hiding the iron behind his back was simple: Wesley looked ready to tackle him. But then he turned the iron over and saw the symbol on the shirt's tag, a little iron outline with two dots inside it, and below the handle's chart, tiny words matched dots to settings. One dot meant low, about 110 degrees Celsius. Two dots meant medium, about 150. Three dots meant high, about 200.

"Wait," Joshua said. "Your shirt has two dots. That's medium, 150 degrees. I had it on cotton, which is the high setting, 200." He tested the idea right there, turning the dial down to the two-dot level and pressing a corner of his own sock. Nothing went shiny. The sock came out smooth and unharmed, which was more than he could say for Wesley's sleeve.

"We could tell people it's a lightning bolt," Wesley said, holding the sleeve up to the light. "Like it's intentional. Influential athletes have custom gear all the time." Joshua did his best to reassure him. "It's small. Nobody at tryouts will be close enough to see it, and if they are, they'll think you iron your own clothes, which is basically true now."

Wesley put the shirt on right there, damp and all, and stood in front of the hallway mirror flexing his arm so the patch caught the light. "Lightning bolt," he said again, and this time he almost sounded convinced. Joshua folded the last towel, set it on the stack, and turned the iron off with two fingers.

Vincent stared at the whiteboard in Ms. Ito's room like it had personally insulted him. The problem was 2x + 3x = 15, and beside him Charlize was already flipping her paper over to start the next one.

"Five x equals fifteen," Vincent said. "So x is three. Done."

Amine leaned over. "Show your work, or Ms. Ito will call it reckless guessing again."

"It's not guessing, it's confidence." Vincent wrote 2x + 3x = 5x anyway, because Amine had a smug face when he was right.

Then the next problem appeared: 2x + 3 = 11. Vincent wrote 5x = 11 without slowing down, and his hand hovered there while something in the back of his brain raised a small polite objection. He frowned at his paper. In the first problem, two x's and three x's were both x's, so they went together fine. But the three in this new problem was just a three. There was no x attached to it. He tried imagining x as a box of pencils. Two boxes plus three boxes made five boxes, sure. Two boxes plus three loose pencils made two boxes and three pencils, and that was that.

"You look like you bit a lemon," Charlize said.

"I wrote something weird." He showed her the 5x = 11. "Is that legal?"

Charlize tapped the 3. "What's the x attached to there?"

"Nothing. It's just three." Vincent erased the 5x and wrote 2x + 3 = 11 again, untouched, feeling a bit foolish and a bit brilliant at the same time. So you couldn't smash them together. Two x plus three stayed two x plus three, and you had to deal with it some other way. He thought about the balance scale Ms. Ito kept on her desk, the one she'd used to argue that whatever you did to one side you owed the other side. Subtract three from both sides. That left 2x = 8, and then x = 4. He checked it: two times four plus three did make eleven. He did a tiny drumroll with his pencil, which flew out of his hand and rolled under Amine's chair.

"Nice hygiene," Amine said, picking it off the floor and wiping it on his sleeve before handing it back.

"That's not what hygiene means."

"Whose pencil landed on the floor?"

Ms. Ito walked past and glanced at Vincent's paper. "I see you and the three are no longer on speaking terms."

"We oppose each other," Vincent said. "It has no x, and I stand for x rights."

She smiled and moved on, and Vincent started the next problem, writing slowly this time, checking every term for hidden x's like a detective. "Four x plus one x plus seven," he muttered. "Five x, plus seven, and the seven just gets to sit there being seven."

Everly spread her flashcards across the library table, careful not to let them slide into the study carrel next to hers.
