"Wait, the actual law?" said Kellan. "Like, with police?"

"With paperwork," said Mr. Chaudhry, and jogged back to the scrimmage.

Eleanor sat with that. A law, written down somewhere, protecting her from her own fastest instinct, which was to say she was fine. It felt like discovering the court had a foundation under it, something solid she'd been standing on without knowing. She tested the idea against what she'd seen: kids pulled for head hits, never for anything else, at every school game she could remember. It fit.

She sustained a headache through the rest of tryouts, and the next day her mother took her to a doctor who signed a form, because that was part of the law too. On Thursday, Mr. Chaudhry posted the roster. Eleanor made the second list, the practice squad, one spot below Yasser.

"You got cut and not cut," Kellan said. "Schrodinger's teammate."

Eleanor grinned and pulled on her sneakers. At the first practice, when Mr. Chaudhry called for someone assertive on defense, she raised her hand so fast it nearly hit Yasser in the chin.

"Careful," he said, ducking. "That could be against the law too."

The community centre's basement smelled of old carpet and burnt coffee, and every Thursday it turned into a blues jam run by Ms. Kovalenko. Asher stood at the edge of the room with his borrowed guitar, watching the older players take turns soloing over the twelve-bar progression. He had practised the scale until his fingers were agile enough to find every note without looking, but tonight Ms. Kovalenko had pointed at him and said, "You're in on the next chorus." Now he was terrified.

"Count the bars," Arian whispered from behind the keyboard. "Four on each chord. When it comes back around, you'll hear it."

Arian's sister Maika started the drums with a steady shuffle, and the whole room leaned into the groove. Asher played his first phrase, then a second, elaborating on the little three-note motif he had rehearsed all week. It sounded almost like the blues. Then somewhere around the seventh bar he stopped counting. His mind went blank, and his fingers kept moving while the chords shifted underneath him like floorboards sliding out of place. He was lost. He had no idea where he was in the form, and he could feel his ears getting hot.

Then he noticed something. The bass walked upward, the keyboard changed, and the whole band seemed to gather itself, like a scavenger spotting the same prize from across the field, everyone turning toward one point. The music climbed and settled, and a moment later the progression started over from the beginning, exactly where it had begun. He had heard that move a hundred times on recordings without ever really hearing it. That was it, the signpost.

"That's the turnaround," Arian said after the tune ended. "End of the form. Lands on the five chord and pulls you right back to the top."

"Does it always?" Asher asked.

"Pretty much. It's how lost soloists find home."

They played two more choruses, and once more Asher lost his place when Maika flipped her drum pattern and threw him off. This time he didn't panic. He hung on a couple of safe notes like a kid treading water, listened for the band to gather and climb, and when he heard the pull back toward the beginning he leapt. His next phrase landed right on the first chord, loud and sure, and Arian grinned across the keyboards.

Ms. Kovalenko raised her coffee cup toward him from her chair by the amplifier and said, "Again from the top."

Aiden had learned the twelve-bar progression in one afternoon, which felt like a victory until he actually played it. The chords were right, the notes of his solo were right, and somehow the whole thing sounded like a microwave beeping. Keagan was coming over at four o'clock to hear the solo, because Keagan had already promised the whole lunch table that Aiden would play it at the talent show sign-up on Friday. That gave Aiden two hours to sound like music instead of a robot.

He played the progression again and listened hard. The notes were correct; he was sure of that. His fingers knew where to go. The problem was something else, something hiding under the notes where he couldn't see it, like the way a floor can look level until a marble rolls to one side. He tried playing louder. He tried playing faster. He tried closing his eyes, which only made him think about how little time was left. His mom called from the kitchen that if he was going to persevere, could he at least persevere more quietly.

Then he put on an old blues track Ms. Vargas had lent him and tapped his foot along. His foot kept wanting to land in the wrong places, splitting some beats and squashing others, and he stopped the song and rewound it twice. He tapped again, clapping each pair of eighth notes instead of the big beats. Long-short. Long-short. Every single pair, long-short, never even. "It's a shuffle," he said out loud to the piano, feeling slightly ridiculous. "The eighth notes are long-short, not even." He had been playing the solo as if the notes were all the same length, and the stiffness hadn't been in his fingers at all. It had been an illusion that playing the right notes meant playing the right rhythm.

He tried it. On the first pass he overshot, so swung that he crashed into the next chord like a shopper with a full cart. The second pass was better. By the fourth pass something happened that he couldn't quite account for: the solo started walking, then limping in an interesting way, and the twelve bars went by before he noticed them. It sounded, for about six seconds, like actual blues. He played it again to make sure he hadn't imagined it.

At four o'clock Keagan let himself in through the back door, as usual, and dropped onto the piano bench. "Okay, disaster check. Can you actually do this by Friday?" Aiden set his hands on the keys and started the progression, long-short, long-short, letting the last note of the solo hang there a little longer than it should have, the way the recording did. Keagan stopped chewing his gum. "Wait. Do that again."

Luke sat in the waiting room of Dr. Patel's office, holding his elbow because his mom had insisted he needed "a check on the sniffles," which was embarrassing enough without Jerry spotting him there. Of course Jerry spotted him there. Jerry was in the corner chair with an ice pack on his wrist from a skateboard attempt he refused to describe.

"Coach says you're starting in Thursday's game," Jerry said, grinning even as he shifted the ice pack. "You excited? Because I told everyone you'd do a victory flip if we win, so that's happening now. Voluntary or not."

"That was voluntary when you promised it. Now it's a trap," Luke said, but he was grinning too. Starting was huge news. He leaned back, then caught a whiff of himself and sat forward again fast. Since when did he smell like a locker room? He'd never needed deodorant before this year, and today he'd forgotten it entirely after gym.

He turned the problem over while a toddler across the room mimic-kicked a soccer ball, narrating her own goal. Fresh sweat couldn't be the culprit, could it? He'd been practically dry after gym, right up until he wasn't. He remembered his older cousin rambling at Thanksgiving: "Fresh sweat has almost no smell. The smell comes when bacteria on your skin break down the sweat from your armpit glands, and those glands kick in at puberty." At the time Luke had nodded the way you nod at relatives. Now it felt like classified information. The pattern fit. New glands, new bacteria buffet, new smell, all starting months ago exactly when his voice went sideways.

So he tested it. He sneaked to the drinking fountain, wet a paper towel, and scrubbed one armpit like it owed him money, leaving the other one as what Cynthia would call the control group, if Cynthia were there, which thankfully she was not. Five minutes later he sniffed each side. The scrubbed side smelled like damp paper towel. The other side smelled like a science experiment. It worked. The bacteria were the problem, and soap was the answer. Probability of him carrying wipes in his gym bag from now on: extremely high.

"Luuuuke," the nurse called.

He stood up so fast he knocked a magazine off the table, and Jerry howled. "Dude, you're more nervous about a checkup than a game."

"I'm not nervous," Luke said, and then, because he couldn't resist telling anyone, "I just solved body odor with a paper towel."

"Put that on the team group chat," Jerry said immediately. "Coach will make you captain for science."

The nurse held the door open and raised an eyebrow at the damp towel in Luke's hand.

"Medical research," Luke told her, and marched in.

Keira counted the boxes in the moving truck one last time, then climbed into the back seat. Her father had taken the new job with a corporation two states away, and no amount of arguing about it in June had changed anything by August. Mael had promised to text every day, and for the first week he actually did.

At her new school, Ms. Li stood at the door on the first morning, distributing schedules to the line of sixth graders. Keira took hers and found a seat near the window. At lunch she stood alone with her tray until a girl named Alexanne waved her over. They ate together, and Alexanne talked the whole time about the soccer team and a science project that involved something volatile that they weren't allowed to touch without goggles. Keira laughed in the right places. Afterward, walking to class, she caught herself thinking that Alexanne was her friend now, and then she thought about Mael, and about how many lunches it had taken with him before she would have told him a secret. Something didn't add up.

That night she searched on her mom's laptop until she found it. A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas had found that it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. She read the sentence twice, then did the math on a sticky note. Lunch was thirty minutes. Fifty hours was one hundred lunches. Almost an entire school year, if you counted nothing but lunch.

So she tested it. The next day she sat with Alexanne again, and the day after that, and she started keeping a tally in the back of her notebook, a small pencil mark for every half hour. She joined the soccer team because Alexanne was on it, which added two hours of practice most days. Some afternoons Alexanne barely talked to her, and Keira marked the hours anyway, the way you mark rainy days in a garden and keep watering.

Near the end of October, Alexanne knocked on her door holding two bus passes. "My mom got extras for the science museum," she said. "Want to come Saturday? It's like four hours, more if we get lost."

Keira looked at her tally page, then folded it in half and shoved it in a drawer. Four hours was four hours, but she was pretty sure they'd already stopped counting.

"Only if we get lost on purpose," she said, grabbing her jacket.

Israel's basement smelled like old carpet and microwave popcorn. He rolled his desk chair sideways so Jackson could reach the second keyboard, and Sky dropped onto the couch with her notebook already open.

"Okay," Israel said. "You said you'd write it yourself. A program that asks for a number and prints whether it's prime. I'm not touching the keyboard."

Jackson cracked his knuckles and typed. He decomposed the problem in his head the way Ms. Qureshi had shown them in math: get the number, then check whether anything divides it, then print the answer. One step at a time. He wrote a loop that tried every number from 2 up to the input, and if it found one that divided evenly, it printed "not prime." Otherwise, after the loop finished, it printed "prime."

"Run it," Sky said, chewing her pen.

He typed 9. The screen said not prime. He typed 7. Prime. He typed 25, 13, 100, 41. Every answer was right. Sky leaned over and frowned at the screen.

"Try 2," she said. "Small numbers are where programs mess up."

He typed 2. The screen said not prime. Jackson sat back. That was wrong, and he knew it, but he couldn't see why. The loop seemed airtight. He read the code line by line, twice, and it looked plausible to him, every part of it.

"Wait," he said slowly. "The loop starts at 2. So for the input 2, the loop divides 2 by 2, it comes out even, and it says not prime. It's testing the number against itself." He highlighted the line. "But for prime, the number only counts if something smaller divides it." He changed the loop to stop before it reached the input itself.

"It's like the loop had a hierarchy problem," he said. "The number itself was sneaking into the check when it shouldn't."

Israel typed 2. The screen said prime. Then he typed 4. Not prime. 6, not prime. 8, not prime. He started typing every even number he could think of, and every single one came back not prime, until he got bored and typed 2 again just to watch it say prime.

"That's weird," Israel said. "It's the only even one that ever says prime."

"That's not the program being weird," Sky said. "That's real. 2 is the only even prime number."

"So every other even number is out," Jackson said, almost to himself. He added one line at the top of the check: if the number is even and bigger than 2, skip everything and print not prime. The program barely had to work at all now. He ran it on 100, and it answered before the rest of the loop even started.

"You just made the program faster by knowing the math," Israel said. "That feels like cheating."

Jackson saved the file under his own name. The screen blinked, and beneath it a new message appeared: one unread email from Ms. Qureshi, forwarded from Israel's account. Subject line: "Extra credit, due Monday."

"You had it the whole time?" Jackson said.

Israel grinned and hit send.

Maya's grandfather kept his old guitar in the hallway closet, and by Sunday afternoon she had claimed it. The recital at the community hall started at seven, which gave her three hours to learn something she had promised the music teacher she could do: improvise a blues solo. Her friend Ross was already set up at the upright piano in the living room, where the afternoon light made everything look tranquil except the two of them.

"Key of A," Ross said, playing a low A to lock it in. "So what are the chords?"

Maya stared at the frets. At home she had practiced with a backing track, and it always worked, but the track had chosen the chords for her. She plucked an A and it sounded right, deep and satisfied, but when Ross tried a minor chord under it, the whole room soured. "No," she said. "Try that one but with the seventh on top." She hummed the note she meant, and Ross found it. The chord suddenly slouched, like it had somewhere better to be.

"That's it," Maya said. "A7. Blues chords want that sound." They hunted for the other two the same way, Ross sliding his hands around the keyboard while she tested notes on the guitar. D7 came next, then E7, and when Ross played all three in a loop, twelve bars at a time, it sounded like actual blues, the kind her grandfather put on the record player while he cooked.

The problem was the solo itself. Every time the E7 came around, Maya froze and played nothing, because at home the track had hidden which chord was which. Here she could see Ross's hands, so she made a deal with herself: watch the hands, and when they jumped to the chord built on E, play fewer notes, save the big bend for right there. She tested it once through and missed, tested again and landed it, and the miss itself told her something. The chords weren't decoration under the melody. They were the ground the melody walked on, invisible unless you looked sideways.

Ross's little brother wandered in, turned the thermostat down to sixty, and wandered out, which meant the piano room would soon be freezing, since Grandpa's furnace took its time. "Fifteen minutes, then we pack up," Ross said, shaking feeling back into his fingers.

On the last run-through, Maya closed her eyes over the E7 and the bend came out clean, hanging in the cold air like it might never evaporate. At the hall that evening, her grandfather sat in the front row. Afterward he said only, "A7, D7, and E7. You found them yourself?"

"With some help," Maya said, and Ross bowed from the piano bench.

Anna slid her basketball stats sheet under her brother's elbow and reached for the mashed potatoes before her mom could distribute them unevenly again. Her dad was already halfway through his chicken, but Anna barely touched hers.

"Loik says he's the best shooter on our team," she said. "He's been telling everyone in the hallway. He was explicit about it, too. One shot, one basket. One hundred percent."

"One hundred percent," her dad repeated, raising his eyebrows. "That's impressive."

"It's one shot." Anna stabbed a green bean. "The whole season. He played two minutes in one game because three people were out sick, and he took one shot, and it went in. Now he's got this perfect percentage and he's saying Amirah should come off the bench instead of him."

Her mom set down her fork. "What's Amirah's percentage?"

"That's the thing." Anna pulled the napkin from her lap and turned it over. "She's taken like forty shots and made twenty-three. I did the division twice. It's a little over fifty percent, and she doesn't even play guard, so most of her shots are hard ones." She wrote 23/40 on the napkin, then 1/1 next to it. "Fifty-something sounds worse than a hundred, if you just read the numbers out loud."

Her brother leaned over to look. "So Loik wins."

"Loik wins on a number that means nothing." Anna tapped the napkin. "It felt like a paradox when I first worked it out, because the numbers say one thing and the truth says another. But it's not really a paradox. It's just a small amount of information pretending to be a big one." She chewed her lip. "The problem is that the number itself isn't wrong, so I can't just tell him he's lying."

"So what are you going to do?" her mom asked.

Anna was quiet for a moment, pushing a pea around her plate. Then she sat up straight. "I'm going to get him to take more shots. We have shooting practice before Thursday's game, the kind where Coach writes down everything. If Loik takes ten shots, the number will fix itself, whatever it turns out to be. And if he really is the best shooter, then fine, he gets to brag with an actual number behind it." She folded the napkin and put it in her pocket. "Either way, the truth shows up."

"Even if he misses all ten?" her brother asked.

"Then he's a one-for-eleven shooter who talks too much." Anna grinned and finally took a real bite of chicken. "And I'm going to text Amirah right after dinner so she can count the shots with me."

Emilie counted under her breath while the backing track looped through the twelve bars for the ninth time. She could play the chords fine, A7, D7, A7, E7, but every time she tried to solo her notes came out stiff, like she was reading them off an invisible list. She wanted her guitar to answer the music, not just stand next to it.

She texted Taya, who had been playing saxophone for two years, and recruited her for an experiment. "Bring your sax," Emilie typed. "I have a theory." Taya arrived within the hour, socks mismatched as usual, and they set up in Emilie's living room with the backing track on the speaker.

"Play something," Emilie said, "and I'll copy it back at you, like a conversation." Taya blew a bendy phrase that slid down like water off a roof. Emilie tried to answer on guitar and it fell flat, too many notes, no shape. She stopped the track. Why had Taya's four seconds of music sounded like a sentence and hers sounded like a spill? She wondered if the problem was invisible, something about the length of the phrase rather than the notes themselves.

They tried again, but this time Emilie counted the bars while Taya played. One, two, three, four, and then it was Emilie's turn, four more bars, back and forth like a tennis rally. She picked one small candidate phrase, three notes that bent, and let it repeat and stretch, elastic, changing a little each time it came around. When Taya answered with a sassy little scooping riff, Emilie answered that instead of her own idea, and suddenly the music sounded like two people talking.

"That's a real thing, you know," Taya said between takes. "It's called trading fours." They grinned at each other and started the track again. This time Emilie didn't plan anything. She listened, counted, and when her four bars came she let her guitar ask a question she didn't know the answer to yet. Taya's saxophone replied with a low growl, and Emilie chased it back up the neck, landing on the one note that felt like a period at the end of a sentence.

Luke spread the ballot slips across the kitchen table, forty little squares of paper he had talked Ms. Doyle into letting him count twice. The class election was over, and Skylar had lost, which was strange, because Skylar and Kassandra had promised almost exactly the same things: longer recess, a suggestion box, a class pet. He was supposed to be finishing a book report where the protagonist survived a blizzard, but the numbers bothered him more.

He counted the way the election had actually gone. Skylar got twelve votes, Kassandra got ten, and a boy whose entire speech had been "vote for me, I'm fun" got eighteen. Skylar and Kassandra had been chronic allies all year, sitting together, agreeing on everything, and together their supporters added up to twenty-two. That was more than eighteen. Luke stacked the slips into three piles and stared at them.

Kassandra arrived first, dumping her backpack on a chair. "I came to complain," she announced. "That's basically my hobby now."

"Look," Luke said, and slid the piles toward her. "The way our election works, whoever gets the most votes wins. It doesn't matter that your votes and Skylar's votes were for nearly the same ideas."

Skylar came through the back door without knocking, which was usual. "Ms. Doyle said you took the ballots."

"Only to count them," Luke said. "Here." He pushed the piles together, then split them a different way. "Pretend you two had been one candidate. Same platform, one name. Twenty-two votes. Fun Guy gets eighteen. You win." He rebuilt the original piles. "Split, he wins. Same people, same votes, different result."

Skylar picked up the winning pile, eighteen slips, and weighed it in her hand. "So being similar to Kassandra is what lost it for me."

"Basically, yes." Luke had spent an hour trying to find some hidden trick in the counting, some mistake, and there wasn't one. The count was clean. The rule itself did it.

"I assumed Kassandra stole my ideas," Skylar said slowly. "I was going to be mad about it all term." She set the pile down. "I'm not, now. It wasn't her."

"There's another way to count," Luke said, pulling over his notebook. He had copied a system from the encyclopedia: if you share out the seats according to each side's share of the votes, it's called proportional representation. "If we ran the class that way, your ideas would still get a voice, because your votes would count toward something." He wrote out a sample count with make-believe numbers so Kassandra could see it work.

Kassandra leaned over the notebook, tapping the page. "So we take this to Ms. Doyle."

"For the next vote," Skylar said. "Not to redo this one. Rules are rules, even bad ones." She was already grinning, though. "But next time, we don't split."

"Or we run on completely different platforms," Kassandra said.

"Or that," Skylar said, and scooped the ballots back into the envelope to return them first thing in the morning.

Clara sat in her grandmother's kitchen with the laptop propped on a stack of cookbooks, because Grandma's Wi-Fi only worked near the window. The program was supposed to be simple. Ask for a number, test it, print whether it was prime. Mr. Weiss had told the class that primes were the fundamental building blocks of numbers, and that they had to write a checker by Sunday. So far, Clara's checker insisted that seven was not prime, thirteen was not prime, and even three was not prime.

"They can't all be not prime," Lyvia said from the phone, leaning against her video call screen. "Three is definitely prime. I'd bet my lunch on it."

"Then my code is calling my lunch," Clara muttered. She scrolled through it again. Ask for the number. Then, for every possible divisor from two up through the number itself, divide and check. She had written it with a while loop that counted all the way up to n, dividing by n at the end.

A memory surfaced from Tuesday. Mr. Weiss had stood by the whiteboard and said, almost offhandedly, "Careful with ranges in Python, everyone. Range of two and n gives you the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1." Then the fire alarm went off for a drill, and everyone had filed outside, sneezing in the pollen, and Clara had never written the rest down. She had assumed she remembered it anyway.

She stared at her loop now, heart tapping a little faster. Her loop divided n by n at the end. Every number divided by itself. Every number got stamped not prime. Her program wasn't broken exactly; it was answering a different question than the one she'd asked.

She deleted the while loop and typed the fix, using range with two and n, her fingers slow and deliberate. She pressed enter. She typed seven. Prime. Eleven. Prime. Eight. Not prime. She was about to shout for Lyvia when a shadow fell across the keyboard.

Grandma stood there with her tea, reading the screen. "You'll want to compress that loop," she said. "One flag variable instead of all those prints."

Clara froze. "You know Python?"

"Python's new to me," Grandma said mildly. "Loops aren't. I wrote payroll code before your father was born, and I still remember the day a range cost me a week." She set down her cup and pulled a chair up beside Clara. "Show me the allergy you wrote for the number one."

Daniel had saved for eleven weeks, and today the pet store was letting him carry out a small brown puppy with one ear that flopped the wrong way. Inara came along to help choose supplies, and she held the list he had written while he counted money at the register.

"Food bowl, leash, puppy kibble," she read. "You forgot treats."

"Did not. Treats are right there." Daniel pointed at a shelf, and while he paid, the cashier slipped a small milk chocolate bar into the bag. "On the house," she said. "For the new owner, not the dog." Daniel laughed and forgot about it.

At home, he set the puppy, Biscuit, on the kitchen floor while he sorted supplies. Biscuit was diligent about one thing above all: finding anything edible. When Daniel turned around, the pup was dragging a paper bag off the counter's edge, and chocolate chips were scattering across the tiles like dark hail. It was baking chocolate, the bag his mother kept for cookies, and Biscuit had already swallowed a mouthful.

Daniel's stomach dropped. He remembered the cashier's joke and thought, it was a joke, so chocolate must be bad, but how bad? A milk chocolate bar versus a bag of baking chocolate did not feel like the same problem. He grabbed the chip bag and called Inara, who looked it up while he watched Biscuit's tail wag, oblivious.

"You have to call the vet," she said. "It says dogs break down something in chocolate really slowly, so it stays in them a long time. And dark or baking chocolate is way more dangerous than milk chocolate."

"The bag calls it theobromine," Daniel said, reading the label with a frown.

Mr. Navarro, the neighbour across the hall, knocked at the sound of the phone call and drove them straight to the clinic, because Daniel's mother would not be home for an hour and the vet said not to wait. In the waiting room, Daniel kept his hand on Biscuit's crate. The vet treated Biscuit, and by evening the puppy was sleepy but fine, curled in a towel-lined box.

At school the next day, Malek asked why Daniel looked so tired. "Biscuit ate baking chocolate," Daniel said. "Milk chocolate would have been less dangerous, but baking chocolate is the worst kind, because of the theobromine. Dogs break it down really slowly." He wrote a note and taped it to the kitchen cabinet at home, right beside the flour: NO CHOCOLATE ANYWHERE BISCUIT CAN REACH.

He also did one more thing. He went back to the pet store, found the cashier, and asked her to trade the joke for a bag of puppy biscuits. "Fair enough," she said, ringing it up. That night Biscuit sat at his feet, ears up, watching him open the bag.

On Saturday morning, a small box sat beside Chloe's cereal bowl with her name on it. Her mom grinned and said, "Happy birthday, almost." Inside was a phone, dark blue and shiny, and Chloe actually shrieked. She spent the whole day taking pictures of the toaster, the cat, and her own sneakers, and by nine that night she was still in bed under her blanket, scrolling through videos with the brightness turned up.

The next morning she dragged herself to the bus stop like her backpack was full of bricks. Averie took one look at her and said, "You look like a zombie." Chloe yawned so hard her jaw cracked. The weird part was that this had happened before, at her cousin's house last summer, when she and Jessy had stayed up past midnight with Jessy's tablet. Chloe remembered lying on the air mattress, eyes wide open, listening to Jessy snore while her own brain refused to shut off. On nights she read paper books instead, she dropped off almost instantly. Both times she'd been tired. Only one variable was different.

At lunch she laid it out for Averie and Jessy like a detective. "Nights with screens, I can't sleep. Nights without, I can. I want to test it properly." She borrowed a notebook from Ms. Charles's classroom shelf and made a chart: five nights, phone off and in the kitchen before bed, and a note each morning about how fast she fell asleep. Her motivation was simple and enormous: the school camping trip was in two weeks, and she did not want to be the kid who lay awake in a tent listening to everyone else breathe.

Night one, she left the phone downstairs and felt like part of her arm was missing. But she was asleep in what felt like ten minutes. Night two, same. Night three, same, and she wrote "wow" in the margin with three exclamation points. Then came the twist. On night four her dad knocked on her door holding the phone. "You left this on the couch," he said. "And I looked something up, because your mom was curious." He read off his own phone: "Blue-enriched light from screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin."

"Melatonin," Chloe repeated. "That's the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening." She said it slowly, like the word was the missing puzzle piece, because it was. It wasn't the videos, it wasn't sinister screen plots to ruin her life, it was light with a lot of blue in it telling her body to postpone sleepiness. She finished night five, and her chart showed five quick fall-asleeps in a row, plus one zombie week before it for comparison.

At the campsite, in her sleeping bag with a headlamp that glowed warm yellow, Chloe propped the notebook open on her knees. Jessy leaned over from the next mattress pad and whispered, "What are you writing?" Chloe showed her the chart and clicked off the lamp. "Rule one," she said. "The phone sleeps in the tent pocket."

Luke sat on his bedroom floor with his spelling list in one hand and his science poster in the other, and his heart would not stop hammering. The poster showed a bee drifting from flower to flower, and across the bottom, in his best lettering, he had written that bees pollinate the apple trees behind Ms. Levy's garden, which was why her branches sagged with fruit every September. He could not make himself study it. Tomorrow was the thing he was not saying out loud, even to himself, and it sat in his chest like a stone.

His phone buzzed. Quentin had sent a message: "Still freaking out? Lionel says use your coping list." Luke typed back "working on it," then stared at the list he'd taped to his wall weeks ago, back when his mom first used the word anxiety at the doctor's office. Deep breaths. Count backward. Set boundaries on worrying, which meant picking one worry time and refusing the rest. He had tried all of it. His hands were still cold, and the bee poster still looked like a smudge.

Then he noticed something odd. He had read the paragraph about bees three times without remembering a word, but when the clock ticked closer to nine, when his worry got acute enough that he could hear the radiator clicking in the corner, he suddenly caught an error he had missed all evening. He had written that flowers pollinate bees. Backwards. His sharpened attention had spotted it instantly, the same way he could hear his dad's van on the street before anyone else did. Luke set down the marker. Maybe the hammering in his chest was not only an enemy.

He decided to test it, because that was what you did with a pattern you weren't sure of. He copied five hard spelling words while calm, breathing slow, keeping the worry behind a boundary. He got two wrong. Then he let himself think about tomorrow on purpose, let the nerves come roaring up, and copied five more. He got all five right. He did it again with the poster facts, and again the worry made his mind grab every detail, quick and tight. His phone buzzed a second time, and this time he answered it out loud.

"Quentin, listen. Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge," Luke said, reading straight off the health worksheet that had been buried under his poster all night. "It says short bursts of it can actually help you focus. Like before a test." There was a pause on the line.

"So your freak-out is doing your homework for you?"

"Basically. Quentin," Luke said, and took the breath he'd been holding since dinner. "Tomorrow's my trumpet solo in front of the whole school. First row of the band, all by myself." The phone was quiet for so long that the radiator clicked twice. Then Luke picked up the trumpet case from under his bed, snapped the latches open, and raised the mouthpiece to his lips.

Mason had six cups of mystery liquid lined on the science fair table, and no idea what was in any of them. Ms. Mansour had labeled them only A through F, shaken each one, and said, "Test them. Tell me acid or base." His palms began to perspire as the first visitors drifted toward his booth.

"We're supposed to dip the litmus paper," his friend Eden reminded him, holding out the little strip of blue paper. "You're just staring at the cups."

"I'm thinking." Mason took the strip and dipped it into cup A. The paper turned pink. He wrote it down, dipped a fresh strip into cup B, and watched that one stay blue. Cup C turned pink so fast the change seemed to snap across the paper like a spark.

Oakley leaned over the table. "So pink means acid, blue means base. Then what's cup D?"

Mason dipped a strip. It stayed blue. He frowned at it. "Base. But Ms. Mansour said something about a scale, the pH scale. She said acids are at the low end and bases at the high end, and seven is in the middle." He checked the color chart taped beside his notebook. Cup D, if the chart was right, was a stronger base than cup B. That meant something invisible was different in the two cups, and the paper was the only way he could see it.

"The paper's doing all the work," Eden said, squinting at a strip like it was under a lens. "Where does it even come from? Nobody makes paper that just knows things."

A woman stopped at the booth, an older woman with a canvas bag, and looked at the strips. "That's litmus," she said. "Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens."

"Lichens?" Oakley said.

"The crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark. The grey patches, like the ones all over my garden wall."

Mason set down his tongs. He had been scraping grey crust off the north side of his grandmother's stone wall just last weekend, thinking it was some kind of dirt. It had a name, and it was hiding in the little strips on his table. He could hardly believe something off a rock could turn pink in lemon juice.

He worked through cups E and F. E turned the paper only a pale pink, a weak acid. F turned it a deep red, a strong one, low on the scale. He lined up all six strips in order beside the cups, and the pattern showed itself, weakest to strongest, like a row of sunset colors.

Ms. Mansour came by with her clipboard. "Verdict?"

"Acid, base, base, strong base, weak acid, strong acid," Mason said. He pointed at the strips. "And I know what the paper is. Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens. The crusty growths on rocks and tree bark."

"Where did you learn that?" she asked, raising an eyebrow.

"A visitor told me." He had been sure all morning that the paper was some kind of plastic invention, and now he was sure he was wrong, and both of those things felt strange and good at once. "Ms. Mansour, after the fair, could I bring some liquid from home and test it? I want to know what my grandma's well water is."

"Bring a sample Monday," she said, and moved on to the next booth.

Mason picked up the deepest red strip and held it up to the gymnasium lights.

The lights went out just as Michael was reaching for the freezer door, and his hand froze in the dark. "Mom, the power's out," he called. She came down the hall with her phone flashlight, and they stood together in the kitchen, listening to the fridge's hum die away into silence.

"The food," his mom said. "That freezer is full of everything for the week." Michael closed the door without opening it, then stopped himself. He had opened it, just once, just a crack, to peek. He told himself a crack didn't count, but the thought kept nagging him.

He went to the window. Across the courtyard, the whole apartment building across the street was dark too, and the streetlights were off, so it wasn't just their building. He knocked on the wall the usual way, and a minute later Daisy knocked back from next door. On the third floor he could see a candle in Nour's window, wobbling.

"Half an hour before you opened that door," his mom said, sitting on the couch with a blanket. "You have to stop opening it." Michael got his notebook and, by phone light, wrote down what he knew: a full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, but a half-full one only lasts about 24 hours, if the door stays closed. He'd read that in the booklet that came with the freezer, back when it was delivered, and had thought it was boring then. Now it mattered. The problem was, their freezer was half full at best. His mom had been planning a big grocery run for Saturday, and today was only Thursday. Twenty-four hours, then, if nobody opened the door again.

He thought about that crack he'd made. It was too late to undo, but he could make the rest of the time count. "Daisy," he said through the wall, "do you have ice?" She laughed. "Our freezer's dead too, genius." But then she said she'd ask her mother about the ice trays, and Nour shouted down the stairwell that her family had two bags of ice from a party. Michael counted on his fingers. If they packed the empty top half of the freezer with Nour's ice, the space wouldn't be half empty anymore. It wasn't quite full, but it was closer.

The stairwell was pitch black. He climbed by feel, one hand on the cold railing, keeping his spine straight against the wall so he wouldn't miss a step. Nour met him at her door with both bags, and Daisy came up behind him carrying her ice trays wrapped in a dish towel. Back in his kitchen, they compressed the ice into every gap around the frozen peas and the bread and the endangered chicken that was supposed to be Sunday dinner. Michael shut the door firmly and taped a note on it: DO NOT OPEN UNTIL POWER IS BACK.

Saturday morning the lights came on with a click, and the fridge started humming again. Michael peeled off the note, opened the freezer, and the cold air rolled out over his face. "Still frozen," he reported. "Every bit of it." Daisy leaned in and poked a bag of peas. "Okay," she said, "I take back what I said about your boring freezer booklet."

Lillian had been staring at the same French worksheet for twenty minutes when she finally raised her hand. "Mr. Sow, if I ask someone for directions in Paris, how do I even get them to stop and listen to me first?"

Mr. Sow smiled but didn't answer. "Listen to the recording from Tuesday again," he said. "The answer is in there." That was typical. He liked to make them hunt for things.

At the table by the window, Masen slid his headphones toward her. "It's the one where the woman asks where the post office is," he said. "Imogen swears she memorized it, but she says the first part sounds like two different words and she can't tell them apart."

Lillian put the headphones on. The woman on the recording began with "Excusez-moi," then asked her question, then ended with "s'il vous plaît." On the second listen, Lillian noticed something the others had missed. The "Excusez-moi" came before the question, every time, and the other word came at the end, like a tag. She rewound it three times. Was one of them just "please"? And if so, what was the other one for?

She tried a test on Imogen, who had lived in Montreal until she was seven. "Pretend you're on a street and I need directions," Lillian said. Then she jumped straight into her question without saying anything first. Imogen blinked at her, startled, and said it felt rude, like being ambushed. "You have to get my attention first," Imogen said. "In French you'd say 'Excusez-moi' before you ask anything. It's how you politely stop a stranger." Then Lillian added "s'il vous plaît" at the end of her second attempt, and Imogen nodded. "See? That one means please."

So the two words had different jobs, and the order mattered. Lillian wrote it on the back of her worksheet with a little arrow diagram, converting the whole recording into three steps: stop the person, ask, be polite. It reminded her of the mock election her civics class had run last month, where you had to sign in, mark your ballot, then hand it over in exactly that sequence. Skip a step and the whole thing fell apart.

On Friday, Mr. Sow set up a game. The classroom became a pretend city with taped streets on the floor, and everyone had to give and follow directions in French while a fan blew papers off the desks in a turbulent rush whenever someone "missed the train." Masen got lost twice, but Lillian walked straight to the paper bakery, stopped her stranger with "Excusez-moi," asked her question, and finished with "s'il vous plaît."

Mr. Sow checked his stopwatch. "Three minutes and nobody had to rescue you," he said. "Where is the bakery, again?"

"A droite, après la banque," said Lillian, pointing at the tape.

The waiting room smelled like mint and something like new crayons, and Victoria kept her hands folded so nobody would see them shaking. She had chipped a corner off a back molar in her sleep, and the dentist, Ms. Virtanen, had asked one question that stuck in her head all morning: "Any chance you've been grinding your teeth at night?" Victoria hadn't known that was a thing a person could do without waking up. It made her wonder what else her body was doing while she wasn't paying attention.

"Open wide," Ms. Virtanen said, her mask fogging slightly. The little mirror clicked against Victoria's teeth like a spoon against a cup. "There it is. Your jaw muscles are tight as wire. That usually means something's been going on for a while, not just one bad night."

Victoria thought about that while the drill whined somewhere far from her mouth, numbed and distant. The swim meet was in nine days, and she'd been jittery about it for weeks, since Coach pinned the roster to the bulletin board. Her stomach hurt at breakfast. She'd stopped reading before bed and just lay in the dark instead, jaw clenched, rehearsing the flip turn over and over. She remembered Freyja at practice on Tuesday, sitting on the gutter with her goggles off, saying quietly, "I've felt awful for weeks. Not nervous-awful. Just awful." Victoria had told her the jitters were normal. Now she wasn't sure that answer had been coherent, or even kind.

Back at school, she found Freyja at the lunch table and slid her tray down beside her. "I need to tell you what I figured out," Victoria said. "Remember how I said the jitters are normal? I think I was only half right. A small amount of stress before a race actually sharpens you. It's stress that lasts for weeks without letting up that hurts you. Mine's been going on so long I cracked a tooth in my sleep." She touched her cheek where the filling was. "So I'm testing something. Four counts in, six counts out, ten times, every night, and lights out at nine-thirty instead of lying there rehearsing. If the jaw loosens up, I'll know it was the stress and not just bad luck."

Freyja turned her juice carton slowly in her hands, like it might symbolize something neither of them could name yet. "Weeks without letting up," she repeated. "That's me."

"Then you should talk to someone," Victoria said. "Not me. The counselor, or your mom. I felt guilty all through lunch for brushing you off on Tuesday, and I'm not doing it again."

"You didn't brush me off. You just didn't know yet."

"Come with me after school?" Victoria asked. "I'll walk you to the counseling office. You can bring the juice."

Sawyer had lost the same race twice, and both times the same thing had happened: a strong first lap, then legs that felt like wet sand on the second. He had decided the problem was that he wasn't trying hard enough. Quincy, who was timing him in the backyard with a stopwatch and a stopwatch only, had decided the problem was Sawyer.

"Sixty-two seconds!" Quincy shouted as Sawyer pounded past the fence post for the first lap of the third practice race. Sawyer raised a hand to show he'd heard, and kept sprinting. At the halfway point of lap two, his legs made an abrupt decision without him, slowing to a shuffle while Quincy jogged alongside, tapping the watch. "You died. Again. Same place as Tuesday."

Sawyer bent over, hands on knees, breathing like a leaky tire. Sixty-two seconds. He'd wanted to go out fast, because fast was obviously better, and twice now fast had turned into a walk by the end. But Quincy's number gave him a strange idea. If the watch showed exactly how fast the first lap had been, then he could tell, right away, whether the lap was faster or slower than planned. He didn't have to guess from how his lungs felt. "Time me again," he said. "And yell the number at the fence post. It's called a split, right? The time for one section."

"A what?"

"A split. My dad says it at meets."

Quincy, who wanted nothing more than to be the kind of person with an official job at a race, straightened up and held the stopwatch like a clipboard. "Fine. Official splitter." Sawyer set off again, and this time, when Quincy bellowed "Sixty-two!" at the post, Sawyer deliberately eased back. "Seventy!" came the shout on the next one, which was too slow, and Sawyer nudged the pace up. Around the final turn his legs still complained, but they carried him across the line at something like a run.

Sawyer walked a slow circle in the grass, doing the math out loud. Sixty-six per lap would be a lot better than one at sixty-two and one at a crawl. He couldn't see the pace itself, but the split made it visible, like footprints in snow. He had been wrong about needing more effort, and it was annoying how long he'd justified sprinting the first lap just because it felt good at the moment. Speed at the start came at the expense of speed at the end, and the watch had finally proven it.

"One more," Sawyer said, lining up at the fence.

Quincy raised the stopwatch. "Official splitter standing by."

The washer hummed like a hive, and Hudson stood in front of it with his mom's instructions scrawled on a receipt: sort, cold water, half a cap of soap. His mom was on nights at the hospital all week, and the basket at home had finally become a mountain, so here he was at Sud City Laundromat on a Saturday morning with nine dollars in quarters and no idea what "sort" actually meant.

"Toss it all in one load," said Tomas, who had tagged along because his own mom said he couldn't sit around the house all weekend. Tomas's family washed everything together, whites and darks and everything between, and he was already loading a lump of mixed clothes into the machine next to Hudson's. "Saves money."

Hudson looked at his own basket. There were his white school shirts, folded flat on top, and underneath them the new red gym socks he'd only worn twice. He dumped everything out onto the folding table and started making piles anyway, because something about the receipt's first word nagged at him. Whites here, darks there, reds in their own small stack. Was that right? He wondered why it would matter. Water was water.

Ms. Rao, who ran the flower shop next door and did her laundry here every Saturday, glanced over from the machine by the window. "Now that's a coherent system," she said, nodding at his piles. "Lights, darks, brights. Most people just shove it all in." She went back to her magazine, and Hudson felt weirdly proud of three lumps of dirty clothes.

He ran the whites first, then the brights, and while the machines churned, Tomas told him about getting his flu vaccine on Monday, which he was dreading. "My arm's going to be sore for two days," Tomas said. "Coach says we don't cease practice for anything, so I'll be doing push-ups with a dead arm."

When Tomas's load finished, he yanked it out and held up a T-shirt that had been white three days ago. It was pale pink now, splotchy across the chest. "What?" Tomas said, turning it around. "How did this happen?"

Hudson peered into Tomas's drum. At the very back, balled up and dripping, was a single new red sock. He remembered his own three stacks, and a question formed in his mind, the kind you could actually test. "Your red sock," he said. "It's new, right? Never been washed much?" Tomas shrugged. Hudson laid the pink shirt on the table next to a still-white one from his own brights load. "Mine went in with the reds, alone. Yours went in with everything. The red sock did something to the water, and the water did something to your shirt." He didn't know exactly how, but the pattern was right there on the table: same sock, different loads, different shirts.

Tomas held the pink shirt up to the light and groaned. "My mom's going to think I tie-dyed it on purpose." He started refolding it, as if pressing hard enough might squeeze the pink back out. Hudson pulled his last load from the dryer while it was still warm, shook out a white school shirt, and folded it along the seams the way his mom did, collar flat, sleeves back. It was white. It smelled like clean. He stacked it on top of the brights and the darks, all of it folded, all of it sorted, and he thought maybe next Saturday he'd try hot water on the towels, just to see.

"Hey," Tomas said, still staring at his ruined shirt. "Next time, show me those piles."

James sat at the computer after dinner, scrolling through baseball stats while his dad washed dishes behind him. He had one goal tonight: prove to Aicha that his favorite player, Marino, was better than her favorite, Ellison. She had laughed at him at lunch and said the numbers settled it, because Ellison's batting average was thirty points higher. James wanted to find something that unsettled it.

He pulled up the season page for both players. Marino was hitting .262, and Ellison was at .294. His stomach dropped a little. Then he noticed the column next to it, the one labeled walks, and Marino's number was huge, way bigger than Ellison's. Why did that matter? He clicked into the fine print at the bottom of the page, the part most people never read, and found the definition. A batting average was hits divided by official at-bats, and walks did not count as at-bats at all.

He leaned closer to the screen. So a batter got no credit for walks. None. Marino had gotten on base over and over without it showing up anywhere in that famous number. James opened a spreadsheet and typed in the numbers himself: hits, at-bats, walks, plate appearances. He did the division twice because he didn't trust himself. When he counted times on base against total times up, Marino was actually ahead of Ellison. It felt like finding a hidden room in a house he'd lived in his whole life.

He snapped a screenshot and texted Aicha. "Marino got on base more often than Ellison. Look." Then he added, "The batting average leaves out all his walks."

Her reply came fast. "That's not a real stat, you drafted that out of nowhere."

"Draft this," he typed, and pasted the numbers. Then, because she would absolutely check, he added the fine print about at-bats so she could see it herself. His dad drifted over, drying a pan, and squinted at the screen. "That's a lot of columns," he said. James explained only the conclusion, not the arithmetic, and his dad nodded slowly. "So the number everybody quotes is kind of predatory, in a way. It hunts the parts that look good and swallows the rest." James laughed at that. He hadn't thought of a stat as something with teeth before.

Aicha's next message took three minutes, which meant she was calculating. "Okay. Fine. But his jersey is still ugly."

"Your whole argument is hormones and ugly jerseys?" he wrote back. He was joking, mostly, but he was also still thinking. If one number could hide something this big, what else was compressed like that? News headlines did it too, he realized, turning a whole season, a whole year, a whole city into a single ranking. He wondered how many invisible walks were hidden inside every number people threw around.

He opened a new tab and started a list: batting average, on-base percentage, everything he could find. At the top he typed one question in bold. "What did this number leave out?"

His dad looked over his shoulder and said, "You're going to be at that computer all night, aren't you."

"Probably," said James.

Zoey had measured the gym floor with a tape measure eleven times, and the ball still refused to cooperate. Her project, "How Fast Does a Ball Really Roll?", needed one clean run: a marble released at the top of a ramp, then timed at one-metre intervals across the smooth floor. At the science fair table, the stopwatch in Toby's hand, she watched the second hand of her whole plan start to wobble.

"Toby, you're flinching before I say go," she said. "That's why your times keep coming out too small."

"I'm not flinching. I'm nervous." Toby set the stopwatch down and straightened his own display, the one about which battery brand lasted longest. He wanted the physics prize more than he had admitted to anyone, and Zoey knew it, because last week in the cafeteria he had shown her the prize ribbon from the year before, frayed at the corner, and said his older brother had won it twice. "If I mess up your timing, I'll never forgive myself."

She remembered then the afternoon her grandmother had taught her to bake bread, kneading the dough in even strokes while saying, "The same push, every time, that's the whole secret." Zoey had thought that was just about bread. Now she wondered whether a ball worked the same way, and whether her graph would prove it.

They tried again. Toby pressed start when she called, and they wrote the numbers together on a napkin: one metre at two seconds, two metres at four, three metres at six. Zoey plotted the points on her graph paper, drew the line through them, and stared. It was straight, and it climbed at one unbroken slant from corner to corner, as if a ruler had been laid along the dots. She checked for a mistake, recalculated, and checked again. "It's straight," she said. "A straight sloping line means constant speed." The ball had rolled at exactly the same speed the whole way, steady as her grandmother's hands on the dough, and the graph had caught it in the act.

Mr. Wright stopped at their table, badge lanyard swinging, and leaned over the paper. "Walk me through it," he said, so Zoey did, pointing at each point: distance along the bottom, time up the side, the slope unbroken. When she finished, he nodded slowly. "Consistent data," he said. "That's rarer than you'd think." Then he noticed Toby hovering and added, "And your battery chart. Fair warning, the judges like a percentage breakdown of results."

"I have one," Toby said. "Sixty-three versus fifty-eight." He flourished the chart out from behind the poster board before he could lose his nerve.

"Then let's go find you a judge," Zoey said, and grabbed his sleeve.

Sydney sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a taxi receipt flattened in front of her like evidence. "Grandma, it says fifteen dollars. Didn't you say the hotel was four kilometres away?"

Her grandmother peeled carrots at the counter. "The driver said six, but he didn't take the pretty route. I never argue with a man holding my luggage."

Sydney frowned at the receipt. Somewhere in those numbers was the truth about how far they had actually driven, and she wanted to find it. On the back of an envelope she wrote what she knew: three dollars just to get in the taxi, then two dollars for every kilometre. She remembered the driver saying it at the curb, and there it was in small print at the bottom of the receipt too.

"So three plus two times the kilometres equals fifteen," she said slowly, and wrote 3 + 2k = 15. "If I could get the k alone, I'd know the distance."

She remembered Ms. Pritchard saying that an equation was like a balance, and that whatever you did to one side you had to do to the other. Sydney took away three from one side, so she took away three from the other. That left 2k = 12. Two k's made twelve, so one k had to be six. She sat back. Six kilometres. The driver had told the truth, and Grandma had doubted him all weekend.

She checked it a different way, because a good result deserved a second test. Three plus two, plus two, plus two, plus two, plus two, plus two. Fifteen. It wasn't a trivial little coincidence either, she decided; it was a rule, and rules meant you could use them again.

"I can infer the route from the money," she announced. "You went six kilometres, not four. Maybe there was a detour, or maybe this receipt is an anomaly and you got a discount you didn't notice."

Her grandmother set down the knife. "A what?"

"Something that doesn't fit the pattern. But it fits here. Six kilometres, fifteen dollars, exactly."

Griffin would not believe this when Sydney texted him. He had told her just last week that math had nothing to do with real life. She took a photo of the envelope and sent it with the message, "Grandma's taxi ride, solved." Then she turned the envelope over and wrote a new question at the top: what if the ride had cost twenty-three dollars?

Her grandmother slid a peeled carrot across the table. "You do the next one," she said, "and I'll check the driver's stories."

Cooper had four index cards, one encyclopedia open to the letter V, and no idea how to start his presentation. The assignment was on the screen of the library computer in green letters: explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War. He knew the treaty had punished Germany after the First World War, but "helped lead to" was the part Mr. Fortin would actually grade.

Sarah-Maude slid into the chair across from him with her own stack of books. "I'm doing the same topic," she said. "Jeanne found a whole chapter in this one. Want to split it?"

"Only if you explain the middle part," Cooper said. "I can get from the treaty to Germany being angry. I can't get from angry to war."

Jeanne arrived carrying a photocopy. "Listen to this," she said, and read aloud in a low voice because they were in the library. "In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles, and Britain and France did not use force to stop him."

"That's it?" Cooper said. "That's the middle?"

"That's a piece of it," Jeanne said. "I don't know what it means either."

While they argued, a boy from their class, the one who always sat near the window, opened a bag of chips behind the reference shelf. Food in the library was against the rules. Mr. Fortin was checking books at the desk ten feet away, and he looked up, and he looked back down at his scanner. Nothing happened.

Cooper watched the boy eat the whole bag without hiding it. Then the boy got up, wandered to the display of new paperbacks marked DO NOT REMOVE UNTIL FRIDAY, and put three of them in his backpack.

"Mr. Fortin," Cooper said, before he decided to say it. "He's taking the new books."

Mr. Fortin went over, had a quiet conversation, and got the paperbacks back. The boy got a warning and a call home. Cooper sat down again, and something clicked into place. "That's the Rhineland," he said.

Sarah-Maude frowned. "The what?"

"The chips," Cooper said. "The rule got broken once and nothing happened. So he tried a bigger one. Britain and France let the first break go in 1936, when it was just troops going into the Rhineland. After that, why would he stop?" He pulled a blank card toward him and wrote rapidly. "It's not that the treaty made the war happen by itself. It's that every time somebody broke it and nobody stopped them, the rules kind of eroded. Wore down. Like a path."

Jeanne turned the photocopy around. "It says here the treaty also made German civilians pay reparations, money taken from ordinary people, not just the government. So they were angry and humiliated."

"So you get anger, then a test, then no pushback," Cooper said, arranging his cards in a line across the table. "Anger, test, nothing. Then more."

Sarah-Maude laughed. "It's ironic. The treaty was supposed to prevent another war by keeping Germany weak, and it basically handed Hitler his script."

Cooper stood and asked Mr. Fortin if he could sign out the projector cart for fifth period on Thursday. Mr. Fortin wrote his name on the clipboard. "What's your topic?" he asked.

"How the Treaty of Versailles helped cause the Second World War," Cooper said. "And how you have to stop the first broken rule, or you'll be stopping the second one a lot harder."

On his way back to the table, he passed the window seats. The boy from class was there, and he looked at Cooper for a long second, then zipped his backpack shut and left it on the floor, empty, next to his chair.

Grayson set the shoebox on the kitchen table and lifted out the photo of his grandfather in his straw hat, holding a fishing pole he never actually used. "It has to be right," he told his mom, who was peeling clementines and not looking at him. "He's only going to get one chance to find his way back."

Ariane arrived at four o'clock with her arms full. She had brought a stack of papel picado her aunt had mailed from Guanajuato, a fat bundle of marigolds from the flower shop, and her little brother Cohen, who wanted to help and kept trying to help too much. "We put it up on November first and second," Ariane said, sliding the paper banners across the table. "My family does it every year. Dia de los Muertos." She was usually quiet in class, the kind of person who let other kids talk over her, but today she was assertive about every detail, like a coach calling plays.

Grayson remembered the summer before last, when his grandfather sat on the porch steps shelling pistachios and telling him about a documentary he'd watched on the tundra, how the caribou knew exactly when to move even though nobody printed them a map. Grayson had asked how they knew, and his grandfather had shrugged and said, "Some things find their way without being told." Grayson had thought that was just something old people said. Now he wanted it to be true.

He built the altar on the sideboard, two wooden crates stacked and draped with a cloth. Cohen handed him the photo and Grayson set it at the center, where his grandfather could look out at the whole room. Then he pulled off marigold petals and scattered them in a line from the front door to the altar, orange against the floorboards like a lit fuse running backward. "The color and the scent guide spirits home," Ariane said, adjusting a candle Cohen had knocked crooked. "That's the whole idea." She wanted this to work too, Grayson realized. Her own grandmother's photo was on an altar in her house right now, and she had looked at it before walking over.

Cohen kept rearranging the food offerings, moving the pan dulce to the left, then back to the right, testing where it belonged. Grayson started to contradict him, then stopped. "Put it where you think he'd find it first," he said. Cohen placed the sweet bread directly in front of the photo, dead center, and stepped back with his hands on his hips like he had solved something.

They sat together as the sky outside went from orange to blue to black. Nobody talked much. Grayson leaned close to the marigolds and breathed in, sharp and dusty-sweet, memorizing it the way you'd memorize a password. If his grandfather was going to follow that smell through the dark, then Grayson wanted to know it himself, in case he ever had to call it back to mind.

The candle flickered once, and Cohen whispered, "He's reading the menu."

The drama room smelled like dust and old curtains, and Mr. Wu had pushed the desks against the wall to make an empty space in the middle. Leo stood at the edge of it with his hands in his pockets. In two weeks the class would perform short improvised scenes for the whole seventh grade, and Leo wanted a good one, but yesterday his scene with Kashton had collapsed in thirty seconds. They had argued about whether they were astronauts or chefs, and the audience had laughed at them, not with them.

"Partners again," Mr. Wu said, reading from his clipboard. "Leo and Pearl."

Pearl walked to the center, rolled her shoulders, and started the scene before Leo was ready. She pinched an invisible cord, made a casting motion, and reeled slowly. "Big one out there today, Grandpa," she said. "Bigger than the one that got away last summer."

Leo heard the words but not the rest. He stared at her empty hands and said, "What are you doing? We're not fishing, we're at a bank."

Pearl's arms dropped. The scene went quiet, and someone in the back snickered. Mr. Wu tapped his clipboard twice, and the class paused.

Leo frowned at Pearl. "You didn't say we were fishing. You just wiggled your arm."

"She did say it," said Kashton from the side. "With the rod. Mr. Wu told us yesterday, remember? An offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, like a place, a name, or a problem. The rod was the place. The lake."

Leo turned it over in his head. Offers could be invisible things, not just words. That was the hidden part, like figuring out which key opened a stuck lock. He thought of a way to test it. He would ignore nothing and see how long the scene could run.

"Same scene," Mr. Wu said. "From the top, and this time, accept it. Yes, and."

Pearl cast the invisible line again. "Big one today, Grandpa."

"Yes, and it's going to demolish the dock if we drag it in," Leo said, grabbing the rod with both hands. "Remember when your antibiotic pills spilled in the tackle box and the whole boat smelled like a pharmacy?"

"Fish loved it," Pearl said. "That patch of water was fertile. Best catches of my life."

They hauled and staggered, and Kashton called out from the side, "The dock is breaking!" so Leo tipped sideways, pulling Pearl with him, and the class clapped while the two of them sprawled on the floor, still holding the rod that wasn't there.

Alexa slid her laptop toward the middle of the table in the library corner where coding club met every Thursday. Mr. Novák had given them one hour before the mini-showcase at four thirty, when each of them would stand up and run a program for the rest of the club. Her objective was small but stubborn: a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime. Her first version worked, but when she typed a big number like 999,983, the little spinner just sat there, thinking, while the clock on the wall ticked closer to the deadline.

Tessa leaned over from the next seat. "Mine keeps saying 9 is prime. Can I look at yours?"

"Watch this, though," Alexa said. She typed 999,983 again and they both stared at the cursor blinking in the terminal, doing nothing. "It's testing every single number up to it. Even ones that can't possibly work."

She wrote the numbers out on scrap paper to think it through. Her loop tried 2, then 3, then 4, then 5, then 6. She circled the even ones after 2 and frowned at them. A number like 999,983 was odd, and every second thing her loop tested was even. She tested a smaller case to be sure, checking whether 15 could divide evenly by 4 or by 6. It couldn't, not once, not ever. After checking whether a number was divisible by 2, a program only needed to test odd divisors, because an odd number could never be divided evenly by an even one. She sat back. Half the loop was pure waste.

While she typed the fix, starting her divisors at 3 and stepping by 2 instead of 1, Mika appeared behind her chair, holding a folded note he had passed across the room like they were in regular class. Alexa unfolded it. "Trade you my variable-naming tips for a look at your loop trick," it read, with a small doodle of a turtle. "My checker takes forever on anything past 1000." She wrote "deal, after showcase" on the bottom, folded it back, and handed it over her shoulder without turning around.

At 4:28 she pressed Enter on 999,983. The answer, "prime," appeared before the second hand finished its trip around the clock face. Mr. Novák called two minutes, and Tessa closed her laptop, still grinning about her own bug, which had turned out to be a missing equals sign hiding in the plumbing of her if-statement. When it was Alexa's turn, she stood, typed one last number into the prompt, and said, "Watch how fast it comes back."

Victoria spread her bank statements across the library table like a detective who had just found a suspicious fingerprint. Five statements, five years, one question that had been bugging her since math class.

"Kylian, look at this. Every single year, the interest is exactly twelve dollars. Not eleven fifty. Not twelve twenty. Twelve."

Kylian leaned over, chewing the end of his pencil. He wanted the library's chess set for lunch period, and Ms. Ndlovu had told him he could have it if he finished his math work first, which was why he was stuck at this table instead of planning his opening moves. "Maybe your bank is just lazy."

"That's what I thought at first." Victoria tapped the page. "But Ms. Ndlovu said there's a rule that governs this, and rules aren't lazy. Rules are rules." She remembered, suddenly, the day her grandfather had opened the account for her. She'd been seven, and he'd slid the paper across the bank counter and said, "Watch this money grow, kiddo," and she'd imagined an actual plant sprouting dollar bills. It had not sprouted. It had just sat there, adding twelve dollars a year like clockwork.

"Okay," she said, sitting up straight. "Test time. If the interest only ever counts my original hundred dollars, then it adds the same amount every year. Watch. Year one, twelve. Year two, twelve. All the way down. It fits." She flipped to a different sheet, one she'd made up herself, with numbers that grew every year instead of staying the same. "But if interest counted the whole balance, the interest itself would grow too. Kylian, my bank is only paying me on the original amount."

"The original amount," Kylian said slowly, "is called the principal. Ms. Ndlovu drilled that into us Tuesday. You were drawing on your shoe."

"I was taking notes artistically." Victoria pulled her shoe closer and, sure enough, there was the word, inked in blue along the heel. She laughed so hard a boy at the next table shushed her with great compassion, as though she were a wounded bird rather than a girl cackling at her own sneakers.

"So compound interest is the one where you earn interest on your interest," Kylian said. "Simple is just principal, principal, principal."

"And my account is the boring one." Victoria sighed. Then she frowned. "Wait. Tuesday, you said the class voted on which bank to use for the fake class savings project."

"Yeah. Mackenzie's group won. They picked compound."

Victoria grabbed her notebook. Mackenzie's group had gotten five extra fake dollars over five years on the very same starting amount. Extra money, from nothing but a different rule. She looked at her own statements, all those identical twelves marching in a row, and felt the future shift under her like a rug being pulled.

"Grandpa's getting a phone call tonight," she said, and began stuffing the statements into her backpack. "Right after I beat you at chess."

"You can't have the chess set. I earned it."

"Then watch me earn something better."

Emilie held the onion like it was a live grenade, which, considering her last attempt, was fair. "Curve your fingers under, like a claw," said Ms. Hu, the camp cook who had already confiscated one bandage box. Emilie bent her fingertips until her knuckles led the way, set the knife against them, and chopped straight down. The pieces were uneven, but all ten fingers stayed where they belonged, so she counted it as a win. Miller gave her a slow clap from across the picnic table.

The real prize, though, was the sauce. Emilie's group had been assigned pasta with sauce from scratch, and she was determined not to serve what Quinn's group served last summer, which everyone still called red water. She diced tomatoes, crushed garlic, dumped it all in the pot with a splash of oil, and set it over the fire with the lid on, because a lid kept things from burning, obviously.

Twenty minutes later she lifted the lid and stared. The sauce was thin. Really thin. Quinn leaned over and said, "Congratulations, you've invented soup." Emilie stirred it and thought about it. When you boil water for tea, the steam fogs up the window, and the pan ends up emptier than it started. Water leaves as steam. Steam can't leave if the lid is on. She did a quick analysis of her own logic: lid on, steam trapped, water stays, sauce runny. Lid off, water escapes, sauce thickens. It was a theory, and theories could be tested.

She propped the lid on a rock beside the fire and let the pot sit uncovered, bubbling slowly. Miller watched the steam curl up into the pines. "It smells more like sauce already," he admitted, which was generous, since it had always smelled like sauce. Emilie stirred every few minutes and marked the sauce line on the wooden spoon with her thumbnail so she could track it.

By dinnertime the spoon told the truth. The sauce had crept down past her thumbnail, thicker, clingier, sticking to the pasta instead of pooling under it. Even the second-in-command taste tester, a kid who usually ate hot dogs and nothing else, asked for seconds. Ms. Hu raised an eyebrow at the empty lid, sitting barren on its rock, and said nothing at all.

"That's my analysis," Emilie announced, ladling out the last of it. "Steam out, sauce thick." Quinn held up his fork. "Less analysis, more pasta."

Ivy's mother had banned screens for the weekend, so naturally Ivy spent Saturday at her mother's office, learning to use one. It was a kind of quiet rebellion: her mother had said "no games," and Ivy had decided that a spreadsheet was clearly not a game.

The task was real. Her mother's team had sold raffle tickets all week, and someone had to add up the columns for each seller and turn them into a bar chart for Monday's meeting. Her mother showed her once, typed "=SUM(B2:B8)" into a cell, and got pulled away to a phone call. Ivy tried it in the next column and got a number that made no sense at all. Liyana, whose mother worked two desks over, leaned in and studied the screen. "Layla's going to accuse you of cheating," she said. "Her chart's going to show her losing to a wrong number."

Ivy stared at the formula. It looked exactly like her mother's. She clicked through the cells one at a time, reading them aloud, and found the problem near the bottom: row 12 sat outside the range, holding sixty-two tickets all by itself. The formula was obeying her perfectly. It was just doing what she'd told it to do instead of what she'd meant. She changed it to "=SUM(B2:B12)," and the total jumped.

"That's the thing about these programs," said a voice behind her. It was her grandmother, who still came in on Saturdays to sort the mail. "They do the arithmetic so you can't argue with it. The first one for home computers was called VisiCalc. Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston wrote it, and it came out in 1979 for the Apple II." She peered at the screen. "Before that, I did budgets on paper, and every total was a small act of hope."

Ivy tested the fix before trusting it. She picked the column with the fewest numbers, added them in her head, and compared. It matched. Then she highlighted the totals, clicked the bar chart button, and watched the bars rise like a skyline, Layla's towering over everyone's except one mystery bar. "Whose is that?" Liyana asked.

They traced the column header up. It was labeled GRANDMA.

Her grandmother raised her hands. "I sold to the whole mailroom."

"You didn't tell me you were in the raffle," Ivy said.

"You never asked."

Luke set his phone face down beside his plate and poked at his noodles. "Dad, I need to say something about the thing you sent me this morning."

His dad looked up. The link had been a blog post claiming that a certain tea could shrink your risk of getting sick by half. Luke had wanted to believe it, because his grandmother drank that tea every day and still caught every cold that went through her building. Something about that didn't fit, and it had bugged him all through school.

"Ocean and I looked it up at lunch," Luke said. "We found the blog post, but then we found a real article in a science journal about the same tea, and the journal one said the effect was tiny, like barely anything." He picked up his fork and held it perpendicular to the table, twirling noodles around it while he talked. "So I asked Ms. Szabó after school what the difference was. She didn't tell me the answer. She just pulled up both articles side by side and said one question would sort it out: who checked each one before it went out."

His little sister reached across for the salt, knocking over the pepper shaker, and their mom set it upright without looking up from her plate.

"The blog post? Nobody checked it," Luke said. "The guy just wrote it and clicked publish. But the journal article, before it got printed, other experts in the field reviewed it for errors. Ms. Szabó said it's called peer review. So one is a story about one person's opinion, and the other is a claim that a bunch of scientists already tried to poke holes in and couldn't. Well, mostly couldn't. The journal one even lists what's still uncertain."

Dad leaned back. "So you're telling me my tea thing is wrong."

"I'm telling you it's untested," Luke said. "There's a difference." His dad laughed, but Luke noticed he slid his own phone over and opened the link again, scrolling slower this time. Luke felt his shoulders, which had been bunched up like a fist, finally start to unclench.

"Grandma should keep drinking it if she likes it," Mom said. "Tastes good, keeps her company. Just don't buy the thirty-dollar kind."
