Then a private message, just from Lola. "can I be honest? you skipped once and it helped. then you skipped again. did it get easier or harder? because from out here it looks harder."

Jaxon stared at the question. He thought about the first time, in the fall, when he'd only felt shaky for one afternoon afterward. The second time, the shakiness had lasted two days. Now, this morning, just reading the word "presentation" had made his chest tight before he'd even decided anything. The pattern was there, plain as the class diagram: every time he avoided it, the next one scared him more, not less.

He typed back, "harder. I just figured that out."

"so what if it's like the flowers," Lola wrote. "they only open when the bee actually shows up. you've never once seen yourself do the presentation, so your brain has no proof you can."

Jaxon sat with that. Tomorrow there was one more presentation slot, for groups doing extra credit. He could sign up. Or he could let the relief win again, and the one after that would be worse. He was still deciding, and he hated deciding.

He opened the chat, found the extra credit sign-up link, and typed his name in the box before he could delete it. His thumb shook a little on the send button.

"There," he said out loud, alone in his room. "Now I have to actually show up."

Lola replied with one word: "finally."

The gym had been transformed, more or less. Crepe paper hung from the basketball hoop like a droopy canopy, and the DJ booth sat directly under it, speakers stacked on folding chairs. Livia stood near the door with Kareem and Ireland, all three of them pretending they came to dances all the time. Then the bass dropped, and conversation became impossible. They ended up right beside the speakers because Kareem said the best spot was close to the music, and nobody argued.

At eleven that night, Livia lay in bed hearing a thin, high whine that was not coming from anywhere. She picked up her phone and typed into the family group chat: "Is the wifi doing something weird? I keep hearing a squeal." Her mom replied with a picture of a shrugging emoji. Her older brother, who had gone to concerts all last year, answered differently: "That's tinnitus. Ringing in your ears after loud music. It means the noise was loud enough to actually damage your hearing. It's a warning sign." Livia stared at the message, then pressed her palms over her ears. Still squealing.

She thought back to the fall, when her cousin's wedding had been held outside under a tent so arid and dusty that the DJ had cranked everything to maximum, and she had heard that same faint whine on the drive home. She had blamed the car. It had never once occurred to her that her own ears were the source, and that the ringing was trying to tell her something. Now the pattern seemed obvious: loud music, then the whine. The whine showed up only after loud music. She wanted to verify it before she believed a group chat at midnight.

On Monday she found Kareem at his locker. "Did your ears ring Saturday?" she asked. He nodded, and then said the thing that made her stomach drop. "They're still ringing. Right now. Like a TV that won't turn off." Ireland came over and admitted hers had rung until Sunday morning. Livia pulled out her phone and showed Kareem her brother's message, and he read it twice without speaking.

"So the speakers," Kareem said slowly. "We were basically leaning on them." He looked down the hall toward the gym doors, as if the speakers might still be lurking there. "There's another dance in March," he said. "I'm standing by the water fountain next time. That's like forty feet away." Ireland said she would join him, and Livia said she would too, but first she was going to ask her brother one more question in the group chat. She typed: "Does it go away?" and watched the screen while the typing dots appeared.

Brayden sat on his bed with the family group chat open on his mom's old phone. The dance was in four hours, and he had typed and deleted the same message six times.

"I don't know how to dance," he finally sent.

His aunt replied first, as usual. "Nobody does. That's the trick."

Then his eccentric uncle, the one who kept ferrets and a telescope on the roof, sent a link. "Watch this before you leave. It changed my whole life philosophy."

The video showed a white bird with a yellow crest on its head, bobbing and stepping as a song played. His uncle's message followed: "In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed."

"A bird," Brayden typed back.

"A bird," his uncle confirmed.

Brayden watched it three more times. Snowball wasn't doing anything fancy. He bounced on one foot, then the other, then shook his head, and when the song slowed down, the bird slowed down too, still landing on the beat. Brayden had an idea, and since there was nobody in the kitchen to watch him fail, he decided to test it there. He put on a song, bounced on one foot, then the other, then shook his head. When the tempo changed, he counted the new beat in his head and adjusted, just like the cockatoo had. It wasn't pretty. But it matched.

At the dance, the gym smelled like floor wax and somebody's older brother's cologne. Yasser was already near the wall, holding a cup of punch like a shield. Lea-Maude stood next to him, doing a small side-to-side step that didn't touch any beat at all.

"Lea-Maude," Brayden said. "Try bouncing. One foot, then the other. And when the song speeds up, you speed up."

"Why?"

"Because it works. I tested it."

She squinted at him, then tried it. On the fourth bounce, she landed exactly with the kick drum, and her whole face changed. "It works," she said, sounding personally offended that nobody had told her sooner.

The DJ put on a slow song and half the gym froze, but Brayden counted the new, slower tempo in his head and slowed his bounce to match. Lea-Maude did the same. Yasser set down his punch and joined them, mostly on beat.

Ms. Rao, on chaperone duty by the door, watched them for a moment. "Where did you three learn that?"

"Family group chat," Brayden said.

"An uncle," Lea-Maude added, still bouncing. "The eccentric one, probably."

"He mentored a cockatoo," Brayden said, which wasn't exactly true, but the beat dropped and there was no time to fix it.

Henry had one class period to get the spreadsheet right, because Mr. Addo had promised that the student with the cleanest budget chart would run the announcement screen at the spring concert. That was the job Henry wanted more than anything, standing at the controls in front of the whole school, so he had claimed the computer next to the window and started typing numbers into column B: what the drama club would spend on costumes, paint, and programs.

"You're doing it all by hand?" Avani asked, leaning over from the next seat. She wanted her chart to have the tallest bars in the room, even if she had to pick categories that made the club look rich. "Mr. Addo said there's a faster way."

Henry typed an equals sign, then SUM, then dragged his cursor down the column of costs. When he pressed Enter, the total appeared at the bottom like it had been waiting there the whole time. "Cool," he said, but he did not trust it. The number looked too big, forty dollars too big, and he could not see why. The formula was hiding whatever was wrong, the way a closed locker hides a mess.

He thought about that for a minute, tapping his pencil on the desk while the lab's old fan rattled in the corner. If the formula really was adding the whole column, then changing any single number ought to change the total too. So he tested it. He clicked on the paint cost, changed 25 to 26, and watched the total jump up by exactly one dollar, all by itself, without him touching the SUM at all. Then he changed it back, and the total dropped again. The formula was working. That meant the problem was in one of the numbers themselves.

He scrolled down the column, one cell at a time, checking each entry against the crumpled budget sheet in his pocket. Near the bottom he found it: the programs cost, which should have read 15, had an extra digit typed after it. He fixed the typo, and the total shrank by forty dollars on its own, instantly, before he even breathed.

"Whoa," Avani said, peering over. "It fixed itself." She looked at her own chart, where she had been padding the decoration budget to make her bars taller, and her shoulders dropped a little. "Maybe mine should just show the real numbers too." Behind them, Mr. Addo paused on his way past and smiled at the screen, mentioning to another teacher that he had built a spreadsheet just like it to watch his own pension after a few volatile years in the market, and that charts helped him sleep at night. Henry highlighted his corrected column, clicked the bar chart button, and watched eight gray bars rise across the screen. "Now label the axes," Avani said, "and then we submit both at the same time."

The cast on Lily's right arm still felt like a stranger, stiff and heavy, and the doctor's words kept circling back to her all week: a fracture of the radius near the wrist, the most common fracture seen in children. She had heard the nurse say it almost cheerfully, as if Lily had joined an enormous club. Now she sat on the low wall by the basketball court, watching Mattea roll her borrowed skateboard back and forth across the cracked pavement.

"I want to learn the kick turn today," Mattea said, pushing off again. "I don't care how many times I stack it. I'll persevere until I get it." Her shoelaces were double-knotted and she'd drawn a tiny flame on the grip tape with marker, because the flame meant the board was equivalent to a race car, at least in her head. Lily suspected nothing could make a wobbly plastic skateboard equivalent to a race car, but she kept that to herself.

"Mattea, wait," Lily said. "How did I break mine?" She held up the cast. "Think about it. I didn't land on my elbow or my shoulder."

Mattea stopped, one foot on the tail of the board. "You put your hands out. You skidded on both palms and then the right one kind of folded."

"Exactly. Falling onto an outstretched hand. That's what does it." Lily stood, warming to the puzzle. She had been turning it over for days, the way you turn over a rock to see what lives underneath. Every skater she could remember falling at the park had done the same thing, hands shooting forward like springs. Was it a rule, then? Did hands always jump out first? "Let's test it. Fall down. On purpose. Softly, onto the grass."

Mattea flopped onto the grass beside the court, arms at her sides, and bounced a little. "Feels weird. My hands wanted to go out even when I knew I was falling."

"I know! Mine too, the whole ride down." Lily noticed Mr. Munro across the yard, winding up the long jump rope for the younger kids, and waved him over. "Mr. Munro, when kids fall off things here, do they mostly catch themselves with their hands?"

He thought for a second, then nodded. "Almost always. Outstretched hands. The wrist pays for it."

"That's what I thought," Lily said. So the rule held even off the board, even on monkey bars and scooters and the icy patch by the doors every January. The hidden cause wasn't the skateboard at all. It was the landing.

"Okay, new plan," Mattea said, brushing grass off her knees. "Teach me to fall on my forearms instead."

They practiced on the grass for the whole recess, Mattea dropping and rolling, tucking her hands in, getting stranger and faster at it. On her last try she landed smooth as a cat and popped straight up.

"Now the kick turn," she said, and stepped onto the board.

Nevaeh stood in Mr. Nur's kitchen with a list of emergency numbers on the fridge and a six-month-old baby on her shoulder, and the baby was screaming like a smoke alarm with opinions. Mr. Nur had left twenty minutes ago for a parent thing at the school, and Nevaeh had already tried bouncing, singing, and a sock puppet named Gerald, who was now sweating from the effort.

The baby's face had gone a dark tomato red. Nevaeh paced the hallway, past the framed photos of Mr. Nur's family and a shelf of shells arranged by size. She thought about her baby-sitting course, the Saturday one with the plastic dolls. The instructor had said something she hadn't fully believed at the time: shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head. Nevaeh had thought, that seems extreme, it's just a little jiggle. But she remembered the instructor's flat, serious voice, and the way the whole room had gone quiet.

She was not going to shake the baby. Obviously. But her arms were doing an impulsive little frustrated bounce without asking her permission, so she made a decision instead. She carried the baby to the crib in the nursery, laid him down on his back, checked that the blanket was below his arms, and stepped out into the hallway. She closed the door halfway and stood there breathing.

Through the gap she could hear the crying continue, drop a little, then continue. She sat on the hallway floor beside a potted plant that was definitely fake, because it had dust on its leaves. "Okay," she whispered. "Think." Crying meant something. Babies didn't cry for no reason, the instructor had said, and Nevaeh decided she could infer the cause if she collected clues like a detective. Not hungry, she'd tried a bottle. Diaper, checked twice, both times heroic. Not tired, because he'd slept before Mr. Nur left.

Then she remembered the sock. When she'd checked the diaper the second time, one sock had been off, and she'd thought nothing of it. But when she took it off, had there been something inside? She crept back into the nursery. The baby was still red-faced but the cries had become grumbly, hiccupy ones. Nevaeh picked up the sock and shook it gently over her palm. A folded hospital bracelet fell out, and a long blond hair, wrapped around the baby's actual sock underneath had been a tiny plastic hospital tag with sharp edges. She hadn't felt it through the sock.

She slid the tag out from the sock, held it up to the lamp, and winced. It had a corner like a shark fin. "Buddy," she said, "you've been walking on a shark this whole time." The baby blinked at her with wet eyelashes and made a sound like a small question.

She freed the hair, removed the tag, put the sock back on, and lifted him up, careful to cup her hand behind his head the way the instructor had drilled into them. He gave one last hiccup and then, insultingly fast, fell asleep against her collarbone, leaving a warm wet patch on her shirt. When Mr. Nur came home an hour later, he found Nevaeh on the couch with the baby asleep in the crib and the plastic tag held up in triumph. "I'd like to open negotiations regarding my fee," she said, "because I solved a mystery."

The war memorial sat on a low hill at the edge of town, a granite soldier staring east over the river, and Jordan's social studies class stood around it in the wind while Ms. Farah-Ali held up a cardboard box. "The historical society lent us this," she said. "Diaries, letters, a land paper. Find a primary source and use it to explain why people moved west." Jordan had wanted the letters, because letters were short. Colton grabbed those first, grinning, so Jordan took the leather diary with the cracked spine and sat on the memorial's bottom step to read.

The handwriting belonged to a man named Amos Reed, who in 1863 wrote that he had nothing in Ohio but debts, and that "the Homestead Act of 1862 offers 160 acres of public land to any settler who will live on it and farm it for five years." Five years, Jordan thought. That was longer than he'd been at his middle school. He read on. Amos had a wife who didn't want to leave her sister, and a boy Jordan's age, and the diary kept returning to that argument the way a tongue returns to a sore tooth.

"Conductor on the train said the plains are turbulent country," Amos wrote in April. "Wind like a living thing. But land is land." Jordan looked up. Brynlee was photographing the engraved names on the memorial, names of men who'd left farms like the one Amos wanted. He thought of his grandfather, who still farms the acres his great-great-grandmother homesteaded. There was a flashback Jordan couldn't shake: last summer, Grandpa had tried to confide something about the farm, said it hadn't come to the family the way everyone believed, then changed the subject and shelled peas instead.

Jordan had assumed, when he chose the diary, that the answer would be simple: people moved west because land was free. That was the sentence he'd planned for his report. But Amos's wife wrote two pages herself near the end, in smaller, steadier letters, and she didn't mention land at all. She mentioned the boy, and the river in Ohio that had flooded their crop twice, and the fact that staying meant owing money to her brother-in-law forever. Free land was the door, Jordan realized, but people walked through it for different reasons, some of which they barely said out loud.

Then Colton leaned over his shoulder. "Reed. That's my mom's maiden name. That's my family." Jordan read the last line again, the one where Amos Reed wrote that his wife had finally said yes, and he hadn't asked twice. "So your family got 160 acres," Jordan said slowly, "for five years of farming." Colton sat down hard on the step beside him. "My grandpa sold it in 1970. Everybody thinks we still have it." Behind them the granite soldier went on staring east, toward everything that had been given up, or taken, or lost. "You should call your mom," Jordan said, and held out the diary.

Noah had been carrying his grandfather's watch in his jacket pocket for three days, wrapped in a paper towel so it would not get scratched. Now he stood at the edge of the cemetery with Wali and Hendrik on either side of him, and the cold came up through his shoes. His mother and aunts stood closer to the grave, near the flowers. Noah kept his hand in his pocket, touching the watch the way you keep checking for your phone, except this was heavier and older and had stopped at 4:17.

"Are you going to put it on?" Wali asked, watching him.

"I don't know." That was the honest answer. He had read somewhere that you were supposed to let go, move on, get back to normal, and part of him wondered whether wearing a dead person's watch every day was the opposite of that. Maybe it was like refusing to believe it happened. His cousin had said grief was contagious, that if you held on to things too tight, everyone around you caught the sadness and nobody got better. Noah had no way to verify that. He could not exactly run an experiment on his whole family.

After the service, people drifted toward the cars, but Ms. Demetriou, who lived two doors down and had known his grandfather from the chess club at the library, stayed behind with him. She saw him turning the watch over in his palm. "I used to think keeping my father's things meant I was stuck," she said. "Then a counsellor handed me a book. Continuing Bonds, from 1996. It argued that keeping a connection to someone who died, through memories, objects, traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving. Not the opposite of it." She shrugged. "I still make his soup every October."

Noah looked down at the watch. So it was not a rule that you had to drop everything and walk away. It was more like a probability: some ways of remembering helped, some probably did not, and wearing a watch that made him think of Saturday chess games seemed likely to be one of the good ones. He buckled it on. It was loose around his wrist, so loose it slid almost to his elbow, and Hendrik laughed and said it looked like a bracelet on a fence post.

"Give it two years," Noah said. "I'll grow into it."

They walked back along the gravel path together, and every few steps the watch slipped down and Noah pushed it up again, the small metal circle catching the low winter sun.

Lea stood at the steel prep counter behind the restaurant's kitchen, an onion in front of her and a knife that had seen better days. On the counter lay a note in Ms. Dhillon's looping handwriting, left there before the dinner rush: "Sauce needs six onions, diced small. If they make you cry, remember the goggles in the drawer." At the bottom, she had added a second line. "Kenneth wants his pasta special on Saturday's menu. Tell him yes or no by five." Lea folded the note into her apron pocket, because Kenneth was already hovering by the stove, waiting for her answer like the sauce depended on it, which in a way it did.

"The special is my recipe," Kenneth said. "My grandmother's. I just need someone to chop proper onion for it. Hamza said he'd stir, but he's voluntary help only, he keeps reminding me." That was true. Hamza had wandered in from the alley, announced he was there voluntarily, and stationed himself by the pot with a wooden spoon.

Lea curled her fingers into the claw grip Ms. Dhillon had shown her, knuckles forward, fingertips tucked away, and pressed down on the onion. The knife slid off without cutting. She pressed harder. It skated sideways again and nearly caught her knuckle, and her breath went shallow. She turned the blade toward the light and saw how the edge had gone dull and rounded, worn down by a year of chopping. Her mind went to the drawer of knives by the sink, the one Ms. Dhillon kept for the sharp ones. If a dull knife needed all that pushing, then a sharp one must need less, and a knife you barely push cannot slip. She fetched a slim blade with a fine edge, and it sank through the onion like the onion wanted it to.

"I'm switching to this one," she said, holding it up. "A sharp knife is safer than a dull one. It needs less pressure, so it won't slip off the food."

"Safer," Hamza repeated, dubious, watching her from the pot.

"Safer," Lea said, and went back to work. The onion dwindled from a whole bulb to a neat pile of even dice, and her eyes barely stung. She swept the pieces into the pan where the oil shimmered, and Kenneth added the tomatoes his grandmother would have used, crushed by hand.

"So," he said, spoon in midair. "Saturday? Yes or no? It's five o'clock somewhere."

Lea wiped the blade, laid it flat, and gave the sauce one slow stir. "Yes," she said. "Tell your grandmother her recipe made the menu."

Muhammad crouched at the electronics bench in the science museum's lower lab, a coil of thin wire in front of him, a battery, a voltmeter, and an ammeter clipped into a tidy circuit. The worksheet on the clipboard asked for one number: the resistance of the wire. All he had to do was measure the voltage across it and the current through it, then divide. Simple, except that the voltmeter kept reading zero.

"Your leads are wrong," Brooklyn said, leaning over his shoulder. "You have to put the voltmeter in line, like the ammeter. Break the circuit and stick it in."

"That can't be right," Muhammad said. "If we break the circuit, the current stops, and then what are we even measuring?" He scrutinized the diagram taped to the bench, a drawing of a battery, a resistor, and two meters. In the picture, the ammeter sat inside the loop, but the voltmeter hovered outside it, connected by its own two little branches. The drawing looked almost lazy, as if whoever made it had forgotten to draw the meter into the circuit properly. Muhammad ran his finger along the lines twice.

Tamara plugged in the battery and the ammeter jumped to life, showing 0.5 amps. So current was flowing. The voltmeter, still reading zero, must be sitting in a dead spot. "In the drawing," Muhammad said slowly, "the voltmeter's leads touch the two ends of the resistor. Not the middle, not the battery. Just the two ends."

He unclipped the red lead and the black lead and moved them so each one touched a different end of the wire, the voltmeter now attached alongside it in its own separate path. The needle swung over and settled at 1.5 volts. "There," he said. "So the voltmeter measures voltage when it's connected in parallel, with its two leads touching either end of the thing you're testing."

"Parallel," Tamara repeated, writing it down. "Okay. Divide."

Muhammad did the math. 1.5 divided by 0.5 was 3 ohms. Then he remembered last summer at his cousin's house, when the porch light kept dimming and his uncle had traced the wire along the railing, hunting for a bad section he couldn't see. His uncle had said the wire would tell on itself if you measured it right. At the time Muhammad had thought that was just something grown-ups said. Now it seemed almost literal. You couldn't see resistance, but the two numbers together gave it away, like footprints.

They tested a second wire, a thicker one with a colorful polymer coating, and got a smaller number, 1 ohm. Brooklyn tried the leads himself, placing them correctly on the first try, and grinned when the needle moved.

Ms. Toussaint wandered by, glanced at their worksheet, and slid a granola bar onto the bench beside Muhammad. "You three missed the lunch talk," she said. "That's nutritious and you earned it."

Muhammad pocketed it and copied the last number onto the sheet in his neatest writing.

Isabelle had volunteered at the soup kitchen for exactly forty minutes, and already she had a mystery. Every Saturday, she had learned from the schedule taped to the fridge, a van arrived with crates of fresh vegetables, carrots still muddy, apples with leaves still clinging to their stems. Fresh produce was expensive. The soup kitchen's budget was small. So where did it all come from? She asked the woman who ran the kitchen, but the woman only shrugged and said, "Ask the driver, hon."

The driver was a college kid with a stable of canvas totes in the back of his van, all labeled with the name of a farm. Isabelle wanted to ask him, but every time she got close, he was already halfway out the door. She decided to verify her first guess, that a rich person donated the money and the kitchen bought the produce. She checked the donation binder by the register. There were plenty of donors, but none big enough for weekly crates of vegetables, and the kitchen's produce orders were all frozen and canned. So her first idea was wrong. Whatever was happening, it wasn't money. It was something else, some rule she hadn't figured out yet.

She wasn't the only one working the mystery. Julien, who had been coming since September, wanted to win the kitchen's volunteer-of-the-month photo on the lobby wall more than anything. He was sure the secret was a famous person who didn't want attention, and he kept trying to peek at the driver's paperwork. "If I find out who it is," Julien whispered, "they'd put my picture up for solving it."

When the van pulled up that Saturday, Isabelle was ready. She carried a crate of potatoes so heavy she had to set it down twice, and she made a point of turning it over. The label didn't say a store or a warehouse. It said Field 4. Potatoes do not come from Field 4 of a store. They come from a farm, and only from a farm, after a harvest.

Her friend Ananya, who had rushed in late from a morning audition for the school play and was still humming her song under her breath, lifted a carrot and frowned at its broken top. "These look like leftovers," Ananya said. "My uncle does this. It's called gleaning. Gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks."

Isabelle stared at the potatoes, dirt still on them, several of them nicked and small, the kind a machine would leave behind. That was the pattern. Not perfect vegetables bought with money. Leftover vegetables picked by hand, by volunteers, the machines having passed over them already. She turned to the driver as he hefted the last crate.

"Do you pick these yourself?" she asked.

"Every Saturday," he said. "You two want to come out next weekend? We could use more hands. Bring gloves."

Julien was already reaching for the signup sheet. "Sign me up twice," he said, and Isabelle laughed and wrote her name right below his.

Jacob had until eight o'clock tomorrow morning to make his science fair project work, and all he had was a water rocket with a sticky piston and a launch pad stuck in the backyard grass. The rocket refused to fly. He pumped and pumped, but the piston jammed halfway up the tube every single time.

Amalia sat on the porch steps eating a banana, and that was the start of the real trouble. "You have flies all over you," Jacob said, swatting the air. "It's the banana," Amalia said. "Rotting fruit just makes them. Everybody knows that. Leave a peach out and boom, fruit flies, straight out of the peach." Jacob stared at her. "Out of the peach? They crawl out of it?" "They appear," Amalia said, like it was obvious.

Jacob went inside and called Fatimah, who owned every book about scientists in the school library. She read to him over the phone, slow and clear: "In 1668, Francesco Redi put meat in jars. Maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat." Jacob wrote it down on his hand because he couldn't find paper. "So if the flies can't get to the rotting stuff," he said, "nothing shows up." "That's Redi," Fatimah said. "You should test it. That's the whole point of a hypothesis. It's a guess you can actually check, and the check can go either way." Jacob looked at the clock. Seven hours until the bus.

He modified his plan fast. Forget the rocket. He set up three jars on the backyard picnic table: one open with a slice of Amalia's banana, one sealed tight with a slice inside, and one covered with gauze held by a rubber band, flies kept off but air getting in. Amalia stood over it with her arms crossed. "This is a counterfeit experiment," she said. "Nothing's going to happen in the sealed one anyway, so what does that prove?" "Then you have nothing to worry about," Jacob said.

At six in the morning, in the gray light, they crouched over the table. The open jar had four tiny flies walking on the banana. The sealed jar had nothing, and Amalia said, "Fine, but that's just because it's airtight." Then Jacob lifted the gauze. Nothing. Not one fly, not one speck, on banana that was brown and soft and as rotten as the first one. Amalia leaned so close her nose almost touched the glass. She looked at the gauze, then at Jacob, then at the gauze again. "Okay," she said quietly. "Okay, fine. They come from outside." Jacob grabbed the jar, the notebook, and the gauze, and ran for the bus.

Alexia spread her notebook across the library table and stared at the assignment sheet for the fourth time. Write a short story with dialogue, a clear climax, and a final draft due Friday. She did not dread writing itself; she dreaded the red pen Mr. Rossi would use on her dialogue, because last time he had circled half her punctuation and written "See me" in the margin.

Julianna dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of graphic novels and her own notebook. "I want mine to be about a soccer tournament," she said. "The championship goal has to be the climax. Obviously."

"Obviously," Alexia agreed, though she wasn't sure what her own climax would be. She had decided on a story about two friends caught in a flood at a summer camp, because at least flood water rising was a problem that got worse on its own.

Haroun arrived last, carrying his laptop and a printout so meticulous it looked like a book page, margins ruled in pencil. "I'm doing a story about an outbreak," he said. "A scientist has to get the vaccine to a town before the sickness spreads. But I need someone to test-read it, because I can't tell anymore if it makes sense."

"I'll read it," Julianna said, always first to volunteer.

Alexia watched her friend's eyes move down the first page. Julianna's reading slowed at the third paragraph. Her lips moved. Then she frowned and slid the paper back across the table.

"Who's talking here?" Julianna asked, tapping the page. "The scientist and the mayor both have lines in this one paragraph, and I got lost. I thought the mayor was the scientist for like four sentences. Is he mad at himself?"

Haroun leaned over and squinted at his own words. "They're all talking in the same place. That's how paragraphs work, right? One topic, one paragraph?"

Alexia pulled the page closer. In her own notebook, she had been copying dialogue out of a library book, a mystery where two detectives argued on a rooftop. She flipped back a page and looked again. Every single time a new person started talking, the book had started a new paragraph. One speaker, one paragraph. Another speaker, another paragraph. It was a pattern, and she could test it.

She grabbed three books off the returns cart, all with dialogue, and dropped them next to Haroun's story. "Look," she said, opening the first one. "Every time a different character starts to talk, a new paragraph starts. Every time. That's how the reader knows who's saying what without you having to write 'the mayor said' every single line."

Julianna picked up the second book and checked. Then the third. "It's true. Every single one."

Haroun was already retyping, his fingers flying. He hit a key, and the scientist's line dropped down into its own paragraph, alone. He read it aloud to himself in a low voice, and this time the argument between the scientist and the mayor sounded like two people instead of one confused person arguing with himself.

"Now I just need my climax," Alexia said, and she wrote at the top of a fresh page: the moment the rescue boat appears, everyone speaks, one at a time.

Julianna pointed at Haroun's screen. "Read me the outbreak scene again."

He started over, and when he reached the scientist's line about the vaccine, he stood up and acted it, holding the printout like a syringe.

Muhammad held the onion like it was a live grenade. "If I cry, don't tell anyone at school," he said.

Brynn's grandmother, Ms. Tang, had declared it Cooking Day at her house, which meant Brynn, Muhammad, and Maci were making pasta sauce from scratch while she supervised from a lawn chair in the kitchen. She was famously eccentric; she drank tea out of a measuring cup and wore a sun hat indoors. "Bend your fingers under, like a claw," she said. "Knuckles forward. The knife slides past them, never toward them."

Muhammad curled his fingers, knuckles bumping the blade as it cut through the onion. Slice, slice, slice. His eyes stung a little, but no tears, and nothing resembled a trip to the emergency room. Maci applauded with a wooden spoon in each hand. He had offered to be Muhammad's tutor for the afternoon, mostly by shouting "CLAW!" whenever Muhammad's thumb drifted.

The sauce came together in the pan: onion, canned tomatoes, a pinch of sugar, salt. Then Muhammad noticed a problem. The sauce was thin and watery, sliding around the pan like a red puddle instead of coating anything. "This is going to drip right off the noodles," he said, frowning at it.

Meanwhile Brynn was draining the pasta over the sink, steam billowing up like a stage effect. Maci lunged across the kitchen and grabbed the pot before the last of the water vanished. "Wait! Save a cup," she said, scooping some of the cloudy liquid into a mug. Muhammad stared at it. The water looked almost milky, which was strange, since it had started out clear. He reasoned that the pasta must have released starch into it while it cooked, and he had read somewhere that starch could make liquids thicker. He tested the idea slowly, splashing a little of the starchy water into the pan and stirring. The sauce tightened around his spoon. He added a splash more, and it clung, glossy and thick, exactly the way sauce was supposed to.

The twist came at dinner. Ms. Tang took one bite, removed her sun hat, and saluted Muhammad with her fork. "Better than the restaurant on Bridge Street," she declared. Muhammad was so proud he stood up and did a small bow, which was a mistake, because his knee hit the table and his fork launched a meatball across the kitchen. It landed, improbably, in the measuring cup of tea.

Brynn looked at the floating meatball, then at Muhammad. "Grandma drinks that," she warned.

Ms. Tang sipped anyway. "Mmm," she said. "Needs more sauce."

Emmett opened the laptop at the kitchen table and found the group chat already buzzing. Three messages from Lilah about the science project, one from Fraser, and then, near the bottom, his own name in a line he had typed an hour ago and forgotten: EMMETT WHERE IS YOUR SLIDE. He had meant it as a reminder to himself, typed into the wrong window in a hurry before dinner, and now it sat there like something dropped in the middle of the room.

Lilah replied first. "why are you yelling?" Then Fraser: "lol emmett calm down." Emmett stared at the screen. Yelling? He hadn't said a word out loud all evening. He read the message again, then read theirs, and a gradual understanding started to form, the way a picture comes up when you turn a Polaroid over. His words were in capital letters, every single one, and somehow that made them read like a shout even though they were just pixels on a screen.

He started to type "I wasn't yelling," stopped, and tried to presume nothing about what they'd understood. Instead he typed it the way he actually felt: "sorry. my little cousin was hammering the keyboard and I didn't check before I sent it. the slide is done, it's the volcano diagram." He kept everything lowercase and calm on purpose, testing whether the letters themselves changed how the message landed.

"ok good," Lilah wrote. Fraser sent a thumbs up. It seemed settled, but it wasn't, because underneath their messages sat one from Mr. Walker, sent to the whole class an hour ago: REMEMBER, PRESENTATIONS BEGIN AT NINE TOMORROW. NO EXCEPTIONS. Emmett felt his stomach tighten. He scrolled back through weeks of messages, looking for the pattern he half suspected was there. Every message from Mr. Walker was in capitals. Every single one, all year, like a wall of loud.

Then came the twist. Lilah typed, "wait. mr. walker never types like that. check the name." Emmett looked closer. The sender was Mr. Walker's name, sure enough, but the email address behind it was a jumble of numbers, not the school address they'd all seen on the syllabus. "Someone's using his name," Fraser wrote. "my mom says that happens. fake accounts copy real ones." The three of them sat in their separate houses, and Emmett could almost feel them all leaning toward their screens at once.

He opened a new message and typed to the real Mr. Walker, using the address from the syllabus, being careful to keep his own letters quiet and ordinary: "Hi Mr. Walker, someone is messaging our class using your name in all caps. We think it's fake. Should we tell the office?" He pressed send and watched the screen, the cursor blinking, the house quiet around him except for the fridge humming in the corner.

The reply came in four minutes, in ordinary lowercase, patient and plain. "Good catch, Emmett. Tell the office tonight. And thanks for not shouting about it." Emmett grinned, screenshotted everything, and reached for his shoes.

The kitchen at her grandmother's house smelled like toasted cumin, and Lea had exactly one hour to get rice, curry, and flatbread on the table at the same time. Her grandmother had twisted her ankle chasing a squirrel off the tomato plants, so she sat by the window giving directions, while Lea did the actual cooking for the first time. Riya had come along, partly to help and partly because she wanted to learn flatbread, since her cousins joked that nobody in her family could make it without turning it into a cracker. "Watch," Riya said, holding up a rolling pin like a knight's sword. "Today I break the stereotype of Riya's flatbread shame."

The rice came to a boil first, so Lea turned the burner down low and started on the curry, chopping onions until her eyes stung. Then the timer went off. "It's done already?" she said, staring at the pot. The rice had absorbed all the water, but the grains still looked slightly firm at the centers when she pinched one. The curry needed another ten minutes, and the flatbread hadn't even been rolled. She pictured the whole meal collapsing like a bad science project. "Grandma, the rice is early and everything else is late."

"Don't panic," her grandmother said from the window. "Think it through."

Lea looked at the pot, at the two burners she had left, at Riya already dusting the counter with flour. The problem wasn't the rice being done. The problem was that she only had two burners and three dishes orbiting them like planets around a too-small sun. Then she noticed something. When she lifted the lid to check the rice, steam billowed out and fogged the window above the stove, leaving it translucent until she wiped it away. There was steam trapped in there. Steam was heat, sort of. Maybe the rice could keep going somewhere else.

She slid the pot onto the cold back corner of the stove and clamped the lid down tight. "What if it just sits there?" she said. "With the lid on. Off the heat." Riya raised an eyebrow but kept rolling her dough into a circle that was more of a lopsided oval. "If you say so. My job is the flatbread."

For ten minutes Lea stirred the curry and watched Riya slap dough onto the hot pan. The first one puffed up like a balloon, and Riya actually did a small victory dance with the spatula. "Tell my cousins," she announced. "Tell everyone." The second one puffed too. When everything was ready, Lea lifted the rice lid, braced for disappointment, and found the grains plump and separate, perfectly cooked all the way through.

They carried the dishes to the table where her grandmother waited, and the old woman leaned over the rice pot and breathed in. "So," she said, spooning some onto her plate, "you figured out the rice rests off the heat with the lid on, and the steam finishes it while you cook the bread." Lea grinned and held up the last flatbread, still steaming. "One pot, one pan, one timing," she said. "Riya, take a picture of that bread before it disappears."

Jonathan pushed his peas around his plate while his father asked the usual dinner questions, and he gave the usual answers, until his father said, "You're doing the thing with the peas again. That means something happened."

"Mr. Georgiou had a garage sale," Jonathan said. "He had a box of old hockey cards. One of them was a Rocco Vale rookie card."

His mother set down her fork. "The one you've wanted since March?"

"The one that was forty dollars at the card shop. Mr. Georgiou wanted ten for it." Jonathan had stood in the driveway holding his allowance, and he had not bought it. That was the part that still hurt. "I offered eight. He said no. I said I'd think about it, and Lola's brother bought it for ten like two minutes later."

His father winced. "Rough."

"There's another one," Jonathan said quickly. "Tayla told me her cousin has one and doesn't even like hockey. She's asking around."

The next day Tayla met him by the fence. "Bad news. My cousin wants twenty. She found out there's a whole group of kids at Riverside who collect Rocco Vale now. Everybody wants that card and there's only, like, four in town."

Four cards, and by Jonathan's count at least nine kids who wanted one. He thought about the card shop, where the same card sat behind glass at forty dollars, unsold, for months. The shop had it, but nobody there was buying at that price. Ten dollars had worked in about two minutes. He chewed on that through math class, through dinner, through the peas.

By Saturday he had a plan, and by the following Saturday the plan had mostly involved waiting, which was the hard part. Then Tayla appeared at his door. "Guess what. Three more Rocco Vale cards turned up. Some guy cleaned out his attic and sold them all to the card shop, and the shop's got a stack now, and they dropped the price to fifteen. My cousin panicked and told me she'd take twelve."

Jonathan counted his money. He had eleven dollars and a jar of coins worth about two more. "Tell her eleven fifty," he said, "or she can watch the shop price keep dropping." It was a gamble, and he knew it. But the cards were getting plentiful, and plentiful things got cheaper. He had watched it happen twice now, in both directions.

Tayla came back an hour later holding the card in a plastic sleeve. "She took eleven fifty. Also, she says you're 'annoyingly right.'"

At dinner that night his father asked what happened to the peas circling. "I got the card," Jonathan said, and set the sleeve on the table between the salt and the ketchup. His mother leaned in to admire it.

His father studied the card, then him. "So the price went down when there were more of them, and up when everybody wanted the few there were. You figured that out yourself?"

"Mr. Georgiou actually told me the name for it, after Lola's brother bought mine," Jonathan said. "When I went back to sulk at his sale. He said the price where buyers want exactly as many as sellers have is called the equilibrium price. Market-clearing price, he said. Whatever. I just call it the pea price." He ate a pea.

His mother raised an eyebrow at "whatever," since clearly he had gone home and written both terms in his notebook. Nobody at the table had to say that out loud.

The twist arrived on Tuesday. Tayla found him at his locker, holding her own Roco Vale card. "Riverside kids moved on. It's some gymnast now. Everyone's trading Vale cards away for nothing." She flipped the card into the air. Jonathan caught it against the locker door, agile for once.

He now owned two of a card that half the school was trying to sell. He put his forehead on the locker door and stayed there for a while.

"Some collector you are," Tayla said.

The phone sat in the middle of the kitchen table like it might bolt if nobody watched it. Paige's dad slid it toward her with two fingers. "Before you touch it, we agree on the rules. Dinner hour is off. Homework first. And I can monitor the screen-time report every Sunday, so no surprises for either of us." Paige nodded so fast her ponytail bounced. She had waited two years for this, and she was not going to lose the phone over a rule on day one.

Her first text went to Charlotte: "Got it!!!" Three exclamation points felt right. Charlotte replied with a row of hearts. Then Paige tried Mael, whose family ran the feed store outside town. His answer came back: "cool. im not doing the agriculture thing." Paige stared at that. Not doing it how? Not doing the homework poster about farming, or not going to the agriculture club meeting, or quitting it forever? The message was ambiguous, and she caught herself inventing three different problems to worry about. She typed "which thing?" and set the phone face down while she waited.

Face down was her own idea. She had noticed, in the first hour, that every time the screen lit up, her eyes went to it even mid-sentence. So she ran a small test on herself: phone face down by the fruit bowl during homework, phone in her pocket after. When she checked later, she had finished her math in twenty minutes instead of her usual forty. "Huh," she said out loud, and wrote the result on a sticky note.

Mael finally answered. "the poster. im still in the club." Then he added, "did you know the first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973?" Paige read it twice. Fifty-some years, and phones in pockets had been around that whole time? Her dad had told stories about waiting by the wall phone in the hallway as a kid, and now she understood why he had never once carried one to school. She looked it up on her new phone, which felt appropriate somehow, and the dates matched.

At dinner she reported everything: the screen-time plan, the face-down trick, the sticky note, Martin Cooper on his New York street in 1973. Her dad laughed until he had to put his fork down. "Text Mael that if a call ever goes that far again, it should at least be pizza related." Paige picked up the phone, then put it back down and picked up her fork first. Rules were rules.

At the gathering after Grandma Dot's funeral, Rose counted the casseroles on the kitchen table and realized she had eaten exactly one forkful of food in two days. Her aunt pressed a plate of scalloped potatoes into her hands and said, "You need to eat, sweetheart." Rose tried. Her throat seemed to close around the second bite, like a door swinging shut.

She found her friends Tabitha and Micaela on the back porch steps. Tabitha had come with her mom, who knew Rose's mother from work, and Micaela lived three houses down and had simply walked over with a plate of cookies. "I think I'm getting sick," Rose told them quietly. "I haven't slept since Tuesday. Not really. And food tastes like paper towels." She laid it out like an equation: sick people can't sleep, sick people can't eat, therefore she must be sick. The math felt solid.

Micaela frowned. "But you don't have a fever or anything?" Rose shook her head. No fever, no sore throat, no cough. That was the strange part. She kept turning the problem over, the way she'd turn a puzzle cube, looking for the side she hadn't checked yet. Then she noticed something. Her uncle, the loud one who usually told three jokes before the soup even came out, was sitting alone in the corner with a full plate, chewing one bite and setting down his fork. Her mother had said she'd been up since four in the morning. Even Cousin Beatrix, who was twenty and usually ate like a horse, was just pushing rice around.

Rose went around the living room, doing a quiet survey. "How did you sleep last night?" she asked her uncle. "Terribly," he admitted. She asked her mother the same question, and got a tired laugh and the word "barely." Rose sat down on the stairs with her notebook and wrote the results in a column. Nearly everyone here was exhausted and not eating. They couldn't all be coming down with the same flu. So the cause had to be something they shared, something that wasn't a virus at all. What they shared was Grandma Dot. Grief, it seemed, wasn't only a feeling. It landed in the body too, dragging down sleep and appetite like a turbulent wind shoving a small boat off course. She had the whole fact now, tested on her own family.

Ms. Vu, who lived next door and had come by with a lemon cake, settled onto the step beside her. "You look like a scientist at work," she said. Rose showed her the column of tally marks. "I thought I was sick," Rose said, "but I don't think so anymore. I think this is what grief does." Ms. Vu nodded slowly and didn't try to reassure her with anything cheerful, which Rose appreciated more than she could say. Instead Ms. Vu said, "Then eating one bite is a victory, not a failure."

Rose looked at her abandoned plate. She picked up the fork and took another bite of potatoes, chewing carefully. It still tasted mostly like nothing, but she swallowed it anyway, and then one more after that. Across the room, her uncle picked up his fork too. Rose raised hers in the air like a tiny flag, and he grinned and raised his back.

Juliette spread the two graphs across the library table and pressed them flat with her pencil case so the fan in the corner wouldn't flip them over. One belonged to the desert, all jagged peaks and dips. The other belonged to the rainforest, and something about it made her frown.

"You're doing the climate project too?" Kael asked, sliding into the seat across from her. He shook rain off his jacket. "Mr. Hassan wants rainfall and temperature compared by Friday, right?"

"Right," Juliette said. "But look at this rainforest graph. I think the photocopier cut it off, or somebody drew the temperature line wrong." She tapped the paper. The temperature line ran almost flat, month after month, like a ruler laid across the page. "Nobody's temperature does that. Even our town goes up in summer and down in winter."

Kael leaned in and squinted. "Maybe it's a misprint. You should ask for another copy."

The bell rang before they could argue about it, and in the hallway Juliette found Timothy by the lockers. His family had come from a place with rainforest at the edge of it, and he kept a photo taped inside his locker door: green crowding up to the sky, mist hanging in the branches.

"Timothy, your heritage, the rainforest part," she said. "Is the weather there different every month, like here?"

He shrugged. "My grandmother writes to me about it. Read this." He pulled a folded letter from his backpack and handed it over. The paper was soft and worn, durable from being read so many times.

Juliette unfolded it. Warm again this month, the looping handwriting said. Warm last month, warm the month before. Your cousin swims in the river every day of the year. Juliette read it twice, then a third time, and her heart started to beat faster. She looked up at Timothy, and the flat line on the graph suddenly looked different.

"It's not a misprint," she said slowly. "The temperature line is flat because temperatures in a rainforest stay warm and change little from month to month. That's what the graph is supposed to look like."

"So you don't need another copy," Timothy said, grinning.

She borrowed the letter. Back at the table, she laid it beside the desert graph, where the temperature line climbed and crashed like a roller coaster, and she wrote her first sentence: The rainforest graph shows a nearly flat temperature line. Then she flipped the rainforest rainfall bars upward, tall and steady, so different from the desert's short stubs.

Kael came back and read over her shoulder. "You solved it with a letter?"

"My grandmother's letter," Timothy said from behind him. "Best source in the library."

Juliette laughed and underlined her sentence twice.

The stadium screen showed the crowd in the arena below, and above the seats a giant photograph depicted the Stanley Cup, silver and dented, with names carved in rings all the way down. Megan squinted at it. The trophy looked like something dug out of a grandparents' attic, not like a prize the best hockey team in the world would fight for.

"Why does it look so old?" Adriana asked, handing Megan a foam finger. "Don't they make a new one every year, like the Lombardi Trophy?"

Colt shook his head. "It's the same one every year. My dad says they pass it around. But I don't know why it's all banged up."

Megan wondered about that. Trophies she knew, the ones at school, were shiny and new because somebody had ordered them from a catalog. She thought about it while the crowd chanted. It couldn't be arbitrary, could it, some team just deciding to keep a beat-up old cup forever? There had to be a reason hidden somewhere, like a rule nobody had told her yet.

"I'm going to ask Mr. Zhu," she said. Their neighbour had a seat three rows down and knew more hockey trivia than the announcers did. She climbed over knees and popcorn, found him, and asked her question straight out. He laughed, pulled out his phone, and turned the screen toward her. "It was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892," he read, "and first awarded in 1893. Oldest trophy in North American professional sports."

Megan's eyes went wide. "Eighteen ninety-three?" That was older than her whole school building. "That's why it's all dented. It's not old by accident. It's old because it's actually old." She tested the idea in her head: if the same cup had been handed to a new team every single spring for more than a hundred years, of course it would look worn. The dents weren't carelessness. They were history, the way the old forest trail behind her house looked worn because a whole ecosystem of deer and rabbits and runners had used it forever.

She climbed back to her seat and told Adriana and Colt the whole thing before the second period started. Colt looked at the screen again, at all those carved rings of names stacked below the bowl. "So it's like a family heirloom," he said slowly, "except the family is every team that ever won it."

"Exactly," Megan said. Down on the ice, the home team scored, and the stadium roared so loud her foam finger vibrated in her hand.

Nolan held up two shirts in the clothing store, one with a sailboat printed on it, the little hull stretching across the chest, and one with a flock of migratory geese flying over a lake. He was eleven and had never once cared what his shirt said, but the school dance was on Friday, and apparently that changed everything.

"Get the geese," said Adem, sliding his sunglasses down his nose even though they were indoors. "The geese say mysterious. The boat says you own a canoe." Vienna, who was there purely to find a headband with a star on it, shook her head. "The boat. Boats are calm. Geese chase people." She had been hunting that headband for three weeks and had dragged them to four stores, and she was not leaving without it.

At the checkout, a bin of glow sticks sat beside the register, and Nolan bought a handful, because the gym would be dark except for them. On Friday night, he found out something odd. The stick he'd kept in his warm pocket all afternoon blazed like a tiny green sun, brighter than anyone else's, but by the second slow song it had faded to almost nothing. Vienna, who had kept hers in her jacket pocket near the cold drinks, had a dimmer stick that was still going strong. Nolan turned his dead stick over in his fingers and thought about it. Warm meant bright and short. Cold meant dim and long.

So he ran a test. He cracked his last two sticks, tucked one into his sock near the cold door where the drinks were stacked, and held the other in his fist the whole next fast song. When the lights came up, the warm one in his fist was already pale, and the cold one still glowed, faint but stubborn, like it was refusing to quit.

"Watch this," Nolan said afterward, when Vienna and Adem came over to his house for snacks. He dropped his last living stick, the cold-tested one, into the freezer and shut the door. Adem pressed his face against the frosty white hull of the freezer like a man peering through a porthole. "If cold makes them last," Vienna said slowly, "then the freezer should transform it into the longest glow ever." At breakfast the next morning, they gathered around, and Nolan pulled open the door.

There it was, pale green, still burning, and Adem whispered, "It survived the night."

Xavier had never done laundry before, and tonight it mattered. His older sister had a job interview at nine the next morning, and she was stuck closing at the diner until eleven, so she had handed him a hamper, two quarters short of a full dollar, and the words "my grey interview shirt is in there somewhere."

The laundromat hummed around him, warm and smelling like soap and hot metal. Mr. Aquino, who ran the place, sat behind the counter fixing a fan with a screwdriver while a portable generator outside rattled backup power to half the machines. Xavier's friends Milan and Hunter had come along mostly to buy snacks from the vending wall, but Milan proved useful, pulling the hamper apart on the folding table. "Dark stuff together," Milan said, "lights together, or the colours bleed." Hunter held up a red sock next to a white towel as evidence. Xavier sorted, thinking his sister had sorted for him for years without him ever noticing. It felt fundamental, like learning how the water got hot in the first place.

He got the wash going and then, while it tumbled, the three of them argued about whether the town should advocate for a later school start time, which ate up forty minutes without anyone conceding anything. When the dryer finally buzzed, Hunter said his mom was picking him up, and Xavier let the load sit. He and Milan played cards on the folding table. The minutes slid by. By the time Xavier pulled the clothes out, the grey shirt was creased all over, sharp lines pressed into the collar and sleeves like it had been slept in.

He hung it up and tugged at the wrinkles, but they stayed. Milan squinted at the shirt, then at the still-warm dryer next to theirs, where another customer's clothes were spinning. "Wait," Milan said. "Remember last month? My hoodie came out fine when I folded it right away, but when I left it overnight it looked like a raisin." Xavier held the wrinkled shirt beside a towel he had pulled out hot and folded immediately, which lay flat and smooth on the table. The difference was obvious. The clothes had cooled crumpled, and cooling crumpled had set the creases.

Xavier ran home, filled the bathroom sink with hot water, and dipped the shirt through it, then hung it straight while it steamed. In the morning his sister found it hanging, nearly smooth, and pressed the last small wrinkles out with her palm. She didn't know about the dryer, or the card game, or the raisin hoodie. She just said, "You actually did it," and Xavier, watching from the hallway, decided not to tell her how close it had been. The front door clicked shut behind her, and he went back to fold the rest of the basket while it was still warm.

The flat tyre lay on the garage floor between Jacob's knees, and Warren stood over him eating the last of the crackers. Jacob had the levers tucked under the tyre's edge, working the second one around the rim. The old tube came out with a soft hiss, and he held it up to the window light until he found the puncture, a pinhole near the valve.

Mr. O'Brien, who owned the garage, had left a new tube and a hand pump on the bench. "You patch it or swap it, your choice," he had said. Jacob swapped it, pushing the new tube inside the tyre and snapping the bead back over the rim with his thumbs. Then came the pumping. He counted the strokes out loud, twenty, thirty, forty, and squeezed the tyre with his hand. It still felt soft, like a loaf of bread that hadn't risen.

"I think it takes about twenty psi," Warren said, still watching. "My dad talks about psi all the time."

Jacob pumped another forty strokes and squeezed again. Barely different. He sat back on the cold concrete and thought. If the tyre looked the same and felt the same after eighty strokes, either the pump was broken or the tyre needed far more than they guessed. He could infer one thing, though: the pump was pushing air, because the hose stiffened on every stroke. So the problem was the target, not the tool.

He tipped the wheel and ran his thumb along the black sidewall, where thin raised letters caught the light. Halfway around he found them, moulded into the rubber: a pressure range, printed right on the tyre, with the numbers given in psi and also in bar. It wanted more than three times Warren's guess.

"That's a lot of pumping," Warren said.

"It's the number printed on the side," Jacob said. "Psi or bar, it says both."

Allie came in from the driveway, where she'd been scraping grey lichen off the wall of the garage with a putty knife because Mr. O'Brien had promised her five dollars for it. She took over the pumping while Jacob counted, and they traded off every hundred strokes. When the gauge on the pump finally climbed into the printed range, Jacob pressed his palm against the tyre. It was hard as a melon.

They wheeled the bike out into the sun and Jacob spun the pedals once with his foot. "Hop on," he said to Warren. "Let's see if it stays up."

Brielle had guessed the food bank would be quiet, but the sorting room sounded like a gymnasium where everyone whispered. Mr. Lewandowski handed her a clipboard with a list of expired codes. "Your job is to enforce this rule," he said, tapping the dates. "Anything past the cutoff goes in the gray bin."

She started on a crate of peanut butter. Angelica, sorting beside her, held up a dented can. "How long have food banks even existed in Canada?" she asked. "Like, a hundred years? Since pioneers?"

"Obviously forever," said Tatum from the next table. "People have always needed food."

Brielle turned a jar over and thought about it. Last summer she had helped her grandmother clean out a pantry and found a jar of pickles with a faded newspaper label. Her grandmother had laughed and said the store had closed before Brielle was born. Things carried their own history if you looked at the edges. "They haven't always existed," Brielle said slowly. "They had to start somewhere. I bet it was recently, like the eighties. Somewhere big, like Toronto."

"Toronto," Tatum agreed. "Everything starts in Toronto."

"You're both wrong," said a voice behind them. Mr. Lewandowski was reading the question off a poster taped to the wall, one Brielle had walked past three times without noticing. It showed a photo of a small storefront with a hand-painted sign. "Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta," he read, then added, "not Toronto. Not even close."

"1981?" Angelica said. "That's before my mom finished school."

"So it's younger than my parents' car," Tatum said, "and their car barely runs."

Brielle kept sorting, but her mind snagged on the number. If the first one opened in 1981 in Edmonton, then somewhere in this room there might be proof. She picked up a dusty box from the bottom of the stack, the kind nobody wanted to lift. Inside, under the canned peas, she found a yellowed volunteer manual with a printing date of 1993 and, on the first page, a short history section. Edmonton. 1981. The words matched the poster exactly. She held it up like a trophy. "I tested it," she announced. "The manual agrees with the poster."

"You did a whole investigation over a bet we didn't make," Angelica said.

"I like being right on principle."

Mr. Lewandowski walked over, looked at the manual, and wrote something on his clipboard. "Saturday crew historian," he said. "Resilient worker, too. That box weighed a ton."

"Resilient," Tatum repeated. "Big word for someone who sorts peanut butter."

"I'm also the narrator of this whole afternoon," Brielle said, gesturing at the room, the gray bin, the clipboard. "When people ask how it went, I decide the story."

"Then make me sound taller," Tatum said.

Brielle dropped another jar into the gray bin and marked her list. "No promises."

Asher slid into his seat in the computer lab just as Ms. Sok said, "Open your spreadsheet, and this time make the chart yourself." On the board she had left two columns of numbers: how many books each homeroom had collected for the library drive. Asher's job was to add each column with a formula and turn the totals into a bar chart. He typed =SUM, dragged his cursor down the column for Room 12, and watched the number appear like magic. Room 12 had 143 books. Room 9 had 149.

"Just six apart," said Maeva, leaning over from the next computer. She was still fighting with her own sum, which kept saying 0 because her formula grabbed an empty cell. Asher showed her how to highlight the right boxes, and she grinned and tried again on her own.

Then he made the chart, and his stomach dropped. The bar for Room 9 towered over the bar for Room 12, three times taller, like a giant next to a mouse. Six books out of more than a hundred, and it looked like Room 9 had crushed them. Keon, whose homeroom was Room 9, was already crowing across the lab. "Look at that! We demolished you!"

Asher stared at the chart instead of answering. Something had to be wrong, but he couldn't see what. Both bars started from the same bottom line, didn't they? He followed the little marks up the side of the chart with his finger and stopped. The axis didn't start at zero. It started at 135. Below that, the chart simply wasn't there, so Room 12's bar could only show the tiny part above 135, while Room 9's bar looked enormous. He remembered the seed experiment in science, how you couldn't judge a seed by its hull until you split it open. This chart had a hull too, and he had believed what was on the outside.

He tested it. In the chart settings he changed the minimum value to zero, clicked apply, and both bars leapt upward, nearly the same height. Room 9 was ahead, sure, but only by a sliver. Then he thought of the fundraising posters in the hallway, the ones that made one grade's total look huge, and wondered how many of those charts started above zero too. A chart could diminish his whole class's work without anyone lying out loud.

"Ms. Sok," he called, waving her over. "Look what happens when the axis starts at 135 instead of zero."

Keon came to look too, arms crossed, his smirk fading to something more thoughtful as the bars evened out. "Huh," he said. "Still ahead, though."

"By six," said Asher.

Keon shrugged, but he pulled his chair over to Maeva's screen. "Hey, your formula grabbed an empty box. Want me to show you what he showed me?"

The car smelled like Grandma Ruth's coffee cake, which sat in a tin on Audrey's lap, untouched since the funeral that morning. Dad drove with both hands on the wheel, quiet the whole way back from the cemetery. Audrey kept thinking about the seven days ahead, when people would stream through their house, and she could not figure out what any of them were supposed to say to her. Sorry your grandma died felt clumsy. Nothing felt right. She opened the tin, closed it again, and watched the houses slide past.

"Dad," she said, "what do I say to people when they come tomorrow?"

He was quiet for a moment. "You don't have to say anything. It's called shiva. It means seven, seven days after the burial, when people come to comfort us."

"So they come just to stand there?"

"Just about."

That did not seem like a plan. Audrey liked plans. She decided to test it, the way she tested things in science class. If the visitors were coming only to be present, then the probability that anyone expected a speech from her was low, maybe one in ten. She would run the experiment tomorrow: stay in the room, say almost nothing, and see whether anyone looked disappointed.

By the second day, the living room smelled of coffee and onions, and Audrey's experiment was failing in a strange way. Nobody was disappointed. Martha came after school and sat beside her on the couch for an hour, and the longest sentence either of them managed was about the cafeteria's new pizza. Martha did not seem to mind. She kept coming back, too, every single day, as if the silence were something worth persisting through.

On the fifth day Diya arrived, hesitant in the doorway, holding a grocery bag with both hands. Diya had moved here in September and had never been to anything like this. She walked over and set the bag on the coffee table. Inside were three boxes of the exact coffee cake Grandma Ruth used to bake, the kind with the swirl through the middle.

"I didn't know what you were supposed to bring," Diya said. "So I brought cake. Is that wrong?"

Audrey looked at the boxes, then at Diya's worried face, and something in her chest loosened for the first time all week. Her experiment had been set up wrong from the start. It was never about testing what she should say. It was about finding out what everyone else was doing, and now she knew: nothing, and everything, just showing up, day after day, until the seven days were done.

"It's the opposite of wrong," Audrey said, and cut them both a slice.

The kitchen table had become a lab. Alexia laid out the battery pack, the multimeter, and a coil of thin copper wire, then smoothed her notebook page where she had written her plan. Fletcher had texted her the setup an hour ago: measure the voltage across the wire, measure the current through it, divide one by the other, and you had the resistance. She could smell the faint warm-plastic odor of the battery pack as she clipped the probes in place.

The multimeter showed 3.0 volts for the voltage, which seemed sensible. Then she switched the dial to read current, and the display flickered and settled on 250. She wrote it down, did the division, and frowned. Three divided by 250 gave her 0.012. That could not be right. A wire with almost no resistance would behave like a dead short, and the battery pack would have gotten hot, but it sat there cool and quiet under the lamp. She pressed her palm against it just to be sure. Nothing.

She texted Fletcher, then sat back and looked at the numbers. The voltage part she trusted; the needle on the meter had been steady. What she could not see was the thing she was actually hunting for. Resistance was invisible, hiding somewhere in that opaque red plastic casing of the wire spool, and she could only infer it from the two numbers on the screen. So if the answer looked wrong, one of the numbers had to be lying. She ran her finger over her notebook and stopped at the 250. Next to the digits, half hidden by her thumb, was a tiny label on the meter's screen: mA. Milliamps. Fletcher's voice, from last week's class, surfaced in her memory: he had emphasized checking units before recording anything, and she had rolled her eyes at him.

She checked the meter again, then rummaged in her backpack for the sheet from Ms. Goh's class. Milliamps had to become amps first. So her reading was not 250 amps, it was 0.25 amps. She erased the old answer, did the division again, and got 12. Ohm's law had been working the whole time; her wire was fine, and the tiny difference in units had shrunk her answer a thousandfold. The twist was that she had spent ten minutes suspecting the copper coil when the real culprit was her own handwriting.

There was a knock at the back door. Ms. Goh stood there holding a plate of cookies, and her eyes went straight to the tangle of wire. "Homework?" she asked. Alexia held up the notebook, tapped the circled 12, and said, "I caught the milliamps before they caught me."

Eve stood between her parents at the edge of the grass, holding a bundle of daisies because her grandmother had a bias toward daisies over roses, always saying roses were for people who wanted to be looked at. The cemetery was quiet except for a wind chime on a stake two rows over, the kind with paper notes hanging from it that read things like Miss your laugh. The pastor said the last words, and then everyone began drifting back toward the cars, and Eve did not follow them.

She knelt and set the daisies against the headstone. That morning, before anyone knocked on her door, she had eaten two pieces of cinnamon toast and watched an old comedy special, and she had laughed out loud at one part, alone in the kitchen. Then she had stopped, mid-laugh, feeling like she had done something wrong. Nine days. It had only been nine days.

At school on Monday, she confided in Kash while they scraped leftover paint from the art room sink traps, a job Ms. Villanueva had assigned them for talking during the demo. "I laughed at a joke," Eve said, watching a blue flake spiral down the drain. "The week she died. Doesn't that make me a terrible person?" Kash was quiet for a second, which was unlike Kash. "My aunt printed out this thing when my grandpa passed. It's still on our fridge. A bunch of names on it."

After school they walked to Kash's house and stood in the kitchen reading the paper clipped to the fridge door under a magnet shaped like a pineapple. It was a page from a counseling office, and near the bottom it said that in 1999, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut had described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. Kash tapped the line above it. "That's what it's called," Kash said. "The dual process model." Eve read the sentence twice. "So the laughing is the getting-on-with-daily-life part," she said slowly, "and it goes back and forth. It's not one straight line where you have to be sad the whole time or you failed." Kash shrugged. "My aunt says some days she only cooks his recipes and cries, and some days she just cooks."

The following Sunday, Eve's family drove back out to the cemetery with candles in paper cups, the small kind with the flammable lids you had to peel off carefully so the wax wouldn't spill. Her father lit one and set it by the daisies, which had gone brown at the edges. Eve stood with her hands in her jacket pockets and thought about the back-and-forth, how in one week she had cried in the shower on Tuesday and then on Thursday helped Alyvia film a video for the science fair, laughing at Alyvia's terrible volcano puns, and both of those days had been real days.

She peeled the lid off a second candle and cupped her hand around the flame while her mother dug a small groove in the soft dirt so it wouldn't tip. "She would have liked these," Eve said, nodding at the candles, and her mother said, "She kept them in the window at Halloween, every single year."

The wind chime two rows over rang once, and Eve watched the little flame bend and straighten, bend and straighten. Then she said, "I'm going to tell Kash about the cinnamon toast thing. The whole thing." She blew out the match and dropped it in the paper cup.

Ms. Toussaint wrote one word on the board, "interpretation," and then read a short paragraph about a boy who shoved past a girl in the hallway without saying a word. "What kind of person is he?" she asked.

"Rude," said Scarlet, without raising her hand all the way. "Total jerk move."

Muhammed, who sat near the window, said nothing. He was staring at his notebook, and Jasmine noticed that his pencil had stopped moving halfway through a sentence. She had a reason to pay attention to Muhammed today. Yesterday she had sworn he'd ignored her on purpose when she waved at him across the cafeteria, and she'd spent the evening being angry about it. Now she wanted to figure out whether she'd been right.

"Maybe he was late for something," Jasmine said. "The paragraph doesn't say what happened before the hallway." A few kids rolled their eyes, and one boy called her idea "controversial," which made no sense to her, since it wasn't like she'd taken a side in a war. Ms. Toussaint just said, "Keep going," so Jasmine decided to test it. She turned her notebook sideways and drew two columns. In one she wrote "jerk," and under it she listed everything that would have to be true for the shove to come from his personality. In the other she wrote "motive," and listed situations that could push even a polite person to shove: bad news, an emergency, a phone call he'd just gotten. The second column filled up faster.

That was when Muhammed finally spoke. "My grandfather went into the hospital this morning," he said quietly. "That's why I didn't wave back yesterday, Jasmine. I was reading the message." The room went still. Scarlet looked at her desk.

Ms. Toussaint pulled a book off the shelf and set it on the front table. "There's a name for what Jasmine just did," she said. "The fundamental attribution error." She passed the book around, and Jasmine read the page herself: the psychologist Lee Ross had named it in 1977. Blaming other people's actions on their personality while underestimating their situation. She copied the sentence into her notebook, then evaluated her two columns again. Every entry under "jerk" now looked flimsy, like a shelf nailed with one screw.

After the bell, Jasmine caught Muhammed at the door. "Is your grandfather going to be okay?"

"He's out of surgery," Muhammed said. "My mom says he's talking again." He pulled his backpack onto one shoulder. "You really made two whole lists about me?"

Jasmine held up the notebook, and Muhammed laughed, and together they walked out into the loud, crowded hall.
