Your seeds were alive the whole time." Levi carried the cup to Cyril's table and set it down in front of him without a word, then got his notebook and, next to his underlined guess, wrote in careful letters: supported.

The gurdwara parking lot was already full when Willow's mother dropped her off, so Willow carried the box of dates herself, careful not to step in the puddle by the steps. Inside, everyone removed their shoes and covered their heads, and Willow did the same, tucking her scarf the way she had learned at last year's open house. A woman at the door pressed her palms together and said, "Sat sri akal," and Willow said it back, even though she always felt she had to calibrate her pronunciation, slow on the first word and quicker on the second.

Her friends Hadi and Imran were already in the langar hall, sitting cross-legged on the floor mats. Beside them sat a boy she didn't recognize, with dark hair and a school jacket from a different school, and a girl who looked like his older sister.

"That's Wiremu," Imran whispered. "New. From New Zealand. His dad's the guest speaker tonight."

Willow set the dates near the serving tables, where volunteers were ladling dal into steel bowls. She had brought the dates because her grandmother always said you never arrive at someone's house or someone's holy place empty-handed, and she wondered if Wiremu's family had a rule like that too. They had. In front of Wiremu sat a paper bag of small green stones, and he was handing them out, one to each person who came near him.

"For the welcome," he said, giving one to Hadi. "We always bring something."

When Wiremu's father arrived, Willow watched him and Wiremu press their noses and foreheads together, gently, for a second. Then the father did the same with his daughter. Willow nudged Imran. "Did you see that?"

"Maybe it's only for family," Imran said.

That was the question Willow couldn't leave alone. If it was only for family, then the greeting was a closed door, and the stones were the open one. But she remembered her own grandmother, who kissed her on both cheeks but only shook hands with strangers, and Willow thought greetings could be doors that opened wider the longer you knew someone. She wanted to know which kind this was.

She calibrate-tested it the only way she could think of: she walked over, stood in front of Wiremu, and leaned in, pressing her nose and forehead against his for a brief second. He didn't pull back. He laughed.

"That's a hongi," he said. "It means we share the breath of life."

Imran tried it next, then Hadi, then two of the volunteers from the kitchen, and by the time the food was served, half the room had shared breath with Wiremu or his sister, and the other half were lining up. Willow sat back down on the mat and remembered the winter her class had a hamster, and how it had escaped and the whole grade seven hallway had organized a search party, and how a single small rodent had made twenty-six kids into a team in one afternoon. One small greeting seemed to be doing the same thing here.

The volunteers served dal and roti, and everyone ate with their right hand, which Hadi explained to Wiremu in a low voice while demonstrating. Willow watched Wiremu's sister tear her roti neatly with her left hand but eat with her right, and Willow thought that every house and every holy place had its own system of rules, learnable if you paid attention to what people's hands were doing. When the karah prasad came around in the steel bowl, Willow cupped both hands together to receive it, the way you were supposed to, and Wiremu copied her, and his sister nodded at him across the mats.

"These dates," Wiremu's father called out from across the hall, holding one up. "Who brought these?"

Willow raised her hand, and he pressed a date to his nose before eating it.

Alexandre had twenty-three dollars in his pocket, saved over five weeks of walking dogs, and he meant to spend it on a basketball jersey at the mall. Ziad and Maxime trailed behind him through the food court, where the smell of sizzling onions mixed with cinnamon from the pastry stand. A giant screen above them showed a famous point guard spinning a ball on one finger. "You gotta try FuelSnax," the player said, winking. "They power my game." Maxime stopped dead. "If he eats them, they work," Maxime said, already digging for his wallet.

At the sports store, a display caught Alexandre's eye before the jerseys did. A banner read "Everyone's Already Switching!" above a rack of socks, with a counter supposedly showing thousands sold today. Ziad squinted at it. "That number just repeats the same digits over and over. I watched it for a whole minute and it never changed." Alexandre felt the pull of the banner anyway, the feeling that everyone else knew something he didn't.

He found his jersey, but beside the register sat boxes of protein cereal with the words "All-Natural Goodness" in golden letters. Natural. Goodness. They sounded strong and safe, and they made him want the box even though he wasn't hungry. He picked it up and turned it over. The ingredient list ran eleven lines long and included things he couldn't pronounce, plus three kinds of sugar. "All-natural," he muttered. "It doesn't even say what's natural about it."

"Ms. Baptiste calls those glittering generalities," Maxime said, peering over his shoulder. Alexandre blinked. "She does?" "Last week. Vague, nice words that make you feel good without saying anything you can actually check." Alexandre looked from the cereal box to the sock banner to the looping basketball video on the food court screen. The sock number was fake, the celebrity was paid, and "goodness" meant nothing he could test. It was like every ad in the mall was using the same three tricks in rotation, consistent as a drumbeat.

He set the cereal down, and on his way past the pastry stand he stopped instead. The woman there was giving Ziad, who had spent all his money on FuelSnax, a free sample of warm bread. "It preserves best if you eat it today," she said with a smile, "but it's real food, from a cuisine my grandmother taught me, not a slogan." Ziad grinned around the mouthful.

Alexandre paid for his jersey, folded it carefully into his backpack, and steered his friends toward the exit. "Next Saturday," he said, "we try every free sample in that food court and rate them for real." Maxime slapped the door handle. "Deal. But Ziad rates nothing until he shares those snacks."

Mr. Sandhu's health class had moved to the unit on growing up, and Gabriella sat in the back trying to make herself smaller. He had just said that puberty meant their bodies would start doing new things, like sweating more, and when he mentioned that everyone would need to figure out their own routines, a few kids laughed. Gabriella didn't laugh, because two days ago, in the middle of a presentation, she had noticed a damp patch spreading under her arm and spent the rest of class holding her binder like a shield. Nobody had said anything about it. Maybe nobody had seen. But how could she know?

She cornered Ariah by the lockers after the bell. "Do you use, like, the white stick or the gel or what?" Ariah shrugged and said her mom bought whatever was on sale, and Tatiana claimed she used nothing at all, which Gabriella was skeptical about, since Tatiana was the fastest runner in gym class and gym was right before lunch. That afternoon, Gabriella got permission to walk to the drugstore two blocks from school, forty minutes of freedom and one specific mission.

The deodorant aisle had an entire wall of options, which should have helped but mostly made things worse. She picked up two sticks and read the labels like they were clues. One said deodorant, and the other said antiperspirant deodorant, which was confusing, because weren't they the same thing? She flipped them over. The plain deodorant never mentioned sweat at all, only odor. The antiperspirant said it reduced wetness. So one of them stopped the smell and one of them stopped the sweat? She turned a third box over, and a fourth, checking whether the pattern held, and it did, every time. "Antiperspirants plug the sweat ducts," she muttered, reading the tiny words on the back. "Deodorants don't stop the sweat." A woman reaching past her for shampoo smiled like she'd heard something funny. Gabriella bought the antiperspirant with her allowance.

The next week, she ran an experiment, though she never called it that out loud. Monday and Wednesday she used nothing, and by gym class her shirt told the story she already knew. Tuesday and Thursday she used the new stick, and the damp patch that usually appeared stayed away, though by Thursday afternoon, when she leaned close to sniff her sleeve, she noticed things starting to deteriorate on the smell front. Interesting. So the wetness and the smell were separate problems, and the stick she'd bought solved only one of them.

Friday morning she set the antiperspirant on the bathroom shelf next to her dad's old deodorant, the green one that smelled like pine. Two different tools, sitting side by side, each doing its own job, like the pipes and the air freshener were separate parts of the same plumbing. She wondered what else about growing up worked like that, one thing that looked like another but wasn't. She rolled the stick on, grabbed the deodorant too, and stuffed both in her backpack, because Monday had a presentation, and she intended to stand in front of the class with both arms moving freely.

Antoine sat cross-legged on Bodie's living room floor with a laptop balanced on a pillow, because Bodie's little sister had claimed the table for a puzzle. "The bake sale report is due to Ms. Rosen tomorrow morning," Antoine said. "She wants our cookie profits typed up, a total, and a bar chart. I've never made a spreadsheet in my life."

"Then you're learning today," Bodie said. "Type the sales in column B, one row per week." Antoine typed in the numbers, then stared at the empty box below them. Bodie leaned over. "In that cell, type equals, SUM, open paren, B1, colon, B7, close paren." Antoine typed it, hit enter, and the column added itself. "Okay, that's magic," he said, and even the puzzle-solving sister looked up.

The chart was harder. Antoine clicked here, dragged there, and the bars appeared crooked and gray. He tried to fix them, but he needed one more number, the total from his own notebook, which he had left at his residence down the street. He called Nina, who had copied his notebook numbers at school. Over the phone she said, "The week with the bake sale total? That's the one I wrote in the box on the second page, C4." Antoine hung up, then frowned at the screen. Nina was reading from her own notebook grid, not his spreadsheet. On his sheet, the letter came first and then the number, so the number he wanted had to live in a cell whose address meant column C, row 4. He tested his idea: he typed C4 into a blank cell, and the spreadsheet showed him exactly the bake sale figure. He'd found the rule. "Cells have street addresses," he announced. "Letter, then number. Like C4 means column C, row 4."

"Congratulations, you converted from confused spreadsheet guy to neighborhood data expert in one afternoon," Bodie said. Antoine laughed, dropped the correct number into the chart, and the bars snapped tall and blue. The biggest bar towered over the others, buoyant as a sail, because the bake sale week had earned almost double the rest.

Antoine saved the file twice, then emailed it to himself, then saved it on a flash drive, then saved the flash drive in his sock. "That's four backups," Bodie said. "Ms. Rosen is going to think you're hiding state secrets." Antoine pulled the flash drive out of his sock and held it up like a trophy. "This," he said, "is what sixteen dollars of cookie data looks like."

Connor had inherited his grandfather's lab notebook, a fat green book full of careful measurements, and today he planned to add a page of his own. Ms. McKenzie had set out five unmarked cups on the long black counter: vinegar, lemon juice, soapy water, baking soda mixed with water, and one mystery liquid nobody could name. The task was to sort each cup as acid or base using nothing but strips of litmus paper.

He tore a strip from the little paper book and dipped it into the first cup. The paper turned pink, sharp and sudden as a struck match. "Acid," he wrote, and moved down the line. The strip in the soapy water flipped the other way, turning blue, and the smell of fake lemons drifted up from the cup beside it, sour enough to make his nose prickle.

Adelie slid over beside him, holding two of her own strips. "Look, vinegar is pH three and lemon juice is pH four," she said. "So vinegar's just a little more acidic. Barely a difference." She started to write "slightly more acidic" on her sheet.

"Wait." Connor frowned at the pH chart taped to the wall. Something about it snagged in his mind. He dipped fresh strips into both cups and laid them side by side on a paper towel, and the vinegar strip's pink was deeper, angrier, in a way that did not look little at all. He thought of his grandfather's notebook, how every entry tested an idea instead of guessing. "I don't think the scale works like that," he said slowly. "I think each whole step is a tenfold change. So pH three is ten times more acidic than pH four. It's not one step of difference, it's ten of them."

Adelie chewed her pen. "Ten times? From one number apart?" But she looked at the chart again, at the way the colors jumped, and crossed out what she had written. "Ten times," she echoed, writing it down.

Ms. McKenzie paused behind them on her way past the fume hood, where the leftover samples from the invasive knotweed experiment were drying on a rack. She glanced at their paper towel and gave a small nod, then kept walking. Adelie grinned and split their last strip in half, since the supply economy of the class meant each pair got only ten, and handed Connor the spare piece for the mystery cup.

Connor dipped it, and the paper turned a pink so deep it was almost red.

The fire station smelled like rubber boots and old coffee, and Ryan stood in the back of the group wondering why he had even raised his hand to come. Joey had begged him, the way he always did, and Ryan had said yes the way he always did, and now here he was staring at a display case while Ms. Nasser counted heads.

The case held things from the station's past: a leather bucket with a long crack down its side, a folded paper roster gone brown at the edges, and a painting of a horse-drawn engine. A small dial sat inside the case with two needles, and Ryan leaned close. One needle had a tiny label that read "humidity." As he watched, it crept upward, then slowly back down.

"Joey," he whispered, tugging his friend's sleeve. "Look at this. The needle moves when the big bay door opens."

Joey shrugged. "It's a thermometer, probably."

Ryan didn't think so. A thermometer would jump when the door let in cold air, and this one moved even when nobody stood near it. He decided to test it. He watched the needle, waited until Ms. Nasser called Samson over to look at the pole slide, then asked the station's tour guide, "What's that dial for?"

"Fire stations like ours keep a little museum corner," the guide said. "Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects. See the bucket? That crack happened before we started controlling the case."

Ryan looked at the bucket again, the split running like a dry riverbed through the leather. So it wasn't age alone. It was the air itself, swelling the wood, shrinking it, swelling it again, a hundred small pulls until something gave. He thought about the warped door in his grandmother's house, the one his dad said he would inherit someday along with everything else in it. All those years, everyone blamed the door. Maybe the door had never had a chance.

Samson pressed his nose to the case. "The painting's got green stuff on the hill."

"Lichen," the guide said. "It grows on rocks and trees, slow as anything. That painter put it there on purpose."

Outside, the afternoon sky had gone the color of a struck match, luminous behind the tower where the brass pole rose. Ryan remembered last fall, when Joey had wanted him to try out for soccer and he'd said no because he was afraid of being bad at it, and how the whole season had gone by without either of them mentioning it again. He still didn't know if saying no had been smart or just safe.

The bay door rumbled open for a returning engine, and the needle inside the case began, slowly, to climb.

The bell on the door of Fortin's Phone Fix rang twice before ten, which meant the Saturday rush was coming. Katherine had been drafted because her mother was friends with Ms. Fortin, and because, as Ms. Fortin put it, "You're thirteen, you know computers." Katherine had not argued. She got to sit behind the counter with the shop's ancient laptop and a mug of hot chocolate, which was better than laundry.

"Here's the job," Ms. Fortin said, sliding a paper across the counter. "Every repair this week, day by day. I need totals and a bar chart, because the accountant says my receipts look like a tsunami hit them." She pointed at column B, Monday's charges. "Add those."

Katherine typed into B11: =SUM(B2:B10). The total appeared, forty-one cells of chaos reduced to one number. She sat back, satisfied, and then did the math on the rest of the week. Five more days. Five more columns. She was going to be here until noon.

Rory, who supervised the front counter on Saturdays and wanted very badly to be promoted to "senior counter associate," leaned over. "You could just type it five more times."

"I could also walk to school on my hands." Katherine stared at B11. The formula said B2:B10. Column C held Tuesday. If she copied the formula one column to the right, what would it say? She had a theory, and theories were free. She copied it, clicked C11, and pasted. C11 read =SUM(C2:C10). Not B2:B10 again. The references had moved with it.

"Oh," she said quietly.

"Oh what?" said Rory.

She dragged the little square at the corner of C11 straight across to G11, and one by one every column total filled itself in. Wednesday. Thursday. Friday. Saturday. Rory made a small sound, like a kettle deciding whether to whistle.

"It's the same formula," Katherine said. "Well, an equivalent one. It shifts."

"Show me that again," Rory said. "Slowly. If Ms. Fortin sees I can do that, she has to make me senior counter associate. There's no counter associate union, but there should be."

Katherine highlighted the totals, clicked the bar chart button, and a chart sprang up, six fat bars leaning sideways like commuters on a train. Ms. Fortin came out of the back, looked at it, and looked at it some more.

"Saturday's the tall one," she said. "Which is strange, because we're closed Saturdays."

Rory and Katherine turned to the chart together.

"Rory," said Ms. Fortin, "what exactly have you been doing here on Saturdays?"

Raphael had signed up to cook Friday dinner for his family ever since his mother enrolled him in the community kitchen's six-week course. Tonight was the last class, and everyone had to send a full meal home: roast chicken, rice, and a salad. The instructor, Ms. Sok, had said the meals had to be packed and out the door by six o'clock, because the kitchen closed at six thirty sharp.

He got the chicken into the oven by four forty-five, which left him time for the rice and the salad. He was proud of the chicken. He had dried the skin, rubbed it with salt and oil, and it was already smelling better than anything he made at home. Zia, chopping carrots two stations over, leaned toward his tray and said it looked exceptional, and she did not hand out compliments often.

At five thirty he washed the plastic cutting board he had used to trim the raw chicken, wiped it with a towel, and set the head of lettuce on top of it. His hand was already reaching for the knife when Avianna, who had finished her salad ten minutes earlier, stopped him.

"You used that board for the raw chicken," she said.

"I washed it," Raphael said. "It's clean."

"It's still how you get cross-contamination," Avianna said. "Bacteria from one food spreading to another. Raw meat on a board, then salad on the same board, and the salad goes straight to the table without any cooking to fix it." She pointed to the stack of boards by the sink. "That's why there's a pile of them."

Raphael stood there with the knife in his hand. He thought about the order of things. The chicken would go into a hot oven and stay there for over an hour, and whatever was on it would be dealt with by the heat. The lettuce would go into mouths exactly as he cut it. It was not a complicated equation: cooked food could take the risk, and ready-to-eat food could not.

He put the board back in the sink, took a fresh one from the stack, and chopped the lettuce on that. Then he thought about the towel he had used on the first board, and he threw it in the laundry bin instead of hanging it back up. He wiped the counter with a clean cloth, found a clean bowl, and finished the salad with cucumber and a squeeze of lemon.

At six ten, Ms. Sok checked each station. When she reached Raphael's, she lifted the lid on the chicken, looked at the salad, and marked something on her clipboard. "Board rotation," she said. "Good." Raphael packed the meal into the insulated bag his father would pick up, snapped the containers shut, and carried it to the door just as his father's car pulled up to the curb.

Lily claimed the back corner of the yard on the first Saturday of spring break, and by lunchtime she had dug two beds, one for tomatoes and one for carrots, with a fence of sticks around them to keep out the dog. "Welcome to the Tomato Growers' Guild," she announced, pinning a paper sign to the fence. "Membership: me."

"Can I join the guild if I only like eating tomatoes?" asked Briella, who had come over to watch and, Lily suspected, to steal the good chair.

"Membership fee is one watering can," Lily said, and Briella ran home to get one.

Their watering routines became a joke between them. Lily soaked her tomato bed once a week until the soil was dark and heavy, then left it alone. Briella, who liked any excuse to be outside, sprinkled the carrots lightly every single afternoon, flicking water around like a chef seasoning fries. "A little drink for the little plants," she declared, and Lily rolled her eyes and let it go.

For three weeks both beds looked happy. Then came the hot week, seven days of sun that made the patio too bright to look at. Briella's carrots drooped first, every single morning, like a row of fainting pencils. Lily's tomatoes sagged a little at noon and stood back up by evening. Lily stood between the beds with her hands on her hips, thinking.

She decided to excavate. With the trowel she dug carefully beside one drooping carrot, then beside one steady tomato, following the roots down with her finger. The carrot's roots were shallow, huddled near the top of the soil, exactly where the sun baked everything dry by midmorning. The tomato's roots ran deep into dark, cool ground.

"Briella, your carrots are lazy," Lily called across the fence. "You've been spoiling them. All that daily sprinkling kept their roots near the surface, where the soil dries fastest. Mine had to go hunting for water, so they grew downward."

"So deep watering less often makes tough roots," Briella said slowly, "and my way makes little spoiled surface babies."

"Exactly. You've been running a carrot spa."

Briella switched to Lily's method, one deep soak and then patience, even though patience was not her best subject. By the end of August the carrots stood straight through the heat, and the guild sign had two names on it, the second written in purple marker. Mr. Demetriou leaned over the fence to admire the tomatoes, calling the setup "very sophisticated for a couple of twelve-year-olds," and Lily handed him the first ripe one, warm from the sun.

Evan sat on the edge of his bed with the new phone warm in his hands, the family group chat already blinking with messages. "Welcome to the twenty-first century," his mom had typed, followed by his grandmother's thumbs-up, which she sent to everything. He had wanted this phone since September, when Valeria and Aubrey had made a video for the science fair and he'd only been able to stand behind the camera, borrowing his mom's old tablet that died if you looked at it wrong.

He typed "thanks everybody" and then started downloading apps. A flashlight app came up first, free, with a million downloads. He tapped Install, and a box popped onto the screen: the app wanted permission to use his contacts. Evan stopped, thumb hovering. His whole address book, for a light. He thought about the group chat, about Gran's number, about Valeria's address sitting in there from when they'd planned that project. He closed the box, and the app worked anyway, a plain white beam across his dark ceiling.

Still, the message nagged at him. In his last class of the year, Mr. Halvorsen had said something Evan had half ignored at the time, something about how apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts. What Evan hadn't known, until he dug around in the phone's settings that evening, was that you could take that permission away later. He found a list of every app and what it was allowed to touch. The video app he'd installed had the camera and the microphone, which made sense. A weather app had his location. He scrolled slowly, checking each one like he was counting his own money.

"What are you doing?" Valeria texted. "Aren't you playing the basketball game yet?"

"Checking permissions," he wrote back. "Did you know you can shut them off in settings?"

"Wait, really? My flashlight app has ALL my contacts. It had them for like a year."

She went quiet, and he pictured her in her kitchen with the same screen in front of her, scrolling. He remembered the science fair again, how he'd let Aubrey post their video without reading what the app asked for, and how he'd felt afterward like he'd signed something without looking. He couldn't decide if that had been careless or just thirteen. Maybe both. The app store page had called the developer "a prestigious software company," which had reassured him at the time and didn't now. Prestigious companies still ask for your contacts to turn on a light.

In the group chat, his grandmother sent another thumbs-up, and beneath it he typed: "Gran, do me a favor. Check your settings tonight. I'll show you how tomorrow."

"Show me what?" she replied.

He picked up the phone and started walking to the kitchen. "I'll show you when I get there," he called out loud, since she was only down the hall.

Camille had circled February 10 on the calendar in red marker, because that was the day of last year's Lunar New Year dinner at Grandma's, and she wanted the class project to match. Archer and Yasser were counting on her. The assignment was to record a family tradition on video, and she had promised them dumplings, red envelopes, and her grandmother's lanterns. When she asked her mother to confirm the date, her mother laughed and said, "It's not February 10 this year. It moves." Camille stared at the calendar. Holidays did not move. Her birthday never moved.

She called Yasser from the kitchen. "Ask your family when Tet is," she said, because Yasser's family also kept Lunar New Year, only they called it Tet. He called back ten minutes later. "January 29." Different again. Archer, whose family did not celebrate it at all, texted a screenshot of something he had found: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20. Camille read it twice. A new moon. She looked out the window at the darkening sky, then at her calendar, and flipped back through the months. The date could land anywhere inside that month-long window, so of course it jumped around.

At Grandma's house two days later, the kitchen smelled like ginger and fried scallions. Camille helped fold dumplings at the counter, pressing the edges with a fork the diligent way her grandmother had taught her, every crimp tight so the filling would not leak. She asked whether Grandma had a calendar somewhere. Grandma wiped her hands and pulled a small booklet from a drawer, printed with moon phases. "We follow the moon," she said. Camille traced the little circles with her fingertip. Dark, then a sliver, then full, then dark again. The new moon, she thought, was the day the circle went black.

She wanted to test it. She texted Yasser: "Look up the new moon for January 29." He wrote back that it matched. Then she found this year's date for the dinner, February 17, and checked that too, hiding her phone under the table so Grandma would not think she was being rude. New moon again. Her idea held. The moving dates were not random; they were a pattern you could not see by looking at a wall calendar at all, because the wall calendar did not track the moon.

Grandma handed her a red envelope and then a plate to conserve, meaning carry it carefully to the dining room without spilling. At the table, Camille told everyone the plan for the video, and Grandma pointed at the painting above the cupboard, horses and mountains from a dynasty long ago, and said they could film that too, since it had come down through the family. On Saturday, Archer and Yasser arrived with the camera, and Camille stood in the doorway holding the booklet of moons.

"Start on this," she said, and held it open to the page where the circle went dark.

Beatrice had forty-two dollars in her pocket, and the star pin at the kiosk by the fountain cost forty. It was a small enamel comet with a tail of real glitter, and there were only twelve of them, according to the sign. The line in front of the kiosk stretched past the pretzel stand. Oceane was already near the front, waving.

"You got here fast," Beatrice said, squeezing in beside her.

"I've been here since the mall opened," Oceane said. "Last month these pins were fifteen dollars. Then the singer wore one, and now everybody wants one, and there aren't many, so the price went up. My brother says that's just how it works."

Andres appeared with a pretzel and a bottle of water. He held both up like evidence. "You know what's weird? This water cost a dollar. It keeps me alive. And yesterday my aunt's ring got appraised at the jewelry store upstairs, and a diamond the size of a crumb is worth thousands." He took a bite. "In this old book, The Wealth of Nations, from 1776, this guy Adam Smith wrote that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal. He noticed it almost two hundred and fifty years ago."

"Because there's water everywhere," Beatrice said slowly, "and diamonds almost nowhere." She looked at the line, then at the price sign. "So if the pins really are everywhere somewhere, the price should fall." She had an idea, and it felt like a piston firing in her brain, one clean push of motion.

She left the line. Behind the kiosk, past the storage door marked with a plastic plant that had somehow grown invasive across the whole wall, Beatrice saw stacked boxes. She asked the cashier, who was restocking, "How many of those comet pins do you actually have?" The cashier laughed. "Six boxes. Two hundred pins. The twelve is what fits on the display." Beatrice walked back to Oceane and told her. "They're not scarce. They're just pretending to be."

Oceane looked at the forty-dollar sign, then at her own empty wallet, then at the line. "So the price should drop when people find out."

It took one weekend. Beatrice came back on Saturday and the display was crowded with pins, the sign now read twelve dollars, and the line had transformed into a loose little cluster of shoppers who strolled up whenever they felt like it. She bought two, one for herself and one for Oceane, and still had money left for a pretzel.

Mr. Pérez, who ran the pretzel stand and lived on her street, leaned on his counter and nodded at her pin. "Nice comet," he said. "You want mustard with that?"

Elliot taped the last poster to the front of the table: ELLIOT, MUSA AND JAYCE, LEMONADE, 50 CENTS. The morning was already warm, and the ice in the cooler was crackling as it settled. In his back pocket he kept the envelope his grandfather had given him last night, with a fancy paper inside that said he now owned one share of Fastline Sneakers.

"Does that mean free shoes?" Musa asked, squinting at the paper between customers. Musa wanted new cleats before Saturday's game, and he'd been saving quarters for three weeks, which was why he'd suggested the lemonade stand in the first place.

"Grandpa says no. He says a share of stock is a small piece of ownership in the company. So if I own a share of Fastline, I own part of the business, and I share in its gains or losses." Elliot paraphrased it as best he could, and Jayce frowned like the words had bounced off him.

"Own part of the business," Jayce repeated slowly. He pointed at the lemonade table. "So if somebody buys our stand, and we had shares of it, we'd get some of the money?"

"Basically, yeah."

Ms. Liu from next door crossed the street with her dog, a fat beagle that pulled straight toward the cooler. She paid with a dollar and told them to keep the change. "Are you boys saving up for something?"

"Musa's buying cleats," Elliot said. "I'm trying to figure out this stock thing. Grandpa also mentioned bonds and said one is riskier, and I have to explain which one at dinner Friday, or no dessert."

Ms. Liu laughed. "I'm a bit biased toward bonds myself, at my age, but I'm not telling you the answer. You'll figure it out." She tugged the beagle away from the ice.

Elliot thought about it while he poured cup after cup, the sugar smell mixing with the hot sidewalk and the sticky ring the pitcher left on the table. He set one cup aside for Musa's little sister, who watched them from her bike every day without ever crossing the street. Then he got an idea. "Okay," he said, turning the paper over and drawing with a pencil. "Say we let people buy shares of our stand. Anyone who owns one gets part of whatever we make. If we sell a hundred cups, they win. If it rains all day and we sell three, they lose. Their money goes up and down with us." He drew a second thing. "But a bond is different. It's just lending money, and the borrower pays it back the same no matter what happens to us. If it rains, the lender still gets paid."

Jayce grabbed the pencil. "So the stock people lose if we lose. The bond people don't. That means stock is riskier." He held up the drawing. "Say that at dinner. Grandpa will think we're a whole dynasty of money people."

"A dynasty of one share," Elliot said, and slid the extra cup across the table toward Musa's sister, who finally wheeled her bike over to claim it.

Gavin boarded the 42 bus with his vocabulary sheet crumpled in his pocket, hunting for a seat. The assignment was due first period: look up the history of one word, write where it came from. He had picked "propaganda" at random, mostly because it sounded cool, and he still had nothing written down. Across from him, Kayden was already glued to a flyer someone in a bright vest had handed out at the stop, the paper still warm from the stack.

"Everybody's signing this," Kayden said, waving it. "The whole school, probably. You don't want to be the only one left out." Above their heads, an ad showed a basketball player Gavin recognized from TV holding a bottle of sports drink, grinning like the drink had personally saved his life. Next to it, a poster warned about a "disgusting, dangerous" new city tax in giant red letters. Three persuasion tricks in one bus, Gavin thought, though he didn't yet have words for the pattern he was noticing.

The man in the vest moved down the aisle, pressing flyers into hands. "Join the movement," he said to each rider. "The smart ones already have." Gavin watched a woman take one without looking, watched two teenagers take two each, watched Kayden nod along. Something about it bothered him, an itch he couldn't scratch. Why did everyone want it more just because everyone else did? He pulled out his phone and typed "propaganda word origin," planning to finish his assignment and maybe illustrate his hunch with the flyer itself.

The screen loaded, and he stopped breathing for a second. He had expected something about politics or war. Instead the entry talked about a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. The bus made an abrupt turn, and Gavin grabbed the pole to steady himself while the fact sank in. The word wasn't born from dictators or rallies at all. It started with a committee whose whole job was persuading people to believe something.

He leaned over to Kayden, suddenly sure of what he wanted to say. "It's from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide. Pope Gregory XV set it up in 1622."

Kayden blinked. "So it's like church advertising?"

"Kind of. And this guy's doing the same thing." Gavin pointed at the vest, the stack, the grinning faces. "Everyone's taking one because everyone's taking one." Kayden looked down at his own flyer, reread it, then made a quick pivot and dropped it into the recycling bin by the door just as it hissed open at his stop.

"You want the last word for your sheet?" Kayden called from the sidewalk. "It's 'sucker.'"

Cameron had borrowed the classroom guitar every lunchtime for two weeks, and his fingertips had gone from sore to tough, like the pads were earning their keep. Today Ms. Leung had asked him to distribute the tuners to everyone before class, small metal clips that hugged the headstock, and Cameron had clipped one to his guitar out of habit.

"It says your E string is flat," said Ria, leaning over from the next chair.

"That's the weird part." Cameron plucked the low string, then pressed down at the twelfth fret, the metal strip almost exactly halfway along the neck. The tuner's needle dropped and shivered. "The tuner says the high one is flat too, but by way more. If they're both E, shouldn't they be wrong by the same amount?"

Ria squinted at the needle. "Maybe you're pressing too hard. Maelle, come look at this."

Maelle crossed the room, still holding her own guitar. "Play the open one." Cameron did. "Now the fret." He did. The two notes rang out, and the second one was unmistakably the same sound, only higher, like the first note's shadow lifted into sunlight.

"They match," Cameron said slowly. "Same note, different height." He measured with his eyes from the nut to the twelfth fret, then from the fret to the bridge. "That's the middle. The string's the same the whole way down, so the only thing I changed was how much of it gets to move." He pressed at the twelfth fret again and watched the length between his finger and the bridge vibrate.

"So when you press the middle," Maelle said, "only half the string is vibrating."

Cameron grabbed a pencil and marked the fret's spot on the whiteboard where Ms. Leung let them sketch ideas. Then he tried pressing at other spots, comparing notes, hunting for the pattern. Ria kept tally marks of which pairs matched and which didn't, like they were working out the probability of a repeat, though Cameron suspected the answer was always going to be the same.

The door opened and Ms. Leung came in carrying a stack of sheet music. She stopped at the whiteboard, where Cameron had written "half = higher" beside his pencil mark.

"Twelfth fret," Cameron said, holding up the guitar. "Want to hear it?"

She set down the stack. "Play it twice."

Connor had been staring into the microscope for so long that his eye ached. The onion skin cells lay before him like pale bricks in a wall, each one neatly outlined. On his worksheet, three labels waited: cell wall, nucleus, and cell membrane. The wall was obvious, the dark dot of the nucleus was easy, but the membrane was nowhere. "Do you see two lines around your cells?" he asked Ria, who was bent over the microscope beside him.

"Two lines?" Ria squinted. "I only see one dark line around each cell. Maybe you forgot to focus." Connor turned the fine adjustment knob slowly, first one way, then the other. The single line around each cell sharpened and blurred, but it never split into two. "Maybe onion cells just don't have a membrane," he said, half hoping she would argue. Ria only shrugged, indifferent to the fate of his worksheet. Behind them, Kylan was already drawing his cells with confident labels, which made it worse.

Connor tried to formulate his problem in words he could test. If the cell wall was the dark outside line, and the membrane was a second line just inside it, then in a healthy cell the two might be squeezed so close together that they looked like one. He remembered the jar of salty water on the supply table at the front of the lab room in the museum's Discovery Hall. Salt water made plants wilt. What would it do to a single layer of onion skin? There was one way to find out.

He walked to the table, took a dropper, and carried it back like it was something precious. "I'm going to put a drop of this on my slide," he told Ria. "If the membrane is stuck against the wall, maybe I can make it come loose." He lowered the drop carefully at the edge of the coverslip and watched through the eyepiece. For a moment nothing changed. Then, cell by cell, something began to peel away from the inside of each dark outline. A thin, faint line pulled inward, shrinking away from the wall like a balloon deflating inside a box.

"There it is!" Connor said. "The cell membrane. It was pressed right up against the wall the whole time, so I couldn't see it as a separate line until now." Ria leaned over to look at his slide and gasped. Ms. Choi, walking past their table, glanced down at his worksheet, where he had written "cell membrane" with an arrow to the shrinking line, and gave him a small nod of approval. When she offered a gentle critique of his drawing and suggested he label the wall as the outer line, not the inner one, Connor just grinned and picked up his pencil. "Kylan," he called across the room, "come look at this. Yours is wrong too."

Michael had the kitchen table to himself until Zayne and Zack arrived, still arguing about whose turn it had been to carry the poster board. He let them argue for a minute, then mediated the only way that ever worked: he put a bowl of chips between them and started laying out his supplies. Litmus paper, a chart he had copied from the library book, a bottle of vinegar, baking soda mixed with water, and, at the far end where his little sister couldn't reach, the drain cleaner his mom had warned him was corrosive.

"Science fair is Saturday," Zayne said, dipping a strip of litmus into the vinegar. It turned pink. "See? Acid. Done."

"That's the problem," Michael said. "It's not done." The rubric Ms. Brown had handed out asked for the pH of each solution, an actual number, and litmus had no numbers in it. It only said acid or base, pink or blue, yes or no. He stared at the pink strip and wondered how you could get a number out of something that only knew two answers. Maybe there was a paper out there that knew more.

Zack flipped through the library book while chewing. "Hey, listen to this." He held it up like he was reading a poem aloud. "Universal indicator changes to a range of different colours, and each colour matches a different pH number on a chart." He turned the book around to show them: a row of colours from red through green to purple, each one sitting above a number.

Michael was already pulling the small bottle from the bottom of his bag. He'd bought it at the hobby shop on Tuesday, on a hunch, without really knowing what it was for. He dropped three drops into the vinegar. The liquid bloomed red, then settled to a deep orange, and when he held it against the chart, it lined up under the number three. Three. Not just acid, but how much acid. He grinned so hard his cheeks hurt.

They tested everything after that. Baking soda water went blue-purple, way up the chart. The drain cleaner went purple, so far to the base end that Michael made Zack hold the chart next to it twice, because it seemed strange that something labeled corrosive could sit on the same scale as soap. Zayne tested lemonade just to see where it landed, and Michael found himself wondering what invisible thing in each liquid made the colours land where they did, like the indicator was translating something he couldn't see.

On Saturday, Ms. Brown stopped at their table, leaned over the row of coloured cups, and asked how they'd chosen their method. Michael held up the chart and the little bottle. "Universal indicator," he said. "Every colour is a different pH."

Jonathan had nineteen tomato seedlings on his windowsill and a plan that could not wait. "We're planting Saturday," he announced at school. "Ms. MacLeod gave me the corner plot at the community garden, and tomatoes take forever, so the sooner they go in, the sooner we eat salsa."

Marc-Antoine and Phoenix met him at the garden gate on Saturday morning with a wagonload of seedlings, including peppers and one ambitious little squash. Ms. MacLeod was watering the rhubarb nearby. "Keen," she said, squinting at the sky. "You know your frost dates?" Jonathan did not want to know his frost dates. He wanted to plant. "The sun's out," he said, and marched to his plot.

They dug fast. Rain from the night before had saturated the soil, so every shovel of dirt came up heavy and shining, and Phoenix kept flicking worms at Marc-Antoine, who shrieked like a kettle each time. By lunch they had planted everything, watered it, and named the squash Gerald. "This alliance," Jonathan declared, standing proudly over the rows, "will produce salsa by July."

That evening the sky turned the color of a bruise, and the radio said the temperature would drop below freezing overnight. Jonathan sat straight up in bed. Freezing. His grandmother had lost her whole garden one year to a late frost. He ran downstairs in his pajamas, grabbed every pot, bucket and recycling bin he could carry, and called Phoenix from the front step. "Cold night. Frost kills tomatoes and peppers and squash. They can't take freezing. Come on!"

Phoenix arrived with a duvet. Marc-Antoine arrived with a colander strapped to his head like a helmet, for reasons he refused to explain. They covered every seedling, tucking the duvet around Gerald like a baby. "My shovel is obsolete," Marc-Antoine said sadly. "We're farmers of buckets now."

In the morning, Ms. MacLeod walked over and tapped a pot. "So you learned about last frost the hard way, or almost." Jonathan admitted he'd been in a hurry. "Next year I wait," he said. "Even if the sun looks perfect. Frost-tender stuff goes outside only after the last spring frost, not one day before."

"That's the most sensible thing you've ever said," said Phoenix, lifting a bucket. Underneath, the tomato seedling stood small and green and entirely alive. Jonathan whooped so loudly that a crow flew off the fence.

Marc-Antoine raised the colander in salute. "To Gerald," he said, "and to salsa in July."

The city had painted a half court onto the asphalt behind the baseball diamond, close enough that a foul ball once dented the backboard, and that was where Felix spent his Saturdays. He was the smallest kid out of the nine who showed up, so Angelo had handed him the ball on the first Saturday and said, "You're the point guard. Boss us around." Felix had not bossed anybody around yet. Today he intended to.

The problem was Alex, who guarded him like Alex was being paid by a corporation that docked his wages for every basket Felix scored. Felix could not get past him. Twice he tried, and twice the ball got swatted into the grass near the pitcher's mound.

He stood at the top of the key and thought about it. Alex stuck to Felix the way a shadow sticks to a shoe. That was the pattern. So maybe the pattern could be used. If Felix ran toward Angelo's defender, that defender would have to step toward Felix, and Alex would follow, and then Angelo would be alone for a second. Felix could not see the second before it happened. He would have to trust it was there.

"Angelo," he called. "Set a screen. Then roll to the hoop." Angelo looked at him, shrugged, and planted himself like a fence post. Felix dribbled off him, and just as Alex and Angelo's defender collided in a tangle of elbows, Felix flicked the pass behind his back. Angelo caught it and laid it in. The net did not even make a sound, it was that clean.

They ran it five more times. It worked four. Ms. Yang, who walked her dog along the outfield fence every Saturday, kept score on a napkin, because she said watching nine kids invent basketball on a baseball diamond was better than television. At the end she read out the totals. Felix had scored two points.

"That can't be right," Alex said. "He ran the whole game."

"He ran the whole game," Ms. Yang agreed, "but an assist is credited to a player whose pass leads directly to a teammate's basket." Angelo, who had scored fourteen, did the arithmetic out loud and found that ten of those baskets had started with Felix's passes. The vote for game MVP was unanimous, all nine kids, even Alex, who raised his hand like it cost him money.

Felix wrote his name and the stat line on the napkin, folded it into his back pocket, and jogged back to the top of the key.

"Same play," he said. "Alex, try to stop it this time."

Elena was still blowing her nose every ten minutes on Thursday when her mother came down with the fever instead. By afternoon, Mom was shivering under two blankets and insisting she would be fine by the weekend. "It's only Thursday," she said. "If I'm not better by Saturday, I'll call the doctor then." Elena sat on the edge of the bed and thought about that. Two days. She remembered the nurse at her own doctor visit saying that the prescription antiviral medicines work best when you start them within two days after symptoms begin, and that this was exactly why you should see a doctor early rather than waiting. If Mom waited until Saturday, she would be right at the edge of that window, or past it.

"Mom, I don't think we should wait," Elena said. "If you go today, they can still give you something that works." Mom groaned, but she let Elena dial the clinic. The receptionist found a slot at five o'clock, and by six Elena was standing at the pharmacy counter with a folded prescription slip, waiting while Ms. Ahmed, the pharmacist who lived on their street, typed at her screen.

"Antiviral," Ms. Ahmed said, reading the slip. "Good timing. Your mom went in quickly?" Elena nodded and explained about the fever starting that morning, and how she had counted the hours on her fingers at home. Ms. Ahmed smiled. "Smart. You caught it in the window." Elena wanted to elaborate, to describe the whole argument she had made in the bedroom, but a line of customers was forming behind her, so she just paid and stepped aside.

Junior was at the magazine rack, supposedly buying cough drops for his grandmother. "Did it work?" he whispered. "Did you actually convince your mom?" "I did math about invisible things," Elena said, feeling pleased. "Like a detective." She peered at the label on the box while they waited for the bus, wondering how anyone had figured out that timing mattered in the first place. Scientists must have watched thousands of patients, she thought, comparing the ones who started early with the ones who started late, until the pattern showed up like footprints in snow.

At home, Mom took the first pill with ginger ale and slept. The next morning her fever had dropped a little, and by Sunday the improvement was gradual but real: she ate toast, then soup, then asked for the crossword. Elena brought her tea and set it on the nightstand. Mom looked up over the rim of her glasses. "Remind me to listen to you sooner next time." "Remind yourself," Elena said. "Two days. That's all you get."

Sophia sat at the kitchen table with her kickboard bag packed for tomorrow's swim meet, staring at the same math page she'd read four times. Her heart kept doing a quick double beat, like a conductor rushing the tempo, and her shoulders had crept up toward her ears without asking permission. She noticed the diagonal crease she'd pressed into the paper from reading it so hard, and she wrote at the top of her notebook: Stressed? Since when?

She decided to test it like a science problem. Jitters before a race, she knew, showed up the day of the race and left after. This feeling had come every night for two weeks, ever since she'd started staying up until midnight studying. She tried the breathing exercise the school nurse had shown her class: slow breath in for four counts, out for six, ten times. On the seventh breath her shoulders dropped on their own. It was like finding a switch that governed the whole humming machine of her body. Then she set a real bedtime, ten o'clock, no screens after nine, and wrote it on the fridge where her dad would see it and hold her to it.

That night a message lit up her phone from Yasmine. "Can I ask you something weird? I've felt sick to my stomach every morning for like three weeks. Not just before tests. All the time. Did breathing stuff help you?"

Sophia sat cross-legged on her bed and thought carefully before typing, because she didn't want to get this wrong. "Breathing helps me a lot. But here's the thing I figured out. Some nerves before a race or a test are normal, they can even make you sharper. It's when the stress stays for weeks without letting up that it's a different problem. Three weeks sounds like the second kind. You should talk to someone about it, like your mom or the nurse."

"Three weeks is the bad kind?" Yasmine typed back. "I thought I was just being dramatic."

"You're not dramatic. Promise?"

"Promise. I'll talk to my mom in the morning."

Sophia plugged her phone in across the room, did her slow breathing until her eyelids felt heavy, and slept until the alarm.

At breakfast her dad slid a note across the table, folded in half. "This came for you yesterday. I forgot." It was from Mr. Bui, her swim coach, written in his tidy printing: "Sophia, you've seemed worn down at practice. I moved you to the second heat so you can swim fresh. Just do your best and enjoy it." She read it twice and laughed, because she'd spent two weeks worrying her tiredness would get her cut from the team, and he'd been quietly watching out for her the whole time.

She stuffed the note in her bag, grabbed her kickboard, and called through the house, "Dad, can we leave five minutes early? I want to warm up slow."

Sawyer slid into the booth at Rosa's Kitchen with his German binder open on his lap. Across the table, Laurel was already eating fries, and Alessandro was balancing a saltshaker on one finger. Mr. Clarke, their neighbour, had promised to quiz them over dinner before Friday's speaking test.

"Ich habe einen Bruder," Sawyer said. "I have one brother. Then I have another brother. And another. And a fourth one." He counted on his fingers. "Plus a sister. In German I have to list all five every time."

"Then your whole turn will be you saying brothers and brothers and brothers," Laurel said.

Mr. Clarke raised an eyebrow but kept stirring his coffee.

Sawyer stared at his notes. Three lines just for siblings, and he still had to describe the dog, the cat, and the rabbit his brother Marco kept in a shoebox. He wondered whether German, which glued words together like "Handschuh" for glove, might have glued something for this too. There had to be a shorter way, and if there was, it would follow the pattern. He texted his cousin in Munich, then set the phone face-up while the waiter brought the pasta.

"Test me while we wait," he told Laurel. She asked about his pets, and he tried "Ich habe einen Hund" until it came out smooth. Alessandro kept dropping the saltshaker and picking it up again, claiming it made his hands agile for the writing section, whatever that meant.

The phone buzzed. Sawyer read the message twice, then grinned. He turned the screen so the others could see it.

"Geschwister," he read. "It means brothers and sisters together, the way English says siblings." He wrote it at the top of his page and underlined it. "One word for all five of them. Ich habe fünf Geschwister."

"That's it? One word?" Alessandro leaned over. "So on Friday you finish your family part in one sentence and get to the dog faster."

"And while you two are still listing," Laurel said, jabbing a fry at them, "I'll have a monopoly on the bonus points."

Mr. Clarke paid the check and gathered his jacket. Sawyer read his new sentence out loud one more time, quietly, under the noise of the restaurant.

"Ich habe fünf Geschwister," he said, and closed the binder.

Audrey carried the rabbit carrier through the gate and set it on the picnic table while her father unlatched the door. Inside the shelter, a rabbit had been waiting three weeks with no name, only a tag that said "found, Front Street." The shelter worker had seemed surprised when Audrey picked her.

"Nobody wants a found rabbit," Ann had said on the walk over. "You don't know where she came from."

"That's the point of finding out," Audrey had said, though she wasn't sure how anyone could. The rabbit had no collar and no tag. She hopped out onto the grass and flattened herself under the picnic table, ears down.

Audrey sat on the steps and made a critique of the facts she had. Rabbits couldn't tell anyone their address. A lost dog at the shelter had gone home in minutes, because the worker had waved a small box over its shoulder and a number had come up. Audrey had asked what the box was for, and the worker had answered with one sentence: "A microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and it holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details." Audrey tried to paraphrase it to Ann later. "Tiny thing under the skin, scanner reads it, owner shows up." Ann had shrugged. But that was for dogs. The rabbit had been scanned too, the worker said, and nothing had come up. Nothing, or something the worker hadn't said out loud?

Audrey's idea was simple. She called the shelter and asked whether the scan on the rabbit had shown any number at all, even an old one. The woman at the desk put her on hold. When she came back she said the scanner had shown a number after the second pass, but the registry page wouldn't load that day, so it had never been entered. She read the number out loud, and Audrey wrote it on her arm with a pen.

At the kitchen table she typed the number into the registry website. A name came up: Biscuit. An address two streets over, a phone number, and a note that said, "Please call any time."

She called from the backyard with the rabbit on her lap. A woman answered, and after a silence she said, "We buried Biscuit's hutch mate in April and she dug under the fence the same week. We thought a fox got her." Then she asked if she could come by with some of Biscuit's old hay, because the rabbit liked to eat only the authentic kind from the farm, not the store kind.

The rabbit's ears went up when the car pulled in beside the gate. A girl got out holding a bag of hay and stopped at the sight of the picnic table. "Biscuit," she said, and knelt down in the grass.

Ariana stood in the wings of the community theatre, holding a folded note from Drake. "I freeze every time," he had written. "Nobody gives me anything to be. If I blank out today, cover for me." She tucked the note in her pocket as Mr. He clapped his hands and called the next pair to the stage.

The rule of the afternoon was simple. Whatever your partner said, you answered with yes, and, then added something new. Ariana had liked the idea on paper, but on stage it felt like walking in the dark. When Dana stepped out across from her and said, "We're on a pirate ship and the wheel is spinning," Ariana's mind went white. She said yes and then nothing, and the scene sagged like a wet tent.

Afterwards she sat on the paint-splattered steps and thought about what had actually happened. Dana's line had not just described a ship. It had quietly made Ariana a sailor, because what else would you be, standing at a spinning wheel? There was a hidden mechanism here, invisible, and she began to test it. In the next practice she told Dana, "Nurse, fetch me the bandages," and watched Dana straighten up at once, suddenly someone with a job, someone with lines to say. Whatever you gave your partner through your words, they became it.

She leaned toward Dana between rounds. "I think it's called endowing," she said quietly. Dana nodded and pointed at the stage, where Drake was shuffling out for his turn.

Drake's partner opened a scene about a broken elevator, and Drake just stood there, blinking, hands loose at his sides. Ariana gripped the note in her pocket. Then she remembered she was supposed to be in this scene too, and she stepped in from the side, straight-backed, and barked, "Captain, the cargo hatch is stuck, and only you can force it open."

Drake's shoulders squared. "Aye," he said, planting his feet. "Stand back, everyone. Yes, and somebody hand me that crowbar." The audience of classmates laughed, and Mr. He smiled and wrote something in his notebook, probably sorting them into some category of "improving." Dana leaned over and whispered that the rescue had been radical, in the best way.

Afterward Drake found Ariana by the costume rack. He started to confide that he had been terrified, but she waved it off and handed him a plastic sword. "Next scene," she said. "You're the captain now. Don't lose the ship."

On the second day of drama camp, Mr. Otieno wrote two words on the whiteboard: YES, AND. He told the circle of campers that their afternoon task was to build a scene with a partner, one line at a time, and that each of them had to accept whatever the other one gave. Then he clapped his hands and sent everyone to the far corner of the gym, near the stacked mats and the basketball hoop with no net.

Emily's partner was Felix-Antoine, who was tall and quick and had already been in two school plays. He started their first attempt by pretending to hold a long rod, casting it out over an invisible lake. Emily, busy deciding what clever thing to say, walked toward him and asked whether he had seen her missing backpack. The scene wobbled and died, like a fish too small to keep. Mr. Otieno, wandering past, only said, "Too bad. That was an offer," and moved on.

Emily stood still and turned the words over. An offer. Felix-Antoine hadn't said anything at all, so it had to be the fishing rod itself, the way he had shown where they were without speaking. She tested the idea in her head. If a place could be an offer, maybe a name could too, or a problem. That would mean every single thing a performer said or did was handing the other person something to use, like passing a ball, and dropping it would eliminate the whole game. She looked over at Aryan and his partner, who were deep in a scene about a haunted bakery, each line adding on to the last, and their laughing sounded contagious, spreading across the gym until even Mr. Otieno grinned.

She went back to Felix-Antoine. "Again," she said.

He picked up the invisible rod and cast it. This time Emily looked at what his hands were telling her. "Yes, and the lake is frozen," she said, "so your line is just sitting on top of the ice." Felix-Antoine's eyes lit up. "Yes, and I've been trying to catch the same fish for three years, because it stole my grandmother's ring." "Yes, and she was the queen of a whole dynasty, so that ring belongs in a museum." They leaned on each other, laughing, and built the scene higher and higher until the fish appeared through the ice wearing the ring like a crown.

When Mr. Otieno called time, he asked each pair to show their favorite moment. Felix-Antoine and Emily walked to the middle of the circle, and he cast the invisible line one more time. Emily crouched, peered down at the floor, and said, "Yes, and he's waving at us."

The lights at Grandpa's house went out at half past seven, right in the middle of Grayson's turn at chess. The whole room dropped into blue darkness, and the old fridge in the kitchen stopped its humming so suddenly that the silence felt loud.

"Power cut," Grandpa said, calm as anything. He felt along the shelf and found the fat candle and the box of matches. "Happens out here when the wind gets up like this. We'll be fine."

Grayson stared at the dark television, the dark computer in the corner, the little lamp his grandpa used for reading. Then he remembered Ciara, back in October, when a storm had knocked out the power on their street for a whole night. She had gone around her house pulling plugs out of the wall, and when he'd asked her why, she had said, "Emergency agencies say to unplug computers and electronics during a power cut, because when the power comes back on, the surge of electricity can damage them." He hadn't really believed her then. It had sounded like one of those rules adults invent for no reason.

"Grandpa," he said, "can I borrow the candle?"

He carried the flame into the corner, warm wax smell following him, and knelt by the desktop computer. He was hesitant at first, because Grandpa loved that machine and Grayson didn't want to look like he was fiddling with it. But he pulled the plug from the wall anyway. Then the television. Then the kettle, the microwave, the radio on the windowsill.

"What are you doing back there?" Grandpa called.

"Unplugging things. Ciara told me the power coming back can send a surge through them and wreck the electronics. So you're supposed to unplug them during the cut."

"Huh," said Grandpa, and Grayson heard him settle back into his chair. "Well, that's one for the city kids to teach us."

They played chess by candlelight after that, hunched over the board, coat buttons cold under Grayson's fingers. Grandpa told a long story about a blackout from decades ago, and about how he had once, at Grayson's age, blamed a friend named Nathaniel for something Grayson himself had broken. "I never did fix that right," Grandpa said, moving his bishop. "Couldn't articulate it at the time. Still can't, really." Grayson wasn't sure what to say, so he just took the bishop.

Around nine, the lights blazed back on. The fridge roared awake, the lamp switched itself on, and everything in the wall sockets jumped at once. Then, from the back room, there was a crack, a pop like a firecracker, and a thin thread of smoke rose from Grandpa's old radio, the one still plugged in by the sofa, the one Grayson hadn't noticed in the dark.

They stood over it together. Grayson's heart was hammering, but underneath the fright was something else: Ciara had been right, and if he hadn't gone around pulling plugs, that crack would have come from the computer too.

"Well," Grandpa said. He put a hand on Grayson's shoulder. "Go get the broom, and then call your friend Ciara and tell her she saved my chess computer."

Grayson was already reaching for the phone.

Alexis sat at the kitchen table with a photocopy of A Midsummer Night's Dream spread in front of him and a pencil that had already gone blunt. Mr. Sánchez had assigned each student one scene to paraphrase into modern English, and Alexis had gotten the part where Helena begs Demetrius to treat her like a dog. His little sister's bug jar sat at the corner of the table, where a fat larva chewed a milkweed leaf, but even that was less confusing than "I am your spaniel; and, Demetrius, / The more you beat me, I will fawn on you." He read it aloud three times and still could not figure out how to say it like a normal person.

"Take a break," his mother said, sliding a plate of toast toward him. "You've been frowning at that paper for an hour." He shook his head. Mr. Sánchez had promised the paraphrases would be performed out loud on Friday, and if Alexis stood up and read nonsense, everyone would hear it. He wanted to get it right, not almost right.

He texted Marielle, who had the same scene. Do you get the "prithee" part? She wrote back a minute later: I keep reading it like the character is weird. Maybe she's cursed? Alexis stared at the word. Prithee. He flipped through his stack of photocopies and found other speeches, hunting for the pattern. Where characters said "I pray thee," they were asking for something. Where they said "prithee," they were also asking for something, in exactly the same spots. He tested it against Helena's lines, swapping one word for the other, and the whole sentence still worked. It was like discovering the two words were squeezed together versions of each other. He typed back: I don't think she's cursed. Prithee means please. She's just being polite, and he's being horrible to her anyway. Marielle sent back a row of exclamation marks and one word: finally.

The doorbell rang. Elly stood on the step holding a folded note, since her phone had been taken away for a week. The note said she had the rude mechanicals' scene and was stuck too, and could she please work at his table, and she promised not to touch the bug jar. She sat down, arranged her paper so its edges were perfectly symmetrical with the table's edge, and got to work.

When Marielle called later, Alexis could hear her reading her paraphrase in a shaking voice: "Please, just let me come with you. I'll follow you even if you're mean to me." Elly nudged him and whispered, "Tell her that's good." He passed it on, and Marielle's voice steadied. Down at the end of the table, the larva had stopped chewing and hung motionless from the leaf. "It's turning into a butterfly," Elly said. "Tonight, maybe." Alexis picked his pencil back up. "Then we'd better finish before it does."

The party spilled across two backyards, Brody's family and Zane's, because their parents had been neighbors long enough to knock down the fence between them. Brody carried a bowl of fruit toward the long table and paused at the stone wall at the far edge of the yard, where pale green lichen had crept over the rocks in rough circles. He wondered how long it had taken to grow, whether it was older than he was. A voice behind him said, "You'll miss the giving of the gifts," and Zane pulled him back toward the crowd.

In Zane's family, gifts weren't ripped open in front of everyone. They were handed over with both hands, received with both hands, and set aside to be opened later, which drove Brody a little crazy. His aunt had already pressed a wrapped box into his palms that way, and he had been watching all afternoon to see if everyone did it, and so far, every single person did. At dinner there was another puzzle: Zane's grandmother served the youngest guests first, and nobody started eating until she lifted her own fork. Brody filed both rules away, the way he collected facts about lichen and weather.

Then he saw the problem. His little cousin, four years old and sticky with cake, was standing beside Zane's uncle, and one of the visiting grown-ups reached out cheerfully to ruffle the boy's hair. Zane moved faster than Brody had ever seen him move in gym class, stepping between them with a plate of mango.

"Sorry," Zane said, "in Thailand the head is sacred, so touching someone's head, even patting a kid, can be rude. My uncle's from Bangkok."

The grown-up pulled his hand back and apologized, and the uncle smiled and waved it off, but Brody noticed he had gone very still for a moment before that. So it mattered, even here, even at a backyard party two yards from the lichen wall. Brody tested it in his head: he had patted his cousin's head a dozen times today, and nobody had said a word to him. Maybe because his cousin wasn't Thai? Or because family was different from guests? He couldn't see the rule itself, only its shadow, and he wanted to know where the edges were.

After dinner he found Zane by the stone wall, supervising a game where the little kids tried to balance pebbles on their palms. "Both hands for gifts," Brody said, counting on his fingers, "grandmother eats first, and no touching heads. Anything else I'm going to get wrong at your birthday?"

Zane laughed and handed him a pebble, flat and gray and perfectly transparent where the sun caught its edge. "Balance this," he said. "I'll tell you when you fail."

Eleanor slid the green binder across the library table until it bumped Joshua's elbow. "Mr. Nguyen says we have to use a primary source," she whispered. "That means something written by a person who was actually there."

Joshua flipped through the photocopies inside. Most of them were dull, a list of supplies, a frugal housewife's account of every penny spent on flour. Then he stopped at one page. "Listen to this. It's from a settler's diary, March 1848. 'Word has reached us of gold in California. My brother talks of nothing else.'"

"California," Eleanor repeated. She pulled the timeline sheet from her folder and smoothed it flat. The paper had a long arrow pointing west with the word MIGRATION printed above it, and a fat cluster of dots near the far edge. "So people moved for farmland. That's what our textbook chapter says."

"Not this guy's brother." Joshua tapped the diary line. "He came for money. Gold fever, that's what the diary calls it."

Eleanor frowned at the timeline. The dots were thickest at the very end of the arrow, but the chapter title said nothing about gold. Maybe the book was just... incomplete? She needed to know what actually pulled all those people west, and one diary line wasn't proof. She raised her hand, and Mr. Nguyen came over.

"I have a question about evidence," Eleanor said. "If one diary says the brother wanted gold, is that enough to explain the big arrow?"

"One source illustrates one family's reasons," Mr. Nguyen said. "What would you need to confirm it?"

Eleanor thought. "More sources? From different people?" She marched to the computer catalog and typed GOLD CALIFORNIA. A memoir by a woman who crossed the plains in 1849 appeared, and she carried the heavy book back to the table. Vada, at the next table, leaned over to see.

"She's finding out why people went west," Vada told Joshua. "Ask her about the diary."

Eleanor flipped the memoir's pages carefully. In the second chapter, the woman wrote that her husband sold their shop after hearing that gold had been discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848. Eleanor read the date twice. Her finger moved to the timeline. The thick cluster of dots sat right after 1848, on the western end.

"It fits," she said. "One diary, one memoir, the dates match up. Gold was found in January 1848, and then all those dots show up." She drew a light pencil line connecting 1848 to the cluster, then checked it against the diary's March entry.

"So the textbook just skipped it?" Joshua asked.

Eleanor grinned. "The textbook gave one reason. The primary sources gave the other one." She started writing her paragraph, then paused and slid the memoir across to Vada, who had been craning her neck. "You can share. There's a good part on page forty about the wagon."

Vada turned to page forty and gasped. "She brought her cat the whole way?"

"Every single mile," Eleanor said, and went back to her pencil.

Taylor discovered the lines on a Tuesday morning, standing in front of the bathroom mirror in her pajamas. They ran sideways across her hips, thin and pale, like the marks a pencil eraser leaves behind on a page. She pulled her shirt down and up three times to check whether they disappeared when she wasn't looking. They didn't.

At school, in Ms. Shin's health classroom, the posters showed diagrams of hearts and food groups, and the word PUBERTY was written on the board in blue marker. Taylor sat between Sarina and Caiden, keeping her hoodie zipped to her chin even though the room was warm and smelled like disinfectant and orange peel from somebody's snack. Ms. Shin was explaining that some changes were voluntary, like choosing to lift your hand or speak up, while others happened on their own, without any decision at all. Taylor thought about her hips. Nobody had asked her permission for those lines.

She passed a folded note to Sarina under the desk. Do you ever get marks on your skin that you didn't put there? Sarina read it, then wrote back slowly, her pencil pressing so hard it tore a little: My sister had them on her legs when she grew like four inches in one summer. She said everybody gets them and they fade. Taylor read the note twice, then a third time, and felt something in her chest loosen, though not all the way. Sarina's sister was seventeen. Seventeen seemed very far away, like an answer written on the last page of a textbook.

After class, Taylor stayed behind while Caiden swept the spilled glitter off the group table, a punishment for flicking it at Sarina during the video. "Ms. Shin," Taylor said, staring at the diagram of the heart because looking at the actual poster was easier than looking at the actual teacher, "are stretch marks normal?" Ms. Shin smiled and said, "Stretch marks? Very common during growth spurts." That was all, and somehow that was enough.

On the bus home, Taylor did the math the way she did equations in her head, lining up the facts like numbers. She had grown two shoe sizes since June. Her jeans that fit in September now stopped at her ankles. Fast growth, lines on skin. It wasn't a mystery with a hidden villain; it was just her body doing what bodies did, faster than her skin seemed to expect. Still, she remembered a girl in fifth grade, the one everyone had whispered about, and Taylor felt a small hot knot of shame when she recalled laughing along. She hadn't known anything then. She knew something now, and knowing made the memory sit differently, the way a word you finally learn makes you hear it everywhere.

That evening her mom knocked on her door and sat on the edge of the bed, holding a folded towel. "You okay? You've been quiet since dinner." Taylor pulled up the hem of her shirt a few inches, just far enough. Her mom looked, nodded, and said, "I had those too, right there. They fade, you know. Mine mostly did." Taylor studied her mother's hips where her sweater hung, and the lines there were so faint she had to squint, like footprints after snow has almost melted.

Later, in her notebook, under the equation homework she'd finished, Taylor wrote a message she might or might not give to the fifth-grade girl if she ever saw her again: I'm sorry I laughed. I have them too now, and they're nothing. She read it over, folded it in quarters, and tucked it into the drawer with her pencils, deciding later whether it would ever be sent. Then she changed into her softest pajamas, unzipped her hoodie for good, and stood in front of the mirror with the bathroom light on, tracing one thin line with her finger until her mom called, "Lights out in ten, sleepyhead, or you'll turn into a bear and hibernate till spring."

The bus smelled like sunscreen and old bananas, which Kate decided was just what a field trip to a historic farm should smell like.
