She roughed up the area with the sandpaper, pressed on a patch, and waited while Reese counted to sixty out loud, twice. Then she seated the tyre back on the rim with her thumbs, and only the levers when it fought her. At the pump she filled it until the tyre felt firm when she pressed with her thumb, then checked it again, harder. Not a temporary fix this time. She wanted it to hold all the way home and tomorrow too.

"That patch has a warranty?" Reese asked. "Nope," Zoey said. "The warranty is me checking the air every single morning." She swung her leg over the frame, and the tyre held a perfect round shadow on the pavement as she rolled out past the carts.

Jayden found the sentence on page 47 of a library book about playgrounds, of all things, while eating cereal at the kitchen table. In 2001, a study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes. He read it twice, then a third time, because his first thought was "so what" and his second thought was not that at all.

"Wesley," he said out loud to nobody, because Wesley was the whole problem. Every day at lunch a couple of kids imitated the way Wesley talked with his hands, and every day about nine other kids watched and did nothing, and every day Jayden was one of the nine. He had been counting himself as furniture. But if other children were there during 88 percent of episodes, then watchers weren't furniture. They were the scenery, and scenery was most of the show. If the scenery moved, the show changed.

He tested the idea on his mom that evening while she washed dishes. "Can I practice something on you?" She said sure, so he stood at the counter and pretended to be a kid at the next table, the one who usually laughed. She stood at the sink pretending to be a kid mocking Wesley's hands. "Cut it out, Wesley's fine," Jayden said, flat, like reporting the weather. His mom raised an eyebrow. "That's it?" "That's it. Not a speech. If I make a big flourish out of it, they'll tease him worse for having a bodyguard." She said that sounded plausible, turned off the tap, and told him he had a weird hobby.

Thursday he came home from school and flopped onto the couch where his dad was reading a memoir by some basketball player. "It worked," Jayden said. "Louis did it too. Somebody said something about Wesley's hands and I just said, 'That's old, find something else,' and Louis said, 'Yeah, honestly,' and the kid stopped." He had watched it happen like a science experiment. One sentence, then a second voice, and the whole table shifted, like turning a light on in a room everyone had been pretending was dark.

"Nine other kids saw it," Jayden added, staring at the ceiling. "Nine. And it only took two of us." His dad set down the memoir. "You want to tell me again slower, because that actually sounded like a plan." Jayden grinned and pulled the library book off the coffee table, opening it flat to page 47.

Matteo sat cross-legged on his grandfather's braided rug, spinning the old globe with one finger while rain ticked against the window. On the kitchen table behind him lay his homework: two graphs, one showing monthly rainfall in the Sonoran Desert, the other in the Amazon rainforest, plus temperature lines that spiked and flattened like uneven skylines. He had promised Ms. Lau he would finish the comparison tonight, and tomorrow morning Lorelei would present their poster with whatever he handed her. He traced his finger over the globe and stopped. The Sahara. He turned it a bit. The Arabian Desert. A little more. The Kalahari, the Australian outback, the Atacama. They weren't scattered anywhere. They lined up in two bands, one above the equator and one below, like a belt worn twice.

"Nonno," he called, "do you have a marker that won't kill the globe?"

His grandfather shuffled in with a coffee cup and handed him a grease pencil. Matteo marked each desert. Then he fetched the atlas from the shelf, found the latitude scale printed along the margin, and measured. Sahara, about thirty degrees north. Arabian, about thirty. Kalahari, about twenty-some south, close to the same belt when he checked the map's finer lines. The deserts clustered near thirty degrees north or south of the equator, two coherent stripes running around the whole planet.

"So that's why the graph for the desert stays flat all year," Matteo said, mostly to himself. "It's not random dryness. It's a rule with an address."

He remembered, suddenly, the science quiz he had bombed in October. He'd guessed that deserts were dry because they were far from the ocean, and Ms. Lau had marked it wrong without comment. He'd been embarrassed, and he hadn't asked why. He glanced at the window. Maybe he should have asked. He still wasn't sure he would have, even now, if the globe hadn't done the asking for him.

He tested the idea against his rainforest graph. The Amazon sat almost on the equator, nowhere near thirty degrees, and its rainfall bars rose tall every single month. He turned back to the globe and spun it to thirty degrees south, over the Australian outback, then to thirty degrees north, over the Sahara again. Deserts there, rainforests not there. The pattern held every time he checked it. He tried to quantify it by counting: on his globe, nine deserts in the two belts, and only one, a small cold one, sitting anywhere else. His grandfather leaned over his shoulder.

"Nine out of ten," Matteo said. "The air must sink there or something. Sink, and dry out." He wrote it in the margin of his poster draft: many hot deserts lie near thirty degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.

"That's more than I ever knew about deserts," his grandfather said, tapping the grease pencil against the Sahara.

Matteo photographed the marked globe for Lorelei, packed the graphs into his backpack, and left the globe on the table, deserts circling it in two thin grey rings.

Mason slid into the chair beside Karter at the library computers and pulled up his spreadsheet with a grin he could not hold back. He had spent three evenings collecting data for the school fundraiser: bottles collected per homeroom, counted and typed into column B, rows stretching down to row ten.

"Watch this," he said. He clicked the empty cell at the bottom of the column and typed SUM(B2:B10). He pressed Enter.

The cell just sat there, showing SUM(B2:B10) in plain text, like a note to himself. Mason stared at it. Karter leaned in and frowned.

"That's not a number," Karter said.

"I know it's not a number." Mason clicked the cell again, then a random cell on Karter's sheet, where a total appeared as 412. Same idea, different result. So something about the two cells was different. He deleted the text and retyped it, letter by letter, watching each character appear. Still text. He looked closer at Karter's cell. In the formula bar at the top, before the word SUM, sat one small symbol Mason had skipped: an equals sign. He had assumed the program would recognize the word on its own, but maybe it needed to be told, right up front, that a formula was coming. Without that sign, the cell treated everything as ordinary words.

He typed =SUM(B2:B10) and hit Enter.

"Six hundred and thirty-eight bottles," he said, both hands in the air. "Karter. Six hundred and thirty-eight."

"Make the chart before you break something," Karter said, laughing. Mason highlighted the homeroom names and the numbers, clicked Insert, and chose a bar chart. Bars sprang up across the screen, one tall column towering over the rest.

"Ms. Szabó's homeroom is destroying everyone," Mason said. "Look at that. Almost double Karter's class."

Behind them, Ms. Szabó herself set down a returned book and peered at the screen. "Is that the bottle drive?"

"Yes, and the winner is obvious," Mason said. "Unless the coach wants to change the criterion to bottles per student, since homerooms aren't the same size."

"That would be arbitrary," Ms. Szabó said. "The rules were posted in September."

"Then I could add a second chart," Mason said, fingers already moving. "One for total, one for average. I can't build both myself by Friday, though."

"I'll take the averages," Karter said. "Delegate. That's what the tall bar means, right? You're the boss of the spreadsheet."

"You're the boss of one column," Mason said, and dragged the chart to the top of the sheet where everyone could see it.

Oliver had one week to figure out the eight hundred metres before Friday's time trial, and his problem was simple: every time he raced it, he died on the second lap. He led the first lap like a champion, and then his legs turned to wet sand and people streamed past him on the final straight. Sahil had watched it happen twice and said nothing, which somehow felt worse than teasing.

On Monday he stood at the track with Terry, watching the older runners warm up. One of them, a boy in a red singlet, tore out fast in his interval and finished slow, wobbling like the last shopper at a closing store. Oliver turned the pattern over in his mind. Two runners, two races, the same shape: fast first lap, terrible second. Maybe the second lap wasn't the problem at all. Maybe the first lap was quietly doing the damage, the way an anonymous vandal smears a wall and disappears before anyone sees the cause. He couldn't watch the energy drain out of his own legs, but he could see its results.

So he ran a test. First lap, all out: fifty-one seconds, then a second lap so slow Terry had to walk alongside him. Next attempt, he held back deliberately, keeping Sahil's claps as a metronome, and ran two laps that felt almost even. When he checked the watch, the slower-starting version was faster overall by nearly four seconds. The whole race transformed just by changing the beginning.

He practiced the controlled pace Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, while Ms. Addo, the coach who supervised the track after school, marked his splits without comment. Thursday evening she only said, "You're not the same runner you were last week," and clicked her stopwatch.

Friday came grey and cool, the lanes freshly painted white. The field of eight loaded into the staggers, and the gun cracked. The boy in lane five surged immediately, five metres clear by the first bend, and Oliver let him go. It felt wrong, like standing still while a carnivore closed in, but he counted his rhythm and held it. Down the back straight of the second lap, the early leader began to shorten his stride. Oliver passed him on the bend, then Terry's brother, then one more runner drifting backwards like a boat losing its engine. He crossed the line second overall, legs burning but still turning over, and bent double gasping at the infield grass.

Sahil jogged over with the watch and crouched beside him. "Two seconds faster than your old best."

Oliver looked up at the scoreboard, at his lane number still glowing there. "Same legs," he said. "Different first lap."

Louis skidded across the polished airport floor and dropped into the plastic chair beside Hayden, who was holding two crumpled sheets of printed graphs like they were treasure maps. "You brought them," Louis panted. "Rainfall and temperature, desert versus rainforest. Best homework ever."

"Mr. Traoré said we had to compare them before the flight," Hayden said, smoothing the pages on his knees. "My mom's taking us to the botanical garden the day we land, the big glass rainforest dome." Their gate announcement flickered overhead, and sunlight refracted through the huge windows onto the graphs, making the little bars glow.

Louis grabbed the temperature sheet. The desert line plunged and soared across the months, twenty degrees of difference between the hottest and coolest. The rainforest line was nearly flat, warm all year. "Easy," he said. "Desert swings, rainforest doesn't. I'd pack shorts for the rainforest and be done." He zipped his backpack triumphantly.

Then his phone buzzed. A message from Aurelia, who was already at her grandmother's village near real rainforest: "Guess what? Days are HOT but nights are COLD here. My grandma made me wear a sweater after dinner. A sweater! In the tropics! Check the daily range, not just monthly." Louis read it twice, frowning. "That can't be right," he told Hayden. "Look, the whole year barely changes."

"The months, yeah," Hayden said slowly. "But she said day and night."

Louis pulled out his pencil and turned the sheet over, sketching a quick test: two little temperature curves, one for a rainforest day. Day up, night down. If nights dropped that far, then the jump between afternoon and midnight could be bigger than the whole spread from the warmest month to the coolest. He stared at his sketch, then laughed out loud. "She's right. The day-night difference can beat the monthly one. I would have frozen."

"You almost did," Hayden said, grinning. "Ready to freeze in a dome?"

Louis unzipped his backpack, pulled out his extra shirt, and stuffed a sweater in beside the graphs, next to the nutritious trail mix his dad had packed and the brochure about rainforest agriculture he'd promised Aurelia he'd read. He patted the bag once. "Sweater for the tropics," he announced. "Aurelia gets the first apology text in history."

"Second," Hayden said, boarding pass in hand. "You'll be apologizing all week."

Louis stood up, shouldered the bag, and said, "Then let's go find out how cold midnight feels under the trees."

Mathis slid the battered copy of A Midsummer Night's Dream across the library table and stared at the page like it had insulted him personally. "Puck, round about, go and watch," he read aloud, then stopped. Ms. Le had said their homework was to paraphrase the scene, to turn each speech into plain modern English, and so far his notebook held exactly one line: "The fairy says something about the earth."

Nimrit dropped into the chair beside him and peered at the page. "You've been on that scene for twenty minutes."

"It's tedious," Mathis said. "Half the words look like typos." He tapped the paper. "And look here. Every so often the script says exit, which is fine, that's obviously the guy leaving. But then it says this other word, exeunt, and it's not even a name. Who is Exeunt? Why does he keep showing up?" He flipped pages, and the word kept appearing, always at the end of the busiest moments, when three or four fairies were crowding the stage.

Nimrit frowned and counted characters on her fingers. "Wait. Look at that part. Puck exits alone, and it says exit. Then Oberon and Titania both leave together, and it says exeunt. Try the crowded one, the scene where all four of them have been arguing." They found it: four speeches in a row, then the word exeunt, and nobody left on stage.

Mathis sat back so fast his chair squeaked. "It's not a person. Exit is Latin for he or she goes out," he said slowly, testing it. "Exeunt is Latin for they go out. It's used when two or more characters leave." He checked it against every scene ending in the book, and it held every single time. "So it's like a stage traffic signal."

"Okay, so now you can actually see who's on stage," Nimrit said. "Can you paraphrase the speeches now?"

Mathis looked at Puck's long speech again. Some of it was still fog, but now he could see the shape of it, who was speaking to whom, who was staying, who was going. He wrote, "The fairy says the earth is so full of vapor from the oceans that clouds form," and crossed out the fog. It wasn't perfect, but it was real English, his English. He turned the page and kept going.

Florence had exactly forty minutes before the 4:15 bus, because her mother's work shirt had to be clean and folded by the time she got home, and the shirt was currently smudged with mustard from lunch. She had offered to do the laundry herself, mostly to prove she could, and now she was standing in the laundry room with her friend Louise, who had come along "for supervision" and was eating crackers on the dryer.

"Sort first," Florence said, reading the crumpled instruction sheet her mom had left. "Darks with darks, lights with lights." She made two piles on the floor, dropped her blue hoodie with the darks, and put the white work shirt in a basket by itself. The mustard stain sat on the pocket like a small yellow flag. Louise leaned over and said her grandmother used something called bleach on stains like that, which sent Florence digging under the sink, where she found a bottle of chlorine bleach and a spray bottle of something labelled "ammonia-based cleaner."

She set the two bottles side by side on the machine and planned it out like a math problem. Bleach for the shirt, the spray for the sink, both before the bus came. She had to budget her minutes: five for spraying, twenty-five for washing, ten for drying and folding. But as she turned the bleach bottle to read the back, her stomach tightened. The label said never mix with ammonia cleaners. The spray bottle's label, when she checked it, said the same thing in the opposite direction.

"What does that even mean, mix?" Louise asked, hopping off the dryer. "You'd just use one and then the other."

Florence stared at the two bottles. Her dad fixed cars, and he called problems like this a variable, something you changed to see what changed after it. She had learned the hard way, with a ruined sweater, that some things in laundry were volatile, that a small wrong move made a big mess. But this didn't feel like a ruined sweater. This felt like a warning written in capital letters for a reason she couldn't see. She thought about pouring a little of each into the sink drain, just to test whether anything happened, and then she thought about the labels again. "Never mix." She put the caps back on both bottles, tight.

"We're not testing that one," she said. "The label says mixing chlorine bleach and ammonia cleaners makes a toxic gas. Chloramine, it's called." She carried the ammonia spray out to the garage shelf, came back, and treated the stain with bleach alone, exactly as the shirt's tag instructed. The washer hummed. At 4:10 she pulled the warm shirt from the dryer, folded the sleeves the way her mom did, and set it on top of the machine like evidence. From the driveway, they heard the bus turn the corner. "Next time," Louise said, grabbing her backpack, "you're teaching me the sorting part."

Rebecca climbed the bus steps holding her ballot for the spirit week vote crumpled in her fist, and the first thing she saw was June sitting three rows up next to Millie, laughing about something, in the exact seat where Rebecca always sat. June didn't even look back. Rebecca compressed herself into an empty seat near the back and stared at the back of June's head. She had texted June twice last night about saving seats, and June had answered neither one. So it wasn't an accident. It was a message.

"You okay back there?" Mr. Li called into his mirror before he pulled the door shut. "Seatbelt's twisted, fix it before we roll."

Rebecca yanked the strap flat. Millie turned around, saw her face, and twisted back around fast, which Rebecca also decided to add to the evidence. By the time the bus stopped at the light by the bakery, she had the whole case built: June wanted to sit with Millie instead, June was ditching her, and the unanswered texts proved it. The worst part was that they were supposed to count the ballots together at lunch, like they did every year. Rebecca decided she would count them alone.

At the next stop, Millie actually got up and walked back, holding the rail against the sway of the bus. She dropped into the seat across the aisle.

"June's phone died last night," Millie said. "Dead dead, she left her charger at her grandma's. She kept trying to get it to turn on this morning. And she saved your seat, but then Marcus tripped carrying his trombone case and knocked your backpack into the aisle and some kid sat on the seat, and June couldn't exactly throw him off the bus."

Rebecca looked at the three-rows-up seat again. June's shoulders were hunched now, and she was glancing toward the back every few seconds the way you do when you're waiting to find out if you're in trouble. Rebecca realized she had read every single thing wrong, and it had happened because when she didn't know why something happened, she had picked the meanest possible reason and treated it like a fact.

"My brother calls that hostile attribution bias," Millie said. "Assuming somebody meant to hurt you when it could just as easily have been an accident."

"Your brother needs to stop reading his psych homework out loud," Rebecca said, but she was already moving up the aisle, one hand on the seats, past Marcus and his endangered trombone case, which the driver was forever warning would be the death of somebody. She slid into the seat across from June.

"Your phone died," Rebecca said.

"My phone died." June held up the dark screen like proof. "I thought you were ignoring me because I ignored you, which I didn't."

"Okay," Rebecca said. "Ballots at lunch?"

"Ballots at lunch," June said, and stuck out her pinky.

The gym smelled like floor wax and sweat before anyone had even sweated, and Ariana wondered if gyms always smelled like the future of tryouts. Ms. Bighorn stood at the door of the gymnasium with a clipboard, and every seventh grader had to say their name before walking through. Ariana noticed that some kids walked in and some kids walked right back out, holding a slip of paper, and she wanted to know why. It wasn't random. She counted. Nine went in, three came out, seven went in, two came out.

"You need a sports physical," Mehar reported when she came back from the door, holding her slip. "A checkup by a doctor or other clinician. That's what the paper says. The signed form has to be in before you can try out or even practice with the team." Mehar's shoulders drooped. "I had my checkup last week. I just forgot the form at home on the counter."

"So it's not that the coach doesn't want you," Ariana said slowly, working it out. "It's a rule. A checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before you're allowed to try out or practice. Every school does it." She looked down the line at the kids still waiting, and a pattern was forming in her head like a constellation. "The kids going back out are the ones who don't have the form. The rule doesn't care how good you are. It only cares about the paper."

"My mom's at work until six," Mehar said. "Tryouts end at five."

Ariana borrowed a pencil from Ms. Bighorn and wrote a message on the back of Mehar's slip, printing the school address in careful block letters. "Text your mom this. Tell her to photograph the signed physical form and email it to the office, or take a picture of the picture, or drive here, or send it by carrier pigeon. Anything. Then run home and get the original if you have to. I'll save you a spot in line." Mehar's thumbs flew over her phone, and Ariana watched her run out through the double doors like the gym was on fire.

The tryout itself was drills first, then scrimmaging. Ariana was fast but her left hand was clumsy, so she made herself dribble only with her left through the whole cone line, missing twice, then not missing. A parliament of eighth graders, the Owls varsity, sat in the bleachers watching, and someone had once told her that a group of owls was called a parliament, which seemed right, because they sat there judging like a tiny government. When Ariana banked in a layup she shouldn't have attempted, one of the Owls nodded, just once, and Ariana felt taller.

At the end, Ms. Bighorn read names for the second day of tryouts. "Ariana. Joshua." Then, "Mehar, pending form, and it just came through, so, Mehar." The team burst into applause so sudden and complete it was unanimous, even the kids who hadn't made it clapping, and Mehar came running back in with the paper held over her head like a trophy. She skidded to a stop beside Ariana, breathless.

"You didn't accuse me of being a bad teammate when I got sent out," she panted. "You just fixed it."

"The rule was the problem, not you," Ariana said. Then Ms. Bighorn asked for everyone's form one more time, just to double-check her clipboard, and Ariana reached into her backpack and found only a granola bar, a bent pencil, and her empty folder where the signed physical was supposed to be. She looked at the clipboard. She looked at the clock.

"Ms. Bighorn?" she said. "Does a photograph of the form count if my dad emails it in the next ten minutes?"

Lea spread the photocopied pages of a settler's diary across the kitchen table and glared at them. Her assignment was to use one primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, but the diary's writer, a woman named Hannah Cole, spent half her ink on weather. "Rain again," one entry said. "The beans did not pollinate, and I fear the bees have gone." Another complained about a wagon that lost part of its cargo crossing a muddy river. Nowhere did Hannah simply announce her reason for leaving Ohio.

On the video call, Martha leaned so close to her camera that Lea could count her freckles. "I found something at my grandpa's house," Martha said, holding up a stiff old paper so fast it blurred. "Hold still," Lea said. When Martha steadied it, Lea read the printed words at the top: it was a land claim, dated 1864, and it mentioned 160 acres of public land, granted under a law that let settlers have it if they lived on the land and farmed it for five years. "Grandpa says it's how our family got the farm," Martha said. "I want to frame it for his birthday, but first I want to know what it actually means, because he keeps saying our whole story started with that paper."

Lea remembered something then. Last autumn, before the unit started, Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya had passed around a ledger page from a ship's cargo and asked them what a receipt could prove about a journey nobody alive had seen. "A document shows you a choice somebody made," he had said, "and choices have reasons hiding under them." So Lea went back to Hannah's diary with a pencil and tried an experiment. She underlined every entry where Hannah mentioned land, then counted the years between Hannah's arrival on her claim and the entry where she wrote, "Today the land is ours by law."

Five years, exactly. Lea flipped to the front and found Hannah's departure date from Ohio, 1863, after the law of 1862. "Martha," she said, holding the diary pages up to her screen, "your paper says 160 acres of public land for settlers who lived on it and farmed it five years. Hannah's diary says she left right after that law, and she counts off five years on her claim. That's why she went west. It was never the weather." Martha whooped so loudly that Lea's cat bolted off the table.

Later, Lea taped one diary page beside her draft and wrote her opening sentence. It felt good, but not as good as what came after, when Martha texted a photo of the framed land paper propped on her grandpa's cake. Lea grinned and typed back, "Tell him happy birthday from Hannah Cole."

"Forty minutes until we cut the cake," Clara's mother called from the kitchen, and Clara had until then to prove her point.

Her little cousin, four years old and sticky from the fruit punch, sat on the rug in the den. Clara had put a marble in a small basket and told him she was going to hide it. "Remember, it's in the basket," she said. He nodded. Then she sent him to the kitchen with Enoch to help carry napkins, and while he was gone she moved the marble into the red box on the shelf.

"You're wasting your cake time," said Braelyn from the doorway. Braelyn was twelve and treated every one of Clara's ideas with the same flat skepticism. "He'll just look in the box. He saw you touch it."

"He didn't see anything. He was in the kitchen." Clara set both containers side by side on the rug. "That's the whole point."

Enoch came back with the cousin and a stack of napkins. "Mr. Sinclair told me to bring these in before the cake," he said, dropping them on the couch. "He says we've got half an hour now, so hurry up."

Clara knelt in front of her cousin. "Where will you look for the marble?"

The boy pointed at the basket. "In there."

"But it's not in there anymore," Enoch said.

Clara shot him a look. "Don't tell him." She waited until her cousin stopped chewing on his sleeve. "Show us. Go find the marble."

He lifted the basket lid, patted the empty bottom, and frowned. Then he checked under the rug, then behind the box. Only when he tipped the red box and the marble rolled out did he grin and hold it up.

"Beginner's luck," Braelyn said. "Ask him where he thought it was."

"Where did you look first?" Clara asked.

"The basket," the boy said, and wandered off toward the punch bowl, indifferent to the three older kids staring at him.

Clara stood up. "That's exactly it. He looked in the basket because that's where he left it, even though it wasn't there anymore. In my psych book it's called the Sally-Anne test, from 1985. Kids from about age four mostly say the character will look where she left her marble, not where somebody moved it while she was away." She counted on her fingers. "He's four, and he did it, and I predicted it before he moved."

Braelyn folded her arms. "You predicted he'd be wrong."

"I predicted what he'd do. Wrong had nothing to do with it."

From the kitchen her mother's voice rose over the noise. "Twenty minutes! Where's the cake knife?"

Enoch was already herding the cousin toward the kitchen, one hand on his shoulder, the napkins forgotten on the couch. Clara grabbed the marble and the basket and followed, and Braelyn, after a moment, picked up the red box too.

"If he asks for the marble at the table," Braelyn said, "I'm telling him you moved it."

Jordan's class had a civics assignment due Monday: pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in his own words. He had put it off all weekend, and now his mom was working at the polling station downtown, so he rode along with his notebook and a pencil.

The gym smelled like floor wax and coffee. Ms. Doyle, the returning officer, had pinned a Charter poster beside the voter list, tall as a door. Jordan stood in front of it while his mom checked people in behind him. Section 2 listed fundamental freedoms: conscience, religion, thought, belief, opinion, expression. Section 3 gave every citizen the right to vote. He copied section 3 into his notebook, then noticed the date printed along the bottom edge. "Proclaimed April 17, 1982," he read aloud.

Griffin was there too, handing out pencils near the ballot boxes because his older sister was a poll clerk. "Why does the year matter?" he asked.

"Because my grandpa voted before 1982," Jordan said. "If the Charter became part of the Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982, then it wasn't part of the Constitution before that. So the right to vote in section 3 couldn't have come from the Charter back then." He wanted to test this, so he wrote a note on a scrap of paper and gave it to Griffin to deliver to his sister at the far table. The message read: "Ask Mom if Grandpa voted before 1982 and what law let him. Send answer back."

Griffin carried it over, waited, and came back with a reply in looping handwriting. "Yes, 1974, federal election. There was an older law, the Canada Elections Act. Grandpa still has his voter card somewhere."

"So voting existed before the Charter," Jordan said. "The Charter didn't create it. It protects it. That's the difference." He crossed out his first draft, which had said the Charter gave Canadians the vote, and started over. "Section 3 means the government can't restrict who gets to vote based on things it shouldn't, like what you think or where your family came from. If a law tries to, the Charter stands in the way."

Griffin leaned over his shoulder. "You should also do a critique of your first draft. You wrote 'gives' twice."

"It was wrong, that's all." Jordan kept writing. Ms. Doyle passed by with a stack of ballots and glanced at the poster.

"Is it feasible to finish that here before we close?" she asked.

"Yes. Ten minutes." Jordan read his new paragraph once through, underlined section 3, and showed it to Griffin. "Say it back to me. If you can explain it, I did it right."

Griffin squinted at the page. "Every citizen gets to vote, and the Charter keeps the government from taking that away."

Jordan closed the notebook. "Exactly. Now I just need Grandpa's voter card for show and tell."

Lillian sat on the gurney with her left arm cradled against her chest, breathing the way the nurse had shown her: in through the nose, out through the mouth. The wrist had gone purple and puffy, and every bump of the wheels on the tile floor sent a hot wire of pain up to her elbow. Roxanne, who had ridden in the ambulance with her because Lillian's mom was stuck in traffic, kept hold of her good hand the whole way.

"It was the ramp," Roxanne said. "The skate park ramp has that crack near the bottom. It's getting worse."

"That's what I thought too," Lillian said. "But watch." She pointed at Roxanne's phone, which showed a slow-motion video Arnaud had taken before anyone dialed 911. "My wheels aren't near the crack. I landed with all my weight on the board at a bad angle. The ramp didn't do it. I did it." She hated knowing that, but knowing was better than blaming a crack that other kids would keep skating over.

The doctor came back with a cart of little tubs, each one a different color. "Time to pick your cast," she said. Roxanne immediately chose tropical orange, but Lillian paused. "Before there were casts," she asked, "what did people do? Just... lie still forever?"

The doctor laughed and pulled up something on the tablet mounted by the bed. "Look this up yourself if you want, but here's the short version. A Dutch army surgeon named Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones, and he published his method in 1852." She turned the screen so Lillian could see the old drawing, soldiers' legs wrapped stiff and pale. Lillian read it twice, mouthing the year. Plaster of Paris. So casts weren't some brand-new invention; they were older than cars, older than light bulbs, and they still worked the same basic way, wet wrapping that hardened around a broken bone.

"Blue," she said. "Blue like the ocean."

While the doctor wrapped layer after layer, Arnaud arrived, out of breath, carrying Lillian's backpack and a slushie. "I figured you'd want your sketchbook," he said. "I got you blue raspberry, but, um, don't slurp too fast or you'll jostle."

"That's the plan," Lillian said. "The slushie is now a slow ritual. One sip every five minutes, left hand stays perfectly still." Roxanne counted the first five minutes on her watch, then held the straw while Lillian drank, careful as someone defusing a bomb.

Lillian flexed the fingers poking out of the blue cast. "Six weeks of this," she said. Roxanne raised her slushie like a toast. "Six weeks of us signing it, starting now."

Alexis slid into the red booth between her dad and her older brother, breathing in the smell of nachos and buffalo sauce. Above the bar, three screens glowed with basketball stats, and the whole place hummed with shouting and laughing. Then she spotted Taya two tables over, waving wildly.

"You're here!" Taya squeezed through the crowd and leaned over the booth. "Guess what. I checked the league site this morning. My shooting percentage is one hundred percent."

"One hundred?" Alexis's brother snorted into his soda.

"Perfect," Taya said, buoyant as a beach ball. "Every shot I took went in."

Alexis felt a flicker of doubt, small but sharp, like a pebble in her sneaker. Taya had barely played this season. "How many shots did you take?"

Taya counted on her fingers, then held up one. "One. Coach put me in for the last minute of the Marshall game, and I made the layup."

"One out of one," Alexis said slowly. She grabbed a napkin and borrowed her brother's pen. In wobbly letters she wrote it out: one made, one attempted, one hundred percent. Then, underneath, she wrote Violette's numbers from the same site, which she remembered because Violette never stopped talking about them: forty-two made out of eighty attempts. She did the division twice on the napkin's corner. Violette's percentage came out to about fifty-three percent.

"So on paper," Alexis said, "your number is better than Violette's. But it's just one shot." She looked up at the big screen, where a scroll of player stats marched past. "All these numbers are like that. They squash a whole season into one figure."

Taya frowned at the napkin. "So my one hundred percent doesn't really mean anything?"

"It means you haven't missed yet," Alexis said. "That's all it can tell anyone." She could infer the rest without saying it: Violette had proven herself over eighty chances, and Taya had proven nothing except one lucky, perfect layup.

Taya's grin came back, defiant. "Then I need more shots. Tomorrow at practice I'm taking fifty." She jabbed a finger at the napkin. "Keep that. I want to see my percentage after."

Alexis folded it into her jacket pocket just as the nachos arrived, steaming and piled high. Taya snatched a chip, pointed it at the glowing screen like a sword, and said, "See you at fifty attempts."

Owen had never noticed the framed poster in Grandpa's study before, but on Saturday afternoon it was the only thing on the wall that mattered. It was a periodic table, faded at the corners, with tiny numbers tucked above each symbol. His science test was Monday, and his own textbook was sitting on the kitchen counter at home, forty minutes away. His mom had said the trip to Grandpa's was temporary, just one weekend, but a test didn't care where your book was.

He copied elements onto a napkin until his pen ran dry, then went looking for a pencil. Instead he found Grandpa in the kitchen holding Owen's phone, which had been buzzing like a trapped wasp. "Your friend Siena has texted you nine times," Grandpa said.

Owen took the phone. Siena was building a model of a sodium atom for the same test, out of a foam ball and pushpins, and she was stuck. "How many electrons do I put on it?" her latest message read. "The sheet just says sodium has atomic number 11. I looked everywhere and it only says protons. I'm going to glue the pins on wrong."

Owen stared at the poster in the study. Eleven protons, sure, that part was easy. But electrons were the mystery. You couldn't see them, couldn't count them, and the poster didn't list them anywhere. He tried to assess the problem like a coach would: what did he actually know? A neutral atom had no charge. An atom with no charge couldn't have extra of anything, or it would be lopsided. If protons and electrons weren't balanced, the whole thing would be off balance. So in a neutral atom, the number of electrons had to equal the number of protons. He sat back. That meant the atomic number told you both.

He texted Siena: "11 electrons. Atomic number counts protons, and in a neutral atom electrons equal protons, so it gives you electrons too." Then he tested it against the poster, hunting through elements to see if the pattern ever broke his rule. Neon, atomic number 10. Ten protons, ten electrons. Carbon, six and six. His hand was shaking a little as he worked, the way it did when a puzzle snapped together.

Then Grandpa appeared in the doorway with two mugs. "That poster," he said, "I hung it when I taught chemistry. Forty years."

Owen gaped at him. Grandpa had always been the grandpa who canned tomatoes and fell asleep during baseball games. Owen realized he'd been working from a stereotype of what an old man in a cardigan knew. "Why didn't you say anything?"

"You didn't ask," Grandpa said. "And you didn't need me. Siena's model will have eleven pins, and you found that out yourself." He set a mug beside the napkin covered in numbers. "Check the bottom right corner of the poster sometime. Element 118."

Owen leaned close. The space was blank except for a penciled note in his grandfather's handwriting: "Still counting."

Hazel slid her draft across the table in Ms. Nair's classroom, where writing club met every Thursday after last bell. Vincenzo read it, frowned, and tapped one line. "This part sounds weird," he said. "'We need to leave now.' Mom said. 'Before the storm hits.'" He read it aloud twice, and both times it came out sounding like three separate people talking.

Hazel looked at the line and felt her stomach knot. She wanted to read her story aloud at the spring showcase, and Ms. Nair had said every story needed a clear climax, the moment everything turned. Hazel's climax was that line, the moment Mom decided to run. If it sounded broken, the whole ending wobbled.

"Try it out loud," Lucca said from the next seat. "Just the quote. Ignore the Mom said part." Hazel tried. "We need to leave now before the storm hits." One breath. One sentence. So the quote was one sentence, even though the tag sat in the middle of it like a rock in a stream. She circled the period after "now" and the capital B on "Before," then erased both. Now she had a comma before the second quotation mark, and "before" started small. The line read smoothly, and when Vincenzo read it aloud this time, it sounded like one person talking through one sentence.

Ms. Nair began to circulate around the room, pausing at each table. When she reached theirs, Hazel held up the draft. "I think when the tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part starts lowercase, because the sentence is still going." Ms. Nair read the line and nodded. "Read it at the showcase," she said, and moved on.

Vincenzo, who had spent three weeks insisting he would never share his own story because nobody would believe a talking dog was plausible, looked at Hazel's page for a long moment. "If your line can get fixed that fast," he said, "maybe mine can too." He pulled his notebook out of his bag.

Hazel remembered the first club meeting in September, when she had written nothing at all and had watched Lucca's pencil move for a whole hour, sure she would never have a story worth fixing. Now her climax line sat on the page, punctuated, whole. She flipped to a fresh sheet and wrote the first line of the showcase introduction: "This is a story about a storm."

Riley stood on the small stage of the community theatre, holding a plastic teacup, while Mr. Kelly wrote "Scene: astronauts on a sinking ship" on the whiteboard. Riley wanted the camp's Friday showcase slot more than anything, but every time he improvised with Elaine, he froze, because once, in last year's talent show, he had planned a whole skit with jokes he'd written at home, and when the audience didn't laugh at the first one, he forgot the rest and just stood there until his cousin pulled him offstage. Planning had failed him, so now he needed to learn the opposite thing.

"Whatever your partner gives you, take it and add to it," Mr. Kelly said. "That's the whole game." He held up a battered paperback with a cracked spine. "Viola Spolin wrote this in 1963. It collects theater games, and people call it the bible of improv teaching." He set it on the edge of the stage and clapped his hands.

Elaine started their scene. "Captain, the hold is flooding and the ship is hibernating for the winter." Riley's instinct was to correct her, because spaceships obviously couldn't hibernate, and he almost said so. But correcting felt like the same trap as scripting, blocking whatever came at him. Instead he tested the opposite. "Yes, and the crew will have to sleep in space suits until spring," he said, "or our hereditary fear of water will wake us up."

"That makes no sense," whispered Roman, who was waiting for the next turn with his arms crossed. "You can't inherit a fear of water."

"Watch," Riley said, and turned back to Elaine. She was pouring imaginary tea with the plastic teacup. "Yes, and this tea will keep the ship drowsy," she said, "but Captain, you have to drink it before the seal leaks." Riley drank the tea, hiccupped a bubble, and floated slowly to the floor as if he weighed nothing at all. Roman laughed for real, not the polite kind.

Afterward, Riley sat on the stage edge and picked up the worn book. He turned pages of games with names and diagrams, games other kids had played since before he was born, and understood that the thing that had saved his scene wasn't luck. There was a rule underneath it, invisible until you tried it, and the rule worked both ways, like a door that swings open and shut. When you blocked, everything stopped. When you took the offer and stacked something on top, the scene kept going whether you were funny or not, and that was the part he'd never believed.

At the showcase, Mr. Kelly called their names. Elaine grabbed the plastic teacup and whispered, "Ready, Captain?"

Riley saluted. "Yes, and the winter is coming early this year."

Jordan posted the photo at 8:42 on Friday night, from the lobby of Siege Harbor, where his squad was waiting for the season tournament to open. It showed him mid-rage, headset half off his head, mouth open, after Asher had stolen his loot for the third time. His location tag was on, the way it always was, so the post read "Oaks Recreation Center, Room 3B" right under his face.

He deleted it ten minutes later, once he'd cooled down and remembered that half his classmates followed his account. Gone. He checked twice, scrolling his own page with his thumb while the lobby music looped and Ireland's voice crackled through his headset asking if he was ready. The photo had retired to nowhere. He queued up and forgot about it.

Saturday morning his phone buzzed against the cereal bowl. Asher had dropped the exact photo into the squad group chat, with a caption: "History cannot be erased." Jordan stared at it, the same open mouth, the same rec center address underneath.

He called Ireland. "How? I deleted that."

"Screenshots," Ireland said. "Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it."

Jordan sat back. He remembered Friday night now, the little flash of Asher's screen in the corner of the video call, the click he'd assumed was a game sound. He opened the chat and counted: Asher had sent it, then two classmates he didn't even know followed his account had shared it onward. Strangers. People whose names he'd never seen, passing around his face and the address of the room where he played every Friday.

He typed a message to Asher: "Delete it."

"Can't," Asher sent back. "Already saved by like six people."

Jordan did the only test he could think of. He posted a new photo, a boring one of his sneakers, location tag still on, and waited. Three minutes later a kid named frostbyte99, whom he'd never met, commented "nice shoes oaks rec center kid." Jordan deleted the post, then messaged frostbyte99: "What photo?" The reply came in seconds: "the sneaker one, saved it, why?"

So that was the rule. He went into his settings and switched off location tagging, then scrolled back through months of posts, checking each one for the address of his school, his street, the rec center. His thumb ached by the time he finished. He untagged, deleted, and closed his account settings.

In the lobby that night, the tournament bracket loaded. Ireland's voice came through: "You ready?"

Jordan pulled on his headset. "Born ready," he said, and hit accept.

Lillian had told Iman three times that she didn't need to bring money, but Iman kept patting her jacket pocket anyway, as if the five dollars might fall out and get lost in the parking lot. The gurdwara smelled of warm dough and cardamom, and the hallway was humid from all the cooking. Through a doorway Lillian could see rows and rows of people sitting cross-legged on the floor, shoulder to shoulder.

"How much is the meal?" Iman whispered, craning her neck.

"There's no charge," Lillian said. "It's called langar."

"Free? For anybody?"

"Every visitor," Lillian said. "Doesn't matter who you are or what religion." She watched Iman do the math in her head, glancing at the strangers, the aunties in bright suits, the man in a Jets hoodie, two little kids squabbling over a spot near the fan. Iman was clearly waiting for the catch. Lillian knew that look, because for years she'd had it too, until her grandmother pointed out that she kept looking for a cash box that didn't exist.

They found a stretch of carpet near the back and sat down. Volunteers moved down the rows with steel buckets, and a woman ladled dal onto Lillian's steel tray, then Iman's, without pausing or asking anything. Iman held her tray stiffly, still in suspense, still waiting for someone to tap her shoulder and say there had been a mistake. When the roti came around, folded in a cloth napkin, she took one and whispered, "This is really good."

Afterward, Iman followed Lillian to the sink to wash hands, but she didn't leave the kitchen doorway. Inside, a man was rolling dough into perfect circles while a woman worked the hot tawa with a long metal turner. A boy about their age, Royce from their science class, stood at a counter stacking roti into cloth bundles, and Lillian hadn't even known he was Sikh.

"Can I help?" Iman asked, so suddenly that Royce looked up.

"There's an empty spot," he said, scooting over. "Just keep them coming to the left side."

Lillian watched Iman take up the stack of warm roti and carry it out to the rows, kneeling beside strangers and offering bread with both hands, the way she'd seen the volunteers do it. When two little kids started arguing over who got to sit closest to the fan, Iman stepped between them and mediated, suggesting they take turns, and somehow they actually listened.

Later, in the parking lot, Iman pulled the five dollars out of her pocket and stared at it. "I didn't need this at all."

"You can keep it for the book fair," Lillian said.

Iman laughed and put it back. "Next time I'm bringing an appetite instead."

Louis crouched at the top of the skate park's biggest ramp with a tennis ball in one hand and his phone in the other, and Laurence stood at the bottom holding a broom handle they had found behind the bins. "When I drop it, start counting seconds," Louis said. "Not with the phone. The phone stopwatch makes you impulsive, you tap it too early." Laurence looked offended but raised the broom anyway, because Laurence was the fastest counter in their class and everyone knew it.

The plan had started that morning in Mr. Pérez's room, where a worksheet about distance-time graphs had seemed like the most boring thing ever invented. Speed equals distance divided by time; draw a line; the steeper the line, the faster the thing. Louis had nearly submerge... no, he had nearly fallen asleep, except Mr. Pérez had said one strange thing on his way past their desk. "A speed in meters per second, times 3.6, gives you kilometers per hour." He had not explained it. He had just kept walking, like he had dropped a coin on the table and left it there.

Now Louis wanted the coin. Vaughn arrived on his bike, skidded to a stop, and asked what they were doing. "Science," said Louis. "We roll the ball, we time it, we find its speed, and then we find out if it beats a person walking." Vaughn frowned. "A person walks about five kilometers an hour, my gran says, she counts everything." He marked a line in the dust with his heel. "So that's the competition. Ball versus gran."

They rolled the ball three times. The ramp to the broom was nine meters; Laurence counted "one-Mississippi" style and got four seconds, then three and a half, then four again. Nine divided by four was 2.25, and Louis did the math twice on the back of his hand because he did not trust his own brain under pressure. Then he remembered the coin. 2.25 times 3.6. He got 8.1. He checked it again. Still 8.1.

"Eight point one kilometers an hour," he announced. Vaughn whooped so loudly that a toddler on a scooter near the bowl turned to stare, and the toddler's dad laughed. "That's faster than your gran!" Vaughn shouted. "Way faster than walking!" Laurence, who was quietly pleased about his counting, said, "So to turn a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, you multiply it by 3.6," just to hear it out loud, and Louis grinned because hearing it made it real.

That evening Louis drew the graph in his notebook, one dot for each roll, the line rising like the ramp itself, and his analysis said the ball was not perfectly steady because his dots wobbled a little. He would tell Mr. Pérez tomorrow. He slipped the notebook under his pillow, then took it out again to look at the dots one more time. "Eight point one," he whispered to the ceiling. "Gran, you never stood a chance."

Matthew had one goal before dinner: prove that Aris was wrong on the class forum. Aris had posted a chart of batting averages and declared that his favorite player, Rico Vance, didn't belong in the top ten because his average was only .261. Matthew's favorite, Vance's teammate Jordy Okafor, sat at .288, and Matthew intended to end the argument for good.

He settled in at the computer and pulled up the stats page, leaning close to scrutinize every column. Hits. At-bats. Average. Then a fourth column he usually skipped: walks. Vance had 84 of them. Okafor had 31. Matthew frowned. Both players had played the same number of games, yet their at-bats were strangely different. Vance had far fewer. He scrolled, read, and scrolled again, and somewhere in a comment thread below the table he found a kid arguing exactly the opposite of Aris. "Vance is underrated," the kid wrote. "A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks don't count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks."

Matthew read the sentence three times. He grabbed a pencil and tried it himself, dividing Vance's hits by his at-bats on scrap paper. The answer matched the .261 on the screen, which meant the comment was describing something real. Vance reached base constantly, but almost a hundred trips to first base had simply vanished from the number everyone quoted. His instinct told him to defend Okafor anyway, because Okafor was his guy, but the numbers were the numbers.

He typed a reply to Aris and then paused, because the phone buzzed. It was Aris himself, calling instead of texting, which he only did when something was wrong. "My grandma's in the hospital," Aris said, voice wobbling. "I can't finish the chart for Mr. Chanthavong by tomorrow. I started it but I'm stuck."

"Send me what you have," Matthew said. "I'm already on that page anyway." He copied Aris's half-finished chart, filled in the missing averages, and while he worked he noticed something that made him sit up straight: the comment defending Vance had been posted by a username, CoachC77, and the profile picture was unmistakable. It was Mr. Chanthavong, their own teacher, arguing about baseball on a stats site at midnight.

Matthew added a final line to the chart, one distinct note at the bottom in bold: "Vance: .261 average, but 84 walks not counted." Then he texted Aris, "Chart's done. Also, wait until you find out who CoachC77 is."

At school the next morning, Mr. Chanthavong collected the charts without a word, but when he reached Matthew's desk he stopped, tapped the bold note, and raised one eyebrow.

"Nice work," Mr. Chanthavong said. "See me after class, Slugger fan."

Noah sat at the upright piano in the music classroom after last bell, working through the same eight measures for the fourth day running. The passage required his right hand to jump a fourth and then cross under, and every time he reached the sixth note his fingers tangled. Mr. Okonkwo had told him the piece was versatile enough to work on either piano or the classroom keyboard, but that didn't help. He ground through it forty more times, hit the same wall, and finally closed the lid.

"You look like despair in a hoodie," said Milania, who was stacking chairs near the door. "That crossing part again?"

"Sixth note. Every single time." He pulled his sleeve down over his hand, as if he could insulate his fingers from their own clumsiness. "I'm going to miss the recital cut at this rate."

At home he practiced once more, badly, and went to bed annoyed.

The next morning he got to school early, before anyone else, and set his backpack on a chair. He told himself he would just check whether the passage was as bad as yesterday, no rehearsing, one run-through. He put his hands on the keys, played the eight measures, and got through them clean, all the way to the end, twice in a row. He had done no extra practice since the night before. He sat there staring at his own hands.

He decided to test it instead of just being glad. He picked a different tricky line from another piece, one he had never practiced, and played it badly that afternoon, fumbling the same spots again and again. Then he left it alone, went home, slept, and did not touch a piano. The next morning he came in early again, and the new line went through without a stumble, no extra practice in between. The same thing had happened twice: a night of sleep after practicing the finger movement made his playing better the next day. He wrote both results in the back of his binder, with dates, so he wouldn't talk himself out of it.

When Milania came in, he was playing the original passage at full speed. She stopped stacking chairs.

"When did you fix that?"

"Last night," Noah said. "I was asleep."

The group chat pinged at 6:47, and Jayden read the first message twice before it made sense. Uriah had written, "It's happening Saturday. Coach picked three of us to take penalty shots in front of everyone at the end of practice." Jayden's thumbs hovered. He knew exactly what Uriah meant, because Jayden was one of the three. He hadn't told anyone yet, not even Michelle, and the anxiety had been sitting in his stomach like a stone since Tuesday, when the coach read out the names and the whole team turned to look.

"You okay?" Michelle typed. "You've been weird in here all week. Like, you start messages and delete them. I can see 'Uriah is typing' happen."

"It's nothing," Jayden sent, then felt bad about it, because it wasn't nothing and Michelle could tell. She'd been trying to organize the science fair group all week, and Jayden kept dodging her, and at some point a friend had a legitimate right to know why. He took a breath and typed the truth. "I'm one of the three taking penalties. Saturday. In front of everybody."

"Wait," Michelle replied. "That's why your messages migrate from topic to topic every time practice comes up. You're steering away from it."

Before Jayden could answer, Uriah sent a photo of a folded note from the goalie, slipped into his locker after practice. The note said: "You looked stressed before tryouts last year and it wrecked your touch. Here's what I do before a penalty shot. I breathe slow and make the exhale longer than the inhale. Slow breathing with long exhales is how I cope before a stressful moment. It settles the body down. Try it before Saturday." Uriah added, "Is this real or is he messing with me? It sounds made up."

Jayden stared at the note. It sounded made up. But he thought about the goalie, about how he never looked rattled, and he decided there was one way to find out. He set a timer on his phone, sat on his bedroom floor, and tried it, in for three, out longer than in, over and over. Nothing magical happened. But his shoulders dropped, and the stone in his stomach got smaller. He did it again Thursday after a rough scrimmage, and again Friday night when he couldn't sleep.

Saturday morning the chat filled up fast. Michelle: "You've got this." Uriah: "Doing the goalie thing in the car. Weirdly works." Then the chat went quiet, because all three of them were walking onto the field.

The coach set the ball down. Jayden took his spot at the arc, and behind him he could hear the whole team shifting on the bench. He didn't look at them. He breathed in, then let the breath out slow, longer than it came in, the way he'd practiced, and the noise seemed to move somewhere behind glass. The keeper rocked on his heels. Jayden pivoted his plant foot and struck the ball.

Declan stood in the synagogue library with his folder open on the table, and the folder had two sections instead of one. The first held his Torah portion, which he had been chanting for weeks. The second held something he had never seen before, a page titled Haftarah. He stared at it until Hugo leaned over his shoulder.

"What's that one?" Hugo asked.

"It's from the books of the Prophets," Declan said slowly, reading the note at the top. "You chant it too. At a bar mitzvah, after the Torah reading." He flipped back and forth between the two sections, counting pages the way he counted anything that scared him. "Hugo. I have two readings to learn. Not one."

Hugo winced. "I thought it was just the one."

"So did I." Declan sat down hard on the chair. Six weeks remained, and the second reading was almost as long as the first.

He thought about the day he picked his date. The synagogue had given his family a list of Saturdays, and his mother had asked which he wanted. He had chosen one nearly at the median of the list, figuring a middle date would give him the most time either way. Now that decision felt like a coin toss he had made with his eyes shut. If he had picked the last Saturday, he would have had four extra weeks. He couldn't know that then, but he kept turning the choice over anyway, like a stone in his pocket.

In the car on the way home, he tested a plan out loud. "The words are what's hard," he told his dad. "But the notes, the trope symbols, those repeat. If I learn the melody patterns once, they should work for both readings. Tropes are versatile like that." His dad shrugged, so Declan tried it that evening at the kitchen table. He sang a phrase from the Torah portion, then the same trope pattern applied to a phrase from the Prophets section. The tune carried the new words. It worked.

The next Sunday he found Mr. Khoury unlocking the sanctuary and asked if he could practice from the bimah, because the acoustics were different up there and he wanted to anticipate how his voice would sound in the big room. Mr. Khoury handed him the microphone. "Go ahead. Sing it like it's the real day."

Declan set both pages on the lectern, took a breath, and began with the haftarah.

Nevaeh had exactly forty minutes before her mother got home, and the math worksheet had to be finished by then. She sat at the kitchen table with a glass of milk, three sharpened pencils, and a problem that refused to behave. Her plan was to solve it like all the others, doing the same thing to both sides, but this one kept doing something strange. The last problem on the page read 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1), and it was the only one left.

She distributed the two on the right side first, and the right side became 2x + 2. Then she subtracted 2x from both sides, the way Mr. Sok had shown the class on Tuesday, and the variables vanished entirely. Both sides of the equation now read simply 2 = 2. Nevaeh stared at it. She anticipated an answer like x = 5 or x = 12, some distinct number she could circle in red, and instead she got something that looked like a joke the worksheet was playing on her.

She called Grey, who was working on the same sheet at his own kitchen table. "Problem twenty is broken," she said. "I did everything right and I got two equals two." There was a pause, and then Grey laughed so hard she had to hold the phone away from her ear. "Mine says four equals four," he said. "I thought I copied it wrong." Nevaeh looked back at her paper. "What do we even write? There's no x left to find."

She tried a number, just to test it. She picked x = 7, put it into the left side, and got 16. She put it into the right side and got 16 again. She tried x = 100, then x = 0, and both sides matched every single time, like two doors leading into the same room. "Grey," she said slowly, "I think it's true for every number. Both sides are just the same thing written differently, so of course they're equal." Grey went quiet, and she could hear him writing. "So what do we write for the answer?" he asked.

Nevaeh thought of her older sister's memoir on the shelf, the one about a summer where nothing went wrong and everything still mattered. Some answers were like that, she decided, true all the way through without pointing at any one thing. She wrote, "True for every number," and boxed it. Then she wrote "same thing, written differently" underneath, because it felt worth saying twice.

At the thirty-nine minute mark, her mother's key turned in the lock. Nevaeh slid the worksheet into her folder and raised her milk glass in a small toast to the empty chair across from her. "Two equals two," she announced to the kitchen, "and Nevaeh equals done."

Luke had been building the dragon for three afternoons in a row, kneeling at the picnic table in Miya's backyard with a bucket of gray clay and a butter knife for the scales. It was going to be his best piece all year, good enough that Mr. Traoré might actually fire it in the school kiln on Friday. The only trouble was the timing. He had finished the body on Wednesday, and the wings on Thursday, and now it was Thursday evening and the dragon still felt cool against his cheek, the way a basement floor feels.

"It's not dry," Miya said, watching him press his thumb into the thickest part of the tail. "Look, it's darker there."

"That's just the slip I used to attach the wings," Luke said, though privately he wasn't sure. Ants had colonized the far end of the table, marching in a tidy line toward a dropped raspberry, and he brushed a few off his sleeve. "It's been out in the sun all day. Sun dries things."

Kira came through the gate with a bag of chips and peered at the dragon. "My mom's a potter," she said. "She fired a bowl once that was still damp inside, and it cracked right up the side. She said leftover water turns to steam when it fires, and steam can burst the whole piece." She crunched a chip. "You don't want steam inside your dragon."

Luke wanted to argue, but he kept thinking about the crack running up his dragon's belly, and how he'd have to explain it to Mr. Traoré. "How do you even tell if it's dry all the way through?" he asked. "I can only feel the outside."

"Warm it up and smell it," Kira said. "Mom checks the smell. Wet clay smells like a creek."

It sounded ridiculous, but it was a test, and a test was better than guessing. Luke carried the dragon to the warm brick step beside the shed, set it on a scrap of wood, and crouched over it with his nose almost touching the clay. The thin wing tips smelled like nothing, like chalk. But when he sniffed the thick middle of the body, there it was, faint and cool: a mineral, river-stone smell. He sat back on his heels.

"It's still damp in the middle," he said. He had been so sure the sun would be enough. "So I can't fire it tomorrow."

"So don't fire it tomorrow," Miya said, so simply that Luke laughed, a short spontaneous bark that surprised even him.

Friday after school, he watched Mr. Traoré load the kiln shelf with Kira's coil pot and the small cups the seventh graders had made, and Mr. Traoré set Luke's dragon on the drying rack instead, pressing it to his own cheek and nodding. "Monday," he said.

"Monday," Luke agreed. At home he emptied the clay water from his bucket into the flowerbed, leaving a gray settlement of fine particles crusted at the bottom, and thought about steam, hidden inside solid clay, waiting. On Monday he carried the dragon to school cradled in a shoebox like something alive, and set it, bone pale and creek-smelling of nothing at all, into Mr. Traoré's outstretched hands.

Blake had made it to the final three of the school spelling bee, and now the librarian's old library book was the only thing standing between him and the regionals.

It had started three weeks earlier, when Mr. Sánchez announced that the winner of the school bee would advance to the regional, then maybe even to the televised nationals. "The nationals are a big deal," he said. "In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde won the whole Scripps National Spelling Bee. She was the first African-American contestant to win it." He said it like it was just a fact on a list, but Blake couldn't stop thinking about it all afternoon.

So he went to the library. Constance was already there, hoarding six books about spelling champions because she wanted to win the bee herself, and she guarded those books like a dragon guards gold. "Those are mine until I read every page," she told him.

"I just want one," Blake said. "The one about recent champions."

Constance narrowed her eyes. "Fine. One. But if you find any good tricks in it, you have to tell me, because I have a system." Her system, she explained, was reading every word in the dictionary that started with Q. "Q words are where people panic," she said. "I will be robust. I will not panic."

Blake sat down with the book and found the chapter about 2021. Zaila Avant-garde had won with the word "murraya," and she juggled basketballs while she practiced, which Blake thought was possibly the greatest thing he had ever heard. Before her, no African-American contestant had ever won the Scripps bee. Ninety-six years of the contest, and she was the first. He read that page four times.

He started testing an idea that afternoon. His theory was that winning spellers weren't people with magic memories; they were people who looked for patterns in how words were built, even when you couldn't see the pattern from outside. He tested it on Tess at lunch. "Spell photosynthesis," he said.

"Uh, P-H-O..." Tess chewed her pretzel. "How would I know? It's some organism thing, plants probably."

"That's the point," Blake said. "If you know it means light putting things together, photo is right there. Photo, light. You don't guess it, you build it." Tess spelled it out, got it, and was so pleased she made him quiz her on ten more words, which she mostly missed, cheerfully.

Now, in the auditorium, under lights that made everything smell warm and dusty, the pronouncer said, "Blake. Your word is murraya."

He almost laughed. Of course. He thought of a girl juggling basketballs, and of how you could look at a word nobody could see inside and still find the pieces. "Murraya," he said. "M-U-R-R-A-Y-A. Murraya." He would cherish this moment even if Constance won, and judging by her furious Q-word flashcards, she planned to.

"Correct," the pronouncer said. "Constance, your word is quay."

Constance froze. Then Blake watched her mouth move, silently, and he knew she was doing the same thing he did: not guessing, building. "Q-U-A-Y," she said. "Quay."

"Correct," the pronouncer said, and Constance turned around in her seat and grinned at Blake like she'd just stolen his lunch.

The pronouncer shuffled his cards. "Blake. If you spell this next word correctly, you advance to the regional. Your word is cherish."

"C-H-E-R-I-S-H," Blake said. "Cherish."

Sebastian was still thinking about the letter at dinner when his dad read it out loud a second time. "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste." His little sister said the whole thing was wrong. His dad said only part of it was. Now Sebastian sat at the computer with the letter open on the screen, trying to figure out which part.

He typed a message to Lia, because she argued about everything and usually won. "How can one sentence be half right?" he wrote. He underlined the sentence in his notebook and drew a line down the middle of it.

Lia replied fast, the way she did when she was eating chips at the same time. "The two million dollars part, somebody can look that up. The waste part is just what the guy thinks." Sebastian stared at the screen. That was it. One half could be checked, like a math answer, and the other half was an opinion, like whether pineapple belongs on pizza. He circled "two million dollars" and wrote CHECKABLE beside it. Beside "waste" he wrote OPINION.

His problem was the essay Ms. Suryanto had assigned, a reply to the editor due Monday, and now he knew exactly what to do with it. He started typing. First he searched for the city budget page and found the parks section, and there it was, the number in the letter, exact. He wrote that the cost could be checked against the public record. Then he wrote that "waste" was the letter writer's judgment, not a fact, and gave his own evidence: the temporary parking lot the skate park had replaced, and the landlord on his street who had complained about kids skateboarding down his driveway until the park opened and they all went there instead.

Kingsley messaged him mid-paragraph. "Did you just call the guy a liar?" Sebastian reread his draft. He hadn't, but it was close, so he softened it. "He's not wrong about the number," Kingsley said. "He just declared the rest like it was a law."

"A law," Sebastian typed back, "like the kind a doctor would prescribe, except opinions don't work that way." Kingsley sent a thumbs up.

On Monday, Ms. Suryanto read the essay aloud to the class and asked Sebastian to explain his method. He held up his notebook with the line drawn down the middle of the sentence. "Cost on this side, waste on that side," he said. "You can check one side and not the other."

Hunter had twenty dollars and one goal: the box of Dragonstrike cards at Ms. Sutton's garage sale. He'd seen the notice taped to a telephone pole, and he'd biked six blocks before the tables were even fully set up. But Kai was already there, holding a shiny Frostfang card up to the light, and behind him stood three other kids from school, all elbowing toward the same cardboard box.

"Ten dollars each for the rare ones," Ms. Sutton said, tapping a hand-lettered sign. "They've been very popular this week."

Ten dollars. Hunter's stomach tightened. Two months ago, at the spring trading fair, the same cards had gone for two or three dollars, because every kid in seventh grade had duplicates spilling out of their backpacks. Back then, nobody wanted Frostfang. Then the game company announced it was discontinuing the set, the supply dried up, and suddenly everyone who'd ignored the cards wanted them desperately. He remembered Haley at lunch, waving her wallet and shouting offers across the cafeteria while kids shoved toward her table. Scarce plus popular equalled expensive. He'd learned that the hard way in November, when he'd traded his own Frostfang away for a sandwich.

Hunter counted the kids at the table. Five buyers, one box. He couldn't change how many cards existed, but maybe he could change his timing. "I'll come back this afternoon," he told Kai, who looked at him like he was insane.

"You'll miss out," Kai warned. "They'll be gone by noon."

Instead of arguing, Hunter biked home, did his homework at the kitchen table while his mom raised an eyebrow, and pedaled back at three o'clock. The sun had shifted across the driveway, and the card table sat almost empty. Haley was there, slumped in a folding chair, trying to sell her own duplicates to Ms. Sutton, who politely declined. The other kids had vanished, their allowances spent, their interest drifting toward whatever the eighth graders were playing now.

"How much for Frostfang now?" Hunter asked.

Ms. Sutton shrugged. "Nobody's touched them in two hours. Two dollars each."

He bought four cards and still had twelve dollars left. On the driveway, Haley stared at the box, then at Hunter's cards, and Hunter watched her change her mind right in front of him. She'd been holding her duplicates, waiting for prices to climb back up. Now she flipped through them and said, "This whole craze is going to crash eventually, isn't it. Like those tulips."

"What tulips?" Hunter asked.

"In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up," Haley said. "Ms. Sutton told me. My English teacher calls it a metaphor for chasing stuff everybody wants."

Hunter thought of the cafeteria scene, of Kai paying ten dollars that morning, of the empty table now. He felt almost impoverished by comparison, having only twelve dollars left, but he handed Haley two of them for her best duplicate. "Trade me your Emberwing too," he said, "and when everybody wants these again, you get first pick."

Haley grinned and shook on it. Down the block, Kai pedaled up, saw the prices on the sign, and let out a groan.

Scarlett had one week before the improv tryout, and her scenes kept dying. She sat on the living room rug with Frances and Lauralie, who had come over to practice, and watched Frances fold her arms for the fifth time.

"Let's try the king and servant again," Scarlett said. "Frances, you're the king. Lauralie, serve the tea."

Frances sprawled on the couch like she owned the palace. "Peasant. My tea is cold. Fetch me another cup, and be quick about it."

Lauralie shuffled forward with an imaginary tray, hunched over. "Yes, Your Majesty. Sorry, Your Majesty."

The scene went nowhere. Lauralie apologized, Frances demanded, and Scarlett stopped them after a minute. "It's not funny. Something's wrong and I can't see what."

She stared at the two of them and thought about it while they drank real lemonade. Frances was sitting high on the couch, Lauralie low on the floor. There was a pattern: whoever sat above the other got obeyed, and the scene just repeated itself. She wanted to test an idea, but she needed information first. Her objective for the afternoon was a scene that actually worked, and she was missing a piece.

The piece lived next door. Mr. Rowe had done theater in college, and when Scarlett knocked on his door and asked how to make a two-person scene interesting, he went to his shelf and pulled down a worn paperback. "Keith Johnstone's 1979 book, Impro," he said, handing it to her. "Read the chapter on status." He didn't say anything else, which was typical of him.

Back in the living room, Scarlett read aloud while Frances and Lauralie listened. The book said characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama. She let that digest for a second, then looked up. "That's it. Frances, you're the high status king, but partway through, Lauralie, you climb. Start giving orders."

"Again from the top," Lauralie said. She took up the imaginary tray, but this time she set it down hard. "Your Majesty, sit up straight. You're slouching in front of the court."

Frances blinked, then snapped upright. "I beg your pardon, I am the king."

"And I'm telling you your tea manners are corrosive to the dignity of the throne. Elbows off the table."

Frances pulled her elbows in. "Yes. Fine. As you were." A pause, and then Frances slid down low in the seat. "Actually, would you show me how to hold the cup?"

Lauralie drew herself up to full height and demonstrated, chin lifted. Scarlett laughed so hard she had to put the book down.

"Same scene tomorrow," she said. "I call the servant."

Leah spread her poster across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with salt shakers. Her assignment was to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death, and she had one column filled: her grandmother's church, heaven, and being with God. The other column was blank because Jaden, who came over every Tuesday, practiced Sikhism, and Leah had promised herself she would get the facts right instead of guessing.
