Grayson's fork stopped halfway to his mouth. Slowly, without a word, he tapped the info button on his own lasagna photo, the button he had not known existed until tonight. The map unfolded. The pin dropped. It stood exactly where he was sitting, above the kitchen, above the blue door on the corner house, above the plate of food going cold in front of him.

He turned the phone toward his mom so she could see the pin, and then looked at the window, where the curtain hung open and the streetlight made a long bright stripe across the table.

"Lock the door," he said.

Mia had built her volcano twice already, and both times it had barely fizzled. Now she stood at the back counter of the science classroom, third volcano in front of her, remembering how she had chosen this project in the first place. Last year she had copied a kit straight from the box, and Ms. Wardak had written "Where is the question?" in red pen across the top of her worksheet. This year there would be a question. Her question was: what actually makes the eruption happen, since nobody could see it?

"It's the gas," Graeme said, tipping baking soda into the crater. "Baking soda, or sodium bicarbonate, reacts with vinegar, acetic acid, and you get carbon dioxide gas. That's the whole push." He said it the way he said everything, like he had read it somewhere and was daring the world to prove it wrong.

"Then more vinegar should mean more gas," Mia said. She had set out four cups on the counter, each with a different amount of vinegar, and a ruler taped to the wall behind the volcano to measure how high the foam climbed. Graeme wanted more than a plain volcano anyway; he wanted a graph. She poured the smallest cup first. The foam rose two centimeters. The next cup, twice as much, sent it nearly to the top of the ruler. She wrote both numbers down, feeling like she was finally doing something instead of just watching something.

Hannah leaned over the tray of paper cups they were using as molds. "Careful, the dried ones get brittle if you leave them overnight," she said, nudging a cracked cup out of the way so it wouldn't obstruct the view of the eruption zone. Mia poured the third cup, the biggest one, and waited for the fountain.

Nothing like it. The foam bulged, sputtered, and dribbled down the side, lower than the second trial. Mia stared at it. The gas had to be there, the same as before, so why had the eruption shrunk? She looked at the crater, then at the cardboard tube inside it, and realized the opening was packed solid with wet baking soda from the earlier trials. She dug it clear with a spoon, ran the same amount of vinegar again, and this time the foam shot past the ruler entirely and splattered Hannah's sleeve. Ms. Wardak looked up from her desk. "Someone will be explaining that graph to the judges on Friday," she said. Graeme was already drawing a second column on the data sheet. "Trial five," he said, holding out the cup.

Joseph was telling everyone on the bus that the city was going to tear down the roller rink and put in a parking garage, and he was enjoying the attention way too much. "My cousin heard it from a guy who works for the city," he said, leaning into the aisle so the kids three rows back could hear. "They already signed the papers."

Justin gripped his backpack strap. The rink was where he and Joseph and Lola had spent every Friday since sixth grade, and last spring he had bailed on Lola's birthday party there because Joseph said the buses on Fridays were "unsafe," which had turned out to mean one kid got sick once. He still felt bad about that. Now he squinted at Joseph and said, "Which guy? What's his name?"

Joseph shrugged. "Does it matter?"

"It matters if it's true," Lola said from the seat behind them. She smelled like the cherry lip balm she put on when she was thinking hard, and she was clicking the cap on and off. "My mom says people say stuff on the bus all day and nobody checks any of it."

"That's an opinion," Joseph said. "I'm allowed to have opinions."

"You said they signed papers," Justin said slowly, working it out. "That's not an opinion. An opinion is like, the rink smells like feet. You can't check that. Papers either exist or they don't." He could see Joseph's jaw tighten, the way it did when a debate started slipping away from him. Joseph wanted to be the kid with the inside story, the one people leaned toward on the bus, and for a second Justin almost let it go.

Instead he pulled out his phone. "My dad and I looked something up last month," he said, "a claim in a TV ad. PolitiFact. It's a fact-checking website, founded in 2007, and it rates claims on a scale called the Truth-O-Meter." Lola leaned over the seat, close enough that he could feel the cold air coming off the window near her sleeve. "It goes from True all the way to Pants on Fire," Justin said. "That's the worst one."

They typed in the rink. The first result was a story from two weeks ago: the city council had voted to keep the rink and renovate it, money already approved. No garage, no papers, nothing signed. Joseph went quiet, watching the phone like it might change its answer.

"It's ironic," Lola said finally, capping her lip balm. "The rink stays open, and the only thing that got torn down was your story." She stood up as the bus lurched toward their stop, one hand on the cold metal rail, and looked back at Joseph. "Friday. Seven o'clock. Bring your skates, and your Truth-O-Meter."

The last pint of strawberries at Ms. Haile's stall had a hand-lettered sign taped to it, and the price had been crossed out and rewritten twice. Lillian stared at the new number. Last week the same berries had cost half as much, and there had been a whole flat of them, red and gleaming, with nobody fighting over the last few. She had spent her money on honey instead, telling herself the berries would still be there tomorrow. Now three people stood in line behind her, and Ms. Haile's forehead had begun to perspire as she counted change fast.

"They were four dollars all June," Lillian said, holding up the pint. "Why eight now?"

"Frost took half the crop up the valley," Ms. Haile said. "Everybody who wants berries this week wants these." She tapped the sign. "Scarce and wanted means dear. Plentiful means cheap. Ask the zucchini people." Behind her, a farmer was practically giving away squash, calling out two for a dollar to anyone who glanced his way.

Jade elbowed up beside Lillian with her dad, who was parking the car at the gas station across the lot. A boy at the pump was tugging his mother's sleeve and pointing at the sign there. "Mom, why is it more than last week?" His mother shrugged, but Jade's dad answered over his shoulder without looking up from the nozzle. "Crude oil got expensive. Crude oil is usually the biggest single part of the price of a gallon of gas, so when crude goes up, pump prices tend to go up too." The boy nodded like he'd been handed the answer to a riddle, and Jade's dad smiled, almost ironic, since he was filling the tank anyway.

Lillian turned the idea over like a lens in her hand, tilting it to see whether it was true. She walked the row of stalls like a scientist, testing. The peach stand had one basket left and a crowd, and the price was high. The lettuce table had crates and crates and a bored farmer, and the price was so low a woman bought four heads. Same rule, two ways. She thought about last Saturday, the honey, the berries she had assumed would wait for her, and she couldn't decide whether she had been patient or just foolish. Maybe both.

She counted her money on the bench near the fountain. Eight dollars exactly, the whole of it, which meant no honey, no peach cider, nothing else all morning. She looked at the pint in her hand, then at the lettuce stand, where four heads would cost two dollars and feed her family a week. The line behind her lengthened. Jade waved from across the lot. Lillian took a breath, pushed through the crowd, and set the strawberries back on Ms. Haile's scale. "Two heads of lettuce," she said, "and the biggest one you've got."

Aiden had a globe, a desk lamp, and one night to figure out the seasons before Mr. Suryanto's science class made their presentations in the morning. The assignment said each student had to explain, with a model, why summer and winter happen. He had tried reading the chapter twice, and both times the words slid off without sticking.

Maelly came over after dinner with a bag of popcorn and her notebook. "My mom had to authorize the sleepover swap, so I can stay till nine," she said, dropping onto the rug beside him. "Show me what you've got."

Aiden plugged in the lamp and set the globe on the floor a step away. "Mr. Suryanto said to use the lamp as the sun," he said. He spun the globe slowly. "So Earth goes around like this, and it turns, and then... seasons." He stopped. He realized he had no idea what came next.

"That's your whole presentation?" Maelly pulled a kernel from the bag. "Mariah brought in a contemporary one off the internet for extra credit, with diagrams. She'll do a whole critique of yours if you just say 'and then seasons.'"

Aiden tilted the globe so its stand held it leaning, the way it sat in the classroom. Then he walked it in a slow circle around the lamp, keeping the lean pointed at the same wall the whole time. At one side of the circle, the top half of the globe caught the light straight on while the bottom half sat in shadow. At the other side, it flipped.

"Look at Canada," he said. "It's lit up like noon. Australia's in the dark." He kept walking the circle. "Now Canada's dark and Australia's bright. Same globe, same lamp. It's the lean."

Maelly leaned in. "So try it without the lean."

That was the part neither of them expected. Aiden held the globe perfectly upright in his fist, no tilt at all, and walked it around the lamp again. Canada caught the light at exactly the same angle on every lap. Australia did too. Every place on the globe got its same slant of light all the way around, lap after lap, and the bright patch never moved north or south. The seasons had simply gone.

"If Earth's axis had no tilt," Aiden said slowly, watching the unchanging light, "sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year." He set the globe down on its tilted stand and did one more lap, watching the light climb and fall. "There'd almost be no seasons at all. It would just be the same weather forever."

At nine, Maelly called her mom from the kitchen. Aiden stood the lamp on his desk where he could see it from bed and walked the globe around it one more time, keeping the lean pointed at the closet door.

"No seasons," he said to the upright globe in his other hand. "Not a single one."

Sydney carried the cardboard carrier through Riverside Park like it held something breakable, which it did. Inside, curled on a towel, was Peanut, her brand-new guinea pig, won after two weeks of arguing her case at the dinner table. Her dad had said pets were a big responsibility. Sydney had said she knew. Now, walking past the duck pond, she wasn't so sure she knew anything at all, because Peanut had barely touched his food this morning.

At the picnic tables by the playground, Tori and Vayda were waiting with the sunflower seeds they always brought. Tori was a veteran pet owner, with two rabbits and a hamster behind her, and she leaned over the carrier immediately. "He's got that hunched-up look," she said. "My rabbit did that when he was sick."

Sydney's stomach dropped. She tried to think backward through the last three days, the way her mom untangled problems at work. She had fed Peanut exactly what the pet store sold her, a bowl of dry pellets, morning and night. She had refilled his water. She had cleaned the cage. Nothing fresh, though. Not one piece of vegetable, because she'd been afraid of giving him something wrong. She remembered the binder from the school library, the one she'd flipped through on the bus during her long commute across town, and one page swam back to her. "Wait," she said slowly. "Guinea pigs can't make their own vitamin C. They have to get it from their food every single day. And I haven't given him anything with vitamin C in it. Pellets alone might not be enough."

"So it's like he got sick from missing breakfast, basically," Vayda said. "Gross breakfast, but still."

It was a guess, but it was a testable one. Sydney dug through the backpack she'd packed like a first-aid kit, just in case: a red bell pepper, bought that morning from the corner store with her allowance. She set a strip of it in the carrier and the three of them crouched on the grass in the shade of an oak, watching, saying nothing, while a jogger thumped past on the gravel path. Peanut's nose twitched. Then he was chewing, fast and greedy, whiskers trembling.

"Okay," Tori whispered, like loud voices might scare the appetite away. "Okay, that's a good sign."

Sydney didn't celebrate yet. She knew one pepper strip wasn't a cure, and she knew that in a few days, if her guess was right, Peanut would perk up, and if it was wrong, she'd be on the phone with a vet. It had been a little vain of her, she thought, to assume the pet store bag held everything a living thing needed, just because it had a picture of a guinea pig on the front. She made a note in her phone: pepper or greens, every day, no exceptions.

Peanut finished the strip and made a sound Sydney had never heard before, a squeaky little wheek aimed straight at her.

"That means he likes you," Tori said. "Or he's begging for more."

"Both," said Sydney, and she opened the backpack again.

The vase was already broken when Jaxon got to the kitchen, which was the only fact nobody argued about. Emilee stood over the shards with a dustpan, and Nevaeh was on her knees trying to glue two pieces together with a glue stick, which was not going to work.

"My grandma's coming at five," Emilee said. "She gave us that vase. We have maybe forty minutes to figure out what happened so we can tell her something."

"That's not much time," Jaxon said.

So they interviewed the household. Emilee's dad said the cat did it, absolutely, the cat had it coming to him for months. Her little brother said Emilee had bumped the table doing a dance move. Emilee said she'd been upstairs the whole time and the brother was blaming her because he'd been dribbling a basketball indoors. Even the grandmother, reached by phone, said the vase had been sitting too close to the edge for weeks, which was practically nobody's fault.

Jaxon wrote all four stories in his notebook and stared at them. Same broken vase, four versions, none of them matching. Something about it tickled the back of his brain, and then he had it.

"My cousin made me watch this old movie," he said. "Rashomon. Akira Kurosawa, 1950. It tells one crime through four witnesses, and every account contradicts the others. Nobody even agrees on what happened."

"So the movie is about this?" Neavaeh said, gesturing at the shards with the glue stick.

"It's about people," Emilee said, in the tone of someone who had consumed an entire documentary series on human nature over spring break. "Everybody sees the thing that makes them feel okay."

Jaxon tested it. He checked the table, which was a solid wooden plateau in the middle of the kitchen, flat and level, no wobble. He checked the shards: the break pattern came from the side facing the hallway, not the stairs, not the living room where the cat slept. A basketball bouncing was probable; a cat leaping four feet sideways onto a heavy vase was not. The brother's story matched the physics, which meant the brother had done it and had still told a lie inside the truth.

"There were two people who could have done it," Jaxon said. "And four stories. That's the weird part."

"Grandma's pulling into the driveway," Emilee said, dropping the dustpan. "Nevaeh, sweep. Jaxon, notebook away. Everybody, casual."

The door opened, and the grandmother walked in carrying flowers for the empty spot.

Maelie stood at the edge of the drama camp stage with her sneakers glued to the floor, which was a problem, because in improv you were supposed to move. The gym smelled like floor wax and old costumes, and somewhere behind her Jaxton was already bouncing on his toes like this was the easiest thing in the world.

"Two of you up," said Mr. Jean-Louis, clapping his hands. "Scene is a garage. Go."

Jaxton launched in. "Hey, look at all this stuff."

"Yeah," Maelie said. "Lots of stuff."

They shuffled around an imaginary garage for a minute, picking up nothing, describing nothing. Jaxton said, "This is interesting." Maelie said, "Sure is." Eventually they ran out of ways to say nothing, and they just stood there while the rest of the campers shifted on the bleachers. Mr. Jean-Louis called time and made a small note on his clipboard. Maelie's ears went hot.

At lunch she sat with Ezekiel, who had been in the morning group and whose scene had actually worked. "What did you do?" she asked, tearing her sandwich into smaller and smaller pieces without eating any of it.

"I said I found a note in my mom's coat pocket," Ezekiel said. "Then my partner had a note to react to. A real one, in her head." He shrugged and stole one of her pickle slices. "You two were just handing each other fog."

Maelie pushed her tray aside and thought about that. Fog. When Jaxton said stuff, she had nowhere to put her hands, nothing to picture, no reason to care. But a note in a coat pocket, that was a thing you could hold. She turned it over the way she turned over the vending machine trick at school, the one where a slow second button press sometimes freed the stuck chips. One test. That was all she needed.

Back in the gym, Mr. Jean-Louis paired them again. Same scene, a garage. Maelie's stomach did a slow flip, but she stepped onto the taped square first this time.

"Careful," she said, lifting a paint can that wasn't there. "Don't knock over Grandma's red bicycle."

Jaxton blinked, and then his whole face changed. He grabbed imaginary handlebars. "This thing? Grandma raced this. She won a trophy on it in 1972, and now it's mine."

"No way," Maelie said. "You promised we'd fix it together. You said we'd ride it to the lake."

"I said no such thing." Jaxton swung a leg over the invisible frame. "But you can ride the basket."

They argued about the basket, discovered a wasp nest in it, and fled the garage screaming with laughter, which was apparently a valid ending, because Mr. Jean-Louis clapped three times and said, "Now that is a scene."

Walking out at the end of the day, Maelie could still feel the shape of that bicycle in her hands, red and wobbling and entirely made up. Jaxton jogged up beside her, still grinning.

"Tomorrow," he said, "Grandma's bicycle has a sidecar."

"With room for Ezekiel," said Maelie.

Hazel held the knife the way Ms. Kapoor had shown her, fingers curled inward like a bear paw, knuckles out front. "This is the claw grip," Ms. Kapoor said, and demonstrated on her own half onion, the blade sliding down and stopping short of her fingertips. "Curved fingers, slow cuts. The knife respects the knuckle."

Hazel respected it too, mostly because the week before, Mathys had gone fast and lost a sliver of thumbnail, and the community kitchen's first aid kit turned out to be one ancient bandage and a cough drop. She cut her onion into even pieces, eyes streaming so hard she had to step back from the board. Corbin, stationed at the next table, watched from a distance usually reserved for people avoiding a virus.

"I don't eat onions," he announced, as if she'd offered him one.

"You're going to," Hazel said. "It's sauce. Onions are the whole base."

"Then I'll eat around them."

Ms. Kapoor set a wide pan on the stove and turned the flame down low, low enough that it looked almost off. "Slow heat, and don't rush it," she said, and moved on to check someone's garlic, leaving Hazel alone with a pile of pale raw onion bits and a pan that seemed to be doing nothing at all.

Hazel waited. The onions sat there, opaque white and stubborn, and she began to suspect the burner was broken. She tried a piece from the cutting board first, raw, and her whole face cramped; it was sharp enough to make her eyes water a second time, which she felt was unfair. Then she poked at the pan. The onions had gone soft and floppy, and a smell was rising that was warm and almost like toast. She fished one out with the wooden spoon, blew on it, and ate it. It was sweet. Golden, soft, sweet, nothing like the sharp thing she'd chewed thirty seconds ago. She stood there recalculating her entire opinion of onions. Same vegetable. The slow low heat had done that. She took another piece to be sure.

She carried the spoon across the room like evidence at a trial and held it under Corbin's nose. "Raw onion tastes like that." She pointed at the cutting board. "This is what happens when you cook it slow. Different vegetable, practically."

"Absolutely not," Corbin said. He looked at the ceiling, the window, anywhere but the spoon. Then his shoulders did something involuntary, and he leaned in and took the smallest possible bite. He chewed. He chewed again, slower.

"There's sugar in there or something," he said suspiciously.

"There isn't. It's just the onion." Hazel was already walking back to the stove. "Told you."

When the sauce was done, bubbling and dark red over the softened onions, Corbin was first in line with his bowl. He came back twice. The second time, he scraped the bottom of the pot with a piece of bread and said, without looking up, "Does this work on mushrooms too?"

Charlie slid into her seat in the computer lab just as the bell finished ringing. Mr. Fraser had put the assignment on the board: build a spreadsheet of the class fund-raiser sales, add the column with SUM, and make a bar chart of each student's total. Charlie wanted hers done by the end of the period, because Yani had promised to trade her a bag of lemon chips for a look at the finished chart.

She typed the names down column A and the dollar amounts down column B, then pasted one more row from the note Yani had sent her, Gracie's total of fourteen dollars. In cell B12 she typed =SUM(B2:B10) and pressed Enter. The number that appeared was 128. She checked it against her paper list, where the total should have been 142.

"Your total's wrong," Yani said, leaning over from the next computer.

"I know it's wrong. I don't know why." Charlie clicked on each cell in the column, one at a time. When she got to B10, the cell with Gracie's fourteen, she noticed something in the formula bar. There were quotation marks around the number, like it was a word instead of a number. She looked at the alignment of the cells too. The other numbers sat on the right side of their cells, but this one sat on the left, the way words did.

"Mr. Fraser," she called, "can SUM skip a cell?"

"If the cell holds text, SUM skips it," Mr. Fraser said, and kept walking between the rows of desks.

Charlie had her idea, then. SUM skipped cells that held text, and this fourteen was being held as text, so it was being left out of the total. She tested it the simple way: she retyped the fourteen directly into B10, with no quotation marks anywhere. The total in B12 changed to 142, exactly what her paper list said. The bar chart updated at the same moment, and Gracie's bar grew taller than Yani's, which had not been true a second before.

"Hey," Yani said, staring at the chart. "Gracie beat me?"

"She beat you the whole time. The spreadsheet just didn't know it." Charlie highlighted the chart, copied it, and pasted it into a new sheet so she could show Gracie in the hallway. Then she held out her hand. "Chips first."

Yani dropped the bag on the keyboard. "That was worth it. You should write this down somewhere, so you remember."

Charlie opened a blank cell at the bottom and typed a short note to herself, the way you might summarize a whole afternoon in one line: check for numbers stored as text. She read it over, decided it was an authentic record of what had actually happened, and saved the file. On her way out, she waved the printed chart at Gracie, who was waiting by the water fountain.

"Fourteen dollars," Charlie said. "You owe me a high five."

Carson had signed up for the art shack at Camp Birchwood mostly because his mother said he couldn't spend another summer indoors, and now he regretted it, because the sheet of paper in front of him showed a street that looked like a flat wall.

"Yours too?" Hunter whispered from the next stool, holding up his own drawing. He had drawn a road running straight back between two rows of lampposts, and every single lamppost was exactly the same height, standing the same distance from its neighbors, like fence posts. The road just stopped being a road.

Mr. Doyle walked between the easels, humming something under his breath. When he reached Hunter's table he paused, tapped the corner of the page, and said only, "Look out the window. Then look at your paper. Then tell me what your eyes know that your hand doesn't." He moved on before Hunter could answer.

Carson looked out the window. Below the art shack, the dirt path ran down toward the lake, and a line of tall wooden light poles marched along the edge of it. The nearest pole was huge, a brown column with a bright lamp on top. The farthest one, way down by the dock, was a stubby little stick, hardly bigger than his thumb at arm's length. He raised his thumb and measured again, walking his gaze back up the line. Pole by pole, each one looked smaller than the one before it, and the gaps between them squeezed tighter and tighter until the last two almost touched.

"Whoa," Carson said. He grabbed a fresh pencil. "Hunter. The poles get smaller the farther away they are."

"That's weird," Hunter said. "They're all the same height in real life. I measured one once."

"That's the point. Same real size, but they look smaller and closer together the farther they go." Carson drew his street again, but this time he made the first lamppost tall as his hand, the next one a little shorter, the next shorter still, and squashed the spaces between them smaller and smaller, until they all shrank down toward one tiny dot near the top of the page where the road vanished. He'd heard Mr. Doyle say the words that morning and hadn't understood them until now. "Vanishing point," he said quietly, almost to himself.

Across the room, Violet leaned over from the still-life table to see what the whispering was about. Her eyebrows went up. "That actually looks like a street," she said. "Like you could walk down it."

Hunter was already erasing his lampposts, tongue poking out the corner of his mouth, shrinking each one row by row. When Mr. Doyle came back around, he stopped at Hunter's table for a long moment and said nothing at all, which Carson was starting to understand was the highest praise the man handed out.

Mr. Doyle set a real challenge on the table before the afternoon was over. The camp director wanted a poster of Main Street for the talent show on Friday, and the three of them would paint it together, buildings and lampposts and all. It would take the rest of the week.

Outside the window, a flock of geese crossed the sky over the lake, the first migratory birds of the season heading south in a long wobbling V. Violet pointed at them and laughed because the V, seen from the side, looked like their street, everything bunched toward a faraway point.

"There's a high probability we ruin the poster," Hunter said, shading another shrinking lamppost.

"There's a probability we don't," Carson said, and picked up his pencil to add a mailbox, small, smaller, smallest, marching down toward the dot.

Owen stood at the starting line of the school track with Bronwyn on his right and Kai on his left. All three of them had signed up for the eight hundred metres for the first time, and Mr. Weiss had given them exactly one instruction: "Save something for the second lap."

Bronwyn laughed. She won every hundred-metre sprint in the district. "Save something? I have plenty." The gun went off, and she was gone, two lanes ahead before the first curve. Kai, who ran cross-country every fall, settled into a smooth, even rhythm beside Owen, and the two of them ran nearly parallel down the backstretch. Owen wanted to chase Bronwyn, but he had a theory. She was sprinting like the race was short, and something about the way she'd gone out made him suspicious.

"The eight hundred is weird," Kai puffed between breaths. "It's like two races glued together. Mr. Weiss says it draws on aerobic energy, that's the kind with oxygen, and anaerobic energy. That kind works without oxygen, but it runs out fast. So it feels like a sprint and a distance race at the same time."

"That's a paradox," Owen said.

"Feels more like a trap," Kai said.

They crossed the first lap with Bronwyn ten metres ahead, arms still pumping. Then the trap sprang. Her stride shortened. Her shoulders rose. By the far curve she was drifting sideways as tiredness invaded her legs, and Owen and Kai went past her one after the other. Owen counted his own breathing, kept his pace even, and held his kick for the last hundred. He finished first, one second ahead of Kai, and bent over with his hands on his knees.

Bronwyn stumbled in thirty seconds later and dropped onto the infield grass. "That race is broken," she announced. "Somebody should fix it."

Mr. Weiss walked over with his clipboard and looked down at her. "The race is fine, Bronwyn. The pacing was broken."

Owen sat down beside her, still catching his breath. Bronwyn glared at the finish line. "Next meet," she said, "I'm running the first lap easy. And then I'm going to sprint the whole second one, and I'm going to win."

"You'll run out again," Kai said from the other side, unwrapping an orange.

Bronwyn folded her arms. "Then I'll sprint half of it. I'll do the math tonight."

Owen watched her get up and walk toward the water fountain, already muttering numbers to herself. Mr. Weiss wrote something on his clipboard and turned toward the next heat. "Lane three," he called. "You're up."

Megan sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with the short story "The Winter Road" spread in front of her and a pencil behind her ear. Tomorrow in Mr. Khan's class everyone had to point out one example of foreshadowing or symbolism and explain what it suggested, and Megan had read the story twice and still had nothing. Lyanna had already claimed the river, which froze solid in the first paragraph and cracked at the end, obviously standing for something. Harrison had texted Megan a whole list of ideas, but Megan suspected he had copied them off the internet, which Mr. Khan would sniff out instantly.

"You're overcomplicating it," Lyanna said from Megan's bed, where she was supposed to be doing her own reading for the assignment. She had her own reason for being there: she wanted Megan to promise they would present together on Thursday, so their grades would be linked and Lyanna's would look stronger. "Just take the crow. The crow is obviously a symbol. Birds mean death in every movie ever."

"I don't want obvious," Megan said. "I want the thing nobody else saw." She flipped back to page one, mostly to avoid Lyanna's eyes, and started reading again even though she'd sworn she was done. The main character, a girl walking to her grandmother's house, stopped to check a loose board in the footbridge. That was it. One sentence. The girl pressed the board with her toe, decided it would hold, and walked on.

Megan sat up so fast the pencil fell out from behind her ear. The bridge. At the end of the story, the girl crossed that same bridge in the dark, running, and the board gave way. On her first read she had sailed right past that early sentence, but now it looked like a lit match in a dark room. She checked the page number of the bridge scene twice, then once more, because she did not want to be the kid who stood up in class and got the whole thing wrong.

"Listen to this," Megan said, and read the sentence aloud. "The clue was sitting there on page one the whole time. Mr. Khan said foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that happens later, and you usually only catch it on a second reading. That's exactly what just happened to me. First time through, nothing. Second time, there it is."

Lyanna put down her book. "Okay, that's better than my crow," she admitted. "So we present together and you lead with the bridge." Megan hesitated, because half of her wanted to say no and keep the discovery to herself. But Lyanna was leaning forward now, genuinely scribbling notes, the way she did when she actually cared, and Megan changed her mind mid-breath. "Fine," she said. "But you do the symbolism part. Your crow is actually competent, if you cut the part about movies." Lyanna grinned and started a fresh page of notes, and Megan flipped back to page one and read the sentence about the loose board one more time, underlining it slowly, twice.

Harper sat cross-legged on Kiara's bedroom floor with Kiara's phone balanced on a stack of graphic novels, while her own phone sat in her lap like a guilty dog. "He actually typed it in all caps?" she asked.

"Every word," Kiara said. "Kasey screenshotted it. Mr. Santoso's message said, 'REMEMBER, THE GROUP CHAT IS FOR HOMEWORK ONLY.' And then twenty people replied with crying-laughing faces, which honestly made it worse."

The class chat was three days old and already a disaster. Someone had posted a video of a cat, then someone else had posted forty links to a game, and then the argument started about whether exclamation points meant you were yelling or just friendly. Harper scrolled through the screenshots Kiara had saved, trying to scrutinize the messages for some hidden rule, some pattern that separated the posts that got laughs from the posts that got people mad. All-caps from Mr. Santoso felt like yelling. All-caps from Kasey felt like a bit. Same letters, different feeling. That made no sense, and Harper wanted it to make sense.

She remembered sixth grade, before anyone had group chats, when she'd passed a folded note to Kiara in math class. The note said something joking about their teacher's tie, and Kiara had laughed out loud right in the middle of a quiz, and they'd both gotten detention. A note was private until it wasn't. A chat felt like the same thing, except a hundred times worse, because the note could only be stolen by one person.

"We need actual rules," Harper said. "Like, written-down rules. But who writes rules for typing?"

"Nobody writes rules for typing," Kiara said. "It's just... typing."

Harper doubted that. Somebody wrote rules for everything, even library whispering and swimming pool walking. She searched on her phone: rules for communicating online. Then: official online manners. Then, feeling a little ridiculous: were there ever official rules for the internet. A result came up that looked like homework from 1995, dry as toast, called RFC 1855.

"Wait," Harper said. "There's a whole thing. One of the first written guides to online manners was published in 1995, and it's a document called RFC 1855."

"RFC like a soccer thing?"

"Like a boring thing. Netiquette Guidelines. Somebody sat down and wrote rules like a legend."

Kiara leaned over her shoulder. "1995. That's before my parents even had a computer."

Harper scrolled. Rule after rule about tone, about not assuming the reader can hear your voice, about public messages versus private ones. It was like someone had read the inside of her head and published it decades before she was born. "So caps from Kasey is a joke because we know Kasey, and caps from Mr. Santoso is a lecture because he's the teacher," she said. "Same public message, different private feelings. The rules were there the whole time, we just never wrote them."

They drafted a list for the class chat: caps only for comedy, homework stuff in the daytime, cat videos allowed on Fridays. Kiara typed it up and read it aloud in her most eloquent news-anchor voice, which cracked them both up. They posted it, signed with both their names.

The twist came at nine o'clock. Mr. Santoso replied in the chat, in careful lowercase: "thank you for this. my daughter suggested the caps lock. I told her teachers need to seem serious. she says I seem like a toaster." Then a single cat emoji.

Harper stared at the screen. "He has a daughter?"

"Two more replies just came in," Kiara said. "Look. He signed one of them RFC 1855."

The farewell party was in full swing in Carter's backyard, which meant that Ryann had already eaten three cupcakes and Jude was trying to win the piñata even though there was no blindfold and no rules. Carter sat on the porch steps beside a kid named, well, a kid whose name Carter honestly could not remember, which was awkward because the kid had come specifically to see him.

"I moved here two weeks ago," the kid said. "My mom said you're the one leaving, so we should hang out before you go."

Carter did the math in his head. Two weeks, one shared lunch period, one group project where they had mostly passed glue sticks. That was maybe four hours total. Something about that bothered him, like a splinter he couldn't see.

Ryann flopped down beside them, cupcake number four in hand. "What's with the face, Carter? You look like you're doing long division."

"I read this thing online," Carter said slowly, testing it out loud. "A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend."

"Fifty hours," the kid repeated. "That's a lot of hours."

"That's why!" Carter sat up. "That's why it feels weird. You and me, we've got maybe four hours logged. We're basically strangers with excellent glue stick teamwork." He pulled out his phone and opened the calculator, which felt very official. "If we played video games for two hours a night, that's twenty-five nights. But I'm moving Saturday."

"Road trip," the kid offered. "If your new town is four hours away, and my mom drives me there twelve times, and I drive back twelve times..."

"You can't drive."

"It's a plan for later."

Jude abandoned the piñata, which had survived everything, and stomped over holding Carter's telescope like a shield. "Okay, party's over for me unless someone addresses the elephant." He thrust the telescope forward. "You're leaving this here. With me. On purpose. And every time I look at the moon I'll envy whoever's looking at it with you in your fancy new town with your fancy new friends." His voice cracked on "friends," and he pretended it hadn't.

"You already have fifty hours with me," Carter said. "Probably three hundred. You're safe. You're the most casual friend I have."

Jude sniffled and aimed the telescope at the piñata. "It does have a warranty, right? If I drop it?"

"It's a telescope, not a toaster. And stop pointing it at the piñata, that's invasive. It's been through enough."

The kid raised his hand like he was in class. "Question. If I get my fifty hours with Carter before he moves, do I get the piñata?"

"It's not mine to give, but yes," Carter said, and they all turned to look at it, hanging there, smug and unbroken, and Ryann went to get the broom handle.

The letter p sat in Sara's piano book like a tiny spy, and she had played it loud for three straight weeks before Ms. Nwosu finally put her hand over the keys.

"Piano," Ms. Nwosu said, tapping the page.

"I am playing the piano," Sara said. "That's sort of the whole problem."

Ms. Nwosu laughed so hard she had to set down her tea. "The word, not the instrument. In music, piano means soft. Little p, quiet hands. And forte means loud." She spun the metronome like a top. "Now, again, and this time listen to yourself."

That was the trouble. Sara had never listened to herself. She had been too busy worrying about the notes, consuming the page one measure at a time while her hands sprinted ahead of her ears. She wanted more than anything to play "The Huntsman's Song" at the spring recital, and Alden, who had heard her practice, had said it sounded like a stampede of very determined cows.

At home that night, Sara tried an experiment. She folded a sticky note in half and wrote SOFT on it, then propped it on the music stand like a tiny road sign. The p in measure four was small and easy to ignore, but a big orange SOFT was not. She played the phrase. The sound came out gentle, almost secretive, like the huntsman sneaking up on something.

Then came measure eight, with the word forte stamped under the staff like a shout. She played it loud, and for the first time she noticed the difference in her own arms, loose for soft, weighty for loud, like shifting a backpack from one shoulder to both. The piece had a shape now. Quiet, loud, quiet again. It was a pattern, a secret code the composer had hidden in Italian.

The next lesson, Ms. Nwosu didn't say a word. She just pulled up a chair in the corner and listened, her fingers conducting little invisible waves in the air. When Sara finished, the room stayed silent for one second, which felt like an hour.

"Well," said Ms. Nwosu. "The cows have been sent to a nicer field."

Alden, waiting outside with his trumpet case, peeked in the door. "Was that actually you?"

"It was the p," Sara said, pointing at the page. "It means soft. It was right there the whole time, being tiny and quiet about it."

"Sort of like you before recital practice," Alden said, and then he ran for it, laughing, before she could swat him with the book.

Lillian clicked through the survey results for the third time and frowned at the screen. Three hundred twelve students had answered the question "How much did you like the fall field trip to the science museum, one to five?", and every answer sat in one long column of numbers that told her nothing.

"You're still on that?" Devyn asked from the next computer. "Just count the fives and be done."

"Counting fives is naive," Lillian said. "The eights who hated it matter too."

Mr. Anderson, walking between the rows of monitors, paused behind her. "Pivot table," he said, tapping her screen once. "Values, rows, and it's under Insert." Then he moved on before she could ask what any of that meant.

She dragged the grade column into Rows, and the spreadsheet folded itself into six neat lines: sixth, seventh, eighth, plus three grades that did not exist, which she deleted. She dragged the rating column into Values and got counts. Big numbers. Useless numbers. She remembered last spring, when she had tallied the book fair survey by hand on paper, one tally mark at a time for two evenings, and had still gotten the seventh grade wrong. She had opposed doing it digitally back then because she thought spreadsheets were for business people, not for someone who just wanted to know whether kids liked pizza day. That choice felt foolish now, sitting in the computer lab with the whole answer one click away.

She right-clicked the count and a menu appeared. Sum. Count. Average. She chose Sum first, because the ratings were numbers, so adding them seemed natural. The spreadsheet gave her totals in the hundreds. Interesting, but not an answer. Then she tried Average.

The numbers changed to small decimals. Sixth grade: 4.6. Seventh: 4.2. Eighth: 3.1. She sat back. "Devyn. The eighth graders liked it way less."

Devyn leaned over. "Wait, how'd you get that? That's not counting anything."

"The average," Lillian said. "Instead of Sum or Count, you switch it to Average. So a column of one-to-five ratings turns into the mean rating for each grade."

"That's it? That's the whole trick?"

Lillian looked at the 3.1 glowing beside Eighth Grade, and thought about her older sister, who had complained the whole bus ride home about the crowds and the boring mineral exhibit. She thought about last spring's paper tallies, about how she had reported the seventh grade's favorite when it probably had not been. Should she have known to ask more than "who picked five"? She did not decide. She printed the pivot table instead.

"Mr. Anderson," she called across the lab, holding up the page. "The eighth graders rated the trip 3.1. What do we do with that?"

He took the sheet and looked at it for a long moment. "That," he said, "is the frontier. Everything past the count is where it gets interesting."

The science fair project was due Monday, and Victoria still needed a poster board, which was why she was at the mall on Saturday with Leonard and Seerat instead of anywhere fun. The supply store closed at six, and it was already quarter past five, but the three of them kept stopping, because the mall was full of screens, and the screens kept shouting at them.

"Everyone's switching," boomed a voice over the shoe store's speaker, above a wall of glowing sneakers. "Join the millions who already know." Victoria slowed down. She counted four different signs saying almost the same thing. Millions, everyone, everybody. Why did the store care whether she thought other people had bought the shoes? She nudged Seerat. "Do you actually want those, or do you just feel like you're the last person on earth without them?" Seerat grinned and kept walking, but Victoria filed the question away, the way she filed things for their class news project.

That project was the real deadline underneath the poster deadline. Mr. Yilmaz had assigned it Friday: find two articles about the same event and present them Monday. Victoria had both headlines saved on her phone, and in the food court, waiting for Leonard to finish his pretzel, she slid the phone across the table. "Same rally, same day, same city," she said. "Look." The first headline called the crowd protesters. The second called the exact same crowd rioters. She watched Seerat's face change as she read each one, falling forward, then hardening. "They're describing the same people," Seerat said slowly. "But I feel completely different about them depending which one I read."

"So that's the poster," Victoria said, her heart going quick. "Same crowd, two words, opposite opinions." It was like the sneaker signs, but sharper. The shoe store had leaned on her with everybody-else-is-doing-it, and the famous athlete grinning from the sunglasses kiosk had leaned on her too, though she'd never once wondered whether he actually wore those sunglasses. The news headlines did something else: they slipped a feeling inside a single word and let it do the pushing. She wondered how many words worked like that, quiet and invisible, like a parasite riding along on a sentence.

At five to six they ran for the supply store, and at the register the cashier pointed at the poster racks. "The foam ones are on sale today only. And laminating is mandatory on the sale price, just so you know." Victoria squinted at the sign. Mandatory was a strong word for something the store simply wanted, and "today only" made her pulse hurry in a way she didn't like being told to feel. She bought the plain board at the regular price, skipped the laminate, and saved four dollars.

Outside, Leonard balancing the rolled-up board under his arm, Victoria said, "Monday, we put both headlines side by side and don't say a word. We just let the class read them." Seerat was already typing the title. "Two Words, Two Opinions," she said.

Layla slid into the booth beside her dad, who was already pointing at the third TV over the bar. "Four hundred metres final," he said. "Replay starts in a minute." Her little brother was busy stacking coasters, and her mom flagged down a waiter to order nachos for the table, since Layla had skipped lunch after her tedious morning of standardized testing.

On the screen, eight runners settled into their blocks. Layla recognized the favourite, a runner in lane four, because his face was on half the posters at school. "He's ranked first in the world," her dad said. "That means he's basically unbeatable."

Layla frowned at that. She had spent the whole week in math class on averages and percentages, and something about "first in the world" bothered her. "Ranked first," she said slowly, "but first by how much?"

"Does it matter?" her dad asked. "First is first."

The gun fired and the bar went quiet except for the fryer. Down the backstretch the runner in lane six, silver-bibbed, crept up on the favourite until they were nearly even. Around the final bend Layla was on her knees on the booth's bench, and half the bar was yelling. The two leaders hit the line together, so close that Layla couldn't tell who won until the replay froze on the finish and zoomed in.

"Second by four hundredths of a second," the announcer said. The silver medalist had lost by less time than a blink. Layla's dad exhaled like he'd been holding his breath the whole race.

"See?" Layla said. "Ranking first doesn't tell you the distance. That guy was first and second was practically on top of him. But first and second could also be a whole minute apart if the race was lopsided, and it would still just say first and second." She assumed everyone at the table would shrug, but her little brother looked up from his coasters.

"So the medal doesn't say how close it was?"

"Exactly. It just says the order." She pulled a napkin and drew two stick figures crossing a line, then wrote "1st" and "2nd" with a tiny gap between them, and beside it drew the same two figures with a huge gap. "Same ranking, totally different race."

Her dad turned his glass slowly. "So when I tell people the favourite always wins, that's a bad premise."

"A shaky one," Layla said, grinning.

Mr. Bautista, their neighbour from two doors down, leaned over from the next booth with his basket of wings. "You just explained why I never trust the sports ticker," he said. "My granddaughter argues the same way. Can I steal that napkin?"

Layla added two more stick figures and slid it across the table to him.

The bus lurched around the corner by the hardware store, and Mason slid down the seat so he wouldn't have to look at Jersey, who was sitting three rows up with the soccer kids. It hadn't always been like this. In sixth grade they'd shared a bench every single morning, arguing about whose turn it was to hold the granola bars. Then Mason joined the robotics club and Jersey made the travel team, and somehow they'd stopped talking about anything that mattered.

Mason kept turning the problem over, the way he turned over a stuck gear in his head. Robots followed rules you could test. If a motor wouldn't spin, you checked the battery, then the wires, then the piston in the little air pump that refused to move. You didn't guess. You tried one thing at a time. So what had broken between him and Jersey? He decided to run a test, to simulate a normal conversation and see what happened.

He waited until the bus hit the long straight stretch past the creek, then moved up and dropped into the seat beside Jersey. "Hey," he said. "Did you see that penalty kick Saturday?" Jersey lit up for a second, and they talked about the game for two stops. Then Mason tried the second half of his test. "Also, my robot finally pushed the block across the table yesterday." Jersey nodded, said "cool," and looked out the window. The pattern was clear. They could still talk about Jersey's stuff. Mason's stuff had gone silent.

Zariah, who rode from the last stop and saw everything, leaned across the aisle. "You two used to be glued together," she said. "What happened?" Mason shrugged. "Different teams, I guess." Zariah pulled out her phone. "We read about this in Mr. Petrov's class. A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end." She scrolled to the page and held it out so he could see it was real.

Mason stared at the sentence. He'd been testing wires and batteries when the actual problem was the whole circuit. It wasn't that Jersey was mad. It was that they'd grown into two different shapes that didn't fit together anymore, unless one of them changed shape a little. He couldn't make himself love soccer, and he couldn't make Jersey love robots. But maybe the fit didn't have to be identical. Maybe it just had to overlap somewhere new.

"Zariah," he said slowly, "what do you actually care about? Like your thing." She grinned. "Statistical stuff, honestly. I made a chart of every free throw our girls' team took last season." Mason's brain sparked like a loose connection snapping back into place. "Wait. I need numbers for my robot. Timing data, distances, everything. And Jersey collects stats for his team in a notebook. All three of us could measure stuff."

He leaned forward and tapped Jersey's shoulder. "You know how you write down every shot your team takes? I want to build something that reads those numbers and predicts the next play. Zariah can check whether it actually works. You in?" Jersey turned around, and for the first time in weeks his whole face was interested. "You could do that with my notebook? For real?"

"I need somebody who knows what the numbers mean," Mason said. "That's you." Jersey grabbed his backpack, unzipped the front pocket, and pulled out the battered green notebook, already flipping it open to a page of neatly boxed scores. "Start with Tuesday," he said. "We took forty-one shots."

The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Connor's homework, and the refrigerator stopped its humming for the first time in his whole life. He heard his mom feel her way to the junk drawer, then a flashlight clicked on. "Candle," she said. "And find the old board games, because this is going to be a while."

Connor sat on the kitchen floor with the flashlight and thought. The whole street was dark; he could see that from the window. On his way home from school, after the storm, Tianna and Monica had stopped dead at the corner of Maple and Third, where a black wire lay across the sidewalk. It wasn't sparking or buzzing or doing anything dramatic. It just lay there, wet and ordinary. Monica had reached toward it, and Tianna had grabbed her sleeve. "Don't," Tianna said. "A fallen line can still be live even when it isn't sparking. My dad says you treat it like it's on, you stay way back, and you tell someone." They had gone the long way around and told Mr. Nakamura, who was out checking his fence. He had thanked them seriously and gone inside to phone it in.

Now Connor formulated a plan. If that wire was the reason the street was dark, then calling the power company's emergency line and telling them exactly where the line was might speed things up. He borrowed his mom's phone, gave the recorded voice the address, and a real person came on. "Yes, we have a crew dispatched to that location," she said. "Tell everyone to stay well away from it."

"There's nothing well away about it," said his sister from the stairs. "It's on the sidewalk where everyone walks to school."

"Then tomorrow morning we put a garbage can on each end of the block," Connor said. "Away from the wire. And we stand there and tell people until the truck comes."

The lights came back at 9:15, all at once, so bright that everyone in the kitchen winced. The freezer shuddered and started up, saving the pierogi his grandmother had taught his mom to make, dough and all, a heritage that went back three kitchens and two countries. Connor's mom declared the rescue of the pierogi a triumph. "Power outages are inevitable in a storm," she said, "but losing dinner is not."

The next morning the wire was gone. Connor, Tianna, and Monica walked the long way anyway, just to check, and Monica kicked a pebble the entire length of Maple Street.

"Next time it storms," she said, "I'm walking with my hands in my pockets."

Austin sat at the kitchen table with a mug of tea, a wad of tissues beside him, and his mother's thermometer on the counter. Three days home from school, and he was tired of being tired. He scrolled on his phone and found a message from Maina: "You missed the science fair meeting. Mr. Ong says pick a topic by Friday."

He typed back with one thumb. "Sick. Got any ideas."

"Pick something about colds, since you're an expert now," she wrote.

He almost laughed, which turned into a cough. Then he actually started thinking. His grandmother claimed the flu shot gave her a cold every winter, and she refused to get it again. His father said that was nonsense. Austin had never known who was right, and nobody at dinner would settle it. A science project might.

He opened the library site on his phone and searched. The first solid result stopped him cold, so to speak. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold. Two hundred. No wonder there was no single cold vaccine; the shot his grandmother blamed couldn't possibly cover all of them. He read further and learned that the most frequent cause was a group called rhinoviruses. He said the word out loud to the empty kitchen. "Rhinoviruses."

He started a note on his phone. He could classify the culprits into groups, list the big families, and put rhinoviruses at the top with the most cases. He found a line about how a famous, prestigious medical journal had published a study on cold viruses, and another paragraph mentioning an old controversy over whether vitamin C helped at all. He wrote both down, then texted Maina a list of what he had so far.

"Good," she answered, "but where's the question? Mr. Ong wants a question, not a report."

Austin stared at his notes. Then he remembered something. Last Friday, before he got sick, he had been at Reese's house, and Reese had been sniffling all through their game. Austin had teased him about it. He scrolled back through their messages until he found the one from Saturday morning: "Can't come today, my throat is destroyed." Austin's own sore throat had started Sunday.

He texted Reese. "Question. When did your cold start, like the exact day?"

"Friday I think? Why."

"So I got it from you." Austin grinned, then stopped. His own symptoms had shown up Sunday, and Reese had been sniffling Friday, which meant Reese caught it first, probably from school, not from Austin. But Austin had been fine until after the sleepover, and the timing fit. He typed, "For my science project. Patient zero. You're going in my notes."

Reese sent back a single word: "Rude."

Austin dragged the thermometer across the counter toward himself and took his temperature again, still writing with his other hand. 99.1. "Maina, tell Mr. Ong my question is: how do you track a cold back to its source?"

Peyton raced down the hall toward the gym with her poster rolled under one arm, dodging a kid carrying a baking-soda volcano. The science fair opened in twenty minutes, and her project on neon was going to be the best one there. She had built a glowing sign with a battery and a small neon tube borrowed from her uncle's shop, and she planned to quiz everyone who stopped by.

"Let me see the poster," said Shania, catching up beside her. They found their assigned table near the door, and Peyton unrolled the poster and weighted the corners with erasers. At the top she had copied the box for neon from the periodic table, with its symbol Ne and the number 10.

A boy from another class, Avi, wandered over with his hands in his pockets. "Ten what?" he asked, pointing at the number. "Ten neutrons? Ten of something, but what?"

Peyton opened her mouth and then closed it again. She realized she had copied the box without ever asking what that small number meant, and her stomach dipped. Her whole poster was about neon, and she could not answer the first question someone asked. "I think it's called the atomic number," she said slowly, "but I don't actually know what that counts."

"Don't guess at people's posters," Shania said, but Peyton was already off her chair.

Mr. McKenzie, who ran the fair, had set up a giant periodic table banner along the back wall of the gym. Peyton drafted Avi and Shania to help her check every element box on it, moving systematically from hydrogen across the first row. "Hydrogen is 1," she said, tapping the box. "Helium is 2. Look, the numbers go up one at a time, all the way across."

"So it's counting something inside the atom," Shania said. "Something every atom of that element has."

They reached carbon, then oxygen, then fluorine, and each box matched the pattern. Peyton felt her pulse quicken, because a pattern that held every single time felt like a rule, not a coincidence. At the reference table by the wall sat an open chemistry textbook that Mr. McKenzie had left out for the judges. Peyton flipped until she found the periodic table chapter and ran her finger down the page. She read the line twice, then spun around.

"Avi! It's the protons," she said. "The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element. Hydrogen has one proton, helium has two, so neon, number ten, has ten protons in every single neon atom. In my tube, in the sign, in every neon sign in the whole world!"

Avi peered at the banner, then at her poster, checking for a contradiction between the two and finding none. "So carbon would be six protons," he said, "and oxygen would be eight. That's actually a cool trick."

When the judges reached her table an hour later, Peyton stood beside her glowing sign, pointed at the 10 in her copied box, and said, "Ten protons, in every atom of neon there is." The judge wrote something on her clipboard, and behind her, Shania gave both thumbs up.

The paper crane collapsed in Arianna's hands for the fourth time, its wings flopping sideways like a bird that had given up on flying. Across the long table at the community art studio, Harleen held up a crane so crisp it could probably cut you.

"Maybe you just need better paper," Harleen suggested.

Arianna didn't think that was it. She was using the same square of silvery foil paper as Harleen, and her folds had been sharp at first. The trouble started partway through, when the model reached a kind of plateau and stopped improving no matter how many times she creased and uncreased. Something invisible was going wrong, and she wanted to know what. She smoothed the failed crane flat and studied the sheet, turning it over, holding it up to the window light.

"Try it with the paper turned the other way," said Leah, who was across the table struggling with a frog. "Like, rotate it ninety degrees before you start."

"You think the paper has a direction?" Arianna asked.

"Paper's made in sheets going one way," Leah said with a shrug. "My grandpa prints stuff and he complains about it constantly. It's like wood. It wants to bend one way and not the other."

Arianna looked at her crease marks. Every fold she'd made across the sheet had come out clean, and every fold down its length had turned mushy and thick. That was a pattern, and patterns meant something. She cut a fresh square from the same sheet of foil paper, rotated it a quarter turn, and began again, creasing slowly and testing each fold before committing to the next one. The sideways folds, the ones that had refused before, slid into place like they'd been waiting for her.

While she worked, Harleen leaned over. "Did you know the word origami isn't about beauty or anything? It means fold and paper. 'Ori' means to fold, and 'kami' means paper." She tapped Arianna's crooked first crane. "So the word literally just describes what you're doing. Folding paper. No magic in it."

"So the magic has to come from somewhere else," Arianna said. "Like direction. Which nobody named in the word." She laughed. "Origami means folding paper, and apparently the paper still gets a vote."

Ms. Ong, the studio's teacher, wandered past with a tray of glue sticks and paused over the half-finished crane. "That one's behaving," she observed.

"It's the same paper as before," Arianna said. "I just turned it."

By the end of the session, Arianna's crane stood on the table with wings that snapped open when she pulled the tail. Leah's frog still looked barren and defeated, a flat green nothing with legs pointing in four directions. Arianna slid her leftover foil paper across the table, turned it a quarter turn, and set it in front of her friend.

"Rotate first," she said. "Then fold."

The laptop cart in Room 12 was so dilapidated that Ms. Das had to jiggle the hinge of every machine just to make the screens stay open. Gabriella grabbed the one with the least cracked casing and carried it to the table beside Sandra, who was already tapping away at hers. They had forty minutes before the talent show auditions at lunch, and Gabriella needed a bar chart of the fundraiser totals for her proposal to Ms. Das. Each row of the spreadsheet held a day of the bake sale, and column B held the money collected. All she had to do was add it up.

"Ms. Das prohibits food in here, so don't bring your audition muffin," Sandra said without looking up. "I'm serious, she confiscated a granola bar on Tuesday."

"I'm not risking my muffin," Gabriella said. She typed the day totals into B2 through B10, nine days of quarters and crumpled dollars. Then, in the very last box of the column, B10, she wrote the total formula, =SUM(B2:B10), because it seemed tidy to keep the answer at the bottom of the list. She pressed Enter and a gray warning box popped onto the screen. Circular reference, it said. She read the words twice. What was circling? Nothing on the screen was moving.

She leaned closer, wondering if the formula was somehow pointing at itself. It included B10, and she had typed it into B10. Was the sum trying to add up its own answer? She decided to test it the simple way: she copied the formula, deleted it from B10, and pasted it into B11, one row below the column. The total appeared instantly, 143 dollars and 75 cents, and the warning vanished. So that was the rule. She hadn't known it had a name until Sandra glanced over and said, "Oh, a circular reference. My brother got that last year."

"That's what it's called?" Gabriella said. "A circular reference."

"Circular reference," Ms. Das confirmed as she walked past, tapping the side of the warning box on Mathis's screen down the row, where the same gray message had appeared. "Move it out of the column, everyone, and check your totals." Mathis groaned and slid his formula down one row, and his sum sprang to life too.

Gabriella highlighted her column, clicked the chart button, and watched nine bars rise across the screen, Tuesday towering over every other day. The lunch bell rang before she could admire it for long. She saved the file, closed the dilapidated laptop, and tucked her muffin deep into her backpack where nobody could confiscate anything. "Coming to the auditions?" Sandra asked, already at the door. "After I show Ms. Das my chart," Gabriella said, and held the screen open one more second so the tallest bar caught the light.

Brielle slid her laptop across the table so Evelina could see the screen. Red squiggles ran through her German paragraph like scratches, under "hund," under "katze," under "schwester," even under her own name. "I typed it the way I say it," she said. "The spell-checker hates everything."

Ms. De Vries leaned over from the next desk, but she only said, "Look closely at what the checker circles. Count them." Then she moved on to help Elsie, whose screen was almost as red.

Brielle stared until her eyes ached. The checker had not flagged "ich," or "habe," or "und," or "ein." She began to isolate the marked words, dragging each one into a list at the bottom of her document. Hund. Katze. Schwester. Mutter. Vater. Then she made a second list of the unmarked ones: ich, habe, und, ist, meine. She read both columns twice, and her pencil tapped faster and faster.

"Evelina," she whispered. "Every word it circles is a thing. A noun. Hund, cat, sister, mother. All the nouns." She opened a fresh line and typed, "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," giving each noun a capital letter at the start. The red vanished, one squiggle at a time, like frost melting off a window. She grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. Her paragraph about her family had looked impoverished before, all errors and no real sentences, but now it said what she meant: that she had a dog named after a baker, a cat who ignored everyone, and a little sister who talked nonstop.

She reached over to Elsie's laptop without being asked. "Try capitals on your nouns," Brielle said. "Watch." She typed "Meine Familie" and the checker stayed silent. Elsie copied the idea, fixing her whole first paragraph while Evelina read hers aloud, halting but real: "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze." When she finished, she looked up, out of breath, and Brielle clapped twice, quiet and fast, so only their table could hear.

At the end of class, Ms. De Vries collected the laptops. "Yours is the only one with no red left," she said to Brielle, and slid it into the cart with the screen still showing the line, "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," every noun tall and gleaming at the front.

Brooke had been stuck on the same page for twenty minutes, sprawled on the floor between the poetry shelf and the front window of Mr. Santos-Reyes's bookshop. "A Midsummer Night's Sleep," she muttered, and Payton, who was flipping through a field guide two aisles over, snorted so loudly the cashier looked up.

"It's Dream," Payton called. "And Mr. Santos-Reyes says we have to paraphrase our speeches into modern English by Friday, so maybe stop insulting the play."

Brooke glared at the page. Hermia and Lysander were arguing, which was fine, but the pronouns kept shifting around like something alive. At the top of the scene Lysander said "you" to Hermia, and then, right in the middle of the fight, he switched to "thee" and "thou," then back again. She counted the switches on her fingers. Five. That couldn't be random.

"Payton, look at this." She held the book up as Payton crossed the aisle, boots squeaking. "He starts polite, then he goes thou thou thou, then when he calms down he says you again. It's like the words flip when he gets mad."

Payton squinted. "Maybe Shakespeare just mixed them up sometimes. He didn't have spellcheck."

Brooke wasn't convinced. "Feasible," she admitted, "but I don't buy it. It happens too neatly." She turned back a few pages to the scene where Hermia talks to her father. There, speaking to a stern duke, she used "you" the whole way through. But Puck, teasing a random workman in the forest, threw "thou" at him instantly. A pattern started to form: thou for friends, family, people below you, and sometimes plain insult, while you stayed polite, for superiors and strangers. If she was right, then Lysander's switches weren't noise at all. They were the fight itself, the exact moments he stopped treating her like a lady and started treating her like someone he could wound.

She read the speech again with that rule in her head, and the modern English came fast. "Basically he's saying, you've ruined my life, you're the reason I'm stuck in this woods, and every thou is a slap." She wrote it in her notebook, then tapped the margin. "For my write-up I can cite the act and scene so Mr. Santos-Reyes can check the switching himself."

"Two things," Payton said. "One, that's actually pretty great. Two, you've been sitting on that caterpillar book for an hour and there's a larva on your sleeve."

Brooke looked down. A small green larva, evidently an escapee from the nature section, was inching toward her collar. She froze, then remembered the field guide Payton had been reading. "Page ninety-two," Payton said, grinning. "It says they're harmless."

She lifted it onto a bookmark and set it on the windowsill, then picked her pen back up. At the bottom of her paraphrase she added one more line, underlined twice: Notice the thou. It's never an accident. Then she flipped to the next scene to see who insulted whom next.

Rosalie arrived at the community center an hour early, because the little library next to the gym was open, and because she had a plan. The spelling bee started at two, and she had already studied four hundred words, but her problem was not memorizing. Her problem was that English spelling made no sense to her. Why "knight" and "night"? Why "island" with an s you never hear? Someone, sometime, must have decided these things, and she wanted to know how.

She told Aedan, who was already setting up chairs in the gym, that she was going to look for the answer. "In an hour?" he said. "You can't learn the whole language in an hour."

"I don't need the whole language," Rosalie said. "I need one pattern. If spellings got settled somehow, maybe there's a way to guess the weird ones."

In the library she pulled down the oldest, heaviest book on the shelf, a reprint of a dictionary from long ago. The cover said it was Samuel Johnson's "A Dictionary of the English Language," published in 1755, and the librarian had tucked a note inside saying Johnson's dictionary helped settle how many English words were spelled. Rosalie sat down on the floor with it. So before 1755, spelling had been looser, and this one book had helped fix it. That meant the strange spellings were not random. They were choices, locked in a long time ago, one by one.

She tested her idea against her hardest words. "Colonel." Johnson's world had already fixed that one, so there was no logic to recover; she just had to know it. But "deceit" and "receipt" had the same sound spelled two ways, which meant the ei and ie words needed checking case by case. She made a quick list of ones that were probable spellings versus ones that were traps, and she found she could usually distinguish the pattern if she said the word slowly and remembered where it came from. Harlan wandered in from the gym and quizzed her with the list until her mother called her to line up.

At the microphone, round five, Ms. Torres, who was reading the words, said, "Defendant."

Rosalie almost smiled. Harlan had drilled that one twice. It ended like "independent," not like the a in "cab." "Defendant. D-E-F-E-N-D-A-N-T. Defendant."

"Correct," Ms. Torres said.

Round eight gave her "gesture," one of her trap words, and round ten gave her "yacht," which she simply knew, the way Johnson must have known it when he wrote it down. When the last boy missed "bizarre," Rosalie got it right, and the gym clapped and Aedan whooped from the back row.

Afterward she found Aedan and Harlan by the water fountain. "So who decides how words are spelled?" Harlan asked. "A judge?"

"No judge," Rosalie said. "No defendant either. Just a dictionary from 1755 that helped settle everything." She held up her worn library card. "It's due back Thursday."

Stella spread her index cards across her grandmother's kitchen table, where the smell of lemon polish and yesterday's coffee still hung in the air. On the first three cards she had written CLAIM, EVIDENCE, WARRANT, because that was what Ms. Charles had drilled into the debate club before the weekend. "A case is a tower," Stella said to herself, "and every point needs all three bricks." Her grandmother set down a plate of warm biscuits and slid it within reach without a word.

The problem was the club's mini-tournament on Monday. Stella wanted the top speaker slot, and Sebastian wanted it just as badly, and he had already beaten her once by poking holes in her evidence until her whole argument folded. This time she intended to build something he could not knock over. So she wrote her claim in careful block letters: The school should restrict phone use to lunch periods only.

She was on her fourth evidence card when her grandmother's old radio, its brass dials cool under Stella's fingers, crackled into a music program. The conductor of the youth orchestra, the announcer said, had changed the program order so the youngest players would not have to wait through two long pieces. Stella smiled at that. She kept writing, filling cards with facts about attention and hallway collisions she had counted herself, three in one week outside the gym.

Then she found the book. It was wedged behind the encyclopedia on the shelf her grandmother kept for rainy days, a thin paperback about argument with a diagram folded inside. Stella traced the diagram with her finger and stopped. There were boxes everywhere. Claim, data, warrant, yes, but three more beside them: backing, qualifier, rebuttal. She counted twice to be sure. Six. Six parts, not three.

"Grandma, come look," Stella called. "I've been building with half the pieces." Her grandmother dried her hands on her apron and studied the diagram, then tapped the qualifier box. "That's the 'unless' box," she said. "Your grandfather used it every time he said he'd fix the fence, unless it rained." Stella laughed and grabbed a fresh card. Her warrant, that fewer phone distractions equal safer hallways, needed backing, which meant the school's own safety report. And the qualifier meant admitting her plan worked only where teachers could supervise. She wrote UNTIL THE NEW WING OPENS and underlined it.

On Monday, Sebastian stood up with his counterargument ready, the one about emergencies, and Stella laid down her rebuttal card before he finished the sentence. Amal, scoring at the side, raised both thumbs. When Ms. Charles read the ballots aloud, Stella's name was on top, and Sebastian leaned over and whispered, "Show me that diagram at lunch." Stella grinned and slid the folded paper across the desk to him.

The smell reached the doorstep before anyone opened the door: broth, ginger, something faintly like toasted seaweed. Riley shifted the gift bag from one hand to the other. He had never been to Dastan's house before, and he had spent twenty minutes in the kitchen at home choosing what to bring, because his mother had insisted you never arrive empty-handed. He finally settled on a box of clementines, which felt safe and unremarkable.

Dastan's mother opened the door and bowed slightly, and Riley, unsure what to do, bowed back. She smiled at that. "Dinner is almost ready," she said, and Dastan grabbed Riley's sleeve and pulled him toward the kitchen, where two enormous pots steamed on the stove. "We're having ramen," Dastan said. "My mom makes it from scratch. She simmers the broth all day, and she dries her own shiitake. It's a fungus, but a good one, so don't make a face."

The noodles went into the bowls last, and Riley watched them sink beneath a translucent slice of pork and a tangle of green onion. At the table, a quiet moment of "Itadakimasu" preceded the first bite, and then something strange happened. Everyone slurped. Dastan, his mother, his father, his little sister: the noodles vanished behind loud, wet, unmistakable slurping sounds.

Riley froze with his chopsticks halfway to his mouth. At his own dinner table, slurping meant someone would say his name in that warning tone. Here, nobody glanced at anybody. His ears warmed as he tried to work out the rule. He tested it carefully, first taking a small, nearly silent mouthful. The noodles were astonishing, but he ate them stiffly, worried about the noise. Dastan noticed. "You okay?"

"Fine," Riley whispered. "Just, aren't you not supposed to slurp?"

Dastan laughed and shook his head. "Not with ramen. With ramen, slurping's fine. Noodles like this and soba too. Watch." He demonstrated, a long cheerful slurp that ended with a satisfied sigh, and his mother nodded approvingly at them both.

Riley considered the evidence: four slurping people, zero frowns, one nod of approval. The rule, he decided, ran the other way here.
