She had asked Luke, of all people, to do one of the readings, which meant he had to know the whole passage by heart, and so far he knew exactly four words of it.

"You look like you're being tortured," said Aariz, who had come over for the afternoon and was now raiding the fridge. "Is that a prayer card?"

"It's a reading. Isaiah something." Luke tapped the card. "Every time I get past the first line, my brain wipes itself clean. I did it twenty times this morning."

Aariz carried a jar of salsa to the counter and sat down across from him. "Twenty times in a row? No wonder. My mom says cramming like that doesn't work. She made me spread out my multiplication tables over a whole week, and she enforced it, too. Timer on the stove and everything."

Luke looked at the timer, then at the card, then at the window where Mr. Tang was watering his tomatoes in the most tranquil way possible, unhurried, humming something. A thought arrived slowly, the way a smell drifts in from another room. Maybe the problem wasn't his memory. Maybe the problem was that he kept testing himself in the same spot, at the same table, in the same tired loop, and his brain had started associating the reading with failure instead of the words themselves. It was like when he'd blamed his bike for a wobbly wheel and then found the axle nut was loose. He couldn't see the loose part. He had to guess and check.

"Okay, new plan," Luke said. He picked up the card and walked to the sink and recited the first line. Then he walked to the stove and recited the first line plus one more. Then the fridge, the window, the pantry door. Each stop added a sentence. When he stumbled at the pantry, he didn't start over. He stayed where he was and repeated only the sentence that had tripped him, three times, until it stopped feeling like a stranger.

"Is that actually helping, or are you just pacing?" Aariz asked, scooping salsa with a tortilla chip.

"Watch. Test me from anywhere." Luke closed his eyes. Aariz picked the window, and Luke reeled off six sentences without stopping, because when he pictured the window his mind showed him the kitchen faucet, and the faucet was hooked to line two, and line two led onward like train cars. The place itself was holding the words for him.

Later that evening his mother came in and found him muttering at the refrigerator, and she laughed until she had to sit down, but she listened to the end and said Marisol was going to cry, the good kind of crying. Luke thought about the morning, all those failed rounds at the table, and couldn't decide whether they had been wasted or whether they had been the ground floor he'd needed to build on. He decided he might never know.

On the day of the Mass, in his stiff shirt, he stood at the ambo and looked out at the congregation, Marisol in the front row in her pale dress. He imagined the kitchen, the sugar jar, the pantry door swinging open, and began. "A reading from the prophet Isaiah," he said, and the rest followed him home.

Jacob pushed his peas around his plate while his dad told the story again, the one about how the town was founded by a man named Hollis Grey who planted a single oak tree in the square and built the first house right beside it.

"Everyone knows that," said Jacob's little sister, mouth full.

Everyone might know it, but Jacob had a problem with it. Everly had shown him the plaque in the square that afternoon, and it said the town was founded in 1847, same as his dad always said. But Lea's grandmother, who had lived here her whole life, swore the first settler was a woman named Ruth Merrin, and that her family still had her letters in a box upstairs. Both stories couldn't be true, and Jacob wanted the true one, because Mr. Chea had promised the best history project in the class would go to the prestigious regional fair in the spring.

"Maybe it doesn't matter," his dad said, reaching for the salt. "It's just an opinion, like who makes the best pizza in town."

"No, it's not," Jacob said. "Best pizza is an opinion because you can't check it. But who founded the town, that's a claim. You can check a claim." He thought about how he'd argued with Everly at lunch, before he'd understood the difference, and how she'd stomped off saying facts were boring. He still wasn't sure he should have pushed so hard.

The next Saturday, Lea opened her grandmother's box on the kitchen table. Inside were letters, brittle and brown at the edges, smelling like dust and old cellar air. One was dated 1847 and signed Ruth Merrin, describing the winter she spent hauling timber while "Mr. Grey keeps to his tent and his larva-collecting jars." Lea laughed so hard she snorted. There was also a folded page from the town's first ledger, an official record of who had paid for which plot of land, and Ruth Merrin's name was first, with the date.

Jacob sat very still. He remembered Mr. Chea saying something once that he hadn't paid attention to at the time, about how the best place to check a claim was a primary source. He'd looked it up later in the library's old newspaper archive: a primary source is a firsthand record from the time, like a letter, a photograph or official data. These letters were exactly that, and so was the ledger. The plaque, he realized, was not; it had been put up decades later by people who hadn't been there.

He felt bad about the twist, in a way. His dad had told that story because his own father had told it to him. But when Jacob laid the letter out on the dinner table that night, his dad read it twice, slowly, and then went to the hall closet and came back with a photograph of Grandpa standing under the oak in the square, grinning.

"So what do we tell people now?" his dad asked.

Jacob folded his hands on the table. "We tell them the lady built the house, and the man collected bugs. Then we ask if they want to see the letter."

Max held the carrier against his chest like a bomb about to tick. Inside was a scrap of gray fur named Biscuit, the kitten his mom had finally agreed to after two years of asking, hinting, and one ill-fated campaign involving a PowerPoint. The pet store smelled like cedar shavings and fish flakes, and Biscuit's eyes were two nervous moons in the plastic window.

At the checkout, Max grabbed the biggest bag of food on the shelf because it was cheap. A kid ahead of him in line, a girl with a volleyball jersey, frowned at it. "That's dog food," she said. "Why is dog food and cat food even different? It's all brown lumps." Her dad shrugged, but the cashier leaned over the counter. "Cats can't make enough of their own taurine," she said. "It's a nutrient in meat. Without it they can get heart disease, even go blind."

Max put the dog food back so fast he thumped his elbow on the shelf. His reasoning felt wobbly but solid at the center: Biscuit was tiny, so a missing nutrient would hit her hardest, and he couldn't see inside her heart or her eyes to check. The problem was invisible. That meant the fix had to be constant, every single day, whether he felt like it or not.

At home, Biscuit investigated the living room in slow, suspicious circles, tail up like a flag. Max opened the new bag of cat food, all meat, and the smell rolled out, rich and salty, nothing like the arid dust of kibble he'd once fed his grandma's goldfish by accident for a whole week. That fish had sulked behind a plastic castle for days. He still felt bad about it. He poured a small mound into a bowl and set it near the radiator, where the floor was warm.

Ria from next door appeared at the door before the bowl even stopped rattling. "He's so small," she whispered, crouching down. Biscuit attempted to pounce on Ria's shoelace, missed, and slid sideways into the table leg, which briefly thwarted her dignity. Ria laughed until she had to sit on the floor.

"She has to eat this every day," Max said. "Forever. It's got the stuff in it she can't make herself."

"Like vitamins?"

"Sort of. Like invisible armor." He tapped the bag. "Meat armor."

Biscuit, deciding the bowl was acceptable, stuck one whole paw into the kibble and dragged a piece out onto the carpet.

Audrey slid into her seat just as Mr. Santoso wrote one word on the board: "Claims." Below it he added a second word: "Opinions." Then he said the class project this term would be to investigate a problem in their own neighborhood and present it, and every group had to pick one today.

"Speeding on Maple Street," Louisa said immediately. "Cars go way too fast by the library. I counted eleven near-misses there last week. Eleven times a car had to brake hard because somebody was crossing."

"That's not even that bad," said Kailey. "The cafeteria is worse. Everyone hates the cafeteria."

Audrey looked back and forth between them. Something felt different about the two arguments, and she turned the feeling over while Mr. Santoso sorted marker pens. Louisa had numbers. Kailey had a feeling that lots of people shared. But were they really different kinds of things? She wondered whether Louisa's near-miss count turned her opinion into something else, like a fact, or whether it was still just an opinion wearing a fancy coat.

She decided to test it. At lunch she took her notebook to the library corner of Maple Street and sat on the low wall for twenty minutes. She tallied every hard brake she saw, the same way Louisa must have, marking little lines in groups of five. She counted three. Twenty minutes was not a week, she knew, so she multiplied in her head and got something in the neighborhood of Louisa's number. The count was real, or at least it could be. Louisa had not made it up.

But when she imagined telling Mr. Santoso, "Cars should slow down on Maple Street, and there were eleven near-misses," she noticed the sentence still began with should. A count could be checked. A should could not. The evidence made Louisa's opinion heavier, harder to push aside, like a backpack full of books instead of one with a single pencil in it. It was more convincing than Kailey's bare statement, but it had not stopped being an opinion. Maybe, Audrey thought, that was the whole trick: opinions and evidence weren't opposites. Evidence just made some opinions worth listening to first.

The next day their group met at the back lab table, where the fertilizer sat in a tray beside the bean seedlings they had planted for a different component of the project. The soil in one pot had gone pale and dry, and Mr. Santoso had already suggested they abandon that pot and start a fresh one, so a half-empty bag of fertile planting mix sat open at the end of the table, smelling like rain.

"Did you actually watch the street?" Louisa asked, eyeing Audrey's notebook.

"Twenty minutes. Three hard brakes. Your eleven in a week makes sense to me."

Kailey groaned. "So we're doing the boring street thing."

"It's not boring, it's checkable," Audrey said. "Nobody can check that everyone hates the cafeteria. I asked eight people at lunch and three of them like the pizza."

Kailey slumped, then sat up again. "Fine. But if we do Maple Street, I want to be the one who counts tomorrow. Maybe I'll get twelve."

Audrey grinned and slid the notebook across the table, open to her neat rows of tally marks.

Arianna slid off her bike at the Sunoco station just as the storm clouds rolled in, and the first thing she noticed was the handwritten sign taped to the cooler: bottled water, two dollars. Yesterday it had been ninety-nine cents. She had fifteen dollars in her pocket from collecting cans all week, and she needed twelve bottles for her soccer team's tournament tomorrow, which meant she suddenly needed twenty-four dollars instead of twelve.

"Nobody's going to pay that," she told Andrea, who was leaning against the ice machine. Andrea shook her head and pointed at the parking lot. A man was carrying out an armful of bottles, and behind him a woman was filling a whole basket. The radio had warned that the storm might knock out the town's water for a day or two, and everyone wanted bottled water at once, while the store had only its one small cooler of it.

Arianna did a quick census of the cooler, counting what was left and who took what. In ten minutes, six people bought water at two dollars, but four people picked it up, saw the sign, and put it back. Yesterday, she remembered, the cooler had sold maybe ten bottles at ninety-nine cents all afternoon, because back then there was plenty and nobody was worried. Now the water was scarce, the price was up, and fewer people were willing to buy it. She whispered her discovery to Andrea like it was a secret code. "When the price goes up, people buy less. When it goes down, they buy more. If nothing else changes."

"My sister calls that the law of demand," Andrea confessed. "She learned it in high school. She raised her lemonade price from fifty cents to a dollar and only half as many people bought it."

Arianna's problem still stood, though. She needed twelve bottles and couldn't afford twenty-four dollars. Then she spotted the shelf above the cooler, stacked with gallon jugs of spring water that nobody was touching. The jugs were still ninety-nine cents each because, she guessed, people wanted the easy little bottles. She grabbed three jugs, plus two bottles for the goalies, and paid eleven dollars and change.

As she wheeled her bike out with the jugs bungee-corded to the rack, Ms. Berg pulled up in her truck and headed straight for the cooler. Arianna pointed up at the shelf. "Jugs are half the price and nobody's fighting over them."

Emile had a rolled-up graph in his back pocket and a granola bar in his fist, and only one of them was going to help him survive the next hour. Ms. Oyelaran had told the class that whoever explained the graph properly at the top of the ridge would get to hold the good binoculars for the walk home, so Emile planned to have it figured out before the switchbacks ended.

"Give me a hint," he said to Harriet, who was marching ahead with the confidence of someone who had already done the reading. "The desert one has these skinny little bars and the rainforest one has fat ones. So deserts are hotter, because taller means more temperature. Obviously."

Harriet snorted so hard she nearly tripped on a root. "You just called a warranty on that theory and it's already broken."

"My theories come with a full warranty," Emile said. "Return anytime."

Behind them, Cole was shining his water bottle at a beetle, watching the light refract through the plastic onto the trail. "Rainforest has more rain," he offered without looking up. "I feel like the bars are rain. That's just my opinion though."

"Rain isn't subjective," Harriet said. "It either falls or it doesn't."

Emile unrolled the graph against a boulder and pinned the corners with two pebbles and one patient thumb. The bars went up and down like a tiny city skyline, and there was a line, too, a thin wobbly line threading across the whole chart like a snake through the bars. He stared at it. The line had numbers on one side that said degrees. The bars had numbers on the other side that said millimeters.

"Wait," he said. "The line is the temperature. The bars are the rainfall. One chart, both things, every month." He traced the desert's line with a finger. "So the desert can be super hot and still barely rain. And look, the rainforest line is lower, but the bars are huge."

"So your tall-equals-hot theory," Harriet said.

"Recalled from the market. Full refund."

At the top of the ridge, Ms. Oyelaran held out her hand for the graph. Emile explained the line, explained the bars, explained how the rainforest was wet and warm while the desert was hot and dry, and Ms. Oyelaran handed over the binoculars without a word.

Emile raised them to his eyes and swept across the valley. "There's a hawk," he announced. "Two hawks. Okay, one hawk and a very committed crow."

"Hand them over," said Cole. "I have a warranty claim."

Hailey knelt in the school garden and patted soil around her tomato seedling for the third time that week, even though she knew the roots would not care. The spring fair was in two weeks, and Ms. Diallo had set up two prize tables in the gym: one for fruit entries and one for vegetable entries. Hailey wanted the blue ribbon for best vegetable, and her tomato plant was the only thing she had.

At lunch, Georges spread his entry form on the bench. "I'm entering my strawberries under fruit," he said. "You should move your tomatoes to the fruit table too. Seeds on the inside means fruit. Everybody knows that."

"They're vegetables," Hailey said. "My grandma sells them at her farm stand next to the carrots and the peppers." Georges said her grandma was just sorting by taste, sweet versus not sweet, and that botanically a tomato was a fruit. He had a dictionary page folded in his pocket to prove it. Hailey felt a dread settle in her stomach, the kind that comes when you might lose an argument and a ribbon on the same day. She signed up for the vegetable table anyway, because moving her form would mean admitting Georges was right before she had checked anything.

That afternoon she took the bus to her grandma's farm stand and asked straight out. "The boy's not wrong," her grandma said, weighing a bag of beans for a customer. "A tomato is botanically a fruit. But back in 1893, the Supreme Court ruled in a case called Nix v. Hedden that tomatoes count as vegetables for import taxes." A man at the stand, holding two beefsteaks, snorted. "Taxes. Not science. Big difference." Hailey copied the case name onto the back of her hand with a pen from the cash box.

On fair day, Mckenzie from her class walked the gym aisles with a clipboard, hunting for entries that had been sorted wrong so she could win the "sharp eyes" prize for spotting mistakes. She stopped at Hailey's tomato on the vegetable table and raised her hand. "That's a fruit. I want the point." Hailey had compassion for her, since Mckenzie had found three real mistakes already, but she did not want to be the fourth. "Botanically it's a fruit," Hailey said. "But in 1893 the Supreme Court ruled in Nix v. Hedden that it counts as a vegetable for import taxes. So it can sit at this table." Ms. Diallo came over, listened, and looked it up in the office. She came back and moved nothing.

The blue ribbon for vegetables went to a wall of snap peas, which Hailey had already figured was inevitable the moment she saw them. But Ms. Diallo handed her a small green ribbon that said Best Argument, and Georges, clutching his own ribbon for strawberries, held his up next to hers. "Fruit table and vegetable table," he said. "Same plant family, more or less." Mckenzie wrote something on her clipboard, crossed it out, and pointed her pen at the snap peas. "Then those judges owe me a point for the carrots next to them."

At dinner, Carter pushed his noodles around his plate while his mom talked about weekend plans. He kept thinking about the group chat. That morning, someone had posted a mean picture of Margaret, the kind where they took her class photo and scribbled on it, and everybody laughed in capital letters. Carter had typed "not funny" and then deleted it before sending, because last time he'd done that, the whole chat turned on him instead, and it got worse for the person he was trying to help.

"You're quiet," his dad said.

"Margaret got teased in the chat today," Carter said. "By the time I wanted to show Mr. Kaur, the messages were gone. Someone deleted them."

His dad set down his fork. "Gone how?"

"The person who posted it can delete it, and they did. So it was just my word against nothing."

Carter remembered Tuesday, when the same thing had happened to Cameron over his stutter. Cameron had gone to Mr. Kaur with nothing on his phone, and Mr. Kaur had asked to see the messages, and Cameron had stood there scrolling through an empty chat while the kid who did it smirked. Cameron wanted a turn on the robotics team so badly that he had persevered through weeks of teasing just to keep showing up, and Carter figured Cameron deserved better than an empty screen.

A thought slid into place, so neat it almost made him drop his fork. The messages were deleted before anyone could see them. But what if they weren't deleted from Carter's phone yet? He had read the mean posts. His phone might still have them.

"Can I be excused for a second?" he asked, and ran to his room. His hands shook a little as he scrolled back through the chat. There it was, the scribbled picture of Margaret, still sitting on his screen with the laughing replies underneath. He took screenshots, one after another, until every mean message was saved. Then he went back to the table and showed his dad, who studied the pictures with raised eyebrows and a dose of healthy skepticism.

"Those could be edited," his dad said.

"They're not," Carter said. "But see, now they can't just vanish. If Mr. Kaur needs proof tomorrow, I have a record."

"Then keep it safe," his dad said, "and show him in the morning."

The next day Carter found Mr. Kaur before first bell and held out his phone. "They deleted the messages," he said, "but I took screenshots. Now you have a record even if the originals disappear."

Mr. Kaur looked through each picture slowly, nodding. "This helps a lot," he said. "Saves everything being just talk."

At lunch, Margaret sat down across from Carter with her tray. "Mr. Kaur talked to them," she said. "They apologized. For real, I think." She paused, then slid a folded napkin across the table. Inside was a doodle of two stick figures giving a high five.

"Your robot arm still glitching in practice?" Carter asked, nodding toward Cameron at the next table.

"Fixed it," Cameron said, grinning. "I persevered."

Carter high-fived him over the napkin holder.

Penelope's fifth sunset looked like mud. She sat on the splintery porch of the art shed at Camp Wyndoo, her brushes soaking in a jar of cloudy water, and stared at the brown smear across her canvas. The first four attempts were lined up against the wall, each one murkier than the last. Tomorrow was the art show, and the whole camp would walk past her table, including her cabinmates Hadley and Riaan, who kept promising her a sunset so orange it would hurt to look at.

"You're doing it again," said Riaan, dropping onto the bench beside her with a popsicle. "You start with that pretty red sky, then you add green for the pine trees, and then it turns into dirt."

"I know," Penelope said. "I mix them a little at the edges on purpose. Every time. And every time it dies." She spread the five muddy canvases in a row on the porch boards. The pattern was sitting right there in front of her: red sky, green trees, brown along every border where the two colors met. She picked up the color wheel chart tacked inside the shed door and spun it slowly on its pin. Red sat at the top. Directly across from it, at the bottom, sat green. She spun it again to check, but the wheel never changed its mind.

"Look at this," she said. "Red and green are opposites on the wheel." She needed a word for that, and she needed somebody to say it, so she marched to the picnic table where Hadley was weaving a lanyard and showed her the chart. "What do you call colors across from each other like this?"

Hadley squinted at it. "Complementary colors. Ms. Greco said that word in the first craft session, the one you skipped for the swim test."

Penelope let that digest for a second. Complementary colors. Opposites on the wheel, like red and green. And when she mixed her red sky and her green trees, she got dull brown, every single time, which meant it wasn't bad luck or a bad brush. It was what opposites did when they touched. "So I have to keep them apart," she said out loud, mostly to herself. "Or find different colors that aren't opposites."

She tested it right there. On a scrap of board she painted one stripe of red beside a stripe of green without letting them blend, and next to it she mixed the two colors into a puddle of flat, dull gray-brown, almost the exact mud from her five sunsets. Then she tried red next to blue. Where they met, the colors stayed clean and bright, no muck at all. Riaan leaned over the scrap, popsicle dripping onto the grass, and nodded slowly.

For her final painting, Penelope kept the fiery red sky floating above a row of dark blue hills instead of green pines, and where she wanted the sharp line between them, she let the paint dry first before adding the next stripe. The orange glow at the horizon she built with yellow and red, layered while they were both wet, because they weren't across from each other on the wheel and she had the scrap board to prove it. By the time the porch light humed on and the mosquitoes came out, the sunset on her easel blazed so hard that Hadley, walking past with a flashlight, stopped in the middle of the path.

"Okay," Hadley said. "Now that hurts to look at."

Grandpa arrived on Saturday with one duffel bag and his old walking stick, and the first thing he did was nearly trip over nothing at all, just a slight catch of his heel on the front step. Jace caught his elbow. That night, Jace noticed the rug that usually sat beside the guest bed was gone, rolled up in the hall closet, and the hallway night light was plugged in. Nobody had said a word about any of it.

He decided to run a quiet experiment. On Sunday he watched Grandpa walk from the kitchen to the porch, counting the places where his feet hesitated: the threshold, the extension cord by the couch, that same front step with its loose board, which rocked like a seesaw under a shoe. Three stumbles in one day, and none of them because Grandpa wasn't paying attention. It was the floor itself, the stuff no one looked at twice.

On Monday, Jace took Grandpa to the park to meet Kaya and Aksil for a picnic. Grandpa planted himself on the bench and announced, "I'm a carnivore today, so save me every sandwich with meat in it," and ate three while telling a story about a dog he'd owned at Jace's age. When Grandpa went to throw away the wrappers, Kaya pointed at the bulletin board by the restrooms, where a health fair flyer was taped up. Jace read it out loud. "Falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged sixty-five and older in the United States." He read it twice, because the words didn't seem like they belonged next to a carnival poster for face painting.

"It's not the big scary stuff," Jace said slowly, mostly to himself. "It's just falling. Tripping over a rug. Catching a heel on a step." Aksil said his own grandma had grab bars in her bathroom, and Jace filed that away too.

That evening, he was assertive in a way he usually wasn't. He put the loose step on the kitchen table like evidence, told his dad about the flyer, about the three stumbles, about the rolled-up rug, and asked for a screwdriver and a Saturday. He refused to just resign himself to watching Grandpa shuffle carefully around a house full of traps for seven days and then go home. His dad looked at the board, then at him, and got the toolbox.

Grandpa came to the door, sandwich in hand, and asked what all the noise was about. "We're fixing your step," Jace said, already kneeling down with a screw in his teeth.

Aubrey sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a photo of her cousin Mattea propped against the sugar bowl, a blank sheet of watercolour paper in front of her. She wanted to give the portrait to Mattea for her birthday, which was in six days, and so far she had managed only a pale yellow blob where the face should be. Her grandmother painted in the corner by the window, saying nothing, which was her way of letting you struggle on purpose.

The blob was the problem. Aubrey had mixed a skin tone, decided it was too dark, and reached for the white paint to lighten it. Before her brush touched the white, her grandmother slid the water jar across the table without looking up from her own canvas.

Aubrey stared at the jar. "You want me to rinse my brush?"

"Try adding water instead of white."

She dipped her brush and let a drop fall into the puddle of skin tone. The colour bloomed lighter, softer, exactly what she had wanted. She tested it again on a scrap, one drop, then two, watching the same paint turn from brick to peach. So that was the rule: you made a wash lighter with water, not white. She thought about the yellow blob, then about the painting she'd seen in her grandmother's studio, a face built from see-through layers, and a new idea took hold. Maybe you weren't supposed to get the skin right in one go. Maybe you started light, almost too light, and added darker washes on top, a little at a time.

She worked all afternoon, laying down the palest layer first, letting it dry, then adding shadow under Mattea's cheekbones with a slightly stronger mix. When she tried to rush and painted over a damp section, the colours bled into a bruise, and she had to blot it with a tissue and start that layer again. It was a dilemma: wait and lose time, or push on and ruin it. She learned to wait.

By evening the face looked like Mattea, if Mattea were made of sunlight. Aubrey held it up. "Is it done?"

Her grandmother put on her glasses, looked, and then did something unexpected. She turned the painting toward the window, tilted it, and pointed at a patch on the forehead that had dried patchy and uneven. "Almost," she said. "One more wash, even across the whole face, will tie it together."

"That'll make it darker."

"A little. That's how it works."

Aubrey mixed the wash, added water until it was barely tea-coloured, and swept it over the face in one steady pass. The patchy spot vanished into the whole. Tomorrow she would paint the eyes, the hardest part, and she wasn't even scared of it now. She set the portrait on the windowsill to dry, and Mattea's face looked back at her, waiting.

Andrew pushed open the metal door of the big brick building on Delmore Street, expecting a line of hungry people stretching to the corner. He'd brought his volunteer slip from Ms. García's class, and he'd imagined handing cans to grateful strangers all morning. Instead he stood in a cavernous room stacked floor to ceiling with pallets of soup, rice, and peanut butter, and not a single customer anywhere. His friend Cayden was already there, tying an apron, looking just as confused.

"Where is everybody?" Andrew asked. "The sign outside said this is where we volunteer."

Cayden shrugged. "Maybe nobody's hungry today."

Andrew didn't buy that. He walked the length of the warehouse, past shelves labeled with numbers, past a forklift parked by the loading dock. If people needed food, they weren't getting it here, and the boxes kept moving somewhere. He noticed the pallets were shrink-wrapped and stamped with the names of neighborhoods, and a clipboard by the dock listed pickup times for vans from churches and schools all over the city. That gave him an idea, and ideas, his dad always said, needed testing.

"Let's verify it," he told Cayden. "We ask the guy with the clipboard where the food goes."

The volunteer coordinator, a wiry man named Merrick who looked about seventeen, laughed when they asked. "You thought people walked in off the street? No, this is a food bank. A food bank is a warehouse that collects and stores huge amounts of food. The places where people actually come pick up groceries are called food pantries, little ones all over town. We ship to them."

Andrew felt his face go warm. He'd had the whole thing backward. He'd pictured himself handing a can of beans to a kid his own age, and instead he was standing in a giant cupboard. For a second he wanted to quit and call his mom to pick him up.

But then Merrick pointed at a map covered in pins. "St. Anne's pantry runs out of boxes by noon every Saturday. Want to ride along?"

They rode in the van, and at St. Anne's Andrew finally got his line of people. He stacked cans on a folding table while a woman with two toddlers chose bread and oranges, and Cayden bagged apples so fast the bagger tore. Andrew had thought the warehouse work didn't count because nobody saw it. Now he understood that the van, the pantry, and his own hands were all one chain, and every link mattered, even the invisible ones.

When they got back, Merrick asked if they'd sign up again next month.

"Both Saturdays," Andrew said, and grabbed a pen.

Leo held up two shirts in the clothing store, one blue and one green, and asked Cora which one looked less terrible. She pointed at the blue, but her eyes had drifted to a rack near the register, where foam earplugs hung in little paper packets beside a card with tiny print. The card said that the U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and that each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.

"Eight hours seems like forever," Cora said. "Why would anyone need these?"

Leo did the math out loud, slowly, because the numbers implied something that surprised him. "Eighty-five decibels is eight hours. Eighty-eight is four. Ninety-one is two. It drops fast." He bought the shirt and, after standing there a moment longer, a packet of earplugs too. The cashier raised an eyebrow but said nothing.

On Saturday, the gym had been transformed into something almost distinct from the place where they ran laps, with streamers and a spinning light and a stage at one end holding giant speakers taller than Mr. Addo, who was standing nearby checking his clipboard. Leo, Cora, and Massimo planted themselves right in front of the speakers because that was where the cool kids stood, and Massimo insisted that closer meant better.

After twenty minutes, Leo noticed a faint ring in his ears, a strange fullness that did not fade when he swallowed. He pulled out his phone and opened a sound meter app he had downloaded the night before. It read 106. He watched the number for a minute, thinking. At that level, the safe time was not hours at all. Each step of 3 halved it again and again, until barely any minutes were left.

"We need to move," he said. "Now, actually."

Massimo groaned, but Cora, who had been pressing a finger against her ear, grabbed his sleeve. The three of them walked to the middle of the gym, and Leo checked the app again. The reading had dropped by more than half. He handed the earplugs to Cora, kept one pair for himself, and offered the last to Massimo, who took it only after the bass hit so hard it rattled the bleachers.

Mr. Addo wandered over during a slow song and glanced at the foam in Leo's ears. "Smart," he said, and tapped his own ear, where a bit of orange foam was already visible.

From across the gym, Massimo shouted over the music, "Best spot in the whole place, and I found it first."

Anthony's plan for the weekend was simple: prove to his dad that his screen time had actually gone down in October, so the November limit should go up. He needed numbers and a chart, because his dad trusted charts the way other dads trusted weather reports. Alek and Imran came over on Saturday with a bag of chips and the family laptop, and the three of them spread out on the living room rug in front of the coffee table.

"Week one, four hours," Anthony read off his notebook. "Week two, three and a half. Week three, three." Imran typed the numbers into a spreadsheet while Alek held the chip bag like a referee holding a whistle. In the empty cell under the column, Anthony typed his first formula, =SUM(B2:B5), and pressed Enter. The number 13 appeared instantly. Alek leaned over and squinted at it.

"That can't be right," Alek said. "Add it by hand." Anthony did, scribbling on the back of a chip receipt, and the total matched. The formula had counted something they couldn't see happening, all four weeks at once, and Anthony felt the laptop almost radiate importance in his hands. The living room lamp hummed. Somewhere the radiator ticked like a brittle stick.

Then came the chart. Anthony highlighted the weeks and the hours, clicked Insert, chose the first option that said Bar Chart, and hit Enter again. The chart appeared with the bars lying flat, sideways, week names running up the side instead of along the bottom. "It's broken," Anthony said. "It came out sideways." He was about to close the whole file and start over when Imran grabbed his wrist.

"Wait. Look at the other buttons." Next to Bar Chart there was a button labeled Column Chart, and its little picture showed upright bars. Anthony clicked it, and the same numbers stood up into vertical columns, neat as fence posts. He looked between the two thumbnails for a long moment, comparing. "Okay," he said slowly. "So in Excel a bar chart has horizontal bars and a column chart has vertical bars. They're both comparing amounts across categories. I picked the sideways kind on purpose. Sort of." Alek laughed so hard a chip flew out of the bag.

On Sunday, Anthony showed his dad the printout, columns climbing left to right, total of thirteen hours in bold at the bottom. He had also added a new factor to his argument: a second column for homework hours, which had gone up. His dad studied the chart, tapped the total, and said he'd think about the limit. Then he asked, quietly, whether the spreadsheet could do the household budget too. Anthony pulled the laptop back onto his knees and said, "Sit down. This is going to take a formula."

Declan pushed his drawing of Main Street across the kitchen table and waited while Avianna held it up to the light, the way Mr. Ma did in art class when he wanted to check whether the lines were true. The assignment was due tomorrow: a street drawn in one-point perspective, every edge aimed at a single vanishing point. Declan had tried three times, and every time the buildings looked like they were falling over sideways.

"Your vanishing point wanders," Avianna said, tapping the spot where the two sides of the street were supposed to meet. "Here it's in one place, and here it's somewhere else. My brother says your pencil rebels if you don't anchor it, you have to pin the point first and make every line obey it."

So Declan drew a small dot in the middle of a fresh sheet and refused to let it move. He lined his ruler up so the curb, the rooftops, the shop windows, and even the stripes on the candy shop awning all pointed at the dot like roads on a map. Slowly the flat paper deepened into a street you felt you could walk down. Avianna, working beside him on her own drawing of the same street, kept glancing at his page and frowning.

"Ours don't match," she said. "Same street, same dot in the middle, but yours looks like the view from the curb and mine looks like the view from the upstairs window of the bakery."

Declan leaned over. She was right. In his drawing, the pavement took up most of the page, tall building faces rising above it. In hers, the street was a thin ribbon squeezed down at the bottom, and you could see the rooftops flat against the sky, with a dry, arid stretch of gravel roof where the bakery's gutters ran. They argued about who had it wrong until Declan noticed something. His horizon line, the flat line running through the vanishing point, sat low on his page. Hers sat high.

"Wait," he said. He grabbed a new sheet, folded it in half to mark the middle, and drew the same street twice: once with the horizon pushed down near the bottom, once with it lifted almost to the top. The low one felt like the street seen from a kid's height, the way it looked when he sat on the curb outside the candy shop. The high one felt like looking down from a window above.

"You sat on the curb when you sketched it," he told Avianna, "and I stood at the bakery window upstairs, remember? Our eyes were at different heights." He flipped his folded sheet over and showed her the two versions side by side. "Mr. Ma is going to lose his mind. We could start a guild, the Horizon Movers, and do the whole class assignment from every floor of every building on Main Street."

Avianna laughed so hard she nearly knocked over the pencil jar, and then she bent over her page and drew a tiny figure sitting on her curb, right at the bottom of the street, waving up at the window.

"There," she said. "Now put me in yours. Window seat, third floor, and I'm holding a cinnamon roll."

Ellie stood at the steel counter in the back of her family's restaurant, rubbing flour between her fingers while the lunch rush rattled the dining room on the other side of the wall. Ms. Nur, who had run this kitchen for eleven years, had put her in charge of one whole meal today: rice, a pot of curry, and a stack of chapatis. "Everything ready at the same time," Ms. Nur had said. "That is the whole trick of cooking. A hungry consumer does not wait." Ellie had nodded like she understood, and she had decided to start with the flatbreads, because they looked like the hardest part.

She rolled and cooked the chapatis first, one after another, laying them on a plate in a neat tower. The rice went on next, then the curry, which needed to bubble for a long while. She stirred it, tasted it, and stirred it again. When the curry was finally thick and fragrant and the rice soft, she carried all three dishes to the pass, proud and ready. Ms. Nur picked up a chapati and bent it. It cracked in half with a dry snap, stiff as a plate.

Ellie frowned at the broken bread. She had watched Ms. Nur make chapatis before, and they were always soft and folded. She tried to remember the order of things on those days. The curry had always been already simmering, the rice already steaming, and Ms. Nur would stand at the griddle at the very end, flipping bread while waiters hovered. That was the pattern. The flatbreads were last, every single time. Ellie looked at the griddle, hot and dry and empty, and thought about how quickly each round of dough had puffed and browned when Ms. Nur cooked it. A minute, maybe two, and it was done.

"The chapatis are no good," Ellie said. "I made them first."

"Then make them again," said Ms. Nur, and turned back to the fryer without another word. It was not a scolding. It was permission.

Ellie mixed fresh dough, rolled it thin, and waited. She let the curry simmer and kept the rice warm, and only when an order came in did she slap a circle of dough onto the dry griddle. It blistered and puffed in under a minute, and she flipped it, counted to ten, and slid it steaming onto the plate beside the curry. The second one took even less time. Luciana, wiping tables on the other side of the pass, leaned over and sniffed. "That smells exceptional," she said. "Can I be your first customer?"

Ellie tore a warm chapati, dipped it into the curry, and set the plate on the pass. "One order," she said, "rice, curry, and bread, all hot at once." Luciana picked it up and carried it out through the swinging door.

Christopher stood in the laundry aisle of Mr. Takahashi's grocery store, holding a bottle of detergent like it might explode. His mother had finally declared that he was old enough to do his own laundry, and she had sent him here with a short list and a shorter explanation.

"Get the kind with the blue cap," she'd said. That was it. No hints about what to do if the blue cap came in six varieties.

"You look like you're choosing a car," said Tessa, appearing beside him with her own basket. She and Bruno had come for snacks, but they found Christopher's suffering more entertaining.

"There are too many choices," Christopher said. "This one converts hard water. This one fights odours. What if my clothes have both hard water and odours?"

"Bold of you to assume anyone can tell," Bruno said, dropping two bags of chips into Tessa's basket.

Christopher took the cheapest blue-capped bottle, feeling he'd won a small battle, and the three of them walked to the checkout where Mr. Takahashi worked the register on Sundays. The store was strangely tranquil, just the hum of the coolers and a radio playing somewhere in the back.

"First load?" Mr. Takahashi asked, scanning the detergent. "You have the face of a boy about to learn something."

"Everyone keeps saying that," Christopher muttered.

At home, he sorted his clothes into piles, darks and lights, the way his mother had described. He checked one or two pockets, found a pencil in a hoodie, and felt proud of his thoroughness. Then he shoved everything dark into the machine, dumped in detergent, and pressed start. He watched the drum spin for a while, like a slow carnival ride, then went to fold his other laundry.

Forty minutes later he opened the machine and stared. Every dark shirt, every pair of jeans, every sock was speckled with white, as though a snowstorm had happened inside the drum. He pulled out his favourite black hoodie and it looked like a negative of the night sky.

He dug through the wet pile and found the culprit: the shredded remains of a paper tissue, dissolved and scattered across everything. One tissue. From one pocket. The pockets he hadn't checked.

He called Tessa. "I checked some pockets," he said. "Some is not enough."

"New consensus: check every pocket," she said, and he could hear Bruno laughing in the background.

Christopher picked the shreds off piece by piece, then ran the load again with nothing in it but water, and most of the specks floated away. When his mother came home, he showed her the hoodie, only slightly snowy still.

"Every pocket," he said. "I'm checking every pocket, every time, forever."

His mother smiled. Christopher took his black hoodie upstairs and hung it on his door, speckles and all, like a flag.

The minivan smelled like airport coffee and the orange peel her dad kept in the cup holder. Victoria sat in the back with her duffel between her feet, watching the highway lights slide past. They had spent nine days at her aunt's house in California, and the flight home had landed an hour ago. Her brother was already asleep against the window, but Victoria's whole body felt wrong, like her bones had stayed three hours behind in another time zone.

"Text me when you land!" she said out loud, remembering Parker's message. She pulled out her phone and typed: landed. feel like garbage. why??

Parker replied fast. weird, u were fine when u flew OUT there. Victoria stared at that. It was true. On the way west she had stayed up late, slept in, and felt normal by the second day. Now, flying east, she was exhausted at seven in the evening and wide awake at three in the morning. She scrolled through Parker's next messages. my mom says most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west. She read it twice. West had been easy. East was wrecking her.

"I'm boycotting the east," she announced to the car. "Direction, that is. When we fly again, we only go west."

"That would make an interesting family," her dad said, checking the mirror. "We'd have to become descendants of people who circled the globe forever." He signaled and changed lanes. "Your grandmother did that once, actually. Never came back east, if I remember right."

Victoria opened her notebook, the versatile little one she used for everything, lists, homework, bad drawings, and made two columns in the dark by the glow of her phone. WEST, she wrote, and under it: felt fine, stayed up later, easy. EAST: awful, awake at 3 a.m., took over a week. Parker's mom's rule fit both trips. It wasn't the airplane, and it wasn't the length of the flight, because both flights were about the same. It was the direction. She decided to test it, in her own small way. School started in two days, and she would keep a chart: what time she got sleepy, what time she woke up, every day, until her body caught up.

The car turned onto their street. Ahead, under the porch light, Ms. Chowdhury from next door was pulling her recycling bin in from the curb, and she raised a hand as they passed. Victoria's dad tapped the horn twice, a short friendly beep, and pulled into the driveway. Victoria grabbed her duffel, pushed the door open into the cold air, and said, "Dad, I need a wall calendar. Tomorrow. It's for science."

The family group chat, labeled "Rivera Household," buzzed at 7:04 a.m. Adam's mom had posted a photo of two concert tickets with the caption "TONIGHT 7pm, me and Dad. Home by 10. Be nice to each other." Adam stared at his phone. Tyler, his best friend since third grade, was coming over at six so they could finish their science project before the deadline tomorrow, except Tyler probably wasn't coming, because they hadn't spoken since Saturday. Adam had sent a message that morning saying "You never keep secrets. You always tell Sam everything," and Tyler had replied with one thumbs down and nothing since.

All day at school Adam collected evidence like a detective. Tyler had, in fact, told Sam one secret, on Friday, one time. But Tyler had kept dozens of others, including the embarrassing one about the pool party in fifth grade. So Adam's message wasn't even true, which bothered him more than the fight itself. In Ms. Francis's class, while she wrote the science project rubric on the board, he flipped through his health textbook and found a page about a researcher named John Gottman. Gottman separates a complaint from criticism, the book said. A complaint targets one specific action. Criticism attacks a person's whole character, and it uses words like "you always" or "you never." Adam copied the page number into his notebook, 214, and underlined it twice.

At lunch Mina slid her tray across from his. "You look like a kid who found out his homework is due an hour early," she said.

"Kind of the opposite." He showed her the page. "I criticized Tyler instead of complaining. That's the word, criticism. A complaint is about one specific action, like 'you told Sam what I said on Friday.' But 'you never keep secrets' goes after who he is."

"So rewrite it," Mina said, shrugging. "You have until six, which is, what, four hours?"

"I also have to integrate his volcano results into the poster before then, which is a whole separate plague."

"Then stop sitting here being negligent about it and go find him," she said, and stole his fries.

The plague metaphor followed Adam through the halls, because eighth graders flooded every route to the gym. He caught Tyler at his locker before the final bell. "One sentence," Adam said. "You told Sam what I said on Friday, and it got back to me, and that's what I was actually mad about. Not 'always,' not 'never.' Just Friday."

Tyler shut his locker slowly. "Sam begged me for twenty minutes. I caved. I was going to tell you myself Saturday, but your message hit first and it stung."

"Fair. Can you still come at six? I can't integrate your lava data without you."

"I'll come at five," Tyler said. "Bring graph paper."

At 6:58, with the poster finished and leaning against the couch, Adam photographed it and dropped the picture into the family group chat with the message "Done. Volcano survives until tomorrow." His mom replied with a fire emoji, and Tyler handed him a marker to sign his name at the bottom.

Brayden had erased his street so many times that the paper was starting to dissolve into gray smudge, and the drawing still looked like a pile of boxes falling downhill. He slumped at the kitchen table, pencil hovering. The assignment was due Monday, and Ms. Kerr had promised it would hang in the hallway outside the art room. His older sister got a drawing hung last year. Brayden wanted his up there too.

The doorbell rang twice, fast, which meant Kailyn. She came in holding her own attempt, a street of shops that somehow got wider as it went back, like the road was walking toward you. "It's broken," she announced. "Mine too," Brayden said. "Mine's so bad I almost recycled it, but then I'd have guilt about wasting paper, so I just stared at it instead."

They laid the drawings side by side. Brayden got the ruler out and ran it along the edges of his buildings, and that was when he saw it. All the lines that should slant, the rooftops, the curb, the shop window ledges, pointed the same wrong way, scattered like dropped chopsticks. "They're supposed to meet," he said slowly. "One point. Everything goes to one point." Kailyn leaned in. "Wait. My mom showed me a picture of this in a museum book. The Last Supper, the giant one by Leonardo da Vinci. The single vanishing point is at Christ's head." She tapped her drawing. "Every edge in that painting points right at him. And get this, there's a tiny nail hole at that exact spot, because Leonardo hammered in a nail and stretched guide strings from it, like spokes, to get his lines straight. The hole is still visible in the painting."

Brayden stared at her. "A nail hole in one of the most famous paintings on Earth? From string?" He grabbed a fresh sheet before the thought could dissolve. "That's it. That's the trick. You don't guess the lines, you build them from one point." He marked a dot at the top center of his page, then, feeling only slightly ridiculous, pressed the pencil point down like a nail. He drew a horizon line through it, laid his ruler from the dot to the bottom corner, and swept a street edge into place. Then another line, then another, all of them running obediently home to the dot.

Kailyn pulled her chair over so fast it banged his. "Do mine next, do mine." She marked her own vanishing point and started twisting her ruler toward it, tongue between her teeth. Her shops leaned backward at first, endangered by her enthusiasm, but she steadied the ruler with two fingers. Brayden added windows, shrinking each one smaller as it climbed toward the dot, and the flat paper suddenly had depth, a real street you could walk down.

They worked until the kitchen went gold with evening light, two streets racing toward two little dots. "Monday," Kailyn said, holding hers at arm's length. "Hallway, here we come." Brayden pressed his pencil tip once more onto the vanishing point, like a nail going in.

"Nobody argues with 'Grandpa's garden has vegetables,'" Alexandre said, waving the paper at the porch table where Leila and Juan sat with lemonade. It was Friday at Grandpa's house, which had somehow become the meeting spot for their writing club, mostly because Grandpa's porch was cool and his dog, Mops, listened well.

Leila frowned at her draft. "It's a thesis. Mr. Iyer said a thesis goes at the end of the first paragraph." She had promised to email her essay to Mr. Iyer by Sunday night, and the new curriculum at school said everyone had to outline a three-point argument before drafting. Alexandre was there to help, and also because Grandpa had promised pie.

"Watch," Alexandre said, and turned to Grandpa, who was watering tomatoes. "Grandpa, your garden has vegetables. Agree or disagree?"

Grandpa squinted. "Agree. Plain as the nose on my face."

"See? Nobody could disagree. A statement nobody would dispute, like a plain fact, gives an essay nothing to argue." Alexandre tapped the paper. "Try a claim a reasonable person could argue against. Then you've got something."

Leila chewed her pencil. Juan, who was supposed to be outlining his own essay about the school's most influential athlete, leaned in. "What about 'Grandpa's garden is better than the farmers market'?"

"Grandpa could disagree with that," Leila said slowly. "The cashier at the market would too. Even my mom might." She grabbed a fresh sheet and started listing points: the tomatoes were fresher, the price was lower, and the drive was shorter. Three points. "That's an argument!"

Then came the twist. Grandpa set down the watering can and cleared his throat. "Fresher, maybe. Cheaper, sure. But the farmers market has a man who sells honey I cannot grow. So I, a reasonable person, disagree." He smiled like he'd just won something.

"That's perfect," Alexandre said. "If even one reasonable person can push back, the thesis works." He was so excited he knocked over the lemonade, and Mops licked it up before anyone could grab a towel.

Leila rewrote her first paragraph right there, reading it aloud while Juan took notes for his own outline. When she finished, she turned to Grandpa. "You're going in my rebuttal paragraph. You and your honey man."

"I'd be honored," Grandpa said. "Now, who wants pie before the market closes?"

Chase turned the photocopied pages of "The Scarlet Ibis" as the school bus rattled past the strip mall. Mr. Santos had promised a reading quiz first period, and the quiz asked one thing: find the foreshadowing and explain what it suggests. Chase could retell the plot fine, but spotting hidden clues inside it felt like trying to see wind.

Toby dropped into the seat across the aisle, unwrapping a granola bar. "You look like the bus ran over your homework."

"The quiz is on this story, and I can't find the clue everyone keeps saying is there." Chase tapped the page. "This brother is ashamed of Doodle, the little brother who can't walk, and then at the end something bad happens. But I can't see what's supposed to warn me."

Shay leaned over the seatback from behind. "Rewind. What shows up earlier that's red and fragile?"

Chase ran his thumb down the margins. There it was, a few pages before the end: a storm blows a scarlet ibis into the family garden, and the exotic red bird dies there in the yard. Doodle, small and fragile himself, buries it. He read the passage again while Toby's granola bar began to decompose into crumbs on the vinyl seat, and the pieces lined up. A red bird, broken by a storm, dies. Then a fragile boy is caught out in a storm too. "The bird," Chase said slowly. "The ibis is the foreshadowing. It's pointing at Doodle."

"That's the whole trick," Shay said. "The bird's not just a bird, it's standing in for him."

Chase tested it out loud, the way he'd have to write it on the quiz. "The dying scarlet ibis foreshadows Doodle's fate, because both are fragile, both are battered by a storm, and both are lost too soon." Saying it made it solid. He underlined the bird's death in pencil, then flipped back and underlined every mention of red: the bird, the bleeding tree, Doodle's name, the scarlet leaves.

"How'd you even get this fast?" Toby asked.

"My mom calls it the family curse," Shay said. "Thinks being bad at math is hereditary. She's wrong, but at least the phrase stuck." She grinned. "Same thing. Once you know what to look for, you see it everywhere. Mr. Santos will probably ask how the quiz revenue from the bake sale's doing, too, so study that order form."

The bus groaned around the last corner toward school. Chase folded the pages, wrote one word at the top of his notes, and slid the pencil behind his ear. "Storm-blown red bird," he said. "Got it."

Anna lay on the living room carpet with three campaign posters spread out in front of her, a glass of juice sweating on the coffee table above her head. Gabriela was running for student council against a boy named Devon, whose posters had appeared overnight like mushrooms after rain. Every single one showed Devon doing ordinary things: eating a sandwich in the cafeteria, tying his shoe by the gym, laughing with a group of kids Anna had never actually seen him talk to. Gabriela's posters, by contrast, listed her ideas in bullet points, and nobody looked at them twice.

"He's going to demolish me," Gabriela said from the couch, where she was cutting out more bullet points. "Everyone keeps saying he seems so normal. So relatable."

"His plan is a mascot and 'better vibes,'" said Hallie, who was sitting cross-legged on the rug, sorting markers by color whether anyone asked her to or not. "My brother voted for him already and the election's not until Friday. He said, and I quote, Devon eats lunch like us."

Anna stared at the poster of Devon with his sandwich. He wasn't doing anything. He was just sitting there, being a regular person, and somehow that was working better than an entire page of Gabriela's proposals about the broken water fountain outside the library. She flipped the poster over, then flipped it back. "He's not winning because of the sandwich," she said slowly. "He's winning because of the sandwich."

"That's what I said," said Gabriela.

"No, I mean it's a technique." Anna scrambled up and dug through her backpack for the media literacy worksheet Mr. Anderson had handed out on Friday, mostly crumpled, still faintly smelling of the bottom of her locker. She smoothed it on the coffee table and ran her finger down the list until she found it. "It's called the plain-folks technique. It presents a politician or a company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as one of us. That's Devon's whole campaign. He's advertising his own normalness."

Hallie capped a marker with great ceremony. "So we make you look normal too? You are normal. Painfully normal."

Gabriela did not thank her for this. But she did grab a fresh poster board, and while Anna held the juice glass safely out of the way, Gabriela drew herself tying her shoe, with one small difference: taped beside it, a strip of paper reading "AND a new water fountain by October." Then she drew herself holding a wrench, which she had never held in her life, and decided that was fine.

They hung the posters in the hallway before first period, and by lunch three people had asked Gabriela about the water fountain, and one person asked Devon what his plan was. Devon said better vibes. Hallie reported this at the living room strategy session that afternoon, sitting exactly where she had been the day before, markers resorted. "He panicked a little," she said. "It was beautiful."

Every November second, Taylor's grandmother turned the side table in her living room into something magical. She stacked wooden boxes into tiers, draped them with an embroidered cloth, and set out candles, marigolds, and little dishes of food until the whole corner glowed. Taylor had helped with the altar since she was seven, but this year she noticed something odd. Her grandmother always placed a bowl of her mother's favorite cuisine, tamales, near the top, and always positioned the candles so their light refracted through a glass of water and scattered orange patterns across the photo of Abuela Elena. But there was a second, smaller frame that went in the very back, turned so slightly toward the wall that you could barely see the face in it.

Taylor wanted to know who it was, and more than that, why it was hidden. Her grandmother never explained the back photo, and Taylor had learned that asking directly got her only a smile and a change of subject. So she tried an experiment. While her grandmother was in the kitchen rolling out dough for pan de muerto, Taylor slipped the frame forward and turned it to face the room.

The photo showed a young man in a soldier's uniform, maybe nineteen, with the same crooked grin as Taylor's grandmother. When her grandmother came back carrying the bread, she stopped in the doorway. She set the plate down slowly, then picked up the frame and held it near the window light.

"His name was Ruben," she said. "My brother. He died when I was twelve, and we didn't put his picture on the altar for many years, because it hurt too much to see it." She traced the edge of the frame with her thumb. "But the ofrenda is for honoring everyone we've lost, so one year I put him in the back, where I could visit him without everyone asking questions."

Taylor's friend Kyra arrived just then with her mother, carrying a jar of marigolds for the altar. Kyra's class had made one at school, and she was full of facts. "Our teacher said the celebration happens in Mexico mainly on November first and second," Kyra announced, "and that these home altars are called ofrendas." She peered at the soldier's photo. "Who's that?"

"My brother," Taylor's grandmother said, and this time she said it out loud, to a guest, without flinching. She set the frame in the front row, right beside Abuela Elena, and adjusted it until the candlelight reached his face.

Kyra's mother asked if they could light the candles together, and Taylor's grandmother handed Taylor the match.

"You do it," she said. "He should meet you properly."

The living room at Ms. Nolan's house was so crowded that John ended up on the floor with a paper plate of nachos balanced on his knee. The championship game had four minutes left, and the score was tied. Theoren sat on the arm of the couch, Rosemary claimed the beanbag chair, and Ms. Nolan's brother, whom everyone just called the uncle, had the best seat in the house and intended to keep it.

Then the running back dove for the goal line, the officials huddled, and everybody in the room winced at once. Touchdown or no touchdown? The referee's arms stayed at his sides while he talked into his headset, and the suspense was so thick that Theoren grabbed a cushion and held it like a shield. "They're checking the replay," Rosemary said. On the screen, the play appeared again, frozen, then run backward, then forward, and John noticed something odd.

He leaned toward the television. The clock in the corner of the picture read 3:41, but the game clock on the score graphic at the top still said 3:52. He nudged Theoren. "Look. Two clocks, two different times. The small one is inside the picture, so the picture itself has to be from before. It's a recording, not live." Theoren squinted, then pointed. "And the left tackle is standing in a different spot. That's the same play from a second ago."

"It's instant replay," the uncle said, without taking his eyes off the screen. "Want to hear something? The first time TV ever did that in a live sports broadcast was the Army-Navy football game, December 7, 1963. A CBS director named Tony Verna made it happen." John stared at him. "You mean before that, if you missed a play, you just missed it?" "For live sports, yes. It didn't exist."

The whistle blew, the referee raised both arms, and the room erupted. Nachos went everywhere. Rosemary jumped up so fast the beanbag chair rolled over Theoren, and the uncle did a lap around the coffee table, which Rosemary's little brother described later as a reckless move for a man his age. Then the kicker lined up for the extra point, and Ms. Nolan called from the kitchen that the pizza was arriving in exactly one minute.

"Hold the pizza," the uncle shouted, "hold everything." The ball snapped, the kick sailed through, and the camera cut to the crowd. A second later the same kick appeared again, from a different angle. "Replay," John said, pointing at the two mismatched clocks before the picture even started moving. "Told you." Theoren threw the cushion at him, and the doorbell rang.

The science fair was eleven days away, and Emile still could not explain the thing on his poster. The heading said "How Nicotine Hooks the Brain," and under it he had taped a diagram of a brain cell with a sad face drawn on it. That was not science. That was a sad face.

He cornered his partner Giuliano in the library after last period. Giuliano had a laptop open to a medical database, scrolling so fast the screen blurred.

"Look," Giuliano said, turning the screen. "Receptors. They're proteins on brain cells." He tapped a diagram. "The brain has its own chemical messenger, called acetylcholine. It fits into these receptors like a key in a lock."

"So the messenger is the key," Emile said slowly.

"And nicotine is a fake key. Same shape, fits the same lock." Giuliano spun the laptop toward him. "Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. That's what they're called, because nicotine fits them too."

Emile sat down so fast the chair squeaked. A fake key. He could see the whole poster suddenly: a door, a real key, a copy of the key, and a brain cell on the other side. He grabbed his notebook and started sketching before the idea could leak away.

Then the problem arrived. Ms. Bautista appeared at their table with her clipboard, which everyone knew meant bad news. "Your display needs a source form signed by a parent before the office will authorize you to use images from that database," she said. "And the fair is Friday setup. I need it tomorrow."

Emile's mother worked nights. She would already be asleep by the time he got home, and she left before he woke up. A signed form was impossible, which meant no diagram, which meant going back to the sad face. He stared at his sketch, and then at his sketch again, and realized something. He did not actually need the database image. He needed the fact, and he already had the fact. The form covered the pictures, not the idea. He could draw his own door, his own keys, his own lock, all from his notebook.

That night he left his mother a note on the kitchen counter.

"Mom. I don't need the form anymore, I'm drawing everything myself. But can you look at my poster sketch on the fridge and tell me if the lock looks like a lock? I'll check before school. Love, Emile."

In the morning the sketch was still on the fridge, and next to it in her handwriting was one word: "Lockish." Underneath she had drawn a tiny arrow pointing at his door and written "add hinges, more exciting."

At setup on Friday, a kid from another class wandered past their table, chewing gum, looking indifferent to every poster in the gym. Then he stopped. "Wait," he said, pointing at the two keys Emile had cut from foil. "The brain makes its own key?"

"Acetylcholine," Emile said. "And nicotine's the fake copy that fits the same lock."

The kid leaned in and tried the foil key against the cardboard lock himself.

Avery slid her flashcards across the desk and waited for Mr. Gupta to call on someone. Around the room, her classmates in Japanese class were whispering practice sentences to each other, and the windows of room 114 rattled whenever the heater kicked on. Today's assignment was family and pets, and Avery wanted to volunteer first, because last week she had frozen when asked to count to ten and Nigel had to whisper the last three numbers to her.

"Okaasan wa yasashii desu," she said when her turn came, sitting up straight. "My mother is kind. We have a cat. Neko ga imasu." She felt pretty good about it, especially the cat part, so the silence that followed confused her. Nigel frowned at his own paper. Richard raised his hand halfway and then lowered it. Mr. Gupta just smiled and said, "Almost. Try again, and this time think about whose mother it is."

Whose mother it is? Avery stared at the word on her card. Okaasan. She had copied it from the board on Monday, when Mr. Gupta had asked Nigel about his weekend and Nigel had said something with okaasan in it. Wait, she thought. Nigel was talking about his own mother on Monday, and Mr. Gupta didn't correct him. She tested a hypothesis in her head: the same word can't be wrong for Nigel and right for me unless the rule isn't about politeness at all, but about who you're talking about. When Nigel spoke to Mr. Gupta about his mother, maybe that made her someone else's mother from the listener's point of view. Which would mean Avery needed a different word for her own.

"Is it... haha?" she asked slowly, and watched Mr. Gupta's face. He nodded once, and she said it again, louder: "Haha wa yasashii desu." Richard leaned over and whispered that he'd made the exact same mistake in his first draft, and Avery felt her ears go warm but not in a bad way. On the board, Mr. Gupta wrote the two words side by side, one for your own family and one for somebody else's, and Avery copied them with a little arrow between them so she'd remember.

After class she quizzed Nigel in the hallway. "Your little brother, mine, same rule?" she asked, and he shrugged and said probably, so they made a game of it, taking turns inventing families. Avery drew a chart in the back of her notebook, two columns, and counted her correct answers against her wrong ones until the ratio stopped mattering because the wrong ones ran out. By Friday, when Mr. Gupta asked for volunteers, her hand was up before he finished the sentence. "Haha wa yasashii desu," she said, "neko ga imasu, and Nigel-san's okaasan makes great onigiri, apparently." Nigel laughed so hard he dropped his pencil.

On her first morning at Camp Windward, Emilia learned three things: the pancake syrup was watery, the mosquitoes were generous, and every swimmer at the waterfront had to have a buddy. Amber had been assigned to her before breakfast, a girl with a sunburned nose and a whistle she'd won in a raffle, which she blew for no reason at all.

"Buddies stick together," Amber said as they walked down to the lake. "When the lifeguards blow their whistles, that's a buddy check. Every pair has to grab hands and hold them up so the staff can count everyone fast."

"Everyone? At once?" Emilia asked.

"Every single swimmer. You'll see."

The water was warm and green, and for an hour Emilia forgot to be homesick. Then she noticed something glittering in the shallows near the reeds, half sunk in the mud. It looked like a compass, or a watch, and it was definitely not hers. She waded toward it, then out of the water entirely, following the shoreline until the glittering thing turned out to be a bottle cap and the swimming area was far behind her. Somewhere a whistle blew, once, sharp. She heard it the way you hear a bird, and kept hunting for the bottle cap's imaginary owner.

The second whistle was longer. Emilia looked up and saw the lifeguards standing on the dock with clipboards, and every swimmer in the lake was holding hands with a partner, arms raised. Except for one gap in the line, one girl standing alone with her hand up and nothing to hold. Amber. Emilia's stomach seemed to dissolve on the spot. She had never seen someone look worried like that, worried in a way that was almost contagious, because now she was worried too, and she was the reason.

She ran. The gravel path had seemed short before; now it stretched like taffy. The lifeguard on the dock was already reaching for the emergency radio, and Emilia did the fastest math of her life: if she didn't get back before that call went out, boats would launch, the whole camp would be searched, and her first day would become a story told at every campfire forever.

"I'm here!" she shouted, splashing into the shallows. "I'm the missing buddy!"

Amber grabbed her hand and hauled it into the air so hard Emilia's arm nearly left its socket. The lifeguard counted the pairs, found the number matched, and lowered the radio. He did not look happy, but he did say, "Nice sprint."

Later, sitting on the dock drying off, Emilia tried to figure out her own mistake, because she wanted a criterion for first-day success she could actually meet, and "never make a mistake" was not going to be it. Maybe the rule was simpler: when you have a buddy, stay where your buddy can see you.

"So what was so important out there?" Amber asked.

"A bottle cap. I thought it was a compass."

Amber laughed so hard she had to lie back on the dock. "Tomorrow we hunt for treasure together. Deal?"

"Deal," said Emilia, and shook on it, one buddy to another.

William had typed the message three times and deleted it twice. "Okay. See you there." He hit send anyway, because Zack had asked twice whether he was coming to the robotics club party, and ignoring it seemed worse.

The next morning in the computer lab, Zack sat two rows away and did not turn around. That alone was strange, because Zack usually talked through the whole class until Mr. Hosseini gave him the look. Today Zack just typed, his shoulders stiff, his face indifferent to the joke Artin was telling about a laptop that caught an infection from a bad download and started sneezing files everywhere. Artin laughed at his own joke, then leaned toward William and lowered his voice.

"It's you he's mad at," Artin whispered. "He showed me your text at lunch. He thinks you don't want to come. He said it sounded, like, angry." Artin had his own plan for the period, a poster for the coding contest he was desperate to conquer, but he kept glancing over at Zack instead of working on it. "Fix it before Friday, or the whole club party is going to be weird."

William stared at his screen. His message had been two words. Two words, and one of them was okay. How could okay sound angry? He opened his sent messages and read it again. Then he opened the message he had sent to Artin the same night, about the game they were both playing: "no way, that boss took me four tries lol." No period. No capital letters. It looked friendly. His message to Zack had a period after every sentence, sitting there like a little closed door.

He had an idea. He typed the exact same message twice and sent one to Artin as a test: "Okay." and then "okay". Artin read them, frowned, and typed back, "the first one sounds like you're mad at me?? the second one's fine." William's pulse ticked faster. It was the period. Same words, different dot, different feeling. He searched the school database, feeling like a detective, and found a news article about a small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers. They had found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one. He read it twice. It wasn't just Zack being dramatic. It was a real thing that had been measured.

He typed fast: "zack. i was NOT mad. i just used periods. a 2016 study from binghamton university says texts with periods at the end actually seem less sincere than the same text without one. no period this time, see" He sent it without any punctuation at the end at all, then sat very still, watching Zack's screen from across the room.

Zack's typing stopped. His shoulders shook once, then again. He turned around and held up his phone, showing a new message he had typed: "okay okay. bring snacks"

"Deal," William said, and behind them Mr. Hosseini cleared his throat and pointed at the clock.

The line outside the arena wrapped around two whole blocks, and Jake had been in it since six in the morning. He clutched the ten dollars he had saved from mowing lawns, because the radio station had promised that the first five hundred tickets to the Silverhawks show would sell for just five dollars each. Behind him, Colt peeled off his hoodie and tied it around his waist, and Ayden shared a granola bar with a girl in front of them who had forgotten breakfast. "It's like a monsoon hit," Ayden said, watching the crowd pour in from the parking lot. "Everybody in town must be here."

"I did the math," Jake said. "The arena holds five thousand, but they're only selling five hundred of the cheap seats. After that, regular tickets are thirty-five dollars." Thirty-five was more than he had, more than he could get before Saturday. He wanted this the way you want things at twelve, completely and without excuses.

The doors opened at ten, and the line shuffled forward in short bursts. Jake watched the board above the ticket window like it was a scoreboard. Cheap seats: 412 left. Then 300. Then 178. Each time the number dropped, his stomach dropped with it. When they were still half a block from the door, the number read 61, and a boy in a Silverhawks shirt came striding out, waving his ticket like a flag. Behind him came a girl with red eyes, holding nothing. "They said there's still regular tickets," she told her mom, "but I only brought ten dollars."

That was the moment Jake understood something he couldn't see but could feel all along the sidewalk. Hundreds of people wanted the five-dollar tickets, and there were only five hundred of them, so most people in this line were going to walk away with nothing. The price was too low for how few tickets there were. "It's a shortage," Ayden said when Jake described it, because Ayden's older sister took an economics class and used words like that at dinner. "That's what they call the gap when more people want a thing than there is of the thing."
