"Can we return her to the stage she was before?"

Parker ignored this. He needed a distraction, and it needed to be good. The book suggested peekaboo, but Ruby could not see his hands from inside her own tantrum. He looked around the room instead. The curtains were camouflage-green, the exact color of his uncle's hunting jacket, and behind them the window looked out on an arid patch of yard where a sprinkler dragged its slow arc across the grass. Water. Babies liked water.

He carried Ruby to the window and pulled the curtain back. Nothing. Then the sprinkler swept past the glass, spraying a fan of drops that caught the afternoon light, and Ruby stopped mid-scream, mouth still open, as if she'd forgotten what the mouth was for.

"Ba," said Ruby.

"Ba," agreed Parker. They stood there through four full sweeps of the sprinkler. By the third one she was laughing, a sound like a small rubber duck being defended.

When the parents came home two hours later, Ruby was asleep in her crib and Parker was on the couch with the book, feeling professional. The mother counted out his pay and glanced at the paperback.

"Did she cry when we left?"

"For a while," Parker said. "Then we watched the sprinkler."

"Separation anxiety," she said. "The sitter before you called it 'the apocalypse.'"

Parker held out his hand for the money. "Book's on page one-fourteen," he said.

Isaac spread his pencils across the kitchen table and checked the clock again. The art contest entries had to be at the community center by four o'clock, and it was already half past two. His drawing, a portrait of his dog Pepper curled on the porch, looked wrong. The shadows were so faint that Pepper seemed to be floating, like a ghost dog.

He frowned at the page. Last night the shading had looked darker. He hadn't changed anything, except that this morning he had knocked the pencil box over and shoved everything back in a hurry.

His friend Cruz arrived, holding a folded note from Billie, who was home with a sprained ankle and couldn't come. Isaac opened it. "You said your dog looks washed out," Billie had written. "Check which pencil you actually grabbed. Not all pencils are the same. My mom got me a whole set and the letters mean opposite things. Billie."

Isaac held his pencil up to the window light. Near the end, in tiny letters, it said 4H. He found another one, a 6B, and made a test stripe with each on the corner of a scrap paper. The 6B went down dark and velvety. The 4H left a mark so pale he could barely see it.

"So that's it," he said. "H must be for hardness. And B is for blackness." He started sorting the whole box, deciding he could categorize them into two groups, the H pile for light lines and the B pile for shadows.

While he worked, Cruz bent the copper wire they were using for the frame of Pepper's collar tag. "This stuff is resilient," Cruz said, snapping it back straight. "You can bend it a hundred times and it doesn't crack. Billie says it's actually an alloy, two metals mixed together."

"Then it can survive the judges," Isaac said. He layered the 6B into the porch shadow under Pepper's chin, then along her back where the evening light faded. The dog sank onto the boards, solid and heavy, exactly the way she looked at dinnertime when she was hoping for scraps.

At ten to four they ran the six blocks to the community center, the drawing in a plastic sleeve, the wire tag jingling against it in Isaac's backpack. The volunteer at the desk pointed to the entry box. Isaac slid his drawing in just as the clock struck four, and Cruz clapped him on the shoulder.

"Ghost dog no more," Cruz said.

Ellie stood at the bathroom sink outside the gym, index cards fanned in one wet hand, and tried to say it out loud one more time before Mr. Halvorsen called her name. "Dopamine release teaches the brain that a behavior is worth repeating," she whispered to the mirror, "and that's how nicotine use becomes a learned habit." The words kept sliding around like soap. She knew them. She just couldn't make anyone feel them.

The bathroom door banged open and Sirine came in, still holding her phone, thumb already moving. "They moved the science talks to after lunch," Sirine said. "Caiden went first and it was a disaster. He just read his cards." She glanced at the screen, frowned, put the phone face down on the sink ledge, and picked it up again ten seconds later.

"That," Ellie said, pointing. "Do that again."

"Do what?"

"Put it down. Watch how fast you pick it back up."

Sirine rolled her eyes but played along, setting the phone down flat. They both stared at it. Her hand twitched toward it twice before she finally snatched it up, laughing. "Okay, that's invasive, your experiment. And I lost."

Ellie felt something click into place, the way a jar lid does when you finally get the right angle. "Don't you see? Your brain got a little hit of good feeling every time you checked for likes. Dopamine. It teaches your brain that checking is worth repeating, so it turns into a habit you don't even decide on." She flipped a card over. "Nicotine does the same thing. The dopamine release teaches the brain that nicotine is worth repeating, and that's how it becomes a learned habit. It's not weakness. It's learning."

Sirine leaned against the stall door, quiet for a moment. "Last week I told my brother he was pathetic for vaping. He tried to quit twice and I said he just didn't really want to." She picked at the edge of Ellie's card. "Maybe wanting isn't the whole thing. Maybe I was judging him for something his brain got taught." She didn't say sorry out loud, but she looked like she was thinking about texting him.

"I was going to stand up there and read cards like Caiden," Ellie said. She dropped the whole stack into the trash can, one by one, like dealing out a hand. "My mom would have to authorize a search party to find my grade after that."

"You're just going to talk?"

"I'm going to talk about her." Ellie nodded at the phone in Sirine's hand. "You're going to lend me your lock screen, and I'm going to make everyone watch your thumb."

Sirine clutched the phone to her chest. "Never. We'd have to sign a treaty."

"Two weeks of me carrying your backpack," Ellie said. "Final offer."

The bell rang down the hall. Sirine held out the phone. "Deal," she said. "Go make Caiden cry."

The flyer on the community centre bulletin board said FREE COMMUNITY BAND, ALL LEVELS, and Quinn had taken that as a personal dare. She'd been playing piano since second grade, but only alone, in her living room, where nobody could hear her mistakes. Now she sat in the third row of the band room with a borrowed keyboard and a folder of music, wedged between Ayesha on flute and Ayana on trumpet, waiting for something to happen.

Something happened. It was the piece, all right, a real one with parts for everyone, and for the first two pages Quinn kept up fine. Then the sheet music did something sneaky. Under the notes it said crescendo, with one of those long skinny angle shapes opening toward the right, and Quinn, who had never seen one before, made a reasonable guess: this must be the part where you get loud. She got loud. So did everyone else, all at once, like a door slamming.

"Whoa," said Ayana, lowering her trumpet. "We sound like a fire alarm."

Ms. Cardinal, who ran the band, held up her hands. "Let's take that bar again. Gentler this time." She did not say what a crescendo was. She mostly said things like "listen to each other" and "try it again," which was either very wise or a way of drinking her coffee while the band taught itself.

Quinn stared at the angle shape. It started skinny and got wide, like a triangle lying on its side, opening up as the music went along. She had guessed "loud," but maybe the shape was the instruction itself, not just a decoration. Gradually getting louder, widening bit by bit, instead of everyone jumping to loud at once like the whole band had been startled by the same bee. She flipped the page and found the shape going the other way, closing down toward skinny, marked diminuendo. If one shape meant gradually louder, the mirror of it probably meant gradually softer. Opposite directions, opposite results. It was almost annoying how sensible that was.

She leaned over to Ayesha. "So crescendo means gradually louder, right? Not just loud."

"Gradually louder," Ayesha confirmed. "And diminuendo is the opposite, gradually softer. Decrescendo too, same thing, they just gave it two names because apparently one wasn't enough."

"Like how we needed two words for trumpet mute and trumpet very muted," Ayana said. "Band is complicated."

They tried the bar again. This time Quinn started quiet and let each measure climb a little louder, and because she was watching Ayesha out of the corner of her eye and Ayesha was doing the same thing, the sound built instead of slammed. When they hit the diminuendo, the whole band eased down together like a tide going out. Ms. Cardinal put down her coffee. That alone felt like a standing ovation.

That night, Quinn texted her grandmother, who had played clarinet in school approximately one hundred years ago.

"Grandma," she wrote, "I was right that crescendo means loud and wrong that it means loud immediately. It means gradually louder, and diminuendo means gradually softer. Also a girl named Ayesha can play flute quietly enough to emphasize a mouse sneeze, which is a legitimate skill."

Her grandmother wrote back within a minute, which meant she had been sitting by her phone. "In my day we called it getting carried away. Proud of you. Did you get your flu vaccine this year? Musicians need lungs."

Quinn laughed, then looked at the sheet music spread across her bed, all triangles and Italian words, and set her alarm ten minutes early to practice the quiet parts. The loud parts, she figured, could take care of themselves.

Thomas had a fence post, a stick of chalk, and a plan that he hoped would make him sound credible when Ms. Weber asked the seasons question on Monday. The question was, "Explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons," and Thomas suspected that "the Earth tilts, so, seasons" would not earn full marks. He needed proof he could point to.

So he stood in his backyard at noon on a bright June day, holding his mother's kitchen timer because he did not trust himself to notice when exactly noon arrived. When the timer beeped, he chalked the tip of the fence post's shadow onto the patio, measured it with a tape measure, and wrote "June noon: 41 centimeters" in his notebook. His friend Chael watched from a lawn chair, eating chips with the focus of a much older man.

"Forty-one," Thomas said. "Now we wait."

"Until December," Chael said. "That's your whole plan? We sit here and conserve our energy for six months?"

"My adversary is not you," Thomas said. "My adversary is the Sun."

Chael pointed out that the Sun was probably not taking sides. Thomas ignored him, because in December they came back. Zak joined them for the second measurement, mostly for the hot chocolate, and the three of them stood around the fence post in their coats while the timer counted down. At the beep, Thomas chalked the shadow's tip, measured, and wrote the number down twice because he did not believe it the first time.

"One hundred and ninety-two centimeters," Zak read over his shoulder. "That's huge. It goes past the birdbath."

"In June it barely got past the patio," Thomas said. He drew two lines in his notebook, one short, one long, and stared at them. "Same post. Same fence. Same noon." He looked up at the low winter sun, squinting, then flipped back to his June page. "The Sun climbs higher in the sky in summer. That's why the shadow's short. And in winter it stays low, so the shadow stretches out." He tapped the notebook. "That's my proof. A fence post doesn't lie."

"A fence post can't lie," Chael agreed. "It's a fence post. It doesn't do anything."

Zak crouched next to the long chalk mark by the birdbath. "So on Monday, you're going to tell Ms. Weber that the seasons are real because of a fence post?"

"I'm going to tell her the Sun sits higher at noon in summer, and my shadow agrees with me," Thomas said. He closed the notebook, tucked it under his arm, and picked up the tape measure. "Also, we're marking the patio again in March. Someone has to check the in-between."

Alexis had been saving her babysitting money for three weeks so she could treat Khaled and Emerson to dinner at Mr. Yamamoto's restaurant, the new one with the paper lanterns that glowed like small orange moons. She had a plan, too: she would order everything in Japanese. She had practiced saying "good evening" on the bus until the driver gave her a strange look, and she had wrapped a box of almond cookies from her grandmother's recipe to give Mr. Yamamoto, because her mother always said you never arrived at someone's place empty-handed.

The greeting worked. Mr. Yamamoto's eyes crinkled when Alexis said it at the door, and he bowed slightly, which made all three of them bow back, Khaled so deeply he nearly clipped a tray of soup. The gift worked even better. He turned the cookie box over in his hands like it was treasure and said he would share it with his wife. Alexis floated to the table feeling like some kind of ambassador for her whole neighborhood.

Then came the rice. Khaled, mid-story about his disastrous science fair volcano, stabbed his chopsticks straight down into his bowl so he could gesture with both hands. "So then the baking soda went everywhere," he said, arms wide, chopsticks standing up from his rice like two little towers. The table next to them went quiet. Mr. Yamamoto, passing with a teapot, stopped. He didn't say anything, but his face changed, the way a room changes when a cloud crosses the sun.

Alexis's stomach dropped. She tried to figure out what had just happened, running through possibilities like cards. It wasn't the noise. It wasn't the gesturing. It was the chopsticks, she realized. It was where they were standing. She remembered the incense sticks her grandmother lit at her grandfather's photo, thin and upright in a little dish, and the cold feeling of that memory lined up perfectly with the look on Mr. Yamamoto's face. "Khaled," she whispered, "lay them across the bowl. Trust me." He did, slowly, like he was defusing a bomb. Emerson leaned in. "Wait, why?" "It looks like incense," Alexis murmured. "You know, offered to the dead." Khaled's ears turned red as the lanterns.

Mr. Yamamoto came back with the teapot and, just like that, the cloud lifted. He topped off their cups and even chuckled at Khaled's volcano story, which Khaled nervously restarted from the beginning. Later, when the tempura arrived, Alexis watched Khaled lay his chopsticks neatly across his bowl every single time he paused, careful as a surgeon. "This table manner thing is controversial," he muttered, "in my house we just have forks." Emerson snorted so hard that rice nearly made a second escape. Alexis raised her teacup. "To ambassadors," she said, and three cups clinked over the steaming bowls.

At dinner on Tuesday, Dad announced that most students at Joseph's school walked to school. He said it the way he said everything, loud and certain, stabbing his fork toward the window for emphasis. Joseph's little sister was pushing peas around her plate, and Mom was already shaking her head, but nobody argued. Joseph set down his glass. "How do you know?" Dad shrugged. "Look at the parking lot. The car line's tiny. It has to be most." Joseph turned his fork over, thinking. "But that's just what you think. It could be checked." His sister rolled her eyes, but Dad leaned back. "Fine. Check it."

The next morning Joseph stood at the front gate with a clipboard and two pencils, because Margot had insisted on a backup. Kate arrived first and grabbed the clipboard. "Are we counting walkers or bus riders?" "Both," Joseph said. "And bikers and car riders. Every student." Margot frowned. "That's the whole school. Nobody's ever done that." "It's checkable," Joseph said, "even if nobody's checked it yet." He had worked that out on the walk over: a thing didn't have to be proven to be provable. They only needed a tally sheet and one morning, or maybe three mornings, in case Wednesday was weird.

Wednesday was weird. A hawk, big and predatory, stooped out of the sky at the soccer field, scattering pigeons, and half the walkers stopped to gawk, which messed up the count. Kate laughed so hard she dropped the clipboard in a puddle. Joseph shared his backup pencil with Margot, whose hands were cold, and lent Kate his jacket sleeve to dry the page. By Thursday they had three clean tally columns and a real answer: 61 percent of students walked. Dad was right. Joseph felt his certainty diminish a little anyway, because it had never been certainty, only a lucky guess.

At Friday dinner, Joseph slid the tally sheet across the table. Dad read it twice. "Sixty-one percent. Huh." He looked almost disappointed. "You know I never checked that," he said quietly. "I just remembered walking when I was your age and figured." Mom smiled at Joseph. "So you proved him right." "I proved it," Joseph said. "He guessed it. Those aren't the same thing." Dad laughed and raised his glass of water to him.

But then Kate texted him a photo of Thursday's sheet, zoomed in on the biker column, and Joseph went still. He had biked on Thursday, for the first time all year, because counting walkers had made him want to try it. Without him, the walking and biking side dropped to 49.5 percent. He had pushed it over "most" himself. He was both the surveyor and, sort of, the result.

At dinner he told Dad the whole thing, and Dad set down his fork and grinned. "So the claim was true because of the kid checking the claim." Joseph's little sister, still pushing peas, said, "That's so weird," and Joseph propped the tally sheet against the salt shaker where everyone could see it. "Next week I'm doing the bus."

Victor sat at the back table in the art room, smudging pencil lines with the side of his hand. Ms. Augustin had told the class to draw a street that looked like it went somewhere, and Victor's street did not. His road edges spread apart as they went back, like a river getting wider instead of thinner.

"You got the chronic slouch again," Adelina said from the next stool, tapping his paper. "Your road's all floppy."

Victor leaned over his page. He had a ruler, and he had an idea. If the road was supposed to get smaller as it went back, then the two edges had to aim somewhere. He laid the ruler along his left edge and slid the pencil along it, extending the line onto a spare sheet clipped behind the drawing. He did the same with the right edge. The two lines crossed at one dot near the top of the spare sheet. Then he extended the sidewalk lines too. One of them crossed the same dot. The other two wandered off to different places entirely.

He looked across the room at Caden's drawing, the one Ms. Augustin had taped to the board as an example. Caden was a veteran of three summer art camps and had drawn a street with shopfronts and streetlights, and everything on it looked like it was actually sinking into the paper. Victor borrowed a viewfinder from the supply shelf and held it up, sighting across the room like a pirate. The ceiling lines above the windows, the shelf edges, even the baseboard all ran toward him in slanted directions. When he marked those slants lightly on a scrap, they pointed at one height, the height of his own eyes.

He went back to Caden's drawing and checked the streetlight on the left against the one on the right, the second-story windows against the doors. With his ruler he found every one of them. "They all go to one point," he said.

"Told you," Caden said from across the room without looking up. "Vanishing point. Everything sits on the horizon line, at your eye level."

Victor erased his floppy road. He drew a straight line across the page where his eye level would be, picked a point on it, and ran every edge toward that point from there. When Adelina and Caden argued about whose turn it was at the good pencil sharpener, he stepped in and settled it with a coin flip before Ms. Augustin could come over, which kept everyone drawing.

At the end of class Ms. Augustin walked the rows. She stopped at Victor's table and picked up the spare sheet, the one with the crossing lines and the dot. "This is the better drawing," she said, and pinned it to the board above Caden's.

Hayden knocked on Sage's door holding his phone like a ticket to somewhere far away. Sage's grandmother, who everyone called Abuela, was visiting from Mexico for two weeks, and Sage had promised that today they would finally practice real Spanish, not the kind from worksheets.

"My motivation is simple," Sage said, pulling him inside. "If I can talk to Abuela without my mom translating, she'll make us churros every single day of her visit."

The kitchen smelled like cinnamon and hot oil. Abuela was already stirring something on the stove. Hayden's heart hammered. He had one job, and he had practiced the sentence twenty times on the bus: "Dónde está la biblioteca?" Where is the library? It was a game they had invented, because Abuela had never been to their town before and Sage thought asking her for directions would be hilarious, since obviously she did not know either.

Abuela laughed when he asked, then played along anyway. "Dos cuadras," she said, and traced a little square in the air with her spoon. "Una cuadra, dos cuadras. Luego, a la derecha." Hayden nodded fast, thanked her, and jogged outside with Sage to test the answer on the actual streets.

"Two streets, then right," Hayden said, counting intersections. But when they hit the second street and turned, the library was nowhere in sight. They found a laundromat, an eccentric old house painted purple with a wind chime made of spoons, and a dog that barked at them like they owed it money. No library.

"Maybe you heard it wrong," Sage said.

"No, it was dos." Hayden stopped on the sidewalk, frowning. She had traced a square in the air. A square. Like a block. He pictured Abuela's spoon drawing its little outline, and something clicked. "Wait. She didn't mean streets. Una cuadra, two cuadras, blocks. In much of Latin America a cuadra is a city block, so dos cuadras means two blocks." He pointed down the street. "We counted streets, not blocks."

They walked one more block, turned right, and there it was, brick and wide and glowing in the afternoon sun like it had been waiting for them. Sage whooped so loudly that a woman watering her roses looked up.

Back in the kitchen, Hayden asked Abuela, in careful Spanish, whether it was really two blocks. She clapped her hands and said yes, that a cuadra was a block, exactly that. Sage slid into the seat beside her and started a sentence in wobbly Spanish, and Abuela reached for the flour.

"Churros?" she asked, raising one eyebrow.

"Churros," Sage said.

The buzzer hadn't even started the game yet, and Eli was already nervous. Coach had handed him the ball at practice and said, "You're running point today. Play the one." Play the one? Eli had grabbed the ball, nodded like he understood, and spent the whole walk to the court at the park trying to figure out what that could possibly mean.

Last summer flashed back to him as he laced his shoes under the crooked rim at the park court. He'd been the worst kid at Ms. Wanjiru's summer clinic, so bad that she'd made him stand at the free throw line and just mimic her footwork for an entire week, over and over, until his pivot foot stopped sliding all over the place. "You learn with your feet before your hands," she'd said. Maybe learning this new thing would be the same: slow, then sudden.

Miller and Andy jogged onto the blacktop, and Andy was already bouncing a ball off his own forehead. "You're point guard now," Miller said. "So call a play, genius. First game to eleven."

"I'm working on it," Eli said. In his head, he turned the coach's words over. Play the one. The point guard brought the ball up, every time. He was the main ball handler, everyone knew that, and if the coach called it a number, then maybe every spot on the floor had a number, like seats in a theater. The one had to be the spot with the ball.

Andy checked the ball to him and the game began. Eli dribbled left, and Miller stepped out from behind Andy and planted himself like a fence. That was a screen. Eli had seen it a hundred times on TV without knowing it had a name, and now it hit him: the screen was the whole play. He could use Miller's body to shake Andy loose, then Miller could pivot and roll toward the basket, and Eli would dish it to him at the last second. A pick and roll. His cousin had yelled it at a Knicks game once, and Eli had copied it into his memory without knowing what it meant.

He tried it. He drove hard off Miller's hip, dragging Andy with him, then whipped a bounce pass behind him to where Miller should have been rolling. The ball skidded out of bounds. Andy laughed so hard he had to hold his knees. "That was an offense this impoverished," Miller wheezed. "We couldn't even feed ourselves."

"Again," Eli said, gripping the ball. The idea wasn't wrong, he was almost sure of that. The pass had failed because Miller rolled one way while Eli threw the other, and that was a problem you could fix with a signal. "Next time I drive, you roll to the rim. Watch my eyes, not the ball."

They ran it again. Miller set the screen, Eli dragged Andy past it, and this time Miller spun and cut hard to the hoop, exactly on cue. Eli's pass arrived a half second before Andy could recover, soft and low, right into Miller's hands. Layup. Miller screamed like they'd won a championship instead of scoring one basket out of eleven.

"One more," Eli called out, already backing up with the ball, already seeing the whole floor in front of him like a map with numbered streets. "Miller, screen left."

Juliette set the soccer ball at the top of the driveway, where the cement sloped gently toward the garage door. "You time it," she told Jeremiah, holding out her mother's stopwatch. "I'll mark where it stops, and we'll do ten rolls for the graph." She wanted the science extra credit, but she also wanted something that looked like a real hill on graph paper, not the flat line her last attempt had produced.

The first roll went fine. The second one did not. Jeremiah called out "2.4 seconds" while Sabrina, timing the same roll on her phone from the porch, said "2.2 seconds." They argued about it until Juliette held up both hands. "Wait. Same ball, same slope, same moment. One of these numbers is wrong, or both are." She made them time three more rolls together, and every time the stopwatch and the phone disagreed by about a fifth of a second, sometimes one way, sometimes the other.

She sat on the front step with her notebook and stared at the two columns of numbers. It was like the disagreement itself was a clue. "It's us," she said slowly. "Your thumb doesn't press the button the instant you see the ball move. Neither does Sabrina's. Our reaction time is about a fifth of a second, and it's in every single measurement." Jeremiah frowned at the stopwatch as if it had betrayed him personally. "So all our numbers are wrong?" "Not exactly," Juliette said. "But the mistake is the same size no matter what we time. So if we timed something longer, the mistake would matter less."

"We could make the run longer," Sabrina said, already looking down the street, where the sidewalk ran flat and straight for half a block to the stop sign. Juliette grinned. A longer run was harder to roll on, but the numbers would be cleaner, and a clean graph was probable to come out of it, which was more than she could say for the driveway mess. "New alliance," she declared. "Same jobs, longer course. And this time I want to replicate each roll at least twice, so we can see if our timings agree."

Mr. Oyelaran, watering his roses next door, watched them chalk a start line at the top of the sidewalk. "Science project?" he asked. "Measuring how fast a ball rolls," Juliette said, "and then drawing it. Distance on one axis, time on the other." He nodded and went back to his roses, but a minute later he called, "My garage has a ramp, if you ever want a steeper one." Juliette said they might take him up on that.

The long rolls worked. When Sabrina's phone said 6.1 seconds and Jeremiah's stopwatch said 6.3, the gap was there but it was small, and the points on Juliette's graph fell into a tidy climbing line. She taped the graph into her notebook and held it up for the others to see. "That," she said, "is our hill." Jeremiah leaned in and traced the line with one finger, from the bottom corner to the top edge of the page.

Sebastian sat on the floor of his half-empty bedroom, surrounded by boxes, holding a stack of letters he had found under his desk. In three days his family would be driving to Rockford, and everything he owned would either come with him or get left behind. He had already said goodbye to Malik and Clemence at school, and the goodbye had felt too short, like a song cut off in the middle.

"What are you doing up there?" his mother called from the hall.

"Packing," Sebastian called back, which was only half true. He was mostly thinking about the mail. His father had filled out the change of address form at the post office that morning, and the clerk had said something Sebastian couldn't stop turning over: a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for twelve months. Not forever. Twelve months. Which meant the postal system would carry his old life to his new house, but only for a while.

He tested the idea before he trusted it. That evening he wrote a letter to himself, addressed it to the old house on Delancey Street, and dropped it in the corner mailbox with his father. If the rule was real, the letter would leave his old address behind, catch up with him, and land in Rockford. If it was not real, the letter would sit in some dead pile in his old town, and he would know the rule had failed. Then Malik called, and Sebastian asked him to send something too, anything, to the old address. "To the old address?" Malik said. "That's the whole point," Sebastian said. "I want to see what happens."

The first week in Rockford was boxes, new streets, and a grocery store where the cashier recommended what she called a nutritious multigrain bread, which turned out to be better than it sounded. Sebastian kept checking the mailbox even though he told himself not to. Six days, nothing. Eight days, nothing, and he started to think his test had failed, that somewhere in Illinois a letter addressed to a boy who no longer lived there was drifting toward oblivion.

On the ninth day his father handed him an envelope with a yellow sticker on it. The sticker showed his old Delancey Street address crossed out above the new Rockford one, and inside, in Sebastian's own handwriting, was the letter he had mailed to himself before they left. He read his own words, standing at the kitchen counter, feeling like he had caught the postal system in the middle of a secret operation.

Two days later a second envelope arrived, thick and lumpy, forwarded from the old address the same way. Inside was a note from Malik and one from Clemence, plus a flattened penny she had put on the train tracks near school. "In social studies we had to elaborate on a topic for two whole minutes," Malik had written, "so I talked about how moving away doesn't end a friendship, it just changes the address on it. Ms. Thompson said it was the best one."

Sebastian carried the letters up to his new room, set the flattened penny on the windowsill where it would catch the morning light, and started writing his reply.

The tent smelled of pine and damp canvas, and rain ticked against the fabric like a slow clock. Kayla knelt on her sleeping bag with her science folder spread open between the lantern and a bag of trail mix. Mr. Kim had assigned the project before the trip, comparing the climate of a desert and a rainforest, and he had made one thing clear: they had to decide for themselves whether their chosen cities really counted. A thick fog settling over the campsite would have hindered anyone hoping to measure the night sky, but Kayla only needed her graphs.

Estelle unzipped the tent flap, letting in a gust of cool, wet air. "Chad's dad says the rain won't stop till morning," she reported, dropping down beside Kayla. "What are you doing with all that paper?"

"Trying to figure out if Singapore is actually a rainforest climate or if I just picked it because it sounded good." Kayla smoothed the rainfall graph flat. The bars rose in a solid wall, month after month, with no dry gap anywhere. Beside it, the temperature line sat high and almost flat across the whole year.

Chad crawled in after Estelle, shaking water off his jacket. "If it rains that much all year, obviously it's a rainforest," he said, reaching for the trail mix.

"Obviously isn't evidence," Kayla said. She flipped through her notes and found the page she'd copied from the climate chapter, the one Mr. Kim had marked with a sticky note that just said check. At the bottom, in her own handwriting, was the rule: every month had to average at least 18 degrees Celsius, and every month had to have at least 60 millimeters of rain. She read it twice, then held the page up to the lantern.

"So I check each month," she said slowly. "One at a time." She put her finger on January. "Eighty millimeters, twenty-six degrees. Good." February. March. April. Her finger moved down the wall of bars like a climber finding holds. Estelle leaned in and started calling out the numbers for May and June while Chad, without being asked, checked the temperature line for July and August. Somewhere outside, water dripped steadily from a branch onto the tent roof.

Near the end of the stack, Kayla stopped. "February only has sixty-two millimeters." She checked the number again, her pulse quick even though she already knew the answer. "Still over sixty. All twelve months pass." She wrote tropical rainforest climate beside the city name and underlined it, then pulled the desert graph toward her, where Cairo's bars barely rose off the bottom of the page.

"Desert next," she said, tapping the thin little rectangles. "This should take about ten seconds."

Jonathan stood in the doorway of Ms. Andersen's classroom with a bowl of his mother's potato salad clutched against his chest, watching the families file in for the international potluck. His family had lived here only three weeks, since his father's job moved them from Lyon, and tonight was supposed to be the night he finally made friends like Abraham and Riaan, who sat in the back row laughing at something on Riaan's phone.

He remembered his last day in Lyon, when his cousin Élodie had shown up at the farewell party and kissed his cheeks twice, then his uncle Alain had arrived and done it three times, and Jonathan had whispered to Élodie that Uncle Alain must be extra sad about the move. She had laughed so hard she had to sit down. That was the trouble with moving: every place had its own invisible rules, and he could not see them until he broke one.

"Jonathan!" Ms. Andersen waved him toward the long table near the windows. "Put your dish anywhere. Abraham brought his grandmother's dumplings, and Riaan brought samosas." Jonathan set down the bowl and hesitated, because back home you never handed food straight to the host. You set it down and let her admire it first, and his mother had spent ten minutes perfecting the parsley garnish so it would flourish properly, green and bright against the yellow. Here, Abraham's dish had landed on the table like a basketball.

At dinner the differences piled up. Riaan's family ate with their right hands only, bread torn small. Abraham's grandmother refused to let anyone start until the eldest guest had taken the first bite. Jonathan, working these out quietly, kept his hands in his lap between courses, and when Abraham slurped his soup without a single glance from anyone, Jonathan filed that away too. His mother would have gasped.

Then Riaan's older brother walked in late, and Riaan jumped up to greet him with a quick, easy back-slapping hug. Something clicked in Jonathan's mind. Back home, friends greeted each other with cheek kisses, la bise, his mother called it, and the number of kisses changed depending on the region, which was exactly why Élodie had laughed. The rule was invisible, and the only way to find it was to watch and guess and get it wrong.

So when Abraham's cousin arrived, a boy from another town, and stood awkwardly holding his container of cookies, Jonathan did not stick out his hand or go in for a hug. He waited, hands loose at his sides, and let the cousin choose first. The cousin nodded. Jonathan nodded back. "Smart move," Riaan said, leaning over. "Last year some kid high-fived him and he just stared at it like it was a dead fish."

Maybe the greeting rules here were permanent, or maybe they shifted from house to house the way the kisses did back home, from two to three with no warning at all. Jonathan could not be sure, and he decided that was fine. He tore a piece of bread, kept his elbows off the table, and slid the last samosa onto Abraham's plate. "Trade you," he said, "for one of those dumplings."

Ariana spread her poster board across the folding table at the edge of the gymnasium, smoothing the curling corners with her palm. Behind her, eighth graders were hanging banners from the bleachers, and the smell of floor wax mixed with the hot glue someone was using two tables down. Her project measured how high a basketball bounced after being dropped from different heights, and her graph was supposed to be the crucial part, the one thing the judges would look at first. She had titled the bottom axis "bounce height" and the side axis "drop height," and she had felt proud of it until Konnor leaned over from the next table.

"Mine looked like that last night," he said, holding up his own poster, which showed a graph with a small rectangle of white paper pasted over one corner. "I had mine backwards. Arabella caught it at her kitchen table when we were redoing our boards."

Ariana felt her stomach tighten. "Backwards how? It's just two lines with dots on them."

"By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis," Arabella said, arriving with a roll of tape dangling from her wrist. She said it fast, like a line she'd repeated all week. "My brother made me say it ten times."

Ariana stared at her poster. She dropped the ball from heights she chose, one meter, two meters, three meters. Those were her choices, the drops. The bounce height was what came out of the experiment, the thing that depended on what she dropped it from. If that rule was true, she had put each thing on the wrong side. She looked up and down the gymnasium, hunting for evidence, and saw Mr. Pelletier setting up the judges' table near the far doors. She didn't want to ask him and look unprepared, so she walked the rows instead, pretending to stretch her legs, inhaling slowly to calm herself while she peeked at other projects. A plant-growth board had days along the bottom. A music-and-heart-rate board had tempo along the bottom. Every single one put the thing the experimenter chose on the horizontal line.

She hurried back to her table and rummaged through her backpack for graph paper. Konnor slid his pencil box across without being asked. She redrew the whole graph, drop heights marching along the bottom, bounce heights climbing the side, and taped the new sheet over the old one just as Mr. Pelletier called, "Fifteen minutes, people."

The first judge stopped at her table, ran a finger along the fresh graph, and said, "Nice, clean axes. Walk me through it."

"Every drop height I chose runs along here," Ariana said, tapping the bottom of the page, "and the bounce it produced climbs up here."

Addison stood on the blocks in lane four, squeezed the excess water from her suit, and told herself the tryout was simple: three heats of two hundred metres, and the top four swimmers made the team. She had left her water bottle on the kitchen counter that morning, and when she reached into her bag between warm-up and the first heat, her hand closed on nothing but a damp towel. Alanna leaned over the rope from lane five.

"You can share mine," Alanna said, holding up a squeeze bottle with a shark sticker on it. "It's mostly full."

"Thanks. After heat two," Addison said, because her stomach felt tight when she drank right before racing. She won the first heat easily. Coach circled her time on the clipboard and wrote "exceptional" beside it with a short pencil.

By the middle of the second heat her arms felt heavy, as though someone had slipped weights inside her suit, and her split times crept up even though she was trying harder. She dragged herself out, breathing hard, and found a message on her phone from Alanna, sent from the bench where she was resting between events: "My sister's a sports-science major and she says swimmers sweat more than they think, even in the water. Losing about 2 percent of your body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce performance, especially in endurance events. DRINK. NOW." Addison read it twice. Nobody had said a word about sweat; the pool kept everyone wet and cool, so it was invisible, like a thermostat set too low in a house where you could not see the dial. But the numbers fit. Her body weight was roughly fifty kilos, and two percent of that was about a kilogram, and she had been in the water for over an hour with nothing to drink. She took Alanna's bottle, drank until her throat stopped feeling like a dried sponge, and then drank a little more.

The third heat was the one that counted. Addison pushed off the blocks, and somewhere around the third turn, instead of fading the way she had before, she found her rhythm again. Her arms turned over smoothly, and when she touched the wall, the scoreboard showed her fastest time of the day. Coach wrote her name on the top line of the team list.

On the bus home, Alanna flopped into the seat beside her. "So are you going to carry two bottles from now on, in case you abandon one again?"

"Three bottles," Addison said. She pressed the cold metal of Alanna's shark bottle against her forehead and grinned. "One for me, one for you, and one for whoever forgets theirs."

Paige stood in Ms. He's garage, which had been turned into a laundry room with two folding tables and a web of drying lines strung overhead like a canopy. Ms. He had left a note pinned to the washer before driving to the airport, and Paige read it again. "Sort darks from lights, wash cold, and whatever you do, iron the yellow shirt last. Trust me. Ms. He." That last line bothered her all afternoon, because Ms. He never wrote anything without a reason, and Paige was the one who had promised to handle the costumes before the school play on Saturday.

She sorted the pile: towels in one basket, Ewan's black drama T-shirts in another, and the yellow nylon costume shirt alone on the table. When she asked Ewan to help, he admitted his real motive right away. "I only came over because I melted my own shirt at home last year," he said, "and if the same thing happens here, I won't be the only one who ruined something." His grin was infectious, but Paige didn't laugh. The whole class would be watching her walk onstage in that shirt.

She ironed the towels first, on high, which worked fine. Then, without thinking, she laid the yellow shirt flat and ran the iron across the shoulder. A shiny, glazed stripe appeared instantly, smooth as tape. Ewan groaned. "That's the exact thing that happened to mine." Paige set the iron down and turned the shirt over, hunting the label. There it was, a tiny iron symbol with a single dot inside.

"One dot," she said slowly. "The towels had labels with three dots, and they took the high setting." She flipped Ewan's ruined-at-home shirt, which he'd brought in his backpack as evidence, and found two dots on its tag. "So the dots tell you the setting. One dot is low, around 110 degrees. Two is medium, around 150. Three is high, near 200." She turned the iron's dial to low, tested it on a hidden seam of the yellow shirt, and the fabric stayed dull and soft.

They worked out a rescue plan together. Ewan held the shirt taut while Paige laid a damp towel over the shiny stripe and pressed gently through it, careful to keep the dial at one dot. The glare faded, mostly. It would pass from the third row of the audience, which was where their classmates actually sat, because everyone knew the front rows stayed empty.

When she finished, Paige folded the shirt along its seams the way Ms. He's note had diagrammed on the back, wrote "one dot only" on a sticky label, and pressed it inside the collar where the next person would find it. Then she hung it from the drying-line canopy and texted Ms. He a photo. The reply came back in a minute: "Told you to iron it last for a reason."

The farmers' market smelled like peaches and hot bread, but Zack walked past all of it with five dollars in his fist and one goal: the last basket of blueberries at Mr. Leblanc's stall. Last week those berries had been three dollars, and the week before that, two. Now a hand-written sign read five dollars, and a line of six people stood in front of him.

"Every basket I brought sold out by ten o'clock," Mr. Leblanc was telling a woman at the front. "Frost took half my crop, so this is all there is." The woman paid anyway. So did the man behind her, and the one after that, even when Mr. Leblanc said, "Sorry, gone up again," and crossed out the five and wrote six. Zack watched the basket shrink to the final few pints, and his stomach dropped. At the peach stall next door, piled high with more fruit than anyone was buying, a sign read two dollars, down from four. Nobody rushed. Nobody lined up.

Zack found his friend Laurent sitting on a hay bale, eating a peach. "You're going to inhale that whole thing, pit and all," Zack said, and Laurent laughed and slowed down. Zack sat beside him and frowned at the crowd still gathered around Mr. Leblanc. "It doesn't make sense. He keeps raising the price and they keep buying. Six dollars a pint now. For berries."

"Maybe they'll stop at ten dollars," Laurent offered.

"They won't. My grandma pays whatever it costs for her berry syrup, because she needs it for her stomach. My mom's the same with Grandpa's heart pills at the pharmacy. The pharmacist said the price went up twice this year and everyone still buys them." Zack stood and paced in a small circle, agile enough to dodge a toddler chasing a pigeon. "The peaches are different. Plenty of peaches, so the price drops until people want them. But berries are scarce, and the people who need them, or the medicine people need, they buy it no matter what. It barely changes."

Seamus strolled over with his cousin, who was arguing about a school project on courtroom trials. "I got to be the defendant," the cousin said, "and Seamus wouldn't stop objecting." Seamus grinned, then noticed Zack staring at the blueberry line. "What?"

"Watch," Zack said. He walked back to Mr. Leblanc's stall just in time to hear him say to the last customer, "Eight dollars, and that's the final pint." The customer counted out the bills without a single complaint.

Laurent appeared at Zack's elbow, peach juice still on his chin. "You were right," he whispered.

Zack unfolded his five-dollar bill and looked at it, then at the empty berry baskets stacked behind the stall. "Mr. Leblanc," he called, "got any rhubarb?"

The market in Cuenca smelled of oranges and fried plantains, and Aaron clutched his notebook like it was a winning lottery ticket. His family had been in Ecuador for five days, and every morning he wrote sentences in Spanish to practice before his teacher, Mr. Owusu, expected a whole recorded presentation when he got home. His brother Marco, who was seventeen and annoying, kept leaning over his shoulder at breakfast to "help."

"Mi hermano está cansado," Aaron read aloud to Adem and Crystal, the twins from the apartment downstairs, who had invited him to the market because their mother sold woven scarves there. Crystal was stacking bracelets, and Adem was attempting to juggle three limes with limited success.

"Wait," Crystal said, squinting at his notebook. "You wrote that sentence with es. Es cansado. My mom says that means he is tired all the time. Like, forever."

Aaron stared at the page. He thought about all the sentences he'd copied: es alto, es cansado, es feliz. The twins' mother waved them over and, between customers, sorted wool with quick fingers. Aaron watched her say "está nublado" about the sky and "es azul" about the wool, and a pattern began to form in his head. He circled every es and every está in his notebook like a detective marking clues. Tall, blue, and happy came with es. Cloudy, tired, and busy came with está.

He tested his idea on Adem. "Tu mamá es amable," he said, pointing at the scarf stall, "y hoy está ocupada." Adem stopped juggling and clapped once. "Sí! That's it. Es for things that stay, está for right now." Aaron grinned and flipped to the sentence about Marco, the one that had started everything. He crossed out the wrong word and wrote the other one above it.

That afternoon, when Marco flopped onto the couch and demanded water, Aaron marched over and recited the corrected sentence. "Mi hermano está cansado. Only today. Not forever." Marco groaned and threw a pillow at him, but their mother laughed so hard she had to sit down, and she let Aaron have the last empanada even though Marco had called dibs.

On the walk home from dinner, Aaron recorded his presentation on his phone, describing his whole family in careful sentences: his mother's curly hair, his father's terrible singing, the dog that was small and white and, today, extremely muddy. When they passed a bakery still glowing at nine o'clock, he bought three rolls with the coins in his pocket and handed one to each of his parents, saving the warmest for Marco, who muttered, "Gracias, hermanito," and split it in half anyway.

Benjamin had three days to figure out one question for Mr. Dela Cruz's class: how did the Treaty of Versailles help lead to the Second World War? Mr. Dela Cruz, whose eccentric habits included pacing the room with a rolled-up map under his arm like a sword, refused to give answers. "You have the library, you have each other," he had said, tapping the question on the whiteboard. "Make me believe it."

At lunch, Benjamin spread his notes across the table in the library corner. Sierra leaned over them, and Lamar dropped his tray down beside hers. Immediately they started arguing about who would do the map and who would write the script for their presentation, so Benjamin mediated, splitting the jobs down the middle before they got loud enough for the librarian's motion sensor to flip the lights off on all of them. Then he pulled the encyclopedia volume toward him and started hunting through 1919.

"Here it is," Sierra said, running her finger down the page. "Versailles. Germany lost land, money, colonies, everything." She flipped to the map and traced a thin strip running to the sea. "Look at this. After the treaty, Germany got cut in two. This bit right here, they call it the Polish Corridor." And at the edge of it sat a city labeled Danzig.

Benjamin copied the shape of the strip onto his own paper, then drew the border from 1914 beside it. Something clicked. Twenty years sat between that map and the war he'd read about last week, and he suddenly needed to know what happened in between. He paged forward, skimming, while Lamar peered over his shoulder. "You look like you found treasure," Lamar said.

"I think I found the bridge," Benjamin said. "Watch." He set two photocopies side by side, the 1919 map and the timeline. "Hitler demanded the return of Danzig and the Polish Corridor. That's the exact land Germany lost at Versailles. And then Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, starting the Second World War in Europe." He tapped the strip on the map, then the date on the timeline. "Versailles didn't start the war. But it's where those places got taken away, and the demand for them back is where it all caught fire."

Sierra grabbed a marker and drew an arrow from the corridor to the date, then circled Danzig in red. "So we start the presentation with this little strip of land," she said, "and we end it with tanks crossing a border."

"Nobody's going to guess it was coming," Lamar said.

"That's the whole point," Benjamin said, and he was already writing their opening line: first, a map that looks boring, and then, twenty years later, a war. He slid the paper across the table so Sierra could make the letters big.

Maelie had promised herself she would not hide in the back room, but by ten o'clock she was still sorting soup cans into crates, and she could hear Mary up front laughing with people in the serving line. Ms. Kamau, who ran the kitchen, patted the crates as she passed. "Pantry first, serving later," she said. "We can't postpone the pantry, or lunch doesn't happen." Maelie stacked another can and thought that was the kind of thing adults said to make chores sound important.

Then a truck rumbled into the alley, and Farhan came sprinting from the loading dock with rain dripping off his sleeves. "It's like a monsoon out there," he said, shaking water onto the floor. "Maelie, come look. That truck isn't from here. The plates say Ohio, but the side says the same thing as our truck."

Maelie followed him to the dock. Their own truck, the one that came every morning, had a green and blue logo on it with the words Feeding America. The new truck, wet and mud-splashed, had the exact same logo. Both drivers were rolling a ramp down together like they did this every day.

"That's weird," Maelie said. "Why would two trucks from different cities have the same logo?"

Farhan shrugged. "Maybe somebody copied it."

Maelie didn't think so. She went to find Ms. Kamau, who was ladling stew at the counter, and asked her straight out. Ms. Kamau smiled without stopping the ladle. "Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks," she said. "We're all one team, coast to coast." Then she called to the next person in line, because the line was long and getting longer.

Maelie stood there turning it over. A network. More than 200. That meant this kitchen in her town and that freezer in Ohio were connected somehow, like plugs in the same outlet. She had a theory, and she wanted to test it, so she marched back to the alley where the drivers were hauling boxes. "Excuse me," she said to the Ohio driver. "Did you come all this way because somebody needed something?"

The driver, a big woman with a whistle around her neck, grinned. "Our freezer broke last night. Called it in, and the closest kitchen with space was you. Forty tubs of soup. You good for it?"

Maelie checked with Ms. Kamau, then pointed the driver to the walk-in cooler. Farhan grabbed a dolly, and together they wheeled tub after tub inside, Farhan pretending each one weighed a thousand pounds. When they finished, he begged Ms. Kamau for a job up front instead of the pantry, because, he admitted quietly, he wanted to meet people, not just cans. She handed him a hairnet and a tray of rolls.

Back inside, Maelie carried two extra pots of soup to the serving line, and Mary waved her over to help ladle. An old man at the counter held out his bowl, and Maelie filled it to the brim, ladle steady, steam rising between them.

"Extra scoop today?" he asked.

"Freezer broke in Ohio," Maelie said. "You're eating soup from out of state."

He looked at her to see if she was joking, then at the full bowl, and laughed so hard the soup rippled.

Audrey had assumed babysitting meant pizza, television, and a kid who could at least say what was wrong. What she got instead was six-month-old Milo, who had been screaming for forty straight minutes in Mr. Pierre's living room while his parents were at a retirement dinner for a colleague two streets over.

On the fridge, held up by a magnet shaped like a croissant, hung a note in looping handwriting. Keep bottles in the fridge, warm 20 seconds, and no matter how frustrated you get, NEVER shake him. An infant's neck muscles are too weak to support his heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury. If you're overwhelmed, put him safely in his crib and step away for a minute. Audrey read it twice. The word "frustrated" being right there in a stranger's handwriting, like it was expected of her, was somehow the most insulting part of the evening.

The bottle hadn't worked. The diaper was dry. She had walked him in circles until her arms burned, sung three songs she normally pretended to be indifferent to, and bounced him on her knee until she understood why professional athletes retire young. Milo screamed through all of it, his face a furious red, his fists like tiny detonators. Audrey felt something hot climb up her own neck, and that scared her more than the crying did. So she did what the note said. She laid him in the crib on his back, checked the blanket was nowhere near his face, and walked into the kitchen, where she stood with her hands flat on the counter and counted the tiles.

From the doorway, she watched him and thought. He'd eaten. He was dry. He wasn't sick; his dad had said so. So what was left? She turned the problem over the way she turned over a math proof. A baby this age, she remembered her cousin saying, hasn't yet developed the adaptation of tuning out noise; everything came in at full volume. Audrey glanced at the kitchen light she'd left blazing and the radio murmuring on the counter, both going the whole time because she'd wanted the apartment to feel friendly.

She went back and switched off the lamp and the radio, until the room held only the gray hush from the window. Then she sat in the rocking chair where she could see the crib and stayed very still. The screaming thinned to grumbling, then to hiccupy breathing, then to nothing but the radiator ticking. Milo lay with his eyes open, watching the ceiling like it was the most interesting thing he'd ever seen.

When Mr. Pierre and his wife came home at ten, they found Milo asleep and Audrey doing homework by phone light. "He cried a lot," she said, "and then he didn't." Mr. Pierre counted out her pay and added two extra dollars. "What was it?" his wife whispered. Audrey shrugged and pocketed the money. "Turns out he just wanted everyone to be quiet, including me."

Joseph had promised the chess club he would figure out exactly how many games each member had won this season, and Coach Reyes kept the results in a shoebox of crumpled score sheets. The club tournament was in three days, and Eugene wanted a poster with real numbers, not guesses. "If we hand in another poster with smudged tally marks," Eugene said, dropping the box on the library table, "Madeleine will never let us hear the end of it."

Mr. Do, who ran the computer lab after school, handed Joseph a laminated sheet of instructions. "Type your wins in column B," he said, "then ask the machine to add them." Joseph typed names into column A and numbers into column B, all thirty-two rows of them. When he tried to add them by hand on scrap paper, his total came out different twice, and he realized he had skipped a row. He decided the program should comply with his instructions exactly, which meant he had to give it exactly the right ones. In the empty cell below his numbers he typed the formula, and the total appeared, instantly, like something had been waiting under the lid of the box.

The bar chart was harder. His first attempt made one enormous bar and eleven skinny ones, and Joseph stared at it until he understood what was wrong: he had included the total row in the chart's range, so the total towered over everything like a giant at a party. He highlighted the rows again without the total, and the chart snapped into shape. Madeleine leaned over his shoulder. "I want the dynasty bar to be red," she said, pointing at the tallest one, which belonged to her. "I've won four years running, since sixth grade."

At home that night Joseph emailed his grandfather, who used to keep accounts for a small hardware store. The reply came the next morning, and Joseph read it at the lab before school:

Dear Joseph, Your chart reminds me of 1979, when I first saw a spreadsheet on a home computer. It was called VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston, and it ran on the Apple II, the first spreadsheet program for personal computers. I remember typing in a column of figures and watching the total change when I fixed one number, and thinking I would never add a long column by hand again. Sometimes I miss doing the sums myself, pencil on paper, because I could see every step. Sometimes I don't miss it at all. I'm still not sure which feeling is the honest one. Love, Grandpa.

Joseph read the letter twice, then tried what his grandfather described. He changed one win from a 3 to a 4, and the total at the bottom shifted on its own. So that was the crucial trick, he thought, the reason Mr. Do kept saying formulas were better than typing totals by hand: the total wasn't a number you wrote, it was a rule the machine followed. He imagined his grandfather in 1979 watching the same thing happen on a machine the size of a toaster, and wondered whether the old spreadsheet had felt like magic or like cheating.

He printed the chart with Madeleine's dynasty bar in red, and carried the poster to the gym, where Eugene was already taping up the bracket. "Check the total," Joseph said, tapping the bottom of the page. "It added itself."

Alexis stared at the postcard on his grandpa's kitchen table, the Grand Canyon glowing orange under a desert sky. Tomorrow he had to explain in science class how a river could carve a canyon that enormous, and his notecard said only one thing he trusted: scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago. "That's it?" he groaned. "That's my whole presentation?"

"Use the sink," his grandpa said, not looking up from his crossword.

"The sink?"

"Water moves dirt. Watch it move dirt."

So Alexis filled a baking pan with packed soil from the garden, tilted it over the sink, and turned the faucet to a trickle. At first nothing happened. He sat back, feeling pessimistic about the whole plan, and nearly quit. Then a thin brown line appeared where the water slid across the soil. He let the trickle run. The line deepened into a groove, and tiny crumbs of dirt piled up at the pan's low edge, a small muddy delta.

"Erosion," Alexis said out loud, "and that pile is deposition." The water hadn't smashed the soil apart; it had carried it away, grain by grain, and dropped it wherever the current slowed.

Zaiden's text arrived just then. Presentation canceled? the message asked. No such luck, Alexis typed back. Found something better.

He timed one minute on the kitchen clock and measured the groove with a ruler. Two millimeters. He did the math twice on a napkin because the first answer seemed impossible. Even a tiny stream, if it never stopped, could dig down astonishingly far over years, and the real river had been at it for those 5 to 6 million years. His little pan was a model, a small honest version of an enormous patient thing.

"You look like your grandmother when she was onto something," his grandpa said, finally setting down his pen. He slid his chair over and squinted at the muddy delta. Then he did something Alexis hadn't expected: he plucked the postcard off the table and turned it over. "Your grandma bought this the summer I guided rafts on the Colorado. Never told you that, did I." He hadn't. Grandpa had never disclosed a single story about being a river guide.

"You steered a boat through that?"

"Twice a week, all summer."

Alexis held up the pan. "Then you already knew the river built all this."

Grandpa tapped the muddy delta with one finger. "Five to six million years, the sign at the rim used to say. Your little ditch here, though, that's brand new."

Alexis grinned and turned the faucet back on.

The market in Cuenca smelled of oranges and wet stone, and Charlotte's mother had already wandered off toward the fabric stalls. That left Charlotte standing in front of a crate of guinea pigs with an old woman who kept saying something to her in Spanish, slowly, the way people talk to a lost dog. Charlotte knew one thing for certain: she had promised to send her class a video describing her family, in full Spanish sentences, by Friday, and so far she had only learned the words for "hello" and "thank you," which would make a very short video.

"Tengo un gato negro," she said to the guinea pigs, practicing. The old woman smiled, so Charlotte tried the sentence again, this time pointing at a black cat dozing on a stack of grain sacks behind the crate. "Un gato negro." The old woman laughed and said it back to her, and it sounded exactly the same, which was either very good or very bad.

Charlotte found Michaela and Anis by the fountain, where they were meticulously arranging their souvenir coins in rows by size. "I think I said it right," Charlotte said, "but I can't tell. She laughed, but she also pointed at the cat, so maybe I accidentally said something about her grandmother." Anis, who had taken exactly two weeks of Spanish before the trip, squinted at her notebook. "You said gato before negro," he said. "In English we'd say black cat. You said cat black."

They tested it. Michaela invented a sentence on the spot, "una casa blanca," and marched up to a fruit seller to point at a white house across the plaza and say it. He nodded. Then she flipped the words, "una blanca casa," and pointed at the same house. This time the man tilted his head, frowned, and looked around, as if a white house might be hiding somewhere behind the bananas. Charlotte exhaled. It wasn't random, then. The noun came first, and the describing word came after it, the opposite of English, every single time. They tried it with a red apple, a small dog, a tall tower, and the pattern held, a perfect one-to-one ratio of nods to right answers.

Back at the hotel, Charlotte filmed her video on her mother's phone, feeling the words line up backwards and somehow land right. "Tengo una hermana pequeña," she said, and then, because Anis was making faces behind the camera, "tengo un amigo ridículo." Behind her, in the doorway, Mr. O'Brien from the room next door raised his coffee cup and said, "Muy bien."

The pool's plumbing hummed under the deck, a low rumble Leah had never noticed until tonight, when everything else had gone quiet. Twelve girls stood along the edge, waiting for Coach to call the next heat. Leah tightened her goggles and glanced at the lane beside hers, where Wali was shaking out her arms the way she always did before a race.

"Fastest two in each heat make the travel squad," Coach said. "Take your marks."

The whistle blew. Leah dove clean, but she heard a splash behind her that was all wrong, a flat smack instead of a cut. When she turned at the wall, she saw Wali in the water near the blocks, holding her head. Wali had slipped on the takeoff and come down hard on the surface, and now the coach was already pulling her out. Leah finished the heat second, but she barely registered it. She climbed out and watched Coach hold up two fingers in front of Wali's face, then move them slowly to one side. Wali tracked them. She said something Leah couldn't hear, and Coach shook her head anyway.

"That's not fair," Leah said to Aydin, who had made the travel squad in the first heat. "Wali looked fine. She followed the fingers. Why pull her?"

"Maybe because she winced when she turned her neck," Aydin said.

Leah couldn't stop thinking about it while she swam her second heat. Wali wasn't dizzy. Wali wasn't confused. So there had to be some other reason, some rule Leah couldn't see, because a coach doesn't pull a girl from her one shot at the team without one. She touched the wall, looked over at the bleachers, and saw Wali sitting with an ice pack, arguing quietly with Ms. McKenzie, the gym teacher who supervised tryouts.

Leah walked over, dripping. "She's fine," Leah said. "You can't just take her out."

"You think I want to?" Ms. McKenzie said. "It's not my choice, or the coach's. Every state in the country, all fifty, plus Washington, D.C., has passed laws about handling concussions in youth sports. A hard hit to the head, the athlete comes out, no exceptions."

Wali stared at her. "There's a law?"

"There's a law."

Leah stood there while the meaning settled over her. It wasn't the coach being cautious, and it wasn't about this pool, or this school, or tonight. The rule was bigger than all of them, and it had been sitting there the whole time, invisible, waiting for exactly this kind of fall.

"Can she try out again next week?" Leah asked.

"If the doctor clears her," Ms. McKenzie said.

Wali looked at Leah and managed a crooked smile. "Save me a spot on that squad."

Leah squeezed the water from her ponytail. "It's saved."

The sign-up sheet said the class debate team tryout would end at 3:15, and it was already 2:50. Elliot stood in the hallway outside Ms. Guo's room, gripping his notes, while Marylou and Niko argued in front of him about who should go first.

"You go," Niko said. "You're the one who said the cafeteria pizza is the worst food in the state."

"That's not something you can test," Elliot said suddenly. "You can't prove it true or false. It's just what I believe, what I feel about pizza." The words came out before he thought about them, and they reminded him of last winter, sitting at the kitchen table while his older brother insisted their uncle's chili was objectively disgusting. His father had leaned over the pot and said, "Give me one test for that, kid." His brother couldn't, and had finally laughed and admitted maybe it was just his tongue against the chili. That night, the whole argument had collapsed into nothing, and everyone had gotten seconds.

Elliot's tryout topic was on the sheet in his hand: "Our school's new rule restricting backpacks in hallways is unfair." He had ten minutes to prepare, and now his notes looked strange to him. "Unfair" was a judgment, the kind of thing evidence couldn't prove. But parts of the rule could be checked. Whether students actually got hurt by backpacks in the hall was something you could count. Whether other schools had the same rule was something you could look up.

When Ms. Guo called him in, he spread his notes on the desk. "I want to argue the backpack rule," he said, "but I have to be honest about what's a claim and what's an opinion. The claim is that hallway accidents dropped after the rule. That can be checked against the accident log in the office, and shown true or false. The unfair part is my opinion. Evidence can't prove it, but it can still be my judgment."

Ms. Guo raised an eyebrow. "You'd give up the easy part, the part that gets applause?"

"It felt naive to think nobody would notice the difference," Elliot said. "Someone on the other team would."

She slid a visitor badge across the desk. "The office closes at 3:15, same as tryouts. If you want that accident log, you have about fifteen minutes." Elliot grabbed the badge and ran, sneakers squeaking on the tile, and behind him he heard Marylou shouting, "Check if they restrict lunch passes too!"

The trouble had started on Tuesday, when Mr. Ndlovu pulled Callan and Michael aside after the drama club meeting and said they would perform a two-person scene at the spring showcase, no script, no plan. Michael had wanted a part with lines he could memorize. Instead he got "improv," a word that sounded like something you did right before falling off a cliff.

By Saturday he was in the living room with Callan and Aanya, a note from Mr. Ndlovu folded on the coffee table. Michael read it out loud for the third time. "Dear Michael. In our game, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem. Your job is to catch every offer and say yes, and. P.S. Your last practice was painful to watch. Sincerely, Mr. Ndlovu." Aanya laughed so hard she slid off the arm of the couch.

"Let's just try it," Callan said, standing up. He pointed one finger at the carpet, reeled an invisible line in with careful, patient hands.

"Hi," Michael said. "What are you doing?"

Callan lowered the invisible rod. "Dude. Seriously?"

Michael replayed the moment later, while Aanya got juice from the kitchen. Two weeks ago, before the showcase was announced, Callan had done the exact same mime in the gym and Michael had ignored it then too, and Callan had stood there fishing at nothing until the game collapsed. The problem wasn't nerves, Michael realized. It was that his eyes treated the rod as random wiggling instead of information. Callan was handing him a place and a problem and Michael kept dropping them, and every dropped offer made the scene worse in a cumulative way, piling up until there was nothing left to act with. He could not see the offers, exactly, the way you can't see wind, but he could see what they did.

Aanya came back with three cups and set them down. "Okay, one rule," she said. "Michael, before you speak, name the offer out loud. Place, name, or problem. Say it, then respond."

Callan picked up the invisible rod again, cast it across the rug toward the bookshelf.

"Offer," Michael said. "We're fishing, and this is a lake. Yes, and I'll bait your hook with this sandwich, because the fish here have expensive taste." He held out an imaginary sandwich, mayonnaise side up.

Callan grinned and reeled faster. "Careful. The last person who fed the fish opened a restaurant, and now the fish expect to see a menu and a revenue report before they bite."

Aanya clapped once. "See? You didn't cite the rule, you used it."

"Shh," Michael said, keeping his eyes on the line. "The big one's coming. Hand me the sandwich."

Beatrice had come to the library for one reason: to prove her uncle wrong. At Sunday dinner he had lifted his wrist, rattled the copper bracelet on it, and announced that it had cured his back pain, and that the company had letters from a hundred satisfied customers. Her cousin Finley had nodded along, but Beatrice had gone home with a strange itch in her mind, the kind that meant a question was not finished with her yet.

She found a table near the window where the afternoon light fell across the wood in long pale stripes. Alizee was already there, spreading out books for their science project, and Beatrice flopped into the chair across from her. "I need to ask you something," Beatrice said. "My uncle says his bracelet fixed his back. How would we know if it actually did?"

Alizee tilted her head. "Did he do anything else that week?" Beatrice thought back. He had started swimming at the community pool, and she remembered her aunt saying he'd finally agreed to see a physiotherapist about his knees, something about worn cartilage and exercises. She wrote both of those on a scrap of paper and stared at them. "So maybe the swimming helped," she said slowly. "Or the exercises. Or it would have gotten better anyway."

"That's a story about one person," Alizee said. "My mom calls that an anecdote." She tapped the library's science database on her laptop and pulled up a proper study, one where hundreds of people wore real bracelets or identical fake ones, and neither group knew which was which. Beatrice read the results twice. The two groups had improved about the same, which meant the copper itself could not take the credit.

The itch in her mind quieted. An anecdote, she decided, was like one footprint in the snow: it told you somebody had passed by, but not which path they had taken or why. A study with many people and tested evidence was more like a whole trail, stamped down from every direction until the pattern showed. It wasn't that her uncle was lying; he genuinely felt better. He had just skipped over the part where other explanations get ruled out.

The next weekend she drafted a note, planning to petition the family for a new Sunday dinner rule: every amazing claim had to survive three questions before anyone was allowed to buy anything. Finley thought it was hilarious and signed first. Her uncle read the note, snorted, and slid the bracelet off his wrist. "Fine," he said, setting it on the table with a small copper clink. "But I'm keeping the swimming."

George had exactly forty minutes to figure out what he was doing wrong before the toasts started at Quincy's sister's wedding.

The reception was in a rented hall behind a Malaysian restaurant, and George was one of only three guests from his school. Quincy had invited him last minute, which meant George hadn't gone to the family dinner where the others had learned whatever they'd learned. He noticed it almost right away: when the flower lady came around, Quincy's grandmother took the little sachet with her right hand. When Uncle somebody passed the tea, he poured and received with his right hand too. George had been handing things back and forth with his left all afternoon, and nobody had said a word, but he caught the grandmother's eyes flick down at his left hand once, twice, and then away.

He remembered a family dinner at Blaine's house in the spring. Blaine's cousin, who was visiting from Kuala Lumpur, had reached for the rice dish with her left hand, and Blaine's mother had touched her wrist and switched the spoon into her right. Nobody explained anything. Blaine had just leaned over and whispered, "In Indonesia and Malaysia, everybody eats and gives and takes with the right hand, out of respect." George had filed it away and forgotten it until now, standing with a gift bag in his left hand and the grandmother heading straight for him.

The problem was the gift. Quincy's family had a table near the front where people were handing over envelopes and boxes before the toasts, and the line was already forming. George had twenty minutes, maybe less. He tested his idea quietly first. When the waiter offered him a satay skewer, George took it with his right hand and said thank you, and the grandmother, watching from her chair, gave him a small nod that looked almost like approval. So it wasn't about being a foreign guest. It was about the hand.

He got in line, shifted the bag into his right hand, and waited. His left palm was sweating around the card he was supposed to pin to the board, which he also moved to his right. When his turn came, he held out the gift with his right hand, and Quincy's sister took it the same way and smiled at him, a real one, not the polite smile she'd given the man before him who had tossed his envelope down with his left.

George walked back to his seat feeling like he'd solved something. Quincy slid over to make room.

"You figured it out," Quincy said.

"Blaine's cousin," George said, and picked up his fork with his right hand, just to keep the streak going.

Jayden sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with his tablet balanced on a couch cushion, sorting through the basketball stats his league had posted online.
