He played nothing but measures eleven through fourteen. Slow, then slower, then fast, then slow again. His little brother wandered in halfway through, humming the four measures along with him until they were stuck in both their heads, which was annoying and also, somehow, helpful. After twenty minutes, Benjamin tried the whole song from the top, and his hands sailed through the jump like it had never been a problem at all. He laughed out loud, alone in the living room.

On Monday after school, he knocked on Mr. Bekele's door. The retired music teacher lived two houses down and had lent Benjamin the sheet music in the first place, excluding from his stack of books anything too advanced. "Did it go badly?" Mr. Bekele asked, seeing Benjamin's face. "No, the opposite," Benjamin said. "I finally fixed it. Four measures, over and over. Not the whole song." Mr. Bekele's grin was infectious, wide and sudden. "Ah, so you learned what most people take years to learn."

At Thursday's recital tryout, Benjamin watched Joaquin flub the same passage three times in a row and stare at his shoes afterward, his ears going red with embarrassment. Benjamin caught him in the hallway. "Which measures are you missing?" he asked. Joaquin showed him, and together they found an empty practice room. "Just these," Benjamin said, pointing at the page. "Nothing else. Watch." He played the four measures slowly, and Joaquin pulled out his clarinet and copied him, measure by measure, until the sun through the window turned orange.

At the end of the hour, Joaquin ran the piece from the beginning. When he hit the hard part and kept going, clean and easy, he looked up and said, "Play it again. I want to hear the whole thing."

The letters on the wall kept going soft. Eleanor squinted at the chart from the plastic chair, and the bottom rows blurred into gray insects. Mya stood in the doorway of the nurse's office, holding both their hall passes like they were tickets to something.

"Read the smallest line you can," the nurse said.

Eleanor read down to the fourth row and stopped. "E, F, P, and then it just smears."

The nurse wrote something on a card. "You'll need an eye exam. You're around twenty-forty, maybe worse." She pulled the chart off its hook and turned it over, and Eleanor saw printing on the back, small and brown with age. "This old thing. I've been meaning to get a new one."

"Wait," Eleanor said, leaning over. "How old is it?"

The nurse tilted the card toward the light. "The print says the design dates to 1862. A Dutch doctor named Herman Snellen came up with it, rows of letters that shrink line by line. We've been squinting at his idea since before anyone's great-grandparents were born."

"That's ancient," Mya said. "That chart is older than the school. Older than the whole town, probably."

Eleanor stared at the fading E at the top, huge and confident, and something bothered her. "If it's that old, the letters might be worn. Maybe I can't read the bottom because it's faded, not because my eyes are bad." It sounded like an excuse the moment she said it, but she wanted to test it anyway. She formulated a quick plan. "Could I try reading something new? Same size, but printed fresh?"

The nurse raised an eyebrow, then smiled. "Sure." She took a sticky note and a marker and copied the smallest row's letters from the chart, P E C Z F, in bold black strokes, and taped the note beside the faded row.

Eleanor looked. The sticky-note letters stayed stubbornly smeared, exactly as blurred as the originals. Same letters, same size, new ink, still soft. It wasn't the chart. It was her eyes. She felt her face go warm, and Mya's hand landed briefly on her shoulder.

"Okay," Eleanor said quietly. "It's me."

Two weeks later she sat in the same chair while the nurse helped her unfold her new glasses, the frames a versatile shade of blue that the optician had promised worked with everything. The sticky note was still taped to the wall. Through the new lenses, P E C Z F stood up sharp and black and certain, every edge clean.

Mya grinned from the doorway. "Can you see the tundra project poster from here too? That's my true test."

Eleanor looked down the hall toward their classroom, where the frost-blue poster hung above the sink, and read the title across its top without a single squint. "Every word," she said. "Even the small print."

At Gage's front door, Maelie stood holding a box of store-bought cookies while his cousin Cecile swept toward her and kissed her right cheek, then her left. Maelie froze, her arms rigid, nearly bopping Cecile in the chin with the cookies. Behind Cecile came Gage's uncle, who kissed her cheek once, twice, three times, and stepped back beaming. Maelie's face burned. At her own house, guests got a wave and a "come in," and she had never once considered that her rules might not be the only ones.

"She does it to everyone," Gage whispered as they headed to the kitchen. "It's called la bise. My cousins do it like saying hi." Maelie set the cookies on the counter, where Gage's aunt took them with both hands and a small bow, and said something in French that made everyone laugh warmly. Maelie laughed too, though she had no idea what the joke was, and that felt like wearing someone else's coat.

At dinner she watched like a detective. Hands on the table, not in laps. Bread torn, never cut with the knife. Cecile said "bon appetit" before anyone lifted a fork, and even Gage's little brother waited. Maelie kept her wrists resting beside her plate and tore her bread carefully, and when she almost reached for the water pitcher before the uncle had been served, she caught herself and pretended to be very interested in the tablecloth. She was not going to be the defendant at dinner court, accused of guzzling water out of turn. That was silly, she knew. She still put the pitcher down.

After dinner she found Cecile alone on the porch steps and tested the question that had been bugging her all evening. "You kissed me twice, but your dad did three. Is he just, like, extra friendly?" Cecile tilted her head. "In his region, everyone does three. Where I live, it's two. It changes from place to place in France." So it was not about her at all. There was a system, a map of kisses she couldn't see, and she had spent the whole afternoon thinking the uncle liked her more than Cecile did. She had tried to decode faces and it had all been postcodes.

"It's two for me," Cecile said, standing and offering her hand like they were closing a deal. Maelie leaned in, right cheek first, and got it right this time, two soft kisses, one on each side. Cecile grinned and went inside. Gage appeared in the doorway, and Maelie raised her hand for a high five, but he laughed and kissed the air beside her cheek twice instead. Her hand hung there, useless and vain, while the porch light flicked on. "Next time," she said, "I'm doing three."

The rain hammering Mackenna's window should have been the most exciting thing in the house, but Scarlett couldn't stop staring at Mackenna's phone. Everyone in town was sharing the same photo: a street turned into a brown river, a mailbox sticking out of the water like a tiny lighthouse. The caption said the creek had burst its banks two blocks from the school.

"That's our street," Mackenna said, her grin infectious. "No school tomorrow, definitely."

Scarlett looked at the water again. Something about it itched at her, the way a word on the tip of your tongue does. The creek didn't flood fast. It crept. And that mailbox looked brand new, no rust, no stickers, when she knew every mailbox on Miller's street wore at least three bumper stickers and a coat of orange stains.

"Can I borrow your laptop?" she asked. "Two minutes. Scientific business."

Mackenna's older brother, sprawled on the couch, muttered, "It's real, it's on the news page."

"Pages can be wrong," Scarlett said. "A page is just a place. It's not proof." She carried the laptop to the kitchen table, saved the photo, and did the thing Miller had shown her back in September, when someone had passed off a shark in a swimming pool as their own pet. "Reverse image search," Miller had called it then, and she did it now: she fed the picture itself into the search bar and let it hunt.

The results bloomed across the screen. The same flood photo had appeared online years earlier, on a weather site, during a storm in a town three states away. It hadn't been taken yesterday, or here, at all.

"Whoa." Mackenna leaned over her shoulder. "So it's old?"

"Older than your mailbox theory," Scarlett said. "Somebody grabbed a dramatic picture and said it was new."

Mackenna's brother sat up. "Wait. People just share stuff because it looks true?"

"Looks true and is true are different animals," Scarlett said. "Kind of like how your dog looks innocent while the trash can is knocked over."

They spent the next hour checking. The photo of the gym with water at the doors was real; the reverse search found nothing older than that morning, and the school's own page confirmed it. The one of a canoe paddling down Main Street turned out to be from a festival four years back, when the town literally closed the street and handed out paddles for fun.

"So what's the criterion, then?" Mackenna asked, chewing a pretzel. "How do we decide which ones to send to the group chat?"

Scarlett considered. "If we can check it, we check it. If we can't, maybe we wait an hour. Boring wins."

"Boring never wins," Mackenna said, but she typed a correction to the group chat anyway: NOT OUR STREET. PHOTO IS FROM YEARS AGO. She added a jellyfish emoji holding a tiny magnifying glass, because, she said, the truth needed a mascot. Scarlett decided the jellyfish could symbolize the whole afternoon: weird, a little see-through, but stinging exactly when it should.

The actual rain kept falling, the actual creek kept creeping, and Mackenna's mom called up that they should check whether school posted anything official. Scarlett closed the laptop and looked out at the gray sheet of water on the glass. Somewhere out there, she thought, was the true story of today, patient as the creek, just waiting for somebody to go looking.

"Tomorrow," Mackenna said, "we fact-check the cafeteria menu."

"Everything," Scarlett agreed, "except the mystery meat. That one stays unsolved."

Khalil leaned over the bean plants on the back counter and pointed at the two trays. "The ones under the red light grew more," he said. "That's a fact." Finnegan rolled his eyes so hard it looked painful. "No, it's your opinion. You just like the red light because it looks like a sci-fi movie."

Eli squinted at both trays. The beans under the red lamp did seem taller, but "seem" was doing a lot of work in that sentence. The science fair judging started in forty minutes, and their poster was supposed to answer a question with evidence, not with whoever argued loudest. Mr. Okonkwo had already stopped by once and asked, "How do you know?" Eli had said "you can just tell," and Mr. Okonkwo had smiled in a way that made Eli want a better answer.

"Maybe we can measure them," Eli said, pulling a ruler out of the drawer. Khalil grabbed his wrist. "We don't have time, the poster isn't even done." "We have forty minutes," Eli said. "Measuring takes five." Finnegan, who had been drawing a volcano on the corner of the poster that had nothing to do with beans, said, "Fine, but if we demolish our whole layout to write numbers on it, that's on you." He said it while sliding the ruler toward Eli, which meant he agreed.

They measured all twelve plants under each lamp and wrote the heights on the board. The red-light beans averaged taller, but two of them were shorter than any of the others, which surprised Khalil. "So I was right," he said. "Sort of," Eli said. "You said they grew more. Now we can actually check it. That makes it a claim, not just something you feel." Finnegan tapped the poster. "So when I say the volcano drawing makes it look awesome, that's different? Nobody could measure that?" "Right," Eli said. "That one's an opinion. Evidence can't prove it true or false. It's just what you believe." Finnegan looked wounded. "It is awesome. That part is authentic volcano shading, I looked at pictures."

With twelve minutes left, they copied the numbers onto the poster and Khalil wrote the heading Results while Finnegan, grudgingly and carefully, colored his volcano smaller so it wouldn't look like propaganda for volcanoes in a bean experiment. When Mr. Okonkwo came back and read the chart, he asked again, "How do you know?" Eli pointed at the ruler and the two rows of numbers. "We checked," he said, and Mr. Okonkwo nodded once and moved on to the next table, where a girl was insisting that her crystals were the sparkliest in the class.

After the funeral, everyone gathered in Grandma's back yard under the big maple, the same tree Carter's grandfather had planted the year he and Grandma bought the house. Carter stood near the picnic table with his hands in his pockets, feeling the old watch on his wrist where it had been all morning. He had taken it from Grandpa's dresser two days ago, before anyone could pack it away. Now he wondered if that had been a mistake, if wearing it meant he was refusing to let go the way a person was supposed to.

He found Claire by the fence, poking at a beetle with a stick. She had come with her mom, and she was clearly bored, which was fair, since she had never even met Grandpa. "You okay?" she asked, glancing at the watch. "You keep looking at it like it might explode."

"Do you think it's weird, wearing this?" Carter asked. "Like, not moving on?" Claire shrugged, so he kept going. "My dad keeps saying we all have to move forward. I don't want to take it off, though. It still ticks."

Claire's face changed the way it did when she was about to win an argument in class. "My mom reads all this psychology stuff. There's a book called Continuing Bonds, from 1996, and it says keeping a connection to someone who died, with memories or objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving. She made me read the first chapter for a report." She said it fast, like she was reciting, then added, "So no, I don't think it's weird. I think it's science."

Carter turned the watch over. The case back was scratched from years of resting on Grandpa's workbench, next to the laser level he used when he built the porch. Every cousin had resented having to hold that board steady while the red line crawled across it, and now Carter would have given anything to hold it one more time. Maybe missing someone was inevitable, and maybe the watch was not a chain, just a bridge. He could test that. If he set it to the correct time and wore it to school tomorrow, and it felt like carrying Grandpa with him instead of hiding from the world, then Claire's book was right about him.

He worked the little crown with his thumbnail until the hands matched his phone. "It's set," he said. "Nine forty-two." Across the yard, his dad was stacking paper plates, and Carter walked over and held out his wrist without a word. His dad looked at the watch, then at him, and put one hand briefly on Carter's shoulder. "He'd be glad it still runs," his dad said. "Wear it to dinner."

Joseph had a globe on his desk, a flashlight, and one night to figure out the seasons before his presentation in Ms. Brennan's class. He had gotten the first part easily enough: Earth's axis was tilted, and the tilt caused the seasons. But when Diya had quizzed him at lunch, she asked why the tilt mattered, and his answer had come out as a jumble. "You said 'the Sun is more direct' about six times," she had said. "What does that even mean?" Now he stared at the globe and its two dotted lines, one above the equator and one below, and wondered what they marked.

He spun the globe slowly. The northern dotted line crossed Mexico, Africa, and India. The southern one ran through Australia and South America. He knew the equator, but these two lines had names, and he could not remember them, which was exactly the kind of thing Ms. Brennan would ask. He texted Khloe, who owned every book in the school library's astronomy section.

She called back within two minutes. "They're the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn," she said. "The one north of the equator is Cancer. Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Around December 21, it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn." Joseph wrote it down, then read it back to her. "Wait, that's it," he said. "That's the whole thing I was missing."

He grabbed the flashlight and propped a book under the globe to keep it stable so it wouldn't roll off the desk. Then he held the flashlight level with the northern line and traced the beam. At that height, the light hit the Tropic of Cancer straight on, but everywhere north of it, the beam struck the globe at a slant, spreading thin and dim. He crouched down and slid the flashlight lower, level with the southern line, and watched the bright spot jump to the other side of the world. It was like the Sun was taking turns standing over each line, six months apart.

The next morning he found Diya at her locker. "Test me," he said. "Ask me why the tilt matters." She raised an eyebrow, game as always. "Fine. Why?"

He held up his hands like a globe and a Sun. "Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. That's where the light comes in straight and piles up, so it's summer there. Around December 21, it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn instead, and everything north of it only gets slanted light. Slanted light spreads out. It's like the beam on my globe last night, wide and weak." Diya nodded slowly. "Okay, that actually made sense."

In class, Ms. Brennan asked for volunteers, and Joseph's hand went up before he could talk himself out of it. He walked to the globe, pointed to the two dotted lines, and said the dates plainly, the way Khloe had said them to him. Ms. Brennan asked one follow-up question about the beam spreading out, and he answered it with the flashlight demo, sweeping the light across the tilted globe while the class leaned forward.

Afterward Diya bumped his shoulder in the hallway. "Good simile, by the way," she said. "The wide, weak beam. It contributed." Joseph laughed and shoved his notes back in his binder, already thinking about what he might present next time.

Jordan had promised his science fair table would not be "just another volcano." By Saturday morning, the volcano itself was done, a lumpy gray cone of salt dough with a film canister buried in its throat, and the actual problem was still unsolved: every test eruption so far had been either a sad fizz or a blob of foam on the ceiling. He sat at the kitchen table with three measuring cups, a bottle of vinegar, and a box of baking soda, devising a plan that would make his project different from the twenty other volcanoes in the gym.

"Are you doing science or making salad dressing?" Lena asked, dropping into the chair across from him. She peered at his notebook, where he had drawn a table with columns for amounts and eruption height.

"Both, kind of," Jordan said. "Watch. Same amount of baking soda each time. Only the vinegar changes." He filled the first cup with a quarter cup of vinegar and dumped it into the canister.

The volcano produced a small burp of pink foam. Lena clapped once, in slow motion, to honor the effort.

"That's the control problem," Angelo said from the doorway, where he had appeared holding a cookie he clearly intended to eat over Jordan's project. "The foam isn't stable. It slides down before you can measure anything."

Jordan ignored the cookie situation and poured half a cup of vinegar for the second trial. This time the foam climbed the slope and actually reached the rim of the paper plate he had placed below. He wrote down the height. One full cup, in the third trial, sent foam over the plate's edge and onto Angelo's sleeve, which Angelo accepted as the cost of participation. The numbers in Jordan's table made a pattern, and he could see it clearly: more vinegar, bigger eruption, every single time.

"So why does it do that?" Lena asked, wiping foam off her elbow.

"My mom said it last night when she was reading my notes," Jordan said. "Baking soda, which is sodium bicarbonate, reacts with vinegar, which is acetic acid, and makes carbon dioxide gas. The gas is what pushes the foam out." He tapped his table of results. "So the factor that matters is how much vinegar I add. More vinegar, more gas, more mess."

"Your mom sounds like she wants a volcano of her own," Angelo said, shaking off his sleeve.

They ran a fourth trial just to be sure, and this time they laid down three paper plates, which turned out to be exactly two plates too few. From the doorway, Mr. Rivera, who had come over to borrow a ladder and never got around to mentioning it, said quietly, "Ceiling again?"

Jordan looked up at the new foam constellation and wrote "trial five: outdoors" in his notebook.

Ivy's web page had a heading that refused to stay in the middle. She had typed text-align: center into her CSS, exactly the way the handout showed, and for one glorious second the words "Ivy's Guide to the Lake Ecosystem" sat right in the middle of the screen. Then she saved the file, refreshed the browser, and the heading slid stubbornly back to the left.

"The tech showcase starts in twenty minutes," said Miles, leaning over from the next laptop. "Ms. Park wants everybody's page up on the big screen."

"I know." Ivy scrolled through her CSS again. There it was, near the top: h1 { text-align: center; }. It was spelled right. She had checked three times. So why did the heading act like she'd never written anything at all?

Neveah wandered over with her own laptop, chewing the last of a granola bar. "Ms. Park said those are more nutritious than the vending machine stuff, but I'm not sure I believe her." She glanced at Ivy's screen. "Still stuck?"

"Watch this," Ivy said. She deleted the word center, retyped it, saved, and refreshed. The heading stayed left, like it was ignoring her on purpose. "The computer is doing something I can't see. There has to be a rule somewhere."

"Maybe it's the page itself," Miles offered. "Like something in the HTML?"

Ivy shook her head. "The HTML worked before lunch. It was centered then." She stopped. It had worked before lunch. What had she done after lunch? She scrolled down through the stylesheet, past the paragraph styles, past the list styles, all the way to the bottom, where she'd added a new section while the other campers were at the lake.

There it was: h1 { text-align: left; }, sitting at the very end of the file.

"You wrote it twice," Neveah said, peering closer.

"I forgot." Ivy stared at the two rules, one at the top and one at the bottom, both aimed at the same heading. The bottom one was winning. But why the bottom? She moved the left rule up above the center rule, saved, and refreshed. The heading stayed left. She moved it back down. The heading went left again. Up, it centered. Down, it went left. It wasn't magic and it wasn't random. When two CSS rules of equal specificity set the same property, the one written later won.

"That's why they call it a cascade," Ivy said, mostly to herself. "The stuff at the end pours over everything before it."

"Ten minutes," Miles warned.

Ivy deleted the left rule entirely. The heading snapped to the center and stayed there. She used the last minutes to modify her list styles, adding a little space between the lines, and to drop in a photo of a turtle she'd taken on Monday. The page looked like a real page now.

When Ms. Park's projector lit up the mess hall wall, Ivy's turtle photo glowed and the heading sat dead center above it. Neveah elbowed her and whispered, "Best one so far."

Ivy grinned and hit refresh one more time, just to watch the heading stay put.

The group chat lit up at 9:04 with a screenshot from Dana: an email sent to the whole class by mistake, sixty addresses crowded into the To field like a bus packed past the doors. "Great," Dana typed. "Now everyone has my email." Someone had already forwarded it to a chat called "everyone but Dana," which was exactly as biased as it sounded, and Dana's replies had gone from jokes to one long silence. Nicholas stared at the screen. His own birthday invitation was sitting in his drafts folder, addressed the same careless way, and his stomach did a slow flip.

He typed into the group chat: "Does anyone know how to send something to a lot of people without showing everybody's address?" Camila answered fast, the way she did when she actually knew something. "Use BCC," she wrote. "BCC means blind carbon copy. People you put there get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses." Nicholas read it twice. He had always thought BCC was some grown-up office button, like CC's serious older cousin, not a door you could actually walk through.

Before he trusted it, he tested it. He sent a dummy email to his own address in the To field, with Camila's address tucked into BCC, and a note that said only "checking something." Then he walked to the kitchen, got a glass of water, and came back to two copies in his inbox. His own copy showed just his address. Camila's reply arrived seconds later: "I can see the email but not anyone else you sent it to. Also this is the weirdest invite I've ever gotten."

He exhaled, long and slow, and opened the real draft. He pasted the class list into the BCC field, one careful line at a time, and typed a short message about Saturday, two o'clock, pizza and games at his house. In the To field, the only name left was his own. It felt strange, like being a diplomat carrying sealed letters instead of shouting announcements down the hallway, but strange in a good way.

He hit send, then went back to the group chat, where Dana had finally posted again, a single shrug emoji. Nicholas typed: "Dana, check your inbox. And everybody, your addresses are safe with me." The typing bubble appeared under Dana's name, disappeared, appeared again. Then it landed: "Okay. What time on Saturday?"

Jace set the shoebox ballot box on the folding table in the city hall lobby and counted the vote slips a third time, because the numbers refused to make sense. His class had been invited to run a mock election for a community open house, and Mr. De Vries had left him in charge of tallying results for the afternoon demonstration. The vote was simple: three imaginary parties, the reds, the blues, and the greens, competing for five seats.

"Okay," said Yann, leaning over his shoulder. "Reds won every seat."

"That's the problem." Jace spread the slips into piles. "Look. Reds got thirty-one votes out of a hundred. Blues got twenty-nine. Greens got forty. The greens actually won the most votes, but the reds took all five seats because their votes were packed into every district." He tapped the district map they had drawn on butcher paper. "Under our rules, whoever gets the most votes in each district wins that seat. Everything else counts for nothing."

Clovis arrived with hot chocolate from the lobby cart and slid one across the table to Jace without being asked, because she had noticed him rubbing his cold hands together. "So change the rules," she said.

"I can't just change them. That's not how it works."

"Then show both ways."

Jace stared at her. She was right. He flipped the butcher paper over and drew a second table, dividing the hundred votes by twenty, so each seat should represent twenty voters. The greens, with forty votes, earned two seats. The blues got one, the reds got one, and the last seat he split by remainder, which took some arguing until Yann and Clovis both agreed the blues were closer. Five seats, three parties represented. He labeled the two tables: first past the post, and proportional representation.

While they taped the paper to the display board, Jace remembered the evening last fall when his mother had let him stay up to watch the real election results roll in. He had pulled up a results page on her laptop and squiggled his finger down the columns, comparing the seat count with the vote percentages, and something had snagged in his mind. He had called his grandfather long distance just to ask about it. One party had won 184 seats out of 338, a majority of the House of Commons, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote. Fewer than four voters in ten, and they ran the whole show. He had sat with that for a long time before going to bed.

When the open house visitors began drifting past, an older woman stopped at the board and studied the two tables. "So this is why people argue about voting systems," she said.

"The green voters would cooperate better under the second one," Yann said, pointing. "Their votes actually add up to something."

Mr. De Vries came by at closing, read both tables top to bottom, and clapped Jace on the shoulder. "The logic holds," he said. "Bring the butcher paper to class on Monday. It's more durable than it looks."

Jace rolled it up carefully and tucked it under his arm like something worth keeping.

Alicia slid her simulation packet across the lab table and read the assignment line again. "Compare a stock and a bond. Explain which is riskier and why." Ms. Jung had set up the whole classroom as a pretend market, with each student holding an envelope of paper assets, and she had just announced that interest rates had risen.

"That's not fair," said Mabel, who sat beside her under the paper canopy of leaves taped to the ceiling for the economics unit. "I already traded for my stuff." Mabel was trying to earn the best grade in the class because her older brother had gotten one, and Alicia knew it, so she passed her friend a highlighter before anything else, because Mabel always forgot hers.

Alicia opened her envelope. She owned one share of Graffiti Robot Company stock, which the market sheet said had jumped in price, and one bond from the city that paid its holder four dollars of interest each round. She had been planning to sell the bond for its face value, ten dollars, and buy a second share of stock. Ayden, at the next table, was shouting that he would pay twelve for any robot stock, and his voice seemed to transmit through the entire room, because suddenly everyone wanted stock and nobody was talking about bonds at all.

She walked to Ayden's table anyway. "Bond for sale. Ten dollars, like the face value says."

"Ten?" Ayden frowned at his market sheet. "The teacher just raised the interest rate. New bonds pay more than four dollars now. Why would I pay ten for yours when I can get a brand new one that pays more?" He offered her seven. She refused and tried the cashier station, then the cluster near the window. Everyone said some version of the same thing. Nobody would pay full price for her old bond, because buyers could get new bonds that paid more interest, and by the last round the best offer she received was six dollars.

Back at her table, she laid out both assets side by side. "Okay," she said slowly, mostly to herself. "My stock went up. My bond went down, and it fell because rates rose, not because the city stopped paying. So the stock could crash to nothing if the company fails, but the bond only dropped a few dollars and still pays interest every round." She had started the day certain that bonds were the safe, boring choice that nobody smart would pick. Now she scribbled on her comparison sheet, crossed out her first sentence, and wrote that each one was risky in a different way, and that a bond's price could fall even when nothing was wrong with it.

Ms. Jung rang the bell for presentations. Mabel leaned over. "So which is riskier?" she whispered.

"Watch this," Alicia said, and stood up holding both pieces of paper above her head like evidence. "Last round, my bond was worth less than it said on its face. I'm going to tell you exactly why."

The trail to the campground was humid, and Audrey's backpack strap stuck to her shoulder like tape. Behind her, her dad argued with her little brother about whether chips counted as a snack or a meal. Ahead, their neighbor from the next campsite, Mr. Qureshi, was already wrestling with a metal box bolted to a post.

"That's the bear locker," Angelique said, catching up. She and her family had arrived at the park the day before, and she had appointed herself tour guide. "Everything goes in there."

"Everything like food," Audrey said.

"Everything," Angelique repeated, and dropped her toothbrush and a tube of sunscreen through the steel door.

Audrey eyed the locker. She had heard about bears her whole life, sort of, in a vague way, the way she'd heard about quicksand. It had never mattered before. Now she stood in a pine forest in a national park where the ranger at the entrance had a clipboard and a serious face, and it mattered a lot. That night, a bear could walk through the campground. She felt a slow creep of dread in her stomach, which was ridiculous, because she was twelve and not afraid of toothpaste.

But that was the thing. She couldn't stop thinking about the toothpaste.

Their first evening, Audrey unpacked the family's food into the locker while her dad set up the tent. She put in the bread, the peanut butter, the trash bag, even the empty wrapper her brother had dropped in the dirt. Then she went back to the tent and stood there holding her toiletry kit, thinking. Angelique had said everything. The ranger pamphlet in the car had said something too. She'd skimmed it, and now she dug it out of the door pocket and read it again, properly this time.

"Anything with a scent counts as food," she read out loud.

"So sunscreen," said a voice. Keagan, Angelique's other friend from the site next door, had wandered over with a bag of marshmallows he was clearly not supposed to have. "Sunscreen, toothpaste, trash. All of it. Basically if a bear could smell it, it's dinner."

"That's grim," Audrey said.

"That's Yosemite rules," Keagan said, and shrugged. "My mom made me put my gum in there."

Audrey marched her whole kit back to the locker: toothpaste, chapstick, the little bottle of bug spray. When she got back, her dad was climbing into the tent with a look of bliss.

"I'm sleeping," he announced.

"Did you put your stuff in the locker?" Audrey asked.

"I don't have food."

"Sunscreen counts. Toothpaste counts. Trash counts."

He groaned the groan of a man who had driven six hours and now had to walk forty more feet. He went anyway, muttering, and came back smelling faintly of citronella and defeat.

The next morning they found muddy prints near the trash barrels two sites down, big ones, and a family standing around a tipped-over cooler looking miserable. Angelique nudged Audrey.

"Told you," she said.

"You're a regular bear diplomat," Audrey said.

"I'm the reason you still have a tent."

Audrey looked at the prints one more time, then went to double-check the locker. Everything with a scent, locked in steel, right where it belonged.

The bus smelled of rain and vinyl seats, and Brielle had the last row to herself until Amina slid in beside her with a paperback held open like a tray. "Ms. García says we have to paraphrase the whole scene by Friday," Amina said, "into words people actually use." She tapped the page, where a Scottish king was busy thinking about murder.

Brielle read the speech slowly, mouthing the words. "If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well it were done quickly." She tried it out loud. "If it was over the moment I did it, I'd better do it fast." That much worked. But something bothered her. Macbeth was saying he wanted to kill Duncan, and there was nobody else in the scene. Lady Macbeth had just left the stage. So who was he talking to? She turned the pages back and forth, checking who had spoken last, checking the stage directions, and found only the word "alone."

"Wait," Brielle said, and recounted the scene to Amina from the top: the king arrives, the guests go to bed, Lady Macbeth exits, and then Macbeth just talks. To the air. "It's a soliloquy," Amina said. "That's what Ms. García called it this morning. The character is usually alone on stage, saying their private thoughts out loud so the audience can hear them." Brielle stared at the page. So the audience was the only witness. Macbeth was telling them a secret he could never tell a living soul, because anyone who heard it would know he was a traitor.

She tested the idea on the next speech. When Lady Macbeth came back and Macbeth said "we will proceed no further in this business," he lied to her face, smooth and stable as anything. But the audience already knew, from the soliloquy, exactly what he wanted and how much he doubted himself. That was the trick of it. The private speech was where the truth lived. She had thought the assignment was about translating old words. It was really about overhearing. She began to write in the margin of her notebook, quick and certain now: He tells us what he won't tell her.

Amina leaned over to read it, and the bus swayed around the corner by the stable yard, where the horses stood nose to nose under the wet roof. "You're ahead of me," Amina said. "I'm still stuck on half these words." Brielle flipped back to the first page of the scene. "Then we've got the whole ride," she said, and clicked her pen. "Start at the top."

The community theatre smelled of dust and old velvet, and the stage lights buzzed so loudly William could hear them from the front row. Ms. Lawson had written two words on the chalkboard in the wing: yes, and. "Whatever your partner gives you," she said, "you take it and add to it. No blocking, no arguing. We'll go until the scene ends itself."

William's hands went cold. Last summer, at the talent show, he had frozen so completely that Darcy later told him he looked like he was trying to hibernate standing up. Forty seconds of silence, then the microphone squealed. He did not want that again, but he had signed up for this class anyway, because the poster said everyone gets better, and he wanted to believe a poster for once.

Darcy went first with Jeremie. "This elevator is stuck," Darcy said, yanking at an imaginary door. "Yes, and we've been in here since Tuesday," Jeremie answered, "so I've already eaten your sandwich." The audience laughed. Ms. Lawson called it good agreement, and the class nodded, reaching consensus without a word.

Then a girl went up and just stood there, staring at the boards. William recognized the frozen look. Her partner scanned the empty stage, then suddenly pointed and said, "Captain, the iceberg is straight ahead!" The girl snapped to life. "Full reverse!" she barked. "Sound the alarm!" William leaned forward. Something had changed her, and it wasn't courage. She had been nobody standing on boards, and then one sentence made her somebody.

"Anyone know what that's called?" Ms. Lawson asked. "Endowing," said Jeremie. "Like, you give your partner a role by what you say. 'Doctor, my arm hurts' makes them the doctor." Ms. Lawson snapped her fingers and pointed to the next pair.

William's turn came fast. He walked out under the transparent gel that turned the light pale blue, and his mind went blank the way it always did, cold and total. His mouth opened. He tried to think of a line and found nothing. His partner, a boy he didn't know, waited, then opened his own mouth, and William saw the freeze spreading.

So William spoke first, at his partner, fast. "Doctor, my arm hurts. It got worse after the whale swallowed us."

The boy blinked, then straightened like a man with ten years of medical school behind him. "Yes, and I told you not to pet the whale, William."

"You told me nothing, Doctor. You were asleep."

The class cracked up, and William felt his feet actually on the boards, warm and planted, and reached for the next line.

The town hall smelled of coffee and damp umbrellas, and Nicolas smoothed his notecards for the tenth time on the folding table. His class had been invited to speak about the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and Ms. Rosen had told him his part was simple: read one right and explain it in his own words. Simple was not the word Nicolas would have chosen. His hands still felt cold from the walk over, even though the room was warm.

A boy from another school, taller, with a lanyard swinging from his neck, grabbed the microphone first. "Freedom of expression," he announced, "means anyone can say anything they want, anywhere, anytime, and nobody can stop them." A few adults clapped. Nicolas felt his stomach tighten, because that was exactly what he had written on his card, in his own handwriting, underlined twice.

Aminata leaned over from the next chair. "Can I see your cards?" she whispered. When he handed them over, she flipped to the back, where he'd copied a section of the Charter for reference, and stood up. "Sorry," she said into the microphone, her voice steadier than Nicolas expected. "Section 1 of the Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society." She read it slowly, then sat down, cheeks pink.

The lanyard boy frowned. "So the rights aren't really rights?" Nicolas stared at his card, and something clicked, like a pattern he'd been staring at without seeing. If the rights were absolute, they would run into each other, one person's freedom crashing into another's safety. The limits weren't a wall against the rights; they were the thing that let the rights work at all. He tested the idea in his head, turning it over the way he turned a puzzle piece before snapping it in. When Ms. Rosen nodded at him, he walked to the microphone.

"Freedom of expression means I can say what I believe," Nicolas said, "and other people can oppose me, out loud, and neither of us gets punished. It's not a hierarchy where the loudest voice wins. It's more like a tranquil lake that everyone gets to drink from, as long as nobody poisons it." The room laughed softly at the lake, and the lanyard boy actually smiled. Afterward, Aminata found him by the cookie table and pushed a napkin with two oatmeal cookies toward him. "You changed your card," she said. "I saw you cross it out." Nicolas bit into the cookie and pointed at the microphone stand, where the lanyard boy was now writing something down, crossing it out, starting again.

Gabrielle balanced the last clay lamp on her grandmother's windowsill and stepped back to inspect the row. Her elbow knocked two of them sideways, and she caught one before it rolled off the ledge entirely.

"Careful," her grandmother said from the kitchen, laughing. "Those are diyas."

"Diyas," Gabrielle repeated, setting the little lamp upright. "Small oil lamps. Got it." She counted them anyway, because the whole afternoon had turned into a job with rules. Nine along the living room window, seven along the bedroom one, and the wicks still had to be checked before dark.

Jeremi and Fernando arrived just as the sky outside went purple, their bikes dropped in the courtyard like the riders had been flung off. Jeremi had never been to a Diwali celebration before and stood squinting at the windowsill as if it were a puzzle.

"Wait," he said. "Your grandma puts fire on the ledge and just... trusts nobody knocks it over? My dad won't even let me light a candle because of the mortgage papers on the desk."

"It's Diwali," Fernando said, tickling a mosquito bite on his arm. "Festival of lights. My family does it too, but we don't put them all in one window."

Gabrielle picked up one of the diyas and turned it in her hand. "The lights go out at night sometimes," she said. "Yesterday the one in the kitchen guttered out, and today the ones by the door. I keep thinking there's a reason, like a pattern." She narrowed her eyes at the window. "The kitchen one is right under the vent. The door ones are where the draft comes in when it opens."

"So the wind blows them out, genius," Jeremi said.

"That's a guess. I want to verify it." Gabrielle slid two lamps away from the drafty corner and placed them closer together near the middle of the ledge. "If these two stay lit longer than the ones I left in the corner, then it's the draft."

Her grandmother came out with a box of matches, chuckling at the three of them crouched at the window like detectives. She lit each wick, one by one, and the humid evening air began to smell faintly of oil and smoke.

"Five days of this," she said, shaking the match out. "You'll have plenty of time to watch your lamps."

"Five whole days," Jeremi whispered, as though the lamps themselves might hear him and get ideas.

They all sat on the floor below the ledge, watching the small flames bend and steady. In the corner, the leftmost diya flickered, sputtered, and went dark.

Gabrielle pointed at it. "Exhibit A."

Emilia had claimed the camp stove the way explorers claim mountains, which meant she stood in front of it with a spatula and refused to let anyone else touch the frying pan. Dinner was her job tonight, all of it, and she'd planned to prove she could handle the whole category of outdoor cooking, from soup to dessert, without a single adult hovering.

"Hovering," her dad said, hovering.

"See? That's the word. You're doing it." She pointed the spatula at the picnic table where Chloe and Meadow sat sorting marshmallows by size, a project Meadow insisted was scientific. "Go sit with them."

He drifted a few steps back, but not far, and Emilia poured oil into the pan for the flatbread she'd been practicing all week. The oil heated, shimmered, and then, when she nudged the pan to even it out, a tongue of flame leapt up from the surface. Chloe yelped. Meadow dropped a marshmallow.

Emilia's first instinct was the blue water jug sitting right there by the stove. Her hand actually went for it before her brain caught up. Two summers ago, Mr. Nasser, their neighbor, had been frying plantains in his driveway when his pan flared exactly like this, and she had watched him calmly reach past the water pitcher and slide a lid over the flames instead. He'd said only one sentence at the time, mostly to himself: "Never pour water on a grease fire." She'd asked why once, later, and he'd shrugged and said the flames would only get bigger, so a lid and no heat was the answer.

So Emilia grabbed the pan's lid, not the jug, slid it over the top, and shut off the burner with a click. The fire underneath dwindled, sulked, and went out, leaving a thin trail of smoke curling from under the rim.

"Whoa," said Meadow. "Why not the water?"

"Water would've made it way worse," Emilia said. "Lid and no heat. That's the move." She lifted the lid a crack, peeked in, and set it back down. "Also, we're having soup."

Her dad let out a breath that sounded like a laugh trapped on its way out. "I wasn't hovering."

"You were hovering at a distance," Chloe said. "There's a whole category for that. Long-range hovering."

"I'm biased," he admitted, holding up his hands, "because my daughter just put out a fire and didn't burn the flatbread." He peered over her shoulder as she lifted the lid again. The pan was scorched but fine. The oil was still hot enough to sizzle when she dropped in the first piece of dough, and it puffed up golden at the edges, perfectly ordinary, as if flames had never happened.

Emilia slid the flatbread onto a plate and held it out. "Dinner, family. Fire show included, no extra charge."

Charlie spread the two graphs across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with salt shakers. One showed a city called Iquitos, with rainfall bars that climbed every month like a staircase to nowhere. The other showed Cairo, where the bars lay flat against the bottom of the page. Ms. Petrov had promised the class would have to defend their answers tomorrow, and Charlie hated being the one who guessed.

Her laptop chimed. Isra's face filled the screen, her own graphs half visible behind her. "Did you finish classifying?"

"No," Charlie said. "I keep switching my answer for Iquitos."

"Then you're violating your own rule," Isra said. "You told us yesterday, stop guessing and use the system."

Charlie pulled up the page in her textbook. The Koppen system, it said, sorted climates by numbers, not by how a place looked. For a tropical rainforest climate, the rule ran down the page like a checklist: every month of the year had to average at least 18 degrees Celsius, and every month had to get at least 60 millimeters of rain. Every single month. No exceptions allowed.

She grabbed a pencil and started at January on the Iquitos graph. Temperature first. January sat at 26 degrees. She drew a light line at 18 across the whole year, like a fence, and checked each month against it. February cleared the fence. March cleared it. She worked through the year month by month, and none of the temperature curves dipped below her line.

"Now the rain," she muttered. She set her ruler at 60 millimeters on the rainfall axis and drew a second fence. This one was harder. January's bar towered past 200. April's bar barely cleared 60, but it cleared it. June, July, August, each one stood above the line. December wavered at what looked like exactly 60, and she squinted, leaned closer, and checked the number printed at the top of the bar. 62. Still above.

"It passes," she said to Isra. "All twelve months pass both tests. Iquitos counts as a tropical rainforest under Koppen."

"Try Cairo," Isra said. "For contrast."

Charlie laid her fences on the Cairo graph. The temperature line dove below 18 in three winter months, and the rainfall bars never once reached 60. Two failures, over and over. Same planet, she thought, same spinning ball of water and air, and one place grew lush green forest while the other grew sand. The graph was the only evidence she had, and it was enough. Somewhere behind those bars was the reason, invisible, but the numbers didn't lie about what it produced.

Her brother thumped past with a box of model airplane cargo, scattering small plastic crates across the table edge. Charlie swept them off her graphs and pinned the last corner down with her coffee mug.

"So tomorrow when Ms. Petrov asks," Isra said, "you'll actually have a method?"

Charlie capped her pencil and smiled at the two graphs, fences still drawn across them. "Every month, both lines. That's my whole defense."

The envelope from Mackenzie was waiting in Asher's backpack when he got to the science museum, and he read it twice while Emerson queued for tickets. "I heard Ms. Virtanen is picking two people to present at the assembly," Mackenzie had written, "and I think it should be you. But you'd better actually understand the seasons, because she'll ask questions in front of everyone. Last year I froze up there and I still think about it." Asher folded the letter carefully. He had said yes to the assembly without really knowing why, and the doubt had followed him all week like a shadow.

The exhibit hall held a giant model of the sun and a rack of globes with little lamps you could wheel around them. A sign challenged visitors: Make winter happen. Asher picked up a globe and started to walk it around the sun, watching the lamp, but nothing changed. The light hit the northern half the same way at every step of the circle.

"You're holding it wrong," Emerson said, though she sounded unsure. She wanted her turn with the globe, and she wanted to be the one who figured it out first; she kept grabbing the base and turning it toward her. Asher held on. He remembered a diagram from the curriculum binder Ms. Virtanen had lent him, one he'd skimmed on the bus. A slanted line through the planet. He tipped the globe sideways, leaning it as he walked the circle, and stopped.

"Look at this spot," he said, pointing at a dot painted near the top of the globe. When the leaning globe was on one side, the dot caught the lamp's light at a shallow, glancing angle. Halfway around, the same dot faced the beam almost straight on. He kept the tilt steady and monitored the dot through a full lap, holding his phone camera up to record it so he could check later. Then, to be sure, he set the globe perfectly upright and walked it around again. The light hit the dot at the same angle every single time. Winter and summer never came. "It's the tilt," he said. "If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year. There'd be almost no seasons."

Emerson leaned over his phone, watching the recording with an infectious grin spreading across her face. "Say that again," she said, reaching for the globe. "Say it slow, and this time let me hold the tilt."

Anna had been to the cultural center for craft fairs and a lunar new year show, but never for this. The hallway smelled of cardamom and butter, and Thomas was already waiting by the doors, bouncing on his heels like the floor was hot.

"You came," he said. "Good. My cousins will outnumber you, but you'll survive."

Inside, the big hall was full of tables, and Anna noticed something odd right away. There were plates stacked everywhere, samosas and dates and some kind of sweet noodles, but nobody was eating. Kids were laughing, aunties were hugging, a man in a bright green robe was arranging a tray of pastries like a general deploying troops. All that food, and not one bite taken. It was a mystery, and Anna loved mysteries more than she loved homework, which is to say a lot.

She watched Thomas's little cousin grab a date, lift it halfway to his mouth, then sigh and put it back. Anna leaned toward Thomas. "Is the food broken? Poisoned? Some kind of decorative food?"

"It's Eid al-Fitr," Thomas said. "That means it's the end of Ramadan, the month where the grown-ups fast. No food from dawn until sunset. A whole month."

Anna did the math slowly, the way she did with riddles. A month of not eating all day. That would explain the tower of pastries, the cousin's dramatic sigh, the man guarding the tray like a dragon. But she wanted proof. "So nobody has eaten since sunrise?" she whispered. "Even the little kids?"

"Some do, some don't," Thomas said. "But my grandmother, never. She says her streak is cumulative. Thirty years of Ramadans, all stacked up."

Then the man in the green robe cupped his hands, the room went quiet, and a voice called out across the hall. The sun had gone down. Anna watched the whole crowd move at once, like one enormous hungry organism with forty arms, and the pastry tray simply vanished, flourishing into nothing while the man in green blinked at his empty hands.

The little cousin ate his date, then five more, then announced to the room, "I have waited my whole life for this," which was three hours, but nobody argued. Thomas's grandmother pressed a pastry into Anna's palm, warm and sticky, and said, "Eat, eat, you are too skinny for a detective."

Anna froze. "How did you know I was investigating?"

"Child, you have been staring at that tray since you walked in." She laughed and patted Anna's cheek. "Next mystery, I suggest the sweet noodles. They vanish fast."

Anna bit into the pastry and turned to Thomas. "So next year, I'm bringing my own plate. And a seat near the front."

Thomas grinned. "Bring a helmet too," he said, and pointed at the empty table where the samosas used to be.

The click started three nights ago, somewhere inside the garage door opener, and it was getting louder. Gabrielle sat on an overturned milk crate in her family's garage workshop, her dad's old workbench behind her, and listened. Click, pause, click. The door went up and down fine, which was the strange part. Something hidden was making the noise, and she wanted to know what.

Elio arrived first, skateboarding up the driveway, then Malek on his bike. They crowded around the opener's metal case while Gabrielle found a screwdriver in the drawer of bolts and drill bits. "It could be the motor," Elio said. "Or a loose screw rattling around." Malek crouched and put his ear against the case. "Do it again," he said, and Gabrielle pressed the button on the wall. The door rumbled upward. Click, pause, click.

"It clicks twice each time, always in the same rhythm," Malek said. "Loose screws don't keep a rhythm." Gabrielle turned the screwdriver and lifted the cover off. Inside she could see the motor, the gears, and a diagonal metal arm that swung as the door moved. She watched it go around, and around, and then she saw it: a small plastic gear with a chip taken out of one tooth. Each time the chipped tooth met the next gear, it slipped, and clicked. "There," she said, pointing. "The gear's broken."

Elio leaned in, frowning. "So how do we know that's really it? We can't watch it every second." Gabrielle thought of the poster she'd made last month for the science fair, the one where she'd written about how plants might respond to sound, and how Mr. Demetriou had looked at it and asked, "How would you test that?" She hadn't been able to answer then, but she'd gone home and figured it out afterward. "You write it as an if-then statement," she said. "Hypotheses are often written as 'If ..., then ...' statements, which name the change being made and the result that is predicted." She picked up a pencil stub and wrote on the back of a sandpaper sheet: If we stop the gear from slipping, then the clicking stops.

"Okay," Malek said slowly. "So what's the change?"

"A little tape won't hold," Gabrielle said, "but if the chipped tooth can't catch on anything, it can't slip." She pressed a small dab of grease onto the broken tooth with a cotton swab, then wiped the swab clean. Elio watched the gears hungrily, as if they might consume the grease and fail anyway. The gear itself was made of a cheap polymer, some kind of soft plastic, which was probably why the tooth had broken in the first place.

Gabrielle pressed the button. The door rumbled down. Silence. She pressed it again, and the door went up through the same quiet, no click, no pause, nothing. Malek pumped his fist. From the driveway, Mr. Demetriou, who had been washing his car across the street, called over, "You three fixed that yourselves?" Gabrielle held up the sandpaper with the if-then sentence on it and grinned. "Tested it," she said. "And the test said we were right."

Paisley dragged the folding table to the middle of the garage and wiped off a smudge of motor oil with an old rag. On Saturday she would tell twenty classmates which cereal tasted better, the name brand or the store brand, and she wanted the answer to be real. Her dad's workbench smelled like sawdust and cold metal, and through the half-open door she could hear a sprinkler ticking across the lawn.

Gibson arrived first, carrying two boxes in a paper bag so nobody on the street could read the labels. "I got the same kind," he said, setting them down. "Toasted oat rings, both of them. One costs almost double." Lia came next with a notebook and a box of small plastic bowls. She lined them up in two parallel rows along the table edge, matched pairs, white and identical.

"Here's the problem," Paisley said. "My brother swears the expensive one tastes better, but he always knows which bowl it's in. He sees the box, and then he decides." She poured milk into a small measuring cup and thought for a moment about how to make him not see.

Lia tapped her pen against her chin. "So don't let him see."

"Right." Paisley carried the boxes behind her dad's old lawn mower, out of sight, and came back with masking tape and a marker. She labeled one row of bowls A and the other row B. Only she knew which row held the name brand, and she wrote the answer on a scrap of paper, folded it twice, and buried it under a coffee can of screws on the shelf. Gibson scooped cereal into the bowls with a serving spoon, careful to make each portion the same size, and Lia stirred a drop of milk into each one so the samples would match.

When the tasting started on Saturday, they set up the garage like a small lab. Ms. Wardak, who lived next door, came over first and tried both bowls, frowning slightly in a way that meant she was thinking hard. "B," she said. Paisley marked it down. Kids from her class filed through the doorway, one at a time, and each one tasted A, drank water, then tasted B. Nobody could tell which was which, so nobody's expectations could sway their answers, which was exactly what Paisley wanted. Gibson called it a blind test, and the phrase felt right, like the whole garage had its eyes covered.

By late afternoon Lia counted the tally marks. Eleven picked A, nine picked B. Paisley dug the folded paper out from under the coffee can, and her hands were a little unsteady as she opened it. The name brand was row B. Nine out of twenty people had chosen the expensive cereal, which was not quite half, and the store brand had actually won. She stared at the numbers while a breeze moved the paper in her fingers.

"We should run it again," Lia said, already flipping to a clean page in the notebook.

Gibson reached for the cereal boxes behind the mower. "Same bowls, new letters?"

Evelyn stood in the garage in front of the washing machine with three baskets around her feet and a folded note from her mom in her hand. The note said she was in charge of her own laundry now, start to finish, and that the white school shirts had to last until June. That was the part that worried her, because Monday's white shirt had come out of the last load faintly pink, and nobody could tell her why.

She dumped the baskets out and sorted. Whites went in one pile, darks in another, and a heap of brights in a third. Then she sat cross-legged and went through the whites piece by piece, wondering what had gone wrong. The pink was even, not blotchy, which seemed strange. If something had spilled, it would have made a spot, wouldn't it? An even colour meant the pink had been everywhere in the water at once.

She dug through the laundry hamper and found it, balled up in a corner: a red sock, brand new, the tag still slightly stiff. On Monday that sock had shared a load with her white shirt. Could a sock give off colour into the water, the way a teabag gives off colour into hot water? She held the sock under the tap and watched the water run pale red. So that was it. New dark or bright clothes could release dye into the wash water, and that dye could tint white and pale clothes. She almost laughed. The sock had been a traitor hiding in the wrong pile.

Her friend Marissa came through the side door with her skateboard under her arm, looking for the helmet she had left on the workbench. "Why are you staring at a sock?" she asked.

"I figured out the pink shirt mystery. This sock leaked dye into the wash, and my white shirt soaked it up. Which is sort of ironic, since the sock was too small to matter and it ruined the biggest thing in the load." Evelyn held it up like evidence in a courtroom.

"That's a whole science happening in your garage." Marissa found her helmet and buckled it under her chin. "Don't hit your head on the dryer door, you'll get a concussion and it'll be my fault for distracting you."

Evelyn set up a test anyway, because guessing wasn't the same as knowing. She put the red sock in a small bucket of warm water with an old white pillowcase, swished it around, and waited while Marissa practiced kickflips on the driveway. After ten minutes the pillowcase had gone pink at the edges. Case closed. She added a cup of white vinegar to the bucket for the sock, made a note to wash new bright things alone from now on, and loaded the machine with pure whites only. As the drum started to turn, she measured out the detergent and said, mostly to herself, "June, here we come."

Nolan crouched at the edge of the pond with a jar in one hand and a worksheet in the other, and both were going badly. The worksheet had three empty boxes labeled cell wall, cell membrane, and nucleus, and the jar was supposed to hold a sample of pond water for the second half of the assignment. Ms. García had set up two microscopes on the folding table by the dock, and she had been clear about the deadline: the bus back to school left at two o'clock sharp, and anyone without a finished sheet was staying behind with her to finish it Monday.

"You're on the onion first," Esme said, waving him toward the table. "I already did mine." She held up her worksheet, and Nolan's stomach dropped. Every box was filled in, and her sketch of the cells looked tidy, like a honeycomb. "I want the pond water slide," she went on. "Asees says there's a paramecium in there, and I want to see it before anyone else finds one. I've been wanting to see one move since sixth grade."

Nolan peeled a paper-thin layer from the onion half Ms. García had left on the tray, laid it on the slide, and lowered the lens. At first he saw nothing but a gray blur. He turned the focus knob a hair at a time, hesitant, because the last time he had rushed it he had cracked a slide in science class and been given the cleanup job for a week. Then the blur sharpened into rows of boxes, wall to wall, like bricks that had been told to colonize every inch of the glass. He could see the thick outer lines easily. That had to be the wall. Inside each brick was a faint rim, which he decided was the membrane.

But the third box was the problem. Somewhere in each cell there should be a dark spot, and he could not find it. He swept the slide, corner to corner, and reasoned it out loud. "The wall and membrane are outlines, so the nucleus is probably a thing floating inside, not a border. Maybe I'm in the wrong category of cell." Esme leaned over, still holding her finished sheet, drumming her fingers because the pond water was waiting for her. "It's the dark blob," she said. "Mine looked like a fingerprint in the middle of each brick. Keep looking, but be fast."

He slowed the sweep and looked for dark instead of looking for shapes. There, in cell after cell, a small dense dot, plain once he stopped expecting something bigger. He wrote nucleus in the last box just as Asees jogged up with the news that the paramecium was, in fact, swimming. "Who even found that first?" Nolan asked, still writing. "Robert Brown," Esme said, grinning. "Some Scottish botanist. He described the nucleus in 1831 looking at orchid cells. Ms. García told me when I asked who first noticed the dark spot." Asees shouted from the dock that the thing was turning left. Esme shoved her worksheet into Nolan's hand for proof of her head start and ran, and Nolan capped his pen at 1:53, following her down to the water.

Bike club met behind the gym on Thursdays, and this Thursday Payton had a problem: her back tyre was flat as a pancake, and the school's Fun Ride was in three days. Mr. Koné dumped a bucket of tyre levers, patches and a pump on the tarmac and said, "Fix it yourselves. I'm only here to convert your groaning into effort." He sat on a crate with his coffee like a king watching peasants.

The tyre levers were the easy part. Payton snapped two of them under the rim, popped the bead loose, and pulled out the old tube with a hiss of dying dignity. Brodie held the wheel steady while Charlee found the hole, spit on the tube, and watched the bubbles. "Culprit located," Charlee announced, like a detective. Then they all stared at the new tube, pale and floppy, like a noodle that had given up on life.

The hard part began when Payton tried to put the noodle back in. Every time she pushed the tyre onto the rim, the tube slithered out of place and got trapped under the bead. She levered, cursed under her breath, started again. Three times the tube bulged out at one spot like a sleepy animal trying to escape. "It's mocking me," she told the wheel.

She stopped and thought. The tube kept twisting because it had no shape, the way a rope tangles but a stick doesn't. If the tube had a shape, it might sit still. There was a pump right there. She hooked it up and put a little air in, just enough that the tube puffed into a rounded circle instead of a sad ribbon. It held its form in the tyre like it had been told to sit up straight. The tyre slid back on in one smooth push, and nothing got caught, nothing got pinched. "It needed a spine," she said, and pumped it up proper.

"Dormant genius activated," said Charlee, offering a solemn high five. Brodie wrote something in his notebook under PAYTON'S LAW, which was a factor he claimed would one day convert the whole school to her fandom.

Then Payton turned the wheel proudly and heard the thin, unmistakable whistle of air escaping from the front tyre, which had been fine all morning. Mr. Koné raised his coffee cup without getting up. "Bucket's still there," he said.

Riley stood in front of the mirror at Trend Junction with three dresses over her arm and twenty minutes before Sami's mom arrived to drive them to the dance. The mall speakers blasted an aggressive jingle about the store's anniversary sale, and Macy held up a fourth dress, silver and short. "This one," Macy said. "It's literally made for a dance."

"Everything here is literally made for a dance," Riley said, but she took it anyway. At the register, wedged between racks of clearance scarves, a bin of glow sticks sat beside a sign: FREE WITH ANY PURCHASE, WHILE SUPPLIES LAST. Riley, who had learned in Mr. Bakker's class to be suspicious of anything free in a place of commerce, took two anyway and slipped one into her pocket.

At the dance she cracked the first stick and clipped it to her wrist, and it blazed so bright that Sami grabbed her arm to make her wave it around. Riley's pocket, though, sat right against the gym's hot radiator through the whole first hour, and when she cracked the second stick later it flared brilliantly and then, by the last song, went dark while the first one still glowed on her wrist. She turned the dead stick over in her hand, thinking. It had been warm in her pocket. The first one had lived in the cool dark of her locker all afternoon, dimmer but still alive. There was a pattern here, she thought, something you couldn't see directly, and only one way to test it.

"Come home with me," she told Macy on the bus. "I need your freezer."

"You need my freezer," Macy repeated. But she came, and Riley retrieved the first glow stick, the dim one, from her jacket and laid it in the ice tray between two cubes of frozen orange juice. "If it's still glowing in the morning, I'm right," she said. "Cold keeps it going longer."

"Why do you care?" Macy asked, flopping onto Riley's bed. "The dance is over."

Riley thought about the silver dress, still hanging in the closet with the tags on because she'd worn Sami's borrowed skirt instead at the last minute, and about the bin at the store. She had taken the free sticks without questioning them, the way she'd said yes to the dance without deciding whether she actually wanted to go. "Because next time I'll know," she said. "Bright and fast, or dim and slow. You have to pick."

In the morning they ran downstairs in their socks. Macy yanked open the freezer door and pulled back the juice cubes.

The glow stick was glowing.

Christopher sat on the spinning stool in front of the mirror and put on the fifth pair of frames, which made him look, in his own opinion, like a startled rodent. "These ones," he declared anyway, because the other four had been worse and his mother was already checking her phone for the third time.

"Those are perpendicular to your eyebrows," said Aviana, who worked the front counter on Saturdays and had opinions about everything, including his hair. "Tilted. Like a crooked picture frame."

"That's a style," Christopher said.

"That's a mistake," she said, and plucked them off his face and handed him a round tortoiseshell pair instead.

While his mother filled out the paperwork, Ms. Henry, the optometrist, came out of the back room with his chart. "Christopher," she said, "before you go, one question. Honest answer. On a normal Saturday, how much time do you spend outside?"

Christopher thought about this very carefully, because a normal Saturday involved a screen, a couch, and eleven straight hours of a game where he was currently ranked in the top two hundred players. "Some," he said. "A decent amount. Outdoors-adjacent."

Aviana snorted so hard she had to pretend to cough.

Ms. Henry just looked at him over her glasses. "Here's the thing. Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood. So when I see a kid your age who needs glasses for distance, I can guess a lot about his weekends."

Christopher felt his face go warm. It was like she'd read his save file. He tested the idea, turning it over. "So if I go outside more now, does that fix it?"

"It's not a magic undo button," she said. "But it's a good habit anyway."

He slid the new frames on and looked at the wall of sunglasses across the store, which was suddenly crisp all the way to the corners instead of soft and foggy, and he had to admit the ceiling tiles had actual lines in them. "Travis is going to nominate me for biggest dork in the grade," he said, pulling out his phone to text him a selfie anyway.

The reply came back in eight seconds: a photo of Travis squinting at his own phone while holding a ruler, and the words "who's blurry NOW."

Aviana leaned over the counter. "Tell him what you learned," she said. "The weekend part. Word for word."

"He'll laugh."

"He squints at everything," she said. "Half the basketball team does. Go count."

Christopher thought of Travis, who never saw a scoreboard until they were three feet away, and of half his class rubbing their eyes after video marathons. He texted: "Up for the park tomorrow? I'll bring the ball. I can actually see the hoop now."

Julia stood on the porch of Emmeline's grandmother's house holding a box of oranges wrapped in paper so shiny it squeaked. Through the door she could hear at least fifteen people talking at once, because tonight was Emmeline's grandmother's birthday, and Emmeline's whole enormous family had come from three different states.

"You take your shoes off first," Emmeline whispered, toeing off her sneakers into a row of sandals by the step. "Everybody does, even Uncle Rob, and he wears size thirteen."

Julia balanced on one foot, then the other, and set her shoes in the row. She had been rehearsing this moment since Tuesday, when her mother said, "You never show up to somebody's grandmother's birthday with your hands empty." Last weekend at her own family's gathering, her cousin had torn the wrapping paper off a gift in two seconds flat and lobbed it over his shoulder, but Emmeline had said that at her grandmother's house, gifts were opened quietly and the paper was folded. Two households, two sets of rules, and Julia meant to learn all of them before dinner.

She pressed the orange box into her hostess's hands with both arms and a small bow, the way Emmeline had demonstrated in the gym on Thursday. The grandmother's eyes crinkled, and she bowed back, lower than Julia expected, and said something that made the whole hallway laugh warmly.

Dinner was ramen, huge steaming bowls of it, and Julia had just lifted her chopsticks when the noise started. Slurrrp. Slurrrrp. It came from every side of the long table, from Emmeline's uncles, from the tiny cousins, even from Emmeline herself, loud and cheerful as a pack of happy engines. Julia froze with her noodles halfway to her mouth. At home that sound meant somebody was about to get the Look from Grandma. She glanced sideways to check whether anyone here was offended, and that was her first clue: nobody was. If slurping were rude, somebody would have frowned. Instead Emmeline's grandfather slurped again and sighed like a man receiving a medal.

So Julia formed a hypothesis, the way Mr. Sadeghi had taught them in science: if everyone did it, and nobody reacted, then the rule itself must be different here, not the people. She would test it once, quietly, and watch what happened. She drew in a modest slurp of broth.

"More," said Emmeline's grandmother, waving a ladle. "Louder! You eat like a shy little microbe!"

"A microbe can't slurp at all," Emmeline said. "I looked it up for Mr. Sadeghi's class. They're too small, and they don't have mouths, exactly."

"Then Julia must not eat like one," the grandmother declared, and the cousins chanted, "Not a microbe! Not a microbe!" Julia laughed so hard she nearly lost a noodle, then gathered up a truly heroic proportional quantity of noodles, about a third of the bowl, and slurped with everything she had. The table erupted in applause. Emmeline's grandfather raised his glass to her. Somewhere down the table an aunt called out that Julia was now officially family, and Emmeline kicked her gently under the table and whispered, "Told you."

After the cake, when the little ones were being herded toward the rooms where they would retire for the night, Emmeline's grandmother found Julia by the door, still holding her folded wrapping paper like a treasure. "Next year," she said, tapping the orange box, "you bring the noodles. I will teach you the big slurp."

Savannah lay on her bed with the family group chat open on her phone, staring at the last message her cousin had sent, a photo of everyone at the lake. She recognized the towels, the cooler, her aunt's terrible hat. What she noticed most was the empty spot on the dock where Jordan usually sat, knees pulled up, grinning.

Jordan had skipped the sleepover on Saturday too. No explanation, just a text that said can't come, sorry, and then nothing for two days. Savannah had typed and deleted four replies. Her final answer had been a thumbs up, which felt cold even as she sent it.

"She just bails on everything now," Savannah said out loud to her phone. "She's become a flake."

Downstairs, her mom called that she was going to the store. A minute later the door shut, and the house went quiet except for the fridge humming. Savannah scrolled back through the chat, looking for proof of her theory. There was Jordan in June, participating in the cousin trivia game until midnight. There was Jordan in July, first to RSVP for the lake day. Then, three weeks ago, the messages just stopped.

That was a pattern, Savannah thought. But a pattern of what? Flakes didn't usually vanish overnight. Something had changed, and it wasn't Jordan's character. It was the situation, except she didn't know the situation.

She thought of Ms. Patel, who lived next door to Jordan and brought their family zucchini bread every August. Savannah pulled on her sandals and walked the two blocks, telling herself she was only returning a Tupperware container.

Ms. Patel answered the door with flour on her hands. "Savannah! Come in. Were you looking for Jordan? She's at the hospital with her grandmother, poor thing. The grandmother tore a tendon in her leg falling down the porch steps, and Jordan's been there every afternoon since, doing the dishes and reading to her."

Savannah felt her face go hot. "Every afternoon?"

"Every single one. She's keeping it quiet because her grandmother hates a fuss."

On the walk home, Savannah remembered a page she had photographed from her sister's psychology textbook because it looked interesting. She found it in her camera roll and read it again: the fundamental attribution error, named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in. She had done exactly that. Twice.

Back in her room, she opened the chat with Jordan, who was not a flake, and who had a grandmother in a hospital bed. She typed slowly.
