"There's a wasp nest by the bridge," the kid said, voice wobbling. "Nobody should clean there without the spray can."

The circle went silent, then erupted. That was exactly the kind of thing they needed. Aaron wrote "wasp nest, bridge" on the agenda under trail cleanup. After that, he kept his eyes moving around the circle, picking raised hands in a pattern he could defend: a new speaker before a repeat speaker. He did let Viviane talk again later, after three others had gone, and she kept it short. Katelynn nudged the Cabin Four kid and offered him the second pair of her own gloves for bridge duty.

By the time they reached the campfire skit item, everyone in the circle had spoken at least twice, and the kid from Cabin Four was volunteering to play the raccoon. Mr. Halvorsen pushed off from the tree, gave Aaron a small nod, and walked toward the dining hall.

"Same time tomorrow," Aaron said, and folded the agenda into his pocket.

Nora's saxophone had a sound like a goose with a grievance, and everyone in the storage room behind the band hall knew it. She was supposed to improvise a blues solo over the twelve-bar progression for Friday's assembly, and so far her solo had four notes in it, all safe, all dull. Maksim sat on an upturned tuba case eating pretzels while she ran the changes again. "That's a solo the way a fence is a vacation," he said.

She glared at him and played the four notes again, louder. The backing track on the classroom's old laptop ground on, guitar chords cycling past in their patient order, and Nora felt like she was standing outside a locked house trying every key on a ring. Rex leaned in the doorway with a trumpet case balanced on his hip. "You're restricting yourself to the pentatonic," he said. "Five notes. Safe. My cousin calls it the fence too, by the way."

"That helps me zero," Nora said, but it helped her a little, because it gave her a thought. She knew the five-note pattern cold. The solo sounded fine and completely unlike the recordings Mr. Popescu played them, the ones with the gritty, scraped-raw sound that had made her want to do this in the first place. Something was in those recordings that was not in her five notes. A stranger's note. She considered the context of everything she'd heard: the players didn't sound like they were breaking rules. They sounded like they were using one she hadn't found.

So she tested a simple idea. She slid down a half step from the fifth note of her pattern and landed on the note just below it, flat where it should have been sharp-edged and clean. Then she played it again, bent and growling, right over the fourth bar. Maksim stopped chewing. "What was that," he said, which was not a question.

"It's the flattened fifth," Nora said. "You add it to the five notes, and it stops sounding like an exercise and starts sounding like the blues." She ran the solo again, and this time the strange note snarled through the middle of every phrase, and even the goose-grief squeak in her low register sounded intentional, almost stylish. Rex raised his trumpet case in a slow salute.

On Friday, in front of an audience that included the affluent families who donated the new risers, Nora stood up for her eight bars. She played her fence of five notes, then let the flat one loose, and heard a woman in the second row say "oh" out loud. Maksim, in the clarinet section, held up one pretzel in silent tribute.

The comment appeared at 9:47 on Tuesday night, in the group chat for the science fair: "Honestly Anabel your poster looks like a kindergartner made it. Maybe let someone with taste handle the design." It was signed, in a way, by the name at the top of the bubble: Walid. Vincent stared at his phone. Walid was the kid who said "excuse me" to desks he bumped into, who had helped Anabel carry her poster board up two flights of stairs that very afternoon.

Anabel didn't reply in the chat. On Wednesday she sat alone at lunch, poking at her pasta, and when Vincent asked if she was okay she said, "Fine," which was obviously not true. He kept replaying the message. The Walid on the stairs and the Walid in the chat couldn't be the same person, could they? But it wasn't a hack; the account had been his for years, complete with his dog in the profile picture.

Vincent decided to test a simple idea: that people act differently in writing than they do in person, and that the difference might be a known thing, something with a name. During study hall he searched "why are people mean online but nice in person." Most of what came up was junk, but one result looked plausible, a paper by a psychologist named John Suler. It described what he called the online disinhibition effect, the way people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. Vincent wrote down the citation so he could show Anabel the source, then screenshotted the paragraph and incorporated it into his notes with the screenshot of Walid's comment, side by side like evidence at a trial.

The next morning he found Walid at his locker. "Did you mean what you wrote about Anabel's poster?" Vincent asked. Walid's face went pale, then red. "I was frustrated about the layout. I typed it without thinking. I would never say that to her, though. Not to her face." That was the part that interested Vincent, and the part that made it worse. It wasn't an impostor. It was Walid, minus whatever stops him in the hallway.

They walked to the computer lab together and found Ms. Lindqvist monitoring the morning crowd. Walid said he would apologize, and he typed it into the chat right there, with his hands shaking a little: "Anabel, that comment was wrong. Your poster is great and I'm sorry." The bubble turned blue and delivered. Then Anabel replied, a single thumbs-up, no words, and closed her phone. At the science fair on Friday she stood beside her poster, which was beautiful, and she thanked the judges politely, and when Walid brought her a cup of punch she took it and said, "Thanks," but she stood a little apart from him the whole evening, and she didn't rejoin the group chat until the following week.

At dinner, Emmett pushed his noodles around the plate while his phone sat face-down beside his glass, buzzing like a trapped wasp. He had posted a video of himself doing a terrible magic trick that afternoon, realized within ten minutes how bad it looked, and deleted it. Now the buzzing wouldn't stop. His dad asked twice whether the chicken needed more salt before Emmett finally flipped the phone over.

The screen showed the group chat with Tristan, Lindsey, and half the soccer team. Lindsey had sent a clip. Emmett tapped it, and there he was again, mid-trick, dropping the cards, his face frozen in the exact moment before the trick failed. He checked his own page first, scrolling fast. The post was gone, deleted, exactly as he'd left it. Yet there it was in the chat, playing on a loop. He typed, "I deleted that," and Tristan answered in seconds: "Lindsey saved it before you did. Anyone who grabs a copy keeps it." Emmett read the line three times. Deleting had felt like slamming a door, but the room had already been photographed.

He set the phone down and tried an experiment in his head. If deleting only cleaned up his page, then anything he posted, photos, his location at the pizza place, everything, could already be sitting in somebody's camera roll, somebody he didn't even know. He picked up the phone and asked Lindsey directly, "Who else has this?" A typing bubble appeared, then vanished, then appeared again. "Just the team," she wrote, which was not exactly an answer. His mom, watching his neutral expression go pale, slid the water pitcher toward him without a word.

"I need to ask people to delete their copies," Emmett said aloud, half to his plate. His dad asked what was going on, and Emmett showed him the chat. "Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it," his dad said, reading Tristan's message back slowly. Emmett nodded. That was the rule, and he hadn't known it existed until it stepped on him.

He messaged everyone in the chat, one at a time, asking politely. Most complied. Tristan sent back a thumbs-up and then, a minute later, "Done." Emmett felt his shoulders drop an inch. Lindsey sent a heart and promised the copies were gone.

At breakfast the next morning, his phone buzzed once. It was Lindsey: "Ask your mom to check the family photo stream." Emmett stared at the message, then opened the app, and there, between his grandmother's birthday cake and the lake vacation, was his own blurry face, mid-trick, cards raining onto the carpet, saved automatically by the cloud. He sighed, grabbed a slice of toast, and went to find his mom. "So," he said, holding up the phone, "how do I delete something I never posted?"

Rebecca spread the photocopied story across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with a jar of pickles and a tin of shortbread. "Book club starts in five minutes," she announced. "Grandma said we could use the kitchen as long as we don't spill anything near her recipes."

Damian arrived first, clutching his copy like a warrant for arrest. "The ending is so obvious," he declared before he'd even sat down. "Page two, Mrs. Vale keeps staring at the locked cabinet. That's foreshadowing. She's the thief. Case closed." Quentin slouched in behind him, eating the last of the shortbread, and shrugged in a way that suggested he had opinions but was saving them.

Rebecca had read the story three times the night before, curled in her grandmother's reading chair while the clock downstairs ticked like a slow heartbeat. Damian's evidence bothered her. The cabinet appeared on page two, sure, and again on page five, and yet the whole story seemed to revolve around the neighbor's greenhouse, where half the conversations happened. Why would the writer keep dragging them back to the greenhouse if the cabinet mattered so much?

"Okay," she said, flipping pages. "Let's test it. If the cabinet is a real clue, then the thief has to have a way in, a reason, and a moment alone with it." She traced the timeline with her pencil. Mrs. Vale never had a moment alone. She was always in the greenhouse, reviving drooping orchids, talking about the flower commerce at the village market, handing out spontaneous advice to strangers. Meanwhile the cousin, quiet little footnote of a character, was mentioned twice bringing in the mail.

Quentin sat up. "The mail. The mail!" He grabbed Damian's copy and stabbed the paragraph. "The key arrives in the mail. Page four."

"The cabinet, though," Damian insisted, but his voice had developed a wobble.

"Think about it," Rebecca said. "The writer put the cabinet right up front, big and shiny and suspicious, so we'd all stare at it and miss the cousin. That's a red herring." Damian opened his mouth, and she held up a hand. "A false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion. Not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing. Sometimes the writer is tricking you."

There was a silence, into which the back door opened and Mr. Lee from next door leaned in, holding a trowel. "Grandmother said something about a book club? I've read that one." He settled into a chair without waiting for an answer. "Fell for the cabinet myself, first time through. Threw the book across the room at the end."

"You too?" Damian groaned, and dropped his forehead onto the table beside the pickle jar. Quentin patted his shoulder with mock solemnity and offered him the empty shortbread tin, as if it were a prize for effort.

Rebecca read the final paragraph aloud, and there it was, the cousin slipping the key into his pocket, hidden in a sentence about orchids. "So what does the greenhouse mean?" she asked, pencil ready. "Because that orchid that keeps nearly dying? I think it's the whole point."

Damian lifted his head. "Explain that again," he said, "slowly, and this time I'm taking notes."

Romy's volleyball team had lost every away game since October, and she was tired of pretending it didn't bother her. What confused her was that the same team, the same passes, the same serves, looked completely different at the community center gym. There they had beaten Riverside in two straight sets, then rolled over Northgate, then won again on Thursday night, a scrappy three-setter against a team that had crushed them on the road 25-12. Romy lay on her bedroom floor afterward, bouncing a ball off the ceiling, trying to digest the idea that the losses and the wins were coming from the same twelve players.

"It can't be the gym," she told Mckinley at practice, spinning a ball on one finger. "A court is a court." McKinley, who kept the scorebook, flipped backward through the pages. Away games: zero wins. Home games: three. "Maybe it's not trivial," Romy said slowly. "Maybe it's a pattern." She grabbed a scrap of paper and went around the community center, asking the Saturday basketball league and the indoor soccer teams one question: how do you do at home versus away? The basketball coach shrugged and said they were about even, maybe a little better at home. The soccer captain said the same thing, better than even, but nobody could say why.

Myla, meanwhile, had her own problem. She wanted to audition for setter, but the coach kept her at libero, saying she was too short to see over the net. Myla practiced sets against the wall every day after warm-ups, fifty in a row, jaw set, until her forearms were pink. "You should just ask for the audition," Romy told her. "Worst thing she says is no." "Worst thing she says is no in front of everybody," Myla said, and served a ball into the bleachers by accident, which made them both laugh so hard Ms. Tremblay, who ran the center, came over to see what was wrong.

The next home game, Romy tested her idea. She played the first set the way she always did, and they won easily. In the second set, she deliberately pretended they were on the road, calling away-game warmups, using the visitors' bench. They lost 25-19. In the third set she gave it up and leaned into the home crowd instead, pointing to Myla after every good dig, and they won the match. Afterward McKinley found something in the community center library, a battered sports book, and read aloud that across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average. "They call it home advantage," McKinley said. Romy grinned. Half didn't sound like much until you counted it over a whole season of everybody's games.

At the last practice of the season, Myla finally raised her hand and asked for her audition. The coach put her at setter for the full scrimmage, and Myla ran the offense like she'd been born there, dumping a sneaky second-touch over the net that fooled even Romy. "That," Ms. Tremblay called from the doorway, "is why I never close this gym early."

The cemetery behind St. Augustine's was the quietest place James knew, so that was where he practiced. He sat on the flat stone near his grandfather's plot with the paper folded in his pocket, saying the words out loud to nobody. His friend Sonia had asked him for help, because in two weeks she would turn fifteen, and her quinceañera, the big Mexican celebration, would begin with a Mass of thanksgiving at the church. Sonia had to do a reading at that Mass, and she could not get through it without stopping.

"You're the one who memorized the whole Gettysburg Address in fifth grade," she had said, handing him the paper. "Figure out why my brain won't hold this."

James had a theory about memorizing, and he wanted to test it. He believed you could not really quantify memory by counting repetitions, the way you'd count jumping jacks. Instead, he thought the brain remembered rhythm and breaks, the places where a sentence turned. So in the cemetery he tried reading the passage in strange chunks, stopping in the middle of phrases instead of at the periods, and then trying the normal way. The strange way was harder, which surprised him. His theory said the pauses were the anchors, and the experiment seemed to prove it.

When Sonia came to the cemetery after school the next day, her entrance was so abrupt that a crow bolted off the fence. "Sorry," she said, breathless. "My mom sent me with the list of everything that still costs money. The hall, the cake, the photographer. She keeps calling the cake delivery a tariff, like the cake is imported from another country." James laughed, then got serious. "Try the reading, but pause wherever I tap." He tapped at odd places, and she tripped over the words, exactly as he predicted. Then he tapped only at the sentence breaks, and the passage rolled out of her like water finding a downhill path.

"That was it," Sonia said, staring at him. "The pauses. When I pause in the wrong spot, I lose the thread and can't find it again."

They met in the cemetery every evening that week, trading lines back and forth while the shadows stretched across the graves. Sonia made mistakes, and James made worse ones, once mangling a line so badly she laughed until she cried. Ms. Quinn, the church's music teacher, passed by on Thursday and heard Sonia run the whole reading clean. "Again," she said simply, and Sonia did it again, perfect.

On the morning of the Mass, James sat in the third pew, his hands folded tight. Sonia walked to the lectern in her pale dress, took a breath, and paused where the pauses belonged. Her voice carried all the way to the back of the church, and James mouthed every word along with her, silently, from his seat.

Sophoria had spent all Saturday morning turning the kitchen counter into a café. She folded a paper menu, arranged her grandmother's old teacups, and taped a sign to the toaster that said SOPEN'S CAFE, which was meant to say SOPHIA'S CAFE but she had run out of room for the A. Deklan was coming over at two o'clock, and technically it was a date, because he had asked, "Do you want to go on a date?" and she had said, "Okay," and then both of them had turned bright red about it.

The problem was money. She had eleven dollars and forty cents in the flowered tin on her desk, and she had worked out a whole algorithm for the afternoon: three dollars for fancy hot chocolate ingredients, two dollars back into the tin for emergencies, and the rest hidden under her pillow where she wouldn't be tempted. But the algorithm had never answered the big question. If Deklan showed up with five dollars of his own, who paid for what? On a date, did one person pay for everything? Would he expect her to? What if he paid and she felt like she owed him a cookie forever?

She called Charly, who knew everything about everything, or at least claimed to.

"Whoever invited the other person pays," Charly said immediately. Then Charly paused, which was unusual. "Or no. My cousin says both people pay. She read it in a magazine."

"That makes no sense. Then it's not even a date, it's just two people buying their own stuff."

"I'm telling you what the magazine said," Charly said. "Ask Ms. He. She's been on like a million dates. Probably. She has a velvet hat."

Ms. He was the neighbour on the corner, an eccentric retired music teacher who wore that velvet hat in all weather and once marched a tuba down the street for no reason anyone ever learned. Sophia envied her a little, the way she did things without seeming to worry about them first. Ms. He was in her garden pulling up something green when Sophia trotted over, and she listened to the whole money problem while holding a carrot like a microphone.

"Well," Ms. He said, "when each person pays for their own share, it's called going Dutch."

Sophia stared at her. "Going Dutch. Like the country."

"That's what they call it," Ms. He said, and went back to her carrots as if she had not just solved the entire afternoon.

At two o'clock Deklan arrived with his hair combed, which was the funniest thing Sophia had seen all week, and Charly showed up ninety seconds later wearing an apron and announcing that she was the waiter and would accept tips in gum. Charly took the fake orders, brought the hot chocolate, and then presented a bill on a folded piece of paper that said 4 DOLLERS, and the awkward moment landed exactly where Sophia had feared. Deklan reached for his pocket. Sophia reached for the tin. Their hands hovered.

"Going Dutch," Sophia said, and slid one dollar across the counter toward Charly, who made a big show of pinching the bill and tucking it into the apron.

"Excellent choice," Charly said, and then dropped the entire tray of cookies on the floor.

Aurora found the diary in the wooden trunk at her grandmother's house, wedged between a quilt and a tin of buttons. The cover read "Journal of H. Tatum, 1849." She texted Clemence and Chelsey immediately, because Mr. Horváth had assigned exactly this: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, and presentations were on Thursday.

"You found an actual diary?" Clemence shouted when they arrived the next morning, bike helmets still on. Chelsey was already pulling on gloves, because Aurora had said the pages were fragile. They spread the diary on the kitchen table while Aurora's grandmother made cocoa, and the three of them leaned over the tiny, slanted handwriting.

The first entry changed everything. "Our farm in Missouri failed two seasons running," H. Tatum had written. "Grain sells for nothing here, and the fever took our neighbor's eldest boy." Chelsey tapped the page. "Those are reasons to leave home." A few entries later, Tatum wrote about letters from a cousin in Oregon describing rich soil and free land, and Clemence threw up her hands. "Those are reasons to go there. It's like the family got pushed out of Missouri and pulled west."

"That's the thing," Aurora said, grabbing her notebook. "Mr. Horváth called them push factors and pull factors. Historians sort reasons for migration that way." She drew two columns and headed one PUSH and one PULL. "Failed crops, no money, sickness, those go on the push side. Free land and good soil, that's pull." She paused. "But some entries don't fit either column. Tatum writes that his wife's brother already went west. Which side is that?"

Chelsey argued it was a pull, because family attracted them. Clemence said it was subjective, that the same reason could feel like a pull to Tatum but nothing at all to his wife, and maybe even a push if staying meant losing her brother forever. Aurora wrote it in a third column labeled QUESTION MARK. "Good," she said. "Mr. Horváth likes when we show the messiness of real evidence. A diary is one person's view, not the whole story."

They worked through eleven entries, and something else surfaced. The Tatums listed their reasons in order, money first, land second, family last. "It's a hierarchy," Clemence said, jabbing the page. "They even ranked their own reasons." Aurora copied the ranked list onto a poster board, then had each of them read one entry aloud so nothing was missed.

When Aurora's grandmother came back with cocoa, she admitted she had never disclosed the trunk's whole history; the diary had come from a great-great-aunt, and there might be letters in the attic, too. Aurora was already halfway up the stairs, flashlight in hand, Chelsey and Clemence pounding behind her. "If we find letters," she called over her shoulder, "we can check whether the Tatums' diary matches what they told the family back home."

Emile held the knife the way Ms. Jung had shown them, fingers curled under like a claw, knuckles forward. The onion sat on the cutting board, pale and smug, waiting to make him cry. Across the counter, Amal was already dicing hers into neat little squares, and Mathew had dismantled his onion into rings without chopping anything at all.

"One more station needs a sauce base," Ms. Jung called out, "so pace yourselves."

Emile pressed down with the knife and the whole board skidded sideways, sliding toward the edge of the counter. He caught it with his hip before the onion rolled off. He tried again, and again the board slid. Amal glanced over. "Yours is going for a walk," she said.

"It does that every time I push down." Emile frowned at the board. It was a durable plastic one, hardly worn, and the counter was clean and dry. That was the thing, he thought. At home his mother's old wooden board never moved, but that counter had a textured surface. This one was smooth as glass. When he pressed, something invisible was letting the board glide, like a tiny sled. He tested it with his palm, pushing gently. Yep, it slid with almost no effort.

He looked around. Mathew was wiping down his station with a damp cloth. Emile grabbed a paper towel, ran it under the tap, wrung it out, and laid it flat under his cutting board. Then he set the onion back on top and pressed down with the knife. The board stayed planted. He chopped once, twice, and the rounds fell away without a single skid.

"Hey, that's clever," Mathew said, leaning over. "A wet towel under the board?"

"Stops it sliding," Emile said, already working the claw grip through the next slice. His eyes stung, but a smaller percentage of the onion was still whole now, which meant fewer fumes rising at once, or so it seemed. Amal came around with her pot, watching him work.

"Half-centimeter pieces," she said. "Those are actually good."

"Sauce crew, assembly in five," Ms. Jung announced.

Emile swept his onion into the pan Amal held out, and the pieces hit the oil with a hiss. Mathew fetched the canned tomatoes, and soon the whole station smelled like something worth eating. Emile chopped a second onion for the pot without once chasing the board across the counter.

"Same towel trick next week?" Mathew asked, holding up the dripping paper towel.

"Every week," Emile said, and dropped it in the trash.

Ms. Hernández wrote one question on the board before the bell had even finished ringing: "Did Marcus do the right thing?" Marcus was a fictional boy from a short story they had all read, a teammate who lied to a coach to cover for his friend Dev, whose grades had slipped. The robotics club had voted on it yesterday and nearly split in two, and Ms. Hernández had clearly decided to make her class do the same thing.

"Vote at the end of the period," she said. "You have forty minutes to figure out why you disagree, not just that you disagree. If you can't tell me that, the whole class loses the debate on Friday." That was the deal, and everyone groaned, because the Friday debate was the fun one.

Cassia went first, arms crossed. "He protected his friend. Dev would have been benched, and Marcus knew it." Titus rolled his eyes so far Nora thought they might not come back. "He lied to the coach. That's it. You don't lie to the coach."

Nora, who had been put in charge of writing down the club's arguments because she was the only one with legible handwriting, started doing what she usually did: listing the facts. Marcus lied. He lied to protect Dev. Dev was benched anyway. The team found out. She read the list out loud, and then something odd happened. Nobody argued with a single item.

"Wait," Nora said. "You both agree on all of this?"

"Obviously," said Titus.

"Obviously," said Cassia, at the same moment, which was the first thing they had agreed on all week.

Nora tried an experiment. She flipped to a new page and wrote Marcus lied to protect his friend at the top, then asked each of them the same question: "What's the bad part?" Titus circled the word lied. Cassia circled the words to protect his friend, then drew a little heart around them, which Nora felt undermined her seriousness, but she let it go.

"You're not arguing about what happened," Nora said slowly, testing the idea out loud before she trusted it. "You're arguing about what matters. Titus cares about the rule. Cassia cares about the friend."

"It's called fairness," Titus said.

"It's called loyalty," said Cassia.

They glared at each other, both correct. Nora looked at the clock. Twelve minutes left. She raised her hand, and when Ms. Hernández called on her, Nora read both circles aloud and proposed an amendment to their plan: instead of arguing who was right, the class would argue fairness versus loyalty itself, incorporating both positions as its own side. Ms. Hernández raised one eyebrow, which from her was applause.

"Vote," she said.

It passed, eleven to nine. Titus and Cassia were the last two hands up, and they raised them at exactly the same time.

Livia had forty minutes before the judges reached her table, and her graph was still wrong. She unrolled the paper and pinned it flat: nine points she had marked last night, scattered like spilled beads instead of sitting in any kind of line. Her project was a rubber ball rolled down the school hallway, timed with a stopwatch at one metre, two metres, three metres and so on. The table beside it read "How Fast Does It Roll?" and so far the honest answer was that she had no idea.

"Your dots are all over the place," said Maximilian, leaning over from the next table, where his robust volcano waited for its final coat of paint. He had supervise duty for the hallway timing yesterday because he owed her for the time she'd covered his paper route, and he had stood there clicking the stopwatch while muttering about it, which had bred in her a small, stubborn resentment she hadn't bothered to argue away.

"The clicks were late," Livia said. "You clicked late."

"Late every single time? Exactly the same amount?" He set down his paintbrush. "Roll it here. I'll time it again, right now, and you watch."

She cleared a path between their tables. The gym floor was smooth wax, better than the hallway's bumpy tile. Livia crouched, called "go," and pushed the ball with the same steady shove she'd used before. Maximilian clicked at each metre mark she'd taped down, and Eli, who had wandered over from the refreshments table, wrote the numbers on a napkin. They ran it three times. The numbers came out close to the first set, close enough that her stomach dropped. It wasn't the timing.

She plotted the new points quickly, one after another, before she could lose her nerve. This time she drew it on fresh paper, distance along the bottom, time going up. When she connected the dots, they climbed in a clean, even path from the lower left to the upper right. No wobble. She checked the old graph again and found the mistake: last night she had plotted two of her metres in the wrong columns, transposed like a bad text message.

"Look at this," she said to Eli, holding up the new sheet. "A straight sloping line. That means the ball is moving at a constant speed." Eli frowned at it, then at the ball, then back at the paper, as if the line and the rubber sphere had to be the same object.

"So it didn't slow down at all? Down a whole hallway?"

"That's what the line says. Same speed the whole way." She picked up the ball and set it at the edge of her table, ready for the demonstration she'd run for the judges, and Eli got out of the aisle just as Mr. Morin called out, "Two minutes, people. Judges are at table four."

Zoey had twenty minutes before the bell, and Mr. Sánchez's assignment glared up at her from her notebook: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. She'd already checked out three websites and closed all of them, because websites weren't primary sources and Mr. Sánchez would know.

"Try the green box," Jamal said, sliding into the seat across from her. He pointed at a plastic tub on the cart by the biography shelf. "Old letters and diaries the librarian keeps for the history classes. My grandpa says our farm came from one of those deals where the government gave people land, so somebody back then wrote things down."

Zoey dug through the box. A settler's diary, 1863, the cover soft as cloth from being handled. She opened it carefully, the way you'd document a crime scene, and there it was, cramped ink: "We have filed our claim. One hundred sixty acres, ours if we stay five years and work the ground."

She read the line twice. "Jamal. Look at this."

He leaned over. "Huh. So they didn't buy it?"

"Not exactly." Zoey's pencil hovered. The diary said the family had left Ohio with almost nothing, the mother sick, two oxen dead on the trail. Nobody crosses that much country for fun, she thought. You cross it because something is waiting on the other side. Her logic was simple: people move when a door opens. The diary was the door, if she could prove it was real and not one family's luck.

Morgan appeared behind them, out of breath. "Ten minutes, Zoey. And the copier is broken, so whatever you're doing, do it in your own handwriting."

"Then stop breathing on me." Zoey copied the line, then hunted the diary's back pages. In March, the writer mentioned a neighbor, a widow with four children, on her own one hundred sixty acres, farming it, waiting out her five years like everyone else. Not one family, then. A pattern. A law, probably, though the diary never named it.

"What's the law called?" Morgan whispered.

"Doesn't say. But it's public land, offered to settlers who live on it and farm it for five years. That's enough to explain the whole moving west thing." Zoey underlined her final sentence, slammed the diary shut, and slid it across the table. "Pages still warm. Run."

Morgan snatched her notebook, and the two of them sprinted for Mr. Sánchez's door as the bell began to ring.

Rosalie arrived at Mr. Santos's classroom with the story half-read and her margins empty. Book club started in four minutes, and Anabel was already at the front table, flipping through her annotated copy like she was shuffling cards.

"You didn't finish it," Anabel said.

"I finished it. I just didn't mark anything."

"You need three annotations to get picked for the discussion." Anabel tapped her own page, which bristled with sticky notes. "Mr. Santos said the top presenter gets to recommend next month's book for the whole club."

That was the part that stung. The club was voting on a prestigious guest author for the spring visit, and whoever presented best this week got to put a book forward. Rosalie wanted that. She sat down and reread the opening paragraph of The Most Dangerous Game, where the sailors talk nervously about an island and Whitney says it has a reputation, bad enough that even tough crew members feel a strange dread as they pass it in the dark.

"Three minutes," said Mr. Santos from his desk.

Samuel leaned over from the next seat. "Just underline words that sound weird. That's what I do."

Rosalie stared at the island's name printed in the first page. "Ship-Trap Island," she read aloud. The name was right there from the beginning, like a label on a box.

"So?" Samuel said.

"So why would Connell name it that? The characters don't know what's coming. But the reader does, kind of. The name does." She thought of the time she'd ignored the warning label on her cousin's old skateboard and ended up with a concussion and a week off school. Warnings mattered. She underlined the name, then the sailors' fear of it, then wrote "the author tells us before the characters find out" in the margin.

"Time," Mr. Santos said. "Who's presenting on foreshadowing?"

Anabel raised her hand and talked about the darkness and the falling sensation Rainsford experiences, which was good, really good. Then Mr. Santos said, "Anyone build on that? Places can foreshadow too."

Rosalie's hand went up before she decided to raise it. "The island is called Ship-Trap Island," she said. "That's not an accident. And the sailors are scared just passing it. The name and the fear both tell you something bad is waiting there before anything bad actually happens."

Samuel turned around in his seat. "I thought it was just a name."

"That's the point. It looks like a name. It's doing a job."

Mr. Santos wrote "place names" on the board. "Strong. Symbolism or foreshadowing from anyone else?"

Anabel looked at her notes, then closed them. "Rosalie covered it better than my page did," she said. "I'll take the next story."

"Then Rosalie nominates next month's book," Mr. Santos said.

She pulled her copy to her chest and wrote the title on the sign-up sheet before anyone could change the subject. "Motion to adjourn," she said.

"Seconded," said Anabel.

George settled into the lobby of Skyfall Arena, headphones on, waiting for the match to fill. He was thirteen minutes early because Paige had messaged him that something weird was happening, and Paige was never weird about a game.

"You see this guy?" Paige typed in the team chat. A player named Vex_444 had joined, and the moment he did, he said: "George, right? Grade eight? You live near the river bridge."

George's fingers went still on the keyboard. His tag in the game was just FallenKite. It said nothing about his grade or his street. He typed back, "lol who's this," and Vex_444 answered with the name of his school and the words "heard you broke your nose at the skate park. Cartilage stuff, rough."

The match started and George played badly, missing shots he never missed, because he kept scrolling back up through the chat. His nose had healed months ago, and he had only told that story to his friends in the lobby, one late night in June. Paige, Lilianne, a couple of others. Nobody else.

After the match he quit to the menu and opened a browser beside the game. He had learned something in Ms. McKenzie's class weeks ago, half-listening, half-drawing: search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so anything posted publicly can turn up in search results. He remembered it now with a cold, specific feeling, because Vex_444 hadn't guessed anything. Vex_444 had read something.

He typed his own name into the search bar, held his breath, and hit enter. The third result was a forum thread titled "funniest lobby chat ever." It was a screenshot. His screenshot, his words, his skate park story in full, posted by an account that had copied the whole conversation from a public lobby archive and pasted it where anyone could find it. Anyone, including a stranger who wanted to act like a friend.

He tested it the only way he could think of. He went back to the lobby, created a second account with a different name, and typed a made-up detail into the chat: "anyone else going to the maroon warehouse Friday?" He logged off, waited an hour doing his homework badly, then searched the phrase. There it was, already in the results, copied and indexed from the public page. His made-up detail, sitting where any stranger could read it.

He wrote to Lilianne first, then Paige, in a group message: don't say anything real in public lobbies, everything gets copied. Then he reported Vex_444, blocked him, and typed one last line into the lobby before closing it, not to the stranger but to whoever else was quietly reading and pretending to be nobody.

"Nice try," George typed. "The warehouse isn't real."

The reply came back in three seconds: "I know. I've known everything else, though."

George stared at the screen, then reached over and pulled the ethernet cable from the wall.

Andrew counted the keys on Mr. Brown's piano for the third time that Tuesday, and every time the number came out wrong in a different way.

"Fifty-two white," he muttered, running his finger along the row. "And the blacks keep moving on me."

"They don't migrate, Andrew," said Warren from the bench, where he was pretending to practice a scale. "They're just small. You skip them when you count fast."

Andrew wanted to know the exact number of keys because of a bet. Beatrix had claimed at lunch that every proper piano had 88 keys, exactly, no matter what. Andrew had said no piano company would build them all the same, because that would be boring. The loser had to carry the winner's trumpet case for a whole week, and Beatrix's trumpet case weighed about as much as a small dog, so the stakes were serious.

At his lesson, he told Mr. Brown he needed to check something before they started. Mr. Brown folded his arms and said he had five minutes, because Czerny waited for no man. Andrew counted the white keys one at a time, touching each with a fingertip so his eyes couldn't trick him. Fifty-two. Then he counted the black keys, which were worse because they sat in little groups with gaps between them, like teeth missing on a comb. Thirty-six. He added the numbers twice in his head. Eighty-eight.

"There's a trick to it," Warren said, watching from the corner. "The black keys come in twos and threes, all the way up. If you count the groups instead of the keys, you don't lose your place."

That was the logic Andrew had been missing. He counted again, tapping each group of two, then each group of three, all the way from the bottom of the keyboard to the top. The pattern held the whole way, stubborn and obstinate, refusing to break even once. He liked that about it. His own fingers were never that reliable.

"So it's really 88," Andrew said.

"It is," said Mr. Brown. "Fifty-two white and thirty-six black, on every standard modern piano you'll meet. Now, hands together, and don't let those black keys scare you. They're only small."

Andrew played his C major scale, hit a B-flat instead of a B, and decided the black keys were scary anyway, whatever Mr. Brown said.

The next day he found Beatrix at her locker and told her the count. She held out her hand, and he shook it, because a bet was a bet. Then she swung her trumpet case onto his shoulder, and it was exactly as heavy as advertised.

"Wait," Andrew said, shifting the case to the other shoulder. "Whose piano did you even count? You don't have one."

"My grandma's. I counted hers twice on Sunday." Beatrix smiled and walked off down the hall. "Fifty-two white, thirty-six black. Grandma says she'll lend it to you if you ever get good enough."

Andrew carried the case to the bus, counted the black keys in his head one more time out of pure habit, and got 36 again.

"Fine," he told the case. "You win."

The floorboard outside the kitchen creaked, and Alexandre froze with his hand on the fridge door. He wasn't supposed to be up. His little cousin's drawing lay crumpled on the counter, a picture of Alexandre with sharp zigzag teeth, and the caption in wobbly letters read, MEAN COUSIN. He smoothed it flat, then pushed it under a newspaper to conceal it, though he wasn't sure why. Nobody had seen him.

All week something had been wrong with him, and he couldn't name it. On Tuesday he had snapped at Darien in the cafeteria over a french fry. On Wednesday he'd left Marvin on read for six hours because a text about a video game felt, for no reason, unbearable. He'd abandoned the model bridge he'd been building for a month, leaving the glue to dry in a gray lump. This morning he had yelled at his cousin for humming, right here in this kitchen, until the kid ran outside near tears. Alexandre tried to remember when it had started, and his stomach dropped as the memory surfaced: Monday morning, gym class, when the coach had pinned a sheet to the bulletin board. Tryouts. Saturday. Two spots.

From the doorway, his grandmother's voice, gentle: "You look like your grandfather did before his surgery. He couldn't sit still either."

"Something's wrong with me," Alexandre admitted. "I keep blowing up at people."

His grandfather appeared in his slippers, holding a mug. "Stress can show up like that. Not just a racing heart. In what you do. Snapping at people, trouble concentrating, losing interest in things you love." He sipped his tea. "Noticing the signs is the first step to managing it."

Alexandre stared at him. The bridge. Darien and the fry. The humming. It wasn't six separate bad moments; it was one thing wearing different masks. Then he thought of the crumpled drawing and flushed hot. "I yelled at her over nothing."

"So fix the nothing," his grandfather said.

In the living room, Alexandre found his cousin building a block tower. He sat down across from her. "I'm sorry about the humming," he said. "You can hum all you want." He breathed in slowly through his nose, counting, then let it out long, the way Ms. Reyes made the class do before tests. He did it again. His shoulders came down from somewhere near his ears.

That night, after a negotiation with himself about whether checking the tryout list online would help or make everything worse, he set his phone on the dresser across the room, away from the bed, and asked his grandmother for an extra blanket. Sleep, his grandfather claimed, was half the battle. In the morning, Alexandre found his cousin's drawing on the kitchen table, uncrumpled, the zigzag teeth erased and redrawn as a wide, careful smile.

On Monday morning Maelie walked into Mr. Pritchard's classroom wearing glasses for the first time, and the world snapped into focus so sharply she stopped halfway to her desk. She could read the tiny handwriting on the schedule card across the room. She could see the cracks in the window putty and every fingerprint on the fish tank. She could also see, for the first time in months, that Cain had dark half-moons under his eyes, and that he'd saved her the seat beside him by piling his books on the other chair.

"How do they feel?" Cain asked, sweeping the books off like a waiter clearing a table.

"Weird. Everything's sharp." She sat down. "The optometrist said I'm nearsighted. It means I can see close stuff fine but far away is blurry."

Behind her, Jayden leaned over his desk. "Join the club. I've had glasses since third grade."

That gave Maelie an idea, and she turned around fully, pencil out. She made two columns on her notebook page: Glasses and No Glasses. Then, while Mr. Pritchard took attendance, she went desk by desk with quiet questions. "Do you wear glasses? What'd you do this weekend, mostly?" Jayden admitted he'd barely left his room, that his weekends could submerge him entirely in games until Sunday night. The kid by the door, no glasses, had been hiking. The girl who drew like a tiny artisan, copying every leaf of the class plant with perfect patience, wore thick frames and said she read indoors all summer. The agile boy who raced everyone at recess, always outside, had perfect vision. When she counted, the pattern held: kids who spent more time outdoors as children were less likely to be nearsighted, and the indoor ones filled her first column.

"See?" she whispered, tilting the notebook toward Jayden. "It's not just bad luck. Outdoor time matters. My mom read the same thing in the pamphlet."

Jayden looked at the columns, then at the window, then back at his screen-worn hands. "So if I'd gone outside more, maybe." He didn't finish it. He straightened his glasses instead.

Mr. Pritchard started the lesson, and Maelie copied the board without squinting for the first time all year. The letters came out clean and even. But when the class turned to silent reading, she glanced at Cain, and the glasses showed her what she'd been missing: he kept blinking at his page, holding the book closer and closer, the way she used to. He hadn't said a word about it.

"Cain," she whispered, "how far away can you read that?"

He held the book at arm's length, then slowly brought it back to his nose. "Don't tell anyone, okay? I'm telling my mom tonight."

She pressed the notebook into his hand. "Take this with you. Tell her to ask about the outdoor thing too."

The bell for third period hadn't rung yet, but Ms. Georgiou was already standing at the whiteboard with her tablet held up. "Before we start the debate unit," she said, "I need you to look at this." On the screen was a photo of a dress, lacy and wrinkled, hanging against a bright background. "Write down what color it is. You have ninety seconds, because the discussion starts at 9:15 sharp."

Ariana leaned closer to the girl next to her, Karina, who had written "white and gold" in big letters. Ariana herself saw blue and black, plainly, the way she saw the whiteboard or the clock. When Dave turned around from the front row, his paper said white and gold too. "You two are messing with us," Ariana whispered. "It's obviously blue." Karina held up her paper and pointed at the screen without a word, as if the photo should speak for itself.

At 9:15, Ms. Georgiou collected the slips and tallied them on the board. Eleven students saw white and gold. Nine saw blue and black. The class split almost down the middle, and the two halves started arguing across the rows, everyone certain, everyone looking at the same picture. "Hold on," Ms. Georgiou said, raising a hand. "This is our debate topic. Not about the dress. About why people can look at one thing and disagree this hard. You have until the end of the period to build an argument."

Ariana couldn't stop staring at the board. Eleven and nine. The split had a strange symmetry to it, almost balanced, like the class had been sorted by a coin flip. But it couldn't be random, she thought, because nobody was guessing. Every single person sounded completely sure. She remembered dinner last week, when her mother and her uncle had nearly shouted at each other over this exact photo on her mother's phone, and how Ariana had assumed one of them was joking. Now she wasn't so sure anyone was joking.

She had an idea, and only twenty minutes to test it. She raised her hand. "Can I walk around and check something? I want to see if people's answers change depending on where they sit, or how far they are from the screen." Ms. Georgiou nodded, and Ariana carried her notebook up and down the rows, asking each person the same short question and recording their answers next to their names. The room was noisy and her notes were sparse, just initials and colors, but one thing became clear: the answers had nothing to do with seats, or the window, or squinting. Karina saw white and gold from every angle. Dave saw white and gold standing on a chair. Ariana herself saw blue and black up close and far away, and she tried to calibrate her own eyes against the screen, blinking hard, tilting her head, refusing to let them shift. Nothing changed.

At 10:05, with two minutes left, Ms. Georgiou clicked to a new slide. "You should know," she said, "this photo went viral in February 2015. The real dress was blue and black." The white-and-gold half of the class groaned; the blue-and-black half cheered, Dave loudest of all now that he'd switched sides in spirit, even though his slip still said white and gold. He spun around in his seat to face Ariana. "Okay, fine," he said. "I believe you saw blue. But you have to believe I saw gold." Ariana laughed and held up her notebook, initials and colors all the way down the page. "Deal," she said. "Same photo, same class, nine different arguments for the debate." Karina tapped her pencil on the desk and said, "I call writing the opening statement."

Florence had never expected to be doing homework in Terminal B, but the flight to Tucson was delayed three hours, and Mr. Bear had said the packets were due the moment they landed. She spread the two climate graphs on the bench beside the boarding gate. One showed the Sonoran Desert, where they were headed, with its temperature line leaping up in summer and plunging in winter. The other showed a rainforest in Brazil. Julianne leaned over her shoulder, chewing gum.

"Which month is best for the rainforest one?" Julianne asked. "We're supposed to classify each place and write a recommendation, like a travel ad." She pointed at the desert graph. "Easy. Go in December, not July, unless you want to bake."

Florence ran her finger along the rainforest's temperature line, then back, then forward again, checking herself. "I can't answer that. Look. January, June, October, they're all warm. All of them. It barely moves." She turned the graph sideways, as if a new angle might reveal a hidden dip, but the line stayed nearly flat from one end of the year to the other. The only thing that jumped around was the rainfall bar chart, heavy some months and heavier others.

Lucille wandered back from the vending machines with a bag of chips. "So every month looks the same for temperature?" she said, peering at it. "Then nobody can pick a coolest month. There isn't one."

"There's got to be a mistake," Florence said, though even as she said it she doubted herself. She remembered, unhappily, a test last spring where she had guessed instead of reading the graph in front of her, and the wrong answer had stared back at her in red pen. She had sworn she would look before concluding this time. So she took out the atlas from her backpack, found the rainforest page, and compared its graph to the handout. The same flat line. The temperature in a rainforest stays warm month after month, she wrote slowly, so the line barely changes. It was the one thing her guess had missed.

For the desert she wrote the opposite: pick your month carefully. Then she added a sentence about adaptation, how cactus wrens and jackrabbits managed the swings that rainforest creatures never faced, and a line about the vigorous summer storms that flooded the dry washes each July. Mr. Bear was walking past, checking his clipboard, and paused at the bench.

"Verdict?" he asked.

"There's no best month in a rainforest," Florence said. "They're all the same temperature. The desert's the picky one." She slid the graphs into her folder as the gate agent finally lifted the microphone.

Eleanor had been practicing one sentence for the entire bus ride to the rink, and by the time she pushed through the doors into the cold, echoing noise of Southgate Ice Arena, she had worn it smooth: "This is my first time here since they finished renovating it." Perfect. Casual. A fact and a question all in one, if Harlan picked up the thread.

He did not pick up the thread. He picked up skates, said his brother had laced a pair for him once with a "cumulative knot," whatever that meant, and then spent the next twenty minutes telling her about his brother. His brother's job, his brother's car, his brother's opinion of the new snack bar. Eleanor nodded so much her neck hurt. She tried three times to steer back, and each time he rolled right over her opening like a Zamboni over fresh ice.

At the rail near the boards, watching Cheikh from math class wipe out spectacularly and bow to the scattered applause, Eleanor started doing the math. Not the school kind. The counting kind. Since they'd sat down, Harlan had asked her exactly zero questions. She had learned that his brother thought the arcade's claw machine ran on some kind of algorithm that decided when to actually let you win, and she had learned nothing about whether Harlan himself could skate, or liked music, or had ever been here before. She was on a date with a person made entirely of facts about somebody else.

So she tested it. Her theory was that he wasn't rude, just nervous, and nervous people talk because silence feels like falling. The test: ask him one real question and see if he could land.

"Wait," she said, as they stepped onto the ice. "You said the claw machine decides when to let you win. How would that even work?"

Harlan stopped so suddenly he wobbled. "Okay, so there's this thing where it only grips hard after enough failed tries," he said, and then, amazingly, he turned it around. "But you've been here before, right? Before they renovated? What was it like?"

"It had a plastic polar bear you could sit on," Eleanor said. "That's it. That's the whole answer."

"A polar bear," he repeated, and laughed in a way that finally sounded like himself. Then he asked a follow-up question, about the bear, and she answered, and it went back and forth like that for two whole laps. Not perfectly. He still told one more brother story, but he caught himself halfway and said, "Sorry, I talk when I'm nervous."

"Me too," Eleanor said. "I planned a whole opening sentence on the bus."

"Was it good?"

"It had the word 'renovating' in it."

He held out his hand as Cheikh flew past, arms windmilling, yelling "WATCH THIS" at nobody. "Teach me to stop," Harlan said, "and I'll never mention my brother again."

"Twice," Eleanor said, and pulled him forward onto the milky, scraped ice.

Kaitlyn stood in Mr. Dang's kitchen with a toddler on her hip and a note on the fridge that read: lunch at noon, nap at one, emergency numbers on the counter. The toddler, Milo, had just presented her with a problem she had not trained for, and she could smell it.

"Okay," she said, laying him on the changing mat. "We can do this." She had watched her aunt change a cousin's diaper once, years ago, at a Thanksgiving crowded with cousins and pie. In that memory, her aunt had hummed something while she worked, slow and steady, hands moving like she had done it a thousand times. Kaitlyn copied the motions as best she could, peeling tapes, folding, wiping, and discovered that the wipes were colder than Milo expected. He howled. She sped up, taped the fresh diaper crooked, fixed it, and held him until the howl shrank to a sniffle.

At the sink, she reached for the soap and paused. Somewhere in the back of her mind was a rule about hands, something she had half-heard in a health video at school. Twenty seconds, that part she remembered, and it had to happen after a diaper change and again before touching food. She wondered if that was really enough, or if the number was just something teachers said. She decided to test it, in the small way she could: she hummed the happy birthday song twice, counting, and kept scrubbing the whole time. The soap went from slippery to almost squeaky. Twenty seconds, it turned out, felt longer than she expected. She did it again before she opened the bread, because lunch was next and the rule said before preparing food too.

Milo ate his sandwich in fistfuls while Kaitlyn built him a tower of plastic cups. Her phone buzzed: a text from Isha, asking if she survived. Barely, Kaitlyn typed back. Did you know you're supposed to scrub for twenty seconds after a diaper change? Isha replied with a single row of laughing faces. Juliet, who was babysitting across town for the first time too, sent: the elastic on my kid's diaper tabs is stronger than my will to live. Kaitlyn laughed, and Milo laughed too, because she laughed.

By one o'clock Milo was rubbing his eyes and fighting sleep with the determination of a small lawyer. She rocked him, and her arms burned with a fatigue she had never felt from soccer practice, a deep slow ache rather than a sharp one. She thought about her aunt again, humming at that Thanksgiving, and wondered whether the humming had been for the baby or for her own counting. Maybe both. Maybe the song was how you enforced the rule on yourself when nobody was watching.

Milo's head tipped against her collarbone, heavy as a bag of rice. She carried him to the crib, set him down without waking him, and stood in the doorway listening to him breathe. Then she went back to the kitchen, looked at the mountain of plastic cups, and began stacking them into a second tower, taller than the first, for when he woke up.

The bus had barely pulled away from the school when Edwin held up a baseball card and announced that Marcus Bell was the most underrated player in the league. "The news keeps emphasizing his batting average like it's everything," he said. "Pure propaganda. The guy gets on base constantly and gets no credit for half of it."

Georgia leaned across the aisle. The card showed .290, which did sound ordinary. But she wondered what a number like that actually counted. "What's it made of?" she asked. "Like, what goes into it?" Edwin shrugged, so she borrowed the back of the card and started reading the small print. Hits, at-bats. "So it's hits divided by at-bats," she said slowly. "Eighty-seven hits, three hundred at-bats." She did the division in the margin of her notebook and got .290, which matched.

Then she found the walks. Sixty of them. "Here's the thing," she said, mostly to herself, because she wanted to see if the idea held together. "What if walks counted? Like, what if they were at-bats where he didn't get a hit?" She divided 87 by 360 instead and got .242. So the walks didn't drag his average down at all. They were simply invisible, sixty times he reached first base, erased from the number. "A walk doesn't count as an at-bat," she said, looking up. "So the average gives him no credit for them. At all. Sixty times, and the number never moved."

"That's what I said!" Edwin looked triumphant, waving the card at Joseph two seats up. "Bell is secretly great. The stat is lying."

Georgia wasn't finished, though, because her notebook was still open and a new question had arrived. All season Edwin had bragged about his own league average, .380, better than anyone in their grade. "Edwin," she said, "how many hits is your .380?" He counted on his fingers and admitted it was eleven. "And your walks?" That took longer, but the answer came out: twenty-three. She wrote it down. Eleven hits out of twenty-nine at-bats, with twenty-three walks the average never saw, never rewarded, never mentioned.

"So Bell's number hides how often he gets on base," Georgia said, "and yours does too. Same trick." Edwin stared at his card, then at her notebook, then out the window at the Stop sign going by. "Twenty-three," he muttered. Ms. Swampy called from the front that they'd better sit down before the pothole street, and Edwin sat, still holding the card at arm's length like it had tricked him personally.

Alexandre scanned the visiting team's lineup as they took the field, counting jersey numbers out of habit. His little sister pointed at the scoreboard and asked why nobody on either team wore 42, and he opened his mouth to answer before realizing he had no answer. "Maybe it's unlucky," he said. Mackenna, two seats over with a bucket of popcorn balanced on her knees, shook her head. "They wear 13 and everything. Try again."

The stadium was packed, the field a lush green stripe under the lights, and between pitches the four screens around the upper deck flashed old photographs in black and white. Alexandre stopped counting the players and started counting the photos. A man sliding into base. The same man shaking hands with teammates. The same man again, and in every single shot the same detail: a 42 on his jersey. "Look at that," he said, nudging Mackenna. "Every picture, number 42. That's not a coincidence."

Mackenna squinted at the screen. "So what? Old teams had old numbers." Alexandre disagreed, and he said so. He reasoned it out loud, fast, because the inning was moving. "If 42 was just old, then some player would wear it now. Numbers get reused. Nobody on either roster has it, and my sister noticed it before I did. It's not reuse. It's blocked. Something happened to that number." To test it, he pulled up the rosters on his phone and checked both teams, top to bottom, every pitcher in the bullpen. Forty-one, forty-three, every number around it, but never forty-two. "It's retired," he said. "Like, for everybody."

"Retired how?" Mackenna asked. Right then the giant screen changed. A message rolled across it in white letters, the same one, Alexandre guessed, that stadiums everywhere showed on this day: a tribute marking that in 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way. The whole crowd stood up. So did Alexandre, still holding his phone with the rosters open.

"That's the guy from the photos," his sister said, tugging his sleeve. Alexandre nodded. He had guessed the mechanism right, one component of it anyway, the blocked number, though he had gotten the reason completely wrong. He had thought it was superstition, like a cursed number teams avoided. Instead a whole league had chosen to lock it away on purpose, everywhere at once, and nobody had needed to tell him for him to find it.

Ms. Villanueva, his old teacher from down the street, was in the next section and waved at them across the aisle. Mackenna cupped her hands and shouted over the noise, "Alexandre figured out the 42 thing before they announced it!" Alexandre sat back down, ears burning, and closed the roster page. On the field the next batter stepped in, wearing 24, and Alexandre's sister read the number out loud to nobody in particular.

Jade leaned over her portrait of Lorie, who was posing at the third easel with a pencil stuck through her bun like a tiny mast. The studio smelled like wet paper and old coffee, and Mr. Chea moved between easels without saying much, which Jade had decided meant he trusted them. Her problem was the shadow under Lorie's chin. While wet, it looked deep and dramatic, like a cave in the painting, and Jade had felt proud of it. She wanted this portrait to be the one she entered in the community show, the one that proved she could do more than doodles of flying kangaroos in her sketchbook.

She remembered the first time she had drawn a marsupial, two years ago in Mr. Chea's Saturday class, when she had painted a sugar glider so dark it turned into a black blot that swallowed the whole tree branch. Mr. Chea had said only, "Look again when it's dry," and Jade had stared at the dried blob, confused, because it had seemed so right when wet. She had been eleven then and had not listened. Now, at thirteen, she tapped her brush against her water jar and looked at Lorie's chin shadow with suspicion. It had been drying for ten minutes. It had dried pale. The cave had become a whisper.

"It's gone," she said to Logan, who was painting a portrait of his own shoe. "The shadow. It was so dark it looked like a doorway to another dimension, and now it's barely there, like the dimension closed."

"Maybe it's shy," Logan said, not looking up.

Jade held the paper up beside Lorie's actual face, near the window where the afternoon light came in gold. There it was: the real shadow under the real chin was much stronger than her painted one. So that was the rule hiding inside the paint. A colour that looked right while wet would not stay that way; it would diminish as it dried, like a tide going out. She could not trust her eyes while the paint still shone. She had to wait, judge the dried paper, and then decide.

She tested it. Mixing a stronger wash, a deeper blue-brown, she swept one careful layer across the chin shadow, watched it gleam dark again, and then set the painting on the rack to dry instead of fiddling with it. "Don't touch it for ten minutes," she told Logan. "That's explicit. Ten minutes, and then we look with dry eyes."

Lorie unbent her neck. "Is my chin still a doorway?"

"Bigger doorway," Jade said, "if the second layer holds." She watched the wet shine sink slowly into the paper, and beside her, Logan quietly set a timer.

The kitchen clock said 7:40, and Marcus had until nine to finish his lab sheet, because the bus came early and Mr. Guo collected homework at the door. On the table lay a battery, a long coil of thin copper wire, a volt meter, and an ammeter borrowed from Mr. Guo's garage, still smelling of sawdust. The assignment seemed simple: measure the voltage across the wire, measure the current through it, then divide voltage by current to get the resistance. His numbers so far read four volts, and zero amps, and zero divided into four was a problem with no answer.

He clipped the volt meter to the two ends of the wire and got a steady reading. Then he clipped the ammeter the same way, onto the same two ends, and the needle sat at zero like it was asleep. He unclipped it, clipped it again, tapped the glass. Nothing. His confidence, which had been high an hour ago, began to dwindle.

He called Aksel, who was doing the same lab across the street. "Mine reads zero too," Aksel said. "I think the meters are broken. Mine and yours, both from Mr. Guo." Marcus was pessimistic about that theory, since Mr. Guo checked his tools the way other people checked lottery tickets, but he didn't say so. "Come over," he said. "Bring your wire."

Aksel arrived with his coil in a plastic bag, and they agreed on a truce: no arguing about whose setup was wrong until they had tried everything twice. They swapped meters, swapped wires, swapped batteries. The voltage reading held steady. The current stubbornly stayed at zero. The clock said 8:15.

Marcus sat back and stared at the circuit instead of the meters. The battery pushed current through the wire, he thought, out one terminal and back to the other, one loop. Then he looked at where the ammeter was clipped. It was attached to the two ends of the wire, the same as the volt meter, sitting beside the loop like someone watching a race from the stands. "The current has to flow through it," he said slowly. "An ammeter has to be in the loop, in series with the wire, or nothing passes through it at all." He pulled the clip off one end, broke the circuit there, and connected the ammeter into the gap so the current ran from the battery, through the wire, then through the meter, then back.

The needle jumped to 0.5 amps. Aksel leaned over the table. "Four volts divided by 0.5," he whispered. Marcus wrote the number 8 in the resistance box, then flipped the paper over and started drawing the loop. "Copy this before you go home," he said, tapping the sketch of the meter sitting inside the circuit. "Mr. Guo's going to ask how we wired it."

The group chat lit up at 9:14 on a Tuesday night. Kennedy had posted a screenshot of a map with a little blue dot sitting on Cameron's street, captioned "guess who's home alone with the good snacks." Cameron stared at his phone. He had never told anyone in the chat where he lived, except Dana, and Dana swore she hadn't said anything. Under Kennedy's message, someone he didn't recognize, a contact saved only as "K's cousin," replied with a single grinning emoji.

At lunch the next day, Cameron showed Dana the screenshot in the computer lab, keeping his voice low because Ms. Singh was helping another student print an essay. "How did Kennedy get a map of my house?" Dana shrugged and started to speculate, maybe Kennedy had followed him home once, maybe somebody's mom had talked, but Cameron kept scrolling back through the chat. The map hadn't come from Kennedy's memory. It had come from an app. Both of them had installed the same treasure-hunt game last month, the one with the sparse desert levels and the daily quests, and Cameron remembered tapping through the permissions without reading a single word.

He opened his phone settings right there at the lab table and found the list of apps. When he tapped the treasure game, a screen came up with three choices for location. He read them out loud under his breath: always, only while using the app, or never. His was set to always. He checked Dana's phone next, and hers said always too, which explained how a dot could appear on a map while the app sat closed in his pocket all evening. He switched his to never, then switched Dana's, and watched the little blue dot on the test map fade away like a porch light going off.

"Wait," Dana said, peering at the screen. "You can pick that? For each app?" Cameron nodded and scrolled through his other apps, setting most of them to only while using, and a few to never. He thought about the photo of the team dinner he'd posted in the chat back in September, the one with the restaurant sign in the background, and how easy it had been to forget that anything posted might sit on somebody's phone forever, ready to be forwarded to a grinning stranger. He couldn't decide if he'd been careless or just twelve. Maybe both.

That night, Kennedy messaged him privately. "Hey, my cousin screen-recorded the whole chat, including your address pic from October. Deleting it now. Where did you even learn to turn that stuff off?" Cameron typed back, "Computer lab. Check your game settings. Location can be always, only while using, or never." The typing bubble appeared, then vanished, then appeared again. Finally Kennedy sent a screenshot of his own settings, the little arrow switched from always to never, and a message underneath: "Send the good snacks tomorrow. Carbs only."

Jasmine had agreed to paint her grandmother's portrait mostly because refusing would have required a longer conversation, and the kitchen table at Grandma's house was already covered in brushes anyway. Her grandmother had been a painter for forty years, and she had announced on Saturday that it was time someone in the family learned a wash, which sounded to Jasmine like a dishwashing technique but turned out to involve laying thin layers of colour over the same face until it looked like a person. The portrait was going to be a surprise, which was difficult, since Grandma kept wandering past the table with her tea.

She had done the drawing on Friday, when her friend Derrick came over to see the house because his little brother had an audition at the music school down the road and Derrick had nowhere else to be. He wanted the portrait to look like him too, or at least like someone cool, and he kept suggesting she make his jaw more significant, whatever that meant. Jasmine told him he could sit beside her so his reflection would end up in the window she was painting behind Grandma's chair. He sat very still for almost four minutes.

The trouble came with the skin. Her first layer of peach went down flat and orange, like a paper bag with glasses. She reached for the white paint to lighten it, the way she would in any other kind of painting, and a dry hand appeared over her shoulder and took the tube away. Grandma set the water jar in front of her instead and said nothing, then went back to her tea. Jasmine looked at the jar, looked at the ruined orange face, and thought about it.

She dipped her brush, added more water to the same peach, and tried the layer again. The colour went on pale and glowing, lighter without a drop of white, and it let the first wash show through underneath like skin actually does. She tested it on the corner of the paper three times, each wash wetter than the last, until she found the tone she wanted. Then she layered the shadow under Grandma's jaw the same way, water instead of white, darker each round, and the face slowly grew a chin it had not had before.

On Sunday, Grandma watered her plants on the porch, which gave Jasmine two clear hours. She painted the grey braid, the reading glasses, the cardigan with the hole at the elbow that Grandma refused to mend because, she said, the cardigan had earned it. Derrick came back to check on his reflection and stayed to watch the final darks go in around the eyes.

When Grandma finally came inside, Jasmine turned the paper toward her and waited. Grandma looked at it for a long moment, set down her tea, and went to the drawer where she kept her good brushes, the ones nobody was allowed to touch. She laid three of them on the table next to Jasmine's hand.

"Same time next Saturday," she said. "Bring the boy who wants a chin. I have a frame."

Claire sat at the kitchen table with her music open to the third page, where her fingers always tangled, and her stomach was doing something complicated. The recital was in two days. Her hands felt cold even though the house was warm.

Her phone buzzed. Sebastien had sent a photo of his sneakers and the message, "I get so stressed before track meets I can barely tie my laces. You nervous too?"

Claire typed back, then stopped. Was she nervous? She kept rereading the same four bars without hearing them. When her mom passed through to start dinner, Claire asked, "Is stress just another word for freaking out?"

"Sometimes it helps you," her mom said, peeling a carrot. "Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge. Short bursts of it can actually help you focus."

Claire turned that over. A response to a challenge. Like her stomach knew about the recital before she'd admitted it. She decided to run a small test on herself. She set a timer for ten minutes and played the hard passage as if the audience were already sitting there, imagining Mr. Bakker from next door in his usual seat, arms crossed. Her heart sped up. Her palms went damp. And her ears, oddly, caught every note, small flaws she never noticed when she played calmly. She scribbled them in pencil.

The next day she tried the opposite. She played the same passage while texting Sebastien with her free hand, relaxed and sloppy, and missed the same mistakes entirely. So the nerves weren't just noise. They were like a lens that sharpened things, at least for a little while. She wondered how much was too much. At her last recital she'd been so shaky she'd frozen at the exact passage she now practiced, and that had been different, worse, like the lens had fogged over. Somewhere between calm and panic there had to be a sweet spot, and she was curious where it was.

That evening Johnathan came over to return her charger and stayed to listen. "Your hands are shaking," he said. "Is that contagious? Because now I'm nervous."

"It's stress," Claire said, almost proudly. "I'm testing it." He looked at her like she'd announced she was testing the weather. Her dad wandered through and set down the little brass whistle he kept on his keyring, the one he said was cheap alloy, not real silver, which was why it had gone dull. Claire picked it up and blew a single note, and the sound was thin but true.

On recital night she stood backstage with her cold hands and loud heart and thought: response to a challenge. She stepped toward the piano, and the stage lights found her.

Isla spread her notes across the library table and stared at the empty space where her conclusion should have been. Her science fair project was supposed to answer whether chewing mint gum helps people concentrate, and so far she had one story: her uncle, at Sunday dinner, holding up a copper bracelet. "Two weeks wearing this, and my back pain is gone," he had announced, tapping the table like a judge. "Proof right here." Isla had asked what else might have changed that month, and he had looked at her as if she had insulted the bracelet personally. She still wondered about that at odd moments, like now.

Elyssa dropped into the chair across from her, dumped a bag of sunflower seeds on the table, and pointed at Isla's laptop screen. "You should write about honey. I had a sore throat last week, my mom gave me honey tea, and the next morning it was basically gone. Honey works."

"Hmm," said Isla. She drafted a question on her notepad: What else might explain a sore throat going away overnight? She thought of her uncle's wrist.

"What," said Elyssa, who wanted credit for the idea and also, ideally, to be quoted in the project as a source. "It worked. That's my evidence."

"It's your story," Isla said. "One person, one time. Maybe your throat was going to get better anyway. Maybe you slept twelve hours. Maybe you drank so much tea the honey never got a chance to do anything."

Liana slid into the third chair, late and unwinding her earbuds. "My brother calls that an anecdote," she offered, stealing a sunflower seed. "A story about one person's experience. He says it can't show that one thing caused another, because other explanations haven't been ruled out." She said it fast, the way she recited song lyrics, and shrugged as if to apologize for having a brother who talked like that.

Isla wrote the word down. Anecdote. It fit her uncle exactly, and it fit Elyssa's honey, and it was somehow satisfying to have a word for the thing that had been bugging her since Sunday dinner.
