Alexia set her phone down on the table like a judge's gavel. "We can settle this. We can ask Ms. Tan, she's right next door, and she knows everything about history." The three of them tore outside, and Ms. Tan was watering her roses like she had been waiting for them. When Alexia asked, Ms. Tan grinned. "Actually, I know this exactly. The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973." She counted off each part on her fingers. "A handheld phone. On a street. In 1973."

"Nineteen seventy-three," Ricky repeated, and Henrik tried to replicate the moment, holding an imaginary phone to his ear and marching around the garden path shouting "Hello? Hello? It's 1973!" Ms. Tan said Cooper had called a rival engineer, which made it even better, like scoring a goal in the other team's net.

Back at the kitchen table, Alexia made her very first call, to her grandmother, who answered on the second ring. "I did it," Alexia said. "It's me, from my own phone, at my own kitchen table." Her grandmother laughed so loudly that Henrik and Ricky could hear it across the room, and Alexia beamed down at the dark blue screen glowing in her hand.

The 42 bus smelled like rain and wet jackets, and Gabrielle had exactly nine dollars in her pocket, which was nine dollars short of the entry fee for the skate competition on Saturday. She had until Friday to find the rest, and so far her only idea was to sell the barely-worn sneakers in her backpack, the ones her aunt had mailed last month in a box with a famous player's face printed on the lid.

Guneet plopped down beside her, holding his phone so close to his face that the screen's glow turned his glasses blue. "Look," he said. "Deon Mack's new commercial. He says these are the best shoes he's ever worn. He laces them up and then he dunks, and the voice says every player in the league is switching over."

"Every player," Gabrielle repeated. The bus lurched around a corner and she grabbed the pole, the worn rubber of her own shoes squeaking against the floor. She was trying to picture every player in the league actually throwing out their old shoes at once, and the picture wouldn't come. It felt like when a magician says "nothing up my sleeve." Saying it didn't make it true.

"I'm getting them for my birthday," Guneet said. "My mom pre-ordered. Everyone at school is getting them." He said "everyone" the way you'd say "the sun rises," like a thing no one could argue with.

Gabrielle looked down at her backpack, where the same shoes, same red stripe, same swooping logo, sat folded in their tissue paper. Her pair was nearly new. If everyone really wanted them, someone on the bus might want to buy hers, and she'd have her entry fee. She stood up, cleared her throat, and held up one shoe. "Brand new," she said to the crowded rows. "Same ones Deon Mack wears."

A woman with grocery bags squinted at the shoe. "Does he, though?" said the man across from her. "My nephew works retail, and he says half the stars couldn't pick their own shoe out of a lineup. They get paid to say it."

Before Gabrielle could answer, the man by the back door looked up from his newspaper. He had grey stubble and a lanyard that read BUI, and he tapped the paper's full-page ad, Deon Mack mid-dunk, mouth open as if about to inhale the whole arena. "I photographed that shoot," Mr. Bui said. "Nice man. They flew him in for one afternoon, handed him the shoes, and he read the line off a card. He'd never seen them before."

Guneet's mouth opened and closed. "But he says they're the best."

"He says what's on the card," Mr. Bui said gently. "That's called a testimonial. Famous face, paid to praise it, whether he knows anything about it or not."

The bus hissed to a stop and half the passengers stood, and Gabrielle felt a strange, acute clarity, like someone had wiped the window she was looking through. The shoes in her hand hadn't changed, but the reason everyone wanted them had just shifted under her feet, and she watched Guneet stare at his phone as if it had lied to him personally.

"So nobody's switching over," Guneet said slowly. "The voice just says they are, so we'll feel left out."

"That part's called bandwagon," Gabrielle said, surprising herself with how steady her voice came out. She turned the shoe over, then held it out to the woman with the grocery bags, who had stayed in her seat. "They're good shoes anyway. Good grip, hardly worn. Fifteen dollars."

The woman looked at the shoe, then at her own cracked soles. "Ten," she said.

"Twelve," said Gabrielle, "and I'll throw in the box with Deon Mack's face on it." Somewhere behind them, Guneet slid his phone into his pocket.

Hudson sat cross-legged on Anya's living room floor, her phone balanced on his knee while she refilled the popcorn bowl in the kitchen. He was supposed to be sending the email inviting their whole class to her birthday party, but his thumb had stopped over the "To" line. If he typed thirty addresses there, everyone would see everyone else's address. Anya had told him last week that a boy named Laurent got teased after his address ended up on a giant class chain, and she'd said it quietly, the way she said things that mattered.

When she came back, he tilted the phone toward her. "If I put everybody in To, they can all see each other's addresses, right?"

"Right," Anya said, setting down the bowl. "My cousin called it a contact disaster once."

"Then what do I do?" Hudson scrolled through the compose screen, hunting. Below the To line sat a small grey link labelled Add BCC. He'd seen the word a hundred times and never once thought about it. Blind carbon copy, he read, in the little pop-up explanation. He tested the idea in his head: BCC people receive the message, but nobody else can see their addresses. If that was true, it solved everything. "Watch," he said, and typed Laurent's address into the BCC field, then his own, then Anya's, all thirty of them, one by one, while she read names off the class list.

He sent the message to himself first as a trial. A minute later his own phone buzzed, and he opened the test email and scrolled through it. The To line showed only his own address. Thirty people would receive the party invitation, and to each of them it would look private, almost personal, as if it had been written to them alone. No hidden list, no shared addresses, nothing opaque about who got it and who didn't.

"The BCC field hides everybody," he told Anya, holding up both phones so she could compare. "People in it get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses. So Laurent's safe."

Anya took her phone back and looked at the sent message for a long moment. "You know, my mom would've just pasted the whole list into To," she said. "You went and found the right door."

They sent the real invitation together, Anya pressing the button at the end so it would come from her account. Replies started arriving within minutes, and the first one was from Laurent: I'm in. Also, nice touch, I can't see half the class's emails for once.

Hudson grinned and let Anya generate the reply, a short message with the time, the address, and a note to bring nothing but themselves. She hit send, and somewhere across town, phones began to buzz.

Cole slid into the corner booth of El Sol, the restaurant where his class met every Thursday for Spanish dinner night, and pulled out his flashcards before his water glass even hit the table. "Tonight," he announced, "I'm describing my whole family in full sentences. Mom already signed the permission slip. I petitioned her for a week."

Rylee dropped into the seat across from him. "You petitioned your own mother?"

"It was a formal request. I wrote it out." He tapped his cards. "Tengo una hermana. I have a sister. Tengo un perro. I have a dog."

"You're doing yours already?" Esther hurried over with her menu and her notebook. "I'm stuck on mine. Our dog is a girl, Lulu, and I want to say she's the best, but I only know perro."

Cole frowned at his card. Perro. He'd written it in September, back when the class had just started, and he'd never once thought about it since. "Wait," he said slowly. "Remember when Mr. Hoffmann called on me and I said la mesa and he gave me that thumbs up? And Danny said el mesa and didn't get the thumbs up?"

"So?"

"So there's a pattern. El and la. Different words. They go with different nouns." He laid his cards out on the table like evidence at a trial. "If el mesa was wrong, then el can't just attach to anything. What if el and la split the nouns into two groups?"

Esther flipped through her notebook. "Mr. Hoffmann said el gato one time. And another time la mesa, la silla."

"Right, so la goes with mesa and silla. And el goes with gato." Cole sat back, feeling something click into place like a gear. "What if it's about the animal itself? A girl dog might not be el perro at all. It might be la perra."

"That sounds made up," Rylee said, but she was grinning.

"I'll test it." Cole shot his hand up. "Mr. Hoffmann!"

Mr. Hoffmann, who ran Spanish dinner night and was currently balancing three plates of tacos, raised his eyebrows from across the room.

Cole pointed at Esther's notebook, where she'd drawn a lopsided picture of Lulu with a bow on her head. "If the dog is a girl," he called, "is it el perro or la perra?"

"La perra," Mr. Hoffmann called back, "for a female dog. El perro is for a male dog."

Esther gasped like she'd won something. "La perra es mi mejor amiga!" she read off her freshly corrected sentence.

"Lulu is your best friend," Rylee said. "Bold."

"She carried my sock around for three days once. She's earned it."

The tacos arrived, luminous with lime and hot salsa, and Mr. Hoffmann set down a bonus plate of churros for the table. "For the student who figured out the groups," he said.

Cole grabbed a churro and held it up like a trophy. "Next week, the whole family," he said. "Every single sentence."

Layla spread her materials across the kitchen table like a general planning a battle: the assignment sheet, two pencils, a granola bar, and a crumpled napkin she had brought home from her grandfather's house on Sunday. On the napkin, in his shaky handwriting, was an outline. Three points, each with evidence listed underneath. He had shown her how he planned arguments before writing, back when he wrote letters to the newspaper.

The assignment was due tomorrow, and she had chosen her topic: the school should replace its dying front lawn with a garden. She had a thesis statement ready, something she'd scribbled on her hand during math: "Our school should replace the lawn with a garden because it would save water, feed people, and teach students science." Three points. Sounded strong. She began copying the outline onto notebook paper, point by point, and under each one she wrote her evidence, exactly the way the napkin showed.

Point one was easy. She'd read that lawns need tons of watering, and a garden of native plants would diminish the school's water use. Point two went quickly too. The food bank on Miller Street took fresh vegetables, and the fourth graders already grew beans in cups on the windowsill. She wrote and wrote, her pencil scratching against the Formica, the kitchen smelling of onion from the pot simmering on the stove.

Then she got to point three. Teach students science. She tapped her pencil. What evidence did she have? She thought about the fungus unit in Mr. Sánchez's class, how they'd grown mold on bread in sealed bags, but that had happened in the classroom, not a garden. She checked her hand. She checked her notebook. Nothing. Her point three sat there with a big blank space underneath it, and something in her stomach went cold.

She picked up the napkin and looked at her grandfather's outline again. Under every one of his points, evidence. Every single one. That was the whole point of the outline, she realized: it showed the weak spots before you wasted an hour writing paragraphs. She had almost spent her whole evening drafting around a hole. Her heart knocked as she stared at the empty space, because the essay was due first period, and it was already dark outside.

Then she remembered. The district website had a page about a school across town with a pollinator garden, and it listed the lessons teachers had built around it. She grabbed her mother's laptop, typed fast, and there it was: a garden study cycle with math, science, and journaling. She wrote "district garden lessons, Bartlett Elementary" under point three and underlined it twice. Then she slid the napkin under her notebook, like a lucky charm, and started her first real paragraph. "Okay," she whispered to the empty kitchen. "Point one."

The rain had not stopped in two days, and everyone in Jack's class was talking about the river. Then Reagan sent him a message with a photo: a street turned into a brown river, a car half underwater, a porch light glowing just above the flood line. "This is by the school," she wrote. "They might cancel tomorrow."

Jack leaned closer to the screen. He did not recognize the street. That was the first thing that bugged him, because he had ridden his bike past the school a hundred times and never seen a porch like that, with a low stone wall and a crooked mailbox. He texted back, "Are you sure it's our school?"

"Viktor says it is," Reagan answered. "He got it from his cousin."

Jack despised being the last to know things, but he despised being fooled even more. Viktor had sent it to everyone in the group chat with the words BREAKING NEWS in capitals, and already three people had replied saying they would not do their homework tonight. It was reckless to spread something like that without checking, Jack thought, though he had done the same thing last month with a fake storm warning.

He tried zooming in on the photo, looking for a street sign, a store name, anything. The image was too blurry. Then he remembered something his older cousin had shown him once, late one night, when they were arguing about a picture of a shark swimming down a highway. Jack had laughed at the shark. His cousin had not.

He called Viktor. "Where did your cousin get that flood picture?"

"Some news page," Viktor said. "Why?"

"Meet me in the chat. I'm going to try a reverse image search," Jack said. "You can drag a picture into it and it shows where that photo appeared online before."

"That sounds fake," Viktor said, but he joined the chat anyway, and so did Reagan.

Jack saved the flood photo, opened the search page, and dragged the file in. The little bar spun. Reagan typed, "Well?" The bar kept spinning. Jack realized he was holding his breath, which felt silly, so he let it out and waited.

The results loaded. At the top was the same porch, the same half-drowned car, the same crooked mailbox. The page it came from was old, years old, from a town three states away, back when that street had actually flooded. Below it were more hits, other pages, other years, the same photo every time. Not our school. Not our river. Not this week.

Jack pasted the link into the chat. For a moment nobody typed anything. Then Viktor wrote, "Oh no."

"I almost told my mom we needed sandbags," Reagan said.

"Delete it," Jack typed, "before someone else thinks it's real." He could already imagine the photo landing on other phones, moving from chat to chat, the whole grade packing up for a flood that had happened somewhere else, long ago.

Viktor sent a single thumbs-up, and the BREAKING NEWS message disappeared from the chat.

Outside, the real rain kept drumming on the window, and Jack turned back to his screen to see if the river gauge was up.

Maya spread her sketchpad on the picnic table in the backyard and checked her phone again. The community studio's street-scene contest closed at four o'clock, and it was already noon. She had drafted three versions of her street that morning, and every one of them looked flat, like buildings pasted onto paper instead of standing along a road.

Mr. Liu, who was weeding his tomatoes on the other side of the fence, leaned over and looked at her drawing. "Ah, perspective," he said. "My grandmother painted streets her whole life. She taught me one rule." He held up two fingers like fence posts. "The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines." Then he went back to his tomatoes, humming, as if he hadn't just handed her the key to everything.

Maya stared at her drawing. Vanishing point, she understood; she had marked a dot in the middle of the page. But which lines ran toward it? She had only drawn the road edges slanting inward. She grabbed a fresh sheet and tried again, this time starting with the dot. From it, she ran her pencil outward. The road edges, yes. But the curbs too, the near edge and the far edge, slanting toward the dot on both sides. And the rooflines, sloping down toward it as the buildings stepped back. Even the shop awnings. It was like the whole street was being pulled by one invisible point.

A squirrel, some aggressive little rodent, darted across the table and knocked her eraser into the grass. Maya rescued it and kept drawing, because now the street was working. The buildings sat back from the road instead of standing on top of it. The road looked like it went somewhere.

Christina arrived at two, bike rattling, to see the entry before they biked it over together. "You didn't shade anything," Christina said. "Last year the winner shaded everything, all the windows, everything."

Maya looked at her clean, hard lines, the orthogonals ruling the page. For a second she doubted it, and she almost reached for her pencil to fill in the windows. Then she set the pencil down. "No," she said. "The lines do the work this time. If I shade over them, they'll disappear."

At the studio, the woman at the sign-in table held the drawing up and looked at it a long moment. "Nice orthogonals," she said.

Maya grinned at Christina. "Told you."

Aaron held the onion like it was a small bomb, which was pretty much how he felt about it. The soup for his family's dinner at the community kitchen had to be on the table by six o'clock, and it was already twenty past five. One chopped onion stood between him and the pot.

"Need help?" Hayley asked, sliding up beside him at the counter. Rafaelle was already peeling carrots at the far end, racing the clock and losing.

"I got it," Aaron said. He brought the knife down, and within four cuts his eyes were stinging and streaming. "Ow. Why is a vegetable doing this to me?"

Hayley grinned and handed him a paper towel. "You look like you just watched the saddest movie ever made."

"It's not funny." He wiped his face, but the tears kept coming. It was like the onion had a plan to humiliate him in front of the whole kitchen. He chopped faster, which made it worse.

"Wait," Rafaelle called over, squinting at them. "Why does it happen, though? Carrots don't do that. Why onions?" He held up a carrot like evidence.

Aaron stopped, eyes burning, and thought back to last Thanksgiving, when his grandmother had chopped onions at the sink wearing swim goggles. Everyone laughed at her, but she didn't cry once. He'd thought it was just a weird grandma thing. Now he wondered. She wasn't protecting her hands or her nose. She was protecting her eyes. So whatever the onion made had to travel through the air and land there. But how did cutting release anything? The whole onion just sat there, harmless, until the knife went through it. Something had to be locked inside.

"Maybe it's in the cells," he said slowly. "Like, the onion only becomes a problem when you break it open. The knife does it." He looked at Hayley. "So it's not the onion itself. It's what gets out when you cut it."

Mr. Hassan, checking the thermostat by the door, raised an eyebrow. "Soup by six, chef. Whatever theory you're testing, test it fast."

"Chill water," Aaron said suddenly. "Grandma kept a bowl of water next to her board." He didn't know why that would help, but the goggle memory made him trust her. He filled a bowl, dunked the onion halves, and cut the rest underwater, lifting them out only at the end. His eyes barely stung at all.

"That actually worked?" Rafaelle said, staring.

Aaron tipped the onions into the bubbling pot and grinned through the steam. "Grandma one, onion zero."

The basement of St. Luke's smelled like cardamom and burnt coffee, because the interfaith welcome dinner always mixed everyone's food on one long row of tables. Avery had come with a jar of her grandmother's pickles, which was their household's rule for gifts: never arrive anywhere empty-handed. She was scanning the room for her friend Flynn when she saw the new family by the door, the ones who had just moved from New Zealand. Their daughter, Mathilde, was in her class at school.

A man from the new family stepped up to Mrs. Okafor, and then he leaned in and pressed his nose and forehead against hers. Avery froze. It looked like a head-bump, an accident, and she half expected both of them to apologize and rub their heads. Neither did. They stayed there for a second, close and unhurried, and then pulled apart smiling, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world.

Flynn appeared beside her, nudging a paper cup of punch toward her since her hands were full of pickle jar. "Did you see that?" he whispered. Avery nodded slowly. She had a theory forming, the way she did when a pattern showed up in math class. If it had been a mistake, it would have happened once. So she watched. When the temple's rabbi greeted the new family, it happened again, nose to nose, forehead to forehead. When the grandmother from the new family greeted Mathilde's teacher, Ms. Kamau, it happened a third time. Same gesture, every time, like a handshake that lived somewhere else on the body.

Avery tested her idea the only way she could think of. She carried the pickle jar over to Mathilde, set it down, held out her hand, and watched carefully. Mathilde shook it, ordinary and smiling. "Your family does the nose thing," Avery said, hoping that didn't sound abrupt. "What is it?"

"A hongi," Mathilde said. "It's a Maori greeting. You press your noses and foreheads together, and it means you're sharing the breath of life." Then she added, "Do you want to try it?"

Avery's stomach did a small flip, but she leaned in. Mathilde's forehead was warm against hers, and for one breath they stood there in the noisy basement, close enough that Avery could smell the cedar smoke that seemed to saturate Mathilde's coat. When they stepped apart, Flynn was grinning at both of them.

At dinner Avery noticed more than she ever had before. The new family waited until everyone at the table was served before eating, while Flynn's family said a quick grace, and Mrs. Okafor broke her flatbread and offered pieces around before touching her own plate. Nobody did it the same way, and nobody seemed to mind. Mathilde leaned over and pointed at the jar of pickles. "Is that a gift? We brought bread from home. My dad says you never visit anyone without bringing something to eat."

"Exactly," Avery said, and slid the jar down the table so it sat between them, half hers and half theirs, like a border nobody needed.

On Saturday morning, Ellie stood in Ms. Warsame's garage, where folding tables held boxes of donated food, and asked the question that had been bothering her since breakfast. "Why would a grocery store give away all these apples? They look perfect." She held one up like evidence.

Ms. Warsame, who ran the little food bank from her garage every weekend, just smiled and handed her a sorting chart. Archie, elbow-deep in a crate of oranges, grinned. "My dad says they dump stuff for the weirdest reasons. Too big, too small, too orange." Ellie rolled her eyes, but she persisted, turning each apple over, checking for the bruise or dent that must be hiding somewhere. Most of them had nothing. She stacked them in the "good" pile until it wobbled like a tiny red tower.

"Here's the thing," Archie said, balancing an orange on his head, which was his way of thinking. "My mom told me the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted. Thirty to forty percent. Of all the food." He let the orange drop into his hand and popped it back in the crate. "So if we had ten of these, like, four would just vanish."

Ellie frowned at the apple tower. Ten apples, four gone. She grabbed a scrap of paper and drew it: ten circles, then crossed out three, then a fourth with a jagged line, right between three and four because nobody knew the exact number. She felt like a detective who couldn't see the crime, only the missing bodies. "Okay," she said. "So I want to test it. We weigh everything that comes in today, and we weigh what nobody takes by closing time. Like erosion, except it's apples falling off a cliff instead of dirt."

They borrowed the bathroom scale, which Archie claimed was inaccurate by exactly two pounds because it hated him. Ellie wrote numbers on the clipboard, quick and agile with the pencil, dodging Archie's attempts to add a zero. Ms. Warsame watched from her lawn chair, pretending to read but obviously eavesdropping.

At closing time, they did the math on the garage floor. Some zucchini had gone soft, a bag of spinach had wilted, and three loaves of bread sat untouched because everybody wanted the sourdough. Not quite four out of ten, but close, and Ellie circled the number twice. "Still a lot of apples falling off the cliff," she said. Archie picked up a leftover zucchini and brandished it like a sword. "Then we fight the cliff," he announced, and saluted the squash.

Henry stood at the edge of the cemetery with a folded index card in his pocket and no idea what was written on it, because he had rewritten it six times and the last version just said PICK ONE MEMORY. His grandfather had kept bees behind the garage for forty years, and everyone expected Henry to speak at the service. Ms. Mansour, who had been his grandfather's neighbor, had asked him gently the day before. "A eulogy," she'd said, "just means a speech speaking well of someone who has died. It comes from Greek roots. Nobody expects a masterpiece." Henry had nodded, but the word had stuck in his head anyway. Speak well of. That was the whole job.

Caius and Lindsay found him near the fence, where gray lichen spread over the stones like slow spilled paint. "Did you pick a memory?" Caius asked. Henry shook his head. "I keep thinking they all need to be in there. The bees, the card games, the time he drove two hours in the rain for my soccer game. But Ms. Mansour said a eulogy is only about speaking well of him, not saying everything about him." Lindsay frowned. "So it's like a highlight, not a biography." Henry had not thought of it that way, and the idea loosened something in his chest.

He decided to test it. "Okay," he said, pulling out the card. "If I can only speak well of him once, what's the best thing I ever saw him do?" Lindsay said the soccer game. Caius said the card games, because Grandpa had let Caius win exactly once and never again, which Caius claimed was respectful. Henry turned each one over in his mind like a stone.

Then he remembered the apple tree. Two summers ago, the blossoms had come and gone and no fruit had followed, and everyone said the tree was dying. His grandfather had refused to cut it down. Instead he had set two of his hives beside it and explained that the bees needed to pollinate the blossoms before any apples could form, and that the windy spring had kept the wild bees away. The next year the tree had been so heavy with apples that a branch had cracked. Henry had thought it was luck at the time. Now he understood it had been his grandfather noticing an invisible problem and quietly fixing it.

"That's it," Henry said. "That's the one." The service began, and when Ms. Mansour caught his eye and nodded, he walked to the front with the card, though he barely looked at it. He told the apple tree story, including the cracked branch, and a ripple of soft laughter went through the chairs. He said the word eulogy once, explained in half a sentence what it meant, because his grandfather would have liked knowing that a fancy Greek word just meant speaking well of somebody, and that was a thing Grandpa had done for everyone, even a dying tree.

Afterward, Lindsay pressed something into his hand: a small synthetic flower, bright yellow, the kind that never fades. "For the tree story," she said. Henry carried it back to the fence and set it on the flat stone where the lichen grew, bright against all that gray. Caius clapped him on the shoulder. "You spoke well of him," Caius said. Henry looked out past the fence at the row of apple trees along the cemetery road, every one of them in bloom.

Eva wanted the last seat at the good lab bench, the one by the window, but Byron had claimed it by arriving five minutes early, and after a short negotiation she agreed to trade him her spare calculator for the period. She set her bag down beside him just as Ms. Virtanen taped an old, yellowed periodic table to the whiteboard. It looked wrong. Half a dozen squares were empty, and one of them had a question mark pencilled inside.

"Why does that one have a hole?" Eva asked, pointing. "Did someone rip it?"

Makai leaned over his binder. "It's not ripped. It's printed that way. My cousin has a poster like it at home."

Ms. Virtanen said only, "Nineteenth-century tables look like that. Work it out," and walked away to unlock the chemical cabinet.

"Great," Byron said. "She abandoned us."

Eva frowned at the poster. The empty squares sat in regular positions, whole rows where an element should have been. Around each gap, the neighbouring elements carried numbers in their corners. On the modern table in her textbook, the same positions were filled: gallium, germanium, scandium, all sitting exactly where the blanks were. She traced one with her finger. In the old table, gallium's square was empty; in the new one it sat at number 31, so it had 31 protons, the same way oxygen at number 8 had 8 protons, which she had learned that morning. Mendeleev, said the caption under the old poster, had left the gaps on purpose. He had known something belonged there before anyone had found it.

A folded note landed on her bench. She opened it. "Did you figure out the blanks or are we all doomed for the quiz? Also you still owe me a calculator. Makai." She wrote back, "Mall table = Mendeleev left gaps for elements not discovered yet. Gallium filled one later. Find the others if you want. Deal stands, you keep the seat." She tossed it across the aisle.

Makai read it, then raised his hand so vigorously his sleeve knocked over a beaker rack. "Ms. Virtanen. Mendeleev left gaps for elements nobody had found yet, and gallium filled one of them."

"That's the whole answer," Ms. Virtanen said.

Makai turned around and slid the calculator back across the bench to Eva. "You win the trade," he said. "That was worth more than a seat."

Eva flipped her textbook to the modern table and started counting empty squares in the old poster against filled ones, tapping each match with her pencil. "Gallium, germanium, scandium," she said. "One down, five to go."

The waiting room smelled like orange cleaner and old magazines. Lillian sat with her hands folded in her lap, trying to look like a person who was not nervous, which was hard because her stomach had been hurting for six weeks and nobody knew why. Ruben sat beside her, bouncing his knee.

"You look like you're plotting something sinister," he whispered, holding up a magazine about sharks.

"I'm not sinister. I'm thinking." She was thinking, actually. She had devised a plan in the car: she would write down everything she'd eaten for six weeks, every day, and hand the list to the doctor, so the doctor would have to find the cause. Hidden causes needed evidence. That was just how it worked, she was pretty sure.

A nurse called her name, and Ruben waved from his chair. "I'll wait. My mom's picking me up here anyway, so I'm basically a captive consumer of these shark magazines."

Inside the small room, the doctor listened to Lillian's stomach, asked questions, and looked at her food list. Then she asked about sleep, and school, and whether anything had been worrying her. Lillian said no a little too fast. The doctor looked at her for a long moment, then said she wanted to check one thing.

"There's a hormone called cortisol," the doctor said, looking at the screen. "It's made by the adrenal glands, and it rises during stress. When stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high." She turned. "That can leave you feeling run down, the way you're describing."

Lillian stared at the ceiling tiles. Six weeks. Six weeks of exactly one thing, which she had not written on any list. The appointment ended with instructions to rest, drink water, and come back. In the waiting room, Ruben handed her a folded note before his mom pulled him away.

"Raegan gave it to me this morning. You're supposed to read it when you're done at the doctor."

Lillian unfolded the letter on the bus home. Raegan's handwriting was cramped into every corner of the page. She had written that she was sorry, that she hadn't meant for the rumor to spread, that somebody had shown Lillian's private messages to half the class, and that she'd been carrying it for six weeks, afraid to say it out loud. "You've been out sick so much," the letter ended. "I keep thinking it's my fault. Please tell me what to do."

Six weeks. The math clicked into place like a lock. It wasn't the food list. It was this, the whole time, this thing she hadn't let herself name.

Lillian got off the bus and stood on the sidewalk with the letter shaking slightly in her hand. Then she pulled out her phone and typed, "We need to talk. Ms. Girma's room, tomorrow, before first bell. I'll be there at 7:45." She pressed send, folded the letter into her pocket, and walked the last block home a little faster than before.

The debate tournament had a surprise event this year: improvised scenes between rounds, and whoever signed up got paired with a random partner. George signed up because Yasmina dared him to, and now he was regretting it. His plan for debates was simple: build a database of arguments, memorize rebuttals, control everything. Improvising had no database. You just stood there and made things up while people watched.

"Here's the one rule," Antony told him in the cafeteria between rounds. "Accept every offer. Say yes, and then add something. If I say the castle is under attack, you don't say no it isn't. You say yes, and the drawbridge is stuck." Antony had read a shelf of theater books and wouldn't stop quoting them. "There's this book called Impro, from 1979, by Keith Johnstone. He says characters play high or low status. A king is high, a servant is low. And shifting status is where the drama comes from."

"Shifting status," George repeated, mostly to get Antony to stop talking.

"Just watch," Antony said. He grabbed a cafeteria tray and held it like a crown. "You're my servant. Bring me grapes."

George shuffled over, shoulders bent, head down. "Grapes, Your Majesty, right away." The kids at the next table glanced over. When George knelt and offered an invisible bowl, Antony examined it, flicked a grape off the tray, and sniffed. It was funny, George had to admit, but it also felt stuck. The king was still being a king. The servant was still serving.

Then Yasmina leaned in from the next seat. "Try turning it around. Make the servant give the orders." George thought about that. If status was the hidden thing running the scene, then moving it should change everything, the way a river changes when you shift one rock. He stood up, kept the bent posture for a second, then straightened his spine and pointed at the tray. "Your Majesty, you left your grapes in the kitchen. Again. Third time this week. And you were late for the war council." Antony's face broke open. He snapped to attention, tray wobbling, and said, "Sorry, sir, it won't happen, sir." The whole table burst out laughing, and the corrosive knot of dread George had carried all morning dissolved just like that.

At the afternoon session, Ms. Morningstar, who was judging, paired George with a girl from another school for a scene about two astronauts. When his partner said, "Captain, the oxygen's leaking," George didn't argue or freeze. He grabbed a hose that wasn't there, said, "Yes, and the repair kit is in your locker from football practice," and let her take command while he fumbled behind her, muttering apologies. They ended the scene with her pinning a medal made of a paper napkin to his shirt while he saluted the wrong direction. The applause was small but real, and Yasmina's voice rose above it.

"Told you he'd persevere," she called out, and Antony held up the tray crown one more time.

Payton slid the tray of cookies out of the oven and stared at them. They were pale, puffy, and dry, more like little cakes than the chewy cookies her grandmother made. Yahya leaned over her shoulder and poked one with a fork. "These are the same cookies you made last week?" she asked. "Because last week's were good, and these look like they lost an argument."

"They did lose an argument," Payton said. "With me."

It was Saturday morning at the community kitchen, and Payton had volunteered to bake a batch for her family's dinner tonight. Ms. Mendoza, who ran the kitchen, had given her the same recipe card both times. Same butter, same sugar, same chocolate chips. That was the maddening part. Two identical recipes, two completely different cookies, and Payton intended to find out why before her little brother ate something that tasted like sweet chalk.

Jasper wandered over with a coffee filter on his head like a tiny hat. "Maybe the oven's haunted," he offered. "That's my official theory."

"Your theories are always controversial," Payton said, "and usually wrong." But she did wonder about the oven, so she checked it. The dial was at the same temperature as last week, and the cookies had browned evenly on the top rack. Not the oven.

She read the recipe again, hunting for anything she might have done differently. Then it hit her. Last week, the flour had already been in the big jar on the counter, and she had spooned it into the cup. Today the jar was empty, so she had dipped her measuring cup straight into the bag, pushing it down into the flour and packing it in. She looked at the bag, then at her cup, then at the kitchen's small scale sitting in the corner.

"Jasper, bring me that vessel of flour," she said, pointing at the jar. She filled her cup by dipping it into the bag, levelled it off, and weighed it. Then she spooned flour gently into the same cup and weighed that. The numbers were not even close. The scooped cup was way heavier. "It's me," she announced. "I've been putting way too much flour in. Scooping straight from the bag packs it down, so the cup holds more than the recipe wants. Weighing it is way more accurate."

Yahya peered at the scale. "So your cookies came out dry because you measured wrong. Not haunted?"

"Not haunted," Jasper admitted, taking the coffee filter off his head with dignity. "I withdraw my theory."

Payton weighed out the proper amount of flour, creamed the butter and sugar, and slid the new dough into the oven. When the timer rang, the cookies came out golden with ruffled edges. Yahya grabbed one, took a bite, and closed her eyes. "Okay, these I would petition the school to serve at every lunch."

Payton packed the cooled cookies into a tin for home and kept two out on a plate. "Those are for the three of us," she said, "as payment for the investigation." Jasper reached for the biggest one, and Payton smacked the back of his hand with the spatula. "Weigh it first," she said. "Biggest by grams wins."

The family group chat lit up at 4:41 on Friday afternoon. Mom: "How many glow sticks do you need?" Dad: "Is this the dance thing?" Payton typed fast, thumbs hammering. "6. Maybe 8. Sonny said the gym goes totally black for the last hour and everyone waves them around." Her grandmother sent a thumbs up, which she sent for everything, including the time Payton broke a toe.

The problem started at the party store, where the cashier pulled the glow sticks from a shelf right beside the sunny window. They were warm in Payton's hand, almost cozy. She remembered her cousin last summer cracking one at a barbecue and it burning out before the fireworks, while the one from the cooler in the trunk still glowed the next day. Warm ones shine brighter, she thought, but do they die faster? She had no way to be sure yet, so she bought eight. A good consumer, her mom liked to say, tests before she trusts, and Payton figured a hypothetical glow stick in her head was worth nothing compared with two real ones on her desk.

At home she cracked two sticks at the same moment and put one on the radiator and one in the freezer, wedged between the frozen peas. Twenty minutes later she took them out. The warm one blazed, a fat green line you could read by. The frozen one was barely there, a pale smudge. She texted the group chat: "Testing. Warm = super bright. Cold = kind of sad. Will report back." Dad replied with three question marks. "It's for science," she typed, and Grandma sent another thumbs up.

She took the warm one and two room-temperature ones to the dance, and she left the frozen one in the freezer on purpose.

The gym went dark at nine, and the ceiling filled with waving green and pink light. Sonny's stick, which he had kept in his back pocket all through dinner, out-glowed everyone's, so bright Aila asked to hold it. "Get your own, I'm a glow stick consumer now," Sonny said, spinning it. By 9:40 his was a dull gray tube. Aila's, which she had clipped into her hair straight from a cold locker bay outside, was faint, but it was faint at 10:15 too, still a steady ember while Sonny sat consoling his dead stick like a lost pet. Payton's room-temperature ones split the difference: medium bright, mostly alive.

At 10:30 Ms. Kang flicked the half-lights on and started sweeping glow sticks off the floor with the edge of her shoe. "Take them or lose them," she called. Payton scooped up the frozen one's three surviving siblings from home in her backpack, no, those were at home; she scooped up her two dim survivors and hers and Sonny's jackets.

That night she checked the freezer before bed. The frozen stick still glowed, faint as a nightlight, stubborn in the dark among the peas. She took a photo and sent it to the family group chat with the caption "still alive." Then she put Sonny's dead stick in beside it, closed the door, and set a reminder on her phone for 7 a.m.

Sonny texted her at midnight: "did u seriously put mine in the freezer." She typed back, "just wait for morning," and fell asleep smiling at the ceiling.

Elliot slid his draft across the library table until it bumped Mary's elbow. "Page four still isn't right," he said. She picked it up and squinted at his handwriting, where a sheriff in a dusty frontier town was interrogating a prisoner named Cole.

"The story stops right when it should get exciting," Mary said. "The sheriff corners Cole in the barn, and then you just write that everything works out. That's not a climax. That's giving up." She tapped the page. "And what is this mark here?"

Elliot looked at the line she meant. His sheriff said, "Your sister told me, 'I saw Cole hide the gold behind the church.'" He had drawn double quotation marks around the sister's words, the same kind he had used around everything else, and now that he stared at it, the page looked like a fence with too many posts. He remembered the afternoon he had skipped the punctuation workshop Ms. Pierre ran at the library because a pickup basketball game had started without him. He had told himself he could figure dialogue out on his own. Sitting here now, with the contest deadline on Friday, he weighed that choice and could not decide whether the game had been worth it.

"Watch my stuff," he said, and he walked to the shelf where the writing guides stood. The first book he opened was three hundred pages of advice about frugal living and had nothing to do with stories, so he shoved it back. The second one had a whole chapter on dialogue. He ran his finger down the page until he found an example where a character repeated what somebody else had said. He read it once, then again. The outer words sat inside double quotation marks, and the quoted words inside those sat inside single ones.

He carried the book back to the table. "Look," he said, pointing at the example. "When someone quotes a quote, the inner one gets single marks."

"Single inside double," Mary said slowly, copying it onto her own notepad. "Wait, that's exactly what you need on page four."

Elliot borrowed a pencil, erased his fence of doubled marks, and rewrote the sheriff's line so the sister's words sat inside single quotation marks. Then he kept going, because the marks had made him think about the scene itself. He crossed out "everything works out" and wrote a real climax instead: the sheriff corners Cole in the barn, Cole tries to evade him by slipping out the hayloft door, and the sheriff is already standing below it, waiting, lantern raised. It was the best thing he had ever written, and it took up half a page.

Anne appeared at the table with her own contest entry and read over his shoulder. "Read the barn part out loud," she said.

Elliot read it in a low voice, doing the sheriff's gravel and Cole's frightened rush of words, and when he finished the last line, the lantern light catching Cole's face as he lands in the dust, Anne said, "Now that's an ending."

Eli crouched beside the garden bed behind the garage, where eight bean plants stood in a stubborn row. Tomorrow morning the science fair boards had to be carried into the gym, and his board was still blank. His hypothesis, printed neatly at the top of his notebook, said that plants watered with sugar water would grow taller than plants watered with plain water, because the extra energy had to go somewhere. He had measured the sugar-fed plants every Sunday for three weeks. They were shorter. Every single one.

"What's that face?" Maxine asked, dropping onto the grass beside him with her clipboard. She was doing her project on which paper airplane design flew farthest, and her results had cooperated, which suddenly seemed unfair. "They look fine."

"They're losers," Eli said. "The sugar ones are four centimeters shorter. My hypothesis is wrong, and I don't have time to redo it." He poked the soil, which smelled damp and faintly of the molasses he had mixed into his watering can. Behind the fence, Mr. Romano was stacking flowerpots, and Eli asked him, half hoping for a miracle, whether he thought the plants might still catch up overnight.

"Plants don't sprint," Mr. Romano said, resting a pot on the fence rail. "That's a result, kid. A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result, and it's worth reporting." He picked up another pot and went back to his stacking, as if he had said nothing more remarkable than the weather.

Eli sat with that. He turned it over the way he turned over a rock in the creek, wondering what might be living underneath it. The fertilizer bag in the shed had bragged about containing a natural plant hormone that boosted growth, and he had read that sugar fed soil bacteria instead. Was that why the sugar plants looked pale and droopy while the plain-water plants stood buoyant and green, their leaves lifting in the evening breeze? He couldn't see the bacteria, but he could see the pattern: more sugar, shorter plants, every time. That was a rule hiding in his own data, and he had almost thrown it in the compost.

He ran inside and printed his board in bold letters: "What Happens When My Hypothesis Was Wrong." He drew a bar graph with the sugar plants low and the plain plants high, and a second panel on how he would budget his time next year to test two groups at once. Maxine leaned over the fence to look, holding a paper airplane.

"You're presenting the failure?" she said.

"I'm presenting the finding," Eli said, and taped the last chart to the board.

The recipe card was smudged, but Violet could still read it: camp biscuits, three cups flour, two tablespoons baking powder, salt, butter, milk. She set the ingredients on the picnic table beside the camp stove while her dad gathered firewood and her little brother threw pinecones at a tree.

The tin marked baking powder turned out to hold four sad grains rolling around the bottom. Violet checked the camp bin, then the car, then the bin again. What she did have was a full box of baking soda. Both cans were orange, both said Clabber something, and the words on the label were vague about the difference. She stirred two tablespoons of the soda into the flour anyway, cut in the butter, splashed in the milk, and dropped six mounds onto the skillet.

The biscuits spread sideways instead of up. They came out flat and soapy-tasting, and her brother spat his into the grass after one bite.

Lucien, from the next campsite, wandered over holding his own plate. "Ours came out right," he said. "My mom packed a fresh can. Baking powder has both things in it, baking soda and a dry acid, so it rises even when the recipe has nothing sour in it." He pointed at her flat biscuits. "Soda alone only works if you add something acidic. Yours had no buttermilk, no lemon, nothing."

Violet looked at the recipe again. Flour, salt, butter, milk. Milk was the only liquid, and milk was not acidic the way buttermilk was. She had swapped in soda without changing anything else, and the batter had nothing to react with. Her first batch was proof.

She lined up the ingredients again and thought through it like a database in her head: recipe, ingredient, what each one did. If she kept the baking soda, she had to add an acid somewhere. She found a lemon in the cooler, squeezed two tablespoons of juice into the milk, and let it sit until it looked slightly curdled. Then she mixed a new batch, soda and lemony milk this time, and dropped the dough onto the hot skillet.

The mounds puffed. Within minutes she had six tall biscuits, golden on the bottom. She split one open and steam came out of the middle, soft and white.

Lucien held out his plate. "Trade you for the flat ones," he said.

"Those are for the birds," Violet said, and handed him a warm biscuit.

Sarah had wanted to learn laundry for weeks, ever since her mom said she was old enough to be in charge of her own clothes, so on Saturday morning she dragged the hamper out to the garage where the washer and dryer hummed against the wall. taped to the dryer was a note in her grandmother's looping handwriting.

"Dear Sarah, use the basket on the left, my wool sweater is in it. Cold water only for that one. Love, Grandma."

Sarah dumped everything onto the folding table. Bently and Tabitha followed her in, because Sarah had promised them all the first warm towels to come out of the dryer. "First we sort," she announced, feeling like a scientist. "Darks, lights, and whites. Bently, you take darks. Tabitha, lights." They worked fast, tossing shirts into three piles, and Sarah held up a red sock like evidence. "This could turn everything pink. It goes with the darks."

Tabitha spotted the basket on the left and the cream-colored sweater folded neatly on top. "What about that?"

"Wool sweater, warm wash, gentle cycle," Sarah said, reading the machine's dial. "Gentle has to be right for something hand-knitted." She piled the sweater in with the darks, set the water to hot, because hot water got things cleaner, and pushed the button. The drum began its vigorous sloshing, and all three of them sat on an overturned milk crate to watch the clothes tumble through the little window like a slow aquarium.

When the cycle ended, Sarah pulled out the sweater and her arms dropped. It was tiny. It would have fit a doll. Bently laughed so hard he slid off the crate, and even Tabitha covered her mouth with both hands. "Grandma is going to lose her reputation as the family knitter if she sees this," Tabitha said, and Sarah felt her stomach flip.

She grabbed her mom's phone and typed in shrunken wool sweater. "Read it out loud," she told Bently, because her own hands were shaking.

"Wool shrinks in hot, sloshing water because tiny scales on each wool fibre open up and lock onto neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter."

"So that's what happened. The hot water opened the scales and they grabbed each other." Sarah scrolled down. "It's called felting," she read aloud. "People do it on purpose to make stuff."

Tabitha picked up the tiny sweater and stretched it between her hands. "Can you undo it?"

Sarah looked at Grandma's note again, at the words cold water only. She raced to the hamper, found the matching wool hat from the same basket, and started a second load with the dial turned all the way to cold. "Test number two," she said. "If cold water keeps the scales closed, the hat comes out the same size, and I know exactly what went wrong."

While the drum turned, she sat at the folding table and wrote a letter.

"Dear Grandma, I put your sweater in a hot wash and now it would fit a cat. I am so sorry. I learned why it happened and I'm doing a cold test with your hat right now. If it works, I will wash everything wool in cold water forever. Can I come over Sunday? Love, Sarah."

She sealed it, propped it against the detergent bottle, and turned back to the machine. "Forty minutes," she said. "Then we find out."

Sydney had read her line from Romeo and Juliet eleven times on the walk to the book club, and she still felt like she was holding the words upside down. Ms. Carvalho had assigned each of them a speech to paraphrase into modern English, and Sydney had drawn Juliet's balcony line. "Wherefore art thou Romeo?" Easy, Sydney had decided. It meant "Where are you, Romeo?" Juliet was up on the balcony, scanning the dark garden, looking for the boy she liked. Who wouldn't look?

Trace was already sprawled on the library carpet with a stack of snacks, and Leandre sat across from him, chewing his pencil like it owed him money. "Okay," said Ms. Carvalho, settling into her chair. "Who wants to go first?" Nobody's hand moved. The radiator ticked. Somewhere down the hall a door slammed, and Sydney inhaled the dusty, arid smell of old carpet and braced herself. "Sydney, you look ready," Ms. Carvalho said, which was unfair, because Sydney was trying to look invisible.

"My line is 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?'" Sydney read it out, then gave her paraphrase. "It's like, 'Where are you, Romeo?' She's up on the balcony trying to spot him." She sat back, satisfied. Across the circle, Leandre stopped chewing his pencil. He flipped through his packet, stopped at a page, and narrowed his eyes at her like a detective in a movie.

"Wait," Leandre said. "I had that page too. Look at the next lines. She keeps talking about his name. 'Deny thy father and refuse thy name.' She's not looking around. She's talking about his name, over and over." Sydney leaned over to see. He was right. Juliet went on about names for another whole speech, like she couldn't stop. Sydney felt something shift in her head, slow and then all at once. If Juliet was stuck on his name, then her question wasn't about where he was. It was about what he was called. "Wherefore means why," Leandre said, tapping the footnote at the bottom of the page. "It says it right there."

"Why?" Sydney said it out loud, testing it. "Wherefore art thou Romeo. Why are you Romeo." She looked at the speech again and the whole thing rearranged itself, the way a Magic Eye picture snaps into shape. Juliet wasn't searching the garden at all. She was asking why the boy she loved had to be a Montague, the one boy her family hated. Sydney had been picturing Juliet squinting into hedges like she'd lost her keys. "I completely staged this wrong," she said. "In my head she was dangling off the balcony going 'Romeo? Romeo? Where are yooou.'"

"Like calling a dog," Trace said, and everyone cracked up, even Ms. Carvalho, who hid it behind her mug. Sydney laughed too, then pulled her notebook over and started rewriting, crossing out her old paraphrase in big strokes. At the top of a fresh page she printed the new version: "Why do you have to be Romeo?" Underneath she wrote, "She's saying: forget your name. Just be you."

Trace crumpled a snack wrapper and tossed it toward the trash can. It bounced off the rim and rolled under the chair. "So the most famous love line in history," he said, "is basically a girl asking a guy to change his name tag." Sydney held up her notebook. "Correction," she said. "The most famous why line in history."

The waiting room at the eye clinic had smelled like plastic and cough drops, and Gabrielle had spent twenty minutes memorizing the poster of shrinking letters before the doctor called her name. Now she was in the back seat of the family car, a new case on her lap, and her mother was pulling out of the parking lot. Inside the case were her first glasses, purple frames with tiny stars on the hinges, and she was afraid to put them on with her mother watching in the mirror.

"Go on," her mother said. "The doctor said to wear them."

Gabrielle slid them on, and the world snapped into focus so sharply that she gasped. The stop sign at the corner had letters on it, actual letters, not a red blur with a white smudge. Every leaf on the oak tree was separate. Last week her cousin Dev, who was visiting from Manchester, had said at dinner that he had "6/6 vision," and Gabrielle had panicked on his behalf, because 6 was clearly less than 20, and less meant worse. She had spent two days worrying that Dev's eyes were failing and nobody was doing anything about it. She had even googled "vision numbers" on her dad's phone, but she'd typed it into a shopping site by mistake and gotten pages of binoculars.

She pulled out her phone and texted Lainey, who was in her class: my cousin says he has 6/6 vision. is that bad? Lainey wrote back almost instantly: my cousin from Singapore says the same thing!! i thought it was some kind of propaganda, like a campaign to make everyone memorize numbers. Then Ananya, who must have been in their group chat, added: wait. i think it's the same as 20/20. countries that use metres write it 6/6 instead.

Gabrielle read that twice. Countries that used metres. Dev lived in England, where road signs said metres, and Ananya's cousin lived in Singapore, and both cousins said 6/6. Both of them could see perfectly. The two numbers were the same eyesight, just written differently, depending on the country. She tested the idea in her head: 20/20 in America, 6/6 where they used metres, and nobody's eyes were bad at all. She laughed out loud in the back seat.

"What's funny?" her mother asked.

"Dev's eyes are fine," Gabrielle said. "I worried for nothing."

Her mother smiled and turned onto their street, and Gabrielle looked out the window. With the glasses on, she could read the numbers on the mailbox at the end of the driveway, the one that had always been a pale square. Then she noticed something that made her sit up straight. The mailbox said 6/6. She blinked, certain her new lenses were playing a trick on her, but there it stayed: number 6, slash, number 6.

"Mom," she said, "did we always live at number twelve?"

Isabelle sat at the kitchen table with a pencil, a ruler, and forty minutes before Makenna arrived to walk to the art drop-off with her. The contest deadline was five o'clock, and her drawing of Camp Willow's main road had to be in the box by then. She had sketched the road twice already, and both times it looked like the street was folding in on itself.

The trouble was the lines. Her road edges angled toward the top left corner. Her sidewalk lines slanted toward the top right. The cabin roofs pointed somewhere else entirely, three different destinations, none of them on the paper's horizon. Last summer Mr. Kang, who ran the camp's art shed, had walked past her easel on the main road and paused. "You're missing your vanishing point," he had said, and kept walking. At the time she had been embarrassed, half convinced he was teasing her, and she had said nothing back. Now she wished she had asked him what he meant.

She laid a fresh sheet on the table and looked at her failed drawing again, hunting for a pattern. She drew a light horizontal line across the middle of the page where the sky met the trees, eye level, where she would be standing looking down the road. Then she tried an idea: she took her ruler and extended the road's left edge upward with a faint line, then the right edge, then the sidewalk lines, all of them drawn out until they crossed. If her hunch was right, they would tell her something the drawing itself was hiding.

Every single line met at one spot on the horizontal line, dead center, where the road vanished into the distance. She sat back. The road edges, the sidewalk, the edges of the rooftops, all of them heading to the same point like cars to one exit. That was the vanishing point Mr. Kang had meant, and it sat on the horizon line right at eye level. She checked her second failed drawing, and there the lines pointed three ways because they hadn't been aimed anywhere at all.

"Isabelle, are you ready?" Her mom leaned in the doorway with the kettle. "Makenna will be here in half an hour."

"Almost," Isabelle said, already ruling lines from the vanishing point outward. She built the street fast, edges slanting in from the point, sidewalks narrow near her and wide up close, a cabin that shrank as it backed toward the middle of the page. A big pine at the roadside would obstruct the view of one cabin, so she let its lines fade behind the trunk. She added a mailbox, small but clear.

Makenna arrived early, out of breath, and leaned over the table. "Whoa. That looks like a real street. What kind of genre is this, anyway?"

"It's just a street," Isabelle said, sliding the drawing into the plastic sleeve, the synthetic sleeve crackling as she smoothed it flat. She thought about Mr. Kang walking past her easel that day, whether he had been trying to help and she had thrown the help away. She still wasn't sure. She capped her pen and said, "Come on, let's go."

Raphael pushed his pasta around the plate while his dad asked about school, which was exactly the wrong question. "The robotics club fell apart today," he said. "Gunner swears the competition bot has to be fast, because all he ever saw was the speed trial video. Spencer says it has to lift things, because he watched the lifting demo twice. I know they're both wrong, because I read the whole rulebook." He had spent three evenings on that rulebook. His ambition was to captain the team next year, and captains knew everything.

"So you told them they were wrong," his dad said.

"I told them the rulebook says the robot gets scored on navigation, mostly." Raphael stabbed a meatball. "Gunner said I made that up. Spencer said I only care about looking smart. Ms. Aydín was standing right there and she didn't even settle it. She just smiled and said, 'Interesting.' How is that interesting? It's a disaster."

His little sister, who was seven and annoyingly lucky, spoke with sauce on her chin. "We learned a story today. The blind men and the elephant, from ancient India. Each man touches a different part, one the trunk, one a leg, one an ear, and they all describe it completely differently. Like one says it's a snake and one says it's a tree."

Raphael stopped chewing. He had expected a baby story about sharing, not a picture of his afternoon. Gunner had touched one part of the competition. Spencer had touched another. No wonder they argued. Then a colder thought tried to submerge itself somewhere below his ribs, and he pulled it back up. He had read the rulebook, but the rulebook was a part too. He had never once watched the speed trial video or the lifting demo. He'd skipped them on purpose, because they looked boring.

"Can I be excused?" he asked. His dad raised an eyebrow, and Raphael explained, fast, that he had three phone calls to make before nine. First Gunner, then Spencer, then maybe Ms. Aydín's school email, if he dared.

He made the calls from the hallway, notebook balanced on his knee. Gunner read him the scoring for speed out loud. Spencer recited the lifting rules from memory. Neither matched the navigation points exactly, and all three lists together looked like nothing any one of them had described. "Okay," Raphael said into the phone, feeling cautiously optimistic for the first time since lunch. "New plan. Sunday, my garage, everybody brings their part."

At the club meeting on Monday, Ms. Aydín pinned something to the bulletin board before anyone sat down. It was a printout of an elephant, drawn with six hands reaching toward it from six different sides, and beneath it her handwriting: "Tell me what you each felt. Then build the whole thing." Raphael stared at it, then at her, and realized she had shown each of them a different demo on purpose, back before any of the arguing started. "You did this to us," he said.

She handed him a marker and said, "Board's yours, captain."

Maelie needed an A on Mr. Marino's erosion project, mostly because she had a reputation for turning in posters with glitter instead of evidence. She also needed somewhere to build her model, and the kitchen table was the only surface her mother hadn't claimed for tax paperwork. So on Saturday morning she carried a baking tray, a bag of sand, and a jug of water to the porch steps, where she planned to carve a canyon in under an hour.

It didn't work. The water rushed across the sand in one wide smear and left a shallow scratch that any self-respecting river would be embarrassed by. Her little brother's plastic dinosaurs stood around the edges watching, neutral as judges.

"You're pouring too fast," said Rio, arriving on his bike with a bag of chips he clearly intended to digest while supervising. "Also, you need more sand. And why is there a T-rex?"

"The T-rex is ambience. And I have to show millions of years, Rio. That's the whole assignment." She stared at the smear. A river that moved slowly enough to cut down instead of across might work, but she couldn't exactly wait a geological age on the porch.

Raylan showed up next, drawn by the chips, and stood squinting at the tray like it owed him something. "You should make it go somewhere," he said. He wanted credit on the project, which he mentioned four times in two minutes, since he claimed to know "basically everything about water."

At the bottom of the yard, the gutter drain trickled into the fish pond, and Maelie noticed something at the spot where the trickle met the still water: a small fan of sand, spread out like a tiny yellow triangle. The water slowed there, and the sand it had been carrying settled out, building up a little mound of new land, slowly making the pond smaller. She crouched over it while Rio ate chips and Raylan asked if he could put his name on the poster.

"That's a delta," she said. "Where a river slows down going into a lake or sea, it drops all the sediment it was carrying, and the land builds up."

"Okay," said Raylan, "but what about the canyon part."

She went back to the tray and tried a slow pour from the jug, moving the stream in one thin line so the water stayed in a single channel. The sand lifted, tumbled, and settled downstream in a small spreading fan at the tray's edge. She did it again. The channel deepened. After the tenth pour there was a groove deep enough to hide a dime in, and at the end, unmistakably, a mini delta fanning out onto the flat sand.

"Millions of years," she said, "condensed into one jug of water."

Rio held up the jug. "Half a jug now. Also your T-rex is drowning."

The T-rex was, in fact, face down in the new canyon, legs sticking up. Maelie left him there and labeled him "fossil evidence."

Alicia pressed the knife into the cutting board at Ms. Sato's market stall, where a demo table was set up with a portable burner and a basket of yellow onions. Her problem was simple and urgent: she had signed up to cook dinner for her family on Saturday, and her little brother refused to eat anything with onions in it. Raw onion, he insisted, tasted like a punishment. If she wanted a real pasta sauce, she needed to solve him first.

"Tuck your fingertips under, like a claw," Ms. Sato said, showing the grip. "The knuckles guide the blade, and the fingers stay out of the way."

Alicia curled her fingers and sliced through the onion, half expecting disaster, but the claw grip worked exactly the way it was supposed to. The pieces fell in neat little rows, and all ten fingers remained attached. Jovan, who had wandered over from the honey stall, watched with his arms crossed.

"Onions are gross," he announced. "That's not subjective, either. That's a fact."

"Maybe," Alicia said, thinking it through. The onion pieces on the board were sharp and harsh; she could smell the sting from a foot away. But the sauce Ms. Sato was stirring had been sitting over a low flame for half an hour, and it smelled nothing like that. It smelled almost like caramel. Same vegetable, completely different smell. What could make the difference? Her logic went like this: the raw onion was sharp, and the only thing that had happened to the cooked ones was slow heat over the burner. If the heat was the hidden cause, then cooking the onions slowly changed something about them, and maybe the change went all the way to the taste. It was a guess, but it was one she could test.

She retrieved a small spoon from the dish rack and held it out to Jovan. "Taste that sauce. Just the sauce."

"I'm not falling for that."

"Fine, then watch me." She tasted it herself first, and her eyes widened. The onions in the sauce were soft and sweet, golden brown, nothing like the fierce raw pieces on the board. She held out the spoon again, and this time Jovan sighed and took the smallest possible taste. Then a bigger one.

"Okay," he said slowly. "Okay, that's weirdly good. Can I have more of that?"

"That's the onions you just insulted," Alicia said. She copied down the steps in her notebook: slice with the claw grip, low heat, patience while the pieces turned golden. Saturday's dinner suddenly looked possible. On Saturday she stood in her own kitchen with the burner on low, and when her brother pushed his plate forward and said, "Is there more sauce?", she slid the pan across to him without saying a word.

The paper was folded into eighths in Gabriella's jacket pocket, and every few minutes she took it out again and smoothed it on her knee. In the front seat, her mother drove with both hands on the wheel and the radio off, which was how you could tell this was a serious day. "Read it to me one more time," her mother said at the second red light, so Gabriella unfolded the page and read the box at the bottom, the one with Grandpa's name at the top in bold.

"William Torres, age seventy-nine. He is survived by his daughter Rosa and his granddaughter Gabriella." She paused, because the next part still surprised her. "Before his long career as a high school janitor, he served four years as a sailor." She looked up. "Mom. A sailor. He never said one word about that. Not ever."

"Sixty years, Gabi. People put things away that long ago." Her mother's voice was careful, the way it had been all week, as if she was afraid of dropping something.

Gabriella had a theory, and she tested it the way she tested things, quietly and with evidence. She pulled up the newspaper website on her phone and scrolled through the other notices on the same page, the contemporary ones, printed that very morning. There was a woman who had worked thirty years as a nurse, loved by her three sons and her church choir. There was a man who collected stamps and was survived by his wife of fifty years. Every single box told who the person was to their family, what work they had done, and what they had cared about. That was the whole point of it, she realized. An obituary was a published notice of someone's death, but it was also a short account of a whole life, told in public, whether or not the person had ever told it to you themselves.

She texted Cynthia, because Cynthia's grandmother had died last spring and Cynthia would know. "Did you know your grandma taught piano before the restaurant thing?" The answer came back fast: "NO?? nobody tells us anything." Then Malorie wrote, "It's like there's a secret file on every grandparent and you only get to open it at the end." Gabriella looked at that for a long moment. It felt almost true, and it also felt like the opposite of what she wanted.

"I should have asked him things," she said out loud. "All those Sunday dinners, I just talked about school."

Her mother reached over and squeezed her hand, a small act of compassion that made the next words easier. "He liked your school stories. But Gabi, he had sixty more years than you. You couldn't have anticipated what was in them." Gabriella thought about arguing that she could have tried, then decided the question would stay open, the way a drawer stays half shut.

At the cemetery gates, a man in a navy cap was waiting by the doors, and when her mother hugged him, he said, "Billy's old crew sends this." He held out a folded flag with an anchor stitched in the corner. Gabriella took it in both hands. "Tell me about the ship," she said.

Maria had promised Ms. Krause a working prime-checker by Saturday, which meant she had five days to figure out how a computer could possibly know that 17 was prime and 18 was not. Computers could not look at a number and just see it, the way people did. They had to be told every step, and Maria did not yet know the steps herself. She had claimed the corner computer at the public library, next to the window, with her notebook open to a page that said, in increasingly desperate handwriting, how does it KNOW?

Jet slid into the chair beside her and read the page upside down. "You could just make a list of all the primes and check if the number's on it."

"All of them?"

"Is that a lot?"

Marc-Olivier, who was at the next computer supposedly doing his geography project, turned around. "It's basically all of them, yes."

Maria typed her program anyway, the part she did understand. It asked for a number, stored it in n, and then did nothing useful with it. She stared at the screen. Somewhere in there, the computer would have to try dividing n by smaller numbers and find out whether any division came out even. But division in Python gave her answers like 2.571428571428571, and she did not want to compare a long ugly decimal against every possible even result. That way, she was fairly sure, lay madness.

She tried it with 18 divided by 7, and got 2.5714285714285714. Then she typed 18 divided by 6 and got 3.0, which was better but still awkward. What she wanted was a way to ask a yes-or-no question: did it divide evenly, or not? She scrolled through the notes Ms. Krause had photocopied for the club, and there it was, one line about the % operator. She typed 18 % 6 and the screen said 0. She typed 18 % 7 and the screen said 4.

"Okay," she said slowly. "The percent sign gives you the remainder. So n % d equals zero exactly when d divides n evenly. No remainder, no leftover piece. That's the whole question, answered." Her reasoning felt almost too simple, so she tested it. 20 % 5 was 0. 20 % 3 was 2. 13 % 2 was 1, 13 % 3 was 1, 13 % 4 was 1, and every one of those little leftover 1s was the program saying no, not this one. A prime would get no after no after no, all the way down. It was a pattern you could not see in the number itself, only in its remainders.

She wrote the loop, ran the program, and typed in 17. Prime, said the screen. She typed 18. Not prime. She typed 91, feeling clever, and the screen said not prime, which startled her until she checked and found 7 times 13. "Huh," she said. "It caught me."

Jet leaned over. "So is it done?"

"One more test." Maria typed 2, the smallest prime, and the tiniest edge case she could think of, the one she suspected would be inevitable trouble.

The screen said not prime. Maria put her forehead down on the keyboard for a moment, then sat up and started rereading her loop.

"That," said Marc-Olivier, "is why you test things."

Friday's cast removal had felt inevitable ever since Dr. Patel said the words, and Alexandre had been dreading it for six weeks. He sat at the kitchen table with his encased arm propped on a pillow, watching a video on his mom's tablet for the fourth time. In the video, a cast saw shrieked through fiberglass and spat white dust everywhere. Cynthia arrived carrying a soccer sign-up sheet and her history textbook, because tryouts were Saturday and her project on the French monarchy was due Monday, and she had decided both problems could be solved at Alexandre's kitchen table.

"You're goalie or we don't have a team," she said, sliding the sheet toward him. "So stop watching that and watch this instead." She queued up a different video, one a girl had filmed in a hospital. In it, a boy yanked his arm away as the saw came near, and the nurse laughed kindly and said, "It vibrates back and forth instead of spinning. That's how it cuts the hard plaster and fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath." Alexandre rewound it twice. He had pictured a spinning blade, like a circular saw, and a spinning blade would go through skin the way it went through everything.

"So the blade isn't sharp sharp," Cynthia said slowly. "It just moves really fast sideways." Alexandre got up and fetched his mom's electric toothbrush. He held the humming head against the palm of his good hand and his skin wobbled like pudding, but nothing stung, nothing cut. Then he pressed it against his cast and the hard shell just buzzed. "To illustrate," he said, grabbing Cynthia's forearm and wiggling his fingertips back and forth on it as fast as he could. She laughed. "That tickles. It doesn't hurt at all."

They were still testing when Mr. Ricci knocked, returning the ladder he'd borrowed. When they told him why the toothbrush was out, he held up his own wrist. "Broke this in '09," he said. He went home and came back with a shoebox, and inside, folded open in two halves, sat his old cast, kept for a bet with his brother. Alexandre turned it over. The cut edges were clean through the shell, and the padding inside was untouched. "Never felt a thing," Mr. Ricci said. "Fell asleep once."

On Friday, when the nurse approached with the saw, Alexandre didn't pull away. He held out his arm, and the noise was as awful as the video, but he watched the dust fly and felt only a warm, buzzing tickle while the cast opened like a shell. Through the door, Cynthia held up the sign-up sheet and grinned. "Goalkeeper," she said.

Emilia sat on the low concrete wall at the edge of the skate park, her right arm resting in a cast on her lap, and watched Blake carve back and forth across the shallow bowl. The morning was warm and the ramps smelled like sun-baked dust. She had been coming here every Saturday for a year, and this was the first one she had spent sitting still.

"Your turn," Blake called, rolling to a stop in front of her.
