He started the onions first because the curry was the longest job. They sizzled in the pan, turning golden, and that was exactly when he realized he had no idea where the cumin was. He dug through the spice cupboard while the onions spat and darkened behind him. By the time he found the jar, the onions had turned black at the edges and the kitchen smelled bitter. He scraped them into the compost and stood there staring at the empty pan.

"Why did that happen?" he asked the air. It wasn't that he couldn't cook. It was that he kept stopping to hunt for things. He texted Shae, whose family cooked every night, and she answered fast: "Mise en place. It's a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place.' You prep and measure every ingredient before you start." Max read it twice. He grabbed a marker and wrote a big amendment across his handwritten schedule at the top: PREP EVERYTHING FIRST.

So he did. He measured the rice into a bowl, chopped every onion, measured out the turmeric, cumin, and salt into tiny dishes, mixed the flour and water for the flatbread, and lined everything up along the counter like a parade. Then he sat with his timer and worked the timing backward, which felt like solving a puzzle he couldn't see the answer to until he tested it. The curry needed forty minutes, the rice twenty-five, the flatbread only ten including resting the dough. So the rice would go in when the curry had fifteen minutes left, and the dough would hit the pan last, while everything else bubbled and steamed.

When Sammy arrived early, Max was already sliding the first flatbread onto the hot pan. "You look like a TV chef," Sammy said, watching the little bowls of spices all measured and waiting. Max flipped the flatbread, watched it puff, and moved it to a warm plate without hunting for a single thing.

The timer beeped and Max lifted lids all at once. Fluffy rice, thick curry, golden bread, all steaming together. His mom took one bite, then another, then nodded slowly and reached for the flatbread. "Okay, chef," she said. "When's dinner tomorrow?"

The clock above the whiteboard gave Ava's group exactly eleven minutes, and Ms. Wright had already circled their desk twice like a shark wearing sensible shoes. Their task sat on the handout: take the scene from Romeo and Juliet and rewrite every speech in modern English, then perform it in front of the class. Delaney had turned "Wherefore art thou Romeo" into "Why are you Romeo" without trouble. Maximiliano had managed "do not swear by the moon" easily enough. But now they were stuck, because the next line read "She hath not seen the change of fourteen years," and nobody knew what to do with that word.

"Hath," Maximiliano said, poking it with his pencil as if it might bite. "That's not even a word. That's a typo with confidence."

"It's a word," Delaney said, "it's just an old word. The question is which old word." She looked at Ava, who was supposed to be the group's ideas person since the incident with the volcano poster, when Ava had single-handedly saved their science grade. Ava stared at the line. Hath. She scanned up the page and found "doth" in an earlier speech, then "thou dost," and then, further down, "she doth teach the torches to burn bright." She noticed something: every time the character was he or she, the verb grew that little th on the end. Thou got st. You got nothing. It was a pattern, and patterns, unlike humidity, could be trusted.

"I think it's a grammar thing," Ava said, tapping the page. "He or she verbs end in eth or th. So doth means does." She pointed at the line. "And hath means has. So it's just, she has not seen the change of fourteen years. She's not fourteen yet."

Delaney gasped like Ava had revealed a family secret. "That's it! That's so boring and normal!" Maximiliano wrote "she is not even fourteen" on the paraphrase sheet with a flourish, then leaned his chair back so far that Ava had to grab his sleeve to keep him from tipping over, which would have eroded what little dignity their group had left, since they were already endangered by the two minutes remaining.

"One minute!" Ms. Wright called, and the smell of old paperback pages mixed with the sharp marker scent of the whiteboard as they ran through their lines once, fast, Ava whisper-correcting "hath means has" every time Maximiliano hesitated. When Ms. Wright pointed at them, they stood up in front of the class in their too-warm corner of the classroom by the radiator, and Maximiliano delivered "She is not even fourteen years old, folks" with the gravity of a man announcing his residence had burned down, and someone in the second row actually laughed, which counted as a victory.

After class, Delaney caught Ava at the door. "So tomorrow, when we get the sonnet, you're doing all the weird words."

"Deal," Ava said, "but if there's another volcano, you're carrying the baking soda."

The planetarium projector emitted a slow river of stars across the dome, and Anna slid down in her seat, trying to make her nervousness settle with the dark. In two days she had to give a science talk on how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, and she still could not picture it. Water seemed too soft to cut anything.

"Sit up," whispered Ariel beside her. "Mr. Kang is going to call on people."

He did not call on her, but he did something worse. He walked the aisles while the dome showed the surface of Mars, so desolate that not even a blade of grass broke the red plain, and said that anyone who wanted bonus points could stand after the show and explain a landform of their choice. Anna's hand went up before she had decided anything.

After the lights came back on, she stood in front of the class with her knees shaking and began with the Colorado River. She said that the river carries sand and pebbles, and that the grinding of that sediment against rock wears the channel down, bit by bit, while the water also carries the loose material away and drops it downstream. She had the concept right, she was almost sure, but a hand shot up near the back. Nikki.

"How deep even is a real canyon?" Nikki asked. "Like, deeper than a swimming pool?"

Anna opened her mouth and nothing came out. Then she remembered the number she had read three times on the bus that morning, because she hadn't believed it the first two times. "The Grand Canyon is 277 miles long," she said, "and over a mile deep at its deepest point. That's 446 kilometers." She held her hands a mile apart, which looked ridiculous, and some kids laughed, so she pointed at the floor. "Imagine our school at the bottom, and the mile of rock that used to be above it, all carried off grain by grain."

"Grain by grain for how long?" Nikki asked.

"Millions of years," Anna said. "That's the whole point. A river is slow, but it never stops."

Mr. Kang nodded once, the small nod he saved for answers he liked, and told her well done. Walking out under the afternoon sun, Ariel bumped her shoulder. "You turned red up there."

Anna grinned. "Only for the first mile."

The votes lay in three shoeboxes on the table at the community centre, one for each party in Ms. González's mock parliament. Alicia counted them twice, because the first time the numbers felt wrong. Purple Party, eleven votes. Orange Party, nine. Green Party, six. Twenty-six students had voted, and Ms. González had promised the afternoon would end with a government.

Anabel leaned over the boxes. "Purple wins. They got the most."

"That's first past the post," Alicia said. "Most votes takes everything. But we learned the other way today. Proportional representation. Purple should get about eleven seats out of twenty-six, Orange about nine, Green about six."

Ms. González had written the rules on the whiteboard, then sat in the corner with her tea and refused to say another word. "You figure it out," she had said. "Pretend I'm the Queen. I only sign things."

So Alicia handed out seats, folding paper strips and writing names on them. Anabel, who led Purple, grabbed her eleven strips and marched to the front table. "We're the government. Everyone else is opposition."

"Wait," said Hiba, from the Green Party. "Count your seats. You need thirteen to govern alone. You only have eleven."

Alicia checked the whiteboard. Half of twenty-six was thirteen. Nobody had thirteen. She ran her finger down the seat list again, slower this time, in case the numbers had shifted while she wasn't looking. They hadn't. The room went quiet except for the hum of the radiators.

"Then nobody's the government," Anabel said. "The Queen can't sign anything. We're stuck forever."

Alicia felt something click, the way a pattern does when you finally see it. "Not stuck. It happened the way the numbers said it would. When seats get shared out fairly, one party hardly ever gets more than half the votes, so the parties have to team up. Coalition. That's the word from the worksheet." She kept her voice steady, though her pulse was going fast. "Purple plus anyone gets past thirteen."

Anabel stared at her eleven strips, then at the Orange table. Orange stared back. The whole room waited.

"You'd want the library period extended," Anabel said at last. "We want the bake sale. Those aren't the same thing."

"They could both be in the budget," Hiba offered, slipping over with her six Green seats, agile in the way of someone who had been waiting all afternoon for exactly this moment. "Six seats is small, but it's enough to matter."

The three parties haggled over the paper strips, trading a library period for a bake sale, arguing about who would summarize the new laws for the Queen. When they finally carried their coalition agreement to the corner table, Ms. González read every line, stamped it, and said only, "About time."

Anabel held up the stamped page like a trophy. "Motion carried," she announced, "thirteen to twelve."

Nicolas stood on Ayat's porch holding a box of oranges his dad had bought on his commute home, and he could not remember whether he was supposed to knock or ring or just walk in. His rain jacket had turned out to be porous in the storm, so his sleeves were damp and the cardboard was going soft, which made the whole thing worse. Ayat opened the door before he could decide, and the first thing she said was "Shoes off, that's the rule here." Nicolas looked down at the row of slippers by the door, then at his wet socks, and laughed. "Good thing I wore clean ones," he said, stepping out of his sneakers.

The kitchen smelled like broth and ginger. Ayat's mother was lifting a huge pot of ramen to the table, and her father was telling Nicolas's dad, who had come up behind him, that the family used to run a small noodle shop before the highway moved and took away half their revenue. "Everyone commuted right past us for years," he said, shaking his head. "Now we just cook for friends." He handed Nicolas a deep bowl with chopsticks on the side, and Nicolas noticed something strange right away.

Everyone slurped. Ayat slurped. Her mother slurped, quite loudly, while reading the label on a jar of chili oil. Her father slurped so hard the noodles vanished in one long pull. Nicolas froze with his chopsticks halfway to his mouth. At home he had been told, more than once, that slurping was rude, and he did not want to be rude here either. But he noticed something else too: the more the family slurped, the faster the noodles disappeared, and the noodles were steaming hot. The quiet way he was eating meant each mouthful sat and cooled before he dared swallow it.

He decided to test his idea. He took one strand, breathed in, and slurped. The noodle zipped up cool and perfect, and his mouth filled with broth. Ayat grinned at him across the table. "Better, right?" she said. "Slurping's fine with noodles. It's just how it's done." Nicolas slurped again, louder this time, and Ayat's father raised his glass of tea like he was giving a toast.

When the bowls were empty, Ayat's mother pressed the last orange from the box into Nicolas's hands for the walk home. At the door, Ayat helped him work his damp sneakers back onto the right feet. "Next time bring your brother," she called from the porch as he stepped out into the drizzle, and Nicolas waved the orange at her.

Gabriella had felt fine the day they flew to the beach, and that was the part that confused her. The flight west had taken half a day, and still she had slept like a normal person that first night, and by morning she was digging in the sand before her dad had even found the sunscreen. Now, three days after flying home east, she was still waking at four in the morning and dragging through every afternoon, and on Monday she had to give her science fair talk at 8:15 sharp. Monday was two days away.

She called Martha from the kitchen, phone wedged between ear and shoulder while she assembled a sandwich that was at least nutritious, turkey and tomatoes and whole grain bread. "I don't get it," she said. "Same plane, same length of flight, one direction I'm fine and the other I'm a zombie."

"It's jet lag," Martha said. "My cousin gets it every time they fly to Europe."

"That's the thing," Gabriella said. "I had jet lag going out too, maybe, but it barely bothered me. Coming home it's like being sick." She looked at her notebook, where she had written two columns: OUT, WEST, FINE. HOME, EAST, MISERABLE. If it were just the flying, both trips should feel the same. Something about the direction itself seemed to matter. She had a candidate theory, scrawled at the bottom of the page: east is worse.

She needed evidence, so she tried an experiment on herself. The problem, she reasoned, was that her body still thought it was three hours earlier than the clock claimed, so bedtime felt impossible at nine. On Friday night she skipped screens, closed her curtains, and lay in the dark anyway, even though she wasn't sleepy. It was awful for about an hour. Then she slept until almost seven, the latest she'd managed since landing.

Saturday she called Martha again, then Jameson, who had a suggestion. "Ask Mr. Whitaker," he said. "He flew to Japan once, remember, for that chess thing." Mr. Whitaker lived two houses down, and when she caught him watering his roses he laughed at her question. "Going over, east, I was a wreck for days," he said. "Coming home, west, I was myself by the second morning. Almost unfair, isn't it." He was still talking about his tournament when she left, but she had what she came for. Her two columns matched his story exactly. Flying east was harder to recover from than flying west, and apparently most travelers found the same, which made her feel less like a broken machine and more like a person with a bad travel direction.

Sunday night she went to bed at eight-thirty, early but not crazy. Monday morning her eyes opened at six-fifteen, one click before the alarm, and she lay still for a moment listening to it. She ate her toast standing up, tucked her note cards into her backpack, and ran the talk in her head one last time on the walk to school. "Good morning," she began, out loud, alone on the sidewalk. "My project is about sleep, travel, and a pattern I tested on myself."

Carter slid his story across the table to Sean and waited. The writing club met in Mr. Jung's classroom after school on Thursdays, and today was the day they traded drafts. Carter's story was about two brothers in a rowboat caught in a turbulent storm, arguing about whether to row for shore or ride it out. He had worked on the argument scene for two full nights, and he was proud of it.

Sean read, frowning. Then he read it again. "Wait, who's talking here?" he asked, tapping the page. "The older brother says row for shore, and then something about the oars, and then something about the lightning, and it's all one big lump. I got lost. I thought the little brother said the lightning part, but then he'd be arguing with himself."

Carter leaned over and looked at his own paragraph. There it was, a solid block of speech with quotation marks stacked end to end, the two brothers trading lines without a break. No wonder Sean had evaporated right out of the story, gone like mist off the water. But how was a reader supposed to know who said what? Carter wondered if there was some trick to it, some pattern in real books.

He grabbed a library book from Mr. Jung's shelf, a novel he'd read twice, and flipped to a conversation. There. Every single time a new character opened their mouth, a new paragraph started. He flipped further. Same thing, page after page. "Look at this," Carter said, and Sean bent in. "A new paragraph begins each time a different character starts speaking."

"So that's how you can tell who's talking," Sean said slowly, running his finger down the page. "You don't even need names half the time."

Carter went back to his draft with a pencil. He broke the argument apart, gave each brother his own paragraph, and read it aloud in a low voice to test it. The words sounded like two people now. Sean listened, then grinned, because he'd been pushing all week to get his own story read aloud at the club showcase, and an argument scene this clear might earn him a spot.

Mr. Jung wandered past their table and skimmed the revised pages. He raised his eyebrows at Carter and said, "Much better. Read it to the group."

At the front of the room, Carter took a breath and began, "Row for shore," the older brother shouted.

Joseph had never swept a gravestone before, and he discovered it was harder than it looked. The brush kept skipping over the carved characters of his grandfather's name, so he slowed down and worked the bristles into each groove while his cousins, Kaius and Emmanuel, pulled weeds from the cracks around the base. Their whole family had driven two hours into the hills that morning, and now dozens of other families dotted the hillside too, all of them sweeping, wiping, and setting out food on the stones.

"Emmanuel says it's called Qingming," Kaius said, crouching beside Joseph with a fistful of grass. "Families visit their ancestors' graves, clean them, and leave offerings. It happens every year around April fourth or fifth." Emmanuel, who was thirteen like the rest of them but acted like he was thirty, nodded from behind the stone, where he was scrubbing off a smear of moss.

Joseph tested the bristles against the deepest groove one more time, then sat back on his heels. He had been thinking about something all morning, and this seemed like the moment to try it. Last spring, before Grandfather got sick, Joseph had chosen to stay home and finish a video game instead of going with him to the noodle shop where Grandfather had eaten every Saturday for thirty years. He had told himself there would be other Saturdays. Now he wanted to know if he could still send something, even one way.

"Grandfather always ordered extra chili oil," Joseph said. "The waiter would warn him every single time, and every single time he'd say, 'I know, that's why I ordered it.'" He pulled from his backpack the small jar he had taken from Grandfather's kitchen cupboard, with his mother's permission, plus a stack of paper bowls he had bought at the corner store after school. His idea was simple: if the families on this hill were leaving offerings of food, then maybe a bowl of noodles with chili oil, mixed the way Grandfather liked it, could go on the stone too.

He assembled it right there. The steam fluctuated in the breeze, curling and straightening, curling and straightening, as if the wind couldn't make up its mind. Emmanuel watched with the expression of a scientist observing a radical new experiment, and Kaius said, "That's the first time I've ever been jealous of a gravestone."

Their grandmother came over, and Joseph held his breath. She looked at the bowl, then at the jar, and something in her face shifted. She said, "He'd complain it needed more chili," and knelt down and added another spoonful herself.

By the time they packed up, the afternoon sun had made nearly a full revolution around the hilltop, lighting the far side of the valley. Whether the noodles reached anyone, Joseph couldn't know, and he decided he didn't need to. He picked up the empty jar to bring home, and Kaius asked, "Same time next April?"

"Same time," Joseph said. "But I'm bringing two jars."

Luke carried the cardboard carrier out of the shelter with both hands, feeling the small weight shift inside it every few steps. His new rabbit, whom he had already named Clover, nosed at the air holes in the corner. The shelter worker had put a folder of care papers in his backpack, and Luke had read the feeding page twice on the bus so he would not forget anything by the time he got home.

He cut through Hollow Creek Park because the path ran parallel to the fence along the creek, and Clover seemed calmer when the carrier swayed gently instead of jostling on the sidewalk. Near the fountain he ran into Kaila, who crouched down to peek through the air holes. "A rabbit," she said. "Nice. I confess I thought your first pet would be something loud, like a parrot."

Before Luke could answer, a small brown terrier trotted out from under a bench, muddy and shivering, with no collar at all. It circled them once and then sat at Kaila's feet as if it had been waiting there all afternoon. "It's lost," Kaila said. "Somebody has to be looking for it." Luke looked around the park, at the empty benches and the far-off swing set, and thought about how the dog could not tell them anything. No tag meant no name, no address, nothing.

Then he remembered a poster by the shelter door. "Dogs get microchips," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "My cousin's dog had one. It's about the size of a grain of rice, and it holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details." Kaila stood up. "Mr. Esposito," she said. "He volunteers at the shelter on weekends, and he walks in this park every day at four." It was ten past four.

They found Mr. Esposito by the duck pond, and he had a scanner with him, a small box like a remote control. He waved it over the terrier's shoulders, and a number appeared on the little screen. "There we go," he said, and tapped the number into his phone. While they waited, Luke set the carrier down on the grass and let Clover sniff a dandelion leaf through the holes, declaring a brief truce between his worry for the terrier and his excitement about his own new pet.

A woman came running across the soccer field before the dandelion leaf was finished, calling a name that made the terrier's ears shoot up. The dog sprang into her arms, tail whirling, and she thanked them three times and shook everyone's hand, even Luke's, who was still holding the carrier. "You did exactly the right thing," Mr. Esposito told him, pocketing the scanner. Luke picked up the carrier and walked home along the creek, and through the air holes he could hear Clover crunching the last of the leaf.

Asher wanted his portrait of the school librarian to look real, the way the ones in the museum catalogue did, with cheeks that had shadow and warmth instead of one flat colour. Ms. Hoffmann had written one word on the board at the start of art club: glazing. She refused to say more. "You'll figure it out," she said, and went to help Brynley unstick a jammed paint tube.

He had painted a pale wash of peach over the whole face and let it dry while he sketched the eyes. Then he mixed a thin rosy wash for the shadow under the cheekbone. Annika leaned over from the next table. "Are you sure it's dry?" she asked.

Asher touched the corner of the paper with his fingertip. It felt dry at the edge, cool and smooth, and he decided the middle must be dry too. He brushed the rose wash across the cheek. The moment the brush touched, the peach underneath bloomed up into it, swirling like ink dropped in water, and the cheek turned a muddy brown-grey blob. His abrupt stroke had dragged the damp layer into the new one, and now nothing was where he had put it.

Annika winced. "That happened to my apple on Tuesday. I painted the highlight over red that was still wet underneath and it all ran together."

"So the surface can feel dry but be wet below," Asher said slowly. He looked at the ruined cheek, then at Ms. Hoffmann's word on the board. He tried the idea out loud. "Glazing. Maybe glazing means brushing a thin transparent wash over a layer that's completely dry, so the colours mix in your eye instead of on the paper." Annika tilted her head, and Brynley abandoned her paint tube to listen.

"Mix in your eye," Brynley repeated. "Like the purple you get when you hold blue film over red film?"

Asher nodded. His impatience had been the real adversary, not the paint. He fetched a hair dryer from the supply shelf and, since Brynley's portrait needed the same treatment, they collaborated, aiming the warm air at each other's papers in turns while the clock ticked toward the end of club. When his page finally felt dry all the way through, dry as toast, he loaded the thinnest possible wash of rose.

The brush glided over the cheek without a single bloom. Underneath, the peach showed through the transparent rose, and where the two overlapped the shadow looked warm and alive. Annika leaned in close to his paper and said, "It's like the colours are stacked instead of stirred."

The new house smelled like paint and cardboard, and Owen stood alone in the middle of his empty bedroom, holding the last box from the truck. In it he found his dad's old college books, which must have gotten mixed in with his stuff. One was thick and boring looking until a folded page fell out. On it, a paragraph was underlined in pencil. It said that in 1950, Leon Festinger and his colleagues studied a student housing complex at MIT, and found that the residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them. Owen read it twice. His dad had drawn a little arrow in the margin beside it, pointing at the word "closest."

Owen carried the book downstairs, where his mom was taping box flaps in the kitchen. "Did you underline this?" he asked. She squinted at the page and laughed. "That's from my first year at college. I marked it because I'd made friends with the girl across the hall and nobody else." She went back to her tape. Owen stood there thinking. His two best friends back home, Mckinley and Joy, had lived one street over and two streets over. He had never noticed that before. The concept seemed almost too simple, but the book said a whole complex full of MIT students had proved it.

So he tested it. He went out the front door and looked at the house directly next door, the one with the moving van still parked outside it too. Whoever lived there was also brand new, which felt like cheating on the experiment somehow, but closest was closest. He knocked, his heart doing something acute and jumpy in his chest. A boy about his age opened the door, still holding a rolled-up poster of a soccer player. "You live next door?" the boy said. "I'm Sanjay." Owen said his name and, feeling awkward, held up the thick book like it could portray a reason for the visit. "My dad's book says people usually become friends with whoever lives closest," he said. "So I figured I should knock on your door before anyone else's."

Sanjay considered this. "That's weird," he said. "But my mom said the same thing yesterday. She picked this house partly because the school's a two-minute walk." He looked back over his shoulder at a wall of boxes. "Want to see my room? It's the one with the best window."

They spent the afternoon unpacking Sanjay's shelf of games and arguing about which one to play first. Owen learned that Sanjay had moved three times already and had a system: he always found the nearest kid before the first week was over, because after that everyone already had plans. "Does the book say anything about a time limit?" Sanjay asked. Owen checked. It did not, which meant they would have to figure that part out themselves. That felt okay. In fact, it felt like the beginning of something. Sanjay tossed him a controller and pointed at the second spot on the couch. "That one's yours," he said. "It's the closest one."

Benjamin had one goal on Saturday: post the photo of his catapult launching a marshmallow across the kitchen before Hank could claim the idea was his. He sat at the computer, opened the app, and hovered over the button. His account was set to private. Only followers could see his posts, and he knew every follower on his list, more or less. He clicked post and went to get a snack.

By the time he came back, a stranger had commented. The account was called marshmallow_fan_2009, and it had written, "Nice catapult. Does your mom know about the ceiling stain?" Benjamin stared at the screen. His mom definitely did not know about the ceiling stain. He checked the photo again. The stain was barely visible in the corner, behind the fridge, which meant somebody had looked closely, and somebody was not on his follower list, because the account was private, or at least it was supposed to be.

He opened his follower list and went through it like a detective, or like a kid with homework avoidance skills, which amounted to the same concentration. There was Mario, his best friend since kindergarten. There was his cousin. There was Ms. Kaur, his neighbour, who followed everyone on the street so she could see whose gardens won prizes. And there was a kid named Dylan from summer camp two years ago, whom Benjamin had accepted because it seemed rude not to. Dylan had never once commented. Suspicious.

Benjamin messaged Mario first. "Did you share my catapult post?" Mario replied with a photo of himself shrugging so hard his shoulders were in the frame. Not Mario, then. Benjamin tested his theory another way. He posted a picture of his left shoe with the caption "Top secret test post." Fourteen minutes later, marshmallow_fan_2009 commented, "Size five. Nice laces." Only followers could see it, and one of those followers had to be passing things along. He wrote to Dylan: "Hey, did you share my posts with anybody?" The typing dots appeared, disappeared, appeared again, and then Dylan's whole account vanished from his follower list, which was its own kind of confession.

Benjamin sat back. He had learned two things. First, setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see. He had assumed private meant sealed, like a vault, and it turned out it was more like a club with a talkative member. Second, marshmallow_fan_2009 knew too much, and he did not intend to abandon the mystery there. He was already drafting a new post for tomorrow: a photo of a blank wall, captioned "The marshmallow was here." If the stranger commented on that, the wall, at least, could keep a secret.

From the kitchen, his mom called, "Whose marshmallow is stuck to my ceiling?"

"Controversial question," Benjamin shouted back, and closed the laptop.

Xavier spread three recipe cards on the kitchen counter like playing cards: rice, curry, flatbread. Lionel and Lauralie were arriving at seven o'clock sharp, and his mother had left for her shift with one instruction, spoken through the car window: dinner has to be on the table when you promised it. He checked the clock. Four forty-five. Plenty of time, he thought, and slid the curry pot onto the stove first because curry sounded like the main event.

By five thirty the curry was bubbling, and it needed forty more minutes. Then he read the rice card properly and felt his stomach drop. Rice, thirty-five minutes. Flatbread, twenty minutes to mix and cook, plus forty minutes for the dough to rest. He grabbed a pencil and started doing the math out loud. "If I work forward, I'll finish the curry at six ten, the rice whenever, and the bread who knows when. That's all wrong." He stared at the clock, wondering if there was a rule hiding underneath all these numbers.

Then it clicked, the way a puzzle piece clicks. "Start with the one that takes longest," he said slowly, "and plan backward from the time you want to eat." He wrote 7:00 at the top of a page and worked downward. Flatbread dough needed to rest starting at six, rice on the stove by five twenty-five, curry, already going, could sit and wait once it was done. His whole schedule rearranged itself in his head like runners moving into parallel lanes, each dish with its own track toward seven o'clock.

He mixed the flatbread dough and set it to rest, then started the rice at exactly five twenty-five. But when he glanced at the dough bowl, a cold feeling hit him. The dough had shrunk slightly, sagging in the middle. Had it failed? His reflex was to panic and throw it out, but instead he poked it with a finger. It sprang back. Whatever had happened, the dough was still alive and working. Maybe, he thought, that's exactly what resting dough is supposed to do. He decided to trust it and kept going.

At six fifty, the doorbell rang. Lauralie burst in first, nose in the air. "Something smells amazing. Is that curry?" Lionel followed, holding a bag of mango chutney like a trophy. "You actually cooked all this yourself?" "Mostly myself," Xavier admitted, and told them about his schedule, the pencil marks still visible on the page by the stove. Lauralie picked it up. "You wrote the ending first," she said. "Seven o'clock, and then everything backward from there. That's clever."

The rice was perfectly timed, the curry hot, and the flatbread came off the pan in blistered golden rounds just as the clock touched seven. Xavier set the last one on the plate and stood back. "Dinner," he announced, "is exactly on time." Lionel reached for a flatbread and grinned. "Then what are we waiting for?"

Ariana taped the agenda to the side of the slide tower at 3:45, right where everyone would see it when they climbed the playground steps. The Skate Spot Club had nine members, and today's meeting was supposed to decide how to spend the fifty dollars they'd earned washing cars. She had written three items on the agenda in her neatest print: new grip tape, a repair kit, and the ramp fund. Her mother had reminded her that morning to enforce the order of the list so nobody's topic got skipped, and Ariana intended to do exactly that.

Only Corey and Brooks had arrived by four o'clock, both of them still holding their boards. It seemed logical to start anyway, since the two of them wanted the same thing she did, the repair kit. "All in favor?" she asked, and three hands went up. She wrote the result in her notebook and was underlining it when Brooks squinted at the page.

"Hold on," he said. "Where's everyone else? Marcy texted me she'd be late because her little brother has a doctor thing about the cartilage in his knee, and the others are coming from detention."

Before Ariana could answer, three more members stomped up the wood chips, and a girl named only in Ariana's mind as the loudest one pointed at the notebook. "You voted without us? That doesn't count. You can't just decide with half the club gone."

Ariana's face went hot, but instead of arguing, she turned back a page in her notebook. At the last meeting, Mr. Campbell, the neighbor who let them use his garage for storage, had watched them argue for twenty minutes about nothing and then said, "Look up quorum, kids. It'll save you some grief." She had looked it up, and the word was sitting right there in her notes: a quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the group's decisions to count. She checked the club rules they'd written in September. Nine members, quorum of five.

"We didn't have a quorum," she said, crossing out the vote. "Only three of us were here. The decision doesn't count."

The loudest one, whose name was actually just what everyone called her because she was always first to speak, folded her arms anyway. "How do we know that's real and not something you made up to redo the vote?"

"Read it yourself." Ariana handed her the notebook and the rules sheet, then climbed two steps up the slide tower so the rest of them could gather below. "Next time we start with a head count. Five or more, we vote. Under five, we talk but we wait. That's fair, isn't it?"

Corey, who had been quiet the whole time, raised his hand. "Can I add something to the agenda? Marcy's brother's knee is why she's late, and the ramp fund money could go toward, like, pads and stuff for people who don't have any."

Ariana wrote it under item three, in the exact spot where it would come up after the repairs. When Marcy finally arrived, breathless with her helmet still on, five more members were counted, the quorum was met, and the vote happened again with everybody's hand in the air.

"Repair kit," Ariana announced, "and four dollars left over to start the pad fund." Corey grinned and slid down the slide, and Marcy raced him to the swings.

Maelie had been in band for three weeks, and the trumpet still made no sense to her. Three valves. Seven fingerings she was supposed to know. But every time she played a C and then a D, something went wrong, and Mr. Mwangi would stop the whole group and ask her to check her fingering again.

After class she stayed behind while Issac packed his trombone and Giuseppe snapped his clarinet case shut. The old trumpet she was borrowing sat on the stand, dented and dull, the one Giuseppe called "the Emperor" because it had belonged to some player who never missed a note, according to legend anyway.

"How do three buttons make all those notes?" she asked.

Issac shrugged. "You just memorize them."

That answer annoyed her. She set the Emperor on her lap and pressed the second valve down, then the first, one at a time, blowing a soft note each time. The second valve made the note a little lower. The first valve made it lower still. She tried pressing the second valve and, right before she blew, pulled its little slide out a few centimetres, like a drawer opening. The note sank even further than before.

"Giuseppe, come listen." She played the note with the slide pushed in, then with it pulled out. "Does the second one sound lower?"

"Way lower," Giuseppe said.

"So pressing a valve isn't magic. The valve just shoves the air down an extra loop of tubing. Longer tube, lower note. And if I pull the slide out, the loop gets even longer." It was the most logical thing she had found all month. If a note was too high, she might be able to salvage it with her slide instead of lipping it down the way Mr. Mwangi kept telling her to.

She tried her C again. It had been sharp all week. She pulled the main tuning slide out a tiny bit, blew, listened, pulled it a little more. On the third try the needle on Issac's tuner app sat dead centre. Her C was finally in tune, and she hadn't changed her lips at all.

Then Issac leaned over and squinted into the bell. "Maelie. Somebody already cranked that slide way out before you. Like, way out. Whoever had the Emperor last was tuning it for a freezing cold room, or they had no idea what they were doing."

Maelie pulled the slide the rest of the way out, turned it over, and found a strip of masking tape with faded writing along the side: DO NOT TOUCH, E.M.

"Who's E.M.?" she asked.

Giuseppe went quiet for a second. "Mr. Mwangi's initials are Elliot Mwangi."

She looked at the tape, then at the door Mr. Mwangi had just walked out of. "Then he's the one who couldn't tune a trumpet."

Issac said, "Play the C again. Right now. Before he comes back."

Gabrielle stood on a chair in the community hall, draping a paper chain along the stage, when her little cousin marched up holding a menorah he had built out of clay and birthday candles.

"Count my candles," he demanded. "I made it perfect."

She counted. One, two, three, all the way to eight. "That's the eight nights," she said. Something tickled the back of her mind, though. Every menorah she had ever seen at their synagogue had one more candle than that, sitting higher or off to the side, like a supervisor. Why would her cousin's look different?

Before she could puzzle it out, the hall doors banged open and Samuelle came in with a foil pan of her mother's latkes. Samuelle had never been to a Hanukkah party before, and she wandered the room like it was a museum, squinting at the dreidels and the sufganiyot dusted with powdered sugar. Then she stopped in front of the big silver menorah on the long table.

"Wait," Samuelle said. "Hanukkah is eight nights, right? So why does that thing have nine candles?"

"That's the question of the evening," Gabrielle said. "My cousin built one with eight and now I'm suspicious of both of them." She lifted the silver menorah down and set it on the table between them. "There has to be a reason. Things in traditions usually have reasons, even weird ones."

She counted the branches out loud, tapping each one with a fingernail. Eight of them stood in a neat row, all the same height. The ninth sat apart, raised above the others like it had won a trophy. Gabrielle turned the menorah slowly, looking at it from every angle, wondering what that odd candle did all by itself. Then she noticed the wax drips. The eight lower cups were clean, barely used. The tall one was caked with old wax, burned down again and again.

"It lights the others," she said slowly. "It's the only one that gets used every single night, so it's the only one that's a mess. The other eight just hold the candles for each night."

Just then the rabbi's wife walked by, balancing a tray of candles, and Gabrielle caught her sleeve. "The tall one, the helper candle, is there a name for it?"

"The shamash," the woman said, and moved on toward the kitchen.

Samuelle tried it out. "Shamash." She grinned. "So the ninth candle is basically the employee of the month."

"The very obstinate employee," Gabrielle said. "It works every night and never gets a night off." She turned to her cousin, who was guarding his clay creation under the treat table like a dragon. "Your menorah needs a ninth branch," she told him. "For the shamash."

"No," he said, arms crossed. "Eight is perfect. Eight nights, eight candles. We made a treaty and I shook on it with myself."

Gabrielle devised a plan on the spot. She traded him a jelly donut for one birthday candle and a lump of his leftover clay, then stood back while he jammed a wobbly ninth candle onto the roof of his creation, higher than all the rest, exactly where a helper belonged.

"There," she said, and lit it first.

Ella found out about the beep test on Monday, when Ms. Kaminski taped a sheet to the gym door listing what Thursday's tryouts would include. Kye read it over her shoulder and groaned. "Not the beep test," he said. "I failed that in thirty seconds last year."

That night Ella called Sloan, who had made the team the year before. Sloan had gone straight to the point. "You run back and forth between two markers, twenty meters apart," she said, "and the beeps come faster at each new level." Then she hung up because her mom was calling her to dinner. Ella sat on her bed turning it over in her head. Last year she had watched Kye sprint the first lengths like a rabbit and then die out by level four. Maybe the problem wasn't speed at all. Maybe it was the pacing. If the beeps sped up, then running flat out early would leave nothing for later, like blowing all your allowance on Monday.

So she devised a plan and wrote it on the back of a cereal box: do not get to the marker early. Get there just before the beep, turn, and go again. Tuesday after school she set out two buckets in the backyard, twenty meters apart, which took some measuring with a tape from the garage and a lot of walking back and forth. Her little brother watched from the porch and offered to honk a bike horn at random, which Ella declined. She used a timer app instead, set to beep at intervals she made shorter as she went. She kept her pace so even it almost felt slow. When the beeps got faster, she let herself speed up, little by little, saving something in her legs.

On Wednesday she did it again, and this time when the clock on the kitchen wall showed the minute hand had made nearly a whole revolution, she was still running. Her legs burned, but she noticed something else too: the intervals she had guessed for the later levels were close to the real ones, because she was still arriving just before each beep instead of long before or long after.

Thursday at tryouts, the gym smelled like floor wax. When the beeps started, Kye shot off the line like it was a sprint race, and by level three he was bent over with his hands on his knees. Ella held back, crossed each line a heartbeat ahead of the sound, turned, and went again. Level five. Level six. The beeps closed in like a tightening net, and she rose to meet them each time.

When she finally missed two in a row, Ms. Kaminski clicked her stopwatch and looked down at her clipboard, then back at Ella. "Level seven," she said. "Same as Sloan last year." Ella walked to the wall, slid down it, and grinned at Kye. "Next time," she panted, "run with me."

The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Anthony's worksheet had one blank line left: Explain one right from Canada's Charter of Rights and Freedoms in your own words. He had written "freedom of expression" at the top, and then nothing, because every time he tried to put it in his own words the sentence fell apart like wet sand.

"You're staring at that line like it insulted you," Lya said, peering over his shoulder in the hallway outside courtroom four.

"It's the 'in your own words' part. Ms. Wong said we can't just copy the Charter. But the Charter already used up all the good words."

Lya sat down on the bench beside him. "My cousins live in Germany, and they showed me their constitution when I visited. It's called the Basic Law, and it's been their constitution since 1949. Guess what Article 1 says. 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'"

Anthony looked up. "Inviolable?"

"Their whole constitution starts with dignity. Ours starts with rights and freedoms." She tapped his worksheet. "Different doors into the same house, maybe."

Ethan slumped onto the bench on Anthony's other side. "This assignment is impossible. There's no right answer, so there's no way to know if you're right." He said it like the day was already ruined, which was how he said most things.

Anthony didn't answer right away. He was thinking about the German line, how a whole country had decided the first thing worth writing down was that nobody could trample a person's dignity. Maybe the trick wasn't to find fancy words. Maybe it was to say what the right actually did. He tested it out, quietly, on the blank line: Expression means you can say what you think, and the government can't shut the valve on it just because it opposes you.

"That's it?" Ethan said, reading it upside down. "That's your answer? It's so... plain."

"That's the point, maybe."

Ms. Wong called them into the courtroom, where a lawyer was waiting to answer questions. When it was Anthony's turn, he read his sentence out loud, and the lawyer said, "That's as good a summary as I've heard. Plain is what the law is supposed to be."

Ethan pulled out his worksheet, crossed out nothing, but kept writing. Anthony watched him fill three lines, then four, then tug Lya's sleeve. "Hey, tell me the German one again. About dignity."

Lya leaned over and whispered it, word by word.

Sebastian stood at the gate of the nature reserve with his mandatory field trip form crushed in his fist, but he was not thinking about the form. He was thinking about the painting he had glimpsed through the window of the old museum barn, because the class was headed there next. In the painting, a dog covered in black spots sat beside a shining red fire engine, and Sebastian could not stop wondering why.

"How can there be a fire station thing out here?" Jamie asked as they walked the gravel path. "This is a nature reserve. There are herons."

"Maybe the barn is older than the reserve," Sebastian said. "Ms. Sok said the land used to belong to a village." That would make sense, he thought. Old places keep old things.

Inside the barn, the engine sat under a layer of dust, and beside it a wooden carriage with tall spoked wheels and long poles where two horses would have stood. Gael pointed at the painting. "Why would they hang a picture of a spotted dog next to an old fire engine? That's the anomaly here. Nothing else in this barn is about dogs."

"Firehouse dog," said the ranger quietly, already moving on toward the paddock. Sebastian did not get more than that, and it bugged him all through the nature walk. A firehouse dog. But why spots? Why a dog at all? He turned it over while the class counted frogs in the marsh, and one detail kept snagging on his mind: the carriage had no motor. The poles meant horses.

At the paddock, two heavy draft horses dozed in the sun. The ranger's own dog, an actual Dalmatian named Pongo, trotted over from the shed, and Sebastian watched closely. He expected the horses to shy, the way they sometimes did at the class's loud voices. Instead both horses lowered their heads toward Pongo, ears soft, and Pongo leaned against a gray shoulder like they were old friends.

That was his clue. "They get along," Sebastian said. "The dog and the horses. Ms. Sok, can I test something?" She nodded, so he asked the ranger if he could walk Pongo along the fence. The dog trotted ahead of him, and when Sebastian stopped, Pongo kept going, running up the path in front of him, turning to check that he followed, clearing the way the way a guide does. Behind him Sebastian heard the horses whinny and pace the fence, wanting to come along.

"So maybe that's it," Sebastian said, half to himself, half to Jamie and Gael, who had followed. "The engines didn't always have motors. Fire carriages were pulled by horses, and the dog got along well with horses and ran ahead, helping clear the way. That's why firehouses wanted spotted dogs." He said it out loud because saying it made the pieces fit, and the painting in the barn suddenly made sense too.

"Prove it," Gael said, grinning. So Sebastian retrieved Pongo's lead rope from the hook by the shed, clipped it on, and walked toward the old carriage barn with the dog trotting out in front of him, exactly like in the painting.

"Look," Sebastian said, pointing at the canvas. "The dog's out front, ahead of the horses. It was always out front."

Jamie leaned closer to the painted wheels and whispered, "I'm never calling a firehouse dog weird again."

Victor stood at the stainless steel counter in Ms. Virtanen's cooking class, staring down an onion like it owed him money. Chopping was mandatory this unit, and the sauce they were making had to be from scratch, no jars, no shortcuts. He curled his fingers into the claw grip the way the diagram on the wall showed, knuckles forward like a boxer's fists, and pressed the knife down. The blade squashed the onion half instead of slicing it. He leaned harder, and the knife slid sideways with a squeak and nearly skated off the cutting board.

Spencer, one station over, watched the whole thing. "You're going to lose a thumb," he said, dicing his own onion in quick, easy strokes.

"My knife is broken," Victor said, holding it up. The edge looked fine, but something about it felt wrong, like a spoon wearing a knife costume.

Ms. Virtanen passed by, glanced at his mangled onion, and swapped his blade for a different one from the rack without a word. Victor set the new knife on the onion, barely pushed, and it sank clean through. A perfect little dice fell away. He blinked. Same hand, same claw grip, completely different result. What had changed? He looked at the two knives, turning them over, wondering if his eyes were missing something they should be able to see.

It reminded him of last summer, when he'd tried to cut a tomato at home with the old knife from the back of the drawer. He'd pushed and pushed, and the blade had skidded right off the slippery skin and jabbed the counter. His dad had handed him the sharp one, and the tomato had opened like it wanted to. Victor had thought at the time that he'd just been clumsy. Now he wondered if the knife itself had been the problem all along. He tested it: with the sharp knife he used almost no pressure, and nothing slipped. With his old one, he'd had to shove, and the shoving was what sent it sliding. A sharp knife is safer, he realized, because it needs less pressure, so it's less likely to slip off the food.

"Dude," Victor said to Spencer, waving the sharp knife like evidence at a trial. "A sharp one is actually the safe one. It doesn't slip because you don't have to push."

"Congratulations," Spencer said. "Now prioritize the sauce before we run out of class time."

The onion hit the hot oil with a hiss, and Victor leaned in to watch it turn glassy and gold.

Jace set the sheet music on the piano stand and read the note taped to the top of the page again. It was from his friend Mahdi, written in his terrible handwriting: "Mr. Whitehead says if we crash at the recital tomorrow because you play the middle part too fast, I will personally hide your sneakers in the gym ceiling. Practice slow. Andante exists for a reason."

The problem was that Jace did not know what andante meant. He knew largo and allegro too, the strange words printed above the staff like tiny road signs, but none of them came with translations. He had guessed before, in band class, that andante meant fast, because the word looked like "athletic." The middle section of the piece had collapsed into a pile of clashing notes, and Bodie, who played trumpet, had leaned over and whispered, "Bro, you just endangered the whole song." That was yesterday. The recital was tomorrow at four o'clock, which gave Jace one evening to figure it out.

He tried an experiment. He set his phone on the piano with a metronome app open and played the largo section first, as slowly as he could stand, letting the chords stretch out like taffy. Slow actually felt right for the opening, grand and heavy. Then he reached the word allegro and pushed the tempo up, quick and bouncy, and the melody came alive. He inhaled, held his breath, and started the andante section at the same fast speed. Within four measures his hands tangled and he lost his place entirely, exactly like in class.

So andante was not fast. That much was clear from the wreckage. He texted Mahdi, and the reply came fast: "my sister says largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively. she says you're welcome. she also says who is the protagonist of that piece, you or the metronome?" Jace laughed out loud in the empty living room. Walking pace. Not a stroll, not a sprint, just walking.

He tried it, tapping his foot like footsteps on a sidewalk, and the middle section finally made sense. The melody had room to breathe between the slow beginning and the flying end. He played the whole piece through three times, and on the third time he only stumbled once, at the page turn.

At nine o'clock he texted Mahdi a photo of the music with all three words circled. The answer came back in seconds: "good. your sneakers are safe for now. see you at four, walking pace."

Landon spread his notebook across the kitchen table and drew a fat parrot beak, a thin warbler beak and a crushing ground finch beak, one above the other. His little sister pulled her chair up beside him because whenever Landon drew anything, she wanted to see it.

"These are finches," he said. "Same birds, different islands. Some islands have big hard seeds, and the birds there have thick strong beaks. On islands with small soft insects, the beaks are thin." He tapped his pencil on the page. "Look how each beak shape corresponds to the food on its island. Like a key matching its lock."

"Why don't the thin-beak birds just move?" she asked.

That was actually a good question, and Landon had to think about it. Ms. Bianchi had made the class memorize three things that all had to be true before you could call something natural selection, and tomorrow there was a quiz. "They don't exactly choose," he said slowly. "Here, help me check." He wrote three boxes. "First, do the birds vary? Do some have thicker beaks than others, even on the same island?"

"Like I'm taller than my friend even though we're the same age," his sister said.

"Right, exactly." He checked the first box. "Second, are beak shapes inherited? Do thick-beaked parents have thick-beaked chicks?"

"The baby birds look like their parents. I've seen that."

He checked the second box and hesitated on the third. He almost wrote it down, then stopped. Maybe he should test it instead of just saying it. He grabbed a handful of dried beans and a handful of rice from the cupboard and put them in two bowls. "Use only these tweezers and pick up beans for thirty seconds. Then use the spoon." His sister clicked the tweezers and got three beans; with the spoon she scooped nineteen. "So on a bean island," Landon said, "the spoon birds survive better and have more chicks. On a rice island, the tweezers win."

"That's the third thing," his sister said. "Some beaks help them survive and have more babies than others."

Landon checked the last box and sat back. All three. Only when all three were true did it count as natural selection, and now he could see why, because if the beaks weren't inherited, or if nothing survived better, nothing would change over time. He copied his three boxes onto a clean page so he could redraw them from memory later.

Their father came through the kitchen, looked at the beans and rice scattered across the table, and raised one eyebrow. "You two are negotiating a peace treaty with the pantry?"

"No," Landon said, grinning. "We're being diplomats between a bean island and a rice island." His sister laughed so hard she knocked over the bean bowl, and the beans rolled everywhere, dormant little seeds waiting for an island that would never come. Landon chased the last one under the toaster and added one more drawing to his page: a spoon-shaped beak.

Jackson taped the two news stories side by side on Ms. Oliveira's classroom door and waited for her with his arms folded. The bell hadn't rung yet, and the hallway smelled like wet snow from everyone's boots.

"Two papers, one poll," he said when she arrived. "This one says the team's free throws went from 40 percent to 50 percent, a rise of 10 points. This one says the same thing, same numbers, but it calls it a 25 percent increase. Ten and twenty-five. Somebody's lying."

Ms. Oliveira read both clippings, then handed them back. "That's a real puzzle, Jackson. But I don't think either reporter made it up. You're welcome to figure it out."

He tried the obvious explanation first: maybe the poll was different, or one paper made a rounding error. He checked the dates, the team name, and every number he could find. Both stories matched exactly. If neither story was wrong, he thought, then both numbers had to be true at once, which felt impossible, like two answers orbiting the same question.

At lunch he dragged his clippings to the corner table where Christine was stacking her tray. "Read these. Tell me I'm not crazy."

She read them twice. "They're both saying the same thing."

"But ten isn't twenty-five," Jackson said. He grabbed a napkin and wrote it out. "Forty to fifty." Christine frowned at the napkin like it might be hiding something.

That afternoon in the gym, the coach had them shoot twenty free throws each, and Jackson counted his makes on his fingers like money. When he missed his last five, Allison laughed from the foul line. "You're plague-level bad today."

"Say that again," Jackson said slowly, an idea turning over in his mind. He walked to the bench and did the arithmetic twice, then a third time, because the first two times it seemed too strange to trust. Then he ran back across the gym floor.

"Ten points and twenty-five percent," he told Christine after practice, holding up his wrinkled napkin. "Same change. Forty to fifty. Two ways of saying it. It sounds like a lie, but it's true." He smoothed the napkin on the bleachers between them.

Christine looked at it, then at him. "So both reporters were right?"

"Both right," Jackson said, and folded the napkin into his pocket like a ticket he'd won.

On Thursday, German class got a new assignment, and Nora copied it into her notebook with a sinking feeling: describe your family and pets in five full sentences, due Monday. She could handle "Ich habe einen Hund" and "Meine Mutter ist freundlich," but five whole sentences felt like a mountain. Mr. Henry had said the trick was not translating English word by word, and Nora wondered what that meant. German had to have its own shortcuts, didn't it? She wanted to find one.

She cornered Mathias at lunch, because Mathias had three brothers and a sister and had been complaining about the same assignment all morning. "I'm going to be writing forever," he groaned, stabbing his fork into his pasta. "Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe eine Schwester. My hand is going to fall off." Nora slid her notebook across the table. What if the language had a shorter path, some formula like the ones in math, where a big thing collapses into one tidy expression? She underlined his four sentences and stared at them, tapping her pencil. Four sentences about siblings. There had to be a way to say it once.

After school they found Mr. Henry loading boxes into his car, and Nora asked him straight out. "Is there one word for brothers and sisters together? Like, all of them at once?" He smiled and shut the trunk. "Geschwister," he said, and spelled it for them. Then he drove off, leaving them standing in the parking lot with the word hanging in the air. Nora wrote it down three times so she wouldn't lose it. So German used Geschwister the way English used siblings, one word covering everyone, and that fact changed the whole shape of her homework. She could describe the relationships in a single stroke and spend her energy on the rest.

The catch was the grammar. Geschwister looked plural to Nora, so she tried "Ich habe vier Geschwister" and then hesitated, because what if the verb changed, or what if it needed different articles than she expected? Getting it wrong in front of the class on Monday would make her feel exposed, vulnerable in a way that answering a math problem wrong never did. She decided to test it. She wrote her sentence, then flipped it around into a question, "Hast du Geschwister?", and practiced it on Elyse outside the library, pretending they were two strangers meeting in Berlin.

Monday arrived. Mathias went first, and Nora held her breath as he said, "Ich habe vier Geschwister," instead of four separate sentences. Mr. Henry nodded and marked something in his book, and Nora let out her breath. When her turn came, she stood up, articulated her five sentences slowly and carefully, and finished with "Ich habe zwei Geschwister und einen Hund." Mr. Henry wrote a check mark beside her name. Walking back to her seat, she caught Mathias's eye and mouthed the new word. "Geschwister," he whispered back.

Saturday morning, Liam stood in his kitchen with his boots still wet from the precipitation that had been falling since dawn, staring at the flyer on the fridge. Volunteer day, the food bank on Miller Street, ten o'clock. He had promised his mom he would try it once, and now that the moment had arrived, he kind of wished the rain had turned into a full snowstorm so staying home would seem reasonable.

The food bank turned out to be a bright room in the basement of a church, with long metal shelves and a smell of cardboard and apples. Ms. Pelletier handed him a clipboard and a pair of reading glasses on a cord. "The dates on the cans are tiny," she said. "Wear these. They magnify the print so you can check nothing has expired." Liam put them on, and the little stamped numbers jumped out at him, sharp and sudden, like the world had leaned in closer. Chase was already at the next shelf, racing through soup cans and calling out dates like a game show host.

Halfway through the morning, Alanna looked up from her box of pasta. "Does anyone know how long food banks have even existed in Canada?" she asked. "Like, are they super old, or new?"

Liam thought about it. The room was in an old church, but the shelves looked new, and the fridge had a shiny sticker from a grocery store fundraiser. "Probably new," he said. "Maybe twenty years? People only started needing them recently, right?"

Chase shook his head slowly. "My grandma talks about them from way back."

Liam decided to test his idea the way he tested anything: find the evidence. Near the door hung a bulletin board thick with old photos, so he went over and worked through them, oldest at the bottom. There were pictures of volunteers in clothes from decades ago, and then, right at the bottom corner, a yellowed newspaper clipping with a headline he read twice. Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta. Beneath it, someone had written in faded marker: It started here later than that, but not much.

"Alanna!" he called across the room. "Come see. Nineteen eighty-one. Edmonton, Alberta. That's the first one." Alanna came over, and Chase too, and the three of them crouched by the board while Liam read the clipping aloud one more time, just to be sure he had it right.

Near closing time, a man with a walker came in and took only a small bag, though Ms. Pelletier had offered him a full box. Liam watched him pause at the door, adjusting his grip, and noticed the handle of a second, empty tote bag folded over his arm. "Would a lighter second bag help?" Liam asked, and fetched one, packing it with the easy-to-carry things, juice boxes and crackers. The man smiled and said, "That's for my neighbour. She can't get down the stairs on Saturdays."

Liam carried the bag out to the bus stop for him, rain spitting lightly, his own hands empty and warm. "Same time next week?" Alanna called from the door, and Liam waved back and said, "Next week."

Riley stood on second base long after the last out, dragging his cleats through the dirt while the parents folded chairs along the foul line. The end-of-season party was supposed to start in twenty minutes, on folding tables behind the backstop, but nobody had moved yet. Koen sat on the pitcher's mound pulling up little tufts of grass, and Ajay was spinning a ball in his glove even though the game was over. Riley had thought everyone would be loud and happy. Instead the team drifted around the diamond like the whole season had left something unfinished.

He walked over and dropped onto the grass beside Koen. "Why does everyone look like we lost? We won." Koen shrugged. Ajay rolled the ball toward them. "It's not the game. Next year there's tryouts again, and half of us won't make the same team. Some kids are moving schools. It won't be this team anymore." Riley frowned. He had felt it too, that heavy quiet, and he had blamed the wind, which came across the brown outfield like cold air off a tundra, flattening everything it touched.

That night he looked it up, because the feeling had a shape to it and shapes had names. His older sister's group-work textbook was still on the shelf, and there it was: a psychologist named Tuckman had stages for how groups form, storm, and settle. Then, in 1977, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, called adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. Riley read it twice. He had assumed something was wrong with them, that winning should feel clean and bright. It was a stage. Teams ended, and feeling strange about it was part of the ending, not a fault in the day.

At the party the next afternoon, behind the backstop, the same quiet hung over the pizza boxes. Riley set his cup down. "Adjourning," he said. Ajay blinked. "That's what it's called. In 1977 these two people, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen, added a fifth stage for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. It's a real thing. It's not just us being weird." Koen laughed, short and relieved. "So we're not sad, we're in stage five." "Basically," Riley said.

Ms. Suryanto, their neighbor who had volunteered as scorekeeper all season, raised her paper cup of lemonade from across the table. "To stage five, then," she said. The team clinked cups, paper against paper, and the quiet loosened. Ajay started retelling the double play from the fourth inning, waving his arms, and Koen argued the ball had bounced. Someone's little brother knocked over the cooler, and everyone rushed to save the ice. Riley bit into his slice, warm and folded, and listened to the voices pile up under the lights, which had not yet been switched off.

Jayden crouched beside the grave marker with a scrub brush in one hand and his notebook in the other. Mr. Morin had asked him to clean the lichen off his wife's headstone before the service at three, and it was already half past two. Shyanne and Payton had come along to help, mostly because Jayden had promised them the leftover donuts from his mom's box.

"I can do the left side," Shyanne said, kneeling and dipping her brush in the bucket. The water had gone gray, and a beetle crawled out from under the stone's base and headed for the grass.

Payton read the dates on the marker out loud. "Fifty-one years. That's a long marriage." He scrubbed at a patch of green with the edge of his sleeve.

A week ago, none of them would have been here. Jayden thought back to Sunday, when he'd sat in the back of Shyanne's church taking notes for his world religions project. He was supposed to compare how two faiths explained what happened after death, and he'd chosen Christianity and Buddhism because they seemed the most different. Then Payton had glanced at his notebook and frowned at the word Jayden had written down.

"What's purgatory?" Payton had asked.

Shyanne had blinked at him. "You don't know purgatory? You go to church every week."

"I've never heard the word in my life," Payton said. "It sounds like a counterfeit word, like somebody made it up to scare people."

That had been the start of the whole argument, and it was still going. The Catholic Church taught purgatory, a state of purification after death before entering heaven. Most Protestant churches, Payton's included, rejected the idea entirely. Jayden had written all this down, but Payton had insisted Shyanne's church must be wrong somewhere, and Shyanne had insisted he ask his own pastor, and somehow the argument had ended with all three of them agreeing to test it.

The test had been Jayden's idea, and it was simple: ask a second source. That was the rule for his project, the same rule that said you couldn't build a whole essay on one protagonist's point of view. So Payton had called his grandfather, who read the Bible every morning, and read him the question straight off Jayden's notebook. His grandfather had paused for a long time and then said, "Some churches teach that, we don't," which settled nothing and somehow settled everything. Two people, same book, different answers. Jayden had underlined that line twice.

Now the cemetery bell rang a quarter chime, and Mr. Morin's car turned in at the gate. The headstone was clean except for one gray patch near the bottom, and Shyanne dumped the rest of the bucket over it, letting the water submerge the stone's base and run off through the grass.

"They can both be right," Payton said suddenly, wringing out his rag. "About the big part, I mean. Heaven."

"Maybe," Shyanne said. "The purgatory part's the part we fight about."

"Write it both ways," Jayden said, snapping his notebook shut as the first mourners walked up the hill. "Two answers, one question."

Mr. Morin stopped beside the marker, put his hand flat on the clean granite, and said, "She'd have liked that you three worked on it together."

At dinner on Tuesday, Lucas pushed his noodles around the plate while his dad talked about the new bridge downtown, how its bones were steel alloyed with other metals to make it stronger than any single metal alone. Lucas wasn't really listening. He was thinking about the group chat, and about Aron.

It had started as a joke, Lucas supposed. Someone posted a picture of Aron's volcano project with a caption about how it looked like a pile of mud, and then everyone piled on, laughing emojis stacking up like a wall. Aron left the chat by fourth period. Lucas had wanted to say something, but every time he typed a message, he imagined the replies turning on him next, so he deleted his words and said nothing. When he finally decided to show the coach, the messages were already gone. Whoever sent them had deleted them, one by one, until the chat looked almost innocent.

"Something on your mind?" his mom asked. "You've stabbed those noodles about forty times."

Lucas set down his fork. "If someone says mean stuff in a chat and then deletes it, is it like it never happened?"

His dad tilted his head. "Depends. Anybody take a picture of it?"

The words landed, and a slow, bright idea opened in Lucas's mind. A screenshot. A screenshot froze the words before anyone could conceal them by deleting them. Messages could vanish, but a picture stayed. That was the pattern he'd been missing: the mean comments kept disappearing before an adult could see them, so no adult ever saw them. It wasn't that nobody cared. It was that nobody had a record.

He texted Adelaide under the table, pretending to check the time. Did you see what they posted about Aron before it got deleted? She wrote back within a minute: saw it, tried to show my sister, it was already gone. Lucas's thumb hovered. Then he typed: If it happens again, don't wait. Screenshot it. Even if it gets deleted, we'll still have proof to show Mr. Pérez. Then we tell him together, so it's not just one person against everyone.

Adelaide sent back a single thumbs-up, and then, after a pause, a longer message: Aron eats lunch in the library now. Somebody should sit with him.

Lucas looked up from his phone. His mom and dad were watching him with the particular patience of parents who know something is going on. "Can I be excused?" he asked. "I want to go online for a few minutes."

"As long as your homework's done," his dad said.

Lucas carried his plate to the sink, then walked back to the table and set his phone down where they could see the screen. "There's a kid in my class getting teased in a group chat," he said. It wasn't an eloquent speech, and his voice cracked in the middle, but he kept going anyway. "Tomorrow I'm going to sit with him at lunch, and if it starts again, I'll be ready."

His mom reached over and squeezed his hand. "Sounds like a plan," she said.

Sarah's band had a chronic problem, and nobody could say what it was. Every time they played "Moonrise March" in Joelle's garage, the song started fine and then fell apart somewhere in the middle, like a cake collapsing in the oven. Maddison blamed the drums. Joelle blamed Maddison. Sarah, who played the old upright piano against the back wall, said nothing, because she had a private suspicion that made her stomach drop: it was her.

She tested the idea at home, playing the march alone and recording it. When she listened back, the opening was steady, but by the second theme the notes were galloping, and by the big dynamic change, where the music was supposed to get quiet and mysterious, she was practically sprinting. So her rushing had to be the hidden cause. The others probably sped up to keep up with her, and the whole thing snowballed. But knowing that didn't fix it. She couldn't hear herself rushing while it happened, which felt like trying to watch her own back.

The next afternoon, Mr. Nkosi from next door was dragging lawn chairs into his truck when Sarah carried the trash out. He heard her humming the march and asked about it, and when she told him the problem, he disappeared into his house and came back with a small wooden box. Inside sat a brass pendulum that clicked when he wound it. "Metronome," he said. "Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815." He set the weight, and the ticking filled the air like a patient, mechanical heartbeat.

Sarah took it to the garage that evening, and the band gathered around it like it was a dragon egg. "What is that thing?" Maddison asked, poking the pendulum and nearly stopping it. Joelle wanted to know if it could do anything cooler than click. "It's from 1815," Maddison said, "so no." Sarah set it ticking at the march's tempo and they started over.

The first run-through was a disaster. Everyone watched the pendulum instead of playing, and Joelle hit a cymbal a full beat late, which sounded like a trash can falling downstairs. Sarah laughed so hard she had to stop. The second time, they ignored the ticking entirely, and the song collapsed at the same exact spot as always. Sarah noticed something then. The collapse always came right after the quiet section, the part where the dynamics dropped way down. When the music got soft, she leaned in, and leaning in made her hands rush, as if quiet meant fast instead of soft.

On the third try she made herself play the quiet section slowly on purpose, letting the click hold her back while the notes shrank to a whisper. It felt wrong, like walking through deep water, but the band stayed with her, and when the march swelled back to loud, they were still together, all four of them, right on the beat.

"Okay," Joelle said, wiping her forehead. "We keep the clicky box. It's in the band now. It can be our dynasty." Maddison reached over and slid the weight down the pendulum, and the ticking slowed, ominously, like time itself taking a nap. "Play it again," Sarah said, and cracked her knuckles.

Ms. Gagnon had taped a tablet advertisement to the whiteboard, and Avery leaned forward in her seat because she wanted that exact tablet for her birthday, which was three weeks away. The ad listed five features in bold letters: a brilliant screen, a fast processor, a slim design, a free stylus, and a huge app store. "Who wants one of these?" Ms. Gagnon asked, and half the class raised their hands, including Zane and Audrey. "Notice how many hands went up," Ms. Gagnon said. "Advertisers notice too."

That was the bandwagon appeal, and Avery wrote it down. Then Ms. Gagnon played an old radio clip where a famous actor praised a brand of soup, calling it the finest cuisine in America, and Avery recognized a celebrity testimonial. Next came a wartime poster with loaded words like "coward" and "hero" splashed across terrified faces. The room smelled of dry-erase marker and the lemon floor cleaner the janitor used, and Avery's pencil was flying across her notebook.

After class, Audrey hurried after her into the hallway, where lockers slammed like thunder. "Did you raise your hand too?" Audrey asked. "For the tablet? Everyone's getting one." Avery hesitated. She had raised her hand, and now she felt an itch at the back of her mind, the same feeling she got when a math answer looked right but something underneath was off. At home that night, she found the tablet's official webpage and read every line. Screen, processor, design, stylus, apps. Five features, same five, over and over. What wasn't there?

She searched the model number plus the word battery, and the results filled the screen. Owners complained the battery barely lasted four hours on a charge, and one review called the screen beautiful but the battery life "a dealbreaker." The ad never mentioned it once.
