Avery sat back, the desk lamp warm on her hands, and understood what she was looking at: the ad showed only the facts that supported it and left out the facts against it, so it seemed stronger than it was. Zane had called it something in class while she was writing. She texted him: what's the word for when an ad only lists the good stuff?

"Card stacking," he typed back.

The next morning she showed her mom the ad, then the reviews. "It's not lying exactly," Avery said. "It's just showing one side." Her mom read both, tapping the counter, and said they'd look at other tablets together on Saturday, comparing everything, good and bad. When Avery told Audrey at lunch, Audrey stared at her tray. "I already told my parents that exact ad," she said, and her voice went small. "They ordered it last night." Avery put a hand on her shoulder to console her. "It's not too late," she said. "Cancel it, then show them what I found." Audrey picked up her phone.

The app was called Sparrow, and everyone in Mr. Hall's fifth period was on it except Nicholas. Beatrix had shown him her feed at lunch, a swirl of drawings and dodgeball videos, and now all he wanted was an account of his own. That evening he typed his real birthday, March 14, and the screen went red. "You must be 13 or older to use Sparrow," it said, in that flat way screens have of not arguing back.

He tried again the next morning in the school library, in case he had mistyped something. Same red message. He leaned over to Meliane, who was two seats away with her tablet. "It keeps asking for my birthday. Why does it even care?"

Meliane shrugged. "My cousin said something about a law. She said websites have to get your parents' permission before they can take your information if you're under 13. That's why most of them just say no one under 13 can join. Easier for them." She went back to her project on hummingbirds, which was due Friday and already six slides long. Nicholas sat with that. A law. From when, though, and who made it? He devised a plan on the back of his math worksheet: he would find the rule in writing, not just in a cousin's retelling.

He typed "why do apps ask if you are 13" into the library search. The answer came up fast, on a page about kids and the internet: the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, a United States law that requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13. He read the sentence twice. So that was the hidden rule under the red message. Sparrow wasn't being mean. It was dodging paperwork. He copied the name of the law into his notebook, letter by letter, because it seemed like the kind of thing a person should know exactly.

At lunch he found Beatrix by the window, defending her hummingbird slide notes from a drippy juice box. "The reason is a law from 1998," he said. "It says websites need parental consent before they collect personal information from kids under 13. So they just make the age limit 13." Beatrix looked at him over her sandwich. "So if you put a different birthday..." "Then they'd be collecting my information without my parents knowing," Nicholas said. "That's the part that feels weird. It's not a lock, it's a rule."

Ms. Adeyemi, on lunch duty, had drifted close enough to hear the last part. She didn't lecture. She just said, "There's a permission form in the office for exactly this. Students use it all the time." Nicholas felt his grin go contagious; Beatrix caught it and grinned back, and even Meliane looked up from her hummingbirds, where a slide about nectar was waiting.

He got the form after last period, folded it into his backpack, and carried it home like something warm. "Mom," he called from the front door, waving the paper, "I need you to sign this."

Beatrice had lost her last three eight-hundred-metre races in the same strange way, and nobody could tell her why. She would lead after one lap, feeling wonderful, and then her legs would turn to something like wet sand and three people would pass her before the finish. Her coach only said, "Save something," which was the kind of advice that sounded like advice and worked like nothing at all.

Since the track was still locked for the season, she trained at the rink, running laps on the rubber walkway that circled the ice, where the cold air kept her from feeling like a boiled potato. Angelique stood by the boards with a stopwatch, shouting her splits, while Tayla sat on a cooler doing what Tayla did best, which was looking things up. "I found something," Tayla said one evening, holding out her phone. "David Rudisha's world record race. The 2012 Olympics. You can watch the whole thing."

They watched it right there, three heads bent over one small screen, while the Zamboni growled past behind them and the smell of cold rubber saturated everything. Rudisha ran from the front the entire way and won in a time so fast it looked like a typo. "Okay, so he never fades," Beatrice said. Tayla shook her head and tapped the lap times. "No. Look. His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second." Beatrice stared at the numbers. The world record holder, the best eight-hundred-metre runner who had ever lived, had also slowed down. Her dying second lap wasn't some freak phenomenon unique to her. It happened to everybody. The question was how much.

She tested it the next evening. Instead of attacking the first lap like a burglar who had forgotten something inside, she ran it deliberately, almost frugally, keeping something back the way her grandmother kept back the good chocolates. Angelique called out the split and Beatrice thought, that's slower than usual, this is a disaster. Then, on the second lap, her legs did not turn to wet sand. They stayed legs. She finished her final lap two seconds faster than she ever had before, and Angelique's shriek echoed off the ice hard enough that Mr. Friedman looked up from the skate rental counter and cupped a hand to his ear.

"You want to know the strangest part?" Beatrice said, hands on her knees, breath fogging in the rink air. "It felt easier and my time was better. That's basically cheating."

"Take it up with Rudisha," said Tayla.

Beatrice straightened up and pointed at the stopwatch. "Again. Right now. Angelique, count me down."

The basketball court behind the school had painted lines all over it, and Raphael had figured out that one full loop around the outside fence was almost exactly four hundred metres, because he had counted his steps and done the math twice. Cindy sat on the bleachers with a stopwatch and a bag of pretzels, and Jasmin stood at the far corner holding a paper cone she had made to shout through.

"Three minutes!" Jasmin bellowed through the cone, which mostly made her sound like a duck. "You have to run eight hundred metres in three minutes by Friday, or Mr. Andersen says you can't be in the meet."

Raphael had been sprinting the first part of every practice run and then dying at the end, wobbling like a shopping cart with a bad wheel. The problem was that he could not see the thing that was beating him. It felt like his legs just quit on the second lap, but that made no sense, because his legs were the same legs he had started with. Something invisible had to be the cause, and he meant to hunt it down.

He devised a plan on the back of his race number, which he had pinned to his shirt inside out so the blank side showed. Three minutes for eight hundred metres on a four-hundred-metre track meant two laps, so he divided and got ninety seconds for the first lap. "Ninety seconds," he said, tapping the number with his pen. "If I do the first lap in ninety, I get the second lap in ninety too, and that's three minutes exactly."

"It feels slow," Cindy warned, when he jogged the first lap instead of charging off like a startled horse. "Like, birthday-parade slow."

"That's the illusion," Raphael puffed as he went by. "It feels easy now because I'm not burning everything up." He rounded the fence by the sagging net, waved at Jasmin, who honked her cone at him, and came through the first lap at ninety-one seconds. Then, instead of turning into a wobbly shopping cart, he stayed buoyant, almost light, and pushed the second lap hard enough to pass a very confused pigeon. He crossed the line, and Cindy pressed the stopwatch and yelled the time.

"Two minutes fifty-eight!" she shouted. "You did it! You did the thing!"

Jasmin ran over, still holding the cone, which now had a bite mark on it for reasons nobody asked about. "So the trick is going slow first?"

"Not slow," Raphael said, holding up the race number with the number ninety written on it, sweaty but readable. "Even. Ninety and ninety. I just have to do it again on Friday, only with seven other kids sprinting ahead of me like maniacs."

"Maniacs who will be walking by the end," Cindy said, and tossed him a pretzel, which he caught in his mouth.

David carried the folded letter in his jacket pocket all the way up the trail, because it was the reason he had dragged Izaiah and Aikam out here on a Saturday at all. The letter was from his cousin in India, who had asked a question David could not stop thinking about: why does the rain arrive right when the heat is worst? He had to explain it in class on Monday, and so far all he had was a page of notes that said "monsoon" about nine times without saying anything else.

"Here," David said, stopping where the trail bent around a wide gray rock. He put his palm flat on the stone, then held it out toward the small stream below. "Rock feels hot. Water feels cold. Same sun all morning." He crouched and touched the stream. "The land heats up faster than the ocean. Like the rock and the water."

Aikam looked from the rock to the stream and back. "So?"

"So imagine the whole country is the rock." David pulled a notebook from his backpack and drew a lumpy shape for land and a wavy line for sea. "In summer, the land gets hot. Hot air rises, like over a campfire. When it rises over the land, air from the ocean flows in to take its place. And ocean air is wet air. That wet air comes in, and that's the rain." He tapped the drawing. "That's why the worst heat and the first rain show up together. The heat itself is pulling the rain in."

Izaiah frowned at the drawing. "You can't see air rising, though. How do you know you're not just making it up?"

David had been waiting for that. He tore off two strips of paper, wet one in the stream, and taped them to sticks a few steps apart, one over the hot rock and one over the shaded ground near the water. "Watch." The paper over the rock fluttered upward within a minute, curling and lifting on the rising heat, while the other strip hung still. "Temporary, it's only a demonstration," David admitted. "But it illustrates the idea. Mr. Farah says you can't see wind either, you see what it pushes."

Then came the twist. Aikam, who had been quiet, pulled out his phone. "My uncle farms rice near Dhaka. I texted him your rock thing last night." He held up the screen. "He says in the wet season the fields need that rain, and in the dry season they need the sun to dry the grain. Both. If the rain failed one year, the rice fails."

David stared at the message. He had been thinking of the monsoon as an answer to memorize, a line for the protagonist of his presentation to say, and here it was deciding whether his friend's family ate. He thought about how easily he could have copied a definition instead of climbing a hill to test it, and he still wasn't sure which choice had been the smarter one, only which one he would remember.

"Monday," he said, folding the notebook away, "I'm opening with the rock."

"You're opening with my uncle," Aikam said, holding the phone higher. "Read it out loud."

The bus groaned into the gravel lot of Willow Creek Pioneer Village just after ten in the morning, and Ms. Sokolov held up a clipboard before anyone could bolt for the gate. "Photo scavenger hunt," she said. "Teams of three, sheet due at the gatehouse at one fifteen, because the bus leaves at one thirty. Not one minute later." Jaxson grabbed Millie and Safa, his usual alliance, and they studied the sheet: a spinning wheel, a hand-forged nail, a working water pump, and one blank line marked "something the villagers did to survive summer."

They found the nail first, then the pump, where Safa took a turn cranking until cold water gushed over her sneakers and she shrieked with delight. Jaxson was already scanning the list again when he noticed the pigs. Behind a split-rail fence, three Berkshire pigs lay stretched in a black mud hole, and a fourth stood pressed against the far rails, trembling, its sides heaving fast. "That one looks sick," Millie said quietly. "It's shaking." The morning had been cool, but by noon the sun had turned the village into an oven, and the gravel crunched like burnt toast under their shoes.

Jaxson couldn't stop thinking about it while they photographed the spinning wheel. At ten, the pigs had all been rooting in the grass, ordinary and busy. At noon, three were buried in mud and one looked miserable. If the pig were sick, it would have acted strange all morning. But it had only gone wrong when the heat did. He compressed his empty water bottle into his pocket, refilled it at the pump, and led the others back to the fence. "Watch," he said, and poured a thin stream of water into a dusty hollow near the rails. The trembling pig heaved itself over, flopped into the wet spot, and rolled until its pink skin was brown.

"Okay, that was the opposite of sick," Safa said. A docent in a straw hat passed with a wheelbarrow and paused at the fence. "Smart pig," she said. "They've got very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days." She walked on, and Jaxson grinned so wide his face hurt. Millie checked her phone and gasped. "Twelve fifty. The gatehouse, now!"

They ran past the print shop, ducked under the low beam of the schoolhouse door, and skidded up to Ms. Sokolov just as the bus driver was starting the engine. Overhead, a wedge of migratory geese honked south across a hard blue sky, and Safa snapped one last picture while Jaxson scribbled on the blank line: "villagers' pigs kept cool in mud." Ms. Sokolov read it, then looked at the mud streaks on Jaxson's shoes and raised an eyebrow. "The pig did that," he said, breathless. "It was practically a science experiment." Millie held up the phone with the rolling pig mid-flop, and the bus doors hissed open behind them.

Victoria raised her hand before Ms. Campbell even finished explaining the game. "So we act out a scene, but nobody gets to plan it first?" Ms. Campbell nodded and said they would each draw a partner's name from the box. Victoria unfolded her slip of paper and read it twice: Samuel. He was the quietest kid in the class, the one who once went a whole week answering only in single words.

They started on the pretend beach, a couple of towels on the stage floor. "I found a message in a bottle," Victoria announced, holding up an invisible bottle. Samuel looked at his shoes. "Okay," he said. Nothing else came. Victoria speculated that maybe he hadn't heard her, so she repeated it louder. "Okay," Samuel said again, and the scene sat there like a car with the engine off. Across the stage, Mason and his partner were already arguing about whether an invisible shark could smell peanut butter, and the whole class was laughing.

Victoria tried three more offers. A seagull attack. A treasure map. A crab that could talk. Each time, Samuel agreed. "Sure." "Yeah." "Okay." The scene stalled every single time, and Victoria started to wonder if saying yes was actually the problem. It didn't make sense, because agreeing was supposed to be polite. But when she listened to Mason's scene, she noticed something. He never just agreed. When his partner said the shark was hungry, Mason said yes, and it was allergic to peanut butter, which is why it kept sneezing. Their scene grew like a snowball rolling downhill, while hers stayed a flat lump of sand.

"That's it," she whispered. Mason caught her eye during the break and grinned. "Yes, and," he said, wiggling his fingers like it was a magic spell. "You take what your partner gives, then you add something." Victoria turned back to Samuel, and instead of feeling annoyed, she noticed his hands were shaking a little, and his eyes kept darting toward the exit. He wasn't refusing her offers. He just didn't know how to build on them, and he was probably terrified of looking foolish in front of everyone.

She sat down beside him on the beach towel. "New plan," she said quietly. "I'll give you something so easy a robot could add to it. Watch." She stood, picked up the invisible bottle again, and held it out. "This message says our class is being attacked by a giant octopus. You're the one with the robust net, the strongest kid on the beach." Samuel blinked, then straightened up like someone had handed him a real job. "And the octopus," he said slowly, "is afraid of jellyfish." Victoria grabbed it instantly. "Yes, and look, a whole jar of jellyfish in my lunchbox!"

The class roared as the two of them chased the octopus around the towels, Samuel declaring himself the antagonist's worst nightmare, waving a net made of nothing at all. When Ms. Campbell called time, Samuel was out of breath and grinning, and Victoria realized the twist: the partner everyone thought would sink the scene had turned out to be the funniest one on the stage. "Same teams tomorrow?" Samuel asked. "Yes, and bring the jellyfish," Victoria said, tossing him the invisible jar.

Madison had forty minutes left before the coding showcase at Camp Birchwood, and her program was broken. She stared at the laptop screen in the craft cabin, where fifteen campers were typing in a hurry, fans humming in the window to push out the heat.

"Mine keeps saying 'not prime' a bunch of times," she said, tilting her screen toward Romane, who sat cross-legged on the bench beside her.

Romane leaned over. On Madison's screen, the number 13 had printed "not prime" fifty times in a column that ran right off the bottom of the window. Thirteen was prime; Madison had checked it on the divisibility chart taped to the cabin wall. Something invisible was going wrong inside her loop.

She read her code line by line, trying to isolate the problem. The loop went from 2 up to 12, checking whether any number divided 13 evenly. For each check that failed, she had typed a print statement saying "not prime." So the program printed it again and again, once for every number that did not divide 13.

"Twelve wrong answers instead of one right one," Zakary said from across the table, peering over. "You're punishing your program for being correct."

Madison laughed despite herself. She flipped her ponytail behind her shoulder and thought about the pattern. What she wanted was for the loop to quit the moment it found one divisor, and to stay quiet otherwise. Her eyes landed on a line in her notes from Tuesday's session with Ms. Islam: break.

"A break statement stops a loop immediately," she said slowly, reading her own handwriting. "So a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor."

She restructured the code. Now the loop would only print "not prime" and then break if it found a divisor; if it finished every check without breaking, it would print "prime" exactly once. Her fingers felt elastic with nerves as she saved the file, and the clock over the door showed nineteen minutes remaining.

She typed 13 and pressed enter. The screen printed a single line: prime.

"Finally," Romane whispered, and patted the bench.

Ms. Islam walked the rows checking progress, pausing behind Madison's chair just long enough to read the output. "Twenty-eight," she said. "Try twenty-eight."

Madison entered it. The program printed "not prime" one time, then stopped, the loop abandoned mid-flight, its work finished early. She ran 97 next, and then 2, and each answer came back clean, single, correct.

When the showcase began on the porch, Madison stood up with her laptop. Zakary gave her a thumbs up, and Romane mouthed "go on." She set the computer on the rail where everyone could see and typed one more number.

The bathroom smelled like pink soap, and Rosalie had been standing at the sink for two full minutes with wet hands, waiting for her heart to stop hammering. In ten minutes she had to walk into the gym and run the assembly slide show in front of the whole sixth grade, because she had let Emelia delegate the tech job to her back when it seemed easy. It did not seem easy anymore. Her hands were cold, her stomach was a stone, and when she looked in the mirror her face was blotchy pink.

She wasn't even sure why she felt this bad. She knew the slides. She had practised twice. That was the part that scared her, actually, that something invisible was doing this to her body and she couldn't point at it.

The door creaked and Emelia slipped in, whispering, "Rosalie? Mr. Kim sent me to find you. He said if you're sick I have to take over." She hesitated in the doorway, taking in Rosalie's white knuckles on the sink. "Whoa. Okay. You're not sick, you're stressed."

"That's helpful," Rosalie said, but her voice came out thin.

Emelia came closer. "My little brother has this before every dentist visit. He does this thing he learned. Put two fingers on your wrist and feel your pulse." Rosalie did, feeling the quick thud, thud, thud. "Now breathe in slow." Rosalie breathed in, and under her fingers the pulse picked up, quicker. "Now out, longer than the in. Like counting to six." Rosalie let the breath go, slow and long, and the beat under her fingers stretched out, softened, slowed. Her heart speeds up a little on every breath in, she thought, and slows down on every breath out. Long out-breaths, then. That was the trick.

They did it together, Emelia counting quietly, "In... two... three... and out, four, five, six, seven." Three rounds of it, and the hammering in Rosalie's chest faded to something she could live with. The irony was not lost on her: she was hiding in a bathroom because of a slide show about healthy habits, of all things.

"One more thing," Emelia said as they pushed open the door. "My brother's thing includes last night. He never sleeps well before the dentist and it's always worse. So tonight you'll sleep, and tomorrow won't be like this."

The gym was loud and bright when they walked in together. Mr. Kim stood at the laptop, relief crossing his face. "There you are. Ready?"

Rosalie flexed her fingers, took one long breath out, and clicked the first slide forward.

The morning bus to the regional bee smelled like peanut butter and nerves. Alexa slid into the seat beside Ashwin, who was reading a folded note for the fourth time. "It's from Odin," he said. "He couldn't come, so he wrote you a pep talk. It's two pages. Front and back."

The note said: Dear Alexa, I know you're worried that only certain kinds of kids win spelling bees, like kids whose parents quiz them every night at dinner. You practice on the bus, which is way harder because the bus is bumpy and smells like peanut butter. Also, I looked up champions at the library yesterday for our bee project. In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee, and she also held three Guinness World Records for dribbling basketballs. So champions can be basketball people too, not just dinner-quiz people. Spell well. Your friend, Odin. P.S. I have changed my mind about the word "mnemonic." It is not pronounced "man-omic." Good luck.

Alexa read it twice, then stared out the window. She had been telling herself a story about spelling bee winners, a quiet little stereotype that lived in the back of her head: winners were kids with fancy word lists and private tutors, kids who practiced in silence, not kids like her. But if a girl who juggled basketballs could win the biggest bee in the country, then maybe the winning kind of kid was just many kinds of kid. Maybe the real pattern wasn't who you were. It was how you worked with words.

She decided to test it. At the library she had noticed that bee-winning words in recent years were often versatile ones, words that could show up in science or geography or old poems, so she had drilled those hardest. Now, on the bus, she asked Ashwin to quiz her only on words that could belong to more than one subject. "Fine," he said, "but if you get 'siphon' wrong I'm eating your spare pencil as a snack." She spelled siphon, and seismology, and brackish, and even mnemonic, which she pronounced correctly on purpose, just for Odin.

At the auditorium, Ms. Augustin checked them in and told Alexa to assess her confidence level honestly, because round one was worth staying calm for. Alexa said seven out of ten, which felt like a true number. Then she stood at the microphone, heard her word, and recognized it instantly as one of her versatile ones, the kind of word that could belong anywhere. She took a breath, looked at Ashwin holding up Odin's two-page note like a banner, and said, "S. I. P. H. O. N. Siphon."

Jasmine was sprawled on the living room rug with the tablet balanced on a cushion when the group chat lit up. Reagan had posted a poll: "Who thinks I should post the porch selfie? YES or YES." Below it sat the photo itself, sent twice, then a third time with the caption "vote now." In the picture Reagan stood on her front steps with her cat, Mr. Whiskers, draped over one shoulder like a scarf, and behind her the porch, the door, and a smudge of white near the railing.

Apollo replied first. "Mr. Whiskers gets my vote. Reagan also yes."

"It's a good picture," Jasmine typed, but she didn't send it yet. Something about the photo kept snagging her attention the way a loose thread catches on a zipper. She pinched the screen and the image magnified until the porch filled the whole display. There, sharp as anything, hung a little white sign next to the door with the number 14 on it, and on the mailbox post, the street name, Wren Street. Anyone in the chat, and anyone the photo got sent to after that, could see exactly where Reagan lived.

She scrolled back through the chat's history to test her idea. Last month Reagan had posted a picture from the school gym, and behind her, stretched across the wall, was the banner with the school's name and mascot. A week before that, a shot at the park with the sign for Wren Street Lake in the corner. Every picture carried its own address, like a return label nobody noticed sticking on.

"Reagan," Jasmine typed, "zoom in on the door in your selfie."

"why"

"Just do it. Look at the sign."

The typing bubble appeared, vanished, appeared again. Then: "oh. that's my house number."

"A stranger could work out where the photo was taken," Jasmine wrote. "Street sign, house number, even the school logo. You've basically posted your address three times."

"I want likes," Reagan replied. "Poppy from summer camp said she'd share it with her whole cabin. That's like twelve people."

Apollo sent a single line of laughing emojis. "Poppy's cabin follows everybody. They followed a pigeon account once."

Jasmine sat up, thinking. The chat was seven kids, but posts could be forwarded, saved, shared on, and once a photo left this little group it was like water going through a net. You couldn't pull it back. "Crop the picture," she suggested. "Cut off everything past the door. Keep you and Mr. Whiskers."

There was a long pause, long enough for Jasmine to notice the porch light was on outside her own window and that her father was humming in the kitchen, steering his way through a new recipe the way a boat drifts without a rudder whenever he stopped reading the instructions.

The edited photo arrived. Reagan stood in a tight square of just steps and cat, background trimmed away, number gone, street name gone. "New poll," she wrote. "Who thinks Mr. Whiskers should have his own account? YES or YES."

"ME," said Apollo.

Jasmine hit send on "Mr. Whiskers 2024" and went to find her father, because from the smell of it, the soup had gone past porous crackers to something resembling paste.

Cameron had surveyed the whole school about lunch food, 214 answers, and now all that data sat on his laptop like a lake that had swallowed a picnic. He wanted to know one thing: which grade liked pizza the most. Heinrich had bet him a candy bar that seventh graders would win, and Cameron intended to collect.

His first attempt was a disaster. He clicked something called PivotTable, and a new empty grid appeared beside a strange floating pane. He dragged the word "Grade" into the middle of the sheet and nothing happened, which felt deeply unfair. Then he dragged "Food" somewhere random and the grid filled with numbers that made no sense at all. Row after row of soggy mystery. "You look like you're trying to drown your own spreadsheet," said his dad from the kitchen doorway.

"The data is submerging me," Cameron said. "Two hundred answers. Zero patterns."

He looked harder at the floating pane. It had four boxes stacked on top of each other, labeled Filters, Columns, Rows and Values, and each box was a slot you could drop a field into. So the pane wasn't just decoration; it was the machine's control panel, and where you dropped a field decided where it showed up in the table. That was a logical way to build a thing, actually. On purpose, he dragged "Grade" into Rows, and the grades listed themselves down the side, six through eight. He tried to drag "Food" into Columns and missed, dropping it into Filters by mistake, and the whole table went blank. He fished it back out. "Filters," he muttered. "So that's what you're for. Not yet."

"Food" landed in Columns at last, and food names marched across the top. Then he dragged "Grade" a second copy, wait, no, he dragged "Answer" into Values, and numbers bloomed everywhere, one count for every grade and every food. There it was, the pattern he couldn't see in the raw lake of answers: pizza row, grade by grade. Seventh grade: forty-one votes. Sixth grade: thirty-six. Eighth grade: thirty-eight.

Cameron took a photo of the screen and texted Heinrich. "Start buying the candy bar." Heinrich replied with a single groaning emoji and the message, "check eighth grade tacos tho." Cameron checked. Eighth grade tacos: forty-four, the highest number in the whole table. Nobody had bet on tacos. "New bet," Cameron typed. "Whoever's grade loses has to eat cafeteria tacos all week." Heinrich answered fast: "Deal. And don't submerge me in screenshots, I already saw it." Cameron dragged "Food" into Filters anyway and clicked taco, just to watch the table rearrange itself one more time.

Xavier stood at the counter with the recipe spread in front of him, a lemony chicken and a big green salad to go with it. His parents would be home at seven, and he wanted dinner ready, not started. He had already sliced the raw chicken breast into strips and scraped them into the sizzling pan. Now he pulled a head of romaine from the fridge and reached for the cutting board, the same one, because it was right there.

He paused, knife in hand. Something about the board bothered him. It looked clean enough, just a few wet smears, but he kept thinking about the chicken juice that had pooled on it a minute ago. Ms. Nielsen had mentioned something once, in the middle of a unit on food safety that most of the class had half slept through. He remembered copying a phrase into his notes, and he dug the crumpled page out of his backpack right there on the kitchen floor.

"Cross-contamination," he read aloud. Raw meat on one board, ready-to-eat food on another, so bacteria from the meat couldn't spread to food that would never touch a flame. That was the whole idea. The lettuce would go straight from board to bowl to table, no cooking, no heat, nothing to stop whatever the chicken had left behind. He turned the wooden board over and squinted at the knife marks. Could stuff hide in those grooves, even after a rinse? It seemed possible, and he didn't want to test it on his family.

So he washed the board in hot, soapy water and set it in the rack, then took the clean plastic one from the cabinet for the salad. He chopped the romaine, diced a tomato, and whisked oil and vinegar in a jar. He decided to incorporate some leftover corn and a handful of croutons, which made the salad look like a real restaurant's. He wondered whether the raw-chicken rule was why restaurants had boards in different colors, and made a mental note to ask Georges, whose family ran a diner.

At seven, his parents walked in sniffing the air. His dad peeked at the pan, and his mom lifted the salad bowl and turned it appreciatively.

"Two cutting boards?" she asked, nodding at the dish rack.

"Yep," Xavier said. "Chicken gets one, salad gets the other. Cross-contamination."

"Where'd you learn that?"

He shrugged and grinned. "School. Who wants salad?"

The spelling bee was three weeks away, and Michael had a plan: read the list of four hundred words every single night until his eyes knew every letter. He read it on the bus, he read it at lunch, and he read it under his blanket with a flashlight until his mother made him sleep. By Friday, his paper had gone brittle at the folds from being opened and closed so many times.

"Quiz me," said Jethro, sliding into the seat next to him before class.

"I don't need quizzing," Michael said. "I've read the list six times."

Jethro shrugged. "Okay. Spell reconnaissance."

Michael opened his mouth. Nothing came out. He could picture the page, the smudge in the corner, even the coffee ring near the top, but the letters had gone blurry in his mind. He tried to retrieve the word and got only "R, E, C" before he stopped, cheeks hot.

"That's what I thought," Jethro said. "My sister made me look something up last year. There was a study in 2006, by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, and they found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it."

"Rereading feels like studying, though," Michael said.

"That's the trap," Jethro said.

That night, Michael handed the list to his mother and made her quiz him out loud. It was worse than reading. He missed chrysanthemum, he missed ghastliness, he missed parallel twice. But every time he got one wrong, she made him spell it three times before moving on, and the misses stung in a way that made them stick.

Ms. Gill held the class bee on a Thursday, and the gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn from the cafeteria. Jane went out on silhouette and gave Michael a thumbs up on her way to her seat. Round by round, the words came, and Michael found that the ones he had missed at his kitchen table now arrived in his head whole, letter by letter, like lights switching on down a hallway.

At the microphone, facing "irresistible," Michael thought of his mother tapping the counter with her pen, night after night, and he smiled. He didn't hear the word from a page in his mind. He heard her voice asking for it.

"I R R E S I S T I B L E," he said.

"Correct," said Ms. Gill. "One word left for the win."

The living room was so full that Hailey had to share the corner of the couch with Elliot, while Landen sat on the floor with a plate balanced on his knees. Everyone was shouting at the screen when the receiver landed in the end zone and the referee waved his arms, signaling incomplete. "His foot was in!" Hailey's grandfather bellowed, spraying popcorn. "They'll show it again," her dad said, and sure enough, the network ran the play back, once in slow motion, once from a second angle. The foot was clearly in bounds, and the whole room roared when the call got reversed.

"Rewind it again," Elliot begged, as if the remote were magic. Grandpa laughed and said something that snagged in Hailey's mind. "You kids think TV always could do that. When I was young, if you missed a play, it was gone. Vanished." Landen frowned. "That can't be right. They replay everything now." Grandpa shrugged. "Somebody had to invent it. I just don't remember who."

Hailey couldn't stop wondering. Somebody had to be first, on some specific day, at some specific game, and it seemed strange that something so ordinary had a beginning nobody in the room knew. She tested a simple idea: if it was a big deal, it would be written down somewhere, the way first flights and first telephone calls were. She borrowed her dad's phone, told him what she was hunting for, and typed in the words instant replay first used. Elliot leaned over her shoulder, and Landen climbed up onto the couch arm so he could see too.

"There," Hailey said, holding the screen out so even Grandpa could read it. The first instant replay in a live sports broadcast happened on December 7, 1963, during the Army-Navy football game, and the director who made it happen was CBS's Tony Verna. "December seventh," Grandpa repeated slowly. "Army-Navy. I would have been about that age." He shook his head, half grinning. "Fifty years I've been watching, and I never once wondered when it started."

Landen turned to Hailey's dad. "Would they even permit something like that today, a director just trying a brand new thing in the middle of a live game?" "Probably not," Dad said. "Too risky. One mistake in front of millions." "So Tony Verna had a reputation for taking chances," Elliot said, and Grandpa snorted, "No, kid, he made one that day." Hailey grinned and passed the popcorn down to Landen, who had the least of anybody, and Grandpa handed Elliot the last soda without being asked.

On the screen the stadium roared through another replay, and Grandpa pointed at the television with his remote. "That machine is keeping history alive," he said. "Rewind it one more time."

Alexandre stood in front of the mirror in the boys' bathroom, holding a stopwatch, and said, "Hello, brain, I have arrived." Nehemiah leaned against the sink and clicked the timer. "Two seconds. Your mouth is closer to your brain than a cigarette is. Barely."

They had a problem. Ms. Ivanova had assigned each pair in health class one question to answer for the fifth graders, and Alexandre and Nehemiah had drawn the worst one: why do people get addicted to nicotine? Briar had gotten "why do your ears pop," which she said was basically a vacation. Alexandre wanted his presentation to be the one the little kids actually remembered, and he had exactly one fact written on his notecard: when smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds.

"That can't be right," Nehemiah said on the way back to class. "I sat next to my grandpa on a six-hour flight. Nothing happened in 10 seconds for that man except sweating."

"Everything about him is slow," Alexandre said. "The doctor told my mom his cartilage is basically vintage. That's not the same as his blood."

They turned into Ms. Ivanova's room, where she was stacking diagrams of a brain on the front table. "Ten seconds," Alexandre said. "Nicotine gets to the brain in about 10 seconds after someone inhales. That's faster than I can find a pencil."

"Look it up in the actual textbook instead of telling me at speed," Ms. Ivanova said, but she said it while sliding the book across the table toward him, which Alexandre took as a good sign.

He and Nehemiah tested the idea at lunch. Alexandre put a random jellybean in his mouth and Nehemiah timed how long until Alexandre could taste it, which was not the same thing at all, Alexandre admitted, but it proved the general principle that stuff travels fast when there's a direct route. Then they tried it again, because the first jellybean was green and Alexandre wanted a do-over. "This is not science," Nehemiah said, eating a third one himself. "This is lunch with a stopwatch."

For the presentation, Alexandre had a plan. He would have five fifth graders stand in a line from the front door of the classroom to the back wall, and he would walk the route while Nehemiah counted the seconds out loud. He practiced the walk twice during recess and got it down to 9 seconds, which he decided was close enough and also extremely satisfying.

On presentation day, Briar went first with her ears-popping talk, which did turn out to be a vacation, and then Alexandre pointed at the door. "Breathe in," he told the fifth graders. "Right now, inhale." They all did, one kid so hard he coughed. Nehemiah started counting, and Alexandre walked the line of kids while the numbers climbed, one, two, three, tapping each of them on the shoulder like a relay. At eight he reached the wall, where Briar had taped a paper brain. At ten, he slapped it.

"That's how fast it happens," Alexandre said. "Ten seconds, and the nicotine's already there, in the brain, in the part that handles rewards. So the brain learns: that thing I did, do it again."

A fifth grader in the front row raised her hand. "My uncle does it the second he's stressed."

"Ten seconds," Alexandre said. "Every time." He tapped the paper brain once more, just for luck.

Jade had signed up for the camp's science showcase thinking she would get to build a volcano. Instead the topic card she drew from Mr. Virtanen's hat read, "How nicotine hooks the brain." Worse, she had forty-eight hours to figure it out, and her only teammates were Gia, who wanted to do a rap about it, and Sawyer, who was currently eating the marshmallows meant for the volcano group.

"You can't rap about neurons," Jade said, flipping through the camp library's one health textbook under a buzzing porch light. "Nobody even knows what a neuron is."

"That's why it's educational," Gia said.

Sawyer leaned over her shoulder, smelling like burnt sugar. "Here's what I don't get. If nicotine is bad for you, why would anyone keep doing it? Your brain isn't stupid."

That was the question, Jade realized, and the answer wasn't in the room. It was hidden inside a skull, too small to see, and she couldn't exactly peek. She persevered through three chapters, chewing her pencil until it tasted like splinters, while mosquitos whined against the screen door. Somewhere in the middle of chapter nine, something clicked. Nicotine, she read, tricked the brain's reward pathway, the system that said "do that again" when you ate a good meal or won a race. Nicotine hijacked it. That was why quitting was so hard: the brain itself had been taught to want more.

The next morning a folded note slid under the cabin door, smelling faintly of the lake. Jade opened it. "Ask the nurse about the nine out of ten thing. Trust me. Signed, a mysterious stranger." Below, in handwriting she absolutely recognized as Gia's, it added, "P.S. It's me, Gia. The nurse is only at the infirmary until lunch."

The nurse, a cheerful woman with a bandana, dug out a laminated sheet from a battered folder. "CDC numbers," she said. "Nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18." She tapped the page. "Think about that one yourself. I'm not allowed to hand you your whole project."

Jade stood in the doorway, the fact turning over in her head like a key in a lock. Nine out of ten. Grown-ups, hooked, and it started before eighteen. Before her age. It was a significant clue: if the brain's reward pathway was still developing in teenagers, then what started young could grab on hard and last for decades. Companies that sold cigarettes had every reason to care about people her age. That was the insight Sawyer's question had been pointing at all along.

At the showcase, under the picnic pavilion, Jade laid out her poster: a drawing of a brain with a little cartoon nicotine molecule pressing the "again, again" button. "Imagine a hijacker in the driver's seat," she said, "except the car is your brain." Gia performed one verse of the rap anyway, which rhymed "reward pathway" with "your brain gets a delay, hey," and even Mr. Virtanen laughed.

Sawyer raised his hand. "So why do companies aim ads at us?"

Jade held up the laminated sheet. "Nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18," she said. "They're not advertising to the smokers they have. They're advertising to the smokers they want."

Mr. Virtanen stopped laughing and wrote something in his notebook, and Gia whispered, "Told you the rap helped."

The fire station smelled like rubber boots and old coffee, and Penelope had exactly forty minutes before the bus left, because Mr. Gill had promised the driver they would be gone by noon. Mr. Gill's worksheet was due on the bus, all five questions filled in, and question four was the one she could not answer: "What does this station preserve from its past, and how?" The tour had rushed past the modern trucks and stopped in the back room, where the guide had waved at a scarred wooden desk and a brass pole before hurrying off to answer someone's question about dalmatians.

Hayden reached out to run his hand along the desk's edge, the way you test a railing. "Don't," Nevaeh said, grabbing his sleeve. "Museums ask people not to touch stuff like this. Oils and salts from your skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces." Hayden pulled his hand back and wiped it on his jeans as if his fingers had already done something wrong. "It's just a desk," he muttered, but he kept his hands in his pockets after that.

Penelope looked at the desk more closely. One end of it was pale and dry, the way old untreated wood looks, but the other end, the end nearest the brass pole, had a dark, shiny patch the shape of a handprint, almost like it had been soaked. She thought about that. If oils and salts from skin built up over time, then the dark patch could be decades of firefighters grabbing that same corner while sliding down the pole, each hand leaving a little behind. It was like a pattern you could read backwards: the stain was the effect, and the hands were the hidden cause.

She decided to test it. The desk was off limits now that she knew the rule, but her own sunglasses in her pocket had a smudge she'd been wiping with her thumb all week. She breathed on the lens and looked at the light: a cloudy print exactly where her thumb always landed, faint but there, building. She had never once seen the oils leave her skin, yet there was proof on the glass. "Okay," she whispered, and Hayden asked what she was doing with her sunglasses in a dark fire station. "Proving something," she said.

She wrote her answer for question four: the station preserves the old desk and pole by keeping hands off them, because skin oils and salts build up over time and stain the surfaces, which is why the shiny patch near the pole looks the way it does. When Mr. Gill collected the worksheets on the bus, he read hers twice. "I've taken three classes here," he said, "and nobody ever noticed the handprint before." Nevaeh leaned over the seat. "Show me," she said, and Penelope turned around as the bus pulled out, pointing back toward the station doors.

The garage smelled like oil and cut grass, and Leah had cleared a lane down the middle of it with two broom handles laid flat as rails. Her science-fair project was due Thursday, and the plan was simple: roll a tennis ball from the workbench, time it with a stopwatch, measure how far it went, and draw a distance-time graph. Ariel sat on an upturned milk crate holding the stopwatch, chewing her pen, because she wanted the job of timer. She had said so twice on the walk over.

"Three, two, one, go," Ariel called. Leah released the ball. It wobbled along the broom handles, past the recycling bins, and knocked softly against the garage door. Ariel clicked the stopwatch and wrote the number on the clipboard: 2.1 seconds for four meters. They did it again. 2.0 seconds. Again. 2.2. Leah plotted each dot on her graph paper, and a line was starting to show, tidy and climbing.

Then the fourth roll went wrong. The ball seemed to hesitate near the paint cans, and the stopwatch read 3.4 seconds. Leah's stomach dropped. She plotted the dot anyway, and it sat far below the others like a stone in a pond. Her whole graph would bend toward it. Tomorrow she had to stand in the gymnasium and explain a crooked line to Mr. Côté.

"That's it," Ariel said, clicking the pen shut. "One weird roll. Just erase it."

Leah stared at the dot. She thought about her neighbor, who had once judged a whole jar of pennies by weighing one handful, and how wrong he had been until he weighed three. She didn't want to erase. "Let's roll five more times," she said. "Same distance, same everything."

Ariel groaned but reset the stopwatch. They rolled and rolled. The readings came in at 2.1, 2.0, 2.2, 2.1, 2.0. None of them looked anything like 3.4. Leah wrote all six numbers in a column and found the average, adding them up and dividing by six. The average was close to 2.1 seconds, and the odd reading barely moved it. It was a small insight with a radical effect on her graph: the line straightened, and the strange dot sat alone below it, obviously wrong, obviously not the ball's real speed.

"Why was that one so slow, though?" Ariel asked.

Leah crouched beside the paint cans. The concrete there was rough, and something small and dark was wedged in a crack. She pried it out with her fingernail. A pebble, sharp-edged, exactly where the ball had slowed. The hidden cause had been sitting there the whole time, invisible until she looked for it.

She dropped the pebble into her pocket, because she wanted it taped to her poster board as evidence. "Average of six rolls," she said, and wrote it in big letters at the bottom of the graph. Then she flicked the ball down the lane one more time, just to watch it run clean.

Andrew spread the poster paper across Colton's kitchen table and weighted the corners with mugs from the cupboard. The sign-language club needed a banner for its booth at the school fair, and Colton had volunteered him because, as he put it, "You have neat handwriting and no other plans on a Saturday."

The design was easy: two hands, blue and gold, and the words JOIN THE SIGN LANGUAGE CLUB in big letters across the top. Andrew had gotten that far when Colton tapped the paper and pointed at the smaller line underneath, the one that read "Open to deaf students and everyone else." Colton wrote something in his notebook and turned it around: Should that d be capital?

Andrew stared at the word. Lowercase seemed right for an adjective, the way you'd write "tall students" or "new students." But Colton's question had a look behind it, like there was a trapdoor under the word and Colton knew exactly where it was. "Does it matter?" Andrew asked, and Colton grinned in a way that meant it absolutely mattered.

They raided Colton's bookshelf, which was stacked with books about sign language and Deaf history, and Andrew found a chapter that mentioned James Woodward. In 1972, Woodward had proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself. Andrew read it twice. So the little d described ears, and the big D described people who belonged to something, a whole culture built around a language, with its own schools and jokes and stories that Colton's family told at dinner with everyone laughing in signs.

Andrew tested his idea out loud. "So if the poster says the club is open to anyone, lowercase deaf covers the condition, but anyone who feels part of the culture can claim the big D." Colton thought about it, then nodded slowly, then shook his head and wrote: Make it capital. The club is about the culture, not about ears. Andrew got it. He had been thinking of deaf as a fact about a person's body, when Colton's club was really about a people.

Mr. Demir, the club's advisor, stopped by to drop off markers, and Andrew showed him the finished banner. "JOIN THE SIGN LANGUAGE CLUB," it read, "everyone welcome, Deaf and hearing." Mr. Demir, who never prescribed rules he could let students discover for themselves, only raised an eyebrow at the capital D and asked, "Whose motivation was that, capitalizing it?" Andrew pointed at Colton, and Colton pointed back at him. "Both of us," Andrew said. Mr. Demir smiled and said the change might be gradual for some people, but the poster looked ready to change a few minds in one afternoon. Andrew rolled up the banner, tucked it under his arm, and carried it out the door.

The lights at the farmhouse went out at suppertime, right in the middle of Connor's math homework. He heard his dad groan from the kitchen and the dog start barking at nothing. Connor found the flashlight in the hall drawer, then dug out a second one and carried it to his little sister, who was sitting very still on the stairs, afraid of the dark.

His dad was already out in the garage, dragging the portable generator toward the middle of the floor. Connor stood in the doorway and watched him set it down near the workbench, close to the door that opened into the kitchen. Dad was reaching for the pull cord when Connor's stomach did a small pivot, the kind it did before a race. Something was wrong here, and he was hesitant to say so, because Dad hated being corrected. Still, his mouth rebelled against staying shut.

"Dad, wait."

"What? Freezing's going to set in, buddy."

"Mr. Ngo did a whole unit on this in science. Generators give off carbon monoxide, so you have to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows. Never in a house or a garage. That's exactly what he said." Connor pointed at the garage walls around them. "And this is a garage."

Dad's hand stayed on the cord. He looked at the generator, then at the kitchen door, then at his son. "Your teacher say that?"

"Twice. He made us repeat it. He said the same rule goes for charcoal grills, too. Outdoors only, away from everything."

Dad straightened up and let out a long breath. "Well. Suppose I'd rather look slightly foolish than extremely sorry." He tipped the generator onto its wheels and rolled it out through the big garage door, across the gravel, and down near the fence at the far edge of the yard. Connor followed with the extension cord coiled over his shoulder, unspooling it behind them. They ran the cord through the window well, and when Dad pulled the cord, the generator coughed to life under the open sky, a safe distance from every door and window of the house.

Inside, a lamp clicked on and his sister whooped from the stairs. Dad set about lighting the gas stove, since the oven wouldn't work, and heated up a pot of soup while Connor spread a blanket on the living room floor. His sister settled between them with her flashlight balanced on her knee like a camp lantern.

Dad slurped his soup, then nudged Connor's elbow. "Tell Mr. Ngo he probably just kept this family warm and safe tonight, all at the same time."

"I'll tell him Monday," Connor said, and passed his sister the last of the bread.

Olivier posted the photo at 4:32 on a Saturday afternoon, standing between the escalators at the mall with his shoe halfway into the fountain. Darren had dared him, and Sonia had been laughing so hard she dropped her slushie. He captioned it "mall fountain legend" and tagged the location, then went to look at sneakers.

At 4:42 he thought better of it. Ms. Chatterjee, his neighbour, shopped at this mall every Saturday, and she knew his mother. He deleted the post, watched it vanish from his page, and felt fine about it. The photo had been up for ten minutes, which seemed like nothing.

On Sunday morning it was in the grade eight group chat. Sonia sent it to him first with a row of question marks. "I deleted that," he typed. "I know," she replied. "Darren screenshotted it before you did. So did three other people, I think." He scrolled up. There it was, with his face and the fountain and the location tag, saved on phones that were not his.

He called Darren. "Why did you keep it?"

"You deleted it, but I already had it," Darren said. "Deleting a post takes it off your page. It doesn't take it off my phone."

Olivier sat with that. So the delete button only cleaned his side of the street. Anything anyone had grabbed was still out there, in their cameras and their chats, and he could not reach any of it. He tried an experiment. He posted a second photo, a boring one of the food court, and asked Darren to screenshot it. Then he deleted it and asked Darren to send the screenshot back. It arrived in four seconds, whole and sharp. The page said the post no longer existed; the copy said otherwise.

On Monday he did a small survey at his locker, trying to be impartial about it instead of just embarrassed. He asked eleven kids whether they thought deleting a post made it gone. Nine said yes. Those nine, he realized, were the same nine who never covered their locker combinations with a hand. He sorted the results into a category he labelled "checks phone, believes phone" and showed Sonia the tally.

"Ms. Chatterjee is in the group chat," Sonia said suddenly, staring at her screen. "Her niece added her. She can see everything."

Olivier looked at the photo of his shoe in the fountain, now viewed by a woman who waved to him over the fence every morning. He pulled out his phone and typed, "Hi Ms. Chatterjee."

The war memorial sat on a hill above the school, its stone arch symmetrical on both sides, with names carved in neat rows. Autumn had a clipboard, a borrowed book from the library, and forty minutes before Ms. Sadeghi's class presentation on why settlers moved west in the 1800s. She had planned to be ready last night, but her poster had collapsed when the glue failed, and now she was rebuilding her whole argument.

Eliott was already there, sitting on the memorial's bottom step with his laptop open. "You brought the textbook?" he asked. Autumn dropped her bag beside him. "Ms. Sadeghi said we have to use a primary source," she said. "I think this counts." She pulled out the library book, a reprint of a diary written by a settler woman crossing the trail, and next to it her modern textbook chapter with its tidy maps.

Mouhamed came running up the hill, out of breath. "The bell rings in half an hour," he panted. "Is it true she won't accept the assignment late?"

Autumn looked down at the diary. The woman had written about bad harvests back home and how her husband wanted new land for agriculture, and how her sister had gone ahead the year before and sent letters that never said to come but never said not to, either. The textbook said the same thing in one flat paragraph: people moved west for farmland and opportunity. It was quicker. It was cleaner. She had quoted it twice in her first draft, and she wondered now whether she had done that because it was easier, or because she had not really understood what she was supposed to find.

"Okay, I have to decide," she said. She laid both books on the flat top of the memorial's base, where the carved names made a line between them. "The diary was written by the person who lived it, at the time. The textbook was written way later by somebody studying it. So the diary is the primary source, and the textbook is the secondary source." Eliott looked up from his laptop. "That's the word she used. Primary source. So quote the diary."

"Show me," Mouhamed said, leaning over her shoulder. Autumn read aloud the entry from October, where the woman wrote that the river had flooded their fields again and they would violate their lease if they stayed and could not pay, so they were leaving in the spring. Three sentences, and they said more than the whole textbook page. The diarist had not explained her reasons in a summary. She had mentioned a flood in passing, a worry about money, a sister out west, all mixed together with a headache and a broken wagon wheel.

"I almost used the easy one," Autumn admitted. She copied the entry onto a fresh card, word for word, and underlined the flood. "Last night I picked the textbook because it was faster. That was a mistake, I think. Or maybe not a mistake, just the lazy road." Mouhamed shrugged. "You found the diary eventually." Autumn packed the books, and the three of them started down the hill toward the school. Halfway down, she stopped and flipped her card over to add one more line, then ran to catch up. "First one to the door gets my extra granola bar," she called.

The waiting room of the eyeglasses store had a chart on the wall with rows of letters that shrank as they went down, and Sofia sat across from it while the optician flipped lenses in a frame that clamped onto her head like a bug. Her friend Lucille had sent her a text that morning: "Good luck. Also, did you finish the science homework? I only wrote two sentences about the extinction of the dinosaurs and Mr. Nwosu will notice." Sofia had typed back that she had written a whole paragraph and left out the part where she had copied half of it.

"Read the smallest line you can," the optician said.

"F, P, T, O, and then it gets fuzzy," Sofia said.

"Right eye, that's 20/40," the woman said, and wrote it on a card.

Sofia stared at the numbers. Lucille had told her once that her own vision was 20/20, and Sofia had assumed bigger numbers were better, the way a score of 40 beats a score of 20. Now she was not so sure, because nobody in the store looked impressed. She decided to test it. The chart hung on the wall and there were floor tiles, so she counted tiles to what she guessed was about 20 feet and stood there. At that distance the F and the P were clear, but when she walked forward to half that distance, they were just as clear and the next line down started to come into focus too. The letter she had been unable to read from across the room was easy up close. So the second number had something to do with how far away the letters were.

She walked back to the chair and asked the optician, "Does 20/40 mean I have to stand 20 feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from 40 feet?"

"That's exactly what it means," the woman said.

So the bigger number was worse, not better. Sofia paraphrased it in her head to make sure she had it: normal eyes read the line at double her distance, which meant her eyes were weaker, not stronger. She felt her ears go warm, because she had told Lucille last week that her eyes were probably better than everyone's. She pulled out her phone and texted: "Correction. 20/40 is not a good score. My eyes are the opposite of good. Also I will help you with the dinosaur thing."

The frame choices were on a spinning rack near the window. Sofia tried on a pair of black rectangles, then a pair of round wire ones that made her look like a substitute teacher. In the mirror, the price tags hung down over her cheeks, and each pair gave her a distinct reflection of the same face, one slightly squashed, one slightly wide. She picked the black rectangles because they stayed put when she shook her head.

The glasses would be ready in an hour, so she and her mother walked to the sandwich place next door. Through the window Sofia noticed that the sign across the street had words on it, actual words, not a gray smear with colored edges. She had been reading that street for years without knowing it was saying anything.

When she picked up the glasses and stepped outside, she stopped on the sidewalk and read the sign out loud. "Lucille," she said to her mother, pointing, "there's a Lucille in that sign. Lucille's Bakery. It's been there the whole time."

The sports bar smelled like fried pickles and shouted opinions, and Alexa slid into the booth between her dad and her little brother, who was already poking at the wall of televisions. On the biggest screen a commentator was saying that a quarterback had thrown for a "near-perfect 156.7." Her dad nodded like he knew exactly what that meant, but her brother frowned.

"Perfect should be a hundred," he said. "Like on a test."

Dad waved a wing at the screen. "Ratings are out of a hundred, buddy. That guy just rounds up."

Alexa didn't think that was right. She had watched the same commentator last week say "a perfect 158.3," and she remembered the number because it looked like somebody's street address, not like a score. A perfect score that wasn't 100 felt like a rule hiding somewhere, and hidden rules bothered her the way a pebble in a shoe bothered her foot. She pulled out her phone and typed "perfect quarterback rating."

Rayne, who had come with her own parents for the Sunday games, leaned over from the next booth. "Whatcha looking up?"

"Trying to conquer a weird number," Alexa said. On the screen, a stat box flashed: completions, attempts, yards, touchdowns, interceptions, all squashed at the end into one big bold number. That was the strange part, she realized. The commentator never mentioned the four little stats again, just the final figure, like they had all been squeezed through a funnel.

The page loaded. She read it twice, then turned the phone toward her dad. "It's called passer rating," she said. "It takes a bunch of passing statistics and combines them into one number, and the scale goes from zero all the way up to a maximum of 158.3."

Her dad squinted at the screen, then at his wing, then back. "Huh. I've been calling it a percentage for years."

"It's not a percentage at all," Alexa said. "It just gets talked about like one. And they rank the quarterbacks by it, so one guy ends up above another guy because of a number that has like four things packed inside it."

"So a hundred isn't perfect," her brother said slowly, like he was deciding whether to be annoyed or impressed. "One fifty-eight point three is."

"That's actually kind of cool," Dad admitted, and he raised his soda toward the screen. "To the weird number."

"Also," Rayne said, grinning, "your team's quarterback is ranked ninth, so maybe don't celebrate too hard."

Dad groaned and covered his eyes. Alexa slid her a handful of napkins and started copying the little stats from the screen. "We'll do the guy from your team next," she said. "Number two in the whole league."

Elijah arrived at his aunt's backyard barbecue carrying a shoebox of index cards, because Mr. Baptiste's assignment was due Tuesday and he had promised himself he would finish it before the potato salad ran out. The project asked students to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death, and he had picked Islam and Hinduism. His problem was simpler and more urgent: he had twenty-two cards, two religions, and no idea how to make the comparison fair.

His cousin Miller spotted the box before Elijah even set it down. "Is that the project? Can I help? I want to be in education when I grow up, so I need teaching experience." Miller was nine and announced his future career roughly once a week, but he was persistent, and Elijah was short on helpers.

They spread the cards on the picnic table between the bean dip and the watermelon. Some cards came from interviews Elijah had done. One, written in his uncle's careful handwriting, said that in Islam each person lives one life, and after death waits for the Day of Judgment. "It's called Yawm al-Qiyamah," his uncle said, drifting over with a plate of ribs. "That's the day everyone is raised and judged, and then sent to paradise or hell." He took a rib and wandered off, leaving Elijah to stare at the card.

"Okay," Miller said. "So how do we organize these?"

Elijah tried sorting the cards by topic first, then by religion, then by which ones had the word "judgment" on them. It kept going wrong. Finally he had an idea he could actually test. "What if we classify them by the number of lives? Islam says one. Hinduism says many. That's the whole difference, right there." He made two piles and held them side by side. One pile had a single straight line: live, die, wait, be raised, be judged, go to paradise or hell. The other pile looped back on itself, life after life after life.

From across the yard, their neighbor Mr. Baptiste, who had come for the pie, leaned over the table. "Careful with that looping pile," he said, tapping it. "Some of my students think reincarnation looks sinister on paper, like a trap. Then they talk to my aunt, who explains it as a journey. Same drawing, different feeling." He smiled at the watermelon. "That's your real comparison, by the way. Not just what happens, but how each story treats getting there."

Elijah wrote "one life, one judgment" beside the first pile and "many lives" beside the second, then drew the straight line and the loop. Miller copied the chart onto a napkin and announced he had "basically co-taught this."

"You made a treaty with me," Miller said. "Helpers get first dessert."

"That was never the treaty," Elijah said, but he was already handing him a slice of pie.

Jack had the twelve-bar blues written on a folded sheet of paper, and he had memorized it wrong, though he did not know that yet. Ms. Foster had put the school's rhythm section together in the music room after last bell: a drummer named Shea, a bass player named Madilyn, and Jack on trumpet, which he had only picked up in September.

"Count the bars," Ms. Foster said. "Don't watch your fingers. Listen to the bass." Then she sat at the piano to comp chords and left the rest to them.

Jack's solo started well. He found a few notes that swaggered, low and bent, and Shea's drums pushed him forward like a hand between his shoulder blades. The music room windows were open, and the sound went out over the estuary behind the school, where the river met the tide in wide brown channels. Jack closed his eyes and thought about that meeting of waters, and he lifted his solo up, reaching for the change.

The change did not come. Madilyn kept plowing along on the same deep note, and Jack's high, bright line landed on top of it like a shoe on a birthday cake. The sound was ugly and distinct, one layer clashing against another, and his ears burned even before he opened his eyes.

"Bar five," Madilyn said, not unkindly. "You went up in four."

"But the pattern repeats every four bars," Jack said. "I counted it."

"That's what contradicts you, though," she said. "In the most basic twelve-bar blues, the band stays on the I chord for the first four bars and moves to the IV chord in bar five." She tapped her bass. "Four bars home, then one bar of change. You have to wait me out."

Jack unfolded his paper and looked at the chart again, and there it was, plain as a stop sign, the IV printed at the top of the fifth bar. He had counted in fours and assumed the harmony counted in fours too. It did not. The band held home longer than he expected, and that was the whole secret.

"Let me try again," he said. "Shea, count the bars out loud."

They ran it twice more. The first time, Jack watched Madilyn's left hand and let her fingers tell him where the harmony lived, and though his solo was careful, almost timid, nothing crashed. The second time he closed his eyes again, and this time he waited. One, two, three, four bars of the low home chord, and only then, on five, when Madilyn's hand shifted, he rose with it, and his line and hers braided together over the drums.

At the end Ms. Foster wrote something on a sticky note and put it on his music stand before she left the room. "That last chorus," it said, "is the one. Same time Thursday."

Jack folded the note into his pocket next to the chart, put his trumpet in its case, and clicked the latches shut.

Norah spread the photocopied diary pages across the library table and flattened the curling corner with her pencil box. The assignment from Ms. Goh said one thing in bold letters: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. The diary, written by a settler named Hannah Barlow in 1846, was supposed to be her evidence. The trouble was that Hannah Barlow wrote about everything, from spoiled bacon to her sister's wedding, and Norah had until Friday to make sense of it.

"Find anything?" Cassia dropped into the chair opposite, holding a page so close to her face that her breath fogged the plastic sleeve. "I just found the word precipitation in here. She complains about it twice. That's my exciting discovery of the day."

"Great. Weather complaints." Norah slid a page across. "I need actual reasons, not complaints."

Jazmin arrived with three granola bars and sat down. "Ms. Goh said my last draft was, quote, competent but not convincing." She tore open a wrapper. "Which is teacher for boring. So I'm starting over, and I'm taking your diary leftovers."

At home that night, Norah read the diary again with a pencil, underlining every line where Hannah explained a decision. On the fourth page, Hannah wrote that the family's Missouri neighbors had all left after the banks failed and the bugs took the corn two years running. On the fifth page, Hannah's father said Oregon soil was supposed to be so rich a man could grow anything, and that land there was nearly free for the asking. Norah stopped. The failures were pushing the family out of Missouri. The land was pulling them toward Oregon. She wrote two columns on a scrap of paper and started sorting every reason she'd underlined into one or the other.

The next morning she showed the columns to Cassia and Jazmin before class. "Push reasons and pull reasons," she said. "The bugs push them out of Missouri, and the free land pulls them west."

"Those are called push factors and pull factors," Cassia said, without looking up from her page. "It was on the board yesterday when you were sharpening your pencil for ten minutes."

"You watched me sharpen a pencil and said nothing?"

"It was a very good pencil. Also, I have this line where Hannah writes she'd rather be eaten by bears in Oregon than stay one more winter in Missouri. Which column is the bear?"

"That's not a factor, that's a mood," Jazmin said, and laughed so hard Ms. Goh looked over from her desk.

On Friday, Norah stood at the front of the room with the diary pages clipped to a poster of her two columns. "I cite the entry from April 1846, where Hannah Barlow writes that the banks failed and the corn was ruined," she said, pointing to the left column, "and the entry from May, where her father describes free land in Oregon." She tapped the right column. "The family was pushed out of Missouri and pulled west, and both kinds of reasons show up in her own words." She stepped back and looked at the poster, then at the class, and waited for the first question.

Jacob spread three cereal boxes across the library table and frowned at them. His problem was real: the school was holding a contest for the best advertisement for the library's new reading club, and the winning poster would hang in the front hall for a whole year. He wanted that spot badly. Mr. Yoon, the librarian, had told the class to persuade people, and Jacob had discovered, after an hour of staring at boxes shouting "NEW!" and "EVERYONE LOVES IT!", that he had no idea how persuasion actually worked.

Selena dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of books. "You look like the boxes insulted you."

"They kind of did. Look at this one. 'Everybody's switching to Crunch-O's.' If everybody switched, why does it need a giant ad?" Jacob turned the box toward her. "And this says 'criminally delicious.' What does that even mean?" He copied the phrases onto his notepad, one per line, and then wrote a heading above them: tricks?

Selena leaned in. "My brother calls that a bandwagon appeal. The ad wants you to feel left out."

That word, bandwagon, snagged something in Jacob's memory. He flashed back to last fall, when his class had stood in the World War II gallery at the museum, in front of a wall of old government posters. He remembered the crowd of faces, the bold colors, the slogans repeating the same idea over and over. Selena had read the placard beside them out loud, slowly, because the words were long. "In March 1933," she had said, "Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda." A whole ministry, just for persuasion, Jacob had thought at the time. Then Matias had whispered, "Public enlightenment and propaganda? Those are basically opposites stuck together," and they had all stood there a little longer than they needed to.

Back at the library table, Jacob had an idea he could actually test. He wrote two identical posters on scrap paper: JOIN THE READING CLUB, and EVERYONE'S ALREADY IN THE READING CLUB, DON'T MISS OUT, plus one celebrity line, "Matias says it's awesome." He showed both to a sixth grader walking past the returns desk and asked which made her want to join. She pointed at the second one instantly. Then he swapped the loaded words out for plain ones and asked again. She hesitated and picked the plain poster. So the tricks worked, he thought, but only when they were there, like lights on a machine. A whole network of posters and radio spots had done the same thing in 1933, and it hadn't been for cereal.

He pulled out a clean sheet. He would advocate for the reading club, but with a poster that showed real kids and real books, not a fake crowd. When he started sketching, the faces he drew were the ones he actually saw every Tuesday: Selena with her stack, Matias with the graphic novels, the sixth grader by the desk.

Mr. Yoon paused behind them on his way past. "Now that one," he said, tapping the blank corner of the page, "I'd put in the front hall."

Aria pushed the flashlight closer to the basketball she had propped on a stack of dictionaries. Her presentation for science was due Friday, and she had decided to explain why Earth's tilt causes the seasons by acting them out in her living room. She tilted the basketball with a chopstick taped to its side, marked a dot for their city, and walked the whole setup around the lamp on the coffee table. When the dot leaned toward the light, the beam landed bright and concentrated. When it leaned away, the same beam spread thin and pale. So far, so good.

The problem showed up on slide four. She had written "June 21, the longest day of the year, is the hottest day of the year," and something about it nagged at her. She remembered August. She remembered lying on the kitchen floor last August with every fan in the house pointed at her, while in late June she had still been wearing a sweatshirt in the mornings. She frowned at the slide. Maybe her memory was just vague, mixed up from too many summers mashed together.

She called Jeremiah, who kept a thermometer log on his windowsill for a project he never finished. "Read me your numbers," she said, and he did, digging through a crumpled notebook while his little sister shouted about markers in the background. The highest temperatures were all from the end of July and the first weeks of August. "So the longest day isn't the hottest," Aria said slowly. "The hottest weeks come later, after the longest day." Jeremiah said that sounded wrong, and then said he had to go find the markers before his sister drew on the wall.

Aria sat with the flashlight and the basketball a long time. She tried to evaluate her whole presentation, not just slide by slide but as a story that would make sense to Sabrina, who asked a question about everything. Land and oceans must take time to warm up, she realized, the way the lake near her grandmother's house stayed cold into July even when the air was warm. The heat built up slowly and hung around. She deleted the wrong sentence and typed a new one, then changed her last slide so it ended with a question for the class instead of a fact she hadn't checked.

There was a knock, and Mr. Liu from next door stood on the porch holding a plate of plum slices because his tree had gone wild again.
