Gavin sat on his grandfather's porch steps with his history notebook open on his knees, staring at the question Ms. Francis had written on the board before vacation: How did the Treaty of Versailles help lead to the Second World War? He was supposed to explain it in a paragraph when school started again, and so far his page held only the word "Because."

"You look like a boy trying to diagnose a car that won't start," his grandfather said, coming out with two glasses of lemonade.

"I have to explain a treaty," Gavin said. "It limited Germany's army after World War One. That's all I know. But then World War Two happened, so did the limit not matter? Was it a bad treaty? I can't figure out what to write."

His grandfather settled into the wicker chair. "Walk with me after your lemonade. There's a memorial at the corner of the cemetery, names from both wars on the same stone."

They walked down the gravel lane, past the fence and the rows of markers. The memorial was a gray obelisk, shorter than Gavin expected. On one face the names from the first war crowded together, and on the facing side, the second war's names started lower down. Gavin ran his finger along them.

"The army was limited to one hundred thousand soldiers," he said slowly. "That's fewer people than a lot of cities. And Germany wasn't allowed an air force at all. So a country that big, told it could barely have soldiers and no planes. That's like taking away someone's lunch every single day."

"Somebody took your lunch once," his grandfather said.

"Andrei did, in fourth grade, before he was my friend. For a week I just took it. Then I got so angry I shoved him into the fence, and we both got in trouble." Gavin looked at the stone again. "The treaty did the first part. It told Germany it was small when it wasn't. Then somebody promised to make Germany big and strong again, and people listened because the anger was already there."

He pulled the notebook out of his back pocket and wrote while standing, hunched over the obelisk's base. Later, back at the house, he read his paragraph aloud over dinner. His grandmother stopped peeling potatoes to listen. His grandfather said it was the most robust argument anyone had made at that table since his uncle debated the whole family about heritage tomatoes versus regular ones.

On the first morning back, Ms. Francis asked for volunteers. Andrei's hand shot up, and behind him Abdullah elbowed Gavin until he raised his too. When Gavin finished reading, his voice steadier than he expected, Ms. Francis said, "You explained cause and effect better than the textbook does."

At recess, Andrei found him by the fence. "You compared a whole country to me stealing a sandwich."

"To you stealing my sandwich," Gavin said, and Andrei laughed so hard he had to sit down on the curb.

Peyton slapped three quarters onto the picnic table beside her lemonade stand and counted the morning's earnings out loud. "Fourteen dollars and fifty cents. Mr. Pelletier, if you buy two more cups, I can hit twenty by noon." Her neighbor chuckled and held out his glass for a refill.

Mustafa pedaled up the driveway on his bike, dropped it in the grass, and grabbed a cup without asking. "Did you hear about Josh?" he said. Peyton leaned forward, napkins still in her hand. "He put all his birthday money into that company everybody was shouting about, the one from the videos. Sixty dollars, every dollar he had." Mustafa drained half the cup. "My brother says the whole thing fell apart. Josh's sixty dollars turned into zero. Nothing left."

Peyton set down the pitcher. Her mouth went dry even with lemonade in it. Last week in Mr. Pelletier's garage, while he fixed her bike chain, he had asked her whether she would rather own a piece of a company or lend money to one. She had shrugged then. Now her brain was racing. Owning a piece, a stock, meant if the company grew, your piece grew. But if the company failed completely, the stock price could fall all the way to zero, and you could lose every dollar you put in. Josh had just lived that.

"Lending is different," she said slowly, watching condensation drip off the pitcher. "If you lend a company money, a bond, you're not owning anything. You just expect to be paid back." She flipped over a paper cup and drew two columns with a marker, stock on one side, bond on the other. "Josh owns a piece of nothing now. Zero." Her conscience pricked her a little, sketching out his disaster on a lemonade cup, but she wanted to understand it before she felt sorry about it.

"That's why stocks are riskier," Mustafa said, peering at the cup. Peyton nodded so fast her ponytail bounced. "Risk isn't just prices wiggling around. It's the whole thing going to zero."

A car pulled up and Josh himself climbed out, holding an empty jar. He walked over slowly. "My mom said I should earn some money back. Got a job for me?"

Peyton looked at her pitcher, half full, then at the twenty-dollar goal written on her sign. She handed him the marker. "Write your name under mine. But first, one rule." She tapped the paper cup with the two columns. "Nobody puts the whole cashbox into one thing. We restrict ourselves to spending on cups and sugar, and we split what's left. Deal?"

Josh uncapped the marker and grinned for the first time all morning. "Deal. Now hand me a lemon."

Taylor crouched beside the fold-up table at the edge of the skate park, holding a multimeter in both hands like it might bolt. Her science project was due Friday, and she had one shot tonight. The idea was simple: measure the voltage across a wire, measure the current through it, divide, and get the wire's resistance. Oceanne had promised to write down every number, and Brayden had promised to keep the skaters from grinding over the equipment.

"Three point four volts," Taylor read off the screen. "Current is one point seven amps. Write it down." Oceanne scratched the number into her notebook while a board rattled past on the concrete behind them. Taylor did the division twice in her head. "Two ohms. Okay, that's our answer. Two ohms."

"Want to check it again?" Oceanne asked. She was the kind of friend who double-checked everything, including her own locker combination.

Taylor ran the test again. Same wire, same battery pack, same clips biting the same spots. "Three point six volts. One point seven amps." She frowned. That came out to a bit more than two ohms. Not much more, but more. She waited a minute, letting a plane drone overhead and the smell of hot rubber drift from the halfpipe, then ran it a third time. The number crept up again.

"That's weird," Brayden said, rolling back toward them with his helmet crooked. "The wire doesn't change. Same wire, same everything. How can the answer change?"

Taylor touched the wire with one fingertip and pulled back fast. It was warm, warmer than the evening air, warmer than it had been when they started. She looked at her three scribbled results. The first reading had come right after they clipped everything together, back when the wire was still cool. The last one came after the current had been flowing for a while. "It's hot," she said slowly. "The wire's hot, and the answer got bigger. Every time."

Oceanne flipped back a page in her notebook. "So when it was cool, we got two. Then a little more. Then a little more again." She tapped her pencil on the numbers like she was playing them on a piano.

Taylor unclipped the battery and let the wire sit. She watched Oceanne sketch a ramp in the margin and Brayden attempt, badly, to distribute the leftover granola bars into three uneven piles. After ten minutes she touched the wire again. Cool. She clipped the battery back on, took one fast reading, and then made herself wait, counting under her breath while the wire warmed, taking readings at each minute mark. The resistance climbed, small step after small step, the whole way up.

"It only holds still when the temperature holds still," Taylor said, copying the numbers into a clean column. "So the steady answer, the real one for a cool wire, is that first quick reading. The rest is the wire heating up under the test." She looked at Oceanne's notebook, then at her own, and felt something settle that felt almost like landing a trick. "We'll take the reading fast, before it warms. And we'll say so right on the poster."

"Mr. Yang is going to think we made that up," Oceanne said, but she was already underlining the column, pressing hard enough that the pencil made a robust, dark line.

"He'll test it himself," Taylor said. "That's the good part." She picked up the multimeter and clipped the leads back on for one more run, just to watch the first number come out clean.

Lincoln sat at the kitchen table wrapped in his grandmother's quilt, staring at the same glass of orange juice he had ignored for an hour. His throat felt like sandpaper, his nose was a faucet, and worst of all, tomorrow was the regional chess tournament, the one he had earned a spot in by beating Nikola twice in the qualifiers. His mom set a bowl of soup in front of him and felt his forehead with the back of her hand.

"Maybe Dr. Patel can call in antibiotics," Lincoln said, spooning steam toward his face. "Nikola got antibiotics last year when he was sick, and he was back at school in two days. If I got some today, I could still play tomorrow."

His mom tilted her head. "You want me to call and ask?"

"Please." He sneezed into a tissue, then added, "It's the tournament. Coach says it's a privilege to be seeded this high, and I don't want to waste it."

While his mom made the call in the hallway, Lincoln heard a knock. Nikola stood at the door holding a thermos and a paper bag, and behind him was Trystan, balancing a chessboard under one arm. They came in and crowded the kitchen, Nikola pouring hot lemon tea that smelled sharp and sweet.

"Nikola," Lincoln said, "when you took antibiotics, what did you actually have?"

"A strep throat," Nikola said. "Mr. Shin explained it to the whole science class afterward, actually. But wait, I thought you missed that day."

Lincoln's brain, foggy as it was, lurched into gear. Strep. He pulled his laptop across the table and typed, sniffling. Trystan leaned over his shoulder. The screen filled with the answer, and Lincoln read it out loud, his voice cracking. "Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they don't help cure a cold or the flu." He sat back. "Strep is bacteria. That's why Nikola got better fast. But this," he pointed at his own red nose, "is a virus. Antibiotics would do nothing. I could take the whole bottle and I'd still be sneezing through the tournament."

His mom came back in, phone in hand. "Dr. Patel said the same thing, honey. Rest and fluids."

Lincoln pushed the soup closer and took a spoonful. It burned pleasantly going down. He tested one small idea out loud, ticking it off. "So if it's a virus, my immune system does the work, and sleeping is basically my move. If I sleep all afternoon and all tonight, maybe I'm functional by nine a.m."

"Functional enough to lose to me in round two," Trystan said, setting up the board. "I registered as an alternate."

"You're infectious, you know," Nikola said, backing up a step and grinning.

Lincoln laughed, which turned into a cough, which turned into Nikola patting his back and sliding the tea closer. "Okay, board away, germ boy. We'll set up a video call tomorrow so you can watch us play."

"Round two," Trystan said, snapping a pawn onto the table, "is mine."

"We'll see," Lincoln croaked, and raised his spoon like a sword.

Peyton loved Saturdays at Grandma's house, mostly because nobody woke her up. She slept until noon, ate cold pizza on the porch, and texted Giselle about nothing in particular. But on Monday mornings back home, her body felt like a phone at two percent battery. Her stomach knotted up before she even got on the bus, and last week she'd nearly cried over a missing math worksheet. She couldn't see what was causing it, which was the part that bugged her most.

"I think you just hate Mondays," Giselle said when Peyton described it at lunch. "Everyone does. It's basically a law."

Peyton didn't dismiss the idea out loud, but she didn't buy it either. Jasleen was fine on Mondays, and Peyton hadn't hated Mondays back in September, when soccer practice had forced her to bed early every night. Something had changed since then. She started keeping a note in her phone: bedtime, wake time, and how her stomach felt before school. By Thursday she had a suspicion, but she needed more data.

That weekend she was back at Grandma's, who was sorting seed catalogs at the kitchen table. "Still planning your vegetable garden?" Peyton asked, picking up a catalog with a cover full of tomato photographs. Grandma nodded and said agriculture had been her whole childhood, waking before dawn to help on the farm, every day, no exceptions. "Even Sundays?" Peyton asked. Grandma laughed. "Especially Sundays. The cows didn't know what a weekend was."

That night Peyton lay in the guest room bed scrolling on her phone, and her stomach was already doing its tight little Monday rehearsal, even though Monday was two days away. She mentioned it to Jasleen on a video call, and Jasleen read something off a health website: keeping the same sleep and wake times every day, weekends included, kept the body steady. "It's called your circadian rhythm," Jasleen said, pronouncing it carefully. Peyton sat straight up. Same time every day. Like the cows. Like soccer season, when she'd gone to bed at ten and gotten up at seven, even after Saturday games, because her dad drove her to early practice. The knot in her stomach had never shown up back then.

So she ran a test on herself. Friday night at Grandma's, she set an alarm for 7:30, turned her phone face down at ten, and did the slow breathing thing Ms. Quinn had shown the whole class after the fire drill: in for four counts, out for six. When the tight feeling crept in, she breathed through it instead of scrolling past it. Saturday morning she woke up tired but not wrecked. Sunday she did it again, even though Grandma offered pancakes at nine and Peyton had already been awake for ninety minutes.

Monday morning, on the bus, Peyton filled in her phone note: stomach, calm; brain, awake. It might be temporary, she knew, one good day out of many bad ones. But she'd already decided. Next Saturday at Grandma's, the alarm was staying on.

"Seven-thirty again?" Giselle texted her that afternoon.

Peyton typed back, "Same time every day. Even weekends."

The library computers were supposed to be for the history project, but Justin had baseball-reference open in one tab and a page about medieval peasants in the other, and the baseball tab was winning. He was supposed to be writing about farming in the Middle Ages, and he had gotten exactly one sentence down, something about how a peasant worked the same strips of field year after year. His friend Mickael leaned over from the next computer.

"Look up David Justice versus Derek Jeter," Mickael said. "Me and my uncle argued about it all weekend. Justice was better in the nineties, no question."

Justin typed the names in. The comparison page loaded, and he scrolled to the batting averages. In 1995, Justice was higher than Jeter. In 1996, Justice was higher again. "See?" Mickael said. "Twice in a row. Case closed."

But there was a third row, the combined line for both seasons together, and Justin stopped with his finger halfway to the screen. Combined, Jeter was higher. He read it twice, then clicked the little button that split the page year by year, thinking maybe the site had made a mistake. It hadn't. Justice won 1995. Justice won 1996. Add them together and Jeter won.

"Lexa," Justin called across the library, not quite loud enough to get them kicked out. "Come look at this. It's broken."

Lexa had her own project on her screen, a poster about flood statistics for the science fair, and she was hunting for a number impressive enough to print in big letters. She dragged her chair over anyway, because Lexa could never resist a puzzle. Justin showed her the three lines. "He beats him both years and loses both years added up. How is that even possible?"

"That's like my flood numbers," Lexa said slowly, tapping the screen. "One big flood year can swing everything, and the headline just squishes it into one number." She narrowed her eyes. "Who decides which number becomes the headline, though? That's what I want to know."

Mr. Bighorn, the librarian, paused behind them on his rounds, but he only looked at the screen, raised one eyebrow, and moved on toward the shelf returns without a word.

Justin sat back. All afternoon, the sports page and the news had been handing him single numbers, and he had just accepted them, the way he'd accepted that the Middles Ages were one gray lump of mud. He wondered how many of those numbers were hiding something the way this one was. Maybe the trick was being systematic, checking the pieces every single time instead of trusting the summary. He couldn't prove that yet, but it felt like the kind of thing a person could quantify, counting how often a headline number matched its own parts.

"Forget my uncle," Mickael said, pulling out his phone. "He's going to lose his mind when I show him this. Text me the link."

"First," Justin said, "help me pick a headline number for Lexa's poster."

Colton stared at his story draft and counted the quotation marks. Seven. Four of them opened dialogue and three closed it, which meant somewhere a character was still talking, possibly forever. Ms. Teo had circled the mess in red and written "Clarify who is speaking!" at the top. The story was about a giant mutant larva that crawled out of the compost bin behind the cafeteria, and it was supposed to be his best work of the year, but right now it read like a ransom note.

"Your larva story?" Reese said at lunch, leaning over his shoulder. She pulled out her own draft and flipped it to the back, where she had sketched a mountain. "Look. I draw my whole plot like this. Rising action climbs the slope, the climax sits at the peak, and everything after falls back down the other side." She tapped the summit. "My peak is when the mask comes off. It's called Freytag's pyramid. Some German guy, Gustav Freytag, wrote a book about drama in 1863, and that's where it comes from."

"That's radical," Colton said. "But where's my peak? My larva just eats stuff for two pages and then it's Tuesday."

"Exactly. You've got a hill, not a mountain. Put something huge at the top and then let it fall." She slid the paper toward him. "Also, new speaker, new paragraph. That fixes half your punctuation."

Colton spent the evening testing her idea on graph paper. He drew the pyramid, wrote LARVA EATS THE PRINCIPAL'S CAR at the peak, and then mapped the falling side: the larva shrinks, the town forgives it, the science club adopts it as a mascot. When his mom asked why he was drawing triangles on his homework, he said, "Plot geometry," and she left him alone. The dialogue he rewrote line by line, whispering each part in a different voice so he could hear where one speaker stopped and the next one started. Whenever a line needed a tag, he added one; whenever two lines in a row belonged to the same mouth, he joined them.

The next morning he handed his draft to Shane, who read it silently and then aloud, doing the larva as a monster truck announcer. Every quotation mark landed where it should. "The car scene gave me chills," Shane said. "Actual chills."

At the end of class, Ms. Teo held up Colton's paper. "This one works," she said. "Strong peak, clean fall, and I can always tell who's talking." Colton grinned at Reese across the room and drew a tiny triangle in the corner of his notebook, then wrote one word inside it: sequel.

Victor tapped the whiteboard marker against his palm and stared at the blank whiteboard like it had insulted him. In twenty minutes, the Geography Club would file into Room 12, and he would run his first real meeting as president. Last month's meeting had been a disaster he still could not diagnose: forty minutes on whether to buy cheese crackers or pretzels for the fundraiser, and then the bell rang before anyone discussed the actual fundraiser. He had replayed it in his head all week and finally landed on a hidden cause. Nobody had written down what else to discuss, so the snack question, being the only question on the table, had swallowed everything.

Paisley arrived first, dropped her backpack on a desk, and eyed the empty whiteboard with open skepticism. "You have a plan this time, or are we voting on crackers again?"

"We are not," Victor said, and he wrote AGENDA in tall letters.

Anouk slid in behind her. "Ooh, official." She pronounced it "ah-GEN-dah," like a spell.

"It's Latin," Victor said. "It means things to be done." He had found that out Tuesday, in the dictionary, while pretending to research rivers. "And it lists the topics in the order we'll discuss them." He wrote 1. Fundraiser, 2. Field trip, 3. Snacks, and put a hard little period after the 3.

"Snacks last?" Paisley said. "Bold."

"Snacks last," Victor said, "because snacks can survive until 3:40. The field trip cannot."

Mr. Tse poked his head in, since the club was technically his to supervise. He studied the board, raised one eyebrow, and said only, "Carry on," which felt like a medal.

The meeting began, and Victor discovered that an agenda was a leash made of paper. When Paisley started a lush, wandering story about her cousin's trip to a rainforest exhibit, Victor tapped item one. "Table that under field trip inspiration," he said, and Paisley grinned and steered back to poster paper prices. When Anouk debated whether the raffle prize should be a globe or an atlas, he pointed to item two, and the field trip conversation absorbed the question like a sponge. Twenty minutes in, they had chosen a poster format, picked the museum, and even settled the globe-atlas fight, because the museum gift shop sold both.

"Item three," Victor announced, feeling like a game show host.

"Cheese crackers," Paisley and Anouk said together, then looked delighted with themselves.

"Pretzels," said Victor, and everyone groaned, and the bell rang before the argument could eat anything but the last four minutes.

Anouk pulled on her backpack and paused at the door. "Same agenda thing next time?"

"Same agenda thing," Victor said, and underlined the 3 on the board one extra time, just for the crackers.

"Where are you from?" asked Ms. Kelly, and the new girl, Isa, opened her mouth and then closed it again.

The class discussion was supposed to be about heritage posters. Everyone had brought one: Kaley had taped up photos of her grandmother's village, and Anais had drawn a map of her mother's hometown with arrows pointing to everywhere the family had lived since. But Isa had come in with nothing, and now she stood at the front of Ms. Kelly's room twisting the strap of her backpack.

"I've lived in four countries," Isa said. "My dad works for a company that moves us. But when people ask where I'm from, I don't know what to say. My parents' home culture isn't mine, really. I wasn't born in most of the places we lived. So." She shrugged and stared at the floor tiles.

Anais's hand went up before she had decided to raise it. Last year a boy had asked her the same question in the cafeteria, and she had said the name of her mother's town, even though she had never lived there, and the answer had felt like a coat that belonged to somebody else. She had thought about that lie for months. "There's a word for it," she said now. "I found it when I was making my poster. My aunt has it too. A sociologist named Ruth Hill Useem, in the 1950s, coined the term 'third culture kid' for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture."

Isa looked up. "Third culture kid. Say it again?"

"Third culture kid," Anais said, and the words sat differently in the room than the map on the wall behind her.

Kaley frowned. "So you're from a country that doesn't exist?"

"Sort of from all of them and none of them," Isa said slowly, like she was testing a bridge with her foot before stepping on it. She pulled a marker from her backpack and went to the whiteboard. "Can I make my poster out of this? Four flags, and then a box in the middle that just says TCK?"

"That's the assignment, more or less," Ms. Kelly said, and moved aside.

Isa drew fast, four rectangles and a crooked box, and under it wrote her name, her real one, the one that had never needed a country attached. She tapped the box twice with the marker and turned around. "Okay," she said. "Next question."

At the Saturday farmers' market, Xavier stood in front of Ms. Lau's stall, where the tomatoes were piled so lush and red they looked like they had been painted that morning. He was on a mission. His grandmother had declared that anyone who wanted dinner at her table on Sunday had to help make it, and he had volunteered for the sauce. That meant onions, and onions meant chopping, which he had never done.

"Take a bag of the Romas," Ms. Lau said, weighing three onions, "and hold the knife like this when you cut." She curved her fingers inward on an invisible onion, knuckles forward, thumb tucked behind. "Claw grip. Your knuckles guide the blade, so it can't reach your fingertips." Xavier practiced the shape with his hand. It felt like a small, stubborn animal.

Back home, he set up on the counter and started to chop. The moment he pressed down, the cutting board shot sideways and the knife skidded off the onion. He tried again, slower. The board slid again, and the blade landed crooked, nowhere near where he'd aimed. He stared at the board. The counter was smooth, the board was smooth, and every push of the knife nudged the whole thing away like a hockey puck. That was the problem, he realized. Not his grip. The board itself.

He thought about what slid and what didn't. A wet bath mat didn't slide. The market's signs didn't blow away when the vendor weighted them with damp cloths on windy days. Maybe wet was the key. He ran a paper towel under the tap, wrung it out, and laid it flat under the cutting board. Then he curled his hand into the claw grip, set the blade against the onion, and pushed down. The board held. He chopped a full slice, then another, and the board stayed planted as if it had been glued. His eyes stung and watered, but he kept going, dicing the whole onion into small, even pieces.

On Sunday, his grandmother tasted the sauce, which had simmered with the market tomatoes, garlic, and a pinch of sugar, and asked where he'd learned to chop like a real cook. Xavier drafted his little cousin over to the counter to demonstrate. He ran a towel under the tap, placed it under the board, curved his fingers into the claw, and handed the boy a butter knife and half a banana.

"Every good consumer of onions should know this trick," he said, and his cousin laughed and chopped a slice clean through.

The spreadsheet was supposed to be easy, but Isla's numbers kept arguing with her. She was entering data for the science fair, burn times for four kinds of fabric, because her project asked which cloth was most flammable and how long each one took to catch. Ms. Rosen had shown the class once, back in September, and now the whole thing hinged on Isla remembering something she had half forgotten. The bell had rung, the lab was nearly empty, and her chart showed a bar taller than the ceiling for cotton and nothing at all for wool.

Then Veronica called from the kitchen, where the two of them had done the actual burning with Isla's dad and a pair of long tongs. "Okay, I found the paper," Veronica said. "Wool, forty seconds, and it's in 4C."

"4C," Isla repeated, and typed 40 into cell 4C, except there was no cell 4C, because the rows were numbered and the columns were lettered, going across. The screen put her 40 somewhere on the wrong side of everything. She stared at it. The columns ran A, B, C, left to right, and the rows ran 1, 2, 3, going down. So an address had to start with the letter. She said it out loud to herself. "C4 is the cell in column C, row 4." She dragged the 40 down to C4, where it belonged.

"Did you say something?" Veronica asked.

"I said your directions are backwards. It's C4, not 4C."

"I was reading it off the paper sideways," Veronica said, which explained nothing and made them both laugh so hard the phone crackled.

Isla checked the rest of the column. Two more numbers had landed in the wrong row because she had rushed, which was why her sum had seemed impossible, and why the bar for cotton had towered over everything like it was trying to oppose the ceiling itself. She fixed each one, then clicked the empty cell at the bottom of the column and typed =SUM(C1:C4). The total appeared, small and believable, like a dog that had finally stopped barking.

The bar chart rebuilt itself as she watched, four bars of sensible heights, denim tallest, wool shortest. Edison leaned over from the next computer, where he was supposed to be logging out. "That's actually a decent chart," he said, which from Edison was practically a standing ovation.

"Tell that to the wool," Isla said, and hit print.

The invitation said Sakura House, and Theodore assumed it was just a restaurant until he pushed through the front door and nearly stepped on a row of shoes. Sneakers, loafers, one small pair of rain boots, all lined up on a lower floor of polished wood that dipped a step below the main level. Beyond it, the whole space opened up: tatami mats, low tables, and a counter where Lou's grandmother was arranging chopsticks like piano keys. Theodore stood at the edge, one sneaker hovering over the wood.

"You're in the genkan," Lou said, appearing from behind a curtain with a stack of menus. "The entrance. Shoes come off here, before you go inside."

Theodore stepped back onto the lower floor and unlaced his sneakers. A pair of slippers sat waiting in a neat spot, and he was almost certain they had not been there a second ago, which meant someone had noticed him coming and set them out on purpose. He slid his feet in. The slippers were slightly too big, but they made a soft shuffling sound that he decided he liked.

Lou's family owned the restaurant, and tonight they were having a celebration dinner for Lou's birthday, which was the whole reason Theodore was there. The problem was the gift. He had wrapped his present, a book about chess, in newspaper because his mother had used all the wrapping paper on her cousin's wedding gift, and now, watching Lou's grandmother present Lou with a small box wrapped in cloth so intricate it looked like origami, Theodore felt the newspaper in his bag like a stone.

At the low table, Theodore discovered more rules. Lou's father clapped his hands together before eating, quick and light, and everyone murmured something together, so Theodore clapped too, half a beat late. When Lou's grandmother poured tea into Theodore's cup, he picked it up and drank, and then noticed that nobody else had touched theirs yet. Lou leaned over. "We wait until everyone's poured. It's how we do it here. At Ivana's house you just start, remember? Her dad gets insulted if you don't eat everything fast."

Theodore filed that away. At his own house the rules were different again: elbows off the table, fork in the left hand because his grandfather said so, and no reaching past anyone's plate. He began to wonder whether there was some hidden pattern underneath all of it, some rule behind the rules. Maybe every family had a list nobody wrote down, and the only way to learn it was to watch for the moment when everyone did the same thing at the same time. He decided to test the idea right there. When the rice arrived, he kept his hands in his lap and his eyes on Lou's father, waiting.

The moment came with the gift. Lou's grandmother handed over the cloth-wrapped box, and Lou received it with both hands, bowed his head slightly, and then set it beside him, unopened. Theodore, who at his own birthday parties had torn paper off in front of everyone within ten seconds, watched carefully. So that was the rule here: gifts got both hands, and they waited. He reached into his bag, and before he could evaluate whether newspaper was too embarrassing, he held the lumpy package out with both hands, the way Lou had received the box.

Lou took it the same way, and his grandmother said something to his father that made them both smile. "She says you learn fast," Lou translated, tucking the present beside him, unopened.

Theodore bowed his head, just a little, and reached for his teacup.

Wyatt sat at the wobbly picnic table behind the art cabin, staring at his drawing of Main Street. He had drawn the road, the shops, and six lampposts, and every lamppost was exactly the same height, evenly spaced like fence posts. Lena leaned over his shoulder.

"It looks like a wall with lampposts glued on it," she said. "Not a street."

Wyatt was skeptical. "They're the same size in real life. Lampposts don't shrink."

Rayden slid his own drawing across the table. His street looked like it went somewhere. His lampposts started tall at the bottom of the page and got smaller and squeezed closer together until they nearly touched a single point far up the road. "Mr. Hu calls it the vanishing point," Rayden said. "All the lines go there."

Wyatt looked back and forth between the two drawings. His eye kept sliding along Rayden's street like it was being transported down the road itself. He took a fresh sheet and drew a horizon line, then one dot in the middle of it. He ran two lines from the bottom corners of the page straight to the dot, like railway tracks, and the space between them became the road.

Then the lampposts. He drew the first one big, right at the bottom edge. The second one he made smaller and put it a little farther along. The third smaller still, and closer to the next one. By the fifth, the lampposts were little more than pencil ticks, bunched together near the dot. It felt wrong, like lying about how tall lampposts were, but he kept going.

He held the drawing up next to Rayden's. Lena walked over and looked at both. "Yours goes back farther," she said. "Mine still looks flat." She took Rayden's pencil and started her own vanishing point.

Mr. Hu came around the cabin with his clipboard. He picked up Wyatt's first attempt, the flat wall one, and studied it. "You drew every post the same height," he said. "Same distance apart, too." Then he picked up the second drawing and didn't say anything at all for a moment.

"That one's mine," said a voice from behind the cabins. A kid Wyatt had never seen before, maybe thirteen, with paint on his sleeves, reached over and took the second drawing out of Mr. Hu's hand. "I left it on the table this morning."

Wyatt stared at the sheet in the kid's hand. He was certain he had drawn it, five minutes ago, on fresh paper. Then he looked down at the table, at the smudge of graphite by the clipboard, and at his own pencil, which had been sharpened that morning and was now suddenly long again.

"Where's my drawing?" Wyatt asked.

The kid flipped the sheet over. On the back, in Wyatt's own handwriting, it said, WYATT, TABLE 4. "Transport yourself to table four," the kid said, "and look under it." Wyatt crouched down. Taped beneath the table was his real drawing, the one with the shrinking lampposts, folded into a paper airplane pointed straight at the vanishing point of the room's far corner.

On Saturday morning, Gabriel stood beside his brother in the lobby of First Regional Bank, holding a garment bag. His brother had a job interview with the branch manager in twenty minutes, and his one good shirt was a disaster.

"It looks like it slept in a ball," his brother said, pulling it out. Creases ran across the front in hard lines, deep ones that no amount of stretching would fix.

Gabriel knew exactly how it had slept in a ball. The night before, he had run his first solo load of laundry while his brother was at work. He had sorted the colours carefully, following the phone call with Flynn, who had opinions about everything. "Separate the darks," Flynn had said, "and hot water shrinking things is controversial, so just use warm." Gabriel had stuffed the shirt into the dryer, heard the buzzer, and then gone to watch a video. He figured he would fold everything in the morning. What was the rush?

That morning, the shirt had come out of the dryer looking like a crumpled paper bag. Gabriel had pulled it out, laid it flat, and tried to smooth it with his hands. The wrinkles stayed. His brother had already left for the bank in his undershirt with a jacket over it, planning to change in the restroom, and he had texted Gabriel to bring the shirt.

Gabriel had an idea. He filled a spray bottle with water, dampened the shirt all over, and ran it back through the dryer for ten minutes while he stood there and watched it tumble the whole time. When the buzzer went off, he took it out immediately and folded it, warm, flat, and smooth. He slid it into the garment bag and rode his bike downtown.

In the bank restroom, his brother changed and looked in the mirror. The collar sat flat. The front was clean. "What did you do?"

"Ran it again and grabbed it the second it stopped," Gabriel said. "I left it in there all night before. That was the problem. You have to take stuff out right away and fold it, or it cools all crumpled."

His brother checked his tie in the mirror, then his watch. Waiting longer would only prolong his nerves, so he opened the restroom door and walked out into the lobby. A woman in a grey blazer was waiting by the desks with a folder in her hand.

"That's her," his brother whispered. "Wish me luck."

Gabriel gave him a thumbs up from the bench by the waiting area and texted Flynn: load one complete. Nobody lost a sock, the towels are folded, and I am never leaving anything in the dryer again.

Behind him, the teller called, "Next in line?" Gabriel stood, gathered the garment bag, and dropped the empty hanger into the trash.

Georgia spread her homework across the kitchen table and stared at the periodic table Ms. Ma had photocopied for the whole class. Tomorrow's quiz asked for the number of protons in an element, and Georgia had exactly one clue: the tiny number above each square. She was pretty sure it mattered, but she could not remember how.

Frederick arrived first, dropping his backpack on the counter and stealing a handful of crackers from the box above the toaster. Chad came next, still holding his lacrosse stick, because Chad brought the lacrosse stick everywhere, even to study sessions he had not been invited to. "You're only here," Georgia said, "because your mom said no screens until your science grade improves." Chad shrugged. "That is a legitimate reason. Also there are crackers."

They bent over the photocopy together. "Okay," Frederick said, tapping the top row. "Hydrogen, then helium. There's a one, then a two." His finger slid down the poster. "Lithium, three. Beryllium, four. It's counting." Georgia felt something click, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. "It counts up by one, all the way across." She flipped to the back of her worksheet, where Ms. Ma had written atomic number in the instructions, and looked again at the little numbers. "So the atomic number for oxygen is eight," she said slowly, "and the quiz wants protons."

She tested it the only way she could. She covered the poster with her hand and asked Frederick to name an element. "Carbon," he said. Georgia moved her hand just enough to peek. "Six. Carbon has six protons." She tried three more, and each time the pattern held, the numbers marching along in order, one more than the square before it. She wrote them down, checking twice.

Chad, meanwhile, had his own plan. "If I memorize the first ten elements tonight, Ms. Ma will let me back on the field by Thursday," he said, pacing the kitchen and chanting, "Hydrogen, helium, lithium." He paused at the window where the neighbor's cat sat watching them. "She's judging me." "That cat is not your colleague," Frederick said. "She has no idea what you're achieving tonight."

When Georgia's dad came in to start dinner, the table was covered with numbered scraps of paper and Chad had made it to neon without stopping. Georgia read her list once more, then again with her eyes shut. Eight protons in oxygen, six in carbon, one in hydrogen, each element exactly one more than the one before it all the way down the table. She slid the paper into her folder and zipped it shut. "Quiz me at breakfast," she said, and Chad, triumphant, said, "Neon. Ten."

Landon stood at the departure gate with his phone in one hand and his notes in the other, trying to explain monsoons to Kiera before their flight to visit his grandmother in Kerala. She was supposed to present with him in Ms. Rajapakse's class next week, and the whole thing depended on him getting it right.

"So the land heats up in summer," Kiera said, squinting at his messy diagram, "and then it rains for months? That part I get. But why does rice farming care?"

Landon glanced at the big window, where heat shimmered off the runway. He tried an experiment. He held his palm above his phone, which had been running warm in the sun, and then above the metal armrest of the chair. The phone felt like a stove; the armrest, which sat in the shade under his bag, stayed cool. "The land is like my phone," he said slowly. "It heats differently than the ocean. That difference is the hidden cause, I think. You can't see it, but it drags the wind, and the wind drags the rain."

"Okay," Kiera said. "But when does it actually arrive? A farmer can't plant rice on a hypothetical date. Rice needs water at the right time or the whole season fails."

Landon wanted to give up. He had rewritten his notes three times already on the flight from school to this connecting airport, and his hand was cramped. "Ask me something I know," he muttered. Kiera persevered anyway, flipping through his notes until she found a photo of a wall calendar from his grandmother's house. Every June, his grandmother circled the first of the month in red pen. When he was small, he had thought it was her birthday.

"That's it," Kiera said, tapping the photo. "That's the date."

Landon remembered his grandmother pointing at the calendar two summers ago, saying, "June 1. The India Meteorological Department calls that the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala, on India's southwestern coast." He had nodded without really listening, the way you do at nine years old. Now the words came back whole, and he wrote them down at the top of his page in careful letters. The farmers in the region, many of them small growers, some barely more than peasants working a few flooded fields, planted when that rain arrived. If it came late, the seedlings died waiting; if it came early, the paddies filled and the season began. The date mattered because everything downstream of it mattered.

"Say the whole thing back to me," Kiera said. Landon took a breath, stood up straight like he would in front of Ms. Rajapakse's class, and began. A family waiting nearby glanced over, and a toddler clapped when he reached the part about Kerala. Kiera held up her phone and hit record. "Again, from the top," she said. "We're going to nail this."

Alexis sat in the back seat with his hands folded in his lap, watching the streetlights slide across the window. The dance started in twenty minutes, and his one real want was simple: to walk through the gym doors without turning around and walking back out. The car slowed at a red light, stopping on the wide grassy median beside the school road, and his mom glanced at him in the mirror. "You'll be fine," she said, which was not the same as helping. Then his phone buzzed with a message from Alanna, and he read it twice.

"Bringing glow stick bracelets for our whole group," she had written, "but one is DEAD. Cracked the whole pack testing them. Save me a slow song?" He typed back "yes" before he could talk himself out of it, and then sat there wondering about the dead one. Why would five out of six work and one not? If the light only shows up when you bend one, he thought, maybe the dead one wasn't really dead. Maybe bending it the first time hadn't done the thing bending is supposed to do. He had no way to check from the car, but he kept turning the idea over like a coin in his pocket.

The car swung into a gas station so his mom could acquire a bottle of water, and Alexis asked for two minutes and came back with a spare pack of glow sticks from the cashier, just in case. His mom raised an eyebrow but said nothing, which he took as permission.

The gym had been transformed. Streamers hung from the basketball hoops, a disco ball spun above the bleachers, and the eighth graders had built an intricate maze of balloons by the door. Alanna met him at the punch table, her arms already stacked with bracelets. She handed him the dead one. "Be my witness," she said. "It's a total dud." Alexis held it up to the lamp and studied it. The good ones he'd cracked all had that snapping feel when he bent them, like something tiny giving way inside. This one had never snapped.

"Can I try?" he asked. He gripped it in the middle and bent it slowly, listening. Nothing. He bent it the other way, pressing harder this time, and felt a faint crack, small as a knuckle pop. The bracelet flickered, then bloomed green along its whole length. Alanna grabbed his arm. "How did you know?" Behind them, Aksil had just cracked his own bracelet and was squinting at it. "Where's the light even coming from?" he asked.

"The bending breaks a little glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside," Alexis said, "and it mixes with other chemicals and a dye. It's called chemiluminescence." Aksil cracked his bracelet again, watching it flare brighter. Alexis slid the green one onto Alanna's wrist. "Save your questions for the next slow song," she said, and pulled him toward the dance floor.

The train swayed through the foothills while Scarlett pressed her forehead against the window and counted pine trees until she lost her place. She and her parents were riding toward Yosemite for a week of camping, and her backpack sat on the seat beside her like a third passenger, stuffed with sunscreen, a toothbrush, a fresh tube of mint toothpaste, and a flashlight with batteries she had checked twice.

Across the aisle, a girl about Scarlett's age was arguing with her little brother. "We can keep the snacks in the tent," the boy insisted. "Bears can't open zippers." The girl, whose name badge from some summer camp read Zainab, rolled her eyes. "That's not how it works," she said, but she didn't sound sure, and their dad just shrugged and kept reading his magazine.

Scarlett turned around in her seat. Last summer, on the same trip with her cousin, she had left her toothpaste in the tent overnight because it wasn't food, so why would it matter? In the morning her mom had marched her back to the metal locker at the campsite and made her put it in. "In parks like this, anything with a scent counts as food," her mom had said, pointing at the locker's painted sign. Toothpaste, sunscreen, even the trash had to go in before bed. Scarlett had stood there feeling foolish, holding her little blue tube while a squirrel watched from the picnic table.

She tested the idea now, the way she had learned to in science class. If the rule counted anything with a scent, then the family across the aisle had a problem bigger than snacks. "Excuse me," she said to Zainab. "Where are you guys camping?" "Yosemite, same as you, I think," Zainab said. "There's a locker at our site." Scarlett nodded toward the brother's daypack. "It's not just snacks. Toothpaste and sunscreen and trash have to go in the bear locker too. I learned that the embarrassing way last year."

The boy groaned like this was the worst news in the world. Zainab, though, leaned forward. "Wait, so even my chapstick?" "If it smells, it goes in," Scarlett said. Zainab began digging through the daypack, pulling out chapstick, a bag of gummy worms, and a wrapper that had already started to migrate toward the bottom of the bag, sticky side out.

When the train slowed at the station, the two families ended up walking toward the same campground shuttle. Scarlett's dad struck up a conversation with Zainab's dad, and somewhere behind them the little brother was still complaining, with vigorous arm waving, about keeping his gummy worms next to his pillow. Zainab caught Scarlett's eye and mouthed, "Thank you."

That night, in the dark tent, Scarlett listened to the wind move through the trees and thought about tomorrow's hike to the waterfall, the part her dad called the climax of the whole trip. Somewhere out there, she knew, the bear locker stood shut and full, holding every scented thing on the site. She smiled, zipped her sleeping bag up to her chin, and whispered into the cold air, "Even the chapstick."

Nathaniel lay in bed staring at the ceiling, listening to his own heart thump like sneakers in a dryer. Tomorrow he had the solo in the spring concert, and every time he imagined the microphone, his stomach did a slow flip. He counted sheep, then counted the glow-in-the-dark stars on his ceiling, then counted how many times his little brother snored. Forty-one. That had to be some kind of record.

Downstairs, the floorboards creaked. His dad appeared in the doorway holding a library book with a cracked spine, one titled with words Nathaniel was too tired to read. "Can't sleep either?" his dad whispered. "Your grandmother swore by something from this book. Dr. Andrew Weil, some doctor with a big reputation for this sort of thing. Want to try it?" Nathaniel groaned, but he sat up, because the alternative was lying there listening to his heartbeat until sunrise.

"Okay, it's called 4-7-8 breathing," his dad said, sitting on the edge of the bed. "Breathe in for four counts." Nathaniel inhaled, his nose whistling faintly like a tiny teakettle. His dad snorted. "Now hold it for seven." The room went very quiet. Nathaniel could hear the refrigerator humming downstairs and a car passing on the wet street, and his chest started to burn at about count five, but he hung on. "Now out, slow, for eight." Nathaniel let the air leak out of his mouth in a long, unglamorous whoosh, like a balloon losing an argument.

"That felt radical," Nathaniel said, flopping back. "In a weird way." They did it three more times. On the fourth round something odd happened: his shoulders, which had been creeping up toward his ears all evening without his noticing, sank into the mattress like they'd given up a fight. His breathing began to regulate itself, slowing down on its own, without counting. His eyelids grew heavy as wet paper towels.

"Wait," he mumbled. "Is this the trick? You get so bored counting to eight that you fall asleep out of self-defense?" His dad laughed, pulled the blanket up to Nathaniel's chin, and turned off the lamp. "Could be," he whispered from the doorway. "Try it tomorrow before the solo. If you get nervous up there, just count." In the dark, Nathaniel practiced one more time: in, four. Hold, seven. Out, eight. His last thought was of the microphone, and this time his stomach stayed perfectly still.

The next morning he found his little brother at the kitchen table, cheeks puffed out like a bullfrog. "In for four," his brother announced, "then you hold it for seven, and then the slow part is eight." Nathaniel stared. "Who taught you that?" His brother pointed at the library book, still lying open on the counter. "Dad left it in the bathroom. I read the whole page."

Mya sat at the kitchen table with her arm propped on a stack of cookbooks, the new fiberglass cast ending just below her elbow. Her friend Hargun had come over with a folder of homework and a printout of her X-ray, which the radiology desk had handed over without being asked.

"Which one did you break?" Hargun asked, tapping the pale shapes on the film.

Mya held the paper up to the window light. Two long bones ran side by side from her elbow to her wrist, and one of them had a thin dark crack near the middle, like a hair stuck to the picture. She wanted to know which bone it was, and not just out of curiosity. The doctor had written a word on her discharge papers, and if she could match the word to the right bone, she could settle an argument she'd been having with herself since the hospital.

She laid her good hand flat on the table, palm up. "The one on the thumb side is the radius," she said, reading from the paper. "The one on the little-finger side is the ulna." She turned the X-ray until the hand in the picture matched her own, thumb toward her, little finger away. Then she traced along the bone that lined up with the thumb side, down from the wrist, until her fingertip stopped at the crack. The radius. That matched the word on the paper too, which made her feel briefly and cautiously optimistic that she had it right.

"Does it matter?" Hargun asked. She was already flipping the folder open, because what she actually wanted was to get the science worksheet done before dinner, and Ms. Haile had said it would incorporate diagrams, labels, and a short written section. "We have to draw the skeletal system today. I was hoping you'd help, cast and all."

"It matters to me," Mya said. She picked up a pencil with her left hand and wrote "radius" on a sticky note, pressing it onto the X-ray next to the cracked bone. Then she wrote "ulna" on a second note and reached for the other bone, but her left hand slid the paper sideways and the note stuck to the table instead.

Hargun peeled it off for her and smoothed it into place. "If you label my diagram that neatly, I'll owe you my mom's monsoon-season soup. She makes it every time it rains hard, and it's the best thing in her whole recipe book."

"Deal," Mya said. She anchored the X-ray under the cookbook stack and picked the pencil back up, resting the cast on the edge of the table where it wouldn't slide.

Outside, the first fat drops hit the window, and Hargun grinned. "See? Perfect timing."

The paper had two headings, and John had only ever read the first one. He stood at the edge of his aunt's backyard, dodging a swarm of relatives who all wanted to pinch his cheeks and tell him how tall he'd gotten, and scrutinized the sheet his mom had printed that morning. Under "Torah portion" was the reading he'd been practicing for three weeks. Under that, in smaller type, was a second heading and a whole block of Hebrew he'd never seen before.

"Four days," his cousin Hana said, appearing beside him with a plate of kugel. "You didn't know about the second one?" She said the word "haftarah" the way you'd say "obviously," and when he stared at her she pointed at the page. "It's a reading from the books of the Prophets. At a bar or bat mitzvah you often chant that too."

"Often," John repeated, as if the word had personally betrayed him. "So it's optional?"

"It's not optional, it's just that nobody told you because everyone assumed someone else did." Hana shrugged and ate a noodle. "Classic family move."

John spent the rest of the afternoon testing a theory. He'd noticed that haftarah passages used the same chant symbols as his Torah portion, mostly, but the tune wandered differently, like the melody kept changing its mind. His theory: if he learned the symbols as a pattern, he could sing the new reading without hearing it first. He hid in the empty guest room, whispered the phrases, and got it wrong in a way that made the neighbor's dog howl. But the second attempt matched the recording on his uncle's phone, and the third was closer, and by the time the cake came out, he could stumble through half of it.

Outside, McKayla, his friend from down the street who had crashed the party for the food, held up the sheet like a referee. "The Prophets one sounds dramatic," she said. "Like a movie trailer." She cleared her throat and chanted, badly, "Thus saaaith the Lord," and John laughed so hard he had to sit down on the cooler.

"Your family is going extinct," McKayla announced, counting the last pieces of cake being divided among nine cousins. "Not enough dessert. Natural causes."

By the end of the night John could do the whole thing, wobbly but real, and he performed it once for the relatives by the fire pit while his grandmother mouthed every word along with him. His uncle's grin was infectious, and even the dog seemed to approve.

"So Saturday," Hana said, "when you chant the haftarah, you'll be fine."

John picked up the last cookie before McKayla could. "The Prophets told me to take it," he said, and took a bite.

William pressed his pencil so hard against the paper that the lead snapped. His street looked like a wedge of cheese, flat and wrong, and the assignment was due at the end of class.

"You keep drawing the road the same width all the way back," said Olivia, leaning over from the next stool. She was already shading her own street, which curved around a corner like it had somewhere to go.

"Streets are the same width," William said. "Nobody narrows a street."

Moses spun his pencil between two fingers, agile as a drum majorette, then dropped it. "Then why does your drawing look like it's falling over?"

William stared at the paper. He thought about the footbridge over the train tracks behind his house, where he and Moses had stood last Saturday throwing pebbles into the weeds. Moses had sworn the rails got closer together near the old water tower. William had said that was crazy. "They'd have to touch," he'd argued. "The train would fall off." Moses had just pointed at the horizon, where the two shiny lines seemed to pinch together like a zipper closing.

"You were right about the tracks," William said slowly. "They look like they meet. But they don't. Not ever. The two edges of a road do the same thing. That's probably why my street looks fake. It's too even."

Olivia scooted her stool over. "So make the edges lean toward each other on the paper. Like the tracks did from the bridge."

William turned to a fresh sheet. He drew a dot in the middle and called it a vanishing point, because he'd read that phrase on Ms. Kim's poster last week and it had finally decided to mean something. Then he drew two lines from the bottom corners of the page, straight toward the dot. The street between them shrank as it went. His brain said impossible; his eyes said perfect.

"Moses, hold the ruler," he said. "I want to elaborate on this. Storefronts, lampposts, maybe a cat."

"A cat on a street?" said Moses.

"An agile cat," William said. "Leaping between rooftops."

"You just wanted to say agile again."

"Every word deserves a second chance."

Olivia laughed so hard she smudged her shading, and William helped her blend it back out with his thumb while Moses anchored the ruler for the lamppost line. The lampposts marched up the page, each one smaller than the last, all leaning toward the dot like commuters toward the last train.

Ms. Kim wandered past their table and looked for a long moment. "Where'd you two learn that?" she asked.

William pointed out the window, toward nowhere in particular, and toward a bridge beyond it. "From a train that never falls off the tracks."

Moses drew the cat anyway, mid-leap, tail like a coat hook.

Brody set his toast crust on the counter on purpose, the way he had every morning that week, and then walked to the doorway and counted to sixty. When he came back, the crust was gone. He had done this four times now, and every time the crust disappeared.

His hypothesis, which he had written on a napkin and taped inside the cupboard door, was that the dog ate it. The problem was that he could not actually see the dog do it. The dog, a small brown mutt named Patches, was shut in the laundry room every morning until Brody's mother left for work, and the crust vanished anyway. So the dog was out. That was the only thing he knew for sure.

He texted his friend Xavier about it after school.

Xavier wrote back: "this is like the swan thing mr joshi put on the board. No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false."

Brody read the message twice, then typed: "so if i watch the crust a hundred times and don't see who takes it, that proves nothing. but if i catch the thief once, i know for sure it wasn't the dog."

"exactly," Xavier wrote. "also you should get a sophisticated trap. flour everywhere. my brother did that for the cookie thief. it was me. i have the face of a criminal on camera."

Brody skipped the flour. Instead, the next morning he set out the crust and stood very still at the far end of the kitchen, next to the fridge, where the counter met the wall in a shadow. He held his phone up like he was checking the time. He waited. Four minutes. Five.

The cupboard under the sink, the one with the gap where the pipe went through the wall, made a small scratching sound. Then a gray mouse came out, walked along the baseboard, stood up on its hind legs at the corner of the counter, and dragged the crust down off the edge. It disappeared behind the toaster with the whole thing.

Brody lowered the phone. He crossed "dog" off the napkin and wrote "mouse" above it. Then he thought about Xavier's message again. He went back and added, at the bottom, "one crust still there would prove dog wrong. one mouse proves dog wrong. a hundred missing crusts prove nothing."

At dinner he told his mother the verdict, and she said they would get traps. Patches, let out of the laundry room, came over and put his chin on Brody's knee.

"Sorry, buddy," Brody said. "Not you this time." He slipped him a piece of crust anyway.

The track behind the school had six painted lanes and one basketball hoop that Mr. Ho wheeled out for the kids who got tired of running circles. Logan had been tired of running circles since September. What he wanted was to be the point guard at Friday's scrimmage, which meant he had one week to learn to call plays, a job he had discovered was harder than it looked the moment he tried it on Tuesday.

"Play twelve!" he shouted, and Matthias, who was supposed to cut left, cut right. Remington, who was supposed to get the ball, stood near the free throw line with his hands up like he was being arrested. The boy guarding Remington, a tall kid from Mr. Ho's homeroom, stayed glued to him the whole time. Every cut Remington made, the defender made too, half a step ahead, as though he'd read Logan's play call off the inside of his own eyelids.

"It's like he's attached to me," Remington said, breathing hard. "With string. Possibly wire."

Logan called a water break and sat on the infield grass, thinking. The problem wasn't Remington's cuts. The problem was something he couldn't see: the defender wasn't watching Remington at all. He was watching Logan's mouth. Every time Logan called a play, the whole defense rearranged itself like a polite audience taking their seats. His own play calls were leaking information. That was the hidden cause, and once he saw it, he couldn't stop seeing it.

He tried an experiment. "Same play," he told Remington quietly, "but this time, Matthias, you stand right in the tall kid's way. Don't move your feet. Just stand there like a mailbox."

"Why?"

"It's a pick," Logan said. "Coach calls it a screen too."

Matthias planted himself in the defender's path, arms folded, radiating a neutral expression of a boy doing absolutely nothing wrong. The tall kid slammed into him like a bird hitting a window. Remington slipped free, took Logan's pass, and laid the ball in off the backboard while the tall kid was still untangling himself and declaring, to no official, that this was unfair.

By Thursday Logan had stopped calling plays out loud entirely. He used hand signals, some of which he invented on the spot, one of which looked alarmingly like he was waving at a helicopter. When Mr. Ho wandered over from the long-jump pit to watch, Logan tried to summarize his week for him. "So I whisper now, and Matthias stands in people's way on purpose."

"A mailbox," Matthias confirmed.

Mr. Ho watched Remington roll off Matthias's shoulder, catch the pass, and score for the ninth time in a row. He nodded slowly, the way a diplomat nods at a treaty he fully intends to honor, and said, "Point guard. Friday." Then he walked back toward the long-jump pit, and Logan turned to his teammates and held up two fingers, then pointed left.

The crack happened right in the middle of Zayd's presentation on sleep, in Mr. Lombardi's health classroom. He said "the brain stays partly awake" and the word awake came out in two pieces, one low and one squeaky, like a skipping record. Somebody in the back row laughed. Zayd's ears went red and he read the rest of his note cards in a flat mumble.

Katherine had been keeping a list in the back of her notebook all semester, ever since her own body started changing and she began wondering whether the boys could feel their changes coming too. Her list had three columns: name, date, and what happened. Yassine's voice had dropped sometime over winter break, so evenly that nobody laughed. A boy in second period had cracked during the pledge. Now Zayd. She had a guess, dormant for weeks, that there was a rule underneath it: the boys whose voices broke gradually were done, and the ones who cracked were still in the middle of something. But a guess wasn't a rule unless you could test it.

At lunch she found Zayd by the vending machines. "Can you hum this?" she said, and sang a low note. He hummed it back, steady. She went up the scale, note by note, like a fire truck climbing. At the seventh note his hum snapped in half. At the eighth, it snapped again. Below that, his voice was smooth all the way down. "It's only the high ones," Katherine said, writing fast. "The low notes work fine."

"So my voice is broken," Zayd said.

"It's not broken. It's under construction."

In the health textbook's chapter on adolescence there was a diagram Katherine had skipped before, a cross-section of the throat with the larynx labeled and two lines inside it marked vocal folds. The caption read that during puberty the larynx grows and the vocal folds get longer and thicker. Katherine sat with that for a minute. Longer and thicker would make a lower sound, the way a thick guitar string sat lower than a thin one. And while the growing was happening, the high notes would fail. That fit her scale test exactly. The rule wasn't about done or unfinished; it was about size changing underneath the sound.

The next day in class, Mr. Lombardi assigned presentations again. Katherine passed Zayd a folded note: low voice, no high words. He opened it, nodded, and pushed his note cards to the bottom of the pile. When his turn came, he stood up and delivered his whole presentation in the lower register, slow and careful, and his voice held. Afterward he sat down beside her and whispered, "Did it work?"

"Every word," Katherine said, and underlined his name in her notebook.

Piper laid her supplies across the kitchen table: a roll of paper towels, a box of baking soda, a bottle of vinegar, a carton of milk, and two small stacks of paper strips she had cut herself, red and blue. Ms. Gagnon had assigned the whole class a pH project for the science fair, and Piper had volunteered to build the booth because she wanted the blue ribbon more than she had wanted anything all year.

Then she found the note tucked inside the box of baking soda. It was from her friend Izabella, who had taken the supplies home the night before to help cut the strips. "Piper," it read, "my little brother got into the kitchen while I was working. I think he mixed up the strips. Some of the red ones and blue ones might have switched stacks. Sorry! Also my family is helping our new neighbours, who are refugees from Syria, so I might be late tomorrow." Piper stared at the two stacks. If the strips were mixed up, her whole demonstration would be wrong in front of everyone.

She sat down and thought. She could not see any difference between the strips just by looking, but there had to be a way to find out what each one was. Then she remembered the one thing she knew for certain: everyone in the class had been unanimous about vinegar during practice. It was an acid. If she dipped a strip in vinegar and it turned red, that strip was the blue kind, because that was the test: blue litmus paper turns red when dipped in an acid, and red litmus paper turns blue when dipped in a base.

She grabbed a strip from the "blue" stack and dunked it in a saucer of vinegar. Nothing happened. It stayed red. So that strip was actually a red one, mixed into the wrong pile. She tested another, and it turned red the moment it touched the liquid, which meant it was truly blue. Strip by strip, she sorted them, dipping and checking, building two honest stacks. Then she tried baking soda mixed with water, and a true red strip turned blue right before her eyes.

When Izabella arrived the next morning, Piper emphasized the pile of tested strips with both hands. "Every single one is sorted," she said. "Your brother actually helped. I understand the whole thing now, and I couldn't say that yesterday." Izabella laughed and hugged her.

At the science fair, a judge stopped at Piper's booth and dipped the blue strip into the vinegar herself. It turned red, clean and bright as a tiny flag.

Julia slid the giant paper periodic table across the lab table and pinned the corner with her elbow before it could curl up again. Mr. Bui had promised that anyone who could correctly find the number of protons in five elements of his choosing would get to run the demo at the front of the room on Friday, and Julia wanted that more than she had wanted anything that week. The rule seemed simple: the atomic number up top of each box told you the protons. Sodium, eleven. Oxygen, eight. She felt almost smug.

Then Mr. Bui's scavenger hunt sheet said "iron," and Julia's whole plan fell apart. She ran her finger down the columns looking for an I. There was iodine, already claiming the symbol I, and there was iridium, smugly wearing Ir, but no iron anywhere. Ember leaned over from the next table, holding her own sheet. "I'm stuck on iron too," she said. "And if I don't finish this, I can't be your partner for the demo, and I already told my little brother I'd bring home the vinegar-and-baking-soda volcano trick." That was Ember's want, and Julia took it as seriously as her own. "Then we collaborate," Julia said. "You take the left side of the table, I take the right, and we look for anything that could mean iron."

Ananya, organizing the beakers at the supply shelf, called over without turning around. "Are you two hunting for iron? Because I found something last night that will make you feel like a peasant who just discovered electricity." She walked over waving a folded note she had written to herself in the margin of her notebook, and Julia read it aloud: "Dear future Ananya, iron is Fe. Not I. It comes from the Latin word ferrum. Signed, present Ananya, who was also confused." Julia laughed and went back to the table.

She found the box labeled Fe, and there it was, atomic number 26. Twenty-six protons, hidden inside every atom of a metal she could see in the door hinge, the chair legs, the fence outside. She tested her idea on another row to make sure the pattern held: gold, Au, also Latin, 79. Silver, Ag, 47. Copper, Cu, 29. Each symbol sat in its box like a nickname with a story behind it, and the number above it kept its promise every time.

By Friday Julia and Ember stood at the front table, filling a bottle while the class counted down. "Twenty-six protons," Ember announced, holding up the steel wool, "in every single strand of this." Julia struck the match, and the wool bloomed into a small, bright, coherent glow that made the whole second row lean forward in their seats.

The last time Simon had sat in this seat, Grandpa had been in the one beside it, complaining that the seatbelt was trying to strangle him and asking Simon to read the road signs out loud because his glasses were "on vacation." Now the seat was empty and Mom was driving them to the memorial dinner, and Simon kept turning his phone over in his hands like it might tell him something.

It did, actually. Ania was visiting relatives in Japan, and she'd sent a photo of a paper lantern glowing on a porch. "This is for my grandma," her message said. "It's Obon. Mid-August here, but July in some regions. During Obon the spirits of ancestors come home for a visit, so we light lanterns to welcome them." Simon read it three times. Grandpa had only been gone since April, and nobody had told Simon there was a schedule for goodbyes.

He decided to devise his own version, right there in the car. He dug through the door pocket and found a birthday candle left over from his sister's cupcakes, and he folded the sandwich bag from his lunch into a lopsided little lantern around it. Mom glanced over. "What are you doing back there?" "Welcoming someone," Simon said, and struck a match from the first aid kit, which he was fairly sure he wasn't allowed to touch.

The flame sputtered and went out. He tried again. It guttered sideways, whipped by the air pouring from the vent, and died again. "Mom, can you close the vent? Please?" She reached over without a word, and the flame caught and held, small and stable, cupped in his hands like something alive. That was the climax of the whole plan, and Simon hadn't even known plans had climaxes until Ms. Diallo taught it in English last year.

He held the lantern up near the empty window. "Hi, Grandpa," he said, feeling ridiculous and not caring. "We're going to dinner. There will be terrible casseroles. You'd have hated them and eaten three." Mom made a sound that was half laugh, half something else, and didn't wipe her eyes until the next red light.

"Ania says in her town it's mid-August," Simon said as they pulled into the parking lot, "but July in some regions, so it depends where you are." He looked at the little flame, then at the empty seat. "I figure we're wherever we are." He blew the candle out gently and carried it inside, cupped in both hands.

The trail climbed through pines until Ms. Whitehead called a rest stop at a granite outcrop, and Layla dropped her pack with a thud. Inside it, rolled tight, were two graphs she'd printed at the library: one for the Sahara, one for the Amazon. Her project was due Monday, and she still couldn't answer the question Ms. Whitehead had written at the top of the assignment sheet. Compare the climates. Explain what makes them different, and why.

The graphs themselves were easy. The desert's rainfall bars were stubs, barely visible except one slightly taller bar in a single month. The rainforest's bars climbed like a wall. The temperature lines told the other half: the desert line zigzagged between scorching days and cold nights, while the rainforest line ran flat and warm, month after month. Layla knew all that. What she didn't know was why. Rainforests huddled near the equator, sure. But deserts weren't at the equator, and they weren't scattered randomly either. She'd noticed something on the classroom globe last week, and she kept turning it over in her mind.

She had stayed late on Tuesday, spinning the globe slowly with one finger while the janitor worked down the hall. The Sahara. Then, below the equator, the Kalahari and the Australian deserts. Then Arabia, and the Atacama on the west coast of South America. She'd grabbed a sticky note and marked them, then stood back. The marks made two belts, one north of the equator and one south, and both belts sat at about the same distance from the middle of the globe. She'd folded the sticky note into her pocket without telling anyone, in case she was wrong.

"Earth to Layla," Conor said, sitting down beside her. He had his binoculars around his neck, the way he'd had them all morning, because he wanted a photo of a pileated woodpecker before lunch. He'd been planning this hike for two weeks and had told her twice that it was not a trivial goal, it was the whole point of walking six kilometres. "You're staring at paper like it owes you money."

"Look at this globe app," she said, pulling out her phone. She opened the map and traced the big deserts with her fingertip. "Tell me what you see."

Conor squinted. "Sand. Lots of sand."

"No, look at where they are. All of them." She waited, letting him find it the way she had, and for a moment nobody spoke. Somewhere downslope, water dripped off a ledge, steady as rain.

"They line up," Conor said slowly. "In two bands."

Layla checked the map's latitude scale with her thumb, the way she'd checked the globe. "About thirty degrees north, and thirty degrees south. That's where they sit." She thought of the graph in her pack, the stubby rainfall bars. It fit, and fitting it made the back of her neck prickle. "Ms. Whitehead said one thing I wrote down. Where air sinks in those belts, it warms up and dries out. So the rain never comes." She said it out loud for the first time, testing it, and it held.

Ms. Whitehead, who had been inspecting the trail register by the old lodge, called back to them that the park service planned to renovate the building next summer, and then asked what they were studying so intently. "Whether that dry-belt thing is a real phenomenon or a coincidence," Layla said. "I'm going to test it tonight. I'll pick three deserts I didn't mark before and check their latitudes on the map."

"If they're all near thirty," Conor said, standing up, binoculars rising, "you've got your answer."

Behind him, a red-crested bird hammered at a dead pine, and Conor spun toward it so fast he nearly fell off the outcrop.

The folding chairs were set up in a ragged line at the edge of the community sports field, close enough to the big screen that the projected game looked almost real. Owen sat between his grandfather and his friend Romeo, a bowl of chips balanced on his knees. The grass beneath their feet was still damp from morning rain, and the field beyond the screen stretched out green and empty, fertile soil that the Parks Department had reseeded just last month.

"They didn't have anything like this in my day," Grandpa said, nodding at the screen. "I remember the very first one, you know. The Packers against the Chiefs. Nobody even knew what it would become."

Owen sat up straighter. "You remember the first one? That was forever ago."

"January fifteenth, 1967," Grandpa said, tapping the arm of his chair. "Green Bay won it going away. Thirty-five to ten."

Romeo leaned over. "No way. Nobody remembers a score from that long ago. My dad can't even remember what he had for breakfast."

"I remember it because we all crowded into Al's Barbershop to watch," Grandpa said. "Half the town in one room."

Owen pulled out his phone and turned it sideways so Romeo could see the screen. "My grandpa says the first one was Packers versus Chiefs, January fifteenth, 1967, and the Packers won thirty-five to ten," he said quietly, typing. Romeo watched over his shoulder, bouncing one knee.

The search results loaded. Owen scrolled once, then twice, and stopped. "It's all here. Every part of it. The date, the score, the teams." He held the phone low so only Romeo could see. "He got it exactly right. He really does remember it."
