By Tuesday of the first week, the phone was dead by lunch. On Wednesday, dead again by lunch. "You're playing games on it all morning," Dalie accused him at the lunch table. "I am not," Gavin said, and he wasn't. He'd only checked the time twice.

Thursday night, sitting cross-legged on Dalie's bedroom floor while Dalie rebuilt a model airplane, Gavin made a list on a napkin. Charged all night. Unplugged at seven. Off by noon. He stared at the numbers and thought about Dalie's brother, who had used this phone for three years, always charging it, always draining it. Emiliano leaned over from the beanbag chair where he was gluing the plane's propeller. "My dad says old phones just do that. The batteries get worn out from being used so long." Gavin looked at the phone. Lithium-ion, it said in tiny print on the box Dalie's brother had left in the closet. The battery wasn't broken. It had just slowly gotten weaker over the years, like a sponge that held less water each time you soaked it.

He tested it. Friday he charged the phone to full, wrote down the percentage every hour, and by fifth period it read eleven percent. Same usage as his friend's new phone, which still showed sixty. That proved it. The battery wasn't his fault.

"It's not my fault," Gavin announced Saturday, back on Dalie's floor, holding up his napkin graph. Dalie frowned. "So you're going to give it back?"

Gavin hadn't thought past proving himself innocent. "No. I'm going to make it work." He ordered a replacement battery online with his allowance, and when it came, Mr. Mensah from next door, who fixed computers in his garage, swapped it in for him in about ten minutes. Sunday night, Gavin charged the phone and wrote 100 percent on a fresh napkin.

Monday at noon the screen still showed seventy percent, and Gavin smiled at it in the cafeteria. Dalie slid into the seat across from him, peering at the screen. "Okay, that's radical," Dalie admitted, then pulled out his own phone, the cracked hand-me-down from his cousin. "Mine dies at two every day. Think you could fix it too?" Gavin looked at the crack, at the old case, at his friend's hopeful face, and put his napkin and his pencil back on the table. "Bring your napkin," he said.

Abigail spread her three library books across the table and checked her notebook for the tenth time. Her science fair project was due Friday, and she still didn't have a claim she could actually support. Yousuf slid into the chair across from her and dropped a shiny copper bracelet on top of her notes.

"My uncle sent me this," he said. "He wore one for a month and his back pain went away. He swears by it. I figured you could put it in your project, since your topic is pain or whatever."

"My topic is evidence," Abigail said. She picked up the bracelet and turned it over. "Yousuf, that's one person's story. It can't show the bracelet caused anything, because other explanations haven't been ruled out."

"Like what?"

"Like maybe his back got better on its own. Maybe he started exercising. Maybe he just wanted it to work." She pulled a worksheet from her folder. "Mr. Do made us sort claims today. A story about one person's experience is called an anecdote. One anecdote isn't evidence, because you haven't ruled anything else out."

Yousuf frowned at the bracelet. "It felt warm when I put it on. That means something."

Abigail glanced toward the front desk, where Mr. Do was checking in a return cart, and an idea landed so hard she almost knocked over her pencil cup. "Wait. We can test it. Not his back, your wrist. You said your wrist aches after gaming."

"So?"

"So we flip a coin. Heads, you wear the real bracelet for a week and write down your pain every night. Tails, you wear this." She dug in her frugal project budget, a slim envelope of allowance money, and counted out coins for the library's lost-and-found bin, where a plain steel ring had sat for months. She'd ask the cashier-priced one at the front, or better, Mr. Do, if she could borrow it. "Same weight, same warmth on skin, no copper."

Yousuf agreed, and they drew a chart with seven boxes each for real and fake. That night he texted her: Wrist pain four out of ten, bracelet on, feels kind of warm. She smiled and logged it.

The week crawled. At school Yousuf reported the pain seemed to diminish by Thursday, which he announced loudly in the cafeteria, and Braydon immediately wanted a copper bracelet too. Abigail kept her face neutral and said nothing, though her stomach tightened every time she thought about Thursday, because of one detail Yousuf didn't know yet. On Monday she had looked up pain studies in the library's medical section and found something that changed everything: in real trials, people wearing fake bracelets reported almost the same improvement as people wearing real ones.

Friday afternoon, they met at the same library table. Yousuf slapped down his completed chart, grinning. "Pain went from four to one. Copper works. I'm telling my uncle he was right."

Abigail slid the chart aside and set the steel ring beside the bracelet. "Flip the coin," she said.

He flipped. Tails.

"You've been wearing the fake all week, Yousuf. No copper at all." She watched his face work through it, the grin collapsing into something between disappointment and wonder. "Your pain got better anyway. So the bracelet can't be what did it, because we didn't rule out it just getting better on its own. That's my whole project. That's the claim with tested evidence behind it."

Yousuf picked up the steel ring and held it next to the copper one, turning them so they caught the window light. Behind them, Mr. Do pushed his cart past the tall shelf, and on the top of it sat a model ship whose cracked hull had been waiting months for repairs.

"Can we run it again next week?" Yousuf asked. "My brother wants in, and he says his knee aches."

Abigail was already drawing a bigger chart. "Tell him to bring his own coin."

Declan's mother had one rule for bring-your-kid-to-work day: stay out of the way. He was doing fine at that until the office printer jammed, and then, while he waited for the repairman, he noticed her screen.

She had a spreadsheet full of numbers, a column of sales for every week of the quarter, and she was adding them by hand. On a calculator. He watched her type a number, press plus, type another, press plus again, all the way down column B, and his fingers itched.

"You know the computer can do that," he said.

"It can?"

"Vihaan showed me once. There's a formula." He leaned over her keyboard, typed =SUM(B2:B10) into the empty cell under her numbers, and pressed Enter. The total appeared instantly, and his mother laughed out loud. "Declan, do you know how many hours I've spent on that calculator?"

He felt tall as anything. Then she ruined it by pointing at the next column over. "Can you do that one too?"

Column C. Then column D. Then E, F and G, all the way across the quarter. Eleven more columns, and he only knew one formula. He remembered Vihaan saying something once about the formula knowing where it was, but he couldn't recall the details, and the repairman was still wrestling with the printer behind them, so Vihaan couldn't be messaged quietly. He tried typing =SUM(B2:B10) into the cell under column C and the total was wrong. Too small. The spreadsheet was totaling column B again, sitting under column C like a liar.

That's when he thought of the copy command. Vihaan had said the formula shifts when it moves. Declan didn't trust it, though. A formula was invisible; you couldn't watch it change the way you could watch a printer repairman yank a crumpled page free. So he decided to test it in a place where it couldn't hurt anything. He copied the cell from under column B, clicked the empty cell under column C, pasted, and clicked into the cell to look.

The formula had changed by itself. It read =SUM(C2:C10). He checked the total against the column above it and it matched. He pasted the same copied cell across the whole row, under every column, and one by one, every week's total appeared, correct, like the spreadsheet was reading his mind.

Later, when the repairman left and Mr. De Vries from the next desk came over to see what the commotion was, Declan showed him the whole trick, the formula, the copy, the chart he'd built from the totals with blue bars for every week. Mr. De Vries was quiet for a moment.

"Could you do that to my numbers?" he asked, pulling out his chair. "They're in a monstrous file. It might compress my week from two days to about ten minutes."

Declan rolled Mr. De Vries's chair over, sat down, and typed.

Katherine sat on her bedroom floor surrounded by crumpled tissues, a box of grape juice, and her phone, which would not stop buzzing. It was Arabella, who had caught the same cold two days before the class trip to the science museum, and Arabella was convinced the trip was doomed.

"LOOK," the message said, with a photo of a tissue that was decidedly green. "My mom says this means bacteria. I need the strong medicine TONIGHT or I can't go Saturday."

Katherine stared at the photo, then at her own wastebasket, where an identical shade of green stared back at her. If Arabella was right, Katherine was doomed too. She pulled her blanket around her shoulders and thought hard. Her dad was at the pharmacy already, picking up her cough syrup. She called him and asked him to do one thing: get the pharmacist talking while she listened on the phone.

"Ask her what the green means," Katherine whispered.

She heard the cashier scanning bandaids in the background, then a woman's voice, patient and quick. "Green or yellow mucus comes from your immune cells, and from an enzyme they release. That's it. The color alone doesn't show whether it's bacteria or a virus. Only a test can sort that out."

Katherine hung up and sat very still, working it through. Her own mucus had turned green on Tuesday, and by Thursday she already felt halfway better. Arabella's had turned green the same day, from the same cold, which everyone knew came from the substitute teacher who sneezed through Monday's math class. A virus, almost certainly. Green didn't mean disaster. Green meant their immune systems were generating whatever that enzyme was, and doing their jobs.

She texted back a short version, then called Arabella for real, because Arabella was pacing her room announcing she'd demand antibiotics at urgent care before it closed at eight. "It's seven fifteen," Arabella said, breathless.

"Listen. Both of us have green. Both of us are improving. Same cold, same sneezing substitute. If green meant bacteria, we'd both need pills, and the pharmacist says it doesn't mean that." Katherine took a sip of juice. "What you need is fluids, sleep, and a flu vaccine in October like Foster's family does, because they never catch anything."

There was a long pause on the line, and then a small, deflated laugh. "So my sophisticated emergency plan was pointless."

"Drink something," Katherine said. "Text me at nine. We'll compare tissues."

Nathaniel had been practicing Addyson's piano piece for two weeks, and today was the day he would finally play it with her, both hands, all the way through. Her living room smelled like popcorn, and the big upright piano sat under a window with a brittle little figurine of a dancer on top, so old that one wrong chord might rattle it off the shelf.

"Start at measure twelve," Addyson said, scooting over to make room on the bench. "That's where it gets tricky."

Nathaniel set his hands on the keys and played. When he reached the letter p printed under the notes, he hammered out a huge, glorious sound, because p had to mean powerful, right? He liked that part best. The dancer figurine trembled.

Addyson winced and stopped him. "That's supposed to be the quiet part. Piano means soft and forte means loud. They're Italian words."

Nathaniel stared at the page. So the p was telling him to shrink, not to shout, and the f he'd been playing gently was asking for a whole different animal. He flipped back a page and found a p he'd been blasting for two weeks. "Wait. So every time I thought the music was saying go big, it was actually saying back off?"

"Basically," Addyson said, laughing. "Try it again, but this time imagine you're sneaking downstairs for a midnight snack during the p part."

He tried it. The soft passage came out whispery and careful, and when the f arrived, the loudness actually meant something, because the quiet had made room for it. It was like the piece was breathing. They ran it three more times, and by the third try Nathaniel could feel the pattern in his hands before his eyes confirmed it.

Her little brother wandered in and asked if he could participate, and Addyson let him hold the sustain pedal, which he did with tremendous seriousness, like a tiny employee of a piano corporation who took pedal duty very seriously.

"One more time," Nathaniel said. "All the way through."

They played it, soft where it asked for soft, loud where it asked for loud, her brother pumping the pedal, the dancer figurine swaying on top of the piano but never quite falling. When they hit the final chord, Nathaniel lifted his hands and found they were shaking a little, in a good way.

"Now the fast part," Addyson said, flipping the page. "Tempo change. Ready?"

He set his hands back on the keys.

Colton held the tweezers like they were a bomb fuse. "If this turns my lemonade red, I'm drinking nothing but water for the rest of my life," he announced, and Ayoub laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the tray of test samples.

Mr. Ba had set out five unlabelled cups on the lab bench and told them to sort acids from bases with nothing but litmus paper. Neve went first, dipping her blue strip into cup one. It came out pink. "Acid," she said, and wrote it down. Colton retrieved his own strip from the box, tore it in half because he was already running low, and tested cup two. Pink again. Cup three, pink. Cup four turned the paper blue, so that one was a base. But cup five was the strange one, and by the time they got to it, they had three cups that all looked exactly the same shade of discouraged pink.

"They can't all be the same," Colton said, squinting at the three strips laid side by side on a paper towel. The mystery sample, the vinegar, and something Mr. Ba had whispered was drain cleaner, all red, all identical. He dipped a fresh strip into the mystery cup, then into the vinegar, then into the drain cleaner, holding them up to the window light where the smell of vinegar mixed with the sharper chemical sting from cup three. Same pink. Same pink. Same pink.

"That's useless," Ayoub said. "It's like a yes-or-no question that won't tell you how much."

"Litmus only shows whether a solution is acidic or basic," Neve read from the worksheet, tapping the line with her pen. "It cannot tell how strong the acid or base is." Colton stared at the three matching strips, and something clicked, the way a jammed locker door finally gives. "So the drain cleaner could eat a hole in the counter and the vinegar could dress a salad, and this paper treats them like twins. We'd need something else to compare them. A scale or whatever." He said it with the guilt-free confidence of a boy whose conscience was clear, mostly because he had not actually tasted anything.

Mr. Ba drifted over, peered at their three pink strips, and raised one eyebrow. "So what have we learned, gentlemen and Neve?"

"We learned that paper is a terrible gossip," Colton said. "It spills one secret and keeps the rest."

"Then perhaps tomorrow," Mr. Ba said, "I will let you meet the pH scale."

Neve wrote a large question mark next to cup five, underlined it twice, and slid the tray toward the window, where the three identical strips dried to the same stubborn shade of pink.

At dinner, Hailey pushed her noodles around the plate and said, "Veronica claims she has a perfect shooting percentage." Her father looked up from his glass. "Perfect? Nobody's perfect." He said it lightly, but Hailey knew he followed basketball closely enough to argue about it. "She told the whole team she's shooting a hundred percent," Hailey said. "She made one shot in the game against Ridgefield. It was her only shot all season." Her little brother laughed so hard he nearly knocked over his milk.

The problem was real. Coach posted the stats on the gym door every Friday, and Veronica's name sat at the top of the percentage column, above players who had scored dozens of baskets. Some of the seventh graders had started saying Veronica was the best shooter on the team, and Zoha had come home from practice with her jaw tight, saying nothing, which was worse than complaining.

Hailey took her plate to the sink and thought about the numbers while she rinsed it. One shot, one make. Two shots, two makes would be the same percentage. But what about someone who took forty shots and made twenty-five? That was a lower percentage, and yet that player had scored twenty-five baskets for the team, not one. The hot water ran over her hands. She counted on her fingers just to be sure the pattern held, and it did. A percentage built on one single attempt could say "perfect" about a person who had barely played.

The next morning she found Zoha at the lockers before homeroom. "Ask Veronica how many shots she's taken," Hailey said. "Not how many she made. Total." At practice that afternoon, Zoha asked, right in the middle of the gym, with the whole team stretching. Veronica said, "One," and then added, "but I made it, so I'm at one hundred percent." Zoha nodded slowly. "So a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots one hundred percent," she said. "Even if she never takes another one."

A few of the seventh graders looked at each other. Veronica looked down at her sneakers. The gym smelled like floor wax and rubber, and the coach's whistle lay silent on the bench. When they ran the shooting drill, Veronica took eleven shots and made four. On Friday the new stats went up on the gym door, and her name had slid down the column. She stood in front of the paper for a long moment, then turned around and said, "Zoha, you take the next practice shots with me. Both of us, ten each."

The bleachers in the gymnasium were packed, and Luke could hear his own heartbeat over the squeak of Jordan's sneakers on the sideline. Six spellers were left, and the word hanging in front of him was "millennium."

"M-I-L-E," Luke began, and then the gym went quiet in a way that felt like falling. He heard the wrong letter leave his mouth and knew, instantly, that the right one was E. His mind raced back to the rules sheet Ms. Suryanto had handed out in the library two weeks ago. He had read one line over and over because it had surprised him: you could start a word again from the beginning, but if you changed even one letter you had already said, it counted as a misspelling. Jordan had shrugged when Luke pointed it out. "Who'd ever need that?" Jordan had said. Now Luke knew exactly who.

He could try to slip the correct E in quietly and hope nobody noticed. But Ms. Suryanto was the judge, and she had a habit of leaning forward with her pen stopped mid-air, watching spellers the way she watched kids trying to sneak a second turn at four square. He remembered the spelling bee last year, when a boy had swapped a letter halfway through and Ms. Suryanto had shaken her head before he even finished. Luke had thought it was harsh then. Now he understood it was just obstinate fairness, the kind that never bends.

"May I start over?" Luke asked.

"You may," Ms. Suryanto said, "as long as every letter you say now matches what you said before."

So the letter could not change, only the rest of the word could. He tested the idea in his head, turning it like a puzzle piece. If he said M-I-L-E again, he was stuck with the wrong E where an N belonged, and the word would die right there. Unless the letters he had spoken could belong to a different word entirely. He thought of Henley's trick from their practice sessions, when Henley would ask for the definition to buy time. Luke didn't need time; he needed a redirect.

"M-I-L-E," he repeated, keeping his voice steady, "N-N-I-U-M." He paused. "Milestone. M-I-L-E-S-T-O-N-E. Milestone."

A ripple went through the bleachers. Ms. Suryanto's pen hovered, then her chin dipped, and she said, "Correct." Jordan pumped both fists so hard he grabbed his own knee, and later he would claim he'd bruised the cartilage under the kneecap, which Luke doubted, since Jordan exaggerated everything.

Back at his seat, waiting for the next round, Luke thought about the boy from last year. If he had simply stopped and started over, keeping his letters, he might have survived another round. Maybe the rule wasn't harsh at all; maybe it rewarded the spellers who noticed their own mistakes instead of hiding them. Luke wasn't sure. He decided he'd ask Henley on the walk home.

"Milestone," Henley whispered from the row behind him. "You nurturing that one for weeks?"

"Since the library," Luke whispered back.

Ms. Suryanto cleared her throat and read the next word.

John flattened the wrinkled poster against the gymnasium table and weighed its corners down with beakers he wasn't supposed to touch. The periodic table printed across it had smudged in his backpack, and three atomic numbers had turned into gray blobs. His whole project, the one that was supposed to save him from a failing grade in science, depended on those numbers.

"You're still fixing that?" Cleo whispered from the next table, where her volcano sat polished and perfect. She wanted the blue ribbon so badly she had practiced her speech on the bus twice that morning. "Judging starts in ten minutes, John."

"I know," he said. He had written quiz questions for the judges, and the third one was ruined. The question asked how many neutrons a certain atom had, and the answer had to come from the poster, but the atomic number had vanished into a smudge. He stared at the grid of squares. He knew the mass number for his element, carbon, sat at the top of the box, a twelve. He had copied that part down last night at his grandmother's kitchen table, along with something she had read aloud from her old textbook: the atomic number counts protons.

A judge in a gray sweater was already drifting toward Cleo's table. Ms. Tran, his science teacher, stood near the door, watching him the way she did when she expected him to quit. John wiped his palms on his jeans. His practice sheet from last night was folded in his pocket, and he pulled it out, hoping the missing number was somewhere in his own handwriting. It wasn't. There was only the twelve, and next to it, the number of protons he'd worked out then, six, because the atomic number was six.

He stopped. Six protons, twelve for the mass number. He mouthed the math. Twelve take away six. If the mass number counted protons plus neutrons, then whatever was left over had to be the neutrons. His pencil hovered. Six. He tested the idea on another element from memory, oxygen, mass number sixteen, atomic number eight, and again the leftover made sense: eight neutrons. It wasn't random guessing; it worked twice, the same rule both times, like a pattern hiding behind the numbers.

"Next table," the judge called, and suddenly he was standing in front of John.

John pointed at the smudged square. "Carbon has six protons," he said, "and its mass number is twelve, so subtracting the atomic number from the mass number gives six neutrons." The judge raised an eyebrow, wrote something on her clipboard, and slid the sheet aside. "Show me on another element," she said.

John's finger moved down the poster and stopped on nitrogen. "Fifteen minus seven."

Zoe had recruited Blaine to quiz her before the Mandarin quiz on Friday, mostly because Blaine was the only person she knew who would actually say "no" when she got something wrong. They sat on the bleachers behind the gym, and Blaine held her notebook like a judge holding a verdict.

"Describe your family," Blaine read. "Full sentences."

"Wǒ yǒu yī gè mèimei," Zoe said. "I have one little sister."

"Good. Pets."

"Wǒ yǒu yī māo."

Blaine squinted at the notebook. "There's supposed to be a little word in there. It says so."

"That can't be right," Zoe said. "It's not in the sentence about my sister."

She tested it anyway, because testing things was faster than arguing with Blaine. She said the sentence both ways, over and over, into her phone's recorder, and played them back. The short one sounded like she was dropping something halfway through, like a stair with a missing step. That night she wrote to her grandmother, who lived two towns over and video-called every Sunday.

Dear Pópo, she wrote. How do I say "I have one cat"? I keep saying it wrong and I don't know which part is missing.

The reply came Thursday, in her grandmother's careful handwriting, scanned and emailed by an aunt. The cat says māo, the letter began, as if Zoe didn't know that. The number goes first, then a small word, then the cat. One cat is yì zhī māo. The small word, zhī, is the one we use for many animals. You would not say the number and then the cat with nothing between them, any more than you would wear an elastic band without stretching it around something. Your sister, by the way, uses a different small word. Ask your teacher.

Zoe read the letter three times. So that was the pattern. Numbers and animals needed something in the middle, and it wasn't the same something for every noun. She made two columns in her notebook, one for sister words and one for cat words, and practiced until her pen ran dry.

Friday, Mr. Robinson walked the rows listening to each student. When he reached Zoe, she pulled off the elastic holding her hair back, because she somehow spoke better with her hands free.

"Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo," she said. "And she is enormous."

"Duì," said Mr. Robinson, and moved on.

Blaine raised a hand. "Settlement of a bet," he announced. "Zoe owes me a cookie. She said the little word didn't matter."

"Cookie," Zoe said, and slid one across the desk.

Payton dragged the laundry basket into the garage and tipped it onto the overturned canoe that leaned against the wall, using the smooth hull as a sorting table. Her mom had left a note on the dryer three days ago: "Learn this. White shirt must be clean by Friday." Friday was tomorrow, and Payton had exactly one load's worth of time.

"Sorting is a waste," she said when Zane and Kaiya biked over and found her staring at the pile. "It's all getting washed in the same machine anyway." Zane shrugged and sat on an upturned bucket while Payton stuffed everything, dark jeans, her new red socks, dish towels, and the white school shirt, into the washer and slammed the lid. Kaiya squinted at the machine like it was a bear trap. "My gran sorts by colour," she offered. "My mom doesn't," Payton said, "and her clothes look fine." The drum rumbled, water beginning to circulate through the window in the lid, swirling soap and clothes into a grey-blue storm.

When the cycle ended, Payton pulled out the white shirt and held it up. It was pale pink. Not uniformly pink, which might have been almost stylish, but blotchy, like a sunset that had given up halfway. Zane laughed so hard he slid off the bucket. "Nice shirt. Very expensive-looking."

Payton laid the pink shirt on the canoe hull and picked up one of the red socks. She thought about the order of events. The shirt had been white when it went in. It came out pink. Nothing else had touched it except water, soap, and clothes, and the only red thing in the load was this brand-new sock. Her gran's new towels had felt damp with dye when she'd hugged them at the store. Maybe, she thought, new dark or bright clothes could let dye go into the wash water, and that dye could tint white and pale clothes. She could test it. She filled a jar with warm water, dropped in the red sock, and set the jar on the workbench where they could all watch.

Within minutes, wisps of red curled off the sock like smoke. "It's bleeding," Kaiya whispered. "So that's the whole point of sorting," Payton said slowly. She had changed her mind completely, and she said so. They found one more clean white thing, an old pillowcase, and laid it flat on the hull. "Neutrals and pale stuff in this pile," Payton said, pointing, "dark and bright in that one. New red sock gets its own jar until it stops bleeding." She reloaded the washer with only the dark load, then held up the pink shirt and studied it, chewing her lip. "Tomorrow," she said, "we find out if pink counts as a school colour."

The comment appeared on the class discussion board at 10:14 a.m., while twenty keyboards clattered in the computer lab. "Nobody wants your stupid robot pictures, Eliana. Delete them." Alex read it twice. The username was RobotKing77, which told him nothing, because everyone in Ms. Sadeghi's fifth period hid behind usernames.

Eliana sat two rows over, staring at her screen, not typing anymore. That was the strange part. Whoever RobotKing77 was, he had watched Eliana post her robot artwork all week, and he had waited until today to strike. Alex thought about Alvin, who sat behind Eliana in every class and told her, just yesterday, that her drawings belonged in a museum. Alvin was so polite in person that he apologized to chairs when he bumped into them. But usernames were like masks, and masks made some people brave.

Alex remembered something from October, a memory that now felt important. He had been at his grandmother's house, and his cousin had typed something snarky about a referee on a fan forum, something the cousin would never yell at an actual game. "It's just the internet," the cousin had said, laughing. At the time Alex had laughed too. Now he wondered if there was a pattern here, some rule he couldn't see.

He opened a search window and typed slowly, evaluating each result before he clicked. A psychology article came up, and he leaned close to read it under his breath. "In 2004, a psychologist named John Suler described the online disinhibition effect. People often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face." He read it again. The words fit Alvin perfectly, but they also fit half the class. He needed proof, not a theory.

So he tested it. He posted, as himself, "RobotKing77, Eliana's robot art is the best thing on this board. Show us yours." Public. Signed. Impossible to hide behind. Then he watched the room instead of the screen, because a comment doesn't write itself; somebody's hands have to do it. Three keyboards went quiet. Somebody coughed. Alvin's hands stayed frozen above the keys, and his ears turned a distinct shade of pink that Alex could see even from across the lab.

The reply came at 10:31. "Sorry Eliana. That was dumb. Your robots are cool." No username attached. The next morning, Alvin left a folded drawing on Eliana's desk, a robot with a tiny crown. Eliana unfolded it, looked at Alvin, and said, "RobotKing, I presume?" Alvin's whole face went red, and she held out her hand and said, "Truce?"

Addison stood outside the Sakura Restaurant holding a wrapped box of maple candies so tightly the ribbon dug into her thumb. Nadia's grandparents had just arrived from Osaka, and Nadia had invited her to dinner, and now Addison had one enormous problem: she had no idea how to greet them. Nadia had drilled her on some things at school, like taking off shoes and not sticking chopsticks upright in rice, but the bowing part was a mystery.

Through the window she watched the door open. Nadia's grandfather bowed to Mr. Mokoena, the owner, and Mr. Mokoena bowed back, and then Nadia's grandmother bowed to a waitress, and the waitress bowed, and everyone in the whole restaurant seemed to be folding at each other like grass in the wind. Addison noticed something. When the grandfather greeted Mr. Mokoena, his bow was quick and shallow, but when Nadia's grandmother met an elderly man by the counter, both of them bent low and held it for a long moment, almost long enough for Addison to have counted to three. A pattern, she thought. Maybe the deeper and longer the bow, the more respect it showed. That was testable.

"Addison! You're early," Nadia said, pulling her inside.

"I have a theory," Addison whispered. "Bowing is like a respect meter. Deep and long means big respect."

"Shh. They're coming. Say konnichiwa. You can do this. I nominate you for bravest friend in the cafeteria."

The grandparents approached. Addison handed over the candy box with both hands, because Nadia had said gifts were given that way and were often refused once or twice before being accepted. Grandmother said, "Oh, you must not," and Addison held on politely, and after the second refusal, exactly as predicted, the gift was accepted with a small bow. Addison bent down low and slow, the way she'd seen done for the elderly man. When she peeked upward, grandfather was smiling, and grandmother bowed back even deeper, so deep that Addison, who had just learned the word in geometry, thought her spine was nearly perpendicular to the floor.

At the table, things got trickier. Addison lifted her bowl of rice to her mouth the way Nadia did, and slurped her noodles, which felt absolutely wrong after years of being told to be quiet at dinner, but grandmother nodded approval and slurped louder, so Addison slurped louder too, and Nadia laughed so hard she nearly dropped her chopsticks.

"So," Nadia said as they waited for tea. "Grandmother says you bowed better than our mail carrier. He waves. Just waves, like he's landing a plane."

"He doesn't know the system," Addison said. "The system is deep bow, big respect."

"Exactly. You figured it out in one minute through a window."

Grandfather leaned over and, in careful English, said, "Your bow was very kind. Next time, maybe not so deep. You are young. You save your knees."

Addison grinned and bowed, quick and shallow, just enough. Grandfather bowed back the same way.

Jasmine stood in her grandmother's kitchen with a photocopied page of Torah verses, and around her the whole family was pretending not to listen while absolutely listening. Her aunt stirred a pot very slowly. Her grandfather set down his teacup with exaggerated care, as if a loud clink might ruin everything.

"Again," said Ms. Ross, the neighbour who had been tutoring her since September. She had come to the gathering on purpose, carrying a cloth bag, because the bat mitzvah was in nine days and Jasmine's confidence kept dwindling every time she stumbled on the same phrase in verse twelve.

Jasmine took a breath and began. She got through verse four, verse seven, even the tricky part she'd nicknamed "the tongue twister." Then her grandmother brought out the real thing, a small Torah scroll borrowed from the synagogue for the occasion, and unrolled it on the table. Jasmine's hands went cold. Somehow reading off parchment was nothing like reading off a photocopy. Her voice shrank, and before she knew it her finger drifted toward the letters, hovering closer and closer, until Ms. Ross gently placed something in her other hand.

It was a slim silver pointer, shaped like a tiny hand at the end. "It's called a yad," Ms. Ross said, and nothing more.

"Yad means hand," Jasmine said slowly, turning it over. "That's why it's shaped like this." Nobody answered, which was how she knew she'd gotten it right. She followed the words with the pointer instead of her finger, and realized something: the reason she'd been stumbling wasn't nerves at all. When her finger hovered over the letters, she was blocking her own view of the line, then losing her place when she moved it. The pointer sat just above the words and traveled with her, steady as a bookmark that walked.

She remembered Brent, her lab partner, laughing about his science fair prototype, a volcano that had gone extinct halfway through the demonstration. "At least it fizzled in front of the class instead of the judges," he'd said. "Practice where you fail." So she practiced right there, in front of twelve relatives and a pot of soup.

Verse by verse, with the yad in her hand, the reading came out clean. When she finished, her grandfather raised his teacup like a toast.

Her little cousin tugged her sleeve. "Can I hold the hand stick?"

"After the ceremony," Jasmine said, "I'll teach you the tongue twister."

Wyatt sat in the third pew of the synagogue with his father's suit jacket buttoned to the top, because Grandma Ruth had always said a boy should look like he cared. At the front, next to the rabbi, stood a small table with her glasses folded on it. Freya slid into the pew beside him and whispered, "My mom said to tell you we're sorry. Also, Leia is parking the bike, so save her a spot." Wyatt saved the spot. He had a plan for the service, which he had written on an index card in his desk the night before: say the mourner's prayer, look at the glasses, remember her voice, feel something. He had tested the plan twice in rehearsal and both times it had worked, more or less.

The week before, he had gone with Leia to a movie because she had won two tickets and had been talking about it for a month. He had laughed hard at the talking dog, and then, walking out into the arid July parking lot, he had felt like he had betrayed someone. He came home and told his father, "I laughed the same week she died. That's wrong." His father didn't lecture him. He only pulled a paperback off the shelf, one with a cracked spine, and said, "Chapter four. Read it yourself, then evaluate whether you're a bad grandson."

The book was by two researchers, Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut. In 1999, they had described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. They called it the dual process model. Wyatt had read the page three times, checking his premise against the evidence: Grandma died on a Tuesday, and he had still eaten breakfast on Wednesday, still done his homework, still laughed at Leia's impressions in the cafeteria. According to the model, that was not betrayal. That was the back-and-forth, the ordinary rhythm of it, loss then life then loss again.

Freya had her own reason for being there. She was collecting signatures on a memory card for Wyatt's family, and she wanted everyone at the shiva afterward to sign it too, which meant she kept slipping out to the lobby with a pen. When she came back the fourth time, Mr. Szabó, who taught science at their school and had known Grandma from the community garden, leaned over the pew. "I heard your father mention the dual process model," he said quietly. "It's why I'm crying and then telling jokes in the same ten minutes."

Leia arrived just as the congregation stood for the prayer. Wyatt's voice shook, steadied, and shook again. Afterward he walked to the small table, picked up her glasses, folded his hand around them, and said, "Thanks for the dog movie, Grandma. You'd have hated it."

The festival crowd in Sevilla was so thick that Luke lost Riley within thirty seconds of stepping through the gate. Worse, he lost the meeting spot too, because the meeting spot had been a giant paper lantern shaped like a bull, and the wind had just knocked it down. His phone was dead, his mom was somewhere near the flamenco stage, and his stomach was doing that desperate thing it did when he had drunk two lemonades at lunch and then walked for an hour.

He had one phrase ready. Ms. Littlechild, his Spanish teacher back home, had drilled it into the whole class before the trip, standing at the whiteboard while the clock ticked toward the bell. "If you remember nothing else," she had said, tapping the marker, "remember this one." Luke had written it on his hand that morning in the hotel, and the ink was still faintly there under the sunscreen: ¿Dónde está el baño? He also remembered Riley grinning beside him, whispering that the blue wristbands Ms. Littlechild handed out symbolized survival, since without them none of them would make it home.

The problem was the answer. He knew how to ask, but when a woman by the paella stand replied in a rapid stream of Spanish, he caught only one word, and it was not a direction. "Le... izquierda?" he guessed, and she laughed kindly and repeated herself, slower this time, pointing with two fingers as if turning a tiny steering wheel. Left. The word must mean left. He said "por favor," the way Riley had practiced with him on the plane, and the woman's whole face softened, and she walked him three steps to a corner and pointed again.

Luke thanked her with the only other word he had, "gracias," and jogged left, where a green sign with a stick figure waited behind a row of flags that symbolized every country represented at the festival. The relief was immediate and enormous. On the way out he spotted Riley by a churro cart, holding two churros like a diplomat holding important documents, his face serious. "I've been negotiating," Riley said. "This nice man only speaks Spanish, and I've been saying 'por favor' at him for ten minutes. I think it means he has to be nice to me now."

"It makes it polite," Luke said, mouth already full of churro. "It's like magic manners." Riley stared at him, then turned back to the churro man and said "por favor" one more time, very slowly, and the man laughed and handed over a third churro, free. Behind them, a loudspeaker announced that the lantern parade, the one mandatory event their whole group had traveled to see, would begin in five minutes. Luke grabbed Riley's sleeve and pointed down the boulevard, where the first paper lanterns were already being lit. "Left is that way. Trust me, I speak Spanish now."

Grandpa's dining room table had become a science lab, and Austin was the scientist who had no idea what he was doing. Spread in front of him were two printed graphs for Ms. Gill's assignment: one showing monthly rainfall and temperature for the Sonoran Desert, the other for a rainforest in Brazil. His job was to compare the two climates, and his pencil hovered over the paper without writing anything.

"I need this to be interesting," Austin muttered, "because right now it's just squiggles."

His cousin Adele slid into the chair across from him, balancing a bowl of popcorn. Adele wanted one thing from the afternoon: to be entertained. "Then make it interesting," she said. "What do the squiggles say?"

"The desert gets almost no rain, and the rainforest gets tons of it. That part's easy." Austin tapped the temperature lines. "But here's the weird part. The desert graph swings from blazing hot months to freezing cold months. The rainforest graph barely moves. Warmest month, coolest month, it's all about the same."

"Sounds boring," Adele said, tossing a kernel at him. "Same temperature forever."

"It's not boring, it's..." Austin stopped. He leaned closer to the rainforest graph. Grandpa, drying dishes at the sink behind them, glanced over but said nothing. Austin flipped through his library book on rainforests and found a chart of hourly temperatures at a weather station. His eyes went down the column, and then he sat back like he'd been poked.

"Adele. Look at this. The days get hot and the nights get cool, right there in the numbers." He grabbed his pencil and circled the day's high and the night's low. Then he circled the warmest month and the coolest month on the other graph and compared the gaps. "The swing between day and night is bigger than the swing between the warmest and coolest months. Way bigger."

"So?" Adele said, stealing her own popcorn back.

"So if somebody was packing for the rainforest, they'd think, it's hot every month, I only need shorts. But the nights are cool. They'd need a sweater. In a rainforest." He laughed. "Ms. Gill is going to think I made this up."

"It does sound made up," Adele admitted. "Show me again."

Austin walked her through it line by line, testing his idea against both graphs to be sure he wasn't fooling himself. It seemed logical, but he'd been wrong before, like the time he'd sworn hail was frozen rain and Ms. Gill had gently proved otherwise in front of the whole class. He checked the book a second time, then a third. The numbers held.

"Fine," Adele said, pointing at his blank worksheet, where despair had been about to set in five minutes ago. "Write it down before you forget it. And draw a little person in a sweater."

"That's not scientific."

"I'll mediate," Grandpa said from the sink, without turning around. "One small sweater person, in the name of science."

Austin grinned and picked up his pencil.

Gavin had forty dollars, and the sneakers in the window of the mall's sportswear store cost one hundred and thirty. He stood there with his vocabulary worksheet crumpled in his back pocket, doing the math twice in case the first answer was a mistake. It wasn't. The shoes glowed under the spotlights like they were radioactive.

"Everybody's wearing them," said Jaxon, who had appeared beside him out of nowhere, holding a smoothie. "The whole eighth grade. Jet has two pairs."

Jet, as it happened, was inside the store, holding up a box and grinning. Gavin went in. The walls were covered with a poster of a basketball player he recognized from TV, mid-dunk, wearing the exact shoe. Underneath, the words read: LIMITED. FEARLESS. REVOLUTIONARY. Elite players demand more. Gavin read it twice. The words felt like they were shouting at him, even though they were printed on paper.

He took out the worksheet, which was for Mr. Anderson's class and due Monday. The assignment was to look up the history of one vocabulary word, and Gavin had picked "propaganda" because it had sounded dramatic. He'd found the entry that morning and it had surprised him so much he'd read it out loud to his mom. "The word propaganda comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622," he told Jaxon, who sipped his smoothie and said, "Huh. I thought it just meant lying."

"It kind of started as spreading an idea on purpose," Gavin said, looking around the store. "Like this." He pointed at the poster. "That's a celebrity testimonial. Jet having two pairs is a bandwagon appeal. And 'fearless' is a loaded word, because shoes can't actually be brave." He felt like a detective who had just exposed a whole criminal operation, except the criminals were posters and the crime was making him want shoes he couldn't afford.

Jet came over, box in hand. "You getting them?"

"I have forty bucks."

"They'd change your whole life," Jet said, and Gavin noticed Jet said it in the exact tone of the TV commercial, which made him laugh until his stomach hurt, somewhere up near his intestine, which he was pretty sure wasn't where stomachaches actually happened but close enough.

The clerk announced over the speaker that the shoes were selling out fast and restocking was not guaranteed. Two kids behind them shifted impatiently. It all felt suddenly inevitable, like a machine designed to end with Gavin's forty dollars in the register.

He tested his idea instead. He turned to the clearance rack, where last year's model sat, nearly identical, for thirty-five dollars. He tried them on. They fit. He carried the box to the register, paid, and walked out with five dollars left for a pretzel.

Jaxon caught up to him by the fountain. "You know those are basically the same shoe."

Gavin held up the box. "Fearless," he said, "and on clearance."

Jack sat in the school library with a folded map of a pretend Chinese town spread across the table. Ms. Romano had set up the exercise for the language club: ask for directions in Mandarin, then follow the answer to find the hidden paper star. Jack had one goal today, and it was not to end up in the pretend river again like last week.

"You went swimming twice," said Jewel, sliding into the chair across from him. "In a map."

"The river was invisible," Jack said. "That's my story and I'm keeping it."

He spread his flashcards and thought about his grandfather. Every summer visit, they walked to the market together, and his grandfather would point at corners and say the same two words over and over. "Zuǒ," he would say, pointing left, and then, turning his hand the other way, "yòu." Each word had its own tone, the way his grandfather said it, one dipping down, one falling like a dropped stone. Jack had repeated them at every intersection for three weeks, and by the end he could navigate the whole neighborhood without his grandfather pointing at all.

He tested the words now, tapping the map. "Zuǒ means left," he said, "and yòu means right. If I actually listen for the tone instead of panicking, I can tell them apart."

Heinrich arrived holding the answer sheet for the round, sworn to secrecy, and Jack asked his question: where was the star? Heinrich answered in Mandarin, rapid and flat, and Jack felt the panic rising, the same panic that had steered him into the river before. He made himself slow down. Two words kept recurring, and one of them dipped down, the way his grandfather's had at the corner by the noodle shop. Dipping meant left. Falling meant right.

"Left at the bridge, then right," Jack said, mostly to himself, and moved his finger along the map. "Twice right at the end, I think."

He traced the path and stopped on the square with the little drawn pavilion. "There."

Jewel leaned over. "You're sure? Because last time you were so sure that you drowned."

"I had a concussion of pride," Jack said. "Not permanent, though."

Heinrich turned over the sheet, and there it was, the pavilion square circled in red. Jack whooped so loudly that Ms. Romano appeared from behind the biography shelf with one eyebrow raised, and Jewel hurried to disclose the whole game before they got kicked out of the library for the second time that semester.

"Keep it down," Ms. Romano said, but she was smiling. "And Jack, next round, try asking me. I lived in Xi'an for two years."

Jack folded his map and grinned. "Zuǒ or yòu, Ms. Romano. I'm ready."

Megan had one goal for the school talent show audition: keep her juggling act a secret until she walked on stage. Three flaming pins, or at least three tennis balls painted to look like flaming pins, depending on how the paint dried.

She practiced behind the gym, where nobody went except the recycling bins. On Thursday she managed eleven catches in a row, a personal record. On Friday, Omar appeared at the corner of the building before she had even picked up the second ball.

"That's your talent?" he said. "Juggling?"

"How did you find me?"

He held up his phone. On the screen was a map of the school, with a little cartoon Megan standing behind the gym. "Snap Map," he said. "It shows your real-time location to your friends. Launched in 2017, I think. My cousin told me."

Megan stared at the little cartoon version of herself. It was wearing a tiny scarf, which she did not own. Otherwise it was uncomfortably accurate, right down to the corner of the building where the map said she was standing, because she was standing there.

"I never installed anything like that," she said.

"It comes with the app. You probably just tapped through it."

That afternoon in Ms. Nair's class, Megan found it in her settings, three menus deep, like something hoping not to be found. There was a list of everyone who could see her: Omar, Issa, and nineteen other names she recognized only vaguely. One was a kid from her old school in another town. She had not spoken to him in two years, and he could apparently watch her move around like weather.

She had an intuition that the little dot updated even when she wasn't posting anything, so she decided to test it. During lunch she left her phone with Issa, walked to the library, and came back. Issa showed her the screen. The dot had made the whole trip without her, faithfully strolling to the library and home again, like a dog that had learned the route.

"You walked past the library, though," Issa said. "You looped by the cafeteria."

"I did. And it saw that too."

After school, Megan turned the whole thing off. Then she went back behind the gym, where Omar was already leaning against the recycling bins, holding his phone up like a reporter.

"Took you long enough," he said. "Your dot's been standing at the flagpole for ten minutes."

"That's the point," Megan said. "The flagpole is where I leave it now." She picked up the first tennis ball, still slightly tacky from the paint.

Omar lowered the phone. "Eleven catches," he said. "You want to make it twelve before Friday?"

Maya pressed her palms against the warm metal tray of soup and followed the line of steam down the counter. Why did the soup kitchen need so many volunteers on a school holiday in January? Her whole class had signed up, and Mr. Doyle had driven five of them over in his van, but nobody had explained why a day off became a day of work.

"You're new," said a woman behind the counter, handing Maya a ladle. "Scoop, pass, smile. That's the whole job."

Beside her, Cullen was already moving like he'd done this for years, sliding bread slices onto trays with meticulous care, straightening each one so the edges lined up. Maya watched a man in a gray coat take his bowl and cup his hands around it, breathing in the vapor before he ate, like the warm air itself was food.

Flashback: last January, Maya had been home on the same holiday, sleeping until ten, and she remembered seeing a news clip where people in orange vests painted a fence and picked up trash. She had wondered then why the reporters kept calling it a day of service. Now, ladling soup in a noisy room that smelled of onions and bleach, she turned the question over. It had to mean the holiday itself asked something of people. She remembered Mr. Doyle saying the word "King Holiday and Service Act" when he passed out permission slips. She tested her idea quietly, the way she tested things: "Cullen, is this why the whole school signs up? Because the holiday is a national day of volunteer service?"

"Since 1994," Cullen said, not looking up from the bread. "The King Holiday and Service Act was signed that year. Made the day into service. My sister's been coming every year since kindergarten."

Maya felt the pieces click. The act, the signing, the date: it was a rule she couldn't see, but she could see its results all around her, a room full of kids on a day off, scooping and passing and smiling.

At two o'clock the crowd thinned, and the woman behind the counter pointed to a stack of dented cans. "Salvage what you can," she said. "Dents are fine, bulges are not." Maya picked up a can and turned it over in her hands, checking the sides, wondering what else in this building had been rescued and given a second job.

Mr. Doyle leaned in the doorway. "Same time next January?"

Maya looked at the empty ladle in her hand. "Can we come in April too, when there's no holiday making us?"

Anthony pressed his nose against the bookshop window, where a dusty sign said they planned to renovate the whole store next month. Inside, a shelf labeled CLASSICS had exactly one copy of The Most Dangerous Game left, and Jayla was reaching for it at the same time.

"I saw it first," Anthony said, grabbing the spine.

"Ms. Holloway needs it for our short story unit," Jayla said. "You can't even explain foreshadowing. That's the whole quiz on Friday."

"Can too." Anthony flipped the book open right there between the shelves. His eyes caught the first page. "Wait. The sailors call it Ship-Trap Island. They're scared of the place, even from far away."

Jayla peered over his shoulder. "It's just a name."

"Names mean stuff, though." Anthony tapped the page. "Ship-Trap. Like the island is a trap made of... ships? Or for ships?" He dug in his backpack and pulled out his notebook. His class had a running list called "sneaky clues," and so far it only had three sad entries from a story about a dog that turned out not to be dangerous at all. He wrote: sailors fear the island before anything happens. It's a warning.

Poppy appeared from the graphic novel section, carrying a book about raccoons. "Ooh, are you being a scavenger for clues? Because I found a raccoon that steals pens."

"Look," Anthony said, and read the opening aloud in his best dramatic voice. A yacht, a dark night, and sailors who felt dread at the mere mention of the island's name. "So if the story is called The Most Dangerous Game, and there's a hunter on board who keeps talking about hunting, then the fear of that island has to hint at danger waiting there."

Jayla frowned. "Hint. Foreshadow. You're doing it."

"I'm doing it." Anthony grinned so wide his cheeks hurt.

They bought the book between the three of them, each paying an approximate third of the price, and Poply threw in an extra nickel so nobody had to wait for change. Outside, the afternoon sun made the sidewalk glow. Jayla held up her palm for a high five, then stopped.

"You still have to explain symbolism," she said. "By Friday."

Anthony looked down at the cover, where the island's dark shape loomed behind the title like something waiting. "The island is a trap," he said slowly. "Maybe the whole island means something. Maybe it's a symbol."

Jayla's hand was still hanging in the air.

"Don't leave me hanging," Anthony said, and slapped it.

Beatrice stood in line at the bank beside her mother, holding a page of homework questions so tightly the paper creased. Question three read: "Which is riskier, a stock or a bond, and why?" She was supposed to interview someone at the bank, but now that she was actually here, her mouth felt dry.

Behind her, two voices were arguing. Beatrice turned and recognized Kiara and Isha from her grade, waiting with a parent of their own.

"It's not fair," Kiara was saying. "My dad put all his money in one company, and the company crashed. He lost basically everything." Her chin wobbled a little, and Isha patted her arm.

"That's the weird part," Isha said. "My grandma had money in that same company too, but hers was inside a fund that holds a whole bunch of different stocks. When the company crashed, she only lost a little."

Beatrice forgot about her dry mouth. "Wait," she said. "Same company, same crash, totally different results?"

"That's what I keep trying to figure out," Kiara said. "I keep imagining it like dominoes. One falls, they all fall."

Isha shook her head. "It's more like the fund spread the dominoes out. That's called diversifying," she said. "Grandma says it means holding many different stocks, so one company going under hurts a lot less than if all the money were in that one stock."

"That's the word my mom uses!" Beatrice flipped her page over and wrote diversifying in big letters, then drew a circle around it. "Okay, so a bond is a promise to pay you back, like a loan. A stock is owning a tiny piece of a company. If the company dies, your piece dies with it. Like, extinct." She tapped her pencil. "So a single stock is riskier, because everything depends on one company surviving."

A woman in a navy blazer opened the counter beside the teller windows. "Beatrice? I'm Ms. Haddad. Your mother said you had questions for a school project." She smiled at all three girls. "Do your friends want to sit in too?"

They trooped after her to a small desk with a bowl of peppermints. Before any question could precede Beatrice's own careful opening line, Kiara blurted, "Is my dad bad with money?"

Ms. Haddad considered this through the lens of long experience, or so it seemed to Beatrice, because she answered slowly and kindly. "No. He put his faith in one thing, and one thing let him down. Plenty of careful people have done the same."

"Then he could put some money in a fund," Isha said. "Like my grandma."

"He says funds are boring," Kiara admitted, but she was digging in her backpack for a pen, and she copied Beatrice's circled word onto her hand.

"Boring survives crashes," Beatrice said, and slid her homework across the desk. "Ms. Haddad, can I write down that bonds are promises and stocks are pieces of companies, and the riskiest thing of all is one single stock with nothing else around it?"

"You may," said Ms. Haddad, dropping three peppermints into their hands. "And tell your teacher the example you found standing in line."

Kiara looked at the word inked on her palm and grinned. "I'm showing my dad tonight."

Grandpa had been in the backyard for ten minutes, holding the tomato seed packet at arm's length and squinting at it like it was a distant hawk. Raphael watched him from the porch, chewing the last of his toast. At the market cafe on Saturday, Grandpa had done the same thing with the menu, stretching his arm out until Raphael finally read the specials out loud for him. Two times was a coincidence, maybe. Three would be a pattern. He wiped his hands on his jeans and went down the steps.

"Grandpa, can you read this?" Raphael held up the watering schedule he'd written, first close to his grandfather's face, then slowly pulling it back the length of his arm. Grandpa blinked at it, frowned, blinked again.

"Stop waving it around like a flag, kiddo. Bring it back a bit." At about arm's length, Grandpa nodded. "There. Whoever heard of a boy writing so small anyway." Raphael inhaled the smell of turned earth and mulch and said nothing, but he marked the distance on the schedule with his thumbnail. It was the same distance as the menu, the same as the seed packet. Whatever was going on, it lived in his grandfather's eyes, and it lived at exactly that range.

Luis came over after lunch, drawn by the promise of the old treehouse ladder, but Raphael showed him the schedule first and explained his test. "So near is blurry and far is fine," Luis said, turning the paper over. "My mom does the same arm thing with her phone." Grandpa, who had been listening from the tomato bed, sat back on his heels and laughed.

"It's called presbyopia," he said. "After about forty, the lens of the eye loses flexibility, and it can't focus up close the way it used to. Reading glasses fix it. I've got a pair somewhere in my suitcase, if I ever unpack it." He brushed dirt off his knees. Raphael remembered being impulsive last summer, laughing when his other grandpa held a birthday card out like that, and how quickly the laughing had stopped when nobody else joined in. He hadn't thought about that in a year, and now here he was, catching the same thing before anyone could tease anybody.

Grandpa never did find the glasses that week, but Raphael left the watering schedule pinned to the shed door in oversized letters, every word big enough to read from across the yard. On Thursday morning Grandpa stood in front of it, hands on hips, and read the whole thing out loud from the picnic table.

"Look at that," he said. "The scavenger who planted these tomatoes also wrote me the only sign in town I can see."

The community centre was holding its first Heritage Night, and Romy had signed up to build the welcome display. She was gluing a balsa-wood model airplane above the sign-in table when Timothy and Philip started arguing beside her, loud enough that she could hear them over the hum of the folding chairs being dragged into place.

"You can't be in the Métis group," Philip was saying. "Your dad isn't Métis. Only your grandma is, and she's not even here tonight."

"My mom says I'm Métis," Timothy said. "She says we're all registered through the nation, and that's that."

"That's not how it works. You have to look the part. You have to be, like, fully from that group."

Romy turned the model over in her hands, checking the propeller she had carved from a coffee stir stick. The blades were set at an angle so they would actually spin. She found herself wondering what rule, if any, decided a question like theirs. You couldn't see belonging the way you could see a propeller or a uniform. Maybe, she thought, there was a written answer somewhere, the way there was a written angle for the blades.

"Ms. Nolan," she called, "is there a computer I can use for ten minutes?"

The activity room had two old laptops. Romy typed in her question about who decides what group a person belongs to. The answer came up faster than she expected. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership. She read the line twice. It meant Timothy's nation decided Timothy's membership, not Philip. She could deduce that from the wording alone, and she wanted to test it before she trusted it.

Back in the gym, she found Timothy alone by the juice table. She showed him the screen. "It's the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples," she said. "Adopted 13 September 2007. It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership."

Timothy read it slowly, and his shoulders came up from where they had been sagging. "So Philip doesn't get a vote."

"Nobody outside your nation does, by the sound of it."

Philip appeared with a paper plate of samosas, because his own family was presenting the food table and he wanted, more than anything tonight, to be the one who knew the most in the room. He read the declaration over Timothy's shoulder, and his face went through several expressions before settling on grudging respect. "Fine. But you still have to come see our table. My grandmother made three kinds, and I helped with two."

By the end of the evening, the gym smelled like frybread and curry, and someone's grandfather was playing fiddle near the stage. Timothy had pinned a small beaded pin to his jacket, one his grandmother had sent. Romy gave the model airplane one last look, flicked the propeller with her finger, and watched it spin.

Sawyer had one job until noon, when the toddler's mother got back from her interview, and that job was sitting on a bench at Riverside Park watching her son push a plastic duck around the edge of the splash pond. The pond was barely a puddle, two inches deep at the most, so at first it had seemed safe to glance at his phone. Then he remembered the line from the babysitting card his aunt had given him, and he stopped glancing.

Matthias arrived at ten, carrying a remote-control sailboat. "This is a descendant of the one my grandfather built," he said, holding it out. "His sank in 1989. This one won't." He crouched at the pond's far side to launch it, and Denise came jogging behind him with a towel, already arguing that the pond was too small for a real race.

The toddler took one look at the sailboat and plunged his arms in after it, laughing. Sawyer scooped him up, dripping. "You have to hold him back," Denise said. "It's two inches of water. He's fine alone for a minute." It sounded naive to Sawyer, the way his own thinking had been naive an hour ago, before he'd really read the card. "Kids can drown in just a few inches of water, and without splashing or crying out," he said. "You can't ever leave them alone near a bath, or anything like one." Denise blinked at him, then at the pond, and didn't argue again.

Then Sawyer's phone rang, and the screen said it was the toddler's mother. Matthias waved him toward the quieter grass, so Sawyer did what the card had drilled: he wrapped the toddler in Denise's towel and carried him along, phone to one ear, wet boy on his hip. He didn't leave him by the water, not even for the length of a call. The interview had moved up, his mother said; she'd be there in ten minutes, not at noon.

Ten minutes. Matthias wanted his race before the sprinklers came on at eleven, because the schedule sheet taped to the pavilion post said the pond drained then, and a drained pond would end everything. So they raced with the toddler on Sawyer's hip, shrieking with delight every time the sail heeled over, Denise running alongside as the official judge even though she'd said the whole thing was silly. The boat crossed the reed they'd stuck in the mud as a finish line a full boat-length ahead of nothing, since it was the only boat, and Matthias raised both fists anyway.

When the toddler's mother hurried up the path, Sawyer handed over a damp, happy boy and a soggy plastic duck. "He never left the water alone," Denise announced before Sawyer could speak. "Not even for a phone call." Behind them, the sprinkler timer clicked, and the pond began to empty.

Rachel had a plan for Saturday morning, and the plan was this: she would do laundry so well that her mother would have to let her do it forever, which meant she would never again wash a single dish. She dragged the hamper into the kitchen, tipped it onto the tiles, and sorted the pile into hills. Dark hill, light hill, towel hill, and a small suspicious hill of things that had once been white but were now the colour of weak tea.

She was patting herself on the back, mentally, when Ophelia arrived in sock feet, holding her phone like a clipboard. "Bryan says you're doing laundry," Ophelia said. "He wants to know if you'll do his too." Rachel said that was a hypothetical question with a very firm answer, which was no. Then Ophelia picked up a cream sweater with wooden buttons from the top of the pile. It was hand-knitted, with a tag sewn inside in her grandmother's looping handwriting. Rachel assumed her mother had left it out for the next wash, since it smelled like campfire and old perfume.

They loaded the machine, poured in the detergent, and Rachel turned the dial to hot, because hot water seemed like the serious, professional choice. The drum thumped. They ate toast at the counter while the machine sloshed and groaned like a stomach ache. When it clicked off, Rachel pulled out the clothes one armful at a time: dark hill, light hill, towels, and then something that made her stop.

The sweater had become small enough for a doll. The sleeves were the length of mittens. Ophelia held it up with two fingers, and the wooden buttons hung on it like coins on a vest. Rachel turned the tag over, and under her grandmother's name, in smaller loops, were the words "WOOL. COLD ONLY." She had washed a wool sweater in hot, sloshing water, and it had shrunk.

"That's called felting," said Ophelia, who was reading from her phone. Rachel frowned and looked at the sweater again, at how tight and stiff the knitting had gone, almost like fabric instead of loops. So something had happened inside the wool itself, something she couldn't see, some invisible thing about the fibres that hot water and sloshing had set off. She narrowed her eyes at the machine as if it had done it on purpose.

She texted her mother a photograph of the tiny sweater, then flattened the rest of the laundry on the kitchen table and started folding towels, since towels could not betray her. Bryan texted back first: HA. Then her mother texted: We'll talk. Ophelia put the little sweater on a jam jar, where it fit perfectly, sleeves dangling like a cardigan for a very small librarian.

"We could say it's a memoir," Rachel said. "Grandma's sweater, in its second life."

"It's a doll sweater now," said Ophelia, and buttoned the top button.

The hockey rink was empty of ice all summer, so Ms. Eze ran a three-on-three basketball clinic on the concrete floor where the zamboni usually parked. Ryan had signed up because he wanted to be a point guard, the one who decided where the ball went. So far he mostly dribbled in circles and hoped.

"Point guards talk," Ms. Eze said on the first Thursday. "If you don't call the play, you're just a kid with a ball." She showed them a pick and roll: one player stands in the defender's path, the ball handler uses that screen, and the screener then slips toward the hoop. Ryan practiced it with Nyla and Maelys until the lights buzzed overhead.

The landlord of the building had left the big garage doors open, and warm air rolled in from the parking lot. On Saturday the older kids showed up, including a tall boy named Devon, and they ran a real game, shirts against skins. Ryan took the point for his team.

He called the play. "Red, Red." Nyla came and set the screen on his defender, and Ryan drove around it, expecting a clear lane. Instead Devon stepped out in front of him. Devon had been guarding Maelys under the hoop, and now Devon was on Ryan. Ryan pulled the ball back out before he lost it, confused. His own defender was trailing somewhere behind the screen, chasing Maelys, who had wandered toward the basket with nobody on her.

At the next whistle he stood at the top and thought it through. It wasn't that his defender had gotten lost. The two defenders had traded who they were guarding. That was the answer to a pick, and it meant the big defender came to the ball. He wanted to test the idea before he trusted it.

"Maelys," he said quietly, "next possession, go set the screen yourself, then roll." He told Nyla to stay wide where her defender would have to choose. Then, to make sure Devon committed, Ryan simulated a hard drive, jabbing his foot toward the paint. Devon moved with him. Maelys screened Ryan's man and cut to the hoop, and the defender who had been guarding Maelys now chased Ryan around the screen. The trade had happened again, exactly as Ryan had guessed, which meant Maelys was open with a smaller player on her.

He fired the pass over Devon's outstretched arm. Maelys caught it, took one dribble, and laid it in off the backboard. Devon called for the ball on the other end, annoyed, and announced that nobody was immune to a good pump fake, which was not at all the same thing, but Ryan let him have it.

"Same play again," Ryan said, backing out to the top. He clapped once and put the ball above his head. "Red, Red."

Andrew sat cross-legged on his grandfather's porch with a folded sheet of Arabic in his hands, mouthing the same line for the ninth time. The ceremony was in three weeks, and he was supposed to recite Surah Al-Fatiha by heart in front of the whole family. So far his tongue kept tripping over one word, and every trip made him laugh, which made him forget even more.

"That word," said his cousin Ravi from the rocking chair, "you're bending it like it's made of rubber. It's not rubber. It's more like cartilage. Firm but flexible."

"You're supposed to be helping, not doing anatomy class," Andrew said. Ravi was twenty, visiting for the summer, and had a habit of turning everything into a metaphor.

"Fine. Say it for me."

Andrew said the whole opening, got through the stubborn word, then blanked completely on the last line. He stared at the porch boards as if the answer might be knotted into the wood grain. "This is impossible. How does anybody memorize anything longer than this?"

Ravi set down his tea. "Recite chapter 36."

"What?"

"Just listen." And then Ravi began, his voice low and steady, verse after verse after verse, rolling out without a single pause or a single page. Andrew slid off the chair and stared. When Ravi finally stopped, ten minutes later, he grinned. "That's one chapter out of the whole Quran. All 114 chapters, and I know every one."

"From memory? All of it?" Andrew's voice cracked on "all," which was embarrassing, so he pretended a bug had flown into his mouth.

"There's a word for someone who's done it," Ravi said. "A hafiz."

Andrew tested something. "Okay, but you finished it once, so it's done, right? Like a video game. You beat it, you close the file."

Ravi laughed so hard the rocking chair squeaked. "Try me tomorrow. Ask me the same chapter again."

The next morning Andrew woke up early and found Ravi on the porch already reciting, eyes closed, fingers tapping his knee. He'd clearly been at it for a while. Andrew flopped into the other chair with his cereal and interrupted at chapter 36, and Rai picked it up mid-verse without blinking. Then Ravi kept going into another chapter entirely, and Andrew realized his cousin did this every single day, the way their grandfather watered the tomatoes every single day whether they looked thirsty or not. The memorizing wasn't a wall you built once. It was a living thing you fed.

"So it's never finished," Andrew said slowly. "Ever?"

"Ever," said Ravi. "Keeping it perfectly takes constant practice. Now stop looking so tragic and give me the Fatiha. And Andrew, if you crack up at that word again, I'm telling Tina you cried over a prayer."

"You wouldn't."

"Recite it properly and we'll never know."

Andrew straightened his back, took a breath that made his ribs creak, and began. The stubborn word came out firm but flexible, exactly like cartilage, and he kept going, one line, then the next, the morning sun beginning to radiate off the watering can by the tomatoes. When he finished the last verse without a single stumble, he opened his eyes and found Ravi holding up one finger.

"Chapter 36. First line. Go."

"Hey, I'm not the hafiz here."

"Not yet," Ravi said. "Porch. Same time tomorrow. Bring the cereal."

Carson pushed his noodles around the plate while his phone buzzed for the third time. Maely had texted again: "Club votes Thursday. You're the tiebreaker. Pick a side."

"Everything all right?" his mother asked.

"The robotics club might split in two." He set the phone face down. "Here's what happened. At the regional meet, Tariq's robot malfunctioned, and he blamed a dead battery. That was a lie. The real reason was that he'd stayed up reprogramming it to cover for Gemma, who'd broken a part and asked him not to say anything. Mr. Visser found out last week."

"So he lied," his mother said.

"He covered for a friend," his father said, not looking up from his plate. "That's different."

"No, it isn't. He lied to a judge." Carson pulled out a sheet of notebook paper where he'd listed the facts. Everyone in the club agreed on all of them. Gemma broke the part. Tariq knew and said nothing. He blamed the battery. The team got a score it shouldn't have. Mr. Visser found out and disqualified them. Nobody disputed a single fact, and yet half the club thought Tariq did the right thing and half thought he betrayed the team. That was the part eating at him. He'd assumed that if people had the same facts, they'd land in the same place, and this was like discovering the sun didn't always rise.

"Both halves know exactly what happened," he said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Same facts. Different answer. So the fight isn't about facts at all. It's about what they value. Maely keeps saying the rules have to apply to everyone or the whole competition is meaningless. Gemma says Tariq was loyal, and you don't sell out a friend." He paused. "They're both valuing something real. Maely values fairness. Gemma values loyalty."

His mother raised an eyebrow. "And you?"

"That's what I have to figure out by Thursday." He told them the club had drafted a kind of contract at the start of the year, promising honesty at competitions, and everyone had signed it, including Tariq. His father argued that a promise to a friend outweighed a piece of paper, and his mother argued the opposite just as firmly, and Carson watched two people who agreed on every fact walk away in opposite directions. Then his phone buzzed again. Gemma: "You're not going to rat out the club at dinner, right?"

He typed back, "Tell Maely I have a proposal for Thursday. Nobody splits. We give back the score ourselves, before anyone makes us. And Tariq apologizes to Mr. Visser without naming who he protected." It wasn't a perfect fix. Someone would still be angry. But if the fight wasn't about facts, then arguing facts forever was pointless, and maybe the only move left was to give both sides something.
