He set the phone down and picked up his fork. His mother slid the bread basket toward him, and his father, after a long moment, nodded. "That's fair," his father said. "And loyal, too."

Declan had planned to finish his climate project at home, in a house with air conditioning and a printer. Instead his grandfather had collected him from the airport and driven him to a place where the mailbox leaned like it was tired, and now the project had to happen here, in a kitchen in the Arizona desert, over a laptop that connected to the internet when it felt like it.

The assignment asked him to compare a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs. His friend Emy-Rose had the easy half. Her grandmother lived in Hilo, Hawaii, and Emy-Rose had already texted him a photo of her rain gauge with water in it, plus the smug caption "day one." Declan's grandfather owned no rain gauge. What he owned was a cactus, a watering can, and a patio that looked like the surface of a planet that had given up.

Declan started with the graphs. He printed them at the library in town: monthly rainfall bars for a hot desert and for a rainforest, and two temperature lines that both ran high. He laid them side by side on the kitchen table and tried to evaluate what he was seeing. The rainforest bars towered over the desert bars, which was almost embarrassing, since some of the desert bars were so short he had to squint to confirm they existed. He found the median monthly rainfall for each place, and the rainforest number was so much larger that he checked it twice, in case the library printer had made a typo.

The temperature lines were the part that bugged him. Both places were hot. If heat meant dryness, the rainforest should have been dry too, and it plainly was not, judging by Emy-Rose's photo of a puddle in her grandmother's driveway that had lasted three days. He needed a way to test the difference, and the laptop kept buffering, so the internet was not going to be influential in his thinking today. He went outside with a measuring cup and poured exactly one cup of water onto the flat concrete beside the patio, marking the puddle's edge with two pebbles.

Then he did what any scientist stuck in a desert does. He sat in a lawn chair and watched water do nothing. By ten o'clock the puddle had shrunk to a dark ring. By eleven the ring was gone, and the concrete was the same pale gray as everywhere else, and the sun was still climbing. He poured a second cup in the shade of the barbecue, out of some sense of fairness. That puddle lasted longer, but even it surrendered before lunch.

He called Emy-Rose that afternoon. "Question," he said. "The sun and dry air at my grandpa's could evaporate way more water in a year than falls as rain here. Like, a puddle I made this morning was gone before lunch. Is your puddle still there?"

"It's been there since Tuesday," Emy-Rose said. "Grandma says it's practically a pond now."

"So that's the whole difference," Declan said. "It's not just how much rain falls. It's how much the sky takes back." He wrote it at the top of his poster in marker, then drew the desert puddle as a ghost with an exit arrow.

That evening his grandfather came out with two glasses of lemonade, looked at the poster, and looked at the dry patio.

"Learn something today?" his grandfather asked.

"Learned you can't keep a puddle in this yard," Declan said, and taped the last graph down before the wind could evaluate it for him.

Henry's problem was simple: Mr. Ramírez wanted a science fair project by Friday, and all Henry had was a dying bean plant on his windowsill and two weeks of nothing. Then Kane came over after school, saw the plant, and asked why it looked so sad.

"Maybe it's bored," Kane said. "My mom plays music for her ferns and they're vigorous. Huge. Practually jungle ferns."

Griffin, who had followed Kane in, shook his head. "That's not a thing."

"It could be a thing," Henry said, and he felt the project forming right there. He took a census of every bean seed in Mr. Ramírez's classroom drawer, twenty-four seeds, and set up six cups of soil with music playing beside them and six cups in silence. Each cup got the same water, the same spot on the counter near the window. "If music matters, the music cups should grow taller. If it doesn't, they'll come out about the same."

Mr. Ramírez walked past the counter on Monday and tapped one of the cups. "Before you go further," he said, "write down what 'no effect' would look like. Then you're testing something." He moved on to unjam the pencil sharpener, which had eaten a crayon again.

Henry stared at the empty line in his notebook. Griffin leaned over. "He means like, if the music does nothing, what happens?"

"Then there's no relationship between music and growth," Henry said slowly. "Same height either way. And the whole point of the experiment is to knock that idea over, to reject it. Like proving it wrong."

"It has a name, actually," Griffin said. "My sister calls it the null hypothesis. It's the statement that there is no relationship between the things you're studying, and your experiment tries to reject it." He paused. "I think that makes us scientists. Or at least people with dirt under their nails."

For ten days Henry measured sprouts with a ruler, recorded heights in milliliters of growth, which he then crossed out because milliliters were for liquid, and rewrote in centimeters. He made Kane stop humming near the control cups after Kane admitted he'd been doing it "for moral support." On day eleven, the music cups averaged 9 centimeters and the silent cups averaged 8.7. Henry looked at the numbers for a long time.

"So do we reject it?" Kane asked.

"Not really. That's basically the same." Henry taped the last measurement into his notebook: 8.7, 9, 8.7, 9. "The music didn't matter. But now we know, and nobody can say we guessed."

"Then I'm never playing the ferns another note," Kane said. "Think of the electricity we'll cease wasting."

"Your mom plays music for plants because she likes the music," Griffin said.

Kane considered this. "Yeah, all right. Hypothesis number two: my mom is the actual scientist."

Henry laughed so hard he knocked over cup eleven. He caught it before the soil hit the floor, and the sprout, silent all its life, kept right on standing.

The note was folded into a tight square and tucked into the side pocket of Adam's backpack, where Max had slipped it during math without saying a word. Adam waited until the group stopped for water, a mile up the trail, before he opened it. "Ask Mr. Hassan to borrow the orange," Max had written. "Willyam already knows. Do not lose this note." Below that, Willyam had added, in handwriting that leaned like it was in a wind, "It's about the science test."

Mr. Hassan was already holding the orange when Adam caught up to him at the overlook, which felt like a trick, though it was probably just that Mr. Hassan liked oranges. "Your classmate failed to explain the seasons on Friday," Mr. Hassan said. "Today you get one more chance before I authorize the retake. Walk with me."

"I know it's about the tilt," Adam said. "I just can't make it make sense."

"That is the whole problem with science," said Mr. Hassan. He handed Adam the orange and his small flashlight. "Make it make sense to us. Right here. If you can explain it on a mountain, you can explain it in a classroom."

Willyam grabbed a sharp twig and pushed it through the orange, straight through from top to bottom. "Axis," he announced, as if he had invented it. Max held the flashlight, standing in for the sun, and shined it while Adam tilted the twigged orange toward the light. One hemisphere glowed bright and direct; the other sat dimmer in the slanted beam.

"Summer up here," Adam said slowly, tipping the top toward Max's flashlight, "and winter down there. Same sunlight. Different angle." He kept the tilt, which was the hard part, and walked the orange around Max in a slow circle. "And it stays tilted the same way the whole way around, so the bright part switches sides halfway through." His heart was going fast. It was working.

Then Willyam said, "Let me try," and took the orange, and held the twig perfectly upright, straight up and down, like a flagpole. He orbited Max with it. Adam watched the lit side of the orange, waiting for the bright patch to slide toward the twig's top the way it had before. It didn't move. It just sat there, in the same spot, the same size, lap after lap around Max.

"Willyam," Adam said, "you broke it."

"I didn't touch anything!"

"You held it straight up. With no tilt, the light hits the same spot at the same angle the whole year. There's nothing to switch. There wouldn't be seasons at all. It would just be the same forever." Adam took the orange back and tipped it again, and there was summer, right where it was supposed to be. Somewhere below them a hawk turned in the warm air, riding the heat the way hawks do.

Mr. Hassan peeled an actual orange from his other pocket and ate it, watching. "Mr. Hassan," Adam said, "can the retake be up here? The curriculum is better on this trail."

"The curriculum," said Mr. Hassan, spitting a seed off the edge, "is wherever you figure things out." Max wrote one more note and handed it over: "You still owe me a flashlight battery, and that's not corrosive, that's a fact."

Alice sat down at Ryerson's piano with the sheet music for "Moonlight Jig" in front of her. She had been practicing the piece for two weeks, and today was the last rehearsal before the school talent show. A stuffed koala grinned at her from the top of the piano, and she gave its grey marsupial face a pat for luck. "Ready?" she asked. Ryerson nodded and lifted the lid of the percussion box he kept beside the bench.

The first half went well. Alice's fingers found the bouncy opening, and Ryerson tapped the tambourine right on the beat, his wrist flicking in time with hers. Then they reached the middle, where the marking "rit." appeared above the staff. Alice slowed down, letting each note stretch out like taffy, and Ryerson followed her. It sounded beautiful, she thought, dreamy and strange. But when the next section began, something felt wrong. Ryerson's tambourine had gone quiet, and when she glanced over, his hand was hovering in midair, waiting.

"You're still slow," he said. "The whole last page is dragging." Alice frowned at the music. She played the passage again and listened hard. He was right. The slow feeling from the rit. had followed her all the way to the end, like mud stuck to her shoes. She bent closer to the page, wondering if there was a clue she had missed. There, printed small above the bar where the dreamy part ended, were two words: "a tempo." She traced them with her finger. "Rit." had told her to slow down. Did "a tempo" tell her something about speed too?

She tested a simple idea. "Play the opening speed," she said to Ryerson, "just the counting, nothing else." He clapped the original beat, quick and bright, and she matched her hands to his claps. Then she played from the "a tempo" marking forward while he kept time, and the melody sprang back to life, bouncing the way it had at the start. "That's it," she said. "A tempo means go back to the original speed after you've slowed down." Ryerson grinned and shook the koala at her like a maraca.

They ran the whole piece once more, and this time when the rit. came, Alice let the notes wander slow and soft, then snapped the speed back exactly where the marking told her to. The change matched the feel of the music, the way a heartbeat corresponds to what a body is doing, fast when it runs and calm when it rests. Ryerson's tambourine came in clean and sure, and by the final chord they were both laughing. Ms. Ramírez, who had come to pick up her nephew next door, stopped on the porch and applauded through the window. "Again," Ryerson said, tapping the tambourine against his palm. "From the top."

Brielle spotted the white tent from the far side of the park, its fabric so translucent that the morning sun shone right through it, glowing like a paper lantern. The whole gurdwara community had moved its celebration outdoors today, and the tent would serve as the prayer space.

"Wait," Dexter said, stopping at the tent flap. "I've never been to anything like this. Am I supposed to do something?"

"You have to take your shoes off first," Brielle said. She knelt and untied her sneakers. "Everyone does. It's like that at mosques and Hindu temples too. My cousin got married at a mandir last spring, and there was a whole shelf of shoes outside, hundreds of them, all mixed up."

Dexter pulled off his sandals, then hesitated, running a hand through his hair. "What about this? Is a hat okay?"

"You need something on your head in a gurdwara. A hat would work, but..." Brielle dug into her backpack and pulled out a folded scarf, bright orange with a thin silver border. "Here. I brought two on purpose."

"You planned this," Dexter said, but he was already twisting it into place, and it sat crooked over one ear.

"I planned it after last time," Brielle admitted. She adjusted his scarf, tucking the loose end so it lay flat. A year ago, before her friend Angela's family had taken her to the gurdwara on Marshall Street, Brielle had marched up the steps in sneakers with the laces still double-knot-hog-tied tight. Angela's grandmother had gently pointed at the shoe rack, and Brielle had spent four embarrassing minutes hopping on one foot while a line of patient people waited behind her. That day she had also turned up bareheaded, and a kind stranger had lent her a thin cotton square that kept sliding off. She'd spent the whole visit learning to interpret the small signals around her: when people bowed, when they sat, when the singing swelled and everyone pressed their palms together. By the end she'd understood that the rules weren't traps for newcomers. They were just things you could know ahead of time, if someone told you or if you watched.

Inside the tent, the ceiling fan turned in slow circles overhead, each revolution stirring the smell of cardamom from the steel pots where volunteers were stirring halva. An uncle nodded at Dexter's scarf and gave Brielle a thumbs up. They found a spot on the carpet beside Angela, who was already sitting cross-legged with her eyes half closed.

"Nice scarf," Angela whispered.

"Brought a spare," Brielle whispered back. "Rule number one of bringing your friend places: carry a backup."

The singers started, and the tabla player's hands blurred, and Dexter leaned over to whisper, "Okay, this is actually amazing," just as the fan swept another warm breath of cardamom down over all three of them.

The food bank shared its parking lot with the neighborhood cleanup, so Emily kept hearing the scrape of rakes and the crash of trash bags while she stood in the cool basement sorting canned beans. She had signed up because Catherine and Japji both claimed it would be fun, though so far the fun consisted of dust, the sour smell of cardboard, and an old sticker on her sleeve that said VOLUNTEER in peeling letters.

Mr. Oyelaran handed her a crate of newly donated corn. "Shelf four, please," he said, and hurried off to diagnose a strange clattering in the ceiling that he suspected was a rodent, possibly the same one that had chewed a box of oatmeal last spring. Emily lugged the crate over. The shelf already held corn, maybe twenty cans in a neat row, so she slid the new ones in front where they would look orderly and full.

When Mr. Oyelaran came back down, he studied the shelf and shook his head. "Redo it, please. New cans go behind." He said it kindly, but Emily's face went hot. Behind? That made the shelf look messy, with the older cans, some dented and dusty, blocking the bright new ones. She was still grumbling inside when Japji appeared with another crate. "He told me the same thing," Japji whispered. "I asked why, and he just said, 'first in, first out.' He's very proud of that phrase."

Emily stood in front of the shelf and turned the words over. First in, first out. The old cans had arrived first, so they left first. If she hid them behind the new ones, nobody would grab them until later, and cans had dates stamped on their lids, dates that did not care about looking orderly. She tested it, moving one dusty can to the front and reading its date aloud to herself, then a new one from the back for comparison. The old one was a year closer to its end. It was like the corn was standing in a line for checkout, and she had been cutting in front of the people who had waited longest.

"I get it," she told Mr. Oyelaran when he passed. "The old cans are endangered. If they hide back there, they'll expire before anyone takes them home." He laughed so hard the clipboard rattled. "Endangered corn. I like that." Upstairs, someone from the cleanup banged on the door, dropping off a bin of donated soup they had collected house to house, and Catherine shouted down the stairs that the rodent in the ceiling was actually just a squirrel, which everyone agreed was only slightly better.

Emily took the soup crate to shelf two, slid the new cans carefully behind the old ones, and straightened the row so the earliest dates stood first in line, right where hands would reach.

Julia crouched at the end of the hallway with a stopwatch in one hand and a marble in the other. Behind her, her dad held one end of a wooden board propped on a stack of dictionaries, making a steep little hill. The plan was simple: roll the marble down, time it, measure how far it went, and turn the numbers into a distance-time graph for Monday's lab report. Her teacher, Ms. Owusu, had been strict about enforcing the rule that every graph needed real measurements, not guesses, and Julia intended to follow it.

"Ready," she called. Her dad let go, the marble flashed down the board and shot across the floor, and Julia stabbed the button far too late. "Zero point two seconds? That can't be right." They tried again, and again, and every time the marble reached the wall before her thumb could catch up. On the fourth attempt she didn't even press the button. She sat back on her heels and groaned.

Amina's face appeared on the tablet screen, propped against the baseboard. She was supposed to be doing the same experiment in her own kitchen, and she wanted their graphs to match so their group could have the best data in the class. "Same problem here," Amina said. "My ball is faster than my thumb. Maybe we should just make up numbers that look nice."

"We can't," Julia said. "Ms. Owusu wants an objective measurement, something that doesn't depend on us deciding what it should be." She picked up the marble and turned it over in her fingers, thinking. Fast was the enemy. If the ball moved slower, she could actually time it. But how did you slow down a rolling ball without touching it? She looked at the board. The steeper the hill, the faster the marble flew. So a gentler slope might mean a gentler speed. "Dad, take away half the dictionaries."

He raised an eyebrow but lifted the stack down until the board lay at a low slant, more of a whisper than a hill. Julia marked the floor with masking tape every thirty centimeters, the way Ms. Owusu had shown them, and set the marble at the top. When her dad released it, the marble crept down the ramp and rolled along the tiles at a pace she could actually watch. She clicked the stopwatch at each strip of tape, calling out, "One! Two! Three!" while Amina scribbled the times on her own sheet of paper, miles away but shouting them back anyway.

They ran it three times to be sure, and the numbers came out almost the same every trial. Julia plotted them on graph paper, distance going up one side, time going along the bottom, and the dots fell into a nearly straight line climbing from the corner. She stared at it. She had expected a wobbly scatter, but the points behaved like they were following a rule she couldn't see, some hidden law of rolling things that only showed up on paper.

Then her dad leaned over her shoulder. "You know, you're not the first person to try this trick. Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, because the ramps slowed the motion enough for him to time it." Julia sat back, amazed that a scientist from centuries ago had faced the exact same problem in the exact same way, without stopwatches or masking tape or a video call.

"Then we did it right," Amina said through the speaker. "Send me a picture of that graph before my dad confiscates my tablet for the night. He claims my science homework is bad for his beauty sleep, which is basically a crime against commerce, since I'm his daughter and he should be investing in me."

Julia laughed and photographed the graph, the line of dots marching upward like a staircase. "Best data in the class," she said, and taped the graph to the refrigerator door, right at eye level, where nobody walking past could miss it.

Arianna had exactly one slide left to fix before math class, and it was the quote at the top: "Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world," attributed to Albert Einstein. She had written it in big letters because it made her poster about savings accounts sound important. But something about it nagged at her, the way a pebble in a shoe nags all the way home.

She found Salma at the lunch table, elbow-deep in a bag of chips. "You know that Einstein quote, the eighth wonder thing? Where did he say it?"

Salma shrugged. "Somewhere smart, probably. A lab. A blackboard place."

"That's not a source, that's a vibe." Arianna pulled out the library tablet and typed the quote in. The first result repeated the saying, but it also mentioned something else: there was no reliable evidence Einstein ever said it. She read the line twice. "It's a fake quote. It's everywhere, and it's fake."

"So you have to cut it from your poster?" Ellie slid into the seat across from them, stealing a chip. "Tragic. Your poster had one celebrity and now it has zero."

"I have to cut it or say what's true. I can't just repeat something nobody can trace back." Arianna tapped the table. "You know what's annoying? The saying still makes a point. Compound interest really does grow faster than simple interest. It just doesn't need a famous dead scientist to vouch for it."

In Ms. Friedman's class, after lunch, they were comparing the two kinds of interest over five years, the exact project on Arianna's poster. Ms. Friedman drew two lines on the board: one straight like a ruler, one that bent upward, curving away from the first like it was escaping. "Somebody give me one difference between them."

"With simple interest, you earn on the money you put in," Arianna said. "With compound, you earn on the money you put in plus the interest you already earned. The two lines look similar at first, then the gap gets bigger every year."

"Good. That's a distinct pattern, not just a bigger number." Ms. Friedman capped her marker. "Arianna, you look like you're about to burst."

Arianna raised her poster anyway. "I was going to open with an Einstein quote about the eighth wonder of the world. Then I checked, and there's no reliable evidence he ever said it. So my new opening is: this graph is cool enough without a fake quote."

The class laughed, and Ms. Friedman smiled. "You just did what mathematicians do. You can infer nothing about a quote's truth from how famous the person is. You have to check the source."

At the end of class, Ellie peered at the two lines on the board, which curved apart with a kind of accidental symmetry, one straight and one bending. "So Einstein never said it, but the graph did all the talking anyway?"

"The graph," Arianna said, rolling up her poster, "never misquotes anybody."

On Monday morning Emmett slid his new phone across the desk so Mouhamed could see it, and Mouhamed whistled low, the way he did when something good appeared in the room. "No way," Harriet said from the next row, leaning over to look. "It's the plan my dad picked," Emmett told her. "Texts and calls are free, and I get some data for the month." He had ridden the bus to school watching videos the whole way, and he planned to do the same thing going home.

By Friday the phone had stopped loading anything unless it was on Wi-Fi. At lunch Emmett sat staring at the little gray bar at the top of the screen. "It worked Monday," he said. "It worked Tuesday morning, too, I think. Then it just stopped." Harriet frowned. "You weren't texting that much, were you?" "Barely any," Emmett said. "A few messages to my dad." He turned the phone over in his hands. Something invisible had run out, and he wanted to know which thing it was.

In Ms. Ramírez's classroom, during the last ten minutes of silent reading, Emmett laid out the week like a math problem on scrap paper. He had watched videos on the bus every morning and every afternoon, except Thursday, when he forgot his earbuds and only texted. The messages were tiny; he'd written maybe twenty of them all week. The videos were the only other thing that used the phone away from home. So it had to be the videos. He thought of a way to test it, though the test felt almost too simple. He raised his hand. "Ms. Ramírez, is the classroom Wi-Fi the school's, not mine?" She nodded. "It's the school's, Emmett. Your plan isn't touched while you're on it."

After school Emmett adjusted his plan for the ride home. While he was still in the building, on the school's Wi-Fi, he downloaded three videos onto the phone. Then, on the bus, he turned off the mobile data and pressed play. The first video opened instantly, without bars, without loading. He watched Mouhamed's face as Mouhamed leaned across the aisle. "Wait, I thought your data died," Mouhamed said. "It did," Emmett said. "But streaming video eats it fast. Texting barely uses any at all. So now I download at school and watch after." It felt like the same bus and the same seat, but from a whole new perspective.

He tried one more thing before getting off. He sent his dad a message asking if they could look at the plan together this weekend, and the message went through on data, small and quick as anything. The phone buzzed back before his stop. "Yes. Also bring the charger." Emmett smiled, put the phone in his pocket, and stepped down into the afternoon.

Matthew sat at the kitchen table while his dad read words from the official list. "Persimmon," his dad said, and Matthew spelled it, and his dad said "Correct," in the same flat voice the judges would use on Saturday. Last year Matthew had gone out in round three on "raspberry," because he had forgotten the silent p, and he had spent a whole year deciding that this time he would not just memorize but understand where spellings came from.

That was why he had gone to the library on Tuesday. While Abdul and Ali quizzed each other near the windows, Matthew had begun to excavate the reference shelf, pulling out heavy books one after another, and at the back he had found something strange: an enormous old dictionary, nearly as tall as his arm was long, with faded brown covers. He had opened it at random and found words spelled in ways he had never seen, some of them with alternatives, two spellings side by side for the same word. Who decided? he had wondered. Somebody must have, at some point, because the list his dad held had only one spelling for every word, and the judges would accept only that one.

He had carried the volume to the desk and asked the librarian about it. She had turned to the front of the book and shown him the page it came from. "Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755," she said. "It helped settle how many English words were spelled." Before that, she said, spellings wandered all over the place, which explained the doubled versions he had found. Matthew had copied the fact into his notebook, and he had read it again on the walk home, feeling the ground shift a little under his memorized lists. The words had not always been fixed. Someone had fixed them.

Now, on Friday night, the kitchen was tranquil except for the ticking clock and the scratch of his pencil. There was a knock, and Mr. Islam from next door stood at the door holding a plate of cookies, because he had heard about the regional bee. "You look like a candidate for some sugar," he said, setting the plate down. "Final round tomorrow?"

"Round six, if I make it," Matthew said. He pushed his notebook toward Mr. Islam, open to the fact he had copied. "Did you know this? That spellings weren't always settled?"

Mr. Islam read it and nodded slowly. "My grandmother used two spellings for the same word in her letters. Drove me crazy trying to read them."

Matthew's dad, drying a dish, glanced over. "So what does that change for you?"

"Nothing," Matthew started to say, and then stopped. He had planned to drill all night, word after word, until his eyes blurred. But if the spellings followed patterns someone had settled, then the patterns were the thing to learn, not just the lists. "Actually, everything," he said. "I'm going to group them. Silent letters together. Double letters together." He swept the flashcards into new piles, reshuffling his whole system with one night to go, his heart pounding at the risk of it.

At the table, Mr. Islam broke a cookie in half and handed a piece across.

"Try one," he said. "Champions eat first."

The elevator in Great-Aunt Lin's building had buttons for one, two, three, and five. Noemie pressed five twice, thinking the first press had not taken, and watched the doors close on her cousins arguing about who would carry the fruit boxes up. Then Thalia nudged her. "It always does that," Thalia said. "There's no four in this whole building. My grandma says the word for four in Chinese sounds almost the same as the word for death, so they just skip it." She shrugged, like skipping a floor was the most ordinary thing in the world, and pressed five again as if to prove it.

Noemie's problem was in her backpack. She had brought Great-Aunt Lin a box of four tea cakes, wrapped in green paper, because her mother had said never arrive at a family gathering empty-handed, and four had seemed like a generous number. Now she counted them in her head and felt the package grow heavier on every floor the elevator did not bother to name. Five, six, seven. Her mother had also said you offer a gift with both hands and the receiver will refuse it once or twice before accepting, which Noemie had assumed was a joke until she saw it happen with the fruit.

At the door, Great-Aunt Lin took one look at the green wrapping and her eyebrows climbed. Noemie had read that green hats meant something unlucky too, so she began unwrapping the cakes herself, quickly, as if speed could fix anything. Then she slid three of them across the table and kept one in her pocket, saying she would eat it on the train home.

"Train home already?" said Great-Aunt Lin. "Sit. Eat first." She waved Noemie to the seat facing the door, the seat of honor, and pointed chopsticks at the lazy Susan. "Turn it toward your grandfather before you take anything. And no standing your chopsticks upright in the rice, that's for other occasions."

"I wasn't going to," Noemie said, though she had been about to.

Her grandfather, who was the conductor of a community orchestra and liked to cite old sayings at dinner, tapped his bowl with his chopsticks. "Three cakes," he observed in English, for her benefit. "Very good number. Three sounds like birth. Life."

"I know," said Noemie, who had known for exactly eleven minutes. She pulled the fourth cake out of her pocket anyway and set it on the lazy Susan, giving it a slow spin.

"Four," said Great-Aunt Lin. "Take that one home, sweetheart."

Noemie ate it on the train, feeling considerably less impoverished of cake than she had planned.

The problem started when Mael refused to believe him. "Summer is hot because Earth is closer to the sun," Mael said, digging his toes into the hot sand. "Everybody knows that." George opposed this idea instantly, mostly because he'd read the opposite in Ms. Sato's science book, but he couldn't actually prove it. Earth's tilt causing seasons was not something you could see from a beach towel.

"We need a flashlight," Albert said. He ran to the lifeguard's station, where Ms. Sato, their neighbour, was reading under an umbrella. She lent him a small transparent plastic one, the kind with a blue casing, and told them not to drop it in the ocean.

George switched it on and held it straight over the sand. "Look. Small circle, and it's bright." He traced the ring of light with his finger. Then he tilted the flashlight at an angle, the way Earth's axis leans, and the light stretched out into a long, pale oval. "Same light," he said slowly, feeling his own mind change as he watched. "But now it's spread over more sand. So each bit of sand gets less." He tilted it further and the glow got wider and dimmer still.

"So in summer," Albert said, crouching down, "the sunlight comes down more straight, like this, and the same light is packed onto a smaller spot, so it heats it more?" George nodded. He stuck one hand in the small bright circle and one in the wide dim oval. The bright patch felt warmer within seconds, though he wasn't sure if that was real or just his imagination. Mael still looked stubborn, so George grabbed a stick and wrote in the wet sand where the waves had just retreated: "Tilt, not distance. Direct light = small + hot. Tilted light = wide + dim + cooler." The foam hissed in and erased it, which Mael said was the ocean disagreeing, but he was grinning when he said it.

That evening George wrote a message on a postcard and left it under a shell on Ms. Sato's porch, since she had asked to know how their experiment turned out. "Dear Ms. Sato," he wrote. "We proved the tilt thing. When the flashlight pointed straight down the circle was small and bright, and when we tilted it the light got wide and dim. So summer is when your part of Earth gets the direct light. Also, the hermit crab in the tide pool had camouflage exactly the colour of the sand, and Mael stepped on a jellyfish but it was fine." He drew a little Earth with a leaning axis at the bottom.

The next morning Ms. Sato caught up with him on the boardwalk, postcard in hand. "One correction," she said. "That was a piece of seaweed Mael stepped on." She held out a thermos. "Hot chocolate for the young scientist?" George took the cup and pointed at the sun climbing over the water. "Direct light," he said. "Small, bright, hot." Mael, from down the beach, cupped his hands and yelled, "Tilt! I believe you now!"

Ellie sat on her bedroom floor with a photocopy of a settler's diary spread in front of her and her laptop open beside it. Ms. Brennan had assigned each student one primary source and one question to answer with it, and Ellie's question was why the Bennett family had left Ohio for the Oregon Trail in 1846. The trouble was that the diary, kept by fourteen-year-old Ada Bennett, never once said why. Ada wrote about oxen, about her little brother's fever, about how her mother cried the first night on the trail. She wrote about everything except leaving.

Ellie's first instinct was to guess that they wanted adventure, because that was the reason in every movie she had ever seen. But when she tried to write it down, the words felt wrong. "They left because it seemed exciting" did not fit a mother crying. She texted Paul, whose source was a letter from a gold miner, and he wrote back that his guy had a reason on every page. Lucky him. Ellie read Ada's first entry again, hunting for anything she had missed, and stopped at a sentence near the bottom: "Father says we can begin again where the land is cheap and no one remembers what we lost."

What had they lost? Ellie read every entry with that question in her head, like a flashlight she was shining backward through the pages. In the third entry Ada mentioned they had sold the spinning wheel, and in the fifth, that Father had taken work hauling stone for other men, which Ada called strange for a farmer with his own fields. Farmers did not haul stone for other men unless something had gone wrong with the fields. It was like finding footprints and trying to picture the animal, Ellie thought. She could not see the cause, only the marks it left.

She searched the diary's introduction, written by a librarian, and there it was in a footnote: the Panic of 1837. Her mom, carrying laundry past the door, asked what a panic was, and Ellie said, "It was a money collapse in 1837 that turned into a long economic depression," reading it almost straight off the page. Then she checked the dates. The diary said the Bennetts lost their farm in 1841, four years after the panic began, right in the middle of the depression. Ruined farmers were heading west looking for cheap, fertile land, and the Bennetts were one of those families. Ellie could finally see the whole shape of it.

Paul called that evening, sounding indifferent to her excitement, mostly wanting to complain about his miner's terrible spelling. "Then swap with me," Ellie said. But when she opened her essay to write her conclusion, she found a twist she had not expected. In the last entry, Ada wrote that Father had a brother in Oregon who had begged them to come for years, even before the farm was lost. So there were two reasons stacked on top of each other, one pulling and one pushing, and the panic alone would not have told the whole story. Ellie highlighted the sentence and asked her mom, "Can a person have two reasons for one decision?"

Her mom set the laundry basket down. "Ask Ada," she said, nodding at the diary. Ellie turned back to the photocopy, pencil in hand, and underlined: "We go because we must, and because Uncle Joseph says the plums there grow as big as your fist."

Declan set his sketchbook on the picnic table in Mehtab's backyard and stared at the pencil outline of his grandfather's face, wishing for the tenth time that he had inherited his mother's talent for art instead of her terrible handwriting. Watercolour kit open. Three brushes. A jar of water so clean it looked like glass. Mr. Hoang, the neighbour whose fence they were technically leaning against, had offered one piece of advice over the fence last week: "Watercolour is transparent, so you work light to dark. Each wash lets the layers beneath show through, because a dark wash can't be covered by a lighter one." Declan had nodded, but he hadn't really believed it. How could paint be like stained glass? Paint covered things. Paint was the covering-est stuff in the world.

So he started with the part that seemed most important: the hair. His grandfather had magnificent silver-black hair, and Declan wanted it bold. He mixed a strong dark wash and painted it in first, feeling very efficient, very systematic, like an engineer. Paige, sprawled on the grass beside Mehtab, watched him lay a pale grey over the hair to soften it. The pale grey vanished. It just disappeared into the dark, like a whisper into a thunderstorm. Declan tried white. Nothing. He tried pale grey again, harder, as if pressing harder had ever fixed anything in the history of watercolour. The highlight he had planned for the top of the hair, that shine that made Grandpa look like Grandpa, would not appear.

"Did the paper eat it?" Mehtab asked, leaning over. "Or did the dark eat it?"

"Nothing ate it," Declan muttered, but he was already wondering. He painted a dark stripe on scrap paper, let it dry, then painted a light stripe over half of it. The light stripe showed up on the white paper and simply was not there on the dark half. Then he flipped the order on a fresh scrap: light stripe first, dark over top. The dark sat on it fine. He did it twice more, because a scientist never trusts one trial. Same result every time. He sat back slowly. It wasn't that his paint was broken. It was that the paint never covered anything. Every layer was a sheet of coloured glass, and glass couldn't hide glass.

"Paint it backward," Paige said. "Face first, skin tones, all the pale stuff, then hair last."

"Like stacking shadows," Declan said. "Lightest shadow first."

He started over. Pale peach washes for the skin, built up in thin patient layers until a nose appeared out of nowhere, which felt honestly like a magic trick. Cheeks, then darker creases, then finally, last of all, the hair, laid down dark over everything and glowing like it had depth because the layers beneath it still showed through. It looked, if he squinted and held it at arm's length, roughly like a human being. Mehtab said it looked like a wizard. Declan decided that was a compliment.

Mr. Hoang appeared at the fence with his watering can and studied the painting. "You learned it the good way," he said.

"The hard way," Declan said.

"Those are the same way," said Mr. Hoang, and watered his tomatoes.

The ad appeared between two videos on Matteo's phone: a man in a suit standing in front of a rocket, saying the new productivity app would "change your life forever." Matteo squinted at it. Behind him, Phillip and Shayan were arguing about whether the cafeteria's mystery meat was actually turkey, which was at least an argument you could settle by asking somebody.

"It changed my life," Matteo said, holding up the phone. "That's what the guy says."

"So it works," Phillip said.

"How would I know if it works?" Matteo said. "He doesn't say what it does. He doesn't say by when. He just says it changes lives."

Shayan leaned over the seat. "Then try it and find out."

"That's the problem," Matteo said. "Even if I tried it, what would I look for? If my life didn't change, they'd just say I wasn't using it right, or it takes a year, or it changes your inner life, whatever that means." He scrolled down, looking for the fine print. "There's nothing here that could ever be proven wrong. That's the trick. It's not even really a claim. It's a claim that can't be checked even in principle, so it gives you nothing to test."

Phillip frowned. "The turkey question we could test, though. We could ask Ms. Kaur. She monitors the lunch line."

"She would know," Shayan agreed. "Or we could follow the delivery truck."

"And the app," Matteo said, "nobody could ever check it. Not you, not the emperor of the whole world, not a scientist with a lab. If you can't check something, you can't argue about it. You can only shrug." He bookmarked the ad anyway, because Ms. Kaur had said their persuasive writing unit started Monday, and he suspected this was exactly the kind of thing she wanted them to notice.

The bus lurched around the corner by the old arcade, the one with the asteroid game where a little ship tried to orbit a dying sun. Phillip pointed at it. "That place is so obsolete it hurts."

"Everything in there changes lives," Matteo said. "Forever. No refunds."

Shayan laughed so hard he knocked his water bottle into the aisle, and it rolled all the way up to the driver's feet and stopped there, spinning slowly, like a tiny planet nobody could argue with.

Jake spread his sketchbook on the picnic table and stabbed his pencil at the blank page. "Today I learn one-point perspective. For real this time."

Florent dropped onto the bench across from him, holding his own pad. "Mr. Pierre says the assignment is mandatory, even for people like me who draw stick figures."

"Then you're lucky you're with me." Jake drew a horizontal line across the middle of his page and marked a dot on it. "See, this is the horizon line, and this dot is the vanishing point. Every edge of the street goes toward it. The sidewalk lines, the rooftops, all of them." He sketched fast, sweeping lines from the edges of the paper straight to the dot, then boxed them in with vertical lines for buildings. A street appeared, flat on the page but somehow deep, like you could walk down it.

Mariah came through the gate with her sketchbook under her arm. "I already started mine. I sat on my front curb this morning and drew our street." She flipped her pad open. Her street looked strange to Jake at first. The road filled most of the page, tall and looming, and the sky was only a thin strip at the top.

"That looks like a giant drew it," Florent said.

"It looks like I'm little," Mariah said. "Because I was. I was sitting on the curb." She tapped her page. "My horizon line ended up way down here, near the bottom."

Jake stared at his own drawing. His horizon line sat in the middle, and the street felt like it belonged to nobody, floating at no height at all. He grabbed a fresh sheet and drew the horizon line high, almost at the top edge, then ran all his lines to the vanishing point again. The street dropped away below, tiny and distant, the way a street looks from upstairs.

"That's like my bedroom window," Mariah said, leaning over his shoulder. "Draw our street from up there, Jake. Then we'll have the same street twice."

"Same street, three views." Jake was already penciling in windows on the far-off buildings, small as rice grains. He held up Mariah's page beside his. "You can't even measure the difference with a ruler, but I bet you could quantify it. Percentage of page that's road versus sky."

Florent snorted. "You two are writing a math problem about a drawing."

"It's better than a poem," Jake said. "A stanza repeats a line with one thing changed. We're repeating a whole street."

Florent pulled his pad closer and drew his horizon line halfway up, then stopped. "Wait. If it's low, I'm a kid on the curb. If it's high, I'm up at a window. Where's mine?"

"Anywhere," Mariah said. "That's the fun part. Where do you want to be standing?"

Florent pressed his pencil down and slid the horizon line to the very bottom of the page. "Curb," he said. "Definitely the curb."

Caleb's German teacher had assigned one page, due Friday: describe your family and your pets in full sentences. Caleb had a mother, a father, a little sister, one dog named Biscuit, and a goldfish that was technically his sister's but ate Caleb's fish food, so he counted it. He typed his first sentence into the class tablets: "Ich habe einen hund und eine katze." He did not have a cat, but Biscuit deserved a companion on paper.

The tablet underlined "hund" and "katze" in wavy red lines, which Caleb took personally. He checked the spelling twice, letter by letter. H-u-n-d. K-a-t-z-e. The spell-checker disagreed anyway, waving its little red flags like a crossing guard who hated him.

Across the room, Hunter was typing fast, capitals scattered through his sentences like birdseed. Caleb leaned over. Hunter had written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," and no red lines anywhere. Not one.

"Your shift key is broken," Caleb whispered.

"It's not," Hunter whispered back.

Caleb looked at his screen, then at Hunter's, then at his own again. He tested something small. He changed "hund" to "Hund" only, leaving "katze" lowercase. The wavy line under Hund vanished. The one under katze stayed. He capitalized "katze." Gone too. So the checker wasn't hunting misspellings, because the letters had been right all along. It was hunting lowercase words that Hunter had uppercase. He scanned more of Hunter's sentences. "Mutter," "Vater," "Schwester," every single one began with a capital. Even "Fisch."

"In German, every noun begins with a capital letter," Hunter said, shrugging. "That's all it is."

Caleb sat with that for a second, feeling the shape of the rule. Not the pets, not the sister, just any noun, big or small. He typed a new sentence about his goldfish and hit capitalize with a kind of ceremony. "Ich habe einen Fisch." Clean. Luminous, even, in its red-line-free way. He began to suspect the humiliation of the past ten minutes had been entirely avoidable.

Then Ms. Choi stopped behind his screen. "Nice work, Caleb. One thing. You wrote that your dog is a cat."

He looked at the sentence. "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze." He had copied Hunter's capitals and, somewhere in the shuffle, Hunter's pets too. Hunter, it turned out, had two cats and no dog, and was watching Caleb now with the calm interest of someone whose homework had just become twice as good.

The line at Kelly's Gas and Go stretched past the air pump before Parker even got his bike parked. Every pump was taken, and a man in a delivery van sat with his engine running, tapping his horn. Serena waved from beside the ice machine, where she and Kole were watching the crowd. "Radio says the ice storm hits at seven," she said. "My mom sent me to fill the spare can for the generator. Yours too?"

Parker held up the five-gallon can. His family's furnace had died that morning, and the repairman couldn't come until next week because he was booked solid with other broken furnaces. The generator in the garage would run the space heaters tonight, but only if there was gas in it by seven o'clock. That gave him just over two hours. He counted the cars. Nine, ten, eleven, and more pulling in off the road every minute.

Mr. Kelly came out with a pole and changed the price sign himself, which he never did. Parker squinted at the new number. Yesterday the regular price had been three dollars and ten cents. The sign now read three eighty-nine. A woman at pump two leaned out her window and shouted at Mr. Kelly, and he shouted back something Parker couldn't hear, and the line barely moved. Kole checked his phone. "Every station in town is jammed. The app says prices are all over the place, going up and down all day." The prices didn't just sit still, Parker thought; they fluctuated, like the numbers on his dad's weather app.

"Watch the pumps," Parker said suddenly. "Not the cars. The pumps." Serena frowned, but Kole got it. At two ninety-nine, the station further down the road, there had been a line a block long, and people were topping off half-full tanks and filling spare cans besides. Here, at three eighty-nine, drivers pumped less. A man shut off his nozzle at fifteen dollars and left with a tank only half full. A teenage driver looked at the sign, swore, and drove off without buying anything. Fewer dollars, fewer gallons, fewer buyers. When the price rose, people bought less. Parker remembered the lemonade stand last summer, when Serena's sister had doubled her price from fifty cents to a dollar and the sidewalk in front of her table had gone empty by noon. When the price fell back, the line came back too.

"It's called the law of demand," Serena said, snapping her fingers. "Mr. Kelly had it on a poster in the back. People buy more when the price drops and less when it climbs, as long as nothing else changes." Parker shifted the gas can to his other hand and checked the sky, which had gone the color of a nickel. The line crawled. Sixty-one minutes to seven. He watched the pump nearest the road, where the man in the van was now arguing with Mr. Kelly about the new price. Mr. Kelly crossed his arms and pointed at the empty half of his lot, the half where the tanks were low, the half that would stay empty until tomorrow's truck came, if the truck could get through the ice at all. "You want it or not?" Mr. Kelly called. "Last can goes to the kid with the generator." Parker stepped forward.

The wind on the back straight of the track had a habit of shoving Maya sideways, and today it was worse than ever. Mr. Buchanan had written her name on the list for the eight-hundred-metre race at Friday's meet, and she had exactly three practices to figure out the one thing that kept ruining her: the first lap always felt easy, and the second lap always felt like her legs belonged to someone else. Piper handed her a folded note as they walked out of science class. "You looked miserable at practice," it read, "so I timed you. Lap one, forty-three seconds. Lap two, sixty-one. Something is eating you alive on that second lap. Also, you still owe me a granola bar from the commerce we did at lunch on Tuesday. Two granola bars, actually, since you never paid up. Piper." Maya laughed, then frowned at the numbers. Sixty-one seconds. Where did eighteen whole seconds go?

She decided to run the practice laps like a scientist instead of a racer. On Monday she went out hard, exactly the way her rebellious legs always wanted to, and paid for it on lap two, dying so badly that Zachariah, jogging beside the fence, called out, "You look like a melted popsicle." On Tuesday she tried going out slow, and although she finished stronger, her total time was still terrible. Neither plan explained the missing seconds. The problem, she realized, wasn't only how fast she ran. It was something invisible that changed from lap to lap.

The wind. On the back straight, where the track curved away from the gym, the gusts hit her full in the face both laps, and she could feel the extra work in her shoulders. But Piper, running just ahead of her on Tuesday, had seemed to float through that stretch. Maya chewed on the puzzle during math class, doodling little arrows in her notebook. The wind blew at everyone. Piper wasn't stronger than her. What was different about where they ran?

On Wednesday she tested it. She tucked in directly behind Zachariah on the back straight, close enough to see the tag on his shirt, and held that spot the whole first lap while he battled the gusts. It felt strangely calm back there, quiet and steady, like running indoors. When she swung out for the second lap, her legs still had bounce in them, and she finished her fastest practice time all week. "You were right on my shoulder," Zachariah said afterward, gulping water. "You were drafting me." "Drafting," Maya repeated, holding the word like a prize. So that was it. Running directly behind another runner sheltered her from the wind, and that meant following someone on the first lap could save her energy for the finish.

At the meet on Friday the wind was howling across the back straight, and Piper was in her heat, seeded one lane and one spot ahead. Maya stayed calm when the gun cracked, letting the field string out, then slid in behind Piper's shoulder at the first turn. Down the back straight the gusts bent the flags sideways, and Maya tucked closer, feeling the calm pocket open up in front of her while the wind worked on Piper instead. Around the final bend, with two hundred metres left, she still had something in her legs. She swung wide, kicked, and heard Piper yell over the wind, "Sneaky, Maya! I'm collecting a granola bar tax for that!" Maya crossed the line, looked up at the clock, and grinned so wide the wind nearly dried her teeth.

Aubrey had signed up for the Saturday printmaking class at the community art studio because she wanted to make a poster for her cousin Dev's birthday, and she was the only twelve-year-old there who hadn't touched a printing press before. Mr. Sultani, who ran the studio, set out pencils, carving blocks, and ink, and told everyone to sketch a design first.

She was halfway through drawing a dragon when she found the note folded at the bottom of her supply bag. It was from Dev, who was seven. "I am not coming to your art thing," it said. "Mom says the studio prohibits eating near the ink, which is fine, but I licked a pencil yesterday at school and I think I have lead poisoning. Please cancel my birthday. Sorry. Dev."

Aubrey read it twice. Then she looked at the pencil in her own hand. She had chewed on pencils her whole life, and so had Krystal, who sat beside her carving a moon into a block, and neither of them had ever gotten sick. If pencils really carried lead, half the kids in her grade would be poisoned by now. That did not add up.

She raised her hand anyway. "Mr. Sultani, do pencils have lead in them?"

"Look in the supply drawer," he said, pointing. "Third one down."

In the drawer she found the box the pencils had come in, and on the side of it, in small print, the word graphite. She turned the box over, and there was more: a short paragraph about how the stuff inside a pencil had never contained the metal lead at all. Early writers had mistaken graphite for a kind of lead ore, and the wrong name had stuck. Aubrey stood there holding the box, thinking about the irony of it. Everyone went around calling it lead, and nobody had ever put lead in it.

"So what's inside?" Krystal asked, leaning over.

"Graphite," Aubrey said. "Not lead. The name came from early writers who mistook graphite for a kind of lead ore."

"Then why does everyone call it lead?"

"Because the mistake never woke up," Aubrey said. "It's been dormant for hundreds of years." She put the box back and pulled out her phone.

She wrote a message to Dev's tablet, since he answered messages faster than letters: "You don't have lead poisoning. Pencils never had lead in them. The gray stuff is graphite. People used the wrong word ages ago and never fixed it. Also I'm still making your poster, and you're still having a birthday." She pressed send.

Then she went back to her dragon, pressed the finished print that afternoon, and mailed it in a cardboard tube with the pencil taped to the outside. On the label she wrote, in careful letters, "Safe to lick. Still don't."

At dinner on Tuesday, Alexander pushed his noodles around his plate and finally said, "Something's wrong with Skyler, and I can't figure out what." She had stopped sitting with them at lunch, and last week she quit the track team right before the big meet. Nothing had happened that he could see. No fight, no falling grade, nothing. It was like watching steam vanish off the pavement and trying to guess where it went. He kept coming back to the question: what was the hidden cause?

"She told me something in September," his mother said, setting down the water pitcher. "She'd been worrying so much for so long that she couldn't sleep, and it was getting in the way of school. So her mom took her to a doctor."

"Like she was sick?" Alexander asked.

"Not exactly like a cold," his mother said. "Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, though. Everybody does."

Alexander frowned. He got nervous before spelling bees, but it passed by the next morning. Skyler's worry hadn't passed. It had lasted a long time, and it was intense enough to knock her off the track team, which was weird because Skyler was the most robust runner in their grade. His father said worry was a common phenomenon, like weather, and Alexander thought that was a strange comparison until he realized weather was invisible too. You only saw what it did to things.

"Mom. If it's normal, why did she need a doctor?"

His mother tilted her head, the way she did when she wanted him to work it out himself. "What did I say about how long it lasted and what it was doing to her life?"

Alexander repeated it slowly, like laying out puzzle pieces. Normal worry comes and goes. Skyler's had stayed, gotten huge, and blocked everything. So maybe there was a point where normal turned into something else, the way a whole fog condenses out of clear air. "There's probably a name for that," he said.

"There is," his mother said. "Skyler told me her doctor diagnosed her with an anxiety disorder."

"Is that bad?"

His mother shook her head. "She said it's treatable. She's been learning ways of coping with it, and she's setting boundaries, like taking a break from the team for a while until things feel steadier."

The next day at school, Alexander slid his tray across from Skyler at lunch, even though she was sitting alone at the far table. "You don't have to talk about it," he said. "But you don't have to eat alone, either."

Skyler looked up, and then at the empty seat, and then back at him. "You're the first one who just sat down," she said. "Everyone else keeps asking if I'm okay."

"I'm working on a theory about that," Alexander said, and handed her a roll.

The campfire had burned down to orange coals when Micheal said the word "tilt," and Paige's whole plan for the evening fell apart. She was supposed to present her science project tomorrow, a talk on why Earth has seasons, and she had counted on one more night of practice. Instead Mr. Nair, who led the camping trip, had gathered everyone around the fire for marshmallows, and now half the class was arguing about whether winter happened because Earth moved farther from the sun.

"That's not it," Paige said, waving her roasting stick. "Earth stays basically the same distance away. It's the tilt of the axis."

Asma laughed so hard she nearly dropped her marshmallow into the ashes. "Tilt? Four seasons? Paige, where my grandmother lives, we would laugh at that. It is hot all year. Near the equator the sunlight stays direct the whole year, so the temperature barely changes. We don't have warm and cold seasons at all. We have wet seasons and dry seasons. That's it."

"Wet and dry?" Micheal said. "That's only two. That's not even half of four."

"Two is plenty," Asma said, "when one of them is rain like a waterfall."

Paige chewed the burnt edge of her marshmallow and thought. Two seasons. No cold. Sunlight direct all year. In her head she held the globe from Mr. Nair's truck, the one with the line drawn around its middle, and she turned it slowly. If the axis tilted, the middle of the globe never leaned away from the light. Only the top and bottom took turns leaning toward it and away.

"I need a flashlight," she said, standing up so fast she almost knocked over the thermos. "And something round."

"Here," Asma said, and held out an orange from the snack bag without being asked, because she had noticed Paige's hands were sticky and gave her a napkin too. Micheal trotted to the tent and came back with his headlamp, its obstinate strap refusing to stay tight until he bit it and yanked the buckle with his teeth.

Paige drew a line around the orange's middle with her finger. "Equator." She shone the headlamp straight down and tilted the orange. "Look. The top leans toward the light, so it's spread out and strong up there. Now watch the middle." The stripe she had drawn stayed bright and direct no matter how far she tipped it. "So near the equator, the light stays direct all year. It never gets weak, never gets strong. Nothing to change the temperature much. So no warm season, no cold season."

"So the rain does the changing instead," Asma said slowly, leaning in. "Wet, then dry, then wet. Like breathing."

"That is so weird," Micheal said. "My brain feels like it's being turned inside out, like an intestine or something."

"Do not compare my orange to an intestine," Paige said. "I'm going to eat this orange."

They were quiet for a moment, the coals popping, moths bumping the headlamp. Paige had been ready to abandon her project and ask Mr. Nair for a new topic an hour ago, and now she had the best part of her whole talk sitting in her palm, tilting in the firelight.

"Can I hold the orange while you do this tomorrow?" Asma asked. "I'll be the equator's lawyer."

"Only if you say wet and dry seasons in that exact voice you just used."

Quinn spread two climate graphs across the kitchen table, one for a desert city and one for a rainforest city, and weighted the corners with mugs from the drying rack. Her project was due Monday, and her plan was simple: look at the bars, decide which place was wetter, write a paragraph. Tim and Rosemary were coming over at three, but she wanted her answer ready before they arrived so she could argue with confidence.

They showed up early, arguing already. "Phoenix is way drier," Tim said, dropping his backpack on a chair. "Look at that rainforest graph. The bars are gigantic."

"No, look at the desert one," Rosemary said, tapping the page. "See how tall the August bar is? That's real rain. That city gets plenty."

Quinn leaned over both graphs, comparing the height of the bars. The rainforest bars were about four times taller, so Tim seemed right. But something bothered her, the way a wobbly shelf bothers you even before anything falls off it. She checked the months, then the temperature lines, then the small print along the side of each graph.

"Wait," she said. She pointed at the numbers stacked beside the rainfall bars. "This one counts by tens. Twenty, forty, sixty. The other one counts by fifties. Two hundred, four hundred." The tall rainforest bar for March topped out at two hundred millimetres. The short desert bar for August stood for sixty. "You can't just look at bar height," she said slowly. "The rainfall axes have to use the same scale, or the bars aren't speaking the same language."

"Then which city is actually wetter?" Rosemary asked.

"The rainforest one, still, but not by as much as it looked. And Rosemary, that August bar in the desert isn't some weird anomaly. It's just a normal summer storm, on a different scale." She grabbed a ruler and drew a fresh set of axes, using the same numbers for both cities, then re-drew the bars so they could be compared fairly. Tim watched over her shoulder and admitted, quietly, that he had nearly written "ten times rainier" in his report.

When Quinn's mother came home, the three of them were taping the new graph to the poster board, and Ms. Almeida from next door was at the door holding a plate of brownies. "Heard there was a science project," she said. Quinn held up the poster. "We verified it ourselves," she said. "Same scale, then compare."

Kaylee spread three books across the library table like she was planning a tiny rebellion against homework itself. "Ms. Mori says we have to compare a desert and a rainforest," she told Andi and Leila, who had come along mostly for the air conditioning. "And she says to use climate graphs. Easy." She flipped to the page on the Sonoran Desert and squinted. "Okay, so the temperature in the desert is super high all year. Look at these bars. Some of them are enormous."

Leila leaned over. "That seems weird. The bars go way up in summer, but they also go way up in the rainforest graph, and the rainforest graph you showed me has tall bars too. The desert can't be as wet as the rainforest."

"It can't," Kaylee said slowly. "That's the whole point of the assignment." She pulled the second book closer, then the third, comparing pages. Both deserts had short bars. Both rainforests had tall ones. "Wait." She traced her finger along a thin line zigzagging across the top of each chart. "There's a line too. I thought it was decoration."

Andi snorted. "Charts don't come with decoration. That would be vigorous decorating." She tapped the line. "Maybe that's the temperature, and the bars are the rain."

Kaylee tested it. In the desert graph, the line stayed high while the bars stayed stubby, which matched what she knew: hot and dry. In the rainforest graph, the line stayed warm and the bars towered, which matched wet. If the bars were temperature, the rainforest would somehow be boiling and the desert would be drowning, and neither made sense. "So the line is temperature," she said, "and the bars are each month's rainfall. They're on the same chart the whole time."

"How do we quantify the difference for the write-up?" Leila asked, hunting for the math. "Do we count bar heights?"

"Ms. Mori said compare, so we compare." Kaylee grabbed a pencil and started a two-column list: line high, bars short for the desert; line steady, bars huge for the rainforest. Andi added a drawing of a very sweaty cactus next to a very smug fern, and Leila labeled them "Team Dry" and "Team Damp."

At the front desk, Ms. Mori glanced at Kaylee's notebook. "So what did the graphs tell you?"

"That I spent ten minutes thinking rain was heat," Kaylee said. "Also that deserts and rainforests are basically opposites."

"Then it was a good ten minutes," said Ms. Mori, and stamped the books with a cheerful thunk. Andi held up the cactus drawing. "He forgives you," she said.

Tristan carried the cardboard box across Ridgeway Park with both hands, because the woman at the shelter had said a puppy could wriggle out of anything. Inside, a black-and-white puppy nosed at the air holes. His parents had made him wait two years for this, and only after he agreed to enroll in the shelter's free puppy-care class the following Saturday. The smell of cut grass and someone's charcoal grill drifted over the path.

Everlee waved from the picnic tables near the fountain, where she was spreading out her lunch. She had texted him three times that morning asking what kind of dog he was getting, because she wanted to be the first to meet it. "Let me see, let me see," she said, and Tristan set the box down on the bench beside her trail mix, which was open in a plastic bag.

The puppy tumbled out, stepped on Everlee's knee, and licked her wrist. She laughed and held up a handful of trail mix. "Want some, buddy? There's raisins in here, he loves fruit probably."

"No, wait." Tristan remembered the shelter woman pointing at a poster on the wall, the one with a bowl of grapes crossed out in red. "Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats." He had thought it was odd, since raisins were just dried grapes, but he had repeated it to himself on the bus anyway.

Everlee froze with her hand in the air. "Seriously?"

"Seriously."

She lowered the trail mix and closed the bag, and Tristan noticed something. There were small purple smears on the puppy's whiskers. His stomach dropped. While he had been reading the adoption papers at the other bench, the puppy had been out of the box, and Everlee's bag had been tipped on its side. A cluster of raisins lay scattered under the table, and three were missing from the pile.

"How many did he eat?" Tristan asked.

"I don't know, I wasn't watching. Two? Three?" Everlee's voice went thin. The park suddenly felt too big and too slow. Tristan picked up the puppy, felt its heartbeat against his palm, fast as a hummingbird, and made a decision. "We have to call the vet. The shelter gave me a number."

Ms. Georgiou, who taught science at his school and was reading on the next bench, looked up. "Is something wrong with that puppy?" Tristan explained, holding out the scattered raisins as evidence. She drove them to the animal clinic in her green hatchback, the puppy whining softly on Everlee's lap the whole way, while Tristan called the vet's office from Everlee's phone and was told to come at once.

The vet gave the puppy something to make it throw up, and it did, right into a metal pan. Then she said he would be fine, because they had come quickly. Tristan sat in the waiting room with the bill in his hand, his first act of commerce as a pet owner, paid partly with his birthday money. He texted his parents, then looked at Everlee.

"From now on, no food on the bench," he said.

"Permanent rule," said Everlee. "I'll check everything. Even my granola bars."

The puppy, sleepy and wobbly, licked Tristan's thumb once and fell asleep in his jacket.

Anais slid the slide onto the microscope stage and clamped it down with the brass clips. The onion skin that Mr. Pham had cut from the inner curve of the bulb was thinner than tissue paper, and she had stained it herself, one careful drop of iodine. At forty times magnification she saw rows of bricks, pale gold and neatly parallel, like a wall built by someone very patient. She turned the knob and the cells snapped into focus, sharp at the edges.

The worksheet had three arrows to label. Cell wall, easy. Nucleus, easy, a dark blot near the middle of each brick. Cell membrane, the third arrow pointed at the outer edge of a cell, and Anais could not find anything there to point at. She looked at the edge where one cell met the next. There was a line, but it looked like a single line, not two. She labeled the wall on that line and left the membrane blank.

Sebastien leaned over from the next stool. "You done?"

"I can't find the membrane." She pulled back so he could see. "Maybe onion cells just don't have one."

"They have one. We're all made of cells, and every cell has a membrane. It's in the book, page sixty."

"Then where is it?" Anais said. She looked again. Sebastien's slide was a different piece of skin, stained darker, and his cells looked the same at the edges. One line. Precious, across the table, had drawn her membrane arrow touching the same line as her wall arrow, which struck Anais as cheating.

She sat with it for a minute. The line at the edge could be two lines lying on top of each other, so close they looked like one. She thought of the track behind the school, where one runner passing another on the inside lane could look, from the bleachers, like a single runner until the moment they separated. If the membrane was pressed right against the wall, it would be invisible as its own line. It would only look missing.

She tested it the only way she could, with the fine focus. She turned the knob a hair at a time, watching the edge of a cell while the focus moved through the thickness of the skin. For one fraction of a turn, the single line seemed to double, just barely, and then it closed again like a mouth. She did it twice more to be sure.

She wrote her labels. Wall and membrane, both on the outside edge, one pressed against the inside of the other. "It's there," she said. "You just can't see it as a separate line, because it's pressed so tightly against the wall." Then she nudged Precious's elbow. "Fix your arrow. Yours is fine, but you're going to want to draw it where mine is."

Madison leaned closer to the screen, where her message from Bennett glowed in the chat window. "My grandpa says Maple Ridge was founded by a guy named Cornelius Vale who gave everyone free land," he had typed. "Ms. Farah-Ali says we need a source for our town history project. Tell me if you find one."

The problem was that half the internet said one thing and half said another. One site claimed Vale arrived in 1841 with a wagon train. Another said the town began in 1848 when a railroad camp turned permanent. A third was so vague it only mentioned "brave pioneers" and "a generous founder," with no names, no dates, nothing she could grab onto. Madison scrolled and scrolled. Which of these, she wondered, was just somebody's opinion, and which was something she could actually check?

Then she remembered what Ms. Farah-Ali had said on Friday, almost in passing: "A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data, and it is often the best place to check a claim." Madison said the words out loud to herself. A letter. A photograph. Official data. Not somebody's website about somebody's website.

The town library's digitized newspaper archive was linked right there on the library page, and it went back to the 1840s. She typed "Vale" into the search box and held her breath. An article from 1847 appeared, written by a reporter who had apparently interviewed Cornelius Vale himself at the land office. Vale had offered parcels at two dollars an acre, the article said, not free. There was even a photograph of the land office ledger, with names and payments inked down the page in careful rows.

So the "free land" story was a claim, and now she had checked it against a primary source. But wait, she thought. What if the newspaper had gotten it wrong too? She searched further and found the land office's official data from the same year, digitized by the county. The numbers matched the ledger photograph. Two different firsthand records from the time, agreeing with each other. That felt like something solid.

She pasted the links into her reply to Bennett. "Primary source says two dollars an acre. Grandpa's story is an opinion," she typed. "Ask him where he heard it. Maybe his grandpa told him." Then she sat back and looked at the photograph of the ledger again, at all those names in faded ink. Somewhere in that list, she realized, might be her own last name. She leaned in and began to read down the columns, one line at a time.

Justin spread his brushes across the library table and stared at the poster he was supposed to finish by Saturday. It advertised the community theater audition on Sunday, and Mr. Doyle planned to hang it right over the returns desk where everyone would see it. The letters were done. The problem was the sunset behind them, which had turned the color of wet dirt for the third afternoon in a row.

"You mixed them again," said Tyrell, sliding into the chair across from him. Tyrell had come to work on his own poster for the summer reading contest, but mostly he was watching Justin suffer.

"I followed the same steps." Justin held up the failed attempt. "I put in the red for the low sky, then I blended up toward the green I mixed for the top, because the poster colors for the audition notice are red and green." Every time the two colors met in the middle, a dull brown smeared across the paper instead of a smooth sunset. He had started to dread picking up the brush at all.

He got up and pulled a book on painting from the shelf, the one with a big circle of colors inside. Red sat on one side. Green sat exactly across from it. He ran his finger around the circle to be sure. "They're opposite each other," he said slowly. "On the color wheel." Tyrell leaned over to look.

"So?"

"So every time I blend them in the middle, I get mud. Watch." Justin took a scrap of paper and touched red to it, then green beside it, then dragged a wet brush through both. The scrap went gray-brown, the exact color ruining his sunset. He tried orange and blue next, and green and red again just to be certain, and each pair darkened the same dull way. "The opposites do it. Every pair I try." He glanced at the book's chart. "Complementary," he read off the page. "That's what they're called when they sit across from each other."

Justin sat back down, flipped to fresh paper, and drew a quick pencil line dividing the sky in two. Instead of blending the red upward into the green, he would keep them apart and let a thin band of dark paper sit between them, like the horizon at dusk. He painted the bottom half red, careful not to cross the line, then measured the top half against the bottom so the two sections stayed proportional. When he set the poster flat to dry, the colors glowed beside each other, clean and bright, no brown anywhere.

Mr. Doyle stopped on his way past with an armload of returned books. He looked at the sunset for a long moment. "Now that," he said, "is going to make people show up on Sunday."

"Two o'clock," Justin told him. "Audition's at two."

Nicholas had promised Mr. Fitzgerald the corrected homework by tomorrow morning, and he was not going to be negligent about it twice. He spread his math sheet on the kitchen table next to his science folder, where a slide of pond water sat waiting under his grandfather's old microscope. He wanted to look for a microbe before dinner, but the math came first, so he pulled his chair close and grabbed a pencil.

The problem stared back at him: 2x + 3x + 7 = 22. Easy, he thought, and he wrote 5x + 7 = 22 in one quick motion. He was on fire. Then the next one: 2x + 3 = 11. He wrote 5x = 8, and something in his stomach went cold.

"Grandma, is this right?" he asked. His grandmother, a retired teacher, was peeling an orange at the counter, and Lucian, who had come over to build a model rocket, looked up from the glue.

She leaned over the page. "In the first one you condensed 2x and 3x into 5x. In the second, tell me, what does the x stand for?"

"Stands for... the mystery number," Nicholas said slowly.

"So 2x is two mystery numbers," she said, tapping the paper, "and 3 is just plain 3. Can you condense those?"

Nicholas stared. Two mystery numbers plus three ordinary ones. You couldn't squash them together. Like trying to add the rocket parts and the glue into one pile. "No," he said.
