Then he sat at his desk with his half-finished trade poster, the one that was supposed to portray a harbor with goods moving in and out and a tariff collected at the gate, and he realized the drawing was due Friday morning, hours before the tryout. Two things, both Friday. He worked on the harbor until eleven, and this time he slept.

Friday came. In the gym, forty kids milled around the far basket while the coach set out cones. Brayden's hands were cold and his heart was loud, and then the coach blew the whistle and threw a ball straight at him, a hard bounce pass he wasn't ready for.

His hands came up before he knew it. Caught it clean.

The future had finally arrived, and it turned out his body knew exactly what to do about now.

Dylan counted the boxes in the living room of apartment 4B. Nine were still taped shut, and his mother had given him until Sunday night, two days away, to unpack the ones with his name on them. Through the wall he could hear the family in 4C, the neighbours he had not met yet, and somewhere below that a dog barked at something he would never see.

Three weeks ago, in his old town, he had stood on Jasraj's porch and promised they would message every single day. They had managed eleven days. Then Jasraj's team made the playoffs and Dylan's messages sat unanswered for hours, and he had typed something sharp about friends who forget people. Jasraj typed back a single word: "Wow." Dylan had inhaled to reply with something worse, then put the phone face down on his desk instead. Neither of them had written since. Calling it a fight felt too big. Calling it nothing felt too small.

In the mail room on Friday he found a girl from 4C sitting on the recycling bin, holding a photograph of a street with tall trees and holding back tears at the same time. "We moved here Tuesday," she said, wiping her face with her sleeve. "It's homesickness," Dylan said. "That's what it's called, being away from home and your people." She looked at him like he had recited a spell. "Does it stop?" He did not know yet, so he said, "Ask me Sunday."

He had a reason to say that. He had been running a quiet experiment on himself, keeping notes in the back of a notebook. Week one, he had wanted to cry at the smell of his grandmother's soup, which his mother had finally made right. Week two, he had still thought about Jasraj at recess but had also learned the shortcut to the corner store. Something was fading, not all at once, more the way a bruise fades. Maybe homesickness worked like that for everyone, easing as you settled in. He wanted proof before he answered the girl.

Saturday afternoon he heard a thump against his door. It was the girl, and a boy from 4C named Stephen, playing hallway football with a rolled-up sock. "You're the endangered one," Stephen announced, pointing at Dylan's feet, which were bare sock territory. Dylan laughed before he could stop himself, a real laugh, the first one in this building. "Truce if you play," the girl offered, holding out the sock like a treaty. He took it. They played until a neighbour on the third floor banged on her ceiling.

Sunday night, boxes unpacked with eleven minutes to spare, Dylan knocked on 4C. The girl opened the door, sock still in hand. "It took me about three weeks to feel better," he said. "Yours might be faster. Or not. But it goes." She nodded slowly, then held up her phone. On the screen was a photo of her new street, bare little trees and all. "I took it today," she said. "For later."

Paisley taped the last photo to the display board at the community centre: a fishing crew on a wide grey bay, a woman in a embroidered parka, a cluster of houses under snow. Her group had one caption left to type, and the deadline was four o'clock.

"Read it back," said Ananya, who was typing on the laptop.

"An Inuit hunter from the photograph, taken in 1962," Ashwin read off the screen.

Paisley frowned. Something about it snagged in her mind, the way a thread catches on a splinter. She had seen the word used differently somewhere, but she could not place where. "Wait. Don't print yet."

"Why?" Ashwin said. "It's due in an hour."

"Because 'Inuit' is the word for a whole group of people. I think. It's like saying 'a French' instead of 'a French person.'" She could not explain how she knew; she had maybe read it on a museum plaque last summer, or heard it at her cousin's school assembly. She needed to check, and the school library was closed on Saturdays.

Ms. Zhou, who ran the community centre's weekend program, was setting out juice and crackers down the hall. Paisley went to find her, passing the smell of wet paint from the art room, and the squeak of sneakers from the gym where a badminton game was going on.

"Ms. Zhou, do you know if it's 'an Inuit' or something else, for one person?"

Ms. Zhou pulled out her phone. "My sister teaches up north. Let me look at her messages." She scrolled, then turned the screen. There it was, in a text about a school pen-pal project: the word Inuit means "the people" in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.

"An Inuk," Paisley said out loud, testing it. That was the missing piece, and it fit the pattern she had half-remembered: the group word and the single word were different, like the threads of the embroidery, whole cloth versus one stitch.

Back at the board, she changed the caption to "An Inuk hunter from the photograph." Ananya printed it, and Ashwin taped it beneath the picture of the man in the kayak.

At three fifty, a woman stopped in front of the display. She was wearing a pin shaped like an ulu, the curved knife Paisley had learned about while researching the fishing photos. The woman read the caption, then looked at the girls.

"You got it right," she said. "Most people don't." She tapped the frame. "That's my father in the kayak."

The health elective at Camp Windrow ended with each camper teaching a five-minute lesson on the stage, and Ava had drawn the hardest topic in the jar: how nicotine hooks the brain. She understood the reward pathway well enough to draw it, dopamine sliding into receptors like a key into a lock. What she could not figure out was why her uncle kept saying his vaping habit used to be one pod a week and was now three. If nicotine worked the same way every time, the amount should stay the same.

She spread her poster on the picnic table while Cedar painted arrows and Nahla arranged red buttons for the dopamine. "The brain adapts," Nahla read off Ava's messy notes from the pharmacy trip last weekend, when they had walked to town for sunscreen. "That's what the pharmacist told you?" Ava nodded. She had asked about her uncle, and the pharmacist had said that with regular use, the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect. Then Ava had asked what that was called, and the pharmacist had smiled and said one word: "Tolerance." That word had been sitting in her pocket all week like a stone.

"But how do I show it?" Ava said, tapping the poster. "Nobody can see a brain adapting." Cedar suggested drawing a brain wearing tiny sunglasses. Nahla suggested a rap. Ava stared at the red buttons instead, and an idea arrived, not slowly but all at once, the way spontaneous ideas do. She scooped the buttons into a cup. "Okay, you're the brain," she told Cedar. "Every time I dump five buttons, that's a puff. You inhale, dopamine floods in, you feel great. Show me great." Cedar spread his arms wide and grinned like a cartoon.

Ava dumped five buttons, and Cedar grinned. She dumped five again, and he grinned smaller. On the fifth dump, Cedar barely smiled. "What if," Ava said slowly, "the brain gets used to it, so the same amount stops working?" She tried dumping eight buttons, and Cedar's grin came back full force. Then ten, then twelve, his grin snapping to full brightness only as the numbers climbed. Nahla scribbled the counts on the poster's edge. By the end of the row, the cup was almost empty and Cedar was grinning at fourteen.

"You realize," Cedar said, still grinning, "you just used up all my buttons being addicted." "That's the whole point," Ava said. "It never gets easier, only bigger." Nahla looked at the scribbled numbers, twelve, fourteen, climbing in a ragged line, and said quietly that her cousin had said almost exactly that in April, laughing like it was nothing.

On the last morning, Ava stood on the stage with her cup and her poster. She pointed at the climbing numbers, said the word tolerance out loud once, and then dumped buttons over Cedar's head while he grinned bigger and bigger and bigger, until the cup was empty and his hands were held out for more.

The school bus rattled over the pothole by the gym, and Mackenzie's word list jumped in her hands. She was down to the last page before the county spelling bee, and the words were betraying her. "Bite," she muttered. "B-I-T-E. Why is that e even there? It doesn't make a sound. It's just sitting there like camouflage, pretending to be useful."

Ali leaned over from the seat across the aisle. "You're the one who signed up for this."

"And I can spell everything except the words with sneaky letters." She tapped the paper. "Bite, bone, home. Then bite's weird cousin, bit. One letter changes the whole sound and I can't see why."

Henley, two rows back, poked her head over the seat. "Maybe the letters used to make those sounds and then stopped. Like, the e used to say something."

Mackenzie stared at her. That was actually a thought. If the e had once been pronounced, the spellings wouldn't be strange at all. They'd be records of something that changed. She flipped her list over and wrote out loud sounds with her pencil, mouthing "bee-nay" for bone just to test it, and Ali burst out laughing so hard the eighth graders turned around.

Mr. Adebayo, riding up front with the team, held up a battered paperback. "You'll want this," he said, and passed it back along the seats. Mackenzie found the page he'd marked. Her eyes went wide. "Listen to this. Between about 1400 and 1700, the long vowel sounds all shifted. It's called the Great Vowel Shift." She read faster. "And here's the twist. Printing had already locked the spellings in, so the letters stayed put while the sounds walked off without them."

"So the e isn't camouflage," Henley said. "It's a fossil."

"A fossil that bites," Ali said, and Mackenzie's grin was infectious; even the eighth graders were smiling now.

The bee that afternoon went three rounds before the announcer said "knife." Mackenzie pictured the word's history like a map, the k that had once been spoken, the strange old spellings that no longer matched the sounds. "K-N-I-F-E," she said. The judge nodded, and in the fourth round, when the word was "mimic," she was so relaxed she almost laughed. "M-I-M-I-C. Mimic."

Afterward Ali pretended to be the announcer, mimicking his deep voice. "Our next word is" and she held up a silent, invisible letter e, floating in the air like a tiny trophy.

Declan stood in his grandma's kitchen for the first time since March, when everything had happened. The house still smelled like her coffee, and that was the problem. His dad was sorting boxes in the living room, and Declan wanted to say goodbye to her somehow, but he didn't know how, and the funeral had happened while he was sick with something contagious and running a fever, so he had never gotten the chance.

"Obstruct the doorway and I'll drop this box," his dad said, so Declan moved. He wandered to the fridge, where her magnets still held a grocery list in her handwriting. Stuck behind the list was a folded page addressed to him. He pulled it free and read it at the table.

"Dear Declan. If you are reading this at the house, then check the cupboard above the stove, the one I never let you open because of the good dishes. Yours is the box marked with a D. Love, Grandma." He got a chair, climbed up, and found a small box. Inside was a sugar skull she had painted with his name, orange and yellow, and a note that said only, "Ask Annie about November."

He texted Annie a photo of the skull. She called back in a minute. "My family does that," she said. "It's called an ofrenda. During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars with photos and marigolds. The color and the scent are said to guide spirits home. It's November 2 today, so if you're going to do it, it's today." Declan thought about that. He couldn't see whether any of it was true, but he could test it the only way available: he could build one and see how it felt to sit beside it.

Annie showed up twenty minutes later with a paper bag of marigolds from the store where Mr. Reddy was working the register on weekends. "He gave me an extra bunch when I told him," she said. On the porch table they set the sugar skull, her framed photo from the mantel, and one of her coffee mugs. The petals Declan scattered in a line from the front door toward the photo, because if the scent was supposed to guide her home, then the path should start where she would come in. Annie argued the petals should go in a circle instead, so they compromised: a path with a circle at the end, like a little landing pad.

They sat until the porch light came on. Nothing visibly arrived, but the smell of marigolds mixed with the smell of coffee still drifting from the kitchen, and Declan told Annie about the time his grandma had called a raccoon a carnivore and then chased it off her bird feeder with a broom. Annie laughed until she had to put her head on the table. Then the wind moved the petals slightly, all together, like something had walked through.

"Okay," Declan said quietly to the photo. "Hi, Grandma."

The bus smelled like sunscreen and peanut butter sandwiches as it rattled up a gravel lane toward the Hartwell Homestead, a historic farm where people in old-fashioned clothes worked the land the way settlers had done almost two hundred years ago. Sydney pressed her forehead to the window. The farmhouse was tall and faded, with a porch swing that creaked even in the light wind, and behind it stood a barn, a garden, and a fenced yard where hens scratched in the dirt.

"The hens get to wander all day," Reed said, leaning across the aisle. "Lucky. Our class hamster just sits there."

Ms. Popescu, their guide for the day, met them at the gate wearing a long gray dress and a white apron. She explained that the homestead showed how a family lived in the 1830s, from the sparse furnishings in the sleeping loft to the heavy iron pots in the kitchen. Sydney noticed that almost everything in the farmhouse had a job, and often two. A bench was also a storage chest. A ladder was also a drying rack for herbs.

Then came the part Sydney had been waiting for. A costumed farmer let the students gather eggs from the nesting boxes along the henhouse wall. The straw smelled warm and dusty, and one brown hen squawked and flapped when Sydney reached beneath her, but the egg was there, smooth and heavier than she expected.

Reed held his egg up to the light and frowned. "Wait. Will this hatch? I haven't seen a single rooster anywhere. Not one, all morning."

Sydney thought about that. She had been watching the yard, too, and Reed was right, there were no roosters, only hens, maybe fifteen of them. But the nesting boxes had been full of eggs anyway, and the farmer had collected them in a basket for the kitchen, not for hatching. She turned her egg over in her hands, wondering. Maybe the hens didn't need a rooster to lay eggs at all. But if that were true, then an egg with no rooster around would never become a chick. She raised her hand.

"Excuse me," she said to the farmer. "The hens here lay eggs even with no rooster, right? So these eggs can't hatch into chicks?"

"That's it exactly," the farmer said, nodding. "We keep only hens at this yard, so the eggs are unfertilized. Good for eating, no chicks coming from them."

"So to get chicks," Reed said slowly, "you'd need a rooster somewhere."

Sydney grinned and tucked her egg carefully into the basket. Somewhere across the yard, a hen burst out of the barn door flapping her wings, and the whole class turned to look.

The gym smelled like floor wax and sweat, and Lea tied her shoes tighter before the second day of tryouts. She had played fine yesterday, she thought, but the coach kept stopping to watch her, and she wondered what he was writing on that clipboard. Maybe nothing. Maybe everything.

During the water break, Brennan leaned against the bleachers. "You see the list the coach taped to the door? Practice squad names go up Friday." Lea hadn't seen it, but she'd heard the eighth graders talking, and something they said had snagged in her mind like a sock on a nail. Every kid they mentioned seemed to have a birthday right after hers, in January or February. Was that a coincidence, or a pattern?

She decided to test it. "Brennan, when's your birthday?" He blinked. "March third. Why?" She moved down the line asking everyone the same question, keeping a mental tally on her fingers like a coach keeping stats. When they formed shooting lines, she counted the older kids in each one and quietly began to monitor which players the coach pulled aside for extra drills. Almost all of them were born early in the year. Nelson, who'd made the team last season, was a September birthday, but he was the tallest kid in the school, which she guessed didn't hurt.

At lunch she found Nelson in the library and explained her tally. He listened with his sandwich halfway to his mouth. "You counted birthdays?" "Half the gym," she said. "Most of the kids who get picked are months older than me. I'm December." Nelson wiped his hands and typed something on the library computer, scrolling, frowning. Then he turned the screen toward her. "Look. Studies of youth sports found that players born early in the selection year get picked more often than players born late. Researchers call it the relative age effect." Lea read the sentence twice. It had a name. It was a real thing, not just her imagination, and something about that made her feel less like a bad player and more like a mystery that hadn't been solved yet.

Still, she felt a flicker of skepticism. Maybe the older kids were simply better, pattern or no pattern. So she designed her own small experiment. At Friday's tryout she decided to count only her own results: made shots, completed passes, loose balls she reached first. Ten minutes in, she had hit seven of nine from the free throw line, and the coach had twice said her name in a voice that sounded like a good sign.

When the list went up, she stood on tiptoe behind Brennan to read it. There, in the middle of the practice squad, printed small and even: Lea. She read it again to be sure, then bounced once on the balls of her feet. "Told you," Nelson said from behind her. "Now quit blocking the door."

The nagar kirtan filled Penelope's whole street with orange. Her little brother rode on her dad's shoulders, and the smell of fried dough drifted from the langar tent at the end of the block. Penelope had invited her classmate Brynlee, who had never been to a Vaisakhi parade before, and Brynlee kept asking questions Penelope could not answer.

"So why is this day such a big deal?" Brynlee asked as a float rolled past with a canopy of yellow flowers.

Penelope opened her mouth and then closed it. She knew it had something to do with a Guru and something that started a long time ago, but she could not put the pieces together. She had a guess, that it was just a harvest festival like the autumn fair, but her guess felt thin. She decided to test it against the one person who always had answers.

"Come on," she said, and pulled Brynlee toward the front of the procession, where her uncle walked beside the truck carrying the Guru Granth Sahib under its embroidered canopy.

A boy about seven years old beat them to it. He tugged the uncle's sleeve and asked, "Why does everybody keep saying today matters?"

"Because in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," the uncle said. "That's the community of initiated Sikhs. Vaisakhi is the day we remember it." He straightened the boy's little turban and kept walking.

Penelope felt her harvest-festival guess fall apart. The parade was not just a party; it was a birthday, sort of, the birthday of the Khalsa itself. She turned it over while a drummer passed them, then another, and she spotted Markus from her class handing out cups of water. He would contradict her the second she got a detail wrong, so she practiced on him first.

"Markus, did you hear why today matters?"

"In 1699, the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," Markus said. "I asked your uncle twenty minutes ago. He told me twice because I forgot Anandpur."

So it held up. Penelope found Brynlee again by the langar tent, where volunteers were laying out paper plates. "I figured it out," she said. "It's not only a harvest thing. Vaisakhi is the day Sikhs remember 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur."

"Credible," Brynlee said, "for someone who just learned it five minutes ago."

"I heard it, I checked it, and Markus agreed," Penelope said. "That counts."

They got in line for food. Ahead of them, an old man who had been complaining to a volunteer about the crowd suddenly smiled and said, "Our landlord is over there serving chole, and last month he claimed he was too busy for anyone."

"Everyone's busy today anyway," the volunteer said, ladling out another bowl.

Penelope handed Brynlee a plate and pointed at the float turning the corner, flowers swaying. "Watch this part. This is the best bit of the whole parade."

Avery had counted the hours until lights-out, and now that it was here, she wished she hadn't. The bunk above her creaked whenever Hugo moved, which was often. Somewhere across the cabin, Cassius was pretending to be asleep, but his breathing was too even, too perfect, like a kid performing sleep for an audience. Avery stared at the underside of Hugo's mattress and thought about her kitchen, where the light above the stove was probably on right now. Was she the only one doing this? It felt like a thing no one would admit out loud, which meant there was no way to know for sure. Unless there was.

The next morning she borrowed a marker from the craft bin and taped a scrap of paper to the inside of the bathroom door, where every girl in the cabin would see it and no counselor would. It said: if you miss home, draw one tally mark. She told herself she was being objective about it, like a scientist counting results instead of guessing. By dinner there were eleven tallies. Eleven, out of twelve girls.

That should have made her feel better, but it didn't, quite. She was the one who had put up the paper, so she knew about all eleven. Everyone else still thought they were alone. That was the problem with hidden things. A feeling nobody shows can't be discovered by accident; something has to happen out in the open.

She found her chance at the campfire. Mr. Desir had just finished a story about an enormous fish and gone off to talk to the lifeguard, and the coals were settling into that stage where you could actually hear yourself think. Hugo was hunched over his marshmallow stick, uncharacteristically quiet, and Avery wondered if he was homesick and if his joking usually hid it. She decided to test the idea out loud.

"I miss my dog," she said, to nobody in particular. "Like, a lot. I keep thinking he's waiting by the door."

Hugo looked up so fast his marshmallow slid into the fire. "You do? I miss my mom's cooking so bad I dreamed about scrambled eggs." Cassius leaned over from the next log. "I wrote my little brother a letter and I'm not even sure he can read."

Then came the twist. Mr. Desir, settling back onto his log, said, "Every summer, kids think they're the only one. But research on overnight camps found most campers feel at least some homesickness, and for most of them it stays mild." He said it like he was remarking on the weather, then asked who wanted seconds on marshmallows, and half the circle raised their hands.

"Wait," Hugo said. "Most? Like, most of everybody?"

"Most," said Cassius slowly, like he was working a math problem. "So it's basically normal. We've all just been hiding it in a way that, like, hindered us from finding each other."

"That's the weirdest use of hinder I've ever heard," Avery said, and the whole log of boys cracked up.

Later, at lights-out, Avery pulled her flashlight out from under her pillow. She didn't need it to find the bathroom paper; she knew the number by heart. But she clicked it on anyway and swept it once around the cabin, a slow circle over eleven sleeping shapes. In the beam each face looked the same: ordinary, breathing, here. Somewhere in her head a thought drifted past, that in a hundred years everyone in this cabin would be gone, a kind of extinction that even tallies and flashlights couldn't reach, and that this was somehow exactly why the tallies mattered now. She clicked the light off.

"Avery?" Hugo's voice came down through the mattress springs. "You still awake?"

"Yeah."

"Tomorrow can we put the tally paper somewhere the boys can use it too?"

Avery smiled into the dark. "Bring a marker," she said.

The rain gauge on the park gazebo read zero, but Chloe checked the sky anyway, because the forecast had promised precipitation by five o'clock and her whole plan needed dry weather. She had exactly forty minutes to fix things with Skye before the storm and before the Friendship Day picnic ended, which was a terrible deadline for something nobody could really schedule.

The fight was three weeks old. Skye had told Mariana that Chloe's volcano project looked like "a melted birthday cake," which it did, but that was not the point. Chloe had heard it secondhand, stopped sitting with Skye at lunch, and the silence had hardened like old glue. Today, though, Chloe was ready to try, because her mom had said something on the drive over that Chloe kept turning over like a stone in her pocket.

"I forgive her," Chloe had told her mom in the car. "But I'm not ready to be best friends again yet. Is that allowed?"

"Totally," her mom had said, eyes on the road. "Forgiving is letting go of the resentment. It doesn't mean you're reconciling."

Chloe had looked the word up on her phone at the picnic table. Reconciling meant rebuilding the relationship, like putting a bridge back up plank by plank. So there were two separate things, not one. You could drop the heavy bag of being mad and still take your time walking back across the bridge. That felt consistent with how her chest actually felt, lighter but cautious, and it gave her an idea she could test.

She found Skye at the horseshoe pit, defending her title against Mariana. Chloe walked up, held out a paper plate with two cookies on it, and said, "Truce. But I'm warning you, I'm only reconciling at, like, medium speed."

Skye took a cookie and squinted at her. "What does that even mean?"

"It means I forgive you, so I'm not mad anymore. But the friendship has to rebuild itself. You can't rush a bridge." Chloe took a bite of her own cookie. "Also, my volcano did look like a melted birthday cake. I'm just saying you could have advocated for me instead of laughing."

Mariana raised her hand. "I would like it noted that I never laughed. I said it looked like modern art."

"You said it looked like a horror movie," Skye said.

"I said it looked like a horror movie with heart."

Skye set down her horseshoe. "Okay, medium speed. But can medium speed include the three-legged race? It starts in ten minutes and Mariana ties the knot too tight and cuts off my circulation."

Chloe pretended to consider it, tapping the cookie against her chin while the first fat drops of rain darkened the gazebo roof across the park. The precipitation had arrived early, which meant the race would be moved under the pavilion, which meant crowded concrete, which meant Skye would definitely stumble and blame Chloe's left leg, as she had every year since third grade.

"Medium speed includes the race," Chloe said, "if you admit my left leg is not the problem."

Skye stuck out her hand. "Your left leg is not the problem. Your left leg is a victim of my hopping."

They shook on it, and then Mariana pulled them both toward the pavilion, shouting, "Team Melted Cake, let's move!"

By the time they reached the starting line, the rain was drumming on the roof and Skye was already hopping.

Florence stood at the front of Room 12 with her hands folded behind her back, waiting for the word that might knock her out. Last year she had lost on "gneiss" in the third round, and for weeks afterward that silent letter had followed her around like a plague, showing up in her dreams and on cafeteria menus. This year she had studied every night, and now only she and Gary were left, the final two spellers in the class bee.

"Your word is 'chrysanthemum,'" said Ms. Ionescu.

Florence traced the letters in her mind, found the tricky spot, and spelled it slowly, the way a careful person crosses a river on stepping stones. Ms. Ionescu nodded. Then Gary spelled "rhinoceros" without even pausing, which struck Florence as reckless, like driving past a sign that said BRIDGE OUT. Round after round went by like that. Clarissa, watching from the second row, whispered something to the boy beside her, and Florence noticed it, because Clarissa never whispered during bees.

At lunch, Florence found out why. "Gary told me he wants to prolong the bee on purpose," Clarissa said, tearing her sandwich in half. "He read that in 2019, the Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. They ran out of words, I guess. Gary thinks if we all keep getting them right, Ms. Ionescu will have to make us co-champions too."

Florence turned this over all through math. Eight winners. A national bee, on a real stage, with eight champions because nobody missed. It had never occurred to her that a bee could end that way, that winning did not require someone else to lose. She thought about last year, when she had whispered "g-n-e-i-s-s" and watched Ravi celebrate. She had wanted him to miss. That wanting had felt ugly even then, and she had done it anyway.

Back in the classroom for the final rounds, she tested the idea. She spelled "vermilion" correctly, watching Ms. Ionescu flip to the next card. Gary spelled "belligerent." She spelled "facetious." Gary spelled "onomatopoeia." The word list in Ms. Ionescu's hand grew thinner with every round, and Florence could see it, a shrinking stack, until there was only one card left.

"Gary, your word is 'serendipity.'"

Gary spelled it right, and Ms. Ionescu looked at the empty stack, then at the two of them. "That's the end of the list," she said. "Florence, you'll take one word from the backup envelope, and Gary the next. If you both get them right, I'll need to check the rules."

Florence took her card. "Momentous," Ms. Ionescu said.

"M-O-M-E-N-T-O-U-S," said Florence.

Ms. Ionescu smiled and reached for her phone. "Clarissa, come read me the third bullet on that bee article. I want to hear it again."

Clarissa stood up, grinning, and read, "In 2019, the Scripps National Spelling Bee crowned eight co-champions."

Aria had saved her allowance for two months to buy four tickets in the upper deck, and now she sat between her dad and her cousin Sofia, who had arrived from England three days earlier. Kaelyn and Myla were one row down, sharing a bag of popcorn and arguing about which team would score first. Below them the field gleamed under the lights, and the players were still warming up.

When Sofia found their seats, Aria had promised her a proper stadium experience, and part of that, in Aria's opinion, was the wave. Around the sixth inning, a section near third base started it. Thousands of people stood, threw their arms up, and sat down again, and the standing moved around the bowl like water sloshing in a giant cup. Aria jumped up with the rest of her section, yelling, then plopped back down, grinning.

"What is this called?" Sofia asked, pointing as the wave came around again.

"The wave," Aria said. "You know, the wave."

"We call it the Mexican wave," Sofia said.

Aria frowned. That didn't make sense. There was nothing Mexican about a baseball stadium in their own city. Maybe Sofia had made a mistake, or maybe she was teasing, the way she had teased Aria about the word "biscuit" at dinner. But Sofia was already standing with the next pass of the wave, so Aria filed the question away and jumped up with her.

She tested the idea the way she tested things, by asking around. "Excuse me," she said to the man with the foam finger at the end of the row. "Do you know why some people call the wave the Mexican wave?" The man shrugged. Myla said she'd heard her grandmother in Colombia say it that way too, though Myla wasn't sure why. Kaelyn was pessimistic about the whole project. "Nobody knows," she said. "You'll just embarrass yourself asking strangers." Aria kept asking anyway.

In the eighth inning, a fan a few seats over, an older woman wearing a scarf from a club team, overheard the girls talking and leaned in. "It got famous at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico," she said. "That's why, in a lot of English-speaking places outside North America, it's the Mexican wave." Aria turned to Sofia. "So it's the same thing, just a different name." Sofia nodded, looking a little smug, in Aria's opinion.

On the walk to the exit after the final out, Aria made a quiet amendment to her mental list of things Sofia knew more about than she did: biscuits, football versus soccer, and now this. Myla was still grumbling that her question had been better. "You didn't even have a question," Kaelyn said. "Yes I did," Myla said. "I asked why the hot dogs cost eight dollars." Sofia laughed so hard she had to stop walking. "Now that," she said, "nobody in the world can explain."

Antoine crouched at the end of the gym hallway with a tennis ball, a meter stick, and a stopwatch he had borrowed from Ms. Mercer, who had one rule that afternoon: no running in the hallways, which prohibited anything but rolling. His problem was simple and stubborn. He wanted to know how fast his ball actually went, and eyeballing it told him nothing. Speed was invisible. You could not watch it, only chase it with numbers.

He had written a note to himself that morning, folded into his pocket like a tiny letter to his future self, and now he smoothed it out on the floor. Measure distance. Measure time. Divide. Annie, who was working beside him with a golf ball, leaned over to read it. "You wrote yourself instructions?" she said. "Last month I did the lab without a plan and got everything backwards," Antoine said. "This time I have a technique. Mark every meter, start the watch at zero distance, record where the ball is at each second." Annie tapped the paper. "Then we'll see if my ball beats yours."

Beatrix stood at the two-meter mark with her own stopwatch, calling out the seconds. At one second, Antoine's tennis ball had gone one meter. At two seconds, two meters. At three, three. Annie's golf ball was slower: one meter at one second, one and a half at two, two at three. Antoine wrote each number down, then drew two axes on graph paper and plotted the points, one line for each ball.

That was where the argument started, because the two lines crossed on his page and Annie insisted the crossing meant her ball had won. Antoine studied the graph. His line climbed like a ramp; hers rose gently, more flat than steep. "Look at yours," he said, tracing it with his finger. "A steeper line means a faster speed. Mine is steeper the whole way. Your ball is slower." Annie frowned at the page, then at the hallway, checking the paper against the world. "Then why did the lines cross?" she asked. Beatrix pointed at the vertical axis. "Because we started the golf ball half a meter ahead, that's all. The lines crossing isn't about speed. The steepness is."

Annie was quiet for a moment, rolling the golf ball back and forth under her palm. "So we didn't tie," she said. Antoine didn't answer right away. He remembered last month's backwards lab, how he had guessed instead of measuring, and how much easier guessing had been. He almost told her the graph might be wrong too. Instead he handed her the stopwatch. "Run it again," he said. "Authentic data, three trials. If your line gets steeper than mine, you win."

Annie set the golf ball on the floor, lined it up with the meter mark, and pressed the button. The ball whispered down the tiles, and Beatrix's voice rang out, "One second!"

Lucas was sitting on Graydon's bedroom floor with Graydon's phone, hunting for an old joke video the two of them had watched about fifty times in fifth grade. The channel that had posted it seemed to be gone. Every search just returned reuploads and dead links. "It has to be somewhere," Graydon said, bouncing a tennis ball off the wall. "The internet keeps everything, right?" Lucas was skeptical about that, because he had lost enough saved games to know that things on screens disappeared all the time. But he kept typing, and on the fourth try he landed on a page he had never seen before. At the top it said Internet Archive, and it claimed that since 1996 it had been saving copies of public web pages.

"That can't be real," Lucas said. Graydon leaned over his shoulder. Under the words was a search box, and Lucas typed in the address of their old school's website, the one that had been redone last year. The page loaded a version from years ago, complete with a photo of the class of that year standing in front of the gym, every face clear and labeled with first names.

Graydon went quiet in a way he almost never did. "Wait. Try my cousin's old blog," he said. "She had one in elementary school and she deleted it, like, forever ago." Lucas typed it in, half expecting a blank error page. Instead the old blog appeared, pink background and all, with a post about a family trip, and, at the bottom, a note about exactly which beach house they had rented, down to the street. "Anyone could read this," Graydon said slowly. "Anyone in the world. Strangers. It's still just sitting there." Lucas scrolled further and found a post full of photos, each one tagged with the park where they had been taken, and the day, and even the time.

"It's like the page is insulated from deleting," Lucas said. "You take it down, but this copy just sits there protected." Then a thought hit him, and his stomach did a small flip. In fifth grade he had kept a blog too, before he knew better, and he had posted a picture of his own house with the street sign visible. He had deleted it two years ago and never thought about it again. His intuition said this archive thing would not have it, because his blog had been tiny and nobody read it. But he had been wrong before.

"Graydon. My blog." He typed his old address with his thumb hovering, almost hoping for an error. The pink and blue page of his eleven-year-old self loaded instantly, complete with the photo of the house, the street sign, and a post that began "Nobody probably reads this but." He stared at it. Then he started copying down the archive's contact page, because it had a link for asking to have things removed. "It might not work," Graydon said. Lucas nodded. "Only one way to find out." He tapped the button that said submit.

Olivier had saved the ranking page on his phone two weeks ago, and every day it bothered him the same way. His favorite player, the one with the strange high leg kick, sat forty-third in the league. Forty-third. Olivier thought he was top ten, and tonight, in the bleachers waiting for Kathleen and Leighton before the game started, he planned to prove it.

"Forty-third is forty-third," Kathleen said, unwrapping a granola bar. "The numbers don't lie."

"The numbers are missing things," Olivier said. "Watch this." He opened his notebook, where he had copied the player's season line by hand. "Look. Hits divided by official at-bats, that's the batting average. But walks don't count as at-bats." He tapped the page. "So a walk gives a batter no credit. None. He gets on base and the average just sits there."

Leighton frowned at the math. "That can't be right. Getting on base helps the team."

Olivier tested it with small numbers right there on the notebook page, because he didn't want to just believe it. Two hits in four at-bats was .500, great. But if the player walked his next three times up, the average stayed .250, because those walks were not at-bats at all. He pushed the notebook toward Kathleen. "He's aggressive at the plate," Olivier said. "Pitchers are scared of him, so they walk him. The ranking punishes him for it."

The gym buzzer went off and the teams ran out. Kathleen chewed slowly, watching the point guard, whose picture Olivier had also printed and taped inside the notebook cover. She had enrolled her in the same fan club Olivier joined in September, before the player got good and the trouble started.

"He should still be higher," she said finally. "You're counting the walks on top of the hits. The average isn't."

Olivier felt his conscience poke him a little, because he had argued the same wrong thing yesterday, that the average must include everything. He had gone home and checked. It didn't.

"Fine," Kathleen said. "I'll write him a letter too."

The point guard drove baseline, got fouled, and stepped to the line while the crowd stomped the bleachers. Olivier held up his notebook so the section could see the cover, and Leighton started the chant first.

Justin knelt at the end of the hallway with a stopwatch, a tennis ball, and a sheet of graph paper that Ms. Sánchez had appointed him to fill in by Monday. The assignment said to measure the speed of a rolling ball, time how long it took to travel a known distance, and draw a distance-time graph. He had put it off all weekend, and now it was Sunday afternoon and the graph was still blank.

He set two pieces of tape on the tile floor, three meters apart, and crouched to push the ball gently from the first mark. He clicked the stopwatch as it crossed each one. Faster than he expected. He did it again, then again, and wrote the numbers in the margin. When he tried to plot them, the points scattered instead of forming a coherent line, and he sat back on his heels, frowning at the paper.

Oceane had done her graph on Friday, he remembered, while he was playing video games. She had asked if he wanted to time it with her, and he had said later. He looked down the empty hallway and thought about that choice for a moment, then got up and went to find his older cousin, who was visiting and reading in the den.

His cousin suggested more intervals. So Justin laid tape every half meter, seven marks in all, and rolled the ball while he ran alongside clicking the stopwatch. Something odd appeared in his numbers. The ball covered the first half meter in almost no time, but each later stretch took longer, until the last stretch took more than twice as long as the first. He checked the ball. Nothing was wrong with it. He rolled it again and watched it the whole way, and this time he saw it plainly: it was still slowing down when it crossed the final mark.

He thought about the ball his grandfather used to keep in the garage, a heavy rubber one that had been handed down like some descendant of an old bowling set, and how it had always stopped short on the mat by the door but rolled forever on the concrete. He looked from the tile to the living room, where the floor turned to carpet. He rolled the ball onto the rug and it stopped within a arm's length, dead, as if it had run out of something.

Back in the hallway, he rolled the ball twice more, wrote the times, and connected the dots. The line climbed steeply and then bent, flattening as it went. He stared at it, then leaned close to the tile and watched the next roll slow, halfway down the hall, still turning, and slowing all the time. "There it is," he said to the empty hallway.

Harrison pressed his pencil so hard against the paper that the street he was drawing began to look like it had been through a storm. Every building leaned the wrong way, and the road refused to narrow into the distance. Ms. Banerjee walked past his desk and tapped the spot where the road should have gone. "Pick your vanishing point first," she said. "Every line that runs away from you has to aim straight at it."

"That's it?" Dylan whispered from the next seat. "One dot controls the whole street?" Harrison stared at his paper. It seemed strange that something invisible, a point that wasn't a real object at all, could be in charge of every edge of every building. He erased his messy lines and tried again, starting with a single dot near the top of the page. The edges of the road aimed at it. The rooftops aimed at it. Slowly the street flattened itself into depth, as if the paper had opened a window.

At lunch he couldn't stop thinking about it. If one hidden point could organize a whole picture, had artists always done this? In the library he found a thick book about Leonardo da Vinci and flipped through it until a page about the Last Supper stopped him cold. He read the paragraph twice, then a third time. "Aleksandra," he called across the table, "come look at this." He waited until she pulled her chair over. "In the Last Supper, the vanishing point is right at Christ's head. And there's a nail hole there, from strings Leonardo stretched to make his guide lines. You can still see it."

Aleksandra leaned in, squinting at the painting. "A nail hole? In one of the most famous paintings on earth?" She sounded as amazed as he felt. "So the whole room in that picture, the walls, the ceiling, the windows, they all point at his head?" Harrison ran his finger along the lines in the book's reproduction, and sure enough, every edge of the room flowed toward that single point. It was like discovering the wire behind a magic trick.

Back in art class, he had an idea and, feeling impulsive, he acted on it before he could talk himself out of anything. He asked Ms. Banerjee for a pin and a length of thread, then pinned one end of the thread exactly at his vanishing point. When he swung the thread across the page, it lay perfectly along his street's edges, his rooftops, his sidewalk. "What's the probability my lines are this straight by accident?" he asked Aleksandra, who had wandered over to watch. She shook her head slowly. "Zero," she said. Harrison grinned and swung the thread again, watching it sweep across his little street like the hand of a clock.

The concert hall smelled like dust and lemon polish, and Savannah's hands were already sweating on her sheet music. In three weeks she would play the middle section of "River Song" on the school piano while Winnie played flute beside her, and Ms. Koné had written one word at the top of the page that was ruining everything: andante.

"What does that even mean?" Winnie whispered, leaning over the music stand on the diagonal aisle that cut from the stage door to the front row.

Savannah had a guess. Italian words looked fancy, and fancy meant fast, at least in her head. "Fast, I think. Like, show-off fast." She set the metronome racing, threw her fingers at the keys, and collaborated with Winnie the only way she knew how, which was to play louder and faster until the melody crashed into the flute part and both of them stopped, breathing hard. The piece had fallen apart, torn right down the middle.

From the third row, Loralie laughed, then covered her mouth. "Sorry. But that was so wrong. My grandma plays this stuff." She hopped up onto the stage edge. "She says largo means very slow. Like syrup."

"Then andante must be slow too," Savannah said, frowning at the page. But that did not fit either, because the next section was marked allegro, and surely the whole piece was not slow, slow, slow. She thought about the words themselves. Largo, she decided, was the slowest. Allegro sounded bright, quick, happy. That left andante sitting in the middle, and she remembered that in her cousin's old exercise book there had been a note next to it, a little drawing of a person strolling down a sidewalk. Walking. Andante meant walking pace, not slow, not racing. She had skipped past it because it seemed too ordinary to matter.

"Let's test it," she said. "Walking speed, but not dragging." She reset the metronome to a steady, unhurried tick, and this time she let the dynamics do the work instead of speed. Soft where the page said piano, swelling where it said crescendo, her hands crossing over each other as the line climbed. Winnie's flute slid in under the melody like it had been waiting there all along. When they reached the allegro, they leapt together, and it felt less like playing and more like flying.

Ms. Koné stood at the back of the hall with her arms folded, and when the last note faded she called out, "Again. Same tempo. More shape."

"Warranty on that?" Winnie asked, grinning.

"None," said Ms. Koné. "Musicians break constantly."

Savannah laughed, flexed her fingers, and set the metronome ticking.

The auditorium smelled like floor wax and nervous popcorn, even though nobody was allowed to eat in there. Alexis stood in line with eleven other spellers, holding her number card like a shield, and next to her Teresa was bouncing on her toes.

"I've got a secret weapon," Teresa whispered. "My cousin in Canada sends me words. She says Americans spell half of them wrong."

"That's not possible," Alexis said, but her stomach went tight. What if it was? The judge, Ms. Farah-Ali, called the first speller, and a boy got out on "restaurant," and the audience did that sad murmur, and Alexis thought about nothing but letters.

Round four, Teresa drew a word and grinned. "Colour. C-O-L-O-U-R." The bell dinged, wrong. Teresa froze. "That's how my cousin spells it! She writes it in every letter!"

"That's the Canadian way," Ms. Farah-Ali said gently. "In the United States we drop the u." Teresa walked offstage, and Alexis felt weird, half glad and half furious on her friend's behalf. Somebody had to be right, but who decided? She budgeted her remaining brainpower carefully: half for her own turns, half for this mystery.

Between rounds, Alexis tested a simple idea. She asked the next three eliminated spellers what they'd missed. "Honour," said one. "Favourite," said another. Every single one had that sneaky u. It was a pattern, like a trap set on purpose. At lunch Alexis had read the dictionary's front pages, hunting for gossip, and she'd found an anecdote about Noah Webster and his 1828 American Dictionary of the English Language. He promoted simpler spellings like "color" instead of "colour," and those became standard in the United States. It wasn't a mistake or a mystery. One man, one dictionary, one country that followed him. Canada just kept the older spelling. Alexis wanted to leap up and tell everyone, but Ms. Farah-Ali was already calling the final round.

Alexis stepped to the microphone, hesitant for exactly one second, then steady. Her word was "neighbor." Teresa's cousin would add a u, and Alexis knew exactly why, and exactly who to thank.

"N-E-I-G-H-B-O-R. Neighbor."

The bell stayed silent. The audience roared, and somewhere in the third row Teresa shouted, "Tell my cousin it was Webster's fault!"

Isla slid the photocopied diary pages across the library table like they were top secret files, which, in her opinion, they nearly were. "This is a real settler's diary from the 1800s," she whispered. "The actual words of a guy walking a wagon trail west. Ms. Whitehead says it's a primary source, so we can build our whole poster on it."

Wynter leaned over, scanning the cramped handwriting. "He complains about the mud for three pages. Three. Pages. Of mud."

"He crossed a whole continent. I think he earned his complaining," Isla said. "This is perfect for why people moved west. He writes about land, and starting over, and how his old town couldn't accommodate their whole family on one small farm." She tapped the word like a game show buzzer. "Evidence!"

Aliza arrived late, breathless, carrying her own notebook. "I found something too. Not a diary. A speech. From one of the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed. A chief talking about wagons rolling through their territory." She set it down between them. "It's a different view of the exact same events."

Isla stared at the two documents side by side. "Wait. So the diary says the trail was empty land waiting for them, and the speech says the land already belonged to people?"

"Yep." Aliza popped the p. "The diary shows one person's view. It rarely tells how the nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events."

"So my poster is only half the story." Isla sat back, feeling the whole project tip over in her head. Then she grabbed a marker and flipped the poster board sideways, drawing a wide brown line down the middle. "New plan. This is the trail. Diary quotes on one side, the chief's words on the other. Same trail, two views."

"That's actually brilliant," Wynter admitted, then pointed at Isla's title, which read WESTWARD HO. "But you have to change that title."

"It's a classic."

"It's a snooze." Wynter snatched the marker and wrote TWO SIDES OF ONE TRAIL, grinning in a way that was frankly contagious, because Isla caught herself grinning back even while defending her honor.

When Ms. Whitehead stopped at their table later, she read both columns, then looked up. "Whose idea was the split poster?"

"Mine," said Isla, "but Aliza found the second source, and Wynter mocked my title."

"A team effort," said Wynter, patting the poster. "My heritage is merciless editing."

Ms. Whitehead laughed and moved on, and Isla bent over the board to letter the chief's words carefully onto the left side, marker squeaking the whole way down.

Caleb's family had finally said yes to a pet, and on Saturday morning he stood in the pet store with a folded list in his pocket. The kitten was already chosen, a gray one asleep in a carrier by the register, but the food aisle had stopped him cold. Dog food and cat food filled opposite shelves, in bags that looked almost the same. "Why is it all separate?" he asked. "It's just kibble."

His friend Thiago, who had come along to help carry things, shrugged. "My uncle says cats can't make enough of their own taurine. It's a nutrient in meat, and if they don't get it they can get heart disease and go blind."

Caleb picked up a bag of dog food anyway, because it was three dollars cheaper and twice the size. Then he put it back. A cat going blind because he saved three dollars was not a trade he wanted to make, even if the money was coming out of his allowance.

At home, the kitten hid behind the couch for the first hour, and the real problem began. The list said to feed her, but the list didn't say how to get a scared cat to eat. Caleb set the bowl down, backed away, and watched. She didn't move. He tried again closer to her, and she still didn't move, though her ears turned toward the bowl when the kibble rattled. That gave him an idea. She wasn't refusing food, she was refusing distance. If the bowl scared her, maybe the food itself could be moved to her instead of the other way around. He took a single piece of kibble and rolled it slowly along the floor, so it stopped just past her whiskers, where she could reach it without leaving her hiding spot. She ate it. He rolled another. She ate that too.

The kitten, whom he had named Pip, still wouldn't come out, but by evening she was eating from a shallow dish that he had pushed halfway under the couch. He wrote this down in a notebook, the way he did for science class, in case the pattern stopped working. Then he thought of a problem he couldn't see. If Pip ate only what she could reach under the couch, she might eat too little, and a cat who ate too little meat wouldn't get enough taurine either, no matter what the bag said. He couldn't watch her all night to find out.

So he set up an experiment. He borrowed his dad's old magnifying lens, propped his phone above the dish on a stack of books, and aimed the lens so the camera could magnify the bowl from across the room. If there was less food by morning, she had eaten when no one was near. He wrote "amendment to plan: check recording at breakfast" on the list his mom had made, and stuck it to the fridge.

On Sunday the kitchen smelled like toast and like his neighbor Ms. Becker, who had come over with a blanket she said every new cat needed. Caleb showed them the recording. At one in the morning, a gray shape crept out, ate for four full minutes, and crept back. Ms. Becker voted the video excellent. His dad voted it excellent. Thiago, watching over video chat, voted excellent too. It was unanimous. Caleb slid the dish a few inches farther from the couch, not too far, just enough to be a small step forward, and pressed record again.

Victor held the cardboard carrier with both hands while Ms. Szabó from the animal shelter slid the paperwork across the counter. "His name is Biscuit," she said, "and he's been waiting three months for a home." Inside, a brown-and-white guinea pig with a white patch over one eye sniffed the air hole and made a sound like a tiny squeaky door. Victor's arms tingled from the weight, which was strange because Biscuit couldn't have weighed more than a bag of sugar.

On Monday, Victor set up the cage in his room: wood shavings, a little wooden house, a water bottle, and a food dish. His friend Mckinley came over after school and pressed her face to the bars. "He's so round," she said. "Like a furry potato." Mckinley wanted a pet of her own more than anything, but her building didn't allow animals, so she had promised herself she would learn everything about guinea pigs anyway, becoming Victor's unofficial mentor on the subject. She had checked out four library books and read two of them already.

The trouble started on Wednesday. Victor heard a metallic rattling in the night, steady as a dripping tap. In the morning he found Biscuit gripping the cage bars with his teeth, gnawing, gnawing, gnawing. "Maybe he's hungry," Victor said, and filled the food dish. Biscuit ate, then went right back to the bars. Mckinley frowned. "He's not hungry. Something else is going on."

Victor decided to test it. He put a carrot stick through the bars, and Biscuit attacked it, gnawing the same way but on the carrot instead of metal. Then a twig from the apple tree in the yard, then a toilet paper tube. Biscuit chewed everything, and his mood turned calm, almost sleepy, afterward. "It's not the cage he wants," Victor said slowly. "It's the chewing itself." They looked it up in one of Mckinley's library books, and there it was: a guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing, so it needs things to chew on to wear them down.

"So the bar gnawing was like an alarm," Mckinley said. "He was telling us his teeth needed work." Victor felt a little embarrassed he hadn't figured it out sooner, but Mckinley just started a chart. At the top she wrote CHEW MENU, and together they listed what Biscuit liked best. The volatile moods Victor had noticed, the squeaky complaining in the evening, settled down once the chewing box appeared next to the cage, stocked with hay twists and cardboard.

On Saturday they brought Zain over to see the results. Zain leaned in, and Biscuit, instead of rattling the bars, calmly picked up a hay twist and dragged it into his little wooden house. Zain raised his eyebrows. "He's like a tiny lumberjack," he said. Mckinley pointed at the chart, and Victor realized he could paraphrase the whole system in one sentence: keep the chew box full, and Biscuit stays happy. He refilled the box that afternoon and set it by the cage door.

Addison had read "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter" once already, and she had hated the ending. Now she sat cross-legged in the reading nook behind the living room couch, her back against the wall, the story open on her knees like she was about to excavate something buried in it.

Ms. Petrov had written one comment in red pen at the bottom of Addison's quiz: "Look for the hints. Reread." That was all. Addison had stared at it for two days, because hints about what? The story seemed simple. A girl named Marta rows out to check the lamp, a storm rolls in, and then, on the last page, the boat is gone and Marta is standing on the rocks, soaked, holding something in her fist. The something was never described. Ms. Petrov had asked the class what Marta held, and Addison had written "a fishhook," which had earned her the red comment instead of a checkmark.

Jada dropped onto the couch above the nook, peering over the back cushion. "You're reading it again? It wasn't even good."

"It was good," Addison said. "Something's hidden in it." She flipped back to page one and started over, slower this time, dragging her finger under each line. On page one, the keeper, Marta's father, winds the lamp mechanism and says the lamp "turns like a slow revolution," and Marta notices a loose screw on the lens housing. Addison's finger stopped. A loose screw. She read the last page again. The lamp had failed in the storm, and a ship had wrecked on the rocks, and Marta was standing there holding something small and metal in her fist.

Her heart started going fast. "Jada. The screw."

"What screw?"

"On page one. The lamp had a loose screw, and nobody tightened it, and then the lamp failed." She checked the middle of the story to be sure. The father says he'll fix it "tomorrow," which in a storm story is like a character saying everything is fine. Addison wrote both clues on a sticky note, then wrote her answer underneath: Marta is holding the screw. The thing that sank the ship is the thing in her hand.

"That's what foreshadowing is, right?" Jada said, squinting at the page. "A hint early on about what happens later. You only catch it the second time through."

Addison hadn't known the word before that moment, and now it felt like a key that fit a lock. She pushed the sticky note into her pocket, grabbed her quiz, and slid out of the nook so fast she banged her knee on the coffee table. The pain was temporary. Ms. Petrov's classroom was four blocks away, and school let out in twenty minutes.

"Where are you going?" Jada called.

"To find out if I'm right," Addison shouted, already pulling on her shoes at the door.

Charles stomped into the backyard carrying his water balloon launcher, which was really just a sling made of surgical tubing lashed between two fence posts. His problem was simple: for the science fair he had to claim how far the launcher could shoot, and yesterday's single test had gone forty-two feet, which felt like a lucky fluke. Today he wanted to know the truth.

Jersey was already sitting on the picnic table with a clipboard, because Jersey liked clipboards more than he liked most people. "Ready," Jersey said. "Trial one."

Charles pulled the balloon back to the knot he had tied in the tubing, let go, and watched the balloon sail over the compost bin and splat against the far fence. Jersey paced it out and marked the distance. Trial two went barely half as far. Trial three flew sideways and exploded on the bird bath.

"That's weird," Charles said, pulling the tubing taut and checking the knot. "I did the same thing every time. Same balloon weight, same stretch."

"Maybe the wind," Jersey said, squinting up. "Or maybe the balloon rolls a little before it settles." Alan leaned over the fence from next door and offered his opinion, which was that the launcher was volatile, since it never did the same thing twice.

Charles thought about that while he reloaded. A single launch couldn't be trusted, because any one throw could be thrown off by something tiny, a gust, a wobble in the tubing, his own fingers slipping. But if he repeated the experiment and averaged all the results together, the weird ones would cancel out and he would get a number he could actually defend at the fair. He could even replicate the whole test tomorrow to check it.

"Let's run it ten times," he said. "Then we average."

They spent the next hour launching, pacing, and recording. One balloon cleared the fence entirely and earned a whoop from Alan, who climbed down from his fence to help refill the bucket. Two landed short and sad. When they finally added the distances and divided, the average came out to thirty-one feet, which was less than his lucky forty-two but steady.

Mr. Rajapakse, watering his tomatoes on the other side of the hedge, called over, "You boys have been at that all afternoon. What did you learn?"

"That one launch means nothing," Charles said, holding up the clipboard, "but ten launches tell the truth."

He turned back to the fence posts, loaded another balloon, and pulled the tubing back to the knot. "Trial eleven," he announced. "Just to be sure."

Gabriel sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with a chrome napkin dispenser on one side and his essay packet on the other. The assignment was due Monday, and Ms. Delgado had been firm about it: no drafting until every student had a thesis statement and three points written out. Gabriel had a thesis. He had three points. The trouble was that something about them felt off, like a picture hung slightly crooked, and he couldn't see which way to straighten it.

"You look like you're solving a mystery," his grandfather said, setting down two glasses of lemonade. He had been a printer for forty years and could spot a crooked line from across a room.

"I sort of am." Gabriel slid the paper across the table. "My thesis is that the school should let kids keep phones in their lockers instead of banning them completely. Point one is that phones help kids contact parents after school. Point two is that phones are useful in emergencies. Point three is that a kid might need to reach his mom or dad in a hurry."

His grandfather read it twice, tapping the table with one finger. "Huh," he said. That was all, which Gabriel had learned was often a lot.

He called Cadence, because Cadence could argue with a fence post and win. She answered on the second ring, and Gabriel read his outline out loud while she drew something on her end, the sound of her pencil scratching through the speaker.

"Stop," she said. "Go back to two and three." He read them again. "Those are the same reason wearing different clothes. If two points say the same thing in different words, the argument really has only two. You've got an emergency point twice."

Gabriel stared at his paper. She was right, and it was strange how the sameness had been invisible until she said it, like a pattern hidden in a random-seeming wallpaper that suddenly resolves into flowers once you see it. He crossed out point three and sat there with the empty space. What was a third reason that didn't correspond to the first two?

He wandered into the living room, where his grandfather's old filing cabinet held the manual for everything in the house, including the toaster and the furnace, each one with its warranty stapled to the front page. Gabriel leafed through them without really meaning to, and then he stopped. The manuals listed reasons in neat numbered sections, and each numbered section was a genuinely different thing: safety, upkeep, parts.

"Grandpa," he called, "how do you decide what goes in a new section?"

"Anything that's its own reason gets its own number," his grandfather called back. "If it's just the last section said again, it doesn't get one."

Gabriel went back to the kitchen table. He wrote a new point three: kids would be more likely to follow a fair rule than a total ban, so lockers would cause fewer confiscations. Then he read all three points in order, listening for that crooked-picture feeling. It was gone. He circled the outline twice, packed it in his backpack, and carried his lemonade out to the porch, where the evening was just starting to cool.

"Cadence," he said, texting her one-handed, "if my next argument only has two real points, I'm making you find it before I do."

Jordan had been waiting all week for the microscope lab, and now he was stuck with a gray smear where onion cells were supposed to be. He twisted the focus knob back and forth, but nothing sharpened. Across the table, Lily-Anne was already sketching little brick-shaped cells into her lab sheet.

"What power are you on?" she asked, leaning over.

"Forty times. The big one." Jordan sat back and exhaled slowly through his nose. "I cranked it to the strongest lens so I could see everything at once. All I get is blur."

Lily-Anne tapped his objective turret, the little rotating wheel that held the three lenses. "Try the smallest one first," she said. "That's how Darwin did it. Find the cells down there, get them sharp, and then switch up."

Jordan turned the turret until the shortest lens clicked into place. He bent over the eyepiece, and there they were: rows of cells like a honeycomb, pale and tidy. He worked the coarse knob in tiny increments until the edges crisped up, then flipped to the next lens. The cells jumped closer, already almost in focus.

"Mr. Rahman," Jordan called, raising his hand. The teacher wandered over, and Jordan pointed at his labeled diagram. "The dark blob in the middle, that's the nucleus, right? And the outer line is the cell wall?"

"Wall on the outside, membrane just inside it," Mr. Rahman said. "Draw the membrane as a second line, thin one. Check the board if you're unsure of the order."

Jordan drew the second line carefully, then hesitated. He glanced at Darwin's side of the table, where Darwin was squinting into his scope with the same defeated look Jordan had worn five minutes ago.

"Start with the lowest-power objective," Jordan told him quietly. "Find them there first, then go up." Darwin rotated the turret, and a second later his shoulders dropped in relief.

"One factor I didn't count on," Jordan said, filling in the last label, "was that the strongest lens would be the hardest one to find anything with."

Lily-Anne slid the box of prepared slides toward him. "There's a rebellious one in there, a cheek cell slide somebody made crooked. Want to try it before the bell?"

Jordan clicked the slide onto the stage and started, as always now, at low power.

Hailey spread six paper airplanes across the workbench in her family's garage, fanning them like cards. The light from the single bulb caught the fold lines, and the smell of motor oil drifted over from her dad's half of the bench. Her project was due in nine days, and she still didn't have clean results.

She had tested every plane that afternoon, throwing each one three times from the chalk mark on the driveway and pacing off the distance. Plane A had gone eleven steps, then seven, then fourteen. Plane D had barely cleared the recycling bin. The numbers were a mess, and the mess was starting to irritate her. She jabbed her pencil at the notebook. "This is supposed to be about wing shape," she muttered. "Wing shape."

A text buzzed on the phone beside the tape. It was from her classmate Haley: "Bad news. Erik says your project is wrong on the board. He says distance is your independent variable, because it's the important one. He was really vigorous about it. Kind of loud. Also, did you know the word for when a species dies out forever is extinction? Random quiz fact from my brother. See you Monday."

Hailey stared at the message, then at her data table. She read her own question aloud, written in marker at the top of the display board: "How does wing shape affect how far a paper airplane flies?" Erik had it backward, she was almost sure. The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect. She changed the wing shape on purpose. She measured the distance.

But then she looked at the planes again, and the almost-sure feeling wobbled. Plane A had narrow wings and thin paper. Plane B had wide wings and thick paper. Plane C had swept wings, thick paper, and a paperclip on the nose. Her hands had stopped halfway through folding, and she set the planes down slowly. She hadn't changed only one thing. She had changed wing shape and paper weight and nose weight all at once, which was exactly why the numbers jumped around. The distance wasn't responding to the wing shape alone; it was responding to everything mixed together.

She spent that evening and half of Saturday refolding. One stack of identical paper, one paperclip on every nose, six planes exactly alike except for the wings. Then she threw them again from the chalk mark, thirty throws in all, while the neighbor's cat watched from the fence with polite interest.

On Monday she found Erik by the lockers. "You said distance is my independent variable," she said. "It's the other way around. The independent variable is the one thing I change on purpose, the wing shape. Distance is the dependent variable. It's what I measure to see the effect."

Erik frowned at her new chart, all six columns lined up in a neat upward slope, wide wings to narrow. He read it twice. "Huh," he said. "That makes more sense than my way." He handed the chart back and tapped the farthest column. "So what flew longest?"

Hailey grinned. "You'll have to come to the fair and find out."

Stella sat at the kitchen table on day four of the flu, wrapped in a blanket, staring at the medicine cabinet through the doorway. Her head ached, her fever had finally dropped, but her whole body felt like it had been squeezed through a rolling pin. She wanted something for the ache, and she wanted it before her mom got home.

She padded to the cabinet on cold feet and opened it. Cough syrup, a thermometer, a box of bandages, and there, a bright orange bottle of aspirin. She reached for it, then paused. Taped inside the cabinet door was a folded note in her mother's handwriting. Stella pulled it free and read it.

"Do not give this to Stella when she has the flu. Ask Mr. Bui if you're not sure why." The note was old, from two years ago, when the neighbor had helped out during a bad flu season. Stella frowned. Aspirin was just pain medicine, wasn't it? Why would it matter whether you had the flu or a headache? She felt a flicker of resentment at being told what to do through a sticky note instead of an actual conversation, and an almost equal urge to take two pills anyway. She was twelve, not a baby. But the note was specific, and her mother was never specific without a reason.

She put the bottle back and knocked on the wall beside the phone. Mr. Bui answered on the second ring, the way he always did, as if he had been waiting by the phone for someone to call about medicine labels or tomato plants or the weather. "Mr. Bui, it's Stella. Can you come over for a minute? I have a question about aspirin."

He arrived in his garden clogs ten minutes later, carrying a small paper bag of oranges that always seemed to accompany him on his visits. Stella showed him the note and the bottle. "I'm not going to take it without asking," she said, "but I want to understand why. Is it because kids are smaller? Like a dose thing?"

"Not a dose thing," Mr. Bui said. He set the oranges on the counter and turned the bottle to read the back, though Stella suspected he already knew what it said. "Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox. It's linked to something called Reye's syndrome." He handed the bottle back. "Rare, but serious. Liver and brain."

"Reye's syndrome," Stella repeated slowly, turning the word over. Rare, but serious, and it involved the liver and brain. So the problem wasn't how much you took, it was when. The same pill that was fine for a headache on a healthy day was off-limits on a flu day. She thought of other medicines in the cabinet. Did they have the same rule? She checked the cough syrup label, then the small box of children's pain reliever in the drawer. No aspirin listed. That, she decided, was probably the point.

Mr. Bui pointed at the kettle. "While you're being a scientist, make tea. For me, and for you." Stella filled the kettle and set it on the burner. On the counter lay her phone, and she picked it up and typed a message to Tatiana, who was home with the same flu: "Did you know we can't have aspirin when we have the flu? Something called Reye's syndrome. Liver and brain. Check your cabinet." The reply came back in under a minute: "We only have the orange pills too. Dhruv is bringing soup tomorrow, I'll warn him."

The kettle began to whistle. Stella poured two cups and carried them to the table, and Mr. Bui peeled one of his oranges in a single long spiral and set half of it on a saucer beside her cup. The steam rose between them, and the spiral of peel curled on the counter like a small bright rope.

The bell over the bookshop door jingled, and Thomas hurried past the shelves of mystery novels toward the back table where the Saturday book club met. Mr. Quinn, who owned the shop, was already setting out chairs, and the clock above the register read 2:41. The discussion started at three, and Thomas had not finished his homework.

"You look like a boy being chased," said Mr. Quinn.

"I have to explain the story to everyone, and I don't get it. There's this red door, and Kaydence says it means danger, and Declan says that's made up, and I have to decide who's right. By three o'clock." Thomas dropped his copy of the story on the table, a thin stapled packet with a dog-eared corner. He had read it twice on the bus and still felt like he was groping around in a dark room.

Mr. Quinn straightened a chair. "Read me the part about the door."

Thomas found the page. The first mention came early, when the main character noticed the red door at the end of the hall and thought it looked out of place, like a warning light in a house that had gone quiet. Then it appeared again when the character's little brother was told never to open it. Then, near the end, on the night of the storm, the door stood slightly open, and cold air propelled the curtains across the floor like reaching hands.

"There," Thomas said, tapping the page. "It's not just one time. The author keeps bringing it up, and every time, something feels wrong."

Declan arrived with Kaydence right behind him, both of them carrying paper cups from the café next door. Kaydence sat down and slid the story toward herself. "I told you, the red door means danger."

"You said it, but you didn't prove it," Declan said. His skepticism was quiet but fixed, the way he held his cup without drinking. "I could say the door means Christmas and it would be just as true."

Thomas raised his hand, then felt silly and put it down. "Kaydence, why danger? Not because you feel it. Because of the words."

She frowned and flipped back to the first page. She read aloud slowly: "Like a warning light in a house that had gone quiet." Then she found the brother, then the storm, then the reaching hands. "It says warning. It keeps showing up when something bad is about to happen. That's three separate places."

"So the door isn't just a door," Thomas said, working it out as he spoke. "It's a symbol, an object that stands for an idea beyond itself. And you can't just announce that. You have to show the details from the story, or it doesn't count."

Declan turned his cup around once, then nodded. "Three details is significant. I'll take it."
