She kept her tally going anyway. Arguments per practice: three, then two, then one.

Here was the twist she did not expect. When the storming faded, the passing got worse, not better, for a whole session. Everyone was so busy being polite that nobody called for the puck. Chloe skated to the bench, flustered, and found Mr. Quinn, the rink manager, eating soup in his usual spot.

"Your ice is weird today," she said, which was not what she meant at all.

"Ice is fine," Mr. Quinn said. "Zamboni and I had a good talk this morning."

"It's us. We fixed the fighting and now we're boring."

Mr. Quinn slurped his soup thoughtfully. "Hmm."

She skated back out and tried an experiment. At the next scrimmage, she deliberately disagreed with Dhruv about a play, loudly, in front of everyone. He argued back. Nizar jumped in. For ten seconds it felt like the old disaster, and then Dhruv grinned and said, "Fine, your way, but if it fails you owe me a slushie."

The play worked. Chloe got the assist, and everyone screamed like they'd won a championship instead of a Tuesday scrimmage.

Afterward, in the lobby, she bought Dhruv a slushie anyway, because his passing had been beautiful. He looked at the cup, then at her. "This makes my record against you look impoverished. You've bought me three this season."

"Enjoy it," Chloe said. "We're performing now."

Nizar grabbed his helmet and pointed at the door. "Practice again Thursday. Bring the marker, in case we need a refill."

Aubrey raced up the steps of the community centre two at a time, trumpet case banging against her leg. The winter concert was only three weeks away, and Mr. Taylor had promised the band a real piece this year, one with dynamics and tempo changes, whatever those were. Inside the gym, Liya was already setting up her flute and Quentin was snapping his drumsticks together like castanets.

"Look at the music," Liya said, sliding a folder across the stand. "There are little letters everywhere. P, f, more p's, more f's." Aubrey squinted at the ending of the piece. Two small f's sat under the final bars, and two small p's floated above the last chord. She had no idea what any of it meant, but she decided on one objective for the afternoon: figure out those letters before rehearsal ended.

They played the piece through, and the ending came out like a thunderclap, every instrument blasting at full volume. Mr. Taylor stopped them and tapped his baton on the stand. "That last chord is marked pp," he said, and waited, arms folded, as if he expected them to solve something.

Aubrey stared at the page. The band had played ff, loud as anything, because the ending felt like it should be huge. But the marking said pp, and they had ignored it. She leaned toward Liya. "I think pianissimo, written pp, means very soft," she whispered, "and fortissimo, written ff, means very loud." Liya's eyes went wide. "So we just played the opposite of the whole ending." Quentin, who had been listening from behind his snare drum, held up his sticks. "You want me to whisper with these?"

To isolate the problem, Aubrey suggested they play only the last eight bars, as quietly as they could manage. The first try collapsed into giggles when Liya's flute squeaked, but the second try worked, a soft, shimmering chord that hung in the gym like frost on a window. Mr. Taylor smiled and made them do it twice more. "Now you sound like a band that reads music," he said, "not a band that attacks it."

After rehearsal, the three of them walked out into the cold, already planning. Liya said her aunt ran a bake sale every December and donated the income to the centre, so maybe the concert could raise money for new stands too. Aubrey hugged her trumpet case and grinned. "Soft ending, loud applause," she said. "That's the plan."

Sydney carried the microscope case down to the pond pavilion, where Ms. Navarro had set up folding tables for the outdoor lab. The school's old scopes were supposed to be obsolete, replaced by digital ones with screens, but Ms. Navarro hauled three of the old brass-and-black ones out every spring. "Nothing beats looking with your own eye," she said, which was exactly why Sydney had shown up. Next week was the audition for the regional science team, and everyone trying out had to prepare a slide and label it correctly. She wanted the practice.

Artin was already there, slicing paper-thin layers of onion with a razor and tweezing them onto glass. Remy sat across from him, squinting into her eyepiece and frowning. "Mine looks like a brick wall," Remy said. "I think I broke something. Cells aren't supposed to look like a wall, right?"

Sydney peeled her own sliver of onion skin, dropped on the iodine stain, and pressed the coverslip down the way the manual said, careful not to violate a single step. If the audition judges docked points for sloppy slides, she would dock them on herself first. She clicked through the objective lenses, starting low, hunting for focus. The pond glittered behind them while she turned the fine adjustment, one tiny click at a time.

Then the image sharpened, and she went still. Rows of rectangles, snug against each other, straight-edged and orderly, exactly like a wall. Her stomach dropped for a second. Had she torn the skin? Folded it into stripes? She lifted her head, checked the slide on the stage, and found it lying flat and perfect. So the pattern was in the onion itself, not in any mistake she had made. That was the strange, wonderful part. She bent down again. Every rectangle held a darker dot near its middle, like a small pale moon floating in each brick.

"Remy," Sydney said, "come look at mine. I think your wall isn't a wall. Look at the edges of each brick. That thick outer border, the dark frame around every single one, that's the cell wall. Each rectangle is one whole cell. That's why they look like rows of bricks."

Remy leaned in, then laughed out loud. "So I didn't break anything. My wall is just a bunch of cells standing in line." She grabbed her pencil and started labeling: cell wall along the thick outer border, cell membrane just inside it, nucleus on the dot. Sydney copied the three labels onto her own diagram, double-checking each one against the image, then checked Remy's slide too and found the same brickyard of cells under it.

Ms. Navarro walked past, peered briefly into Sydney's eyepiece, and gave her a thumbs-up without a word. Sydney sat back and looked at the pond, at the water that looked like plain water, and wondered what a drop of it would show under the lens tomorrow. She pulled a clean slide from the box and set it on the table, ready.

Max lay on the living room couch with his plastered arm propped on a pillow and a notebook balanced on his chest. Three weeks into the cast, the sharp pain had faded into a deep, itchy ache, and that change bothered him. He had a theory: if the bone was actually knitting itself back together under all that plaster, the ache should follow a pattern, not just drift around randomly. So every evening he recorded where it hurt and how much, on a scale of one to ten, because a single night of notes told you nothing but the cumulative record might.

Noemi arrived after school with her phone and a folding tripod, because she had her own plan. "I'm making a video called Four Weeks in a Cast," she announced, arranging the tripod at the foot of the couch. "Nobody at school has ever narrated their own broken arm before. You talk, I film, and by the end we show everyone what it's really like." She wanted it for the school media club contest, and she had already story-boarded six scenes on graph paper.

Max held up the notebook. "Then start here. I've got data." He narrated the first three weeks for her camera, tracing the ache's path with his good hand. "Week one, sharp jabs right where I landed on the stairs. Week two, the jabs moved outward, like a ring. Week three, it's a dull throb across the whole break." He paused, studying the page. "Something in there is doing something. I just can't see it."

On Thursday he tested his idea the wrong way. Reaching for the remote with his bad arm, he knocked his elbow hard on the end table, and the throb flared back to a sharp jab that lasted two days. His log broke its pattern. He decided the consequence was obvious: he had ruined the healing, reset everything to week one, and he sulked about it until Elsa came over on Saturday with a metallic marker to collect cast signatures.

"You don't know that," Elsa said, printing her name in careful block letters above the spot where the stairs had gotten him. "You guessed a pattern from three data points. In science, that's like, nothing." She wanted her signature to be the first one everyone noticed, so she added a small lightning bolt under the E.

At the follow-up visit on Monday, Max spread his notebook on the exam table and told the doctor everything, including the knock. The doctor clipped the new X-ray to the light box and pointed with a pen. There, over the break, sat a fuzzy gray lump. "See that cloud there?" the doctor said. "That's your callus." Max leaned close. The doctor tapped the lump on the film and added, "A mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends. It means the bone is healing."

Max studied the fuzzy shape, then checked his notebook. The ring of ache, the outward spread, the dull throb, even the flare after the knock. It had all been the callus building itself, invisible the whole time. "It was there the entire time," he said. "My knock didn't reset anything." Outside in the waiting room, Noemi was already rolling, and Max held the X-ray copy up to the light. "Scene seven," he said. "The lump has a name."

Camille leaned over the aquarium in Ms. Mwangi's room, tightening the little valve on the air pump so the bubbles slowed to a lazy trickle. Behind her, Darwin dropped into a chair with a magazine and slid it across the table.

"Look at these," he said. A basketball player named Rashad Cole grinned up from the page, lacing a pair of silver-and-orange sneakers. "The GritLine 3. Everybody's getting them. Emerson already has a pair, and half the team says they're the best shoe ever made. Elite. Legendary. That's what the ad says."

"They're a hundred and sixty dollars," Camille said. "That's your whole birthday money plus four weeks of dog-walking."

"I know, but Rashad Cole wears them." Darwin tapped the photo. "If they're good enough for him, they're good enough for me. He wouldn't wear junk."

Camille looked at the tiny print under the picture. She had to tilt the magazine toward the window to read it. "Paid partnership," she said slowly. "Darwin. It says he got paid."

"So? He still wears them."

"Does he?" Camille turned the page and found a smaller ad for a different brand of sneakers, with a different star, also grinning, also lacing them up. Then a third. Three stars, three brands, three claims of legendary greatness. She felt something click into place, like the valve finally seated. "If Rashad thinks one shoe is the best, why does the other guy think a totally different shoe is the best? They can't all be right."

"Maybe they're all good," Darwin said, but he frowned.

Camille flipped back to the tiny print. Paid partnership, again. "It's called a testimonial," she said. "A famous person saying something's great, even if they don't actually know anything about it, and even if they got paid to say it. We did ads in Ms. Mwangi's class last month. Remember the poster with the word 'crucial' on it in huge letters?"

Darwin slumped. "So he might not even like them."

"He might. Or he might just like the money." Camille watched the bubbles rise in the tank, slow and even now, the water calm. "Here's what we could do. Don't buy them yet. Tomorrow, look at everybody's actual shoes at practice. Ask Emerson if his feet hurt. Ask the guys on other teams. Then decide with your own eyes."

Darwin was quiet for a moment. "Emerson's been saying they're durable, but he also said everybody has to get them or you're basically nobody. That part made me feel kind of bad."

"That's them trying to humiliate you into buying," Camille said. "Nobody's nobody because of shoes." She slid the magazine back. "Check feet tomorrow. Report to me."

Darwin grinned and stood. "Field research," he said, and saluted her on his way out the door.

Ariana stood at the top of the basement stairs with a hamper on her hip, reading the note her mother had taped to the door before her shift upstairs at the bank. "Dark load first. Cold water. Check every pocket. Fold while warm. I'll prioritize the laundry this weekend if it's too much, but you wanted to learn, so learn." Below her, in the little staff room behind the vault, the bank kept an old but durable washer and dryer for the night cleaners, and Mr. Pelletier had said she could use them as long as she was careful.

She dumped the hamper on the folding table and sorted the way her mother had shown her: darks in one pile, whites in another, anything red and suspicious on its own. Inara and Layla had come along, mostly for the vending machine, but Inara was actually helping. Layla sat on the dryer eating cheese crackers and offering commentary.

"You have to check pockets," Inara said, holding up a pair of jeans. "My dad ruined a whole load once."

"Ruined how?" Ariana asked, but she was already halfway through the pile, and she was sure her pockets were empty. She'd emptied them yesterday. Hadn't she? She thought about the grey hoodie, worn all week, the one she'd stuffed with napkins at lunch and tissues during the sneezing fit in math class. She couldn't remember taking them out. That was the thing about pockets, she thought; you couldn't see inside them, so you had to reason from what you'd done, not from what you could see. She checked the hoodie. Two tissues, crumpled soft as clouds.

Layla slid off the dryer. "Okay, that's actually weirdly satisfying."

"Put them in," Ariana said. "And next time I check everything, even the ones I'm sure about."

While the washer filled, Mr. Pelletier came down for his coffee mug and paused at the table. "When my daughter was your age she skipped the pockets once," he said. "One paper tissue, whole load of dark clothes came out speckled white. Every single item." He lifted his mug toward the washer. "Shreds everywhere. That's why we check."

Ariana peeled the two tissues apart and dropped them in the trash, then leaned against the washer and felt it start to tumble. She thought about all the times she'd tossed clothes in at home without looking, and how many speckled loads she might have caused and never known about, and whether her mother had quietly picked white shreds off everyone's shirts and never said a word.

The cycle beeped its long final beep, and Ariana pulled the dark load out warm, laid it flat on the table, and folded each piece while Inara matched the socks. Layla held up a black shirt, turned it toward the light, and said, "Not one white speck on it."

"Two tissues," Ariana said. "That's how close it was."

John had signed up for the community kitchen class for one reason: Mr. Buchanan had promised that everyone would leave knowing how to make pasta sauce from scratch. So far John had learned two things. First, that onions could make a thirteen-year-old boy cry like a toddler at a birthday party, and second, that there was a way to hold your fingers so you kept all ten of them.

"Curl your fingertips under, like a claw," said London, who had taken the class twice before and acted like a chef with forty years of experience. "Knuckles guide the knife. Fingers stay out of the blade's way."

John curled his fingers and chopped. The onion halves came out uneven, half cubes and half onion confetti, but all ten fingertips survived. Across the table, Marshall was wiping his eyes with his sleeve and pretending he wasn't. "It's allergies," Marshall said, and John and London both said "Sure it is" at the same time.

By five o'clock the sauce was bubbling on the stove, and Mr. Buchanan set out plates for the families arriving at six. John stirred, tasted, and frowned. The sauce was thin. It slid off his spoon like red water and pooled at the bottom of the bowl. London leaned over and looked too. "Mine's runny as well," she said. "Mr. Buchanan's sauce last week was thick enough to hold a spoon upright. What did we do differently?"

John looked around the kitchen, thinking. Last week's pot had been on the back burner. Theirs was on the front. He walked over to Mr. Buchanan's old pot, still sitting on the back burner, and noticed the lid hanging on its hook beside it, dry and clean. Then he looked at their own pot. The lid was on. It had been on the whole time, since the very first bubble.

He lifted the lid off their pot and stood there a second, watching the steam curl up toward the vent. "The lid," he said. "It's been trapping everything in there. With the lid off, the water gets out as steam, and the sauce gets thicker the longer it cooks." London tilted her head, considering, then found a wooden spoon and propped the lid on the counter, well out of temptation's reach.

They could not postpone dinner, so the six families would just have to wait twenty extra minutes, which Marshall announced to the room like a peasant heralding the king: "The sauce requires patience! Snacks will be served!" Mr. Buchanan, who was spontaneous about very little, calmly sliced bread. By ten past six the sauce clung to the spoon, glossy and slow, and Mr. Buchanan held the spoon upside down over the pot to show the whole room. Nothing fell. Marshall stood on his chair and applauded, and John, grinning, handed him the first plate.

Rebecca stood at the camp stove with three pots and a problem. The rice would take twenty minutes, the curry thirty, and the flatbread only five, and somehow all of it had to land on the picnic table at six o'clock sharp, because the whole cabin group would come tramping back from the lake starving and loud. Ms. Wu had handed her a dented pot, a bag of rice, and one sentence: "Tonight you cook, I watch." Then she had sat down on a log with her thermos like it was the best show in the county.

Reem was already at her elbow, measuring rice into a cup with the focus of a scientist. "Two cups," she said. "My mom does it this way, you don't just guess." She leveled the cup with her finger and poured it into the pot. Sebastien crouched by the cooler chopping onions for the curry, sniffling dramatically. "I'm crying," he announced, "but like, in a brave way. This is a robust onion. Possibly two onions in trench coats."

The rice was the puzzle. Rebecca had only ever watched her dad boil pasta in a huge storm of water, then dump it all into a colander in the sink with steam billowing up like a dragon. So when the water in her pot started to bubble, she picked up the pot and swung it toward the sink. "Whoa, whoa," Reem said, grabbing the handle with both hands. "You don't drain it. It's the absorption method. All the water gets soaked up. There's nothing left to pour off." Rebecca frowned at the pot. "All of it? Where does it go?" "Into the rice," Reem said. "That's the whole point."

Rebecca lowered the pot back onto the burner and peered through the steam at the grains swimming around. How could each little grain drink its share, exactly, like tiny camels? She put the lid on and set a timer, and while she waited she worked backward on the rest of the meal, which felt like a math problem she actually wanted to solve. The curry needed thirty minutes, so it went on first. The rice needed twenty, so it went on ten minutes later. The flatbread dough she could mix now and cook last, five minutes in the hot pan. She wrote the schedule in the dirt with a stick, then a mosquito landed on the word "flatbread" and she had to rewrite it.

The middle part was the hard part, because nothing looked like it was happening. The curry burbled and smelled like cumin and coconut, but the rice just sat there under its lid, quiet as a secret. Rebecca lifted the corner of the lid exactly once and a puff of steam rolled up her glasses. "We don't peek," Reem said. "It's like a closed-envelope system." Sebastien, from across the table: "It's like the rice has a constitution and the lid is the law." Rebecca snorted. Fine. No peeling back the lid. But she pressed her ear close and heard the faintest hiss and crackle underneath, like tiny rain on a tiny roof, and she decided that was her evidence. Something was happening in there.

At minute nineteen she started the flatbread, slapping the dough between her palms the way Ms. Wu had shown her until it flopped like a lazy frisbee. The first one hit the pan and blistered up in fat bubbles that she couldn't help but cherish, each one a small triumph of heat and dough. When the timer dinged, she lifted the rice lid and stared. No water. Not a puddle, not a drop. The grains stood there plump and steaming, having somehow swallowed every last bit of it, and she felt like she'd caught a magician pulling off the trick.

The three dishes made it to the table at 6:02, which Sebastien declared "close enough for a first attempt, and honestly the flatbread alone could fix a bad day." The campers descended, and Rebecca watched her pot of rice empty out fast, which was its own kind of proof. Ms. Wu held up a forkful and said, "Same meal tomorrow?" Rebecca was already thinking about whether the timing would change if she doubled the rice, and she said, "Only if I get to figure out the doubling part."

Nevaeh had been dreading third period all morning, because third period was when the new girl arrived. The new girl was from France, she had lived in three different cities before her family moved, and Nevaeh had been assigned to show her around. Nevaeh was terrible at meeting people. She usually said "hi" too quietly and then stared at the floor.

The new girl walked into Mr. Rowe's room before the bell, spotted Nevaeh by the science counter, and crossed the room fast. Then, without a word, she leaned in and pressed her cheek against Nevaeh's, once, twice, making a small kiss sound in the air each time.

"Uh," said Nevaeh. Her face went hot. Chanelle, watching from the window seat, mouthed the word weird.

"It's how we say hello," the new girl said. "We call it la bise."

At lunch, things got stranger. Nevaeh brought the new girl to the table where Hayden and Chanelle were already sitting, and the new girl gave each of them the same two kisses. But when Nevaeh picked up her slice of pizza with her hands, the new girl stared, then quietly demonstrated cutting hers with a knife and fork, the way Nevaeh's grandmother did with fried chicken. Fine. Different houses, different rules; Nevaeh's own family thought elbows on the table were a crime. She could live with that.

The mystery came after school. A young man was waiting at the front steps, and the new girl ran to him and hugged him, and then they kissed cheeks three times. Nevaeh counted. She stood behind the mailbox by the flagpole and counted again, in case she'd imagined one. Three.

"So?" Chanelle said, catching up. "Maybe she likes him more than us."

"That's not it." Nevaeh thought about motive the way Mr. Rowe had taught them in the detective story unit. If liking people was the reason, she'd give her cousin three every day. But she'd given two to everyone at lunch, teachers included, without hesitating, like she wasn't deciding anything at all. Which meant the number wasn't about feelings. It was about something else, some rule Nevaeh couldn't see. She had one idea, and it felt almost rebellious to march over and ask a stranger about it, but she did it anyway.

"He's my cousin," the new girl said. "From the south. He'd be lost in Lyon. We do three there, my cousins do, and here at home we always did two." She smiled like the whole thing was the most ordinary fact in the world.

Her cousin offered his hand and a two-cheek hello, so Nevaeh leaned in and carefully gave him back three.

"Two dollars a basket," said the woman behind the tomato stand, and Jack counted out quarters while Abdullah held the bag and groaned about being used as furniture.

"My mom sent me to find someone," Abdullah said. "A teenager selling a bond. Don't ask why, she's doing some errand thing." He pointed across the market, past the honey jars and a man arguing with a very calm goat, to a folding table with a hand-lettered sign: BOND FOR SALE, PAYING 2 PERCENT, ASKING FULL PRICE.

The teenager at the table, whose name was not on the sign and stayed off it, looked miserable. "Nobody will pay full price," he said. "It's worth full price. It says so on the paper."

Jack picked up the bond and turned it over, as if the back might contain better news. He was supposed to be learning this stuff for a class project with Constance, who was already marching toward them carrying a sack of peaches like a trophy.

"Here's my reasoning," Jack announced. "Constance, you're the bank today."

"I'm the peach vendor."

"You're whatever I need you to be." He held up the bond. "This pays 2 percent. Now pretend the bank, which is Ms. Le's stall over there, is selling brand-new bonds at 3 percent."

Constance squinted at him, then at Ms. Le, who was weighing squash and minding her own business. "Fine. I'm a bank that sells peaches and bonds."

"If you can buy a new bond that pays more interest," Jack said, "why would you pay full price for this old one?"

The teenager slumped. "Because it's already printed?"

Abdullah patted his shoulder with mock solemnity. "The paper does not symbolize the money, my friend. My grandmother taught me that after I tried to pay for ice cream with a drawing of ice cream."

Jack tried a quick test. He walked to Ms. Le's stall and asked, loudly enough to be overheard, "If interest rates go up, what happens to the prices of old bonds?"

"Old bonds get cheaper," Ms. Le said without looking up from her scale. "Everyone wants the new ones that pay more. Eggs are three fifty."

The teenager heard it. He looked at his sign, took out a marker, and crossed out FULL PRICE, writing LOW PRICE instead, with a little frowny face. Two customers wandered over within a minute.

"See?" Jack said. "Rates up, old bond prices down. It's like the inevitable fate of every tomato at closing time. Somebody's going to get a deal."

Constance handed him a peach. "You're buying this. You dragged me into being a bank, and banks get paid." Jack dug into his pocket and came up with one quarter, two bottle caps, and a rubber band. Abdullah tried to pay with the rubber band, and the peach negotiation began again.

The group chat lit up at 7:04 p.m., right after dinner. Nylah had typed, "We need a crosswalk on Maple Ave before school. Sign my petition." Aedan replied with seventeen pizza emojis and the words, "We need new cafeteria pizza. Sign MY petition." Elliot lay on his bed with his tablet on his chest, watching the two arguments stack up like rival towers.

"Those aren't the same thing," Nylah wrote. "The crosswalk is a claim. You can check it. I counted twelve near-misses on Maple Ave this month. Twelve kids almost getting hit. The pizza thing is just an opinion." Aedan shot back, "It's a FACT that the pizza is bad." Elliot snorted so hard his tablet slid off his chest and bounced onto the rug. He typed, "Says who?" and Aedan answered, "Says me, a person with taste."

Elliot scrolled up through the chat. Nylah's messages had numbers, times, and a photo of the corner where the crossing guard's post stood empty every Tuesday. Aedan's messages had exclamation points and one blurry picture of a rectangle that might have been pizza. Elliot tried an experiment. He typed, "Aedan, what would change your mind about the pizza?" Aedan wrote, "Nothing. It's gross." Then Elliot typed, "Nylah, what would change your mind?" and she answered in seconds: "If the near-misses stopped. Then we wouldn't need the crosswalk."

That was the difference, Elliot realized, drumming his fingers on the rug. Nylah's argument was still her opinion, in a way, because a crosswalk was what she thought should happen. But twelve near-misses made it a stronger opinion than Aedan's, which came with no reasons at all, just a flat "it's gross." Elliot typed slowly, spelling it out: "Aedan, an opinion with evidence is still an opinion. But it's more convincing than one with no reasons. Give me one reason. One." The chat went quiet. Then Aedan sent a photo of the cafeteria invoice showing the pizza cost nine dollars a slice and was labeled "peasant bread with cheese product." Below it: "That's my reason."

The next morning Mr. Choi stopped them at the classroom door, holding a printed copy of the petition. "Twelve near-misses," he said, tapping the page. "I was one of them. A driver nearly clipped my bike there last week." He smiled, and the smile turned out to be infectious; even Aedan grinned and added his name under Nylah's thirty-one signatures. At lunch, Aedan slid his untouched pizza slice onto Elliot's tray and said, "Nine dollars. Tell me that's an opinion."

Riley had one job before dinner: find a photo for the class project on migratory birds. He typed his own name into the search box first, mostly because Aleksandar had bet him a fruit roll-up that nothing would come up.

Riley lost the bet in four seconds. Third result down, there it was: a comment on a birdwatching forum, posted when he was eight, signed with his full name. He had forgotten writing it, but there it was, public as a billboard. "Why is it still here?" he asked the empty kitchen. "I wrote that ages ago."

He clicked around the forum and found a page about how the site worked. A short paragraph mentioned that search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages. So something posted publicly could turn up in search results, even years later. Riley leaned back. Little robot readers, he thought, copying everything they could reach. He wondered how many of them had consumed his comment, carried it off, and filed it somewhere.

Then he noticed the twist. The comment showed his username, but the search result also offered a cached copy of the whole thread, and in that thread, someone had replied with a photo of a park. Riley squinted. He recognized the fence, the crooked bench. It was the park two streets from his house, and the person who posted it had written the date and the time they were there. A stranger, sharing exactly where and when they stood, without seeming to notice.

Riley tested a quick idea. He searched the park's name plus the word "sighting." More posts came up, from different strangers, and a surprising percentage of them mentioned locations: a street corner, a school field, someone's backyard with the house number visible in the photo frame. Each post was harmless on its own. Stacked together, they were a map nobody had meant to draw.

He screenshotted everything for himself, then went to find his dad. "Can you delete my old comment?" he asked. "And can we check what's public about us?"

His dad pulled up a chair. "Let's look."

At school the next morning, Riley found Aleksandar at the lockers. "You owe me a fruit roll-up," Aleksandar said.

"You can keep it," Riley said. "But search your own name tonight. Then ask me about the crawlers."

Mia pressed her pencil harder against the paper, but the shading still looked like fog. Her wolf sketch for the community studio's spring show was supposed to be the best thing she'd ever made, and so far the animal looked more like a ghost. Riaan leaned over from the next easel, his own drawing of a soccer ball halfway done.

"Yours is so light," he said. "Are you using a magic eraser instead of a pencil?"

"Very funny." Mia turned her pencil over and squinted at the letters stamped near the end. 4H. She dug through the studio's shared box of pencils and pulled out another one, a 6B, its tip worn soft and round. She remembered the studio's poster had something about these letters, and Riaan had mentioned it once. "H is hardness," she said slowly, "and B is blackness."

"Blackness," Riaan repeated, grinning. "Like a heavy metal band."

Mia dragged the 6B across a corner of scrap paper, and a dark, velvety stripe appeared, like night against the 4H's thin gray whisper. If 4H was hard and pale, then 6B was soft and dark, and that meant she could build her wolf's shadowed fur with the B pencil and save the H for the pale moonlight on its back. It was a radical change to her plan, but she decided to test it on the scrap first: fur strokes in 6B, a few light hatch marks in 4H, side by side. The scrap wolf leg looked alive.

Ms. Murphy came by with a stack of fresh paper for the studio's refugee art class, which met on Thursdays and shared the same big room. She paused at Mia's easel. "That's much stronger than last week's fox," she said. "Whatever you changed, it's working."

"I picked the wrong pencil before," Mia said. "4H for everything. It wouldn't go dark no matter how hard I pushed."

Riaan held up his own pencil, squinting at it. "Mine says 2B. Is that halfway to a heavy metal band?"

Mia laughed and showed him her scrap test, then went back to the wolf. She worked in careful layers, 6B for the deep shadows behind the ears, 4H only where the moon touched the fur. Her hand began to ache, and she shook it out and kept going, because good shading took time to sustain through a whole drawing. When the studio's clock showed closing time, she stepped back. The wolf stood in real darkness now, eyes bright against the deep 6B night. Riaan leaned over, tapped the edge of the paper, and said, "Okay, that one actually looks like it could bite somebody."

Camille had been practicing the canoe rescue drill all morning, and now her heart was pounding so hard she could feel it in her ears. Her hands shook on the paddle, and her breath came quick and shallow, like she had sprinted up the hill to the dining hall. She crouched on the dock of Camp Birchwater and stared at her fingers. "Myla, do I look sick to you? I feel weird."

Myla squinted at her. "You look fine. Maybe you're just nervous. Musa got like that before the talent show last week, remember? He couldn't even hold the microphone."

That made Camille think. She hadn't felt sick at breakfast, and she hadn't felt sick during warm-ups. The shaky feeling had started the moment Mr. Owusu said her group would perform the drill in front of everyone after lunch. She turned that over while she coiled the rope. Sick didn't wait for announcements. Sick didn't care about audiences. Whatever this was, it did.

She found Musa hauling a bucket of paddles up from the beach and told him about her heart and her shaking hands. He nodded like she'd said something obvious. "That's the fight-or-flight response," he said. "When your brain senses a threat, your adrenal glands release adrenaline, and that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing quicker." He'd read it in a book his aunt gave him, and it was why he'd spent the talent show breathing slowly in the bathroom before he went on stage. It wasn't sickness. It was her body getting ready, like an engine revving.

Camille decided to test it. If quick breathing and a pounding heart meant her brain thought there was a threat, then maybe slow breathing would convince it otherwise. She sat on the dock, planted her feet, and breathed in for four counts and out for six, the way Musa described. After the third round, her heartbeat settled from a drumroll into something steadier. Her hands still trembled a little, but less.

That night, after lights out, she lay awake replaying the afternoon. The drill had gone fine, not perfect, and she wondered whether her breathing had helped or whether she would have calmed down anyway. Last summer she'd hidden in the infirmary during the whole swim test, convinced she was ill, and no one had ever told her otherwise. Maybe she'd wasted that whole day for nothing. She thought about her younger self with an uneasiness she couldn't quite sort out. There was no fixing it now, but there was tomorrow's overnight hike, and the night after that.

She set a plan in her mind, a candidate routine to try: no talking after ten, slow breathing in her sleeping bag, and her flashlight turned away so its beam wouldn't refract off the tent's mesh ceiling and keep her brain awake. In the next tent, Myla was still giggling with someone, the sound warm and infectious even through the canvas. Camille smiled in the dark, breathed out for six counts, and closed her eyes.

John's grandfather had sworn by his new ginger tea. On Sunday, after two days of what he called the worst headache of his life, he drank a cup and woke up Monday feeling fine. "That tea is a miracle," he told John at breakfast, and he meant to buy three more boxes.

At school, John found Meghan and Stefan cleaning out the crayfish tank in Ms. Hosseini's room before class. Good hygiene in a science classroom meant gloves and fresh water, and Ms. Hosseini had made it clear that anyone who skipped the gloves also skipped the crayfish. John pulled on a pair and said, "Can I ask you guys something weird? If you have your worst headache ever, and then you take something, and the next day you're fine, does that prove the thing worked?"

Stefan shrugged. "It worked for your grandpa. That's proof enough for me."

"It worked for him," Meghan said slowly, rinsing a net. "One person. That's a story, not a claim."

Ms. Hosseini, who had been writing on the board, turned around. "That's the most interesting sentence I've heard all morning. What's the difference, John?"

John stared at the tank. "A claim needs, like, testing? Lots of people, not just one?"

"Tested evidence," Ms. Hosseini agreed. "So how would you test your question? You can't see a headache, and you can't see why it went away. You have to look for a pattern."

That gave John an idea. He asked Stefan to collaborate with him at lunch, and they made a chart. For one week, they asked everyone in their grade who got headaches to rate the pain from one to ten every day, and to write down any remedy they used. They did not tell anyone what to take. By Friday they had thirty-six sheets of paper covered in numbers.

The pattern was hiding in plain sight. People mostly took remedies on their worst days, the nines and tens. And almost every time, the next day was better, whether the remedy was tea, a cold cloth, or nothing at all. Even the kids who just waited usually dropped back to a three or a four. John highlighted the rows in yellow until his marker ran dry.

"There's a name for this," Meghan said on Monday, holding up her tablet. She had looked it up after he told her the results. "Regression to the mean."

"Unusually bad days are usually followed by more ordinary ones," John read over her shoulder, "so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing." He copied it into his notebook, then wrote underneath: Grandpa's tea, maybe not a miracle. Maybe just a bad day ending.

He decided to call his grandfather anyway. "Grandpa," he said when the phone picked up, "keep drinking the tea if you like it. But I need to tell you about my experiment."

Hunter had thirty minutes to finish the spreadsheet project, and the part he dreaded most was still ahead of him: the bar chart. Ms. Zhou had assigned each student a column of fundraiser sales data, and Hunter's job was to add a total and turn the numbers into bars. Landen, two seats over, was already dragging his chart into place with the calm of someone who had done this before.

Hunter remembered last week, when he had tried to build a graph of his Pokemon card collection and ended up with a chart shaped like a staircase to nowhere. He had closed the laptop that day and told himself spreadsheets were invented to punish people. Today he was being slightly less pessimistic, mostly because Ms. Zhou had said the project counted as a test grade.

He typed his sales numbers into column B, rows two through ten. Then he clicked on cell B10, where his last number sat, and typed =SUM(B2:B10), thinking he could put the total right there at the bottom of the list, like a tidy ending. The moment he pressed Enter, a warning box popped onto the screen, announcing a problem with the formula.

"Your computer hates you," Aaden said from across the room, not unkindly.

"It doesn't hate me. It's telling me something." Hunter read the warning again. The word in the message was "circular reference." He said it out loud. "Circular reference."

Landen leaned over. "My cousin got that once. It means the formula includes its own cell. Like adding B10 into a total that lives in B10."

Hunter stared at the screen. His total formula was trying to swallow itself, like a snake eating its own tail. He tested the idea the way he tested everything, by changing one thing and watching what happened. He deleted the formula from B10, put the same =SUM(B2:B10) into B12, one row below the data, and pressed Enter. No warning. The number appeared, correct and ordinary, as if nothing had ever gone wrong.

"Diagnosed and fixed," he announced, feeling like a surgeon who had used a laser instead of a hammer. He selected his data, clicked the chart button, and watched ten honest bars rise up the screen. He dragged the chart beside the numbers and studied it. The tallest bar belonged to the sixth-grade bake sale, which surprised no one.

Ms. Zhou paused behind his desk. "Nice chart, Hunter. And nice recovery."

He saved the file twice, just in case. Then he turned the laptop so Landen could see it. "Look," he said. "Snake, officially un-eaten."

Charlie had typed the same line four times, and the heading still sat at the left edge of the screen like it was glued there.

"Ms. Mokoena said our fan pages have to be finished before the bell," said Yuvraj from the next computer. His page was about the Raptors, and his heading floated neatly in the middle. "Yours is about the Raptors too, right? Copy mine."

"No way. Mine has to be better than yours." Charlie wanted her page to be the one Ms. Mokoena picked to show at assembly, because the winner got to skip the lunchtime homework club and help run the school website instead. She looked at her CSS again. She had written text-align: centre; exactly the way her mother, who painted signs for a bakery, had taught her to spell centre on every menu and birthday banner in the house.

Yuvraj leaned over and squinted. "Weird. Yours looks the same as mine." He compared them line by line, his finger hovering over the screens. "Wait. You wrote centre. I wrote center."

"That's not a real difference," Charlie said, though a small wondering feeling opened in her chest. Could a computer care about one letter? She had learned in science that you have to calibrate your instruments before you trust your measurements, so maybe code was the same: you had to test one small thing at a time and watch what changed.

She deleted the r and the e, swapped them, and typed text-align: center; then hit refresh. The heading slid to the middle of the page like it had been waiting for permission.

"It moved!" Yuvraj grabbed his own screen. "That's so arbitrary. One letter, and the whole computer just ignores you?"

"CSS uses the American spelling," Charlie said slowly, trying the idea out loud. "So the browser just ignores centre. Only center works." She typed centre again on purpose, just to watch the heading flop back to the left, then fixed it. Cause, effect, cause, effect. It was like the experiments they did with plants, except this one answered in half a second.

Ranveer appeared behind them, holding half a granola bar. "Can I borrow someone's page as a template? I spent the whole class on my pictures and forgot the heading."

"Only if I get your crickets for lunch," Yuvraj said. "You always get the good carbohydrates and I get soggy fries."

"Deal." Ranveer sat down and copied Charlie's now-perfect lines, his own page about cricket players taking shape screen by screen.

When Ms. Mokoena walked the rows, she paused at Charlie's monitor. "Centred heading, working image, clean colours. Nicely tested, Charlie. Show the class how you debugged it."

Charlie stood up, typed centre one last time on the projector for everyone to watch the heading drift left, and said, "Now watch this."

Annabelle sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her laptop balanced on a stack of homework, typing her first real program. The assignment from Mr. Sow's coding club was to write a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime. She had the loop working, the remainder check working, and a triumphant little "is prime" message ready to go. Across town, Cayson was almost certainly doing the same thing, because he had announced at lunch that he would finish first and demo his program at Thursday's club meeting before she could.

She tested her program slowly, the way a conductor might cue one section of an orchestra at a time. She typed 7 and got "prime." She typed 9 and got "not prime," which felt right. She typed 12, then 13, then 97, and each answer came back correct. Then, just to be thorough, she typed 1, because 1 was small and easy and she expected the machine to breeze past it.

The screen said "prime."

Annabelle frowned. One couldn't be prime, could it? She tried to assess where her reasoning had gone wrong. Her loop started at 2 and checked every possible divisor up to the number itself, and since nothing divided evenly into 1, the program never found a factor, so it printed "prime." The computer had followed her instructions perfectly. The mistake was in her head, not in the loop. She stared at the word on the screen, and it started to look almost ominous, sitting there so confidently, so wrong.

She opened her math notebook and wrote out factor trees to think. 12 broke into 2 times 2 times 3. 30 broke into 2 times 3 times 5. Every number she tried had exactly one way of being written as a product of primes. Then she wrote 1 equals 1, and 1 equals 1 times 1, and 1 times 1 times 1, and the pattern wobbled. If 1 counted as prime, the uniqueness broke, because you could tack on any number of ones and get a new answer. That was it. Mathematicians left 1 out on purpose so that every whole number had only one way of being written as a product of primes. She added one line to her program, an if statement guarding the door, and ran it again.

On Thursday, Cayson went first, just as he had promised, and typed 1 into his own program with a flourish. "Prime," his screen announced. Annabelle raised her hand while the room was still quiet. "One is not prime," she said. "It's excluded so every number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." Mr. Sow turned slowly from the projector and smiled.

Olivia spread her poster board across the kitchen table and weighed the corners with mugs. The science fair was in nine days, and her project had a problem: she still had a question instead of a hypothesis. She had written "Music is good for plants" on a napkin, and Ms. Zhao had circled it and written "How would anyone prove you wrong?" in red pen.

Whitney arrived with a bag of sunflower seeds and her own agenda. "I want my name on this," Whitney said, dropping into the chair. "I did the watering last time, and nobody even said thanks." Olivia said that was fine, then held up the napkin. "Ms. Zhao says a hypothesis has to be testable. That means an experiment could actually show it's wrong." Whitney squinted at the napkin. "So 'music is good for plants' is no good because there's no way to break it?" Olivia nodded and picked up a fresh index card.

They tried out wording while eating crackers. "If plants get music," Olivia said slowly, writing, "then they'll grow taller than plants with no music." Whitney read it over her shoulder. "That one you could break. If the music plants come out shorter, you're wrong." They agreed to grow twelve seeds in two groups on the windowsill, identical soil, identical water, one group next to Olivia's speaker playing the same playlist every morning. Whitney labeled the pots W, because she wanted her initial on something permanent, not a temporary scribble on a napkin.

The first four days, nothing sprouted, and Whitney speculated that the seeds were dead. Olivia refused to guess in that direction. "We can't just speculate without anything to look at," she said. "Give them three more days." On day six, five green hooks broke the soil, three of them on the music side. Whitney leaned in so close her breath fogged the window. "It's working. Music wins."

Day nine brought the twist. The tallest sprout, the one Whitney had been measuring every morning with a ruler, was on the quiet side, and by half a centimeter. Whitney stared at the numbers in the log, then closed the notebook. "I wanted music to win," she said. "I even picked the songs." Olivia tapped the index card. "That's the whole point. If the experiment could show we're wrong, then it actually counts when it shows something." Whitney opened the notebook again and wrote the new number down.

By Friday the two quiet-side sprouts had pulled further ahead, and Olivia wrote "Results did not support the hypothesis" on the poster in blue marker. Ms. Zhao stopped at their table at the fair, read the line, and said, "This is my favorite kind of project." Whitney pointed at the W on the pots. "I measured those," she said. "Every single morning."

The rental car smelled like sunscreen and pretzels when Hudson spotted the first yellow sign: WARNING, FLOOD RISK AREA. They were in the middle of a desert, hours from anything green, and the road outside was so dry it had cracked like old paint. "Flood signs in a desert," he said. "That's like putting a shark warning in a cow pasture." Rebecca, wedged beside him with her notebook of climate graphs, snickered without looking up.

Rebecca wanted an A on their climate project, and she'd brought two printed graphs to prove she deserved it: one for a rainforest, one for this desert. The rainforest graph looked like a comb, with tidy bars of rainfall every single month. The desert graph looked like a mouth missing most of its teeth. "See," she said, tapping it, "my graph shows the rainforest gets rain every month, all year. The desert gets almost nothing." Hudson frowned at the desert's lopsided spikes. Almost nothing, except one tall bar that stood alone like a flagpole. He remembered, suddenly, the trip two summers ago, when his uncle had recounted the story of a canyon flash flood, how a wall of water had roared through on a day with not a single cloud overhead. Hudson had thought the man was exaggerating back then. Now he wasn't so sure.

"Wait," Hudson said. He pulled out a marker and drew a dotted line on Rebecca's graph, connecting the empty years to that one spike. "What if the desert doesn't just get less rain? What if it's unreliable? Like, years with almost no rain at all, and then one storm dumps a whole bunch at once." Rebecca tilted her head. "That would explain the flood signs." "It would explain the flood signs," Hudson agreed, and they grinned at each other the way you do when a mystery cracks open in the back seat.

At the next gas stop, Mr. Chea, their neighbor and the official driver of this expedition, went in for coffee while Hudson studied a poster by the register. It showed a dry wash with a phone number and the words: REPORT YOUR RAIN SIGHTINGS. YOUR TESTIMONY HELPS US WARN OTHERS. While he waited, Hudson texted his dad, who was stuck at home working: "You will not believe this. Desert flood warnings are real. Not subjective opinion. Scientific fact, with graphs." His dad sent back a single message: "Then why did Mr. Chea pack an umbrella? Check the trunk."

Hudson lifted the trunk lid. There, folded beside the jumper cables, sat a compact umbrella, looking smug. He held it up as Mr. Chea came out jingling his keys. "Expecting a flood, Mr. Chea?" Mr. Chea took the umbrella, popped it open over his head in the blazing sun, and walked back to the car like a dignified beetle. "Insurance," he said. On the horizon, a single gray cloud was beginning to stack itself up.

Maeva sat cross-legged on the living room rug with her laptop balanced on the coffee table, a blanket over her knees because the radiator had gone quiet again. On the screen were three hundred and twelve survey answers about cafeteria food, one row per student, with columns for grade, favourite lunch, and whether they'd eat it again. Ms. Gagnon had asked for a summary by grade, and Maeva had promised to have it by Sunday. She'd been dragging cells around for an hour, and the numbers kept sliding into the wrong places like socks in a drawer.

Her dad came through with a mug of tea and stopped behind the couch. "Pivot tables," he said, pointing at a menu at the top of the screen. "Drag your grade column there and your lunch column there, and it counts for you. I remember when those were brand new. Pito Salas invented them, working on a spreadsheet program called Lotus Improv. It came out in 1991, and everyone in my office thought it was magic."

Maeva tried it. Grade went into Rows, favourite lunch into Columns, and a grid bloomed across the screen, every count already correct. "That's it? That's all it does?" It felt almost too easy, like the spreadsheet was doing her homework for her. But when she checked the totals, something was wrong. Grade 8 showed two hundred and four respondents, and there were only about ninety kids in Grade 8. She pulled the blanket tighter and frowned at the numbers. Something invisible was doubling the count, and she meant to find it.

A message popped up from Nassim: "Did you finish?? Brooklynn says the Grade 8s all picked poutine, is that true? Because I don't believe it, they're not that different from us."

Maeva typed back: "My table says poutine won by a landslide in Grade 8 but the count is messed up. Investigating." She decided to decompose the problem: one grade at a time, one row at a time. She filtered the sheet to Grade 8 only and sorted by name, and there it was. Every Grade 8 student appeared twice. The gym teacher had handed out the paper survey on two different days, and half of them had answered twice because they'd forgotten. She deleted the duplicates, counted the unique rows, and rebuilt the pivot. Grade 8 dropped to eighty-nine, and poutine still won, but only by four votes over the synthetic meatballs, which apparently tasted better than they sounded.

She sent Nassim the corrected numbers, then sat back and looked at the grid glowing in the dark room. It had taken one pivot table, one filter, and one stubborn hour to catch a mistake nobody else had noticed. On Monday she'd show Ms. Gagnon both versions, the doubled one and the true one, and explain the difference.

Her dad leaned over the couch again. "So who's the Grade 8 poutine champion?"

"Nobody," Maeva said. "It was a ghost army. I deleted them."

Theo sat at the kitchen table with his math book open, pencil hovering over the equation 3x + 5 = 17, and he could not make the x come loose. He had subtracted five from one side once, in class, and Mr. García had circled the mistake in red. "Both sides, Theo," he had written in the margin, and Theo had folded that page away, embarrassed, and never asked about it.

From the living room came the sound of his grandmother's television, too loud, and the smell of onions browning on the stove. She had left a note propped against the fruit bowl before she started cooking, because she never interrupted a simmer at the wrong moment. He unfolded it. "Dear Theo, your mother says you are stuck on the homework. I checked the old dictionary on the shelf, the green one, second drawer of the desk. Look up the short word with two lines. Love, Gran." Below that she had drawn two neat parallel strokes, like the rails of a tiny train track.

Theo found the dictionary and, tucked between its pages, an even older pamphlet about the history of numbers. He read it while the onions hissed. The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, and he had chosen two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal. Theo read the sentence twice. Two lines, the same length, the same distance apart, forever. Recorde had drawn a picture of fairness itself.

"So it's a promise," Theo said out loud. The two sides of 3x + 5 = 17 were equally true, equally heavy, and whatever he did to one side he had to do to the other, or the promise broke. He tested it. Subtract five from the left, subtract five from the right: 3x = 12. Divide both sides by three: x = 4. He checked it by plugging four back in, and it complied, twelve plus five turning into seventeen exactly. The pencil had cramped into his thumb tendon, and he shook his hand out and laughed once, alone, surprised.

His friend Nelly knocked on the door with her own worksheet, wanting help because Mr. García had promised extra credit for whoever could explain why you do the same thing to both sides, and she had only a vague answer that she admitted was not plausible. Theo pushed the pamphlet across the table to her. "Read the middle paragraph," he said. "Then tell me those two lines aren't the best idea anyone ever had."

Nelly ran her finger along the page. "Recorde," she said slowly. "Welsh. 1557." She picked up her pencil, drew two careful parallel lines at the top of her worksheet, and started on the first problem.

Antoine spread his notebook across the library table, next to a stack of books about story writing. His short story was due Friday, and Ms. Morin had written one comment at the top of his draft: "Dialogue needs correct punctuation, and I still can't find your climax." He understood the climax part, sort of. The protagonist of his story, a kid who finds a lost dog, needed one big moment. The punctuation was the mystery.

Lainey dropped into the chair across from him with her own draft. "What's with the frowning?" she asked.

"Commas and quotation marks," Antoine said. "I keep guessing where they go, and Ms. Morin keeps marking it wrong." He slid his paper toward her. His line read: "Where are you going"? He asked.

Lainey tilted her head. "Mine looks different, but I don't know why. It's the most probable reason I got marked down too."

Antoine pulled a published short story from the stack and flipped to a page full of talking. He ran his finger down the lines, hunting for question marks. There, in the middle of the page: "Where did you get that?" she asked. He stared at it. The question mark sat inside the quotation marks, and the word after it, asked, began with a lowercase letter. That felt wrong to him, like starting a sentence with a small letter on purpose. He flipped further and found another: "Are you coming?" he said. Same pattern.

"So the question mark goes inside," he said slowly, "and then he asked has a lowercase h?" He tested it against his own line, which did the opposite. That was probably why the red marks kept appearing. He copied the pattern into his draft: "Where are you going?" he asked. It looked strange and correct at the same time, like a door that opened the wrong way but still led somewhere.

"That has to be the rule," Lainey said. "Ms. Morin will enforce it, whatever it is."

Now Antoine had a different problem, the one Ms. Morin had called the missing climax. His dog story wandered from scene to scene without a peak. He read it over, then took out his pencil and wrote a new middle section where the kid finally spots the dog across a busy street just as the light changes. Then the kid runs. The whole story pointed at that moment now, and the dialogue could carry the ending: "Where have you been?" he asked.

He packed up as the library lights dimmed for closing. At the door, Lainey waved her own paper. "Read mine tomorrow?"

"Only if you check mine," Antoine said, and pushed out into the cold evening with his notebook under his arm.

The backyard smelled of grilled corn and cinnamon, and Gavin's cousin Rosario kept disappearing behind the garage with a folded paper in her fist. At the long table under the string lights, their grandmother was telling everyone that a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving, which was why Rosario had to stand up in front of the whole church and deliver a reading. Gavin watched his cousin slump in her chair, poking at her rice, looking lethargic in a way that had nothing to do with being tired.

"Want me to quiz you?" he asked, following her behind the garage with two paper plates of flan.

"I freeze," Rosario said. "I know it at home, then I open my mouth in front of people and it's gone." She read the line aloud again, flawless and quick, then groaned. "See? Alone I'm fine."

Gavin chewed and thought about that. At home the words came; in front of people they vanished. So the problem wasn't the words, it was the eyes on her, which meant practicing the words alone was like practicing swimming on dry grass. He remembered last summer, when he'd had to recite a poem for Mr. Hughes's class and had bombed it in front of thirty kids. Afterward, his mother had made him perform it three times for the family in the kitchen, and by the third time his voice had stopped shaking, because the scary part had been the audience, and he had gotten used to one.

"Okay, new plan," Gavin said. "Don't practice alone. Practice on us." He dragged two lawn chairs into the space behind the garage and set them facing the paper-plate "congregation." "Every time you finish, the crowd gets flan." Rosario laughed, but she stood, spread her feet like she was bracing against wind, and began. She stumbled on the second line. He made her start over. She stumbled again. He waved the flan like a bribe.

By the fourth try, the words stopped hiding. When Rosario inhaled before the last sentence, Gavin noticed she wasn't staring at the paper anymore, she was looking over his head at the fence, steady as a fence post. "One more," she said, "with everybody." She marched around to the yard, where the aunts and the little cousins were still eating, and climbed onto the low wall by the grill.

"Attention, consumers of my grandmother's cooking," she announced, and the whole table turned. She began the reading, slow and clear, her voice carrying past the corn smoke to the dark edge of the yard. When she finished, their grandmother was already on her feet.

"Again," Grandma said, wiping her eyes with the corner of her apron. "And louder."

The living room smelled like popcorn and salsa, and every seat was taken except the floor. Evelyn sat cross-legged in front of the television with her friend Isobel, while Donald sprawled across the couch between Mr. Sharma, their neighbour, and Evelyn's dad. On the screen, the championship game was tied with two minutes left, and everyone was shouting at once.

During a timeout, Donald pointed at the hoop. "Okay, serious question. Why do we even call it a basket? It's a net. Nobody calls a soccer goal a sock."

"It's just what it's called," Isobel said, reaching for the popcorn.

Evelyn frowned. That answer felt like a door someone had painted shut. Words usually came from somewhere. She thought about it while the announcer read a commercial, and then she pulled her dad's laptop off the coffee table and typed the question into the search bar. "If I can document this, you have to get the next round of snacks," she told Donald.

"Deal," he said. "I'm not scared of a computer."

She scrolled, and the answer appeared in black and white. "It's a basket because the first goals were actual baskets. Peach baskets." She read the rest of the page twice to be sure she had it right. "James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, and he used peach baskets as the goals."

Donald sat up so fast he nearly knocked over his soda. "Peach baskets? Like, real peaches came in them?"

"That's where the word comes from," Evelyn said. "He nailed them up and the ball had to go in." She turned the laptop so everyone could see the old photograph on the screen, men in wool uniforms standing under wooden peach baskets nailed to a balcony.

Mr. Sharma leaned forward, squinting. "Look at that. No holes in the bottom either. Somebody must have climbed a ladder every time a point was scored."

"Imagine pausing an NBA game so a guy could fetch the ball out of a peach basket," Isobel said, laughing.

The page went on, and Evelyn read quietly for a moment. Naismith had worked with young men who had no income in the cold Massachusetts winter, kids from impoverished neighborhoods with nowhere to go, and the game had given them something to do inside. She thought about her own gym class, rainy days, and the battered ball in the garage. "So the game basically started because a teacher needed something for his students to do indoors," she said.

"He'd faint if he saw this," Donald said, gesturing at the sold-out arena on the TV, the fireworks, the roaring crowd.

The buzzer sounded, the game came back on, and everyone leaned toward the screen. Donald slid off the couch and headed for the kitchen without being asked.

"Snacks!" Isobel called after him. "You lost the bet!"

"Two bags of chips coming up," Donald called back, "but only because of the peach baskets."

Bennett had been at Camp Tamarack for exactly four hours, and already the dining hall smelled like burnt oatmeal and bug spray. He sat at the end of a long table with his cabin group, tray untouched, listening to Iyla from Cabin 6 argue that the morning's campfire had been left perfectly safe.

"It was out," she said. "Gray ash, no flames. Done."

"Then why did Mr. Singh make everyone go back?" Bennett asked.

Iyla shrugged. "He likes bossing people around."

Lisa leaned across the table. "He made them pour water on it twice. And stir it with a shovel. Then pour again. My brother was in that group last year."

Bennett turned that over. Pour, stir, pour. That was a rule, not a mood. Mr. Singh was making the whole group redo something they thought was finished, which meant the counselor believed a fire could look dead and not be dead. That was a hidden cause, invisible, the kind of thing you couldn't settle by staring at it. You'd have to test it somehow.

After lunch, Bennett found Mr. Singh stacking cups behind the counter. "How do you actually know when a campfire is out?"

Mr. Singh looked at him for a second. "You feel for heat with the back of your hand. If it's too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave."

That was the whole answer, and it had a comparison built into it, one Bennett filed away. He walked back to the tables thinking about the camp's evening skit, which his cabin was supposed to perform at the Friday campfire. They'd been arguing all morning about which skit to do, and Mr. Singh had finally made them vote by ballot, folded papers and all, because Iyla refused to yield on her talking-squirrel idea. Iyla had also announced that a campfire skit would be impossible now, since Mr. Singh was clearly going to ban campfires forever after the morning's disaster.

Bennett had voted for Iyla's skit anyway, mostly because the other option was forty minutes of knock-knock jokes. He found her by the juice machine.

"If the fire gets a total ban," she said, "we do the skit in here. In the dining hall. Around the ketchup."

"Mr. Singh isn't banning anything," Bennett said. "He's just making sure the fire is actually cold before anyone leaves it. That's all it was. You pour water on it, stir it, pour again, then feel for heat with the back of your hand. Too hot to touch means too hot to leave."

Iyla chewed on that. She'd spent four hours believing the counselors had invented a punishment just for her group, and the simpler explanation, that the fire had only looked dead, was somehow more annoying. "Fine," she said. "Skit at the fire. But I'm checking it myself first. Back of my hand."

Friday night came, and the fire burned down to coals while the squirrels delivered their punchlines. When the crowd filed out, Iyla stayed behind, cup in hand. She poured, stirred with the shovel, poured again, then hovered her hand over the ash.

"Cold," she announced, sounding almost disappointed.

Bennett held out his own hand anyway, and she smacked it away. "Back of the hand only," she said. "House rules."

The poster outside the gym had been up for three weeks before Alexander actually read it. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, it said, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He read it twice because he was waiting for Robyn, and Robyn was late again.

Robyn had stopped eating lunch at their table on Tuesdays and Thursdays. At first Alexander thought it was a schedule thing, but she was in the cafeteria those days, sitting alone near the windows, headphones in, picking at a pretzel. When he waved, she lifted two fingers and went back to the window. He remembered the fall, before any of this, when Robyn had run the announcements and laughed so hard at Billie's impression of Mr. Clarke that she had to leave the room. That was the Robyn he knew. Something had changed, and the change had been gradual, so gradual he hadn't noticed until it was already done.

He tested his first idea on Wednesday. If it was stress about the science fair, she would talk about the science fair. He sat down across from her and asked how her display board was coming. "Fine," she said, and folded the pretzel bag into a small square, then a smaller one, like it was a ritual she did without thinking. "It's fine." That idea was wrong.

So he stood in the hallway and looked at the poster again. Emotional. Psychological. Social. He tried to work out which one had broken. Not emotional, exactly, because she didn't seem sad when Billie did something dumb in class; her mouth still twitched. Not psychological, or at least not in any way he could check. Social. She was pulling away from people, a little at a time, and nobody had said anything because nobody had a rule for when to say something.

He found Billie at the water fountain and told him about the Tuesdays and Thursdays. "She's coping somehow," Billie said. "Coping means dealing with it, right? That's what my sister's counselor says." Alexander said maybe, but coping alone by a window with headphones seemed different from coping with your friends. He wanted to say it more clearly, but he couldn't paraphrase the poster fast enough, so he just said, "Social is part of it too. Being around people. It counts."

On Thursday he didn't ask about the science fair. He put his tray down across from Robyn and said, "Billie's bringing his telescope Friday. He says Saturn's up. You in?" She looked at him for a long moment, then at the window, then back. "I get anxiety in crowds now," she said. "Even the cafeteria kind." "Then we'll do the roof," Alexander said. "Four people is not a crowd." Robyn unfolded the pretzel bag and folded it once more. "Okay," she said. "Friday."

Autumn sat on the back porch steps at her grandmother's house, holding a folded square of newsprint that her father had pressed into her hands that morning. Relatives milled around the yard with plates of potato salad, and somebody's uncle kept refilling the punch bowl, but Autumn barely looked up. The paper was the obituary, the notice that had run in the town paper about her grandfather's death, and she had read it four times already. It said he was survived by his wife, three children and five grandchildren. It said he had worked thirty years at the hardware store. And in one short line near the bottom, it said that in his youth he had been a sailor, and that he never lost his love of the sea.

A sailor. Grandpa, who got seasick on the ferry to the island, who kept a robust coil of rope in the garage even though he never went on a boat that she knew of. Autumn flipped the paper over, as if the back might explain more, but there was only a coupon for mulch. She had spent whole summers at his kitchen table while he consumed crossword puzzles one clue at a time, and he had never once mentioned the sea. That bothered her more than the sadness did, somehow. A person could hold a whole hidden life and never let it slip.

Melody arrived after lunch with her mother, a plate of lemon bars, and the careful face people wear at these things. "I'm really sorry," she said, sitting down beside Autumn on the step. "Is that him?"

"It's his obituary," Autumn said. "It's a published notice about someone's death, and it has a little account of their life. Family, work, interests. That kind of thing." She tapped the last line. "It says he was a sailor. He never told me that. Not once."

Melody leaned over to read. "Maybe he forgot to tell you. Or maybe he told your dad."

That was the thing to test, Autumn decided. If Grandpa had really loved the sea, there should be evidence somewhere, some trace of it, because a person's interests leak into their stuff whether they talk about them or not. She stood up, brushed crumbs off her skirt, and went inside to the garage. Melody followed.

The garage smelled like oil and old newspaper. Autumn pulled open the bottom drawer of Grandpa's workbench, the one she had always assumed was full of junk. Inside was the coil of rope, tied in a strange, complicated knot she had never seen anywhere else. Beside it lay a brass compass, green with age, and a photograph of a very young man in a sailor's cap standing on a ship's deck, grinning like he had just gotten away with something. It was Grandpa. It was unmistakably Grandpa, fifty years younger.

Autumn carried the photograph out to the yard and found her father by the fence. "You never said he was a sailor," she said.

Her father looked at the picture for a long moment. "He got a concussion falling from the rigging when he was nineteen," he said. "After that he came home and never went back. He didn't like to talk about it." He put his arm around her shoulders. "But he kept everything, didn't he."

Autumn held the photograph up so the light caught the ship's white rail and the boy's crooked grin. "I'm going to learn that knot," she said, and went back for the rope.

The courthouse hallway smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Riley's knee would not stop bouncing. In twenty minutes his team would stand before a judge in Room 4B and argue that the school's class elections should switch from first-past-the-post to proportional representation, and every team before them had been torn apart by the same question: "Show me one country that actually made the change." Nobody on the judges' panel wanted a theory. They wanted proof.

"We could just make something up," Gurfateh whispered, adjusting the tie he'd borrowed from his uncle, which was roughly the size of a seatbelt. "Judges love confidence."

"They love facts," Naima said. She flipped through their binder one more time, past the sample vote count they'd worked out on pizza night. Under first-past-the-post, their imaginary Class of thirty voters gave the Purple Party eleven seats, even though most people had voted against Purple. Under proportional representation, the seats actually matched the votes. The numbers were right there. It was the missing piece that scared Riley, the country that had done it for real, and it felt like something dormant buried in the back of his brain, waiting for a jolt to wake up.

Flashback to that pizza night: flour on the counter, Naima assigning jobs, Riley insisting he could eat a slice while doing long division. He had knocked over a cup, and while mopping it with his sleeve he'd caught a snippet of a documentary his dad was watching in the next room, something about elections, an island country, a change in how people voted. He hadn't written it down. He'd been too busy discovering that cheese and cartilage don't mix, after biting into something on his slice that his little brother had smuggled in from a science kit. "Ow," he'd said. "That's it. I'm going to look it up later." He never had.

Room 4B's door opened, and Ms. Santos-Reyes, who had driven them to the courthouse and prescribed rest, water, and no arguing in the van, leaned toward them. "Two minutes," she said. "Judges are running ahead of schedule." She did not offer facts or advice. She only straightened Riley's note cards, which were curling like old leaves.

"That documentary," Riley said suddenly, grabbing Naima's sleeve the way Gurfateh's tie grabbed his whole torso. "An island country. New Zealand, maybe? They voted on it. A referendum. And they replaced first-past-the-post with the proportional system. MMP." He wasn't sure. It could have been Australia, or a dream, or a commercial for kiwifruit. Gurfateh was already typing on the ancient tablet they'd brought, and Riley watched the loading bar crawl while the door to 4B opened again and the clerk inside called, "Team four."

"Confirmed," Gurfateh whispered, eyes wide. "New Zealand, 1993 referendum, replaced it. And they first used the new system in the 1996 election." Naima jammed the tablet into Riley's hands and shoved him toward the door.

The judge looked up from her glasses. "Young man, before you begin. Has any real country ever actually switched from first-past-the-post to a proportional system?" Riley held up the tablet, screen still glowing. "Yes, Your Honor. New Zealand. A 1993 referendum to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP. They first used it in the 1996 election." The judge raised one eyebrow, glanced at the screen, and nodded slowly. "Proceed."

Alexis crouched beside the workbench in Mr. Ivanova's garage, staring at the multimeter in her hand. On the little screen, next to the number, sat a symbol that looked exactly like a tiny horseshoe. "Why does it say my wire has three horseshoes?" she asked.

Sarah laughed from the doorway. "It doesn't. That's not a horseshoe." But she wouldn't say what it was, which Sarah seemed to think was hilarious. Behind her, Aidan shifted the toolbox he was carrying and checked the clock on the wall. "Twelve minutes," he said. "The science fair judges start at ten sharp."

The premise of their project was simple: prove that a thin wire had more resistance than a thick one. Alexis's job was the measuring, and the measuring had to be done right now, because Mr. Ivanova needed his garage back at ten for a repair job. The meters, the spools of wire, the whole table had to be cleared out. Alexis clipped the meter leads onto the first wire, read the numbers, and wrote them in her notebook. Voltage. Current. But the horseshoe symbol kept showing up beside every reading, and she could not shake the feeling that it mattered.

"It's the omega symbol," Sarah finally said, bouncing on her heels. Sarah wanted credit for the answer, Alexis could tell, wanted to be the one who got to say it. "Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter omega." She said it slowly, like she was handing over a prize.

Alexis looked at the screen again. Three ohms. Then it clicked into place, the whole hidden chain of it: the meter could not show her resistance directly, but it could show voltage and current, and if she divided one by the other, the answer would come out in those little omegas. She had been treating the symbol like decoration when it was the key to the entire calculation. She grabbed her pencil and worked through the thin wire: six volts, two amps. Three ohms. The meter agreed with her arithmetic, and her stomach did a small flip.
