"Or," said Kaden, "the toothbrush whispers during the dance. In front of everyone. Mouth full of toothpaste."

Natalie laughed so hard she knocked over the crackers. "That's disgusting. That's perfect." She started writing before the crumbs even hit the floor, and Ms. Greco leaned over her shoulder, read two lines, and quietly slid the rest of the crackers into her desk drawer.

Penelope stood at the edge of her aunt's backyard with her phone hidden in her sleeve, mouthing words under the sound of the dhol drum. In three weeks she would stand before the Panj Pyare at her Amrit Sanchar, the Khalsa initiation ceremony, and she was determined to recite Japji Sahib perfectly, all of it, from memory.

"You're perspiring," said her cousin, fanning her with a paper plate. "It's not that hot."

"It's not the heat. It's line forty." Penelope whispered the troublesome words again, then lost them again, like water slipping through her fingers. She had tried reading the prayer fifty times, but somehow her brain only held what she heard.

Then she noticed something. Her grandfather, a veteran of every family wedding and funeral for sixty years, sat by the mango tree reciting along with the aunties, eyes closed, never missing a word. He wasn't reading. He had never once, in her whole life, seen him hold a gutka at a gathering like this. He knew Japji Sahib the way he knew how to breathe.

Her idea arrived like a firecracker. If she stopped reading and only listened, over and over, maybe the words would stick the way they stuck for him.

"Play the recording," she told her cousin, and instead of staring at her phone screen, she closed her eyes through the whole recitation. When the aunties started the verses again for the elders who had arrived late, she kept her eyes shut and let the rhythm pour in. Musk from the incense drifted past. Her sandals stuck slightly to the grass. And then, on the third repetition, her own lips were moving half a second ahead of the sound, the hidden pattern suddenly clear, every verse locking onto the one before it like puzzle pieces she had been holding upside down.

"You got it," her cousin whispered, poking her arm. "You actually got it!"

Payton and Lucas appeared at the fence gate, waving. "We biked over," Payton panted. "Did you finish learning your prayer?"

"Line forty and everything," Penelope said, grinning so wide her cheeks ached. "And I found out something. My mom said the same prayer is recited at the initiation itself. So when I stand there, I won't just be saying something I practiced alone. I'll be saying what everyone says, all together."

Lucas leaned his bike against the fence. "So it's like a secret code you already know."

"More like a song the whole family knows," Penelope said, and she took a deep breath and began, right there in the backyard, the first verse rolling out steady and sure.

On Saturday morning Arianna sat at her mother's desk in the corner of the office, because the library was closed and the rec-center spreadsheet project was due Monday. Marvin had come along, mostly for the vending machine on the third floor, but he pulled a chair up beside her and watched the screen. The center wanted to know which Saturday classes had the most sign-ups so they could order supplies, and Coach had asked for numbers, not guesses.

Arianna typed the class names into column A and the sign-up counts into column B, then clicked the empty cell at the bottom of the numbers. She remembered the formula from the handout and typed =SUM(B2:B9). The cell showed 186, which matched the total she'd added by hand on paper, so the adding part was done. Now the chart. She highlighted the names and numbers, clicked Insert, and chose the chart that said Bar.

The chart appeared, and the bars ran sideways. Coding stretched across the page, Pottery hung below it, Fencing below that, each one reaching out to the right like arms. "It's lying down," Marvin said. "The whole thing's sideways. Did you break it?"

"No, it's not broken." Arianna leaned closer. The names sat on the left side of the chart, one per row, and every bar grew out to the right from its name. She scrolled through the chart menu again and found a second button, the one that said Column. She was hesitant to click it, since she'd already made a chart and didn't want to lose it, but there was an Undo button if it went wrong. She clicked.

The new chart stood the bars upright. The same names now ran along the bottom, and the bars grew upward, Fencing tallest, then Coding, with Pottery and the rest in a row beside them. "Oh," she said. "They're different. That one's a bar chart, so the bars go across. This one's a column chart, so they stand up." Marvin looked from one version to the other. "Same numbers," he said. "Same amount of tall either way."

Ms. Banerjee, who worked at the desk across the aisle, rolled her chair over and introduced herself as a neighbor who didn't have a home office. She asked to see the chart, said the standing bars would read better in the email to the rec-center board, and added that the numbers needed one small amendment, since the Chess Club count had gone up by four after Thursday. Arianna changed the 12 to a 16, and the total cell jumped to 190 and the Chess bar stretched taller, all by itself. Marvin pointed at the screen. "It fixed its own chart. Now that's going to propel me straight to the vending machine, because I earned it."

The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Lea sat with her ankle propped on the chair across from her, because she had twisted it jumping off the bleachers during lunch. The jump itself had seemed like a fine idea at the time. Her friend Giuseppe had said, "Don't," and she had said, "Watch me," and now here she was, waiting for Mr. Sánchez to look at a ankle she could have predicted would go sideways.

Her mother had gone to the front desk to sort out the insurance card, so Lea was alone with a rack of pamphlets. She picked one up mostly because the cover showed a brain drawn in blue crayon colors. YOUR DEVELOPING BRAIN, it said. She flipped past the parts she already knew from health class and stopped on a page about the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses. It keeps developing through the teenage years, the pamphlet said, and into a person's twenties.

Lea read the sentence twice. She looked at her ankle, swelling inside her sneaker, and thought about the bleachers. She thought about the boots. Two weeks ago she had taken sixty-three dollars out of the shoebox in her closet, money she had been saving since September for the class trip to the river caves, and spent all of it on silver boots she had seen through a shop window for exactly four minutes before buying them. The boots now sat under her bed, and she was vain enough, she had to admit, to keep wearing them even though Anabelle had pointed out they matched nothing Lea owned. Planning. Controlling impulses. Apparently the part of her that was supposed to handle those jobs was still under construction.

She pulled out her phone and typed a message to Anabelle: "At doctor for ankle. Bleacher thing. Also I read something. The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into your twenties. So basically I have construction equipment where decisions should be. Does this mean I can charge the boots to my brain?"

The reply came in three bubbles. "That is the most convenient excuse I have ever heard." Then: "But also, my cousin is 24 and he still eats cereal out of a mixing bowl, so maybe it's true." Then: "Are you still coming to the caves? Because the deposit is due Friday."

Lea looked at the deposit line. Fifty dollars, nonrefundable. The boots had cost sixty-three. She could return them, she realized; the receipt was still in the box, and the store took returns within thirty days. Thirteen dollars would not cover fifty, but babysitting Saturday could contribute the rest if she started now.

The door opened and Mr. Sánchez came out in his white coat. "Lea? Left ankle, I hear. What happened?" His eyes went to the pamphlet still in her hand. "Doing some light reading?"

"Bleachers," she said. "I jumped off them even though my friend said not to." She held up the pamphlet. "Turns out my planning department is a work in progress."

Mr. Sánchez laughed and waved her toward the hallway. "Then we'd better get that ankle sorted so you can plan on walking to the shoe store," he said. "Sounds like you've got boots to return."

Lea limped after him, already typing Anabelle back: "Boots going back tomorrow. Caves are on."

Lauren stood at the dessert table at her cousin's graduation party, next to a tray of lemon bars her grandmother had made from a recipe on the back of a flour corporation's box. Her uncle Ray took one, bit into it, and made a face.

"Too sour," he announced to the whole backyard. "Nobody likes these."

Lauren looked down the table. Aunt Priya had taken two. Two of the little cousins were eating theirs down to the crumbs. She thought about the science unit Ms. Nowak had assigned before summer break, the one where the class had surveyed 200 students about cafeteria snacks. Lauren had surveyed only her three friends first, and all of them had said they loved the veggie chips, so she'd written that everyone did. Then the big survey came back with different numbers, and Jasmine had laughed so hard she knocked over Ariya's glue. Ms. Nowak hadn't lectured. She'd just handed back both charts side by side and let Lauren look.

She exhaled slowly and counted the plate of lemon bars. Twelve pieces had been set out. Seven were gone, and the party had been going for an hour. Two whole bars sat untouched on her uncle's napkin beside his soda, abandoned after one bite.

"Uncle Ray," she said, "how many people did you actually ask?"

He shrugged. "I asked your dad. He made the same face."

"So that's two people out of, what, forty here?" She pointed at the tray. "Seven bars gone in an hour. And Aunt Priya took seconds."

"The kid did a whole survey," Aunt Priya said from behind them, waving her half-eaten bar. "Look at her, counting everything."

"I'm not doing a survey," Lauren said, though her notebook was already out of her back pocket, the same one she'd carried all spring. She flipped past the snack chart to a clean page and wrote the tally: eaten, refused, unknown. Her uncle watched her with his arms crossed, but he didn't walk away.

"There's melted ice cream on your collar," he said at last, pointing at a molten streak of vanilla running down toward her sleeve.

Lauren blotted it with a napkin and kept counting. Two more people came up for bars while she stood there, one of them the graduate herself, who took a piece in each hand. "Grandma only makes these once a year," the graduate said. "You trying to figure out if she should make them more?"

"Sort of," Lauren said. "I'm trying to figure out what's actually true."

Her uncle picked up his second abandoned bar, turned it over, and took another bite.

The bus to Camp Wenaki left at seven in the morning, and Hudson had until sundown to prove to himself that he could handle two weeks away. That was why he was at the canoe launch with Ronan and Addisyn, dragging the old aluminum canoe down to the water while the sky turned orange over the far shore. The canoe belonged to the landlord of the marina, who rented it out for five dollars, and Hudson had paid with quarters he had been saving since spring.

"The thing I'm worried about isn't the food or the bugs," Hudson said, steadying the bow. "It's getting lost. My mom says the camp is huge, with a lake and trails everywhere. What if I'm out somewhere at night and I can't tell which way is back?"

Ronan shrugged. "They'd give you a map. Or a counselor."

Addisyn tipped her chin toward the water. "My brother went last year. He said no phones allowed, not even at night. They do this thing where everyone lies on the dock and finds north with just the stars."

"Find north?" Hudson let the canoe drift against the gravel. "How? The stars are everywhere."

"Wouldn't know," Addisyn said. "He wouldn't tell me. He said it would embarrass him to admit he remembered anything from camp."

They paddled out and back, then hauled the canoe up and stayed as the light drained out of the sky. The three of them lay on the wooden planking of the launch, shoulders touching, and Hudson scanned for anything familiar. The Big Dipper came out first, its seven stars bright and easy, hanging above the tree line like a giant ladle.

"There," he said. "But that doesn't tell me anything. It just sits there."

He stared harder. Four stars made the bowl, and he traced them with his finger, one edge, then the other. One side of the bowl ran parallel to the other side, neat and straight. Then he tried something. He lined up his arm with the two stars at the outer edge of the bowl, the ones on the far lip, and slid his hand outward, away from the handle. His arm crossed a stretch of dark sky and stopped at one lone star, brighter than the scattered ones around it, sitting almost exactly where his hand pointed.

"That star," Addisyn said, sitting up. "My brother drew it on a napkin once. He called it Polaris, the North Star."

"It works," Hudson said, half whispering. "The two stars at the edge of the bowl. They point right at it. Every time I trace it, I land on the same star." He did it again to be sure, and again, and his arm stopped in the same place, steady over the trees.

"Great," Ronan said. "Now point south."

Hudson turned his back to Polaris and jabbed a finger toward the dark water below the launch. "That way. And in two weeks I'll be doing this on a dock in the middle of nowhere."

Addisyn flopped back down beside him. "Then find it one more time, so you don't forget."

Hudson raised his arm to the bowl and traced the line, slow and careful, out to the lone steady light.

Nathaniel sat on the kitchen counter swinging his legs while his mom peeled the sticker off the new glasses case. The problem had started two weeks ago, in the back row of Ms. Karimi's class, where the board had turned into a soft gray smear. He could read his phone perfectly, which had briefly made him suspect the board itself, maybe dry-erase markers of terrible quality, maybe a chalk conspiracy. Then he'd borrowed Elia's notes and realized the smear followed him everywhere that was far away.

"It's called nearsighted," Marielle had told him at lunch, matter-of-fact, because she'd had glasses since fourth grade. "Light from far stuff focuses in front of your retina instead of on it." She'd tapped her own lenses. "Usually because your eyeball is a tiny bit too long."

"Your eyeball is too long," Nathaniel had replied, and they'd laughed until milk came out of Elia's nose.

Now the glasses were here, and Nathaniel had a theory to test before he even put them on. If the problem was distance, then things up close should look the same either way. He held up his phone with one hand, glasses in the other. Text, sharp. He slid the glasses on. Text, still sharp, maybe smaller. Then he looked out the window at the mailbox across the street, which for weeks had been a friendly blue blob. The mailbox had a flag. The flag was up. "Whoa," he said. "The mail came."

His mom raised an eyebrow. "You thought the mailman was a raccoon?"

"I had no data on the mailman."

He got systematic about it. He walked to the end of the driveway and back, testing the street sign, the neighbors' porch numbers, a squirrel on the fence that turned out to be two squirrels. He made a mental chart. Far things: fixed. Near things: unchanged. Which implied, he decided, that Marielle was right and his eyeballs were, in fact, slightly too long. He went inside and told his mom this with great dignity.

"Congratulations," she said. "Also, since you can see the mailbox now, you're in charge of the mail, which means you'll be the first to see the checks. Our household revenue depends on your new glasses."

"The revenue of this entire house rides on my eyeballs being too long?" He adjusted the glasses, striking what he hoped was a heroic pose. "Then I accept the burden."

He trotted back down the driveway, flags and squirrels and porch numbers all crisp around him, and pulled the mail from the box with a flourish. "Two checks and a pizza menu!" he announced to the whole street.

Jared's basement smelled like popcorn and old carpet, and his laptop sat propped on a milk crate between two sleeping bags. "Okay," he said, tapping the keyboard. "Ms. Becker said our project has to run by Friday. Yours asks for a number and says if it's prime. Mine has to do factorials, which is way worse." Jasmine pulled her chair closer, practically bouncing. She had been thinking about prime numbers all day, and tonight she was finally going to make the computer decide them for her.

She typed fast, reading each line out loud as it appeared. "n equals int, input, give me a number. Then for i in range of 2 and n, if n percent i equals zero, print not prime." It felt like casting a spell. "Then print prime at the end," she finished, and hit run before Jared could even grab another handful of popcorn.

The screen asked for a number. Jasmine typed 7, her all-time favorite. "Not prime," the screen announced. She stared at it. "Seven is absolutely prime. Try five." Jared typed 5. Not prime. He typed 11, then 13, then, just to be ridiculous, 2. Not prime, not prime, not prime. "Every single number," Jasmine said. "It thinks nothing is prime. Nothing in the whole world."

Jared flopped backward onto a sleeping bag and groaned at the ceiling, but Jasmine's instinct told her the bug was small and sneaky, hiding somewhere she couldn't see it. She traced the loop with her finger on the screen, her attention suddenly acute. "Wait," she said slowly. "When I type 7, the loop checks i. And range of 2 and 7 goes 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. It stops right before 7 itself." She counted on her fingers to be sure. "So it tries every possible divisor except 1 and n itself." Jared sat up so fast the milk crate wobbled. "Then where does it get the idea that 7 divides by something?"

They stared at the code together, and then Jasmine saw it: her final line, the "print prime" one, was sitting inside the loop by mistake, so the program printed "prime" over and over and then "not prime" last, and the last word was all they'd been reading. "It was saying prime the whole time," she shouted, laughing. "We just watched the wrong part!" She yanked the last print statement out of the loop, aligned it with the "for" line, and ran it again. Seven went in. Prime, said the screen, once, clean and certain. Jared held up the popcorn bowl like a trophy, and Jasmine reached over and typed 97, just because she couldn't wait to see it one more time.

Rachel had been staying at Grandma's house for three days, and she had one clear objective: learn to do an entire load of laundry by herself before her mother arrived on Saturday. Grandma had shown her the sorting part on Monday, dark clothes in one pile and light clothes in another, and Rachel had felt optimistic about the whole project until she opened the bleach bottle that afternoon.

The striped shirt was the problem. It was Ahmed's, borrowed for a paint fight at Jericho's birthday party, and now it was streaked with grey smudges. Rachel figured bleach would brighten it right up, but when she flipped the shirt over, she found a care label with a triangle crossed out with a big X. She stared at it. On her own white socks, the label showed a plain empty triangle, no X at all. So the symbols were opposites. The crossed one had to mean no bleach, and the empty one had to mean bleach was fine. She set Ahmed's shirt on the far side of the counter, away from the bottle, feeling like she had cracked a secret code.

Then she found the note on the fridge, held up by the magnet shaped like a trout. "Gone to the garden centre," Grandma had written in her looping hand. "Monitor the washer, it makes a clicking sound on the spin cycle but it's harmless. Your friend's shirt is on the counter, don't bleach it, the label says not to." Rachel laughed out loud. Grandma had known about the shirt the whole time.

But when Rachel went back to the counter, the striped shirt was gone. She checked the hamper, the sofa, even the freezer, because Grandma sometimes put things in strange places. Nothing. Then she heard the clicking sound from the laundry room, a steady tick like a clock with a limp, and noticed the washer's round window full of swirling water. Floating inside, unmistakably, were Ahmed's stripes. Rachel pressed her forehead to the cool glass. Grandma, in her hurry, must have tossed it in with the whites and, worse, Rachel could smell the sharp bleach smell already in the room.

She yanked the dial to drain and pulled the shirt out, dripping and smelling like a swimming pool. The stripes were still stripes, thank goodness, but faintly faded at the collar. Rachel laid it across the porch railing in the sun to dry, and when Grandma's car rattled up the driveway, Rachel was standing beside it, holding the bottle of bleach like evidence.

"I read the label before you did," Rachel said. "The crossed-out triangle means don't bleach."

Grandna picked up the shirt, turned it over, and squinted at the label. "Well," she said slowly, "then we'd best write Ahmed an apology and ask him what he wants for dinner when he comes Friday."

Rachel went inside to find a pen.

Grandpa's tropical fish tank hummed in the corner while Emmett stared at his phone, reading Otto's messages for the third time. At lunch today, some kids had mimicked the way Kaliyah talked with her hands, and Emmett had just sat there, frozen, until the bell rang. Otto had laughed along, which somehow felt worse.

"You're wearing a hole in that couch," Grandpa said from his armchair.

"Kaliyah got teased today. I didn't do anything." Emmett turned the phone over. "Otto laughed. I didn't even say stop."

Grandpa set down his newspaper. "Tomorrow's another lunch."

That night Emmett lay awake testing an idea, the way he tested things in science class. If he yelled at the teasers, they'd just switch targets, probably to him, and then there'd be two people getting laughed at. If he did nothing again, Kaliyah would keep eating alone. There had to be a move in between. He thought about the fish tank, how the little striped fish always swam near the slow one, not fighting the bigger fish, just staying close so it wasn't alone.

At lunch the next day, he got his chance. The same kids started up again, copying Kaliyah's hand movements. Emmett walked over and sat down directly across from her.

"Kaliyah, did you finish the science questions?" he asked, loud enough to carry. "I got stuck on number four."

The mimicking stuttered and stopped. Kaliyah blinked, then flipped open her notebook. "Number four? That one took me forever. I'll show you." One of the teasers tried another wave of his hands, but with Emmett there asking real questions, nobody laughed, and enforcing the joke suddenly took too much effort. The kid shrugged and turned back to his own table.

Otto lingered, looking unsure.

"Sit or don't," Emmett said. "But knock it off either way."

Otto sat. He even asked Kaliyah about the science homework, and by the end of lunch his ears were red with embarrassment, though he kept talking anyway.

In Ms. Ong's class that afternoon, they discussed a news story about a student who had filmed a bullying incident instead of helping. "Someone who only watches is a bystander," Ms. Ong said, "but someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated is called an upstander."

Emmett raised his hand. "So an upstander doesn't have to fight anybody? They can just, like, sit with the person?"

"That counts," Ms. Ong said.

After class, Otto caught up with him in the hall. "So at lunch, when you sat with her. Was that being an upstander?"

"That was the whole idea," Emmett said, and shoved open the door to the bus loop, where Kaliyah was waiting with her notebook, already flipped to number four.

Nora had never been to her grandmother's town before, and she arrived in Japan in the middle of August, which felt like the worst possible timing. Back home, her teacher Ms. Ramos had told the class about a festival honoring ancestors, and Chanelle had looked it up later and said it happened in July. Nora had stared at her phone for a whole minute, thinking she had missed her one chance. "I thought I'd be too late," she told Ayden on a video call the night before they left Tokyo. "If it's in July, then Grandma already came and went, and I wasn't even here."

Ayden leaned closer to his screen. "So ask somebody there. Maybe it's like time zones."

"That's not a real thing," Nora said, but the idea propelled her downstairs anyway, where her aunt was folding yukata cloths into a bag.

Her aunt laughed a little, the way people do when a worry turns out to be smaller than it sounded. "In some regions it's July," she said. "Here, and in most of Japan, we do Obon in mid-August. Your grandmother's spirit is believed to come home for a visit. You haven't missed anything." Nora let out a breath she felt like she'd been holding since the funeral, three months and one ocean ago.

The temple grounds were crowded by the time they arrived, lanterns strung between wooden posts, drummers tuning their rhythm behind a raised platform. Nora held the paper lantern her aunt had bought and turned it over in her hands, checking for instructions. A woman at the long table, notorious in the family for never letting anyone skip a step, showed Nora how to write her grandmother's name with the brush. Chanelle had texted that morning: "Light it good, ambassador of our whole friend group." Nora had rolled her eyes, but now, carefully painting each character, she sat up straighter, as if her whole class might somehow see her.

She had a theory, and she tested it quietly while she worked. If spirits come home for a visit, she thought, then they must need a path, and that must be what the lanterns were for, a trail of light from the temple back to the house where Grandma lived. So after lighting hers, Nora watched which way the older families carried theirs, and she walked the same direction, holding her lantern up, letting its small flame bob beside her aunt's.

At her grandmother's house, her aunt set her own lantern by the gate. Nora put hers next to it, then looked up at the dark windows. "She'll know it's mine," Nora said. "I used the good brush." Her aunt bumped her shoulder gently, and together they stood in the lantern light, listening to the drums drift down from the temple.

Isaac had claimed the big table by the library window, the one with an outlet, because his science fair project required a lamp, two trays of bean sprouts, and a certain amount of dignity. His hypothesis, printed neatly on an index card, said that the sprouts under the lamp would grow taller than the sprouts in the dark corner by the biographies. It was an influential hypothesis, at least among the four people who had heard it. Marco had declared it "basically guaranteed," which Isaac now understood was not a warranty of any kind.

The problem was the ruler. The dark-corner sprouts were winning. Not by a little, either. The tallest one had gone pale and weird and stretched almost nine centimeters, while the lamp sprouts sat there being green and short and smug about it. Isaac measured them twice, hoping he had measured wrong, and then a third time, which was the scientific version of asking the question again until you liked the answer.

"I could just switch the trays," Marco said, leaning over the table. "Nobody would know."

"The ruler would know," Isaac said. He did not actually believe the ruler had opinions, but at this point he wasn't ruling anything out.

He was carrying the trays toward Ms. Rahman's desk, possibly to confess, possibly to ask if the library had a book called What To Do When Nature Embarrasses You, when she looked up from a return cart and said, before he even spoke, "Let me guess. Wrong direction?" She examined his index card, then his trays, and shrugged. "A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting." Then she went back to scanning books, as if she hadn't just handed him the only useful sentence of his entire week.

Isaac sat down and thought about that while Marco tried to dismiss it. "So you're going to stand up there and tell everyone you were wrong?" Marco said. "In front of the judges?"

"The judges are scientists," Isaac said. "Half their papers are probably titled Well, That Didn't Work." He crossed out nothing on the index card. Instead he wrote a new line under the hypothesis, in careful print: RESULT: OPPOSITE. TALLER IN DARK. He taped the pale nine-centimeter sprout's photo next to it, because the thing had earned its portrait.

At the fair, the judges stopped at his table longer than at anyone else's. One of them leaned in, read the crossed-out prediction and the honest result, and asked Isaac what he would test next. Isaac slid a fresh index card across the table. It said: WHY DO THEY STRETCH? He tapped it twice.

Sarah stood in her grandfather's driveway with the front wheel of her bike in her hands and exactly three hours before the trail ride with Josiah and Nikolai. The tyre was as flat as a dropped pancake. She had assumed she would need a whole new tyre, which the bike shop in town might not even have, and the shop closed at one.

"You could dismantle it and look inside," her grandfather said from the porch, and then he went back to his newspaper, because he believed people learned better when nobody hovered. Sarah found a plastic tub under his workbench labelled TYRE STUFF, and inside it were three flat plastic levers, a hand pump, a tin of patches, and a folded note in her grandfather's handwriting.

"Turn the wheel and look for what punctured the tyre," the note said. "If you find glass or a thorn, leave it in that spot. Then take the tyre off and find the hole. Most tyres have a separate inner tube inside that holds the air, so the flat is usually a hole in the tube, not the tyre. Patch the tube. Grandad."

Sarah read the note twice. So there was a tube hiding in there, and that was probably all that was broken. She pushed one lever under the edge of the tyre, then a second, and the tyre loosened enough for her to peel it back. A rubber tube sat inside, grey and sad and soft. She pulled it out and felt along it with her fingers while the clock in the kitchen ticked toward noon. Nothing. She was about to pump air into it and listen for a hiss when she remembered the note's advice about looking for the cause. She spun the wheel slowly, and there, wedged in the tread, was a tiny sliver of glass, thin as a fingernail clipping. It was almost invisible until the sun caught it.

"Got you," she said out loud. She marked the spot with her thumb, pulled the glass out with tweezers, and matched that point on the tyre to the same stretch of tube. When she dipped that section into a bowl of water and squeezed, a thin chain of bubbles rose up, showing the hole like a secret being told.

She roughed the spot with sandpaper, stuck on a patch, and pressed until her thumbs ached. It seemed hopeless pressing a sticker onto rubber and expecting it to hold air, but her grandfather had once told an anecdote about crossing the whole county on a patched tube, so she kept at it. She worked the tube back inside the tyre, tucked the edge under with the levers, and pumped until the tyre was firm. When she squeezed it, it held, round and stubborn.

Josiah rang the doorbell at half past one, two and a half hours early, with his own bike and Nikolai's in tow. "We thought you'd be walking to the trail," he admitted. Sarah carried the wheel out, dropped it into the forks, and spun it. It hummed.

"Tube's patched," she said. "Let's go."

The cardboard carrier wobbled in Theodore's hands as he crossed the backyard, and something inside it yawned so loudly that Kimberly laughed from the porch steps. The kitten was a scrawny gray thing the shelter had named Pocket, and Theodore had spent his savings on her because nobody else wanted a cat with a notched ear. There was only one problem, and it sat in the middle of the kitchen table like a stone: his whole family was vegetarian, and his mom had already said the kitten could just eat what they ate. Lentils, rice, vegetables.

"It's a dilemma," Theodore admitted to Kimberly and Elisha, who had come over to see the new arrival. He let Pocket out onto the grass, where she stalked a falling maple seed with terrifying seriousness. "Everybody at home thinks it's fine, but she's not everybody. She's a cat." He had a vague feeling about it, nothing he could point to, just the memory of Pocket ignoring the shelter worker's offering of bread crust while demolishing a bowl of meat food in ninety seconds flat.

Elisha crouched down and offered Pocket a piece of carrot. Pocket sniffed it, sneezed, and walked away with her tail up like a flag of contempt. "Okay," Elisha said. "That's data."

Theodore had brought out the small bag of food the shelter had sent home, and he read the label aloud on his knees in the grass. "Cats are obligate carnivores," he read. Kimberly frowned, so he said it again, slower. "Obligate carnivores." Whatever it meant, the word obligate sounded like something you couldn't argue with, like a law. The label went on in smaller print, and it said plainly that cats depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet. He read that part twice, feeling the sentence settle over him. It wasn't an opinion. It was the same for every cat that had ever lived.

"So I have to allocate part of my allowance to real cat food," Theodore said. "Every week. Meat food, even though we don't eat it." He did the math in his head, then out loud for Kimberly to check, and she nodded. It would cost most of what he earned walking Ms. Zhang's dog, but he could do it.

That evening he set two bowls on the back step: one with leftover rice and beans, one with the shelter food. Pocket circled both, sniffed the beans, and then drove her whole face into the meat bowl, purring so hard her notched ear trembled. From the kitchen window his mom watched, arms crossed, and finally called through the screen, "Add it to the shopping list. The good kind."

Mr. Campbell-Brown had written two words on the board in capital letters: FORESHADOWING and SYMBOLISM. "Your essay is mandatory," he said, "and no, you cannot write 'the paw is spooky' three hundred times and call it done." Wyatt slumped. Reading had never intimidated him before, but explaining hidden stuff on paper felt like being asked to describe a smell over the phone.

At lunch, Miriam and Manha spread the photocopies across the cafeteria table. "Okay," Manha said, tapping the page, "our story is The Monkey's Paw, by W. W. Jacobs, from 1902. This soldier guy, Sergeant-Major Morris, shows up at the family's house with this dried old monkey's paw."

"And he literally warns them," Miriam said, reading out loud, "'the wishes bring terrible results.' Then he chucks it into the fire." She flipped the page. "And the dad goes and fishes it out anyway. Like grabbing a hot coal because you like the color."

Wyatt stared at the fire scene for a long moment. "Wait," he said slowly. "That's the foreshadowing, isn't it? Morris didn't just tell them the wishes were bad. He warned them and threw the paw into the fire before they even made one wish. So when everything goes wrong later, you can't say nobody saw it coming. The story told us everything up front."

Manha grinned. "And the fire bit is symbolism too. Getting thrown into the fire is like the paw getting rejected, and the dad rescuing it is like him ignoring the warning." She paused. "That sounded smarter in my head."

"It sounded smart out loud too," Miriam said. "Write that down before one of us forgets it."

Wyatt scribbled notes so fast his pen tore the paper a little. Then he stopped. "Here's my test. If the foreshadowing works, then the dad should have known better. He rescued the paw with his own hand after a soldier who'd actually seen the results told him it was terrible. So every bad thing after that is on him." He looked up. "Is that an argument or am I just being mean to a fictional dad?"

"That's an argument," Miriam said. "A brutal one, but an argument."

On Monday, Mr. Campbell-Brown handed the essays back. Wyatt got an A minus, with one comment in red ink: "Strong reasoning. One deduction for calling Mr. White 'a Paw Goblin of poor choices.'" Wyatt held it up for the others to see, and Manha laughed so hard she knocked over the class plant.

"Symbolism," Wyatt said solemnly, rescuing the pot from the floor. "The fall foreshadowed your detention."

The message pinged at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, while Jasmine was supposed to be finishing her math homework. It was a screenshot from Mikaella, dropped into the group chat with no caption: a glossy ad for the VivaTab Plus. Five feature bubbles floated across the page. Fastest processor in its class. Superthin design. Award-winning screen. Free streaming bundle. Six-month warranty.

"OK this is the one," Mikaella typed. "I'm asking my parents for it for my birthday."

Jasmine leaned closer to her phone. Something about the ad felt too shiny, the way a lake looks smooth until you poke it with a stick. She typed back, "It does look good. But isn't it weird that there are exactly five great things and nothing else? Like, where's the price of the bad stuff?"

"What bad stuff?" Mikaella replied.

"That's the thing. We don't know. That's what I want to find out."

Marie-Soleil popped into the chat a minute later. "My cousin works at an electronics store. Want me to ask her what people complain about?" Jasmine did want, very much. Mikaella sent a shrug emoji and said, "It has five awards though. Five."

Jasmine chewed on that. Why did the number five keep being mentioned, and why did it make the tablet seem so great? She imagined a corporation somewhere choosing exactly which five facts to put on the page and quietly not choosing the others. It was like the five coolest kids at school saying a party was amazing while nobody mentioned that the music stopped at nine. She typed, "Do you think they listed everything about it, or just the good parts?"

"Obviously just the good parts," Mikaella wrote. "It's an ad."

"But that's the trick," Jasmine typed. "They only show the facts that support their side and leave out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is. There's a name for it. Card stacking."

"Like stacking a deck," Marie-Soleil replied. "So the good cards are always on top."

"Exactly. So let's flip the deck over."

Jasmine opened a review site and searched for VivaTab Plus problems. The first three results made her sit straight up. Owners complained that the battery drained in about four hours. Four! The ad never mentioned battery life at all, not once, and now she understood why. It also ran hot if you watched videos for more than an hour, and the streaming bundle auto-charged your card after three months unless you cancelled. She pasted the links into the chat.

Mikaella was quiet for a long moment. Then: "four hours?? my brother uses his tablet the WHOLE bus ride there and back."

"Plus homework time," Jasmine typed. "The battery would be extinct before dinner."

Marie-Soleil's cousin texted her the same thing: customers came back complaining about the battery more than anything else. "My cousin says the company that makes it probably knows and just doesn't put it in the ads."

"Because they don't have to," Jasmine wrote. She stared at her screen, almost pleased with the feeling of having caught something that had been designed not to be caught. It was a little like finding the hidden picture in one of those magic-eye posters.

The next morning Mikaella came to school with a new plan. "I showed my dad the complaints and the ad side by side, and he said if I can wait for the sale, I can get a different one with a real battery. He says he'll cherish the money I just saved him." She dropped into her seat and pulled out her phone. "Now help me check the ad for the other one. Ten to one they stacked that deck too."

Dominic had been waiting for Sky's birthday party all week, and the second he walked through the door he spotted the bouncy castle in the backyard, the table of arcade prizes, and Arvin, standing alone near the snack table while two kids from another school circled him like seagulls around fries.

"Nice glasses, four-eyes," one of them said. "Can you even see through those things?"

Dominic's stomach tightened. He wanted to shout at them, but shouting had backfired in fourth grade when he'd yelled at a teaser on the bus and made everything worse; the kid had just gotten louder, and the teased kid had gotten teased for needing a bodyguard. So he stood there, holding his gift bag, thinking hard. Why did teasers keep going? Because they liked the audience, he decided. The whole room was watching Arvin, and the two kids were performing. If the audience looked somewhere else, would the show stop?

He needed to test it. He scanned the room. In the kitchen, Sky's dad was pulling a giant sheet cake out of the fridge, candles still in a box beside it. Dominic took a breath and marched to the middle of the party.

"Everybody!" he called. "They're cutting the cake, like, right now! Come on!"

The whole room turned. Kids stampeded toward the kitchen, and the unanimous rush of sneakers on the tile swallowed everything else. Even the two teasers jogged over, suddenly more interested in frosting than in Arvin. Dominic hung back, and Arvin drifted over to stand beside him, pretending to inspect a poster of the solar system on the wall.

"Thanks," Arvin said quietly. "You didn't have to do that."

Dominic shrugged, though inside he felt like he'd won a prize. "I just changed the subject. Distraction. It works better than yelling at them, I think."

Sky appeared with two plates of cake, thundering over like a small storm. "Did you see that cake? My dad spent an hour installing the candles, he had to use this special holder thing for the number eleven, it goes right down the spine of the cake, all eleven candles in a row." She handed them each a fork. "Best one yet, right?"

"Definitely," Arvin said, and it was the first full sentence he'd said all afternoon.

Later, out in the bouncy castle, the two teasers tried again. One of them pointed at Arvin's glasses and opened his mouth, and Dominic, mid-bounce, didn't even look at them. He just launched into the biggest cannonball of his life, and the whole castle wobbled like jelly. Every kid shrieked and scrambled to copy him, and by the time the bouncing settled, the teasers had bounced away to the other side.

Arvin caught Dominic's eye and grinned. "Cannonball distraction," he said. "You're getting good at this."

Katherine exploded off the line like the eight hundred metres was a fifty-metre sprint. For one glorious lap she was in front, her sneakers slapping the gym floor, Gregory's shout ringing behind her. Then the second lap began, and her legs turned to wet sand. She crossed the line in fifth place and had to lean against the bleachers just to stay upright.

Her objective for the next three weeks was simple: figure out what happened in that second lap. She couldn't see the problem, because her legs weren't hurting on purpose and nobody was tripping her, but something invisible was stealing her energy. So she started writing down lap times after every practice run in the gym, hers and Jayda's, on the back of her homework planner.

Jayda always finished stronger than she started. Katherine always faded. One afternoon they compared their splits from the same practice race, and the pattern jumped out at her. "You ran the second lap faster than the first," Katherine said, tapping the numbers. "Every single time. I do the opposite." Jayda grinned and said, "Ms. Moretti calls that a negative split. When you run the first half faster, like you, that's a positive split." Katherine stared at the paper. The names felt backwards, but the times didn't lie.

So she tested a simple idea. In the next practice, she would hold back on the first lap on purpose, keeping Jayda's shoulder a few steps ahead of her, and save everything for the second. It felt wrong at first, like standing still while a race happened somewhere else. When the bell that marked the halfway point rang, she adjusted her stride, pushed her arms harder, and began to hunt.

Gregory, jogging the outside lane as a pacer, yelled, "You've got more than you think!" Her breathing was ragged but her legs still answered. She passed two classmates on the far curve, then a third on the straight. She didn't win, but her second lap was two whole seconds faster than her first, written in her own handwriting in the planner afterward.

At the next time trial, she did it again, and this time she won her heat. Jayda thumped her on the back, and even the coach, who rarely said much, nodded from the doorway. Katherine was starting to believe she had the constitution of a distance runner after all, not because she was the fastest girl in the gym, but because she could wait when waiting was the harder thing.

She stood at the line for the final practice of the unit, planner tucked under her arm, and glanced at Jayda in the next lane. "Watch my second lap," she said, and settled into her crouch.

Chase had six dollars in his pocket and one plan: strawberries for his mom's birthday shortcake. At the first stall in the farmers' market, the baskets were piled high and red, more baskets than he had ever seen in one place. A hand-written sign read three dollars each. He stared at it, because last month, the Saturday he'd forgotten his wallet, the same baskets had been six dollars. He checked the sign twice, as if the number might be shy and change back when noticed.

"Something wrong with them?" he asked the farmer, a woman in a sun hat.

"They're fine. Best ones of the year. I've got more than I know what to do with right now."

Chase walked on to think, past a stall where a tiny wind turbine spun on a pole, powering a fan that kept the greens crisp. The whole market smelled like peaches and kettle corn. He turned the price over in his head. Six dollars last month, three dollars today. It wasn't the strawberries that had changed. They looked better than ever. Something behind the sign had changed, something he couldn't see: how many the farmers had to sell. When there were tons of them, the price dropped. When there were only a few, it climbed. He felt like he'd found a hidden lever under the whole market.

He found his friend Lionel by the honey stall, guarding a jar like it was treasure. "Lionel. Test my theory. Ask the blueberry people what they cost in July."

"July's when blueberries are everywhere," Lionel said. "My grandma freezes bags of them. She calls it stock-up season."

"So in July they're cheap because everybody's got them, and now they're expensive because hardly anybody does." Chase counted on his fingers, adding it up like a cumulative score. "It works for strawberries too. June strawberries, three dollars. They cost double that before, when the stands had just a few."

"You've been doing math on a Saturday," Lionel said. "Voluntarily. I'm telling Mr. Das."

Mr. Das, their neighbor, was two stalls down buying tomatoes, and he raised an eyebrow when the boys told him. "You two figured that out from baskets of fruit? Some people take an economics class to learn it." He held up his tomatoes. "Want to know what these cost me in August?"

"Cheaper," both boys said at once. "Peak harvest."

Chase went back to the strawberry stall and bought two baskets, then a third, because at three dollars he could. The farmer threw in a few bruised ones for free, which would go in the smoothies he'd make to prolong the birthday weekend into Sunday. On the way out, he passed the pie stall, where a line stretched ten people long and the pies were eight dollars each. He nudged Lionel.

"Only so many pies, all those people. You know what that means."

Lionel groaned. "It means we'd better get in line now, before the price finds out."

Savannah stood in the baking aisle holding two bags of flour and a small kitchen scale that cost more than her allowance for two weeks. Last Saturday her chocolate chip cookies had come out dry and cakey, more like biscuits than cookies, and her little brother had eaten exactly one and pushed the plate away. She was in charge of dinner and dessert tonight while her parents worked late, and she did not want a repeat.

Mr. Wu from next door turned into the aisle with his cart, and she felt a flash of relief at seeing a familiar face.

"Buying a scale?" he asked, nodding at the box.

"My cookies were wrong," Savannah said. "The recipe said two and a quarter cups, and I measured exactly that. Two and a quarter cups, level with a knife and everything." She caught herself remembering how she had dug the measuring cup straight down into the flour bag, packing it full, and how proud she'd been of the neat flat top. Now that memory provoked an uneasy feeling, like she'd checked the wrong answer twice and called it right.

Mr. Wu smiled. "My grandmother broke me of scooping flour straight from the bag. She weighed everything."

Savannah frowned. Scooping did something? She turned the flour bag over in her hands, thinking. If she pushed the cup down into the bag, the flour would get packed down, and a packed cup could hold more flour than the recipe expected. More flour than the recipe wanted. That would make cookies dry. Dry and cakey. She looked up at Mr. Wu, and he gave her the small nod of a man watching a jury reach a verdict.

"Could I borrow your scale tonight?" she asked. "I'll bring it back tomorrow."

"You can borrow mine and keep the one in your cart," he said. "Two scales, two tests."

At home, she laid both scales on the counter and set out two identical measuring cups. Into the first cup she scooped flour straight from the bag, digging deep and leveling it off. Into the second she spooned flour gently, the way the recipe book's small-print note suggested, and leveled that too. Then she weighed them. The scooped cup was heavier, a lot heavier, close to a whole extra half cup's worth of flour hiding inside what looked like the same measurement. She wrote both numbers on the back of a receipt, because her brother, who was already circling the mixing bowl with his spoon, would never believe her otherwise.

She weighed the flour for the new batch straight into the bowl, no cups at all, checking the number against the recipe. The dough came out softer and shinier, and it smelled like actual cookie dough instead of paste. Her brother hovered nearby, spoon raised, his judgment momentarily vulnerable to the smell of butter and brown sugar.

"Try one," she said, sliding the first warm cookie off the sheet.

He bit into it, chewed, and pointed the spoon at the plate. "Make these forever."

Every morning that week, Gabriella had found the strawberries in her backyard patch half-eaten, and this morning two whole berries were gone. She crouched over the flattened leaves and called across the fence, "Zackery! Get over here! We have a mystery."

Zackery bolted through the gap in the hedge, still holding his toast. "Raccoons," he said. "Definitely raccoons. That's my theory."

"Your what?" Gabriella squinted at him.

"Theory. Like, a fancy guess." He shrugged. "My brother says scientists don't know anything anyway. He says evolution is just a theory, so it's basically a guess."

Gabriella ran inside, grabbed her science notebook, and came back flipping pages. Earlier that year Ms. Castillo had made them copy a sentence from the board, and Gabriella had underlined it twice. She held it out. "Look. It says a theory is not a guess, it's an explanation that's been tested over and over and supported. A hypothesis is the idea that's still being tested."

"So a hypothesis is the guess part," Zackery said slowly, "and a theory is the part that already passed the tests?"

"Right. So your raccoon thing isn't even a theory. It's a hypothesis. And we can test it." She was already pacing the length of the patch. "If raccoons did this, they'd climb the fence, so we'd find muddy prints on the rails. If it was birds, they'd peck from above and leave the top of the berries torn up. These bites are on the side, low, near the ground."

Zackery checked the fence rails. "No prints. That contradicts raccoons."

They tested it that night. Gabriella's dad adjusted the thermostat on his way out to the porch, muttering that he wasn't sitting in the cold, so the porch light glowed warm and yellow over the garden while they hid behind the shed with a thermos of cocoa. Elliana squeezed in beside them at ten o'clock because she'd heard about the stakeout and refused to miss it. "If it's rabbits," she whispered, "there'll be droppings by morning. My aunt says check for droppings."

At 10:40 the grass rustled. Something small and brown hopped out of the dark, sat up on its hind legs, and plucked a strawberry clean off the plant with its teeth.

"Rabbit!" all three of them hissed at once, and the rabbit froze, then vanished into the hedge with the berry still in its mouth.

Gabriella wrote in her notebook by porch light: Hypothesis, raccoons, overturned. Hypothesis, rabbits, supported. Not a theory yet. Not until we test it again. "Tomorrow night," she said, "we put a low fence around the patch and see if it holds. If the berries survive, that's test number two."

Elliana grinned. "And if a rabbit gets in anyway?"

"Then we make a new hypothesis and start over." Gabriella snapped the notebook shut. "Science isn't one big guess that stays a guess forever. It's guesses you keep checking until they can't be knocked down."

Zackery raised his cocoa. "To test number two," he said. "No permanent conclusions until the rabbits say so."

Rachel sat at the kitchen table with a blank page and a pencil that had already been sharpened twice. Her assignment was to write an argument for why the school should start a compost bin, but Mr. Zhou had refused to let anyone draft a single sentence yet. First they needed a thesis, then three points, then an outline. Rachel had a thesis: "Our school should compost its cafeteria waste." She had scribbled four possible points and crossed out two. What she did not have was any idea how the outline was supposed to hold together.

The doorbell rang, and Charlee came in still holding her lacrosse stick, because she wanted Rachel's dad to drive them both to Saturday's game. He wasn't home yet, so she flopped into the chair across from Rachel and peered at the page. "You have three things written here," Charlee said. "What do they do?"

"They're my points," Rachel said. "Composting cuts trash, teaches science, and gives the garden free fertilizer." She stared at the list. Three points, and then a whole essay to write, and no clue how to connect them. She assumed each point would just turn into sentences somewhere, floating around in the draft until it looked long enough.

A scratchy sound came from the back porch, then silence. Rachel stood very still, listening. The yard looked tranquil in the late light, the compost bucket beside the door with its lid on tight. The sound came again, closer, and Charlee gripped her stick. Something was out there, and neither of them could see it.

Rachel ignored it for one more minute because an idea had just landed in her head, whole and shining. She grabbed a clean sheet and wrote her thesis at the top. Then, under it, she wrote the first point and started a paragraph. The paragraph opened with "First, composting cuts our school's trash in half," which was a sentence that tied the point back to her thesis. She did the same for the second and third points, and suddenly she saw it: each point got its own paragraph, and each paragraph opened with a sentence that linked back to the thesis. "Give me your highlighter," she said, and Charlee dug one from her bag. Rachel marked the first sentence of every paragraph.

"Read only the yellow parts," she said, and held out the page. Charlee read the thesis, then the three highlighted sentences, and her eyebrows went up. "I skipped everything else and I still got your whole argument. It's like a skeleton."

"The first sentences are topic sentences," Rachel said. "I just tested it on you." The scratchy sound came again, and Charlee was already at the window. "Rach," she said. "Your compost bucket lid is moving."

Luke pressed his nose to the glass case and read the label twice. "Mystery liquids," it said. "Use the litmus paper to test each one." A science museum was not where he had wanted to spend his Saturday, but his mother had dropped him off with Paxton and Maddie anyway, and Mr. Mokoena from next door had promised to pick them up at four. That gave them three hours and one puzzle: twelve bottles, no labels that helped, and a stack of thin paper strips beside a color chart numbered zero to fourteen.

"Red means acid," Maddie said, pointing at the chart. "Blue means base. Middle is neutral." She was reading fast, the way she did before anyone could beat her to an answer. Paxton had already dipped a strip into bottle one, which fizzed faintly. The strip turned pink.

Luke picked up bottle seven, which looked like plain water but smelled faintly of soap. He thought of his grandfather's bathroom sink, where a sliver of white soap sat in a dish and the whole room smelled like that. One evening last week he had run the water over the sliver and dropped in one of the litmus strips from his backpack kit, just to see. The strip had turned blue, deep blue, and the chart in his kit had put it around nine or ten. Vinegar, which he had also tested, turned red and sat way down near the other end. Soapy water and vinegar were on opposite sides of the scale. He hadn't believed it at first, because soap feels gentle and acid sounded like the dangerous one.

"Bet it's neutral," Paxton said, leaning over bottle seven. "Looks like water."

"It won't be," Luke said. "Watch." He dipped the strip, counted to five like the chart instructions said, and held it up. Blue. He laid it against the chart. "Nine, maybe ten. Most regular bar soap is basic, around nine or ten on the pH scale." Paxton squinted at the strip, then at the chart, then back at the strip.

"Okay," Paxton said slowly. "I thought acids were the strong ones. Soap's on the opposite side from vinegar, and it's still up there." He grabbed bottle eight and a fresh strip, suddenly in a hurry to test his own guess about the dish soap inside it. Maddie wrote "7: soap, 9-10" in the little notebook she carried everywhere, then ruled a line for bottle eight and waited, pencil ready.

By the time Mr. Mokoena arrived, they had worked through all twelve bottles. Maddie had filled six notebook pages, Paxton had changed his mind about three guesses, and Luke was explaining that bacteria could colonize the drain in the museum's fountain display, which was why the water smelled strange, though that was a test for another day. Mr. Mokoena asked what an extravagant afternoon of chemistry had cost them, and Luke held up the plastic bag of used strips like a trophy.

"Nothing," he said. "We didn't even break anything."

Kate sat on the counter stool at Mr. Rahimi's phone repair shop, her laptop open next to a tray of tiny screws. She had spent two weeks collecting survey answers from students about the school cafeteria, and now she had to turn three hundred rows of responses into something the principal would actually read.

"You said a pivot table would summarize them," she said. "By grade."

Mr. Rahimi wiped his hands on a cloth and came over. "Make a column for grade, a column for the answer, then drop them into the rows and values. It counts for you." He pointed at a cracked phone on his bench. "While you try it, I'm going to simulate a drop test on that one. It's hypothetical until the screen actually cracks."

Kate selected her data, inserted the pivot table, and dragged "Grade" into the rows area and "Favorite cafeteria meal" into the values area. The summary appeared instantly. She scrolled down the short list: Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8.

Then she counted again. Grade 6 had 112 responses. Grade 8 had 104. Grade 7 showed only 41, and below it sat a second row, "Gr 7," with 43.

"That's wrong," she said. "Grade seven only shows forty-one, but I collected eighty-four of those."

Mr. Rahimi leaned over without touching the keyboard. "Looks like your table thinks you have six grades."

Kate stared at the two rows. They looked the same to her. Then she went back to her raw data and sorted the grade column. The entries scrolled past: Grade 6, Grade 6, Gr 7, Grade 8, Gr 7, Grade 6. Some students had typed it one way, some the other. She hadn't noticed because on paper the difference was small.

She tested a simple idea. She used find and replace, changing every "Gr 7" to "Grade 7", then refreshed the pivot table. The two rows merged into one that read 84.

"So it wasn't counting wrong," she said. "It was treating them as two different grades because the words weren't typed the same."

"Exactly," Mr. Rahimi said. "The table only knows what the words say, not what you mean by them."

The door chimed and Alanna came in, shaking rain off her jacket. "Did you finish the numbers? Hillary wants to know if pizza actually won."

"Pizza won in grade six and eight," Kate said, turning the screen. "But grade seven picked the noodle bar by ten votes, and I almost missed it. Half their answers were hiding in a separate row."

Alanna frowned at the screen. "Why would it split them?"

"Because 'Gr 7' and 'Grade 7' count as two different things. I had to make them match first." Kate copied the finished table into her report, then saved the file twice, once to her laptop and once to a drive in her backpack, next to a paperback with a cracked spine she kept meaning to tape.

Mr. Rahimi set the dropped phone back on the bench, its screen intact. "Hypothetical no more," he said.

Kate zipped her bag. "Tomorrow I'm checking every column before I summarize anything. Hillary's survey is next, and she spells 'seventh' three different ways."

Eleanor's laptop sat on the kitchen table next to a bowl of cereal she had stopped eating an hour ago. On the screen was her Python program, which was supposed to ask for a number and print whether it was prime, and which currently believed that 9 was prime.

"You typed equals-equals, right?" Gurshaan said over video call. "Last week Japji spent forty minutes on one equals sign."

"I typed it right," Eleanor said. "It's the loop. Watch." She entered 9 again, and the program printed "prime" with total confidence.

Japji leaned closer on his screen. "It only checks 2, then it stops."

Eleanor read her own code. She had written the loop to test divisors 2, 4, 6, and so on up to the number itself. If the number wasn't divisible by 2, it sailed through the rest of the even divisors untouched and got declared prime, because 9 was never going to be divisible by 4 or 6 or 8 either.

"Wait," she said slowly. "That's why 9 passed. Nine isn't even divisible by any even number at all."

"So make it count by ones," Gurshaan said.

"I could." Eleanor was already typing. "But if it has to check every single number up to a million, it'll take forever. Ms. Li said ours would be the fanciest prime checker in the grade, and I intend to acquire that title." She paused. "After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, a program only needs to test odd divisors. An odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one."

There was a silence while Gurshaan and Japji considered this.

"So you check 2 once," Japji said, "then 3, 5, 7, and skip everything even?"

"Half the work, gone." Eleanor changed her loop. "My premise is that 9 gets caught by 3." She ran it.

9: not prime.

She tried 7. Prime. She tried 25, which got caught by 5, and 97, which survived every odd divisor she threw at it and came out prime, correctly, for the first time all afternoon. Then she entered 1000003 and the program chewed on it for a moment and said prime.

"That's the one Ms. Li will test," Gurshaan said. "She loves the big ones. She'll call it prestigious if it's fast."

"It's fast," Eleanor said. "It's doing half of what it did before and getting better answers."

Japji held up his hand toward his camera, and Eleanor held up hers toward his pixelated blur. Gurshaan, two screens away, did the same.

Eleanor saved the file, then entered one more number, 2, just to be sure. The program thought about the loneliest prime of all and printed its answer.

"Prime," she read aloud, and closed the laptop over a finally cold bowl of cereal.

The itch started on Tuesday, three days after Lydia broke her arm jumping off the shed roof. It was deep under the cast, in a spot she could not reach, and by Friday it had become the only thing she could think about. She sat at the kitchen table with her homework untouched, flexing her fingers inside the plaster, trying to press her skin against the wall of the cast.

She got up and found a ruler in the drawer. It was thin enough to slide down the gap between her thumb and the cast edge, and she was already lifting her arm to do it when she remembered the doctor's words from the office visit. He had said it plainly: never slide pencils, sticks, or anything like that into a cast to scratch an itch, because it can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining. She had nodded then without really listening. Now she set the ruler down on the table and stared at it.

Her friend Mohamad rang the doorbell that afternoon, holding a bag of sour candies and his own homework. "You look terrible," he said, which was his way of asking how she was.

"There's an itch," Lydia said. "Deep down. It's been going for hours and it's going to drive me insane. I almost used a ruler, but the doctor said not to put sticks in, because you can scrape your skin and wreck the lining." She tapped the cast with her knuckle. "I need another way to hit that spot."

Mohamad tipped his head. "Can air get in there?"

They tried the hairdryer on its cool setting, Mohamad holding the nozzle while Lydia angled her arm. A thin stream of air slid down the gap, and Lydia felt it move along her skin like a cold finger. It reached the itchy patch and the feeling quieted, though it did not vanish entirely. She made him hold it there for a full minute, and when he finally lowered the dryer his arm was trembling from holding it steady, as if he had been serving a heavy tray.

"That actually worked," she said. "It's still there, but it's calmer. Like it went from aggressive to just annoying." She flexed her fingers again. "The itch means the bone is healing, I think. Mom said itching is part of it, so it's a good sign, even if it's the worst good sign ever invented."

"So it has to sustain itself for how many more weeks?" Mohamad asked, unwrapping a candy.

"Five. Five weeks of this." Lydia pulled her sleeve over the cast edge. "Can you come back tomorrow with the hairdryer?"

He held up the sour candy bag. "I'll bring two."

Benjamin sat alone at the end of the lunch table, turning his tray so the pizza wouldn't stare at him. Across the cafeteria, Mohammed was laughing with Rafael about something, probably the rocket they'd promised to build together, the one Benjamin had found out about only because Rafael had left the plans on the lab table with Benjamin's name crossed off the materials list. That stung worse than the pizza.

His dilemma was simple: say nothing and let the friendship rot, or say something wrong and finish the job himself. Last night he'd written a note on a napkin. It started, "You ditched me," which felt satisfying and probably would start a war. He crossed it out. Then he remembered a page from the old counseling booklet Mr. Navarro kept on the shelf behind his desk, the one Benjamin had flipped through while waiting to be excused from gym. A psychologist named Thomas Gordon had come up with something in the 1960s called an "I-message," a sentence that describes the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." Benjamin hadn't believed a single sentence could matter that much. Now he had a chance to test it.

He wrote slowly, testing the idea like a hypothesis. "You ditched me" got crossed out. "I felt left out when I saw the rocket plans without me" went underneath. It felt invasive at first, like showing everyone the inside of his backpack, but it was his own feeling, not an accusation. He folded the napkin, carried his tray across the room, and stopped at their table.

"Can I sit?" he asked.

Mohammed scooted over without looking up. "Sure. There's room."

Benjamin put the napkin between them. "Read it before you yell at me."

Mohammed read it twice. His ears went pink. "We didn't ditch you. We were going to tell you. Rafael said we should test the fins before the third person got sucked in, because last time you ended up in the hedge."

"The hedge was one time," Benjamin said.

"The hedge had your outline in it," Rafael said. "Like a cartoon."

Mohammed slid the napkin back. "I'm sorry it looked like ditching. I should have just said something."

"Me too. I felt left out," Benjamin said. "That's an I-message, by the way. Gordon, nineteen sixties. It's in Mr. Navarro's booklet, next to the hedge incident, probably."

Mohammed laughed, then tore a piece of napkin and scribbled on it. He held it up: "I promise to preserve one hedge and one best friend." He tucked it into Benjamin's pocket. "Now come look at the fins. You're on parachute duty."

"Parachutes fail," Benjamin said, already following him.

"Not in the hedge they don't."

The gym smelled like rubber and floor wax, and Mackenzie's left knee had started aching again by the second drill. It was a strange ache, always in the same spot, just below the kneecap, and it showed up halfway through every practice lately. She glanced down at her legs. Both knees looked symmetrical, same shape, same scrapes, but only the left one complained.

At water break she found Lexa by the bleachers. "Does your knee ever hurt? Like, right here?" Mackenzie pressed the spot below her own kneecap.

"After jump rope day, sometimes," Lexa said. "Why?"

Mackenzie didn't answer right away. She was counting in her head. Last week they had done two hundred jumps, then layups, then box jumps. The week before, almost the same. The ache never came on game days, when they jumped less and rested more. It came after the practices with the most repetitions. "I think it's not random," she said slowly. "I think it's the amount."

"Amount of what?"

"Jumping. Same thing every time. Like a pattern."

Lexa shrugged. "Tell Coach."

Instead, Mackenzie tried an experiment on herself. At the next practice, when Ms. Nowak set up the box jump station, Mackenzie did half the reps everyone else did and spent the extra time working on her passing. If the jumping was the hidden cause, the ache should stay away. By the end of the hour, her knee was quiet for the first time in three weeks. She felt something loosen in her chest, though she also felt a little guilty, like she'd been keeping a secret.

She hadn't been the only one watching reps. Markus, who wanted the starting point guard spot more than he wanted lunch some days, had been hoarding the ball all season, taking extra shooting drills after everyone left. Today his right elbow was wrapped in ice, and he sat on the bench while the scrimmage ran without him. Mackenzie sat down beside him.

"What happened?"

"Youth league baseball, last spring," Markus said. "I was a pitcher. Coach made me stop mid-game because I'd hit my pitch limit for the day. I thought it was so unfair. Then the doctor said my growth plates were still open." He shifted the ice pack. "Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of kids' bones. They're weaker than the bone around them. That's why they put limits on young athletes, all that repetitive stress." He looked at the court. "I kept shooting anyway this season. Now my elbow's the one saying stop."

Mackenzie told him about her knee, and the half-reps, and how the ache had vanished. "I was going to keep testing it," she said. "Two more practices, half the jumps, see if the pattern holds. But maybe I should just tell Ms. Nowak."

"Tell her," Markus said. "I wish I'd told somebody in April."

The scrimmage ended, and Ms. Nowak walked over with her clipboard. Mackenzie stood up, knees wobbling just a little, and said, "Coach, can I talk to you about the jump drills?"

Beatrice sat cross-legged on Brynley's bedroom floor with Brynley's phone balanced on her knee, because her own phone was at home charging and this could not wait. The new app everyone at school was using had a green sign-up screen, and it had just asked for her birthday for the third time.

"I put my real birthday," she said. "Twice. It just kicks me back to the start."

Brynley leaned over her shoulder, chewing a strand of her hair. "What did you put?"

"September fourteenth. I turned eleven in September."

"Put thirteen," Brynley said, like it was obvious.

"I'm not lying about my age on the internet." Beatrice said it primly, then immediately felt how prim it sounded, which was ironic, since Brynley's mom had told them both twice not to be on the phone past eight. She tried the real birthday one more time anyway, holding her breath. The screen blinked and showed the same green form, empty again, asking for her date of birth.

"That's not a glitch," she said slowly. "It's doing it on purpose. It only rejects kids under thirteen."

Brynley flopped backward onto her rug. "My cousin says the app hates kids. She's dramatic."

Beatrice turned the phone over in her hands, thinking. Her dad explained internet rules at dinner sometimes, and something was tugging at the back of her memory, a word he had used. Children's something. She typed the phrase into the search bar: websites collecting personal information from children under 13, parental consent. The answer came up before she finished typing. "It's a law," she said. "The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998. Companies have to get parental consent before they collect personal info from kids under thirteen. That's why so many sites say you have to be thirteen. The app isn't being mean. It's following the law."

"So the app is being boring on purpose."

"Basically." Beatrice had a private little flare of pride in her chest, the kind she never showed at school. She had found the rule hiding behind the green screen. But she also understood, in a distant and slightly annoying way, that knowing the rule did not change the rule. She was eleven until September, and September was a long way off.

Brynley sat up. "So just wait? That's your big solution?"

"No." Beatrice scrolled to the bottom of the sign-up page and found a small link that said parental consent options. She clicked it. There was a form a parent could fill out, with permission and a signature. She turned the phone toward Brynley. "Can I ask your mom to call my dad?"

"You want to document permission. Like a permission slip for the internet."

"It's kind of a concept, isn't it? Permission slips for everything." Beatrice was already composing the text to her father in her head, deciding which words sounded the most responsible. She typed out the first line, showed it to Brynley for approval, and pressed send.

Avery had never set foot in the dilapidated community theatre before Tuesday, and now she was there four afternoons a week, rehearsing for the summer showcase. Mr. Perera supervised the rehearsals from a folding chair in the third row, calling out notes while the kids worked through their scenes. Avery's scene kept dying. Every time Graydon offered her something, like "Quick, the dragon is coming," she answered with "No, there's no dragon," and the scene fell flat like a dropped curtain.

"Say yes, and add something," Mr. Perera called. "That's the whole game."

That part she could fix. The harder problem was that even when she said yes, her scenes with Graydon still felt like two people reading a cereal box. On Thursday, hunting for a prop crown in the dusty storeroom, she found a battered paperback taped shut with a note folded inside the back cover. The note read: "To whoever finds this: the answer is in chapter five. High or low, the shift is the engine. Trust it. Signed, a kid who was terrified here in 1986." The book was Impro, by Keith Johnstone, 1979, and the margins were full of someone's pencil scribbles.

Avery read the chapter twice on the bus. Characters in a scene played higher or lower status, the book said, and shifting status created drama. That was the hidden pattern she'd been missing, and she had an idea for testing it. At Friday's rehearsal, she and Graydon ran the scene Larissa had written for them, a king and a servant. Avery played the king, ordering Graydon around, and the scene limped along, safe and boring. Then, on her next line, she flipped it. "Fetch my soup," she said, and then she lowered her eyes. "Unless... you think I should get it myself."

Graydon blinked, straightened up, and pointed at her. "Yes. You should get it yourself. And my laundry too."

Larissa laughed so hard from the front row that she slid off her seat, and Mr. Perera leaned forward in his chair for the first time all week. The scene got funnier the more orders the servant gave, because the king kept shrinking while the servant kept growing. Avery felt the insight land in her bones: the shift was the engine, just like the note said.

Afterward she found Graydon alone by the water fountain, staring at his shoes. "I was scared," he admitted. "Being the boss up there, that actually helped." She handed him the old paperback. "Chapter five," she said. "Keep it till Tuesday."

Ms. Ahmed had put a stack of old magazine ads on the history classroom table and told the class to sort them into piles. "One pile for ads that use famous people," she said, walking between the desks. "One for ads that use loaded words. One for ads that try to convince you everyone is buying the thing. I'll be around to supervise, but I want your own ideas first."

Luca picked up a faded ad from 1978. A television star stood beside a cassette player, grinning. "Celebrity testimonial," he said, and dropped it on the first pile. Haley held up another one. "This one says 'the car everyone trusts.' That's the everyone pile, right?" Malik read a shampoo ad aloud. "'The amazing, luxurious formula for gorgeous hair.' Those are the loaded words. They sound great but they don't actually say anything."

"They're tricks," Malik said.

"Not tricks exactly," Ms. Ahmed said. "More like techniques. People who write these know how our minds work."

Luca's family wanted a new television, and his mother kept saying she'd buy the brand "everybody knows is the best." Luca had asked her how she knew, and she'd said she just knew, that she'd heard it again and again. He wanted to figure out whether that was a real reason or not, because the other brand cost sixty dollars less.
