Nicholas had spent six weeks learning to eat cereal with his left hand, and now that the day had finally come to get the cast off, his little brother refused to sit next to him in the waiting room. "That saw is going to cut your arm off," his brother whispered, edging toward the far end of the bench.

Nicholas flexed his fingers inside the stiff fiberglass, thinking. He remembered the sound from the day they put the cast on, a buzzing roar like an angry hornet, and he remembered that the nurse had touched the blade flat against her own palm first, right in front of him. "See?" she had said. "The blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning. That lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath." He had believed her, mostly, but he still didn't fully understand how something could tell the difference between his arm and the cast.

He tested his thinking on the drive home afterward, holding the idea up to the light like a mystery novel. At the kitchen table, he grabbed Maxime's electric toothbrush, which Maxime had brought over along with Kabir and a bag of chips to celebrate the arm's return. Nicholas pressed the bristles against the back of his other hand and turned it on. His skin just wobbled. Then he pressed the vibrating handle against a stale piece of bread crust on the counter. The crust trembled, too, but it didn't break apart either, which proved nothing, and Kabir laughed so hard he sprayed chips.

"You're biased toward your own experiment," Maxime said, wiping the counter. "That's a toothbrush."

"It's a vibrating thing that didn't cut my skin," Nicholas said. "That's a pattern. Rules have patterns."

The next morning his brother still wouldn't stop worrying, so Nicholas had to prioritize: he could sleep in, or he could show a scared kid that his big brother still had both arms. He knocked on his brother's door holding two butter knives, one he spun like a tiny wheel and one he wiggled back and forth against his palm, buzz, buzz, buzz. "Which one would plow right through your skin if it touched you?" he asked. His brother pointed at the spinning one immediately.

"Right," Nicholas said, pulling up his sleeve to show the pale new arm, whole and unmarked, with the faint ghost of the cast still printed around it. "The loud one wiggles. It's all noise." His brother poked the arm once, twice, checking for hidden damage, then held up his own wrist. "So if I ever break mine, I get to pick the color?"

"Orange," Nicholas said. "Definitely orange."

Mya spread three kinds of seeds across the picnic table in her backyard: tiny poppy seeds, medium sunflower seeds, and big dried beans. Beside them she laid four tools, a straw, tweezers, a clothespin, and a nutcracker. Her little brother had asked her last night why his teacher called finch beaks "natural selection," and she had promised to show him instead of just telling him.

"You're a bird," she said. "Your beak is one of these. Pick up as many seeds as you can in thirty seconds."

Hawa had come over to help time the rounds, and Markus wanted to play too, though he tried to dismiss the whole thing at first. "It's just picking up seeds," he said.

"Then it should be easy for you," Hawa said, and started the timer.

Markus grabbed the nutcracker and cleared out every bean on the table but couldn't pinch a single poppy seed. Mya, with the tweezers, swept up the small seeds and left the beans behind. Her brother, working the straw, got nothing at all and complained until Mya showed him the straw could stab a bean like a fork. In three rounds, each tool beat the others at its own seed, and each one failed somewhere else.

"So on one island the food is small seeds," Mya said, "and on another island it's big hard ones. Now the part that matters." She held up the straw. "If a bird with a straw beak moves to the bean island, does it get to trade tools?"

"No," her brother said.

"Right. It's born with it. Baby finches get their beak shapes from their parents." She wrote the word inherited on the back of a seed packet. "And before that, we needed the first thing: the birds aren't all the same. Tweezers, nutcrackers, straws, all mixed together in one flock." She wrote varies above it. "Then the island picks the winner. Birds whose beaks match the food survive and have more babies, and the ones that don't, don't." She wrote the last line underneath and turned the packet so her brother could read all three.

Her brother was quiet for a moment. "So nobody chooses?"

"Nobody chooses."

The neighbor's cat slid along the fence then, low and predatory, eyes fixed on the sparrows at the feeder. The sparrows scattered instantly, all but one that had been sleeping, and the cat came away with nothing. Markus pointed at the cat and said its motivation was pretty obvious, and that it had failed the survival part of the test.

Mya laughed and gathered the seeds back into their cups. Her brother was still holding the straw, stabbing beans one at a time, very slowly, refusing to quit.

Matthew set the sheet music on the piano stand at the community centre and played the first four bars of the piece for the third time, and for the third time he sped up without meaning to. It was like his fingers had their own opinion about the tempo. In the next room the band rehearsal was starting, and he could hear Jack arguing with Evander about who got to play the timbales.

"You're rushing again," said Evander, leaning in the doorway with a granola bar. "You always rush. Last week Mr. Rodríguez stopped the whole ensemble twice because of you."

That was true, and it stung. Matthew remembered the winter concert, the flashback he kept trying to shake off: him at the keyboard, barreling through the quiet middle section while the trumpet player shot him a look, the music tumbling forward like a shopping cart with a bent wheel. He had practised that piece diligently for weeks, every day after school, and it had still fallen apart in public. Practising more clearly was not the answer. Something hidden was going on, some rule inside his own hands, and he could not watch it happen because it happened too fast to notice.

"Maybe the problem isn't your practising," Evander said, mouth full. "Maybe it's that you have no clock in your head. Have you tried that thing?" He pointed to a shelf near the window, where somebody's wooden box sat gathering dust. A little brass pendulum hung inside it, and a sticker on the lid said MAELZEL, 1815.

"What is it?"

"A metronome. Maelzel patented it in 1815. It ticks a steady tempo. Wind it up and see."

Matthew lifted it down, turned the crank, and set the sliding weight near the bottom of the pendulum. Tick. Tick. Tick. Slow, patient, stubborn. He played the first line along with it and discovered something odd: the ticking did not feel fast, but his hands were still arriving early, sneaking ahead of each click like kids cutting a lunch line. So the rushing was real, and it was measurable. Then he tried a simple experiment. He played the line without the metronome, stopped, and tried to guess how many seconds had passed. He guessed four. The clock on the wall said nearly six. His internal sense of time ran quick, like a scale that always weighed light.

He recruited Jack from the rehearsal room to sit beside him and clap the ticks while Matthew played the dynamics, soft in the middle passage, loud at the end, and Jack's clapping held him back like a leash made of sound. When Mr. Rodríguez passed through on his way to check the first aid kit, he paused in the doorway and listened to all forty bars arrive at the finish line together.

"Somebody's found the metronome," Mr. Rodríguez said.

"Somebody found out he can't trust his own head," Matthew said, and set the weight one notch slower.

Easton sat at his dad's desk on a Saturday, staring at a spreadsheet full of numbers that made his eyes feel like raisins. His dad had challenged him: track the recycling totals for all four floors of the office building, add each floor's column with a formula, and turn it into a bar chart by lunch. The prize was a milkshake. Easton wanted that milkshake more than he had wanted almost anything that week.

He typed numbers into column B, then tried to mimic what he had seen his dad do, clicking the little fx button and writing =SUM(B2:B9). When the total appeared at the bottom of the column all by itself, he actually laughed out loud. "It counted them for me," he said to the empty office. "Like magic, except with math." Then he highlighted the totals and clicked Chart, and four bars climbed up the screen. Floor Three's bar towered over the others like a skyscraper next to garden sheds.

"Whoa," said a voice behind him. It was Sana, whose mom worked down the hall and who always showed up when there were snacks involved. "Floor Three is crushing everyone."

Easton frowned at the screen. Something felt off, the way a picture of a friend can look strange if it's stretched. He looked at the actual numbers. Floor Three had 96 bottles. Floor Two had 92. That was only four more, barely anything. So why did the bars look like a mountain versus a pebble? "That's weird," he said. "The numbers are almost the same."

He leaned closer and noticed tiny marks along the side of the chart. The bottom of the bars didn't start at zero. They started at 90. Easton rubbed his chin like a detective in a movie he'd seen once. What if the bars started at zero instead? Would that fix it? There was only one way to find out. He right-clicked the axis, hunted through the menus, found a box that said "minimum," and typed 0.

The bars collapsed. All four of them turned into nearly equal towers, like a row of apartment buildings built by the same architect. Sana burst out laughing. "It was faking! Floor Three looked like a giant and it's only ahead by four bottles."

"So the chart wasn't lying exactly," Easton said slowly, watching the honest new bars. "But if the axis starts above zero, small differences look way bigger than they really are." He felt like he had pulled a curtain back on something sneaky, which was ironic, because he had made the sneaky chart himself. He wondered how many charts in newspapers and on TV did this exact trick, and whether anyone ever noticed.

Just then his dad came around the corner with a raised eyebrow. "Any word on an amendment to my recycling report, or are you two just decorating my computer?"

"It's done," Easton said, and hit print.

Sara had lost the eight hundred metres three times this season, and every time it happened the same way. She exploded off the line, led the whole first lap, and then her legs turned to wet sand on the second while other runners streamed past her. Tonight, in the empty school gym, she stood at the marked indoor oval Mr. Koné had taped onto the floor and stared at the two lap lines like they were a puzzle. Something invisible was beating her, and she wanted to see it.

"Trying to figure out why you die at four hundred?" Mohamed asked, dribbling a basketball nearby. Anna sat on the bleachers with her laptop, unwrapping a granola bar and offering half to Sara without a word.

"I run fast," Sara said. "That should be good. So why does fast lose?"

"Maybe fast isn't the crucial thing," Anna said. "Maybe it's fast at the right time." She turned the laptop around. "I found the world record race. Want to watch how a champion paced it?"

They crowded around the screen and watched David Rudisha run the men's eight hundred metres at the 2012 London Olympics. Sara leaned close to the split times, and something clicked. "Look at that," she said slowly. "His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second. The fastest man ever slowed down on purpose, kind of. He didn't save everything." She looked up. "So it's not slow first, sprint second. It's just slightly less fast first."

Mr. Koné, locking the equipment cage, raised an eyebrow. "You going to test that, or talk about it all night?"

Sara borrowed the stopwatch Mohamed tossed her and ran lap after lap while Anna called out splits and Mohamed jogged beside her the last fifty metres each time, shouting that she had more left than she thought. On her first attempt she went out too hard anyway and finished gasping. "You're excited, not calculating," Anna said gently, handing her a water bottle. "Try forgetting the girl next to you exists."

The next time, Sara counted her steps through the first curve, held herself back a whisper's worth, and told herself the leader of lap one was not the winner of the race. When she crossed the second line, her lungs burned but her legs still answered, and Anna shouted, "Negative split by a hair!" Sara bent over, laughing between breaths. "So that's the factor I was missing," she said. "Not effort. Placement of effort." Mohamed held up his hand, and she slapped it, still catching her breath.

At the meet on Saturday, two girls surged ahead of her in the first curve, and for one second every muscle begged to chase them. Sara let them go. She kept her rhythm, her whisper's worth held back, and when the bell rang for the final lap she was still whole. Coming off the last bend she found another gear she had left in storage, passed one girl, then the other, and hit the tape with her arms up. Anna's voice cracked yelling her name from the fence. Sara walked over on shaking legs, took the water Anna held out, and said, "Tell me my splits."

The cultural center's social hall smelled of matzo ball soup and candle wax, and Sophia found her family's table near the window, right beside the ones Paris and Santino from school had saved for their own families. Her little cousin Benjie, who was seven, sat clutching a folded paper under his napkin like it was something he'd smuggled in. He had been muttering at breakfast all week, whispering in the car, and once Sophia had caught him practicing to the bathroom mirror.

"You look like you're going to be sick," she whispered, sliding into the chair beside him.

"I'm not sick," Benjie said, but he didn't let go of the paper.

Sophia thought about last year, when she had been the youngest at the Seder and it had been her turn. She remembered standing up with her knees shaking and her voice cracking on the second question, and how her grandmother had smiled the whole way through anyway. She had almost offered to take Benjie's place this year, the way an older cousin supposedly could, but she'd decided against it and still wasn't sure that had been fair of her.

She tested a theory quietly. "Is it because of the part where everyone stares at you?" she asked.

Benjie shook his head. "It's because I'll mess up the Four Questions and everyone will know the youngest kid couldn't do it."

Sophia leaned back. So that was it. He didn't mind the crowd; he minded being the one who was supposed to know. "The youngest one always asks them," she said. "That's how it works. It's not a test you can fail. Even if you skip a word, it still counts."

He looked at the paper, then at the candles, then at her. "Even if my voice goes squeaky?"

"Even then."

Down the table, her uncle was telling the story of the Exodus from Egypt, and her aunt was describing how the center had asked families to donate extra grape juice and horseradish for the guests who came without any. The horseradish, the bitter herb, was notorious at their table for making Grandpa's eyes water every single year, and by the time the plagues were recited, sure enough, he was dabbing his face with his napkin while everyone pretended not to notice.

At last the moment came. Benjie stood up. The paper shook in his hand and his voice wobbled on the first question, squeaked badly on the third, and dropped so low on the fourth that Sophia's mother leaned forward to hear. But nobody laughed, nobody corrected him, and when he sat down, Paris, three tables away, gave him a little wave.

"That was pretty good," Sophia told him.

Benjie refolded the paper very carefully and put it in his pocket. "Next year I'm doing it without the paper," he said, and reached for a piece of matzo.

The science museum's chemistry hall had a wall-sized periodic table, and Edouard's class had twenty minutes before the bus left. Mr. Abdi handed out a quiz sheet with one question left blank on purpose: "If an oxygen atom somehow lost a proton, what would you have then?"

"Trick question," Jaylen said. "It would just be broken oxygen."

Edouard wasn't so sure. He stood in front of the wall and traced his finger along the boxes until he found oxygen. In the top corner of the box sat the number eight. Next to oxygen was nitrogen, with a seven. He had skimmed the little label under the table that morning, but he hadn't really read it, and now he leaned in again. Above the boxes it said: atomic number. He stared at that word, then at the eight, then at the seven.

"Okay," he said slowly, "so oxygen is number eight and nitrogen is number seven."

Priya came over from the hydrogen display, where she had been trying to make her reflection contract into the curved mirror beside it. "So what?"

"So the numbers are the protons." He tapped the wall. "That's the whole point of the number. And if oxygen somehow lost one proton, it wouldn't be broken oxygen. It would have seven protons." He dragged his finger one box to the left. "It would be nitrogen."

Jaylen shook his head. "That can't be right. Oxygen is oxygen because of what it does, right? It's the stuff you breathe."

"Any atom with eight protons is oxygen," Edouard said, reading the panel under the display case, which repeated it in plain print. "An atom with seven protons is nitrogen. That's what makes it that element. The proton count decides."

Jaylen looked at the wall for a long moment. His shoulders dropped. "So the quiz answer is nitrogen. Losing one proton turns it into a totally different thing." He rubbed his eyes. "I was sure it was a trick question. I changed my mind, and I hate that."

Mr. Abdi walked by collecting the sheets. "Answers, gentlemen, ladies. Bus in five."

Jaylen wrote his answer, then held the pencil up. "From your perspective this is fun. From mine it's disturbing. You're telling me the air is one proton away from being wrong."

"You'll live," Priya said. "You've had a chronic case of being wrong since September, and you keep surviving it."

On the bus, Edouard watched the museum shrink in the window and thought about how something nobody could ever see, one proton, was the only thing standing between two boxes on a wall. He pulled out his notebook, wrote 8 at the top of a page and 7 below it, and drew an arrow between them.

"One," he said, and underlined it twice.

The drum kit took up half of Shania's garage, and the old upright piano, inherited from a grandfather nobody remembered, took up most of the rest. Scarlett sat at its bench with the sheet music for "Moonlight Over Water" propped against the music stand, her fingers hovering above the keys. Shania twirled a drumstick and waited.

"From the top," Scarlett said. "And watch me this time, because we keep rushing the middle."

They had practiced the piece for two weeks, and it still fell apart in the same place every single time. The opening sounded fine, dreamy and rolling, but by the ending the whole thing turned into a wall of noise. Shania hit the cymbals like she was trying to provoke the neighbors into calling about it, and Scarlett pounded along to keep up, and the last eight measures dissolved into mush.

Shania's mom had even knocked on the garage door once, holding her ears, which Shania had treated as a compliment. That was the problem, Scarlett thought. Shania wanted the performance to end big and loud, a finish that would make the audience sit up. She wanted the drums to be the rudder of the whole piece, steering where it went. Scarlett just wanted it to sound right.

She looked at the last page again. Under the final measures sat two tiny letters, and above them, near the loud part in the middle, two different ones. She had assumed they were smudges or some kind of printing mistake. But now she noticed the same letters turning up in every piece in the folder. She fetched her music dictionary from her backpack, the one she'd bought at the used book sale and never opened, and looked up the first one.

"Shania," she said slowly, "come look at this."

Shania leaned over the piano, drumstick dangling from her fingers. "What?"

"Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft." Scarlett tapped the page. "That's what's marked on the ending. Very soft. Not louder. And ff means very loud. That's the middle part. We've been playing the whole thing exactly backward." She felt strangely buoyant, the way she did when a puzzle suddenly snapped together. All this time there had been a pattern hiding on the page, and they had stomped right past it.

"So the ending is supposed to shrink?" Shania looked wounded. "That's the opposite of a grand finish."

"Try it once," Scarlett said. "Just once. If it's terrible, you can hit everything as hard as you want."

Shania sighed like the weight of the world had landed on her shoulders, picked up her brushes instead of sticks, and counted them in with a whisper. Scarlett let her right hand drift down to almost nothing, and the last notes of "Moonlight Over Water" faded out like a tide going still.

"Okay," Shania admitted, brushing a cymbal so lightly it barely breathed. "That's kind of amazing. Do it again."

The away team's goalie had just made his thirty-second save when Nikhil leaned across the bleachers and asked the question that had been bothering Felix all week. "Okay, so a perfect passer rating in the NFL is 158.3. Why not 100? Who picks a number like that?" Felix pulled his toque down over his ears. The rink was cold enough that his breath hung in front of him, and the scoreboard above the ice showed shots on goal: 32 for one team, 9 for the other. "Somebody had to pick something," Ulysse said, without looking up from the game. "They couldn't just say he's good."

Felix could not stop thinking about it, even while the home team's best player flew down the wing and rang a shot off the post. On the drive home, his dad had the sports radio on, and a voice said that a quarterback had a rating of 112.4. "That's out of 158.3," the voice added. Felix stared out the window at the streetlights. He tried an experiment on Monday at school. He wrote 112.4 on a scrap of paper, drew a line under it, and wrote 100 under that. Then he crossed it out and wrote 158.3 instead, because that was the ceiling, the way 100 percent was the ceiling on a math test.

At lunch he showed the paper to Nikhil and Ulysse in the cafeteria. "Here's a hypothetical," Felix said. "A quarterback throws one pass, and it's a touchdown. Perfect, right? But his rating isn't 158.3, because the number isn't for one throw. It squishes a whole pile of throws into one number, like how the scoreboard last night said the goalie made 32 saves, but that doesn't tell you if the saves were easy or impossible." Nikhil squinted at the paper. "So the weird number is weird because it's doing a weird job." "Basically," Felix said. Ulysse stabbed his fork into his pasta. "This is why I like goals. One goal equals one goal."

Ms. Ho overheard the last part when she came by to collect trays. She had coached Felix's floor hockey club the year before, and she knew about numbers, too, because she kept the standings for the city league. "You three should see how the league ranks teams," she said. "People always modify the rules when one number isn't telling the whole story. It drives the parents wild." She handed them a printed standings sheet. Felix ran his finger down the columns: wins, losses, goals for, goals against, and then a single percentage at the end. The team in first place had fewer wins than the team in third. "How?" Nikhil said. "Games in hand," Ms. Ho said, and walked off with the tray cart rattling behind her.

That evening Felix did his test. He took the standings sheet home, got out his calculator, and worked out each team's percentage from its own wins and games played, not from the wins alone. Third place rose above first. The percentage had been hiding the pattern the whole time, the way stamina hides under a player's jersey, unseen until the third period when he's still skating and everyone else is gripping their knees. Felix texted a photo of his recalculation to Nikhil, who replied with a single message: "so the number was telling the truth but not the WHOLE truth."

At Thursday's floor hockey practice, Ms. Ho taped the corrected standings to the gym wall, with Felix's percentages beside each team. Ulysse looked at it, then at Felix, and pointed his stick at him. "Congratulations," Ulysse said. "You're now the kid who does math for fun." Felix picked up a ball and dropped it at centre floor. "Faceoff first," he said. "We'll settle the rankings the old way."

Luca sat on the crinkly paper of the nurse's cot, holding his new prescription slip like it might bite him. The words OD and OS were typed beside two numbers, and beside those, in Mr. Bekele's careful handwriting, was a note that the glasses would arrive Thursday. Luca had read the slip eleven times since the eye doctor's office on Saturday, and every time the letters looked worse.

"OD," Lucien whispered from the doorway, because Lucien had promised to walk to the nurse's office with him and then refused to leave. "You know what that stands for? Ocular Disease." Luca's stomach dropped. "OS has to be Ocular Something worse," Lucien went on. "Why else would they hide it in Latin?"

That was exactly the part that bugged Luca. Nobody hides good news in Latin. But Mr. Bekele was already coming back with the folder, so Luca did the only reasonable thing, which was to shove the slip under his math workbook and pretend to examine the poster about lichen on the wall, which had nothing to do with anything but gave him somewhere to point his eyes. The poster said lichen was actually two organisms living together, a fungus and an alga, and Luca's brain snagged on that even in the middle of his panic. Two things, one word. Two letters, one slip.

He thought about Latin class. Oculus meant eye; he was almost sure. He'd seen dexter before too, in a word for right-handed. And sinister meant left, which was unfair to left-handed people but that was Latin for you. He tried it out against the paper, covering one letter at a time. If OD meant the right eye, then the number beside it belonged to his right eye, and the doctor had said his right eye was the blurrier one at the board. Luca covered his left eye and squinted at the eye chart hanging on the wall. Blurrier. Right. The letters weren't a disease at all; they were an address label.

"Mr. Bekele," Luca said, holding up the slip before he could lose his nerve, "on here, does OD mean my right eye and OS my left eye? Like, oculus dexter and oculus sinister?"

Mr. Bekele smiled and tapped the two letters. "OD is the right eye, OS is the left. Straight from the Latin."

Lucien's mouth fell open. "So it's not a disease?"

"It's an address," Luca said, and it felt inevitable, the way the whole terrifying code had cracked open the second he stopped guessing and started testing. The two boys compromised on what to do next: Lucien wanted to go look up more Latin, and Luca wanted to walk to the window to see whether the tree across the yard had leaves he could actually count. They did both, fast, and Luca counted eleven leaves on one branch before the bell even rang.

Tristan crouched at one end of the science lab with a marble in his hand and ten minutes left before the bell. Mr. Kim had set the challenge at the start of class: measure the speed of a rolling ball, draw a distance-time graph, and have it on his desk by the end of the period. Aryan had already finished his graph, all neat columns and confident lines, and Tristan's paper was still blank.

"Want me to time it?" Zia offered, holding the stopwatch. "But I'm impartial, so no arguing if your numbers are terrible."

"Deal," Tristan said. He marked the tile floor with chalk every fifty centimetres, set the marble at the zero line, and gave it a push. Zia called out the times as it crossed each mark, and Tristan scribbled them down. The marble moved fast at first, then slower, and by the last chalk line it was barely crawling. When he plotted the points, they didn't make a straight line at all. They curved, flattening out like a hill levelling into a plain.

"That can't be right," Tristan said. "Aryan's graph is straight."

Aryan leaned over from the next bench. "I rolled mine on the counter. Smooth surface. Yours is on the floor, right by the carpet square where the stools sit?"

Tristan looked down. His chalk line ended a hand's width from the ragged square of carpet Mr. Kim kept there to stop the stools scratching the tile. His marble had rolled the whole course on tile, but the last run of the day before, when he'd tested it before setting up, had stopped almost immediately on the carpet. Why had that one quit so fast? He had an idea forming, but he couldn't quite articulate it yet.

"Five minutes," Zia warned.

"Roll it on the carpet," Tristan said suddenly. "The whole course. I'll move the carpet out and lay it flat." They dragged the carpet square into the open, chalked new marks on its edge, and rolled again. The marble crossed the first mark at a decent speed, then the second much slower, and died halfway to the third. Tristan grinned. It wasn't that the tile made the ball fast. It was that the floor was quietly taking the ball's energy the whole time, and the carpet took it much faster. On smooth tile the ball kept going a long way; on carpet it stopped quickly. That was why his graph curved. The ball had been slowing down the entire time.

He drew the curved line carefully through his points, labelled it, and dashed the graph onto Mr. Kim's desk just as the bell rang.

Mr. Kim looked at the curve and raised an eyebrow. "And what does this shape tell you, Tristan?"

"The ball was losing the whole time," Tristan said, out of breath. "I just couldn't see it until I watched where it stopped."

Parker had eleven dollars in his pocket and a five-year plan taped to his bedroom wall, and today he was going to spend every dollar at the farmers' market on tomatoes. Not to eat. His mother had said that if he saved the money instead, she'd help him open a savings account, and Parker wanted to see the actual numbers first.

He found Mr. Kim at his vegetable stall, because Mr. Kim was the only adult Parker knew who kept a calculator clipped to his apron. "If I put ten dollars in a savings account at six percent," Parker asked, "how much do I have after five years?"

"Simple interest or compound?" said a voice behind him. It was Londyn, from his class, holding a bag of peaches and grinning like she'd caught him doing homework in public.

"What's the difference?" Parker said.

Mr. Kim sold a bunch of carrots to a woman with a wagon, then leaned on his scale. "With simple, the bank pays you sixty cents a year on ten dollars, every year, the same. Five years, three dollars extra. But with compound, the bank pays interest on your interest. Try it on my calculator."

Parker typed. After one year, ten dollars and sixty cents. After two, eleven dollars and twenty-four cents, because the sixty cents earned interest too. By year five he had thirteen dollars and thirty-eight cents. Thirty-eight cents more than simple. It wasn't much, and he said so.

"That's because ten dollars is small," Londyn said. "My cousin saves for a mountain bike, and she's obsessive about compound interest. She taught me the rule of 72."

"The what?"

"The rule of 72," Londyn said. "You divide 72 by the percentage rate, and that's about how many years your money takes to double. At six percent, 72 divided by 6 is 12, so it takes about 12 years."

Parker did the math in his head. "I'm eleven. My money would double by the time I'm twenty-three." He stared at the calculator like it had contradicted him, which was silly, because calculators can't argue. "Twelve years. That feels like forever."

"That's the contradiction of saving," Londyn said, biting into a peach. "The boring years are the ones doing all the work."

Tara wandered over from the honey stall, heard the whole thing, and asked what happens at twelve percent. Parker divided 72 by 12 in his head. "Six years to double. Twice as fast." Tara looked at Mr. Kim. "Is he right?"

Mr. Kim shrugged. "The rule says so, and the rule's been around longer than my carrots."

They were unanimous, then: Parker should keep his eleven dollars, let his mother open the account Friday, and come back next week to buy tomatoes for the plan instead of the pocket. He put his money away and picked up one perfect tomato anyway.

"For research," Parker said, and paid Mr. Kim a quarter.

Brooke spotted the problem the moment her mother parked the car. Tessa was already waiting on the sidewalk outside the gurdwara, and Tessa was wearing flip-flops, which was fine, but she was also bareheaded, which was not. Brooke had explained the rules twice on the walk to school yesterday: everyone took off their shoes, and everyone covered their head. Tessa had nodded, but nodding was not the same as remembering.

"I forgot a scarf," Tessa said, before Brooke even reached her. "I had one on the counter this morning and then my little brother invaded my room and now it's probably in his dinosaur bin."

Inside the entrance, the shoe shelves stretched along one wall, and Brooke counted the rows of sandals and sneakers while she unlaced her own shoes. "You can borrow mine," she said. "The scarf, not the shoes. My shoes would swallow you whole." Tessa laughed, which was the point of saying it.

Her mother patted her bag. "I brought two scarves, just in case. One of them is tropical, very loud parrots."

"That one's mine," Brooke said immediately.

They dropped their shoes on an empty shelf and pinned the scarves over their hair. In the main hall, the singing had already started, and the smell of food drifted down from the langar hall upstairs. Tessa leaned close. "This is like a siege," she whispered. "There are so many aunties guarding the door to the kitchen and they all want to feed me."

"That's not a siege," Brooke whispered back. "A siege is when nobody lets food in."

Colton appeared beside them with his little brother trailing behind him like a duckling. "Brooke, your grandmother is looking for you," he said. "She says you promised to help carry the trays of karah prasad, and she says, and I quote, don't hide behind your friend." He grinned. "I told her I didn't know where you were, but she looked at me like I was a very bad liar."

Brooke ducked behind Tessa, then peeked out. "Okay, okay, I'm coming." She turned to Tessa. "Watch. When they pass out the sweet pudding, hold both hands like a bowl. And if a grandma gives you a second helping, just take it. Trust me."

"Third helping," Colton said. "It's always three."

Upstairs, Brooke's grandmother pressed a tray into her hands, warm through the metal, and steered her toward the rows of people waiting with their palms open. Tessa followed with the parrot scarf slipping sideways over her hair, and Brooke reached back without looking and tucked the corner straight again.

"Hold it steady," her grandmother said.

"I've got it," Brooke said, and stepped into the line of light from the kitchen doorway, tray first.

The bus rattled over the pothole by the gym, and Logan's finger slid down the page of his worn copy of Romeo and Juliet. Ms. Thompson had assigned each student eight lines to paraphrase into modern English by tomorrow, and his eight lines were a jumble of thees and thous that refused to line up. He read them under his breath, tapping the edge of the book against his knee.

"You look like the bus ran over your homework," Maiya said, dropping into the seat across the aisle.

"Worse. 'But soft, behold what light through yonder window breaks?' Fine, I get that part. But then it's 'She speaks yet she says nothing' and suddenly everything is thou this and thee that. Why does the word keep changing?"

Maiya leaned over and squinted at his page. "Maybe they're two different words for two different jobs?"

Logan stared at the lines. A pattern flickered at the edge of his thinking, like something moving behind a curtain. He tried reading the speech out loud twice, then held his pencil under one word at a time. "Okay, watch. 'The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars.' Then, 'It is my lady, O it is my love, O that she knew she were.'" He paused. "But over here, 'See how she leans her cheek upon her hand, O that I were a glove upon that hand, that I might touch that cheek.'"

"So?" said Maiya.

"So it's like when I say 'I' and 'me.' You don't say 'touch I's cheek.' You say 'touch my cheek.'" He flipped back a page, hunting. "Here. 'I love thee.' That has to be 'I love you.' You wouldn't say 'I love thou,' the same way you wouldn't say 'she loves I.'" His pencil moved faster now. "Thee is the object form of thou, like me is the object form of I. Thou does the action. Thee gets it done to them."

Maiya pulled out her own copy and ran her finger through her assigned lines. "Then my whole paraphrase is wrong. I translated every single thee as though." She groaned, then started scratching out words with her eraser, the paper shivering under her hand.

Logan copied his version into his notebook, testing each line against his new rule. Some guesses still felt shaky, and he scribbled question marks beside two of them for Ms. Thompson. When the bus hit the next pothole, he barely noticed; he was too busy wondering whether other old words bent like this too, and whether he could find more of them hiding in the play before anyone told him.

At his stop he swung his backpack over one shoulder and held the book open against his chest. "Tomorrow I'm going to ask Ms. Thompson if there's a whole list of these," he called back to Maiya.

"Good luck," she said, already erasing her third line.

The bell over the door gave its usual tired jangle, and Austin slid onto the stool beside the slushie machine, where he always sat while his mom paid the electric bill at the counter next door. Mr. Karimi's store was tranquil in the late afternoon, shelves humming with refrigerator noise, nobody in line. Austin spread his math retake sheet on the glass counter and stared at the first problem: 2x + 3x + 4 = 24.

He had to pass this one. Fail again and he'd be pulled from Friday's basketball game, and Loick was counting on him to play point guard while Loick's brother recovered from a concussion at the last game. Austin wrote quickly: 2x + 3x is 5x, so he penciled 5x, then looked at the + 4 and kept going. 5x + 4. His pencil drifted toward combining those too, and he wrote 9x = 24, because that felt like the same move. He got x = 24 over 9, a weird decimal, and something about it made the back of his neck prickle.

"Check it," said a voice. Loick had come in for gum and was reading over his shoulder. "Plug it back in."

Austin tried. If x was that decimal, then 5x plus 4 should equal 24. It didn't. It came out wrong, off by more than a little, and Loick tapped the spot where Austin had merged the terms. "You can't do that there. Look at the next one." Loick flipped Austin's practice sheet, which his teacher had marked in red: 2x + 3 = 9. Beside it, red pen: "What does the x stand for?" Austin had written 5x = 9, and gotten it wrong. That was the exact mistake, again, hiding in tonight's problem.

He stared at the + 4. It was just a number, sitting alone, no letter attached. The x terms had letters. 2x and 3x were like coins of the same kind, stackable, but the + 4 was a different kind of coin. Austin erased his work and formulated a new plan: combine only the matching terms first, 2x + 3x into 5x, leave the + 4 alone, then do the same thing to both sides. Subtract 4 from each side. Divide each side by 5. x = 4. He checked it and it landed perfectly on 24.

Mr. Karimi came over to restock the gum and glanced at the paper. "So you changed your mind about that step," he said.

"I did," Austin said, and boxed the answer twice. "Five x. Not nine. Four is just four."

Loick paid for his gum and held the door. "Friday, point guard. Bring that brain."

Florence spread the notebook page across the lunch table and pinned the corner with her milk carton before the breeze could invade the cafeteria and carry it off. On the page were two columns of numbers, game by game, for Lisa and for Issa.

"The tournament sheet is due to Mr. Ho tomorrow morning," Lisa said, tapping the deadline circled twice in red pen. "He only takes one of us as Florence's doubles partner. So make it fair."

Florence had watched both of them play basketball all season, and she had kept score in her notebook because arguments about who was better always turned into shouting. Now she added each column of points and divided by the number of games, twice, checking herself. Both averages came out the same. She slid the notebook to the middle of the table.

"You're identical," she said. "Eight points a game, both of you."

"That can't be right," Issa said. She leaned over the columns, her braid dropping into the milk puddle. "Look. Lisa scored eight every single game. Eight, eight, eight, like a robot. I had a sixteen, and a twenty, and then a two, and a zero." She pointed at the zero. "That was the day I twisted my ankle. And the two was the game right before the science trip, when I was up until one in the morning finishing my poster."

"Your poster," Florence said. "The one with the owl?"

" nocturnal animals, yes. Three weeks of work. I was a zombie at practice."

Florence looked at the columns again. Same total, same average, but Lisa's numbers sat in a tight line while Issa's leapt up and crashed down like a roller coaster she could almost hear. An average, she realized, squashed all those separate games into one number, and once it did, the shape of them disappeared. Two players could match on average and still be nothing alike.

"Here's what I keep thinking," she said slowly. "In the tournament, we play four matches in one day. Whoever I pick has to show up four times in a row."

Issa sat back. "So you're picking Lisa."

"I didn't say that." Florence pulled out a pencil. "I said I want to test something. Tomorrow morning, before the sheet is due, both of you shoot twenty free throws. Not one average score. I write down every single shot, each one, in order."

Lisa frowned. "Why does the order matter?"

"Because I want to see the spread," Florence said. "I want to see whether you go make, make, make, or miss, miss, hot streak, collapse. One number can't tell me that."

The next morning the gym smelled like floor wax, and Mr. Ho unlocked the door at seven fifteen and watched from the bleachers with his coffee, saying nothing. Lisa shot first: fifteen makes out of twenty, evenly spaced, steady as rain dripping off a gutter. Then Issa, rested and ankle taped, hit her first nine in a row, missed five straight, and finished with six more makes. Florence wrote down every shot.

"Same count," Lisa said, counting the marks. "Fifteen each."

Florence ran her finger down Issa's column, over the cold streak in the middle. "You're the better pick when you're hot, and the worse pick when you're not," she said. "And I can't know which one walks onto the court."

Issa bounced the ball once, twice. "So it's Lisa?"

Lisa picked up the pen and turned the sign-up sheet toward them. "Write both our names in the alternates line," she said. "Florence picks her partner the morning of the tournament, game by game, and I shoot first."

The moving truck idled in the driveway while Beatrice climbed into the cargo area between the boxes. Her father had said she could ride in the back as far as the corner store, where he would stop and let her up front for the long highway stretch. She counted the boxes around her: nineteen, and only three had anything written on them.

"You should have labeled them," said Brenden, who had come to say goodbye and had lingered until the loading was done. He was standing at the tailgate with his hands in his pockets. "My dad labels every box with the room it belongs in and what's inside it. When we moved, the movers carried each box straight to the right place."

"Then it's the irony of my life that we did it the other way," Beatrice said. She looked at the wall of brown cardboard, all of it identical, and thought about the new house she had seen only once, in photographs. "Three labeled, sixteen blank."

She tried to work out which box held her bedsheets. She could not see inside them, so she tested what she could observe. She pressed the top of the nearest box and felt something soft and folded, which could be sheets but could also be winter coats. The second box rattled, so that was desk stuff. She rocked the third and it shifted like books. The pattern was clear, in a useless way: soft, loud, heavy, and no way to tell the sheets from the coats. Mr. Tanaka, the neighbor from across the street, leaned over the tailgate with a marker in his hand. "Found this behind your recycling bin," he said. "You dropped it yesterday."

Beatrice took the marker. The truck would leave in ten minutes, before her father finished the paperwork, so she had ten minutes and a decision. She chose the soft box, opened the flaps, and found coats. Under the coats, folded flat, were her sheets, which meant the sheets and the coats had been packed together and the box would have to be opened twice at the other end, once for her bedroom and once for the hall closet. She wrote BEDROOM on it, then added COATS AND SHEETS. One by one she thumbed boxes open, checked the contents, and wrote the room and everything inside. It was not systematic, the way Brenden's dad had done it, because she was doing it backwards, opening boxes instead of labeling them as they were filled, but by the time her father rapped on the side of the truck she had covered fourteen of the sixteen in thick black letters.

At the new house, after dark, the hallway filled with boxes. The two unlabeled ones sat in the middle of the floor while every marked box went straight upstairs, straight to the kitchen, straight to the bathroom, carried by movers who never asked a single question. Beatrice found the marked box, pulled out her sheets, and made her bed before she unpacked anything else. From the doorway, her mother said, "Dinner in twenty minutes."

"Tell me where the plates are," Beatrice called back, "and I'll show you which box."

The science room smelled like vinegar and old chalk, and Mr. Adebayo had set out five unmarked cups along the back counter. Eli leaned over them with Kelly, who was already copying the color chart onto her wrist with a pen. "Blue litmus turns red for acids," she muttered, "red turns blue for bases, and purple means neutral. That's the whole map." Eli tore two strips of paper from the packet, careful not to touch the ends, because the last time they did this Tyler had fingerprinted a mystery cup and ruined the results for the whole row.

Tyler's cup was the problem. He had grabbed the second one from the left, sniffed it, and announced, "It's lemon juice, and lemon juice is neutral, because it's food. Nobody puts acid in food." Kelly raised an eyebrow but said nothing. Eli wanted to prove him wrong, but more than that, he wanted to be sure himself. He had a plan: dip the blue strip, dip the red strip, and if both stayed the same color, the cup was neutral. If the blue strip turned red, that meant acid, and then he could check the pH number against the chart Mr. Adebayo had taped to the window. That was the part Eli liked. The invisible thing, the acid itself, left a mark you could read, like footprints from something you never actually saw.

Outside the window, the sixth graders were pulling up invasive vines along the fence, the ones that had crept over the native bushes all spring. One of them held up a fat larva in a trowel of dirt and carried it to the compost bin like it was treasure. Eli dipped his strips. The blue strip went red, bright and instant, like it had been waiting. The red strip stayed red. He laid both strips on a paper towel and slid the pH chart over until the color matched.

"Two," he said. "It's about a two."

Kelly leaned in, frowning at the chart. "That's really low. Low numbers mean strong acid, right?"

Tyler crossed his arms. "It's still food."

"Okay, but lemon juice has a pH of about two," Eli said, tapping the chart. "That makes it strongly acidic compared with most things people drink." He lined the cup up beside Kelly's sample, plain water, which had barely changed either strip, and beside the cup of soapy water that had flipped red paper to blue in a lazy, slow way, as if it were thinking it over.

Tyler stared at his lemon juice for a long moment, then at the red strip that had been blue a minute ago. "So my teeth are sitting in acid every time I drink this?"

"Not explaining teeth," Eli said quickly, before anyone could start. Mr. Adebayo drifted past their table, glanced at the strips laid out in order, and gave a single approving nod without breaking his stride. Outside, the vine pile grew taller, and the kid with the trowel waved the larva at the window one last time before tipping it gently into the compost.

Kelly capped the pen and held out her marked-up wrist. "Okay, genius. Cup four. What's your prediction?"

Eli picked up a fresh blue strip, hovered it over the mystery cup, and said, "Watch this."

The trouble started before the aquarium even came into view, because Mr. Santos made everyone walk the last two blocks from the bus. Halfway there they passed the old fire station, and London stopped dead in front of a painting by the garage doors. It showed a black-and-white spotted dog sitting beside a gleaming old engine. "Why would a fire station hang up a picture of a dog?" London asked. "Did it save somebody? Was it a mascot?" Tegan guessed it won a contest. Brooklyn guessed nothing, because she honestly had no idea, and that bugged her the way an itch bugs you inside a cast.

Mr. Santos clapped his hands and herded them along, but Brooklyn kept thinking about it. At the aquarium he handed out a scavenger hunt sheet with a bonus question worth ten points: "Find the history room and solve the spotted dog mystery." Ten points. Tegan, who was failing science by exactly the width of a shrimp, grabbed Brooklyn's sleeve. "You're the one who always advocates for the weird exhibits. Advocate for the history room."

"Not the weird exhibits," Brooklyn said. "The good ones."

The hunt itself was fun for about twenty minutes. They found a temporary exhibit on jellyfish, where London said the moon jellies drifted like slow glowing dinner plates, then immediately asked if that counted as a simile for English class. Tegan said no, it counted as showing off. They ticked off octopus, eel, and the tank where a hermit crab switched shells while everybody cheered like it was a soccer goal. But the bonus question stayed blank, and Tegan's grade drooped in Brooklyn's imagination like a sad anemone.

The history room turned out to be one small alcove near the seahorses, with old photos of the aquarium from a hundred years ago. Brooklyn scanned them fast. There was the building under construction. There was a whale skeleton being assembled. And there, in a faded photo, was the aquarium's original water pump wagon, pulled by two horses, with a spotted dog out in front of them, ears back, clearly running. Another photo showed the same dog nose-to-nose with one of the horses, both looking delighted about it. Brooklyn's brain did the thing it did in math class when pieces finally fit. The dog and the horses were friends. The dog ran ahead of the carriage. It was clearing the way.

"That's it," she said, dragging Tegan and London over. "Look. Dalmatians got along well with horses, so they ran ahead of the horse-drawn fire carriages and helped clear the way. That's why fire stations have them." She pointed at the running dog, then the smiling horse, then back. "The painting wasn't about a contest. It was about the horses."

Tegan wrote it down so fast the pen squeaked. London squinted at the photo. "So the dog was basically a siren with legs."

"A very spotted siren," Brooklyn agreed.

On the walk back to the bus they passed the fire station again, and London saluted the painting. "Nice work, buddy," he told the dog. "Clear the way."

Connor wanted a new bike before summer, but the money he would inherit from his grandfather, fifty dollars in a savings account, would not be released to him until he turned thirteen in June. When Ms. Wijaya announced that the class would compare two savings accounts over five years, Connor leaned forward, because this was suddenly personal.

"Each pair gets graph paper," Ms. Wijaya said. "Account A earns simple interest. Account B earns compound interest. Plot both balances, year by year, and tell me what you notice."

Connor sat with Jaden, who groaned at the stack of numbers on the worksheet. They calculated Account A first: the balance rose by the same amount every year, so the points landed in a neat row. When Connor connected them with his ruler, the line came out perfectly straight. "That's the boring one," Jaden said, tapping it.

Account B behaved strangely. In the first year it grew a little, in the second year a little more, and by the fourth and fifth years the numbers jumped by bigger amounts than before. Connor plotted the points, and when he drew the curve through them, it bent upward, climbing away from the straight line. He frowned, checked the subtraction twice, and got the same result. "I think I messed up," he told Jaden. "It can't gain more each year than the year before. That's not logical."

Jaden borrowed his calculator and redid the fifth year. "It's right," he said. "Look at the graph, not the numbers. The lines start together, then they slowly pull apart. The straight one just keeps going straight. The curvy one keeps bending up."

Connor stared at the two lines. He had expected them to match, or at least to run parallel, but the gap between them widened every year. Then he asked Ms. Wijaya if he could test the idea on his own account. She handed him a fresh sheet and said, "Show me."

He imagined the school's backup generator humming behind the gym, steady and unchanging, like the straight line of simple interest. His grandfather's compound account was more like a snowball, and when he sketched a guess of where it might be by now, he drew the curve sweeping upward past where the straight line would have been. He showed Ms. Wijaya the page, and she nodded once, which felt better than a whole paragraph of praise.

That evening, Connor asked his mother to call the bank. She read him the current balance, and it was higher than his straight-line guess by exactly the kind of jump his curve had predicted. He did a quiet lap around the kitchen table. "Fifty dollars isn't fifty dollars anymore," he said. She laughed and said, "Then maybe wait a little longer." Connor looked at the graph folded in his pocket, at the line still bending upward, and said, "One more year. Then the bike."

Dominic sat at the library table with the shoe magazine open in front of him, though he was supposed to be finishing his homework. On the page, the basketball star Marcus Hale stood on a court, pointing at the sneakers on his feet. The headline read, "The best shoe in the game." Dominic had read the page four times. The sneakers cost more than any pair he had ever owned, and his birthday was in three weeks.

Dastan dropped into the chair across from him and looked at the magazine. "Those are the Marcus Hales. Ines has a cousin who has them. Half the team at my old school had them too." He tapped the page. "Everyone's getting them."

"Everyone," Dominic repeated. He turned the page. There was a full-page spread showing twenty kids at a bus stop, all wearing the same sneakers, with the words "Join the millions" printed across the top. Dominic frowned at it. Somehow the picture made the shoes seem even better, and he noticed that it did that without saying anything about the shoes at all.

He got up and found Ms. Fitzgerald at the reference desk. "Do you have anything about how ads work?" he asked. She led him to a shelf and pulled out a thin book called How They Persuade You. Back at the table, he opened it and started reading. One section was called "The Testimonial." He read it twice, then looked up.

"It's called a testimonial," he told Dastan, holding up the book. "It's when they use somebody famous to say a product is good. But the person might not know anything special about it, and they might be getting paid." Dastan leaned over to read the page himself. "So Marcus Hale gets paid to wear them?" Dominic shrugged. "Maybe. Maybe not. The book says you can't tell from the ad."

He decided to test it. At the computer station he typed Marcus Hale's name and the sneaker brand together. The first result was a news story from two years earlier: the brand had signed a deal with Hale worth millions, and after that he wore their shoes in every game. Dominic read the number twice to calibrate his expectations; a paid deal that big meant the shoes were a job, not a choice. He clicked back to the brand's own site and found a smaller item, a quote from the team's equipment manager saying the shoes were versatile enough for guards and centers alike. That was a person whose whole job was knowing shoes, and he had chosen a plain word, not a headline.

Dominic copied the page numbers onto his hand and walked back to the table. Ines had arrived and was looking at the magazine. "Those are so cool," she said. "Marcus Hale wears them."

"He gets paid to wear them," Dominic said. He slid the book across the table to her. "Page twelve."

Xavier had come to Mahi's house for one reason: to get his board game back before Saturday. He found it under a pile of jackets, but he couldn't leave, because Mahi was standing in the hallway with her fists clenched and her cousin's broken headphones in her hand.

"He says I broke them because I'm careless," Mahi said. "I didn't even touch them. He left them on the stairs, and then he says it's my fault." Her cousin had already gone home, and now Mahi's mother thought somebody was lying. If Mahi couldn't prove anything, she'd lose her weekend screen time, and Xavier knew she'd been saving that weekend for a project. She wanted the truth, and she wanted it before dinner.

Xavier sat on the stairs where the headphones had been and texted Valerie, whose older sister took a psychology class. "Two people saw the same thing and each thinks the other one is being unreasonable," he typed. "How can they both be so sure?" Valerie wrote back, "My sister has a word for that. Hang on." Then a second message: a photo of a page from her sister's notebook. Mahi leaned over his shoulder and read it out loud. "Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased."

Xavier stared at the words. That was it, exactly. Mahi was certain she was right; her cousin was certain she was wrong; each one figured the other had to be careless or dumb or lying. Neither of them had considered that they'd each seen only one slice of what happened. Xavier began to generate a plan on the back of a homework sheet. He would not ask anyone what happened. He would only ask what each person saw, from where, and when. He called the cousin, who admitted he'd been in the kitchen when the headphones fell. He asked Mahi where she'd been, and she said the living room, the whole time, doing her project.

They could both be telling the truth, Xavier realized, and both be sure the other was wrong. Then Mahi's dog trotted past them with a chewed cord hanging from its mouth, and Mahi burst out laughing so hard she had to sit down. "We were both wrong about each other," she said, wiping her eyes. Xavier felt a small twist of guilt for assuming the cousin had just been biased. "Don't be pessimistic about him," Mahi added, "he's actually okay." From the kitchen her mother called, "Dinner in five," and Xavier grabbed his board game and ran.

Colton pressed the same key on the piano for the tenth time, and it still sounded wrong. The piece Ms. Chan had assigned them, a duet he was supposed to play with Dakota, had a slow middle section marked "Largo," and every time he reached it, his hands sped up like they had somewhere better to be.

"You're rushing again," Dakota said from across the music room, where she was assembling her snare drum. "The slow part sounded exactly as fast as the fast part."

"That can't be true," Colton said, but he knew it was close. He flipped to the page and stared at the tempo marking at the top of the slow section. Sixty. There was a little note beside it that said the number meant beats per minute, but that didn't help him feel it. He couldn't see a beat. It was like trying to catch something invisible.

Then he noticed the wall clock above the door, its second hand ticking around the face. He watched it for a while, tapping one finger against his knee each time the hand jumped. Tick, tap. Tick, tap. Even and unhurried. When he counted out loud along with it, the counting felt proportional to the clock, each tap spaced out like fence posts in a row. "Dakota, come look at this. Sixty beats in a minute means one beat every second. The clock is doing it for free."

Dakota set down her drumsticks and joined him under the clock. "Play the slow part and I'll watch the second hand," she said. "If you're with the clock, you've got it." He played the first line and rushed it so badly that his last chord landed two whole seconds ahead of the hand. On the second try he finished one second early. On the third, his final note landed exactly on the tick, and they both shouted at the same time.

"Now the loud part," Dakota said, pointing at the marking that said "forte," then back at the soft opening marked "piano." "You have to convey the difference, not just hit the keys harder. Make the soft part actually sound careful, like mushrooms of fungus growing quietly in a corner, and then the loud part will knock people over." Colton laughed at the image, but he tried it, hunching close to the keys for the soft bars and sitting tall for the forte, while Charleigh, who had wandered in to grab her flute, clapped from the doorway.

Ms. Chan looked up from her desk and smiled without saying anything, which Colton took as a good sign. He played the piece through one more time, eyes flicking between the page and the clock, the slow section steady as a heartbeat, the dynamics rising and falling like waves.

"Tomorrow we take it at full speed," Dakota said, spinning a drumstick. "Sixty and counting."

The clock over the lab read 2:14, and Hayden had already snapped two onion slides, both of them cracked. He was the only one at his table without a picture on his lab sheet, the one that had to show the cell wall, the cell membrane, and the nucleus, each labelled with a straight little arrow. Alessandro across the table had finished his twenty minutes ago and was now leaning back like a defendant who knew he was getting off easy. "Chronic slide-breaker," Alessandro said, tapping his own perfect sketch. "That's what they'll put in your file."

"You finished because you rushed," Francesca said. She wasn't hurrying. She wanted her drawing good enough to hang in the showcase outside the science room, the one Mr. Whitehead filled every month, and a rushed sketch wouldn't make it. She peeled a paper-thin layer from the inside of the onion with tweezers, laid it flat in a drop of water on her slide, and lowered the cover slip so slowly that Hayden could hear himself breathe. "Your turn. Careful this time."

Hayden exhaled, cut his smallest piece yet, and floated it onto the glass. The cover slip settled without a single crack. He carried the slide to the microscope like it was made of frost, clipped it on the stage, and cranked the objective down. Francesca leaned in beside him, pencil ready. The table went quiet except for the radiator ticking.

The circle of light was nearly blank. There were faint lines, maybe, ghost-edges of something, but nothing he could point to, nothing he could label. "It's empty," Hayden said. "The onion's broken." He turned the fine focus back and forth until his eyes ached. Alessandro drifted over, looked, and shrugged. "Mine wasn't empty." Francesca frowned at her slide, untouched on the counter, and then at the empty one under the lens. Same onion. Same water. Same method. So something they couldn't see had to be the difference, and it had to be in Alessandro's slide.

"Wait," Hayden said. "What did you put on yours?" Alessandro thought, then pointed at a brown dropper bottle at the far end of the counter, half hidden behind the lens paper. "That stuff. Mr. Whitehead said use a drop. Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so iodine stain makes the nucleus and cell wall easier to see." Hayden lifted one edge of his cover slip with the tweezers, let a single brown drop wick underneath, and set it back down.

He bent over the eyepiece and turned the focus one slow notch, then another, afraid to hope. The blank circle filled as though ink were spreading through it: neat brick-shaped cells, their walls sharp and dark, and inside each one a small dense dot. The nucleus. He found the membrane hugging the inner edge of the wall, and his hand was steady enough to draw three clean arrows. Francesca leaned in, whispered "perfect," and started her showcase sketch, and Hayden slid his chair closer to see it.

The bus smelled like wet jackets and orange peel, and Kayla had to shout over the engine just to be heard by Gordon, who was two rows back and holding his phone up like a laser pointer aimed at her face. "Justice or Jeter," he said. "Pick one. For real, pick."

"For what?" Kayla slid across the sticky seat until her knee bumped the cold metal wall. The bus lurched around the corner by the field house, and Gordon's phone nearly hit Ibrahim in the ear.

"Because my uncle says Justice was better and my dad says Jeter, and they've been arguing since Thanksgiving." Gordon turned the screen toward her. "Look. Nineteen ninety-five. Justice hits three point two five. Jeter hits two point five zero. Justice wins, easy."

Ibrahim leaned over the seat, breath smelling of the orange. "And ninety-six?"

"Nineteen six," Gordon said, scrolling slowly, like he was afraid of the number. "Justice, three point one one. Jeter, three point one four." He paused. "Wait. That's Jeter winning."

Kayla frowned. "So Justice wins the first year, Jeter wins the second."

"Right. So they're even. Unless..." Gordon's thumb hovered over the screen. Down the aisle somebody's binder slid and slapped the floor, and the driver yelled something about feet out of the aisle. "Unless you put both years together. My dad says the combined numbers don't work out even. He says Jeter's ahead."

"That's impossible," Ibrahim said flatly. "If you win both halves, you win the whole thing. That's like, the most basic thing in the universe."

Kayla didn't answer. She was thinking about Ms. Morningstar's class, the poster about surveys, the sentence she'd read twice because it didn't seem to fit inside her head. Something tugged at her, an idea she couldn't see directly, the way you can't see the wind but you can see the bag it pushes down the street. "Just add them," she said. "Combine the years. Show me."

Gordon's face went stiff. He tapped the screen once, twice, and the bus went quiet for Kayla, the engine fading under the waiting. The numbers came up. She read them, then read them again, and a laugh escaped before she could stop it.

"Justice," she said, "higher in ninety-five. Higher in ninety-six. But when you put the two years together, Jeter's average is higher."

Ibrahim grabbed Gordon's wrist. "Show me that. Show me it right now, because you made that up." He stared at the screen until his eyes watered. "But he won both years. Both! How does he lose?"

"I don't know," Kayla said, "but it's right there. Averages don't add up the way you think. The whole thing squishes down to one number and the number doesn't care who won the parts." She thought of the standings on the gym wall, every player flattened into a single decimal, hiding everything underneath.

"Wait till my uncle sees this," Gordon said. He raised the phone and snapped a picture of the screen, grinning. "He's going to oppose this with his whole soul."

"Good," Ibrahim said, peeling the last of his orange. "I want to hear the eloquent version of losing."

The bus hissed to a stop, and Gordon was already typing, thumbs flying.

The group chat lit up at 7:14 in the morning, and Aiden read it from under his blanket, where he had been lying since 6:50 telling himself he had a sore throat.

Brady: presentation order posted. you're after deanna

Deanna: aiden you're literally going to pretend to be sick again

Aiden: not pretending. throat feels weird. low voltage. like a dying battery

Brady: that is not how throats work

Aiden knew exactly how throats worked. His throat was fine. The rest of him was the problem, the sick-hot feeling that showed up every time Mr. Nolan said the word "presentation." In September he had faked a dentist appointment and skipped the first one, and it had felt amazing, like pressing an ejector seat button. In October he'd skipped the second one with a stomachache. By December he was skipping them with no excuse at all, just a note his mom wrote saying he wasn't feeling well, which was technically true in a way she didn't ask about.

The weird part, the part he turned over while pretending to drink tea, was that each skip felt better than the last, and each upcoming presentation felt worse. In September the sick-hot feeling had been small. Now, thinking about Wednesday, it was big enough that he'd actually practiced his speech zero times, because even opening his notes made his hands sweat. He lay there doing the math on it. If skipping made him feel better, then the next one should feel easier, not harder. Something about his own system wasn't adding up, like a machine that ran fine until you checked the output.

Deanna: mr. nolan asked where you were btw. i said throat thing. he did a face

Aiden: what kind of face

Deanna: the kind where he knows

That afternoon, after school, she messaged him alone, outside the chat. "Can I tell you something without you doing the dying battery thing," she wrote. "I used to hide in the bathroom before swim meets. Whole season. My coach thought I had a nervous stomach. Then one meet the bathroom was locked and I had to just swim, and it was awful for about four minutes and then it was over and I realized it had been awful every single time I didn't swim too, just spread out longer." She added, "My mom called it anxiety and said I was coping by avoiding, and the avoiding was making it worse. That's a thing apparently."

Aiden stared at the screen. It fit his math. Every skip was relief, quick and certain, and every next presentation came bigger than the last. The fear wasn't staying dormant; it was training, like it did push-ups every time he stayed home. He tested the idea against September, October, December. It held.

Aiden: ok. wednesday. i'm doing it

Brady: seriously?

Aiden: seriously. but if my voice cracks someone has to console me at lunch

Deanna: deal. bring cards

Wednesday came anyway, the way Wednesdays do. Aiden stood by the door of Mr. Nolan's room while Deanna presented on red tides, and his hands were sweating, and his heart was doing something a drummer would call ambitious. When his name was called, his legs carried him up front without consulting him.

"Mine is on sleep," he said, and his voice did crack, right on the word sleep, which at least made three people laugh with him instead of at him. He kept going. The slides were out of order and he found the right one anyway. Four minutes later, it was over, and the sick-hot feeling was still there but smaller, like it had shrunk to fit the actual room instead of the imaginary one.

At lunch Deanna dealt the cards without a word. Brady looked up from his sandwich and said, "Voice cracked." Aiden flipped his first card onto the pile. "Shocking voltage, is what that was."

Hannah typed her own name into the search bar, mostly because Mckenzie had dared her to at lunch. "Everybody's got something out there," Mckenzie had said, spinning her spaghetti with her fork. Hannah had always assumed her internet self was small, a few school announcements and one blurry team photo from the swim club. Then the results loaded, and there it was, third from the top: a comment she had written in third grade on a public class blog, the one where the whole neighborhood had argued about whether the park should get a dog run. Her old username was right there, along with the sentence "I think dogs are loud and Alden smells like his hamster." She had written it when she was eight. She was twelve now, and Alden was in her science class, and the page said anyone could see it.

She clicked the link. The blog was still online, still public, still showing the date. That was the part that made her stomach flip. She hadn't thought about that blog in four years, but it hadn't gone anywhere. It had just been sitting there, waiting to be found. She remembered Mr. Visser, their computer teacher, saying one sentence about this back in the fall, something she had barely listened to. She dug out her notes. "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers," she had written, "to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results." Crawlers. She said the word out loud to the empty living room, and it gave her a plan.

If the crawlers had found her, they would have found other people too. She typed in Alden's full name, and on the second page of results there he was, age nine, holding a giant zucchini at the farmers market, with the caption "Spontaneous zucchini eating contest winner!" The photo radiated joy, his grin enormous, but it also had the name of their whole town attached to it. Then she tried her swim coach, and found a roster from two seasons ago listing her own event times, her age, and the pool address, all in one place. The pattern held every single time.

She opened her messages and started typing to Mckenzie.

"I found the dog comment. Third grade. It's the third result when you search me. Try searching your own name and tell me what shows up, then check Alden. I want to see if it's everybody or just us. Also I'm going to write to the blog's contact address tonight and ask them to take my comment down."

Mckenzie's reply came fast: "omg. searching now."

While she waited, Hannah found the blog's contact page and wrote a short polite note explaining that she had written the comment when she was eight and would like it removed. She read it twice before sending. Three days later, an answer appeared from the blog's owner, agreeing to delete it and thanking her for asking nicely.

On the fourth day she searched her name again, and the comment was gone from the results. Alden's zucchini was still there, though, so she showed him the photo at school. "My mom entered me in that," he said, laughing a little. "I didn't know strangers could find it." Hannah pulled out her phone. "Okay, so, before we post anything ever again, we search our names first. Deal?" Alden stuck out his hand. "Deal."

Eli had promised his grandmother he would grow her a real vegetable garden behind her house, the kind she used to have before her knees got bad. By the second week of June, the corn seedlings were up, the bean seeds were sprouting, and the squash had sent out its first wide, prickly leaves. The problem was the weeds. They were aggressive, coming up between every row faster than he could pull them, and each afternoon he found more.

Daniel came over on Saturday and stood at the edge of the plot with his bike helmet still on. "You planted everything mixed together," he said. "My uncle keeps his corn in one bed and his beans way over there. Yours looks like a jungle." Eli pulled a weed and tossed it on the pile. "It's supposed to look like this," he said, though privately he wasn't sure. "There's a system. I just can't tell if it's working."

What he could not see was the part that bothered him. The beans had curled little stems that seemed to be reaching sideways, hunting for something, and he didn't know whether they were failing or waiting. He thought about it that night at his grandmother's kitchen table while she sliced tomatoes. Maybe the beans needed something to grab. He decided to postpone pulling any more weeds near the corn until he had watched for three days, just to see what the beans did when they touched the stalks. If his grandfather's old seed box had been right about anything, it was that.

On Monday morning Eli crouched in the dirt and saw it. A bean vine had wrapped itself around a corn stalk, spiraling upward, tight as a spring. He ran his finger along it and the vine held firm. Two rows over, another bean had latched on and was climbing higher than the leaves he could reach. He took a photo to show Daniel. Then he looked down at the ground under the squash plants, where the big flat leaves lay like umbrellas, and noticed something else: almost no weeds there. Where the squash leaves shaded the soil, the weeds had stopped. The parts of the bed without squash were still thick with them.

Daniel rode over after school and Eli walked him through row by row. "My grandpa's neighbor called it the Three Sisters," Eli said. "Corn, beans, squash." He pointed at the corn holding the bean vines upright, then at the squash leaves lying over the bare soil. Daniel knelt down and touched the shaded ground, then the weedy ground beside it, comparing.

"That's actually kind of amazing," Daniel said. Eli grinned and handed him a pair of gloves. "You can pull the ones by the fence," he said. "The sisters have got the rest covered."

Leah stared at the three recipes taped to the counter and felt like a general planning a battle. The rice had to simmer for twenty minutes, the curry needed fifteen, and the flatbread cooked one at a time, two minutes per bread. Ms. O'Brien had said the whole meal had to land on the table together, hot, at exactly twelve fifteen.

"It's like a transport schedule," said Zoya, squinting at Leah's notes. "Everything leaving different stations, arriving at one time."

"Exactly," Leah said, sketching a timeline. Rice first, then curry while the rice bubbled, then breads last, flipped out of the pan one after another. Charles-Olivier claimed the bread station and started mixing dough before Leah had even measured her rice, because he said waiting was obsolete, a word he had learned from his older brother and used about everything.

The first bread puffed up beautifully in the pan, golden and spotted. Charles-Olivier slid it onto an open plate and cheered. "Look at that! Flawless!" By the time the second bread came off, the first had gone stiff and cool, curled at the edges like an old leaf. He poked it. It cracked. The third bread went onto the plate and began hardening almost immediately, steam drifting off it into the air and vanishing.
