The problem was that Zion's ideas were good, so nobody wanted to shut them down, and there was nowhere to put them. An idea with nowhere to go just circles the room like a fly.

She held up her hand, palm out, and Zion stopped mid-sentence. "I just remembered something," she said. "My mom runs meetings at work, and she keeps a parking lot."

"A what?" Laila asked.

"A parking lot. It's a list where the meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later instead of derailing the current item."

Zion frowned. "So my ideas get parked?"

"Your ideas get saved," Quinn said. "Nothing gets thrown away." She turned to a fresh page, wrote PARKING LOT at the top, and under it: "Zion: herb sale at spring fair, money for rain barrel." She looked up. "Item one. The cleanup. Date?"

"Saturday the fourteenth," Laila said, and Zion nodded, because his idea was sitting right there on the page where he could see it.

They finished three agenda items in twenty minutes. Quinn could speculate all she wanted about why it worked, but watching Zion glance at the parking lot page twice, checking that his basil sale was still there, she thought she already knew. When they reached the end of the agenda, she said, "Now the parking lot. Zion, tell us about the spring fair."

Zion stood up so fast his chair scraped the floor. "Okay, so," he said, "imagine a table, right, and it's covered in little pots of basil."

Ms. Nakamura raised her mug. "I'll take two," she said.

Oliver had forty dollars of birthday money in his pocket, and the tablet kiosk in the middle of the mall was calling his name. The screen above the counter flashed five huge bullet points: FASTEST PROCESSOR, CRYSTAL CLEAR SCREEN, THOUSANDS OF APPS, ULTRA LIGHT, LOVED BY MILLIONS. A video played on loop showing a famous singer holding the tablet and saying, "I never leave home without mine." Behind him, a wall of photos showed crowds of smiling customers, and a banner read, "The amazing tablet everyone is buying."

Ajay and Roxane had come along to keep him honest, though so far they were mostly being no help. "The singer has one," Ajay said, staring up at the screen. "And millions of people bought it. It must be good."

"That's the point," Roxane said. "They want you to think that. Mr. Lim told us ads do that. He called one of them a celebrity testimonial."

Oliver pulled out the phone his mom made him carry and searched the tablet's name. Every review mentioned five things, the same five on the poster. But he noticed something odd. He checked a second review site, then a third, typing in the words "problems" and "battery." There it was. On a forum, user after user said the battery lasted barely three hours, and when Oliver found a photo of the box in small print, it listed the battery specs that the ad never once mentioned.

"They're stacking the deck," he said slowly. "It's called card stacking. Showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it. That's why the ad seems stronger than it is."

"So it's not a lie," Ajay said, frowning at the poster. "Fastest processor is probably true."

"It's true," Oliver said, "but it's not the whole truth." He had been one tap away from handing over his forty dollars as a deposit. He turned to the counter and asked the cashier, "What's the battery life on this?" The cashier paused just long enough for all three of them to notice, then said two and a half hours, maybe more if the screen was dim.

Ajay changed his mind right there. "Okay, I wanted one because everyone has one. That was dumb."

"It wasn't dumb," Roxane said. "You checked before you bought it. That's the whole trick."

On the way to the food court, they made it systematic, walking past store windows and calling out the tricks they spotted: the sneaker ad with a basketball star, the energy drink poster shouting "the greatest taste ever." They even mediated a small argument about whether "greatest" counted as a loaded word, and settled it by looking up what loaded meant. By the time they reached the climax of the afternoon, the soft pretzel stand, Oliver still had his forty dollars.

"Next weekend," he said, "we research first, then buy." He held up his phone and snapped a picture of the pretzel stand's sign, which claimed the best pretzels in the universe. "Starting with this."

Lincoln stood in his grandfather's hallway with the reading for his coming-of-age ceremony folded in his back pocket. In two weeks he had to recite all fourteen lines from memory, in front of both sides of the family, and so far he could manage four. He had read the lines aloud maybe fifty times in his bedroom, and each time they seemed to slide back out of his head the moment he closed the page.

"I'm pessimistic about this," he told Jet, who had biked over to keep him company. "I'm going to stand up there and say the second half first."

Jet was looking at the photographs on the wall. "Your grandpa's house is huge. How many rooms is this?"

"Eight, plus the sun porch." Lincoln followed his gaze down the hallway. The kitchen at the front, the living room, the dining room, the study, the two bedrooms, the bathroom, the porch. Rooms he had walked through since he was four years old.

He unfolded the paper and read the first line again. Something about beginning. He walked into the kitchen and set the line there in his mind, on the counter next to the cookie jar, the way you might set down a set of keys. Then he walked to the living room and placed the second line on the mantel under the clock. Third line went on the dining room table. Fourth line, the study desk. He kept going, room by room, until the last line sat on the porch rail beside the watering can.

Then he walked back to the front door, closed his eyes, and moved through the house in his mind. Kitchen, cookie jar, first line. Mantel, clock, second line. It worked. The lines came out in order, the way houses come in order when you walk through them.

Lauriane arrived just then with her grandmother's recipe cards, and Lincoln explained what he had done. "My mom calls it the method of loci," she said. "She memorizes her speeches that way."

"By putting the words in places?"

"Along a route you already know. Then you walk the route in your head and the words are waiting there."

Lincoln grinned. He tried it again, start to finish, with Jet timing him on his phone. Forty seconds, no mistakes. When Jet asked what he would do if he got nervous and his mind went blank at the ceremony, Lincoln said he had a plan for that too. "Panic is like an invading army. It only takes territory nobody's guarding. Every line in that house has a guard on it."

"That's a metaphor," Jet said.

"It's the truth," Lincoln said, and walked the hallway again, touching each doorframe as he passed.

Bennett raced along platform four so fast his backpack bounced like a second heartbeat. His grandfather was arriving on the 3:40, and Bennett had the whole week planned: model rockets on Saturday, the science museum on Tuesday, and tonight, chili dogs. When the train doors slid open with a hiss, Grandpa stepped out holding a duffel bag and a paper cup of tea that had gone cold somewhere outside the city.

"There he is," Grandpa boomed, and Bennett grinned so wide his cheeks ached. On the drive home, though, Bennett noticed things. Grandpa kept his coat zipped all the way up, even with the heater running. His hands, when he pointed at a billboard, looked pale, almost translucent in the late light, like paper held up to a window. And at the house, Grandpa settled into the recliner in the den, the coldest room in the whole place, without saying a single word about it. That was the part that bothered Bennett most. Grandpa would complain about the referee, about the price of licorice, about Bennett's shoelaces. Not about cold.

At school the next morning, Bennett leaned across the lab table toward Jensen. "Do old people get cold differently?" Jensen shrugged, but Gracie, who was sorting index cards, looked up. "My aunt's a nurse. She says older adults are at greater risk of hypothermia than younger adults. That's a dangerous drop in body temperature. Her unit treats somebody every winter." Bennett repeated the word under his breath. Hypothermia. Grandpa, sitting calm and quiet in a chilly room, not complaining. He had a theory, and he knew exactly how to test it.

That afternoon he borrowed the classroom thermometer from Ms. Robinson, promising to return it by Friday. At home, he set it on the den table, watched Grandpa do the crossword, and wrote down the reading every twenty minutes. Sixty-three degrees, then sixty-two. Grandpa said nothing. Bennett's stomach tightened. He marched to the thermostat and cranked it up, then dragged a space heater beside the recliner and draped his own fleece blanket over Grandpa's knees like he was tucking in a king.

Grandpa lowered the crossword. "What's all this?" Bennett exhaled, then explained about Gracie's aunt, about hypothermia, about the readings in his notebook, his voice getting faster as he went. Grandpa was quiet for a moment, and Bennett braced for teasing. Instead Grandpa said, "Sixty-two, huh? No wonder my tea kept going cold." Then came the twist: he pulled his phone from his pocket and held it up. On the screen was a note titled BENNETT'S WEEK, and item one said, Let the kid fuss over me a little. "Your grandmother told me you'd been studying up," Grandpa said. "She said, 'He'll figure it out. He always does.'"

Bennett laughed until he had to sit on the arm of the couch. Then he grabbed a second blanket, because even a scheming grandfather deserved two, and announced, "Chili dogs. Kitchen. Five minutes."

The bus rattled toward the county bee, and Rebecca flipped through her word list for the hundredth time. Across the aisle, Carmelo was bouncing his knee so hard the seat shook. "I just want to beat Mikayla," he said. "She beat me in the geography fair, the science fair, and the rock-paper-scissors semifinal. This is my year."

"Your year, and also the year of the fourteen other candidates on this bus," Rebecca said, nodding at the seats full of spellers from other schools. One boy was whispering words to himself like a haunted calculator.

Mikayla leaned over the back of her seat. "Quiz me. Go." Rebecca read, "Insulate." Mikayla spelled it perfectly, then added, "It means to cover something so heat or electricity can't get through, like the foam in this bus's walls, which are clearly failing, because I'm freezing."

Rebecca laughed, but inside she felt the old knot tighten. Last year she had gone out on "saguaro," and she hadn't even tried to figure it out. She had just stood there, guessed a couple of vowels, and walked off the stage. Later, lying awake in her arid, air-conditioned bedroom, she had replayed it and realized she'd given up without using any of her options. She'd heard other spellers ask questions at the microphone, but she'd never paid attention to what was allowed.

"Ms. Halvorsen," she called to the teacher up front, "at the real Scripps bee, what are spellers allowed to ask for?"

Ms. Halvorsen turned around. "You may ask for the definition, the part of speech, the language of origin, or a sentence using the word. The judges have to answer." She smiled. "County bees follow the same rules."

Rebecca's heart sped up. A definition. A sentence. Language of origin. She remembered the kid who had spelled "schtum" last year only after asking where it came from, and it suddenly made sense: German words had German patterns. If she knew a word came from Spanish, she'd know there was no silent k. It was like being handed a map right before walking into a maze.

"Ask me one," she told Mikayla. "Something impossible."

"Bougainvillea."

Rebecca closed her eyes. "May I have the language of origin?" she asked, playing both parts. "French, from a botanist's name," she answered herself, "so it's probably spelled the French way, with all those letters sitting together like passengers on a crowded bus." She spelled it out, letter by letter, and Mikayla shrieked, "Correct!"

Carmelo groaned. "Great. Now I have to beat both of you."

The bus groaned too, downshifted, and pulled into the parking lot behind the auditorium. Rebecca zipped her word list into her backpack and stood first in the aisle, fingers already curled around an invisible microphone.

Zoey sat at the kitchen table with her German notebook open and a pencil that had already lost its eraser. Her assignment was to describe her family and her pets in full sentences, and so far she had written one sentence about her dog, Biscuit, and then crossed it out because she was not sure if Biscuit was masculine or feminine in German. Down the hall she could hear her three little brothers racing toy cars, and her sister was singing the same four lines of a song over and over. The house was not a quiet place for homework.

She tried again. "Ich habe einen Hund," she wrote, and then came the hard part. "Ich habe drei Brüder und eine Schwester." She counted the words and frowned. In English she could just say "four siblings," which was short and done. In German she seemed stuck spelling it all out, and if she had to read her paragraph out loud in Mr. Petrov's class tomorrow, she would be standing there forever while Kyson and Dave smirked from the second row.

Then she remembered something. Last week Mr. Petrov had said a word on the board and moved on quickly, and she had copied it without knowing why. She flipped back two pages. There it was: Geschwister. She squinted at it, then tested a simple idea. She texted Dave, who was also in the class and annoyingly good at vocabulary. "Does Geschwister mean brothers and sisters together? Like one word for all of them, the way English uses siblings?"

"Ya," Dave texted back. "Geschwister. You didn't know that?"

Zoey grinned and wrote her new sentence: "Ich habe vier Geschwister." Two words instead of five, and it even covered her sister without a separate sentence. It was a small insight, but it felt like finding a shortcut through a hedge. She kept going, describing her mother as helpful, her father as tall, and Biscuit as loud, which was generous to Biscuit.

Her brother Theo wandered into the kitchen holding a broken toy car. "Can you fix it?" he asked. Zoey was tempted to say no and be pessimistic about it, since the wheel had vanished somewhere under the couch and was probably gone forever. Instead she said, "Delegate. You find the wheel, I'll fix the axle." Theo dropped to the floor and searched, and when he held up the wheel triumphantly, she snapped it back on for him. He hugged her leg and ran off, and she went back to her paragraph feeling like the whole evening had gone two words shorter than expected. She read her last sentence out loud to the empty kitchen, and Biscuit barked in agreement.

Hazel dumped the duffel bag onto the table in the school's family-studies room and stared at the mountain of clothes Mr. Kapoor had left for the laundry unit. Her partner, Liam, pulled out his hockey jersey first and held it up like a trophy. "This has to be perfect by Friday," he said. "Coach says if we look sloppy, we play sloppy."

"Then let's not turn it pink," Hazel said. She began sorting, whites in one pile, darks in another, colours in a third. A red sock lurked near the bottom, and she fished it out before it could orbit its way into the whites and ruin everything.

Liam's stack included a white shirt with blue stripes, and next to it a truly grey practice shirt. "These need bleach," he said, reaching for the bottle on the shelf. "The striped one's gone dull."

Hazel caught his wrist. Something was nagging at her. The striped shirt was new, and she'd seen tiny printed symbols stitched into the seam. She turned the shirt inside out and found the care label, a little strip of writing with a row of small icons. There was a tub, an iron, and a triangle with a cross through it. The grey practice shirt's label showed a plain, empty triangle instead.

"That's a contradiction," Hazel said slowly. "Same kind of shirt, same fabric almost, but the symbols don't match." She held the two labels side by side. "The empty one has to mean it's okay, and the crossed-out one has to mean no. It means it must not be bleached."

"Then what do we do about my striped shirt?" Liam asked, deflating a little.

"Hot water and detergent, and a good long soak," Hazel said. "No bleach. If it doesn't work, you wear it dull." Liam opened his mouth to argue, then looked at the crossed-out triangle again and closed it. "Fine," he said. "But the jersey gets the full treatment."

They loaded the machine, measured the detergent, and started the wash with only the grey shirt and a few true whites in the bleach load. While it churned, they folded towels from the finished load, and Hazel found that vigorous shaking before folding made the towels lie flat instead of bunching into lumps.

When the cycle ended, Liam held up the grey shirt, bright and clean, and then his striped one, soaked and hung to dry, its blue stripes still exactly blue. He grinned. "Dull stripes, alive colours. I can live with that." Hazel slid the bleach bottle back onto the shelf, label out, so the next person would know to check the triangle first.

The baby monitor crackled at 10:58, three minutes after Grayson had settled onto the couch with his homework. He listened. A thin, rising wail came through the speaker, the kind that would not stop on its own. Ms. Kobayashi had left him a list on the fridge, written in tidy blue ink, and next to the words "diaper change" she had added a note in the margin: "Wash hands after, before food. Twenty seconds. Sing the chorus twice." He had read it twice earlier, wondering why she bothered to write something so obvious, but the wail got louder, so he carried little Ben up to the changing table and got to work.

It was worse than he had pictured. When it was over, he stood there holding his breath, arms damp, and considered his options. He could rinse quickly under the tap and get to the bottle warming on the counter. Or he could follow the note exactly, soap and all, through a whole twenty seconds of scrubbing before he prepared Ben's lunch. He looked at his hands under the hallway light. They looked clean. But looks, he thought, were exactly the problem. Whatever was on them, if anything, was too small to see, which meant he could not judge by looking. That was the part that interested him, in a restless, uncomfortable way.

So he tested it. At the kitchen sink, he pumped soap onto his palms, turned on the water, and hummed the chorus of the song stuck in his head, once, then twice, checking the clock above the stove. Two choruses came out to just past twenty seconds. He kept scrubbing the whole time, between his fingers, around his thumbs, backs of his hands, then rinsed and dried them on the clean towel before he touched the bottle.

Ben ate sweet potato with his fists and thrived on it, smearing orange across the high chair tray and grinning like he had discovered something wonderful. Grayson found himself grinning back. "You're a mess," he said, "but at least I did the math on my hands before your lunch." Ben banged the tray in reply.

At noon the door opened, and Ms. Kobayashi came in shaking rain off her coat. "How did it go?" she asked. "The diaper, I mean. First-timers usually look shaken."

"It went fine," Grayson said. "But why twenty seconds exactly? And why the chorus twice?"

She smiled as she lifted Ben out of the chair. "Twenty seconds of scrubbing is what health agencies recommend, after a diaper change and before preparing food. The chorus just fills the time." She shrugged. "Sing anything you like."

Grayson nodded slowly, filing that away. Then he pointed at the counter. "There's still half a jar left, and I already washed. Want me to warm it while you take off your boots?"

Charles sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table with his left arm propped on a pillow, the cast already itching in three places he couldn't reach. Taylor sat on the plastic chair by the window, turning the fact over out loud, because that was what Taylor did. "The doctor said it's only partly broken. How can a bone be partly broken?"

"A greenstick fracture," Charles said, using the words the doctor had written on the paper in his file. "That's what it's called."

"But what does it mean?" Taylor leaned forward. "Greenstick. Like a stick that's green?"

Charles had been wondering the same thing since Monday. The doctor had said the bone cracked on one side and bent on the other, and that it happened mostly in kids because their bones were more flexible, like a young green branch. That part stuck in his head and wouldn't let go. Cracked on one side, bent on the other. Which side cracked? The outside of the bend, or the inside?

"Think about it," Charles said. "When you bend something, one side gets stretched and the other side gets squished." He held up his good hand and curved it like a bow. "So which side breaks first?"

"The squished side?" Taylor guessed.

"That's what I thought. But wait." Charles looked around the room. On the counter sat a box of wooden tongue depressors, and next to it a clipboard the receptionist had asked his mom to authorize, signing the forms for the follow-up visit. Charles reached with his right hand and took one wooden stick. "Don't tell," he said, and bent it slowly, watching both sides the way you watch a kettle before it boils. The outside of the curve went pale and split into tiny lines. The inside just compressed. When he bent further, the outside snapped through while the inside stayed connected, bent.

"The stretched side," he said. "The outside of the bend cracks, and the inside just bends. Green stick. Because a dry old stick snaps clean through both sides."

Taylor took a fresh depressor and tried it, and then a third, in vain, trying to get one to break on the inside of the curve instead. Every single one cracked on the outside first. "So your bone did this," Taylor said, holding up the split-but-hinged stick, "on your arm."

"And it happens to kids mostly, not grown-ups, because our bones are still bendy." Charles turned his cast arm over, imagining the hidden line inside it, one side cracked, one side bent, mending in there where he couldn't see. He wondered whether the two sides healed at different speeds. He decided he would ask.

The door opened and Mr. Tremblay from next door poked his head in, there for his own appointment, holding his hat. "Still in one piece, Charles?"

"Mostly," Charles said, and held up the bent tongue depressor. "Want to see a picture of my arm?"

The deadline was Sunday morning, and it was already Thursday night when Willow stood in her grandmother's kitchen holding a photocopied booklet like it might bite her. In three days she would stand among the adults at the Gurdwara and recite Japji Sahib from memory as part of her preparation for Amrit Sanchar, and so far she could get through about four lines before her brain went blank.

"You are chewing your lip again," her grandmother said, sliding a cup of chai across the counter. "That habit is toxic to your concentration."

Willow laughed despite herself. "Everything is toxic to my concentration. The words all sound the same when I panic. Ek onkar satnam, karta purakh, and then static." She flipped the pages, forty stanzas of Gurmukhi she could read slowly but not yet hold in her head.

Her cousin Otis wandered in from the living room, headphones around his neck. "Why does it have to be this prayer, anyway? Why not something short?"

"Because it's recited at Amrit Sanchar," their grandmother said simply, and went back to stirring the pot. "That is the Khalsa initiation ceremony. When you take amrit, Japji Sahib is part of it. So you learn it before, and you learn it well."

Willow stared at the booklet. She had known the ceremony was coming, known she was nervous about it, but she hadn't connected the two things until that moment. The morning prayer wasn't just homework her grandmother had invented. It was the same words that would be spoken during the initiation itself, which meant that every line she learned now would be waiting for her there, already inside her, like friends in a room she hadn't entered yet. Otis saw her face change and raised an eyebrow, but she just said, "I need your phone."

She had an idea she wanted to test. Instead of staring at the page, she recorded herself reading one stanza, played it back while walking the length of the hallway and back, then tried to say it before listening again. One stanza, ten laps. Her grandmother watched from the kitchen doorway as Willow muttered and stumbled and restarted. "You look like a pigeon," Otis said, and Willow threw a cushion at him without breaking her rhythm.

By Friday night she had eight stanzas. On Saturday she noticed something: the booklet's page had a symmetry to it, the way certain phrases returned in mirrored places across stanzas, and once she saw the pattern, whole chunks locked together like puzzle pieces. When a line slipped away from her at the sink on Sunday morning, she stopped, walked seven steps the way she had practiced, and the words came back on their own.

At the Gurdwara, standing with the others while Japji Sahib rose around her, she found she did not have to grab for the lines. They sustained her, carrying her forward while her heart pounded, all the way to the final stanza.

Afterward Otis found her in the hallway. "So? Did you get through it?"

Willow held up the worn booklet. "Forty stanzas, ten hallway laps each," she said. "You owe me four hundred laps of pigeon-watching."

Bentley slid his new glasses on in the back of Ms. Clarke-Williams's classroom, and the whole room sharpened at once. He could read the tiny copyright line on the poster by the window. He could count the tiles in the ceiling. He could see that Aryan had drawn a tiny rocket on the corner of his homework.

"Let me try," said Youssef, and Bentley handed them over, though his instinct said no, not my new glasses. Youssef squinted, blinked, and handed them back fast. "The floor is way too close."

Bentley thought about Saturday. He remembered the optometrist's office, the chair that leaned back, the row of letters shrinking line by line until they looked like ants. His dad had mentioned that Bentley spent all weekend indoors, every weekend, on screens. The optometrist had nodded and said, "Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood." Bentley had filed that away. Now he turned it over. Was that why his eyes went wrong, all those weekends of screens and no sky? There was no way to see it directly. He would have to test it.

At recess he found Aryan and Youssef on the blacktop. "Question," Bentley said. "Who here has glasses?" Aryan raised his hand. Youssef shook his head. "And who spends weekends outside?" Youssef pointed at himself. Aryan shrugged. "Xbox," he said. "Basically dawn to dinner." Bentley grinned so wide the glasses slid down his nose. Two kids was a small sample, sparse evidence, but the pattern held, and he wanted more of it. He made a chart in his notebook that afternoon: every kid in class, glasses or no glasses, indoors or outdoors. He knew the survey would have to precede any real conclusion, so he asked everyone the same two questions and kept careful tally marks.

By Friday the pattern was still holding, more or less, and Bentley had decided that weekend number one of the new outdoor life would start immediately. Then came the twist. Ms. Clarke-Williams stopped by his desk, looked at his chart, and laughed. "Interesting project, Bentley. I've worn glasses since I was eight." He checked his column for her, and there it was, written in his own neat pencil: Ms. Clarke-Williams, no glasses.

"You have contacts," Bentley said.

"I do. And I grew up on a farm. Outside all day, every day, and I still ended up nearsighted." She tapped his chart. "So your pattern has a hole in it."

Bentley stared at the tally marks. So being outdoors made nearsightedness less common, but it was no guarantee, more like a coin that landed heads more often than tails. He drew a small arrow from Ms. Clarke-Williams's row to the margin and wrote, exception, test more people.

"Saturday," he announced to Aryan at the door. "Park. Bring the Xbox controller if you have to, but leave it in your pocket."

Chase stood guard over the biggest box of his life: four dozen samosas, two giant jugs of mango juice, and a tray of sweets, all labeled CARGO in his dad's marker. The community hall smelled like onions and excitement, and tomorrow the whole pile would ride in the van at the front of the Vaisakhi procession.

"Watch it," his dad had said. "Last year, half the sweets vanished the night before."

That was the mystery Chase intended to solve. Somebody in this hall was a sweet thief, and he was going to catch them. He recruited the first two people he saw: Kelsey, who lived three houses down, and Edie, who could stare at a wall for ten minutes without blinking, which made her ideal for surveillance work.

"Nobody's getting past me," Edie said, sitting on a folding chair facing the box.

They took shifts while the aunties cooked and the uncles argued about parade route maps. By dinner, the mystery had already begun. The tray of sweets, which Chase had counted twice at eleven in the morning, now held exactly six fewer pieces.

"Somebody's stealing at daylight," he whispered. "Or they're nocturnal. Like a raccoon."

"Raccoons don't like burfi," said Kelsey, who knew this because a raccoon had once rejected her sandwich entirely.

Chase had a plan for the morning. Before anyone touched the cargo, he had laid a thin line of flour across the floor in front of the table, one his dad wouldn't notice. His theory: the thief had to walk, so the thief had to leave tracks. He crouched and squinted at the flour line, and there they were, tiny prints, five toes, raccoon-shaped, leading from the flour to the wall and stopping at a loose vent panel near the floor.

"It IS a raccoon," he said, feeling like a champion detective.

Edie peered at the prints. "Chase. Look at the size of them. That's the biggest raccoon in the world, or..."

Or footprints in socks. Human socks. The prints doubled back and vanished behind the stage curtain.

Chase crept over and yanked the curtain aside. There sat the janitor's kid, a small boy maybe five years old, with flour-socked feet and a burfi crumb on his chin, guarding a tower of stolen sweets like a dragon on gold.

"Twist!" Edie announced, pointing.

They returned the sweets, mostly, except the part that could not be returned for evidence reasons. The little boy's mother promised to keep him away from the cargo, and Chase taped the vent shut anyway, just to be safe.

Outside, the drums were warming up for tomorrow. Kelsey tugged her uncle's sleeve as he carried a banner toward the truck.

"Why does this day matter so much?" she asked him. "Everyone keeps saying it's the big one."

He grinned. "Vaisakhi. In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur. That's why the whole city will be out there tomorrow."

"So it's a birthday," Kelsey said.

"Sort of," her uncle said. "Now grab that end of the banner, detective. You too, raccoon catchers."

Chase and Edie each took a corner of the cloth, and the gold letters of the banner snapped open into the evening air.

The running track circled the hockey rink like a balcony, four laps of hallway carpet above the ice, and in the cold air Payton could hear skates scraping below while the cross-country team warmed up. She had entered her first eight-hundred-metre race on Saturday, and Ms. Okonkwo had let the team use the rink track after practice. Payton's problem was simple and stubborn: both times she had time-trialed the distance, she flew through the first lap and then died on the second, finishing slow and gasping. Something invisible was going wrong, and she meant to find it.

Angela jogged up beside her with the stopwatch. "Want to try again?" she asked. Payton nodded and turned over the paper race number she had pinned to her shirt. On the back, in pencil, she had written her math from the bus that morning: to finish eight hundred metres in three minutes on a four-hundred-metre track, a runner must average ninety seconds for each lap. "So my target is ninety for lap one," Payton said. "Not ninety-five, not eighty. If I hit ninety, I have a shot at three minutes."

The first attempt, she went out hard the way instinct told her to, and Angela called the split at sixty-four seconds. Payton's second lap was one hundred and eleven. "See?" she panted, hands on her knees, watching the zamboni glide below. "Going fast early doesn't conceal the problem. It makes it worse. The fast lap steals from the slow one." Brady, stretching against the railing, grinned. "So don't be a hero for one lap," he said. "Be boring twice."

She tried again, and this time she counted her steps and held back even when her legs begged to sprint. Angela called "ninety-one" at the lap, and Payton kept her rhythm, arms easy, breath even. Coming off the last curve she still had something left, and she spent it all in the final straight. Angela clicked the watch and held it up: three minutes, one second.

"One second off," Payton said, but she was smiling. Brady clapped his mitten-covered hands together. Below them, a goalie tapped his stick on the ice, and the sound rang up through the cold.

"Ninety and ninety-one," Angela said, reading the splits off the watch. "That's the whole secret, isn't it?" Payton folded the race number and put it in her pocket, the pencil numbers facing in. "Ninety and ninety," she said. "On Saturday."

Fox's kitchen smelled like burnt popcorn, but nobody mentioned it, because Fox's science project was due Monday and the bean seeds had failed to germinate even though he'd watered them twice a day for two weeks. "They're dead," Fox said, sliding his phone across the table to Samuel. "But that's not my problem. This is my problem."

On the screen was a half-written email: a birthday invitation for Saturday, addressed to exactly one person, Tiana. "I want to invite the whole class," Fox said. "All twenty-six of them. But last time I sent a group email, everybody hit Reply All for three days. Nolan replied 'ok' to twenty-six people. Twice."

Samuel picked up the phone and looked at the fields above the message. To. CC. And under those, a third one, grayed out like it was waiting for something. BCC. He'd seen it a hundred times and never once tapped it. "What's this one do?"

"Blind carbon copy," Fox said, reading the label out loud with a shrug. "No idea. Sounds like a spy thing."

Samuel tapped it anyway. A new field opened up, translucent in the way the phone showed empty boxes, and he typed Tiana's address there instead of in the To line. The To line still needed something, so he put Fox's own address in it. "Test it," he said. "Send that to Tiana and to your mom's account. Then we check what your mom's account shows."

Fox sent it. Then he logged into his mother's laptop at the counter, next to the hummingbird feeder, where a bird was dipping its beak into the nectar so fast it was mostly a blur. The email was there, from Fox, subject and all. Fox's mother's address sat alone in the To line. There was no sign of Tiana anywhere.

"She's invisible," Fox said slowly. "Tiana got it, though. She's already typing."

Samuel scrolled on the laptop and found the proof. Forward, he thought. If somebody forwarded the message, the whole list would come with it, but the list only had one name. Twenty-six people could get the invitation, and no one would see anyone else's address. He felt the idea settle in his chest like a seed that had finally been in the right soil. "Okay. Put every address in BCC. Put your own address in To. Nobody sees anybody."

Fox grabbed the phone and started typing, hunched over the counter while the feeder's sugar water caught the afternoon light. But he stopped halfway through the class list, his thumb hovering above the screen.

"What about Tiana?" he asked. "She told me she doesn't want her address going anywhere. That's why she never signs the group birthday card. She thinks people save them."

Samuel looked at the To line, then at the empty BCC field, and then he grinned. "That's the whole point. She can come, and nobody gets her address. Not even the other kids."

Fox finished the list, double-checked it, and hit Send. The phone buzzed almost immediately with a reply, and he turned the screen so Samuel could see it.

From Tiana: "Saturday. I'll be there. And whatever you just did, tell me how."

Emilia pressed her pencil so hard against the paper that the vanishing point turned into a smudge. She had drawn her street three times already, and every time the shops looked wrong, like the whole block was sliding downhill toward the dot in the middle.

"Ms. Bondarenko's going to pick two drawings for the hallway display on Friday," Jerry said from the next table. He was outlining his bakery again, tracing the same lines over and over so they would look bold. "I want mine chosen so bad my grandma could see it at open house."

"You'll get it," Emilia said, but she was staring at her own paper. Her bakery had a door and two windows, and she had slanted every single edge toward the vanishing point, just like the road. The roofline, the doorframe, even the window tops all leaned inward, and now the front of the building looked like it was toppling over sideways.

Cloe leaned across the aisle. "Whoa. Yours look like they're falling."

"I know," Emilia said. "But the road works, and the roofline works, so why not the windows?" She flipped back to Ms. Bondarenko's example sheet, the one with a neat street and one dot. In the example, the road edges slanted toward the dot, and the rooftops slanted toward it too. But the window tops were flat. So were the tops of the doors. Every line on the fronts of the buildings ran straight across, perfectly horizontal, or straight up and down, perfectly vertical. Emilia's stomach did a small flip. The lines that faced her squarely, straight on, weren't supposed to lean at all. Only the sides of the buildings, the ones angled away, ran toward the vanishing point.

She tested it before she told anyone. On a scrap sheet she drew one shop front with slanted windows and another with flat ones, side by side. The flat one looked solid and calm. The slanted one looked like it was about to precede its own roof into the gutter. She almost laughed out loud.

"Okay, watch," she said to Jerry and Cloe. She erased her window tops, laid her ruler flat, and redrew them horizontal. She squared the doorframes vertical. When she held the paper up, the bakery stood firm at the corner of her street, and the road still raced away toward the dot.

"Whoa," Jerry said. "Show me that again, slow." He had already ruined two windows on his own bakery by slanting them. "Flat for the fronts, angled for the sides."

"Right," Emilia said. "The vanishing point gets the road and the rooftops, but not the fronts."

Cloe frowned at her own paper. "So my whole row of shops has been falling over since Tuesday, and I thought I just couldn't draw." She grinned and started erasing. "Fixing ten windows is not trivial, by the way. You owe me a pencil."

"I'll sharpen you a whole case," Emilia said, and drew her last window, flat and true, while Jerry measured his doorframe twice.

The stage lights at the community theatre hummed so loudly that Livia could hear them from the wings, where she stood watching Dion fail. He and Calista were supposed to improvise a two-minute scene about a rainy day, and every time Calista said "Yes, and," Dion just nodded and said "Okay" and the scene died like a radio losing signal. Ms. Santoso, who ran the Saturday workshop, clapped her hands and called a break, but Livia barely noticed. She was thinking about last spring, when she had quit the workshop the day before the showcase because she was afraid of freezing in front of a crowd. That fear had sat dormant in her all summer, like something waiting under ice, and she had only just come back.

During the break she wandered past the prop table, where a plastic ship's wheel leaned against a painted backdrop of a spaceship hull, dented and silver. Calista flopped into a folding chair beside her. "Dion keeps stalling," Calista said. "I offer him stuff and he just stands there."

"He's not saying no," Livia said slowly. "He's saying nothing." She turned the ship's wheel with one finger. Something about the prop was snagging in her mind. Last week Ms. Santoso had mentioned a trick in passing, half a sentence tossed over her shoulder, and Livia hadn't caught all of it. Something about how what you say can hand your partner a whole role, like telling them "Doctor, my arm hurts" and suddenly they are the doctor. Livia hadn't understood it then. Now she wondered if the wheel was an answer.

"Can I try a scene with you?" she asked Calista. "Right now, before break ends. I have an idea."

They stepped onto the stage. Livia took a breath and said, "Yes, and it's good thing you showed up, Captain, because the ship's hull is cracked and we're taking on water." She picked up the wheel and held it out.

Calista blinked, then straightened her spine and took it. "Aye. Everyone to stations. And you, First Officer, seal that leak before we lose the cargo." Just like that, Livia was the first officer, and she knew exactly what to do, because Calista's words had made her into it. She knelt by the backdrop and pressed her palms to the painted metal. "Yes, and the sealant is holding, Captain, but there's something moving in the hold."

Dion, watching from the front row, leaned forward. "How did you do that?" he called up. "Calista froze for me every time."

Livia hesitated, half-tempted to keep the trick to herself after how he'd hogged the spotlight in the fall play. But she remembered quitting, and how keeping her fear private had fixed nothing. "It's called endowing," she said. "You give your partner a part through what you say. Watch."

She turned back to Calista. "Captain, we need to disclose what's in that hold before we dock. Should I open it?"

"Open it, First Officer," Calista said. "Whatever's down there has been dormant long enough."

Bennett stood in Willa's garage, which her dad had strung with paper lanterns for the farewell party, and tried to memorize everything at once. The folding table with the dented punch bowl. Alden attempting to juggle three dinner rolls and failing gloriously. He was leaving in six days, and he had a theory that if he collected enough of this, packed it in his head like souvenirs, the move would hurt less.

Willa slid next to him by the chip bags. "You're doing the staring thing," she said. "You did it at the science fair too, right before your volcano won."

"I'm recruiting memories," Bennett said. "For the move."

Willa frowned, which meant she was actually thinking. "That's backwards. When we moved here in fourth grade, I cried at a photo of my old street for like a month. Homesickness, my mom called it. Being away from home and all your familiar people." She grabbed a chip. "It didn't stop until I got used to things here. You can't stockpile against it, it just... happens, and then it fades while you settle in. My mom said it's really common, like almost everybody gets it."

Bennett didn't want to believe her. He'd been feeling quietly rebellious about the whole move anyway, refusing to pack his bookshelf, and part of him felt a smoldering resentment toward his dad's new job, even though his dad hadn't done anything wrong exactly. If Willa was right, then his memory-collecting was pointless, like bringing an umbrella to stop it from raining. He decided to test it. He closed his eyes for ten whole seconds in the middle of the party and tried to burn the garage into his brain. When he opened them, Alden had stacked all the dinner rolls into a wobbly pyramid on Bennett's head.

"Science," Alden said solemnly.

Bennett laughed so hard the rolls cascaded onto his shoes, and Mr. Mwangi from next door poked his head in, saw the rolls, and quietly added one more to the pile before anyone could stop him.

Later, when the lanterns were being taken down, Bennett thought about a choice he'd made back in fourth grade, before Willa arrived. There had been another new kid that year, a quiet boy who ate alone, and Bennett had never sat with him. He'd told himself the boy seemed fine. Now he wondered. Had that kid gone home and cried over some street he missed, while Bennett, who could have helped, just watched?

He found Willa pulling a lantern off its string. "When I get there," he said, "I'm going to find whoever eats alone. Just so you know. That's my plan."

"Recruit them into your pyramid of science?" she said.

"Obviously."

She handed him the lantern, the green one, still warm from its bulb. "Take it. Put it in your new room."

He held it by its wire loop, careful, like it might remember this night as long as he did.

Ivy set the greeting card on the picnic table and pressed the fold with her thumb. The thick card cracked along the crease in a jagged white line, and the paint on the outside flaked off in little chips, like frost. It was the third card she had ruined that afternoon. Her mother's birthday was tomorrow, and the folded cards in the craft store would cost more than the money in her jar.

She sat on the back step and thought about last winter, when Edmond's father had rebuilt the fence. Edmond had watched him work and told Ivy about it later, laughing at his own memory of it. His father had run a tool along each plank before bending it around the fence post, a dull-edged thing pressed in a straight line, and the wood had folded smooth as bread dough instead of splintering. Ivy had not understood it then, but the picture stayed in her head.

Maybe card worked like that too. She went back to the table, where the lawn smelled of cut grass and the ice in her lemonade had melted to a thin ring. She found a butter knife with a rounded, worn edge, laid a ruler across the card, and drew the blunt tool along the line once, firmly, like a piston moving in a single steady stroke. Then she folded the card. The crease came out clean and straight, with no cracks and no bumpy lumps along the fold. She ran her finger over it and grinned.

"That's the one," she said out loud.

Jayden leaned over the fence a few minutes later, chin on his arms. "Why is yours flat and the other ones all ugly?"

"You score it first," Ivy said. "You run a blunt tool along the line before you fold, and the fold comes out straight instead of cracked."

Jayden squinted at the ruined cards in the grass, then at the new one. "Huh. That's actually kind of great." He pointed at her paint set. "Can you do a lily on it? Mom likes lilies." Ivy revised her plan for the front of the card, sketching lightly in pencil before she touched the brush to it. The petals came out the way she wanted, soft and a little crooked, but right.

By evening the card stood finished on the kitchen counter, propped against the sugar bowl, folded edge crisp as a book's spine. Ivy's mother came in from the garden with dirt on her hands and saw it there. She picked it up, opened it slowly along the clean crease, and read the words inside twice.

"You made this?" her mother asked.

"All by myself," Ivy said. "Every fold of it."

Felix stood on Ibraheem's porch with a folded note in his hand, breathing in the smell of rain that had rolled through an hour ago. The grass was lush and dripping, and mist still hung over the backyard like slow-moving vapor. He had written the note last night, after the fight, and now he had to actually give it to someone.

The fight was with Brynlee. On Tuesday he had knocked her volcano project off the lab table, laughed with Ibraheem about the mess, and then told everyone in the cafeteria that she had overreacted. She hadn't spoken to him since. He wanted his best friend back, and the note was his plan.

Inside, Ibraheem was spreading clay across a cardboard base, building his own model for Mr. Levy's class. "You came," he said. "Sit down. Tell me what that is."

"It's an apology," Felix said. He unfolded it and read it out loud. "Brynlee, I'm sorry if you got upset about the volcano thing."

Ibraheem set down his clay tool. "Read that again." Felix did. "Sorry if you got upset. That's weird. It makes it sound like it's her fault for being upset, not yours for knocking it over."

Felix read it a third time, slower. He was starting to see what Ibraheem meant, like noticing a pattern hidden in a sentence he had already checked twice. "My sister watched this video," Ibraheem said, rolling a ridge of clay. "She said that's called a non-apology. It's sorry about your feelings, not sorry about what you did." Felix copied the word onto his palm with a finger, then hunted through his backpack for a pen.

"So the note's not really an apology at all," he said. "It's a fake one." He spread the paper flat on the table, next to Ibraheem's half-built mountain, and crossed out his old line. The pen tore through once and he smoothed the page and started over on the back.

He tried writing it out several ways. "I'm sorry your project broke" still blamed the project. "I'm sorry the accident happened" blamed the accident. Finally he wrote, "I'm sorry I knocked over your volcano and laughed. That was my fault, both parts." He read it aloud, and it felt different in his mouth, harder to say and more true.

"Better," Ibraheem said, but then he pinched off a piece of clay and illustrated the problem with it, squashing it flat under his thumb. "Except you laughed about it with me, at lunch, in front of everyone. The note fixes Tuesday morning, not Tuesday lunch."

Felix stared at the flattened clay. He had been thinking about the volcano and forgetting the cafeteria completely, like a person who fixes one broken window in a house and ignores the hole in the roof. "Then I go say it there," he said. "Where I did it."

They found Brynlee at her locker before first period. Felix held out the note, but he didn't hand it over, because he wanted her to hear the words from him. "I'm sorry I knocked over your volcano and laughed," he said. "That was my fault, both parts. I'm sorry I did it in front of everyone, too."

Brynlee looked at the paper, then at him. "That's a real apology," she said. "Not a sorry-if one." She slung her backpack over her shoulder. "You can help me rebuild the lava flow at lunch. It takes two hands anyway."

Eva had exactly forty minutes before the judges reached her table, and her bean plants were acting strange. Two weeks ago she had started them for her project, and one pot by the window had sprouted tall and green while the other, on the shelf by the door, sat there doing basically nothing. The whole fair buzzed around her in the gym: a kid named Brogan was testing whether his polymer balls could bounce higher off concrete than off carpet, and Channing was trying to negotiate a second extension from Mr. Sadeghi because her volcano kept leaking. Eva waved them both over.

"Look at these," Eva said, pointing at the pots. "Same seeds, same water, same soil. So why is this one winning?"

Brogan leaned in until his nose almost touched the leaves. "Maybe it likes you better. Plants can sense stuff."

"Plants can't sense stuff."

"Then explain the window pot, genius."

Channing peered at both pots, then at the poster Eva had propped up, which read, in giant hopeful letters, PLANTS LIKE MUSIC. "Wait," she said. "What does that even mean? How would you know if a plant likes music? It can't clap."

Eva opened her mouth, then closed it. Her poster had a nice drawing and a title she'd made at eleven o'clock the night before, and absolutely nothing else. A judge with a clipboard was already circling nearer, pausing at each table, and the clock above the bleachers showed thirty-one minutes.

"Mr. Sadeghi," Channing announced, and dragged him over before Eva could stop her. He read the poster, then looked at Eva with the mild smile that meant trouble.

"Interesting claim," he said. "Tell me, how would you test it?"

Eva's mind went blank, then scrambled. Test it. A plant couldn't say yes or no, so you had to make it show you somehow. "You could play music for one plant and not another," she said slowly, "and then see if they grow differently."

"Better. But what exactly will you look for? Guess what will happen first, in one sentence."

Eva stared at the pots. A guess you could actually check. "If I play music for one plant and not the other, then... the music plant will grow taller." She said it out loud and felt something click into place. "That's a real hypothesis. If, then. The change, and what I predict."

Mr. Sadeghi nodded once and moved on, but Eva wasn't done, because the shelf plant still made no sense, and now she had a tool. If light were the difference, then moving the shelf plant to the window should fix it. She carried the pot over, set it beside its rival, and marked both with tape labels so no judge could accuse her of cheating.

At the twenty-minute mark, Brogan wandered back holding one of his polymer balls, which had somehow gotten stuck in his hair. "Your hypothesis has a problem," he said, chewing gum with great seriousness. "I watered your shelf plant Tuesday. With soda. It looked thirsty and I felt bad."

Eva grabbed his sleeve. "How much soda?"

"Like half a can. It was orange."

So there was her hidden cause, sitting there the whole time, sweet and orange and patient. She yanked a fresh poster board from under the table and wrote fast: her if-then sentence, the shelf plant, the soda confession signed by a guilty witness. When the judge finally stopped at her table, Eva pointed at the tall pot, the struggling one, and Brogan, who raised his hand like he was swearing on a Bible.

"The data," she said, "is durable. The witness, less so."

Liam arrived at the street festival just after four o'clock, carrying a box of small clay lamps his grandmother had sent. He was supposed to set them up at the community table, but when he got there, the organizer pointed at the sky and said the lamps had to be burning before dark, and dark came at six. Liam had about forty lamps and one strip of ledge along the festival stage to work with.

Archie and Marissa found him counting lamps out of the box. "What are those?" Archie asked.

"They're called diyas," Liam said. "Little oil lamps. You light them for Diwali, the festival of lights." He held one up so they could see the shallow bowl and the cotton wick lying inside.

Marissa picked up a lamp and turned it over. "You need oil for all of these? We have two hours."

"There's a jug behind the stage," Liam said. "But if we pour one at a time, we'll never make it." He thought about the problem. Instead of filling lamps one by one, they could coordinate the jobs: one person poured oil, one placed wicks, one carried finished lamps to the ledge and spaced them out. He told Archie and Marissa the plan, and they set up an assembly line on the folding table, moving the lamps left to right like cars through a car wash.

They had filled about thirty when a man from the next booth complained that the lamps were too close to his stall. The festival organizer came over, looking like a judge about to rule on a case, and Marissa whispered, "You'd better argue well, defendant." The man said fire near his paper decorations wasn't safe, and Liam pointed out that the ledge ran along the stage, not the booth. The organizer measured the gap with his arm, said it was fine, and told the man to move his decorations back a foot.

By ten to six, the last lamp sat on the ledge, and a woman from the temple went along the row with a long match, tipping each flame alive. As the sky turned grey, the diyas glowed one after another, a bright line against the darkening street. Liam's grandmother had told him on the phone that this was only the first night, and that the festival would go on for five days, with the lamps lit again each evening. He would come back tomorrow, and the day after, with the same box.

"Look at that," Archie said, and pointed to where a little girl in a gold dress was holding her hands near the flames, not touching, just feeling the warmth.

Joseph sat on Martha's kitchen floor with her phone balanced on his knee, scrolling through photos from Saturday's soccer game while Martha microwaved popcorn in the next room. He stopped at a picture of himself mid-jump, mouth open, eyes crossed, looking like a startled frog. He had never seen it before. Martha's account was private, he knew that, because she'd made a big deal of it last month. Only followers could see her posts, and she'd bragged that she'd counted every one of them.

"Martha," he called. "When did you take this?"

She came in shaking a bag of popcorn. "Saturday. Why?"

"It has forty likes." He held up the phone. "You have like thirty followers."

Martha frowned and took the phone. She tapped the picture, scrolled, and her eyebrows went up. The likes kept loading. Then she opened her messages, and there it was: her private post, forwarded by a boy named Dylan from another school, sent to a group chat with eighty people in it. "I didn't even know Dylan followed me," she said slowly. "I accepted him forever ago because he commented on my cat video."

Joseph leaned over her shoulder. "So being private doesn't matter?"

"It limits who sees my posts," Martha said. "But anyone I already accepted can still copy or share what they see." She said it like she was reading it off a wall, and Joseph could tell she'd just figured it out too.

He thought about that while she chewed popcorn. He had his own account, also private, with a follower named Catherine from summer camp, a girl he'd spoken to exactly twice. If she could forward anything he posted, then his embarrassing trip-and-fall video from the pool party last week wasn't as safe as he'd believed. He borrowed Martha's phone to check, since his own was dead at home, and yes, there was Catherine, still on his list, still able to see everything.

"What are you doing?" Martha asked.

"Testing something." He went to his page through her account, saved the pool party video to her camera roll with a few taps, and then deleted it. The copy stayed in the photos. That was the part that made his stomach drop. Even if he deleted a post, anyone could have already saved it, and he would never know. He showed Martha the saved video sitting there on her phone like evidence.

"So what do we do?" she asked.

Joseph made her go through her followers one by one, unfollowing anyone she couldn't actually name. When she got to Dylan, she hesitated, then pressed remove. He did the same thing later at home, starting with Catherine. It seemed plausible that most of his followers were fine, but "seemed plausible" wasn't the same as knowing, so he checked each one anyway.

On Monday, a kid from Mr. Ramos's homeroom stopped Joseph in the hall and grinned. "Nice frog face," the kid said. Joseph just looked at him and kept walking. At lunch, Martha slid her phone across the table, showing him she'd made a new account. "Private from day one," she said. "And this time I know every follower's actual face."

"Show me how you set it up," Joseph said, and pulled out his phone.

Jace spread his notebook across the library table and wrote, in careful letters, "Does the brand name change how cereal tastes?" His project for the science fair was due in nine days, and so far all he had was a question and two boxes of corn flakes in his backpack, one famous and expensive, one from the store's own shelf. He had asked Audrey and Anaya to meet him in the back corner by the biography section, because the librarian let you talk there as long as you whispered.

"Here's the problem," Jace said when they arrived. "If you hand people a bowl and tell them it's the fancy brand, they'll probably say it's better. That's not really a taste test. That's a test of the box." Audrey frowned at the two boxes poking out of his bag. "So don't show them the boxes," she said. "Hide them. Pour the cereal, label the bowls A and B, and don't tell anyone which is which." Anaya tapped the table. "Then nobody's expectations can sway their answers. It's called a blind test. My sister did one for her project last year." Jace wrote it down fast, feeling the shape of a real experiment forming at last.

They set up right there. Audrey took both boxes behind the study carrel, out of everyone's sight, and came back with two unlabeled bags. She filled six bowls, marked A on three and B on three, and shuffled their positions when Jace wasn't looking. Anaya fetched water cups. One by one, they tasted, rinsed, and wrote their scores on slips of paper that Jace folded without reading. A man at the next table watched them crunching and whispering, and once the librarian drifted over, but she only raised an eyebrow and moved on.

Jace unfolded the slips at home that night, and his stomach dropped. Six out of six picks favored bowl B. He stared at the pile, sure he had messed something up, because B had to be the cheap one. He was certain of it. Certain, that is, until he opened his backpack and found a folded note tucked into the famous brand's box.

"Dear detective," the note read, in Audrey's looping handwriting. "You checked my bags twice but never the boxes. I swapped the cereal before you even got to the library. The flakes in the famous box came from the store-brand bag. Your labels were never right, and that's the twist for your board: if you can't trust the box, how can you trust your tongue? Bring eight dollars to lunch. I had to buy both bags. Audrey."

He laughed out loud in his dark kitchen. His first experiment had failed in the most useful way possible, and that insight was better than any result: the labels themselves could lie. He would need a more sophisticated setup for the fair, numbered samples, sealed envelopes, someone else holding the key. He sat back down, opened his notebook to a fresh page, and began writing the story of how bowl B won.

The spelling bee was down to three people, and Aiden wanted the dictionary that Mr. Cardinal kept on his desk, the big one with the ribbon bookmarks, promised to the winner. Marko had spelled "prohibit" without pausing, and Leela, who wanted the trophy that came with the dictionary more than she wanted the dictionary itself, had gotten through "fungus" and "extravagant." Now it was Aiden's turn.

"Chorus," said Mr. Cardinal. "Language of origin: Greek."

Aiden stared at the chalkboard behind Mr. Cardinal's head. The k sound. He thought about the word list he'd studied with his mother, where he'd tripped over "chef" twice. Chef had the sh sound spelled c-h, and next to it in the notes his mother had written "French." Chef was French, and it used c-h for the sh sound. If French used c-h for sh, then Greek might use c-h for the k sound. He had never seen it written down; he was guessing from the pattern.

"C-h-o-r-u-s," he said. "Chorus."

"Correct," said Mr. Cardinal.

Leela clapped once, then pressed her hands flat on her desk. Her word was "chef." She asked for the language of origin, the way spellers did, and Mr. Cardinal said, "French." Aiden watched her mouth move. She started with c, then hesitated, changed it, and said "s-h-e-f." The bell on Mr. Cardinal's desk rang.

Marko went out on "chaos," trying s-h at the front, so it was Aiden and Leela. She got "chimney" right, glaring at the ceiling while she spelled it. Then Aiden had "orchestra." Greek again, Mr. Cardinal said. The k sound after the vowel. If the pattern held, it was c-h here too.

"O-r-c-h-e-s-t-r-a," Aiden said. "Orchestra."

"Correct," said Mr. Cardinal. "One more. Leela, 'chef.'"

She closed her eyes. "C-h-e-f. Chef."

"Correct," Mr. Cardinal said, and wrote both their names on the board side by side. "We'll settle it Monday." He slid the dictionary an inch toward the center of the desk. Leela leaned over and touched the cover, once, like she was checking it would still be there.

"Chorus," she said to Aiden on the way out. "I never would have tried c-h."

"Chef," Aiden said. "You almost lost it and you didn't."

She pulled the trophy off the shelf by the window and held it up so he could see his reflection in the bowl of it. "Monday," she said. "Bring your pattern."

The family group chat, which was called FAM JAM because his uncle thought he was funny, lit up at 4:32 on Friday afternoon, and Eli grabbed his phone off the bus seat like it was on fire.

"First dance TONIGHT," he typed. "I cannot dance. This is an emergency."

His mom answered first with seventeen exclamation points. His dad sent a thumbs up, which helped nobody. Then his grandmother, who had learned to send videos that spring, dropped in a clip of a white bird with a yellow crest bobbing its head, stomping, and swinging its neck in perfect time while a pop song played. Eli watched it four times. Under the video his grandmother had typed, "If this bird can do it, so can you."

Eli read the caption next to the video twice. In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel had shown that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed. He sat up so fast he banged his head on the bus window. The bird didn't just bounce around. It kept the beat, and when the beat slowed down or sped up, the bird slowed down or sped up with it. He screen-recorded the clip and forwarded it to Kade and then, after a long minute of deciding, to Sia, because Sia had told him at lunch that she was "probably just going to stand near the punch" and had said it while looking at her tray like it might save her.

"Scientific proof that rhythm is learnable," Eli texted. "This bird changed speed when the song changed speed. It adjusted. It ADJUSTED, Sia."

Kade replied with "lol" and then, a minute later, "wait that's actually kind of great."

Sia sent one message back: "A bird. Really."

At the dance, the gym smelled like floor wax and the banner hung perpendicular to the wall, sagging a little in the middle, and the DJ was terrible in the best possible way. Eli and Sia stood near the punch for two whole songs, and then the speakers switched to something slow at first and then quicker. Sia tilted her head. "Okay," she said. "Tempo change. If the bird can adjust, I can adjust." She started small, just shifting her weight, then matched it when the song sped up, and Eli matched her, and it worked, it actually worked, and Kade spun past doing a move that made him look like a startled kangaroo, some kind of bouncing marsupial, and Sia laughed so hard she nearly stopped dancing but didn't.

Later there was a brief argument about whose fault it was that Kade's elbow had knocked two cups of punch onto the floor, and Eli mediated by declaring that both of them had to help the coach mop, which they did, still keeping time to the music.

In the bathroom mirror, holding his phone at a careful angle, Eli took a photo of his sweaty, grinning face and sent it to FAM JAM with one word: "Snowball."

His grandmother replied in under a minute. "That's my boy."

The Saturday skate session was Nolan's whole plan for the weekend, and at 9:04 a.m. he opened the group chat to confirm it. Three messages sat there already. Kellen had written, "meet at the park at ten?" Ludovik had replied with a thumbs up and a photo of his board with new wheels. Nolan typed, "I'll be there" and then, worried his plain little message would get buried before anyone read it, deleted it and typed again in capitals: I WILL BE THERE.

Ludovik answered within a minute. "why are you yelling?" Nolan stared at the screen. Yelling? He had been sitting silently on his bed, not making a sound. He typed, "I'm not yelling, I'm at home," and Ludovik sent a single laughing emoji, then, "all caps = shouting, everyone knows that." Kellen added, "you sounded like a coach blowing the whistle, lol."

Nolan set the phone down and walked to the window, thinking it over. So the letters themselves carried a voice. He scrolled back through weeks of messages, testing the idea against the evidence, and found a pattern: whenever Ludovik's mother made him log off, his last message was always something like "I HAVE TO GO." Those messages did read like shouts, even though Nolan had never pictured it before. Mr. Banerjee from next door had once sent a notice to the whole street email list about the parking rules, all in capitals, and three people had written back sounding offended before he apologized and sent it again in lowercase. Same words, different letters, different feeling. It was like a principle of some kind, hidden inside the typing itself.

Still, part of Nolan opposed the whole idea. He had used capitals just to be noticed, not to be loud, and nobody had asked him that. He felt hesitant about typing anything else now, in case he got it wrong twice in one morning. He decided on a test. He sent a private message, just to Kellen: "in caps i meant please see my message. was that annoying?" Kellen replied, "kind of, yeah, but it's fine. just use regular letters, people will see it."

Nolan typed, "ok. see you at ten. bringing the ramp." Then he paused, and added one more line in the group chat, in careful lowercase: "sorry for shouting at you guys." Ludovik sent back, "we forgive you, don't do it at the park or the little kids will cry." Nolan grabbed his helmet and shoved the phone in his pocket, already out the door and halfway down the stairs.

The swim team had a problem, and it had a name that Henry didn't know yet. For the first three weeks of the season, the relay squad did nothing but argue. Abygael insisted the backstroke swimmer should go second. Megan wanted the fastest kid to anchor, even though that was Henry's spot, and she said so at every practice in the indoor pool behind the community centre. The water in the shallow end seemed to fluctuate between calm and chaos depending on who was yelling loudest on the deck.

Henry wanted that anchor leg more than he wanted almost anything. But he also wanted the relay to stop falling apart, because at the end of the month there was a real meet, and a team that fought at the wall would fight at the handoff too. He started paying attention, not to the arguments themselves but to the pattern underneath them. Week one, everyone had been shy and polite, learning names, copying the older swimmers. Week two, the politeness cracked open. Week three, the fighting felt almost organized, like it was settling into lanes.

He mentioned it to Mr. Tesfaye, who ran the pool and lived as a tenant in the apartment upstairs, coming down most evenings to check the chlorine. "It's like the team has stages," Henry said, dragging the kickboard back to the rack. "First everyone's nice, then everyone fights, then maybe something else."

Mr. Tesfaye smiled and said only, "There's a book in the lost-and-found box that might interest you. Nobody's claimed it since autumn." He did not say anything more, which was typical of him.

The book was a fat paperback about how groups work, and Henry found the page that night at his kitchen table. Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. He read it three times. The next morning at school he showed Megan the page. "See? Forming, storming, norming and performing," he said. "We're in the storming part. It's supposed to happen. The fighting isn't the end, it's a stage."

Megan squinted at it. "So if it's a stage, we just have to get through it?"

"That's my idea," Henry said. "But it won't just be time. We have to make the norming part happen. Mr. Tesfaye says the pool temperature is cumulative, little changes adding up all day. I think trust works like that too. Small things, stacked."

So at the next practice Henry stopped defending his lane and started stacking. When Abygael fumbled her goggles, he fished them off the bottom before she even finished her lap. When Megan's split time was bad, he told her what was good about her turn instead. Megan, who secretly wanted to be the one organizing everybody, grabbed the whiteboard from the office and drew the order of the relay, then handed the marker to Abygael. "You decide the backstroke spot," Megan said. Abygael wrote her own name second, and nobody argued.

At the meet, their handoffs were clean, one after another, and when Henry touched the wall at the end of the anchor leg, Megan was already reaching down to pull him out. "Told you," she said, grinning at the scoreboard. "Norming."

Olivier had noticed a pattern. On the nights before a math test, his stomach hurt, and on test mornings it hurt again. He had started keeping track on the back of his planner, and the bad-stomach days correspond exactly with quiz days. So it was not the cafeteria food, and it was not a virus. Something invisible was going on, and he wanted to know what.

He mentioned it to Calista while they were fighting with his locker, which had become rebellious lately and refused to open on the first three tries. "Does your stomach hurt before tests?" he asked. "Or is that just me?"

Calista got the locker open on the fourth yank. "Not my stomach. My brain does this loop where I imagine every way I could fail." She shrugged. "My mom calls it anxiety. She says everyone gets it, some people just get it louder."

That word rang a small bell. Mr. Ferreira had used it in homeroom last week, in the middle of a lesson on extinction, of all things. He had been explaining why the passenger pigeon died out, then paused and said some students had looked anxious about the science fair, and that anxiety was a normal response to stress. Olivier had mostly been drawing a pigeon at the time. Now he wished he had listened better.

So he ran a test of his own, the way he would test any rule. Thursday was the unit test, and on Wednesday night he did three things differently: he went for a bike ride around the block twice, he got in bed an hour earlier than usual, and he told his dad the whole thing, even the part about the planner chart. His dad didn't solve anything, he mostly listened and said the chart was smart. Thursday morning Olivier's stomach was quiet.

At lunch he found Calista and Rafael at the far table. "It worked," he said, sitting down. "Exercise, extra sleep, and talking to my dad. No stomach ache."

Rafael looked up from his tray. "Wait, what works?"

"Coping," Olivier said. "It means the ways you handle stress. I always thought it just meant, like, surviving. But there are actual strategies, and you can test them like a science experiment." He tore his chicken sandwich in half and offered a piece to Rafael.

"Next time I loop," Calista said, "I'm telling my mom instead of staring at my ceiling."

"Eleven tonight," Rafael said. "Basketball at my driveway. Bring the ball, mine's flat."

Olivier pointed at Rafael's tray. "Deal. Now eat your green beans."

Cole had thought the ball was moving fast, but the numbers said otherwise. He had watched Emerson bowl an old soccer ball down the flat concrete channel between the ramps at the skate park, and it had looked quick, so quick that his first guess at its speed had been way off. Now he crouched at the top of the channel with a tape measure in one hand and his phone stopwatch in the other, because Mr. Vargas's science assignment was due Monday, and the assignment asked for a distance-time graph of something that rolled.

"You're doing homework at a skate park," Anis said, rolling up beside them on his board.

"I'm doing homework on you guys," Cole said. "I need a ball, a distance, and a time. The graph I can draw at home."

He stretched the tape along the channel and marked three meters with a scrap of chalk. Three meters, no more, no less, because a short negotiation with Emerson had settled it: Emerson wanted a longer run so the ball would speed up on the slope, but Cole needed a flat, measured stretch or his graph would be wrong before he started. Emerson had finally agreed it was more feasible to roll on the flat and keep the measurement honest.

"Start it when I say go," Cole said. He crouched at the chalk line. "Not before, not after. Exactly on go."

Emerson set the ball down and steadied it. Anis leaned on his board to watch. Mr. Vargas, who had come down to the park with his dog, stopped near the fence but said nothing, which suited Cole fine.

"Go."

Emerson released the ball. Cole's thumb hit the stopwatch the instant it crossed the chalk line, and he watched it travel, counting silently, the ball rotating over the gray concrete. It crossed the three-meter mark and he stopped the timer. He looked at the screen. Two seconds.

"So how fast was it?" Anis asked.

Cole did the division on the back of his hand with the chalk. The ball had gone three meters in two seconds, so each second it had covered one and a half meters. "One point five meters per second," he said. "That's its speed. Three meters, two seconds, one point five."

"That's it? It looked way faster."

"That's the average," Cole said. He wrote the numbers on his hand: 0 seconds, 0 meters; 2 seconds, 3 meters. At home he would connect the two points and the slope of the line would be the speed. A steeper line would mean a faster ball, a flatter line a slower one, and the line for this ball sat exactly where the math put it, not where his eyes had.

Emerson rolled the ball again, and this time Cole called the numbers out loud as he clicked the stopwatch: "Three meters, two seconds, one point five." The chalk on his palm had already begun to blur, so he pressed his hand flat against his notebook before it could fade.

The sign on the diner door read CLOSED, but inside Mr. Chatterjee's kitchen, everything was hot and loud and moving. "Fifty minutes," Mr. Chatterjee announced, tapping the big clock above the stove. "The food critic arrives at six, and my sauce cook called in sick. You three wanted a real job? Here is your real job." Declan rolled up his sleeves. So did Nora and Khalid, though Khalid looked like he was rolling them up for a funeral.

Declan's first task was the onions. He gripped the knife somewhere between confidently and dangerously, and Mr. Chatterjee slid a cutting board toward him. "Claw grip," he said, curling his own fingers like a bear paw. "Fingertips tucked, knuckles forward. The knife respects knuckles. It does not respect fingertips." Declan curled his hand into a claw and pressed the onion with his knuckles while the blade whispered past them. "I feel like a very cautious crab," he said, and Nora snorted so hard she almost dropped a garlic clove.

While the onions sizzled, the sauce went wrong. Declan had crushed the tomatoes, added the garlic, and let it bubble, but it looked thin and sad, like soup that had given up on life. Worse, it refused to stick to anything. He drizzled some over a test noodle and watched it slide right off into the bowl. "The critic will write that our sauce has commitment issues," Khalid said, poking at it.

Then Declan noticed something. The pot of pasta next to him had a cloudy, almost slippery look to the water, and when he fished out a spoon and let it cool, it felt faintly gluey between his fingers.
