Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, he thought, and starch was the thing that made sauces thick, wasn't it? He remembered his aunt's gravy going lumpy from flour. Maybe the water itself could do a job like that. "Don't dump that pot!" he shouted, just as Khalid lifted it toward the sink. Khalid froze mid-lift, like a statue of a man betraying his friends. "A splash of that starchy water helps the sauce thicken and cling to the pasta," Declan said, ladling a bit in and stirring. Nora saved a whole cupful, "in case of emergencies, or in case you're wrong."

He was not wrong. Within a minute the sauce turned glossy and smooth, and when he dragged another test noodle through it, the sauce clung on like it never wanted to let go. Khalid changed his mind about the whole plan with dramatic speed. "I take back every doubt," he declared. "You are a pasta genius. I am merely a pasta apprentice."

At 5:58 the plates went out. The critic, a small woman with a large notebook, twirled her fork, took one bite, and closed her eyes. Mr. Chatterjee peered through the pass-out window, gripping the counter. When the critic finally wrote something down, she held the notebook up so they could read it. Three words: "Sauce. Perfect. Again?"

Hunter had until tomorrow morning to make his street drawing look like a street instead of a flat wall, and the lampposts were winning. He had five of them across the page, each exactly the same height, standing in a neat row like fence posts. He stared at the sketch at the kitchen table, then at the reference photo Ms. Demetriou had handed out, then back at his page.

"If they're the same height in real life, why do they look like that in the photo?" he asked Elie, who sat across the table working on her own version of the assignment. She leaned over and squinted at his lampposts. "In the photo they shrink," she said. "And they get squished together, kind of. Like they're huddling for warmth." Hunter grabbed a ruler and held it against the photo, measuring each lamppost. He had never tried to quantify a drawing before, but numbers felt safer than guessing. The closest one measured tall. The farthest one barely cleared the ruler's first mark, and the gaps between the posts shrank the deeper into the picture they went.

He remembered Tuesday then, the day Ms. Demetriou had drawn the street on the whiteboard while the class was supposed to be quiet because the refugee family visiting from the front office was being introduced down the hall. She had drawn one dot in the middle of the board and called it the vanishing point, and every line of her street had leaned toward it like it owed the dot money. Hunter had been half listening, doodling what he later told Elie was "definitely a snake and not a squiggle." Now he wished he'd paid more attention, because the snake was not going to save his grade.

"One-point perspective," he said slowly, tapping his pencil on the blank part of his page. "So all my lines go to one point, and the lampposts shrink toward it too." He erased his fence-post row, drew a small dot in the center of the page, and fanned faint lines out from it. Then he drew the nearest lamppost big and bold, and each one after it smaller and squeezed closer to its neighbor. Elie watched him work, chewing the end of her marker. "If you fail this," she said, "I'm telling everyone the snake was venomous and it distracted you. Self-defense. Very tragic."

"It was a squiggle," Hunter said, "and squiggles are harmless." He held the page up to the kitchen light. The street ran away from him, deep and real, the little posts marching toward the dot and shrinking the whole way, and for the first time all night it looked like somewhere you could actually walk. Elie leaned over, nodded once, and said, "Okay, now draw the snake on the corner. The street deserves it."

The toast sat untouched on Brooke's plate for the third morning in a row, and last night she had stared at the ceiling until the numbers on her clock read 2:47. She pressed the back of her hand to her forehead like her grandmother used to do. No fever. She wasn't stuffy, either, and her throat didn't hurt. So why did she feel like her bones were made of wet sand?

At school, Elly slid her tray across the table in the cafeteria. "You didn't eat your granola bar again," Elly said. "That's the whole week, basically." Brooke shrugged. "I keep thinking I'm coming down with something, but I can't find any symptoms." Mr. Otieno, who was on lunch duty, must have overheard, because he told her the nurse's office was open if she wanted to check in. He added that the nurse couldn't give out so much as a cough drop without a parent authorizing it first, but she could talk.

The nurse's office smelled like soap and paper towels. A small pamphlet rack stood by the cot, and while Brooke waited, she read the titles out of curiosity. One booklet was called When Someone Dies. Inside, one sentence caught her and wouldn't let go: grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping, or changes in appetite. She read it twice. Three things, and she had all three. She checked them off against herself like a scientist tallying data. Tired: yes. Trouble sleeping: two forty-seven in the morning, yes. Appetite: the toast, the granola bar, yes.

If that was the cause, then it wasn't a virus, and it couldn't be measured with a thermometer, like the sensor in the hallway smoke detector that beeped when it couldn't see clear air. This was something happening in her that no instrument could catch. She thought of a night last summer at Grandma's house, when the moon had come through the kitchen window so luminous on the floor that they'd turned off the lamp and eaten ice cream by moonlight alone. Grandma had said it was the best lighting in town and it was free.

That evening, Brooke put a photo of Grandma on her nightstand, just to test an idea. She ate half the toast, then the other half, slowly, tasting it. She asked herself whether grief might work like weather, something that arrived, did what it did, and eventually moved on. Sleep still came late, but it came.

In the morning, she slid the photo into her backpack to show Elly, and zipped it snug against her lunch.

On the second day of canoe camp, Ms. Morales announced that a storm was imminent, so the whole group had to haul the boats out of the water before the first fat raindrops landed. Charlotte was helping flip a canoe over when she heard the joke. "Nice paddling, Kyra," said a boy from the other cabin. "You steered us straight into the reeds like a human propeller." A knot of kids laughed, and Charlotte laughed too, a small snort she almost didn't notice making.

Kyra went red and pretended to be very busy with a paddle strap. The boy tried another joke, then another, each one a little meaner, and Charlotte noticed something odd. After every joke, he didn't look at Kyra. He looked at the laughing group, quick as a bird checking a feeder. It was like he wasn't really performing for Kyra at all. Charlotte started to wonder whether the laughs were the actual fuel, and whether the jokes would stall out without them. There was one obvious way to find out.

The next morning the sky was clear and the water was so flat it looked like a mirror that hadn't woken up yet. The boy drifted over to the dock where Kyra was untangling a rope. "Need help? Or are you going to tie yourself to the propeller again?" Charlotte, standing with Annabel nearby, kept her face perfectly still, like a person watching paint dry. Annabel glanced at her, caught on, and studied her shoes instead. The boy waited. The silence stretched out so long that a loon called somewhere just to fill it.

He tried again, louder. "I said, tie herself to the..." Annabel shrugged. Kyra, to everyone's surprise, said, "Ropes are actually hard, want to learn the knot?" That was worse for him than any insult. He mumbled something about going to find his water bottle and left at nearly jogging speed. "Did you see that?" Annabel whispered. "He kept checking if we were laughing. We stopped and the whole thing just died." Charlotte felt a grin spread across her face. "It's like teasing is a campfire. Take away the audience and you isolate the flame. No fuel, no fire."

Kyra walked over holding the untangled rope like a trophy. "So are you two going to teach me this knot, or just stand there looking smug?" "Smug," said Charlotte. "Definitely smug," said Annabel, and Kyra laughed so hard she dropped the rope in the lake and had to fish it out with a paddle.

The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Alicia kept her eyes on the clock above the reception desk. School started in fifty minutes. If they weren't called back in the next ten, she would miss the bus, and her mother would have to drive her, and her mother had already driven her twice this month.

"Why are you so twitchy?" whispered Cian, who had come along because his own appointment was right after hers. He flipped through a magazine about wind energy, stopping at a picture of a giant white turbine on a hillside. "Look at this thing. It's taller than the school."

"I'm not twitchy," Alicia said. But her hands were folded so tight her knuckles had gone pale, and her stomach had that hollow, rolling feeling again. It had come every morning for three weeks now, always before school, always gone by lunch. She had started keeping a list in her notebook: what she ate for dinner, what time she went to bed, whether her stomach hurt the next morning. That was her idea. If she could find the pattern, she could fix it.

"You should ask Mr. Whitaker to postpone the science quiz," Cian said. "He does stuff like that."

"It's not the quiz." Alicia ran her finger down the page of her notebook, and then she stopped. Toast on Monday, hurt. Soup on Tuesday, hurt. Pizza at Eliot's on Wednesday, hurt. On Saturday, the same toast, the same pizza, and nothing. It wasn't the food. It was only ever school mornings. Something she couldn't see was doing this, and she was looking straight at the shape of it.

The door clicked open and a nurse called, "Alicia?" and her mother stood up, and that was when the twisting feeling jumped into her throat. Behind her, she heard Cian say quietly, not to her, almost to the magazine, "That's how it started with my sister. The stomach stuff." Alicia turned around. "What do you mean?"

"She thought it was the cafeteria food," Cian said. "It was anxiety. Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but hers was so bad for so long it got in the way of everything, so the doctor said it was an anxiety disorder." He shrugged. "It's treatable. She talked to the doctor about it, and now she's way better."

In the exam room, the doctor asked why she had come in, and Alicia's mother started to say, "Stomachaches, we thought maybe something she's eating," and Alicia heard herself say, "Can I go first?" She showed the doctor her notebook, all her careful columns, and pointed at the empty Saturday rows. "I tested the food idea and it's wrong. It's only school mornings. Every single one. Could it be anxiety?"

The doctor looked at the pages for a long moment, then back at Alicia, and pulled her chair closer. "That's good detective work," she said. "Let's talk about it."

"Alicia," her mother said, "why didn't you tell me?"

"Because I thought it was just stomachaches," Alicia said. Then, quieter: "And because I thought I was supposed to just cope with it."

"You don't have to just cope," the doctor said. "That's what we're here for." She tapped the notebook, still open to Alicia's neat rows of dinners and bedtimes, and the clock on the wall showed they had already missed the bus.

Muhammad slid his worksheet across the table at the tutoring centre, hoping the problem would somehow evade him the way the smell of pencil shavings evaded everyone else. It didn't. x + 7 = 12 sat there in bold print, and under it, 5x = 35. He had missed the lesson on equations because he'd been home sick with a fever, and now the whole page looked like a tsunami of letters and numbers about to crash over him.

"You look like you're guarding a secret," said Laura, dropping into the seat beside him. She was there every Tuesday, and her actual reason for coming was the opposite of Muhammad's dread: she wanted to be the first in her class to finish the algebra booklet, because her older sister had framed hers and hung it in the hallway. She wanted a frame too. She leaned over his paper. "Oh, those are easy. Well, once you see the trick."

"Then tell me the trick," Muhammad said, but Marius, who was folding a paper airplane two seats down and listening more than he let on, spoke first. "It's not a trick, it's like locked doors. My dad changes the locks every year and keeps the old keys."

Laura rolled her eyes at Marius, then turned back to Muhammad. "Think about it. Somebody added seven to your x. What undoes adding seven?"

Muhammad stared at the equation. Something added. To undo it, take it back off. "Subtracting seven?"

"Subtraction undoes addition," Laura said, nodding. "And going the other way, division undoes multiplication. That's the whole booklet, basically." She tapped the second problem with her pencil. "So try your idea. See if it works."

Muhammad subtracted seven from the left side, then, remembering what she'd said about doing the same thing to both sides, from the right side too. x = 5. He checked it in his head: five plus seven really did make twelve. On the next one, 5x = 35, someone had multiplied x by five, so he divided both sides by five. x = 7. Five times seven, thirty-five. He felt like he'd found the old key after all, the one that still fit the lock.

When Ms. Lombardi came by to collect the worksheets, she paused at Muhammad's page, all six problems correct, and gave him a small nod before moving on. Marius launched his paper airplane and it swooped low over Muhammad's head, and Muhammad, feeling frugal with nothing but time now, picked up the next booklet from the stack. "What's this one called?"

"Two-step equations," said Laura. "Bring it over. I'll race you."

The phone store smelled like new plastic and hope, and Katherine stood at the counter while her mom signed the papers. "Two gigabytes a month," the cashier said, sliding the box across. "Plenty, unless you stream a lot."

"That's what Vihaan said before his plan died," Janice whispered beside her. "Remember Tuesday?"

Katherine did remember, though it had been months ago, before she had a phone at all. Vihaan had slumped onto the gym bench holding his dark screen like a dead fish and announced that his data was gone in one week, all from watching videos on the bus every morning. At the time she had laughed. Now she clutched her own box a little tighter.

The first week was heaven. She texted Janice forty times, took photos of the neighbor's suspicious cat, and helped mediate a fierce argument between Janice and Vihaan about whose turn it was to pick the game at recess. Texts, photos, calls. Then, on the school bus, she got bored and opened a video of a raccoon opening a jar. Then another. By Thursday she was watching a whole series about a talking toaster, one episode per pothole.

On Saturday morning, her phone refused to load anything at all. She stared at the little bars at the top, full of signal, and yet nothing worked. She thought about Vihaan on the gym bench. Texts had cost him almost nothing, all month. Videos had cost him everything, in a week. It wasn't the phone, and it wasn't the signal. It was the plan itself, used up, and she could prove which part had eaten it.

She borrowed her mom's phone and sent Vihaan a message: "Emergency. Did you text a lot the month your data ran out, or mostly watch videos?"

"Videos," he wrote back. "Bus videos. Why?"

"Same. Bus videos. I have to survive until the first of the month."

Vihaan replied with a strategy that had clearly been hard-won: "Download episodes at home on Wi-Fi. Then the bus is free. Also the toaster series gets weird in episode six, so you're not missing much."

Janice, hearing the whole plan at recess on Monday, held up her own phone. "An anonymous number called me twice last night and hung up. I think it's the toaster people." Katherine snickered until Ms. Do, monitoring the lunch line, gave them the look that meant quiet, but with a small smile underneath it.

That afternoon, in the store's little service alcove below the office of the building's other tenant, a dentist, Katherine asked the cashier one careful question: "So videos away from Wi-Fi are the expensive part, and texts barely count?" He nodded, and she set a rule for herself, three downloads at home, zero videos on the bus, and wrote it on a sticky note for the phone's case.

Four weeks later, on the last day of her plan, her phone still loaded everything, and she stood at the bus stop holding it up like a trophy as Vihaan climbed on. "Still alive," she said, and pressed play.

Theodore's pencil hovered over the diagram, stuck on the third blank. He had found the cell wall easily enough, a thick dark outline around every brick-shaped cell, and the nucleus sat in the middle like a small gray dot. But the worksheet said to label the cell membrane too, and he could not find it anywhere.

"Maybe onions just don't have one," Reid said from the next stool, not even looking up from his own microscope. "That's my answer. Drawing an arrow to nothing."

"That's not an answer, that's giving up," Theodore said. Dax laughed without lifting his head. The three of them had been assigned the same slide, a whisper-thin layer of onion skin stained purple, and Ms. Ross had told them their diagrams were due before the bell. Theodore adjusted the fine focus, scanning the edge of one cell. One line. Only one line. If there were a membrane, shouldn't it look like a second line, just inside the wall, like a fence inside a fence?

He thought about last week, when he had wrecked his first slide by cranking the stage up too fast and cracking the coverslip. Ms. Ross hadn't scolded him; she had just said, "The lens is closer than you think, Mr. Theodore. Most things you break, you break because you can't see the distance." He had been careful ever since, and that memory was what made him stop and think now instead of guessing.

Maybe the membrane was there, just closer than he thought. Pressed right up against something. He turned the light adjustment down until the field dimmed, and the thick wall went soft and pale. Then, at the very inner edge of the wall on one cell, a single faint line appeared where the wall was, no second line beside it, no gap, nothing separate. He turned the light back up. Gone. He did it again. There.

"Look," he said, grabbing Reid's sleeve. "Dim your light and watch the edge of a wall."

Reid squinted. "I still only see one line."

"Exactly. In a healthy onion cell the membrane is pressed tight against the inside of the wall, so you can't see it as its own line. It's there. It's just hiding against the wall." His heart was going fast, the way it did when a math problem cracked open all at once.

"So how do I label it?" Reid asked.

"Same arrow as the wall. Point to that edge and write both."

Reid actually did it, then held up his worksheet. "If you're wrong, we're both wrong."

"You two realize grading isn't subjective, right?" Dax said, not looking up. "There's a right answer. Ms. Ross prescribed the exact labels on the sheet. Wall, membrane, nucleus. This isn't art class."

"It's not wrong if we can defend it," Theodore said, and raised his hand. "Ms. Ross? Question about the membrane."

She came over, and Theodore pointed at the dim circle of light under his lens. "We could only find one line. The membrane's pressed against the wall, so it isn't a separate line in a healthy cell. Is that right?"

She leaned down, looked, and straightened up. "Label it on the edge, then, like you told your friend there. Nice work." She moved on toward the window row, where someone had knocked over a beaker.

Reid wrote his arrows slowly, tongue between his teeth. "First one I've gotten right all semester," he said. "Don't tell Dax I said that."

"I heard it," Dax said. "It's going in the history books. Reid's diagram, the start of a whole dynasty."

"Then label your dynasty carefully," Theodore said, and dimmed the light one more time to check.

Savannah had three measures of "Ode to Joy" left to learn before Friday's assembly, and the clarinet in her hands still squeaked on the high F like an angry duck. Mr. Nikolaidis had posted the sign-up sheet for the assembly on Monday, and her name was on it, in her own handwriting, which suddenly felt like a terrible decision.

"You sound like a dying goose," said Phillip, who sat two chairs over and never let anyone forget he had played since third grade.

"Thank you," said Savannah. "Very helpful."

Esteban leaned across his music stand. "How much did you practice this week?"

"Two whole hours. Last night." She held up her reed case as proof, as if the worn reed could testify for her. "I played that F at least a hundred times and it still squeaks."

Esteban frowned and turned his own trumpet over in his hands. "I only practiced twenty minutes a day this week. Total, that's less than your two hours." He lifted the trumpet and played his whole solo line, clean, every note landing where it belonged.

Savannah stared at him. The same total time, spread differently, and his notes came out right while hers squeaked. She turned the idea over the way she turned the clarinet keys, testing whether it was really solid. If it was true, then one long desperate night was the wrong tool entirely, and several shorter sessions spread across the days would build the skill better. She thought about the bake sale the band had run in October, how the income from it had paid for the new music stands only after weeks of small sales adding up, not one giant day. Small amounts, spread out, did the work.

That afternoon she found Mr. Nikolaidis stacking chairs and petitioned him to open the music room before school for the rest of the week. "Voluntary practice," she said. "Just for anyone who wants twenty minutes of quiet. I'll unlock it myself if you sign the form."

He raised an eyebrow. "Twenty minutes?"

"Twenty minutes, every morning, until Friday."

He signed. On Tuesday morning she played the F forty times and it squeaked thirty-nine of them. On Wednesday it squeaked twenty-two times. On Thursday morning, Phillip wandered in with his flute, pretending he had just happened to be early, and played his part beside her. The room filled with the sound of two imperfect instruments learning to be less imperfect together.

Friday morning, twenty minutes before the assembly, Savannah stood at the window with the clarinet assembled and the reed wet. She breathed in, set her fingers on the keys, and played all three measures through, slow and even. The high F came out round and clear, and Phillip lowered his flute long enough to mutter, "Finally."

The camp handbook had been sitting on Raphael's desk for three days, unopened, while he packed. Now it was six o'clock, the van left at seven, and he had a duffel bag whose contents were roughly proportional to its importance, which meant the flashlight was buried under four extra T-shirts nobody would ever see him wear.

Nikita arrived with a bag of chips and no luggage of his own, which seemed unfair. "You're going to a month of bad cuisine," he said, crunching. "Beans from a pot. Beans from a different pot."

"It says here there's a cook." Raphael had finally opened the handbook, mostly to avoid the flashlight excavation. A page near the front had a short history of the place, and a photo of a plaque by the lake. He read it twice. "Huh. It says the Gunnery camp started in 1861. This Connecticut schoolmaster, Frederick W. Gunn, took his students on a hike to a camp by the sea. It's usually considered the first organized American summer camp."

"So?"

"So I thought camps were invented, like, forty years ago by people who hated children. This thing's older than Canada." He checked that. It was. "You're telling me some guy in 1861 decided a hundred and whatever students should walk to the ocean and sleep outside, on purpose, and now I have to do it too."

Nikita peered at the plaque photo. "That contradicts my whole theory of camps."

"Which was?"

"That they were punishment." Nikita ate another chip. "Your theory is also that. You packed like it's punishment."

Raphael looked at the duffel. He had packed for a disaster, not for a month by a lake. The 1861 guy had hiked to the sea with, presumably, less than four extra T-shirts. Raphael tested a simple idea: if camp had worked since before his grandmother's grandmother, the bag did not need to contain everything ever manufactured. He dumped it out. The flashlight rolled under the bed, which felt like a sign.

At seven, his father honked. Alena ran over from next door with a ziplock of cookies and a note card. "For the bus," she said. On the card she'd written "1861" and drawn a little hiker. "You said the schoolmaster guy hiked to the sea. First one ever to do the whole thing."

"I'm not the first one ever to do anything," Raphael said, hauling the lighter bag.

"You're the first Raphael at that camp," said Alena.

From the van window, he waved the note card like a ticket, and his father pulled out before Nikita could say anything about beans.

Nevaeh slid the birthday card across the kitchen table and read the note inside for the third time. Her grandfather had written that he would hold her one thousand dollars for five years at 5 percent simple interest, and that she should figure out for herself what that meant. "Figure it out," she muttered. "Thanks, Grandpa."

She called Neil first, because Neil loved money the way other kids loved dinosaurs. "A thousand dollars," he breathed into the phone. "You could buy the new racing game, the headset, AND the controller with the extra buttons." That was Neil's whole plan for her money, of course, since his own allowance had gone extinct two weeks after he spent it all on stickers. "But what happens if you just leave it with your grandpa?" she asked. Neil yawned. "Nothing happens. Money just sits there."

That answer bugged her all through dinner, so after dinner she excavated her notebook from the bottom of her backpack, where it had been buried under three old permission slips, and started doing math. If five percent meant fifty dollars for every hundred, then a thousand dollars earned fifty dollars in a year. She wrote it down: year one, one thousand fifty. Year two, one thousand one hundred. She kept going, adding fifty each time, until year five ended at one thousand two hundred fifty dollars. Two hundred fifty dollars for doing nothing. Neil was wrong, and she couldn't wait to tell him.

The next morning she found Ms. Nikolaidis on her porch, sorting mail. Ms. Nikolaidis was the kind of neighbour who had opinions about everything, including the weather, which she called corrosive to her garden fence. Nevaeh laid out her numbers and asked the question that had kept her up. "Is there a way money grows faster than that? Like, if the interest got added in and then the whole bigger amount earned the next fifty?" Ms. Nikolaidis tapped the paper. "That's compound interest, dear, and yes, banks do that. Your grandfather's way is simple, the same fifty every year." Nevaeh stared at her own handwriting. So the fifty could stack on top of other fifties somewhere else. Somewhere, money was doing that without her.

She ran two blocks to Neil's house and knocked until he opened the door in his socks. "Two hundred fifty dollars," she announced. "After five years I'll have one thousand two hundred fifty. That's the deal." Neil leaned against the doorframe. "So buy the game now, have fun now." Nevaeh shook her head slowly. "If I wait, I get the game AND two hundred fifty dollars. That's like the game paying me to wait." Neil squinted at her, and she could almost hear the gears grinding.

At school on Monday, Nevaeh cornered him by the lockers with a new page of math. She had spent Sunday trying compound interest with a calculator, and the five-year answer came out bigger than one thousand two hundred fifty, though she still wasn't sure she'd pressed the buttons right. "I'm going to ask my mom about a real bank account," she said. "One where the interest compounds." Neil sighed the sigh of a boy watching a fortune slip away, then held out his hand. "Fine. But when you're rich, I get one snack." Nevaeh shook it. "You get half a snack."

Ellie stood at the kitchen counter with a slice of toast she couldn't eat. Tomorrow was the piano recital, and her heart was pounding so hard she could feel it in her throat. Her hands shook when she picked up her water glass. She pressed her palm against her forehead. No fever, but something was wrong with her. She wondered if she should tell her mom she was too sick to perform.

Instead she sat down, took out her phone, and texted Damian, whose older brother was something of a veteran at recitals and auditions. "My heart is going crazy and my hands are shaking. Am I getting sick?" Damian replied three minutes later: "No. When the brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing quicker." Then a second message: "It's called the fight-or-flight response. Your body thinks the recital is a bear." A third: "Unless you actually see a bear at the recital, in which case, cancel."

Ellie laughed, which felt strange with her heart still hammering. So her body wasn't broken. It was doing a job, just the wrong one. She decided to test it. If adrenaline was making her breathing quick, maybe slow breathing could signal that things were fine. She set a timer for two minutes, sat up straight in the kitchen chair, and breathed in for four counts and out for six. In, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four, five, six. Halfway through, her shoulders dropped. By the end of the timer, her hands were steadier, and her heart no longer felt like a drum solo.

She found a sticky note and wrote herself a plan: breathe before bed, no screens after eight, lights out by nine, and repeat the breathing in the morning. Sleep mattered too. She had read that a tired brain felt more vulnerable to stress, and tomorrow she did not want her brain mistaking an audience of parents for a pack of wolves. She stuck the note on the refrigerator under a magnet shaped like a pineapple.

The next evening, Ellie stood backstage with her sheet music. Her heart picked up speed, exactly as predicted. She breathed in for four, out for six, and the pounding slowed enough that she could walk to the piano without dropping anything. She played the first piece with two small mistakes and the second one clean. Afterward, Ms. Santoso caught her arm in the hallway and said, "Steady hands at the end there." Ellie held up her phone, showing Damian's bear message, and said, "Emergency instructions."

Gavin had never thought much about laundry until Mr. Njoroge announced a life-skills week and wheeled a washing machine into the classroom like it was a game show prize. "By Friday," Mr. Njoroge said, "each of you will run a full load, start to finish." Gavin's mom was going to be thrilled. She'd been telling him for a year that he could learn this at home, and for a year he'd been responding by lying very still on the couch.

Kayden dumped a bin of practice clothes on the table. There were towels, gym shorts, a stack of white school shirts, and one bright red sock so new it still had a tag on it. Bianca started making piles immediately, darks in one, whites in another, her lines running parallel like parking spaces. Gavin figured one big pile would save time, so he shoved everything in together, added soap, and pressed start before anyone could stop him.

Forty minutes later, the white shirts came out pale pink. Not dramatic pink. Not flamingo. Just a soft, sneaky, uniform pink, like a sunset had leaned on them. "What did you do," Bianca said, holding one up to the light. Gavin stared at the red sock, which had come out of the machine looking completely innocent. He had a theory forming, and it felt a bit like being a detective, except the suspect was footwear.

He ran a test. He filled a clear bowl with warm water and dunked the red sock in it all by itself, no shirts allowed. Within a minute, the water had a faint red haze drifting through it, like smoke trapped under glass. The sock was letting dye loose into the water. That had to be it. The dye went into the wash water, the water went everywhere, and the white shirts soaked it up. New sock, new dye, and the tag still on it. Gavin felt his brain make a small clicking sound.

"So the pink shirt was the water's fault," he announced. "The dye got into the water, and then the water shared it with everything. Like a bad group project." Bianca snorted. Kayden proposed a treaty: he would stop hiding Gavin's sneakers if Gavin never mixed a load again. Gavin shook on it, then folded the pink shirts into a neat stack and carried them to Mr. Njoroge's desk like evidence.

Mr. Njoroge held one up, raised an eyebrow, and said, "Nice fold."

"Check the water bowl," said Gavin. "I caught the criminal red-handed. Well. Red-socked."

Dad had barely finished serving the noodles when Mom slid her phone across the table. "Look at this," she said. "A man froze his batteries for a day, and they lasted three times longer in his remote. I already put the new ones in the freezer."

Brooke chewed slowly. One man, one remote, one time. That didn't sound like much of anything, and tomorrow she was supposed to hand in a current science topic to Mr. Weber, a real one, with a source that would not fall apart the second someone looked at it. This might be her chance to solve both problems at once.

"Can I test it?" she asked.

Mom sighed the sigh of a woman who had already bought the batteries. "Fine. But don't use the good remote."

That afternoon Brooke sat in the library with Lianna and Maria, two identical remotes on the table, one battery fresh from the freezer and one from the drawer. While they waited for something to happen, Lianna pushed a journal article across the table, one she had found for her own topic. It was about battery performance, and it was dull, dense, and full of charts. Next to it lay the blog post Mom loved, which had exclamation points. Maria frowned. "Why does this one look so much more official?"

"Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors," Lianna said, tapping the article. "It's called peer review." The blog, as far as any of them could tell, had been reviewed by nobody except the man's enthusiasm.

The test itself took all evening. Brooke set the two batteries upright in identical remotes, turned the volume up on both, and taped the buttons down so each one drained at the same rate. She arranged them on her desk perpendicular to each other so she could tell them apart in the dark, then checked every twenty minutes and wrote down the times. The frozen battery died at 9:42. The regular one died at 9:51. Nine minutes. Barely a shrug.

At dinner the next night she brought the notebook, the remotes, and both articles. Dad reached for the bread just as she opened to her data table, which she suspected was his version of an escape plan.

"Nine minutes," she said. "That's it. And the journal article, the one where actual experts checked it before it got published, tested way more batteries than two and found basically nothing."

"So the freezer was a waste of space," Mom said.

"The freezer was a waste of space. The blog was one guy who probably had a good battery to start with."

Dad grinned. "Should I tell your grandmother her ice-cube diet is next on Brooke's list?"

"Dad. Do not embarrass me in front of the data." She slid the peer-reviewed article toward Mom, who put down her fork and started reading the charts, pausing only to take the batteries out of the freezer.

Christopher's grandfather had died in June, and the apartment still felt wrong in small ways. His chair at the table was empty. His crossword pen sat in the jar by the phone, and nobody moved it. Christopher wanted to do something, anything, that would make the goodbye feel finished, but he couldn't figure out what.

On the first Sunday of August, Aksil called from Japan. He was staying with his grandparents' neighbors in a town outside Kyoto, and the video connection made his face wobble. "It's Obon here," Aksil said. Christopher asked what that meant. "It's a festival," Aksil said. "Mid-August in most regions, July in some. The spirits of ancestors come home for a visit."

Christopher sat up straighter. "Home. Like, here?"

"Like wherever home is," Aksil said. He turned the phone toward the window, and Christopher saw paper lanterns glowing along a street, small orange moons in a row. Aksil's voice came back close to the speaker. "We lit one for my grandmother. First Obon without her."

That night Christopher lay awake reasoning it through. He couldn't see a spirit arrive. Nobody could. But if the whole thing worked on a rule, spirits returning during the festival, then the lantern was the part you could test. If the rule was real, a lantern at his own window should count as home too. Grandpa had lived in this apartment for nine years before he moved to the care home. If any place was home, this was it.

On Monday he found Curtis at the park and tried to summarize the idea out loud, because saying it to someone made it more real than thinking it. "It's like a door," Christopher said. "The festival is when the door is open, and the lantern is how you say which door is yours." Curtis scratched his chin. "So build one. You could use that contemporary lamp kit from science club, the one with the LED and the paper shade." Christopher hadn't thought of that. He'd been picturing candles, which his mom would veto in about two seconds.

They built it in Christopher's kitchen. Curtis held the paper cylinder while Christopher taped the seam, and the LED inside made the whole thing glow warm yellow, close enough to the lanterns in Kyoto. His mom came home while they were testing it and didn't veto anything. She stood in the doorway with grocery bags still in her hands and looked at it for a long moment. Then she went to Grandpa's crossword pen and set it beside the lantern on the sill, as if it belonged there.

At school Ms. Bouchard had them write short research pieces that week, and she reminded everyone that facts needed a citation, the place where you found them. Christopher wrote about the festival and put Aksil's call down as his source. Ms. Bouchard read it, then read it again, and asked him quietly if the lantern had worked. Christopher said he didn't know yet. The festival days in his region were mid-August, and that was still a week away.

On the night in the middle of August, he set the lantern in the window facing the street. He turned it on and sat on the floor beside it with the crossword from that morning's paper, Grandpa's pen in his hand. He filled in one across answer, 7 Down, then 22 Across, and left the rest of the grid blank on purpose, the way they used to do when they ran out of time. The little light glowed steadily against the dark glass. Down on the street a car passed, and then it was quiet, and Christopher whispered, "The door's open."

Raphael climbed onto the bus holding his phone like it was evidence in a trial, which, in a way, it was. Amar was already in the third row, leaning across the aisle to show Diego a photo of a brown river swallowing a street. "Downtown's under water," Amar said. "My cousin posted it. School's definitely closing."

Raphael sat down and scrutinized the picture. Water to the top of a stop sign, a kayak paddling past a mail truck. It looked dramatic. It also looked, somehow, already seen, the way a joke you've heard twice does. "When did your cousin take this?" he asked.

"She didn't. She shared it." Amar was optimistic about floods the way some kids are about snow days; a disaster was just a day off with better scenery. "It says breaking news right on it."

"Anyone can type breaking news," Raphael said. "That's an opinion with a font."

Diego frowned. "So it's fake?"

"I didn't say fake. I said nobody's checked it." Raphael knew the difference now, because Ms. Paquette had spent one entire Tuesday on it: some things you could only argue about, and some things you could actually look up. Whether downtown was flooded was the second kind. He copied the image, opened a search engine, and pasted it in. Amar watched over his shoulder, breathing loudly, the way people do when they want the answer to be yes.

The results loaded. The same kayak, the same mail truck, the same stop sign, on pages that were years old. "Wait," Diego said. "What did you just do?"

"Reverse image search," Raphael said. "It shows where a photo appeared online before." Which, in this case, was everywhere, and years ago. Amar took the phone and scrolled, his day off dissolving one result at a time. He handed it back without a word.

"So my cousin shared an old picture," Amar said finally. "She didn't know."

"She could check it the same way I did," Raphael said. "Forward her the link."

The bus hissed around the corner by the senior residence, where two old men sat on the dry porch arguing over a crossword. Amar was already typing to his cousin, thumbs going fast. "If there's ever a real flood," Diego said, "how will we know?"

Raphael pocketed his phone. "Same way," he said. "We'll look."

The church basement smelled of dust and coffee, and the folding chairs had been pushed against the walls to make room for the music ministry's Saturday practice. Violet sat on a metal chair with her trumpet on her lap, watching Ms. Pham count off the band. Three weeks ago, when she had first wandered down after the Sunday service, she had only wanted somewhere to practice that wasn't her thin-walled apartment. Now she was being asked to solo.

"Blues in B flat," said Dominik, who played keyboard and seemed to know everything. "Twelve bars, then it starts over. One time through all twelve bars is a chorus." He said it the way he said most things, quickly, like he was handing her a pencil.

The chord progression was invisible. That was the problem. Nothing in the room showed her where the music was except Dominik's left hand, and he moved it too fast. She had missed her entrance twice already because she counted bars the way she counted pages in a book, and somewhere between bar four and bar five her mind drifted into the arid stretch of the progression where every bar sounded the same to her ear. She could hear the chords, but she could not see the shape underneath them.

She thought back to math class, to the unit on ratios. Twelve bars, she remembered thinking, was like a ratio of chord to bar, three chords spread over twelve bars, and if she tapped her foot the whole time, every twelve taps meant she had traveled the whole shape once and landed back at the beginning. On her last try she had tested it, tapping quietly against the chair leg, and when her count reached twelve, Dominik's hand had jumped back to the same chord as before. The pattern was real. It circled.

"When Violet's ready, she takes two choruses," Ms. Pham said, tapping her music stand twice.

Two choruses. Twenty-four bars. Violet stood, raised the trumpet, and the cold mouthpiece touched her lips. She stopped thinking about notes and started thinking about the shape, the invisible circle she was traveling. The band propelled her forward through the first chorus, and she let a few notes spill out, low and cautious, then climbed a little when the progression climbed underneath her. Somewhere around bar nine, her stomach tightened, but her foot kept tapping and her count held. Twelve. The circle started over, and she heard Dominik's hand jump back to the first chord exactly when she expected it.

The second chorus braver, she bent one note the way the saxophone player had bent his, a small curved sound that surprised her. She reached bar twenty-four and stepped back from the microphone. The basement went quiet except for the hum of the old refrigerator in the corner.

"That," said Dominik, "was two whole choruses."

Violet grinned and wiped the mouthpiece on her sleeve. "Can I have three next time?"

Grandma Ruth arrived on Sunday with one suitcase and a bag of mint candies, and by Tuesday Sydney had figured out something odd. At the kitchen table, Grandma caught every word, even when Sydney mumbled. But in the backyard, while the sprinkler hissed across the grass, Grandma kept tipping her head and saying, "Say that again, dear?" Sydney wanted the week to go well, so she decided to find the pattern.

At first she blamed herself. Maybe she was talking too fast out there, or standing too far away. So she tried an experiment on Wednesday. She stood at the same distance from Grandma in both places and said the same sentence at the same speed. In the quiet kitchen, Grandma laughed at the joke about Ms. Ricci's runaway chalk. In the backyard, with the neighbor's leaf blower roaring, Grandma only smiled and nodded, and Sydney could tell she hadn't caught a thing.

That was a clue. It wasn't the words and it wasn't Sydney. Something invisible was changing. She thought about the sprinkler, the leaf blower, the crows that argued in the maple every morning. She remembered the airport in the summer, how Grandma had gone silent for the whole layover even though she'd been chatty at home on the porch. Sydney had assumed Grandma was tired back then. Now it seemed more probable that the noise was the problem, not the words and not the tiredness.

On Thursday she tested it. She invited Aurora and Sulaiman over, and they planned a backyard picnic. Sulaiman wanted the portable speaker on. Sydney said no, and when he asked why, she said, "Grandma's hearing, it's the background noise that gets her." Then Sydney did the opposite of the usual plan: she moved the picnic to the far corner of the yard, away from the sprinkler line, and asked her dad to hold off on the mower. Aurora brought a quilt and they all sat close, in a tight little circle.

It worked. Grandma told them about her own grandmother, who had crossed an ocean with two spoons and a photograph, and how every descendant in the family still made her jam recipe wrong. She told a story about nearly submerging a canoe at summer camp, and Sulaiman laughed so hard he fell off the quilt. Sydney watched her grandma's face, quick and bright, no more nodding and smiling through guesses.

Later, when the sprinklers clicked on and Grandma's replies went vague again, Sydney stood up and turned the timer dial until the water stopped. Grandma raised her eyebrows.

"Rain check," Sydney said, "for the grass."

The lights went out just after Beatrice set her homework on the kitchen table, and the whole farmhouse went quiet in a way it never did in daylight. The hum of the refrigerator stopped. The clock over the stove went dark. She heard her grandmother's chair scrape in the living room, then footsteps feeling their way along the hall.

"Power cut," her grandmother called. "I'll get the candles."

Beatrice sat still for a second, listening. Outside, the wind pushed against the barn and the power lines swayed where she knew they ran along the road, though she could not see any of it. That was the thing about a dark house, she thought: the cause of the trouble was out there somewhere on those lines, invisible, and she could only guess at it from the sound of the wind. Her mind did the same trick in reverse when she tried to picture the fuse box in the cellar. She knew its shape, its cold metal door, but not what had tripped inside it tonight.

"Wait," she said, standing up and finding the counter by memory. "Don't light those." She remembered Mr. Goldberg, who had come to her class back in the spring with a crate of safety gear. He had not given a lecture. He had held up a flashlight in one hand and a candle in the other and let the class argue about which one belonged in a power cut. Beatrice had argued for the candle, because it seemed braver, and she had been wrong. Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, she had copied into her notebook, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house. It had felt like a paradox at the time, the thing that made light also being the thing that could burn the place down.

Her grandmother was hesitant at the hall closet, matches already in her hand. "Candles got us through forty years of storms, Bea."

"I know. But we have three flashlights in the drawer by the sink." Beatrice bumped her hip on a chair, apologized to it out loud, and slid the drawer open. Her fingers found rubber grips, cold and certain. She clicked one on and the kitchen reappeared, pale and smaller than she expected. She clicked the second one and handed it over.

Her grandmother turned the flashlight over in her hands, studying it the way she studied a new calf. Then she blew out the match she had been saving and set the candle box back on its shelf, high and out of reach.

"Good girl," she said. "Go see if the one in the mudroom still works."

Beatrice padded to the door, swept the beam across coats and boots, and found the third flashlight tucked behind the umbrella stand. She thumbed the switch, and a thin circle of light landed on the window, where the wind was still busy with the wires she could not see.

"There you are," she said.

The book club met in the back corner of the library, where the radiators ticked and the window looked out on the arid stretch of gravel behind the parking lot. Luke had read "The Monkey's Paw" twice, and he still couldn't say what the paw was supposed to mean. Jordan could. Jordan had written a whole page about it.

"Okay, my turn," Jordan said, flipping his notebook open. "The paw is a symbol. It stands for greed, or maybe fate, and the fact that it's a monkey's paw means humans are grabbing at things that aren't meant for them."

Ms. Sandhu nodded slowly and looked around the circle. "Anyone want to build on that or push back?"

Luke looked down at his copy of the story. He had circled three places where he'd felt something odd in the wording, though he couldn't have said why. "There's the part where the sergeant-major throws the paw in the fire," he said. "Before anybody even makes a wish. I kept thinking that had to mean something."

Nada sat forward. "That's foreshadowing. He's warning them."

"He's literally warning them," Luke said. "It's not even hidden. Sergeant-Major Morris says the wishes bring terrible results, and then he throws the paw into the fire, and the dad goes and grabs it out anyway." He tapped the page. "So the story warned everyone before the first wish was ever made. Whatever happens after that, we can't say we didn't see it coming."

Jordan frowned at his notebook. "So then the symbol is... the fire? Fire is supposed to cleanse stuff, and the dad thwarted that by rescuing the paw."

"That works," Nada said. "Or the paw itself is the warning, and they just ignore it."

Luke tried an idea out, the way you test a loose tooth. "Maybe that's the trick of it. Foreshadowing isn't the author whispering. Sometimes a character just comes out and says it, and the scary part is nobody listens." He read the line aloud, the one about the man who wished for death, and the room went quiet enough that they could hear the radiator tick three times.

Ms. Sandhu smiled. "That's a claim worth writing down, Luke. Can you defend it with two more moments from the text?"

Luke flipped pages, hunting for his circled spots. "Give me a minute," he said. "I know they're in here somewhere."

Jordan slid his pen across the table. "Use mine. Ink, not pencil."

"Thanks." Luke started to write, then stopped. "Wait. The chess bit at the beginning. The dad loses at chess because he takes a risky move. That's it, that's the other one. Everything in this story is somebody taking a risk they were warned about." He underlined it twice, and the pen made a small satisfying scratch against the paper.

Autumn sat cross-legged under the climbing dome with a battery pack, a coil of thin wire, and her brother's multimeter, which she had borrowed without asking and felt slightly vulnerable about, since he counted it among his treasures. Elena hung upside down from the bars above her, watching.

"You said the science fair was in two weeks," Elena said. "Why are we at the playground?"

"Because the garage smells like gasoline and my mom keeps asking if I need help." Autumn clipped the wire to the battery and touched the multimeter probes to each end. "Watch. 6.0 volts." She unclipped one probe and moved it so the current meter sat in the loop instead. "0.4 amps."

"So what does your mystery wire do?"

"That's the thing. I can't see resistance. It's inside the wire, like a hidden property. But if voltage pushes and current flows, I can infer it." She wrote 6.0 divided by 0.4 on the back of her hand and got 15. "Fifteen ohms."

Elena dropped down beside her. "Ohms. Like the name?"

"That's what I wondered. Why would a unit of electricity have a person's name?" Autumn flipped through her notes. Mr. Weber, her science teacher, had written one sentence on her proposal sheet: Ohm's law is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm, who published it in 1827. She had circled it twice.

"A German guy figured out the rule before the Civil War," Autumn said. "Almost two hundred years ago. So the unit got his name."

"That's the irony," Elena said. "He's famous for something invisible."

Autumn tested it. Her idea was that a longer wire should have more of that hidden resistance, so she clipped in twice the length and measured again: still 6.0 volts, but now 0.2 amps. She divided and got 30. Double the length, double the resistance. The rule held.

Francesca arrived with a slushie and peered at the setup. "You're doing homework at a playground."

"It's not homework, it's detective work," Autumn said. "I'm hunting something I can't see by looking at what it does to things I can see."

Francesca squinted at the numbers. "I thought science fair projects had to have explosions or volcanoes."

"I thought so too," Autumn said. "I was going to do the baking-soda volcano. But this is better, because nobody built a volcano in 1827 and got a rule named after them." She wound the extra wire back onto its spool and wrote the heading for her poster: The Hunt for the Hidden Number.

Elena swung back up onto the bars. "Fifteen ohms!" she called down. "Invisible and famous!"

Autumn packed the multimeter into her backpack, zipped it, and ran for the swings.

The pharmacy closed at nine, and it was already twenty past eight when Paisley's mother dropped her at the door with a crumpled ten-dollar bill. Paisley's head still ached from the flu, her throat felt like sandpaper, and the fluorescent lights made everything buzz a little. Somewhere between the cough syrup and the vitamins she found the shelf of pain relievers, and she began to coordinate her three needs in her mind: her headache, her fever, and the ten dollars, which would not stretch to everything.

She reached for the aspirin first, because it was the cheapest and the box looked conventional, the kind of thing her grandmother kept in her kitchen drawer. Then she flipped it over and squinted at the fine print on the back. The label said not to give it to children or teenagers during flu or chickenpox, because it was linked to something serious. She read the line twice. Her ears were blocked and hot, and the small letters seemed to swim.

"Ms. Martínez?" she croaked, waving toward the pharmacist at the counter. "This aspirin box says kids shouldn't take it with the flu. But it doesn't really say why. Is it just a rule for little kids, or me too?"

Ms. Martínez came around the counter and looked at the box, then at Paisley's red nose. "It's linked to a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain," she said. "It's called Reye's syndrome."

Paisley stood very still while the words sanked in. Rare, but serious. Liver and brain. She was eleven, which meant she counted as a child, and she had the flu right now, which meant the warning applied to her exactly, not to somebody else. She thought of the bottle of aspirin sitting in her own bathroom cabinet at home, the white pills her mother sometimes handed out for headaches. Her mother might not have read the back of that bottle in years. Old bottles probably had old labels, and old labels might not carry the warning at all.

"Can I borrow your phone charger?" Paisley asked. "Just for a second. My phone's dead." At the outlet by the photo machine, she plugged in, waited through the longest thirty seconds of her life, and called home. "Mom, don't take the aspirin from the cabinet for me. Not while I have the flu. Get the acetaminophen, the blue box, second shelf." Her mother asked why, and Paisley said, "It matters. I'll explain when I'm back."

She bought the acetaminophen with four minutes to spare and pushed through the doors into the cold night air, where the wind on her feverish face felt, from her droopy perspective, almost wonderful. Her mother's car idled at the curb, and through the window Paisley could see the blue box already sitting on the passenger seat, held out like a prize.

The bus dropped Alice's class at the nature reserve just after nine. Mr. Mercado handed out maps and read the day's plan aloud: a hike on the ridge trail in the morning, and after lunch, a tour of the old ranger station, which had been turned into a small museum. Alice folded the map into her pocket and followed Tabitha toward the trailhead, where Leanna was already waiting with a water bottle in each hand.

The hike was fine until Leanna twisted her ankle on a loose rock half a mile in. Mr. Mercado wrapped it and let her sit on a fallen log while the rest of the group continued to the overlook. When they came back down, Leanna held out her phone. "I wrote you a note," she said. "Since I can't walk fast, read it when you do the tour." The message said: "Look for the secret. There's a place in the ranger station where a hundred years of hands left a mark. Find it and tell me what it is."

Alice was hesitant to leave Leanna on the log, but Mr. Mercado promised to stay with her, so Alice joined the line into the ranger station. Inside, the guide pointed out the old wooden desk where the first ranger had written his reports, and a wooden railing that ran along the entry hall. Behind her, a boy in a red jacket reached out to drag his hand across the desk's surface. Tabitha caught his wrist. "Don't. Museums ask visitors not to touch things because oils and salts from skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces." The boy pulled his hand back and wiped it on his shorts.

Alice thought about what Tabitha had said all the way down the hall. Oils and salts from skin. Build up over time. She stopped at the railing and looked at it closely. The rest of the wood was dull and grey, but the top of the railing, exactly where a hand would grip it, was dark and slightly shiny in a smooth band. She put her face close without touching. The shine ran the whole length, at hand height, and nowhere else.

She turned around and walked back to the desk. It sat behind a rope, but she could see the same thing on its edge: a dark patch on the front lip, right where a person would rest a hand while sitting. She raised her hand. "Is that dark spot on the desk from people touching it?" The guide nodded. "That's the hand print of every ranger who ever worked there, one on top of another."

After the tour, Alice hiked back up the trail fast enough to make her lungs burn. She found Leanna on the log, finishing the sandwich that was meant to consume the last of her appetite before the ride home. "It was the railing," Alice said. "A hundred years of hands left a shine on it, and the same mark on the desk." Leanna grinned and tapped her phone. "I already took the picture. Look."

The 42 bus was late again, and John sat on the bench with a paper grocery bag between his knees. Inside was the sweater, folded as flat as he could make it, which was not very flat.

"What's in the bag?" Luc asked, dropping onto the bench beside him.

"Evidence," John said. "Of a crime I committed."

Philemon leaned over from the other side. John peeled the bag open. Luc pulled out the sweater, held it up, and stared. It was small enough for a doll, its cables puckered and stiff, its sleeves hardly longer than thumbs.

"Whose is that?" Philemon asked.

"Mine. My grandma knit it for me last winter. It came down past my hips." John took it back and turned it over in his hands. "Saturday was my first time doing a whole load by myself. Mom's got her arm in a sling, so it was me or nobody. I sorted the darks from the lights, checked pockets, everything. Then I shoved it all in on hot, because hot water has to be better, right? More hygiene. More cleaning power."

Luc winced. "And?"

"And I came back after the spin cycle and found this." John held the sweater up again. "Everything else was fine. The towels were great. Only the sweater turned into this."

The bus appeared at the far corner, then vanished behind the bakery, which meant it wasn't the 42. Philemon tossed a pebble at the curb. "So hot water shrinks sweaters. Mystery solved."

"That's what I thought," John said. "But then I got curious. I ran a test." He pulled a scrap of paper from his pocket, a list written in pencil. "I took a square of the same yarn from grandma's leftover ball and washed it in cold, gentle water. It barely changed. Then I tried a square in hot water in a bucket, but without sloshing it around. Also almost fine. It was the hot water plus the moving that did it. Hot and still, no. Cold and sloshy, no. Hot and sloshy, tiny doll sweater."

Luc frowned. "That makes no sense. Water isn't alive. How does water know?"

"That's what I couldn't figure out," John said. "I called my grandma. She wasn't even mad, which was worse somehow. She said every wool fibre has tiny scales on it, and in hot, sloshing water the scales open up and lock onto the neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter and tighter. She said it's called felting."

"Felting," Philemon repeated, as if testing the word. "So the sweater grabbed itself smaller."

"Basically the whole sweater shrank itself," John said. "Nobody did it to it. It did it to itself." He looked down at the ruined cables and thought about the months of knitting, the arid weeks of January when he had worn it every single day to the bus stop, this very bench, pulling the collar up against the wind.

"So you're taking it to her to fix?" Luc asked.

"She says she can't undo it. But she said she'd teach me to knit, and I could make something new out of the felt. A mitten, maybe." John shrugged, then straightened. "Actually, I already started. Last night I did the cast-on row four times until it worked. And I've done two loads of laundry since, both cold, both fine."

Philemon grinned. "So next Saturday you'll be the laundry expert and a knitting apprentice."

"Grandma says experts elaborate. Apprentices just have a lot of wool."

The 42 rounded the corner at last. John stood, tucked the little sweater back into the bag, and shouldered his backpack. "Tell your moms," he said, stepping onto the bus, "cold and gentle for anything knit."

Mason slid his phone across the dinner table the moment his father sat down. "Look at this dress. What color is it?"

"White and gold," his father said, without even putting down his fork.

Mason turned to his mother. She leaned over, squinted. "Blue and black. Obviously."

"Obviously?" His father set down the fork after all. "It's white. With gold lace. I'm looking right at it."

Mason looked at the same screen and saw blue and black, same as his mother, which was strange because his father was the one in the house who noticed everything, like the day the neighbor moved her mailbox three feet to the left. His father did not miss things. Yet here he was, calmly describing a completely different dress.

Mason had a plan. He texted Mathieu, who lived two streets over and would answer anything, and then Edmund, who would answer anything but wrongly. Mathieu replied in nine seconds: white and gold, are you blind? Edmund replied: blue and black, why do you even ask. That made it two against two, and the four of them had looked at the same photo on four different screens. So it wasn't the screen. He turned his brightness up and down and held the phone at arm's length. His father still said white and gold. His mother still said blue and black.

"Maybe you're all messing with me," Mason said.

His mother put her hand on her chest, wounded. "I would never. That is blue."

"It is white," his father said, with the patience of a man being reasonable at a lunatic.

Mason needed more evidence. He walked next door and rang Mr. Adebayo's bell, holding the phone out before the door was fully open. Mr. Adebayo studied it, then laughed. "This again. My whole family split over that thing in February. My brother threatened a household amendment, no dress talk at dinner. Half the internet fought about it, you know."

"And the actual dress?" Mason asked. "The real one, in a store."

"Blue and black. There's a photo of it somewhere. It went viral because everybody saw it differently."

Mason walked home slowly, turning this over. He had assumed there was one right answer and one wrong one, and that the wrong one belonged to his father. But his father wasn't wrong about what he saw. He was wrong about the dress, but right about the white and gold, if that made any sense at all. Maybe it didn't have to.

At the table, his parents were still going. His mother had pulled up the photo of the real dress, royal blue with black lace, and his father was leaning in with narrowed eyes, like a man approaching a legitimate court exhibit.

"Huh," his father said.

"That's an apology," his mother said.

"That's a 'huh.'"

Mason set his phone face down between the salt and the green beans. "New rule. We vote on something we can actually settle. Like whether Edmund counts as a reliable witness."

"Edmund," said his mother, "is the boy who told you gummy bears grew on trees until fifth grade."

"He retracted it," Mason said, and passed the potatoes.

On Saturday morning Christopher stood at the gate of the community garden holding a paper bag of gloves that Ms. García had handed him, wondering what he had agreed to. Behind the vegetable beds, volunteers were sorting crates of tomatoes, carrots, and slightly bruised apples into boxes marked for the food bank distribution table. His friend Emerald waved him over to the sorting station, where a boy named Mathias was pulling soft oranges out of a crate one at a time.

"These came from the grocery store on Fifth Street," Emerald said. "They donate the stuff that looks weird, or that didn't sell fast enough. Apples with bumps. Carrots with two legs." She held up a carrot that split like a pair of scissors at the bottom, and Mathias laughed so hard he dropped an orange.

Christopher picked up the orange and turned it over. It was a little soft on one side, but the rest felt fine. "If a whole store gives away this much," he said, "how much never gets eaten anywhere? Like, everywhere in the whole country?" He was already trying to work out how you'd even count that, since nobody could see all the food in America at once.

Mathias shrugged, but Emerald pulled out her phone. "My mom made me memorize a fact for the food drive poster at school," she said, and scrolled through her pictures. She turned the screen around. In big green letters it said the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted.

Christopher stared at the number. "That's like four out of every ten apples just gone," he said. He glanced at the crate of soft oranges, then at the line of neighbors already forming at the distribution table near the gate. Maybe the pile in front of him wasn't the whole story. Maybe most of the wasted food never even made it to a garden like this, and what he was seeing was an illusion of plenty. He wanted to know if the soft oranges could still be used, because if they could, that was a small piece of the problem he could actually fix.

"Ms. García," he called, "could we cut around the soft spots instead of throwing these out?" She said that would be feasible if they had enough knives and cutting boards, so Christopher asked Mathias and Emerald to collaborate with him on a trimming station. Ms. García found three plastic knives, and soon they were carving good halves out of bad oranges while neighbors at the table picked up the pieces in little bags. A woman with a stroller took four halves and said her kids loved oranges but she never bought the ugly ones because they cost the same as the pretty ones.

By noon the crate was empty except for peels, and Christopher felt his legs aching from standing. Then Ms. García came over holding a clipboard and a strange look on her face. "I called the store to thank them," she said. "Turns out they've been donating for two years, and nobody ever told us they had a whole cold room of bread and eggs in the back. They thought we couldn't handle it." She set the clipboard down. "Would you three be willing to come back next Saturday with a van?" Christopher looked at Emerald, who was already grinning, and at Mathias, who raised his plastic knife like a sword. "We'll be here," Christopher said, and he pulled the gloves back out of the bag.

The morning after the moving truck left, Everly sat in a classroom where every desk had a name tag except hers. Mr. Charles handed her a blank tag and a marker, and she wrote her name in block letters while twenty-eight students watched. He pointed to an empty seat beside a girl with braids, who slid her pencil case over to make room.

At lunch the girl, Adelina, asked where Everly had lived before. "Fairview," Everly said. "My best friends there are Margaux and Priya." Adelina said the equivalent of that at her old school had been two boys she'd known since kindergarten, but when her family moved last spring, she never heard from them again. "It's like we just stopped existing to each other," she said. Everly pushed her tray around and thought about that all through afternoon math.

That evening she called Margaux, who was sorting comic books into boxes. Everly had an idea and she wanted to test it. "Adelina lost her old friends because they moved and nobody kept in touch. So let's do the opposite. Every Sunday at four, video call. If we do it regularly, we stay close. That's the whole plan." Margaux said her mother would never let her miss it if it were on the calendar, so they made it official and wrote it on the wall planner in orange marker.

The first Sunday, Priya joined too, and they all drew the same dragon from a tutorial, comparing results on camera. The second Sunday, Margaux's internet went out, so she called from the library and held her phone up to a book about fantasy, which was the only genre all three of them read. Everly began to incorporate pieces of Fairview into her new life, telling Adelina the jokes Margaux made and showing her the drawings Priya sent.

By October, Everly noticed a pattern in Adelina. Adelina texted her cousin in another state every single day, and that cousin was still her closest friend. But Adelina's old neighbor had moved two years ago, there had been no calls, no messages, no visits, and now Adelina couldn't remember the neighbor's last name. Two friendships, two different results, and the difference was contact. Everly wrote it in her notebook like a science observation, then felt silly and crossed it out.

In November, Mr. Charles assigned a project on communities, and Everly chose to survey students about friends who had moved away. She asked one question: do you still talk to them, and how often? Out of nineteen answers, the eleven students who called, messaged, or visited their old friends said they were still close. The other eight mostly shrugged.

The day before winter break, Everly's Sunday call came through with snow falling behind Margaux's window. Priya held up a painted figure and said, "Next week you're drawing with us, no excuses." Adelina leaned into the frame from the couch beside Everly and waved.

Isla sat cross-legged on Emmitt's bedroom floor while he dumped a bag of chips between them and passed her his phone. "You have to see Marisol's video," he said. "She posted the science fair volcano exploding and it has, like, two hundred comments." The app was called Flicker, and Isla had been wanting an account ever since the whole group chat started moving there. She tapped Sign Up.

The first questions were easy. Username, password. Then a white box appeared: Date of Birth. She typed her birthday, September 14, and the phone buzzed and the screen went gray. A message in small print said accounts could not be created for users under 13. "That's weird," she said. "I'm twelve. My birthday's in two weeks."

Emmitt leaned over her shoulder, breathing chip smell onto her cheek. "Just lie," he said. "Nobody checks." Isla stared at the box. She could type anything, and the phone would believe her. But something about it snagged in her mind, the way a thread catches on a nail. She scrolled down and found a long page of rules nobody ever reads, and near the middle was the answer: a law, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, said websites had to get parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13. That was why so many sites made you say you were 13.

"So they ask your birthday," she said slowly, "because if you're under thirteen, the whole app would be too invasive. They'd have to call your parents first." Emmitt shrugged. "Then put thirteen. Marisol did it, I bet. Everybody does it." He was already back to watching the volcano video with the sound turned up, the plastic hiss of bubbles almost real through the speaker.

Isla started a little experiment. She cleared the form and typed a birthday that made her twelve years and ten months old. Gray screen. She tried twelve years and eleven months. Gray screen again, the same flat buzz, like the phone was shrugging her off. She tried thirteen years exactly. The screen bloomed green, and suddenly there was a place for her profile picture, her interests, her school. The app wanted to invest her in it right away, little prizes for filling in every blank. Her thumb hovered.

Down the hall, a door opened, and Ms. Li called, "Emmitt, is Isla staying for dinner?" Emmitt yelled back something with his mouth full. Isla looked at the green screen, then at the blank where it asked for her school, her real name, her city. Two weeks, she thought. In two weeks she'd be thirteen and it would all be true anyway. She pressed the back arrow until the form disappeared.

"Forgot my password," she told Emmitt, and slid the phone across the carpet toward him.

Alexis slid a crumpled flyer across the dinner table so his father could see it. "The game convention is Saturday, and there are only two hundred holographic Dragonheart cards, and one kid at school is selling his for forty dollars." He had saved twenty-two dollars from raking leaves, which had felt like a fortune until this week.

His father stirred his soup and looked at the flyer. "Forty dollars for a card. You know what we paid for water today? A whole case of bottles for three dollars." He held up his glass. "You can't live without water, but it's cheap. A tiny diamond costs thousands and nobody needs one to survive."

"That's weird," Alexis said, chewing slowly. He thought about that instead of the card for a moment. "Water does everything, and it's almost free. A diamond just sits there." He remembered Ms. Lawson mentioning something like this in class on Tuesday, so after dinner he dug out his notes. There it was, underlined twice: In The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal. So people had noticed this puzzle almost two hundred fifty years ago, and it was still true at his own dinner table.

The next morning he found Celina at her locker and told her the whole thing. "Ms. Lawson talked about it, remember? Adam Smith, 1776, The Wealth of Nations." Celina laughed and said, "Only you would turn a card into homework." But she frowned at the flyer thoughtfully. "So if everyone wants the card and there are only two hundred, the price goes up. Like the diamond. If there were a million of them, it would cost as much as water."

"Exactly. So the price isn't about how good it is. It's about how many there are compared to how many people want one." Alexis decided to test it. He made a small poster for his locker: TRADING DRAGONHEART? MEET ALEXIS. By Friday, three kids had offered theirs, and the lowest price was eighteen dollars. He bought that one, keeping four dollars to spare, and felt like he'd solved something.

At Saturday's convention he spotted Ainsley near the entrance staring at a display case with a frail, hand-drawn banner sagging over the table. A canopy of balloons swayed above the vendors, and beneath it Ainsley pointed at a glass box. "Look. The card's in there. Signed by the artist."

Alexis leaned closer. There were thirty identical cards fanned out under the glass, each one holographic, each one signed, and the sign above them read: TEN DOLLARS EACH, LIMIT TWO PER PERSON. He looked at his card, then at the case, then at the empty space in his wallet where eighteen dollars used to be. Ainsley grinned and said, "I'd hurry. There's already a line."

Samuel wedged his knee against the seat in front of him and studied the worksheet Mr. Sutherland had handed out on the bus. The field trip was to the fire station, and the whole visit would run on a tight schedule: one hour, then back on the bus, because the firefighters had a real call drill at eleven.

"Question six is impossible," said Zackery, leaning over the aisle. "It says, 'Why would you crawl instead of run in a smoky hallway?' I put 'because you'd trip.'"

Nimrit, who sat by the window with her binder open on her knees, tapped her pencil against question six. "My cousin's a firefighter. She says something about the air down there. I can't remember what."

Samuel turned his pen sideways and rolled it between his fingers. He was thinking about the fog machine from the school haunted house last October. The haze had hung at the top of the gym first, thick and gray, and only later had it settled. Everyone said the machine was broken, but maybe it wasn't broken at all. Maybe that was just what smoke did. If the air near the floor was cleaner and cooler, because smoke and heat rose upward, then crawling wasn't about tripping at all. He scribbled a draft answer and covered it with his hand. "I've got a guess," he said. "But I want to check it before the bus gets there."

The bus rattled over a pothole, and Mr. Sutherland stood up at the front. "When we arrive, the station will accommodate us in groups of ten," he said. "Booths, gear, and a practice tunnel. And yes, you may bring your worksheets."
