At Alexis's house the poster went fine until Alexis's mother announced dinner in twenty minutes, which meant the project had to be done by then. That was when Alexis frowned at her own phone and said, "Thierry was going to text me the citation for that bird website. He promised. Nothing's come through." They waited. Alexis tapped the screen, held the phone up toward the window like she could catch a signal in her hand, and even turned the phone off and on again. Still nothing, and the clock on the wall crept toward dinner.

Ruby thought about her own new phone, still in her pocket, and about how Alexis's phone had been silent since they started gluing feathers onto the poster. She remembered something she'd noticed in the store, a tiny airplane icon in the corner of the display model's screen. She had tapped it once out of curiosity and seen the signal bars disappear, then tapped it again and watched them return. Now she leaned over Alexis's shoulder and looked at the top of the screen. There it was: the same little airplane. "Airplane mode," Ruby said, pointing.

Alexis stared at the icon. "My little brother had my phone in the car," she said slowly. "He must have turned it on." She tapped it off, and before she even set the phone down it buzzed twice, fast, like a held breath finally let out. Thierry's messages scrolled in, one right after another, along with the link they needed. Alexis read the citation out loud while Ruby wrote it at the bottom of the poster in her neatest letters, and the last feather was glued down just as Alexis's mother called from the kitchen. Ruby felt her own phone buzz once in her pocket, and she grinned at Alexis without checking it yet. "Ten more minutes," Alexis's mother said from the doorway, holding up the timer.

Florence pushed her peas around her plate while her dad told her grandfather about the new tenant in the upstairs apartment, a quiet man who fixed bicycles in the garage. She was only half listening. Her mind was back in the school library, at the Nature Club meeting she had run that afternoon, where Blakely and Zoe had ended up shouting over each other about the fund-raiser until the bell rang and nothing got decided. Next week she had to run it again, and the thought made her stomach tight.

"Something wrong with the peas?" her grandfather asked. He always noticed.

"The club meeting," Florence said. "I'm president, but I can't get anyone to stop talking at once. Zoe thinks we should sell seed packets. Blakely wants a bake sale. Mr. Watanabe says if we can't decide by Friday, the school will give our table at the spring fair to the chess club." She set down her fork. "It's like everyone gets louder and nobody gets heard."

Her grandfather chewed slowly, then pushed back his chair. "Come with me a minute." He led her to the bookshelf in the hallway, the one with the dusty top rows nobody touched, and pulled down a small brown book so old its spine was soft. "This was your great-grandmother's. I nearly gave it away last spring. See what you think."

Florence opened it on the hall table. The pages smelled like cedar. It was a guide to running meetings, all about agendas and motions and taking turns so every person got to speak once before anyone spoke twice. "Robert's Rules of Order," she read on the title page. "It says here it was first published in 1876. By a U.S. Army officer named Henry Martyn Robert." She looked up. "An army officer wrote a book about being fair at meetings?"

"Goes back further than your club does," her grandfather said. "Take it home."

That week, Florence wrote an agenda on a sheet of loose-leaf: old business, then the seed packets, then the bake sale, then a vote. She made a rule, borrowed straight from the book, that anyone wanting to speak raised a hand and got called on, and that discussion of one item had to cease before the next one began. When Zoe started to interrupt, Florence said, "Hold that thought, it's next on the agenda," and Zoe actually sat back and waited. Blakely got her whole argument out without a single shout. Then Zoe did. The vote was close, six to five, seed packets, and Blakely shrugged and said, "At least I got to talk."

On Friday, Florence carried the old book to Mr. Watanabe's classroom and set it on his desk so he could see they had a plan now. He read the title page, then raised his eyebrows at her. "This is a loaner," Florence told him. "Temporary. Grandpa says it stays in the family."

Caleb stood at the starting line in the school gym, where cones marked four laps of a short oval because the track outside was still buried in snow. He had lost the eight-hundred-metre race at the last meet by blowing up halfway through, and today he intended to figure out why. The problem was invisible. He couldn't see his energy draining away, but he could see the results: a fast first lap, then legs like wet sand on the second.

Davin jogged up beside him. "I've been thinking about our race," Davin said. "Your first lap was way faster than mine, but I caught you at the end. My second lap was quicker than my first. Running the second half faster than the first is called a negative split. Running the first half faster is called a positive split." He pulled a crumpled paper from his pocket with both their lap times on it, which they had copied off the results sheet outside the caretaker's residence next to the gym.

Caleb studied the numbers. His first lap had been three seconds quicker than his second. Davin's second lap had been four seconds quicker than his first. So Davin had run a negative split, and Caleb had run a positive split, and Davin had won. Caleb couldn't see the pattern working inside his own legs, but he could see it on paper, and it repeated exactly. "I want to test something," he said. "Next time trial, I run the first lap slow on purpose. Deliberately slow. If I die on the second lap anyway, the idea is wrong."

Pascal, who was holding the stopwatch, laughed. "That's backwards. Everyone knows you go out hard and hang on." Caleb said that maybe everyone was biased, because going out hard felt brave and slowing down felt like quitting, even if it won races. Pascal shrugged and agreed to time it anyway.

Ms. Kowalski blew her whistle from the stage at the end of the gym, and the three of them set off. Caleb counted his steps and held himself back while Pascal and Davin surged ahead. It felt awful. At halfway he was trailing by half the gym, but his breathing was even and his legs still answered when he asked them to go. He began to pick runners off. He passed Davin on the third lap, and on the last stretch he caught Pascal two cones from the finish and leaned across the line first.

Afterward, all three of them sat on the bleachers with the stopwatch, and Caleb made them read out his laps. First lap slower, second lap faster. A negative split, on purpose, and it had worked once. It might not work every time, and he would have to evaluate it again at the next time trial before he trusted it. Davin clapped him on the shoulder. "Same race next week," Davin said. "This time I'm racing your way."

The arrivals board at the airport flipped from DELAYED to LANDED, and Luke stood on his toes even though it changed nothing about his view. His grandmother was coming to stay for a whole week, and he had promised his mom he would hold the sign he'd made, mostly so she could find them in the crowd. GRANDMA FRIDA, it said, in letters so large that a man beside him asked whether she was famous. "Only to me," Luke said, which made the man laugh. Then the doors opened, and there she was, dragging a suitcase with one wheel that spun in the approximate direction she never intended to go.

At home, things went well for two days. Then, on Tuesday morning, Luke found her standing at the kitchen counter, frowning at a plastic box with seven little lids in a row. "Did I take my morning pills?" she asked. "I can't remember, and I don't want to take them twice." Luke picked up the box and turned it over in his hands, curious how anyone was supposed to solve a problem like that. It was like trying to figure out whether the fridge light goes off when the door closes. You couldn't see the answer directly. You had to look for evidence.

He opened the lid marked MON and found it empty, and the lid marked TUE was empty too. The WED compartment still held its little cluster of pills, and so did THU through SUN. "Wait," he said slowly. "If you'd forgotten Monday, that compartment would be full. Two empty compartments means two doses already taken. It's Tuesday, so today's is the empty one." His grandmother peered at the box. "You mean the box remembers for me?" "The box testifies," Luke said grandly. "If my teacher asks me to cite my sources, I will cite a plastic container." She laughed so hard she had to sit down.

At school that afternoon, Luke told Yanis and Mathew about it during lunch. Mathew said it was like a metaphor for memory, a machine doing the remembering for you. "Not a metaphor," Luke said. "An actual box. Metaphors don't have lids." Yanis pointed out that the whole thing only worked if she loaded it correctly at the start of the week, which was the part Luke found the most interesting. A system was only as good as its weakest Sunday night.

The next morning Luke came downstairs and found his grandmother opening WED, shaking the pills into her palm. "Tuesday's compartment was empty," she announced, "so I knew it was Wednesday." She looked rather pleased with herself. Luke grinned and got the orange juice. "So," he said, sliding the glass across the counter, "same time tomorrow?"

The court behind the rec center had one good rim and one bent one, an impoverished patch of asphalt with cracks running through the key. Addison was running point for the first time in a real game, and her team was losing 8 to 6. The other team's best player, Zachariah, kept calling for the ball and then holding it, dribbling in place, letting the clock on his phone tick away whole minutes while nobody scored.

"That's not even basketball," Elaine said, wiping sweat off her forehead. "He's just standing there."

Addison had been watching anyway, not the ball but the other team. Every time she called for a screen, their big man switched onto the roller and their guard stayed with the ball. But when Elaine set a screen without Addison signaling, nobody switched, and Elaine slipped free under the rim twice. The pattern was invisible unless you compared the two situations, and Addison thought she had it: the defense was reading her voice, not the movement itself.

"Give me the ball," she said. She took it to the top, and this time she called nothing. Elaine set the screen silently, and the defenders both stayed on the ball, exactly as Addison predicted. Elaine rolled, Addison fired the pass between two arms, and Elaine laid it in. 8 to 7. Zachariah called timeout out of pure frustration.

"We should get a shot clock," Elaine shouted across the half court. "Like the NBA."

"We don't have a clock," Zachariah said.

"Use your phone. The NBA adopted a 24-second shot clock for its 1954-55 season," Elaine said. "You have to attempt a shot within 24 seconds of getting the ball. So you can't just stand there."

"You made that up," Zachariah said. "Basketball didn't always have clocks." But he couldn't contradict her with anything specific, and his own teammates were tired of standing around, so one of them held up a phone and started the timer. Zachariah got the ball and, for the first time all afternoon, had to attack.

Addison kept her discovery quiet for two possessions. Then, with 14 seconds on the clock and her team down 8 to 9, she brought the ball up and called the play out loud anyway. "Elaine, high screen!" The big man switched just like she expected, and instead of using the screen, Addison split off the opposite way into the space he had abandoned. She pulled up at the free throw line. The ball hit the back rim, bounced straight up, and dropped through.

Elaine grabbed her by both shoulders. "You called it out loud on purpose?"

"Nine to nine," Addison said, backing toward the top of the key. "Watch the phone. Twenty-four seconds."

Claire carried her clipboard down to the lake dock like it was made of gold, because taped to it was the first official agenda of the Camp Birchwood Trading Post Club. Item one: opening remarks. Item two: what to do with the club's fifteen dollars. Item three: vote. She had been meticulous about it, rewriting the whole thing twice because the first version had put the vote before the discussion, which Dahlia said was like chewing before the sandwich arrived.

"Order!" Claire called, standing on a flat rock that served as the podium. Nine campers sat on the dock, plus Adele, who was lying on the dock with her hat over her face. "We'll go down the agenda one item at a time, and everyone who wants to talk gets a turn before we move on. Raise hands, and I'll keep a list."

It worked better than she'd hoped, mostly. Item two produced a flood of ideas: a telescope, a repair kit for the canoes, a giant watermelon for the end-of-camp party. Then Marco, who could not sustain interest in any topic for more than two minutes, moved that they buy the watermelon, and Mr. Adeyemi, the nature counselor who had wandered over to watch, seconded it just to keep things moving.

"All in favor of the watermelon?" Claire counted five hands. "Opposed?" Four hands, including Adele's, whose hat slid off as she shot her arm up. Marco immediately demanded a recount, then changed his mind halfway through and said, "Wait, no, the recount will make us miss swimming."

"Then it passed, right? Five beats four," said Dahlia.

"Hold on," Claire said. Two people hadn't voted at all. She counted the dock again, tapping each head with her pencil. Eleven members, five yes, four no, two nothing. She remembered the rule from the dusty club handbook she'd found in the craft cabin, the one nobody else would touch because a spider lived in it. "A majority vote means more than half of the votes cast. Not more than half the club. Just the votes actually cast."

"So five out of nine," Adele said, sitting up, suddenly interested. "Nine votes cast, and five is more than half of nine."

"It passed!" Marco pumped both fists and nearly rolled off the dock.

"But what if the two who didn't vote show up tomorrow and hate watermelons?" asked one of the non-voters, looking worried.

"Then they should have voted," Adele said. "That's the whole trick of it. You have to show up."

Claire wrote MOTION PASSED, 5-4 on her agenda, feeling like a real chairperson, whatever that was. "Next meeting, Thursday, same rock. Item one will be assigning someone to carry the watermelon."

Marco raised his hand. "Point of order. Can the watermelon be my co-chair?"

"It can be whatever you want," Claire said, "as long as it doesn't try to run the meeting."

Jules's bedroom smelled like hair spray and mint gum, and Hailey sat on the bed holding a diagonal-striped dress she wasn't sure about. The dance started in forty minutes. Her stomach had been doing a strange floating thing since lunch, and she wanted to know why.

"Your hands are freezing," Jules said, grabbing one. "Mine too. And my stomach feels like it's full of moths."

"That's the exact feeling," Hailey said. She had been thinking about it all afternoon. "Hayden said his stomach flips and his heart pounds before he even gets somewhere scary. At his last game, before the whistle, his heart was going so fast he could hear it." She frowned. "Why would a stomach and a heart both act weird at the same time? They don't even do the same job."

"Maybe you're just hungry," Jules said, chewing her gum.

Hailey tested that idea by eating half a granola bar. The floating feeling stayed exactly where it was, so hunger wasn't the cause. Something else had to be making it happen. She counted her own pulse with two fingers on her wrist, watching the clock, and got ninety-four beats in a minute. Sitting still on a bed, that was fast. Her heart was racing like she'd been running laps, only she hadn't moved.

The doorbell rang, and Hayden came in still wearing his soccer warmup, holding an ice pack to his head. "Missed a ball at practice," he said. "The coach thinks it might be a concussion, so my mom has to watch me tonight. She's driving us to the dance and staying in the parking lot the whole time."

"You're still coming?" Jules said.

"Skipping the first dance of middle school? No." He sat down heavily in the desk chair. "Also my stomach is doing the flip thing again, and my heart is thumping like crazy. I haven't even walked in yet. Am I sick?"

Hailey leaned forward. She lined up what she knew like clues. Fear of the dance, then racing heart, then the floaty stomach, always together, always before something scary, never during something calm. "I think it's one thing causing all of it," she said slowly. "When you're nervous, your body lets out something called adrenaline. It speeds up your heart. And it pulls blood away from your stomach. That's the flip. People call them butterflies."

"Wait, so the butterflies are real?" Hayden said.

"They're a real feeling with a real cause. Nothing's actually wrong with you." Hailey checked her pulse again, thinking. "So if being nervous makes it, then being less nervous should stop it. What makes you not nervous?"

Jules and Hayden looked at each other. "Music," they said at the same time.

Jules turned on her speaker, loud, and Hayden drummed the ice pack against his knee in time to the beat. They jumped around for one whole song, the diagonal dress forgotten on the bed, and when the song ended Hailey took Hayden's wrist and counted. Eighty-two.

"It's going down," she said, grinning. "It actually works."

"Then we petition the DJ for this exact song," Hayden said, "the second we get in."

In the car, all three of them were quiet until the gym doors came into view, glowing. Hailey's stomach floated once more, high and light, and this time she just smiled at it.

"Ready?" Jules asked.

Hailey opened the car door. "Butterflies and all."

Something was eating Logan's tomatoes, and it had excellent taste, because it only took the best ones. Each morning he found another perfect red fruit gnawed down to a green ring, always on the low branches, always overnight.

"Raccoons," said Kellan, leaning over the fence between their yards. "Big ones. Possibly a bear."

"It's not a bear," Logan said. "It's something smaller. And it comes at night." He couldn't see the culprit, so he decided to do what Ms. Bakker called working like a scientist: guess, then test. His guess, his hypothesis, was that the eater was a bird, because the bites were high on the fruit and messy, like pecking. Caius, who was over by the shed holding a garden fork like a knight, had a different hypothesis. "Mice," he said. "They climb."

"Then let's test it," Logan said. He had overheard Ms. Bakker next door telling someone about her students' plant experiment, and one phrase had stuck in his head: a fair test keeps everything except the one thing you're testing exactly the same, same amount, same temperature, same timing. He figured that rule could work here too.

They set up two tomato plants in pots, side by side in the middle of the garden, with the same amount of water, in the same temperature, checked at the same time each morning. On one plant they stretched netting over the top, tall enough that a bird couldn't reach through. The other stayed bare. If the birds were guilty, the netted plant would be safe and the bare one would get eaten. If the mice were guilty, both plants would get eaten, because mice would just climb the netting, and Caius would get to look smug.

The first morning brought an ominous discovery: the bare plant had two bites taken from it, and the netted plant was untouched. Logan felt a flicker of triumph but refused to diagnose the case as solved on one night of evidence. That felt like deciding a whole season from one at-bat, as his coach would say. They repeated the setup, same amounts, same spot, same timing, for three more nights. Same result each time.

"It was birds," Kellan said, in the tone of someone who had guessed wrong and was now guessing after the answer was known.

"That's what the test says," Logan said. He felt a small obligation to be fair about it, since Caius had been wrong and was taking it with more dignity than expected. Caius was still holding the fork.

Ms. Bakker looked over the fence on her way to her car, nodded at the two pots, and said, "One variable, everything else the same?" Logan held up two fingers. "Four nights." She gave him a thumbs-up and drove off, which felt like the highest grade he'd received all year.

That evening he netted the whole row, every plant, and stood back to admire it. Somewhere overhead, a fat robin watched him from the power line, un-netted, patient.

"We'll see about tomorrow," Logan told it.

The bus hummed along the highway, and Adam ran his finger down the list of words for the fifth time. The regional bee started in forty minutes, and his brain felt like a thermostat set too high, overheating on every vowel. "Chrysanthemum," he whispered. "C-h-r-y-s."

Keenan slid into the seat beside him and held out half a granola bar. "You skipped breakfast. I saw you in the hallway with your nose in that book instead."

"I had to budget my time," Adam said, taking the bar anyway. "Forty minutes of review beats ten minutes of cereal." He flipped open the library book he'd carried all week, the one about the Scripps National Spelling Bee and its champions. A folded page marked the chapter he had read four times.

Aubree leaned over the seat in front of them. "What's so good about that part? You keep going back to it."

"In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde won the whole Scripps bee," Adam said. "First African-American contestant ever to do it." He tapped the photograph of her holding the trophy, her smile enormous. "She was thirteen. She practiced maybe a thousand words a day. And she played basketball, too."

"So she wasn't just a spelling robot," Aubree said.

"That's what I keep thinking about. She probably got words wrong along the way. The book says she missed some at other bees before that." Adam closed the book and looked out the window at the flat, frozen fields. "I've been treating every word like it has to be perfect. Maybe that's backwards. Maybe you just keep going through the misses."

Ms. Petrov stood at the front of the bus and raised her voice over the engine. "Ten minutes, spellers. Jackets, water bottles, and your courage." When she passed Adam's seat she paused, glanced at his book, and smiled at the photograph. "Good choice of reading," was all she said.

The parking lot was windy and bright. Keenan zipped his jacket and pointed at Adam's thin sweatshirt. "You're going to freeze in that. Take mine till we get inside."

"I'm fine."

"You're shivering. It's practically tropical weather for you in here, maybe, but not out there." Keenan draped his coat over Adam's shoulders before Adam could argue.

Inside the auditorium, the seats filled up fast. Aubree squeezed Adam's arm. "Number fourteen. That's you. Third row."

Adam sat, laid the book on his knees, and opened it one last time to the folded page. The announcer stepped to the microphone and said, "Our first speller, contestant number fourteen."

Adam stood, left the coat on the chair, and walked toward the bright lights.

The rumor said the vending machine in the east hallway had taken Maisy's dollar and given her nothing back, and it had spread so fast that by Wednesday half the seventh grade was refusing to buy anything, which was a problem for Bentley, because he had spent his entire allowance on a candy resale scheme that depended on that machine's reputation.

He sat in Ms. Moretti's history classroom trying to figure out where the rumor had come from. Nobody had actually seen Maisy lose the dollar. Maeve said she'd heard it from a kid in gym, who heard it from someone else. Bentley counted on his fingers under the desk. He had heard the story five separate times himself, and he'd caught himself telling it twice.

"You only believe it because you keep hearing it," he whispered to Maeve. "That's it. That's the whole reason."

"So?"

"So it's like when they play the same cereal commercial over and over and then you think the cereal must be good." He leaned closer. "People did a study in 1977. Lynn Hasher and some other researchers. They found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true."

Maeve looked skeptical. "Where did you learn that?"

"Ms. Moretti's propaganda unit. Yesterday. I was actually listening, for once."

Ms. Moretti rapped the board. "Moving on. Wartime posters. Notice this one says everyone is buying war bonds. That's a bandwagon appeal. It doesn't give you a reason; it just says everyone's doing it, so you should too." She pointed at a poster with a famous actor's face. "And here's a celebrity testimonial. And this headline calls the enemy 'savage.' Loaded words."

Bentley raised his hand. "Is repeating something a lot also one of those?"

"It can be, yes. Advertising works partly on it." She moved on to agriculture posters from the same era, full of waving wheat and words like "abundance."

At lunch, Bentley ran his test. He told Maisy, loudly, that the machine had been inspected by the district and was totally fine, then got Maeve to mention it to two kids at the next table, then asked a seventh grader to bring it up one more time by the water fountain. By the end of the day, three separate people had told Bentley the machine was fine as if they'd known it all along. One of them had been spreading the original rumor at breakfast.

"You repeated it," Maeve said, catching him by the doors. "You used the exact trick you were complaining about."

"I know," Bentley said. He fed his last dollar into the machine and pressed B4. The candy bar dropped, and the change clinked down, and a kid behind him in line said, "See? Everybody's using it again."

The community centre math club met on Thursdays in the room with the broken radiator, and Vincent had missed three weeks because of his paper route. Now he sat hunched over a worksheet, pencil ticking, trying to remember what Mr. Chukwu had taught about equations. He knew the rule well enough to say it: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. Subtract three from both sides, and the sides stay balanced like a scale. Divide both sides by four, same thing. But the problems in front of him kept coming out wrong, and he could not see why.

"Try number seven," said Willem, sliding his chair over. Willem finished worksheets the way other kids finished crisps, in about ninety seconds. "Just get x alone."

"I know that part," Vincent said. "It's after that it falls apart."

Across the table, Irene was waving a page in the air. "Mr. Chukwu, I proved one equals two. Look." She read it out, step by step, starting from a equals b. Multiply both sides by a. Subtract b squared. Factor. Divide. And there it was, 1 equals 2, tidy as anything.

Mr. Chukwu raised an eyebrow and told her the proof was counterfeit, and that finding the hidden flaw in it would earn her a place at the regional team table. That was the table Vincent wanted. The team had four seats, and the tryouts were in two weeks, and Willem already had one.

That night Vincent copied Irene's proof onto graph paper and dismantled it line by line, testing each step the way you test a bridge, one plank at a time. Every line looked legal. Multiply both sides, fine. Subtract from both sides, fine. Factor, fine. Then he stopped at the division. Divide both sides by a minus b. He frowned at it. He plugged in numbers. If a equals b, then a minus b equals zero. He wrote it out, circled it, and sat very still.

The next Thursday he got there early and found Irene by the whiteboard. "Line five," he said. "You divide by a minus b. But if a equals b, that's zero. You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer."

Irene stared at the proof, then at him, then burst out laughing. "You sneak. I checked every line."

"You checked them forward," Vincent said. He picked up the marker and drew a fat circle around the sneaky step. The nib squeaked against the board.

Mr. Chukwu came in with the tryout list in one hand and read the whiteboard over their shoulders. He said nothing, but he wrote a second name at the top of the list, and slid it across the table. Vincent's name sat beside Willem's.

"First practice is Saturday," Mr. Chukwu said. "Bring the marker. And bring that circle."

Emmett floated home from the first basketball practice of the season. His legs felt springy, his shot felt smooth, and he told his dad that tryouts had been nothing. "Easiest practice of my life," he said. On Wednesday, two days later, he woke up and nearly fell over trying to climb the stairs. His thighs burned like someone had filled them with sand. He hobbled into the kitchen gripping the railing.

At school he found Marylou and Cayden at the lunch table. "Walk it off," Cayden said, chewing his sandwich. But Emmett was frowning at the ceiling, thinking. Practice had been Monday. He'd felt fine Monday night, fine Tuesday morning, and now Wednesday he could barely sit down without lowering himself with both arms on the desk. Why hadn't it hurt right away? "That's weird," he said. "If the practice caused it, the soreness should've shown up right after. Unless it's like a delayed reaction." Cayden offered his testimony: the same thing had happened to him after his first week of swimming lessons, fine that day, wrecked two days later. "Three kids on my old team said that too," Marylou added, and Emmett wrote the pattern in his notebook: fine first day, worst on day two or day three.

That night he searched the internet and found the name for it. "Delayed onset muscle soreness," he read out loud to himself. Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaked twenty-four to seventy-two hours later, not right away. He sat back. So that was the rule. Then his stomach dropped, because the first game was Saturday, and if the pattern held, today and tomorrow would be the worst days, right up against tipoff.

He had an idea and decided to test it. Thursday, Mr. Qureshi supervised the open gym hour, so Emmett asked if he could use a side hoop. He didn't sprint or jump. He jogged gentle laps, took slow set shots, and stretched while Marylou timed him. His theory was simple: if the soreness was already peaking, moving lightly couldn't make a new peak, because he wasn't doing anything new or hard. By Friday afternoon the sand in his legs had drained away. He climbed the bleachers two steps at a time and grinned down at Cayden.

Saturday morning the team bus rolled up to the neutral gym across town, where neither side would have home fans, and Emmett bounced on his toes in the layup line. His legs felt light and quick. "Whatever you did," Cayden whispered, "do it before every game." Emmett spun the ball on his finger, caught it, and said, "Science, my friend. Science." Then the whistle blew, and he broke toward the basket.

Cameron crouched beside the stone wall of the war memorial, holding his phone flat against a faded plaque. His history project was due Monday, and it had to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, using a primary source. The problem was he had picked the museum's modern textbook, all shiny pages and timelines, and Ms. Charles had shaken her head at his draft.

"You need a primary source," she had said, and nothing more.

"That's the museum one," said Allegra, dropping onto the wall beside him with a granola bar. The wind off the memorial lawn smelled of cut grass and cold metal. "I did mine on the letters. A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event. Like my letters from the soldier."

"So the textbook doesn't count?"

"The textbook's written later, by someone studying it. That makes it a secondary source."

Cameron scrolled through the museum's digital collection and found a settler's diary, scanned page by page, the ink brown and spidery. He read it aloud while pigeons argued on the cannon nearby. "May the 14th. Rain again. Thomas says the land here is tired, and the soil in the west is black as coffee. We will follow the birds." He looked up. "Follow the birds?"

Eesa leaned over from the other side of the wall, where he had been copying names off the memorial into his notebook. "Migratory birds. They go west in spring, don't they? Maybe he watched which way the geese flew."

Cameron tested the idea. He flipped through the diary pages, hunting for the same pattern, and there it was again: a sketch of geese in a V, pointing west, and beside it, "good land lies where the birds rest." So the settler's motive wasn't just soil, it was the birds as a sign. He could eliminate the textbook now, cross it off his source list, because the diary was the thing made at the time by someone who lived through it. The textbook could still back him up later, but the diary was the heart of the argument.

He started his new draft right there, notebook on his knees, wind flapping the pages until Allegra pinned them down with her granola bar wrapper. "Paragraph one," he said, printing hard. "A settler's diary from the trail. Quote the geese."

Eesa peered over his shoulder. "Better than mine. I just have names."

"Yours matters too," Cameron said, and he meant it, then bent back over the page and wrote the first line in ink that wouldn't blow away: The birds knew the way before the people did.

Juliette had five dollars and one plan: the glass prism on Mr. Byrne's folding table. She had seen it from the sidewalk, throwing a small rainbow onto the pavement when the sun hit it. By the time she crossed the lawn, a boy was already holding it up, turning it so the light refracted onto his shoe.

Mr. Byrne had penciled a new sign and clipped it to the front of the table. The old one, THREE DOLLARS, lay crumpled in the grass. The new one said EIGHT DOLLARS. "Three people asked for it in ten minutes," he told the boy. "Only one like it here." Juliette looked down the table. There were four boxes of paperbacks, a bucket of spoons, and one bowl of heavy glass doorknobs, marked fifty cents each. She had five dollars. The prism was out of reach unless the boy walked away, and he was counting out eight ones.

Behind her, Malia was working a card table with a pitcher of lemonade and a sign that said TWO DOLLARS A CUP. Two kids looked at the sign, looked at their single dollars, and drifted next door, where Anaya stood beside her own pitcher, handwritten sign reading ICED TEA, ONE DOLLAR. Anaya poured cup after cup. "Tea's basically a substitute," Malia said, arms crossed. "Same job on a hot day, half the price." By eleven o'clock Anaya's pitcher was empty and a line of kids stood in front of her, waiting for her mother to carry out the backup jug from the kitchen. Malia stared at her own full pitcher, then got a marker and scratched out the two.

Juliette watched all of it and turned back to Mr. Byrne's table with a new idea. The prism's price had jumped because everyone wanted the one fancy thing. But the doorknobs would do the same job, splitting sunlight into color. She picked one up, held it to the sun, and got a wobbly rainbow across the paperbacks. It worked. Not as sharp, but it worked. She put two more in her hand and brought all three to Mr. Byrne.

"Fifty cents each," he said, reading his own sign. Then he paused, because the boy with the prism was gone and two girls from the line at Anaya's table had wandered over. One of them pointed at the bowl of doorknobs and asked what they cost. Mr. Byrne looked at the empty spot where the prism had been, then at the bowl, and said, "A dollar each now." Juliette set her three down on the scale. "You said fifty. I picked these out before she came over." He rubbed the pencil mark on the sign, seemed to consider, and said, "Fair enough. Fifty for you. Dollar for everybody after."

She paid a dollar and fifty and carried the doorknobs home in her backpack just as the clouds stacked up, heavy and green like a monsoon sky. On her front steps she lined them up along the railing and waited for a break in the light. When the sun cut through, three crooked rainbows fell across the porch boards. Malia came up the walk with her pitcher, still unsold, and stopped to look. "Okay," Malia said. "I'm dropping my price to a dollar before the weekend. And I'm buying one of those."

Blaine's basement smelled like popcorn, and his laptop glowed on the ping-pong table between them. Kenan leaned in from the other side.

"See?" Blaine said, turning the screen around. "VelocityWater dot com. It says professional athletes drink it and their injuries heal in half the time. My cousin wants me to buy a case with my birthday money."

The website really did look impressive. There were photographs of runners, a video with dramatic music, and a quote from somebody called Dr. Harlan Voss. "It seems real," Rachel admitted. She scrolled through the About page, and everything there was polished too, which almost convinced her.

Then she stopped. Something about it felt like the time her neighbour Mr. Rao had shown her a flyer for a roofing company that vanished after one storm. She opened a new tab and typed the company's name into a search. In another tab, she searched for "Dr. Harlan Voss." The results were strange. Nobody outside the website mentioned him at all. Then she found a news article from two years earlier: the company selling the drink had been warned for making up health claims. The whole amazing website, every last page of it, was run by the people profiting from it.

"It's like checking what other people say about somebody instead of just asking the person themselves," Rachel said slowly. Kenan nodded. "Mr. Rao calls that lateral reading. He does it before he trusts any website about mortgage rates, since scam sites love that topic." Blaine typed it into his notes.

"My cousin's going to say the website looks so professional," Blaine said.

"Then show him what you found in the other tabs," Rachel said. She scrolled back to the news article, where a lawyer had called the company negligent for ignoring safety warnings, and a reporter described how their fake review pages had been thwarted by a regulator who demanded they publish a correction. "It's all right here."

Blaine copied the link and texted it to his cousin. Then he closed the laptop halfway, like he was shutting a door on a salesman.

"He already answered," Blaine said, holding up his phone. "He says thanks, and he's buying a water filter instead."

Levi carried the cardboard box the whole six blocks home, even though his arms ached, because the puppy inside kept trying to climb out. His neighbor Mr. Ortiz had found the litter behind his garage, and after a week of posted signs nobody claimed the wriggling brown one with the white sock feet. "He's yours now," Mr. Ortiz had said, and those words had propelled Levi down the sidewalk faster than his bike ever had. The puppy, who he was calling Biscuit, rode home quietly for once, watching the houses slide past.

Levi set the box on the kitchen counter only long enough to grab the water bowl from under the sink, and that was his mistake. When he turned back, Biscuit had tipped out of the box, landed on the counter somehow, and was chewing through a plastic bag with his whole face buried in it. The bag was the dark baking chocolate his mom used for cookies. Half a square was already gone. "No, drop it," Levi said, and Biscuit dropped it and wagged, thrilled by the new game.

Levi's stomach went cold. He had read one thing about dogs, on a flyer at the pet store, and it had said something about chocolate being bad. But he'd also seen Ryleigh's lab eat a dropped M&M at the park and be fine, so maybe it was all exaggeration. Then he remembered the flyer's exact words, which he'd thought were weird at the time: dogs break down the stuff in chocolate, which was called theobromine, very slowly, so it stays in them. And dark chocolate and baking chocolate were far more dangerous than milk chocolate, because they had more of it. Biscuit had just eaten baking chocolate. The M&M hadn't mattered. This did.

He tested his reasoning out loud, walking in a circle. "Milk chocolate, small amount, fine. Baking chocolate, half a square, not fine." He called Ryleigh to check, and Kurtis was there too, since they'd been planning to come see the puppy. "Yeah, my aunt's dog got into cocoa powder once," Ryleigh said. "They called the vet right away. The vet said the dark stuff is the dangerous stuff." Kurtis added, "It's called theobromine, that's what the vet said it's called." Levi hung up and dialed the vet's number with shaking fingers, and a calm voice on the line asked how much, what kind, and how much the puppy weighed. "Bring him in now," she said.

At the clinic, they took Biscuit through a door Levi couldn't follow him through, and he sat in the waiting room gripping the empty chocolate bag like it was evidence. Forty minutes later a tech carried Biscuit out, sleepy but walking on his own four sock feet, and said he'd be stable and fine by morning. Levi held him against his chest all the way home, and at the counter he swept every bag of chocolate into the highest cabinet, then pushed the box of dog biscuits to the front where Biscuit could see them. "Yours," he said. "The chocolate is mine."

The mystery liquids sat in two unlabelled beakers on the counter, and Mr. Santos had promised a homework pass to whichever group identified them correctly. Benjamin dipped a strip of blue litmus paper into beaker one, and both strips, his and Danika's, turned the same shade of red. He dipped a fresh strip into beaker two. Red again, exactly as red as the first.

"So they're the same," Andrei said, already reaching for the worksheet to write "identical liquids" in his scrunched handwriting.

"Wait." Benjamin held the two strips side by side against the fluorescent light. "The paper only shows whether a solution is acidic or basic. It can't tell how strong the acid or the base is." He'd read that line twice last night, partly because he'd been avoiding his math homework, and he was glad now of that small dishonest choice. "Both of these are acids. But one could be way stronger and the paper would still just say red."

Danika frowned at the strips like they had betrayed her personally. "So our big clue is basically a light switch. On or off. Nothing in between."

"Basically," Benjamin said. "We'd need another test to compare them. A pH number, maybe." He remembered his father's aquarium kit in the garage, translucent plastic tubes and a color chart, but that wouldn't help him here at school. He tried a different angle. "What if the strength shows up somewhere else? Like, how they react with something?"

Andrei looked around the lab with the expression of a man recruiting an army from whatever was nearby. "Baking soda," he said, pointing at the supply shelf. "Mr. Santos said we could use anything on that shelf."

They measured a pinch of baking soda into each of two small cups. Benjamin poured a little from beaker one onto the first pinch, and it fizzed politely, a thin foam that settled after a few seconds. Danika poured from beaker two, and the second cup erupted like a furious root beer, foam climbing the sides and spilling over onto the counter while Andrei yelped and jumped back.

"Okay," Benjamin said, mopping up with a paper towel, grinning. "Not identical."

"Definitely not identical," Danika said, holding up her worksheet. "So what do we write?"

Benjamin thought for a second, watching the last bubbles pop in the second cup. "Beaker two: acid, strong. Beaker one: acid, weaker. Evidence: the fizz." He paused. "And maybe a note that litmus paper got us halfway and quit."

Andrei wrote it all down, then added at the bottom, in his terrible handwriting, "Danika owes me a new sleeve."

Grandpa's trumpet sat on the piano bench like it had been waiting for Joshua all summer. He lifted it, turned it in the light, and blew until his lips buzzed and a wobbly note finally squeaked out. He wanted to be ready for band tryouts in September, and Grandpa had promised to teach him everything.

"First you read music," Grandpa said, sliding a beginners book across the piano. "Start with this page." Joshua stared at the five lines, the black dots, and the swirly symbol at the start that looked like a fancy ampersand. Every time he tried to name a note, he guessed. G? C? He couldn't tell, and guessing wouldn't cut it when the band director handed out real music.

Then he noticed something. The swirl at the beginning of the staff curled around one line and circled it, like a lasso. He traced it with his finger, again and again. The second line from the bottom. What if the swirl was pointing to a specific note on purpose? He counted up from the bottom line, then dug out the little chart taped inside the book cover. The second line was G. The swirl circled G. "Grandpa, is that why they call it the G clef?" he asked. Grandpa grinned and said, "That's exactly why, the treble clef is the G clef." From that moment, Joshua could find G anywhere on the page, and he climbed the alphabet from there, naming notes faster and faster until the lines stopped being a mess and started being a map.

Agam came over the next day, skeptical as usual. "You learned to read music in one afternoon? Sounds like propaganda to make me feel slow." Joshua slid the book across the porch steps. "Count up to the second line and tell me what you see." Agam traced the curl, checked the chart, and his eyebrows went up. "It circles G. Every single time." He'd been sure it was luck, but now he couldn't refute it; the pattern held on every page, every song.

Mr. Brennan, the neighbor, heard them practicing on the porch and wandered over with his coffee. "Explicit instructions from the swirl itself," he said, tapping the page. "Can't argue with that." Joshua raised the trumpet, found his note, and blew a clean, round G that rang out across the yard.

Nevaeh stood at the kitchen counter with the biggest knife her mom would allow, an onion, and a printed recipe she'd found on a cooking site. The recipe had been posted by someone anonymous, just a username with a pot emoji, but hundreds of people had commented that the sauce was better than anything from a jar. That was her objective for the evening: chop the onion, build the sauce from scratch, and serve it over pasta before her little brother started whining about being hungry.

First she had to survive the onion. Her eyes were already stinging from the first cut, and her grip felt clumsy. She curled her fingers on the onion like claws, knuckles forward, so the blade could only bump against bone instead of fingertips. It was slower than she expected. The pieces came out uneven, some thin as paper, some fat as dice, and she wondered whether the sauce would still work with onion bits of every size.

Then the counter betrayed her. She reached for the salt, her elbow knocked the knife, and it slid toward the edge. Her whole body wanted to snatch it out of the air. Instead she jumped backward, and the knife hit the floor with a bang, blade down, quivering in the gap between her sneakers. She stood there breathing hard, staring at it, remembering Malachi telling her about his cousin at camp last summer. "A knife slid off the picnic table," Malachi had said, "and his uncle grabbed for it. Six stitches. His uncle says you never try to catch a falling knife, you step back and let it drop." Nevaeh had thought that sounded backwards at the time. Now her toes, all ten of them uncut, made a pretty good argument for it.

She picked the knife up carefully, washed it, and got back to work. The anonymous recipe said to cook the onion slowly until it turned soft and golden, so she lowered the heat and gave the sauce time, stirring it now and then, tasting, adding a pinch of sugar when it tasted sharp. Her mom drifted through the kitchen and peered over her shoulder. "Smells like somebody's nurturing that pot," she said, and Nevaeh laughed, because that was exactly what it felt like, patience and attention and the willingness to keep showing up.

When the pasta was drained and the sauce ladled over the top, her brother took one bite, then another, then a third without saying a word. Nevaeh watched him, spoon paused halfway to her own mouth. He looked up. "Can you make this again tomorrow?"

Bentley had turned his dad's garage into a lab, which mostly meant dragging a card table next to the lawnmower and taping a hand-lettered sign to it that said SCIENCE. Sahil and Sara sat on overturned buckets while Bentley lined up six clear cups. "Today we test acids and bases," he announced. "Mr. Shin gave me litmus paper from his hardware shop. Blue paper turns red in acid, and red paper turns blue in base."

"If it's neutral, nothing happens," Sara said. "Like plain water. Water's neutral, pH 7."

"Exactly." Bentley dropped a strip of blue paper into the vinegar cup and they watched it flush pink. Lemon juice did the same. Sara contributed a splash of her mom's leftover coffee, which turned the paper a distinct brick red, darker than the vinegar had. Sahil wrote it all down in a notebook, frowning at his own spelling of "phenomenon."

Then Bentley stirred a spoonful of baking soda into a cup of water. "This one's easy," he said, feeling smug. "Baking soda in water. It's basically just water with powder in it. I'd say the probability of it testing neutral is about a hundred percent." He dipped the red paper in and waited for nothing to happen.

The paper turned blue.

"That's not nothing," Sahil said. "That's very much something."

Bentley leaned over the cup like it might confess. He dipped the blue paper in too, and it stayed blue, calm as anything. "So it's not acid," he said slowly, thinking out loud, "because acid would have turned the blue paper red. It's a base. The baking soda did that. Baking soda dissolved in water makes a mildly basic solution." He fished out the box and squinted at it as if it had been keeping a secret from him all along. "Powdered betrayal," he muttered, and Sara laughed so hard she nearly fell off her bucket.

They ran the test three more times, and every strip came back blue. Sara checked a chart on Bentley's notebook cover and held it up. "Mildly basic, it says, pH of about 8 to 9." Bentley exhaled, long and dramatic, and wrote the numbers in Sahil's notebook in his biggest handwriting. Then he uncapped the vinegar and, with great ceremony, dripped it into the baking soda cup. The fizz climbed the side and overflowed onto the card table, and all three of them scrambled back, laughing, while the puddle hissed quietly between the battery charger and the lawnmower.

The bus jolted over the pothole by the elementary school, and Elliot had three stops left to figure out what to do about Karson. Every morning for a week, Karson had been calling Izaiah "Radio Tooth" because of the gap between his front teeth, and every morning Izaiah just stared out the window and took it. Yesterday, Izaiah had finally fired back with a clever comeback about Karson's haircut, and the whole back of the bus had howled. Elliot had expected that to end things. Instead Karson came back twice as mean, and by afternoon he had two other kids chanting the nickname too. Elliot turned that over all day. The comeback had been funny, but funny gave Karson something new to hit back at. It was like the teasing had its own hierarchy, and a punchy insult just moved Izaiah up to a bigger target.

Elliot had written a note during math and folded it into his pocket, and when Izaiah slid into the seat across the aisle, Elliot passed it over. The note said, "Meet me at the back before Karson gets on. I have an idea." Izaiah read it twice, gave a small nod, and moved.

Karson boarded at the corner by the pharmacy, loud from the first step. "Morning, Radio Tooth. You broadcasting today?"

Elliot's first try came out too abrupt, almost like a shove in words. "Karson, your haircut looks like a lawnmower lost a fight with you." Karson's grin got wider, not smaller, and Elliot felt his stomach drop. Wrong move. He could see it happening again, exactly like yesterday, the teasing inflating because he'd handed Karson fresh material.

He took a breath and tried the other direction. "That's not funny. Stop." Four words, flat and calm. Nothing in them to fight about.

Karson blinked. "What, are you his bodyguard now?"

"That's not funny. Stop," Elliot said again, same tone, and Izaiah, catching on, repeated it too. "Not funny. Stop."

Karson looked for a hook and found nothing to grab. He muttered something about boring people, put in his earbuds, and turned toward the window. The two chanting kids glanced at each other, uncertain now that there was no show.

At the next stop, after Karson shuffled down the steps without a single word about teeth, Izaiah leaned over. "Where'd you get that?"

"Figured it out after yesterday," Elliot said. He had almost confided the whole thing to Ms. Otieno after class, the note about Karson still crumpled in his pocket, but he'd wanted one more try on his own first. Now he was glad he'd waited.

"Same bus tomorrow?" Izaiah asked.

"Same seat," said Elliot, and pressed the note flat into his pocket.

The movers carried the last box on Tuesday, and by Thursday Rebecca was standing in Room 12 with her schedule in her hand. She counted eleven desks before Mr. McKenzie called roll. At lunch she sat at the end of a table of girls who already knew one another's jokes, and by Friday she had learned exactly one name, and that was only because it was printed on a worksheet: Shyla.

At her old school it had taken her three weeks to become friends with the girl next door, and that was only because they kept meeting at the same bus stop every morning. Rebecca wrote this down in her notebook so she could see it: friends came from seeing the same people over and over. Random lunch tables didn't work because the people changed every day. She needed one place, one group, meeting regularly, so that a friendship would have time to grow, the way seeds needed a whole season. A class where everybody shared one interest would be even better, because then there would be something to talk about besides the weather.

She found the list of clubs taped beside the office: art, robotics, drama, chess. Chess met Tuesdays and Thursdays in Room 9. Her grandfather had taught her the game two summers ago, and she could still beat him about half the time. She wrote her name on the sign-up sheet.

On Tuesday, Room 9 held six kids and a folding table with three boards set up. A girl with short braids looked up. "I'm Ellie. You know the rules? I need a real opponent, everyone here plays wrong." Ellie was entering the county tournament in November and couldn't practice properly against people who moved their knights sideways. Rebecca sat down and captured Ellie's bishop on the ninth move. Ellie stared at the board, then grinned. "Thursday. Same time. Don't forget."

They played again Thursday, and the Tuesday after that, and the one after that. Rebecca brought granola bars because Ellie claimed she played worse without carbohydrates in her system, and Ellie traded her a laminated sheet of openings she had copied from the library. Between games they argued about whether the knight or the bishop was worth more, and one afternoon Ellie mentioned that the club was exactly the reason she'd stopped eating lunch in the bathroom last year.

In November Rebecca rode with Ellie's mother to the tournament and sat in the third row during the final game. Ellie won on time, held the small plastic trophy over her head, and pointed straight at Rebecca from the stage. On the bus home, Ellie leaned against the window and said, "Next year we both enter." Rebecca looked out at the highway lights going by and said, "Okay. I'll document every game we play, so we can study them." She opened her notebook and started with the date.

The library was quiet except for the pencil sharpener grinding somewhere near the biography section. Noemie spread her worksheet on the table and stared at the problem Ms. Francis had circled in red: x divided by 3 equals 5. She had solved every other one, the ones like x plus 4 equals 9, just by undoing the plus. This one had a fraction sitting in the way, and she did not know how to move it.

Tatiana dropped into the chair across from her and slid over a wrinkled receipt. "Augustin's at the vending machine," she said. "We owe him. He paid for all three of us at the cafe after the science fair, and now we have to pay him back, but the receipt got wet and the total smeared." The bottom of the paper was a molten gray blot where the ink had run. Tatiana tapped the surviving line above it. "My share was 5 dollars. We split it three ways, so we each paid the same."

"So the total is some number," Noemie said slowly, "and if you divide it by 3, you get 5." She pulled the receipt toward her and wrote on the back, where the paper was still clean. "That is the same as my worksheet. X divided by 3 equals 5." She looked at the smeared blot, then at her pencil. The total was hidden, but if she could work backward from the share, she could find it.

She tried things out loud. "If the total were 12, each share would be 4, because 12 divided by 3 is 4. That does not coincide with 5 dollars, so 12 is wrong." She tested 18 in her head; 18 divided by 3 was 6, still wrong. Then she wrote a 3 next to both sides of her equation, one on the left and one on the right, like weights matched on a scale. The fraction on the left cleared away, and on the right, 3 times 5 stood alone. "Fifteen," she said. "The total is 15 dollars." She checked it the opposite direction: 15 divided by 3 was exactly 5.

Augustin came back from the vending machine cracking open a bag of pretzels. Tatiana held out the receipt. "Fifteen dollars," she said. "Five each, three of us." Augustin counted on his fingers, shrugged, and dug into his pocket.

Noemie turned back to her worksheet. She copied the same move onto the circled problem, wrote a 3 on both sides, and watched the fraction disappear. Ms. Francis passed the table on her way to the reference shelf, glanced down, and put a small check mark next to it with her red pen. Noemie flipped to the next problem, which had a 4 in the denominator instead, and picked up her pencil again. "Four goes on both sides," she said to Tatiana. "Watch."

Charles had taped his hypothesis to the top of the display board in big letters: seeds watered with leftover tea will sprout faster than seeds watered with plain water. The science fair was two days away, and the evidence said otherwise. Every plain-water cup on the windowsill of the science classroom had a green hook of a sprout poking through the soil. Every tea-water cup held nothing but damp dirt.

"No, no, no," Charles said. He leaned over the tray until his breath foged the plastic wrap. He had done everything right. Same soil, same number of seeds, same squirts from the same dropper. He lifted a tea cup and sniffed it, getting a bitter wet-teabag smell, and set it down harder than he meant to.

Ludovik looked up from his own project across the lab table, where he was gluing cotton balls to a poster about static electricity. "Maybe they just need more time."

"They got the same time as the others. That's the whole point." Charles rubbed the back of his neck. Something he couldn't see had to be going on in those cups, or something he hadn't thought of. Maybe the seeds were duds. He dug one out of the dirt with a pencil tip and found it swollen and split, exactly like the sprouting ones. So the seeds were alive. The tea itself had to be the difference, though he couldn't watch that part happening. He planted six fresh seeds, three in each group, watered them, and labeled them "Trial Two" with a shaking marker.

Alexi came in from gym class still carrying the smell of the locker room and peered at the trays. "Why does half your window look like a graveyard?"

"Because my hypothesis is wrong, probably." Charles said it quietly, like testing whether the words were true.

By the next morning, Trial Two had copied Trial One exactly. The plain-water seeds had cracked open and pushed up pale white stems; the tea seeds had swelled and stopped. Charles sat down on the radiator and put his head in his hands. His Saturday, his careful notes, all of it had gone toward proving himself wrong, and it felt like he had nothing to show.

Ms. Oyelaran stopped at his table on her way to unlock the supply cabinet. She looked at the board, then at the trays, then at him. "Present it," she said.

"Present a fail?"

"A wrong result is still a real result," she said, and moved on to argue with Ludovik about the cotton balls.

Charles stared at his notebook. He had recorded every watering, every measurement. Nobody else would know this, that too much tea stops sprouts cold, or whatever it was doing down there in the dark. It was a small thing to know, but it was real, and he had proved it twice. Being vain about his first guess would be the actual failure.

He picked up the marker, crossed out nothing, and printed a new line under the old hypothesis: "Prediction not supported. Findings reported." Then he stepped back to look at the board, the ghost of the tea smell still on his fingers.

The whistle blew, and the cones at each end of the gym looked very far apart, like they were trying to depict the distance across an actual desert. Beatrice stood on the starting line with eleven other girls, all of them trying out for the track team, and waited for the first beep.

"Twenty meters," Mikaela whispered beside her. "You run to the far line before the next beep, then back. It's the multistage fitness test, but everybody just calls it the beep test."

"What happens after a while?" Beatrice asked.

"New levels. And the beeps come faster at each one."

The first beep sounded, and everyone shuffled forward at an easy jog. It was almost funny, how slow it felt. Beatrice had finished her sprint warm-ups early just to be first in line, and now she had nothing to do with all that energy. Last spring, at soccer tryouts, she had sprinted the opening drill like a maniac, gasped her way through the middle, and been cut before the final round. The coach had said something about pacing, and she had hated hearing it.

The beeps guided them back and forth, back and forth. At level two, Beatrice noticed she was arriving at each line several steps early, standing there waiting. So was a tall girl named Ryerson, bouncing on her toes. Ahead of them, a few girls ran hard every single leg, arriving exactly on the beep, breathing like they'd already run a race.

Beatrice thought about the pattern she could feel but not see: the beeps were a clock, and the clock was speeding up. If the beeps came faster at each new level, then the girls sprinting now were spending something they would need later. But waiting too long was dangerous too, because once the beeps outran a comfortable jog, she would have to sprint just to survive, with no cushion left.

She tested it. For the rest of level two, she aimed to arrive two steps before each beep, no more. It took constant adjusting, like pouring water into a glass without spilling. Ryerson, beside her, kept bursting and stopping, bursting and stopping.

Level four arrived with an ominous silence, then a quicker rhythm. The sprinters ahead began to look ragged. One girl missed a beep twice and was waved to the side. Ryerson reached level five but shook her head, hands on knees, and stepped off.

By level six it was just Beatrice and two others, and there was no pacing left, only running. Her lungs burned. The far line swam toward her, then away, then toward her again.

The final beep she caught by a lunge, one hand slapping the floor.

"Good," said Ms. MacLeod, checking her clipboard. "Wednesday, four o'clock, first practice."

Beatrice walked to the water fountain on legs that felt like static, and Mikaela was already there, holding a cup out to her.

Alicia sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office with a tissue pressed to her nose, trying to breathe through the congestion and failing. Her mother had finally dragged her in after four days of fever, and now she had time to think. Her thoughts kept circling back to the sleepover at Shania's house, six days ago. Everyone had been perfectly healthy that night. They had eaten pizza, watched a movie, and shared one big bowl of popcorn, passing it around the circle.

"Pizza and popcorn, that's it," said a voice, and Alicia looked up. Sebastian was sitting two chairs down, red-nosed and miserable, wrapped in his own coat.

"What are you doing here?" she asked.

"Same thing you are, probably. My mom says it's the flu." He sneezed into his elbow. "Weird, because Shania's sleepover was the only place I went all week, and nobody there was sick."

Alicia frowned. That was the strange part. Shania had hosted them all, and she had seemed fine, full of energy, doing handstands in the hallway. But Sebastian had the flu, Alicia had the flu, and by now she knew from the group chat that two other girls from the sleepover had it too. Four out of five guests, and the one who wasn't sick was Sebastian's little sister, who had fallen asleep early and hadn't shared the popcorn.

"Wait," Alicia said slowly. "Four of us got sick and we all arrived the same day. If we caught it there, somebody had to have it at the sleepover."

"Nobody was coughing," Sebastian said.

"But what if you can spread the flu before you even know you have it?" Alicia pulled out her phone and typed carefully, and there it was: people with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms. She held the screen so Sebastian could see. "So Shania could have been coming down with it that night and looked totally healthy."

Sebastian groaned. "Then Shania got us sick without knowing. She's going to feel awful."

"She didn't do anything wrong," Alicia said. She tried to console him. "It wasn't like she was careless. She didn't even know."

The nurse called Sebastian's name first, and he stood up, shrugging his coat back onto his shoulders. "When we're better, we should tell everyone at school. People always blame whoever sneezes, but it might be the person who looks fine."

Alicia nodded and pulled up the group chat. She started typing a message to Shania, asking how she was doing, and added a thumbs-up emoji at the end before pressing send.

The music room smelled like valve oil and old carpet, and Mr. Bautista had written twelve empty boxes on the whiteboard. "Count them as we play," he said. "Blues form is twelve bars, then it starts over." Annabelle had her trumpet on her lap. She had never made up a solo before, and every note she knew suddenly felt like it belonged to someone else.

Ira sat at the piano, which was the problem, because Ira wanted the solo for himself. He had asked twice already, and Mr. Bautista had said the same thing twice: "Annabelle's turn today. You comp the chords." Ira plunked the first four bars with his whole forearm, sulky, then settled down and used actual chords. Behind them, Eliot tapped the rhythm on his knees and told a long anecdote about his cousin who once got lost during a concert and played the wrong song for a whole minute. "That will not happen to me," Annabelle said, and then it did.

She lost count somewhere in bar six. She kept playing, but her notes stopped matching what Ira's hands were doing, and the sound went wrong in a way she could hear but not see. She stopped, mouthpiece at her lip, and listened. The chords moved through a pattern, round and round, and near the end the sound seemed to lean, as if the whole progression were tipping forward. "There," she said. "What's that bit?"

"The turnaround," Eliot said.

She watched Ira's hands through the next chorus and tracked it. The turnaround was the end of the twelve-bar form, and it landed on the V chord, which pulled the music back to the start of the next chorus. She had a theory: if she got lost again, she didn't need to count, she only needed to wait for that tipping sound and jump in when the form started over. She could test it right now, before the fear of getting lost went extinct in her mind the way courage sometimes did, five minutes after you needed it.

"Take it from the top," she said. "And Ira, play the turnaround loud so I can hear it coming." Ira had changed his mind about the solo, or at least about her having it. He played the twelve bars clean and strong, and at bar twelve he leaned into the V chord like a door swinging open. Annabelle came through it on an F, loud, right on the downbeat of the next chorus, and held it until the room went bright around her. "Again," she said.

Evelyn spread the photocopy across the library table so flat that the corners stopped curling. It was a page from a settler's diary, written in 1846 by a woman named Margaret Hale, and Evelyn's assignment was to explain why the Hale family left Missouri for Oregon. The trouble was that the diary didn't come out and say why. Nobody in 1846 wrote essays for thirteenth-grade students to digest.

"Read this part again," Leilani said, dragging her chair closer. She tapped a paragraph with one finger. "'The bank took our claim in the spring, and Josiah cannot find work in Hannibal. Yet the papers say Oregon soil is black as coffee and a man may hold six hundred acres.'"

Madelynn arrived late, holding a note from the coach and still in her practice jersey, because she wanted to keep her eligibility and that meant showing Ms. Rao she was actually studying. She dropped into the third chair and squinted at the page. "That's two different kinds of reasons," she said. "Bad stuff at home, good stuff out there."

Evelyn wrote two columns in her notebook. At the top of one she wrote AWAY, and at the top of the other she wrote TOWARD. "The bank taking the claim goes under away," she said. "It pushed them out. The free land goes under toward. It pulled them." She worked down the diary, sorting line by line. The fever that took the baby went under away. The letters from a cousin in Oregon went under toward. Then she hit a sentence about wolves and hesitated, because wolves in Missouri could push you, but so could wolves in Oregon pull you back. "Madelynn, which column?"

Ms. Rao passed behind them on her way to the returns cart and paused just long enough to see the page. "There's a name for those," she said. "Push factors and pull factors." Then she went on shelving, which was her way of saying figure out the rest yourselves, and Evelyn underlined the two words at the top of her columns.

By the last paragraph Evelyn noticed something that made her sit back. The pull factors were the ones Margaret Hale wrote about longest, the black soil, the six hundred acres, but the push factors were what got them moving. Her own family had moved two years ago, and Evelyn had always told people it was because of the new job, which was a pull factor if anything was. But her mother had also been laid off, and somehow they never mentioned that part. It felt arbitrary, which reason you named when people asked. Maybe there wasn't one true reason. Maybe there was a whole column.

"There's a third problem," Leilani said, pointing at the diary's last line. "'We turned back at the river and will try again in spring.'" Evelyn looked at it for a long moment, then wrote one more heading under her columns: TOO SCARED TO MOVE YET. Madelynn laughed so loudly that Ms. Rao looked over, and Evelyn slid the notebook out of view and started copying the columns onto her poster paper.

The recipe card on Anna's station had three jobs on it: rice, curry, flatbread. All three had to reach the table at the same time, which meant the rice had to start first because it took twenty minutes, the curry in the middle, and the flatbread last, cooked fast in the dry pan. She wrote the order on the back of her hand with a pen she'd negotiated off Freyja in exchange for the last of the paprika.

"That's not a plan, that's a tattoo," Freyja said.

"It's an algorithm," Anna said. "Step one, step two, step three, and dinner comes out all at once."

Ms. Henry moved between the stations, saying nothing unless someone's pan was actually on fire, which so far it wasn't. Anna got the rice bubbling, then turned to the curry and read the first line again. Heat the ghee, add the cumin seeds, fry them briefly until they darken, then add the onions. She frowned at it. Why fry the seeds first, alone in the fat, instead of stirring them in later with everything else? They were going to get cooked anyway. She thought of last term, when she'd dumped cinnamon straight into her porridge and tasted nothing but pale powder. Maybe the seeds had to go into hot fat on their own for some reason she couldn't see.

"I'm going to test it," she told Theodore at the next station. "Half the cumin now, the way it says, and half stirred in at the end. Then we taste both."

"Science," Theodore said solemnly, "with curry." He held out a spoon as if knighting her.

The seeds hit the ghee and within seconds the smell changed, warm and toasty and suddenly everywhere, like the pan had woken up. Freyja leaned over from her station. "My gran calls that tadka," she said. "Frying the whole spices in hot oil first." Anna filed the word away and kept going, because the onions were not going to wait for anyone's grandmother.

The flatbread was its own small crisis. The dough stuck to the rolling pin, then to itself, and Anna remembered her mother telling her to let dough rest and Anna, impatient at nine years old, refusing. She had pounded out flatbreads that came out like shields. This time she covered the dough with a cloth and let it rest while the curry simmered, and when she rolled it, it moved like it wanted to cooperate.

The timing nearly collapsed anyway. The rice finished early, the curry needed five more minutes, and Anna negotiated with the clock by wrapping the pot in two tea towels to hold its heat, a trick she'd seen Ms. Henry use without ever being told it was allowed. The flatbreads puffed in the pan, one after another, and then everything landed on the counter in the same minute: rice, curry, three warm breads.

The tasting was the real test. Anna took two spoons of curry, the tadka batch and the late-cumin batch, and did not say which was which. Theodore chewed the first spoonful, then the second, then went back to the first like a man returning to a good room. "This one," he said. "The other one tastes like... cumin that never got the message."

Anna tasted it herself. The seeds stirred in at the end were sharp and a little raw, standing apart from everything, while the fried ones had melted into the whole dish, the flavour riding through the ghee into the onions and the sauce. So the fat had to come first. The pan had to teach the spices before anything else joined them.

"What's the word again?" Theodore asked, already reaching for the last flatbread.

"Tadka," Freyja said, and Anna got there half a second behind her, both of them saying it at once, and Freyja laughed so hard she nearly dropped the curry spoon.

The ferry's engines hummed under Jasmine's sneakers as she leaned on the rail, watching the mainland shrink to a brown smudge. Delaney stood beside her, and Lamar had claimed a bench where he was attempting to photograph a seagull that refused to cooperate. "Beach day," Delaney said, holding up a bottle. "My mom works for a corporation that makes sunscreen, so we get it free. I have six bottles." Jasmine had put on sunscreen that morning at the house, before the long drive to the dock. She figured she was set.

Their neighbor Ms. Tan was on the ferry too, knitting in the shade of the cabin. "You two are going to roast out there," she said, not looking up from her needles. "Sunscreen doesn't last all day, you know." Jasmine nodded politely and didn't believe her. How could something you put on at nine in the morning just quit? It was still on her skin, faintly coconut-scented. It must still be working.

They hit the beach before noon. Jasmine checked her phone at eleven, at twelve, at one, and did the math: two hours had passed, then more. She was proud of herself for noticing, in a distant, filing-it-away sort of way. Then she and Delaney and Lamar spent the rest of the afternoon in and out of the waves, racing to the buoy, dragging each other off the paddleboard, towel-drying, going back in. Nobody reapplied anything. Lamar said the water would preserve whatever protection remained, like wax on a car, and that sounded scientific enough that nobody argued.

That evening, back on the ferry for the return trip, Jasmine's shoulders began to sting. By the time the lights of the harbor appeared, they were the color of the boiled ham her grandmother made, a distinct, glowing pink that hurt when her jacket brushed it. Delaney's nose had peeled already, a little white flap like a price sticker. Lamar, mysteriously, was fine, and he would not stop mentioning it.

Jasmine sat down across from Ms. Tan, who took one look and raised her eyebrows over her knitting. "It wears off," Jasmine said slowly, working it through. "It doesn't last the whole day. You have to put it on again every two hours out there. And right after swimming, or sweating, not later. Right after." She counted backward on her fingers: morning application, hours of sun, hours of waves. The whole afternoon had been one long expiration notice she hadn't read.

"You could have told me straight out," she added. Ms. Tan snipped her yarn. "I did, dear. Twice." Delaney appeared with one of her six bottles and set it solemnly in Jasmine's hands. "For tomorrow," she said. "We leave at nine. I'll set an alarm." Lamar leaned over the rail and shouted, "Two hours!" at the seagull, which, for once, did not argue.

Mia spread her survey papers across the workbench in the garage, weighting the corners with wrenches so the fan in the window wouldn't scatter them. Fifty kids had answered her two questions: did you eat breakfast this morning, and what did you get on the last math quiz? Her poster was due Friday, and Mr. Wright had already warned her that a science fair project needed more than a pretty chart. She'd been meticulous about the data, checking every name against every number twice, and the pattern was clear. Kids who ate breakfast scored higher. Almost every time.

"So breakfast makes you smarter," said Jayden, who had biked over to help her glue the title letters. He held up a B and squinted at it. "Done. Can we eat now?"

"It's not done." Mia tapped the graph with her pencil. "What if breakfast isn't the thing doing it?"

Jayden stuck the B on crooked, then peeled it off again. "What else would it be? The cereal has, like, magic vitamins?"

That was the problem. Mia kept thinking about last year, when she'd blamed her dying pepper plant on the new fertilizer and switched back to the old one, and the pepper had died anyway. It turned out the neighbor's tree had grown in and shaded the whole pot. Two things had changed together, the fertilizer and the shade, and she'd picked the wrong one to blame.
