The statement listed two numbers that refused to match, an interest rate and, beside it, a slightly higher figure labelled APY. "Why are there two?" she asked, tapping the paper. "Which one is mine?"

Her grandfather shrugged and went back to his coffee. "You're the one taking the math elective. You tell me." Mia, who had come along to help clean out the attic, leaned over Katherine's shoulder. "Maybe the bank made a printing error," Mia said. "Or maybe one of them is a trick." Katherine felt her whole plan hinge on the answer, because she had promised herself she would compare what her money could do over five years before she opened the account.

She fetched her notebook and worked the simple version first: five percent of two hundred dollars, added up year by year, would not accelerate anywhere exciting. Then she tried letting each year's interest join the pile before the next year was counted, and watched the total creep higher than the simple version. Not by much, but by something. When she divided to find what that worked out to per year, the answer landed almost exactly on the smaller printed number, the APY, not the interest rate. "It's not a trick," she said, half to herself.

"Prove it," Mia said, defiant on the bank's behalf, arms crossed. So Katherine looked it up on her grandfather's old laptop while he watched from his chair. The page said that under the Truth in Savings Act of 1991, banks in the United States have to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, and that the APY includes the effect of compounding. "See," Katherine said, turning the screen toward Mia. "The APY is the honest number. Compounding is already baked into it."

She copied both five-year totals into her notebook, one for simple interest and one for compounding, and drew a box around the difference. "Eleven extra dollars," she announced. "That's two sandwiches and a bus ticket, for doing nothing but leaving the money alone." Her grandfather laughed and slid his pen across the table so she could underline the winner. "Then go open the account," he said. "And put my ten dollars in with it."

The bleachers were folded against the wall because the workers were coming to renovate the gymnasium over spring break, so the whole spelling bee audience sat in folding chairs that creaked every time someone shifted. Ella stood in line with Ashlynn and Philip, holding her number card, number fourteen, and going over the list of words she had copied from the library the night before. She had gone to the library looking for practice words and had pulled a heavy old volume off the bottom shelf instead, a copy of Samuel Johnson's "A Dictionary of the English Language." The librarian had told her it was published in 1755 and that it helped settle how many English words were spelled. Ella had sat there a long time, turning the brittle pages, thinking it was strange that spellings had ever needed settling at all, that somebody had to decide.

Now Mr. Kaur, who was running the bee, tapped the microphone. "We'll go through the lineup once, then sudden death rounds until we have a champion. You have ninety seconds per word." Ninety seconds. Ella folded her hands.

Ashlynn went out on "gregarious," missing a letter near the end. Philip survived "conscientious" by whispering it to himself twice before starting. Ella got "melancholy," and then, three rounds later, it was down to her and a boy from another class whose card said number two.

Mr. Kaur looked at his card and read, "Simile." Ella asked for the definition, and he said it was a comparison using like or as. That was easy, and she spelled it slowly, correctly, and watched the boy swallow.

His word was "abrupt." He started too fast, added a letter that didn't belong, and stopped halfway through with an abrupt silence. Ella was the champion. People clapped, Mr. Kaur handed her a small trophy, and a woman from the front row stood up to take a photo for the school website.

"Champion," the woman said, "tell us your secret. Hours of drills?"

"One night," Ella said. "I found an old dictionary."

"A spelling book?"

"Not exactly. Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language.' It was published in 1755, and it helped settle how a lot of English words were spelled." She lifted the trophy. "I figured if I knew who decided the spellings, I'd know what to expect."

Mr. Kaur was stacking his index cards at the microphone, and he cleared his throat. "Ella," he said, holding up the deck, "you should know I wrote these rounds from the modern district list. Every word you missed in practice came from that old dictionary of yours, and every word you got right was one the district added after they decided to renovate the library this summer and toss the bottom shelf." He dealt the cards onto the table like evidence. "The book you studied from is the one leaving the building."

Ella looked at the trophy, then at the door where two workers were already rolling in tarps. "Then I'd better take it home tonight," she said, and she went to pull it off the shelf before the bell.

The farm smelled like wet hay and motor oil, which was not what Gabriella had expected from a science field trip. Ms. Fraser had set up a folding table beside the barn, and on it sat three microscopes in padded cases that had clearly cost the school a great deal of expense, because the principal had mentioned it twice during announcements. Each student had to peel a paper-thin layer off an onion from the farm's storage shed, stain it with iodine, and find the cells.

Gabriella's layer tore twice before she got a piece small enough to lie flat on the slide. Through the eyepiece, at first, she saw nothing but a pale smear. Then she turned the fine focus, and the smear broke apart into neat brick-shaped cells, row after row of them, like a wall built by someone very patient.

"There's no way this is only fifty times," Rory said from the next microscope. "My cells look bigger than my thumb."

"Fifty times," Nash said. "It says ten on the eyepiece and forty on the lens thing. Ten plus forty is fifty."

Gabriella lifted her head. "Why would you add them?"

Nash shrugged. "Because they're both magnifying."

She looked down at her own microscope. The eyepiece, the part her eye touched, had 10x printed on it in tiny silver letters. The rotating metal nosepiece held four objectives, and the one clicked into place over her slide read 40x. She thought about it while an irritated chicken paced the barn doorway, watching the class with what she could only describe as predatory attention, as if the onion slides might be edible.

"I think you multiply," she said. "Ten times forty. That's four hundred."

"You can't just decide that," Rory said.

"Watch me." Gabriella swapped to the smaller objective, the one marked 10x. Through the eyepiece the cells shrank to a faint mesh. Ten times ten would be one hundred, and one hundred looked like this. She clicked back to the 40x lens, and the brick wall swelled into place again, four times wider than before. "See? If adding were right, going from forty to ten on the objective should shrink it a little. It shrinks it a lot. Four times."

Nash checked his own eyepiece, found the same silver 10x, and said nothing for a moment. "Fine. Four hundred," he said, in the voice of someone conceding a point at the expense of his dignity.

Ms. Fraser drifted past, looked at Gabriella's slide, and raised one eyebrow. "Wall, membrane, nucleus. All three, in your sketch, before the bus leaves." She moved on without another word, which was either high praise or a threat. With Gabriella it was often hard to tell.

Gabriella bent over the eyepiece again and began to draw. The cell wall was the outer rectangle, easy. The membrane hugged it just inside, thin as a rumor. The nucleus took longer to find; she nudged the slide a fraction, and there it was, a small dark circle orbiting the middle of one cell like a moon that had decided to sit down. She labeled all three, then sat back and looked at the chicken, which was now standing directly on Nash's notebook.

"Your predator has my data," Nash said.

Natalie spread her supplies across the library table: a pencil, a roll of tracing paper, and the flyer for the library's anonymous postcard contest. The rules said entrants could not sign their names, which suited her fine. She wanted her art judged on its own, not on who made it. She had chosen a design of a compass rose made entirely of tiny pencil-drawn stars.

She had barely started when a boy from her street slid into the seat across from her. He was eight, and he was holding his hand up like he'd been burned. "I poked myself," he said. "With a pencil. Am I going to get lead poisoning?"

"You washed it?" Natalie asked. He nodded. "Then you're fine." He didn't look convinced. He kept staring at the small gray smudge on his palm, and Natalie could see that telling him to calm down would only obstruct the conversation rather than help it. Eight-year-olds needed proof.

She remembered something from a book she'd read here last year, something about pencils, and she wasn't sure she had it right. She raised her hand toward the reference desk, and Ms. Tremblay came over. Natalie asked where the books on pencils and drawing materials would be, without mentioning the boy, and Ms. Tremblay pointed her to a shelf near the window. Ms. Tremblay had a way of answering the question you asked instead of the one you were really asking, which was exactly the compassion Natalie needed at that moment.

Natalie pulled a thin book about the history of drawing tools and found the page in under a minute. She read it twice, then carried it back. "Okay," she said, setting the book between them. "Pencil lead has never contained the metal lead. It's graphite." The boy frowned at the word. "The black stuff in your pencil. People used to mistake graphite for a kind of lead ore, and the name stuck. So there's no lead in there at all. Nothing to poison you."

The boy looked at the page, then at his palm, then at the book again. "Never?" he asked. "Not even a little?"

"Not even a little," Natalie said. He wiped his hand on his jeans anyway, and then, reassured, he leaned over her postcard and told her that one of her compass points was crooked. She checked it against the edge of the table. He was right. She erased the star and redrew it.

Colton had been typing for eleven minutes and the little cursor in the terminal just blinked at him, waiting. His program asked for a number, then divided it by 2, 3, 4, 5, and so on until it found a factor or ran out of patience. He had typed in 999,999,937, a number Maia had dared him to try, and now the computer lab smelled like thirty warm monitors and nobody was talking.

"It's frozen," said Maia, leaning over from the next seat. "Restart it."

"It's not frozen. It's thinking." Colton pointed at the fan humming inside the machine. "It's on, like, divisor forty thousand by now."

Maia did not care about divisors. Maia cared about the app she was building for the young entrepreneur contest in March, a homework tracker that buzzed at you with increasing urgency, and she needed Colton's prime checker as a small part of it, for reasons she had explained twice and he had forgotten twice. "Every second you sit here is a cumulative loss for my launch date," she said. "That's a business term."

He ignored her and stared at his loop. Divide, check, divide, check. Then he thought about what a factor actually was. If 999,999,937 was a times b, both of them couldn't be huge, because two huge numbers multiplied together would blast past 999,999,937. One of them had to be small. Small meant no bigger than the square root of 999,999,937, which was somewhere around thirty-one thousand, a number he could reach in a blink.

He cut the loop off at the square root and ran it again. The answer appeared so fast he thought he had broken something. "Prime," the terminal said, instantly, as if it had known all along and had merely been waiting for Colton to catch up. Maia refused to believe it. "That can't be right. It just skipped a million numbers." So he tried to refute it himself, typing in 999,999,929, and the program printed "divisible by 9401" just as fast, which meant the short loop was really checking, not guessing.

"That's actually useful," Maia admitted, already sketching a buzz schedule on her notebook cover. "Fast prime checks, that's a selling point. I'm putting you in the credits."

Ms. Santoso came around the lab collecting the exit tickets, and stopped at Colton's screen. "Nice work. You know the assignment only asks about numbers up to a hundred, though." She smiled at his eleven-minute martyrdom on the terminal behind her, still faithfully dividing nothing.

Colton saved his file anyway. "Ms. Santoso," he said, "what's the square root of extra credit?"

Jonathan had never been inside Sakura House, the little Japanese restaurant on Miller Street, and he was nervous about two things: the gift in his backpack, and the fact that Leyla's family knew exactly how to act there and he did not. Leyla's grandmother owned the place, and after weeks of Leyla tutoring him in math for free, his mom had insisted he bring something to thank her. The wrapped box of green tea had seemed like a legitimate choice at the store. Now it felt like a test he hadn't studied for.

"Grandma lives upstairs," Leyla said when they arrived, holding the side door open. "We eat in the kitchen sometimes." Jonathan stepped in and stopped. The floor just inside the door was lower than the rest, a shallow trench of tile, and a neat row of shoes sat along its edge, toes pointing out. Beyond it, the floor rose a step to a hallway carpeted in pale runners. Two pairs of guest slippers waited there, lined up like they had been expecting him.

William, who had invited himself along, walked straight past the shoes and onto the raised hallway in his sneakers. "Come on, we're late," he said. Leyla's grandmother appeared from the kitchen, and Jonathan watched her eyes drop to William's feet. She didn't say anything, but her smile went thin at the edges, and William suddenly seemed to notice the row of shoes behind him all at once. His ears turned red.

Jonathan tested his idea before moving. The shoes came off in the low area, so that patch must be where it happened, and the slippers must be for after. He unlaced his shoes, set them beside the row facing the door, and stepped up into the slippers. "Genkan," Leyla said quietly, nodding at the sunken tile. "That's what my grandma calls it." William backed up, nearly tripping into the trench, and switched to the other pair of slippers with the careful movements of someone dismantling a bomb.

In the apartment kitchen, Jonathan handed over the tea with both hands because that seemed safer than one. To his surprise, Leyla's grandmother did not open it. She set it on the cabinet shelf, said something warm in Japanese, and pressed a small wrapped parcel into his hands in return. He had assumed gifts got torn into right away, like at his own birthday parties, and the fact that she hadn't made him wonder if he'd picked the wrong thing. But Leyla was smiling at him, and the parcel in his hands had real weight.

Dinner was tempura and rice, and the three of them demolished it. William, who had spent the whole walk bragging about knowing chopsticks, kept dropping his shrimp; Leyla, without a word, slid the little chopstick rest toward him and demonstrated a slower grip. Jonathan noticed how her grandmother watched all of it, the dropped shrimp, the corrections, the way nobody mentioned William's earlier mistake. Then she leaned across the table and pointed her chopsticks at William's plate.

"You try," she said. "Slow is better than fast."

William looked at her for a second, then at his hands, and started over.

Parker slumped onto the bench outside the gym, holding his phone like it was evidence in a trial. Tenley had gone silent on him at lunch, and he had spent all of sixth period trying to figure out why. His best guess: she had found out that he had read her texts when she left her phone on his desk Friday. He had only meant to check the time, but one message had led to another, and now his stomach was doing that anxious flip it did before tests he hadn't studied for.

"Mr. Wright says stress lives in the body," said Subhan, dropping down beside him and offering half a granola bar. "That's why your face looks like that. So, what did you do?"

"I don't know yet. That's the problem." Parker took the granola bar anyway, because eating something was his mom's coping trick and it sometimes worked. "She was fine Friday morning. She was weird Friday after school. Something happened in between, and I was with her the whole time except for the phone thing."

Subhan raised an eyebrow. "The phone thing."

"Okay, the phone thing might be the hidden cause. But here's my test. If she's mad about the phone, she'll still be mad today but not mad at you. If she's mad about something else, like the canceled trip, she'll be mad at everyone. So go say hi and report back."

"You want me to be your lab rat." Subhan stood up anyway, brushing crumbs off his jeans. "If I get excluded from the group chat because of this, you owe me lunch for a week."

Tenley was at her locker, and Parker watched from the bench like a detective who had accidentally made himself the suspect. She said hi to Subhan. Then she said something longer, glancing toward Parker, and Subhan walked back slowly, like a man approaching a dragon, or worse, a girl with a grievance.

"She says you read her messages," he reported. "Also, and I quote, tell him I'm not an adversary, this isn't a duel, I just want him to understand."

Parker crossed the hallway. His mouth was dry, and his heart was doing a rhythm that would have impressed the band teacher. "I did read them. I'm sorry. I should have asked first."

"Yeah, you should have." Tenley shut her locker. "It's about boundaries. A boundary is a limit I set about what I'm comfortable with, like how people treat me, touch me, or use my stuff. My phone, my bag, my journal. You ask first, even for the time."

"So it's not that you hate me."

"It's that you crossed a line without noticing there was a line." She almost smiled. "There was a very clear line, Parker. It had, like, seventeen flags on it."

He held up both hands. "No flags crossed from now on. I'll ask before I even look at your pencil case. I'll send a formal request in writing. I'll get it notarized."

"That's a lot of paperwork for a pencil."

"I'm thorough."

Tenley laughed then, the real kind, and Subhan, who had crept closer pretending to check the lost-and-found board, gave a spontaneous round of applause that made a passing sixth grader join in for no reason at all.

"Tomorrow, bring your phone to lunch," Tenley said, slinging her backpack over one shoulder. "I'll set a password you can't guess, and we'll test whether you've really learned self-control."

"It'll be the easiest test of my life," Parker said. "Except for the time I sneezed during the fire drill."

The beach at Yellowstone Lake was nothing like the ocean beach back home, but Lily spread her towel on the gray sand anyway and dared her brother to stick a toe in the water. He yelped. She laughed. Their parents were still unloading the cooler, and her friends Maika and Rylen, whose family had come on the trip with them, were trying to salvage their sandwiches from a raiding band of gulls. "Sophisticated birds," Rylen said, shaking out a bag of chips the gulls had opened with two precise jabs. "They wait until you look away."

That night there was a campfire talk at the amphitheater, and the park ranger, Mr. Berg, walked the rows of folding chairs with a microphone asking questions. He handed out Junior Ranger badges for correct answers, and Lily wanted one badly. She had answered three questions right already, from the booklet she'd read in the car. Then Mr. Berg asked one that emptied every raised hand in the crowd. "What was the first national park in the United States, on what date did it become one, and which president signed it into law?" Her parents guessed Yosemite. Maika's parents guessed the Grand Canyon. Rylen whispered something about Abraham Lincoln. Nobody got it, and Mr. Berg moved on without telling them, which Lily thought was almost mean.

She couldn't stop turning it over on the walk back to the tent. The answer was hiding somewhere, she figured, the same way the gulls' plan had been hidden until they struck. Parks put their own history on display. That was a rule she could test. So the next morning, while everyone else slept, she took the flashlight and walked to the visitor center, which opened early, and went plaque by plaque along the stone arch outside.

The big bronze plaque near the door read like a birthday card. Established March 1, 1872. She copied it into her notebook. The park's own name was carved above the entrance, so that part was settled too, but the president was still missing. She dug the folded five-dollar bill out of her shoe, where she kept it at the beach, and smoothed it flat under the flashlight. The face on it belonged to Ulysses S. Grant. It was a guess built on a pattern, and she would have to test it out loud.

At the next campfire, Mr. Berg asked the same stumper again, and Lily's hand went up before he finished. "Yellowstone," she said. "It became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law." Mr. Berg froze with the badge halfway to her hand, then pressed it into her palm. A parliament of owls called from the pines behind the amphitheater as she sat down, and Rylen leaned over and whispered, "The five-dollar bill, wasn't it?" Lily just held the badge up so it caught the firelight.

Andrew stood on the stage in the drama room with his arms crossed, which was part of the problem. Mr. Nolan had spent two weeks teaching the class to improvise with a partner by accepting every offer with "yes, and," and Andrew still couldn't make a scene last longer than thirty seconds. Nova, his partner, would say something like, "We're lost in the woods," and Andrew would say, "Yes, and we have a map," and then the scene would just stop, like a wind-up toy that had run down.

After class he went to the school library and searched the shelf behind the biography section, where the theater books were hidden. He found a battered paperback called "Impro," written by a man named Keith Johnstone in 1979. He sat on the floor between the shelves and read the chapter about status. The book said characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama. Andrew read the sentence twice. He had never thought about a scene having levels before, like a stack of steps where somebody stood on top and somebody stood below.

He had an idea, and he wanted to test it before Friday's performance. The class had been assigned a prototype scene, a simple king and servant sketch meant to teach basic structure, and Andrew's plan was rebellious in a small way: instead of keeping the king on top the whole time, the servant would start giving orders halfway through. If the book was right, the shift would make the scene come alive. If it was wrong, he would look like an idiot in front of everyone.

On Friday, Nova played the king and sat on a chair that stood in for a throne. Andrew entered with an imaginary tray. "Your soup, Your Majesty," he said, bowing so low his knees bent.

"Yes, and it's cold," Nova said, waving him away. "Take it back."

"Good, because I seasoned it myself, and you'll eat it while I take your carriage to the market." Andrew straightened up and pointed at the door. The audience, which had been silent, started laughing. Nova blinked, then leaned forward in the throne.

"Yes, and you may take the carriage," Nova said, "but the driver obeys me."

"The driver obeys me now," Andrew said. "I gave him a raise."

The laughing got louder. Mr. Nolan, who had been writing on his clipboard, looked up and did not write anything for a moment. When the scene ended, he walked over. "That was the first time your scenes didn't cease after two lines," he said. "What changed?"

Andrew held up the paperback, its cover soft from forty years of hands. "This book says shifting status creates drama."

Nova took it and flipped to the dog-eared page. "Keith Johnstone, 1979," Nova read aloud, and tapped the paragraph. "Can I borrow it after you?"

The bleachers were half empty for the time trials, but Justin's stomach was as tight as it would be at a real meet. He had one job today: run eight hundred metres without dying in the second lap, the thing that had happened at every race since September. Mr. Nikolaidis had told them to bring a plan, and Justin's plan sat folded in his pocket like a secret.

"Remember," Fatima said, stretching beside him on the infield, "you don't have to beat Drayden today. You have to beat your old time." Drayden was already at the start line, bouncing on his toes, fast out of the blocks the way he always was. Justin had watched enough races to see a pattern in Drayden's losses too: brilliant first lap, collapse in the second. Something invisible was at work, and Justin was starting to think it could be measured.

The whistle blew. Justin hung back on purpose, letting Drayden and another boy migrate to the front while he sat third, feeling controlled, smooth, strong. Too strong, maybe. His legs felt fantastic, and the track unrolled under him so easily that he stopped counting his effort and just ran.

"Sixty-two!" Mr. Nikolaidis shouted as Justin came through the first turn of the second lap. Sixty-two. Justin's mind snagged on the number. He had planned something around seventy. He tried to remember what the coach had called the shouted time at the last meet, when a runner in the outside lane had gone out crazy fast. He hadn't asked then. He asked now, gasping as he passed the bench.

"Your split," Mr. Nikolaidis called. "One lap, sixty-two seconds."

A split was the time for one section of a race, then, one lap of it, and a runner's four-hundred-metre split showed right away whether the first lap had been faster or slower than planned. Justin's first lap had been way faster than planned. Way faster. His legs confirmed it before his brain did, flooding with heaviness exactly where the backstretch began. Drayden was ten metres ahead and wobbling, arms punching the air, slowing so visibly it looked like he was running uphill. Justin was slowing too, but less, and the gap shrank metre by metre.

He crossed the line behind Drayden and bent double, hands on knees, watching the grass blur. Fatima jogged over with her clipboard, ready to deliver her usual critique, which was blunt but fair. "You went out too hard," she said. "Sixty-two. Your plan said seventy."

"I know," Justin wheezed. "I felt great, so I forgot the plan." He straightened up and looked down the track at Drayden, who was still walking it off in small circles. Two boys, two identical mistakes, one distinct number to explain them both. "Next time," Justin said, "somebody shouts my split at the first lap, not the second. Then I can fix it while it's still fixable." He looked at Mr. Nikolaidis, who raised his stopwatch and nodded once.

Antoine spread the periodic table across the kitchen table and held it flat with two mugs, one on each corner, because the printout refused to lie still. Ms. Liu had promised a quiz tomorrow: she would name an element, and they had to give the number of protons in its atoms. Antoine had figured out that part fairly quickly. The atomic number sat right above each symbol, and the atomic number matched the proton count, so gold, number 79, meant 79 protons. That rule felt solid. The problem was the symbols themselves, which behaved like a code written by someone who wanted to confuse him personally.

The phone buzzed. Dan had sent a photo of his own printout with the message, "Iron. Timed. Go." Antoine ran his finger down the left side of the table. He found hydrogen, lithium, sodium, all making sense. He kept going, hunting for a big capital I. There was iodine, which had apparently stolen the letter, and there was iridium, but no I standing alone for iron. He checked twice, then a third time, dragging his finger so slowly it was like trying to excavate a fossil from rock with a teaspoon.

"Twenty-six," he typed. Then, before Dan could reply, he sent another message. "Wait. I guessed. I can't find iron on this thing."

"Found it," Dan wrote back a minute later. "It's Fe. My dad says it's from Latin. Ferrum. So Fe for iron."

Antoine stared at the little square. Fe, number 26. Of course it wasn't I. Of course the table would hide iron behind a language he didn't speak. He checked the atomic number anyway, because guessing had nearly fooled him once already. Twenty-six, so 26 protons, and the answer he had blurted out out of pure luck was actually right. He laughed at himself, alone in the kitchen, which felt slightly ridiculous.

Angel texted the group next: "Is anyone else finding these symbols ambiguous? K is potassium? Who decided that?" Antoine sent back a picture of the iron square with "Fe. Ferrum. Latin. Dan's dad is a legend." Then he made himself a new game. He would call out an element, Dan and Angel would answer with the proton count, and nobody could check the table until they had committed to a number. Silver caught Angel, who said 47 after a long pause and turned out to be exactly right. Tin caught Antoine, who said 22 instead of 50, and Dan typed a single crying-laughing face at him.

By ten o'clock Antoine had gone through the whole table twice, and the once-impossible squares had started to feel like characters he knew. He thought of iron as the protagonist of the metals, the one everybody leaned on, hiding behind Fe like it had a secret identity. He texted one last challenge to the group. "Fe. Protons. Five seconds." Before he even put the phone down, the screen lit up with two answers, both reading 26.

Arthur waited until the science room emptied before he unpacked the shoebox, because the multimeter inside belonged to his uncle, who had lost his repair shop in the recession and now fixed toasters in the garage. "Borrow it as long as you need," his uncle had said, which Arthur understood to mean forever, or close to it.

The science fair was in three days, and Arthur's project was a mess. He had clipped the meter to a length of copper wire, pushed current through it, and written down five pairs of numbers: voltage and current, over and over. On their own the numbers were ambiguous. Divide one pair and he got a slightly different answer from the next pair, so which was the resistance of the wire, the number everyone was supposed to report? He had tried averaging, which felt like guessing with extra steps.

Shiloh leaned over his shoulder at the lab table. "Just pick the biggest one."

"That's not a method," Arthur said. "That's a shrug with math on it."

Mr. Desir drifted past on his rounds and tapped the graph paper lying blank beside the box. "Graphs nurture better thinking than tables do," he said, and moved on before Arthur could ask what that meant.

Arthur decided to try it anyway. He drew an x-axis for current and a y-axis for voltage, then plotted all five points. Something clicked in his chest. The points fell into a nearly perfect line, and when he held his ruler up and extended the line backward, it ran straight through the origin, through zero on both axes. Every reading, all at once, was telling him one thing instead of five confusing things. He grabbed his pencil and worked the slope, the rise over the run, using two points that were far apart so his measurement would be clean. When he divided, the number matched his best pair almost exactly.

Miguel came back from washing his hands, saw the graph, and frowned at it. "So which reading wins?"

"None of them," Arthur said. "Together they win. The slope is the resistance."

Miguel squinted at the line through zero, then at the shoebox meter, then back at the line. "So your uncle's toaster shop is basically why your project works."

"Basically," Arthur said, and drew a second wire's points on the same axes, watching them climb a steeper line than the first.

Joshua set the folding table on Grandma's porch before anyone arrived, because the last meeting had fallen apart when three people talked at once and nobody could hear the vote. He had an agenda written in his grandfather's careful block letters: call to order, minutes, field trip vote, closing. When Kevin and Emerson climbed the porch steps, Joshua tapped the paper. "We follow this. One speaker at a time."

Grandpa's garage smelled like oil and cut lemons from the tree outside, and the boys dragged lawn chairs into the shade while Joshua read the agenda aloud. Kevin immediately pushed for the lake trip. "Canoes. All day. My uncle can drive." Emerson shook his head and raised his hand, which surprised Joshua, since Emerson never raised his hand. "The planetarium," Emerson said. "The new dome show is only on Saturdays, and Saturday is the one day my mom works, so she can't drive anywhere."

Both sides made sense, so Joshua called the vote. Kevin put up a hand. Emerson put up a hand. Joshua, who had planned to vote last so he wouldn't push anyone, looked down at his own hand and froze. "If I vote for the lake, it's two to one and we go to the lake."

"No," Emerson said, leaning forward. "You're the chair. If you vote, it's two to two." He said it flat, like a door closing. Joshua had read a chapter of Grandpa's old club handbook, the one with the cracked spine, and now he flipped through it fast, pages whispering. There it was, under motions and votes. He read the line twice under his breath.

"A tie vote means the motion fails," Joshua said. He emphasized the last word, and the porch went quiet except for a wasp ticking against the screen door. "It hasn't won more than half the votes cast, so it just doesn't pass. That's the rule." Kevin slumped. "So no lake?" "And no planetarium," Emerson said, which was an abrupt end to a whole afternoon of arguing, and both of them stared at Joshua like he had made it up.

Joshua thought about it, testing the idea against what he'd read. The rule wasn't the problem. The rule was just telling them something they already knew but hadn't said out loud. He picked up his pencil. "New motion. We table the trip vote until next meeting, and before then we ask the planetarium if they do weekday shows for groups." Kevin sat up. Emerson drummed his fingers on the chair arm, then nodded once. "Write it in the minutes," he said. Joshua wrote it, and the pencil scratched a small, steady line across the page.

On Thursday afternoon, Quinn sat at the upright piano in the music classroom and missed the same six notes for the eleventh time. The passage sat in the middle of her recital piece, a quick run that crossed her left hand over her right, and every time she reached it her fingers bunched up like dropped spaghetti. Ty leaned on the piano from the other side, watching. "You're slowing down right before it," he said. "Maybe stop being scared of it." Cassandra, who was waiting for her turn on the xylophone, was skeptical. "That's not it. She slows down because her hands don't know it yet. Watching harder won't fix that."

Ms. Whitehead came over and told Ty his bus would leave without him if he didn't commute to the gym for practice, so he left, but before he went he said, "Don't practice all night. Sleep on it." Quinn stayed another twenty minutes. She played the run slowly, then faster, then got it wrong, then got it wrong again, then packed up and went home with her practice sheet pressed flat in her bag.

That evening she did not touch the piano. She thought about Ty's advice and decided to test it, since her usual method, repeating the passage until her hands ached, had produced nothing all week. She ate dinner, read two chapters of a book about weather anomalies, and went to bed at nine. Lying in the dark, she felt the shape of the six notes in her fingers without moving them, then fell asleep.

On Friday morning the music classroom was open early, and Cassandra was already there tuning the xylophone. Quinn took the same bench, set the practice sheet on the stand, and played the passage straight through. Her left hand crossed over her right and landed on the exact keys, clean, twice, three times in a row. Cassandra put down her mallet and stared. "When did you practice that?"

"I didn't," Quinn said. "Not after Thursday. I slept on it, like Ty said. A night of sleep after practicing a sequence like this can make it better the next day without any extra practice." She said it plainly, the way she had read it in the science magazine at her dentist's office, because Cassandra was already frowning.

"That's an anomaly," Cassandra said.

"It happened, though. Watch." Quinn set her hands on the keys and played the six notes again, faster this time, and this time she did not slow down at all.

The living room was so packed that Addison had to sit on an overturned laundry basket, and the smell of her father's chili had begun to saturate every corner of the house. On the screen, two teams walked out onto the pitch for the final, and that was when the argument started.

"Brazil," said her uncle, pointing his spoon at the television. "Brazil won the first World Cup. Everyone knows that."

"Argentina," said Braylon, who had come over with a bowl of popcorn and a lot of confidence. "My grandfather told me. Argentina, all the way back."

Addison frowned. Something about both answers bothered her, though she couldn't have said why at first. She kept thinking while the announcer's voice filled the room, and then it clicked: nobody had actually named the country that hosted the very first tournament. Hosting and winning weren't necessarily the same thing, but if she could find out who hosted it, she'd be closer to the truth. She raised her hand like she was in Ms. Boateng's class and said, "Does anyone know where the first one was even played?"

"Europe somewhere," her uncle said vaguely.

The wifi was out because of the storm, so the plumbing of the internet, as her mother called the router in the hall closet, was useless. Addison went to the basement instead, where the family's old encyclopedias lived on sagging shelves. Carina followed her with a flashlight. "You really think it's down here?" Carina asked.

"It's a temporary blackout, not the end of information," Addison said, and pulled the volume with the right letter off the shelf. They knelt on the cold concrete floor and turned the thin pages until Carina sat back on her heels and read aloud: "First World Cup, 1930. Hosted and won by Uruguay, who beat Argentina four goals to two in the final."

They ran upstairs. "Uruguay," Addison announced, holding the book above her head like a trophy. "The first World Cup was in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina four to two."

Braylon stared at her. "My grandfather is going to be so upset."

"He can take it up with the encyclopedia," Addison said.

At halftime, her uncle slid the book toward himself and read the page twice, his lips moving. Then he closed it gently, stood up, and unclipped the spare key from his keyring. "Temporary custody," he said, laying the key in Addison's palm. "The trailer has the rest of the set. Go get the S through Z before your mother donates them."

Carina was already grabbing the flashlight.

Grandpa's kitchen smelled like sawdust and lemon dish soap, because the downstairs bathroom was being renovated and everyone had to wash up at the sink by the back door. Evan spread his science kit across the counter: a stack of litmus paper, a chart of the pH scale, and five little jars he'd brought in his backpack.

"Ms. Krause said we have to test real things, not just stuff from the lab," Evan said. "So I'm testing everything in this house."

Lee pulled a bottle of vinegar from the pantry. Yazan found baking soda under the sink and grinned. "These two are going to fight each other. I've seen my mom do it."

Evan tore a strip of litmus paper in half and dipped one piece into a cup of vinegar mixed with water. The paper turned red. He checked the chart. "Three," he said. "Acid. Now the baking soda." He stirred a pinch of it into a fresh cup and dipped the other strip. It turned blue. He lined the two papers up on the counter like evidence.

"Try the soap," Lee said, nodding at the pink bar in the dish by the tap. "My grandpa swears by that stuff. Says his hands are a chronic mess from the machine shop and it's the only soap that cleans them."

Evan held the bar under the running water, worked up a puddle of suds in a cup, and dipped a fresh strip. He waited. The paper turned blue, a deeper blue than the baking soda had given him.

"That's weird," Evan said. "Soap should be neutral. It's just soap."

"Test it again," Yazan said.

"I tested it. Look." He laid the strip beside the others and measured it against the chart. "Nine. Maybe ten." He counted the boxes between the vinegar's three and the soap's nine, six whole squares on the scale, on the opposite side from the acid. "Most bar soaps are basic, around nine or ten," he said slowly, reading it off the chart's fine print. "This one's right there."

"So the stuff you wash with is on the base side of the scale," Lee said.

"Opposite from vinegar." Evan wrote it in his notebook, then looked up. "Grandpa!" he called toward the living room. "Your soap is a base!"

His grandfather appeared in the doorway with a cookie in one hand. "It's a what?"

"A base. Like the opposite of vinegar. Look." Evan held up the blue strip next to the red one. Grandpa leaned over the counter, squinting, and crumbs fell onto the pH chart.

"Huh," Grandpa said. "All these years." He went back to his chair, and Evan heard him tell someone on the phone, "The boy says my soap's a base."

Yazan was already eyeing the fish tank in the hall. "Can we test that next? There might be larva in the water from those plants."

Evan tore off three more strips and followed him.

Rose stood at the low stone wall of the war memorial, her notes flapping in the wind, and tried to say her presentation out loud for the fourth time. "The Treaty of Versailles," she began, "punished Germany after the First World War, and the Rhineland was supposed to stay demilitarized." That was as far as she got before her own voice faded. She could recite the facts, but she could not yet explain how a treaty signed in 1919 helped lead to a second war. It felt like tracing a river underground. She knew where it started and where it ended, but the part in between was hidden.

She tried again, walking slowly along the wall of carved names. "In March 1936," she said, "Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles." She paused by a name worn almost smooth. "And Britain and France did not use force to stop him." That part she could say perfectly. What she could not answer was Mr. Hernández's question from class, the one he had written on the board in his cramped handwriting: so what?

Behind her, Paul and Manraj were supposed to be copying names for their own assignment. Paul, though, had climbed onto the base of the memorial to rub a chalk impression of a name, even though the sign by the gate said clearly not to touch the stone. Mr. Hernández, who was helping another student across the lawn, didn't notice. Paul jumped down, grinning. "See? Nobody said anything."

"Because he didn't see you," Manraj said. "That's not the same as it being fine."

Rose watched Paul study the sign, then study Mr. Hernández's turned back, and she felt something click, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. A rule broken once, with no consequence, and now Paul was looking at the memorial's tall centrepiece, the one fenced off completely, and testing whether he could get away with more.

"Try it and Mr. Hernández will actually do something this time," Rose said. "You're not negotiating with a sign. You're negotiating with whether he acts."

"Feasible, though," Paul said, one hand on the fence. "I could get up there."

"That's not the point." Rose came closer, and the idea she had been chasing all morning finally lined itself up. What if 1936 worked the same way? Not the treaty itself, she thought, but what happened after it was broken. The treaty drew a line, and then the line got crossed, and the people who could have stopped it did not use force. She could distinguish between the rule and the response to the rule, and that was exactly the difference her presentation needed. The punishment in the treaty wasn't the whole story. What mattered was what the other countries did when it was broken.

She flipped her notes over and wrote on the blank back of the page, fast, while the sentences were still hot: the line was crossed in March 1936, and when crossing it cost nothing, the next crossing became thinkable. Paul was already halfway up the fence when Mr. Hernández's voice cracked across the lawn like a whip.

"Down. Now." Paul slid back to the grass, ears red, and Rose capped her pen. She walked to the gate with her notes against her chest and read the new paragraph once more. "So that's the so what," she said to Manraj, and pointed back at Paul, who was still apologizing. "Watch him. Now he'll never try the fence again. Now imagine nobody had said anything."

The computer lab at Camp Lac des Pins smelled of pine and warm keyboards, and Maeva had claimed the seat by the window because the afternoon light made the screen easier to read. Her Python program was almost done. It asked for a number, tested whether anything divided it, and printed PRIME or NOT PRIME. She had been at it for three days, and today she wanted to finish before the swimming block so she could show Matthieu.

Rachel leaned over from the next computer, her own program still a blank file. "Type in a one," she said. "Test the weird cases first. That's what my sister does."

Maeva typed 1 and pressed Enter. The screen said PRIME. She frowned, because the little knot in her stomach said otherwise. She waved Matthieu over anyway, since he had promised to try her program, and he typed 7, then 9, then 100, and the answers all looked right. Then Mr. Jean-Louis, the activity leader, stopped behind them with his mug of coffee and peered at the screen through his transparent glasses, which fogged slightly at the edges.

"Try one," he said.

Matthieu typed it. PRIME. "See, it works," he said, but Mr. Jean-Louis only raised an eyebrow and waited, the way he did when he wanted campers to excavate the answer themselves instead of handing it to them. Maeva stared at the screen. She knew her loop checked divisors from 2 upward, so of course nothing divided 1, and the program called it prime. But something nagged at her. She grabbed the scrap paper by the keyboard and wrote out small numbers as products: 6 is 2 times 3, 12 is 2 times 2 times 3, 8 is 2 times 2 times 2. Every one had its own building blocks. Then she tried to write 1 that way and got nothing but a bare, lonely 1.

"Oh," she said. "One is not a prime number. Mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." She said it slowly, testing it as she went, and Mr. Jean-Louis nodded once and drifted off toward the canoe group. Maeva felt her cheeks go warm with a flash of embarrassment at her mistake, but Rachel was already grinning at her, and that made it easier.

"Your turn is coming," Maeva told her, adding the fix to her program, one line that turned 1 away at the door before the loop even began. She saved the file, spun her chair toward Rachel's blank screen, and dragged it closer. "Okay. First word of the day: print."

The community centre piano room smelled of floor polish and old coffee, and the radiator by the window ticked like a slow metronome. Noemie spread her new sheet music on the stand, a short piece by a composer she had never heard of, printed with Italian words scattered between the staves. Her friend Aniya leaned over her shoulder, tapping one of them with a chipped fingernail.

"Andante," Aniya read. "That one's got to be fast, right? It sounds fast. Like running."

Noemie wasn't so sure. The word sat over a row of long, unhurried notes, half notes and whole notes, the kind you couldn't rush even if you tried. "Maybe it means something else," she said slowly. "There's a guy who plays here on Saturdays. He had a tote bag once with all these words printed on it."

Aniya rolled her eyes. "We're not going to interrogate a stranger about his tote bag."

They were saved from that particular controversy by Mr. Ong, who ran the Tuesday evening keyboard group and was stacking chairs in the corner. He wasn't a piano teacher exactly, more the person who kept the room booked and the radiator from flooding, but Noemie had seen him humming along when she practiced, so she raised her hand anyway.

"Mr. Ong, do you know what andante means? I think it might mean walking speed, but Aniya thinks fast." She had guessed it from the notes themselves, the way they strolled instead of sprinted, like someone crossing the community centre lobby without hurry.

Mr. Ong set down a chair. "Andante, a walking pace," he said. "Largo is very slow. Allegro is fast and lively." Then he went back to his chairs, offering nothing more, which was his way.

Noemie slid onto the bench. She played the opening, which was marked largo, and let each note sink into the room like a stone into still water. When andante arrived, she imagined her feet on the linoleum hallway outside, steady, unhurried, and the melody picked itself up and walked with her. Then the page turned and allegro flashed at the top, and her fingers had to leap, light and quick, like they'd been pollinated by something that made them suddenly busy.

Aniya had been right about one thing, sort of. "Okay," she admitted, from her seat on the radiator, "I would have played that walking part like a racehorse. The whole piece would have fallen apart by bar eight."

"It would have," Noemie agreed, "because you'd have been at allegro speed during andante." She played the passage again, this time shaping it even more, soft in the largo, fuller where the notes clustered lush and close together in the middle section, bright and skipping at the allegro. The room held the sound the way the window held the last of the evening light.

Mr. Ong stopped stacking chairs. He stood near the doorway with the last chair still in his hands, listening.

"You know," he said, "we could use a keyboard for the spring concert. Saturday mornings."

Noemie looked at the music on the stand, at all those Italian words she could now read like a map. "I'll be here," she said, and turned back to the first page, hands ready over the keys.

Isabelle pressed her eye to the microscope at the museum's wet lab station and saw nothing but a pale gray blur. Behind her, Jannah was already sketching her slide, and the worksheet in Isabelle's pocket had three empty labels waiting: cell wall, membrane, nucleus. The class had forty minutes before the bus left, and Ms. Rahimi had made it clear that a finished worksheet was the price of the trip counting for science credit. A legitimate excuse, like a broken scope, might earn mercy, but nobody was going to believe a blur.

She twisted the coarse focus one way, then the other, slow as turning a safe dial. On the third try the blur sharpened into a lattice, rows of brick-shaped cells fitting edge to edge like a honeycomb flattened by a thumb. Isabelle blinked. The cells had been there the whole time, hidden inside an ordinary onion, waiting under a square of glass no bigger than a stamp.

"That's the cell wall," Jannah said, leaning over from the next stool. "The thick outer lines. The membrane's the skinny line hugging inside it." Isabelle copied the labels, then stopped at the dark dot floating in each cell. "And that's the nucleus," Charli said from across the bench. "That dark spot." Isabelle squinted at it. Somebody had to be the first person ever to notice that spot, she thought, back when nobody knew what a cell even was. She raised her hand. "Ms. Rahimi, do you know who first saw the nucleus?"

"Robert Brown," Ms. Rahimi said. "A Scottish botanist. He described the cell nucleus in 1831, while he was studying orchid cells." Isabelle wrote it in the margin of her worksheet. Charli leaned over to read it and frowned. "No way. People couldn't even see germs back then, so how did they figure out what caused infections? I thought all this stuff was modern." Isabelle tapped the margin with her pencil. "They didn't know about germs, that's the point. Brown saw the spot before anybody knew what it did. It took a whole lot longer, like a century, before doctors had an antibiotic to cure infections." Charli chewed her lip, looking from the margin to her own slide. "Huh. I guess you can find a thing long before you understand it." She crossed out something in her notes and started over.

Isabelle went back to her microscope, wanting to excavate every detail before the clock ran out, the faint membrane line, the nucleus like a small dark moon in each cell. But when she reached for the fine focus, her sleeve caught the stage and the slide skidded sideways. The image collapsed into blur again. Ms. Rahimi called five minutes from the doorway, and there was no time to re-center it properly. Isabelle got the wall back, just barely, and traced a shaky line where the membrane should be, but the nucleus had drifted to the edge of the field, half swallowed by shadow. She labeled it anyway, arrow pointing at the half-visible dot, and slid the worksheet into her folder as the lights over the benches clicked off.

On the bus, Jannah passed her a perfect drawing of all three labels, offering to let her copy it. Isabelle looked at it for a long moment, then handed it back. "Mine's a mess," she said, "but it's my mess. And I got the margin note." She turned to the window, where the museum was shrinking behind the trees. "Robert Brown, orchids, 1831," she said quietly, like a spell she didn't want to forget.

Alexandra stood in the humid kitchen with her speech cards fanned across the counter, rehearsing for the fourth time. On Monday she had to give a five-minute talk in front of her whole history class, and Mr. Moretti had asked for two volunteers to be candidates for the regional speech contest. She had raised her hand before she thought it through, and now her heart hammered every time she pictured the room.

Courtney came through the back door with Nyla behind her, both of them still carrying their gym bags. "You look like you're about to be sick," Courtney said, dropping her bag on a chair.

"I'm fine," Alexandra said, which was obviously not true. Her hands were shaking enough that the cards rattled.

Nyla picked up one of the cards and read it. "You've got anxiety written in the margin. Twice."

"That's my mom's word. She's been saying I need coping skills, not just more practice runs in the kitchen." Alexandra squared the cards. "But she's at work and I don't actually have any."

Nyla sat down. "My brother's a goalie. He does this thing before penalty shots. He breathes out slow, longer than the breath in, like he's fogging a window with one long stream. He says everybody on his team does it before a stressful moment because slow breathing with long exhales calms the body's stress response. It's the most boring trick in the world and it works."

Alexandra tried it right there. In for three counts, out until her lungs felt empty, the kitchen air warm and damp around her. After the fourth exhale her hands had stopped rattling the cards. She read the opening line and her voice came out level.

"Okay," Courtney said. "Now set a boundary with yourself. One more run-through, then you stop for the night. My mom says rehearsing past midnight just makes it worse."

"One more," Alexandra agreed. She set the timer on the stove, breathed out slow and long, and started at the top. When she finished, Nyla was holding up a score card made from a napkin that said ten, and Alexandra laughed and dealt the cards onto the counter like a magician.

"Monday," she said, and exhaled again, slow and long.

At dinner, Sadie set her notebook next to her plate and pushed the green beans around with her fork. Tomorrow morning she had to hand in her survey project for Mr. Flores, and right now it was wrong.

"Smells good," she said, mostly to herself. Her mother had made the spicy noodle casserole from the box labeled with the school logo, the same snack the cafeteria was considering adding next month. Sadie had surveyed three people: Sami, Kate, and her older brother. All three loved it. She had written her conclusion in bold letters: "Everyone loves this snack."

Her dad spooned a second helping onto his plate. "Two people at my office tried it today," he said. "One spit it into a napkin."

Sadie put down her fork. Three out of three loved it, but one out of two hated it. The numbers were pointing in opposite directions. She flipped to her results page and stared at her three tally marks. Then she remembered Kate saying something at lunch about Mr. Flores's class survey, the big one taken during first period.

"Can I use the phone?" she asked, already reaching for it. She texted Sami: "Did you do Flores's class survey about the noodle thing?" The answer came back a minute later with a photo of the results sheet. Two hundred students had answered. One hundred and eighteen said "okay," forty-one said "love it," and the rest said "no."

Sadie ran the numbers twice. In two hundred people, "love it" was the smallest group. Her survey of three had made it look like everyone. She picked up her pencil, crossed out her bold conclusion, and started writing new lines: a claim about what people think needs tested evidence, and a story about three friends tasting something is not that. Three people can all happen to love it, she wrote, but in two hundred the differences even out.

She paused over the word "evidence," then circled it. Her claim would be: "Most students think this snack is just okay." The big survey was her evidence, and she could quantify exactly how it backed her up. Her brother's glowing review now looked ambiguous, one voice that could mean anything.

"Bed by ten," her mom said, clearing plates. "Deadline's at eight-thirty, not midnight."

"I know." Sadie copied the results onto a fresh page. Her dad, a veteran of twenty years of Friday-night office snack orders, leaned over her shoulder.

"Two hundred answers beat three," he said.

"That's the whole point," Sadie said, and stapled the pages together.

Mason had promised Mr. Hughes he would stay after class on Tuesday, and it was Tuesday, so he stopped in the doorway of the empty science room while the humid air from the hallway pushed past him like it wanted out too.

"You failed the elements quiz," Mr. Hughes said, sliding a paper across the desk. "But you're not stupid, Mason. You just quit halfway through."

Mason looked at the red marks. He had guessed every question that mentioned protons. "I didn't quit. I just don't get what the numbers are even for."

"Then get it." Mr. Hughes stood up and pulled a folded poster from his cabinet, one giant grid crammed with boxes and letters. He spread it on the table. "Homework. Pick any object in your house, find what it's made of on here, tell me tomorrow." He tapped the top corner of one box. "Start with what the box tells you."

That evening Mason sat at the kitchen table with the poster propped against the sugar bowl, tracing boxes with his pencil. Above each box sat a number. Carbon had a six. Oxygen, an eight. Gold, a startling seventy-nine. His phone buzzed: a message from Ezekiel, "did u figure the quiz out." Mason typed back, "working on it," which felt like a lie, because he was mostly staring.

Then he turned his pencil over and read the tiny label on the side. Graphite. He knew graphite was carbon; everyone knew that, it was practically the first thing anyone learned about pencils. He hunted the poster until he found the C box again, with its six at the top. Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus. That was what the small print under the number said. He read it three times. The number at the top, the atomic number, wasn't decoration. It told you the protons.

He needed to be sure. He grabbed his mom's copper-bottomed pot from the stove and found copper on the poster, twenty-nine. So every copper atom had twenty-nine protons, all of them, every single atom in the pot. It was strange and a little thrilling, like holding a secret count of invisible things. He texted Ezekiel: "pencil = carbon. atomic number 6. six protons. copper pot = 29. I think the top number IS the protons." Ezekiel replied with a row of exclamation points and then, "wait does that mean my braces??"

Mason laughed and looked up titanium himself: twenty-two.

The next afternoon he walked into Mr. Hughes's room carrying the pencil and the pot, which was heavy and absurd and exactly why he'd brought it. He set both on the desk. "Pencil lead is carbon. Atomic number six. Every carbon atom in it has six protons in its nucleus." He slid the pot forward. "And this is copper, twenty-nine."

Mr. Hughes picked up the pencil and turned it slowly, letting the light refract off the painted yellow surface. "Retake Friday?"

"Retake Friday," Mason said, and carried the pot back out like a trophy.

Juliette was at her desk with the computer glowing in the dark room when she took the dares thread a step too far. Adam had written, "post a video of yourself singing the school song in your frog hat," and she had been the one to say yes. She filmed it, uploaded it, and sat back feeling brave and hilarious all at once.

Then ten minutes passed, and the brave feeling curdled. She imagined Moses seeing it. She imagined the whole eighth grade seeing it. Her fingers moved fast, and she deleted the post. The page went clean, just her old photos of the science fair, where she had used a prism to split the hallway lamp into a rainbow for her project on light. Gone, she told herself. It was up for ten minutes, that was all.

The next morning her phone buzzed and buzzed again. In the class group chat, Adam had posted the frog hat video. "Blink and you missed it," he wrote, "except I didn't." Moses replied with a row of crying-laughing faces. Juliette stared at the screen on the bus, her stomach dropping through the floor. She had deleted it. She checked her page again from her phone, and it was still gone, still clean, and yet there it was in the chat, whole and looping, her voice cracking on the second verse.

She tested it, because she needed to be sure it wasn't some trick of the app. At home that evening she posted a photo of her desk, waited two minutes, and deleted it. Then she messaged the photo to Adam directly and asked him to save it before she removed it. "Already did," he wrote back. After the deletion, he sent her the file again. Her page showed nothing. His chat showed everything. So that was the rule, and nobody had ever told her: deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.

She thought about Ms. Cruz, who had once kept a jar of dead bees on the windowsill and explained how insects pollinate the flowers along the fence, how one small visit spreads pollen everywhere without the flower ever seeing where it goes. Juliette had thought that was just science. Now it felt like a description of her frog hat, drifting from phone to phone, landing who knew where. Strangers could have it. She could not see them, and they could see her.

She wrote a message to Adam that was long and angry, and she deleted that too, remembering just in time. Then she wrote a short one. "Not funny. Please take it down." She watched the three dots appear.

"It's already everywhere," Adam wrote. "Moses sent it to the soccer group. I can delete mine, though."

Juliette leaned back and looked at her clean page, at the photo of the prism throwing its quiet rainbow, and wondered which version of herself was the real one out there: the girl who had dared, or the girl who had tried to take it back. Adam's message said, "Done. Deleted it. For real this time." She typed, "It's still not gone, is it," and pressed send.

Caleb had been playing the piano for four years, but nothing had prepared him for the twelve-bar blues sheet Mr. Perera had handed out at the community centre on Tuesday. The chords were simple enough, just three of them looping around and around, and Mr. Perera wanted each of them to improvise a solo over the loop by Friday. Caleb cherished challenges like this, the kind you could grind at until something clicked, but every time he tried, his solo sounded like a robot reading a grocery list. The notes were right. That was the sinister part. Right notes, wrong everything else.

"You sound like a metronome," said Sylas, who played trumpet and had no sympathy whatsoever. He leaned against the community centre's battered upright piano while Saif nodded from the drum throne he had claimed even though he didn't play drums. "Mr. Perera's demo sounded nothing like that."

"That's because Mr. Perera is good," Caleb said, and played the loop again, stiff as ever.

Saif started tapping his foot along with Caleb's playing, then stopped, then started again, frowning. "Wait. Play the melody line again, just the melody." Caleb played it. Saif shook his head. "When Mr. Perera played it, the notes were uneven. Like, the first of each pair hung around longer, and the second one hurried to catch up."

Caleb's hands paused over the keys. Uneven. He thought about the recording on the community centre's old laptop, the one Mr. Perera had played of a woman singing the blues. He'd assumed the piano was just... vibrating, or something. But what if the unevenness was the whole point? He tried it: played each pair of eighth notes long-short, long-short, letting the first note stretch like taffy and snapping the second one quick.

Sylas actually stood up straight. "There it is!" He pointed at Caleb with his trumpet like a sword. "Do that again."

Caleb did it again, and then, heart pounding, he launched into his solo over the twelve-bar loop with the lopsided feel underneath. The same wrong-right notes from Tuesday now slunk and swung, bending toward something that sounded, unmistakably, like the blues. Saif had found a pair of drumsticks in the lost-and-found bin and was clicking them on the piano frame in the same crooked pattern, grinning like a maniac.

Mr. Perera poked his head in from the hallway, one eyebrow up. "Somebody's found the shuffle rhythm," he said.

"Is that what it's called?" Caleb asked.

"That's what it's called," said Mr. Perera, and disappeared back toward the gym.

Caleb played the loop once more, all the way through, feeling each pair of notes lean long-short, long-short, and Sylas lifted his trumpet to try a solo of his own.

Ayah's kitchen had been turned into a café, complete with a hand-lettered chalkboard menu and napkins folded into triangles. "Le Café d'Ayah," Ivy read aloud, "open for one customer only, which is me." Ayah's father had made omelettes, so real food sat under the warming light while the two of them practiced, because on Friday their French class was taking over the school cafeteria and Ms. Owusu would only respond to students who ordered in French. Ivy wanted the crepe station more than anything, and she intended to get through the whole line without freezing.

"Bonjour," Ayah said from behind the counter, sliding into her waiter voice. "Qu'est-ce que vous désirez?" Ivy managed the order part quickly; she had drilled it all week. "Je voudrais une crêpe au fromage, s'il vous plaît. Combien ça coûte?" Ayah told her the price, and Ivy counted out buttons from a jar they'd decided were euros. That was when it all fell apart, because Ivy had no idea how to ask for the bill. She tried "La note, s'il vous plaît," and Ayah's eyebrows went up. "That means like a grade, or a note you pass in class. A waiter would look at you funny." Ivy tried "la facture," and Ayah shook her head again. "That's the word on an electricity bill. Not this."

Ivy stared at the chalkboard, frustrated. Somewhere in the back of her notebook she remembered a page she'd skimmed and thought she'd never need, the restaurant vocabulary list from October. She flipped through it, past all the food words, and there it was. "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," she read slowly. "It means 'the bill, please.'" Ayah grinned and wrote it on the chalkboard in big letters, right under the prices.

They ran the scene again, and this time the whole thing felt different. Ivy ordered, asked the price, and finished with "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," and Ayah presented a napkin with the buttons counted out on it, bowing like a waiter in a movie. Ivy thought about how she'd nearly skipped that vocabulary page because it seemed boring at the time, and she wondered what else she'd skipped that might matter later. She couldn't decide whether she was lazy or just human, and she left the question alone.

"My dad says French is versatile," Ayah said, stacking plates. "You can use it in Senegal, Belgium, Haiti, half of Africa." She flicked the towel toward Ivy. "He's proud of his heritage, so he advocates for us learning it even when we complain." Ivy laughed and pocketed a button as a souvenir. "Then tomorrow I'm advocating for the crepe line moving faster." Ayah pointed at the chalkboard. "Only if you remember the magic words." Ivy stood, squared her shoulders, and said it perfectly: "L'addition, s'il vous plaît."

Muhammad set the microscope on the picnic table in the backyard, careful to keep it in the shade of the umbrella so the sun wouldn't glare through the lens. Ms. Rivera, his neighbour and a retired lab technician, had lent it to him for the weekend along with a box of slides, a bottle of stain, and a note that read, in her neat handwriting, "Onions are patient teachers." His friend Jad had already claimed the second chair, and Marilyn sat cross-legged on the grass with a purple onion in her lap like a small cannonball.

"Ms. Rivera says we have to see the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus," Muhammad said, unfolding the diagram she had photocopied for him. "And label all three."

Jad peeled a layer of skin off the onion while Muhammad fetched a cup of water from the kitchen. His mother was at the doctor's getting a prescription refilled, so the backyard belonged entirely to the three of them and the wasp that kept circling the lemonade. Marilyn laid the thin slice of skin on the slide with tweezers, added a drop of stain, and then lowered the coverslip flat, straight down, like a lid on a pot.

Under the lowest magnification, the field of view filled with round shapes, dark-ringed and scattered everywhere. "Those are the cells," Marilyn said, turning the fine focus. "Look, they're everywhere. That was easy."

Muhammad leaned in and looked for a long moment. Something bothered him. The shapes had no edges that met, no neat rows like the diagram, and each one was a perfect circle with a thick black ring. "Cells have straight sides in the picture," he said slowly. "These are round. And they're all different sizes, even in the same spot." He straightened up. "I don't think those are cells. I think they're bubbles. Air bubbles."

Marilyn lifted the coverslip off, tilted the slide toward the light, and squinted. "Then where are the cells?"

"Under the bubbles, maybe. Or squished somewhere." Muhammad thought about the coverslip. When Marilyn had dropped it flat, it must have trapped air underneath. He looked at the next blank slide, then picked up the tweezers with a fresh piece of onion skin. "Let's try putting it down at an angle, one edge first, and lowering it slowly."

Jad supervised the drop of stain, holding the dropper steady while Muhammad touched the edge of the coverslip to the liquid and let it fall in a slow hinge. "Keep going," Jad said. "Nice and easy." Muhammad lowered it until it lay flat, and not one circle rose up under the glass.

Marilyn looked first. She was quiet for a second, then said, "Muhammad. Come look."

The field of view was full of rectangles, brick-shaped and fitted together in tidy rows, each with a darker outline. Muhammad turned to the higher magnification and focused until a small dense spot appeared near the centre of one cell. "That's the nucleus," he said. "And the dark outline is the wall. The membrane is right inside it, thin, like a second edge." He pulled the diagram close and printed the three labels in pencil beside his drawing, then drew a fourth label with an arrow pointing at nothing: "bubbles, gone."

Ms. Rivera came out to take back her lemonade pitcher that evening and peered through the eyepiece. She was quiet in her neutral, careful way, and then she said, "Brick wall. Textbook quality."

"Angle first," Muhammad told her, holding up the slide. "One edge, then down slow."

The desks in Ms. Andersen's room had been pushed into a horseshoe, and in the middle, draped with a paper tablecloth, sat the "restaurante." Charles had a real reason to care about this practice. His family was spending spring break at his aunt's house in Mexico City, and he had promised himself he would order his own food there, in Spanish, without pointing at the menu like a little kid.

Alayna played the waitress first, holding a notepad and looking far too pleased about it. Charles cleared his throat. "Quiero un taco de pollo," he said. "Y, uh, cuanto cuesta?" Alayna told him the price in quick Spanish that he mostly missed, but he caught "veinte" and nodded like he'd understood all of it. Leanne, sitting beside him, snorted. "You just agreed to pay whatever she said."

Then came the real test. Charles had a debate meet right after school that day, and he needed to eat on the bus, so his order had to travel. He asked for his taco and a lemonade, and Alayna walked away and came back with everything arranged on an actual ceramic plate, complete with a cloth napkin folded like a swan. "You're supposed to say the magic words," she said, tapping the plate. "Otherwise they think you're staying."

Charles stared at the plate and turned the problem over in his mind. He'd noticed something earlier, when Leanne ordered: she had added two words, and her food had come wrapped in foil. The words revolved through his memory until they lined up. "Para llevar," he said slowly, testing each syllable. Leanne grinned and mimed walking away with a bag. "Para llevar," she confirmed. "To take away. That's the phrase."

He tried again from the top, more smoothly this time. "Quiero un taco de pollo, para llevar, por favor. Cuanto cuesta?" Alayna scribbled on her notepad and vanished behind the bookshelf that served as the kitchen. She returned with a foil packet and a paper cup with a lid, and even though it was all pretend, Charles felt his shoulders drop. It had worked.

"That's basically how you survive my abuela's kitchen," Leanne said, "except hers is an invasive level of feeding. You say you're full and she brings a second plate." Charles laughed. "Then I'll say para llevar and be the one carnivore who takes his tacos on the road." He copied the phrase onto his hand in pen, because the bus left in an hour and he had a lunch line to face, one that revolved around exactly this question: staying or going. He slid his foil packet into his backpack and headed for the door.

The rink smelled like cold rubber and popcorn, and Olivia had checked her phone four times since Julian texted that he was parking. Abygaelle had insisted on coming too, "just for ten minutes, so it's not weird," but ten minutes had turned into forty, and she was still circling the ice like a random satellite.

"You could just confess that you're nervous," Abygaelle said, leaning on the boards beside her. "It's not against the law."

"I'm not nervous. My hands are cold. That's different."

It wasn't different. Julian was laughing with the skate rental guy, and every time Olivia looked at him her stomach did something she could only describe as voltage, a live wire jumping under her ribs.

They skated two slow laps, and then he took her hand to steady her around the corner, and that part was easy. She liked it. She'd imagined it all week, actually, the exact weight of his glove against hers. They raced Abygaelle to the far end and lost. They split a pretzel. When the Zamboni came out, they sat on the benches with their skates dangling, and Julian's shoulder touched hers, and neither of them moved away.

Then the lights flickered toward closing time, and Julian stood and held out his arms for a hug. Olivia had wanted this all day. But he was grinning at Abygaelle too, and his friends from math class were shoving through the exit doors right behind them, already looking, and suddenly she didn't want an audience for it.

She stepped back. "Not here."

Julian's arms dropped. For a second his face went flat, and Olivia braced for him to push, to say come on, to lean in anyway the way boys did in the shows she wasn't supposed to watch.

Instead he said, "Okay. Another time, then, when it's just us."

"Really?"

"You said no. That's kind of the whole deal." He shrugged and picked up his skate bag. "Either of us can say no to that stuff, any time, and the other person just deals with it. You didn't know that?"

Olivia realized she had known it, somewhere in the back of her head, but she had never once seen anyone actually do it. She had always pictured saying no as the beginning of an argument, not the end of one.

Outside, the cold hit their faces, and Abygaelle caught up with her scarf flapping. "So that went terrible, right? You hugged, he freaked?"

"We didn't hug. I said no, and he just... accepted it."

Abygaelle stopped on the sidewalk. "Wait. You turned down Julian Kim?"

Olivia pulled her hat down over her ears and started walking. "Text me tomorrow. I have a date to finish planning."

Jayden crouched beside the creek with a plastic bag, peeling the papery skin off a wild onion Luis had spotted near the trail. "One layer," Mr. Çelik had told them, "the thinnest one you can pull off whole." If the layer was too thick, the microscope in Jayden's backpack would show nothing but a brown smudge, and tomorrow's lab report, with its three labeled parts, would be blank.

"Got it!" Jayden held up a piece of skin so thin he could see the shadow of his fingers through it. Braxton, who had already found a rotting cork fragment washed down by the erosion on the bank slope, waved it in the air. "Mr. Çelik says mine might work too. Old cork, thin slice, same idea."

Back at the wooden picnic table at the trailhead, Jayden laid the skin on a slide, added one drop of water, and pressed the cover glass down. He leaned into the eyepiece. At first there was only a gray fog, and his stomach dropped. Then he turned the fine focus, one tiny click at a time, and the fog snapped into a grid, rows and rows of neat little boxes like a brick wall stretching off the edge of the view.

"Look, look!" Braxton shoved in, and Jayden pulled out the diagram folded in his pocket, the drawing of cork he'd photographed from the science museum wall last summer.
