"In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team," he read slowly. "It was the first time any professional athlete was honored that way."

"Wait, so no player in the whole league can ever wear it again?" Cian asked.

"Not on any team," Elijah said. "That's why we couldn't find it. It's not that nobody picked it. Nobody's allowed to." He sat back, and the idea kept unfolding like a map. A number, just a number, banned everywhere so one man would be remembered. He wondered how many players put it on before 1997. He wondered what it felt like to be the last one wearing it.

"How did you figure that out?" Grayden asked, reaching for the chips.

"I didn't figure it, exactly. I noticed the pattern first, then tested it." Elijah grinned. "Same technique as the coin thing. Look for what's missing, then find out why."

Cian raised his soda can. "To number forty-two."

They all tapped their cups together, and on the screen the shortstop dove for a ground ball and came up grinning with the ball in his bare hand.

Layla sat cross-legged in the langar hall of the gurdwara with a photocopied page of Japji Sahib balanced on her knee, and for the tenth time that week she got stuck at the same line. "Ik oankar," she whispered, "sat naam, karta purakh, and then... something." The ceiling fan hummed like it was laughing at her.

Azalea slid into the seat across from her with a paper cup of chai and a granola bar. "Still dying?"

"It's forty pauris, Azalea. Forty." Layla flipped the page over as if the words might hide on the back. "My uncle takes Amrit in three weeks, and he asked me to recite it for the family beforehand. Me. The girl who forgot the words to 'Happy Birthday' at her own party."

"You did forget. We all stood there clapping in silence." Azalea pulled the page back and squinted at the small print at the bottom. "Hey, listen to this. It says Japji Sahib is also recited at the Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar."

"That's the one my uncle is going to," Layla said slowly. So that was why he kept saying she should really learn it, not just skim it. The prayer wasn't just for her little performance at home; it belonged to the ceremony itself. She chewed on that. If the words mattered that much, then everyone at the ceremony would know them, and she would be the only one mouthing along like a goldfish.

She came up with a test. The next morning she set her alarm for six, and the morning after that too, because she'd read that people recite it at dawn. Her mouth felt like an arid desert by day three, but her lips were starting to move on their own, ahead of her brain, like her feet on the way to school. She made a prototype out of index cards, one pauri per card with only the first letter of each word, and Luca, who was visiting his grandmother next door, offered to supervise her run-throughs in exchange for half her cookies. He held up the cards with great ceremony, wearing his sunglasses indoors for no reason Layla could determine.

"You skipped a whole line," he announced on Thursday, lowering the sunglasses.

"I did not. You turned two pages at once, genius." But when she checked, he was right. She laughed so hard she had to start over, and this time the words came out whole, all the way to the end, in the sunlight coming through the langar windows.

On the morning of the ceremony, her uncle straightened his turban in the hallway and asked, "Ready?"

Layla patted her pocket, where the index cards were, just in case. "Race you to the door."

Joshua had one job before dinner: find the photo Kiana sent him yesterday and turn it into the banner for their group's fundraiser page. The fundraiser was Kiana's idea, a livestream marathon where viewers would donate money every hour the three of them kept playing. She wanted it to look professional, and she had texted him the photo twice already, with the message "make it cool" both times.

He dragged the file onto the desktop and right-clicked it, hunting for the resize option. Instead he clicked something called Properties, and a panel opened with more information than he expected. Camera model. Date. And then a tab labeled Location, with a small map. A pin sat on the map, and when he zoomed in, streets appeared that he recognized. It was Kiana's street. Not her neighborhood, her street, the corner where the blue mailbox stood, four houses down from her front door.

"Whoa," Rae said over the voice call. "Wait, do it to mine." Joshua had the call running through his headphones while he worked. He pulled up a photo Rae had sent last week, of the glitchy scoreboard from the game night at his house. Same thing: a pin, sitting right on Rae's block. He checked a third photo, one he had taken himself at the park. A pin on the park.

"So every picture is doing this?" Rae said.

"It's writing it into the file," Joshua said. "Hidden data. It's called EXIF metadata." He had found the words at the bottom of the properties panel, small and gray, like a stamp on the back of a postcard nobody was supposed to read. Location services on, GPS coordinates in, every single time. He sat back. That meant the photo he was about to upload, the one Kiana wanted as the banner, would carry her street address to anyone who downloaded it. Anyone. The page was going to be public, because Kiana insisted public meant more donors.

"Kiana's going to say just post it," Rae said. "She's been planning this stream for two weeks. She keeps talking about how many followers she'll get."

"She can get followers without her house attached," Joshua said. He opened the file in an editing program and tried saving it as a new image, then checked the properties of the copy. The map tab was gone. He tried it again with Rae's photo, same result. Whatever the editing did, it wiped the pin out.

He texted Kiana a screenshot of the map, pin and all, and typed: "I can fix the banner. But you should see this first."

Three dots appeared. Then they vanished. Then they appeared again.

The keyboard on his screen stayed silent, and somewhere across town, on a street a pin could name, Kiana was deciding what to say.

Rose had gotten the seasons question wrong twice, and Mr. Han had a rule: third wrong answer meant you taught the topic to the class yourself. She stood in the science room after last bell, staring at the model globe on the counter by the window, trying to figure out how she was going to explain seasons without embarrassing herself a third time.

"It's the tilt," said Audrina, who had stayed to sweep glitter off her lab table from an unrelated incident. "You know that, right?"

"That's what the textbook says," Rose said. "I can say the words. I just can't say why." Last year she'd given an answer about distance from the Sun, and Juniper had laughed so hard she knocked over a beaker, and Rose had pretended to laugh too, which she still regretted. The globe on the counter was leaning, she noticed now. Not standing straight. Leaning, like it had been set down carelessly, except nothing in Mr. Han's room was ever careless.

She borrowed a protractor from the drawer and held it against the globe's stand. The metal pole sticking out of the top, the axis, was off from straight up by about 23.4 degrees. She checked twice, because the first time her hand was shaking slightly.

"Was it always like that?" Audrina asked.

"It's supposed to be," Rose said slowly. She turned the globe and watched the desk lamp Mr. Han used for grading, holding it where the window was, pretending the lamp was the Sun. When the globe's lean tipped the half she was looking at toward the lamp, the light spread across it wide and direct. When she turned it halfway around, the same lean tipped that half away, and the light went thin and slanted across the surface. Same lamp. Same distance. Different angle. She tried it a third time with the lamp moved closer, and the angle mattered more than the distance did, by a lot.

The next day Mr. Han called on her anyway, before she volunteered, which was exactly like him. Rose walked to the model, tilted it so the class could see the lean, and said Earth's axis was tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun. Then she did the lamp demonstration, sweeping the light across the globe's north half and south half in turn. "That's why they're opposites," she said. "Our summer is their winter."

Juniper raised her hand. "So last year when you said it was distance, you were just, like, completely wrong?"

"I confess," Rose said. "Completely." Half the class laughed, but it was a different laugh from before, and afterward Mr. Han said her model was going on permanent display, leaning exactly as it was, next to the sign he lettered that afternoon: 23.4 degrees. Check it yourself.

Emma had been counting on the cows all week. The nature reserve had a small working dairy farm at its edge, and Ms. Malik had promised the class they could watch the morning milking. On the bus, Emma leaned across the aisle to Johan and Aida and said, "I'm going to figure out how much milk one cow gives. For my science project. If I time it and measure the pipes, I can calculate it."

"Sure," Johan said, though he was already looking out the window at the pines.

The milking barn smelled of warm hay and something sharp and grassy, and the pipes overhead hummed while machines clicked in a steady rhythm. Emma counted the cows in the stalls. Fourteen, all with swollen udders. She pulled out her notebook and started sketching the layout, but a thought snagged her, the way a loose thread catches on a nail. Every cow here had milk. But how? Last summer, at her grandmother's village, Emma remembered a goat named Pepper who had milk only after her twins were born. Before that, Grandmother had said, Pepper gave nothing at all. Emma had been seven and had thought it was strange, then forgotten it.

She looked down the row of stalls again. Beside the far end, past the last milking cow, there was a separate pen, and in it stood a cow with no calf, and her udder was flat. Emma felt her stomach do a small flip. "Johan," she whispered, "look at that one. She's not being milked."

"So? Maybe she's sick."

Emma tested a hypothetical idea out loud, keeping her voice low. "Maybe a cow only makes milk if she's had a calf." Johan shrugged. Aida, who had been listening, frowned and said, "But then every cow in this barn must have had a calf. All fourteen." It sounded like a paradox to Emma, milk everywhere but only because of something absent, something you could not see, the calves who were somewhere else. She revised her whole plan in her head. Timing pipes was useless. She needed to know where the calves were.

She walked to the fence and asked the farmer, a woman in green boots, "Where are the calves?"

"Some in the hutch pens past the barn," the farmer said. "That first-year heifer there hasn't calved yet, so there's no milk from her."

Emma wrote it down with cold fingers: a dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf. The whole hidden rule, sitting right there in her notebook. She turned and waved her pen at Johan and Aida. "Come on. We're going to the hutches."

The community hall smelled like onions and warm bread, and Jade pulled her friend Alexis past the shoe rack before Alexis could change her mind. "My mom's inside helping cook," Jade said. "You don't have to do anything. Just come."

"I don't have any money on me," Alexis whispered, hanging back at the doorway. Rows of people sat cross-legged on the floor on long mats, and volunteers moved between them carrying buckets of dal and trays of roti. "I can't just take food from your temple."

Jade had wondered the same thing the first time her grandmother brought her, years ago. She had counted the visitors who looked like they weren't Sikh at all, tourists in hiking boots, a woman with a camera, two teenagers in soccer jerseys, and none of them had paid. She'd even asked her dad to check whether there was some hidden charge, some box at the door. There wasn't. She'd tested it herself once, sitting at the end of a row where nobody knew her, and the roti still arrived.

"That's the whole point," Jade said. "It's called langar. Everybody eats, no matter who they are. Nobody pays." She pointed at the mats. "See how everybody's sitting on the floor together? My dad says that's on purpose. Like, a CEO and a homeless guy sit the same way."

Alexis still stood in the doorway, so Jade tried an experiment. "Fine. Don't eat. Just sit with me and watch." They found a spot near the back, and within a minute a volunteer with a steel bucket set two steel bowls of dal in front of them, the way she did for every row, and a man in an orange turban placed roti in their palms with a small smile. Alexis looked at the roti like it might be a trick. Then she took a bite, and then another.

Afterward Alexis tugged Jade's sleeve. "Okay, that was the best bread I've ever had. Can I do something? Anything?" Jade led her to the kitchen doorway, where they washed their hands and joined a line of volunteers rolling dough. Alexis's first roti came out lopsided and thin on one side, but the woman next to her, who had flour up to her elbows, laughed and said the flat ones cook fastest, and by the tenth one Alexis could make the dough flourish under her palms in a wide, even circle. "My mom's going to ask where I was all afternoon," Alexis said, stacking her rotis. "She's going to think I'm making this up. Free food, and they let strangers cook."

"Tell her to come next month," Jade said. "I'll keep a list. She can be entry number two in my database of people I dragged here." Alexis grinned, but then her phone buzzed and her face changed; her mom wanted her home early to babysit, and Alexis had to go before the trays she'd made came back around. Jade watched her leave, then carried the lopsided first roti out to the mats herself, still warm, and set it in an old man's bowl. He tore off a piece and nodded at her. "Dhan vaad," he said, and Jade sat down in his row until the next bucket came.

Ethan slid his story across the table in Room 12, where the writing club met every Thursday after last bell. "Read the dog one," he said to Riya. "It's got a climax. Ms. Siddiqui said every story needs one, and mine has it on page two. Big rescue. Storm drain, flashlight, the works."

Riya read fast, which was her way, because she wanted her turn on the good chair by the window before anyone else claimed it. "The dog gets carried out of the drain, and then it ends," she said. "So what happened to the dog after? Does it go home? Does the kid keep it? You can't just stop." Loukas, sitting across from them, grinned. "He can. It's called quitting."

"It's called a cliffhanger," Ethan said, though he wasn't sure that was true. Riya flipped the pages back and forth like the missing part might fall out of them. She pointed at the last line, where the kid in the story holds the shivering dog up over the grate while rain comes down. "Everything before this builds to it. That's the climax. But after the climax, the story isn't over. The falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends." She said it like she was quoting someone, and she was; the sentence was underlined twice in her notebook from last week's notes.

Ethan took the story back and read his own ending again. She was right, and he could see the hole now, the same way you see a missing stair once someone trips on it. He borrowed Ms. Siddiqui's red pen from the supply box without asking, which was a risk, since she had once threatened to ridicule anyone who left the cap off. On the back of his last page he wrote three lines: the kid takes the dog home, the family puts up one poster and nobody calls, and the kid's dad, who had said the whole search was a waste of a Tuesday, lets the dog sleep on the couch. Then he checked his quotation marks, because the coach in his story had dialogue and he had put the comma inside the quotes, then outside, then inside again on the same page.

He read the new ending aloud to the table. Riya listened all the way through before she reached for the good chair, which for her was a standing ovation. Loukas tapped the page where the dad came around. "That's the best part. He was like a diplomat the whole time, negotiating where the dog could sleep, and then he just gives in." Ethan looked at the sentence and realized his story about an impoverished kid with no flashlight batteries had turned into a story about a family letting something in.

"Write yours next," he told Loukas. "But give me my pen back first."

Loukas held the pen above his head. "Trade you the pen for the dog story. I want to copy the ending trick."

"Write your own couch," Ethan said, and grabbed it.

Mackenzie stared at her draft and wondered if stories could have rules that hid themselves on purpose. Her character, a night guard in a museum, kept asking questions, and every time she wrote one, the next line looked wrong somehow. The motion sensor on the classroom ceiling clicked the lights back on whenever someone waved a hand, and that gave her an idea. Maybe punctuation worked like that, invisible until you moved through it.

She read her line out loud to Gracelynn, who sat cross-legged on the desk beside her. "Where are you? He asked." Gracelynn winced. "Why is He so big? It looks like a new sentence started." Mackenzie tapped her pencil. "But the question mark ends the quote, so shouldn't the next word be a capital?" She tried it the other way, lowercase, and squinted at it. "Where are you? he asked." It looked strange and correct at the same time, like a door that opened the wrong way but still opened.

Eliot leaned over from the next row, holding his own story about a haunted aquarium. "Mine has a question too," he said. "Do fish sleep? she whispered." He had already written it with the lowercase, without even thinking about it. Mackenzie copied both versions onto a sticky note and carried them to the board, where Ms. Becker had posted a page from a published story. She found a question there. The question mark sat inside the quotation marks, and the tag after it began with a lowercase letter. "It's not just Eliot being weird," she announced. "Real authors do it too." Now she had a pattern from three separate places, and patterns, she had learned, were how hidden rules gave themselves away.

She went back and fixed every question in her draft, and then she found the bigger problem Ms. Becker had circled in green: her story had no clear climax. The guard wandered, the lights flickered, nothing built. "What if the sensor fails?" Eliot suggested. "Total darkness, and the guard hears something moving in the dinosaur room." Mackenzie liked that. She could sustain the tension for a whole paragraph, letting the guard feel her way past display cases while the reader wondered what was ahead.

When she read the finished story aloud on Friday, the room went quiet in the way that meant nobody was indifferent to what happened next. At the final line, the guard spun around, flashlight raised, and asked, "Who's there?" she demanded, and somewhere in the dark, something answered with a low, patient hiss.

The cultural festival had taken over the whole park, with tents for food, dancing, and crafts, but Blake walked past all of it toward the synagogue's booth, where a rehearsal table waited. In two weeks he would read from the Torah scroll for his bar mitzvah, and he had spent a month practicing from a printed book that portrayed the words with vowels and little musical marks above and below the letters. Elisha and Caelan came with him, partly for support and partly because the booth was giving out free honey cake.

Ms. Yilmaz, who ran the booth, set a wooden case on the table and opened it. Inside lay the actual scroll Blake would read from, its parchment a warm cream color, the handwritten letters sharp and black. Blake leaned close, and his stomach dropped. There were no vowels. There were no musical marks at all. "How am I supposed to know the tune from this?" he asked.

"Look again," Caelan said. "Read the letters out loud, slowly."

Blake did. Something strange happened. As he moved along the line, the melody from his practice book rose in his head by itself, attached to the shapes of the words. The printed book had not just shown him the music; it had stitched the tune into his memory of the passage. "The scroll doesn't have the notes," he said slowly, testing the idea, "because I'm supposed to already know them. From the book." He tried a full phrase, chanting it, and it came out right, the rise and fall landing where the marks would have been.

Elisha grabbed his arm. "That's why your practice book exists! It's like a cheat sheet you memorize so the real thing can be blank."

Blake tried another verse and stumbled on one word, then laughed at himself and tried again. Ms. Yilmaz smiled and turned the scroll to his actual portion. "Whenever you're ready."

That night Blake wrote a message to his grandfather, who lived too far away to attend.

Dear Grandpa, you won't believe what happened today. The real scroll has no vowels or musical marks, so everything I learned from my practice book has to live in my head. At first I panicked, but it turns out a month of practicing every night actually worked. I was biased against my own memory, I guess. I thought I needed the marks on the page, explicit and right in front of me, and I didn't. Caelan and Elisha cheered so loud that people at the falafel tent turned around. Two more weeks. I'll call you after.

The morning of the ceremony, Blake stood in front of the open scroll, took a breath, and began to chant.

Elena's mother had been in the hospital for two weeks, which was how a thirteen-year-old came to be standing in the Blue Ribbon Laundromat on a Saturday morning with a garbage bag of clothes and no plan. Her dad had said "just throw it all in," but she had watched her mother separate loads her whole life, so she sorted on the folding table: darks in one pile, whites in another, towels in a third. The darks were the biggest pile, mostly her father's work shirts and her own black leggings, so she fed those into the machine first, dumped in the detergent, and pressed the button like she was launching a rocket.

Dillon was there too, because Dillon was always wherever something was happening. He had set up a folding stand by the door with a hand-lettered sign that said "DILLON'S FOLDING SERVICE, 50 CENTS AN ITEM" and he wanted, more than anything, a first customer. "You have a lot of items," he said hopefully, nodding at her garbage bag. "It would be feasible for you to hire me. Very feasible."

"I can fold my own clothes," Elena said, though she was not entirely sure that was true. She presumed the dryer would do most of the work anyway. Behind them, an old man was arguing with a machine that had eaten his quarter, and the air smelled like warm cotton and lemon soap, with a hum underneath it all like a hive of sleepy bees.

When she pulled the dark load out, every single piece was speckled with white. Her dad's navy shirt looked like it had been caught in a snowstorm. Dillon laughed so hard he knocked over his sign. Elena stood there holding a shredded mess and thinking, and then it clicked: nothing in the pile had been white going in, so the white had to come from inside the load. She dug through the speckled clothes, and down in one of her dad's jacket pockets she found the remains of a paper tissue, torn to pieces. One forgotten tissue, she realized, had broken apart in the wash and scattered shreds over everything in the whole load. That was why her mother always checked pockets. Nobody had ever told her that. She had to find it out the snowy-shirt way.

She picked every shred off by hand, which took forty minutes and made her fingertips numb, and Dillon folded six of her dad's shirts for a quarter because, as he put it, "first customer discount, plus I feel bad for you." Her conscience twinged a little about paying him with quarters from her dad's laundry fund, but she figured she had earned it. The second load was her whites, and before it went in, she went through every single pocket, one by one, even her own, and found a movie stub and a gum wrapper. That load came out clean, no shreds anywhere, and she stood in front of it for a second, proving her theory to herself.

At home she laid the speckled work shirt over the back of a chair, the one piece she hadn't been able to save. Her dad would notice, and she would have to explain it, and he would probably laugh and probably also be tired. She folded the clean shirts into a neat stack the way her mother did, collars lined up, and set them where they always went. Then she texted him: "Laundry done. Mostly."

Anna sat cross-legged on the living room floor with the remote balanced on her knee, waiting for the 100-metre final to start. Asma flopped onto the couch beside her, still holding the printout they'd made in the library that afternoon.

"Your dad's going to want the TV," Asma said.

"He's out. We have till seven." Anna turned the volume up.

On the screen, eight sprinters settled into their blocks. The commentator's voice conveyed urgency even in the seconds of silence before the gun, leaning on words like "rivalry" and "fastest field ever assembled." Then the crack, and the runners rose together and tore down the track.

It ended in a blur. Two of them crossed nearly as one, and the stadium noise swallowed everything else. The scoreboard flashed gold beside one name and silver beside another, then the times: 9.81 and 9.82.

"A hundredth of a second," Asma said. "That's less than a blink."

Anna rewound it and paused on the finish. The two bodies were almost a single shape. She looked at the medal table on Asma's printout, where the silver medalist now sat second in the rankings, one place behind the winner and one place ahead of the bronze.

"Look at this," Anna said, tapping the column of finishing positions. "First, second, third. Same as always."

"So?"

"So the second-place guy lost by a hundredth of a second today. But in the semi-final, the girl in third lost by almost a whole minute in the steeplechase. Both of them get the same thing on paper. A two and a three." Anna grabbed a pen from under the couch cushion and drew the medal table again, this time with the gaps stretched out to scale. First and second were a hair apart. Second and third were a canyon. "The ranking shows you the order. It doesn't show you the distance."

Asma leaned over the drawing. "So when my dad says our school is ranked second in the district, that could mean anything."

"It could mean barely second. It could mean almost first." Anna thought of the swim rankings posted outside the gym, her own name sitting ninth. She'd been treating it like a fact about how fast she was. Now she wanted the times themselves, not the order. "Can we get the actual results from the meet?"

"They're online. The commentary's pretty sparse, though, just splits and numbers."

"Numbers are all we need. Bring your laptop down here."

Asma climbed the stairs two at a time, and Anna pulled the coffee table closer and cleared a space for it beside the paused TV screen, where two runners still hung frozen, a hundredth of a second apart.

Ava sat at the corner table in the school library with her notebook open to a page of squiggles that were supposed to be quotation marks. Her story was due tomorrow, and her climax kept going flat. In her draft, a girl named Marisol races home through a turbulent storm to tell her family that she won the art contest, and Ava wanted Marisol's words to feel like thunder. Instead they sat on the page like wet paper.

"I keep messing up the part where Marisol repeats what her brother said," Ava told Adalyn, who was working two seats away on a poster that was supposed to symbolize courage for a health project. Adalyn leaned over, chewing the end of a grape-scented marker. The line read: Marisol shouted, "Dad, Mateo told me, you draw better than anyone!"

"That looks wrong," Adalyn said. "But I don't know why."

Ava stared at it. She remembered sitting at her grandmother's kitchen table last summer, copying sentences from an old paperback while the fan rattled and the smell of burnt toast drifted from the kitchen. In one of those sentences, a character had said, "She called it 'the long goodbye.'" Ava had copied it twice, backward and forward, without thinking. Now the memory surfaced like a coin glinting at the bottom of a pool. The book had used little marks inside the big ones. She hadn't invented that; she had seen it.

She had a way to test it. Mr. Nielsen's writing shelf held a stack of novels, and Ava pulled one off and flipped until she found a character quoting someone. There it was again: double marks outside, single marks inside. She grabbed a second book, then a third, checking every time someone repeated another person's words. Same pattern every single time. Her insight felt solid enough to stand on, so she went back and rewrote the line: Marisol shouted, "Dad, Mateo told me, 'You draw better than anyone!'"

"That looks right," Adalyn said, tapping the single marks with her marker. "Like smaller doors inside bigger doors."

Ava rewrote her climax so the storm, the shouting, and the single marks inside the double ones all crashed together on the last page, and when she read it aloud under her breath, she could almost hear the rain. She was still grinning when Mr. Nielsen stopped by the table, glanced at her page, and slid a printout in front of her. The contest rules were printed at the top, and under format it said: entries must be handwritten in ink, final drafts only, no computer corrections. Ava looked down at her notebook, at the beautiful corrected line, and then at her left wrist, still in a brace from the skateboard fall that made handwriting hurt.

"First clean copy in the morning," Mr. Nielsen said, and walked away.

Ava picked up her pen with her right hand and wrote one shaky word. "Marisol."

Brooklyn sat in the waiting room of the vet clinic with her science poster across her knees, and the poster was still blank. Tim had brought in a shoebox with a limp sparrow his cat had caught, and while Ms. Bighorn, the vet, examined the bird behind the counter, Brooklyn had exactly one hour before her mom picked her up. The presentation on natural selection was due tomorrow morning, and the first period bell would not wait.

"You could do moths," Tim offered, peeking over the half door. "Moths that match the trees. Everyone does moths."

"I want to do the finches," Brooklyn said. She flipped through her notebook, where she had sketched three beaks: one thick like a nutcracker, one long and thin, one curved like a tiny parrot's. "Darwin collected birds on the Galápagos Islands, and the beaks are different on different islands. Thick beaks where the seeds are big and hard. Thin beaks where the bugs hide in bark. I just can't figure out how to show it."

Skylar slid into the chair beside her, back from the front desk with a pamphlet about bird feeders. "The problem is you can't see it happening. Nobody watched a beak change."

"That's the part that's bugging me," Brooklyn admitted. She tapped her sketches. "It's like a hidden cause. The beaks don't change on purpose. But why would Darwin's own birds fool him? He was this famous observer, and he didn't even know what he had." Skylar frowned at that, so Brooklyn made a note to check it, because half-remembered facts were worse than none.

"Actually," Skylar said, reading further in the pamphlet's small print, "there's a story in here. In 1837 an ornithologist named John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were actually a new group of closely related finches."

"Wait. He thought they were wrens? Blackbirds?" Brooklyn leaned over to see the paragraph herself. "So the birds looked so different that Darwin mislabeled them, and a bird expert had to sort it out. That's almost better than my idea." She felt oddly relieved, too, because last week at the community garden she had called a warbler a sparrow, and Skylar had laughed for a whole bus ride. Even Darwin had gotten birds wrong, and Darwin kept finch skins in jars.

Then she had it. "The feeders," she said, pointing at the wall behind the counter, where the clinic sold tubes of seed and little dishes of nectar. "Ms. Bighorn, can I borrow two kinds of seed? Big striped ones and tiny ones. Just for a demo."

Ms. Bighorn came out with the sparrow cupped in her hands, blinking but alive, and set a scoop of striped sunflower seed and a scoop of millet on the counter. Brooklyn grabbed tweezers from her pencil case and a binder clip from her poster bag. "Tim, you're the thin beak with the tweezers. I'm the thick beak with the clip. Same bowl of mixed seed, thirty seconds. Go."

The tweezers snatched millet grains quickly but could barely crack a striped seed, and the clip crushed the big seeds easily but fumbled the tiny ones. They ran it twice to make sure, and it came out the same both times, which was the logic of the whole thing written in seed hulls. For her poster Brooklyn drew the tools as beaks, arrows from each island's food to each island's bird, and a bold caption to emphasize the point: beaks match the job.

At the bottom she taped her sketch of a small brown bird and wrote, "Counterfeit blackbird. Actually a finch, according to John Gould, 1837. Darwin got fooled too." Skylar laughed when she read it, then took out a pen and drew a tiny speech bubble on the bird that said, "Gotcha."

Ms. Bighorn carried the sparrow past them toward the door, still blinking. "You three want to release him outside? He's ready." Tim grabbed the shoebox, Brooklyn rolled her poster, and Skylar held the door as the bird whirred up into the maple tree and landed, squarely, on the sunflower feeder with the big striped seed.

Caleb spread his science fair notebook across the library table and tapped the page where he had written, in big letters, "Which hot chocolate tastes best: brand X or the store brand?" Heather dropped into the chair across from him with three books about medieval history, because she was in the library's after-school history guild and had promised the librarian a report by Friday.

"Nobody will pick the cheap one honestly," she said, reading his plan. "They'll taste it, see the fancy label, and say the expensive one is better because they expect it to be better." Caleb argued with her for a minute, then stopped, because he remembered his brother swearing a headache medicine worked, and then swearing the same thing about a sugar pill their mom had given him by mistake. The medicine had not been the thing doing the work. The believing had been.

"So we hide the labels," Caleb said. "Cups marked A and B." Heather shook her head and pulled his notebook toward her. "Not enough. What if you pour the cups? You know which is which. You could hand somebody the good one with a bigger smile." She looked at him until he got it. He rewrote the plan so that Youcef, who was meeting them at the library in twenty minutes, would mix up the cups himself and write the code on a card he would seal in an envelope. Caleb wouldn't know, the tasters wouldn't know, and even the person handing out the samples wouldn't know. "My mom calls that a double-blind trial," Heather said. "Neither the testers nor the people running it know who's getting which." He asked her to paraphrase that in his notes, and she wrote it in one clean sentence.

The twist came at four o'clock, when Youcef arrived with the carton of brand X already opened. "I had to test it at home," he admitted. "So I know which cup is which by smell." That broke the whole plan, and for a moment Caleb thought the project was dead. Then he found the solution in the library's little kitchenette: paper cups with lids and straws. If nobody could smell the cocoa, Youcef's accidental knowledge couldn't leak out. Youcef poured, shuffled the cups in a random order, and sealed the answer card while Caleb turned his back to prove it.

Nine tasters from the history guild participated, mostly because Heather bribed them with the leftovers. Caleb called out "A or B?" and tallied votes. Seven out of nine picked the store brand. When Youcef slit open the envelope, the cheap cocoa had won, and Caleb felt a strange mix of triumph and disappointment, because his family had been paying extra for the fancy carton his whole life.

"Want to co-author the write-up?" he asked Heather, sliding the notebook toward her. She was already writing. "You owe me," she said. "My medieval guild report is due Friday, and I just spent my afternoon on chocolate." Youcef raised a lidded cup in a small toast. "To science," he said, and drank.

The driving school sat in a strip mall between a nail salon and a vacant shop with a faded FOR LEASE sign, and behind the classroom, in a little back room with a sink and a folding table, Ms. Morales kept a washer and dryer. "The landlord lets me have them back here," she told Noah on his first day, "as long as I keep the door shut during lessons." Noah's mother worked late on Tuesdays, so after class he waited forty minutes in that back room, and that was where he was standing when his brother called.

"I need the blue shirt for my interview tomorrow morning," his brother said. "The one I washed last night. It's still in the dryer, I think. Can you fold it and put it on my bed?"

Noah opened the dryer and pulled out the shirt. It was a disaster. Deep creases ran across the chest and the sleeves looked like crumpled paper. He shook it out, he smoothed it flat on the table with both palms, but the creases stayed, set hard into the fabric. He called his brother back. "It's wrecked," he said. "It was in there all night."

His brother groaned, and Noah heard him pacing. "Hang on," Noah said. He was thinking. His brother's other good shirt, the grey one, was in the hamper unwashed, and Noah had never done a load of laundry in his life, but he had watched his mother sort colours, and he had two hours. He dug through the hamper, kept the grey shirt away from a red sock and a muddy towel, measured the detergent the way he remembered, and started the washer. Then he sat on a plastic chair with his permit manual and read about right-of-way until the cycle ended.

Lux, who was waiting for a ride too, wandered in while the dryer was still tumbling. "You have a fertile imagination if you think that grey thing is going to save him," Lux said, pointing at the wrinkled blue shirt still lying on the table. "Maybe," Noah said. When the dryer buzzed, he was standing right beside it. He pulled the grey shirt out while it was still warm and soft, laid it on the folding table, and smoothed it flat. Where the blue shirt had hardened into ridges, the grey one came out smooth and stayed smooth. Noah folded it into a neat square, then a rectangle, and it looked like something from a store shelf.

Ms. Morales came back to lock up and found him still studying the two shirts side by side. "The one I took out right away," Noah said, holding up the grey, "and the one that sat in there overnight." He slid the folded grey shirt into his backpack, careful not to crush it. "Tell my brother I'm on my way," he said to no one in particular, and jogged out to the curb to wait for the headlights.

Jasmine had agreed to watch the neighbor's baby for exactly ninety minutes, which had sounded manageable until she was actually standing in the park with a stroller, a cooler, and the baby's eight-year-old brother Knox, who had brought a walkie-talkie for no reason she could determine. On the hill beyond the playground, a wind turbine turned its slow white circle, and Knox narrated every rotation like a sports announcer. The baby, Rohan according to the instructions, was supposed to eat at one o'clock, and it was one o'clock.

Jasmine dug through the cooler. Inside was a small jar of oatmeal, a bottle, a plastic bag of crackers, and a squeezable honey bear. A note from the parents was taped inside the lid. She read it while Knox attempted to climb the slide backwards.

The note said: "Feeding plan attached. IMPORTANT: no honey for Rohan until he is 12 months old. Honey can contain bacteria spores that grow in a baby's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism. Yes, even a tiny taste. Yes, even mixed into things." There was a smiley face drawn after this, which Jasmine felt did not match the content at all.

She had been about to stir honey into the oatmeal, on the theory that babies preferred things sweet. She put the honey bear down on the bench like it was a live grenade. "Do your parents leave notes like this a lot?"

"Mom leaves notes on everything," Knox said. "The microwave has a note. It's her whole personality."

Jasmine thought about the spores, invisible things sitting in the honey, waiting. You couldn't see them. The only way to know the rule existed was to read it, and she almost hadn't. She fed Rohan the plain oatmeal instead, and he ate it with enormous enthusiasm, smearing most of it into his own hair.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Yasmina, who babysat for another family on this street and had offered backup advice.

Yasmina: "how's it going? btw if Knox tries the red berries by the fountain, those are toxic. also did you check the parents' note? the LAST sitter gave that baby honey. she felt so bad she cried at the block party."

Jasmine typed back: "I checked it. Nobody is germinating anything in anybody's gut on my watch." She was pleased with that sentence. She was less pleased a minute later, when she turned around and found Knox had taken off his shoe and was attempting to plant a dandelion seed in it, explaining that it would germinate by Friday. The walkie-talkie crackled with static from his pocket.

The parents arrived at 2:40. The mother inspected Rohan, found one shoe, one cracker, and a large quantity of oatmeal in his hair, and declared the afternoon a success. Then she sat down on the bench, unscrewed the honey bear, and squeezed a long golden ribbon into her own thermos of tea.

"More for me, then," she said.

Alexandra set her phone timer on the kitchen counter, next to a bowl of eggs and a half-eaten piece of toast. "Three minutes," she said to Libby, who was perched on a stool by the fridge. "That's how long I have to explain the whole thing to Mr. Nakamura tomorrow. Nicotine, the brain, why people can't stop."

Libby tapped the counter. "Pretend I'm him. Go." Alexandra took a breath. "Okay. Deep in your brain there's a reward pathway. It's the part that says, do that again, that was good. Food, friends, music, all of it runs through there. Nicotine sneaks into that system and cranks the dial way up. The brain gets used to the bigger signal, so normal things start to feel flat, and now you need the nicotine just to feel okay." She paused. "That's the addiction part. Wanting it isn't weakness. The pathway itself got rewired."

She had almost forgotten where she first learned it. Back in October, at Harry's cousin's birthday party, someone had passed around a slim silver vape on the back porch. Harry had held it out to her, casual, like offering gum. Alexandra had said no before she really knew why, and Harry had shrugged and said, "Probably smart. My sister says your brain keeps building until you're about twenty-five, so kids get hooked way easier than adults." She had stared at that little silver tube afterward, thinking about a brain still under construction, rooms being built inside her own head.

"Time," Libby announced, and Alexandra slumped. "Two minutes forty. I can do it faster." She paced between the counter and the table, trying the explanation again, and this time she tripped over the middle part. "The... the receptor thing. Ugh, cramming all this in one night might actually hinder me." Libby grinned. "That's a vocab word and you know it." Alexandra threw a dish towel at her, laughing, and the laugh was contagious; soon they were both wheezing while the eggs sat forgotten.

Then the kitchen door opened and Mr. Nakamura himself walked in, carrying a casserole dish, back early from the potluck next door because the landlord had called about a flooded basement. He blinked at the two girls, timer still ticking on the counter. "Practicing your presentation? I'm your audience tomorrow, you know." Alexandra went pink. Then Harry stepped in behind him, holding the silver vape from the party, and set it on the table. "It's a prop," he said quickly. "Empty. It's for your talk. I figured a real one would make everyone actually listen." Alexandra picked it up, turned it over in her hand, and looked at Mr. Nakamura. "Want the two-minute version now, or should I wait until I beat three minutes?"

"Beat the clock," he said, settling onto Libby's stool and folding his hands. "I'll count."

Emilia pushed a fresh sheet of paper across the art room table so fast that her pencil rolled off the edge and bounced under the stool. Today Ms. Sokolov had promised the class they would learn to make a flat page look like a real street, and Emilia had been waiting for this lesson since September. London leaned over from the next table, already sharpening three pencils at once like she was preparing for surgery.

"Start with your vanishing point," Ms. Sokolov said, walking between the tables. "One dot. Then draw your orthogonals first." She tapped the air above Melody's paper and moved on without another word.

Emilia froze, pencil hovering. Orthogonals. She had written the word in her sketchbook that morning, circled it twice, and still had no idea what it meant. Melody raised her hand, but Ms. Sokolov was already across the room helping someone tape down a curling corner. The class rule was that a question could only go to the teacher twice per period, and Emilia had already used one asking whether the horizon line had to be straight. She needed to be objective about this, not just guess and waste her second question.

She looked at the example sketch Ms. Sokolov had pinned to the board. A street ran back toward a single dot, and faint pencil lines still showed beneath the ink. Slowly, Emilia traced them with her eyes. The road edges, the curbs, even the rooflines of the buildings on both sides, every one of them slanted toward that same dot. They weren't random. They were the bones of the whole picture, the lines that ran back toward the vanishing point. "Those are the orthogonals," she whispered, and felt like she'd found a hidden door. She drew her dot, then ran four lines toward it from the corners of her page, light as breath. The street appeared on her paper like it had been waiting there all along.

Then came the twist. Melody slid her own drawing over, grinning, and Emilia saw that Melody had put her vanishing point dead center, so the street ran straight and flat, like a road sitting on the equator instead of curving through a real town. "Yours looks alive," Melody said. "Mine looks like a diagram." Emilia tilted Melody's paper, then grabbed her eraser. She could fix this. She regulated her breathing, the way she did before a free throw, and moved the dot off to the left with one careful nudge.

"Now redraw your road edges," Emilia said, tapping the paper. "Curbs, rooflines, all of it, back to the new dot."

Melody's pencil was already moving.

Piper got to the coffee shop ten minutes early, which she decided was the correct amount of early: enough to choose the good table by the window, not so much that she looked like she had been waiting since breakfast. The radiator under the window clicked and hissed, baking the air until the whole corner of the room felt as arid as a desert. She set her water glass in front of her like a prop, then moved it, then moved it back.

Liam arrived at exactly four o'clock, held up a thumb, and got in line for the counter. He came back with two hot chocolates, one for her, and said, "I guessed whipped cream. If that's wrong, the date is cancelled." She laughed, which was a good sign, and then she made a joke about the radiator being a dragon, and he laughed too, a real snorting laugh, and she felt her face go hot.

She knew what it was. She had read it in a library book about the body that nobody had ever borrowed before her: blushing happens when blood vessels in the face widen and let more blood flow near the skin. The warmth she felt was that extra blood doing its thing, right there under her skin, announcing itself to the entire coffee shop. She put her hands over her cheeks, which was like locking the barn after the horse had already ordered a latte.

In the bathroom she ran cold water over her wrists. If widened vessels meant more blood near the skin, then cold ought to work the other way, tightening things up. She held her wet wrists to her cheeks like two fish and stared at herself in the mirror. The red faded, slowly, the way a stain gives up. "Okay," she told the mirror. "Okay."

Genesis was at the sink, drying her hands. "Are you sick?" she asked. "Because if you have an infection, I'm standing very far from you."

"It's not an infection," Piper said. "It's just blushing."

"From what?"

"From a date. Table by the window. Don't look."

Genesis looked immediately and at length. Then she came back and said, "He's stacking whipped cream on his spoon like a tiny tower. I approve." When Piper sat down, Liam slid his whipped cream tower across the table to her.

"It collapsed," he said. "Like all towers."

She felt her face go warm again, and this time she just let it. "Your turn to blush," she said. "Tell me a joke and I'll laugh really hard at it, and we'll see if we can replicate the experiment."

"Replicate the experiment," Liam repeated, grinning. "On our first date."

"Only date," she said, "that comes with a control group," and she pointed her spoon at his cheeks, waiting for pink.

Sofia wanted the last spot on the morning announcements crew, and so did Arjun. Ms. Bighorn said they would have to negotiate between themselves before Friday, which meant Sofia needed something impressive to trade or to show.

For her social studies project, she had picked two articles about the same downtown march. She spread them on the library table after school, with Arjun across from her and Adelie beside him, eating crackers. One headline said "Thousands of Protesters Fill Main Street." The other said "Rioters Disrupt Downtown." Sofia read both stories twice and frowned. The details matched almost exactly: the same street, the same crowd size, the same broken window near the end.

"That's weird," she said. "Same event. Completely different feeling."

Adelie leaned over. "The second one made me picture people smashing things. The first one made me picture people holding signs."

Arjun pointed at the words. "Protesters. Rioters. That's the whole difference. Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd protesters or rioters can push readers toward opposite opinions." He shrugged. "My brother talks about this stuff at dinner."

Sofia tested it. She copied both headlines onto slips of paper, swapped the words, and slid them across the table to Adelie without saying which was original. "React to each one. Fast." Adelie read "Thousands of Rioters Fill Main Street" and said it sounded scary, like a curfew kind of thing. Then she read "Protesters Disrupt Downtown" and said it sounded annoying but basically normal. Same facts, opposite reactions, both times. Sofia wrote the results in her notebook with a pencil that was running out of voltage in its little electric sharpener, so the letters came out gray and streaky.

For her presentation, she made a versatile display board, one side for each headline, with the matching photos hidden behind flaps. When she lifted the flaps at the same moment, the class saw identical images of the same intersection. Ms. Bighorn stopped writing in her grade book and looked at the board for a long moment. "Where did you find the second article?" she asked. Sofia told her, and Ms. Bighorn wrote something down without explaining it.

After class, Arjun caught up with her in the hallway. "That was good," he said. "Trade you. You can have the announcements spot if I get to co-present the project at the district fair." Sofia thought about the fair, the microphone, the audience of judges, and how a headline could tilt a whole room before anyone read a single sentence. She stuck out her hand. "Deal," she said. "But you're carrying the board."

The computer lab at Camp Windrow smelled like pine from the open window and warm keyboards from twenty laptops running at once. Florence sat in the back row with her screen tilted away from Randy, not because she was hiding anything, but because she wanted to type her program herself. Their counselor had given them the task that morning: write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. Florence had a plan, and she wanted to follow it without anyone leaning over her shoulder.

Her plan was simple. If a number can be divided evenly by two, it is not prime, so her loop would check every number from two upward and flag the ones that divided evenly. She typed it out, and when she ran it the first time it asked for a number just the way it was supposed to. That felt like a small victory, so she allowed herself a grin before testing further.

Then the trouble started. She entered seven, and the program said prime. She entered nine, and it said not prime. So far so good. But when she entered two, the screen said not prime, which was wrong, because two was the very first prime number she had ever memorized back in fourth grade. "Oh, come on," she muttered. Randy looked over. "What did you violate this time?" he asked. "Some law of mathematics, apparently."

Ms. Wilson walked past and glanced at the screen, but she only said, "Test a few more numbers and see what they have in common," and moved on, which was her way of making the campers do their own detective work. Florence tried four, six, eight and ten, and every single one came back not prime. Then she tried three, five and seven, and those were prime. The pattern was gradual at first, like fog clearing, but then it snapped into focus: two was the only even prime number, because every larger even number could be divided evenly by two. Her loop was punishing two for being even, and that was the bug.

She fixed it by making her program treat two as a special case before the loop ever started. When she ran it again, the screen said two was prime, and she sat back so fast her chair squeaked. Randy leaned over. "So what was it?" "Two," she said. "My own program was the jury, and it convicted the wrong number." He laughed and pulled his chair closer, copying her special case into his own code while Florence watched the cursor blink on her screen, waiting for the next test.

Gabriel curled his fingers into what the video had called the claw grip, knuckles forward like a tiny armor, and lowered the knife toward the onion. Daniela leaned on the counter beside him, watching with the patience of someone who had already been told twice not to touch the blade. "Slower," she said. "The onion isn't going anywhere." Gabriel moved the edge down and felt it bite through the layers, and his eyes began to sting so badly he had to resign himself to chopping half-blind, trusting the claw to keep his fingertips out of the blade's path. A tear slid down his cheek anyway. "How does it even know?" he muttered. "It's a vegetable."

The sauce was Mr. Romano's idea, sort of. He had come over to fix the porch light, smelled garlic from the kitchen, and poked his head in. "From scratch?" he'd said. "Good. Restaurant sauce is just ketchup wearing a suit." Gabriel had decided to take that as a compliment to his ambitions. Now he had a pan of crushed tomatoes bubbling, and the pasta was boiling in the big pot, and the whole kitchen smelled like something sophisticated that he had made himself.

The sauce looked thin, though. Watery at the edges. Gabriel tipped the pot toward the sink to dump the pasta water, all of it, the cloudy frothing mess swirling against the lid.

"Wait." Daniela grabbed his wrist. "Save a cup of that." Gabriel stared at her. "The gray water? It looks like dishwater." "It's not just water," she said. "Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta." He squinted at the cloudy surface. So the fog in the pot was the hidden thing, the reason the water looked wrong, and maybe the reason his sauce looked wrong too.

He ladled out a cup, dumped the rest, and added the splash slowly, stirring. He watched. The sauce turned glossy where the water went in, then seemed to tighten around the spoon. He added a little more, testing, and the bubbles changed from flat and sloppy to slow and round. "It's clinging," he said. "Look at it. It's actually clinging."

They took their bowls to the porch steps and ate while the sky went orange. Mr. Romano, packing up his toolbox, paused on his way to the truck and leaned over for a look. "Sauce from scratch, onions chopped by a boy who still has ten fingers," he observed. "Consensus around here is you'll do it again next week?" "I'll do it again Friday," Gabriel said, and twirled his fork.

Riley stood backstage at the community center gym with a stack of index cards shaking slightly in his hand. In five minutes the regional spelling bee would begin, and he was stuck on the same word he had missed at practice for a week: "bite." He kept wanting to write B-I-T, because that was how the short word sounded in his head. The silent e felt like a trap set on purpose. Octavia, waiting beside him in line, leaned over. "You're mouthing it again," she whispered. "You looked like a goldfish."

"I can't figure out why there's an extra letter nobody says," Riley whispered back. "There has to be a reason." He refused to abandon the question, even though his coach had told him to just memorize and stop wondering. Before the bee, Eleanor had slipped a folded note into his jacket pocket, saying it might help with his vowel problem. He hadn't had a chance to read it yet. He ducked behind the bleachers and opened it.

"Riley," the note read, "I looked it up after you complained on Tuesday. Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift, and that happened after spellings had started to become fixed. That's the big reason English spelling often doesn't match how we say things. So 'bite' isn't a trick. The letters just stopped moving before the sounds did. Good luck. Eleanor."

Riley read it twice, and something clicked. The e in "bite" was like a fossil, a mark left behind by an older version of the word. The spelling was a photograph of how people used to talk. It wasn't random, and that made it easier to remember. He folded the note, slid it into his pocket, and walked back to the line just as Ms. Nakamura, the bee coordinator, called his name. He crossed the gym floor to the microphone, and the judges conferred and then were unanimous on his first word: "height."

"H-E-I-G-H-T," Riley said slowly. In his mind he pictured the word as an old artifact, sounds that had drifted while the letters stayed put. The judges nodded, and the announcer's voice rang out over the gym. "That is correct." Riley grinned and looked toward the bleachers, where Octavia gave him a thumbs up, and he whispered, "Two hundred years of history says I can spell."

Alexandre had one goal for his lunch break in the library: convince Ms. Ramos, who ran the student council, that the school needed a petition for a crosswalk on Maple Street. He had his argument ready. "It's dangerous," he announced, dropping his books on the table where Maddison and Braydon were already sitting. "Everyone says so."

Maddison looked up from her notebook. "Everyone says the cafeteria pizza is dangerous too." Braydon snorted so hard he knocked over his pencil cup. Ms. Ramos, shelving books three feet away, gave them a look that seemed to govern the whole room, because both boys straightened up at once.

"That's different," Alexandre said. "The pizza is just gross. That's an opinion." He paused, because the word felt slippery. "I mean, saying the street is dangerous is also an opinion, isn't it?"

"That's where you're wrong," Maddison said, and turned her notebook around. She had drawn a grid with tally marks filling four rows. "I stood at the corner after school for three days. Twelve times a car screeched or swerved while somebody was crossing. I counted. Twelve near-misses." Braydon leaned over and whistled. Alexandre read the numbers twice, and something clicked into place, like when his grandfather's clock prescription finally arrived in the mail and the old gears began turning again with a soft, luminous glow behind the glass. The count was real. He could picture each mark becoming a screech of tires.

"So your opinion has evidence," Alexandre said slowly. "It's still an opinion, but it's a more convincing one than mine, because I gave no reasons." Maddison nodded. "Exactly. Try it again."

Alexandre stood, took a breath, and spoke as if Ms. Ramos were actually listening instead of pretending to alphabetize biographies. "I think the city should build a crosswalk on Maple Street. Twelve near-misses in three days is my reason." He heard Braydon mutter "ooh, data boy" under his breath, which was annoying but also kind of great.

"Better," said Ms. Ramos, sliding a biography of Marie Curie onto the shelf. "But I have a question for you, data boy." She turned around, holding a city map. "If your numbers came from the wrong corner, would they still be evidence?" Alexandre felt his stomach drop. He looked at Maddison, whose tally sheet suddenly seemed very small. "Which corner did you watch?" he asked. "The one by the bakery," she said. Braydon pointed at the map and grinned. "The bakery's on Oak Street."

Alexandre stared at the map for a long moment, then grabbed a fresh pencil. "Same method," he said. "Right corner. Tomorrow, three o'clock." Maddison was already drawing a new grid.

The corner store smelled like oranges and floor cleaner, and Ivy had claimed the stool by the window because it was the only place in the neighborhood where she could think without her little brother asking to play. She spread her math homework across the counter space Mr. Chea let her use, a worksheet on solving equations, and stared at the first problem until the letters blurred. Across the aisle, Jessy was reading the label on a can of tropical fruit salad and arguing with a boy from their grade about whether pineapple belonged in the same category as mango.

The boy, whose grandmother owned the store, had his own math on a scrap of paper. He wrote fast, tongue between his teeth, and then shoved the paper toward his grandmother at the register. "Done. 2x plus 3, that's 5x."

His grandmother, a small woman with reading glasses on a chain, picked up the paper and frowned at it. Then she turned to the shelf and started restacking cans, leaving him standing there. "My grandma was a teacher," the boy said to Ivy, half proud and half embarrassed. "She won't just tell me. She asked me what the x stands for and then went back to work."

Ivy looked at her own worksheet. She had done the same thing two problems ago, squashing 2x + 3x into 5x with no trouble, and then hesitating when she hit 2x + 3. She pulled her pencil down the margin and wrote both expressions side by side. Two x's and three more x's, that was five x's, like putting four cans of tropical fruit with one more can and getting five cans. But 2x and 3 were not the same kind of thing at all. You could not add cans of soup to bags of rice and call it all soup.

"I think I get it," she said slowly. "They're like terms, the x ones. The plain numbers are a different kind."

"Like sorting," Jessy called over, not looking up from her can. "You categorize things before you count them."

The boy erased his 5x. He tapped his pencil, wrote 2x + 3 again, and left it alone. Then he flipped his paper toward his grandmother once more, and this time she looked at it for a long moment and gave him a single nod before turning back to the customer at the register.

Ivy went back to her first problem, which had 4x + 7 + x on the left side of the equals sign. She combined the x's into 5x, wrote it down, and then did the same thing to both sides, subtracting seven from each. The equation shrank under her pencil until x stood alone, equal to a number she could actually check. Outside, a delivery truck pulled up with crates of winter apples, a small piece of agriculture rumbling to the curb, and Mr. Chea went out to meet it.

"Twenty minutes till closing," the grandmother called.

"Then I have twenty minutes," Ivy said, and turned the page.

The reception line moved slowly, and Sara's gift bag sweated in her hands. Julianne had said her family's weddings ran long on ceremony, but Sara hadn't expected the bride's grandparents to stand at the front greeting every single guest, one by one.

"That's Obaachan and Ojiichan," Julianne whispered. "They came over from Kyoto last week. You'll bow."

"Bow how?" Sara asked, but the line was already pushing her forward, and Julianne got swallowed by a hug from a great-aunt.

Sara watched. That was the only thing she could do, so she did it properly, counting in her head like she was running an experiment. A cousin shook the grandmother's hand and gave a small nod, barely a dip of the chin. The grandmother nodded back the same size, quick and light. Then an older man in a grey suit stepped up, pressed his gift forward with both hands, and bent from the waist in a slow, deep bow that held for what felt like ten seconds. The grandfather answered with a bow just as long and just as deep. Then a teenage boy, clearly in a hurry, mumbled something and ducked his head about an inch, and the grandmother's returning nod was small and fast, almost clipped.

So there was a pattern. A shallow, quick bow got a shallow, quick bow, and a long, deep one got a long, deep one. The reasoning came together in Sara's head: the bow was like a mirror, but it was also like a measurement. The longer and deeper it was, the more respect it carried, which meant she had to decide, right now, how much respect she wanted to show. Too shallow and she'd look like the hurried boy. Too deep and she might look like she was pretending to be somebody important.

Her turn. She handed the gift with both hands, the way the man in the grey suit had done, because that part she could verify had worked. Then she bent from the waist, slow and steady, and held it, counting to five, terrified she'd misjudged.

When she straightened, Obaachan was smiling. She bowed back, long and deep, and said something to Julianne's mother, who laughed and translated: "She says you have better manners than half the relatives."

At the dinner table, Sara sat between Hayden and the teenage boy, who turned out to be named Ken and to be the bride's cousin, not rude at all, just jet-lagged and lethargic from the flight. He showed her how to hold her chopsticks to take food from the shared plates, and she showed him the trick of balancing a dinner roll on the butter knife, which made him laugh so hard he had to put his water glass down.

Later, when the dancing started, Obaachan caught Sara's eye across the room and gave her one more small, careful bow. Sara bowed back, exactly the same size, and held it until she heard the old woman laugh.

The porch boards at his grandfather's house still smelled of cedar oil, and Edouard sat cross-legged on them with his notebook, listening to the screen door bang behind Kallie. She had ridden her bike over with a red pen stuck behind her ear and a claim that made his stomach drop. "I marked every period before 'she said' in your draft," she said, flipping to the last page. "Every single one. It's an infection of periods, Edouard. It spread through the whole story."

He took the notebook and saw the red circles, twenty-three of them, crowding his dialogue like ants at a picnic. His story was due at tomorrow's writing club meeting, and Ms. Sun had said the assignment needed correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax. He had spent all week on the climax, a scene where two brothers argue during a storm on a lake, but he had not thought once about commas.

Kallie leaned against the porch rail and munched a stolen plum from the bowl by the door. She was not going to tell him the rule straight out; that was her way, and it had hindered him more than once, though it also made him remember things better. She pointed at his first line, where he had written: "I'm not turning back." she said. Then she wrote her own sentence on the corner of the page: "I'm ready," she said. "Compare them," Kallie said. "Look what happens when the tag comes after."

Edouard stared at the two sentences until his eyes ached. In hers, the spoken part ended with a comma sitting inside the quotation marks, not a period at all, and then "she said" followed in lowercase. The speaker's sentence flowed into the tag like a river into a wider river. He thought about last year, when he had guessed on every punctuation question and earned his worst grade of middle school. He had promised himself he would stop guessing. So now he tested it, being systematic the way his grandfather was when he sorted screws into jars: he wrote five new lines of dialogue, each with the tag after the spoken words, each ending with the comma inside the quotation marks. Kallie checked them one by one and shrugged, which meant they were right.

"Wait," he said suddenly. "Then the period only goes there when nothing follows. When the tag comes after, it's the comma instead." Kallie grinned and split the last plum in half with her thumb, offering him the bigger piece. Somewhere in the garden his grandfather's sprinkler ticked on, and Edouard picked up his pen and went back to the brothers on the lake, fixing the first red circle on the page. "I'm not turning back," he wrote, "she said." Then he crossed it out, and wrote it again the right way.

The boarding call for Denver wasn't for another forty minutes, but Dylan's mother kept checking the gate screen anyway, so Dylan had time to sit with his backpack in his lap and think about the rock.

It was in the front pocket, wrapped in a sock. Rose-colored, flecked with something that caught the light, about the size of a plum. He'd found it last summer on the trail above the lake, when his family had come west before, and he'd slipped it into his pocket without saying anything. His sister had seen him do it. She was younger, but she'd gone quiet on the whole hike home, and for a year Dylan had assumed she was just being annoying. Now he wasn't so sure. This morning at breakfast she'd gone quiet again the moment he mentioned this trip, the same exact silence, the two mornings sitting in his memory like parallel lines, and that pattern made him think the silence had a cause he hadn't looked for. Something to do with the rock.

He pulled out his phone and texted Noam, who had gone to a different park with his uncle in the spring. Noam had talked about it for a week afterward.

Noam's reply came fast, as if he'd been waiting. "You mean you took a rock OUT of a park? That's against the rules. My uncle made me memorize them. Leave No Trace. It's seven principles. Like 'dispose of waste properly.' And 'leave what you find.'"

Dylan read the message twice. Leave what you find. He unzipped the pocket and looked at the rock, and the guilt he'd been carrying around without naming it suddenly had a name. He typed: "What if you already took it? A year ago?"

"Then you take it back," Noam wrote. "Uncle says that's the fix."

Dylan looked at the gate screen. Twenty-five minutes. They were flying to Denver and then driving north, and if he checked the map right, the drive passed within an hour of the same lake. It could work. He turned to his sister, who was slouched beside their mother with her headphones half on.

"Hey," he said. "You remember that rock I took? From the lake trail?"

She pulled one headphone off. Her eyes went straight to his backpack, which told him everything. She had known all along. "You still have it?"

"Yeah. And I'm taking it back. On this trip. Putting it back where I found it."

She studied him for a long moment, the way she did when deciding whether a promise was real. "The exact spot," she said finally. "Not just anywhere."

"The exact spot."

The gate agent picked up the microphone, and Dylan zipped the pocket shut, stood up, and held his backpack against his chest with both hands.

Willow spread the photocopy of the Canadian Charter across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with mugs. The assignment from Mr. Grant was due tomorrow: pick one right, explain it in your own words, and be ready to say something true about it that nobody else in the class would know. Her eyes kept snagging on the small print under section 15, the equality rights. Every other section had the same start date, 1982. Section 15 said 1985.

"That's a misprint," her mother said, passing through with laundry. "Photocopies always mangle something."

Willow didn't think so. The date was printed cleanly, and it appeared twice, in both the English and French columns. A misprint wouldn't be that consistent. She grabbed her phone and called Janelle.

"Drop everything," Janelle said before Willow spoke. "I'm making a poster about freedom of expression and I need it to look eloquent. Like, judges-quoting-me eloquent."

"Janelle. Why would one part of the Charter start three years later than the rest?"

"Three years? That's weird. That's like everybody's birthday except yours showing up late."

Willow frowned at the page. Janelle's joke wasn't a joke, actually. The rest of the Charter had come into force in 1982, and section 15 waited until 1985. That gap had to mean something. She thought of her science class, where you tested an idea by changing one thing and watching what happened. Her simple test: look up whether other official documents had delayed sections. If section 15 were the only one, the delay was about section 15 itself, not about printing schedules or a lazy clerk.

She typed, read, typed again. The pattern held. Governments had been given time to update their laws before the equality rights took effect. So the delay wasn't an accident; it was deliberate, built into the document.

Her palms began to perspire against the phone. This was the thing nobody else would know. She could stand up in Mr. Grant's class and say it.

"Found something?" Janelle asked.

"The equality rights, section 15. They came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws."

"Update them for what?"

"That's the part I have to explain in my own words," Willow said. "Mr. Grant wants our own words, not the textbook's." She paused. "Want to hear my try?"

"Only if you listen to my poster after."

"Section 15 means the law has to treat everyone as equal. And the three-year wait means even governments needed practice before they had to prove it."

Janelle was quiet for a second. "Huh. That's actually better than eloquent. That's true."

Willow wrote the sentence at the top of a fresh page. Outside, a delivery truck rattled past, and somewhere down the block a screen door banged twice.

"What's your poster line?" she asked.

Janelle cleared her throat. "I may not agree with your poster, but I will defend to the death my right to make mine."

"That's a famous quote, Janelle."

"It's a famous quote with my name on it now," Janelle said, and Willow laughed so hard she knocked a mug off section 2.

Aaron sat at the kitchen table with his phone face down beside him, staring at a crumpled napkin where he had written his fourth attempt at a text. Kameron had not spoken to him since Friday, when Aaron had found out about the sleepover he was not invited to, and every draft so far started the same way. "You ditched me." "You left me out on purpose." He crossed them out so hard the pen tore the napkin. None of them would work. He knew that much, even if he could not yet explain why.

While hunting for a clean sheet of paper, he dug through his binder and found a worksheet from Ms. Campbell's class that he had never bothered to evaluate properly, since it had been handed back with a check mark and shoved in the back pocket. On it, in his own handwriting from weeks ago, was a note about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon, who in the 1960s coined the term "I-message": a sentence like "I felt left out" describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." Aaron read it twice. So that was why every draft had felt like a thrown rock. He had been aiming every word at Kameron, and a person who feels attacked ducks.

He decided to test the idea, because it seemed almost too simple. He wrote "You ditched me" on one line, then rewrote it underneath as "I felt left out when I heard about the sleepover." He read both aloud to the empty kitchen. The first one put his fists up. The second one, awkward as it sounded, left a door open. There was still the matter of actually sending it, which felt like an obligation he could not shake, so he picked up the phone before he could talk himself out of it.

The reply came while he was pacing the arid, sun-baked back porch, where the potted plant his mom kept forgetting to water had gone crispy at the edges. "Come outside," Kameron wrote. "Backyard. Now."

Kameron was standing by the fence, holding a lopsided posterboard that read HAPPY EARLY BIRTHDAY, with the B drawn backwards. "It was supposed to be a surprise party," he said, ears going red. "That's the sleepover. Wallace was helping me plan it. That's why nobody told you anything."

"You could have just said that," Aaron said, though his voice cracked halfway, which ruined the effect.

"You could have just asked instead of going quiet for three days," Kameron said, and then, quieter, "I got your text. That I-message thing."

"You know about those?"

"Ms. Campbell taught us that in September. You were absent," Kameron said, and grinned. "It's a good one, though. Handmade birthday posters with the wrong date on them, apparently, need a strong opener too."

Alexander had promised Mr. Swampy, the farmer down the road, that he would not set foot in the barn again after the incident with the goat and the feed bucket. That promise was why he was now crouched beside the barn door on a milk crate, holding a microscope Mr. Swampy had lent him, with a fresh onion in his lap.

"You look like a diplomat negotiating a peace treaty with that onion," said Dominique, perched on the fence. Collin sat beside her, unwrapping a sandwich he had clearly brought for moral support.

"I'm being careful. Mr. Swampy prohibits barn entry, not barn-adjacent entry. There's a difference." Alexander peeled a translucent layer from the inside of the onion, the part thin enough to read a newspaper through, and laid a square of it on a slide. His assignment was due Monday: draw the cells and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. He'd left it until Sunday, which Dominique had described, twice, as "a choice."
