If the pounding only showed up before presentations and not during, say, gym class, then the trigger really was the presentation and not his heart itself. He thought back: the science fair, the tryout for the basketball team, the day he'd asked Malaika if she wanted to study together. Pounding, pounding, pounding. Dodgeball on Friday, nothing at all.

"Here's the thing," the doctor said, handing him a printout. "There are coping strategies. Slow breathing, practiced beforehand. And it helps to set some boundaries, like not taking on five presentations in one week just to prove something."

Cole remembered the science fair. He'd volunteered for it alone, in front of everyone, mostly because Mr. Farah had said it would look good on scholarship applications someday. At the time it had felt brave. Now he wondered if it had just been a bad trade, trading three nights of sleep for a line on an application. He still couldn't decide.

On the way out, he passed the scale in the hallway and stopped. His heart was hammering again, badly, worse than before the presentation. He checked his watch and counted. Fastest yet.

The only dangerous thing in the room was the blood pressure cuff he was about to dodge.

"Do I have to get that too?" he asked the nurse.

Ella sat at the kitchen table with her Spanish paragraph spread in front of her. Mr. Tremblay had circled one word in red ink and written "See me" beside it. The paragraph was about her plans for next year, and the circled word was "teneré" in the sentence "El año que viene teneré un perro."

She had written it the way she wrote every other future tense verb. "Hablar" became "hablaré," "visitar" became "visitaré," so "tener" should become "teneré." But the red circle said otherwise. Her mom set a glass of milk on the table and asked what was wrong. "Mr. Tremblay circled one verb," Ella said, "and I can't figure out why. Everything else is fine."

She pulled out her phone and texted Zara, who was in the other Spanish class. "Did you get anything circled on the plans paragraph?" Zara wrote back a minute later: "Yes! My 'poder' came back circled too." Ella frowned at the screen. "Poder" should become "poderé," the same way everything else worked. Two circled verbs, both wrong, and the pattern, whatever it was, hid somewhere she couldn't see it directly.

She got out a fresh sheet of paper and made a chart. Down the left side she listed regular verbs like "hablar" and "comer," and down the right side she listed "tener," "poder," "venir," and "salir." Then she opened her textbook to the future tense chapter and hunted for sentences. "Saldré mañana," one exercise said. "Vendrán en junio," said another. The regular verbs kept their stems whole, but the ones in her right-hand column all lost something. "Tener" didn't become "teneré" at all. It became "tendré."

She texted Alejandro, who had spent a summer in Mexico with his cousins. He replied fast. "It's tendré, not teneré. Tener becomes tendré, it means I will have." Ella wrote it at the top of her chart. The stem changed and the e turned up in the ending. She fixed her sentence: "El año que viene tendré un perro." Then she added two more sentences to the paragraph for good measure, one about how she would donate her old bike to the shelter, and one about how she and the dog would be agile enough by spring to join the weekend agility class at the park.

The next morning she handed the corrected paragraph to Mr. Tremblay before the bell. He read it, looked up, and pulled a red pen from his pocket. "One more thing," he said. "You wrote that you'll feed the dog like a scavenger. Vulture, Ella." Ella took the paper back and crossed out "buitre," laughing. "Fine. Next year I'll feed him dog food."

Jordan stood in the middle of Grandpa's garage, which now held a washer and dryer instead of the old woodworking bench, staring at three garbage bags of laundry his mom had left there with one instruction: "Figure it out before Sunday." He was supposed to be learning to do a whole load from start to finish, and he'd promised Malaika he could handle it, but the bags held everything mixed together: towels, jeans, T-shirts, and, folded in paper at the bottom of the second bag, Grandpa's hand-knitted cream sweater with a note that said, "Wash gently, please."

His first move was to classify the pile into heaps on the garage floor: darks, lights, whites, and a fourth heap he wasn't sure about, which held the sweater and a woolly pair of socks. He texted Malaika a photo of the heaps, and she wrote back, "The mystery pile is wool, obviously. Wash it cold or don't wash it." Loukas, who came over to help in exchange for snacks, shrugged and said everything could just go in on hot, because hot water got things cleaner.

They compromised on science. Jordan had a theory that whatever made wool different had to be invisible, something about the yarn itself, and that hot water might be the trigger. To test it, he took one of the woolly socks and ran it under the hottest tap water in the garage sink, sloshing it around in a bucket for a few minutes while Loukas timed him. The sock came out noticeably smaller, tight and dense where it had been stretchy, almost like felt. The other sock, swished in cold water, stayed exactly the same size. "So it's the hot water plus the sloshing," Jordan said, laying the two socks side by side. "Something in the wool reacts."

Malaika arrived just then with her phone, and after a search she held it up. "It's called felting," she said. "Tiny scales on each wool fibre open up in hot, sloshing water and lock onto the neighbouring fibres, and that pulls the knit tighter." Jordan looked at his shrunken sock, which now would barely fit a doll, and felt both sick and relieved. Sick because he'd ruined a sock, relieved because the sweater was still sitting clean and dry in its paper, and because the pattern was clear. Wool meant cold water and no sloshing, and now he knew why the note said "gently."

The rest of the day went better than the start. He ran the darks and towels on hot, the lights on warm, and washed the sweater alone in cold water, squeezing it gently instead of wringing it, the way you'd handle something porous that could soak through and change. When everything came out of the dryer, he and Loukas folded it into a lopsided but real stack on the workbench, and Jordan laid the two socks on top like evidence. He took a photo of the whole load, folded sweater included, and sent it to his mom with the words, "Sunday is handled."

Then he dropped the little shrunken sock into his pocket, deciding he'd keep it as a prototype for a keychain or just as proof of what he'd figured out, and switched off the garage light.

Mya slid two photocopies across the dinner table, one in each hand, like she was dealing cards. "Dad, you're the British soldier. Mom, you're the colonial militiaman. Vada, read the time out loud."

Vada, still holding her fork, raised an eyebrow. "This is why you invited me to dinner?"

"Just read it."

Vada cleared her throat. "April morning, 1775, Lexington. Both witnesses say the same thing happened at the same spot. Both say the other side fired first."

"Right." Mya tapped the left page. "The British witness says a colonist hiding behind a wall fired first. The colonial witness says a British soldier fired first. Historians still don't know who actually fired that shot. Nobody does. Not after two hundred and fifty years." She looked around the table. "So here's my test. Dad, Mom, read your accounts out loud, but don't say which side is yours."

Her dad frowned but read. Her mom followed. Same green, same smoke, same crack of muskets in the pale light. Then they argued, gently, about who sounded like the villain of their page.

Mya leaned forward. "Which one is the British account?"

Her dad pointed to the right page. Her mom pointed to the left. Vada pointed at both and then pulled her hand back.

"You can't tell," Mya said. "That's the point. Each account is robust on its own. It has details, it sounds honest. It's only when you put them side by side that they contradict." She had spent three days on this, ever since Mr. Tran had handed the history club the two accounts and said only, "Notice whatever you notice." She'd assumed the answer would pop out. It hadn't. So tonight she'd built a test around a simple principle: if you strip away the labels, a fair reader still can't pick the truth.

Vada set down her fork, which she had been loading with rice the whole time. "Wait. This matters for my thing. For my essay." She pulled a crumpled assignment sheet from her pocket and smoothed it on the tablecloth. "I have to write about a fight on the bus last week. I was going to write what I saw. But Tanya told me the eighth graders started it, and she was sitting closer than me."

"So who started it?" Mya's dad asked.

"I don't know," Vada said slowly, like the words surprised her. "I was going to say the eighth graders, because that's what everyone says. But I only actually saw the middle of it." She looked at the photocopied pages, then at Mya. "Can I borrow these? I want to interview two people from the bus before I write anything."

Mya pushed both pages across. "Verify everything."

Her mom laughed and started stacking plates. Vada was already writing questions on the back of her napkin, and outside the window a streetlamp buzzed on.

Rosalie kept a small blue notebook under her mattress, and tonight she wrote in it with a flashlight: "Day 41. Nothing yet." Her older cousin had gotten her first period at ten, which had seemed ancient history until Rosalie turned twelve in March and started counting. The notebook was her way of testing a theory, though she hadn't called it that yet.

At Kenzo's house on Saturday, she found Kenzo and Daniyal at the kitchen table with a bowl of popcorn between them. Kenzo's older sister was on the phone in the hallway, laughing about something with her friend. Rosalie caught the words "my period" and looked away, feeling like she'd read someone's mail.

"My sister got hers at fourteen," Kenzo said, once the sister had wandered upstairs. "She was the last of her friends. She used to keep a calendar with little stars on it, like she was waiting for a bus that was always late."

"My sister got hers at ten," Rosalie said. "Ten."

Daniyal shrugged. "My mom's a nurse. She says there's this big CDC survey, like huge, thousands of girls, and the middle age, the median, is about twelve. But she said the normal range around it is really wide, so basically anytime is normal-normal." He ate a fistful of popcorn. "Which, if you think about it, means nobody can predict anything, which is the most annoying kind of fact."

Rosalie turned that over all the way home. A median of about twelve meant half the girls in her grade were probably before her and half after, and a wide range meant even ten and fourteen both fit inside normal. So her cousin being early told her nothing about herself, and neither did the notebook's forty-one empty days. The data was one thing she couldn't see directly, but she could test her own small piece of it. That night she made a treaty with herself: stop counting days, keep three supplies in her backpack, and act like it was a bus that would come whenever it came. Sealing the treaty required chocolate, so she ate the last of the Easter candy concealed behind the vegetable drawer, where her dad thought nobody looked.

On Monday she took the notebook out from under the mattress anyway. She didn't write a day number. Instead she wrote "wide range" and drew a crooked bus, then added a window with no driver in it, because the schedule was clearly not up to her. She slid the notebook into her backpack next to the supplies, zipped it shut, and went downstairs for breakfast.

Kenzo met her at the corner, agile as always, hopping the puddle from last night's rain. "Still waiting on the bus?" she asked.

"Stopped checking my watch," Rosalie said. "Want my fruit roll-up? I'm not hungry."

The bleachers in the gymnasium were folded against the wall, and the whole seventh grade sat on the floor in wobbly rows while Mr. Siddiqui set up the microphone at the free-throw line. James stood backstage with six other spellers, card number four pinned to his shirt, and watched Calla pace between the volleyball standards. She had beaten him in the classroom bee on the word "silhouette," and she had beaten him in the school bee last year on "camouflage." If she beat him today, it would be three years in a row, and that pattern felt like a rule he couldn't break.

Kingsley leaned against the stage curtain, chewing a straw. "You look like you're solving a math problem," he said.

"I am, sort of," James said. "Every time it comes down to me and Calla, she wins. I keep trying to figure out why."

"She reads more than you."

"That's not a reason, that's an insult." James pulled at his card. What he wanted wasn't just to win. He wanted to know whether the pattern was real or whether last year and the year before had been luck dressed up as destiny.

The bee began. A boy misspelled "legible," and a girl from second period went out on "gratitude." Mr. Siddiqui's voice rolled up into the rafters, calm as a radio announcer. When James stepped to the microphone, his first word was "retrieve," which meant to go and get something back, and he spelled it slowly, like he was carrying it a long way. Calla got "hereditary," as in a trait passed down through a family, and James thought, of course she did, like her winning was hereditary too.

By round nine it was only the two of them. Calla spelled "organism." James spelled "resilient." Round ten: she got "threshold," he got "vacant." Round eleven, round twelve. Mr. Siddiqui kept flipping to the last page of his word list, and James noticed something: the pronouncer's forehead was shiny, and the list was getting thin. The words weren't running out because the spellers were failing. They were running out because the spellers kept getting them right.

"I know what happens now," Kingsley whispered from the curtain, loud enough for James to hear. "In 2019 the Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. Eight of them. They just gave up and crowned everybody."

James felt something loosen in his chest. The pattern of Calla beating him wasn't a rule at all. It was just what had happened before, and what happened before could stop.

Round fourteen came. Calla spelled "turbulence" without a wobble. James stepped up and received "apparent," and spelled it with the double p and double r, and heard the bell stay silent.

Mr. Siddiqui looked at his final page, then at his watch, then out at the rows of seventh graders sitting cross-legged on the glossy floor. He cleared his throat. "Ladies and gentlemen," he said, "it appears we have two champions." He held up the nearly empty list like a referee holding up a card.

Calla turned to James and stuck out her hand. "Trophy's at the display case," she said. "I say we make them fit both our names on the little plaque."

Adam stood in front of a glass case in the history museum, staring at a small leather book with cracked binding. Inside was the diary of a settler named E. Hobbs, written in faded brown ink in 1873. His worksheet asked him to use a primary source to explain why people moved west, and he had forty minutes before the bus left.

"You're on your third paragraph of nothing," said Jan, leaning over his shoulder. Marie-Soleil was already scribbling on her own sheet two cases away.

"I don't get what the diary is supposed to tell me," Adam said. "It just says they crossed a river and a wheel broke."

Mr. Shevchenko, the museum guide, passed by and said, "Read like a detective. What does the writer notice? What does he never mention?" Then he moved on to help another group.

Adam bent closer. Hobbs counted his oxen, described the grass, mentioned his wife's cough. Then, on the fourth page, a line jumped out: "If we hold the claim five years, the land is ours, all one hundred and sixty acres, and no landlord can take it back."

Adam froze. He had seen that number before. Last summer, in his grandfather's attic, he had opened a tin box while looking for badminton rackets and found a stiff paper document with a wax seal. His grandfather had held it up to the window and said, "This is how our family got the farm." The paper had said the same thing, 160 acres, five years. Adam had thought it was trivial at the time, just an old receipt. Now he wondered if it was the whole answer.

He tried a small test. If land was the reason people moved, then the diary should mention land more than anything else. He made tallies in his notebook, a way to classify each entry: weather, repairs, illness, land. Land won, nine mentions against three for everything else.

"Marie-Soleil," he whispered, "does your diary mention the Homestead Act?"

She scanned her pages. "Mine calls it the Act. Same thing?"

"Maybe." Adam read again. Hobbs wrote about "filing at the land office" and "proving up." It fit, like a vessel filling with water, every line finding its level around one central fact: people moved west because the United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.

He wrote his answer, then copied Hobbs's exact sentence as evidence, including the broken wheel, because that detail showed how badly they wanted the land and kept going anyway.

On the bus, Adam texted his grandfather a photo of his finished worksheet. The reply came before the museum was out of sight: "Come by Saturday. I'll show you where the fence corners met, all four of them."

Parker slid his chair up to the table just as Mr. Martínez set a folded receipt in the middle of it. "Warm-up problem," Mr. Martínez said. "First team to crack it gets the window seats."

Anita grabbed the receipt before anyone else could. "This is my grandma's," she said. "From the taxi on Saturday. She thinks the driver overcharged her, and she wants proof." Her voice was tight. Anita did not like being wrong, and she liked losing even less.

Parker read over her shoulder. The paper showed a base charge of three dollars, then two dollars per kilometre, and a total of fifteen dollars at the bottom. Across the table, Jeremie was already scribbling guesses. "Five kilometres," he said. "Two times five is ten, plus three is thirteen. Close."

"Close is wrong," Anita said. She tried six. Two times six was twelve, and twelve plus three was fifteen. "It's six kilometres." She reached for Mr. Martínez's answer sheet, but Parker put his hand flat over it.

"Wait," he said. "You guessed it. Guessing won't work next time." He turned the receipt over and wrote in his most meticulous handwriting: 3 + 2k = 15. "My sister does this. You're allowed to take three off, but you have to take it off both sides, or the equals sign breaks." He drew a line down the middle of the equation. "It's like symmetry. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other."

Anita frowned at the line. "Both sides."

"Watch." He crossed out the three on the left, then crossed out a three on the right, turning fifteen into twelve. "Now it's just 2k equals twelve."

"So k is six," Jeremie said slowly. "Because two times six is twelve."

"Same answer," Anita admitted, "but his way doesn't depend on luck." She pulled the receipt back toward herself and checked the trip meter her grandmother had written on the back: 6 km. The numbers matched. Anita copied Parker's equation onto a fresh sheet, careful this time, and slid it into her folder. "I'm showing my grandmother tonight. She can take this to the company and ask for her money back if it doesn't match."

Mr. Martínez walked past, glanced at Parker's crossed-out threes, and gave a single nod. He did not disclose the answer on his sheet, but he did move two chairs to the window. "Window seats," he said. "Earned."

Parker sat down and looked at the equation still on the back of the receipt. Then he wrote a new one underneath, 3 + 2k = 21, just to see if the trick would hold twice.

Grandma's kitchen smelled like onion soup, which Ivy decided was perfect, since tonight the whole house was going to become a restaurant in Paris. Grandma had printed a menu, taped it to the pantry door, and put on her reading glasses, which apparently turned her into a French waiter. Ivy had a plan, too: by Sunday she wanted to order lunch in French on her class trip, all by herself, without her notebook.

"Bonsoir," Grandma said in a dramatic voice, gliding over with an invisible notepad. "What will Madame have?"

Ivy had practiced on the bus and in the bathtub, so she went first with the words she knew best. "Je veux le poulet," she said. "Et... combien ça coûte?"

Grandma's eyebrows shot up. She put one hand on her hip like an insulted actor. "Madame!" she gasped. "Out of my restaurant! We do not serve people who talk like that!"

Ivy sat back, staring at the pantry menu. She hadn't dropped a plate or used a wrong number; her question about cost had even come out smoothly. So the problem had to be hiding in the first sentence, in the tiny word "veux." It was the only part she'd changed since yesterday, when Grandma had smiled and poured her pretend water. She tested the idea, swapping in the other phrase from her worksheet. "Je voudrais le poulet, s'il vous plaît. Combien ça coûte?"

Grandma's whole face softened. "Ah, magnifique. Right this way, Madame." She scribbled on the air with her invisible pen.

"Wait," Ivy said, laughing. "That's it? One little word?"

Rose, who was watching through a video call propped against the sugar bowl, shook her head. "My brother told me that. 'Je voudrais' means 'I would like,' and 'Je veux' means 'I want.' One sounds polite and one sounds like you're demanding chicken."

"Like the chicken owes you money," Grandma added, straightening her glasses. She went to the counter and picked up a small paper bag from the pharmacy, tucking her prescription inside it so it wouldn't get lost in the restaurant chaos. Then she returned, calm and official, as if no one had ever been thrown out of a Paris bistro in her kitchen.

They ran the scene again, Ivy ordering soup, bread, and even dessert, asking the price each time. Grandma transmitted each imaginary dish to the imaginary kitchen with a little bow. When Ivy ordered her made-up chocolate mousse, she leaned forward and asked, very politely, whether it came with two spoons.

"Deux cuillères," Grandma said, and slid an empty bowl toward her with both hands.

Zoe had cancelled three appointments since September, and today the receptionist had refused to let her reschedule again. So now she sat in the waiting room of Dr. Iyer's office, gripping a magazine about dinosaurs that she wasn't reading. Beside her, Tia flipped through the same issue and read aloud that sauropods were the largest herbivores ever to walk the earth, which seemed to Zoe like a strange thing for a doctor's office to care about.

"You're doing that thing with your thumb," Tia said. "The wringing thing."

"I'm fine," Zoe said, and her thumb kept going.

The problem was needles. In September the shot had seemed like a small, ordinary thing, and she'd skipped it anyway because it was easier. In October just walking through the door had felt worse. By November she'd made her mother call and cancel from the car, and today her heart was doing something vigorous against her ribs, like it was trying to leave before she did. She had begun to suspect the dates mattered. She pulled out the little appointment card and checked: the three cancelled dates corresponded exactly to the three times the fear had grown bigger. Every time she ran away, the next time was scarier. She was teaching herself something, and it wasn't the right thing.

"That's backwards," she said out loud.

"What is?"

"I keep dodging it so I'll feel better, and I do, for like an hour. And then the next appointment is worse. It's like the dodging is the thing making it grow." She looked at the card. "I want to test it. Today I stay, and I look right at it. If I'm right, staying should make the next one easier."

Tia lowered the dinosaur magazine. "You're going to look at the needle? Voluntarily?"

"That's the experiment."

The nurse called her name before she could lose her nerve. In the exam room, Dr. Iyer was an older man with brisk, vigorous movements, snapping on gloves and swabbing Zoe's arm before she had finished sitting down. He asked about school, about sleep, about whether she worried a lot. She admitted she did, that her stomach dropped before every presentation, that she'd been skipping things. He said the words for it, anxiety and stress, the way he'd say asthma or a sprained ankle, and asked what she did to cope. "Not coming here," Zoe said, and told him her theory about the cancelled dates lined up with the fear getting worse each time.

"That lines up with what we see," Dr. Iyer said. He didn't make a speech about it. He just said, "Some things you can't outrun forever," and lifted the syringe.

Zoe kept her eyes open. She watched the whole thing, which lasted about four seconds and felt like a mosquito with better aim. Her body had braced for something enormous, and what arrived was small, and her body had no idea what to do with the mismatch.

"See?" Tia said in the hallway afterward, holding the door. "Nothing to it. I told you." Then Tia, who had given the speech about bravery, who had never skipped anything in her life, looked at Zoe's tiny bandaged arm, turned a spectacular grey colour, and sat straight down on the floor.

Zoe went to get the nurse, trying not to laugh, and heard herself say, "Don't worry. It only looks scary the first hundred times you look away."

Charles slid his stool closer to the lab bench, where Ms. Ramos had taped a photocopied periodic table beside the gas taps. The paper smelled faintly of toner, and the morning light caught the dust on the window fume hood. On the whiteboard she had written three questions, and the first one read: "How many protons does gold have?" Charles wanted the answer, because Ms. Ramos was keeping a leaderboard for the unit, and Kingston was already two points ahead of him.

He traced his finger along the rows of small boxes. Each box held a symbol, a name, and a number in the top corner, and at first the numbers looked random, like locker combinations. Then he noticed that gold's number, 79, matched a second smaller number printed below the symbol. He checked oxygen. Eight and eight. He checked carbon. Six and six. So the top number, the atomic number, was a key. If it told him the number of protons, he could find the protons for any element on the table without asking anyone.

He tested it in the margin of his notebook. Oxygen, eight protons. Iron, twenty-six. He was on neodymium when Kingston leaned over from the next bench. "You figured out the protons thing?" Kingston whispered. Charles nodded and covered his margin with his palm, because the rule felt like a treasure he wanted to keep for the quiz on Friday.

The room reminded him of the science museum his class had visited last fall. There had been a long timeline on the wall near the entrance, and Kaylie had stopped in front of an old chart with gaps in it, like a checkerboard missing squares. She had read the caption out loud. "Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869," she had said, and then she had counted the empty spaces with her finger. Charles remembered standing there thinking the table had always existed, complete, like a map of a country that was finished. Learning that it had once been smaller and unfinished had made the boxes on the classroom wall feel newer, almost fragile.

He went back to his sheet. Beside the modern table, Ms. Ramos had pinned a black-and-white copy of that old chart, its edges curling. Charles thought that Mendeleev must have reasoned the same way he just had, hunting for a pattern in numbers he could not see with his eyes, the way you could not see protons themselves, only the clues they left behind. In the corner of the lab, the red dot of the spectroscope laser blinked on and off as the student there adjusted her settings, and someone at the far bench laughed at a beaker that had turned an unexpected shade of green. Ms. Ramos had mentioned last week that some of the older equipment in the room, the wooden balance in the cabinet, was nearly obsolete, replaced by digital scales, though she still kept it because she liked it. Charles thought a table from 1869 was not like that. It had been modified over the years, boxes added, but the pattern underneath still worked, and the proof was right there in his margin, in his own careful rows of numbers.

He raised his hand for Ms. Ramos to check his answers, then lowered it again. Better to double-check one more element first, he decided, and he ran his finger along the bottom rows toward uranium.

The group chat lit up at 9:04 on a Tuesday night, right when Quinn had promised herself she would hibernate under her blanket until morning.

Matis: HAVE YOU SEEN THE NEW FROSTLINE DUNKS. Trennon Blake wears them. THE Trennon Blake.
Maxwell: those are so sick
Matis: everyone on the travel team is getting them. literally everyone. you'll be the only one in old shoes.
Quinn typed back: How much?
Matis: 180
Quinn: one hundred eighty dollars because a basketball player wears them?

She set her phone down, then picked it up again. Matis had been saving allowance money since June for a new skateboard, and now every dollar was about to march off toward sneakers. Something about it bugged her, the way a wrong answer bugs you before you figure out why it's wrong.

Quinn: question. did Trennon Blake pick those shoes himself?
Matis: he obviously picked them, they're HIS signature
Maxwell: wait my cousin works at the sports store. she says the company designs them and pays him to wear them
Matis: paid?? source??
Maxwell: she showed me a magazine ad once. it says "Trennon Blake" in tiny letters at the bottom but under that it says he's paid to be in it
Quinn: so it's a testimonial. a famous person endorsing something, even if they don't actually know anything special about it, and they might be getting paid.
Matis: he's a BASKETBALL PLAYER. he knows shoes.
Quinn: does he know shoemaking? or just running around in them like everybody else?

There was a long pause, three dots appearing and vanishing. Quinn decided to run a test, the way Mr. Lombardi had them test ideas in science. She sent a screenshot of the shoe ad next to a screenshot of another ad, one where a famous singer held a brand of motor oil.

Quinn: would you buy motor oil because she says so?
Matis: no that's dumb, she's a singer
Quinn: so why shoes because he says so?
Maxwell: yo

The chat went quiet again. Quinn chewed her thumbnail. She hadn't meant to embarrass Matis in front of Maxwell, and for a second she worried she had. Then she sent one more message, careful this time.

Quinn: I'm not saying they're bad shoes. I'm saying "everyone has them" isn't a reason, and "Trennon Blake wears them" isn't either. we could look up actual reviews. like, systematic. read twenty of them and count how many mention the heel falling apart.
Matis: ...fine. do it at lunch.

At lunch the next day, Matis slid his tray down next to hers with the dignity of someone who had lost an argument but refused to admit it out loud. "Seventeen out of twenty," he muttered, pulling out his phone. "Seventeen reviews say the heel wears out in three months."

"Maxwell's cousin says the old model lasted a year," Quinn said, "for half the price."

Matis stared at the screen for a long moment. Then he opened his banking app, the one where his skateboard fund lived, and looked at the number for a while.

"Okay," he said. "New plan." He tapped the screen twice, like casting a ballot in an election only he could vote in. "Skateboard first. Shoes when these ones actually fall apart." He paused, then grinned. "And when they do, I'm getting whatever brand Maxwell's cousin says lasts longest, not whatever Trennon Blake gets paid to jump in."

Quinn raised her chocolate milk. "To evidence."

"To evidence," Matis said, and clinked his juice box against it.

The church smelled of pine polish and lilies, and the wooden pew creaked every time Taylor shifted her weight. On the folding table near the front sat a photograph of Grandma June holding a garden trowel, her hat crooked as always. Taylor's mother had asked her last night, quietly, if she would say a few words at the service, and Taylor had said yes before she could think too hard about it. Now the program in her hands felt like a live thing.

At the top of the program, in sparse gold lettering, was the word eulogy. She turned the paper over, turned it back, and stared at it. Kassidy slid into the pew beside her, tugging her skirt straight. "You still don't have one?" Kassidy whispered. "A memory. You said you'd pick one by this morning."

"I had nine this morning," Taylor whispered back. "Now I have none. They're all too small. She taught me to whistle through grass. That's not a speech." Her throat tightened, and she told herself the prickle behind her eyes was just a hormone thing, the way Kadence's older sister was always saying, crying over nothing, and she blinked hard until the front of the church came back into focus.

After the first hymn, Ms. Romano, who had been Grandma June's neighbor for twenty years, walked to the lectern. "I learned something from June years ago," she said. "She was the only person on our street who knew where words came from. She told me a eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died, and the word comes from Greek roots meaning to speak well of." She smiled down at Taylor for a second, then went on, but Taylor had stopped hearing the rest.

Speak well of. That was it, she realized. Not a list of accomplishments, not the biggest moment. The rule hiding inside the word itself. Her grandmother collected words the way some people acquired teacups, dusting them off, showing them to anybody who stood still long enough. Taylor suddenly knew which memory to pick, and she knew how to test it. She leaned toward Kassidy. "When I go up there, listen for whether I'm praising her or just listing stuff. If I'm listing, kick the pew."

"You're going up there?" Kassidy's voice cracked. "You have to tell Kadence, she's been dying to hear what you picked." Two rows ahead, Kadence twisted around, and Taylor held up the program and pointed at the word eulogy. Kadence frowned, then shrugged. Kassidy cupped her hands around her mouth. "Greek," she whispered loudly. "It means speak well of."

Kadence nodded slowly, like a puzzle piece had dropped into place for her too.

When Ms. Romano finished, the pastor called Taylor's name. Her knees felt borrowed, but she walked up anyway, and the lectern smelled like lemon cleaner and old varnish. "My grandma taught me words," she said, and her voice wobbled, then steadied. "She said whistling through a blade of grass was a lost art, and she made me practice until I got it, and when I finally did, she said, well of me. She said it exactly like that, like it was an old phrase. So here's the grass, and here's the whistle." She pulled a fat blade from her pocket, set it between her thumbs, and blew until a thin, reedy note floated up into the rafters, where the pine smell and the dust motes hung together in the light.

From the third pew, Kassidy kicked the wood once, softly, and Kadence was laughing and crying at the same time. Taylor folded the grass blade back into her pocket and said, "That one's for you, Grandma."

Mila pulled a sweater the exact green-gray of lichen off the rack and held it up, but she wasn't really seeing it. In her head she was already in the gym next Friday, under the paper streamers, with everyone watching her stand stiff as a fence post while the music played. She could not dance. That was the whole problem, and no amount of shopping was going to fix it.

"Try the blue one," said Kierra, who was holding three dresses over one arm like she was on a mission. "Blue is authentic. It looks like it came from your grandmother's closet on purpose."

Antony, who had been dragged along and kept drifting toward the shoe section, held up his phone. "Okay, you two have to see this before you decide anything." He turned the screen toward them. On it, a white cockatoo with a yellow crest was bobbing its head and lifting its feet, clearly dancing. "His name's Snowball," Antony said. "He's a sulphur-crested cockatoo. In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed he could move in time to music. And when they sped the song up or slowed it down, he adjusted. He matched the new tempo."

Mila leaned closer. The bird wasn't just twitching. It was stepping left, right, swaying, landing on the beat. "Wait. Really? A bird?"

Kierra lowered the dresses. "If a bird can keep the beat, Mila, you can keep the beat."

Mila thought about that. Snowball couldn't read a dance manual. Nobody taught him steps. He heard the music and moved with it, and when the tempo changed, he changed too. Maybe keeping the beat was the actual secret, and everything else was decoration. There was only one way to find out. "Antony," she said, "play a song. Any song."

He started something fast, and Mila stood there in the aisle between the racks, shifting her weight side to side, counting the pulse under the music. One-two, one-two. When Antony secretly thumbed the speed control and slowed the song down, her swaying slowed with it, and when he cranked it up again, she caught back up, laughing now, half a step behind and then locked on.

"Ha!" Antony said. "It worked. You adjusted, like Snowball."

"It worked," Mila agreed, still moving. The stiff fence post in her imagination had turned into a person who could find a rhythm and hold it.

At the register, Kierra and Mila disagreed over which dress to buy, and Mila's mom, who had been waiting by the mirrors, mediated by suggesting they flip a coin. Kierra won the coin toss, but then she studied the blue dress again and changed her mind. "Actually, get the one you picked. You were the one dancing in it." Antony, who had sworn he would never go to the dance, tapped his phone and said, "Save me a song. Something with a tempo I can adjust to."

The morning they landed at the beach, Luca felt perfect. Ten hours on a plane, a whole ocean behind them, and he had slept fine and eaten the weird airplane noodles and even helped carry his little sister's bag. "Jet lag," his dad had warned before they left, "it'll get you." But it never did. On the second day Luca and Mira, the girl from the rental house next door, dug a moat around a lopsided sandcastle and gave it a guard made from a stick wearing a shell hat. "He's a peasant," Mira decided, patting the stick into the wet sand. "He guards the castle but nobody ever thanks him." Luca added a second stick beside him, defiant against the incoming tide, and they laughed when the water flattened both guards and the peasant's shell hat floated away.

The trip went too fast. Luca postponed packing until the last night because, he told himself, a packed suitcase meant the trip was really ending. When the taxi came, Mira ran down the sand barefoot to hand him the shell hat. "For the peasant's replacement," she said, and her ears went pink.

They flew home the next day, east, back over the same ocean. And this time Luca felt wrecked. At the beach he had bounced out of bed at dawn; now, home, he lay staring at the ceiling at two in the morning, wide awake, then couldn't drag himself up when morning actually came. His stomach grumbled at the wrong hours. He was grumpy at breakfast, sleepy at lunch, alert at midnight. "What's wrong with me?" he complained to his mom. "It was the same length flight both ways."

That was the part that bugged him. Same plane, same hours, same ocean, but only one direction had flattened him. He got a pencil and drew two arrows across a sketch of the world in his notebook, one pointing left to the beach and one pointing right to home, and stared at them until his eyes hurt. On the fourth sleepless night he found Mira online and told her his theory. "Going out, we flew west. Coming home, east. Same distance. So it can't be the flying itself."

Mira sent back a link from her own search, then a single line: "It says most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west." Luca read it twice, then checked a second site, then a third. All the same. It wasn't the plane, or the hours, or the noodles. It was the direction, and somehow he'd been lucky on the way out.

He took the shell hat out of his backpack and set it on his windowsill, ragged edge facing east. Somewhere behind the rooftops, past the whole dark ocean, the tide would be crawling up the ruined castle. "Guard it," Luca told the shell, and turned off his lamp.

Levi slouched in front of the computer, clicking through a website his science teacher had assigned. The banner at the top said "MiracleGroMax: Doubles Your Tomato Yield, Guaranteed!" Below it, a farmer held an enormous tomato in both hands like a trophy. Levi leaned closer. He had a science project due Friday about claims and evidence, and this ad seemed too good to be true.

He scrolled down and found a testimonial from a man in Ohio who said he'd used the fertilizer and grown the biggest tomatoes of his life. "See, it works," Levi muttered, then stopped himself. One man's story wasn't the same as a tested claim. He remembered the unit on agriculture from class, the part about ancient farmers who saved seeds from their best plants, and how scientists later figured out which fertilizers actually helped by running careful trials. One farmer's lucky season could be good weather, rich soil, or plain luck.

He opened a chat window and typed, "Kassandra, you awake?"

"Barely," she wrote back. "What?"

"MiracleGroMax. The ad shows one farmer. How would they actually know it works?"

"Test it?" she suggested.

Levi thought about that. He imagined two identical pots of tomato seedlings on his windowsill. If he gave one pot the fertilizer and the other pot nothing, that would be a mess, because the fertilized pot might also get more sunlight by accident, or better soil. Then it hit him: the pot without the fertilizer had to get everything else exactly the same. Same soil, same water, same spot on the sill. He typed quickly, describing both pots, and added, "The one without fertilizer is called a control group."

"Like in class," Kassandra wrote. "Mr. Kovalenko would be proud."

Blaine joined the chat a minute later. "Just spray it on everything and see if stuff grows," he typed, which made Levi grin. He explained why that wouldn't tell you anything, because without a control you couldn't link the growth to the fertilizer itself. Any difference between the two groups had to come from that one thing, the fertilizer, if everything else stayed identical. Blaine sent back a thumbs up and, "Okay, I get it. Buy two pots."

The next morning Levi placed the pots side by side, labeled A and B, and measured each seedling with a ruler. "Thirty days," he told them. "Then we'll know." He watered both with the same small cup, set the fertilizer packet beside pot A, and took a photo to transmit to Mr. Kovalenko for approval. His phone buzzed with Kassandra's reply to the morning's picture before he even sat down: "My mom just bought the same fertilizer for her whole garden. All of it."

The poster outside Mr. García's classroom showed the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and the afternoon sun through the hallway window refracted off its plastic covering, scattering small bright patches across the words. Alexa stopped to read it for the third time that week, because on Friday every student had to stand up and explain one Charter right in their own words, and she still did not have hers.

"Still hunting?" Adnan asked, coming down the hall with his debate binder under his arm. He already knew his: the right to a lawyer, which he planned to deliver like a courtroom speech, since the debate team had a tournament next month and he wanted the practice.

"It's not the explaining that's stuck," Alexa said. She tapped the bottom corner of the poster, where a date sat in small print. "April 17, 1982. That's when the Charter became part of Canada's Constitution." She frowned at it. "Before that, what did people have? Nothing? Something else?"

"You could just pick section seven and be done," Adnan said. "Everyone does section seven. It's the conventional choice."

"That's why I don't want it." She copied the date into her notebook and stared at it while the light shifted on the glass. Her idea was simple: if the Charter had a birthday, then something must have existed before the birthday, the way a house exists before the renovation. She wanted to test it.

In the library she found a thick blue book on government, and Adnan found her there twenty minutes later, hunched over the index. "You were right to wonder," she said. "Before 1982 it wasn't that people had no rights at all. But the Charter, this exact list, only came in when it was proclaimed that day in April." She turned the book so he could see the printed date. "So when I explain my right, I can say it's written down in the Constitution, and that's been true since 1982. Before that, the same words didn't exist anywhere."

Adnan slid into the chair across from her. "Fine, but which right?"

Alexa pointed to the section on life, liberty and security of person, and under it the line about a fair hearing within a reasonable time. "This one. In my own words: the government can't just decide things about you in the dark. If it comes after you, you get to see the case, face your adversary, and answer back."

"That's yours," Adnan admitted. "I'm keeping the lawyer one."

On Friday, when her turn came, Alexa stood in front of the poster, the sunlight still moving across the plastic, and said the date first: "April 17, 1982, the day the Charter became part of the Constitution."

Hannah slumped into a chair at the public library and spread her materials across the table: three books about South Asia, a printed article, and a note from Mr. Vargas that said, in red ink, "Your explanation of the monsoon is still wrong. Presentation Thursday. Try again."

The problem was that nobody in her sources came out and said why the rain arrived. They all agreed it did. One book had a picture of farmers wading through flooded rice paddies, and one had a diagram with big curved arrows, but the arrows just floated there like decorations. Kendrick dropped into the chair across from her and stole a grape from her snack bag.

"Still fighting the weather?" he asked.

"It fights back," Hannah said. "Mr. Vargas prohibited us from just reading our slides out loud, so I actually have to understand this thing." She pushed the diagram toward him. "Look. The arrows point from the ocean toward the land. In summer. Why would air do that?"

Kendrick squinted. "Air has somewhere better to be?"

Hannah laughed, then stopped laughing, because that was actually a thought. She flipped to the section on land and sea and read it twice. "Okay," she said slowly. "In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean." She put one hand flat on the table, like the land, and curved the other over her water bottle, like the sea. "So the land gets hot, hot air rises over the land, and then moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it." She dragged her curved hand toward her flat one. "That's the arrow. The ocean air is wet. It comes in, and it rains."

"That's it?" Kendrick said.

"That has to be it. It explains why the rain arrives right when the heat is worst. My cousin in India always complains about exactly that." She checked the clock above the reference desk and winced. The library closed in forty minutes, and her rough draft was one wrong sentence away from nothing. Brady arrived, out of breath, with a bag of rice from the school supplies box for their model, and for ten minutes they poured and swept and poured again while Hannah talked through her hands, summer after summer, ocean air flowing in and falling as rain onto the rice.

On the walk home, Hannah held her notes against the wind. "It matters," she said. "The rice needs that flood. Farmers plan everything around it." She grinned. "Kendrick, you fixed my whole presentation with one dumb joke."

"It's a gift," he said, and held the door.

Nicholas had never done his own laundry before, and he was determined to get it right. His mother was home sick with a fever, and the basket in the hallway had grown into a small mountain, so he carried it three blocks to Mr. Hussain's laundromat with a list in his pocket: sort, wash, dry, fold. His friend Romane came along because her own wash was backed up too, and because she wanted the good dryer, the one near the window that she claimed ran hotter than the rest.

First came sorting. Nicholas spread the clothes across two plastic tables and tried to distinguish the darks from the lights, which was easy until he reached a grey towel that seemed to belong to both piles. Romane leaned over, plucked a red sock from his whites pile, and waved it like evidence. "This turns everything pink," she said. "Trust me. My whole soccer uniform is rose coloured now." He moved the sock, then checked a shirt pocket and found a crumpled receipt and one dime, which he pocketed with a small sense of victory.

While the first load sloshed, Nicholas scrubbed a table where somebody had spilled something sticky. Under the sink he found two spray bottles, one marked chlorine bleach and the other marked glass cleaner with ammonia. He was about to pour a splash of bleach into the cleaner bottle to make one super cleaner when Mr. Hussain hurried over from the counter. "Stop," he said, holding up both hands. "Never mix those two."

Nicholas read the labels again, frowning. "Why not?" he asked, because the warning on the back only said do not mix with ammonia-containing products, which told him nothing.

Romane pulled out her phone, typed for a moment, and held up the screen. "It says here chlorine bleach mixed with ammonia-containing cleaners releases chloramine, and it's a toxic gas." She looked from one bottle to the other. "So if you'd poured them together, we'd all be coughing out on the sidewalk." Nicholas set the bleach down slowly, the way he might set down something with teeth. He had been about to mix two ordinary cleaning bottles, the kind of thing that looked harmless, and the danger had been completely invisible until the words on the labels connected.

Right then the lights flickered and died, and the washing machines shuddered into silence. Mr. Hussain groaned, then disappeared through a back door, and a moment later a generator roared to life somewhere behind the wall. The machines woke up one by one, drumming again, and the laundromat filled with warm humid air that smelled of soap. Romane got her dryer by the window after all, and she did a little diagonal dance across the tiles in celebration.

When everything was dry, Nicholas folded his mother's shirts the way she liked, sleeves crossed over, then folded in half, and stacked them so the edges lined up straight. He kept back her softest blanket and a clean pillowcase for her fever, and on the way home he stopped at the corner store for lemon tea. Romane carried the basket up the stairs for him, and he pushed open the apartment door with his shoulder. "Mom," he called, "your laundry's done, and I brought tea."

The rumor reached David on Tuesday, in the locker room before practice, when a teammate said Riverside's best runner had been declared ineligible for Saturday's meet. "My cousin heard it from somebody who goes there," the teammate said. "They're going to have to forfeit." David wanted it to be true so badly he could taste it. Riverside had beaten his school three years in a row, and the thought of them losing without a race even being run made him grin all through warm-ups. He told Aiyana about it at lunch, and he told Hailee, and by Wednesday half the eighth grade was repeating it as fact.

Aiyana was the one who frowned. "Who actually checked?" she asked. "Not who heard it. Who checked?" David shrugged, but the question stuck to him like burrs on a sock. He realized he had passed the story along without asking a single question, which was, he had to admit, a little reckless. He also realized something stranger: when Hailee had said the rumor might be wrong, he had felt annoyed, as if she were taking Riverside's side. That feeling seemed worth investigating.

On Thursday he found the Riverside roster online, and there was the runner's name, still listed, with a time from a meet held the previous Saturday. Then he found the league rules, which said eligibility was reviewed before the season, not during it. The roster and the rumor couldn't both be true. One of them was a flat contradiction, and only one of them came from a person he could message. He sent a note to the Riverside student council page, feeling a bit foolish, and by that evening a reply came back: the runner was fine, the rumor had started as a joke in a group chat.

"You know there's a name for what you did," Aiyana said on Friday, when he told her. "Confirmation bias. You believed it because it fit what you already wanted." David winced, but she said it without smugness, just handing him the word the way you hand someone a bandage.

The hard part came after. At practice he had to stand in front of teammates and say the story wasn't true, and a couple of them looked at him like he'd ruined something. One boy muttered that it might still be true, that Riverside was probably hiding it, and David recognized that exact feeling, the one that wants the good news so much it refuses the bad.

Saturday came, and Riverside won again, their runner crossing the line four seconds ahead of David. He stood at the fence afterward, breathing hard, watching the other team celebrate. Aiyana handed him his water bottle. "Next rumor," she said, "we check first." He nodded, still watching the runner, who was doing a victory lap he had absolutely earned.

The bus jolted over the railway tracks, and Laurence's word list nearly slid off her knee. She caught it and kept drilling. The regional bee was in forty minutes, and Sydney had already beaten her twice on "pronunciation," which was frankly humiliating.

"Give me one from the bonus sheet," she said.

Morgan flipped the pages, hunting. "Here. Color. C-O-L-O-U-R."

"That's wrong," Laurence said.

"It is not." Morgan held the sheet like evidence in court. "My cousin lives in Ottawa. She spells it colour every day at school and gets full marks. Your way is the wrong one, or hers is, and it's not hers."

Laurence stared at the two spellings side by side. They couldn't both be right for the same bee, which meant somewhere there was a rule deciding which one counted here, and she didn't know it. She took out her phone, and after a minute of searching while the bus made an abrupt turn that nearly dissolved her grip on the seat, she found it.

"Noah Webster," she read. "In 1828 he published the American Dictionary of the English Language, and he pushed simpler spellings. Color instead of colour. His versions became standard in the United States."

Morgan leaned over. "So in Canada it's still the old way?"

"Looks like it. So your cousin isn't wrong. She's just not spelling for this bee." Laurence set the phone down. "That means the judges here want Webster's version. Color, no u." It was an adaptation, she thought, words changing shape for a new country, and now she knew which shape to use. She wrote it three times on the back of her hand in marker that she hoped wouldn't sweat off.

Morgan was quiet for a stop or two. "I've been telling my cousin her spelling is backwards for two years," Morgan finally said. "I owe her a phone call and probably an apology."

"You can call after I win." Sydney, two rows back, snorted at that, and Laurence turned around in her seat. "You want to test me on it right now?"

"Fine," Sydney said. "Spell it."

Laurence took a breath. "C-O-L-O-R. Color."

Sydney's marker tapped twice against the seat, keeping score.

Ava stood in the food court of the mall, phone hot in her hand, staring at a photo she had posted two days ago: her and Romain goofing around in front of the fountain, with the caption about her audition for the jazz ensemble. Her account was private. She had checked the setting twice. Yet the photo was here, on a stranger's page, reposted with a caption that said, "Found this kid who thinks she can play trumpet."

"Okay, breathe," said Ahmad, sliding into the seat across from her with a tray of nachos. "Tell me the whole thing, from the start. Don't jump around."

Ava forced herself to slow down. She described accepting a follower request a month ago from someone with the username lkelly_04, someone she vaguely remembered from a summer recreation program. Then the audition, then the post, then this. Ahmad tilted his head. "So your page is private, but they follow you."

"That's it," Ava said, and the pieces began to fit together like the sections of a symmetrical origami shape she'd folded in art class: two halves she had thought matched, but one side had a fold she'd missed. "Private means people who don't follow me can't see it. But anyone I already accepted can see everything, and they can take a screenshot and post it wherever they want. It's like the greenhouse Ms. Tesfaye showed us when we studied agriculture. The walls keep most things out, but anything already inside can carry seeds back out."

Ahmad wiped cheese off his fingers. "So lkelly_04 saw it and forwarded it."

"Only one way to test that," Ava said. She posted a new photo, a boring shot of her sneakers, and waited. Ninety minutes later, it appeared on the stranger's page too, same angle, same gray laces. "Confirmed," she whispered. She unfollowed and removed lkelly_04, reported the page, and asked Romain to do the same with any follower he barely knew.

Then came the part that actually helped. Ava messaged the stranger directly: "This is my photo, posted from a private account, and I did not agree to share it." The stranger's page vanished within an hour. When she told Ms. Tesfaye about it at the music room the next afternoon, Ms. Tesfaye nodded slowly and said, "You decomposed the problem instead of panicking. That's exactly how I want you to approach a difficult passage in your audition piece, too."

At the audition on Saturday, Ava lifted her trumpet, the metal cool against her lips. In the third row of chairs, Romain gave her a thumbs up, and beside him Ahmad held up his phone with a note on the screen that read: Playing for us, not for strangers. Ava smiled, took a breath, and began.

Jordan blew his nose, dropped the tissue in the trash can by the couch, and counted. That was the ninth one since breakfast. Tomorrow was Elisha's birthday party, the one with the pizza and the rooftop terrace, and he was not going to miss it over a runny nose. The problem was his mother, who stood in the doorway with a thermometer like a guard holding a key.

"I'm fine," he said. "It's basically gone."

"You were shivering last night." She checked the thermometer again even though she'd already read it. "You have the constitution of a wet paper towel in this family. Every cold finds you."

"It's not every cold. It's one cold."

She went back to the kitchen, and Jordan picked up his phone. He texted Leanna, because Leanna had been sick two weeks ago, right before he was, and they'd shared a booth at the pizza place the day she came back. If they'd had the same thing, then why was he sick now and she wasn't again? He typed, "what were your symptoms," and waited, sniffling, until the three dots appeared.

"Sore throat, fever, couldn't swallow," she wrote. "Why?"

His throat was fine. His was all nose and cough. Weird. He opened the laptop on the coffee table and searched why no cold vaccine. The first result made him sit up. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold. Not two, not ten. More than two hundred. And the most frequent cause was something called rhinoviruses. He said the word out loud to the empty living room. "Rhinoviruses."

He called Leanna. "You gave me your cold," he said when she picked up.

"I got better two weeks ago. You can't catch it from me now."

"That's what I mean. We probably didn't even have the same one." He walked to the window with the phone wedged against his shoulder, watching the street. "There's more than 200 different viruses that cause colds. Rhinoviruses are the most common. Your sore throat thing could be one virus and my nose thing could be a different one entirely. That's why there's no single shot for it. You'd need like two hundred shots."

"So you're saying it's not my fault?"

"I'm saying I can't prove it's your fault."

"That's the most romantic thing you've ever told me."

He laughed, then coughed, then laughed again. Here was the part that mattered. He grabbed a notebook from his backpack and wrote a plan: fluids, rest, no staying up, extra vitamin whatever was in the kitchen. He incorporated a walk around the block at four o'clock, because he'd read that light movement helped and he needed to prove to his mother he could function. The fever reading was crucial; if it was gone by morning and he kept the plan tonight, he had a case.

At dinner he set the notebook next to his plate. His mother read it, chewing slowly.

"A walk?" she said. "Tonight?"

"Thirty minutes. Then straight to bed."

She looked at the thermometer on the counter, then at him. "If you have no fever at seven a.m.," she said, "we'll talk about the party."

Jordan was already writing seven a.m. at the bottom of the page.

Liam sat at Milania's kitchen table with her laptop open in front of him, a paper list of numbers beside it. They were counting bird sightings for Ms. Teo's science project, and Milania had volunteered her house, her laptop, and her mother's promise of pizza afterward. "You put the numbers in column B," she said, peeling an orange. "Then you make the computer add them."

"I don't know how to make a computer do anything," Liam said. He typed the sightings anyway, ten rows of them, then found the SUM button in the toolbar. The cell filled itself in, and he copied it to the total row the way the menu suggested. Except the cell where the answer should have been didn't show a number. It showed SUM(B2:B10), plain letters sitting there like a label.

"That's not a total," Milania said, leaning over his shoulder. "That's just words." She tried clicking things, then deleted the cell and retyped it by hand, letter by letter, and the same words came back. Liam stared at it. The cell wasn't refusing to add; it was treating his formula like an ordinary sentence. Somewhere in the program there had to be a signal, some mark that told the cell to calculate instead of just display. He thought about the first cell, the one the toolbar had filled in before he copied it, and scrolled up to look.

The original cell started with an equals sign. His retyped version didn't. He deleted his text, typed the equals sign first, then SUM(B2:B10), and the number 47 appeared instantly. "Every formula starts with the equals sign," he said. "Without it, the cell just shows what you typed." Milania slapped the table. "So the equals sign is like raising your hand. It's how the cell knows you're talking to it." They made the bar chart next, and Liam kept adjusting the chart type until the bars came out symmetrical, ten even columns across the screen, one for each day of counting.

Ms. Teo's class would see the chart on Monday, and it looked good, better than good. But Milania's mother called from the hallway that pizza was ready, and Liam understood, watching Milania close the laptop lid over his chart, that the project was shared now, and the grade would be shared too, even though he was the one who had found the equals sign. Her father's colleague had donated the binoculars they'd used, and Milania reminded him of that twice on the way to the kitchen. At the table she slid the biggest slice onto his plate without a word, and Liam, chewing, kept seeing the chart behind his eyes, the bars rising evenly, and hers.

The gym doors opened at 7:20, and the cold air hit Ellie like a wall. "This place is a tundra," Nizar said, rubbing his arms as they walked in. The banners above the far hoop portrayed a snarling wolf, the school mascot, and Ellie looked at it while she laced her shoes. Day one of tryouts. Twelve girls, ten roster spots.

Monday's drills were all new: lunges across the length of the court, defensive slides, box jumps until their legs shook. Ellie went home tired but fine. She texted Nizar that she felt great and went to bed early.

Tuesday morning, she reached the school stairs and stopped halfway up. Her thighs burned so badly she had to take the last steps sideways, one hand on the rail. In the hallway she found Nizar gripping a water fountain, wincing. "I thought I pulled something," he said. "I felt fine yesterday." Ellie lowered herself onto the bench beside him and thought it through. She hadn't fallen, hadn't twisted anything. Every girl who had lunged hard on Monday was walking like a robot today. The two returning players, who had done these drills all last season, moved fine. It wasn't injury. It was something about doing an unfamiliar workout.

"You'd know if you tore something," said Lexy, dropping onto the bench's other end. Lexy was a guard, quick and loud, and she wanted the last spot badly; everyone knew it. "My sister gets it every season. It's called delayed onset muscle soreness. Nobody's immune." She stood, tested her knees with a squat, and winced. "Worst between 24 and 72 hours after. So tomorrow will be even uglier."

Ellie filed that away and made a plan. In the gym, while the others jogged stiffly, she did a long, slow warm-up, then spent the drills choosing her moments instead of chasing every ball. When a loose rebound bounced toward the sideline in the last scrimmage, she didn't sprint for it; she angled, cut off the passing lane, and stole the outlet pass instead. The layup was easy. Mr. González blew his whistle. "Ellie, switch to the first group."

Lexy's head turned at the call. They both knew what the first group meant.

At the end of practice, Mr. González read the names for Wednesday's final session. Ellie heard hers, then Lexy's, then Nizar's, though Nizar only made the manager list and stood there holding the clipboard like it might break. Lexy walked over to Ellie by the door, still moving carefully, and put out her fist. "Last spot tomorrow," she said. "May the least sore legs win."

Nicolas was sitting on Priya's bedroom floor with her phone balanced on his knee when she yanked it back and stared at the screen like it had insulted her.

"Look at this," she said. "Benson texted me an hour ago, 'Are you still coming to the game?' and I wrote back 'Yeah' and he sent 'Okay.' With a period. Capital O, whole word, period." She dropped the phone on the rug between them. "That's angry. That's the angriest text I've ever gotten in my life."

Nicolas picked it up and read the exchange twice. "It just says okay."

"Exactly. It says okay like a door slamming."

He looked at the little row of messages above it, from earlier that day, when everything seemed fine. Priya had sent Benson a joke about their science teacher, Mr. Clarke, and Benson had replied "haha" with no punctuation at all, then "you coming tonight?" also with nothing. Both of those texts had felt friendly. Only the last one had the period. Nicolas drummed his fingers on the carpet. Maybe it wasn't what Benson said but how it looked on the screen. He thought about how his mom signed her work emails with full sentences and periods, all formal, while his friends never used periods at all.

"Let's test it," he said. "Send me a text. Same word, twice."

Priya grabbed her phone, pulled up Nicolas's contact, and sent "fine" with nothing after it, then "Fine." with the period. Nicolas watched both arrive on his own phone. He read them out loud. The first one sounded like fine. The second one somehow sounded like it had a temper behind it, though it was the same four letters sitting on the same screen.

"I think the period is doing it," he said. "It's not you being paranoid."

He typed "why do periods in texts sound mad" into the search bar, and after a minute of scrolling he found something from Binghamton University. "Listen," he said. "Researchers there did a study in 2016. Messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one." He read it again to make sure he had it right. "Same message, exactly the same, and the one with the period loses."

"So Benson isn't mad at me?"

"He might not be. He might just punctuate like a grown-up." Nicolas thought of Mr. Clarke, who put periods in every text he sent the debate team, even "See you Tuesday." Everyone used to joke about it. Nobody had actually thought Mr. Clarke was furious at all of them.

Priya's worry seemed to evaporate a little, though not entirely. The whole evening hinged on whether she showed up at the game or sat home rereading one punctuation mark. She started typing, deleted it, and typed again. Then she handed the phone to Nicolas so he could see before she hit send.

"Okay!! coming at 7, save me a seat"

She pressed send, and they watched the three dots appear almost immediately.

The note was taped to Ms. Berg's refrigerator, right above the handle where Hudson could not miss it. "Back by nine sharp. Owen's bedtime is eight. There's mac and cheese in the fridge. He's been fussy when we leave, but don't worry. We'll pay you double for the trouble. The Bergs." Hudson read it twice, then looked at Owen, who was eleven months old and banging a spoon on the high chair tray like it owed him money.

The trouble started the second Ms. Berg and her husband picked up their coats. Owen stopped mid-bang. His face crumpled, and the scream that came out of him was enormous, way too big for such a small person. The front door clicked shut behind them and Hudson stood in the kitchen holding a plastic spoon, feeling like the worst babysitter in the history of the world. He checked the note again, as if it might have grown a new paragraph of instructions. It had not. Seven thirty-five. Owen was supposed to be asleep by eight, and at this rate he would still be screaming when he turned forty.

Hudson presumed Owen was hungry or hurt, but the screaming did not sound like either. It sounded like grief. Then he remembered his cousin's baby, and something his aunt had said at Thanksgiving while everyone else was eating pie. He texted his cousin Chanel, who babysat all the time: "Baby losing it when parents left. Normal?" Her reply buzzed back fast: "Totally. It's called separation anxiety. It's a normal stage. Starts around the second half of the first year." Hudson stared at the message. Owen was eleven months old, which fit, and it was normal, which meant it was not his fault. Best of all, Chanel added one more line: "Distraction works. Try something new."

So Hudson tested it. He did not try food, because food was not new. Instead he pulled the colander out of the drawer, put it on his own head like a helmet, and marched around the kitchen table while humming the wrong notes to a song he half knew. Owen hiccupped, sniffled, and stared. Hudson marched the other direction. Owen made a sound halfway between a sob and a laugh. By the third lap the crying was gone entirely, replaced by a squeaky giggle that Hudson would have felt proud of if the colander strap were not cutting into his ears.

Owen fell asleep at 7:58, two minutes to spare, and Hudson lowered him into the crib with the concentration of a bomb technician. Then he sat in the kitchen and ate the mac and cheese alone, and found it tasted like being trusted with something that mattered. When the Bergs came home at nine and pressed the extra money into his hand, Ms. Berg said, "You'll babysit again? Permanently, we hope?" Hudson said yes. He did not mention that he would miss his Saturday nights, or that the colander was now, as far as Owen was concerned, a hat.

Jasmine set the microscope on the kitchen table exactly the way Ms. Banerjee's note had described, because the note was all she had. "Bring your slide back Monday," it read in Ms. Banerjee's tidy handwriting, "and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. Careful with the focus knob. Do not modify the settings I marked with tape." The tape was still there, two green strips on the coarse knob, so Jasmine only touched the fine one.

Teagan sat across from her, chin on her hands. She had brought the onions, three of them, because she wanted first look. "I'm basically nocturnal during swim season," she said, "so a Friday night microscope party is perfect for me. But I get to see the cells before you draw them. That's my price."

"Deal," Jasmine said, though she regretted it the moment the light snapped on.

Under the lens the onion skin looked like a brick wall made of living things, each cell a tidy rectangle. Teagan took her turn first, as promised, and hogged the eyepiece for a full minute. "There are little dark dots," she reported. "Like somebody sneezed pepper on it."

Jasmine's stomach dropped. Ms. Banerjee wanted the nucleus labeled, and if the dots were dirt, she would label a speck of dust on her drawing and hand in a mistake for the whole class to see. She thought about it while Teagan kept looking. Dirt would land wherever it landed, in clumps, in streaks, in some cells and not others. She leaned in and checked. One dot per cell. Every single rectangle had its own small, round, darker spot, sitting there like it belonged.

"That's not dirt," Jasmine said slowly. "Dirt wouldn't be so neat. That dot is the nucleus. It's in every cell because every cell needs it. It holds the DNA."

"What's DNA?" Teagan asked.

"The genetic material. Like the instructions for the whole onion."

She drew the cells on graph paper, wall on the outside, membrane drawn just inside it, nucleus as its careful round dot. Her labeling was going to be the best in the class. Then she remembered the deal and slid the paper aside so Teagan could copy the shapes too, which meant Teagan's Monday would look almost as good, and Jasmine's mom called down that lights out was in ten minutes, before she could label the last three cells.

Teagan grinned and picked up the pencil herself. "I'll do these ones," she said. "I'm the nocturnal one, after all."

Dylan had signed up for the Saturday shift at the community kitchen because his grandmother used to volunteer there after she retired, back when her pension was small and the work made her feel useful. Now he stood at a steel counter beside Zac and Kathryn, six onions in front of him and a note card from the coordinator in his pocket. The card read: "Dylan, you're on sauce today. Mr. Romano will show you the knife work. Chop small, cook slow, and the soup line eats at noon." He read it twice, because noon sounded very close.

Mr. Romano put a chef's knife in Dylan's hand and an onion on the cutting board. "Claw grip," he said, curling Dylan's fingertips under so only the knuckles faced the blade. "The knife rides against your knuckles. The fingertips stay out of the way." Dylan pressed down and the onion split with a crack, and the smell hit him right away, sharp enough to make his eyes water. He kept his wrist moving the tip in a smooth rock, the way Mr. Romano had shown, and the cubes came out small and fairly consistent, all about the same size, which apparently mattered because they would cook at the same rate.

Zac was on garlic at the next board. Halfway through his pile he reached for a bowl at the back of the counter and his elbow knocked the handle of his knife. The blade slid off the edge. Zac's hand shot out to grab it.

Dylan had seen this before. Last summer at the lake, a kid named nothing anyone remembered now had swept a paring knife off a picnic table reaching for marshmallows, snatched at it midair, and opened a gash across three fingers that ruined the whole trip and meant a long drive to the clinic. Dylan had stood there watching it happen and done nothing. This time he grabbed Zac's sleeve and yanked him back a step. The knife hit the floor handle first, bounced, and lay still. Nobody was bleeding.

"Sorry," Zac said. "Instinct."

"That's how people get cut," Dylan said. "You just step back and let it drop."

Mr. Romano picked the knife up, checked the edge, and set it down flat on the board. "Falling knife, empty hands," he said, and went back to the stove.

Kathryn had the tomatoes going in the big pot, and the kitchen filled with the smell of them collapsing into oil and onion, sweet and a little smoky where the bits on the bottom browned. Dylan stirred with a wooden spoon longer than he thought necessary, tasting at the end, adding a pinch of salt, tasting again. When the sauce finally tasted like something he would want on pasta, not like watery tomato, he understood why the note card said cook slow.

At noon the line formed. A man Dylan recognized from the bus stop took the first bowl and said the sauce was good, and a woman asked if there was extra for her neighbor. Mr. Romano told them the kitchen was able to donate twenty extra portions this week because the sauce had stretched farther than planned. Dylan washed the boards and knives at the sink, drying each blade and laying it flat, well back from the edge.

His grandmother had told him once that the kitchen would teach him more than chopping. He hadn't believed her, but he put her note card, the one she'd left him, back in his pocket next to the day's schedule, and carried the last pot to the line.

"Same time next Saturday?" Zac called after him.

"Bring your own knife," Dylan said. "Just don't catch it."

Evan hunched over the team laptop behind the robotics table, typing and deleting the same line for the third time. The competition gym smelled like burnt coffee and floor wax, and in twenty minutes the judges would walk by to score their display station. Their robot worked fine. The trouble was the little quiz program Ms. Kang had suggested as a bonus station, a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime, and Evan had promised he could build it.

"How's the wizard coming?" Thomas asked, sliding into the next chair. He wanted that bonus point badly, because his robot arm had jammed during the obstacle run and the quiz station was his only chance to impress the judges today. "Two minutes, I swear," Evan said, though his screen showed nothing but an input line and a blinking cursor. He knew primes were numbers that only divided by one and themselves. What he didn't know was how a program could possibly check whether a division came out even.

He typed a few guesses. If he divided 9 by 3, the answer was 3.0, and dividing 10 by 3 gave 3.3333333. Maybe he could turn the answer into letters and check for the dot? That felt wrong, and anyway it made his embarrassment flare hot enough that he was glad Thomas couldn't see the screen. Then he noticed a symbol in his notes from class, a percent sign, and an old line he had copied off the board: n % d == 0.
