Jace spread the science project across the kitchen table like a detective laying out evidence. The assignment was due tomorrow: draw a model of a sodium atom, label the particles, and show his work. He had the paper, the colored pencils, and a printout of the periodic table. The only problem was that the paper was blank, because he had no idea how many electrons to draw.

He called Nahla, who lived two floors up in the same building.

"How many electrons did you draw for yours?" he asked the moment she picked up.

"I'm not telling you the answer," Nahla said. "Mr. Girma would know. But I'll come down and sit with you while you figure it out. Ten minutes."

She arrived with her own binder and a granola bar, which she broke in half and pushed the bigger piece across the table to him, because she knew he always forgot to eat when he was stuck. She settled into the chair their tenant usually sat in on Sunday mornings and waited.

Jace dragged his finger across the printout. "Okay. Sodium. Atomic number eleven. So that means eleven protons, I got that part. But electrons?" He squinted at the tiny square as if it might whisper the answer. It looked faintly sinister, sitting there in its little box, keeping its secret.

"Draw what you do know," Nahla suggested. "Start with the protons in the middle."

He drew a cluster of eleven small plus signs in a nucleus, then sat back. "A neutral atom," he said slowly, reading off the top of his notes, where Mr. Girma had written it on the board and underlined it twice. "Neutral. Not positive, not negative." He tapped his pencil against the table. "If the protons make it positive, and electrons make it negative, and the whole thing is neutral..."

Nahla reached over and stole one of his blue pencils to start her own drawing, just so he wouldn't feel watched.

"Then they have to cancel out," Jace said. "Eleven protons means eleven electrons. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. So the atomic number gives you both."

He allocated the electrons to their shells the way the textbook diagram showed, two in the first ring, eight in the second, one lonely electron spinning in the outermost orbit. He labeled it carefully, then checked sodium's square one more time. Eleven. Protons, eleven. Electrons, eleven. It balanced.

There was a knock at the door. Mr. Girma from down the hall stood there holding a plate of cookies. "I heard pencils moving through the wall," he said, peering past Jace at the drawing. "Is that sodium?"

Jace held it up. "Eleven protons, eleven electrons, neutral atom."

Mr. Girma smiled and set the plate on the table next to the half granola bar. "I'll leave you two to it, then. Save me a cookie."

Nahla was already copying the diagram into her own binder, her pencil moving fast. "Jace," she said without looking up, "check nitrogen for me. Number seven?"

Jace ran his finger down the column, found it, and picked up a fresh cookie.

The clock on Cristian's basement wall said 6:40, and the coding club showcase started at 7:30, which meant Kaitlyn had fifty minutes to make her program stop lying. She had written a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime, and it worked fine for 7 and 11, but when she typed 9, it proudly announced PRIME.

"That's wrong," Cristian said, leaning over her shoulder with a soda radiating cold against her arm. "Nine is three times three."

"I know what nine is," Kaitlyn said, but her cheeks went hot anyway. Karim was sprawled on the couch with a marker and a big sheet of graph paper, drawing a grid of numbers from 2 to 50 for the club's poster. "I checked every number by dividing by two. If it doesn't divide by two, it's prime, right?"

Karim snorted without looking up. "Fifteen doesn't divide by two."

Kaitlyn stared at the screen. Fifteen. Three times five. Her whole method was built on one test, and one test could not cover everything. She needed to divide by more numbers, but which ones, and how far? She tried dividing by every number up to n, and that worked, but for 47 it took forever, and the showcase needed the program to answer fast while people watched.

"Wait," she said slowly. "Karim, what are you doing to that grid?"

"Crossing out multiples," Karim said. "Two, so four, six, eight, all gone. Then three, so six, nine, twelve. Then five. It's called the Sieve of Eratosthenes, some old Greek thing. Ms. Shapiro showed us." He circled 2, then 3, then 5, then 7, and pointed at the survivors scattered across the paper like islands. "Whatever's left is prime."

Kaitlyn grabbed the sheet and pulled it close. Every number crossed out was a multiple of some smaller number, and every number still circled was immune to being crossed out, because no smaller prime divided it. And here was the part that made her bounce in her chair: by the time Karim reached 7, the next unmarked number after it, 49, was seven sevens, and everything smaller than 49 that wasn't prime had already been crossed out by 2, 3, or 5. She did not need to test every divisor. She only needed the primes up to the square root of n.

She typed fast, deleting her old loop and writing a new one that divided only by small numbers and stopped early. Cristian read the line out loud as she finished it, and Karim abandoned the poster to watch.

"Try nine," Cristian said, like a game show host.

She typed 9. NOT PRIME. She typed 25. NOT PRIME. She typed 97, held her breath, and the screen said PRIME so fast it felt like an echo. Karim checked it against his grid, where 97 would have sat far past the last row, uncrossed if he ever extended the paper.

"Forty-seven's still prime?" Cristian asked.

"Forty-seven has always been prime," Kaitlyn said. "My program just didn't know it yet." She saved the file twice, closed the laptop halfway like it was something breakable, and pointed at the stairs. "Grab the poster. We have twenty minutes."

Karim rolled the grid into a tube. "The Sieve of Eratosthenes, ladies and gentlemen."

"Move," Kaitlyn said, already three steps up.

Hannah crouched on the garage floor next to Ms. Chen's workbench, holding a coil of copper wire in both hands like it might bolt for the door. She needed a science project that would actually work this time, not another baking-soda volcano that fizzled out in front of everyone. "So I measure the voltage across the wire, then the current through it," she said slowly, reading from her notebook, "and the resistance is the ratio of one to the other."

"That's the plan," Ms. Chen said. She clipped the wire into the circuit and spun the dial on her multimeter. "Tell me what the screen shows."

Hannah leaned in. The number was 4.7, and beside it sat a strange symbol, a looping shape like a horseshoe standing on end. "Four point seven horseshoes?" she said. Everett, who was sprawled on an old lawn chair recording data, snorted so hard he nearly dropped the pencil.

"It's not a horseshoe," Ms. Chen said, smiling. "That's omega, the Greek letter. Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter omega." Hannah wrote it down, drawing the loop twice until it looked right. It reminded her of last spring, when she had stood at the whiteboard convinced her answer was correct because it "felt" right, and Ms. Chen had said that science was not about feelings, because feelings were subjective and the universe did not care what felt true. Hannah had flushed to her ears that day. Now she measured things twice.

"Okay," she said. "So if the resistance is voltage divided by current, and I change the voltage, the resistance should stay the same, because it's a property of the wire. If my numbers violate that, I did something wrong." Everett sat up straighter. "Wait, that's actually a test? Like the wire can't lie?" "That's exactly what it is," Hannah said, and her heart beat a little faster.

They ran the experiment five times. At 3.0 volts and 0.31 amps, then 6.0 volts and 0.62 amps, then 9.0 and 0.93, the division came out to almost the same number every single time. Hannah checked each result on her calculator while Everett read the meter aloud, and Ms. Chen watched from her stool without saying a word. On the fifth run the answer jumped to 40, and Hannah frowned at the clips before realizing one had slipped loose and was touching the paint of a coffee can. She fixed it, reran it, and got 9.9.

"Ten ohms," Everett said, pointing at the little omega on the screen. "Give or take." Hannah copied the number into her notebook, drew the symbol one more time, and then held the wire up to the garage light, turning it slowly. "You were hiding this the whole time," she told it. Everett laughed and clicked the pen closed.

At the Japanese booth at the cultural festival, Ellie stood in front of a menu written in both English and Japanese, holding a crumpled practice sheet in her pocket. Maika had promised to teach her enough Japanese to order lunch, since Ellie's family was visiting Tokyo in the spring and she wanted to surprise her grandmother by ordering on her own. The plan was simple: three phrases, one order, one question about the price. Ivana had already ordered a plate of yakisoba by pointing at the menu, which felt like cheating to Ellie, though Ivana said it was efficient.

The booth had been set up like a tiny restaurant, with paper lanterns strung along the front and a man in an apron taking orders behind a counter. Maika leaned close and whispered the first phrase, and Ellie repeated it, then wrote it out phonetically on her sheet. When she tried the second one, the word for "how much," she kept slipping into the rhythm of English, and Maika laughed so hard the paper lanterns above them swayed.

"You have to let the sounds land soft," Maika said. "Like dropping a pebble in water, not throwing it."

Ellie tried again, slower this time. The man behind the counter looked up and nodded, so she stepped forward, heart tapping, and said the whole order in one careful line. The words came out smaller than she had practiced, but they came out. Then she asked the price question, and he answered with a number she almost missed. She counted out the bills exactly, added a little extra, and left the coins on the counter beside her tray, the way her family always did at restaurants back home.

She had taken three steps toward the tables when the man came around the counter and caught up with her. He held out the coins in his open palm and shook his head, polite but firm, as if she had dropped her keys. Ellie stared at the shiny coins, and a principle assembled itself in her mind: what looked like politeness at home looked like a mistake here. She remembered a travel show where a server ran a whole block to return change a family had left on the table, and suddenly that scene made sense. Tipping was not part of it at all.

"Keep it," she started to say, then stopped, because Maika was already translating something the man said, quick and gentle.

"He says thank you, but this is the exact price. Nothing extra is expected."

Ellie took the coins back and bowed a little, which made the man smile. Ivana, watching from a table with her yakisoba, raised her chopsticks in salute. Ellie sat down and turned the practice sheet over, writing a new note to transmit to her future self in Tokyo: pay the exact amount, and do not leave money on the table, because someone will always run after you to give it back.

"Next time I'm ordering dessert too," Ivana said. "In Japanese, if you teach me."

Ellie looked at the dessert case behind the counter and folded the coins into her pocket. "Mochi," she said. "I already know that word."

Jordan had discovered the trick by accident at his cousin's birthday party the summer before. A kid named Tomas was getting grilled about his stutter, a circle of boys leaning in like it was a show, and Jordan had simply grabbed his sleeve and said they needed help carrying the snacks. The circle broke apart the second the two of them walked into the kitchen. Nobody had to be brave in that hallway. The audience had just left.

Now it was October, and Blaine was the one in the circle. It had started near the lockers before science, Vladimir doing most of the talking, a small crowd doing the laughing. Blaine's science folder had slid open and his volcano diagram, the one with the monsoon of red marker arrow labeled "lava flow" pointed the wrong direction, was being held up like evidence in a trial.

"Even the volcano's ashamed of it," Vladimir said, and the crowd supplied the laughter again, right on cue.

Jordan stood there holding his own folder and thought about the party. The problem, as far as he could figure it, wasn't really Vladimir. Vladimir had been mediocre at best before eighth grade, but he'd learned that teasing Blaine worked, and it worked because the crowd kept showing up. Take the crowd away and the whole thing might just deflate, the way it had in that kitchen with Tomas. Jordan wasn't sure. It was a theory, and like Mr. Zhou kept saying about their lab experiments, you didn't know until you ran it.

He crossed the hall. "Blaine, come on, let's go," he said, nodding toward Mr. Zhou's door. "Mr. Zhou said he wanted help setting up the erosion demo before class."

Blaine blinked at him. "He did?"

"He did," Jordan said, with what he hoped would convey certainty rather than total invention. Blaine glanced once at the diagram still in Vladimir's hand, then let it drop to the floor and followed.

Jordan kept talking about the erosion demo, inventing details about sand trays and a spray bottle, and by the time they reached the classroom doorway he looked back. The circle had come apart into two kids checking phones and one wandering off. Vladimir was left standing there holding Blaine's volcano diagram with nobody to show it to, which was its own kind of punishment.

Inside, Mr. Zhou was stacking sand trays, and it turned out he actually did need help with the erosion demo. He handed them a spray bottle and asked where they'd been. Blaine opened his mouth, then looked at Jordan.

"We were helping carry stuff," Jordan said.

Mr. Zhou looked at the two of them for a moment longer than necessary, then at the spray bottle. "Start with the slope at thirty degrees," he said. "And, Jordan, next time you invent an errand, pick one I haven't already assigned you."

Blaine snorted. Jordan picked up the sand tray.

Aubrey pushed the coffee table against the wall so the living room had room for two actors and one imaginary dragon. Loukas flopped onto the couch with his script, which was useless, because tonight there was no script. Tomorrow was the drama camp showcase, and Mr. Rao had put them together as a pair for the improv section.

"Remember the rule," Aubrey said, retrieving two hairbrushes from the kitchen drawer to use as microphones. "It's called 'yes, and.' You accept what your partner gives you, and then you add something new."

"I know, I know." Loukas popped up, took a brush, and grinned. "Start."

Aubrey held her brush to her mouth. "Good evening, we're live at the world's largest pickle festival."

"Yes," said Loukas, nodding.

She waited. He kept nodding. The silence stretched until the imaginary crowd probably left. "And?" she finally said.

"And... yes?"

"That's the problem. You keep agreeing but you never add anything, so the scene just stalls, like a car with no gas." She tried again. "Good evening, we're live at the world's largest pickle festival, where a giant pickle has just come to life."

"Yes," said Loukas.

"Add something! Anything! The pickle is doing something."

"Yes... the pickle is standing there."

Aubrey groaned and dropped onto the couch cushion beside him. It was like playing catch with someone who caught the ball and then sat down with it. She stared at the ceiling and thought. Loukas was diligent, honestly. He'd memorized every line of the camp skit in one night. Maybe the problem wasn't effort. Maybe the problem was that he thought agreeing was the whole job, when agreeing was only half.

"Okay, new plan," she said. "Whatever I say, you say yes, and then you make it weirder. Weirder than my weird. Can you do weird?"

"Excuse me, I am a champion of weird."

"Prove it. Scene: we're two astronauts landing on Mars."

"Yes, and the Mars rover is our tour guide and it only speaks in knock-knock jokes," Loukas said immediately.

Aubrey blinked, then laughed so hard she snorted. "Yes, and the first joke is so bad it knocks over a rock, and the rock rolls downhill and reveals a door."

"Yes, and the door has perfect symmetry, two handles, two windows, and it opens from both sides at once."

"Yes, and behind it is a whole pickle festival, which means we never left Earth!"

They went back and forth for twenty minutes, building a Mars hotel run by a pickle with a clipboard, and the scene never once stalled. When Aubrey's mom leaned in from the kitchen to say it was almost time for Loukas to head home, they both looked up, startled, like they'd actually been on Mars.

"Same time tomorrow before the showcase?" Loukas asked, setting his hairbrush microphone down with great ceremony.

"Yes," said Aubrey, "and bring the dragon."

Hazel slid her practice sheet across the library table and frowned at the first problem: x + 7 = 19. Tomorrow was the makeup quiz, and if she failed it, she would be benched for Saturday's track meet. Kyrie had already aced his test, and Zachery claimed the equations were easy, which made it worse.

"You take the seven off the left," Kyrie said, tapping the paper, "but you have to take it off both sides. Same move, both sides."

"Why both?" Hazel asked. "The seven is only on one side." She looked up at the shelves behind them, where Mr. Popescu was pushing a cart of returns. The library smelled like pencil shavings and old paper, and the radiator under the window ticked as it cooled.

Mr. Popescu set down a book called Mathematicians: A Memoir of the Great Minds and let it fall open near their table. "Look who drew that," he said, pointing at a page, and walked away before Hazel could ask him anything. She leaned over. There was a picture to illustrate the old notation, the strangest equals sign she had ever seen, long and slanted. "Listen to this," she said slowly. "The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557. He chose two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal." She ran her finger under the printed line, reading it twice to be sure she had it right.

"Parallel," Zachery said, "like train tracks. Never touching, always the same distance apart." Hazel stared at the sign in her own equation. Two sides. The same, all the way down. She tried a small experiment, something she could test: she took x + 7 = 19 and subtracted seven from the left only. She got x = 19 on one side and a lopsided 12 on the other, which could not be right, because if the sides were equal before, they had to stay equal after. So she subtracted seven from both sides instead. x = 12. She checked it: 12 plus 7 was 19. It balanced, like the two parallel lines, like a scale with a weight on each pan.

Her pencil moved faster down the sheet. She tried 3x = 15 and divided both sides by three, and then 5x minus 4 = 26, adding four to both sides before dividing by five. Each answer fit when she checked it, every single one. Zachery flipped a page of the memoir and found a picture of Recorde's actual book, the slanted lines printed there in ink gone brown with age. "This guy invented a symbol the whole world still uses," he said.

Hazel wrote one more equation at the bottom of her page, x minus 3 = 9, then drew a careful equals sign, two straight parallel lines, and whispered, "No two things could be more equal." She picked up her pencil and solved it in a single clean line.

The message popped up at 9:14, right after James finished his math homework: "EMERGENCY. Did anyone see what happened in the east hallway after last period?" Thalia had sent it in all caps, which meant trouble. Mathieu answered first. "I saw it. Marcus and that kid from Mr. Barrett's class slammed into each other going full speed." James typed back that he'd been near the water fountain, maybe ten meters away, and it hadn't looked that fast to him. Marcus was limping, sure, but people bumped in that hallway every day.

Thalia's next message arrived in pieces, the way she typed when she was worked up. "My mom asked me how fast they were going when they smashed into each other. She thinks the other kid should be suspended. She's going to email the school tomorrow." James stared at the screen. Something about the word "smashed" bothered him, like a stone in his shoe. He remembered the sound, and it had been more of a thud.

"I'm going to verify this," he typed. "What exactly did your mom ask you?" He waited, thumbs hovering. Mathieu sent a shrug emoji. Thalia replied, "She asked how fast they were going when they smashed into each other. Why?" James didn't answer right away. Instead he opened a search page and typed: do the words people use change how you remember something?

He found it within a minute, on a page about memory research. In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer had run a study. People who were asked how fast cars smashed into each other gave higher speed estimates than people who were asked how fast cars hit each other. Same films. Different verb. James read it twice, then a third time, his door rattling as his sister laid siege to it wanting the charger. "Not now," he called.

He copied the sentence and pasted it into the chat. "So here's the thing," he typed. "Nobody actually knows how fast they were going. Thalia, your mom asked you with the word smashed. Mathieu, you said full speed. I said bump. And we all saw the same hallway." The typing bubble appeared under Thalia's name, vanished, appeared again. She was hesitant; James could almost see her chewing her lip.

"Okay," she finally sent. "But my mom already wrote the email. It's in her drafts." James called her, holding the phone to his ear while he paced. "Tell her to reread her own question," he said. "Then tell her what Mathieu said when nobody used that word yet." There was a pause on the line, then Thalia's voice went muffled, and he heard her say, "Mom? Before you send that, can I ask you something about how you asked me?"

Paisley sat in the waiting room of the animal clinic with her cat carrier on her knees and her science homework balanced on top of it. The sheet said to draw an onion cell and label the cell wall, the cell membrane, and the nucleus. She had the wall, easy, a thick brick-colored outline. She had the nucleus, a dark dot like a swallowed peppercorn. But the membrane was nowhere. She had redrawn the same cell four times.

"That's a microscope, isn't it?" Rayyan said, pointing through the doorway into the back room, where a squat gray machine sat on a counter between shelves of sample jars. Rayyan was there with his gecko, Reginald, who had stopped eating crickets. What Rayyan wanted, mostly, was to see that microscope up close, and possibly to look at something disgusting through it.

"My grandma's cat needs his teeth checked," Zaiden said from the next chair. "I'm the lucky escort." He leaned over Paisley's drawing. "Why is there an arrow pointing at nothing?"

"That's the problem. The membrane's supposed to be there and it isn't. Maybe onion cells don't have one."

Mr. Adebayo came out with a clipboard, and when Paisley's mother explained that their old cat, Muffin, was being seen for drinking too much water, he nodded and said it would be a few minutes. Paisley asked, in a rush, whether the clinic's microscope might be free.

He looked at her worksheet, then at the clock, and said they had time between patients, but she had to be careful and not dismantle anything. She carried the slide like it was a soap bubble. In the back room, on a counter beside a jar labeled only anonymous, she set the onion skin under the lens and squinted. Wall. Nucleus. Between the wall and the inside, nothing but a clean empty gap where the line should be.

Rayyan had his face practically on her shoulder. "Told you. No membrane."

"Everything alive has a membrane," Zaiden said. "We learned that. It's like the skin under the shell. It has to be there."

Paisley stared at the flat gray bricks of the cells. Then she thought about the one thing she knew: the membrane had to be pressed right up against the inside of the wall. She traced the wall's inner edge with her pencil, pressing hard, then lifted the pencil and looked. The wall now looked like two lines, a thick one and a thin one, tight together. "It's not missing," she said slowly. "It's hidden. It's squeezed against the wall so you can't see it as a separate line unless you know where to look." She drew both lines and labeled the thin one, her hand steady.

Mr. Adebayo looked in from the doorway. "Nice work. Muffin's ready now, and I'll be honest, we need to run more tests."

Paisley carried her finished drawing back to the waiting room, and behind her Rayyan was already asking, "So what's the ratio of weird stuff you could look at under that thing? Like, ear wax?"

Paisley sat down next to the carrier and slid her finger through the mesh door. Muffin blinked at her, slow and yellow-eyed.

"Tomorrow we'll know more," her mother said.

The last box of Frost-Cola cereal sat alone on the top shelf, and the price tag beneath it made Lincoln stop so fast his sneakers squeaked on the floor. Six dollars. Last month the same box had cost three. He looked down the aisle at the pyramid of plain oat cereal, stacked to his shoulder, marked two for five dollars. Something was going on here that he could not see, some rule working behind the prices like gears inside a clock.

He found his mother by the strawberries, which were piled in red heaps and selling cheap, and beside her stood Gurshan with his own cart. Gurshan held his phone out. "You see this?" On the screen was a marketplace post offering a Strato-Dragon card for eighty dollars. "Same card I traded you my extra for in December. Everyone wants one. There are only like ten in the whole school."

Lincoln took the phone and studied the post, the smell of strawberries sweet and cold in his nose. He remembered the poster in Ms. Visser's classroom, the one about the Dutch Republic, and the line he had copied into his notebook because it sounded impossible. "In the winter of 1636 to 1637, rare tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic cost more than people could believe," he said slowly. "Then in February 1637 the prices collapsed. Buyers just stopped showing up." Gurshan stared at him. "So the same thing could happen to the Strato-Dragon." Lincoln nodded. "Cheap thing, lots of it. Rare thing, everybody wants it. Then the wanting stops, and the price falls off a cliff."

They decided to demonstrate the idea right there in the store. Gurshan became the buyer, Lincoln the seller, and the two forlorn bottles of spicy mango soda on the endcap became the rare bulbs. "Five dollars each," Lincoln announced, holding them up. Gurshan, playing an obstinate shopper, shook his head and bargained down to four, and a woman reaching past them for orange juice laughed. Then Gurshan wheeled his cart into the juice aisle, where gallons stood in crowded rows, and offered Lincoln one dollar for the next bottle Lincoln touched. Nobody wanted what was everywhere. The pattern held. It held all the way to the registers, where a man ahead of them paid nine dollars for the second-to-last bag of storm-tracked ice melt, and the cashier said, "Rain's coming, everybody wants it."

At school the next morning Gurshan grabbed Lincoln's sleeve before first period. His face was pale. "The Strato-Dragon. Lily-Rose found out there are two hundred of them. Somebody opened a whole case from the mall this weekend. They're not rare at all." Down the hall, Lily-Rose was already waving a Strato-Dragon in the air like a flag, and behind her came a boy Lincoln had never traded with before, holding out a card and saying, "Eighty dollars. Take it or leave it, but I need the money today."

Mya arrived at book club carrying her copy of the story flat against her chest, like a shield, because she had not finished it. She had read to the middle on the bus and then fallen asleep, and now Syeda and Magalie were already arguing about the ending at the little table by the library window.

"You're biased," Syeda said, "because you guessed wrong." Magalie had guessed the lottery would be for a prize, which, to be fair, was a reasonable thing to guess.

Mr. Baptiste held up his hand. "Before anyone spoils anything further, we have a member who hasn't finished. Mya, go read the last three pages in the corner. We'll wait. We'll be quiet, which will be hard."

It was hard. Mya read the ending with her back to them, and when she turned around her face apparently said everything, because Syeda pointed at her and said, "See."

"Okay," said Mr. Baptiste. "Now the real work. Reread the first paragraph. The very first one, the calm one, from The New Yorker, 1948. What does Jackson put there?" He would not say more. He had this policy of standing by the window and drinking his terrible coffee while they floundered, and he seemed to enjoy it.

The paragraph was full of sunshine, grass, flowers, boys running around gathering stones. Mya read it twice. On the bus it had seemed like set dressing, the literary equivalent of a welcome mat. Now it sat there like a loaded water pistol in a cheerful family photo. She assessed it line by line, the way she'd been taught, hunting for anything that didn't belong at a picnic.

"The stones," she said slowly. "The kids are piling them up in the corner. Nobody explains why. And the whole story goes by and nobody explains why, until..." She stopped, not wanting to say the ending out loud, as if it could still be un-happened.

"Until the lottery," Magalie finished.

"It was there the whole time," Mya said. "Page one. First paragraph. She basically told us, and I read right past it." She felt like a scavenger who had walked over buried meat all afternoon and then complained there was nothing to eat. "So that's foreshadowing. And the stones aren't just stones. They mean the whole tradition, probably. Something old and ordinary and awful."

"Write that down," said Mr. Baptiste, "before you get shy about it."

Mya wrote it in the margin of her copy, in pencil, small. Syeda leaned over to read it, then flipped to the first page and read the paragraph a third time with narrowed eyes.

"Children," Syeda said. "Piling up stones. On a sunny day." She looked up. "I'm never trusting a sunny day again."

"Reasonable," said Mya, and turned the page back to the ending.

Zoey stood in the aisle of the pharmacy on Willow Street, holding a box of tissues and staring at a shelf of cough syrup like it might stare back. She had been home with the flu for four days, and tomorrow was the tryout for the spring play, the one Hazel had promised they would audition for together since November. If she missed it, there would be no other chance.

"Mom, can we just ask the pharmacist for the strong stuff?" Zoey whispered. Her mother was comparing two bottles of fever reducer, and behind them a boy about Zoey's age leaned on the counter, talking to Mr. Nikolaidis, the pharmacist who also lived on their street.

"My doctor won't give me antibiotics," the boy was saying. "I have a soccer game Saturday. I need to be better by then."

Mr. Nikolaidis tapped the counter. "You can't rush this one with antibiotics. Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses. A cold or the flu is a virus, so they won't help cure it."

Zoey turned the box of tissues over in her hands. So that was why the doctor had just told her mother to wait it out. She had been thinking of the flu like a splinter, something you could pull out if you found the right tool. It was more like a storm; you could only hold on until it passed.

"Then what does work?" the boy asked.

"Rest, fluids, time," Mr. Nikolaidis said. "Boring, but true."

Zoey stepped up to the counter. "Mr. Nikolaidis? If I've been resting for four days, is that enough time? I have a tryout tomorrow."

He looked at her over the rim of his glasses, as if adjusting a lens to bring her into focus. "How's the fever?"

"Gone since this morning."

"Then your body's winning. You might not feel lush and green tomorrow, but you'll be standing."

On the drive home, Zoey texted Hazel: Can you ask if I can audition last, like at the end? Might give me a few more hours.

Hazel replied with a row of exclamation marks. Already did. You're slotted after me. Rest, weirdo.

Zoey slept until dinner, woke to soup, and slept again. In the morning her throat was still scratchy and her legs felt like they wanted to hibernate through another week, but her head was clear. Hazel met her at the auditorium door and pressed a bottle of water into her hand.

"Your voice sounds like a rusty gate," Hazel said.

"Perfect for the villain," Zoey said, and walked toward the stage.

Rosalie sat down in the computer lab with the fundraiser notebook open beside the keyboard. Ms. Castillo had given her one job before Friday: turn the class bake sale records into a spreadsheet with a column total and a bar chart, so the principal could see what each table earned. Ameera had already typed the numbers, and now it was Rosalie's turn to make the sheet do the math.

She clicked the empty cell under the column of earnings and typed =SUM(B2:B9). Eight tables, eight numbers. The total appeared: forty-one dollars and fifty cents. Rosalie frowned. She assessed the column again, adding the figures in her head the slow way, table by table. When she got to fifty-five dollars, she stopped. The machine was short by thirteen dollars and fifty cents.

"Can't you just type the right number in?" said Maika, leaning over from the next computer. "The principal won't check."

Rosalie shook her head. "If the total is wrong, the chart is wrong, and then the whole thing is a lie." She looked at the cells one at a time. Seven of them sat snug against the right edge of their boxes, but the number for Table 4, thirteen fifty, huddled on the left side, exactly where words sat. She remembered Ameera pasting that one in from a text message because the Table 4 kids had sent their earnings by phone.

She deleted the cell, typed 13.50 fresh, and pressed Enter. The number jumped to the right edge, and the total at the bottom changed on its own to fifty-five dollars. So that was the rule, she thought, and she felt it click into place like a locker: SUM skipped anything that wasn't a real number, no warning, no red mark. A pasted figure could look like a number and still be nothing but text to the machine, quietly left out.

Then she built the chart. She selected the table names and the earnings, clicked the bar chart button, and the bars rose across the screen. Table 3's bar stood tallest, tall enough to look almost aggressive next to Table 5's stubby little block. She added a title, Class Bake Sale Income, and printed one copy for Ms. Castillo and one for the bulletin board outside the office.

At the door she ran into Ameera, who read the chart upside down and then right side up. "Table 4 did all right," Ameera said. "I thought they'd earned nothing."

"They did earn something," Rosalie said. "The sheet just didn't know it yet." She folded the extra copy and put it in her binder, next to the notebook with all the messy original numbers, the ones she wasn't ready to recycle. Ameera was already walking off down the hall with the good news, and the paper still smelled faintly warm from the printer.

Piper slapped the crumpled sign on Mr. Rowe's desk before the bell finished ringing. "The bookstore by the mall banned backpacks. That's a violation of my Charter rights. Section 8, unreasonable search."

Mr. Rowe picked up the sign and read it. "Assignment's due Friday, Piper. You have to explain a right in your own words. This is a start."

"Better than a start. It's real." She pointed at the small print: NO BACKPACKS. NO EXCEPTIONS. "They searched Loic's bag last Saturday. Made him open it right at the counter."

After class she found Loic and Terrence at the lockers and laid out her plan. "If the Charter protects us, we test it. We walk in with the backpacks and cite the section. If they back down, the rule doesn't restrict us anymore."

"Or we get banned from the only bookstore we can walk to," Terrence said.

Loic shrugged. "I'm in. I still want my money back anyway."

Saturday, Piper led them through the door with her backpack straps gripped tight. The same clerk stepped in front of the counter. "Read the sign."

"I did. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms says you can't search us without reason."

The clerk folded his arms. "Kid, we're not the government. The Charter applies to governments, not to us."

Piper froze. She had read the whole document twice for the assignment and never once thought about who it was aimed at. The clerk waited, arms still crossed, and she realized he wasn't guessing. "You're sure?"

"My sister's a lawyer. I've heard the speech a hundred times."

They bought nothing and walked out. Terrence kicked a pebble across the parking lot. "So we can't do anything?"

"There's still the assignment," Piper said slowly, pulling out her phone. She searched the Charter's text, scanning for the words that mattered. Governments. The word sat there in her notes from Monday, circled twice, and she had skipped right past it. "Okay. New idea. The sign isn't a Charter problem. But the city bus kicked me off last month for the same reason, and the bus is the government. That's my example."

"You're going to write about yourself?" Loic asked.

"I'm going to write about the difference." She was already typing notes. "Friday, Mr. Rowe's going to ask who did their project on a real event. Mine's going to be the only one with a twist."

Terrence squinted at her. "What twist?"

Piper held up the phone, showing a photo she'd taken of the bookstore's front window. Below the NO BACKPACKS sign sat a smaller plaque: PROPERTY OF THE CITY LIBRARY BOARD.

Loic leaned in. "Is a library board the government?"

Piper grinned and pocketed the phone. "Ask my essay."

The note on the fridge said everything Avery needed: feed at seven, crib is in the corner room, call if anything seems wrong, back by ten. Mrs. Okafor had paused at the door with the diaper bag over her shoulder and said, "Do you want me to clarify anything before I go?" Avery had almost said no, just to sound confident, but instead she asked about the bottle warming and the nap schedule, and she was glad she did, because the answers mattered.

The baby, a chubby three-month-old named Pip, stared up at her from the blanket on the floor like she was the most interesting thing that had ever happened. For the first hour, everything was easy. Pip chewed her fist, kicked her legs, and let out small delighted hoots whenever Avery made a face. Avery texted Mahee: This is the best job ever. Fifteen dollars for playing with a baby. Mahee texted back: The median babysitting rate in our town is probably twelve, you're rich.

Then, at eight o'clock, Pip started to cry. Not the polite fussing from before, but a red-faced, air-raid siren wail that went on and on. Avery walked her, bounced her, sang a song she made up on the spot, checked the diaper, offered the bottle again. Nothing worked. Her arms ached and her ears rang, and a hot, frantic feeling climbed up her neck.

Her phone buzzed. Mahee again: lol just shake her till she stops. Avery's stomach dropped. No, she typed back fast. Never. My babysitting class said shaking a baby can seriously injure her brain. Their neck muscles are too weak to hold up a heavy head. Mahee replied with a horrified face and "I WAS KIDDING," but Avery was already moving. She laid Pip gently on her back in the crib, made sure the blanket was loose and away from her face, and stepped out to the hallway to breathe. Five minutes, the instructor had said. The baby is safe in the crib. You can take five minutes. That was the rule, and now it made complete sense.

From the hallway, she heard something through the baby monitor that made her freeze. The crying wasn't steady at all. It came in waves, and right before each wave, there was a tiny clicking sound. She crept back to the doorway and watched. Pip's face was scrunched, her knees pulling up to her belly, and her fists were clenched tight. Avery had read a page about this, and suddenly the pieces snapped together. Gas. Tummy trouble. It wasn't her fault, and it wasn't random.

She remembered the dryer humming in the laundry room, a low warm rumble, and the way Mrs. Okafor had mentioned Pip sometimes calmed with noise and motion. Avery scooped her up carefully, supporting that heavy head with her whole hand, and carried her into the laundry room. She flipped the empty dryer on and swayed. The machine thumped and rolled behind them, vibrating faintly through the floorboards, and the smell of clean towels hung in the warm air.

Pip gave one last hiccupping wail, then a shudder, then went quiet. Her eyes drifted shut mid-cry, like the nap had been completely spontaneous, and Avery stood there in the humming dark feeling like she had solved a mystery worthy of a whole detective agency.

At ten, Mrs. Okafor came through the door and tiptoed over to peek at the crib. "She's asleep? After her fussy evening?" Then she looked at the running dryer and laughed softly. "You found it. Her dad does the same trick." Avery grinned all the way to the kitchen, where her fifteen dollars waited on the counter, and Mahee's next text was already lighting up her phone: TELL ME EVERYTHING.

Felix set the meter stick across two stacks of books and propped one end on Grayson's binder, making a ramp that leaned like a frail cardboard hill. "Ms. Ricci said we measure distance and time, then draw the graph ourselves," he said. "I want the steepest ramp in the class."

"That's a mistake," Grayson said. "A steep ramp means the ball goes fast the whole way, so the graph will just be one straight line, up like a wall. You should oppose my idea if you want, but I'm telling you, straight ramp, straight line."

Charles-Etienne was timing with the stopwatch app on his phone, and Felix had taped a long paper strip along the floor marked every twenty centimeters. "We call out each mark as the ball passes it," Felix said. "Charles-Etienne writes down the time. Then we plot it." He glanced at the wall poster of a deer labeled HERBIVORE: EATS ONLY PLANTS, which had nothing to do with physics but made the lab feel like the lab.

They released the marble. "Twenty!" called Felix. "Forty!" Charles-Etienne's thumb hammered the lap button. "Sixty! Eighty!" When they plotted the points, Felix drew the line through them and frowned. It was not straight. It began almost flat, then bent upward, growing steeper and steeper toward the end, like a slide that scooped down.

"Your graph is wrong," Grayson said. "You missed a mark." They ran it again, and then a third time, and each graph came out the same shape, curving up, getting steeper. Felix tapped the paper. "The line starts shallow because the ball is slow at the top. It ends steep because the ball is going fastest at the bottom. The curve means it's speeding up the whole way down." He ran his finger along the bending line. "A steeper part is a faster moment."

Grayson leaned over the points for a long moment, then set down his pencil. "I change my mind," he said quietly. "I wanted a straight line because it was easier to draw. But the curve is better. It tells more."

That evening Felix wrote a note to leave on Grayson's desk before class.

"Grayson, I looked at our three graphs again. Every one curves upward, steeper at the end, even though we dropped the ball from different heights each time. It's never a straight line when the ball speeds up. Tomorrow I want to try a flat track on the floor, because I think that one won't curve. If I'm right, the flat-track graph will prove the ramp graph. Your friend, Felix."

The next morning Grayson was already at the lab bench, the ramp rebuilt, the paper strip smoothed flat, two stopwatches lined up beside the marble. He looked up when Felix came in. "I borrowed a second stopwatch from Ms. Ricci," he said, "so we can check each other's times." He rolled the marble down the ramp one more time, and both of them watched it fly off the end and across the floor.

Ethan's fingers hit the last chord of "The Little Peasant Dance" a full eight seconds before the recording ended. He pulled his hands off the community centre piano and stared at the clock on the wall. Mr. González had given every piano student a spot in the Friday recital, but at this rate Ethan would finish his piece while everyone else was still settling into their chairs. Why did he always rush? He didn't feel fast inside. The music felt slow to him, steady even, yet somehow the clock said otherwise.

"You did it again," said Mouhamed, who was sprawled on the bench beside him with his trumpet case open. "Giuliana timed you. Sixty-one seconds. She says the recording is one minute and ten."

"Maybe the recording is wrong," Ethan said, though he doubted it. Giuliana appeared from behind the upright piano in the corner, holding her phone like a piece of evidence.

"The recording is fine. You're impulsive. You play every loud part faster." She tapped her phone. "Watch. You cruised through the middle section where it gets loud."

Ethan played just the middle section while she timed him, then played it again while pretending it was quiet, like a whisper. The quiet version took longer. That was strange. The notes were exactly the same in both versions. Same fingers, same keys, same everything. Somehow the loudness itself was dragging him forward, like a dog pulling a leash. But how could you notice something happening inside your own hands? It was like trying to watch your own eyes blink.

Then he remembered the shelf in the supply room, where Mr. González kept old method books and a strange pyramid-shaped brass box with a sliding weight on a metal arm. Mr. González had called it a metronome once. Ethan fetched it, wound the key, and set the weight the way Mr. González had shown a younger student last month. Tick, tick, tick. The sound was stubborn and even, refusing to hurry no matter what.

"Play with that," Giuliana said. "We'll verify it. You against the machine."

Ethan started the piece, matching his notes to the ticks. Whenever he pulled ahead, the tick landed behind him like a reproach, and he eased back. When the loud middle section arrived, he felt the old tug, but now he had something outside himself to check against, something that couldn't be charmed into speeding up. He finished, breathing hard. Giuliana looked up from her phone. "One minute and nine seconds."

Mouhamed leaned over the brass box. "Who even invented this thing?"

"Mr. González said a guy named Maelzel," Ethan said. "Johann Nepomuk Maelzel. He patented it in 1815."

"Patented? Like an invention?"

"Like an invention." Ethan slid the weight a notch lower, and the ticking slowed to a patient walk. He wondered what it would feel like to master a slow tempo instead of just surviving it. He set his hands on the keys again.

"Count me in," Giuliana said, thumb hovering over the timer. "Ready? Go."

Levi stood at the top of the driveway with the ball on his hip, counting the cones Ms. Virtanen had set out as pretend defenders. Brodie planted himself beside cone three, ready to screen.

"Call something," Brodie said. "You're the point guard. Point guards talk."

Levi knew the words. He had watched his cousin run a pick and roll a hundred times on TV, and he could picture it: Brodie would step out and block Levi's defender, Levi would dribble past, and then Brodie would roll to the basket. The problem was calling it out loud. His voice had a way of disappearing when other kids were listening, and today Asees was watching from the porch steps, arms crossed, waiting to be impressed or disappointed.

"Pick and roll," Levi finally said, too quiet.

"What?"

"Pick and roll!" He pointed at Brodie, then at the rim, drawing two parallel lines in the air like the two paths they would take, side by side and then splitting apart.

Brodie jogged over and set the screen. Levi rubbed off it, and Asees, playing defense from the porch, jumped out to cut him off. Levi spun and found Brodie rolling hard to the hoop, but Asees's little sister had wandered onto the court, and everyone froze so nobody plowed her over.

"That's a switch," Asees said, walking the girl back to the sandbox like a mother marsupial carrying its young. "I picked up Brodie now. You got the little kid's spot." She grinned, because Brodie was a head taller than her, and she looked tiny beside him.

Levi's first thought was that the play was ruined. His second thought was the interesting one. Asees was quick, the quickest defender out here, and she was guarding the tallest player on the driveway. That did not seem like a problem for the defense. It seemed like a problem Asees had just handed him.

"Same play again," Levi called, louder this time. "Brodie, deep post."

Brodie looked confused but ran it. Levi came off the screen, and when Asees stepped out to meet him, Levi lobbed the ball over her outstretched hand. Brodie caught it high, turned, and laid it in off the backboard. The little kid in the sandbox clapped like it was a fireworks show.

"See," Levi said, bouncing the ball once. "When you switch, you're on Brodie. That's the mismatch. I just have to find it."

Asees rubbed her chin like a detective. "Run it again, then. But this time I'm not switching."

"Then I'm taking the lane myself," Levi said, and he slapped the ball hard against the pavement.

The group chat lit up at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, and Jayden typed fast, because his little cousin was coming over Saturday and he had a plan. "does anyone remember that video Ms. Cruz showed us with the marble and the basket," he wrote. "the Sally-Anne thing from 1985." Charlie-Rose answered first: "the one where the kid says she'll look in the basket?? i thought that was fake." Riya sent a single eye emoji, which meant she was interested but pretending not to be.

"it's not fake," Jayden wrote. "kids from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away." He explained the setup: Sally-Anne puts her marble in her basket and goes out. While she's gone, someone moves the marble to a box. Then you ask where she'll look. His cousin was three, which meant, if the video was right, she'd probably point at the basket. "i want to try it for real. i need one of you to recruit as the marble mover. saturday, 2pm, my kitchen."

Riya thought it was a strange idea. "isn't that kind of a trick on a three-year-old," she wrote. "you'd basically be setting her up to be wrong." Jayden read the message twice. He hadn't thought of it that way; he mostly wanted to see whether the pattern held with an actual kid he knew, someone who shared his grandmother's laugh and called ducks "quack-quacks." He wrote back, "we make it a game and she gets the marble either way. lots of compassion, zero tricks." Charlie-Rose added, "i'll bring cookies as backup fairness."

Saturday afternoon, the chat filled with photos. Charlie-Rose had hidden the marble in the box while the cousin was in the hallway watching Jayden's dad stir soup. Then the cousin came back, and Jayden asked the question slowly, the way you talk to someone balancing on a curb. "Where will she look for her marble?" The cousin pointed at the basket without hesitating, then ran to check inside it, found nothing, and frowned at the box until Charlie-Rose let her "discover" the marble there, which turned into a game of hiding it four more times.

The last photo showed the cousin asleep on the couch, the marble loose in her fist, and under it Jayden wrote: "basket. she said basket. exactly like the video." Riya replied, "so she thinks people know things they can't know. that's kind of turbulent for a tuesday." Charlie-Rose sent, "she's three. she'll figure out people can be wrong eventually." Jayden set his phone face down on the counter and watched the marble roll a little in his cousin's fingers as she breathed.

Ryder pushed his noodles around the plate while his mom talked about Thursday. Basketball tryouts were Thursday, three days away, and his stomach had been sour since Monday morning. He had not eaten much at lunch either. He noticed that, and he noticed something else: whenever Coach Griffin said the word "tryout" in the gym that afternoon, the sour feeling jumped, as if someone had poked it.

"So how was school?" his mom asked.

"Fine," Ryder said. Then, because the word was already on his tongue, he added, "Griffin posted the tryout list."

"That's good, isn't it?"

He shrugged. "It's three days away. Nothing's even happening yet."

After dinner he carried the recycling out and found Mr. Nasser on his porch, sorting seed packets into a shoebox. Mr. Nasser was retired and knew a little about almost everything, including, it turned out, the mind. Ryder mentioned the tryout, and the sour stomach, and how weird it was that a game that did not exist yet could make his body act like it did.

"Ah," Mr. Nasser said. "Psychologists separate fear from anxiety. Fear is a reaction to a threat happening now. Anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future." He held up a seed packet. "Fear is what you feel when a dog is barking at you. Anxiety is what you feel for three days before the dog might bark at you."

Ryder turned that over on the walk back inside. His mom was at the table paying bills, and the quiet ticking of the kitchen clock gave him room to think. So the sick stomach was not about anything real in front of him. It was about a maybe. That meant it might be testable, like the time he and Caelan figured out which locker was rattling by listening at each door in turn.

He sat down across from his mom. "Can I try something?" he asked. "Close your eyes and count to ten with me."

She raised an eyebrow but did it. Ryder closed his eyes too and deliberately pictured the gym on Thursday, the whistle, Griffin with his clipboard, the other boys stretching on the line. His stomach clenched. Then he pictured the gym right now, empty, the lights off, no tryout happening anywhere on Earth at this moment. The sour feeling loosened, just a little, like a knot half undone.

"It's smaller," he said, opening his eyes. "When I make it now instead of later."

His mom said it sounded like he had found a way of coping, and that he should tell her before it turned into cumulative sleep loss instead of just three bad dinners. Ryder laughed. He said Griffin had told the team that a good player adapts to the situation in front of him, and maybe a good stomach did the same thing.

At the table later, doing homework, he wrote a note to Caelan and underlined one line twice: Not a dog yet. Just a maybe dog. When he read it back, he grinned and taped it inside his binder where he would see it Thursday morning.

Matteo sat on his bedroom floor with his history notes spread across the carpet, and the chat window on his laptop kept lighting up. Chloe had a piano recital in three days, and she had sent the same message eleven times: "I'm quitting. I have anxiety. Sell my tickets." Jude replied with a random photo of a cat wearing a tiny hat, which was his way of coping, and then added, "You said that before the last recital and you won a medal."

Matteo had his own problem. The chapter test was tomorrow morning, and whenever he thought about it his stomach tightened and his hands went cold. He had been trying to classify the feeling all week: was it the kind that made him want to hide under his desk, or the kind that made him actually sit down and work? He texted Chloe instead of answering her directly. "When you get nervous before you play, does your playing get worse or better?"

She typed for a long time. "Better, I think. I hear every note more. Everything gets sharp."

Matteo stared at the screen. So the tightness in his stomach might not be an enemy. Maybe stress, the body's response to a demand or a challenge, could do something useful, at least in short bursts, the way it sharpened Chloe right before a recital or a runner before a race. He needed to test it. He set a timer for twenty minutes, closed every chat window, and read the chapter straight through. His hands were still cold, but he noticed he wasn't rereading the same sentence four times. The facts stuck. Napoleon, the coal mines, the whole boring parade of dates.

The timer went off and Chloe called him, which broke the boundaries he had just set for himself, but he answered anyway. "I decided I'm not quitting," she said. "But I need you to come Saturday. If I look at you in the second row I won't spiral. Also I need you to hold my backup sheet music, which is a big responsibility, and if you lose it you owe me a piano, no warranty, final sale."

"That's not how warranties work," Matteo said. "Also I can't afford a piano."

"Then don't lose the music."

Jude's message popped up under the call: "I'll be there with the cat hat." Matteo hung up, reset the timer, and opened the chapter again. His stomach still felt tight, but now it felt like a hand on his shoulder, pointing at the page. He read until his mom knocked on the door and told him lights out. He turned off the lamp, put the notes under his pillow like some kind of guarantee, and said to the dark ceiling, "Napoleon, 1812."

The message that ruined Tuesday afternoon was short: "Ms. Chan assigns the most homework of any teacher in the entire school, maybe on Earth." Muhammad had typed it as a joke, but jokes, he was learning, did not always travel well through a screen.

Killian replied first. "Seriously? I'm going to complain to my parents." Then Florence: "Wait, is that real? She gave us that worksheet today, I thought it was reasonable." Within ten minutes the group chat had gone from joking to planning, and Florence had actually started a list of every assignment Ms. Chan had given since September. Muhammad stared at his phone, thumb hovering. Nothing in his message had said "just kidding," because out loud his voice would have done that for him.

He remembered the science trip last spring, when the class stood at the edge of the parking lot while Ms. Chan pointed at the crusty green patches on a stone wall. "That's lichen," she had said. "It looks dormant, but it's alive and working." Then, because a wasp had flown at Killian's head, everyone laughed, and even the teacher smiled, and no one had misunderstood anything, because everyone could see everyone's face. Muhammad thought about how laughter used to arrive at the same time as the words, and how in the chat it seemed to have ceased arriving at all.

He typed: "That was a joke, sorry." Too late, the planning had its own momentum now. Florence had written "Meeting at lunch, we should say something to the principal." Muhammad closed the app, then opened it again, and decided to test an idea: if he could not send his tone, maybe he could type it.

He searched "jokes taken seriously online" and scrolled past forums and articles until he found a page about the very first emoticon. On September 19, 1982, a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman proposed :-) on a Carnegie Mellon University message board so readers could tell which posts were jokes. Muhammad read it twice. Somebody, forty years before he was born, had hit exactly the same problem and solved it with three characters. He copied the little sideways face and pasted it into his message: "Ms. Chan assigns the most homework of any teacher in the entire school, maybe on Earth :-). Also that was a joke. Killing the lunch meeting, please."

Florence replied within a minute. "Oh. I took that completely seriously. Nice face, by the way." Killian sent a row of laughing emojis, and the plan quietly dissolved. Then Florence typed, "Does that thing have a name?" Muhammad answered, "It's called an emoticon," and added a winking one, just to make sure.

Ruby had until Saturday to stand up in the community centre's main hall and explain one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in her own words, and so far every attempt had come out sounding like she was reciting a cereal box. Ms. Vogel, who ran the youth rights club on Thursday evenings, had been clear about the rules: no reading from the pamphlet, no copying a definition, just plain words that proved you understood it.

Ruby spread the pamphlet across a wobbly table near the window. She had chosen section 2, the freedom of peaceful assembly, mostly because it sounded less complicated than the legal rights. Dan dropped into the chair across from her, already talking.

"I'm doing the US one," he said. "My grandma lives in Detroit and she mailed me a booklet. She's coming Saturday, and she said she wants to hear me say something true about it." He slid the booklet across the table. "The first ten amendments to the Constitution are called the Bill of Rights, and they were ratified in 1791. Two hundred years before I was born."

"That's extravagant," Ruby said, turning the thin pages. "Two hundred years of people arguing about ten sentences."

She read his amendments and then her Charter section again, and a pattern started to bother her. The American words talked about Congress not making laws against assembly. The Charter said everyone has the freedom. She began to hypothesize that the difference was about who the rule was aimed at: one document told the government what it couldn't do, and the other told people what they could do. She couldn't see it directly, though. It was a guess about a hidden shape.

"I need a test subject," she said. Dan raised his hand immediately, since he wanted the practice anyway. "Don't use the booklet words. Just say it like you'd tell your grandma." She took a breath. "Peaceful assembly means you and other people can stand together in public for something you believe in, as long as you're not hurting anyone or smashing things. The government can't just scatter you because it doesn't like your sign."

Dan frowned, then nodded slowly. "So the rule isn't really about standing. It's about who's allowed to stop you." That was it, exactly the piece she'd been missing, and it had come out of her own mouth before she'd even noticed it was there.

Ms. Vogel paused beside their table on her way past. "Five minutes till we clear the room, and the hall is booked for a birthday party after this, so no lingering." Ruby began gathering the papers, then stopped at Dan's booklet, its corner bent, his grandmother's name written inside the cover in careful blue ink.

"Can I borrow this overnight?" Ruby asked. "I want to read all ten before Saturday."

"Bring it back," Dan said, "or my grandma will ask you about it, and she's more of a quiz than a person."

Theodore's mother had to postpone her lunch break, so he sat at the empty desk beside hers with his math project spread out: three hundred survey answers about cafeteria food, dumped into a spreadsheet, and no idea how to make sense of them. His table just went on and on, row after row of Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8, pizza, pasta, pizza, sushi.

"You're going to type all of that by hand?" said Asma, who had come along to use the office wifi. She leaned over his shoulder. "That's radical levels of boring. Use a pivot table."

"A what?"

She clicked through the menus, dragged Grade into the rows, dragged Food into the columns, and dragged Answer into the values box. The endless table collapsed into a tidy grid: every grade down the side, every food along the top, counts where they crossed. Theodore sat back. It was like watching three hundred students get sorted into seats in one second.

"Okay, that's actually amazing," he said. "But I want to look at just Grade 7 without rebuilding the whole thing."

Asma squinted at the toolbar. "There should be buttons somewhere. I saw them in a video once."

They searched together. Theodore found a button labeled Slicer and clicked it, and a small gray box with three buttons, Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8, appeared beside the table. He pressed Grade 7 and the grid narrowed instantly to that one grade. He pressed it again and the full table came back.

The man from the next cubicle wandered over with his coffee. "Careful, that file's old," he said. "Slicers didn't exist before Excel 2010. They were added in 2010. If someone opens that on the ancient version downstairs, the buttons won't be there."

"Then I'll check the version first," Theodore said. He was already pressing Grade 6, then Grade 8, watching the numbers swap in and out. Grade 8 liked sushi almost as much as pizza, which nobody would have guessed from the raw rows.

Ms. Levy, his math teacher, had said the project needed a pattern, not just a pile of answers. Theodore had planned to count by hand all weekend, and he'd told Ireland it would be miserable. Now Ireland texted: still counting? and Theodore sent back a photo of the slicer buttons.

Ireland replied with three question marks.

"Come Monday," Theodore typed, "I'll show you. It's like a network of switches. Press one, the whole table listens."

He dragged Food into the rows instead, just to see what would happen, and the grid rearranged itself again, foods down the side now, grades across the top, still filtered to Grade 8.

"Save it," Asma said, pointing at the screen. "Before your mom's computer eats it."

Theodore hit save and pressed Grade 7 one more time, watching the numbers flicker into place.

Jessica pushed the folded poster board down the hallway toward Room 12, where the sign-language club met on Thursdays. Fraser had asked her to make the poster because her lettering was the neatest in grade eight, and the club needed members or it would be cancelled. She had lettered WELCOME TO THE DEAF CLUB in big blue capitals, and now she stood in the doorway holding it up.

Fraser's face went strange, half pleased and half worried. "Almost," he said. "Can you change one thing?"

Jessica frowned at her own work. She had spent two evenings on the swan curves of the F's. "Which thing?"

"Deaf has to be capital D." Fraser's hands moved while he talked, because that was how he talked with his cousin, quick shapes like birds taking off. "Lowercase deaf is the hearing condition. Capital D is the community, the culture, the sign language, all of it. James Woodward proposed that in 1972."

"Who's James Woodward?"

"No idea. My cousin told me. He said everybody in the club would know, and some people feel strongly about it."

Jessica sat down at the craft table with her pencil and eraser. She had made an assumption, she realized, that the word was just a word, and she felt vulnerable holding up her mistake in front of the whole room. The laminator smelled like warm plastic, and someone's phone was playing music too quietly to name the song.

She erased the lowercase d and redrew it tall, matching her other capitals. Then she tested the idea on Francois, who was taping the doorway and pretending not to eavesdrop. "If I write Deaf with a capital, does that include you, even though you can hear?"

Francois considered this while smoothing a wrinkle out of the tape. "I think that's the point. I'm learning sign because my grandmother went deaf at forty, small d. But me coming here, that's the big D part."

Jessica looked at the poster again, and a doubt crept in. She turned to Fraser. "So it's not wrong to write deaf lowercase ever?"

"It depends what you mean," Fraser said. "My cousin uses both about himself."

The adviser, Mr. Wiśniewski, leaned over from the next table where he was fixing the popcorn machine, and Jessica braced for a lecture. He only shrugged and said, "Ask them yourself," and nodded toward the door, where three students she had never met were peering in at the poster.

The tallest one read it slowly, lips moving, then looked at Jessica. "Who made this?"

"I did," she said, holding it a little tighter. "Should I change it back?"

The student smiled, but did not answer right away.

Aaron pushed the grocery cart down the laundry aisle while his dad limped behind him, rubbing his knee. "The cartilage in there is complaining," his dad said, "so you do the reaching." That was fine with Aaron, because the reaching was the whole point. Three days ago he had offered to do his own laundry, a voluntary offer that had seemed like a good idea until he opened the washer and found every one of his dark shirts speckled with tiny white flecks, like snow that had stuck and refused to melt.

He had stared at that load for a long time before he started thinking like a detective. The flecks were soft and thin and tore when he pinched them. Nothing in the machine was white and soft. But his hoodie had a pocket, and when he turned the pocket out, he found the answer: the corner of a paper tissue, the only survivor of the one he had forgotten there. The tissue had broken apart in the wash, he realized, and its shreds had scattered over every single item in the load. That had to be why his mom always checked pockets before washing. Nobody had told him. He had worked it out himself, and now he was here to fix the evidence.

He reached for a bottle of stain remover, then stopped. Would stain remover even work on this? The flecks were not stains, exactly. They were pieces of something sitting on top of the cloth. He put the bottle back and picked up a lint roller instead, rolling the sticky sheet over his own sleeve to test the idea. It lifted fuzz instantly. If the shreds were only clinging to the surface, the roller should pick them up, and the clothes might be fine after a run through the dryer, where the lint trap would catch whatever loosened.

"A lint roller?" said a voice. Ayana from science class was at the end of the aisle, holding a box of dryer sheets. "Laundry emergency?"

"Tissue in a pocket," Aaron said. "One tissue destroyed an entire load of dark clothes."

Ayana winced. "My mom checks every pocket in our house for that exact reason. She found a whole receipt in my dad's jeans once."

"That makes sense," Aaron said. "It's the hidden stuff that gets you." He dropped two lint rollers in the cart, one for now and one for the future.

At the checkout, Mr. Bouchard from next door was ahead of them in line with a small bag of oranges. He glanced at the lint rollers and smiled. "Been there," he said. "My load of black socks looked like a blizzard hit it."

At home, Aaron spread the dark clothes across his bed and rolled, sheet after sticky sheet, until the roller was furred white and his shirts were dark again. He folded them into neat squares, checked every pocket twice, even the empty ones, and stacked them in his drawer. Then he peeled off the used sheet, stuck it to the edge of the trash can, and stood back to admire the pile.

The group chat lit up at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, which meant August had found something in his grandmother's photo box again. This time it was a birthday card his grandfather had sent her in 1994, signed in careful blue ink: "Szabó István." August posted a picture of it with the caption, "My grandpa signed his own name wrong?? On a CARD???" Cade replied with three crying-laughing faces and the words "one job," and then the two of them began composing a corrective reply to a man who had been dead since 2009.

Lillian typed "wait" three times before anyone stopped. She was staring at the signature, and something about it was snagging in her brain the way a sleeve catches on a nail. In her history class, Ms. Yilmaz had put a roster on the board for a unit on family trees, and half the names had looked backwards to Lillian too: Kim Ji-ho, Wang Mei, Tanaka Aiko. Ms. Yilmaz had called roll that day and said the second name first, every time, without stopping to explain. So Lillian went to the class site, pulled up the unit, and found the worksheet she'd half-ignored in September. There it was in the margin, in her own handwriting because Ms. Yilmaz made them copy the tricky bits: In Hungarian, the family name comes before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.

"It's not wrong," she posted. "Hungarian puts the family name first. Same as Chinese, Japanese and Korean names. Szabó is his last name." The chat went quiet for a full minute, which in group-chat time was roughly a geological era. Then August sent a single "??????" and Cade wrote, "so his name is István Szabó and he wrote it the Hungarian way? on purpose?" Lillian confirmed it, and August replied that he had spent nine years of his life calling his grandfather "Grandpa Szabó" at family dinners while apparently using the correct order entirely by accident.

The next message was a photo of another card, this one from 2001, signed "Kovács Erzsébet," which August had always assumed was some aunt he'd never met. "That's my grandma," he wrote. "She's alive. I'm texting her." Ten minutes later he reported back: she had replied with a paragraph about the village where she grew up, where a peasant farmer on her street had been the only person with a telephone, and where she had nurtured a habit of signing her name properly because her schoolteacher had rapped knuckles over anything less. She closed, August said, by hoping he wasn't becoming one of those people who found handwriting obsolete, since a typed name told you nothing about a person.

Cade asked whether this meant he'd been filing Japanese names backwards in his head all through elementary school, and Lillian said basically yes. August changed the group chat name to "Szabó István Memorial Correct Order Society" and pinned the photo of the card to the top. Then he posted one more picture: his grandmother's reply, ending with the line, "Tell your friends the phone is not always right, but grandmothers usually are."

Grandpa's kitchen smelled like toast and chlorine, because Romy had hung her swimsuit over the radiator and it was still damp. She had a swim meet on Saturday, and her stomach had been knotted since Tuesday. She sat at the table, stacked and restacked the jam jars, and could not eat.

"Your hands are going again," Grandpa said, pointing his butter knife at her drumming fingers. "Same as before your music exam."

Romy looked down. He was right. She drummed when something was coming, some deadline or race, and she had never noticed it before. She tried an experiment: she counted the jam jars, breathed in for four counts and out for six, the way the school nurse had shown her class in September, and drummed the table only once more before her hands went still. Her stomach unclenched a little too. Interesting. The jitter had a purpose, she thought, like a warm-up. It arrived before the thing itself and then it left.

That was not true for everyone. Her friend Juno had texted every night for three weeks, saying she felt heavy and could not sleep, kept waking at odd hours, dreading things she could not name. Romy had assumed it was random, but three weeks was not random. Three weeks was a pattern. On Wednesday night Juno came over to Grandpa's, and the two of them built a fort of sofa cushions in the lounge. "The night before a race, my nerves actually help me," Romy said, breathing out slowly. "They sharpen me up. But yours has lasted for weeks. That's different." She got Grandpa's hot water bottle and set a rule: no screens after nine, warm milk, lights out at the same time every night, and ten slow breaths before Juno closed her eyes. Juno fell asleep before the tenth.

On Saturday morning Romy stood on the pool deck in her cap and goggles, and the big crowd did not intimidate her the way it had last season. Her heart hammered, but she recognised it now as the sharp kind, the kind that came and went with the race. She breathed in for four, out for six, and dove clean off the block.

Afterward, dripping, she checked her phone. Juno had slept through the night, twice in a row. And she had done something else: she had written down her worries on a page, found one clear motive behind the heavy feeling, a friendship that had gone wrong at school, and told her mum about it. Romy read the message twice, then typed back, "Grandpa says come Sunday. Bring your own suit."

The rain had driven everyone inside Rayna's garage, where her dad had set up a ping-pong table and an old space heater that rattled like it was chewing gravel. Gavin was losing, as usual, when Lux started in on a kid from their science class who wasn't even there to defend himself. "Did you see what Marcus wore on the field trip? He looked like a substitute teacher on vacation." Lux grinned and popped a chip in his mouth, then glanced sideways at the group.

Gavin laughed. It was a small laugh, mostly air, the kind you do when you don't want to seem like the one person who didn't get the joke. Rayna laughed too. Lux's grin widened, and he came up with another one, and then a third, each one a little meaner than the last. Gavin noticed something odd: after every joke, Lux looked over at them. Not at Marcus's empty chair, not at the ceiling. At them. It was like the jokes weren't really aimed at Marcus at all; they were aimed at the audience, waiting to see if they landed.

"Wait," Gavin said, mostly to himself. He missed an easy return and let the ball roll under the heater. Lux told another joke, and Gavin watched carefully this time. Joke, then the glance. Joke, then the glance. He began to resent the way he'd been laughing along, because now he could see what his laughing was doing. It wasn't harmless. It was approval, and approval was the mechanism that kept the whole thing running. Every laugh was a little fuel line running straight to Lux.

So Gavin tested it. When the next joke came, he kept his face still and said, "He's actually pretty good at science. He helped me with the volcano write-up." Rayna, catching on, said, "Yeah, mine too." Neither of them laughed. The room went quiet except for the space heater, still chewing its gravel. Lux told one more joke, glancing over hopefully, and when nothing came back he shrugged and started talking about the Raptors game instead. Just like that, the Marcus material dried up.

Later, while they gathered their backpacks, Rayna nudged Gavin with her elbow. "So we're unanimous on this, right? No more laughing at his jokes?" Gavin nodded and zipped his bag. "Unanimous," he agreed. "Although if he starts on the Raptors, I can't make any promises." Lux rolled his eyes and tossed the empty chip bag at the trash can. It bounced off the rim and landed on the floor, and all three of them stared at it for a moment before anyone moved.

Michael sat on the wooden bench outside courtroom four, holding a photocopy of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms so tightly the pages creased. In twenty minutes, each student in Ms. Leung's civics class had to stand up in the courtroom, which a judge had lent them for the morning, and explain one right in their own words. Michael had drawn fundamental freedoms. He had read the section six times on the bus and still could not say it out loud without stumbling.

"Which one did you get?" Diana asked, dropping onto the bench beside him.
