Jonathan had been practicing in his grandfather's garage every afternoon for a week, and every afternoon the same thing went wrong. He would tune the guitar, play the open E string, and then press down at the twelfth fret, and the note would come out sour instead of matching.

Meliane sat on an overturned milk crate, eating leftover noodles from a container. "You're pressing too hard," she said. "My cousin does that."

"No, it's not pressure." Jonathan played the open string again, listening. The garage smelled like motor oil and old cardboard, and a spider had built a web in the window corner that nobody wanted to disturb. "Watch this." He pressed the twelfth fret and plucked. The sour note buzzed through the quiet.

Baby, who lived next door and had wandered in as he always did, leaned against the workbench. "Sounds like a dying goose," he said cheerfully.

"Thanks." Jonathan laid the guitar flat on his lap and studied the neck. He knew the twelfth fret was supposed to give him the same note, one octave higher. That part he had learned from a poster at the music shop, and it made a strange kind of sense to him: the string was pressed exactly at its halfway point, so only half the length vibrated. Half the string, one octave up. He measured with his eyes, fret by fret, from the nut to the bridge. Something was off, and it was something he couldn't see directly.

"The string's too old," Meliane suggested.

"That would make it dull, not sharp." He tested the idea. If the fret sat in the wrong place, then the note would be wrong by the same amount every single time, and the errors would pile up, cumulative, as he climbed the neck. So he checked the fifth fret against the next string, then the seventh, then the ninth. The lower notes matched almost perfectly. The trouble only appeared near the top.

"The bridge," he said suddenly. He turned the guitar over. The bridge had shifted, just barely, toward the bass side, loose enough to slide when the strings were tightened. That was the hidden cause. He borrowed his grandfather's small screwdriver from the pegboard and nudged the bridge back until the twelfth fret note landed true, the same as the open string, only higher.

"Play the dying goose again," Baby said.

Jonathan played a slow scale up the neck. Every note rang clean. "That refutes the dying goose theory," he said, and Meliane laughed so hard she nearly dropped her noodles.

They stayed until the light through the window turned orange. Baby asked if Jonathan could play something for the neighborhood party where his mother was cooking Thai cuisine, and Jonathan said he could try, now that the guitar agreed with him.

"Half a string, one octave," Meliane said, plucking the twelfth fret herself. "Weird."

"Yeah," Jonathan said. "But it works."

The phone store smelled like new plastic, and Jacob held the box with both hands while the cashier rang it up. His mom had said the phone was his, and his alone, which meant the mistakes would be his alone too. Kye and Jax had come along, and they crowded around as Jacob peeled off the shrink wrap right there at the counter.

"First app," Kye said. "Get a flashlight."

Jacob searched for it and tapped install. A box popped up on the screen. The flashlight app wanted permission to use his camera, his microphone, and all his contacts. He stared at it.

"Why would a flashlight need my contacts?" Jax asked. "It's a light."

Jacob thought about it. A flashlight did one job, and that job did not involve calling anyone. He could not see why the app wanted those things, and he did not like not being able to see why. He imagined everyone in his contacts list, all his aunts and his teachers and Mr. Berg from next door, being handed over to some app for no reason. He tapped deny, deny, deny, and installed it anyway. The flashlight worked fine.

Later that week, he was still thinking about it. If an app had to ask before it could use the camera, microphone, or contacts, then somewhere in the phone there had to be a record of what he had said yes to. He went into settings and dug around until he found a list of every app and what it was allowed to do. There it was. He scrolled through and diagnosed the problem right away: a weather app he had installed on Tuesday had permission to use his microphone, and he had agreed without reading. He tapped the little switch next to microphone and turned it off. He checked the camera and contacts too, and switched those off wherever an app had them but did not seem to need them.

At school on Monday, Kye brought it up again. "You were so paranoid at the store," he said.

"It asked for my contacts," Jacob said. "A flashlight."

"So what did you do?"

"Denied it. And I can take it back later in settings, if I ever say yes by accident."

Jax pulled out his own phone, found his app list, and went quiet. His flashlight app had contacts, camera, and microphone all switched on. He turned them off one by one, and his ears went red, but nobody said anything about the humiliation of it, because Kye was too busy checking his own phone.

At home, Jacob's mom asked how the phone was going. He said it was fine, and that he was keeping the settings screen handy. Then he took the phone out, opened the flashlight, and shined it at the ceiling.

"Are you sure you don't want to wear the blue dress?" Mya's mom had texted the family group chat for the third time, attaching a photo of the dress hanging on Mya's closet door. Mya typed back "the green one" and muted the chat, because Grandma would chime in next with eleven exclamation points, and her stomach was already doing enough flip-flops for one evening. The dance started in an hour, and a small, loud part of her kept saying she could still fake a headache.

Tiana arrived at seven sharp, holding two hair ties and a plan. "Emery's going," she said, in the tone of someone stating a fact she intended to enforce. "You're dancing with him at least once, even if it's one random slow song in the middle. That's the whole mission." Mya said maybe, which in Tiana's language meant yes, and finished zipping the green dress.

In the car, Mya's little brother sat wedged between them on the way to his friend's house first. He stared out the window and said his stomach felt weird and his heart was going really fast, and he hadn't even done anything yet. Mya almost told him to stop making things up, but then she noticed he wasn't joking. She'd read something in Ms. Gallagher's class about how nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach and causes that exact flip-flopping feeling. She'd thought it was boring then. Now she looked at her brother's pale face and thought it might be the most useful thing she'd ever learned.

"You're not sick," she told him. "You're nervous, and your body released adrenaline. It makes your heart race and pulls blood away from your stomach. That's the butterflies." He frowned. "Then it's a false signal?" "It's real, it's just not a stomach bug," she said, and made him breathe slowly with her until they reached his friend's driveway. By the time he climbed out, his color was back, and he even waved instead of slouching.

Mya sat quietly for the last few blocks, testing the idea on herself. Her own stomach was still twisting, but if that was just adrenaline and racing blood, then nothing was actually wrong with her either. She checked the family group chat: Mom had texted a thumbs-up, Grandma had sent eleven exclamation points on schedule. She typed "going in" and put the phone away.

Tiana grabbed her hand at the gym doors, where the music thumped and Emery was already visible near the punch table, pretending not to look over. "One slow song," Tiana whispered. Mya took a breath, felt her heart hammering, and recognized it for what it was. Then she walked in anyway.

Nathan stood in the snack aisle gripping his list, which said, in his mother's handwriting, "usual granola bars." The tag under the usual granola bars read $7.49. Last month it had been $4.99. He checked the tag twice, flipped it over, and even looked behind it, as if a cheaper price might be hiding there.

Jolie appeared beside him with a basket on her hip. "Seven forty-nine? Did they dip them in gold?"

"There has to be a mistake." Nathan scanned the shelf. "Or a reason. Stores don't just add three dollars for fun."

"They kind of do."

He didn't believe that. Stores were run by people who counted things, and people who counted things had reasons. He walked the aisle slowly, reading tags like a detective. The fancy yogurt in the cooler had gone up too, and so had the almond crackers. But the store-brand crackers, two shelves down, were the same price as always, and the shelf was packed so full the rows looked like cargo stacked in a ship.

"Interesting," Nathan said.

"That's a weird thing to say about crackers."

"Look. Everything that got expensive is half gone. Everything that's still cheap is stacked to the ceiling." He pointed at the oat bars, a different brand, doing the same job as granola bars, sitting fat and plentiful at $3.29. "I think when a price goes up, everybody just... switches. They buy the other thing. The substitute."

Jolie picked up a box of oat bars. "Substitute. Like a substitute teacher, but for snacks."

"Exactly. It does the same job." Nathan tested the idea by watching people. A man in a yellow jacket glanced at the granola price, made a face like he'd bitten a lemon, and dropped two boxes of oat bars into his cart. A woman with two kids did the same thing, twice as fast, because the kids were chanting for snacks in voices that shattered the tranquil hum of the store.

"It's happening right now," Nathan whispered. "Watch. Price up, everyone runs to the substitute. The substitute gets popular."

"Popular and still cheap," Jolie said. "For now."

At the checkout, Mr. Banerjee from next door was ahead of them, unloading his cart. Nathan spotted six boxes of oat bars. "Mr. Banerjee, did you switch from the granola ones?"

"The granola ones went up three dollars," Mr. Banerjee said. "The oat ones do the same job. My wallet voted." He laughed at his own joke so hard the cashier looked up.

Nathan bought four boxes of oat bars with his mother's money and exact instructions broken. At home he set them on the counter, and when his mother frowned, he held up the receipt like a trophy.

"Half the price," he said. "And I still have change."

She turned the box over, read the label, and bit into one.

Maeva finished her first soccer practice of the season feeling great. She had sprinted until her lungs burned, taken a hard tackle from Greyson, and walked home through the park with her cleats swinging from one hand. "That wasn't so bad," she told Hussein at the water fountain. "I was worried I'd be too sore to move after sitting out all winter."

Hussein laughed. "Just wait two days." He was a veteran of the league, three seasons in, and he said it the way people say things they've learned the hard way. Maeva didn't believe him. Her legs felt fine, strong even, and she figured soreness was like sunburn: it showed up right away or not at all.

The next morning she was still fine, and she smirked about it on the bus. Then day two arrived. She woke up, swung her legs out of bed, and let out a yelp that brought her dad running. Her thighs burned like someone had wrung them out. She had to lower herself onto the toilet seat with both hands on the counter, and the stairs at school turned into a slow, sideways shuffle. Greyson clutched his own legs and groaned in sympathy at lunch. "Mine started this morning," he said. "I thought I'd dodged it."

Hussein slid his tray over. "It's called delayed onset muscle soreness," he said. "Hits 24 to 72 hours after, not right away. New or hard exercise, that's what does it." He shrugged. "Nobody told me my first season either."

Maeva turned that over all through math class. If the soreness peaked later instead of right away, then feeling fine after practice told you nothing about the real cost. Which meant Coach had been smart to make Saturday an easy recovery session, and it also meant something else, something about the tryout she'd skipped last fall. She'd told herself she was too tired that day, but maybe she'd just never pushed hard enough to know what tired meant. She couldn't go back and check. The choice was already made, and she still wasn't sure whether it had been caution or something closer to quitting.

There was a game on Saturday, and she intended to be there. On Friday evening she tested her idea in the park near her house. If the soreness followed its own schedule, easing off today wouldn't necessarily make it vanish by tomorrow, but it might keep it from getting worse. So she did one slow lap, easy jog, no sprints, and stopped while her legs still felt like legs. Her dad watched from a bench, arms crossed. "Hussein's family swears leg cramps are hereditary," he called out. "His uncle, his grandmother, apparently everybody." Maeva waved that off. This wasn't cramps, and it wasn't inherited. This was her own body keeping score.

Saturday morning she stood at the midfield line, thighs still aching but bearable, and bounced on her toes to feel it out. The referee raised the whistle. Greyson looked over from the far sideline and shouted, "Stairs still killing you?" Maeva grinned and shook her head once. Then the whistle blew.

The text from Haley glowed on Juliette's phone screen: "sorry if you got upset at lunch." Juliette read it aloud to Kamden, who was sprawled on his bedroom floor rebuilding a model bridge, toothpicks everywhere.

"That sounds like it's my fault for being upset," Kamden said, not looking up. "Like you're sorry I have feelings." He pushed a toothpick into place. "It's not sorry for what you did. It's sorry I felt a way about it."

Juliette stared at the words. She had meant them kindly. But reading them again through that lens, the way Kamden did, she saw it: the sentence never said she was sorry for spilling the secret about Haley's tryout solo. It only said sorry "if" Haley got upset. The "if" made the whole thing conditional, like maybe Haley had imagined the whole day.

"Is there a name for that?" she asked.

"Mr. Côté called it a non-apology last year," Kamden said. "He said half the apologies in movies are non-apologies."

Juliette set the phone down on the carpet. She thought about lunch, the way Haley's face had gone stiff when Priya mentioned the solo, the way Juliette had laughed and said, "Yeah, she's been practicing that one forever." She could still hear the sound of Haley's tray scraping back from the table.

She tried to paraphrase her own text into something true. "I'm sorry I told Priya about your solo. That was your news to share, not mine." She said it out loud to the toothpick bridge. It felt heavier than the text, like it cost something.

"Just send that," Kamden said. "Actual words. Not the immune version where nothing touches you."

Juliette typed it with her thumbs, deleted "I think," because that was another escape door, and typed it again. Before she could lose her nerve, she pressed send. The phone sat silent for so long that Kamden handed her a toothpick and put her to work on the suspension cables.

The bridge was half a tower tall when the phone buzzed. "Come over?" Haley had written. "I have the solo memorized. You're the only one who's heard it."

Juliette pulled on her jacket at the door. "Tell your mom I'm eating at Haley's," she called back to Kamden, and she was already down the front steps.

Ms. Hosseini had built a stream table in the corner of the science room, a long plastic tray filled with packed sand and tilted on wooden blocks, with a hose that ran from the tap through a small brass valve. Romy stood in front of it with her notecards and nothing on them but a question mark.

"You go Thursday," Halle reminded her. "Same as the rest of us. You're not getting an extension."

"I know when I go." Romy turned the valve a quarter inch. Water slid down the tray and curled into the sand. Within a minute a channel had opened, a small canyon with steep little walls, exactly like the diagram of the Grand Canyon in the textbook. But something bothered her. She measured the channel with a ruler. Then she measured the pile of sand at the bottom end of the tray, where the water slowed and spread out.

"Where'd all this come from?" Koen leaned over her shoulder, fogging the glass of the window behind them so it condense into a grey film he drew a face in.

"It came from the canyon," Romy said. She checked the numbers again. "The channel lost exactly as much sand as the pile gained. Nothing vanished." She dug her finger into the pile. "The water carried it. That's the wearing away and carrying off part. Erosion." She pointed at the heap at the tray's end. "Then it dropped it here, because the water slowed down. Deposition. The dropping of the material somewhere else."

"So the canyon's just the hole where something used to be," Koen said.

"And the pile is where the something went." Romy turned the valve further, and Koen said, "Whoa, reckless," as the flood collapsed a sand wall and dumped half the canyon into the delta in three seconds. She shut the valve and stared at the wreckage.

"It still balances," she said quietly. She measured again, and it did.

On Thursday she stood at the front while Ms. Hosseini opened the tap. Romy turned the valve herself, one careful quarter inch, and let the class watch a river begin its work. "Millions of years at this speed," she said, "and you'd get something you could hike into. Watch the bottom of the tray." The first grains of sand tumbled loose, rode the current, and settled at the far end in a tiny, brand-new beach.

Owen pressed his museum worksheet against the glass case and frowned at the little square marked C. Six, the square said, in a corner above the word carbon. Somewhere behind him, Hareem was already two exhibits ahead, and the first one to finish all ten elements won the extra planetarium ticket Ms. Tang had promised.

"How do you even know what that number means?" Kyra asked, catching up with her pencil clicking.

"It counts the protons," Owen said. He had figured that out at the second exhibit, where a brass plate explained that the small number on every square was the atomic number. Each element had its own, and the protons were what made it that element. He checked carbon again. Six protons. He wrote it down, feeling the paper go soft under his sweaty palm.

Then he reached the case with the skeleton of a horse and a label about carbon-14, and his pencil stopped. Carbon-14. But fourteen did not match six. His stomach dropped, because if the second number was also protons, then he had gotten every answer wrong, and Hareem was going to win by default. He stared until the words blurred. Maybe the plate at the start had said something about neutrons. He turned around and jogged back through the echoey hall, past the humming model of a volcano, the smell of dust and machine oil warm in his nose.

Kyra followed him and read the plate out loud over his shoulder. "Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These versions are called isotopes."

"Isotopes," Owen repeated, and the whole thing snapped into place like a latch. Carbon-14 still had six protons, because six was carbon, always. The extra stuff was neutrons, and neutrons were the factor that could change without changing what the element was. He could not see a single proton or neutron, not through the glass or anywhere, but the numbers on the table let him quantify them anyway, which felt almost like a superpower. He ran the test in his head: hydrogen with one proton and hydrogen with an extra neutron would both still be hydrogen. It worked. He turned to Kyra, grinning so hard it hurt.

"Write this down before I forget," he said, and she did, in her durable gray notebook with the bent spiral, while Hareem's voice rang out from three cases away, asking if anybody had found element ten yet.

Juliette set the microscope on the kitchen table and peeled a paper-thin layer from the inside of an onion, the layer so translucent she could read the cereal box through it. Her worksheet had three empty boxes: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. So far she had found one of them.

"Is that the wall or the membrane?" Maina asked, leaning over her shoulder. Maina had biked over with the salt shaker from her own kitchen, because Juliette's mom had used all theirs for the pickles.

"That's the wall," Juliette said, tracing the brick-like outline with her pencil. "The straight edges. But the membrane is supposed to be right against it, and I can't see any line between them." She turned the fine focus one more revolution, and the image sharpened, but still there was just the wall and a smooth gray inside. No membrane, no dark dot for a nucleus. She squinted. "How can something be there and be invisible?"

Maina tapped the worksheet. "Ms. Ba said our grade comes from labeling all three."

Juliette sat back and remembered fourth grade, when she'd been sure her snowflake had melted before she could draw it. Her grandfather had shown her that if she caught it on dark wool instead of her warm glove, it lasted long enough to see. Sometimes you had to change the thing around the thing you wanted. She chewed her pencil. The cells were full of water. What if she changed the water?

"Onion cells are sitting in water," she said slowly. "What if the water isn't plain anymore?"

Maina held up the salt shaker. "You want me to?"

"One drop. At the edge of the cover slip."

Maina sprinkled salt into a spoon of tap water, stirred, and let a single drop touch the slide. Juliette watched through the eyepiece, hardly breathing. For a moment nothing happened. Then, like a curtain being pulled back, the inside of each cell shrank. A thin skin peeled away from the wall and crinkled inward, and there, unmistakable, was the membrane. Inside the shrunken skin, a small dark circle appeared: the nucleus, which had been pressed flat against everything else before.

"Look, look!" Juliette yanked Maina down by the sleeve. "It's pulling away from the wall! The membrane! And the nucleus!"

Maina stared. "The salt did that?"

"It drew the water out of the cells," Juliette said, already writing labels with her pencil, arrows pointing to the wall, the shrunken membrane, the dark nucleus. She flipped her notebook over and found the word printed at the bottom of the chapter she'd skimmed. "It's called plasmolysis."

"Sounds like a superpower," Maina said.

Juliette tilted the lamp, and the light refracted through the drop on the slide, throwing a wobbling rainbow across the table. She leaned down to the eyepiece again, grinning.

"Salt shaker," she said, holding out her hand. "One more drop."

Emile had planned to spend Saturday at his grandfather's kitchen table anyway, because Grandpa kept a tin of lemon biscuits within reach of anyone who sat there, and because the essay was due Monday. The prompt was simple: should the school cut funding for the robotics team to save the music program? His class had argued about it for two days, which was longer than anyone had argued about anything except whether the cafeteria pizza counted as pizza.

He spread out his notes next to the biscuit tin. At the top of the page he had written a thesis, the sentence that was supposed to hold the whole essay up, and under it, three points: robotics costs more, music serves more students, and the school promised both programs last year. He had circled it all in blue pen the way Mr. Mendoza had shown them, and now he sat looking at it while the kitchen radio fluctuated between a weather report and something in a language he didn't recognize.

Timothe had texted him a photo of his own outline, and Charles had sent four texts, none of them about the essay. The last one said, "did u even start." Emile typed back "obviously" and turned his phone face down, because obviously was a strong word for one circled sentence and a biscuit.

Then he noticed something. His second point, music serving more students, was the argument he actually cared about, so he had moved it first in his outline, then felt bad for the cost argument and moved it up too. Now the outline read music, costs, promise. But his thesis still said the team cost too much, that music reached more students, and that the school had made a promise. The two lists didn't match. He read the thesis aloud to the empty kitchen. "It's like a menu that lists the courses in a different order than they're served," he said, and Grandpa, passing through with a watering can, said, "At my restaurant we served the soup whenever the customer asked for it," which was not helpful but was probably true.

Emile fixed the thesis so it named the points in the same order his paragraphs would discuss them: music first, costs second, promise last. Then he tested it. He wrote the paragraph topics in the margins of his outline, one word each, and checked them against the thesis like a man matching socks. Music, music. Costs, costs. Promise, promise. He did it twice, because the first time felt too easy, and things that felt too easy in Mr. Mendoza's class usually meant he'd missed something.

He sent Timothe a photo of the corrected page with the message "your thesis has to list your points in the same order you're going to argue them." Timothe replied with a single thumbs up, which Emile chose to interpret as gratitude. The fatigue in his right hand from all the circling was starting to feel like a real injury, and the cost argument still seemed kind of trivial compared to two hundred kids losing their orchestra, but the structure held. He straightened the pages, took one more biscuit, and started writing the first body paragraph, music first, exactly as promised.

Keira stared at the practice sheet on the kitchen table. If she got every problem right tonight, her mother would let her go to Kaleigh's movie marathon on Friday. If she missed even one, she stayed home. The last problem on the page looked like a trap: 5x + 2 = 3x + 10. The x was on both sides, like a cat sitting in two doorways at once, refusing to pick a room.

She pulled out her phone and typed a message to Kaleigh. "The quiz is Monday and I still don't get the ones with x on both sides. Which x am I supposed to move first?" While she waited, she made a quesadilla and ate it too fast, the molten cheese burning the roof of her mouth, so she sat there fanning her mouth with the edge of her napkin and thinking about the problem instead.

Kaleigh's reply came in three bubbles. The first one said, "idk, I got that one wrong." The second disclosed something Keira hadn't known: "Harlyn says she moved the wrong one on purpose and still got the right answer. Ms. Müller just wrote 'ok' on it." Keira read that twice. Moving the wrong x on purpose? How could wrong still lead to right?

She set her pencil down and tried it. First she subtracted 3x from both sides, because 3x was the smaller one and somehow that felt polite. On the left, 5x minus 3x left 2x, and the 2 stayed put, so 2x + 2 = 10. She wrote that down. Then she subtracted 2 from both sides, and divided, and got x = 4. She checked it: 5 times 4 plus 2 was 22, and 3 times 4 plus 10 was 22 too. She actually said "ha" out loud, alone in the kitchen.

Then she tested Kaleigh's claim. She crossed out her neat work and started over, this time subtracting 5x from both sides instead. The left side became just 2. The right side became 10 minus 2x, so 2 = 10 - 2x. It looked worse, like she'd wrecked it, but she kept going, subtracting 10 from both sides and getting negative numbers that eventually turned themselves around, and there it was again: x = 4. Both roads, same answer. She flipped to the front of her sheet and did the same experiment on an easier problem, just to be sure the pattern held.

She texted Kaleigh one more message before bed. "You can move either x. I tried it both ways and got 4 both times. It's like both doors lead to the same room." Then she wrote out the whole last problem one final time, clean and slow, in her best handwriting.

The next morning her mother checked the sheet at the counter, problem by problem, while Keira buttered her toast. When she reached the last one she paused, then slid the page back across the counter with a small amendment to the deal: movie marathon, plus Kaleigh's house for dinner afterward, if Keira showed Ms. Müller the double-check trick on Monday. Keira grinned, folded the sheet into her binder, and zipped it shut.

The gym was so cold that Livia called it the tundra, and she wasn't entirely joking, because she could see her breath near the water fountain by the doors. She pulled her sweatshirt tighter and found a spot on the bench beside Terrance, who had a pencil behind his ear and a folded piece of paper on his knee.

"Keeping stats again?" she asked.

"Somebody has to," Terrance said. "The box scores in the paper never name anyone but the starters." He drew a grid with careful lines, frugal with the space because it was his last clean sheet of paper.

On the court, Serenity was warming up, bouncing once, twice, then letting a shot fly. It rattled in. From the bleachers behind them, a girl named Priya's little sister stood on the third row and shouted, "My sister is the best shooter on this team! She's one hundred percent this season!"

Livia turned around. "One hundred percent of what?"

"Of her shots," the girl said, as if that settled everything. "She never misses."

Terrance flipped back a page in his notebook. "She took one shot," he said. "First game. It went in."

Livia thought about that all through the first quarter. One shot, one make. The number was true, and yet it felt like a trick. If Priya had missed that single shot, she'd be at zero percent, and nobody would be shouting anything. The percentage wasn't telling them much about Priya at all. She watched Serenity take six shots, sink three, and miss three, and Terrance marked every one, and fifty percent started to feel like a sturdier fact, because it rested on something.

At halftime, Livia wandered down to the fence behind the bench. Priya was sitting at the end of it, still in her warm-up jacket.

"Your sister says you're a perfect shooter," Livia said.

"I know." Priya grinned. "One for one. Can't argue with the math."

"Sure I can," Livia said. "One shot is like one raindrop deciding whether it's a rainy day." She pointed at Serenity, who was practicing free throws, calmly dropping in five of eight. "She's at fifty today, but she took real shots. Somebody tried to thwart her with that stat already, you know. Terrance read it out loud."

Priya's grin faded into something more thoughtful. "So if I never shoot again, I stay perfect forever."

"You stay perfect and useless," Livia said. "The number only means something if you feed it."

Priya chewed on that, then stood up and jogged to the scorer's table to check in for the second half. Livia went back to her seat and told Terrance to keep his pencil ready.

It took four minutes. The ball swung around the arc, and Priya caught it at the elbow, hesitated, and launched. It clanked off the back rim, and her little sister in the bleachers made a sound like a deflating balloon. Priya, though, laughed, held up one finger to the crowd as if to say, that's one data point, and got back on defense.

The next possession she caught the ball in the same spot and shot without hesitating. It dropped through clean, and Terrance wrote something down with great ceremony.

"What's her percentage now?" Livia asked.

"Fifty," he said. "The most honest number she's had all year."

"Perfect is overrated anyway," Priya called from the court. "I'm going for a hundred attempts."

The community room at the back of the bank had two washers, a dryer, and a long folding table, and Mr. Ho let the entrepreneurship club use it on Saturdays. Noemie was in charge of laundry day, which meant forty club t-shirts had to be clean, folded, and ready to sell at the farmers' market on Sunday morning. She had never done a full load on her own before, so she stood in front of the table with Jayson and Cameron and a heap of shirts on either side of her.

"Darks over here, lights over there," she said, sorting. "Mr. Ho said the red ones run the first few washes, so they get their own load." Cameron held up a grey shirt. "Grey's a dark," Noemie decided, and he tossed it over. Jayson wrote the price tags. They loaded the first batch, and while the washer drum thumped, the three of them packed jars of the nutritious trail mix the club was selling alongside the shirts. Mr. Ho leaned in the doorway and said the club account was doing well, and if the market went the way last month's had, their little business would flourish by spring.

The trouble started with the dryer. Noemie's older brother had come by earlier and asked them to wash his one good shirt for his bank interview, the interview at this very branch, at nine the next morning. His washer was broken and he had to work until closing. Noemie had said yes without thinking twice. But when the dryer buzzed, Cameron was elbow-deep in trail mix and Jayson was arguing about whether to raise the price of a large shirt to twelve dollars, and the shirts stayed in the drum, heaped and steaming, while the three of them counted the cash box and packed the car. By the time Noemie remembered, the load was cold.

She pulled out her brother's shirt and her stomach dropped. Creases ran across it in deep lines, sharp enough to look deliberate. A few club shirts from the same load were just as bad, but a stack she had pulled out early and folded flat was smooth. She laid her brother's shirt beside a folded one on the table and stared. "These were in the same load," she said. "The only difference is I got these out right away." Jayson frowned. "So they wrinkle while they're sitting there?"

"As they cool," Noemie said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Left crumpled in there after the cycle ends, they wrinkle as they cool. Take them out promptly and fold them, they stay smooth." Cameron groaned, because it was nearly six and the bank locked its community room overnight. Noemie looked at the dryer's control panel, then at the clock. One more cycle. She rewashed the creased shirts, and this time she made Jayson stand beside the dryer with a timer while she and Cameron kept folding table space clear. The moment the buzzer went off, she pulled everything out piece by piece, snapped each shirt flat, folded it, and stacked it. Her brother's shirt came out last, and it cooled smooth and straight on the table under her palm.

Sunday morning her brother wore it to his nine o'clock interview, and Noemie watched him cross the lobby of the bank beside a row of neatly folded shirts in club bins. When he came out at half past, he walked straight to the community room and pointed at his own collar. "Not a crease on it," he said. "You're doing my laundry forever."

Everly had been trying to write a story in her grandmother's back room all afternoon, and the notebook page was still almost barren except for one dense paragraph where her hero and the old lighthouse keeper argued about a storm. When Kim arrived for the sleepover, Everly shoved the notebook across the table. "Read this part and tell me if it works."

Kim squinted at the page. "Okay, so the keeper says the boat can't leave, and then he says the storm's too close, and then he says the radio's dead. Wait, who said the radio's dead? Was that him or the hero?" She flipped the notebook upside down, as if the answer might fall out of it. "I'm lost. Who is talking?"

Everly leaned over the page. Every line of speech sat in the same long paragraph, jammed together with commas and quotation marks, and she could see why Kim couldn't tell the voices apart. "I hypothesize that the problem isn't the words," she said slowly. "It's the shape. All the talking is stuck in one blob."

To test the idea, she copied the scene onto a fresh page, but this time she broke it apart. Every time the hero finished a line and the keeper began, she pressed return and started a new paragraph. She kept the ratio of narration to speech about the same, half description and half talking, so the only change was where the paragraphs fell.

"Now read it," she said.

Kim read aloud, and her voice swung back and forth without stumbling once. "The hero says go. Then a new paragraph, and it's the keeper saying no. It's obvious who's talking, because a new paragraph begins every time a different character starts speaking. Why didn't you do that before?"

"Because I didn't know it mattered." Everly laughed and grabbed the pen again. "Okay, that fixes who's talking. Now the other problem is that nothing big happens at the end. Mr. Rossi says a short story needs a clear climax, and mine just... trails off."

Kim tapped the window, where rain had started to hammer the glass. "Make the storm actually hit. Make the keeper choose between the radio and the boat."

Everly wrote fast, one speaker per paragraph, and when she finished the last line, the keeper shouting into the wind, she slid the notebook back across the table.

Kim read it in silence, then looked up. "Read me the next one tomorrow."

Arthur stared at the blank line where his paragraph was supposed to be. Mr. Zhu wanted five sentences in Spanish about plans for next year, and it was due at the end of class. Twenty minutes left.

He knew his plans easily enough. He would join the track team. He would write to his pen pal, Mateo, in Madrid. He would speak Spanish every day, or at least try. The trouble was the verbs. Every time he wrote a plan, the sentence fell apart on the ending.

He wrote "hablar con Mateo" and frowned. That meant "to speak with Mateo," not "I will speak." He chopped the word down to "habl" and stared at the scraps, as if the missing piece might fall out of his pencil. Nothing came.

"Stop grinding your eraser," Yahya said from the next desk. "You're going to wear a hole in the paper."

"I can't figure out the future," Arthur said. He kept his voice low, because Mr. Zhu was walking between the rows and the room was supposed to be quiet. "I need I will speak. In Spanish."

Yahya leaned over and looked at Arthur's sentence. Then he flipped back a page in his own notebook, where he had copied a model paragraph off the board. His eyes went from his page to Arthur's and back, twice, like he was checking a pattern.

"You're cutting it up," Yahya whispered. "Don't. Look at how I wrote estudiar for next year. I wrote estudiaré. The whole infinitive stays, and the ending goes on the end. So for yours, hablar becomes hablaré."

"Hablaré," Arthur repeated under his tongue. He wrote it, then "hablaré con Mateo cada día." It looked longer than he expected, but whole. He tried the next one. "Correré en el equipo de atletismo." Then "estudiaré mucho." His pencil moved faster now, agile on the page, and the sentences stacked up like dominoes that finally stood.

At home that night he prolonged his practice, writing three extra sentences past the assigned five, because Mateo deserved a real letter and not a sad little paragraph. When his mother asked why he was still at the kitchen table, he said he had a friend in Madrid who would notice if he quit halfway.

The next morning he slid the paper onto Mr. Zhu's desk. Mr. Zhu read it, raised one eyebrow, and drew a small arrow beside the last sentence.

"Read this one to me," he said.

Arthur looked down at the line he had written without checking. "Viajaré a España," he said slowly. "I will travel to Spain."

Mr. Zhu set the paper down. "Ask your parents about summer," he said, and moved on to the next desk.

The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and coffee, and Isabelle gripped her birthday money, two hundred dollars, in a zippered bag because she did not trust her backpack pocket. Caylee and Arianna had come along for the walk, mostly for the free lollipops at the counter, but they crowded behind her at the desk where a woman in a navy blazer waited.

"Hi, I'm Ms. Asante," the woman said. "Opening a savings account?"

"Yes. But first I have a question." Isabelle unfolded the paper where she had worked everything out the night before. "Your sign says six percent interest. If I leave two hundred dollars for five years, simple or compound, which one gives me more?"

Ms. Asante's eyebrows went up, just a little. "Which do you think?"

"Compound. Because with simple, you only earn interest on the two hundred every year, over and over. With compound, the interest earns interest too." Isabelle traced her columns. "Simple gives me sixty dollars more after five years, so two hundred sixty. Compound gives a little more than that, like sixty-eight dollars. But I couldn't figure out when my money would actually double."

Arianna popped her lollipop out of her mouth. "Why double? You'll be rich by then anyway."

"Four hundred dollars is not rich," Caylee said.

Ms. Asante slid a printed sheet across the desk. It showed the same two columns Isabelle had made, simple and compound, and the compound number beat simple by exactly the gap she had guessed. But at the bottom was a line she had never seen: Rule of 72. Isabelle stared at it.

"What's the rule of 72?" she asked.

Ms. Asante smiled and tapped the words but said nothing else, the way a teacher does when she wants you to find it yourself. Isabelle muttered, "Seventy-two divided by something." She tried dividing by years. Then she divided 72 by 6, the percentage rate.

"Twelve," she said slowly. "Twelve years to double. I'm thirteen now, so I'd be twenty-five."

"That's the rule," Ms. Asante said. "Seventy-two divided by the yearly percentage rate. At six percent, about twelve years."

Arianna leaned over the counter. "Twenty-five is so old. You'll be, like, paying rent."

"You'd have four hundred dollars you didn't lift a finger for," Caylee said.

Isabelle pushed the bag of money across the desk. "Compound, please. I can persist with it. Twelve years is long, but I'm not spending it anyway."

Ms. Asante typed, and the machine hummed. "You know," she said, "some people think interest is a trick because they can't see it working. You built yourself a little algorithm on paper instead. That's more credible than most grown-ups who walk in here."

The printer clicked out a single blue receipt with a starting balance of two hundred dollars. Isabelle folded it into her pocket, next to her worn calculation sheet, and Caylee asked if there were any grape lollipops left.

Cooper spread the newspaper clipping across the library table and read it aloud to Adelie and Leela. "'The new skate park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste.'" He tapped the page. "This guy says our park is a waste."

"My dad says people write letters like that when they don't skate," Adelie said, dropping her backpack onto a chair.

Cooper pulled out his debate notebook. He had signed up to argue at the next city council meeting, and Ms. Girma had told him the library kept the meeting minutes in the reference section. His argument needed to be solid, not just loud. "If I'm going to answer this letter, I have to know which parts of it I can actually refute."

"Refute how?" Leela asked, flipping the clipping toward herself.

"Like, prove wrong. But look." Cooper drew a line down the middle of a fresh page. On the left he wrote "two million dollars" and underlined it. "That's either true or it isn't. Somebody can look it up. The city budget would show it." On the right side he wrote "a waste" and stared at it. "But that part, I can't look that up anywhere. There's no budget line for waste."

Adelie leaned over the notebook. "So one sentence, but two different kinds of thing in it?"

"Right." Cooper stood and went to the reference shelf. The minutes from last spring were bound in blue folders, and he found the vote on the skate park without much trouble. There it was: the contractor's bid, two million dollars, approved six to one. He carried the folder back to the table. "The number checks out. So the letter writer got the cost right, and I can't refute that part no matter how much I want to."

Leela frowned at the clipping. "Then what do you argue?"

Cooper copied the bid number into his notebook, then the vote count, then the date the park opened. He wrote slowly, because he was thinking. "The 'a waste' part. That's just his opinion. It can't be checked. But the number of people who use the park, that can." He looked up. "If I count skaters on a Saturday, that's a checkable number. My whole Saturday, gone, but it's a real count."

"Then his 'waste' claim has to stand against actual numbers," Adelie said.

"Exactly. And here's the weird part." Cooper tapped the original sentence again. "One sentence can mix both. The cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion. Same sentence." He grinned and closed the folder. "Leela, you're good at counting. I'll need a tally sheet."

"Bring two pencils," she said. "And my board."

Alyssa spread her notebook on the flat rock at the edge of the pond and weighted the pages with two pebbles, because the wind off the water kept flipping them. She had promised Denise and Harleen she would have the finch project figured out by Saturday, and Saturday was today. Her plan was simple: bring the girls to the pond, act out the birds, and see whether her idea about beaks even made sense.

"Bigger beaks are better," she said when they arrived, lugging a shoebox. "That's what I thought, anyway. Big beak, big advantage. So I devised a test." Inside the box were kitchen tongs, tweezers, and two bags of seeds, one holding large hard ones and one holding tiny soft ones. She pointed at the mud below the willows. "Tongs are big beaks. Tweezers are small beaks. We pick up seeds for thirty seconds each and count."

Denise took the tongs first, and Harleen called time from the bench. With the big hard seeds, the tongs crushed it. Alyssa's tweezers fumbled, dropping seed after seed, and the score was not even close. "Told you," Alyssa said, stacking her seeds in a little cattail-leaf cup.

Then Harleen said, "Wait, your notes say something weird." She turned the notebook toward the light. Alyssa leaned over and read the page out loud, slow, so it would stick. "After the very wet El Niño year of 1983 brought many small, soft seeds, selection on Daphne Major's medium ground finches reversed, favouring smaller beaks." Denise frowned. "Reversed? How can small be better?" Alyssa looked at the second bag of seeds and said, "Let's just try it."

They scattered the tiny soft seeds in the grass at the pond's edge. This time the tweezers darted and plucked, quick as anything, while the tongs knocked the little seeds around like an obstinate bull in a narrow doorway, gripping three at best out of every ten tries. Denise counted out loud from the bench, and when time was up she held up two piles: a heap of tweezers seeds and a sad pinch of tongs seeds. "Okay," she admitted. "Smaller beaks won. That's a total contradiction of round one."

"That's the point," Alyssa said. "It's not that one beak is better forever. It flips depending on the seeds. Big hard seeds, big beaks win. Then that rainy year came, 1983, and all those small soft seeds showed up, so on that island, Daphne Major, the medium ground finches with smaller beaks ended up doing better." She copied the numbers into her notebook, then underlined the year twice. Harleen was already scooping the leftover seeds toward the ducks, and one drake, unimpressed by anyone's beak, snatched the whole pile in a single gulp.

The field trip bus rattled up to the Henderson Heritage Farm, a historic site so old that the guide claimed the barn had stood since before the town had a name. Scarlett stepped off behind Zachery and Alexi, still holding the worksheet Ms. Villanueva had handed out, and the first thing she noticed was that the place smelled like wet straw and dust.

The guide split them into groups, and Scarlett's group got the chicken yard. Their job was to collect eggs from the nesting boxes and carry them in a basket to the farm kitchen, where a woman in a long apron would show them how people had cooked a hundred and fifty years ago. Zachery lifted a warm brown egg out of the straw and frowned at it.

"Will this hatch?" he asked. "If we put it back, could a chick come out?" He looked around the yard, counting the birds. "I don't see a rooster anywhere. Not one."

Alexi shrugged and kept gathering eggs, but Scarlett couldn't stop thinking about it. If the whole flock was hens, then where would chicks come from at all? On the bus, she had read one of the plaques by the gate, a faded sign about the farm's breeding flock, and it had said the farm kept a "notorious" rooster named Barnaby in a separate pen across the road, away from the visitors, because he chased people. She hadn't understood why that mattered until now.

"Wait," she said. "If the rooster is over there, and the hens are over here, then these eggs can't hatch. No rooster means no chicks. But the hens still lay eggs anyway, every day, whether he's here or not. So the eggs would just be eggs." She turned one over in her palm. "That's why the farm can collect them for cooking without stealing future chickens."

"That's a guess," Zachery said.

"Then let's test it." Scarlett carried the basket to the kitchen, where the aproned woman had set up an old lamp in a darkened corner. She showed them how farmers used to hold an egg up to the flame to see inside, a trick that worked best in a room with no windows. Scarlett lifted an egg toward the light. The shell glowed a plain, clear gold, empty of the shadowy veins a chick would have. She tried a second egg, then a third, and each one was the same.

"So none of these would ever be chicks," Zachery said slowly. "Not because they went cold, but because they never could be."

The woman in the apron nodded without saying anything more and slid the eggs into a bowl of flour. Outside, through the open door, Scarlett could see the far pen across the road, where a large bird with burning red feathers strutted along the fence, keeping his distance from everyone.

"There's Barnaby," she said, pointing. "Not even he can help those eggs now. They're already in the batter."

Zachery laughed and wiped his hands on his jeans. "Then I'm eating the evidence."

Dinner was chicken and rice, and Ms. Holloway from next door had brought over a casserole dish because she wanted her pan back and stayed to eat. She also wanted Aaron on her library quiz team, which was the third time she'd asked this month.

"I'll think about it," Aaron said, which was what he'd said the other two times.

"You look tired," his dad said.

Aaron pushed rice around his plate. "The doctor says I'm fine. She said the tiredness is probably from being stressed so long." He repeated it the way the doctor had said it to him. "Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress. When stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high." That was the whole explanation. No infection, no low iron, just chemistry that had been running hot for weeks.

"So it's not like a valve that opens and closes," his dad said. "More like a tap somebody left on."

"I guess." Aaron didn't want to guess. He wanted to know, and the doctor hadn't tested anything. So he decided to run his own test. If long stress kept cortisol high, and high cortisol made him feel run down, then cutting the stress should change something. He could measure that. Every day after school he'd rate his energy from one to ten in his notebook.

Ms. Holloway leaned forward. "You take on a great deal, Aaron. Basketball, jazz band, that robotics thing with Hafsa."

"Hafsa and Hallie both quit robotics," Aaron said. "They said they were setting boundaries. That's the word Hallie used. She said no to Tuesdays and Thursdays and her anxiety got better."

"Sounds like coping to me," Ms. Holloway said. "You could speculate all night about which activity is draining you, or you could find out."

He found out. He skipped jazz band for two weeks, just Tuesdays, and told Mr. Delaney it wasn't forever, only an experiment. His energy numbers climbed from threes to sixes. When he went back the following Tuesday, the number dropped to four. Basketball, dropped from the schedule the week after, made no difference at all; his numbers stayed at six.

At the next dinner, the notebook lay open beside his plate, graphs penciled in the margins. "It's jazz band," he told his dad. "Not the practicing. The performing."

"So what's the plan?"

"Bounditions," Aaron said, and Ms. Holloway laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water.

"Boundaries," she corrected.

"Right." He tore off a corner of napkin and wrote it down. "Tuesdays only, and I'm telling Mr. Delaney tomorrow. And Ms. Holloway, if the quiz team meets on Thursdays, I'm in."

She raised her glass of water toward him. "Thursday it is."

Emilia sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field, her left arm in a bright green cast that ended just below her elbow. Mr. Ma had put her in charge of the stopwatch, since she couldn't play, and she was learning that watching a game from the sidelines showed you things you never noticed while running. For one thing, players fell constantly, and almost every single one of them threw a hand out to catch the fall.

She started keeping a second column on her clipboard, next to the sprint times. Tally marks for every tumble. Nearly all the falls ended the same way: palms slapping the grass, wrists bending back. It made her wonder. Her own fracture, the doctor had said, was of the radius, the bone on the thumb side of the forearm, right near the wrist, and it had happened exactly that way, when she'd pitched off her scooter and landed on an outstretched hand. The doctor had also mentioned that this was the most common fracture seen in children. Emilia looked at her tally marks, then at the green cast on her arm. Could she infer a rule from all this? It seemed like kids' wrists and the ground had some kind of standing appointment.

During the water break she found her classmate Jay, who was attempting a skateboard trick on the paved path beside the field, even though Mr. Ma had told him twice to knock it off. "Try to land on your forearm and slide," she said. "Not your hand. Trust me."

"That's radical advice from someone on a bench," Jay said, but he nodded.

She explained what she had figured out, pointing at her clipboard. "Radius, near the wrist. Most common fracture in kids. And you know how it happens? Falling onto an outstretched hand. Everybody does it. Watch." She nodded toward the field, where a midfielder had just gone down, hand out, wrist snapping back. Tally mark.

Jay attempted his kickflip anyway. He got most of the rotation, landed crooked, and pitched forward, and Emilia's stomach dropped as she watched both his hands shoot out in front of him like they belonged to somebody else. He sat on the pavement cradling his right wrist, which was already puffing up. An hour later he was in the emergency room, and the next morning he showed up at school with a sore, swollen wrist wrapped in a blue cast that ended just below the elbow.

"Radius, near the wrist," he said grimly, holding it up. "Falling on an outstretched hand, just like you said. You should charge money for that advice."

"Consider it free," Emilia said, "no warranty included." She was still laughing when the office aide came to find her, holding a note from her doctor. Her bone had healed ahead of schedule, and the cast could come off that very afternoon. She looked at Jay's fresh blue plaster, and then at her own green one, and held out her arm to admire it one last time.

"Enjoy the bench," Jay said. "I'll be keeping your tally marks warm."

Antoine stood in the doorway of the synagogue's social hall with a box of grape juice bottles balanced against his hip, wondering which table belonged to his aunt and uncle. The room smelled of chicken soup and candles. It was his first Seder without his grandmother, who had always hosted it in her cramped kitchen, and everything here felt too big and too bright.

He found his family near the window. His little cousin Zoe sat with a wrinkled paper in front of her, moving her lips without sound. Zoe was seven, the youngest kid at the table, and she had been practicing the Four Questions all week. Antoine knew because he had heard her through the wall of their shared hotel room, whispering the same Hebrew words over and over until he could almost recite them himself.

"Antoine," she whispered, grabbing his sleeve as he sat down. "What if I mess up?"

"You won't."

"But what if I freeze? In front of everybody?"

He looked around the hall. Forty people, maybe more. The rabbi was already pouring the first cup. Zoe's hands were shaking so badly the paper rattled against the tablecloth.

Antoine's mother lit the candles and said the blessing, and then the Seder began to move through its order, plate by plate, cup by cup. Zoe kept glancing at the paper, folding one corner, then another, until it looked as brittle as an old leaf. Antoine watched her and began to formulate a plan. If she panicked, someone had to be ready.

So he tested an idea, quietly, on his knee. While the adults sang, he mouthed the first question under his breath, the words he had absorbed through the hotel wall without meaning to. He got through the first line, stumbled on the second, and tried again. Next to him, his uncle's friend Mr. Anderson, a broad man with a loud laugh, gave him a curious look.

"You practicing too?" Anderson asked.

"No. Just in case."

"In case of what?"

Antoine didn't answer. Zoe was staring at the paper like it might bite her.

When the moment came, when his uncle lifted the matzah and nodded at her, Zoe stood up. She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. The whole hall waited. Her eyes went white and wide, and her paper slipped from her fingers onto the floor.

Antoine stood up beside her.

He started the first question, half a step behind the melody but close enough. Zoe's head snapped toward him. He kept going, a little slower, and on the second line her voice crept in under his, then rose above it. By the third question he wasn't leading anymore. He sat down and let her carry it alone through the fourth, clear and strong, while Mr. Anderson thumped the table and half the hall hummed along.

When she finished, Zoe dropped into her chair, grinning. She picked her paper up off the floor and smoothed it flat.

"You knew it the whole time?" she whispered.

"Only from listening to you."

She stared at him. "You could have just told me you'd do that."

"You'd have worried about me instead."

At the end of the night, after the last cup and the last song, his uncle caught Antoine at the coat rack. "That was quick thinking," he said. "Your grandmother would have done the same thing." He pressed a piece of afikoman into Antoine's hand, wrapped in a napkin, still a little warm.

"Split it with Zoe," Antoine said.

From across the hall, Zoe was already waving the paper at him. "Next year," she called, "I'm teaching you the whole thing."

Edouard slammed his notebook onto the lab table so hard that the beaker of water wobbled. "The ad said the mayor cut the bus budget in half," he told Lea-Rose and Nael. "My grandpa believed it before the commercial even finished. He said he's voting for the other guy now."

"Maybe she did," Nael said, stacking petri dishes because Mr. Bighorn had assigned cleanup duty and nobody wanted to salvage a detention on a Friday.

"She didn't. I just know it." Edouard tapped his pencil. The problem was that knowing and proving were not the same thing, and Mr. Bighorn had spent the whole week driving that point home. Last Tuesday he had made them drop steel wool into two test tubes, one capped and one open, and asked which one rusted and why. Edouard had figured out that something invisible in the air had to be causing it, even though nobody could see the cause directly. "You can't see air," Mr. Bighorn had said. "So you test what it does."

Lea-Rose leaned over her phone. "My mom does this thing when an ad makes her mad. She looks it up on PolitiFact. It's a fact-checking website, and it's been around since 2007." She scrolled, then turned the screen so both boys could see. "Look, they rate claims on a scale."

Nael squinted. "They call it the Truth-O-Meter," he read off the page. "It goes from True all the way to Pants on Fire."

Edouard grabbed the phone. There it was, the bus budget claim, with a little cartoon meter pointing almost to the bottom of the scale. The website hadn't just said the mayor was innocent, either. It showed the actual budget numbers, year by year, from records anyone could request. The budget had barely moved. The ad had taken one small cut and blown it up. That was the hidden mechanism, like the invisible something rusting the steel wool. A claim could look solid on the surface and still be corroded underneath.

"So it's not just that Grandpa's wrong," Edouard said slowly. "It's that somebody built that ad on purpose to make him wrong." It seemed ironic that a thirty-second commercial could do more work than months of real governing, and that people trusted the commercial.

On Monday, Edouard printed the fact check and brought it to his grandfather's apartment. He didn't lecture. He just set the pages on the kitchen table beside the coffee mug and said, "Look at the meter, Grandpa. Almost Pants on Fire."

His grandfather put on his glasses, read for a long time, and finally looked up. "Well," he said, "I still don't like her roads policy. But at least now I'm angry about a real thing."

"That's all I wanted," Edouard said, and slid the sugar bowl across the table.

Samantha leaned over the sink in the second-floor bathroom and held her note cards at arm's length, because the fluorescent light made the ink look like it was floating. Tomorrow she had to explain, in four minutes, how nicotine hooks the brain, and right now her cards said things like "reward pathway = dopamine?" with a question mark she'd added at lunch.

"You're hiding in here again," said Courtney, coming in with her gym bag. "Mr. Watanabe said he'd allocate five minutes at the end of class for anyone who wants to practice."

"Four minutes. He said four, and I need all of them." Samantha set the cards down on the sink's edge, where a drip from the tap threatened the bottom one. Courtney noticed and slid a folded paper towel under them without saying anything about it.

"Okay, start over," Courtney said, and perched on the radiator by the window, which rattled when the wind came through the arid gap where the frame didn't quite meet the wall.

Samantha took a breath and began. "So nicotine gets into the brain and tricks the reward pathway, the same system that makes food taste good and makes you want to see your friends again. It floods it. The brain doesn't like being flooded." She stopped, staring at her cards. "And then... this is where it falls apart. My uncle stopped smoking three times. The last time he went from half a pack to a whole pack and I never understood why he didn't just stay at half."

Courtney's older sister vaped for a year before quitting, so Courtney leaned forward. "He needed more to feel the same thing?"

Samantha froze. She heard the pharmacist's voice from the counter where she'd stood with her uncle in March, him picking up patches, her waiting. The pharmacist had said, as she rang up the box, "With regular use the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect. That's called tolerance." Her uncle had nodded like he already knew, which maybe he did, in his own way, and Samantha had mostly been reading the candy display. But the line had stuck.

"That's it," she said now, scribbling on the back of a card. "The brain adapts. An adaptation, like the whole system recalibrates around the nicotine, so the old amount stops working. He wasn't choosing to smoke more. His brain was demanding it." She looked up. "That's the trap part. That's why quitting is hard, and that's the middle of my whole talk."

"Say the whole middle section to me," Courtney said, hopping off the radiator. "I'll time it."

Samantha squared the cards, tapped them once on the porcelain, and started talking to the mirror.

Every strawberry that had ripened in Rachel's garden had a neat bite taken out of it, always overnight, always from the side facing the fence. She crouched by the bed and turned a half-eaten berry in her fingers while Lilith peered over her shoulder. "My mom says it's birds," Lilith said. "Rohan says it's rabbits. He's so sure." Rachel wasn't sure of anything yet. She had a guess, though, that something was coming through the gap under the fence, and a guess, she figured, was only worth anything if you could test it. "That's called a hypothesis," she said. "A guess you can check."

She set up her test at dusk. Six ripe berries, three placed near the gap and three by the patio, each one dusted with flour so that anything touching it would leave tracks. In the morning she found tiny three-toed prints on the patio berries and nothing at all by the fence. Rabbits were out. The flour marks were so faint, though, that she couldn't yet distinguish real tracks from scratches the wind might have made, so she repeated the whole thing the next night, and the night after that. Three mornings in a row, the same pattern.

Meanwhile Rohan had brought his toy cars to the garden wall and built a ramp from an old plank. His red car beat Lilith's blue car once, and he crowned it on the spot, holding it overhead like a trophy. "Fastest car, proven forever," he announced. Rachel frowned. "You ran it one time." They raced again and the blue car won, then won twice more, and Rohan's champion turned out to be counterfeit, a title from a single lucky roll down the plank. "You have to run it several times," Rachel said, "or you can't tell a real winner from one that just happened by chance." Rohan looked at his car like it had lied to him.

On the fourth morning Rachel hid behind the shed before dawn, wrapped in her jacket, and watched the strawberry bed through the network of bean vines climbing the trellis. The thief came at last, and it wasn't a bird or a rabbit. It was Lilith's little sister, in pajamas, carefully biting one berry from each plant and leaving the rest, the neat three-toed prints explained by the plastic dinosaur clutched in her fist, dragging through the flour as she reached.

Lilith went pale when Rachel told her. "She's been sneaking out at night? Mom will freak." They made a deal: the little sister would get two berries each evening, picked honestly, and Rachel would keep the flour tests going one more week to be certain the pattern held. It meant giving up her best berries every night, and it meant Lilith walking home stiff and quiet, but the next morning the fence gap stayed untouched, and the patio berries ripened whole.

Charlie had one goal for the zoo field trip: win Mr. Perera's mystery-object challenge. Every quarter he picked a student who solved it, and that student got to feed the seals. She had lost twice to Sam already, and today she intended to fix that.

The class followed Mr. Perera past the insect house, where Arya stopped to press her magnifying lens against a case of jewel beetles. "If the mystery is another beetle," Arya said, "I'm keeping the lens."

"No beetles today," said Mr. Perera. He led them to a brick building tucked between the reptile house and the aviary, where a shiny brass pole ran from a hole in the ceiling all the way to the floor. "This building is the old fire station that used to stand here, before the zoo grew around it. That is the original pole, from Chicago's Engine Company 21. The question is: why did firefighters use a pole instead of stairs? Guesses, everyone."

"To look cool," said Sam immediately.

"To slide down carrying a cat they rescued," someone offered.

Charlie frowned at the pole. She had guessed wrong once before, about a turtle shell, and the memory still stung. But her history teacher had mentioned fire stations last week, and something was trying to germinate in her memory, a small seed of a fact pushing up through everything else she'd crammed for the quiz. Something about 1878.

"Was it speed?" she said slowly. "Like, in 1878, a firefighter at Chicago's Engine Company 21 slid down a pole, and he got down faster than the others who took the stairs?"

Mr. Perera raised an eyebrow. "You're not guessing, are you. You're remembering."

"That's cheating," said Sam, grinning.

"It's called learning," said Arya. "Look it up."

"It's not cheating, and it might not be right," Charlie said. She pointed at the metal stairs spiraling up beside the pole. "We could test it. Somebody climbs the stairs and somebody slides. Time both."

"With what?" said Sam.

Arya held up her phone. "I've been timing the sea lion show for my sister. My timer is very consistent. Two seconds, every time I test it."

Mr. Perera checked that the coast was clear, then gave permission. Sam clumped up the stairs while Charlie gripped the pole, and Arya counted down. Charlie dropped, slid, and landed with a squawk that made a passing peacock answer. Arya called out the times, and the slide beat the stairs by seconds, again and again, trial after trial.

"So the pole stayed because one man in 1878 was faster sliding than the others were on the stairs," Charlie said. "And it spread from Engine Company 21 to stations everywhere."

"Feeding time," said Mr. Perera, holding out a bucket of fish, and the whole class groaned as Charlie took it and jogged toward the seals, grinning at Sam over her shoulder. "Tomorrow," Sam called after her, "I'm memorizing the entire reptile house."

The chili crisp shelf at Hartley's Grocery was almost bare, and the one jar left had a bright new sticker on it. Ellie leaned close and squinted. Last month the same jar had been five dollars. Now it said nine. She snatched it up anyway, because the cooking contest was Saturday and she needed it for her noodles, but the price itched at her all the way down the aisle.

She passed the pharmacy counter, where a man was arguing that his prescription should have been ready an hour ago, and the itch turned into a thought. "Maika's bracelets," she said out loud. A woman pushing a cart gave her a look, but Ellie didn't care. Back in September, Maika had sold her woven bracelets at the fall fair for eight dollars each, and every single one had sold out by noon. Two weeks later, Jaycob was selling bracelets, and the girl down the street, and even a table of them at the farmers market. When lots of people wanted something and there wasn't much of it, the price shot up. And when the price shot up, more people started selling it, because at eight dollars a bracelet it was suddenly worth your Saturday. She could still see Maika counting her money, grinning, while Jaycob studied her knots and said, "I could make these."

By the pasta aisle, Ellie had a plan. More sellers showing up wasn't some accident, it was inevitable, like the bracelets proved. If the chili crisp price had jumped, then somewhere, someone was deciding to make more of it and get in on that nine dollars. She just had to find that someone before Saturday. She put the expensive jar back on the shelf to conserve her allowance, which felt very brave, and hurried toward Mr. Tang's house two blocks over, because Mr. Tang made his own chili crisp in giant batches every autumn and the whole street knew it.

"Sold out," Mr. Tang said at his door, holding up empty hands. "Everyone wants it since that video went around. But," and he paused, rubbing his chin, "my cousin wants some of that nine-dollar money too. He's making a batch Thursday. Me, I'm making double my usual."

Ellie nearly bounced off the porch steps. Double! Her idea had been right, and now it had proof. "Can I reserve two jars?" she asked. "For the contest. I'll pay whatever you usually charge, not the store price."

Mr. Tang laughed and told her five dollars a jar, the old price, because she'd helped him carry boxes in the summer. On Thursday, Ellie stood in his kitchen while he ladled glowing red chili crisp into jars, the smell so sharp her eyes watered. She counted out her ten dollars, hugged the warm jars to her chest, and raced home to practice her noodles.

At the contest on Saturday, three other kids had brought chili crisp dishes, and one of them leaned over Ellie's table and whispered, "Where did you even find it? The store was cleared out and the price was crazy."

"Mr. Tang," Ellie said, spooning a little more over her noodles, "and get there early next time. He made double."

Vincent had been diligent about his watercolour portrait for exactly three days, and today the cheeks were going to ruin everything. He had mixed what he thought was a soft rose for the blush on his subject's face, but the wash had gone on dark as a strawberry, and it was drying fast.

"It looks like she ran a marathon," said Keenan, leaning over from the next easel in Ms. Lindqvist's art room. "In the desert."

"Thanks. Very helpful." Vincent stared at the paper. Ms. Lindqvist had drilled one rule into them all week: build the portrait light to dark, layer by layer, because watercolour was unforgiving. He'd assumed unforgiving meant permanent, which meant the portrait was finished before it started.

Inaaya appeared behind him with her damp brush in hand. "Hold on. Watch this." She touched a clean tissue to the too-dark cheek and pressed lightly, then again with a corner of the tissue. When she lifted it away, the blush was lighter, the edge softer, and the strawberry had turned into something closer to a real blush.

"Wait. You can extract the paint? After it's on?" Vincent grabbed his own brush, wet it, and dabbed it against his subject's other cheek, then pressed tissue to the spot. Paint came up into the tissue, leaving the paper paler. He laughed out loud, and the kid across the room looked over to see what was so exciting.

"It's not a miracle," Inaaya said. "Ms. Lindqvist mentioned it Monday. You were probably staring at your palette."

He had been staring at his palette, actually. He'd spent the whole week treating watercolour like a treaty he couldn't break, one wrong move and the deal was off, portrait over. Now he was renegotiating. He dabbed again along the jaw where the shadow had gone too heavy, testing how much pressure lifted how much colour, how far he could push it before the paper started to fuzz.

"We should sign something," Keenan said, holding up his own ruined background, a sky gone stormy grey when he'd wanted pale morning. "A formal treaty. You teach me the dabbing trick, I give you my last chocolate milk at lunch."

"Done," Vincent said, and shook on it, already wetting his brush for Keenan's sky.

Emma slid the microfilm reel into the reader, and the newspaper page from 1847 glowed green on the screen. Her project was due Friday: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. She had chosen the diary of a settler named Ruth Carver, kept in the library's glass case, and she had copied out three pages of it in her notebook.

"There," said Leen, pointing at Emma's transcription. "Ruth writes that a fever went through their wagon train on June the third and her sister almost died." Leen frowned at the newspaper. "But this paper from June the third says the trains at that crossing were delayed by flooding, and lists no sickness."

Ms. Haile, the librarian, wheeled a cart of document boxes past their table. "Something wrong?" Emma showed her the two dates, and Ms. Haile said only, "Historians check a diary against other sources, such as letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate," and kept pushing the cart.

Emma stared at the screen. She had assumed the diary was right because Ruth had been there. But maybe Ruth had written the entries later, from memory, and had gotten the date wrong. She formed a simple test: if the fever happened at that time, other sources should mention it somewhere nearby. She scrolled the newspaper forward, day by day, the pages flickering and the machine humming warm beside her elbow.

On June the tenth she found it: a notice that a party of emigrants had halted at the crossing, "several persons ill of fever." Emma then checked the government land records in the orange box Ms. Haile had left on the hold shelf. Ruth's family filed their claim two weeks later than the diary said they arrived. One date in the diary, Emma saw, was off by a week. The other details, the flooding and the sickness, matched. Ruth had not lied; she had just misplaced the date.

"So the diary is wrong and the paper is right?" said Aliyah, arriving with her backpack still on.

"Half wrong," Emma said. "The fever was real, just not when Ruth said." She wrote at the top of her notes: never trust one source alone, because an assumption is not the same as evidence. Then she copied the June the tenth notice onto her page and underlined the word "fever" twice. Aliyah leaned over her shoulder and read the sentence out loud, and Emma slid the notebook across the table so she could see the microfilm screen herself.

Brody stood in the kitchen with three piles of clothes on the floor and a folded note from his mom, who had left for a two-day work trip. The note said, "You wanted to do your own laundry. Prove it." He had begged for this after she shrunk his favourite hoodie, but now the washing machine glinting in the corner looked less like freedom and more like a corporation of buttons waiting to laugh at him.

He sorted the way he thought made sense: darks, lights, and a suspicious middle pile he decided to dismiss entirely by shoving into the dark load. Then he spotted his striped shirt, the one with the mystery ketchup stain from lunch. The stripes were white and navy, so bleach seemed like the obvious move. He carried the bottle toward the machine, then hesitated. His mom once ruined a red sock situation by guessing, and guessing had not gone well. He checked the little tag inside the collar, where a triangle with a cross through it stared up at him. "What does that even mean?" he muttered.

He texted Gordon, whose reply came in three seconds: "idk, my dad handles that." Brynlee answered a minute later with a photo of a label from her own shirt. Hers had an empty triangle, no cross. "mine says the plain one means any bleach is fine," she wrote. Brody laid both facts side by side in his head. If an empty triangle meant any bleach may be used, then the crossed-out triangle on his striped shirt meant the opposite: it must not be bleached. It was like the tag was warning him in code, and he had almost cracked the code the wrong way. He put the bleach back under the sink and ran the shirt through with ordinary detergent instead, setting the machine by matching the dial to the words on his mom's note.

While the wash churned, Ms. Ferreira, the neighbour whose kitchen window faced his, knocked on the screen door. "Your machine sounds like it's doing gymnastics," she said. Brody invited her in, and she watched him move the load to the dryer with an air of amused inspection. "I once bleached a whole load of my husband's socks," she offered. "Every one came out yellow." "Yellow?" Brody said. "That's not even a bleach colour." "Exactly," she said. "Respect the tags."
