Tyler put his left foot on the side of the canoe, the curved edge closest to the dock, because that seemed like the obvious place. The canoe tipped instantly, hard, and cold lake water sloshed over his sneaker. He grabbed the dock, heart hammering, while Amir made a sound like a deflating balloon.

"You almost went in," Amir said. "Full clothes. Phone in your pocket."

"That's not funny." But a small resentment toward the canoe itself had already started forming in Tyler's chest, the way you can resent a door that sticks or a bike chain that comes off. It was just wood and plastic. It still seemed to be out to get him.

He crouched and studied the thing. When he pressed down on the side, it tipped. When he pressed in the middle, it barely moved. The canoe rocked around its center, he realized, the way a seesaw rocks around its middle bar, and the middle bar of a seesaw is exactly where you want to sit. "I should step into the middle," he said slowly, "not onto the side." He remembered his cousin once saying people keep their weight low and centered in a canoe, that's the whole trick, and now the words finally meant something.

"So step in the middle," Harlyn said.

"I'm interpreting the situation, thank you." Tyler put one foot, then the other, straight into the center of the canoe, crouching low like a crab, and the boat settled under him, steady as a table. He sat down on the bottom, knees bent, paddle across his lap, and let out a breath. It worked. It really worked. Mr. Schneider climbed in behind him without a single wobble, and they paddled a long slow loop past the reeds while Tyler practiced steering, feeling more ready for camp by the minute.

Back on shore, wringing out his sock, Tyler found Harlyn reading the camp brochure he'd left on the dock. She looked up with a strange expression.

"Tyler. This year's canoeing block is kayaks."

Tyler stared at his duffel bag, then at the green canoe, then at Harlyn. "Then what do I do with everything I just learned?"

Amir pointed at the water. "Learn to tip a kayak."

Eva had promised the whole coding cabin that by Friday demo night her program would ask for a number and say whether it was prime, and right now it said that 9 was prime, which it was not. She sat at the long pine table with her laptop open, running the loop again and watching the wrong answer blink at her. Kash leaned over from the next seat, grinning. "Nine is prime now? You've discovered new math."

"Don't humiliate me before I've had breakfast," Eva said, but her ears went hot anyway. Hana pulled her chair around so she could see the screen.

The problem was the flag. Eva had set a variable called found to zero, and inside the loop she changed it when a divisor appeared, and after the loop she checked it, except the check kept happening too early, or the flag kept its old value from the run before, or something she couldn't see. That was the worst part. The loop did its work somewhere she couldn't look, and the mistake was hiding in there like a bird in a hedge.

"Birds," Hana said suddenly, pointing at the poster taped to the cabin wall, a map dotted with arrows. "Migratory routes. That one crosses the equator twice, look, it goes all the way down and back." Eva looked, mostly to rest her eyes, and thought about how the map showed where the birds went but not why they knew to go there. Her program was like that too. It showed the answer but not the reason underneath.

Then Mr. Chowdhury, the mentor who ran the cabin, came by with his coffee. He read her screen for a moment, took the marker, and wrote four lines on the little whiteboard beside the table. Her loop, but with the word else tucked under it, and her print statement moved inside that block. He tapped the marker once against the board. "Else," he said, and went to refill his coffee, because he never explained anything twice or even once if he could help it.

Eva stared at it. "A loop gets an else?" she said. Hana frowned. Kash shook his head slowly, which meant he didn't know either, which meant nobody at the table knew, which made Eva feel a little better and a lot more curious.

She traced it with her finger on the screen. The else sat under the for, the way an else sits under an if, and the print was inside it. "So if the loop breaks, the else gets skipped," she said, "and if it never breaks, if it checks every number and finds nothing, then the else runs." No divisor found, so the number is prime. She deleted the flag, typed the else, and hit run.

9: not prime. 7: prime. 11: prime. 25: not prime.

"Run it on a million," Kash said. Eva typed it in.

The gym smelled like floor wax and cold coffee, and the line for the student mock election snaked past the bake sale table. Nevaeh stood with her sample ballot and a problem: her grandmother had said this morning, flat and tired, "I've voted in every election since I was eighteen, and my vote has never counted once." Nevaeh wanted to prove her wrong before dinner.

Mr. Nowak, who ran the polling station and the chess club, had taped a poster to the bleachers. "Sample district results," it read. "Party A: 34 percent. Party B: 33 percent. Party C: 33 percent. Winner: Party A. Seats: Party A, one." Christina squinted at it. "Thirty-four beats thirty-three. So A wins the seat."

"Look at the whole district, though." Nevaeh counted on her fingers. "Sixty-six percent voted for B or C. That's most of the voters, and they get nothing." She drafted a quick tally chart on the back of her ballot, three columns, and stared at it. Somewhere behind the numbers there was a reason her grandmother felt invisible, and she meant to find it.

Naomie arrived with a pretzel from the bake sale and her own agenda: she wanted the mock election switched to proportional seats so her party, always squashed in third place, could finally win something. "My cousin says other countries do it differently," she said. "Seats by share of the vote. Can we test it?"

Mr. Nowak handed them a fresh tally sheet. "Try it. Same numbers, both ways."

Nevaeh ran it. First-past-the-post: A took the seat, and every ballot marked B or C elected nobody, all sixty-six percent of them stacked in dead columns. Then she divided the seats by share, and B and C each pulled one. The same votes, counted two ways, produced two different parliaments.

"Grandma votes for C," Nevaeh said quietly. "Always. In her district." She pointed at the dead columns. "Those are wasted votes. That's what they're called. That's her, every single time."

Christina frowned at the chart. "So she's right and wrong. Her vote is counted, but it never elects anybody."

Nevaeh copied both tallies onto a napkin, folded it, and put it in her jacket pocket. Naomie was already drafting a petition for proportional seats, ten signatures or bust.

"Where are you going?" Christina called.

"Home," Nevaeh said, pushing through the double doors. "Grandma's making dinner. She's indifferent about my opinion on her cuisine, but not about this."

The assignment was Adam's idea, which meant it was his job to coordinate it: Yara would handle the interviews, Thalia would bring her grandmother's prayer book, and Adam would find a place to start. He chose the old cemetery behind St. Brigid's, where the stones went back over a hundred years and the caretaker, Mr. Campbell-Brown, let students in after school as long as they closed the gate.

"Grandma's stone is this way," Thalia said, leading them past a row of leaning markers. She stopped at a granite slab with a small crucifix carved at the top, a figure on the cross with her head bowed. Yara found her own family a few rows over, at a plain cross with nothing on it, just clean lines. Adam wrote both descriptions in his notebook and stood between the two graves, tapping his pencil.

"Okay, so here's my theory," he said. "The crucifixes mark the Catholic graves and the plain crosses mark the Protestant ones. If the symbols are different, maybe the teachings are different too. So, Thalia, what does your church say happens after you die?"

Thalia brushed lichen off the edge of her grandmother's stone while she thought. "We go to heaven, but first most people go to purgatory," she said. "It's a purification. Like being cleaned up before you go in."

Yara frowned at her. "My church never says that. We go straight to heaven if we're saved. Pastor Ruiz says purgatory isn't in the Bible at all." The two of them stared at each other, and Adam could almost see the surprise traveling between them, because they had sat three seats apart in homeroom since fifth grade and never once guessed their churches disagreed on something this big.

Mr. Campbell-Brown came around the corner with a spray bottle and a stiff brush, working on a marker crusted with green. "Careful where you stand," he said. "This cleaner's corrosive. It'll eat through your shoe laces faster than the moss." Adam stepped back and asked him about the symbols, and the caretaker nodded slowly. "Catholics put up the crucifix, mostly, and the others keep it plain. Been that way longer than me."

Adam flipped to a fresh page and drew two columns, one headed with a crucifix and one with a plain cross. Under the first he wrote purification first, then heaven, and under the second, straight to heaven, no middle state. Then he added a third line at the bottom, for the question he would ask in class on Monday: what else do the two churches see differently that nobody has told us about? Yara borrowed his pencil to underline it, and Thalia zipped her grandmother's prayer book back into her bag as the shadows of the stones stretched long across the grass.

The radiator next to the study carrel clanked like a spoon in a pot, and Emilie spread her photos across the table so Janelle and Mathew could see the disaster. "Ms. González says our presentation on monsoons has to answer why they matter," she said, "and all I have is a paragraph about wind and a picture of rice fields that look like somebody flooded the farms on purpose."

Mathew picked up the photo and held it to the light. "Maybe it's a mistake," he said. "Maybe the river rose." Janelle leaned over his shoulder and sniffed. "Smells like a lake in there. Or like your lunch." Mathew elbowed her, and the photo fluttered into the map drawer, which slid open with a groan that made half the library turn around.

Emilie retrieved it and sat very still, which was what she did when she was thinking. The water in the picture wasn't deep, just a few inches, and it lay perfectly flat between the green rows, like a mirror laid down on purpose. If the river had flooded the fields, the water would be muddy and uneven, wouldn't it? And the plants looked healthy, not drowned. She flipped through the other photos. Field after field, all standing in shallow water, all neat. Nobody lets an accident repeat itself in every picture. She wrote in her notebook: water on purpose. Then she needed proof, and proof meant the shelves.

She left Janelle and Mathew arguing about whether rice was a carbohydrate the same way bread was, and walked the agriculture aisle fast, running one finger along the spines. The tense part was the clock: the library closed in forty minutes, and Ms. González was already at the front desk stamping returns. Emilie found the book. It was thick and smelled like dust and rain. She paged through it with her heart tapping, past diagrams of winds, past a chart of approximate rainfall totals, until she reached a picture identical to her photo, and one short sentence underneath it.

She carried the book back at a speed that did not technically permit running, and slid it onto the table. "They flood them on purpose," she said. "Rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies. The standing water helps keep many weeds from growing."

Janelle blinked. "So the rice is swimming on purpose."

"So the monsoons matter," Emilie said, tapping the rainfall chart. "The rain fills the paddies. That's the whole answer. No monsoon, no water, no rice."

Mathew held up the photo again. "Then this isn't a disaster. It's dinner."

"Approximately," said Janelle, and stole his pencil.

The sugar wouldn't brown. Jacob stared into the pot at the community kitchen, where he'd signed up to make dessert for his family's Friday dinner, and the white grains just sat there in a pale puddle, refusing to turn gold. Tanya leaned over his shoulder, sniffing the pot.

"It's supposed to be caramel," Jacob said. "Golden, then amber. Mine's just... warm sugar water." He'd volunteered to participate in the community kitchen's family-meal night mostly so he could brag about making dessert from scratch, and now the bragging was in danger.

"Give it more heat," Tanya said. "Browning is browning, right? Like when Mr. Demetriou did that roast last week and the crust went all brown and crackly."

Jacob stopped stirring. Something about that bothered him. The roast had browned in the oven, dry heat, no sugar at all. His pot was nothing but sugar and a splash of water. Could they really be the same thing? He remembered Mr. Demetriou saying a word while he carved the roast, something French-sounding, and Jacob had written it on his recipe card because it sounded cool. He dug the card out of his backpack. There it was: Maillard. Next to it, in his own handwriting, "needs amino acids, the stuff in meat." His pot had no meat, no amino acids, nothing but sugar.

"So this can't be Maillard," he said slowly, feeling his heart pick up. "It's sugar alone being heated. That's a different reaction." He turned the burner up anyway, testing the idea, because if he was wrong the sugar would stay pale forever. Within a minute the puddle blushed gold, then deepened to amber, and the smell changed to something toasty and sweet. Seerat, at the next station, rushed over. "Jacob! Yours worked! Mine's still gray, and I followed every step." She showed him her pot: milk, butter, sugar, and a pinch of salt. It was browning unevenly, pale in patches.

"Seerat, is your crust the same as the roast crust?" Jacob asked her.

"No idea," she said. "Is it?"

"The roast one is the Maillard reaction," Seerat read off his card before he could answer, squinting at his handwriting. "It also needs amino acids." She frowned at her pot. "Milk has that stuff in it. So mine's doing both browning at once and going weird."

The fundamental difference between the two brownings had ruined her fudge and saved his caramel, all in the same ten minutes. Jacob laughed so hard he nearly dropped the spoon, then helped Seerat scrape her pot and start again with plain sugar, teaching her his technique while she stuck out her tongue at him.

"Just remember," he said, tipping his finished caramel into a jar, "when my family oohs and aahs tonight, tell them the part where mine almost failed too."

"Sure," said Seerat, already stirring her new batch, which was turning a perfect gold. "Right after I tell them mine's the second-best caramel this kitchen has ever seen."

The jar was still warm in Jacob's hands when Seerat held up her pot, amber and gleaming, and shouted, "Yours is now second!"

Louis had written the same first sentence four times, crossed it out four times, and was now drawing a small tank in the margin of his notebook. The prompt on the board read: Should the school replace the asphalt courtyard with a garden? Take a position and defend it with three points. Mr. Reyes had said the draft was due at the end of the period.

Ria leaned over from the next desk. "You've written nothing."

"I'm deciding how to word it," Louis said.

Aisha, on his other side, slid her paper toward him. She didn't have sentences either. She had three lines: "Garden better. One: cools the yard. Two: kids actually use it. Three: storm water. Thesis: garden helps school more than asphalt." Below that, a few quick bullets under each line.

"That's not an essay," Louis said.

"It's not supposed to be. It's the plan. My brother says decide what to say before you worry about how to word it. The outline is the deciding part. The sentences come after."

Louis looked at his tank. He had been trying to plan his argument and craft his sentences at the same time, and each half kept wrecking the other. He flipped to a clean page and wrote: "Garden, three points." It took him two minutes to list them. Shade cuts the heat, students eat lunch out there, and the beds soak up rain instead of letting it flood the walkway. Then one line at the top: "The garden does more for us than the asphalt does."

He stared at it. That was a thesis. He hadn't struggled over it at all, because the deciding was already done.

He drafted fast after that. When a sentence came out clumsy, he crossed it out without panic, because the plan underneath was still standing. It was like a rudder; the outline held his direction while the wording swung back and forth.

Mr. Reyes walked the rows. He paused at Louis's page, read the three lines at the top, and nodded once. "Structure first. Good."

At the end of class Louis had two full paragraphs and the start of a third. Aisha held up her paper, which was three sentences long but had the whole skeleton on it. "Want to compare at lunch? I think my storm water point could demolish your shade point."

"Bring the lunch data," Louis said, and copied his outline onto the back of his hand so he wouldn't lose it before fifth period.

The problem started on Tuesday, when Mr. De Vries moved Lincoln to the back row. "Chatty section," Mr. De Vries said, pointing at the desk behind Makai, and Lincoln dragged his bag down the room like it was full of bricks. From there the board was a smear of white chalk. He could read his phone perfectly, though, even with the brightness turned low, and that made no sense to him. The board was huge. The phone was the size of a sandwich. Something had to be wrong with the light, not with the board, and he meant to find out what.

He ran a test at lunch. He had Callie hold up a menu from across the cafeteria while he squinted through a hole he'd punched in an index card. The tiny letters sharpened. Then he tried the same card trick on the menu held at arm's length. No change, because near things had already looked fine. "You look like a spy," Callie said. "A spy who needs glasses," Makai said, and Lincoln grinned, because the test had told him something: only far things went blurry. Light from far objects was landing somewhere wrong in his eye, and near objects were not.

Mr. De Vries called home that afternoon. His mother booked an appointment before dinner, and on Thursday an optometrist flipped lenses in front of Lincoln's face while a machine hummed. "Your eyeball is slightly too long," the man said, marking a chart. "So light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina instead of on it. We call that nearsighted." Nearsighted. Lincoln said the word twice, testing it. It fit everything: the blurry board, the perfect phone, the pinhole that squeezed the light back onto the right spot.

He picked out frames the same day, black with a thin orange line along the top, even though his mother said the second pair was pushy. "It's my face," Lincoln said, and she laughed and paid. Walking out, he kept bumping his own excitement into things, pointing at street signs he could suddenly read from half a block away, at individual leaves on trees that had been green fog that morning.

Back at school, Mr. De Vries looked up from his roster with an ominous expression, like he was about to assign seats again. "Front row, Lincoln. Fair warning." "No need," Lincoln said, sliding the glasses on. "I can read the board from the ceiling now." Makai raised a hand. "Can we delegate the chalk-erasing to him, since he can see it?" "Denied," said Mr. De Vries.

At lunch Callie offered him half her cookie as a truce for the spy joke, and he took it. He looked down the hallway toward the gym doors, forty feet away, and read the tiny sticker on the trophy case glass. "Trobie Case, 1987," he said. "It's spelled wrong. It's supposed to say Trophy."

"How long has that been there?"

"Nobody knows," Lincoln said. "Nobody could see it."

Olivier had exactly twenty minutes before Ms. Bianchi collected the worksheets, and he had not answered a single question. The periodic table hung on the wall above the sink, a huge grid of colored squares with tiny numbers in each corner, and he was supposed to find the number of protons in an element from something called the atomic number. He had been absent on Monday, so whatever the rest of the class knew, he did not.

"Hurry up," said Maxwell, who sat next to him and had already filled in half his sheet. "The clock is not going to slow down for you."

"You were here Monday. What's the atomic number?"

Maxwell shrugged. "Some number in the box. I just match them up." He slid his paper an inch toward Olivier, then pulled it back. "Ms. Bianchi will call it copying. She said that last week."

Olivier looked at the wall again. At the back counter, Imogen was labeling petri dishes from an old experiment, checking whether the bacteria had begun to colonize the agar overnight. She held one up to the light. "Two out of five," she reported to no one in particular. "The others are still empty."

Empty. That was the problem with the periodic table too, Olivier thought. Nobody had ever seen a proton. They were inside the atom, too small to see, and yet the worksheet wanted him to count them. He decided on a test. If the table really was a table, and not just decoration, then the simplest element should be somewhere obvious. The simplest thing would be the thing with the least of whatever the numbers measured. He ran his finger along the top row of the giant chart, starting from the left, where the numbers would be smallest, if they were ordered at all.

His finger stopped in the top left corner. Hydrogen. The little number above the letter H was 1. He checked the box next to it, helium, which showed 2, and then lithium, 3, all the way across and down, the numbers climbing in order like seats in a theater. He wrote on his worksheet: hydrogen, atomic number 1. Then, underneath, in the column for protons, he wrote 1 again. If the atomic number gave you the protons, then hydrogen, being number 1, had exactly one proton. Every hydrogen atom, one proton. He checked the next question, which asked about helium, and wrote 2.

"Where did you get that?" Maxwell asked, leaning over.

"Top left corner," Olivier said. "Hydrogen has atomic number 1, so every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton." He tapped the chart. "It's the simplest one on the whole table."

"Motivation at last," said Ms. Bianchi from the front, collecting Imogen's petri dishes. "Olivier, since you're so interested, you can guess which dish Imogen thinks will colonize fastest, the one near the window or the one near the radiator."

Olivier walked over and looked at the two dishes, then at the thermometer taped to the window frame. He picked up the one from the radiator tray and held it beside the other.

"This one," he said.

The lobby filled up fast that evening, avatars clustering around the spawn point while the matchmaking timer counted down. Alexis had exactly one goal: get his squad, which included Emy-Rose and Iman, through the raid on the northern settlement before his internet cut out at nine. What he did not have was a plan for what his cousin had posted from his account an hour earlier, a photo of Alexis in his dinosaur pajamas, captioned "age 14, still afraid of the dark."

He deleted it in a panic. Ten minutes, that was all it had been up. He checked his page twice, scrolled, refreshed, and confirmed the post was gone, wiped clean off his profile like it had never existed. Then he joined the voice chat and tried to sound normal, which mostly meant saying "ready" when Mr. Halvorsen's neighbour's kid, who somehow always ended up in their lobby, asked if everyone had their gear.

"Nice pajamas, by the way," Iman said.

Alexis's stomach dropped. "What?"

Iman sent a link. The screenshot was crisp, the dinosaur pattern fully preserved, the caption and everything, and it was sitting in the squad's group chat where at least forty people could see it. Alexis stared at it, then went back and looked at his own page again. Empty. The post was not on his page, but here it was anyway, glowing on his screen in someone else's chat.

He thought about that for a second. Deleting had removed it from his profile, he had watched that happen. But Iman had already grabbed a copy, and a copy in Iman's hands was a copy Iman could send to anyone. So deleting it late was like locking the barn after something had already walked out the door carrying a photo. The only fix was to ask, which was going to require being assertive in a way that did not come naturally to him at all.

"Delete that," Alexis said, aiming for calm and landing somewhere near strangled. "Please. Actually, not please. Delete that."

"Too late," Emy-Rose said cheerfully. "The kid from the settlement raid already saved it. He saves everything. He's like a museum of embarrassing posts."

In his headphones, Alexis could hear the countdown for the raid beginning, the timer ticking toward a fight he was suddenly much less worried about. Somewhere out there, a copy of the dinosaur pajamas was traveling from phone to phone, and all he could do was mute himself and press ready.

"Two minutes," Iman said. "Also, I'm keeping mine."

The Saturday portrait class met in the back room of the gallery, where Ms. Adebayo had hung the students' watercolours along one wall like a miniature revolution, because until this term nobody in town had taught kids to paint faces. Romy wanted hers to look like her grandmother, who was coming to visit in two weeks, and she wanted the cheek to have that soft shadow under the bone, the one that made a face a face.

Levi wanted something different. He kept glancing at the doorway because his little brother's school had prohibited siblings from the adult classes, and Levi had promised to film a few seconds of the lesson so his brother could watch at home. He set his phone on the paint table, propped against a jar of brushes, and checked the battery twice.

Romy laid her first wash, pale peach, the way Ms. Adebayo had shown. Then she mixed a thin violet for the shadow and brought her brush toward the cheek.

"Wait," Levi said, "I'm not filming yet."

She didn't wait. She touched the brush to the paper, and the violet bloomed outward into the peach, feathers of grey crawling through it, until the cheek looked bruised, almost venomous, a greenish swelling where a face should be. Romy stared at it. "That's not a shadow," she said. "That's a swamp."

She looked around the room. Danae, two tables over, had three dried layers on her portrait, each one darker than the last, and Danae's shadow sat cleanly on the cheek like breath on glass. Romy leaned closer. The layers were separate, one over another, like sheets of coloured film stacked up. She pressed her fingertip to her own paper. Cool and damp. She pressed Danae's. Dry.

"Is that the trick?" she asked Danae. "You let each one dry all the way?"

"Glazing," Danae said. "That's what it's called."

Romy set her muddy portrait on the windowsill in the sun and started a second sheet, laying the peach wash, then waiting, checking with her fingertip, waiting more, while Levi filmed the drying paper for his brother and narrated in a whisper. When the paper was finally dry, she brushed the thin violet over the cheek. It sat on top of the peach, and her eye did the mixing, soft and warm, exactly the shadow she had imagined.

Ms. Adebayo paused behind her. "That one you can hang," she said.

"Hang it facing the doorway," Romy said, "so my grandmother sees it the second she walks in."

The smell of Grandma's spare room hit Alexis the moment he opened the door: old paper, dust, and the sharp honey-sweet scent of her watercolour set, the same set she had used since she was his age. "Grandma's hereditary talent skips a generation, apparently," his dad liked to joke, which meant Alexis was the lucky one, and today he was going to prove it. He had one week at her house, one portrait to paint, and one plan: layer thin washes from the lightest tones to the darkest, exactly the way her old notebook described.

He started with pale washes, letting each dry before adding the next, watching the face of his subject, Carter from a photo on his phone, slowly deepen like a photo developing in a tray. By the third afternoon he had a real nose, real cheekbones, real shadows under the eyes, and he raced downstairs to show her.

"You're building it right," Grandma said, tapping the paper's edge. "But be careful with water on top of your darks."

He didn't ask what she meant. He should have. That evening his friend Iyla came over with her own portrait, and when she brushed clean water across her dried background to soften a sky, her whole wash smeared and bloomed grey-blue across the page. "Why would it do that?" she said, holding the ruined corner up. "It was dry. It was completely dry."

Alexis remembered the sticky sweetness of the paint set and suddenly had an idea worth testing. He dropped a dried blob of leftover paint, hard as a pebble, into a cup of water and swirled it. Within seconds the waterclouded with colour. The paint was coming back to life. He grabbed the little label from Grandma's box of pigments and read the ingredients out loud. "Gum arabic," Iyla said slowly, sounding it out. "So that's what's binding it." The gum held the pigment together, Alexis thought, and apparently it let the pigment dissolve again even after it had dried. That was why Grandma had warned him. Water was both the maker and the unmaker here.

The twist came at midnight, when he was trying to fix a dark smudge on Carter's forehead. If dried paint could dissolve again, then water could take it away. He wet a clean brush, touched it to the smudge, and blotted with a tissue, once, twice. The smudge lifted, leaving a soft highlight that made the forehead look round and lit. He laughed out loud in the dark kitchen. His mistake had handed him a technique.

In the morning, Iyla arrived early, and their visits happened to coincide at the front door, both of them clutching paintings. He showed her the lifted highlight, and she gasped. Grandma leaned in the doorway with her tea and studied the portrait for a long moment. "I'd frame that one," she said. "The nose alone is worth a frame."

Blake had one week to write his first real argument essay, and the only thing on his page was the word "Thesis" underlined three times, like underlining might accelerate the ideas out of his pencil. Writing club met on Tuesdays in Mr. Sharma's room, which smelled of dry-erase markers and someone's forgotten banana, and today Mr. Sharma had written a single sentence on the board: "Three points, three body paragraphs." Blake copied it down, then copied it again, because copying felt like working.

He spread out his draft on the table, and Taliyah leaned over. "What's your argument?" she asked.

"That my landlord should let us have a dog."

"You're thirteen. Your parents are the landlord's tenants."

"My argument is that the building should allow dogs," Blake said with dignity. "Three reasons. One, dogs make people calmer. Two, they get neighbors talking to each other. Three, our building is the only one on the street that says no."

Hashim slid into the next chair, chewing the string of his hoodie. He was in a famously pessimistic mood because his own essay topic, "Why Mondays Should Be Illegal," had been rejected twice. "You realize," he said, "that nobody reads a whole essay. Mr. Sharma grades like forty of these. I bet he skims."

"That's a terrible theory," said Taliyah.

"It's a great theory," said Hashim. "Test it. Give me your paragraphs, and I'll read only the first sentence of each one."

So Blake wrote fast, three paragraphs, one for each reason, and slid the pages across. Hashim covered the rest of each paragraph with his forearm and read only the opening line aloud: "Dogs lower stress in apartment buildings." Then, "Second, dog owners meet their neighbors on the sidewalk." Then, "Finally, every other building on our street allows dogs." Hashim sat back. "Okay. I get your whole argument. Every reason, in order, and they all clearly back up your dog thesis. It's almost annoying how well that works."

"You skipped all my best sentences!" Blake grabbed the pages back, then stopped. He looked at his first lines. Each one carried one reason, and each one pointed back at his main point, like signposts. "Wait," he said slowly. "So the first sentences are the argument. The rest is just... proof delivery."

"That is the most beautiful thing you've ever said," said Taliyah.

Mr. Sharma drifted past their table and tapped the board. "Hashim, stop reading with your arm." Then, quieter, "Though it does make you wonder how I actually grade, doesn't it?" He walked on, smiling at the wall.

Hashim leaned toward Blake. "I'm going to test it on him. A note, tomorrow, before class." He tore a corner from his notebook and wrote: "Dear Mr. Sharma, if you only read the first sentences of this note, then you will never know that Blake is planning to bring a dog to writing club on Tuesday. Sincerely, a concerned citizen."

"Delete that," said Blake, reaching across the table, and Hashim held the note over his head, grinning.

Dominic curled his fingers into a claw over the half onion and set the knife edge against his knuckles, exactly the way his grandfather had shown him at the kitchen table. "Curved fingers restrict the blade," his grandfather had said, "so it can't reach your fingertips." Dominic pressed down, and the onion split into neat rings, which he then chopped into pieces, sliding each pile aside like a median down the center of the cutting board.

Khadija and Marilou were already at the stove with the canned tomatoes. "Your grandpa said six o'clock sharp," Khadija said, checking the clock above the window. "That's fifty minutes." Marilou dumped the tomatoes into the pot, and Dominic carried over the onions, breathing through his mouth because his eyes were streaming.

They set the pot to simmer and clapped the lid on to keep it safe from spatters. Then they got to work on the pasta. It had been naive of Dominic, he realized later, to think the hard part was the knife work. The hard part was waiting.

At five forty, Marilou lifted the lid to stir and frowned. "It's still really soupy." She dipped a spoon, and the tomato water ran off it in a thin red stream. Dominic leaned over the pot. It looked exactly the same as when they'd started, and by his reasoning it should have been thicker by now. Something had to be wrong with the pot, the heat, or the tomatoes, and only one of those was easy to test.

He lifted the lid and held it up. The underside was dripping wet, and steam curled off it in a slow ribbon. Steam, he thought. Water turning into steam. If the lid was on, the steam hit the lid, turned back into water, and dripped home into the sauce. Nothing could get out.

"We take the lid off," he said.

"For twenty minutes?" said Khadija. "It'll spit everywhere."

"It has to," Dominic said. "Simmering with the lid off lets the water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker. With the lid on, we've been trapping it all in there." He set the lid on the counter like evidence.

Marilou dragged the pot half off the burner to restrict the spatter to one side, and they waited, stirring, watching the bubbles. By ten to six the spoon stood up on its own, and the sauce clung to the pasta in thick red coats. They plated four bowls just as headlights swept the driveway.

The front door opened, and their grandfather came in, sniffing. He picked up a bowl, twirled his fork, and took one long bite while the three of them held their breath.

"Perfect," he declared. Then he reached for the water pitcher and filled his glass three times. "Thickest sauce I ever had. Now, who's making me something to drink it with?"

Anthony had twenty-three dollars from selling his old skateboard, and he was carrying it around the farmers' market like it was on fire. He needed it for a school project. Mr. Cohen had told the class on Friday that whoever could explain, by Monday, which was riskier, a stock or a bond, and why, would present at the assembly. Anthony wanted that spot more than he wanted the honeycrisp apples he could smell from the cider stand.

He found Teresa and Graham arguing beside a table of peppers, and Mr. Cohen himself buying bread two stalls down, which gave Anthony an idea. "Ask him," Teresa said, but Anthony shook his head. Mr. Cohen never answered project questions directly. Last time, he had just smiled and said the market would teach him, and Anthony had spent a week thinking about actual grocery stores.

What actually happened was stranger. Graham's mother ran a jam stand, and next to her a retired banker had a card table with a hand-lettered sign: "Ask me about money. Free." Graham spotted the sign first. "Total civilian," he whispered, "some guy with nothing to sell." But Anthony noticed the man's hands, ink-stained and steady, and the way he listened to the pepper seller's complaints about rain like he was reading a report.

Anthony asked his question anyway, and the man answered with a question. "If someone borrowed ten dollars from you, and someone else offered to pay you twice the usual interest, which borrower would you trust more?" Anthony chewed on that while a customer's sugar packet dissolved into the man's coffee, little white clouds spiraling down. Twice the usual interest. Nobody paid extra for nothing. The borrower paying double was the one more likely to fail to pay you back at all, because otherwise nobody would need to lure lenders that hard. "Those are called junk bonds," the man said, tapping the table. "High-yield, some people say, to be polite." Anthony felt the whole thing click sideways, like a door he'd been pushing the wrong way. Stocks could crash, sure, but a junk bond was a promise from someone the interest itself told you was shaky. The risk was hiding inside the reward, printed right there in the yield.

Mr. Cohen appeared at the table, holding his bread, and raised an eyebrow at Anthony's grin. "Found something at the market?" he asked. "Whether it's worth twenty-three dollars is subjective," Anthony said, "but I think I just bought a presentation." Mr. Cohen laughed and pointed at the jam stand. "Better buy some jam too, then. Graham's mother is watching."

Julia had finished dead last in the first time trial because she sprinted the whole first lap like it was a hundred metres, and by the second lap her legs felt like they belonged to someone else. Ms. Paquette hadn't lectured her about it. She had only handed her a folded note at the end of practice, and Julia had read it twice on the bus home. "Watch Renee's race tomorrow," it said. "Don't watch her legs. Watch the gap between her and the others, lap by lap. Tell me what you notice." That was the whole message, no signature, which was very Ms. Paquette.

So on Saturday, Julia stood at the corner of the soccer field where the track looped around the outside of the grass, squinting past the glare that refracted off the puddles from last night's rain so the lane lines seemed to double. Renee was in lane three. When the starter's whistle went, a girl from the other school shot out like a rocket, five metres clear by the first turn. Julia's stomach did the thing it always did, the wanting-to-chase thing, but she held her ground and counted, the way she'd practiced in her head all week. Renee sat fourth, even, unhurried, running the diagonal backstretch like she was saving something for later.

Lap one ended. The fast girl was still leading, but Julia could see the truth now, the pattern Ms. Paquette had wanted her to find: nobody who went out that fast could hold it. By the far curve the leader's arms were pumping too high, her stride shortening, and one by one the pack began to close. It wasn't that they sped up, exactly. It was that she slowed, sharply, like a toy with a dying battery.

Renee passed her on the final straight and won by four strides. Afterward, Julia found her by the fence, hands on knees, gasping. "You went out slow on purpose," Julia said. Renee grinned through her breathlessness. "If you can't hold the pace for both laps, the first lap is a lie. That girl borrowed energy she had to pay back." Julia nodded slowly, the whole shape of the race rearranging itself in her mind. Then, because Renee was still shaking, she jogged to the team cooler and brought back the last water bottle, and Renee poured half of it over her own head and offered the rest back.

"That's yours," Julia said.

"Split it," Renee said. "You've got your own race in an hour, and now you know the secret."

Julia took a long drink, tucked the note deeper into her pocket, and walked toward the starting line.

Alyssa had one week to learn the ending of "March of the Silver Bells" before the garage band's first real performance, and the ending was the problem. She sat at the old upright piano in Bruno's garage, the sheet music propped against a stack of paint cans, while Jesse tuned his guitar and Bruno messed with the drum kit. Every time they played the final eight measures, the band blasted through them at full volume, and it sounded wrong. It sounded like a parade crashing into a wall.

"It says something right there," Jesse said, leaning over her shoulder. "Those little letters under the notes."

Alyssa traced the marking with her finger. Two small f's at the start of the section, then two p's at the very end. She'd skipped past them all week because the notes themselves were easy, and easy notes got all her attention. But markings like that had to mean something, or why would the composer bother writing them?

She tried an experiment. "Play it like we always do," she told the boys, "but watch my hand." At the double f's she played the loudest chords she could manage, so loud the strings inside the piano buzzed, and the garage was saturated with sound that bounced off the concrete floor and the dusty shelves of tools. Then, at the double p's near the end, she dropped to a whisper, barely touching the keys. Bruno, watching her hand instead of his music, dropped his sticks to a tick. Jesse caught on and let his last chords fade like a bell dying away.

"Whoa," Bruno said. "It's like the song walks away instead of slamming a door."

The next day at school, Alyssa found Ms. Koné in the music room and asked about the letters. "Fortissimo means very loud," Ms. Koné said, "and pianissimo means very soft." Alyssa grinned. She had guessed the pattern right: the loud letters matched the loud sound, the soft ones the whisper. It felt like cracking a code that had been sitting in front of her the whole time.

On Saturday they ran it six times in the cold garage, Jesse in gloves with the fingertips cut off, the old thermostat on the wall cranked as high as it would go. On the seventh run Alyssa's fingers were stiff and brittle from the chill, and she fumbled the soft ending, laughing so hard she could barely finish. Bruno counted them in again. This time the loud part rang out big and bold, and the last notes faded until the garage was almost silent, just the heater humming.

Jesse held up both fists like a champion. "One more time from the top."

The argument started over a dented trash can lid, which Daniel thought was a strange thing for two best friends to fight about. He had come to Blaine's house to work on their science project, but instead he was standing in the kitchen watching Blaine and Lorelai glare at each other across the counter.

"He slammed it on purpose," Lorelai said. "You were mad about the group grade and you took it out on my project."

"I set it down and it rolled off the table," Blaine said. "You just assume the worst because you're still sore about the grade."

"You're the one being unreasonable."

Daniel remembered the previous Saturday, when he had watched the whole thing happen from the porch. Blaine had been carrying an armful of display boards, and the lid had slid off the pile when he turned too fast. He hadn't even been looking at it. But when Daniel said, "I saw it, it was an accident," Lorelai just folded her arms, and Blaine muttered, "See? Even Daniel agrees with me," which somehow made everything worse.

Daniel retreated to the living room, where Blaine's older sister was doing homework at the coffee table. He asked her how two people could watch the same trash can lid and see two different events. She slid a psych textbook across the couch toward him without looking up. "It's called naive realism," she said, and went back to her notes.

He read the page twice. Naive realism was the belief that we see the world as it really is, so anyone who disagrees with us must be uninformed or biased. Lorelai wasn't lying and Blaine wasn't lying. Each of them was certain the truth was obvious, and each one decided the other was the problem. Daniel set the book down and thought about his plan for the science project, which involved testing an idea you couldn't see directly. You could do that with people, too.

He marched back into the kitchen and made them each a vigorous argument for the opposite side, Blaine's accident story delivered to Lorelai, Lorelai's motive theory delivered to Blaine. Then he offered a treaty: they would both participate in rebuilding the display for the class presentation, and nobody had to admit anything about the lid.

Lorelai was the first to crack a smile. "You're saying we're both sure we're right, and both positive the other one is being ridiculous."

"That's exactly what I'm saying," said Daniel, and handed her a glue stick.

Emile pushed the folding table across the gym floor until it screeched against the volleyball line, and Emilien dumped a shoebox of notecards beside him. "This is our case," Emilien said. "Unbeatable." Ms. Henry had taped a sign to the bleachers that read CLAIM, EVIDENCE, WARRANT, and under it, in smaller letters, if you can't say the warrant, you don't have a point. Emile picked up the first card. It said, in Emilien's sprawling handwriting, "Cousin Jules failed math because of video games."

"Where's the evidence?" Emile asked. Emilien tapped the card. "It's right there. It happened. I watched it happen." Emile thought back to September, when his mother had blamed a broken dishwasher on the new detergent, and his father had quietly run it twice more with the old detergent before saying a word. It had still been broken. One try had proved nothing either way, his father said later, over the last clean plates they owned. Emile hadn't understood why that mattered until now.

He flipped through the rest of the shoebox. Every card circled back to Cousin Jules. "Your whole case," he said slowly, "is one guy." Emilien frowned. "One guy with a dramatic story." From the free-throw line, Maurice called over that his uncle had eaten video games for breakfast, basically, and done calculus in his sleep. Emilien shouted back that Maurice's uncle didn't count because he was "a statistical monster," which was somehow the funniest thing anyone had said all week, and even Ms. Henry, shelving the pinnies, put a hand over her mouth.

Emile laid the cards out in rows, like a coach drawing a play. "Look. Claim: games hurt grades. Evidence: Jules. That's it. There's no warrant connecting one cousin to every student in the school." He picked up a fresh card. "We need to quantify it. Survey thirty kids, games and grades, count them." "Counting is boring," Emilien said. "Counting wins," Emile said. "Ms. Henry's whole system is about being systematic. Claim, evidence, warrant, every single point, no skipping." He glanced up at the sign on the bleachers. "And there's a word for your cousin thing. Anecdotal evidence." Emilien squinted. "Is that an insult?" "It's a category," Emile said. "The category of stories that prove nothing."

Emilien looked at his shoebox, then at Jules's card, then at the empty gym, where thirty desks' worth of students would show up for the debate on Friday. He groaned the groan of a boy about to do real work, and Maurice jogged over with a clipboard he had clearly stolen from the equipment room. "Survey?" Maurice said. "I'll do the hallway before lunch. That's my zone." Emile handed him a pencil. "Fifteen before, fifteen after," he said. "And Jules?" Emilien held up the card, studied it one last time, then clipped it to the bottom of the stack, face down. "Backup material," he said. "For the emotional finale."

Muhammad had agreed to babysit for Ms. Katz mostly because she paid ten dollars an hour and mostly because he wanted the money before Saturday. The plan seemed simple: watch the baby, feed the baby, keep the baby alive until Ms. Katz got home at nine. The whole evening, he discovered, would revolve around a small person named Rose who could not say a single word but had strong opinions anyway.

Ms. Katz's son Zack was supposed to be at his friend's house, but his friend got sick, so Zack was there too, lying on the couch with a comic and pretending he did not need a babysitter. He was eight. Muhammad decided not to argue about the chain of command.

At six o'clock Rose started making a specific sound, a cranky huh huh huh that Muhammad quickly learned was her signal for hunger. He found the jar of baby oatmeal on the counter and the note Ms. Katz had left taped to the fridge. He mixed the cereal with warm water, tested it on his wrist like she'd shown him, and offered the spoon. Rose clamped her mouth shut. He tried again. She turned her whole face away, which for someone who could not sit up on her own was a fairly clear statement.

Muhammad looked around the kitchen for ideas. On the shelf above the stove sat a bear-shaped bottle of honey, and he remembered his own mother stirring a spoonful into his little brother's tea when the boy had a sore throat. Sweet things made food better. He reached for the bottle.

"You can't," Zack said, not even looking up from his comic.

"Why not?"

Zack pointed the corner of his comic at the fridge note. Muhammad leaned in and read the part he had skipped, the part in capital letters. NO HONEY. He read it twice. Babies under twelve months should never have honey, because it can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism.

"Huh," Muhammad said. He set the bear down on the shelf, feeling as though he had almost done something without ever knowing it was a something.

"So she hates the oatmeal," he said. "What do we do?"

"Try it warmer," Zack said. "Mom heats it up more than that. She says it's a thing."

Muhammad tested his theory. He warmed the bowl another thirty seconds, offered the spoon again, and Rose opened her mouth like a small pink trapdoor and ate the entire serving. When Ms. Katz came home, she found the kitchen clean, the baby asleep, and Zack taking full credit for the temperature.

"He was going to use the honey," Zack announced.

Ms. Katz looked at Muhammad. Muhammad held up the empty oatmeal jar. "Read the note twice," he said. "That's the whole job."

The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and the folding chairs were arranged in rows facing a low stage where Ms. Gauthier sat with a stack of index cards. Kaylee sat in the third row between Victor and Alisa, her number pinned to her shirt, waiting for her turn in the school spelling bee. The winner would retrieve the district trophy from the front office cabinet, where it had sat since last year, and Kaylee wanted it.

Words came and went. Victor spelled "nutritious" correctly, and Alisa went out on "salmon." Then Ms. Gauthier called Kaylee's word. "Chorus. It comes from Greek." Kaylee froze. She heard a k sound at the start, but k could be spelled several ways. Then she thought about "chef," which Alisa's grandmother, who was proud of her French heritage, said all the time. In "chef" the sh sound came from French. This word was Greek, not French. She remembered her word list at home, the Greek column, where k sounds kept showing up as "ch." She decided to test that pattern right now.

"Chorus. C-H-O-R-U-S. Chorus."

"Correct," said Ms. Gauthier.

Two rounds later, only Kaylee and a seventh grader were left. The seventh grader stepped up, and Ms. Gauthier read the next card. "Chef. The language of origin is French." The seventh grader frowned. "C-H-E-F," he said slowly. "Wait. C-H-E..." He stopped, started over, and spelled it with a k at the end. The buzzer sounded.

Ms. Gauthier turned to Kaylee for the winning word. "There's a word on this card I wasn't planning to use until the district bee," she said, almost apologetic. "Monarch. It comes to us through French."

Kaylee's mouth went dry. The middle of it had that k sound. She had just watched French break her pattern in front of everyone, because in "chef" the special spelling was the sh, and the k sound in "monarch" might follow some rule she didn't know. She stood at the microphone while the whole gym waited.

"M-O-N-A-R-C-H. Monarch."

Ms. Gauthier looked at the card, then at her, and reached slowly for the buzzer.

The problem sat in the middle of Gavin's kitchen table like a dare: an assignment sheet from Ms. Kapoor that said, Explain why people moved west in the 1800s, and you must use a primary source. He had his textbook open, and the textbook had a whole chapter on the westward movement, but every time he tried to start his paragraph, the assignment sheet seemed to stare back at him.

He called Lydia first. "What does primary even mean?" he asked. "The textbook is, like, the main book."

"Wait, I think my sister did this," Lydia said. "Hold on." He heard her shouting upstairs, then she came back breathless. "Okay, a primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through it. Like a settler's diary. And a secondary source is written later by someone studying it."

Gavin looked at his textbook, which was printed three years ago about events from two hundred years ago. His stomach did a slow flip, the same one he'd felt in fourth grade when he realized he'd been feeding the class hamster twice a day and nobody else was feeding it at all. He had been about to write his whole report on a secondary source. He closed the textbook with a thud.

Sia arrived with her backpack and a folder of printouts. "The library had scanned pages online," she said, spreading them across the table so they covered the wood, the smell of the printer's warm ink still rising off them. "Diaries from people on the trail. Some are hard to read."

Gavin leaned over a page where faded ink had saturated the paper until the letters bled into each other. He squinted at one entry, sounding it out: "June the third. The mule is lame and we have only half the flour we left with, and still my husband insists we go on, for the land in Oregon is said to be free to any who will work it."

"That's a reason," Sia said, tapping the page. "The land. And the mule thing, that's what it cost them."

"Ms. Kapoor said the most influential details are the ones that show why," Gavin said slowly, "not just what happened." He tested it out on another diary, an 1852 entry from a woman describing a lawyer she'd met on the trail who kept a list of every family passing his camp. A lawyer counting families, families who had left schools and shops and colleagues behind in Missouri. That was a pattern he couldn't see directly, but here it was in ink: people had whole lives already, and they left them anyway, for land.

He opened a blank document and typed the first sentence: A settler's diary shows why families moved west, even when the trip nearly broke them.

"There," Sia said.

He read the June third entry one more time, then started typing the second sentence.

Mr. Goldberg made outlines mandatory before anyone wrote a single word of the persuasive essay, and he had taped a sample outline to the board at the front of Room 12. Bentley stared at it while the radiator ticked and the smell of chalk dust settled over the desks. His topic was due by the end of the period, and the sheet in front of him was still blank except for his name.

He wanted to argue that the school should keep its old oak tree instead of cutting it down for the new parking lot. He knew what he felt about it. What he did not know was how to squeeze a whole argument into one sentence at the top of the page, the way Mr. Goldberg kept asking for.

Kaden leaned over from the next desk. "Why do the numbers on that thing look like the ones on a clock?" he whispered. "Is that a three, or a weird letter?"

Bentley looked again. The sample outline had a I, a II, and a III marching down the left side, each marking one of the three main points, and under each main point sat a capital A and a capital B for the details. It was strange, but the strange parts were orderly. The big points got the clock-like numbers. The smaller stuff got plain letters.

He tried it himself. At the top he wrote his one sentence: the school should save the oak tree because it shades the building, it is home to birds, and it is older than the school itself. That was the whole argument folded flat, like a map. Then he wrote I and put the shading point next to it, with A for the afternoon temperature readings Mr. Goldberg had let the class take outside last week, and B for the shade over the benches where kids ate lunch. II got the birds, with A for the nest Anabel had photographed in May and B for the list of species the class had counted. III got the age, with A for the date on the old photograph in the hallway and B for the ring count the principal had mentioned.

It was like testing a rule. If the outline held together, he could write the essay straight down the page, point by point, and nothing would wander. He slid the paper toward Anabel, who sat in front of him. "Does this demonstrate that I actually have a plan, or does it just look like one?"

She read it upside down for a second, then turned around and took it properly. "It's a plan. Each point has its own evidence under it. Also, that part about the benches is good, it's like a simile without actually being one, the tree doing the protecting."

Mr. Goldberg walked the rows, pausing at desks, nodding at some papers and tapping others. When he reached Bentley, he read the outline all the way through, both hands in his pockets. "Roman numerals and letters, in the right places," he said. "And a thesis that actually makes a claim. Start drafting."

Bentley picked up his pen and wrote his first sentence, following the map he had just drawn.

Michael stood at the edge of the drama room carpet, chewing the inside of his cheek. Ms. Campbell had written two words on the board: yes, and. Their assignment was to improvise a scene with a partner, and in one hour they would perform in front of the whole class. His partner was Yohan, who was already pacing and muttering to himself, because Yohan wanted the lead in the spring play and believed this class was his audition.

They tried a practice scene on the spot. "Welcome aboard," Michael said, steadying an imaginary wheel. "The sea is rough tonight."

"We're not on a boat," Yohan said. "This is a cafeteria."

Michael felt the scene drop like a cut string. He had nowhere to go. The floor was just a floor again. They tried twice more, and both times Yohan denied whatever Michael offered, and both times the scene died before it started. "It's like you're slamming a door," Michael said. Reagan, who was practicing nearby, looked over. "In drama that's called blocking," she said. "You reject or ignore what your partner gives you, and it stops the scene from moving forward."

Michael turned the idea over. Nobody could see a rule like that; it was invisible until you broke it. But he had watched it happen three times in a row, so he decided to test it. "One more," he said. "Whatever I say, don't deny it. Build on it. Yes, and."

Yohan rubbed the back of his neck. "Fine. But if you make me a talking sheep, I quit."

"Welcome aboard," Michael said again. "The sea is rough tonight."

"Yes," Yohan said, slow at first, "and the captain lost his hat overboard."

"And the hat," Michael said, "was a gift from my grandmother, who happens to be a shark."

Yohan laughed, a real one, and then leaned into the wheel like a man fighting waves. Suddenly they had a grandmother shark, a hat, and a storm, all of it invented out of nothing. Michael could feel the difference, like current in a wire. When Ms. Campbell clapped and called time, Yohan was still grinning.

Later, while the class lined up, Yohan slid next to Michael. "The thing is," he said quietly, "I kept saying no because I thought whoever controlled the setting would look like the leader. That was dumb. It was arbitrary, like deciding the scene by coin flip." Michael shrugged. "You didn't look like a leader. You looked like a guy in a cafeteria arguing about a boat." Yohan winced, then laughed. When their turn came, they stood back to back, and Michael opened his palms like a book. "Ready to hear the strangest library rule ever?"

"Rules are eroding everywhere, my friend," Yohan said, "and this library is next."

Kaylee sat cross-legged on the floor of Genesis's bedroom with a laptop balanced on a binder, because Genesis's desk was buried under laundry and half a model volcano. On the screen was a spreadsheet of their science-class fundraiser: thirty rows of candy sales, one column for the money each student brought in. If they could total it and turn it into a bar chart before Monday, Mr. Holloway would let them present the results to the whole class. Kaylee wanted that more than she had wanted anything since the audition for jazz band.

"Type the total here," Genesis said, pointing at a blank cell near the bottom of the numbers. Kaylee scrolled, picked a spot, and entered =SUM(B2:B10). She pressed Enter.

The screen flickered and a warning box appeared, gray and sudden, with an exclamation mark inside a diamond. Kaylee's stomach dropped. "What did I do?"

Genesis leaned over her shoulder, which only seemed to magnify the problem, since now two people were staring at a message neither of them understood. "It says something about a circular reference," Genesis read slowly. "What is that?"

Kaylee looked at the cell where she had typed the formula. Then she looked up at the formula bar, and her eyes moved between them twice. She had entered the sum in cell B10, the very last cell in the range she was adding. The formula was adding up B2 through B10, and it was sitting inside B10, trying to add itself. She could not see the machine thinking, but she could see the pattern, like guessing there was a wire crossed behind a wall.

"Wait," she said. "I think I get it. It's in its own sum. It's eating its own tail." She deleted the formula, moved down one row to B11, and typed =SUM(B2:B10) again. The warning did not come back. In its place sat a number, the whole fundraiser total, plain as anything.

"It worked," Genesis said, and Kaylee laughed so loudly that a spontaneous round of applause broke out from the doorway, where Leslie had been watching the whole time with a bag of chips.

"Chart time," Kaylee said, and highlighted the column. "Mr. Holloway is going to lose his mind."

The message landed at 4:32 on a Tuesday, right when Christopher was supposed to be meeting Joey and Kurt at the basketball courts behind the school. He pulled out his phone under the bleachers and saw it glowing at the top of the group chat: WHERE ARE YOU, in letters so big and black they seemed to jump off the screen. It was from Kurt. Below it, Joey had already replied, "why are you yelling? lol."

Christopher typed back "omw 5 min" and started jogging. On the way he scrolled up through the chat, because something felt off. Kurt never wrote in capitals. His usual messages were all lowercase, drifting and lazy, things like "maybe i'll come" and "idk might be tired." Today there were three caps messages in a row. WHERE ARE YOU. THEN FORGET IT. NOT WAITING HERE ALL DAY.

At the courts, Kurt was sitting on the far bench with his hood up, spinning a ball on one finger. He didn't look up when Christopher jogged through the gate. Joey was shooting free throws, and he mouthed "good luck" with a grin that said he was planning to enjoy this.

"Hey," Christopher said. "Got held up in science. Mr. Iyer kept us late because half the class turned in, like, one paragraph."

"Whatever," Kurt said, still spinning the ball.

Christopher sat down on the bench. He had a theory forming, and he tested it the way he tested things, carefully, out loud. "You wrote in all caps today. Joey thought you were yelling at us."

"I was not yelling," Kurt said, finally looking up. "It's just typing."

"Kind of yelling, though," Joey called from the foul line. The ball clanked off the rim. "Everybody reads caps that way. It's like shouting on a screen."

Kurt frowned at his phone like it had betrayed him. "Nobody answers my normal messages," he said. "I type 'anyone at the courts' and it just sits there for an hour. I type it big and you two show up in five minutes."

Christopher checked the chat history to be sure, scrolling back two weeks. He counted. Kurt's lowercase messages got answered, on average, maybe once in five, a rough ratio of one reply for every five sent. Then again, half of those had been sent at ten at night, when everyone else's phones were off, so quiet hours and being ignored often coincided. The caps messages had been sent at peak time, right after school. That was probably the whole difference. "It's not the size," Christopher said. "It's the timing. You text us at ten p.m. and expect us to answer. Nobody's awake. My phone is off and I'm lethargic by then anyway, half asleep on the couch."

"So I shouted for nothing," Kurt said.

"You shouted and it worked out badly," Joey said, jogging over. "Christopher showed up because you texted at the right time, and now we all think you're mad."

Kurt pulled his hood down. There was a silence that was almost funny, the three of them standing there while the truth sat in the middle of the court like a loose ball nobody wanted to pick up. "I wasn't mad," Kurt said. "I just wanted to play."

"Then next time type like a normal person," Christopher said, "with one or two question marks, and maybe wait longer than nine minutes before declaring an emergency."

"Nine minutes," Joey repeated, delighted. "It was nine minutes."

"Fine, fine." Kurt stood up, bounced the ball once, hard. "First to eleven. Losers explain group chat etiquette to Mr. Iyer."

"He already knows," Christopher said, taking position at the top of the key. "He's the only one who types in lowercase and still gets answers."

The banners at the cultural center were so orange they made Alexander squint, which was saying something, because he had spent the whole drive here squinting at his little sister's karaoke. His father had been hired to transport the sound equipment for the Vaisakhi celebration, and Alexander had been dragged along to carry cables. His friends Iris and Charles had come too, mostly for the food, though Charles claimed he was there "for cultural research," which meant he wanted to watch the drummers.

"So what's the big deal about today?" Charles asked, nodding at the stage where a man in a bright turban was testing a microphone. "Is it like a harvest thing? My mom said something about harvest."

"That's what I thought," Alexander said. "But look." He pointed at a long banner near the entrance. It showed a painted scene of a crowd gathered around one man on a hillside, and the crowd looked serious, not harvest-y at all. Nobody carries swords to a wheat festival, Alexander reasoned, unless it is a very strange wheat festival. He decided to test his harvest theory. "If it's just harvest, there'll be wheat everywhere. Let's count the wheat."

They counted. Iris found wheat on one poster, painted behind some dancing figures. Charles found wheat in a mural, small and golden in the corner. But in the middle of the mural stood a man raising a sword, and around him, five figures. No wheat touched them at all. Alexander's harvest theory was wobbling like Charles after the merry-go-round incident in third grade.

"Okay, new plan," Alexander said. "We find someone who actually knows and we eavesdrop politely."

"Eavesdrop politely," Iris repeated. "That's called listening."

They drifted toward the food tables, where a girl about seven was tugging her uncle's sleeve. "Why does this day matter so much?" she asked. "Everybody keeps saying Vaisakhi, Vaisakhi."

Her uncle smiled and crouched down. "It's the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," he said. "That's the story those banners are showing. That's why this day matters."

Alexander felt like a locker had swung open in his brain. Not harvest. A founding. The swords, the five figures, the crowd on the hill, all of it clicked into place like the last piece of a puzzle, except the puzzle had been hiding under the table the whole time.

Charles raised his hand as if in class. "So when we eat the food, are we honoring the Khalsa or the wheat?"

"Both," the uncle said, laughing. "The wheat doesn't mind sharing."

A drummer hit a deep, buoyant boom that rattled the juice cups, and Iris grabbed both boys by the sleeves. The procession was forming near the stage, orange flags lifting like small sails, and the three of them dove into the crowd just as the drums rolled forward.

Romy had six minutes to figure out how the new student should be greeted, and her spreadsheet of welcome ideas had failed her completely. She sat in the empty computer lab, scrolling through a school database of international student records that Ms. Joshi had left open on the desktop. Faris, transferring from a school in New Zealand, was arriving today, and Romy, as head of the welcome committee, wanted the greeting to be right. Not an approximate guess, but right.

She had one clue. In the notes column of his file, a previous teacher had written a single strange line: "greets with hongi." Romy searched the word and found a photo of two people pressing their noses and foreheads together, eyes almost closed. She read that it was a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand, and that it meant the sharing of the breath of life. She read it twice, because it sounded made up, like something Kabir would invent for a bet.

She decided to test it. If she offered her hand and Faris expected a hongi, the moment would go stiff and wrong, and a whole year of awkward homeroom mornings would be thwarted before it began. So at the door of the gym, when Faris arrived with his aunt and a box of mangoes for the class, Romy leaned in and pressed her nose and forehead gently against his. For a second he was completely still. Then he smiled so wide that his aunt laughed, and Kabir, holding the banner behind them, nearly dropped it.

"You know the hongi," Faris said.

"It's for sharing the breath of life," Romy said. "Right?"

He nodded and handed her a mango, and she gave him the welcome folder she had decorated, because in her grandmother's house no guest ever arrived without a gift and no host ever let one leave without one. Faris turned the folder over in his hands like it was something rare. In return his aunt insisted Romy keep a mango, refusing three times before Romy understood that refusing back was part of the game.

At lunch, Faris sat with his elbows off the table, waiting until everyone was served before he ate, while Kabir tore his parantha with his fingers and reached across for the pickle. Romy watched them both and realized politeness was not one rule but a hundred different ones, and the only way to learn them was to lean in, nose first.

"Same time tomorrow?" Faris asked, lifting his mango.

"Same time tomorrow," Romy said, and pressed her palm flat on the table like a promise.

Michael sat at the kitchen table with a photocopy of "The Scarlet Ibis" by James Hurst, a story from 1960 that Mr. Mercer had assigned on Tuesday. The quiz was tomorrow, and Michael had read the thing twice without knowing what he was supposed to see in it. He slid the pages around, read the part about the red bird again, and dragged his chair over to the laptop to message Bethany.

"Did you figure out what Mercer wants us to notice?" he typed.

She answered with a shrug emoji, which helped nobody. Michael frowned at the page. In the story, a storm had blown a red bird into the family's garden, and the bird died there. Then the story went on about Doodle, a fragile boy, and Michael had a feeling the bird was not just a bird. He began to speculate. Maybe the dead bird was a hint about what would happen to Doodle a few pages later. He checked the last page first, which felt like cheating, and then he saw it: Doodle's fate matched the bird's. The bird had come before, the way a weather report comes before rain.

He tried the idea out like a mechanism, turning it over. The author could not just come out and say what would happen, so he put a signpost in early. It was like the birds that used to flock over the fields near his grandfather's town and were now extinct; people knew something was wrong only because of what they noticed and remembered. If you paid attention to the pattern, you could see what was coming.

Bethany showed up at four with her own photocopy, wrinkled from her backpack, and a bag of chips she did not share. "Jules says the bird is just there to be sad," she said, dropping into the other chair.

"Then why is it red? Why does a storm blow it in? Why is it in the garden, of all places?" Michael tapped the page. "The bird dies in the garden. Then look what happens to Doodle. It's a setup. The first thing tells you about the second thing."

Bethany read the ending, chewed a chip, and read it again. "Okay," she said. "That's creepy and also kind of great. What do we call it, though? Mercer will want the word."

Michael scrolled through his notes until he found the term from Monday's class. "Foreshadowing. The bird foreshadows what happens to Doodle." He wrote it in his notebook, then wrote the sentence again in case the first one looked accidental.

They drilled each other until dinner. Bethany quizzed him on the year, the author, the bird, the garden, the storm, and Michael got them all right, even upside down with his eyes closed, which he demonstrated and immediately regretted when he knocked his water onto the photocopy. He dried it with a paper towel, and the red bird on the page smeared into a pink blur that looked, Bethany said, like the one thing the quiz would definitely ask about.

"It's a sign," Michael said, holding it up. "Even the water is foreshadowing."

Elena squeezed the last toothpaste-coloured ribbon out of her yellow paint tube and flattened the empty thing with her thumb, like pressing a tiny piston until nothing was left inside. Across the studio, Dakota was already halfway through her portrait, and hers looked amazing: silver hair, dark eyes, a proud grandmother staring out of the paper.

"How did you get the hair so dark already?" Elena asked.

"I did it first," Dakota said, "so I wouldn't have to fuss with it later. Now I'm adding the highlight down the middle, that bright grey streak."

Elena watched her friend load a pale wash on her brush and drag it across the dark hair. Then she watched the pale wash vanish. Dakota tried again, heavier, and again the dark swallowed it, the way a lake swallows a dropped coin. Dakota stared at her brush as if it had lied to her.

Elena looked down at her own portrait, which was barely started, just a faint peach glow where her grandfather's face would be. She had been about to jump straight to his grey beard so it would look like something. Now she paused. Something invisible was going on here. She dipped her brush in clean water and painted a square of pale yellow on scrap paper, let it dry, then brushed a darker orange over half of it. The yellow glowed up through the orange like firelight through a curtain. She tried the reverse, orange first, then yellow on top. The yellow did nothing. It was like trying to unring a bell.

"Dakota," she said slowly, "watercolour is transparent. Whatever's underneath shows through."

"So my highlight is trapped under the dark hair."

"Under, nothing. It's gone. You can't cover a dark wash with a lighter one. You have to go light to dark." Elena turned back to her grandfather and began, for the first time, in the right order. A whisper of yellow. A breath of pink for the cheeks. She layered wash after wash, each one a little deeper, and the face rose up out of the paper as though it had been hiding there all along, waiting to be let out in the correct sequence.

Outside the window, a wedge of migratory geese cut across the grey sky, headed somewhere warm. Mr. Campbell-Brown, who was retiring from the studio at the end of the month and kept saying so, wandered past with his coffee mug and stopped behind Elena's easel.

"Well," he said. "Somebody's been doing her experiments."

Behind him, Dakota flipped her paper to the blank side and started again, whispering, "Light to dark, light to dark," like a spell.

The bus smelled like old vinyl and orange peel, and Brooke had her word list balanced on her knees, going through it for the fourth time. Sabrina sat beside her, flipping through a library book about the Scripps National Spelling Bee that she had borrowed mostly to keep Brooke company. The regional bee was in forty minutes, at the middle school across town, and Brooke's biggest rival, Aryanna, was two rows back mouthing words to herself.

"You should read this," Sabrina said, turning the book around. "In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee." Brooke looked at the photograph, a girl her own age holding a trophy nearly as tall as she was, and something in her chest shifted. She had assumed the champions were always the same kind of kid, the kind with tutors and five thousand hours of practice, but Zaila had practiced with a spreadsheet her dad made. An ordinary girl, and then not ordinary at all.

"How did she handle the hard ones?" Brooke asked. Sabrina paged backward. "It says she thought about where words come from. French words, Greek words. Each language has its own fingerprint." Brooke chewed on that. She noticed her own list had a pattern she had never seen before: the French words, like crotchet and ricochet, all ended in that soft sliding sound, while the Greek ones, like xanthoma, carried distinct clusters of letters that barely looked like English at all. Was that a real rule, or just a trick her eyes were playing?

She decided to test it. "Sabrina, quiz me on the ones I marked F." Croissant, demiurge, cortege, one after another, and every time the French spelling came out of her pencil the way it sounded, glidey and quiet. Then the Greek ones, and those she built like blocks, consonant by consonant. It held. The pattern was real, hiding inside her own list the whole time, waiting for her to notice.

The bus lurched around the last corner and shuddered to a stop in front of the other school. Aryanna was already in the aisle, so Brooke made a quick pivot into her seat to let her pass, then folded her list and slid it into her jacket pocket.
