She could let go of the resentment without promising the sleepovers and the shared locker and all of it, not yet, maybe not ever in the same shape. She crossed the playground, and Chantelle saw her coming and stopped pretending the fence was interesting.

"I forgive you," Hazel said. "For the negligent thing. Which, by the way, I did six slides."

"Five," Chantelle said. "But one of them was really good."

"I'm not saying we go back to how it was, though. Not today. My mom calls that reconciling, and it takes longer."

Chantelle considered this, then held out her fist, and Hazel bumped it. "Partial credit," Chantelle said. "Very you."

Ms. Rahimi, on yard duty, watched them from the door and gave a small nod, as if she'd been keeping score. Hamza's next free throw actually went in, which nobody could believe, and Chantelle yelled "witnessed!" so loudly that a seagull left the roof in a hurry.

Alice stood outside the gym with her speech cards sweating in her hand, listening to the buzzer sound every thirty seconds. In four minutes she had to give her debate summary in front of the whole class, and her heart was hammering so hard she could feel it in her ears. Bree leaned against the wall beside her, chewing the end of her pencil.

"You look like you're about to pass out," Bree said.

"I'm not. It's just anxiety," Alice said. "My body thinks a class presentation is a bear attack." She tried to laugh, but it came out thin.

Inside the gym, Mr. Cardinal was running the soccer unit at the far end, and through the open door Alice watched the goalie, a girl from another class, crouch down in front of a penalty shot. The whole gym went quiet. Instead of freezing, the goalie let out one long, slow breath, so slow Alice could almost count it, and then settled into her stance. The shooter kicked, the goalie dove the right way, and the ball thumped into her gloves.

Alice stared. "Did you see that? She breathed out forever before the shot." Bree shrugged, but Alice's mind was already working. Maybe the long exhale wasn't just a habit. Maybe it was a coping skill, something you did on purpose before a stressful moment to calm the body's stress response. She had read those exact words on a poster in the counselor's hallway and thought they were decoration, but the goalie had used it like a tool. There was only one way to find out if it actually worked, and she had about two minutes to run the test on herself.

She pressed her back to the cool metal of the locker and breathed in through her nose, then let the air out slowly through her mouth, longer than the inhale, the way she remembered a coach describing to the goalie. "Slow breathing, long exhales," she muttered. "Fine, body. Let's see." Her chest still felt tight, but by the third breath the hammering had dropped to something she could think over. Her hands stopped shaking. It wasn't magic; it was more like turning the volume down.

"Alice, you're up," Mr. Cardinal called from the doorway, clipboard in hand.

She was still hesitant at the front of the room, and her first sentence came out wobbly. But she kept the slow exhales going between points, and by the time she reached her closing argument her voice was steady. Dalia caught her eye from the second row and gave a small thumbs up.

Afterward Mr. Cardinal read his critique aloud to the class, the way he did for everyone, and Alice braced herself to be humiliated. "Strongest closing so far," he said. "Shaky start, though. What happened?"

Alice glanced at Bree, who was grinning. "I figured something out in the hallway," Alice said. "Ask the goalie."

Alexander had been at camp for exactly one day, and he already knew three things: the lake was freezing, the counselor's whistle was loud, and his buddy was a kid named Calvin who talked with his whole face. They had been paired at the waterfront that morning, which meant, as Calvin explained cheerfully, "We're a buddy pair, so at a buddy check you have to find me fast and hold up your hand." Alexander had nodded, but he'd been busy watching a heron stalk the reeds at the far end of the beach, and he hadn't really listened.

After lunch there was free swim again. Alexander put on his suit, waited for the whistle, and then slipped back to the cabin to grab the crumpled letter his mom had tucked into his duffel. He read it twice, found a granola bar in his pocket, and came back down the hill eating it, feeling pleased with himself. That was when he heard the whistle blast three times, short and sharp, and saw the whole beach erupt. Swimmers scrambled out of the water in pairs, arms shooting up, fingers raised in twos.

Staff moved along the shoreline counting heads. Alexander spotted Calvin standing alone in the shallows, scanning the sand with a face gone pale and tight. "Where were you?" Calvin shouted the moment he saw him. "At a buddy check we have to find each other quick so they can count everyone, and I couldn't find you anywhere. They were about to clear the whole lake."

Alexander raised his hand, fingers up in a two, and Calvin slammed his own hand against it like they'd won something. A counselor jogged over, counted them, and moved on, though he gave Alexander a long look. "I was in the cabin," Alexander confessed, quieter than he meant to. "I didn't think it mattered if I wasn't swimming."

"That's the thing," Calvin said. "I'm your buddy whether you swim or not. Every camper at the waterfront is paired with a partner. You could've been the strongest swimmer here and it wouldn't be equivalent to being counted. Nobody's counted without their buddy." Mr. Sandhu, the waterfront director, waved them toward the towel rack and told the group that anyone who left the beach had to sign out with a buddy or a counselor, so no one would ever be a missing-person candidate by accident.

Alexander promised to sign out next time. He even meant it. Then, on the way back up the hill, Calvin stopped dead beside the waterfront shack, squinting at the sign-out sheet clipped to the board. At the top of the page, in someone's careful printing, was the day's first entry: Calvin's own name, signed out to the nurse's cabin at nine that morning, and never signed back in. "I forgot I did that," Calvin said weakly. "I made them search the lake for me."

Alexandra spread her flashcards across the library table so fast that two slid off the edge and landed face down, which felt like a bad omen. On Saturday her family was going to Grand Harbor, a real Chinese restaurant, and she had promised her grandmother she would order the dumplings herself, in Mandarin, without pointing at the menu like a lost tourist. The problem was that she could say "I want dumplings" but had no idea how to ask the price, and if the total came to more money than she had, she would be standing there with her wallet open like a jar of dust.

"You look like you're defusing a bomb," said Patience, dropping into the next chair with her own homework.

"I'm defusing embarrassment," Alexandra said. "Which is worse."

Jeff leaned over from the other side and picked up a card. He read it out in a pronunciation so terrible that Ms. Wanjiru, shelving books two aisles away, made a small sound like a kettle deciding not to whistle. "That contradicts everything on the card," Alexandra told him. "You just said 'I would like a small haircut of soup.'"

"Sounds delicious," Jeff said, and Patience snorted into her sleeve.

Alexandra flipped through the cards again. Every card had a word, a meaning, and a small drawing, because she learned better with drawings. There was the card for dumplings, with a fat little moon of a dumpling on it. There was the card for rice, with a bowl. There was the card for tea, with a cup so stained-looking that she suspected the previous owner had actually used it as a coaster. The corners of the cards were soft and frayed, the lamination gone at the edges; the erosion of careful thumbing by every student who had checked out this set before her. She found that oddly encouraging. Other people had needed this too.

Then she found a card at the back that someone had written by hand, in pencil, in looping letters: "Duōshǎo qián? It means How much money? Say it like: dwaw-shao chyen. Trust me, this is the everyday way to ask a price. Signed, a survivor of the Grand Harbor line." Alexandra read it three times. Whoever the survivor was, they had faced the exact dragon she was facing, and they had left behind the sword.

She tested it immediately, because a card could lie. "Patience, ask me how much something costs, any language."

"How much is this sandwich?"

"Duōshǎo qián?" Alexandra said, and Jeff gasped like she had pulled a rabbit from her ear.

At lunch she took her practice to the cafeteria line, which she declared to be a restaurant, and Patience played cashier with a milk crate as the register. Jeff ordered in his haircut-of-soup voice and was charged one imaginary million dollars. When Alexandra reached the front, she asked, "Duōshǎo qián?" and Patience, deadpan, said, "Six dollars," and Alexandra counted out six grapes, and the whole line applauded, which for a cafeteria meant three people clapped while the rest stared.

On Saturday, Grand Harbor smelled of star anise and steam. The fish tank near the register glowed luminous green, and the dumpling stall behind it was crowded. Alexandra joined the line, and while she waited she said the question under her breath, over and over, her lips moving like a tiny engine. When she reached the front, the woman in the tall white hat raised her eyebrows. Alexandra pointed at the dumplings and said, clear and whole, "Duōshǎo qián?" The woman smiled and held up eight fingers, and Alexandra paid before her brain could panic. Walking back to the table with the steaming box, she caught her grandmother's eye and grinned.

"Duōshǎo qián?" her grandmother asked, nodding at the box.

"For you, free," Alexandra said, and set it down in the middle of the table.

Abigail spread her poster board across the bleacher seats at the far end of the gymnasium, where the science fair tables were already marked with tape. Her title read, in tall blue letters, "Music Is Good for Plants." Yasmin plopped down beside her with two granola bars and handed one over without being asked, because she knew Abigail forgot to eat when she was working.

"That's your whole project?" Yasmin said, chewing. "Four words?"

"It's a hypothesis," Abigail said. "Ms. Mori told us a useful hypothesis has to be testable. That means an experiment could actually show it's wrong. Like a prediction. You're supposed to write it 'If... then...'"

"So write it that way."

Abigail stared at the poster. If music is good for plants, then what? She tried, "If music is good for plants, then a plant near music will grow taller than one without music." Saying it out loud made something click. Good was a feeling word. Taller was a number she could measure and maybe be wrong about. She grabbed the marker and crossed out the old title, then wrote the new sentence along the bottom edge of the board, her handwriting getting smaller as she ran out of room.

Yasmin leaned over to clarify one thing. "Taller than what, though?"

"Than a plant with no music. Same pot, same window, same water. Everything the same except the music." Eliana arrived with her own project, a baking soda volcano trailing a smell of vinegar, and asked what they were doing. Abigail explained, and Eliana frowned.

"But what if they grow the same? Then you're wrong in front of everybody."

"Then I'm wrong in front of everybody," Abigail said. "That's kind of the point. If nothing could prove me wrong, it's not really an experiment."

Eliana considered this while adjusting her volcano's paper cone. "That's actually the most systematic thing I've ever heard you say. Usually you lose your shoes twice a day."

Abigail's older cousin had offered to tutor her in science after midterm grades came out, and honestly the sessions were starting to feel worth the Saturday mornings. She checked her seedlings, three in pots lined up in a shoebox by the gym door, all of them a stubborn two centimeters tall so far, music or no music. Two weeks until the fair. Plenty of time to be right, or to be interestingly wrong.

Ms. Mori walked past, glanced at the rewritten sentence, and gave a small nod. Abigail uncapped the marker again and added a column to her data table labeled "no music, control," while Yasmin held the poster steady against the breeze from the propped-open door.

Isaac's fingers kept tripping over the same four measures in the garage, where the old upright piano lived between the lawnmower and a shelf of paint cans. Daven sat on an overturned bucket, wincing every time Isaac flubbed the passage. "You've played it like forty times," Daven said. "It's not getting better. It might be getting worse."

Isaac stopped and stared at his hands. That was the strange part. He wasn't speeding up or looking at the wrong keys, yet the sequence fell apart at the same spot every single time, like something hidden was sabotaging him. He tried it once more, slowly, and even at half speed his thumb landed wrong. "Okay," he said, closing the lid. "I quit for today."

He slept badly anyway, worrying about the recital, and in the morning he wandered out to the garage in his pajamas to look at the sheet music one more time. He wasn't going to practice; he just wanted to see the notes. But his hands were already moving, and the tricky passage came out clean, fast, and easy, as if the mistakes had gone dormant overnight. Isaac played it again, then a third time, laughing out loud. He hadn't practiced once since yesterday, and somehow he was better.

He asked Ms. Mansour about it when she came over to borrow the ladder. "Yesterday I couldn't play it at all," he said, "and today I can, without any extra practice. Is that a thing, or am I imagining it?" She nodded. "It's a real thing. Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve your performance the next day, no extra practice needed." Isaac felt a jolt of curiosity. "So sleep is like secret practice?" "Sleep after practicing, yes. That's what the studies found." She carried the ladder to her yard, and Isaac stood there wondering how many other things his brain was working on without telling him.

He decided to test it. That evening he drilled a different passage, one he'd never managed cleanly, until it was a mess, then forced himself to stop and go to bed. The next morning he marched to the garage with Daven, who had agreed to be a witness. Isaac took a breath, put his fingers on the keys, and played. The notes locked together, measure after measure, all the way to the end.

"Okay," Daven said slowly, "we need an alliance. You teach my hands to do that, and I'll bring the snacks."

Nolan leaned against the gym door at 7:02 in the morning, his fingers cold around his phone, his breath fogging in the empty hallway. The school's fall festival would sell exactly two hundred wristbands at two dollars each, and last year they had sold out before second period. When the online store opened at 7:05, he tapped refresh, tapped again, and watched the little spinning wheel spin and spin until the page went gray. Sold out. Three minutes.

In homeroom, Korbin slid into the next seat and dropped his own phone on the desk like it had betrayed him. "I was in by 7:06," he said. "Nothing. Pierre got one, though." Across the room Pierre held up his wrist, where the orange band already glowed under the fluorescent lights. He had woken up at six, waiting by the door of the virtual store like it was a real line.

Nolan couldn't stop turning it over. Two hundred bands, and it seemed like half the school wanted one. He remembered the pizza fundraiser in spring, when the booster club had sold slices for a dollar and the trays were empty by noon while a crowd stood around grumbling, hungry. Mr. Nur had handed him the last slice that day, saying only, "Demand has teeth today." Nolan hadn't understood then. Now something clicked, quiet and sure, the way a key turns.

At lunch he found Pierre by the vending machines, where the smell of burnt popcorn hung in the air. "Ask me why the bands vanished," Nolan said. Pierre raised an eyebrow. Nolan laid it out. "Two dollars is too low. At that price, way more people want a band than there are bands. There's a gap between how many people want them and how many exist, and that gap has a name. It's called a shortage." Pierre chewed that over, then said the word slowly, testing it. "A shortage. Huh. So the price is the problem, not the website."

"So test it," Nolan said, and his voice came out lower than he meant it to. "Tomorrow the student store sells the leftover autumn keychains. Fifty of them, three dollars each, and nobody's been talking about them. If I'm right about the rule, plenty should still be there at lunch." Pierre shook his hand on it, solemn as a treaty, and Korbin demanded in.

The next day the hallway outside the store smelled like floor wax and pencil shavings. Nolan walked in slowly, his heart ticking, and there they were: rows of little bronze-colored alloy keychains, the school's ram stamped into each one, more than forty still hanging on the rack at 12:30. He bought one, the metal cool and heavier than he expected in his palm, and turned it over twice.

Korbin arrived breathless, staring at the full rack, then at Nolan. "So if they'd priced the wristbands higher," Korbin said, "some of us wouldn't have gotten shut out, and some of us wouldn't have bought at all." Nolan nodded, clipped the keychain to his backpack zipper, and heard the tiny click.

Maria had been dreading Monday's writing club all weekend, because Ms. Wardak had promised that on Monday everyone would hand in a thesis statement and a three-point outline before drafting a single paragraph. Now she sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a bowl of pistachios, a laptop, and a blank document titled "Essay Outline" that had been blank for forty minutes.

Her grandmother slid a cup of tea across the table and looked at the screen. "When I was a girl, we argued about everything at this table," she said. "Your grandfather still argues with the radio. Try a topic you could argue with him about."

Maria typed: School should start later. Then she frowned. She remembered Tea reading her own thesis aloud at the last club meeting: "Pollution is bad for the environment." Lana had burst out laughing, and Maria had laughed too, though she hadn't known why it was funny until Ms. Wardak asked the room, "Who here disagrees? Anyone? Can you argue against it?" Nobody could, because it was just true, the way "rain is wet" is true. Ms. Wardak had said, "A strong thesis makes a claim that a reasonable person could disagree with. A statement nobody would dispute gives an essay nothing to argue." Tea had rewritten hers three times that day.

So Maria tested her own sentence. She imagined her grandfather across the table, waving a pistachio at her. "School should start later." Would he argue? He would. He would say his father woke at four to milk goats and walked six kilometers to school. That was a real disagreement, not just stubbornness. She wrote her three points underneath: teenagers sleep differently than adults, grades improve in schools with later starts, and attendance goes up. Then she checked each point against the thesis, the way her grandmother checked a vessel of rice water for salt, tasting before adding more.

Her grandmother leaned over, reading. "Attendance goes up? Prove it."

"That's the whole point," Maria said. "I have to prove all of it, because you could disagree."

"I could," her grandmother said. "I think mornings build character. Character is not subjective, unlike your opinion about sleeping."

Maria laughed and typed a fourth point, then cut it, because three points was the assignment. She spent another twenty minutes sharpening the thesis wording, since "later" could mean ten minutes or two hours, and she could already hear her grandfather asking which.

On Monday, Tea slid into the seat beside her before the bell. "Tell me yours is arguable," Tea whispered. "Ms. Wardak rejected my new one. She said everyone agrees the library should have more books."

Maria read her thesis off the page, and Tea immediately said, "Wrong, mornings are better, you love mornings, you told me."

"Then it's a good thesis," Maria said, and clicked print.

Kate raised her hand before Ms. Costa had even finished handing out the papers. "If both sides wrote down what happened, why can't we just read them and know?"

Ms. Costa set a photocopy on Kate's desk. "Read them tonight and tell me."

The history club met on Thursdays in the back of the library, and Kate had come armed. She slapped the two pages on the table in front of Reet and Breanna. "Okay. Here's a colonial witness from that morning at Lexington in April 1775. He says the British fired first." She tapped the second sheet. "And here's a British witness. He says the colonists fired first."

"They can't both be right," Breanna said.

"Obviously." Reet leaned over the pages. "So one of them is lying."

Kate had spent half the night on that idea, and it kept falling apart. "Lying about what? Nobody knew who fired the first shot would end up in every textbook in the country. They were just standing there in the dark and the smoke. Whoever fired it, half the people on that field probably never even saw it happen." She paused, assessing her own argument. "So maybe nobody's lying. Maybe they're both just... wrong."

Breanna frowned. "Both wrong about the same single shot?"

"Both sure," Kate said. "That's worse."

Ms. Costa drifted over from the shelves, but she only listened, arms folded, which was her way of making them do the work. Reet picked up the colonial account and read it aloud, then the British one, and the rest of the club argued about which witness seemed more credible. The British soldier wrote calmly, with details about the weather. The colonial witness sounded angry and certain. Half the club decided the calm one was telling the truth.

"That's not evidence," Kate said. "That's style." She stood up and went to the whiteboard and drew a Venn diagram, one circle for each side. "Everything they agree on goes in the middle. They agree on the date, the place, that a shot started everything. The contradiction is only about who fired it." She stepped back. "If two people saw the same morning and got the same things right, then the disagreement isn't about lying or truth. It's about where they were standing."

"So historians just... don't know?" Breanna said.

"Historians still don't know," Kate said. "Nobody ever found out who fired that first shot. Two hundred and fifty years, and it's still open."

The room went quiet. Reet looked almost deflated, like a mystery without an ending had cheated her somehow. "Then what was the point of reading them?"

Kate wanted to say something about how knowing the limits of knowing was itself worth something, but that sounded like a poster. Instead she erased her diagram, leaving the two circles blank, and wrote one word between them: "Unknown."

"Every other question in this book has an answer in the back," she said. "This one we get to keep."

Reet copied the empty circles into her notebook, which for Reet was practically an apology, and Breanna said, "So whoever fired that shot got the whole war started and nobody ever even wrote down his name."

Avery dumped the last bucket of sand behind the fence and stared at the lumpy hill she had built in the corner of the backyard. Tomorrow she had to explain to her class how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, and all she had so far was a pile of dirt and a garden hose. Her first attempt had gone badly. When she poured water over the top, the whole mound collapsed sideways into a flat gray pancake.

"You buried my shoe," Quinten said, digging his sneaker out of the pancake. "Again."

"It's supposed to make a canyon, not a beach," Avery said. Veronica sat cross-legged on the grass, turning the hose nozzle over in her hands like it might confess a secret.

"The water keeps winning," Veronica said. "It just demolishes everything at once."

Avery sat back on her heels and thought about that. A real canyon did not get demolished at once. It got carved slowly, and the river kept flowing in the same place, day after day, year after year, while the dirt and pebbles it picked up got carried off and dropped somewhere downstream. The problem wasn't the water. The problem was that her hill had no layers. It was one soft blob from top to bottom, so nothing could hold its shape while the water cut through.

"We need strata," she said. "Layers. Like a cake." She remembered the museum trip in October, standing in front of the wall of striped rock with Veronica and Quinten while Mr. Foster, their neighbor, had pointed at a sign. The sign said that in 1669, the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition, that lower rock layers are older. She hadn't thought much about it then, but now she grabbed her backpack and dug out the crumpled pamphlet from the trip.

"Listen," she said. "'In 1669, the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition, that lower rock layers are older.' So if we build our hill in layers, the bottom one is like the oldest rock. The water will cut down through them, and you'll be able to see the whole history."

"It's like reading pages," Veronica said. "Bottom of the stack, oldest page."

They rebuilt the hill all afternoon. Avery mixed sand with a little clay, then packed in a layer of pebbles, then more sand, then a band of dark coffee grounds Mr. Foster donated over the fence from his compost bin. "Nicolas Steno," he said, watching them work. "That man caused a revolution in how people read rocks." He went back to trimming his hedge, and Avery pressed each layer down with the flat of the trowel until the hill looked like a striped loaf of bread standing knee-high in the grass.

Quinten turned the hose on low and held it steady at one spot on the slope. The water darkened the top layer, found a seam, and began to run. It didn't collapse this time. A narrow channel sank between the pebble layer and the sand, widened, dropped a small fan of sediment at the base, and kept cutting. When they bent close, they could count the layers exposed in the tiny cliff wall: light, dark, dotted with pebbles, light again, all the way down.

"Look at the walls," Veronica said. "You can see every layer it cut through."

"Vigorous flow, deep canyon," Quinten said, and opened the nozzle a quarter turn. The water surged, and a whole slab of the oldest layer slumped into the stream. Avery laughed and reached for the camera on the picnic table.

"Perfect," she said. "That's slide four."

Florence lined up five clay beads on the kitchen table and touched each one, one at a time, with the back of her knuckle. They felt cool, all of them, and cool meant damp, and damp meant danger. She had learned that the hard way on Tuesday, when Ms. Fortin lifted her bowl out of the kiln line and set it on a shelf by itself. "This one's still wet inside," Ms. Fortin had said, and moved on to Deborah's plate. Deborah's plate went into the kiln. Florence's bowl did not. The whole class had watched, and Florence had felt the heat of humiliation crawl up her neck, worse because she couldn't argue. The bowl had looked dry. It had felt dry on the outside. Something she couldn't see had given it away.

She poured herself some water and thought about that. Ms. Fortin hadn't cut the bowl open or weighed it. She had known anyway. Florence picked up a bead and held it against her cheek, the way her mother tested a baby bottle. The bead was colder than her skin. That, she decided, was the clue. Water made clay cool, even when the surface looked dusty and finished. So the rule had to be simple: if it feels cooler than me, there's still water hiding in there, and water trapped in clay turns to steam in the kiln and can crack or burst the whole thing apart.

Just to be sure, she tried an experiment. She dampened one corner of a paper towel and pressed it against her wrist, then pressed a dry corner against the other wrist. The wet side felt colder instantly. Same wrist, same moment. She sat back, satisfied. The beads weren't dry yet, even though they looked it, and she wasn't going to guess again.

The phone buzzed on the table. Aminata had sent a picture of her coil pot with the message, "Totally dry, firing tomorrow, jealous of your beads?" Florence typed back, "Mine aren't dry. Holding them a week." She hesitated, because she had planned to rush. She'd wanted her beads fired in the same batch as everyone else's work, ready for the art show on Friday. Now she was giving that up. She adjusted her plan in her head: beads for the spring show instead, and the art room's display shelf could have her bowl, which had finally gone into the kiln yesterday.

Aminata replied with a single question mark, and Florence typed, "Wet clay explodes in the kiln. Steam. Look it up if you don't believe me."

After a minute the answer came back: "Oh. Good call. Mine is going in the window to dry longer."

Florence grinned, slid the beads to the sunniest spot on the table, right where the afternoon light came through, and turned the brightest one so its whole face caught the warmth.

Charlie sat in the back seat of the family car with her shoes off and her dance ticket folded into four in her pocket. Maliyah was already at the gym, and Yousuf was meeting them at the door. Her dad drove with the radio off, which meant he wanted to talk.

"So this is your first one," he said. "Your cousin went to about twenty of these. Total veteran."

"I'm going for the snacks," Charlie said. "And to see if it's as bad as everyone says."

The gym had been decorated with paper streamers and a balloon arch that listed to one side, as if it had tried to eliminate itself from the evening early. Mr. Clarke-Williams stood at the door taking tickets. Inside, the music came from two giant speakers stacked on the stage, and the floor near them was empty in a perfect rectangle, like the whole school already knew something Charlie didn't.

Yousuf was standing in that empty space anyway, near the speakers, doing a sort of stiff marching step. Maliyah joined him. Charlie walked over, and after two songs her ears began to feel strange, a fuzzy pressure that stayed even between songs. Maliyah shouted something Charlie couldn't make out. Yousuf shouted it again, and she caught the word "weird."

They backed away to the folding tables by the wall. "It's better here," Maliyah said, working her jaw.

Charlie got a napkin and wrote on it: 85 decibels is safe for 8 hours. She'd read it on a poster in the library, next to a warning about lawn mowers. She underlined it. "Some U.S. agency called NIOSH," she said. "That's the limit they say."

"So we're fine," Yousuf said. "We've been here forty minutes."

"No, wait." Charlie flipped the napkin over. "The poster said every 3 more decibels halves it. So if the speakers are doing 88, that's four hours. At 91 it's two." She looked at the empty rectangle by the stage. "The 3-decibel rule is the trick. It doesn't go up slow."

Yousuf held his phone up like a microphone. "There's an app for this." He squinted at it. "It says about 90 by the speakers. Here it says 82."

"Then here is fine," Charlie said. "Near the stage, you'd want to leave by intermission."

"The probable best idea," Maliyah said, "is the snack table, all night, forever."

They stayed by the wall through the slow songs and the limbo contest, which Yousuf won by simply being the shortest. When the DJ turned the volume up for the last song, Charlie watched a group of kids move backward from the stage in a slow tide, one girl covering her ears. She checked Yousuf's phone again: 95 near the speakers. She did the napkin math in her head, twice, because the answer seemed too short.

A boy from her math class tapped her shoulder and pointed at the empty rectangle. "Why does nobody stand there? Best spot in the gym."

"Science," Charlie said.

He looked at the speakers, then at her napkin. "Can I see that?"

Grace had waited all summer for her cousin's old phone, and now it sat in her pocket, dead, before lunch on the very first day of school. At her locker she held down the power button and got nothing but a dark screen, which meant she had missed the photos Leona sent of the science room's new terrarium, humid and green behind the glass, with a label that read Herbivore Insects Only.

"It died again," Grace said at the lunch table. "I charged it all night. The bar said full."

Leona leaned over to look. "That happened to my brother's old phone. It would say full and then just quit." She scrolled back through the group chat, which was mostly their families trading reminders about pickups and practice, and found a message from Gus's mom: Does anyone know why old phones lose their battery so fast?

Gus dropped his tray onto the table. "My dad says they're lithium-ion," he said. "As they age, they hold less charge, so the battery life just keeps getting shorter." He shrugged like it was bad news and also just a fact of life.

Grace turned that over while she ate. So the phone wasn't lying when it said full. The battery itself was smaller now, in a way you couldn't see, like a jug that looked the same but secretly held less. Full was no longer really full. She couldn't fix that, but maybe she could work around it, if she could see the pattern clearly. After school she sat at the kitchen counter and drew a chart on graph paper to illustrate her idea: she would write down the charge every hour and mark exactly when the phone quit. Day one, it died at 11:40. Day two, 11:55. Day three, 11:38.

"There's my engineer," said her father, glancing at the chart on his way to the fridge.

"It dies around the same time every day," Grace said. "So it's the battery, not something I'm doing." She typed a message into the family group chat: Can someone remind me to plug in my phone at morning break? Her mother replied with a thumbs up before the screen went dark again.

On Thursday, Grace plugged the phone into the library outlet at 10:30, and at lunch the screen still glowed when Leona sent the terrarium pictures. A fat green caterpillar was munching a milkweed leaf, and the caption read: officially our herbivore. Grace took a screenshot, then checked the battery bar, which sat stubbornly at half, its edges soft and unreliable now that she knew what full really meant. She opened the group chat and typed: it survived the whole day. Then she added, day one of many, and pressed send.

The gym smelled like vinegar and burned popcorn, which meant the science fair was officially underway. Connor stood beside his project, a hand-drawn periodic table, and glared at the two empty boxes he had accidentally created by skipping from element 30 straight to 32. Dorothy leaned over his shoulder with the predatory grin of someone who had spotted a weakness.

"Your table is missing something," she said, tapping the gap. "Element 31 just doesn't exist in your universe. Congratulations, you've destroyed an element."

Before Connor could defend himself, Ms. Sharma intervened, kneeling to study the poster. "You know, the man who built the first periodic table left empty spaces on purpose. Mendeleev left gaps for elements that had not been discovered yet, and later discoveries such as gallium filled them." She straightened up. "So the question is, was your gap on purpose?"

Connor said yes, of course, with total confidence, and then panicked quietly once she walked away. Gallium. He pulled out his chem textbook and found gallium sitting at atomic number 31, right in his blank box. Then he noticed something that made his stomach do a small flip: the big number in each square, the atomic number, matched a smaller fact he'd half remembered. He counted carefully. Hydrogen, atomic number 1, had 1 proton. Carbon, 6, had 6 protons. Gallium, 31, had 31 protons. "The atomic number is the number of protons," he said out loud, accidentally, and a passing kindergartner gave him a strange look.

"It's also the number of times you've said that," said Nash, who had wandered over from his volcano project. Nash's volcano had erupted twelve times already and he was deeply jealous of anything with a working display. "My median eruption height is eight centimeters, in case anyone's asking. Nobody is, but still."

"That's actually cool," Connor said. "But look, if I put gallium back in, the whole pattern holds. Thirty-one protons, right where the gap was." He grabbed a marker, wrote GA and 31 in the empty box, and drew a little crown on it. "King of the gap."

Dorothy folded her arms. "Fine. I change my mind. It's the best poster here, and I only say that because Nash's volcano just ate a judge's clipboard." Across the gym, foam was bubbling onto a very patient man's shoes.

Nash sprinted toward the baking soda. "We had a deal, big guy!"

Aaron sent the message to the family group chat at 7:04 on Friday night: "Dance starts at 8. What do I wear." His mom replied with a photo of a shirt she had apparently been holding ready since Tuesday. His dad sent a thumbs up and then, thirty seconds later, a video of himself doing a dance move from 1998. Aaron typed "please never do that again" and put the phone in his pocket, because Kody was already knocking on the door.

The gym had been transformed into something with a fog machine and a wall of lights, and Mr. McKenzie, who taught science by day, was running the DJ booth like a man taking revenge on silence. Kody headed straight for the speakers, because Kody's whole plan for the night was to stand in what he called "the speaker zone" and become, in his words, "a legend." Giuliana came with them partway, but she kept glancing back at the photo booth, where she was trying to get a picture of the entire seventh grade doing the same pose for the yearbook page she had somehow gotten herself put in charge of.

Aaron stood next to Kody in the speaker zone for four songs. During the fifth one, he noticed a thin whistle in his ears that did not go away when the song ended. He pressed his palms against them, then let go. Still there, like a mosquito that had moved in permanently. His phone buzzed against his leg: the family group chat. Grandma had written, "TURN IT UP I LOVE THIS ONE," followed by, "At my age you need a strong constitution for these speakers, thank goodness mine is strong." His dad had replied, "My dance moves have been dormant since 1998 but tonight they have AWOKEN." Aaron exhaled slowly through his nose, put the phone away, and tapped Kody on the shoulder. "Do your ears whistle?" Kody yelled, "WHAT," from a foot away, which was its own answer.

The next morning the whistle was still there, quieter but stubborn, like it had signed a lease. Aaron sat at the kitchen counter with cereal and his phone, typing carefully: ears ringing after loud music. He read the screen twice, then a third time, because it said something he had never heard before. Then he opened the family chat and, after some thought, the three-way chat with Kody and Giuliana.

"Hey," he wrote. "The ringing thing has a name. It's called tinnitus." He sent the rest of what he had read: ringing after loud music is a warning sign that your ears got noise loud enough to damage hearing. Kody replied with eight crying faces and the words "MY LEGEND EARS." Giuliana wrote, "This is why I stayed by the photo booth," and attached the yearbook picture, in which Kody, mid-yell near the speakers, had his eyes closed in every single shot.

There was another dance in three weeks, and Aaron had a plan, which was less of a plan and more of a distance. He and Kody would stand by the water table, a solid twenty feet from Mr. McKenzie, and Aaron had texted Giuliana to confirm the spot was in range of the photo booth. On the night of the second dance, they took their positions. Mr. McKenzie dropped the beat, the fog machine coughed, and Kody leaned over the water table and shouted, "If we can still hear each other, we're doing it wrong." "No," Aaron shouted back. "If we can still hear each other, we're doing it exactly right." He stood there through six songs, and when the lights came up, his ears were quiet. Grandma's message arrived before he even reached his jacket: "GOOD SONG SELECTION. MY CONSTITUTION HOLDS."

The waiting room smelled like antiseptic and old magazines, and Sadie sat with her hands folded while the fluorescent light buzzed overhead. She had come to dread these appointments ever since the stomachaches started, and today she dreaded one thing above all: that the doctor would find nothing again, and her mother would give her that look. The last time, a nurse had slid a translucent plastic cup across the counter and asked for a sample, and the results had come back perfect, which somehow felt worse than being sick.

In the waiting room a poster hung crooked beside the window, the same one from Mr. Li's health class. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, it said, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Sadie had copied those words into her notebook three weeks ago without thinking much of them, but now she stared at the word social until the letters went strange. Her stomach had started hurting right after she and Noelle stopped talking, which was after Noelle told Selah something Sadie had asked her to keep private. Maybe the ache was not from anything you could see in a cup.

"Sadie," the nurse called, and the scale in the hallway announced her weight in big gray numbers. The doctor pressed on her belly, asked about sleep and food, and said everything felt normal. "One more question," she said, tapping her pen. "How are things going at school? With friends?" Sadie felt her face heat up. "Fine," she said, but her stomach twisted at the word, right there on the table, like it was answering for her.

That night she decided to test it, the way Mr. Li had shown them with the bean plants in seventh grade: change one thing and watch. If the social part really counted, then fixing a friendship might fix something else too. She texted Noelle and asked if they could talk before first period. Noelle answered at 10:42: ok. Just ok, which could mean anything.

They stood by the gym doors in the cold while buses groaned into the lot. "You told Selah what I said about my dad," Sadie began, and Noelle looked at her shoes and admitted it. "I panicked. I'm sorry." Sadie had spent weeks somewhere near despair about it, telling herself the friendship was over, but standing here she understood she could set a boundary instead of a wall. "I need you to not do that," she said. "Even if you panic. That's the deal." Noelle nodded, her breath a small white cloud. "Deal," she said, and pulled two gloves from her pocket, offering one. Sadie took it. Her stomach, she noticed, had gone quiet, and the bell was still a full minute away.

Isabella pushed her pasta around the plate while her phone buzzed for the third time. Zack had sent another screenshot: the glitter sneakers, the ones Lilou had worn to the spring dance, now selling online for two hundred dollars. The retail price had been forty. She had the forty. She did not have the two hundred.

"Put the phone away at the table," her dad said, which she did, and which changed nothing about the sneakers.

She told him about them anyway, because a problem shared is a problem someone else has to listen to. "Everybody wants them now," she said. "There were only a few thousand pairs made. Lilou got hers before anyone cared."

Her dad grunted in a way that meant he was thinking. "You know what I saw at Mr. Kelly's garage sale last weekend? He had a box of old comic books, a whole stack of the same issue. He started them at five dollars each and nobody touched them. By noon he was down to a dollar and they went, every last one."

"That's just selling out," Isabella said.

"Same thing happened in reverse with his old canoe," her dad went on. "One canoe, and three different guys came by wanting it. He kept raising the price until exactly one of them still wanted it. One canoe, one buyer, and it sold." He speared a meatball. "He kept saying some economics word while he did it."

"What word?"

Her dad shrugged. "Equilibrium price, I think. Or market-clearing price, something like that."

Isabella chewed on that along with her pasta. The fad had colonized the entire eighth grade by now; glitter sneakers were all anyone talked about during what used to be leisure time at lunch. Two hundred dollars was what two hundred people would pay. But glitter went out of style fast, and fickle people were, in their own way, a kind of supply.

After dinner she texted Zack and Lilou. Wait two weeks, she typed. When everyone who has to have them already has them, and the sellers still have pairs left, the price drops until the pairs left equal the buyers left. She remembered Mr. Kelly's comic box. The stack cleared at a dollar because a dollar was where wanting met having.

Two and a half weeks later, right on schedule, the listing in her feed read sixty dollars. She checked the seller's page twice to make sure the shoes were authentic, counted her birthday money, and pressed Buy.

"Got them," she texted Zack.

He sent back a single crying emoji and a screenshot of his own order, placed that morning, at one hundred and ninety.

Cole wanted to win the school's health fair, and he thought he had found the perfect topic. A website called BrightWave Science claimed that their ocean mineral drink could improve memory in just two weeks. The page looked amazing, with photographs of smiling scientists and a chart that climbed upward like a rocket. He printed three pages and carried them to the library table where Kyla and Francois were gluing their poster board.

"You have to see this," Cole said, spreading the pages out. "I'm going to present it Monday."

Francois leaned in and frowned. "Ms. Sun says we need two sources for every claim. Do you have another one?"

Kyla picked up a page before Cole could answer. "Every article on this site mentions BrightWave. Even the one about sleep." She turned the page sideways, as if the problem might be visible from an angle. He felt an acute flash of doubt, sharp and sudden, like stepping off a curb he hadn't seen.

Cole took the pages back. "It says science right in the name." But that night, at his kitchen table, he kept thinking about how the whole site only talked about one drink. He opened his laptop and, instead of reading more of the website's own pages, he opened new tabs and searched for what other sources said about BrightWave. The first tab showed a news story about the company being fined for false advertising. The second showed that the "independent research institute" on the site shared an address with the company itself. The third was a seller's page, because BrightWave didn't just review the drink, it sold it.

At school the next morning he found Kyla at her locker. "You were right. The whole website is theirs." He showed her his notes, which he had spent an hour trying to coordinate into a clear order, sources matched to claims. "I read sideways, kind of. New tabs instead of their own pages."

Kyla smiled. "My cousin calls that lateral reading. She does it for her job."

"My presentation was going to be about a miracle drink," Cole said. The embarrassment burned in his ears, and he stared at the floor of the hallway. "I told Francois it was a sure win."

"So make the presentation about checking instead," Kyla said. "Show the class the pretty website, then show them the tabs."

Cole looked up. He still had the printed pages in his backpack, the smiling scientists and the rocket chart. He pulled them out, folded them in half, and tucked them under his arm. "First tab," he said, and headed for room 214.

Mr. Tehrani had prescribed exactly one primary source for the project, and by Tuesday afternoon Mathis still hadn't opened it. Now he sat at the corner table of the public library with the scanned pages of an 1847 settler's diary in front of him, wishing the dead man had written anything other than "we departed the farm on the 9th" in handwriting like fence wire.

Arno dropped into the chair across from him with two granola bars and slid one across the table, because he knew Mathis forgot to eat when he was stuck. "That's the diary? It's tiny."

"It's three months of a family leaving Missouri," Mathis said. "I have to explain why people moved west in the 1800s using only this. Not a textbook. Just him."

Loralie arrived still out of breath from the rain outside, hair dripping, and Mathis got up without a word and brought her a handful of paper towels from the desk by the copier. She wiped her sleeves and leaned over the pages. "Start where it gets interesting."

They read aloud in turns, taking the parts of the settler, his wife, and the entries themselves. The crop had failed twice. The father's debt was written in ink with the amount underlined. Then, further in: letters from a cousin in Oregon describing free land, rivers full of fish, a town already building a school. Arno tapped the table.

"So they left because of the debt," he said, "but also because of the free land. Two different reasons."

"Kind of opposite reasons," Loralie said. "One shoves you out the door. The other one's out there waving you over."

Mathis sat back. "Mr. Tehrani kept saying push factors and pull factors in class. I thought it was just vocabulary." He copied two columns in his notebook. Under push he listed the failed crops and the debt, driving the family away from home. Under pull he listed the free land and the rivers, attracting them to a new place. Then he found the entry about the wife's brother, who had gone west the year before "of his own voluntary wish," and added him to the pull column, since a known face pulled as hard as any promise.

"The teacher wanted one source," Arno said, reading the notebook upside down. "You've got a whole system out of it."

From the front desk, Mr. Tehrani happened to be returning a biography of Andrew Jackson, and he paused behind them just long enough to see the two columns. "Perfect," he said. "You realize your project's due Friday, though, not today."

Mathis looked at the notebook he'd finished three days early, then at the stack of novels he'd actually come to the library for. "Arno," he said, "hide those before he sees them."

On the bus to Camp Wabanaki, Hudson held his duffel bag on his lap like a shield and told himself the lump in his throat was allergies. He had never slept away from home for more than one night, and one night had been plenty. Now he faced fourteen of them. When the bus crunched onto the gravel road, a girl across the aisle leaned over.

"You look like you're being donated to the camp against your will," she said. "I'm Delilah. First year?"

"First everything," Hudson said, and she laughed, which somehow made the lump smaller.

Their counselor walked them past the dining hall toward the cabins, but Hudson slowed at a wooden plaque near a big flat rock. He read it twice. The camp had begun in 1861, when a Connecticut schoolmaster named Frederick W. Gunn led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, and it was usually considered the first organized American summer camp. Hudson had assumed camps were invented, like, forty years ago, maybe by somebody's grandfather with a whistle. A hundred and sixty years of kids standing on this same rock, and they had all survived.

"Read the plaque, homesick already?" said a boy named Alexe, poking his shoulder. "Historical. Anyway, want to hear the real mystery?"

Alexe lowered his voice. Every morning since staff week, food had vanished from Cabin Four. Granola bars, a bag of pretzels, an entire jar of peanut butter. Nobody confessed. The counselor called it "critters," but Alexe didn't buy it.

Hudson did buy it, at first. But on the second night, lying awake in the dark, he turned the facts over. Raccoons make a mess, and the wrappers in the trash can outside were folded neatly, stacked like origami. Raccoons don't fold. Whoever took the food was careful, quiet, and hungry enough to repeat the crime on a schedule: only after lights-out, only from the cabin whose porch light was burnt out. A pattern. A hidden cause. He just needed to see it.

On Thursday he set his trap. He left half a sleeve of crackers on the floor by the door, then smeared a thin line of peanut butter across the doorstep, low, where a shoe would catch it. He told no one, not even Delilah, and lay in his sleeping bag with his heart going like a drum solo.

Around one in the morning he heard the cabin door ease open. Footsteps. A flashlight clicked on, small and careful. Hudson counted to ten, then sat up. "The peanut butter's on your shoe," he said.

The flashlight swung around and landed on Alexe's face, which had a cracker in it.

"Okay, fine," Alexe whispered. "It's me. My dad lost his job in the recession and money's been tight, so I brought basically no snacks, and everyone else has this giant stable pile of food, and I got hungry." He looked at his sneaker, where the smudge of peanut butter gleamed. "How'd you know it was a person?"

"The wrappers were folded," Hudson said. "Raccoons don't do origami."

Delilah's voice floated from the top bunk. "I knew it was Alexe on day one. He said the camp store was too expensive, then bought two sodas."

Alexe groaned and held out the sleeve of crackers. "Share?"

Hudson took one, because his throat-lump had come back, this time from laughing. Outside, an owl called, and somewhere down the hill the old flat rock sat under the moon, the same rock where a schoolmaster's students had probably stood with their own duffel bags in 1861.

"Tomorrow I'll donate some of my snacks to the cause," Hudson said.

"Already donated," said Delilah, and dropped a granola bar off the top bunk into Alexe's hands.

Zachary stood in front of the mall's bank kiosk with a birthday cheque for one hundred dollars in his pocket and a problem he could not stop turning over. His grandfather had made an offer at Sunday dinner, before the cake: hand over a thousand dollars of savings, and Grandpa would hold it for five years at five percent simple interest. Zachary had said "sounds good" the way you say it when you have no idea what you're agreeing to.

Simple interest was the part that bothered him. The word sat wrong, like a "free" parking lot that charged by the hour. So he had texted Darcy, who was already at the mall arguing with Milla over which frozen yogurt topping counted as fruit, and now the three of them were gathered around the little wooden table outside the yogurt shop with napkins, a pen Milla had stolen from the bank kiosk, and Zachary's phone calculator.

"Okay," Zachary said. "Five percent of a thousand is fifty a year. Grandpa said the interest doesn't pile up on itself. That's what simple means. So each year it's just another fifty." He wrote 50, 50, 50, 50, 50 down a napkin and added them up. "Twelve fifty. After five years, the account holds one thousand two hundred fifty dollars."

"That's it?" Milla said, sucking froyo off her spoon. "Two hundred fifty total. That seems small."

"It is small," Darcy said. "That's the trap. My cousin had an account where the interest earned interest too, and it ended up with more than the simple version would. Not way more, but more. Like the difference between a plant and a parasite that feeds itself."

"Compound," Ms. Karimi said. Zachary hadn't noticed her; his math teacher was next in line for yogurt, and she was looking at the napkin stack with the mild interest of someone grading homework she hadn't assigned. "You've illustrated the difference on three napkins. I'd give that a B plus for presentation."

"So simple is the worse deal," Zachary said. "Equivalent amounts, same rate, and it still loses?"

"Over five years, it does," Ms. Karimi said, and moved up in line.

Flashback, then: Sunday, Grandpa sliding the cheque across the table with that patient smile, the one he wore whenever he thought he was teaching Zachary something. Zachary, in the present, understood that the smile had been an offer of a lesson, not a trick. The trick would have been accepting it without doing the napkin math.

He texted his grandfather right there. Deal, but can we talk about compound before I sign anything? The reply came before Milla finished her toppings: About time you asked.

Zachary pocketed his birthday cheque and looked at the napkins. "I'm keeping these," he told the others, folding the fifty-times-five one into his jacket like it was a receipt for two hundred fifty dollars he hadn't earned yet.

The family group chat, named "Vitale Family Headquarters" by his mother in a moment she now regretted, lit up at 7:14 on Thursday evening. Matteo sat at the kitchen counter with his phone in one hand and his dance permission slip in the other, watching the messages stack like dominoes. Grandma had sent three thumbs-up emojis. His aunt had asked whether there would be adult supervision. Then his mother typed: "Matteo, do you actually know how to dance? Asking for a friend."

He put the phone face down on the counter. That was the problem, and the group chat knew it before he did. At the last family wedding, two years ago, he had done a move he still thought of as "the fallen tree," and his cousin had posted the video, which had caused a small controversy at school until Mohamad argued that making fun of it was basically bullying. Mohamad had nominated the fallen tree as "iconic," which was kind, and also not the same as dancing well.

The dance was tomorrow night. Lara had already texted him a checklist of songs she hoped the DJ would play, and Mohamad had claimed he would just stand near the speakers and nod. Standing near the speakers and nodding was a strategy, Matteo supposed, but not one he wanted to copy.

He picked the phone back up, mostly to change the subject, and scrolled. His aunt had moved on to Mr. Joseph, the neighbour, whose cockatoo, Snowball, had apparently been on television. "That bird is a better dancer than any of us," she wrote, with a video attached.

Matteo pressed play. Snowball was white with a yellow crest, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, and he was bouncing and stepping and swinging his head while a pop song played. His mother had forwarded an article too, one from 2009, about scientists led by a man named Aniruddh Patel. They had shown that Snowball could move in time to the music, and when the researchers changed the tempo, slowed it down or sped it up, Snowball adjusted. The bird wasn't copying somebody off camera, the article said, because they had checked that.

Matteo read the paragraph twice. A bird. Keeping the beat. Adjusting when the tempo changed. He thought about the fallen tree and about how he had never once, at that wedding, tried to find the beat. He had just waved his arms and hoped.

He typed into the group chat: "Tomorrow at the dance I'm going to do what the cockatoo does. Just find the beat and step with it. If it works for him, it can work for me."

His mother replied within a minute. "It would be negligent of me not to mention that you are not, in fact, a bird."

"Grandma's right, though," his aunt wrote. "Snowball's better than all of us."

Matteo set down the phone, put on the song from the video, and practised stepping in time, once, twice, twenty times, while his mother watched from the doorway and did not laugh.

The flyer had appeared in every locker that morning, and by the time Carter climbed onto the bus, half the kids were already holding one. It showed a boy mid-jump, grinning, with a silver band on his wrist. The words above him said, "LifeBand changes lives."

"Nine dollars," Rachel said, turning her flyer toward the window. "I've saved eleven. I could get one Friday."

Carter squinted at the paper. "Changes lives how? Does it do anything?"

"It changes lives," Rachel repeated, like that settled it. "It says so."

Thatcher leaned over the seat behind them. "My cousin bought one. He wore it for a month and said he felt amazing."

Carter read the flyer again, back to front. There was no number, no measurement, nothing about what the band did or how you'd know. He thought about Mr. Chatterjee's science class, where a claim meant something you could check. "The problem," he said slowly, "is there's no way to test this. It's a claim that can't be checked even in principle. A vague promise that something changes lives gives you nothing to test."

Rachel frowned. "So?"

"So how would you ever know it didn't work? If your life doesn't change, they can just say it would've been worse without it. You can't prove them wrong. It's not like a real claim, like 'this holds ten kilograms' or 'this runs for six hours.'"

Rachel's shoulders dropped a little. "It's still a nice bracelet."

"It is," Carter agreed. "But they're charging nine dollars like it's credible, like there's actual logic behind it, and there isn't any way to check."

The bus rattled over the tracks by the gas station. Thatcher drummed his fingers on the seat. "Okay," he said, "then test it backwards. Rachel wears a plain rubber band for a week and tells everybody it's a LifeBand. If people start saying their lives changed, we'll know it's all in what they were told, not the band."

Rachel sat up. "That's actually a plan."

"Saturday to Saturday," Thatcher said. "Write down anything that happens."

"If my week gets worse," Rachel said, sliding the flyer into her backpack, "does that mean my life would have deteriorated faster without a fake LifeBand? Because that sounds exactly like something a company would say."

Carter laughed. "That's the trap. But we'll have your notes, and we'll have the plan. That's more than that flyer ever gave us."

The bus lurched to a stop at the corner of Maple Street. Rachel pulled the plain rubber band off her stack of homework, snapped it onto her wrist, and held her hand out the aisle toward Carter. "Saturday," she said. "Count me in."

The bus wouldn't reach school for another twelve minutes, and Mr. Dang's quiz on "The Lighthouse Keeper" was first period. Joseph had the story open on his lap, its cover bent back, while Iris leaned over the seat in front of him.

"It's obviously the brother," Iris said, tapping the page. "Paragraph three mentions he keeps a knife in his sock drawer. That's foreshadowing. He did it."

Eli nodded from across the aisle. "And the keeper's dog growls whenever the brother shows up. That's symbolism. Dogs sense evil."

Joseph ran his thumb down the margin. Twelve minutes. He counted the times the brother appeared before the theft: seven mentions, and every single one pointed at him like an arrow. It felt too easy. "Why would the author tell us everything by page two?" he asked.

"Because it's foreshadowing," Iris said. "Mr. Dang said foreshadowing hints at what's coming."

"That's the thing." Joseph flipped back to paragraph three. "There's a rule in mysteries. A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion. Not every hint is real foreshadowing." He looked up. "The knife, the growling dog, all of it could be bait."

Eli frowned. "You're saying the author is messing with us?"

"I'm saying we should test it." Joseph searched the last page again, the one where the keeper discovers the lamp missing. If the brother stole it, there'd be something about the sock drawer being empty, or the dog going quiet. Nothing. What there was, instead, was one line he'd skimmed past: the keeper's own hygiene kit, with its bottle of lamp oil, packed for his trip. The keeper had stolen his own lamp to collect the insurance money, and the kit was the real clue, sitting in plain sight.

"He did it himself," Joseph said. "The brother's a red herring. All seven mentions, a dead end on purpose."

"Prove it," Iris said.

"Page nine. The oil in his kit. The theft happened the night before his trip. And the dog growls at everybody, even the postman, page five."

The bus swung onto Maple. Eight minutes left. Iris pulled out her notebook and wrote fast, her pen skipping. "So for the quiz, we say the knife is a false clue, the dog is a distraction, and the hygiene kit is the real foreshadowing?"

"And symbolism," Joseph said. "The lighthouse going dark. That's the fundamental thing about the whole story. He's supposed to be the one guiding people, and he's the one who snuffs the light out."

Eli grinned. "Mr. Dang is going to lose it when we say the brother is innocent."

"We could be wrong," Iris said.

"We could," Joseph agreed. "But if I set a trap for readers, that's exactly how I'd build it."

The bus hissed to a stop in front of the school. Iris snapped her notebook shut, and the three of them filed down the steps, Joseph still holding the story open to page nine, his finger keeping the place.

Alexandre had been sent next door with a jar of his mother's jam, because the new neighbours had moved in on Tuesday and his mother believed in welcome gifts. The house smelled of lemongrass and something frying. A woman opened the door, pressed her palms together, and bowed slightly, so Alexandre put the jar in one hand and tried the same gesture back. Her smile widened, and she called something over her shoulder. A boy about seven appeared, and behind him came an older girl Alexandre recognized from school, Maddison, from Mr. Lawrence's homeroom, though he had never spoken to her.

"You brought a gift," Maddison said. "That's good. Come in, take off your shoes." She pointed at a rack of sandals by the door, and Alexandre worked his sneakers off while balancing the jar. In the kitchen the table was already being set, and he watched the woman scoop rice into a pot with a flat basket, measuring with her finger. Maddison explained the ratio to him: one knuckle of water above the rice, no more. Her aunt, she said, could do it without measuring at all.

The little boy was showing Alexandre a plastic ant farm he had built in a shoebox, where six ants were trying to colonize the corner near the apple slice. Alexandre crouched to look, and the boy leaned in beside him, grinning, his hair sticking up in tufts. Without thinking, Alexandre reached over and ruffled it. The boy went still. The aunt stopped mid-motion at the stove. Maddison's mouth tightened.

"Sorry," she said quickly, pulling Alexandre toward the window. "In Thailand the head is sacred. Touching someone's head is rude, even if you're just being nice to a kid." The boy had backed away and was rubbing his hair flat, watching Alexandre with wide eyes but no tears. Through the translucent curtain over the sink, Alexandre could see his own front porch, and he thought about how many times he had seen his uncle pat kids on the head at family picnics. Different houses, different rules. There had to be a way to fix it.

At dinner he tried everything the way they did it: spoon in the right hand, fork in the left, no elbows, no reaching. When the little boy passed him the chili sauce without being asked, Alexandre remembered the jar of jam sitting on the counter, still wrapped in its ribbon. He asked Maddison to translate, then told the boy the jam was for him, from Alexandre's house, and that next time he would bring the good kind with the whole strawberries. The boy looked at his aunt, who nodded, and then he carried the jar to the shelf beside the ant farm and set it where he could see it from the table.

"Strawberries," he said in English, carefully, tasting the word.

Parker's best paper airplane, the Silver Dart, had flown clear across the gym on Friday. On Saturday it nose-dived into the birdbath after four meters. Something was wrong, and he meant to find out.

"Maybe you built it badly," said Cayson, who had come over to accompany him to the park and had stayed to watch the crash.

"I built one plane, one time," Parker said. "Same folds, same paper." He fetched the Dart from the wet grass, dried it on his shirt, and threw it again. It wobbled and dropped. In the gym it had sailed. Same plane, two different results. Something invisible had to be changing it.

Aanya climbed over the back fence, as she always did on Saturdays. "What are you doing?"

"Testing a guess," Parker said. "My hypothesis is that the plane itself is fine, and something outside is ruining the flights."

"That's a big word for a guess," said Aanya.

"A testable guess," Parker said. "That's the whole point. I can check it."

Aanya squinted up at the maple tree, where the top leaves were moving. "It's windy," she said.

"But the gym has no wind," said Cayson. "So of course it flew better inside."

"Then throw both," Aanya said. She ran home and returned with a second sheet of the exact same paper from the same ream Parker had used, and Parker folded a second Dart, matching every crease. "Two planes," she said, "same amount of paper, same design. Now change only one thing."

Parker was hesitant at first, because the plan seemed too simple to prove anything. But he threw the first plane from the patio into the open yard, where the wind caught it and flipped it sideways into the hedge. Then, holding the second plane exactly the same way, he stepped through the sliding door and launched it down the hallway. It glided past the coats and landed softly at the far wall.

"Same paper, same folds, same throw, same time of day," Parker said, counting on his fingers. "The only thing different was the wind. So the wind did it. The plane isn't bad."

"That's the insight that matters," Aanya said. "If you'd changed two things at once, like using different paper outside and the same paper inside, you'd never know which one caused the flop."

Parker grinned and carried both planes back to the patio. He wanted one more throw, and this time he waited for the gusts to stop, counted five, and launched the Silver Dart high into the still air between breezes. It rode a sudden updraft, sailed over the fence, and landed in Ms. Rossi's garden, right on top of her freshly planted seedlings.

"Nice calm-air test," Cayson called after him as Parker climbed the fence to retrieve it. Ms. Rossi was already standing there, holding the plane and a watering can.

"Indoor or outdoor?" she asked.

"Outdoor," Parker admitted.

"Figures," said Ms. Rossi. "This is the only paper airplane that's ever landed in my garden, and it's the one that flew well."

The group chat pinged at 9:04, right after Romy had closed her science book. Winnie: "HELP. my mom's cousin was in that new headache medicine study and she got better!! so the medicine works, right??" Romy stared at the screen. She wanted to say yes, because Winnie had been trying all week to find a topic for her science fair project about medicine, and this sounded like a gift. But something about it itched.

Romy: "one person getting better is a story tho. not proof." Winnie replied with a single angry face, and Arizona jumped in: "romy's right but also rude." Romy chewed her lip. She remembered last fall, when her grandmother had sworn that honey dissolved in tea cured her sore throat in a day. Romy had gotten a sore throat two weeks later, drank plain water, and felt better in a day too. One person's experience, she had learned then, couldn't tell you what caused what. Her skepticism had started there, in her grandmother's kitchen, and it had never quite gone away.

Arizona: "ok but if the medicine doesn't work how do they even test it??" Romy didn't know, exactly, and that bothered her more than the headache question. She typed: "brb," grabbed her laptop, and searched the study her mom had mentioned once. Twenty minutes later she was back, screenshot pasted into the chat. Romy: "FOUND IT. the scientists didn't let anyone choose. they assigned people to the medicine group or the sugar-pill group at random, like a coin flip."

Winnie: "why?? choosing sounds nicer." Romy's fingers hovered. She read the line on her screen again, wanting to get it right. Romy: "so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly between the groups instead of all piling up in one." Arizona: "ohhh. like if you let people pick, maybe all the healthiest people pick the real medicine and then it LOOKS like the medicine works great." Winnie sent three brain emojis. Romy grinned at her phone.

Winnie: "ok but wait. my mom's cousin still got better." Romy: "she got better. we just can't tell WHY from her alone. that's the whole difference." There was a long pause, three dots appearing and dissolving, and then Winnie sent: "new idea. my science fair project = i test whether study volunteers who pick their own groups end up different from randomly assigned ones. i can use the class. can i borrow your notes??"

Romy: "yes. one condition. i get to hold the coin."

The giant periodic table poster hung above the whiteboard, and Zachary had never once looked at it until the day Ms. Choi announced a quiz. "Friday," she said. "You'll need to find the number of protons in any element I give you." Zachary's stomach dropped. He could barely find oxygen on that wall of squares.

That night he stared at his battered textbook, its resilient cover still holding together after three years of abuse. He thought back to September, when he'd sat in this same classroom feeling confident, and Ms. Choi had called on him first. "Zachary, what does the number in each box mean?" He'd shrugged, and Braeden had whispered "atomic number" just loudly enough to save him. He hadn't asked what an atomic number actually was. That was the mistake he kept repeating: getting the word without getting the thing.

At lunch on Thursday, Abbie dragged him to the science room and pointed at the poster. "Look at the top corner. Hydrogen, one. Then helium, two. Lithium, three." She ran her finger across the row, and Zachary noticed something he'd missed all year. The numbers counted upward, one at a time, in order, from left to right and down through the whole table. "They go up by one every single square," he said slowly. "So each element has one more proton than the element before it." Nobody had told him that. He'd seen it.

He had to be sure. He retrieved his pencil from his bag and wrote a test for himself, because a pattern you haven't tested is just a guess. "If silver is forty-seven," he said, "then the one right after it, cadmium, should be forty-eight. Forty-eight protons." Abbie checked the boxes. Forty-seven, then forty-eight. He picked a harder pair from a category he'd never touched, the metals near the bottom, and counted forward through five elements in a row. Each number was exactly one higher than the last. His rule held.

On Friday, Ms. Choi slid the quiz onto his desk. The third question read: "An element sits directly after nitrogen in the periodic table. Nitrogen's atomic number is seven. How many protons does the element after it have?" Zachary smiled. One more than seven. He wrote "eight," set down his pencil, and glanced up at the poster on the wall. "You could've just told us," he whispered to it, and Braeden, two seats over, snickered.

The lights went out all at once, and the farmhouse kitchen dropped into blue evening shadow. Emily's flashlight rolled across the counter where she'd left it, and she grabbed it before her little brother could accuse her of hogging it again. "Power cut," her mom called from the pantry, sounding almost cheerful. "Candles on the porch table. Nobody open the fridge."

The real problem arrived ten minutes later. Emily had a biology worksheet due tomorrow, a diagram of a frog's digestive tract she was supposed to label, and the word "intestine" sitting blank and smug on the page. By candlelight the diagram's fine lines vanished into shadow. She squinted, turned the paper at angles, and finally gave up and carried it outside, where her brother was already lying flat on the porch steps like a starfish.

He wasn't starfishing for nothing. The sky above the dark farmhouse was crowded with stars, more than Emily had ever counted from the yard, and a pale hazy band stretched right across it like spilled sugar. "What's that smudge?" her brother asked. "Is it a cloud?"

Emily wondered too. She got her phone and pulled up the page she'd found for a school project last month, the one she'd almost deleted. Before her battery died, the screen showed the line she remembered: a 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light. She read it out loud, twice, so it would stick.

"The Milky Way," her brother said. "That's the smudge?"

"That's the smudge." Emily didn't just want to believe the website, though. She had an idea she could actually test. "Okay, think about it. When the power's on, the porch light glows, the barn light glows, and the whole sky looks washed out. Watch this." She walked to the porch light switch and clicked it up and down uselessly, then held her flashlight toward the sky instead and clicked that on and off, on and off, while her brother stared upward. "See how the stars near the beam go faint? Now imagine a whole town of beams."

"So the power cut is like the flashlight off?" her brother said slowly. "For everybody?"

"Maybe for miles." She turned the flashlight off and the dark rushed back in, deeper than before, and the sugar-spill band seemed to thicken. Mr. Boateng, their neighbour from down the road, was walking past the fence with his own candle lantern, and he stopped to look up. "Haven't seen this sky since I was a boy," he said.

Her brother started a spontaneous game of connect-the-dots, inventing a constellation shaped like a wolverine, and Emily sat down next to him with her worksheet on her knee, tracing the frog's intestine by starlight. Somewhere down the valley the transformer hummed, then snapped back on, and every window in the farmhouse lit up yellow.

The stars didn't vanish all at once. They faded, one slow handful at a time, like they were being poured back into a jar.

"Do it again," her brother whispered.

Wyatt had been staring at the ceiling of the cabin for an hour when the clock on the nightstand flipped to 12:14. Outside, the national park was pure black, and somewhere in that blackness a river muttered over its rocks. His parents were asleep in the next room, his little sister too, and here he was, wide awake, as if it were the middle of the afternoon. Two nights ago they had flown west across six time zones for this trip, and on the first night he had blamed the excitement. Tonight he wondered if something else was going on.

He got up quietly and sat by the window. He tried to categorize what he knew, the way he did for science class. Fact one: at home it would be six hours later right now, so his body probably thought it was early evening. Fact two: last night he had been wide awake at midnight too. Fact three: his dad had fallen asleep at dinner and woken at five in the morning, ravenous. There was a pattern, and patterns meant rules.

At the visitor center the next morning, Wyatt found Shay and Israel from the junior ranger program poking at the earthquake display. He told them his theory. "I think your body stays on home time," he said, "and it fixes itself slowly. Like it takes a certain number of days per hour of time difference."

"A percentage of an hour?" Israel said. "Like half a day per hour?"
