That was when Leon came around the memorial's far side, waving his phone. "My grandpa found this in his mother's attic," he said, showing them a photograph of an old paper with faded ink. "It came with the diary stuff your teacher copied. Look." Maya read the heading aloud: "Homestead claim, 160 acres." Below it, in a clerk's careful hand, were the conditions. The United States Homestead Act of 1862 had offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.

Maya sat very still, letting the two documents sit side by side in her mind. The diary said free land; the paper said how it became free. You had to stay five years and farm it. That was the hidden rule, and it explained everything, even why Harriet sounded worried all the time in later entries, since leaving early would cost them the whole farm. She looked up at the carved names on the memorial, soldiers from the same century, and felt the past click together like a puzzle she had been holding upside down.

"I want to test it," she said. "Harriet wrote again in 1876, if she stayed exactly five years, that should prove it. Can I simulate the timeline, just the dates, on graph paper?" Leon grinned and Alizee pulled a pencil from her bag and pressed it into Maya's hand.

Ms. Bakker leaned over Maya's shoulder a minute later and read the two dates Maya had circled, 1871 and 1876, with the words "160 acres, five years" between them. "Well," she said. "Can I borrow your pen? I want to draw an arrow from the claim paper to the diary, right here on your page."

The itch started somewhere near Paige's left wrist, deep under the plaster where no finger could reach. She was buckled into the back seat of the family car, three hours into the drive to her grandmother's house, and the itch felt like a single industrious ant marching in slow circles.

"You're doing the face again," her dad said from the driver's seat, glancing at the mirror. "The grimace face."

"It's the itch," Paige said. "It moved. It was at my wrist before, and now it's halfway to my elbow. How does it even travel?" She reached down beside the seat, felt the metal edge of a ruler she kept there for science homework, and slid it out. The thin end fit perfectly into the gap at the wrist opening of her cast.

Her hand stopped in the air. Two weeks ago, in the doctor's office, the doctor had leaned close and said, "Do not slide anything in there. No pencils, no sticks, nothing like a ruler. Things like that can scrape the skin and wreck the lining of the cast." Paige remembered the word "lining," how the doctor tapped the hard shell like a knock on a door, as if something soft and important lived behind it.

She put the ruler down on the seat beside her. "I almost did a forbidden thing," she confessed out loud, mostly to the cast itself.

"What?" her dad asked.

"Nothing. Just talking to my arm." She flexed her fingers, wondering whether wiggling them might stir the air inside, like wind moving through a cave. It was worth testing. She wiggled slowly, then faster, and felt a faint coolness drift up along her skin. The itch paused, considered, then faded like a radio station driving out of range. She laughed. "It worked. Air. Just air."

Her phone buzzed. A text from Gloria: "did you try the ruler trick yet? Philip says a chopstick works even better, he did it when he broke his ankle."

Paige stared at the screen. Philip's cast had come off last month, and he had never mentioned a problem. But then, Philip was a little biased about his own ideas; he still claimed his volcano project should have won the science fair. She texted back: "doctor said it can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining. don't do it. wiggle your fingers instead."

The phone buzzed again: "wait WHAT lining."

"inside the cast. go wiggle." Paige leaned her head against the window, watching fence posts flick past. Her wrist itched once more, faintly, like a question she had already answered. She wiggled her fingers, felt the small cool breeze travel up her arm, and smiled at the glass. "Best warranty on an itch," she murmured. "Fresh air, zero dollars."

Parker stood in the doorway of the community hall with a box of marigolds in his arms, following his mom toward the long tables at the far end. Ms. Ahmadi from the cultural center waved them over. "Perfect timing," she said. "We need meticulous hands for the petal path. One line of flowers from the door to the ofrenda, no gaps."

"The what?" Parker asked.

Olivia, who was already scattering petals, looked up. "The ofrenda. It's the altar." She pointed to the tiers at the head of the table, where candles, pan dulce, and little clay skulls waited to be arranged. "Día de los Muertos," she added. "It happens November first and second, and it's for people in your family who died."

Kurtis arrived with a stack of framed photos and set them down too hard, and one frame slid off the table. He caught it, but the backing popped loose, and a folded paper fell out. Parker picked it up. It was a letter, old and soft at the creases, written in looping cursive.

"Give it here," Olivia said, but Parker had already started reading, because the photo in the frame was a young man in a soldier's uniform, and the letter was addressed to him.

"Dear Tomas," Parker read under his breath. "The corn is in. Your mother saves the first tortilla for you every night, and she says you will find your way home by following the smell." He looked up. "Tomas is Olivia's great-grandfather, right? She said so when she brought the picture."

Ms. Ahmadi tilted her head toward the ofrenda. "Put the letter back where it belongs."

Parker didn't move. Something wasn't fitting. He looked at the petal path he was supposed to build, the unbroken line of orange from the door to the altar, and then at the letter in his hand. His mom had told him the petals were just decoration, but decoration didn't need to be one continuous line with no gaps. A path needed to go somewhere. And a letter that said "you will find your way home" needed a road.

"Ms. Ahmadi," he said slowly, "is the petal path for the people who died? So they can find the ofrenda?"

She smiled and said nothing, which was answer enough.

He knelt and laid the first marigold at the threshold, then worked backward toward the altar, checking each petal against the last, the way Kurtis was being meticulous about straightening the photo frames. Kurtis, meanwhile, had picked up the letter again, and his face had gone strange.

"Olivia," he said. "The signature. It's signed Papa. But Tomas was your great-grandfather. Your great-great-grandfather must have written it, and it was never sent." Kurtis held it out so they could both see. "It's dated the year after he died."

Olivia took the letter and stood very still, then placed it on the ofrenda beside the photo of the young soldier, smoothing the folds flat with two fingers.

"There," she said. "Now it arrived."

Alexis had a spreadsheet open on the kitchen laptop, 400 rows of survey answers stretching down the screen like a road with no end. She and Rae had spent a whole week collecting answers from students about the school cafeteria, promising everyone a report by Friday, and now all Alexis had was a shapeless pile of data. "How am I supposed to count these by hand?" she said to the empty room. Her dad suggested takeout as consolation, but she waved him off and kept staring.

Rae arrived after dinner with a bag of chips and zero ideas. "You could sort by grade," she offered, leaning over Alexis's shoulder. Alexis tried it, and it helped a little, but the list was still enormous, and every time she counted a section she lost her place. "There has to be a better way," Alexis muttered. "Mael said something about this once. He recruits half the school for his gaming club, so if anyone knows how to handle 400 people, it's him."

She texted Mael, and he called back from his uncle's porch, where he'd been helping string lights through the canopy of trees overhead. "Insert a pivot table," he said. "Drag the Grade field into Rows, then drag another field into Values. That's all I'll tell you, because I want to see if you can actually do it."

"It's not a battle, Mael."

"Everything's a little bit a battle."

Alexis clicked through the menu, half expecting disaster, and dropped Grade into the Rows area. The screen flickered and the whole wall of 400 answers collapsed into three neat rows running down the left side of the table: one for seventh grade, one for eighth, one for ninth. Each grade appeared exactly once, no matter how many hundreds of answers sat behind it. Rae grabbed her arm. "Wait, where did everything go?"

"Nowhere," Alexis said slowly, testing it. "It's all still there. The table just shows each different grade one time." She dragged the survey answer into Values, and counts bloomed beside each grade like she'd flipped a light on. Seventh grade, 152 answers. She sat back, grinning at the small tidy table that had swallowed a mountain.

Rae was already copying the numbers into their report. "This changes everything for Friday."

Alexis saved the file twice, then a third time to be sure. "Mael gets the first slice of whatever we're celebrating with."

"He'll demand synthetic cheese flavor," Rae said, snapping the chip bag shut.

The computer lab was humid from thirty machines running all afternoon, and Hayden's program still refused to cooperate. He had written it himself, line by line in Python, following the plan from the whiteboard: ask for a number, test whether anything divides it, print "prime" or "not prime." It worked for 7. It worked for 15, which correctly came out not prime. Then Caelan leaned over his shoulder and typed 2, and the screen said not prime.

"That's wrong," Hayden said. "Two has to be prime. There's nothing to divide it by except one and itself." He scrolled up through his loop, looking for a mistake. Caelan pointed at the first line of the test, where Hayden had told the program to reject every even number before doing anything else. It seemed sensible when he wrote it. Even numbers felt like the opposite of prime.

Lorelai pulled her chair over from the next station. "Run it with eight," she said. He typed 8, and the program said not prime. Then 9, and it said not prime, because three divides nine. He tried 10, 12, 14. All not prime, all correct. The program was getting the big evens right and the small one wrong, which was a contradiction he couldn't ignore. Something about the number 2 was different from every other even number, and the difference was invisible in his code.

He whispered the sequence to himself, testing each even number in his head like the program would. Four. Six. Eight. Every one of them could be split into equal halves, which meant something divided each of them besides one and themselves. But when he reached 2, the splitting stopped. There was nothing left over to divide it. He sat back. "Two is the only even prime number," he said slowly, "because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2."

"Then fix the loop," Caelan said.

Haydan deleted the line that threw out all evens and added a special case instead: if the number is 2, print prime. He ran the program again and typed 2. The word prime appeared in green, and he transmitted a screenshot to the club's shared folder so Lorelai could check it from her machine. Ms. Yoon walked past and paused at his screen, but she only nodded and kept moving.

He tried 2 one more time, then 97, watching both answers come back. "Okay," he said to the screen. "Now try to break it."

Piper plugged her practice amp into the garage wall and set her feet on the cold concrete, guitar on her knee. The chord chart lay on an overturned milk crate beside her: twelve bars, the same loop over and over. Mr. García had told her to improvise a solo on top of it, and for three nights she had played nothing but safe notes that all sounded the same.

Oaklyn sat cross-legged on the old workbench, tapping the beat. Merrick had claimed a lawn chair and was spinning a drumstick like a tiny, versatile baton, which was his way of saying he was ready to keep time on the plastic buckets behind him. "Play something wild," Oaklyn said. "You're doing scales, not a solo."

"It's the blues," Piper said. "It's supposed to sound like something."

She thought about her grandfather's records, the way the guitar on them cried and bent and sagged. Those notes slid around, half of them not even real notes. She looped the progression again, and this time, on the fourth bar, she pushed the third string sideways with her finger, hard.

The note squealed, sharp and sour, like a rodent caught in a trap. Merrick winced. Oaklyn laughed so hard she nearly fell off the workbench. Piper froze, staring at her own finger. She had pressed the string sideways and it had stretched tighter across the fret, and the pitch had climbed way past where she wanted it. She tried again, gently, and the note rose just a little, a smooth little lift, like a voice asking a question instead of giving an answer. So that was the trick. She could control it, as long as she didn't oppose the string too hard.

"Again," Oaklyn said, and Piper looped the twelve bars once more. This time she bent on purpose, small on one bar, wider on the next, letting each note sag back down after it rose. Merrick dropped his drumstick and slapped a lazy shuffle on the buckets to match her. She hit one bend too far, sour again, but she let the sour note hang there on purpose, then slid down out of it, and somehow that sounded even bluer than the clean ones.

Her grandfather had quit piano lessons at twelve because a teacher told him he was playing it wrong, and Piper had never known whether to think that was brave or a waste. She decided she could worry about that later. The progression swung back around to bar one, and she leaned into the bend that had made her cry the first time she heard it on his old record, easing the string sideways until the note floated up and hung there, trembling, over Merrick's buckets.

"Right there," Oaklyn whispered. "Do that one again."

Anais had one objective for Saturday: walk into the Wongs' housewarming with the perfect gift. She had been to their old apartment only once, for Mael's birthday, and she remembered how Mrs. Wong had pressed a second helping of noodles onto her plate before she'd finished the first, and how Mr. Wong had greeted her with both hands around his teacup, a small bow that made her feel suddenly very formal. The new house had a wide porch and a persimmon tree, and Anais wanted the gift to match.

At the shop she found a clock shaped like a bird, brass, with a soft tick she could hear from across the aisle. "Mael, look at this," she said, holding it up. "Their kitchen has that empty wall by the stove."

Mael went quiet in a way she had learned to diagnose like a change in weather. He set down the mug he'd been examining. "Get something else. Anything else."

"Why?"

He glanced toward the counter, then said it low and plain. "In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death."

Anais put the bird clock down slowly, the way she'd seen people set down evidence in the courtroom shows she watched with her dad, like she was afraid the defendant would object. Her ears went hot. "You couldn't have mentioned this before I fell in love with it?"

"You fell in love with it ninety seconds ago." He picked up a lacquered tea tin and sniffed the jasmine through the lid. "This says the same thing. Welcome to your home, sit down, stay a while."

Anais tested the idea against what she remembered. Nobody in the Wong household had ever mentioned clocks, but there had been a moment at the birthday party when someone gave Mr. Wong a pocket knife and Mrs. Wong laughed and handed him a single coin in return, saying it made the knife a purchase, not a gift. So the family noticed things like this. Rules she couldn't see, but real ones. She bought the tea, plus a tin of almond cookies, and wrapped both in red paper because Mael said red was lucky.

At the gathering the steam from the dumplings fogged the kitchen window, and the little cousins were made to greet Anais with two hands around their juice cups like tiny ambassadors. When she presented her gift, Mrs. Wong held it in both palms and said, "So thoughtful, so thoughtful," and Anais felt her shoulders drop an inch.

Then Uncle Peter arrived, loudly, carrying a wrapped box with a bow. "For the new house!" he announced. "Everyone needs to know what time dinner is!"

It was a clock. A rooster, brass, ticking softly.

Mrs. Wong took it from him with both hands, smiling, and carried it straight to the empty wall by the stove, where she hung it and stepped back to admire it. "Perfect," she said. "We bought it for ourselves last week."

Grandma's violin had been sitting on top of the wardrobe since at least last Thanksgiving, and Victoria had claimed it the moment she walked in the door. "You can keep it," Grandma had said, "if you can make it sound less like a duck in a dispute." That was the challenge, and Victoria intended to win it before Sunday dinner.

She tuned the A string carefully, bracing the scroll against the couch cushion so the old pegs would behave. Judah sprawled on the rug with his phone, offering expert commentary. "That sounds like a fire alarm with feelings," he said, and Victoria flicked his ankle with the bow. Alexa, cross-legged in the armchair, hummed the note back at her, then hummed it again a minute later, and Victoria noticed something odd. Alexa's hum had slid downward, and when she bowed the string again, hers had dropped too. The note was sinking on its own, slow as a melting ice cream cone.

Victoria refused to believe her playing was so bad the violin was losing the will to vibrate. She stared at the peg and formed a theory: the peg was loosening by itself, little by little. "So if the peg turns, the note changes," she said. "Tighter one way, looser the other. That's the pattern." To test it, she turned the peg a tiny amount in one direction and bowed. The pitch climbed higher, like a doorbell being stretched. She turned it back the other way and the note dropped low and grumpy. Faster vibration made the higher pitch; slower made the lower one, and the sneaky peg was choosing slow. "It's not me," she announced. "It's physics committing crimes."

They set up a stakeout. Alexa hummed the note every minute like a human thermostat, keeping the pitch stable, while Judah watched the peg and Victoria held the violin steady in the lamp light. When Alexa's hum slid down again, Judah shouted, "It moved! It's turning by itself!" The peg had crept backward a whisper. Victoria pushed it in snugly, and this time the note held, round and steady as a coin on a table.

At dinner, Grandma asked how the duck dispute was going. "The duck has been replaced by a swan," Victoria said, "though the swan occasionally squawks." Grandma laughed so hard she had to set down the mashed potatoes. After dinner, Victoria carried the violin back to the living room and played her three stable notes over and over, and Judah, who had given up mocking her, hummed along. "You know," he said, "that peg could symbolize every instrument that ever needed a good grip." Victoria pressed the peg in one more firm quarter turn, lifted the bow, and said, "Then hold on tight, swan."

The school bus rattled over the bridge, and Hailey went through her word list for the fourth time. "Verrucose," said Violet, reading off the cards she'd made. "B-u-c-c-a-n-e-e-r. No, wait, I'm the one who spells. You just say them."

Hailey spelled it wrong twice, then right, and stared out the window at the gray river below. The regional spelling bee started in forty minutes, and she was the last qualifier from her school. Annabelle, two rows back, kept saying she should have been the one to go, and the worst part was that Hailey half believed her.

"Who even decided these spellings?" Hailey muttered when Violet gave her "rhythms," a word with no proper vowels in the middle. "Somebody had to pick. Somebody sat down and chose y instead of i."

Violet shrugged. "Old dead guys, probably."

But Hailey remembered now, the way you remember a locker combination in the middle of the night. Last week, killing time in the library before the school bee, she had pulled a fat blue volume off the shelf just because it looked ancient. Inside, the preface mentioned Samuel Johnson and a dictionary of the English language, published in 1755, and she'd read that it helped settle how many English words were spelled. She had stood there in the quiet stacks thinking that every weird spelling on her list had passed through a book like that. Now, on the bus, she tested the idea against her hardest words. If spellings had been settled in a book, then they weren't random, and random was what scared her. She drilled the trickiest ones by asking why they might have landed that way, and "rhythms" stopped looking like a trap and started looking like a decision somebody made.

Annabelle leaned over the seat. "You're going to freeze up there," she said. "You froze in the class bee, I saw it."

"Maybe," Hailey said. "But I figured something out. Want to hear it?" She told Annabelle about the old dictionary, about 1755, about how the spellings had been helped along by one printed book instead of being pure luck. Annabelle listened all the way through, which she almost never did.

The gym at the other school smelled like floor wax, and the first three rounds chewed up eleven spellers. Hailey spelled "potpourri" and "gherkin" and a boy in a green jersey went out on "liaison," his face a picture of despair. In round six Annabelle, watching from the bleachers, gave her a small thumbs up, and Hailey thought, she changed her mind about me, or maybe I changed it. Then the judge said her word: "samovar."

In the second before she spoke, she felt the old panic rise, the freeze. She thought of the fat blue volume, of Samuel Johnson deciding letters one by one, and the panic loosened its grip. Someone had settled these spellings so that they could be learned, and she had learned them.

"S-a-m-o-v-a-r," she said, and her voice came out steady, almost defiant, as if daring the word to be spelled any other way.

"That is correct," the judge said, and somewhere behind her Violet started clapping before the applause rule could stop her.

Aiden spread three newspapers across the library table, and Jemma leaned over his shoulder. Their class project was due Friday, and Ms. Gauthier had told them to compare how different sources reported the same event: a rally downtown last Saturday over the new parking rules.

"Look at this," Aiden said, tapping the first headline. "Thousands march for fair parking." He slid the second paper over. "And this one says Mob disrupts downtown traffic." He read both articles twice. Same day, same street, roughly the same crowd. The first paper called the people protesters; the second called them rioters.

"Those words mean different things," Jemma said, frowning. "Protesters sounds calm. Rioters sounds scary."

"That's the whole trick," Aiden said. He flipped to the back of the first article, where a list of local business owners supported the march, and then to the second, which quoted only one angry driver. He wrote in his notebook: loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd protesters or rioters can push readers toward opposite opinions. "If you only read one paper," he said, "you'd think either everything was fine or the city was on fire."

Sandrine arrived with a stack of magazines and dropped them on the table. "I found the ads," she said. "Ms. Gauthier wanted examples of persuasion too." One ad showed a famous basketball player holding a sports drink and grinning. Another claimed that everyone was switching to a certain phone brand. A third described a competing snack as a pathetic, wasteful excuse for food.

"This one uses a celebrity," Sandrine said, tapping the basketball player. "If he drinks it, people think it must be good." She pointed to the phone ad. "And this one says everyone is buying it, so you should too." Aiden noted that down as well. The third ad he read out loud, and even the word pathetic made Jemma wince.

"That's another loaded word," Aiden said. "It's not just describing the snack, it's making you feel bad about it." He circled the two headlines in his notebook and drew an arrow between them. "It's the same move. Push your feelings so you don't check the facts." He checked the clock and started budgeting their remaining time: twenty minutes to draft the poster, ten to proofread, five to pack up.

Ms. Gauthier stopped at their table on her way past. "How's it going?" she asked, and Aiden showed her the two headlines side by side. She read them, raised an eyebrow, and said, "That's a nice catch. Which article is true?" Aiden looked at the papers, then at his notebook, and realized he had spent all his energy on the words and none on checking what actually happened at the rally.

"Both," Sandrine said. "Some people marched, and some people blocked an intersection. The papers just picked the half they wanted us to feel."

"Then that's our poster," Aiden said. He picked up the marker and uncapped it. "Which headline do we put on top?"

The group chat lit up at 7:42 on a Tuesday night. Juno had joined Ms. Sok's homeroom that morning, and by lunch Maya already knew three things about her: she had an accent that shifted depending on who she talked to, she had lived in four countries, and she would not answer the question everyone kept asking.

Saanvi: ok but for the project we need to put everyone's hometown on the map. Juno where do we pin you??

Juno: hard to say

Maya: you have to be from somewhere

Juno: I'm from the airport, basically

Maya stared at her phone. Everyone else laughed and moved on, pinning their own dots on the shared map, but Juno's answer snagged in her mind like a zipper on a coat. People didn't dodge a question that simple unless the question wasn't simple. Maya tried to work out the hidden cause. Maybe Juno was embarrassed about one of the countries. Maybe she thought the chat would judge her. She scrolled back through the messages and noticed a pattern: whenever anyone asked where are you from, Juno answered fast, almost relieved, with a joke. It was the sincere follow-ups, the "no but really" ones, that shut her down.

Maya: not making fun. genuine question. you lived in four countries. which one feels like home

The typing bubble appeared, then vanished. Appeared again. Maya waited, chin on her fist, while her mom called something indifferent from the kitchen about dishes. Then Juno sent a single line.

Juno: none of them. and all of them? my parents say Seoul but I've never lived there

Saanvi: wait there's a word for that. my cousin is one. third culture kid

Maya: meaning what

Saanvi: some sociologist came up with it. Ruth Hill Useem. american. in the 1950s. it's for kids raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture

Juno: THAT. that's me. I've never had a word for it before

Maya sat back. She had guessed wrong about the cause. Juno wasn't hiding anything or ashamed of anything. The question itself was broken, like asking someone to choose one stanza from a poem and call it the whole poem. Maya thought about her own grandmother's recipes, the ones she would inherit someday, and how Juno's inheritance was scattered across four kitchens in four time zones. Nobody had put a name on that before the 1950s, and now the name existed, and Juno had just found it in a group chat at 7:51 on a Tuesday.

Maya: so for the map, want me to make you a pin that's just a dot in the ocean between all four?

Juno: yes. dead center. label it Juno

Saanvi: on it

Maya opened the map, zoomed out until the continents looked small, and dropped the dot where the lines would all cross. She typed one more message before her mom reached the doorway.

Maya: welcome home, Juno.

The photo showed Isobel's new bike leaning against her garage, and under it she had typed "guess who saved up ALL summer." Lucas was sitting on her couch, scrolling, while she made popcorn in the kitchen. He tapped the picture to make it full screen, then tapped the little "i" in the corner just to see if it would tell him when it was taken.

It did. It also showed a small map with a pin on it, and beneath the pin a street name he recognized, because it was Isobel's street, with her house right there under the pin. He checked the next photo she had sent, one of the lake where they'd all swum in July. Another pin, on the shore of that lake, a forty-minute drive away.

"Isobel," he called. "Come look at this."

She came in carrying the bowl and stood over him, chewing. "That's my house. Why is my house on there?"

"Your phone put it there. When it takes a photo with location services on, it writes the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file." He scrolled. "It's called EXIF metadata."

"That's creepy. So everyone I sent that to knows where I live?"

Lucas tested it. He opened a photo from his own phone, one he'd taken at his grandmother's kitchen table, and checked the details. A pin sat on her street, three blocks from the school. He had sent that photo to the whole group chat last week, and the group chat had fourteen people in it, some of whom he barely knew. He deleted the message from his side, but he already understood that deleting it on his phone did nothing about anyone else's copy. Photos, once sent, got stored and passed around, and the hidden data traveled inside them like a passenger.

His reasoning ran ahead in a way he didn't like. Isobel had posted the bike picture to her public page an hour ago. Anyone scrolling could tap those details the way he just had.

"Okay," Isobel said. "So I take it down."

"That's step one." He went into her phone's settings with her, and they found the camera section and the location switch, and she turned it off. "New photos won't get tagged. The old ones still have the pins baked in."

"So the bike photo is a problem even off my page."

"It can be shared by anyone who saved it. Strangers included."

She stood there a moment, then took the phone from him, deleted the post, and pulled up her camera. "Take one more picture of the bike. No pin this time." She aimed at the garage through the window, snapped it, and handed the phone back to him. "Check it."

He tapped the "i" and looked. The screen where the map had been was sparse now, just the date and the file size, an empty white space where her street used to be.

"Nothing there," he said. "Clean."

"Good," Isobel said, and shoved the popcorn bowl at him. "Now help me figure out what to do about the fourteen people in your grandmother photo."

Mr. Bear wrote one word on the board and underlined it twice: perspective. Kaylee slumped in her seat, because she knew where this was going. Yesterday her mother had asked, "Did you really smash into that boy in the hallway?" and Kaylee had said yes, fast, hard, her fault probably, and now Remington wasn't speaking to her. But she remembered it as barely a bump. Both memories couldn't be true, and she wanted the real one back.

"Let's try something," Mr. Bear said, splitting the class in half with a wave of his hand. "Group A, look at the screen. Group B, turn around and face the wall." He showed Group A a photo of two crumpled cars and asked, "How fast were these cars going when they smashed into each other?" Kaylee, in Group A, wrote forty miles an hour. When the groups switched, he showed the same photo to Group B and asked, "How fast were the cars going when they hit each other?"

Janessa, who wanted to win every class game ever invented, leaned across the aisle. "Fifteen," she whispered to Kaylee. "I wrote fifteen. What did you put?" Kaylee showed her paper. Forty. Same photo. Same two cars. Janessa's eyes went wide, and she started collecting everyone's answers in a pile like a detective gathering evidence.

"Nice work," Mr. Bear said. "In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer ran this exact experiment, and the people who heard the word smashed gave higher speed estimates than the people who heard hit." Kaylee copied it down, then sat very still. Her mother hadn't seen the hallway. Her mother had only chosen a word, and the word had built the memory, like a propeller spinning air into something solid that hadn't been there before. She raised her hand. "Can you revise what you remember? Or is the original gone, like, extinct?"

"Try it," Mr. Bear said. "That's your homework."

At lunch Kaylee found Remington at the vending machines. "What did you actually see?" she asked. "Not what your mom asked you. What did you see?" Remington frowned. "She asked if you slammed me into the lockers." "And what did you tell her?" He was quiet a moment, turning his water bottle in his hands. "That you knocked my books down. Maybe I made it bigger after." Janessa appeared with her pile of class data and slapped it on the machine between them. "Evidence," she said. "Somebody's memory is on trial."

Remington picked up the papers, looked at the two columns of numbers, and slid one of Kaylee's books out of his backpack, where it had been all along. "Truce?" he said.

Christopher had been fighting with the same sheet of paper for twenty minutes, and the street he was drawing still looked flat as a pancake. The community art studio smelled like pencil shavings and the coffee Mr. Bear kept in a dented thermos, and the big windows let in the smell of rain off the sidewalk outside.

"Watch," said Mr. Bear, drawing one quick demonstration. "All your lines run to one point. One-point perspective. The vanishing point sits on the horizon line, and every edge of every building leans toward it." Then he wiped his hands on his apron and went to help Rowen, who had knocked over a jar of brushes.

Christopher stared at his vanishing point, a small dot in the middle of the page. He ruled his lines again, slow and careful. The buildings began to lean inward like they were listening to each other, and the street seemed to run away from him. It was finally working, except for one thing he couldn't name. The street felt wrong, like he was floating above it.

Across the table, Ludovick was drawing the same street, the same corner of Maple and Third, from the same reference photo. Ludovick's street felt low and close, like you could step off the curb into it. Christopher leaned over. "Your horizon line is way down at the bottom," he said.

"So's yours, way up high," said Ludovick. "That's why mine looks like you're standing on the sidewalk."

Christopher thought about that. A low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, like you're small on the curb. A high one looks down from a window above. He hadn't put his horizon low on purpose; he'd just drawn it in the middle of the page and then slid it up when the buildings got crowded. That was the hidden cause of the floating feeling. He tested it right away, sketching a second small version with the horizon pushed down near the bottom edge. The buildings rose tall above it, and suddenly he was standing in the street instead of hovering over it. It wasn't some trivial fix; it changed the whole drawing.

"It's like Rowen's window," Ludovick said, waving Rowen over. Rowen, who had drawn the street from the studio's upstairs window last week, held up her sketch, and the three of them formed a little alliance of bent heads, comparing where each horizon line sat. Mr. Bear drifted by and said nothing, only nodded.

Christopher started his good copy. He would draw the street from the curb, because that was where he really stood every day, small and looking up. His pencil whispered across the paper, ruling the first long line toward its waiting dot.

The washing machine behind the front desk of Rahimi's Driving School rumbled like a car idling in first gear, which Jake figured was about the only connection between the two businesses. His mother taught parallel parking out in the lot until six, and Jake did the family laundry in the little utility room so he would not be home alone. He had the system down: dark pile, light pile, towels separate, one capful of detergent. Ms. Rahimi called him "the most robust thirteen-year-old washer I have ever met," and she had seen decades of nervous students, so he took it as a real compliment.

Today there was a new item, a cream-coloured sweater his grandmother had knitted him for his birthday, the one he was supposed to cherish because she had made it stitch by stitch with her arthritic hands. It smelled like her house, lavender and toast. He had a whole flashback about it: sitting at her kitchen table in February while she held up the half-finished sleeve and said, "This is the ratio I always use, three parts cream to one part oatmeal, so it will not look too yellow." He had nodded like he understood wool the way she did. He did not.

The hot tap was already running, and the machine was set to heavy duty, big sloshing waves, because that was what he always used for towels. He stood there holding the sweater, and something nagged at him. His grandmother had once said her words for washing instructions were "cool water, gentle, like washing a cat." But why would temperature matter? He could not see anything happening inside wool, no moving parts, nothing. Then he remembered the doll-sized sock his cousin had once pulled from a hot wash at a family reunion, and how his grandmother had clucked over it like it was a tiny casualty. Maybe there was a rule hiding in there: hot water plus lots of motion equaled shrinkage. Cold water plus gentle cycle would test it. He switched the dials and laid the sweater in like it was a sleeping animal.

Just then Emerson and Jaden burst in from the parking lot, arguing about who had almost hit the orange cone. Emerson's tee shirt had a giant grease smear across it from leaning on the practice car's hood.

"Jake, emergency wash," Emerson said, holding the shirt out like evidence. "Hot. Boiling. Whatever kills grease."

"Hot's fine for cotton," Jake said. He pointed at the machine churning through its gentle cycle. "Not for that. It's my grandma's knitting."

Jaden peered through the round window at the pale sweater drifting in the cool water. "What happens if you boil a sweater?"

"It felts," Jake said. "It shrinks down doll-size." He did not know all the why of it yet, but he knew the pattern was real, and the sweater floating safely past the window proved his test had worked.

Ms. Rahimi appeared in the doorway with two bottles of water. "One for the washer boy, one for the shirt boy," she said, and Jake caught the cold bottle she tossed him. By five thirty the sweater lay flat on a towel, air drying, still smelling faintly of lavender, still big enough for a boy and not a doll.

"There," Jake said, folding Emerson's shirt, which had come out clean and exactly the same size as before.

George knelt on the patio with a drawing pad, a ruler, and a pencil that had already lost its eraser somewhere in the grass. His assignment was to draw a street using one-point perspective, which meant every line had to run toward a single dot called the vanishing point. The problem was that his street kept looking like a wedge of cheese.

"Your buildings are doing a Parliament impression," said Gurman, leaning over the fence with a slice of toast. "All leaning at different angles, arguing about it."

"Very funny." George flipped the pencil around and stabbed at the paper. "If I could keep the lines straight long enough to sustain one decent road, I'd be fine."

Kelvin arrived through the gap in the hedge, skeptical as always, arms crossed like he was auditing the whole backyard. "My cousin says you can't fake this stuff. He says the old painters used strings. Actual strings, pinned to the wall, to pull the lines toward the point."

George stopped. Strings. He tried to picture it and couldn't, so he decided to test it. "Gurman, hold this." He grabbed a ball of garden twine from the shed, a hammer, and one nail, which he poked into the middle of the fence panel at eye level. Then he clipped a sheet of paper to the fence right over the nail. He tied one end of the twine around a second pencil and looped the other end around the nail.

"Now pull the string tight and draw along it," he said. Gurman tugged the twine taut and dragged the pencil. The line shot perfectly toward the nail, dead straight, like magic. Kelvin took a turn, then George, spinning the string like a compass to fan lines out from the dot. Within ten minutes the sheet had a road, two rows of buildings, and windows that all obeyed the single point. It looked like an actual street. The three of them stood back and admired it the way you'd admire a rocket you built yourself.

"You know who did this for real?" said Kelvin. "Leonardo. In the Last Supper, all the lines vanish at one point, right at Christ's head. He stretched strings from a nail to get it right." He pointed at the fence. "And get this. The nail hole is still visible there. In the painting. After all these years."

George leaned close to his sheet of paper. There, dead center, sat a small ragged hole where the nail had pushed through behind it. His vanishing point had a wound in it, right in the middle of the road.

Gurman squinted, then grinned. "Congratulations. Five hundred years from now, that's going to be worth millions."

"Half of it's mine," said Kelvin. "I pulled the string on the left sidewalk."

"Fine," said George. "But the nail stays on my fence."

Mason stood on the front step holding a box of almond cookies his mom had shoved into his hands in the parking lot, and he could not figure out one thing about the doorway. The whole family was gathering here because his uncle's mother was visiting from Japan for two weeks, and Mason had never met her. But the door was already open, and in the little entry area just inside, instead of a rug, there was a low wooden step with a whole row of shoes lined up neatly on it, heels facing the door. His grandmother's slippers, his aunt's flats, even his uncle's giant sneakers, all parked like cars in a lot. Nobody had walked past that step with shoes on.

"You too," his uncle said, jerking his thumb downward. "Shoes off in the genkan." Mason didn't ask what that meant. The word matched the spot itself, and a pair of cloth slippers sat waiting on the floor past the step, sized, he guessed, for him.

He tested it. He eased off one sneaker and set it on the wooden step beside the others, then stepped up in his sock foot onto the polished floor. Nothing happened. No alarm, no frown. His grandmother was watching from the hallway, and when he took off the second shoe and put on the slippers, she gave a small nod and something that might have been a smile. So that was the rule: shoes stopped at the step, and the genkan was where they stayed. He filed it away the way he filed away locker combinations.

The kitchen was loud with cousins and casseroles. Kolby, his cousin's friend from down the street, had been dragged along to even out the table and was now on drink duty, trying to submerge the soda cans in a cooler of half melted ice. "How do you know when to bow and when to shake hands?" Kolby whispered as the grandmother came near. "You don't," Mason whispered back. "You watch." He watched. She put her hands together and said something short and warm to Ms. Whitehead, the neighbor who had brought over a casserole; Ms. Whitehead, who had never bowed at anything in her life, bowed back anyway, too deep, and everyone pretended not to notice except the grandmother, who looked delighted.

At dinner, Mason kept sneaking glances at the grandmother's hands, the way she turned her chopsticks to pick from the shared plates, the way she waited until the oldest person at the table lifted their bowl. He copied her half a beat behind, and when he passed the rice toward Kolby and set the spoon down with its handle facing out, exactly as she had done, she said something to his uncle. "She says you have careful eyes," his uncle translated. Kolby grinned. "Careful eyes is a metaphor, right? Like, you notice stuff." "Yeah," Mason said. "Like that."

Later, out on the porch with the cookies finally opened, Mason asked his uncle when she flew back. "Sunday," his uncle said. Mason looked down the street, which had gone quiet and almost desolate, all the porch lights off except theirs. Five days, and he had just now learned where the shoes went. Inside, through the window, the grandmother was teaching Kolby to fold a paper crane, and Kolby's was coming out mangled, and she was laughing anyway, and Mason pushed the cookie box across the porch rail toward the empty seat beside him.

Wyatt's cousin's graduation party was spread across his grandmother's tranquil backyard, with folding tables under the maple tree and a cooler of lemonade sweating in the shade. Wyatt had promised Mr. Shevchenko a science fair project idea by Monday, and so far all he had was a blank notebook. Then his uncle Bill started in again about the honey-ginger tea he drank every night for his bad knee.

"I'm telling you, two weeks after I started, the tendon stopped aching," Uncle Bill said, slapping his leg. "That stuff works."

Wyatt wrote it down. Then he thought about it, turning his cup in his hands. One person, one knee, no test. Lots of things could have changed in two weeks. "How do you know it was the tea?" he asked.

"Because I felt better after I drank it," Uncle Bill said, like that settled everything.

At the dessert table, Wyatt found his friends Madeline and Mohamad, who had come with their families. He laid out his idea: a taste test to see if people could really tell the fancy brand-name lemonade from the store brand. He had both, and Grandmother had pitchers and paper cups. Mohamad poured two batches into identical cups and shuffled them behind a card table. But when he handed them out, he kept grinning at Madeline, and Madeline laughed before she even sipped, because Mohamad's face gave away which cup was which every single time.

"Stop," Wyatt said. "We have to violate our own rule and fix it. Mohamad can't know either." So they found his aunt, who had been sitting nearby, and asked her to pour. She shuffled the cups where nobody could see, and only she checked the code on the bottom of each pitcher, writing letters on a napkin she folded and tucked in her pocket. Neither the tasters nor the person serving knew which cup was which. Mohamad tasted his pair, frowned, guessed, and got it wrong. So did Madeline. So did Uncle Bill, twice.

"Hey," Uncle Bill said, staring at his empty cups. "So my tea thing. Was that just me expecting to feel better?"

Wyatt shrugged, but his pen was already moving across the notebook page, printing the words double-blind trial at the top, because when neither the tasters nor the server knew who was getting the real thing, nobody's expectations could sway the results, and that was exactly what he'd tell Mr. Shevchenko.

Mohamad read over his shoulder and said, "You're testing the tea next, aren't you."

Wyatt turned to the dessert table and began stacking cups.

The computer lab smelled like warm plastic and the lemon wipes Mr. Ma used on the keyboards at the end of every day. Nevaeh sat two seats from the back, next to Japji, both of them supposed to be finishing a social studies assignment on primary sources. Japji was not finishing anything. Japji was laughing at her screen with her hand over her mouth.

"Look," Japji whispered, turning the monitor. "Look what I found."

It was a blog. Purple background, a cartoon cat in the corner, and a title in a font that should have been illegal: Japji's Awesome World. The last post was dated six years ago. It was a photo of Japji, age eight, in a swimsuit, standing in front of a lake house with the town's water tower visible behind the roof.

"I deleted that blog," Japji said. "Years ago. My mom made me. It's still here."

"Where is here?" Nevaeh asked. She leaned over, and under the cartoon cat she read the words Internet Archive, and next to those, Wayback Machine.

"Since 1996 it's been saving copies of public web pages," Japji said, scrolling. "And this thing lets anyone look at old versions of websites. Anyone. I looked it up after I stopped screaming."

Nevaeh's stomach did something quiet and slow. Because three years ago, before her parents split, she had kept a blog too. She'd written about her street, her school, which door of the gym she used, the name of her cat. Then her dad moved and her mom said start fresh, so Nevaeh had deleted everything and told herself it was gone, the way you close a drawer and the drawer is over.

"Type in an address," Japji said. "If it was public, it might be there."

Nevaeh typed the old address. Her fingers remembered it even though she'd half convinced herself she'd forgotten. The screen thought about it, then produced a calendar with dates on it, small blue circles like a handful of pennies. She clicked one. Her blog appeared. Same green header, same posts, including the one from her eleventh birthday where she'd listed, for reasons that now escaped her, her exact bus stop and the fact that she was home alone until five.

"So anyone could read this," she said.

"Anyone," Japji said. "Strangers. Your future boss. My future boss. Everyone's future boss."

Mr. Ma drifted past their row. "Screens on the assignment, please," he said, and kept drifting, because Mr. Ma's interest in enforcement had dwindled steadily since October and was now mostly a courtesy.

Nevaeh stared at the old post. The archive was objective about her, that was the thing. It didn't know she'd changed. It just held the page, patient as a filing cabinet, and anyone who knew where to look could open the drawer. Her house was still on the same street. Her cat was fatter but recognizable.

She thought about the foundation of the whole thing, how she'd always imagined the internet as a river where you could drop something and watch it go. Apparently it was also a basement.

She clicked through her old posts and copied down every one that mentioned a place, a time, a door. Twelve. Then she opened a new tab and found the archive's page for requesting that copies of a URL be removed. There was a form. There was a wait time. It was better than nothing.

"Doing homework?" Japji asked.

"Kind of," Nevaeh said, and started filling in the first line.

Gavin had walked past Bryan's house every school day for three years, and every single time the door had opened before he reached the porch. Today the door stayed shut. His sneakers scuffed the sidewalk, and he kept his eyes on the crack where the concrete slabs met, right at the spot where Bryan had taught him to land a skateboard trick last summer.

The fight had happened on Friday, quick as a snapped shoelace. Gavin had waited outside the corner store for twenty minutes while Bryan played basketball with Harry and some other kids, and when Bryan finally strolled over, Gavin had said, "You ditched me. You always ditch me when Harry shows up." Bryan's face had gone flat and closed, like a window with the blinds pulled, and he had walked home alone.

Ms. Leung had a poster on her classroom wall that Gavin had never really read until Monday, when he was avoiding looking at Bryan two rows over. It said that psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term "I-message" in the 1960s, and that a sentence like "I felt left out" describes the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." Gavin copied the words into his notebook, then dug out the crumpled note from his pocket, the one that started "You ditched me." He crossed it out and tried again: "I felt left out when I was waiting." It sounded almost too simple. He wrote a second version, then a third, trying to sound honest without sounding like a kid in a workbook.

"How's the peace treaty coming?" Harry asked him at lunch, peering at the notebook. Gavin flipped it shut.

"Did you know there's a whole name for it?" Gavin said. "It's called an I-message." Harry shrugged and stole a fry, but Gavin noticed he said it louder than he needed to, loud enough for the next table to hear.

On Thursday he stopped at the corner store and bought two popsicles with his last crumpled dollar, then walked up Bryan's street, his stomach tight. The sky smelled like rain coming, and someone's mower droned three houses down. He climbed the porch steps and knocked before he could talk himself out of it.

Bryan opened the door halfway, one hand still on the knob. Gavin held out a popsicle, already sweating in the warm air.

"I felt left out on Friday," Gavin said. "That's all I wanted to say. Not that you ditched me. That I felt left out."

Bryan looked at the popsicle, then at the sidewalk, then somewhere past Gavin's shoulder. The mower stopped, and in the sudden quiet Gavin could hear his own heartbeat.

"You could have just texted that," Bryan said, but he took the popsicle and pulled the door open wider.

Ryder sat on the edge of the bathtub in his grandmother's downstairs bathroom, still wearing his socks, listening to the house tick and settle around him. Tomorrow was the social studies exam, the one Ms. Chea had warned them about for two weeks, and his brain would not stop. His thoughts seemed to revolve around the same three worries: the tariff question she had promised would be on the test, the definition he might mix up, and Dev, who had studied three days longer than he had and still looked nervous. Ryder had been meticulous about his flashcards, color-coded and everything, but lying in the guest bed his heart had pounded like he was running laps.

He remembered, then, the last time he had felt this way, before the math final in the fall. That night he had stayed up until two in the morning rereading everything, and the next day his mind had gone blank on question one. Stephanie had found him in the hallway afterward, staring at his shoes, and she had said something he hadn't liked: "Cramming all night made it worse, not better." He had argued with her at the time. Now, on the cold rim of the bathtub, he was less sure he'd been right.

There was a soft knock, and his grandmother's voice came through the door. "Ryder? The light's been on for an hour."

"I can't sleep," he admitted. "The exam."

The door opened a crack. She was holding a small paperback book, its cover soft from years of hands. "My doctor's been after me to slow my breathing," she said. "There's a trick in here, from Dr. Andrew Weil. It's called the 4-7-8 breathing exercise. In for four counts, hold for seven, out slowly for eight." She sat down on the closed toilet lid across from him. "Want to try it with me?"

Ryder counted it out. Four counts in through his nose, which felt like forever. Seven counts of holding, where his chest complained a little. Then eight counts of letting the air out, slow, like air leaking from a tire. "That's a long exhale," he said.

"That's the point," she said. "Again."

They did it four more times, and by the fourth, Ryder noticed something odd. His shoulders had dropped without his permission. The tariff question was still in his head, but it was just sitting there instead of spinning. He thought about Stephanie again, and how he'd rolled his eyes at her, and he decided that tomorrow he would tell her she'd been right about the sleep thing. Maybe she had a point about breathing too.

His grandmother stood and pulled a towel from the shelf to put in his arms. "Now, no flashcards in bed. Lamp off in ten minutes."

"Yes, Grandma," Ryder said, and switched off the bathroom light.

On Monday Sadie wore her new glasses to school for the first time, and by lunch she had counted eleven things she had been missing, including the basketball hoop, the numbers on the scoreboard, and Lilou's face across the courtyard. "They're purple," Lilou said, pointing at her own glasses, which Sadie had never once noticed. "We match. Kind of." At recess a small crowd formed around Sadie near the swings, because Calum had announced that Sadie now had 20/20 vision, and everyone wanted to look at the lenses. "Actually," said a boy visiting from his cousin's school, "my cousin moved from overseas and the eye doctor there told her she has 6/6 vision. Six out of six. She says it like it's good, but that can't be good. Twenty out of twenty is perfect. Six out of six is only six."

Sadie pushed her new glasses up her nose and thought about that. If the cousin's doctor had written 6/6 on a real chart, in a real clinic, it seemed unlikely he was announcing bad eyesight. Her intuition said the numbers were measuring the same thing in different ways, like how a liter and a quart are different numbers for the same amount of juice. She needed evidence, though. "What country?" she asked. "Do they use metres there?" The boy frowned. "Yeah, kilometres and everything. My cousin says the speed signs look funny."

So Sadie proposed a test. She would stand at the fence and read the banner taped over the gym door, first with the glasses on, then off, and the group would vote on whether her vision was perfect or terrible either way. The vote to try it was unanimous, mostly because nobody wanted to go back to the four-square game while a mystery was unsolved. With her glasses on, she read every letter down to the tiny line about the spring fundraiser. Without them, the banner turned into a grey smear with a butterfly shape in the middle. "Same banner," she said, blinking. "Two different numbers could describe those eyes. Twenty twenty here, six six there. It depends on the ruler, not the eyes." She felt her ears go warm, because half the playground was listening and she was talking like Ms. Owusu during a science lesson.

The boy squinted at the fence, then at her. "So my cousin's eyes are perfect and I sent her a get-well card?" "You sent a get-well card?" said Lilou, and the crowd dissolved into laughter that was mostly with him and only slightly at him. He shrugged and said he would write a follow-up card that would preserve her dignity, something like "Congratulations on your eyes, disregard previous letter."

Ms. Owusu came out to see what the crowd was about, and when they told her, she looked at Sadie over the top of her own glasses and said that a girl who reasoned like that ought to be able to see what was sitting on her own head. Sadie reached up and found her old pair, the ones she'd been hunting for all weekend, perched on her hair like a second set of antennae. Lilou took a photo before she could take them off.

Aria spread her papers across the picnic table in her backyard, weighting the corners with pebbles because the wind kept lifting them. She was folding a paper crane for the library's origami contest, and so far she had made four cranes with crumpled wings and one that looked like it had flown into a window. Levi dropped through the gate with his own square of paper and a granola bar, and behind him came Harris, who set his phone on the table and immediately moved it again when the metal surface, already a conductor of the morning sun, grew hot under it.

"The contest rules are pretty explicit," Harris said, scrolling. "It says origami. Nothing else. So does that mean no cutting?" Levi tore the corner off his granola bar wrapper and shrugged. "My brother says origami just means paper craft. Cutting counts." Aria frowned at her fifth crane. She had a feeling that was wrong, but a feeling was not proof, and contest judges did not give points for feelings. "If the word itself tells us," she said slowly, "then we could actually know instead of arguing."

Levi leaned in, interested despite himself. Aria pulled up the library website on Harris's phone and typed the word into the search box. The entry appeared, short and plain. "Origami," she read, and then grinned. "Ori means fold, and kami means paper." Levi sat back. "So it literally means folding paper. Not cutting paper. Folding paper." Harris looked at the crumpled cranes on the table, and all three of them said it at the same time: "Start over."

They did, but Aria wanted to be sure the rule held in practice, not just on a screen. She folded one crane using only creases, and Levi made one by snipping two small cuts for the wings. They set both in the middle of the table just as dew began to condense on the cold lemonade glasses, and the wind, patient as a judge, knocked Levi's cut crane flat while Aria's folded one stayed standing. Levi laughed, but a little sadly, because he had spent twenty minutes on his. Aria slid her remaining squares of gold paper across the table to him. "You fold fast," she said. "You just got the rules wrong."

By noon there were seven cranes lined up along the table's shaded edge, one slightly lopsided but all of them made of whole paper, folded and folded and folded again. Mr. Huang, watering his tomatoes over the fence, peered at them and asked how many they were entering. "All of them," Aria said, and Levi held up his gold one, still creasing the final wing flat with his thumbnail.

The retake was at eight the next morning, and Caleb had one evening to dismantle his reputation as the kid who failed the equations quiz. He spread his notebook across the library table, where Alizee was already waiting with two pencils and a look that said she expected disaster.

"Show me what you did," she said.

He flipped to the quiz. Ms. Koné had circled one line in red: 2x + 3 = 5x. Kolton leaned over from the next chair and whistled. "You just added them? Bold move."

"It made sense at the time," Caleb said. "Two things plus three things is five things."

Alizee slid the paper back. "Try it with an actual number. Say x is ten. What's 2x + 3?"

"Twenty-three."

"And 5x?"

He stopped. "Fifty." He stared at the red circle like it was taunting him. "So they're not the same thing at all."

Ms. Koné passed their table with a cart of returns and paused long enough to tap the corner of his page. "The library closes in forty minutes," she said. "Plan accordingly."

Kolton spun his pencil. "I'm pessimistic about your chances, but go on."

Caleb wrote 2x + 3x at the top of a fresh page. This time he tested it the new way. If x was ten, that was twenty plus thirty, which was fifty, and 5x was fifty too. He tried x equal to four. Eight plus twelve was twenty, and 5x was twenty. It worked every single time, which felt almost suspicious.

"So the ones with x can combine," he said slowly, "but a plain number can't join them. It's like the x is a label. Two apples plus three apples, fine. Two apples plus three, that means nothing."

"Two apples plus three rocks," Alizee said. "You still have five objects, but you can't call them five apples."

"Right." He copied the failed quiz problem and started over: 2x + 3 = 5x became 3 = 5x minus 2x, which became 3 = 3x, and then he divided both sides by three and got x = 1. He checked it. Two plus three is five, and five times one is five. He actually laughed out loud, and a kid at the next table shushed him.

"She shushed him," Kolton whispered. "He's under siege and she shushed him."

"Do another one," Alizee said, dealing problems like cards. "Fast."

He did four more, stacking the solved pages like evidence for a trial. On the last one, 4x + 2 + x = 17, he combined the 4x and the x into 5x first, left the 2 alone, and had the answer before the clock on the wall hit the quarter hour.

Ms. Koné appeared at the desk and flicked the light switch once, the universal signal. Caleb packed his bag, then paused at the door and pointed at the last page through the window of his mind, the 5x sitting there clean and correct.

"Tomorrow," he told Alizee, "I'm getting that circle in red for a whole different reason."

Leah had been at Kessler Middle School for exactly four days, and she had already learned that the cafeteria had a conductor of sorts, a girl named Justina who waved people toward tables the way a train officer waved passengers aboard. On the fourth day Justina waved Leah toward a seat beside Campbell, who was drawing a map of the old Kessler building on her folder. "It used to be over on Pine Street," Campbell said. "They moved us all here two years ago." Leah looked at the map, then at her own lunch tray, and did not say that two years sounded like nothing at all.

That night she wrote a message to her best friend back in Marlow, because a phone call would make her voice shake. I keep thinking the hallway smells wrong, she typed. Like floor cleaner instead of rain. That's a weird thing to notice, right? She sent it before she could delete it. The reply came fast: not weird. My cousin says that's called homesickness. Leah stared at the word. It had a name, which meant other people had felt it too, which meant it was a thing that happened to people and not a flaw in her. She decided to test it like a science problem. If homesickness came from being away from familiar people, then the cure should be people becoming familiar, and that should take time, not willpower.

So she made a plan and stuck it inside her locker door. Rule one: say one true thing to a new person every day. Rule two: no rereading old group chats after nine o'clock, because rereading only prolonged the ache. Rule three: keep score, honestly, in the back of her notebook. Wednesday she cried in the bathroom over a photo of her old street, the crooked oak and the painted fire hydrant, and she wrote that down too. Cried, 4 minutes. It felt ridiculous, writing it, but it was data.

The next Wednesday, Mr. Eze kept her after band to ask if she would run the metronome for the flutes. "You count steady," he said. "Steady counters are rare." She counted, and Campbell mouthed a joke across the pit about a flute player who had once fallen asleep mid-note, and Leah laughed so hard she lost the count, and Mr. Eze made them all start over. That night she opened her notebook to compare. Wednesday one: four minutes of crying. Wednesday two: zero crying, one joke, one actual job. The difference was significant enough that she circled it twice.

The twist came on Friday, when Justina slid into the seat across from her and unfolded a map of Pine Street, hand-drawn, with the old school circled in marker. "I found it in my drawer," Justina said. "I looked at it every day for a month when we moved. Then I just stopped needing to." Leah understood then that the pain had a schedule, and that everyone got the same schedule, just on different days. She wrote one more message to Marlow, short this time: It gets smaller. I'm timing it. Then she closed the notebook, picked up her tray, and waved toward the empty seat beside Campbell.

Amelia stood at the edge of the school parking lot, holding her phone like a ticket she was afraid to lose. On the screen was a message from Massimo: "I'm in the car with my dad. My stomach keeps flipping and my heart is pounding like I ran a mile. Can you actually be sick from a dance before the dance?" The gym doors glowed yellow behind her, and the bass from inside thumped against the parked cars.

She typed back, "You're not sick. Mr. Kaur told us last week. It's adrenaline. When you're nervous your body lets it out, it speeds up your heart, and it pulls blood away from your stomach. That's the butterflies feeling." She paused, then added, "Come anyway. If it's still happening in an hour, we'll find your dad."

Inside, Gaelle was assessing the snack table like a general planning a battle. "Brownies first, then punch," she announced. Amelia scanned the room for a way to test her own idea, because her stomach had been doing the same slow flip since seventh period. If the butterflies really came from blood being pulled away from her stomach, then getting her stomach busy with something else ought to change things. It was a concept she could actually check. She took a brownie, ate half, and waited.

By the time the DJ played the third song, her stomach had settled. She danced with Gaelle, badly, and then with a boy from science class, also badly, and laughed both times. Her heart still beat fast, but fast from jumping around, which felt completely different. She began to think the flip in her stomach might not be so inevitable after all, or at least not permanent.

Then Massimo appeared in the doorway, hair combed, shoulders up around his ears. He looked like a boy walking into a test he hadn't studied for. Amelia waved him over and pointed at the snack table. "Eat something," she said. "It works. I tested it." He gave her a skeptical look, so she told him about her stomach, and about the brownie, and how the butterflies had gone quiet.

"Adrenaline," he repeated, chewing. "Pulls blood away from the stomach. Weird that knowing it helps." He didn't finish the brownie, but he did stay. When the slow song came on, Gaelle dragged them both into a circle of friends, and Massimo's shoulders came down from his ears a little at a time, like ice melting. Near the end of the night, he leaned over during a fast song and shouted, "My heart's racing, but it's the good kind now!"

Amalie's dad was parked under the far light when the doors opened onto the cold parking lot. Massimo climbed into his own car and rolled down the window. "Text me before the next dance," he called. Amelia pulled out her phone under the streetlight and started typing.

Braden's kitchen felt like the inside of a sock, humid even with the fan blowing papers off the counter, and Chase had until eight o'clock to finish. The science club needed a spreadsheet showing each team's snack-stand revenue from the fall fundraiser, and as treasurer Chase had promised to email the chart to Ms. Bautista before the meeting tomorrow. He had never built one before.

"Type equals, then SUM, then open paren," Braden said, leaning over his laptop. Chase typed carefully, highlighting the column of weekly totals for Team Falcon. When he pressed Enter, the number 212 appeared at the bottom of the column, and something about seeing it add itself made him grin.

"That's the whole semester," Chase said. He did the same for Team Kestrel, which came to 218 dollars. Six dollars apart, out of more than two hundred. He clicked the chart button, chose a bar chart, and the bars appeared on the screen. Then he sat back. The Kestrel bar towered over the Falcon bar, nearly three times as tall. "That can't be right," he said.

Braden glanced at it and shrugged. "Six dollars is six dollars. Kestrel crushed you." Chase started to dismiss it and move on, but something snagged in his mind. He clicked on the chart and stared at the numbers running up the left side. They began at 200, not zero. He dragged the axis settings down so the scale started at zero, and the two bars snapped to almost exactly the same height, like two kids standing back to back.

"Look at that," Chase said quietly. "A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are." He turned the laptop so Braden could see the two charts side by side, the tall dramatic one and the honest one. "The first one makes it look like Kestrel doubled us. It's the same six dollars either way, but the picture lies."

Braden pulled out his phone and scrolled to the club's group chat. "Carmelo sent this chart last week. He started the axis at fifty." Chase leaned over and looked at the image, at the two bars, one looming over the other. He saved his own chart, attached it to the email, and typed a single line to Ms. Bautista: "Here are the real numbers, from zero." Then he hit send.

Maria snapped at Bastien before breakfast, and it wasn't even about anything. He had taken the last pancake, and she had said, "Great, thanks a lot," in a voice that made Darwin look up from his oatmeal like she'd thrown it at him.

"You okay?" Darwin asked.

"I'm fine," Maria said, which was obviously untrue, since she had also lost the knot-tying contest twice this morning when she'd won it every day last week. She kept forgetting the rabbit went over the mountain, not under it. She'd skipped evening canoe practice yesterday, too, even though the regatta was Saturday and canoeing was her whole reason for choosing this camp. She had told everyone she was tired. She had not told anyone that paddling had started to feel like a test she'd already failed.

At the picnic table she made a list on her napkin. Snapping at Bastien: check. Forgetting knots: check. Skipping canoeing: check. She stared at it. Ms. Sun, the water-safety instructor, was arguing with a raccoon over a bagel two tables away, so Maria leaned toward Darwin. "If you snapped at your little cousin over nothing," she asked, "what would you think?"

"I'd think my cousin was annoying," Darwin said. Bastien kicked him under the table.

"No, I mean over nothing nothing. Like he breathed too loud."

"My cousin did that once," Bastien said slowly. "Turned out he was stressed about soccer tryouts all week and didn't know it. Stress shows up in your behavior, not just in your head. Snapping at people, can't concentrate, don't want to do the stuff you normally love." He shrugged. "My mom's a nurse. She says noticing the signs is step one."

Maria looked back at her napkin. Every single box. She felt like she'd been handed a verdict by a very small judge. "So I'm not turning terrible overnight. I'm stressed about Saturday."

"Radical discovery," said Darwin, deadpan. "The favorite canoeist is nervous about the race. Shocking."

That night, Maria tried an experiment, because a theory needed testing. She skipped the flashlight tag game, did ten slow breaths in the pattern Ms. Sun used before water drills, in for four, out for four, and got into her sleeping bag before the counselors had to yell lights-out. She did the same the next night, even when Bastien tried to lure her out by claiming he'd seen a moose, which was almost certainly Darwin in a hat.

By Friday morning she tied the knot in nine seconds flat, and at practice she caught herself grinning halfway across the lake. At breakfast she slid her own pancake onto Bastien's plate. "Truce," she said.

"I want syrup too," said Bastien.

"You're violating the truce," said Maria, and took it back.

The group chat had gone quiet in a strange way, the kind of quiet that felt louder than typing. Theo sat in the back of the science room during lunch, phone under the desk, staring at a screenshot Zara had posted in the robotics team chat. It showed a private conversation between Ellia and someone whose name was blurred out, and in it Ellia had written that Zara "always takes over everything and nobody can stand it."

"That's from a private chat," Zara said, dropping into the seat beside him. Her voice was flat, careful. "Someone sent it to me."

Theo studied the screenshot again. Ellia loved private messages; she was always typing little side comments during class, thumbs flying. She thought of them as whispers, as words that vanished. Theo had a slow, ominous feeling that he knew exactly what had happened, and it was simpler than anyone wanted to believe. A private chat was not really private, because whoever received it could screenshot it and pass it on. He tested the idea in his head: the message had reached Zara without Ellia sending it to Zara, so at least one other person had read it and forwarded it. The blur meant that person was hiding.

"Can I see who sent you this?" he asked.

Zara shook her head. "It came from a number I don't have saved. But I want to know, Theo. I want to know who's passing it around more than I even care about what she wrote."

He got that. Being talked about was bad, but being watched by someone invisible was worse, like an infection spreading through the team, quiet and unseen.

When the bell rang, Theo found Ellia at her locker. She looked pale, and her books were hugged against her chest like a shield. "Zara's not speaking to me," she said before he could open his mouth. "I said something dumb. I didn't think anyone would see it."

"Who did you send it to?"

Her eyes flicked down the hall, toward the gym doors where the team was gathering for the design workshop. "Just one person. To complain. It was stupid."

"Then it's not really Zara's problem yet," Theo said. "The screenshot came from your one person. That's where it started."

Ellia stared at him. The hallway was thinning out, sneakers squeaking somewhere far off, and Mr. Ferreira leaned out of his classroom door calling that the collaborators for the bridge project should get a move on. Ellia shut her locker with a clang.

"Come on," she said, tucking her phone into her pocket, screen down. "I'll ask Zara to show me the number."

The restaurant smelled of sesame and grilled fish, and Ryder stood in the doorway holding a wrapped box that was starting to feel heavier than it actually was. His classmate Emilee had invited him to dinner with her host family, a Japanese exchange student named Kenji and Kenji's grandparents, who had flown in that morning. Ryder had never met grandparents from another country before, and he wanted to make a good impression, which was exactly why his stomach was in a knot.

Kenji's grandfather saw him first. The old man stood, turned to face Ryder, and bowed, bending low from the waist and holding it for what felt like a long moment. Ryder panicked and stuck out his hand. The handshake happened anyway, awkward and parallel to nothing, and the grandfather took Ryder's fingers gently, the way you'd hold a small bird. A waiter trying to pass had to sidestep around them both, the tray of soup obstructing his view, and Ryder's ears went hot. Emilee caught his eye from the booth and mouthed, bow.

Ryder slid in beside her and put the gift on the table, which turned out to be wrong too. Kenji's grandmother frowned at it, and Kenji leaned over and whispered, "She'll take it later, when we leave. You give gifts with two hands, and she has to pretend it's too much." Before Ryder could ask what that meant, the grandmother had slid it into her bag, nodding thanks, and he decided not to test the wrapping question out loud. Instead he watched.

He watched the way Kenji served his grandfather first, the way nobody stuck chopsticks upright in the rice bowl, the way the grandfather bowed again when the tea arrived, deeper this time than before, longer too. Ryder started noticing a pattern: the shallow quick bows went to the waiter, and the deep slow ones went to the grandfather's old friend who stopped by the table. It was like the bow itself carried a measurement. Emilee saw him counting. "Kenji told me," she said under her breath. "In Japan, bowing is how you say hello, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows."

So when dinner ended and the grandparents rose to go, Ryder stood up, turned to face them, and bowed, slow and low, the way you'd mean it. The grandfather's face opened into a wide, surprised smile, and he bowed back even deeper, which made the grandmother laugh behind her hand. Kenji clapped Ryder on the shoulder. The cost was small and real at once: Ryder never got the handshake he'd practiced, and the box he'd chosen so carefully went into a bag without being opened, unwitnessed, maybe to be saved or maybe to be quietly given away. Outside, through the restaurant window, the grandfather bowed once more to the whole table, and Ryder bowed back from the sidewalk, alone.
