Kaylie leaned over. "You know you can't, right?"

"Watch me. I'll test a hundred numbers at a time."

She pulled a math book out of her bag, the one Ms. Nwosu kept on the shelf for early finishers, and flipped until she found the page. "Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers." She slid the book across so he could see the page himself.

Vincent read the sentence twice. "Infinitely many. So there's no biggest one."

"There's no last one. It says proved, so it's not a guess."

He sat back and looked at his program. The prompt still blinked on the screen, waiting. If the primes never stopped, his plan to compress all of them into one final answer was dead. But a different idea came to him, and he tested it right there. He changed the program so that instead of asking for one number, it counted upward on its own and printed every prime it found. Then he added a line so it would never stop.

"Try 13,055," said Linkin from the next row, wandering over. "My cousin says it's exceptional, whatever that means."

The counter was in the nine thousands. They watched the primes scroll past, 9341, 9343, 9371, while Linkin pulled up a chair. When the counter reached 13055, the program printed not prime.

"Your cousin lied," Vincent said.

"Or the number lied." Linkin pointed at the screen. "It's still going, though. How long will it run?"

"Until the bell," Vincent said. "Euclid says it won't run out."

Piper slid the paper across the counter at the eyeglass store and read it again while the clerk typed into the computer. It said -2.00 under the word sphere, and next to that, OD and OS, which she guessed meant right eye and left eye. She turned to Maia, who was leaning on the counter beside her.

"I got a minus two," Piper said. "On my eyes. That can't be good. What happens if you get all the way to zero?"

Maia peered at the paper. "It's not a score. My cousin has glasses. It's how they measure lens strength, in diopters. The minus sign means nearsighted, and a plus sign means farsighted." She tapped the counter. "So minus two just means your lenses are a certain strength, that's all."

Piper wanted to test that. If minus meant nearsighted, then nearsighted people should see far away badly but close up fine. She walked to the end of the store, where a rack of sunglasses stood by the entrance, and looked back at the eye chart hanging behind the counter. The big E at the top was clear, but the second line was a gray smear. Then she pulled her library book from her backpack and read the tiny copyright page from eight inches away, easy. Far blurry, near fine. Minus fit. She walked back.

"There you are," Maia said. "I've been doing a census. Nine people came in while you were gone, and six of them were picking up glasses. That's a lot for one store."

"You counted them?"

"I want to prove to Francisco that half the kids in our grade wear glasses. He says it's only a few. He's at the book display by the fountain if you want to argue with him."

While the clerk fitted the new frames to Piper's face and bent the arms behind her ears, Maia texted Francisco. The frames were thin and blue, and when Piper looked up, the store sharpened all at once, like someone had cleaned a window. She could read the sale sign across the aisle. She could read the small print on the lens cleaner box.

They found Francisco by the fountain, next to a traveling exhibit from the science museum, a glass case of live orchids with a card about the bees that pollinate them, and a model of a venomous snake with a warning never to touch a real one. Piper stopped in front of the exhibit sign at what had to be forty feet.

"That sign says the bees visit each flower twice a day," she said. "It's printed in letters this big." She held up her thumb and forefinger, a tiny gap between them.

Francisco squinted at the sign. "There's a sign?"
"How many kids in our grade wear glasses?" Maia asked him.
Francisco looked from the sign to Piper's new blue frames. "Okay. Maybe more than a few."

The mosque hall smelled of cardamom and fried bananas, and Paige stood near the door holding a tin of her mother's lemon squares like it was a bomb about to go off. Dastan had invited her to the open house after Friday prayers, and she had said yes before thinking it through. Now she was surrounded by people who all seemed to know exactly what to do, and she did not know anything. The evening felt sophisticated in a way she couldn't name, full of small signals she couldn't read yet. She wished she were back home helping her dad with the leaky plumbing under the kitchen sink, where at least a problem was a problem and not a mystery.

Dastan appeared beside her with his little cousin hanging off his elbow. "You came! Come meet my grandmother." Paige followed him across the hall, rehearsing what to say. When they reached a small woman in a green headscarf, Paige remembered the tin and held it out. The grandmother smiled, but Dastan's aunt, standing nearby, caught Paige's wrist gently and murmured, "The other hand." Paige stared down. She had offered the gift with her left hand. Nobody had said a word about hands, and yet somehow she had already gotten it wrong.

At the long table afterward, Paige decided to verify her suspicion. She watched each person in turn, the way her dad watched a pipe joint before declaring it fixed. Every single one of them took the rice with the right hand, passed the mango drink with the right hand, waved away extra chicken with the right hand. Even Dastan's cousin, who was maybe five, did it. It wasn't random. It was a pattern, a rule she could actually learn, and learning a rule was something Paige knew how to do. When the satay platter came around, she reached for it with her right hand, and Dastan's grandmother gave her a nod so small that Paige almost missed it.

"So the right hand for everything," Paige said quietly to Dastan as they cleared plates. "Eating, giving, taking." He shrugged. "In Indonesia and Malaysia, it's a sign of respect. My whole family does it." She filed that away, feeling the evening loosen around her. She was about to carry a stack of cups to the kitchen when Dean came skidding in late from soccer practice, still in his muddy shorts, holding a box of dates as a gift.

Dean spotted Dastan's grandmother, walked straight up to her, and thrust the box out with his right hand, because Paige had already texted him the rule twice. The grandmother looked at the box, then lifted her arm, and Paige saw for the first time the plaster cast running from wrist to knuckle. "Thank you," the grandmother said, taking the dates carefully in her left hand. Behind her, Dastan whispered, "She broke it bowling." Dean looked at his own clean right hand, then at her full one, and said, "Next time I'm bringing two boxes, one for each."

The water at Camp Windrow had been pulling back all week, and by Tuesday the swim dock stood a full meter above the recession line, so the whole afternoon group had been herded to the archery range instead. Jaxon was fitting his third arrow when he heard the laughter start near the equipment shed. Henri was standing there holding a bow with a grip bent almost sideways, and a kid from another cabin was saying, "They gave the broken one to the kid who talks to arrows." A ring of maybe ten campers stood around, and every single one of them watched and nobody moved.

Jaxon nocked his arrow and pretended to aim while his brain churned. Last summer he had read a thing in his sister's psychology book, something about crowds. He couldn't remember the name of it at first, only the shape of it: the more people watching, the less likely any one of them was to do anything, because everybody figured somebody else would go first. He had thought it was nonsense then. Standing here now with his string half drawn, he wasn't so sure. He looked at Aydan, two targets over, who was clearly listening and clearly not moving. Aydan glanced at Jaxon, then at the ground.

The name surfaced at last, arriving the way forgotten homework does, all at once and too late to matter. "It's the bystander effect," Jaxon said quietly, mostly to himself.

"What?" Aydan said.

"Nothing. I think," Jaxon said, and lowered the bow. "If I go stand next to Henri, watch what happens." He set the arrow in the rack and walked over, slow, like he had a reason, and stopped at Henri's shoulder. "Hey," he said. "Trade you bows. This one's got a weird flex to it, I want to see something."

Henri blinked at him. "It's broken."

"I know. I'm testing an idea." Jaxon took the bent bow and turned it over with a small frown, as if it were genuinely interesting. The kid who had made the joke looked around, seemed to realize nobody was laughing anymore, and drifted back toward his own target.

Then Aydan came over, and after Aydan a girl from the third cabin, and then two more campers, until there were five people around Henri asking to see his stance, and the moment had folded itself up like a map and blown away. Jaxon kept his voice light and his eyes on the warped grip. One person moves, he thought, and the spell breaks. Or maybe the joke would have died anyway, and it was all ambiguous, cause and effect tangled up like fishing line. He filed that under things he couldn't prove.

Mr. Leblanc came by at the end of the hour to collect the equipment. He picked up the bent bow, turned it exactly the way Jaxon had, and said, "Who found this?"

"Henri did," Jaxon said. "It wasn't his fault it snapped."

Mr. Leblanc looked from Jaxon to Henri, then at the small crowd still hanging around Henri's target, helping him count his arrows back into the quiver. "Funny," Mr. Leblanc said slowly. "Usually nobody reports broken gear. It just turns up in the pile." He rested the bow against the shed and pulled out a clipboard. "Henri, you want to help me log it? You're the one who thrived out here today, three bullseyes on a crooked target."

Henri smiled for the first time all afternoon. "Bring the broken one," he told Jaxon, already walking. "I want to see your weird flex."

The guidance counsellor's office smelled like pencil shavings and old paper. Natalie sat across from Mr. Chen's desk, twisting the strap of her backpack, while he rummaged through a drawer. On the desk between them sat a little tin airplane with a propeller that spun whenever the heater kicked on, and a poster on the wall showed faces with labels underneath: worried, calm, stressed. Mr. Chen was helping her with her schedule, but he kept getting interrupted, because Larissa had come in too, and Larissa could not stop talking about the swim tryouts on Thursday.

"I can't eat," Larissa said. She picked up the tin airplane and set it down again without spinning the propeller. "I keep thinking about the diving block. What if I false start? What if I freeze and everyone stares?" She had been saying things like this since Monday, and it was only Wednesday. Natalie watched her friend's hands open and close around the airplane and thought about her dog at home, who barked like the world was ending whenever the mail slot clattered. The dog forgot the mail slot the second it went quiet. Larissa's problem was different, and Natalie wanted to know why, because if she could name it, maybe she could fix it.

"The diving block isn't even in front of you right now," Natalie said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "There's no water in this room. But you're acting scared." She looked at the poster, at the face labelled anxious. Then a memory surfaced, something her aunt had said once: psychologists separate fear, which is a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, which is worry about a threat that might happen later. The dog had fear. Larissa had anxiety about something days away. Natalie decided to test it.

"Okay, hear me out," she said. "When that dog lunged at you at the park last spring, you were scared, but it was over in ten seconds and you were fine by dinner." Larissa nodded. "The tryout is Thursday. It hasn't happened. So this isn't the same kind of scared. Your brain is fighting a race that hasn't started." Larissa stared at her, then laughed, a small surprised sound. "That's weirdly better," she said. "Can we do something about it, though? My mom keeps telling me to calm down, and that signifies nothing."

Mr. Chen, who had been listening while pretending to sort files, raised one hand. "Boundaries, first," he said mildly. "I need to be explicit: this is my lunch break, so you two get ten minutes and the leftover pretzels." He slid the bag across the desk. Natalie grabbed a pretzel and pointed it at Larissa like a pen. "New rule. Every time you imagine the dive, you picture the tin airplane instead and say one true thing that's happening now. Warm office. Pretzel. Friend." Larissa picked up the airplane, spun the propeller with her thumb, and watched it blur. "Ten minutes," she said. "Teach me the airplane rule before the bell."

Liam had never been inside city hall before Saturday, and the echo of his sneakers on the marble floor made him feel like he was going to get in trouble for something. Mr. Lin met them at the bottom of the staircase, holding a stack of ballots and a shoebox with a slot cut in the top. "Youth council mock election," he said. "Every vote gets counted today, right here in the council chamber. You three are my counting team."

Harley dumped out the ballots on the long wooden table where the real councillors sat on real meeting nights. There were forty of them, and Liam sorted them into piles by candidate while Reagan kept tally on a clipboard. The room smelled like dust and lemon polish. When the last ballot was sorted, the piles read twelve votes for the skateboard park, eleven for the community garden, and seventeen for the esports lounge. Reagan circled the seventeen. "Esports wins. That's it, then."

"Wait," Harley said, jabbing a finger at the piles. "Seventeen out of forty is less than half. Twenty-one would be half. So most people picked something else, and the esports lounge still gets everything?" Reagan was skeptical, recounting twice, but the numbers refused to change. Liam, who had privately despised the esports campaign from the start, was surprised to feel his stomach go wrong anyway. It wasn't only about losing. Twenty-three ballots had gone the other way, and they were all about to be swept into the shoebox like they'd never existed.

He lined the piles up like bars of a graph, which is what he did with everything, even the times he found organisms under his microscope at school. "What if we split it up instead," he said slowly. "Forty votes, and the esports lounge got close to half, and the garden and the park got close to a quarter each. There are four spots on the youth council budget. So the lounge takes two spots, and the garden and the park each take one." Reagan frowned. "That's not how elections work, though." Liam turned to Mr. Lin, who had been listening from the doorway with his arms folded, and asked whether both ways had names. "Yours is proportional representation," Mr. Lin said. "Reagan's is first past the post."

Mr. Lin wouldn't tell them which was fairer, because of course he wouldn't. So Liam proposed a deal he didn't love: keep first past the post for naming the youth council president, since Reagan pointed out somebody had to actually be in charge, but split the budget money proportionally, by the piles. Harley agreed for the garden side, Reagan agreed because the esports lounge still came out on top, and they wrote it all on the clipboard and carried it to Mr. Lin like a treaty.

The council chamber emptied out through the big doors and the lights clicked off in sections, each one a little clap of dark. Outside on the steps, Harley bumped his shoulder against Liam's. "Good fix." Liam looked back at the building, where somewhere inside his losing ballots were still sitting in the shoebox, unrecorded in any official tally, and where he'd also just handed the thing he despised the biggest share of the money. "Half a fix," he said. "Come on, I'll race you to the bus stop."

Brooklyn sat on the floor of Guillaume's basement with a camera lens in her lap, waiting while he hunted for batteries. The lens was his dad's, heavy as a soup can, and she kept her eyes on it so she would not think about the lines on her hips. She had seen them that morning in the mirror, thin and pale, like scratches that did not hurt. She had pulled her shirt down fast, before her brain could start guessing.

"Found them," Guillaume said, holding up two batteries. "Drew's coming with popcorn. His mom is frugal, so it's the store brand, but it's fine."

They were making a stop-motion movie about a LEGO knight who fought a vacuum cleaner. Brooklyn fit the lens onto the old camera and squinted through it. Everything looked closer and stranger, the knight's painted face full of tiny cracks. She liked that. Behind a lens, small things became important and big things became small.

Drew arrived with the popcorn and news. "Guess what. My sister had a total meltdown yesterday over her legs. She found these little lines on them and thought something was wrong with her skin."

Brooklyn's hands stopped on the camera. "What kind of lines?"

"Thin ones. Like little white threads. My mom said relax, it happens when you grow too fast for your skin to keep up." Drew shrugged and ate a handful of popcorn. "She says hers faded after a while."

Guillaume clicked the vacuum cleaner on for the knight's battle scene and its motor made everything rattle. Brooklyn did not laugh at it this time. She was thinking. She had grown two inches since September; Ms. Huang had said so at school when they got measured in gym, and Brooklyn's leggings had gone from long to short without her noticing the day it happened. Fast growing, then lines. She tested the idea quietly, matching it against what she knew. Drew's sister had shot up recently too; everyone said so.

After the movie was done, the knight victorious on a hill of popcorn kernels, Guillaume walked her to the door. "Same time next week?" he asked.

At home, Brooklyn found her mom folding laundry. "Mom, are the lines on people's skin, the thin ones, do they have a name?"

"Stretch marks," her mom said. "Lots of people get them during growth spurts, and they usually fade over time."

"Okay," Brooklyn said. That night she looked once more, quick, then pulled her shirt down and did not check again until Sunday. The lines were still there. She nodded at them the way you nod at a neighbor, and went to find her sketchbook to draw the knight.

Arthur had rehearsed the plan three times on the bus: buy two hot chocolates, find Philip near the fence behind the away bleachers, and watch the fourth quarter together. It was the first date either of them had been on, and Arthur wanted it to go smoothly, which was exactly why he kept checking the plan like homework. He asked Philip earlier that day to clarify one detail, whether they were meeting at the fence or at the ticket booth, and Philip had said the fence, laughing a little, because of course the fence.

The game was close. The home team, whose mascot was a gray kangaroo suit with a sagging pouch, kept fumbling, and every time the marsupial slumped against the goalpost the crowd groaned along with it. Arthur and Philip stood shoulder to shoulder in the cold, steam rising off the paper cups, and when the home team recovered a fumble on the thirty-yard line Philip grabbed Arthur's sleeve without seeming to notice he'd done it. Arthur noticed. He noticed the whole drive, through the cold smell of mustard and wet metal bleachers, all the way to the field goal that sailed through the uprights and won the game.

Then Philip let go of the sleeve and said, "You can hold my hand, if you want. That's allowed." Arthur reached over. Halfway there he stopped, because something occurred to him. "Can either of us change our mind? Like, say no halfway through, or at the end, whenever?"

Philip nodded. "Either of us. Any time. And the other one just accepts it, no pressure, no asking why."

Arthur closed the last few inches and took his hand. It was warm from the cup and a little sticky from the cocoa. They walked out with the crowd, past the ticket booth where the cashier was counting quarters, past the mascot sitting on a cooler with the kangaroo head in its lap.

At the corner where they usually split up, Arthur turned toward Philip for a hug. Philip stepped back, just slightly, just enough. "Not tonight," he said. "Hand was good. Hug, no."

For one second Arthur felt the pull to make it a joke, to say something that would nudge Philip into changing his answer. He let the second pass. "Okay," he said. "See you Monday."

He walked home with his hands in his pockets, and his phone buzzed twice before he reached his block. The first text said, thanks for not making it weird. The second said, the kangaroo wants a rematch next Friday. Same fence?

Arthur typed one word back, "Fence," and hit send.

The dryer at home had gone completely silent that morning, and Romy decided it was extinct, like the dinosaurs, except with more lint. She dragged her bulging laundry bag to the bus stop and plopped it down on the bench just as Keaton skidded up beside her, breathless.

"Is that your entire wardrobe?" he asked, poking the bag. "What did you do, lose a bet?"

"Mom's home at six, and she said if the laundry isn't done by then, I'm the defendant in a trial I will lose. The dryer makes a buzz and then nothing. It's dead."

Keaton leaned on the bus stop sign. "Or it's faking. My grandma's toaster used to do that."

The bus wasn't due for eleven minutes, and the schedule seemed to fluctuate depending on the driver's mood, so Romy had time to think. She'd passed the laundromat a hundred times, and taped to its window was a poster she'd never actually read. She read it now, mentally: failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect. Lint. Airflow. Heat. She thought about the filter at home, which she had never once touched in her entire life, and a cold, prickly feeling crept up her neck. Nobody in her house had ever pulled that thing out. Ever.

"Change of plan," she said, hoisting the bag back up. "We're walking home. Two blocks. You're my witness."

"You just said the dryer is dead."

"I said extinct. Extinct animals sometimes turn out to be frogs in a hole. Come on."

At home she yanked open the dryer door, slid out the lint filter, and stared. A mat of grey fuzz sat on it, thick as a slice of bread, dense enough to bounce a coin off. Keaton made a noise like a startled goose. Romy peeled the whole felted slab away in one piece, held it up like evidence, and dropped it in the trash. Then she restarted the dryer. It buzzed, hesitated, and began to tumble with a low, healthy rumble.

"Your defendant," Keaton announced, "is found not guilty."

"Not guilty of being extinct," Romy agreed, feeding towels into the washing machine and starting the whole load from scratch, sorting darks from lights like she'd actually been paying attention all along. She folded the first warm shirt into a lopsided square and held it up. "Mom will never know. This stays between us, the dryer, and the lint."

"Your secret's safe," Keaton said, patting the machine gently on its corner. "So long as you feed it, it won't burn the house down."

The community kitchen smelled like toasted cumin and hot oil, and Camille stood at the counter with three timers in front of her and no idea how to use any of them. Her curry bubbled on the back burner, the flatbread dough rested under a damp cloth, and the pot of rice sat on the front burner with its lid rattling. The whole point of tonight's lesson, Mr. Islam had said, was that everything should arrive at the window together, hot, at the same moment. If the rice finished early it would go cold. If it finished late, the curry would thicken into paste.

Last week had been a disaster, and Camille remembered it in a quick, stomach-dropping flash: Patience standing over the rice pot, lifting the lid every two minutes to check on it, saying "just looking," while Kamden shouted that the flatbread was burning. Every dish had finished at a different time. The rice had come out crunchy in the middle, and they had eaten standing up, in shifts, and Camille had gone home with the sour feeling that she had missed something she should have seen.

She thought about that crunchy rice all week. The pot had been on the heat for the right amount of time. The water had been measured. So why had the grains stayed hard? She turned it over while walking to school, while washing dishes at home. The difference was Patience's lifting, again and again. Something was escaping each time that lid came off. Steam. The steam was part of the cooking, and Patience had been letting it out.

"Patience," she said now, "don't open that pot. Trust me on this one." Patience's hand was already halfway to the handle.

"But I can't tell if it's working," Patience said. "It's an illusion, just sitting there doing nothing."

"That's what it looks like, but it's not nothing. Last week you kept checking and the rice came out crunchy." Camille slid a strip of tape across the lid and the pot rim, sealing it like a tiny door. "We leave it alone."

Patience looked wounded, so Kamden leaned over to reassure her. "You can be in charge of the flatbread instead. That one actually needs watching." He flipped a puffed golden round onto the plate and she grabbed the spatula, and soon she was too busy turning bread to glance at the taped pot at all.

Camille timed the curry down to its last ten minutes, dropped the flatbread rounds onto the griddle so they'd be warm and soft when the rice was done, and then, when everything was close, she pulled the tape free and lifted the lid herself. Steam rolled up in one thick white cloud, fragrant and perfect, and the grains below were separate and tender all the way through. She spooned rice onto three plates, ladled curry beside it, and slid the warm bread on top just as Mr. Islam called time.

"All together," Patience said, staring at the three plates.

Camille picked up the first plate and carried it to the window.

Bentley had been setting up the hanukkiah on the kitchen windowsill when the doorbell rang, and now Shanaya was standing in the hallway with her boots still on, holding a plate of her mother's biscotti. "My mom said to bring these," she said. "Also, I have a question, and it's been bugging me since class on Monday."

"Ask it after the candles," Bentley's father called from the stove, where the latkes were frying.

"No, now," Shanaya said. She pointed at the menorah. "Hanukkah is eight nights, right? We learned that. So why does that thing have nine spots for candles?"

Bentley looked at the hanukkiah. He counted the branches with his eyes, touching each one with a fingertip. Eight across, in two rows of four, and one taller branch standing apart in the middle. Nine. He had lit it every year of his life, and he had never once counted. "Huh," he said.

"Don't ask me," his father said, flipping a latke. "You're the one who wants to be an engineer. Figure it out."

Bentley picked up a box of candles and tipped them out onto the table. He placed one candle in each of the eight lower branches, then held up the ninth. Shanaya watched him with her arms crossed, waiting. He looked at the tall middle branch, then at the candles in his hand, and then at the box, where the word shamash was printed in small letters beside a picture of a single candle set slightly apart from the rest. "Shamash," he said slowly, reading it. "I've heard my grandma say that word. It's the helper candle." He set the ninth candle in the tall branch. "Eight for the eight nights," he said, "and this one lights the others. That's why it's taller. So you can tell it apart."

"So you'd never light the eight with a match?" Shanaya asked.

Bentley realized he had never actually watched closely enough to know. He had always been busy holding the door open or fetching his little cousins. "Let's find out," he said. "Tonight's the fourth night, so we do four plus the shamash."

When his father finally turned off the stove, the whole family crowded into the kitchen. Bentley's grandmother struck the match and touched it only to the shamash, then lifted the shamash out of its branch and carried its flame to the first candle, then the second, then the third, then the fourth, chanting the blessing while the flames wobbled. Shanaya leaned in beside Bentley, close enough that he could hear her breathing. The candles guttered and steadied, and the oil smell from the latkes condensed on the cold window above them into a faint fog.

After the blessings, the adults drifted back to the table for dinner, but Bentley and Shanaya stayed by the window, watching the flames. Steam condensed on his juice glass, too, and he drew a crooked star in it with his thumbnail. "It's cumulative," Shanaya said. "Like, every night you add one more, so by the last night the whole thing is lit, all eight plus the helper."

"That's kind of the point, I think," Bentley said. "It gets brighter the whole way through."

"I like that," Shanaya said. She picked up a biscotti and pointed it at the hanukkiah like a baton. "Same time tomorrow? I want to see the fifth one."

"Bring more of these," Bentley said, and took one for himself.

Sophia stabbed her noodle and slid her phone across the table to Harper. "Look at this invite. My aunt's wedding is Saturday, and it says wear white if you can. My mom says I can't."

Harper leaned over, chopsticks frozen midair. "Weird. Since when does a wedding want everyone in white?"

"That's what I said. But look at the photo." Sophia enlarged it. The bride, Great-Aunt Mei, stood in a red dress with gold stitching, glowing like a lantern. "She's not wearing white. Everyone else is, in the picture from her first ceremony announcement."

Louis reached across and scrolled. "So the guests wear white and the bride wears red? That's backwards."

"Maybe it's a theme," Harper said. "Like a white party."

Sophia's mother set down a bowl of soup and shook her head. "Not a theme. Your great-aunt is honoring tradition. In our family's culture, white is worn for mourning at funerals." She spooned dumplings into Louis's bowl without pausing. "So the bride does not wear it. But your cousin Clara's fiancé's family is American, and for them the bride wears white at weddings. Same color, opposite meanings."

"Wait," Louis said. "The same color can mean two opposite things?"

"Apparently," Sophia's mother said, and went back to the kitchen.

The three of them sat quietly for a moment. Sophia turned her fork over, thinking. Everyone at that wedding would be looking at the same white dress and seeing something completely different, depending on where they came from. Her mom hadn't explained why the traditions existed, and Sophia didn't ask, because the important part was already clear: meaning wasn't in the color itself. It was in the people looking at it.

"So what do I actually wear?" Sophia pulled up photos of her closet on her phone. "I have until Friday to decide. If I wear white, Clara's side thinks I'm festive. If Aunt Mei's side sees it that way too, because they chose this, fine. But what if some older relatives didn't get the memo?"

Harper grinned. "Test it. Text your mom's cousin and ask what everyone wore at the engagement party."

Sophia did. The reply came back fast: a photo of a room full of guests in white and ivory, laughing, with Aunt Mei in red at the center. Sophia counted the faces, then tried to quantify her worry on a scale of one to ten and decided it had dropped to about a two. "It worked for them," she said. "The families already negotiated this."

"Negotiated a color," Louis said. "That's like commerce for clothes."

Saturday morning, Sophia buttoned the white dress she'd borrowed from Harper and felt cautiously optimistic. At the reception, Clara's grandmother complimented her outfit, and Aunt Mei's brother gave her a thumbs-up from across the room. Two sides of one family, one table, one color doing double duty.

Sophia found Aunt Mei near the cake. "I almost didn't wear this."

Aunt Mei smoothed Sophia's sleeve and smiled. "White for the guests, red for me. Everyone sees what they hoped to see."

"Which did you see?" Sophia asked.

Aunt Mei lifted her champagne glass. "I saw a girl who asked a good question before she got dressed."

Sebastian jogged the chain-link loop that circled the community pool, counting strides while Caroline timed him from a folding chair by the gate. Eight hundred metres was two laps of the loop, and every time he raced Greyson after school, he died on the second one. "Two twenty-one for the first lap," Caroline called, "and then you basically walked." She was studying for her lifeguard written test between splits, flashcards about chlorine levels spread across her knees, because she wanted the summer job more than anything and needed to pass by Friday.

"You're starting too slow," Greyson insisted from the deep end, where he was treading water between sets. "You save too much. Then you sprint at the end like it's a hundred."

Sebastian didn't think so. He had watched the men's eight-hundred-metre world record race from the 2012 London Olympics on his phone three times the night before, David Rudisha running alone at the front, and something about it had snagged in his head. He asked Caroline to watch it with him now, the phone propped on her chair, the pool's gutter dripping behind the audio. On the second viewing she paused the screen and tapped the split that flashed after the first lap. "Look at this. His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second." Greyson hauled himself out to see, dripping on the concrete. "The world record, and he slows down at the end?" He sounded almost offended.

Sebastian ran it again in his head. The champion went out fast, faster than his finishing pace, and still won the world. Maybe the problem wasn't that Sebastian started too fast. Maybe he started too slow, spent the whole first lap trapped behind his own caution, and then had nothing left because he panicked and surged at the wrong moments. There was no way to see pacing, no way to hold it in your hand, but you could test it. "One more time," he told Caroline. "First lap, I'm going out like it's a four hundred. Don't yell at me."

He went through the first lap so hard the roar of his own pulse drowned the pool filter, past the barren shade of the empty baby pool, through the chlorine smell at the gate, his legs already heavy when Caroline shouted the split. Two fifteen. His best opening ever. The second lap hurt more than anything he could remember, and he gripped the fence and gasped, certain he had ruined it. "Two twenty-two," Caroline called, and then, checking her watch twice, "Three thirty-seven total. You just took eleven seconds off."

Greyson stood there with his towel forgotten over one shoulder. "Do it again Tuesday?" Sebastian was already walking the curve to cool down, one hand pressed to his aching side, grinning so wide it hurt worse than his legs. "Bring the flashcards," he told Caroline. "I'll time you on the written stuff while I recover."

Ellie's science grade was currently a C minus, which her mother described as "room to grow" and which Ellie described, privately and more accurately, as a problem. Mr. Marino had assigned the final project: explain how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands. Kai was building a pioneer settlement for social studies and kept offering her leftover fence posts. Benoit said he was doing his on volcanoes, which was not even the right unit.

Ellie started with a shoebox and some clay birds, but the birds all looked like pigeons with identity issues. Worse, she could not actually say what she was supposed to say. The textbook had a picture of a small scrubby island called Daphne Major and a paragraph she had read four times. During a severe drought in 1977, the small seeds ran out, and medium ground finches with larger, deeper beaks survived better because they could crack the large, hard seeds that were left. She could recite it. She could not explain it to a six-year-old, and Mr. Marino had announced that anyone who could not explain it to a six-year-old did not understand it themselves.

"Then be the six-year-old," she told Kai on Thursday, dragging him to the cafeteria table where she had dumped a bag of birdseed and two pairs of pliers.

"I'm twelve."

"Pretend." She sorted the seed into two piles, small soft ones and large hard ones, then took the small pile away. "Drought. Small seeds are gone. Pick a bird." She handed him the pliers with the narrow tips and kept the wide-jawed ones for herself. Benoit sat down uninvited, which was how Benoit sat down anywhere.

They cracked seeds. Kai's narrow tips slipped off the big hard ones, and after a minute he was grinding the same seed against the table with an expression of personal betrayal. Ellie's wide jaws split them, one after another, though she had to regulate her grip carefully because squeezing too hard just launched the seed kernel across the cafeteria. A kernel hit Benoit in the ear. He ate it.

"So the big-beaked ones ate, and the other ones didn't," Kai said, spitting out a crushed seed. "And then?"

"And then the survivors had babies, and the babies had the useful beaks, and the island full of birds slowly had different beak shapes than the finches on the other islands." She lined up her clay lumps, which still looked like pigeons, and squeezed the front of each one forward into a stubby deep wedge. They now looked like pigeons with unfortunate noses, but the noses were the point.

On presentation day, Mr. Marino watched her pliers demonstration without expression, arms folded, the way a bench watches a chess match. Then he asked the class who survived the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, and Ellie answered before anyone else could, "Medium ground finches with larger, deeper beaks, because they could crack the large, hard seeds after the small ones ran out." Mr. Marino wrote something in his book.

"A minus," he said, and turned to Benoit's volcano, which was already leaking baking soda onto the floor.

The tutoring centre smelled like pencil shavings and old carpet, and Alexia had been staring at the same problem for ten minutes. On her worksheet, in her own handwriting, it said 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, and she had no idea which x she was supposed to deal with first.

"If I get this wrong again, Ms. Johansson will think I wasn't listening," she whispered to Mehtab, who sat beside her with a science textbook open, drawing labelled arrows toward a picture of a microbe.

"Then don't get it wrong," Mehtab said, without looking up. "But you won't learn anything if I just hand you the answer."

Alexia slid her paper toward him anyway. "Look. There's an x on the left and an x on the right. Which one moves?"

Mehtab finally closed the textbook. "Try one. Pick either."

"That's ridiculous. One of them has to be the right one."

"Try the right side first. Take away the 3x."

Alexia wrote it out, crossing off the 3x with a careful line. Then, because Ms. Johansson had drilled it into the whole room that whatever you did to one side you did to the other, she subtracted 3x from the left too. She looked at what remained and sat back. Both x's had gathered onto one side, and the whole thing had shrunk to 2x + 2 = 10.

"That's it?" she said. "That's the whole trick?"

"Now do the other way," Mehtab said. "Take away the 5x instead."

She started a fresh line. When she subtracted 5x from both sides this time, she got negative numbers, but the x's still ended up alone on a single side. It was messier, and she wrinkled her nose at the minus signs, but it worked too. Either x. Both ways. She checked by finishing the first version: 2x + 2 = 10 meant 2x = 8, so x = 4. She plugged 4 back into the original problem, and both sides came out to 22.

Ms. Johansson drifted over and scanned the page. "Two methods, both correct, and a check. Nicely done, Alexia."

Faith leaned across from the next table, where she had been muttering that fractions were toxic. "Wait, it works both directions? Show me that on mine."

Alexia pulled Faith's paper over and uncapped her pen. "Okay, yours is 6x + 3 = 4x + 11. Watch what happens when I take away 4x."

Ariana had been watching the same page for a week: Avah's handmade bracelets, woven from silver thread and blue beads, listed at eighteen dollars each in the school's online marketplace. On Friday night, Ariana checked one last time before bed, feeling almost nocturnal the way she kept waking to refresh the page, and every single bracelet was gone. Sold out. At eighteen dollars.

"I want to hypothesize something," she told Noa at lunch on Monday. "If Avah can sell thread and beads for eighteen dollars, could we?" Noa shrugged and said her cousin had a law of supply poster in her shop. So Ariana and Noa spent their savings, plus the ten dollars Ariana's grandmother sent from her pension every month, on supplies. They listed ten bracelets at sixteen dollars.

They sold out in two days. Ariana raised the price to eighteen, then twenty, and the bracelets still went fast. It felt like discovering an invisible rule, something she couldn't see directly but could test. "Watch," she told Noa. "The price is high, so I predict more people will start selling."

By the next week, her prediction had come true in a way she hadn't expected. Ms. Kerr, who lived two streets over, posted a page of beaded bracelets. Then two girls from the chess club. Then a boy Ariana had never met, selling woven bracelets at fifteen dollars, then twelve. The marketplace page that had shown only Avah's work now scrolled on and on. Ariana checked her own listing. Two bracelets sat unsold for three days straight.

"So that's it," Noa said, scrolling beside her. "When the price went up, everybody started offering more. That's the law of supply." Ariana nodded slowly. The rule she had guessed at was real, and it had a name, and it was now working against her. She couldn't change how many sellers there were. But she could change what she made.

That weekend Ariana and Noa didn't weave bracelets. Instead they braided keychains with tiny lightning bolts worked into the pattern, something nobody else on the page was selling. They listed five at ten dollars each. By Monday morning, three had sold, and a message waited in her inbox from the boy with the fifteen-dollar bracelets.

"Hey," it read. "Where did you get those bolt beads?"

Emmett crouched at the mouth of his garage, holding a marble against the sloped ramp he had built from an old shelf board and two paint cans. Ayaan stood beside him with a stopwatch, and Aksel crouched farther down the driveway with a second stopwatch and a strip of masking tape stuck to the concrete.

"Same roll, two timers," Emmett said. "One of these numbers has to be lying."

Ayaan's dad had offered the garage for the project because it had the only smooth, level floor on the street, and because rain was coming. Emmett needed a distance-time graph for Monday, which meant he needed real distances and real times, not numbers he invented at his desk. A graph built from made-up points would be counterfeit science, and Mr. Torres had a nose for that sort of thing.

He let the marble go. It hissed down the ramp, crossed the tape, and rattled into a rolled-up towel Aksel had placed at the end.

"Two point one two seconds," Ayaan read off.

Aksel squinted at his own screen. "One point nine five."

They ran it again. Two point zero nine and one point eight eight. A third roll gave two point three one against two point one four. Every time, Aksel's number came out smaller, and the gap between them stayed about the same, close to a fifth of a second, whether the marble ran fast or slow.

"It's not the marble," Emmett said slowly. "The marble doesn't care who's watching it."

Ayaan frowned. "So it's us."

Emmett made them both close their eyes and try to snap their fingers the instant he clapped. Aksel snapped almost with the clap. Ayaan snapped late, every single time. It was small, that delay, but it was there, like a hiccup in the middle of the count.

Ayaan's face went pink. "I'm messing up your whole project."

"You're messing it up the same amount every time," Emmett said, and then he stopped, because the idea arrived all at once. "Wait. That's the thing."

He grabbed the chalk they had been using to mark distances and drew a new start line way back near the garage door, tripling the run. "We take a census," he said, waving at the tape marks, "of lots of rolls, the long ones, and your late click gets spread out. It's a fifth of a second, so on a short run it eats a huge bite of the answer. On a long run it barely matters."

They rolled the marble ten times down the full length. Ayaan's times and Aksel's times came out nearly twins, two tenths apart at most, and often closer. Emmett wrote each pair in his notebook, averaged them, and plotted the points on graph paper taped to the garage wall. The dots climbed into a nearly straight line.

"That's the speed," he said, tapping the slope with his pencil. "Right there."

Ayaan leaned in and ran a finger along the line. "So my slow thumb didn't ruin anything."

"It's part of the data now," Emmett said. "Every scientist has a thumb."

Aksel set up the ramp again without being asked, and outside the first fat drops began to slap the driveway.

"One more roll," Emmett said, pressing the marble to the board. "On three."

Aiden stood in his grandfather's study with a photocopied page of Hebrew in his hand and a month until his bar mitzvah, and the letters refused to stay in order. His grandfather had read from the Torah scroll at his own bar mitzvah, decades ago in a synagogue that no longer existed, and he had promised Aiden one thing: he would teach him the way he had been taught, with the scroll itself.

"Tomorrow you'll practice on the real thing," his grandfather said, laying a velvet cover over the scroll on the desk. "Tonight, again from the page."

Aiden read the blessing aloud twice, stumbled on the same phrase twice, and wondered whether his tongue was simply obstinate or whether the words moved around when he blinked. He tried closing his eyes between lines to see if the pattern would settle. It didn't. He tried tapping the rhythm on the desk with two fingers, and that helped a little, the way a drumbeat holds a marching line together.

The next evening his grandfather unrolled the scroll across the long table, and Aiden leaned over the parchment. The letters were square and black, the columns neat as a field after planting. He began to read, following his place with his eyes, but as the tricky phrase came near, his finger drifted up and hovered an inch above the page, tracing the words as if his hand could steady them. His grandfather reached into the desk drawer without a word and held out a slim silver rod with a hand-shaped point at the tip.

"Use the yad," he said. "It means hand."

Aiden took it. The metal was cool and heavier than it looked. He set the pointing finger under the first word of the phrase and read on, and this time the letters held still, as though something about touching the place without touching had anchored them. Was it the yad, or was it that he now had to monitor two things at once, the words and the pointer, so his mind couldn't wander off and drag the syllables with it? He decided to test it. He read the next verse using the yad, then one without it, then one with it again. Without it, his finger crept toward the parchment; with it, his place stayed locked.

"Why not just touch it with a finger?" he asked.

"The parchment isn't touched," his grandfather said, and rolled the corner of the scroll back a little. "Not by hands."

On Saturday, in front of everyone, his mother in the second row and his classmates Tanner and Carys squeezed beside her, Aiden stood at the reading table. The rabbi handed him the yad, its silver hand catching the light from the windows. He set it beneath the first word and read, all the way through, without a single stumble, and when he finished, the whole room rose around him, and his grandfather's voice was the loudest one there.

Antoine had been practising his wheelie for twenty minutes when Troy started in on Katie's dinosaur backpack.

"Nice bag," Troy said, loud enough for the kids on the swings to hear. "Did you dig it up yourself?"

A few kids laughed. Katie stood by the climbing wall, holding one strap like she was thinking about bolting for the gate.

Antoine's first idea was to say something clever back, but he'd tried that last week and it had turned into a ten-minute insult contest that Troy won. So he sat on his bike and thought instead. Troy wasn't even looking at Katie when he joked. He was looking at the kids on the swings. That was the interesting part. It was like the teasing needed people watching it, the way a fire needs air. Take away the audience and the whole thing might just go out.

He ran a quick test in his head. If he yelled at Troy, everyone would gather closer, and Troy would have to keep going to save face. If he did nothing, Katie stood there alone. There was a third door, though.

Antoine dropped his bike in the grass and walked over to Katie like he hadn't heard any of it. "Come on, let's go," he said. "I need help with the water fountain. It's got an intricate system of buttons and I can't figure out which one actually works."

Katie blinked, then caught on. "The one on the left," she said, following him. "Everyone knows the left one."

"Left, right, up, down," Antoine said as they walked off. "It's like a whole curriculum in fountain studies. There should be a test."

The swings had gone quiet behind them. By the time they reached the fountain, Troy's joke had nobody left to land on, and it just sort of evaporated, the way a balloon goes floppy when you let go of the neck.

At the fountain, Katie pressed the left button and it sprayed Antoine's shoe. "Oops," she said, grinning for the first time all recess.

Tuesday morning, Antoine found a folded note tucked into his backpack pocket. In Katie's handwriting it said: "Thanks for yesterday. Troy cornered me by the buses but nobody was around, and he gave up after like ten seconds. Weird. Anyway, dinosaur backpack forever. K." Antoine read it twice, then added it to the small collection of important papers in his desk at home, next to a library card and a drawing of a shark wearing a hat.

At recess, Troy came over to the basketball court, bouncing a ball with more force than the situation required. "Okay," he said. "The fountain thing. That was actually pretty smooth, and now everyone thinks I'm the boring kid who can't keep a joke going."

"You could sustain a joke for weeks," Antoine said. "That's not your problem."

Troy spun the ball on one finger, watched it wobble, and caught it. "Fine. But if I'm going to be funny, I'm going to be funny at someone who deserves it. Like Mr. Pell, who assigns homework on Fridays."

"That's a bold target," Antoine said.

Katie appeared beside them with her dinosaur backpack swinging. "For Mr. Pell, you're going to need a better plan than a backpack joke," she said, and passed Troy the ball.

Mr. Leblanc handed the stories back on Tuesday, and Landon's had one comment in red at the bottom: "Your dragon attack is great, but I got there too fast. Fix the middle." Landon read it three times during lunch, scowling at the page while Hope peeled an orange beside him.

"My story's fine," he said. "The knight fights the dragon on page one. That's the best part."

Hope shrugged. "Then why did he write fix the middle?"

That afternoon Landon asked Malachi to read it, mostly to prove Mr. Leblanc wrong. Malachi read fast, the way he did everything, then flipped back to the first page. "It's all fight," he said. "The knight wins, story over. There's nothing to be scared of. It's like when we watched that movie trailer that showed the whole movie."

Landon took the pages back. That night he tried an experiment. He took his sister's favorite book, the one with the prism on the cover that split light into rainbows on her wall, and copied its shape. Not the words, just the pattern: small trouble, bigger trouble, worst trouble, then the huge moment. He wrote the pattern out on a sticky note like a diagram. Page one, the knight's village loses its water. Page two, a stranger takes the last horse. Page three, the knight's brother is taken. Then the dragon.

The next morning he left a note in Hope's locker because he got to school before she did. "Read this version. Don't look at page one first. Tell me if your stomach hurts before the end." After first period she found him by the water fountain, holding the pages like evidence. "Page two," she said. "When the brother gets taken, I actually gripped the paper. That didn't happen yesterday."

"So it works," Landon said.

"What do you call that part? The stacking-up part?"

Landon had looked it up the night before, in the writing handbook Mr. Leblanc kept on the shelf by the window. "Rising action," he said. "It's the series of complications that raise the stakes and build tension before the climax." He said it fast, the way you recite something you just learned, and Hope nodded like it was obvious.

In class, Mr. Leblanc read the new draft silently, his face neutral, and Landon could not tell anything from it. Then Mr. Leblanc slid the paper across the desk. "Better. Could you replicate this structure in your next one, without copying the plot?" Landon said he could, and he meant it, because now he understood it wasn't about the dragon at all.

At lunch Malachi grabbed the pages out of his binder before Landon could stop him. "You added a brother?" Malaci read, and read, and for once in his life he did not rush. When he finished the last page he looked up and said, "Read me the water part again. I want to hear how you did that."

Julia stood at the folding table in the community room of Maple Court, the seniors' residence, trying to remember which crate held the canned peas. A hand-lettered sign above her read Community Food Bank, and beside it a poster with a stylized bowl logo she'd never paid attention to before. She was hesitant at first about handing out the wrong thing, but the woman in the purple cardigan waiting in front of her just smiled and said she'd take whatever Julia had.

"If you like peas, these are good," Julia said, and the woman took two cans and moved on to Forrest, who was bagging bread at the next table.

Outside, a white truck backed up to the loading door, and Julia squinted at it. The same bowl logo from the poster was printed on its door, and under it, in small letters, a city name from two states away. She nudged Forrest. "Why is that truck from Ohio? Isn't this our town's food bank?"

Forrest shrugged and went back to sorting oranges. Ty, who had been hauling boxes since seven, said maybe the truck was just lost. But Julia kept thinking about it while she restocked crackers. A second truck arrived at ten, from a different city entirely, and it had the same logo too. Lost trucks didn't travel in pairs with matching paint.

During the lull before lunch, she found Ms. Shapiro, the volunteer coordinator, checking clipboards near the kitchen. Ms. Shapiro governed the whole operation from a desk no bigger than a cookie sheet, deciding who worked which table and what got unloaded first. "Can I ask you something?" Julia said. "Both trucks today have that bowl logo, but they're from different places. Are they all the same food bank?"

"Same network," Ms. Shapiro said. "It's called Feeding America. More than 200 food banks, all across the United States, in one nationwide network."

Julia turned that over while she stacked juice boxes. One network, more than 200 food banks. That meant the crates of peanut butter weren't random; they had come through a system bigger than this one building. She decided to test it. The next time a driver came through the door, she asked to see his paperwork, and there it was again, the bowl logo at the top of a delivery slip from yet another city.

"See?" she said to Forrest, holding up the slip. "It's not our food bank and their food bank. They're all connected."

At the end of the afternoon, the woman in the purple cardigan came back for the last loaf of bread. Julia set it in her bag and added a jar of applesauce from the surplus crate. "I saved this for you," she said. "I noticed you took the small cans last time."

The woman patted her hand. "You watch out for people, don't you."

Julia taped the delivery slip, logo up, onto the edge of her folding table.

Jacob had never needed deodorant before this year, and that was the part that bugged him. He sat on Tony's front step with a bottle of water, shirt stuck to his back, after forty minutes of driveway basketball in the heat. Tony's older cousin, who was staying with them for the summer, dropped into the chair beside him with his own bottle.

"You reek," the cousin said to Tony.

"So do you," said Tony.

"I don't, actually." The cousin held out his arm and sniffed it. "Fresh sweat has almost no smell. Body odor shows up when the bacteria on your skin break down the sweat from your armpit glands. Those glands don't even turn on until puberty."

Jacob looked down at his own soaked shirt. "So we're just old enough to be a lunch buffet for germs now."

"Pretty much," the cousin said, and went inside.

Jacob carried the thought home the way you carry a rock in your shoe. Two days later he had a plan. He took two clean washcloths, wiped one across his forehead right after running, and tucked it into a plastic bag. Then he wiped the second one under his arm and put it in a second bag. He labeled them with tape and a marker: forehead, armpit. He set both bags on top of the heating vent, because the thermostat in the hallway said the house was cold and the vent was the warmest spot he knew. Warmth had to matter. His gym clothes only smelled bad after they sat crumpled in his locker, never right after class.

At Tony's house that afternoon, he explained the experiment. Tony's mom let them use the kitchen timer. Ariella came over because Tony texted her, and she leaned on the counter examining the bags like they were evidence.

"So your theory," she said, "is that it's not the sweating. It's what happens after."

"If I'm right, the armpit cloth will smell and the forehead cloth won't, even though both got sweat on them at the same time," Jacob said. "The forehead kind of sweat was fine last year. The armpit kind is the new stuff."

Tony wrinkled his nose. "You're doing science on your own stink."

"Somebody has to."

They waited an hour, and when the timer beeped, Jacob opened the forehead bag first. He sniffed, then passed it around. Nothing. Ariella smelled it twice and shrugged. Then Jacob opened the armpit bag, and Tony recoiled so fast he knocked his chair over. The smell was sour and unmistakable, like the whole locker room in one square of cloth.

"So the bacteria eat it," Ariella said slowly, "and that's the smell. The sweat itself is innocent."

Jacob taped both cloths to a sheet of paper and wrote the date underneath. He had a whole row of questions now. He wondered whether washing actually removed the bacteria or just scattered them, and whether the same trick would work on his gym shoes, which had been a mystery to him since October. He also wondered about the second gym shirt in his locker, the one he'd crumpled up wet on Monday and forgotten about until Friday. He looked at the taped cloth, then at his backpack hanging on the chair.

"Nobody touch anything," he said. "I have to go check on something."

The rumor arrived on a Tuesday, in the seventh-grade group chat someone had optimistically named Homework Help. "Everyone knows Liliana took the fundraiser money," Ayaan wrote, and then three other people said some version of the same thing. By Thursday the message had been reposted, screenshotted, and restated so many times that Harper couldn't scroll past it without seeing Liliana's name attached to the word "sketchy." Nobody posted a receipt. Nobody posted a photo of an empty cash box. They just kept saying it, and the saying itself seemed to be the proof.

Harper noticed something odd about herself, though. On Tuesday she had thought the rumor was ridiculous, because Liliana had once chased her half a block to return a dropped bus pass. By Thursday, some quiet part of her brain had started to feel that it was plausible. Not proven. Just... likely. And she couldn't point to a single new piece of evidence, because there wasn't one. What had changed was the number of times she'd read the sentence.

She decided to run a test. In the chat she posted, in a casual tone, "fun fact: the vending machine on the second floor is being removed because it sold expired yogurt." Then she logged in as nobody in particular and repeated it. She reworded it slightly the second time, because a good scientist modifies the conditions a little, and waited. By lunch, someone had replied, "yeah I heard that too," and someone else had written, "my cousin goes here and she said the yogurt thing is real." Harper had invented the yogurt thing eleven minutes earlier.

She looked up what was going on and found a stack of search results. "Listen to this," she typed to Ayaan in a private message. "In 1977, Lynn Hasher and her colleagues did a study and found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true." Ayaan replied with a single wide-eyed emoji, then: "so the chat has basically been running the experiment on us for free."

Harper went back into the main chat and posted her evidence, screenshots and all: the invented yogurt rumor, the timeline, the original posts about Liliana with no source behind them. She pointed out the loaded words, the "everyone knows," the way a kid had even claimed some streamer had mentioned it, as if a person with a million followers would know what happened in their cafeteria. The typing dots bubbled up and vanished several times. Then a message landed from Ms. Chowdhury, who had apparently been added to the chat at some point and reading silently, which was its own kind of horror: "Harper, see me after class. Bring the screenshots."

Ayaan sent her one last message before the bell. "Expired yogurt," he wrote. "Never change."

Max had forty minutes until the rehearsal at Hartwell Concert Hall, and one page of music that might as well have been written in code. The title, "Morning Walk," was followed by a scattering of Italian words: largo, then andante, then allegro near the end. Mr. Watanabe had handed out the sheets that morning and said only, "Trust the words, not your habits." Max had shoved the pages into his durable black folder and forgotten about them until now.

He found Jaya and Rose in the third row of the hall, already assembling their music stands. The place smelled like dust and lemon polish, and the stage lights transmitted a warm amber glow across the empty seats. Max climbed up beside them and set his folder on the stand. "I think I've got it," he said. "Largo must be the big finish, right? It sounds like 'large.' And andante sounds quick, like 'ante up.' So we start fast and get bigger."

Rose frowned at her page. "The citation at the bottom says the arranger lived in Milan. Maybe the words are just, like, style names."

"Style names, speed names, same thing," Max said. "Let's just play it."

They counted in together, Max on piano, Jaya on flute, Rose on snare drum. Max launched into the opening at a gallop, loud and proud, and the whole thing collapsed within eight bars. Jaya's flute line wandered off, Rose's rim-taps scrambled to catch up, and the melody that was supposed to unfold gently became a stampede. Mr. Watanabe's voice floated down from the balcony. "Again. Slower. Read the page."

Max stared at the sheet, cheeks hot. The problem wasn't his fingers; they knew the notes. The problem was something invisible on the page, some rule hiding inside those words. He thought about the title again. Morning Walk. A walk. Andante. Walking pace. He flipped his pencil over and wrote the words in a column: largo, andante, allegro. If andante was walking speed, then largo, sitting before it, had to be even slower, and allegro, at the end, had to be the fast part. The piece was a story that sped up, not one that started fast.

"Andante means at a walking pace," he said slowly, testing it out loud. "That's why it fell apart. I was running through a walk." Jaya tapped the first measure. "So largo is very slow, like barely moving, and allegro is fast and lively at the end." Rose grinned and loosened her drum key a quarter turn. "Finally, a plan."

They played it again. The opening stretched out, long and quiet as fog over a field. When the andante section arrived, Max let his hands settle into the easy rhythm of footsteps, and Jaya's flute floated in on top of it. By the allegro, the hall itself seemed to wake up, Rose's drum snapping like popcorn, the last chord ringing out into the high dark ceiling. Mr. Watanabe came down the stairs applauding, and Jaya slid her flute case over so there was room for him to sit.

"Same time Thursday," he said. "And Max, bring the pencil. It's doing good work."

Aubrey sat at the kitchen table with her math notebook open to a page that said, in her own handwriting, PROBLEM SET FROM HELL. She was supposed to solve linear equations by doing the same thing to both sides, which had seemed easy in class and now seemed like a trick someone was playing on her specifically. Her dad had told her the practice would pay off in a cumulative way, all the skills stacking up. She had said "mm" and taken her notebook to the kitchen, where the snacks were.

She had just gotten x to equal 4 on her third try when Neil texted her a photo. It was a photo of the whiteboard from math club, which had preceded her dad's kitchen by forty minutes in her evening, and which she had skipped to eat leftover pizza. On the board, in Neil's handwriting, was a "proof" that 1 equals 2. Below it, Marlowe had written CHECKMATE, MATH.

Aubrey set down her pencil and copied the steps onto her own page. Start with a equals b. Multiply both sides by a. Subtract b squared from both sides. Factor. So far so legal; she checked each line by doing the operation to both sides, the way Ms. Clarke had drilled into them until it was basically muscle memory. Then the proof divided both sides by a minus b, and one line later declared that 1 equals 2, with a little flourish.

Aubrey stared at the step. She tried it with real numbers. If a equals b, say both of them are 5, then a minus b is 5 minus 5, which is 0. She wrote it out. The proof had divided both sides by zero. She remembered Marlowe, of all people, saying it at lunch last week, mouth full of sandwich: "You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer." Aubrey had assumed Marlowe was quoting a fortune cookie. Apparently it was load-bearing.

She texted back: division by zero, step 5. Also she's right, and I owe Marlowe a cookie. Then, because the kitchen table was right there and the pizza was gone, she went back to her problem set. The equations behaved now that she watched what she did to both sides, dividing only by actual numbers, never zero, like she was checking a label for something she was allergic to and had wisely skipped the antibiotic.

Neil texted back a single word: traitor. Aubrey picked up her pencil and solved for x.

Anthony had one job on a Saturday afternoon at the mall: find a birthday present for his mother before her dinner at seven. He had twenty dollars and an hour, and Axton had tagged along because he was bored.

In the electronics store, Gurleen from his homeroom was standing at a display laptop, typing fast. "Look at this," she said when she saw them. "Remember my old craft blog from fifth grade? I found it. Every single post."

"How?" Anthony asked. "You deleted it last year. You said so."

She turned the laptop toward him. The page looked old, the banner crooked, a photo of her bracelet instructions sitting there like it had never left. "Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages," she said. "This part of it is called the Wayback Machine. Anyone can look at old versions of websites. Axton, try yours."

Axton typed the address of a video channel he had abandoned in sixth grade. A saved copy came up, dated three years back, complete with a map widget on the sidebar showing his old neighborhood. "That was my location thing," he said quietly. "I forgot I turned that on."

Anthony pulled out his phone and typed in the blog address he had used in fifth grade, the one with his skateboard tricks. The page loaded. There was his face, twelve years old, grinning in front of his house with the street number visible on the door. Below it, a post that read "gone to Riverside Skate Park every Saturday, come find me." He had written that when he was naive enough to think only his friends read it. Strangers could have read it too, at the time, and they still could, because here it was, saved.

"It's like donating something without knowing," Gurleen said. "I put that stuff up, and some archive took a copy and stored it. I never agreed to that exactly, but it's public, so it happened anyway."

Anthony tested it. He went to the top of the page and clicked through the list of dates, and the site had been saved eight separate times, each one a snapshot, like the mall directory board that photographed the food court every hour. Nothing he did on his phone now could remove those copies. His Saturday location, posted by his twelve-year-old self, was still findable by anyone with his old web address.

He screenshotted the page for himself, then closed the phone and got back to the present problem. In the candle shop near the escalator he found a lavender candle for fourteen dollars, paid the cashier, and still had time left.

"At least we know now," Gurleen said, catching up with him by the fountain.

"Yeah," Anthony said. "Check your old accounts before you post anything new." He dropped the candle in his backpack and headed for the exit doors.

Easton dug through his backpack on his grandfather's tiled porch, trying to excavate his pocket money from under a paperback and a tangle of earbuds. He came up with eight euros in coins, which should have been plenty, but he could not be sure, because he had never once ordered anything in French. Across the courtyard, his grandfather's kitchen window stood open, and the smell of coffee drifted out into the warm afternoon.

"Are you going to stare at your money all day?" Tristan called from the gate. Tristan had spent two summers at this house before and had one clear goal: to reach the crêpe stand in the square before the best flavors sold out, and he wanted Easton to do the ordering for both of them. "You promised. You've been practicing all week."

"I've been practicing words," Easton said, pocketing the coins. "Saying them to an actual person is different." His assumption had been that everyone at the stand would switch to English the moment he stumbled, which would make the whole thing pointless. Tristan shrugged and said that had not happened to him last year, so they would find out.

The square was quiet, with plane trees dropping dappled light onto the stone, and the crêpe stand had a short line. Easton listened while he waited. The man ahead of them, a local, pointed at a crêpe and asked, "C'est combien ?" and the vendor answered with a price. Then a woman at the other end of the counter asked, "Combien ça coûte ?" about a bottle of cider, and got an answer too. Two different questions, Easton thought, and the vendor had treated them the same way, so both must mean "How much is it?" He filed that away like a coin he could actually spend.

When their turn came, Easton stepped up. "Bonjour. Un crêpe au chocolat, s'il vous plaît," he said, and the words came out steadier than he expected. The vendor nodded and started pouring batter. Easton hesitated, then tried it. "C'est combien ?"

"Quatre euros cinquante," the vendor said. Easton did the math quickly. Four fifty for his, and Tristan wanted lemon and sugar, probably cheaper, so his eight euros would cover both with change to spare. He ordered the second crêpe, paid, and collected the warm paper sleeves.

"You did it," Tristan said, already tearing off a corner of his crêpe. "Better than my first try, honestly."

"Next time I'm going to try it the other way," Easton said, taking a bite. "Combien ça coûte?" He pointed at a bottle of cider sitting by the counter, and the vendor laughed and told him.

Justin had never built a spreadsheet before, and the empty grid on Mr. Ramírez's classroom computer looked like a piece of graph paper waiting to embarrass him. The tech club was keeping score for the sixth-grade reading challenge, and whoever built the tracker got to present it at Friday assembly. Justin wanted that job. He typed each class's book count into a column, then hunted through the menus until he found SUM and dragged it across the cells. A total appeared at the bottom, and he leaned back so fast his chair squeaked.

Then Quinn leaned over his shoulder. "That total's wrong. Room 12 read 43 books, not 34. You flipped the digits." Justin checked her list and groaned. He clicked on the cell with 34, typed 43 instead, and before he touched anything else, the grand total at the bottom changed on its own. He stared at it. He changed the number back to 34, watched the total drop, then typed 43 again and watched it climb right back. "It's watching the whole column," he said slowly. "Change anything inside it and the total fixes itself."

He had to be sure. He picked a harmless cell at the top, added ten to it, and the total went up by exactly ten the instant he pressed enter. He put it back. Myah, who was building the chart next to him, had been quiet this whole time, the way she got when she was concentrating. "Make the bars now," she said. "The chart reads the same numbers, so it should follow them too." Justin highlighted the column and inserted a bar chart, and five bars jumped onto the screen, the tallest one belonging to Room 9.

That night he couldn't stop thinking about it, so he texted Quinn. "I fixed the typo and the total changed before I even asked it to. SUM watches the range." Her reply came fast. "So if Mr. Ramírez adds books tomorrow, the chart updates too?" He wrote back, "Try it. Change one cell, watch the bar." In the morning, sunlight through the window refracted off the screen while Quinn tapped in a new number, and the bar for her class grew taller without either of them touching the chart.

At Friday assembly, Justin stood in front of everyone with the projector glowing behind him. "One typo taught me the best part," he said. "Fix the number, and the total and the chart fix themselves." Afterward Myah nudged him. "Told you typing stamina pays off." Justin laughed and said, "Mistakes are inevitable. Fixing them is automatic."

The mirror in the girls' bathroom had told the truth that morning, and the truth had three red bumps along Rebecca's chin. Nothing like this had happened last year, which was the part that bugged her most. She spent all of math class sketching a timeline in her notebook: smooth skin in September, one tiny bump in February, three bumps now. Something had changed, and she meant to find out what.

After school she marched into Murphy's Pharmacy with her allowance crumpled in her pocket. Maddox had promised to meet her there, and he was already leaning against the shelf of face washes like he'd been waiting for hours.

"They multiply at night," Rebecca whispered, pointing at her chin. "Every morning there's more. It's like they're nocturnal."

Maddox peered at her face with scientific seriousness. "Maybe you sleep on a dirty pillowcase."

"That was my first theory. I changed it. Didn't help." She grabbed two bottles and turned them over. "So now I'm reading labels, because labels have to tell you what's actually in there."

The first bottle said it fought oil. The second said it removed excess oil gently. She flipped to the back panels and found tiny words like salicylic acid and oil-free. Then, on a pamphlet tucked behind the shelf, she found a paragraph that made her stop dead. Hormones in puberty, it said, make the oil glands in the skin produce more oil, and that extra oil is called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.

"Sebum," she read aloud. "That's the actual word for it."

"So it's not my pillowcase theory," Maddox said.

"It's not dirt at all. It's me. My own skin started making extra oil because of puberty." She felt a strange, buzzing relief. The cause was invisible, but it had a name, and named things could be fought.

She picked the face wash that said oil-free, paid the cashier, and practically bounced out the door. Halfway home she spotted Ms. Berg on her porch, arguing on the phone with her landlord about a leaky pipe, and waved so hard she nearly dropped her bag. Ms. Berg covered the phone and mouthed, "Tomorrow?" Rebecca nodded. Tomorrow was Saturday, and Maddox and Caroline were coming over to build the model volcano for science class, the one they'd decided would accelerate baking soda and vinegar with a secret extra ingredient.

That night Rebecca washed her face exactly as the bottle directed, twice, and studied the three bumps in the mirror like a general studying enemy territory.

"Okay, sebum," she said. "I know your name now."

She snapped off the light and grinned at the dark.

Megan had claimed the window seat with a blanket, two granola bars, and a photocopied story called "The Scarlet Ibis" that Ms. Takahashi had handed out on Friday. Monday's assignment sat underlined twice at the top of the page: find the foreshadowing, find the symbolism, explain what each one suggests. Megan had read the first three pages at the kitchen table, where her little brother kept invading her space to ask if she knew where the tape was, so she had retreated to the nook and pulled the curtain half shut behind her.

The narrator's little brother, Doodle, was small and fragile and not supposed to live long, though he did. Megan got that far easily. Then, on page six, a red bird blew in with a storm and dropped out of the tree into the family garden, and the family crowded around it, and the bird died there among the flowers. Megan read the paragraph twice. A strange bird in a strange garden, red as blood, dying right in front of the fragile boy. She texted Emelia.

"Is a bird dying in the garden supposed to mean something or is it just a bird"

Emelia texted back fast, which meant she was also avoiding homework. "Ms. T said stories don't waste ink. If it feels too obvious it's on purpose."

Megan chewed her pen. Too obvious, maybe, or too ambiguous to prove. She flipped ahead to test the idea, since guessing was cheaper than rereading. At the end, the narrator ran through a storm, and Doodle, fragile Doodle, fell behind, and when the brother went back for him, Doodle was under a bush, and the narrator described him in a way that made Megan close the book for a second.
