"That's actually smart," Violet admitted, and she felt a small pang, because Layton always had the smart ideas and she was the one who stayed up late with paint on her knuckles. She traded him a cookie for the sorting, which felt like a fair price, though it wasn't.

The three of them painted in a silence broken only by the scrape of brushes. When her blue bled into the yellow and made a smear of green, Violet nearly cried, but Layton blotted it with a paper towel before it spread. The wheel survived, mostly.

It was Mr. Dhillon, their neighbor, who cracked the question open. He came by to return Violet's mom's casserole dish, noticed the painted circle on the table, and said only, "You know, Newton has a whole book about color. It's on the shelf in my garage if you want it." He did not explain further, which was his way.

Violet found the book that evening, an old fat copy of Opticks, first published in 1704. She turned the pages at her own kitchen table, past diagrams of prisms, until she reached a drawing that stopped her cold: the colors of the spectrum arranged in a circle, an early form of the color wheel. Isaac Newton, the gravity man, had drawn this shape before anyone else thought to. She sat with that for a long moment, feeling oddly cheated and oddly thrilled at once, because now her wheel was a copy after all, and every wheel ever made was too.

She painted a tiny N in the center of her own circle, small enough that only she would notice it. Then she texted Bradley a photo of the page and waited, brush hovering, for the three dots to appear.

Maya stood in the laundry aisle of the grocery store with a crumpled list in her hand. Her mother was working a double shift, the basket at home was overflowing, and Maya had decided she would learn to do laundry herself before school on Monday. She picked up a bottle of detergent, read the back, and put it back. The second bottle promised something about colours, so she took that one.

At the end of the aisle, Ms. Ortiz from next door was comparing two boxes of dryer sheets. "First load?" she asked, nodding at the detergent.

"First load ever," Maya said. "I sorted everything into darks and lights already. I'm doing the darks first."

"Good plan," said Ms. Ortiz, and nothing more, which Maya appreciated. She paid at the register, lugged the bottle home, and loaded the washing machine with the pile of dark clothes: jeans, black t-shirts, her navy hoodie, and Rafaelle's grey hoodie, which he had left in her locker on Friday and told her she could borrow all weekend.

While the machine filled, Maya went through her own pockets by habit. A hair tie, a receipt, four cents. She dumped everything on the counter and shut the lid. The machine ran for forty minutes, and she used the time to fold a load her mother had left in the dryer, redoing a fitted sheet twice before the corners gave in. Folding, she decided, took more stamina than it looked like it would.

When she pulled the dark load out, she stopped. Every single item was speckled with tiny white shreds, dotted across the jeans, clinging to the hoodie sleeves, packed into the seams. She held up Rafaelle's grey hoodie and turned it over. Shreds everywhere. She turned her own pockets inside out, one by one. Clean. All clean.

She stood in front of the machine and thought. The shreds had to come from somewhere. They were on every item in the load, so whatever had made them had been inside the machine with the clothes. She had checked her pockets, so it had not been hers. Which left one hoodie she had not checked, because it was not hers to check.

She went back to Rafaelle's hoodie and felt along the front pocket. Inside, stuck to the lining, was the remains of a paper tissue, half dissolved, still shedding. It had broken apart in the wash, and its shreds had scattered over everything else. That, she realized, was why people checked pockets before washing, even pockets that belonged to other people.

She shook each item over the trash can, then ran the whole load through again with an extra rinse. Some shreds came off. The navy hoodie still held a few stubborn specks in its intricate stitching along the cuffs. She picked at them with tweezers and revised her plan for Monday: get the hoodie back to Rafaelle before he looked closely, or tell him first.

Monday morning, she found him at his locker with the hoodie folded over her arm, one last white speck still caught in the cuff. She held it out.

"You did laundry?" Rafaelle said. "Nice." He took the hoodie and started to put it on, then paused, his thumb finding the speck. "What's this?"

Maya took a breath. "Okay, so, whose tissue was in your pocket?"

Harrison had always thought the clock in Grandpa's hallway was broken, because its ticking never matched the one in the kitchen. Now the house was quiet for a different reason, and both clocks had been stopped by an aunt with careful fingers, and Harrison stood between them not knowing what to do with his hands.

Saad and Walid had come with his mother for the gathering after the funeral, and the three of them ended up at the kitchen table, where a stack of folded papers sat beside a bowl of walnuts nobody was eating. "What are those?" Walid asked. "The one from the newspaper," Harrison said. "It's the obituary. It's the notice that runs in the paper when someone dies, with a short account of their life, their family and work and things like that." Saad pulled one from the stack and unfolded it, and Harrison read over his shoulder, expecting the version of Grandpa he already knew: retired machinist, three grandchildren, loved his garden.

Then he hit the word sailor.

"He was in the merchant marine," Harrison said slowly. "Two years. It says here he crossed the Atlantic eleven times." He looked up. "He never told me that. Not once. Not even when I did my boat project in fifth grade and he helped me sand the hull." Walid frowned. "Maybe the paper got it wrong. Papers get things wrong." Harrison stared at the small grey column, feeling the ground shift a little, because if the paper was right, then there was a whole Grandpa he had never met, and the only person who could ask was gone.

"So test it," Saad said. "If he was a sailor, there'd be stuff. Sailors leave stuff behind."

They started in the attic, where the July heat pressed down through the pink insulation between the rafters and everything smelled of cedar and dust. Under a trunk lid that took all three of them to lift, they found a folded chart of the North Atlantic with a soft crease worn molten-shiny from being opened and closed hundreds of times. They found a brass compass in a leather case, and a notebook with tide tables copied out by hand. "He kept this," Harrison said, turning the compass so the needle swung and settled. "He kept all of it, and he never said a word."

Downstairs, Mr. Chatterjee from next door was helping carry chairs, and when he spotted the compass in Harrison's hand he stopped in the doorway. "I wondered where that had gone," he said. "Your grandfather taught me to read that chart the summer I retired. Said a man who'd crossed an ocean eleven times could stand to teach one old neighbour a little navigation." He smiled at Harrison's face. "He never talked about it at the fence, though. Said the sea was private."

Harrison looked at the compass, then at Mr. Chatterjee. "Would you teach me now?" he asked.

"Every Saturday," Mr. Chatterjee said. "Bring the chart."

Leo had signed up to volunteer at the community food bank that operated out of the annex behind the animal shelter, mostly because his mother had said he needed to do something useful over spring break. He had expected the place to smell like kibble, since the dogs were right through the connecting door, but the annex smelled like oranges. Three crates of oranges, a bin of lettuce with brown edges, and a shelf of dented canned soup covered most of the floor.

"Grocery store donations," said Kayson, who had been volunteering there since January and clearly considered himself an expert. "We sort the good from the bad, box up the good, and Mr. Oliveira takes whatever people won't eat over to the animals. Pigs get a lot of it."

Leo picked up a bag of grapes with one squashed bunch at the bottom. "So this whole bag counts as bad because of one bunch?" he asked.

"That's the rule."

That seemed bizarre to Leo. He pulled the squashed bunch out, set it aside, and looked at the rest of the grapes, which were fine. If stores threw away whole bags because of one bad part, no wonder there was so much food here. He started keeping count on the back of a receipt, one tally for every container where only part of the food was spoiled. By the time he hit nineteen, only four containers were spoiled all the way through.

"I hypothesize the store just doesn't want to pay someone to pick through it," Leo said, tapping the receipt. "It's faster to toss the whole thing."

"You hypothesize?" Kayson said, grinning. "You sound like my science teacher." But he came over and looked at the tallies anyway. On the wall by the sink there was a poster with smiling vegetables on it, and Kayson read the small print out loud. "The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted." He whistled. "Thirty to 40 percent. That's almost half."

Leo stared at his tally sheet. Part of that number had to be bags like this, whole containers tossed for one soft bunch. He tested his idea on the next crate of lettuce. Instead of throwing the brown-edged bin out, he stripped the outer leaves off each head and put the pale green centers in the people box. He got eight good heads out of it, enough for eight families.

Mr. Oliveira came through the connecting door with an empty wheelbarrow, looked at the two boxes, and raised an eyebrow at the tallies on the receipt. "You want to write down the numbers every week? If we can show the store how much is still good, maybe they'll sort it before it comes to us." He slid the wheelbarrow over for the outer leaves and the squashed grapes, which the pigs apparently would not mind at all.

Leo said yes before he finished thinking about it. That night he sat at the kitchen table trying to finish an English assignment, a poem about his week, and found himself writing a stanza about oranges and lettuce heads and the smell of dogs through a doorway. He read it once, crossed out two lines, and wrote a better one underneath.

Luke sat cross-legged on the floor of Paul's bedroom, holding Paul's phone with both hands, staring at the group chat.

WHERE ARE YOU, the message said. He had typed it himself, all capitals, thirty seconds ago.

"You have to admit it stands out," Paul said, peeking over his shoulder. "Everything else in that chat is lowercase. Kendra writes entire sentences without a single capital. It's kind of a revolution in laziness."

Three dots appeared at the bottom of the screen. Then Kendra's reply came through: "why are you yelling at us?"

Luke frowned at the phone. "I wasn't yelling. I was typing."

"Doesn't matter," Paul said, taking a chip from the bag between them. "Everybody reads caps as shouting. That's just how it works. Type it again like a normal human."

Luke thought about that. The two of them were supposed to meet Kendra at the skate park at three, and it was already two-forty, and nobody had answered his first message, the polite lowercase one that said "hey we still on for today?" That message had sunk into the chat like a stone into a pond. The all-caps one had gotten a reply in under a minute.

So there was a rule here, and the rule had two sides. Quiet messages disappeared. Loud messages got noticed, but the people who noticed them thought you were angry at them. He could not see Kendra's face, could not hear her voice, and somehow the shape of the letters was doing the job of a tone of voice.

He tried an experiment. He typed: "sorry, not yelling, just late. are you still coming?"

Then, after a pause, he added a second message, all capitals: "AND BRING THE EXTRA WHEEL."

"See, now that second one just sounds like you're furious about a wheel," Paul said.

But the reply came fast. "lol ok. and why were you screaming at your phone earlier?" Then a string of laughing faces. Kendra had understood. The capitals were loud, but when you put them next to a calm message, the loudness turned into a joke instead of a fight.

Luke leaned back against Paul's bed and thought through what had just happened, because it felt bigger than one afternoon. At the park, Kendra would hear his actual voice, and his tone would come along for free. On the phone, tone had to be built out of letters and punctuation, and everyone had agreed on the meanings without ever saying them out loud. A period at the end of "ok" could feel cold. All caps could eliminate every other message on the screen. None of it was proportional to anything; nobody had actually raised a voice, and yet people got hurt or laughed or answered, all depending on shapes.

He typed one more message to test the idea: "MEETING AT THE USUAL SPOT."

Kendra answered before he even set the phone down. "stop SHOUTING and yes we're leaving now."

Paul grabbed his board off the wall hooks and pulled open the bedroom door. Luke stood, pocketed the phone, and followed him down the stairs into the bright afternoon.

"NEXT TIME," Luke said in his loudest voice, "I'LL JUST SEND A PIGEON."

"THAT'S STILL SHOUTING," Paul yelled back, and his little sister, passing through the kitchen, told them both to knock it off.

Norah had fifteen minutes before her mom picked her up, so she spread her math sheet on the counter of the corner store beside the slurpee machine and got to work. The sheet was due tomorrow, and she had gotten every question right until the last one, which had brackets in it, and something about brackets made her brain fold in half.

Eliana slid in beside her with a bag of chips. "That one's easy. It's just three times x plus two, so three x plus two." She snapped a chip in half for emphasis.

Norah wrote 3x + 2, solved it, and got x equals three. Then she did what Ms. Chaudhry had drilled into them all week: she checked it. She substituted three back into the original equation, and the two sides came out different. Not close. Different. She erased so hard the paper went thin.

"See, it doesn't check," Norah said. "So something before the solving step went wrong." She looked at the brackets again. The three sat outside them like a guard. Maybe it wasn't just multiplying the x. She tried multiplying both things inside, so 3(x + 2) became 3x + 6, and solved from there. This time, when she substituted her answer back, both sides matched exactly.

"Wait, why?" Eliana leaned over the counter, chip forgotten.

"Because the three multiplies both terms inside," Norah said. "Not just the x. The two gets it too."

Charles-Edouard appeared from the magazine rack holding a wildlife magazine with a kangaroo on the cover. "That's a marsupial," he said, tapping the picture, "and that's the only thing I understand in this store." He squinted at their paper. "The cover says the photos depict animals in their natural habitat, which is more than I can say for math homework in a corner store."

Norah laughed, then copied the corrected steps into her notebook so she would remember. She wrote it out explicit and plain: clear the brackets first, then solve. She left out the part about feeling stupid, because she didn't, really. She had found the error herself, with the check, before the teacher could circle it in red.

Ms. Chaudhry came in for her evening coffee and paused at the counter. "Homework in my store now, Norah?"

"Last question," Norah said. "It almost beat me." She held up the sheet so the brackets showed. "But I got it. Want to check it?"

Ms. Chaudhry took a pen from behind the counter and substituted the answer back in, right there beside the candy display. "Checks out," she said, and dropped a coin on the counter for her coffee.

Maria's problem was simple: on Friday she had to stand in front of Mr. Tang's science class and explain why we have seasons, and she did not understand it herself. She only knew the sentence she was supposed to memorize, which was about the tilt of Earth's axis, and memorizing felt like cheating.

On Tuesday she stayed after school with Hussain, who wanted the classroom's old globe for the chess club display he was building. He carried it to their table, and while he wiped dust off the stand with his sleeve, Maria turned the sphere slowly. Two dotted lines circled it, one above the equator and one below.

"What are these for?" she asked.

"No idea," Hussain said. "They're on every globe, though. My grandpa has one in his shop with the same lines."

Aedan, who was passing on his way to basketball practice and could never resist stopping where people were arguing, leaned over. "Those mark something. I read a page about it once." He pulled out his phone, tapped for a minute, and read aloud. "Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Around December 21, it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn."

"So the top dotted line is the Tropic of Cancer," Maria said, "and the bottom one is the Tropic of Capricorn." She stopped turning the globe. The dates were June 21 and December 21. She knew those dates; they were the first day of summer and the first day of winter, at least where she lived. And the Cancer line was north of the equator, on her side of the world. She traced it with her finger, then the southern one. "When the Sun is overhead here, it's summer here. When it moves down to the other line, it's our winter."

"That's contagious, your face right now," Aedan said. "You look like you actually get it."

She borrowed the flashlight from Mr. Tang's desk, with a promise that returning it was an obligation she would not forget. She held it level and shone it straight down over the Tropic of Cancer, watching the light bunch into a small bright circle on the globe's surface. Then she kept the flashlight level and slid it down until the beam hit the Tropic of Capricorn. The bright circle followed. In her mind she added the axis, tilted, always tilted the same way, and saw the northern half leaning toward the light in one position and away from it in the other.

That night she wrote a message to Hussain, because he had taken the globe to chess club: "Don't let anyone draw on it. I need the two dotted lines visible on Friday. If your display contract with Mr. Tang says you can keep the globe all week, bring it to Room 12 before first period anyway. Maria."

On Friday she stood at the front with the globe and the flashlight. She shone the beam onto the dotted line in the north, said June 21, then moved the light to the southern line and said December 21, and watched Mr. Tang nod.

Benjamin sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field with his arm propped on his knee, the white cast making him look like he was wearing half a suit of armor. The doctor had printed out his X-ray, and he'd been staring at it all through math class, then through lunch, and now here, while his teammates ran drills without him. Hawa dropped onto the bench beside him, sweating and holding out half her granola bar.

"Look at this," Benjamin said, pointing at the film. "The bones glow white, and everything else is basically invisible. My whole arm, gone, except the bones." He turned the film toward the low sun, frowning. "I asked my little brother why, and he said the machine paints them. That can't be right."

Hawa leaned over and squinted. "My mom's a radiology tech. She told me once. The calcium in your bones absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them, so the bones show up white." She bit her granola bar. "Basically the machine can't see through the calcium, so that part stays white on the picture."

Benjamin went still. He stared at the X-ray again, and this time he wasn't looking at the forearm bones at all. He was looking at a small white smudge near his wrist, one he'd assumed was part of the break. "Hawa. Calcium is in the bone. So a white spot has to be something dense." He tapped the smudge with his finger. "That's separate from the fracture line."

"So? It's bone stuff," Hawa said.

"No, because." He stopped, thinking hard, the way he did in science when a whole chain of reasoning had to line up before he could say a word. "Three days after they put the cast on, the itch near my wrist drove me crazy, and I pushed a bottle cap under the edge to scratch with it. Then I couldn't get it out. I tried to incorporate it into my life, like, fine, I live with a bottle cap now. But metal is dense too. Denser than calcium, even."

Hawa snatched the film and held it up. "Benjamin. That is absolutely a bottle cap."

They ran, well, Benjamin jogged with his good arm pumping, straight across the field to where Ms. Johansson was coaching the younger kids. He explained, breathless, holding out the X-ray, and she laughed so hard she had to sit on her heels. At the clinic the next morning, the doctor tilted the film, looked at Benjamin over her glasses, and said, "Most kids draw on their casts. You gave me a mystery." She cut a small window, and out slid a battered bottle cap, defiant to the last.

Hawa held it up like a trophy. "Evidence," she said. "Case closed."

The temple smelled of sandalwood and marigolds, and Mia held her notebook against her chest so nobody would see the heading she had written at the bus stop: AFTER DEATH, TWO ANSWERS. Her grandmother had been buried nine days ago, and Mia's mother had said heaven, plainly, like closing a door. Then Courtney had said something about ghosts in science class, and Mia had begun to suspect that nobody actually knew. So when Raya invited her to the gathering for Raya's grandfather, Mia brought the notebook and a plan.

She found Raya by the shoe shelves, stacking sandals in pairs. "I'm sorry about your grandfather," Mia said.

"He'll be back," Raya said.

"Back from where?"

Raya picked up a stray sandal. "Back here. Another life." She said it the way Mia's mother said heaven, like a fact you didn't check.

Mia kept her skepticism to herself and followed Raya into the hall, where plates of food were being passed down long rows. She watched Raya's grandmother set a bowl of rice in front of a framed photograph, fold her hands, and stand there. Mia nudged Raya. "Is she monitoring something? Like, waiting for a sign?"

"She's offering food," Raya said. "For his next journey."

Mia wrote: not gone to a place, going to another life. She tested the idea out loud. "So your grandfather isn't in heaven watching you. He's going to be a baby somewhere."

"Maybe not a baby," Raya said. "But the soul gets born again. The cycle is called samsara."

"How does it pick?" Mia asked. "Where you go, what you become?"

Raya looked at her, then at the photograph. "Karma," she said. "What you did, what kind of person you were, that decides the next life. My grandfather was good, so it will be a good one."

Mia sat with that. A rule you couldn't see, working like gravity, sorting every soul after every death. Her grandmother had made jam for the whole street and never said a harsh word about anyone. Under Raya's rule, that had to count for something. Under her mother's rule, it counted too, just in a different place. She turned to a clean page and drew two columns, headed them both with her grandmother's name, and wrote heaven on one side and samsara on the other.

"It's for school," she said, when Raya leaned over her shoulder.

"It's for your grandmother," Raya said, and tapped the notebook. "What are you putting under karma?"

Mia thought of the jars of plum jam still lined up in the pantry, labeled in her grandmother's careful hand. She wrote: gave everything away. Then she underlined it twice, closed the notebook, and went to help carry the rice to the photograph.

The bus home from school smelled like wet boots and oranges, and Evan had his laptop balanced on his knees, flipping between two baseball pages. He wanted to settle an argument with Hendrik once and for all: which player was better, David Justice or Derek Jeter, back in the nineties? He had the numbers, and numbers didn't lie.

"Look," Evan said, turning the screen toward Audrey, who slid into the seat across the aisle. "In 1995, Justice had a higher batting average than Jeter. And in 1996, Justice beat him again. Two years, two wins. Hendrik owes me a pop."

Audrey leaned in, chewing the end of her pencil. "Show me 1996." She squinted. "Okay, yeah. Justice, higher. Both years." She sat back, looking vaguely ominous, like a math teacher about to hand back a test nobody passed. "So case closed."

Evan grinned and started typing, planning to add the two seasons together for a victory chart, the kind with bars. He was already imagining the picture he'd text to Hendrik. Then he stopped typing. He ran the addition again. He ran it a third time, because the screen was telling him something that couldn't be true: Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher than Justice's.

"That's broken," Evan said. "The site's broken."

"It's two sites," Audrey said, pulling out her phone to check a different one. A minute later she held it up. "Same thing."

A kid a few rows back yelled something about a snow day, and the driver's wipers squeaked against the drizzle, but Evan barely heard any of it. He stared at the numbers. Justice won 1995. Justice won 1996. Put the seasons together and Jeter won. It felt like a magic trick with no magician in sight. Somewhere in his head, an idea began to germinate: maybe combining years wasn't the same as adding up wins, maybe the seasons themselves were doing something he couldn't see from the two averages alone. He grabbed a napkin from his lunch bag and started copying figures, testing one small idea after another, crossing most of them out.

"You realize," Audrey said, watching him scribble through a pothole, "that you can't actually send Hendrik a victory chart now."

Evan laughed, though it stung a little. That was the irony of the whole afternoon: he'd gone hunting for proof he was right and come home with proof the question was wrong. "I'm sending him this instead," he said. "Both seasons and the combined one. Let him lose sleep over it."

The bus lurched around the corner by the corner store, and Evan slid the napkin into his binder, careful not to smudge it. "First one to figure out why it works buys the pop," he said.

Anna had been standing at her grandfather's grave for ten minutes and still did not know what to do with her hands. The cemetery was quiet except for a crow somewhere behind the cedar hedge, and the granite marker in front of her looked the same as it had in March, gray and neutral and stubborn, as if it refused to admit anything had changed. She had brought tulips because her mother said flowers, and a scrub brush because she guessed dirt, but nobody had told her the order. Should the flowers come first, or the cleaning? She wondered whether there was a wrong way to do this, and whether her grandfather, who had opinions about everything from lawn mowing to lasagna, would let her feel it if she got it wrong.

Two rows over, a family of six appeared with rakes, buckets, and cloths, and they began working on an older grave as though they had done it a hundred times. Anna watched them sweep the stone, pull weeds from around the base, and wipe the carved letters until the names came back to life. Only after all of that did they set out small dishes of food and light sticks of incense. So that was the pattern: the cleaning had to precede the offerings. It made a kind of sense to her, the way you wash dishes before you set the table, and she felt a small spark of curiosity about where such a custom came from.

A girl about her own age knelt to brush leaves from the stone. Anna walked over, mostly to ask, and partly because watching them felt like borrowing someone else's courage. "Do you do this every year?" she asked.

"Every Qingming," the girl said, and when Anna's face must have looked blank, she added, "It's our festival, usually April fourth or fifth. Families go to their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings."

Anna thanked her and walked back to her grandfather. Her grandmother had died in February, and her grandfather had followed in June, and this whole year was a house with the furniture rearranged. She tested the idea she had just borrowed: she swept the brush across the top of the stone and watched dust and old rain streaks slide away. She worked the letters of his name one by one, GRAY letters first, then the rest, and the stone began to look like itself again. Her grandmother's name was on there too, underneath, and she cleaned that line as well, twice, carefully.

Then she set the tulips down and spoke out loud, quietly enough that only the crow and the granite could hear. "Okay. Now you." She stood with her palms flat on the warm stone until the other family's incense smoke drifted over on the breeze and curled around her wrists.

Grace counted the survey rows for the third time and got a different answer again. Two hundred and six students had answered the question "Should the cafeteria serve tacos every week?" and Ms. Patel wanted the results summarized by grade before Friday's assembly. Grace had been highlighting rows and tallying by hand, and every tally came out different.

"You're going to wear a hole in that trackpad," said Louie, leaning over from the next computer. "My dad says nobody does it this way anymore. At his office they use something called a pivot table."

"A what?"

"A pivot table. That's the actual name. He says a guy named Pito Salas invented it, back when he was working on a spreadsheet program called Lotus Improv. It came out in 1991." Louie shrugged. "He got all excited telling me. Said his colleagues still cherish the day they learned it, because it turned a whole afternoon of counting into two minutes."

Grace opened the help menu and found the pivot table option, half hidden under a menu she had never clicked. She dragged the grade field into the rows box and the taco answer into the values box, then hit refresh. The spreadsheet reorganized itself instantly: grade six, forty-one yes; grade seven, fifty-three yes; grade eight, thirty-eight yes. The rest were no votes, split neatly by row.

"Wait," said Akram from across the lab, wheeling his chair over. "Why does grade eight have so many more no votes than the others? Last year grade eight was the grade that petitioned for pizza Fridays." Grace stared at the numbers. She remembered that the grade eight survey had gone out the same week the cafeteria had raised prices, right when everyone was annoyed about everything. Maybe the tacos weren't really the issue. She wondered if the results were biased by timing, so she ran a filter to see which day each grade's answers had come in, and sure enough, most of the grade eight no votes were from the price-hike week. She tested it by separating the answers into two pivot tables, one for each week, and in the second week grade eight flipped to mostly yes.

Ms. Patel walked the aisle, stopped behind Grace's screen, and read the two tables side by side. "So what do we tell the assembly?"

Grace highlighted the second table. "Tell them tacos won. But if anyone asks why the first week looked weird, blame the price hike, not the tacos."

The restaurant's big screen filled the whole back wall, and every table near it was packed. Laurence had saved seats for her parents, her little brother, Nash, Leyla, and her cousin Leo, who had flown in that afternoon from Nigeria. On the screen, the stadium camera panned across thousands of fans as the game went to a tense half-time break.

Then the crowd did the wave. A whole section stood, threw up their arms, and sat down, and the motion swept around the stadium like water running through a channel. Her brother scrambled onto his chair and shouted, "Do it here! Do the wave!" Nash stood. Leyla stood. Half the restaurant stood, and the wave wobbled its way down the counter and died somewhere near the kitchen door.

"It's called the Mexican wave," Leo said, sitting back down. "That's what everyone at home calls it."

"No way," Nash said. "It's just the wave."

"It's the Mexican wave," Leo insisted. "Ask anyone."

Laurence watched the screen instead of arguing. The commentators were replaying the crowd shots, and she noticed the ticker at the bottom, a line about the World Cup. A thought assembled itself in her head, slow and then sudden: if the move picked up its name at a World Cup, then people in different countries would have all learned it at the same time, from the same giant tournament, and their name for it would stick in their region. Leo calling it the Mexican wave and Nash calling it the wave wasn't a fight about who was right. It was two languages for the same thing, like two doors into the same room. She couldn't see the reason directly, but she could test it. She pulled out her phone under the table.

"Cheating," Leyla said.

"Researching." Laurence typed fast. There it was: the wave became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, which was why so many English speakers outside North America called it the Mexican wave. She held the screen up. "Look. Same move, different name, depending on where you watched it from. They're equivalent."

Nash read it twice and frowned. "So we're both right?"

"That's my consensus," Laurence said, and Leyla laughed so hard she knocked over the ketchup.

Leo looked almost disappointed. "I wanted to win."

"You can win the next round," Laurence said. "The waiter's coming, and I'm going to prescribe you the milkshake with the chili powder in it. House rule."

On the screen the second half kicked off, and the whole restaurant stood up again.

Hunter crouched in front of his sketchbook on the gallery bench, glaring at his drawing of Main Street. The road looked like it had melted. The buildings leaned toward each other like tired old men, and nothing went where it was supposed to go.

"You've erased that corner four times," said Isaak, who was supposed to be taking photos for the school newspaper before the gallery closed at five. "Also, your street is haunted."

"It's not haunted, it's crooked." Hunter flipped his pencil sideways and squinted down it like a tiny carpenter. "Mr. Fernando said something today about lines all going to one point. I was doodling a shark at the time."

"That shark was lush, though. Best shark I've ever seen."

"Thanks. Totally useless shark."

They had come to the gallery because Mr. Fernando had given the class a challenge: draw a street in one-point perspective, due tomorrow morning, and the only hints he'd offered were "come look at the big wall in the west room" and "bring a friend, less moping." It was quarter to four now, and the west room held a huge print of Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper.

Hunter stood in front of it. Long table, thirteen men, windows behind. He traced the ceiling lines with his finger in the air, then the tapestry edges on the walls, then the table's side. Every line, if he extended it in his head, ran to the same spot. He walked closer, then closer still, until a guard cleared his throat meaningfully.

"Right there," Hunter said. "The ceiling, the walls, the table. It all aims at his head."

"Whose head?"

"The guy in the middle. They all meet at the same point. That's what Mr. Fernando meant. One point. A vanishing point, like the street goes into it and disappears."

Isaak leaned in with his camera, hunting for his newspaper shot, and zoomed way past polite distance. "Wait. There's a tiny hole. Like somebody poked it with a pin. Dead center."

Hunter's brain did a fast, joyful tumble. If every line led there, and there was a hole there, then somebody had pinned something at that exact spot. Strings. Guide strings, stretched from the hole outward to keep the lines true. A tiny nail hole, still visible, in one of the most famous paintings on Earth.

He ran back to the bench and excavated his pencil case from the bottom of his backpack, sharpened the pencil with his teeth like a barbarian, and started a fresh street. He marked one dot first, then made every roofline, curb, and doorway run obediently toward it. The buildings stood up straight. The street went somewhere and vanished.

"Done," he announced at 4:58. "Photograph it before they kick us out."

Isaak snapped the picture, then offered a settlement: he'd text Hunter the photo, but only if Hunter drew him one lush shark, in perspective, by Friday.

"Deal," Hunter said, and drew a dot for the shark to vanish into.

Dylan had promised Mr. Yip a poster for the community centre's heritage night, a big pie chart of the origins of people in a small town in Manitoba. He had the numbers from a census website, and they were broken. Scottish, 34 percent. Ukrainian, 22. English, 19. German, 12. Filipino, 11. He added them twice on the whiteboard in the craft room and got 98 percent both times, which was fine. Then he noticed he'd skipped a line. With the last two entries included, the total was 127 percent.

"You drew the pie wrong," said Vivienne, looking over his shoulder. "Or the town's impossible. One of those."

"It's not my pie," Dylan said. He drew a circle on the whiteboard and tried to decompose it into wedges that added up to more than the whole thing. It couldn't be done. A circle was a circle. Unless the wedges overlapped, which pies, in his experience, did not do.

Lina arrived with the glue gun and took the defiant view that the website was simply lying to them, the way websites did. She suggested he cut the extra 27 percent and go home. Dylan instead went to the computer room and searched until he found a page about the census. He read one line out loud, slowly, like a person checking a receipt: "The census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population."

Vivienne frowned. "Since 1981? That's, what, before my dad was even bald."

"So a person can be Scottish and Ukrainian at the same time," Dylan said. He wrote it on the whiteboard and drew two overlapping circles, like a Venn diagram, which was not a pie at all. "The wedges overlap. That's why it's over a hundred." He felt the particular joy of a rule discovered rather than told, and then the particular deflation of a poster to redo.

He stayed late, cutting new shapes. Instead of a pie he built overlapping circles with the community centre'spopulation written along the bottom, and in each overlap he taped a small photo of a real person from the centre. Mrs. Ocampo in the Filipino-Ukrainian overlap. The twins from swim practice in three circles at once. Mr. Yip came in at the end, looked at the poster for a long moment, and said, "So who's the antagonist here, the pie chart or the census?"

"The pie chart," Dylan said. "It started the fight."

Stella sharpened her pencil three times before she even touched the paper. Mr. Rodríguez had written "one-point perspective street scene" on the board and drawn a single dot in the middle of an example, and now everyone in the art room was supposed to make their own street plunge back toward that dot. Stella wanted hers to look like the road to her grandmother's house, with a bakery on the corner, but her first attempt had come out flat as a pancake. The buildings sat on top of the road instead of beside it.

"You look like you're about to boycott this assignment," Paige whispered from the next easel.

"I might," Stella said. "My street is broken."

Mr. Rodríguez walked past and paused at her table. He tapped the empty air above her drawing with one finger. "Draw your orthogonals first," he said, and moved on before Stella could ask what on earth those were.

Stella stared at the dot he had told her to mark, the vanishing point, sitting in the middle of her page like a tiny moon. Paige leaned over and slid a torn piece of sketchbook paper across the table. In round pencil letters it read: "I looked it up while he was talking. The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines. That's the whole secret. Your road edges have to aim at the dot. Claira already figured out the rooflines. Hurry up."

Stella read it twice. Then she looked at her drawing and saw the problem plainly: her road edges ran straight up and down the page, parallel, going nowhere. She flipped to a fresh sheet, marked her dot, and this time she started with those lines alone, the two road edges angling in toward the dot, then the curbs above them, then the long slope of a roofline on the bakery. It felt strange to draw a street with no buildings in it yet, only these slanted bones, but the bones were what held everything up. Where she had guessed wrong before, she could see it now: every line that was supposed to recede had been refusing to move.

She filled in the bakery between two rooflines, added the corner where her grandmother's mailbox would go, and even let herself draw a small green awning for the bakery window, carefully following the slant. At the next table Claira held up her own drawing so Stella could check it against hers. The toxic-yellow pencil Claira had used for her bus shelter looked almost warm against the gray street. Stella smiled and slid Paige's note back with one word added at the bottom: "Leisure is over. Look."

Paige read it, laughed quietly, and turned back to her own paper, drawing her first line straight toward the dot.

Sofia dragged the folding table out of the garage at eight in the morning, before the sun had fully cleared the rooftops. Her lemonade stand was not really about lemonade anymore. It was about the twenty dollars she had promised to add to Grandpa's birthday present, a frame for the old photograph of his father holding a bank book from 1929. For her history project she had found a record showing that after the 1929 crash, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 89 percent from its September 1929 peak to its low in July 1932. Her great-grandfather had put his savings into stocks right before that, and the money had never come back. She kept thinking about the number as she squeezed lemons: 89 percent, gone.

Ali arrived on a bike with a dented basket, skidding to a stop in the gravel. "You said you needed help. Is this about the project, or the money?"

"Both. I have to explain which is riskier, a stock or a bond, and why, and I keep getting tangled." Sofia poured a cup for the mail carrier, who waved and kept walking. "Ms. Clarke-Williams said to imagine explaining it to somebody at a lemonade stand. So I thought, actual lemonade stand."

Ryker showed up at ten with a notebook full of practice problems, because Ryker showed up to everything with a notebook. "Okay, test me," he said, holding out a cup. "Stocks and bonds. Bonds first."

"Ms. Clarke-Williams says bonds are like lending the stand ten dollars and it pays you back with a little extra," Sofia said. "Stocks are like owning a piece of the stand itself."

"Then stocks seem better," Ali said. "If the stand does great, your piece is worth more."

"Unless the whole town decides nobody wants lemonade ever again," Sofia said slowly. An idea was forming, and she reached for a marker and the cardboard sign. "Wait. I can test this."

She wrote two columns on the sign's blank side and labeled them with her neatest printing. Then she asked Ali to be the bond. "You lent the stand five dollars. Whatever happens, you get five dollars and a quarter back. Ryker, you own a tenth of the stand." She counted the morning's cash: eleven dollars and some coins. "Ryker gets a tenth of everything, good day or bad."

They played it out three times with imaginary days, a busy Saturday, a rainy Tuesday, a heat wave. Ali's nickel never changed. Ryker's take swung wildly, sometimes a pile of quarters, sometimes almost nothing. "So you can't just categorize one as good and one as bad," Sofia said, drawing an arrow between the columns. "The bond is a promise. The stock is a bet on the stand itself."

"The prototype of risk," Ryker said, pointing at the stock column.

Ali frowned at the sign. "But how bad can a real bet get?"

Sofia told them the number, the whole thing, the crash and the peak and the low. Ali was quiet for a moment, staring at the photograph sticking out of Sofia's binder, the bank book and the face above it. "Eighty-nine percent," Ali said. "That's like the stand burning down and taking Ryker's tenth with it, and then the lot going empty for three years."

"And the bond holder still gets paid back," Ryker said, "if whoever borrowed doesn't vanish."

"Unless," Sofia said, and wrote that word on the sign too, smaller, in the corner.

Ms. Clarke-Williams stopped by on her walk that afternoon and bought two cups. She read the cardboard sign, both columns, the arrows, the small word in the corner. "This is a market," she said, indicating the table, the cups, the line of neighborhood kids.

Sofia counted out Ryker's tenth of the day's earnings, four quarters and a dime, and dropped them into his palm. "Owing beats owning," he said, and Ali held up her fixed nickel like a trophy.

Elizabeth slid the Mandarin grammar book across the library table so fast it thumped into Francis's elbow. "Help," she said. "The paragraph is due Friday, and I can't find the future tense anywhere."

Francis rubbed his elbow and pulled the book toward his stack of notes. "It has to be in here," he said. "Spanish had a whole chapter on it. I need the same one, because my paragraph is about joining the robotics club next year, and Ms. Menon said it has to be about our real plans."

They flipped pages together while the radiators ticked and rain streaked the tall windows. Elizabeth found chapters on measure words and tone marks, but no chart of future endings. She sat back, frustrated. "Maybe the book is missing pages," she said. "Maybe someone tore them out."

"Nobody tore out a grammar chart," Francis said. He was already checking the index, which was its own kind of help, because it gave Elizabeth an idea.

"If the pages aren't missing," she said slowly, "maybe there's nothing to find. Maybe the verbs don't change at all." She grabbed a pencil and wrote the sentence she remembered from Monday's reading, the one about pandas being nocturnal, since their insulation of thick fur kept them warm even at night. Then she wrote her own sentence: next year she would join the art club. She looked at the two sentences side by side. The verb looked exactly the same in both. Same characters, same shape.

She found the difference somewhere else. The panda sentence had no time word. Her sentence had "míngnián," which meant next year, right at the front, doing all the work. She tested it, saying both sentences out loud under her breath while Francis watched. "The time word carries it," she said. "The whole future rides on that."

"So there's no future ending," Francis said, "because the verb never changes?"

"Right. And look." She pointed at a second word in her notes, "huì," sitting before the verb in a dialogue example. "This one helps too. It means will." Francis copied both words onto his palm with his marker, since he kept losing his index card, and wrote his robotics sentence with "míngnián" at the start.

They worked until the librarian flicked the lights once, her signal that the library closed in ten minutes. Elizabeth packed her bag, then saw Francis still frowning at his paragraph. She pulled out her grammar book and slid it across the table to him.

"Take it home," she said. "I've got what I need. Page forty-one, the panda part, in case you forget."

Francis grinned and zipped the book into his backpack just as the lights went dark. "Next year," he said, "huì," and held the door for her.

Naomi sat in the lobby of Castlefall, refreshing the clan list for the third time, because the Emberhawks had one open slot and tryouts closed at nine. Her headset crackled.

"You're the girl from the picture, right?" said a player whose tag was VexNine. "Karlee's friend. The one at the lake, blue kayak?"

Naomi's hand froze on the mouse. She had never seen VexNine before in her life. "How do you know about the kayak?"

"Someone posted it. Public clan album, like two years ago. It's got your whole names in the caption. Naomi plus last name."

She dropped out of the queue and opened a search engine in another window. She typed her own full name, half expecting nothing. The fifth result was a comment she had written in fifth grade on the Castlefall forums, calling a character named Lord Bramble the best antagonist ever written and signing it with her real name and her town. Below it, a link to the kayak photo, captioned by Karlee: "Naomi and me at Pine Lake!" The lake name was right there. Anyone who read it knew where she swam in summer.

Ronald joined the party channel. "You dropped queue. Tryout's in ten."

"Someone found a photo of me. From a public post Karlee made." She kept scrolling, systematic about it now, checking each result, working out which posts had her name and which didn't. The pattern was simple: the public stuff showed up, the private clan chat didn't. She ran a test, typing a phrase from an old private message into the search bar. Nothing came back. She typed a phrase from the public forum comment. First result.

"It's crawlers," VexNine said. "Automated programs that copy public pages so search engines can index them."

"So anything public gets copied," Naomi said slowly. "And it stays findable."

She messaged Karlee, who was offline, then went into her own old account and deleted the forum comment, all forty-one of them, one by one. The kayak photo she couldn't touch; it was Karlee's post. She rejoined the queue with four minutes left, won her duel, and got the Emberhawk slot.

Afterward she celebrated with Ronald in voice chat, though it felt thinner than she'd imagined. Then a clan notification popped up. The Emberhawks' roster page was public, and her full gamertag, which contained her real first name, had just been published to it. She watched the page load, knowing that somewhere a crawler was already on its way.

Gavin spread his boxes across the driveway at seven in the morning: old comics, a bin of plastic dinosaurs, three board games with all their pieces counted twice. His goal was fifty dollars for the robotics kit he'd seen online, and by eight he had made four. The problem, he decided, was not what he was selling. It was the price.

His neighbour Mr. Singh ran the garage sale next door, and Mr. Singh had the crowd. He had a crate of glass marbles, nothing special, and he had taped a sign to it that said TWENTY-FIVE CENTS EACH. A line of kids stretched past the mailbox. Gavin watched a boy buy eight marbles, come back ten minutes later, and buy six more.

"Those are just marbles," Gavin said to his friend Kane, who had shown up to help and was eating chips on the porch steps. "My dinosaurs are better."

"Then charge more for the dinosaurs," Kane said. Kane wanted a cut of the profits, ten percent, because he had carried the boxes from the basement and planned to stand at the curb shouting at cars all morning. Gavin told him he could have five percent if the shouting worked.

The shouting did not work. At a dollar per dinosaur, nobody touched them. At three for a dollar, a woman with a stroller bought six, but that was it. Gavin sat on the steps and tried to think it through the way his math teacher talked about quantifying things, putting actual numbers to a guess instead of just feeling that something was true. Fewer buyers at a higher price. More buyers at a lower one. The same box of dinosaurs both times, the same driveway, the same sky. Only the number on the sign had changed.

He looked over at Mr. Singh's table again. The marble line was gone, and Mr. Singh was reading a newspaper with his feet up. Gavin walked over. "What happened to your customers?"

"Sold the crate," Mr. Singh said. "A man came by and offered to take every marble I had. Volume business. When I first opened, though, I charged a dime each, and I could barely keep the jar full. Kids were back three times in an hour." He folded the newspaper. "Law of demand," he said, and went back to reading.

Gavin went back to his driveway and made a new sign. DINOSAURS, TEN CENTS. By ten o'clock the bin was nearly empty, and Jillian from his science class was arguing that the triceratops should cost more than the others because it was the only one with all three horns intact. Kane stood at the curb yelling "Aggressive deals, prehistoric prices!" at every passing car, which Gavin decided was worth the five percent. When the last dinosaur sold, Jillian held out a dime for the triceratops, and Gavin slid it across the table to her for free, because she'd been right, and because a kid who knew a bargain was worth keeping around.

Audrey pressed her sketchbook against the railing on the gallery's mezzanine and stared down at the big photograph on the far wall. It showed an empty street running straight back between two rows of buildings, and it was exactly the kind of picture she wanted to draw for the summer art contest. The theme was "My Street," and the deadline was Sunday, which gave her three days.

Her problem was simple and enormous: her streets looked wrong. Last night she had drawn the road outside her house four times, and every time it came out like a wedge of pie floating in the middle of the page. She had shown the drawings to her dad, who said they were nice, but nice was not the same as right.

"Audrey! Over here!" Ayana waved from the other end of the mezzanine, with Hendrik beside her holding a lemonade. The three of them had walked to the gallery after Ms. Nguyen had given them free passes from the community center.

"Look at this photo," Audrey said as they reached her. "The street looks like it goes back for miles, but it's flat paper. Flat paper with lines on it."

Hendrik leaned over the railing. "The buildings on the sides aren't smaller in real life."

"Right!" Audrey flipped her sketchbook to her failed drawings. "And my road edges are doing this." She traced them with her pencil. Both edges slanted inward, but they were aimed at different spots, and her sidewalk lines wandered off toward a third. Three different directions, none of them meeting anywhere.

Ayana squinted at the photo, then at Audrey's page, then at the photo again. "In the picture, the road edges come together. Like, actually together. Somewhere near that far door."

Audrey grabbed a fresh page. "One point. What if all of them, every line going back, they all have to hit the same point?" She held her pencil at arm's length toward the photograph, lining it up with the left road edge, then the right, then the sidewalk lines, then the rooflines of the buildings. The pencil kept landing on the same tiny patch of gray near the horizon, right where a distant door glowed in the street's far end. She felt a revolution start in her chest, like someone had flipped a drawing inside out.

"Here," she said, and drew a horizontal line across her page, then a single dot on it. "Vanishing point." She said the word out loud and it felt like a key turning. "And the line it sits on, that's where the horizon is. It's eye level. If I'm standing on the street looking straight ahead, that's where it goes."

She drew fast now. Road edges from the bottom corners straight to the dot. Sidewalk lines to the dot. Building edges to the dot. Then she drew the verticals, the fronts of buildings, standing straight up and down, and the whole street dropped into place on the page like it had been waiting there the whole time. She could not stop grinning.

"That's it," Hendrik said. "That's actually it."

"Ms. Nguyen said the gallery closes in ten minutes," Ayana said, tugging her sleeve.

"Ten minutes is three buildings." Audrey was already ruling the next line toward the dot, her pencil rushing to keep up with the street appearing under it.

William had fifteen dollars in his pocket and one text left to send before his phone died. He stood near the ticket booth at the football field, watching for Priya's blue jacket, and typed fast: "Going to the game with Priya and Arthur and Titan. Home by nine." His mom answered with a thumbs-up before he could even worry about it.

The plan had started in science class, of all places. Titan had leaned over during a worksheet and said, "My sister texts my mom everything before she leaves. Where she's going, who she's with, when she'll be home. Every single time, like a reflex." William had filed that away, and this morning he had tested it by asking his mom, casually, what she'd want to know if he went somewhere Friday night. She listed the same three things without hesitating. That settled it. Three facts, sent in advance, and nobody could say he hadn't been careful.

Priya arrived at the gate with Arthur trailing behind her, carrying a bag of popcorn he had clearly already started. They paid and pushed through the turnstile into the noise of the crowd. The bleachers were packed, so they migrated toward the empty seats at the far end, near the fence, where the sound of the game reached them a beat late. William bought two hot chocolates, since Priya's hands were cold, and managed not to drop either one.

In the third quarter his phone buzzed with a low battery warning, and then it died for good. He felt a small twist of panic, then reminded himself that the whole point of the earlier text was that the plan already existed somewhere outside his phone. His mom knew where he was. She knew who he was with. She knew nine o'clock. He didn't need to explain anything to anyone.

At two minutes to nine, they walked to the parking lot together. Priya's older brother was already idling at the curb. "Text me when you're home," she said, and Arthur made a face like he might be sick, and Titan laughed so loudly that a man walking past looked over.

William's mom was in the driveway when the brother's car pulled up. She was holding her car keys, not her phone, and the porch light was on. "You made it with two minutes to spare," she said. Then, quieter, "Thanks for the text. That's how I knew exactly where to come if I'd needed to." A strand of Stadium lights still glowed orange behind the trees at the end of the street.

The community centre homework club met in the room behind the gym, where the windows looked out on a lush wall of ivy that nobody ever trimmed. Evelyn spread her worksheet on the long table and read the first problem again: 2x + 3x = 25. She wanted a spot on the school math team, and Ms. Asante had told her that today's practice sheet was the tryout, collected at four o'clock sharp.

"You look like you're defusing a bomb," said Peyton, sliding into the next chair.

"Feel like it." Evelyn tapped her pencil on the paper. She knew the rule was to do the same thing to both sides, but 2x + 3x had two pieces on the left and she didn't know what to do with them first.

Across the table, Emilien wrote something fast and confident. Evelyn leaned over, hoping for a hint, and her stomach dropped. He had written 5x = 25.

"How did you get that?" she asked.

"Easy. Two plus three is five."

Before she could answer, Ms. Asante passed behind them and set a battered binder on the table. "Loaner binder," she said. "Pages in the back are loose. Mind the envelope, it's not mine." She moved on to the far table, and Evelyn forgot about the envelope because Emilien was already copying his answer onto the tryout sheet.

She couldn't let him turn that in. If he did, the whole room would ridicule him when it came back marked wrong, and she knew how that felt. But she didn't know why it was wrong, only that something about it itched. Two x's and a plain three. She thought of the ivy outside: vines and bricks. You could add vines to vines, but bricks were something else.

She opened the binder to hunt for a similar problem. The loose pages crackled and the envelope slipped out, sealed, with her name on it. Her actual name, Evelyn, in handwriting she almost recognized. She tore it open.

Dear whoever gets this binder, the note began. I failed the tryout last year because of one thing, so I'm writing it down for you. 2x + 3x becomes 5x. Like terms combine. But 2x and 3 cannot be combined, because one has a variable and one does not. There is no x to add to the 3. It was signed with only a smiley face, and Evelyn sat very still, because Emilien had just done the exact thing the letter warned about.

"Emilien," she said, keeping her voice low, "what does your x stand for?"

He looked at his page. "Something I don't know yet, I guess."

"So you're adding three of something you don't know to two of something you don't know. Then tell me what the 3 is three of."

He stared at his pencil. Peyton pulled the letter across the table, read it twice, and said, "Who wrote this?"

Evelyn turned the envelope over. On the back, in the same handwriting, was a single line: I got the next one right.

She slid the letter to Emilien, picked up her own pencil, and wrote 5x = 25 on the first problem, where both terms had x's. Outside, a breeze moved through the ivy, every leaf shifting at once.

Ava stood at Kaia's kitchen counter, which Kaia had declared "the restaurant," and tried to remember the word for water. It was Friday, and on Tuesday their French class would take a bus to a real crêpe place across town, where they had to order entirely in French. Ava's grade depended on it, and so did her pride, because she had told Colin she would order for both of them.

"Bonjour," said Kaia, holding a notebook like a waiter's pad. "Que voulez-vous?" She had stacked the counter with cereal boxes and a plate of toast, and their friend Colin sat at the table as the only other customer, drumming his fork against his glass.

"Je veux une crêpe," Ava said, proud of herself. She had practiced that sentence all week.

Kaia put her hands on her hips. "Excuse me?" she said, in English, stepping out of her waiter role. She looked genuinely annoyed, which surprised Ava, because Kaia never got annoyed at anything.

"What did I say?" Ava asked. Colin stopped drumming.

"That was so rude," Kaia said. "You basically barked at me." She flipped her notebook open to a page where she had copied sentences from their textbook. "Try again."

Ava frowned. She replayed the moment in her head. She hadn't shouted, and her pronunciation had been fine, she was almost sure of it. So what had changed the room? It had to be the verb. She thought about English for a second: nobody at a real restaurant said "I want water." They said "I would like." Maybe French worked the same way. She tested the idea the only way she could.

"Je voudrais une crêpe," she said, slower this time.

Kaia's whole face changed. "Perfect!" she said. "See, 'Je voudrais' means 'I would like.' 'Je veux' just means 'I want.' Big difference." She turned back to her pad. "C'est combien?" she added, tapping the cereal box as if it had a price.

"Um," said Ava, and her mind went blank. "Combien... ça coûte?" It came out as a question, but Kaia nodded so hard her braids bounced, and Colin clapped once, which made him knock his glass over. It rolled off the table and landed on the rug without breaking.

"My neurons are fried," Colin announced, rubbing his temples, "but you've got it. Say the whole thing to me. I'm the waiter now."

"Je voudrais une crêpe au chocolat," Ava said to Colin, standing straighter. "C'est combien?"

"Cinq euros," Colin said, in the worst accent Ava had ever heard, holding up five fingers arranged in a line almost perpendicular to his palm, like a tiny fence.

On Tuesday, when the real waiter came to their table, Ava heard her own voice come out steady. "Je voudrais une crêpe au fromage, s'il vous plaît." The waiter smiled and wrote it down. Across the table, Colin raised his water glass and mouthed, "C'est combien?"

Cameron stood at the white line of the school track, the morning sun warming the rubber under his shoes and the smell of cut grass drifting from the football field. Mr. Diallo clicked his stopwatch and held it up.

"Eight hundred metres, two laps. Go when you're ready."

Last Saturday's race still stung in Cameron's mind. He had blasted off the line like a rocket, arms pumping, and led the whole first lap while the crowd shouted his name. Then his legs turned to concrete on the back straight of lap two, and three runners streamed past him before the finish. Damian had won, and afterward, in the changeroom, Damian and Davis compared lap times.

"First lap sixty-two, second lap seventy-one," Damian said, reading from his phone.

Davis whistled. "Mine was the other way around. Sixty-eight, then sixty-four. My second lap was faster than my first."

"That's a negative split," Damian said. "Running the second half faster. Mine was a positive split, faster first half."

Cameron had stared at the floor, because his own splits were the worst of all. Sixty, then seventy-eight. His legs hadn't just faded, they had collapsed, and there had to be a reason he couldn't see. It wasn't that he lacked speed. Something hidden was eating it. He turned the two sets of numbers over all week and formed an idea: if the fastest first lap made the slowest second lap, maybe the trick was to hold something back on purpose, like saving the best slice of pizza for last.

Now he raised his hand before the start. "I'm going to try running the first lap slower on purpose."

Davis, leaning on the railing with a water bottle, groaned. "I need you to pace me for my time trial next week. If you jog the first lap, that ruins my pacing." Davis had his own plan: he wanted a negative split so big that Mr. Diallo would pick him for the city relay team, and he needed a rabbit, someone to chase.

"Fine," Cameron said. "Chase me anyway. I'll be just ahead."

Mr. Diallo's whistle cracked the air. Cameron went out controlled, legs light, lungs easy, holding a rhythm that felt almost too comfortable. Davis hammered past him at the bend, exactly as planned, and Cameron let him go, counting his own effort like coins in a pocket. He crossed the first lap right behind Davis's shoulder.

Then the test. Cameron lifted his knees, drove his arms, and found, to his amazement, a whole tank of fuel still waiting. He surged past Davis on the final curve, spikes gripping, the wind cold on his teeth, and sprinted the home straight so hard his vision narrowed to the finish line.

Mr. Diallo called out the splits. "Sixty-nine, then sixty-three. Second lap faster than your first. Negative split, Cameron."

Cameron bent over, laughing between breaths. "It works!"

Davis jogged up, grinning. "Do that at my trial. Stay one metre ahead of me the whole way."

"Deal," Cameron said, and shook on it, sweat cooling on his neck.

Avery stood in Cloe's bedroom while Cloe dumped a shoebox of glow stick bracelets onto the bed. The dance started in an hour, and the theme was Glow Night, which meant everyone would be walking around like fireflies.

"My mom bought these because she's frugal," Cloe said, sorting the stiff plastic tubes into piles. "Ones already cracked are half price, but half of them don't work."

Avery picked one up. It was dark, just a pale tube. She bent it anyway, and nothing happened. A second one, nothing. The third gave a faint green flicker and died.

"They're not broken batteries," Avery said slowly. "Something inside has to mix. When you bend it, you must be breaking something." She held a dead one up to Cloe's lamp, squinting. "I can't see a seam or a vial or anything. But every one that works, works after a hard snap. Every one that doesn't, doesn't."

"So snap harder," Cloe said.

Avery pressed the dead tube against the edge of the bed frame and pushed until she felt a tiny click, like a seed cracking. Green light spilled across the comforter.

"Told you," Cloe said.

At the dance, the gym was so dark the bleachers looked like they'd vanished. Israel appeared beside them with a bracelet glowing orange on his wrist. "Where's the light even coming from?" he said, turning it over. "There's no bulb. I checked."

"You crack a little glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside," Avery said. "It mixes with other chemicals and a dye, and the reaction makes light. It's called chemiluminescence."

Israel stared at her. "How do you know that?"

"She tested it," Cloe said. "On my bed frame. With science."

Halfway through the night the principal walked the floor with a clipboard, and Avery watched him stop a group of eighth graders near the door. One of them was shaking a glow stick like a maraca, flinging drops. The liquid speckled the gym floor in little orange dots.

"That's a citation," Israel whispered. "He's getting a citation."

Avery laughed, then caught herself. A splatter of orange had landed near her shoe. She wiped it carefully with her sleeve and held her own bracelet up high, where its glow washed green across her knuckles. "Come on," she said, and pulled Cloe toward the music.

Isla spread her homework across the kitchen table: a worksheet, her history textbook, and a shoebox her grandmother had mailed from the attic. The assignment said, "Use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s." Isla underlined primary twice. What did that even mean?

Inside the shoebox, wrapped in a dish towel, was a thin booklet with a cracked leather cover. Her grandmother's note said it was a copy of a diary kept by one of their ancestors, a woman named Ruth who had walked part of the trail west when she was sixteen. Isla turned the brittle-feeling pages, which were actually reprinted paper, and read the first line out loud. "We left because the land was tired and Papa said Ohio would let us thrive." She frowned. Thrive. The land was tired? How could land be tired?

She reached for the textbook instead, because textbooks had answers. She found a chapter with a tidy paragraph about people moving west for farmland, opportunity and railroads. It was clear and organized, and she copied two sentences before stopping. Something felt off. Why did Ruth say the land was tired, and the textbook say nothing about tired land?

A memory surfaced from last month, the field trip to the history museum. Their guide, Mr. Gill, had held up an old letter behind glass. "This is called a primary source," he had said, "something made at the time by a person who lived through an event." Then he'd pointed at a poster on the wall. "That poster is a secondary source, written later by someone studying it." Isla had been half listening, wondering if the letter smelled like old paper, but now the words came back sharp and clear.

She looked at the diary, then at the textbook, then at the diary again. Ruth wrote her words while walking west, while living it. The textbook was written a hundred years later by somebody who studied it. So the diary was the primary source, and the textbook wasn't. That meant the assignment wasn't asking for the neat summary. It was asking for Ruth.

Isla texted her friend Tiffany: is the textbook a primary source?? Tiffany wrote back, duh, it's the main book. Isla stared at the message, then typed: no, it's a secondary source because it was written later. Ruth's diary is my primary source. She made it, and she lived it. Tiffany replied with a single word: oh.

Isla started a fresh page. She copied Ruth's line about the tired land, then flipped ahead. In one August entry, Ruth wrote that rain finally came down like a monsoon after weeks of dust, and that the oxen drank until they shook. Random details, Isla thought, but not really random. Tired land, dust, no rain, then rain. Ruth's family wasn't chasing some big idea. They were hungry for good ground. That was a reason, hiding under the dust of the page, and Isla had dug it out.

She wrote her paragraph, quoting Ruth twice. Then she propped the diary against the salt shaker so the cover faced her while she worked.

"You're the primary source," she told it.

Colton crouched on the back porch steps, holding his sketchbook at arm's length and squinting at it. The assignment was due Monday: draw the old oak tree in the yard, and he had promised Ms. Mori it would be his best work. But the tree on the page looked like a ghost, all pale gray scratchings, none of the deep shadow in the knots and under the branches.

He thought about last spring, when he'd given up on a portrait of his grandmother because it came out "washed out," as his dad said. He'd blamed the paper, blamed the light, blamed himself, and shoved the sketchbook in a drawer for weeks. He didn't want that to happen again, so this time he decided to actually figure out what had gone wrong.

"Whatcha doing?" Aleksandar called, dropping his bike on the grass and coming over. He peered at the page. "That's the tree? It looks kind of faint."

"I know." Colton turned the pencil in his fingers and read the letters stamped on the barrel. He had grabbed it from the coffee can of pencils without looking, the way he always did. It said 4H. Then he dug through the can and found another one, a 6B, and a memory surfaced: Karen, of all people, leaning over his desk in art class saying, "On drawing pencils, H is hardness and B is blackness." He'd ignored her because he'd been in a bad mood that day, and now he felt his ears go warm.

He had a theory. Maybe the faint tree wasn't his fault as an artist; maybe the tool itself was the hidden cause. He tested it by hatching a small patch of shade with the 4H, then a patch with the 6B right beside it. The 6B patch came out dark and velvety, almost like charcoal, while the 4H stayed stubbornly pale even when he pressed hard.

"So the 6B is the black one," Aleksandar said, watching. "H for hardness, B for blackness. Huh."

"Blackness," Colton repeated, and grinned. He started over on a fresh page, blocking in the trunk with the 6B, letting the soft graphite drag thick and dark across the paper. The smell of cut grass drifted over from the neighbor's mower, and a squirrel scolded them from the oak's lowest branch, almost as if it approved.

Later Karen stopped by to return a lacrosse stick, and they showed her the finished drawing, the two of them voting his new tree better than his old portrait. It was unanimous, two to one, once Karen added her hand. She laughed and said he should have listened to her months ago, and Colton couldn't argue. He thought about all the drawings sitting faint and half-finished in his drawer, drawings a different pencil might have provoked into something better. He tapped the 6B against his knee and said, "Come on, I want to show you something in the garage."

Declan's bedroom smelled of pencil shavings and cold pizza, and on his desk sat the worst science grade he'd ever gotten: a red C-minus on the seasons quiz. Mr. Rosen had written one comment at the top. "You told me what happens. Not why." Tomorrow he'd let students retry the question out loud, and Declan wanted that chance badly, because his father, who worked on engines all day and called pistons the honest part of any machine, had said over dinner, "Anybody can memorize. Understand it, and nobody can take it from you."

Isha came over after school carrying her dad's camping lantern and a beach-ball globe from the dollar store, the kind so cheap the countries were already obsolete, their borders printed crooked. She plunked the lamp in the middle of the room. "You're the Earth. Walk around it and show me winter."

Declan held the tilted globe and started his orbit, taking slow steps around the lantern, and it began to irritate him almost immediately, because every time he rounded the lamp he turned the globe so it always faced the light the same way, spinning it in his hands like a steering wheel. "There," he said. "Now the top half gets less sun."

"That's summer," Isha said. "You just made the top lean toward the lamp."

He stopped. He walked it again, and this time he forced himself to keep the globe's axis pointing at the same spot on the wall, at the closet door, no matter where he was in his circle. When he stood on one side of the lamp, the top half of the globe leaned toward the light, bright across all its crooked countries. When he shuffled around to the far side, still aiming the axis at the closet, the top half leaned away and the light struck it thin and slanted, like late afternoon in December. "It's not pointing at the Sun," he said slowly. "It's pointing at the same direction in space the whole year. The whole orbit. That's why the seasons flip." He grabbed a marker and drew a lopsided circle on a pizza box, an arrow poking off the globe, straight and unchanging.

The next day Mr. Rosen called on him, and Declan walked a chalk eraser around the desk lamp, axis aimed stubbornly at the window, and Mr. Rosen nodded and said, "That's the explanation. B plus." Two points short of the A, because the quiz still counted, but standing at his seat with chalk dust on his sleeve, Declan drew the crooked circle in his notebook anyway, and beside it he wrote, for his father, "nobody can take it from you."

The chemistry lab on the second floor of the science museum smelled faintly of vinegar, and Cole liked it immediately. Mr. Ferreira had set out six cups of liquid, a stack of blue and pink strips, and a chart with numbers from zero to fourteen. "pH scale," he said. "Test each cup, write your result, and don't guess. The paper does the guessing." Dahlia, beside Cole, was less interested in the paper than in the prize table across the room, where the day's best lab sheet won a glow-in-the-dark mug. She had already measured her handwriting smaller so her sheet would look neat.

They worked through the cups quickly. Vinegar turned the blue paper pink, so it was an acid. Soapy water turned the pink paper blue, a base. Plain water left both strips unchanged, neutral, right in the middle at seven. Cole began to feel confident, the way you do when a pattern holds. Then Dahlia slid the last cup toward him. "Baking soda water," she said. "Bet you five points off my sheet it's neutral, same as plain water. It's mostly water anyway."

Cole dipped a blue strip. It stayed blue, which felt like half a win for her. He was about to write "neutral" when he remembered the other test. He dipped the pink strip, and it turned blue, slow and unmistakable, like sunrise deciding to happen. He held it up to the chart. "It's not neutral. Look, it's basic. Mildly basic, somewhere around eight or nine." Dahlia frowned at her cup as if it had lied to her personally. "It's an illusion," she said. "It looks exactly like water." Cole grinned. "Water with a secret."

Dahlia refused to give up on her mug so easily. She made Cole test three more strips from the same cup, watching each pink strip turn blue like the first one, and made him initial each result as a witness. When Mr. Ferreira strolled past, she flagged him down and pointed at her sheet. He checked the numbers, nodded, and slid the glow-in-the-dark mug across the table. Dahlia held it up to the light like a trophy. "See? Persevere," she said. "You were pessimistic about my five points."

"I was right about the baking soda," Cole said. "That's worth something."

"Fine." She poured him a little of the solution into a paper cup and handed him one last strip. "Prove it again."

At 7:04 on Tuesday night, Cameron's phone buzzed so many times it nearly slid off his desk.
