Then she jumped up, opened the freezer, and wedged hers between the ice trays. "If cold makes them last longer," she said, "this one might still be glowing at breakfast."

"Nine o'clock, my kitchen, everyone bring sunglasses," Eloi said.

In the morning, frost had feathered the freezer door. Lilah peeled the stick out with a dish towel and held it up to the window. A thin green pulse still burned inside the plastic, and Cooper leaned in until his nose almost touched it.

Harper stood on Oakley's porch holding a box of mochi she had picked out herself, because her mother had said never arrive at a family dinner empty-handed. She rang the bell twice before she understood that the second ring had been a mistake, and when the door opened, Oakley's grandmother pressed her palms together and bowed. Harper, clutching the box like a shield, did not know whether to bow back or shake hands or wave. She chose a small bow, and the grandmother smiled and took the mochi with both hands, which made Harper wonder if she had done something right on the first try.

Inside, the table was already set for ramen. Oakley's father came in from the kitchen carrying a steaming bowl in each hand, setting them down one at a time, and everyone said what sounded like "itadakimasu" before touching their chopsticks. Harper copied the word half a beat late, like a singer joining a song in the middle. Then the slurping began.

It started with Oakley's little brother, a polite-looking kid who suddenly inhaled his noodles with a sound like a drain unclogging. Harper froze with her chopsticks halfway to her mouth. In her own house, slurping was practically a crime, the kind of thing her grandfather commented on for the rest of dinner. Yet here Oakley's mother slurped, and her father slurped, and even the grandmother, so small and dignified, produced a noise that would have launched a siege of corrections at Harper's table. Nobody glanced at anybody. Nobody apologized. It was the equivalent of saying please and thank you, done with the whole face buried in the bowl.

Harper decided to test it. She lifted a tangle of noodles, waited a second, and slurped as quietly as she could manage, trying to evade notice while still doing the thing. Oakley looked up. "You don't have to be shy about it," Oakley said, laughing. "In Japan, slurping ramen and soba is acceptable. It's not rude like at your house."

Harper slurped again, louder this time, and the sound she made was enormous, and nobody flinched. Oakley's father nodded at her approvingly, and the grandmother refilled her tea before Harper had even asked.

Later, sitting on the floor of Oakley's room while they waited for the mochi, Harper thought about all the dinners where she had whispered "excuse me" for sounds ten times smaller than this. Maybe the rules she had memorized were only one family's rules, one house's. She unwrapped a piece of green tea mochi and took a bite. "Next time at my place," she said, "we're definitely having ramen."

Aaron slumped at his lab table in the science classroom and watched Mr. Yip write a question on the board: "How do students at our school really get to school?" Behind him, Riaan was already talking. "Most students walk," Riaan said. "Everybody knows that."

"Everybody thinks it," said Clementine, without looking up from her notebook. "That's not the same."

Aaron felt the familiar dread of being asked to sort out an argument, because Riaan and Clementine never stopped until someone sided with one of them. He turned around anyway. "How do you know most students walk?"

"I see tons of kids walking every morning," Riaan said.

"That's an opinion," Clementine said. "You saw some kids. Some isn't most."

Aaron picked up his pencil and rolled it between his fingers. He was thinking about the mock trial they had done in social studies, where the defendant had been declared innocent only after the jury saw actual evidence, not just what witnesses felt sure about. "Here's the thing," he said slowly. "Riaan's claim could be checked. Like, actually counted. Nobody has checked it yet, but it could be. That's different from an opinion."

Mr. Yip, who had been straightening the beakers at the front bench, walked over. "Go on," he said, which made Aaron nervous, because Mr. Yip usually only said that when he wanted more than Aaron had.

"We could do a survey," Aaron said. "Ask every student how they get here. Walk, bus, car, bike. Then count it up." He wrote the word survey on the corner of his notebook and underlined it twice.

Riaan leaned back on his stool. "Fine. But you can't ask the whole school in one day."

"We can ask our grade today," Clementine said. She was already folding a sheet of paper into a tally chart with three columns. "Start at lunch."

At lunch, the three of them stood at the end of the cafeteria line with the chart. Riaan asked the questions, Clementine made the marks, and Aaron kept a running total on his calculator. Some students gave strange answers. One boy said his dad drove him on rainy days but he walked otherwise, and a girl named her route as if it were a hereditary trait, saying her whole family had taken the same path for thirty years. Aaron counted her as a walker, then crossed it out, then counted her again as half.

By the end of lunch they had forty-three responses, and walkers were winning by six. Aaron looked at the tally marks and at the three grades they hadn't even started on. "We need the seventh graders," he said, and headed for the door.

Amelia sat cross-legged on her grandmother's carpet, the afternoon light making the room smell like warm dust and cardamom from the kitchen. In her lap lay the page she was supposed to memorize, the same surah she would recite at her coming-of-age ceremony in three weeks. Every time she reached the middle verse, the words slipped away like water through her fingers.

"Again," she whispered, and got halfway before the line dissolved.

Last summer, she remembered, her cousin had sat on this exact carpet and recited for what felt like an hour without opening a book. Amelia had been ten then, half listening, half amazed, and she had assumed his memory was simply better than hers, a random gift some people got and others didn't.

Now her grandmother's front door opened and the cousin himself walked in, older, carrying a duffel bag. "Amelia! Still fighting with that surah?"

"You made it look easy," she said.

He laughed and sat down across from her. "You know I didn't learn it from a page like that."

She frowned. "What do you mean?"

He tapped his temple. "Everything. The whole Quran, all 114 chapters, up here. Took years." He said it plainly, not bragging.

"There's a word for that," her grandmother called from the kitchen, and then her cousin said it at the same time: "Hafiz."

Amelia leaned forward. "But you learned it years ago. It stays just like that?"

He shook his head slowly. "I recite every single day. If I skip even a week, pieces start to blur. It's like the bank and a mortgage, the grandmother put it later at dinner; you have to keep paying or you lose the house."

Amelia decided to test this. That evening she recited the surah from memory once, then locked the page in her grandmother's wooden cabinet and promised herself not to peek until morning. At breakfast she stood by the window, the smell of buttered toast thick around her, and tried the middle verse. It was gone, exactly where it always vanished. She tried walking the length of the rug while reciting, saying the verse forward and then backward, and on the fourth pass the missing words rose up whole, surprising her like a fish breaking the surface of a pond.

At the ceremony three weeks later, she stood in front of everyone with her hands shaking and delivered every line without a single mistake. Afterward, her grandmother pressed the old carpet's corner into Amelia's hands, a rolled piece to take home, and said quietly, "It was always meant for the one who kept trying."

Amelia carried the roll to the car, knowing she would have to recite every day now, forever, or watch it all slip away. From the porch her cousin called out, "Same time tomorrow?"

Raphael's first soccer practice of the season ended with him sprinting laps until his lungs burned, and he jogged home feeling great. He flopped onto the backyard grass, peeled off his cleats, and texted Kayleigh: "Coach is tough but I'm fine. Barely tired." She replied with a suspicious row of question marks, which he ignored.

Two mornings later he woke up and nearly fell down the stairs. His thighs ached so deeply that he had to lower himself onto the couch one leg at a time, gripping the railing. He limped into the backyard, where Charbel was waiting to practice passing. "What happened to you?" Charbel asked. "You were fine Monday." Raphael lowered himself onto the picnic bench like an old man and frowned. He hadn't been hurt at practice. Nothing had twisted or snapped. The soreness had arrived out of nowhere, a whole day later, which made no sense to him.

"Maybe you're sick," Charbel said. Raphael shook his head. No fever, no sniffles, just muscles that screamed when he tried to stand. "A virus needs an organism to spread in," he said, thinking aloud, "but nobody else on the team texted that they were sick, and I'd be running a fever." He dragged himself up and tried a slow lap around the yard. The movement hurt at first, then loosened him a little. He stopped, eyes narrowed. "Wait. I felt nothing Monday. It peaked today. Two days after." Charbel pulled out his phone and typed fast. "My cousin's a trainer. She says it's called delayed onset muscle soreness. New or hard exercise, and it peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away." Raphael pointed at him. "That's exactly what happened. Not a virus."

He turned the idea over while he poked a ball back and forth with Charbel, slowly, wincing less each minute. The timing implied something useful: if Monday's practice had planted this soreness, then Wednesday's soreness had been set in motion before he even felt it. Which meant Friday's practice would plant Saturday's misery. So Thursday, he decided, he would warm up gently, stretch, and tell the coach his legs were still recovering from the first session, instead of pretending to be invincible and sprinting himself into next week's pain.

Friday's practice still hurt, but not like Monday's, because Raphael paced himself and drank water between every drill. On Saturday morning he walked downstairs normally, smiled at the banister, and carried his ball out to the backyard, where the morning light turned the dew opaque silver on the grass. Kayleigh was already there, juggling the ball on her knees. "Stairs?" she asked. Raphael trapped the ball under his foot and grinned. "Stairs are nothing. Watch this."

William climbed onto the 42 bus with his vocabulary sheet folded in his back pocket, holding the pole as the doors hissed shut. His assignment was to look up the history of five words, and four of them had been boring. The fifth word, propaganda, was supposed to be his last stop before Kalen's house, where they were building a model bridge out of coffee stirrers. The bus smelled like rain and vinyl, and a man near the front was humming along with his headphones even though nobody else could hear the song.

Above the windows, an ad showed a famous basketball player holding a purple sports drink. "Everybody's switching," the ad said in enormous letters. William stared at it. Everybody was a strong claim for a bus. He tried to picture everybody, all the people in the world, holding purple drinks, and decided the probability of that was close to zero. The player was grinning like the drink had personally rescued him from something.

Two rows ahead, Kameron from his science class sat with an older boy William didn't know, and Kameron was nodding along as the boy talked. "That neighborhood is full of criminals," the boy said, loud enough that a woman with a grocery bag glanced over. "Total disaster. Everyone knows it." William noticed how the words did work, heavy words, pushing a feeling onto a place William had never even visited. Kameron nodded again, faster.

At his stop, William found Kalen at the kitchen table with the laptop already open, glue on his fingers. "Look," Kalen said, spinning the screen around before William could even sit. He had found the word history first. "Guess where propaganda comes from. Guess." William guessed a war, a president, a newspaper. Kalen shook his head, grinning. "A church committee. The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622, for spreading the faith."

William sat down slowly. "So it started as just spreading an idea, like seeds or something." He thought about the basketball player, and the boy on the bus, and the enormous word everybody. "The drink ad never cites any proof that the drink works. It just says a star likes it and that everyone's doing it. That's the same trick, kind of. A gradual one, where you don't even notice." Kalen dotted glue along a stirrer and pressed it into the bridge. "So tomorrow, when Kameron repeats that criminal stuff, what do you say?"

"I ask him where he heard it," William said. "And whether he's ever actually been there." He picked up a stirrer and held it against the tower, checking the angle. Kalen handed him the glue.

"That side's going to sag," Kalen said.

"Only if we let it," said William, and pressed the stick down until it held.

Riley crouched beside the long ramp in the gymnasium, marking it with tape every half meter, because her project was due at the science fair in exactly two hours and her first ramp had turned out to be crooked. The gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn from the concession table. Leyla held the meter stick steady while Catalina, who had appointed herself timekeeper, clicked the stopwatch experimentally.

"Do it again," Riley said. "You stopped the clock before I let go of the ball."

"That's called anticipation," said Catalina. "Athletes have it."

They ran the ball down the ramp six times. Riley recorded each trial in her notebook, distance in meters along the left column and time in seconds along the right, then plotted the points on graph paper. When she connected them, the line was nearly straight, climbing steadily from the origin, and she felt a small quiet satisfaction. A straight line through the origin meant the ball's speed had stayed constant, which meant she could actually calculate it. She took her best trial, two meters in 1.6 seconds, and divided. One point two five.

"Point two five what?" Leyla asked, peering over her shoulder.

"Meters per second. That's my speed." Riley frowned at the number anyway. Something about it bothered her, and she tried to formulate exactly what. The units themselves were the problem, she decided. Meters per second meant nothing to most people walking past a poster.

"You know what you should do?" said Catalina, who had wandered over from the popcorn table with a full bag. "Figure out if your ball beats a person walking. Like a race. People get that."

Riley considered the context. A walking person went about five kilometers per hour, her dad had once said on one of their hikes, and she happened to know her ball's speed in meters per second, and the two had to be comparable somehow. There was a conversion, she was almost sure. She flipped through her math notebook from the beginning of the semester, past the fertile pages of half-finished homework where good ideas had sprouted and then been abandoned, until she found it in her own handwriting, circled twice: to change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply by 3.6.

She did it twice to be sure. One point two five times 3.6 came out to 4.5 kilometers per hour. She sat back on her heels. The walking person won. Her ball, which had looked so swift rolling down the ramp, would lose a race to someone strolling to the bus stop.

"Well?" Catalina crunched popcorn.

"Four point five kilometers per hour," Riley said. "A walker does five."

Leyla laughed so hard she had to put down the meter stick. "Your ball loses to my grandmother."

Mr. Haile, checking tables down the row, paused at theirs. "You converted that yourself?" he asked, tapping the notebook page. Riley nodded. He looked at her graph, then at the ramp, and asked whether the ball would go faster on a steeper one, and whether her graph would still be a straight line.

Riley looked at the stack of books under the high end of the ramp, then at the clock. Ninety minutes until judging. Catalina was already pulling out the bottom book.

Tyler kept his notebook open on his knee as the school bus rattled past the hardware store. In it he had copied the box score from last night's basketball game, because Raelynn insisted Devonne was the best player on the team and Tyler thought she was wrong. Devonne averaged fourteen points a game. Marcus averaged eleven. But Tyler had watched every game this season, and something about those numbers felt like a photograph of a room where all the furniture had been moved.

"You're counting again," Raelynn said, dropping into the seat across the aisle. Aryanna leaned over her shoulder to look. "Fourteen beats eleven. That's just math."

"Fourteen is one number for eight games," Tyler said. "It squashes everything together." He tapped his pencil down the column of Devonne's points: 28, 3, 25, 6, 30, 2, 24, 14. Half the games were huge and half were nearly nothing. Marcus's column was boring and steady, 10, 12, 11, 9, 13, 10, 12, 13. Tyler circled the middle numbers. "The median tells a different story. Devonne's is about fourteen, same as his average. Marcus's is 11, same as his. That's not it either." He chewed the pencil eraser. So what was he actually trying to see?

He thought of his uncle at the sports bar two weeks ago, the night the whole family had crowded around the screen. "Read this," his uncle had said, sliding a paperback across the table. "Michael Lewis wrote it. Moneyball, 2003." Tyler had flipped it over while his uncle kept going, quieter now, almost to himself: "The Oakland Athletics, back in 2002, used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." A low-budget team competing with rich teams by looking at numbers nobody else trusted. Tyler had been hesitant to believe it at the time, one number outperforming millions of dollars, but the idea had stuck to him ever since, orbiting his brain like a satellite he couldn't shake.

"What's on-base percentage?" Aryanna asked now, reading his mind, or maybe his face.

"How many times a player gets on base instead of making an out," Tyler said. "It counts walks. Points don't." He looked back at his notebook, and the page seemed to rearrange itself. He had a column for shots but not one for passes. Devonne shot every time he touched the ball. When the score was close and the shot missed, the ball seemed to orbit the rim and bounce out, and Devonne's teammate would be standing alone under the basket, unguarded, every single time. Tyler started a new column with a ruler, straight and careful, and headed it with Marcus's name.

"Whatever you're doing," Raelynn said, "you're doing it at the tournament too."

"Get me the stat sheet," Tyler said, already flipping to a clean page as the bus hissed to a stop.

Amelia sat at the kitchen table with her German book open to a blank page. The assignment was simple enough: a paragraph about her plans for next year, all in the future tense. Mr. Ho had written one example on the board before the bell, and she had copied it down without really looking at it. Now she looked. "Ich werde Deutsch lernen." Two words she recognized, werden and lernen, and the rest she would have to build herself.

She tried her first sentence. "Ich werde gehe nach Berlin." Something about it felt wrong, the way a crooked picture frame feels wrong before you see the tilt. She read it aloud, and her voice slowed at gehe. It sounded like she had said "I will go go." She flipped back through her notes and found the example again. In Mr. Ho's sentence, the verb lernen sat at the very end, after Deutsch. In her sentence, gehe sat in the middle, right after werde, like it belonged there because English worked that way.

Her phone buzzed. Musa had sent a photo of his own paragraph, and his sentences had the same shape as hers, verbs crowding the middle. She typed back, "Look at the example he wrote. The main verb goes last." Then, to verify it, she checked two more sentences in the textbook chapter. Ich werde ein Buch lesen. Ich werde meine Oma besuchen. The pattern held every time: werden, then everything else, then the infinitive at the end.

Outside the window, the gray stone wall of the house was spotted with lichen, pale green circles that had spread since the rainy month. Her dad had said last spring he would scrub it off and then never had, and the wall had quietly gone on growing its own map. Amelia thought about how often she did the same thing, saying she would do something and then letting it slide. Last term she had been almost negligent about German homework, leaving it until the bus ride, and now here she was, the night before, doing exactly that again. She smoothed the page and kept writing anyway. "Nächstes Jahr werde ich nach Berlin fahren." She read it aloud. "Next year I will to Berlin travel." It sounded strange in English, but in German it had a rhythm, like the verb was a stone dropped at the end of a line.

She finished the paragraph, all six sentences, each one holding its shape. Then she read Musa's reply: "He posted a new example. Check the class page." She opened it. Mr. Ho had added a note under his own example sentence. It said, "Remember, ich werde Deutsch lernen means I will learn German." Amelia stared at her page, at her careful verb-final sentences, and wondered whether she had actually understood the rule or only copied a shape.

The kitchen light hummed. She picked up her pen again and hovered over the last line, then wrote, "Ich werde mehr studieren."

The train had been moving for twenty minutes before Landon stopped staring out the window and started doing math in his head. They had left the campsite at nine, and Dad was staying behind to pack the van and lock up the trailer. He planned to be on the road by eleven. That gave him two hours, which sounded like plenty, except Landon kept picturing the fire pit. They had put it out in a hurry that morning, before the rain started. He had dumped one bucket of water on it, everyone had piled into the car, and nobody had stirred anything.

"You're doing your worried face," said Valentina, who was sitting across from him with her feet on her backpack. She and her mom were taking the same train east, which was the only fun part of the whole trip. "What's wrong?"

"The fire," Landon said. "I only drowned it once. There was still smoke coming off the edge when we walked away." He had learned the right way back in June, from a booklet at the ranger station: to put out a campfire you drown it with water, stir the ashes, and drown it again, and you keep doing that until everything is cool to the touch. One bucket and no stirring was not that. It wasn't a trivial mistake either, the kind you shrug off. Buried under grey ash there could still be an ember, and he couldn't see it from a moving train, which was the whole problem. Hidden causes were like that, his science teacher would have said, though Mr. Pelletier would also have made them diagram it.

"Call your dad," Valentina said.

Landon retrieved his phone from the side pocket of his pack and found one bar of service flickering between hills. He dialed anyway. It rang four times, long enough for him to imagine the van already pulling onto the highway, the fire pit abandoned with its secret heat.

"Dad, wait. Before you leave. The fire pit."

"I'm looking at it right now," Dad said.

"You have to drown it, stir the ashes, and drown it again. Keep going until everything's cool to the touch. Not just warm. Cool."

"I know," Dad said. There was a scraping sound, metal against stone. "I did the first round an hour ago, and I've been back twice since. The sticks were hissing when I stirred them, so I poured a whole second bucket. I was about to do a third because the big log at the back still feels warm to my hand." A pause, then the sound of water splashing, and the line crackled. "There. Everything's cool now. Even the ring."

Landon let out a breath. "Okay. Good."

"Goodbye, Landon. Train's fine?" Dad asked, and Landon said it was, and they hung up.

Valentina raised her eyebrows. "So your dad was already on it."

"Yeah." Landon slumped back against the seat. Two hours of worrying over an ember he couldn't see, and Dad had been standing in the rain, patiently drowning a dead fire. Valentina started laughing, and after a second he did too.

"Next time," she said, "call before the train leaves."

Cameron had a tray of dirt on the kitchen table, a jug of water, and one very suspicious cat. He was supposed to be writing a paragraph about the Grand Canyon for Monday, and the paragraph was supposed to include how long the river took. He'd written "a while" and then crossed it out.

The trouble had started that afternoon in Ms. He's class, when she'd held up a postcard of the canyon and asked them to explain how a river could carve a hole that deep. Cameron had said, confidently, "It's basically a big flood." Alicia had looked at him the way you look at a pizza that's fallen cheese-side down. Kruz had just said, "Sure, a flood that lasted forever," which was somehow worse, because it made Cameron's answer sound wrong twice at once. Ms. He hadn't corrected anyone. She'd only said, "Find out," and Cameron suspected she enjoyed that.

Now, at home, he poured a slow stream of water across the tray of dirt. At first nothing happened. He tilted the tray, and the water found one groove and sank into it, widening it, dragging tiny crumbs of dirt downhill in a muddy smear. It wasn't dramatic. That was the thing. It was slow, patient, almost boring, and yet the groove got deeper every minute. He nudged the tray steeper, remembering a video he'd watched where a scientist said the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago. Five to six million years. His groove had taken four minutes. He tried the math on the back of his hand and decided not to write the number down, in case it was ridiculous, which it was.

Last summer, at his grandfather's house, there had been a gully behind the fence that the grown-ups all complained about after every storm. Cameron had thought the storm made it, because the storm was volatile, all thunder and drama, while ordinary days seemed to conceal their work completely. But now he looked at his tray and understood he'd had it backward. The loud thing moved the dirt, sure, but the quiet water was the one that never stopped. The gully was the storm's plan, carried out by the drizzle.

He built a flat-topped ridge of dirt, a little plateau, and cut a channel down its middle, then ran the water again. Sediment piled up at the bottom where the slope eased, a tiny muddy delta, deposition happening right there between the salt shaker and the cat.

"Enjoying the show?" he asked the cat. The cat blinked. Cameron wrote one sentence at the top of his page: "Rivers don't tear things open; they persuade them, grain by grain." Then he poured again, and the plateau's edge, ever so slightly, crumbled.

The fire station sat at the edge of town, and beyond its back fence Maelie could see a small farm where three pink pigs stood panting in a shaded corner of their pen. The class had come to see the trucks, and Mr. Halvorsen, who once worked here and still had a key, was letting them climb aboard Engine 4. "One at a time," he said. "There's a hierarchy to these things. Driver, officer, then everybody else." Dane groaned because he wanted the driver's seat, and Skyla, who was third in line, kept checking her phone battery like the photo she planned to take might expire.

Maelie took her turn in the officer's seat, but her eyes kept drifting out the window. It was the hottest day of the summer so far, and the pigs were plastered in mud so thick and opaque that she couldn't tell where the mud ended and the pig began. Were they just messy animals? she wondered. But why would they stand in muck on purpose on a day like this, when the whole rest of the pen was clean and shaded?

While the others lined up at the pole, Maelie slipped to the back fence with her water bottle from lunch. If the pigs were dirty because they liked dirt, they'd ignore water. She poured a splash into the dry dirt near the fence, making a small puddle, and waited. The biggest pig trotted over, flopped down, and rolled until its whole side glistened. It wasn't the dirt, Maelie thought. It was wet. The mud was just a way to stay wet longer.

She found Mr. Halvorsen by the hose rack. "The pigs next door," she said. "Are they rolling in mud to cool off?" He nodded. "Pigs have very few working sweat glands," he said, "so they wallow in mud or water on hot days." Maelie wanted to verify that, so she asked if she could borrow the small hose for a minute. He checked with the duty firefighter, who shrugged and said the connection by the back gate was fine.

She sprayed a thin arc over the fence while Dane, having finally claimed the driver's seat, leaned out the truck window to watch. The three pigs jogged to the fence, and when the water pooled in the low spot of their pen, they lay down in it one by one, grunting, ribs heaving, cooler already. Skyla squeezed through the gate with her phone raised. "Move the hose a little left," she said. "I want the rainbow in the picture."

Alexandre had one hour before the mall's gaming tournament started, and he meant to spend it finding the leak. Two weeks ago he had posted a photo of his sneakers here, at Riverside Mall, and by that evening three strangers had commented asking if he was "the kid who hangs out by the fountain every Saturday." He had never written that. He had never posted a schedule. Yet somehow the pattern was out there, stored somewhere, visible to people he did not know.

Cassidy met him near the fountain, phone in hand. "So what's the plan? You check the photo itself?"

"The photo's just a picture," Alexandre said. "But when I posted it, the app knew where I was. That's my inference. Something on my phone is telling them." He scrolled through his settings while shoppers streamed past the storefronts, and found the screen he'd only half-remembered. Each app had its own choice, app by app: whether it may use his location always, only while he was using it, or never.

"Wait, you can pick that?" Cassidy leaned over. "Per app?"

"Always, only while using, or never," Alexandre read. "Every app, one by one." He tapped into the map app he used for bus times. Only while using. Fine. His camera. Never. Then a free puzzle game, one Cassidy had begged him to try last month, the one with the cheerful cartoon monsters. The little arrow beside it said Always.

"Every Saturday," Cassidy said slowly. "You play it while we wait for the tournament line."

"And it's been telling the game's company where I am, even when I'm not playing." Alexandre felt the floor tilt a little, the way it does when something ordinary turns out to have been watching you. He changed it to Never, and the arrow went gray.

At the tournament table, Penelope waved them over, and a boy Alexandre didn't recognize was already there, wearing a counterfeit jersey with a crooked logo stitched over the number. "You're the fountain guy," the boy said. "I saw your picture. Cool shoes. You here every week, right?"

Alexandre looked at him, deciding in one breath. "Not anymore," he said. "Same mall, but you won't know when." It wasn't a lie exactly, though it cost him something to say it, because the fountain line had been the good part of Saturdays, the part strangers had shared with him without his knowing.

After the matches, he checked the game's app one more time, half expecting the setting to have crept back to Always, the way some things quietly do. Never, it still said. He slid the phone into his pocket and turned toward the fountain, where Cassidy was saving his place in line, and where nobody, as far as he could tell, was keeping count anymore.

Penelope sat on the porch of her grandfather's house with a sketchpad on her knees, trying to draw the street that curved past the front gate. Her first attempt lay beside her, and every time she looked at it, her stomach sank a little. The street didn't look like a street at all. It looked like a flat wall with lines painted on it. She had drawn the lampposts marching down the middle, every single one the same height, evenly spaced like fence pickets, and the whole picture had refused to lie down flat on the page.

She thought about her grandfather, who had spent his whole life in agriculture and who could look at a field of wheat and tell you, without walking out to it, whether the far rows were healthy. When she'd asked him how, he said the far rows looked different, lighter and closer together, and your eye learned to mediate between what you saw and what you knew was there. She had laughed at him then. Now she wondered whether drawing a street worked the same way, like there was a rule hiding somewhere that her eyes hadn't learned yet.

Pierre-Olivier pedaled up the drive and dropped his bike in the gravel. "That's not a street," he said, looking over her shoulder at the flat wall. "It's a picture of a street that got squashed."

"I know it's wrong," Penelope said. "I just can't see where it went wrong." She flipped to a fresh page and drew two lines that started wide at the bottom of the page and slanted toward each other until they nearly touched near the top. Then she made a small dot where they almost met. She had heard the word once, in a hallway, from a kid who took art on Tuesdays. "Vanishing point," she said, mostly to herself.

She set her pencil at the top of the nearest lamppost and drew a faint guide line from it to the dot. Then she tried the same thing from a lamppost farther down the street, and the guide line cut lower across the page. She placed a dot where it landed and drew a post there, smaller. She did it again, farther along, and again, and the posts came out smaller and closer together the deeper into the page they went, even though she knew they were all the same real height, because she could see them standing equal outside the gate.

When she finished, she held the pad out at arm's length. The street ran away from her, deep and real, the posts shrinking into the distance exactly the way the real ones did past the gate. Pierre-Olivier leaned in, then looked up at the actual street, then back at the page. "It goes back," he said. "Mine never did that." He ran inside to get his own paper, and Penelope heard him calling for a pencil before the screen door had even banged shut.

At the end-of-season party in Lillian's backyard, nobody was eating the cake. The Rockets had gone undefeated in soccer, Coach had brought a trophy the size of a toaster, and still everyone stood around the picnic table like they were waiting for something bad to happen. Lillian watched Ishaan kick a pinecone against the fence, over and over, and watched Sophie turn her water bottle slowly in her hands without drinking. It didn't make sense. They had won. So why did the whole team feel like a plate someone had tapped, that brittle hum right before it cracks?

"It's not the losing teams that cry at awards day," Lillian said to Sophie. "I checked. The winning ones cry too."

Sophie shrugged. "Maybe everybody's just tired."

Lillian didn't think so. That night she dug through her older sister's old books from a business class, the ones with chapters about how people work in groups, and there it was. A researcher named Tuckman had described the stages a group goes through, forming, storming, norming, performing, and for years that was where it ended. Then in 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage. It was called adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. Lillian read the page twice, then closed the book carefully, like it might fall apart in her hands.

The next morning she called Ishaan. "Meet me in the backyard at ten. Bring Sophie."

When they came, she had a plan. If the sad feeling was really the fifth stage, then it should show up wherever a group broke up, not just their team. "I'm going to document it," she said, holding up a notebook. "Every team, every club, everything that ends. We test it." They made a list. Ishaan's cousin had worked at a corporation all summer in an office and had moped for a week when her project team finished and everyone went back to different desks. Sophie's book club had ended in June, and the members still texted each other photos of books they thought the others would like. Even Lillian's dad's garage band, which had practiced for years, had gone quiet for a month after their last gig.

"That's four out of four," Ishaan said, counting the notebook pages.

"Five," Lillian said. "Counting us."

So on Saturday she brought the notebook to the field where the Rockets were having their last pickup game before summer. She stood in front of the team, feeling her ears go hot, and said, "It's called adjourning. It's the last stage. In 1977 this guy Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added it, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. That's what's happening to us. That's why the cake party felt so weird."

Nobody laughed, which she had feared. A girl named Ishaan passed the ball to Sophie, who trapped it and looked at Lillian for a long second.

"Then we're in it right now," Sophie said. "Last game. Everybody in?"

They played until the grass stains went past their knees. Afterward, sweating and laughing, they crowded around the notebook, and one by one every player signed the page under the word Lillian had written at the top: Adjourning.

The dance started in ninety minutes, and Nicolas was lying on Samira's living room floor with a pillow over his face. "Everyone already has a partner," he said through the pillow. "Aleena's going with that kid from her math class. You have a partner. I have nothing."

Samira snatched the pillow away. "Get up. You've been doom-spiraling for twenty minutes and we still have to get ready." Her little cousin was in the corner of the room, doing something with her feet that looked like a mix of marching and hopscotch. She stomped, clapped, turned, stomped again, all facing the big window.

Nicolas watched her. "What is she doing?"

"A line dance. My aunt taught her. It's from her side of the family, part of her heritage, and she will do it anywhere, including the grocery store." Samira raised her voice. "Show him the whole thing."

The cousin lined up three stuffed animals beside her, all facing the same direction as her, then did the steps again. Stomp, clap, turn, stomp. The animals just sat there, but somehow it looked like a group.

"Wait," Nicolas said slowly, sitting up. "She's not dancing with anybody. She's just doing the same steps as everyone else, facing the same way. If a whole crowd did that, nobody would need a partner at all." He counted on his fingers. "There are what, four moves? Four moves and you're dancing with thirty people."

"Line dances," Samira said, "let a whole group do the same steps together facing the same direction. Nobody needs a partner. That is literally the entire point." She pulled him to his feet. "So you have a job now. Learn four steps before the car leaves."

They pushed the coffee table aside to accommodate a practice area, which mostly meant the cousin shouting "AGAIN" every time Nicolas messed up the turn. The footwork felt intricate at first, like his shoes were tied together, but by the tenth try his feet found the pattern. Stomp, clap, turn, stomp. He did it facing the couch, facing the kitchen, facing the front door, just to prove it worked in every direction, and Samira cracked up when he whispered "stomp, clap" at her mother's houseplant.

In the car, Nicolas practiced with his hands on his knees. At the gym doors he could already hear the bass, and his stomach did one slow flip. Then the music changed, and a voice on the speakers called out, "Okay, everybody, line up!"

The whole floor turned the same direction at once, strangers and couples and kids from every grade, and Nicolas slid into the back row just as the stomping started.

"Stomp, clap," he said out loud, and grinned at Samira across the gym.

Sophie had taped her periodic table poster to the gym wall six times before it finally stayed put, and by the time the science fair doors opened, she could hear the poster paper flapping like it wanted to escape. Her project was called "Counting the Invisible," and the whole idea had come to her three weeks ago when she'd realized that no one, not once, had ever actually seen a proton. Yet there they were on every element card, counted as confidently as candies in a jar.

"Table four, table four," said Emerson, who was stationed at the next table with a homemade volcano. "The judges are heading this way, and one of them has a clipboard, which we all know means business."

Sophie straightened her element cards. She had made one for every element in the first three rows, and on the back of each she had written a single number. Carbon had a 6. Neon had a 10. Sodium had an 11. The trick, she had discovered, was hiding in plain sight on the front of each card: the tiny number in the corner of each box on the periodic table was the atomic number, and the atomic number was exactly how many protons the element had. She had tested it on a dozen elements with the library's reference book, and every single time the numbers matched.

The clipboard judge stopped at her table. "So, young lady, what's invisible here?"

"Protons," Sophie said. "You can't see them, but you can count them. Pick any card."

The judge picked oxygen. Sophie flipped it over: 8. "Eight protons. The atomic number tells you, every time, no guessing. That's the pattern nobody had to discover by looking, because you can't look."

Behind the judge, a boy from another school, Nicolas, was leaning over the museum timeline Ms. Clarke's class had brought as a display. "Hey," he called out, pointing at a faded reproduction of an old handwritten chart. "This thing only has about sixty elements on it. Were people just lazy back then?"

Sophie came around the table to look. The timeline card under the chart read: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869.

"That's Mendeleev," Sophie said. "The early version. They hadn't found them all yet."

"Found them, or made them?" Nicolas asked.

"Found. Some of them are hiding in rocks, in tiny amounts, and chemists had to extract them, like digging a marble out of a bucket of sand." She tapped the chart's empty gaps. "And look, he left blanks. He thought there should be something there."

The clipboard judge was writing fast now. "You tested your proton rule against reference data?"

"Twelve elements," Sophie said. "I want to do all of them. I figured out how, too. If I line up my cards by atomic number and find the median, I can split them into two piles and check each pile the same way."

Ms. Clarke appeared behind the judge, arms crossed, smiling in that way she had when she was deciding something. "Sophie, the regional fair is in March. Registration closes Friday."

The poster chose that moment to peel loose and swing down over the timeline. Nicolas laughed, Sophie grabbed for it, and the judge said, "Hold that thought, I'm coming back with the head judge."

Sophie smoothed the poster flat and looked at all those numbered boxes, sixty in Mendeleev's chart, more in hers, the whole invisible world lined up and counted. "Friday," she said to Emerson. "I'm registering tonight."

Charlie had exactly twenty minutes to figure out the Grand Canyon before Mr. López collected everyone at the museum exit, and she was not going to waste one of them.

"Look at this," she said, dragging Aksel and Winter toward the stream table in the erosion hall. Workers had installed it that morning, a long slanted tray with a hose at the top and a ramp of sand, gravel, and little pebbles waiting to be carved. Aksel grabbed the hose handle before she could.

"Watch," he said, and opened the valve wide. Water rushed down the tray, and within seconds a channel began to cut into the sand, branching like lightning. Charlie leaned over it, nose almost touching the glass. "It's working! The canyon's forming!" The water quickened at the steep middle section, and she noticed something odd. Pebbles that had been sitting near the top were hopping, tumbling, riding the current. But the fine sand barely moved at all from up there. It just slid slowly, in little clouds.

"Wait," Charlie said. "The big rocks are moving and the sand isn't? That's backwards." She snatched the valve from Aksel and slowed the flow to a trickle. The pebbles stopped instantly, dropping where they were, halfway down the tray. But the muddy water kept drifting on, thin and brown, all the way to the bottom of the slope, where it pooled and went still. Only then did the haze settle out, coating the lowest inch of the tray in silky smooth mud.

Winter crouched at the end of the table, eyes wide. "So the pebbles got dropped first and the mud got carried the whole way. That's why they're in different places." Charlie felt her heart thumping like she'd won something. Faster water could haul the heavy stuff, and the moment it slowed, the water let it go, biggest pieces first, finest stuff last. She flipped the valve wide again, then slow, watching the deposits rearrange themselves, pebbles high, mud low, over and over, like the table was telling her a secret in code.

"That's the whole canyon," she said. "Millions of years of this. The river carries, then it slows, then it drops." Mr. López appeared behind them with his clipboard, indifferent to their discovery, already counting heads. But Charlie wasn't moving until the last grain of mud settled. "Ten more seconds," she begged, and Aksel turned the hose on full.

Joshua's hands were damp on the keys when Ms. Romano set the small wooden box on top of the piano. "Try it once more," she said, "with the machine." The night before, he had found a note folded into his sheet music, in Leyla's round handwriting: "Cory says you rush the fast part every rehearsal. I don't hear it, but he's not wrong about things like this. Please check. Also I saved you a seat at the concert. L." He had read the letter three times, half grateful and half stung, and practiced until ten o'clock without solving anything.

The box had a pendulum inside and a slider you could move up and down. When he set it going, it ticked like a patient insect. Ms. Romano said only, "Maelzel patented this in 1815. It's called a metronome." Then she sat back and let him work.

He started the piece at the slow marking, sixty ticks a minute, and by the eighth measure the ticking and his hands had drifted apart, his fingers running ahead like water finding a downhill path. There it was. He couldn't feel the rushing at all while he played, but the machine could see it for him, or hear it. It was like the time in sixth grade when his bike wobbled and he blamed the road, until his dad pointed at the loose front wheel. The wobble wasn't the road. The rushing wasn't the piece. It was him.

He tried a small experiment. Instead of playing the whole song, he took just the loud, quick passage and set the metronome slower than it should ever go, glacially slow, so every note had room. Then, measure by measure, he raised the tempo by small steps, calibrating the slider until the ticking matched the marking on the page. The speed wasn't a variable he could leave to his mood anymore; it was fixed outside him, steady while his excitement rose and fell. When he finally played the passage through, loud where the dynamics said loud, soft where they said soft, it came out coherent for the first time, all one piece of music instead of pieces glued together.

Ms. Romano smiled at the last chord. "That," she said, "is what I wanted you to find yourself."

At Thursday rehearsal, Cory kept time by tapping his sneaker against the floor, and when the fast part arrived, Joshua stayed with him, note for note, all the way to the end. Leyla caught his eye across the music stand and raised her eyebrows. He tapped his pocket, where he'd written 1815 on a scrap of paper. "New machine," he mouthed, and turned the page.

Mr. Lin set the timer for twenty minutes and said the paragraph had to be about plans for next year, all in the future tense. William stared at his lined paper. He had already written his first sentence: "Next year I will be in grade eight." The problem was the French half of the page, which was blank.

"You can't still be on sentence one," Lucca whispered from the next desk. "I've got four lines."

"Because you're writing about pizza," William whispered back. "You only need 'I will eat.'"

Lucca shrugged, as if that were a reasonable strategy. William looked at his verb chart, the one with the endings for the future tense. He knew how to build it. You took the infinitive, added the ending. Parler plus ai made parlerai, I will speak. Finir plus ai made finirai. So "to be," which was être, should give him êtreai. He wrote it down and stopped.

It looked wrong. It sat on the page like the fungus growing on the bread in the science corner, something that shouldn't be there and definitely wasn't French. He crossed it out and wrote it again. Still wrong.

Madalyn leaned over the gap between their desks. "You're making that face."

"There's no such word as êtreai," William said.

"So don't use it."

"I have to. My whole paragraph is about being in grade eight. Being is the first sentence."

He thought about his verb list from September. Avoir, to have, future stem aur. Aller, to go, future stem ir. Those hadn't come from the infinitives either. He'd memorized them without noticing, the way he'd memorized the route to school. So maybe être did the same thing, shed its whole body and grew a new stem. He tried sounds in his head. Ser? He wrote "je serai" in careful, meticulous letters, then checked it against nothing, because there was nothing to check it against. Only the timer, which showed nine minutes left.

At the bell, Mr. Lin walked the rows. When he reached William's desk he paused, tapped the page once, and said, "Je serai. Good."

"You knew that was a guess," William said.

"Doesn't matter. You tested it." Mr. Lin moved on to Lucca's paper. "Lucca. You cannot eat pizza every day next year. Variety."

William slid his paragraph into his binder and looked at Madalyn. "Next year," he said, "I will be the one who finishes first."

"In French?" she said. "Say it in French."

"Je serai," said William, and zipped the binder shut.

Xavier leaned closer to the poster outside Mr. Harper's classroom, tracing the white shape in the middle with one finger. "It's a vase," he said. "Obviously a vase."

Karson crossed his arms. "It's two faces. Two profiles, like they're about to kiss. There's a nose and a chin on each side."

"They can't both be right," Xavier said, though even as he said it, he could feel something shift. The vase seemed to fold inward, and suddenly the curves he'd been following turned into a forehead and a tip of a nose. He blinked hard and the vase came back, but only after he stopped trying to see the faces. "Wait. I see the faces now. But when I see them, the vase is gone."

Stanley wandered over from the water fountain, still wiping his mouth on his sleeve. "Mr. Harper put that up yesterday. It's called a Rubin vase." He tapped the small caption at the bottom of the poster. "Some Danish psychologist named Edgar Rubin came up with it, back in 1915. It can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same time."

Xavier read the caption twice. That was the strange part, the part that made his brain itch. He covered the black part with one hand and the white part popped out as a vase. He covered the white edges with his fingers spread wide, and the faces appeared like they'd been hiding there the whole time. He tried to force both at once, staring until his eyes watered. Nothing. It flicked from one to the other like a light switch with no middle position.

"So who's right?" Karson asked.

"Maybe both of us," Xavier said slowly. "We're looking at the exact same poster and seeing totally different pictures." He thought about the argument he'd had with his dad last week, both of them describing the same awful, turbulent car ride home in completely different ways, each one certain the other was wrong. Maybe that worked the same way. Maybe neither of them was lying. "Hold on. I want to try something."

He grabbed a marker from the bin by the door and wrote beneath the caption: WHAT DO YOU SEE? VASE OR FACES? Then, careful to isolate his handwriting so it wouldn't touch the poster itself, he added a tally chart with two columns and left the marker resting on the ledge.

By lunch, the chart was full. Nine tallies for vase, eleven for faces, and a sticky note in messy printing that said, I CAN SWITCH! IT JUST TAKES A SECOND. Karson stood beside him, counting the marks. "Eleven people saw faces first. That means you owe me a chip."

"One condition," Xavier said, snapping the cap back on the marker. "Tomorrow we ask them if they can see the other one too."

Karson handed him the bag anyway.

Cooper sat in the corner of the gaming store with his tablet balanced on his knee, logged into the lobby where his squad always met at four o'clock. His controller had died during first period, and the only replacement cable in town was on the rack three feet away, still sealed in its translucent plastic. He had exactly nine dollars, and the cable cost eleven, which was the problem driving everything else.

"There he is," Samara's voice came through his earbuds, crackling a little. "Ready for the tournament match?"

"Sort of," Cooper said. "I'm at the mall, actually. I can't play unless I get this cable, and I'm two dollars short." He said it fast, hoping the embarrassment would slide past everyone.

"You're at the mall?" Samara said. "In the game store, right? The one next to the pretzel place, standing by the accessories rack?"

Cooper looked up so fast he nearly dropped the tablet. He had not told anyone where he was. The store window faced the food court, and through it he could see Maddison at a table with her phone, which meant she might have guessed. But Samara was at home, miles away, and she had known his exact position. There had to be a hidden cause, something he could not see directly, and he decided to test it. He walked two aisles over, to the sports games section.

"You moved," Samara said. "Now you're by the sports games."

"How do you keep doing that?" Cooper asked.

Maddison's voice joined the lobby. "It's Snap Map. It's been on Snapchat since 2017, and it shows your real-time location to your friends on a map. Samara's watching your little icon walk around the store."

Cooper pulled out his phone and found the map. His own dot glowed in the middle of a building labeled with the mall's name, and around it he could see Samara's dot at her house and Maddison's dot at the food court, close enough that he could picture her table exactly. He had never thought of it before. A stranger could not see him, but every friend could, any time, whether he wanted them to or not.

He opened his chat and typed a message to Maddison: "Can I borrow two dollars for the cable? I'll pay you back Monday. Also, turning off my map now. It feels weird being a dot."

He pressed send, found the setting, and switched his location to ghost mode. His dot vanished from the map, though Samara would probably tease him about it later.

A reply popped up. "Deal. Meet me at the pretzel place. I'll insulate you from Samara's jokes. She's already typing."

Cooper walked toward the food court, cable money in reach, one invisible thing on his phone finally under his control.

The museum's Second World War gallery smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Madison had exactly forty minutes before Mr. Nakamura's class reassembled at the front doors. She stood in front of a display case with a copy of the Treaty of Versailles inside, her notebook open to a blank page.

"I don't get it," said Brennan, peering over her shoulder. "We have to explain how one treaty helped start a whole other war. That's like saying a scraped knee caused a broken leg."

"Mr. Nakamura said to find the factor nobody notices," Madison said. She read the panel beside the case twice. Then she saw it, a short paragraph about Article 231, and she copied the number down and underlined it. "Listen. Article 231 made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war."

"So what? Somebody always signs the papers."

Madison tapped the glass. "Everybody blamed Germany. Only Germany. They even called it the war guilt clause." She said the words slowly, because something was clicking into place, the way a math problem suddenly worked when you stopped rushing. "Imagine our group project fails, and the teacher blames only you. Not me, not Amari, just you."

Brennan frowned. "I'd be furious. Especially if we all messed it up."

"And would you want to work with that teacher again?" Madison asked. She was testing the idea the way she tested a hypothesis in science class, pushing on it to see if it held. "Would you trust anything they said afterward?"

"No way." Brennan paused. "Wait. So the treaty blamed Germany alone, and the whole country felt like..."

"Like you just did. Except a hundred times bigger." Madison scribbled fast, then crossed out a line and rewrote it. "That's the hidden part. You can't see resentment in a photograph. But it's there, and it's a factor in what came next."

Amari appeared from the WWI room, chewing the last of a granola bar. "Those cafe things are actually nutritious, unlike the vending machine. What'd I miss?"

"Madison figured out our whole presentation," Brennan said.

"Not the whole thing." Madison showed them her page. Three arrows ran from the treaty to the anger to the later war, and beside Article 231 she had written her group-project comparison. "When we present, I'll cite the article by number, and then I'll tell the class the project story. Mr. Nakamura said evidence plus a good analogy."

Amari read the page and nodded. "You should open with the blame part. Start small, then zoom out to the country."

The chime for regrouping sounded down the hall. Madison closed her notebook, hugged it against her chest, and headed for the doors with her two friends flanking her.

"First line," Amari said. "Say it to us like we're the class."

Madison took a breath. "Raise your hand if you've ever been blamed for something a whole group did."

Eve stared at three charts she had copied from the board, one for verbs ending in -ar, one for -er, one for -ir, and her hand already ached. Ms. Bautista had assigned a paragraph about plans for next year, all in the future tense, due at the end of class. Around her the language room smelled like dry-erase markers and somebody's grape gum, and Lux was drumming his pencil against his desk like a tiny, irritating woodpecker.

"I'm going to fail," Lux whispered. "Three charts. Twenty-something endings. My brain is a tsunami and everything I memorized is underwater."

Eve had written exactly one sentence: El año que viene yo comeré más verduras. Next year I will eat more vegetables, which was a lie, but at least it was a grammatical lie. She flipped back a page in her notebook and found a sentence from yesterday's homework: Yo viviré con mi abuela. I will live with my grandmother. She wrote both verbs side by side and squinted at them.

Comeré. Viviré. One ended in -er and one ended in -ir, but their endings looked the same. That couldn't be right. Teachers loved making things complicated, and Eve had learned the hard way that when something looked easy, it was usually a trap.

She tested it. On a scrap paper she took hablar, an -ar verb, and mashed the -é onto the end the way she had with the other two. Hablaré. Then she checked her chart. Hablaré. Identical. She tried three more, filling the scrap paper with crooked columns, and every single one matched. The three charts on the board were really one chart wearing three costumes.

"Psst. Lux." She slid the scrap paper across the aisle. "Look. Regular verbs share the same future endings whether they end in -ar, -er or -ir. One set. Not three."

Lux stared at it the way people stare at a vending machine that has given them two candy bars. "Then why did I memorize three charts last night?"

"Because we copy what's on the board without looking." Eve grinned, then felt the grin fade a little, because she had lost a whole evening to those charts too, an evening she could have spent at Alyvia's pool.

Alyvia leaned over from the next row, sniffing the paper as if the secret might smell like something. "Show me," she said, and Eve walked her through it once, quietly, while Ms. Bautista helped a boy who had written the same verb four times in a row.

Eve wrote her paragraph fast after that. El año que visitaré a mi abuela en México. Aprenderé a cocinar con ella. Hablaré español todos los días. The words poured out, and for once her pencil kept up with her head. She even added a joke at the end about how she would definitely, honestly eat vegetables, which Alyvia read over her shoulder and snorted at.

At the door, though, Ms. Bautista caught her. "Eve, I saw that scrap paper. Three charts erased, one kept." She held up Eve's notebook. "You crossed out two pages of notes."

"I didn't need them," Eve said, and heard how it came out, half proud and half like she'd thrown away something she'd paid for.

Ms. Bautista handed the notebook back with a small smile. "Keep the crossed-out pages anyway. Sometimes it helps to remember what things cost." Eve slid the notebook into her backpack, the dead charts still faintly visible under the lines of ink, and followed Alyvia out into the hall, where the bell was already ringing.

Jace sat on the floor of Stephanie's living room with her phone balanced on his knee, tapping through the photos she had just sent to the group chat. Stephanie wanted him to help her pick the best shot of the science fair volcano, because the class had been asked to nominate one picture for the school website, and the deadline was tonight. The fake lava had turned out great, orange and blurry with motion, but something else caught his eye before he could choose. When he swiped up on one of the photos Patience had sent from her house, a little map appeared at the bottom of the screen. He leaned closer, smelling the lemon cleaner on Stephanie's floorboards, and saw a red pin sitting on a street he recognized. It was Patience's street, exactly, down to the block.

"Stephanie, come look at this." She crawled over, chewing the last of a granola bar, and frowned at the pin. "Why does your phone know where Patience took her picture?" she asked. Jace tapped the info icon again, and a page of small grey text opened up. It showed numbers, a latitude and longitude, and near the top a label that read EXIF metadata. "That's what it's called," he said slowly. "EXIF metadata." Stephanie read the coordinates out loud like they were a spell.

Jace felt a small, acute worry tighten in his stomach, the same sharp feeling he'd had last summer when his cousin's photo of a scraped knee had somehow shown up on a stranger's account and everyone spent a week arguing about how it spread, like an infection moving through the group chat, one share at a time. "So if Patience sends a picture to the website," he said, "anyone who downloads it could see this? Like, strangers could see exactly where her house is?" Stephanie shrugged, but her thumb had stopped scrolling. "Check one of mine," she said, and pulled up her own volcano photo.

He tapped the same info page on her picture. No pin, no coordinates, just the date and the camera settings. "You must have location off for the camera," he said. He tested it twice more, opening Patience's photo, then Stephanie's, then Patience's again, and the pattern held. Location services on meant the map appeared; off meant nothing. That was the rule, and it was invisible unless you went looking.

Jace texted Patience: turn off location for your camera, then send the volcano again. Two minutes later a new photo arrived, and when he swiped up, the screen showed only the time it was taken. No red pin, no street, no numbers.

"Send this one to the website," Jace said, holding the phone out to Stephanie. She hit send, and the volcano's orange glow lit up the dark screen between them.

Brody leaned closer to Abdul's basement computer, where the desk lamp made a small island of light in the desolate, unfinished corner of the room. Abdul had promised to teach him Python tonight, and the notebook between them held three lines of code: ask for a number, divide it by everything smaller than it, and print "prime" if nothing divided it evenly. It had seemed so simple when Abdul explained it at school. Now Brody watched the cursor blink on a number he had typed in, nine digits long, and the program just sat there, thinking.

"Is it broken?" Brody asked. He pressed a key just to see if the screen would react. It did, so the computer was alive; something inside his program was grinding away. He felt a flicker of dread, the kind he got when a math test had five minutes left and two problems to go. Abdul shrugged and sipped his soda.

Brody stared at the loop in the notebook. For a divisor, it counted from two all the way up to the number itself, one at a time. Millions and millions of trial divisions, all invisible. He began to wonder what the divisions were actually doing. If a number was, say, 6, that was 2 times 3, and if it was 12, that was 3 times 4. Both factors, never both huge. He scribbled on the back page: 2 times 18 is 36, 4 times 9 is 36, 6 times 6 is 36. Every pair he wrote had at least one small number in it. Was that a rule? If a number was a times b, one of them always had to be small, no bigger than the square root of the whole thing. He tested another pair to be sure: 5 times 7 is 35, and 5 is smaller than the square root of 35. The small factor never vanished.

"So I only need to check divisors up to the square root," Brody said slowly. "If nothing up there divides it, nothing above it will either, because one of any pair is always that small." He felt like he had found a hinge and swung a heavy door open with one finger. He changed one line, capping the loop at the square root, saved the file, and typed the nine-digit number again.

The answer flashed onto the screen before he finished letting go of the Enter key: not prime. Brody laughed out loud. "It was fast because the answer was hiding in the small divisors the whole time," he said. "I just made the program search the whole desert when the well was near the house."

Abbul pulled his chair over. "Okay, that was wild. Try it on something with twelve digits."

Brody cracked his knuckles and started typing.

The envelope had been waiting on the kitchen table that morning, and now the phone sat heavy in Olivia's pocket on the school bus, its screen still showing the setup wizard she hadn't finished. She slid into the seat beside Willow, who peered over immediately.

"Did you integrate your contacts yet?" Willow asked. "Took me forever. Half the numbers in my mom's database came out wrong."

Olivia laughed, but before she could answer, the phone buzzed. A message glowed on the screen: a six-digit code, and above it the words: Your verification code is. She hadn't asked for any code. She hadn't even made an account yet.

"What's that?" Charley leaned over the seat from behind them.

"Nothing," Olivia said, locking the screen. Her stomach had gone tight. A minute later, another buzz. A different code. Then a third.

She remembered something Mr. Gupta had said in the computer club back in September, when he'd helped them set up the club's shared drive. Two-factor authentication, he'd called it, which asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account. At the time she'd thought it was just an extra annoying step. Now she turned it over slowly, staring at the fogged window. Somebody was trying to get into an account. And whoever it was already had her password, because otherwise the codes wouldn't be coming at all. Her password was the school one, the one she'd used everywhere since sixth grade.

"Whoa," Charley said, watching her face. "You look like you saw a ghost."

"Somebody has my password," Olivia said quietly.

Willow's eyes went wide. "Your email?"

The bus rumbled around the corner toward the school. Olivia opened her school account settings, thumbs shaking slightly, and changed the password to something long and new. Then she waited, the phone flat on her palm, watching the screen like a held breath. The bus hissed to a stop. No buzz. No code. She waited through the whole line of kids getting off.

"You're going to miss our stop," Willow said.

"One more second." The screen stayed dark. Whatever had been knocking at her account couldn't get in anymore, not without a second proof, and the second proof came only to her phone, in her hand.

"Ironic," Charley said, climbing over the seat. "The codes that told you something was wrong are the same thing keeping them out."

Olivia stood, dropped the phone into her pocket, and stepped down off the bus into the cold morning air. "New rule," she said. "Different password for everything, starting today."

Anais had babysat exactly zero babies before Saturday, which was why she kept the parents' note in her back pocket and checked it every ten minutes. The baby, Milo, was eight months old, and they were spending the morning at the park by the duck pond because Milo liked watching the ducks and Anais liked having something to look at besides her own nerves. Her little brother's friend Grant had tagged along to feed the ducks, which he claimed was impartial diplomacy between the mallards and the geese, though really he just liked throwing bread.

Milo got fussy around eleven, so Anais settled him in the stroller and dug out the jar of food his mom had packed. Milo refused the spoon, clamping his mouth shut and turning his head like a tiny, determined door slammed shut. Anais thought about it. Babies liked sweet things, everyone knew that. In the pantry at home, her mom kept a squeeze bottle of honey, and Anais remembered she had a packet of honey crackers in her bag from lunch. She reached for the crackers, thinking she could crumble one into the jar and make the food taste better.

"Wait," Grant said, pointing with his bread hand. "Isn't there a note?" Anais pulled the folded paper from her pocket. The parents had written it that morning, and she had only skimmed it.

"Do not give Milo honey," she read. "No honey for babies under 12 months old. It can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism. Not even a little. Not even in crackers." She lowered the note. Her stomach did a slow flip. She had been about to do the exact thing they warned against, and she had walked right up to it without knowing.

"I was going to mix honey into his food," she said. "I was that close." Grant whistled. "So the spores just sit there in honey until a baby digests it, and then, boom?" Anais nodded slowly, then remembered she shouldn't nod like she'd known all along. "Something like that. The note says they grow in his gut." Grant looked at the ducks, then at Milo. "So honey's like a trap that only works on babies. That's the weirdest supervillain origin story ever."

Anais texted her older cousin, who had two kids, to double-check. The reply came fast: "Yep, no honey before their first birthday. Under 12 months, their gut can't handle the spores. After a year it's fine. You did the right thing asking." Anais read it twice, then put the phone away feeling steadier.

The actual problem was still in front of her: Milo was hungry and refusing plain food. She tried warming the jar between her palms first, which her cousin had also suggested in a follow-up message, and then offered the spoon again. Milo considered her with deep suspicion, opened his mouth like a small eager bird, and ate the whole jar. When she burped him, he patted her arm with one fat hand, gently, as if approving her work. Grant fed the last of the bread to an enormous goose and said, "You're basically a professional." Milo burped again, louder this time, and Anais laughed so hard she had to sit down on the bench.

Elizabeth pulled her shin guard out of her locker, and a folded note fell out with it. The locker room smelled like rubber mats and orange peel, and Kaley was already lacing her cleats on the bench beside her. The note was written on a torn corner of the tryout sign-up sheet, in Jiya's loopy handwriting: "Check the birthdays on the posted roster. Count them. Trust me."

"Jiya's being mysterious again," Elizabeth said, waving the note.

"Jiya's always being mysterious. Yesterday she told me my shoelaces were tied in a pattern. They were just tied."

At the wall by the showers, the list of girls who had made the soccer team hung crooked on a pushpin. Elizabeth had missed the cut, and her name was not on it, which was bad enough. But under each name, someone had written the player's birth month for a team-birthday chart the coach was making. She read them off. Sophie, January. Priya, March. Amelia, February. One girl had an October birthday, and one had a November, and then Elizabeth herself, December. She counted twice. Most of the kids who made the team were born early in the year, and the ones born late, like her, mostly had not.

"Maybe the older kids got picked more," she said slowly. "They're not better. They're just months older."

Kaley frowned. "That sounds fake."

"My arm's sore," Jiya announced, bursting in from the hallway and rubbing her shoulder. "Flu vaccine yesterday. Also, I read about your mystery. Kids born early in the selection year get picked for teams way more than kids born late."

"What's that called?" Elizabeth asked.

"The relative age effect," Jiya said, with the smugness of someone who had practiced saying it in the mirror.

Elizabeth exhaled, long and dramatic, and sat down on the bench. Then she stood up again. "Okay. Test. Coach ranked us on speed and skills, but I only got two touches on the ball in the scrimmage because Sophie hogged it. I was hesitant in the drill, sure, but nobody passes to a girl they don't know." She marched to the coach's office door, which had a sign-up sheet taped to it for a second tryout for the practice squad, added that morning.

She wrote her name at the top, then turned around. "Jiya, you're doing my birthday chart next time, and it better say December, in glitter."

"Fine," said Jiya, "but only if you score on Sophie."

Elizabeth grinned and pulled her cleats back on.

The sliding doors of Hilltop Grocery exhaled cold air onto Alex's face as he pushed through with the Saturday-morning crowd. In his backpack sat a half-finished sheet for Mr. Hoffmann's class: compare a stock and a bond, say which is riskier and why, due Monday. He had two days, and so far the page held only a doodle of a dollar sign wearing sunglasses.

His mother handed him a list and sent him toward the cereal aisle while she queued for the deli. That was where he ran into Eleonore, who was weighing oranges like they were treasure and reading a battered pamphlet at the same time.

"Don't tell me you finished the Hoffmann thing," Alex said.

"Almost. My grandpa gave me a savings bond years ago, so I asked him about it. Want to hear?" She put an orange back and lowered her voice, as if sharing a secret. "A bond is a loan from an investor to a government or a company. It promises to pay interest and to repay the original amount on a set date."

Alex stared at her. "Wait. A loan? I thought the government loaned you the money."

"No, it's the other way. Grandpa lent the money when he bought the bond. The government borrowed it."

A memory floated up, tranquil and sharp at once: sitting at his grandfather's kitchen table three summers ago, holding a crisp paper bond with his own name on it, feeling rich without understanding what he owned. He had thanked Grandpa, stuck it in a drawer, and never thought about it again. Now he turned the memory over like an orange in his hand. He had been the lender all along. The town, with its roads and library and school, had borrowed from him.

"So a stock," he said slowly, walking with her past the bread racks, "is when you buy a tiny piece of a company, and it can go up or down or vanish. But the bond promises to pay interest and pay back the original amount on a set date."

"Right. Now which is riskier?"

Alex tested it out loud. "Nobody promises you anything with a stock. The company could boom or flop. The bond promises." He paused by the dairy case. "So the stock is riskier. No promise."

"That's what my grandpa said."

At the checkout, Alex's mother was already unloading the cart, and the cashier, who commuted in from two towns over every Saturday, was scanning soup cans at lightning speed. Alex helped bag, still turning the problem over. He remembered Grandpa once saying he wished he'd bought more bonds and fewer stocks before the market dipped years back. Maybe that was wisdom. Maybe it was just a man steadying himself against an old regret. Alex couldn't decide, and Eleonore's shrug in the parking lot said she couldn't either.

Monday felt closer than Monday should. Alex folded the pamphlet Eleonore had lent him, slid it into his bag between the cereal and the milk, and said, "Let's write it tonight."

The car smelled like his dad's coffee and the pine air freshener that had died sometime in October. Cameron sat in the back with his tie stuffed in his pocket because wearing it for the whole ride felt like too much commitment. Outside, the gym windows glowed yellow, and he could see shapes moving inside, kids, actual kids, dancing or standing near a wall that the art club had covered in paper stars meant to depict a night sky. His stomach flipped so hard he pressed a hand against it.

"Motion sickness?" his dad asked, glancing in the mirror.

"No. My heart's going fast too, like I ran a mile, but I've been sitting still the whole time." He checked his pulse with two fingers, the way Patience had shown him in science class when they were being meticulous about counting heartbeats per minute. Fast. Really fast, for a person doing nothing but holding a tie.

His phone buzzed. Leonard: "im by the door dont leave me hanging."

Cameron stared at the message and thought it through. His heart was racing and his stomach felt hollow, the feeling everybody called butterflies, even though nothing was flying around in there. When he ran laps in gym, his heart raced like this, but his stomach never felt like this. So the running wasn't what caused the flip. What was different right now? He wasn't moving. He wasn't sick.
