"More than 200 different viruses. And the most frequent ones are called rhinoviruses."

"No wonder we get colds all the time," Emery said. There was a pause, and Lucas heard typing in the background, which meant Emery was only half listening. "So, um. The science fair thing. Ms. Novák picked lab partners today. You got me, obviously. But I already told her our topic. Is that okay? I mean, you're not mad?"

Lucas realized Emery hadn't texted to check on him at all. Emery had texted because he felt guilty. "What topic?" Lucas asked.

"Vaccines," Emery said quickly. "How they work. It's a legitimate project, it has real research, I checked. And now you're literally an expert because you looked all that stuff up while dying on your couch." Emery laughed a little, then stopped, waiting.

Lucas thought about it. A vaccine project with a partner who had already chosen it wasn't what he'd planned. But two hundred viruses was a real hook, a question a judge couldn't guess the answer to. "Fine," he said. "But I want the part where we explain why nobody's ever cured the cold. And you owe me all the notes from today's meeting."

"Deal," Emery said. "I'll bring them over tomorrow. My mom says soup helps, so I'm bringing soup. From the corporation-sized can, so don't worry, there's plenty."

"Bring crackers too," Lucas said, and pulled his notebook closer to start a page titled with a fat number: 200.

Emily spread her science fair notebook across the library table and tapped the page titled "Can People Tell Name-Brand Cola from Store Brand?" The taste test was in three days, and she still had one column blank.

"Twenty people," Alexandre said, reading over her shoulder. "Ten get the name brand first, ten get the store brand. You write down what they say."

"That's the problem." Emily turned her pencil over and over. "What if they guess right just because of how I hand them the cup? If I smile when I give them the good one, that's a clue."

Kaley slid into the third chair with her backpack still on one shoulder. "So don't smile."

"Faces leak," Emily said. "Everything leaks. The way you pour it. Which cup you reach for first."

Mr. Han, the librarian, came by with the cart of returns. He paused at the word "leak." "Testing people?" he asked.

"Taste test," Alexandre said. "For the science fair. My cousin did one last year, and every single person guessed right. He said his brand was just better."

"Was it?" Emily asked.

Alexandre shrugged. "He poured it for them. He wanted his brand to win, so who knows how he poured it."

Emily wrote "cousin" in the margin and crossed it out. She stared at the two columns on her page, one labeled "sample" and one labeled "what they said." Then she drew a third column and labeled it "who knew."

"What if I don't know which cup is which either?" she said slowly. "Then I can't give anything away, because I don't have anything to give."

Kaley frowned. "Then how do you keep track?"

"Someone labels them and leaves." Emily's pencil moved fast now. "My mom pours the cups tonight. She puts a mark on the bottom, like A and B, and writes down which is which on a card. She seals the card in an envelope. Tomorrow she's not even at the fair. She complies with the rule that she can't be in the room when people taste."

"She won't like that rule," Kaley said.

"She'll like it fine. It's for science."

Alexandre took the envelope idea further. "The people tasting can't know either," he said. "If they think the name brand is in one specific cup, they'll believe they taste it, even if it isn't there."

"So nobody knows," Emily said. "Not them, not me. Only the envelope." She flipped to the back of her notebook and found the term in a book she'd read about medicine trials. "It's called double-blind. Neither the participants nor the researchers know who's getting the real thing."

"Then your cousin's test wasn't fair," Alexandre said.

"His test was a story about one person. Mine will be a claim with evidence." She underlined the last line of her plan.

On Saturday she set up her table near the biography section, with its quiet rows and the smell of old paper. The two coolers sat side by side in perfect symmetry, each with plain white cups, and Emily served sample after sample without a clue in her head about what she was pouring. A man in a跑步 jacket tasted cup A, then cup B, and said the store brand was the name brand, absolutely certain. A girl Emily's age got both right. By noon, fourteen of twenty-two people had guessed wrong, which was close to what pure chance would look like.

At two o'clock Mr. Han cut open the envelope with the library's scissors and read the card aloud. Emily tallied the final score: nine right out of twenty-two. She looked at the number for a long moment, then laughed out loud in the middle of the quiet library.

"So nobody could tell," Alexandre said. "Not even you."

"Not even me," Emily said, and wrote it down.

The bus smelled like sunscreen and pretzels by the time it reached Old Fort Hastings, where a guide in a tri-corner hat was waiting to show them the barracks, the powder room, and the guard tower. Jaxson had been skeptical about the whole trip, mostly because the permission slip mentioned a fire safety drill, which sounded like something for little kids. "Thirteen years old," he muttered to Jaya as they filed through the gate, "and they're teaching us how to duck."

The surprise came in the guard tower's lower chamber, where a firefighter had set up a machine that pushed out a harmless gray haze, like fog escaping a cooler. The plan was for each student to cross the room through the haze and reach the far door. Hailey went first, walking upright, coughing and waving her arms the moment she hit the wall of gray. The room filled fast, and the haze hung thick near the ceiling while a thinner layer drifted at knee height. Jaxson watched from the line and noticed something: the fog rolled upward when it came out, piling along the top of the room first.

He turned the observation over while the line crept forward. In a real fire, he reasoned, the hot air would act like that machine's fog, carrying smoke upward, which would leave the lower air clearer and cooler than the air above it. That would explain why the drill wanted them low, and it refuted his earlier theory that crawling was just about staying under the smoke's height like limbo. It wasn't only about height. It was about which air was cleaner and cooler, near the floor, where the smoke and heat hadn't pooled.

When his turn came, he stood up straight for exactly three steps, just to test it. His eyes stung and he tasted something acrid, and the heat of the demonstration lamps near the ceiling pressed down on him like a hand. He dropped to his hands and knees and the world changed at once. Below the haze he could see the floorboards, the door frame, even Jaya's sneakers ahead of him. The air felt cooler there too. He crawled fast, and when he pushed through the door he was grinning instead of coughing.

Mr. Bakker met them on the tower steps, clipboard in hand. "Well, Mr. Stand-Up-Straight," he said. "Learn anything in there?"

"Smoke and heat rise," Jaxson said, "so the cleaner, cooler air is down near the floor. That's why you crawl low under it." He looked back at the doorway, where Hailey was still blinking the sting out of her eyes. He jogged up the steps, unclipped his own water bottle, and held it out to her.

Zoe curled her fingers into what the cookbook called the claw grip, knuckles forward, and set the blade against the onion. "If I cut myself," she said, "I want it noted that I opposed this project from the start."

"You proposed this project," said Kristopher from his perch on the dilapidated stool by the window, the one that wobbled like it was deciding whether to keep being a stool. "On Tuesday. In writing. There was a list."

There had been a list. Number three was "make pasta sauce from scratch, not from a jar," and Zoe had underlined it twice, which at the time had felt like commitment. Now the onion was making her eyes stream and Kristopher was reading out her own list back to her, which she felt was a misuse of the document.

She got through the onion, uneven cubes sliding across the cutting board, and dumped it into the pan with the garlic and a glug of oil. She turned the heat to high because high seemed faster. The kitchen smelled good for about ninety seconds. Then it smelled like something had gone wrong in a way she couldn't see. The sauce, when she stirred and tasted it, was bitter, a flat acrid taste that no amount of stirring fixed.

Kristopher tasted it too and made a face he tried to hide, badly. "It's a new genre of sauce," he said. "Sauce, but punishing."

Zoe stood over the pan and thought. The onion looked fine, soft and golden. She fished out a piece of garlic and looked at it. Dark. Really dark, almost brown at the edges, while the onion beside it had barely colored. They'd gone into the pan at the same moment, on the same heat, and only one of them had burnt. The garlic was in smaller pieces, sure, but Kristopher's onions on taco night got smaller than that and never turned bitter. So maybe it wasn't size. Maybe garlic just couldn't take the heat the way onion could, and it burnt while the onion was still softening, and burnt garlic was what the whole pot now tasted like.

She dumped the batch, rinsed the pan, and started over. This time the onion went in alone, and she waited, scraping and turning, until the pieces went soft and translucent. Only then did she mince the garlic and slide it in, stirring fast. Thirty seconds later the smell was completely different, warm and sweet instead of sharp.

She dropped in the tomatoes, lowered the heat, and handed Kristopher the wooden spoon. "Taste in ten minutes," she said. "And if it's good, we're crediting me twice on that list."

Sophia had babysat plenty of times before, but never for the Hendersons' little boy, Eli, who was almost two. Mrs. Henderson showed her where the diapers were, where the snacks were, and then pointed at the upstairs hallway. "Bath is at seven. He loves his ducks."

At seven, Eli sat in the tub with three rubber ducks and about four inches of water, slapping the surface and shrieking with joy. Sophia knelt beside him on the bath mat, keeping one hand on his slippery shoulder. Downstairs, the phone rang. She glanced at the door, then back at Eli, who was reaching for the soap.

Her mother had drilled one rule into her before she ever watched a child: a toddler can drown in just a few inches of water, and it can happen without any splashing or crying out, so a child should never be left alone in or near the bath. Not for a phone call, not for anything. Sophia had rolled her eyes at the time, but standing there with the phone ringing and Eli wobbling forward on his knees, the rule suddenly felt like the edge of a frontier, and she had no idea what lay past it. She was not going to find out.

She yanked the big frog towel off the hook, lifted Eli out of the water even though he protested in a small, furious voice, and wrapped him up like a burrito. Then she carried him, dripping and squirming, down the stairs. "I know," she told him. "Bath is fun. We'll go back." She answered the phone on the fifth ring. It was Mrs. Henderson, checking in.

"Everything okay? I heard the water running."

"Yes, we're in the middle of bath time," Sophia said, bouncing Eli on her hip. "He's taking a break in a towel. He's never alone near the water, not even for a second. That's my rule."

There was a pause, and then a warm sound on the line. "Good girl. That's exactly right."

After the call, Sophia lugged Eli back up and set him on the bathroom floor while she added a little warm water. He was small and still so frail compared to his big sister, Madelyn, who lived next door and sometimes carried him around like a sack of potatoes. Sophia had texted Madelyn earlier: "First night with your brother's twin, the Henderson kid." Madelyn had replied with three laughing faces.

When Eli was dry and in pajamas, Sophia read him the book about the moon three times. On the third time he fell asleep against her arm, one duck still clutched in his fist. She lowered him into the crib the way she had practiced with a pillow an hour before Mrs. Henderson left.

When the headlights swept the front window, Sophia was downstairs writing a note about how many duck books they had read. Mrs. Henderson came in quietly, read it, and smiled. "I have to confess something," she whispered. "I left the phone ringing on purpose. It was a test."

Sophia stared at her. "You did not."

"I did. And you carried him out wrapped in a towel." Mrs. Henderson set her keys in the dish by the door. "Same time next Friday?"

Sophia grinned and picked up her backpack. "Only if the ducks come too."

The trail climbed in switchbacks above the creek, and Evelyn kept her phone in her pocket, which was hard, because her whole science grade was living inside it. She had a presentation due Monday about monsoons, and so far her notes said only "WIND? + RAIN? + RICE???"

"Are you muttering at the dirt again?" Penelope asked, catching up. "Because the dirt can't help you."

"It's not dirt, it's evidence." Evelyn pointed at the hillside, where the grass had gone crunchy and yellow in patches. "The creek's low, the grass is brittle. That's what happens when the rain comes late."

Santino swung his water bottle by its strap. "So your presentation is about dry grass."

"It's about monsoons." She had read the word a dozen times and still couldn't quite picture it. "In South Asia, the wind changes direction in summer and it pours rain for months. But last year the monsoon came late, and it was weak, so..." She stopped. "Wait. If the rain is late and small, the farmers can't plant their rice on time."

"Boo, rice," Santino said. "Rice is boring."

"That's what I thought too," Evelyn admitted. "But then my mom bought rice on Tuesday and stood in the aisle making a face at the price. It had gone up since last month. She said the news mentioned the weak monsoon, and I thought, that can't be a coincidence."

Ms. Liu, walking at the back of the group, raised an eyebrow but said nothing, which was her way of saying keep going.

Evelyn crouched by the creek and wet her finger, then held it up. Penelope copied her, and so did Santino, though he looked like he was saluting something.

"What are we doing?" Penelope asked.

"Feeling which way the wind blows. If the wind pivots, like it does when a monsoon starts, it comes from a different direction than before. I want to feel a pivot." She closed her eyes. The breeze slid past her wet finger from the uphill side. "Okay. From the ridge. If it pivoted tomorrow and blew from the creek side instead, that would be the kind of switch that pulls moisture in."

Santino frowned at his own finger. "Mine feels cold from every direction."

"That's because you dipped your whole hand in the creek, genius," Penelope said.

Evelyn laughed, then sat down on a rock and started writing fast: late monsoon means delayed planting, weak monsoon means smaller harvest, smaller harvest means the rice costs more, which is why her mom had made the face. It was like a chain, and you couldn't see the first link from a grocery store. You had to reason backward, from a price sticker all the way to a wind that pivots an ocean away.

"You're muttering again," Penelope said.

"I'm drafting. It's different."

On the hike down, Santino kept asking questions. Did the farmers just wait? Could they store water to conserve it for a bad year? Was there any crop that handled a late monsoon better? Evelyn answered what she could and wrote down the rest. "Rice isn't boring," Santino announced at the trailhead. "Rice is a whole detective story."

That night she rehearsed the presentation in the kitchen, using a squirt bottle as the ocean, and her dad applauded with a sandwich in one hand.

Monday morning, she stood up in class with her diagrams, took a breath, and said, "My topic is dry grass."

Ms. Liu said, "Evelyn."

"Monsoons," Evelyn said. "I was testing you. Anyway, it starts with a price sticker."

Sydney stood in the shoe-lined hallway of the gurdwara with her phone in her pocket, turned off like Ms. Cho had asked, and tried to get the first line of Japji Sahib to stick in her head. Her best friend Larissa was being initiated next month, and she had asked Sydney to help her learn the morning prayer by heart before then. That was a bigger job than Sydney had expected. The words were in Gurmukhi script, and even in the English transliteration they rolled and folded in ways her tongue kept tripping over.

They sat cross-legged on the carpeted floor of the langar hall after the morning service, a shared notebook open between them. "Okay, from Ik Onkar," Larissa said, closing her eyes. She got through four lines, then her memory dropped off a cliff. She opened one eye. "Your turn to catch me."

Sydney had noticed something while listening that morning. The recitation hadn't been one flat string of sound. Certain phrases came back again and again, the way a chorus returns in a song, and the people reciting grew louder and steadier each time. She wondered if the prayer had a shape she couldn't see from the outside, some hierarchy of parts, with the repeated lines holding the smaller ones together. "Do the parts that repeat come at regular intervals?" she asked. "Like, is it consistent?"

Larissa counted on her fingers along the printed page, tapping each heading. "Sunhil, sunh," she murmured, tapping, tapping. "Yeah. The sections all end with the same kind of closing phrase." She looked up, surprised at her own discovery, as if the pattern had been hiding in her mouth all those years of listening and only now showed itself.

They drilled the first five sections that way, with Sydney tapping the carpet at every returning phrase like a metronome. It worked better than plain repetition. When Larissa could say all five without dropping a word, they went to find Ms. Cho, who was stacking steel cups in the kitchen. "She's ready for the whole thing," Sydney said.

Ms. Cho smiled and dried her hands. "Do you know why we take extra care with Japji Sahib?" she asked, and then shook her head before either of them could answer. "No, I won't tell you. Ask your grandmother, Larissa."

They found Larissa's grandmother by the door, wrapped in her shawl. "It is recited at Amrit Sanchar," she said simply, "the Khalsa initiation ceremony. When you take amrit, Japji Sahib is part of it." Larissa went quiet, and Sydney let the information digest. The prayer her friend was memorizing wasn't just a morning habit. It would be spoken on one of the biggest days of her life, in front of everyone.

"Then we'd better not mess it up," Sydney said. She flipped the notebook back to the first page. "Ik Onkar. Again."

Larissa closed her eyes.

Bentley sat on the piano bench in Mr. Huang's studio, but the instrument in his lap was a guitar he had borrowed from his cousin, and it was winning. He had spent a week practicing the chord changes for the recital piece, and in the practice room at school the chords had sounded almost clean. Here, under Mr. Huang's ear, every chord buzzed like a parliament of angry magpies arguing over a crumb.

"You're pressing too hard," Mr. Huang said, which was strange, because in the practice room Bentley had been told he wasn't pressing hard enough.

"I don't get it," Bentley admitted. "Same guitar, same me. Why does it sound different here?"

Alycia, who was waiting for her lesson on the bench by the window, looked up from her phone. "Maybe your cousin's guitar is haunted."

"Very helpful."

She grinned, but Bentley kept turning it over. Something was different between the two rooms. He hadn't changed. His hands hadn't changed. The songs hadn't changed. In the practice room he sat in a low chair; here he perched on a tall piano bench, guitar sliding off his thigh. His left hand stretched at a steeper angle, reaching, and a stretched hand clamps instead of presses.

"Mr. Huang, can I try the chair?"

Mr. Huang raised an eyebrow, then waved him toward the folding chair by the door. Bentley sat, planted his feet, and played the same chord that had buzzed thirty seconds before. It rang clean, and he laughed out loud.

While Mr. Huang fetched the metronome, Bentley, feeling bold, plucked the open low string and let it hum. Then he pressed down at the twelfth fret, halfway along the neck, and plucked again. The sound was the same note, only higher. He tried it three more times, pressing at the exact middle of the string each time, and every time the open string's note came back, lifted. He could feel something invisible working, a rule hiding inside the wood and wire.

"Mr. Huang, why does the middle sound like the same note, just higher?"

"That's called an octave," Mr. Huang said. "Rest your finger directly over the twelfth fret and touch lightly, don't press."

Bentley tried it. The string whispered out a bell-like note, pure and floating, the octave again without his finger even pressing down. Alycia left her phone in her bag and came to stand beside him.

"I have to confide something," she said, low enough that only Bentley could hear. "I've been terrified of the recital for two weeks. I was going to fake being sick."

Bentley played the harmonic one more time. "Sit in the chair," he said. "It helps."

Jordan had meant to resent the whole assignment, and he told his grandfather so while carrying the box of old science books up from the basement. "Mr. Munro says we have to memorize the atomic numbers of twenty elements by Monday," he said, setting the box on the kitchen table. "Twenty. And half of them I can't even pronounce."

His grandfather, who was frail enough now that climbing the basement stairs took him a while, lowered himself into a chair and started flipping through the box. "Have a look at this one," he said, pulling out a thin paperback with a cracked spine. "I bought it secondhand when I was about your age. The landlord of the bookshop practically gave it away."

Jordan opened it and found a folded chart at the back, a periodic table printed in faded ink. Most of it looked familiar, rows of boxes with letters and numbers. Then he noticed something strange. Several boxes were empty. Just blanks with dashes where names should be, sitting in neat positions among the filled ones. "Why would anyone print a table with holes in it?" he asked. "Was it a misprint?"

"That's what I wondered too," his grandfather said, tapping the page but saying nothing more, which was his way of making Jordan work for things.

Jordan pulled out his phone and texted Angelica, who was the one person in his class who actually enjoyed this stuff. He wrote: old periodic table with blank boxes, why? While he waited, he tried something with the chart itself. He found carbon, saw the number 6 at the top of its box, and counted: six protons. He checked neon, atomic number 10, and thought ten protons, which felt obvious once he looked. Then oxygen, number 8. It worked every time, like a rule hiding under the numbers. The atomic number wasn't just a label. It told you something you couldn't see, something about particles way too small to look at, and the chart gave you a way to count them anyway.

Angelica texted back a long message, and Jordan read it out loud. "Mendeleev, the guy who built the first table, left gaps in it on purpose. He predicted elements nobody had found yet." Jordan ran his finger over the empty boxes again. So they weren't mistakes. They were guesses, waiting. He scrolled down in her message. "One of the gaps got filled by gallium when somebody finally discovered it. It fit right where the blank had been."

Jordan looked at his grandfather, then back at the chart, then grabbed a pencil. "Can I keep this book?" he asked. "I want to figure out which gap gallium filled."

His grandfather smiled and pushed the salt shaker aside to make room. "Start counting," he said.

The science museum was hiring junior docents for the summer, and the interview was simple: stand at the big water table in the River Power exhibit and explain to visitors how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. Brooke had signed up because the job came with a name tag and free admission, but now she had a problem. Mr. Cardinal, who ran the program, had watched her rehearse with Shea and Shania and said her explanation sounded like she was reciting a card. "Learn the table first," he said. "Then talk."

The table was a long basin of pale sand with water pumped through it from one end to the other. You could shape the sand with your hands, and a crank let you change the speed of the current. Brooke bent the sand into a single curve, like a letter C lying down, and turned the crank to medium. Shea stood on her left, Shania on her right, both leaning over the glass.

"Watch the outside of the bend," Brooke said. She dropped a pinch of confetti near the top of the curve, and they all followed it. The pieces shot along the far bank, the outside wall of the curve, moving so fast they blurred. Confetti dropped near the inside bank crawled, barely drifting. "Fastest on the outside," Brooke said. "Slowest on the inside."

Within a few minutes the sand showed it. The outside bank, where the fast water hit, steepened into a cut wall, collapsing in small slices and washing downstream. The inside bank grew a smooth apron of pale sand and fine gravel that widened every time they looked. Shania pointed at it. "It's building a little beach." Brooke nodded. "That's deposition," she said. "The slow water drops what it's carrying, right there on the inside." Shea traced the deep channel hugging the outer wall with one finger above the glass, not quite touching.

Brooke tested it twice more. She made a tighter curve and the outside bank eroded faster; she made a gentler one and it eroded slower, but always on the outside, never the inside. The pattern held every time. She straightened up and looked at the whole table, the cut bank and the beach sitting opposite each other on the same bend, and thought about millions of years of this, the river swinging side to side, chewing down and laying down at once.

She turned the pump off and the water went opaque with stirred silt, so she waited for it to settle. Mr. Cardinal came back with a clipboard. "You have five minutes," he said. "Show me." Brooke pointed at the bend. "The water runs fastest on the outside of the bend, so it erodes that bank. On the inside it's slowest, so it drops its sand and gravel there. A river doing that over millions of years carves a canyon." Mr. Cardinal looked at the table, then at her. "Better," he said. "Now say it to a stranger." The first stranger through the door was a boy with a juice box, and Brooke stepped forward and asked, "Want to see a canyon get started?"

The birthday party was in Addison's backyard, which smelled like charcoal and sunscreen, and Levi was on his second slice of cake when Kenneth started in on a kid named Milo from their class. Milo had worn the same dinosaur backpack since fourth grade, and Kenneth thought this was hilarious in the way that only seventh graders can. "Nice backpack," Kenneth said, loud enough for the whole picnic table. "Does it commute to school with you, or does it walk?" A couple of kids laughed. Milo stared at his plate.

Levi knew the feeling. Two weeks ago, at lunch, some kids had gone after his friend's shoes, and Levi had sat there chewing, pretending to be deeply interested in his milk carton. The next day Ms. Villanueva's class had a discussion about it. She'd said one sentence and then moved on, and it had stuck in Levi's head like a burr: "An upstander is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander." Levi had spent the rest of the day wondering which word described what he'd done at lunch. Bystander, obviously. He'd been a bystander with a milk carton.

Here was the thing, though. He'd also learned, from a failed attempt on the bus, that yelling "Leave him alone, jerk" just gave everyone a better show. The teasing moved to him, then doubled back on the original kid, and the whole thing got worse. So there was a rule in there somewhere, invisible but real: attention was the fuel. If you made a big loud thing of it, you fed the fire. His idea was that the opposite might work. Don't attack. Don't lecture. Just quietly move the attention somewhere harmless.

He picked up the water balloon from beside his chair. "Milo," he said, "you still owe me a rematch from the arcade. I've been practicing." This was not exactly true, but it was true enough. Milo looked up, cautious, like a dog checking whether the stick was real. "You did not practice anything," Milo said. "I watched you lose to a claw machine on Saturday." The table's attention drifted toward the claw machine story, which involved Levi, a plastic penguin, and a certain amount of public humiliation that was safe because he was telling it himself. By the time he finished, Kenneth had wandered off toward the piñata, and nobody was looking at the backpack.

Later, Milo found him by the drinks. "That was decent of you," Milo said. "You didn't have to do the whole balloon thing." Levi shrugged. "I've been thinking about that word Ms. Villanueva said. Upstander. I figured there's probably a dumb way and a smart way to be one." Milo considered this, sipping his punch. "So which were you?" "The smart way," Levi said. "Obviously." Milo tipped his cup, and a single red drop landed on Levi's shoe.

Ms. MacLeod handed out the copies of Romeo and Juliet, and Victoria slid hers to the corner of the desk where the shadow from the window wouldn't fall across the words. Jayden groaned beside her, but quietly, because Ms. MacLeod had already assigned parts. Victoria had the servant, a part with almost no words at all, which was why she'd wanted it. She still remembered last year, when she'd frozen during the class play and Alejandro had to whisper her whole line to her. She wasn't going to be the person who froze again, even if it meant taking the smallest role in the room.

Then she read her part and frowned. The servant had one word. Three times, whenever someone called from offstage, the servant shouted "Anon!" at the door. That was it. "Anon, anon!" Jayden read the calling lines in a big dramatic voice, and Victoria said "Anon!" and felt ridiculous, because she had no idea what she was saying.

She tried a hypothetical version in her head: what if "Anon" were the servant's name? It didn't fit. Nobody called him that. They called "Boy!" and "What, ho!" and he answered "Anon, anon!" every single time. Victoria tapped her pencil and looked at the pattern. Someone calls. He answers with the same word. Then he shows up. She remembered the French word "à présent," which her grandmother used on the phone, always meaning now, soon, on my way. What if "Anon" worked like that? She wrote "Coming right away!" in the margin, small, in pencil so she could erase it if she turned out to be wrong.

"Okay," Ms. MacLeod said, "paraphrase your speeches into modern English, in your groups. Victoria, you first, since your servant has the least to say."

Victoria took a breath. "When they call him, he says 'Anon,' and I think it means at once or soon. So a servant calling 'Anon!' is saying, coming right away." She gripped the desk, ready to be wrong.

Jayden flipped to the footnotes at the back of the book and ran his finger down the page. He couldn't refute her; the note said the same thing, right there in tiny print. "You got it," he said, and Alejandro held out his fist for her to bump.

"Read it again," Ms. MacLeod said. "With the meaning this time."

Jayden bellowed his line from across the room, and Victoria called "Anon! Coming right away!" at the door, loud enough that the class in the next room probably heard her.

Alice leaned on the chain-link fence behind first base, pressing her palm against her sore right shoulder. Nahla jogged over from the pitcher's mound and dropped her glove on the dirt beside her.

"It's the lactic acid," Nahla said. "My brother says that's what makes you sore after you pitch."

Alice frowned. "We pitched yesterday at practice. If lactic acid were the problem, it should have showed up right away, not today." She had read something about this in the sports medicine book Ms. Lin kept on the shelf in the equipment shed, and one detail stuck with her: lactic acid returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise. She turned that over in her head. "So your arms should have felt fine by the time we walked home yesterday. The soreness started this morning."

"So it's not lactic acid at all," Nahla said. "It's something else."

"It's something that happens later. A day later, maybe." Alice picked up her glove. "Which means it's not something you can fix by resting for an hour after pitching."

Avianna called from the dugout. "Are you two planning to play, or are you taking a science class out here?"

They took the field. Alice played second base, and by the fourth inning her legs were heavy with fatigue, though nothing hurt the way her shoulder had hurt that morning. When a ground ball skipped toward her, she kept her glove low, fielded it cleanly, and threw to first without trying to be aggressive about it. The runner was out by two steps.

Between innings she crouched beside Avianna near the water cooler. "Yesterday after practice I sat around for an hour and then biked home," Alice said. "If lactic acid caused the soreness, that rest should have cleared it, because it's back to normal within about an hour after exercise. But I woke up sore anyway. So sitting still after pitching doesn't help."

"Then what does help?" Avianna asked.

"Moving, maybe. Gently. Not sitting." Alice stood and swung her arms in slow circles. "Ms. Lin had us walk laps after the hard practice last week, remember? I wasn't sore the next morning."

Nahla jogged over from shortstop. "You're revising your whole warmup based on this?"

"I'm revising my whole cooldown," Alice said. "Walk it off tomorrow, don't just collapse on the couch."

In the seventh inning, with the tying run on third, Alice ranged to her left, backhanded a line drive that most players would never have reached, and fired to first to end the game. Her legs ached, but her shoulder felt loose. On the walk to the fence she turned to Nahla.

"Tell your brother he's wrong about the lactic acid," she said. "And tell him he owes me a slushie."

Lincoln had the phone in his hand for twenty minutes before he texted Blair. "It died," he typed. "The whole thing. Like a minute in." He and Maina had gone to the coffee shop after school, and it had started fine, and then he had asked if she liked Mr. Pemberton's class, and she said no, and he asked if she liked the school play, and she said yes, and then they both drank their hot chocolates until the cups were empty. He had walked her home anyway, and she had said "see you," which could mean anything.

"You asked yes-or-no questions the whole time," Blair texted back. "Everyone does that when they're nervous. It's like a quiz."

Lincoln stared at the message. He scrolled back through the afternoon in his head, counting. Do you like school. Do you have brothers. Is the hot chocolate good. Blair was right. Every question he'd asked could be answered in one word, and every one had been. It was like there was a hidden rule running the whole conversation, and he'd been following it without knowing it existed. Maybe, he thought, if a question couldn't be answered with yes or no, it couldn't be answered in one word either. It was worth testing. Maina had said see you, so he texted her, apologized for being weird, and asked if she wanted to try again Saturday.

She said yes.

Saturday, at the same table by the window, Lincoln was ready. When the drinks came, instead of asking if hers was good, he asked what she would order if the coffee shop had no menu and she had to invent a drink. Maina put down her cup. "Okay, so. It would have to have caramel," she said, "but also something weird, like black pepper, because my grandma puts pepper on strawberries and everyone thinks she's insane but it's actually amazing." That led to her grandma, which led to the summer Maina's family had boycotted the whole grocery store over a fight about a dented can, which led to her dad standing in the parking lot holding a hand-lettered sign. She talked so long Lincoln's hot chocolate went cold, and he barely noticed.

He kept it going all afternoon. What was the most gullible thing she'd ever believed, he asked, and she confessed she had believed in the tooth fairy until fifth grade because her mom kept leaving extremely detailed notes in tiny handwriting. He asked what she would do if she could skip one year of school entirely, and she said seventh, without hesitating, and then went quiet and told him why, and he listened. An hour and a half went by like ten minutes. When they finally left, she held the door for him and said, "You're way easier to talk to than you were last time."

He was still glowing about it on Monday until Blair cornered him by the lockers, grinning. "So how'd your experiment go, scientist?"

"Perfect," Lincoln said. "She did almost all the talking."

Blair clapped him on the shoulder. "Then she asked me Thursday night what your favorite song is. Said she didn't want another silent car ride. Guess you'd better come up with an answer."

Lauren spread her essay drafts across the corner table of the Sunhill Cafe, three napkins weighing down the curling pages. The topic stared back at her: Should the voting age be lowered to sixteen? Her teacher wanted a thesis statement and an outline with three supporting points before anyone wrote a full draft, and Lauren had a draft anyway, which was the problem.

"You're doing it backwards," said Edith, sliding into the seat across from her with a hot chocolate. "Ms. Owusu said thesis first."

"Ms. Owusu doesn't have to read my handwriting," Lauren said, but she pulled out a fresh sheet of paper. She had written three body paragraphs last night. One argued that sixteen-year-olds pay taxes on their part-time jobs, so they should have a say. One argued that they can already drive, which is more dangerous than voting. One argued that other countries let them vote at sixteen, so it clearly works.

She wrote her thesis at the top of the page: Sixteen-year-olds should get the vote because they pay taxes, they can already drive, and other countries have proved it works. Then she numbered her points one, two, three to match. Perfect. She leaned back and drank her lukewarm tea.

Dereck arrived twenty minutes late, shaking rain off his jacket, and read over her shoulder while he waited for his muffin. "Your driving paragraph is way stronger than the taxes one," he said. "Start with it. My brother says always open with your best punch."

Lauren reread the paragraphs. He was right about which was stronger. She picked up her pen, drew arrows, and reordered the outline: driving first, taxes second, other countries third. Then she looked back up at her thesis and stopped. "Wait," she said. "My thesis says taxes, driving, other countries. But my outline now goes driving, taxes, other countries."

Edith frowned at the page. "So the reader hits the driving paragraph first, but the thesis promised taxes first?"

"Right." Lauren read the thesis again, mouthing it. It wasn't wrong exactly, but it was like a table of contents that listed the chapters out of order. She crossed out the old version and wrote a new one, moving the words around the same way she had moved the paragraphs: Sixteen-year-olds should get the vote because they can already drive, they pay taxes on their jobs, and other countries have proved it works. The order in the sentence now matched the order in the outline, point for point.

The cafe owner, who was planning to retire at the end of the year and had told every regular customer about it at least twice, brought Dereck his muffin and glanced at the paper. "Homework about the parliament? You kids are ambitious."

"It's about voting," Lauren said. She copied the reordered thesis onto a clean card so it wouldn't get lost under the napkins. Monday she would hand in the outline, and for once the whole thing would line up.

"Read it to me one more time," Edith said.

Lauren held up the card. "Sixteen-year-olds should get the vote because they can already drive, they pay taxes on their jobs, and other countries have proved it works."

"Conventional," Dereck said, mouth full of muffin, "but solid."

Beatrice sat on the low concrete ledge at the edge of the skate park with a battery, a thin coil of wire, a voltmeter, and a multimeter borrowed from her uncle's toolbox. Her homework was due Monday: measure the voltage across a wire, measure the current through it, and calculate the resistance. The trouble was that her numbers kept coming out wrong, and she could not see why, because resistance was not something you could watch like a skater wiping out on the half-pipe.

"You look like you're doing surgery on a sandwich," said Romy, rolling to a stop beside her, wheels grinding grit across the pavement. Zainab coasted up on the other side, eating a popsicle that dripped orange down her wrist.

"I'm trying to diagnose my circuit," Beatrice said. "Something's hiding in there. Every time I run it, the resistance answer changes, so something I'm not controlling must be a variable." She frowned at the coil. Last night the wire had sat dormant in her backpack, cold and untouched, and this morning it had warmed in the sun on the ledge. She laid her palm against it. Warm. She wondered whether heat could be the hidden cause, the thing she could not see directly.

She ran the test again, holding the wire up out of the sun so it stayed cool, and this time the numbers held steady. Voltage divided by current gave the same resistance twice in a row. "Ha!" she said, and did a small seated victory bounce that nearly knocked the multimeter off the ledge.

"Okay, explain like I'm a popsicle," Zainab said.

"Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance is what the wire pushes back with," Beatrice said, packing up. "The meter measures voltage in volts. Guess who that's named after? Alessandro Volta. An Italian physicist. My uncle told me at the science museum last summer, there was a whole battery exhibit with his name on it."

Romy squinted. "So if I get shocked on the rail over there, is that a volta?"

"That's just static, and also please don't." Beatrice clipped the leads together and stood, slinging her backpack over one shoulder. She looked at the long metal rail gleaming in the afternoon light, then at the battery in her hand. "Tomorrow I test the same wire cold and hot, three runs each, and graph it."

"Science at a skate park," Zainab said, dropping her stick in the trash. "Mr. Dang would faint."

From across the bowl, Mr. Dang, who coached the Tuesday beginners group, cupped his hands and called, "Homework on my ledge means you owe me a lap!"

Beatrice laughed and picked up her board. "Fine, but I'm timing it, and don't blame me if the slope is the variable."

The heritage wall went up on Friday, and every student had to hand in a card with three words describing where they were from. Zachary had written his in two minutes: Portland, Oregon, the whole time. The new kid, Monroe, sat with a blank card in front of him for most of Thursday's class, tapping his pencil like it might start writing on its own.

"You lived in Brazil, right?" Zachary said at lunch. "Just put Brazil."

"I lived there for two years. Also Singapore, Germany, and Egypt. Four countries." Monroe tore the crust off his sandwich. "Everybody keeps asking where I'm from, and when I start listing places, their eyes kind of glaze over."

Frederick leaned across the table. "Pick the one you liked best. That's your answer."

But Monroe said the question felt like a shirt that restricted him, like it only came in one size and he didn't fit it. Zachary thought about that all through afternoon classes. There had to be a name for people like Monroe. Kids who moved like that couldn't be the first ones ever. Somebody, somewhere, must have noticed the pattern and called it something. After the last bell, he asked Ms. Andersen if he could use the library computers before it closed, and she said he had twenty minutes because the building locked at four.

He typed in words like "kid who lived in many countries." That gave him travel blogs. He tried "growing up abroad." That was closer. One result mentioned a sociologist, an American named Ruth Hill Useem, who had coined a term back in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture. Zachary read the phrase twice. Third culture kid. It sounded strange and right at the same time, like a name for a thing you'd seen your whole life without knowing it had one. He copied it onto his hand with a pen, because his notebook was in his locker and the librarian was already jingling her keys.

Friday morning, Zachary found Monroe at the blank wall outside Ms. Andersen's room, card still empty, deadline ten minutes away. "Try this," Zachary said. "Third culture kid."

Monroe stared at him. "Say it again."

"Third culture kid. It's a real thing. A sociologist came up with it."

Monroe wrote it down, then added three more words underneath: adaptable, tired, lucky. He pinned the card between Frederick's Ireland card and a girl's card about her grandmother's village in Kerala. Ms. Andersen walked by, read Monroe's card, and nodded once, the way she did when something was exactly right.

At recess Monroe was telling three kids from second period about his school in Singapore, how the lunch breaks were longer and how everyone swapped languages in the middle of sentences. He had more stamina for the story than Zachary expected, like the question had been holding all of it in. When the bell rang, Monroe turned around, walking backward toward the door.

"You know what the weird part is?" he called. "I didn't know there was a word for me either."

Nicolas pressed the doorbell of number fourteen with his thumb, then wiped his palm on his jeans. Ms. Rodríguez opened the door with a toddler on her hip and a folder of papers under her arm. "You must be Nicolas. The emergency numbers are on the fridge, and my sister's coming by nine." She set the little girl, Pia, down on the carpet, handed him a bag of crackers, and hurried off to a late meeting at the school where she taught.

For the first ten minutes, babysitting was exactly what Nicolas had imagined. Pia stacked blocks, knocked them over, and laughed like each crash was a brand-new invention. Nicolas stacked a tower of his own to see if she would copy it, and she did, which made him feel like a genius scientist. Then he got up to refill her sippy cup, and when he came back from the kitchen, the living room had gone quiet in a way that made the hair on his arms stand up.

Pia was on her hands and knees near the coffee table, reaching for something. Nicolas crossed the room in three steps and saw a bottle of orange vitamins sitting right at the edge, low enough for her small fingers to brush the cap. He remembered his mother saying the words once at their own house, medicines and cleaning products up high, out of reach, because little kids explore by putting things in their mouths. Pia, meanwhile, had already proven the point: she was chewing on the remote control with great focus.

He lifted the bottle to the highest shelf of the bookcase, then checked the room like a detective. Under the bathroom sink he found a spray bottle of cleaner behind a stack of towels, low and easy to grab, and he carried that up high too. To keep himself honest, he took out his phone and photographed each spot before and after, planning to document everything so Ms. Rodríguez could see exactly what he had moved and why. Pia supervised from the doorway, cracker in each fist, shouting a word that might have been "up."

The sister arrived at nine, but Ms. Rodríguez came home ten minutes later, tired and carrying a paper bag of leftovers. "How was she?" she asked, and Nicolas showed her the photos. She scrolled through them slowly, and her tired face changed. "The vitamins were on the coffee table? I could have sworn I put them away." She looked at the high shelf, then at Pia, who was attempting to eat the remote again. "You just earned yourself a regular job, Nicolas. A distinct improvement over my last sitter, who spent the whole evening on his phone." Nicolas grinned. "Actually, I was on mine. But only for evidence." Ms. Rodríguez laughed and held up the bottle of vitamins. "Next time," she said, "I'll put these so high even I can't reach them."

Kenza wanted an answer by nine o'clock, because at nine she was going to post a photo of her new house, street sign and all, so her cousins could find her after the move. "Just tell me if it's a bad idea," her message said. Lea typed back that she'd check something first, though she wasn't sure what.

An hour earlier, Trace had sent her a link with the words "you won't believe this." It led to a blog Lea had written in fourth grade, the one she'd deleted two years ago, complete with a photo of her in front of her old school and a post that said exactly which park she went to every Saturday. "How is it still there?" she had asked Trace. Trace said he didn't know, but that his brother had found some site that keeps old pages. "It's called the Wayback Machine," Trace wrote. "You just put in an address."

Lea pulled up the site. In the search box she typed her old blog's address, half expecting an error. Instead a calendar appeared, dotted with dates. She clicked one from three years ago, and there was her nine-year-old self, announcing to the entire internet which bench she sat on and when. Anyone, anywhere, could be reading it, and had been able to for years without her knowing. She felt her face go hot. Deleting had seemed so final at the time.

She thought about Kenza's photo. The street sign wouldn't just reach the cousins; it would sit there, waiting, the way Lea's park post had waited. Maybe it would even get copied into an archive, though she didn't understand how that worked. She decided to test it the only way she could: she opened the archive again and searched a few other pages she remembered, including a site Trace had made and abandoned. The Wayback Machine had that too. Whatever this thing was, it had been quietly saving copies of public web pages since 1996, and it wasn't picky.

At 8:41 Lea called Kenza. "Don't post the street sign," she said. "Send your cousins the picture in a message instead. It turns out stuff doesn't really go away. I found my old blog, the one I deleted, still readable." There was a pause on the line.

"Still readable? Like, strangers could see it?"

"Anyone. That's how I found it." Lea heard Kenza breathing, thinking.

"Okay," Kenza said slowly. "New plan. No sign, just the house. And Lea? See if you can find my old swim team page in that machine. I want to know what's out there."

Lea grinned, cracked her knuckles, and started typing.

The cones were still wet from morning rain when Matthew lined up on the far curve of the soccer field, which Mr. Owusu had measured into a rough four-hundred-metre loop. He had one job today, and it was not to run fast. "First lap, steady," Billie called from the sideline, clipboard in hand. "Remember what happened last time." Matthew remembered it well: he had charged out like the finish line was two hundred metres away, and by the second lap his legs had turned to rope.

At the whistle he went out hard anyway. It felt controlled, it felt easy, and that was the trap. When he thundered past the start line at the end of lap one, Mr. Owuso's voice cut across the field. "Fifty-eight seconds!" Matthew's stomach dropped. He had planned sixty-six. Billie sprinted alongside him for a few strides, holding up the watch. "That's your split, Matt. Fifty-eight. Way faster than you meant to go."

He tried to fix it on the spot. Instead of surging, he shortened his stride and counted his breaths, four steps in, four steps out, testing whether the count could hold him together. His arms burned, but the count held. Behind him he heard Samir yelling, "You're not dying, you're just scared you're dying, which is different!" That made him laugh, which cost him a breath, which somehow helped.

He crossed the line in two minutes and eleven seconds, and then he bent over with his hands on his knees while the drizzle began to saturate his shoulders. Billie read the clipboard. "So the split tells you right away. Fifty-eight means the first lap was faster than planned. If it had come up slow, that's the other problem." Matthew nodded, still gasping. Fifty-eight. Faster. He could see now that the first lap had lied to him, that feeling easy at the start was not the same thing as being on pace.

They ran it twice more. On the third try he counted from the very first stride, and when Mr. Owusu shouted "Sixty-five!" at the line, Matthew felt something loosen in his chest, because sixty-five was almost exactly the number he had chosen. The second lap still hurt, a vigorous, full-body hurt, but it was a hurt with room left in it. He finished strong enough to pass Samir, who was jogging the loop just to keep him company. Afterward Mr. Owusu clapped him on the back and said the van was leaving in ten minutes, and Matthew had an obligation to help load the cones. He picked up the nearest one, tucked it under his arm, and grinned at Billie. "Same time Thursday?"

Gabriel spread his science notes across the kitchen table and stared at the empty box where the answer should have been. Question fourteen wanted the number of protons in selenium, and selenium was not on the torn half of the periodic table he had copied in class. Ms. Mensah, whose kitchen this was, had taken him in after school twice a week since autumn, and she had said he could work at her table as long as he kept the noise reasonable. He pushed a bowl of tangerines aside and laid down the crumled poster she had lent him from the back of her junk drawer.

Arianne arrived first, shaking rain off her jacket, and Ayan came a few minutes later with his little brother's flashcards still in his pocket. "Quiz tomorrow," Arianne said, dropping into the chair opposite Gabriel. "Fourteen questions, and Ms. Mensah's tea smells like cinnamon, which is the only good part of this afternoon."

"It's rooibos," said Ms. Mensah from the stove, "and the basil on the windowsill has finally flowered. Leave it alone, please. The bees come by in the afternoon and pollinate it, and then I get seeds for next year."

Gabriel pulled the poster flat and pinned the curling corners with salt shakers. He ran his finger along the top row of boxes. Hydrogen, then helium, then lithium, one after another. "Wait," he said. "Look at these little numbers." Each box had a small number above the symbol. Hydrogen had 1, helium had 2, lithium had 3, beryllium had 4. He traced onward, and the numbers climbed steadily, all the way across the row, then kept climbing on the next one.

Ayan leaned in, his finger hovering a centimetre above the paper. "They count up by one. Every single box." Arianne frowned and checked a stretch herself, phosphorus to argon, 15, 16, 17, 18. "So the table is in order," she said slowly. "Increasing atomic number. Whichever element comes next has exactly one more proton than the one before it."

"That's it," Gabriel said, sitting back. "The atomic number is the number of protons. I kept trying to memorize them one by one and it's just counting." He looked back at question fourteen. Selenium was missing from his torn copy, but on the poster he found arsenic at 33, and right beside it, in the next box, sat selenium. Thirty-four. He wrote it down and underlined it twice.

Ayan smiled and dealt the flashcards between the three of them. "My uncle taught me chemistry with a stick in the dirt," he said quietly. "We came here as refugees the year I turned ten, and I thought I'd lost all my schooling. Turns out the periodic table is the same in every country." Ms. Mensah set down a plate of sliced tangerines, and Gabriel felt buoyant enough to attempt question fifteen, which asked about bromine, three boxes further along. He counted, wrote 35, and reached for a slice of fruit.

Arianne pointed at the last question on the sheet. "Technetium," she read out loud. "Guess what's not on this poster at all."

"Then we count from the box that is," Gabriel said, tapping molybdenum with his pencil.

The clock on Mr. Smith's desk said 2:58, and Jeremy stared at it like it might run backward if he wished hard enough. In two minutes he would be sitting across from Mr. Smith, the guidance counsellor, explaining why he had thrown a pencil sharpener at the gym door. He hadn't hit anyone. That was the one good thing. The bad thing was that everyone had seen him do it, including Adriana, whose opinion of him mattered more than he wanted to admit.

"Jeremy," Mr. Smith said, gesturing to the squishy blue chair, "before we get to the sharpener, tell me about tryouts." Mr. Smith was an influential figure at their school, the one teacher even the eighth graders listened to, and somehow he already knew everything. "Soccer, right? Saturday?"

Jeremy sat. "Goalie tryouts." His hands were sweating again, the way they had all week. "I keep messing up in practice. My stomach hurts, my hands shake, and I can't think. Maximiliano says I'm just nervous, but it feels bigger than that."

"That sounds like stress," Mr. Smith said. "Sometimes anxiety shows up in the body before you notice it in your head." He wrote the word anxiety on a sticky note and slid it across the desk. "And this?" He tapped a poster on the wall that said COPING SKILLS in block letters. "These are things people learn to do before a hard moment. Not medicine, nothing a doctor prescribes. Just skills."

Jeremy studied the poster. Box breathing. Counting. Slow breathing with long exhales. He thought about Saturday, about facing a penalty shot, and a memory surfaced that he hadn't connected to anything until now. His uncle, who had served overseas and now coached a youth league in a civilian neighborhood two towns over, always stood behind the net before shootouts. Jeremy had watched him once, breathing out slowly, so slowly, through puckered lips, while the shooter lined up.

"Wait," Jeremy said slowly, testing the idea like ice on a pond. "My uncle breathes like that before every penalty shot. Long exhales. I thought it was superstition, like not stepping on the foul line." He stood up. "It's not superstition. It's a skill. It calms the body down before the stressful moment." He tried it right there, in the office, a slow breath in and a long breath out, and his stomach unclenched just a little, enough to notice.

Mr. Smith smiled and mentioned boundaries, about knowing what was his to control and what belonged to the coach's decisions, but Jeremy was barely listening. He asked to borrow the poster. On Saturday, standing in the goal, Jeremy took one slow breath and let it out so long that the shooter paused and looked at him, confused. The ball sailed straight into Jeremy's gloves, and from the sideline he heard Adriana shout, "Nice save, superstition boy!"

Romy sat at the kitchen table with a pencil, a ruler, and a blank page that was starting to feel like an enemy. Her art teacher, Mr. Bouchard, had promised the class that anyone who mastered one-point perspective could design the backdrop for the spring play, and Romy wanted that job more than she had wanted anything since the talent show in grade five. The trouble was the vanishing point. Every time she drew her street, the buildings looked like they were falling over sideways.

She called Fatimah, who showed up ten minutes later with her own sketchbook and a bag of pretzels, because Fatimah never went anywhere without snacks. "Okay," Fatimah said, dropping into the chair across the table, "show me the disaster."

Romy turned her page around. Fatimah leaned in to scrutinize the drawing, tilting her head first one way and then the other. "The road edges are wrong," she said at last. "They don't go to the same place."

"They do too," Romy said, but she grabbed her ruler and laid it along one edge, then the other. The two lines crossed somewhere off the corner of the page. Fatimah was right. "They're supposed to meet at the vanishing point," Romy muttered, "but I put the point in two different spots without noticing."

Fatimah pulled out her phone and swiped through her photos until she found one from last summer, a shot of train tracks taken from the footbridge near her grandmother's house. She slid the phone across the table. "Look at this. The rails look like they touch way out there."

Romy peered at the picture. "They look closer in the distance, sure."

"No, they look like they meet," Fatimah insisted. "Like they actually come together."

"They can't meet," Romy said. "They're parallel. Rails are the same distance apart the whole way, or the train would fall off." Fatimah frowned at the photo, clearly not convinced, so Romy took the ruler and measured the rails near the bottom of the picture, then the same rails farther back. Near, the gap was wide; far away, it shrank to almost nothing. "See? They only look like they meet. Parallel lines like railway tracks, or the two edges of a road, look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet."

Fatimah grabbed a pretzel and chewed on it along with the idea. "So that's why my drawing looked flat," she said. "I drew the road edges the same distance apart the whole way." She had been hoping for the backdrop job too, and suddenly her shoulders drooped.

Romy looked at her friend's sketchbook, then at her own ruined street. "Draw with me," she said. "We'll both get good at it, and whoever wins, the other one helps paint." Fatimah's face brightened. They pushed the pretzels aside, taped a fresh sheet to the table, and marked a single dot in the middle of the page.

"Every edge of the road goes to that dot," Romy said, and drew her first line straight toward it.

Katherine had the graphs spread across two airport seats while the departure board flickered from ON TIME to DELAYED. Rainfall bars for a rainforest station rose like green towers every month, while the desert station barely showed a sliver all year, and the temperature lines told their own story, one steady and warm, the other swinging between baking days and cold nights. Her worksheet asked her to compare the two climates, but the second page had a climate map of the world with strange letter codes printed over each region, Af here, BWh there, and she had no idea what they meant. If she did not finish before they boarded, Ms. Kovalenko would mark it late, and Katherine refused to be negligent about the one assignment she actually found interesting.

Ziyad dropped into the seat beside her with two pretzels and handed her one. "Stuck?"

"These codes," Katherine said, tapping the map. "Af, BWh. They must mean something, because the rainforest is always Af and the deserts are always B, but I can't test that if I don't know who made the rules or why."

Teagan leaned over from the other side, chewing. "Ask your phone."

"It's in my checked bag with my charger," Katherine said, which was exactly the kind of planning she could not justify to anyone. She looked around the gate area instead, and spotted the tiny airport bookshop with its rack of atlases. She ran over, found a world atlas, and flipped to the climate map section, following the tiny print to a note at the bottom.

"Listen to this," she said, hurrying back and reading aloud. "The codes are called the Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today. It was developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany."

"So Af isn't random," Teagan said slowly.

"It's a system. Koppen looked at rainfall and temperature together, the exact things on my graphs." Katherine laid her hand flat over the map, covering the rainforest band. "See, everywhere with year-round rain and steady warmth gets Af. Every desert gets a B and something about how dry." She checked her graphs against the map three times, and the pattern held each time. She wrote her comparison, and then, feeling bolder, added the note about the codes and who invented them.

Ms. Kovalenko walked past, glanced at the paper, and smiled. "You did the bonus question. I hadn't even assigned it yet."

Katherine grinned and looked up just as the board changed again. The flight was cancelled, and their class trip to the rainforest would have to wait for tomorrow, leaving Katherine with a finished assignment comparing two climates, and no airplane to get to either of them. Teagan held out the last pretzel. "Deserts, at least, wait for everybody."

Payton stood in the school parking lot with Jenny, both of them holding their dance tickets so tightly the paper had gone soft at the corners. The October wind smelled like someone's fallen leaves and bus exhaust, and through the gym doors they could already hear the thump of music.

"I'm not going in if it's going to be like last year's field day," Jenny said. "I hid in the restroom for an hour."

Payton remembered field day too. She flashed back to that afternoon in the parking lot, the exact spot where she was standing now, when the coach had asked her to run the relay anchor leg and she had frozen while the whole grade watched. She had spent the whole ride home trying to digest what had gone wrong, and she still wasn't sure. "This time we walk in together," she said. "We find a wall. Walls are safe."

Inside, the gym had been transformed. Somebody had hung a mirror ball from the ceiling, and the gym was full of small spots of light that swept across the floor, the bleachers, and the backs of everyone's heads. Payton and Jenny pressed themselves against the wall by the water fountain, exactly as planned.

Then Payton noticed something. When the ball turned, the spots all moved together, like a school of fish. She watched the single spotlight in the corner, the one Mr. Nikolaidis was adjusting on its stand, and then watched a spot of light slide up her own sneaker. When he switched the spotlight off, every spot vanished at once. When he switched it back on, hundreds of spots reappeared. So it wasn't hundreds of lights up there. Each little mirror tile on the ball caught that one beam and threw it in a slightly different direction, which was why the whole gym sparkled from a single bulb.

"Watch this," Payton said, and she waved at Mr. Nikolaidis, then pointed at the spotlight and made a turning motion with her finger. He grinned, gave a thumbs up, and spun the ball faster. The spots raced across the floor in long streaks.

"Okay, that's actually amazing," Jenny said. "How did you know he'd do that?"

"Because I watched what happened when he turned the light off and on. One spotlight, all those spots. It has to be the ball."

Imane wandered over from the snack table, where she claimed to have a monopoly on the pretzels since nobody else was eating them. "Are you two going to stand there all night studying physics, or are you going to dance?" She grabbed Jenny's wrist.

The opening notes of a song they all knew started up, and the spots of light came sweeping toward the wall like a wave. Payton pushed off the wall and stepped into the middle of them, sneakers and all, and called over her shoulder, "Come on, Jenny. Walls are for people who don't know how light works."

Every Saturday morning, Ava swept the floor of Mr. Xu's clock shop, dusted the shelves of tiny brass gears, and earned twelve dollars, which she carried straight to the bank on the corner. She had been doing this since September, and by spring she had saved two hundred and forty dollars. Her plan was simple: keep saving until she could buy the leather satchel in the window of the artisan shop down the street, the one the leatherworker had stitched by hand, with a brass clasp that matched the clock gears she spent her mornings dusting.

One Saturday the teller handed her a slip of paper with her balance, and Ava stared at it. Last month the bank had paid her interest, one dollar and twenty cents. This month it had paid one dollar and twenty-one cents. "That's bizarre," she said. "I didn't put anything extra in." She checked the deposit column twice, thinking she would find a mistake, a number she had forgotten. There was nothing. The same deposits, the same two hundred and forty dollars, and yet the interest itself had grown.

She took the problem to Harriet, who was waiting outside the shop with a bag of pistachios. "Look," Ava said, holding out the slip. "Same money in, more interest out." Harriet chewed a pistachio and squinted at the numbers. "Maybe the bank just felt generous," she said, which was exactly the kind of answer Harriet always gave. Ava shook her head. She remembered her grandmother once choosing an account that paid simple interest, the same flat amount every year, and regretting it, and Ava had never understood why until now. She flipped the slip over and found a small paragraph of fine print, and read it slowly, following the words with her finger.

Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, she read, so the interest itself starts earning interest. She read it again. The one dollar and twenty cents from last month hadn't just sat there like a coin under a mattress. It had joined her two hundred and forty dollars, and together they had earned the extra penny. Her money was growing money. She thought about her grandmother's flat account, the same dollar every year for five years, never a penny more, and about the five years ahead of her own account, where each month's interest would climb onto the last month's and earn again.

"It's like the shop," she told Harriet, waving toward the window where the brass gears turned. "Each gear grabs the one beside it. The second one only moves because the first one moved." Harriet popped another pistachio. "So your money is a gear," she said. "Weird. But okay." Ava folded the slip and put it in her pocket, next to the satchel fund total she kept in her head. On the walk home she stopped in front of the artisan's window, looked at the brass clasp, and then kept walking, because she had just decided to leave her money where it could orbit on its own. "Five years," she said to Harriet. "Watch it turn."

The sign on the cooler said BOTTLED WATER $1.00, except the one had been crossed out and replaced with $2.50 in thick marker. Zachary stared at it through the glass door of the gas station while his dad filled the tank outside. It was ninety-six degrees, the kind of heat that made the parking lot shimmer, and he had exactly two dollars in his pocket.

Inside, the cooler told the whole story. Six rows of soda, untouched. One lonely bottle of water on the top shelf, sweating like it knew it was popular. A man in a paint-splattered shirt grabbed it, looked at the sign, and set it back down with the expression of someone who had been personally insulted. Behind the register, the cashier shrugged and turned a small fan toward her own face.

Zachary's friend Remington was there too, leaning against the slushie machine with a book called Economics for Beginners tucked under his arm, because that was the kind of person Remington was. "She raised it twice today," Remington said, nodding at the sign. "Every time the shelf got emptier, the price went up. Watch what happens when she's stuck with the last one at closing."

Zachary decided to test it. He had two dollars, and the water cost two fifty, so his plan was to stand there being hot until the price came to him. He examined the beef jerky. He read the entire display of air fresheners, which hang in the shapes of pine trees and little crowns. The man in the paint shirt came back, paced, and left again. A woman bought gas and a soda, because soda was still a dollar and plentiful as gravel.

At five o'clock, the cashier walked over with her marker, scratched out the 2.50, and wrote 2.00. Zachary pounced. Then, right beside him, Ms. Hoang from down the street reached for the very same bottle, and the two of them stood there in a silence that lasted exactly long enough to be awkward. Zachary let her take it, mostly because she was his neighbor and partly because she had once consoled him for an entire afternoon after his hamster died, and you do not outbid a person like that. She paid, then looked at the empty shelf and the new price, at the marked-up sign still faintly showing one dollar underneath. "Amount people want equals the amount she's got," she said. "Remington, doesn't your book call that the equilibrium price? The market-clearing price, something like that." Remington looked genuinely wounded that she had gotten to say it first.

The twist came a minute later, when the cashier opened the back cooler to restock and carried out an entire case of water. She set the bottles in neat rows, took her marker, and wrote $1.00 on the sign again, big and cheerful. Zachary bought two, one for himself and one for his dad, and felt oddly buoyant, like a diplomat who had just avoided a war nobody knew about. Outside, he handed his dad the bottle. "Two fifty an hour ago," his dad said. "What happened?"

"Cooler happened," Zachary said, and cracked it open.

Lincoln could hear the drums before he reached the park gates. It was Vaisakhi, and the whole community had spilled out of the gurdwara onto the grass, with stalls of food, kids chasing each other between blankets, and a stage where a group was singing. His mother had sent him with a bag of rice to donate, and she was somewhere behind him arguing cheerfully with an aunt about who made better pakoras.

At the edge of the crowd, Lincoln spotted Jessy from his science class, standing awkwardly near a shoe rack piled with hundreds of pairs of shoes. "You came," Lincoln said, surprised. Jessy shrugged. "You said there'd be food. Also I'm supposed to write about a cultural celebration for Ms. Mori's class, so this counts as research."

"We have to go inside the gurdwara to drop off the rice," Lincoln said, toeing off his sneakers and setting them on the rack. "You take your shoes off too. Everyone does, everywhere, in mosques and Hindu temples and gurdwaras. It's a respect thing." Jessy looked down at his battered shoes, whose laces had gone a strange greenish color from winter puddles, like something corrosive had been at them. He pulled them off anyway.

At the next door, Lincoln paused. He'd forgotten the one part that always tripped him up. A volunteer was handing out thin orange scarves, and every single person who passed through covered their head, whether they were a grandfather or a girl Jessy's age. Lincoln had gotten this wrong at Diwali two years ago, walking in bareheaded until his cousin yanked him back by the collar, and he wasn't going to let Jessy make the same mistake. "Here," he said, taking two scarves. "In a gurdwara you cover your head. Everyone, no exceptions." He tied his own the way his grandfather had taught him, a quick knot at the side.

Jessy fumbled with his, dropping one end in the dirt, and Lincoln stepped in and helped him loop it. "Like a concept in physics," Jessy said, adjusting it. "Once you know the rule, you can predict what happens at every door." They carried the rice inside, where the smell of dal and warm bread rolled over them, and a man with a kind face waved them toward the kitchen.

Later, on the grass, Jessy ate his third plate of food and scribbled notes for Ms. Mori, filling a whole page about shoes and scarves and the kitchens that feed anyone who shows up. "This is going to be the best report in the class," he said. Lincoln stole a piece of his bread and grinned. "You're welcome. Next time, dig deeper. There's a whole library in there." Jessy pointed his pen at him and said, "You mean excavate the truth?" and Lincoln laughed so hard the plate nearly slid off the blanket.

Asher stood at the back of the community hall with his practice book open to page twelve, humming the melody his cantor had marked in pencil. Around him the cultural festival filled the room with the smell of fried dough and cardamom, and his classmates Johan and Elisha were working the ticket table. In three weeks Asher would chant his bar mitzvah portion in front of everyone, and he had practiced until the tune played in his head even in the shower.

Ms. Vogel, who ran the festival's exhibit of sacred texts, waved him over to a long table near the stage. "We're doing scroll demonstrations on the hour," she said. "Your rabbi said you could rehearse on the real one before the hall opens." She lifted the velvet cover from a Torah scroll and unrolled it to the place Asher recognized from his book, the same words from Genesis.

He leaned in and stopped. The parchment had letters, yes, but no little dots, no vowels, and none of the squiggles above and below the words that told him which tune to use. His practice book had everything printed plainly; the scroll had nothing but consonants in black columns. "Where did the marks go?" he asked.

"They don't go anywhere," Ms. Vogel said. "A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks."

"So how does anyone chant from it?" Asher asked. She only smiled and pointed at his book, so he sat down on the stage step to work it out. The book had the vowels and the tune marks printed in it. The scroll did not. That meant the melody had to live in the person, not on the page. He had assumed the reading and the singing came from the scroll together, but the fact was you learned the chanted melody in advance, from the printed book, and carried it to the scroll by memory. He tested it: he covered the vowel marks on page twelve with his hand and tried the first line from the bare consonants alone. The tune arrived on its own, the way he knew the school song without reading it.

That evening his grandmother, who could not travel for the ceremony, sent him a message: "I chanted from a scroll in 1968 with nothing but the letters in front of me. Halfway through my portion my mind abandoned the melody completely, and my rabbi had to whisper the next phrase. Don't be gullible about your own memory, Asher. Test it the hard way."

The next morning he taped a sheet of paper over the vowel marks in his book, stared at the bare letters, took a breath, and began the first verse with no help at all.

Alex had said "I plead the Fifth" eleven times that week, mostly to avoid taking out the trash, and it had worked exactly zero times, so he decided to find out what the phrase actually meant before the constitutional rights fair at city hall on Saturday.

Ms. Wiśniewski had assigned the fair weeks ago. Each student had to pick one right from the constitution, read it aloud, and explain it in their own words at a table in the rotunda, where real city employees would wander by and listen. Alex had drawn the Fifth Amendment out of the paper bag, and Abdulrahman had drawn the Second, and Dev had gotten the Tenth and kept mispronouncing it as "the Tent," which Alex privately found funnier than it was.
