"In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller," she said. "It has a name and everything."

"So it's real," Mr. Côté said. "Now what are you going to do about it?"

Aubrey had thought about that all weekend. The conventional answer, working harder, wouldn't work, because nobody knew when they were easing off. The problem was invisible. So at the next practice she clipped the spring scale to the team rope and called out numbers while everyone pulled, each puller hearing their own reading as it happened. Eliott's number sagged every time he stood beside Evan, and once he knew it, he held steady. Evan improved within two pulls. By the end of the hour the six of them were dragging the picnic table across the lawn, scale pinned high, everyone shouting readings like a rowdy crew.

At the tournament their first match lasted eleven seconds. Aubrey lay back in the grass afterward, rope burns stinging her palms, and started uncoiling the scale from her bag. "Next pull," she said. "I want numbers on the big rope too."

Isabella had enrolled in the summer water basketball league at the community pool, and today was the first real game in the shallow end. She was the point guard, which meant she brought the ball up and decided what everyone would do. The coach had taught the team one play all week: the pick and roll, where Camille blocked Isabella's defender and then spun toward the hoop. It was crucial that the timing be exact, or the whole play fell apart.

"Camille, set the pick!" Isabella shouted on the first possession. Camille planted herself in front of the defender, and Isabella darted around her, but the defender slid over before the roll even started. The pass got knocked away. The next time, Isabella yelled it again, louder, and the same girl stepped into the passing lane and stole the ball.

During the break, Isabella floated near the pool wall, thinking. How did the other team always seem ready? Nobody on their side was that fast. Was something else going on? She remembered the September before, when her class had played a guessing game and she had ruined it by reading the answers off the board the teacher forgot to erase. The memory stopped her. Of course. She was announcing the play out loud, standing three meters from the girl guarding her. Every shout was a gift.

"I think I figured it out," she said to Alison and Camille, gripping the concrete edge of the pool. "They're not guessing. They're hearing me. I call the play in plain words, right next to their ears."

"So don't say anything," Alison said.

"Real point guards call plays with a hand signal, a number, or a code word," Camille said, "so your team knows the play and the defense doesn't."

Isabella grinned. That was it exactly. She turned the pick and roll into a number. "When I hold up two fingers, that's the pick and roll," she whispered. "Two fingers. Nothing else. If I hold up a fist, we just pass it around." Alison nodded. Camille nodded.

The next possession, Isabella swam to the top of the arc and raised two fingers, casual as someone adjusting goggles. The defender tensed, watching the ball, watching Isabella's eyes, looking for any clue about what would happen next. Camille drifted over as if she were just finding space. Then she set the pick, hard and legal, and rolled. The defender, who had heard nothing at all, was a full step late. Isabella fired the bounce pass off the water and Camille laid it in over the rim.

The scorekeeper called out the new score, and Alison splashed water straight up into the air like a fountain.

Bennett set six bean plants on the kitchen table in a row, all in matching yogurt cups. The science fair was in five days, and his project claimed that fertilizer made plants grow faster. The problem was that all six plants had been fertilized since day one, and while they were tall and green, Matilda's question from yesterday kept bugging him. "Faster than what?" she had asked, tilting her head at his poster. He had said "than normal," and she had said "like what normal?" and he had said "just normal," which even he could tell was a terrible answer.

"You're staring at beans like they're going to confess," said his little sister, dropping her backpack on a chair.

"They might have to," Bennett said.

His mom's plant sat on the windowsill above the sink, a scraggly little bean in plain dirt that had never gotten a drop of fertilizer. Bennett looked at it, then at his six, and felt something click. His plants weren't proof of anything. If he'd never raised a bean without fertilizer, then even the scraggly windowsill plant couldn't save him, because it had different dirt, a different window, different watering. Everything about it was different, so any difference in height could come from any of those things, not just the fertilizer. What he needed was plants treated exactly like his six, same cups, same window, same water, except for the one thing being tested. He grabbed his notebook and wrote it down before the idea could escape.

He called Matilda. "I'm starting over," he said. "Eight new beans. Four get fertilizer, four don't. Everything else identical."

"Those are called a control group," Matilda said. "Lyla did one for her mold project. Four untouched, four gross."

"Four gross," Bennett repeated gravely. "That's basically a metaphor for my whole week."

Five days was tight but a bean in a wet paper towel could sprout in three, and Ms. Szabó had said late entries could show growth charts instead of finished plants. On Saturday morning, he lined up the new cups on the table, measured his windowsill plant for the hundredth time, and texted Matilda a photo of two identical sprouts, one labeled F and one labeled N. He titled it "The showdown is imminent." She replied with a bean emoji and the words "my money's on the plain one."

By Monday, all eight had poked up through the soil, and the plain ones were, annoyingly, slightly ahead. Bennett grinned anyway and wrote the numbers down. The data was doing exactly what data was supposed to do, which was refuse to agree with him yet. "Grow," he told the control group. "Or don't. Either way, I finally have something to measure."

The computer lab at Camp Winnoway smelled like hot plastic and bug spray, which Victoria thought was fitting, since she was fighting a bug of her own. Her program was supposed to ask for a number and print whether it was prime. Instead it printed "not prime" for everything. She typed in 7. Not prime. She typed in 13. Not prime. She typed in 2, which even her little brother knew was prime, and the screen said no anyway.

Veronica leaned over from the next keyboard, chewing the end of a pen. "Maybe the camp just wants you to feel bad about math."

"It's not the camp. It's me. I did something." Victoria scrolled through her eight lines of code like they were a ransom note. She had a loop, a check for remainders, and a print statement, all of which looked innocent enough that one of them had to be lying.

She tried tracing it by hand, which Ms. Rahimi had suggested on the first day without ever explaining anything useful. Take 7, Victoria thought. The program divides 7 by 2, 7 by 3, and so on, and if any division comes out even, it declares the number not prime. So which one was coming out even? None of them should. Unless the loop was dividing by something it shouldn't. She counted on her fingers what the loop actually went through, starting at 2 and stopping before the number itself, and then looked at her code again. She had written range(2, n+1). Her loop tried n itself. Seven divided by seven leaves no remainder, so every number in the universe turned out to be not prime, including the primes. The primes were getting framed. She fixed the line to range(2, n) and hit run.

That night she wrote it all down in a letter to her grandfather, the only person she knew who would care. "Dear Papa," she wrote, "you donated twenty dollars so I could come to coding camp, and today I finally earned some of it. My program said every number was not prime because it divided each number by itself. Range from 2 up to one less than the number tries every possible divisor except 1 and the number itself, and I had gone one too far. In other news, the lake water tastes like pennies and Brayden started a rebellion at lunch by refusing to hand in his swim buddy card. It lasted four minutes. His rebellion, unlike my primes, was frail."

The next morning, Brayden dropped into the seat beside her with the wounded dignity of someone who had lost to a lifeguard. "What are you doing now?"

"Testing the fix." She typed 9 and the program said not prime. She typed 11 and it said prime. She was about to type 97, her favorite, when Ms. Rahimi paused behind them and looked at the screen.

"That's a nice prime checker," Ms. Rahimi said. "I've been trying to write one all week for my own class."

Victoria slid her chair over, one careful inch. "Eight lines. I charge in popsicles."

Ms. Rahimi pulled out her wallet. "Do you take camp store credit?"

Keira stood at the French booth with her notebook pressed against her chest, trying to look like she belonged. She had one job at the festival: collect a custom from every booth for her class project, and the French booth was giving her trouble. Her cousins, Angel and Kelly, had come along, but they had already drifted toward the food trucks, leaving her alone with a long table of pastries and a family from Lyon who kept greeting each other in a way she couldn't quite follow.

The mother of the family pressed her cheek to a friend's cheek and kissed the air twice, once on each side. Then an older man arrived, and she did it three times, left, right, left. Keira's pencil hovered. Two kisses, then three kisses, same woman, one minute apart. She flipped to a fresh page and wrote both numbers, because a pattern you can't see is still a pattern, and patterns usually have a reason hiding underneath.

She tested her first idea right away. Maybe the older man got three because he was older, so she watched a boy about her age greet the mother. Two kisses. That fit, but it felt too easy, so she kept watching. A woman with a sunburned nose and a Marseille tote bag embraced the older man and gave him three kisses. The same woman turned to the boy and gave him three as well. Age was out. Keira crossed it off.

Angel and Kelly came back with paper cones of fries. "What are you staring at?" Angel asked, following her gaze.

"Counting kisses," Keira said. "The people from Lyon give two. The people with the Marseille bags give three. Watch the aunt over there. She just did three to the sunburned woman and two to the Lyon mother, back to back."

Kelly watched, chewing. The aunt moved down the line, and it happened again, exactly as Keira had predicted. "How did you know?" Kelly whispered.

"I didn't, at first. I thought it was age. But it isn't. It's where they're from." A girl Keira's age turned around, and Keira asked her, feeling her face go warm, "What do you call that? The cheek kisses."

"La bise," the girl said, laughing kindly. "And where I'm from, we do two. My grandmother does three. She says we're not from the same place." She said it the way you'd say the sky is blue, like it was too trivial to argue about, and turned back to the pastries.

Keira wrote it all down, fast, before the details could leak out of her head. Angel leaned over her shoulder. "Yesterday I thought this project was going to be boring," Angel said. "I was wrong."

Keira had thought so too, and she was glad to change her mind. She copied her tally for Angel, and when Kelly grumbled that her fries had gone cold, Keira tried to console her by offering the last pastry from the Lyon table, held out in both hands the way the French family had passed everything, never one hand, never grabbed. Kelly took it properly, and the three of them stood there eating while the aunt worked her way down the booth, two kisses, three kisses, two kisses, as regular as a code being spoken aloud.

Liam sat on the lakeside dock with his duffel bag between his knees, watching the camp bus fold its doors shut behind the last arrivals. Two weeks. He had never been away from home for more than a sleepover, and even that one had ended with his mom driving over at ten at night. His cabin assignment slip was crumpled in his fist. He smoothed it out and read it again, as if the letters might change.

Iyad was already sitting near the end of the dock, skipping flat stones. "You're in Cabin Four too," he said, holding up a matching slip. "Coach said they'd let us vote later on a cabin mascot. Ballot and everything. I'm going with the otters." He tossed another stone; it hopped three times and sank. Liam tried one of his own and it plopped straight down, and for a second he almost laughed, which surprised him.

That night, after lights out, a voice from the top bunk, Isobel's cousin's sleeping bag empty beside it, said quietly, "Anybody else missing home?" Nobody answered at first. Then a kid named Iyad from the next bed said, "Me. A lot, actually." One by one, all six of them admitted it. The counselor had told them at dinner, not as a lecture but as a shrug, that research on kids at overnight camps had found that most campers felt at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stayed mild. Liam had assumed he was the only one, the worst one, the kid who would have to call home. Instead he lay there listening to five other voices saying the same thing, and the tight feeling in his chest loosened, though it did not disappear.

The next morning Liam had an idea he wanted to test. If everybody felt it a little, then keeping busy together might be what kept it mild, so he proposed that the cabin incorporate a dock visit into every evening, ten minutes of stone skipping before bed. "Otters are versatile," Iyad argued, "but so is a plan like that." They voted by paper ballot, and the dock plan won, five votes to one. The one dissenting voter wanted card games instead, and he grumbled about it all the way to the lake.

By the fourth evening, Liam could skip a stone four hops. Isobel, who had joined their cabin's ritual after her cousin's empty bunk got filled, managed two. Liam still thought about his mom's kitchen at night, still kept her postcard tucked inside his pillowcase, and he understood now that those two weeks would hold both things at once: the missing and the stones. He wound up and threw. The rock skimmed five times, farther than any of them, and then dropped into the darkening water. "Again," said Iyad, handing him another.

Ms. Dang put a photocopy of the Last Supper on the board and told the class they had ten minutes of sketching time before she took the computers away for the quiz. Michael stared at his own drawing of a street, which looked like a stack of boxes that had fallen over, and thought about the time he had told his grandfather he wanted to be an artist. His grandfather had smiled, said artists hibernate in cold apartments, and laughed at his own joke until he coughed. That had been in March, before the hospital, before a lot of things.

"Your street's crooked," said Simon, leaning over from the next stool. "The buildings look like they're drunk."

"I know," Michael said. "I can't figure out where the lines go."

Simon tapped the photocopy. "Guillaume told me about this painting. In the Last Supper, the single vanishing point is right at Christ's head. All the lines in the room go there." He squinted. "And get this. There's a nail hole, a real one, still visible at that exact spot. Leonardo hammered in a nail and stretched strings from it to guide his lines."

"A nail hole? In the most famous painting ever?"

"Tiny," Simon said. "But it's still there."

Michael looked at the photocopy. Every edge of the ceiling and the walls seemed to lean toward that one point, like iron filings dragged toward a magnet. Invisible lines. Lines nobody drew, but that the eye followed anyway. He pulled his mechanical pencil, its barrel of thin alloy clicking as he extended the lead, and made a dot in the middle of his own paper. Then he drew a dot where his street should disappear.

He tested it. He ruled a line from the top corner of his first building straight to the dot, then the bottom edge, then the window ledges. The building popped backward into depth like a stage set. He did the next one, and the one after that, and the street opened up in front of him, wide at the bottom and narrow at the far end, exactly the way a real street did when you stood in the middle of it. His hands actually felt warm.

"Better," Simon admitted. "Although your lamppost is still pretending to be a tree."

"That's a tree," Michael said, and they both laughed until Ms. Dang looked over.

He worked through lunch. He wanted to keep the drawing, maybe give it to his grandfather for the hospital wall, something permanent, and he asked Ms. Dang for a sheet of good paper. She said the good paper was locked up for the exam portfolios. So he cut his practice sketch carefully out of the notebook, and in the corner of the new sheet, before starting over, he pressed the pencil tip down and made one small hole.

"What's that for?" Simon asked.

Michael stretched his ruler from the hole to the edge of the page and drew his first line. "Ask Leonardo."

Hailey sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a notebook, a pencil, and a problem. Her story was due Monday, and Ms. Foster had written one thing at the top of last week's draft: "Where is your climax? Something has to happen!" Hailey had read that sentence eleven times, and it still hadn't told her what to do.

"You look like the pencil insulted you," her grandmother said, sliding a cup of cocoa across the table.

"My character just talks. The whole story is talking. Ms. Foster says nothing happens." Hailey tapped the page. "I'm going to devise a plot where my hero actually does something. Maybe she saves the neighbor's runaway parrot."

Her grandmother laughed so hard she had to sit down, which Hailey took as a sign the plot was a good one. She wrote a vigorous opening scene, all flapping wings and shrieking, with the parrot racing past the hedge and her hero sprinting after it in slippers. Then she hit the wall. Her hero was supposed to shout what her little brother had told her earlier: "He said, 'The parrot bites.'" Hailey stared at it. Did she need two sets of marks? Which ones? She tried commas, then colons, then wrote the whole thing in double quotation marks twice and immediately crossed it out because it looked like the sentence was wearing two hats.

She decided to test it. "Grandma, read this out loud," she said, holding up the notebook. Her grandmother read it twice, once slowly, and said, "I can't tell where his voice stops and yours starts." That was the clue Hailey needed. Her reasoning went like this: the outside voice, the hero's, got the big double marks, so the inside voice, the brother's, must get something smaller and different. She tried single marks tucked inside the doubles and read it aloud. "He said, 'The parrot bites.'" The sentence worked. You could hear the two voices, one folded inside the other, like a note inside an envelope.

On Monday Ms. Foster read the story in front of the class, all the way to the part where the hero cornered the parrot on the garage roof with a crackers. "Best climax of the pile," Ms. Foster announced. "And that nested quotation is perfect." Prince leaned over from the next desk and whispered, "I put my inside quotes in double marks. Twice."

"Two hats," Hailey whispered back.

"What?"

"Your sentence was wearing two hats. I'll show you at recess." She slid her notebook toward him, and at the bottom of her page, in red pen, Ms. Foster had drawn a small parrot wearing a tiny hat.

The lights went out just as Abigail opened her science book. She sat for a moment in the sudden dark, listening to the refrigerator stop its hum, then got up and felt her way to the kitchen drawer where the flashlights lived. Through the window she could see that the whole street was black. No porch lights, no glow from the TV in the Hendersons' front room, nothing. That told her something. If only her house had gone dark, the problem might be a tripped breaker or a blown fuse, something she could check herself. But a whole street meant the trouble was somewhere out there, somewhere she couldn't see.

She recruited her little brother to hold the flashlight while she looked for the candles, promising him the biggest slice of the leftover banana bread if he didn't wave the beam around. He agreed, mostly. Their parents were still driving back from her grandmother's, so for now the house was just the two of them and the rain ticking against the windows.

While her brother searched for matches, Abigail stood at the front window and thought about the walk home from school. She and Elissa had cut through Maple Court after the storm, and there, lying across the sidewalk, was a power line. It had come down with a branch, and it wasn't sparking or humming or doing anything that looked dangerous. Elissa had started to step over it, and Abigail had grabbed her sleeve.

"Don't," she'd said. "It can still be live even when it isn't sparking. We stay well away and tell an adult."

They had backed up to Mr. Virtanen's porch, and he had called it in right away, reporting it to the utility while the girls stood with him, well back from the wire. Abigail hadn't needed anyone to explain it twice. A wire you couldn't trust was a wire you treated as live, always.

Now she looked toward Maple Court from the window, though it was too dark to see that far. That wire could be the very reason her street was black. She found her phone and called Elissa, who answered on the second ring.

"Your power out too?" Abigail asked.

"Whole block. My dad says they're working on it."

"Mr. Virtanen reported the downed line, right? Before it got dark?"

"He showed me the confirmation number. They know about it."

"Good," Abigail said. "Keep everyone away from it, okay? Even if it looks dead, nobody touches it or steps over it. It has to be treated as live until the crews say otherwise."

Elissa promised, and Abigail hung up feeling steadier. She lit three candles, set them on the table, and got out the book she'd been reading before the lights failed, a thick one about wildlife. By candlelight she read a chapter on the wombat, a stubborn, burrowing marsupial that dug its tunnels even through land overtaken by invasive weeds. Her brother leaned against her arm, flashlight forgotten in his lap.

When the porch lights across the street blinked back on, he pointed at the window and shouted, "They're back!"

"Then let's go see if the fridge survived," Abigail said, and blew out the first candle.

The new house was completely empty, and every footstep Adam took echoed like he was walking around inside a drum. He had claimed the upstairs room with the window facing the street, and now he sat on the floor of it, holding his phone, waiting for the video call that Benny and Benson had promised.

Last summer, before anyone knew about the move, the three of them had biked to the creek behind the school and Benny had lost his shoe in the mud. Benson had fished it out with a stick and held it up like a trophy, shouting, "Behold, the legendary shoe of Benny, recovered by a master scavenger of the creek!" Adam had laughed so hard he had fallen off his bike. He kept replaying moments like that in his head, and this morning he had even cried a little over a photo of his old street, which embarrassed him, so he had wiped his face and told no one.

His mother had said something on the drive here, though. She had not made a speech about it, just one line while they passed a water tower: "Being sad because you're away from home and the people you know, that's homesickness. It's common. It eases as you settle in." Adam had shrugged at the time, but now, sitting in the empty room, he decided to test whether she was right. His test was simple: keep doing things, and see if the heavy feeling shrank.

So he carried boxes upstairs, labeled his door, and dragged his mattress to the corner with the best light. When the call finally buzzed, he answered fast. Benny's face filled the screen, and behind him was Benson, holding up a shoe. "We found a shoe at the creek," Benson announced. "It is not mine, it is not Benny's. It symbolizes your absence, Adam. Someone else is losing shoes now."

Adam laughed so suddenly that he snorted, and the empty room echoed it back at him, twice. They talked until his mother called him down, and when he hung up the heaviness was still there, but smaller, like it had moved from his chest to somewhere behind his ribs.

At the front door stood a man holding a plate of food, a neighbor who introduced himself as Mr. Chukwu. "Welcome to the street," Mr. Chukwu said, glancing at the bare walls. "New houses look like this at first. Empty. You'll fill it."

Adam took the plate and looked back up the stairs at his room, where the mattress already sat in the corner with the good light.

"I started," he said. "Want to see my labels? I spelled one wrong on purpose so Benny would notice."

Austin sat at Xander's kitchen table with his Spanish book open to a blank page. The assignment was due Monday: one paragraph about plans for next year, all in the future tense. Xander's grandmother had offered to check their work, and Xander, who had spoken Spanish since he was small, kept leaning over to peek at Austin's paper.

"You wrote 'yo jugo fútbol el año que viene,'" Xander said. "That's not future tense. That's like saying you already juice soccer."

Austin erased the sentence so hard the paper ripped a little. The problem was that he couldn't find the future anywhere. He flipped to the verb charts in the back of the book. In Spanish, the future was built right onto the verb itself, an ending you could see and hear. Then a question slid into his mind and wouldn't leave. He tried it out loud. "Wait. What's the future ending in English?"

Xander stopped chewing his granola bar. "What?"

"The ending. Like Spanish has one. What is it for English?"

Xander opened his mouth, closed it, and stared at the table. "There isn't one," he said slowly, like he didn't trust his own answer. His grandmother, stirring soup at the stove, laughed and said something in Spanish that made Xander's ears go red.

Austin grabbed a napkin and wrote three sentences: I will run. I am going to run. I run tomorrow. He looked for the ending on "run" in every one of them. Nothing changed on the verb. The future lived somewhere else entirely, in the words sitting in front of it. Will. Going to. That was the whole system. He tested it against the window, the fridge, Xander's dog snoring under the chair: the chair will break, the soup is going to boil. It held every time. The insight felt like finding a trapdoor in a floor he'd walked across his whole life.

"So English just borrows helper words," Xander said, reading over his shoulder. "Spanish incorporates the future right into the verb. That's actually kind of cool."

Austin started his paragraph over. He wrote about next year in careful Spanish, attaching the future endings where they belonged, and when he got stuck he checked the napkin. His plan was modest: he would join the Spanish club, he would learn to cook his grandmother's rice, he would visit the affluent neighborhood across town where his cousin lived, because his cousin had promised him a tour. When he finished, Xander's grandmother read the whole thing and nodded.

"Buen trabajo," she said, and set a bowl of soup in front of him. Austin picked up his spoon, then paused. "The soup will be amazing," he said, and grinned at Xander. "See? No ending. Just a helper."

Stella's new phone was two years old when she got it, because it was actually her cousin's old phone, mailed across the country in a padded envelope with a note that said "treat it kindly." That night, her mom added her to the family group chat, renamed it Stella Has A Phone Finally, and Stella sent her first message, "hi everyone," at 8:47. The phone was dead by morning.

In homeroom she showed the phone to Malachi, who poked at the battery icon. "Four percent? You charged it overnight."

"I did." She plugged it into the wall by the window and watched the number crawl. At lunch she tried again to post in the group chat, where her uncle had already sent eleven photos of his cat, and the screen went black mid-typing. Dead again. Same time as yesterday.

She remembered last summer, visiting her cousin, how the phone had lived all day on one charge back then, streaming music through lunch and still glowing at midnight. So it wasn't the phone's settings. Something had changed inside it in two years, something she couldn't see. She had a few plausible theories: her charging cable was bad, the group chat was eating power, the phone itself was broken. She decided to eliminate them one at a time.

That evening she ran the test. She borrowed her mom's cable and charged to full, then left the phone asleep on her dresser, doing nothing. By morning it had dropped to half. A phone doing nothing shouldn't lose half a battery overnight. She checked her mom's brand-new phone, also asleep all night on the same shelf. Ninety-six percent. So it wasn't the cable, and it wasn't the chat. It was the phone's own battery, somehow worse than it used to be.

"Text her and ask," Natalia said on the bus, reading over her shoulder. "Cousins tell each other stuff."

The reply came during fifth period, buzzing in Stella's pocket until she could look: "oh that battery lol. it's lithium-ion. they chemically age, so they hold less charge than when they were new. battery life just gets shorter over time, nothing you did."

Stella read it twice. So the phone wasn't broken and she hadn't ruined it; it was just old, in a slow way that happened to every phone like it. She typed back, "how much longer do i have with it," and watched the typing dots appear, then disappear, then appear again.

Down the aisle, Mr. Sandhu was collecting permission slips. The dots were still going.

"Stella, phone away," he said.

She slid it under her binder, screen up, just as the reply landed.

Carter slid his story across the library table and checked the clock above the biography shelf. The writing contest entries had to be emailed by three fifteen, and it was already two forty.

"Read it fast," he said. "It's about a volcano that eats homework."

Deacon picked up his red pen like a knight drawing a sword. "I nominate myself official punctuator." He read, and his pen began to strike. Every time a character spoke and then the words "he said" or "she said" followed, Deacon circled the period and wrote NO in the margin. By the second page there were seven circles, like tiny red craters.

"You're wrong," Carter said. "Periods end sentences. That's the one rule I actually know."

Deacon turned the draft around and tapped the page. "Then why does every book in this place do the opposite?"

Carter looked. Deacon looked. They both looked at Skyla, who was shelving returns with a cart and pretending not to hear. She pushed the cart a little closer, which was her way of joining.

So Carter tested it. He pulled three novels off the shelf at random, opened each where characters were talking, and laid them side by side. In the first, "'I'm ready,' she said." In the second, "'Run,' he said." In the third, "'It's molten rock, you goofball,' said the guide," which fit Carter's volcano theme so well he copied the word down. Three books, three commas, all sitting inside the quotation marks before the tag. When a dialogue tag follows a spoken sentence, that was a comma's job, not a period's.

"My whole neuron just rewired," Carter said. "Every page. It's a pattern."

Deacon crossed out his seven red NOs with a flourish. "I punctured your punctuation with confidence," he said. "For that, I apologize in writing." He tore a page from his notebook and wrote a note, which he folded and slid across the table like a spy passing secrets. Carter unfolded it. "Dear Carter: Your commas were right and my pen was wrong. My pen will undergo retraining. Yours, Deacon." Below that, Skyla had already added, in different ink, "He showed me this note first. It was longer. He cut the part where he cried."

"That was a draft," Deacon said. "Drafts are sacred."

Carter laughed, fixed nothing, because there was nothing to fix, and typed the story with two minutes to spare. He hit send and leaned back.

Then Mr. Tse appeared beside the table, holding a clipboard. "The contest deadline," he said apologetically, "was yesterday."

There was a silence. Carter looked at his sent email glowing on the screen.

"So," Deacon said slowly, tapping his red pen, "you'd like to volunteer a first-place entry for next year?"

"No," said Mr. Tse. "We'd like to nominate Carter as a judge."

The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and tape, and Thomas's hands were shaking as he set his poster on the folding table. His project measured how much weight a paper bridge could hold before it sagged. He had tested six bridges, added washers one at a time, and counted them all. His graph showed the results. It looked wrong.

Salma leaned over from the next table. "That line goes down. Heavier weight should mean more sag, right?"

"More washers, more sag," Thomas said. "The line should climb."

Elise came around the table and studied the poster. "How did you set it up?"

"Washers on the bottom, sag on the side." He traced the line with one finger. The paper with the most washers showed the most sag. The paper with the fewest washers showed the least. Every measurement was right. The line still fell instead of rising.

"You swapped it," Elise said. "My brother did that last year."

"Swapped what?"

"The axes." She pointed at the bottom of his graph, then the side. "By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis."

Thomas stared at her. His washers were the thing he chose, the thing he controlled at each test. The sag was the thing that answered back. He had put the answer on the bottom and the choice on the side. "So the washers go across the bottom," he said slowly, "and the sag goes up the side."

"That's the rule," Elise said, and went back to her own table, where her display about erosion in a sandbox was already drawing a crowd. She had built a drip system that carved tiny valleys into the sand, and she had documented every stage with photographs.

Thomas sat down on the floor behind his table, pulled a pencil from his bag, and flipped his poster over. He could hear Mr. Johansson at the door checking clipboards, which meant judges were close. He drew a new set of axes, quick but careful, and plotted his six points again, the same numbers in new places. Then he drew the line.

It climbed.

Every point sat exactly where his tests had put it, and the line rose from the lower left toward the upper right, steady and systematic, one clean sweep. He taped the new graph over the old one just as Mr. Johansson stopped at his table.

"Tell me about your results," Mr. Johansson said.

Thomas stood, brushed pencil dust off his knees, and pointed at the rising line. "The more weight I add, the more it sags. Here, watch this part." He picked up his spare bridge and began stacking washers, one by one, waiting for the paper to contract into a shallow curve under the load.

The cafeteria had been turned into a restaurant called El Sol, with paper tablecloths and a chalkboard menu, and Ms. Farah-Ali stood at the door collecting imaginary reservations. Brayden's grade depended on ordering a full meal in Spanish and asking what it cost. That was the whole assignment. It sounded easy until he remembered he had exactly one week of restaurant vocabulary and a tendency to say the first word that came into his head.

He sat down across from Cleo, who was rehearsing under her breath like the menu might be confiscated. At the next table, Sirine was already playing server for another group, pad in hand, wearing the unimpressed expression of someone working a double shift.

"Quiero el taco," Brayden said when his turn came. Sirine wrote it down without looking up. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

"Seis dólares." Flat. Businesslike. She moved to the next table.

Brayden watched her take Cleo's order, and something bothered him. Sirine hadn't been rude exactly, but she hadn't smiled either, and he'd seen her smile at the table before his, twice. He ran the orders back through his head. The boy at the first table had said something longer, something with a soft sound at the front. Quisiera. Brayden had written it in his notes and then, in the margin, "???"

He had a theory. Maybe the word itself carried the attitude. He'd noticed in English that "I want" and "may I have" got different reactions from his mother, and his mother was one person, but here was a second data point. One server, two words, two faces. That wasn't proof. But it was testable.

He waited until Sirine looped back to take dessert orders. Cleo went first, said "quiero el flan," and got the same polite blankness. Then Brayden leaned forward and tried it.

"Quisiera el helado," he said. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

Sirine's pad stopped midair. She smiled, an actual smile, and said, "Tres dólares, y muy buena elección," which he understood well enough to feel his ears go warm.

"So that's the trick," Cleo whispered. "Quisiera."

"Means 'I would like,'" Brayden whispered back. "I want versus I would like. Watch." He raised his hand and called Sirine over one more time, purely for research. "Quisiera agua, por favor." Smile. Then, quietly, just to check, "quiero una servilleta." The smile thinned to a professional line. The pattern held. Two trials, same result, both directions.

After class, Ms. Farah-Ali stopped him at the door. "You ordered three times, Brayden."

"I wanted to preserve the data," he said. "Science." She looked at him for a moment, then wrote something in her grade book that was probably good.

Cleo caught up with him in the hall. "Tomorrow I'm trying it on the lunch lady."

"She doesn't speak Spanish."

"The attitude translates," Cleo said, and pushed through the doors toward the cafeteria.

Elijah sat at the upright piano in the music room after school, staring at the top of the page where Mr. Mensah had circled the tempo marking. "Largo, 60," it said, in pencil. He had been playing the piece all week, and every time he got to the quiet, slow middle section, something felt wrong. It didn't sound sad the way it was supposed to. It sounded ordinary.

He tried the section again, playing the notes softly, the way the dynamics told him to. Still ordinary. He slammed the lid shut, then opened it again, because slamming pianos was the kind of thing that got you banned from the music room, and he needed this room.

Annabella came in to retrieve her flute case from under the chairs. "You're playing it too fast," she said, without even stopping.

"I'm playing it slow," Elijah said. "Slower than the rest of the piece."

"Not slow enough." She buckled her case and left, and Elijah sat there thinking about that. She had said it like it was obvious, but how slow was slow? The marking said 60, but he had no idea what 60 meant when it came to his own hands. He couldn't hear his own rushing, because from inside, his playing always sounded the way he imagined it, not the way it actually was.

Then he noticed the wall clock above the door, the old one with a second hand that ticked as it swept around. His grandmother had one just like it, and he remembered sitting in her kitchen years ago, bored, counting the ticks while she talked on the phone. Sixty of them, he'd figured out back then, one whole trip around the dial. He looked at the pencil marking again. Sixty. That couldn't be a coincidence.

He set his hand on middle C and watched the second hand. Tick. He pressed the key. Tick. Press. Tick. Press. One beat each second, exactly. So the composer wanted this section to move like a clock, like time itself, steady and unhurried. The concept wasn't about the notes at all. It was about the space between them. He had been playing at maybe twice that speed, which meant the quiet middle section, the part that was supposed to decompose the melody into single, isolated notes floating in silence, had been crushed together into a shuffle.

He tried it with the clock, one note per tick, and the section opened up like a room with the curtains pulled back. The dynamics made sense now too. When the tempo was truly slow, a soft note had time to hang in the air, and the next note arrived like a step in the dark. It sounded sad. It sounded like the piece finally had something to say.

Mr. Mensah appeared in the doorway, keys in hand, and listened with what Elijah thought was a neutral expression, though it was hard to tell with him. When Elijah finished, the teacher just nodded and said, "Same time tomorrow."

After he left, Elijah wondered whether he should have figured this out a week ago, before the recital sign-up sheet filled up, instead of the day after. He set his music on the stand, watched the second hand sweep once more around the dial, and started again from the very first measure.

Tyler dragged two chairs over to the computer lab table, and Loic followed with a stack of printed surveys that smelled like pencil shavings. The room hummed with the noise of thirty machines, and the afternoon sun made a hot stripe across the keyboard.

"We asked four hundred kids," Loic said, fanning the pages, "and the eighth graders win every single question. More pizza, more field trips, more dance. It's not even close."

Tyler frowned at the spreadsheet on the screen. Mr. Santoso had told them to summarise the survey answers by grade using pivot tables, and Tyler had figured that part out. He dragged Grade into Rows, dragged Answer into Values, and the counts appeared. Grade six: 118 students. Grade seven: 124. Grade eight: 158. The eighth grade column towered over the others on every question.

"That's it, then," Aditya said, leaning over from the next seat. "Eighth graders just like everything more."

"Or they have more people," Tyler said slowly. He counted the grade totals twice, tapping his pencil on the desk. Eighty-one eighth graders wanted the field trip. But sixty-five sixth graders wanted it too, and there were only 118 of them in the whole grade. He scribbled on the back of a survey page, dividing numbers, and the obstinate gap in the raw counts started to look like a trick. "They don't win. They're just bigger."

Loic squinted at the scrap paper. "So how do we make the spreadsheet see that?"

Tyler right-clicked on a count inside the pivot table. A menu unfolded, and near the bottom sat an option called Show Values As. He hovered over it and found % of Column Total. When he clicked it, every count changed into a percentage of its column, so each grade's answers were measured against its own students. The eighth grade's 81 shrank to a fair share, and grade six's 65 jumped up beside it. Sixth grade was actually the biggest slice of its column.

"Look at that," Tyler said, turning the screen toward them. "Sixth graders want the field trip more, per kid. It just looked like eighth grade before because they had more people."

Aditya laughed and dragged his chair over. "So the pizza question too?"

They rebuilt the pivot table for pizza, and then for the dance, and the percentages kept flipping the story around. Grade seven took the pizza. Grade eight kept the dance, but barely. When Mr. Santoso walked past and glanced at their screen, he nodded once and kept going, and Tyler felt the insight settle in his chest like a locked door clicking open.

"We should present it this way," Loic said, highlighting the percentage columns.

"Every question," Tyler said, and hit print.

Sydney had been accused of turning the classroom globe into a weapon once, so Mr. Delgado watched her a little too closely when she picked up the model Earth at the planetarium's hands-on table. "Just tilting it," she said. He nodded anyway, the way a coach nods when he expects the tendon to snap any second.

The problem was this: on Saturday she had to stand in front of her class and explain why we have seasons, and every time she practiced in the mirror she said something like "we're closer to the sun in summer," which her cousin Aisha, on a video call from Jakarta, had laughed at for a full minute. "Orbit's an ellipse, but that's not it," Aisha had said. "Everyone gets that wrong." Sydney needed to actually see it, and the planetarium's dome was the closest thing to seeing space without a rocket.

Haider and Pascal from her class were there too, mostly for the gift shop, but she'd bribed them with popcorn to hold the flashlight. "You're the sun," she told Haider. He stood very still and radiated. Pascal held the tilted globe while Sydney walked it in a slow circle. Summer, winter, summer, winter. She stopped halfway around. "Wait. There's a spot where neither pole leans toward him."

Pascal squinted. "That's the equinox," Haider said, because of course he'd read the plaque by the door while everyone else was buying popcorn. "Around March twentieth and September twenty-second."

Sydney pulled out her phone and messaged Aisha, who was twelve time zones away and, at this hour, probably eating breakfast. When the sun sets for you tonight, tell me the time. Aisha replied an hour later: six fifteen. Sydney checked her own sunset forecast for the same date: six twenty. Close enough to make her grin at the ceiling.

"See, around the equinoxes day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth," she said, pacing in front of the two of them like it was Saturday already. "Jakarta, here, everywhere. Same date, both places. If it worked for Aisha, it works for the whole planet, and it's not because we're closer to the sun." She spun the globe and watched its eccentric wobble on its stand. "It's the lean. It's always the lean."

Mr. Delgado drifted over, looked at the flashlight, the globe, the two boys holding their poses without complaint, and Sydney standing between them like she owned the solar system. "Closer to the sun," he said, testing her.

"The lean," she said, and walked the globe another quarter turn.

Grace pushed her peas around her plate while her grandmother sorted a stack of mail at the end of the table, muttering about her pension form for the third time that week. At the other end, Dad ladled out seconds of soup and asked how the Robotics Club had gone that afternoon. Grace set down her spoon.

"Terrible," she said. "Himmat swears we voted to spend the snack fund on a new battery pack. Junior swears we voted to save it for the competition entry fee. They argued for twenty minutes and then Mr. Bianchi poked his head in and asked if we were okay because we were shouting about chips."

Dad laughed into his soup. "So who's right?"

"That's the thing. Nobody knows. There's no record. It's like the meeting evaporated." Grace pulled her notebook out of her backpack and flipped to a page of doodles, a robot with too many arms. "I'm supposed to run the next one, and if I can't even settle a chip argument, the club will fall apart before regionals."

Her grandmother slid the pension form aside and tapped the table with one knuckle. "At the community centre, every meeting has minutes. That's how we know who promised to fix the hall clock in 1998. Harold. Still not fixed."

"Minutes?" Grace said. "Like, minutes of time?"

"A secretary takes them," her grandmother said. "They're the written record of a meeting, what was decided, not every single word everybody said."

Grace looked at the notebook, then at her soup, then at the notebook again. If nobody had written anything down, then Himmat and Junior could both be honestly remembering two different half-meetings, or one of them could be inventing a decision that never happened, and she couldn't see which from the outside. But the idea itself was testable. She wrote TUESDAY, 3:15, LIBRARY in big letters and underlined it twice.

"Can I practice on you two?" she said. "Right now. This dinner is a meeting. Dad, you're Himmat. Grandma, you're Junior, except nicer."

"Nobody has ever called me nice," her grandmother said, and stole a roll off Grace's plate to prove it.

Grace read out her plan for Tuesday. "First, an agenda. Snack fund, competition entry, whose turn to monitor the clean-up rota. One item at a time. And a secretary, someone who writes down what we decided. Himmat's handwriting is notorious, it looks like a spider fell in ink, so I'll ask Junior." She demonstrated on the notebook, printing neatly: DECIDED: review the pension of the snack fund, then laughed at herself and crossed it out. "DECIDED: count the snack fund. VOTE: 4 for, 2 against. That's it? That's minutes?"

"Grandpa once spoke for forty minutes about guttering," her grandmother said, "and it took one line in the minutes. Gutters: deferred."

At Tuesday's meeting, Grace held up the notebook before anyone could open their mouth. "We start with the agenda, we end with minutes, and the battery-versus-entry question gets settled by a real vote that Junior writes down." Himmat groaned, Junior saluted with the pen, and when the vote came out five to one for the entry fee, Himmat studied the page, shrugged, and said, "Fine, but I want it noted that I was robbed."

Junior printed it, word for word, and Grace let him, because it was, technically, a decision.

Isla stood in the hallway with one heel jammed against the wall and stared at the pencil mark her mom had just made above her head. Two months ago the mark had been at her chin's twin, the old one, and now there was a gap between them wide enough to slide a book through. But her jeans still puddled at the ankles like always, and that was the part that made no sense to her.

Her shoes were the worst of it. In September her mom had bought her new sneakers because the old ones pinched, and now, in November, the new ones pinicked too. She'd worn them to school anyway, and by last period she'd been slipping them off under her desk while Phoenix whispered that her feet were going to smell like Prince's gym bag. Isla had kicked him under the table, which only made her toes complain louder.

That night she took out a notebook and made three columns: shoes, jeans, sleeves. Under shoes she wrote "September, too small. November, too small again." Under jeans she wrote "still fine." Under sleeves she wrote "still fine." It looked like a mistake, like two of the columns had gotten mixed up, because how could her feet shoot ahead while everything else stayed behind? She remembered Phoenix complaining in October that his shoes had stopped fitting twice already that year, and she'd laughed at him, and now she was doing the same thing. Maybe, she thought, it wasn't a fluke. Maybe feet went first, and hands too, and the rest of a person caught up afterward, like runners who started before the whistle.

She decided to test it. Every Sunday she measured her right foot with a ruler, traced her hand on the notebook page, and checked whether her sleeves reached her wrists. She wrote the numbers down like Ms. Tang had taught them for science, in a table, so a pattern would germinate on its own if there was one to find. Six Sundays later the pattern was there, plain as a percentage on a test: her foot had grown a whole size and a half, her hand traced out past the first outline by a finger's width, and her sleeves and inseams had barely moved. Hands and feet first, she wrote in the margin. Arms and legs and everything else, later.

She showed the notebook to her mom, who read it twice and then got quiet in a way Isla recognized. "I had a growth chart too," her mom said finally. "Your grandmother drew it on the kitchen doorframe. I fought her about it every single year."

"Why?"

"Because I wanted to stay the size I was." Her mom smiled at the doorframe, not at Isla, and Isla understood there was more in that answer than her mom was saying. She thought about the old sneakers, and about laughing at Phoenix, and about how her mother's face had looked just now, and she didn't decide what any of it meant yet.

"New shoes this weekend," her mom said, standing up. "Big ones. And you can tell Phoenix his feet aren't weird, they're just early."

Hailey slid her worksheet across the table at the tutoring centre and tapped problem seven with her pencil. "I've done this one six times. It keeps falling apart."

Elias leaned over from the next seat, still chewing the end of his own pencil. He had a maths test on Friday and had begged his mum to let him come tonight, though he kept getting distracted by the clock on the wall. "Show me."

"Fine. Watch." Hailey wrote the equation out again. "x plus one equals x plus two. So I subtract one from both sides, like Ms. Charles taught us. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other." She worked it through, then stared at the result. "x equals x plus one. That's useless."

"So subtract the x," Elias said. "From both sides."

She did. Zero equals one. She sat back. "That's not a solution. That's just wrong."

Renaud, two seats down, looked up from his notebook. "Maybe you copied it wrong off the board."

Hailey checked her phone photo of the board. The equation was exactly as she'd written it. She tried plugging in numbers anyway, because trying felt better than sitting there. If x was five, the left side was six and the right side was seven. If x was a hundred, the sides were a hundred and one and a hundred and two. The gap never closed. Every number she picked came out one too small on the left. She wrote a quick column of test values and circled the differences, and every single answer came out the same.

"Elias," she said slowly, "I don't think there's any number that works. Not one. No number can be one more and two more than itself at the same time."

Elias frowned at his own sheet. "Every equation has an answer, though. They gave us twenty minutes for ten problems, and we've spent most of it on this."

"That's the trap," Hailey said. She raised her hand. "Ms. Charles? Question seven has no solution. I checked a bunch of numbers and the sides are never equal, and when I subtract everything away I get zero equals one."

Ms. Charles walked over, looked at the page, and nodded once. "Good. That one's on purpose." She moved on down the row of tables.

Elias copied the phrase no solution at the top of his sheet, then glanced at the clock and sped up on his remaining problems.

Renaud slid his chair back. "I wanted to be the one to catch it," he said, gathering his books as the timer on the desk began to beep. "Next time, the trick question is mine."

"Race you to problem eight," Hailey said, and flipped the page.

Lillian met Macey and Nizar by the fountain in the mall food court, carrying the shoebox that held their science project: a banana, a slice of bread, and a plastic bag of soil full of decomposers, the worms and fungi that would break the food down over the next three weeks. The group had been unanimous about the plan in class, voting with raised hands, and Ms. Grewal had told them to document every stage with photos. Lillian was in charge of the photos.

She had already posted the first set on her account, the one she used for the project. It was private. Only people she'd accepted as followers could see it, which she'd always assumed meant her pictures stayed inside a kind of locked room. So when Nizar slid his phone across the table and said, "Look, my cousin found your banana photo," her stomach dropped. She didn't know his cousin. She'd never accepted him.

"Who sent it to him?" she asked. Nizar shrugged. "Some kid named Tyler, I think. Said it got forwarded to a group chat." Tyler. Lillian scrolled through her follower list until she found him, a boy from her old school who had followed her two years ago and never said a word since. She had accepted him back then because it felt rude not to.

She stared at the banana. The problem wasn't the banana, really; it was that this account also had photos of her street, her front door, the mall entrance where she waited every Friday. If Tyler could pass along a project photo, he could pass along those too. She thought about it while Macey poked the soil and asked whether the worms were asleep. Private meant only followers could see it, that much was true. But it didn't stop a follower from copying what was right there on their screen and sending it anywhere at all.

She tested it to be sure. She posted a plain picture of the mall fountain and waited. Twenty minutes later, Nizar forwarded it to his cousin, who sent back a thumbs up from three towns away. That settled it. Lillian opened her follower list and removed Tyler, then a dozen other names she barely recognized, one by one. "Cleaned out," she said, and set the phone face down next to the shoebox.

They spent the rest of the afternoon photographing the banana from four angles, and Lillian saved every picture in a folder marked SCIENCE, deciding she'd share them in person at school instead. When they packed up, Macey held the box while Lillian folded the map of the mall back into her pocket, and Nizar said, "Same fountain next Saturday?" "Same fountain," Lillian said, and hitched her backpack higher on her shoulder.

The old piano in the basement of the mosque sat under a poster about Friday food drives, and every Saturday Hannah commuted forty minutes by two buses to get to it. Nobody else wanted the slot. The instrument was badly out of tune and one key stuck if you played it twice in a row, which was inconvenient in a piece where that key appeared four times.

She was supposed to play it at the community interfaith evening in three weeks, a short piece with soft parts and loud parts marked in the sheet music. The soft parts were fine. The loud parts came out like a door slamming, no matter what she did. At home she'd watched videos, but the videos all assumed your piano lived somewhere other than a basement and had all its keys.

Isra, who came along mainly for the bus ride and the samosas, sprawled on a folding chair behind her. "You're pounding," Isra said. "Mr. Somsak is going to hear you upstairs and think we've knocked something over."

"I'm not pounding. The music says forte, so I have to play forte." Hannah put her hands in her lap and glared at the page, which offered no further advice. The problem, she decided, was not her hands. The problem was that forte was somehow the same action as whispering, just bigger, and she couldn't figure out what actually changed between the two. She tried an experiment. She played the loud section three ways: arms tense, arms loose, and a version where she let her fingers fall from higher up. Each one sounded different. Not better, exactly, but different in a direction she could hear.

Mr. Somsak came down at four to lock the storage room, found them still there, and paused at the doorway with his keys. He was the caretaker, and according to Isra he had once played organ somewhere in Bangkok, though he never mentioned it. He listened to Hannah's fourth attempt, the one with falling fingers, and said only, "Better. The instrument can do that. It's built for it."

"What do you mean, built for it?"

He tapped the fallboard once, on the word painted there. "Pianoforte. It means soft-loud." Then he went upstairs with his keys, apparently considering that a complete answer.

Hannah lifted the fallboard and looked at the letters again. Soft-loud. Not soft OR loud, like the piano came in two categories the way the food drive boxes came in cans and dry goods. Soft-loud, one word. The whole point of the machine was that the same key could do either, depending on how hard you struck it, and until now she had been playing as if the loud parts belonged to some reckless separate piano she had to summon by brute force. She put her hands back on the keys and played the passage again, thinking not louder but harder-then-released, letting each note arrive with weight and leave quickly.

The sound that came out was big without being a slamming door. Isra sat up straight, which for Isra was a standing ovation. "Do that part again," she said.

Hannah did it again, and the stuck key stuck on purpose this time, ringing out under her hand like a bell.

Lauren had the phrase written on her palm in gel pen, which she now realized was a mistake, because it had smeared into something that looked like "¿Cuánto castella?" and the festival started in forty minutes.

The school library was supposed to be empty on a Saturday, but Gia was at the corner table with a Spanish textbook open, copying vocabulary like a machine. "You're going to the festival," Gia said without looking up. "You're going to walk up to the food stall and freeze."

"I'm not going to freeze. I just need to clarify one thing." Lauren sat down and held out her hand. "Can you read that?"

Gia studied the blue smear. "I can read that you write on yourself. What's it supposed to be?"

"Something like 'how much does it cost.' Mr. Ba wrote it out for me after Spanish club, but I was rushing and I didn't check it, and now I can't tell if the last word says cuesta or castella, and castella isn't even a word I know."

"Then it's probably not the word." Gia turned to the back of the book. "There's a glossary."

"That's vague. There are a million entries."

Gia ran her finger down the C's anyway. Lauren watched, then noticed something. The book had a whole section of sample dialogues, and one was a restaurant scene: a customer pointing at a single dish, asking the price, then ordering it. She flipped to it and read the line out loud. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

"That's it," Gia said. "That's how you ask the price of one item. It's the usual way."

Lauren copied it onto a fresh index card, and then, because her embarrassment over the smeared palm was still fresh, she copied it two more times and made Gia quiz her. "¿Cuánto cuesta?" she said, until the words stopped feeling like a puzzle.

At the festival, the line at the food stall was long and loud. Edith from her Spanish class was ahead of her and pointed at the empanadas. "How much are these?" she asked the man in English, and the man smiled, shrugged, and held up his hands. Edith pointed again. He held up three fingers, but nobody could tell if that meant three dollars or something else, and the people behind them shifted their weight.

Lauren stepped up, pointed at one empanada, and said, "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

The man's face changed completely. "Tres dólares," he said, and tapped the little sign.

"Gracias," said Lauren, who had at least learned that much properly, and she paid, took her empanada, and turned around to find Edith still holding three dollars and looking at her like she'd performed a magic trick.

"Teach me," Edith said.

Rebecca spread her outline across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with the salt shaker and a mug of cold cocoa. The prompt, printed at the top in her careful printing, read: Should our school switch to a four-day week? She had written her thesis at the bottom of the page: Our school should switch to a four-day week. Below it sat her three points: it saves money on buses, it cuts energy costs, and it lowers spending on electricity. The clock over the stove ticked while she read them over.

Mr. Hu had said the outline governed the whole essay; whatever she put in those three lines would decide every paragraph that came after. So she wanted to get them right before drafting a single word. She slid point one to the top and tapped the pencil against her teeth.

Her phone buzzed against the wood. It was Titus, whose class had done the same assignment last period. He had offered to trade reviews, so Rebecca photographed her outline and sent it, then pulled his toward her. His essay argued for keeping the school garden, and his points were that gardens teach science, that gardens need water to grow, and that gardens attract bees. She frowned at that and typed: your point two isn't a reason, it's just a fact.

His reply came fast. Yours is worse. Look at two and three.

She read them again. Cuts energy costs. Lowers spending on electricity. The cocoa had gone bitter at the bottom of the mug, and she took a sip anyway while she stared. Both of those said the school spends less money. The words were different, but the reason underneath was one reason wearing two shirts. She counted on her fingers: bus money, energy money. That was it. Two.

She tried a fix. If point three had to be truly different, she needed a reason that wasn't about money at all. She thought about Skyler, who took care of her little brothers every day and still made honor roll; a free day might help students like her, or it might strand them. Rebecca turned the pencil over and erased. New point three: a longer weekend gives students time for jobs and family. That was a different kind of reason, and the classroom suddenly felt like fertile ground in her mind, full of examples she could actually use: Skyler's schedule, the farm stand on Route 9 that hired eighth graders on Saturdays.

She texted Titus back: you were right, two of mine were the same reason in disguise. Do I get to fix yours? She wrote under his outline: if gardens need water, then your job is to prove the school can afford the watering, so merge that into point one. Then find a second real reason. He sent back a thumbs-up and a photo of his dog asleep on his homework.

Rebecca copied her outline onto a clean sheet, all three lines sitting level under the thesis like fence posts the same height. She read them aloud in the quiet kitchen, and the third one made her think of Skyler again, and of the empathy Mr. Hu kept asking them to show for readers who disagreed. Fine, she thought, she would answer the skeptics too. She sharpened the pencil with the little sharpener screwed to the wall and started her first draft, "Our school should switch to a four-day week, because it saves money on buses, lowers energy costs, and gives students time for work and family."

Hayden had to write a paragraph for Mr. Boateng's class explaining why people moved west in the 1800s, using a primary source instead of a textbook. That was the whole assignment, and it was due Monday. He was at his grandpa's house for the weekend, so Grandpa had dug a shoebox out of the hall closet and set it on the kitchen table. "Great-great-great-uncle Elias," Grandpa said. "He kept a diary crossing the trail in 1852. Knock yourself out."

The handwriting was cramped and brown with age. Hayden copied out a few lines about the oxen going lame, about river crossings, about how tedious the days had become, one dusty mile after another, month after month of walking beside the wagon. Then he found what he expected: land, cheap land, a place of their own. He felt a little smug. Mystery solved, paragraph done.

"Wait," he said out loud, mostly to himself. "There's a second booklet under the diary." It was slimmer, and the handwriting inside was different, loopier, younger. Elias's daughter Ruth, Grandpa confirmed, peering over his glasses. Ruth's first page was dated 1870. She described leaving the farm and heading back east to live near an estuary town where her husband had found work at the docks. And then Hayden read a line that made him sit up straight. She had not gone by wagon. The trip that had eaten her father's whole summer had taken her only days.

He flipped back and forth between the two booklets like he was checking a math answer. Elias: months on the trail, 1852. Ruth: days, 1870. Something had changed in between, and it was not the land or the people. He texted his classmate Nikola, who was a rail fan and kept saying so at lunch. Nikola sent back one line: "The transcontinental railroad, finished 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah. Changed everything." Hayden looked at the date in Ruth's diary, one year later, and grinned. He delegated the boring part of the job to his phone, setting a timer for a five-minute break, then got back to reading.

His paragraph almost wrote itself after that. People moved west for land, yes, but the diary showed something the textbook page never had: the same journey could be a grueling march or a short ride, depending on the year. Even the reasons people gave for going seemed to shift once the going got easier.

On Sunday evening, Grandpa drove him home with the shoebox buckled into the back seat. "Keep it a week," Grandpa said. "Ruth wrote more later on." Hayden lifted the lid to peek and found, tucked beneath everything, a folded map with a rail line inked across it in Ruth's looping hand, and beside the summit, in tiny letters, the word "Finally."

Bennett clutched his phone on the number 14 bus, thumb hovering over the orange BUY button for the DropZone X sneakers. The ad had everything: the rapper D-Low grinning in the shoes, the words "revolutionary" and "unstoppable" stamped across the screen in white capitals, and a counter that said 4,000 pairs had sold in the last hour. Four thousand. His whole grade would be wearing them by Friday, and he would be the one kid still standing in his scuffed gray pair from last year.

Oakley leaned over from the seat beside him, buoyant with excitement. "I already ordered mine. Chiara did too. You're literally the last one."

"I'm deciding," Bennett said, though his finger was already tired from deciding. He had sixty-eight dollars from mowing lawns all September, and the shoes were sixty-five. That was the math that made his stomach tight, but the counter kept climbing on his screen, 4,003 now, and D-Low's smile said everyone who mattered already knew the answer.

Chiara, two rows back, wasn't looking at shoes. She was watching a review video with the sound low, and then she scrolled down and stopped. "Wait. Look at this." She held her phone between their seats. On the screen a girl was gushing about the DropZone X, calling them the best shoes ever made, when in tiny gray letters at the end of the caption sat two characters: #ad.

"So?" Oakley said.

"So in the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something," Chiara read off the article she'd pulled up. "That hashtag is the disclosure. She got the shoes for free."

Bennett looked back at his own screen. He scrolled the ad down, past D-Low, past the loaded words, past the climbing counter, until he found the caption. There it was, small as a patch of lichen on an old wall: Paid partnership with DropZone. D-Low hadn't bought those shoes. D-Low had been handed them, plus probably a check, and told to smile.

Here was the thing Bennett could now test. He tapped over to a different reviewer, a guy who ran a channel full of boring, honest sneaker teardowns, the kind who measured the sole thickness with a ruler. Bennett scrolled his caption. No #ad, no partnership tag, nothing. And that guy's verdict, in a video from last week, was that the DropZone X used the same cheap foam as a forty-dollar shoe. Bennett could infer the rest: the ad was counting on him never scrolling down.

The bus hissed to a stop at Maple Street. Bennett closed the orange screen, and his sixty-eight dollars stayed safely in his pocket.

Oakley stared at him. "You're seriously not getting them?"

"Four thousand pairs in an hour," Bennett said, stepping down onto the curb. "From an ad where nobody scrolls."

Chiara waved from the window. "Meet me at the library," she called. "I found a whole video on this stuff."

The art shack at Camp Windrow smelled of pine sap and pencil shavings, and Jonathan had claimed the stool by the window because it gave him a view of the dirt road that curved past the mess hall. He wanted his drawing to look like a real street, with depth that pulled you in, but his first attempt had come out flat as a pancake. Mylo leaned over his shoulder and squinted at it.

"Looks like the road is standing up," Mylo said. "Like a wall with lines on it."

"Thanks," Jonathan said, but he knew it was true. Ms. Johansson, the art instructor, had pinned a handout to the corkboard that morning showing a street scene with a single dot in the middle of the page and straight lines running out from it in every direction. At the bottom of the sheet, in her looping handwriting, was one instruction: "Draw your orthogonals first." She was outside now helping Avianna stretch a canvas, so there was nobody to ask.

"Orthogonals," Mylo read over his shoulder. "What are those, the lines?"

Jonathan studied the handout. The dot was labeled the vanishing point, and every line that touched it was some edge that ran away from the viewer: the two sides of the road, the curbs along it, the tops of the roofs on either side. Lines that went across the page, like the fronts of the buildings, never touched the dot at all. That was the pattern. He tested it by laying his ruler from the dot to the edge of his paper, then to another edge, then to a spot where a roofline would sit. They all angled back toward that one point like roads merging. "The lines that run back toward the vanishing point," he said slowly, "road edges, curbs, rooflines. Those are the orthogonals." He said the word out loud just to hear how it fit.

He started over on fresh paper, sketching the dot first, then sweeping his ruler four times to set the road edges and curbs, then adding the rooflines so they ran to the same point. The road immediately stopped being a wall and became a road, sliding away from him. Avianna came in with wet canvas on her arm and stopped mid-step.

"Oh," she said. "That one goes somewhere."

"It's an illusion," Jonathan said, grinning. "The paper's flat. My eyes don't think so, though."

Mylo sat down beside him with his own paper, which was sparse compared to Jonathan's, almost empty except for one careful dot. "Lend me your ruler," he said. "I want mine to go somewhere too."

Jonathan slid the ruler across the table, and Mylo's pencil whispered its first line toward the vanishing point.

Paisley spread the ballots across the ping-pong table in the games room at the community centre. There were thirty-three of them, one for each student who had voted yesterday in the mock election Mr. Walker had organized. The Green Team had won seventeen seats out of thirty-three on the classroom map, even though most of the ballots did not say Green.

"That's not fair," said Clarke, dropping into the chair across from her. "Green got almost every riding."

"Ridings are the whole problem," Paisley said. She sorted the ballots into piles by colour. Green had eleven. Blue had nine. Orange had eight. Purple had five. "Eleven out of thirty-three is a third of the vote. But look at the seat chart." She slid Mr. Walker's hand-drawn map across the table. Green had taken seventeen of the thirty-three ridings because its voters were spread out, just enough of them in each one to win it.

Ruben arrived with a laptop and set it down beside the ballots. "Mr. Walker said to look up a real one," he said. "Canada, 2015, federal election." He opened the results page and turned the screen toward them. Paisley leaned in and found the numbers. The Liberal Party had won 184 of 338 seats, a majority, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote.

"Thirty-nine and a half percent," she said slowly, "and they got more than half the seats. More than half." She wrote the two numbers side by side on the whiteboard by the vending machines. "So the same thing happened for real. A third of our voters gave Green more than half our seats, and under forty percent gave the Liberals a majority."

"That's the conventional way we vote, I guess," said Clarke. "Most places do it like that."

"So it's normal," said Ruben.

"Normal isn't the same as fair." Paisley did not want to resent the Green Team, exactly, since nobody had cheated, but she felt something sour sitting in her chest anyway, and she decided to test it. "Ruben, if we counted proportionally, what would Green actually get?"

Ruben divided on the laptop. "Eleven out of thirty-three votes is about a third, so eleven seats."

Paisley rewrote the seat chart on the whiteboard. Green dropped from seventeen to eleven, Blue rose from seven to nine, Orange from six to eight, and Purple from three to five. Nobody had a majority anymore. "Under the first way, Green runs everything on a third of the votes," she said. "Under the second way, they'd have to make a deal with someone."

"That's proportional representation," Ruben said, reading the heading on Mr. Walker's worksheet. "It's right there on the page."

Paisley stood back and looked at the two charts. "My inference is that the seat map hides the real votes," she said. "You can't see the piles just by looking at who won each riding. That's why it felt wrong before I counted."

Mr. Walker came in carrying a box of juice boxes and stopped at the whiteboard. "You found the 2015 numbers?"

"Liberals, 184 out of 338 seats, with about 39.5 percent of the votes," Paisley said. "A majority."

"Hm," said Mr. Walker, and set down the box. "So which system do you three want to argue for on Friday?"

Paisley capped her marker and pointed at the second chart. "This one. And I can prove it with thirty-three ballots."

The first thing Sarah learned about hosting a dinner party was that thirteen-year-old boys eat like seagulls. Her cousin had devoured four rolls before anyone else had finished buttering one, and now he was turning his attention to Inaaya, who had just admitted, very quietly, that she couldn't swim.

"Everyone can swim," her cousin said, mouth half full. "Even my dog can swim. What do you do at the pool, just stand there?"

Sarah's stomach did a small, turbulent flip. Across the table, Larissa caught her eye with a look that said, do something. Sarah put down her fork.

"Stop it," she said. "That's rude."

"Oh, I'm rude?" Her cousin straightened up like a lawyer who had just been handed a winning case. "I'm just asking a question. It's a free country." He turned back to Inaaya. "So do you wear floaties? Do you have little arm floaties?"

Inaaya stared hard at her plate. The plan had backfired. Sarah had challenged him head-on, and now he was twice as loud, because arguing had turned a small tease into a performance with an audience.

Mr. Li, their neighbor, had come over with a lemon cake, and Sarah suddenly remembered it sitting on the counter behind her. She had exactly one piece of information that her cousin wanted more than anything in the world. She took a breath and stood up.

"Grandma's cutting the cake," she announced, loud enough to reach every chair at the table. "The lemon one. Whoever gets the end piece gets the extra frosting."

Her cousin's head whipped around so fast his napkin slid off his lap. "The end piece? That's mine. I called it in the car."

"Nope," said Larissa, catching on instantly. "I called it first. I texted Sarah at four o'clock."

"You did not. That's not a real call!" Her cousin was already half out of his seat, and the swimming topic had gone completely out of his head, like a balloon let go outdoors. Inaaya looked up, and then, to Sarah's surprise, she laughed.

"He fell for the frosting," Inaaya said. "Like a cartoon villain."
