"That's just joking," Alexis told herself, remembering a poster from last year about bullying that she'd barely read. But something nagged at her. She tried to recall the exact words: hurtful behavior that is repeated, and involving an imbalance of power, unlike a one-time argument between equals. This was repeated, sure, every day at the playground after school. And the imbalance part, Marcus was bigger, older, and always had an audience, while Eunice stood alone. A one-time argument between equals was different, like when she and Jasmin had screamed at each other over a borrowed hoodie last spring and made up by Friday. This wasn't that. The contradiction between what Marcus called joking and what kept actually happening bothered her all through dinner.

The next day, Alexis devised a test. If it was real joking, Eunice could joke back and everyone would laugh, including Marcus. That was the rule with her friend Jasmin, who called Alexis "drip tray" for the smoothie she'd spilled in sixth grade, and Alexis called her "flagpole," and it evened out because they each had one. So at the playground, Alexis wandered over and said loudly, "Eunice, you should hide his backpack next time. Fair trade." Marcus's smile went flat. He didn't laugh. He said, "Watch it," and suddenly Eunice's backpack was back in her hands and Marcus was shooting hoops alone.

"Interesting," Alexis murmured. A real joker could take a joke. He couldn't, which meant he wasn't one.

Eunice walked over to the swings and sat down without saying anything for a minute. Then she said, "You didn't have to do that. Now he might come after you."

"Then we'll both be worth coming after," Alexis said. "Also I'm extremely competent at holding my own backpack, so you'll have backup." Eunice snorted, which turned into a real laugh this time, the slow kind. Jasmin jogged over from the monkey bars and asked what was so funny, and Alexis just pointed at Marcus, missing his shot for the third time in a row.

"There's a word for him," Eunice said quietly. "Bullying."

"Repeated," Alexis said, "with a power imbalance. Not just a one-time argument between equals. I checked."

Jasmin squinted at the court. "So what do we do about it?"

"We tell someone tomorrow, together," Alexis said. "But today..." She hopped off the swing, picked up Eunice's backpack, and held it out like a trophy. "Today, Eunice holds it herself and nobody takes it."

Eunice grabbed the strap and slung it over one shoulder, chin up, and the three of them walked past the basketball court toward the water fountain.

Ray slid a newspaper across the library table with one finger, like it might bite him. "Third page. Swimmer bitten off Cape Cod. Right before our trip." He was supposed to come with Lauren's family to the coast on Saturday, and now he said he wasn't going in the water, maybe not going at all.

"You're being reckless in the other direction," Lauren said. "Staying home because of one story?" Mr. Ahmadi, shelving returns two aisles over, gave them the look he gave kids who got loud, so she lowered her voice. She went to the front desk and asked him how to retrieve old newspaper articles on the computer, and he showed her the search screen, then wandered off to help a toddler who was trying to climb the picture-book shelves.

Lauren typed in shark attack and counted. Then she typed in dog bite. Then bee sting. The screen filled up faster than she'd guessed, column after column. She tapped the glass. "Ray. Come look. If examples of shark attacks jump into your head easy, but bee stings barely do, you'll think sharks are the big danger, even when they're not. That's why the story scared you. It's easy to remember."

"Fine," Ray said, but he didn't move. Lauren kept digging and found a magazine article from years back, yellow-edged in the bound stacks. She read out loud, "Two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, described this in 1973." She squinted at the page. "It has a name. The availability heuristic. People judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind."

"That's exactly what happened to me," Ray said. He finally came over and read the article himself, chewing the strap of his backpack. After a while he said, "Okay. I'll swim. But not at dawn, and not near seals, and that's not a negotiation, that's an amendment to the deal."

"It's not a deal, it's a beach," Lauren said, but she was already writing her source list for Monday's current events class. That was the cost of the whole afternoon; her original plan had been to finish her essay, and now the essay was untouched and the library was closing in twenty minutes. She printed one page and paid ten cents for it at the desk, and Mr. Ahmadi slid her change across the counter along with a bookmark she hadn't asked for.

Saturday morning the ocean was gray and flat, and Ray stood at the edge of the surf for a long time with his arms crossed, reading the water like it was a page he didn't trust. Then a wave caught his ankles and he yelped and grabbed Lauren's arm, laughing, and waded in up to his knees.

"First one in," he called over his shoulder, already deeper than her.

At dinner on Tuesday, Sarah pushed her peas around her plate and finally said it out loud. "The club meeting was a disaster. We spent forty minutes arguing about snacks and never got to anything else." Her father paused with his fork halfway to his mouth. "Nobody wrote down what you were going to discuss?" Sarah blinked. That was exactly it. Zariah had wanted to talk about the river cleanup, Anouk had a plan to donate old textbooks to the library, and neither of them had said more than two sentences before the snack debate swallowed the whole room.

"Mr. Huang told me once that you write the topics down before the meeting," her mother said, ladling more soup into Sarah's bowl without being asked, because she knew Sarah forgot to eat when her mind was racing. "A list, in the order you'll take them up." Sarah nodded slowly, but something still bothered her. At the last meeting she had tried to keep order, and it hadn't worked. Why would a list change anything? She couldn't see how a piece of paper could stop six people from talking over each other. Maybe the problem wasn't the paper. Maybe the problem was that nobody, including her, knew whose turn it was next, and a list would give every topic a visible place in line.

The next day she hunted through the dictionary in the library, mostly because Zariah had laughed and called the list "a boring old word, agenda," and Sarah wanted to catch her friend being wrong for once. She found the entry and grinned. At dinner that night she announced it to her parents. "Agenda. It's a Latin word meaning things to be done." Her father laughed into his water glass. "So when Zariah says your agenda is boring, she's literally calling things that must be done boring."

She made a test of it, because an idea you haven't tested is just a wish. At Thursday's meeting she wrote three items on the whiteboard before anyone sat down: snacks, textbooks, river cleanup, in that order, snacks last. She gave each item ten minutes by the clock on the wall. When Anouk started drifting onto the subject of the bake sale, Sarah tapped the board and said, "That's not on the agenda," and Anouk sat back down, looking almost relieved. Zariah got a full five minutes on the cleanup, and two people volunteered to donate gloves and trash bags before the snack discussion even began.

The twist came at the end. When Sarah reached item three, snacks, the room went quiet, and Anouk raised her hand. "Actually, can we skip it? The meeting ran so well I don't want to wreck it with forty minutes of arguing about chips." Everyone laughed, and they voted to end early. Walking home under the streetlights, Sarah felt the brittle evening cold on her face and thought briefly about her conscience, which had pricked her at the start when she'd wondered if controlling the meeting made her bossy. Zariah bumped her shoulder. "Same agenda next month?" she asked. "Same agenda," Sarah said, and held up her crumpled list like a trophy.

The first time Audrey ran the eight hundred metres, she sprinted the whole first lap because it felt amazing to be ahead, and then the second lap swallowed her whole. Her legs turned to cement somewhere around the final bend, and Samantha passed her, and then two girls from the other school passed her, and she crossed the line in a blur of embarrassment. She walked to the fence afterward and promised herself she would figure out how the race actually worked.

That night she watched the record race from the 2012 London Olympics on her laptop, pausing it with her finger hovering over the space bar. David Rudisha ran the men's eight-hundred-metre world record that day, and she timed his laps with her phone. "His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second," she said out loud to the empty kitchen, and she rewound and timed it again to be sure. The fastest eight-hundred-metre runner ever did not run even laps. He banked speed early, then fought to keep what was left. That felt like a hidden rule, something you could not see from the stands, and she wanted to test it on her own legs.

At the track the next afternoon, Malory was already stretching by the first lane, bouncing on her toes. "Coach says the relay spots get decided Friday," Malory said. "I want the anchor leg so bad I can taste it. Are you doing pacing work? Can I run with you?" Audrey had come to negotiate an arrangement: Malory would call out lap splits from the sideline while Audrey ran, and in exchange Audrey would help her practise baton exchanges until dark.

The first test was ugly. Audrey went out hard, hit the two-hundred mark flying, and died exactly where she had died before. "That's not it," she panted, hands on her knees. She thought about Rudisha again, about the difference between fast and reckless, and adjusted. On the next attempt she aimed for a first lap only slightly quicker than what she believed she could hold, treating the gap like a metal alloy, a blend rather than two separate metals bolted together. The first lap had to melt into the second.

The third run felt different from the inside. She rounded the bend with something still in the tank, and instead of the usual wall she found a manageable ache, and she drove through the finish line with her arms pumping. Malory jogged over waving her phone. "You negative split less, but you held on. You were three seconds faster overall."

"And you're going to be anchor," Audrey said, picking up the baton from the grass. "Come on. Hand me the stick, hit my hand, don't look back."

The sun hung low and tropical over the far bleachers as they ran the exchange again and again, two quick slaps of hand on palm echoing down the straightaway.

"Read the first paragraph again," Mr. Lau said, tapping the page. "All the way back to the top."

Matteo flipped the pages of his copy of The Lottery and found the opening, the one they had skimmed two days ago. Sunny morning, flowers blooming, and the kids of the village running around while school let out for the summer. He had barely noticed it the first time. Now the ending sat in his head like a stone in his shoe.

Hawa leaned over from the next desk. "You look like the story bit you."

"It kind of did." Matteo read the paragraph again, slower this time. "Bobby Martin had a pocket full of stones, and the other boys soon had their stones." He looked up. "They were piling up stones. Right there. In paragraph one."

Elsa spun her pencil. "So? Kids collect rocks. I had a rock monopoly on my street when I was nine. Nobody touched the good ones without trading."

"Sure," Matteo said, "but this story was published in The New Yorker in 1948. Shirley Jackson put those stones there on purpose." He tapped the page twice. "It's like the author left the ending on the first page and nobody told us."

"That's foreshadowing," Hawa said. "I think."

"It is," said Mr. Lau, walking past, and kept walking, because Mr. Lau was stubborn about making them do the work themselves.

Matteo tried an experiment out loud. "If you took out the stones, paragraph one would be pure sunshine. Flowers, green grass, summer. Extravagant niceness. With the stones in it, it still sounds calm, but something's off, like a smile that's too big."

Elsa frowned at her page. "So the calm is fake?"

"Not fake," Matteo said. "The town really is calm. That's the creepy part. They pile up stones like it's a game, and at the end the stones aren't a game at all." He underlined the line in pencil. "It's a clue that only works backwards. You can't see it until you've finished."

"That's cheating," Hawa said. "Authors should warn us."

"They kind of did," Elsa said, grinning. "You just read the warning as a weather report."

Matteo wrote "stones = ending, p. 1" in his notebook, then added a question mark after it, because he wanted to ask Mr. Lau whether every object in the story was a clue or just the stones. The black box. The stool. The slips of paper. He raised his hand.

"Mr. Lau, is the black box a clue too, or do I have to sustain this level of paranoia for the rest of the year?"

Mr. Lau smiled and picked up a piece of chalk.

Natalie spread the crumpled taxi receipt on the library table and smoothed it flat with her palm. "Fifteen dollars," she said. "Grandma swore the ride was only four kilometres, but the driver charged her for six. She wants to prove it before she calls the company."

Noelle leaned over the receipt. "So prove it. That's what the quiz is about tomorrow, isn't it? Mr. Nwosu's going to make us turn words into equations."

Reem pulled her chair closer and tapped the receipt with her pencil. "It says three dollars base fare plus two dollars per kilometre. I used to ride that taxi with my uncle all the time." She wrote 3 + 2k on the corner of Natalie's notebook. "The k stands for the kilometres, the thing we don't know."

Natalie stared at the letters. Under them she wrote 15, the total on the receipt, and then she sat back. "It's like a sealed box," she said slowly. "The k is hidden inside. I can't see it, but whatever I do to one side, I have to do to the other, or the balance breaks." She tried it out loud, testing the idea the way Mr. Nwosu kept telling them to. "If I take three away from the left side, I take three away from the right side too." She wrote 2k = 12 underneath.

"That's the whole algorithm," Noelle said, copying the steps into her own notebook. "Undo one thing at a time, same operation on both sides, until only the k is left."

"Then divide both sides by two," Reem said. Natalie did it, and k = 6 sat at the bottom of the page in her careful handwriting. Six kilometres. Not four, not five, but six, exactly what the driver had charged for. Somewhere in the middle of the ride they must have looped past the market, which would add the extra distance. Natalie checked it by running the equation forward: three plus two times six, which came to fifteen, which matched the receipt exactly. "Grandma was wrong," she said, almost laughing. "She's going to argue anyway."

Mr. Nwosu stopped by their table on his way to the reference shelf and glanced at the notebook. "Taxi problem?" he asked. Natalie nodded and slid the page toward him. He read it, nodded once, and said, "Good. You balanced it." He moved on without another word, and Natalie felt the warmth of that single nod spread through her whole chest.

She copied the work onto a fresh sheet for her grandmother, numbering each step so it would look official, and folded it into her backpack next to the receipt. "Six kilometres," she said again, zipping the bag shut. "She can call the company now, but they're going to tell her the same thing."

Norah had spent her entire Saturday morning refilling the bulk bins at Mr. Kang's grocery store, and her pay for the day was fifty-two dollars. She slid the envelope into her backpack and biked home thinking about the jar on her dresser, the one marked NEW PHONE, into which she had already stuffed one hundred and thirty dollars.

In the kitchen, her mother was looking at a bank flyer. "They called it compound interest," her mother said. "You put money in, and it grows." Norah frowned, because her math class had just plotted two savings accounts on graph paper, and the two lines had not grown the same way at all. In Mr. Wheeler's assignment, one line rose steadily, step after step, exactly the same amount every year, while the other started close behind and then bent, climbing a little more each year than the year before, until by year five it had pulled far ahead. The steady one was simple interest. The bending one was compound.

"Can I see that?" she asked, and took the flyer to her room.

The phone she wanted cost four hundred dollars. She had one hundred and thirty, and if she added fifty dollars every month from her job, the jar would get there in about five and a half months. That was the simple way, and it felt inevitable that she would just do that. But the graph from class provoked a question she could not leave alone: if she put the money in a compound account instead, would the curve do some of the work for her?

There was a problem, though. The class graphs had covered five years, and her phone was a five-month goal. She could not see five years from here, and that was her real dilemma. So she did what Mr. Wheeler had taught them: she tested a smaller version. She took out a fresh sheet of graph paper, drew axes, and plotted her own two lines, one rising straight, one bending upward, gaining more each interval than the one before. Then she wrote five years across the bottom and stared at the gap between the lines at the end.

On Monday she found Loic stacking chairs after school. "You know how our graphs curved?" she said. "The compound one pulls away more and more the longer you leave it. So the money I'd earn in five months is tiny. But if I leave it for five years, it's a lot." Loic tilted his head. "So you're not buying the phone?" Norah laughed. "I'm buying the phone. But after that, every paycheck goes in the account, and I don't touch it. I want to be standing where the curve is."

That afternoon she rode back to Mr. Kang's store and asked if she could work Thursdays too. He checked the schedule taped behind the register, then nodded and handed her an apron. "Bins first," he said, and pointed at the oatmeal.

Julia stood on Khadija's porch holding a box of dates in her left hand, because her right hand was busy ringing the doorbell. When Khadija's grandmother opened the door, Julia passed the box over with her left hand without thinking. The grandmother took it, but Julia noticed something odd: the woman reached across herself with her right hand to receive it, and her smile went thin for just a second before warming up again.

"Come in, come in," the grandmother said, and Julia followed Khadija down the hallway, past framed photographs and the smell of coconut and lemongrass from the kitchen. Julia kept replaying that small moment on the porch. She remembered, suddenly, a flashback from school last autumn: a new student from Indonesia had handed Mr. Brown a permission slip, and Mr. Brown had joked, "Right hand, right on," and the boy had laughed and said, "In Indonesia and Malaysia, we use the right hand for eating and for giving and receiving things." Julia had assumed he was only talking about himself. Now, watching Khadija's family, she wondered if the rule ran through the whole household, invisible like a current under still water.

At dinner, the table crowded with dishes, Julia tested her idea. She kept her eyes low and her hands still, and she watched. Khadija tore flatbread with her right hand. Her father spooned curry with his right. Her little brother reached for the water pitcher with his left, and Khadija's mother caught his wrist and steered it across to the right, saying nothing, as if correcting a wobble in a beginner cyclist. Nobody said the rule out loud. It was just there, the way the rule at Julia's own house was that you took off your shoes at the door and that elbows never touched the table, rules her friends always got wrong the first time.

When the bowl of rice came around, Julia passed it with her right hand, careful and deliberate. The grandmother looked at her, really looked, and nodded once. "You noticed," she said. Julia felt her ears go hot. Khadija leaned over and whispered, "It's a sign of respect. Grandma will talk about you for a week now."

Later, when the plates were cleared, Khadija's father mentioned that they were hoping to buy the house next door, if the mortgage on it wasn't too heavy, and that the neighbors' moving sale seemed imminent. Khadija pulled Julia out to the porch to look at the fireflies. "You know, when I went to your house, I gave your mom my gift with my right hand and she took it with her left," Khadija said. "Did I insult her?"

Julia thought about her mother, who waved hello with whichever hand was free. "I don't think she even noticed," she said.

Khadija frowned at the fireflies. "So it matters here and not there," she said. "How do you know which place you're in?"

Julia watched a light blink on and off above the hedge. "Maybe you just watch, like I did tonight," she said. "Or maybe you get it wrong first."

"Getting it wrong sounds terrible," said Khadija.

Julia laughed. "It's only a hand."

The automatic doors of the pharmacy sighed open, and Adam walked in with his hands still shaking a little. He had not slept at all last night. The science project was due this morning, and he had stayed up until sunrise gluing labels onto his model of the water cycle, and then the alarm had gone off before his eyes ever closed. On the bus, Kenneth had flicked Adam's ear as a joke, and Adam had grabbed Kenneth's wrist so hard that Nicholas had to say, "Whoa, calm down." Adam was here now to buy plasters for the cut on his thumb, which he had gotten from the project's wire frame, and he could not stop replaying the bus.

Mr. Papadopoulos was behind the counter, sorting boxes. "Late night?" he asked, glancing at Adam's face.

"How could you tell?"

"You have the look of every parent who comes in after a newborn." He slid the plasters across the counter. "Rough day too?"

Adam paid for them, then noticed a magazine rack by the window. One cover said YOUR BRAIN ON NO SLEEP in yellow letters. He picked it up while Mr. Papadopoulos helped the next customer, a woman with a cough. Inside, he found a short article. He read one line twice: In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala, a brain area that responds to threats. He whispered the strange word to himself. "Amygdala."

"Did you say something?" Mr. Papadopoulos asked.

"There's this part of the brain, the amygdala. It responds to threats. And in the study, people kept awake for a whole night reacted about 60 percent stronger to upsetting pictures." Adam looked up. "So Kenneth's joke this morning, maybe my brain thought it was a real threat. Because I'm exhausted."

Mr. Papadopoulos shrugged. "I sell plasters, not brains. But you look like you just solved a mystery."

It did feel like solving something, the way finding a hidden wire explains why a model tilts. The ear flick had been temporary, tiny, and his reaction had been huge. Maybe his brain's whole alarm network had been turned up loud by the sleepless night. Adam wondered: could he test this? He decided on a small experiment. Tonight he would do the opposite of last night, same bedtime three nights in a row, phone in the kitchen, and he would see whether small jokes felt small again.

Before leaving, he tried one more thing. He stood by the rack, put a hand on his stomach, and breathed in slowly through his nose for four counts, out for six, the way the magazine suggested. His shoulders dropped half an inch. The shaking in his hands did not vanish, but it did diminish, going quiet like a radio turned down.

At school the next morning, Kenneth flicked Adam's ear again. Adam turned, grinned, and flicked him right back.

Nicolas stood in the wings of the community theatre, holding a slip of paper that read "beach trip" and wishing he had never signed up for the improv workshop. The empty stage intimidated him more than any audience ever had, because on stage you couldn't hide behind a script. Ms. De Vries clapped her hands and explained the rule: whatever your partner says, you accept it and add to it. "Yes, and," she said. "That's the whole game."

His first scene, with Adnan, fell apart in thirty seconds. "We're at the beach," Nicolas offered, and Adnan said, "Yes, and we brought some stuff." They passed an invisible box back and forth, calling it "things" and "supplies," until neither of them knew what to do next. The audience of other kids giggled in the embarrassed way that means they were glad it wasn't them. Renee, sitting in the front row, wasn't giggling. She wanted the funniest scene of the afternoon, because the two funniest people got to perform at the spring showcase, and she already had a bit about a seagull she was saving for it.

Backstage, Nicolas turned the failed scene over in his mind. Adnan had said "some stuff," and the scene had died. In the scene before theirs, a girl had said "Grandma's red bicycle," and suddenly her partner was ringing the bell and yelling about the busted brake. It wasn't talent, he decided. It was the words themselves. Vague words gave you nothing, but specific words, like "Grandma's red bicycle" instead of "a bike," gave your partner something real to grab. He tested the idea quietly, mouthing beach words until he found a sharp one.

"Renee, go with me this time," he whispered, and she shrugged like it cost her something, seagull bit and all. On stage, Nicolas began immediately. "Yes, and the estuary we're wading in is full of crabs," he said, "and one of them has my grandmother's wedding ring in its claw." Renee's eyes lit up. "Yes, and the crab speaks French," she said, "and he'll trade the ring for a croissant." Nicolas dug in his pocket and produced an imaginary croissant so warm he described the butter dripping. The kids in the audience were laughing for real now, leaning forward, and Adnan shouted from the front row that he wanted to be the crab's lawyer.

Ms. De Vries watched with her arms folded and a small smile, and when the scene ended she said, "Nicolas, that was eloquent for a guy wrestling a crustacean." Renee grabbed his sleeve. "Showcase," she said. "You and me. Crabs and everything."

Nicolas bowed, and the paper slip reading "beach trip" drifted out of his pocket and landed on the stage boards like a dropped ticket.

The gymnasium smelled like hot glue and floor wax, and the air was so humid that Easton's display board curled slightly at the corners. He smoothed it flat and taped it down again, then stood back and stared at the word he had lettered across the top in blue marker: HYPOTHESIS. His project asked which brand of battery kept an LED burning longest, and his guess had been that the expensive brand would win. It had not. The cheap battery was still glowing on his table after nineteen hours, and the fancy one had died at midnight.

Kiaan leaned over from the next table, where his volcano oozed baking-soda foam onto a tray. "You look like your dog died."

"My hypothesis was wrong," Easton said. He said the word slowly, like a stone in his mouth. Last month he had nearly skipped writing one at all. Mr. Gagnon had circled the empty spot on his rough draft and written one word back: why? Easton had stayed up late that night making something up, just to fill the box, and he had envied Kiaan, whose volcano needed no guessing at all. Now the guess he had invented to please a teacher was the thing being proven wrong in public, under fluorescent lights, with judges walking the aisles.

Amina wandered over with her clipboard, judging sheet and all, because she had signed up as a student marshal for the extra credit. "What does that word even mean? Hypothesis?"

Easton opened his notebook to the page where he had looked it up for the board. "It comes from ancient Greek," he said. "It literally means putting or placing under."

Amina frowned. "Placing under? Under what?"

"That's what I asked. I thought I'd copied it wrong." He turned the notebook so she could see the printed page. "A hypothesis is something you place under your experiment. Like a foundation. You build the test on top of it." He had read that three times in his kitchen, the window open, a train horn far off, before it finally clicked.

"So yours was placed under and then crushed," Kiaan said, grinning.

"Basically." Easton looked at the little LED, still burning, stubborn and orange. Here was the part he kept turning over: if he had never written the guess, he would have run the same test and gotten the same result. But he would not have felt the result land anywhere. The wrongness needed something to be wrong about. He wasn't sure yet whether that made the guessing worth it or just painful, and he didn't try to settle it while the judges were circling.

Mr. Gagnon stopped at his table and read the whole board, top to bottom, including the part where Easton had written in red marker: My hypothesis was overturned. The cheap battery lasted longer. Then he tapped the still-glowing LED with one finger, like ringing a tiny doorbell.

"That one," Easton said, "still hasn't quit."

The park benches were sticky with humid air, and Michael kept wiping his palms on his jeans while he waited by the fountain. His first actual date. Leah was meeting him here in ten minutes, and the plan was simple: walk through the park, then catch a movie at the theater on the far side. The problem was which movie.

Jaiveer had come along to keep him company until Leah arrived, and now he was being Jaiveer about it. "You can't just say 'let's see a movie,'" he said, elaborating with his hands the way he did when he thought something was obvious. "You have to already know what you're both allowed to see. That's consumer research. My sister calls it that."

Michael frowned at the fountain. He had never wondered about movie ratings before. They had just always been there, stamped on posters and trailers like weather. But now it mattered, because half the movies playing were rated one thing and half another, and he only had a ten-dollar bill and one shot at this. Was there even a rule? PG meant kids could go, R meant they couldn't, but what about everything squeezed in between? He tried to remember anything his dad had said and came up with nothing.

"Wait," he said slowly. "There's a middle one. I've seen the tag on trailers. Between PG and R."

"You mean PG-13?"

Michael pulled out his phone and searched for it, scrolling fast, because Leah's bus stopped at the corner in five minutes and a plan without a movie was no plan at all. He read the result twice. "It says here the PG-13 movie rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984. A whole separate rating, added right between PG and R." He looked up. "That's why it exists. Somebody put it there."

"So you're saying there's a whole rating that exists just for movies like this one?" Jaiveer squinted at the theater marquee across the park, where the titles gleamed in the haze. "Then that's your answer. If the movie's PG-13, you're fine."

Michael tested the idea against the marquee, matching letters to ratings, until he found one that worked for both of them and started at the right time. He had just worked it out when he heard the bus hiss to a stop behind him.

He turned around, and Leah was already waving.

Landon's grandfather had turned the sunroom into a stage of sorts: two folding chairs, a lamp on a crate, and a notebook full of writing prompts. Landon and Alistair had come to practise before Monday's drama camp audition, because the director was going to pair them up and make them improvise a scene with no script at all.

"We're a spaceship crew," Alistair said, launching in. "The engine's broken."

Landon crossed his arms. "No we're not. We're knights."

Alistair tried again. "Fine, knights. Our castle is under siege."

"No, it isn't."

The scene collapsed. Alistair sat down on one of the folding chairs and spun the notebook toward Landon. "We're doing it wrong. The good campers do something and I can't tell what it is. I've been trying to infer it from watching the older kids, but every scene I watch, all I notice is they never argue."

Landon flipped through the notebook. His grandfather had written notes from an acting class he took in 1974, back when the neighbourhood was affluent enough to have its own little theatre. One line was circled twice: "Yes, and." Landon read it, then read the scribble beside it. "It's called 'yes, and,'" he said slowly. "You say yes to whatever your partner set up, then you add something."

"Add something how?"

"Like this." Landon stood and gestured at the lamp. "Alistair, this lighthouse is ours, and the bulb just died."

Alistair's shoulders came up. "Yes, and there's a ship coming toward the rocks right now."

"Yes, and I think the keeper's old flare gun still works."

"Yes, and it's in the flooded cellar." Alistair grabbed an umbrella from the coat rack and held it like a torch. He waded across an imaginary cellar, and Landon could hear him breathing harder, the way he only did when a game was working. They built the scene for ten straight minutes: the flare, the ship, a sailor with a broken arm carried up the stairs.

When they finally stopped, Landon understood what he'd been missing before. Saying no had been a signal to Alistair that his ideas were worthless, so Alistair stopped offering any, and the scene starved. Every "yes, and" handed his friend a new brick, and his friend kept building.

They ran it three more times, trading who started. On the last round Alistair opened with, "We're two guys in a sunroom, and the audition is in two days." Landon picked up the flare gun umbrella and aimed it at the window. "Yes, and we're going to be ready."

Aurora had a green notebook full of French phrases, and by Saturday morning she had crossed out three of them. "Un croissant, s'il vous plaît" had worked fine at the bakery on Rue Vernet in her imagination, but asking for the bill had gone wrong twice. She'd written "La note, s'il vous plaît" first, because "la note" sounded like a bill to her, and then "La facture," which her dictionary said meant an invoice. Neither felt like something a waiter would actually say, and the restaurant test was Monday night at Chez Margot, where Ms. Kaminski had booked a table for the whole class.

Martin flopped onto her kitchen floor with his own notebook. "I've got the food part down," he said. "Croque-monsieur, salade, une limonade. It's the money part that scares me. What if I just hold out my wallet and point?"

"Then you'd survive," Aurora said, "but you'd look like a tourist." She flipped her laptop toward him and opened a video of a French family finishing dinner in a real bistro. She'd decided to test an idea: if "la note" and "la facture" were wrong, some other word had to be right, and it ought to show up in real restaurant scenes. She watched the waiter's hands, not his mouth, then played the clip again with the sound magnified.

That was when she caught it. The waiter set down the small tray, and the man at the table said something quick and polite. Aurora backed the video up, listened three times, and wrote it down carefully: "L'addition, s'il vous plaît." She found two more videos, and in both of them, there it was again, the same phrase, every single time. Not "la note." Not "la facture." "L'addition." She underlined it twice, and Martin leaned over her shoulder to copy it, muttering it under his breath like a spell.

Lina arrived at Monday's dinner rehearsal still shaking her head. "I practiced 'la note' all weekend," she said, "because my cousin in Montreal told me that's what she says." But when the waiter came, Lina went first anyway, took a breath, and said, "L'addition, s'il vous plaît." The waiter smiled and brought the tray without a single confused blink, and Lina turned back to the table with her arms up like she'd scored a goal.

Aurora ordered last, all the way through: "Un croque-monsieur et une limonade, s'il vous plaît." When the plates were cleared she looked straight at the waiter and said the phrase she'd dug out of all those videos. He nodded, and a moment later the little tray appeared in front of her with the paper bill folded on top. Ms. Kaminski, watching from the end of the table, raised her water glass. "Well," she said. "The verdict is in, and I think you all just paid for your own dinners. In French."

Martin slipped his copy of the phrase into his shirt pocket for next time. "Chez Margot," he said, "won't know what hit them."

Jack stood at the white line of the running track with a race number safety-pinned to his shirt and a problem he could not stop turning over. In three weeks he had to run eight hundred metres in under three minutes to make the county team, but every time he tried, the first lap felt wonderful and the second lap felt like wading through wet sand. Ms. Malik had watched him last Tuesday and said nothing except, "Think about where your legs go before they go there." Jack had a suspicion the trouble was invisible, hiding somewhere between his stopwatch and his enthusiasm.

He flipped his race number over on the bus and worked it out with a pencil stub borrowed from Emil. Eight hundred metres was two laps of the four-hundred-metre track. Three minutes was one hundred eighty seconds. He wrote it small, then smaller, and the answer arrived on the paper like something that had been waiting: to finish eight hundred metres in three minutes, he had to average ninety seconds for each lap. Not one number, but the same number twice. Emil leaned over his shoulder and read it aloud, then checked it with his fingers, counting the seconds in tens.

The next morning King held the stopwatch at the line. "Ninety seconds, then ninety more," Jack said. "If I come through the first lap fast, slow me down. Yell if you have to." King nodded and clicked the watch. Jack went out, and the hard part was that the first lap felt terrible on purpose, like holding a horse back at a gate. He wanted to fly. Instead he complied with the number on the paper, watching King's raised hand at the two-hundred-metre mark, where a small crowd of walkers had gathered by the fence.

He crossed the line for lap one at ninety-one seconds. King shouted it, and Jack felt a strange calm settle over him, because now the second lap was a race he could actually win. He pushed hard up the back straight, and on the final bend he found something left, a vigorous burst that carried him past the imaginary runner he was always chasing. King clicked the watch. Two minutes, fifty-two seconds. Eight seconds to spare. Jack lay on the infield grass, laughing at the clouds.

Emil jogged over holding the race number. "There's a problem," he said slowly. "You pinned this on upside down this morning. Look at the back." Jack took it. Under his pencil marks, in printed ink he had never noticed, was a small chart of suggested splits, and next to it a line saying the target pace for his age group had been changed this season to three minutes and two seconds, not three minutes flat. His pencil math had been aimed at a time nobody had asked him for.

Jack sat up and looked down the track, empty now except for the walkers drifting away. Three weeks until the race, and two different numbers in his head. He turned the paper over and over, then folded it into his pocket and stood. "Same time tomorrow," he said. "Bring the stopwatch."

Anais had been on the Miller's Creek trail exactly four times in her life, and today she was pretending it was practice for the wilderness. "Two miles," she announced to Tenley, who was hiking beside her with a granola bar already half gone. "That's nothing. Camp Wanderhawk is a whole week of trails like this. Real ones, with bears."

"Bears," Kiaan repeated from behind them, delighted. "Probably just raccoons."

"Raccoons can thrive anywhere," Anais said. "Bears need real forest. That's the difference." She was carrying a daypack loaded with everything she'd packed and repacked three times last night: flashlight, water bottle, the laminated list her mom had printed, and one notebook where she planned to record every skill she learned before camp even started.

That was why she'd begged Mr. Kim to come along. He lived two houses down, and he hiked this trail every Saturday, and once, a long time ago, he had been a camp counselor himself. Today he had promised them lunch at the creek and one demonstration.

At the gravel clearing by the water, he set down his pack and got out a small shovel, a bucket, and a single match. "Sit," he said. "You wanted lessons. Lesson one happens before any fire ever starts."

He built a fire no bigger than a dinner plate, and they roasted the last of the marshmallows Tenley had smuggled in. When the flames had died to grey coals, Mr. Kim kicked a little dirt over the pile and stood up. "There," he said. "Out. Let's pack up."

Kiaan reached for the bucket, but Anais stopped him. Something wasn't right. She crouched at the edge of the fire ring and stared at the ashes. The smoke had stopped, sure, but the wind kept shifting one thin feather of it back up, in a pattern, like the pile was still breathing underneath. Dirt on top could hide heat. That was the whole trick of it.

"It's not out," she said. "I think the middle's still hot under the dirt. We can't see it, so we have to test it another way."

Mr. Kim folded his arms, but he was smiling. "Go on, then."

Anais remembered a poster from the ranger station at the trailhead, the one with the bear in the ranger hat. She'd read it twice while waiting for Tenley to tie her shoe. "Drown, stir, drown again," she said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "Then feel for heat. If it's too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave." She grabbed the bucket, sloshed the whole thing over the coals, and stirred the black mess with the shovel until it looked like soup, then dumped her water bottle over it too.

"Now the touching part." She waved her palm slowly above the wet ash. Warm. She waited, waved again. Warm, but less. A third time, and her hand stayed still. Cool. "Cold," she reported. "Cold all the way through. Now it's actually out."

"And that," Mr. Kim said, "is the one rule they'll drill into you at Wanderhawk until your whole cabin can say it in one coherent sentence. Fire safety has a hierarchy, and feeling for heat is at the top of it."

Anais wrote it in her notebook in big letters, underlined twice, and drew a small bear in a hat beside it. She was going to be the kid in her cabin who already knew everything. She jogged to catch up with the others on the trail, notebook bouncing against her hip, already planning what she'd teach them first.

Alexis spread two boxes of cereal on the picnic table in his backyard: Sparkle O's, the name brand, and Round Marts, the store brand his mom bought to save money. His science fair project was due in nine days, and he had a question he actually wanted answered. Did people really taste a difference, or did they just taste the box?

Bodie arrived first, riding his bike over the gravel alley and skidding to a stop by the fence. Youcef came next, carrying a notebook and a pen he clicked constantly. "So we're the taste testers?" Bodie asked, already reaching for a box. Alexis pulled both boxes away and carried them inside. When he came back, he held a tray with four bowls, each labeled with a letter on masking tape: A, B, A, B. Youcef wrote the letters down.

"Wait," Bodie said. "Which one is the expensive one?" Alexis shook his head. "That's the whole point. If I tell you, you'll say the name brand tastes better because you think it should." He had read about it in his library book the night before, sitting at the kitchen table long after his mom had told him to sleep. The book called it a blind test, because the people tested don't know which sample is which, so their expectations can't sway their answers. That exact sentence had made him sit up straight. He explained it in one line: "It's a blind test. You don't know which bowl is which, so you can't be biased."

Bodie ate a spoonful from A, then B, then A again, frowning like the frown itself was data. "B is better. B tastes more like actual oats." Youcef tasted both and chose A. Alexis recorded every answer, plus three more from neighbors who wandered over when they smelled cereal in the backyard, and by evening he had eleven results. Nine of the eleven picked the store brand, or the name brand, or said they were identical, and when Alexis finally revealed which letters matched which boxes, even he was surprised. Bodie had chosen the cheap one. Bodie, who swore up and down that Sparkle O's were the only cereal worth eating.

"You tricked me," Bodie said, but he was grinning. Ms. Hamdan, the neighbor whose garden ran along the back fence, had been one of the eleven, and she called across the rows of tomato plants, "Would it be a privilege to see your results at the fair? I'd like to know if my own answers fooled me too." Alexis said it would, and he meant it.

That night he taped his data sheet to the garage wall, all eleven rows of letters and choices, and thought about how the answer had been hiding inside people the whole time, invisible until he covered the boxes. Nine days was still enough time to test soda, and maybe chocolate chips, and Bodie had already volunteered to comply with any future experiment involving snacks. Alexis pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward him and wrote at the top: Experiment Two.

Everly sat on the bench at the bus stop with her gym bag open in her lap, turning her white school shirt over in her hands. It wasn't white anymore. The collar and one whole sleeve had come out of the wash a pale, cloudy pink, like a sunset that had given up halfway. She held it up to the light from the streetlamp and frowned.

"That looks like a failure," said Emelia, dropping onto the bench beside her with her own bag. "What happened to it?"

"I washed it. That's all. My mom's away this week, so I did my own laundry for the first time." Everly dug through the gym bag and pulled out a single red sock, still damp, and laid it on the shirt. The pink patches lined up almost exactly with where the sock had been tangled in the sleeve. "I found this stuck inside the shirt when I pulled everything out."

Emelia leaned over. "So the sock did it? It's brand new, isn't it?"

"Got it Saturday." Everly turned the sock in her fingers, then rubbed a damp corner of it against her wrist. A faint smudge of red came off onto her skin. "It's still letting dye go. The sock must have bled dye into the wash water, and the shirt soaked it up." She stared at the sock, working it through. New clothes, dark or bright ones, gave up dye. That dye sat in the water. Anything white or pale in that same water drank it in. Which meant the sorting her mother always did, the piles on the basement floor, wasn't just fussiness. It was a rule with a reason behind it.

"So that's why my mom separates everything," she said slowly. "I dumped it all in one load because it was faster. Darks, whites, everything." She folded the ruined shirt over her arm. "Next time I sort first. Colours with colours, whites on their own, at least until a new thing's been washed a few times."

"Could you fix the shirt?" Emelia asked.

Everly considered it. "I could wash it again on its own and see if the pink comes out. If it doesn't, it deteriorates into my painting shirt for art class." She smiled a little at that. "Ms. De Vries says we shouldn't ruin good clothes in the studio anyway. This way I'd have one that's already half-ruined and sort of an artisan tie-dye, and I wouldn't have to care."

The bus rounded the corner, its headlights sweeping across the wet road, and Everly zipped the sock into a side pocket by itself, away from everything else. "Travelling alone," she told it. "You're a menace."

Emelia laughed as they stood. "You're going to be so careful with laundry now."

"Careful and smug," Everly said, and slung her bag over her shoulder.

Mya spread the stat sheets across the lunch table outside the gym, weighting the corners with her water bottle against the wind. The three-on-three tournament started Friday, and each team could add one player from the spare list. Two names kept circling in her head: Dani, who was not on the allowed list of named friends but whose numbers were right there, and a boy whose row Mya tapped with her pencil. "Both average ten points a game," she said to Isa. "Exactly the same. Ten and ten."

Isa leaned over the game-by-game column. "Look at this, though." She traced her finger down the page. The boy had scored two, then eighteen, then zero, then twenty. Up and down, up and down, like a heartbeat monitor. Dani's column read nine, ten, eleven, ten, nine. "Same average," Isa said slowly, "but one of them swings between great games and terrible ones."

Mya wrote both columns out again on a napkin, testing the idea. If she picked the steady one, her team could plan around a reliable ten points every game. If she picked the other, she might get twenty, or she might get nothing at all. The average hid all of that. It squished every game into a single number, the same way the news said the class average was 78 percent without saying who struggled and who breezed through. On the pollinate poster in the science hallway, the numbers about the bees hid the same kind of thing, she thought: the bees that visited a hundred flowers one day and slept the next. She crossed out the swingy column and circled the steady one.

Marc-Antoine dropped his tray next to hers, glanced at the napkin, and grinned. "You're overthinking it. I'll take the swingy one, and Mr. Das can put you down for steady." He signed the roster first, sliding it across the table toward the coach's office, which used to be the old residence of the caretaker before the school converted it. Mya signed beneath him and added Dani's name in careful block letters.

"It's not overthinking," she said, folding the napkin into her pocket. "It's the most fundamental decision of the whole tournament."

Saturday morning, in the first game, Marc-Antoine's pick threw up an air ball, missed two layups, and sat down with his hood up after four points. Mya's Dani scored nine, exactly as always, and their team won by one. Then Mya went out for the second game, took her first shot, and banked in a three she hadn't meant to bank, then missed everything else until the final buzzer. Marc-Antoine leaned over from the next court. "Ten points a game," he called out. "Same average as Dani."

Isabella crouched over a narrow stream of seawater that ran across the sand toward the ocean, carrying tiny grains with it in a hurry. Her science notebook lay open beside her towel, and at the top of the page, in letters she had pressed so hard the pencil had nearly torn the paper, were the words: Explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. Tomorrow. Out loud. In front of everyone.

"You look pessimistic," said Alessia, dropping down beside her with a slushie. "Like the slushie is going to spill on your notebook."

"The slushie might spill on my notebook," Isabella said. "But that is not my problem. My problem is that I have to explain something that takes millions of years, and I have one night, and every time I try to picture it my brain shows me a river holding a chisel."

Valentina waded over from the shallows, shaking water off her ankles. "Then don't picture a chisel. Watch your little river. It's doing the whole thing right now, just small." She knelt and dug her finger into the stream's path. The current slid around the blockage, then slowly, grain by grain, undercut the sides of her finger-dam until it collapsed and swept the sand downstream.

Isabella sat up straight. She grabbed a handful of wet sand and packed it into a wall a little farther along. "Okay. Test." The stream pushed against the wall, thinning it, pulling grains off the upstream face and carrying them away. Where the water slowed on the far side, the grains settled out and built a small sandy fan. "It took stuff from one place and dropped it in another."

"That's erosion," Alessia said, pointing at the worn wall. "Wearing away the rock and soil, and carrying it off."

"And deposition," Valentina said, pointing at the fan. "Dropping the material somewhere else."

Isabella wrote both words in her notebook, then drew arrows. "So a real river does this forever. Millions of years. Little scratches turn into a canyon this deep." She held her hands apart, then wider, then comically wider, until her arms were stretched like a bird about to take off, and Alessia laughed so hard she nearly spilled the slushie, which Isabella snatched off the sand just in time.

"There is an irony here," said Ms. Pritchard, the lifeguard, walking past with her thermos. "The girl worried about one night of homework just discovered something that takes a million years by playing in a puddle."

That evening, back at the beach to verify her idea one more time, Isabella found her notebook gone. She spun in a circle, heart pounding, until she spotted it fifteen meters down the beach, dry and undamaged, sitting on a low ridge of sand. The tide had come in, pulled sand from one stretch of beach, and dropped it right there, building the ridge around her book. She picked it up, hugged it, and ran up the slope, calling over her shoulder, "Alessia! The ocean just deposited my homework!"

Dominic stood at the starting line of the school gym with his heart already running faster than his legs. Mr. Levy had taped four orange cones into a rough oval across the floor, and today was the last practice before Friday's eight-hundred-metre race against Riverside. Two laps around the cones, all-out, and Dominic had lost every time trial for three weeks by blowing up on the second lap.

"You went out like your shoes were flammable," Sahib said, clicking the stopwatch after the last attempt. "First lap forty-two seconds, second lap sixty-one. You died out there."

Ricky flopped onto the bleachers beside them, still breathing hard from his own trial. He held up his phone, where he'd typed both his laps. "Look at mine. First lap fifty-five, second lap fifty-three." He grinned through his sweat. "Running the second half faster than the first is called a negative split. Running the first half faster is called a positive split. Coach said that's why I passed you at the end."

Dominic stared at the two sets of numbers. In every race he'd ever lost, the pattern was the same: fast first lap, crawling second. He had always blamed his legs, or the stuffy air in the gym, or the squeak of his sneakers on the polished floor. But maybe the problem wasn't his legs at all. Maybe the hidden variable was how he spent the first lap, like pouring out the whole bottle before the race was half over. He needed a test.

"One more," he told Sahib. "Count my first lap out loud. If I'm under fifty, I'm going too hard, and I'll ease off until you say fifty-one."

Sahib raised an eyebrow but got the stopwatch ready. The gym smelled like floor wax and old rubber, and the afternoon light through the high windows made long stripes across the cones. Dominic crouched, started, and forced himself to hold back even when his body begged to sprint. "Forty-nine," Sahib called. Dominic shortened his stride. "Fifty-two at the lap." He had never run a first lap that slow on purpose, and it felt almost wrong, like tiptoeing when everyone else was running.

Then the second lap began, and his legs still had something left in them. He pushed through the final turn, arms pumping, lungs burning but working, and crossed the line without staggering. Sahib stared at the watch. "Fifty-one and fifty. You almost even split. And your total time? Two seconds faster than your best."

Ricky jogged over, phone in hand. "Dude. If you can persevere through one more week of going out slow, you might actually negative split on Friday."

Dominic looked down at the stopwatch, at those two small numbers side by side, the second one smaller than the first. His whole plan for the race had just flipped inside out. "Same pace tomorrow," he said, and picked up the cones.

Adam had one goal in art class: draw the dragon street from his favorite game, the one where buildings lean in from both sides and every window glows like a hundred small furnaces. Ms. Bondarenko had written "one-point perspective" on the board and drawn a single dot in the middle of a rectangle, but Adam was already three pencils deep into his own version, and something was wrong.

The buildings on the left of his drawing looked fine. The ones on the right looked melted, like they had been left in the sun. Samantha leaned over from the next table, squinting. "It looks like the street got scared and ran away sideways."

"Maybe I just need to modify the windows," Adam said, and he redrew them, tilted the other way. Worse. Now the dragon street looked like it had two broken hips.

Ryerson strolled by with his coffee-stained thermos, because eighth graders apparently had a census of every bad drawing in the room and he was conducting it. "Nice attempt. Not plausible. Not even a little."

Adam ignored him, which was hard, because Ryerson was annoyingly often right. Adam sat back and stared at the dot on the board. All the guide lines in Ms. Bondarenko's example ran to that one point. Straight lines, like train tracks converging somewhere impossibly far away. Then he thought about the actual corner near his house, where he'd stood last weekend sketching. He had been standing at the corner, looking down one street with another street shooting off to his left. Two streets. Two directions. One dot. He counted on his fingers, which Samantha noticed and generously did not mention.

"That's it," he said. "You can't draw a corner with one vanishing point. One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street. The fronts of the buildings face you, like flat cards, and everything else, the roofs, the road, the sides, all of it recedes to that single point behind." He said it fast, like the words were escaping before he could lose them.

He flipped to a fresh page and imagined himself standing in the middle of the dragon street instead of at its corner. He drew the dot first, right in the center, then made the flat fronts of the buildings, then let every angled edge race toward the dot. The road narrowed to a spear point. The glowing windows shrank as they went. Far down at the dot he placed one tiny door, and behind it, he decided, the dragon.

Ms. Bondarenko paused at his table, tapped the page once, and said, "You discovered that the hard way, didn't you."

"Two broken hips," Adam said, "and a corner near my house."

Ryerson leaned in for a closer look at the little glowing door. "So what's behind it?"

Adam grinned and drew one golden eye peeking out at the vanishing point.

The camp bus smelled like sunscreen and granola bars, and William had spent the first hour memorizing the back of the seat in front of him. His mother had packed his duffel with the optimism of an entrepreneur who believes every product will sell, including three ponchos for a week of forecast sun. Across the aisle, Lennox was holding court about the camp brochure. "Nightly tick checks," he said. "The whole cabin lines up and somebody looks behind your ears. I'm skipping it. Ticks only get you if you're, like, wrestling a deer."

Lauralie, two rows up, turned around. "My cousin goes to this camp. She says the ticks there are blacklegged ticks. Some people call them deer ticks." She shrugged. "Different name, same tick. And in this part of North America they can give you Lyme disease, so everybody checks."

"Everybody but me," Lennox said. "I'll stay on the gravel."

William looked out the window at the fields rolling past, waist-high grass everywhere, and thought about it. If ticks lived in tall grass, then anybody walking through grass could pick one up, not just deer wrestlers. It was a rule you couldn't see working; you'd have to test it. When the bus stopped at a rest area with a picnic area framed by a sea of grass, he had his chance.

"I'm going to demonstrate something," he announced, and walked straight into the grass while Lennox watched from the safety of the pavement. William counted to sixty, came back, and sat on the curb. He pulled off one sneaker, then the sock, and turned the sock inside out in the transparent light of the afternoon sun. Near the toe, small as a sesame seed, something dark was crawling.

"Okay," Lennox said. His voice had gone up half an octave. "Okay, that's on your sock, that doesn't mean anything."

William flicked the tick onto the pavement and put his sock back on, methodically, like a scientist filing data. He didn't say anything, which was the whole trick. The bus driver called everyone back aboard, and as they filed on, Lennox studied the grass along the path with the expression of a man rethinking his entire worldview. He had walked through that same grass when he'd gone to look at the vending machines.

At the campground, when Ms. Sharma, the cabin leader, called for the nightly tick check, Lennox was second in line, ahead of William. "Check behind my ears twice," he said. "And my hairline. And everywhere else."

"First-timer?" Ms. Sharma asked, already parting his hair with two fingers.

"Let's just say I've revised my position," Lennox said, holding still, eyes closed, like a man praying.

Antoine raised his hand halfway, then lowered it. Mr. Cohen had asked the class to talk about where their families came from, and Antoine was still thinking about Sunday dinner, when his cousin visiting from Germany had laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her glass. The family kept calling her country Germany, and every time they did, she said "Deutschland" back, like she was correcting a nickname she hated. Antoine had not understood the joke, and it bothered him for three days.

"Antoine?" Mr. Cohen said. "You look like you're somewhere else."

"I'm here," Antoine said. "I just have a question. My cousin laughs when we say Germany, because she calls it Deutschland. Why do we have a word for a place that the people who live there don't use?"

Francesca turned around in her seat. "My mom does the same thing. She's from Côte d'Ivoire, and she gets annoyed when people say Ivory Coast."

"That's an exonym," Ross said suddenly, sitting up straighter. "A name outsiders use for a place or a group. The name a group uses for itself is an endonym. I read about it last week." He had been quiet all class, but now he was leaning forward over his notebook. "I was going to do my presentation on my grandpa's village, and I wanted the real name in it, not the English one. I looked it up."

Mr. Cohen nodded but said nothing more, which Antoine took as permission to keep going. Antoine flipped his notebook to a blank page and wrote two columns. At the top of one he wrote "their own name" and at the top of the other he wrote "our name." He tapped Ross's shoulder. "Test it. Go around the room."

Ross asked Francesca first, then the boy by the window, then Antoine himself, whose grandmother still called her island by its old name in her language while the atlas said something else. The columns filled up. Every single time, the two names were different. Antoine stared at the page and felt the pattern click into place, like a lock turning. It wasn't that his cousin was correcting them, exactly. She was just using the door she had always used, and his family was using the one built on the outside of the house.

"I thought she was being fussy," Antoine said slowly. "I'm going to stop saying Germany when she's here. I'll say Deutschland."

"It feels weird in your mouth at first," Francesca said. "But my mom lights up when someone tries." Ross grinned and drew a star next to the real name of his grandpa's village in his notebook, deciding on the spot that it would be the mandatory first slide of his presentation, the principle he'd build everything else around.

Antoine copied his two columns onto a clean sheet to show his cousin after school. At the bottom he wrote, in careful letters, "Deutschland," and underlined it twice.

Lillian counted the broken toothpicks on the lab table and wrote down the number before she forgot it. The science fair was on Friday, and her bridge model still sagged in the middle like a tired hammock. Across the table, Teresa was supposed to be recording data, but she had filled the whole margin of the notebook with tiny spirals.

"Third trial," Lillian said, laying the last toothpick across the span. The bridge groaned and collapsed. Teresa didn't even look up.

That was the third time this week. Teresa, who last year had won the fair with a volcano she had rebuilt four times, now spent lunch in the library and flinched when the bell rang. Lillian wondered what had changed. It wasn't the project, because Teresa still knew every formula. It wasn't her family, because her little brother still waved at her through the gym window every Tuesday. Maybe it was something Lillian couldn't see at all, something running underneath like a wire inside the bridge.

On Thursday, Lillian tried a small test. She set a timer and simulated the fair, calling out like a judge would. "Contestant, explain your structure." Teresa's hands started shaking so hard she knocked over the glue bottle. She fled to the hallway, and Lillian found her sitting against the lockers with her knees pulled up.

"I'm not being dramatic over something trivial," Teresa said before Lillian could speak. "I keep telling myself it's just a bridge, it's just a crowd, but my heart pounds anyway. It's been like this since October. I couldn't even go to Angelica's party."

Lillian sat down beside her. "That's not trivial. That's a long time."

Teresa wiped her eyes. "My mom took me to a doctor last month. I told her everything, and she said it's an anxiety disorder. That's what it's called when the anxiety is really intense and it lasts a long time and it gets in the way of daily life." She picked at her sleeve. "Feeling anxious sometimes is normal. Everybody gets that. Mine just went past normal. The good part is it's treatable. I started seeing someone for it, and some days are already better."

"So it can get better," Lillian said slowly. It was like finding the actual weak joint in the bridge instead of guessing. "Then we build around it. Tomorrow I'll present our data, and you stand next to me and hold the notebook. If a judge asks you something, you can squeeze my elbow and I'll take it. Deal?"

"Deal," Teresa said, and almost smiled. "Also, your load is off center. That's why it keeps failing."

On Friday, Mr. Rossi paused at their table, nodded at the rebuilt span, and said it reminded him of his pension planning, "boring but sturdy, built to hold up for years." Teresa held the notebook steady through the whole presentation, and when the ribbons were handed out, theirs was red. Lillian felt the squeeze on her elbow, but this time Teresa was just pointing at the ribbon, saying, "Third place. We built that."

Andrew laced his skates on the cold bench outside Rink 2, where the hockey tryouts were supposed to start in twenty minutes, and tried not to look at the list pinned to the door. Forty-one names. Nineteen spots. His reputation at the rink was exactly one thing: the kid who fell through the bench door during last year's exhibition game and got waved at by the whole visiting team.

"Relax," said Mayson, who had come to watch even though she'd made the swim team on Monday. "You're fast when you stop thinking."

"That's the problem. I never stop thinking." He pointed his stick at her. "Speaking of which. That new girl, Rowan, said her old school time was two seconds faster than your tryout time, and now everyone says she's taking your spot in the medley relay."

Mayson's jaw tightened. "Her school had a fancy pool."

Andrew had never seen Rowan's school, but he chewed on the problem while the zamboni groaned past. Swimmers didn't slow down for no reason, and Rowan wasn't lying, he was pretty sure. So something invisible had to be different. He skated over to where Rowan was waiting for the figure skating session and asked her straight out how long her old pool was.

"Fifty meters," she said. "Our meets there were all long course."

"Ours is twenty-five yards," Mayson said, arriving with her bag. "Short course. Coach calls it that all the time."

Andrew held up his hands like he was measuring two different windows in the air. "So you're not comparing the same thing at all. Olympic swimming races are held in fifty-meter pools, long course, and our pool is half that, short course. It's like my old stick time from a rink with bigger ice. You can't just put the numbers next to each other."

Rowan looked almost relieved. "Nobody at my old school ever said that out loud."

They carried the idea to Ms. Shevchenko, who ran the pool schedule, and she nodded and posted both girls' times in separate columns with a note. By Tuesday the coaches were rethinking the relay. Mayson hugged Andrew so hard she knocked his helmet off, and Rowan got the backstroke leg after all, which meant Mayson gave up her favorite event to keep her.

At Thursday's hockey cut, Andrew survived the first round and then got spun into the boards during the last drill, and when the final list went up, his name was twenty-first. One spot short. He stood there while the zamboni came out again, and Mayson stood next to him, not saying anything helpful.

"Coach," Andrew called across the ice, "is the list final, or do you need a manager who knows how to measure things?"

The coach looked at him for a long moment, then tapped the clipboard. "Locker room, Monday. Bring a stopwatch."

Mr. Karimi handed out the story on Tuesday, four pages about a kingdom whose old dynasty was falling apart while an enemy army prepared to colonize the valleys to the south. He told the class to read it once for Tuesday and twice for Thursday. Alicia read it once Tuesday night, thought it was fine, and forgot about it until Thursday morning.

"Twice is pointless," she told Julianna in the hallway before class. "It's the same words both times."

"Then why'd he say it?" Julianna asked.

Alicia didn't answer, but in class, when Mr. Karimi asked them to write about how the author planted the ending early, she went back to page one just to prove nothing was there. In the first paragraph, the young prince kept a dead falcon on a shelf in his room, one whose wing had never healed right. She had skimmed past it Tuesday. She turned to the last page, where the prince's own broken messenger bird failed to fly, and the army arrived before any warning could be sent. She flipped between page one and page four three times.

"Jaycob," she whispered across the aisle. "The dead falcon at the start. Was that there the whole time?"

He leaned over. "The shelf bird? Yeah. I noticed it the second read. Foreshadowing."

"That's the word," Alicia said, and wrote it down. The falcon wasn't just a bird; it stood for the messenger system itself, winged and already failing, and the author had put it in the prince's bedroom before anything went wrong. She underlined the line about the unhealed wing and wrote "symbol of the whole kingdom" in the margin.

When Mr. Karimi called on her, she said the first-page falcon hinted at the ending, and that she had only caught it on the second reading because the first time she was rushing to find out what happened. He nodded once and wrote her example on the board.

After the bell, Julianna caught up with her at the lockers. "So the twice thing?"

"It's real," Alicia said. "The hint's sitting on page one and you walk right past it." She slung her backpack over one shoulder and pulled out the story again, turning back to the first page to see what else she had missed.

Nathan had one afternoon to figure out his history presentation, and the school library had nothing but the internet, which kept giving him the same three sentences over and over. So he took the bus downtown to the city archive, where his friend Fares had once found his grandfather's name in a list of refugees from 1948. Fares had said the place smelled like dust and patience, and he was right. Behind the front desk, Mr. Santos was misting a tropical fern that leaned toward the window as if it missed somewhere warmer, and he raised an eyebrow when Nathan asked for "anything about Versailles, I guess."

"You guess," Mr. Santos repeated, but he was smiling, and he led Nathan to a long table and set down a folder of reproductions. "The maps are the good part. Start there." Nathan spread out a copy of a 1919 map of Europe and frowned at it. Germany looked like a vase that had been chipped on purpose. A thin strip of land ran from East Prussia down to the sea, cutting German territory in two, and two words were printed along it. Danzig. Polish Corridor.

Emy arrived twenty minutes later, out of breath, because she was his partner on the presentation and had sprinted from her piano lesson. "You started without me," she said, dropping her bag, then she saw the map and went quiet the way she did in museums. She put one finger on the corridor. "This is what he wanted back," she murmured, mostly to herself. Nathan leaned in. "Who wanted what back?"

She flipped open her notes, photocopies of newspaper pages from 1939. "Hitler demanded the return of Danzig and the Polish Corridor, the land Germany lost at Versailles." She traced the strip with her finger, up to the city on the coast and back down again. "And when Poland said no, Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. That started the Second World War in Europe." Mr. Santos, passing by with his watering can, paused long enough to nod once, then kept walking.

Nathan sat back. He had been writing his presentation as a list of complaints, reparations, army limits, lost land, and it had felt like a pile of unrelated facts. Now the map showed him something he couldn't see on the screen at home: a strip on paper from 1919 turning into tanks twenty years later. He pulled out his notebook and drew the border himself, badly, then labeled it. "That's my first slide," he said. "The map first, then the demand, then the invasion." He underlined the date twice to emphasize it, hard enough that Emy winced.

"Don't kill the notebook," she said, and slid the 1939 clipping across the table so the two pages sat side by side, the border and the war touching at the edges. Mr. Santos came back with a second folder and set it down gently between them. "Keep going," he said. "You've got the shape of it."

Hayden pushed through the pool doors on Tuesday feeling like a champion, which lasted exactly until he reached the stairs to the bleachers and his legs announced they were on strike. He gripped the railing and took the steps sideways, like a crab in swim trunks.

"You too?" Alma said from three steps up, lowering herself with both hands on the rail. "Yesterday after tryouts I felt amazing. I walked home. I had a snack. I ruled the world." She winced as she sat down. "Now I can barely fold myself into a chair."

Brodie arrived behind them, walking like a robot with low batteries. "Do not make me laugh," he said. "Laughing uses my stomach." He lowered himself onto the bench in one careful motion, then looked around the pool with narrowed eyes. "Something weird is going on. Everyone who swam hard Monday is hobbling today. The kids who didn't come Monday are fine. Is the pool cursed? Did someone put a hex in the deep end?"

Hayden had been wondering the same thing, sort of, minus the hex. He watched the other swimmers, counting. His sister had complained once after her first soccer practice of the season, but not that night. It hit her the day after, and worse the day after that. "I think it's not the pool," he said slowly. "I think it's timing. The soreness shows up late. Like a delayed package."

"A delayed package of pain," Alma said. "Worst mail ever."

At that moment a kid named Theo, who had felt so great Monday evening that he'd done a victory lap around the parking lot, attempted to climb the block for warm-up and made a noise like a startled goose. Mr. Pérez, the coach, just nodded as if he'd seen this exact thing every season for twenty years. "Anyone who says the word 'delayed' today gets out of treading-water drills," he called, and then pretended he hadn't said anything.

"Dude," Alma whispered, poking Hayden's arm, which he felt everywhere. "What's the word for when it hits later like this? My mom said it once. Delayed onset something."

"Delayed onset muscle soreness," said a girl from the next row, without looking up from stretching her calves. "It's usually worst 24 to 72 hours after a workout your body isn't used to." She flexed one foot and grimaced. "So tomorrow might be even worse than today. Plan accordingly." She said it like a weather report, then hobbled off toward the blocks, deeply buoyant despite everything, practically floating on her own smugness.

Hayden tested the idea in his head like a math problem. Monday was the hard, unfamiliar workout. Tuesday was one day later, and half the pool was walking like penguins. So Wednesday and Thursday, days two and three, could be the peak of the disaster. Factor in the fact that today's tryout would give their muscles new work to complain about, and Friday's final cut might happen right when everyone's legs were at their most dramatic. Which meant the swimmers who paced themselves, who migrated to the easier lanes and saved their arms, would look fresh exactly when it counted.

"Okay," he said, standing up in stages like a collapsing tent in reverse. "New plan. We go hard enough to make the team today, but we save the hero stuff. Our real competition is Thursday, when everyone else is noodle-legged."

Alma saluted, which hurt her shoulder, which made Brodie laugh, which hurt his stomach, which made Theo laugh from the blocks, which made him wobble, which made the whole pool go briefly, gloriously quiet.

"Steady," Mr. Pérez said, but he was smiling.

Hayden took the stairs down one careful crab-step at a time.

The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Tristan walked through the empty living room, his sneakers echoing off the bare walls, and found a folded piece of paper taped inside the kitchen cabinet. Somebody had left it behind on purpose, he decided, because the tape was fresh and the fold was neat.

He opened it. "Dear whoever," the note read. "I'm Wassim. I lived here for six years and now I live in Arizona. I'm leaving you my bike lock combo (it's 22-10-7) and one piece of advice. There was a study in 2018 by Jeffrey Hall at the University of Kansas. He found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. I timed it with my best friend and he was right, almost to the hour. Good luck. P.S. There's a kid named Jasmin two houses down who is worth every minute."

Tristan read the note twice. Fifty hours. He had been dreading this move for weeks, ever since his dad announced the new job, because leaving his friends felt like a door slamming shut.
