The cutting board was balanced on the counter's edge because the toaster was hogging the flat part, and every time Kaylee set the onion down and touched the knife to it, the onion rolled. It rolled left, then right, then clear off the board and bounced onto the floor. Jett picked it up and handed it back. "It's like it's alive," he said, wiping the onion on his shirt. Kaylee stared at it. Whole and round, it rolled. But the recipe card had a note in the corner in her grandmother's loopy writing: halve it from top to root first. She turned the onion so the little pointy top faced up and the scraggly root faced down, and cut straight through the middle. Then she laid each half flat side down on the board. She nudged one with the knife tip. It didn't move. She nudged harder. Still steady, like a little boat sitting on its keel. Halved from top to root, flat side down, an onion could not roll at all.

"We slice the halves now," she said. "See? Flat side down, and it stays put." Jett tried to console her about the floor bounces with a joke about the onion wanting freedom, but she was already slicing, claw grip protecting her fingers, thin half-moons falling away in neat rows. Jett's eyes started streaming when it was his turn, and he laughed while he cried, which made Kaylee laugh so hard she had to set her knife down.

The sauce came together slowly, tomatoes collapsing into the oil, garlic going golden, the onions melting soft and sweet. When Jett tried to sneak the last of it straight from the wooden spoon, they got into a small argument about tasting rights, and Kaylee settled it with a fair settlement: one spoon each, and Jett dried the dishes. Her grandmother's card called it the authentic way, the old way, and Kaylee thought it tasted exactly like Sunday afternoons at Grandma's table.

When her parents came home, the whole kitchen smelled like the real thing. Kaylee's dad lifted the pot lid, breathed in, and reached for a spoon.

"That's mine," Kaylee said, and slid the wooden spoon out of his reach.

The hardware store smelled like sawdust and paint, and Brooke headed straight for the plumbing aisle with her shopping list in her fist. For the science fair she was testing whether plants could grow faster under colored light, and she needed PVC pipes to build a frame that would hold her grow lamps parallel to the shelf. Her hypothesis: red light would make the beans thrive while plain white light would leave them scraggly.

She was comparing elbow joints when she heard a familiar voice crack behind the paint cans. It was Ronald from her science class, and he was holding a notebook with both hands like it might fly away.

"It's ruined," he was saying to Mr. Hussain, the retired teacher who worked weekends at the store and who both of them knew from the community garden. "I predicted the plants would lean toward the window, and every single one of them grew straight up. Straight up! All forty of them. I measured twice." His voice climbed. "The fair is Friday and I have nothing."

Brooke watched Mr. Hussain set down his box of screws. "Forty plants, all measured twice," he said. "Sounds like careful work to me."

"Careful work that proves me wrong!" Ronald's notebook drooped. "I can't stand up there and say I was wrong."

Brooke turned the elbow joint over in her hand, thinking. "My mom does inventory at the warehouse," she said slowly. "She says the boxes she counts are cargo whether or not the manifest predicted them. The data is the data. If all forty plants grew straight up, then that's what plants do in your setup, and nobody else in class knows that yet."

Ronald stared at her. "So I'd present the wrong part?"

"You'd present what you found," Brooke said. "A result that shows your hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result. It's worth reporting." She shrugged. "Mr. Hussain just told me basically that at the garden last week, when my tomato cages fell over."

Mr. Hussain smiled at his screws. "I said no such thing about tomatoes."

"You said it about the compost," Brooke said. "Same idea."

Ronald looked down at his notebook, and something in his shoulders let go. "I could make a chart. Forty plants, all vertical. And write about what I'd test next." He said it like he was testing whether the words held weight, and they did, because he straightened up. "Maybe whether they'd lean if the window was the only light source at all."

"That's a real follow-up question," Mr. Hussain said.

Brooke put her elbows and pipes on the counter, and Ronald insisted on carrying her bag to the door because she'd stayed to talk instead of grabbing her parts and rushing off. At the register he was already sketching his chart on the back of the receipt.

"Good luck Friday," Brooke said.

"You too," Ronald said. "Hope your red lights win."

"If they don't," she said, hoisting the bag onto her shoulder, "I'm charting that too."

Juliette had a talk to give on Monday about how a river carves a canyon, and she had exactly one idea: build a river in the kitchen sink. She layered sand, dirt from the flowerpot, and flour into a glass baking dish, pressing each layer flat. Flour on the bottom, sand in the middle, dirt on top. It looked like a sad dessert.

Zac arrived just as she turned on the faucet. "What are we supposed to be learning from this?" he asked, dragging a stool to the counter.

"Watch the water." She angled the dish so a thin stream cut across the layers. At first nothing happened, which was annoying. Then the stream found a low spot and began to chew into the top layer, carrying brown crumbs downstream in a muddy plume. Where the water slowed at the far end, the crumbs settled into a tiny fan. "There," she said. "The river digs where it's fast and drops stuff where it's slow. It's erosion and deposition at the same time."

Zac leaned in. "Okay, but if it keeps cutting, it gets down to the sand. Then the flour. Then what?"

"Then I get in trouble for using all the flour." She watched the stream sink deeper, though, because he had a point. The canyon wasn't just getting wider. It was cutting through, top to bottom, like it was reading downward. She turned off the tap and got out her phone.

The search took a while because "rock layers pages" mostly gave her an ad for mattresses. But she found a museum page with a picture of striped rock and a sign that made her sit up straight. The sign said the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition in 1669. "It's called the law of superposition," she read aloud, "and it means lower rock layers are older."

"Older," Zac repeated. "So the bottom of your dish, the flour, that's the oldest."

"The first thing down." She tapped the glass. "So when a river cuts a canyon, it's slicing through time. The bottom rock got there first, and everything else piled on top, layer by layer, and then the river came along and cut through all of it." She started the water again, slower this time, and they watched the stream work its way down one millimeter at a time.

"Can we incorporate something with more drama?" Zac said. "Like a rockslide?"

She set a pebble at the top of the stream. The water carved around it, split into two channels, and left the pebble sitting on a tiny island of dirt while everything downstream turned brown. "Fine," she said. "Nature's providing drama for free." On her notepad she wrote "pebble = million years, approximately," then crossed out "approximately" and wrote "definitely."

Her mother came in, looked at the counter, and adopted a neutral expression. "Is my herbivore in that dish?"

"One fossil snail," Juliette said solemnly, pressing a macaroni shell into the flour layer. "Bottom layer. Oldest one. Steno says so."

Christopher had read the same line nine times, and his tongue still tripped over it every single time. He sat at the kitchen table with the photocopied pages of his Torah portion spread in front of him, a pencil, a glass of grape juice, and a deadline that was starting to feel like a wall. His bar mitzvah was in five weeks, and Ms. Sharma, his tutor, would arrive in an hour.

"You sound like a robot with low batteries," said Elijah, who had come over to practice his own portion at the same table. Elijah's bar mitzvah was two months after Christopher's, and they had agreed to drill each other. Elijah dropped his copy of the reading on the table, making the juice wobble.

"I can't feel where the phrases end," Christopher said. "On the page they're just letters."

Elijah leaned over. "When I mess up, I cover the line with my hand and say it to the ceiling. If I can say it without seeing it, I actually know it."

Christopher tried it. He covered the first verse, stared at the ceiling, and recited it, halting at first, then steadier. The second verse came out almost smooth. The third one collapsed at the same word as before. "It's that word. Every time."

"Then it's not the whole portion," Elijah said. "It's one word. That's a smaller problem."

Christopher worked on the stubborn word alone, saying it slowly, then quickly, then tucked inside the full sentence. It was like the time he'd fixed the dilapidated shed door at his grandfather's house: the whole door had seemed broken, but only one hinge was loose. When Ms. Sharma rang the doorbell, he could recite four verses without the paper.

"Good," she said, unpacking the practice scroll she kept in a canvas bag. "Now read from the parchment itself. It has no vowels, so your ear has to carry the tune." She set the scroll on the table, and Christopher bent close, reading the first verse aloud. His voice wobbled but held. On the second verse, his hand crept forward, his index finger drifting toward the parchment to hold his place.

Ms. Sharma didn't say stop. She simply placed something in his other hand: a slim silver pointer with a small hand shape at its tip. "A yad," she said. "It means hand."

Christopher laid the yad's fingertip under the words instead of his own, and the verse came out clean, right through the word that had been defeating him all afternoon. His finger never touched the parchment at all.

"Again," Elijah whispered, grinning across the table, and Christopher guided the yad back to the start of the verse.

The moving truck smelled like cardboard and old carpet, and Luca loved it anyway. He sat cross-legged between a rolled-up rug and a box marked KITCHEN, holding the box with his chess set balanced on his knees. Behind him, wedged into the gap between his bike and a garbage bag of winter coats, sat Hubert, who had talked his mom into riding along for the last hour of the drive so the goodbye could stretch as long as possible.

"Open it," Hubert said, pointing at the chess box. "One game. Winner keeps the trophy."

"What trophy? We never had a trophy."

"We do now." Hubert dug through his backpack and pulled out a tiny plastic dinosaur, a prize from the arcade where they'd spent every Friday since sixth grade. "Winner keeps Rex until Christmas break. Then you come back and we play for him again."

Luca flipped open the box. The pieces were still in a grocery bag, wrapped in paper towels so they wouldn't rattle, because his mom had packed them at midnight after loading the truck in the rain. He set up the board on a crate, and the truck swayed around a corner and knocked over both kings before he'd finished. Hubert laughed so hard he slid down the coat bag.

"You know nobody at this new school plays chess," Hubert said, resetting his king. "You'll be the chess kid. That's like being the desolate guy who eats lunch in the library."

"They have a chess club." Luca moved a pawn. "I checked the website last night. It meets Tuesdays and Thursdays in Ms. Zhou's room." He had done more than check. He had emailed the school and asked which clubs still had space, and chess was the one that met twice a week, every week, all year. His old friendships had taken years of Fridays and summers to build, but they'd had one thing in common to grow around. A club worked the same way, he figured: same people, same interest, over and over, until you knew each other. He hadn't told his mom that was the real reason he'd signed up.

"So you'll thrive in the library, eating lunch with the chess team. Great plan."

"That's exactly the plan." Luca advanced his bishop and took Hubert's knight. "Here's the thing. New kids make friends by accident, waiting around hoping someone talks to them. I'm not waiting. I'm showing up somewhere on purpose where the same people show up too."

Hubert was quiet for two moves. The truck rumbled over a bridge, and the whole load shifted and creaked like a ship. "What if the chess club is full of people you hate?"

"Then I'll hate them every Tuesday and Thursday until I don't anymore."

Hubert snorted and sacrificed his rook to set a trap, and Luca, watching the board and not the road, walked straight into it. "Gotcha," Hubert said, sliding his queen down the long diagonal. "Rex rides home with me."

They reset the pieces and played again, faster this time, bumping shoulders every time the truck braked. Somewhere past the second bridge Luca won, and Hubert pressed the little dinosaur into his palm. "Christmas break," Hubert said. "Don't lose him before then. And don't lose, either." Luca closed his fingers around the plastic spine and tails of the tiny T-rex and slid him, carefully, into the chess box with the kings.

Cooper plugged his guitar into the amp Mr. Chowdhury kept in his garage, and the cord crackled like something waking up. Ross was already behind the drums, tapping his sticks together, and Barrett tuned his bass with his ear nearly pressed to the strings.

"Same plan?" Ross asked. "Twelve bars, then you solo."

"Same plan," Cooper said, but his stomach flipped. He had been practicing all week, and he still got lost every time he tried to improvise. The chords rolled along without him, and by the time he found a note he liked, the pattern had already moved on and left him behind.

Last Saturday flashed back into his mind: Mr. Chowdhury sitting on an overturned milk crate, nodding while Cooper stumbled through the progression for the first time. "You stopped at bar ten," the neighbor had said. "You were almost home." Cooper had stared at his fingers, wondering how anyone could count and play at the same time.

Now Barrett counted them in, and the twelve bars swung past, turbulent and fast, like a river Cooper kept trying to jump into midstream. Then it was his turn. He played three notes, lost his place, and shut his eyes in frustration.

"Wait," Cooper said. He held up a hand. "I keep counting from wherever I start. But the bars don't care where I came in. The pattern just goes around." He traced a circle in the air with his pick. "Twelve bars, then it starts over."

Ross grinned. "Mr. Chowdhury calls that a chorus," he said. "One whole time through."

"One time through the whole twelve bars is a chorus," Cooper repeated, and the word felt like a handle he could grab. He tried again. This time he counted silently, one-two-three-four all the way to twelve, and when the pattern swung back around, he was still there, riding it. He bent a note, let it wail, and heard Barrett laugh with delight.

"Take two choruses," Ross called out over the cymbals. "Two whole times around. Can you hold on that long?"

Cooper leaned into the amp and let the second chorus carry him somewhere he had never been. "Count me in," he said.

Harper spread her French notes across the kitchen table while her mom distributed lemon slices into three glasses, one for Harper and one each for Tristan and Gavin, who had come over to finish the paragraph Ms. Pierre had assigned. The task was simple on the surface: write eight sentences about plans for next year, all in the future tense. The problem was that Tristan and Gavin had been arguing about it since the bus ride home.

"I'm using the futur simple," Gavin said, tapping his pencil. "Voyagerai. It sounds fancy."

"It sounds like a robot," Tristan said. "Nobody talks like that."

Harper slid her notebook toward them. "Listen to this." She read aloud from a page she had copied off the board last week. "Je vais voyager. Je vais visiter ma grand-mère."

"Voyager," Gavin repeated. "Where's the future in that?"

"It's the vais," Harper said. "French has a near future made with aller plus an infinitive. 'Je vais voyager' means 'I am going to travel.'"

Gavin frowned at his own paper. "So I could say... je vais jouer au soccer?"

"Try it out loud," Harper said. She had a theory, and she wanted to test it. If the near future sounded natural in every sentence they wrote, then that was the form they should use for the whole paragraph. She flipped to the back of her workbook, where Ms. Pierre had printed a page of sample sentences from real French magazines, and read them one by one while Tristan kept score with tally marks. Nine of the eleven sentences used aller plus an infinitive.

"That's not proof," Gavin said, but his voice had lost its assertive edge.

"It's a pattern," Harper said. "Ms. Pierre gave us those on purpose."

Tristan leaned over Gavin's draft. "Rewrite your first line. Instead of j'irai, put je vais."

Gavin erased slowly, crumbs of pink rubber scattering across the table, and wrote the new version. Then he read both out loud, one after the other. The second one rolled off his tongue the way the magazine sentences had. He grinned and pulled a fresh sheet toward himself, and the hinge of his binder squeaked as he opened it flat.

They worked until the window went dark and the lemonade glasses sat empty with seeds stuck to the bottom. Harper read the finished paragraph aloud once more, all eight sentences steadied by that same little vais, and Tristan clapped twice, soft, so the neighbors wouldn't hear through the wall. Gavin slid his paper across the table to her.

"You check it," he said. "You're the one who figured out the trick."

"It's not a trick," Harper said, picking up her pencil anyway. "It's just how they say it."

Livia stood outside the pretzel shop at the mall and typed a message to her mother: Going to the bowling alley on Level 2, with Brent from science class, home by 5:30. Her mother had made her repeat the rule so many times it ran through her head like a song: tell a parent where you are going, who you will be with, and when you will be home. All three parts, every time. She sent it, put her phone in her jacket pocket, and walked toward the arcade entrance where Brent said he would be waiting.

Here was the problem she could not stop turning over. She and Brent had only ever talked online, through the group chat for the science fair. She had seen one blurry photo of him. Plenty of kids at school met people this way, but she had learned in health class that a stereotype like "everyone online is dangerous" was not the same as actual thinking. The pattern she wanted to test was simple: did the person at the arcade match the person in the chat? She could not see honesty directly. She could only look for signs of it.

She had also sent a message to Ashlyn, and she read it once more before she went in. "If I don't text you every half hour, call my mom and tell her exactly where I said I'd be. Also, you're on standby at the bookstore by Level 2 if I text the word pretzel." Ashlyn had replied with a thumbs-up and "Feasible plan, detective," which was Ashlyn's way of saying it would work.

Brent was there, holding two tokens for the skee-ball lanes. He was shorter than the photo, and his laugh was exactly like it was in the chat, quick and then gone. He did not ask her to go anywhere else. When she checked the time at three, he noticed and said, "Texting your mom? Mine makes me do the same thing. Where I'm going, who I'm with, when I'll be back. I sent it before I left the house." She felt the knot in her stomach begin to loosen, and then, because she was still testing her idea, she kept watching anyway.

They bowled two games. At the second check-in he said, "You keep texting." Livia decided to stop being indirect about it. "I don't really know you yet," she said. "So I told my mom and my friend Ashlyn the whole plan, and they're both a text away." She waited to see what his face would do. He nodded. "Good," he said. "My coach says a plan stops working the second you hide it." At the counter, he bought the pretzel she had been staring at, and when she reached for her wallet he said, "Next time it's on you."

At 5:15 they walked to the bus stop together. Livia texted her mother, "On my way, on time," and texted Ashlyn, "All clear, cease surveillance." Ashlyn wrote back one word: "Pretzel?" Livia held up the paper bag with the last warm piece inside and shook it so Brent could see. "Split it," she said, and broke it in two.

The gate to Louis's backyard sagged on one rusted hinge, the last piece of the old dilapidated fence his dad kept promising to replace. Louis crouched beside the garden bed anyway, because that was where the mystery lived. The bean plants near the fence were brown and stunted. The ones in the middle of the yard stood green and tall, and it made no sense, because he watered them all the same.

"Same soil, same seeds," said Charlee, kneeling next to him with a notebook. "So what's your hypothesis?"

Louis liked that word. "My hypothesis is that something in the fence is poisoning the near plants."

Giovanni had arrived on his bike, and now he dropped it in the grass. "How would you test it?"

Last week, Louis remembered, he had flipped through a battered science book at the library while waiting for his mom to finish work. He couldn't commute home with her until five, so he'd had an hour to kill. In that hour he'd read about a philosopher named Karl Popper, who argued in a book first published in 1934 that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong. Louis had read the page twice. It had stuck to him like a burr.

"Popper," Louis said now, pulling weeds away from the base of the brown plants. "He said an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong."

"So," said Charlee, catching on, "if nothing could ever prove your fence idea false, it's not really science."

"Right. So here's what could prove me wrong." Louis held up a plastic cup. "If I test the soil near the fence and it's the same as the soil in the middle, my idea dies. If it's different, my idea survives." He dug into the dirt with a spoon, packed two cups, and carried them next door.

Ms. Wanjiru taught chemistry at the high school, and she let them use her old soil test kit on the porch step. She watched without saying much, arms folded, while Giovanni squeezed drops into each sample.

The cups turned different colors. The fence soil showed a pH the middle soil didn't.

"It was the fence all along," Charlee whispered, as if the fence might hear.

Louis grinned and wrote the numbers down, then stopped. "Wait. Old treated wood can leach stuff. Tomorrow we test soil from the other side of the fence too. If that one's clean, then it's the wood and not something coming from Ms. Wanjiru's yard." He capped the pen. "Same rule. If her side is bad too, I'm wrong, and I start over."

Ms. Wanjiru handed him one more test strip. "Bring me the result either way."

The bus smelled like sunscreen and pretzels, which Matteo considered a good omen for a field trip. The science center had a new exhibit called Farm Physics, and his class had forty minutes there before lunch. Mr. Njoroge handed out scavenger hunt sheets and said, "Stay with a partner. No exceptions."

Matteo paired up with Maya, who wanted to see the giant microwave that made marshmallows inflate. But on the way, they passed a small barn with a real fence around it, and inside the fence stood a real cow. A placard said her name was Dandelion. Beside Dandelion, a machine display showed a model udder with a lever. A sign read TRY IT: PULL TO MILK.

Andrei was already there, yanking the lever. Nothing came out. "It's broken," he announced.

Matteo pulled the lever too. The model udder stayed dry as chalk. He frowned and looked at Dandelion, who was chewing with the calm expression of someone watching a boring movie. A second sign, smaller, hung near the fence: ASK OUR FLOOR AMBASSADOR ABOUT DAIRY DAYS. A teenage volunteer in a green vest was stacking hay nearby.

"Excuse me," Matteo said. "Is the milking model broken?"

The volunteer, whose badge said Floor Ambassador, laughed. "It works. There's a trick to it."

Maya pulled twice more, then declared she was boycotting the lever forever, because clearly the lever was against her. Andrei tried holding it down. Matteo stepped back and watched instead. The lever wasn't the problem, he decided, because it moved smoothly. Something upstream had to be blocking it. Like when the class fish tank pump stopped and it turned out a pebble was jammed in the tube. There was a hidden cause, and hidden causes had rules.

He studied the barn. On the far wall hung photos of cows with small tags under each one. He read them. Dandelion's photo was there too, with a calf lying beside her in the picture. Every single cow in the photo wall had a calf in her frame. Every one. He counted nine.

"Wait," Matteo said slowly. "Dandelion had a calf." He looked at the volunteer. "Do all the cows here have calves?"

"Every cow in our barn," the ambassador said. "That's how it works. A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf."

Matteo turned to the model. Near its base sat a small button he had not noticed, labeled CALF BORN. He pressed it. Somewhere inside, a tiny bell dinged, and when Maya pulled the lever, white liquid splashed into the little pail.

"Finally!" Maya cheered. "I un-boycott the lever."

Andrei pressed the button about forty more times, and the model cow moaned a recorded moo, which made a kindergartner in line laugh so hard she fell over.

Mr. Njoroge found them there, and Matteo showed him the trick. "You know," Mr. Njoroge said, gazing at tranquil, chewing Dandelion, "you three argued with that lever for ten minutes."

"Five," said Andrei, pressing the button again.

The postcard shop in Quito sat three doors down from the hotel, and Matteo had already walked past it twice before he worked up the nerve to go in. He was supposed to be writing to his pen pal, Andrés, in Spanish, about his plans for next year, and he had promised Ms. Leung he would mail the letter from Ecuador itself. The problem was his draft. He had written "hablé con Andrés el año que viene," which felt wrong the moment he looked at it, and he could not figure out why.

Gideon found him at the counter with the letter spread out between two postcards of the equator monument. "You've been staring at that for ten minutes," Gideon said, leaning over his shoulder. "What's hablé supposed to be?"

"I will speak with him next year," Matteo said. "But hablé sounds finished. Like it already happened."

Gideon tapped the word with one finger. "That's because you chopped hablar down to habl- and stuck the wrong thing on it. My cousin in Bogotá drilled me on this all summer. In Spanish, the simple future adds an ending to the whole infinitive. You keep hablar and put the ending after it."

Matteo grabbed the pen and wrote "hablaré" in the margin, then read it out loud. "Hablaré con Andrés el año que viene. I will speak with Andrés next year." The word sat there on the page like a small door swinging open. He tested it on the next verb, visitar, writing "visitaré los museos," and then "aprenderé," and each one worked the same way. The infinitive stayed whole. The ending rode along behind it like a tail.

He bought a stamp from the cashier with his limited, careful Spanish, and when the man answered in fast, buoyant sentences, Matteo caught "va a escribir" and grinned because he understood it. Gideon marched him down the block to the mailbox, and Matteo dropped the letter in before he could second-guess a single accent mark.

Back at the hotel, Ms. Leung was in the lobby with her tea. "Mailed it?" she asked.

"Hablaré con Andrés," Matteo announced, as if it were the headline of the year. "Next year. That's the whole plan, right there in one word."

"Then next year is already started," she said, and raised her cup to him.

The satellite images were printed on two sheets of paper, January and July, and Nolan spread them across the backseat of the van as the highway hummed past the window. His father drove, and up front his little cousin Emrick kept turning around to stare at the papers like they were a puzzle somebody had dropped.

"You're supposed to be learning something for Monday," Emrick said. He was eleven, and his whole want in life, as far as Nolan could tell, was to seem older than he was. "Ms. Zhao says if you can't explain it, you don't actually understand it."

Nolan traced the thick band of clouds near the equator in the January image with his finger. Then he looked at July. The band had moved. It sat far to the north, draped over South Asia like a wet blanket someone had dragged up a staircase.

"Emrick, look at this. Same planet, same band of clouds, different spot."

"So? Clouds move." Emrick leaned over the seat, close enough that Nolan could smell his fruit snacks. "That's not an explanation. Even I know that."

Nolan ignored him, which was a mistake he had made before, at Summer's birthday party, when he had ignored her question about the science project and she had ended up partnering with somebody else. He still wondered whether he should have just answered her. He put both sheets side by side and thought out loud anyway, because thinking out loud was how he found things.

"In January the band's near the equator. In July it's up over South Asia. That's northern summer." He tapped the July sheet where the land was. "So during their summer, the rain moves in." He remembered his grandmother's story about the rice fields, how everyone waited for the rains the way kids around here waited for snow days. Rice needed the water. If the rains came late, the whole season could fail.

"Here's my test," he said. "If the rain band moving north is what makes the monsoon, then in southern winter it should be sitting south, away from South Asia, and that's their dry season. That's why farmers plant rice when the rains arrive."

Emrick squinted at the papers for a long moment. "What's the band even called?"

"Summer says it's called the Intertropical Convergence Zone. It's a belt of rising air, and in northern summer it shifts north over South Asia and brings the monsoon rains with it."

"Say that to Ms. Zhao on Monday and she'll think you're a genius," Emrick said.

Nolan folded the papers carefully. He would ask Summer to be his partner on the next project, and this time he would explain things the first time she asked. Up front, his father glanced in the mirror and smiled.

"For the record," his father said, "I only printed those so you'd stop fighting over the radio."

The hotel room in Lisbon had two beds and a balcony that looked out over red rooftops, and Ariana had claimed the one nearest the window before her dad even set down the suitcases. That first evening, she video-called Myriam, who had stayed home. "You sound weird," Myriam said. "Like you're not tired at all."

"That's the strange part," Ariana said. "We flew west all day and I feel basically normal. I went to bed at the right local time and woke up at the right local time." She stretched, feeling vigorous enough to climb the seven hills of the city if anyone asked her to. Her dad, meanwhile, had fallen asleep at dinner, his fork still in his hand.

The trip itself was about heritage. Her grandmother had grown up in a village two hours north, and they spent three days there, walking through the churchyard where her great-grandparents were buried and eating bread that a cousin pulled steaming from a wood oven. Ariana took notes so she could summarize it all for Emilee, who was doing a family history project and had begged for details.

Then came the flight home, east across the ocean, landing at dawn. Ariana had expected the same easy adjustment as before. Instead she sat in the taxi with her eyes burning, and by dinnertime she was asleep on the couch, waking at midnight, groggy and furious. The next day at school she yawned through every class. "I don't get it," she told Myriam at lunch. "Same length flight, same me."

She decided to test something. On the trip out, her dad, flying west, had been the wrecked one while she felt fine. Now, flying east, she was the wrecked one. She checked with Emilee, who had flown to California and back last summer. "Coming home was way worse," Emilee said. "Going out there, I was fine in a day." Ariana drew a little chart in her notebook: every westbound person had bounced back quickly, every eastbound person had dragged for days. The pattern held. Flying east was simply harder on travelers than flying west, and that was all there was to it.

The problem was what to do about it. Her family was already planning the next trip, east again, for spring. So Ariana made a plan and took it to Mr. Ndlovu, who lived across the hall and worked night shifts at the hospital, a man who knew a great deal about strange sleeping schedules. She showed him her chart, and he studied it, nodding slowly.

"So," she said, "starting a few days before we fly, I want to shift my bedtime earlier, bit by bit, and get sunlight in the morning. Can I borrow your light therapy lamp for a test run this week?"

Mr. Ndlovu smiled and went to get it.

Carson had one job at the cultural festival: collect six stamps on his passport booklet from six booths, then trade it for a samosa. He was on stamp five when he spotted the last table, wedged between a calligraphy display and a very determined man playing the oud. Behind the table sat Maxine from his geography class, arranging little cards that read "Ask me anything."

"Anything?" Carson said. "Okay. What happens after you die? In your faith, I mean."

Maxine folded her arms. "Bold choice. Most people ask about the food."

"Charbel already told me what Christians believe," Carson said, patting his pocket where he'd scribbled notes. "Heaven, hell, judgment. My grandpa's funeral was like that too. But my uncle just died, and I don't know what he believed, so I don't know where he is. That's the part that plagues me."

"Okay," Maxine said, gentler now. "In Islam, there's a stage called barzakh. It's an Arabic word for barrier. It's where the soul passes through between a person's death and the resurrection."

"So it's like a waiting room," Carson said.

"Don't call it a waiting room in front of my grandmother."

He copied the word down, then frowned at it. "But Charbel's version doesn't have a middle part. His goes straight to judgment. Yours has a barrier in between. One of those has to be wrong, right? You can't both be right about a place nobody can see."

Maxine considered this, chewing a card of dried apricot. "You could ask everybody at the festival and count."

So he did. He asked the Sikh booth, the Buddhist nun, a very enthusiastic man with a table about Day of the Dead. Every booth had a different map of the invisible world, drawn with total confidence. Carson filled three pages. By the end, the stamp lady gave him his samosa out of pity, since he'd forgotten to collect stamp six.

He found Maxine packing up the table as the oud player finally stopped. "I counted," he said. "Nobody agrees. Not even a little."

"And?"

"And I think maybe the map isn't the point," Carson said slowly. "My uncle was a guy who'd talk your ear off at every party. Wherever he is, whoever's got the map right, he's not somewhere silent." He paused. "That's not an answer, though. It's just... me deciding not to let the question plague me."

"It's a decent answer anyway," Maxine said. She handed him one of the little cards, the one that read "Ask me anything," and on the back she wrote barzakh in careful Arabic letters. "Here. Barrier. For your pocket."

Carson slid it in beside Charbel's notes, two maps of the same nowhere, and ate his samosa walking home under the indifferent stars.

The bus home was loud, which was why nobody did anything at first, or so Noemie told herself. Three rows back, a kid from another class was flipping Cheikh's hood up and down over his head, calling him a ghost every time it flopped. Everyone watched. Nobody said a word.

Noemie turned around in her seat. Beside her, Hank was staring too, his mouth open, thumbs frozen over his phone. That was the strange part. Hank despised this kind of thing; last month he had broken up a shoving match in the gym in about four seconds flat. Now he just sat there.

Then she remembered the poster outside Mr. Sutton's room. She had read it twice because it seemed backwards. People are less likely to help when many others are watching, because each person assumes someone else will act. It even had a name, and the name had stuck in her head all week.

She tested it. She counted the watchers: seven kids, not counting her and Hank. Seven people, all waiting. She elbowed Hank and kept her voice low. "Bystander effect."

"What?"

"That poster. Everyone's waiting for someone else to go first."

Hank blinked at the row behind them. "I was going to, in a second."

"Sure," she said. "So was everyone."

The hood went up again. Cheikh pulled it down and stared at his shoes, knuckles white on his backpack strap. Noemie's first idea was to shout at the kid, but she had tried that in sixth grade and it had only made things worse, turned the whole bus into a show. So she tried the opposite. She stood, stepped into the aisle, and sat down in the empty seat right beside Cheikh, shoulder to shoulder, like it was a random empty seat she happened to pick. "You still have my geometry notes?" she asked him, loud enough to carry.

Cheikh looked up, startled. "I gave them back Friday."

"Right, the ones with the diagram." She held out her hand, palm up, waiting.

After a beat, Cheikh understood and started digging in his bag. The kid with the hoodie had nowhere to put his hands now. He tried one more flip, but Noemie's head was in the way, and she just kept talking about the diagram, and Hank slid across the aisle into her old seat so the three of them filled the bench like a wall.

By the next stop the kid had turned around and was bothering no one. Hank leaned over. "So we've got a treaty now? Somebody sits next to him every ride?"

"Somebody sits next to him," Noemie said, "and everybody else stops waiting."

Cheikh zipped his bag and slid the notebook toward her, the diagram page open. "Keep them till Monday," he said.

Sofia smoothed the graph flat on the table and weighted its corners with bowls of sugared almonds. Across the top of the booth, Ms. Chan had strung extravagant paper lanterns, gold and crimson, that swayed whenever anyone walked past. The graph was Sofia's contribution to the festival's heritage display: a bar chart of every ethnic and cultural origin reported in their town, taken from the census numbers Ms. Chan had printed for her. It looked wonderful, except for one thing that had been nagging Sofia for two days.

"The percentages add up to one hundred and sixty-three," she said when Yahia arrived with a crate of cups. "That's impossible. You can't have a hundred and sixty-three percent of people."

Yahia leaned over the bars, counting under his breath. "You didn't add wrong. I rechecked it at your kitchen table, remember? Twice."

She had rechecked it three times. Now she needed to know whether the numbers were wrong or whether something else was going on, some rule she couldn't see. She pushed a jar of dried beans across the table. "Help me simulate it. Each bean is a person. I'll ask people walking by where their families are from, and we'll drop a bean in a dish for every origin they name. Then we count beans and count people."

Kim showed up just as the festival gates opened, wearing a shirt with Ukrainian embroidery over jeans, carrying a tin of shortbread her grandmother had made. She eyed the dishes. "You want me to be a bean?"

"Two beans, maybe," Sofia said. "What do I mark you as?"

Kim's fingers picked at the embroidery on her cuff. "At my gran's house I'm the Canadian one. At school I'm... I don't know. Sometimes it feels like camouflage, like I blend into whatever room I'm in and belong to none of them." She said it lightly, but she didn't look up.

"Then pick all of them," Sofia said, and held out the jar.

Kim hesitated, then took three beans and dropped them one by one. "Ukrainian. Scottish. And Metis, on my dad's side." A couple behind her, overhearing, laughed and said they'd need six beans, and their toddler got two.

By mid-afternoon the dishes held far more beans than people who had passed the booth, and the pattern matched the graph exactly. Sofia was staring at her chart when Ms. Chan stopped to buy a coffee, following her gaze.

"They let people report more than one origin on the census," Ms. Chan said. "It's been that way since 1981. That's why the totals run higher than the population."

Sofia looked at Kim, then at the crowded dishes, and reached for a marker to fix the graph's title. "Every bean counts," she said. "Grab a dish, Kim. We're not done counting."

The garage smelled like sawdust and old paint, and Maeva had claimed the workbench for the most important project of her life: a model of a sodium atom due Monday. Sebastien sat on an overturned crate, holding a shoebox full of Styrofoam balls they had painted the night before. "The glue gun's hot," he said. "How many electrons do we stick on?"

That was the problem. Maeva stared at the printout Ms. Yoon had given her, a periodic table squished onto one page. She had circled sodium, and she knew the big number 11 in its box was called the atomic number. Eleven protons, she had written in her notes. But the assignment said the model had to be a neutral atom, and she had no idea how many electrons that meant. She couldn't count them. Nobody could see electrons, that was the whole frustrating thing.

"You could just put a random amount," Sebastien said, testing the glue on a scrap of wood. "It's a model." Maeva said that if the numbers were random, the model wasn't science, it was decoration. She flipped the printout over, where she had copied the sentence Ms. Yoon had underlined on the board: in a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. She read it twice, then looked up so fast she nearly knocked over the paint water. "Sebastien. The atomic number is eleven. Eleven protons. So if it's neutral, it's eleven electrons too." The atomic number told you both.

"Prove it," Sebastien said, which was fair, because Maeva had been wrong about the beaker thing last week. She tried it on another element to test the idea. Carbon, atomic number six: six protons, so six electrons in a neutral atom. Oxygen, atomic number eight: eight and eight. The rule held every time she checked it, like a pattern hiding inside the table, waiting for her. She counted out eleven small balls and handed them to Sebastien. "Two go on the first ring," she said, "and the rest on the outer ones. That part's in the book."

From the doorway, Ms. Yoon, who had come across the yard to borrow a ladder, watched them glue the last electron into place. "You know," she said, "sodium's the one you isolate from salt, and it will actually ignite if you drop it in water." Sebastien leaned back from the model. "Venomous?" he asked. "Not exactly," Ms. Yoon said, laughing. Maeva turned the finished atom slowly in her hands, all eleven electrons in their rings, and carried it toward the house, holding it level like something that really might ignite.

Vincent set the folded newspaper next to his plate before he even sat down, and his father raised an eyebrow at it but said nothing until the spaghetti had been served. "You've been carrying that thing around since Tuesday," his father finally said. "Somebody die?" "Somebody wrote a letter," Vincent said. "About the skate park."

He smoothed the page flat between the salt shaker and his glass. The letter was short, and he had read it so many times he could almost recite it, but he read it aloud anyway, slower this time. "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste." His mother twirled her fork and waited, the way she did when she suspected there was more coming.

There was more coming, but Vincent wasn't sure yet what it was. That was the problem. The letter had landed like a small bomb at school on Wednesday. Randy had marched around the cafeteria saying the writer was totally right, the whole thing was a boondoggle, while Ivana had pulled out her phone and started hunting for the town budget like a detective. Vincent had mostly watched them argue, feeling something he couldn't name, and then last night, lying in bed, he had grabbed a pencil and done something odd. He had drawn a line straight down the middle of the sentence.

"The two million dollars part is checkable," Ivana had said in the cafeteria, before the flash of the lunch lights and the clang of trays, and Vincent had nodded without really hearing her. Now, at the table, he heard it. He picked up his pencil, still tucked in the newspaper's fold, and drew the line again where his parents could see it. "Half of this sentence, you could go look up," he said. "The money part. Either the park cost two million dollars or it didn't, and the town records would say." He tapped the second half. "But this part, 'is a waste.' How would you check that?"

His father chewed for a moment. "You couldn't," he said slowly. "Somebody could think it's a waste and somebody else could think it's the best thing the town ever built, and both of them would just be saying what they think." "An opinion," Vincent's mother said. "The cost is the fact, and 'a waste' is the opinion." Vincent felt the pencil-line idea click into place, like the truce he and his cousin had once declared over a disputed Lego bin, each side keeping its half.

He thought of Randy tomorrow, still hot about the letter, and how Randy might resent being told his favorite argument was half made of fog. But Ivana would get it instantly. She already half had, in the cafeteria, with the porous afternoon light streaming through the window while she scrolled. Maybe he could just draw the line on a photocopy and hand it to both of them.

"So it's one sentence," Vincent said, "but it's doing two different jobs at the same time." His mother refilled his plate without being asked. "Pass me that pencil again," his father said. "Show me exactly where the line goes."

The folded paper landed on Lea's lab stool just as the bell finished ringing. Inside, in Esteban's blocky handwriting: bet you can't explain the finches without saying "evolved" more than twice. She crumpled it into her pocket and looked up at the board, where Mr. Esposito had taped photographs of four finches side by side, each with a different beak.

"Islands," he said, tapping the map. "Same ancestor, different islands, different food. Your job today is to explain the beaks." He set a dish of sunflower seeds, a cup of sugar water, a bowl of dried nectar powder, and a tray of small hard beans on each bench. "Tools are on the side counter. Tweezers, pliers, nutcrackers, pipettes. Choose."

Lea's team got the beans. Zayn grabbed the pliers. "This is easy," he said, cracking three beans in a row. Lea picked up the tweezers and failed, twice, the beans skittering across the bench and rolling onto the floor. Her cheeks went hot. The bell would ring in twenty minutes, and she still had nothing for the bet, nothing for the write-up.

Esteban leaned over from the next bench, watching her fail with the tweezers a fourth time. "So the finches just grew bigger beaks to survive," he said. "Like, they needed them, so they got them."

"Think about it," Lea said. "My fingers didn't get stronger from failing just now." She held up the tweezers. "A single finch can't grow a bigger beak because it needs one. That's not how it works."

"Then where did the big beaks come from?"

Lea looked down the row of benches. At the nectar station, a girl was drawing liquid up through a pipette, quick and efficient, while her partner with the pliers dripped and fumbled. At the seed bench, Zayn's pliers flew. Every bench had a tool that won and tools that lost. She pulled her stool closer to Esteban.

"Some finches are just born with bigger beaks than others," she said. "Like, some are small, some are big, all in the same flock. It's random. Then the island decides."

"Decides how?"

"Look at Zayn." On their own bench, the pliers were crushing beans while her tweezers sat useless. "The ones with the right beak get the food. They survive, they have chicks, and the chicks get their beaks." She wrote it in the margin of her lab sheet, arrows branching out from one flock into many. "So the individual bird doesn't change. Not one bird. It's the whole population, over generations, that changes. That's the part that evolves."

Esteban frowned at his own paper. "So on the bean island, the big-beaked birds were the only ones that had chicks."

"And on the flower island, the skinny-beaked ones that could reach the nectar." Lea underlined her last line twice. Mr. Esposito walked past, paused, read over her shoulder, and moved on without a word. At the nectar bench, the pipette girl was doing a vigorous, splashy victory dance.

Lea tore a strip off the bottom of her lab sheet. She wrote one word, folded it, and flicked it across the aisle onto Esteban's bench. He opened it and found his own bet returned to him, with a tally mark underneath: she had used the word exactly once.

"Rematch on Friday," he whispered.

"Bring better tweezers."

Autumn arrived at her grandmother's house just as the sun was leaning low, carrying a box of small clay lamps that clinked together like teacups. The whole family was already there, aunts in the kitchen, uncles dragging chairs onto the porch, her little cousin circling the sweet table like a shark. Grandmother met Autumn at the door and put the box in her hands. "Line them along the window ledge before dark," she said, "and leave room for tomorrow."

Autumn set out the lamps carefully, one by one, curl of wick resting in each little clay bowl, until the ledge looked like a row of waiting boats. Tomorrow puzzled her. Festivals, as far as she knew, happened once and then ended, like birthdays. She counted the lamps, then counted the clay lamps still stacked in the box, and found that the box held many more than the ledge could hold in a single night. She counted the small bottles of oil too. Twelve. The ledge took only eight lamps. If the lamps were all meant for tonight, why bring enough oil for days?

She went to find her grandmother, who was in the kitchen telling an aunt exactly how much cardamom went into the syrup. "We call them diyas," Grandmother said when Autumn held one up, "the little oil lamps." Then she added, without stopping her stirring, "Diwali isn't just tonight. It goes for five days, and we light them each evening." Autumn did the arithmetic in her head. Eight lamps a night, five nights, and enough oil left over for mistakes. That was what the box had been telling her all along. She felt the same satisfaction she got when a math tutor at school showed her a shortcut and the numbers suddenly agreed with each other.

Next door, Mr. Papadopoulos was sweeping his porch, and he paused to watch the lamps begin to glow in the blue twilight. Autumn saw him standing there and carried a spare diya over the low wall between the yards, holding it carefully so the flame wouldn't gutter. "For your porch," she said. "It's Diwali, five nights of lights." He took it with both hands and set it on his step, where it burned small and steady beside his door.

Inside, her little cousin had excavated the bottom of the sweet tin, hunting for the last coconut barfi, and was holding it aloft in triumph when Autumn came back in. Grandmother was already at the window with the match, moving down the row, and one by one the ledge filled with light. "Tomorrow," she said, "you arrange them in the shape of a lotus." Autumn looked at the empty shelf below the window, already planning how the petals would go.

Rosalie spread three jars on the garage workbench, each with a chunk of overripe banana inside, and pulled the gauze toward her like it was treasure. The whole thing had started at lunch, when Eugenie had banged her tray down and declared that rotting fruit made fruit flies all by itself, no flies needed. "The banana just turns into them," she had insisted. Rosalie couldn't stop thinking about it on the walk home, because if that were true, fruit flies were appearing out of nothing, and something about that bugged her more than the actual flies.

"You're building a fruit fly fortress," Samir said, ducking under the half-open garage door with a roll of masking tape. He had texted her that he wanted to see the experiment, and he had brought a headlamp for no reason Rosalie could figure out. She set jar one open on the bench. Jar two got a gauze cover, tied tight with string so nothing could sneak in or out. Jar three got a solid lid, completely sealed. "If flies come from the banana itself," she said, "then all three jars should get maggots. The cover shouldn't matter."

"But if flies come from flies," Samir said, "then covering the meat thwarts them." He pointed at jar two. "They'd land on the gauze and not get through." Rosalie nodded, though she hadn't thought of the word thwart. She had been calling it "blocking." Samir reached up to grab the string from a high shelf, and the headlamp slid off the workbench and cracked him square on the shoulder. He rubbed it, laughing. "Almost a concussion. That would have been a significant injury, and I would have sued your garage."

Mr. González, who was fixing a lawnmower two driveways over, wandered over when he saw the jars. He leaned against the doorframe, wiping his hands on a rag, and listened while Rosalie explained. "You know," he said, "a fellow named Francesco Redi did this back in 1668, only he used meat. Maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the ones he covered with gauze that kept the flies off the meat." He tapped jar two with one finger. "Same design, though. You'll see." Then he went back to his lawnmower without another word, which Rosalie appreciated.

For three days she checked the jars every afternoon, drawing what she saw in a notebook. The open jar grew wiggling white maggots on the banana. The gauze jar grew none, though on the second day Rosalie spotted two flies pacing across the mesh like tiny frustrated guards. The sealed jar grew nothing either, but it also smelled so terrible that Samir gagged and almost knocked it over holding his nose. On Thursday Eugenie showed up, arms crossed, and stared at the notebook for a long minute. "Okay," she said slowly. "Okay, so it's the flies." Rosalie slid the gauze jar toward her and said, "Your turn to make a guess we can test."

George had been running himself empty for three weeks, and every time he crossed the line in the eight hundred metres he finished last while his lungs burned. The problem was invisible. Nobody was pushing him, nothing was broken, yet halfway through the race his legs turned to sand. He stood at the edge of the track after practice and watched the older runners, and he noticed something: the ones who won did not look fast at the start. They looked almost lazy.

Henrik jogged over with two water bottles and handed him one. "You went out like a rocket again," Henrik said. "You were leading after the first lap. Then you died."

George frowned. "The first lap. That's four hundred metres, right?" He counted the lanes in his head. The outdoor track looped back to the same white line every four hundred metres, so the whole race was exactly two laps. Two laps meant the race really had two halves, and he had been spending his whole budget on the first one. "It's not a sprint," he said slowly. "It's a first lap and a second lap. I have to save something for the second one."

To test it, he asked Ms. Perera if he could run a time trial before class the next morning. She agreed, holding the stopwatch with her coffee in the other hand. George ran the first lap deliberately behind Henrik, and it felt wrong, like walking past an unopened birthday present. His tendon above his heel twinged at the bend, so he shortened his stride and kept the pace steady. On the second lap he still had legs left. He passed Henrik at the final curve, and the clock showed a time four seconds faster than his best.

At lunch, Arjan spread out the sign-up sheet for Saturday's meet and tapped the eight hundred. "You're doing it," he said, and Henrik nodded so hard it was unanimous before George even opened his mouth.

On Saturday, the starter raised the gun. George reminded himself one more time: two laps, save the second. The gun cracked and the field surged ahead of him, and he held back while every nerve in his body screamed that they were getting away. At the bell, the runner beside him surged wildly toward the far straight, arms pumping like a finish. George blinked. That was one lap too early. The runner looked around, realised his mistake, and groaned out loud. George stayed even, waiting, holding the last of his strength in his legs like a coin in a closed fist. The final curve came up ahead, and George leaned into it.

Hazel slid onto the piano bench in the music room and set the sheet music on the stand before anyone could grab the seat. Rehearsal didn't start for ten minutes, but she wanted to look at the spot in measure thirty-four one more time, the spot where the whole band had fallen apart yesterday.

"Move over," said Donovan, nudging her with his elbow. He balanced his trumpet case on the edge of the piano. "Ms. Yip wants me on the melody today, and my grandma is coming to the concert, so I can't sound like a dying goose."

She shifted to make room. Donovan talked about the concert every single day, and his grandmother had already promised to wear her good purple hat, which apparently was a big deal. "You won't sound like a goose," Hazel said. Then she pulled out the crumpled note she'd found taped to her locker that morning and smoothed it flat on the music stand.

Half the band slows down at the rit. and half doesn't, the note read. That's why it sounds like a train wreck. Not a trumpet problem. Signed, someone in the back row.

Donovan leaned over to read it. His shoulders dropped an inch, like a weight had come off them. "So it's not us?"

"It's the word." Hazel tapped measure thirty-four. "See this? Rit. It's telling us something." She'd noticed the pattern yesterday: the flutes and the low brass dragged behind the beat right at that measure, while the trumpets and percussion charged ahead. Two different speeds, one piece of music, total disaster. She had a guess about what the three letters meant, but she wanted to test it before she said anything out loud.

"Rit. means gradually slowing down," said Cody, appearing behind them with his drumsticks. He pointed at the marking. "And accelerando means gradually speeding up. They're basically opposites. My cousin told me when she took piano."

Hazel stared at the page. If rit. meant slowing down, then the players who were slowing were actually following the music correctly, and the ones who kept the old tempo were wrong. "So the fix isn't compromise," she said slowly. "The trumpets just have to come with us. We slow, they slow. All together, bit by bit, not all at once."

When Ms. Yip raised her baton, Hazel caught Donovan's eye and tapped the sheet music, then made a slow sinking motion with her hand. He grinned and passed it along the trumpet section like a secret. At measure thirty-four the whole band eased back together, note by note, like a wave rolling onto a beach and settling into sand. Cody's drumsticks followed them down gently instead of charging ahead, reckless and loud as they had been all week. For the first time, the ending of the piece sounded like an ending.

Ms. Yip lowered her baton and blinked at them. "Well," she said. "Whatever you did, do it again."

Donovan's grandma was going to hear something worth the purple hat. Hazel turned the page and set her fingers on the keys, ready to go again.

The gym smelled like vinegar and baking soda, because somebody's volcano was going off two tables down. Xavier straightened his periodic table poster for the tenth time and checked his stack of element cards again. Carbon, number 6. Oxygen, number 8. All night he had drilled the rule until it felt solid: the big number on each square, the atomic number, told you the protons. He wanted the blue ribbon more than he wanted lunch, and lunch was pizza day.

Dereck leaned over from the next table, where his own poster showed water evaporating from an estuary in careful blue marker arrows. "Judge at three o'clock," he whispered. "She's stopping at everybody."

The judge stopped at the volcano first, then at Dereck, nodding along while he gave a vigorous defense of his arrows. Then she reached Xavier's table, picked up the carbon card, and turned it over slowly. "Tell me about carbon-14," she said. "Is that still carbon?"

Xavier's mind went white. His cards only had plain numbers. Fourteen was not six. If the protons changed, it would be a different element, wouldn't it? But nobody would call something carbon if it wasn't carbon. He stared at the card so long that the judge's pen clicked once, then twice.

A folded square of paper landed on his table. Jemma's handwriting was on the outside fold, and she was watching from the water-quality display with her thumbs up. Xavier's hand drifted toward it, then stopped. Ms. Nasser had said the rules twice this morning: help from a classmate during judging means disqualification. He pushed the note to the corner of the table and turned back to the judge. "It has to still be carbon," he said slowly, testing each step as he said it. "The atomic number, six, that's the protons. That's what makes it carbon. So if carbon-14 is called carbon, the protons are still six. Something else changed." He glanced at the card. "Maybe neutrons. Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons." The judge raised an eyebrow, so he kept going. "Those versions are called isotopes. Same protons, always the same protons, different neutrons."

The judge wrote something on her clipboard and moved on without a word. Xavier waited until she was across the gym, then unfolded Jemma's note with shaking fingers.

"You looked like you were going to evaporate," it read. "P.S. I taped the answer under your carbon card yesterday. You never flipped it over."

Xavier turned the card. There it was in Jemma's handwriting, small and neat: "Same protons. Different neutrons. Isotopes."

"I didn't even need you," he called across the gym, and Jemma just grinned and pointed at the judge, who was writing his table number on something blue.

Savannah came back to school on Tuesday with a bright green cast from her wrist to her elbow, and by first recess half the playground had gathered around the bench where she sat.

"Which bone did you break?" Cedric asked. "There's more than one in there, you know."

"There's two," Lauralie said. "I saw my cousin's X-ray."

Savannah looked down at her cast. At the hospital, the doctor had held up the film and pointed, but she had been too busy staring at the white line on the black picture to listen. "I don't remember what he said it was called," she admitted. "I just know it was the skinny bit near the middle."

"That's radical," Cedric said, tapping the green plaster with one finger. "But which one is it? They have names, don't they?"

Savannah thought about the X-ray again. She remembered two long pale stripes running side by side, one next to her thumb and one next to her little finger. The doctor's finger had tapped the one on the thumb side. She wiggled her thumb inside the cast, and the muscle pulled tight along the exact place where the ache lived. When she stretched her little finger instead, the pull came from somewhere lower, somewhere that felt fine.

"I think I broke the one on the thumb side," she said slowly. "On the X-ray, the broken one ran along where my thumb is. The other one, the little-finger one, is the one that still feels solid."

"The radius," said Ms. Whitehead, who had crossed the yard on duty and caught the last words. "The thumb-side bone."

"That's it," Savannah said. "He said radius. And the other one is the ulna." She pointed down the cast toward her little finger. "Ulna, that side."

"Prove it," Cedric said.

So Savannah stood up, walked to the water fountain, and turned the handle the way Ms. Whitehead told her to, palm down. Nothing. Then she flipped her arm over, palm up, and pressed the handle with the little-finger side of her cast, and a hot wire of pain shot up toward her elbow. She winced and let go, and the fountain dribbled to a stop.

"That's the ulna side," she said, half laughing, half grimacing. "Definitely the ulna side that still works."

Lauralie wrote "radius, thumb side" on the cast in blue marker, right over the spot where the ache lived, and drew a small crack beside it like a badge.

Colton lined up five glasses on the kitchen counter like a tiny laboratory: water, vinegar, baking soda mixed in water, lemon juice, and the dregs of his dad's sports drink. His kit from the science shop had arrived two days ago, a pack of litmus paper strips and a color chart, and he had been waiting all week for a Saturday with nothing else in it. Mustafa had come over, mostly to eat the leftover pizza, but he drifted toward the counter when Colton started tearing strips apart.

"Watch this," Colton said. He dipped a strip into the vinegar and held it up. The paper turned pink-red. "Acid. Blue litmus turns red in acid, and red litmus stays red." He dipped a fresh strip into the baking soda glass, and it stayed blue. "And that one's a base. Red litmus turns blue in a base." He felt like a detective who could interrogate suspects that never said a word out loud.

Mustafa squinted at the chart on the box. "So vinegar's a three and lemon juice is a two." He picked up the lemon juice glass. "Big deal. Three, two, they're neighbors. Two's only a little more acidic than three."

"No, wait." Colton grabbed the chart and read the fine print twice. "It says each whole step is a tenfold change. So pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4." He looked up. "Ten times. Not a little."

Mustafa shook his head. "It's one number apart. One."

Colton took the sports drink glass, which had tested at a 4, and the vinegar at a 3. He couldn't show ten times anything with the strips, since they only gave the number, not the strength. He thought about it while pacing between the counter and the fridge. "You know how you can't see a hormone working, but a tiny amount of it changes a whole lot? This is like that. The scale hides the size of the change." He held up the chart. "pH 3 isn't just one step from pH 4. It's ten times more acidic, right here in the rules."

Mustafa took the lemon juice and vinegar glasses and sniffed each, then set them down slowly. "So lemon juice is ten times more acidic than vinegar." He rubbed the back of his neck. "I told my little sister coke was 'basically water with flavor' yesterday. I'm never going to hear the end of this."

By afternoon they had conquered the whole chart, testing dish soap, rainwater from the windowsill, even a drop of hot sauce Mustafa swore was practically venomous. Every glass sat on the counter with a labeled strip beside it. Then Colton's dad came home, glanced at the row of experiments, and pointed at the sports drink glass. "That was mine, wasn't it."

Colton looked at the pink strip lying next to it. "It was a four."

His dad sighed, picked up the glass, and drained it anyway. "Ten times more acidic than the soap water, and I drank it," he said. "Show me the hot sauce one."

Colton handed him the strip and the chart.

Scarlett stood at the steel counter in the back of Mr. Mercer's restaurant, three recipes spread out in front of her. Mr. Mercer had said she could use the kitchen on Sunday nights, when the place was closed, as long as she cleaned everything. Hector and Pierre-Olivier were coming at seven o'clock for the dinner she had promised them: curry, flatbread, and rice.

She read the times first. The curry needed forty minutes. The rice would take twenty. The flatbread was fastest, ten minutes to mix and cook in the hot pan. At first she planned to make them in that order, because that was the order on her list. Then she counted backward on her fingers. If she started the curry at six twenty, it would finish at seven. But if she started everything at six twenty, the flatbread would be cold and stiff by the time they sat down.

She pulled a marker from her pocket and wrote a schedule on a paper towel. They would eat at seven, so the flatbread, the fastest thing, should go in the pan last, at about six fifty. The rice should start at six forty, and the curry, the one that took longest, should be first, at six twenty. She copied the times onto the edge of each recipe so she could not lose them.

While the curry simmered, she checked the little cups of mung beans she had left on the windowsill. Two of them had begun to germinate, tiny white roots poking out of the seeds. She had brought them to show Hector, who insisted you could not grow anything in a restaurant kitchen, and she planned to set the cups on the table as proof.

The rice went on at six forty, and she measured the water twice, because Mr. Mercer had said rice fails on water. At six fifty she mixed the flatbread dough, which she had not planned for. Mixing and rolling took longer than cooking it did, and while she worked, she listened for the rice pot. When the lid rattled, she turned the heat down.

Hector and Pierre-Olivier arrived at seven, right on time. Pierre-Olivier brought a bottle of mango juice and put it in the middle of the table like it was a centerpiece. They argued about whether raisins belonged in curry, which Hector called a controversial opinion and Pierre-Olivier called obvious.

At two minutes past seven, everything came to the table together. The flatbread was warm, the rice steamed, and the curry had thickened exactly as the recipe picture showed. Scarlett watched her friends load their plates and reached for a flatbread while it was still soft.

"Start with the one that takes longest," she said, mostly to herself. Hector looked up, and she pointed at the paper towel schedule hanging over the counter, pinned under the salt shaker. "That's the whole trick."

Aaron had ruined four portraits since Monday, and camp ended on Saturday. Ms. Visser's art shed smelled like lake water and old paper, and every afternoon Aaron sat at the wobbly table trying to paint his grandfather's face. The problem was simple and terrible: he kept painting the skin in one thick coat, and it came out flat as a paper plate.

"You're doing it backwards," said Micaela, leaning over from the next easel. "Ms. Visser said light to dark. Like, the pale wash is the foundation, and you add darker layers on top for the shadows."

Aaron looked at his paper plate grandfather. "So the light stuff goes on first."

"Obviously. You've been going dark to light like some kind of cave painter."

He retrieved a fresh sheet from the supply shelf, taped it down, and mixed a pale peach wash, so pale it looked like water pretending to be paint. He brushed it over the whole oval of the face. Then, because he was impatient, he loaded his brush with a darker tone for the shadow under the jaw and touched it straight onto the wet paper.

The shadow did not stay a shadow. It bloomed outward like a drop of juice in a glass of milk, edges going fuzzy, crawling across the cheek. Aaron yelped and grabbed a paper towel, which smeared everything into a pink cloud.

"Whoa," said Parker from the window, where he was supposed to be sketching but was mostly watching other people fail. "It spread like a rumour."

Aaron stared at the cloud. His first four failures had been crisp and flat. This one was blurry, but soft, almost like real skin in bad light. He thought about it while the paper dried. The paint had spread because the paper was still wet. That was the only thing different. On his ruined sheets before, the paper had been dry each time he added a layer, so every edge stayed hard. He needed hard edges for the eyes and the mouth. But for skin, for cheeks and shadow, soft might actually be right.

"Wet-on-wet," he said, mostly to himself. "That's what it did."

"What's what did?" said Parker.

"Paint on paper that's still wet. It spreads out all blurry."

He tried again. Pale foundation wash first. Then, while the paper still shone with damp, he touched the shadow tone under the jaw and let it bloom. It made a soft gray pool, not a line, exactly like shadow on a real face. For the eyes he waited until the paper was dry, and those came out crisp and dark. It was a system. It was, he thought, almost a cheat code.

By Friday the portrait was passable. Micaela said it looked like his grandfather had been sitting in fog, but nice fog. Parker said it looked like his grandfather was dreaming, which Aaron decided to take as a compliment. When Ms. Visser walked past, he covered it with his hands, then moved them, quick, before he could lose his nerve.

She looked for a long moment. "The jaw shadow," she said. "Do that again."

Aaron picked up his brush.

Georgia stood in the Hendersons' backyard at 7:58 p.m. holding a squalling baby, and the note in her pocket said the parents would be home at ten. Ten was the deadline. Baby Milo had to be asleep before then, or the Hendersons would come home to a red-faced hurricane and never hire her again.

The note, which Mrs. Henderson had taped to the fridge, read: "Milo's bottle is warm. Safe sleep: back to sleep, firm flat mattress, no pillows, no blankets, no toys. Monitor is on the kitchen counter. Our number is on the back." Georgia read it three times while Milo yanked her earring. Eight months old, and already a meticulous planner of his own escapes.

She got him inside, fed him, burped him twice, and carried him to the crib in the nursery. On the chair beside it sat a fluffy yellow blanket with a duck on it, soft as a cloud, and Georgia reached for it automatically. Her hand stopped in midair. The note. No pillows, no blankets, no toys. She looked at the duck blanket, then at the empty crib, then at the duck blanket again, as if the duck might argue its case. "Sorry, buddy," she told Milo. "You get a bare crib and a firm, flat mattress. That's the whole deal." Milo blinked at her like she had personally cancelled fun.

He screamed anyway. Georgia paced the backyard with him in the dark, whispering every song she half knew, and Jaya texted her from next door: "Is the baby alive? I can hear him from my window. That's impressive." Georgia texted back one-handed: "Barely. I'm not." Jaya replied, "Want backup? I'll monitor him on the monitor while you two stare at the stars. It's very relaxing out here." Georgia, rocking Milo by the rusting swing set, noticed the metal frame was cool and smooth, some silver alloy that never seemed to warm up even in summer, and Milo, cheek against her shoulder, was going heavy and slow.

She laid him down on his back, center of the mattress, tucked nothing around him, and tiptoed out. Through the monitor came one small snort, then quiet breathing, like a tiny accordion. Georgia and Jaya sat on the porch steps with the monitor between them, and at 9:52 the Hendersons' car slid into the driveway. Mrs. Henderson tiptoed in, peeked, and came back whispering, "Asleep on his back, nothing in the crib. You read the note." Georgia nodded solemnly. Jaya raised her hand and said, "I monitored."

Naomi sat at Tiago's kitchen table with her Spanish textbook open to the chapter on plans for next year. The textbook only taught one future form, the kind with endings bolted onto the verb, and her paragraph was due Monday. She had written three sentences and erased two of them.

"Stop staring at it," Tiago said, sliding a glass of juice across the table. "It's not an adversary. It's a paragraph."

"Easy for you to say." She was hesitant to admit it, but she wanted to tell someone, so she did. "I got a C on the last one because I guessed at the forms. I'm not guessing this time."

Tiago's grandmother came in from the garden with a basket of tomatoes and asked, in Spanish, what they were doing. Naomi tried her question out: next year, what would she do? The grandmother answered without pausing. "Voy a estudiar," she said, and then more words Naomi didn't catch, something about a garden and a trip.

Naomi wrote the phrase down fast. She had seen "ir" before, the verb that meant to go, and she knew an infinitive when she saw one. Her textbook chapter never mentioned putting them together like that. She looked at her notes, then at the grandmother, who was still sorting tomatoes. Could Spanish speakers really talk about plans with "ir a" plus an infinitive? It sounded like English, saying you were going to do something, but she had been wrong before when things sounded like English.

She tested it. "Voy a jugar?" she asked, holding up her draft, and pointed at a line about playing on the soccer team next fall. The grandmother nodded and corrected nothing. Naomi tried a third one, "Voy a viajar," and got another nod, plus a smile that suggested she was saying it well enough for a person who talked to tomatoes.

By the time the paragraph was finished, five of her six sentences used the new pattern, and each one had survived the grandmother. Naomi copied the final version into her notebook while Tiago teased her about taking over his kitchen.

Monday, Mr. Gagnon handed back the paragraphs at the end of class. Naomi's came back with a red circle around her first sentence and a single note: "We don't cover this until spring. Where did you learn it?"

She thought of the basket of tomatoes and almost laughed. "Next year," she said, "I'm going to ask your questions earlier."

The kitchen at Lyam's house smelled like popcorn and someone's spilled root beer, and James was stacking cups by the sink when he heard the laughter change pitch across the room. A boy from his science class had Jayla's phone in his hand, holding it above her head, reading her game notifications out loud in a squeaky voice. "Ooh, level forty in Cat Garden, everybody." A ring of kids had formed around them, and every time Jayla jumped for the phone, the circle laughed again.

James felt his face go hot. He had promised himself after the incident in the cafeteria last month, when his sharp comeback had only made things louder, that he would handle the next moment differently, though he had not figured out how. He watched the boy's eyes flick toward the audience after every joke, checking for laughs the way a performer checks a crowd. That was the pattern. The teasing was not really about Jayla's phone at all. It was about the circle of faces, feeding it. Take away the audience, James thought, and there might be nothing left to perform for.

He crossed the room anyway, skeptical of his own theory, and tried a joke first. "Give it back, man, your solo act is bombing." The circle laughed, but at him now, and the boy grinned wider because a second performer had joined the show.
