The receiver caught the ball at the sideline, or maybe he didn't, and the whole room started shouting at once. Then the screen cut to a replay, and everyone leaned forward.

"He was in," Salim said.

"His toe was on the line. Look at it," Ralph said.

The replay ran three times in slow motion. The room voted, argued, voted again, and finally agreed the catch counted. Then the uncle leaned back and said, "You know, when I was a kid, we would have just fought about it until the game was over. Nobody would ever know."

Carter looked at him. "What do you mean? TV always shows replays."

"Not always," the uncle said. "Somebody had to be first."

That idea stuck in Carter's head for the rest of the quarter, and he kept turning it over while Ralph and Salim argued about whether the kicker was any good. If replays had a first time, then there was a specific game, a specific day, when a director tried it once and everything after that was different. The problem was that the moment itself was gone. You couldn't watch a broadcast from before instant replay and see what TV looked like without it, at least not the whole picture. It was like trying to prove the rule of a game by watching people play before the rule existed.

Carter pulled out his phone at the commercial break and searched. He found it fast, but the first page was vague, just "some game in the sixties," and a second page seemed to contradict it with a different year. He scrolled until two sources agreed. Then he checked the date against a third one, because a contradiction meant somebody was wrong, and he wanted to know who.

"Grandpa," Carter said, "do you remember where you were on December 7, 1963?"

Grandpa squinted at him. "I was thirteen. Why?"

"Because that's when it happened. The Army-Navy game. A CBS director named Tony Verna used instant replay in a live sports broadcast for the first time. That was the first one ever."

The uncle sat up in the recliner. "Army-Navy. I've heard that. That's the one."

"So you were the same age I am now," Carter said, "when the first replay ever showed up on TV."

Grandpa was quiet for a second, watching the screen where the kicker was lining up. "I didn't know it was first. I just knew that one season we argued and the next season we pointed at the set." He turned the volume up. "Kick's coming. Watch close, because you're only going to get to see it live once, and then you're going to get to see it forever."

The outfield grass was still wet when Mr. Kaminski clicked his stopwatch and pointed at the foul poles. "Two laps around the whole diamond," he said. "Eight hundred metres. Tryouts end at noon, so this is your one shot today." Henry crouched at the backstop beside Heinrich, who was bouncing on his toes like a piston, ready to explode.

The whistle blew and Heinrich took off like the fence was on fire. Henry forced himself to hold back, even when Rebekah, stretching by first base, called out, "Heinrich's already ten steps up!" Henry kept his own count, the one he had practiced all week: not fast, not slow, a rhythm he thought he could hold twice. Around second base, around third, Heinrich hit the lap mark flying while Henry crossed it three seconds behind, feeling annoyingly fresh.

The second lap changed everything. Heinrich's legs, which had portrayed pure speed on the first circuit, now looked heavy and confused, as if they belonged to someone else. He shortened, then shortened again, and by the time they came out of the turn into the final straight, Henry was on his shoulder. Heinrich's arms were windmilling. "Go," Heinrich gasped, and Henry went, passing him clean and leaning through the finish.

Mr. Kaminski stopped the watch and showed Henry the split. "Your two laps are almost identical. That's what I want to see." Henry walked back and put a hand on Heinrich's back while Heinrich stood with his hands on his knees. "I burned everything in the first lap," Heinrich said. "I had nothing left." Henry nodded. "Same thing happened to me last week. I went out hard, then I slowed way down on the second one, like my legs just quit. Somebody passed me right at the end, just like I passed you."

Heinrich straightened up, still breathing hard. "So the trick is not going as fast as you can at the start?" "The trick," Henry said, "is going the fastest speed you can still hold for both laps. It has to be one coherent pace, not two different races." Mr. Kaminski checked his clipboard. "Heinrich, the backup group runs at eleven thirty. That's your second chance." Heinrich looked at the clock on the scoreboard, then at the track of flattened grass ringing the diamond. "Okay," he said. "This time I'm staying with you."

Rebekah tossed Henry his water bottle from the fence, and Heinrich was already jogging to the backstop to wait for the whistle.

The bus smelled like sunscreen and old vinyl by the time it rolled through the gates of Hartwell Living History Farm, where people in bonnets and suspenders pretended it was still 1852. Lea pressed her forehead to the window. She had wanted this trip all month, mostly because of one rumor: the farm let visitors collect eggs from the chicken yard.

Ms. Wanjiru counted heads twice, then handed out activity sheets. "Free exploration for forty minutes," she said. "Stay in sight of the big barn." Lea was already moving, with Eliza and Gage trailing behind her, past a woman churning butter and a man who insisted on calling the farm's ox "His Majesty," like the whole barnyard was a monarchy and the ox sat on the throne.

The chicken yard was loud and dusty, and a woman in a striped apron handed Gage a woven basket. "Six eggs," she said, "from the nests along the fence." Gage crouched by the first nest, lifted a brown egg into the basket, and then froze. He looked around the yard, squinting at every feathered body. "Wait. There's no rooster anywhere. None of these are big ones with the tail feathers. So if I put these eggs somewhere warm, would they hatch?"

Eliza shrugged. "Probably? That's how chicks happen, right? Egg, then warm, then chick."

Lea watched the hens scratching in the dust. Something about the question snagged in her mind. If eggs needed a rooster to become chicks, then every egg a hen ever laid would need one, and hens here were laying eggs with no rooster in the yard at all. Did the hens even know the difference? She turned the idea over. Maybe the hens laid eggs no matter what, and the rooster only mattered for what came after. "I don't think they'd hatch," she said slowly. "I think hens lay eggs whether or not there's a rooster. But without a rooster, the eggs can't turn into chicks. They're just eggs."

"That's a big claim," Eliza said. "Can you justify it, or are you guessing?"

"There's a test," Lea said. She asked the woman in the striped apron, "Do you keep a rooster in this yard?" The woman shook her head. "The rooster lives in the pen across the lane. These hens haven't seen him in months." And yet the nest boxes were full, six brown eggs sitting in the straw with no rooster anywhere near.

"So the eggs happen anyway," Gage said, staring into his basket, "but these ones could never be chicks."

"That's kind of amazing," Eliza said. "They look exactly like the other kind. You can't tell by looking."

"Maybe you can't," Lea said. "Maybe it's subjective, whether an egg seems special. But it either has a chick in it or it doesn't."

At the farmhouse kitchen, the cook cracked one of Gage's eggs into a bowl for a demonstration on nineteenth-century baking. The yolk sat round and golden and empty of any beginning. Gage held the basket a little tighter for the rest of the afternoon, and Lea kept glancing at the hens, wondering what else they did without anyone noticing.

Grace had exactly four dollars and fifty cents in her jacket pocket, and the new SneakFleet sneakers cost way more than that, but she rode the bus home from school anyway, staring at the ad above the window. It showed a crowd of thousands, all wearing the shoes, with giant letters that said "JOIN THE MILLIONS WHO ALREADY SWITCHED." Behind her, Harlow leaned over the seat.

"See?" Harlow said. "Everybody has them. Madelyn got hers Saturday. If we don't get them before the dance, we'll be like the only two people there in regular shoes. They'll practically exclude us from the whole seventh grade."

Grace looked at the ad again. "What do they actually do better? It just says millions of people switched. It doesn't say one thing about the shoes."

Harlow shrugged. "It doesn't have to. That's the point. It's a big crowd."

The bus shudders around a corner and Grace kept thinking. Millions of people could mean anything. If the company sold a shoe to every kid in every school in the country, that would be millions, and it still wouldn't tell her whether the shoe lasted one month or fell apart in the rain. She turned the idea over, testing it. A big number of buyers wasn't a reason. It was just a picture of a crowd.

"They're doing a trick," she said slowly. "It's called a bandwagon appeal. It makes you want to buy because everyone else did, so you feel like you belong, instead of giving you a real reason."

Harlow frowned. "So you're not getting them?"

"I want to belong too," Grace said. "I just don't want to pay ninety dollars for a feeling."

At their stop, Ms. Ramos was waiting to board with her grocery bags, and Grace held the door. "Excuse me, Ms. Ramos," she said. "You're a teacher. If an ad just says join the millions who already switched, and never says what the thing does better, is that a real reason?"

Ms. Ramos smiled. "Sounds like you already answered yourself."

That weekend Grace counted the ads in the magazine at the dentist's office. Eleven of them. Nine used a famous basketball player saying the shoes made him a champion, or words like "revolutionary" and "legendary" that sounded amazing and meant nothing. Only two ads mentioned anything the product actually did, and one of those was a percentage claim about battery life. She copied them both into her notebook.

On Monday she found Harlow at her locker. "I can't afford SneakFleets anyway," Grace said, "so I'm going to prove they're not magic. Madelyn's had hers a week. If they're really revolutionary, they'll still look new by the dance." Madelyn, walking past, held up one foot. The toe was already scuffed gray. Harlow stared at it, then laughed.

"Okay," Harlow said. "New plan. We show up in whatever we've got, and we dance anyway."

Owen locked the bathroom door and set his hands on the edge of the sink. In the mirror his face was pale, and when he held one hand flat against the counter, it trembled anyway. His heart was slamming like he'd sprinted up three flights of stairs, though all he'd done was walk down the hallway to this bathroom, fifteen minutes before the geography bee was supposed to start. He pressed two fingers under his jaw and counted. Too fast. Way too fast.

He was getting sick. That was the obvious answer. People got the flu in November, and the cafeteria pizza at lunch had been heavy enough that his stomach still hadn't managed to digest it, and now his whole body was quitting on him. He should find Ms. Villanueva and tell her Noemi would have to take his spot on the team. She'd been alternate for a reason, though, and he'd studied the rivers of South America for two weeks. He opened the cabinet to look for something, anything, and found only his mother's prescription for her migraines, label faded, and a box of bandages. Nothing for a racing heart.

There was a knock on the door. "Owen? They're doing name tags." It was Alejandro, who had the locker next to his and never knocked on anything quietly.

"In a minute," Owen called back. His voice came out thin. He turned on the tap and splashed cold water on his face, and standing there dripping, he started to think instead of panic. Sick people got a fever, or a sore throat, or a stuffy nose. He had none of that. What he had was a fast heartbeat, quick shallow breathing, and shaking hands. Exactly like last spring, before the piano recital, when he'd been sure he was coming down with something and had felt completely fine by the next morning.

His mother had said something then, standing in the kitchen with her tea. "When your brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline," she'd said, "and that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing quicker." He'd asked what threat, since nobody was chasing him, and she'd shrugged. "It's called the fight-or-flight response. Your body can't tell a recital from a bear." He hadn't really believed her. His body couldn't be that dumb.

But here it was again, the same pattern, and if his mother was right, then he wasn't sick at all, and if he wasn't sick, then maybe he could do something about it. His brain thought the geography bee was a bear. Fine. He couldn't reason with a bear, but he could work the other end, the breathing. Slow breaths in, long breaths out, the way the gym teacher had them do after sprints. He breathed in for four counts and out for six, resting his hands on the cool synthetic marble of the counter so the shaking had something steady under it. He did it again. And again. Slowly, his breathing lengthened, and then, like something settling, his heartbeat came down with it. Not all the way. But enough.

The sleep part he'd have to fix later, because that was the other thing he could see now, looking back over the past week: two nights of flashcards past midnight, one night of staring at the ceiling. No wonder his body had run out of ways to stay calm. He'd trade the studying for sleep next time, maybe, and that felt like a loss too, because the flashcards were why he knew the Amazon had the largest discharge of any river on Earth.

He dried his face, checked the mirror once more, and unlocked the door. Alejandro was leaning against the wall with a marker and a blank name tag. "Thought you fell in."

"Almost," Owen said, and held out his hand for the tag. It was still trembling, just barely, so he took another slow breath, in for four, out for six, right there in the hallway, and followed Alejandro toward the gym.

The funeral was for Romy's great-aunt Ida, and the priest's voice carried over the rows of headstones like a stone skipping water. At the very end he said the congregation looked forward to "the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come," and everyone repeated it, even Romy's mother, even the cousins who hadn't been inside a church in years. Romy mouthed along but didn't say the words. She was too busy noticing them.

Afterward, while the adults clustered around the flower cart, she found Sean sitting on the low stone wall that ran along the cemetery's east fence. His grandfather was buried somewhere in the back rows, under a Star of David, and Sean had told her once that his family said kaddish for the dead, a prayer in Aramaic that never once mentioned dying. "How does your side explain what happens after?" she asked him. "Yours just promised resurrection and a world to come. That's a lot of detail."

Sean shrugged. "Ours doesn't really do detail. You praise God, that's the kaddish. Nobody hands you a map." He picked at a piece of moss on the wall. "Why, does it matter to you?"

Romy had been turning that over all week, ever since her mother mentioned the funeral. Her grandmother was Catholic and her father's family was Jewish, and she had never thought to compare them side by side, like two answers to the same homework question. Her idea, and it felt almost too simple to be plausible, was this: if she could stand in each tradition's holy place and listen for what people actually said about the dead, she could assess the difference for herself instead of guessing. "Come with me Sunday," she said. "My grandmother's church, then your synagogue. Just to listen. We'll test the logic of it."

On Sunday they sat in the back pew of St. Brigid's, and when the congregation stood and recited the creed, Romy heard it again, whole and unmistakable: the Nicene Creed, the one from the funeral, ending with the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. At the synagogue afterward they stood beside Sean's father while he prayed, and Romy listened hard for anything like a promise. There was praise, there was peace, there was God's great name. There was no map, exactly as Sean had said.

Walking home through the cemetery shortcut, past great-aunt Ida's fresh stone, Romy stopped and read the carved dates. Two traditions, two ways of standing at a grave: one looking forward to a world to come, one sanctifying the world that already was. She couldn't see either one from here, and that, she decided, was the interesting part. "Next," she said, pulling her notebook from her backpack, "we find out what the Muslims say."

The poster on the wall said "Stress" in big letters, but the S had peeled off, so it said "tress," and Maeva kept staring at it because looking at Ms. Van Dijk's door was easier than looking at Fynn. Fynn sat beside her with his elbows on his knees, and he had lost the track meet on Tuesday and then slept through Wednesday's quiz, and today he had asked her to come here, so here she was.

"Sit anywhere," said Ms. Van Dijk, waving at the squishy chairs. "Fynn, you wanted to talk about the last few weeks?"

"I keep being tired," Fynn said. "Like, all the time. Even when I sleep."

Maeva had a theory, and she had spent all of lunch testing it against what she knew. Fynn's dad had been in the hospital for six weeks. Six weeks of worrying before every phone call, before every afternoon. She turned it over like a math problem. If a bad day made you tired, that was one thing. But this was weeks, and weeks was different. She remembered the nurse at the hospital, the one who had stopped to talk to them in the hallway while they waited, and what she'd said.

"Cortisol," Maeva said. "That's the hormone thing. Remember? The nurse said it's made by the adrenal glands and it rises during stress." Fynn nodded slowly. "And she said when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high. Six weeks is a long time."

Ms. Van Dijk leaned forward. "That's what the doctor told your dad's nurse to pass along, isn't it, Fynn? Not a diagnosis, just a reason."

"Yeah." Fynn rubbed his eyes. "She said that's why I feel run down. My anxiety's been running the whole time, like a faucet nobody shut."

"A valve," Maeva said. "And nobody shut the valve." It came out sharper than she meant, and she heard what was underneath it. She was angry. Not at Fynn. At the kids in their group chat who had sent him forty messages about the meet, at the ones who kept asking if his dad was going to be okay, at everyone who kept opening the valve.

"So here's the test," she said. "If weeks of stress keep the cortisol high, then less stress is the thing to try. Coping, the nurse called it. Real coping, not just waiting." She pulled out the notebook she had filled during last period. "I wrote down everything that hits you in a day. The group chat. The hospital calls after nine. Candice asking you to cover her paper route."

"Boundaries," Ms. Van Dijk said. "That's the word for the shut-off part."

Fynn looked at the list. He took the pen out of Maeva's hand and drew a line through the group chat. Then through the paper route. Then through after-nine calls, and he wrote his aunt's number there instead, because she was already at the hospital and didn't need to be told twice.

"One week," he said. "Then we see if I'm still a zombie."

"Seven days," Maeva said. "I'm counting."

Ms. Van Dijk turned the notebook around to face them both and wrote nurture across the top of the page, under the word Monday.

The basement of the old synagogue smelled like dust and candle wax, and the piano in the corner hadn't been tuned since anyone could remember. Violet sat down anyway, because tonight was the Hanukkah concert rehearsal and she was playing the solo in the middle of the piece. She had only six days to learn it.

Ms. Karimi had handed out the sheet music on Sunday, then gone home with a fever, so the rehearsal was just Violet and her friends Jan and Brogan, who would sing the second part. At the top of the page sat three strange words: largo at the beginning, andante in the middle, allegro at the end. Brogan leaned over her shoulder and squinted. "Those are Italian, I think. My cousin invests in opera tickets, he says Italian is everywhere in music."

"Probably just decoration," Jan said, shrugging.

Violet decided andante sounded the most impressive, like something fast and brilliant, and she played the middle section that way, flying through the runs at top speed. The whole thing collapsed. Her fingers tangled, Jan came in at the wrong moment, and the final chord landed like a dropped tray of dishes. Brogan laughed so hard he knocked over a folding chair. "That was predatory," he gasped. "Like a hawk attacking the keyboard."

Violet stared at the page, her ears still hot. Last spring she had skipped reading the rules of the science fair too, and her volcano had erupted sideways onto a judge's clipboard. She had promised herself she would stop guessing and start looking things up, and here she was, guessing again. "There's a dictionary in the office upstairs," she said. "The rabbi keeps one next to the prayer books."

She found it and carried it back down, flipping pages while Jan held the flashlight on her phone. The entries were short. Largo: very slow. Andante: at a walking pace. Allegro: fast and lively. So the words were instructions about speed, not decoration at all, and she had played the whole middle backwards, slow where it should walk and fast where it should crawl. No wonder it fell apart.

They tried it again, this time with Violet dragging the opening out until it felt almost too long, letting the middle stroll, then letting the end run. Something clicked. The melody rose out of the untuned piano like it had been waiting there the whole time. Jan's voice settled into it, and even Brogan stopped joking and hummed along.

When Violet hit the last chord, Ms. Karimi was standing at the bottom of the stairs, still pale, coat over her pajamas. She had come to check on them despite the fever. She listened to the ending echo off the stone walls and nodded slowly. "Play the largo even slower," she said. "Make them wait for it."

Megan stood at the edge of her grandmother's backyard with the folded paper in her hand, the same paper she had carried around for two weeks. The reading for her quinceañera Mass was printed on it, and in three weeks she would stand in front of everyone she knew and say it without the paper. At the long table under the string lights, her cousins were arguing about who would donate the flowers for the church, and her aunt was telling someone that the guest list had to be proportional to the size of the hall, half as many chairs as invitations sent.

"You've been staring at that thing since lunch," Haniya said, sliding onto the bench beside her. "My mom says hi, by the way. She couldn't come today."

"I keep losing the middle part," Megan said. "The beginning is fine and the end is fine, but the middle just falls apart every time."

Haniya tapped the paper. "So say it here. Nobody's listening."

Megan started strong, her voice steady through the first lines, and then, exactly where she predicted, the words slid away from her. She stopped, frowned, and started the middle again. It collapsed again at the same word.

"That's weird," Haniya said. "It's the same place every time."

Megan looked at the paper, then at the yard. Her little cousins were running laps around the lemon tree, shouting a counting rhyme. She watched them for a moment. "They remember the rhyme because they move while they say it," she said slowly. "Maybe my brain needs something to hang the middle on." She held up the paper. "I'm going to walk. One lap of the yard for the whole reading, and if I hit the bad spot, I'll mark where my feet are."

She walked the perimeter of the grass, saying the reading out loud, and this time when she reached the middle her feet were passing the rosebush by the fence. She stumbled, stopped, and stood there. On the second lap she slowed her steps as she came to the rosebush, and the words came with her, one line for every two steps, all the way through the part that had been crumbling. She finished the last sentence at the porch steps and turned around, grinning.

Ms. Sharma, the neighbor who had come over for the cake, was watering her side of the hedge and had clearly heard everything. "The Mass of thanksgiving will be lucky to have you," she said. "My reading at my own wedding fell apart until I did it while washing dishes."

"Every day, then," Megan said. "One reading, one walk around the block."

Haniya held out her hand for the paper. "Fold it up. You don't need it anymore."

Megan folded it along its worn creases and put it in her back pocket. "Lap three," she said, and set off past the lemon tree.

Gavin had written one sentence in forty minutes, and he had crossed it out twice. The essay prompt sat on the kitchen table in front of him: Is the school's morning news program propaganda, or a fair source of information? He was supposed to state his position in a single thesis sentence, then build a three-point argument before drafting. He kept starting the thesis and getting tangled in the wording, and every time he crossed it out, the blank page seemed larger.

Alaina came in through the back door, dropped her backpack on a chair, and leaned over his paper. "You've been on that since I texted you."

"I can't get the first sentence right," Gavin said. "If the thesis sounds weird, the whole essay is weird."

"So skip the sentence part." She slid a glass of water across the table toward him, and sunlight refracted through it, laying a wobbling stripe of light across his notebook. "Do the plan first. My cousin calls it the bullet-point outline. You write down what you want to say, then worry about how to word it later."

Gavin frowned at her. "Mr. Lewandowski said thesis first."

"He said thesis, outline, then draft. He didn't say you have to word the thesis in perfect sentences right away. Write it ugly."

Gavin turned to a fresh page. Under a heading that just said ARGUMENT, he scrawled three fast bullets: morning news only shows one side of the fundraiser fight; the anchors never interview anyone against it; the principal picks every story himself. No sentences, no punctuation, half of it abbreviations. It took him four minutes.

Then something shifted. Staring at the three bullets instead of a blank page, he could suddenly see the shape of the whole essay, and the thesis came out almost whole: "The morning news program is not an impartial source because it shows only one side, silences opposing voices, and lets one person decide what counts as news." He read it to Alaina.

"That's propaganda, right there," she said, tapping his third bullet. "One guy controlling all the stories. Use that word."

Gavin wrote it in. Behind the glass of water, the stripe of light had crawled up the wall, and his outline was still ugly, and it didn't matter anymore. He flipped to a clean sheet and started the draft.

The community centre had been a polling station all day, and now that the real voters had gone home, Mr. Rao was letting the student volunteers run a mock election with pretend ballots. Leo had drawn the tally sheet himself. He sat at a folding table near the window, sorting ballots into three piles, one per candidate.

"Forty for Red Party," he announced. "Thirty-five for Blue. Twenty-five for Green." Paisley wrote the numbers on the board while Madelyn stacked the ballots so Mr. Rao could classify them again if anyone disputed the count. One hundred ballots, three parties, no argument about the arithmetic.

"Red wins," Paisley said, and circled the forty.

Leo looked at the board. Something about it bothered him, the way a noise you hear every night bothers you only when you finally listen. He counted again, this time adding the two losing piles together. "Wait," he said. "Sixty people picked Blue or Green. Only forty picked Red. Red wins anyway?"

"That's first-past-the-post," Madelyn said. "Most votes takes the seat."

"Most out of the three," Leo said. "Not most out of everybody." He took a fresh sheet and drew a long rectangle divided into three sections, sized to match the numbers: forty percent, thirty-five, twenty-five. "If it worked like this, like the seats match the votes, then Red wouldn't just take everything. Blue and Green would get something too."

"Proportional representation," Paisley read off the sample ballot's back page, where the mock election rules were printed. She had known the whole time, Leo realized. She had circled Red's win without a word just to see if he would notice. "Mr. Rao said to let you find it," she admitted. "He said you'd get there faster if we didn't hand it to you."

Rain started against the window, the first of the monsoon season, loud enough that they had to raise their voices. Mr. Rao came over with the boxed real ballots under one arm, ready to seal them for the night. He glanced at Leo's rectangle and the three piles on the table.

"So," Mr. Rao said. "Same hundred voters, two different results. Which one do you want to present at Monday's assembly?"

Leo tapped the rectangle. "This one. But I'll show them the piles first, and let them count it themselves." He slid the forty Red ballots across the table until they sat apart from the sixty others. "Sixty here, forty there," he said. "Then I'll ask who won."

The waiting room smelled like antiseptic and old magazines, and Alice sat between Yusuf and an elderly man with a cast on his wrist. Her own arm, wrapped in fresh plaster from the fall off the bleachers, rested in a sling. Yusuf was reading a poster about bone health out loud in an assertive announcer voice, which made the elderly man chuckle.

"Six weeks," the man said, tapping his cast. "That's what they told me. Six weeks in this thing. What did they tell you?"

Alice held up two fingers, then decided that looked like a peace sign, then said, "Three, maybe four. The doctor said probably three." She hadn't thought about it until now. Same building, same kind of break, the man had said, a clean break near the wrist. Yet his number was nearly double hers. Yusuf shrugged when she glanced at him, but the question had already settled into her mind like a stone in a shoe.

She tested her idea the only way she could, by gathering evidence. She asked the man how old his granddaughter was, and he said she'd broken her ankle last summer. "Four weeks in a cast," he said, and then, before Alice could ask, "they told me I'd need longer than her, and they were right. Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break. That's what her doctor said, anyway." He said it like testimony, a hand raised in a courtroom, and Yusuf laughed so hard the receptionist looked over. Alice wrote the words on the fogged window with her good hand, watching them condense into little droplets and run.

"Wait," she said slowly, working it through. "So it's not about how careful you are, or how bad the break looks. It's just... age. You heal slower because you're older, and I heal faster because I'm fourteen." The man nodded, looking a little rueful about it. "Faster isn't always better, though," he said. "My granddaughter was back on the soccer field in a month and a half, and she re-injured the same ankle by October. You'll be out of that cast before the season even starts." Alice thought of the gymnastics meet she'd missed, the one where Isabella had taken her spot on bars and scored higher than Alice ever had. Fast-healing bones wouldn't fix that.

When the nurse called her name, Alice stood up, and the man raised his good hand in a small salute. "Four weeks, tops," she said to Yusuf, and walked through the door.

The reading was eleven lines long, and Hayden had to recite it from memory at his grandmother's house on Saturday, in front of the whole family. He had been mouthing the words for two days and kept losing them around line six. On Thursday he rode his bike to his grandfather's place, a dilapidated yellow house at the end of Fell Street, and spread the paper on the kitchen table.

"The words won't stick," he told his grandfather. "I say them and they slide right off."

His grandfather was watering a fern by the window. "When I was your age, I put each line in a room of this house," he said. "Line one at the front door. Line two on the stairs. When my turn came, I walked the whole route in my head and the lines came with it."

Hayden frowned. "You walked the house in your mind?"

"That's the method of loci," his grandfather said. "You link each part of the text to a place along a route you know, then walk that route to recall it."

Hayden tried it. He taped the paper inside the front door and read line one there until the words and the peeling paint belonged together in his head. Line two went on the third stair, where the carpet was worn pale. Line three sat on the kitchen table next to the thermostat, which his grandfather kept at seventy because he claimed the furnace could not accelerate fast enough on cold mornings. By the time Hayden placed line six on the bathroom sink, he noticed something: the rooms were doing the remembering for him. He only had to picture the hallway and the words arrived, attached to each doorway like coats on hooks.

On Saturday the living room filled with aunts and cousins, and Mikaela from his class slipped in at the back because he had invited her. She caught his eye and tapped her temple twice. When his name was called, Hayden closed his eyes, stepped onto the front porch in his mind, and started walking. Door, stair, table, sink. The lines came out in order, all eleven, and he opened his eyes on the last word to see his grandfather nodding once, quickly, the way he did.

Afterward Mikaela found him by the food table. "Teach me that," she said. "I have fifty vocabulary words for Monday."

"Fine," Hayden said. "But you have to walk me through your house first."

Jack stood at the edge of the school parking lot, holding the corsage box so tightly that the ribbon bit into his thumb. The gym doors glowed yellow at the far end of the lot, and music thumped through them like a second heartbeat. He had been standing there for eleven minutes. He knew because he was counting, which was the problem, because counting was all he ever did instead of moving.

Ayaan found him first, leaning against a light pole with his tie already loosened. "You're boycotting the dance from out here?" he asked. "That's not how boycotting works. You have to actually not go in."

"I'm going in," Jack said. "I'm waiting for Gracelyn."

Gracelyn was waiting too, on the other side of the lot, near the monsoon of noise pouring from a science classroom where the AV club was testing speakers. She had told Jack at lunch that she wasn't sure about the dancing part. Jack had made the mistake of saying, "You don't have to dance," which was the same thing as saying don't, and she had gone quiet on him. He'd replayed that moment all week, weighing whether he should have said something else, or nothing at all. He still didn't know.

He crossed the lot to her, and she held up her phone before he could apologize. "Look at this," she said. On the screen, a white cockatoo with a yellow crest was bobbing and stepping to a pop song, perfectly in time. "Snowball," Gracelyn said. "Ayaan found the video. He's notorious for it."

"He's a bird," Jack said. "Birds can't dance."

"He can. In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball could move in time to music." She swiped to a second clip. "Watch. When they change the tempo, he adjusts."

Jack watched the bird slow down and speed up with the beat, crest bouncing, and something in his chest untangled a little. If a cockatoo could find the rhythm and follow it when it changed, then the rhythm was real, out there, something you could find and hold onto. It wasn't a talent you were born with or without. It was a rule you could test.

"So here's my theory," he said, keeping his voice steady. "You don't have to be good. You just have to find the beat and match it. If Snowball can adjust when the tempo changes, we can adjust when the song changes."

Gracelyn looked at the gym doors, then at the corsage box, then at him. "That's your big idea? Be like a parrot?"

"Be like a scientist's parrot."

She laughed, and the laugh decided more than either of them said out loud, because the thing she'd actually been waiting for all week was a sign that Jack would meet her halfway instead of managing her. She took his arm and they walked across the lot together, Ayaan falling in behind them like a bodyguard.

Inside, the floor was packed and the music was terrible and wonderful. Jack found the beat with his foot, counting, and then stopped counting and just moved. When the DJ changed the tempo mid-song, Gracelyn caught his eye and slowed with it, matching him step for step, and Jack realized she had been able to dance the whole time.

"You waited outside because of me, didn't you," he said over the music. "Not because you were scared."

Gracelyn kept dancing. "Figure it out, Patel."

Hunter's table at the camp science fair had a shoebox, three marbles, and a hand-drawn map of the brain that his little cousin could have done better. He had signed up to explain why his grandpa had struggled for ten years to quit smoking, and so far the only person who had stopped at his table was Mira, and she had only come to steal his duct tape.

"It looks naive," Mira said, tapping the drawing. "Like a potato drew it."

"It's a prototype," Hunter said. "That means a first version." He pointed at a pathway he had colored gold, running from the front of the brain to the middle. "This is the reward pathway. Watch." He rolled a marble down a groove so it struck a lever, and the lever flipped a paper flap that read FEELS GOOD. "That's what nicotine does. It hits the cells in there and they release dopamine."

"What's dopamine?" Gia had wandered over, chewing a granola bar.

"A chemical messenger," Hunter said. "Linked to pleasure and motivation." He rolled the marble again, and the flap flipped again. "The brain likes it. So the brain wants it again. Grandpa said that's why quitting was the hardest thing he ever did. His brain kept asking."

Gia frowned at the shoebox. "But you can't see any of that happening. It's all inside."

"That's the problem," Hunter admitted. His first plan had been to saw a skull in half, but the camp director, Mr. Saleh, had said no. So Hunter had spent the evening trying to make something invisible visible. The marble was his best idea so far, and it rolled crooked every third time.

Mr. Saleh stopped at the table, arms crossed. "Elaborate," he said. "Show me more than one roll."

Hunter took a breath. He grabbed a second marble, then a third, and rolled them one after another, faster and faster, until the flap was flipping like a startled bird. FEELS GOOD, FEELS GOOD, FEELS GOOD. "See? The brain gets the message over and over, and it starts to expect it. Grandpa said that after a while his brain panicked when the marbles stopped." He let the last marble roll and settle, and the flap hung still.

A knot of campers had gathered. One kid asked whether coffee did that, and Hunter said he honestly didn't know, which made Mr. Saleh nod like Hunter had said something brilliant. Gia borrowed a marble and rolled it herself, then rolled it again, and again, and then a fourth time.

"Okay, that's mine now," Gia said, pocketing the marble.

"You're proving my whole point," Hunter said. "You can't stop."

"Exactly." Gia grinned and held the marble up to the light. "Now I know how your grandpa felt. Except my dopamine is blue and costs nothing."

Mr. Saleh pinned a blue ribbon on the potato-brain drawing and reached past Gia to pocket a second marble for himself.

Harrison had been standing by the climbing bars for ten minutes before he noticed the pattern. Randy was teasing Eesa about his accent, the way he said "thirty" like "tirty," and after every joke Randy's eyes flicked sideways, quick as a clock hand, toward the three boys laughing beside the slide. Harrison was one of them. He had laughed too, just a small snort, because it seemed safer than standing there with a flat face.

"Say it again," Randy said. "Tirty. Come on, it's great." Eesa's shoulders had drawn up around his ears, but he smiled a little, the way you do when you hope smiling will end something.

Harrison thought about the flicking eyes. If Randy kept checking the laughing group, maybe the laughing was the fuel, the way a generator needs gas before it will run at all. Take away the fuel and the machine ought to sputter out. He could presume that, at least. It was a small idea, easy to test. The next joke came, something about Eesa ordering "tirty tacos," and Harrison let his mouth stay closed. He looked at the ground, then up at the sky, like a kid checking the weather.

Randy told another one anyway. But this time the glance toward the group was longer, and when the laughter came back thinner, one boy distracted by a phone, Randy's voice lost a little of its bounce. The jokes had been getting the group's approval, and Harrison had been part of that without ever deciding to be. Laughing to fit in was its own kind of signal, like waving a green flag he hadn't meant to wave.

"Hey, Randy," Harrison said, walking over. He kept his voice easy, hands in his pockets. "Eesa's got that new deck of cards in his bag. The ones from Istanbul. You want to see them or what?"

Randy blinked. Jokes needed an audience, and now Harrison was offering a different show entirely. "I guess," he said.

Eesa unzipped his bag slowly, watching Harrison out of the corner of his eye, and spread the cards on the bench. The backs were painted with vines and gold birds, delicate work, nothing like the plain decks everyone else had. Even the kid with the phone drifted over. Randy picked up a card and turned it over twice, as if the picture might change.

"They had them at this shop near my grandmother's," Eesa said. His shoulders had come down from his ears.

"Deal us in," Harrison said, and sat down on the bench between his two classmates, the cards flashing gold in the afternoon light.

The potato salad was nearly gone when Lucas cornered his cousin by the porch railing. "Okay, one question. Who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775?" Amara shrugged. Jonah, mouth full of chips, said, "The British. Obviously."

"It's not obvious," Lucas said. He pulled out the two photocopies Ms. Foster had given the history club before summer break. "I've been reading these all week." Last Tuesday at the library, he'd set the pages side by side, expecting one to fall apart. Instead, both sounded completely sure.

"Read this one," he said, handing Amara the first sheet. "That's a colonial witness. He says the British fired first." He gave her the second. "That's a British witness. He says the colonists fired first." Amara read, frowning. "So somebody's lying."

"That's what I thought too," Lucas said. He glanced toward the picnic table, where Ms. Foster, his neighbor, was balancing a paper plate. She'd been drafted into the party because she was the only adult who would talk about history longer than his uncle would talk about his lawn. She raised an eyebrow at him but said nothing.

Here was Lucas's test, the one he'd been building toward. "What if nobody's lying?" he said. "What if both sides believed it was the other guy?" He thought of the smoke, the noise, a hundred frightened men on each side of a green at dawn. His idea was simple: memory fills in whatever fits what you already fear. "Think about the probability," he went on. "Two armies facing each other, everyone jumpy, a shot rings out in the confusion. Nobody can prove who violated the peace first, because every witness saw it from behind their own line."

Jonah swallowed his chips. "So we'll never know?"

"Historians still don't know," Ms. Foster said, finally setting down her plate. "That's the honest answer."

Jonah, who had announced at the start of the summer that history was just dates, looked at the two pages again. "So the truth just... got lost?" Lucas nodded. For a second nobody spoke. Then Jonah said, "I changed my mind, by the way. History isn't boring. It's a mystery nobody solved." He grabbed another handful of chips. "Still not doing your club poster, though. I'm negligent about posters. It's my whole style."

Lucas laughed. From the yard, his uncle yelled that the sparklers were lit, and the three of them ran for the grass before the flames burned out.

The eye clinic sat between a smoothie shop and a shoe store, and Jessica had been past it a hundred times without ever once going in. Today she stood at its counter while her mother filled out forms, and Jessica stared at the chart on the far wall, squinting until the letters blurred back together. The top line said E. She was almost sure it said E.

"Jessica Vance," called a man in a white coat. His name tag read Mr. Xu. "Come on back. We'll get you sorted before your audition, don't worry."

"It's at four o'clock," Jessica said, checking her phone. "The school talent show tryouts. I'm singing." She still had two hours, but the bus took forty minutes, and lately she'd been walking right past her stop because she couldn't read the number on the sign until the bus had already pulled away. That was the whole reason she was here.

Her friend King had come along, mostly for the food court afterward, and he leaned in the doorway of the exam room. "My cousin visiting from Australia says she has six-six vision," he said. "I told her that's impossible, twenty-twenty is perfect."

Mr. Xu didn't answer. He just flipped the lens machine in front of Jessica's face and slid one dial after another. "Better or worse?" Each time, Jessica had to decide, and each time the letters sharpened or softened like the focus on a camera. It was strange, she thought, that nobody could see her eyesight except her. The optometrist could only measure it and trust what she reported.

Then it hit her. "Wait," she said. "Australia uses metres. My cousin from England says six-six too, and England uses metres." She looked at Mr. Xu. "Six-six and twenty-twenty are the same thing? Two different measuring systems, same eyes?"

"Six-six in metric countries, twenty-twenty here," Mr. Xu said with a small nod. "Both describe the same eyesight." He slid one more lens into place. "How's this?"

"Better. A lot better." The chart jumped into focus so sharply that she laughed out loud, because the second line didn't just say F, it said F P T O Z, and there was a third line, and a fourth. She could see the dust on the chart's frame. She turned to King. "Your cousin has perfect vision. She just measures it in metres."

"Told you nothing was wrong with her," King said, though he hadn't, and Jessica let it go because it didn't matter.

Choosing frames took forever. The sophisticated titanium pair looked amazing but cost more than her mother's shoes budget for the year, so Jessica adjusted the simpler wire pair on her nose in the mirror and decided they'd do. Mr. Xu promised the lenses would be cut in twenty minutes, which left just enough time for King to run to the smoothie shop and bring back a mango one, which he handed her without being asked, extra napkins tucked under the lid because he knew she always spilled.

The glasses came ready at 3:20, warm from the lab, and the whole mall snapped into detail as she slid them on: price tags, sale signs, a baby's sock dropped by the fountain. On the bus, she read her stop number from half a block away and pulled the cord in time. At the audition, she stood on stage, saw the piano keys clearly across the room, and sang.

Ms. Ricci had written two sentences on the board and asked the class to sort them: "Pickle pizza is delicious" and "Our classroom fern gets watered every Tuesday." Brooklyn copied both into her notebook, which was more than Royce was doing. Royce was drawing a shark with laser eyes.

"Obviously the pizza one is an opinion," he said before Ms. Ricci had even finished passing out the lab sheets. "And the fern thing is just, like, my opinion too. I mean, who says it's Tuesday? Time is basically a feeling."

Brooklyn looked at the fern. It sat on the windowsill between two bean seedlings the class had planted last week, and both seedlings were slumped over like they'd given up on the semester. She raised her hand anyway. "The fern thing can be checked. We could ask who waters it, or look at the schedule, or hide a camera."

"That's surveillance," Royce said. "Also my opinion."

"It's not an opinion if it can be checked," Brooklyn said. "It's a claim. Like if I said the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin. That's not my opinion. That's just wrong. I could check it, and it would be false."

Royce opened his mouth, then closed it, which for Royce was practically a scientific event. Ms. Ricci wrote the word "claim" on the board without comment and moved on to the bean seedlings, which was convenient, because Brooklyn actually cared about the beans. The seedlings in jar A were thriving. The ones in jar B were dying, and both jars sat in the same window with the same water. Something unseen was doing this.

She had a hypothetical cause: maybe the seeds in jar B had been stored near the radiator over winter, so their stored carbohydrate, the food a seed lives on before it sprouts, had been used up or ruined while the jar A seeds stayed cool. It was a guess about something she couldn't see, the inside of a seed, so it needed a test. She took four fresh seeds from each jar, laid them on wet paper towels in labeled bags, and put them in the cabinet where Ms. Ricci kept the preserve jars and the smells of vinegar that clung to everything. If the jar B seeds sprouted fine in the cabinet, her radiator idea was wrong. If they flopped again, she was onto something.

The pizza, meanwhile, had not gone away. Royce brought it up at lunch, waving a hypothetical slice he described in unnecessary detail, and Cameron, who had heard about the fern, asked Brooklyn whether liking pickle pizza could ever be false. "No," Brooklyn said. "It's just taste. It can't be checked. There's nothing to check." Cameron nodded slowly, like a man receiving bad news about a sandwich he'd already eaten.

Three days later she opened the cabinet. The jar A seeds had fat white roots curling through the paper towels. The jar B seeds had done almost nothing, one brave sprout and three shrugs. She carried both bags to Ms. Ricci's desk, and behind her Royce said, quietly, "Okay, so the tower thing. The Eiffel Tower is not in Berlin."

"Correct," Brooklyn said, and pinned the B bag to the board next to the word "claim."

The lobby chat filled with small yellow messages while Rachel adjusted her headset. "Team Sunset Dynasty, ready to lose?" Nicholas typed, which was his way of saying good morning. Rachel grinned and queued them up, but her eyes kept drifting to the side of the screen, where her friend Soraya had just posted a photo to the team's shared board. It was a selfie on a porch, a victory pose with her new rank badge held up like a trophy. Rachel zoomed in without really thinking about it, the way she did with any screenshot, looking for detail.

The porch was nice. The railing, the welcome mat, a potted plant. And behind Soraya's smiling face, small but sharp, a house number on the door frame, and beside it a street sign at the corner of the block, just visible over the hedge. Rachel sat back. She thought about the eleven thousand players in this game's community, some of whom she had never met, and how the photo was set to public because Soraya never touched her settings. A stranger could zoom in the same way Rachel just had. A stranger could look at a house number and a street sign and work out exactly where the photo was taken. That part was simple. The part that made her stomach tighten was what came after.

She took a screenshot of her own zoom, cropped it to just the door frame and the sign, and sent it to Soraya with a single message: "Look what I can see."

The next round started without her. Nicholas's character got eliminated twice while Rachel stared at the chat window, waiting. Then Soraya's reply appeared: "What am I looking at?"

"Your house number. And your street," Rachel typed. "The photo's public. Try to find my house from this." She attached a test photo she had just taken of her own porch, but this time she had angled herself against the blank garage door, nothing behind her but smooth gray. If Soraya could find Rachel's house from that, Rachel would stop worrying. If she couldn't, the worry was worth something.

Soraya spent six minutes trying. She asked for the town, and Rachel gave it, being as impartial as a referee, offering no hints either way. Soraya found nothing. No number, no sign, no school logo on a hoodie, nothing. "Okay, you win," she finally typed. "Deleting the porch one. Should I retake it in front of the garage like yours?"

"Or the fence," Nicholas cut in, having clearly been reading the whole time. "The fence is very dramatic. Very mysterious. Like a dynasty that fell because everyone could see its address." Rachel laughed out loud, and in the lobby two teammates asked what was so funny.

Soraya posted the new photo an hour later, taken against the fence, and beneath it she wrote that she had gone into her settings and turned the board to friends-only besides. Then she sent Rachel a private message: "There are four other people on the team with porch photos. Want to help me check them?"

Rachel exhaled, sat up straighter, and opened the board. One by one, zoom by zoom, she and Soraya messaged each teammate, and by the end of the evening every background had been checked and two more photos had been retaken. Ms. Sok, whose nephew apparently played on their team under the name FalconGirl88, sent a message too: "Nice work, team. Falcon's photo was all fence before I even asked."

"We run a tight dynasty," Nicholas announced in the lobby.

"A mysterious one," Rachel said, and started the next round.

Chloe pushed her chair in at the family dinner table and slid a folded paper across to her dad. "Guess what happened at the garden club today."

"You finally got the marigolds planted?" her mom asked, passing the potatoes.

"Better. I fixed the meetings." Chloe unfolded the paper, which had AGENDA written across the top in her careful handwriting. "Every meeting we've ever had turns into Milena and Ronald arguing about fundraisers while everybody else just sits there. Last week, Mr. Mwangi came to advise us and he couldn't even get a word in. I figured there had to be a reason meetings kept going like that, some kind of pattern, and I wanted to find the rule underneath it."

Her dad raised an eyebrow. "And you found this rule where?"

"The library shelf behind the bake sale box. There's this old book, dusty, falling apart. It's called Robert's Rules of Order, a guide to running meetings fairly. It was first published in 1876 by a U.S. Army officer named Henry Martyn Robert. An army officer, Dad. Writing meeting rules."

"Soldiers have meetings too," her dad said, grinning.

"Anyway," Chloe said, waving her fork, "I read half of it last night. It's actually kind of sophisticated. You keep a list, an agenda, and people raise hands, and nobody talks over anybody. So today I budgeted exactly ten minutes per topic, and I ran the whole meeting with the book right next to me like a referee."

Her little brother snorted. "Did Ronald follow the rules?"

"That's the best part. He tried to interrupt Milena about the car wash, and I said, 'Ronald, you're on the list for after her.' And he actually sat back down. He looked a little shocked, like the chairs themselves had spoken." Chloe laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her milk. "Then Milena finished her point in two minutes because nobody was racing her, and this quiet kid who never talks suggested we sell herb seed packets, and everybody loved it. We voted and everything. A real vote, with hands."

"So the old book worked," her mom said.

"It worked because it's fair, that's the thing," Chloe said. "It's not me being bossy. The rules don't care who's loudest. I have this ambition now, this plan. Next meeting, I'm teaching everyone else the basics so the club keeps running this way even when I'm not president anymore." She refolded the paper and tucked it into her back pocket.

"Chloe," her dad said, "you just made an 1876 army officer the hero of the garden club."

She stood up and grabbed the old book from her chair. "He's not the hero. He's the coach." Then she was already halfway to the stairs, calling over her shoulder, "Meeting notes to write!"

The screen above the counter filled half the wall of Marconi's, and every seat in the place faced it. Lucy slid into the booth between Ella and Alina, her dad on the outside with a basket of garlic knots, and on the screen the Comets were ten minutes from finishing the championship game.

"Say it now," Ella said, "so I can enjoy it. Comets win because they're the better team."

Alina looked skeptical. "They've played every playoff game at home. Put them on a neutral field and I'm not sure."

"That's such an excuse," Ella said.

Lucy chewed a garlic knot and thought about last spring, when she'd insisted her debate team only lost because the judges were unfair. Later she'd found the recordings and heard her own stumbling opening. She had never said that out loud to anyone, and it still sat wrong with her.

"They do seem different at home," Lucy said slowly. "But is that a real thing or just a story people tell?"

"Look it up," Alina said, mouth full of pizza.

Lucy pulled out her phone under the table, careful of Ms. Nguyen, whose booth was across the aisle. Ms. Nguyen taught science at their school and had once confiscated Alina's phone for a week. Lucy typed fast. Then she read it twice.

"Okay, this is real," she said. "In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games. It even has a name. Home advantage."

"Ha," Alina said, not even pretending to be quiet.

"But wait," Lucy said. She turned the phone so Ella could see. "More than half isn't all of it. It's a tilt, not a wall. The Comets could still be better."

Ella sat back. "So the truth is annoying. Both things at once."

On the screen the Comets' striker took a ball off a defender's foot, cut inside, and buried it in the far corner. The restaurant erupted. Lucy's dad knocked over the parmesan shaker trying to high-five Ella, and a waiter came jogging over with a stack of napkins like he was responding to a plumbing emergency.

"Sorry, sorry," her dad said, mopping.

Ella reached over and consoled the shaker, patting its top. "It's okay, buddy."

Lucy was still holding her phone, scrolling. Some teams showed bigger home advantages than others, season to season, and none of it settled whether this team, tonight, deserved it. She closed the phone and put it face down.

"Here's what I think," she said. "They were good at home all season. That counts. But next year, first away game, I want to watch."

Alina raised her soda. "To away games."

"To evidence," Ella said, and clinked her cup against it.

From the next booth, Ms. Nguyen leaned over without looking up from her salad and said, "For what it's worth, that's the best sentence I've heard all year."

Alex had texted Zackery three times before the Tomas family's kitchen light finally felt less scary: I'm babysitting, what if she cries, what if I ruin everything? Zackery's last reply still glowed on the screen: "You'll figure it out. You always do." Two-year-old Mia banged a plastic spoon on the high chair tray and grinned at him, and Alex decided that maybe Zackery was right.

He had made a systematic plan, written on a napkin and taped above the sink: snack at six, blocks at six thirty, bath at seven, bed at seven thirty. He was proud of the napkin. He followed it exactly. He had not planned for what happened at 6:42, when he turned to rinse the snack bowl and heard a cupboard door click open behind him.

Mia stood by the counter holding the spray bottle of surface cleaner, and the trigger was loose in her fist, and there was a wet stripe down her chin. Alex's whole body went cold. He took the bottle gently out of her hands, kept his voice light, and set her on the high chair where he could see her. Then he crouched and studied the label, but the tiny print swam in front of him. For one second despair pressed down on him, and he almost called his mom at work, but she was two towns away and Mia was right here, with something on her face that might be cleaner or might be just drool.

Then he remembered the fridge. Down at the bottom, under a cartoon magnet, hung a strip of paper with numbers on it. He peeled it off. At the top, in the mother's handwriting, it said POISON HELP, and under that: 1-800-222-1222. Alex grabbed his phone and dialed. A woman answered before the second ring finished.

"Hi, my name is Alex, I'm babysitting, and a toddler got hold of a cleaner bottle," he said. "I don't know if she swallowed any."

"You did exactly the right thing calling," the woman said. "This number, 1-800-222-1222, is the Poison Help line, and it connects you to your local poison control center at any hour, even right now." She asked what the bottle said, whether Mia was coughing, whether she was acting normal. Alex read the label out loud, letter by letter, while Mia chewed the spoon and watched him. The woman told him what to watch for and said to call back any time, for any reason, even if he just felt unsure. He said thank you twice.

Mia went to bed at 7:30 exactly, right on schedule. Alex sat at the kitchen table and texted Zackery: "I handled it." Then he took the napkin plan off the wall, smoothed it flat, and wrote one more line at the bottom, 1-800-222-1222, and taped it up where he would never miss it.

Piper stood at the bathroom sink with her flashcards propped against the mirror, rehearsing her health presentation for the fourth time. On Monday she had to explain, in two minutes, how nicotine hooks the brain, and Mr. Hughes had said her first attempt sounded like she was reading a dictionary. Behind her, water dripped from the faucet with a steady plink.

Her uncle had given her the best material without meaning to. At his doctor's appointment last week, he had asked why he reached for a cigarette the second he got stressed, and the doctor had answered that when smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about ten seconds. Piper had written it on an index card in red pen. Ten seconds. She scrutinized the card, turning it over, looking for what made it important. It was fast. Faster than almost anything else. But why did fast matter?

She tried out an answer in the mirror. "Your brain learns by connecting." Her voice bounced off the tile. She turned on the tap and let cold water run over her wrists, which is what she did before quizzes. "If something bad happens and you feel better almost right away, your brain links them. If the gap is ten seconds, the link is tight."

A knock rattled the door. "Piper, some of us need the bathroom," her brother called.

"One minute." She flicked the water off. Her idea still needed a test. She grabbed her phone and set a timer for ten seconds, then started it and stood still, counting the drips from the faucet. Four. Five. Six. Ten seconds was nothing. If her uncle felt relief within that window, his brain would barely have room to notice anything else that might have helped, like walking outside or taking a breath. The cigarette always got the credit.

She flipped through her cards to the part about dopamine and the reward pathway, which she had copied from a site her school library listed as a prestigious research institute. Then she found her facts about money, because Mr. Hughes liked presentations that answered "so what." Cigarette sales produced billions in revenue for tobacco companies every year, and those companies counted on brains that had learned, in ten seconds, to want more.

At the door she heard her brother again, and behind him Ibraheem's voice, who had come over to time her run-throughs. "Tell her Jason says even his mom quit and she's the most stubborn person alive," Ibraheem said. Piper opened the door with the cards fanned out like a poker hand.

"Ibraheem, sit on the tub," she said. "You're my class. Question one. Somebody hands you a cigarette and says one won't hurt. You have ten seconds. Go."

Jan scooped a hole in the sand and set a beach ball in it, standing upright. "Okay, Miss Science Fair. Explain the seasons again, but this time so I actually believe you."

Sarah crouched beside the ball and stuck a wooden skewer through it at an angle, like a lamppost leaning in the wind. "The Earth is tilted," she said. "Not toward the sun all the time, just sometimes. When our half leans in, summer. When it leans away, winter." She remembered the day she'd gotten this wrong, back in September, when she'd told the whole class that the Earth must swing closer to the sun in June. Ms. Sinclair had only raised an eyebrow and said, "Then why is it winter in Australia right now?" Sarah had gone home red-faced and spent two evenings with a flashlight and a grapefruit until the pattern finally turned over in her mind. She had come to cherish that grapefruit, dented as it was.

Jan spun the ball slowly, watching the skewer's shadow crawl across the sand. "Here's my problem," Jan said. "My grandmother lives near the equator. Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so temperatures change little. She laughs when I talk about four seasons. Her town has wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones. Winter coats, snowmen, none of it. She says a cold day there means she wears a long-sleeved shirt."

Sarah stopped with her hand on the ball. That had never come up in any of her books. She pictured the tilted skewer again, tilting toward the sun, away, toward, away, and then she imagined standing right where the skewer pointed, straight under the flashlight beam no matter how the ball leaned. "Then it works," she said slowly. "If the light barely changes all year, the temperature wouldn't either. So it isn't that her seasons are wrong. They're just driven by rain instead of warmth."

"So who's right, you or your grandmother?" Jan asked.

"Both. Maybe neither of us is the whole story." Sarah judged herself fairly, like an impartial referee between her grapefruit and Jan's grandmother, and had to admit the verdict might be a tie. She picked up the skewer and tilted the ball toward the imaginary sun. "Say the sun is that lifeguard chair. Stand on the equator line I drew and tell me what you notice about your shadow."

Brooke stood at the kitchen counter at ten thirty on Tuesday night, staring at the math worksheet she had barely started. Her heart was doing a fast, shallow drumroll, and her shoulders were up near her ears. She had snapped at her mom at dinner over nothing, and she could still feel a low simmer of resentment about it, which was unfair, since the snapping had been hers.

Her phone buzzed. Anastasia, from across the street: "You up? Science test still."

"Still," Brooke typed back. "Can't focus. Heart racing. Weird."

"Same last week. My cousin made me count my sleep. Try it."

Brooke pulled out a notepad. She had gone to bed at midnight, waking at six thirty for school. She counted on her fingers: six and a half hours. She counted the last three nights, and they were all about the same. She wrote the number down and stared at it, because it looked wrong, like something had been quietly taking a cut of her nights. She had assumed she was tired because of the test. Now she wondered whether the test was going badly because of the tiredness, and the idea felt like finding a leak under a sink.

A second text arrived, this one from Maxton, the twelve-year-old next door whose kitchen window faced hers. He was up gaming, his screen glowing blue across the yard. "Why are your lights on," he asked when she waved him over by phone.

"Doing sleep math," she said when he came to the back door. "I get six and a half hours. Teenagers are supposed to get eight to ten."

He frowned. "How much for kids?"

"Nine to twelve if you're six to twelve," she said. "I read the whole chart during dinner."

Maxton leaned on the counter and did his own arithmetic out loud. Midnight to seven, for a week. "That's way under nine," he said, and shut his game off without being told, which Brooke found unexpectedly eloquent, a whole argument in one click.

"Sit down," she said. "Before bed, you're supposed to breathe slow. Four counts in, hold, six out." She set the kitchen timer and did it with him, both of them at the table, the worksheet pushed aside. Her drumroll heart slowed, beat by beat, like something settling.

That night Brooke plugged her phone in downstairs, set her alarm for ten, and put a note on her pillow: test tomorrow, brain tonight. She counted the hours until morning and got nine and a half.

At breakfast the next day, her mom slid eggs onto her plate. Brooke smiled first, before anything could go wrong, and said, "Sorry about yesterday. I figured out what it was."

"What was it?"

Brooke held up nine and a half fingers. "Bedtime. Nine fifteen tonight, deal?"

The tutoring centre smelled of pencil shavings and old carpet, and Nathaniel had been staring at x + 7 = 12 for four whole minutes. Across the table, Aurelie was already on problem six, her pencil whispering along like she'd been born knowing this stuff.

"How are you doing that so fast?" he asked.

"Doing what?" She didn't look up.

"The letter thing. It's a letter, Aurelie. Since when do letters equal numbers?"

She tapped his page with her eraser. "It's a mystery number. Something plus seven gives you twelve."

Nathaniel slumped back. He'd skipped breakfast to get here on time, and now his stomach was staging a small rebellion against the whole morning. Outside the window, Mr. Fitzgerald's garden looked lush and green in the June heat, which only reminded him that everyone else in the world was outside.

"Five," Aurelie said.

"I don't want the answer. I want to know how."

She finally looked at him. "You know how you got 12 in the first place? You'd take the mystery number and add seven. So think backwards."

Nathaniel wrote the equation again. He thought about his locker combination at school, how he'd once locked his gym shoes inside and the janitor had to undo the lock, turning it back the way it came. The lock had gotten to that state by turning forward, so turning backward got it out.

"Subtraction," he said slowly. "Subtraction undoes addition. So if seven got added, I can take seven away."

"From both sides," Aurelie said. "It has to stay balanced, like a seesaw. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other."

He wrote x + 7 = 12, then minus 7 under both sides. On the left, the sevens cancelled each other. On the right, 12 minus 7 was 5. x = 5. He checked it: 5 plus 7 really was 12.

"Wait," he said. "Does this work for everything? What if it's multiplication?"

Aurelie pushed her sheet toward him. "Try 3x = 15."

He stared at it. Three times something is fifteen. So something got multiplied by three, and to undo multiplication you'd divide. He wrote it out, dividing both sides by three, and there it was: x = 5 again. He laughed out loud, too loud for the quiet room, and a kid two tables over shushed him.

"Sorry," Nathaniel whispered, grinning. "It's just, I skipped toast for this."

"Sustain yourself on algebra," Aurelie said, deadpan, and went back to problem seven.

Nathaniel flipped to the next page, where the equations got longer and stranger, and squared his shoulders over problem one.

Vincent had claimed the corner of the garage behind the bicycles, where an old workbench held nine bean plants in paper cups. Each cup had a strip of masking tape with a letter on it, A through I, and a notebook lay open beside them with two weeks of measurements inside. His science fair project was supposed to answer one question: which of three fertilizers made beans grow fastest? The trouble was that his results made no sense at all. Plants A, B, and C had the blue fertilizer and had grown an average of four centimeters. Plants D, E, and F had the pink one and grown almost the same. G, H, and I had the green powder, and they had barely grown at all.

Aditya crouched beside the cups on Saturday morning, reading the notebook over Vincent's shoulder. "They're all basically the same," he said. "Except the green ones, which stink."

"That's the problem," Vincent said. "If all three fertilizers give the same result, my project is a poster that says nothing." He picked up cup B and turned it toward the window light. The stem was pale and leaning hard toward the glass.

Megane arrived with her skateboard under her arm and stopped in the doorway. She looked at the cups, then at the notebook, then at the watering can on the floor. "Wait," she said. "Which ones just get plain water?"

Vincent blinked. "None of them. They all get something."

Megane set her skateboard against the wall. "In my sister's project she had a control group," she said. "It gets no change at all, so you have something to compare against."

Vincent sat down on an upturned milk crate and stared at the cups. If every plant got fertilizer, then he could never tell whether the fertilizer was doing anything, because he had nothing to compare it with. Maybe beans grew four centimeters in two weeks no matter what. He thought about the seed packets in the drawer, the ones Ms. Leblanc had handed out in class, still sealed. He could start three more cups today with only plain water and call them his control group. The fair was in twelve days, which was tight, but beans sprouted fast in the warm garage, especially in the tropical heat that pooled near the window every afternoon. A late start might still show a difference if he checked them every morning and let the warmth accelerate the sprouting.

He filled three new cups with soil, pressed a seed into each, and watered them from the tap. Then he wrote "control" on their tape strips and started a fresh page in the notebook.

By the morning of the fair, the control plants had grown five centimeters, taller than every fertilized plant on the bench. Vincent propped his poster beside the cups, titled "Which Fertilizer Wins? None of Them." Ms. Leblanc stopped at his table, read the chart twice, and smiled.

Aditya leaned in and whispered, "So the best fertilizer is water?"

"Cheaper, too," Vincent said, and straightened the tallest control cup so everyone could see it.

The poster hung beside the trophy case outside the gym, where Justin stopped every day on his way to math. It showed a smiling man holding a piggy bank, and beneath him two numbers: an interest rate of 3.90 percent and, in smaller type, an APY of 3.98 percent. Justin had walked past it for two weeks without noticing. Today he stopped, because Ms. Shevchenko had just assigned a project on saving money over five years, and he had nothing yet.

He found Emile and Callan at the long table by the library windows. Callan was consuming a bag of pretzels so fast that crumbs dotted his history homework. "Look at this," Justin said, holding up his phone, where he'd snapped a picture of the poster. "Same bank, same account, two different rates. One of them has to be wrong, right?"

Callan leaned in, chewing. Emile pulled out a pencil and copied both numbers onto the margin of his notebook. "Maybe it's a typo," Callan said. "Banks make typos." But Justin doubted it. A bank that could afford a poster that size could afford to check two numbers, and the poster looked diligent about everything else, right down to the fine print. "There's a word here," he said. "APY. I've seen it at my dad's bank too, always a little higher than the rate."

Emile squinted at the small letters at the bottom of the picture. "It says something about a law. Truth in Savings Act of 1991." He read it aloud twice. "It says banks in the United States have to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield." "An annual percentage yield," Justin repeated, writing it down. "The APY. So they're not allowed to just show the plain rate. It includes compounding, whatever that means."

They tested it right there. Justin imagined a hundred dollars in the account, and Emile worked the plain rate first, 3.90 percent, year after year for five years. Then Callan, who had finally stopped eating, tried the APY of 3.98 percent the same way. The second pile ended up bigger, though not by a fortune. "So the APY is the honest number," Justin said slowly. "The other one's smaller because it leaves something out. The law makes them show the bigger one so nobody gets fooled." It felt like finding a hidden rule that had been posted on the wall the whole time.

Ms. Shevchenko passed their table on her way to the printer. "You three have been at this for forty minutes," she said. "More stamina than you show in gym, Callan." She glanced at their margins, crowded with numbers, and at Justin's phone still open to the poster. She didn't say anything else, which Justin took as a good sign.

He still had to build the five-year chart for Monday, column by column, plain rate beside APY, so the difference showed up on the page. His grandfather had promised him a hundred dollars if he mowed the lawn all summer, and suddenly the account in the poster seemed like a real place that money could go. He borrowed a library pencil, opened a fresh page, and wrote "Year 1" at the top.

Callan looked over his shoulder. "Which number are you using?" Justin tapped the APY twice with the eraser end. "The one the law likes."

Adam typed the joke fast, before he could lose his nerve. "Our class project is so good we should submit it to the principal as a hostage situation." He hit enter in the school computer lab chat, where Ms. Rosen had asked everyone to post feedback on the group presentation.

Liv replied first. "Adam, that's not funny. We could actually get in trouble for that." Three other classmates typed careful, neutral replies about maybe softening the wording. Adam winced and scrolled up and down, looking for some way to take it back. It was a joke, obviously a joke, but the screen gave nothing away. Words just sat there, flat.

He leaned over to Asiya's monitor. "Can they tell I'm kidding?"

She read the thread and winced too. "Not even slightly. Tone doesn't travel."

Adam opened a new tab and searched how to show you are joking in text. The first result stopped him cold. A computer scientist named Scott Fahlman had proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. He read it twice. Someone had invented the smiley face for exactly his problem, decades before he was born, and the reason was printed right there in one line.

"That's it," he said. "That's the whole thing. Somebody made this on purpose."

Liv slid her chair over, arms crossed, skepticism all over her face. "So you're going to fix a bad joke by sticking an emoji on it?"

"A classic," Adam said. "The original. Fahlman used a colon and a parenthesis."
